In 455 CE, the Vandals under King Gaiseric (GY-seh-rik) sacked Rome far more thoroughly than Alaric had.

The Vandals (a Germanic people who had migrated from central Europe to Spain to North Africa, conquering the wealthy province of Africa and its crucial grain supply) looted Rome for two weeks, stripping temples, palaces, and public buildings of everything portable, including (according to tradition) the treasures that Titus had taken from the Temple of Jerusalem nearly four centuries earlier.
The word "vandalism" derives from their name, though the connection is a later invention and probably unfair to the actual Vandals, who were organized raiders, not mindless destroyers.
The final decades of the Western Empire were a parade of puppet emperors manipulated by Germanic generals.
The real power lay with the barbarian commanders who controlled what was left of the Western army.
When Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus in 476 CE, he was not overthrowing a functioning state.
He was tidying up a formality.
The Western Empire had already ceased to exist in any meaningful sense.
Its provinces (Gaul, Spain, Britain, Africa) had been taken over by Germanic kingdoms.
Its army was Germanic.
Its treasury was empty.
Its capital had been sacked twice.
The last emperor ruled little more than the Italian peninsula, and even that was contested.

In 438 CE, near the end, Emperor Theodosius II in Constantinople had ordered the compilation of the Codex Theodosianus, the first official compilation of Roman imperial law, systematizing centuries of legislation into a single collection.
The Codex would profoundly influence medieval European law and the later Justinian Code compiled in the sixth century.
Even as the Western state crumbled, the legal tradition survived, embedded in the institutions that the Germanic successor kingdoms would adopt and adapt.
Roman law did not fall with Rome.
It endured, and it shaped every legal system in continental Europe.
Why did the Western Roman Empire fall?
The question has generated more scholarly debate than almost any other in history.

Edward Gibbon's The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire (published 1776-1789) attributed the collapse partly to the enervating effects of Christianity, which diverted energy from civic life to otherworldly concerns.
Modern historians have proposed dozens of explanations.
The honest answer is that no single cause is sufficient.

The fall was overdetermined — so many things went wrong that the real question is not "what caused it?" but "why did the western half collapse while the eastern half survived the same pressures for another thousand years?" Start with the military.
The Germanic migrations and the Hunnic invasions put sustained pressure on frontiers that the empire could no longer adequately defend.

The army was smaller, less well-funded, and increasingly composed of barbarian foederati whose loyalty was to their own chiefs, not to Rome — because the chiefs, not the emperor, had recruited them and led them in battle.
But Constantinople faced the same pressures (and also the Sassanid Persians) and survived.
Military pressure alone does not explain the difference.
The money explains more.
The western provinces were poorer than the east to begin with, and every territorial loss made things worse.
When the Vandals seized Africa after 439 CE, Rome lost the grain that fed its capital and the tax revenue that paid its soldiers.
The Visigoths in Spain and southern Gaul, the Burgundians in eastern Gaul, the Franks in the north — each carved out a kingdom that still looked vaguely Roman but sent no taxes to the Western court.

Each loss of territory made the remaining territory harder to defend, which led to further losses, in a vicious spiral that the eastern empire, more compact and centered on Constantinople's impregnable position and the Aegean as its internal sea, never entered.
Then there was the political rot.
The western court was paralyzed by factionalism, assassination, and the dominance of Germanic generals who used the emperors as puppets.
The eastern bureaucracy, professional and insulated by Constantinople's triple walls, maintained institutional continuity that the west could not match.

And the simple geography mattered: defending the long western frontiers (the Rhine, the Danube, the British coast, the African coast) required more resources than the shrinking western tax base could generate.
Constantinople had to defend the Danube and the Euphrates.
Ravenna had to defend everything else.
What about Christianity?
Gibbon's argument has not aged well in its simplest form — the eastern empire was equally Christian and survived for a millennium.

But Christianity did redirect resources (wealthy Christians donated to the church rather than to civic building projects), create a parallel power structure (bishops competed with imperial officials for authority), and encourage a theology that devalued earthly power in favor of heavenly reward.
Whether this weakened the state or merely filled the vacuum the state was already leaving behind is a question that generates more heat than light.
The most honest answer is probably the most unsatisfying.

The Western Empire fell because too many things went wrong simultaneously, and the system, which had survived individual crises repeatedly (the Gallic sack, the Punic Wars, the Crisis of the Third Century), finally encountered a combination of crises that exceeded its capacity to recover.
The eastern half survived because it was richer, better positioned, and better governed.
The western half, poorer, more exposed, and more politically dysfunctional, could not absorb the same shocks.
But here is the question the simple narrative of "fall" obscures: what exactly fell?
The Roman state in the west ended in 476 CE.
Roman civilization did not.

The Germanic kingdoms that replaced the empire spoke Latin (or learned it), adopted Roman law (or adapted it), worshipped in Roman churches (using Roman liturgy), and governed through Roman administrative structures (or imitations of them).

The Frankish king Clovis, who united Gaul in the early sixth century, was baptized as a Catholic Christian, took a Roman title, and governed through a bureaucracy staffed by literate clergy trained in Roman traditions.
The Visigothic law codes were written in Latin and drew heavily on Roman legal principles.

The Pope in Rome, the bishop who had inherited the prestige of the old capital, became the spiritual authority of the western world, conducting business in Latin, preserving Roman texts in monastery libraries, and maintaining an administrative structure modeled on Roman provincial government.
The roads endured.
The aqueducts lasted (some are still functioning).
The legal principles survived in every European legal system.
The Latin language evolved into French, Spanish, Portuguese, Italian, and Romanian.
The calendar Augustus and Caesar gave the world is still in use.
The concrete domes are still standing.

The Catholic Church, the institution that most directly inherited Rome's organizational genius, still governs from Rome, still uses Latin in its liturgy, and still calls its leader Pontifex Maximus, the title of Rome's chief priest.
Rome did not fall.
It transformed.
The empire became the church.
The legions became the feudal armies.
The provinces became the nations.
The language became the romance languages.
The law became the common inheritance of Europe.
The roads became the routes of medieval commerce.

The idea that a single civilization could unite diverse peoples under common law, common language, and common institutions became the aspiration of every European empire that followed, from Charlemagne to Napoleon to the European Union.
The real question is not why Rome fell.
It is how a cluster of mud-brick huts on a marshy riverbank became a system so durable that we are still living in its shadow, fifteen hundred years after the last emperor handed over his crown.

chapters.title: The Valley Before the Mountain
sentences: The Valley of Oaxaca (wah-HAH-kah) is shaped like an upside-down Y.
Three long arms of flat, fertile valley floor converge at a single point in the southern highlands of Mexico, roughly 300 miles (480 km) southeast of modern Mexico City.
The northern arm is called the Etla (ET-lah) Valley.
The eastern arm is the Tlacolula (tlah-ko-LOO-lah) Valley.
The southern arm is the Zimatlán (see-maht-LAHN) Valley.

Together they form one of the most productive agricultural zones in highland Mesoamerica: roughly 600 square miles (1,500 square kilometers) of valley floor, ringed by mountains that rise to 10,000 feet but open enough to catch the summer rains that water the maize.
The elevation is about 5,000 feet (1,500 meters), which means warm days, cool nights, and a climate that has been friendly to farmers for at least 10,000 years.
And right at the center, right where the three arms meet, there is a mountain.
Not a towering peak, but a long, flat-topped ridge rising about 1,300 feet (400 meters) above the valley floor, commanding views in every direction.
You can see the entire valley from the top.
You can see who is coming from the Etla arm, the Tlacolula arm, the Zimatlán arm.
You can see everything, and everyone can see you.
Around 500 BCE, someone decided to flatten the top of that mountain and build a city on it.
That city was Monte Albán (MON-tay al-BAHN), and it would remain continuously occupied for more than 1,200 years, making it one of the longest-lived urban centers in the ancient Americas.
But we are getting ahead of ourselves by a thousand years.
The mountain was still covered in scrub and rock in 1500 BCE.

The people who would eventually build on it were living in small farming villages in the valley below, growing maize and squash and beans, making pottery, arguing with their neighbors, and slowly, generation by generation, building the social complexity that would one day require a capital city on a mountaintop.

Before we go further, a note about "firsts." The Zapotec are credited with developing one of the earliest writing systems in the Americas, possibly the earliest calendrical notations in Mesoamerica, and one of the first planned urban spaces in the Western Hemisphere.
Some of these claims are solid.
Some are actively debated by scholars who would assign some of those honors to the Olmec (Olmec Civilization Ch 7) or the Maya instead.
And all of them carry the caveat that belongs in front of every ancient history: "first" in archaeology means "first surviving evidence of." The Zapotec had neighbors.
Some of those neighbors built with perishable materials.
Some of their sites haven't been excavated.
And the humid soils of Mesoamerica destroy organic materials that drier climates in Egypt or Mesopotamia would have preserved for millennia.
When this book says "earliest known," it means exactly that: the earliest we have found so far.
Keep this in mind.
The Valley of Oaxaca was not empty when the Zapotec story begins.

People had been living there since at least 8000 BCE, hunting deer and rabbits, gathering wild plants, and gradually domesticating the crops that would become the Mesoamerican agricultural trinity: maize (corn, domesticated from a wild grass called teosinte), beans, and squash.

The three crops together provide a complete diet (carbohydrates from maize, protein from beans, vitamins from squash) and they grow well together in the same field, a system called milpa (MEEL-pah) farming.
By 1500 BCE, the valley's residents had been full-time farmers for centuries, and they were starting to build the kind of permanent villages that farming makes possible.
The earliest phase of settled life in the valley is called the Tierras Largas (tee-EH-rahs LAR-gahs) phase, roughly 1500–1150 BCE.
During this period, small farming hamlets dotted the valley floor, most of them clusters of a few dozen wattle-and-daub houses surrounded by maize fields.

The pottery was simple but distinctive: a grayware tradition (gray-colored clay vessels fired in oxygen-reduced kilns) that would become a hallmark of Zapotec material culture for the next three thousand years.
Every Mesoamerican region developed its own pottery style, and the Valley of Oaxaca's grayware was as recognizable as a fingerprint.
When archaeologists find Oaxacan grayware at a distant site, they know Zapotec trade goods or Zapotec people were there.
One village grew faster than the others.

San José Mogote (san ho-SEH mo-GO-tay), in the Etla arm of the valley, was already the largest settlement in the Valley of Oaxaca by around 1400 BCE, with a population that would eventually reach over 1,000 people.
That might not sound impressive.
Compared to contemporaries in the Old World, it wasn't.
Babylon had tens of thousands of residents by this time.
The New Kingdom pharaohs ruled millions.
But in the context of Mesoamerica around 1400 BCE, a village of a thousand people with public buildings and specialized craft production was a significant center of power.

Across the Gulf Coast lowlands, about 300 miles (480 km) to the northeast, the Olmec were building San Lorenzo (Olmec Civilization Ch 2) on a grander scale, but in the Oaxacan highlands, San José Mogote had no rival.
What made San José Mogote different from the other villages in the valley?
Three things.
First, it had public architecture.

By around 1150 BCE, the residents were constructing lime-plastered ceremonial platforms oriented to astronomical alignments, structures that required organized labor and planning beyond the household level.
A large temple mound called Structure 28, standing over 15 feet (4.5 meters) tall with stuccoed walls and a stairway, was one of the earliest monumental constructions in highland Mesoamerica.
Someone was organizing communal labor projects.
Someone was directing resources toward buildings that served the community, not individual families.
That "someone" implies leadership, hierarchy, and the kind of inequality that turns a village into a chiefdom.
Second, San José Mogote had specialized craft production.

Workshops at the site produced polished magnetite mirrors, objects so labor-intensive to make (grinding iron-ore crystals to a flat, reflective surface using sand and water) that they could only be the work of full-time specialists supported by surplus food.
These mirrors were not just for local use.
They were trade goods, exported hundreds of miles through Mesoamerican exchange networks.

Third, San José Mogote had connections. magnetite mirrors, marine shell ornaments, and obsidian (volcanic glass, the sharpest cutting material available in pre-metal Mesoamerica) linked the Valley of Oaxaca to distant regions, including the Olmec heartland on the Gulf Coast.
Around 1100 BCE, Olmec-style artifacts begin appearing at San José Mogote: carved greenstone figurines, specific pottery motifs, and the distinctive iconography of the Olmec art tradition.
Did the Olmec politically control the Valley of Oaxaca?
Almost certainly not.
Did they trade with it, influence it, and share religious ideas?
The evidence says yes.
The Zapotec were not Olmec.
They were their own people, speaking their own language (part of the Oto-Manguean family, as different from the Olmec's language as English is from Chinese), developing their own cultural traditions.
But they were in contact with the Olmec world, and some ideas flowed along the trade routes.
By around 900 BCE, the Valley of Oaxaca had developed a political landscape that would look familiar to anyone who has studied early chiefdoms anywhere in the world.
The three arms of the valley had become three rival territories.
San José Mogote dominated the Etla arm.
Smaller centers competed for influence in the Tlacolula and Zimatlán arms.

Warfare, or at least the threat of it, was part of the political environment: some settlements moved to more defensible hilltop locations during this period, and burned buildings appear at several sites.
The three-valley rivalry would simmer for four centuries before someone found a drastic solution.
That solution was Monte Albán (Chapter 2).
But before the mountain, the valley produced something that would become one of the most debated objects in Mesoamerican archaeology.
Around 600 BCE, at San José Mogote, someone carved a stone slab that would later be known as Monument 3.
It shows a human figure in an awkward, contorted position, naked, with closed eyes and an open mouth, and between its feet, two glyphs.
The figure looks like a dead person.

The glyphs appear to be a calendrical name, a name composed of a day sign from the 260-day ritual calendar, identifying the figure by their birth date, a practice that was widespread in later Mesoamerican cultures.
If the glyphs are what they appear to be, then Monument 3 is one of the oldest written texts in the Americas, possibly the oldest in Mesoamerica.
That "possibly" carries a lot of weight.
The Olmec Cascajal Block (Olmec Civilization Ch 7), a tablet with 62 carved symbols found near San Lorenzo, may date to around 900 BCE, which would make it older.

But the Cascajal Block's date is disputed, its symbols have not been securely linked to any known writing system, and some scholars question whether it qualifies as "writing" at all versus a system of symbols.
Monument 3's glyphs, by contrast, are clearly part of the same writing tradition that would develop into the full Zapotec script over the following centuries.
The debate over which Mesoamerican civilization wrote first, the Olmec or the Zapotec, is genuinely unresolved.
What is not debated is that both were writing centuries before the Maya, whose earliest texts date to around the third century BCE.
Monument 3 matters for another reason.
The contorted, naked figure with closed eyes is not a dancer, not a celebrant, not a worshipper.
It is almost certainly a dead or sacrificed captive, displayed as a trophy.
The glyph between the feet is the captive's calendrical name, a way of identifying the victim.

If this interpretation is correct, then Monument 3 is the earliest known example of a practice that would define Zapotec political culture for the next thousand years: carving images of defeated enemies into stone and displaying them publicly as propaganda.
The Danzantes of Monte Albán (Chapter 3) are the same tradition scaled up from a single stone to over three hundred.
The valley was getting more complex, more competitive, more violent.
It needed a center.
Around 500 BCE, it got one, on a mountain that nobody had previously considered building on, because the amount of labor required to make it habitable was, by any reasonable estimate, insane.

Cross-civ check: the Tierras Largas and San José Mogote phases (1500–500 BCE) overlap with the Olmec heartland civilization on the Gulf Coast (Olmec Civilization Ch 1–6), the rise and fall of San Lorenzo (~1200–900 BCE) and the flourishing of La Venta (~900–400 BCE).

In the Old World, this period spans from the late Shang dynasty in China through the entire Zhou dynasty's Western Zhou period, the Neo-Assyrian Empire in Mesopotamia, the New Kingdom and Third Intermediate Period in Egypt, and the Greek Dark Ages transitioning into the Archaic period.
In the Andes, the Norte Chico civilization had already risen and fallen, and the Chavín culture was emerging (Early Andean Ch 4–5).
The Zapotec were developing in parallel with, but independently from, both the Olmec and these distant civilizations.
Mesoamerica was not a single invention radiating from one center; it was multiple societies experimenting with complexity simultaneously.

chapters.title: Building Monte Albán
sentences: Around 500 BCE, something happened in the Valley of Oaxaca that had no precedent in the region and very few parallels anywhere in the ancient Americas.
A group of people, possibly a coalition from multiple valley communities, possibly a faction from San José Mogote that imposed its will on the others, decided to build a city on a mountain.
Not on a gentle hill.
Not on a natural plateau.
On a jagged mountain ridge, 1,300 feet (400 meters) above the valley floor, at the exact point where the three arms of the Valley of Oaxaca converge.
The location was strategically brilliant: visible from everywhere, defensible from every direction, and neutral in the sense that it belonged to none of the three valley arms individually.
But it was also, by the standards of any reasonable construction project, absurd.
The mountain's summit was rough, uneven, and far too small and rocky to support a city.
The nearest water source was at the bottom of the mountain.
There was no farmland on the summit.
Everything, every meal, every drop of water, every building material, would have to be carried up the slopes on human backs.
They did it anyway.
The Zapotec didn't find a mountain with a flat top.
They made one.
The construction of Monte Albán was one of the most ambitious landscape-engineering projects in the pre-Columbian Americas.

The builders leveled the mountain's summit, cutting down rocky peaks and filling in ravines to create a vast, roughly rectangular platform about 1,000 feet (300 meters) long and 650 feet (200 meters) wide.
The Main Plaza that resulted was one of the earliest planned urban spaces in the Western Hemisphere, a public arena flanked by temple platforms, administrative buildings, and residential terraces.

The engineering required moving hundreds of thousands of tons of rock and earth, all by hand, all on human backs, up slopes that are still a stiff climb for tourists with hiking boots and water bottles.
To put this in perspective: the Olmec at San Lorenzo had reshaped a natural plateau around 1200 BCE, adding artificial extensions and carved terraces (Olmec Civilization Ch 2).
That was impressive.
But San Lorenzo worked with a natural landform.
Monte Albán's builders essentially created an artificial mesa on top of a mountain.

One useful comparison is the Persians leveling the terrace at Persepolis around the same time (Persian Empire Ch 2), but Persepolis used the wealth of an empire that stretched from Egypt to India, and Monte Albán's leveling took centuries of cumulative work, not a single imperial construction campaign.
The Zapotec did it with the resources of a single mountain valley.
Why build here?
The question has occupied Mesoamerican archaeologists for decades, and the answers tell us about the political conditions that made Monte Albán necessary.

The most widely accepted model, proposed by the archaeologist Richard Blanton (an American scholar who led the Valley of Oaxaca Settlement Pattern Project in the 1970s–80s), is that Monte Albán was a disembedded capital: a new political center deliberately placed in neutral territory to unite previously rival communities.
San José Mogote had dominated the Etla arm, but it could not have served as a capital for the entire valley without the other two arms viewing it as an imposition.
Monte Albán, sitting at the junction where the three arms meet, belonged to no arm and therefore could belong to all of them.
It was a compromise location, a political creation, a city built not because people needed to live there but because people needed a shared center of authority.
The alternative model is simpler: Monte Albán was built by the winners of a war.

San José Mogote's rulers, having defeated or intimidated their rivals, chose the mountain for its defensive advantages and established a new capital that proclaimed their dominance over the entire valley.
This model is supported by the militaristic imagery that dominated Monte Albán from its earliest days: the Danzantes carvings (Chapter 3) are essentially a wall of defeated enemies.
The truth probably involves elements of both.
Monte Albán may have been founded as a coalition project with a significant component of coercion.

Either way, the result was the same: by around 450 BCE, Monte Albán was a functioning city with a permanent population of several thousand, growing rapidly, and already producing the carved stone monuments that are its most famous and most disturbing legacy.
The first structures at Monte Albán were built during what archaeologists call Period I (roughly 500–200 BCE), and they established the template that the city would follow for the next millennium.

The Main Plaza was the spine of the city: a long, open rectangle oriented roughly north-south, flanked by stepped temple platforms on its east and west sides, with the massive North Platform complex closing off the northern end.
The plaza was not paved (it was packed earth), but it was deliberately kept clear of buildings.
This was public space, a stage for ritual, for political display, for the gatherings that held a young state together.
On the hillsides below and around the Main Plaza, residential terraces cascaded down the mountain slopes.
Over the centuries, more than 2,000 terraced platforms were carved into the hillsides, each supporting one or more houses.
The terraces transformed the rough mountain slopes into a staircase of habitable surfaces, each one leveled and retained with stone walls.

The labor investment was immense, but the result was a city that could accommodate a growing population while keeping the ceremonial center on the summit reserved for temples, tombs, and the ruling elite.
At the heart of Period I Monte Albán, there was a building that made a statement.

Building L (the letter designation comes from Alfonso Caso's archaeological survey; the original Zapotec name is unknown) was constructed on the west side of the Main Plaza, and its walls were covered with over 300 carved stone slabs depicting human figures.
These are the Danzantes (dahn-SAHN-tes), Spanish for "dancers," a name given by early observers who thought the contorted figures were performing some kind of dance.
They were not dancing.
They were dead, or dying, or mutilated, or all three.

The Danzantes are the subject of the next chapter, but their presence at the founding of Monte Albán tells us something important: this city was built by people who wanted their enemies to know what happened to people who resisted.

One of the most enigmatic structures at Monte Albán is Building J, an arrow-shaped building near the center of the Main Plaza that is oriented at a roughly 45-degree angle to every other structure on the site.
Every other building at Monte Albán faces the plaza in a neat, orderly arrangement.
Building J points off at an angle, like a compass needle ignoring the grid.
The shape is unusual: a pointed front, widening to a broader rear, with a narrow tunnel-like corridor running through the interior.
Why the odd orientation?
The leading theory, proposed by the archaeoastronomer Anthony Aveni, is astronomical.

Building J's pointed end aligns with the position on the horizon where the bright star Capella rose around 275 BCE (though some scholars question whether this alignment is intentional or which celestial target was the actual referent), and the building may have been used to observe the zenith passage of the sun, the two days each year (in May and August at this latitude) when the sun passes directly overhead and vertical objects cast no shadow.
Zenith passages were deeply significant in Mesoamerican cosmology, and several Mesoamerican sites have structures aligned to observe them.
If Building J was an observatory, it would be one of the earliest purpose-built astronomical structures in the Americas.
But Building J had another function that is not debated at all.
Its exterior walls were decorated with over 40 carved stone slabs, each showing a place-name glyph (a hieroglyphic symbol identifying a specific location) accompanied by an upside-down human head.
These are the conquest slabs: records of places that Monte Albán had conquered, with the inverted head symbolizing a defeated ruler.
The conquest slabs are the earliest known territorial conquest records in Mesoamerica.
They are political propaganda in stone: a public inventory of military victories, meant to be read by anyone walking through the Main Plaza.
They told visitors, allies, and potential enemies exactly how many communities had tried to resist Monte Albán and what had happened to their leaders.

The conquest slabs also contain some of the earliest examples of the Zapotec writing system in its mature form: a combination of calendar signs, name glyphs, and place signs that could record specific historical information.
This is writing, not decoration.
It encodes meaning.

And it raises the question that has driven some of the most heated debates in Mesoamerican archaeology: who wrote first? (Chapter 3.) By the end of Period I (roughly 200 BCE), Monte Albán had transformed the Valley of Oaxaca.
The three-valley rivalry that had simmered for centuries was over.

Monte Albán dominated the Etla arm completely, had absorbed or neutralized the major centers in the Tlacolula and Zimatlán arms, and was beginning to project power beyond the valley itself, establishing frontier outposts in the Cuicatlán Cañada (kwee-kaht-LAHN kah-NYAH-dah, a narrow canyon corridor to the north) and the Mixteca Alta (meesh-TEH-kah AHL-tah, the mountainous region to the west).
The valley's population may have reached 50,000, with Monte Albán itself housing several thousand on the hilltop and surrounding terraces.
Water was a constant challenge.
The mountaintop had no natural springs, no river, no reliable water source.

The Zapotec solved this through a combination of cisterns (stone-lined basins that collected rainwater), carried water from the valley floor (an exhausting daily task for the city's lower classes), and, eventually, canal systems that may have directed water from higher mountain slopes to catchment basins near the city.

The logistical difficulty of water supply alone would have limited Monte Albán's growth, and the fact that the city eventually housed 25,000 people (Chapter 4) on a waterless mountaintop is a testament to the organizational capacity of the Zapotec state.
Every drink of water in Monte Albán was an act of infrastructure.
The transformation took roughly three centuries: from a coalition project on a bare mountain around 500 BCE to the unchallenged capital of a unified Zapotec state by 200 BCE.
The pace is remarkable.
The Olmec heartland had taken roughly 300 years to develop its first major center at San Lorenzo (Olmec Civilization Ch 2), and that center had been built on a natural plateau.
Monte Albán achieved comparable political dominance in the same timeframe while constructing its physical infrastructure from scratch on the least convenient building site imaginable.
Whatever was driving the Zapotec, they were in a hurry.
The city's expansion beyond the valley also began during Period I.

Zapotec forces pushed into the Cuicatlán Cañada, a narrow river canyon corridor leading north toward the central Mexican highlands, and established frontier outposts that controlled the trade route and collected tribute from local communities.
To the west, they exerted influence over communities in the Mixteca Alta, though the extent of Zapotec military control outside the valley during this early period is debated.
What is clear is that Monte Albán was not content to dominate its own valley.
From its earliest years, the city was projecting power outward, using military force to control strategic trade routes and buffer zones.
The Danzantes on Building L (Chapter 3) and the conquest slabs on Building J were not bluffs.
They recorded real campaigns against real places, and the communities depicted on those slabs had real reasons to take the message seriously.
The writing was on the walls, literally.
The next chapter looks at what it said.

chapters.title: The Danzantes and the First Writing
sentences: The figures on the walls of Building L at Monte Albán are not dancers.
This needs to be stated clearly because the name has stuck for over a century, and it is completely wrong.

The more than 300 carved stone slabs set into the walls of Building L depict human figures that are naked, that are shown in contorted postures with limbs at unnatural angles, that have closed eyes and open mouths, and that in many cases show clear evidence of mutilation: streams of blood flowing from wounds, genital mutilation, scrolls of blood or viscera emerging from the body.
Some have calendrical name glyphs carved near them, identifying the individual by their birth date in the 260-day ritual calendar.
Some have additional glyphs that may record place names or titles.
These are not dancers.
They are dead or dying captives, displayed as public monuments to Zapotec military power.
The nineteenth-century scholars who named them "Danzantes" were interpreting the contorted postures as dance movements.

Modern scholars, with better parallels from across Mesoamerica and a clearer understanding of the visual conventions, recognize the postures as those of slain enemies: the limp limbs, the closed eyes, the bloodletting are consistent with sacrificial victims or killed prisoners of war.
The Danzantes are the earliest large-scale program of conquest propaganda in Mesoamerica.
Over 300 individual figures were carved, each apparently depicting a different person (the faces and body types vary), each displayed on the wall of a building in the most public space in the city.
The message was blunt: these are the people who opposed Monte Albán, and this is what happened to them.
It is, in effect, a gallery of the dead.
The tradition of carving conquered enemies into stone did not begin at Monte Albán.
It began at San José Mogote, with Monument 3 (Chapter 1), the single carved slab showing a naked, contorted figure with a calendrical name glyph between its feet, dating to around 600 BCE.
Monument 3 is the prototype.
The Danzantes are the same idea scaled up to industrial proportions.

The fact that the practice appears at San José Mogote before it appears at Monte Albán, and that San José Mogote is in the Etla arm of the valley while Monte Albán sits at the junction of all three arms, is one of the strongest pieces of evidence for the theory that Monte Albán was founded by people from San José Mogote who brought their artistic and political traditions with them.
The Danzantes also tell us about early Zapotec religious and political practices.
The mutilation depicted on many figures, particularly genital mutilation, suggests that captives were subjected to ritual humiliation before or after death.
The calendrical names attached to the figures indicate that the Zapotec cared about identifying specific individuals, not just displaying generic enemies.
This was personal.
Each slab was a specific person, named and displayed, their humiliation made permanent in stone.

The practice has parallels in later Mesoamerican traditions: the Maya carved images of bound, named captives on their stelae (stone monument pillars), and the Aztecs displayed the skulls of sacrificial victims on skull racks called tzompantli (tsom-PAHNT-lee).
But the Danzantes predate both of these traditions by centuries.

The glyphs on the Danzantes bring us to the Zapotec writing system, and to a debate that has generated more scholarly heat than almost any other question in Mesoamerican archaeology: who invented writing in the Americas?
The Zapotec script was a logographic writing system, meaning it used symbols to represent words or concepts rather than individual sounds (as an alphabet does) or syllables (as the Maya script does).

Zapotec writing combined three types of signs: calendar signs (symbols from the 260-day and 365-day calendars, used for dates and personal names), name glyphs (symbols identifying specific people, usually by their calendrical birthday), and place signs (symbols identifying specific locations, often shown as stylized hills or mountains with identifying features).
Together, these elements could record historical information: who conquered whom, when, and where.

The script appeared in its earliest form at San José Mogote around 600 BCE (Monument 3) and matured at Monte Albán over the following centuries, reaching its fullest expression in the conquest slabs of Building J (Chapter 2) and the genealogical stelae of the Classic period (Chapter 4).
The Zapotec writing system was used for at least a thousand years, from roughly 600 BCE to at least 500 CE, making it one of the longest-lived writing traditions in pre-Columbian America.
But was it the first?

The candidates for "earliest writing in the Americas" are, in chronological order of claimed dates: the Olmec Cascajal Block (possibly 900 BCE, but the date and the status of the symbols as "writing" are both contested; Olmec Civilization Ch 7), the San José Mogote Monument 3 (roughly 600 BCE, with clear calendrical glyphs that are part of a continuous writing tradition), and the earliest Maya inscriptions (roughly 300–250 BCE, in the fully developed hieroglyphic system that would become the most sophisticated writing in the pre-Columbian Americas).
If the Cascajal Block's early date is accepted and its symbols are considered writing, the Olmec win.
If not, the Zapotec's Monument 3 holds the title.
The Maya developed the most complete and expressive system, but they started later.
The honest assessment is that writing in Mesoamerica probably developed in multiple places roughly simultaneously, with mutual influence between regions.
The Olmec, the Zapotec, and the peoples of the Isthmian region (who would later produce the Epi-Olmec script) were all experimenting with symbolic notation between 900 and 400 BCE.

Claiming a single "inventor" of Mesoamerican writing is probably as misguided as claiming a single inventor of Old World writing, where Mesopotamia, Egypt, and the Indus Valley all developed scripts within a few centuries of each other with unclear lines of influence.
What can be said with confidence is this: the Zapotec writing system is the earliest Mesoamerican script that can be traced as a continuous tradition from its earliest examples to its mature form.

Monument 3 at San José Mogote and the Danzantes at Monte Albán are demonstrably part of the same writing tradition that produced the conquest slabs, the genealogical stelae, and the tomb inscriptions of the Classic period.
The thread is unbroken.
That claim is not contested.
Alongside writing, the Zapotec developed one of Mesoamerica's most sophisticated calendar systems.
The foundation was the piye (PEE-yeh), a 260-day ritual calendar that combined 20 named days with 13 numbers.
Each day had both a number (1 through 13) and a name (one of 20 day signs), producing 260 unique combinations before the cycle repeated.

A person's birthday in the piye was their calendrical name for life: someone born on the day "1 Jaguar" was called "1 Jaguar." This system of calendrical naming is visible on the Danzantes and on Monument 3, where the defeated captives are identified by their piye names.
It is the same 260-day cycle used across Mesoamerica by the Olmec, the Maya, and the Aztecs, though each culture used different names for the day signs.
Whether all Mesoamerican 260-day calendars derive from a single invention or represent independent developments from a shared agricultural or astronomical logic is debated.
The Zapotec also used the yza (EE-sah), a 365-day solar calendar divided into 18 months of 20 days each, plus a residual 5-day period considered dangerous and unlucky.
The yza tracked the agricultural year, the seasons, and the solar cycle.
When combined with the piye, the two calendars produced a Calendar Round: the number of days it took for the same combination of piye and yza dates to recur.
This happened every 52 solar years (18,980 days), creating a cycle that was the longest unit of time the Zapotec calendar could express without starting over.
The Calendar Round was shared across Mesoamerica.

The Maya went further, developing a Long Count calendar that could track time across millions of years (Olmec Civilization Ch 7), but the Zapotec, like most Mesoamerican civilizations, operated within the 52-year cycle.

Cross-civ check: the development of Zapotec writing and calendrics (~600–300 BCE) is roughly contemporary with the Greek alphabet spreading across the Mediterranean, the Persian Empire using Aramaic as its administrative script (Persian Empire Ch 3), the late Zhou dynasty in China producing the classical philosophical texts (Zhou Dynasty Ch 6–8), and the Brahmi script emerging in India (Vedic Period Ch 7).
In the Americas, the Olmec were in their late phase at La Venta and Tres Zapotes, and the earliest Maya settlements were forming in the lowlands of Guatemala and Yucatán.
The Zapotec were not writing in isolation.
They were part of a Mesoamerican world in which multiple societies were experimenting with notation, record-keeping, and the systematic tracking of time.
The Zapotec language itself, called Diidxazá (deeth-ah-SAH) by its speakers, belongs to the Oto-Manguean language family, one of the oldest and most diverse language families in Mesoamerica.

Oto-Manguean is completely unrelated to the Mayan language family, the Mixe-Zoquean family (which the Olmec probably spoke), or the Uto-Aztecan family (which includes Nahuatl, the language of the Aztecs).
The distance is not one of dialect: these are separate language families as unrelated to each other as Chinese is to Arabic.
The Zapotec were linguistically, and likely ethnically, distinct from every other major Mesoamerican civilization.
They shared the same cultural toolkit (the 260-day calendar, the ballgame, maize agriculture, pyramidal architecture) but they were not the same people, and their language is the proof.
Over time, as Zapotec populations spread across the mountainous terrain of Oaxaca, the language diversified into multiple regional variants, some of them mutually unintelligible.
Modern linguists recognize at least four major Zapotec language clusters, with dozens of local variants.
This linguistic fragmentation reflects centuries of political fragmentation: when communities are isolated by mountains and governed by separate city-states, their languages diverge.

The same process happened in ancient Greece, where the mountainous terrain produced dozens of Greek dialects, and in the Maya lowlands, where independent city-states spoke related but distinct Mayan languages.
The Zapotec called themselves Be'ena' Za'a (beh-EH-nah SAH-ah), meaning "Cloud People," and they believed their ancestors descended from clouds, rocks, trees, and jaguars.
The origin tradition, recorded by Spanish friars after the conquest, explains the Zapotec preference for mountaintop settlements: the Cloud People came from the sky, so they lived close to it.
It is a beautiful myth, and Monte Albán, perched above the valley with its summit often wreathed in cloud, was its perfect physical expression.

chapters.title: Monte Albán at Its Height
sentences: By around 200 BCE, the military and political consolidation of the Valley of Oaxaca was essentially complete.
Monte Albán had absorbed or conquered every rival center in all three valley arms.
The frontier outposts in the Cuicatlán Cañada and the Mixteca Alta were established.
The Danzantes on Building L had made their point.

And the Zapotec state entered a period that archaeologists call Period II (roughly 200 BCE–200 CE), transitioning into Period IIIA (roughly 200–500 CE), together representing Monte Albán's golden age: the centuries when the city reached its maximum extent, its greatest architectural ambition, and its most complex political relationships.
The city grew relentlessly.
By around 400 CE, Monte Albán's population had reached an estimated 25,000 people, making it one of the largest cities in Mesoamerica.
The hilltop itself could never hold that many people.

The Main Plaza and its flanking temple platforms were the ceremonial and administrative core, but most of the population lived on more than 2,000 terraced residential platforms carved into the hillsides radiating out from the summit in every direction.

The city sprawled down the mountain slopes for more than a mile in some directions, a cascade of stone-walled terraces, each one laboriously leveled to create a building platform, connected by stairways and paths climbing up and down the mountainside.
To feed this population, the Zapotec had to intensify agriculture in the valley below.
Engineers constructed canal irrigation systems to water the maize fields of the valley floor, channeling water from streams and springs to extend the growing season and increase yields.
The valley's three arms each had their own agricultural infrastructure, feeding their produce up the mountain to the capital.
Monte Albán was, in this sense, a parasite on the valley: the city produced nothing except political authority, religious ritual, and military security.
The valley fed it, and in return got a center of governance, a place of worship, and protection from external threats.
The architecture of Monte Albán at its height was not flashy by Mesoamerican standards.
There are no towering pyramids here, no massive temples soaring above the landscape.
The Zapotec built lower, wider, more restrained structures than their contemporaries.
The Main Plaza was flanked by platforms typically 20 to 30 feet (6–9 meters) tall, faced with cut stone and stucco, painted in reds and whites, with temple buildings on their summits.

The overall effect was horizontal rather than vertical: a long, open plaza framed by a regular rhythm of platforms and stairways, the whole composition emphasizing order, symmetry, and the controlled public space of the plaza itself.
Compared to the towering pyramids of Teotihuacan or the ornate temple facades of the Maya, Monte Albán was understated.
The mountain did the work of height.
The buildings did the work of order.
The North Platform was the exception.
The largest structure at Monte Albán, the North Platform was a massive elevated complex at the northern end of the Main Plaza, accessible by a grand staircase of carved stone.
This was the elite precinct: the residence of the ruling family, their administrative buildings, and some of Monte Albán's most important tombs.

The North Platform was expanded repeatedly over the centuries, each new ruler adding to its mass and complexity until it became a small acropolis, a city within a city, elevated above even the hilltop summit.
The ball court, an I-shaped playing field set into the northeast corner of the Main Plaza, was one of the earliest formal ball courts in the Oaxacan highlands.

The Mesoamerican ballgame (played with a solid rubber ball, using hips, shoulders, and forearms to keep the ball in play) was one of the defining cultural practices of the entire Mesoamerican world, shared by the Olmec (who may have invented it; Olmec Civilization Ch 4), the Maya, the Aztecs, and dozens of other cultures.

The game had deep religious significance: it reenacted cosmic struggles, it could determine the fate of captives, and in some traditions the losing team (or the winning team, depending on which scholar you ask) was sacrificed.

Monte Albán's ball court was smaller and less elaborate than the great courts at Maya and Aztec sites, but its presence confirms that the Zapotec participated fully in this pan-Mesoamerican tradition.
The most remarkable development of Monte Albán's golden age was not anything the Zapotec built at home.
It was a relationship with a city 250 miles (400 km) to the northwest that was, for several centuries, the largest city in the Western Hemisphere.
Teotihuacan (tay-oh-tee-wah-KAHN), in the Valley of Mexico (modern-day Mexico City's northern suburbs), was a metropolis of 100,000 to 200,000 people at its peak around 400–500 CE.
It was the New York of the ancient Americas: a cosmopolitan center that drew people, goods, and ideas from across Mesoamerica.
Its Pyramid of the Sun (over 200 feet (65 meters) tall) was one of the largest structures in the pre-Columbian world.
Its influence was felt from Guatemala to the American Southwest.
And it had a very specific relationship with Monte Albán that archaeologists have spent decades trying to understand.
The evidence for Zapotec-Teotihuacan contact is concrete and bilateral.

At Teotihuacan, archaeologists have identified a distinct residential neighborhood, the Oaxaca Barrio (Zapotec Quarter), where Zapotec people lived, used Oaxacan-style grayware pottery, built Oaxacan-style tombs, and deposited Zapotec funerary urns.
This was not a few isolated immigrants.
It was an established community, possibly a permanent diplomatic or merchant enclave, maintained for several centuries.

At Monte Albán, the reverse evidence exists: a few buildings in the city show the talud-tablero (tah-LOOD tah-BLEH-ro) architectural style (a distinctive combination of sloping base panel and vertical framed panel) that is the signature of Teotihuacan construction.
Teotihuacan-style pottery and artifacts appear at Monte Albán in small but consistent quantities.
What did this relationship look like?
The key question is whether Teotihuacan dominated Monte Albán politically or whether the two cities were diplomatic equals.
The evidence points more toward the latter.
Monte Albán shows no signs of conquest or violent disruption during the period of Teotihuacan contact.
The Zapotec did not adopt the Teotihuacan writing system, religion, or political structure.
The talud-tablero buildings at Monte Albán are a stylistic influence, not a sign of occupation.
And the Oaxaca Barrio at Teotihuacan looks like a diplomatic enclave, not a hostage community.

The most likely interpretation is that Monte Albán and Teotihuacan maintained a formal diplomatic relationship, possibly involving trade agreements, mutual recognition, and the exchange of elite personnel, but that the Zapotec remained politically independent.
Two great cities, aware of each other, trading with each other, respecting each other's power, but each running its own affairs.
This is unusual in Mesoamerica.

In many cases, Teotihuacan's influence on distant cities was more aggressive: the Maya city of Tikal experienced what looks like a Teotihuacan-sponsored regime change around 378 CE, and several other Maya cities show evidence of Teotihuacan military intervention.
Monte Albán, apparently, was strong enough to maintain a relationship of equals.
The Zapotec capital on its mountain was not easily pushed around.
The greatest surviving artistic legacy of Monte Albán's golden age is its tombs.

The Zapotec elite buried their dead in elaborate stone-lined chambers beneath their residences, a practice rooted in the belief that the dead remained active participants in family life, interceding with the gods on behalf of the living.
Elite families reopened their family tombs repeatedly over generations, depositing new burials alongside the old, adding offerings, and maintaining a continuous relationship with their ancestors.
This was not passive remembrance.
This was ancestor veneration as a functioning political institution: a family's legitimacy derived from the prestige of its ancestral dead, and the family tomb was the physical proof of that lineage.
Tomb 104, dating to around 200 CE, is the most famous example.

Located on a hillside residential terrace, Tomb 104 is a stone-lined chamber entered through a doorway topped by a large ceramic funerary urn depicting a richly dressed figure (probably a deity or a deified ancestor).
Inside, the walls are covered with polychrome murals, the finest surviving examples of Classic Zapotec painting.
The murals depict processional figures in elaborate costumes, deities identified by their distinctive headdresses and attributes, and calendrical signs recording dates and names.

The colors (red, yellow, blue, and green on a cream background) are vivid, the draftsmanship is confident, and the overall effect is of walking into a painted world designed not for living eyes but for the dead.
Tomb 104's murals show the Zapotec at the peak of their artistic and intellectual sophistication.
The figures are dressed in costumes that identify them as specific deities or as priests performing specific rituals.
The calendrical inscriptions record dates in the piye and yza systems (Chapter 3), tying the burial to specific moments in the ritual calendar.

The ceramic urn at the entrance, with its elaborate headdress and seated posture, is typical of the Zapotec funerary tradition: urns depicting deities or ancestors, placed at tomb entrances as guardians or companions for the dead.
Over a thousand of these urns have been recovered from Monte Albán, and they constitute one of the richest traditions of ceramic art in the ancient Americas.
The Zapotec rulers who commissioned these tombs legitimized their authority through carved stone stelae (upright stone slabs, STEE-lee) recording their names, parentage, conquests, and ritual acts.
The genealogical stelae are the written record of Zapotec political history in the Classic period.
They name specific rulers, identify their parents, record their ritual titles, and sometimes depict them performing acts of authority: taking captives, conducting ceremonies, or receiving tribute.

The inscriptions are in the Zapotec script (Chapter 3), and while the script has not been fully deciphered, enough of it is understood to extract basic historical information: names, dates, relationships, and places.
The stelae reveal a political system in which hereditary kingship was the norm: rulers inherited power from their parents, and they legitimized that inheritance by recording it in stone.
This is different from the earlier Danzantes tradition, which was about military conquest and the display of defeated enemies.

By the Classic period, Zapotec political propaganda had shifted from "look at who we killed" to "look at who our ancestors were." The shift suggests a more settled, more dynastic political order, one in which legitimacy came from bloodline rather than battlefield.

Mesoamerican archaeologists see a similar transition in the Maya world, where early monuments emphasize warfare and captive-taking while later ones emphasize dynastic genealogy and ritual performance.

Cross-civ check: Monte Albán's golden age (200 BCE–500 CE) coincides with the Roman Republic's transformation into the Roman Empire, the Han dynasty in China, the Maurya and early Gupta periods in India, and the Teotihuacan domination of central Mexico.
In the Maya lowlands, the great Classic-period cities of Tikal, Calakmul, Palenque, and Copán were rising during the later part of this period.

Monte Albán was not the only great city in Mesoamerica, but it was one of the oldest and most stable, its continuity of occupation unmatched by Teotihuacan (which collapsed around 550 CE) and rivaled only by a few Maya cities.

chapters.title: The Classic Zapotec World
sentences: The period that archaeologists call Monte Albán IIIB (roughly 500–700 CE) is the Zapotec civilization's autumn.
Not its fall.
The city was still large, still occupied, still the center of Zapotec political and religious life.
But the peak had passed.
The population may have already begun to decline from its 25,000 maximum.
The great building projects had slowed.
And beyond the valley, the Mesoamerican world was shifting in ways that would eventually pull the ground out from under Monte Albán's 1,200-year run.

But before we trace the decline (Chapter 6), the late Classic period deserves its own chapter because this is when we see the Zapotec world most clearly: the gods they worshipped, the art they made, the tombs they painted, the daily life they led.
The political history of Monte Albán is a story of power, conquest, and diplomacy.
The cultural history is the story of what the Zapotec built their power to protect.

The Zapotec religious world was organized around a concept called Pitao (pee-TAH-oh), a term that scholars translate variously as "great time," "infinity," or "the breath of the cosmos." Pitao was not a single god.
It was the underlying creative force of the universe, manifesting through specific deities who governed specific domains of life and nature.
The concept has rough parallels in other Mesoamerican cosmologies: the Maya notion of a living, animate universe, or the Aztec concept of teotl (divine force pervading all things).
But the Zapotec articulated it in their own way, and their pantheon had its own distinct personalities.
The most important Zapotec deity was Cocijo (ko-SEE-ho), the god of lightning, rain, and fertility.
Cocijo was the dominant figure in Zapotec religious art, appearing on ceramic funerary urns, carved stone reliefs, temple facades, and painted tomb walls more often than any other deity.

He is depicted with a distinctive forked serpent tongue (representing lightning), an elaborate headdress (often featuring the glyph for rain or cloud), and a fierce expression that combines human and supernatural features.

Cocijo was the Zapotec equivalent of the Maya rain god Chaac (CHAHK) and the Aztec rain god Tlaloc (tlah-LOHK; the Aztecs were the last great Mesoamerican empire, 14th–16th centuries CE, Chapter 8), all three belonging to a pan-Mesoamerican tradition of rain deities that can be traced back to the Olmec (Olmec Civilization Ch 4).
In a mountain valley where agriculture depended on seasonal rains, a rain god's prominence makes perfect practical sense: Cocijo controlled the water, and the water controlled the harvest.

Other important deities included Pitao Cozobi (pee-TAH-oh ko-SOH-bee), the god of maize and sustenance, who represented the food supply on which the entire civilization depended; Coquihani (ko-kee-HAH-nee), the god of light and the sun; and a goddess of death and the underworld whose Zapotec name is uncertain but who appears frequently on urns and in tomb murals, typically depicted with a fleshless jaw and skeletal features.
The Zapotec underworld, called Lyobaa (lee-OH-bah, meaning "place of rest" or "place of the dead"), was not a place of punishment.
It was where the dead went to continue their existence, and the family tombs beneath elite residences were understood as literal entrances to this realm.
The city of Mitla, which would later become the Zapotec religious capital (Chapter 7), was believed to be built directly above the entrance to Lyobaa.
The artistic peak of the Classic Zapotec world is visible in the tomb murals and funerary urns that are Monte Albán's most distinctive artistic legacy.
The urns deserve particular attention.

Over a thousand ceramic funerary urns have been recovered from Monte Albán and other Zapotec sites, and they constitute one of the richest and most varied ceramic art traditions in the pre-Columbian Americas.
A typical urn is a cylindrical vessel (designed to hold offerings for the dead) fronted by a seated figure, usually a deity or a deified ancestor, wearing an elaborate headdress and costume.

The figures are modeled with remarkable detail: individual feathers in headdresses, woven patterns on clothing, jewelry, ear ornaments, pectoral plates, and the characteristic attributes of each deity (Cocijo's serpent tongue, Coquihani's solar disc, Pitao Cozobi's maize ears).
The urns were placed in tombs, at tomb entrances, and in offerings beneath buildings, serving as companions, guardians, or intermediaries for the dead.
The artistic range is enormous.
Early urns (Period I–II, roughly 500–200 BCE) are relatively simple: seated figures with minimal costume detail, modeled in the gray clay that is the Zapotec ceramic fingerprint.
Classic-period urns (IIIA–IIIB, roughly 200 BCE–700 CE) become increasingly elaborate, with multiple layers of headdress, intricate costume elements, and polychrome paint applied after firing.
Some urns are individual masterpieces of ceramic art.
Others are clearly mass-produced, using molds to replicate standard deity types.

The variation tells us something about the social function: the finest urns were commissioned by elite families for their most important tombs, while simpler versions were available to lower-ranking households who still needed a deity figure for their family burial.
Alongside the urns, the tomb murals of the Classic period represent the Zapotec at their most visually ambitious.

Tomb 104 (Chapter 4) is the most famous, but dozens of other painted tombs survive, their walls decorated with processional figures, deity portraits, astronomical signs, and the geometric patterns that would reach their ultimate expression at Mitla (Chapter 7).

The painting style is flat and linear (figures shown in profile with no attempt at depth or perspective, similar to Egyptian tomb painting or Maya vase painting), with bold outlines filled with flat color.
The palette is rich: reds, yellows, blues, greens, and blacks applied over a white or cream plaster ground.
The murals were not meant to be seen by the living.
They were painted for the dead, inside sealed chambers that were covered with earth after the final burial.
The art was functional, not decorative: it created a painted environment for the dead to inhabit, a portable version of the world they were leaving.
What did daily life look like for the people who were not buried in painted tombs?
The archaeological evidence from the residential terraces of Monte Albán and from smaller Zapotec towns across the valley gives us a picture of a stratified but functioning society.
Most people were farmers.

They lived in wattle-and-daub houses (wooden frames filled with mud plaster, thatched roofs) on the terraced hillsides below the monumental center, grew maize on the irrigated valley floor, supplemented their diet with beans, squash, chili peppers, avocados, and wild game, and made the distinctive Oaxacan grayware pottery for cooking, storage, and serving.

Life centered on the household compound: a cluster of buildings around a shared courtyard, housing an extended family, with a small shrine or offering deposit in one corner and, for families with some status, a burial chamber beneath the floor where ancestors were interred.
Social stratification was visible in the housing.
Elite residences on the upper hillsides and near the Main Plaza were larger, better built (stone foundations, plastered floors, multiple rooms), and associated with richer tomb offerings.
Commoner residences lower on the slopes were smaller and simpler.

The gap was significant but not as extreme as in some contemporary Mesoamerican societies: the architectural difference between a Monte Albán elite house and a commoner house was less dramatic than the gap between a Maya palace and a Maya farmer's hut.
The city's economy was based on agriculture, craft production, and tribute.
Specialist potters, obsidian workers, and shell ornament makers operated workshops in specific neighborhoods.

Obsidian (volcanic glass, the sharpest cutting material available) was imported from distant sources: the Zapotec did not have local obsidian deposits, so all of it came through trade, primarily from the highlands of central Mexico.
Cotton textiles, probably produced in the lowland areas outside the valley, were another important trade good.
And tribute, collected from conquered communities beyond the valley, flowed into Monte Albán and supported the ruling elite.
The Zapotec also had a developed system of markets.

While the archaeological evidence for marketplaces is indirect (markets don't leave obvious architectural traces), the distribution of goods across the valley, the presence of standardized pottery types, and later Spanish colonial accounts describing Zapotec market traditions all suggest that periodic markets, perhaps weekly, served as the primary mechanism for distributing goods beyond the household level.
This is consistent with the broader Mesoamerican pattern: both the Maya and the Aztecs organized their economies around periodic markets, and the Zapotec appear to have done the same.
One aspect of Zapotec religious life that the archaeological record documents without ambiguity is human sacrifice.
The Danzantes (Chapter 3) are the earliest evidence: captives killed, mutilated, and displayed as political trophies.
In the Classic period, sacrificial practices continued but appear to have been more ritualized and less theatrical than the mass sacrifices the Aztecs would later practice.

Archaeological evidence from Monte Albán includes decapitated skulls deposited as offerings beneath buildings, sacrificial burials in tombs (servants or attendants killed to accompany their lord into the afterlife), and iconographic depictions of bloodletting rituals in which rulers pierced their own tongues or earlobes with obsidian blades and offered the blood to the gods.

Bloodletting by rulers, a practice shared with the Maya (who documented it in extraordinary visual detail on their lintels and painted ceramics), was understood as a form of communication with the supernatural: royal blood opened a channel to the gods, and the pain of the ritual was the price of divine attention.

The scale of Zapotec sacrifice appears modest compared to what the Aztecs would later practice (the Aztecs sacrificed thousands of captives in single ceremonies at Tenochtitlan's Great Temple), but the practice was real, continuous, and central to Zapotec political-religious life.
The Danzantes were not an aberration.
They were the founding statement of a tradition that lasted over a thousand years.
The Zapotec relationship with the jaguar and the puma deserves a note.
Across Mesoamerica, the jaguar was the supreme symbol of royal power and the supernatural, a tradition that can be traced back to the Olmec (Olmec Civilization Ch 4).
The Zapotec participated fully in this tradition.
Rulers were depicted wearing jaguar-skin garments, sitting on jaguar thrones, and adorning their bodies with jaguar imagery.
Jaguars appeared on ceramic urns, carved reliefs, and tomb murals.
The jaguar was associated with the earth, the night, the underworld, and military power.
It was the ruler's animal, the shaman's companion, and the predator whose authority no one in the natural world questioned.
A Zapotec king wearing jaguar skin was making the same statement as a European king wearing a crown: I am at the top of the hierarchy, natural and supernatural.

Cross-civ check: the Classic Zapotec world (500–700 CE) coincides with the fall of the Western Roman Empire and the Early Medieval period in Europe, the late Gupta period and the beginning of medieval India, the Sui and Tang dynasties in China, and the rise of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula.

In Mesoamerica, the great Maya Classic-period cities were at their height, Teotihuacan had recently collapsed (around 550 CE), and the political vacuum left by Teotihuacan's fall was reshaping alliances and trade networks across central Mexico.
Monte Albán, remarkably, survived Teotihuacan's collapse.
The diplomatic partner was gone, but the city on the mountain endured for another two centuries.
That resilience is part of what makes the Zapotec extraordinary: they outlasted the biggest city in their world and kept going.

chapters.title: Monte Albán Falls Silent
sentences: Cities don't die the way people do.
There is rarely a single moment, a definitive end, a line you can draw and say: this is when it was over.
Cities thin out.
They get quieter.
Neighborhoods empty.
Buildings are abandoned, then reused as quarries for their stone, then collapse into rubble that slowly fills with soil and weeds.

The process takes generations, and for the people living through it, the decline may have felt less like a catastrophe and more like a series of small disappointments: one fewer family on the terrace above, one more building falling into disrepair, one more year when the ceremonies felt a little less grand and the plaza a little more empty.
Monte Albán's decline unfolded over roughly 200 years, from around 600 to 800 CE.
The city didn't fall to an invader.
It wasn't destroyed by war or natural disaster.
It simply lost its reason for being.
What went wrong?
The honest answer is that we don't know with certainty, but several factors converged.
First, the loss of Teotihuacan.
When that great metropolis collapsed around 550 CE (from some combination of internal unrest, environmental stress, and perhaps external attack), it sent shockwaves through the Mesoamerican world.
Teotihuacan had been the hub of a trade and diplomatic network that reached from Guatemala to the American Southwest.
Its collapse didn't just remove one city from the map.
It severed trade routes, disrupted political alliances, and created a power vacuum that destabilized the entire central Mexican highlands.
Monte Albán had maintained a diplomatic relationship with Teotihuacan for centuries (Chapter 4).
With Teotihuacan gone, Monte Albán lost its most important external partner, its most reliable trade connection, and its primary point of contact with the wider Mesoamerican world.
The Zapotec capital survived the initial shock.
Monte Albán was still occupied, still functioning, still the center of the valley when Teotihuacan was already in ruins.
But the long-term effects were corrosive.
Trade declined.
Exotic goods (obsidian from central Mexico, green obsidian from Pachuca, marine shell from the coasts) became scarcer.
The economic networks that had sustained elite power at Monte Albán weakened.
Second, the valley itself may have been under agricultural stress.
Thirteen centuries of intensive cultivation, canal irrigation, and population growth had taken a toll on the Valley of Oaxaca's soils.
There is some evidence (debated) of soil erosion on the hillsides, reduced crop yields on overworked valley floor lands, and the expansion of farming into more marginal areas.
The valley was probably still productive enough to feed a large population, but feeding it at the levels required to maintain a city of 25,000 on a mountaintop may have become increasingly difficult.
Third, and perhaps most fundamentally, the secondary centers in the valley had grown strong enough to challenge Monte Albán's dominance.

During the centuries of Monte Albán's golden age, the city had maintained its authority over the entire valley partly through military power, partly through religious prestige, and partly through the practical advantages of being the center of a trade network.

As the trade network weakened and the military advantage of the hilltop location became less relevant in a world where the main threats were from within the valley rather than outside it, the secondary centers began to assert their independence.
Why send your tribute up the mountain when you could keep it for yourself?
The process was not dramatic.
It was bureaucratic.

Over the course of the seventh and eighth centuries, the political authority that had been concentrated at Monte Albán gradually dispersed to several smaller centers in the valley, each claiming some portion of the power that had once belonged to the hilltop capital.
Lambityeco (lahm-bee-TYEH-ko), a center in the Tlacolula arm of the valley, grew to prominence during Monte Albán's decline.

Its palaces were decorated with remarkable stucco friezes: paired portrait heads of a ruling couple, modeled in three-dimensional relief on the building facades, plus large Cocijo masks flanking the entrances.

The portraits are among the most lifelike representations of specific individuals in all of Zapotec art, and they make a pointed statement: here are our rulers, named and displayed, not on a distant mountaintop but right here in our own city.
Lambityeco was claiming legitimacy on its own terms.

Jalieza (hah-lee-EH-sah), a large hilltop settlement in the southern arm of the valley, also grew during this period, its terraced hillsides housing thousands of people and its workshops producing cotton textiles for regional trade.

Yagul (yah-GOOL), in the Tlacolula Valley, began its transformation from a modest settlement into a major center with a hilltop fortress, a palace complex, and one of the largest ball courts in the Oaxacan highlands.
Each of these cities was becoming what Monte Albán had once been for the whole valley: a self-sufficient center of political authority, trade, and religious life.
Yagul deserves closer attention.

Located on a dramatic rocky outcrop in the Tlacolula Valley, Yagul combined the defensive logic of Monte Albán (a hilltop site with commanding views) with a more practical approach to daily life (the fortress on the summit, the residential and ceremonial areas on the lower slopes, close to water and farmland).

Yagul's ball court was one of the largest in the Oaxacan highlands, and its Palace of the Six Patios, a complex of interconnected courtyards surrounded by rooms, was one of the most impressive residential structures in Postclassic Oaxaca.

The palace's layout suggests a multi-family elite compound, a physical embodiment of the shared-power arrangements that characterized the post-Monte Albán political order: not one ruler in one palace, but several elite lineages living in connected but separate quarters, cooperating through proximity.
By around 750 CE, Monte Albán had ceased to function as a political capital.
The Main Plaza was no longer maintained for public ceremonies.
The North Platform's elite residences were abandoned.
The terraced hillsides, which had once housed over 20,000 people, were thinning out as families moved to the valley floor or to the rising secondary centers.
The construction of new public buildings stopped.
No new stelae were carved.
No new conquest slabs were installed.
The city was dying not with a bang but with a long, slow exhalation.
The physical evidence of the abandonment is sobering.

Excavations show that residential terraces on the hillsides were gradually stripped of their usable materials: roof beams pulled out for reuse, stone walls dismantled for building material elsewhere, ceramic vessels removed or broken.
The people leaving Monte Albán did not leave in panic.
They left methodically, taking what they could use and leaving behind what they couldn't carry.
The process looks less like a flight and more like a moving day repeated across decades, one family at a time, until the mountain was quiet.
But Monte Albán was not forgotten.
Even after it ceased to be a living city, it remained a sacred site.
Zapotec and later Mixtec elites continued to use its tombs for burials, reopening ancient chambers to deposit new offerings alongside centuries-old bones.
The hilltop became a pilgrimage site, a place where the living came to honor the dead and to draw legitimacy from the prestige of the ancient capital.
Monte Albán was too important to abandon entirely.
It became a cemetery, a shrine, a memory palace where the past was kept alive through burial and ritual.
This pattern, a city declining politically but retaining sacred significance, is common in Mesoamerica.

The Maya city of Tikal experienced a similar transformation in the ninth century CE, and the great pyramid complex at Teotihuacan remained a pilgrimage destination for centuries after the city's collapse.
Monte Albán's transition from capital to sacred site was part of a broader Mesoamerican pattern in which the power of a place outlasts the power of the people who built it.
The end of Monte Albán was not the end of the Zapotec.
This is the critical distinction.
The city fell silent, but the civilization did not.
The Zapotec language continued to be spoken across the Valley of Oaxaca and beyond.
Zapotec pottery traditions continued unbroken.
Zapotec religion, with Cocijo and Pitao Cozobi and the ancestor cult, continued to structure daily life.
The Zapotec calendar, the piye and the yza, continued to mark time.
The Cloud People did not disappear when their mountain capital declined.
They dispersed, fragmented, and reorganized around new centers of power.
The civilization was more durable than any single city.
The next four centuries, from Monte Albán's abandonment through the arrival of the Aztecs, would be the most politically chaotic period in Zapotec history.
But chaos, for the Zapotec, was survivable.
They had been building their identity for over a thousand years, and no amount of political fragmentation could erase that.

Cross-civ check: Monte Albán's decline (600–800 CE) coincides with the Tang dynasty in China, the rise of Islam across the Middle East and North Africa, the Early Medieval period in Europe, and the late Classic Maya period, which was itself entering a series of collapses that would depopulate the great lowland cities by the tenth century.

The Classic Maya collapse and Monte Albán's decline are often discussed together as part of a broader pattern of Late Classic-period urban crises in Mesoamerica, though the specific causes were different in each case.
The Maya collapse involved warfare, deforestation, drought, and political fragmentation across a vast lowland region.
Monte Albán's decline was more localized, driven by the loss of regional trade networks and the political maturation of rival valley centers.
Both ended the same way: great cities emptied, and political power scattered into the hands of smaller, more numerous successors.

chapters.title: The Mixtec Wars and Mitla
sentences: The Valley of Oaxaca after Monte Albán was a place of competing city-states, shifting alliances, and one very persistent question: who was in charge?
The answer, from roughly 900 to 1521 CE, was: nobody, exactly.
Or rather, several someones simultaneously, none of them powerful enough to dominate the valley the way Monte Albán had for a thousand years.

The Postclassic period in the Valley of Oaxaca was a time of political fragmentation, military rivalry, cultural mixing, and some of the most extraordinary art and architecture the Zapotec world ever produced.
It was also the period when the Zapotec stopped being alone in their valley.
The Mixtec (MEESH-tek) were coming.
After Monte Albán's decline, political power in the Zapotec world split along two lines.
The secular (political and military) authority centered on Zaachila (sah-ah-CHEE-lah), a city in the Zimatlán arm of the valley whose rulers claimed descent from the ancient Monte Albán dynasty.
The spiritual authority centered on Mitla (MEET-lah), a city in the eastern Tlacolula Valley that became the seat of the huijatoo (hwee-hah-TOH), the Zapotec high priest.
The huijatoo was not a king.

He was the supreme religious authority in the Zapotec world: the chief diviner, the oracle, the guardian of the entrance to Lyobaa (the underworld, Chapter 5), and the person who presided over the burials of kings and nobles.
Spanish friars who encountered the institution after the conquest compared the huijatoo's authority to the Pope's, and the comparison is not entirely wrong.
The division between secular and religious power was explicit and institutionalized.
Zaachila governed the living.
Mitla governed the relationship between the living and the dead.
Mitla itself is one of the most architecturally distinctive sites in all of Mesoamerica.
Its palaces and temples were decorated with something found nowhere else in the pre-Columbian Americas: geometric stone mosaic panels.

Thousands of precisely cut stone pieces, each one individually shaped and fitted without mortar, were assembled into repeating patterns of interlocking frets, stepped spirals, zigzags, and geometric meanders.
The panels cover entire walls, wrapping around doorways and along building facades, creating surfaces that look more like woven textiles translated into stone than like conventional architecture.
