The buildings they left behind in the canyons, the great houses and cliff dwellings and kivas and roads and petroglyphs, are not the ruins of a vanished people.
They are the early chapters of a story that is still being written.
When a Hopi elder visits Chaco Canyon, he is not visiting someone else's ruins.
He is visiting his ancestors' home.

Cross-civ context: the Ancestral Puebloans' story challenges one of the deepest assumptions in popular history: that when a civilization's monuments are abandoned, the civilization has "fallen." Rome fell.
The Maya collapsed.
Angkor was swallowed by the jungle.
These are satisfying narratives with dramatic endings.
But many civilizations did not end.
They relocated, adapted, and continued under new names in new places.
The Ancestral Puebloans are perhaps the clearest case: the buildings were abandoned, but the people were not lost.
They walked south, carrying their languages, their ceremonies, their clan structures, and their identity, and they rebuilt.
They are still here.
The ruins are not an ending.
They are a waypoint.

chapters.title: Aztlan and the Eagle on the Cactus
sentences: The most powerful empire the Western Hemisphere had ever seen began as a band of refugees that nobody wanted.

In 1519 CE, when Spanish conquistadors first crested the pass between the volcanoes Popocatépetl and Iztaccíhuatl and looked down into the Basin of Mexico (the high-altitude bowl, ringed by mountains, that holds modern Mexico City), they thought they were dreaming.

Below them, on a chain of islands in a vast salt-and-freshwater lake, stood a city of stone causeways, whitewashed pyramids, and floating gardens, with a population somewhere between 150,000 and 250,000.
It was larger than any city in Spain, larger than Rome, larger than Paris, larger than London.

The chronicler Bernal Díaz del Castillo (a foot-soldier in Cortés's army who later wrote the most readable eyewitness account of the conquest, finishing his book in his eighties in Guatemala) wrote that some of the soldiers asked whether what they were seeing was real, or a vision out of the romance novels they had read as boys.
It was real.
It was called Tenochtitlan (teh-nohch-teet-LAHN, "the place of the prickly pear cactus").
And it was, by any measure, one of the great cities the world has ever produced.
Two hundred years earlier, the people who built it had been so poor and so despised that other tribes drove them off their land for fun.
They were not natives of central Mexico.
They were latecomers, immigrants, a people on the run, stuck doing the worst jobs for the worst pay, the kind of group that other settled peoples treated as a problem rather than a partner.
How they got from there to running the largest empire in the history of the pre-Columbian Americas is one of the most remarkable rags-to-riches stories on record.
It also took less time than the Roman rise from city to empire by a margin of several centuries.
Their name, the one they used for themselves, was Mexica (meh-SHEE-kah).
The label "Aztec" comes from a different word, Aztlan (AHST-lahn), the legendary homeland they claimed to have left, and it was applied to them mainly by 19th-century historians.
The Mexica themselves rarely used it.
We use it because the empire they built drew in many peoples beyond the Mexica proper, and "Aztec Empire" has become the standard name in English.

Where this narrative needs to talk specifically about the people of Tenochtitlan, it will say "Mexica." Where it needs to talk about the imperial system that included their allies and the dozens of tributary peoples, it will say "Aztec." That distinction matters more than it sounds.
A note on what we know and don't know.

The Aztec Empire is unusual in this series because it ends in 1521, on the cusp of the modern era, and because two parallel literate traditions (Aztec painted books and Spanish narrative writing) overlap for the final century.
We have far more material than we have for any earlier American civilization.

We also have a particular kind of distortion: the Mexica themselves rewrote their own past more than once, the Spanish wrote about them with a mix of admiration, contempt, and propaganda, and the most influential single source, the Florentine Codex (a twelve-volume encyclopedia of Aztec culture compiled by the Franciscan friar Bernardino de Sahagún, sah-ah-GOON, between roughly 1540 and 1577 from interviews with Aztec elders), was assembled fifty years after the conquest by a Spaniard whose Aztec informants had every reason to color what they remembered.

"First" claims and confident dates in this narrative carry the same caveat that applies to every TL in this series: we are looking at the past through whatever lens survived, and the lens has fingerprints all over it.
The Mexica's origin story begins with a place called Aztlan, "the place of whiteness," somewhere to the north of the Basin of Mexico.
Aztlan was an island in a lake, with seven caves at its center where the seven Nahua-speaking peoples (the Mexica and their linguistic cousins) emerged.
Or possibly Aztlan never existed and the whole thing is a charter myth invented later to give the Mexica a homeland to be proud of.
Modern archaeologists are split.
Some place it in the modern Mexican state of Nayarit.
Others place it in the American Southwest.
Most accept that the Mexica did migrate from the north, but the literal Aztlan with the seven caves is probably mythology dressed up as geography.
What is reasonably solid is the language family.
The Mexica spoke Nahuatl (NAH-watl), a language belonging to the Uto-Aztecan family, which also includes Hopi, Comanche, Shoshone, and the languages of the Tarahumara of northern Mexico.

Uto-Aztecan is a different family from the Mayan languages of the southeast (Maya Civilization Ch 1) and from the Oto-Manguean languages of the Zapotec and Mixtec to the south (Zapotec Civilization Ch 1).

The distance between Nahuatl and Yucatec Maya is comparable to the distance between English and Persian: same continent of language families in the abstract, but mutually unintelligible and culturally distinct.
The Mexica arriving in central Mexico were not coming home to people who already spoke their language.
They were strangers.

Around 1100 CE, give or take a century, the Mexica left Aztlan, prompted (or so they later said) by their patron god Huitzilopochtli (wee-tsee-loh-POACH-tlee, "Hummingbird of the South" or "Hummingbird on the Left," a war god, in this period a relatively narrow tribal patron rather than a major cosmic figure — Chapter 3 covers the later promotion that turned him into the sun itself).
Huitzilopochtli was carried in a portable shrine on the back of one of his priests, and he gave directions: keep going south, keep going south, and one day I will give you a sign.
The migration took over two centuries.
They stopped at place after place.
They were thrown out of place after place.
They walked, they fought, they ate what they could.
The setting they were walking into was the wreckage of a much older civilization.

The Basin of Mexico had been the heart of a great regional system since at least 100 BCE, when the city of Teotihuacan (teh-oh-tee-WAH-kahn) had risen to become the largest city in the Western Hemisphere, with a population of 125,000 to 200,000 (Teotihuacan Ch 1).
Teotihuacan had collapsed in flames around 550 CE, and in the centuries afterward, a confusing succession of smaller polities had risen and fallen.
The most prestigious of these was the city of Tula, the capital of the Toltecs (TOLE-teks), a Nahuatl-speaking people who had dominated central Mexico from roughly 900 to 1150 CE.
By the time the Mexica arrived, Tula too had been destroyed and abandoned.
But the memory of Toltec rule was the gold standard of legitimacy in the Basin of Mexico.
Anyone claiming to rule needed Toltec descent.
The Mexica, who had no such descent, would have to invent it later.
When the Mexica wandered into the Basin of Mexico, sometime in the late 13th century, the basin floor was already crowded.
Dozens of city-states (each called an altepetl, ahl-TEH-petl, "water-mountain," the basic Mesoamerican political unit, a city plus its territory) competed for land, water, and labor.
The major players included Culhuacan, Azcapotzalco, Texcoco, Xochimilco, Coyoacan, Tlacopan, and many others, none of them friendly to newcomers.
The Mexica showed up uninvited, and the existing residents made it clear they were unwelcome.
Around 1248, the Mexica settled briefly at Chapultepec (chah-POOL-teh-pek, "grasshopper hill"), a wooded hill on the western shore of Lake Texcoco that had reliable freshwater springs.
Chapultepec was a good location, which is exactly why the existing inhabitants of the basin objected to having Mexica squatters there.
A coalition of nearby city-states attacked, drove the Mexica out, and killed many of their leaders.
The survivors fled south.
Their refuge was the city-state of Culhuacan (kool-WAH-kahn), an old altepetl on the southern shore of the lake whose ruling family claimed direct descent from the Toltecs.
The Culhua took the Mexica in, but the hospitality was barbed.
They settled the refugees on Tizapan (tee-ZAH-pahn), a stretch of stony, snake-infested ground that nobody wanted, on the assumption the snakes would solve the Mexica problem.
The Mexica, however, ate the snakes.
Within a generation they were thriving, intermarrying with their hosts, and serving as Culhua mercenaries in the constant low-grade warfare that filled the basin's politics.
This period, the Mexica vassalage at Culhuacan, mattered for two reasons.
First, intermarriage with Culhua nobles gave the Mexica a thin but real claim to Toltec blood, which they would lean on heavily for centuries afterward.
Second, it ended in disaster.
The Mexica, asked by the Culhua king Cocoxtli to provide a daughter for what the Mexica understood as a marriage alliance, instead sacrificed and flayed her in honor of a goddess.

The detail varies in the sources (one tradition says the priests believed she was meant to become a deity; another says they were trying to flatter Cocoxtli with the highest religious honor they could imagine), but the outcome was the same.
Cocoxtli's father attended the ceremony, saw a Mexica priest dancing in his daughter's skin, and called for blood.
The Mexica fled.
They had nowhere to go.
To the west and north, the Tepanec confederation (the dominant power in the basin at the time) was hostile.
To the east, Texcoco was an ally of the Tepanec.
To the south, Culhuacan now wanted them dead.
The only direction left was into the lake itself.

In 1325 (the date is conventional, drawn from later Mexica chronicles, and might be off by a few years either direction), Mexica priests sighted the sign Huitzilopochtli had promised them more than two centuries earlier.

On a small, rocky island in the marshy western lobe of Lake Texcoco, a giant eagle perched on a prickly pear cactus, devouring a snake. (The image survives today on the Mexican flag; the cactus and eagle are the national emblem of Mexico, and the lineage from Mexica founding myth to modern coat of arms is direct.) This, the priests announced, was the place.
The wandering was over.
The site was, by every objective measure, terrible.
It was a mosquito-ridden marsh in the middle of a salty lake.
There was no farmland.
There was no fresh water (Lake Texcoco was brackish in its central portions, drinkable only at the freshwater inflows around the edges).
There was no stone for building.
There was no timber.

The only assets were defensive: the surrounding water made the island hard to attack, and the existing powers in the basin had not bothered to claim it because nobody else thought it was worth claiming.
That last point was decisive.
The island fell within the formal territory of Azcapotzalco, the Tepanec capital.
The Mexica negotiated permission to settle there in exchange for tribute and military service.
They became, formally, vassals of the Tepanec king Tezozomoc (teh-zoh-ZOH-mok), an aging warlord who would dominate the Basin of Mexico for the next half-century.
The Mexica agreed because they had no other option.

They named their new home Tenochtitlan, "the place of the prickly pear cactus." A short time later, a faction split off and founded a sister city, Tlatelolco (tlah-teh-LOL-ko), on a neighboring island just to the north.
Tlatelolco would later become the empire's greatest marketplace; in 1325, it was just another mud island.
The Mexica started building.
They drove wooden piles into the lake bed, piled mud and reeds on top to extend the available land, and laid out the first version of a plan they would refine for the next two centuries.

They built a small temple on the highest point of the island, a shrine to Huitzilopochtli that would, six rebuildings later, become the Templo Mayor (TEM-plo MAH-yor, "Greater Temple," the twin-pyramid that anchored the city).
The first version was a modest wooden hut.
By 1521, the seventh version would be 200 feet (60 meters) on a side at its base and 150 feet (45 meters) high, the tallest structure in the city.
Cross-civ check: 1325, the conventional founding date of Tenochtitlan, sits in the middle of a remarkable century.
In England, the Hundred Years' War with France was about to begin (1337).
In China, the Mongol Yuan dynasty was on its last legs (Ming would replace it in 1368).
In West Africa, the Mali Empire was at its height under Mansa Musa, who had just made his famous gold-distributing pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324.
In the Andes, the Inca were still a small mountain kingdom around Cuzco, just beginning their own expansion (Andean Kingdoms Ch 8).
The Maya in the Yucatán were in their Postclassic period, with Mayapan as the dominant city after the collapse of the great Classic-era centers (Maya Civilization Ch 7).
The Aztecs and the Inca, the two American empires the Spanish would conquer in the 1520s and 1530s, were both founding their capitals within the same generation.
They never knew the other existed.

The Mexica in 1325 were a small client kingdom on a salty island, paying tribute to a Tepanec king they hated, building reed huts on mud they had piled up themselves, and worshipping a hummingbird-shaped war god who had told them they would one day rule the world.
Almost no one in the Basin of Mexico would have bet on them.
Within a hundred years, almost no one in the Basin of Mexico would dare bet against them.

chapters.title: From Vassal to Hegemon
sentences: The Mexica spent their first century in Tenochtitlan as someone else's hired help.

For a hundred and three years, from 1325 to 1428, they paid tribute to the Tepanec capital of Azcapotzalco (ahs-kah-poh-TSAHL-ko, "place of the anthills," on the western shore of Lake Texcoco) and fought as Tepanec mercenaries in the wars that the aging tyrant Tezozomoc waged against his neighbors.
They were good at it.

The Mexica had no farmland of their own and no traditional craft industry (the chinampa system that would later feed the city was not yet built out at scale, and Tlatelolco's market was still developing), so military service was the main thing they had to sell.
They sold it well, and they got paid in territory: small grants of land in conquered towns where Mexica warriors could collect their own tribute, separate from what the Tepanec king collected.
By the early 15th century, individual Mexica nobles had become wealthy on these grants, and Tenochtitlan itself had grown from a few thousand people to perhaps 30,000.
But mercenaries who get too rich start to look like rivals.
And the Mexica, for all their loyal service, were never going to be Tepanec.
They had their own god, their own dynasty, their own ambitions.
The longer they served, the more dangerous they became.
Tezozomoc, no fool, kept them dependent through a system of close marriage alliances that worked, until his death, and then catastrophically failed.
Before that crisis broke, the Mexica needed kings, and they got them.
In 1376, the city's elders selected Acamapichtli (ah-kah-mah-PEACH-tlee, "handful of reeds"), a Mexica noble whose mother was a Mexica princess and whose father was Culhua.
The half-Culhua descent was not optional.

The Mexica needed an external claim to legitimacy, and Culhua blood meant Toltec blood, which meant a credible claim to descend from the prestigious civilization (Chapter 1) that all Nahuatl-speaking peoples used as the gold standard of royal pedigree.
Acamapichtli became the first tlatoani (tlah-toh-AH-nee, "speaker," literally "he who speaks well," the title of the Mexica king).
The plural is tlatoque, and within a generation, the title would be applied to the rulers of every altepetl in the basin.
For now, Acamapichtli was the first of his line.
Acamapichtli's reign (1376–1395) was unspectacular by design.

He consolidated the Mexica royal household, fathered children by women of multiple Mexica calpulli (Chapter 6) to bind the city's clan factions to the throne, served Tezozomoc loyally in Tepanec wars, and oversaw the second major construction phase of the Templo Mayor.

When he died, the elders elected his son Huitzilihuitl (wee-tsee-LEE-witl, "Hummingbird Feather," not to be confused with the god Huitzilopochtli — the names share the hummingbird element but the deity is "Hummingbird of the South" while the king is "Hummingbird Feather"; Mesoamerican naming conventions used a small set of bird and animal motifs in many recombinations).

Huitzilihuitl reigned from 1396 to 1417 and made the most important political move of the early dynasty: he married a daughter of Tezozomoc, formally embedding the Mexica royal line into the Tepanec ruling family.
This was the same political logic that had guided Acamapichtli's descent from the Culhua, applied to the current dominant power.
Huitzilihuitl's son by this marriage, Chimalpopoca (chee-mahl-poh-POH-kah, "Smoking Shield"), would inherit the throne and, by blood, would be Tezozomoc's grandson.
That blood was supposed to protect the Mexica.
Instead, it killed Chimalpopoca.
In 1426, Tezozomoc finally died, after ruling Azcapotzalco for over fifty years.
Tepanec power had been built around him personally, and his death triggered the kind of succession crisis that authoritarian states with no clear inheritance rules tend to produce.
The throne should have gone to his designated heir, but a younger son named Maxtla (MAHKS-tlah) seized it instead, killing his brother in the process.
Maxtla then turned on every relative he distrusted, and the half-Mexica grandson of Tezozomoc, sitting on the throne of Tenochtitlan, was high on the list.
In 1427, Chimalpopoca was assassinated.
The sources disagree on the details (some say Maxtla's agents had him killed in his palace; others say he was captured, imprisoned, and committed suicide in detention).
What is clear is that the assassination left Tenochtitlan without a king, surrounded by enemies, and one strong push away from being wiped out altogether.

The Mexica elders met in emergency session and chose Itzcoatl (eets-KOH-ahtl, "Obsidian Serpent"), the son of Acamapichtli by a slave woman, an older man with a reputation as a war leader and a stubborn pragmatist.
Itzcoatl was not a member of the legitimate royal line by the standards of his time (the slave-mother lineage was a serious mark against him).
The elders chose him anyway because he was the only candidate willing to fight.
The legitimate heirs argued for surrender to Maxtla; Itzcoatl argued for war.
The Mexica went to war.
They were not going to win it alone.
Tenochtitlan's army, even by generous estimates, numbered at most a few thousand fighting men.
Azcapotzalco could put ten or fifteen times that number in the field.
What Itzcoatl had was a network of grievances.
Maxtla had alienated his own family, attacked his neighbors indiscriminately, and made enemies of the surviving heirs of the Tepanec confederation.
Most importantly, he had attacked Texcoco (tesh-KO-ko, the major altepetl on the eastern shore of Lake Texcoco) and driven its young king-in-exile into hiding.
That king's name was Nezahualcoyotl (neh-zah-wahl-KOH-yotl, "Fasting Coyote"), and he was about to become the most famous individual in Aztec history, depending on which Aztec city you asked.
Nezahualcoyotl was a remarkable person, the kind who shows up once in a generation in any culture, and the only individual in this entire narrative who could plausibly be called a philosopher-king.
He was born in 1402, the son of Texcoco's ruler Ixtlilxochitl I, who had been killed by Tezozomoc's forces when Nezahualcoyotl was a teenager.
Hidden in the mountains by loyal nobles, Nezahualcoyotl spent his early adulthood as a fugitive, hunted by Maxtla's assassins, moving from refuge to refuge while plotting his return.
By 1428, he had built a coalition.
Itzcoatl, recognizing an obvious ally, made the deal.

In 1428, Tenochtitlan, Texcoco (under Nezahualcoyotl), and the smaller Tepanec city of Tlacopan (tlah-KOH-pahn, on the lake's western shore) formed the Triple Alliance, the pact that would become the political core of the Aztec Empire for the next ninety years.
The terms were carefully calibrated.

Tenochtitlan and Texcoco would each receive two-fifths of all conquered tribute, and Tlacopan (the junior partner, included to give the alliance a foothold on the western shore and to break up what remained of Tepanec power) would receive one-fifth.
The 2:2:1 ratio was the central political arithmetic of the empire, and it held, with some erosion in Tlacopan's share, until the Spanish arrived.
Why did the alliance work?
The mechanism was simple but effective.
Each capital ran its own internal affairs, kept its own king, and maintained its own military traditions.
They jointly agreed on which towns to conquer, jointly campaigned, and divided the spoils by formula.
There was no central capital and no common citizenship.
A Texcocan was not a subject of Tenochtitlan, and vice versa; both were members of an alliance that had agreed to exploit everyone else.
Crucially, the three capitals were close enough geographically (all within sight of each other across the lake) to coordinate effectively, but distant enough to maintain separate identities.

The arrangement avoided the trap that has destroyed many federations: nobody had to accept being absorbed into anybody else's system, and the predictable payoff of joint conquest gave everyone a continuing reason to cooperate.
The alliance's first target was Maxtla.
The combined armies besieged Azcapotzalco for 114 days in 1428, sacked the city, and captured the tyrant himself.

Maxtla was sacrificed at the founding ceremony of the Triple Alliance, his heart cut from his chest with an obsidian blade and burned as an offering to Huitzilopochtli, in front of the assembled armies of the three allied cities.
The Tepanec confederation collapsed.
Azcapotzalco was demoted to a tributary.
The market that had been Mesoamerica's premier slave market for a century was relocated.
And the Mexica, in the space of a single year, transformed themselves from a vassal city-state into one of three co-ruling capitals of an emerging empire.
Itzcoatl spent the next twelve years (1428–1440) doing the unglamorous work of consolidation.

With Texcocan allies on his eastern flank and Tlacopan blocking the western approach, he conquered the freshwater-lake cities to the south of Tenochtitlan one after another: Xochimilco (sho-chee-MEEL-ko, "field of flowers," famous for its chinampas, Chapter 4), Cuitlahuac, Mizquic, and Coyoacan.
These conquests gave the Mexica direct control over the most fertile chinampa zones in the basin, which solved the food-supply problem that had haunted Tenochtitlan since its founding.
The southern lakes were freshwater, perfect for chinampa agriculture, and the conquered towns now owed tribute payable in maize, beans, and squash.
For the first time in their history, the Mexica did not need to import every grain of corn they ate.
Itzcoatl also did something stranger and more telling.

Around 1430, he ordered the burning of the codices (a codex in Mesoamerican usage was a long folded screen of bark paper or deer hide, painted with pictographs and phonetic glyphs, used for histories, ritual calendars, tribute lists, and divination — the closest thing the Aztecs had to a book): the destruction of older painted books that recorded Mexica history.

The justification, recorded later by Aztec elders, was that the existing histories were inaccurate, that they portrayed the Mexica as the impoverished migrants and mercenaries they had been, and that "it is not fitting that our people know these pictures.
Our people, our subjects, will be lost and our land destroyed, for these lies are many." The codices were burned.
New histories were commissioned to replace them.

The new histories backdated Mexica greatness, claimed Toltec ancestry more directly, recast Huitzilopochtli as a major cosmic deity rather than a minor tribal spirit, and generally constructed the propaganda that would sustain Mexica imperial identity for the next ninety years.
This is one of the more important political acts in the empire's history, and it deserves to be flagged for what it was.
Itzcoatl's regime did not just write its own version of history.
It deliberately destroyed the older versions to prevent comparison.
The Mexica we know about, the empire of cosmic destiny and Toltec ancestry and divinely sanctioned conquest, is in important ways a creation of the post-1430 propaganda program.

Where the older histories said "we were poor wanderers nobody wanted," the new histories said "we were always destined to rule." Where the older histories said "Huitzilopochtli was a tribal patron god," the new histories said "Huitzilopochtli is the sun, and the sun requires our service." The man behind much of this rewriting was Itzcoatl's nephew and chief advisor, who held an office Itzcoatl had created specifically for him: the cihuacoatl (see-wah-KOH-ahtl, "Snake Woman," a title not a gender; he was male, the office name referred to a goddess associated with childbirth and the earth, framing the cihuacoatl as the feminine domestic complement to the warrior-king).
His name was Tlacaelel (tlah-kah-EH-lel), and he would hold the office for nearly sixty years, outlasting four tlatoani.
He is the closest thing to a Cardinal Richelieu the Mexica produced, and probably the single individual who did more than any other to define what the Aztec Empire ultimately became.
When Itzcoatl died in 1440, he left a Mexica state that was unrecognizable from what he had inherited thirteen years earlier.
From a vassal of the Tepanec, paying tribute and providing mercenaries, the Mexica had become co-rulers of the most powerful alliance in the Basin of Mexico.
From a city of perhaps 30,000 people on a salt-marsh island, Tenochtitlan had grown into an emerging metropolis fed by chinampa tribute from a dozen subject towns.
From a tribal religion, Huitzilopochtli had been promoted to a cosmic role that justified continuous warfare.
The empire was not yet built.
But the engine that would build it was running.

chapters.title: Tlacaelel and the Engine of Conquest
sentences: The man who made the Aztec Empire what it was never sat on the throne.

Tlacaelel (tlah-kah-EH-lel, "Sad-Hearted One" or "Manly Heart," depending on the etymology you trust) was the half-brother and chief advisor of Motecuzoma I, the nephew of Itzcoatl, the cousin of Acamapichtli's other descendants, and through marriage and family politics he was related, somehow or other, to nearly every important Mexica noble of his generation.
He held the title of cihuacoatl, the vice-royalty Itzcoatl had invented for him in 1428, and he held it from then until his death around 1487 — fifty-nine years, across four reigns.

He directed the empire's bureaucracy, managed the judicial system (Chapter 6), commanded the army when the tlatoani was elsewhere, and (the role that history remembers most) reformed the state religion so thoroughly that the Aztec Empire of 1500 was, in important ways, a religious revolution that he had personally engineered.
He was offered the throne three times, after Itzcoatl's death in 1440 and again in 1469 and 1481.
Three times he refused.
The Aztec sources, all written long after his death, treat this as a sign of supernatural humility.
The more cynical reading is that he had figured out that being kingmaker was a more durable position than being king.
Kings die in battle, get assassinated by rivals, get poisoned by their advisors; advisors who outlast four kings tend to keep their heads.
Tlacaelel kept his.

His religious reforms, which he began under Itzcoatl and pushed through fully under Motecuzoma I (moh-tay-koo-ZOH-mah, "He Who Frowns Like a Lord," sometimes spelled Moctezuma or Montezuma — the original Nahuatl was Motēuczōma; "Motecuzoma" is the closest English approximation, and we'll use it throughout for both Motecuzoma I and Motecuzoma II), reframed the basic relationship between the Mexica and the cosmos.

Before Tlacaelel, Huitzilopochtli was a relatively narrow tribal deity: the patron god of the Mexica specifically, a war god, a guide who had brought them out of Aztlan and led them to the eagle-on-cactus prophecy.
After Tlacaelel, Huitzilopochtli was the sun.
He was the deity whose daily rising required cosmic maintenance, and the maintenance required human blood.

Specifically, it required the blood of brave warriors, which meant the Mexica needed to fight wars constantly, capture brave warriors constantly, and sacrifice them constantly, or the sun would not rise.
This was, in cosmological terms, an enormous promotion.
A regional war god was now the literal motor of the universe.
The promotion was paired with a creation story, the Five Suns mythology (Chapter 5 covers it in detail), in which the gods themselves had sacrificed their lives to set the current sun in motion.
Aztec religion was not asking humans to invent a new obligation; it was asking them to honor an existing one, to repay a cosmic debt the gods had voluntarily contracted at Teotihuacan.
The debt-and-payment framing was politically effective because it made sacrifice feel like an inheritance rather than an imposition.
The Mexica were not killing strangers because they enjoyed it; they were keeping the universe running because someone had to.
The mechanism was beautifully constructed, in a horrible way.
By making the central state god the sun itself, Tlacaelel made every act of imperial expansion a religious obligation.
Refusing to wage war would be refusing to feed the sun, which would mean cosmic collapse.

The sacrificial demand could only be met by capturing live warriors in battle (regular slave-trading and famine-driven self-sale of slaves provided plenty of bodies, but Huitzilopochtli specifically required warriors taken in honorable combat, so the regime had to keep fighting wars).
Imperial expansion stopped being optional.
It became a sacrament.
The reform package included more than the sun-god promotion.

Tlacaelel oversaw the second great wave of codex-rewriting (after Itzcoatl's initial burning, Chapter 2), establishing the Mexica as the chosen people of the sun and backdating the sacrificial cosmology so that it appeared to have been Mexica practice from the beginning rather than a 15th-century innovation.
He standardized the monthly festival cycle (Chapter 5), institutionalizing the eighteen public sacrificial events that turned the calendar into a year-round ritual machine.
He formalized the Flower Wars (more on these below) as a permanent mechanism for replenishing the captive supply when conquest campaigns slowed.

And he shaped the priesthood itself: the calmecac school system (Chapter 6) educated the noble boys who staffed the temples, and Tlacaelel's reforms tightened the link between high-priestly office and the state bureaucracy he ran.
Some scholars argue this is too clean a theory and that the real reforms were messier and slower than the Aztec sources make them sound.

There is fair reason for the skepticism: most of what we know about Tlacaelel comes from histories written by his great-grandson, Hernando de Alvarado Tezozomoc (writing in the late 1500s, several generations after the events), who had every reason to make his ancestor look like an architect of empire.
Other scholars argue the reforms are well-attested in multiple independent sources and that the sun-god framing of Huitzilopochtli is genuinely a 15th-century innovation.

The current scholarly reading lands somewhere in the middle: Tlacaelel did substantially reshape Mexica religion, the sun-god promotion of Huitzilopochtli is real, but the reforms were more gradual than the legendary single-handed transformation the post-conquest sources describe.
Either way, by 1500 the cosmology of imperial sacrifice was the Mexica state ideology, and Tlacaelel's name was attached to it.
The Flower Wars deserve a section to themselves, because they were where Tlacaelel's machine became most visible.

Beginning around 1455 (during the worst drought of the century, the One Rabbit famine, when sacrificial demand was running ahead of the conquest pipeline), the Aztec state institutionalized a recurring, ritualized form of warfare against the city-states of Tlaxcala, Cholula, and Huejotzingo on the eastern side of Popocatépetl.
The war was scheduled.
The combatants knew each other.

The objective was not territorial conquest but the capture of high-quality warriors for sacrifice, with both sides agreeing to constraints (set times, set locations, no mass civilian casualties) that limited but did not eliminate the violence. xochiyaoyotl (sho-chee-yah-OH-yotl, "flower-warfare") was the formal Nahuatl name; the "flower" referred to the captured warrior, who would "bloom" by giving his life on the altar.
What were they for?
The conventional explanation is religious: ritual battles to feed the sun.

Modern scholarship adds practical functions: they kept the army in fighting trim, they pressured the Tlaxcalans without the cost of a full conquest that the rugged terrain would have made expensive, and they served as the empire's primary military training program for young warriors.
All three readings are probably true at once.
What matters for understanding Tlacaelel's machine is the structural function: the Flower Wars guaranteed a steady supply of sacrificial victims even when conquest campaigns went quiet.
The system never had to stop.
The sun would always be fed.

And in pulling Tlaxcala into a permanent state of low-grade war rather than absorbing it, the empire created the eighty-year reservoir of grievance that would, in 1519, hand Cortés his decisive ally (Chapter 8).
Tlacaelel built the machine to last.
He did not foresee what would happen when the machine met something it had never been designed to absorb.
The kings he served were, by and large, capable men.
They had to be.
Motecuzoma I (r. 1440–1469) is sometimes called Motecuzoma the Elder to distinguish him from his more famous great-grandson.
He was Itzcoatl's nephew, Tlacaelel's brother, and the first tlatoani who got to rule a Mexica state that was already powerful rather than building it from scratch.

His campaigns pushed the empire well beyond the Basin of Mexico for the first time: east into the Huastec (WAHS-tek) lowlands of the northern Gulf Coast (which lay roughly 200 miles east of the Basin of Mexico, across the eastern mountain ranges, in the lowland zone where rubber and vanilla grew), south into Oaxaca where his armies conquered Huaxyacac (wahsh-YAH-kahk, the predecessor of modern Oaxaca City) and the surrounding Mixtec and Zapotec territories (Zapotec Civilization Ch 8).
The conquests brought rubber, cotton, vanilla, gold, jade, and cochineal (the carmine-red dye produced from a cactus-eating insect) into Tenochtitlan's tribute lists.
They illustrated the machine Tlacaelel had built — every campaign yielded both economic tribute and live captives for the temples — but they did not invent it.
The machine ran the campaigns; the campaigns did not make the machine.
Motecuzoma I also presided over the calamities that defined his reign in Aztec memory.

In 1449, a catastrophic flood inundated Tenochtitlan, and Nezahualcoyotl (Chapter 2), now the firmly established king of Texcoco, designed and supervised the construction of a 10-mile-long dike across the lake — the Albarradón de Nezahualcoyotl, the largest hydraulic engineering project in the pre-Columbian Americas, faced with stone, sluice-gated, and stout enough to separate the brackish water of the eastern lake from the freshwater chinampa zone (Chapter 4).
Without it, Tenochtitlan would not have survived another century.

In 1454, the One Rabbit famine (the worst drought of the 15th century) collapsed harvests across central Mexico for four consecutive years; the chronicles describe people selling themselves into slavery, parents giving children to coastal Totonacs in exchange for maize, and the population genuinely believing the world was about to end.

The famine reshaped Aztec society — slavery expanded permanently (Chapter 6), tribute from outside the basin became indispensable, and the New Fire Ceremony of 1455 was remembered as the most terrified calendrical transition in Mexica history (Chapter 5).
By 1469, when Motecuzoma I died, the Aztec Empire stretched from the Gulf Coast to parts of the Pacific, with tribute flowing from over 200 conquered towns.
The empire's basic shape was set.
The dike protected the capital.
The Flower Wars supplied the sacrificial pipeline.
Tlacaelel was still in his office, planning the next round, and would outlive his brother by nearly twenty years.

chapters.title: The Floating City
sentences: We need to talk about the city itself.
By the 1490s, Tenochtitlan was the largest city in the Western Hemisphere, larger than any city in Spain or France, and one of the four or five largest cities on earth.

Estimates of its population vary because we have no census: archaeological reconstruction of the city's residential footprint, combined with figures recorded by Spanish observers in 1519, points to between 150,000 and 250,000 residents at the moment of contact.

Even the low end of that range makes it bigger than London (about 50,000 in 1500), Paris (around 200,000 but on the high end of contemporary estimates, and probably overstated), and Seville (about 70,000).
The high end makes it comparable to Constantinople or Beijing.

Add the sister-city Tlatelolco, which by 1473 had been administratively absorbed under Tenochtitlan's rule but remained a distinct urban center, and the metropolitan complex on the lake's central islands held perhaps 200,000 to 300,000 people.
This was not normal for the Americas.
Outside Tenochtitlan, the largest Aztec city was Texcoco, with maybe 60,000 residents.
The next tier of cities (Cholula, Tlaxcala, Huexotzingo) held 20,000 to 40,000.
After that, you dropped quickly to towns of a few thousand.

Tenochtitlan was an outlier within its own empire by a factor of three or four, supported by a tribute system that pulled food and labor from a region of perhaps five to six million people across central Mexico.
The city was built on islands, and the islands were mostly artificial.
The natural high ground in 1325 amounted to a few rocky outcrops totaling perhaps half a square mile.
By 1500, the urbanized area was over five square miles.
The difference was made by Chinampas, dredged earth, and pile-driven fill.
The Mexica had spent two centuries growing their city outward into the lake, by hand, one wicker-and-mud platform at a time.
Chinampas (chee-NAHM-pahs, sometimes called "floating gardens" in popular accounts, though they don't actually float) were the agricultural foundation of the city.

The technology predates the Mexica by centuries (it was practiced at Xochimilco well before the Mexica arrived in the basin), but the Mexica scaled it up dramatically after 1430, when they conquered the southern lake towns and gained direct control of the chinampa zones.
Here's how a chinampa works.
You stake out a rectangular plot in the shallow freshwater portion of the lake.
You weave a fence of wicker around the perimeter.
You shovel mud, lake-bottom muck, and decomposed vegetation inside the fence until you've built up an island three or four feet above the water level.
You plant willows along the edges; their roots grow downward and lock the chinampa in place.
You plant your crops on top: maize, beans, squash, chili peppers, amaranth, tomatoes, flowers.
The water table sits within an arm's reach of the surface, which means the crops never need to be irrigated; the roots simply tap into the lake.

The canals between chinampas (typically about 10 feet wide) double as transport corridors and as fertilizer reservoirs: when canals silt up, you dredge them and pile the rich black mud on top of the chinampas.
Each chinampa might be 30 feet by 200 feet, and a family could work several.
The yields were astonishing by pre-modern standards.
A well-managed chinampa could produce up to seven harvests per year (compared to one for a typical European wheatfield), feeding perhaps fifteen people per acre under intensive cultivation.
The chinampa zone south of Tenochtitlan covered roughly 35 square miles at its peak, which is to say, roughly twice the size of the developed island of Manhattan.

The Aztecs were running the most productive agricultural system in the Americas, and possibly in the world, in the middle of a salty highland lake at 7,400 feet elevation, on a foundation of mud and willow roots.

The system fed Tenochtitlan in years when the basin's hill-slope farming failed, and it continued to feed Mexico City through the colonial period; small chinampas are still worked at Xochimilco today, the lone surviving fragment of the system.

The Maya had developed a structurally similar raised-field system in the lowland swamps of the Petén centuries earlier (Maya Civilization Ch 1), and the Andean cultures around Lake Titicaca had built their own version on the altiplano (Early Andean Civilizations Ch 1) — three independent inventions of the same basic idea, in three radically different environments.
The city itself was laid out with a precision that the Spanish chroniclers, accustomed to medieval European street plans, found uncanny.

Tenochtitlan was divided into four quarters (campan), oriented to the cardinal directions and meeting at the Sacred Precinct (huey teocalli, way teh-OH-kahl-ee, "great temple" or "great holy place," the walled complex at the center of the city that contained the Templo Mayor and dozens of other temples).
The four quarters were further subdivided into calpulli (kahl-POOL-lee, neighborhood-clan groups, Chapter 6), each with its own local temple, school, and council.
Streets and canals ran in a regular grid, both designed to be used: the streets for foot traffic, the canals for canoe traffic.
The Spanish chroniclers compared it to Venice, which is the right comparison in spirit, but Tenochtitlan's canal network was more extensive than Venice's by an order of magnitude.
Bernal Díaz wrote that the canals were so busy you could not throw a stone without hitting a boat.
Three great causeways connected the island to the mainland: one running west to Tlacopan, one running south to Iztapalapa (with a branch to Coyoacan), and one running north to Tepeyac.

Each was about 15 to 25 feet wide, raised eight feet or so above the lake surface, paved with cut stone, and punctuated at intervals by removable wooden bridges over channels left for water flow and (more pointedly) for defensive use.
The bridges could be lifted out, isolating Tenochtitlan from the mainland, which was the single most important defensive feature of the city.
The Spanish would learn this the hard way during La Noche Triste (Chapter 8).
The causeways were not the only links.
Two aqueducts brought freshwater into the city, since Lake Texcoco itself was too brackish to drink.
The first, the Chapultepec Aqueduct, was designed by Nezahualcoyotl himself and completed around 1466.

It was an extraordinary piece of engineering: a double-pipe system running about 2.5 miles from the freshwater springs of Chapultepec hill to the city, made of stuccoed stone troughs supported on a low causeway.
The two pipes ran in parallel so that one could be cleaned while the other carried water; this wasn't a luxury but a necessity, since the system was prone to silt and algae buildup.
Drinking-water vendors in Tenochtitlan filled their canoes at the aqueduct's terminus and paddled the water through the canal network to households that wanted it.

The Chapultepec Aqueduct fed the city for fifty years, until it was destroyed by Cortés during the siege of 1521, and the Spanish later rebuilt it on the same alignment because no one could think of a better design.

A second aqueduct, the Acuecuexatl (ah-kway-kway-SHAHTL, from the Coyoacan springs), was built by Ahuitzotl (whom we'll meet properly in Chapter 7 — for now: the warrior-king who pushed the empire to its maximum extent in the 1490s) in 1499.
It was an engineering ambition that exceeded the engineering capacity.
The flow was too strong, the channels too unprotected, and in 1500 the system overflowed into Lake Texcoco, raised the water level several feet, and flooded large sections of Tenochtitlan.

Ahuitzotl, by some accounts, died of injuries sustained when a low doorway collapsed on him as he fled the rising water (the connection between the flood and his death two years later is debated, but he certainly never fully recovered, and the construction failure haunted his last years).
The flood is a useful reminder that Aztec engineering, brilliant as it was, was not infallible.
The same hydraulic system that fed the city could also drown it.
The center of everything was the Sacred Precinct, a walled enclosure roughly 1,300 feet on a side at the heart of the city.
By 1500, the precinct contained 78 separate buildings, most of which we can identify only from descriptions in the Spanish chronicles and from the foundations excavated in modern Mexico City.

These included the Templo Mayor (Phase VII by 1500, the seventh successive enlargement, built over the ruins of the previous six), temples to Quetzalcoatl, Tezcatlipoca, Coatlicue, and dozens of lesser deities, the great tzompantli (tsom-PAHN-tlee, "skull rack" — a wooden frame on which the heads of sacrificial victims were displayed in rows), a ceremonial ball court, and the calmecac school for noble boys (Chapter 6, the academy where the sons of the nobility were trained).
Archaeological excavation of the tzompantli in the 2010s recovered hundreds of skulls from the foundation of the rack and confirmed the historical accounts.

The whole complex was enclosed within the coatepantli ("serpent wall," a low stone wall topped with sculpted serpent heads) and entered through four gates corresponding to the four quarters of the city.
The Templo Mayor itself was the seventh and largest version of the original 1325 shrine.
By 1487, when Ahuitzotl rededicated it, the pyramid stood about 150 feet (45 meters) tall, with two parallel staircases, each over 100 steps, leading to twin shrines at the summit.

The southern shrine, painted red and white, housed Huitzilopochtli; the northern, painted blue and white, housed Tlaloc. the painted polychrome was the city's signature visual: Aztec architecture was not the bare stone we see in ruins today but the same kind of brilliantly painted plaster surface that had defined Teotihuacan a thousand years earlier (Teotihuacan Ch 2).

When Spanish observers tried to describe Tenochtitlan, they kept reaching for the word "white" to capture the lime-plastered surfaces, but they noted the "great red and blue temples" rising above the white.
From the lake, the city would have been a ridge of color — white walls, red and blue pyramid summits, painted murals on every important building, all reflecting in the lake water.
The dedication of the Phase VII Templo Mayor in 1487 by Ahuitzotl is one of the more contested episodes in Aztec history.
The Mexica chronicles claim that 80,400 victims were sacrificed over four days at the rededication, with the lines of captives stretching out of the city for miles and the priests working in shifts.

The number is almost certainly exaggerated; modern estimates cluster around 4,000 to 14,000, and even the lower figure assumes industrial-scale ritualized killing that would have required a specific organizational apparatus to manage.

What is not in doubt is that the rededication was unprecedented in scale, that captives from many recently conquered Gulf Coast and Oaxacan towns were sacrificed (a deliberate political gesture: the rededication asserted Mexica dominance over the new tributaries), and that the event was remembered for generations as the moment Aztec sacrificial practice reached its full public scope.
Ahuitzotl was the kind of ruler who liked his statements grand.

At the foot of the Huitzilopochtli stairway, set flush with the plaza floor, lay the Coyolxauhqui Stone, a circular relief eleven feet across that depicts the moon goddess Coyolxauhqui (koy-ol-SHAH-wkee, "Bells on Her Cheeks," sister of Huitzilopochtli) at the moment of her dismemberment: limbs splayed, head severed, body curled into a circle.

The myth behind the image: their mother, Coatlicue, conceived Huitzilopochtli by a feather that fell from the sky; Coyolxauhqui, scandalized, conspired with her four hundred star-brothers to kill their mother before the new child was born; Huitzilopochtli leapt from the womb fully armed, killed Coyolxauhqui, and dismembered her on a hill where her limbs scattered.
The architecture and the myth lined up exactly.

Sacrificial victims, after their hearts were cut out at the temple summit, were tumbled down the steps to land on her image — every sacrifice reenacting the cosmic battle, every victim playing the role of Coyolxauhqui falling, every body that landed on the stone a renewed assertion of the warrior-sun-god's victory over the moon.

The stone was rediscovered in 1978 by electrical workers digging near the cathedral in central Mexico City, an event that triggered the Templo Mayor Project, the long-running modern excavation directed by Eduardo Matos Moctezuma (eh-DWAR-doh MAH-tos mok-tay-ZOO-mah, by descent related to the Aztec royal line, and the central archaeologist of his ancestors' temple) that has progressively uncovered the temple foundations beneath the colonial city.
More new evidence about the late Aztec Empire has come from this single excavation than from any other in Mesoamerica.
The Tlatelolco Market, on the sister island just north of Tenochtitlan, was the empire's commercial heart and one of the largest marketplaces in the world.

Bernal Díaz, who saw it firsthand in 1519, wrote that some of his fellow soldiers, who had traveled in Constantinople and Rome, said they had never seen a market so well-organized or so full of people.

The numbers given by various Spanish observers (40,000, 60,000, 80,000 daily visitors) are guesswork, but the lower estimate is plausible and represents a foot traffic that few European cities of 1519 could match.

The market sold maize, beans, chili peppers, tomatoes, salt, cacao, vanilla, rabbits, dogs, turkeys, fish, frogs, salamanders (axolotls were eaten in Tenochtitlan in great numbers, until the Spanish found them disgusting and they fell out of fashion), feathers, jade, gold, silver, cotton, henequen fiber, sandals, cloaks, slaves, medicinal herbs, and dozens of other categories.
Each commodity had its own section.
Each section had its own court of magistrates that adjudicated disputes on the spot.
Cheating, defective merchandise, and price gouging were grounds for criminal prosecution.
The market ran on cacao beans as small-denomination currency.
A turkey cost 100 beans.
A tamale cost 1 bean.
A canoe cost about 1 cotton quachtli (KWACH-tlee, a standardized cotton cloth that served as the larger-denomination currency, equivalent to about 65 to 300 cacao beans depending on quality).

The system worked because cacao was both a luxury beverage and a durable, divisible, portable commodity, and because the empire's tribute system funneled cacao production from the Soconusco coast (Chapter 7) into central Mexico in industrial quantities. cacao-as-currency was not a Mexica invention; the Maya had been using cacao beans as a standardized medium of exchange across the lowland markets for centuries (Maya Civilization Ch 2), and the Aztecs had inherited the convention along with the trade routes.
The Spanish, seeing the market for the first time, were dumbfounded: an economy this large running without coin or letter of credit, ordered by traditional law and visual inspection.
The market was also where the pochteca (poach-TEH-kah, the long-distance merchant guild) operated their warehouses and conducted their business.

The pochteca were one of the most curious institutions of the empire: a hereditary class of professional merchants, with their own neighborhoods, their own gods, their own dress, their own legal courts, and their own complicated relationship with the imperial state.
They will get a chapter of their own (Chapter 6).
What did everyday life feel like in this city?
Loud, crowded, and largely outdoors.
Houses were one-story adobe-and-stone constructions for commoners and two-story plastered compounds for nobles.

Most domestic life happened in interior courtyards, since the climate at 7,400 feet is mild year-round (Tenochtitlan's average annual temperature is about 60°F; nights can be cold but freezes are rare in the city center).
Cooking was done over clay hearths fueled by wood and charcoal, both increasingly expensive as deforestation around the basin progressed (Chapter 8).

The diet centered on maize prepared as tortillas and tamales, with beans, squash, chili, amaranth, sage seeds, and prickly pear as supplements; meat was occasional and came mainly from turkey, dog, fish, and the lake's astonishingly varied small game (frogs, salamanders, lake-fly larvae, even dragonfly nymphs).

The Mexica drank water, atolli (ah-TOH-lee, a thick maize gruel), pulque (POOL-kay, the fermented sap of the maguey cactus, mildly alcoholic, the everyday alcoholic drink of central Mexico), and, for the wealthy, xocolatl (sho-KOH-lahtl, the bitter cacao beverage that gave the modern English word "chocolate").
Public drunkenness on pulque was severely punished, in theory; the elderly were exempt and could drink as they pleased.
The smell of the city was distinctive.
Spanish observers, who knew European cities were filthy, were impressed at how clean Tenochtitlan was.
The streets were swept daily by a corps of municipal cleaners.
Public latrines were available.
Human waste was collected in canoes for use as fertilizer in the chinampas, an integrated nutrient-recycling system that European cities would not match for another four centuries.
The air would have smelled of burning copal incense from the temples, cooking maize, lake water, and, on festival days, blood.
Compared to contemporary Seville, Tenochtitlan would have been startlingly clean and startlingly bloody at the same time.

chapters.title: The Sun That Demanded Blood
sentences: Aztec religion was the most theatrical in the ancient world.

Other civilizations sacrificed humans (the Mesopotamians and the Shang both practiced it at certain periods, the Carthaginians did, the Maya did, the Andean cultures did, a number of European prehistoric cultures did), but no other civilization staged human sacrifice on the scale, with the regularity, or with the cosmological elaboration that the Aztecs did.
The Templo Mayor was the most actively used sacrificial site in human history.
The state religion required the regular spilling of human blood as the literal mechanism that kept the universe running.

And the religion was performed publicly, on the highest pyramid in the city, in front of crowds, by costumed priests, with formal liturgies and choreographed processions, every single month of the year.
This is uncomfortable material, and it deserves to be presented with as much honesty about the evidence as the rest of the empire's history.

The basic facts (regular sacrifice, the Templo Mayor as the central site, the connection between warfare and sacrificial supply, public ritual performance) are not seriously disputed; they are documented in Aztec sources, Spanish sources, and the archaeological record (skull racks, sacrificial knives, butchered remains in temple contexts have all been recovered).
What is contested is scale: how many sacrifices per year, how many at major dedications, how the demand interacted with imperial expansion.
The Aztec sources, written by descendants of the priestly elite, tend to inflate the numbers as a sign of religious devotion.
The Spanish sources, written by people who needed to justify the conquest, tend to inflate the numbers as a sign of barbaric darkness.
Modern estimates range from a few thousand sacrifices per year across the entire empire on the low end to twenty thousand or more at peak.
We will probably never have a definitive count.
What we can say is that the practice was systematic, pervasive, and central to the imperial state, and that calling it "occasional" or "ceremonial" misses the point.
We should also resist the modern temptation to read Aztec religion as either uniquely barbaric or as a kind of misunderstood purity.
It was a real religion, with internal logic, performed by people who genuinely believed they were doing necessary cosmic work.

It was also a system that benefited a specific political class (the priestly and warrior elites who organized and consumed the rituals) at the expense of vast numbers of conquered peoples and slaves whose bodies fed it.
Both things are true.
The Aztec sources are explicit that human sacrifice was a religious necessity, that cosmic destruction would follow if it stopped, and that the gods needed blood to function.
The same sources are explicit that the war machine that fed the sacrificial system also expanded the empire, enriched the elite, and intimidated potential rebels.
Religion and politics were not separable; they were the same engine.

The cosmology, in summary form: the Aztecs believed that the world was now in its fifth age (or "fifth sun"), and that four previous worlds had been destroyed in succession (by jaguars, wind, fire, and water).
The current age was created at Teotihuacan, where the gods had gathered after the destruction of the fourth world to bring up a new sun.
The gods sat around a great fire, and the question was who would throw himself in to be reborn as the new sun.
A wealthy, beautiful god named Tecuciztecatl volunteered first but lost his nerve on the threshold of the flames.
A poor, scabrous god named Nanahuatzin, by contrast, threw himself in without hesitation, and was reborn as the sun.

Tecuciztecatl, shamed, then jumped in too and was reborn as the moon, but the gods threw a rabbit at his face to dim his brightness (which is why the Aztecs saw a rabbit on the moon, the way other cultures see a face).
When the new sun rose, it would not move; it sat there glaring at the world, demanding that the other gods sacrifice themselves so it would have the energy to begin its daily journey.
All of them.
And ever since, the sun's daily movement across the sky has required the same kind of sacrifice that originally set it in motion: blood, freely given, by the creatures of the world.
This was, on Tlacaelel's interpretation (Chapter 3), the foundational reason for human sacrifice.
The Aztecs were repaying the cosmic debt incurred when the gods sacrificed themselves at Teotihuacan.
The current world, the fifth sun, would last only as long as the cycle of sacrifice continued.
When it stopped, the sun would stop, the world would end, and another age would begin.
And the Mexica, as the chosen people of Huitzilopochtli (the sun himself, in his warrior aspect), bore the primary responsibility for keeping the cycle going.
The fact that the Aztecs literally walked among the ruins of Teotihuacan when they made these arguments is one of the strangest things about their religion.
They knew the ruins existed.
They had named them ("the place where the gods were born").
They collected artifacts from the site, mostly green obsidian objects, and reused them in their own rituals.
They incorporated Teotihuacan into their creation mythology as the literal birthplace of the current world.
But they did not know who had built it (Teotihuacan Ch 8 covers the absence of a name for the original builders).
To the Aztecs, the great pyramids 30 miles to the northeast were divine architecture, evidence of the gods' presence at the moment of cosmogenesis.
They made pilgrimages to the site, they performed rituals there, they wrote it into their sacred geography.
Teotihuacan, dead for nearly a thousand years by the time the Mexica encountered it, had a second life as an Aztec religious site.
The pantheon was crowded.

The Florentine Codex catalogs hundreds of named deities, ranging from major cosmic figures down to local patron gods of individual neighborhoods, and the relationships among them were tangled enough that even the priests disagreed on the details.
A handful of the major figures, though, dominated public worship and the calendar of festivals.
Huitzilopochtli, the war god turned sun god (Chapter 1, 3), the patron of the Mexica themselves, was the demanding center of state religion: he wanted warrior captives, and he wanted them constantly.

Across the twin shrines at the summit of the Templo Mayor, his shrine faced that of Tlaloc, the ancient rain god, identifiable across more than a millennium of Mesoamerican iconography by his goggle eyes and fanged mouth.

Tlaloc had been worshipped, under the same iconography, at Teotihuacan a thousand years earlier (Teotihuacan Ch 7) and traces back further still to Olmec storm-deity imagery (Olmec Civilization Ch 4) — a continuous lineage of more than two thousand years.
The pairing of war-and-sun with rain-and-agriculture at the apex of the city's religious architecture was not arbitrary.
It reproduced, in stone and paint, the empire's two ultimate dependencies: military success and reliable rainfall.
Tlaloc demanded children, particularly during the dry season, on the belief that their crying would bring more rain.

This is one of the more disturbing facts of Aztec religion, attested in multiple sources and archaeologically confirmed by the buried remains of sacrificed children in deposits beneath Tlaloc's shrine.
The other great cosmic powers ran along complementary axes.

Tezcatlipoca (tes-kah-tlee-POH-kah, "Smoking Mirror") was the sky-and-night counterpart to Huitzilopochtli's solar warrior: a trickster god of sorcery, royalty, and discord, often depicted with an obsidian mirror in place of one foot.

Quetzalcoatl (ket-sahl-KOH-ahtl, "Feathered Serpent") was the deity of wind, learning, priesthood, and creation, and the oldest continuous figure in the Mesoamerican pantheon — feathered serpents appear in Olmec iconography over a thousand years earlier (Olmec Civilization Ch 4), the Maya knew him as Kukulkan (Maya Civilization Ch 7), and he had a major temple at Teotihuacan (Teotihuacan Ch 3).

His trajectory is itself a small drama: his cult was politically suppressed at Teotihuacan around 250 CE (Teotihuacan Ch 3 and Ch 7), then revived by the Toltecs at Tula, then inherited by the Aztecs, who turned the legend of his eastward departure into a cosmological end-times prophecy.
A god the people of Teotihuacan once tore down had, a thousand years later, become the deity whose return the Aztecs feared above all others.

The Aztecs gave him a major role in their creation mythology — he descended into the underworld to retrieve the bones of humanity and give them new life — and they kept the older Toltec story about his departure eastward across the sea, with a vow to return in a year called One Reed in the cyclical calendar.
The Year One Reed of the early 16th century corresponded to 1519.
We will come back to that.
The mother and earth and underworld powers were as important as the sky deities, and as fearsome to look at.

Coatlicue (koh-aht-LEE-kway, "She of the Serpent Skirt") was the earth and mother goddess, mother of Huitzilopochtli, Coyolxauhqui, and the four hundred star-brothers (Chapter 3, Chapter 4); her surviving eight-foot basalt sculpture, commissioned around 1490 and now in the National Museum of Anthropology in Mexico City, wears a skirt of writhing serpents and a necklace of human hands and hearts.

The statue is one of the most powerful objects in pre-Columbian art, and one of the most disturbing: when it was first excavated in 1790, the ecclesiastical authorities of Mexico City ordered it reburied as a pagan object too dangerous to leave on display.
It was excavated and reburied multiple times before finally entering the museum in the 19th century.

Xipe Totec (SHEE-pay TOH-tek, "Our Lord the Flayed One") presided over springtime renewal — the year shedding its old husk like a snake shedding skin — and his annual festival, Tlacaxipehualiztli (tlah-kah-shee-peh-WAH-leets-tlee, the second of the eighteen monthly festivals), was the most disturbing event in the regular ritual cycle.

Captives were sacrificed, then their priests wore the flayed skins for the next twenty days as the skin progressively rotted away, symbolizing the new green corn stalk emerging from the dry husk of the old.
This is documented in detail in the Florentine Codex and confirmed by archaeological remains.

The priests believed they were enacting a vital agricultural metaphor on which the next year's corn crop depended; modern observers should not pretend the ritual was less than it was, and also should not pretend it was simply gratuitous.

Coyolxauhqui (Chapter 4) was the dismembered moon, Huehueteotl (way-way-TEH-otl, "Old Old God") was the ancient fire deity also worshipped at Teotihuacan, and dozens more — neighborhood patrons, deities of pulque and birth and rain and travel — filled out a pantheon in which there was always one more god to feed.
The Aztec calendar was a parallel cosmological apparatus, a clockwork that organized when each ritual was due.
The system used two interlocking calendars that turned together like gears.
The tonalpohualli (toh-nahl-poh-WAH-lee, "count of days") was the 260-day ritual calendar, made by combining 20 named days with 13 numbers.
The 260-day cycle dates back to at least the Olmec period (Olmec Civilization Ch 7) and was shared across Mesoamerica; the Maya used the same cycle (Maya Civilization Ch 2).

Each day had its own divinatory meaning, and skilled priests (known by the title tonalpouhque, "counter of days") used the calendar for naming children, scheduling weddings, predicting outcomes, and diagnosing illness.

The xiuhpohualli (shee-oo-poh-WAH-lee, "count of years") was the 365-day solar calendar, made of 18 months of 20 days plus 5 final "useless" days (nemontemi) at the end of the year, considered unlucky.
Each of the 18 months had its own festival, with its own deity, its own ritual sequence, and (almost without exception) its own form of human sacrifice.

The Toxcatl festival in May, dedicated to Tezcatlipoca, featured the sacrifice of a young man who had been chosen a year in advance to live as the living embodiment of the god, dressed in his regalia, attended by servants, accompanied by four wives in his final twenty days, before climbing the temple steps and having his heart cut out at the summit.
The next day, a new young man was selected to begin the year's incarnation.

The festival of Ochpaniztli in autumn, dedicated to Toci (the grandmother of the gods), involved the sacrifice and flaying of a woman whose skin was then worn by a priest performing a ritual sweeping of the temple.
The cycle of monthly sacrifices was continuous, with no calendrical gap.
The two calendars (tonalpohualli of 260 days, xiuhpohualli of 365) interlocked into a larger cycle of 52 years, called xiuhmolpilli (shee-oo-mol-PEEL-ee, "binding of the years").
After 52 years, both calendars returned to their shared starting position.
The transition between cycles was the moment of greatest cosmic vulnerability in the entire Aztec calendrical system.
The Aztecs feared that at the end of one bundle of years, the world might fail to begin a new one, and the fifth sun would simply expire.
To prevent this, the priests performed the New Fire Ceremony (xiuhmolpilli, "binding of the years," the same word used for the 52-year cycle itself).
The most elaborately documented New Fire Ceremony was that of 1507, recorded in the Codex Borbonicus.
The ritual unfolded as follows.
In the days before the ceremony, all fires across the empire were extinguished.
Hearths were swept clean.
Pottery was broken.
Pregnant women were locked in granaries with masks of maguey leaves on their faces, on the belief that if the world did end, pregnant women might turn into demons that would devour the survivors.
Children were kept awake all night by their parents, who pinched them every time they nodded off, on the belief that any child who slept through the New Fire would turn into a mouse.
The priests, dressed in the regalia of all the major deities, climbed to the summit of Huixachtlan hill (wee-shahk-TLAHN, the "Hill of the Star," about 7 miles southeast of Tenochtitlan) at sunset.
They watched the constellation Pleiades.

When the Pleiades reached zenith, signaling that the world had not ended, the head priest laid a sacrificial victim on the altar, opened his chest, and drilled new fire on his sternum using a wooden fire-drill on a wooden hearth, the ancient method.
When the spark caught (and it always caught, the priests being expert in this), it was set into a torch, then carried by relay runners to every temple and household in the empire.
Within hours, the entire central Mexican plateau was relit from a single flame, drilled on a single human chest, on a single hilltop.
The world had survived another 52 years.

The Mexica chronicles record three New Fire Ceremonies during the imperial period: 1403 (under Huitzilihuitl), 1455 (under Motecuzoma I, during the One Rabbit famine, especially fraught), and 1507 (under Motecuzoma II, the most elaborately documented).
A fourth would have occurred in 1559 if the empire had survived; instead, the Catholic missionaries in colonial Mexico did everything they could to suppress the ceremony, with mixed success.

The ceremony is one of the most striking examples of public ritual in the ancient world, and it should be set alongside the Roman Saecular Games or the Egyptian Sed Festival as a comparable performance of cosmic renewal.
The Romans renewed their state every 110 years; the Egyptian pharaoh renewed his rule every 30; the Mexica renewed the world itself every 52.
The scale of belief was, by any standard, enormous.

chapters.title: Ladders and Cages
sentences: Aztec society had a structure that was rigid by some measures and surprisingly mobile by others.
At the top sat the tlatoani of Tenochtitlan, who by 1500 was the most powerful individual on the continent.

The tlatoani was not strictly hereditary: each successor was elected by a council of senior nobles from a pool of eligible candidates, all of whom belonged to the royal lineage descended from Acamapichtli.
Election usually fell to a brother, son, or nephew of the previous ruler, but the council could and did skip candidates considered unsuitable.

The system was a mix of hereditary monarchy and oligarchic election; in practice, it produced a string of capable warrior-kings, with two notable failures (Tizoc, the brief reigning fifth tlatoani in the 1480s whom we'll meet in Chapter 7, was considered too weak and was probably poisoned; Cuauhtémoc, the last tlatoani who would face Cortés's siege in 1521, ruled in collapsing circumstances and could not have saved the empire even if he had been a genius).
Below the tlatoani came the pipiltin (pee-PEEL-teen, the noble class, plural of pilli).
The pipiltin were defined by descent: anyone who could claim direct descent from a tlatoani or from one of the empire's founding lineages.

They held the senior offices in government, the priesthood, and the military, were exempt from manual labor, owned land in their own right (most other land was held communally by calpulli), wore distinctive clothing (cotton fabrics and dyed mantles forbidden to commoners), and received the best education at the calmecac schools.

They were also, in theory, held to higher standards: nobles caught in adultery, drunkenness, or theft faced harsher penalties than commoners, on the principle that those who wielded the empire's authority should be its strictest exemplars.
In practice, justice was probably more flexible than the ideal.
Below the pipiltin came the macehualtin (mah-seh-WAHL-teen, the commoner class).
The macehualtin were the vast majority of the population: farmers, artisans, soldiers, fishermen, market sellers, porters, builders.
They held land through their calpulli (kahl-POOL-lee, the neighborhood-clan group, originally a kin-based unit but by 1500 more of a residential and occupational organization).
The calpulli was the basic unit of Aztec civic life.

It allocated chinampa plots to its members, organized labor levies for state projects, ran its own school (the telpochcalli), maintained its own local temple, and selected representatives to the city's senior councils.
Each calpulli had a council of elders that adjudicated minor disputes and set local rules.
The calpulli system distributed power widely enough that ordinary Mexica had a real stake in the empire's success, and they could draw on their calpulli for support in times of crisis.
The macehualtin were not stuck where they were born.
The Aztec system included a working ladder of social mobility centered on warfare.

A commoner who captured one enemy warrior in battle received a small honor; capturing two or three increased his rank; capturing four entitled him to the title of eagle warrior or jaguar warrior (the elite military orders, distinguished by their costumes — eagle-feather suits with bird-headdress helmets, or jaguar-pelt suits with snarling-jaguar helmets).

At the highest level, a commoner who distinguished himself sufficiently in warfare could be elevated to the rank of cuauhpilli (KWAH-oo-PEEL-lee, "eagle noble"), a kind of meritocratic nobility that was distinct from the hereditary pipiltin but enjoyed many of the same privileges.
The system was a working channel for social mobility, and it was the empire's primary mechanism for incorporating talented commoners into the warrior elite.

The Roman Empire, comparable in scale, maintained a similar system of military advancement (although nothing as formalized as the Aztec eagle and jaguar orders), and the structural logic was identical: a continuously expanding empire produces opportunity for ambitious commoners, which keeps the lower orders invested in the system rather than rebelling against it.
Below the macehualtin came the mayeque (mah-YEH-keh), a smaller class of landless commoners who worked land owned by nobles in exchange for a share of the produce.
The mayeque are sometimes described as serfs, but the analogy is imperfect; they were free in person but tied to land obligations.
At the bottom were the tlacotin (tlah-KOH-teen, slaves).
Aztec slavery was different from racial chattel slavery in the Americas after 1500.
The tlacotin were not a hereditary class; their children were born free.
Slavery resulted from specific causes: criminal punishment, debt, or self-sale during famine.
Slaves could own property, marry, save money, and purchase their own freedom.
They were not racially differentiated from their owners.
The institution was real and exploitative, but it operated more like Roman or Mediterranean slavery than like the colonial-Atlantic slavery that would replace it after 1521.
A subcategory, tecpan tlacotin, were slaves attached to noble households and palace administration.

Captives taken in war, who would become sacrificial victims, were not classified as tlacotin; they were a separate category, considered already given to the gods, distinct from the regular slave population.
Children were schooled in one of two institutional systems, depending on their birth.
The calmecac (kahl-meh-KAHK, "house of lineage" or "house of the noble line") were schools attached to the major temples in each city.
They educated the sons of the pipiltin and a select group of commoner boys destined for the priesthood.

The curriculum was demanding: religious ritual, calendar mathematics, astronomy, the painting of codices (the Aztec script was a mix of pictographs and phonetic glyphs, complex enough that mastering it took years), Nahuatl rhetoric, history, law, and military discipline.

Calmecac students lived at the school, slept little, fasted often, performed self-mortification (cutting their tongues, ears, or genitals with maguey thorns to draw blood as offerings), and were beaten for infractions.
Graduates filled the empire's administrative, religious, and high-military offices.
The calmecac was the institutional core that reproduced the elite generation after generation.
The telpochcalli (tel-poach-KAHL-lee, "house of the youth") were neighborhood schools attached to each calpulli.
They educated commoner boys in martial combat, civic duty, communal labor, and the basics of religious participation.
Graduates of the telpochcalli formed the bulk of the Aztec army and the trained labor pool that built the empire's roads, canals, and pyramids.

The schooling was less academically demanding than the calmecac but no less rigorous physically; telpochcalli students worked on public construction projects, performed sweat-bath rituals, and were trained from childhood in handling the macahuitl (the wooden sword edged with obsidian blades, the standard Aztec weapon — obsidian is volcanic glass, sharper than steel when freshly knapped, though brittle; central Mexico had abundant high-quality obsidian sources, and the empire's whole edged-weapon tradition rested on them).
Girls received less formal schooling but had their own institutional paths.
The most studious might become cihuatlamacazqui, female priestesses attached to certain temples, who could be married or celibate depending on the institution.
Most girls learned weaving, cooking, household management, and religious ritual from their mothers and from local female elders.
Aztec gender roles were strict by modern standards but allowed more autonomy than was typical in early modern Europe.
Women owned property in their own names, could initiate divorce, ran market stalls, and could become priestesses, healers, or midwives.

The most educated noble women, like Macuilxochitzin (the daughter of the cihuacoatl Tlacaelel), composed Nahuatl poetry and were celebrated for their literary work; her surviving poems are among the most beautiful texts in the Aztec corpus.
Marriage was monogamous in legal form for commoners but polygamous for nobles, who could maintain multiple wives in separate households.
Sexual conduct was strictly regulated: adultery was punishable by death, applied to both men and women, and enforced.
Public drunkenness was, in theory, also a capital offense for the young, though the elderly were exempt.
