The legal system was harsher than Roman law in its written code but probably patchier in its enforcement, particularly in remote tributaries.
The judicial system was relatively sophisticated.

Cases proceeded through a hierarchy of courts: local calpulli councils handled minor disputes, district courts handled serious crimes, and the tlatocan (tlah-TOH-kahn, the supreme council of the tlatoani) served as the empire's high court.

Judges were full-time professional specialists, drawn from the calmecac graduates, paid by the state, and held to strict standards: bribery of a judge was a capital offense, and judges who took bribes were executed publicly as a deterrent.

The 80-article legal code formalized by Nezahualcoyotl of Texcoco around 1445 was widely admired and partially adopted across the empire; it specified penalties for murder, adultery, theft, official corruption, battlefield cowardice, and other offenses, with detailed gradations based on the social status of victim and perpetrator.

Texcoco, under the long reigns of Nezahualcoyotl (1431–1472) and his son Nezahualpilli (1472–1516), became the most legally and intellectually sophisticated polity in central Mexico, and it served as the cultural counterweight to Tenochtitlan's military and religious dominance.
Nezahualcoyotl deserves a sketch of his own.

He was a poet, an architect, a hydraulic engineer (the Albarradón that saved Tenochtitlan from flooding was his design), a religious skeptic (his philosophical poetry rejects the dominant sacrificial cosmology in favor of a more abstract, possibly monotheistic conception of "the giver of life"), and a working king who held one of the empire's three capitals for forty-one years.
His court at Texcoco was a center of poetry, scholarship, and royal patronage that drew artists, philosophers, and scientists from across central Mexico.
About thirty of his Nahuatl poems survive in collected manuscripts compiled after the conquest.
They are not what one expects from a 15th-century warrior king.

Sample lines, in an approximate translation that follows the spirit of Miguel León-Portilla's standard scholarly renderings rather than any single one of them word-for-word: "Truly do we live on Earth? / Not forever on Earth; only a little while here. / Although it be jade, it will be broken. / Although it be gold, it is crushed. / Although it be a quetzal feather, it is torn asunder. / Not forever on Earth; only a little while here." The voice is thoroughly Mexican and unmistakably medieval-Mesoamerican; it is also a voice that the Renaissance Italian humanists, working in the same century on the other side of the Atlantic, would have recognized as a fellow practitioner of philosophical lyric.
Petrarch (1304–1374) and Nezahualcoyotl (1402–1472) are roughly contemporaries, and their concerns overlap.
The pochteca were one of the most distinctive institutions of the empire and require explanation, because nothing comparable existed in the contemporary Old World.
The pochteca were the long-distance merchant guild, a hereditary class of professional traders who organized armed expeditions to distant markets and brought back luxury goods.

They lived in their own neighborhoods (the Pochtlan and Acxotlan calpulli of Tenochtitlan), worshipped their own patron god (Yacatecuhtli, "Lord of the Vanguard"), wore distinctive plain dress, kept their own legal courts (Chapter 4), and operated under a strict guild discipline.

They were technically commoners, but the wealthiest pochteca families rivaled the nobility in their material wealth, and by the late empire, the line between rich pochteca and poor pipiltin had genuinely blurred.

The state simultaneously valued them (for the goods they brought) and resented them (for their independence and wealth), and the relationship was managed through a combination of formal recognition and informal tension.
A pochteca expedition was a serious undertaking.
A typical caravan included perhaps fifty to two hundred merchants, with porters carrying loads on tumplines (forehead-straps; Mesoamerica had no pack animals), interpreters, and armed guards.
The merchants traveled in disguise when crossing hostile territory, learning the local dialects and customs to pass as foreigners.

They carried specific Tenochtitlan products outbound (cotton cloth, obsidian blades, slave-grade copper, rabbit-fur capes, dyestuffs) and returned with luxuries that Tenochtitlan could not produce: cacao beans (the bulk currency, but also the high-grade dark-roasted beans for the elite chocolate trade), quetzal feathers (the iridescent green tail feathers of the resplendent quetzal, the supreme prestige material in Mesoamerica), jade and obsidian ornaments, jaguar pelts, gold dust, amber, rubber, and tropical bird feathers of every color.

They also gathered intelligence: pochteca expeditions were the empire's primary source of information about the political condition of distant kingdoms, and pochteca who returned reporting that a particular tributary was preparing rebellion or a particular independent kingdom was vulnerable to conquest were rewarded with tlatoani audiences and noble titles.

The pochteca network reached from the Aztec heartland in central Mexico to the Soconusco (or Xoconochco, sho-koh-NOACH-ko) cacao coast on the Pacific, on the border of modern Guatemala (Chapter 7), to the Maya region of Yucatán in the southeast (where pochteca traders may have witnessed the late Postclassic Maya cities firsthand, Maya Civilization Ch 8), and reportedly as far north as the American Southwest.

Goods of unmistakably Aztec character (specific copper bell types, cotton fabrics, mosaic mirrors) appear in late prehistoric sites in modern New Mexico, suggesting that pochteca trade reached at least as far as the Pueblo cultures, although direct pochteca presence that far north has not been confirmed.

On the eastern side of the continent, a contemporaneous prestige-exchange network centered on Cahokia moved copper, marine shell, and ceremonial goods comparable distances through non-market gift exchange (Mississippian Culture Ch 6).
The shape of the system, viewed from a height, comes back to the chapter's title.
Aztec society was a series of ladders set inside a series of cages.
A macehualli could climb to cuauhpilli on captured warriors.
A talented commoner boy could land in the calmecac and rise into the priesthood or administration.
A merchant could outearn a noble.
A clever woman could become a priestess, a healer, a market judge, a poet.
The ladders were real.
They were also bounded.
Hereditary nobility kept the highest offices for itself.
The pochteca, for all their wealth, never sat at the top of the empire's political order.
The mayeque worked land they would never own.
The tlacotin remained tlacotin until their debts were paid.
And the engine that drove the whole structure — Tlacaelel's machine of warrior capture and cosmic obligation — required a constant supply of bodies that the system itself produced and consumed.
Mobility for some was made possible by constraint for many.
The arrangement worked, for almost a century, because the empire kept growing and the rewards kept arriving.

When the growth stopped, in the early 1500s under Motecuzoma II (Chapter 7), the ladders started to feel less like opportunities and more like the bars of a cage that everyone, suddenly, was inside together.

chapters.title: Ahuitzotl and the High Tide
sentences: Three rulers brought the empire to its zenith.
Axayacatl (ah-shah-YAH-kahtl, "Water Mask," r. 1469–1481) succeeded his grandfather Motecuzoma I at age 19.
He was vigorous, ambitious, and a competent if not brilliant general.
His reign opened with the conquest of Tlatelolco in 1473.
Tlatelolco, the sister city on the neighboring island, had remained politically separate from Tenochtitlan for nearly 150 years, with its own ruling line and its own market.
By the 1470s, the relationship had soured: Tlatelolco's tlatoani, Moquihuix, had attempted to build an anti-Tenochtitlan coalition.
Axayacatl crushed it.
Moquihuix died in the assault on the Templo Mayor of Tlatelolco.
The market, the most important commercial institution in central Mexico, was annexed under Tenochtitlan's administration.
Tlatelolco never recovered its political independence, but its market continued to flourish under the unified administration, and its calpulli structure remained intact.
Axayacatl also pushed the empire to one of its catastrophic limits.
In 1479, he led a major campaign against the Tarascan Empire of Michoacán, the most powerful kingdom in Mesoamerica that the Aztecs never conquered.

The Tarascans (also called the Purépecha, poo-RAY-pay-cha, after their own name for themselves) ruled from their capital at Tzintzuntzan (tseen-TSOON-tsahn, "place of the hummingbirds," coincidentally similar to a Nahuatl-style name despite being in a completely unrelated language) on the western shore of Lake Pátzcuaro.

The Tarascans had a number of advantages: defensible mountain terrain, skilled metalworkers (the Tarascans were among the few Mesoamerican civilizations to master copper and bronze metallurgy, putting them centuries ahead of the Aztecs in metal weaponry), and a centralized state that mobilized armies efficiently.
At Tlaximaloyan in 1479, the Aztec army of perhaps 32,000 men met a Tarascan army of perhaps 50,000.
The Aztecs were routed.
Estimates put their losses at over 20,000 men, the worst military defeat in Mexica history.
The frontier between the two empires froze along a line of fortified Aztec border towns, and no later tlatoani would attempt the conquest.
The Tarascans remained independent until they made their own arrangement with the Spanish in 1522, after the fall of Tenochtitlan.

In 1479, Axayacatl also commissioned the Sun Stone (sometimes called the Aztec Calendar Stone), a massive basalt disc nearly 12 feet in diameter and weighing 24 tons, carved with the central deity Tonatiuh (the sun) surrounded by symbols of the four previous cosmic ages, the twenty named days of the tonalpohualli, and decorative borders showing the cosmic ordering of the world.
The stone was intended for a ceremonial platform in the Sacred Precinct, where sacrificial victims could be slain on top of it.

It was buried after the conquest, rediscovered in 1790 in the Zócalo (the central plaza of colonial Mexico City), and is now the most famous single object of pre-Columbian art, displayed in the National Museum of Anthropology.
Axayacatl died in 1481, possibly of injuries from the Tlaximaloyan defeat.

His successor was his older brother Tizoc (TEE-sok, "He Has Drilled Holes"), a weak king whose two campaigns ended in embarrassing failures and whose ill-attended military expeditions returned without enough captives for proper religious obligations.

Tizoc was almost certainly assassinated by poison in 1486, after just five years on the throne, in what may have been the only successful coup against a sitting tlatoani in Mexica history. (The poisoning is documented in multiple sources but the details are uncertain.
It was probably orchestrated by Tlacaelel, the cihuacoatl, who at this point was in his eighties and had outlasted four kings; the political logic suggests his hand.

The Mexica state did not formally acknowledge the assassination, but the speed of Tizoc's replacement and the absence of any official mourning campaign points strongly to the conclusion.) Tizoc did manage to commission one major monument: the Tizoc Stone, a massive sacrificial slab carved with 15 conquest scenes showing himself dragging captives by the hair.
The propaganda was wildly ahead of his actual accomplishments, but the stone is a beautiful piece of late-Aztec sculpture and it survives.
Ahuitzotl (ah-WEET-sotl, "Water Beast," r. 1486–1502) was the youngest of the three brothers (Axayacatl and Tizoc both being his elders), and he was the empire's greatest general.
He took the throne, by all accounts, with the explicit goal of erasing his brother Tizoc's failures, and he proceeded to do so on a scale that nearly doubled the empire.
Ahuitzotl rededicated the Phase VII Templo Mayor in 1487, the four-day ceremony with thousands of sacrificial victims (Chapter 4).
He pushed the empire's frontiers in every direction.
To the southeast, he conquered the Gulf Coast Huastec territories that had rebelled against Motecuzoma I.
To the south, he extended Aztec rule deep into Oaxaca, completing the conquest his great-grandfather had begun (Zapotec Civilization Ch 8 covers the receiving end).
To the southwest, in 1494, he pushed Aztec armies all the way to the Tehuantepec isthmus and onto the Pacific coast, conquering the wealthy Soconusco region.

Soconusco (Chapter 4, Chapter 6) was the source of the highest-grade cacao in Mesoamerica, and bringing it under direct Aztec administration meant that the Tlatelolco market suddenly had a guaranteed supply of luxury cacao at tribute prices.
The cacao trade alone justified the campaign.
Ahuitzotl's reach was, by any measure, the maximum extent of the empire.
By 1500, the Aztec Empire covered roughly 80,000 square miles of central and southern Mexico, organized into about 38 tributary provinces, drawing tribute from over 300 conquered towns.

The annual tribute (catalogued in detail in the post-conquest Codex Mendoza, a pictorial manuscript commissioned around 1541 by the first Spanish viceroy of Mexico — a viceroy being the king's personal stand-in for governing a colony — to document the Aztec tribute system the Spanish were inheriting) included over 7,000 tons of maize, beans, and chia seeds; 200,000 mantles of cotton cloth; 32,000 reams of paper; 16,000 rubber balls; 20 lip-plug ornaments of jade; thousands of warrior costumes; tens of thousands of cacao beans (the small-denomination currency); and an extraordinary range of specialized products from each region.

The system was the most extensive tribute network in the pre-Columbian Americas, and it ran on a rough division: subject towns owed quarterly or annual deliveries, plus emergency levies during major construction projects or imperial events. the contemporary Inca Empire, building its own continental-scale state at the same time on the other side of the Americas (Andean Kingdoms Ch 8), ran the opposite system: rather than extracting goods, the Inca state extracted labor through the mit'a rotation, in which subject communities owed periodic stretches of agricultural and construction work to the state.
Two empires, neither aware the other existed, had landed on radically different solutions to the same problem of extracting value from a tributary periphery.
The empire was not a unitary state.
It was a layered network of subject polities, with wide variation in their relationship to the center.

Some tributaries were directly administered by Aztec governors (the calpixque, kahl-PEESH-keh, tribute-collectors stationed in major regional centers, who managed the assessment and collection of goods).
Others were left under their own kings, who paid tribute and provided military service when called but otherwise governed their own affairs.
A few key strategic locations were directly settled by Mexica colonists.

The diversity of arrangements is one reason the empire collapsed so quickly: when the center was attacked, many tributaries had no particular reason to defend it, and several actively joined Cortés in 1519 (Chapter 8).
Ahuitzotl's last years were shadowed by the Acuecuexatl flood of 1500 (Chapter 4).
He died in 1502, possibly of injuries sustained during the flood.

The succession went to his nephew (Axayacatl's son), a quiet, devout, and bookish man named Motecuzoma II Xocoyotzin (sho-koh-YOH-tseen, "the Younger" — the suffix distinguishes him from Motecuzoma I).
The elders chose him because he was Ahuitzotl's nearest qualified male relative who was not a military disappointment.
They got something other than what they expected.
Motecuzoma II (r. 1502–1520) is one of the more debated figures in 16th-century history.
The traditional Spanish-tinted version, which dominated the narrative for centuries, portrays him as superstitious, paralyzed, weak, and ultimately complicit in the empire's destruction.

The revisionist version, increasingly favored by modern Mesoamerican scholarship, portrays him as a competent administrator who reorganized the empire, centralized its bureaucracy, expanded its scribal apparatus, and did exactly what most rulers in his situation would have done in the face of an unprecedented and (to him) inexplicable foreign invasion.
Both versions probably contain truth, and the more interesting reading is the one that holds them together.
The Motecuzoma II of the first decade of his reign was the most administratively ambitious tlatoani the empire had ever produced.
He centralized the bureaucracy, replacing many of Ahuitzotl's provincial governors with men loyal to himself.

He expanded the codex tradition — the painted books recording tribute, history, ritual, and law — to the point where his scribes effectively built the documentary base on which the post-conquest Codex Mendoza would later be drawn.

Around 1507, his scribes produced the Codex Borbonicus, the most beautiful surviving Aztec calendar codex (Chapter 5), recording the ritual calendar and the New Fire Ceremony of that year in painted detail.

He restructured the imperial elite: noble titles that had been awarded loosely under previous kings were standardized, and access to the highest court positions was tightened to keep them within a small group of high-ranking pipiltin.

The cumulative move was toward a more centralized, more documented, more legible state — the kind of bureaucratic consolidation that ambitious early-modern monarchs were attempting at the same moment in Europe and Asia.

Imperial expansion continued in parallel, though at a slower pace: campaigns into Oaxaca to consolidate Ahuitzotl's gains, the inconclusive Flower War rhythm against Tlaxcala continuing, expeditions onto the southern Pacific coast.
The empire reached its maximum extent under his rule, but the rate of new conquests had clearly slowed.

The system was hitting the natural limits of pre-modern logistics — the further from Tenochtitlan, the harder a campaign was to supply — and the rewards of expansion were thinning out for the cuauhpilli warrior nobility, the very class that the tightening of court access had also alienated.
The administrative confidence broke, by the testimony of every surviving source, in the second decade of his reign.

Aztec sources record eight omens in the years 1509–1519: a comet that appeared every night for a year; a temple that caught fire by itself; a lightning strike on another temple in a clear sky; a comet during the day; the lake boiling without cause; a weeping woman heard at night through the streets, calling "my children, my children, where shall I take you?"; a strange bird with a mirror in its head, captured by fishermen and presented to Motecuzoma, in which he saw warriors riding on the backs of unknown beasts; and twin men with two heads who appeared and then disappeared.

The omens are recorded primarily in the Florentine Codex, fifty years after the events they describe, and there is no way to separate genuine pre-conquest portents from post-conquest narrative reconstruction.
What is consistent across the sources is the shape of Motecuzoma's reaction: the centralizing, documenting, codex-commissioning king of the early reign turned inward.
He withdrew.
He consulted astrologers and priests with increasing desperation.
He spent more time in private chambers and less in the council halls.

The same impulse to control and standardize that had served him as an administrator now expressed itself as an obsessive search for the right ritual, the right reading, the right portent that would tell him what was coming.
What was coming, the calendar was helpful enough to underline.

The Year One Reed in the 52-year cycle corresponded to 1519 in our calendar, and according to the legend told and retold for generations, the god Quetzalcoatl (Chapter 5) had departed eastward across the sea long ago, vowing to return in a year called One Reed.

The legend was older than the Aztecs, present in Toltec tradition, and was probably not understood as a literal political prophecy — more as a cosmological cycle that might or might not turn out to have political significance.

Modern scholars reasonably argue that the post-conquest sources amplified the Quetzalcoatl-return narrative to provide a face-saving explanation for why the Aztecs failed to crush Cortés on first contact.
Motecuzoma probably did not literally believe Cortés was Quetzalcoatl.

But he knew the legend, the year was Year One Reed, and the appearance of strange men with strange beasts on the eastern coast in that specific year would have been deeply unsettling to anyone who could read a calendar.
The administrative reformer and the haunted reader of omens were the same man, in sequence, in the same chair.
The post-conquest Spanish accounts of Motecuzoma in 1519 — frozen, indecisive, alternately conciliatory and remote — have been understandably read as the portrait of a weak king.

Read alongside the picture of his early reign, they look more like the portrait of a strong administrator whose tools had stopped working: a man who had spent a decade tightening every lever in the imperial machine, only to find that the lever he most urgently needed was not on the board.
He responded to Cortés the way he had responded to everything else, by reaching for documentation and consultation and ritual control.
Those reflexes, which had built the most centralized bureaucracy in Aztec history, were exactly the wrong reflexes for the moment in front of him.
Inca Atahualpa, half a generation later, would receive Pizarro under similar pressure of cosmic uncertainty (Andean Kingdoms Ch 8), with similar paralysis, with the same eventual outcome.

In April 1519, lookouts on the Gulf Coast brought news to Tenochtitlan that men with white skin and beards had landed at Veracruz, riding animals taller than dogs, carrying weapons that spat fire and thunder, accompanied by a Nahua-speaking woman who served as their interpreter.
They were marching west.
Whatever this was — Quetzalcoatl returning, a foreign embassy, an invasion — it was the largest test the empire had ever faced, and it had arrived in the year the calendar had warned about.

chapters.title: The End of the Fifth Sun
sentences: In April 1519, Hernán Cortés landed near modern Veracruz with about 530 men, sixteen horses, ten cannon, and a small number of large dogs.

He was 34 years old, a minor Spanish noble of unimpressive birth, a failed law student, and a regional administrator on Cuba whose patron, the Cuban governor Diego Velázquez, had given him command of an exploratory expedition and then changed his mind and tried to recall him.
Cortés sailed anyway, in defiance of orders, and he understood that his political position depended entirely on succeeding spectacularly enough to retroactively justify his insubordination.

The 500 men with him were not picked troops; they were a mix of soldiers, sailors, and adventurers, equipped with steel armor and edged weapons, but few of them had any combat experience above small skirmishes.
Against the 200,000-soldier Aztec military, on paper they should have lasted weeks at best.
They lasted long enough to win because Cortés understood something Motecuzoma II did not.
The Aztec Empire was not a unified state.

It was a tributary system extracting goods and warriors from hundreds of subject peoples, many of whom hated it, several of whom were willing to fight on the side of anyone who would help them break free.
Cortés's first political move was to land near the Totonac city of Cempoala (sem-poh-AH-lah).

The Totonacs were a non-Nahua people of the central Gulf Coast, ethnically and linguistically distinct from the Mexica, who had been conquered by Motecuzoma I some seventy years earlier (Chapter 3) and had owed Aztec tribute since.
Cempoala itself was a recent and uneasy tributary, close enough to the coast to receive the brunt of Aztec tax pressure.
The Totonacs hated Aztec tribute collectors.
They saw an opportunity.

Cortés had Aztec collectors who happened to be in Cempoala arrested in front of the Totonacs (then secretly released them to maintain the option of negotiating with Tenochtitlan), and then declared the Totonacs free of Aztec tribute under his protection.
The political message was clear: the Spaniard was offering to break the Aztec system.
Within weeks, the Totonacs had pledged thousands of warriors.
Cortés had his first allies.

He then scuttled his own ships in the harbor at Veracruz, eliminating the option of retreat for his 500 Spaniards, founded the Spanish settlement of Villa Rica de la Vera Cruz (the legal jurisdiction that gave him independent authority from Cuba), and marched inland.
The march from the coast to Tenochtitlan covers about 200 miles (320 km) over difficult terrain, including the high passes between the volcanoes Popocatépetl and Iztaccíhuatl.
Cortés took six months.
The reasons were diplomatic and political, not logistical.

He needed to convert the 500 Spaniards plus a few thousand Totonac auxiliaries into a force that could realistically take Tenochtitlan, and the only way to do that was to find more allies along the route.
The crucial alliance was with Tlaxcala.
The Tlaxcalans, eighty years deep into the Flower War with Tenochtitlan (Chapter 3), had cut a particular kind of grim deal with the Aztec Empire.
They had remained nominally independent but at the cost of being raided continuously for sacrificial victims, tens of thousands of their men taken to the Templo Mayor over generations.

They were surrounded on three sides by Aztec tributaries, salt and cotton and other essentials had been embargoed by the Aztecs for decades, and their accumulated grievances were as deep as any in Mesoamerica.
When Cortés appeared on their borders in September 1519, however, they treated him as another invader.

The Tlaxcalans first attacked Cortés's column with 30,000 to 50,000 warriors, in some of the most brutal fighting of the entire campaign; the Spaniards held formation by murderous use of their cannon and crossbows, but several Spanish soldiers were killed and more captured for sacrifice.
After two weeks of inconclusive battle, Tlaxcalan leaders met to debate.
The hawks wanted to destroy the strangers.
The doves, led by the elderly senator Xicotencatl the Elder, argued that the Spanish were a tool that could be used against Tenochtitlan, and that the Tlaxcalans should ally with them.
The doves won.
Tlaxcala became Cortés's most important ally in the conquest, eventually contributing tens of thousands of warriors to the final Siege of Tenochtitlan.
The Tlaxcalan-Spanish alliance was the single political fact that made the conquest possible.
Without Tlaxcala, Cortés's 500 Spaniards would have been cut off and destroyed.
With Tlaxcala, the conquest became a civil war within Mesoamerica, with the Spanish providing technological and tactical edge but the bulk of the fighting force being Mesoamerican.
Two other figures from the early phase of the conquest deserve to be named.

Malintzin (mah-LEEN-tseen), known to the Spanish as Doña Marina and to later Mexican history as La Malinche, was a Nahua woman who had been sold into slavery as a child by her own mother (a noblewoman of Coatzacoalcos who, after remarrying, wanted to clear the way for her new husband's children to inherit).
She ended up among the Maya of Tabasco, where she learned Yucatec Maya in addition to her native Nahuatl.
The Maya gave her, along with nineteen other women, to Cortés as a peace offering after a battle.

Cortés, who already had a Spanish-Maya interpreter (a Spanish friar named Jerónimo de Aguilar, who had been shipwrecked in the Yucatán years earlier and had learned Maya in captivity), realized within days what Malintzin's bilingualism meant: he could communicate with any Nahuatl-speaking polity through a two-step translation chain (Spanish to Maya through Aguilar, Maya to Nahuatl through Malintzin).
Within months, Malintzin had learned enough Spanish to translate directly.
She became Cortés's translator, advisor, lover, and eventually the mother of his son.
Her role in the conquest is enormous: she negotiated alliances, decoded political situations, and probably saved Cortés's life multiple times by detecting plots before they unfolded.

Modern Mexican opinion of Malintzin has shifted multiple times: from villain (the woman who betrayed her people) to victim (a slave forced into impossible choices) to political agent (a survivor who navigated unprecedented circumstances and shaped them as best she could).
All three readings have a basis in the evidence.
The Mexican word malinchismo, meaning "preference for foreigners over one's own people," derives from her name and is still in use as a political insult.

Cuitláhuac (kweet-LAH-wahk, "Excrement Owner," a respectful name in Nahuatl, where bodily references carried no shame), Motecuzoma's brother and the king of Iztapalapa (one of the lake-shore cities), was the principal Aztec hawk in the high command who consistently advised aggressive resistance to the Spanish, was overruled by Motecuzoma II repeatedly, and eventually replaced his brother as tlatoani after Motecuzoma's death (see below).
His brief reign would last 80 days.

Cortés reached Cholula (cho-LOO-lah, the great pilgrimage city to the southeast of Tenochtitlan, with a pyramid larger by volume than the Pyramid of the Sun at Teotihuacan, Teotihuacan Ch 2) in October 1519.
Cholula was nominally independent but strongly aligned with Tenochtitlan.
Cortés camped in the city and spent several days there.
Then, on October 18, 1519, he ordered his troops to massacre several thousand Cholulan nobles and warriors in the temple plaza.

The pretext was that Malintzin had warned him of a Cholulan plot to ambush the Spanish at Motecuzoma's order; the existence of the plot is debated by modern historians (some sources strongly suggest it was real, others suggest Cortés invented it as cover for a calculated act of terror).
What is clear is that the Cholula massacre sent a brutal political signal across central Mexico: the Spanish would respond to even suspected resistance with extreme violence.
Tributary cities along Cortés's route that had been hesitating now hurried to declare for him.
On November 8, 1519, Cortés met Motecuzoma II on the southern causeway leading into Tenochtitlan.
The meeting is one of the most photographed-in-the-imagination encounters in world history.

Motecuzoma rode in a litter borne by nobles, dressed in the regalia of a tlatoani (cotton mantles trimmed with gold, gold sandals, a turquoise diadem on his forehead, and rich plumes of quetzal feathers).
Cortés was on horseback in steel armor.
They exchanged formal greetings through Malintzin.
Motecuzoma escorted the Spanish into the city and installed them in the palace of Axayacatl, an old royal compound near the Templo Mayor.
The decision to admit Cortés to the city, rather than fight him on the causeways, has been called the most consequential single mistake in Mexican history.

Motecuzoma's reasoning is unrecoverable; the explanations range from Quetzalcoatl-return paralysis to a calculated decision to neutralize the Spanish threat by bringing it inside the walls where his army was strongest.
Whatever his thinking, the decision was catastrophic.
Within two weeks, Cortés had taken Motecuzoma II hostage in his own palace.

The mechanism was simple intimidation: Cortés visited Motecuzoma with armed soldiers, accused him of complicity in an attack on Spanish coastal positions, and demanded that the tlatoani come live as a guest in the Spanish quarters as proof of good faith.
Motecuzoma went.
The senior Aztec nobility was divided on what to do; the tlatoani's instructions, transmitted through Cortés's hands, were to maintain calm.
For seven months, Cortés effectively ruled the Aztec Empire through Motecuzoma, with tribute being collected normally and the city government continuing under Spanish supervision.
Then everything fell apart.
In May 1520, Cortés had to leave the city.
A second Spanish expedition, sent from Cuba by Velázquez specifically to arrest Cortés for his earlier insubordination, had landed at Veracruz under the command of Pánfilo de Narváez.
Cortés took half his force and marched east, defeated Narváez's larger but disorganized army at Cempoala (and absorbed most of Narváez's men into his own command), and headed back to Tenochtitlan.
In his absence, his lieutenant Pedro de Alvarado (the red-haired Spaniard the Aztecs nicknamed "Tonatiuh," the Sun) managed the Spanish position in the city.

On May 22, 1520, during the festival of Toxcatl (the great festival of Tezcatlipoca, Chapter 5, when 600 to 1,000 of the empire's senior nobles and warriors gathered unarmed in the Sacred Precinct for the choreographed dances), Alvarado ordered his troops to seal the gates of the precinct and slaughter every Aztec inside.
The Massacre at the Templo Mayor killed several hundred to several thousand Aztec nobles in a single afternoon, depending on which source you trust.

Alvarado's stated justification was that the Aztecs had been planning an attack on the Spanish; modern historians are skeptical, and the more likely explanation is that Alvarado, with too few men and too many enemies, attempted a preemptive decapitation of the Aztec leadership.
Whatever his reasoning, the result was that the Aztec population finally turned on the Spanish openly.
When Cortés returned with his reinforced army, he marched into a city in open revolt.

The Aztec command structure had been damaged by the massacre but not destroyed; the surviving nobles selected Motecuzoma's brother Cuitláhuac as their war leader, and the entire population of the city had risen to fight.

Cortés tried to use Motecuzoma to calm the crowds; according to Spanish sources, the captured tlatoani went to a balcony of the Spanish quarters and tried to address his people, who responded by hurling stones and arrows at him.
Motecuzoma was struck and died of his wounds three days later, on June 29, 1520. (Aztec sources give a different account: that Motecuzoma was murdered by the Spanish when his usefulness ended.
The truth is contested; the Spanish version is uncorroborated, but the projectile-strike account is the more economical reconstruction of events.
Either way, the empire's tlatoani was dead at Spanish hands, in custody, in the middle of his own city.) With Motecuzoma's death, Cortés's leverage over the city evaporated.
The Spanish position became militarily impossible.
They were 500-plus men in a city of 200,000 that had finally and decisively turned hostile.
On the night of June 30 – July 1, 1520, Cortés ordered a desperate retreat from Tenochtitlan, west along the Tlacopan causeway.
The Aztecs had pulled out the wooden bridges; the Spanish had built portable wooden bridges of their own to span the gaps.

The Spanish withdrew through driving rain in the dark, weighed down by the gold and treasures they had stolen during their seven-month occupation (Cortés had ordered that any soldier could carry as much gold as he could manage; many soldiers stuffed their armor and clothing with gold ingots, an act of greed that would prove fatal when they had to swim or fight).
The Aztecs attacked from canoes on both sides of the causeway.
Spanish soldiers, weighed down by gold, fell into the water and drowned.
Spanish prisoners taken alive were sacrificed at the Templo Mayor over the following days.
The night is remembered in Spanish history as La Noche Triste ("The Sorrowful Night," from a tradition that Cortés sat under a tree on the western shore at dawn and wept for his dead).
The Spanish lost about 600 of the roughly 1,300 Spanish soldiers (now reinforced by Narváez's men), thousands of their indigenous allies, and almost all of their cannon, gunpowder, and gold.
Several days later, the Aztecs hauled drums up to the Templo Mayor and beat them while priests sacrificed the captured Spanish soldiers, in full view of the surviving Spanish on the lake shore.
Bernal Díaz, who was there, never forgot the sound of the drums; he wrote about them decades later as the most terrible noise he had ever heard.
It was, in conventional military terms, a Spanish disaster.
Half the European force had been destroyed in a single night.
The Aztecs had retaken their city.
The empire still held its tributary network.
The Tlaxcalan alliance was untested by serious defeat.
Any reasonable observer in July 1520 would have concluded that Cortés's gamble had failed, that the Spanish should withdraw to Veracruz and accept the loss, and that the Aztec Empire would survive.
Bernardino de Sahagún would write later that this was the moment when the empire could have been saved.
The Spanish retreat to Tlaxcala took two weeks of hard fighting.
They were down to about 400 Europeans and a few thousand Tlaxcalan auxiliaries.
Aztec forces under Cuitláhuac followed them, attacking as they could.
At the Battle of Otumba in July 1520, Cortés's depleted force met an Aztec army roughly 40,000 strong on an open plain.

Cortés's cavalry, the few remaining horses he had managed to bring out of Tenochtitlan, broke the Aztec center by killing the Aztec commander and capturing his battle standard (the loss of the standard, in Mesoamerican military convention, signaled defeat regardless of the actual military situation).
The Aztec army withdrew.
The Spanish reached Tlaxcala alive.
And then the empire's other enemy arrived.

Smallpox, a disease the Americas had never seen before, was reportedly introduced to the Mexican mainland in April 1520 by an African slave who came over with the Narváez expedition; the chronicles name him Francisco de Eguía, though the patient-zero attribution to a single individual is contested by modern historians and was probably a tidied-up account constructed after the fact.
What is not in doubt is that Smallpox arrived with the Narváez landing.

The virus, against which indigenous populations had no immunity, spread westward through central Mexico through summer and autumn 1520, reaching Tenochtitlan during the post-Noche-Triste recovery period.
The Aztec sources describe it as huey zahuatl ("great rash"), a disease that had no name in Nahuatl because nothing like it had ever existed in the Americas.
The mortality was catastrophic.
Estimates of population loss in central Mexico from this single 1520 epidemic range from 25 percent to 50 percent.
The disease did not discriminate by class or military function: peasants died, nobles died, priests died, generals died, the tlatoani himself died.

Cuitláhuac, who had ruled for only 80 days, died of smallpox in late November 1520, ending one of the most brilliantly led military campaigns in indigenous American history before he could finish the job he had started.
The empire's command structure was wrecked.
The military leadership, the administrative class, the priesthood, the experienced officers, all of them had been disproportionately exposed during the epidemic and disproportionately killed.
The Aztec sources describe villages where there were not enough living people to bury the dead, and corpses were pulled from houses and dumped into mass graves or left where they lay.
Tenochtitlan, a city of 200,000 that depended on a complex labor and food-distribution apparatus, faced food shortages because too many of the people who ran the system were dying.

Cuitláhuac was succeeded as tlatoani by his cousin Cuauhtémoc (kwah-oo-TEH-mok, "Descending Eagle"), the last tlatoani, a young man (probably about 25) who had survived the epidemic and who was determined to fight for the city.
By his accession, the world was already largely lost.
In Tlaxcala, Cortés rebuilt his army.

He drew on Tlaxcalan auxiliaries (perhaps 50,000 to 100,000), additional reinforcements from Cuba, fresh gunpowder and cannon, and (most consequentially) thirteen brigantines (small sailing-and-oared warships) that he had ordered built in Tlaxcala from the timbers of his scuttled coastal ships, transported overland in pieces, and reassembled on the lakeshore.
The brigantines were the first European warships ever launched on a New World inland lake, and they would be decisive.
They allowed the Spanish to control Lake Texcoco, cut off canoe traffic in and out of the city, and bombard the causeways from positions the Aztecs could not reach.

The Siege of Tenochtitlan began on May 26, 1521, with about 700 Spanish soldiers and somewhere between 75,000 and 200,000 indigenous allies (Tlaxcalans, Texcocans, Totonacs, and a growing number of formerly subject Aztec tributaries who saw which way the war was going).
The Spanish cut the Chapultepec aqueduct, eliminating Tenochtitlan's main freshwater supply.
They blockaded the causeways.

They began grinding through the city quarter by quarter, fighting through canals and over rooftops, demolishing buildings as they advanced (so that the Aztec roof-jumping defensive tactics would have no platforms).
The Aztecs fought brilliantly, as they always had.

They sacrificed captured Spanish soldiers atop the Templo Mayor in full view of the besieging army, hauling captives up the steps and removing their hearts in plain sight, then rolling the bodies down the steps onto the Coyolxauhqui Stone.
Spanish soldiers in the besieging army watched their comrades die this way and described it as the most terrible thing they had ever seen.
But the city was starving.
Smallpox was killing more defenders than Spanish weapons were.
The supply of fresh water was gone.
The chinampas were cut off from access.
After 75 days of siege, on August 13, 1521, Cuauhtémoc attempted to escape the city by canoe with a small group of nobles and family.
He was intercepted by a Spanish brigantine and captured.
The same day, the city formally surrendered.

The Aztec sources describe what was left as "a city of corpses." The most famous Aztec lament for the fall of the city, recorded in the Cantares Mexicanos (the early colonial-era anthology of Nahuatl poetry), reads in part: "Broken spears lie in the roads / We have torn our hair in our grief / The houses are roofless now, and their walls / are red with blood." Cuauhtémoc was tortured by Cortés (the Spanish poured boiling oil on his feet) to make him reveal the location of Tenochtitlan's gold treasury.
According to the Aztec tradition, Cuauhtémoc bore the torture without breaking; according to the Spanish tradition, he revealed nothing because there was less treasure than the Spanish had hoped for.
He was kept alive as a puppet for several years and finally executed in 1525 during Cortés's expedition to Honduras, on charges of plotting rebellion.
Modern Mexico considers him a national hero, and his statue stands at the head of one of Mexico City's main avenues.
The empire was over.
Tenochtitlan was a ruin.
The Spanish founded Mexico City on top of it, deliberately demolishing the temples and using the stones to build the cathedral and the colonial palaces.
The Templo Mayor was buried beneath the colonial central plaza (the Zócalo), where it lay for 450 years until the 1978 rediscovery of the Coyolxauhqui Stone (Chapter 3).

The chinampas were drained over the next century, the lake itself progressively reduced and finally eliminated by 19th-century drainage projects, and the basin floor that had once held one of the largest cities in the world became one of the largest cities in the world again, in an entirely different form.
What survived?
The Nahuatl language survived.
Over a million people in modern Mexico still speak it as a first language; it is one of Mexico's official indigenous languages.

Many Spanish words come from Nahuatl, and from Nahuatl into English: avocado (ahuacatl), chocolate (xocolatl), tomato (tomatl), chili (chilli), coyote (coyotl), peyote (peyotl), tequila (from a place name), Mexico itself (Mexihco).
The Mexican flag still carries the eagle on the cactus devouring the snake, the Mexica's founding sign.

The chinampas survived in fragmentary form at Xochimilco, where farmers still maintain a network of canals and floating gardens that look essentially as they did in 1500, and which is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
The codex tradition partially survived.

Most pre-conquest pictorial books were destroyed in the conquest or in early colonial book-burnings (the Spanish friars considered them devil's works), but a handful (the Codex Borbonicus, the Codex Borgia, the Codex Mendoza, the Codex Florentine, perhaps two dozen others) survived in libraries in Europe and Mexico.

Combined with the post-conquest manuscripts compiled by Sahagún, by Aztec elders working in the colonial period, and by Spanish chroniclers, they preserve a fraction of pre-conquest Aztec knowledge — far less than what was lost, but more than survives for any other indigenous American civilization except the Maya.
The medical tradition survived in fragments.

The Badianus Manuscript, written in 1552 by an Aztec physician trained at the colonial Colegio de Santa Cruz de Tlatelolco and translated into Latin by another graduate, preserves illustrated descriptions of pre-conquest Aztec herbal medicine.
It is the oldest medical text from the Americas.

Aztec medicine was, in many areas, more advanced than European medicine of the same period — botanical pharmacology in particular, where the Aztec ticitl healers maintained working knowledge of over a thousand medicinal plants.
The poetry survived.

The Cantares Mexicanos and the Romances de los Señores de la Nueva España preserve Nahuatl poetry from before and immediately after the conquest, including Nezahualcoyotl's poems and the great laments for the fall of Tenochtitlan.

The genetic legacy survived: most modern Mexicans descend from the Mexica and their neighbors, and the Spanish-Indigenous mestizo population that emerged in the colonial period now numbers over 100 million people across Mexico and the United States.

What did not survive was the political fact of an indigenous Mesoamerican imperial state, the religious cycle of public sacrifice, the calendrical apparatus that organized cosmic time, and the trade networks that had connected central Mexico to the Pacific cacao coast and the American Southwest.

These were destroyed deliberately by the Spanish authorities in the decades after the conquest, and, less directly, by the demographic catastrophe that followed European contact: the population of central Mexico fell from perhaps 12 million in 1519 to roughly 1 million by 1605, a loss greater than the Black Death in any European country.
The empire was destroyed by smallpox, by Tlaxcala, by Cortés, and by Motecuzoma's hesitations, but the civilization beneath the empire was destroyed by the diseases that came with Cortés's ships.
A final cross-civ check.

The fall of Tenochtitlan in 1521 sits in the same century as the Protestant Reformation (Luther's 95 Theses, 1517), the rise of the Ottoman Empire under Suleiman the Magnificent (succeeded 1520), the Mughal conquest of India (Babur's victory at Panipat, 1526), the consolidation of the Ming Dynasty's mid-period in China, the late Inca expansion (Andean Kingdoms Ch 8 — the Inca Empire was at its peak when Pizarro arrived in 1532, eleven years after Tenochtitlan's fall, and would be destroyed by the same combination of factors), and the European Renaissance entering its mature phase.

A related but distinct version played out in the eastern woodlands of North America, where Hernando de Soto's entrada of 1539–43 carried epidemic disease into the still-functioning Mississippian chiefdoms (Mississippian Culture Ch 9).
The early 16th century was a global hinge: the closing of the Old World's isolated regional histories, the beginning of an integrated global system.

The Aztec Empire, which had risen from a vassal city-state to one of the largest and most sophisticated states in the world in less than two centuries, was caught at the moment of its greatest extent by the first wave of European-American contact, and it did not survive the encounter.
Neither did most of the populations that the empire had ruled.

The conquest was not the Spaniards' achievement alone; it was a catastrophic intersection of microbial biology, internal Mesoamerican politics, technological mismatch, and individual human decisions, and any of those factors changed in another direction would have changed the outcome.
But once the encounter had begun, no realistic alternative outcome would have left the empire intact in its 1519 form.
The Fifth Sun set in 1521, and the world that came after was a different world.
The Mexica had told themselves, generation after generation, that the cosmos required regular blood to keep functioning.
They were not, by the standard of all the previous cosmic ages they remembered, wrong.
The cosmos had ended four times before.
It would, they knew, end again.
They had hoped, and labored, and sacrificed, to push that ending as far away as they could.
It came in the year One Reed.
They had had advance warning of that for centuries.
They were prepared for it as well as they could be.
It still ended them.

chapters.title: The Empire That Wouldn't Die
sentences: There is no Byzantine Empire.
Or rather — there was, and they did not know it.
Nobody in this entire 1,123-year story ever called themselves a Byzantine.
They called themselves Romaioi (roh-MY-oy, Greek for "Romans").

They called their state Basileia ton Romaion, "the Empire of the Romans." Their emperors styled themselves Imperator, Augustus, Basileus — Roman titles, sometimes in Latin and sometimes in Greek translation.

When their last emperor died fighting on the walls in 1453, he was, in his own mind and in the minds of his soldiers, the Roman emperor in Roman Constantinople defending the Roman Empire from a foreign invader.
The word "Byzantine" was invented by a German scholar named Hieronymus Wolf in 1557 — a hundred and four years after the empire was already gone.

Wolf needed a label that distinguished the Greek-speaking medieval state from the Latin-speaking ancient one his own readers identified with, and he reached back to Byzantion (BIZ-an-tee-on), the small Greek colony that had stood on the site of Constantinople before Constantine arrived.
The name stuck for the same reason a lot of historiographic conventions stick: it was useful.

It gave western European writers a way to talk about an empire they wanted to think of as decadent, schismatic, and Other — separate from "real" Rome, which they preferred to imagine as the ancestor of the West.
Throw the label out and the picture changes.
There was no fall of Rome in 476 CE (Ancient Rome Ch 10).
There was a fall of the western half of the Roman Empire.
The eastern half — older, richer, more populous, with better fortifications, better tax revenues, and a far more impregnable capital — kept going.
It kept going for almost exactly a thousand years after Romulus Augustulus handed his crown to Odoacer.
During those thousand years, it called itself Rome.
It used Roman law.
It maintained Roman administrative titles.
It traced its emperors in unbroken succession back to Augustus.
And it watched, with a mixture of bafflement and amusement, as the barbarian kingdoms of western Europe slowly forgot how Rome had worked and started reinventing it badly.
This narrative will use "Byzantine" anyway, because that is the word the reader knows.
But every time you see it, mentally translate it as "Roman." The people in this story were not the descendants of the Romans.
They were the Romans.
They just happened to live in a Greek-speaking eastern Mediterranean and to have stopped wearing togas around the time you stop wearing one to your job.
A note before we go further: dates in this narrative are CE (Common Era, the secular equivalent of AD) unless otherwise noted.

The Byzantine state itself dated events from "the creation of the world" — Anno Mundi — using a chronology that placed the creation in 5509 BCE, which means a Byzantine reading this in 1453 would have called it the year 6961.
We will spare ourselves that.
The story starts with one man, one battle, and one decision.

The man was Constantine I (later "the Great"), born around 272 in modern Serbia, son of a Roman officer who rose to become one of the four co-emperors of the Tetrarchy (the four-emperor power-sharing system that Diocletian had set up in 293 to manage an empire that had become too large for one ruler — Ancient Rome Ch 8).
The Tetrarchy worked while Diocletian was personally enforcing it and collapsed the moment he retired in 305.
Constantine spent the next eighteen years fighting his way through a series of civil wars against rival claimants.
The decisive moment came on October 28, 312, at the Battle of the Milvian Bridge outside Rome, where Constantine destroyed the army of his rival Maxentius and took the western half of the empire.

Constantine claimed that on the eve of the battle he had seen a Christian symbol in the sky — the Chi-Rho (KY-roh, the first two letters of "Christ" in Greek, superimposed) — accompanied by the words In hoc signo vinces, "in this sign you shall conquer." Whether the vision happened, whether Constantine actually believed it happened, or whether the whole story was retrofitted by Christian biographers afterward is one of those questions the surviving evidence cannot settle.

What is not in doubt is that the next year, in 313, Constantine and his eastern colleague Licinius (lih-SIN-ee-us) issued the Edict of Milan, which legalized Christianity across the empire and ordered the return of confiscated church property.
After three centuries of being a persecuted underground sect, Christianity was suddenly the favored religion of the Roman emperor.
The pattern was an old one in the ancient world: a ruler builds legitimacy by liberating a previously persecuted monotheistic community and casting himself as that community's divinely chosen patron.
Cyrus the Great had done this for the exiled Jews 850 years earlier, releasing them from Babylonian captivity and inscribing his benevolence on the Cyrus Cylinder (Persian Empire Ch 1).
Constantine's Edict of Milan was the same move at the same scale — the Roman emperor declaring himself the protector of a persecuted monotheist faith, and reaping the political reward.
Then in 324, Constantine defeated Licinius and reunited the entire empire under one ruler for the first time in a generation.

And then, in 325, he did something that would shape religion in Europe for the next sixteen hundred years: he convened the First Council of Nicaea (nye-SEE-uh, a town in northwestern Anatolia, modern İznik in Turkey), the first ecumenical (empire-wide) gathering of Christian bishops, summoning over 300 bishops from across the empire to settle a doctrinal dispute that was tearing the new state religion apart.

The dispute was about the nature of Christ — specifically, whether the Son was co-eternal with the Father (the position of the bishop Athanasius of Alexandria) or whether the Son had been created by the Father at some point and was therefore subordinate (the position of an Alexandrian priest named Arius, whose followers were called Arians).

The council sided with Athanasius and produced the Nicene Creed — the statement of faith still recited every Sunday in Catholic and Orthodox churches today, which begins "We believe in one God, the Father almighty… and in one Lord Jesus Christ… begotten not made, of one substance with the Father." Most readers raised in a Christian context will recognize the creed and assume the dispute was a minor theological argument.
It was not.
The Arian controversy nearly destroyed the eastern half of the empire over the next century.
Emperors picked sides.
Bishops were exiled, restored, exiled again.

Mobs rioted in the streets of Antioch and Alexandria over the placement of a single Greek letter (the difference between homoousios, "of the same substance," and homoiousios, "of like substance," is one iota — literally the Greek letter that gives English "iota" — and the most famous theological controversy of the fourth century turned on whether Christ was homo-ousios or homoi-ousios with the Father).
The Greek-speaking East cared about theology in a way the Latin-speaking West did not, and the cost of that caring would become a recurring theme.

Constantine's son Constantius II (con-STAN-tee-us, ruled 337–361) was an Arian who reversed his father's pro-Nicene policy and persecuted Athanasius mercilessly — the iota war ran for fifty years before Nicene Christianity finally won permanently.
The decision that made Byzantium possible came in 324, the same year Constantine reunited the empire.
He decided to build a new capital.

The site he chose was a small fishing town called Byzantion — a Greek colony founded in 657 BCE on a triangular peninsula on the European side of the Bosporus, the narrow strait connecting the Sea of Marmara to the Black Sea.
The location was, in retrospect, the most defensible major-city site in the Mediterranean world.
Three sides of the peninsula are surrounded by water (the Bosporus to the east, the Sea of Marmara to the south, an inlet called the Golden Horn to the north).
Only the western side, facing the Thracian plain, is overland — and the western side is short enough that a single line of walls can seal it off.

The Bosporus is also the gateway between two seas (the Black and the Mediterranean) and two continents (Europe and Asia), meaning whoever controls Byzantion controls the most important trade chokepoint between northern grain, Russian fur, Anatolian metal, and Mediterranean shipping.
Constantine renamed it Constantinople ("Constantine's city") and dedicated it on May 11, 330.

Or rather: he formally rededicated it as "New Rome" — the official name on the inaugural inscription was Nova Roma, and the city was given a Senate, free grain distributions, seven hills (the geography was kindly cooperative), and every major Roman institution copied or transplanted from the original.
The intent was not to abandon Rome.
The intent was to give the empire a second capital, equal in dignity to the first, but better positioned to rule the wealthier eastern provinces.
Within a few decades the practical reality of imperial administration would shift the center of gravity east, and within a few centuries the western capital would be a memory.
Constantine also began the urban program that would eventually make Constantinople the largest city in the Christian world.

He built the Hippodrome — a U-shaped chariot-racing arena modeled on the Circus Maximus in Rome, capable of seating up to 100,000 spectators. (We will come back to the Hippodrome in nearly every chapter, because it is impossible to overstate how central the racing track was to Byzantine politics.

Imagine if every American presidential candidate had to formally appear before the crowd at the Super Bowl, and if the Super Bowl crowd routinely rioted, deposed presidents, and lynched generals.) He laid out broad colonnaded avenues, a great central forum, and the foundations of an imperial palace complex that would grow over the next eight centuries into a labyrinth of throne rooms, chapels, gardens, and ceremonial chambers covering a quarter of the peninsula.
He also began stripping the Mediterranean world of its art treasures to fill the new capital.
Pagan statues from Athens, Delphi, Ephesus, and Rome itself were carted to Constantinople and erected as decorations in the Hippodrome and the forums.

The most famous — a bronze column of three intertwined serpents, originally cast in 479 BCE from melted-down Persian armor as a thank-offering after the Greek victory at Plataea (Persian Empire Ch 3) — was uprooted from Delphi and stood in the spina of the Hippodrome.
Its lower section is still there.
Modern Istanbul, walking past it, has not always known what it is looking at.
Constantine died in 337.

He was baptized only on his deathbed, by an Arian bishop, which has caused some consternation for later Catholic and Orthodox traditions that prefer their first Christian emperor to have been clearly orthodox.
The Eastern Orthodox Church canonized him as a saint anyway, calling him Isapostolos — "Equal-to-the-Apostles" — for his role in legalizing the faith and convening Nicaea.
His mother Helena, who had made a pilgrimage to Jerusalem in 326–328 and reportedly discovered the True Cross of the Crucifixion buried under a pagan temple on Golgotha, was canonized too.
The True Cross would become the most important relic in the empire and a recurring character in the chapters ahead.
The fourth century was a long, slow argument about whether the empire was really Christian.
Constantine had legalized Christianity but not made it the state religion.
His sons mostly favored the Arian faction.

His nephew Julian (called "the Apostate" by Christian writers, ruled 361–363) was the last pagan emperor — a thoughtful, philosophically trained ruler who had been raised as a Christian, hated it, converted privately to traditional Greco-Roman polytheism, and on taking the throne tried to roll back Constantine's revolution.
Julian restored animal sacrifice, reopened pagan temples, withdrew Christian privileges, and wrote bitter polemics against the church.

He also tried to revive the Jerusalem Temple — partly out of philosophical sympathy with Judaism, partly because rebuilding the Temple would have falsified Jesus's prophecy that not one stone would be left on another.
Julian's attempt was abandoned when an earthquake (or, depending on the source, a fire) destroyed the construction site.
He died less than three years into his reign, struck by a spear during a poorly-planned invasion of Sasanian Persia (Persian Empire Ch 9).

His last words, according to the hostile Christian tradition, were "Vicisti, Galilaee" — "You have conquered, Galilean." This line is almost certainly a later invention, but it captured what Julian's failure meant: paganism's last imperial champion was dead, and there would be no second attempt.

The pagan rollback ran out of steam, and seventeen years after Julian's death, on February 27, 380, Emperor Theodosius I issued the Edict of Thessalonica, which made Nicene Christianity — the version that had won at Nicaea fifty-five years earlier — the official state religion of the Roman Empire.
Pagan sacrifice was banned in 391.
The Olympic Games, which had run continuously every four years since 776 BCE, were abolished in 393 (or possibly 426; the exact date is debated).
The temples were closed, looted, or rededicated as churches.
The Library of Alexandria's pagan elements (what was left of them) were dispersed.
A thousand-year religious civilization, the entire intellectual and ritual world of classical antiquity, was officially dissolved in a single generation.
Theodosius was the last emperor to rule both halves of the empire.

When he died in 395, the empire was split between his sons: Arcadius (ar-KAY-dee-us) took the East with its capital at Constantinople, Honorius (hoh-NOR-ee-us) took the West with its capital first at Milan and then (after 402) at Ravenna.

The split was not new — the empire had been divided into eastern and western administrative halves for a century, and it would technically remain a single state in legal theory for centuries afterward.
But after 395, no single person would ever rule both halves again.
The two courts grew apart.
The two churches grew apart.
The two languages grew apart, as Latin retreated in the East and Greek became the daily working language of administration.
This is the conventional date — 395 — for the start of the Byzantine Empire, even though no Byzantine ever knew that.
They thought they were just Romans whose empire happened, for administrative reasons, to have its operational capital in the east.
What kept the East alive while the West collapsed was a combination of geography, economy, and one extraordinary piece of architecture.
The geography is the simpler half.
The Eastern provinces were richer.
Egypt alone produced enough grain to feed Constantinople and pay a substantial chunk of the imperial budget.
Syria and Anatolia had bigger populations, more cities, and better-developed agriculture than anywhere in the West outside Italy.
The major eastern frontiers (the lower Danube and the upper Euphrates) were shorter than the western ones (the Rhine, the upper Danube, the British coast, the African coast).
When Goths and Huns and Vandals swept across Europe in the fifth century, they were attacking a western state that had to defend a longer perimeter with a smaller revenue base.
The same migrations broke against the eastern frontier and were either deflected — onto the West, where they could do worse damage — or absorbed.
The economy followed from the geography.
Constantinople sat on a major trade hub and could collect customs duties from anyone shipping through the Bosporus.
The eastern Mediterranean's network of cities — Alexandria, Antioch, Ephesus, Thessalonica, Caesarea — generated a tax base unmatched anywhere in the West.
The empire could afford a professional standing army.
It could afford a professional bureaucracy that did not need to be staffed by aristocratic amateurs.
It could afford an enormous engineering project to seal off its capital from any imaginable land assault.
That engineering project was the Theodosian Walls.
Constantine's original wall had become inadequate as the city grew.

So in 408–413, during the long reign of Theodosius's grandson Theodosius II (ruled 408–450 — child emperor for most of his reign, dominated first by his sister Pulcheria and then by his pious wife Aelia Eudocia), the imperial regent Anthemios ordered a new fortification line drawn farther west, sealing off the entire landward approach to the city.
The Theodosian Walls were not a single wall.

They were a layered defense system: a wide ditch (filled with water from cross-walls when needed), an outer wall (about 30 feet or 9 meters tall), a terrace, a higher inner wall (about 40 feet or 12 meters tall and 16 feet or 5 meters thick), and 96 towers spaced at regular intervals so that any approach to one tower was within bowshot of two others.
The whole system stretched roughly four miles (6.5 km) across the peninsula, sealing the city off from the Thracian plain to the west.
The Theodosian Walls would not be breached by a foreign army for over a thousand years.

They survived sieges by Avars (a Eurasian steppe confederation) in 626, Arabs in 674–678 and 717–718, Bulgars repeatedly, Rus' in 860, and a coalition of European Crusaders in 1203–1204 (and even the Crusaders in the end did not breach the land walls — they got in via the sea walls along the Golden Horn).

Constantinople did not fall to a land assault until 1453, and even then only because the attackers had something the previous attackers had not had: gunpowder cannons — specifically the massive bronze bombards cast by the Hungarian engineer Orban for Mehmed II, which breached the walls that had held for over a millennium (Ottoman Empire Ch 4).
For more than a millennium, the Theodosian Walls were the most formidable defensive system in the world.
They are the single most important reason the eastern half of the Roman Empire outlived the western half by a thousand years.
The fifth century did its worst to the empire and the empire absorbed it.
In 410, Visigoths under Alaric sacked Rome (Ancient Rome Ch 10).
The shock was psychological, not strategic.
Constantinople was unaffected.
In 451 the Hunnic confederation under Attila ravaged the Balkans and extracted enormous tributes from Constantinople before turning west and attacking Gaul.

Eastern emperors paid Attila off rather than fight him on his own terms — a recurring Byzantine tactic that western moralists have always found contemptible and that Byzantine accountants always found cheaper than war.

The same year, Emperor Marcian (ruled 450–457, an old soldier who had married Theodosius II's pious sister Pulcheria after her brother's death and become emperor through that marriage) refused to continue paying Attila tribute and convened the Council of Chalcedon (kal-SEH-don, a town across the Bosporus from Constantinople, modern Kadıköy in Istanbul).
Chalcedon was the fourth ecumenical council, and it was supposed to settle a different theological war that had succeeded the Arian controversy.
The argument now was not about whether Christ was divine — Nicaea had settled that.
The argument was about how Christ was divine and human at the same time.
Two wings emerged.
The Monophysites (moh-NOF-ih-syts, "single-nature" Christians, dominant in Egypt and Syria) held that Christ had one composite divine-human nature.
The Dyophysites (dy-OF-ih-syts, "two-nature" Christians, dominant in Rome and Constantinople) held that Christ had two distinct natures, divine and human, united in one person.

Chalcedon sided with the Dyophysites and produced the Chalcedonian Definition that is still the official doctrine of the Catholic, Orthodox, and most Protestant churches: Christ in two natures, "without confusion, without change, without division, without separation." The losers refused to accept the verdict.

Egypt and Syria — the Monophysite heartlands — broke off into their own churches, which still exist today: the Coptic Orthodox Church of Egypt, the Syriac Orthodox Church, the Armenian Apostolic Church, the Ethiopian Orthodox Church.
The schism was permanent.
Sixteen hundred years later, these churches still reject Chalcedon.

And the political consequence — that the empire's two richest provinces, Egypt and Syria, would never again feel fully loyal to the Constantinopolitan church or state — would matter enormously when the Arabs arrived in the seventh century.
The locals welcomed them.
Why fight for an empire that had spent two centuries persecuting your bishops?

The Henotikon, an attempt by Emperor Zeno (ruled 474–491) in 482 to paper over the Chalcedonian split with a vague compromise edict, made things worse: it triggered the Acacian Schism (ah-KAY-shun, named after the Patriarch Acacius) — the first formal break between the churches of Rome and Constantinople, lasting from 484 to 519.
The Acacian Schism was eventually patched up.

The pattern it set — Rome and Constantinople drifting apart on doctrinal questions, then reconciling, then drifting apart again — would repeat for the next six centuries until the breach became permanent in 1054 (Chapter 7).
Meanwhile, in the west, the empire was disintegrating.
Vandals took North Africa in 439, cutting off the western grain supply.
Visigoths took Spain and southern Gaul.
Franks moved into northern Gaul.

Anglo-Saxons crossed into Britain (the Angles, Saxons, and Jutes from the North Sea coast and the society they built is the subject of the Anglo-Saxon England narrative; the Scandinavian pre-Viking world that shares their cultural language is the subject of the Vendel Age narrative).

In 476, the Germanic general Odoacer deposed the last western emperor, the unfortunate teenager Romulus Augustulus, and sent the imperial regalia east to Constantinople with a message: there was no need for a separate western emperor any longer.
Odoacer would rule Italy as a king, nominally under the eastern emperor's authority.
The eastern court accepted the regalia, recognized the new arrangement, and went on with business.
To Byzantines, 476 was not a fall.
It was an administrative consolidation.

The empire was again a single state with a single emperor in Constantinople, and the western provinces were under barbarian governors who would eventually, presumably, be brought back into proper Roman administration.
The fact that this view was politically convenient does not mean it was wrong, exactly.
It does mean that the next emperor capable of seizing on it would try to make it real.
That emperor was Justinian.

chapters.title: Justinian's Reconquest
sentences: Justinian was an unlikely candidate to rule the world.
His uncle Justin I (ruled 518–527) was an illiterate Thracian peasant who had walked into Constantinople in his youth as a pig farmer's son looking for work in the imperial guard.

By the early sixth century he had risen, through a combination of competence, ruthlessness, and the kind of luck that catches every veteran soldier who outlives his rivals, to command the Excubitors — the elite palace guard regiment.
When Emperor Anastasius I (ruled 491–518) died without an heir in 518, Justin was the man with troops in the room, and he became emperor by acclamation.

He was around 68 years old, semi-literate (according to Procopius's hostile Secret History — the only source for the detail — he had to sign documents using a stencil with the word legi, "I have read," cut into it for him to trace; no friendlier source confirms this and it may be polemic), and entirely uninterested in the kind of sophisticated cultural projects his nephew would pursue.
What Justin had was good political instincts and a brilliant nephew.

The nephew was Petrus Sabbatius, born around 482 in a village in modern North Macedonia, brought to Constantinople as a teenager, and educated at his uncle's expense in law, theology, history, and Greek philosophy.
By the time Justin took the throne, Petrus — now using the regnal name Justinian — was already running the actual administration.
When Justin died in 527, Justinian formally inherited a throne he had effectively held for years.
He was brilliant, exhausting, and obsessed.
He worked through most nights.

The historian Procopius of Caesarea (proh-KOH-pee-us, c. 500–570) called him "the sleepless emperor." Procopius was the greatest Greek historian of the period, and served as legal secretary to Justinian's leading general — about whom much more shortly.

His ambition was simple and fixed: to restore the Roman Empire to its full territorial extent, reconquer the lost western provinces, codify Roman law, build the greatest church in Christendom, and fix the Chalcedonian schism.
He achieved most of these goals, broke the empire's economy doing it, and left successors who would spend two centuries cleaning up the consequences.
Justinian's reign begins not with a battle but with a wedding.
In the early 520s, while still co-emperor with his uncle, Justinian fell in love with a woman named Theodora (theh-oh-DOR-uh).

The complete biography of Theodora is unrecoverable because the only detailed source for her early life is Procopius's Secret History (the Anekdota, written around 550 but not published in his lifetime — a manuscript that savaged Justinian, Theodora, and the general Belisarius in unsparing prose, surviving by chance in a single Vatican copy that was rediscovered in the seventeenth century).

Procopius reports that Theodora was the daughter of a bear-keeper at the Hippodrome, that she became an actress and possibly a prostitute, that she traveled to Egypt and back, that she was famous on the Constantinopolitan stage for an obscene mime routine involving trained geese and Leda.
How much of this is true and how much is the disgruntled invective of a man who had to write panegyrics to the imperial couple by day and was venting in private by night is impossible to know.

What is clear is that Theodora came from outside the aristocracy — that she was, by the standards of the imperial court, scandalously low-born — and that Justinian had to get the law against patrician-actress marriages changed before he could marry her in 525.

Theodora was crowned co-empress when Justinian took the throne in 527 — not the consort of an emperor but an empress in her own right, with her own court, her own seal, her own diplomatic correspondence.
She was central to Justinian's government for the next twenty-one years, until her death from cancer in 548.
She protected Monophysite bishops despite her husband's official Chalcedonian policy.
She funded a monastery for former prostitutes.
She pushed through legislation expanding women's rights — making it harder to divorce a wife without cause, criminalizing forced prostitution, giving women fuller property rights.
Whether or not Procopius's biographical details are accurate, the policy record is unambiguous: she used imperial power to protect women in ways no previous Roman empress had.
The single moment that made Theodora a legend came in January 532, in the worst political crisis of Justinian's reign.
The Nika riots began as a dispute between the two great chariot-racing factions — the Blues and the Greens.
The factions were not just sports teams.

They were para-political organizations with their own organized militias, their own neighborhoods, and their own quasi-religious affiliations: Blues were Chalcedonian and aristocratic, Greens were Monophysite and populist.
On January 10, 532, the city prefect attempted to hang seven faction members for murder.
Two of them — one Blue, one Green — survived the gallows when the rope broke and were sheltered by sympathetic monks.
Their factions, normally hostile, united to demand pardons.
When Justinian temporized, the unified factions began rioting, sweeping through the city with the chant "Nika!" — "Conquer!" — that gave the riot its name.
Within days, half the city center was on fire.
The original Hagia Sophia (a smaller wooden-roofed basilica, the second of the name; the first had burned in 404) was destroyed.
The Senate House burned.
Senators caught up in the chaos elected an alternative emperor — Hypatius, a nephew of the late Anastasius — and acclaimed him in the Hippodrome.
Justinian, holed up in the imperial palace with Theodora, his generals, and his closest advisers, prepared to flee by ship.
Theodora stopped him.

The exact words Procopius records may not be verbatim — these speeches almost never are — but the substance is well attested: she told the council that exile was worse than death, that the imperial purple was a fine shroud, and that she would not run.
The line Procopius gives her — "Royalty is a good burial-shroud" — is one of the most quoted in Byzantine history.
Justinian stayed.

His generals Belisarius and Mundus then led an armed force into the Hippodrome through the imperial passages, while the eunuch Narses (NAR-seez, a court chamberlain who would prove to be one of the most extraordinary military commanders of the age — his story comes back) bribed key Blues to abandon the rioters.
The trapped crowd in the Hippodrome was massacred.
Procopius reports 30,000 dead, though the number is suspect by ancient standards.
Hypatius was executed.
The riots ended.

Justinian's throne was secure for the next thirty-three years, though every emperor in Constantinople for the next thousand years would remember that the Hippodrome could turn into a deathtrap for an unpopular ruler in a single afternoon.
The destroyed city center now needed to be rebuilt.
Justinian seized the opportunity.
He started with the law.

By the sixth century, Roman law was a thousand years of accumulated mess — overlapping statutes, contradictory rulings, opinions of long-dead jurists treated as binding precedent, imperial edicts that nobody had bothered to reconcile with each other.
Practical lawyers operated by tradition and connection rather than by any orderly code.
Justinian commissioned a panel of legal scholars under the jurist Tribonian (trih-BOH-nee-an) to fix this once and for all.
