The result, completed in stages between 529 and 534, was the Corpus Juris Civilis — "the Body of Civil Law" — a four-part compilation that has shaped almost every legal system in continental Europe.

The four parts: the Codex (a streamlined collection of imperial edicts, replacing all earlier compilations); the Digest or Pandects (a fifty-book compilation of the writings of the great Roman jurists, condensed and edited to remove contradictions); the Institutes (an introductory textbook for first-year law students, still readable, still in print); and the Novels (Latin Novellae, the new laws Justinian and his successors issued after the original codification was complete).
The cultural impact of the Corpus is hard to overstate.

After the Latin West rediscovered the Digest at Bologna around 1070, it became the foundational text for the medieval revival of Roman law — taught in every European law school, cited in every continental court, ancestor of the legal codes of France, Germany, Spain, Italy, the Netherlands, Quebec, Louisiana, Latin America, and Japan.

Most modern legal systems outside the English-speaking common-law tradition descend, more or less directly, from a project a Constantinopolitan emperor commissioned to clean up his clerks' filing system.
The Corpus is also where the Latin tags every English-speaking lawyer learns come from: res ipsa loquitur, nemo iudex in causa sua, audi alteram partem.
Justinian's legal staff did their work in Latin, the language of Roman law, even as the empire around them was switching to Greek for everything else.
The Latin text is part of the time capsule.
He continued with architecture.

Five days after the Nika riots ended, Justinian ordered the construction of a new Hagia Sophia (HAH-yah soh-FEE-ah, "Holy Wisdom" — the cathedral was dedicated not to a saint but to one of the divine attributes of Christ, who is the Wisdom of God in the Greek theological tradition).
The architects were two mathematicians — Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus — chosen for their command of geometry rather than their building experience.
The construction took five years and ten months.
Up to ten thousand workers labored in shifts.
Marble was shipped in from quarries across the empire (purple porphyry from Egypt, green marble from Thessaly, golden marble from Numidia).
The completed building was dedicated on December 27, 537.

According to a legend that may even be true, Justinian walked into the empty cathedral after the ceremony and exclaimed "Solomon, I have surpassed thee!" — a comparison to the Jerusalem Temple that became the most quoted line of his reign.
Hagia Sophia is a work of architectural daring that no Roman engineer had ever attempted at this scale.
The central feature is a dome — but not the kind of dome the Romans had built before, which always sat on a circular drum (like the Pantheon in Rome, Ancient Rome Ch 7).
Hagia Sophia's dome sits on a square base, which means the architects had to solve a geometric problem: how do you transition from four walls to one circle?

Their solution — possibly invented for this building, possibly borrowed from earlier Persian or Syrian experiments — was the pendentive (PEN-den-tiv): a triangular concave surface that fills the corner between two walls and curves up into the dome above.
The four pendentives smoothly transfer the weight of a circular dome onto a square set of supporting piers.

This invention made it possible to put a dome on top of any rectangular space, and it became the standard feature of every later Byzantine, Ottoman, and Russian Orthodox church, from the Süleymaniye in Istanbul to St.
Peter's in Rome to St.
Basil's in Moscow.

The dome itself spans 102 feet (31 meters) and rises 180 feet (55 meters) above the floor — at the time, the largest enclosed interior space in the world, a record it held for nearly a thousand years until the completion of Seville Cathedral in the early sixteenth century.
The original dome partially collapsed in an earthquake in 558 and was rebuilt — slightly higher and steeper — by Isidore the Younger, the original architect's nephew.
The interior was clad in marble revetments and gold mosaics that, lit by hundreds of windows around the dome's base, gave the impression that the dome was floating on a ring of light.

Hagia Sophia would become the model that Ottoman architects spent a century trying to surpass — the chief Ottoman architect Sinan explicitly designed the Selimiye Mosque in Edirne (1574) to exceed it by several feet of dome diameter (Ottoman Empire Ch 5), making the building part of a 1,000-year architectural conversation rather than a period endpoint.

The Byzantine writer Procopius, in his Buildings (a panegyric to Justinian's construction projects, the opposite-mood book to his Secret History), wrote that the dome appeared "not to rest on solid masonry but to cover the space with its golden dome suspended from heaven." When the Ottomans took Constantinople in 1453, they kept Hagia Sophia standing and converted it to a mosque, adding minarets and Islamic calligraphic medallions but leaving the structure essentially intact.
When the Turkish Republic secularized it in 1934, it became a museum.
In 2020 it was reconverted to a mosque.
It has been continuously roofed and continuously functional for fifteen hundred years.
Almost no other major building in the world can say that.

While Hagia Sophia was rising, the empire was also rebuilding the Hagia Eirene (eer-EE-nee, "Holy Peace") — another church burned in the Nika riots, dedicated to a different divine attribute, completed in 548.
Hagia Eirene survives today as one of the two oldest substantially original Byzantine churches in Istanbul.

Justinian's reconstruction of his capital was not just a political flex; it was a wholesale rewriting of the city's monumental skyline, on a scale and to a quality that would not be matched in Europe for nearly a millennium.
And then he turned to the West.
In 533, Justinian sent a small army across the Mediterranean to North Africa.
Its commander was Belisarius (bel-ih-SAR-ee-us, c. 500–565), a young general from Thrace who had already distinguished himself in the eastern wars and during the Nika riots.

The target was the Vandal Kingdom, the Germanic state that had ruled North Africa since Gaiseric's conquests in the 430s (Ancient Rome Ch 10; how the Vandals crossed the Rhine, crossed Spain, crossed to Africa, built a Mediterranean fleet, and sacked Rome twice is told in the Migration Period narrative).
The Vandals were Arian Christians who had spent a century persecuting their Catholic subjects, taxing them heavily, and getting fat on the wealth of the African provinces.
They were also, by the 530s, militarily soft — a small ruling caste of Germanic warriors whose grandsons preferred chariot races and country villas to actual fighting.
Belisarius landed with about 15,000 men, marched on Carthage, and won two pitched battles in three months.
The Vandal king Gelimer fled into the Atlas Mountains and surrendered the following year.
The entire Vandal kingdom — North Africa, the western Mediterranean islands (Corsica, Sardinia, the Balearics) — was Roman again.

Belisarius returned to Constantinople and was given a triumph — the first triumph since Augustus's day (Ancient Rome Ch 6) for a non-imperial general — riding a chariot to the Hippodrome at the head of his troops with the captured Gelimer walking before him.
The North African campaign had taken less than a year.
Justinian, encouraged, ordered Italy next.
This was a much harder target.

The Ostrogothic Kingdom (OS-troh-goth-ic, "Eastern Goths") had ruled Italy since 493 (the full Ostrogothic story, from the Danube to Italy, is told in the Goths narrative) under their king Theodoric the Great, who had governed competently, kept the Roman institutions running, employed Roman bureaucrats (including the philosopher Boethius, beh-OH-thee-us, who wrote the Consolation of Philosophy in prison while awaiting execution by Theodoric for treason — Boethius's book is one of the most important works of medieval philosophy and one of the last great Latin texts of antiquity), and kept his own Gothic warriors out of the locals' way.
By the 530s Theodoric was dead, his successors were weaker, and Justinian saw an opportunity.
Belisarius landed in Sicily in 535, took the island in months, crossed to the mainland, and captured Naples and then Rome itself in late 536.

He held Rome through a year-long Gothic siege in 537–538 — a brilliant defensive campaign in which a much smaller Roman force pinned the Goths against the Aurelian Walls and starved them into withdrawal.
He then advanced north and took Ravenna, the Ostrogothic capital, in 540, capturing the king Vitiges and most of his court.
It looked like the reconquest was done.

The Goths, having lost a king, immediately raised another — Totila, a brilliant cavalry commander who reorganized Gothic resistance and turned what should have been a mopping-up operation into a twelve-year nightmare.

Belisarius was recalled to Constantinople and sent east to fight the Persians (the Sasanians under Khosrow I had taken advantage of the western distraction to invade Syria in 540, sacking Antioch and dragging its population into Mesopotamia — a Sasanian-Roman war that would consume the empire's eastern attention for the next decade).

Justinian, paranoid about Belisarius's popularity and possible imperial ambitions, kept his most capable general on a short leash for years afterward, depriving him of the resources he needed to actually finish either war.
The Italian war ground on.
By the late 540s Totila had recovered most of Italy, including Rome itself (which he took, lost, and took again).
Belisarius was eventually returned to Italy with a tiny force and told to manage.
He did what he could.
By 552, after Belisarius had again been recalled, Justinian sent the elderly eunuch Narses — the same court chamberlain who had bribed the Blues during the Nika riots — to finish the job.
Narses was around 75 years old, had no formal military training, and turned out to be one of the most gifted generals of late antiquity.
He destroyed Totila's army at the Battle of Taginae in 552 and the Gothic remnant under Totila's successor at the Battle of Mons Lactarius in 553.
The Ostrogothic Kingdom was extinguished.
Italy was Roman again.
The reconquest had taken nineteen years instead of the projected one or two.
It had cost more than the empire could afford.
And the Italy that Narses delivered to Justinian was a smoking ruin.

Rome itself had been depopulated — its population, reportedly half a million in the early imperial period, had crashed below 50,000 by the mid-sixth century, with whole neighborhoods reverting to pasture inside the Aurelian Walls.
The senate had ceased to meet.
The aqueducts had been cut by besiegers and never properly repaired.
The cultural life that had survived the Gothic kingdoms collapsed under the weight of the war that was supposed to restore it.

Justinian also seized the southeastern corner of Spain from the Visigoths in 554, creating the province of Spania — a strip of coast from Cartagena to Cadiz that Byzantium would hold for about seventy years before the Visigoths recovered it.
Briefly, the Mediterranean was again a Roman lake.
The bill came due in two installments.

The first was the Plague of Justinian, which arrived in Constantinople in 541 and killed an estimated quarter of the eastern Mediterranean's population in successive waves over the next two centuries.

The disease — almost certainly bubonic plague caused by Yersinia pestis, the same pathogen as the later Black Death — apparently originated in central Asia or the Horn of Africa, traveled along the grain ships from Egypt to Constantinople, and from there spread to every Mediterranean port.

Procopius, who lived through the first wave, wrote a clinical description in his Wars that medical historians still recognize: bubonic swellings in the groin and armpits, sudden fevers, vomiting blood, hallucinations, death within days.
He estimated 10,000 deaths a day at the peak in Constantinople.

Modern estimates put the total mortality of the first wave at 25–40% of the city's population, and the cumulative effect of the subsequent waves at around 50% of the eastern Mediterranean's population over two centuries.
The economic damage was permanent.
Tax revenues collapsed.
Cities shrank.
The army could no longer be filled with native recruits and increasingly relied on barbarian foederati.
Justinian himself caught plague in 542 and recovered.
The empire as a whole did not.
The second installment was the Three Chapters Controversy of 553.

The "three chapters" were three sets of theological writings — by Theodore of Mopsuestia, Theodoret of Cyrrhus, and Ibas of Edessa, three Syrian bishops dead more than a century — that the Monophysites considered tainted with Nestorianism (the doctrine, condemned in 431, that Christ's divine and human natures were almost two separate persons).

Justinian, still trying to patch the Chalcedonian schism that was alienating Egypt and Syria, convened the Fifth Ecumenical Council at Constantinople and pressured it into condemning these three long-dead theologians — a gesture meant to placate the Monophysites without formally repudiating Chalcedon.
The gesture failed in both directions.
The Monophysites were not satisfied (they wanted Chalcedon repudiated outright).
The western church was furious (it considered the condemnation of long-dead theologians a violation of due process).
Pope Vigilius was effectively kidnapped to Constantinople and bullied into signing off, and his successors spent decades trying to walk it back.

The schism between Constantinople and Rome was not formally renewed, but the Three Chapters mess deepened the western perception that the Eastern emperors meddled in church matters in ways no proper Christian ruler should.
One last small story from Justinian's reign deserves mention because of the chain of consequences it set off.
Around 552 — the same year Narses was finishing off the Ostrogoths — two Nestorian Christian monks arrived in Constantinople from the East.
Nestorians (NES-tor-ee-anz) were yet another wing of Christianity, distinct from Chalcedonians and Monophysites.
Condemned at the Council of Ephesus in 431, they had spread eastward into Sasanian Persia and beyond.

They had been living in China — Procopius calls the source country Serinda, "the country of the Seres," meaning the silk-producing land — and they reported that they could break the Chinese monopoly on silk production.
China had kept the secret of silk for over two thousand years (Ancient China Ch 5; the silkworm and the mulberry-leaf process were a state secret enforced by capital punishment).
The monks claimed they could smuggle the eggs out and start production inside the empire.
Justinian financed them.
They returned with silkworm eggs concealed in the hollow chambers of bamboo walking sticks.
The eggs were brought to Constantinople, hatched, and bred.
Within a generation Byzantine silk production was a state-controlled industry, eventually centered on Thebes in Greece and Constantinople itself.

The Byzantine state imposed a strict monopoly: silk dyed in imperial purple could only be made in the imperial workshops and could only be worn by the emperor and senior officials. (This is also where the modern sense of "royal purple" comes from: the dye, a deep red-purple known as Tyrian purple, was extracted from the murex sea-snail in a process so labor-intensive that an ounce of dye required tens of thousands of snails.
The Byzantines preserved the Phoenician craft (Phoenicia Ch 4) and made it the marker of imperial dignity for nine hundred years.) The Chinese silk monopoly was broken.
The Silk Road shifted.
The Byzantines became the silk merchants of the Mediterranean for the next five hundred years.
And it all happened because two anonymous monks walked into the imperial palace in 552 with hollow walking sticks and a proposition.
The Byzantines had a gift for these moments — for converting a chance arrival into a state industry, for taking an institution they did not invent and running it better than the inventors had.
Silk is a small story by the standards of Justinian's reign.
It is also a Justinianic story in miniature: Roman ambition meeting Greek cleverness, financed by an emperor who could not stop pulling at every thread he encountered.
Justinian died in 565, after thirty-eight years on the throne.
He had reconquered North Africa, Italy, and southern Spain.
He had codified the law.
He had built Hagia Sophia.
He had survived a riot that should have killed him and a plague that did kill half his subjects.
He had also bankrupted the treasury, bled the army, and left behind territorial commitments his successors could not meet.
Within a generation, the Lombards (yet another Germanic people) would invade Italy and seize most of what Belisarius and Narses had reconquered.
Within a century, the Sasanian Persians and then the Arabs would strip Egypt and Syria from the empire entirely.
Most of what Justinian achieved did not last.
But Hagia Sophia is still there.
The Corpus Juris Civilis is still there.
The pendentive dome is still there in every major Byzantine, Ottoman, and Russian church.
The silk industry he founded survived as long as the empire did.
He overreached spectacularly, and even what he overreached for left foundations the empire would build on for nine more centuries.
When his successor Justin II (his nephew, ruled 565–578) opened the imperial treasury after his uncle's death, he reportedly found it empty.
The bill for restoring the Roman Empire had come due, and Justinian's heirs were going to pay it.

chapters.title: The Heraclian Convulsion
sentences: The fifty years after Justinian's death were an exercise in trying to hold on.
His successors — Justin II (565–578), Tiberius II Constantine (578–582), Maurice (mor-EES, 582–602) — were competent men handed a fiscally exhausted empire and an overextended frontier.

They lost most of Italy to the Lombards (lom-BARDS, a Germanic people who invaded in 568 — within four years they held everything north of Rome and Ravenna, and within a century the only Byzantine holdouts in Italy were the Exarchate of Ravenna, the south, and Sicily).
They lost ground to the Avars and Slavs in the Balkans.
They held the eastern frontier against the Sasanians at enormous cost.
Maurice, the longest-reigning of the three, was a soldier-emperor of real ability.

He intervened successfully in a Sasanian civil war in 591, restoring the legitimate king Khosrow II to the Persian throne in exchange for territorial concessions in Mesopotamia and Armenia — a diplomatic coup that gave Byzantium two decades of peace on the eastern frontier.
He wrote a military manual called the Strategikon, a practical handbook on how to run a Roman army that survives and is still readable.
He also tried to fix the empire's fiscal problem the only way that mathematically worked: cutting army pay.
This was a mistake.
In 602, the Danube army mutinied over a winter campaign Maurice had ordered, refused to obey a recall, marched on Constantinople, and acclaimed a centurion named Phocas (FOH-kus) emperor.
Maurice, his wife, and his five sons were captured and executed — the sons forced to watch their younger brothers die before their own turn came.
It was the first violent overthrow of a Byzantine emperor in two centuries, and it began a pattern of palace-coup instability that would haunt the empire for the next four hundred years.
Phocas was a disaster.
He had no political experience and no clear constituency.
He purged the senatorial aristocracy.
He let the Danube frontier collapse.
He provoked Khosrow II — who had been a personal friend of Maurice and had sworn vengeance for his murder — into invading the eastern provinces in 603.
Within five years the Sasanians were across the Euphrates.

Within a decade they had taken Antioch (611), Damascus (613), and Jerusalem (614, sacking it and carrying off the True Cross that Helena had reportedly discovered three centuries earlier — Chapter 1).
By 619 the Sasanians had completed the conquest of Egypt.
The empire was reduced to Anatolia, the southern Balkans, and a handful of Italian holdings, and even those were under continuous Avar and Slav pressure.
In 610, before the worst of these losses, the Exarch of Carthage's son Heraclius (heh-rah-KLEE-us) sailed east with the African fleet, took Constantinople, and overthrew Phocas.
The mob lynched the deposed emperor on the steps of the imperial palace.
Heraclius was acclaimed in the Hippodrome and inherited an empire that was, by any objective accounting, finished.
He did not act like it.
Heraclius's first move was to switch the empire's official language from Latin to Greek.
This sounds like a footnote and was actually one of the most consequential administrative decisions in the empire's history.

The Eastern Roman Empire had been functionally Greek-speaking for centuries — Greek was the everyday language of the streets of Constantinople, of the merchants of Antioch, of the theologians of Alexandria, of the army's enlisted ranks.
But the official language of the imperial chancery, of the law, of the highest court rituals had remained Latin, the language Constantine had brought with him in 330.
Heraclius, around 620, formalized what had already been true on the ground: the empire was a Greek state.
Imperial documents were now to be issued in Greek.
The emperor's title shifted from Imperator to Basileus (BASS-ih-lyoos, the Greek word for "king," previously used only of foreign monarchs but now claimed by the Roman emperor as his own).

The legal codes would still be written in Latin (Justinian had codified them less than a century earlier, and the Latin texts were not going to be retranslated en masse), but everything new was in Greek.

This is the line modern historians sometimes use to mark the actual transition from "Roman Empire" to "Byzantine Empire." The Byzantines themselves did not see it that way, but it was a real change — by the eighth century, knowledge of Latin in Constantinople was a specialist skill, the way knowledge of classical Greek is in modern English-speaking universities.
The two halves of Christendom were now also two halves of language, and theological disputes were increasingly carried out by people who could not read each other's documents in the original.
In 622, twelve years into his reign, Heraclius did the thing that nobody had expected him to be able to do.
He counterattacked.
The Sasanian war by this point had been running for nearly two decades.
The Persians held everything from Armenia to the Egyptian desert.

They had besieged Constantinople in 626 (in coordination with an Avar attack from the north — the city was saved by the Theodosian Walls, by Greek fire on the Persian fleet across the Bosporus, and by a Marian intercession that Constantinopolitans credited to a citywide procession of icons, which gave the Marian veneration central to Eastern Orthodoxy a particular boost).
Heraclius's response was unconventional.

Rather than defend the eastern provinces in detail — which the empire could no longer afford — he embarked on a series of audacious counter-offensives, taking the war directly into the Persian heartland.
He sailed from Constantinople with an army in 622, landed in northwestern Anatolia, and crossed into Armenia.

Over the next six years he maneuvered through the Caucasus, Azerbaijan, and Mesopotamia, alternately threatening Khosrow's western capital at Ctesiphon (TES-ih-fon, on the Tigris near modern Baghdad — Persian Empire Ch 9) and burning Sasanian shrines.
He allied with the Western Turks (a steppe confederation — a tactical innovation that Byzantine and Sasanian rulers had previously disdained) and with the Khazars.
He recovered Armenia.
He pushed into Azerbaijan and burned the great Zoroastrian fire-temple at Adur Gushnasp, retaliating for the Persian sack of Jerusalem.

The decisive moment came on December 12, 627, at the Battle of Nineveh — fought, in a coincidence that no Byzantine could have missed, at the same site as the great Mesopotamian capital that the Medes and Babylonians had destroyed twelve hundred years earlier (Mesopotamia Ch 12).

Heraclius personally led the Roman cavalry, killed three Persian commanders in single combat (according to the Byzantine sources — these accounts are exactly as reliable as you would expect), and routed the main Sasanian field army.
Khosrow II was overthrown by his own nobles a few months later, executed, and replaced by his son, who promptly sued for peace.
The Sasanians evacuated all the conquered provinces, including Egypt.
The True Cross was returned.

In March 630, Heraclius rode into Jerusalem in the most theatrical religious pageant of late antiquity, personally carrying the recovered cross of the Crucifixion to the Church of the Holy Sepulchre — the church Constantine's mother Helena had built three centuries earlier on the supposed site of the Resurrection.
The Byzantine sources describe him entering the city barefoot, in a hair shirt, surrounded by chanting clergy.

The triumph was the high point of his reign and one of the most celebrated moments in Byzantine history, commemorated annually thereafter as the Feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross — a feast still observed in the Eastern Orthodox calendar.
It was also, in retrospect, the moment of maximum overreach.
The empire had won a twenty-five-year war, recovered all its territory, restored its most precious relic, and humiliated its eternal rival.
Both Byzantium and Sasanian Persia were exhausted by the effort.
Their armies were depleted.
Their treasuries were empty.
Their populations were demoralized by decades of war and plague (the Plague of Justinian had returned in additional waves throughout the early seventh century).
The two great empires of the ancient world had spent their reserves fighting each other, and neither had any cushion left for what came next.
What came next arrived from Arabia.

Six years after Heraclius's triumph in Jerusalem, an Arab army defeated the main Roman field army at the Battle of Yarmouk (yar-MOOK, August 636 — fought along the Yarmouk River near the modern Syria-Jordan border).

The Arab commander Khalid ibn al-Walid (KAH-lid IH-bin al-wah-LEED, the most gifted general the early Arab armies produced — possibly the most gifted general the seventh century produced anywhere) lured the Roman force into a battle in difficult terrain, exploited a sandstorm, and shattered an army that on paper outnumbered his perhaps two to one.
The Roman commander, an Armenian eunuch named Vahan, was killed or captured.
The defeat ended Roman power in Syria.

Within two years the Arabs had taken Damascus (a second time, this time permanently), Antioch (whose fall ended six centuries of Roman rule in the city Augustus had governed personally), and Jerusalem (which surrendered to the Caliph Umar in 637, the holy city changing hands for the second time in a generation).
Egypt fell next.

The Arab general Amr ibn al-As invaded in 639 with a small force, took Babylon Fortress at the apex of the Nile delta in 641, took Alexandria itself in 642, and within a few more years had completed the conquest of the empire's wealthiest province.
The Coptic Christians of Egypt, who had been Monophysites under heavy Constantinopolitan pressure for two centuries (Chapter 1), did not resist the Arab takeover with any enthusiasm.
Their bishops negotiated terms.
The Greek-speaking ruling class largely fled.
The Arabic-speaking Muslim minority who took over taxation and high administration found that the existing Coptic-speaking bureaucracy continued to function smoothly under new management.
Egypt would never again be Roman.
The pattern was the same in Syria.

The local population, Monophysite or Jewish or unaligned, had no particular reason to fight for an empire that had spent the past two centuries persecuting their preferred theology and taxing them mercilessly.

The Arab invaders offered lower taxes and freedom of worship for non-Muslims who paid the jizya (a head tax on non-Muslim subjects, lower than the Byzantine taxes the same populations had been paying).
They were welcomed in many places.

The Christological hairsplitting that had dominated imperial politics for three centuries had finally produced its political consequence: the empire had alienated half its tax base, and when an outside power offered better terms, the alienated half went over.

The protected-minority arrangement that began here — Christians and Jews paying the jizya in exchange for legal autonomy — was the direct ancestor of the Ottoman millet system, which institutionalized the same logic into the most elaborate minority-management framework in world history, with each recognized community governed by its own patriarch under its own law (Ottoman Empire Ch 6).

By the time Heraclius died in 641 — broken in mind and body, his last years marked by erratic behavior, religious experimentation, and an incestuous second marriage to his niece Martina — the empire had lost everything he had recovered.
The True Cross was evacuated to Constantinople before Jerusalem fell again.
The recovered provinces were gone.
The empire was reduced to Anatolia, parts of the southern Balkans, the Italian holdings, and the great city itself.
But Heraclius had bought the empire something more important than territory.
He had bought it a reorganization.

The theme system (THEEM-uh, from Greek thema, meaning "a placement" but used in Byzantine administration for both a military district and the army stationed in it) is the institutional adaptation that allowed the empire to survive what would otherwise have been a fatal loss of territory and revenue.
The traditional Roman administrative system separated military and civilian power.
A province had a civilian governor for taxes and law and a military commander (a dux, the word that gives English "duke") for the army.
The army was a salaried professional force, paid in cash from central revenues, equipped by central workshops, deployed wherever needed.
The seventh-century crisis broke that system.
Tax revenues from Egypt and Syria were gone.
The empire could not pay a salaried professional army out of what was left.
So it improvised.

The themes were large military districts in Anatolia, each commanded by a strategos (strah-tay-GOSS, "general"), who was simultaneously the military commander and the civilian governor of his district.
The soldiers stationed in each theme — instead of being paid in cash they could not receive — were granted military lands (stratiotika ktemata) in exchange for hereditary military service.
A soldier got a farm.
His son inherited the farm and the military obligation.
The army became a force of citizen-soldier farmers who supplied their own equipment, fed themselves from their land, and reported to the strategos when called up.
The state paid only a small cash supplement and provided weapons in time of war.

The system began informally under Heraclius — historians used to date it precisely to 640, but the current scholarly consensus is that it evolved gradually from emergency expedients in the 620s and 630s and was not really systematized until Constans II's reign in the mid-seventh century.

By the end of the seventh century there were four themes covering Anatolia: the Anatolikon (the largest, in central Anatolia), the Armeniakon (in the northeast), the Opsikion (around Constantinople), and the Thrakesion (along the Aegean coast).
Each was simultaneously a province, an army, and a tax-collecting unit.
The theme system did three things at once.
It saved the army, by paying it in land instead of cash.
It saved Anatolia, by giving the local peasantry a stake in defending it.

And it produced, eventually, a new aristocracy — the strategoi and their officer corps, who would gradually consolidate large estates from the theme lands and become the military aristocracy that would dominate Byzantine politics from the eighth century onward.
It also did something less measurable.
It made the empire smaller and tougher.
The empire that emerged from the seventh-century crisis had given up its ambition to control the southern Mediterranean.
It was now a Greek-speaking, Anatolia-centered state with its capital at Constantinople and its religious identity defined by Chalcedonian Orthodoxy.
The Monophysite provinces were gone.
The Latin West was a different country.
The empire had finally become what posterity would call Byzantium — and it would survive in this form for another eight hundred years.
A small theological epilogue closes the chapter.
Heraclius and his successors made one last desperate attempt to mend the Chalcedonian schism that had cost them Egypt and Syria.

The compromise was called Monothelitism (mon-oh-THEL-it-iz-um, "single-will-ism") — the doctrine that Christ had two natures (preserving Chalcedon) but a single will (the unity that the Monophysites wanted).
It was an elegant attempt to thread a needle, and like Zeno's Henotikon two centuries earlier, it satisfied no one.
Rome rejected it.
The Monophysites had already been lost to the Arab conquests and no longer cared what Constantinople taught.
The Greek east was divided.
The fight was carried by an unlikely figure: Maximos the Confessor (mak-SEE-mos, c. 580–662), a former imperial secretary turned monk who became the leading theologian of his age.

Maximos rejected Monothelitism, was tried for treason in Constantinople in 654, refused to recant, was tortured (his tongue and right hand were cut off — these being the instruments of his offense, since he had spoken and written against imperial policy), and exiled to the Caucasus, where he died in 662.

Nineteen years later, the Sixth Ecumenical Council of 680–681 formally repudiated Monothelitism, vindicated Maximos posthumously, and even anathematized a sitting pope — Honorius I, who had endorsed Monothelitism in correspondence — in a ruling that would haunt later Catholic theology of papal infallibility.
The lesson of the seventh century, written in the bodies of Maximos and the lost provinces, was that Byzantine theology was no longer a tool for managing the empire's eastern populations.
The eastern populations were gone.
Theology was now a question of how the empire's remaining population — Greek, Chalcedonian, Anatolian — defined itself.
The answer would shape everything that followed.

chapters.title: The Iconoclast Century
sentences: The empire that emerged from the seventh century was a smaller, harder, more religious thing than the one that had entered it.
The lost southern provinces had been the empire's wealthiest tax base and its most heterodox population.
What remained — Anatolia, Thrace, Greece, the Italian holdings — was overwhelmingly Greek-speaking, Chalcedonian, and accustomed to siege.
It was also under continuous attack.

The Umayyad Caliphate (oo-MY-ad, the first hereditary Arab dynasty, ruling from Damascus from 661 onward), having absorbed Syria, Egypt, Persia, and most of North Africa within thirty years of Muhammad's death in 632, now considered Byzantium the next obvious conquest.
Two great sieges of Constantinople defined the late seventh and early eighth centuries.
The First Arab Siege of Constantinople ran from 674 to 678 — a four-year naval blockade in which Umayyad fleets repeatedly attempted to force the Bosporus.
They were defeated by an invention that would protect the empire for the next four hundred years: Greek fire.
Greek fire was the most feared weapon in the medieval Mediterranean.
The traditional account credits its invention to a Syrian Greek refugee named Kallinikos of Heliopolis, who arrived in Constantinople around 672 carrying the secret.

The exact composition was a state secret so closely guarded that no ancient source preserves the formula in full — it was lost when the empire fell, and the recipes circulated in modern histories are scholarly guesses rather than documented fact.

The leading reconstructions propose some combination of crude petroleum (skimmed from natural seeps in the Caucasus), pine resin, sulfur, and quicklime, heated in a copper container and pumped through a bronze siphon onto enemy ships.
The mixture ignited on contact with seawater (the quicklime reaction), continued burning on the surface of the water, and could not be extinguished by ordinary means.
Imagine a flamethrower mounted on a warship, projecting a stream of burning liquid that floated on the sea and stuck to whatever it touched.
The Arab fleet of 678 was destroyed by it.
The fleet of 717–718 was destroyed by it.
Russian fleets in 941 were destroyed by it.

The Greek fire monopoly was a strategic asset comparable to any nuclear deterrent of the modern age, and the Byzantines guarded it accordingly: the formula was held by a single family, the manufacturing was done in a single workshop in the imperial palace, and the operators were sworn to secrecy on pain of death.
The Second Arab Siege, in 717–718, was the empire's near-death experience.
The Umayyad caliph Sulayman sent his brother Maslama with an army of perhaps 80,000 men and a fleet of 1,800 ships to take Constantinople once and for all.

The Byzantine emperor at the moment of crisis was Leo III (called "the Isaurian," from the rugged southeastern Anatolian region of Isauria where his family came from — though "Isaurian" may be a later Byzantine simplification, and his family appears to have come originally from northern Syria).
Leo III had taken the throne in March 717 in a palace coup against the previous emperor, who had panicked at the approaching Arab armies.
Leo had less than five months to prepare his city.
The Theodosian Walls did most of the work.
The Arabs could not breach them and could not storm them.
The siege ground on through the unusually severe winter of 717–718, during which the Arab army camped in tents on the Thracian plain froze and starved by the thousand.
A Bulgarian army arrived from the north — bribed by Leo to attack the Arab rear — and inflicted further losses.
The Arab supply fleet, manned partly by Egyptian Christian conscripts who deserted to the Byzantines on contact, was destroyed by Greek fire in successive engagements.
By August 718 the surviving Arab forces lifted the siege and retreated.
Of the 1,800 ships that had sailed against Constantinople, only five returned to the Caliphate.
The siege was the largest pre-modern military operation ever launched against the city, and it had ended in catastrophic Arab defeat.
The historical consequence is hard to overstate.
If Constantinople had fallen in 718, the Arab armies would have had a clear path into Europe via the Balkans, and the entire trajectory of European history might have looked different.
As it happened, the failure of the second siege effectively halted Arab expansion into Europe by sea.
The Caliphate would never again attempt an assault on Constantinople.

The defeat also contributed to the Umayyad dynasty's credibility crisis: after 718 the Umayyads could no longer promise the conquests that justified their rule, and the internal tensions this created were one of the factors that brought the Abbasid revolution of 750 to power (Islamic Golden Age Ch 1).

Fourteen years later, on the other side of the Mediterranean, the Frankish ruler Charles Martel would defeat an Umayyad raid in southern France at the Battle of Tours, which is the moment European textbooks usually credit for stopping the Arab advance into western Europe.
Tours mattered, but Constantinople in 718 mattered more.
Leo III, having saved the empire, decided to break it.
In 726 — the date is approximate; the sources are Iconoclast-hostile and the chronology is contested — Leo issued an edict against the use of religious images in Christian worship.
Specifically, he ordered the removal of the famous icon of Christ above the Chalke Gate of the imperial palace and its replacement with a plain cross.
This single act started a controversy that would consume the empire for the next 117 years and that would permanently alter the relationship between the Byzantine state and the Roman papacy.
To understand why, you need to understand what icons were in eighth-century Christian practice.
An icon (from Greek eikon, "image") was a painted image of Christ, the Virgin Mary, or a saint, used as an aid to prayer and veneration.

Icons had been a central feature of Eastern Christian piety for centuries — every Byzantine church was full of them, every Byzantine home had its private icons, every Byzantine peasant had a personal relationship with the painted figure of his or her favorite saint.
People kissed them, lit candles before them, addressed prayers to them.

Some icons were believed to be miraculous (the Hodegetria, an image of the Virgin reportedly painted from life by Saint Luke himself, was carried in procession around Constantinople's walls during the 626 Avar siege and was credited with the city's deliverance).
Some were even believed to have appeared without human hands (the acheiropoieta, "not-made-by-hands," like the Image of Edessa, a cloth that supposedly bore the imprint of Christ's face).

The theological argument against icons drew on the Old Testament prohibition of graven images (Exodus 20:4) and the Islamic example: Islam's stark prohibition of religious images had given the Caliphate an austere visual culture that some Byzantines openly admired.
The argument was also political.
Leo III believed — or argued — that the empire's recent military disasters were divine punishment for the idolatrous worship of images.
Stripping the empire of icons would restore divine favor and military success.

There was a class element too: the icon-veneration tradition was strongest among ordinary people and the urban populace, while the iconoclast movement found its core support among the Anatolian military aristocracy and the army itself, both of which had been shaped by long contact with Islamic neighbors.
The argument for icons drew on the Incarnation: Christ had become a human being with a face, and to forbid the depiction of that face was to deny the reality of his humanity.
The leading defender was John of Damascus (yo-HAN of dah-MASS-kus, c. 676–749), who is one of the most important figures of the period and one of the great ironies of the iconoclast controversy.

John was a Christian priest and theologian whose family served as administrators for the Umayyad caliph in Damascus — meaning that the most influential defense of Byzantine icon veneration was written by a Christian living safely under Muslim rule, beyond the reach of the Byzantine emperor he was theologically opposing.

John's Three Treatises on the Divine Images laid out the careful theological distinction that would eventually win: a distinction between veneration (proskynesis, the honor due to a saint or to Christ depicted in an icon) and worship (latreia, the absolute adoration due to God alone).
One could legitimately venerate the image of Christ, John argued, because the honor passed through the image to its prototype.
One could not worship the image, because the image was not God.
This distinction is still official Catholic and Orthodox doctrine.

Leo III's son Constantine V (ruled 741–775, called "Kopronymos" — KOP-roh-NEE-mos, "name of dung," by his enemies, who claimed he had defecated in the baptismal font during his christening; this is a polemical slur, almost certainly invented by his iconodule biographers) was a more militant iconoclast than his father.
He hated monks — monks were the strongest icon defenders, and the great monasteries were the major centers of icon production.
He persecuted them brutally.
He convened the Council of Hieria (hye-ER-ee-uh) in 754, which assembled 338 bishops and condemned icon veneration as idolatry.
The council declared itself the Seventh Ecumenical Council, claiming to settle the question definitively.
It did not.
The papacy — Pope Stephen II in 753 — had already broken with Constantinople over the iconoclast question, an act that had enormous political consequences.
Stephen could no longer rely on the Byzantine emperor for protection against the Lombards in Italy.
He turned instead to the Franks, traveling personally to the court of Pepin the Short in 754 and securing a Frankish military alliance.

Pepin invaded Italy, defeated the Lombards, and donated the conquered territory in central Italy to the papacy, creating the Papal States that would form the temporal power of the Pope for the next eleven centuries.
Pepin's son Charlemagne would extend this arrangement.

On Christmas Day 800, Pope Leo III (a different Leo III — not the iconoclast emperor, but the contemporary Pope, a confusion the careful reader will need to track for the next sentence) crowned Charlemagne Imperator Romanorum in Saint Peter's Basilica, creating the Holy Roman Empire as a Latin Christian counterweight to Constantinople.
The Byzantine reaction was outrage: the Romans had a Roman emperor, in Constantinople, and there was only one of him.
The Frankish empire, in Byzantine eyes, was a usurpation.
But the practical reality was that the western half of Christendom now had its own emperor, its own pope-emperor relationship, and its own institutional independence from Constantinople.
The schism of 1054 (Chapter 7) was already implicit in 800.
The iconoclast controversy, in other words, did not just split the Byzantine church.
It split Christendom into the eastern and western halves that have remained divided ever since.
The first iconoclast wave was reversed in 787 by an unlikely figure: Empress Irene (eye-REE-nee, formally Irene of Athens, c. 752–803).
Irene had married Constantine V's son Leo IV in 769.
When Leo IV died in 780, she became regent for their nine-year-old son Constantine VI.
She was a committed iconodule (icon-supporter), and within seven years she had engineered the reversal of imperial policy.

The Second Council of Nicaea in 787 — actually convened twice, after a first attempt in 786 was broken up by iconoclast soldiers — restored icon veneration on the basis of John of Damascus's distinction between veneration and worship.
The Council is recognized as the Seventh Ecumenical Council by both the Catholic and Orthodox churches today, replacing Hieria 754 in the official sequence.

Constantine VI grew up under his mother's domination, attempted to assert his independence, was repeatedly outmaneuvered by Irene, and was finally arrested, blinded, and deposed by his mother in 797 — in the same room of the Sacred Palace where she had given birth to him twenty-six years earlier.

Irene then ruled in her own right as Basileus (the masculine form — she insisted on the male title, signing imperial documents as "Irene, the great basileus and autocrator of the Romans") from 797 to 802.

She is the first woman to rule the Byzantine Empire as sole monarch — a status the western papacy treated as so anomalous that Pope Leo III used the alleged "vacancy" of the imperial throne (because no emperor was a woman, in the western view) as part of the justification for crowning Charlemagne in 800.
Irene's reign ended in a coup in 802.
She was exiled to Lesbos, where she died the following year.
The Eastern Orthodox Church, which had benefited from her restoration of icons, canonized her as a saint despite her having blinded her own son.
Saints in the Byzantine tradition are not required to be morally unblemished.
They are required to have done the right thing on a sufficiently important question.

The second iconoclast wave began in 815 under Emperor Leo V the Armenian (ruled 813–820, an iconoclast military emperor of Armenian origin who restored iconoclasm at the Synod of Constantinople in 815).

It continued under his successors Michael II and Theophilos (theh-OH-fih-los, ruled 829–842) — Theophilos being one of the most attractive personalities of the iconoclast period: a learned, aesthetically sophisticated emperor who hated icons but loved court ceremony, mathematics, and Arabic-influenced palace architecture.

He commissioned the scholar Leo the Mathematician (c. 790–870) to design mechanical automata for the imperial throne room — golden lions that roared and lashed their tails when foreign envoys approached, mechanical birds that sang from a golden tree, a throne that rose toward the ceiling when the emperor was seated upon it.

These were not just luxuries; they were a Byzantine version of statecraft, designed to stun ambassadors with the technological superiority of the empire and to make foreign visitors uncertain whether they were being received by a man or a god.

Bishop Liutprand of Cremona, visiting Constantinople in 949, described them in detail and was duly impressed; the Byzantine writer Constantine VII Porphyrogennetos (Chapter 5) recorded their use as part of imperial protocol.
Leo the Mathematician also designed an optical telegraph system that could transmit messages from the eastern frontier to Constantinople in under an hour using synchronized fire-beacons.
The iconoclast court was many things, but it was not unsophisticated.

The chief intellectual defender of icons during the second iconoclast wave was Theodore the Studite (THEE-oh-dor, 759–826), abbot of the Stoudios Monastery in Constantinople and one of the great monastic reformers of the medieval world.

Theodore wrote prolifically against iconoclasm, was repeatedly imprisoned and exiled for his opposition, and rebuilt the Stoudios Monastery into the most influential religious community in the empire.

The Stoudite Rule he composed for his monks — strict, communal, intellectually serious — became the template for monasticism throughout the Byzantine and Slavic worlds, and many of the monasteries of Mount Athos still follow it in modified form today.
Theophilos died in 842, leaving his three-year-old son Michael III on the throne.

The regent was Theophilos's widow Empress Theodora (a different Theodora — not Justinian's wife, who had died three centuries earlier; the Byzantines reused names mercilessly, and a reader needs to track each separately).

This second Theodora had been a secret iconodule throughout her husband's reign — she reportedly hid her icons from Theophilos behind a mirror — and on his death she immediately set about restoring icon veneration.

The formal restoration came on the first Sunday of Lent, March 11, 843, in a great procession in Constantinople that has been celebrated ever since as the Triumph of Orthodoxy, the Sunday of Orthodoxy.

It is still the major liturgical feast of the first Sunday of Lent in every Eastern Orthodox church, marking the date the iconoclast crisis ended and the icon-rich worship of contemporary Orthodoxy was definitively established.
Why did the iconoclast controversy matter?
Why did the Byzantine state spend more than a century tearing itself apart over the question of whether painted images of saints could be venerated?
Three answers, none of them complete on its own.
First, the controversy was about the relationship between divinity and matter.
The iconoclasts believed that the divine could not be represented in matter without compromising its transcendence.
The iconodules believed that the Incarnation — God taking on human flesh — had sanctified matter and made the depiction of Christ not just permissible but theologically required.
The argument was, at its core, about whether God could be touched.
Second, the controversy was about the balance of power between the state and the church.
The iconoclast emperors were trying to assert imperial authority over religious doctrine — to make the emperor's theological judgment binding on the church.
The iconodules, including monks like Theodore the Studite and theologians like John of Damascus, were defending the church's independent authority on matters of doctrine.
The iconodule victory was, among other things, a victory for the principle that the emperor did not have unilateral theological authority.
The institutional consequences — a more independent patriarchate, a stronger monastic movement, a more distinct division between sacred and secular spheres — were lasting.
Third, and most consequentially, the controversy split Christendom permanently.

The iconoclast period drove the papacy into Frankish arms, created the Holy Roman Empire as a rival institution, and accelerated the linguistic, theological, and institutional divergence between the Greek East and Latin West.

The Byzantines emerged from the iconoclast period with a richer, more developed icon-centered piety than they had entered it with — and with a Latin neighbor who increasingly considered them schismatic foreigners rather than fellow Romans.
The empire that came out of 843 was, however, ready for its golden age.

chapters.title: The Macedonian Renaissance
sentences: The years between 843 and 1025 are the closest thing to a golden age that the Byzantine Empire ever experienced after Justinian.
The icons were restored.
The Arab armies had been pushed back.
The frontier was stabilizing.
The economy was recovering.

And the imperial throne was occupied, more or less continuously, by a remarkable succession of capable rulers from a single dynasty that had taken its name from the Macedonian theme of northern Greece (modern Greek Macedonia, not the ancient Macedonia of Alexander the Great, though the geographic overlap was considerable).
The dynasty's founder was, in some respects, an unlikely candidate.

Basil I (called "the Macedonian," ruled 867–886) was an Armenian peasant who had been brought to Constantinople as a teenager, found work as a stable groom, and risen — through his startling physical strength, his good looks, and his willingness to do dirty work — to become the trusted companion of Emperor Michael III (the same Michael who had been a child during the icon restoration of 843, now grown into a reckless young man with a serious drinking problem and a habit for Hippodrome chariot racing).
Basil murdered the emperor's chief minister in 866 with imperial connivance, was adopted by Michael as co-emperor, and then, in September 867, murdered Michael himself in his bedchamber.
The legitimate Macedonian dynasty thus began with a regicide.

Byzantine sources written under his descendants worked hard to soften this — Basil was, after all, the founder of the longest-lasting and most successful dynasty in Byzantine history — but the basic facts were impossible to obscure.
What Basil and his successors then did with the throne was extraordinary.

The first major project of the Macedonian period was the Photian Schism — and "schism" here means not a permanent split but a sharp confrontation between Constantinople and Rome that prefigured everything that would come in 1054.

Photius (FOH-tee-us, c. 810–893) was one of the most learned men of the ninth century — a scholar, philosopher, and lay civil servant who became Patriarch of Constantinople in 858 despite never having taken holy orders before his elevation (he was rushed through six holy orders in six days, a procedural irregularity Rome refused to accept).

His Bibliotheca — a collection of summaries and critiques of 279 ancient books, many of them now lost — is one of the great works of Byzantine scholarship and a major source for our knowledge of vanished classical literature.

His patriarchate was twice contested by Rome (which preferred his rival Ignatius), and the resulting Photian Schism of 863–867 — a mutual exchange of excommunications between Pope Nicholas I and Patriarch Photius — rehearsed every argument that would later be deployed in 1054: papal supremacy versus conciliar authority, the Filioque clause in the Nicene Creed (a Latin addition stating that the Holy Spirit proceeded "from the Father and the Son," which the East considered a heretical alteration of the original creed), the use of unleavened versus leavened bread in the Eucharist, clerical celibacy versus clerical marriage.
The schism was patched up.
The grievances were not.
Photius's tenure also overlapped with one of the most consequential missionary projects in European history.

In 862, the Slavic prince Rastislav of Great Moravia (a Slavic state in central Europe, in what is now the Czech Republic and Slovakia) sent a request to the Byzantine emperor for missionaries who could preach Christianity to his people in their own language.
Photius assigned two brothers from Thessalonica — Cyril (originally named Constantine, c. 826–869) and Methodius (c. 815–885) — to the mission.
Cyril, a brilliant philologist, invented an entirely new alphabet for the Slavic language: the Glagolitic script (gla-goh-LIT-ik, named from the Old Slavic word glagol, "word").
The script was specifically engineered to capture the sounds of Slavic, which had no native written tradition.

The Glagolitic alphabet was eventually superseded by a simpler script developed by Cyril's disciples in the late ninth century — the Cyrillic alphabet (named after Cyril, though he did not create it personally), which adapted Greek letters with additional symbols for distinctively Slavic sounds.
Cyrillic became the script of Bulgarian, Serbian, Macedonian, Russian, Ukrainian, Belarusian, and a long list of smaller languages.

The brothers also translated the Bible and the Orthodox liturgy into Old Church Slavonic — a Slavic literary language that became the Latin of the Orthodox Slavic world, used in churches from Ohrid to Moscow for the next thousand years.
This was a Byzantine cultural achievement on the scale of the Hagia Sophia.

Rome had insisted on Latin as the only legitimate language for liturgy in western Christendom, with disastrous consequences for the long-term retention of converted peoples (English, German, French, Polish, and Hungarian Christians all worshipped in a language they did not understand for the next thousand years).
Constantinople, by contrast, had translated its religion into the language of its converts.
The Slavic peoples received Christianity in their own tongue, with their own alphabet, with their own translated scriptures.

The result was that Slavic Orthodoxy took root much more deeply than Latin Christianity ever did in northern Europe — and that the Slavic world became, by the eleventh century, a culturally autonomous Byzantine satellite extending from the Adriatic to the Volga.
The Macedonian dynasty also benefited from a steady recovery of military strength.
Constantine VII Porphyrogennetos (kon-stan-TEEN, "Born-in-the-Purple," c. 905–959) was Basil I's grandson and one of the most attractive personalities to occupy the Byzantine throne.

He spent most of his life as a co-emperor pushed aside by stronger men — most notably the admiral Romanos I Lekapenos (roh-MAHN-os, lek-ah-PEH-nos), who muscled his way into power as senior emperor from 920 to 944, married his daughter to Constantine, and effectively ran the empire while Constantine remained a figurehead.
Romanos I was a competent emperor in his own right.

He successfully fought the Bulgarians, brought the empire's relations with neighboring states onto a more stable footing, and issued land legislation protecting small landholders against the encroachment of large aristocratic estates — the so-called dynatoi, "the powerful ones." But Constantine VII outlasted him, finally taking sole power after Romanos was deposed by his own sons in 944 and dying in obscurity.
What Constantine VII did with his decades of forced leisure was write.
Constantinople under his patronage became one of the great scholarly centers of the medieval world.
He commissioned a series of encyclopedic compilations on imperial administration, court ceremony, military strategy, agriculture, and history.
Three of these survive and are among the most important sources we have for tenth-century Byzantium.
The De Administrando Imperio ("On the Administration of the Empire," composed around 952) is a confidential manual on geopolitics, written by Constantine for his son Romanos II's instruction.

It contains ethnographic descriptions of every neighbor — Pechenegs, Khazars, Magyars, Rus', Bulgarians, Serbs, Croats, Arabs, Lombards, Franks — with practical advice on how to play them off against each other.
The book is the closest thing the medieval world produced to a modern intelligence briefing, and it includes details about peoples like the early Rus' that survive nowhere else.

The De Ceremoniis ("On Ceremonies") describes the imperial court rituals in obsessive detail: which day of the year requires which color of imperial garment, how foreign envoys are to be received, what music is played at which moment of an imperial banquet, how the throne is to be approached.
Most readers find this book intolerably dull.
But it is a unique window into the theatrical machinery of Byzantine power, the way the empire used spectacle to overawe both subjects and foreigners.

The De Thematibus is a less successful work — a description of the empire's military themes that is now considered partly inaccurate — but it preserves administrative information that would otherwise be lost.

Together, these three books are the foundational documents of what historians call the Macedonian Renaissance: a deliberate, state-sponsored revival of classical learning in tenth-century Byzantium, parallel to and a century earlier than the more famous Carolingian Renaissance in the Latin West (the Frankish revival of classical scholarship under Charlemagne and his successors).
The Macedonian Renaissance was not just official scholarship.

It produced the Souda (SOO-duh) — a massive 30,000-entry Greek-language encyclopedia compiled around 980, organized in alphabetical order, covering history, biography, literature, philosophy, philology, geography, and grammar.

The Souda is the single most important source for our knowledge of ancient Greek literature, because it preserves quotations and biographical details from hundreds of works that have not otherwise survived — an enormous fraction of what we know about pre-Christian Greek civilization comes through the Souda.
It produced Photius's Bibliotheca, mentioned earlier.

It produced manuscripts of classical Greek literature copied in the new minuscule script (a flowing cursive form of Greek writing, more compact and faster to write than the older majuscule script, that became standard in the ninth century and dramatically increased the rate at which classical texts could be transmitted).
Most of the Greek classical texts that survive into the modern world reach us through Macedonian-era copies.
The Athens of Plato is preserved by the Constantinople of Constantine VII.
The military recovery accelerated under Constantine VII's successors.

Nikephoros II Phokas (nih-KEH-foh-ros FO-kus, ruled 963–969) was a brilliant general from the Anatolian military aristocracy who had already reconquered Crete from the Arabs in 961 — a campaign that was the empire's most important military success in two centuries.
Crete had been Arab since 824 and had been used as a base for Aegean piracy that had devastated Byzantine coastal trade for over a century.
Nikephoros's reconquest restored Byzantine naval supremacy in the eastern Mediterranean.
Two years later he took the throne in a coup and turned his attention east.
In 969, Nikephoros recaptured Antioch — one of the great cities of late antiquity, the seat of one of the five original Christian patriarchates, lost to the Arabs in 638.
Its reconquest was the symbolic culmination of three centuries of Byzantine military recovery.
He pushed the eastern frontier deep into Syria, recovering territory that had been Arab since the seventh century.

He was assassinated later that year in a palace coup organized by his wife Theophano and her lover John I Tzimiskes (TSIM-iss-keez), who succeeded him as emperor and continued the offensive — pushing into Mesopotamia and reportedly threatening Jerusalem itself before being recalled by an unrelated crisis.
Tzimiskes was probably poisoned by his own minister in 976, opening the way for the man whose name dominates the rest of the Macedonian period.
Basil II (ruled 976–1025) is the great warrior emperor of medieval Byzantium.
Tall, plain-faced, austere, never married, ruling for forty-nine years, he transformed the empire into the dominant power of the eastern Mediterranean.
Procopius wrote about Justinian.
Anna Komnene would write about her father Alexios (Chapter 8).
Nobody wrote a comparable hagiography of Basil II, partly because he was personally so unappealing — he had no court life, no literary interests, no taste for ceremony, no interest in being praised.
He is described as wearing dyed-purple robes only in battle and ordinary military gear in the palace.
He probably preferred this.
Basil II is the only Byzantine emperor for whom the documentary record consists almost entirely of his administrative and military acts, with his personality emerging only by inference.

His first decades were spent fighting an internal civil war against the Anatolian military aristocracy, which had assumed it could control the boy emperor and was disabused of this assumption violently.
By the late 980s Basil had crushed the rebels and asserted personal control.
He then turned to the Bulgarians.

The First Bulgarian Empire had emerged on the lower Danube in the late seventh century when the Turkic-speaking Bulgars (a steppe people from the Pontic region, originally Turkic-speakers but rapidly Slavicized) crossed the Danube and conquered the local Slavic populations.
Under successive rulers it had become the major rival to Byzantium in the Balkans.
Tsar Symeon the Great (ruled 893–927) had been Constantine VII's principal antagonist, repeatedly defeating Byzantine armies and nearly capturing Constantinople itself.
Under Symeon's successors the empire had fragmented but remained dangerous.
Under Tsar Samuel (SAM-yoo-el, ruled 997–1014) it had reconsolidated and was again threatening Byzantine control of Greece.
Basil II decided to destroy it.
The Bulgarian war ran from roughly 1000 to 1018, eighteen years of grinding mountain warfare in the rugged terrain of modern North Macedonia, Bulgaria, Albania, and Serbia.
Basil's signature tactic was relentless persistence — annual campaigns, year after year, never resting on a victory, never accepting a partial settlement.
The decisive engagement came on July 29, 1014, at the Battle of Kleidion (KLY-dee-on, the "Pass of the Keys" in Bulgarian Klyuch, in what is now southwestern Bulgaria).
Basil's army surrounded a Bulgarian force of about 15,000 men in a narrow mountain pass and captured nearly all of them.
What he did next made his name.

According to the Byzantine chroniclers — and these accounts are detailed enough and contemporary enough to be substantially credible, though the specific number is debated — Basil ordered all 15,000 prisoners blinded, leaving one man in every hundred with a single eye to lead the others home.
The 99% who were fully blinded were tied together in groups of a hundred, each led by a one-eyed guide, and sent back to Tsar Samuel.
Samuel reportedly suffered a stroke and died two days after seeing his army return in this condition.
The sobriquet Boulgaroktonos — "Bulgar-Slayer" — was attached to Basil II afterward, though it was not used in his lifetime; the earliest attestation is about a century later.
Some modern historians have argued the blinding story is exaggerated or invented.

The Byzantines did practice mass blinding as a punitive measure — it was a standard penalty for treason and for usurpers (less terminal than execution, but it disqualified a man from being a candidate for the throne, since the empire required physically perfect rulers).
Whether the Kleidion blinding was on the scale tradition records is not certain.
What is certain is that the Bulgarian Empire collapsed within four years of the battle.
By 1018 the entire Bulgarian state had been absorbed into Byzantium.
The Balkans were Byzantine again, for the first time in four centuries.
Two other achievements of Basil II's reign deserve mention.
The first was the Christianization of Kievan Rus' in 988.

The Rus' (ROOS, an early medieval Slavic-Norse confederation centered on the Dnieper River, the ancestor of modern Russia, Ukraine, and Belarus) had been raiding Byzantine territory periodically since the ninth century.
The most spectacular raid had been in 860, when a Rus' fleet had appeared in the Bosporus and threatened Constantinople itself before withdrawing.

The raid of 907, led by Prince Oleg of Kyiv, had been more strategic — it ended with a treaty granting Rus' merchants advantageous trading terms in Constantinople, terms that built up a substantial Rus' merchant community in the Byzantine capital and that required regular diplomatic management for the next century.
But the Rus' as a whole remained pagan, and their relationship to Byzantium remained transactional.

In 988, Prince Vladimir of Kyiv (VLAH-dih-meer, c. 958–1015), who had reached out to Basil II for marriage to the emperor's sister Anna Porphyrogennetos in exchange for military aid against an internal Byzantine rebellion, agreed to convert to Orthodox Christianity as a condition of the marriage.

The Rus' chronicle the Primary Chronicle records that Vladimir had previously sent envoys to investigate the world's religions — the envoys reported that Islam was unacceptable because it forbade pork and wine ("drinking is the joy of the Rus'," Vladimir is said to have declared, "we cannot exist without that pleasure"); that western Christianity was unimpressive ("we beheld no glory there"); and that the liturgy at Hagia Sophia in Constantinople was so beautiful that "we knew not whether we were in heaven or on earth." The story is almost certainly stylized, but the political logic is real: Byzantine Christianity offered Vladimir more than Latin Christianity did — translated scriptures, autonomous metropolitan organization, the prestige of marriage to the imperial family, ongoing diplomatic and economic ties.
He chose Orthodoxy, mass-baptized his population in the Dnieper, and brought the entire Rus' state into the Constantinopolitan religious and cultural sphere.
The Christianization of Rus' was the single most consequential religious transition in Eastern European history.

It locked Russia, Ukraine, and Belarus into Orthodox Christianity rather than Latin Christianity, gave them Cyrillic rather than Latin script, oriented their high culture toward Greek rather than Roman models, and laid the foundation for what would later become the Russian claim to be the Third Rome (Chapter 12).

When the Russian state began calling Moscow the Third Rome in the late fifteenth century, it was claiming an inheritance that had been assembled, deliberately and patiently, by Constantinople over the previous five hundred years.

As part of the marriage agreement, Vladimir sent Basil II a force of 6,000 Norse-Rus warriors — heavily armed axe-wielding northmen who became the elite imperial bodyguard known as the Varangian Guard (VAR-an-jee-an, from the Old Norse varingjar, "sworn companions").
The Varangians were not just decoration.

They were the imperial last line of defense, fanatically loyal to whoever currently held the throne (their loyalty was to the office, not the man — they switched smoothly from one emperor to the next, even when the new emperor had murdered the old one).

They were also a recruitment magnet for adventurers from across the northern world: after the Norman Conquest of England in 1066, large numbers of Anglo-Saxons fleeing the new Norman regime traveled to Constantinople and enrolled in the Varangian Guard, which by the late eleventh century was substantially Anglo-Saxon.

The Varangians served the empire for over four centuries, and the famous Norwegian king Harald Hardrada served in the Guard before returning to Scandinavia and dying at the Battle of Stamford Bridge in 1066.

The Varangian arrangement embodies a logic the Ottomans would carry to its extreme institutional conclusion: foreign soldiers without local connections make more reliable guards than native troops with land and kinship at stake.

The Ottoman devshirme applied this insight not just to a bodyguard corps but to an entire governing class, recruiting Christian boys from the Balkans and raising them as loyal servants of the sultan with no other identity (Ottoman Empire Ch 6).
The second achievement was that Basil II left the empire fiscally healthy — the only Byzantine emperor between Anastasius I and the Fall who can plausibly claim that distinction.

He had filled the treasury through systematic taxation, military success, and an aggressive policy of resuming aristocratic land grants that had been used to deprive the small landholders of the theme system.
When he died in December 1025, the empire stretched from southern Italy to Armenia, the borders were secure, the army was strong, and the central treasury held enough gold to sustain a major war.
There would never again be a moment when so much had been so consolidated.
His successors threw it away in fifty years.

chapters.title: Ceremony, Silk, and the Hippodrome
sentences: This chapter is a pause.
Six hundred years have gone by — Constantine to Basil II — and the political narrative will continue to grind forward in the next chapter.
But before it does, there is a question worth asking.
How did the machinery of Byzantine civilization keep running through six centuries of plague, civil war, foreign invasion, and theological crisis?

Emperors fell, dynasties rotated, provinces were lost — but the silk weavers kept weaving, the imperial workshops kept minting gold, the patriarchs kept performing the liturgy, the bureaucrats kept collecting customs duties on the Bosporus.
Something more durable than any single emperor was holding it all together.

The argument of this chapter is that the empire's daily institutions — its court, its currency, its commerce, its monasteries, its ceremony — were the durable thing, and that the political crises we have been tracking played out on top of a substrate that the crises did not reach.
What did it mean to wake up in tenth-century Constantinople?
How did a Byzantine eat, dress, work, fight, pray, and die?
The empire was, throughout its existence, the most urban, most literate, most ceremonial society in the Christian world.

Constantinople in 1000 had perhaps 400,000 to 500,000 inhabitants — by far the largest city in Europe (Paris had perhaps 20,000 in the same period; London perhaps 15,000) and second in the world only to Baghdad, the Abbasid capital, which was at this point larger than Constantinople by a wide margin and was the only city in Eurasia that surpassed it. (Tang Chang'an had been comparable in size before its sack in 904; by 1000 the eastern Eurasian primacy had passed to the cities of Song China.) The next chapter will continue the political story.
This chapter will linger inside the city for a moment.
Start with the emperor.
The Byzantine emperor was, in theory, the absolute monarch of a Christian empire ordained by God.
In practice, his power was constantly contested — by the senate, the church, the army, the great aristocratic families, the urban populace, and the chariot factions of the Hippodrome.
The Byzantine state had no orderly mechanism for imperial succession.
An emperor reigned until he died, was deposed, was murdered, or abdicated.
Of the eighty-eight emperors between 330 and 1453, perhaps a third died violently — assassinated, blinded and deposed, killed in battle, or executed after a coup.
The throne was, in this sense, a far more dangerous job than the papacy or the caliphate.
What the emperor wore was prescribed by ceremony to a degree no modern monarch matches.

The full imperial regalia included the loros (a long jeweled stole wound around the body in a complex figure-eight pattern), the skaramangion (a long brocaded silk tunic), the tzangia (purple boots — only the emperor could wear purple shoes), the stemma (an arched crown set with precious stones, with pendant strings of pearls hanging beside the face).
Variations of these garments were prescribed for every day of the liturgical and civil year, and the emperor's wardrobe was one of the major operating expenses of the imperial household.
What the emperor did was equally choreographed.

The De Ceremoniis describes his daily schedule in painful detail: when he rose, when he prayed, which icons he venerated and in what order, when he received foreign ambassadors, when he dined, when he attended church, when he went to the Hippodrome, when he processed through the city.
Almost every public action was a ritual.

The most famous ritual was the proskynesis (pros-kih-NEE-sis, "prostration") — the act of full prostration before the emperor, with the supplicant lying flat on the floor, forehead touching the marble.
Foreign envoys were required to perform proskynesis before being received in audience.

The Western European bishop Liutprand of Cremona (a tenth-century Lombard diplomat who served as ambassador to Byzantium and wrote two memoirs of his visits) described his reception by Emperor Constantine VII in 949: he prostrated himself three times before the throne; the throne, by the previously-mentioned mechanism designed by Leo the Mathematician, then rose toward the ceiling, with the emperor wearing different robes when it descended again.
Mechanical golden lions roared.
Mechanical birds sang.
A choir of eunuchs chanted hymns of praise.
Liutprand was, despite his determined western contempt for the Byzantines, impressed.
This was theater, but it was theater with a purpose.
The empire was perpetually outnumbered, outflanked, and overstretched.
Spectacle compensated for what military force could not always deliver.
Ambassadors who had been overawed in the throne room were less likely to recommend war on their return home.
Subjects who had seen the emperor in his terrifying glory were more likely to obey his administrators in their unglamorous offices.
Around the emperor was a court of extraordinary complexity, and at the center of it was a class of officials unique to Byzantium: the eunuchs.
Eunuchs in the Byzantine court were not slaves.
They were not prisoners.
Many came from respectable families.
Some were castrated as children specifically to qualify them for high office.
Others were made eunuchs as adults, voluntarily, to enter the imperial bureaucracy.

The empire had perhaps a dozen senior offices reserved exclusively for eunuchs — the parakoimomenos (the emperor's chamberlain, an enormously powerful office), the protovestiarios (in charge of the imperial wardrobe and treasury), the praepositus sacri cubiculi (master of the sacred bedchamber).
These were not minor offices.
The parakoimomenos in the late ninth century could effectively run the empire while the emperor slept.
The eunuch general Narses (Chapter 2) had defeated the Ostrogoths.
The eunuch Joseph Bringas had run the empire under two emperors in the mid-tenth century.
Why eunuchs?

The Byzantine answer was practical: eunuchs could not father children, which meant they could not start dynasties, which meant they could be trusted with positions of personal access to the emperor and his family without fear that they would seize the throne for their descendants.
