Eunuchs were also legally barred from becoming emperor themselves, which meant their loyalty was structurally directed toward the current ruling family rather than toward their own line.

The eunuch class was, in this sense, an institutional answer to the problem of dynastic succession: a class of high-functioning officials whose interests were aligned with the throne's stability rather than with their own perpetuation.
The Byzantines were also more comfortable with the third-gender quality of eunuchs than later Western Europeans would be.
Court eunuchs occupied a recognized social role with its own dignity, its own dress code, its own career path.
They were not seen as failed men or as objects of pity.
They were seen as a specialized administrative caste, and they were treated as such.
This is a feature of Byzantine society that has often been treated as scandalous or grotesque by later writers.

It is more usefully understood as one of several institutional adaptations the empire developed to manage its peculiar combination of absolute monarchy, dynastic instability, and large bureaucratic state.
The other distinctive Byzantine institution at the heart of city life was the Hippodrome.
The Hippodrome was a chariot-racing arena built by Septimius Severus in the late second century and expanded by Constantine.
By the tenth century it sat along the eastern flank of the Great Palace, in the heart of the imperial city.

Its U-shape, modeled on the Circus Maximus in Rome, was about 1,400 feet long (430 meters) and 380 feet wide (115 meters), with a central spina decorated with monuments looted from across the Mediterranean — the Serpent Column from Delphi (Chapter 1), an Egyptian obelisk dedicated by Theodosius I, a bronze statue of Hercules (later destroyed by the Crusaders in 1204).

Races were the central public entertainment of Constantinople — eight to twenty-four chariot races on race days, four chariots per race, with charioteers (mostly slaves or freedmen, often famous, sometimes wealthy) competing on behalf of the four traditional racing factions: the Blues, the Greens, the Reds, and the Whites (the Reds and Whites had withered to insignificance by Justinian's day; from the sixth century onward only the Blues and Greens really mattered).
The factions had organized fan clubs, dressed in faction colors, controlled neighborhoods, ran organized claques in the Hippodrome itself, and functioned as semi-official political institutions.

The Blues drew their support disproportionately from the aristocracy and the Chalcedonian establishment; the Greens drew theirs from the urban populace and the Monophysite-leaning artisan classes (a connection that lingered even after the Monophysite question had been resolved by the Arab conquests).

The emperor attended major races in person, seated in the kathisma — an imperial box connected by a private staircase to the Great Palace, allowing him to enter and leave without exposing himself to the crowd.
From the kathisma he could be acclaimed by the populace, heckled by the populace, or — in extreme cases like the Nika riots of 532 (Chapter 2) — directly threatened by the populace.
The Hippodrome was where Byzantine emperors learned what their subjects thought of them, and where Byzantine subjects learned which of their wishes the emperor was prepared to grant.
Successful charioteers were celebrities on the order of modern athletes.

Porphyrios of the Greens, the most famous Byzantine charioteer (active in the late fifth and early sixth centuries), had statues erected in the Hippodrome and bronze monuments in his honor that survived into the early modern period.
His fans — and the rival fans of his Blue counterparts — produced elaborate carved monuments documenting their respective heroes' victories.
We know more about Porphyrios than we do about most Byzantine emperors of his century.
Outside the imperial palace and the Hippodrome, the city was a working metropolis on a scale Western Europe had not seen since classical Rome.
Constantinople's harbors — the Neorion and the Theodosian Harbor on the Sea of Marmara, the Prosphorion and the Boukoleon on the Golden Horn — handled thousands of merchant ships a year.
The customs duties from Bosporus traffic were one of the empire's largest single revenue streams.

Goods came through from everywhere: Russian fur and amber from the Black Sea ports, Indian pepper and Chinese silk via the Red Sea and Egypt, North African grain (until 642), Italian timber, Danubian salt fish, English tin, Arab perfumes and incense.
The city's manufacturing base was concentrated in the silk industry.

Justinian's smuggled silkworms (Chapter 2) had matured by the tenth century into a state-controlled production system based around imperial workshops in Constantinople and provincial centers in Greece (Thebes, Corinth, Patras).

The state monopolized the production of certain silk grades — particularly the deep-purple "blattai" reserved for imperial use, dyed with murex purple in a process inherited from the Phoenicians (Phoenicia Ch 4).
Lower grades were produced for export and for the domestic market under tight regulatory supervision.

The Book of the Eparch — a tenth-century regulatory manual for the city's guilds, surviving in a single Geneva manuscript — describes the rules in detail: who could buy raw silk, who could weave it, who could sell finished garments, what prices could be charged, what penalties applied to violations.
The picture is of a remarkably regulated commercial economy, far more formalized than anything in contemporary Western Europe.
The other major industry was gold.

The bezant — the western European name for the Byzantine gold solidus, a coin originally introduced by Constantine and standardized at 4.5 grams of nearly pure gold — was the international reserve currency of the Mediterranean for over seven centuries.
Foreign rulers from Britain to India hoarded bezants as a store of value.
The bezant's stability — maintained, with one important exception we will come to in Chapter 7, from the fourth through the eleventh century — was a major source of Byzantine soft power.
A ruler who could pay in bezants could buy mercenaries, allies, treaties, and intelligence anywhere in the known world.
Anastasius I's currency reform in 498 had also restored the bronze coinage, creating clearly denominated follis coins for daily transactions.

The Byzantine monetary system was, by medieval standards, sophisticated — a tri-metallic currency (gold for international and high-value transactions, silver for medium transactions, bronze for daily small transactions) with consistent denominations and reliable purity.

Western Europeans who came east on diplomatic missions or pilgrimages were routinely astonished by the wealth of Constantinople — by the casualness with which gold was used, by the marble and the gilding and the silk and the perfumed water and the orchestra of musicians during dinner.
Education in Constantinople ran on two tracks.

The University of Constantinople had been founded in 425 by Theodosius II — a cluster of imperially endowed chairs in Greek and Latin grammar, rhetoric, philosophy, and law, with about 31 chairs in total.
It functioned more or less continuously from the fifth century to the fifteenth, though its prestige and funding fluctuated.
In the ninth century, the scholar Leo the Mathematician taught at the Magnaura School in the imperial palace, training a generation of officials and clergy in geometry, music theory, and astronomy.
In the eleventh century, Michael Psellos (Chapter 7) reorganized higher education around philosophy, with himself as hypatos ton philosophon ("consul of the philosophers") at its head.
The University was never a degree-granting institution in the modern sense, but it produced trained civil servants, lawyers, physicians, and clergymen for the empire's institutions.
The other track was the monastery.
Byzantine monasteries were not just religious communities; they were schools, hospitals, libraries, scriptoria, agricultural enterprises, and pension homes for retired aristocrats.
The Stoudios Monastery in Constantinople, reformed by Theodore the Studite (Chapter 4), was the most influential, but there were hundreds of others scattered across the empire.
The greatest concentration was on Mount Athos (AH-thos, a remote peninsula in northern Greece dedicated to monastic settlement from 963 onward, when Athanasios the Athonite founded the Great Lavra).

Mount Athos remains today the largest surviving Eastern Orthodox monastic community, a self-governing peninsula of twenty monasteries occupying about 130 square miles (330 km²) — and women have been forbidden from entering since 1046, an interdiction that is still in force.
Monasteries copied manuscripts, preserved liturgical practice, trained clergy, and provided alternative careers for men and women who did not wish to or could not marry.
They were also enormously wealthy, accumulating lands and endowments over centuries until they became major economic actors in their own right.

The Byzantine state had a complicated relationship with monastic wealth — sometimes confiscating it (Constantine V during the iconoclast period was particularly aggressive about this), sometimes endowing it lavishly (almost every emperor founded at least one monastery as part of his personal patronage).
By the eleventh century, the largest Constantinopolitan and Athonite monasteries were among the most economically significant institutions in the empire.
Religious life in Byzantium was the constant background hum of every other aspect of life.

The Orthodox liturgical year structured the calendar — every day was a saint's day, every week had its fasts (Wednesdays and Fridays, plus the four extended fasting periods around Christmas, Easter, the apostles' feast, and the Dormition).
Every Christian Byzantine was supposed to fast for roughly half the year.
Animal flesh, dairy products, and (during the strictest periods) olive oil were forbidden during fasts, with elaborate exceptions for the sick, the pregnant, the very young, and travelers.
The combined effect was a national diet built around bread, vegetables, legumes, fish, and seafood, with meat and dairy as celebratory foods rather than daily staples.
The Hagia Sophia was the centerpiece.

The full Divine Liturgy of John Chrysostom — the standard Byzantine eucharistic service, with chanted hymns, processions of clergy in elaborate vestments, clouds of incense, and a continuous antiphonal exchange between priests and choir — took roughly two hours.
On major feast days the service expanded to include vigils, processions through the city, and ceremonial acts involving the emperor.
The visual environment was overwhelming: gold mosaics, marble columns, hundreds of oil lamps, banners, colored silks.

Byzantine writers describe walking into Hagia Sophia as walking into a vision of heaven — the building was deliberately designed to overwhelm the senses, to make the worshipper feel that the boundary between earthly and divine had become thin.
For ordinary Byzantines, the most important religious activity was probably the veneration of personal icons.
Every household had its private icon corner.
Travelers carried small icons in their luggage.
Soldiers carried icons into battle.
Mothers gave birth with icons in the room.
Dying Byzantines kissed icons in their last moments.

Icons were not, in the post-iconoclast theological consensus, worshipped — they were venerated as windows onto the saints they depicted, as channels through which the divine reached into the human world.
After the iconoclast crisis, this distinction was understood and cherished.
Byzantium had decided, definitively, that the divine could be touched, and that touching it through the medium of paint and wood was a normal part of being a Christian.
The empire would face fresh disasters in the next chapter — a fiscal collapse, a battlefield catastrophe, and a final formal break with Rome.
But its institutions, its city, its theology, its court, its commerce, its monasteries, and its faith had reached a coherent maturity by the early eleventh century.
What followed would gradually erode these things, but they were not lost.
Even in the empire's worst moments, the silk weavers of Thebes were still weaving silk.
The monks of Stoudios were still copying manuscripts.
The icon painters of Constantinople were still producing the small wooden panels that would survive long after the empire fell, and that today fill the world's great museums.
Byzantium produced a civilization whose physical artifacts you can hold in your hand.
That civilization was already in place by the year 1000.

chapters.title: The Slow Crack
sentences: Basil II died on December 15, 1025, in the imperial palace, planning a campaign to reconquer Sicily from the Arabs.
The campaign never sailed.

Within fifty years his consolidated empire had fragmented, its currency was halved, its army was a wreck, and the most prestigious title in Christendom had been transferred from the Roman emperor in Constantinople to whoever was fighting his way to the top of a chaotic court.
This chapter is about the rapid deterioration that turned the strongest medieval state in Europe into a wounded empire begging for outside help by 1071.

It is also about the formal break between the Greek and Latin churches that took place in the middle of that deterioration, in 1054 — an event whose long-term consequences would dwarf its immediate impact.
The deterioration was not military at first.
It was fiscal.
The Macedonian dynasty had run the empire on a strict gold standard.

The nomisma (no-MIZ-mah, the Greek term for the gold solidus, also called the bezant in the West) had been minted at 4.5 grams of essentially pure gold for over six hundred years — an extraordinary monetary stability with almost no parallel in pre-modern history.
Then, around 1030, the gold content of the coin began to slip.
By the 1040s it was about 90% pure.
By the 1050s, 80%.
By the 1060s, 70%.
By the 1070s, around 30%.

The currency that had been the international reserve of the Mediterranean world was now visibly debased, lighter than its old weight, redder in color from the increased copper alloy, less trusted in foreign markets.
Why did the empire debase its currency?
The simple answer is that it was running out of money.

The aristocratic families who had been kept in check by Basil II were now back in control of the imperial court — their fortunes were vast, but the imperial treasury depended on tax revenues from peasant landholders, and the aristocrats had spent the post-Basil years buying up peasant lands, converting tax-paying smallholdings into tax-exempt aristocratic estates worked by tied tenants.
Tax revenue collapsed.
The army, the bureaucracy, and the court still needed to be paid.
Successive emperors filled the gap by reducing the gold content of the coin and using the saved metal to pay their bills.

This worked in the short term and was disastrous in the long term: the debasement broke confidence in the currency, accelerated inflation, hollowed out the army (whose soldiers' pay no longer purchased what it used to), and undermined the empire's standing in international trade.

The aristocratic resurgence had a name: the dynatoi (dih-NAH-toy, "the powerful ones"), the great landed families of Anatolia and the European provinces — the Phokas, Skleros, Doukas, Komnenos, Argyros dynasties that supplied generals, governors, and emperors for the next two centuries.
These families were rich, well-connected, militarily competent, and politically dangerous.
Basil II had spent his life suppressing them.
His successors were either incapable of doing so (because they were not soldiers) or unwilling (because they had married into the same families).
The political instability was theatrical.

Between 1025 and 1081, the empire was ruled by a parade of inadequate emperors, most of whom came to the throne by marriage to the same elderly empress: Zoe Porphyrogennita (ZOH-ee, c. 978–1050), Basil II's niece and the legitimate heir to the Macedonian dynasty.
Zoe was 50 years old when she first married.

She married three times in succession (Romanos III Argyros, who probably murdered her first husband; Michael IV the Paphlagonian, who definitely had Romanos III drowned in his bath; Constantine IX Monomachos, after Michael IV's death), with brief interludes in which she ruled alongside her sister Theodora as joint empresses (the only time in Byzantine history that two women ruled simultaneously in their own right).
Each husband took the throne by virtue of marriage to her.

The third, Constantine IX, was a feckless aesthete who funded the magnificent monastery church of Hosios Loukas in Boeotia (whose mosaics from this period are among the finest surviving Byzantine works) but spent his reign losing border provinces, allowing the army to decay, and presiding over a court culture obsessed with eunuch favorites, theological speculation, and elaborate festivals.
Constantine IX's reign also produced the empire's most influential intellectual: Michael Psellos (PSEL-os, 1018–1078).

Psellos was a scholar, philosopher, and palace insider whose Chronographia is one of the great Byzantine literary works — a memoir of the emperors he served, written in luminous Greek prose, full of psychological observation and dry court gossip.

Psellos was also the chief proponent of a Byzantine revival of Platonic philosophy, an enthusiasm that would worry his more orthodox contemporaries (Plato's pagan metaphysics and Christian theology had been awkwardly co-existing for centuries; Psellos pushed the Plato side harder than was conventional).
His student John Italos would be tried for heresy in the next century for taking the Platonic revival further still.
The intellectual ferment of the late Macedonian period was real and impressive.
It just did not translate into political competence.
While the court drifted, two formal breaks occurred that would shape European history for a thousand years.
The first was the Great Schism of 1054.
The breach between the Roman papacy and the Patriarchate of Constantinople had been building for centuries.
The Photian Schism of the 860s (Chapter 5) had rehearsed the major arguments.
The iconoclast period had driven the papacy into Frankish arms (Chapter 4).

The Filioque clause — the Latin addition to the Nicene Creed stating that the Holy Spirit proceeded "from the Father and the Son" — had been adopted in Frankish liturgy in the eighth century, condemned by Photius in the ninth, and was by the eleventh century the universal practice of the Latin church and a standing grievance of the Greek church (which considered any addition to the original creed of 381 a heretical alteration).

The use of unleavened bread (azymes) in the Latin Eucharist, the Latin requirement of clerical celibacy, the Latin claim of papal supremacy over the universal church — these were the standing differences, and they were getting harder to paper over.

In 1054 the Patriarch of Constantinople, Michael Cerularius (sair-oo-LAH-ree-us), and the papal legate Cardinal Humbert of Silva Candida got into a shouting match over these issues during a diplomatic visit.
The argument escalated.
On July 16, 1054, Humbert marched into Hagia Sophia in the middle of the Divine Liturgy and laid a bull of excommunication against Cerularius and his clergy on the high altar.
Cerularius excommunicated Humbert in return.

Both men, in strict canonical terms, had exceeded their authority — Humbert was acting on a papal commission whose pope (Leo IX) had died three months earlier, while Cerularius's counter-excommunication was a personal act rather than a synodal one.
Neither anathema was formally aimed at the entire opposing church.
But the symbolic impact was enormous.

The Latin and Greek churches had been formally severing communion in the persons of their respective leaders, in the most prestigious church in Christendom, in the middle of the central rite of Christian worship.
Whatever the legal niceties, the schism was now public, theatrical, and irreversible.
Within a generation, the two churches had stopped recognizing each other's sacraments.

By 1100, the Greek and Latin churches had become two distinct Christian communions — communions that have remained divided for nearly a thousand years, despite multiple attempts at reunion (most notably the Council of Florence in 1439, which we will reach in Chapter 11).
The mutual excommunications of 1054 were formally lifted by Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras in 1965, in a Vatican II-era gesture of reconciliation.
The actual schism is still in place.
Catholics and Orthodox can today attend each other's services with mutual respect, but they cannot share communion, and the underlying theological and ecclesiological differences remain unresolved.
The second break came on August 26, 1071, on a high plain near the town of Manzikert (MAN-zih-kert) in eastern Anatolia (modern Malazgirt in eastern Turkey).

The opposing forces were the army of Emperor Romanos IV Diogenes (ruled 1068–1071, the latest soldier-emperor pulled in to fix the empire's military problems) and a large Seljuk Turkic force commanded personally by Sultan Alp Arslan (alp ar-SLAN, "Heroic Lion," ruler of the Great Seljuk Empire).

The Seljuks (SEL-jooks) were a Turkic dynasty originating from Central Asia who had moved into the Iranian world in the early eleventh century, converted to Sunni Islam, and conquered most of Iran, Mesopotamia, and Syria within a generation.
By the 1060s they were raiding deep into Byzantine Anatolia.
Romanos IV's campaign of 1071 was supposed to push them back.
It went catastrophically wrong.
The two armies were comparable in size — perhaps 40,000 men each, though estimates vary.
Romanos's army was a mixed force of regular Byzantine themes, Norman mercenaries, Pecheneg auxiliaries, and Armenian troops — a coalition with mutually suspicious commanders.
Alp Arslan's force was a more cohesive Turkic cavalry army, fighting on terrain it knew well.
The battle began with conventional maneuvering.

Then, at the moment of decision, Romanos's reserve corps under the command of Andronikos Doukas (a member of the rival aristocratic faction) deliberately withdrew from the field rather than support the emperor.
The withdrawal turned the battle into a rout.
Romanos's main army was surrounded and destroyed.
Romanos himself was captured — the first Roman emperor since Valerian eight centuries earlier (Persian Empire Ch 8) to be taken alive on a battlefield.
Alp Arslan treated his captive surprisingly well.

There is a famous (probably apocryphal) exchange between sultan and emperor after the battle: Alp Arslan asks Romanos what he would have done if their positions had been reversed, and Romanos answers, "I would have killed you, or paraded you through the streets of Constantinople." Alp Arslan replies that his own punishment is harsher: "I will release you." The release was strategic — Alp Arslan wanted the empire weakened by a returning emperor whose authority was contested, not destroyed by a power vacuum.
He extracted a peace treaty involving territorial concessions and tribute, and let Romanos go.
The aftermath proved Alp Arslan's calculation correct.
While Romanos was traveling back, the Doukas faction in Constantinople deposed him, blinded him, and installed their own candidate Michael VII Doukas as emperor.
The civil war that followed lasted years.
The peace treaty Romanos had signed with Alp Arslan was repudiated.
Anatolian provincial governors stopped sending tax revenues to the central government.
The frontier collapsed.
Within a decade of Manzikert, Turkic nomads had spread across the entire Anatolian plateau.
The Sultanate of Rum (ROOM, "the Sultanate of Rome") was established at Iznik (the old Nicaea) by 1077, a hundred miles from Constantinople.
It was a Turkic state ruled by the Seljuks of Rum, a junior branch of the Great Seljuk Empire; they took the name "Rum" because they had moved into territory whose inhabitants were Romaioi, Romans.
The cities of central Anatolia — Caesarea, Iconium, Sebasteia, Melitene — fell one by one.
The peasant population, the manpower base of the theme system, was uprooted, scattered, or killed.

The Turkmen nomads who arrived behind the Seljuk armies converted Anatolia from a Greek-speaking, Christian, settled-agrarian region into a Turkish-speaking, Muslim, partly-pastoral one over the next two centuries.
The transformation was not complete; substantial Greek Christian populations remained until the twentieth century.
But the demographic balance had shifted in a way that the empire could never reverse.
Manzikert is the moment that, in retrospect, ended the medieval Byzantine state and began the long Byzantine decline.
It was not the worst military disaster in absolute terms — the loss of Egypt and Syria in the 630s and 640s had been worse in territorial terms.
But Egypt and Syria had been peripheral provinces dominated by Monophysite populations indifferent to imperial fortunes.
Anatolia was the empire's heartland.
Losing Anatolia was losing the manpower base, the recruiting ground, the agricultural base, and the strategic depth that had allowed Byzantium to weather the seventh-century catastrophe.
After Manzikert, the empire was a Balkan state with a few coastal Anatolian footholds.
It was not a Roman empire of the eastern Mediterranean any longer.
It was something smaller, more European, and on a long downward trajectory.
The chaos of the 1070s ended in 1081, when a young general from one of the great Anatolian aristocratic families seized the throne and put a partial brake on the slide.
His name was Alexios Komnenos, he was 24 years old, and he is the subject of the next chapter.

chapters.title: The Komnenian Restoration
sentences: Alexios I Komnenos took the throne on April 4, 1081, in a coup so quick that the soldiers he had bribed to admit him to the city celebrated by sacking the wealthy quarters of Constantinople for three days.
He was a member of the Komnenos family, an Anatolian military aristocratic dynasty that had already produced one short-reigning emperor (Isaac I, 1057–1059) before being pushed aside.
Alexios's mother Anna Dalassene was a politically ferocious woman who had spent the previous decade planning her sons' rise to power.

By the early 1080s Alexios had outmaneuvered his rivals, married into the Doukas family (the rival aristocratic clan, securing political reconciliation through marriage to Irene Doukaina), and assembled the resources to seize the throne.
The empire he inherited was in extremis.
Most of Anatolia was under Turkic occupation.
Robert Guiscard (gee-SKAR), the Norman duke of southern Italy, had landed an invasion force in the Balkans and was advancing toward Thessalonica.
The Pechenegs (PEH-cheh-negz, a Turkic nomadic confederation) were raiding across the Danube.
The treasury was empty.
The army that had fought at Manzikert no longer existed in any meaningful form.
Foreign coin had largely replaced the debased nomisma in domestic transactions, a humiliation for an empire that had supplied the Mediterranean's reserve currency for seven centuries.
Alexios spent the next thirty-seven years — until his death in 1118 — putting the empire back together.
He did this by combining diplomacy, military improvisation, fiscal reform, and a willingness to make distasteful deals with the foreigners his predecessors had alienated.
The Komnenian Restoration is not a recovery of imperial greatness.
The empire that emerged would never again be a major Mediterranean power.
But it would survive, and its survival was Alexios's achievement.
His first move was monetary.

In 1092, after a decade of preparation, Alexios introduced a new gold coin, the hyperpyron (hee-PEER-puh-ron, "super-refined") — a 4.5-gram coin with about 87% gold purity, replacing the catastrophically debased nomisma.
The hyperpyron would not be quite as pure as the old solidus, but it was reliable enough to restore confidence in Byzantine money.

It became the new international currency of the eastern Mediterranean, holding its value for the next two centuries (it would be debased again under Alexios's later Komnenian successors and finally collapse in the thirteenth century, but for the moment it bought Alexios time).
His second move was diplomatic.
In 1082, before the hyperpyron was issued, Alexios made the bargain that would haunt Byzantine commerce for the next century.
He needed naval help against the Norman invasion.
The only naval power with the capacity to provide it was Venice — a small Adriatic city-state that had been a Byzantine vassal for centuries but had grown wealthy and independent through trade.

Alexios offered the Venetians a deal: in exchange for naval support, Venice would receive sweeping commercial privileges throughout the empire — exemption from most Byzantine customs duties, dedicated quarters in Constantinople and other major ports, the right to trade freely in territories where their Byzantine competitors had to pay full tariffs.
The arrangement was enshrined in a Chrysobull (KRY-soh-buhl, "golden bull," an imperial document sealed with a gold seal) issued in 1082.
The Chrysobull of 1082 was the death warrant of Byzantine commercial independence.
The Venetians took the privileges and turned Constantinople into a Venetian-dominated commercial hub.

Within a generation Italian merchants — Venetians, Pisans (granted comparable privileges in 1111 by Alexios's son John II), and Genoese (granted privileges in 1155) — controlled the carrying trade, the long-distance commerce, and most of the high-value commodity trade of the eastern Mediterranean.
Byzantine merchants, paying full tariffs at home while their Italian competitors paid none, were squeezed out of their own markets.
The empire's commercial economy gradually became a tributary of the Italian maritime republics.
The fall of Constantinople in 1204 (Chapter 9) and the ultimate fall of 1453 (Chapter 11) were both carried out by states whose commercial dominance had been handed to them by the Komnenoi.
But in 1082 Alexios needed ships, and the Venetians had ships, and the long-term consequences were a problem for whoever came next.
His third move was the appeal that produced the First Crusade.
By 1095, with the Norman threat handled and the eastern frontier stabilized, Alexios decided to attempt a partial reconquest of Anatolia.
He needed manpower.
The empire's domestic recruiting base was inadequate — Anatolia, the traditional source of theme troops, was under Turkic occupation.
Alexios sent a diplomatic mission to Pope Urban II in March 1095, asking for western mercenary contingents to assist in a campaign against the Seljuks.
What Alexios got back was something he had not asked for.

Urban II, at the Council of Clermont in November 1095, transformed Alexios's mercenary request into a call for a general Christian war of liberation — to recover not just Anatolia but the Holy Land itself, including Jerusalem, which had been under Muslim rule since 638.
Urban offered participants a plenary indulgence (full remission of the temporal penalties for sin).
He framed the campaign as a pilgrimage with weapons.
He called on every Christian capable of bearing arms to "take the cross." The response was overwhelming — far larger than anything Alexios had imagined.
In 1096, three successive waves of crusader contingents converged on Constantinople.

The People's Crusade under Peter the Hermit was the first — a disorganized mass of perhaps 40,000 untrained pilgrims who arrived at Constantinople in summer 1096, were ferried across the Bosporus by a relieved Alexios, and were promptly massacred by the Seljuks within weeks of crossing.

The Princes' Crusade that followed was more serious — armies under Godfrey of Bouillon, Bohemond of Taranto (the son of Alexios's old enemy Robert Guiscard, which was awkward), Raymond of Toulouse, and Hugh of Vermandois.

Each leader and his army arrived separately and was received by Alexios in elaborate ceremony, fed at imperial expense, and required to swear an oath of fealty to the Byzantine emperor — promising to return any conquered territory that had previously been Byzantine.
The crusader leaders found Constantinople bewildering.
The wealth astonished them.
The court ceremony was alien.
The Greek language was incomprehensible.

Alexios's daughter Anna Komnene — born in the imperial purple chamber in 1083, age 13 at the time of the First Crusade — described the crusader princes in unsparing terms: greedy, treacherous, easily provoked, suspicious of every Byzantine kindness.
She would later write the great history of her father's reign, the Alexiad.
Anna's Alexiad, completed around 1148, is one of the great works of medieval historiography and the first major historical work known to have been written by a woman in the European tradition.

It is also a one-sided document — Anna detested the crusaders and never lost an opportunity to record their faults — but it is a near-contemporary account of one of the most consequential moments in medieval history, and it has been a primary source for crusade historians ever since.
The crusader armies crossed into Anatolia in 1097.
They besieged and took Nicaea (the old Byzantine city, now a Seljuk capital), which Alexios then claimed as a Byzantine recovery — to crusader fury, since they had expected to plunder the city.
They marched across the Anatolian plateau, suffering terribly from heat, thirst, and Seljuk harassment.

They besieged Antioch for nine months in 1097–1098, took it after horrific casualties, and then, instead of returning the city to Byzantine control as their oaths required, kept it for themselves — installing Bohemond of Taranto as Prince of Antioch.
Alexios was not amused.
He considered the crusader betrayal of their oath a permanent grievance that justified Byzantine non-cooperation in subsequent crusades.
The crusaders considered Alexios's failure to march to their relief at Antioch a permanent grievance that justified their later treatment of Byzantium.
Both sides were partly right.
Both sides spent the next century and a half nursing the grudge.
In July 1099, the surviving crusader forces took Jerusalem and massacred most of the Muslim and Jewish population.
The Kingdom of Jerusalem was established.
The other crusader states — the County of Edessa, the Principality of Antioch, the County of Tripoli — were carved out from former Byzantine and Arab territory in the Levant and northern Mesopotamia.
The crusaders had achieved their stated goal.

They had also created a network of Latin Christian states in territory the Byzantines considered legitimately their own — and they had set up the structural conflicts that would, over the next century, drive Byzantium and the Latin West into outright war.
Alexios died in 1118.
His son John II Komnenos (ruled 1118–1143, called Kalojohannes, "John the Good") is one of the most quietly impressive Byzantine emperors.

He is also one of the least studied, because he had no Anna Komnene daughter writing his biography and because his reign produced no spectacular failures or successes — just steady, methodical extension of the empire's recovery.

He campaigned almost continuously: against the Pechenegs (whom he destroyed at the Battle of Beroia in 1122, ending Pecheneg power forever), against the Hungarians, against the Serbs, against the Seljuks of Rum, against the crusader states in Cilicia.
He recovered more Byzantine territory in Anatolia, restored Byzantine suzerainty over the Principality of Antioch, and pushed Byzantine forces into the Holy Land itself.
He was on a campaign in Cilicia in 1143 when he was wounded by a poisoned arrow — accidentally, in his own quiver, while hunting boar — and died of the resulting infection.
The accident was so improbable that contemporaries suspected assassination, but no plausible plot has ever been documented.

His son Manuel I Komnenos (ruled 1143–1180) was a more theatrical version of his father — a charismatic, multilingual, aesthetically sophisticated emperor who pursued an ambitious foreign policy on multiple fronts.
Manuel's reign was the high-water mark of Komnenian recovery.
He intervened in Italian politics, attempting to manipulate the German emperor Frederick Barbarossa and the papacy.
He maintained close diplomatic relations with the crusader states.
He patronized Latin court culture, inviting Western knights to Constantinopolitan tournaments — a move that scandalized conservative Byzantines who considered jousting an unseemly western barbarism.
He married a Western princess (Maria of Antioch, of the crusader Antiochene house).
He married his children to Western royals.
The Constantinopolitan court of the 1170s was the most cosmopolitan it had been since Justinian's day.
It was also overstretched.
Manuel's ambitious foreign policy required a level of military and diplomatic activity the empire could no longer easily sustain.
The decisive setback came on September 17, 1176, at the Battle of Myriokephalon (mee-ree-oh-keh-fah-LON, "Place of a Thousand Heads," a mountain pass in southwestern Anatolia).
Manuel had assembled a massive expedition to retake the Anatolian interior from the Seljuks of Rum.
The force was perhaps the largest Byzantine army to take the field since Manzikert.
It was ambushed in the pass by Sultan Kilij Arslan II of Rum, suffered heavy casualties, and was forced to retreat in disarray.
Manuel survived and successfully extracted the surviving force, but the campaign's strategic objective was dead.
The dream of recovering the Anatolian interior — the dream that had animated Byzantine military policy since Manzikert a century earlier — was abandoned.
Manuel reportedly compared his defeat to Manzikert in his subsequent communications with the western powers; he was not exaggerating.
After Myriokephalon, Anatolia was permanently Turkic.
Byzantium would never again seriously attempt to reclaim it.
Manuel died in 1180, leaving the throne to an eleven-year-old son, Alexios II.

The regency was managed by Manuel's western widow Maria of Antioch and her favorite Alexios Komnenos (a different Alexios from the boy emperor — a cousin), and it provoked widespread Greek resentment of Latin court influence.

In 1182 a coup brought to the throne the most colorful and most disastrous of the Komnenian emperors: Andronikos I Komnenos (ruled 1183–1185), a cousin of Manuel I, a man who had spent most of his life in spectacular adventures across the medieval world.

He had escaped prison, hidden among Turks, romanced the wife of the Antiochene prince, fathered children by his own niece, contracted a Western dynastic marriage for his teenaged son — and so on for sixty-five years.
He had finally returned to Constantinople in his old age determined to take the throne.
Andronikos's coup was bloody.
He arranged the murder of the regent Alexios.
He had Maria of Antioch strangled.
He married the eleven-year-old Alexios II's twelve-year-old French widow Agnes of France (forty-five years his junior).
He then strangled Alexios II personally.

Once on the throne, he turned on the wealthy Constantinopolitan elite, executing aristocrats, confiscating estates, and pursuing fiscal reforms that would have helped the imperial treasury if they had not been carried out with such public cruelty that they made him universally hated.
The single most consequential act of his reign came before his coup.

In 1182, during the regency unrest, the population of Constantinople had risen up and massacred the Latin merchant community — perhaps 60,000 Italians (mostly Pisans and Genoese), killed or sold as slaves over the course of several days, with Latin priests singled out for particular cruelty.
The massacre was a delayed reaction to a century of resentment over Italian commercial privileges.
It was also a permanent stain on Byzantine relations with the Italian republics, who would not forget.
The pogrom of 1182 is one of the immediate causes of the Fourth Crusade two decades later.

Andronikos's reign ended in September 1185 when a Norman invasion fleet from Sicily took Thessalonica (with great brutality, sacking Byzantium's second city in retaliation for the 1182 massacre), and the Constantinopolitan populace, already terrorized by Andronikos's purges, rose against him.

He was caught fleeing the city, dragged back, and lynched in the Hippodrome over the course of three days — his eyes gouged out, his right hand cut off, his teeth pulled, his skin peeled, his body hacked apart by the same crowd that had cheered his coup three years earlier.
He was the last Komnenian emperor.
His death is sometimes cited as the moment the Byzantine state lost its final reservoir of legitimacy.
The dynasty that had restored the empire after Manzikert had ended in mob justice.
The aristocracy was leaderless.
The Latin west was furious.

The next twenty years of Byzantine history would be a blur of weak emperors from the Angelos dynasty (Isaac II, Alexios III), losing territory, losing money, losing competence, until the climactic disaster of 1204.

chapters.title: The Catastrophe of 1204
sentences: In April 1204, Christian crusaders from western Europe stormed the walls of the largest Christian city in the world, sacked it for three days, and destroyed in a single week more of the surviving heritage of classical antiquity than any other event between the burning of the Library of Alexandria and the Reformation.
They carried off mountains of gold and silver, looted churches, melted down bronze statues for coinage, raped nuns in their convents, and installed a Latin emperor on the throne of the Romans.
The city would not be Greek again for fifty-seven years, and it would never again be what it had been.
The Fourth Crusade is one of the strangest events in medieval history.
It started as a campaign to liberate Jerusalem and ended as a campaign to install a Catholic emperor in Constantinople.
It was carried out by Christians against Christians, in violation of explicit papal prohibition, with the Latin and Greek churches in nominal communion at the time.
It happened because of a chain of contingencies, miscalculations, and outright frauds, with each step seeming locally rational and the cumulative outcome catastrophic for everyone involved.
Here is how it happened.

In 1198 the new Pope Innocent III called for a Fourth Crusade to recover Jerusalem (which had been retaken by the Muslim sultan Saladin in 1187, in a campaign that destroyed the original Kingdom of Jerusalem and gave rise to the Third Crusade — the unsuccessful one with Richard the Lionheart and Frederick Barbarossa).
The strategic plan was to attack Egypt first, since Egypt was the wealthy core of the Ayyubid sultanate and a victory there would force Ayyubid concessions in the Holy Land.
Egypt could only be reached by sea.
The crusaders, mostly French nobles led by Boniface of Montferrat, contracted with Venice to provide transport ships for the expedition.
The contract — negotiated by the doge Enrico Dandolo in 1201 — committed the crusaders to pay 85,000 silver marks for ships sufficient to transport 33,500 men and 4,500 horses.
The crusaders did not show up in the numbers they had promised.
When the expedition assembled at Venice in summer 1202, perhaps a third of the projected force was present.
The crusaders could not pay the contracted price for the ships they had requested.

Dandolo, who was 90 years old and blind but politically formidable, presented the crusaders with an ultimatum: they could not leave Venice without paying, but he would reduce the debt if they helped Venice retake the Adriatic city of Zara (modern Zadar in Croatia), which had recently rebelled against Venetian control and was now under the protection of the King of Hungary — a Catholic king who had himself taken the cross.
The crusaders agreed.

The Pope was furious — attacking a Catholic city under crusader protection was an explicit violation of crusade vows — but his condemnation arrived too late to prevent the storming of Zara in November 1202.

Innocent III excommunicated the entire crusade and then, when the practical implications dawned on him, conditionally lifted the excommunication for everyone except the Venetians (who he held primarily responsible).
The crusade was now operationally compromised but technically still in progress.
While the crusaders wintered at Zara, a Byzantine prince showed up offering them a deal.
Alexios IV Angelos was the son of the deposed and blinded Byzantine emperor Isaac II Angelos (who had been overthrown by his brother Alexios III in 1195).

The young Alexios had escaped to the West and was now offering the crusaders 200,000 silver marks, 10,000 troops for the Egyptian campaign, the submission of the Greek church to Rome, and a permanent garrison of 500 Byzantine troops to maintain the Latin Kingdom of Jerusalem — all in exchange for crusader assistance in restoring his father (and himself as junior co-emperor) to the Byzantine throne.

The deal was structurally absurd — Alexios had no resources to make any of those payments, and his proposed coup against Alexios III was politically delusional — but it solved the crusaders' immediate cash flow problem, and Boniface of Montferrat had personal ties to the Angelos family that made the proposal seem more credible than it should have.
The crusader leaders accepted.
In June 1203 the crusader fleet arrived off Constantinople.
The city was still the largest in Christendom, ringed by the Theodosian Walls (which had repelled every assault for eight centuries) and the sea walls along the Golden Horn and the Sea of Marmara.

The Byzantine navy was a wreck — Andronikos I had let it decay decades earlier, and successive emperors had relied on Italian fleets for everything important — but the city was still apparently impregnable.
Alexios III, the reigning emperor, mismanaged the crisis comprehensively.
He refused to negotiate.
He failed to defend the harbor chain across the Golden Horn (the Venetian fleet broke through and entered the inner harbor).
When the crusaders launched their first major assault in July 1203, his army did not engage.
Within weeks Alexios III had panicked, taken what gold he could grab, and fled the city.
The blinded Isaac II was retrieved from his prison and reinstated.
His son Alexios IV was crowned as co-emperor.
Now Alexios IV had to pay what he had promised.
He could not.
The Constantinopolitan treasury did not contain 200,000 marks.

Greek attempts to raise the money — including melting down church plate, levying special taxes, and forced loans from the aristocracy — produced perhaps half the contracted amount and unleashed widespread popular fury.
Alexios IV's government became increasingly unpopular as winter set in.
The crusader army camped outside the city demanded payment.
Riots broke out in the city.
In late January 1204 a Greek nobleman named Alexios Doukas Mourtzouphlos ("Bushy-Eyebrows") seized the throne, strangled Alexios IV, and let Isaac II die of fright.
The new Alexios V Mourtzouphlos repudiated the agreement with the crusaders.
The crusader leaders held a council in March 1204.
They resolved that since the Greeks had broken their agreement, the only remaining option was to take Constantinople by storm and install a Latin emperor.

The deal among the crusader leaders divided the future spoils in advance: a Latin emperor would be elected by an electoral committee, three-quarters of the loot would be split between the Venetians and the French crusaders to settle the contract, and the territory of the empire would be partitioned among the leading crusaders.
The assault began on April 9, 1204.
The crusaders did not attack the land walls — those had never been breached and were probably not breachable.
They attacked the sea walls along the Golden Horn, where Venetian ships armed with siege ladders could pull alongside the wall towers.
The first day's assault failed.
The crusaders regrouped, renewed the attack on April 12, and broke through near the Petria Gate.
Alexios V Mourtzouphlos fled the city.
By nightfall on April 12, organized Greek resistance had collapsed.
The crusaders entered Constantinople.

What followed was three days of systematic looting that contemporaries — including the Greek bishop and historian Niketas Choniates (nih-KEE-tas khon-ee-AH-teez), an eyewitness — described in horrified detail.
The great churches were stripped of their gold and silver liturgical implements.
Tombs were opened and their occupants' jewelry torn from their bodies.
The bronze monuments of the Hippodrome — including the famous Lysippus Hercules, the Heracles by Lysippos — were melted down for coinage.
The four bronze horses that had decorated the spina were carted off to Venice, where they still stand atop the Basilica of San Marco (the originals are now indoors; replicas are visible from St.
Mark's Square).
Hagia Sophia was looted of its silver iconostasis, its gold lamps, its ceremonial vestments.
A prostitute was placed on the Patriarch's throne and made to sing obscene songs.
Niketas Choniates fled the city in disguise and recorded what he had seen, as a primary source whose horror is, even nine centuries later, undimmed.
The damage was permanent.
The accumulated wealth and artistic patrimony of nine centuries of Byzantine civilization was largely destroyed in three days.

What was not melted down was carried off as relics and treasure to western European cathedrals, where some of it survives — the Crown of Thorns now in Notre-Dame in Paris, fragments of the True Cross in Limburg Cathedral, the Pala d'Oro altarpiece in St.
Mark's Venice, all of these were Constantinopolitan loot.
The Byzantine state lost its capital, its dynasty, its treasury, and its cultural inheritance simultaneously.
The crusaders elected Baldwin of Flanders as the new Latin Emperor of Constantinople.
The Latin Empire would last from 1204 to 1261.
It controlled Constantinople and its hinterland, parts of Greece, and a network of Italian-administered ports.

The crusader contingents seized lordships across the former Byzantine territory: the Duchy of Athens (under the de la Roche family), the Principality of Achaea in the Peloponnese (under the Villehardouin family), the Triarchy of Negroponte (Euboea, divided among Venetian families).

Venice itself took the lion's share — Crete, Modon and Coron in the Peloponnese, the Cycladic islands, and a quarter of Constantinople itself, including Hagia Sophia (which was converted to a Latin Catholic cathedral).
The empire that Justinian had imagined as the universal Christian state was now a patchwork of Frankish lordships and Italian colonies.
Greek resistance reformed in three exile states.
The Empire of Nicaea was established in 1204 by Theodore I Laskaris (las-KAR-is, son-in-law of Alexios III), centered on Nicaea in northwestern Anatolia.
Theodore I and his son-in-law and successor John III Doukas Vatatzes (vah-TAT-zeez, ruled 1221–1254) made Nicaea the most successful of the exile states.

John III was a sober, methodical ruler who built up agricultural self-sufficiency (he reportedly issued chickens and grain to peasant villages to encourage food production), invested in domestic textile industries, restored a competent army, and gradually pushed the Latin Empire out of Asia Minor.

Under his rule Nicaea became the de facto Byzantine state — recognized by most of the Orthodox world as the legitimate successor, with the Patriarchate of Constantinople reestablished in Nicaea and continuing to consecrate Greek bishops as if from the original see.

The Empire of Trebizond (TREB-ih-zond, on the Black Sea coast of northeastern Anatolia) was founded in 1204 by Alexios I Megas Komnenos and David Komnenos, grandsons of Andronikos I, with Georgian backing.

Trebizond was a smaller state with a maritime focus, ruled by the Grand Komnenoi dynasty for the next two and a half centuries — outlasting Constantinople by eight years before falling to Mehmed II in 1461.
Trebizond's culture was distinctively its own, a Byzantine fragment that had developed its own court traditions, its own historiography, and its own foreign policy.
The Despotate of Epirus (eh-PYE-rus, in northwestern Greece and southern Albania) was founded by Michael I Komnenos Doukas, an illegitimate cousin of Alexios III.

Epirus had a brief moment of greatness under Theodore Komnenos Doukas (ruled 1215–1230), who recovered Thessalonica from the Latin Empire and crowned himself emperor — claiming to be the legitimate Byzantine ruler in opposition to the Nicaeans.
Theodore's claim collapsed when he was captured by the Bulgarians at the Battle of Klokotnitsa in 1230, after which Epirus became a regional power without imperial pretensions.
The recovery of Constantinople was carried out by Michael VIII Palaiologos (pah-lay-oh-LOH-gos, ruled 1259–1282 as Byzantine emperor, 1261 onward in Constantinople).
Michael was an Anatolian aristocrat from the Palaiologos family who had served as a general under John III Vatatzes and had risen to be regent for the boy emperor John IV Laskaris in 1258.
In December 1258 Michael arranged his own elevation as senior co-emperor; in 1261 he completed the political transition by having the eleven-year-old John IV blinded and shut away in a monastery.
The reconquest of Constantinople itself was almost an accident.
On July 25, 1261, a Nicaean force under the general Alexios Strategopoulos had been sent on a small reconnaissance mission near Constantinople.
Strategopoulos discovered through local contacts that the city's Latin garrison had been mostly evacuated to attack a Venetian rival in the Black Sea, leaving the walls almost undefended.

He led his small force — perhaps 800 men — through a postern gate at night, took the city without significant resistance, and welcomed Michael VIII to the Byzantine capital fifteen days later, on August 15, 1261.
The Latin Emperor Baldwin II fled to western Europe to spend the rest of his life trying to organize a counter-crusade that never materialized.
The recovered capital was a wreck.
Constantinople in 1261 was a city of perhaps 35,000 inhabitants — down from at least 400,000 before 1204.
Whole neighborhoods were depopulated.
Churches were in ruins.
The aqueducts had been sabotaged.
The harbor walls were collapsed.

Hagia Sophia, when Michael VIII entered it for his triumphal coronation, was a stripped Catholic cathedral missing most of its gold mosaics, its silver iconostasis, its furniture, and its liturgical vessels.

Michael VIII spent the rest of his reign — twenty-one more years — trying to consolidate the recovered empire and prevent western European powers from organizing a second crusade to retake Constantinople.

The most dangerous threat came from Charles of Anjou, the brother of King Louis IX of France, who had been installed as King of Sicily in 1266 and who spent the 1270s assembling an alliance to invade Byzantium.
Michael's diplomatic response was layered.

He concluded the Union of Lyons in 1274 — a formal reunion of the Greek and Latin churches under papal supremacy, opposed by virtually the entire Greek clergy and population, but useful as a tool for keeping the Pope from blessing Charles's invasion.
He funded a Sicilian rebellion against Charles in 1282 — the Sicilian Vespers, a successful uprising that destroyed Charles's invasion plans by removing the staging base.
The Union of Lyons was repudiated by Michael's son Andronikos II immediately after Michael's death, but the diplomatic gambit had worked: Constantinople had survived the immediate post-1261 crisis.
But the empire that Michael VIII left to his son in 1282 was a shadow.
It controlled Constantinople, parts of western Anatolia, parts of Thrace, and the southern Greek mainland.
It had no functioning navy.
Its army was substantially mercenary.
Its treasury depended on Italian merchant presence for tax revenue.

The Anatolian frontier was crumbling — by the 1280s, Turkic emirates were emerging across the old Nicaean territories, and one of them, an obscure principality on the northwestern Anatolian frontier ruled by a chieftain named Osman, would by the next generation be calling itself the Ottoman Beylik.
The Byzantine restoration after 1261 had recovered the ceremonial form of empire.
It had not recovered the substance.

chapters.title: Palaiologan Twilight
sentences: The last two centuries of the Byzantine Empire are the slowest collapse in medieval history.
After the recovery of 1261, the empire kept getting smaller, weaker, and poorer.
Its emperors traveled across Europe as supplicants.
Its generals lost battles to opponents whose grandfathers had been raiding herders.
Its theologians wrote brilliant works while the territories they wrote in were incrementally swallowed up by Ottoman expansion.

And yet — this is the strange thing about the Palaiologan period — Byzantine high culture experienced one last efflorescence in these decades, producing some of the most original Greek writers, painters, and theologians since late antiquity.
The empire was dying creatively at its peak.

This chapter covers the period from Michael VIII's death in 1282 to the eve of the Ottoman siege of 1422 — about a hundred and forty years of contraction, civil war, theological controversy, and a precarious diplomatic dance between the Latin West, the Slavic Balkans, and the rising Turkic powers of Anatolia.

Michael VIII's son Andronikos II Palaiologos (ruled 1282–1328) was a learned, pious, fiscally cautious emperor who happened to be in charge during one of the worst possible moments in Byzantine history.
He inherited a state with a ceremonial empire and a real budget shortfall.
His response was to cut spending.
The single most consequential cut was the dismantling of the Byzantine navy — Andronikos II saved money by laying up the imperial fleet and contracting maritime defense to Genoese mercenaries.
The decision had immediate consequences and long-term ones.

The immediate consequence was that the Genoese, paid to protect Byzantine shipping, used their position to dominate Black Sea and Aegean commerce — establishing a fortified colony at Galata (the district of Constantinople across the Golden Horn from the imperial city, which became a Genoese walled enclave with its own laws, its own taxes, and its own fleet, all explicitly outside Byzantine sovereignty).
The long-term consequence was that Byzantium permanently lost the capacity to defend itself by sea.
Every Byzantine emperor after Andronikos II had to ask Italians for naval help.
The other major Andronikos II disaster was the Catalan Company.

In 1303, with the Anatolian frontier collapsing under Turkic pressure, Andronikos hired a force of about 6,500 Catalan and Aragonese mercenaries — the Almogavars, veterans of the Sicilian Vespers wars, commanded by the unstable Roger de Flor — to push back the Turks.
The Catalans were spectacularly effective in their first campaign, breaking Turkic siege lines and recovering territory.
They were also impossible to control.
They demanded enormous wages, plundered the Byzantine countryside they were supposed to be liberating, and got into murderous quarrels with their Byzantine sponsors.
In April 1305, Andronikos's son and co-emperor Michael IX arranged the assassination of Roger de Flor at a banquet.
The Catalans took this as license for open war.

They sacked Thrace and Macedonia for the next four years — the so-called Catalan Vengeance — and finally moved south, seized the Duchy of Athens from its Frankish ruler in 1311 at the Battle of Halmyros, and ruled it as the Catalan Duchy of Athens for the next seventy-seven years.
The empire had succeeded in pushing one foreign occupier off its territory only by hiring another and then losing control of him completely.
Then came the civil wars — and this is where the empire signed its eventual death warrant.

The single most consequential decision of the entire Palaiologan period was made by a Byzantine claimant during one of these civil wars, when John Kantakouzenos invited the Ottomans across the strait into Europe to fight on his behalf.
The Ottomans came, won the war, and then refused to leave.
Every detail of the genealogical complexity that follows is in service of one outcome: a Byzantine emperor handed the Turks their permanent European foothold, and the empire never recovered from it.
Track who is fighting whom if you can; if you can't, just hold onto that single fact.

Andronikos II's grandson Andronikos III rebelled against him in 1321, kicking off seven years of intermittent civil war that destroyed what was left of imperial finances and dragged Bulgarian and Serbian armies into Byzantine domestic politics.

Andronikos III finally won in 1328, reigned competently until 1341, and then died at age 45, leaving the throne to his nine-year-old son John V Palaiologos under the regency of John's mother Anna of Savoy and the senior nobleman John Kantakouzenos.
The regency arrangement collapsed within months.

Kantakouzenos and the regency council fell out, and the dispute escalated into the Byzantine Civil War of 1341–1347 — a six-year conflict that did the empire more damage than any external war since 1204.
The civil war was simultaneously a dynastic dispute (regency vs.

Kantakouzenos), a class conflict (rural aristocracy vs. urban populist movements, with the Zealot revolutionary government taking control of Thessalonica from 1342–1349 in a remarkable experiment in popular government), and a theological dispute (about which more in a moment).
The fighting drew in Bulgarians, Serbs, and — most consequentially — Ottomans.
It was during this civil war, in 1346, that Kantakouzenos invited Ottoman mercenaries from the emir Orhan to fight on his behalf.
Kantakouzenos married his daughter Theodora to Orhan as part of the alliance.
The Ottoman troops crossed into Europe to support Kantakouzenos's faction — the first Ottoman armies to fight on European soil.
They returned to Anatolia after their initial campaigns, but the precedent had been set.
In 1352 Kantakouzenos called them back for a renewed civil war.
This time they did not fully leave.
In 1354 a major earthquake destroyed the walls of the Byzantine fortress at Gallipoli on the European side of the Dardanelles.
Orhan's forces, conveniently nearby, occupied the ruined fortress and refused to give it back.
The Ottomans had their permanent foothold in Europe, and they had it because a Byzantine emperor had hired them, married into them, and called them across the strait twice.
The empire had handed its eventual conquerors a bridgehead.
The civil war also destroyed the empire economically.
The currency was debased again and again.
The army was in tatters.
The Italian merchant communities — Genoese in Galata, Venetian in their own enclave — extracted more privileges in exchange for emergency loans.

By the time Kantakouzenos finally took the throne as John VI in 1347 (and then graciously stepped aside in 1354 to retire as a monk and write his own apologetic history of the war), the empire he had won was not worth winning.
The same year John VI took the throne, the Black Death arrived in Constantinople.
The Black Death was the second great plague pandemic — the same disease (Yersinia pestis, bubonic plague) that had caused the Plague of Justinian eight centuries earlier (Chapter 2).
The Constantinopolitan outbreak of 1347 killed between a third and half of the city's surviving population.
The empire's already collapsed tax base contracted further.
Repeated plague outbreaks over the following decades kept the population suppressed.
The Black Death was the worst demographic catastrophe in Byzantine history.
The civil war was tangled with one of the most distinctive theological controversies in late medieval Christianity: Hesychasm (HESS-ih-kazm).
Hesychasm was a contemplative monastic practice — derived from the Greek hesychia, "stillness" — that had been developing on Mount Athos for centuries.
The practice involved silent prayer (the Jesus Prayer: "Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me"), repeated continuously, often coordinated with breathing.

Advanced practitioners reported that this practice could produce visions of an uncreated divine light — the same light that the disciples Peter, James, and John had seen at Christ's Transfiguration on Mount Tabor, according to Hesychast theology.
The light was not a physical phenomenon nor a metaphor; it was, the Hesychasts argued, a direct experience of the uncreated energies of God.
This claim provoked a storm.

A Calabrian Greek monk named Barlaam (BAR-lahm) attacked Hesychasm as superstitious and theologically incoherent — God's essence is unknowable to created beings, Barlaam argued, and any claim to direct experience of God's light was either a hallucination or heresy.
The Hesychast response came from Gregory Palamas (PAL-uh-mass, c. 1296–1359), a Mount Athos monk who would become Archbishop of Thessalonica.

Palamas developed a sophisticated distinction between God's essence (ousia, fully transcendent and unknowable) and God's energies (energeia, the activities and operations through which God interacts with creation, knowable to humans through grace).
The uncreated light was an energy, not the essence — and direct experience of the uncreated energies was therefore both possible and theologically orthodox.

The Hesychast controversy ran through the 1330s and 1340s, intersected with the civil war (Kantakouzenos was a Hesychast supporter, the regency tended Barlaamite), and was finally settled in Palamas's favor at a series of councils at Constantinople in 1341, 1347, and 1351.
Palamism became official Eastern Orthodox doctrine.
Palamas himself was canonized in 1368, less than a decade after his death.
The intellectual stakes here are larger than they might appear.
Palamism resolved one of the deepest tensions in Christian theology — between God's transcendence and God's accessibility — in a way that would shape all subsequent Eastern Orthodox spirituality.
The Western Catholic and Protestant traditions did not adopt the essence-energies distinction, and it remains one of the defining theological differences between Eastern and Western Christianity.

The contemplative Hesychast tradition Palamas defended also became the dominant spiritual practice in Russian, Romanian, and Greek monasticism, producing a continuous lineage of spiritual writers — most famously the eighteenth-century compilation called the Philokalia — that remains the heart of Orthodox spiritual practice today.
That all of this happened during the worst political collapse in Byzantine history is one of the strangest features of the Palaiologan period.
The empire was dying.
The theology being produced inside it was as ambitious and as influential as anything in the Christian tradition.
Outside the theological sphere, the empire's political deterioration accelerated.
In 1331 the Anatolian city of Nicaea — the empire's wartime capital from 1204 to 1261, the city of the First and Second Ecumenical Councils — fell to Sultan Orhan of the Ottomans.
The fall of Nicaea was a profound symbolic blow.
The empire that had taken its name from the city for half a century had now lost it permanently to the Turks.
Andronikos III had attempted to relieve the city in 1329 at the Battle of Pelekanon (peh-leh-kah-NON, on the southern shore of the Sea of Marmara) and had been defeated by Orhan personally.
Pelekanon ended any realistic Byzantine hope of reconquering northwestern Anatolia.
By 1340 the Ottomans had taken Nicomedia (NI-koh-MEE-dee-ah, the old eastern capital under Diocletian, the city where Constantine had died — modern İzmit) and most of the Bithynian coast.
The empire's Anatolian provinces were reduced to a handful of coastal footholds.

The other major external threat was the Serbian Empire under Stefan Dušan (DOO-shan, ruled 1331–1355), a brilliant Serbian king who exploited the Byzantine civil war to expand Serbian rule across most of the Balkans — taking Macedonia, Albania, Epirus, and parts of Thessaly, and crowning himself "Emperor of the Serbs and Greeks" in 1346.
Dušan's empire briefly rivaled Byzantium itself in extent and was, by the 1340s, the major power of the southern Balkans.

He died unexpectedly in 1355 at age 47, possibly poisoned, and his empire fragmented within a few years — but his reign had permanently broken Byzantine control of the southern Balkans, and the Serbian successor states that emerged from his death were weak enough that they could not effectively resist Ottoman expansion either.
In 1369 the Ottomans took Adrianople (modern Edirne in European Turkey) and made it their new capital.

Adrianople had been a Byzantine city for over a thousand years — site of the disastrous Roman defeat by the Visigoths in 378 (Ancient Rome Ch 9; how a starved and cheated refugee nation destroyed a Roman field army and changed the empire's relationship with barbarian peoples is told in the Goths narrative), of the major Bulgarian victory over Krum's army in 813, of countless other Byzantine military campaigns.
Its loss meant that the Ottomans now controlled the entirety of Thrace except for Constantinople itself.

The empire was reduced to its capital, a few coastal cities (Thessalonica, briefly recovered for the empire in the 1370s), and a few exclaves in Greece (the Despotate of the Morea, in the Peloponnese, ruled by Palaiologan princes).
Constantinople was a Byzantine island in an Ottoman sea.
In 1389 the Ottoman victory at the Battle of Kosovo over the Serbs eliminated Byzantium's last potential Balkan ally.
The Bulgarian state had already been destroyed (Tarnovo fell to the Ottomans in 1393).
The Byzantine emperor became, in formal terms, an Ottoman vassal — required to pay tribute, provide troops for Ottoman campaigns, and travel to the sultan's court when summoned.
This was the most humiliating arrangement in nine centuries of Byzantine sovereignty, and it was the price of Constantinople's survival.
A small intellectual aside before this chapter ends.
The Palaiologan period produced, despite its political miseries, an extraordinary cultural renaissance.

Demetrios Kydones (kih-DOH-neez, c. 1324–1398) was an imperial minister and translator who rendered Thomas Aquinas's Summa Theologiae into Greek — opening Latin scholastic theology to Byzantine readers and provoking a generation of Greek engagement with Western philosophy.

The mosaics and frescoes of the Chora Church in Constantinople (now the Kariye Mosque, restored to mosque status in 2020) were completed in the early fourteenth century under the patronage of Theodore Metochites and represent the artistic peak of Byzantine icon painting — sophisticated, emotionally intense, technically brilliant.
The historian John Kantakouzenos, after his abdication, wrote a four-volume history of his own civil war that is one of the most readable late Byzantine works.

The philosopher Nikephoros Gregoras wrote a contemporary Roman History covering 1204–1359 that, despite being a defeated Barlaamite polemic, contains essential historical information available nowhere else.
And in the 1390s, in the Despotate of the Morea, the most original Byzantine philosopher of the late Middle Ages began his career: Gemistos Plethon (PLEH-thon, c. 1355–1452).

Plethon was a Platonist who pushed the Byzantine engagement with classical philosophy further than anyone before him — eventually proposing, late in life, a return to a reformed version of Greek polytheism as the basis for a renewed Hellenic civilization.
His more conventional contemporaries considered him a crypto-pagan.

His later influence on Italian Renaissance Platonism — through his appearance at the Council of Florence in 1439 and his impact on the young Cosimo de' Medici, who would found the Florentine Platonic Academy on his account — would be enormous (Chapter 12).
Plethon is one of the strangest figures in Byzantine intellectual history, and one of the most consequential bridges between the Byzantine and Renaissance Italian worlds.
The empire's last reprieve came from an unexpected direction.

On July 28, 1402, at the Battle of Ankara in central Anatolia, the Ottoman sultan Bayezid I ("the Thunderbolt") was decisively defeated by Tamerlane — Timur (TEE-moor, c. 1336–1405), the Turkic conqueror who had built a vast empire stretching from Anatolia to India and was now sweeping through the Anatolian heartland.
Bayezid was captured and died in captivity the following year.
The Ottoman state fragmented into a civil war among Bayezid's sons that ran from 1402 to 1413, with each son claiming the sultanate from a different city.
For Byzantium, Tamerlane's victory was an unexpected gift.
The pressure on Constantinople collapsed.
The Byzantines, who had been on the verge of being besieged in 1402 — Bayezid had been preparing the assault — were suddenly safe for the first time in two generations.

Emperor Manuel II Palaiologos (ruled 1391–1425), who had spent the years 1399–1402 traveling through western Europe (Venice, Paris, London) trying to drum up military support against the Ottomans (and being received with respectful sympathy but no concrete aid), returned to a city that had been spared by an entirely external event.

Manuel II's tour is itself a striking piece of Byzantine history — the Roman emperor traveling as an honored guest through cities that had once been Roman provinces but were now sovereign states whose rulers he had to flatter for favors.
He spent Christmas 1400 at the court of Henry IV in London.
He was painted in his imperial robes by an English manuscript illustrator.
He met scholars across Italy and France.
He returned having extracted nothing concrete but having impressed the Latin West with the dignity and erudition of the dying empire.
Tamerlane died in 1405.
The Ottoman civil war ended in 1413 with the victory of Mehmed I (1413–1421), who reconsolidated the Ottoman state.
By 1422 his son Murad II had besieged Constantinople for the first time.
The siege failed — the Theodosian Walls held, as they always had — but it was the first time in nearly a century that the Ottomans had directly assaulted the imperial city.
The reprieve was over.
The next siege would be the final one.

chapters.title: The Last Hundred Years and the Fall
sentences: The empire's last half-century is the most thoroughly documented period of its history.

Eyewitness accounts of the final siege of 1453 survive in remarkable abundance — Greek chronicles, Italian merchants' diaries, Ottoman annals, Spanish military reports — and the events have been picked over by historians for five and a half centuries.
What follows is the conventional outline, briefly extended where the documentary record is particularly rich.
The fall of Constantinople is one of those events where the actors knew, at the time, that they were participating in a historic catastrophe.
The contemporaries who wrote about it described it as the end of an age.
They were not exaggerating.

Whether you take 1453 as the symbolic end of the Middle Ages, the real end of the Roman Empire, the start of the Renaissance, the start of the Age of Exploration (the closure of the eastern Mediterranean to European Christian shipping was a major motivation for Iberian exploration of the Atlantic in the late fifteenth century), or simply the disappearance of a particular medieval Christian civilization that had been continuously present since 330 CE — every framing has its merits, and they are all true at once.
This chapter is the story of how it happened.
Manuel II's son John VIII Palaiologos (ruled 1425–1448) inherited a diminished and frightened empire.

The 1422 siege had failed, but Murad II had subsequently taken Thessalonica (in 1430, after a long Venetian-administered defense) and had reduced Byzantine territory to Constantinople, the Despotate of the Morea, and a few coastal exclaves.
John VIII spent his reign on a single strategic gamble: securing western military aid by submitting the Greek church to Roman papal authority.
This was the Council of Florence, held intermittently between 1438 and 1445 (originally convened at Ferrara, then moved to Florence due to a plague outbreak).
It was the most ambitious church council since Chalcedon nearly a thousand years earlier.

The Greek delegation included Emperor John VIII himself, Patriarch Joseph II of Constantinople, the leading Byzantine theologians (including Bessarion of Trebizond, who would become the most consequential Greek scholar in Renaissance Italy, and Mark of Ephesus, who would lead the resistance to union), and the elderly Plethon, who attended as a court philosopher and used his time in Florence to give lectures on Plato that would profoundly influence Cosimo de' Medici.
The theological negotiations were conducted in good faith.
The Greeks and Latins discussed the Filioque clause, papal supremacy, purgatory, the use of unleavened bread in the Eucharist, and several smaller points of difference.
They reached a series of compromises that the Greek delegation signed at the formal Decree of Union on July 6, 1439.

The decree affirmed papal supremacy ("the Roman pontiff is the successor of Peter, prince of the apostles, and true vicar of Christ"), accepted the Filioque as an orthodox formulation in either creed, and acknowledged the Catholic doctrine of purgatory.
Mark of Ephesus refused to sign.
The Greek populace, when the delegation returned to Constantinople, refused to accept the union.
The leading anti-unionist theologian George Scholarios (later Patriarch Gennadios II) preached against it.

The famous quip — attributed (probably apocryphally) to the Byzantine grand admiral Loukas Notaras — captured popular sentiment: "Better the Sultan's turban in the city than the Cardinal's mitre." The Greek clergy, except for the bishops who had personally signed in Florence, refused to commemorate the Pope in their liturgies.
The Union of Florence became dead letter within a few years of being signed.
The price the Greeks were supposed to receive was western military aid.
They received some — Pope Eugene IV organized a crusade in 1443–1444 led by the Polish-Hungarian king Vladislav III and the Hungarian general John Hunyadi.

The crusade made initial progress in the Balkans but was destroyed by the Ottomans at the Battle of Varna on November 10, 1444 — Vladislav was killed, the crusader army shattered, and any prospect of large-scale European military intervention against the Ottomans evaporated.
The Union had been signed without producing the promised aid.
The Greeks had compromised their religious autonomy for nothing.
The unionist cause was now hated by the Greek population while the empire remained as exposed as before.
Murad II died in February 1451.
He was succeeded by his nineteen-year-old son Mehmed II — the man who would take Constantinople.
Mehmed II is one of the most studied conquerors in medieval history.

He was extraordinarily intelligent, extensively educated (fluent in Turkish, Arabic, Persian, Greek, and Hebrew, with serious interests in Greek philosophy, geography, and military engineering), ruthless, ambitious, and from the moment of his accession committed to one specific goal: the conquest of Constantinople.
His grandfather Bayezid I had besieged it.
His father Murad II had besieged it.
