His own first reign — he had briefly held the throne as a teenager from 1444–1446 before being pushed aside by his father — had ended in part because he had been considered too inexperienced to attempt the siege.
Mehmed had returned to the throne determined to finish what his ancestors had started.
His preparations took two years.

He built a fortress called Rumeli Hisarı (roo-MEH-lee hee-SAH-ruh, "the European Castle") on the European side of the Bosporus in 1452, opposite an existing Ottoman fortress on the Anatolian side, sealing the strait between the Black Sea and Constantinople — meaning that no grain could reach the city from the Black Sea ports without Ottoman permission.

He commissioned a Hungarian engineer named Orban to cast the largest cannons the world had ever seen — bronze monsters firing stone balls weighing up to 1,200 pounds, requiring teams of sixty oxen to move them.
The largest, called the Basilica, had a 27-foot barrel and could throw a stone ball nearly a mile.
Orban had originally offered his services to the Byzantines, who could not pay his price; he had then approached Mehmed, who could.
Mehmed assembled an army of perhaps 80,000 to 100,000 men.
He assembled a fleet of perhaps 100 to 150 ships.
He had the new gunpowder weapons.
He had time — the Hungarians, the Venetians, and the Pope were all distracted by their own concerns and would not provide major aid.

The defenders inside Constantinople numbered perhaps 7,000 men, including 700 Genoese mercenaries under Giovanni Giustiniani Longo, a Genoese soldier of the Lomellini family who had volunteered to come and fight — bringing his own troops at his own expense — in what he correctly understood as the great Christian cause of the age.
Other Italian volunteers swelled the total.
The Byzantine citizen militia could perhaps add a few thousand more.
The Theodosian Walls and the Golden Horn chain were the empire's last assets.
The emperor was Constantine XI Palaiologos (ruled 1449–1453), John VIII's brother, who had been Despot of the Morea before being summoned to Constantinople on his brother's death.
Constantine XI was an experienced soldier, a personally brave man, and — perhaps most importantly — a recognizable figure of dignity in a moment that demanded one.
He had inherited an impossible task.
He performed it with a kind of doomed integrity that has made him the most legendary of Byzantine emperors.
The siege began on April 6, 1453.
For fifty-three days the Ottoman army and fleet pressed against the city.

The cannons hammered the Theodosian Walls at multiple points, opening breaches that the defenders desperately repaired with rubble, earth, and bundled timber overnight, only to have the same breaches opened again the next day.

The Ottoman fleet, blocked by the Golden Horn chain (a great iron chain stretched across the harbor mouth from Galata to the imperial city, supported by floating logs), tried to force the entrance and was beaten back by Greek fire and superior Christian seamanship.

In an extraordinary feat of engineering on the night of April 22, Mehmed's engineers built a greased wooden ramp over the hill behind Galata and dragged seventy ships overland into the upper Golden Horn, neutralizing the chain and adding a new front to the siege.
The defenders had to spread their already-thin manpower thinner.

The pivotal events of the siege are well-documented in eyewitness accounts: Nicolò Barbaro, a Venetian surgeon and ship's officer who kept a daily diary of the siege, recorded the cannon fire, the failed assaults, the morale of the defenders, the desertions, the flares of hope and despair.
His account is dry, practical, and detailed.

George Sphrantzes (sfrant-ZEEZ), Constantine XI's secretary and lifelong friend, survived the fall and wrote the Memoirs — a Byzantine chronicle of the last decades that includes intimate details of life inside the besieged palace.
Sphrantzes was an unusually reliable witness; his account of the emperor's last days has been the basis for every subsequent treatment.
Leonard of Chios, a Latin archbishop present in the city during the siege, wrote a letter to Pope Nicholas V immediately after escaping that summarized the fall in considerable tactical detail.
Leonard was hostile to the Greek defenders (he considered them inadequately committed to the union of 1439) and his account is biased, but it is contemporary.
Tursun Beg, a young Ottoman official who was present, wrote a Turkish chronicle of Mehmed's reign that includes a sympathetic Turkish-side account of the siege.
These sources are largely consistent on the major facts.
Constantinople was running out of men, ammunition, food, and morale.
The walls were breaking down faster than they could be repaired.

The Genoese in Galata maintained an officially neutral stance — declining to fight on either side openly — while clandestinely passing information and supplies to both sides, an approach that infuriated everyone involved.
The Italian volunteers and the Greek defenders fought together with surprising solidarity given the deep unionist-anti-unionist tensions of the previous decades.
Constantine XI personally rotated through the threatened sections of the wall, encouraging the defenders, sleeping in armor, eating what his men ate.
The siege had become an endurance contest that the Byzantines were slowly losing.
The final assault came on the night of May 28–29, 1453.
Mehmed had been planning a single concentrated attack to overwhelm the exhausted defenders.
The assault began about an hour before dawn on the 29th.
The first wave of irregular Ottoman troops — the bashi-bazouks, expendable forces sent in to wear down the defense — was thrown against the walls and largely destroyed.

The second wave of Anatolian regulars achieved a partial breach but was repelled by Giustiniani's Genoese counterattack at the Saint Romanus Gate — the section of the walls where the most concentrated cannon damage had occurred and which had become the primary point of pressure.
Then the Janissaries went in.
The Janissaries (yan-iss-AIR-eez) were the elite Ottoman infantry corps and Mehmed's personal guard — his last and best assault force.

They were recruited through the devshirme system: Christian boys from Balkan villages were taken from their families, converted to Islam, given specialized military training, and made to serve as the sultan's personal slave-soldiers.
The system produced extraordinarily disciplined and fanatically loyal troops.
Led by the sultan in person, they pressed through the breach, encountered exhausted defenders, and broke them.
The decisive moment, according to the eyewitness accounts, was the wounding of Giovanni Giustiniani Longo.

Hit by an Ottoman bullet in the chest, Giustiniani gave the order for his Genoese troops to evacuate him to the inner walls — a decision that, in the chaos of the assault, was taken by other troops as a general retreat.
The Greek defenders, seeing the Italians fall back, broke also.

Constantine XI rode to the breach personally to try to rally them, was unable to hold the line, and — according to legend, which is consistent with several eyewitness accounts though no one survived who actually saw it — threw off his imperial purple robes and rushed into the press of Ottoman troops to die fighting as a common soldier.
His body was never definitely identified.
There have been periodic later "discoveries" of imperial remains that have all been disputed.
The most likely truth is that Constantine XI was killed in the breach, his body stripped and lost in the general slaughter.
The Ottomans poured into the city.
Resistance collapsed.
The Hagia Sophia, full of refugees praying through the night, was broken open.
The men were killed or taken as slaves; the women and children sold.

Mehmed had ordered three days of plunder by custom but cut it short to one day on the evening of May 29 itself — his troops had become uncontrollable, and he wanted to preserve as much of the city as possible for his new capital.
He rode to the Hagia Sophia in the late afternoon and ordered the building consecrated as a mosque.
The first Islamic prayers in the cathedral were performed on Friday, June 1, 1453.
The Byzantine Empire was over.

A few details from the immediate aftermath, since they came up in earlier chapters and deserve closing: The grand admiral Loukas Notaras, the leading Byzantine official who survived the siege, was initially treated honorably by Mehmed and offered a position in Ottoman service.
He refused.
He was executed several days later, along with his sons, after a series of incidents whose exact nature is disputed.

Bessarion, who had signed the Florence Union and converted to Catholicism, settled in Italy as a cardinal, founded an important academy of Greek studies at his home in Rome, and donated his great library of Greek manuscripts to Venice — the Biblioteca Marciana, which still holds thousands of Byzantine texts that would otherwise have been lost when Constantinople fell.
George Scholarios, the leading anti-unionist, was named Patriarch Gennadios II by Mehmed himself a few months after the conquest.

Mehmed wanted a stable Greek Orthodox church in his new capital and considered the unionist faction discredited; the anti-unionist Scholarios was the obvious candidate to head the surviving Christian institutions under Ottoman rule.
Trebizond, the last remaining Byzantine successor state, fell to Mehmed in 1461.
Its ruler, David Komnenos, was executed with most of his family.
The line of the Grand Komnenoi was extinguished.
The Despotate of the Morea, ruled by Constantine XI's brothers Demetrios and Thomas Palaiologos, fell to the Ottomans in 1460.
Thomas escaped to Italy with his children.

His daughter Zoe Palaiologina (later renamed Sophia) eventually traveled north and married Grand Duke Ivan III of Moscow in 1472 — a marriage that gave the Russian princes a credible claim to the Byzantine inheritance and that supplied them with the Byzantine double-headed eagle as the symbol of the Russian state, which is still on the Russian flag today.
The empire was gone.
The story of what came after — the cultural, religious, and political afterlife of Byzantium — is the subject of the final chapter.

chapters.title: The Inheritance
sentences: When something dies after eleven hundred and twenty-three years, it does not disappear cleanly.
The Byzantine Empire's physical territory was erased from political maps in May 1453.

Its institutions, its texts, its art, its religion, its political ideas, and a substantial fraction of its population continued to exist — in Ottoman territory under new management, in Italy as Greek refugees, in Russia and the Slavic Orthodox world as the senior partner in a shared faith, in Western Europe as a recovered classical inheritance newly available to scholars who had never been able to read it.
This chapter is about the afterlife.

It is shorter than the others because most of it has been alluded to throughout the book — every chapter has been pointing at the empire's eventual disappearance and its eventual influence on the world that followed.
What this chapter does is collect those threads into one place.
Byzantium did not so much fall as scatter.
The fragments are still around us.
Start with the Greek scholars in Italy.
The fall of Constantinople accelerated a migration that had been happening for decades.

From the Council of Florence in 1438–1439 onward, Byzantine scholars had been traveling to Italy in increasing numbers — sometimes for diplomatic missions, sometimes to teach Greek to Italian humanists, sometimes as religious refugees fleeing Ottoman expansion.
After 1453 the trickle became a flood.
Scholars who had survived the siege escaped to Italy with whatever manuscripts they could carry.
Byzantine families that had cultivated Greek scholarship for generations relocated to Florence, Rome, Venice, Padua, Ferrara.
The cumulative impact on Italian culture was enormous.
Italian humanists had been recovering Latin classical literature for two centuries — that was the Renaissance as it had existed up to 1450.
But Greek had been functionally inaccessible.
Plato existed in fragmentary Latin paraphrases.
Aristotle existed in Latin translations from Arabic translations from Greek originals.
The major works of Greek philosophy, drama, history, poetry, and theology had not been read in the Latin West since the early Middle Ages.
The Byzantine refugees brought the originals, knew the language fluently, and were willing to teach.
The figures involved are well-known to historians of the Renaissance.
Manuel Chrysoloras (kris-oh-LOH-ras, c. 1355–1415) had taught Greek in Florence as early as 1397 and trained the first generation of Italian Greek scholars.

Bessarion (Chapter 11), now Cardinal Bessarion, established a Greek manuscript collection in Rome that became the largest in the West and donated it to Venice on his death — over six hundred manuscripts, the foundation of the modern Biblioteca Marciana, preserving texts that would otherwise have been lost.

Gemistos Plethon, attending the Council of Florence as an old man, gave lectures on Plato that so impressed Cosimo de' Medici that Cosimo founded the Florentine Platonic Academy under Marsilio Ficino, which translated Plato's complete works into Latin for the first time and produced the Renaissance Neoplatonism that would shape European philosophy for the next two centuries.
John Argyropoulos (ar-jeer-OH-poo-los) taught Greek at the universities of Florence and Rome.
Demetrius Chalcondyles edited the first printed edition of Homer in 1488.

Aldus Manutius, the Venetian printer, employed Cretan Greek refugees to produce the Aldine editions of the Greek classics in the 1490s and 1500s — the books that gave the rest of Europe its first reliable access to Plato, Aristotle, Sophocles, Euripides, Aristophanes, Thucydides, and the other foundational Greek texts.
The standard claim that the fall of Constantinople "caused" the Renaissance is too strong — the Italian Renaissance had its own deep roots, and the recovery of Greek was already underway before 1453.
But the Byzantine refugees of the 1450s and 1460s accelerated and shaped that recovery.

They brought the manuscripts, the linguistic competence, and the philosophical traditions that turned the Italian Renaissance into a serious engagement with Greek thought rather than a mostly-Latin enterprise.
The Byzantine scholars who fled the dying empire were the indispensable middlemen of one of the largest cultural transmissions in European history.
The second major inheritance was religious.
The Eastern Orthodox Church survived the fall.
Mehmed II, with characteristic political acumen, recognized that the Greek population of his new capital and his Balkan territories needed continued ecclesiastical leadership.

He appointed George Scholarios as Patriarch Gennadios II in 1454 and granted him civil authority over the Christian populations of the empire — an arrangement called the Rum millet (the "Roman community," using Rum in its Ottoman sense as a designation for the Greek Orthodox Christians).

Under the Ottoman millet system, the Patriarch of Constantinople became the head of an autonomous Christian community within the Ottoman state, with jurisdiction over religious affairs, family law, education, and most internal matters of the Greek population.

The Patriarchate continued to function in Constantinople — operating from new premises since the Hagia Sophia was now a mosque — and it continued to function as the senior see of the Eastern Orthodox communion.

This Ottoman-era patriarchate was the institutional vehicle through which Greek Orthodox identity, language, and culture survived the centuries between the fall and the Greek War of Independence in 1821.
The Patriarchate was politically constrained, financially squeezed, and periodically harassed by Ottoman administration, but it kept functioning.

It maintained the liturgical traditions, the canonical texts, the educational institutions, and the historical memory of Byzantium under conditions where independent Greek political existence was impossible.

When modern Greek nationalism emerged in the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, it drew its sense of continuity directly from the Patriarchate — the institutional bridge between the Byzantine past and a modern Greek future.

The patriarchates of Antioch, Alexandria, and Jerusalem — the other ancient Eastern Orthodox sees — had continued under Muslim rule since the seventh century and continued under Ottoman rule afterward.
They formed, with Constantinople, the four ancient Eastern patriarchates of the Greek-speaking Orthodox world.

Their existence and continuity meant that Eastern Orthodoxy — distinct from both Roman Catholicism and Protestant traditions — survived as a major Christian communion through the post-Byzantine centuries.
The third inheritance was Russian.

The marriage of Zoe Palaiologina to Grand Duke Ivan III of Moscow in 1472 (Chapter 11) gave the Muscovite princes a credible claim to the Byzantine succession at the moment when Russian territorial expansion and political consolidation were beginning in earnest.
Ivan III adopted the double-headed eagle as the symbol of the Russian state.
He took to using imperial Byzantine ceremonial protocols at his court.
His grandson Ivan IV (Ivan the Terrible) took the title Tsar — the Russian form of Caesar — in 1547 in a self-coronation explicitly modeled on Byzantine imperial ritual.
The Patriarchate of Moscow was established in 1589, with Constantinople's reluctant approval, formalizing Russia's claim to be an autocephalous (independent) Orthodox church.

The doctrine that Moscow was the Third Rome — first formulated by the monk Philotheus of Pskov in a letter to Grand Duke Vasily III around 1510 — became central to Russian political-religious identity.
The argument went: the first Rome had fallen to barbarians and heresy in the fifth century.
The second Rome (Constantinople) had fallen to Turks because of the Greek capitulation to Catholicism at the Council of Florence.
The third Rome was Moscow, the last surviving seat of true Orthodox Christianity, the rightful heir of the imperial Christian tradition.

"And a fourth there shall not be." The argument shaped Russian political and religious self-understanding from the sixteenth century onward, and it surfaced repeatedly through the imperial period — every time a Tsar claimed the right to intervene in Balkan or Middle Eastern politics on behalf of Orthodox Christians, the Third Rome argument was somewhere in the background.
The Russian Orthodox Church — the largest of the modern Orthodox churches — is, in this sense, the institutional descendant of Constantinople.

Its liturgical practice, its theology, its monastic tradition (much of it transplanted from Mount Athos via the medieval Russian monasteries), its iconography, and its self-understanding all derive directly from Byzantium.
The same is true, in different proportions, of the Romanian, Bulgarian, Serbian, Ukrainian, and Georgian Orthodox churches.
Roughly a quarter of a billion Christians in the world today belong to churches that trace their religious inheritance directly to medieval Constantinople.
The fourth inheritance was Ottoman.
This is the inheritance Western Europeans have been most resistant to acknowledging, but it is real and substantial.
Mehmed II was an admirer of Byzantine institutions.
He preserved the Patriarchate, the millet system, the city's basic administrative geography, and many of its trade relationships.
He kept Hagia Sophia standing rather than demolishing it.
He commissioned the historian Critobulus of Imbros to write a history of his own conquests in classical Greek, modeled on Thucydides.
He patronized Italian Renaissance painters (the famous portrait of Mehmed by Gentile Bellini, made on commission in 1480, was the first realistic European portrait of an Ottoman sultan).

He saw himself, plausibly, as the legitimate heir of the Roman imperial tradition — taking the title Kayser-i Rûm ("Caesar of Rome") and treating Constantinople as the natural seat of his expanding empire.
The Ottoman state that grew out of Mehmed's conquests retained many Byzantine features.
The administrative geography — the sanjaks and provinces — followed Byzantine themes in their broad outlines.
The agricultural taxation system inherited Byzantine surveys and assessment practices.
The Greek Orthodox clergy continued to perform functions for the Greek population that Byzantine clergy had performed before.

The Ottoman court ceremony, while heavily influenced by Persian and Turkic precedents, also borrowed from Byzantine protocols — particularly in the elaborate reception of foreign ambassadors, where the Ottoman ceremony of the elevated throne and the silent corps of officials owed something to the Byzantine machinery of intimidation.

The classical Ottoman style of mosque architecture — exemplified by the works of Mimar Sinan (mee-MAR see-NAHN) in the sixteenth century — was a direct descendant of Hagia Sophia, with its central dome on pendentives, its half-domes on the four sides, and its ring of windows lighting the interior.

The Süleymaniye Mosque (1557) and the Selimiye Mosque in Edirne (1574) are not just Hagia Sophia's children; they are arguably its best children, more rationally laid out, structurally more sophisticated, more elegantly proportioned.
Sinan was working in a tradition Anthemius and Isidore had founded ten centuries earlier.

The Greek-speaking population of Anatolia and the Balkans continued to live in Ottoman territory, often in the same villages and cities they had inhabited before the conquest, often speaking the same Greek dialects, often worshipping in the same churches under the new millet arrangement.
The Ottoman conquest was not a population replacement.
It was a change in management, with substantial continuity at the local level.

By the time the Ottoman Empire itself collapsed in the early twentieth century, the Greek population of Anatolia had been there continuously for nearly three thousand years — through Hittites (Hittite Empire Ch 8), Phrygians, Lydians, Persians, Alexander, the Hellenistic kingdoms, Romans, Byzantines, Seljuks, and Ottomans.
The Greek-Turkish population exchange of 1923 — when 1.2 million Greeks were expelled from Anatolia and 400,000 Turks from Greece — was the final, brutal end of that continuity.
The fifth inheritance was legal.

Justinian's Corpus Juris Civilis — the codification of Roman law that had been completed in 534 (Chapter 2) — became the foundation of European civil law in a process that began in the late eleventh century and continued through the early modern period.
The rediscovery of the Digest at Bologna around 1070 launched the medieval revival of Roman law.
The Bologna law school became the major center of legal education in medieval Europe.
Italian civilians (lawyers trained in the Justinianic tradition) taught at every European university in the late Middle Ages.

The codified legal systems of France, Germany, Spain, Italy, the Netherlands, Quebec, Louisiana, Latin America, and Japan all derive — through complex chains of transmission — from Justinian's commission.

The English-speaking common law tradition is the major exception to this pattern, and even it has been substantially influenced by Roman law concepts (much of the law of contracts, trusts, and equity has Roman roots, and several common-law jurists trained on the continent imported Justinianic principles directly).

Most of the world's legal systems today — every system except the common law and the various Islamic, Confucian, and traditional African and Asian systems — descend from a project initiated by an emperor in Constantinople fifteen hundred years ago.
The empire is gone.
The law it codified is the operational legal system of about half the planet.
The sixth and most diffuse inheritance is iconographic.
Western European Christian art, particularly Roman Catholic art, drew constantly on Byzantine models from the early Middle Ages onward.

The development of devotional images of Christ, the Virgin, and the saints in Western Europe followed Byzantine iconographic conventions for centuries — the seated Theotokos and Child, the Crucifixion, the Last Supper, the Pantocrator, the standard saint poses, the gold backgrounds.
Italian altarpieces of the late medieval and early Renaissance period (Cimabue, Duccio, the early Giotto) are deeply indebted to Byzantine icons.

The transition from "Italo-Byzantine" to specifically Italian Renaissance painting — beginning with Giotto in the early fourteenth century — was a transformation of an existing Byzantine pictorial tradition rather than its replacement.
The iconographic traditions of the Eastern Orthodox world remained closer to their Byzantine origins.
The icons painted in seventeenth-century Russia or twenty-first-century Greece follow recognizably the same conventions as the icons painted in twelfth-century Constantinople.
The painters worked from manuals derived from Byzantine treatises.
They used the same gold backgrounds, the same gesture vocabulary, the same color symbolism.
Eastern Orthodox liturgical visual culture is a continuous tradition stretching from Justinian's Constantinople to today.
This is the inheritance most casual visitors notice without realizing it.
Anyone who walks into a Greek or Russian Orthodox church in the modern world, anywhere in the world, sees a visual environment that was set by Byzantine artists more than a thousand years ago.
The aesthetic survives the death of the political state that produced it.
What did Byzantium leave us?
A city that is still standing.
A mosque-cathedral that is still operational.
A book of laws that became the law of half the world.

A church that is still holding services in a language that is now the academic specialty of a few thousand scholars but was once the everyday language of one of the great civilizations of human history.
A diplomatic tradition that taught Western Europe how to conduct business with foreigners.
A monastic tradition that survives unchanged on Mount Athos and in countless other Orthodox monasteries from the Aegean to Alaska.
A textual inheritance — Plato, Aristotle, Sophocles, the New Testament, the Greek Fathers, the Souda — without which the European intellectual tradition would be unrecognizable.
An iconographic vocabulary that still defines what religious art looks like for hundreds of millions of people.

A claim about the relationship between divinity and matter — the Incarnation, defended at Nicaea, defended at Chalcedon, defended at the Triumph of Orthodoxy in 843, defended at the Hesychast councils in the fourteenth century — that has shaped Christian theology for two thousand years.
There is also, finally, an idea.

Byzantium spent eleven centuries demonstrating that a multilingual, multiethnic, multidoctrinal Christian state was possible — that Roman institutions, Greek language, and Christian religion could be combined into a single durable polity governed by law and tied together by a shared imperial identity that did not depend on a single ethnic group or a single linguistic community.
The empire absorbed Slavs, Armenians, Goths, Bulgars, Norse, Anglo-Saxons, Arabs, Jews, and dozens of other peoples into its administration, its army, its church, and its cities.
It did not always do this gracefully.
It often did it badly.

But it did it, for an extraordinarily long time, and the institutional template it left behind — that universal Christian empire could be a real political form, not just a theoretical aspiration — shaped the imperial ambitions of the Holy Roman Empire, the Russian Empire, the Habsburg Monarchy, and (in inverted form) every modern European nation-state that has had to define itself against the Byzantine model.
The empire fell on May 29, 1453.
The civilization is still here, scattered across Greek monasteries and Russian cathedrals and Italian libraries and Turkish mosques and the legal codes of two-thirds of the world.
The Byzantines, who were nothing if not stubborn, would probably consider that survival a partial victory.
The empire that had refused to die for eleven centuries had finally been killed.
But it had not stopped being inherited.
The Romans who never stopped calling themselves Romans had won the only kind of victory their long defeat allowed them.
Their world was over.
Its inheritance was permanent.

chapters.title: The World Before the Raids
sentences: The horned helmet is a 19th-century opera invention.
Start with that, because it is the single most important fact about the Vikings that almost everyone gets wrong.

The fearsome, bull-horned helmet that Wagner's costume designer Carl Emil Doepler put on the heads of his Ring Cycle singers in 1876 has nothing to do with anything anyone wore in the North Sea between 793 and 1066 CE.

There is exactly one intact Viking-era helmet known to archaeology — the Gjermundbu helmet (YEHR-mund-boo), found in a Norwegian grave from the tenth century — and it is a plain iron skullcap with an eye-guard and a pointed crown.
Horns on a battle helmet would catch sword strokes and rotate the helmet sideways to break the wearer's neck.
Anyone who has ever swung a stick knows this.
Doepler did not consult any sailors.
He consulted a stage director.
The point is not pedantry.
The point is that the actual Vikings — the people who actually lived this story — are more interesting than the costume.

They were farmers who became sailors who became raiders who became settlers who became kings who became, eventually, the Russians, the Normans, the Icelanders, and a chunk of the genome of every English-speaking person reading this.
They reached Baghdad.
They reached Newfoundland.
They sold each other's relatives in slave markets that stretched from Dublin to Damascus.
They wrote poetry so technically dense that scholars still argue about how to translate it.

They named one of their kings Harald Bluetooth (his teeth weren't actually blue — the nickname blátǫnn may refer to a dark dead tooth, or to a hereditary discoloration, or to a misreading of an old word for "dark-skinned"; nobody knows), and a millennium later the Swedish engineers who invented short-range wireless networking named the protocol after him because he had unified Denmark and Norway the way they were trying to unify computers and phones.
The Bluetooth logo on every device on earth is a bind-rune of Harald's initials in the Younger Futhark alphabet.
This is the world we are walking into.

It is more peculiar than the cartoon, and it is darker than the cartoon, and it ends with a Norman duke (himself a great-great-great-grandson of a Viking) winning the Battle of Hastings on a Saxon hilltop in October 1066, four hundred miles south of the coastal monastery where the whole thing started.
Before we go any further: a caveat.
"First" in early-medieval history means "first surviving evidence of." The Viking Age was a literate age in a region that was overwhelmingly oral.
The people we are about to meet wrote in runes, on stone and wood, in short formal inscriptions; they did not keep tax registers or court chronicles.

Most of what we know about them comes from three kinds of sources: their victims (Christian monks who wrote in horror about being raided), their trading partners (Arab travelers and Byzantine bureaucrats), and themselves at one remove — the Icelandic sagas, which are prose narratives composed in the 12th and 13th centuries about events that had happened two or three hundred years earlier.
The sagas are wonderful and they are also, in places, fiction.
The archaeology is wonderful and it is also full of holes.
Some of what we think we know about the Vikings is wrong.
We don't always know which parts.
The setting is Scandinavia, the long northern peninsula that separates the North Sea from the Baltic.
Today it holds Denmark (the flat, low country at the southern end), Sweden (the long forested middle), and Norway (the mountainous, fjord-cut Atlantic coast).

Those three are Scandinavia proper (the North Germanic core, with closely related languages and a shared Norse descent), and they are not the same thing as the Nordic countries, a wider grouping that also takes in Finland and Iceland.

The distinction matters here because Viking-Age Finland was Finnic (a different language family and a different people, Finno-Ugric rather than Norse) and sits largely outside this story, even though Swedish traders and raiders worked its coast.
In the 700s CE these were not countries.
They were patchworks of small kingdoms, free farms, and forested pagan backlands, governed by chieftains whose authority rested on personal loyalty and the redistribution of plunder.

The total population of all three regions was probably around 1.5 to 2 million people — about the population of modern Phoenix, Arizona, spread over a region roughly the size of Texas plus California.
The geography shaped everything.

Norway is a wall of mountains falling straight into the sea, fractured by long deepwater inlets called fjords (FYORDS, drowned glacial valleys carved by Ice Age ice and never refilled by sediment), and the only flat land is in narrow strips along the coast and at the heads of the fjords.
You cannot grow wheat there reliably.
You can grow oats and barley and you can keep cattle and sheep and you can fish, and that was the life of an ordinary Norwegian farmer.
Denmark is the opposite: low, flat, sandy, the rolling glacial moraine of Jutland and a sprinkle of large islands (Zealand, Funen, Bornholm) commanding the entrance to the Baltic.
Denmark could grow more grain than Norway, which is why Denmark would become the political center of the Viking world.
Sweden sits between, a vast country of pine forest and lake systems, looking east toward the Baltic and the Russian river network rather than west toward the Atlantic.
The climate was, for once, on their side.

The period from roughly 950 to 1250 CE is called the Medieval Warm Period (MWP), a stretch of mild northern temperatures that opened sea lanes and lengthened growing seasons across the North Atlantic.
Iceland was actually warm enough to grow some barley.
Greenland's coastal margins genuinely were green in summer.
The pack ice retreated.
Storms were no kinder than usual but the navigable season was longer, and the kind of long-distance ocean voyage that would have killed everyone in the year 600 was achievable by the year 900.
The Vikings were lucky in their century.
Their descendants in Greenland, who would be ground out by the colder Little Ice Age in the 1300s and 1400s, would be unlucky in theirs.
The basic unit of Norse society was the longhouse.

A longhouse is exactly what it sounds like: a long, narrow, single-room building, typically 50 to 100 feet (15–30 m) long and 15 to 20 feet (5–6 m) wide, with thick earthen walls, a peaked timber-and-turf roof, and a long central hearth running down the middle.

Cattle and people often lived under the same roof, with the animals at one end and the family at the other — body heat from the cattle helped warm the human end during the worst of the winter, and the cattle benefited from being indoors rather than dead in a snowdrift.
There were no chimneys; smoke rose to the rafters and seeped out through gable openings.
There were almost no windows; the building was lit by the hearth and by oil lamps fed with seal blubber or fish oil.
Inside, on either side of the central hearth, raised wooden platforms ran the length of the room, and these platforms served as bench, table, workbench, and bed.
You sat on them by day, ate on them by night, and slept on them under woolen blankets and animal skins.
Everyone in the household — owner, family, servants, slaves — slept in the same long room.
This is the texture of Viking domestic life.
Smelly (the cattle, the lamps, the unwashed wool, the open fire).
Built to keep the wind out.

A longhouse was a fort against the climate, and a Norwegian winter is a serious adversary: the sun barely rises north of the Arctic Circle in December, temperatures sit below freezing for months, and the prevailing storm pattern is a sequence of Atlantic depressions delivering snow, sleet, and gale-force winds week after week.
A house that did not keep its inhabitants warm was a house full of corpses by spring.
The longhouse worked.
Variants of it would be built across the entire Norse diaspora: in Iceland, in Greenland, briefly in Newfoundland, in the Hebrides, in Yorkshire.
Wherever you find a long earthen rectangle with a central hearth, you are looking at the architectural fingerprint of a Norse household.
The longhouse was also the seat of authority.

A chieftain (Old Norse goði, GO-thee, originally meaning something close to "the man who performs the rites") was a hybrid figure — part secular warlord, part priestly officiant — who hosted the seasonal sacrifices for his region, mediated lawsuits among the free farmers who owed him loyalty, and led them to war when raiding season opened.

The role was hereditary in practice but never sacrosanct: a goði who could not perform the rites well, give out gifts generously, win lawsuits cleanly, or lead a successful raid would lose his following to a rival.

He ran his hall, and the warriors who owed him loyalty came to feast there in the long winter nights, drinking ale and mead from horns, listening to skalds (court poets, Chapter 6) recite verses about ancestors and famous battles.

A chieftain held authority not by coronation but by performance: he was generous (he gave out gifts, weapons, gold arm-rings, slaves), he was successful (he led raids that returned with plunder), and he was personally formidable (he could fight, and he had killed people).
A chieftain who stopped being any of those things was replaced.
Sometimes he was replaced by his son.
Sometimes he was replaced by an axe in the back.
The system was direct.
Above the chieftains, in the larger regions, sat the early kings — but the word "king" in 800 CE Scandinavia meant something much smaller than what it would mean in 1100 CE.
A Norse konungr (KO-nungk, our word "king") might rule a single fjord system, or a cluster of islands, or a portion of Jutland, with revenues that would not impress a Frankish bishop.

Real territorial kingship — the kind where a single ruler controls the entire country and collects systematic taxes — would only arrive in Scandinavia with Christianity and the writing technologies the Church brought with it (Chapters 5 and 7).
Norse society was built on oaths.
There were no written contracts.
There were no notarized property deeds.
There were no police.
What there was, instead, was a dense web of personal sworn loyalty, witnessed by community and by the gods.
A warrior swore an oath of loyalty to his chieftain.
A chieftain swore an oath to his king.
Two parties agreeing to a deal swore the deal in front of witnesses, sometimes with hands clasped over a sacred ring kept on the temple altar.
Marriage was a contract between two families, sealed by oath and bride-price. manumission of a slave was an oath.
Adoption of a son was an oath.
The legal world ran on memorized commitments enforced by reputation and the threat of violence.
Break an oath, and you were níðingr (NEETH-ing-ger) — a person without honor, whom anyone could kill without consequence.

The Norse word for an honorless oath-breaker survived into modern Scandinavian languages and into English in fossil form: an outlaw is someone outside the law — someone whose life is no longer protected by the oath-network of the community.
This is important context for everything that follows, because it explains why Viking armies could function.
A Viking warband was not a state institution.

It was a network of personal oaths radiating out from a war-leader (the war-band, or comitatus, originates in the Iron Age Germanic world; its Vendel-Age Scandinavian form, the hall, the ring-sword, and the sworn retinue, is the subject of the Vendel Age narrative).

Men followed a chieftain because they had sworn to follow him, because he had given them gifts, because he was likely to give them more, and because killing him while their oaths still bound them would mean a permanent loss of standing among everyone who knew them.
The whole structure was social, not bureaucratic.
It bound the warband together more tightly than any payroll ever could, and it dissolved instantly when the chieftain died.
This is also why Viking armies often disintegrated after a victory: the leader had been killed, or he had run out of plunder to distribute, and the oaths went slack.
Now, the central question.
What is a "Viking"?
The word "Viking" describes a thing you do, not a person you are.
This is a crucial distinction that almost every popular source gets wrong.
The Old Norse phrase fara í víking means "to go on a viking" — to go on a raid, an overseas plundering expedition.
A man who did this regularly was a víkingr.
The word may come from the Old Norse vík (a bay, a creek, an inlet), suggesting "the men of the bays" — sailors who lurked in coastal hideouts.
It may come from the Old English wíc (a camp).
The etymology is contested.
What is not contested is that "Viking" was a job description.
The vast majority of people in 800-CE Scandinavia were not Vikings.
They were farmers, fishermen, blacksmiths, weavers, traders, slaves.
They lived in longhouses, milked cows, hauled nets, raised children, and never went to sea in anger.
The Viking minority — the men who went raiding — were a small and seasonal fraction of the population.
A young man might do a season or two of raiding to win a marriage portion and then come home, marry, and farm for the rest of his life.
A wealthy chieftain might lead raids for a couple of decades and then settle down to govern.
The activity was bracketed within a normal agricultural life, not opposed to it.
This is why the modern phrase "Viking culture" is somewhat misleading, the way "pirate culture" would be a misleading way to describe 18th-century Britain.
The Vikings were one (highly visible, highly violent) outgrowth of a broader Norse society that was mostly doing other things.

When we talk about Viking religion, Viking ships, Viking law, Viking poetry, we are really talking about Norse religion, Norse ships, Norse law, Norse poetry — the cultural matrix from which the raiding minority sailed.
The book is conventionally called the Viking Age because the raids are what wrote the Norse onto the world's literary record.
Nobody on the Continent took notice of Norse weaving traditions.
They took notice of Norse fleets coming up the river.
And the fleets are where everything begins, because the Viking Age does not happen without one specific piece of technology.
The longship is the keystone of the entire era.
It is the reason a marginal frontier people on the rim of Christendom suddenly appeared everywhere from Iceland to the Caspian Sea within three generations.
It is the reason the Carolingian and Anglo-Saxon defensive systems failed.
It is the reason the Vikings could reach North America five hundred years before Columbus.
Without the longship, none of the rest of this story happens.
The breakthrough was not invention; it was refinement.
Northern Europeans had been building wooden boats with overlapping plank construction — called clinker-built in English, klinkbygget in Norwegian — for centuries before the Viking Age.
Clinker construction means that each plank of the hull overlaps the plank below it (like clapboard siding on a house), and the planks are riveted together and caulked with tarred wool or animal hair.
The hull this produces is light, flexible, and surprisingly strong.
It bends with the waves rather than fighting them.

A modern fiberglass hull is rigid; a clinker hull flexes, twisting up to several inches across its length in heavy seas, and that flex is the secret to taking a relatively light wooden boat across an ocean.

What changed in the late 700s was the addition of the keel as a deep, structural backbone — a single long timber, sometimes carved from one enormous oak, that ran the entire length of the boat and extended below the waterline as a rigid spine.

The keel did three things at once: it kept the boat tracking straight in the water rather than skidding sideways under sail, it stiffened the hull longitudinally so it could carry a heavy mast, and it allowed the boat to take a square sail.
Earlier northern boats had been rowed (the sailless clinker hull is the burial vessel at Vendel and Valsgärde, and the Vendel Age tells when and how the sail was finally added).
Late-eighth-century longships could be sailed, with rowing as backup for windless days and harbor maneuvering.
A square sail on a deep-keeled clinker hull is the package that made open-ocean voyages possible.

A Viking longship of the classic period — the kind that would attack Lindisfarne, sail up the Seine to Paris, ferry the Great Heathen Army across the North Sea, and reach Iceland — was typically 65 to 100 feet (20–30 m) long, 15 feet (4.5 m) wide, drew only 3 feet (90 cm) of water (which meant it could be beached anywhere with a sloping shore, and could navigate rivers and shallows that no contemporary Mediterranean ship could enter), carried a crew of 30 to 80 men, and could be rowed at about 5–7 knots and sailed at 10–15 knots in good wind.
The hull was so light that the crew could carry the ship overland on rollers between river systems if necessary — a tactic the Rus' would use to portage between the Volga and the Don (Chapter 4).
The ship was fast, shallow, oceangoing, river-capable, beachable, and portable.
No other vessel in the world combined those qualities.
The two great surviving Viking ships found by archaeologists tell the story.
The Oseberg ship (OH-seh-bayr), excavated in 1904 from a burial mound in southern Norway, dates to about 820 and was used as the funeral vessel for two high-status women buried in 834.

It is shorter and lighter than a battle longship — probably a coastal craft, a yacht for a queen — but it shows the technology in flower: a deep keel, a tall mast step, elegant overlapping planks, and prow and stern carved in interlaced animals.

The Gokstad ship (GOK-stad), found in 1880 in another Norwegian burial, dates to about 890 and is a true ocean-going longship: 76 feet (23 m) long, 17 feet (5 m) wide, with a mast amidships and 16 oar holes per side.
A modern reconstruction of the Gokstad ship sailed across the Atlantic in 1893 in 28 days, proving that the technology was up to the job.
The Vikings reached America in this kind of boat.
They did not need anything else.
The longship was not just transport; it was also burial.

Both the Oseberg and Gokstad vessels were funerary deposits — the most spectacular ship burials of the Viking Age — and the Ladby ship in Denmark and a scatter of smaller Norse ship burials show the same pattern: when a great chieftain died, you buried him in a boat.
The ship carried the dead onward, the way it had carried the living to plunder.
The metaphor was not subtle.
One more thing about the longship that gets understated: it was a slave ship.
The slave trade was central to the Viking Age economy.
We will return to this in Chapter 7, when we get to the great Norse commercial centers at Hedeby and Dublin.
For now, the foundational fact: a longship raid was, among other things, a labor-procurement expedition.

When Vikings sacked a coastal village or a monastery, they took portable wealth (gold, silver, vestments, books — the books for their gem-encrusted covers, which they ripped off; the parchment was used to wrap fish), and they took people.
Young men and women, mostly.
The captives were tied, loaded into the boats, fed enough to survive the voyage, and sold at one of the great northern slave markets.
For most of the Viking Age, the largest single market was Dublin (Chapter 3).

For some Norse traders, the slaves went east instead of west, down the Russian rivers, ending in the markets of Constantinople and Baghdad in exchange for the Abbasid silver dirhams (the Islamic-world coinage) that flooded Scandinavia for two centuries (Chapter 4).
The romantic account of the Vikings — the brooding longship slicing through arctic mist, the fierce blue-eyed warrior with his battleaxe — leaves the slaves out.
They are not optional.
The economic system that sustained the raids depended on them.

Roughly a quarter of the population of Viking Age Iceland, by some recent genetic estimates, was descended from women who had originally been Irish and Scottish slaves taken on raids — which is to say, the entire Icelandic founding population was substantially a slave-taking economy made flesh.

The English word thrall (a slave, a person held in bondage) is a direct loan from Old Norse þræll (THRALL), and the Norse legal codes carefully distinguished the rights of free men, freedmen, and thralls.
Slavery was not an embarrassment.
It was a category of property, and it was the category that paid for the gold rings on the chieftain's arm.
So: the world before the raids.
A patchwork of small kingdoms in a region where farming was hard and the sea was easy.
A society organized around the longhouse, the oath, the chieftain's hall, and the warrior's loyalty.
A pagan religious world (Chapter 5) that we will get to.
A climate that was, just then, kinder than usual.

And a single piece of marine technology — the deep-keeled clinker-built longship under square sail — that allowed, for the first time, a small band of armed men to step out of a Norwegian fjord on a spring morning and arrive on the coast of Northumbria a couple of weeks later, fully fed, fully armed, and fully prepared to take whatever they could find.

Cross-civ check: the Viking world that was about to explode (~793 CE) coincides with the Carolingian Empire at its peak under Charlemagne, the Abbasid Caliphate at its high tide in Baghdad under Harun al-Rashid (himself a contemporary of Charlemagne — they exchanged ambassadors), the Byzantine Empire struggling through the Iconoclast controversy, the Tang dynasty in China, the early Heian period in Japan, and the late stages of the Maya Classic period in the Yucatán.
The longship arrived in a connected world.
It was about to make the connections shorter.

chapters.title: Lindisfarne and the Western Raids
sentences: On the morning of June 8, 793, Northumbrian monks at the monastery of Lindisfarne, on a tidal island off England's northeastern coast, saw something they had never seen before: dragon-prowed wooden boats running up the beach.

The chronicler Symeon of Durham, writing about three centuries later from monastic records, describes what happened next in the medieval scriptorial register that makes everything sound slightly more dramatic than it probably was: the heathens "miserably ravaged God's church on Lindisfarne with plunder and slaughter," dug up the altars, killed some of the monks, dragged others into the sea and drowned them, and carried off the rest in chains.
The treasures of the church were stripped.
The relics were desecrated.
And then the boats vanished back into the North Sea as fast as they had come.
In purely military terms it was a small event.
A handful of monks killed, a small island monastery sacked, perhaps a dozen captives taken.
The total monetary value of the plunder was probably less than what a successful Frankish merchant cleared in a year.
But Lindisfarne is the conventional starting date of the Viking Age because of what it meant, not what it took.

Lindisfarne (founded 635 by the Irish monk Aidan, mother house of northern English Christianity, location of the most beautiful illuminated manuscript in Europe — the Lindisfarne Gospels, made around 715) was the most spiritually prestigious site in the Anglo-Saxon north (the Northumbrian golden age and Alcuin's letters of horror are covered in detail in the Anglo-Saxon England narrative; the Vendel-Age society that produced the raiders is the subject of the Vendel Age narrative).
A Raid on Lindisfarne was an attack on the foundational sacred geography of Northumbrian Christianity.
And the raiders had not bargained, had not threatened tribute, had not negotiated.
They had simply turned up out of an empty sea and taken what they wanted.

The Anglo-Saxon scholar Alcuin of York (AL-kwin, ~735–804, an English-born theologian who had moved to the court of Charlemagne and become the leading intellectual of the Carolingian Renaissance) wrote a horrified letter from Charlemagne's court when the news reached the Continent.
"Never before has such a terror appeared in Britain as we have now suffered from a pagan race.
Behold the Church of St.

Cuthbert spattered with the blood of the priests of God, despoiled of its ornaments." Alcuin's letter is the Anglo-Saxon equivalent of the September 12 newspapers: the moment when a literate civilization realized that its assumptions about the geography of safety had been wrong.
The sea, which had always been a barrier, was now a highway, and somebody on the other side was using it.
Why monasteries?

It is worth explaining the target selection, because monasteries were the perfect targets for the kind of force the early Vikings could project, and it is not an accident that most of the early raids hit them rather than secular settlements.
A monastery in 8th-century Britain or Ireland was, in modern terms, a combination bank, art gallery, university, and lightly defended manor house.

Centuries of donations from kings, nobles, and pious commoners had piled up in the form of gold-and-silver liturgical vessels (chalices, patens, reliquaries), illuminated manuscripts bound in gem-encrusted covers, embroidered vestments shot through with gold thread, and stockpiles of food and ale.
The monastery was the most concentrated unit of portable wealth in its region.
And — this is the critical part — it was located, by religious convention, in remote places.
Lindisfarne sat on a small tidal island visible from miles of empty coast.
Iona was on a wind-swept Hebridean isle.
Skellig Michael was a literal Atlantic crag.

The whole architectural premise of early Insular Christianity was that monks should be apart from worldly society, in places where nothing ever happened, where the only neighbors were sheep and seabirds.
This was a wonderful theological choice and a catastrophic strategic choice.

A coastal monastery was undefended (monks were unarmed, by their vows), located precisely where a longship could beach, contained portable concentrated wealth, and could be reached, looted, and exited within the same daylight tide.
It was the eighth-century equivalent of a rural ATM with no security camera.
The Vikings looked at this map and made the obvious calculation.

For three decades after Lindisfarne, raid after raid would work the same playbook: a small fast fleet of two or three longships, an unscheduled landing on a remote stretch of coast, a quick strike on a known monastic target, and a withdrawal before any local force could assemble.
The Carolingians saw it coming and could not stop it.

Charlemagne (Frankish king from 768, Holy Roman Emperor from 800, ruler of an empire stretching from the Pyrenees to the Elbe) ordered coastal defenses and a fleet around 800, but the Carolingian state was a land empire.
It had no navy in any serious sense, no system of coastal watch towers, no warning network.
The empire's military strength was in heavy cavalry and infantry mobilized from its great estates — slow to assemble, slower to deploy.
By the time a Frankish levy had been raised in response to a Viking landing, the Vikings had been gone for three weeks.

The very feature that made the longship deadly — its speed, its shallow draft, its ability to ascend rivers fifty miles inland and then escape on the next tide — was the feature that the existing defensive systems of Latin Christendom had no answer for.
The Carolingian Empire was a cathedral built to withstand siege, not a coast guard.
Two years after Lindisfarne, the raiders hit Iona (eye-OH-nuh) in 795 — the great monastery off the western coast of Scotland founded by St.
Columba in 563, the cradle of Irish-Scottish monasticism, the home of the Book of Kells (which the monks would eventually evacuate to Ireland for safekeeping).
The raid on Iona was repeated.

Vikings came back in 802, in 806 (when 68 monks were killed in a single attack), and finally in 825 — the Second Sack of Iona — when the abbot Blathmac (BLATH-mak) refused to reveal the hiding place of St.
Columba's silver shrine and was tortured to death on the altar.
The original Iona community largely abandoned the island after that and relocated inland to Kells in Ireland.
The Book of Kells went with them, which is why it is called the Book of Kells today, and not the Book of Iona.
The raids escalated in tempo and ambition through the first half of the 9th century.
Hedeby (HAY-deh-bee) in southern Denmark grew explosively in this same period as Norse merchants channeled stolen wealth into a long-distance trade network we will return to in Chapter 7.
The Frankish frontier was nibbled.
Frisian coastal communities (the low coast of what is now the Netherlands) were raided repeatedly in the 810s and 820s.
Birka in central Sweden, founded around 750 and prospering by the 820s, became the eastern counterpart to Hedeby — a Baltic trading hub where Slavic, Frisian, Arab, and Norse goods all changed hands.
In 829, the Frankish missionary Ansgar (AHN-sgar, ~801–865, sent by Emperor Louis the Pious as the first Christian missionary to Scandinavia) sailed to Birka and built a small church there.
The mission lasted, intermittently, for decades and converted very few people, but it was the first serious Christian foothold in Sweden.
The conversion of Scandinavia (Chapter 5) was going to take another two centuries.

In 834, in southern Norway, two high-status women — one elderly, one in her fifties — were buried in the Oseberg ship, which would lie undisturbed in its turf-covered mound for over a thousand years until Norwegian archaeologists excavated it in 1904.

Whether the older woman was a queen, a high priestess, a renowned witch, or all three is unknown. (Her companion may have been a sacrificial attendant — strangled to accompany her into the afterlife, in a pattern echoing the Scythian royal kurgans, Scythians Ch 3.) The grave goods — a sledge with carved animal heads, a four-wheeled wagon, looms, beds, kitchen tools, four ornate dog-sled-style sleighs, and the elegant ship itself — make the burial one of the richest finds of the Viking Age.
The Oseberg ship is not a warship.
It is a court vessel, a yacht, a thing for a great person to be seen in.

It is also, today, the single most important physical artifact for understanding what Viking material culture actually looked like, because organic materials that would normally rot — wood, textiles, leather — were preserved in the waterlogged blue clay of the burial mound.
In 841, a Norse fleet established a permanent fortified beachhead — a longphort in Old Irish — on the south bank of the River Liffey at the mouth of an Irish harbor.
They called the place Dublin (Old Norse Dyflinn, from the Irish Dubh Linn, "black pool," referring to a tidal pool in the Liffey).

Dublin would grow within a century into the largest slave market in northern Europe (Chapter 7) and the political capital of a Norse-Irish kingdom that controlled the central Irish Sea for two hundred years.
Other Norse longphorts followed: Limerick, Waterford, Wexford, Cork.
Pre-Viking Ireland had no cities.
The Vikings built Ireland's first cities, on the coast, with their own walls and their own laws, and the Irish were not consulted.
The peculiar fact is that Ireland's modern urban backbone — Dublin, Cork, Limerick, Waterford, Wexford — is essentially the map of the original Viking longphorts.
These were never Irish creations.
They were Norse trading enclaves planted on Irish soil, and the Irish around them spent the 9th and 10th centuries alternately fighting and intermarrying with the foreigners.
By the year 1000, "Norse-Irish" was a coherent ethnic category, with its own language, its own legal habits, and its own kings (Norse warlords with Irish wives and Gaelic-speaking children).

The Battle of Clontarf in 1014 — when the Irish high king Brian Boru defeated a Norse-Irish coalition outside Dublin — is sometimes called the end of Viking Ireland, but the truth is that the Vikings were already half-Irish by then.
They didn't leave; they melted in.
Then came the rivers.

The genuinely terrifying escalation of the 840s was the discovery, by Norse fleets, that they could sail up the rivers of Continental Europe and strike inland targets that had never had to think about coastal defense.
Paris, by the standards of 845, was an inland city.
It was 100 miles up the Seine from the sea.
It was protected by no walls capable of stopping a serious assault, because it had not been seriously assaulted in the lifetime of anyone living.
The walls it did have were Roman remnants, repurposed as a quarry by generations of locals.

In March 845, a Viking fleet of 120 ships under a leader the Frankish chronicles call Ragnar (possibly the same legendary Ragnar Lothbrok later sagas would lionize, possibly someone else entirely whose name has been retroactively glued to the legend) sailed up the Seine, brushed aside Frankish resistance, and sacked Paris on Easter Sunday.
The shock to Frankish prestige was enormous.

King Charles the Bald (Charlemagne's grandson, ruler of West Francia, the kingdom that would become France) paid an enormous Danegeld (DAYN-geld, "Dane-gold," tribute paid to make Vikings go away) of 7,000 pounds (about 2,500 kg) of silver — the first major Danegeld in Frankish history, though by no means the last.
The Vikings took the silver and went home.
They came back.
The same year, 845, another Norse fleet sacked the newly founded archbishopric of Hamburg in northern Germany, forcing the missionary Ansgar to flee for his life.
The Frankish Empire — ruler of half of western Europe, heir of Rome — was now paying its enemies to leave it alone and watching its archbishops abandon their sees.
Paris would be besieged again in 885–886 by an even larger fleet, perhaps 700 ships, under the joint command of several Viking warlords.
This time the city had walls, and a young Frankish count named Odo held the bridge over the Seine at the Île de la Cité through nearly a year of siege.
Odo's defense was so notable that he was elected King of West Francia in 888, displacing the Carolingians for the first time.
The Vikings eventually withdrew up the Seine to plunder Burgundy after extracting another large Danegeld.
The takeaway, for everyone watching: the Vikings could reach any river city in Christendom, the Carolingian state could not stop them, and the only reliable response was to pay them off.
In the 850s, the raiding fundamentally changed in character.

Overwintering became normal: instead of sailing home to Scandinavia in the autumn, Viking fleets started to seize defensible river islands or coastal forts and dig in for the winter, raiding from a fixed local base year-round.

This is the strategic shift that converts the Viking Age from a series of seasonal robberies into something much more dangerous — a permanent armed Norse presence operating from forward bases inside Continental and Insular territory.
From an overwintered position, you could strike at greater depth, accumulate plunder more efficiently, and project force into a region in a way that mere summer raiding never could.
The classic 9th-century Norse overwintering camps were on the Loire, on the Seine, on the Thames, and on a series of islands and estuaries up and down the European Atlantic.
The Vikings were no longer guests.
They were squatters, and they were heavily armed.
The most ambitious raid of the period demonstrates how far and how creatively the Norse were willing to operate.

In 859, the Norse warlords Hastein (HAS-tane, also spelled Hasting or Anstign) and Björn Ironside (a son of Ragnar Lothbrok in the legendary tradition; whether he was a historical individual is debated) led a fleet of 62 ships out through the Strait of Gibraltar into the Mediterranean.
This was unprecedented: a Norse fleet entering the inland sea where Romans, Byzantines, and Muslims had assumed they were the only naval powers.

Hastein's fleet raided the coasts of Iberia (then partly under the Umayyad emirate of Córdoba, partly under the Christian kingdom of Asturias), spent a winter in the Camargue at the mouth of the Rhône, ascended the Rhône to plunder Provence, sacked the city of Pisa on the Italian coast, and raided as far as the southern coast of France and Morocco before turning around and heading back through Gibraltar in 862.
By the time they returned to Brittany three years after they had set out, half their fleet was gone.
The expedition was a disaster financially.
It was also a statement: the Norse could go anywhere with a coast.
The Hastein expedition marks the apex of the long-range, free-lance Viking raid.
After the 850s, the energy shifts: the raids stop being one-off plundering trips and start being conquests.
The crews stop going home in the autumn.
They send for their wives.
They start to think about land.
The watershed is 865.

In the autumn of 865, a Norse force unlike anything that had come before — bigger, better-organized, and led not by a single chieftain but by a coalition of warlords — landed in East Anglia on the eastern coast of England.
The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, the contemporary court chronicle of Wessex, called it the mycel hæþen here — the Great Heathen Army.

Modern scholars argue about the actual numbers (estimates range from 1,000 to 3,000 men, with later landings boosting the total), but everyone agrees that this was an order of magnitude beyond anything the Vikings had committed to England before.

The army wintered in East Anglia, requisitioning horses from the local Anglo-Saxon king (who, lacking other options, complied), and then in 866 it marched north and took the city of York (Old Norse Jórvík, YOR-veek), the capital of the kingdom of Northumbria.
York fell on November 1, 866 — All Saints' Day.
The Northumbrian kings Aelle and Osberht, who had been fighting each other, briefly reconciled and tried to retake the city in March 867.
Both kings were killed.
Northumbria became, effectively, a Viking kingdom.

According to a legend that the Icelandic sagas would tell three centuries later, the leadership of the Great Heathen Army was the sons of Ragnar Lothbrok — among them Ivar the Boneless, Halfdan, and Ubba — who had come to England specifically to avenge their father's death at the hands of King Aelle.

Aelle, the saga says, was put to death by the blood eagle (a particularly horrible ritualized execution where the victim's ribs were cut from the spine and folded outward like wings, and the lungs pulled through the gap; whether the blood eagle was an actual practice or a poetic flourish from later Christian chroniclers describing pagan Vikings is one of the genuinely unsettled debates of Viking-Age scholarship).

The historicity of Ragnar himself is contested — he is far more legend than man — but the historicity of his "sons" leading the Great Heathen Army is reasonably solid: contemporary sources do name Ivar and Halfdan as commanders, and Ubba appears in the Anglo-Saxon record.
Whatever the truth about the patriarch, the family enterprise was real.
The Great Heathen Army would spend the next fifteen years reshaping the political map of England.
East Anglia fell in 869 (the East Anglian king Edmund was tied to a tree and shot full of arrows, becoming Saint Edmund the Martyr, England's first patron saint before St.
George took the role centuries later).
Mercia, the central English midland kingdom, was carved up in 874.
By 875, of the four traditional Anglo-Saxon kingdoms — Northumbria, East Anglia, Mercia, Wessex — three had been destroyed or reduced to vassal states.
Only Wessex in the southwest still had a functioning native crown, and the Heathen Army was about to come for it.
The crown belonged to a 22-year-old named Alfred, who was about to become the most consequential king in English history.

Cross-civ check: the Great Heathen Army's invasion of England (865) coincides with the end of the Tang dynasty's stability in China (the Huang Chao Rebellion would erupt in 874), the height of the Abbasid Caliphate's intellectual flowering in Baghdad, the early Pala dynasty in Bengal, the Heian court flourishing in Japan, and the Maya Terminal Classic collapse in the southern lowlands.
While Saxon kings died in the rain at Northumbrian battlefields, Baghdad scholars were translating Aristotle into Arabic.
The world was bigger and stranger than either of them knew.

chapters.title: Conquest and Settlement
sentences: In May 878, in the marshy fenlands of Somerset in southwestern England, a king who had been hiding in the swamps for four months emerged with a small army and won a battle that saved the English language.
That is not an overstatement.
If Alfred the Great (king of Wessex from 871 to 899) had lost the Battle of Edington to the Viking warlord Guthrum, there would be no kingdom of England as a continuous Anglo-Saxon political entity.
The whole of England would have become, within a generation or two, a Norse-speaking province of a wider Scandinavian world.

The language we are reading right now — English, the Germanic-Romance hybrid that grew out of the Anglo-Saxon dialects of Wessex — would have been replaced by Old Norse the way Latin replaced Etruscan.
None of this was inevitable.
It came down to one battle in a swamp.

The setup: the Great Heathen Army had spent the early 870s reducing the rest of Anglo-Saxon England, and by 875 the remaining Norse force in England was led by Guthrum, a Danish chieftain who had carved out a power base in East Anglia.

In January 878, Guthrum launched a surprise winter attack on Wessex — winter campaigning was rare in early-medieval Europe because armies dissolved without supplies, but Guthrum's force was based locally and could feed itself off Wessex farms.
The attack caught Alfred at his hunting lodge at Chippenham during the Twelfth Night celebrations.
Alfred barely escaped.

The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle describes him as fleeing with a small bodyguard "through woods and fen-fastnesses" to the Isle of Athelney, a small dry rise in the Somerset marshes, where he built a fort and waited.

The story that he burned the cakes — that, in hiding at a peasant woman's hut, he was so distracted by his thoughts that he failed to watch the cakes she had asked him to mind, and was scolded for letting them char — is from a later medieval chronicle and is almost certainly invented.

What is not invented is that Alfred genuinely was reduced, in the spring of 878, to a refugee king with a bodyguard, hiding in a swamp, while the rest of his kingdom was occupied by people who wanted to kill him.
He was 28 years old.
He had been king for seven years.
He had a hereditary illness (probably Crohn's disease, based on his contemporary biographer's medical descriptions) that gave him intermittent agonizing intestinal pain.
And he was, somehow, going to win.
In the spring he sent runners to summon the levy of three Wessex shires: Somerset, Wiltshire, and Hampshire.
The men came.
In May 878, Alfred met Guthrum's army at Edington in Wiltshire.

The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle says Alfred "fought against the whole army and put it to flight, and pursued it as far as the fortress." Guthrum and his survivors were besieged in Chippenham for two weeks, ran out of food, and surrendered.
The peace terms — the Treaty of Wedmore, signed at Wedmore in Somerset later that year — were extraordinary.
Guthrum agreed to convert to Christianity.

He stood as godfather to himself in Alfred's presence at his baptism, taking the Christian name Æthelstan (no relation to the later King Æthelstan of England, but a politically loaded choice — the name meant "noble stone").
Alfred and Guthrum then negotiated a partition of England: Wessex and western Mercia for Alfred, eastern and northern England for Guthrum and the Norse settlers.

That partition, formalized in a separate treaty around 886, created the Danelaw — the territory of England under Norse legal custom, stretching roughly from the line of the River Thames east of London north to the River Tees in Yorkshire, and including the cities of York, Lincoln, Leicester, Nottingham, Stamford, Derby, and Norwich.
Within the Danelaw, Norse customary law applied: legal procedures, weights and measures, land-tenure conventions, and (crucially) place-names became Scandinavian.

Modern English place-names ending in -by (a Norse word for "village" or "farm" — Derby, Whitby, Selby, Grimsby), -thorpe (a satellite settlement — Scunthorpe, Grimsthorpe), and -thwaite (a clearing — Bassenthwaite, Crosthwaite) are the linguistic fingerprint of the Danelaw, still legible on modern Ordnance Survey maps a thousand years later.
England outside the Danelaw is a country of -tons, -hams, and -hursts — Anglo-Saxon endings.
Inside the Danelaw, you cannot drive ten miles without hitting a Norse place-name.
The map is a map of conquest.
The English language itself was permanently altered by the Danelaw.
Old English and Old Norse were closely related Germanic languages — about as different as modern Dutch and German, mutually slow but possible to follow with effort.
After three or four generations of bilingual contact in the Danelaw, English absorbed an enormous vocabulary from Norse.
The pronouns they, them, their are Norse, replacing the original Old English hi, hem, hera.
The everyday verbs take, give, get, call, cast, die, want are Norse.
Sky, skin, skull, egg, husband, window, knife, leg, root, cake, fellow, gift, law, outlaw — Norse.

The structure of English grammar simplified during this period, partly because the simplest mutual-intelligibility move when two related languages are in contact is to drop the case-endings that don't agree.
The English language we are reading now is a creole of Anglo-Saxon and Old Norse, with French painted on top after 1066.
Without the Danelaw, English would have ended up much closer to modern German.
The Vikings who lost at Edington won the battle for the language anyway.
England was the loud half of the story.
The Danelaw farmers, the Edington battle, the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle's blow-by-blow account — these are the parts of the Viking Age that medieval Christian Europe wrote down and remembered.
But the same generations that produced Alfred and Guthrum also produced a quieter and more astonishing set of voyages, made by Norse men and women who never bothered Wessex at all.
They sailed the other way: not south to plunder old kingdoms but west into empty water, looking for land nobody owned.
The same longships that ferried the Great Heathen Army across the North Sea could, with a steadier nerve and a fairer wind, cross hundreds of miles of open ocean to islands no European had ever seen.

While the southern half of the Norse diaspora was reshaping England, a different branch was doing something almost no one in the Mediterranean world believed was possible: settling the open North Atlantic.

The chronology of the North Atlantic settlement is, in outline: Around 825, Irish monks (the Papar, "fathers" — tiny groups of Celtic anchorites looking for desert islands to be solitary on) reached Iceland but did not settle in numbers.
The 12th-century Icelandic Landnámabók ("Book of Settlement") would later record them as the first arrivals.

In 860, a Norwegian named Naddodd sighted Iceland accidentally during a storm-blown passage to the Faroe Islands and named what he saw "Snowland." In 868, Floki Vilgerðarson sailed deliberately to Iceland with three sacred ravens that he released at intervals to find the way (the first one flew back to the Faroes; the second flew up and returned; the third flew on, and Floki followed it).
Floki gave the island its modern name, Ísland — Iceland — after a particularly hard winter.
He was the first to overwinter there.

In 874, Ingólfr Arnarson became the first confirmed permanent Norse settler, founding the homestead that would become Reykjavík (RAY-kya-veek, "Smoky Bay," named for the volcanic steam vents in the area).

The Landnámabók says he threw his high-seat pillars (carved wooden posts that flanked a chieftain's seat in a longhouse, treated as a sacred clan possession) into the sea as he approached the coast and built his hall where they washed ashore.
The story — pagan ritual divination guiding the founding of a homestead — sets the tone for how Iceland was settled.
What followed, between 874 and roughly 930, is called the Landnám ("land-taking") period in Icelandic tradition.

Approximately 9,000 to 20,000 Norse colonists — mostly from southwestern Norway, but also from Norse Ireland, the Hebrides, and the Northern Isles — arrived in waves and claimed every habitable patch of the island.
By 930, the Landnámabók records, all the available land in Iceland was taken.
The total population was probably about 60,000 by the year 1000.
A great deal of the immigration was driven by political pressure back home.

Harald Fairhair (Harald Hárfagri, c. 860–933) — the first king to attempt to unify all of Norway under a single crown — had defeated his rival petty kings at the Battle of Hafrsfjord around 872 and demanded the submission of the surviving aristocracy.
Many Norwegian chieftains preferred emigration to subjugation, and Iceland — empty, far away, and beyond Harald's reach — was the obvious destination.
The Icelandic sagas would later mythologize this as "the freedom-loving Norwegians fleeing tyranny," which is partly self-serving but partly accurate.
Iceland was a refuge for the kind of independent-minded chieftain who did not want a king.
So in 930, the settlers did something extraordinary: they convened a national assembly and declared a republic.

The Althing (Old Norse Alþingi, AL-thing-ee, "general assembly"), founded in 930 at Þingvellir (THING-veh-leer, "Assembly Plains," a dramatic geological site at the boundary of the North American and Eurasian tectonic plates, where a long fissure rift forms a natural amphitheater), is one of the longest-running parliamentary institutions in the world.
The Icelanders met every June at Þingvellir for two weeks.

They appointed a Lawspeaker (Old Norse lögsögumaðr, LERG-sergh-oo-mathr, "law-speaking man"), whose job it was to recite the entire body of Icelandic customary law from memory in three-year cycles, a third each summer (which is how a non-literate society stored its constitutional law: in the head of one specialist, refreshed annually).
The Lawspeaker did not rule; he merely remembered.
Disputes were arbitrated by panels of free farmers.
Major decisions of the commonwealth — including the conversion to Christianity in 1000 (Chapter 5) — were taken by acclamation at Þingvellir.

This was not quite democracy in the modern sense (slaves and women had no voting power, and the system was dominated by a class of about 36 chieftains who held the goðorð offices), but it was a remarkable functional achievement: a stateless commonwealth running for 330 years on customary law, oral tradition, and the personal authority of the Lawspeaker, with no king, no standing army, no royal court, no taxation.
