The Icelandic Free State persisted until 1262, when civil wars among the leading clans drove the country into the arms of the Norwegian crown.
Three centuries is a long run.

By way of comparison, the Roman Republic lasted just under five centuries (Ancient Rome Ch 4), the United States is currently 250 years old, and the original Icelandic system held together for longer than the British constitutional monarchy has been in its modern form.
Iceland was, in early-medieval terms, an experiment that worked.

The Grágás ("Grey Goose") laws — the body of customary law of the Icelandic Free State, named possibly for the goose-quill on which they would be written, possibly because the Old Norse word for goose connoted ancient wisdom — were finally committed to writing in 1117–1118, after Iceland had Christianized and acquired the Latin alphabet through the church.

The Grey Goose laws are dense, precise, and procedurally elaborate: they regulate inheritance, dowry, manslaughter compensation, slave manumission, ship ownership, fishing rights, wood-cutting rights, cattle trespass, beached whales (a serious matter in a deforested island where any timber, even a piece of driftwood, was valuable), and the etiquette of formally calling on a neighbor to witness a legal transaction.
They are also, between the lines, a portrait of an entire society that had decided to do without kings.
A note on something that does not get enough attention: a great many of Iceland's founding settlers were women, and several of them came as the heads of their own households.

The most famous is Aud the Deep-Minded (Old Norse Auðr djúpúðga, EWTH the deep-OOTH-ga; sometimes called Unn the Deep-Minded in different manuscripts), an Irish-Norse noblewoman whose career reads like a saga because it is one.
Born probably in the Hebrides in the 830s, she was the daughter of a Norse chieftain and the wife of a Viking king of Dublin (Olaf the White).

When her husband and son were both killed in different battles in Scotland and Ireland, Aud — by then in her sixties — gathered up her remaining family, freed her slaves, distributed dowries to her granddaughters, organized passage on a knarr (a wider, deeper Norse merchant ship for cargo and emigration, distinct from the slim warship-style longship), and led a household of perhaps fifty people across the open Atlantic from Scotland to Iceland in the late 880s.
She established her family at Hvammr in western Iceland, became one of the most respected matriarchs of the early commonwealth, and converted to Christianity before she died.
The Landnámabók devotes substantial space to her descendants, who included some of the most powerful Icelandic families.
Aud is not unique.

The settlement records list other woman-headed households, female priests of the pagan gods (the female counterpart of the goði was the gyðja, GITH-ya), and women whose dowries gave them control of substantial estates.

Norse society was patriarchal in the standard early-medieval sense, but it was not as patriarchal as its Mediterranean Christian contemporaries; women had significant property rights, could initiate divorce, owned the keys to the household stores (a literal Norse symbol of female authority — the keys were worn on a brooch), and could lead emigration parties when their husbands died.
The Vikings did not invent female autonomy, but they preserved a Germanic-pagan version of it that the Christianizing Continent had largely buried under Roman legal categories.
Iceland was the first true open-ocean colony of the Viking Age.
It was the first time a substantial population had been transferred across hundreds of miles of open Atlantic to a previously uninhabited landmass.
This was not coastal hopping.

Iceland is 600 miles (960 km) from Norway across some of the most dangerous water in the world — the Norwegian Sea, the Iceland-Faroes Ridge, the cold Atlantic depressions that come barreling east off Greenland.

To sail to Iceland and back you needed the longship, the open-ocean sailing rig, the sun compass and sunstone for navigation in the absence of compasses (Chapter 4 notes the Norse may have used calcite crystals to find the sun's position on overcast days), the dead-reckoning skill of generations of fishermen, and a willingness to lose a quarter of your fleet to weather as a normal cost of business.
The Norse had all of those, and they paid the price.
Iceland would, in turn, be the launchpad for the next move.
In 982, an Icelandic chieftain named Erik the Red (Old Norse Eiríkr rauði, EYE-reek-er ROW-thee) was outlawed from Iceland after killing several men in a property dispute.
Outlawry was a heavy sentence: an outlaw could be killed by anyone without legal consequence, his property was forfeit, and he was to leave the country at the next sailing season.
Erik had already heard rumors of a land to the west — sighted, supposedly, decades earlier by a Norwegian named Gunnbjörn during a storm-blown passage.
Erik decided to use his three-year exile to find it.
He found it.
The sailing was rough; he made landfall on the southwestern coast of what we now call Greenland and spent three years coasting and exploring.

He named the place Greenland — Grænland — because, in his own quoted words from the Saga of Erik the Red, "men would be more readily persuaded to come there if it had a good name." This is the first explicit recorded act of marketing in Norse history.
Greenland is not, in fact, particularly green.

The southwestern coast does have summer pasture — meadow grasses and birch scrub in the protected fjords — and you can pasture cattle and sheep there during the brief Arctic summer, which is what the colonists did.
But the interior is a continental ice sheet over a mile thick, and the coast outside the southwestern fjords is a rampart of black rock and floating ice.
Erik had picked the one habitable strip and was selling it as if the whole island looked like that.
The marketing worked.
In 985 (or possibly 986), a fleet of 25 ships set out from Iceland for Greenland.
Fourteen ships made it through; the others were lost or turned back.
The survivors founded two settlements: the Eastern Settlement (Eystribyggð) near the modern town of Qaqortoq, and the Western Settlement (Vestribyggð) further north near modern Nuuk.
The total population eventually reached perhaps 2,000 to 3,000 at its 12th-century peak.

The colonists farmed sheep and cattle, hunted seals and walrus (the walrus tusk was the Greenland economy's main export, a prestige material in Continental Europe — a chunk of carved walrus-tusk ivory could cross half of Europe in trade — and the small island chess set with figures of carved walrus-tusk known as the Lewis chessmen, found on a beach in the Outer Hebrides in 1831, is probably a Greenland export that washed up halfway home), and traded with passing Icelandic and Norwegian ships.
They built turf-roofed longhouses and stone churches.
They held annual assemblies.
They went on hunts deep into the Arctic, leaving runic graffiti on rocks above the 73rd parallel.
Greenland would persist, against the steadily worsening climate of the Little Ice Age, until the late 1400s.
The Western Settlement was abandoned around 1350; the Eastern Settlement vanished sometime between 1450 and 1500, leaving no clear written record of how.
The last documented contact was a wedding at Hvalsey Church in 1408, recorded in a letter to the Icelandic bishop.
After that, silence.
When Hans Egede, a Danish-Norwegian missionary, reached southwestern Greenland in 1721, he found only ruins.

The Greenland colony is the longest-lived European colony in the New World that ultimately failed: nearly five hundred years of pasturing sheep on the edge of an ice sheet, ended by climate, isolation, and the slow attrition of a population too small to replenish itself.

It is also, in its own way, one of the great human stories of adaptation — a few thousand farmers held an Atlantic foothold through the Medieval Warm Period and could not hold it through the Little Ice Age.
The lights went out one winter at a time.
But before they went out, the Greenlanders made one more move.

Around the year 1000, the year the Althing voted to Christianize Iceland, Leif Erikson — son of Erik the Red, born in Iceland, raised in Greenland — sailed west from the Greenland settlements toward an even further coast that traders had glimpsed years earlier.

He coasted the eastern shore of what we now call North America and landed at three places he named Helluland ("Stone-Slab Land," probably Baffin Island), Markland ("Forest Land," probably Labrador), and Vinland ("Vine Land" or "Wine Land," probably the northern part of Newfoundland, where wild grapes do not actually grow but other vines do, and the name may reflect a misidentification of berries or a deliberate marketing flourish in the family tradition).
At a bay on the northern tip of Newfoundland, the Norse built a small encampment.
The site was found in 1960 by the Norwegian explorer-archaeologists Helge and Anne Stine Ingstad, working from clues in the sagas.

L'Anse aux Meadows (lans-oh-MEH-doh, French for "Bay of Meadows") sits on the windswept tip of Newfoundland — three turf-walled longhouses, a workshop, and a small smithy, dated by radiocarbon to around the year 1000, with iron nails forged from local bog iron in a Norse style and butternut shells indicating that the inhabitants had ranged at least as far south as New Brunswick.
It is the only confirmed Viking site in North America.
It is conclusive proof that the Norse reached the New World five centuries before Columbus.
Why did Vinland fail?

The sagas describe escalating conflicts with the indigenous Skraelings (Old Norse Skrælingjar, SKRAY-ling-ar; a derogatory Norse term that probably referred to the Beothuk or other northeastern coastal peoples) — first trade, then trade gone bad, then violent skirmishes.
Thorfinn Karlsefni, an Icelandic merchant, led the most ambitious colonization attempt around 1010 with 160 settlers and three ships.
They lasted three years.

Freydis Eriksdottir (Erik the Red's formidable, controversial daughter) led a final expedition that ended in internal Norse violence — the sagas tell a story of Freydis personally killing five women on the expedition with an axe, though whether this is history or saga drama is unresolved.
By about 1015, the Vinland project had been abandoned.
The Norse had reached America.
They could not hold it.

Without the population base to send hundreds of settlers, without the iron and steel weapons that gave 16th-century Spaniards a decisive technological edge, and against a substantial indigenous population that did not want them there, the Norse settlements in Newfoundland were small parties of lightly armed colonists facing the same problem the English at Roanoke would face six hundred years later.
The lesson, looking back at the whole western expansion: the Vikings had reached the absolute limit of what their technology could do.

From a longhouse in Norway in 793, Norse society had pushed across the open Atlantic, founded one of the world's longest-lived republics on a previously uninhabited island, established the first European colony in the New World, and bumped up against the edge of what longships and pre-industrial population numbers could sustain.
The Vikings stopped not because they ran out of ambition.
They stopped because they had run out of physics.

chapters.title: East and the Rus'
sentences: While the western branch of the Norse diaspora was settling Iceland and bouncing off Newfoundland, a different and arguably more consequential branch was going in the opposite direction.

Sweden in the 9th century was less politically prominent than Norway or Denmark, but it had a geographic advantage that neither could match: it faced east, across the Baltic, into the headwaters of the Russian river system (the earliest hard evidence for this eastward push is the Salme boat-grave on Estonia, circa 750, roughly forty years before Lindisfarne and the first physically attested Scandinavian sea-raid).

From a Swedish trading post on the Baltic coast, you could row a small boat into the Gulf of Finland, ascend the Neva to Lake Ladoga, work up the Volkhov to Lake Ilmen, and reach Novgorod — a distance of about 200 miles inland, navigable in days.

From Lake Ilmen, you could portage south to the headwaters of either the Dnieper (NEE-per) or the Volga, the two great rivers that drained the East European Plain south to, respectively, the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea.

By drag-and-row, the Swedish merchant-warriors discovered, you could connect the Baltic to two of the richest commercial worlds in 9th-century Eurasia: the Byzantine Empire centered on Constantinople, and the Abbasid Caliphate centered on Baghdad.
The Swedes spent the next two centuries doing exactly that, and it changed both Russia and the Norse world forever.

Slavic-speaking and Finnic-speaking peoples on the Russian rivers called these eastern Vikings the Rus' (ROOS) — a term whose etymology is disputed, but which probably derives either from the Old Norse Rōþskarlar ("rowing men," the men who plied the rowing routes) or from the Finnish Ruotsi ("Sweden"), and which would, by an extraordinary linguistic accident, become the root of the words Russia and Russian.
The country that would eventually call itself Russia is named after a Norse rowing crew.
More on that in a moment.
The eastern Norse expansion ran in parallel with the western raids and settlements but was driven by a different logic.
The west was about plunder and farmland.
The east was about trade — specifically, about silver.
The Abbasid Caliphate in the 9th century was the wealthiest single political entity on earth.

From its capital at Baghdad (founded in 762, the largest city in the world by 800 with roughly 700,000 inhabitants), the Abbasids minted enormous quantities of high-quality silver coins called dirhams — heavy, thin, broad coins struck with Quranic calligraphy and the issuing caliph's name and date.

The Abbasid mints produced tens of millions of dirhams across the 9th and 10th centuries, and the dirhams flowed outward through trade as the dominant currency of the entire Islamic and Eurasian commercial world.
They were the dollar of their century.
And from about 800 onward, an extraordinary number of them flowed north, up the Volga, into the Norse world.
The Islamic Golden Age Ch 8 covers the economic context — the Caliphate's silver mining, trade revenues, and monetary policy — that made this flood of dirhams possible in the first place.
Archaeologists have recovered hundreds of thousands of Abbasid silver dirhams from Viking-Age hoards across Scandinavia, the Baltic, and northern Russia.
The largest hoards — from Gotland (a Baltic island that became the great Norse silver vault), from Hedeby, from Birka — contain tens of thousands of coins.

The Spillings hoard, found on Gotland in 1999, contains about 14,000 silver coins (mostly Abbasid, some Sasanian, some Byzantine) weighing 67 kilograms (147 pounds) — the largest single Viking silver hoard ever recovered.

Multiply that by the dozens of large hoards and the thousands of small ones, and the scale becomes clear: the Norse world imported, by some estimates, well over a hundred tonnes of silver from the Islamic Caliphate during the 9th and 10th centuries.
That is a structural fact about the Viking economy.
Most of the silver that the western raiders extracted from Frankish and English Danegelds was minor, in volume, compared to the eastern flow.
What did the Norse trade for the silver?

Furs (especially sable, ermine, and fox, prized at every point on the route — the medieval Mediterranean had no fur of its own to speak of, and the cold luxury market was dominated by the Russian boreal forest), walrus ivory from Greenland, amber from the Baltic shores, honey, wax, and — overwhelmingly — slaves.
The Old Norse term mansal meant "the sale of human beings," and this was the central commerce of the Volga route.

Norse raiders took captives in the western raids on Britain and Ireland, in the Baltic against the Slavs and Balts, in the Russian forests against the Finno-Ugric and Slavic peoples; the captives moved south down the Russian rivers in chains and were sold in Itil (the Khazar capital on the lower Volga) and Bulghar (a major Volga trading entrepôt) into the Islamic world — where the Abbasid demand for household servants, concubines, and slave soldiers sustained the market at scale (Islamic Golden Age Ch 8).
Some ended up in Baghdad.
Some ended up in Cordoba.

The Arab geographer Ibn Fadlan (a 10th-century Abbasid envoy whose 922 travelogue describing his journey to the Volga Bulghars is one of the great primary sources for the Rus') described the Rus' merchants on the Volga in detail: tall, tattooed men carrying axes and seaxes; wealthy in dirhams; and accompanied by women in bondage whom they bought, sold, and abused under his appalled gaze.

Ibn Fadlan also witnessed and described in horrifying detail the funeral of a Rus' chieftain on the Volga, including the strangling and ritual stabbing of a slave girl who had volunteered (or been volunteered) to follow her master into death.
His account of the Rus' is one of the great pieces of 10th-century reportage.
It is also, quietly, an inventory of what slavery looked like at the receiving end.
The political crystallization of the Rus' begins in the 860s, with a figure named Rurik.

According to the Primary Chronicle (the 12th-century compilation of Kievan Rus' historical traditions, written in Old Church Slavonic by Christian monks long after the events it describes), Slavic and Finnic tribes around Lake Ladoga and the Novgorod region invited a Varangian (Norse) chieftain named Rurik and his brothers to come and rule them, because "our land is great and rich, but there is no order in it." "No order" meant something concrete: the local tribes had been paying tribute to other Varangian raiders, then driven them off, then started fighting among themselves, with rival chiefs raiding each other's villages and no recognized arbitrator to settle blood-feuds or enforce treaties.

What the chronicler is describing is a stateless region with no monopoly on violence — the same problem the Norse themselves had at home, only worse, because there was no shared kinship network or assembly tradition to fall back on.
The remedy proposed was, in effect, to import a chieftain from outside who would be too high above the local quarrels to take sides.

This is the classic invitation legend; whether anyone actually invited anyone is doubtful, and the Primary Chronicle's framing — "we asked the Vikings to come and govern us" — is suspiciously convenient for later generations of Rus' rulers who wanted to legitimize their dynasty.

What is not doubtful is that around 862, a Norse-led polity coalesced at Novgorod ("New City"), with Rurik or someone like him at its head, and that this polity would, within a generation, expand to dominate the entire Russian river system.
In 882, Rurik's successor (or kinsman; the genealogies are fuzzy) Oleg (Old Norse Helgi) moved the Rus' political center south from Novgorod to Kiev on the middle Dnieper.
Kiev was a much better commercial site than Novgorod: it sat on the main southern river, it commanded the trade route to Constantinople, and it had richer agricultural land around it.

Oleg's seizure of Kiev — he is said to have killed the two existing Rus' chieftains there by tricking them into a meeting — and his declaration that Kiev would be "the mother of Rus' cities" is the conventional founding date of Kievan Rus', the medieval state that would, over the next two centuries, evolve from a Norse trading enterprise into a Slavic Christian kingdom and ultimately into the cultural foundation of all three modern East Slavic nations: Russia, Ukraine, and Belarus.
The trajectory deserves a pause.
It is one of the great cases in world history of an immigrant warrior elite assimilating into the population it ruled.

The early Rus' rulers were Norse — their names were Norse (Rurik, Oleg, Igor, Olga, Svyatoslav, Vladimir all derive from Old Norse Hrørek, Helgi, Ingvarr, Helga, Sveinald, and Valdamar respectively), their warband ethos was Norse, their longships were Norse.
By the third generation, they were marrying Slavic and Khazar princesses.
By the fifth, they spoke Slavic at home.
By the sixth, the dynasty was indistinguishable from the population it governed except by lineage.

The Rurikid dynasty would rule the lands of the Rus' for the next seven centuries — until 1610 — and would govern, by the late medieval period, an empire that no early-medieval Norseman would have recognized as having anything to do with Scandinavia.

The mechanism is one of the cleanest examples in history of how a small warrior elite can be culturally swallowed by the people it conquers: marry into them, learn their language, adopt their religion, and within a few generations the only thing Norse about you is the family tree.
Rus' diplomacy with Constantinople ran on a peculiar mix of raids and trade treaties.

Constantinople in 860 was the largest city in Christendom, a million-plus inhabitants behind the most formidable land walls in the world (the Theodosian Walls, three concentric defensive lines stretching across the peninsula on which the city sat — Persian Empire Ch 8 for the Byzantine context).
The city sat at the junction of the Black Sea and the Mediterranean, controlled the Bosporus, and ran a Mediterranean trading economy that would make any Norse merchant's mouth water.
The Vikings looked at this city, calculated, and went for it.

In June 860, while the Byzantine emperor Michael III was campaigning in Anatolia, a Rus' fleet of about 200 ships emerged out of the Black Sea, descended on the unprepared Bosporan suburbs, and plundered them for ten days.
The city itself, behind its walls, was untouched, but the shock to Byzantine prestige was enormous — and it was reciprocated by the shock to Norse imagination.
The Rus' had now seen Constantinople.

The patriarch Photius, who watched the raid from the walls, preached two surviving sermons about it, calling the raiders "an obscure nation, a nation of no account, a nation ranked among slaves, unknown, but which has won a name from the expedition against us." The "nation of no account" had just become a player.
The raids became a recurring feature.

Oleg led a major expedition against Constantinople in 907 that resulted in a celebrated trade treaty: Rus' merchants got the right to trade tax-free in Constantinople, to be lodged at imperial expense for six months a year, and to take a fixed monthly stipend of bread, wine, fish, and meat — extraordinary commercial privileges, the kind of thing the Byzantines did not extend to anybody.
The treaty cemented the Dnieper trade route as the great Rus' artery to the Mediterranean.
In 941, Igor of Kiev (Oleg's successor) launched another major attack on Constantinople.

This one ran into the Byzantine secret weapon — Greek fire (a flammable liquid mix, possibly petroleum-based, projected through bronze siphons mounted on the prows of Byzantine warships, which clung and burned even on water and could not be extinguished by normal means; the formula was a Byzantine state secret so closely guarded that it was forgotten by the 13th century and has never been definitively reconstructed).
Igor's fleet was burned to the waterline.
He limped home with a fraction of his ships and his men.
But he was undeterred enough to mount another raid in 944, and the Byzantines, weary, signed a fresh and slightly less favorable treaty.
Igor was killed in 945 by the Drevlians (a Slavic tribe) when he tried to extort a second tribute from them.
His widow Olga — a Norse-Slavic queen with a saga-worthy ferocity — took the regency for their young son and avenged him with a campaign so brutal it became legendary even in a brutal era.

According to the Primary Chronicle, Olga buried alive the first Drevlian envoys, burned a second delegation in a bathhouse, killed 5,000 Drevlians at her husband's funeral feast, and burned down the Drevlian capital with the help of pigeons whose tails she set alight (the pigeons flew home to their roosts and ignited the thatched roofs of every house in town).

The pigeon story is almost certainly fictional; the rest may be exaggerated; but Olga's campaign of revenge was real enough that the Drevlians ceased to exist as an autonomous people and were absorbed into the Kievan Rus'.
She was a person you did not cross.
In about 957, in one of the most consequential individual decisions of the Viking Age, Olga traveled to Constantinople and accepted Christian baptism.
The Byzantine emperor Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus (who left a court-protocol manual describing her visit in detail) stood as her godfather.
She returned to Kiev a Christian.
Her son Svyatoslav refused to convert — his warband would have laughed at him, he said — but Olga had set in motion a process that her grandson would complete.
The grandson was Vladimir, and Vladimir's conversion in 988 is one of the great hinge moments in European religious history.
The Primary Chronicle preserves a wonderful (and almost certainly stylized) story about how Vladimir picked his religion.

Faced with the question of which monotheism to adopt — Kievan Rus' was now wealthy enough to need a state religion, the old Slavic-Norse paganism was no longer adequate to a multiethnic territorial kingdom, and the neighbors all had options on offer — Vladimir is said to have sent envoys to investigate the great faiths.

The Volga Bulghar Muslims were rejected because their ban on alcohol was "incompatible with the joys of the Rus'" ("Drinking is the joy of the Russians; we cannot live without it" is Vladimir's reported line; whether he actually said it or not, it is now permanently associated with him).
The Khazar Jews were rejected because their having lost Jerusalem suggested God had abandoned them.
The Western Roman Christians were rejected because their churches lacked beauty.
The Byzantine Orthodox envoys, taken to a service at Hagia Sophia in Constantinople, sent back the report: "We knew not whether we were in heaven or on earth." Vladimir picked Orthodox Christianity.
The choice mattered.
A different ruler picking Roman Catholicism would have placed Russia in the Latin West rather than the Greek East.
A different ruler picking Islam would have integrated Russia into the Dar al-Islam.

By choosing Constantinople over Rome and Constantinople over Baghdad, Vladimir aligned the Rus' permanently with the Byzantine cultural sphere — the Cyrillic alphabet (developed by 9th-century Byzantine missionaries Saints Cyril and Methodius for converting Slavs), Orthodox liturgy, Byzantine architectural styles, Greek-derived theological vocabulary, and the political theology of Caesaropapism that the Russian tsars would borrow wholesale a millennium later.
Russia is Russian today in a culturally specific way because of choices made by a Norse-descended prince in Kiev in 988.
The longshot is hard to overstate.
Vladimir followed his decision with mass action.

According to the Chronicle, he ordered the wooden idol of the thunder god Perun (the Slavic equivalent of Thor) to be tied to a horse's tail, dragged down to the Dnieper, and beaten with sticks by twelve men until it could be thrown into the river.

The population of Kiev was then ordered into the Dnieper for mass baptism. ("If anyone fails to come, let him be considered an enemy of the prince.") The conversion was top-down, fast, and not voluntary in any modern sense.
But it stuck.
Within a generation, Kiev had Byzantine-trained bishops, stone Orthodox churches, and a literate clergy producing the first Old Church Slavonic manuscripts.
There is one more eastern thread to follow, because it loops the Norse world all the way back to itself.
In 988, the same year Vladimir was baptizing Kiev, the Byzantine emperor Basil II was facing a serious revolt by Anatolian generals.
Vladimir, as part of a marriage alliance that gave him the emperor's sister Anna, sent Basil 6,000 elite Norse warriors as imperial bodyguards.

These men formed the founding cohort of what would become one of the most prestigious military units in the medieval world: the Varangian Guard, the emperor's personal household troops, recruited overwhelmingly from Scandinavia, the Rus' lands, and (later) Anglo-Saxon England.
The Guard fought at Constantinople for nearly five centuries, until the city's fall to the Ottomans in 1453.
They were paid in gold.
They wore distinctive battle-axes.
They spoke Old Norse on duty into the 13th century.
And they served as the route by which dozens of Norse warlords made fortunes in Byzantine service and then went home.
The most famous was Harald Sigurdsson — better known to history as Harald Hardrada ("Hard-Counsel," HARD-rah-da, c. 1015–1066), half-brother of King Olaf II of Norway.
After Olaf's death at Stiklestad in 1030 (Chapter 5), Harald, then 15 years old, fled east and joined the Varangian Guard in Constantinople.
He spent the next decade fighting Byzantine wars in Sicily, Bulgaria, the Caucasus, North Africa, and Anatolia, accumulating an enormous personal fortune in pay and plunder.
By the time he returned to Norway in 1045 and claimed his inheritance, he was one of the wealthiest individuals in the Norse world — and one of the most experienced soldiers.
He would rule Norway for the next twenty years and die at Stamford Bridge in 1066 (Chapter 8) trying to take a kingdom that wasn't his.
Harald is the cleanest example of how the eastern and western branches of the Norse world were connected.

A Norwegian king, a survivor of his half-brother's failed Christian campaign, fled east, joined the imperial guard of the most cosmopolitan city on earth, fought in Sicily within sight of North Africa, retired with a fortune in dirhams and Byzantine nomismata (gold coins), came home to claim a Norwegian crown, and died trying to take an English one.
He carried a Norse longsword and a Constantinople pension into the same battle.
The world was bigger than any one chapter could contain, and Harald saw most of it.

Cross-civ check: the Rus'-Byzantine dirham-flow age (~860–970) overlaps with the Macedonian Renaissance in Constantinople (a flowering of Byzantine art, scholarship, and military success), the Buyid dynasty in Iran (Persian Empire Ch 9 — Shia rulers controlling Baghdad while leaving the Abbasid caliph as a figurehead), the Samanid dynasty in Central Asia (the great patron of Persian-language poetry, Bukhara as a rival to Baghdad), the Liao dynasty in northern China, and the Mayan Postclassic transition in the Yucatán.
The dirhams that paid for Norse longships originally came out of silver mines in Khurasan and Central Asia (Persian Empire Ch 9) and reached Scandinavia by river.
The Viking Age was a Eurasian-scale economic system.
It was not a local European drama.

chapters.title: The Gods and the New God
sentences: The Norse worshipped a family of gods who fought monsters, drank too much, lied, schemed, slept with each other's spouses, knew that they were doomed, and went into the final battle anyway because dying well was the point.
Norse mythology, as we know it, comes to us from two main sources.

The Poetic Edda is a collection of about 30 anonymous mythological and heroic poems, composed in Iceland and Norway in the Viking Age and the centuries immediately following, preserved in a single 13th-century manuscript called the Codex Regius (Latin: "Royal Book"), which spent four hundred years in private hands until it was rediscovered in 1643 by an Icelandic bishop, presented to the Danish king, and survived World War II in a Copenhagen vault.

The Prose Edda is a 13th-century systematic textbook of Norse mythology written by the Icelandic statesman, scholar, and saga-writer Snorri Sturluson (1179–1241) for the use of skalds (court poets) who needed to understand the old myths in order to compose properly even after the conversion.
Snorri is our best single source on Norse cosmology.

He was also a Christian writing 200 years after the official conversion, working from oral tradition and surviving poems, and his accounts have been smoothed and rationalized in places that we cannot always identify.

Caveat: the Norse cosmology described below is the system as Snorri wrote it down, which is the closest we can get, but the actual Viking-era pagan religious experience was almost certainly more local, more variable, and less neatly structured than Snorri's textbook makes it look.
With that caveat, here is the system.

The cosmos contains nine worlds, arranged around or upon a vast world-tree called Yggdrasil (IG-druh-sil, "Odin's Steed," because Odin is said to have hung on the tree to gain wisdom — more on that in a moment).
Yggdrasil is an enormous ash tree whose branches extend over all the worlds and whose roots reach down into the underworlds.

It is sustained by the Well of Urd (the Well of Fate), where the Norns (three female fate-spinners, vaguely paralleling the Greek Fates and the Slavic Rozhanitsy, who carve the destinies of gods and men into the wood of the tree) tend its waters.

The tree is gnawed by serpents at its roots, plagued by a dragon named Níðhöggr at its base, and crowned by an eagle who drops gossip to a squirrel named Ratatoskr, who runs up and down the trunk carrying insults between the eagle and the dragon.
This is a cosmology with a sense of humor.

The nine worlds are arranged on three rough levels — gods above, humans in the middle, monsters and the dead below — and most of the action in the surviving myths happens by characters traveling between them.

The names that matter most for the stories are these: Asgard — the home of the Æsir (EYE-sir), the principal sky-gods (Odin, Thor, Tyr, and so on) Midgard — Middle-Earth, the world of human beings (Tolkien borrowed the word and the concept directly) Jotunheim — the home of the Jötnar (YERT-nar, often translated "giants" but really an older race of cosmological forces, often hostile, sometimes not, frequently the romantic partners of the gods) Hel — the realm of the unhonored dead, ruled by a goddess named Hel, half a beautiful woman and half a corpse Muspelheim — the world of fire, ruled by the fire-giant Surtr, who will burn the cosmos at Ragnarök The other four — Vanaheim (an older lineage of fertility gods who fought and made peace with the Æsir), Niflheim (cold and mist), Alfheim (light-elves), and Svartalfheim (dark elves or dwarves) — fill out the system but rarely drive a story.
The principal gods of the Æsir: Odin (in Old Norse Óðinn, OH-thin), the All-Father, god of war, wisdom, poetry, magic, and ritual ecstasy.
Odin is one-eyed (he gave his other eye to drink at the Well of Mimir for wisdom).
He hangs himself on Yggdrasil for nine days and nights, pierced by his own spear, in order to learn the secret of the runes.
He has two ravens, Huginn ("Thought") and Muninn ("Memory"), who fly out across the world each day and return to whisper news in his ears.
He has two wolves, Geri and Freki.

He keeps a hall in Asgard called Valhalla ("Hall of the Slain"), where the slain warriors brought to him by the Valkyries (VAL-kuh-rees, "choosers of the slain" — armored female spirits riding through battle who select which warriors will die and join Odin) feast all night and fight all day in preparation for the final battle.
Odin is the patron god of kings, of warriors, and of poets.

He is also untrustworthy — he is the god most likely to break an oath, and the warriors who follow him know that he will eventually betray them, because he needs them dead and in Valhalla for his army at Ragnarök.

Thor (in Old Norse Þórr, THORE), the thunder god, son of Odin, the most popular deity in the Viking Age by a wide margin (Thor's-hammer pendants are by far the most common religious amulet in Norse archaeology, especially in the late pagan period when they appear as a deliberate counter-symbol to the Christian cross).
Thor is a red-bearded, hot-tempered, immensely strong protector — of the gods, of humans, of the cosmic order against the giants.
He drives a chariot pulled by two goats.
He wields the hammer Mjölnir (MYERL-neer), which always returns to his hand after being thrown.
Thursday is named for him.
Freyr (FRAYR) and his sister Freyja (FRAY-yah), the great Vanir gods of fertility, peace, and prosperity.
Freyr controls rain and harvest.

Freyja is associated with love, sexuality, gold, war (she gets half the slain; Odin gets the other half — a detail that gives a sense of her stature), and a magical art called seiðr (SAYTH, a kind of ritual divinatory magic that was generally considered women's work, and that was associated with shamanic practice; Odin himself could practice seiðr but it was considered effeminate for him to do so).
Freyja drives a chariot pulled by two cats.
Friday is named for her.
Tyr — the older war god, originally the principal sky-god of the proto-Germanic pantheon, demoted by the Viking Age to a supporting role behind Odin.
He has only one hand, having sacrificed the other to bind the great wolf Fenrir.
Loki — not exactly a god, more of a trickster figure, the father of monsters (the wolf Fenrir, the world-serpent Jörmungandr, the goddess Hel).

Loki is hilarious, treacherous, and ultimately catastrophic; he engineers the death of Odin's beloved son Baldur and is bound in a cave with a serpent dripping venom on his face until Ragnarök, when he will break free and fight against the gods.

And looming over the whole cosmology, the central feature that distinguishes Norse mythology from almost every other religious system in the world: Ragnarök (RAG-nar-erk, "Doom of the Gods" or "Twilight of the Gods").
The gods know that they are going to die.
The Norns have foretold it.

The whole cosmic order will end in a great battle at the end of time: the wolf Fenrir will break his chains and devour Odin; Thor will kill the world-serpent and walk nine paces and fall dead from its venom; the fire-giant Surtr will burn the world; the sun will be eaten; the stars will fall.
After Ragnarök, a new world will rise from the sea, and a small remnant of gods and humans will repopulate it.
But the present cosmic order — the gods we know, the heroes we know, the world we know — is doomed.
The warriors in Valhalla are training for a battle they will lose.
The heroism is in fighting anyway.
This is a religion of doomed nobility, and it shaped the Viking warrior ethic in concrete ways.
A man fated to die cannot avoid his fate.

The honorable thing is to face it well — to die with weapon in hand, with one's name on the lips of the next generation. (Whether the conventional Viking concept of Valhalla as "the warrior heaven" was as central to lived practice as the sagas suggest, or was sharpened in the post-conversion saga literature, is debated.) The poem Hávamál ("The Sayings of the High One"), the longest of the Eddic poems, contains lines that became proverbial: "Cattle die, kinsmen die, the self must also die; / I know one thing which never dies: / The reputation of each dead man." A reputation outlasts a body.
Die well; live in your descendants' memory; that is what immortality is.
The lived practice of Norse paganism centered on blót (BLOTE) — sacrifice.
A blót was a public ritual of animal slaughter (occasionally human, in extreme circumstances), conducted at major seasonal festivals to honor specific gods and seek their favor for the coming season.
The slaughtered animal's blood was sprinkled on the altars, on the temple walls, and on the participants.
The meat was cooked and eaten communally; the worshippers drank the blood (or, more commonly, an ale toasted in the names of the gods); and the rest of the carcass was burned.

The chief blóts of the year: Sigrblót (Victory-Blót) in early spring, dedicated to Odin, asking for victory in the coming raiding season Miðsumarblót at midsummer, dedicated to Freyr, asking for a good harvest Vetrnætrablót (Winter-Nights-Blót) in October, beginning the winter half of the year Jólablót at midwinter (the origin of the word Yule, the great midwinter festival that Christianity would absorb and rebrand as Christmas) The Dísablót was a midwinter sacrifice specifically for the dísir — collective female ancestral and fertility spirits.
The Dísablót was particularly observed in Sweden, where the central royal cult site at Uppsala (uhp-SAH-la) hosted national-scale sacrifices into the late 11th century.

Adam of Bremen, a German cleric writing around 1075 (one of our key non-Norse sources for Viking-Age religion, though he is reporting at second hand from Saxon and Danish informants and is hostile to paganism), described the Great Heathen Temple at Uppsala in vivid and somewhat horrified detail: a wooden temple decorated with golden chains, containing three large wooden statues of Odin, Thor, and Freyr (Thor in the central position, with Odin and Freyr on either side); a sacred grove next to the temple where the bodies of sacrificial victims — humans, dogs, and horses — were hung from the trees; and a great festival every nine years at which 99 of each kind of victim (humans, dogs, horses, cattle) were sacrificed.
Adam was repeating reports, and parts of his account — especially the human sacrifice details — may be exaggerated by his Christian informants.

What is reasonably solid is that Uppsala was the central Swedish royal cult site, that animal sacrifice was a major part of Norse religious practice there, and that the temple persisted, against mounting Christian pressure, until the late 11th century.
Uppsala was probably destroyed and replaced by a Christian cathedral around 1090.
The temple at Uppsala is the great late holdout of Norse paganism.
By the time Adam was writing, every other major Scandinavian region had nominally converted.
Sweden was the last domino, and its national royal cult held on for another century beyond the others.
The conversion of Scandinavia was not a single event.
It was a 250-year process, full of false starts, reversions, forced baptisms, and political compromises.
But the pivotal moments cluster in a roughly fifty-year window: the late 950s through the early 1000s, when most of the great Norse polities went officially Christian.
Denmark went first.
Harald Bluetooth (Harald Blátǫnn, ruled c. 958–986) is the king who flipped Denmark, and he made sure everyone knew it.
Harald was the son of Gorm the Old, the first historically attested king of a unified Denmark, and he was a politically capable, religiously pragmatic, and territorially ambitious ruler.
Christianity had been seeping into Denmark for over a century, brought by Frankish missionaries (Ansgar in the 820s) and Christian merchants in the trading towns.

By the 960s, Harald was under increasing pressure from the Holy Roman Empire (the German-led successor to Charlemagne's empire, then under Otto I) to convert his country, partly because Otto wanted to claim suzerainty over Denmark and a pagan kingdom was a legal target for crusade.

Harald accepted baptism around 965 — the Saxon historian Widukind tells a vivid story about how a missionary named Poppo proved the Christian God's superiority by carrying a red-hot iron in his bare hand without injury, which convinced Harald, though the story is conventional and occurs in many medieval conversion narratives.
Harald commemorated his reign and Denmark's conversion with one of the most extraordinary monuments of the Viking Age: the Jelling Stones at the royal cult site of Jelling in central Jutland.
Harald's father Gorm had erected an earlier, smaller runestone there for his queen Thyra.

Harald topped his father's monument with a much larger one — a great runestone about ten feet (3 m) tall, on three faces of which is carved (in beautifully executed Viking-era runic script) the inscription: "King Harald ordered these monuments made in memory of Gorm his father and Thyra his mother.
That Harald who won for himself all of Denmark and Norway, and made the Danes Christian." On one face is carved a writhing serpent-and-lion battle scene (a Viking animal style of high quality).
On another face is carved one of the earliest depictions of Christ in Scandinavia — Christ outstretched against a tangle of vines, simultaneously crucified and triumphant.

The Jelling Stone is, in effect, Denmark's baptismal certificate: a public state monument announcing the country's conversion, in the language of pagan runestones, with Christian imagery, planted in the old royal pagan cult site, by the king who unified the country.
It is a propaganda masterpiece, and it works as a propaganda masterpiece a thousand years later: tourist buses still stop there.
Harald's son Sweyn Forkbeard (Sveinn Tjúguskegg) revolted against Harald around 986 and exiled him; Harald died of his wounds the same year.
Sweyn was a more pragmatic Christian than his father and a more aggressive king.
He would, two decades later, become the first Danish ruler of England.
Norway went next, less peacefully.
Olaf Tryggvason (995–1000), a great-grandson of Harald Fairhair, returned from a youth of raiding in the Baltic and the British Isles and seized the Norwegian crown.

Olaf had been baptized in England (probably in 994, following a major Viking raid that ended in a peace and a Christianization deal with the English king Æthelred) and he came home a fervent and violent convert.

Over a five-year reign he campaigned across Norway forcibly Christianizing region after region — destroying pagan temples, killing recalcitrant chieftains, threatening farmers with mutilation if they refused baptism.
He founded the city of Trondheim as a new Christian Norwegian capital.
And he sponsored conversion missions to Iceland, Greenland, and the Faroes from his court.
Olaf was a Christian crusader-king in the literal sense, and his campaigns were ferocious enough to leave a permanent mark on Norwegian historical memory.
He died at the Battle of Svolder in 1000, betrayed and ambushed by a coalition of Danish, Swedish, and Norwegian rivals, leaping into the Baltic in his armor rather than be captured.
His campaigns had succeeded in Christianizing the coastal regions; the inland Norwegian valleys would take another generation.
Olaf's successor as Christian crusader-king of Norway was his (probably distant) kinsman Olaf Haraldsson (1015–1028, later canonized as Saint Olaf).

The second Olaf was a more systematic ruler and a more brutal Christianizer than the first — he sent missionaries (or warbands) into the inland valleys to destroy idols and force baptism, codified the first Norwegian Christian laws, and consolidated royal authority around the new church.

He was overthrown by a coalition of Norwegian chieftains backed by Cnut the Great of Denmark in 1028, fled east into exile, returned with an army to reclaim his throne, and was killed at the Battle of Stiklestad on July 29, 1030.
Stiklestad was a tactical defeat that became a strategic victory.
Within a year, miracles were being reported at Olaf's grave.
Within a generation, he had been declared a saint — Norway's first and only national patron saint.

The cult of Saint Olaf spread rapidly across Scandinavia, the Norse diaspora, and as far as the Anglo-Saxon and Russian churches; medieval pilgrim routes across Norway converged on his shrine at Nidaros Cathedral (NEE-dah-ros, the medieval name for Trondheim, where Olaf's body was eventually interred).
The man who had fought to impose Christianity by force became, in death, the saint whose cult sealed the conversion he had tried to win in life.

The mechanism is not unique — the same dynamic created the cult of Edmund the Martyr in England — but it is one of the cleanest examples of how a violent Christianization could eventually become a beloved national identity.
Iceland converted in 1000, and the Icelandic conversion is one of the most remarkable in religious history because it was accomplished by a single act of constitutional procedure.

By the 990s, Iceland was split between an increasingly large Christian minority (converts from voyages abroad, contacts with Norway, missionaries sent by Olaf Tryggvason) and a still-dominant pagan majority.
The two factions were on the edge of civil war.
Pagan and Christian Icelanders refused to honor each other's legal proceedings.
Marriages were collapsing along religious lines.
Olaf Tryggvason was holding Icelandic hostages at his court in Norway and threatening to refuse trade to a non-Christian Iceland.
In the summer of 1000, the Althing met at Þingvellir under enormous pressure.

The Lawspeaker that year was Þorgeirr Ljósvetningagoði (THOR-gay-ir LYOSS-vet-nings-go-thee, "Thorgeir the Priest of the People of Light-Lake"), a respected pagan chieftain. Þorgeirr was asked, by both sides, to render a judgment that would prevent the country from breaking apart.
He withdrew under his fur cloak, lay down on the grass, and refused to speak or move for a day and a night. (No one knows what he was doing under the cloak.
The traditional Christian interpretation is that he was praying or meditating.

The traditional pagan interpretation is that he was performing útiseta, "outside-sitting," a Norse divinatory practice in which a person sat outside in silent communion with spirits to receive guidance.
Modern scholars cannot say which it was.) When Þorgeirr emerged from the cloak, he announced his ruling: Iceland would adopt Christianity as its public religion.
All Icelanders would be baptized.
Public pagan worship would cease.
But — and this was the brilliance — private pagan practice would be tolerated.
People could still worship the old gods at home, eat horse meat (a pagan ritual food banned by the church), and expose unwanted infants (a pagan custom that the church banned in principle).
The compromise gave the Christian faction the public victory it needed and gave the pagan faction time to convert organically.
Iceland was therefore Christianized by parliamentary vote in 1000, brokered by a pagan Lawspeaker, with pragmatic concessions on both sides, with no executions, no battles, and no martyrs.
The Icelandic conversion is the cleanest, most procedural, and least violent religious transformation of the Viking Age.

It is also, not coincidentally, the conversion that most thoroughly preserved the cultural memory of the pagan past — Iceland would, three centuries later, produce the Eddas and the sagas, the documents in which Norse mythology survives.
The country that converted gently kept its old stories.
The countries that converted by sword forgot more.
Sweden held out longest.
The Swedish royal kingdom did not formally Christianize until the early 11th century under Olof Skötkonung (995–1022), the first Swedish king to be baptized (around 1008).
But pagan practice persisted at the great central temple at Uppsala for another seventy years, into the 1080s, when the temple was finally destroyed and replaced by a Christian church.
The Swedes are a useful reminder that the Viking-Age conversion was not a single switch.
It was a long, regional, generation-by-generation process, and pockets of organized paganism survived until well after the conventional 1066 end-date of the Viking Age.
The conversion mattered in concrete ways beyond the religious.

Christianity brought writing — the Latin alphabet replaced runes for serious documentation, kings began to issue charters and laws, monasteries became centers of literacy, and Iceland in particular took to the new technology with extraordinary energy.

Christianity brought stone churches, which were built on top of old pagan cult sites in a pattern repeated all across Scandinavia (the present-day cathedrals of Lund, Trondheim, and Uppsala all sit on or next to old pagan sacred sites).

Christianity brought diplomatic respectability: a Christian Norse king could marry a Christian Frankish princess, sign treaties with Christian kingdoms as a recognized political peer, and integrate his kingdom into the broader European political order.
The conversion was, in part, a process of accreditation.
To be Christian was to be admitted to the diplomatic club of Latin Christendom.
The Norse were tired of being outside it.

Cross-civ check: the great Norse conversion window (~960–1030) overlaps with the Cluniac monastic reform movement in Latin Christendom (the great spiritual renewal centered on Cluny in Burgundy that would shape European church politics for two centuries), the Buyid rule of Baghdad (Persian Empire Ch 9), the Song dynasty's founding in China (960), the Fatimid Caliphate at the height of its power in Cairo, and the Toltec ascendancy in central Mexico.
Iceland's conversion of 1000 happened in the same year that Leif Erikson reached Vinland and that the Hungarian king Stephen I was crowned a Christian king of Hungary by the Pope.
The whole western edge of the steppe and Atlantic worlds was being absorbed into Latin Christendom in the same generation.
The Vikings' century-long conversion was one front of a continental religious shift.

chapters.title: Skalds, Sagas, Runes
sentences: The Vikings were the most prolific creators of vernacular written texts in early-medieval Europe.
That sentence is almost the opposite of what most people assume.
The popular image is of a non-literate culture, an oral world of beardy men shouting at each other across mead-halls.

The reality is that Viking-Age Scandinavia produced more written texts in the local language — runestones, runic inscriptions on small objects, runic graffiti, eddic and skaldic poetry preserved in later writing — than any other corner of Europe in the same period.
Latin Christendom in 900 wrote almost nothing in the vernacular; everything serious was in Latin.
The Vikings, lacking Latin and lacking the political will to use it, wrote in their own language, in their own script, on their own surfaces.
This chapter is about that body of text.

There are three traditions to cover: runestones (monumental writing on stone), skaldic poetry (formal court verse, oral, transmitted by memory through generations of professional poets), and eddic poetry (anonymous mythological and heroic verse, also oral, eventually written down in Iceland after the conversion).
Each is a distinct technology of cultural memory.
Together, they constitute one of the most distinctive vernacular literary traditions of the Middle Ages.
Runes were the writing system of the Norse and other Germanic peoples.
The earliest runic inscriptions, in the Elder Futhark alphabet of 24 characters, date from around 150 CE — five centuries before the Viking Age proper.
By the early Viking Age, the runic alphabet had been simplified and reformed into the Younger Futhark of 16 characters (the reform happened in stages around 700–800 CE).

The Younger Futhark was an awkward writing system on purpose: 16 characters had to do the work of representing all the sounds of Old Norse, which meant some runes did double duty (the same rune for p and b, for example), and reading a runic inscription required context to disambiguate.
The reform made the runes faster to carve but harder to read.

A runestone is a memorial monument: a standing stone, typically 5 to 10 feet (1.5–3 m) tall, carved with a runic inscription that commemorates a person — usually a male relative who has died abroad — and frequently mentions the journey he was on when he died.

The classic runestone formula is: "X had this stone raised in memory of Y his [son/brother/comrade], who died in [foreign location]." Sweden has the largest single concentration of Viking-Age runestones — over 2,500 of them, the great majority erected between about 950 and 1100.
They cluster in the Lake Mälaren region around modern Stockholm, the heartland of the Swedish commercial elite who sent their younger sons east to the Volga and to Constantinople.
The runestones are an extraordinary body of social-historical evidence.

They tell us where Norsemen went (the inscriptions name Garðaríki — Russia; Miklagarðr — "the Great City," Constantinople; Serkland — the Caliphate; Englaland — England; Langbarðaland — the Lombard country, northern Italy), they tell us how they died (in battle, by drowning, by treachery), they tell us about family structures (women erecting stones for husbands, mothers for sons, brothers for brothers, sometimes joint stones for a whole family), and they tell us about the early reach of Christianity (later runestones often have crosses carved into them and end with prayers for the soul of the deceased).

The Rök runestone in Östergötland, Sweden, carved around 800, contains the longest known runic inscription — about 760 characters, on all five faces of the stone, in a mix of standard runes and several encrypted runic ciphers.
The inscription was raised by a man named Varin in memory of his dead son Vaemod, and it references heroic legends, ancient kings, and what appears to be a riddle or cryptographic challenge.
Modern scholars have argued for decades over the meaning.

Recent interpretations have suggested that the inscription is responding to a climate catastrophe — possibly the Late Antique Little Ice Age of 536 onward — by invoking ancestral heroes against renewed climatic anxiety.
Whatever its meaning, the Rök stone is the most ambitious piece of Viking-Age vernacular literature surviving on a non-perishable medium.

The Jelling Stone (Chapter 5) is the most politically loaded runestone — Harald Bluetooth's monument to his own kingship and Denmark's conversion, with its trilingual visual program of runic inscription, animal-style serpent-art, and Christian crucifixion imagery.

The Berezan' runestone, found on a small island at the mouth of the Dnieper in the Black Sea, was raised by a Swede named Grani in memory of his comrade Karl, who died on the way home from a Byzantine expedition.

The Berezan' stone is, in geographic terms, the southernmost Viking-Age runestone yet found, and it nicely illustrates the eastern Norse reach: a Swedish memorial inscription, in Old Norse runes, on a Black Sea island within sight of the Anatolian coast.
The complete runestone corpus — about 6,000 inscriptions across Scandinavia and the Norse diaspora — is one of the largest bodies of vernacular epigraphy from any pre-modern European culture.
The Vikings did not have parchment manuscripts.
They had stones, and they made the stones speak.
Skaldic poetry (skáldskapr, SKAHLD-skahpr, "the craft of skalds") is the strangest, densest, and most technically demanding tradition of court poetry produced in any medieval European vernacular.
A skald was a professional court poet — usually Icelandic by the late Viking Age, since Iceland produced the great majority of skalds — attached to a king's or chieftain's hall.
The skald composed praise-poems for the patron, commemorating his battles, his ancestry, his generosity, and his enemies.
Skaldic poetry was paid; a successful skald received gold rings, weapons, ships, and land in exchange for verses.
It was also performed, at feasts and assemblies, in front of the warband.
A successful praise-poem was retold for generations and could establish or destroy a king's posthumous reputation.
The political stakes were real.
What makes skaldic verse extraordinary is its formal density.

The standard meter, dróttkvætt ("court-meter"), is one of the most metrically constrained poetic forms ever devised: Each stanza has eight lines Each line has six syllables Lines pair into couplets, with strict rules about which syllables alliterate with which (the alliteration patterns are mathematical) Internal rhymes within each line follow further strict rules (full-rhyme in even lines, half-rhyme in odd lines) The grammar is freely word-orderable to fit the meter, which means a skaldic stanza is often syntactically scrambled almost beyond recognition; understanding it requires unscrambling the word order On top of this, the lexicon is dominated by kennings — compound metaphorical descriptors that substitute for ordinary words.
A kenning is a two-element noun phrase that names something obliquely.

Some examples: "the whale-road" — the sea "the swan-bath" — the sea "the storm of swords" — battle "the fire of arms" — gold "the feeder of ravens" — a warrior (because warriors leave corpses for ravens to eat) "Odin's mead" — poetry (from the myth in which Odin steals the mead of poetic inspiration from a giant) "the sky of the helmet" — the head "the icicle of blood" — a sword Many kennings are nested: a sword is "the icicle of blood" or "the fire of arms," but in a kenning chain it might become "the icicle-of-blood storm" (battle), and a warrior in that battle might be "the feeder of the icicle-of-blood storm's swans" (the swans of battle being ravens, the feeder being the warrior).
A complex skaldic stanza may contain six or seven kennings, all packed into 48 syllables, with the word order scrambled and the syntax distributed across multiple metrical clauses.
Reading skaldic verse is a three-step process: unscramble the syntax, decode the kennings, identify what they refer to.
A trained 11th-century skald could compose this on the spot in the patron's hall, and a trained audience could follow it.
Why this density?
Two reasons.

First, the formal difficulty was the point — skaldic verse was an explicit display of intellectual mastery, a way for a poet to demonstrate that he had spent years memorizing the Norse mythological corpus (because every kenning depended on the listener knowing the relevant myth) and the technical rules.
A bad skald couldn't compose a single stanza.
A good skald could improvise.

Second, the density made memorization easier in a particular way: the alliteration and internal rhyme constraints were so rigid that a memorized stanza could only be reconstructed in one form, which meant the verses could be transmitted orally across generations without textual corruption.
Skaldic poems composed in the 9th century were still being recited in the same wording in the 13th century, and the metrical lock made it possible.
The form is the preservation technology.

The most famous skald — the one whose life and work the Icelandic sagas would later celebrate — was Egill Skallagrímsson (EH-gil skahl-ah-GREEMS-son, c. 910–990), a 10th-century Icelander who was simultaneously a fearsome warrior, a savage berserker, an awkward man, a tender father, a devoted son, and the greatest poetic genius of his generation.
Egill killed his first man at age seven (over a children's ball game, according to his saga).
He raided across the Baltic and England.

He composed a legendary praise-poem called Höfuðlausn ("Head-Ransom") for his enemy King Erik Bloodaxe of York in a single night to save his own life — Egill had been captured by Erik, was due to be executed in the morning, and bought his head back with one of the great poems in the language.
He also composed Sonatorrek ("On the Loss of My Sons"), a long lyric lament after the deaths of two of his sons, including drowning.
Sonatorrek is one of the most personally moving poems in early-medieval European literature.
Egil's Saga, written by Snorri Sturluson around 1230 from oral tradition and surviving Egill verses, is one of the masterpieces of the saga tradition.
Egill is the proof of concept of the Norse poet-warrior: the same hands that swung the axe wrote the lyrics.

The eddic poems are different in character: anonymous, mythological, narrative, in much simpler meters than skaldic verse, transmitted orally and finally written down in Iceland in the late Viking and post-Viking period.
The Codex Regius (Chapter 5) preserves about 30 eddic poems, covering Norse mythology and heroic legend.

The major mythological poems include: Völuspá ("The Prophecy of the Seeress"), the great cosmological poem in which a dead seeress, summoned by Odin, recites the entire history of the cosmos from creation to Ragnarök and the new world afterward.
Völuspá is the single best literary source for Norse cosmology.

Hávamál ("Sayings of the High One"), Odin's collected wisdom — a long string of proverbs, runic lore, courtship advice, and reflections on mortality, including the section in which Odin describes his self-sacrifice on Yggdrasil to learn the runes.

Vafþrúðnismál ("Sayings of Vafthruthnir"), a wisdom-contest between Odin and a giant. Þrymskviða ("The Lay of Thrym"), the comic-mythological story of how Thor recovered his hammer from the giants by dressing up as the goddess Freyja and going through with a fake wedding.
Lokasenna ("Loki's Quarrel"), in which Loki crashes a feast of the gods and insults each of them in turn, revealing scandals and weaknesses.

The heroic poems of the Codex Regius retell stories from the broader Germanic legendary tradition — the Volsungs, Sigurd the dragon-slayer, Brynhild the valkyrie, Atli (Attila the Hun) — and these stories would be reworked by other Germanic-speaking peoples into the German Nibelungenlied and ultimately, twelve centuries later, into Wagner's Ring Cycle.
The Norse versions are older and stranger and contain the rawer version of the cycle.
The eddic poems are the foundation document of Norse mythology.
Without them, we would know the Norse gods only from outsider sources (Adam of Bremen and the like) and from kennings in skaldic verse.
The Codex Regius is the reason we can talk about Yggdrasil and the Nine Worlds and Ragnarök at all.

The third great Norse literary tradition — the Icelandic family sagas — is technically post-Viking-Age, written in the 12th and 13th centuries (after the conversion, after the Latin alphabet, after the establishment of monastic scriptoria in Iceland), but its subject is the Viking Age proper, and its authors were drawing on living oral tradition that ran continuously from the Settlement period to their own day.

The Icelandic family sagas are anonymous prose narratives — typically novel-length, in cool, terse, dialogue-heavy realist prose — that recount the lives of Icelandic chieftain families across the 9th, 10th, and 11th centuries.

The most famous include Egil's Saga (about Egill Skallagrímsson, mentioned above), Njál's Saga (a sweeping multigenerational epic of feud and burning), Laxdæla Saga (a tragic love-and-feud story centered on a powerful matriarch, Gudrun Osvifsdottir), The Saga of the Volsungs, and the so-called Vinland Sagas — The Saga of the Greenlanders and The Saga of Erik the Red — which together describe the Norse voyages to Vinland that we covered in Chapter 3.
The sagas are extraordinary literature.
They are written in a calm, distancing, almost cinematic prose that lets the reader judge character through action rather than authorial commentary.

They are interested in the pressure-points of small communities: feuds that smolder for decades, marriages that fail across multigenerational fault lines, the way an oath made by a grandfather binds a grandson into a killing he doesn't want to do.
They contain dialogue that feels modern.

They contain character drawing of a sophistication that Western European literature would not match for another four centuries — the next time you find anything like the psychological realism of Njál's Saga in European prose, you are in 17th-century France.
Are they reliable history?

The sagas were written 200 to 350 years after the events they describe, by Christian authors working in a literate court culture, drawing on long oral tradition that had certainly been reshaped along the way.
The skeleton of named characters, family lines, and major events is largely confirmed by other sources (the runestones, the Landnámabók, foreign chronicles).
The dialogue, the small-scale politics, and the precise sequences of events are partly oral memory and partly artful reconstruction.

Modern scholars treat the sagas as a unique blend of remembered tradition, family lore, written record, and outright literary invention — useful, beautiful, but never to be cited as straightforward fact.

They are the medieval Norse equivalent of historical novels: full of real people and real places, written about a period the author never lived through, and impossible to fully separate from the author's imagination.

The body of saga literature is enormous — approximately 40 family sagas, dozens of legendary sagas, the great kings' sagas (Snorri's Heimskringla — the saga of the Norwegian kings — runs to over 800 pages), and a series of bishops' sagas, contemporary sagas, and shorter tales.

By volume of vernacular prose produced relative to population, Iceland in 1200 outproduced any European country; the only comparable medieval vernacular literary corpus is the Arabic literary explosion of the same period.
So: the Vikings wrote, and what they wrote was distinctive.
Runestones for monumental memorialization.
Skaldic verse for political praise and personal display.
Eddic poetry for the mythological canon.
Sagas (later) for family memory and historical reconstruction.

The whole package is the literature of a culture that took oral tradition seriously as a technology — that built memorization aids into its meter, that used public stones as memorials when manuscripts were unavailable, and that, when manuscripts finally became available, produced a vernacular prose literature that the rest of medieval Europe would not match for centuries.
The popular image of the Viking as a non-literate brute is exactly backwards.
The Viking world was built around words.
The words just weren't in Latin.

Cross-civ check: the body of Norse vernacular literature (~800–1300) overlaps with the Tang and Song Chinese poetic traditions (the great age of Chinese lyric, when Li Bai and Du Fu and Su Shi are writing); the classical Persian poetry of Ferdowsi (whose Shahnameh, completed around 1010, is roughly contemporary with the Eddic poems' likely composition); the Arabic poetic golden age of the Abbasid court; and the late Sanskrit court poetry of medieval India.

The Norse tradition's distinctiveness is not its existence — every literate culture had court poetry — but its medium (runic stone, oral memorization rather than parchment) and its formal density (skaldic dróttkvætt is in a class of its own).

chapters.title: The North Sea Empire and the Long Reach
sentences: In December 1013, the Anglo-Saxon king of England, Æthelred II (often nicknamed "the Unready" — actually a mistranslation; the Old English unræd means "ill-counseled" or "no-counsel," a pun on his name Æþelræd, "noble counsel"), fled to Normandy with his wife Emma and their children.
The kingdom he was abandoning had just been conquered by the Danish king Sweyn Forkbeard.

Three years later, in 1016, Sweyn's son Cnut (the Anglicized form of Old Norse Knútr, KNOOT, often written Canute in older English) finalized the conquest, defeating the brief revival of Anglo-Saxon resistance under Æthelred's son Edmund Ironside.
Cnut would rule England until 1035.
He would also, simultaneously, rule Denmark (from his father's inheritance) and Norway (after he conquered it from Olaf Haraldsson in 1028).

For a period of roughly seven years — 1028 to 1035 — Cnut was king of England, Denmark, and Norway at once, the ruler of the North Sea Empire, the most extensive single political unit ever to have a Norse-speaking ruler.
He was not just a great Viking.
He was, briefly, an emperor.
How did the Viking Age get from a 793 monastery raid to a 1016 multi-kingdom monarchy?

Through about a hundred years of consolidating Scandinavian state formation, escalating Danegeld payments out of England, and a Norse military-economic complex that was both more sophisticated and more brutal than the early raiding period.
To get to 1016 we have to back up and walk through the century in order.

The chapter follows that order: first the trading towns that made the Norse rich (the 800s), then the new Scandinavian states that organized them (the late 900s), then the second great wave of attacks on England (the 990s and 1000s), then Cnut's North Sea Empire (1016–1035).
The thread running through all four scenes is the same — silver, slaves, and the gradual replacement of warband chieftains by territorial kings.
Scene one: the trading towns, 800s onward.
Long before Cnut, the economic muscle of Viking-Age Scandinavia was concentrated in a small number of trading towns that formed the commercial backbone of the entire diaspora.
Three of these matter most.
Hedeby (HAY-deh-bee, also called Haithabu) was the largest.

Located at the southern end of the Jutland peninsula at the head of the Schlei fjord, in what is now the German state of Schleswig-Holstein, Hedeby sat at the geographic chokepoint where North Sea trade met Baltic trade.
The Danish king Godfred relocated merchants there from the trading town of Reric in 808 to consolidate Danish commercial control of the region; the move is recorded in the Frankish royal annals.

Hedeby grew within a century into a town of perhaps 1,500 to 2,000 permanent residents (a large town by 9th-century European standards), with a defensive semicircular rampart, a network of plank-paved streets, hundreds of pit-houses and craft workshops, and a harbor ringed with quays.

Hedeby produced glass beads, comb-makers' wares, iron tools, leather goods, and silver ornaments at a quasi-industrial scale, and it brokered exchange between the Frankish-Carolingian commercial sphere, the Norse Baltic, and (via the Russian rivers) the Islamic world.

The Arab traveler At-Tartushi — a 10th-century Andalusian merchant whose surviving travelogue is one of the few outside descriptions of a Norse town — visited Hedeby in the 960s and left a horrified account: a noisy pagan town where wives could initiate divorce, women wore their eyes painted with kohl, and the inhabitants held a great seasonal feast in honor of Sirius (probably the autumn blót) at which they sacrificed cattle, dogs, and the occasional human being to honor their gods.
He thought the town was awful.
He also thought it was unprecedentedly large for a Northern European settlement.
Birka in central Sweden, founded around 750 on a small island in Lake Mälaren about 18 miles (30 km) west of modern Stockholm, was the eastern counterpart to Hedeby.
Birka sat where the Baltic met the inland Swedish lake system and the headwaters of the trade routes east.
It handled Slavic, Frisian, Arab, Anglo-Saxon, and Norse goods.

Excavations of Birka cemeteries have produced thousands of graves containing Abbasid silver, Byzantine silks, Frankish swords, Anglo-Saxon coins, and Slavic pottery — a single woman's grave may contain artifacts from four distinct cultural zones thousands of miles apart.
Birka was where the Volga route emptied into the Baltic.

Its decline began around 970, probably because of shifting trade routes after the collapse of the Khazar Khaganate — a Turkic-Jewish steppe kingdom on the lower Volga that had been the gatekeeper of the Volga trade route for centuries.
The Rus' prince Svyatoslav destroyed Khazaria in 968, after which the Volga route became less stable and the silver dirham flow began to dry up.
The end of the Khazars killed Birka.
The Swedish trading center moved to Sigtuna, a more inland, more Christian site, around 980.
Dublin (Old Norse Dyflinn) was the largest western Norse town and the linchpin of the Norse-Irish slave economy.

By 950 it had a population of perhaps 5,000 — making it one of the largest cities in Atlantic Europe — surrounded by an earthen rampart, with a planned street grid, a working harbor, and a permanent slave market.
The economic rationale of Dublin was specific and grim: Norse warbands raided Irish, Scottish, English, and Welsh coasts and brought captives to the Dublin market.

Slaves were sold to Norse-Icelandic colonists (who needed labor for their farms), to Norse-Irish dynasties (who used them domestically and on land), to Continental European buyers, and — in the largest numbers — to merchants going east to feed the Islamic and Byzantine slave markets.
The Dublin slave trade ran for nearly two centuries, from the 840s through the 1100s, and it was central to Viking Age economics.

Dublin slave market had become a bottleneck institution: Norse fleets concentrated their captives there, Norse buyers arrived there, Continental and Mediterranean traders came there, and a single price-setting mechanism formed for human beings across the entire Norse commercial zone.
This is not the Vikings as romantic seafarers.
This is the Vikings as the operators of one of the most efficient slave markets in early-medieval Europe.

A note on the slave economy that the cartoon-Viking image leaves out: a substantial fraction — by some recent estimates one quarter to one third — of the founding population of Iceland was descended from female slaves taken in raids on Britain and Ireland.

Genetic studies of modern Icelanders have found that about 60% of their female-line mitochondrial DNA traces back to women from the British Isles, while about 75% of their male-line Y-chromosome DNA traces back to Norway.
The implication is straightforward and brutal: the Norse men who settled Iceland brought with them, in large numbers, women who had not chosen to come.
The whole demography of Iceland is a population built on a slave-taking economy.
The same dynamic operated, on smaller scales, throughout the Norse Atlantic.
The rings of gold buried in chieftains' graves across the Viking world were, in part, monetized human beings.
The Dublin slave economy also functioned as the Atlantic mirror of an older Mediterranean pattern.

The Phoenician city of Carthage had run Mediterranean slave hubs from about 800 BCE onward (Phoenicia Ch 7); a thousand years later, Dublin became the equivalent maritime entrepôt for the northern waters, fed by raid networks and feeding the Islamic and Byzantine markets via the Volga route.
Different sea, different century, same business model: a fortified port with a harbor, a market, a price-setting authority, and a hinterland of raiders.
Scene two: state formation, 950–980.
By the second half of the 10th century, the wealth flowing back from the trading towns and the raids was hitting Scandinavia hard enough to reshape its politics.

State formation was driven by three overlapping forces: the wealth coming back from raids and trade, the military pressure of unified neighbors (the Holy Roman Empire to the south, the Anglo-Saxon kingdom to the west, the Rus' to the east), and the unifying institutional infrastructure of Christianity (Chapter 5).
Around 950–980, three large new royal projects took form.

In Denmark, Harald Bluetooth consolidated central royal authority not just by accepting Christianity (Chapter 5), but by undertaking some of the most ambitious public-works projects in Viking-Age Scandinavia.

Around 975–980 he ordered the construction of a network of identical ring fortresses across Denmark — at Trelleborg, Fyrkat, Aggersborg, Nonnebakken, and Borgring — each a perfectly circular ramparted enclosure laid out with breathtaking geometric precision: identical diameters (ranging from 460 to 790 feet, 140 to 240 m), identical four-quadrant interiors with identical longhouse barracks arranged in symmetric squares, identical four-gate cardinal-direction entrances, identical proportional ratios between rampart, ditch, and inner courtyard.
The ring fortresses were laid out by people who shared a single architectural plan and the precise instruments to execute it.
They are unique in early-medieval Europe: nobody else was building anything like them.
