Whether they were primarily royal garrison strongpoints, military training centers for the conscript-based Danish royal levy, or central-place administrative nodes is debated.
What is not debated is what they signal: a Danish kingdom capable of organized statecraft on a scale no previous Norse polity had achieved.
Denmark in 980 was the first Scandinavian country with a real state.
The ring fortresses are its concrete signature.
In Norway, the state-formation work begun by Harald Fairhair (Chapter 3) was completed, in fits and starts, by the two Saint Olafs, by Magnus the Good (1035–1047), and by Harald Hardrada (1046–1066).
By the mid-11th century Norway had a unified crown, a Christian church, a developing cathedral system, and increasingly written laws.
It was no longer a patchwork of fjord-kingdoms.
In Sweden, the consolidation was slowest.
The royal authority around the great cult site at Uppsala remained nominally pagan, regionally limited, and informal in structure until the late 11th century.
Sweden was the last Scandinavian country to fully Christianize, the last to develop a centralized monarchy, and the last to produce written laws.
Scene three: the second wave on England, 980s–1016.
The new Scandinavian states were better-organized than their predecessors, and what they organized first was a renewed assault on England.
The second great wave of attacks, beginning in the 980s, produced the largest sustained tribute extraction in early-medieval European history.

By the time Æthelred II came to the English throne in 978 (at age 12, after his half-brother Edward had been murdered, probably with the connivance of Æthelred's mother — a fact that haunted Æthelred's reign), the political situation had shifted.
Norse Scandinavia was no longer a patchwork of warbands.
It was producing organized royal armies funded and led by kings like Sweyn Forkbeard.
The English defenses, last seriously tested under Alfred a century earlier, had eroded.
The Anglo-Saxon fyrd (the regional militia levy) was slow to assemble and unevenly equipped.
The new Viking armies arriving in the 980s were faster, better-equipped, and operating with state backing.

The pattern repeated through the 990s and 1000s: a Danish or Norwegian fleet would arrive, raid coastal districts, defeat any local English force that came against it, and then accept a large Danegeld payment to leave.

The first major payment was 10,000 pounds (about 3,600 kg) of silver in 991, after the Vikings won the Battle of Maldon on the Essex coast — a battle commemorated in one of the great surviving Old English poems, The Battle of Maldon, which celebrated the heroic doomed defense of the English ealdorman Byrhtnoth (he died on the battlefield, his bodyguards refused to flee, and the poem makes their last stand into a meditation on loyalty: "Heart shall be the harder, mind the keener, courage the more, as our strength lessens").
The Danegeld payments escalated. 16,000 pounds in 994. 24,000 pounds in 1002. 36,000 pounds in 1007. 48,000 pounds in 1012.
By the end of Æthelred's reign, the English crown had paid out perhaps 250,000 pounds (90,000 kg) of silver to Viking armies — far more than the entire English royal annual revenue.
The economic damage was crushing.

The political damage was worse: every Danegeld payment confirmed that the English crown could not defend its own kingdom and that its subjects were paying a state tax to be transferred to its enemies.
This was, in mechanism, an old story playing out on a new sea.
Eleven hundred years earlier and four thousand miles to the east, the Han dynasty in China had faced exactly the same problem with the steppe nomads of the Xiongnu confederation (Xiongnu-Huns Ch 3).

After Han forces were humiliated at Baideng in 200 BCE, China settled into a system the Chinese called heqin — "harmonious kinship" — under which thousands of rolls of silk, large quantities of grain and gold, and an imperial princess every generation were sent north as tribute, in exchange for the chanyu's promise not to raid.
The Han paid heqin to the Xiongnu for nearly seven decades.
The English paid Danegeld to the Vikings for about three.

The settled-state arithmetic was identical: a wealthy agricultural kingdom, a fast-moving military culture that could appear anywhere along an enormous frontier, and a calculation that buying off the raiders was cheaper than fortifying every coast or border.

In both cases the calculation was wrong in the long run — heqin failed to stop Xiongnu raids, Danegeld did not stop Sweyn — and both societies eventually had to choose between conquest and being conquered.
The English chose poorly.
The most infamous moment of Æthelred's reign was the St.

Brice's Day Massacre on November 13, 1002. Æthelred, infuriated by the ongoing Danish raids and apparently fearing a fifth-column rising by the Danish settler population in eastern England, ordered the killing of all Danes within his kingdom on St.
Brice's day.
The chronicles report that the order was executed in some places with appalling thoroughness — at Oxford, Danes who took refuge in St.
Frideswide's church were burned alive in it.

The number of dead is unknowable; estimates range from a few hundred to many thousands, and the order was probably enforced unevenly across England (in the Danelaw itself, where the Danish-descended population was the majority, it was largely ignored; in Wessex and the south, where Danes were a vulnerable minority, it appears to have been carried out).
One of the people killed in the massacre was Gunhilde, the sister of Sweyn Forkbeard of Denmark.
This was the trigger.

Sweyn launched a sustained war of conquest against England that ran from 1003 to his death in early 1014. Æthelred fled to Normandy in 1013 (where his marriage to Emma of Normandy, sister of the Norman duke, proved consequential — that connection was the legal basis for William of Normandy's later claim to the English throne, Chapter 8).
Sweyn died unexpectedly in February 1014, just weeks after being acclaimed king of England, and Æthelred briefly returned, but the situation was hopeless.
Sweyn's son Cnut, then about 19, finalized the conquest in 1016 after a year-long civil war against Æthelred's son Edmund Ironside (so nicknamed for his armored ferocity).
Edmund was killed (or possibly murdered) in November 1016, and Cnut became king of all England.
Scene four: Cnut and the North Sea Empire, 1016–1035.
Cnut, ruling England from 1016 and Denmark from 1018 (after the death of his elder brother Harald), was a different kind of Viking king.
He was barely a Viking at all in the raiding sense.

He was a Christian (he had been baptized as a youth), he was politically sophisticated (he kept many of the existing English administrative structures, retained many Anglo-Saxon nobles in positions of power, and married Æthelred's widow Emma of Normandy as a matter of statecraft, neutralizing both her Norman family and her sons by Æthelred), and he was a serious participant in mainland European politics.
He attended the imperial coronation of the Holy Roman Emperor Conrad II in Rome in 1027 and walked away with formal acknowledgments of Danish royal status.
He minted his own coins in England with a sophisticated minting infrastructure inherited from the Anglo-Saxon state.
He governed England through a system of earldoms — large regional governorships — that consolidated previous arrangements.
He was, in short, a competent king of a Christian kingdom, not a free-ranging raider.
In 1028, Cnut conquered Norway from Olaf Haraldsson (Chapter 5), adding the Norwegian crown to his portfolio.
At this point — for about seven years, 1028 to 1035 — he was simultaneously king of England, Denmark, and Norway, plus suzerain of parts of Sweden and Pomerania.
The North Sea Empire was a real political entity, with Cnut as its central ruler, governed by a system of earls, regional kings, and personal loyalty oaths.
It was the largest state ever built around a Norse-speaking core.
It also did not last.
Cnut died in 1035 at age 40.
His sons quarreled.
His Danish-English-Norwegian inheritance fragmented within seven years of his death.
By 1042, Edward the Confessor — Æthelred's son by Emma — had reclaimed the English crown.
By the same year, the Danish and Norwegian crowns had passed to other dynasties.
The North Sea Empire was a single-generation construction.
Its political infrastructure had not had time to outlast its founder.
But the precedent — that a single Norse-derived ruler could govern all the major Scandinavian and English territories at once — was a permanent fixture of European political imagination.
It was the closest thing Northern Europe had to a counterpart of the Carolingian Empire, and it was built by the great-grandson of a Viking pirate.
There is one more thread to pull before the final crisis of 1066.
In Norway, Cnut's Norwegian conquest was reversed by Olaf Haraldsson's son Magnus the Good (1035–1047), who succeeded Olaf as king of Norway.
Magnus shortly thereafter inherited the Danish throne in 1042 from Harthacnut (Cnut's son by Emma of Normandy and the last king of Cnut's English-Danish line, who died childless that year).

For a brief moment Norway and Denmark were united again under Magnus, and Magnus was preparing to invade England to claim Cnut's old crown when he died in 1047 — possibly from a riding accident, possibly poisoned.

Magnus was succeeded in Norway by his uncle, who had recently returned from the Varangian Guard in Constantinople with an enormous fortune, military experience that made him the most feared commander in Northern Europe, and a new nickname earned in his foreign service: Hardrada, "Hard-Counsel." This was the man who would, twenty years later, sail to Yorkshire to claim a kingdom and die under a hail of Saxon arrows on the bridge at Stamford.

Cross-civ check: the consolidation phase of Viking-Age Scandinavia (~960–1066) coincides with the Song dynasty stabilizing China after the Five Dynasties period (Song China would become the wealthiest single state on earth by 1100), the early Seljuk Turk expansion across Persia and Anatolia (Persian Empire Ch 9), the Fatimid Caliphate at the height of its Egyptian power, the Western Chalukya dynasty in southern India, the Cluniac monastic reform shaping Latin Christendom, and the early stages of the medieval European agricultural and demographic boom that would sustain the high Middle Ages.
Cnut's North Sea Empire was a peer of the Christian Holy Roman Empire and a player in the wider European order.

It was also an outlier — there would not be a comparable Northern European maritime empire under a Scandinavian ruler again until the Danish crowns of the late medieval period, and even those would be different in character.

chapters.title: The Year of Three Kings
sentences: In January 1066, the English king Edward the Confessor (the son of Æthelred II and Emma of Normandy, restored to the English throne in 1042 after the dissolution of Cnut's North Sea Empire) lay dying in Westminster, the new abbey he had built on a marshy island upriver from the City of London.
He had no children.
He had no obvious heir.

He had been a deeply religious, politically ineffective, and possibly celibate king who left the practical governance of his realm to a network of competing earls, the most powerful of whom — Harold Godwinson, Earl of Wessex — was the brother of Edward's queen Edith and was, by 1066, the de facto regent of England.

When Edward died on January 5, 1066, the Witenagemot (WITT-en-uh-geh-moht, the council of leading English nobles and bishops, the closest Anglo-Saxon institutional equivalent of a royal council) elected Harold Godwinson king of England the next day.
He was crowned at Westminster on January 6, the day Edward was buried.
The choice was contested before the crown was even on Harold's head.

There were three live claimants to the English throne in January 1066: Harold Godwinson himself, the new king, who had been chosen by the Witenagemot, was personally formidable, was the senior earl of the kingdom, and had been Edward's right-hand man for the previous decade.

Harald Hardrada of Norway, the former Varangian Guard commander, the most experienced military leader in Northern Europe, who based his claim on a tortuous chain of inheritance from the deceased Magnus the Good (who had been promised the English throne, in some accounts, by Harthacnut, the last king of Cnut's English line).
The claim was thin in legal terms.
Harald did not care; he had a fleet and an army, and he intended to take what he wanted.

William, Duke of Normandy (also called William the Bastard, and in the future William the Conqueror), great-grandson of the Viking Rollo — a Norse warlord granted the territory of Normandy by the Frankish king Charles the Simple in 911 in exchange for converting and defending the lower Seine.
Rollo's descendants had governed Normandy ever since, gradually assimilating into French language and culture while retaining Scandinavian dynastic memory.

William claimed that Edward had promised him the English throne during a 1051 visit, and that Harold Godwinson had personally sworn an oath in 1064 — under unusual and possibly coerced circumstances — to support William's claim.
The Norman version of this oath, depicted later in the Bayeux Tapestry, shows Harold swearing on a chest of holy relics.
The English version of events is silent or actively contradicts the Norman one.

Whatever the truth about whose claim was strongest in legal terms, William's reaction to Harold's coronation was unambiguous: Harold was an oath-breaker and a usurper, and William would take England by conquest if he had to.
Three men, three armies, one crown.
The year that followed was the climax of the Viking Age and the moment when it ended.
The first to move was Harald Hardrada.
In late summer 1066, Harald assembled a fleet of about 300 ships and roughly 9,000 men at the Solund Islands off the western coast of Norway.

He was joined by Tostig Godwinson — Harold Godwinson's exiled younger brother, who had been Earl of Northumbria until his subjects revolted against his harsh rule in 1065, who had been expelled from England, and who had spent the past year in Flanders and Scotland looking for foreign backing to restore him.
Tostig had visited Hardrada earlier in 1066 to propose a joint invasion.
The two men sailed together for England in early September.
The invasion fleet rounded Scotland, raided the northeast English coast, and landed in the Humber estuary around September 18.

Hardrada and Tostig advanced inland, defeated a hastily assembled English northern army at the Battle of Fulford on September 20 (just outside York, where the Earls Edwin of Mercia and Morcar of Northumbria — Harold Godwinson's brothers-in-law — were routed and probably suffered serious casualties), and accepted the surrender of York on September 24.
Hardrada's army was now in possession of the second-largest city in England and the political center of the old Viking Kingdom of York.
Harold Godwinson was in the south of England, watching the Channel for William's expected invasion.
The news from York reached him around September 21.
He moved fast.
He gathered his housecarls (his elite household troops) and the thanes of southern England, and force-marched north along the old Roman road.

The march was a logistical wonder of the period: roughly 200 miles (320 km) in five days, an average of 40 miles per day, possible only because much of the army was mounted and the road network through the East Midlands was Roman-built and well-maintained.
By September 24 — the same day York surrendered — Harold Godwinson and his force were entering Yorkshire.
He covered the last 8 miles to the village of Stamford Bridge on the morning of September 25.

Hardrada and Tostig had pulled most of their force back from York to a meeting point at Stamford Bridge, where they expected to receive hostages and tribute from the surrounding shires under the terms of York's surrender.
They were not expecting an army.
According to the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle and the much later (and more dramatic) Norse account in Heimskringla, many of the Norse troops had left their armor on the ships at Riccall, eight miles away.
It was a hot late-September day.
They were resting on the bank of the River Derwent.
They saw, in the distance, what looked like a glittering sheet of moving metal — the English army marching up the road in full armor.

The Battle of Stamford Bridge on September 25, 1066, is one of the great forgotten battles of European history because it would be eclipsed three weeks later by the more famous battle that decided the kingship.
But Stamford Bridge is, in its own way, the more telling of the two.
The English caught the Norse half-armored and divided.

There is a famous saga story of a single Norse warrior holding the wooden bridge over the Derwent against the entire English army for some time, killing forty Englishmen with an axe before being killed himself by an English soldier who floated under the bridge in a half-barrel and stabbed him from below.
Whether this story is true (it appears only in the later saga sources, not in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle) the bridge was eventually crossed.
The main battle on the eastern bank was a long, brutal, full-scale fight.
Harald Hardrada took an arrow through the throat early in the battle and died.
Tostig Godwinson was killed soon afterward.
The Norse army was annihilated.
Of the 300 ships that had come into the Humber, only about 24 were needed to carry the survivors home.
The Norwegian invasion of England was finished.

Harald Hardrada's body was buried in York, near the cathedral, in unconsecrated ground because of his pagan past — the Christian crusader-king of Norway, a Varangian Guard veteran of Constantinople, dead under a hail of English arrows in a Yorkshire pasture.
Stamford Bridge, September 25, 1066, is the battle conventionally dated as the end of the Viking Age.

The reasoning is not that it ended Norse activity — Norse polities would continue, Norse kings would rule, Norse colonies would persist for another four centuries — but that it ended the structural pattern of the Age: large Scandinavian armies launching seaborne invasions of major European kingdoms in pursuit of conquest.
Hardrada was the last great Viking conqueror of the classical model, and at Stamford Bridge he died a classical Viking death: spear, arrow, axe, in armored ranks on a meadow.
After Stamford Bridge, the Scandinavian kingdoms turned inward; the new model of European political competition was Norman feudal warfare, not Norse longship raiding.
The technology and the social structure of the longship-warband were obsolete.
But that judgment is in retrospect.
From the perspective of Harold Godwinson, lying in his battle camp in Yorkshire on the night of September 25, the Viking threat had just been crushed.
He had won.
He could go home.
Then a rider came from the south.
Three days earlier, on September 22, a tide change at the mouth of the Somme had finally favored a Norman invasion fleet that had been waiting weeks for the right wind.

William of Normandy had crossed the Channel with about 700 ships, 7,000 men, and 2,000 horses (a Norman cavalry-heavy army, a fundamentally different kind of force from anything the Vikings had ever fielded).
William's fleet had landed at Pevensey on the Sussex coast on September 28, three days after Stamford Bridge.

The Norman army had immediately moved up the coast to Hastings, where William fortified a base camp and began ravaging the surrounding countryside — burning villages, slaughtering livestock — to draw Harold south.
The strategy worked.
Harold Godwinson, two weeks after one of the great victories in English military history, had to march south over 250 miles (400 km) to face a fresh Norman army.
His own army was exhausted.
His housecarls had taken serious casualties at Stamford Bridge.
The southern fyrd had partially demobilized.
Many of his troops were not arriving in time.
But Harold had to act, because Norman raiding was destroying the southern English economy and the longer he waited, the worse the damage would be.

He left London around October 11 with whatever forces he could assemble and met William's army at a ridge called Senlac Hill about 7 miles (11 km) inland from Hastings on the morning of October 14, 1066.

The Battle of Hastings has been described in detail in dozens of sources — the Bayeux Tapestry, the Carmen de Hastingae Proelio (a Latin verse account written within a year or two of the battle, probably by a Norman bishop), William of Poitiers' biography of the Conqueror (William of Poitiers was a Norman cleric who had been in William's household and wrote his Gesta Guillelmi around 1071–1077, the closest thing to an authorized Norman version), the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, and the Latin chronicle of John of Worcester (a 12th-century English monk who compiled an annalistic history drawing on lost earlier sources, generally read as the most balanced of the surviving accounts).

The basic shape: English infantry holding a shield wall on the ridge, Norman cavalry repeatedly charging up the slope, neither side gaining decisive advantage through the morning, the Norman infantry and archers wearing down the English shield wall through the afternoon, the death of Harold Godwinson late in the day (an arrow through the eye, in the Bayeux Tapestry's famous depiction; possibly a hacking sword wound, in some textual accounts; possibly both) followed by the collapse of English resistance.
Harold's two younger brothers, Gyrth and Leofwine, also died on the field.
By dusk on October 14, William of Normandy was the master of the battlefield.
The whole defending core of the English aristocratic class was dead in two battles three weeks apart.
There was no replacement available.
By Christmas Day 1066, William had been crowned king of England in Westminster Abbey, on the same spot where Harold had been crowned eleven months earlier.
The Norman conquest of England was complete in formal terms; the consolidation of Norman rule across the country would take another five years of vicious provincial campaigns.

But England's Anglo-Saxon political class was effectively destroyed at Hastings, and over the next generation the Norman ruling class — speaking Norman French, building stone castles, holding land in feudal tenure — would entirely replace the Anglo-Saxon thane class as the governing stratum of English society.
This is the conquest that brings about three quarters of the French vocabulary in modern English.
It is also the conquest that ends the long Anglo-Saxon era and begins the medieval English kingdom.
The peculiar and wonderful irony is that William himself was a Viking.
Not in name or language, but in blood.

He was the great-great-great-grandson of Rollo — a Norse warlord who had taken Normandy from a Frankish king in 911, three generations before Cnut had taken England, ten generations before William's own reign.

The Norman aristocracy who would, after 1066, rule England were the assimilated descendants of Vikings who had settled the lower Seine, learned French, become Christians, adopted continental cavalry warfare, and reinvented themselves as a French knightly nobility while retaining a residual Norse dynastic identity.
The conquest that ended the Viking Age in England was led by a man whose ancestors had begun it.
The Viking world had folded in on itself. 1066 is the conventional end-date of the Viking Age.
It is a usefully clean date, and the events of that year do mark a real structural shift.
But it is worth taking a moment to look at what continued.
Iceland continued.

The Icelandic Free State persisted for another 196 years after Stamford Bridge — through the great age of saga writing in the 12th and 13th centuries, until the Sturlung-era civil wars drove the country into Norwegian royal hands in 1262.
The Norse colony in Greenland continued, perhaps for another 400 years; the lights only went out around 1450.

The Norse-Irish kingdoms of Dublin and the Irish-Sea world continued; Magnus Barefoot of Norway would mount the last serious Norse military expedition into the Irish Sea zone in 1098–1103, dying in an Irish ambush on Ulster's coast.

The Rus' continued — and in fact reached a peak under Yaroslav the Wise (1019–1054), who codified the Russkaya Pravda (the foundational law code of medieval Russia, modeled in part on Scandinavian and Byzantine legal traditions), built the Saint Sophia Cathedral in Kiev (modeled on Hagia Sophia in Constantinople), and forged dynastic alliances across Europe.
Yaroslav's daughters married the kings of France, Hungary, and Norway (Anne of Kiev became Queen of France; her signature in Old Cyrillic is still preserved on French royal documents).
The Rurikid dynasty would govern Russia until 1610.
Modern Russia is, in a real and unbroken sense, a downstream descendant of the eastern Norse expansion of the 9th century.
The Varangian Guard continued, though its character changed.
After Stamford Bridge, displaced Anglo-Saxon nobles fled east across the Channel, across Europe, and into Constantinople, where they joined the Guard alongside the Rus'-Norse component.
By 1100, the Varangian Guard was substantially Anglo-Saxon.
By 1300, the cultural identity had shifted.
The Guard finally dissolved when Constantinople fell in 1453 — having served the Byzantine emperors for 465 years, longer than the United States has existed.
Norman descendants of the Vikings continued conquering things long after 1066.
Other Norman warlords took Sicily and southern Italy from the Byzantines and Muslims in 1060–1130, founding the Norman Kingdom of Sicily.
Normans ran the First Crusade to Antioch in 1098.
Normans served as elite mercenaries across the Mediterranean.
The Viking diaspora's most successful descendants spent the next two centuries reshaping Mediterranean Europe.
So the end of the Viking Age is real but partial.
The seaborne raiding and conquest model ended at Stamford Bridge and Hastings.

The political, dynastic, and cultural legacies of the Norse expansion continued for centuries afterward — in Russia, in the Norman Mediterranean, in Iceland, in the Anglo-Saxon-Norman fusion that would eventually produce modern English political culture.
The longship-borne Viking warband as a strategic actor in European politics ended in 1066.
The downstream effects of the Viking Age have not yet ended; some are still running.
A final thought, returning to the helmet.
The Viking Age was 273 years long — from Lindisfarne in 793 to Stamford Bridge in 1066.
That is shorter than the United States has existed, and noticeably shorter than the Roman Republic, the Tang dynasty, or the Pharaonic New Kingdom of Egypt.

In that span, a marginal northern people sailing out of pre-state fjord-kingdoms reached Newfoundland, Constantinople, Baghdad, Rome, and the gates of Egypt; founded the political ancestors of Russia, Iceland, Normandy, and Norman Sicily; placed Christian kings on the thrones of Denmark, Norway, Sweden, England, and Kievan Rus'; created one of the densest vernacular literary traditions in pre-modern European history; established the slave-trading and dirham-flow trade networks that connected the Caliphate to the North Atlantic; built ring fortresses, longhouses, stave churches, and the longship; and ended their Age with the great-great-great-grandson of one of their own warlords riding up Senlac Hill to take the crown of England.

It is one of the most successful three-century runs of any people in human history, and the absurd thing is that the popular memory of it is dominated by a costume detail invented by a German opera company in 1876.
The actual Vikings were less colorful and much more interesting.
They were mostly farmers.
They worked dirty, dangerous, profit-making jobs.
They held themselves and each other to oaths because they had no state to enforce contracts.
They wrote terse poetry with mathematical structure.
They sold each other's relatives.
They built parliaments.
They reached parts of the world that no other Europeans of their era reached.
They did all of this without horns on their helmets, and they would, every single one of them, have laughed at the picture.

Cross-civ check: the year of three kings (1066) coincides with the Northern Song dynasty at its commercial and demographic peak in China; the early Seljuk Empire consolidating Anatolia after the Battle of Manzikert (just five years later, 1071, when the Seljuks would shatter Byzantine military power and open the way for the eventual fall of Constantinople and the Crusades); the Almoravid rise in North Africa and Iberia; the Chola dynasty at the height of its naval reach across the Indian Ocean; and the founding of the Toltec capital at Tula in central Mexico.

The world that the Vikings exited in 1066 was about to become the world of the Crusades, the high medieval European agricultural revolution, the rise of the universities, and the great commercial expansion of the Italian city-states.
The Viking Age was over.
The medieval world that replaced it was, in many of its most important components, the Viking Age's direct inheritance.

chapters.title: The Steppe Before Temüjin
sentences: In the middle of the twelfth century, on a landscape that no surviving map of the time bothered to describe in any detail, a child was born into a world that had no business producing the largest land empire in human history.

The world in question was the Mongolian plateau (the eastern half of the great Eurasian grassland belt, the same belt that had earlier produced the Scythians in Chapter 1 of the Scythians narrative and the Xiongnu in Chapter 1 of the Xiongnu-Huns narrative).
It was geographically enormous, ecologically harsh, and politically a mess.
Multiple tribal confederations occupied overlapping pastures.
Some had been Buddhists or Nestorian Christians for generations.
Some still followed older shamanic traditions.
They raided each other for horses, livestock, women, and revenge.
They formed alliances and broke them within a year.
They had never been unified, and most observers in the settled world (Chinese, Persian, Russian, European) assumed they never would be.
Within a single human lifetime, that assumption would be wrong by more than any prediction in recorded history has ever been wrong.

This is the story of the Mongol Empire (the political project that began in 1206 with a tribal assembly in northern Mongolia and ended in 1368 with a deposed emperor fleeing his Chinese capital), and during which the Mongols conquered more territory in two generations than Rome had managed in four centuries.

It is the story of a civilization that destroyed cities so completely that some of them never reappeared on any map, and of the same civilization sponsoring the most ambitious astronomical observatory in the medieval world.
It is one of the darkest stories in this app, and one of the most consequential.
The Mongols did not create the Eurasian world we now describe as connected.
But they were the moment when that connection, after thousands of years of being merely possible, became overwhelmingly real.
A note on "firsts" before we go further.

The Mongols are credited with creating the largest contiguous land empire in history, the first true intercontinental postal system, the first state-issued paper currency widely circulated outside China, the first attempt at a Eurasia-spanning system of religious tolerance enforced by law, and (more darkly) the first medieval pandemic carried along an inter-civilizational trade network.
Most of these claims are solid.
All carry the standard caveat that "first" in history means "first surviving evidence of." The Mongols did not invent every technique they used.
They were the first to combine them on a scale that matched the size of their empire.
To understand why the Mongols mattered so much, you have to understand why no one had done what they did before.
The Eurasian steppe is a belt of grassland stretching roughly 5,000 miles (8,000 km) from Hungary to Manchuria — wider than the continental United States.
Its eastern half, the Mongolian steppe, is the harshest stretch.
Winters routinely hit minus 40 degrees (the same in Fahrenheit and Celsius, the one point where the two scales meet).
Summers are short and hot.
The terrain is rolling grass broken by mountain ranges (the Altai in the west, the Khentii in the north and east, the Khangai in the center) and cut by rivers that freeze solid for months.
The people who lived on it practiced pastoral nomadism: they did not grow food, they grew herds, and they followed their herds in seasonal circuits across the grass.
Their wealth was livestock — sheep, goats, cattle, camels, and above all horses.
Their homes were the ger (a circular felt tent on a wooden lattice frame; "yurt" is a Turkic word that English borrowed for the same structure).
Their political units were tribes and clans bound by kinship, marriage, and the personal authority of a chief.
This was an old way of life on the steppe, a thousand years older than the Mongols.
The Xiongnu had practiced it.
The Turks had practiced it.
The Khitans (a Mongolic-speaking people who ruled the Liao dynasty across northern China and southern Mongolia from 916 to 1125, before being overthrown by the Jurchen-led Jin) had practiced it.
So why hadn't anyone before the Mongols built an empire that lasted?
The blunt answer is that the steppe naturally fragmented.
Every successful chieftain produced multiple sons, each of whom inherited followers and pastures, and each of whom had reason to fight his brothers.
The harsh ecology kept any one tribe from accumulating overwhelming surpluses.

Foreign powers (China, Persia) were practiced at playing the tribes against each other through tribute, marriage alliances, and selective trade access — the Han dynasty (Han Dynasty Chapter 5) had perfected this strategy more than a thousand years earlier, and the technique still worked.
The result was a steppe that was politically incoherent for most of its history.
There were brief moments of unification — Modu's Xiongnu confederation around 200 BCE, the Göktürk Khaganate in the sixth century — but they fragmented within a few generations.
The default was tribal competition, not empire.

To unify the steppe permanently you would need to do several things that no one had ever managed at once: defeat every rival confederation in turn, replace tribal loyalties with personal loyalty to a single ruler, codify a body of law that all tribes accepted, organize the warrior population into a single coordinated army, and survive long enough to see your sons inherit the system rather than tear it apart.
In the twelfth century, on the eve of the Mongol unification, the steppe contained roughly five major confederations whose names matter for what follows.
The Tatars (TAH-tars) occupied the eastern Mongolian plateau near the Khingan mountains.

They were the largest and most prestigious confederation, allies of the Jin dynasty in northern China (the Jurchen-led empire that had displaced the older Liao dynasty), and frequent enemies of the Mongols proper.

The name "Tatar" is the one that would later be projected onto all the steppe peoples by Europeans and Russians, even though the Mongols themselves destroyed most of the actual Tatars early in Genghis Khan's career.
The slippage is one of history's stranger naming accidents — what Europe called "the Tatar Yoke" was overwhelmingly Mongol-led.
The Kereit (keh-RAIT) controlled the central plateau around the modern Mongolian capital.

They were Nestorian Christians (a branch of Christianity that had spread east from Persia in late antiquity, named after the fifth-century theologian Nestorius and rejected as heretical by both Catholic and Orthodox churches but flourishing along the Silk Road for centuries).
The Kereit ruler Toghrul (TOH-grul) held the Chinese honorific Wang Khan (WAHNG khan, "Prince Khan"), bestowed by the Jin court for his services against rivals.
The Naiman (NYE-mahn) occupied the western plateau toward the Altai.
They too were largely Nestorian.

The Naiman court used a Turkic dialect and the Uyghur script (a writing system the Naimans had borrowed from the more sophisticated Uyghur Khaganate, which had ruled the steppe two centuries earlier — the Mongols would borrow it in turn, and it remains the basis for the traditional Mongolian script today).
The Merkit (MEHR-kit) lived in the forested zone north of Lake Baikal.
They were not exactly nomads (the forest steppe required a different way of life) but they were warlike enough to count.
And the Mongols proper, the smallest and least prestigious of the five, occupied a stretch of grass and forest along the Onon and Kerulen rivers in the north-central plateau.
They were divided among multiple clans, of which the Borjigin (BOR-jih-gin, "blue-grey wolf") was a senior lineage but not, in 1162, a particularly powerful one.
The Mongols had been tributaries of the Tatars and clients of the Kereit.
They were, in modern terms, the underdogs.
The man who would change all of this was born into the Borjigin clan in roughly 1162 (the date is debated; some sources say 1155 or 1167, but 1162 is the most common scholarly figure).

His name at birth was Temüjin (teh-MOO-jin), reportedly named after a Tatar chieftain his father had killed shortly before his birth — naming a child after a defeated enemy was a steppe custom intended to transfer the enemy's strength to the child.
The boy who would become Genghis Khan was, before he was anything else, a child named for revenge.
A few things to understand about the steppe economy and military, because they are the operating system of everything that follows.
The Mongol horse was the linchpin of the entire system.

The steppe horse (sometimes called the Mongol pony today) was small by European or Persian standards — roughly 13 to 14 hands, about the size of a large modern pony — but it was extraordinarily tough, able to survive Mongolian winters by pawing through snow to reach frozen grass, willing to drink from any water source, and capable of covering 50 to 60 miles (80–100 km) per day for weeks.
A Mongol warrior on campaign brought three to five remounts and switched horses through the day to keep them fresh.
No infantry army could match the pace, and no settled cavalry tradition (which depended on grain-fed horses too expensive to bring in large numbers) could match the logistics.
Every Mongol man was a warrior.

Children learned to ride before they could walk in any meaningful sense, and they learned to shoot the composite bow (the same recurved bow tradition the Scythians had perfected fifteen hundred years earlier — layered wood, horn, and sinew, glued and cured for months, short enough to use on horseback but as powerful as much longer bows of single materials) before they were ten.
Hunting was a year-round practice that doubled as military training.

The annual winter hunt was conducted as a slow-shrinking circle of riders that drove game into a central kill zone — exactly the same maneuver, scaled down, that Mongol armies used to envelop enemies in the field.
What this meant in practice: the steppe could mobilize a far higher fraction of its population for war than any settled society.
A Chinese empire of fifty million people might field an army of a hundred thousand professional soldiers, which is roughly two-tenths of one percent of the population.
A Mongol confederation of one million people could field an army of a hundred thousand without disrupting daily life — ten percent of the population.
The math was lopsided in the steppe's favor for any kind of warfare that did not depend on holding cities.
The settled world's only consistent advantages were technology (siege engines, walls, manufactured weapons in volume) and numbers in static defense.
When you combined a steppe army's mobility with siege technology — by integrating captured engineers, which is what the Mongols would do — the settled world's advantages disappeared.
No one had quite seen the implications of this combination yet.
The Mongols would.

Cross-civ check: 1162, the year of Temüjin's birth, is roughly contemporary with the Twelfth-century Renaissance in western Europe, the Komnenian dynasty's revival of the Byzantine Empire, the Ayyubid sultan Saladin consolidating power in Egypt and Syria, the Southern Song dynasty in China managing a brilliant economic and technological golden age behind a defensive line on the Huai River, and the Pala dynasty's decline in eastern India.
In the Andes, the Chimú were building their adobe capital at Chan Chan (Andean Kingdoms Chapter 2).
In Mesoamerica, the Toltec had collapsed and the Maya cities of the Yucatan were entering their post-classic phase.
None of these civilizations knew about each other in any meaningful way.
Within sixty years, one Mongol empire would be in direct contact with most of them simultaneously.

chapters.title: Becoming Genghis Khan
sentences: Temüjin was eight or nine years old when his father was poisoned.
This is where every account of Genghis Khan's life begins, including the Secret History of the Mongols (the anonymous Mongolian-language chronicle composed around 1240).

The Secret History is the only narrative source in the Mongols' own language and the closest thing we have to an authorized internal version of the foundation story; it was eventually preserved in a Chinese phonetic transcription after the original Uyghur-script Mongolian copies were lost.
Without the death of Temüjin's father, the Mongol Empire would not exist.
With it, the boy who became Genghis Khan was forged.
The father in question was Yesügei (yeh-SOO-gay), a chieftain of the Borjigin clan and a battle-tested warrior who had killed enough Tatars to earn the lasting hatred of the entire confederation.

Around 1171, Yesügei was traveling home after delivering young Temüjin to the family of his betrothed bride — steppe custom required a boy to live with his future in-laws for several years before marriage, partly to bond with the new family and partly as a kind of gentle hostage.
On the journey home, Yesügei stopped at a Tatar encampment to share a meal.
The Tatars recognized him.
They poisoned his food.
He made it back to his own camp before dying.
What happened next was not unusual on the steppe, but it is brutal to read.
Yesügei's followers — the warriors who had served him out of personal loyalty — abandoned his widow Hoelun and her children.
The clan stripped them of livestock, refused them a place at the seasonal migrations, and left them to starve on a stretch of steppe near the Onon River.
Hoelun, by every account, kept her family alive by foraging for roots, fishing, and shaming her sons into hunting marmots and small game.
They lived in a single ger with no men of fighting age, no herds worth mentioning, and no political standing whatever.
Temüjin, the eldest, was at this point perhaps ten years old.
The Mongol Empire's founder spent his formative years closer to homeless than to royalty.
The early teenage years contain one episode that the Secret History records and that historians take seriously as character-forming.
Temüjin's older half-brother Begter, the son of Yesügei's second wife, had been bullying the family — hoarding food, claiming dominance.
Temüjin and his younger full brother Khasar ambushed Begter while he sat watching the horses, shot him with arrows, and killed him.
Hoelun reportedly raged at Temüjin for hours, comparing him to wild animals that eat their own kind.

The episode is often cited as evidence that Temüjin understood power as something that had to be consolidated absolutely, even within a family, and that he would not tolerate rivals close enough to threaten him.
The pattern would repeat at imperial scale.
Temüjin's first move toward something larger than survival came around 1184.
He was twenty-two years old.
He had reclaimed his father's bride Börte (BUR-teh) from her family's keeping and brought her to his small encampment.

The marriage was a serious one — Börte would later bear his four legitimate sons, all of whom would rule major shares of the empire, and she would remain his most senior wife for the rest of his life.
A few months after the wedding, the Merkit raided the camp.
The raid was specifically a revenge attack.
Years earlier, Temüjin's father Yesügei had himself kidnapped Hoelun from a Merkit man on her wedding day — that was how Temüjin's parents had met.
The Merkit had not forgotten.
When they learned that Yesügei's son had taken a wife of his own, they rode to take her in compensation.
They succeeded.
Börte was carried off and given to a Merkit warrior.
Temüjin escaped on horseback and lost his bride in the same night.
Temüjin's response was the first act of leadership his career produced.
He rode to the camp of his father's old sworn brother Toghrul, the Wang Khan of the Kereit, and called in the alliance Yesügei had once secured.
He also called on his anda (AHN-dah, sworn brother) Jamukha (jah-MOO-khah), a charismatic Mongol of equal status who would be Temüjin's closest friend and bitterest rival across the next two decades.
Toghrul provided several thousand Kereit warriors.
Jamukha provided several thousand Mongol warriors.
Temüjin himself contributed a much smaller force.

Together they fell on the Merkit, recovered Börte, and demonstrated a principle that Temüjin would build the rest of his life around: alliances are the only thing that makes a small force into a large one, and a leader who can call in alliances is more dangerous than a leader who only commands his own followers.
Börte was rescued pregnant.

The child she bore a few months later, Jochi (JOH-chee, "guest" or "visitor" in Mongolian, a name that historians believe references the uncertainty about his paternity), was raised as Temüjin's eldest son.
Whether Jochi was actually Temüjin's biological son or the son of the Merkit captor was a question the family avoided in public and addressed never.
It would become important after 1227, because Jochi was the senior heir by birth order, and the doubt about his paternity gave his brothers ammunition.
The Mongol Empire's first succession crisis had its roots in a single missing season of 1184.
The next twenty years are, for the reader's purposes, a sequence of escalating tribal wars in which Temüjin slowly defeated every rival on the steppe.
The detailed political ledger is not what the chapter is for — the Secret History spends hundreds of paragraphs on the names of allies and betrayers, and most readers do not need the granularity.
The pattern is what matters.
Temüjin's method, refined across two decades of practice, had several distinct features that contemporary steppe politics did not.
He absorbed defeated peoples instead of just looting them.
Conventional steppe warfare worked on a "raid-and-retire" logic: you defeated a rival tribe, took their herds, killed their warriors of fighting age, and went home.
Temüjin instead distributed the defeated warriors among his own units, where they fought as full members under Mongol commanders.
The losers became part of the next campaign's army.

This is the same mechanism the Romans had used to absorb Italian peoples a thousand years earlier (Ancient Rome Chapter 2), and it produced the same result: an army that grew with every victory rather than shrinking from casualties.
He promoted on merit rather than lineage.
Temüjin's senior commanders — Subutai (soo-buh-TAI), Jebe (JEH-beh), Mukhali (moo-KHAH-lee), Boorchu (BOH-or-choo) — were not Borjigin nobles.

Jebe was a former enemy who had once shot Temüjin's horse out from under him in battle and who Temüjin spared on the explicit reasoning that a man who could shoot that well was worth more alive than dead.
Subutai was the son of a blacksmith.
Such people would never have led major formations under any other steppe ruler.
Under Temüjin they led campaigns that conquered continents.
He punished betrayal with consistent ruthlessness, but rewarded loyalty across former enemy lines.
When the warriors of the defeated Tayichiud clan brought their captured lord to Temüjin in hopes of reward, Temüjin had them executed for betraying their own master.
When a single Tayichiud warrior refused to surrender his fleeing lord and confessed it openly, Temüjin made him a general.
The message — made loudly and publicly, every time — was that loyalty was the supreme virtue, regardless of who you had originally been loyal to.
After enough public examples, men who switched sides started fighting harder for Temüjin than they had for their original chiefs.
He declared the Mongol identity to be larger than the Borjigin clan.
This is subtle and important.
Under earlier steppe leaders, a confederation was a temporary alliance of tribes who kept their own identities.
Under Temüjin, all the conquered peoples — Tatars, Kereit, Naiman, Merkit, the various Mongol clans themselves — were progressively reassigned to military units that mixed their origins.
After a decade of this, "Mongol" stopped being the name of one tribe and became the name of the new political community.
By 1206 there was no separate Tatar people in any meaningful sense; the surviving Tatars were Mongols.
By 1203 the Kereit were defeated and Toghrul, the old Wang Khan, was dead — the alliance from 1184 had ended in a falling-out and a war.

By 1204 the Naiman were defeated at the Battle of Chakirmaut (chah-keer-MOWT), which incidentally delivered to Temüjin the Naiman scribes and the Uyghur script, giving the Mongols a writing system for the first time in their history.

By 1205 Jamukha — Temüjin's old anda, who had become his most determined rival — was captured, refused mercy, and was executed in the noble fashion (without spilling his blood; for the steppe peoples, the soul lived in the blood, and bloodless execution by smothering or back-breaking was an honor).
In 1206, Temüjin called a kurultai (a great assembly of all the tribal leaders of the unified plateau) at the headwaters of the Onon River, where he had been born forty-four years earlier.
The Kurultai of 1206 is the foundational moment of Mongol history.
A kurultai (KOO-rul-tai) was a steppe institution of long standing — an assembly of tribal leaders convened to elect a new ruler, ratify major decisions, or coordinate military campaigns.
The Xiongnu had held them.
The Turks had held them.
Every steppe confederation worked through some version of the same process.

What was different in 1206 was scale and permanence: every chief on the plateau was present, no rival confederation existed any longer, and the man being acclaimed was not a conventional steppe ruler but a new kind of leader proposing a new kind of state.
The assembly raised Temüjin on a felt carpet (a steppe enthronement ritual) and acclaimed him Genghis Khan.
The name's exact meaning is debated.
Chinggis Qa'an (CHING-gis kah-AHN) is the more accurate Mongolian transliteration; "Genghis" is a Latinized form that English uses by convention.

Most scholars accept the translation as something close to "oceanic ruler" or "universal ruler" — chinggis possibly meaning "ocean" (the steppe word for the largest body of water imaginable), with the implied claim being authority over all the lands the ocean touched.
It was a cosmically large title for a man whose father had been a minor chieftain.
The kurultai also ratified several institutions that would define the Mongol state for the rest of its existence.
The Yassa (YAH-sah, the Mongol legal code attributed to Genghis Khan) was promulgated as the empire's written law.

The Yassa is one of those documents that is famous for existing without anyone alive today knowing exactly what it said — no complete copy survives, only fragments and references in Persian, Arabic, and Chinese sources.
What the references agree on is that the Yassa codified rules on theft, murder, military discipline, hunting, water rights, religious practices, and the conduct of leaders.
It made the dropping of food on the ground a punishable offense (a steppe-survival rule taken seriously).
It mandated religious tolerance — clergy of all faiths were exempt from taxation and military service, and persecution of any recognized religion was a capital crime.
It established that the death penalty applied equally to everyone, including members of the imperial family.
The Yassa was not a constitution in the modern sense; it was a king's set of rulings.
But it functioned as one, and for the first generations of the empire it was treated as binding on all Mongol rulers.

The decimal military system was formalized: every man in the empire was enrolled in an arban (a unit of ten), ten arbans formed a zuun (a hundred), ten zuuns formed a mingghan (a thousand), and ten mingghans formed a tumen (ten thousand, the largest standard formation).
Every level had a commander appointed by Genghis Khan personally and answerable up the chain.
The decimal system was not new — the Xiongnu had used it (Xiongnu-Huns Chapter 2) and most steppe empires before the Mongols had imitated it — but Genghis enforced it across deliberately mixed units.
A tumen would contain men from a dozen former tribes, all serving under the same commander, all answering to the same chain.
Tribal loyalty was being structurally replaced by army loyalty.
For the rest of the empire's existence, the Mongol military was the only steppe army that could not be unmade by tribal defection.
The Keshig (KESH-ig) — the imperial guard — was expanded from a personal retinue into a formal institution of ten thousand men, drawn from the sons and brothers of the senior commanders.
The keshig served as the khan's bodyguard, his administrative staff, his pool of future generals, and (not incidentally) his hostage system.
A commander whose son served in the keshig had a strong motivation not to rebel.
The Nine White Banners (nine spear-shafts hung with white horsetails) became the empire's symbol.
The number nine was sacred in Mongol shamanic tradition (the heavens were said to have nine layers), and the white horsetails referenced the steppe's most valuable possession.
The banners would be carried at every kurultai for the next two centuries.
The empire that Genghis Khan ratified at the kurultai of 1206 contained perhaps one million people.
It was militarily strong but economically modest — pastoral nomads producing meat, milk, hides, and felt, with limited access to manufactured goods and almost no tax base in the conventional sense.
To survive, Genghis needed either trade or conquest.

Trade required cooperation from the great settled empires bordering the steppe — the Jin dynasty in northern China, the Western Xia in the Tangut zone southwest of Mongolia, the Khwarezmian Empire in Central Asia and Persia.
Conquest required almost the same thing: the army needed somewhere to go.
Genghis chose conquest, but he started by inviting trade and watching to see whether it would be honored.
It was not.

chapters.title: The Eurasian Whirlwind
sentences: Genghis Khan was forty-four years old at his coronation, and he had twenty-one years left to live.

In those twenty-one years he and his generals would conquer or destroy: the Western Xia kingdom, the Kara-Khitai (a Buddhist Khitan-led successor state in modern Xinjiang and eastern Central Asia, founded by Liao-dynasty refugees in the 1130s after the Jin destroyed the Liao in north China), the Khwarezmian Empire, the northern half of Jin China, fragments of the Russian principalities, large portions of the Caucasus, and the eastern half of the Persian-cultural sphere.
Geographically this is roughly the area from the Pacific Ocean to the Caspian Sea, north to south from the Siberian forests to the Indus River.
The campaigns proceeded simultaneously on multiple fronts.
They produced casualties on a scale not previously documented in any source the survivors of any of the involved civilizations left behind.
This chapter is what the whirlwind sounds like from inside a written tradition.
The first target was Western Xia (also called Xi Xia or, in the Mongol sources, Tangut — TANG-uht — after the Tangut people who founded the kingdom).
Western Xia was a semi-Sinicized kingdom of Tangut-speaking people in the upper Yellow River valley, roughly modern Ningxia and Gansu in northwestern China.

It controlled the Hexi Corridor, the narrow strip of habitable land between the Gobi Desert and the Tibetan Plateau through which all overland trade between China and Central Asia had to pass — the same corridor that had triggered the original Han-Xiongnu wars more than a thousand years earlier (Han Dynasty Chapter 4).

Western Xia was militarily competent, economically rich on Silk Road tolls, and strategically vulnerable: it sat between the Mongol steppe and the much larger Jin dynasty, and any time the Mongols moved south Xia was the first kingdom they encountered.
The first Mongol campaign against Western Xia in 1209 was, in Genghis's evident reasoning, a rehearsal.
He needed to test his armies against a settled enemy with walled cities.

Western Xia surrendered after the Mongols diverted the Yellow River to flood the capital city's defenses (the diversion did not work as planned and apparently flooded the Mongol camp instead, but the political effect was achieved).
Xia agreed to pay tribute and accept Mongol overlordship without being formally annexed.
Genghis turned his attention to the larger prize.
That prize was the Jin dynasty, the Jurchen-led empire that ruled northern China from the Yellow River to the Korean border.
The Jin had displaced the older Liao dynasty about a century earlier.

They were, by any measure, the larger and more sophisticated power: a population in the tens of millions, a tax base in the hundreds of thousands of pounds of silver per year, walled cities in the dozens, and an army that included native Chinese, Khitan auxiliaries, and Jurchen heavy cavalry.
Genghis invaded in 1211 with a force that was probably no larger than ninety thousand men.
The campaign would last twenty-three years.
What the Mongols brought to the Jin war that no previous steppe army had brought was a willingness to integrate the technical specialists of conquered cities into their own system.
The first Jin city to fall in 1211 was Datong.
The Mongols took the surviving engineers, siege specialists, blacksmiths, and gunpowder technicians, organized them into specialized units, and used them against the next city.
The next city's specialists were added to the next campaign.

Within a few years the Mongol army was conducting siege warfare with trebuchets (counterweight catapults capable of throwing 200-pound stones), fire-lance weapons (bamboo or paper tubes filled with gunpowder and projectiles, the immediate ancestors of firearms), and mines and counter-mines under city walls — none of which the Mongols had possessed five years earlier.
The army was a learning organization in a way that ancient armies almost never were.
The Jin capital Zhongdu (modern Beijing, then called Zhongdu — JONG-doo — the "central capital") fell in 1215 after years of intermittent siege.

The fall produced one of the war's most consequential events at the human-individual scale: a Khitan official named Yelü Chucai (YEH-lyoo CHOO-tsai), a serious scholar of Confucian classics and a poet, was captured among the bureaucratic survivors and brought to Genghis Khan.
Yelü Chucai was tall, bearded, fluent in multiple languages, and possessed of a kind of cool dignity that the steppe court immediately registered as authority.
Genghis kept him on.
Over the next two decades, Yelü would talk multiple Mongol khans out of policies that would have left north China a depopulated pasture, arguing that taxation produced more wealth than slaughter.
He is plausibly responsible for several million lives.
The Mongol Empire's habit of recruiting captured administrators rather than killing them is not a small detail of the period.
It is the reason the empire grew rather than collapsing under the weight of its own destruction.
In 1218 the western front opened in a way the Mongols had not particularly intended.
Far to the west of the Mongol heartland, beyond the Tian Shan mountains, lay the Khwarezmian Empire (kwah-REZ-mee-an, sometimes spelled Khorezm or Khwarazm).
Khwarezm was a powerful Turkic-Persian state that had emerged in the previous century, ruled in 1218 by the ambitious and politically inept Shah Muhammad II.
Khwarezm's territory was vast — modern Iran, Afghanistan, Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, and parts of Kazakhstan.
It contained some of the most sophisticated cities of the medieval world, including Samarkand, Bukhara, Urgench, Merv, Nishapur, and Herat.

The empire was Persian-cultured (Khwarezmian elites spoke Persian, patronized Persian poetry, and ran their administration in Persian — the cultural-resurrection pattern that the Persian Empire narrative documents at length, Persian Empire Chapter 10).
It was the richest and most populous state in the eastern Islamic world.
Genghis Khan, having spent the better part of a decade fighting the Jin, was not initially interested in Khwarezm.
He sent a trade delegation — five hundred merchants, goods and gold, a request to open commerce between the two empires.
The delegation reached the Khwarezmian frontier town of Otrar on the Syr Darya river.
The local governor, Inalchuq, decided the merchants were spies.
He had them all executed and confiscated their goods.
This was the kind of provocation that Genghis Khan responded to as if a religious obligation were involved.
He sent envoys to Shah Muhammad demanding Inalchuq's punishment.
Muhammad executed one of the envoys and sent the others home with their beards shaved off — a deep insult in the Islamic and steppe worlds alike.
In 1219, Genghis Khan invaded Khwarezm with an army that contemporary chroniclers estimated at a hundred and fifty thousand men.
The number is probably exaggerated; modern estimates suggest a hundred thousand or fewer.
Either way, Genghis's force was smaller than the army the Khwarezmian Shah commanded on paper, and it was operating a thousand miles from its supply base.
Shah Muhammad chose to garrison every major city separately rather than concentrate his army for a field battle, on the theory that the Mongols could not sustain multiple sieges.
The strategy was disastrous.
The Mongols took the cities one at a time, and they had become, by 1219, the most devastatingly effective siege army in the world.
The campaigns of 1219 to 1221 are difficult to summarize without slipping into pure horror.
Bukhara fell in 1220.
The city's congregational mosque survived but was used as a stable.
Genghis Khan reportedly mounted the pulpit and told the assembled survivors: "I am the flail of God.

If you had not committed great sins, God would not have sent a punishment like me upon you." Whether he actually said it is uncertain — the line is preserved in the Persian historian Juvayni's account a generation later — but the city's craftsmen were deported to Mongolia, the garrison was massacred, and a portion of the population was used as a human shield in the assault on Samarkand.
Samarkand fell shortly after.
The same pattern: craftsmen extracted, garrison massacred, defensive walls dismantled, population reduced.
Samarkand had been one of the great cities of the Islamic world, a center of Persian poetry and Hanafi legal scholarship.

It survived the Mongol conquest physically, but its character would not recover for nearly two centuries (Timur, claiming Mongol descent, would make Samarkand his capital in the 1370s, and by then the city had to be rebuilt almost from scratch — Chapter 9).
Urgench, the Khwarezmian capital in the lower Amu Darya delta, was the most ferocious siege of the war.
The city held for months.

When it finally fell in 1221, the Mongol commanders divided the population among the army for systematic killing — every soldier was given a quota — and then diverted the Amu Darya river through the city's foundations to wash the ruins flat.
Contemporary sources claimed casualties of well over a million.

Modern historians regard those figures as inflated propaganda (medieval armies could not actually count deaths at that scale), but accept that the Urgench massacre was one of the largest organized killings in pre-modern history.
Nothing called Urgench would exist on the same site for centuries afterward.

Nishapur in eastern Iran (the home city of the Persian poet and mathematician Omar Khayyam, who had lived and died there a century earlier) was destroyed in 1221 after a Mongol prince was killed by a stray arrow during the siege.
The avenging force, commanded by Genghis's youngest son Tolui, was ordered to leave nothing alive.

The city was taken, the population killed, the buildings demolished, and the fields salted with skulls — chroniclers describe pyramids of severed heads built outside the gates: men's heads, women's heads, children's heads, separately.
The horror was the point.
The Mongols had developed an explicit doctrine: cities that resisted should be destroyed so completely that other cities would surrender at the first summons.
The doctrine worked.
Many Khwarezmian cities surrendered without resistance and survived.
The ones that resisted did not.
Shah Muhammad II himself fled west across his crumbling empire and died of exhaustion on a small island in the Caspian Sea in 1220 or 1221, sources differ.
His son Jalal ad-Din Mingburnu kept fighting.
Genghis personally chased Jalal ad-Din across Afghanistan and finally cornered him at the Indus River in late 1221.

Jalal ad-Din made his last stand with about thirty thousand men, lost the battle, and saved his life by spurring his horse off a cliff into the river and swimming to the Indian bank with his sword still in hand.
Genghis Khan reportedly watched from the cliff and remarked to his sons that this was what a true man looked like.
Jalal ad-Din lived another decade as a fugitive in northern India and Iraq before dying of less impressive causes.
The Khwarezmian Empire, which had been the richest state in the eastern Islamic world three years earlier, was over.

While Genghis was destroying Khwarezm, Subutai and Jebe — two of his most capable generals — undertook a reconnaissance expedition that turned into one of the most extraordinary military campaigns in history.
They were sent west to chase Shah Muhammad's remnants.
They kept going.

They rode around the southern shore of the Caspian Sea, defeated the Georgians in the Caucasus, crossed into the Pontic steppe, and at the Battle of the Kalka River in 1223 destroyed a combined army of Russian princes and Cuman steppe nomads who had marched against them.

It was the first contact between Mongol forces and any state that European writers documented — Russian chronicles of 1223 describe the appearance of an unknown people from the east, who came, fought a battle, and disappeared.
Subutai and Jebe rode back to Mongolia having scouted everything between the Caspian and the Dnieper.
Twenty years later their report would be the basis of the great western campaign (Chapter 4).
In the meantime, they had circumnavigated the Caspian Sea on horseback and conducted an entire war on the side.
No campaign in Roman or Persian military history compares in distance covered.
By 1226, Genghis Khan was approximately sixty-four years old, and the campaigns had taken a physical toll.

He returned to Mongolia and turned his attention to Western Xia, which had refused to send troops for the Khwarezmian campaign — a refusal that, under Mongol political logic, was a declaration of independence and therefore a declaration of war.
Genghis personally led the final Western Xia campaign in 1226–1227.

The kingdom was destroyed; the dynasty's name was struck from the official Chinese historical record (Western Xia is the only major Chinese dynasty that does not receive a standard official history); the Tangut population was systematically reduced — though not, as is sometimes claimed, eliminated, since Tangut identity persisted into the Ming period.
In August 1227, Genghis Khan died.
The cause is not certain.

Contemporary sources offer competing explanations: a fall from a horse during a hunt the year before, a wound that became infected, a natural illness, even (in one Persian account, almost certainly false) an injury inflicted by a captured Tangut princess in revenge.
The Secret History says simply that he ascended to heaven during the final siege.
He was sixty-five years old.
His generals kept his death secret until Western Xia surrendered.

The body was taken north to a location that has never been publicly identified — Mongol custom required that a great khan's burial site be kept secret, and the soldiers escorting the body were said to have killed every person they encountered on the route to prevent the location from being known.

Legend, recorded in several later chronicles without primary-source corroboration, says the funeral cortège killed every person it encountered along a route of hundreds of miles to keep the burial location secret; some traditions put the death toll in the thousands.
The grave has not been found.
It is one of the most determined searches in modern archaeology, and it has produced a great many candidate sites and zero verified ones.
The man who controlled the largest empire in history is buried somewhere in northern Mongolia, and no one alive knows where.
The empire he left covered roughly 13.5 million square miles (35 million km²) — about four times the size of the modern United States.
He had been reigning for twenty-one years.
His four legitimate sons by Börte had to figure out how to inherit it.

chapters.title: The Sons of Genghis
sentences: The Mongol succession system was, on paper, simple.
The empire was divided into ulus (OO-loos, "people" or "appanage") — territorial allocations to each of Genghis Khan's four legitimate sons by Börte.

The eldest, Jochi (JOH-chee, the disputed-paternity son from Chapter 2), received the westernmost lands — the steppe and forest zones north of the Aral and Caspian seas, what would become the Golden Horde.
The second son Chagatai (CHAH-gah-tai) received Central Asia from the Tian Shan mountains to the Aral, including the great cities of Samarkand and Bukhara.
The third son Ögedei (UH-geh-day) received the Mongol heartland in the Altai region, plus the position of Great Khan over all the others.
The youngest son Tolui (TOH-loo-ee), per Mongol custom that the youngest son inherits the family hearth, received the Mongol heartland in central Mongolia plus the bulk of the army.
In practice, the system was intricate and politically combustible.
The four ulus were not equal in wealth or military power.
The election of the Great Khan required a kurultai of all senior Genghisid princes, and that kurultai could disregard the founder's wishes.
Jochi died (probably of natural causes) in 1227, six months before his father, leaving his own sons — including the future Batu Khan — to claim his ulus.
Tolui died in 1232, possibly poisoned, possibly from drinking himself to death after a shamanic ritual in which he had volunteered to take on his older brother Ögedei's illness.
The founding generation cleared out fast.

The empire that came out the other end was governed for the next thirty years by a sequence of Great Khans who managed simultaneously to expand the empire's territory and to create the political fractures that would eventually break it apart.
Tolui's regency (1227–1229) was a brief interlude per Mongol custom, since Tolui as the youngest son held the family hearth pending the formal kurultai.

Tolui used the regency to complete operations against the Jin dynasty, and in particular to test the integration of Khitan and Chinese specialists into the Mongol command structure that Yelü Chucai (Chapter 3) had been advocating.
The model worked.
By 1229 the Mongol war machine was running on a hybrid steppe-and-Chinese institutional base.
The kurultai of 1229 elected Ögedei Khan (reigned 1229–1241) as Great Khan. Ögedei was, by Mongol-court standards, a moderate.
He was personable, generous, alcoholic, and (when sober) shrewd.
He continued his father's expansionist policy on every front while also building the institutions the empire would need to survive its own size.
The most important institution-building was the construction of Karakorum (kah-rah-KOR-um) as the empire's capital city.
Genghis had used Karakorum as a base camp; Ögedei built actual walls, a palace, official residences, religious buildings, and a market district.
This was a substantial step away from steppe tradition, which had no fixed capitals — every previous steppe empire had governed from rolling encampments or annual gathering points.
Karakorum was a deliberate signal that the Mongol Empire intended to govern, not just raid.
It contained Buddhist temples, mosques, a Nestorian church, and a substantial population of foreign craftsmen, engineers, and clerics imported from across the empire's territory.

The city's most famous fixture was the Silver Tree, a fountain commissioned by Ögedei from a French silversmith named Guillaume Boucher (a Parisian who had been captured during the Hungary campaign and brought back to Mongolia, one of dozens of European specialists in Mongol service).
The Silver Tree had four spouts that dispensed wine, mead, rice wine, and grape wine on demand, powered by a bellows operated by a mechanical angel at the crown.
The fountain stood for the entire conceit of Karakorum: a steppe capital staffed by global specialists, dispensing the world's products to anyone who arrived at the court.

The European Franciscan friar William of Rubruck (the Flemish missionary who reached Karakorum in 1253 as the personal envoy of King Louis IX of France) saw the Silver Tree in operation and wrote one of the only Western descriptions of the medieval Mongol court.

His account, the Itinerarium, is the source for almost everything Europeans of the period knew about how the Mongol capital actually functioned. Ögedei also formalized two infrastructure projects that would matter enormously for the next century.
The first was the Yam (also called the örtöö), a relay postal and travel system with stations roughly every 25 to 30 miles (40–50 km) along all major imperial roads.
Each Yam station maintained a stable of fresh horses, food, and lodging, available to any traveler who carried a paiza (PYE-zah) — a metal pass in gold, silver, or wood depending on rank.

The Yam allowed messages to cross the empire at unprecedented speed (a courier could cover 300 miles in a day under emergency conditions, switching horses every station) and gave merchants and diplomats a degree of secure travel that had not previously existed across most of Eurasia.

The closest historical parallel is the Persian Royal Road's relay courier system under Darius (Persian Empire Chapter 3), which carried messages from Sardis to Susa in seven days using mounted relays at fixed stations — the same mechanism, scaled up by the Mongols across a vastly larger geography.
The Yam was the operating infrastructure of the Pax Mongolica that would emerge by mid-century (Chapter 7).

The second was Sorghaghtani Beki (sor-GHAGH-tah-nee BEH-kee), Tolui's widow, a Nestorian Christian Kerait noblewoman who emerged after her husband's death as one of the empire's most capable administrators. Ögedei, recognizing her abilities, made her responsible for the Tolui ulus.
Sorghaghtani would over the next twenty years educate her four sons — Möngke, Kublai, Hülegü, and Ariq Böke — in administration, multiple languages, and political patience.
All four would eventually rule major Mongol states.
Three of them would be Great Khan (Möngke and Kublai) or founders of khanates that became their own dynasties (Hülegü).

She is plausibly the most consequential woman in the Mongol Empire's political history, and her quiet positioning of her sons across two decades is the reason the Toluid line displaced the Ögedeid line in the empire's second generation.
The military expansion under Ögedei was even more dramatic than Genghis's.
In 1234, the Jin dynasty finally collapsed.
The last Jin emperor committed suicide as the Mongol-Song combined army stormed his last refuge at Caizhou.
Northern China was now Mongol territory.
Whether the Mongols would govern it as a steppe-style tributary zone or as a Chinese-style empire was a question that would split the next generation.
In 1236, Ögedei dispatched the Great Western Campaign — the largest single military operation in Mongol history.
The army was commanded jointly by Batu Khan (Jochi's son, claiming the western ulus his father had been promised) and Subutai (now in his late sixties, the most experienced general in the empire).
Their combined force was roughly 150,000 men, drawn from across the empire's territory and reinforced by Turkic auxiliaries from the western steppe.
Their orders were to subjugate everything between the Volga and the Atlantic.
They came close.
The campaign destroyed the Volga Bulgars in 1236, the Cumans (a Turkic steppe people of the Pontic-Caspian zone) over the next two years, and then turned on the Russian principalities.
Riazan fell in 1237.

Vladimir (the dominant principality of northeastern Rus') fell in 1238 after a long siege; the city was burned, the cathedral set on fire with the population sheltering inside, and the surrounding region depopulated.
Kiev (KEEV, also spelled Kyiv), the symbolic mother-city of Rus' culture, fell in December 1240.

The Italian friar John of Plano Carpini (the papal envoy who traveled overland through these territories five years later, leaving the first detailed European report on the Mongols) described the post-Mongol Russian landscape as fields of bones with no living men to bury them.
The phrasing is rhetorical, but the demographic effect was real.
The Mongol force then split.
One column under Batu marched into Hungary.
Another under Subutai's lieutenants marched into Poland.
The Battle of Legnica (LEG-neet-sah) in April 1241 destroyed a combined Polish-Silesian-Teutonic Knight army under Henry the Pious of Silesia.
The Mongols left a hill of severed ears as the body count: nine sacks, by the Polish chronicler.
The defeated knights' commander died on the field; his head was paraded on a pike to the next siege.

Two days later — and this is the timing that should be impossible without the Yam communication system — Subutai and Batu defeated the Hungarian army at the Battle of Mohi (MOH-hee), more than three hundred miles to the southeast.
King Béla IV of Hungary escaped.
His army was destroyed.
The Mongol force pursued, sacking cities across Hungary through the summer and probing into Croatia and the Adriatic coast.
In the spring of 1242, the Mongol army stopped, turned around, and marched home.
The reason was that Ögedei Khan had died in December 1241, alone in Karakorum, of (probably) acute alcohol poisoning during a drinking party.
The succession kurultai required the attendance of all senior Genghisid princes, including Batu and Subutai.
They obeyed the protocol.
Europe was saved by a steppe drinking culture and a constitutional procedural rule.
How far the Mongols would have gone if Ögedei had lived another five years is one of the great counterfactuals of medieval history.
The Holy Roman Empire's defenses were weak.
Italy was politically fragmented.
