The geography to keep in mind is this: by 1100, the Islamic world was a chain of major polities running from the Atlantic to the Indus, with three caliphates (one fictional in the political sense, two real), perhaps a dozen substantial regional dynasties, and a single broadly shared scholarly culture overlying the political fragmentation.

The Golden Age happened across this fragmentation, partly because the fragmentation itself created multiple competing patrons and prevented any single political center from imposing intellectual orthodoxy on the rest.

chapters.title: Cordoba and the West
sentences: The Islamic conquest of Spain happened fast and almost incidentally.

In 711, an Umayyad raiding force under the Berber commander Tariq ibn Ziyad (TAH-rik IB-n zee-YAHD) crossed the strait that separates North Africa from southern Spain and defeated the Visigothic king Roderic at the Battle of Guadalete.
The crossing point would later be named for him: Jabal Tariq ("Mount of Tariq"), corrupted in modern English to Gibraltar.
Within seven years, the Umayyad forces had conquered most of the Iberian Peninsula; only a narrow strip along the northern Atlantic coast remained under Christian control.

The new province was called al-Andalus (al-AHN-dah-loos — the etymology is contested; one theory traces it to the Vandals who had ruled Spain briefly in the fifth century, another to a pre-Roman geographic name), and it was governed as a province of the Umayyad Caliphate from Damascus until the Abbasid revolution made that arrangement obsolete.
The province was peripheral to the Damascus-based Umayyad administration.
It was not peripheral to what would happen there.
After the Abbasid massacre of the Umayyad family in 750, Abd al-Rahman I escaped (Chapter 1) and arrived in al-Andalus in 755.
He found a province in chronic civil war among rival Arab tribal factions.

Within a year, he had defeated the local governor and established himself as emir (independent ruler) at Cordoba (KOR-do-bah, an old Roman city on the Guadalquivir River — the river name is an Arabic transliteration of the older Latin name Baetis, but with the Arabic definite article al- added: al-Wadi al-Kabir, "the great river").

For the next century and a half, Cordoba was the capital of an independent Umayyad emirate that recognized no caliphal authority — neither the Abbasids in Baghdad, whom the Umayyads had every reason to reject, nor any other claimant.
Al-Andalus was politically anomalous: a Muslim polity outside the recognized caliphal order.
In 929, Abd al-Rahman III ended the anomaly by claiming the caliphate himself (Chapter 6).

The Cordoban Umayyads now had every theological qualification their Abbasid rivals had — descent from the Quraysh (the Prophet's tribe), territorial sovereignty, control of mosques, command of armies.
Abd al-Rahman III ruled for forty-nine years (912–961), the longest reign of any medieval Iberian ruler.
By the time he died, Cordoba was probably the largest and richest city in Europe.
The numbers for Cordoba's tenth-century peak are extraordinary and need calibration.
Contemporary Arab sources give population estimates in the hundreds of thousands; some claim a million.
The realistic estimate is somewhere between 100,000 and 300,000, with 200,000 as a defensible middle-of-the-road figure.
By comparison, the largest Christian European cities of the same period — Rome, Constantinople aside (Constantinople was probably larger, 400,000–500,000) — were smaller.
Paris in 1000 had perhaps 20,000 inhabitants.
London had perhaps 10,000.

Cordoba was at minimum five to ten times the size of any Latin Christian city, and the gap was visible in everything: paved streets (which medieval Paris would not have for another 200 years), public baths, street lighting, water supply by aqueduct, a public sewer system, hundreds of mosques, dozens of public libraries.

The most striking single piece of architecture was the Great Mosque of Cordoba, begun in 784 by Abd al-Rahman I on the site of an earlier Visigothic church (which had itself been built on the site of a Roman temple — the layering is typical of Iberian sacred architecture).

Successive emirs and caliphs expanded the mosque four times over the next two and a half centuries, each expansion roughly doubling the area, until by the late tenth century it covered about 200,000 square feet (the size of a modern American mall).

The interior is one of the most distinctive spaces in any religious tradition: a forest of approximately 850 columns of marble and granite, mostly recycled from older Roman and Visigothic buildings, supporting double-tiered horseshoe arches in alternating bands of red brick and white stone.

The visual effect is hypnotic — the columns repeat in seemingly infinite patterns in every direction, the alternating arches ripple overhead, the proportions feel intentionally non-rationalist (the eye cannot find a single focal point and is forced to keep moving).

The motivation for the design — never explicitly explained in surviving sources — was probably to create a sensory environment of overwhelming abundance, in which the worshipper experienced the divine through bewildering plurality rather than focused contemplation.

The Great Mosque was one of the earliest fully-realized statements of a distinctive Islamic Iberian aesthetic that would eventually flow into Mudejar architecture, Christian Spanish baroque, and through them back into the wider European tradition.
The mosque was converted into a Catholic cathedral after the Reconquista capture of Cordoba in 1236.
It is still a cathedral.
The columns and arches are still there.

A Renaissance choir was built into the middle of the mosque-cathedral in the sixteenth century, an intervention that the Holy Roman Emperor Charles V — visiting the building shortly after the choir's construction — reportedly criticized: "You have destroyed something unique to build something common." The criticism was correct.
The Great Mosque of Cordoba is one of the architectural masterworks of medieval Islam, and the modern visitor still walks through it.
Abd al-Rahman III also built a new royal city.

Madinat al-Zahra (mah-DEE-naht az-ZAH-rah, "City of the Bright One" — named, according to the standard story, after his favorite concubine Zahra) was begun in 936 and built over the following twenty-five years on a hillside about three miles (5 km) west of Cordoba.

It was designed as a royal capital separate from the older city — a deliberate echo of Abbasid Samarra (the Iraqi royal city built a century earlier) and an explicit statement that the Cordoban caliph was sovereign over his own affairs.

The complex covered about 280 acres (115 hectares) on three terraces, with the caliph's palace at the top, gardens and reception halls in the middle, and the mosque, barracks, and administrative buildings at the bottom.

Surviving descriptions speak of an enormous reception hall with mercury fountains in the floor (so that sunlight, refracted through the moving liquid metal, played across the walls in patterns that astonished visitors), gold-and-marble bathing complexes, and gardens of imported plants from across the Mediterranean.
Madinat al-Zahra was not a long-lived capital.
It was built as the seat of Cordoban caliphal authority, and when the Cordoban caliphate collapsed in 1009–1031, the city was looted, burned, and abandoned.
The site was buried under farmland for nine centuries.
Excavations beginning in the early twentieth century have recovered enough to identify the basic plan and some of the decorative elements.
It is now an archaeological park and a UNESCO World Heritage site.
Less than 10% of the site has been excavated.
What is visible today is a small fraction of what was once one of the most spectacular royal complexes of the medieval Mediterranean.
Cordoba's intellectual life paralleled Baghdad's, on a smaller scale but at comparable quality.
The Library of Cordoba was the largest library in medieval Europe.

Caliph al-Hakam II (ruled 961–976), Abd al-Rahman III's son and successor, was a bibliophile who reportedly maintained agents across the Islamic world tasked with locating and acquiring rare manuscripts.
The library catalog at his death, according to contemporary reports, ran to 44 volumes describing over 400,000 individual manuscripts.

The figure is striking — by comparison, the largest contemporary monastic libraries in Christian Europe had perhaps a few hundred manuscripts — but it is plausible given Cordoba's resources and population. (For perspective, the famous library of the Abbey of St.
Gall in Switzerland, considered one of the great Christian European libraries of the period, had about 400 manuscripts in 850 CE.

Cordoba's library was a thousand times larger.) The library survived the city's political collapse for some decades but was dispersed during the eleventh-century chaos, with parts of the collection traveling to Christian Toledo (where it would feed the translation movement, see below) and parts disappearing.
Cordoban scholarship covered the full range of Islamic intellectual disciplines.

Ibn Hazm (IB-n HAZM, 994–1064) was probably the most original Cordoban thinker of the Golden Age — a polymath who wrote on jurisprudence (he founded a small Zahirite legal school that emphasized strict literal reading of texts and rejection of analogical reasoning), comparative religion, and the psychology of love.
His most famous book is the Tawq al-Hamama ("Ring of the Dove," c. 1022), a treatise on love and lovers in Islamic Spain.

The book combines theoretical analysis (the stages of falling in love, the signs by which a lover can be identified, the proper response to unrequited affection) with autobiographical anecdote and quoted poetry.

It is a deeply personal book in a tradition that did not generally encourage personal disclosure, and it provides one of the most vivid extant pictures of Andalusian aristocratic life — the assemblies, the gardens, the slave-girls trained as poets and singers, the elaborate codes of romantic behavior, the alternating piety and licentiousness of high society.

The European troubadour tradition that emerged in southern France in the eleventh and twelfth centuries, with its distinctive vocabulary of courtly love, has been argued to have absorbed elements from the Andalusian Tawq tradition through cross-cultural contact across the Pyrenees.
The scholarly consensus on the strength of this transmission is mixed; some elements are clearly shared and some are independent developments.
But Ibn Hazm at minimum represents the same psychological-romantic tradition that would find its echo in Provençal poetry a century later.
Ibn Tufayl (IB-n too-FAYL, c. 1105–1185), working a century after Ibn Hazm, produced what may be the strangest book of the Andalusian Golden Age.

The Hayy ibn Yaqzan ("Living Son of Awake," composed in the 1160s) is a philosophical novel — yes, a novel; the form is hard to categorize but "novel" is the closest modern term — about a child raised alone on a desert island, with no human contact and no inherited culture.

The protagonist Hayy grows from infancy through stages of development, observing the world around him, reasoning about it, and gradually deriving from his observations and his unaided reason a complete metaphysical system that arrives at the existence of God, the structure of the cosmos, and the duties of the moral life.

He never meets another human being until he is a grown adult; the philosophical truths he discovers, the novel argues, are accessible to any rational being using sense observation and careful reasoning, without requiring revelation, scripture, or social tradition.

When he eventually meets a religious scholar from a nearby inhabited island, the two exchange views and discover that the truths Hayy has derived independently are largely identical to those preserved in revealed religion — except that the religious tradition has clothed them in symbolic and mythological forms accessible to ordinary believers, while Hayy has the bare philosophical substance.
The book is a vision of the harmony of reason and religion.
It is also, by implication, a defense of the philosophical project against al-Ghazali's attack (Chapter 5).
The Hayy ibn Yaqzan was translated into Latin by Edward Pococke the Younger in 1671.
It was widely read in seventeenth-century Europe.
John Locke owned a copy.
Daniel Defoe is generally believed to have known it, and Robinson Crusoe (1719) borrows the desert-island frame, though Defoe transformed the philosophical content into something quite different.

Some scholars have argued that Hayy ibn Yaqzan contributed directly to the Enlightenment's project of grounding knowledge in unaided reason — the idea that an uncorrupted human mind, given access to nature, could derive truth without ecclesiastical authority.
The line of influence from twelfth-century al-Andalus to eighteenth-century Europe is real, even if its weight is debated.
The most striking individual scholar of late Andalusian Islamic Spain was, in fact, not a Muslim.

Maimonides — properly Moshe ben Maimon (mo-SHEH ben mai-MON, 1138–1204) — was a Jewish scholar born in Cordoba shortly before the Almohad conquest disrupted the convivencia of the Cordoban caliphate's late centuries.

The Almohads (Chapter 6) were less tolerant of religious minorities than their predecessors had been, and Maimonides's family fled al-Andalus in the 1150s, eventually settling in Cairo, where he served as a court physician to Saladin's vizier and later to Saladin himself (Chapter 9).
He wrote in Arabic for most of his career, using the Arabic-Hebrew script of medieval Sephardic Jewish intellectual life.
What he produced was foundational for the entire Jewish religious tradition.

The Mishneh Torah ("Repetition of the Torah," completed 1180) was a fourteen-volume systematic codification of all Jewish religious law, arranged by topic and accessible to ordinary readers — the first major attempt to make the vast and unstructured Talmudic tradition navigable.

The Guide for the Perplexed ("Dalalat al-Ha'irin" in Arabic, Moreh Nevuchim in Hebrew, completed 1190) was a philosophical treatise that integrated Jewish theology with Aristotelian-Avicennan philosophy, arguing that Jewish religious texts had to be interpreted in ways consistent with what reason could establish about God and the world.
The Guide was written in Arabic, then translated into Hebrew, then into Latin in the early thirteenth century, where it influenced Thomas Aquinas and the entire Christian scholastic project.
Maimonides was, by training and intellectual orientation, a product of the Islamic Golden Age.
His Arabic was the Arabic of the Cordoban scientific community.
His Aristotelianism was that of Ibn Sina and al-Farabi.
His method of synthesizing religious tradition with philosophical reason was the method that al-Ghazali had attempted within Sunni Islam and that Ibn Rushd was attempting at the same moment.
The achievement of medieval Sephardic Jewish intellectual life — and Maimonides is its tallest peak — was not a separate achievement from the Golden Age.
It was an integral part of the Golden Age, conducted in Arabic, on the same intellectual framework, with the same shared scientific and philosophical inheritance.
Medieval Spain produced one civilization that wrote in two scripts (Arabic and Hebrew) and worshipped in three traditions (Muslim, Jewish, and Christian).

The convivencia — the long Spanish word that has become standard in modern historiography — is the Spanish term for "living together," and it is used to describe the religious pluralism of Islamic Iberia during the Cordoban Umayyad caliphate's peak.

The standard idealized picture is of three faiths coexisting in mutual tolerance under enlightened Islamic rule, sharing scientific projects and aesthetic forms, building together a civilization that ranks among the most admirable accomplishments of human history.

The standard cynical picture is of three faiths in chronic mutual suspicion, occasional pogrom, and structural inequality, with the "tolerance" amounting to lower-status protection of subordinate Christians and Jews who paid the jizya (the discriminatory tax on non-Muslims under Islamic rule) and were excluded from the political-military elite.
The truth is between these and varies sharply by period.

Under Abd al-Rahman III and al-Hakam II in the tenth century, Cordoba was unusually pluralistic — Christian and Jewish scholars served at court, intermarriage was common (always one-way: Muslim men could marry non-Muslim women, but not the reverse), Hebrew poetry flourished in Arabic-speaking Jewish communities, and the Christian community produced its own Arabic-language religious literature.
Under the Almoravids and especially the Almohads in the twelfth century, Christian and Jewish communities were under severe pressure, with major waves of forced conversion and emigration.
The convivencia was real but conditional.
It depended on the specific religious-political stance of the rulers, and when that stance hardened (as it did under the Almohads), the pluralism collapsed.
The Cordoban Umayyad Caliphate ended badly.

The dynasty's last decades, after al-Hakam II's death in 976, were dominated by a brilliant general named al-Mansur ibn Abi Aamir (al-mahn-SOOR, "the Victorious" — a Cordoban regent two and a half centuries after, and entirely unrelated to, the Abbasid caliph al-Mansur of 762 who founded Baghdad; al-Mansur was a generic honorific that multiple medieval Muslim rulers chose for themselves) who effectively ruled the caliphate as a regent during the boyhood of the next caliph and never relinquished power.

After al-Mansur's death in 1002, his sons attempted to inherit his role, the formal Umayyad caliphs reasserted themselves, civil war broke out, Madinat al-Zahra was sacked, and by 1031 the caliphate was formally dissolved.

What followed was the Taifa period (TAY-fah, from Arabic ta'ifa, "faction" or "party" — the name later applied collectively to the small kingdoms that emerged from the Cordoban caliphate's fragmentation).

For about sixty years, al-Andalus was divided into perhaps thirty small Muslim kingdoms — Seville, Toledo, Zaragoza, Granada, Valencia, and others — each ruled by a local dynasty, some Arab, some Berber, some Slavic (descended from the slave-soldiers brought from eastern Europe to serve in the Umayyad guards).

The Taifa courts were culturally productive — much of the most sophisticated Andalusian poetry was written under Taifa patronage, the smaller scale of each court producing intensified competition for scholarly and artistic talent — but militarily they were each individually weak.
This was the moment the Christian kingdoms of northern Spain seized.
The Reconquista ("reconquest") was the centuries-long process by which Christian rulers reclaimed the Iberian Peninsula from Muslim rule.
It was not a coordinated movement; it was a series of opportunistic advances, alliances, betrayals, and reversals over more than seven centuries (722–1492).

The Christian kingdoms — Castile, León, Aragon, Navarre, and Portugal as it emerged — alternately fought each other and the Muslim states, and the religious framing of the wars was much more inconsistent in the medieval period than the post-medieval ideology of the Reconquista presented it.
Christian rulers often allied with Muslim rulers against other Christian rulers; Muslim rulers often allied with Christian rulers against other Muslim rulers.

The famous El Cid (al-SID, c. 1043–1099, born Rodrigo Díaz de Vivar), commemorated in Spanish national epic as the great Christian hero of the Reconquista, in fact spent much of his career fighting for Muslim rulers against Christian ones.
The military realities did not match the ideology that would later form around them.
The decisive Christian advance during the Taifa period was the capture of Toledo in 1085 by Alfonso VI of León-Castile.
Toledo had been a major Taifa capital and one of the great centers of Andalusian scholarship.
Its capture was a strategic disaster for the Muslim states; it brought a Muslim panic that summoned the Almoravids from North Africa to intervene (Chapter 6).
It was also one of the more important cultural transmission events in European history, because the Christian conquerors of Toledo did not destroy the city's Arabic libraries.

What happened in Toledo from the late eleventh century through the thirteenth was the Toledo School of Translators — a sustained program of Arabic-to-Latin translation organized under the patronage of successive Christian kings of Castile.

Gerard of Cremona (c. 1114–1187), an Italian scholar who came to Toledo specifically to learn Arabic, translated some 87 major works from Arabic into Latin during a thirty-year career, including Ptolemy's Almagest (the standard astronomical text of the medieval world), al-Khwarizmi's Algebra, Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine, al-Razi's medical works, and Aristotle's natural philosophy.
Robert of Chester translated al-Khwarizmi.
Michael Scot translated Ibn Rushd.

The scale of the Toledo translation project was comparable to the original Greek-to-Arabic translation movement of ninth-century Baghdad, and its consequence was equally significant: the Latin Christian world finally acquired access to the unified scientific corpus that Arabic-speaking scholars had been working with for three centuries.
Most of what European universities would teach in medicine, mathematics, astronomy, and natural philosophy from 1200 to 1500 came through the Toledo translations.

The cultural transmission was thus running, by the twelfth century, from the dying Cordoban tradition into the rising European universities, mediated through the bilingual scholarly culture of Toledo and its smaller counterparts (translators worked in Sicily, Pisa, and Provence as well).
The European Renaissance, when it eventually happened, was substantially powered by texts that had been preserved, translated, refined, and commented on in Arabic over the previous five centuries.
The Cordoban caliphate ended politically.
Its libraries, partly preserved through Toledo, kept producing intellectual descendants for centuries.
The Reconquista accelerated through the thirteenth century.
Cordoba itself fell to Ferdinand III of Castile in 1236.
Seville fell in 1248.
Valencia fell in 1238.
By 1264 the Christian kingdoms had reclaimed almost all of the Iberian Peninsula.
The only remaining Muslim polity was the Emirate of Granada, in the southeastern mountains, ruled by the Nasrid dynasty as a Christian-tributary state.

Granada would survive for another 248 years — long enough to build the Alhambra, the Nasrid palace complex above the city, which is the most visited site in modern Spain — and would finally fall to the combined armies of Ferdinand and Isabella in 1492.
The 1492 fall of Granada is conventionally taken as the end of Islamic Spain.
It is also the year Columbus sailed for the Americas under Castilian patronage.
The two events are not unrelated.

The completion of the Reconquista freed the Castilian monarchy to direct resources and military attention overseas; the wealth that had built Cordoba and the technological sophistication that had run through Toledo were already being redirected toward Atlantic exploration.
The seven centuries of Islamic Spain end with the Catholic Monarchs taking Granada and immediately turning around to fund Columbus.
The medieval Mediterranean Islamic civilization and the early modern Atlantic European civilization meet in 1492 at the gates of the Alhambra.

The Cordoban caliphs would have considered the European Renaissance powered by their libraries an underwhelming legacy compared to the political empire they were aiming for; from the twenty-first century, it looks like the more substantial inheritance.

chapters.title: Trade and the Dirham Flood
sentences: The most underrated single fact about the Islamic Golden Age is that it was funded.
Scholarship costs money.
Translators have to be paid.
Manuscript copying takes labor.
Hospitals require buildings, staff, and supplies.
Observatories need instruments.
Universities need professors who do not have to farm.

The intellectual work described in the previous six chapters happened because the Caliphate's economy could underwrite it, and the Caliphate's economy could underwrite it because the Islamic world sat astride the densest commercial network the medieval world had yet seen.
Two trade systems converged in Abbasid territory.

The first was the Silk Road, the overland route system connecting the Mediterranean to China through Central Asia, which had existed in some form since the Han dynasty (Han Dynasty Ch 5) but reached new commercial intensity under the Abbasids.
The second was the Indian Ocean trade network, which connected East Africa, Arabia, India, Southeast Asia, and South China through monsoon-driven sea routes.
The Abbasid Caliphate sat at the western end of both systems.
Goods from Tang and Song China, from Gupta-successor India, from the spice islands of Indonesia, and from the East African coast flowed through Baghdad and Basra to Mediterranean buyers.
Silver from Iranian mines, dates from Iraqi orchards, glass from Syrian workshops, and steel from Damascus forges flowed back the other way.
The taxes on this trade, collected through the muhtasib system of market inspectors and the customs houses at major ports, were the financial foundation of the Caliphate.
This chapter sketches the major trade systems and the cultural-political consequences that came with them.
The Indian Ocean trade was the older and probably the more important of the two.

It had existed in some form since at least the first century CE, when Greek merchants from the Roman province of Egypt had sailed to southern India for spices and pearls (the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, a Greek navigational manual from around 50 CE, describes the route in detail).
Under the Sasanians it had been a Persian-dominated trade system, with merchant communities in southern Arabia, the Persian Gulf, and the western coast of India.

The Arab conquests inherited the system intact; the religion of the merchants changed from Zoroastrianism (and miscellaneous Christianity) to Islam, but the routes, the ships, and the commodities remained the same.
The technical foundation of the trade was the monsoon wind system.

The Indian Ocean has a uniquely predictable seasonal wind pattern: from May to October the winds blow from the southwest (carrying ships from Arabia or East Africa east toward India), and from November to April they blow from the northeast (carrying ships back the other way).
A merchant who sailed from Basra in the spring could reach the Malabar Coast of India in two months, do business through the summer, and return home in late autumn.
The schedule was fixed by the climate.
Once you knew the timing, you could trade across the Indian Ocean as reliably as a modern shipping line.
The standard ship of the trade was the dhow (DOW), a type of wooden vessel with one or two triangular lateen sails.

The lateen sail is a triangular sail mounted on a long yard at an angle to the mast; its great advantage is that it allows sailing closer to the wind than older square sails, making travel against the prevailing wind possible if difficult.

The lateen probably originated in the Indian Ocean and spread to the Mediterranean, where it became the dominant sail type for medieval Italian shipping and through that route the standard sail of the European late-medieval merchant ships that opened the Atlantic.
Dhows were sewn rather than nailed — the wooden planks of the hull were stitched together with coconut-fiber rope, with seams caulked with pine pitch.

The technique sounds primitive but was actually well-suited to the warm Indian Ocean: a stitched hull was flexible enough to absorb impact (running aground on a coral reef, for instance, did not split a stitched hull the way it would split a nailed one), and the absence of iron nails meant no rust in saltwater.
Dhows came in a range of sizes, from small coasters of perhaps 30 feet (9 meters) to ocean-going merchant vessels of 150 feet (46 meters) carrying several hundred tons of cargo.
The commodities were diverse.

Eastward from the Arab world flowed: dates, gold and silver coins, glass, fine textiles, copper, horses (highly valued in India, where the Indo-Gangetic plain was poor horse country), and the products of Mediterranean and European agriculture.

Westward from India and beyond flowed: spices (black pepper from the Malabar Coast, cinnamon from Ceylon, cloves and nutmeg from the eastern Indonesian islands, ginger and sugar from various sources), textiles (the famous Indian cotton, plus silk re-exported from China), gemstones and pearls, ivory, ceramics (Chinese porcelain was already a luxury import in ninth-century Baghdad), aromatic woods, dyes, and a small but consistent flow of medical drugs and rare books.

The annual value of this trade was substantial enough that medieval Arab geographers like Ibn Hawqal (10th century) and al-Muqaddasi (also 10th century) wrote detailed economic geographies of the major trading cities, with quantitative information about commodity prices, customs duties, and trade volumes that would not be matched in European economic geography until the early modern period.
The trade had cultural consequences.
Muslim merchant communities established themselves along the coasts of India, Southeast Asia, and East Africa.

By the eleventh and twelfth centuries, there were settled Muslim populations on the Malabar Coast (modern Kerala), in the Maldives, on the Swahili Coast of East Africa, in the spice islands of Indonesia, and in southern China (the Guangzhou Muslim community, descended from Arab and Persian merchants, dates from the eighth century — Tang Dynasty Ch 6).
Most of these communities began as trading enclaves and gradually expanded through intermarriage and conversion.

The Swahili coast (the East African coastal strip from Somalia to Mozambique) is the clearest case: by the twelfth century, a chain of trading cities — Mogadishu, Mombasa, Kilwa, Sofala — was running an Indian-Ocean-facing commercial culture in which the Bantu-language-speaking African population had absorbed Arab linguistic influence (the Swahili language is a Bantu language with substantial Arabic loanword content), Islamic religion, and Arabic literacy.
The trade routes converted populations.
The Silk Road complemented the Indian Ocean trade.

Where the maritime route specialized in bulk goods (spices were heavy in volume, textiles too), the overland route specialized in lighter, higher-value cargo — the items where the per-pound value justified the substantial transport cost of camel caravan over thousands of miles.
Silk itself was the original signature commodity (hence the name), but the trade by Abbasid times included gold, silver, gemstones, drugs, books, and the most important non-physical category: ideas.
The Abbasid silver currency — the dirham (DIR-ham, derived through Arabic from the Greek drachma) — was the monetary backbone of much of medieval Eurasia.

Silver was mined in Iran, Central Asia, and (later) Spain at substantial volumes; the Caliphate's mints at Baghdad, Damascus, Cairo, and Cordoba struck millions of dirhams each year, with high silver content (typically 95%+ pure) and consistent weight standards.
The dirham was, for several centuries, one of the most stable and most widely accepted currencies in the world.
The geographic spread of dirham finds is one of the more striking pieces of medieval economic history.
The Vikings came south for silver.

The Volga trade route was the riverine system by which Scandinavian merchants — operating from bases at Birka (BEER-kah, near modern Stockholm), Hedeby (HED-eh-bee, in southern Denmark), and Staraya Ladoga (just south of modern St.
Petersburg) — moved south through the river systems of European Russia to reach Islamic markets.

The route ran from the Baltic up the Volkhov River, across Lake Ilmen, down the Volga, and finally into the Caspian Sea, where Volga Bulgar and Khazar trading cities provided the interchange between Scandinavian goods and Abbasid silver.
This was a real, operating commercial system from approximately 750 to 950 CE — not a romantic literary trope but an industrial-scale trade flow with measurable volume and dating.
What did the Scandinavians sell?

Furs, mostly — the cold forests of northern Russia were the world's premier source of high-quality fur in the medieval period, and Islamic urban markets had a substantial demand for sable, ermine, marten, and squirrel for luxury garments.
Honey and beeswax were the second most important export.

Slaves were the third — captives taken in Scandinavian raids on the Frankish and British coasts, transported east through the Baltic and the Russian rivers, sold to Islamic markets for use as servants, soldiers, or concubines.

The slave trade is the morally darkest part of the picture and is fully documented in both Scandinavian and Arabic sources; some of the Russian river-cities that grew up along the Volga route — including the early settlements at Novgorod and Kiev — derived a substantial portion of their early income from slave-trading.
What did the Scandinavians buy?
Specifically, dirhams.
The numbers are staggering.

The total quantity of Islamic dirhams found in archaeological hoards across Scandinavia, Russia, the Baltic, and the North Sea coasts is estimated at well over one million coins, and that is only the surviving hoards.

The actual flow during the trade's peak period (around 800-950) is estimated at several hundred million dirhams over the two centuries — a quantity of silver large enough to constitute a significant portion of the Caliphate's silver production.

The single largest known hoard, found at Spillings on the island of Gotland in 1999, contained over 14,000 silver coins (most of them Islamic dirhams) along with substantial silver bullion, weighing 67 kilograms in total.
It is the largest Viking-age silver hoard ever discovered.
Gotland alone has produced over 700 documented hoards from the Viking-age silver flow.
The flood of dirhams shaped the Viking Age (Viking Age Ch 4 traces this from the Scandinavian end).
The substantial silver income from the eastern trade was one of the major factors enabling the rapid expansion of Scandinavian commercial and military activity in the eighth and ninth centuries.
Viking longships were partly funded by Abbasid silver.
The Russian state (the early Kievan Rus) emerged in part as the local power that taxed the river trade.

The Khazars — a Turkic people of the steppe whose ruling class converted to Judaism in the eighth century, occupying the lower Volga and the Caspian frontier — controlled critical chokepoints on the route and grew wealthy on the transit fees.

The arrival of Islam in Scandinavia was not a religious phenomenon (the Vikings did not convert) but an economic one — Islam, in the form of dirhams pouring north, transformed the economy of an entire region two thousand miles away.
The flow ended around 950, when the Samanid silver mines of Central Asia were largely exhausted and the Caliphate's silver production declined sharply.

The Vikings, having become dependent on the silver income, redirected their attention west — toward the Frankish and English coasts, which is why the late Viking Age is more about western Europe than eastern.
The cessation of the silver trade is also one of the proximate causes of the decline of the Khazar state and the consolidation of the early Russian principalities.
The dirham flood was a formative force in northern European history.
It also documents, in physical artifacts retrievable from the ground a thousand years later, just how vast the Caliphate's economic reach really was.
A different stream of evidence comes from a closet in a Cairo synagogue.

The Ben Ezra Synagogue in Fustat (the older part of Cairo, distinct from the Fatimid royal city of al-Qahira) maintained, from about the ninth century onward, a geniza (geh-NEE-zah, a Hebrew term for a storage room where used Jewish documents are kept; rabbinic tradition forbids destroying any document containing the divine name, so old documents are stored rather than discarded).

Over the following thousand years, the Cairo geniza accumulated something like 400,000 fragments of Jewish documents in Hebrew, Arabic-with-Hebrew-script (Judeo-Arabic), and a handful of other languages.
The documents were forgotten.
The room was sealed.
The collection sat undisturbed in the synagogue's attic from roughly the eleventh century until the late nineteenth.

In 1896, the Scottish twin sisters Agnes Smith Lewis and Margaret Dunlop Gibson brought a manuscript fragment they had purchased in Cairo back to Cambridge, where it was identified by the rabbinic scholar Solomon Schechter as a fragment of a previously unknown Hebrew text.
Schechter traveled to Cairo, gained access to the geniza, and shipped its entire contents (about 280,000 fragments) back to Cambridge, where they remain in the Taylor-Schechter Genizah collection.
The remaining fragments are scattered across libraries from Oxford to St.
Petersburg to New York.
The Cairo geniza is the single most important documentary collection for the social and economic history of the medieval Mediterranean world.

It contains everything from the formal — Bible commentaries, legal contracts, theological treatises — to the maximally informal: shopping lists, love letters, business accounts, marriage contracts, divorce proceedings, immigration records, tax receipts, school exercises by Jewish children learning to write Arabic in Hebrew letters.
The historian S.

Goitein, working from the 1950s through the 1980s, produced a five-volume Mediterranean Society (1967–1988) that reconstructed the daily life, commercial networks, and cultural texture of medieval Mediterranean Jewish communities — and through them the broader Islamic world they lived in — with a granularity that no other medieval documentary source allows.
What the geniza shows about the Islamic Golden Age is detail.

Specifically: a Jewish merchant family in twelfth-century Cairo running business operations through correspondents in Tunis, Sicily, Palermo, Aleppo, Yemen, and the Malabar Coast, communicating in Judeo-Arabic, settling accounts with bills of exchange that allowed long-distance commerce without physical transport of bullion, conducting their affairs under Fatimid (then Ayyubid, then Mamluk) Islamic legal cover, and producing the textile, foodstuff, and spice trade volumes that powered Egypt's economy.
The geniza Jews were not isolated.

They were one community within a multi-religious commercial world that ran on shared commercial law (the Cairo geniza shows Jewish merchants using Islamic legal forms when convenient, just as Muslim merchants used Jewish moneylenders when convenient), shared shipping networks, shared currencies, and a shared culture of long-distance credit that operated centuries before its European equivalents.
The medieval Mediterranean was a single commercial space.
The geniza is the densest documentary evidence of that fact.
The Indian Ocean trade had its own great traveler, working at the very late end of the Golden Age.
Ibn Battuta (IB-n bat-TOO-tah, 1304–1369) was a Moroccan Maliki legal scholar from Tangier who left home in 1325, at age 21, to make the hajj to Mecca.
He returned home in 1354, having traveled approximately 75,000 miles (120,000 km) over twenty-nine years across most of the known Islamic world and beyond.

His itinerary included: North Africa, Egypt, Syria, the Hejaz (multiple times), Iraq, Persia, the Arabian Peninsula, East Africa as far south as Mombasa, the Anatolian Turkic states, the Crimea and the Golden Horde, Central Asia, India (where he served for several years as a judge in the Delhi Sultanate under Muhammad bin Tughluq), the Maldives (where he served as a judge for another period), Ceylon, China (he probably reached at least southern China; some details of his Chinese itinerary are debated), Sumatra, and finally Spain and West Africa across the Sahara to the Mali Empire.
The total mileage exceeds Marco Polo's contemporary travels by a comfortable margin.

He dictated his account, the Rihla ("Journey," literally; the Arabic word can also mean "travel narrative" as a literary genre that had developed by Ibn Battuta's time), to a court secretary in Morocco after his return.

The book is the single most detailed travel record of the medieval Islamic world, and it documents what the Indian Ocean trade looked like at ground level: the merchants in every port, the ships, the courts of the local rulers, the legal systems, the religious practices, the infrastructure of caravanserais and bath-houses and mosques.

Ibn Battuta could travel from Morocco to China and find Muslim scholars who shared his Maliki legal training, kindred merchants who could host him, mosques where he could pray, judges who would recognize his credentials and offer him judgeships, networks of mystical orders that included branches in every major city.
The Islamic world by his lifetime was a connected cultural-economic space that no Christian European had a comparable analog of.
Marco Polo had traveled through a foreign world and returned with marvel-tales.
Ibn Battuta traveled through a familiar world and returned with detailed administrative observations.
The Rihla is a late-Golden-Age document — Ibn Battuta lived after the Mongol sack of Baghdad and the political collapse of the Abbasid caliphate.

But what he documents is the cultural Islamic world that survived the political collapse: still vast, still connected, still running the commercial and intellectual networks the Abbasid centuries had built.
The institutions persisted because they were rooted in trade, language, religion, and law rather than in political unity, and trade language religion and law are more resilient than dynasties.
The economic foundation of the Golden Age was always plural.

Iranian agriculture (the Sawad and the Iranian plateau), Egyptian agriculture (the Nile valley), Andalusian agriculture (the Guadalquivir basin and the Granadan huertas), Mediterranean trade, Indian Ocean trade, Silk Road trade, the Saharan gold trade with West Africa, the Volga silver trade with the Vikings — all of these contributed simultaneously and reinforced each other.
The Caliphate did not depend on a single revenue source.
When the Iranian silver mines declined around 950, Egyptian gold and Andalusian agricultural surplus picked up the slack.

When the political center of gravity shifted east after the Mongol invasions (Chapter 10), the Mediterranean trade through Cairo and the surviving North African trade with West Africa carried the Islamic commercial world forward.
The redundancy of the economic base is one of the major reasons the cultural unit survived the political disasters of the eleventh through thirteenth centuries.
The next chapter turns to those disasters.

chapters.title: The Seljuk Eclipse and the Crusades
sentences: The Abbasid caliph who sat on the throne in Baghdad in 1100 was a man named al-Mustazhir bi'llah.
You have probably never heard of him.
This is not your fault.
By 1100, the office of caliph had been almost entirely ceremonial for a century and a half.

The actual government of the eastern Islamic world was being conducted by a rotating cast of regional sultans and viziers who used the caliph's name as a formal legitimation device but did not consult him on policy.
The political history of the late Golden Age is, accordingly, the history of those sultans and viziers — Buyids, Seljuks, Khwarezmians, Ayyubids, Mamluks.
The caliph remained in his palace.
The empire moved on without him.
The shift began in 945, when a small Iranian dynasty called the Buyids (BOO-yids, sometimes spelled Buwayhids) took Baghdad.
The Buyids were Twelver Shia Muslims from the Caspian region of northern Iran.

They were originally mountain warlords from the Daylam (a rugged region south of the Caspian Sea) who took service under Iranian and Iraqi rulers in the early tenth century, gradually accumulated military force, and by the 940s controlled most of Iran and parts of Iraq.

In 945 the Buyid amir Mu'izz al-Dawla (moo-IZZ ad-DAW-lah, "Strengthener of the State" — the al-Dawla honorifics were a Buyid innovation that future regional rulers would emulate) entered Baghdad with his army, deposed the existing political establishment, and installed himself as the de facto ruler of the Caliphate's heartland.
The arrangement that followed was peculiar.
Mu'izz al-Dawla and his Buyid successors did not abolish the Abbasid caliphate.
They could have — they had the military force, and they had ideological grounds, since they were Shia and the Abbasid was a Sunni institution.

Instead, they preserved the caliph as a formal ruler, took the title amir al-umara ("commander of commanders") for themselves, controlled the Caliphate's armies, taxes, and administration, and let the caliph maintain ceremonial functions and the religious symbolism of the office.

The Buyid logic seems to have been pragmatic: the Sunni population they ruled would not accept a Shia caliph; abolishing the caliphate would create a religious-political vacuum they could not fill; far easier to rule through the existing institution while reducing it to a shell.
The Buyids ruled the Caliphate's heartland for 110 years (945–1055) without ever attempting to replace the caliph.
The Buyid period was, intellectually, productive.
The Buyid courts at Baghdad, Rey, Shiraz, and other cities patronized scholarship enthusiastically.

Several of the Golden Age figures from earlier chapters worked under Buyid patronage — including Ibn Sina (Chapter 4), who served various Buyid courts before moving on, and al-Biruni (al-bee-ROO-nee, 973-1050), the great polymath geographer and astronomer who produced his Kitab al-Hind (a remarkably penetrating comparative study of Indian science and religion, written after he accompanied Mahmud of Ghazni on campaigns into India).
Buyid Shi'ism was relatively non-aggressive; Sunni scholars were not persecuted, and most of the great Sunni religious institutions of Baghdad continued to operate normally.

The Caliph al-Qadir issued the Qadiri Creed in 1018, a formal Sunni doctrinal statement responding to Buyid Shi'ism and Mu'tazilite rationalism, which the Buyid amirs allowed to circulate without suppression.
The political shift to Shia rule did not reshape religious life on the ground.
What it did do was demonstrate that the Caliphate was no longer a unified state.
After 945, the political authority that had once flowed from Baghdad outward had reversed direction.

Local dynasties — Samanids in Khorasan, Ghaznavids in Afghanistan, Fatimids in Egypt, Buyids in Iraq and western Iran, smaller dynasties everywhere — were now running their own affairs, occasionally consulting Baghdad for legitimating gestures, but otherwise functioning as independent states.
The Caliphate had become, in modern terms, a confederation of local rulers united by a shared religious institution rather than a unified empire.
The Buyids were displaced in 1055 by a new force: the Seljuk Turks.

The Seljuks were a confederation of Turkic-speaking peoples from the steppe north of the Aral Sea — descended ultimately from the Oghuz Turks who had moved into the Central Asian frontier of the Caliphate in the ninth and tenth centuries, converted to Sunni Islam, and gradually assimilated to the urban Islamic culture they encountered.

The Turkic language family — distinct from both Iranian and Semitic, related at distance to Mongolian; the Turkic-speaking peoples are linguistically as different from Persians and Arabs as English-speakers are from Hindi-speakers, even though they had been Muslim for several generations and were culturally Persianate in important respects — had been gradually expanding into Iran and the Islamic east for some time.
The Seljuk dynasty, founded by Tughril Beg (TOO-gril, ruled 1037-1063), was the first Turkic political force to seize central control of the Caliphate.
Tughril Beg's army entered Baghdad in 1055 at the invitation of the Sunni Caliph al-Qa'im, who had been chafing under Shia Buyid domination for over a century.
The Buyids were expelled.

Tughril Beg was given the title Sultan ("authority" or "ruler" — sultan had previously been a generic term but now became the formal title of the supreme political ruler holding power in the Caliphate's name) and married the caliph's daughter.
The arrangement was the same as the Buyid arrangement in legal form: caliph as religious authority, sultan as political authority, separation of functions, shared sovereignty.
The difference was that the Seljuks were Sunni.
The Caliphate now had a Sunni political protector for the first time in over a century.
The Seljuks were also expansionist in a way the Buyids had not been.
By 1071 they had taken control of most of the Iranian plateau, Iraq, and Syria, and were pushing into Anatolia.
The most consequential single battle of the late Golden Age was fought in 1071 in eastern Anatolia.

The Battle of Manzikert (MAN-zih-kert, fought near Lake Van in modern Turkey, August 26, 1071) pitted the Seljuk sultan Alp Arslan (ALP ar-SLAN, "Heroic Lion," ruled 1063-1072) against the Byzantine emperor Romanos IV Diogenes (ro-MAH-nos di-OG-ehn-eez).

The Byzantines had been pursuing a policy of pushing eastward into Armenia and Mesopotamia for several decades; Romanos had assembled a large army (perhaps 40,000 men, including mercenaries) for what was supposed to be a decisive campaign against the Seljuks.
The Seljuks responded with a smaller but more mobile force.
The battle was a disaster for the Byzantines.

A combination of mercenary defections, tactical mistakes, and Seljuk skill at the steppe-style feigned retreat resulted in the destruction of the Byzantine field army and the capture of Romanos himself.
He was the first Roman emperor to be taken prisoner in battle since Valerian had been captured by the Sasanian king Shapur I in 260 (Persian Empire Ch 8).
Alp Arslan, displaying the chivalric gestures that medieval Islamic and steppe traditions both valued in conquerors, treated his captive honorably, signed a peace treaty, and released him.
Romanos returned to Constantinople to find that his political faction had been overthrown in his absence; he was blinded, exiled, and died of his injuries the following year.
The strategic consequence of Manzikert was the opening of Anatolia to Turkic settlement.

The Byzantine theme system (Byzantine Empire Ch 3 — the system of military-administrative provinces under regional generals that the empire had used to garrison and tax its Anatolian heartland since the seventh century) had been holding eastern Anatolia together for four centuries, and the destruction of the field army at Manzikert (covered in detail from the Byzantine side in Byzantine Empire Ch 7) was the moment that system broke.

Turkic tribes streamed into the Anatolian highlands over the following decades, settling among the indigenous Greek-speaking population, gradually converting them or displacing them, and over the next four centuries transforming Anatolia from a Greek Christian province into the Turkish Muslim heartland that would eventually become the Ottoman Empire (Byzantine Empire Ch 7-11).
What we now call Turkey is the result of Manzikert.
Without the battle, modern Turkey would not exist as a Turkic-speaking nation.
The other strategic consequence was the call for help from Constantinople to Western Europe.

The Byzantine emperor Alexios I Komnenos (ko-NEE-nos, ruled 1081-1118), inheriting an empire shrunk by Manzikert and threatened on all sides, sent envoys to Pope Urban II in 1095 asking for Western military aid against the Seljuk advance.
Alexios wanted what we would now call a mercenary force — Western European heavy cavalry to be incorporated into Byzantine command and used to retake lost provinces.
What he got was something else.
In November 1095, Pope Urban II preached a sermon at the Council of Clermont in central France calling for a Western Christian military expedition to recover Jerusalem from Muslim rule.

The sermon's exact text does not survive (we have several reconstructions written by chroniclers afterward, all subtly different from each other), but its basic structure is clear: Urban framed a campaign to assist the Eastern Christians as a meritorious religious act, offered participants the remission of sins, and connected the recovery of Jerusalem to the broader cause of Christian unity.
The response was unexpected.
Within months, tens of thousands of Western Europeans had taken the cross — the symbolic vow of pilgrimage with military intent — and were preparing to march east.
The First Crusade (1096-1099) was the first major military intervention by Western Europe in the Islamic world since the Carolingian campaigns three centuries earlier.
It was, by any reasonable measure, an astonishing success — for the Crusaders.

A peasant force called the People's Crusade was massacred in Anatolia early on, but the main armies of Frankish nobles successfully crossed Asia Minor (with reluctant Byzantine logistical support; relations between the Crusaders and Alexios soured almost immediately, neither side trusting the other), captured the city of Antioch in 1098 after a long siege and a famous battle in which the Crusaders, their food running out, sortied against a relief army and won an unexpected victory, and reached Jerusalem in June 1099.
The siege of Jerusalem lasted six weeks.
The city fell on July 15, 1099.
The Crusaders sacked it.
The sack was unusually bloody even by the standards of medieval city captures.

Contemporary Crusader sources — proudly — describe the killing of Muslim and Jewish inhabitants en masse, with chronicles citing knights riding through streets where the blood reached their horses' bridles.

The numerical claims for casualties are inflated by both sides for their own reasons (Muslim sources to dramatize the atrocity, Crusader sources to celebrate it), but the consensus modern estimate is that several thousand to perhaps tens of thousands of inhabitants were killed in the days following the city's fall.
The Muslim population of Jerusalem was effectively eliminated.
The Jewish population was either killed or expelled.
The Eastern Christian population was largely tolerated but had a difficult relationship with the Latin Crusaders.
The Crusaders established four Crusader states along the eastern Mediterranean coast: the Kingdom of Jerusalem, the County of Tripoli, the Principality of Antioch, and the County of Edessa.

These were small Latin Christian polities embedded in a much larger Muslim world, surviving on European reinforcement, control of the coastal ports, and the chronic political division of the surrounding Islamic states.

They were not ideologically central to the wider Islamic world's military-political agenda for most of the next ninety years — the Seljuk and Fatimid struggles for control of Syria absorbed most local attention — but they were a chronic irritant.

While the Crusader states were establishing themselves on the Levantine coast, the eastern part of the Islamic world was undergoing an institutional transformation that had begun a generation earlier and would shape its intellectual and religious life for centuries — and would, by the time of Saladin, supply the ideological infrastructure for the Sunni response to the Crusades.
Nizam al-Mulk (nih-ZAHM al-MULK, "Order of the Realm," c. 1018-1092) was the great vizier of the Seljuk sultans Alp Arslan and Malik-Shah I.

He served as the de facto chief minister of the Seljuk Empire for nearly thirty years, during which he reorganized the empire's administration along Sasanian-Persian lines (the same Persianizing tendency that had marked the early Abbasids — Chapter 1; the Iranian administrative tradition kept getting reused), wrote a famous mirror for princes — the Siyasatnama ("Book of Government," c. 1090) — that became a standard reference for Islamic political theory for centuries, and founded the institutional system that would define Sunni higher education for the rest of the medieval period.
The institution Nizam al-Mulk founded was the madrasa (mah-DRAH-sah, "place of study" — the Arabic noun derived from the verb "to study").
Madrasas as informal religious teaching institutions had existed for some time, but Nizam al-Mulk created the first network of state-funded, standardized, residential teaching colleges.
The flagship was the Nizamiyya of Baghdad, founded in 1065, with branches established over the following years in Nishapur, Isfahan, Mosul, Basra, Marv, Herat, and other major cities.
Each Nizamiyya was endowed with land or commercial revenues sufficient to support a faculty of professors, a residential community of students, a library, and a mosque.
Students received free education, room, and board.
The curriculum focused on Sunni law (especially the Shafi'i school, which Nizam al-Mulk personally favored) and Ash'ari theology, both taught according to standardized texts and methods.
The Nizamiyya network was the first state-funded higher education system in any civilization.

It pre-dated the European universities (the University of Bologna, conventionally dated to 1088, was contemporary with the late Nizamiyya foundations; but the European universities developed organically from earlier cathedral schools rather than as a planned state initiative).
It standardized Sunni religious education across the Caliphate.
And it employed many of the great late-Golden-Age scholars — including al-Ghazali (Chapter 5), who taught at the Baghdad Nizamiyya before his nervous breakdown.
The Nizamiyya system also institutionalized the Ash'ari-Ghazalian theological synthesis as the standard Sunni orthodoxy.
The professorial line at each madrasa enforced doctrinal continuity — a Nizamiyya graduate had a specific theological training that was the same in Baghdad as in Nishapur.
Sunni Islam, by 1150, had acquired through the Nizamiyya system the doctrinal uniformity it had previously lacked.
The fragmentation of legal schools (the four madhhabs) was preserved; what had become standardized was theology.

By the time Saladin emerged a century later, the Sunni religious-political world he operated in had been shaped by the Nizamiyya — its judges, its preachers, its theologians had been trained on a common curriculum, and the call to confront the Crusader presence could be framed in the unified Ash'ari-Sunni terms the madrasa network had taught.
Nizam al-Mulk himself was assassinated in 1092 by a Nizari Ismaili Assassin (Mongol Empire Ch 5) sent by Hassan-i Sabbah, the founder of the Order of Assassins at the mountain fortress of Alamut.

The Assassins were Nizari Ismaili Shia (Chapter 5) — a splinter of the Fatimid tradition that had organized into a militant order specializing in the targeted assassination of Sunni political and religious leaders.

They had emerged in Iran in the late 1080s, established a string of mountain fortresses including the famous Alamut in the Alborz mountains north of modern Tehran, and conducted a 170-year campaign of high-value political assassination across the eastern Islamic world.
Nizam al-Mulk was their first major victim.
They would kill many more before being eliminated by the Mongols in 1256 (next chapter).
The Islamic political response to the Crusader presence took most of a century to organize, and when it came it was led by an unexpected figure.

Salah al-Din Yusuf ibn Ayyub (sah-LAH ah-DEEN, "Righteousness of the Faith," c. 1137-1193) — known to Western Europe as Saladin — was a Kurdish military commander whose family had served the Seljuks in northern Mesopotamia.
The Kurds are an Iranian-speaking people of the highlands of eastern Turkey, northern Iraq, and western Iran; the Kurdish language is Indo-European, related to Persian, but distinct from it.
The Kurds had been Sunni Muslims since the early Caliphate, but they retained a distinct ethnic identity and produced their own military aristocracy in the medieval period.

Saladin's family rose under Seljuk patronage and then under the patronage of the Sunni Syrian ruler Nur al-Din (noor ah-DEEN), who had built a powerful Syrian state in the mid-twelfth century in opposition to both the Crusaders and the Shia Fatimids in Egypt.
Saladin was sent to Egypt by Nur al-Din in 1169 as part of an expedition to support a Fatimid faction in Cairo's internal politics.
Through a combination of political skill and luck, he ended up as the Fatimid vizier — a Sunni Kurd running the central administration of a Shia caliphate.
In 1171, on the death of the last Fatimid caliph, Saladin formally abolished the Fatimid Caliphate, restored Sunni control of Egypt, and proclaimed allegiance to the Abbasid caliph in Baghdad.
The Friday prayer in Cairo's mosques, after 262 years of Fatimid Shia recitation, returned to the Sunni form.

The change was massive — Egypt had been Shia for nearly three centuries and the institutional architecture of the country had been built around Shia legitimacy — but Saladin pulled it off without major popular resistance.
The largely Sunni population of Egypt seems to have welcomed the shift; the Fatimid-loyalist faction in Cairo was small and isolated.
When Nur al-Din died in 1174, Saladin extended his control to Syria, marrying into Nur al-Din's family to claim political legitimacy.
By 1186 he was the ruler of a unified Egyptian-Syrian state that surrounded the Crusader Kingdom of Jerusalem.
He had also secured formal investiture from the Abbasid caliph as Sultan, giving him recognized Sunni political legitimacy across the Islamic east.
In 1187, Saladin invaded the Crusader states.
The decisive engagement was the Battle of Hattin (HAH-teen, July 4, 1187), fought in the hills above the Sea of Galilee.

The Crusader army, under the inept king Guy of Lusignan, was lured onto a waterless plateau, denied access to springs, surrounded by Saladin's forces, and destroyed over two days of fighting in summer heat.
Most of the Crusader military aristocracy was killed or captured.

Saladin reportedly executed the Knights Templar and Hospitaller prisoners (the two military religious orders, considered the most ideologically committed Crusaders) but spared most of the nobles for ransom.
Within three months he had taken every major Crusader city in the Levant except Tyre.
Jerusalem fell on October 2, 1187 — the Hijri date was the anniversary of the Prophet's Night Journey to the Temple Mount, a coincidence both sides noted.
Saladin's treatment of Jerusalem on its surrender was the moral inverse of the 1099 Crusader sack.
The Christian inhabitants were not killed.
They were allowed to leave on payment of ransom, with the poor (those who could not pay) released without payment after Saladin's brother contributed funds.
Christian holy sites were preserved.
Eastern Christian inhabitants — Greek and Armenian — were allowed to remain.
The Muslim and Jewish populations who had been expelled or killed in 1099 were invited to return.
The contrast between the two captures of Jerusalem was so striking that medieval European chroniclers — even crusader ones — sometimes acknowledged it.

Saladin became, in European literary tradition, a kind of paragon of Islamic chivalry, eventually appearing in Dante's Inferno in Limbo (the section reserved for virtuous non-Christians) and serving as a sympathetic character in nineteenth-century Walter Scott novels.

The Christian response was the Third Crusade (1189-1192), led by Emperor Frederick Barbarossa of Germany (who drowned crossing a river in Anatolia before reaching the Holy Land), King Philip II Augustus of France (who returned home early), and most prominently King Richard I "the Lionheart" of England (1157-1199, the Plantagenet king of an Anglo-French realm covering much of modern France and England).
Richard fought Saladin to a stalemate over three years of campaigning, recovered the coastal strip from Acre to Jaffa, but failed to recapture Jerusalem.
The Treaty of Jaffa in 1192 ended the Crusade with Christians keeping the coastal Crusader states (substantially reduced from their 1187 peak) and Saladin keeping Jerusalem.
The Crusader presence in the Levant would persist for another century, but it was now a coastal-strip residue rather than a major regional force.
Richard and Saladin never met in person, but a long-running medieval European tradition fictionalized chivalric exchanges between them.

The most famous — Richard's horse killed in battle, Saladin sending him a replacement — is probably apocryphal but captures the genuine mutual regard the two commanders developed during the campaigns.
Both were exceptional military leaders, and each recognized the other.
Saladin died in Damascus in 1193, six months after the Treaty of Jaffa.

His family — the Ayyubid dynasty — divided his empire among its various branches and ruled Egypt and Syria as a fragmented confederation for the next sixty years, sometimes hostile to the Crusader states, sometimes in alliance with them, always in chronic internal conflict among Saladin's relatives.
A final note on the Khwarezmian Empire, because its story sets up Chapter 10.
The Seljuks themselves declined through the twelfth century, fragmenting into smaller successor sultanates as the dynasty's central authority weakened.

By the late twelfth century, the dominant power in the eastern Islamic world was the Khwarezmian Empire — a successor state founded by the family of a Seljuk vassal who had originally governed the Khwarezm region (the same area along the lower Amu Darya from which al-Khwarizmi had hailed; the Iranian-speaking heartland of Central Asia).

Under Ala ad-Din Muhammad II (1200-1220), the Khwarezmian state controlled most of Iran, Afghanistan, Transoxiana, and parts of the Iraqi border — an empire larger than the Seljuk empire had been at its peak.
The Khwarezmian sultan was, in 1218, the most powerful Muslim ruler in the eastern world.
The Abbasid caliph in Baghdad was a religious figurehead.
The Ayyubids in Egypt and Syria were dealing with the Crusader successor problems.
The Seljuks of Anatolia (the Seljuks of Rum) were a regional power.
The Khwarezmians outranked them all.
In 1218, a small caravan of Mongol merchants arrived at the Khwarezmian frontier town of Otrar carrying trade goods and a request for normal commercial relations.

The Khwarezmian governor of Otrar — apparently acting on the sultan's orders, or at least with the sultan's tacit approval — accused the merchants of being spies, executed them, and seized their goods.
Genghis Khan, the Mongol ruler whose envoys these had been, sent a second delegation requesting an explanation.
The sultan had its members beheaded.
Genghis Khan now had what he later called the cause for the most destructive single military campaign in human history.

chapters.title: The Mongol End
sentences: The Mongol invasion of the Islamic world is documented exhaustively from the Mongol side in the Mongol Empire narrative (Mongol Empire Ch 3).
What this chapter offers is the view from inside the world that was being destroyed.
The Khwarezmian Empire collapsed within two years of Genghis Khan's invasion.
The Mongol army crossed the frontier in the autumn of 1219.
Otrar fell in early 1220 — the governor who had murdered the Mongol envoys was reportedly executed by having molten silver poured into his eyes and mouth, the Mongol response to greed.
Bukhara fell in February 1220.
Samarkand fell in March 1220.
Merv fell in 1221 — the population was massacred so systematically that the Persian historian al-Juvayni, writing forty years later, gave a casualty figure of 1.3 million.
The figure is implausibly high (Merv probably had at most 500,000 inhabitants), but it captures the contemporary impression of comprehensive destruction.
The major cities of Khorasan and Transoxiana — the heartland of eastern Islamic culture — were systematically depopulated.
Agricultural infrastructure (irrigation canals, stored grain, water wheels) was destroyed.

The casualty figures from these campaigns are debated among modern historians; the reasonable consensus is that total deaths in the Khwarezmian campaign and its immediate aftermath probably ran to several million, with proportionally heavy population losses in Khorasan and Transoxiana.
The eastern Iranian world did not recover for centuries.
Some specific cities — Merv, Nishapur, Balkh — would never recover their pre-Mongol prominence at all.
The cultural losses were comparable.
The library of Bukhara, one of the great collections of the eastern Islamic world (the library that the young Ibn Sina had read his way through, Chapter 4), was burned.
The libraries of Samarkand, Merv, and Nishapur were destroyed.
Manuscripts not lost outright in the cities were lost in the disruption of the trade and copying networks that had kept them in circulation.
The intellectual continuity that the Caliphate had built up over five centuries was breaking in real time.
Sultan Ala ad-Din Muhammad II died in 1220 on a small island in the Caspian Sea, hiding from the Mongol pursuit.

His son Jalal al-Din continued resistance from base in Afghanistan and India for another decade, conducting a guerrilla campaign that occasionally won battles but could not reverse the strategic position.
He was finally killed in 1231 by a Kurdish bandit who did not recognize him.
The first phase of the Mongol invasion ended in the early 1220s with the death of Genghis Khan in 1227 and the recall of the main Mongol forces to deal with succession matters in Mongolia.
The eastern Islamic world had a thirty-year reprieve.
It was used badly.
The political fragmentation that had characterized the previous century continued; no Islamic power assembled the coalition that might have allowed coordinated resistance to the next Mongol wave.

The Ayyubids continued their internal squabbles; the Seljuks of Rum dealt with regional concerns; the Abbasid caliph in Baghdad continued to be a religious figurehead; the Mamluks would not exist as a state until 1250.
The next Mongol wave came in 1253-1258 under Hulagu Khan (HOO-lah-goo, c. 1217-1265, the grandson of Genghis Khan and brother of the new Great Khan Mongke).
Hulagu's campaign had two strategic objectives: the destruction of the Nizari Ismaili Assassins, and the destruction of the Abbasid Caliphate.
The Assassins had been an irritant to every Sunni political authority in the Islamic east for 170 years.
Their fortress network across Iran was the most successful long-term insurgency in medieval history.

They had killed Nizam al-Mulk, multiple Seljuk sultans, multiple Crusader leaders (including Conrad of Montferrat in 1192), and probably had attempted to kill the Mongol commander Mongke Khan himself in 1254.
The Assassin grand master at Alamut, Rukn al-Din Khurshah, was a young man with limited political experience who attempted negotiations with the advancing Mongol force.
The negotiations failed.
Hulagu's army arrived at Alamut in November 1256.
The garrison surrendered on December 15, 1256.
The Mongols dismantled the fortress — the first time in the 170-year history of the order that Alamut had been taken.
They executed the garrison and Khurshah's family.
The Assassin library at Alamut was largely destroyed, with a small selection of scientific texts saved by one of the captured scholars, Nasir al-Din al-Tusi (Mongol Empire Ch 5).
Al-Tusi, recognizing the Mongol commander's interest in mathematics and astronomy, talked his way out of execution and into Mongol service.
He would become the most consequential single intellectual under Mongol patronage.

The career-saving act of intellectual flexibility that resulted in al-Tusi joining the Mongol court is one of the more remarkable individual stories of the period — and the Maragha Observatory (later in this chapter) would not exist without it.
Hulagu's army then turned to Baghdad.
The destruction of Baghdad in February 1258 is the conventional terminal event of the Islamic Golden Age, and the description from the Mongol side is given in detail in Mongol Empire Ch 5.
From the Baghdad side, the relevant facts are these.
The reigning caliph was al-Musta'sim bi'llah (mus-TAH-sim bee-LAH, ruled 1242-1258, the thirty-seventh and final Abbasid caliph).
His vizier was Ibn al-Alqami, a Shia who has been blamed by some later Sunni historians for treacherously underestimating the Mongol threat in order to serve Shia interests.
The accusation is probably unfair; the actual evidence suggests that Ibn al-Alqami was a competent administrator whose advice the caliph mostly ignored.

The caliph and his court substantially underestimated the Mongol threat, made no serious preparations for siege, and failed to call for help from the surrounding powers (Mamluks, Ayyubid remnants, Seljuks of Rum) until far too late.
Baghdad in 1258 was no longer the Baghdad of the eighth-century peak.
The city had declined substantially during the political fragmentation of the previous three centuries.
Its peak population of perhaps a million in the ninth century had reduced to perhaps 400,000 by the mid-thirteenth.

The Round City of al-Mansur was a memory; its walls had been dismantled centuries earlier and modern Baghdad was a sprawling complex of neighborhoods, mosques, markets, and palaces along both banks of the Tigris.
The city was still the largest Muslim city in the world by some measures and still the religious capital of Sunni Islam, but it was no longer the unrivaled center it had been.
The siege began in late January 1258.

The Mongol force outside the walls was perhaps 150,000 men — substantially larger than the Baghdad garrison, better equipped, and with siege engineering provided by Chinese siege specialists who had accompanied Hulagu west.
The Caliphate's defenders fought competently for several weeks, but the walls were breached on February 5, the garrison surrendered on terms, and the city was given over to the army on February 13.
The killing lasted approximately a week.
The lower estimates of casualties are around 100,000 to 200,000 civilians killed in a city of perhaps 400,000 — meaning that one in four or one in two of Baghdad's inhabitants died in the sack.
The higher estimates run to 800,000 or even a million but are not credible at the population scale of the city.
The libraries were thrown into the Tigris.

The contemporary witness Ata-Malik Juvayni — who was actually a senior administrator working for the Mongols, but who wrote a substantial account of these events — described the river running black with the ink of dissolved manuscripts.
The story is probably exaggerated for literary effect, but the underlying fact is real: the major manuscript collections of Baghdad were destroyed.

The Bayt al-Hikma had at this point not been the same active research institution it had been in the ninth century — its peak as a translation center had been four centuries earlier — but it remained a major manuscript library, and in the late Abbasid period it was one of perhaps a dozen specialized libraries in the city that contained accumulations of Arabic, Persian, Greek, Indian, and Syriac texts not preserved in this concentration anywhere else.
Some of those texts existed only in Baghdad.
When the libraries burned, those texts were gone.
The caliph was captured.

The Mongol custom that forbade the spilling of royal blood was honored: al-Musta'sim was rolled up in a felt rug and stamped to death by horses, or kicked to death, or crushed under his own treasury, depending on which contemporary account you read.
He died bloodlessly.
The Abbasid Caliphate, which had anchored Sunni political legitimacy for half a millennium, was finished.
The medieval institutional consensus that had defined Sunni religious-political order ceased to exist in February 1258.
So what continued?
A great deal, actually.

The "end of the Islamic Golden Age" is real in the sense that the political-cultural center at Baghdad had been destroyed, but it is misleading in the sense that the broader Islamic civilization survived, adapted, and in some respects continued to flourish.
The terminal event of the Caliphate was not a terminal event of Islamic culture as a whole.
Several things continued in important ways.
The Persian intellectual tradition continued under Mongol patronage.

The Ilkhanate — the Mongol successor state in Iran, founded by Hulagu after his campaigns and ruled by his descendants until the early fourteenth century (Mongol Empire Ch 7) — became a major center of Persian-language scholarship within a single generation.
The Mongol court at Tabriz patronized Persian poets, historians, and scientists.
Nasir al-Din al-Tusi, the Persian polymath whom Hulagu had spared at Alamut, was given resources to build the Maragha Observatory in northwestern Iran in 1259 — within months of the Baghdad sack.

Maragha was, for the rest of the thirteenth century, the most sophisticated astronomical research institution in the world, equipped with instruments larger and more precise than any used in Baghdad, staffed with scholars from across the Islamic world and beyond (including some Chinese astronomers who arrived via the Mongol cross-Asian connections), and producing astronomical work — including al-Tusi's Tusi couple, a geometric device for modeling planetary motion that would feed forward into Copernicus's heliocentric model three centuries later — that built directly on the Abbasid mathematical tradition.
The institutional center of Islamic science had moved from Baghdad to Maragha within eighteen months of the destruction of the former.
The pattern of scientific continuity through political catastrophe is one of the more remarkable features of the late Golden Age.
The Mongol rulers of the Ilkhanate converted to Islam within two generations.
Ghazan Khan (ruled 1295-1304) was the first Mongol ruler of Iran to convert; his successors followed.

The conversion entailed the partial dissolution of the Mongol-Persian distinction — Mongol elites took on Persian court culture, married into Persian aristocratic families, patronized Persian-language scholarship, and within a few generations were culturally indistinguishable from their Persian subjects.
The pattern is the same one Persian Empire Ch 10 documents repeatedly: the Iranian cultural tradition absorbing its conquerors.
Mongol rule in Iran was destructive in its first generation and culturally generative in its later generations.
The poet Rumi (1207-1273) wrote his great Persian Sufi poetry during the Mongol invasion period itself.
Sa'di (1210-1291) wrote his classic Persian prose works under Mongol-affiliated patronage.
The Persian literary tradition that the Mongols had partially destroyed was, by 1300, being patronized by the Mongol descendants who had settled into Persian court culture.
The Mamluk Sultanate of Egypt held the western Islamic line.

The Mamluks — a slave-soldier military class who had taken political control of Egypt in 1250 — defeated a Mongol force at Ayn Jalut in Galilee in September 1260 (Mongol Empire Ch 5), establishing the limit of Mongol westward expansion in the Near East.
