The Mamluk Sultanate would rule Egypt and Syria from 1250 to 1517, providing political continuity for the Islamic religious-cultural tradition in the western half of the Islamic world.
Cairo, under the Mamluks, became the most important single Islamic city after the destruction of Baghdad.

The Mamluk court patronized scholarship, built monumental mosques and madrasas, maintained al-Azhar (Chapter 6) as a major center of Sunni learning, and supported the migration of scholars from the destroyed eastern centers.
Many of the late-Golden-Age scientific figures — including Ibn al-Nafis (Chapter 4) — worked in Mamluk Cairo.
The Mamluks also installed a relative of the murdered Abbasid caliph as a ceremonial Abbasid in Cairo in 1261.
This shadow caliphate had no political authority but provided a ceremonial Sunni religious continuity until the line was extinguished by the Ottoman conquest of Egypt in 1517.
The Ottoman sultans subsequently claimed transfer of the caliphate to themselves, though the historicity of that claim is debated.

The Sunni caliphate as an institution thus had a continuous formal existence from the Prophet's death in 632 to the Turkish Republic's abolition of the Ottoman caliphate in 1924 — 1,292 years — though its actual significance varied wildly across that span.
The North African and Andalusian traditions continued for another two centuries after 1258 with little Mongol involvement.

The Almohad caliphate had collapsed earlier in the thirteenth century, but successor dynasties (Marinids in Morocco, Hafsids in Tunisia, Zayyanids in Algeria, Nasrids in Granada) continued to govern; al-Andalus continued to produce scholarship until the fifteenth century; the Toledo translation movement continued to feed into European universities through the entire late medieval period.
The political collapse in Iraq did not interrupt the western Islamic intellectual tradition at all.
The European reception of Islamic learning continued unbroken.

The Latin translation of Arabic scientific texts, begun in earnest in twelfth-century Toledo (Chapter 7), continued through the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries and shaped the curriculum of every European university into the early modern period.

The Mongol destruction of Baghdad did not affect this — the texts that mattered for the European reception had already been transmitted, and the late-Andalusian translation pipeline was independent of events in the east.

The European Renaissance happened with no awareness that the original Arabic intellectual culture had partly collapsed in the meantime; the Latin Christian world was inheriting a tradition whose mainland source had been damaged in ways most European scholars never knew about.
So how should we read the Mongol sack of Baghdad?
The honest reading: it was a catastrophic event that ended the institutional center of one of the most productive intellectual cultures in human history, but it was not the end of that culture.
The Islamic Golden Age, as defined by the Abbasid Caliphate's central role in patronizing scholarship, ended in 1258.
The broader Islamic intellectual tradition — Persian, Egyptian, Andalusian, North African, increasingly Anatolian and Indian — continued.

Some specific things were permanently lost: manuscripts that had existed only in Baghdad's libraries, institutional networks that depended on the city's political-economic centrality, generations of scholars whose careers were truncated.

Other things continued, transmitted, evolved, and built new traditions: the Persian tradition under the Ilkhanate and later the Timurids and Safavids, the Mamluk Egyptian tradition, the Andalusian-Maghrebi tradition, the Ottoman tradition that would emerge in Anatolia and the Balkans.
The Islamic civilizational sphere remained, after 1258, the largest culturally connected zone in Eurasia.

Its productivity in the sciences would slow over the following centuries — the reasons are complex and contested — but its religious, legal, philosophical, and literary traditions continued and remain alive into the present.

What was specifically lost was the unified intellectual ecosystem that had centered on Baghdad — the system in which al-Khwarizmi could send his algebra to Andalusian scholars, Hunayn ibn Ishaq could collect manuscripts from Byzantine territory for Iraqi readers, Ibn Sina's Canon could move from Khorasan to Cairo without translation, and a single set of references in Arabic could reach scholars from the Atlantic to the Indus.
After 1258, the Islamic world became a more polycentric system, with separate intellectual ecosystems in Cairo, Samarkand, Cordoba (until 1492), Delhi (after 1206), and elsewhere.
The polycentric system was vibrant but had a less efficient knowledge-circulation network.
The scientific productivity that had peaked in the unified system declined as the system fragmented.
There is also a second-order effect that matters.

The ending of the Caliphate as a real political institution coincided with — and may have partly caused — the consolidation of religious authority in the ulema class rather than in any central institution.
After 1258, with no caliph and no central state, Sunni religious authority became permanently distributed across the legal schools and the regional madrasa networks.
This was a stable arrangement that has persisted for centuries.
It also made centralized intellectual reform difficult.
The kind of state-funded research enterprise that the early Abbasid caliphs had run could not be reconstructed, because there was no longer a political authority capable of running it.

The Ottoman sultans of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries patronized scholarship enthusiastically, but the model was court patronage of individual scholars, not the systematic state-funded research program of the Bayt al-Hikma.
Whether this institutional shift contributed to the relative scientific decline of the Islamic world after 1500 is one of the major debates of comparative civilizational history.
Both sides have something to say.
The scale and ambition of the early Abbasid translation movement was, in any case, never repeated.
The Islamic Golden Age covers roughly five centuries, and it is one of the most productive single cultural periods in human history.

What was accomplished during it can be summarized in a list that risks sounding like name-dropping but is in fact understatement: The translation into Arabic of almost the entire surviving corpus of Greek scientific and philosophical literature, plus substantial portions of the Persian and Indian intellectual traditions.
The synthesis of these traditions into a unified scientific corpus accessible across the Islamic world in a single language.
The invention of algebra as a systematic discipline (al-Khwarizmi).
The transmission westward of the decimal place-value numeral system with zero, which the modern world uses for all arithmetic.
The development of trigonometry as a working computational tool with sine and cosine functions (al-Battani).
The most accurate astronomical observations of the medieval period, with planetary models that fed forward into Copernican astronomy (al-Battani, al-Tusi).
The first systematic public hospital and teaching-hospital system in any civilization.
The most comprehensive medical encyclopedia of the medieval world (Ibn Sina's Canon), which was the standard European medical text for six centuries.
The first systematic experimental method in optics, with controlled experiments and quantified observations (Ibn al-Haytham).
The first systematic clinical case-history medicine (al-Razi).
The first state-funded higher education system (the Nizamiyya madrasas).
The synthesis of philosophy, theology, jurisprudence, and mysticism into a coherent religious culture (al-Ghazali).
The most influential medieval commentaries on Aristotle (Ibn Rushd).
The codification of Sunni legal pluralism into the four-school system that has held for a thousand years.

The development of the Persian literary tradition that has produced some of the world's greatest poetry (Firdawsi, Rumi, Sa'di, Hafez — the last two, working in the late thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, are after our period but on the same continuous tradition).

The construction of monumental architecture across two continents (the Great Mosque of Cordoba, the Alhambra, the Cairo madrasas, the Samarkand monuments) that represents one of the great architectural traditions of human history.
The development of the most extensive trade networks of the medieval world, connecting the Atlantic to the Pacific and underwriting the prosperity that funded all of the above.

The Latin Christian world that took up many of these accomplishments and built its own civilization on them — the world that became the modern West — would not have done so without this prior tradition.
The European Renaissance was a Latin reception of Greek-Arabic-Persian scientific learning.
The modern scientific method has roots in Ibn al-Haytham.
The mathematics of the modern technical world descends from the algebra of al-Khwarizmi and the decimals of Aryabhata-via-Baghdad.
The medical institutions of the modern world have their first pre-modern parallel in the Abbasid bimaristans.
The university as an institution has its first pre-modern parallel in the Nizamiyya madrasas.
The five centuries between 750 and 1258 were not a "preservation" of Greek learning by an Islamic intermediate, as the older textbook formulation has it.

They were a productive intellectual culture in their own right, drawing on Greek, Persian, Indian, and earlier Mesopotamian sources, synthesizing and extending them, and producing a body of scientific, philosophical, and literary work as substantial as anything the medieval world produced anywhere.
The Mongol sack of Baghdad ended the institutional center of that culture.
It did not end the culture itself.
The civilizations that came after — Mamluk Egypt, Ilkhanid and Timurid and Safavid Iran, Ottoman Turkey, Mughal India, the modern Islamic world — are continuous with the Golden Age.
The chain is unbroken.
The sack of Baghdad was a hinge, not an ending.

What the modern world has inherited from the Islamic Golden Age it has inherited not because of the Caliphate's destruction but in spite of it, through the libraries that survived, the texts that had already been transmitted west to Toledo and Sicily, the Persian poets who kept writing under Mongol patronage, the scholars who carried the tradition through every successor dynasty, and the children in every Muslim community for the next eight hundred years who learned to read by reading the Quran and then went on to read everything else.
The five centuries are over.
The civilization they built persists.

chapters.title: The Frontier Beylik
sentences: The Ottoman Empire begins, by tradition, with a man, a dream, and a small flat-roofed town in northwestern Anatolia.
The man was Osman I (oss-MAHN, c. 1258–1326), the chieftain of a small Turkic warrior band on the western frontier of the collapsing Sultanate of Rum.

The dream came to him while sleeping at the house of his future father-in-law, the Sufi shaykh Edebali (eh-deh-bah-LEE): a vision of a tree growing from his chest until its branches covered the world.

The town was Söğüt (suh-OOT, "the willow"), a frontier settlement in the foothills of the Bithynian highlands, about ninety miles southeast of where Constantinople still flickered as the wounded capital of the dying Roman Empire.

The dream is a thirteenth-generation Ottoman court legend recorded centuries after the event by writers who already knew how the story ended, and it is almost certainly a piece of dynastic propaganda.
The town is real.
The man is real, in the sense that he existed and was the ancestor of every Ottoman sultan who followed, but almost nothing about Osman's life can be reconstructed from contemporary sources.
Even the date of his death is uncertain.

What is not uncertain is that during Osman's adult lifetime, the political order of Anatolia broke into pieces, and that he was one of the dozen or so warlords who happened to be in the right place when it did.
The right place was the Bithynian frontier — the wedge of northwestern Anatolia where the Sea of Marmara, the Black Sea, and the inner plateau meet.
The frontier had been a contested zone for centuries.
The Byzantine Empire had ruled it from Constantinople for nine hundred years (Byzantine Empire Ch 1–10).

The Seljuk Sultanate of Rum (a Turkic dynasty that took its name because it ruled territory whose people were Romaioi — Romans — Byzantine Empire Ch 7) had taken most of the Anatolian interior after the Battle of Manzikert in 1071, leaving the empire with only a strip of coastal cities.
By the late thirteenth century both sides were exhausted, and a third party had broken both of them: the Mongols.

The Mongol Ilkhanate (the Persia-based khanate of the four Mongol successor states, Mongol Empire Ch 7) had crushed the Seljuks of Rum at the Battle of Köse Dağ (KUH-seh DAH, "Bald Mountain") in 1243, reducing the sultanate to a tribute-paying vassal that decayed steadily for the next half-century.
By Osman's youth the Seljuk sultans were Mongol puppets; by his old age the sultanate had ceased to function in any meaningful sense.

What replaced it across Anatolia was a patchwork of perhaps two dozen beyliks (BAY-liks, "principalities," from Turkish bey, "lord") — small Turkic warrior states under chieftains who had been Seljuk frontier commanders or who had taken advantage of the chaos to set up shop on their own.
Each beylik controlled a few towns and a stretch of grazing land.
Each was theoretically Muslim and Turkic.
None controlled enough territory to call itself an empire.
Most have been forgotten by everyone except specialists.
Osman's beylik was one of the smallest and most peripheral.
It sat at the western edge of the beylik zone, with the Byzantine fortified towns of Bithynia immediately to the west and the larger Germiyanid beylik to the south.

Osman's father Ertuğrul (er-TOO-rool) had reportedly been granted the Söğüt district by a late Seljuk sultan in exchange for military service against the Byzantines and against rival Turkic chieftains.
Ertuğrul died around 1280.
Osman, then in his early twenties, inherited what amounted to a few hundred horsemen, a town, and a license to raid westward.
He did so for about forty years.
The license to raid westward had a name and an ideology.

The name was gaza (gah-ZAH, Arabic for "raid" or "expedition"), and in the frontier zone of late thirteenth-century Anatolia it had hardened into a specifically religious concept: an organized armed expedition against a Christian or pagan enemy on behalf of Islam, conducted by frontier warriors known as ghazis (GAH-zees).

The ghazi tradition was old in the Islamic world — it had been a feature of every Muslim-Christian frontier from al-Andalus to the Caucasus — but on the Anatolian frontier it had a particular sharpness.
The Byzantine villages just over the hills were reachable, lightly defended, and rich.
The Bithynian fortified cities (Bursa, Nicaea, Nicomedia) were tougher targets but enormously richer if they could be taken.
A ghazi leader who could promise plunder, glory, and (theologically) salvation could attract recruits from across Anatolia.
This is the crucial fact about the early Ottoman state.
It was, in its first generations, not really a state at all.
It was a magnet.

Osman and his successors offered something the other Anatolian beyliks did not: an open frontier, an active raiding zone, a chance for any Turkic horseman with a horse and a bow to ride west and become wealthy.
Recruits came from across Anatolia.
Some were Sunni Muslim warriors looking for gaza.
Some were nominally Muslim Turkmen tribesmen who were really still pagan or shamanist and were following the fighting because it paid.
Some were defectors from neighboring beyliks.
A surprising number, in the first century, were Christian warriors — Greek and Slavic and Albanian fighters who had fallen out with their own lords and joined the Ottoman side as paid auxiliaries.
The early Ottomans cared about loyalty, courage, and competence.
They did not yet care much about religious purity.

The state that emerged from this magnet would look very different a hundred years later, but at the founding moment it was a multi-ethnic, multi-confessional armed company organized around a frontier raiding license.
Osman's Sufi connections mattered for this.

The shaykh Edebali, whose daughter Osman married (her name is given variously as Bala Hatun or Mal Hatun in later sources — even his wife's name is contested), was a leader of the Babai (bah-BYE-ee) Sufi network, a heterodox dervish movement that had spread across Anatolia in the wake of the Mongol disruption.
The Babais were not orthodox urban Sunnis.
They were itinerant mystics who moved easily across confessional boundaries, spoke Turkish rather than Arabic or Persian, and had a long history of frontier organizing.
Their support gave the early Ottomans religious legitimacy without forcing them into the doctrinal narrowness of the established Islamic schools.
Sheikh Edebali was, by all accounts, the political theologian of the Ottoman founding, and his role is one of the better-documented features of an otherwise obscure period.
What Osman actually did is harder to recover than what he meant.
The contemporary sources are almost entirely Byzantine, and they are not interested in him personally — he appears as one of several Turkic warlords harassing the Bithynian frontier.

The Ottoman chronicles that name him as the founder of the dynasty were composed in the fifteenth century, more than a hundred years after his death, and they project the dynastic clarity of the later empire backward onto a chaotic frontier period that did not, at the time, look like the founding of anything in particular.
What can be reconstructed is approximately this.

Around 1299 — the traditional foundational date, though it is conventional rather than precisely documented — Osman declared his independence from any nominal Seljuk overlordship, minted a coin in his own name (or had one minted; the surviving examples are problematic), and began calling himself an autonomous bey.
By the early 1300s his band had grown large enough to fight pitched battles.
In 1302 he won a notable victory over a Byzantine force at the Battle of Bapheus (BAH-fee-us, near modern İzmit), the first time his beylik had defeated a regular Byzantine army in the open field.

The Byzantine defeat at Bapheus shocked Constantinople and drove the empire to hire the Catalan Company (Byzantine Empire Ch 10) — a desperate move that, as the Byzantine chapter records, made things worse.
The Catalans pushed Osman back briefly but could not be controlled and turned on the Byzantines themselves, leaving Osman free to resume his expansion.
By the 1310s the Ottoman beylik controlled most of the Bithynian countryside.
The walled cities held out longer.
Bursa (BUR-sah, the major Byzantine city of Bithynia, called Prusa in Greek), surrounded by Ottoman forces from roughly 1313 onward, finally surrendered in 1326.
Osman was already dying by the time the city fell — he reportedly heard the news on his deathbed — and the credit went to his son.
The son was Orhan (or-HAHN, c. 1281–1362), and he is the figure in the early Ottoman story whose actions can actually be tracked.
Orhan inherited the beylik on Osman's death in 1326 and ran it for thirty-six years.
Under his rule, the Ottoman state crossed the threshold from raiding band to organized polity.
He took Bursa and made it the dynasty's first proper capital.
He minted Ottoman silver coins (akçes — AHK-ches — small flat silver pieces that became the standard imperial denomination for the next three centuries) systematically rather than sporadically.

He commissioned the first identifiably Ottoman architecture — modest mosques, schools, and bath complexes in Bursa and the surrounding towns, in a style that drew on Seljuk precedents but was beginning to develop its own character.
He took the title Sultan for himself in some inscriptions, though the usage was inconsistent and the practical meaning uncertain.
Orhan also took the city of Nicaea in 1331 — a moment of major symbolic importance.
Nicaea (modern İznik) had been the temporary capital of the Byzantine government-in-exile during the Latin occupation of Constantinople from 1204 to 1261 (Byzantine Empire Ch 9).
It was the city of the First and Seventh Ecumenical Councils.
It was the second city of the Greek-speaking Orthodox world.
Its fall to the Ottomans was a blow that Constantinople could not absorb.

Orhan made it a center of Ottoman religious learning, founded a madrasa (a Muslim religious school) within the captured walls, and integrated Nicaea's Greek population into the Ottoman administrative system on terms remarkably generous by the standards of the age.
Most converted to Islam over the following generations; some did not, and continued to live as Orthodox Christians under Ottoman rule.
The pattern that would later be formalized as the millet system (Chapter 6) was already in operation in rough form.
Orhan also took Nicomedia (modern İzmit) in 1337, completing the Ottoman conquest of Bithynia and giving the beylik a coastline on the Sea of Marmara.
The geography mattered.
Once the Ottomans held the Marmara coast, they were within sight of Europe.

The strait at the Sea of Marmara's western end — the Dardanelles (also called the Hellespont, the narrow passage between the Aegean and the Marmara) — separated Anatolia from the European province of Thrace by less than a mile of water at its narrowest point.
The European shore was Byzantine territory in name and almost completely undefended in fact.
The Ottoman beylik now had the option, if it could find a pretext, of crossing into Europe.
The pretext arrived in 1346.
The pretext was a Byzantine civil war.

John Kantakouzenos, the senior aristocrat who had been regent for the boy emperor John V Palaiologos and had fallen out with the regency council, was fighting a six-year war for control of Constantinople (Byzantine Empire Ch 10).
He needed military allies.
The Ottomans had cavalry.

Kantakouzenos married his daughter Theodora to Orhan in 1346 — a Christian Byzantine princess given as a bride to a Muslim Turkic sultan, an arrangement scandalous to traditional Byzantine sensibilities but accepted as the price of military aid.
Orhan sent troops across the strait to fight on Kantakouzenos's behalf.
They fought, won, and went home.
In 1352 Kantakouzenos called them back for a renewed phase of the civil war.
They came again.

This time they fought in Thrace and the southern Balkans, and they began to notice that the territory they were riding through was lightly defended, agriculturally rich, and full of Christian peasants who had no particular reason to fight for an emperor in Constantinople they had never seen.
In March 1354 a major earthquake destroyed the walls of the Byzantine fortress at Gallipoli on the European side of the Dardanelles.

Orhan's eldest surviving son Süleyman Pasha (soo-LAY-mahn pah-SHAH, not to be confused with the later Süleyman the Magnificent — the Ottomans reused names mercilessly across centuries, and a reader needs to track each generation separately) happened to be conveniently nearby with a force of perhaps ten thousand men.
He occupied the ruined fortress, refused to leave when Byzantine envoys arrived demanding the territory back, and began rebuilding the walls under Ottoman control.
This was the turning point.
The Ottomans now had a permanent foothold in Europe, and they had it through a combination of opportunism, family alliance, and timely seismic activity.
Süleyman Pasha died in a hunting accident in 1357, but the foothold held.
Orhan, now seventy-six years old and frail, designated his second son Murad as heir and watched Ottoman raids spread across Thrace.

When Orhan died in 1362, the Ottoman beylik had grown from a few hundred horsemen at Söğüt to a state controlling Bithynia, parts of western Anatolia, and an expanding bridgehead in southeastern Europe.
It had a capital, a coinage, a developing administrative system, and a religious infrastructure of mosques and madrasas.

It was still smaller and less powerful than the largest of the rival Anatolian beyliks (the Karamanids of central Anatolia, who claimed direct succession from the Seljuks of Rum, were considered the senior power by most contemporary observers).
But it had something the other beyliks did not: an open frontier into Christian Europe and a religious-ideological framework — gaza — for exploiting it.
The Karamanids were doing nothing of the sort.
They were squabbling with their Turkic neighbors over towns in central Anatolia.
The Ottomans were riding across Thrace toward the Bulgarian border.
A note on what makes the early Ottoman story unusual is worth pausing on, because it bears on everything that follows.
Most successful conquering states in world history have started from a unified ethnic or religious base and expanded by absorbing other groups.
The Ottomans did the opposite.

They started as a magnet for everyone willing to ride west, with no particular ethnic or even religious unity, and they only gradually acquired the consolidated Sunni-Muslim-Turkic identity that the later empire would project.
This is documented in the surviving chronicles, sparse as they are.
The early Ottoman armies contained Greek Christians, Slavic Christians, Albanian Christians, and Turkic-speakers of every shade of Muslim observance.

The early Ottoman administration borrowed heavily from Byzantine fiscal practice — the tax rolls of the conquered Bithynian cities continued to function under Ottoman management, and the Byzantine officials who had been running them were often kept in place.
The early Ottoman religious establishment was Sufi-influenced, syncretic, and tolerant of practices that would later be condemned as heretical.
The early Ottoman court contained Christian wives, Christian advisors, and Christian soldiers.
What changed this was not Osman or Orhan.

What changed it was institutional consolidation under their successors, particularly Murad I — the next chapter's protagonist — and the gradual evolution of the Ottoman state from a frontier raiding band into a centralized military empire with its own theology, its own bureaucracy, and its own slave-soldier corps.
By 1450 the Ottoman state would look entirely different from the one Orhan had handed off in 1362.
But the founding magnet is part of why the empire grew so fast: it was easier to join than to fight, and the price of joining was low.

Cross-civ check: Osman's lifetime (c. 1258–1326) was the height of the Pax Mongolica (Mongol Empire Ch 7), when the four Mongol khanates were maintaining a continental trade system from China to Persia.
Marco Polo was traveling to Kublai Khan's court while Osman was raiding Bithynia.
The Yuan dynasty in China was at its peak.

The Mamluk Sultanate in Egypt — the slave-soldier state that had repelled the Mongols at Ayn Jalut in 1260 — was the dominant Sunni power of the Mediterranean world; the early Ottomans were a backwater compared to it.
The Ilkhanate in Persia was about to convert to Islam under Ghazan Khan in 1295.
In Europe, Dante was writing the Divine Comedy during Osman's last years.
In England, the Magna Carta had been signed forty years earlier.
In China, the Song dynasty had recently fallen to Kublai's Mongols.

The mid-thirteenth and early-fourteenth centuries were one of the more crowded moments in pre-modern history, and the tiny Ottoman beylik on the Anatolian frontier was, at the time, one of the least important things happening in it.

chapters.title: Conquering the Balkans
sentences: By 1362, the Ottomans had a foothold in Europe.
By 1396, they had most of the Balkans, the Janissary corps, and a reputation that would terrify Christian Europe for the next three centuries.

The transformation took thirty-four years, two sultans, and a series of battles that did to the medieval Balkan kingdoms what the Mongols had done to the Sultanate of Rum: broke them faster than they could organize a coherent response.
The agent of most of this was Murad I (mu-RAHD, ruled 1362–1389), Orhan's second son, who took the Ottoman throne at around thirty-six and spent twenty-seven years methodically extending it.

Murad was the first Ottoman ruler whose actions we can track in detail — Byzantine, Bulgarian, Serbian, Italian, and early Ottoman sources all converge on him, and the picture they produce is consistent.
He was a careful, patient strategist with a particular gift for institutional design.

The Ottoman state's transformation from raiding beylik to organized empire happened on his watch, and most of the institutional features that would define the empire for the next four centuries were either invented or formalized by him.
Murad's first major act was to take Adrianople in 1369.
Adrianople (modern Edirne in European Turkey, sometimes spelled Edirne in modern usage and Adrianople in older Western sources) was a Byzantine city of considerable importance.
It sat on the Maritsa River in eastern Thrace, about 130 miles northwest of Constantinople, at a strategic crossroads where the main land routes from the Balkans to Constantinople converged.
The Roman emperor Hadrian had refounded it in the second century and given it his name.
The Visigoths had defeated the Roman emperor Valens there in 378 (Ancient Rome Ch 9), one of the most catastrophic Roman defeats of the late imperial period.
The Bulgar Tsar Krum had won a major victory there in 813.
The Byzantine Empire had recovered it in the early twelfth century and held it more or less continuously since.

In 1369 Murad's forces took the city, probably without a major siege — the Byzantine garrison was too small to hold against a serious Ottoman investment, and the surrounding Thracian countryside was already under Ottoman control.
Murad made Edirne his new capital.
This was a significant decision.
Bursa remained the dynastic-religious center, where Osman and Orhan were buried and where the great early Ottoman mosques stood.
But the working capital — the city where the sultan held court, where the army assembled, where the bureaucracy operated — was now in Europe, not Anatolia.
The Ottoman state had crossed psychologically as well as militarily.
It was a European empire with Anatolian roots, and it would remain so until 1453.
The choice of Edirne also had a strategic logic.
From Edirne, Ottoman armies could march in any direction across the Balkans.
Northwest into Bulgaria.
North into Wallachia (the principality that became part of modern Romania).
West into Macedonia and Serbia.
South into Greece.
Each campaigning season, the army assembled at Edirne and rode out.
Each campaigning season returned with more territory.
The Bulgarian campaigns came first.
The Second Bulgarian Empire — the medieval Bulgarian state that had reformed in 1185 after a long period of Byzantine occupation — had been weakening for a century.
It had lost its Black Sea ports to the Genoese.
It had been pummeled by Hungarian invasions from the north.
By the 1360s it was effectively three competing kingdoms, each ruled by a different Shishman family member, none capable of mounting a coordinated defense.
Murad picked them off one at a time.
The Tsar of Tarnovo accepted Ottoman vassalage in 1373.
The smaller principalities of Vidin and Dobrudzha followed within a few years.
By 1380 the Bulgarian state, in any meaningful sense, had ceased to exist.
Its full incorporation into the empire would happen under Murad's successor, but the work was already done.
The Serbian campaigns followed.

The Serbian Empire of Stefan Dušan (Byzantine Empire Ch 10) had been the dominant Balkan power in the 1340s, but Dušan had died young in 1355, and his empire had fragmented within a few years into competing Serbian principalities.
The largest, ruled by Prince Lazar Hrebeljanović (la-ZAR hreh-bell-YAH-no-vich, c. 1329–1389), controlled what is now central Serbia.
The others were already paying tribute to Murad by the early 1380s.
Lazar tried to organize a Serbian-led coalition against the advancing Ottomans, drawing in Bosnian, Albanian, and minor Bulgarian forces.
The decisive battle came on June 15, 1389, on the Field of Blackbirds (Kosovo Polje in Serbian, KAW-soh-voh PAW-lyeh, in what is now southern Kosovo).
The Battle of Kosovo is one of those events that has been so heavily mythologized that recovering the actual military engagement is almost impossible.
The contemporary sources — Serbian, Bulgarian, Bosnian, Italian, and Ottoman — agree on a few facts and disagree on most others.

What can be reconstructed: the Ottoman and Serbian-led armies were comparable in size, perhaps thirty thousand each; the battle was fought through the day of June 15; both Murad I and Prince Lazar were killed; the Ottoman side eventually held the field, but the casualties on both sides were so severe that it is contested whether the battle should be classed as a tactical Ottoman victory or a draw.

The Serbian tradition holds that Murad was killed by a Serbian noble named Miloš Obilić (MEE-losh oh-BEE-lich), who feigned defection, was admitted to the Ottoman camp on the eve of battle, and stabbed Murad to death in his tent before being cut down by guards.
The Ottoman tradition holds that Murad was killed during or after the battle by a wounded Serbian found among the bodies.
Several versions of each story circulate.

The political fact, regardless of the specific mechanism, is that the Ottoman sultan was killed at the close of an engagement that was more costly than expected, and that the Ottoman command structure had to be improvised on the field.
The improvisation worked.
Murad's elder son Bayezid (BYE-eh-zeed) was present at the battle.

Within hours of his father's death, Bayezid had his younger brother Yakub strangled — eliminating the rival claimant to the throne and consolidating his own succession before the surviving Ottoman commanders could organize an alternative.
The Ottoman army was held together.
The Serbian survivors, leaderless after Lazar's death, fragmented.
Lazar's widow Princess Milica accepted Ottoman vassalage on her dead husband's behalf and married her daughter to the new Ottoman sultan as part of the settlement.
Serbia became a tribute-paying Ottoman vassal, contributing troops to subsequent Ottoman campaigns.
The Battle of Kosovo did not destroy Serbia in 1389.
But it broke any prospect of Serbian-led resistance to Ottoman expansion, and it began a cultural memory that would, six centuries later, still be operating in Balkan politics.
The Serbian Orthodox tradition canonized Lazar as a martyr.

The Battle of Kosovo became the founding myth of Serbian national consciousness — every nineteenth-century Serbian nationalist text, every twentieth-century Serbian political speech invoking the suffering of the nation, every twenty-first-century rally about Kosovo, traces back to that single afternoon in 1389.
The historical reality was murkier.
The mythological reality is one of the most consequential facts in modern Balkan politics.
The new sultan was Bayezid I (1389–1402), and he was a different kind of Ottoman from his father.
Murad I had been patient.
Bayezid was not.

He was nicknamed Yıldırım (YUHL-duh-ruhm, "the Thunderbolt"), reportedly for the speed at which he moved his armies — Ottoman forces under Bayezid would appear in front of a fortified city days before the defending commander knew he was on his way.
He was personally brave, occasionally reckless, and possessed of a strategic ambition his father had carefully avoided.
Murad had built an empire in Anatolia and the Balkans by careful pressure on weaker neighbors.
Bayezid wanted to take Constantinople, conquer the rest of the Balkans, dominate Anatolia outright, and project Ottoman power as far as Hungary and the Black Sea.
In the eight years between 1389 and 1396, he came close to doing it.
He blockaded Constantinople from 1394 onward, building a fortress on the Asian side of the Bosporus (the Anadoluhisarı, "Anatolian Castle") to control the strait.

He campaigned aggressively in Anatolia, conquering several rival beyliks (the Karamanids, Aydinids, and Saruhanids) and absorbing their territories — moves that doubled the empire's Anatolian holdings but offended the Turkic religious establishment, which considered war between Muslim states unseemly.
He pushed the Balkan frontier north to the Danube, putting pressure on Hungary.
And in 1396 he provoked, and crushed, the largest Christian crusader army that had been raised against the Ottomans up to that point.
The crusade was organized by King Sigismund of Hungary (SIG-iss-mund, who would later become Holy Roman Emperor), with substantial French, German, English, Bohemian, and Burgundian contingents.
The strategic plan was to march down the Danube to Constantinople, relieving the Byzantine capital and breaking Ottoman power in the Balkans simultaneously.
The expedition was widely advertised across Europe as a holy war, attracting volunteer knights from as far as Scotland.

By summer 1396 the crusader army assembled — the Christian sources put it at over fifty thousand men, which is probably an exaggeration; the modern estimates run from twenty to thirty thousand, still the largest western European force to operate in the Balkans for a generation.
The crusaders besieged the Ottoman frontier fortress of Nicopolis (nih-KOH-poh-liss, on the Danube in modern Bulgaria) in September 1396.
Bayezid, who had been blockading Constantinople, raced north with about fifteen thousand Ottoman regulars and a substantial Serbian vassal contingent under Stefan Lazarević (Prince Lazar's son).
The two armies met on September 25.
The crusader cavalry charge, led by the French and Burgundian knights, hit the first Ottoman line and overran it.

The knights then continued forward into terrain Bayezid had specifically chosen for the engagement — a slope studded with sharpened stakes that disabled cavalry — and were met by the Ottoman reserve, including the Serbian heavy cavalry.
The Christian knights, heavily armored and now without horses, were systematically slaughtered.
The Battle of Nicopolis (September 25, 1396) was the worst Christian defeat against the Ottomans since Manzikert.
Sigismund escaped down the Danube.
The French and Burgundian commanders were captured.

Bayezid had several thousand prisoners executed in cold blood the next day, in a deliberately staged spectacle witnessed by the surviving captive commanders — the message being that western European nobles who took up arms against the Ottoman state would not be ransomed under any conventional code of medieval chivalric warfare.

The high-ranking French prisoners (including John the Fearless of Burgundy) were eventually ransomed for enormous sums, but the scale of the executions among lower-ranking knights ended any prospect of further large-scale European intervention for a generation.
After Nicopolis, no major western crusade was organized against the Ottomans for nearly fifty years.
Bayezid returned to Anatolia, resumed the blockade of Constantinople, and began making preparations for what was supposed to be the conclusive Ottoman siege.
He never got to launch it.
While he was preparing to take Constantinople, a different conqueror was preparing to take him.
Before that story (Chapter 3), one more institutional development from Murad's and Bayezid's reigns deserves explicit attention, because it would shape the empire for the next four centuries.
The Janissary Corps (yan-iss-AIR-eez, from Turkish yeni çeri, "new troops") was created during Murad I's reign, probably around 1363.
The Ottomans had already been recruiting non-Turkic soldiers — primarily Greek and Slavic prisoners of war — and converting them to Islam to serve as imperial troops.
What Murad did was systematize the practice and turn it into a permanent corps with its own organization, training, pay structure, and esprit de corps.
The earliest Janissaries were Christian boys captured in raids or surrendered as tribute by conquered Christian populations, converted to Islam, and trained for military service.
The corps was small at first, a few thousand men.

It would grow to be the elite infantry of the empire, the institution that took Constantinople in 1453, the force that brought down the Mamluk Sultanate in 1517, the unit that made the Ottoman army a different kind of fighting force from any of its rivals.

The recruitment system that fed the Janissary corps had its own name: the devshirme (DEV-shir-meh, "collection"), and it was formalized under Murad I as a regular tribute imposed on the empire's Balkan Christian subjects.

Boys aged eight to eighteen were collected from Christian villages, taken to Edirne (and later Istanbul), converted to Islam, given Turkish names, and sorted into educational tracks based on aptitude.
The most able became palace administrators or eventually grand viziers.
The rest became soldiers.
The full mechanics of the system are detailed in Chapter 6, where they fit the larger institutional picture better.

What needs noting here is that the institution that would dominate the Ottoman army through the empire's classical age was already in place by the time Bayezid was preparing to take Constantinople, and it was being staffed by the children of the empire's Balkan Christian subjects.
By 1400 the empire had absorbed most of the Balkans, controlled most of Anatolia, was blockading Constantinople, had a slave-soldier corps with no European parallel, and looked unstoppable.
It was about to be stopped.

Cross-civ check: at the moment of Nicopolis (1396), the Ming dynasty was in its first generation under the Hongwu Emperor (Mongol Empire Ch 8); the Mali Empire in West Africa was past its peak under Mansa Musa's distant successors; the Aztec Triple Alliance in central Mexico was just consolidating, with Tenochtitlan founded only seventy years earlier; Timur was finishing his second great campaign through Persia and India; Korea was about to enter the Joseon dynasty in 1392; and the Hundred Years' War between England and France was in a relatively quiet phase between Crecy and Agincourt.
The Ottoman Empire of Bayezid I was, by 1400, one of the largest and most aggressive of the world's expanding powers.
Within two years it would briefly cease to exist.

chapters.title: The Tamerlane Catastrophe
sentences: The conqueror who stopped Bayezid was Timur (TEE-moor, c. 1336–1405), known in Europe as Tamerlane (a corruption of Timur-i Lang, "Timur the Lame," a nickname referring to a permanent battlefield injury).

He was, by any reasonable measure, the most consequential warlord of the late fourteenth century, and his sudden interest in Anatolia in 1402 was the worst thing that could have happened to the Ottoman state.
Timur's career is told in detail in the Mongol narrative (Mongol Empire Ch 9), so the summary here is brief.

He was a Turkic-speaking warrior from the Barlas tribe of Transoxiana (the region between the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers in modern Uzbekistan), who claimed Mongol descent through a Genghisid maternal line and ruled in the name of puppet Chagatai khans.

From his capital at Samarkand, he had spent the previous thirty years rebuilding a Mongol-style empire across the Iranian world — conquering Persia, the Caucasus, much of Mesopotamia, and parts of northern India.
By 1400 he ruled the largest single state in Eurasia outside the Ming dynasty.
He was sixty-four years old and not slowing down.
What brought him to Anatolia was a combination of refugees and arrogance.
Several Anatolian beyliks that Bayezid had absorbed had sent their displaced rulers to Timur's court, asking for restoration.

The most consequential was Sultan Ahmad Jalayir of Baghdad, whose Jalayirid dynasty Timur had crushed and who had fled to Bayezid for refuge — exactly the reverse of the displaced Anatolian rulers' pattern.
Timur and Bayezid exchanged a series of increasingly hostile letters in 1399 and 1400.
Each accused the other of harboring his enemies.
Bayezid's letters were particularly aggressive, addressing Timur with deliberately insulting language.
The exchange has the quality of two confident conquerors stress-testing each other — but Timur was the more experienced commander, and Bayezid had not understood what he was provoking.
In 1400 Timur sacked Sivas in central Anatolia, in a brutal demonstration of what he was capable of.
Bayezid's young son Ertugrul was reportedly among the casualties.
In 1401 Timur sacked Damascus and Baghdad, eliminating his other strategic concerns.

In summer 1402 he marched west into Anatolia at the head of an army that contemporary chronicles put at over a hundred thousand men — likely an exaggeration, but the force was certainly larger than anything Bayezid could put in the field, and it included the heavy battlefield component that had made Timur's army the most feared on the continent: war elephants, brought from his Indian campaigns.
Bayezid lifted the blockade of Constantinople — the city would have fallen within a year had he kept it up — and rode east to meet Timur on his own ground.

The Ottoman army was a smaller, more regionally specialized force: perhaps 70,000 men, including the Janissary infantry, the Anatolian and Rumelian feudal cavalry, and a contingent of his Serbian vassal Stefan Lazarević.

The Ottoman army's strength was its discipline and the quality of its individual units; its weakness was that several of its components were ethnically and politically unreliable in the specific situation now unfolding.
The two armies met on July 28, 1402, on the Çubuk Plain outside Ankara (modern Turkey's capital, then a regional Anatolian city) in central Anatolia.
Bayezid had marched his army hard for several days through a hot, dry late-July landscape, and his troops arrived already exhausted.
Timur had reached the field first, taken up a defensive position near a freshwater stream, and forced Bayezid to fight without water in midsummer heat.
The first significant Ottoman tactical disaster was thirst.
The second was defection.

The Anatolian feudal cavalry contingents that Bayezid had absorbed by force when he conquered the rival beyliks contained large numbers of soldiers who recognized the deposed beys riding in Timur's army.
Some of these troops switched sides during the battle, going over to Timur's wing.
The Ottoman left flank collapsed.

The Janissary infantry held their ground in the center — they had nowhere to defect to, and they fought with the discipline that would become their hallmark for the next two centuries — but they were now isolated.
The Serbian vassal contingent on the right under Stefan Lazarević also fought hard.
The center and the right could not save the day.
By late afternoon the Ottoman army was disintegrating.
Bayezid himself, with a small bodyguard and his sons, fought through the wreckage trying to escape.
He was overtaken, knocked from his horse, and captured alive.
The Battle of Ankara (July 28, 1402) was the most catastrophic Ottoman defeat in the empire's six-century history.
The Ottoman army was destroyed.
Most of Bayezid's sons escaped, but they were now scattered across Anatolia and the Balkans without a coordinating central authority.
The Ottoman state, as a unified polity, ceased to exist for the next eleven years.

What Timur did with Bayezid is one of the most-discussed episodes in late medieval history, partly because the contemporary sources contradict each other and partly because later European writers added so many embellishments that recovering the original treatment is hard.

The Ottoman tradition, written under Bayezid's restored descendants, holds that Timur kept Bayezid in a golden cage paraded behind his army as a humiliation, and that Bayezid eventually died of grief and despair within months of his capture.
The Timurid sources are gentler — they describe Bayezid as treated honorably and dying of natural causes the following March, perhaps from a stroke.

The European tradition, working from secondhand reports, picked the most colorful version: Bayezid in a cage, used as Timur's footstool, his wife Olivera (a Serbian princess, Stefan Lazarević's sister) forced to serve naked at Timur's banquets.

Most modern historians consider all three details — the cage, the footstool, and the Olivera humiliation — to belong to the same category of European literary embellishment, surfacing in late-medieval and early-modern Christian sources writing about a triumphant Muslim warlord and a fallen Christian-married Muslim sultan, rather than in the contemporary Timurid or Ottoman record.

What is well established: Bayezid died in Timur's custody on March 8, 1403, less than eight months after his capture; he was approximately fifty-four years old; he had been the unstoppable conqueror of the Christian Balkans, and he had ended his life as a captive of a Turkic warlord he had never expected to face.
Timur did not stay in Anatolia.
He had no interest in administering the territory or replacing the Ottoman dynasty.

He installed his preferred candidates among Bayezid's sons as nominal vassals, restored several of the beyliks that Bayezid had absorbed (the Karamanids, in particular, recovered their independence and would be a thorn in Ottoman flesh for the next eighty years), and then withdrew his army eastward in late 1402.
He died in February 1405 while preparing an invasion of Ming China, leaving a Timurid succession war that consumed his own empire for the next several decades and ended his territorial unity.

What Timur left behind in Anatolia was a power vacuum that the Ottomans had to climb back out of, with no help from anyone, while every neighboring power — Christian and Muslim — tried to take advantage of their weakness.
The eleven years between 1402 and 1413 are known in Ottoman historiography as the Interregnum (Turkish Fetret Devri, the "Era of Discord").
Bayezid's surviving sons fought a four-cornered civil war for the throne.

The four main contenders were: Süleyman Çelebi (CHEH-leh-bee, an honorific roughly equivalent to "lord" or "noble"), Bayezid's eldest surviving son, based in Edirne and controlling the Balkan provinces.
Süleyman had escaped from the Battle of Ankara and made his way to Europe, where the Janissary corps and most of the Balkan vassals supported him.
He was a competent but heavy-drinking ruler, and his court became known for its corruption.
Isa Çelebi, based in Bursa and controlling the Bithynian heartland.
He fought a brief war against his brother Mehmed, lost, and was eventually eliminated.
Mehmed Çelebi, based in Amasya in north-central Anatolia, controlling the Black Sea-facing provinces and the Anatolian feudal cavalry.
He was the youngest of the major contenders, the most patient, and the eventual winner.
Musa Çelebi, who switched sides repeatedly, allied with Wallachian and Byzantine forces, and at one point briefly held Edirne.
He had a sharper military aptitude than his brothers but was politically less adept.
The fighting was intricate, multi-front, and protracted.
Süleyman ruled the Balkans from 1402 to 1411, when he was overthrown by Musa with Wallachian backing.
Musa held Edirne briefly in 1411–1413, alienating the Janissaries with high-handed treatment.

In summer 1413 Mehmed crossed from Anatolia into Europe, allied with the Janissary corps and the senior Ottoman commanders Süleyman had alienated, defeated Musa at the Battle of Çamurlu in central Bulgaria on July 5, 1413, and reunited the empire under his own rule.
Musa was strangled with a bowstring after the battle.

Mehmed I (ruled 1413–1421) then spent eight years cleaning up the wreckage: restoring central authority over the Anatolian feudal lords who had reasserted independence during the Interregnum, putting down a series of rebellions among Sufi networks (the most famous being the Sheikh Bedreddin uprising of 1416, a syncretic religious-social movement that combined heterodox Sufism with peasant grievances against the Ottoman fiscal system; Bedreddin was hanged at Serres in 1416), restoring tribute relationships with the Balkan vassal states, and rebuilding the army and treasury.
The Ottoman state Mehmed I left to his son in 1421 was smaller than Bayezid's empire had been in 1400 but functional.
It had survived the worst near-death experience any Islamic state had endured since the Mongol conquest of Baghdad in 1258.
It still controlled most of the Balkans, most of western Anatolia, and the strategic Bosporus-Marmara region.
Constantinople was once again a Byzantine vassal under Ottoman pressure.
The recovery had been a near-run thing.
It would not have happened without Mehmed I's patient consolidation, and the Ottomans of the next generation would speak of him as the second founder of the dynasty.

Cross-civ check: while the Ottoman Interregnum was tearing the empire apart, the Ming dynasty in China was completing its consolidation and dispatching the great fleets of Admiral Zheng He to the Indian Ocean (1405 onward — the first Zheng He voyage left the Yangtze the same year Timur died).
The Council of Constance (1414–1418) was meeting in central Europe to resolve the Western Schism of competing popes.
The Hussite Wars were beginning in Bohemia.
Joan of Arc would be born in 1412, the year Musa took Edirne.
The Inca Empire was beginning its expansion under Pachacuti's father in the central Andes.
And the Aztec Triple Alliance was about to launch its major imperial expansion under the first Moctezuma.

The early fifteenth century was a period of consolidation across Eurasia after the disruption of the late fourteenth, and the Ottoman recovery from Ankara was one of the more dramatic stories of the moment.
Mehmed I died in May 1421, possibly from a stroke, possibly from a chronic illness contracted during the Bedreddin campaign.

He was succeeded by his seventeen-year-old son Murad II (ruled 1421–1444 and 1446–1451 — he abdicated once and returned), who would carry the empire from recovered backwater to the brink of its greatest conquest.
Murad II was, by Ottoman dynastic standards, an unusual figure.

He was thoughtful, given to introspection, twice tried to retire to a Sufi lodge in Manisa to spend his life in religious contemplation, and twice was pulled back to the throne by court factions and military emergencies.

He was also a very competent battlefield commander when he had to be, and his reign saw the first serious attempts to take Constantinople since the Interregnum — the failed siege of 1422, in which the Theodosian Walls held against Ottoman cannon for the first but not the last time.
The 1422 siege was significant for what it foreshadowed.
Murad II's army included the first real Ottoman gunpowder artillery — bombards capable of throwing stone balls weighing several hundred pounds at the city walls.
The technology was still primitive.
The cannons fired slowly, were prone to bursting, and could not be aimed precisely.
The Theodosian Walls absorbed the bombardment and held.
But the principle had been demonstrated: gunpowder weapons could, in theory, breach masonry walls that no previous siege technology had been able to crack.
The Ottomans took the lesson seriously.
Over the next thirty years, they would invest steadily in artillery development, hire the best European gun-founders they could find, and build the largest cannon park in the world.
By 1453, Mehmed II would have the artillery park his grandfather had begun developing.
Murad II also fought the last major medieval crusade.

In 1444, encouraged by a Hungarian-Polish king named Władysław III (vlah-DEE-swahf, also called Vladislaus or Wladyslaw in older sources), a coalition of Hungarian, Polish, Wallachian, and Bulgarian forces marched south, allegedly in violation of a peace treaty Murad had just signed.
Murad — who had abdicated earlier that year in favor of his twelve-year-old son and gone back to his Sufi retreat at Manisa — was begged by his viziers to return.
He came back.
The two armies met at Varna on the Black Sea coast of Bulgaria on November 10, 1444.
The Christian forces were initially successful; the young king Władysław led a personal cavalry charge that nearly reached Murad's tent.
Then the charge was caught by the Janissaries, Władysław was killed, his head was put on a spear and paraded around the battlefield, and the crusader army disintegrated.

The Battle of Varna ended any further crusader hopes in the Balkans, eliminated the most credible Christian field army the Ottomans would face for the next century, and rendered Constantinople's diplomatic isolation complete.
A second Christian coalition under the Hungarian general John Hunyadi (HUN-yah-dee) tried again at the Second Battle of Kosovo in October 1448.
Murad II won that one too, in a three-day engagement that destroyed Hunyadi's reputation and forced Hungary to abandon active resistance to Ottoman expansion in the Balkans.
Murad died in February 1451, at the age of forty-six, after a cerebral hemorrhage during a banquet in Edirne.
He was succeeded — for the second time — by his now nineteen-year-old son.
The son was Mehmed II.
The next chapter is his.

chapters.title: The Conquest of Constantinople
sentences: Mehmed II is one of the most-studied conquerors in medieval history, and the basic outline of his reign needs little embellishment.
He took the throne in 1451 at nineteen years old.
He took Constantinople in 1453 at twenty-one.

He spent the next twenty-eight years remaking the Ottoman state into a world empire, taking the title Kayser-i Rûm (KAY-ser-ee ROOM, "Caesar of Rome") and treating the city he had conquered as the natural seat of a renewed Roman imperial tradition, with himself as the Roman emperor's legitimate successor.

By the time he died in 1481, the Ottoman Empire was the most powerful state in the Mediterranean basin, and the medieval world that had centered on Constantinople for eleven hundred years had been replaced by something different.

What made him capable of all this is, at least in part, accident of timing — his predecessors had built the army, the institutions, and the artillery park he inherited — but it is also genuine personal capacity.

Mehmed was multilingual (Turkish, Arabic, Persian, Greek, and probably some Hebrew and Italian), heavily educated by the standards of any fifteenth-century court, and possessed of an unusual combination of strategic patience and sudden tactical aggression.
He was personally capable of designing fortification systems, conducting siege engineering calculations, and discussing Greek philosophy with captured Byzantine scholars.
He was also ruthless to a degree that shocked even his Ottoman contemporaries.

The fratricide law that the Ottomans formalized under his reign — empowering a sultan upon accession to legally execute his brothers and nephews to prevent succession wars — was, on Mehmed's part, a calmly considered policy decision, not an emotional reflex.
He was the first Ottoman ruler whose ambition was global rather than regional, and he was the first Ottoman ruler with the institutional and technological tools to pursue that ambition effectively.
The siege of Constantinople, told in detail in the Byzantine narrative (Byzantine Empire Ch 11), can be summarized here from the Ottoman side.
Mehmed's preparations took two years.
His first move was to build a fortress on the European side of the Bosporus, directly across from the existing Ottoman Anadoluhisarı (which Bayezid I had built in the 1390s).

The new fortress was called Rumelihisarı (ROO-meh-lee-hee-sah-RUH, "the European Castle"), and it was constructed in the spring and summer of 1452 in just over four months — an architectural feat made possible by mobilizing thousands of laborers and cutting stone from the surrounding hillsides on a massive scale.
With both castles operating, the Ottomans could close the strait between the Black Sea and the Sea of Marmara at will, controlling all maritime traffic.
Any merchant ship trying to reach Constantinople from the Black Sea grain ports — the city's principal source of food — now had to ask Ottoman permission.
The Byzantine emperor Constantine XI Palaiologos could see the new castle from his palace windows.
He understood what it meant.
He sent envoys to Mehmed pleading for a withdrawal.
Mehmed's reply, recorded in the Greek sources, was that the Bosporus belonged to him and that further Byzantine interference would be treated as an act of war.
His second move was the artillery park.

Mehmed hired a Hungarian engineer named Orban (or-BAHN), a master gun-founder who had originally offered his services to Constantine XI and been turned down because the Byzantine treasury could not pay his fee.
Mehmed could pay.
Orban moved to Edirne and supervised the casting of the largest cannons the world had yet seen.

The biggest, called the Basilica (a Greek loan-word, which the Ottomans pronounced Şahi), is reported in the post-conquest Greek chronicles to have had a barrel about twenty-seven feet long and to have thrown a stone ball of around twelve hundred pounds — figures that may be inflated, since the surviving sources are post-facto accounts written by chroniclers describing a weapon they wanted readers to find legendary, but the orders of magnitude are at least plausible against later sixteenth-century Ottoman bombards that survive intact.

The casting and transport were themselves engineering challenges: the Basilica required a team of sixty oxen to move, and a road crew of two hundred men and the engineering corps to grade the path between Edirne and Constantinople in advance.
Several smaller bombards were also cast.
Together, the artillery park represented the largest concentrated investment in gunpowder weaponry up to that point in human history.
His third move was the army.

Mehmed assembled approximately eighty thousand to a hundred thousand men — Janissary infantry as the elite shock force, Anatolian and Rumelian feudal cavalry as the conventional army, irregular volunteers (bashı-bozuks, BAH-shuh boh-ZOOKS — literally "spoiled heads," a term for unruly or undisciplined troops, used here for the cannon-fodder tier sent in to wear down the defenders) as the expendable assault force, and a fleet of perhaps a hundred to a hundred and fifty ships gathered in the Sea of Marmara.

The defending Byzantine garrison numbered perhaps seven thousand, supplemented by Italian volunteers — most importantly seven hundred Genoese under Giovanni Giustiniani Longo, who had crossed from Genoa with his troops at his own expense.
The siege began on April 6, 1453.
The fifty-three days that followed are among the most-narrated sieges in history.

The major events fit the broad outline already sketched in the Byzantine chapter: the cannons hammered the Theodosian Walls, opening breaches that defenders desperately repaired overnight; the Ottoman fleet failed to force the entrance to the Golden Horn, blocked by the great chain stretched across the harbor mouth; on the night of April 22, Ottoman engineers built a greased wooden ramp over the hill behind Galata and dragged seventy ships overland into the upper Golden Horn, neutralizing the chain and creating a new front; the defenders had to spread their already-thin manpower across multiple threatened sections of wall; the cannon damage at the Saint Romanus Gate eventually became unrepairable; the Italian volunteers and the Greek defenders fought together with surprising solidarity given the deep theological tensions of the previous decades.
The Ottoman sources add a few details that are useful for understanding what was happening on the besiegers' side.

The Janissary corps was Mehmed's last and best assault force, and he held them in reserve through most of the siege, throwing in the bashı-bozuks and the regular Anatolian troops first to wear down the defenders.
By late May, after seven weeks of failed assaults, morale in the Ottoman camp was uneven.

Several senior viziers — most prominently the longtime grand vizier Halil Pasha, who was the senior military advisor inherited from Murad II's reign — counseled Mehmed to lift the siege and negotiate terms.

The siege was costing more than expected; the European powers were rumored to be assembling a relief fleet (in fact, only a small Venetian squadron sailed and arrived too late); the Ottoman regular soldiers were exhausted.
Mehmed listened to the arguments, considered them, and rejected them.
He gave the order for a final concentrated assault, with the Janissary corps committed in person, for the night of May 28–29.
The Fall of Constantinople (May 29, 1453) is the event whose name everyone in Christendom remembered for the next four centuries.
Mehmed's troops broke through at the Saint Romanus Gate after Giustiniani was wounded and his Genoese began withdrawing.
Constantine XI was last seen rushing into the press of Ottoman troops near the breach, having reportedly thrown off his imperial purple.
His body was never definitely identified.
The plunder was authorized by Ottoman law and custom for three days.
Mehmed cut it short to one.

By the evening of May 29 he had ridden into the city, taken control of his own troops, and proceeded to the Hagia Sophia — full of refugees who had fled there praying through the previous night — to claim his greatest physical prize.
He ordered the cathedral consecrated as a mosque.
The first Islamic prayers were performed there on Friday, June 1, 1453, three days after the assault.
The Christian inscriptions and figurative mosaics were eventually plastered over rather than destroyed; the building was reused, not demolished.

Mehmed II is reported to have walked through the empty cathedral after the ceremony and quoted a Persian couplet about the impermanence of imperial glory: "The spider weaves the curtain in the palace of the Caesars / The owl calls the watches in the towers of Afrasiab." It is one of the more melancholic moments of triumph in conqueror's history.
The Ottoman state was now in possession of Constantinople.

Mehmed renamed it nothing, formally — the city remained "Konstantiniyye" in Ottoman official usage for the next four hundred years, with the name "Istanbul" (a corruption of the Greek eis ten polin, "into the city," which Greek speakers had been using as a colloquial shorthand for centuries) as a parallel popular name that gradually displaced the formal one.
In 1930 the Turkish Republic standardized "Istanbul" as the official name.

From 1453 onward the city was the working capital of the Ottoman Empire, the largest and richest city in the Mediterranean, and the symbolic center of an Islamic imperial project that consciously inherited Byzantine and Roman precedents.
What Mehmed did with the captured city in the months and years after the conquest is at least as interesting as the conquest itself.
His first task was repopulating it.
Constantinople in May 1453 was a depopulated wreck — the city's population had been declining for centuries, and the siege casualties and post-conquest enslavements had reduced it further.
Mehmed needed bodies.

He pursued an aggressive policy of forced and incentivized resettlement: Greek Orthodox families from across the empire were ordered to relocate to Constantinople; Armenian families from eastern Anatolia were brought in; Sephardic Jews who would soon be expelled from Spain (Chapter 5) were welcomed; Anatolian Turks were resettled in entire neighborhoods.
By 1480 the city's population had recovered to perhaps a hundred thousand.
By 1530 it would be the largest city in Europe.
By 1600 it was probably the largest city in the world, with roughly seven hundred thousand inhabitants — larger than Beijing, larger than Cairo, larger than Paris and London combined.
His second task was building.
The city of Constantinople had not had a major construction program for two centuries.
Mehmed launched one.
Topkapı Palace (TOHP-kah-puh, "Cannon Gate Palace," named for the gate near which it stood), begun in 1459, became the working residence of the Ottoman sultans for nearly four hundred years.
It was not a single grand structure on the Western European model.

It was a complex of pavilions, courtyards, and gardens, organized around three successive courtyards of increasing privacy, with the inner courtyards reserved for the sultan, his family, and his most senior administrators.

The architectural model was as much Persian and Central Asian as Byzantine — pleasure gardens, water features, kiosk-style buildings — and it gave the Ottoman court a distinctive character that contrasted sharply with the heavy stone palaces of European monarchs.
Topkapı was a working capital, a school, a treasury, and a religious institution all at once.
The Sultan's private quarters, the harem, the divan (the council chamber where the grand vizier conducted state business), the imperial kitchens, and the palace school were all on the same grounds.

The Fatih Mosque Complex (FAH-tih, "the Conqueror's Mosque"), begun in 1463 on the site of the former Church of the Holy Apostles (which had been the burial place of Byzantine emperors since Constantine the Great — Mehmed's choice of this specific site was symbolically deliberate), was the first major imperial mosque complex in the new capital.

Like later Ottoman imperial complexes, it was a kulliye (kool-LEE-yeh) — a unified institutional cluster combining a mosque, a hospital, a soup kitchen, multiple madrasas, and a tomb-mausoleum, all built and endowed as a single charitable foundation.
The kulliye model was an Ottoman institutional invention, and it would shape the urban geography of every major Ottoman city for the next four centuries.
The original Fatih Mosque was destroyed in an earthquake in 1766 and rebuilt in a different style; only fragments of the Mehmedian original survive.

The Grand Bazaar of Istanbul (KAH-pah-luh CHAR-shuh, "Covered Market") began as a small structure in 1461, expanded under Mehmed's successors, and grew into one of the world's largest covered markets — a network of sixty-one streets and over four thousand shops, sheltered under multiple domes, organized by guild and trade.

By 1500 the Bazaar was the central commercial node of the Ottoman Mediterranean, with rooms for foreign merchants, banks of money-changers, and a strict regulatory regime overseeing prices, weights, and quality.
It is still operating, six centuries later, on roughly the same footprint.
His third task was institutional consolidation.
Mehmed issued the Kanunname (kah-noon-NAH-meh) of 1477 — an imperial law code organizing Ottoman administrative and criminal practice into a single corpus.
The Kanunname's most discussed provision was the fratricide law: "And to whichever of my sons the sultanate shall pass, it is fitting that for the order of the world he shall kill his brothers.
Most of the ulema (religious scholars) have approved this.
Let them act accordingly." The provision was not a literary flourish.

It was the formal legal basis for what would become standard Ottoman succession practice: upon ascending the throne, a new sultan was authorized to execute his brothers (and any potential rival nephews) to prevent the kind of civil war that had wrecked the empire after Bayezid I's death.

The cost of this in human terms was real — sultans through the sixteenth century routinely had several dozen relatives strangled with bowstrings on their accession — but the political effect was that the Ottoman state did not have a major succession war for two centuries.
The Kanunname also organized the timar system, the Ottoman variant of the Byzantine theme system (Byzantine Empire Ch 3).

Like Byzantine stratiotika ktemata, timars were land grants given to soldiers — primarily to the sipahis (SEE-pah-hee, the Anatolian and Balkan feudal cavalry) — in exchange for hereditary military service.
A sipahi held his timar from the sultan, drew its revenue, and was obliged to report for military duty with a specified number of additional armed retainers when called up.
Unlike European feudal grants, timars were not full property; they were revocable and reassignable, and the sultan retained ultimate ownership.

The timar system, combined with the Janissary corps (Chapter 6), gave the Ottomans an army of roughly fifty thousand cavalry plus ten to twenty thousand professional infantry, drawn from the empire's own land base, paid through institutional rather than monetary means, and far more flexible than the comparable European feudal armies.
It would be the institutional foundation of Ottoman military power for the next two centuries.
Mehmed's later campaigns extended Ottoman control across the eastern Mediterranean and the Balkans, and the highlights are worth tracking briefly.

In 1461 he eliminated the Empire of Trebizond (Byzantine Empire Ch 11), the last surviving Byzantine successor state — a small Pontic kingdom on the Black Sea coast under the Komnenos dynasty that had outlasted Constantinople by eight years.
Trebizond surrendered after a brief siege; the last emperor David Komnenos was executed two years later along with most of his sons.
In the same year the Ottomans completed the absorption of the Despotate of the Morea, the Peloponnesian fragment ruled by Constantine XI's brothers.
Thomas Palaiologos escaped with his family to Italy.

His daughter Zoe Palaiologina (later Sophia) eventually married Grand Duke Ivan III of Moscow in 1472, a marriage that transferred the Byzantine imperial inheritance to Russia and laid the groundwork for the Russian "Third Rome" doctrine (Byzantine Empire Ch 12).

Mehmed's wars with Venice (1463–1479) ended with Ottoman gains across the Aegean: Negroponte (modern Euboea, the long island off the eastern coast of Greece) fell in 1470, after a violent siege that shocked Christian Europe; Venice ceded several Aegean islands and Albanian coastal cities; the eastern Mediterranean balance shifted decisively against the Italian maritime republics.

Albanian resistance under Skanderbeg (skan-der-BEG, born George Kastrioti — c. 1405–1468, an Albanian noble who had been raised at the Ottoman court as a hostage and Janissary trainee, then defected when Murad II sent him to Albania to suppress a revolt; he turned the suppression into a twenty-five-year-long Albanian insurgency that became one of the legendary resistance movements of late medieval Europe) was a serious irritant during the 1450s and 1460s, but it was personal to Skanderbeg himself and dissolved after his death in 1468.
In 1480 Mehmed launched two major operations that, had they both succeeded, would have remade the Mediterranean again.
The first was the Siege of Rhodes — an attempt to take the heavily fortified Hospitaller stronghold in the Aegean that controlled shipping lanes between the eastern Mediterranean and the Levant.
It failed; the Knights Hospitaller, dug in behind impressive walls, repelled the Ottoman fleet and army.

The second was the invasion of Otranto in southeastern Italy — an Ottoman expeditionary force under the Albanian-born admiral Gedik Ahmed Pasha that took the Italian town of Otranto in August 1480, slaughtered most of its male population, and held a beachhead on the Italian mainland for thirteen months.
Pope Sixtus IV briefly considered fleeing Rome.

The invasion of Italy was abandoned in late 1481 only because Mehmed II had died on May 3 of that year (probably from natural causes, though contemporary rumor suggested poison administered by his own son Bayezid II), and his successors had to consolidate the throne before continuing the campaign.
Otranto was recovered by Christian forces.
The Italian invasion was never resumed.
Mehmed's reign had transformed the Ottoman Empire.
He had inherited a state recovering from the Interregnum, with one major Christian capital still independent.
He left a state that ruled most of the Balkans, all of Anatolia and the Aegean, and a working empire centered on the city that had been the symbolic seat of Roman Christendom for eleven centuries.
His self-styled title — Kayser-i Rûm — was not delusional.

By the standards of the institutional and territorial inheritance, he was the legitimate Roman emperor of the eastern Mediterranean, ruling from the same throne in the same city, with continuity in many of the same administrative practices, and a court that included Greek Orthodox patriarchs, Armenian merchants, Italian humanist painters (he commissioned Gentile Bellini to paint his portrait in 1480 — the first realistic European portrait of an Ottoman sultan), and Persian astronomers.
He had ended one civilization and become the senior partner of its successor.
His tomb in the Fatih Mosque complex was inscribed with a verse comparing him to the prophet Sulayman — Solomon, in the Ottoman court tradition, was the ideal of the just and wise universal monarch.
The next great Ottoman ruler would be named after that prophet, and he would push the comparison further than anyone had imagined.

Cross-civ check: 1453, the year Constantinople fell, was also approximately the year Johannes Gutenberg finished printing his first Bible in Mainz — the technologies that would shape the next century of European thought were emerging at the same moment as the Ottoman political consolidation.
The Hundred Years' War between England and France ended the same year (October 1453, at the Battle of Castillon).
In China, the Ming dynasty under the Jingtai emperor was recovering from the Tumu Crisis of 1449.
In the Andes, the Inca Empire was beginning its great expansion under Pachacuti.
In Mesoamerica, Moctezuma I was the Aztec emperor, presiding over a major expansion of the Triple Alliance.
Mehmed II's conquest of Constantinople is often described as the event that ended the Middle Ages in European historiography.
From a global perspective, it was one of several great political events of the 1450s, all of them reshaping their respective regions, all of them happening in parallel.

chapters.title: Selim, Süleyman, the Lawgiver
sentences: If Mehmed II's reign was the moment the Ottoman Empire became a world power, the seventy-five years between his death in 1481 and the death of his great-grandson Süleyman in 1566 were the moment it was at its operational peak.
The empire doubled in size.
It absorbed the Mamluk Sultanate of Egypt, the Hijaz (with the holy cities of Mecca and Medina), most of Iraq, Syria, the North African coast as far as Algeria, Hungary, and most of the Balkans.

It built the architecture by which Ottoman civilization would be remembered — the imperial mosques of Istanbul, the great kulliye complexes, the unified visual vocabulary of dome, half-dome, minaret, and tilework.
It codified the legal system that would harmonize Islamic religious law with secular imperial decree across three continents.

It produced the cultural idiom — Ottoman Turkish poetry on Persian models, miniature painting at the imperial workshop, Iznik tile and ceramic, court music — that would become the standard of refined taste from Sarajevo to Baghdad to Cairo.
This chapter covers the three rulers who presided over this expansion: Bayezid II (1481–1512), Selim I "the Grim" (1512–1520), and Süleyman I "the Magnificent" (1520–1566).
Three sultans, three temperaments, one trajectory.
