Bayezid II is the least studied of the three, partly because he ruled between two more dramatic father-and-son figures and partly because his reign was deliberately calmer than the campaigns surrounding it.

He was Mehmed II's elder son, took the throne after a brief succession struggle with his younger brother Cem (JEM) — a struggle which ended with Cem fleeing to Christian Europe, where he became a high-value diplomatic hostage shuttling between the Knights Hospitaller, the French king, and successive popes for the next thirteen years until his death in 1495 in suspicious circumstances.

Bayezid II spent the early years of his reign consolidating institutional gains rather than launching new conquests, and his diplomatic skill in keeping Cem's potential as a rival neutralized while not provoking a Christian crusade in his name was one of the more delicate political achievements of the late fifteenth century.
His reign produced one of the most consequential humanitarian decisions in Ottoman history.
In 1492, the Catholic monarchs Ferdinand and Isabella of Spain issued the Alhambra Decree, ordering the expulsion of all Jews from Spain who refused conversion to Christianity.
Around 200,000 Sephardic Jews were forced to flee — to Portugal, to Morocco, to the Italian city-states, and across the Mediterranean to anywhere that would accept them.
Bayezid II opened the Ottoman Empire to them.
He reportedly sent ships to Iberian ports to facilitate the migration and ordered Ottoman authorities to receive Jewish refugees with dignity.

The Sephardic Jewish community established in cities across the Ottoman world — Salonika (modern Thessaloniki, which by 1500 had become the largest Sephardic Jewish city in the world, with the Jewish population outnumbering Greeks and Turks combined for the next four centuries), Istanbul, Edirne, Sarajevo, Smyrna (modern Izmir) — would shape Ottoman commerce, medicine, finance, and printing for the remainder of the empire's existence.
The political logic of Bayezid's decision was genuine pragmatism.

The Sephardic Jews brought commercial networks across the western Mediterranean, technical skills (especially in medicine, mathematics, and metalworking), and an established expertise in printing — the first Hebrew printing presses in the Ottoman Empire were established by Sephardic refugees in the 1490s, decades before Arabic-script printing was permitted (Chapter 9).
But the decision was also shaped by Bayezid's reading of the situation.

Later Ottoman tradition attributes to him a remark that Ferdinand was considered a wise king but had impoverished his own country and enriched Bayezid's — a perfectly crafted aphorism that probably owes more to subsequent polishing than to a contemporary record, but that captures the policy logic accurately.
The Spanish expulsion was, by any rational political calculus, an act of national self-mutilation.
The Ottoman gain was Spain's loss, and Bayezid was clear-eyed about both halves of that equation.
The Sephardic resettlement was part of a larger pattern.

The Ottoman state in the late fifteenth century was the most religiously diverse polity in the Mediterranean basin — Sunni Muslim majority, with substantial Greek Orthodox, Armenian Christian, Jewish, Catholic, Druze, Alawite, and Yezidi populations, plus various smaller heterodox Sufi communities.
The institutional framework that managed this diversity (the millet system, Chapter 6) was already operational in rough form, and Bayezid's reign was when it began to be formally codified.

The empire was not a tolerant state in any modern sense — non-Muslims paid additional taxes (the jizya head tax and the harac land tax), faced legal disabilities in Islamic courts, and could not bear arms — but it was a structured pluralist state, and within its limits, the Ottoman framework offered protections that no Christian European monarchy of the period could match.
Bayezid II also began the Ottoman state's serious engagement with maritime science.
The Ottoman admiral Piri Reis (PEE-ree RAY-ess, c. 1465–1553), nephew of an earlier Ottoman corsair, served in the eastern Mediterranean fleet during Bayezid's reign.
He is the figure whose work would, in 1513, produce the most discussed cartographic document of the early sixteenth century: the Piri Reis World Map.

The map (or rather the surviving fragment of it, found in the Topkapı archives in 1929) shows the western coastline of Africa, the eastern coastlines of the Americas, and a portion of Antarctica — with annotations in Piri Reis's own hand acknowledging that he drew on more than twenty source maps including Christopher Columbus's lost original chart of the Caribbean.

The Antarctica appearance is overstated in popular accounts; what the map actually shows in that region is harder to identify and may represent a misunderstood or distorted depiction of the South American coastline.

What is genuinely remarkable about the Piri Reis map is the speed at which the new geographic knowledge from Iberian voyages had reached an Ottoman naval officer's drawing table — the Americas had been encountered in 1492, and within twenty years Piri Reis was incorporating them into a synthesis with classical Ptolemaic geography.
The Ottoman state was a participant in the Age of Exploration, even if its naval commitments were primarily Mediterranean.
Bayezid II abdicated in 1512, under pressure from his son Selim and the Janissary corps.
He died one month later, possibly poisoned by Selim, possibly of natural causes — the historical sources are uncertain.
Selim I (ruled 1512–1520), called Yavuz (yah-VOOZ, "the Stern" or "the Grim") in Ottoman tradition, was the shortest-reigning of the three sultans in this chapter and arguably the most consequential.
He took the throne by displacing his father and executing his brothers and nephews.
He spent the next eight years on campaign almost continuously.

By the time he died of an infected boil in 1520, he had doubled the empire's size, claimed the Caliphate, and absorbed the Mamluk Sultanate of Egypt — the dominant Sunni Muslim state of the eastern Mediterranean for the previous three centuries.
His first major campaign was eastward, against the Safavid Empire of Persia.
The Safavids were a new force in the early sixteenth century.

The dynasty had been founded in 1501 by Shah Ismail I (iss-mah-EEL, c. 1487–1524), a charismatic young Turkmen warrior-poet from the Safaviyya Sufi order in Azerbaijan, who had united the Turkic tribes of northwestern Iran under a militant Twelver Shi'a ideology and conquered most of Persia within a decade.

The Safavid state was, in its first generation, an explicitly Shi'a state — Shah Ismail had imposed Twelver Shi'ism as the official religion of his empire, persecuted Sunni populations, and aggressively recruited from heterodox Turkmen groups in eastern Anatolia.

Many of the recruits came from the Qizilbash (kuh-ZUHL-bahsh, "Red-Heads," named for the red headgear that marked them as Safavid loyalists) — Turkmen tribal warriors whose Sufi-influenced religious practice was a direct competitor to the Sunni-centered Ottoman religious establishment.
This was an existential challenge.

The Ottomans were a Sunni state; the great religious authority they claimed was Sunni; their eastern Anatolian provinces were full of Turkmen populations whose loyalty was now being competed for by the Safavid Shah.
In 1511 a major Qizilbash uprising in eastern Anatolia (the Şahkulu rebellion) had nearly destabilized the entire province before being suppressed.
Selim, on taking the throne in 1512, identified the Safavid threat as the most serious facing the empire.

He ordered a massive purge of suspected Qizilbash sympathizers within the eastern Anatolian Turkmen population — modern estimates of the killed run as high as forty thousand — and then prepared for war with Ismail.
The two armies met on August 23, 1514, at Chaldiran (CHAHL-dur-AHN, in northwestern Iran near modern Maku).
The Ottoman force was about sixty thousand, with the Janissary infantry, the timar-based cavalry, and a substantial artillery park.
Ismail's force was about forty thousand, almost entirely Qizilbash cavalry, with no artillery of his own.
The battle was decided by the Ottoman cannons.
The Janissaries took the Safavid frontline cavalry under sustained fire from chained-together field guns, opened gaps in the line, and let the Anatolian sipahis exploit the breaks.
Ismail himself was wounded and barely escaped.
The Safavid army was shattered.

The Ottomans took Tabriz, the Safavid capital, briefly — they could not hold it through the winter — and demonstrated that gunpowder weaponry would, from now on, be the difference between Ottoman and traditional Islamic military forces.
The Battle of Chaldiran is one of those events whose immediate consequences and long-term consequences are different.

The immediate consequence was Ottoman security on the eastern frontier — the Safavid expansion into Anatolia was halted permanently, and Shah Ismail spent the rest of his life avoiding pitched battles with the Ottomans.
The secured eastern flank is also what allowed Selim to pivot south and destroy the Mamluk Sultanate within three years, giving him Egypt, Mecca, and the Caliphate.
The Safavid perspective on this battle — the trauma of defeat, the loss of Tabriz, and the long recovery under Shah Tahmasp — is covered in Safavid Persia Ch 3.

The long-term consequence was the institutionalization of the Sunni-Shi'a sectarian divide as the operative religious geopolitics of the Islamic world, with the Ottomans as the Sunni superpower and the Safavids as the Shi'a counter-state.
This divide is still operative in the politics of the modern Middle East.

Iraqi-Iranian relations, Saudi-Iranian relations, the Lebanese sectarian system, the Bahraini civil tensions — all of them trace, in some part, to the Ottoman-Safavid rivalry that became unbridgeable in 1514.
Selim's second major campaign was southward, against the Mamluk Sultanate.

The Mamluks (mam-LOOKS, "owned ones," from the Arabic word for "slave") were a slave-soldier dynasty that had ruled Egypt and Syria since 1250 — a roughly contemporaneous slave-soldier state to the developing Janissary system, but with deeper roots and a longer institutional tradition.

The Mamluks had defeated the Mongols at Ayn Jalut in 1260 (Mongol Empire Ch 5), expelled the last Crusaders from the Holy Land in 1291, and ruled the eastern Mediterranean as the dominant Sunni Muslim power for the previous two and a half centuries.
Their empire included Egypt, the Levant, the Hijaz with the holy cities of Mecca and Medina, and the trade routes connecting the Indian Ocean to the Mediterranean.
By 1516 the Mamluk state was institutionally exhausted.
The slave-soldier recruitment system — which had relied on Circassian and Turkic boys imported from the Black Sea region — was being throttled by Ottoman control of the Black Sea trade.

The Mamluk military had not adopted gunpowder firearms or artillery to any significant extent, holding instead to the heavily armored mounted archery model that had defined Mamluk warfare for centuries.

The Mamluk economy had been undermined by the Portuguese Indian Ocean voyages that had begun in 1498 — Vasco da Gama's arrival in Calicut had opened a maritime route around the Cape of Good Hope that bypassed the Egyptian-Mediterranean spice trade, costing the Mamluks a major share of their revenue.
Selim moved fast.

The Ottomans defeated the main Mamluk army at Marj Dabiq (MARJ dah-BEEK) in northern Syria on August 24, 1516 — a battle decided, like Chaldiran, by Ottoman gunpowder superiority over a force that fought as if firearms had not been invented.
The Mamluk Sultan Qansuh al-Ghawri was killed in the battle (probably from a stroke during the engagement, though the sources disagree).
The Ottomans took Damascus, then Aleppo, then the rest of Syria.
They marched south through Palestine into Egypt.
The successor Mamluk Sultan Tuman Bay II tried to organize a final resistance at Ridaniya, just outside Cairo, on January 22, 1517.
Cairo fell.
Tuman Bay was captured several weeks later and hanged from the Bab Zuwayla gate of his own capital.
In the conquest of Egypt, Selim acquired three things of fundamental importance.
The first was the Hijaz, with the holy cities of Mecca and Medina.
The Mamluks had been the guardians of the Two Holy Cities since 1250.
The Hijaz was now Ottoman.
The annual pilgrimage caravan (the hajj) and its security infrastructure passed under Ottoman authority.
The Sharif of Mecca acknowledged Ottoman sovereignty.
The sultan's title became "Servant of the Two Sanctuaries" — a designation that gave the Ottomans a unique religious legitimacy across the Sunni Muslim world.
The second was the Caliphate.
The Caliphate had been a contested institution since the Mongol sack of Baghdad and execution of the last Abbasid Caliph in 1258 (Mongol Empire Ch 5).

A surviving Abbasid line had been kept as ceremonial puppet caliphs at the Mamluk court in Cairo since then, with no real authority but with the symbolic weight of three centuries of formal continuity.
Selim, on taking Cairo, reportedly received the formal transfer of the Caliphate from the last shadow Abbasid, Al-Mutawakkil III, who was brought to Istanbul and pensioned.

The historicity of this transfer is debated — there is no contemporary documentary evidence of a formal ceremony, and the doctrine that the Caliphate had been transferred in 1517 was probably elaborated retrospectively in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.

What is clear is that from 1517 onward, the Ottoman sultans claimed the title Caliph of the Muslims in addition to their other titles, and the claim was widely accepted across the Sunni Islamic world.

The institutional fusion of sultanate and caliphate would become a central feature of Ottoman political theology for the next four hundred years, and its eventual abolition in 1924 (Chapter 12) would close one of the longest-running theological-political institutions in human history.
The third was Egypt's tax base.
The Egyptian treasury, even in its weakened sixteenth-century state, was one of the largest single revenue sources in the Mediterranean basin.

The Egyptian grain economy continued, after a brief disruption, to feed Istanbul's growing population — the same role Egypt had played for Constantinople's growing population a millennium earlier (Byzantine Empire Ch 1).
The Egyptian textiles, the Indian Ocean trade routes, the customs duties on the Suez and Alexandria trade — all of these now flowed into Ottoman coffers.
The empire's annual revenue roughly doubled overnight.
The Janissary corps could be expanded.
The fleet could be rebuilt.
The artillery park could be modernized.
Selim's territorial conquests had paid for the next half-century of Ottoman expansion.
He died in September 1520 of an infected boil on his back, while preparing what would have been his next campaign.
He was forty-nine.

His son Süleyman I (ruled 1520–1566), called the Magnificent in the West and Kanuni (kah-noo-NEE, "the Lawgiver") in the Ottoman tradition, took the throne at twenty-six and ruled for forty-six years — the longest single reign in Ottoman history.
He inherited the empire at the moment of maximum institutional and territorial momentum, and he ran it through what every subsequent Ottoman generation would treat as the empire's golden age.
Süleyman's reign was so comprehensively productive that summarizing it is difficult.
His military campaigns alone took up most of every year for most of his reign — he led thirteen major campaigns in person, more than any other Ottoman sultan.
The institutional, legal, and architectural achievements of his reign would shape the empire's character for the next three centuries.

His personal correspondence with European monarchs (especially with King Francis I of France, with whom he forged the Franco-Ottoman alliance of 1536, the first formal diplomatic agreement between a Christian and Muslim European power, and one that would shape European politics for the next two centuries) gave him a reputation in western Europe as the most formidable monarch of his age.
The court of Süleyman was the place where Ottoman classical culture reached its concentrated peak.
Take the campaigns first.
In 1521, the year after his accession, Süleyman captured Belgrade — the Hungarian fortress at the confluence of the Danube and Sava rivers that had been the strategic key to defending central Europe.
Mehmed II had failed to take Belgrade in 1456.
Süleyman took it in his first major campaign.
The road to Hungary was now open.
In 1522, he took Rhodes — the Hospitaller stronghold his great-grandfather Mehmed II had failed to capture in 1480.
The siege lasted six months and cost the Ottomans heavily, but the Knights Hospitaller eventually surrendered on negotiated terms and were allowed to evacuate to Sicily and eventually Malta.
With Rhodes Ottoman, the eastern Mediterranean shipping lanes were secure.
In 1526, at the Battle of Mohács (MOH-hahch) in southern Hungary on August 29, Süleyman destroyed the Kingdom of Hungary.
The Hungarian king Louis II was killed (drowned in a swamp during the rout).
Most of the Hungarian aristocracy died with him.

Hungary fragmented into three pieces over the next several years: the central plain became an Ottoman province administered from Buda (the western half of modern Budapest, taken in 1541); the eastern portion became the Principality of Transylvania, an Ottoman vassal under a Hungarian noble dynasty; the western strip remained under Habsburg rule.
Hungary as an independent kingdom ceased to exist for the next 150 years.
In 1529, Süleyman besieged Vienna — the first Ottoman attempt on the Habsburg capital.

The siege was a stretch — the Ottoman supply lines were over a thousand miles long, the campaign season was running out, the autumn rains were beginning to make Hungarian terrain impassable for siege artillery — and after three weeks of unsuccessful assaults, Süleyman lifted the siege on October 14 and withdrew.
The First Siege of Vienna marked the practical limit of Ottoman expansion into central Europe.
Habsburg forces would never push the Ottomans back as far as the Hungarian plain in Süleyman's lifetime, but the Ottomans would never get further west than the suburbs of Vienna either.
The European-Ottoman frontier had stabilized along a line that would not move significantly for the next 150 years.
In 1534, Süleyman took Baghdad from the Safavids — a campaign that brought all of Iraq under Ottoman control.
The Tigris-Euphrates valleys, which had been the heart of the Islamic world under the Abbasid Caliphate, were now Ottoman.
The Twelver Shi'a holy cities of Najaf and Karbala fell into Ottoman hands.

The acquisition was symbolically enormous — the Ottoman sultan now ruled the city the Caliph had ruled — and it gave Süleyman additional grounds for the Servant of the Two Sanctuaries title his father had claimed.

The Ottoman-Safavid wars of 1532–1555 never produced a decisive battlefield result because the Safavid Shah Tahmasp I refused to fight one — he abandoned Tabriz multiple times rather than risk a pitched battle, using a scorched-earth strategy that denied the Ottoman army food and forage while the Iranian winter did the rest.
The strategic asymmetry (Ottoman firepower vs.
Safavid strategic retreat) is the defining military theme of the era.
The Peace of Amasya in 1555 stabilized the frontier without resolving the sectarian rivalry.
The Safavid side of these wars — and how Tahmasp eventually rebuilt the army Abbas I would use to recover Baghdad — is covered in Safavid Persia Ch 3.

Throughout the rest of his reign, Süleyman alternated campaigns against the Habsburgs in Hungary, the Safavids in Persia and Iraq, the Portuguese in the Indian Ocean (Ottoman fleets repeatedly tried to expel the Portuguese from the Red Sea and the Persian Gulf, with mixed success), and various Christian states in the Mediterranean.

The naval war was largely managed by Hayreddin Barbarossa (HYE-reh-din bar-bah-ROH-sah, c. 1478–1546, an Aegean-born corsair-turned-Ottoman-admiral whose Mediterranean fleet dominated the central and western Mediterranean for two decades), whose victory at the Battle of Preveza in 1538 destroyed a combined Christian fleet under the Genoese admiral Andrea Doria and gave the Ottomans naval supremacy in the Mediterranean for the next thirty years.
Now take the institutional and cultural side.
Süleyman's title Kanuni ("the Lawgiver") came from his comprehensive codification of Ottoman secular law.
The Ottoman legal system rested on two pillars.

The first was sharia — Islamic religious law, derived from the Quran, the hadith (the recorded sayings and actions of the Prophet Muhammad), and the centuries of juridical commentary developed by Sunni legal scholars.

The second was kanun — secular imperial law, issued by the sultan to handle areas where sharia was silent or where administrative practicality required additional rules: taxation, land tenure, military organization, criminal procedure for non-religious offenses, market regulation.
The two systems coexisted in tension.
Sharia was the universal religious-moral framework.
Kanun was the practical operating code of the empire's administration.

Süleyman's chief jurist, the Sheikh ul-Islam (the highest religious authority of the empire — the office had been formalized under Mehmed II) Ebussuud Efendi (EH-boos-SOOD), spent decades of careful work harmonizing the two systems.

Ebussuud's interpretive method was to find sharia-compatible justifications for kanun provisions where possible, and to acknowledge the sultan's authority to legislate in areas not explicitly addressed by sharia.
The resulting Kanun-i Osmani (the systematic codification of Ottoman secular law completed during Süleyman's reign) became the operational legal framework for the empire across three continents.
Ottoman judges in Cairo, Damascus, Sarajevo, Buda, Sofia, and Istanbul applied a single legal code, with regional adaptations, to populations of every religion.
By the standards of any sixteenth-century legal system, this was remarkable.

The architecture is the other defining feature of the period, and its great figure was Mimar Sinan (mee-MAR see-NAHN, c. 1490–1588) — the Ottoman chief architect for fifty years and one of the most consequential builders in human history.
Sinan was, like many of the Ottoman state's senior officials, a devshirme recruit.

He was born in the Ottoman Anatolian province of Cappadocia to an Orthodox Christian (probably Armenian or Greek) family, taken in the devshirme around 1512, converted to Islam, trained in the imperial palace, and assigned to the Janissary corps as a military engineer.
He served on Süleyman's campaigns for over twenty years, building bridges, roads, fortifications, and siege engines across the empire.
He was appointed chief imperial architect in 1539, at about age forty-nine, and held the post for the next forty-nine years.

The buildings he designed and supervised during that period — about three hundred and fifty across the empire, of which over a hundred survive — established the visual vocabulary of Ottoman classical architecture.

Sinan's central problem was the same one Justinian's architects Anthemius and Isidore had faced ten centuries earlier (Byzantine Empire Ch 2): how do you cover a large central interior space with a single dome, while keeping the worshipful interior lit, structurally sound, and aesthetically coherent?
Anthemius and Isidore had invented the pendentive — the triangular concave surface that transitions from a square base to a circular dome — as their solution at Hagia Sophia.
The pendentive remained the structural basis of Byzantine and Ottoman dome architecture for the next thousand years.
Sinan's contribution was to refine, rationalize, and extend the system across an entire family of imperial mosques.
His great early work was the Şehzade Mosque (sheh-ZAH-deh, "the Prince's Mosque"), completed in 1548, built for Süleyman's deceased son Mehmed.
The Şehzade is symmetrical in plan, with a central dome supported by four half-domes — the first time this exact configuration had been attempted, and a step beyond the Hagia Sophia model.

His acknowledged masterpiece in Istanbul was the Süleymaniye Mosque (soo-lay-mah-NEE-yeh), completed in 1557 — a massive imperial complex containing the mosque, four madrasas, a hospital, a soup kitchen, a primary school, a hammam (public bath), and various other charitable institutions.
The Süleymaniye's central dome is 173 feet high and 86 feet across, supported by two half-domes on the longitudinal axis.
It is a more rationally proportioned, structurally cleaner descendant of Hagia Sophia.
Sinan said of it that it was the work of his apprenticeship.
His self-proclaimed masterpiece was the Selimiye Mosque in Edirne, completed in 1574, when he was about eighty-four years old.

The Selimiye's central dome is 108 feet across — surpassing Hagia Sophia by about six feet — and supported by eight piers arranged in an octagon, an entirely new structural system that allowed the dome to appear as if it were floating without visible support.
Sinan considered it the work of his maturity.
He may have been right.

The Selimiye is now a UNESCO World Heritage site and is generally considered, by serious students of architectural history, to be one of the supreme achievements of the medieval and early modern world.
The ornament was as important as the structure.

The interior of the Süleymaniye and Selimiye mosques used Iznik tiles — the polychrome ceramic tiles produced in the imperial workshops at Iznik (the old Byzantine Nicaea) from the early sixteenth century onward, with their characteristic blue, turquoise, red, and green floral and arabesque motifs against a white background.
Iznik tilework set the visual standard for Ottoman religious and palatial decoration for the next two centuries.
The light filtered through stained-glass windows.
The calligraphic medallions inscribed with Quranic verses provided the major focal points.

The sound of the mu'addhin's call to prayer floated from the minarets — Sinan typically used four minarets for an imperial mosque, with multiple balconies (şerefe) corresponding to each minaret's height ranking.
Sinan was eighty-eight when he died in 1588.
He had designed mosques, palaces, mausoleums, baths, bridges, aqueducts, hospitals, and schools across an empire stretching from the Danube to the Tigris.
He had trained generations of architects who would continue the tradition for the next century.

His tomb is in a small mausoleum he designed for himself, near the Süleymaniye complex, with an inscription giving his name in plain Arabic script and his title — "Mimar Sinan" — without further elaboration.
He had not needed to elaborate.
Anyone walking past it knew what he had built.

Süleyman's wife Hürrem Sultan (HUR-rem) — born Roxelana in Ruthenia (modern western Ukraine), captured as a teenager in a Tatar slave raid, brought to the Ottoman harem, and rising through the harem hierarchy to become Süleyman's principal favorite — would change the structure of Ottoman dynastic politics for the next century, and her story properly belongs to the next chapter where the post-Süleyman world is shaped by her precedent.

What needs noting here is that Süleyman, in 1533 or 1534, freed Hürrem from slave status and married her in a public legal ceremony — the first time an Ottoman sultan had legally married a woman since the early fifteenth century.
The previous practice had been concubine relationships, with the mothers of potential heirs deriving their status from their sons rather than from formal marriage.
Süleyman's marriage to Hürrem was unprecedented and shocked court traditionalists.

It also concentrated political power in the imperial harem in a way that had not existed before, and the long-term consequences would become one of the defining features of post-Süleyman Ottoman politics.
Süleyman died on the night of September 6, 1566, during the siege of the Hungarian fortress of Szigetvár (SIG-et-var).
He was seventy-two years old.
The grand vizier Sokollu Mehmed Pasha kept his death secret from the army for six weeks, finishing the siege successfully and getting the body back to Istanbul before the news broke.
The transition to the next sultan went smoothly.
The empire's institutional momentum was so strong that Süleyman's death was, organizationally, almost a non-event.
The empire he left was the largest, richest, and most institutionally sophisticated political entity in the world outside the Ming dynasty.
It controlled the Balkans, all of Anatolia, the Levant, Egypt, the Hijaz, Mesopotamia, the North African coast as far west as Algiers, and substantial parts of the Caucasus.
It had a population of perhaps thirty million.
It had the most professional army in Europe, the largest navy in the Mediterranean, and a working multi-religious legal and administrative system that no other contemporary state could match.
It had just produced, under Sinan, an architectural achievement that would not be surpassed for centuries.
The next two hundred years would be a story of slow erosion of all of this.
The institutions would prove brittle.
The frontier would stop advancing.
The court would become increasingly self-absorbed.
The empire would, eventually, begin to lose territory it had taken centuries to acquire.
But none of that was visible in 1566, when the Ottomans were burying their longest-reigning sultan and the Janissaries were chanting their loyalty oath to his son.

Cross-civ check: the year of Süleyman's death (1566) was approximately when Akbar the Great of the Mughal Empire — the Persian-Mongol-descended dynasty in India — was beginning his major reign, when Elizabeth I of England had been on the throne for eight years, when the Counter-Reformation in Catholic Europe was reaching its peak, when Ivan the Terrible of Russia had been declaring himself Tsar for nineteen years, when the Spanish Empire under Philip II was at its territorial peak in the Americas, and when the Ming dynasty under the Jiajing Emperor was in its long mid-period decline.
The Ottoman Empire of the mid-sixteenth century was contemporary with most of the early modern world's great political consolidations.
It was as large as any of them and structurally as sophisticated as the most sophisticated.

chapters.title: The Janissaries, the Devshirme, the Millet
sentences: This chapter is a pause.

The political narrative of Chapters 4 and 5 has been driving forward through campaigns and conquests, and the next chapter will resume that drive through the slow disintegration of the post-Süleyman court.
But before it does, three institutions are worth examining in detail, because they were the operating mechanisms by which the Ottoman state ran.

None of them are unique inventions — each had earlier precedents in Islamic, Byzantine, and steppe practice — but the Ottoman versions were more developed, more systematized, and more durable than their counterparts elsewhere.

They are the slave-soldier corps of the Janissaries, the recruitment system that fed it (the devshirme), and the religious-pluralism framework that managed the empire's non-Muslim populations (the millet system).
These three together explain how a state ruling thirty million people of dozens of ethnicities and several major religions could function as a coherent administrative entity for four centuries.
The political stories are easier to remember.
The institutional stories are why the political stories were possible.
Start with the Janissary corps.

The Janissaries (yan-iss-AIR-eez, from Turkish yeni çeri, "new troops") were the standing professional infantry of the Ottoman Empire from approximately 1363 (under Murad I) to 1826 (when Mahmud II destroyed them, Chapter 9).
For most of those four hundred and sixty-three years, they were the most consistently effective infantry force in the world.
They were the first Ottoman troops trained from childhood to use firearms in coordinated formations.

They were the units that took Constantinople, defeated the Mamluks at Marj Dabiq and Ridaniya, won at Mohács and Chaldiran, marched on Vienna twice, and stood as the personal guard of every sultan from Murad I to Mahmud II.
What made them distinctive was the recruitment pattern.
The Janissary was not a free Muslim subject who had volunteered for military service.
He was a kapıkulu (kah-puh-koo-LOO, "slave of the Porte" — the Ottoman name for the slave class of the imperial household).

He had been taken from a Christian family in childhood through the devshirme, converted to Islam, given a Turkish name, trained and educated in the imperial system, and made the personal property of the sultan.
His legal status was technically slavery.
His operational reality was an elite military profession with steady pay, organized barracks life, hereditary recognition, and access to the most senior positions in the Ottoman state.
The institutional logic was Byzantine, Mamluk, and Abbasid.

Both the Byzantine tagmata (the elite professional units of the imperial guard) and the Mamluk slave-soldier system had demonstrated that personally loyal slave-soldiers, owing their entire training and status to the ruler, made better elite troops than aristocratic levies whose loyalty was complicated by family interests.
Slaves had no families in the original sense — their families had been left behind — and could not start dynasties to compete with the ruling one.

The Safavid Empire independently developed the same institutional logic under Shah Abbas I, creating a ghulam corps recruited from Georgian, Armenian, and Circassian boys in the Caucasus — the same geographic zone, a different recruitment method, but an identical structural rationale (Safavid Persia Ch 4).
The parallel shows that the slave-soldier solution to the loyal-army problem was a shared early-modern Islamic response to a shared structural challenge, not a uniquely Ottoman invention.
They were, in this sense, structurally analogous to the Byzantine eunuchs (Byzantine Empire Ch 6) and the Mamluk corps in Egypt and Syria.
The Ottomans took the slave-soldier idea, refined it, and turned it into the central pillar of their military system.
The corps was organized in regiments called ortas (OR-tahs), each of about a hundred men, with elaborate insignia and traditions.
The Janissary commander (the Ağa of the Janissaries) was one of the senior officials of the imperial court, with direct access to the sultan and a major voice in succession politics.
The corps had its own legal jurisdiction, its own internal discipline, its own pay structures, and its own ceremonial roles.
Janissaries fought on foot in close formations, primarily armed with arquebuses (early matchlock firearms) from the late fifteenth century onward.

They were trained in coordinated volley fire — entire ranks discharging muskets simultaneously and reloading in sequence — at a level of coordination that European armies would not match for another century.
They were paid in cash from the central treasury, supplemented by ceremonial gifts from the sultan on his accession, on military victories, and on major holidays.
The cohesion of the corps came from the bektashi Sufi order, which functioned as the spiritual home of the Janissaries from the late fifteenth century onward.
Every Janissary was nominally a Bektashi member.

The order's syncretic theology — drawing on Sufism, Twelver Shi'ism, and folk traditions — gave the slave-soldier corps a specific religious identity that distinguished them from both the orthodox Sunni religious establishment and the Christian populations from which they had been recruited.
Bektashi rituals, songs, and food (the pilav, the rice-and-meat dish that became symbolic of Janissary identity) were part of corps culture for centuries.
By the mid-sixteenth century the Janissary corps numbered about twelve thousand men.
By the early seventeenth century it had grown to about forty thousand.

The expansion was driven by Ottoman fiscal needs: as the timar-based feudal cavalry became less militarily relevant against gunpowder-armed European armies, the central government compensated by expanding the cash-paid Janissary corps.

The expansion would, eventually, be the corps's undoing — by the eighteenth century, the Janissaries had become a hereditary urban guild more interested in protecting their pay and privileges than in military training.
But in the period of Ottoman peak power (roughly 1450 to 1600), the Janissary corps was the most disciplined, best-trained, and best-equipped infantry force in the Mediterranean basin.
Now the recruitment system.

The devshirme (DEV-shir-meh, "collection" or "gathering" in Ottoman Turkish) was the institutionalized recruitment of Christian boys from the empire's Balkan provinces for conversion to Islam and service in the Ottoman state.

It was a tribute, in the technical sense — a tax paid in human beings rather than in money or goods — and it was levied on the empire's Balkan Orthodox Christian populations approximately every four to seven years from roughly 1380 to 1638.

By the time the system was effectively abandoned in the seventeenth century, it had brought somewhere between two hundred thousand and two hundred fifty thousand boys into the Ottoman state apparatus.
The mechanism was carefully regulated.
A senior Ottoman official (typically a Janissary commander) would arrive in a Balkan province with an imperial warrant authorizing the levy.
He would assemble the local Orthodox priests, who had access to baptismal records, and require them to identify boys aged eight to eighteen who met the criteria.

The criteria were specific: only sons of Christian families, with a strong preference for second sons (the eldest was usually exempt to keep the family's farm running), unmarried, physically sound, intelligent, of good character.

Recruiters were specifically forbidden from taking only sons, married youths, married converts to Islam, gypsies, Jews, Armenians, or boys from urban families with administrative connections — the levy targeted the Orthodox Christian peasantry of the rural Balkans almost exclusively.
The selected boys were taken to assembly points (typically Edirne or Istanbul), examined by court officials, and divided into two streams.
The first stream, comprising the most physically capable but less academically promising, was assigned to Turkish village families in Anatolia for several years.
Here the boys learned Turkish, basic Islam, agricultural and military skills.
They were not slaves in this period — they lived as members of their host families — but they were under Ottoman state oversight and could not return home.

After several years they were assembled at the imperial barracks in Istanbul and inducted into the Janissary corps as acemi oğlanlar (ah-jeh-MEE oh-lahn-LAR, "novice boys"), where they completed military training and were eventually assigned to active Janissary regiments.

The second stream, comprising the most intelligent and physically attractive, was sent directly to the Enderun — the Inner Palace School at Topkapı, established by Mehmed II around 1455 and refined by his successors.
The Enderun was the elite educational institution of the empire.

Its curriculum included Ottoman Turkish, Arabic, Persian, mathematics, calligraphy, music, archery, swordsmanship, riding, falconry, Islamic theology, history, and the elaborate court etiquette required for service in the imperial household.
The school operated in conditions of strict discipline and genuine intellectual rigor.
Pupils lived in the palace under the close supervision of senior pages and palace eunuchs.
They progressed through a hierarchy of seven academic-administrative chambers, each with its own specialization.

Graduation, after fourteen to twenty years of training, led to assignments in the imperial bureaucracy, the diplomatic corps, the provincial governorships, the military command structure, or the imperial household itself.
The most successful Enderun graduates rose to the highest offices of the empire.
Of the approximately 215 grand viziers in Ottoman history, more than half were of devshirme origin.

Sokollu Mehmed Pasha (so-kol-LOO meh-MED pah-SHAH, c. 1505–1579), who effectively ran the Ottoman state from the late 1560s until his assassination in 1579 and who was perhaps the greatest grand vizier of the entire imperial period, had been taken as a devshirme boy from a Bosnian Serbian Orthodox family in approximately 1518, at about age thirteen.

Pargalı Ibrahim Pasha (par-gah-LUH ee-brah-HEEM, c. 1495–1536), Süleyman the Magnificent's favorite and grand vizier for thirteen years, had been taken from a Greek family from the western Greek coast.
Mimar Sinan, the architect of the Süleymaniye and Selimiye mosques, was a devshirme graduate (Chapter 5).

The military commanders, the grand admirals, the provincial governors — the highest administrative class of the empire — were largely a slave class, recruited as children from the conquered Balkan Christian populations and trained in the imperial palace.
The ethical complexity of this system was real and is difficult to summarize without sliding into either condemnation or apologetics.

From a modern human-rights standpoint, the devshirme was a forced child levy, a violation of religious freedom, a separation of children from their families, and a system of slavery — even if the form of slavery was unusually privileged by historical standards.

From a sixteenth-century perspective, the system offered the recruited boys access to opportunities that would have been unimaginable in their home villages: education, social mobility, careers at the highest levels of one of the world's great empires.
There are well-documented cases of Balkan Christian families bribing Ottoman officials to include their sons in the devshirme rather than to exclude them.
There are also well-documented cases of families hiding their sons, or marrying them off underage, to avoid the levy.
Both responses existed simultaneously, and the relative balance varied by region, period, and family circumstance.
The boys themselves, once recruited, generally identified as Ottomans rather than as their birth peoples.

The senior devshirme graduates were, by the mid-sixteenth century, the institutional core of the empire — a class with their own esprit de corps, their own marriage patterns (devshirme graduates often married daughters of the imperial family or of senior Ottoman aristocrats), and their own political interests.

Many maintained connections with their home villages — sending money, building mosques and schools, occasionally returning to visit — but their primary loyalty was to the imperial system that had made them.

The devshirme was, in this sense, a remarkably effective integration mechanism: it took the empire's most marginal subject population (rural Balkan Christian peasants) and transformed them, individually, into the empire's most powerful administrative class.
The system declined in the seventeenth century for reasons that had little to do with its inherent design.

The Janissary corps gradually became hereditary — the legal prohibition against Janissaries marrying was relaxed, then ignored, and Janissary sons increasingly inherited their fathers' positions without going through devshirme training.
The free Muslim population, growing in proportion to the Christian population, increasingly demanded access to Janissary careers and successfully pushed for inclusion.
The administrative ranks were increasingly filled by free Muslim graduates of the empire's growing madrasa system rather than by devshirme alumni.
By 1638 the regular devshirme levies had ended.
By the late seventeenth century, the institution was effectively gone.

What remained was a Janissary corps that had lost its slave-soldier basis, was no longer centrally trained, and was increasingly a hereditary urban guild — an institution that had outlived the recruitment system that had originally given it its quality.
Now the system that managed the empire's non-Muslim majority — and majority is the right word for most of the empire's territory and most of its history.
The Ottoman Empire was, in 1500, about half non-Muslim, with substantial Greek Orthodox, Armenian Apostolic, Jewish, Coptic, Syriac Christian, and Druze populations.
In 1700 it was still about forty percent non-Muslim.
The system that managed this religious diversity was the millet (mil-LET, "nation" or "religious community" in Ottoman Turkish, from the Arabic milla).
The millet system was not a sudden invention.

Its precedents went back to Mehmed II's appointment of Patriarch Gennadios II as the head of the Greek Orthodox community in 1454 (Byzantine Empire Ch 12), and beyond that to early Islamic precedents for organizing dhimmi (DIM-mee, "protected") non-Muslim populations under their own religious authorities.
What Ottoman practice did was systematize and extend the model.

By the sixteenth century, the major non-Muslim communities of the empire were organized into formally recognized millets, each headed by its religious leader, each enjoying internal autonomy in matters of personal status (marriage, divorce, inheritance, education), each responsible for collecting its own taxes for transmission to the imperial treasury, and each granted recognized legal protections.

The four classical millets were: The Rum millet (the Greek Orthodox community, named Rum from the Arabic-Ottoman term for "Roman" — a designation that the Ottomans inherited from the Byzantine self-identification, Byzantine Empire Ch 1).

The Patriarch of Constantinople was the head of the Rum millet, with jurisdiction over the Greek Orthodox populations of the empire — a community that included not only ethnic Greeks but Bulgarian, Serbian, Romanian, and Albanian Orthodox Christians (the national Orthodox patriarchates of Bulgaria, Serbia, and the Romanian principalities all came under the Constantinople patriarch's jurisdiction at various points in the Ottoman period).
The Rum millet was the largest single non-Muslim community in the empire, with perhaps eight to ten million members at peak.
The Armenian millet.
The Armenian Apostolic Church, with its own patriarch in Istanbul (separate from the Rum patriarch), governed the Armenian Christian population.
The Armenian community was concentrated in eastern Anatolia, the Caucasus, and the major commercial cities (Istanbul, Izmir, Aleppo).

It had its own ecclesiastical structure, its own legal traditions, and its own commercial networks — Armenian merchants dominated the empire's silk trade, the Persian-Indian trade routes, and substantial portions of the international banking system.
The Jewish millet.
After the Sephardic resettlement under Bayezid II (Chapter 5), the Ottoman Jewish population was the largest in the world.
It was organized under a chief rabbi (the Hahambaşı) in Istanbul, with regional chief rabbis in the major Jewish cities.
The Jewish community combined Sephardic, Romaniote (the older Greek-speaking Jewish population that predated the Sephardic arrival), and Ashkenazi populations.

Jewish merchants, doctors, financiers, and translators were enormously important in Ottoman commerce and diplomacy — the imperial physician was almost always Jewish from the late fifteenth through the seventeenth centuries.

A fourth, smaller community was the Catholic millet, organized later (formally in the early nineteenth century) for the Latin-rite Catholic populations — primarily Italian merchants in Istanbul and Izmir, and the Maronite Catholic communities of Lebanon.
The Maronite-Catholic relationship with Rome and France gave this community a particular geopolitical weight that increased through the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.
Each millet operated according to its own internal religious law for matters within the community.

A Greek Orthodox merchant disputing an inheritance with another Greek Orthodox merchant would have his case heard in the Greek Orthodox ecclesiastical court, applying canon law and Byzantine civil law (the tradition descending from Justinian's Corpus Juris Civilis was preserved in the Greek Orthodox legal system, Byzantine Empire Ch 12).
An Armenian merchant marrying his daughter to another Armenian dealt with the Armenian church.
A Jewish family sending a son to school dealt with the Jewish community organization.
These were not merely private matters — they were legally recognized public functions of the religious authorities, with enforcement support from the Ottoman state.

Cross-community matters — disputes between members of different millets, criminal cases, taxation, property issues touching multiple communities — went to the Ottoman state courts, applying sharia and kanun.
A Greek Orthodox merchant suing a Muslim merchant went to a sharia court.
A Jewish-Armenian commercial partnership disputing a debt went to the Ottoman judge.
The millet system had important limitations that should not be glossed over.
Non-Muslims paid additional taxes (the jizya head tax, the harac land tax).
They could not, in principle, ride horses or bear arms.
They were required to wear distinctive clothing or markings (the requirements varied by period and region; in some periods they were enforced strictly, in others ignored).
Their houses could not be taller than Muslim houses on the same street.
They could not testify against a Muslim in an Islamic court.
New non-Muslim places of worship could not be built without sultanic permission, though existing ones were generally protected.
Conversion from Islam to another religion was a capital offense (the reverse direction, conversion to Islam, was actively encouraged and rewarded).
Non-Muslims were excluded from the Janissary corps after the early period, from the senior religious offices, and from the highest courtly positions.
But within these limits, the system offered protections that no contemporary Christian state matched.
There were no Inquisitions in the Ottoman Empire.
There were no organized expulsions of religious minorities (the Sephardic Jews fled to Ottoman lands, not from them).
There were no forced mass conversions on the Spanish-Inquisition model.

There were periodic local persecutions and occasional anti-Christian or anti-Jewish riots, but the systematic state-sponsored persecution that characterized parts of late medieval and early modern Christian Europe was not a feature of Ottoman governance.

A Greek Orthodox Christian, an Armenian, or a Jew living in fifteenth- or sixteenth-century Ottoman Istanbul lived under more durable legal protections than the same person would have lived under in Catholic Madrid, Anglican London, or Lutheran Wittenberg.
The millet framework also explains how the empire could function across such enormous religious diversity for so long.

By organizing non-Muslims as legally recognized corporate communities with internal autonomy, the Ottoman state outsourced the management of religious diversity to the religious communities themselves.

The state did not have to adjudicate Greek Orthodox marriage disputes or Armenian inheritance cases or Jewish divorce procedures — those were handled by the relevant patriarch, archbishop, or rabbi, with the state providing only enforcement when needed.
The system was administratively efficient, ideologically coherent (within the Islamic theological tradition of dhimmi protection), and remarkably stable.
It survived for four centuries with substantial structural continuity.
Three of the most distinctive Ottoman institutions, then, share a common feature: they were ways of integrating populations the empire ruled but did not wish to assimilate.

The Janissary corps integrated young Christian boys into the empire's most elite military and administrative class, while keeping them as a structurally separate slave-soldier caste with their own discipline and esprit de corps.

The devshirme system extracted talented children from the Balkan Christian peasantry, converted them to Islam, trained them at imperial expense, and channeled them into careers at the highest levels of the state — while explicitly not requiring or expecting their birth communities to convert as a whole.

The millet system organized the empire's non-Muslim majority into recognized religious communities with internal autonomy, allowing them to maintain their religious, legal, and cultural identities under Ottoman sovereignty without forcing assimilation to Islamic practice.
Each system was, in its own way, a recognition that the empire's unity did not require the empire's homogeneity.
The Ottoman approach was the opposite of the homogeneity-driven nation-state model that would emerge in nineteenth-century Europe.
It was an imperial framework — pluralistic, hierarchical, multi-ethnic, multi-religious — that operated by managing differences rather than by erasing them.
This is also, ultimately, why the empire's nineteenth-century encounter with European nationalism would be so destabilizing (Chapters 9 and 10).

The institutional framework that had managed religious and ethnic diversity for four centuries was specifically incompatible with the nation-state model that European powers were exporting to the Ottoman world.

The Greek Orthodox communities of the empire, organized as a religious millet, would gradually transform under the influence of Greek nationalism into a national community demanding political independence.
The same would happen, in different forms, for Bulgarians, Serbs, Romanians, Armenians, and eventually Arabs and Turks themselves.
The institutional brilliance of the millet system in 1500 was its capacity to manage diversity without political fragmentation.
The institutional brittleness of the same system in 1850 was its incapacity to absorb the new ideology of national self-determination.
The framework that had been the empire's strength for four hundred years became the empire's weakness in its last century.

chapters.title: The Sultanate of Women and the Cage
sentences: Süleyman the Magnificent died on September 6, 1566, at age seventy-two, in his command tent during the siege of Szigetvár in southern Hungary.

The grand vizier Sokollu Mehmed Pasha kept his death secret from the army for six weeks, finishing the siege successfully and delivering the body to Istanbul for burial in Süleyman's own mosque complex.
The empire passed smoothly to Süleyman's son Selim II (ruled 1566–1574).
It would never again be ruled by a sultan who personally led major battlefield campaigns.

Of the eighteen Ottoman sultans between Selim II and the empire's collapse, perhaps two — Murad III's son Ahmed I (briefly) and Mahmud II in the early nineteenth century — exercised the kind of personal political mastery that Süleyman had embodied.
Most of the rest were figureheads.
Some were children.
Some were mentally unstable.
Some were conscientious but unprepared.
None had come of age on military campaign with a senior commander as a tutor, the way Süleyman had come of age riding with his father Selim I and his grandfather Bayezid II.

What replaced sultanic personal rule, in the period from 1566 to roughly 1700, was a different model of governance: a court-based bureaucratic system in which the grand vizier ran the imperial administration on a daily basis, the harem ran the politics of dynastic succession, and the senior religious authority (the Sheikh ul-Islam) ran the religious-legal apparatus.
The sultan in this system was a ceremonial-religious figure whose personal capacity mattered less than the court coalition supporting him.
The system worked surprisingly well for surprisingly long.
It also produced two distinctive features that Western observers found scandalous and that Ottoman traditionalists found troubling: the Sultanate of Women and the Cage system.

Both deserve careful attention, because they reshaped how Ottoman power operated for over a century, and because the conventional Western narratives about them are usually more dramatic than accurate.

The Sultanate of Women (Kadınlar Saltanatı in Ottoman Turkish) was the period from approximately 1533 to 1683 during which the women of the imperial harem — particularly the valide sultans (vah-LEE-deh sool-TAHNS, "mother sultans" — the mothers of reigning sultans) and senior favorites — exercised major political power, often dominating decisions on appointments, foreign policy, taxation, and succession.
The phenomenon began with Hürrem Sultan, Süleyman the Magnificent's wife (Chapter 5).

Hürrem was the first formally married wife of an Ottoman sultan since the early fifteenth century, and her elevation to that status broke the previous pattern in which the mother of a potential heir held political power only in proportion to her son's prospects.
Hürrem held political power because Süleyman loved her, listened to her, and brought her into the inner circle of his policy-making.

Her surviving correspondence with Süleyman, with her son-in-law (the grand vizier Rüstem Pasha, who was married to Hürrem and Süleyman's daughter Mihrimah), and with various foreign monarchs (she corresponded with the Polish queen, with the Persian shahbanu) shows her engaged in detailed political calculation.
She was not running the empire from behind the scenes, but she was a senior member of the policy-making apparatus, and her political weight was unprecedented.
After Hürrem's death in 1558, her institutional precedent persisted.

The senior women of the harem — the valide sultan, the favored consorts of the reigning sultan, and the sisters and daughters of the imperial family — continued to operate as a coordinated political bloc.
Their power varied with the personal capacity of each sultan and the specific dynamics of each generation, but the basic pattern was set.

The two figures who most clearly embody the Sultanate of Women are Nurbanu Sultan and Kösem Sultan, the latter of whom is among the most consequential individual figures in seventeenth-century Ottoman history.

Nurbanu Sultan (NOOR-bah-noo, c. 1525–1583) was a Venetian-Greek noblewoman, born Cecilia Venier-Baffo on the Aegean island of Paros, captured by Ottoman corsairs as a teenager, brought to the imperial harem in Istanbul, and rising through the harem hierarchy to become the favored consort of Selim II.
When Selim II died in 1574, her son Murad III took the throne and Nurbanu became valide sultan.
She held that position until her death in 1583, during which she effectively shared decision-making authority with her son and the grand vizier.
Her surviving political correspondence — including a remarkable exchange with Catherine de' Medici of France — shows her negotiating Ottoman foreign policy directly.
She is also notable for her sustained patronage of mosque construction; the Atik Valide Mosque in Istanbul, built by Mimar Sinan in 1583, was her commission.
Kösem Sultan (KUH-sem, c. 1589–1651) is the most consequential of the harem-based political figures.

Born Anastasia to a Greek Orthodox priest's family on the island of Tinos in the Aegean, captured around age fifteen and brought to the harem, she became the favored consort of Ahmed I (ruled 1603–1617).
She had multiple sons by Ahmed I.

After Ahmed's death she became the valide sultan when her son Murad IV took the throne in 1623, retained influence under her son Ibrahim (ruled 1640–1648), and emerged as the senior valide sultan during the minority of her grandson Mehmed IV in 1648.
For most of the period from 1623 to her assassination in 1651, Kösem was the most politically powerful figure in the empire.

She managed grand vizier appointments, controlled foreign policy negotiations, mediated between rival factions of the Janissary corps and the religious establishment, and personally directed major imperial decisions during the chaotic mid-seventeenth century.
Kösem's reign within the harem is also notable for its internal contestation.
When her grandson Mehmed IV came to the throne in 1648 at age six, his mother Turhan Sultan (a Ukrainian-born harem favorite, of similar background to Kösem herself) became the formal valide sultan.
Kösem, as the senior valide of the previous generation, retained substantial independent authority.

The two women became rival power centers within the harem, and the conflict was eventually resolved by Kösem's assassination in September 1651 — strangled in her bedchamber, on the orders or at minimum the approval of Turhan Sultan, by harem eunuchs and senior court officials.
Kösem was approximately sixty-two years old.
She had been a major political figure for over forty years, the longest individual political career of any woman in Ottoman history.
The Sultanate of Women is sometimes treated, in older Ottoman and European historiography, as a corrupting feminization of imperial politics that was a major cause of Ottoman decline.
This narrative is not credible on closer inspection.
The harem-based political system worked well or poorly depending on who was running it, in exactly the same way the sultan-led political system had worked well or poorly depending on who was sultan.
The genuinely effective valide sultans (Nurbanu, Kösem in her better moments, Turhan) ran the empire competently through periods when the formal sultan was a child or otherwise incapacitated.
The genuinely incompetent ones (and there were several) damaged the empire in proportion to their power.
What the Sultanate of Women does represent is a genuine institutional shift: from rule by warrior-sultans on military campaign, to rule by court-based coalitions in which the harem was a major node.
The shift was not a corruption of an earlier ideal.

It was an adaptation to the realities of governing a fully formed multicontinental empire from a single capital, where the sultan's capacity to lead campaigns in person had become physically and politically impractical.

The court-based system was, in its way, a more institutional and less personal form of governance — one that relied on collective decision-making among the senior figures of the imperial household rather than on individual sultanic genius.
The other distinctive institutional development of this period was the Cage system (Turkish Kafes, kah-FESS, "cage").
The system needs to be understood against the backdrop of the fratricide law that Mehmed II had codified in 1477 (Chapter 4).

For the previous century and a half, the standard procedure on the accession of a new Ottoman sultan had been the immediate execution of his brothers and nephews — typically by strangulation with a silken bowstring — to prevent succession wars.
The procedure was institutionally efficient.
It also became increasingly difficult to justify as the empire's fertility patterns produced more royal sons.
Mehmed III, on his accession in 1595, executed nineteen of his brothers in a single ceremony.
The strangulation of nineteen children at a single moment — the youngest were toddlers — generated enormous popular outrage.
Even the religious establishment, which had endorsed the fratricide law for over a century, expressed concern.
The institutional response, formalized under Ahmed I in 1603, was the Cage system.

Instead of executing all of the new sultan's brothers and nephews, they would be confined to a specific apartment complex within Topkapı Palace — the Kafes — where they would live under permanent house arrest, with limited contact with the outside world.
They would receive personal servants (carefully selected to be loyal to the reigning sultan), food, books, music, and certain harem privileges.
They would be denied military training, administrative responsibility, contact with potential supporters, and any role in state affairs.

They would remain in the Kafes for their entire adult lives, unless circumstances required them to be brought out — most commonly when the reigning sultan died without an adult heir, in which case the most senior surviving brother or uncle from the Kafes would be brought out, dressed in imperial robes, and elevated to the throne.
The Cage system was less brutal than mass fratricide.
It was also institutionally disastrous, in ways that took several generations to become apparent.

A sultan who had spent his entire adult life — sometimes thirty or forty years — in a small palace apartment with eunuch servants and decorative concubines was not prepared to govern an empire when the throne suddenly fell to him.

Ibrahim I (ruled 1640–1648), brought out of the Kafes at age twenty-five after his elder brother Murad IV had unexpectedly died, was so traumatized by the transition that contemporary sources describe him as initially refusing to leave his room — he was convinced the messengers announcing his accession were assassins sent by his brother to lure him to his death.

When he did emerge, his subsequent eight-year reign was characterized by mental instability, erratic decision-making, and a court life dominated by a series of harem favorites whose political influence was even more direct than that of the formal valide sultans of previous generations.
He was eventually deposed by a coalition of the Janissaries, the religious establishment, and his own mother Kösem, and executed in August 1648.
Mustafa I (ruled 1617–1618 and 1622–1623) had been confined to the Kafes for fourteen years before his first accession at age twenty-six.
His mental state was such that he could barely speak coherently in his first audiences.

He was deposed within ninety-six days, sent back to the Kafes, brought out a second time four years later when Osman II was assassinated, found again to be incapable of governing, and deposed a second time after sixteen months.
He died in the Kafes a few years later.

The historical sources are sympathetic to him — he was clearly a victim of the institutional system rather than an architect of his own incapacity — but he was not a functional sultan, and his two brief reigns were periods of administrative paralysis.
The aggregate effect of the Cage system, across the seventeenth century, was a dynasty of sultans whose preparation for office was systematically inadequate.
Some of them were intelligent men whose intelligence had been wasted by decades of confinement.
Some had genuine mental illness exacerbated by the conditions of their captivity.
None had any practical experience of administration, military command, foreign relations, or even routine social interaction with people of varied status.
The court-based system of governance — the grand vizier, the valide sultan, the senior bureaucrats — adapted to fill the vacuum, and the empire continued to function.
But the institutional brittleness was real, and the consequences would compound over time.

The Safavid Empire fell into the same trap almost simultaneously: Shah Abbas the Great had confined his sons inside the Isfahan palace to prevent coups, and the resulting generation of princes had no administrative experience — producing Safi I, Soleyman I, and Sultan Husayn, who presided over the dynasty's slow collapse (Safavid Persia Ch 7).
The political narrative of the post-Süleyman period needs to be summarized briefly, because it sets the stage for the empire's first major territorial losses.
Selim II (1566–1574), called the Sot for his serious drinking problem, ruled through his grand vizier Sokollu Mehmed Pasha.

The major event of his reign was the Battle of Lepanto on October 7, 1571 — the largest naval battle in the Mediterranean in centuries, in which a coalition Christian fleet under the Spanish prince Don John of Austria destroyed the Ottoman Mediterranean fleet off the western coast of Greece.
The Christian victory was real — perhaps two hundred Ottoman galleys sunk or captured, twenty-five thousand Ottoman sailors and soldiers killed — but its strategic consequences were limited.
The Ottoman state rebuilt its fleet within a year.

Sokollu reportedly remarked to a Venetian ambassador that "in cutting off our beard, you have only made it grow back stronger; in cutting off your arm at Cyprus, we have done you permanent harm." Cyprus, taken by the Ottomans in 1570 just before Lepanto, remained Ottoman for the next three centuries.
Lepanto's psychological impact on Christian Europe was enormous; its operational impact on Ottoman power was modest.
Murad III (1574–1595) ruled through Sokollu until the grand vizier's assassination in 1579, then through a series of less competent successors.

The Long Turkish War with the Habsburgs (1593–1606) was the first major Ottoman conflict in which the empire's military advantage over the Habsburg armies had clearly disappeared — the war ended in stalemate with the Treaty of Zsitvatorok, the first treaty in which the Ottomans formally recognized the Habsburg Holy Roman Emperor as an equal sovereign rather than a tributary.
Mehmed III (1595–1603) executed his nineteen brothers on his accession (described above).
His death in 1603 led to the formal institution of the Cage system under his son Ahmed I.
Ahmed I (1603–1617) was sympathetic, religiously sincere, and relatively competent.

His commission of the Sultan Ahmed Mosque (the Blue Mosque) — built by Sinan's pupil Sedefkar Mehmed Aga between 1609 and 1616, with six minarets and an interior covered in over twenty thousand blue Iznik tiles — produced one of the architectural climaxes of the late classical Ottoman period.

The Blue Mosque was deliberately built directly opposite Hagia Sophia, on the site of the former Byzantine Great Palace, with the intent of creating a paired architectural complex unmatched in any contemporary capital.
Murad IV (1623–1640) was the last Ottoman sultan to lead a major field campaign in person.
He took Baghdad back from the Safavids in 1638 — the city had been lost to Shah Abbas I in 1623 — and stabilized the eastern frontier.
He was also a notably violent ruler, given to executing courtiers and citizens in person on minor pretexts, and his reign produced widespread popular fear of the imperial court.
He died at age twenty-seven, possibly from cirrhosis (he had inherited the family drinking problem) or possibly from the effects of long-term mercury treatment for syphilis.

After Murad IV came the disastrous Ibrahim I (described above), and after Ibrahim came the long minority of Mehmed IV (1648–1687), during which the empire was rescued from administrative collapse by the institutional intervention of a single grand-vizieral family.
The Köprülü (KUH-pruh-loo) family was a late-flowering example of Ottoman administrative recovery.

The patriarch, Mehmed Pasha Köprülü (c. 1575–1661, of Albanian-Christian devshirme origin), was appointed grand vizier in September 1656 at age eighty-one, on conditions that he himself dictated to the court: full authority over all imperial appointments, the right to confiscate property without specific imperial sanction, immunity from harem political interference, and complete control of military operations.

The Köprülü appointment was, in effect, an institutional recognition that the empire was being run by the central court coalition rather than by the sultan personally, and that decisive grand-vizieral authority was needed to halt the administrative drift.
Mehmed Köprülü ran the empire for five years until his death in 1661.
He executed several thousand officials he considered corrupt or disloyal.
He ended the Cretan War of attrition with a Venetian peace settlement that recovered most of Crete.
He restored the empire's finances.

He was succeeded by his son Fazıl Ahmed Pasha Köprülü (1635–1676), who continued the same authoritarian-reform pattern for fifteen years and is sometimes considered the most effective grand vizier of the late seventeenth century.

Together, the two Köprülüs gave the empire what amounted to a generation of competent central administration, during which the territorial losses of the previous decades were halted and some recoveries were made.
By the early 1680s, the empire under the Köprülü system was institutionally stable, militarily formidable, and apparently positioned for renewed expansion.

The grand vizier in 1683 was Kara Mustafa Pasha (KAH-rah moos-tah-FAH, son-in-law of Mehmed Köprülü, married to a Köprülü daughter, considered a Köprülü-faction figure even though he was not a blood relative of the dynasty).
He decided that the moment had come to do what no Ottoman commander since Süleyman the Magnificent had attempted: to take Vienna.
The siege he launched in July 1683 would be the turning point of the empire's three-and-a-half-century military trajectory.
The next chapter is its story.

Cross-civ check: the seventeenth century was the period of the Thirty Years' War in central Europe (1618–1648), the English Civil War (1642–1651), the Manchu conquest of Ming China and the founding of the Qing dynasty (1644 onward), the Mughal Empire's peak under Aurangzeb (after 1658), and the consolidation of the Tokugawa Shogunate in Japan.

The Ottoman seventeenth century was, by contrast, a period of court-based bureaucratic governance under sultans of varying capacity, with the Köprülü family providing the institutional rescue at the end.
By the standards of seventeenth-century governance worldwide, this was not exceptionally bad.
By the standards of Süleyman's reign a century earlier, it was a long disappointment.

chapters.title: The Long Defeat
sentences: The story of Ottoman territorial decline is conventionally dated from 1683 and the failure to take Vienna.
The decline was real, but the causal story is more complex than a single battle.

What changed in the late seventeenth century was not the empire's military capacity in isolation — Ottoman armies remained large, well-equipped, and capable of defeating most non-Habsburg European forces well into the eighteenth century.

What changed was the relative balance with the Christian European powers, which were experiencing a sustained military, fiscal, and technological transformation that the Ottoman state could not match.
The empire did not collapse.
It stopped advancing.
Eventually, after a series of major wars, it began to retreat.

This chapter covers the period from 1683 to 1730, which is the period during which the empire's strategic posture shifted from offensive to defensive, during which it lost its first major territories to Christian powers in over three centuries, and during which the first hesitant attempts at institutional reform began.
It is not a period of dramatic catastrophe.
It is a period of slow, sustained pressure that the Ottoman institutional system could not relieve.
The Second Siege of Vienna began on July 14, 1683.

Kara Mustafa Pasha had marched a massive Ottoman army out of Belgrade in May, gathering vassal contingents along the way (Crimean Tatars, Wallachian and Moldavian forces, Hungarian rebel units under Imre Thököly, who had risen against Habsburg rule and made common cause with the Ottomans).
The total force, by early July, was approximately one hundred and twenty thousand men with three hundred cannon — the largest Ottoman field army assembled since Süleyman's day.

The Habsburg Emperor Leopold I evacuated Vienna with his court on July 7, leaving the city in the hands of a garrison commander named Ernst Rüdiger von Starhemberg with about eleven thousand soldiers and the Viennese militia.
The siege lasted just over two months.
The Ottoman engineering corps dug parallel siege trenches in textbook fashion, brought their cannons within range of the city walls, and began systematic bombardment.
By mid-September the Ottoman mines had brought down significant sections of the walls, and the city was on the verge of falling.
The defenders were exhausted, food was running short, and the next coordinated Ottoman assault was likely to succeed.
What broke the siege was a relief army.
Pope Innocent XI had spent the previous year mobilizing a coalition of Christian powers — the Holy League — to defend Vienna and roll back Ottoman power in central Europe.
The coalition included Habsburg Austria, Poland-Lithuania, several German principalities, Venice, and (later) Russia.
The largest field component was the Polish army under King John III Sobieski (yon SOH-byes-kee), one of the most effective commanders in late seventeenth-century Europe.
Sobieski's force linked up with German contingents under Charles V of Lorraine at the Danube north of Vienna in early September and marched south to relieve the city.

On September 12, 1683, the combined Christian relief army — about eighty-five thousand men — attacked the Ottoman besieging force from the rear and right flank, on the slopes of the Kahlenberg (a hill northwest of Vienna).
The attack caught Kara Mustafa unprepared.

He had assumed that the Ottoman covering screen would delay any relief force long enough for him to take the city first; he had not accounted for the speed of the Christian coalition mobilization or for the tactical flexibility of Sobieski's hussar cavalry.
The Ottoman besieging army was routed within several hours.
Sobieski's famous letter to the Pope — "Venimus, vidimus, Deus vicit," "We came, we saw, God conquered" — became one of the iconic statements of the Christian-Ottoman conflict.
The casualties were substantial — perhaps fifteen thousand Ottomans killed, including most of the senior staff officers and a significant portion of the artillery park.
The withdrawal was disorganized.
The siege equipment, the camp treasury, and Kara Mustafa's personal tent (with its luxurious furnishings, including the green ceremonial banner given to him by the sultan) were all captured.
The relief armies followed up with a counter-offensive that pushed the Ottoman frontier deep south of the Danube within weeks.

Kara Mustafa retreated to Belgrade, where on December 25, 1683, he was strangled with a silken bowstring on the orders of Sultan Mehmed IV — the standard Ottoman fate for grand viziers who had presided over major military disasters.
His head was sent to Istanbul as proof of execution.
The Köprülü era of competent grand-vizieral governance had ended in catastrophe.
The Second Siege of Vienna, in retrospect, was the high-water mark of Ottoman expansion.
The empire would never again threaten central Europe with serious force.
The military momentum that had carried the Ottoman frontier across the Balkans and into Hungary for three hundred years had finally exhausted itself.
What followed was the Great Turkish War of 1683–1699, in which the Holy League pursued the Ottoman retreat across Hungary, the Peloponnese, the Crimea, and Wallachia.
The Habsburg armies, freed from the Vienna siege and reinforced with imperial troops, took Buda in 1686 — ending one hundred and forty-five years of Ottoman rule over the Hungarian capital.
Belgrade fell in 1688 (the Ottomans recovered it in 1690 in a brief counteroffensive, then lost it again later).
The Venetians recovered most of the Peloponnese in 1685–1687.
Russian forces under Peter the Great's predecessors began pushing south against the Crimean Tatars and the Black Sea Ottoman provinces.
The war was the longest single conflict in Ottoman history (sixteen years) and one of the most disruptive.
The empire lost not just territory but operational confidence.
The Janissary corps mutinied repeatedly during the war, in some cases refusing to leave Istanbul to fight.
Provincial governors increasingly operated as semi-independent warlords.
The treasury was emptied.
