The currency, the silver akce that had been the empire's standard for three centuries, was debased to roughly one-third of its former silver content.
The administrative coherence of the empire, which had been the legacy of the Köprülü reforms, fragmented under the pressure.
The war ended at the Treaty of Karlowitz (now Sremski Karlovci in Serbia) in January 1699.
The treaty was negotiated under English and Dutch mediation — itself a remarkable indicator of the empire's diminished diplomatic position.
Under its terms: The Ottomans ceded Hungary and Transylvania to the Habsburgs (apart from a small slice retained around Belgrade and the Banat).
They ceded Podolia (in modern western Ukraine) to Poland-Lithuania.
They ceded most of the Peloponnese, the Aegean islands of Aegina and Lefkada, and the Dalmatian coast hinterland to Venice.
They ceded Azov (on the Black Sea coast at the mouth of the Don) to Russia.
The territorial losses were the first substantial Ottoman losses to Christian powers since the empire's founding three centuries earlier.
The European frontier had moved south for the first time in Ottoman history.

What the Treaty of Karlowitz also represented, for the first time, was an Ottoman acknowledgment that they were now operating in the same diplomatic system as their European counterparts — bound by treaty obligations, subject to international mediation, fighting wars that ended in negotiated settlements rather than in the surrender of a defeated enemy.
The Westphalian state system that had emerged in central Europe after the Thirty Years' War was being extended to the Ottoman frontier.
The empire had to learn to operate within it.
The empire's first response to Karlowitz was a generation of attempted reform under a new grand vizier — and the political ambivalence of that response is the second main feature of this chapter.
Sultan Ahmed III (ruled 1703–1730) presided over the period that Ottoman historians call the Lale Devri — the Tulip Era — running roughly from 1718 to 1730.

The era took its name from the fashion among the Ottoman elite for elaborate tulip cultivation, with new tulip varieties bred competitively at imperial gardens, individual prized bulbs sold for prices that would have astonished any seventeenth-century Dutch tulip speculator, and entire palace complexes designed around tulip gardens for nighttime viewing illuminated by candles set on the backs of trained tortoises (a detail that the European visitors of the period reported with disbelief but which the Ottoman sources confirm).

The court of Ahmed III at the Sa'dabad Palace, built on the upper Golden Horn in 1722–1723 in a deliberately European-influenced style, was the most cosmopolitan and most leisure-oriented Ottoman court since Süleyman.

The grand vizier driving the Tulip Era's cultural programs was Damat Ibrahim Pasha (DAH-mahd ee-brah-HEEM, "Ibrahim the Son-in-Law," married to a daughter of Ahmed III), who had concluded the Treaty of Passarowitz with Austria and Venice in 1718 (which had cost the empire additional Balkan and Aegean territories but had stabilized the frontier) and who was using the post-treaty peace to attempt a series of cautious modernizing reforms.

The reforms were ambivalent — partly serious institutional engagement with European models, partly aristocratic fashion-following, partly genuine cultural openness to Western European arts and sciences.
The most consequential of the Tulip Era reforms was the introduction of printing to the Ottoman Empire.
The Ottoman delay in adopting printing technology is one of the more discussed features of the empire's institutional history, and it is worth a brief explanation.
Printing presses had been operating in Ottoman territory since the late fifteenth century, but only for the empire's non-Muslim communities.
Sephardic Jewish printers had been printing Hebrew books in Salonica and Istanbul since the 1490s.
Greek Orthodox printers had been printing Greek liturgical books from the early sixteenth century.
Armenian printers had operated since 1567.

What was prohibited was the printing of texts in Arabic script — books in Arabic, Persian, and Ottoman Turkish, the three languages of Islamic religious scholarship and Ottoman administrative practice.

The prohibition was not absolute legal ban but a combination of factors: the religious establishment's preference for traditional manuscript culture (which had developed sophisticated calligraphic standards over centuries and which was associated with the manual labor of religious scribes), a guild-economic interest of the manuscript copyists' guild in Istanbul (estimated at perhaps eighty thousand professional copyists in the seventeenth century), and a general administrative caution about the reproduction-control implications of printed texts in a multi-religious empire.

The first Ottoman press in Arabic-script Turkish was established by Ibrahim Müteferrika (mu-teh-fer-ree-KAH, c. 1674–1745), a Hungarian-born Ottoman convert to Islam who had taken Ottoman service and worked as a translator and diplomatic functionary.
With imperial endorsement, Müteferrika opened his press in Istanbul in 1727 and began producing Ottoman Turkish books — primarily history, geography, and political science.

His first major publication was a Turkish translation of a classical Arabic dictionary; his most famous was the Cihannüma (the Universal Geography), a comprehensive geographical reference incorporating recent European cartographic knowledge.
Müteferrika's press operated successfully for fifteen years, producing seventeen titles in twenty-three volumes.
After his death in 1745 the press was inactive for several decades before being restarted under different management.

Ottoman printing remained a niche activity until the early nineteenth century, when commercial pressures from European imports and state-sponsored newspapers finally drove the institutional adoption of large-scale printing.
The Tulip Era also produced the empire's first systematic engagement with European scientific and military literature.

Ottoman diplomats sent to Paris, Vienna, and Madrid produced detailed reports on European institutions, technology, and military organization — the Yirmisekiz Çelebi Mehmed Efendi mission to Paris in 1720–1721, which produced the Sefaretname (a diplomatic memoir of the Paris embassy that became one of the most-read Ottoman travel books of the eighteenth century), is the most famous example.
Translations of European technical works on mathematics, fortification, and gunnery began to appear in Ottoman scholarly libraries.
But the reforms were also resented.

The Tulip Era's conspicuous luxury — the elaborate gardens, the European-style architecture, the imported French goods, the social practices borrowed from foreign embassies — alienated the Janissary corps, the religious establishment, and the urban poor.
The economic crisis of the late 1720s (a combination of currency debasement, inflation, and a major plague outbreak in 1726) sharpened the political tension.

The Janissaries, who had been losing their military relevance for over a century but retained their nuisance value as an urban political force, were particularly hostile to a reform program that they correctly perceived as eventually intended to replace them.
In September 1730, a Janissary irregular named Patrona Halil — an Albanian-born former bath attendant turned Janissary auxiliary — organized a popular uprising in Istanbul.

The trigger was a combination of war taxes (Ahmed III had ordered a campaign against Persia, requiring new levies), economic distress, and accumulated resentment of the Tulip Era's conspicuous court culture.
The uprising spread rapidly through the city.

Within forty-eight hours, the Sa'dabad Palace had been sacked, the Tulip gardens burned, and thirty senior officials of the Damat Ibrahim Pasha government — including Ibrahim himself — executed by the mob.
Sultan Ahmed III was deposed and confined to the Kafes (where he died eight years later).
His nephew Mahmud I was placed on the throne.
The Patrona Halil revolt ended the Tulip Era abruptly and demonstrated the political limits of top-down modernization in the Ottoman context.
The revolt was suppressed within several months — Patrona Halil himself was arrested and executed in November 1730 — but the damage had been done.
The reforms were rolled back.
The reformers were dead.
The empire's first sustained engagement with European institutional models had failed.
For the next half-century, no Ottoman administration would attempt comparably ambitious reforms.
The empire entered the eighteenth century with intact institutions but diminished capacity.
It would lose more wars to Russia and Austria over the next several decades.
It would cede further territories.
It would sink, gradually, into the strategic position that nineteenth-century European observers would call the Sick Man of Europe.

The institutional rescue, when it eventually came, would be more radical than anything Damat Ibrahim Pasha had attempted, and it would arrive only after the Ottoman state had run out of other options.

chapters.title: Reform and Backlash
sentences: The hundred years between the Patrona Halil revolt of 1730 and the formal launch of the Tanzimat reforms in 1839 are, in Ottoman historiography, the period of the empire's deepest institutional crisis.
The territorial losses continued.
The economic gap with western Europe widened.
The administrative coherence of the central state weakened, replaced increasingly by the autonomous power of provincial governors (the ayan) and the religious establishment.
Three sultans in this period — Selim III, Mahmud II, and Abdülmecid I — attempted serious institutional reform.
The first was killed for it.
The second succeeded by destroying his own elite military corps.
The third launched the most sustained reform program in Ottoman history.
This chapter is their story.

It is also the story of the institutional violence required to break the empire out of its eighteenth-century paralysis — and of the limits of that violence, since the reforms ultimately failed to halt the empire's geopolitical decline.
The eighteenth century brought a series of military defeats that reshaped Ottoman strategic geography.
The Russo-Turkish War of 1768–1774 ended with the Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca (kuh-CHOOK ky-nar-JAH), one of the most consequential treaties in Ottoman history.

Russia, under Empress Catherine the Great, had defeated the Ottomans repeatedly in Romania, the Crimea, and the Aegean (where the Russian fleet had sailed all the way from the Baltic to defeat the Ottoman navy at the Battle of Çeşme in 1770).

The treaty's terms included Ottoman cession of significant Black Sea territories, Russian recognition as protector of Ottoman Orthodox Christians (a provision that would be invoked repeatedly over the next century to justify Russian intervention in Ottoman internal affairs), and the practical Russian annexation of the Crimea (formalized in 1783).
The loss of the Crimea was strategically devastating.

The Khanate of Crimea, an Ottoman vassal since the late fifteenth century, had been the Tatar northern bulwark of the empire — a horse-warrior society that had repeatedly raided Russian and Polish-Lithuanian territory and whose armies had supplemented Ottoman field forces in Balkan campaigns.
With Crimea gone, the Ottoman Black Sea was an open sea, and the empire's northern frontier was permanently vulnerable.

The Russo-Turkish War of 1787–1792, the Greek revolutionary disturbances in the Aegean of the late 1820s, the loss of Algiers to France in 1830, and successive smaller wars and territorial adjustments through the early nineteenth century all extended the same pattern.
The empire was losing wars to states it had once dominated.

The institutional explanation was clear to senior Ottoman observers: the empire's military and administrative systems, designed in the sixteenth century, could not match the more centralized, technologically advanced, and bureaucratically rationalized states that European modernization had produced.
The first sultan to attempt a serious institutional response was Selim III (ruled 1789–1807).

Selim III had been deeply read in European political and military literature during his time in the Kafes (he was confined there from age four to age twenty-eight, during the long reign of his uncle Abdülhamid I).
He came to the throne convinced that the empire required fundamental institutional reform along European lines.
His reform program, called the Nizam-ı Cedid (nih-ZAHM-uh jeh-DEED, "the New Order"), was the most ambitious modernization project the empire had attempted.

The centerpiece was a new infantry corps — also called the Nizam-ı Cedid — recruited from free Anatolian Muslim peasants, trained on European models with European drillmasters (mostly French officers brought in for the purpose), equipped with modern uniforms and modern firearms, and paid from a separate dedicated treasury.

The corps was deliberately structured to be parallel to and eventually a replacement for the Janissaries, whose military uselessness was now obvious to everyone but who still constituted the empire's largest single military expenditure.

Selim III also reformed the timar-based provincial cavalry system, attempted to standardize tax collection across the empire, opened technical schools for naval engineering and military medicine, established new printing operations, and sent diplomatic missions to Paris, London, Vienna, and Berlin with instructions to study and report on European administrative practice.

The first permanent Ottoman embassies in European capitals dated from his reign — a major institutional innovation, since Ottoman diplomatic practice had previously relied on temporary missions rather than resident representation.
The Janissaries hated all of it.
The Nizam-ı Cedid was a direct existential threat to their institutional position.
The reform-funding diversions from the central treasury reduced their pay.
The new bureaucratic procedures eroded their political influence.
The European-trained officer corps was a competing source of military prestige.
By the early 1800s, the Janissary corps in Istanbul and across the empire was openly hostile to the entire reform program.

In 1807, a Janissary uprising in Istanbul, supported by the religious establishment and several senior Ottoman officials who had personal grievances against Selim's reform circle, deposed Selim III and placed his cousin Mustafa IV on the throne.
Selim was confined to the Kafes.
The Nizam-ı Cedid was dissolved.
The reform program was cancelled.
Several months later, in a counter-coup organized by reform-aligned officials, Mustafa IV ordered Selim's execution to prevent his restoration.
Selim III was murdered in the Kafes in July 1808.
The counter-coup that killed Selim also deposed Mustafa IV, executed him a few months later, and placed his half-brother Mahmud II on the throne.
Mahmud was twenty-three years old.
He had spent his childhood in the Kafes.
He had been an admirer of his cousin Selim's reform program.
And he had just witnessed, in concentrated form, the institutional violence that any serious reform attempt would require.
Mahmud II (ruled 1808–1839) is one of the most consequential Ottoman rulers of the late empire, and his reign is best understood as a long, patient preparation for a single decisive act.
The act was the destruction of the Janissary corps.
The institutional analysis Mahmud II conducted in the early years of his reign was clear-eyed.
The Janissaries were the central obstacle to any serious modernization.

Their political power was largely a nuisance value rather than military value — they were no longer effective field troops by the early nineteenth century — but their capacity to organize urban riots, to depose sultans, and to mobilize the religious establishment against reform programs had been demonstrated repeatedly.
Selim III had tried to bypass the Janissaries by building parallel reformed units.
The strategy had failed.
Mahmud II concluded that the only solution was complete elimination.
The preparation took eighteen years.
Mahmud II spent the period from 1808 to 1826 carefully building his political base.
He consolidated personal control over the central administration.
He secured the support of the senior religious establishment by pursuing an explicitly Sunni-orthodox religious policy and by patronizing major religious scholars.

He cultivated alliances with the ayan — the provincial notables whose autonomous power had grown during the eighteenth century — by formally recognizing their local authority in exchange for military and fiscal cooperation.
He rebuilt the central artillery corps under reformed leadership.

Critically, he worked carefully and quietly with reform-minded Janissary officers to identify and replace the corps's most committed traditionalists, while leaving the bulk of the corps unaware of what was being prepared.

In June 1826 Mahmud announced a new reform: a parallel infantry unit called the Eşkinciyan (esh-kin-jee-YAHN), structured similarly to Selim III's Nizam-ı Cedid but with stronger institutional backing.
The Janissaries — predictably — interpreted the announcement as a threat and began organizing a revolt.
On June 14 and 15, the Janissary corps in Istanbul rose in armed rebellion, exactly as Mahmud had calculated they would.
They occupied their barracks, issued demands for the cancellation of the new corps, and prepared to march on the imperial palace in the standard pattern of Janissary revolts going back centuries.
What they did not know was that Mahmud had spent the previous several years preparing for this exact moment.
The Sheikh ul-Islam issued a religious fatwa declaring the Janissary revolt to be religiously illegitimate.

Mahmud's reformed artillery corps surrounded the Janissary barracks and bombarded them with cannon fire — including the use of grapeshot at point-blank range when individual Janissaries tried to escape.
The barracks were systematically destroyed.
The Janissaries inside were killed or burned alive.
Across Istanbul over the following days, identifiable Janissaries were rounded up and executed; their bodies were left in public places.
Janissary officers in provincial garrisons were arrested and executed in coordinated operations across the empire over the following weeks.
The death toll has never been precisely established.

Modern estimates range from six thousand to twenty thousand Janissaries killed in Istanbul alone during the four-day Auspicious Incident (Vaka-yı Hayriye, vah-kah-yuh hi-REE-yeh — the Ottoman official designation for the event, deliberately framed as a positive moment of imperial restoration).
Several thousand more were killed in provincial operations.
The entire institutional structure of the corps was systematically dismantled.
The Janissary regimental insignia and traditions were officially banned.
The Bektashi Sufi order, which had been the Janissaries' spiritual home, was suppressed and its lodges closed.

The four-hundred-and-sixty-three-year-old institution that had taken Constantinople, defeated the Mamluks, and stood as the personal guard of every sultan since Murad I was eliminated within a single summer.
The Auspicious Incident was the most violent single act of state-on-state institutional destruction in Ottoman history.
It was also the prerequisite for everything that followed.
With the Janissaries gone, the path to comprehensive modernization was open.
Mahmud II spent the remaining thirteen years of his reign building the institutional foundation for the Tanzimat reforms his son would launch.
The remaining Mahmud II reforms are easier to summarize.
He created a new conscription-based standing army modeled on European lines.
He reformed the central administration into something resembling modern ministries.
He standardized the imperial currency.
He instituted the first imperial census in 1831.
He commissioned new official histories.
He patronized translation projects to bring European technical and scientific literature into Ottoman Turkish.
He built new schools, including the precursors of what would become the Imperial Medical School and the Imperial Engineering School.
He sent dozens of young Ottomans to Paris, Vienna, and Berlin for European-style higher education, building the cohort of European-trained officials who would run the Tanzimat administration.
He also faced two major crises that would have ended a less skilled ruler.
The first was Greek independence (1821–1832).

The Greek War of Independence began as an uprising of the Phanariot Greek elite of Constantinople and rural Greek populations in the Peloponnese, mobilized by philhellene sentiment in western Europe and supported by Russia.
The war was brutal on both sides.
The Ottomans called in Egyptian forces under Ibrahim Pasha (the son of Egypt's quasi-autonomous governor Mehmed Ali Pasha) for the suppression.
By 1827 the Egyptian-Ottoman forces had largely defeated the Greek rebels.

Then a combined British-French-Russian fleet intervened, destroying the Ottoman-Egyptian fleet at the Battle of Navarino in October 1827 in one of the more decisive naval engagements of the nineteenth century.

The result was the establishment of an independent Greek state in 1832 — the first major successful nationalist secession from Ottoman rule, and the template that other Balkan independence movements would follow over the next century.
The second was the Egyptian Crisis of 1831–1833 and 1839–1841.

Mehmed Ali Pasha (also written as Muhammad Ali, MEH-med ah-LEE, 1769–1849, an Albanian-born Ottoman commander who had been appointed governor of Egypt in 1805 and had built it into the most modernized province in the empire), encouraged by the Greek War complications, demanded compensation for his contributions to the Greek campaign and was refused.
He launched an invasion of Ottoman Syria in 1831 and defeated successive Ottoman field armies.
By 1832 his son Ibrahim Pasha had taken Damascus and Aleppo and was advancing on Anatolia.
The Ottoman state was, briefly, on the verge of military collapse.

The empire was rescued only by Russian intervention — Tsar Nicholas I sent a fleet and an army to defend Istanbul, in exchange for which the Ottomans signed the Treaty of Hünkar İskelesi (hoon-KAR is-keh-leh-SEE) in 1833, granting Russia exclusive naval rights in the Bosporus straits and effectively making the Ottoman Empire a Russian protectorate.

The British, alarmed by Russian dominance over the Ottoman state, intervened diplomatically in subsequent years to roll back the Hünkar İskelesi terms and to push Mehmed Ali back into Egypt — which was accomplished after a second crisis in 1839–1841 with the Convention of London.

The settlement granted Mehmed Ali hereditary governorship of Egypt (effectively making it a separate state under nominal Ottoman suzerainty, an arrangement that would last until British occupation in 1882) but stripped his other territorial gains.
The Ottoman state survived, but only because the great powers of Europe had decided that its survival was strategically preferable to its collapse.
The empire had become an object of European great-power management rather than an independent political actor in its own right.
Mahmud II died in July 1839, in the middle of the second Egyptian crisis.
He was fifty-three years old.
His reform program had eliminated the Janissaries, modernized the army, restructured the administration, and laid the foundations for further institutional development.

He had also failed to halt the empire's geopolitical decline, and his legacy was a state that was institutionally stronger but strategically more dependent on European patronage than at any point in its previous history.
He was succeeded by his son Abdülmecid I (ruled 1839–1861), who at sixteen years old took the throne with the empire still in the middle of the Egyptian crisis.

The young sultan was guided by a circle of senior reformers who had grown up in Mahmud II's bureaucratic system — most importantly Mustafa Reşid Pasha (mu-STAH-fah reh-SHEED, 1800–1858), an experienced Ottoman diplomat who had served as ambassador to Paris and London and who was the architect of the Tanzimat program.

On November 3, 1839, three months after Abdülmecid's accession, Mustafa Reşid Pasha read the Gülhane Hatt-ı Şerifi (GUL-hah-neh hat-tuh sheh-REE-fee, the Imperial Edict of the Rose Garden) in front of the assembled imperial court, foreign ambassadors, and senior religious authorities at the Gülhane gardens of Topkapı Palace.

The edict announced a comprehensive program of legal and administrative reform: equal protection of life, property, and honor for all Ottoman subjects regardless of religion; an end to arbitrary execution and confiscation by imperial decree; tax reform to replace tax-farming with regular state collection; military conscription on a regularized basis; and the formal end of the millet-based legal disabilities for non-Muslim subjects in matters of state law (though sharia continued to apply in religious matters).
The Gülhane edict launched the Tanzimat (TAHN-zee-maht, "Reorganizations") period — the most sustained institutional reform program in Ottoman history, running from 1839 to roughly 1876.
The story of what the Tanzimat reforms accomplished, what they failed to accomplish, and how they interacted with the rising tide of Balkan nationalism is the subject of the next chapter.

Cross-civ check: the early nineteenth century was the period of the Napoleonic Wars and their settlements (1799–1815), the independence movements in Spanish America (1810–1825), the Greek War of Independence itself, the Industrial Revolution in Britain entering its second phase, the early consolidation of the Qajar Dynasty in Iran, and the late Mughal Empire falling under increasing British control.

Mahmud II's reforms in the Ottoman Empire were contemporary with similar institutional modernization programs in Egypt under Mehmed Ali Pasha, in Persia under the early Qajars, in Japan under the late Tokugawa shogunate, and in China under the late Qing.
Each of these states was attempting to adapt to the increasing institutional and military pressure from western European powers.
Each was succeeding, in its own way, partially.
The Ottoman case was neither uniquely successful nor uniquely failed — it was one variant of a global early-modern state-modernization pattern, with its own specific successes and limitations.

chapters.title: The Sick Man of Europe
sentences: The phrase "Sick Man of Europe" was attributed (in a private 1853 conversation with the British ambassador) to Tsar Nicholas I of Russia, describing the Ottoman Empire as a dying patient whose territories should be partitioned among the European great powers before its final collapse.

The phrase was not original to the Tsar — variants had been circulating in European diplomatic correspondence for decades — but it captured what had become, by the mid-nineteenth century, the standard European framing of the Ottoman state.
The empire was, in this framing, a polity in terminal decline, holding together only because the European great powers could not agree on how to divide it.
The framing was both true and false.

It was false in the sense that the Ottoman state of 1850 was institutionally stronger than the Ottoman state of 1750 — the Tanzimat reforms had produced a more centralized, more bureaucratic, more militarily capable empire than the eighteenth-century version.

It was true in the sense that the empire's relative position vis-à-vis the European great powers had continued to deteriorate, and that the strategic survival of the Ottoman state was now genuinely dependent on European patronage rather than on Ottoman power.

This chapter covers the period from 1839 to 1908 — the seventy years of the Tanzimat reform era, the autocratic counter-reform under Sultan Abdülhamid II, and the Young Turk Revolution that ended the autocracy.

It is a period of substantial institutional change, recurring military disasters, accelerating territorial loss in the Balkans, and the gradual emergence of a new political ideology — Turkish nationalism — that would eventually replace Ottomanism as the empire's organizing principle.
The Tanzimat reforms of 1839–1876 produced more institutional change than any previous reform period in Ottoman history.
The most consequential changes came in three domains.

The legal transformation imported French criminal and commercial codes, established secular state courts (the nizamiye courts) running in parallel with the sharia courts, and abolished both the death penalty for apostasy and (after 1857) the slave trade — fundamentally rebalancing the relationship between religious and secular law that Süleyman's Kanunname had originally negotiated three centuries earlier.

The administrative transformation centralized provincial governance on French departmental lines, ended the autonomous ayan system that had run the empire's interior since the eighteenth century, and built a state council on European parliamentary models.

The civic transformation, formalized in the Hatt-ı Hümayun edict of 1856 issued at the end of the Crimean War under explicit British and French pressure, granted non-Muslim subjects full legal equality in state law and opened state administrative careers to them.

Alongside these came the educational and military pillars — state primary and secondary schools (the rüşdiye and idadiye networks), the French-language Galatasaray Imperial Lyceum (founded 1868) whose graduates would dominate the late Ottoman administration, the Darülfünun (the precursor of Istanbul University) in 1863, conscription-based military forces trained on European lines, and a navy and artillery park modernized through partnerships with European arms manufacturers.
The reforms were genuine, comprehensive, and sustained.

By the 1870s the Ottoman Empire had a unified administrative structure, a partially codified secular legal system, a growing public school network, a regular army, and a state bureaucracy staffed by European-educated officials operating in something approximating modern administrative routines.
The empire was not, by 1875, the same kind of state it had been in 1825.

What the reforms did not accomplish — and this is the more important point for the chapter's argument — was halting the territorial losses in the Balkans, addressing the rising European-supported nationalist movements among the empire's Christian populations, or modernizing the Ottoman economy fast enough to keep pace with European industrial growth.
The institutional reforms produced a more capable state.
The geopolitical situation continued to deteriorate.
The two trends ran in parallel, and the second one, by 1878, would matter more than the first.
The major Ottoman foreign-policy event of the mid-nineteenth century was the Crimean War (1853–1856).

The war began as a Russian-Ottoman dispute over the protection of Christian holy sites in Palestine — Russia claimed the right to protect Orthodox Christians under the terms of the 1774 Küçük Kaynarca treaty; France claimed similar rights for Catholics under separate older agreements; the Ottomans tried to balance the two and ended up alienating the Russians sufficiently to provide Tsar Nicholas I with a pretext for war.
The Russians invaded the Ottoman Romanian principalities (Wallachia and Moldavia) in mid-1853.
The Ottomans declared war in October 1853.
What made the war historically distinctive was the European intervention.
Britain and France, alarmed by Russian expansion against the Ottoman state, declared war on Russia in March 1854 and committed major military forces to the campaign.
The Sardinian Kingdom joined the alliance in 1855.

The combined Anglo-French-Ottoman-Sardinian forces fought the Russians primarily in Crimea (the war's geographic name), where the Siege of Sevastopol (October 1854 to September 1855) became one of the most costly and famous military operations of the nineteenth century — the engagement during which Florence Nightingale transformed military nursing, William Howard Russell of the Times invented modern war correspondence, and the Charge of the Light Brigade (October 1854) became one of the most romanticized military disasters in English-language poetry.
The war ended with the Treaty of Paris in March 1856.
Russia ceded territory and was prohibited from maintaining a Black Sea fleet.
The Ottoman Empire's territorial integrity was guaranteed by the great powers.

Most consequentially for Ottoman internal affairs, the empire was formally admitted to the Concert of Europe — the diplomatic system of the major European powers — and the Hatt-ı Hümayun reform edict of 1856 was issued in part as a response to British and French pressure for further reforms in exchange for European protection.

The Crimean War was an Ottoman victory in the conventional sense — the Ottomans had survived a Russian attempt to dismember them, retained their territories, and entered the European diplomatic system as a recognized member.
It was also a demonstration of the empire's complete strategic dependence on European patronage.
Without British and French intervention, the war would have been lost.
The empire's survival was now structurally dependent on the great powers' willingness to defend it.

The Tanzimat era reached its climax under Sultan Abdülaziz (ruled 1861–1876) and his successor Murad V (ruled briefly in 1876 before being deposed for mental incapacity), during a period of accelerating institutional change and accelerating Balkan crisis.
Abdülaziz's reign is bookended by two major projects that capture the period's contradictions.

The Dolmabahçe Palace (DOL-mah-bah-cheh, "Filled-In Garden" — the palace was built on landfill at the upper Bosporus), commissioned by Abdülmecid I in 1843 and completed in 1856, became the new imperial residence.
It replaced Topkapı as the working palace of the sultans.

Architecturally it was European Baroque-Rococo on a vast scale — fourteen tons of gold leaf in the ceilings, the largest crystal chandelier in the world (a gift from Queen Victoria, weighing four and a half tons), French furnishings, German silver, English textiles.
It was deliberately European in style, and it represented the Tanzimat-era Ottoman elite's aspiration to be recognized as part of European civilization.
The palace was also catastrophically expensive, contributing significantly to the imperial debt that would eventually become unmanageable.
The other project was the Bulgarian Massacres of 1876.
In the spring of 1876, a poorly organized Bulgarian nationalist uprising broke out in the central Bulgarian highlands, encouraged by Russian agents and exiled Bulgarian intellectuals.

The Ottoman regular army was occupied with similar insurgencies elsewhere in the Balkans, so the suppression was conducted primarily by bashi-bazouk irregulars and Circassian refugees who had been settled in the area after fleeing Russian conquest of the Caucasus in the 1860s.

The suppression was extraordinarily brutal — entire villages massacred, churches burned with congregations inside, the towns of Batak and Perushtitsa subjected to atrocities that contemporary investigators (including the American journalist Januarius MacGahan, whose dispatches for the London Daily News produced detailed eyewitness accounts) documented in horrifying specificity.
Estimates of the dead range from twelve thousand to thirty thousand, mostly Bulgarian Orthodox civilians.
The events became an international scandal.

William Gladstone, the British Liberal leader, published a pamphlet called Bulgarian Horrors and the Question of the East that became one of the most-read political pamphlets in nineteenth-century Britain and that fundamentally shifted British public opinion against Ottoman support.
The combination of fiscal collapse (the empire formally defaulted on its foreign debt in October 1875), the Bulgarian crisis, and rising Russian pressure produced a coup in May 1876.
Abdülaziz was deposed by a coalition of reformist officials and senior military commanders.
He was found dead a week later — officially a suicide; almost certainly murdered.
His nephew Murad V was placed on the throne, suffered a mental breakdown within weeks, and was deposed in turn after a brief reign.
The throne passed to Murad's younger brother Abdülhamid II.
Abdülhamid II (ruled 1876–1909) is the most controversial Ottoman ruler of the modern period.

The standard nineteenth- and twentieth-century European framing painted him as the Red Sultan — a paranoid autocrat who reversed the Tanzimat reforms, suppressed the Ottoman press, ran a vast secret police network, and presided over the Hamidian Massacres of Armenian Christians in eastern Anatolia in 1894–1896.
The standard framing was, in important respects, accurate.

The more recent revisionist scholarship has argued that Abdülhamid II was also one of the most institutionally productive Ottoman rulers of the nineteenth century — that his reign saw substantial expansion of railway, telegraph, education, and industrial infrastructure, and that his autocratic methods were a rational response to genuine threats to the empire's coherence.
Both readings can be true simultaneously.
Abdülhamid II was, in his political instincts, a rigorous autocrat who distrusted the constitutional and parliamentary institutions the Tanzimat reformers had attempted to establish.
He was also genuinely committed to the institutional development of the empire and presided over substantial modernization that the constitutionalist reformers had not been able to achieve.
His first major action was paradoxical.

In December 1876, he promulgated the first Ottoman Constitution — a document drafted by the senior Tanzimat reformer Midhat Pasha, providing for a parliament with both elected and appointed chambers, a bill of rights, and significant limitations on the sultan's authority.
The Constitution was the most ambitious Ottoman institutional reform of the nineteenth century.
The first parliament met in March 1877.
Abdülhamid II then suspended the Constitution and dissolved the parliament in February 1878, citing the Russo-Turkish War of 1877–1878 as a national emergency requiring autocratic governance.
The Russo-Turkish War of 1877–1878 was the second major Russian invasion of the empire's European territories in a generation.
The Russians took most of Bulgaria, the Ottoman Caucasus, and substantial portions of eastern Anatolia.

The Treaty of San Stefano (March 1878) imposed brutal terms on the Ottoman state: full Bulgarian independence (with Bulgaria including most of Macedonia and substantial Aegean coastline), Romanian independence, Serbian and Montenegrin independence with substantial territorial expansion, autonomy for Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Russian annexation of Ottoman Caucasian territories.

The treaty's terms were so favorable to Russia that the other European great powers refused to accept them, and at the Congress of Berlin (June 1878) the European powers under Otto von Bismarck's mediation revised the settlement: Bulgaria was reduced in size (Macedonia returned to Ottoman control); Bosnia-Herzegovina was assigned to Austrian administration (under nominal Ottoman sovereignty); Cyprus was assigned to British administration as compensation for British support of Ottoman positions.
The Ottomans lost approximately one-third of their European territory and roughly twenty percent of their total population in the war and the resulting settlement.
The Berlin settlement was a watershed.
The Ottoman state had now lost effective sovereignty over Bulgaria, Romania, Serbia, Bosnia, and Cyprus within a single decade.
The Balkan provinces that had been the empire's European heartland for five centuries were largely gone.
What remained — Albania, Macedonia, Thrace, the Aegean coast — would be lost in the Balkan Wars of 1912–1913.
The Ottoman European Empire that had been built by Murad I, Bayezid I, and Mehmed II between the 1360s and the 1450s was, by 1878, a few decades from complete dissolution.
Abdülhamid II's autocratic methods after 1878 were comprehensive.

He ran the imperial administration personally from his palace at Yıldız (YUL-duz, "Star"), a complex of pavilions and gardens on the European hillside above the Bosporus that he had built specifically as his political headquarters and that he very rarely left.
He maintained an extensive secret police and intelligence network.
He suppressed the Ottoman press, particularly any commentary on constitutional or political topics, with strict censorship.

He cultivated relationships with the senior religious authorities of the empire, presenting himself as the Caliph of Sunni Muslims worldwide and developing a pan-Islamic ideology as the new ideological basis for Ottoman political coherence.
He maintained close personal control over senior appointments, security operations, and major foreign-policy decisions.
He also presided over substantial institutional development.

The Hijaz Railway, built from Damascus south to Medina (eventually extended to Mecca but completed only as far as Medina before the empire's collapse), was completed in 1908 and became the most ambitious Ottoman engineering project of the period — a religiously legitimated project funded by donations from Muslims around the world, intended to facilitate the hajj and to extend Ottoman state authority into the Hijaz.
The telegraph network was built out across the empire.
The Imperial Naval School, Military Medical School, and Mülkiye (the imperial civil-service academy) produced a generation of European-educated technocrats.
The empire's first modern universities, technical schools, and professional academies dated from his reign.
The state developed a relatively functional postal service, modernized cartography, basic public health institutions, and the early beginnings of an industrial sector.
The dark side of his reign was real and is best documented by the Hamidian Massacres of 1894–1896.
The eastern Anatolian provinces had a substantial Armenian Christian population — perhaps two million people in the 1890s — concentrated in the highlands of the empire's eastern frontier zone.
Armenian nationalist movements, influenced by similar Balkan independence movements and supported by Armenian communities in the Russian Caucasus, had emerged in the 1880s.

Ottoman authorities, particularly Abdülhamid II personally, viewed Armenian nationalism as an existential threat — Armenian autonomy or independence in eastern Anatolia would, they correctly calculated, encourage further European intervention and accelerate the empire's territorial dissolution.
The response was systematic violence.

From 1894 to 1896, organized massacres of Armenian populations were conducted across eastern Anatolia by Hamidiye irregular cavalry (Kurdish tribal levies organized by the imperial state for frontier security) and by Ottoman regular troops.
Cities and villages were attacked, churches burned, populations killed in coordinated operations that bore the institutional fingerprint of state organization.
The death toll is contested but credible estimates range from one hundred thousand to three hundred thousand killed across the three-year campaign.
The European press reported the events extensively.
Western European public opinion was outraged.
Western European governments were unable or unwilling to intervene effectively.
The Hamidian Massacres established the pattern that would be extended catastrophically during World War I.
The Ottoman state had identified its Armenian Christian population as a politically unreliable population whose loyalty to the empire could not be assumed in a crisis.
The state's response combined administrative pressure, demographic engineering, and organized mass violence.
The full institutionalization of this approach — and its escalation into a systematic genocide — would happen under Abdülhamid II's eventual successors.
The pattern began under his rule.
The end of Abdülhamid II's autocracy came from within his own institutional system.

The Young Turks (a loose translation of Jön Türkler, in turn a Turkish rendering of the French Jeune-Turcs) were a movement of European-educated Ottoman intellectuals, military officers, and administrators who had emerged during Abdülhamid II's reign.

They were the products of the institutional developments of the period — graduates of Galatasaray Lisesi, the Imperial Military College, the Mülkiye, and the European universities where Ottoman students had been studying since the Tanzimat era.
They were committed to constitutional government, secular state institutions, modernization on European lines, and the preservation of the empire as a coherent multi-ethnic polity.

The most consequential Young Turk organization was the Committee of Union and Progress (CUP, İttihat ve Terakki Cemiyeti), founded in 1889 by medical students at the Istanbul Imperial Military Medical School and gradually expanded into a broader political movement.

The CUP combined a relatively traditional intellectual constitutionalist faction (centered in Paris and Geneva, where many leaders lived in exile) with a more activist military faction concentrated in the Ottoman Balkan army.

By 1907 the CUP had organized cells across the Ottoman officer corps, particularly in the Balkan garrisons stationed in Salonika (which was an unusually cosmopolitan multi-ethnic city — a major center of Sephardic Jewish, Greek, Bulgarian, and Turkish populations, with a substantial German and French commercial presence — and which became the operational headquarters of the CUP's military faction).
In July 1908, several CUP-affiliated army units in the Balkan provinces launched a coordinated mutiny, demanding the restoration of the 1876 Constitution.
The mutinies spread rapidly across the Ottoman army.
Abdülhamid II, faced with the prospect of a general military uprising, restored the Constitution on July 24, 1908, and recalled parliament.
The Young Turk Revolution had succeeded in its initial constitutional demand within several weeks.
What followed in 1908–1909 was a complex political struggle.
Abdülhamid II attempted a counter-coup in April 1909, organizing a religious-conservative uprising in Istanbul.
The CUP-led Action Army marched on Istanbul from Salonika under General Mahmud Şevket Pasha, suppressed the uprising, and deposed Abdülhamid II on April 27, 1909.
He was confined to a villa in Salonika (and later, after 1912, returned to Istanbul under house arrest, where he died in 1918).
His brother Mehmed V Reşad was placed on the throne as a constitutional monarch.
The CUP took effective political control of the empire.
The Young Turk era (1908–1918) would be the empire's last decade, and the next chapter is its story.

Cross-civ check: the late nineteenth century was the period of the Meiji Restoration in Japan (1868 onward), the Self-Strengthening Movement in late Qing China, the rise of European imperialism in Africa and Asia, the consolidation of nationalism as the dominant European political ideology, the American Civil War and Reconstruction, and the late stages of the Industrial Revolution.
The Ottoman experience was one variant of a broader pattern of non-Western state response to European industrial-imperial ascendancy.
Some of these responses — Meiji Japan, in particular — produced remarkably successful modernizations that allowed the state to retain full sovereignty.
Some — Qajar Persia, the late Qing — produced partial modernizations that left the state weakened but surviving.
The Ottoman case fell in the second category.

The state survived to 1918, but it survived as a smaller, weaker, more dependent version of itself, with the institutional foundations for a different kind of post-imperial successor state being slowly assembled by the European-educated reformers who would eventually become the founders of the Turkish Republic.

chapters.title: The Great War and Aftermath
sentences: The decade between the Young Turk Revolution of 1908 and the Mudros armistice of 1918 is the most compressed and catastrophic period in Ottoman history.

In ten years the empire fought four major wars (the Italian War of 1911–1912, the First Balkan War of 1912–1913, the Second Balkan War of 1913, and the First World War of 1914–1918), lost almost all its remaining European territory and most of its Arab provinces, presided over a systematic genocide of its Armenian population, and effectively ceased to exist as a functioning state.
The Ottoman state that walked into the November 1918 armistice was a shell.

The recovery and transformation that followed in 1919–1923 produced not a restored Ottoman Empire but a fundamentally different state — the modern Republic of Turkey — which is the subject of the final chapter.
This chapter is the wartime story.
The Young Turk government's first decade (1908–1914) was politically chaotic.
The CUP had won constitutional restoration but had not yet consolidated political power.
Three major political crises shook the new constitutional regime in its first years.
The Italian-Ottoman War of 1911–1912 saw Italy invade and conquer the Ottoman provinces of Tripolitania and Cyrenaica (which became the Italian colony of Libya).

The Ottoman military response was inadequate — the empire could not project power across the Mediterranean against a serious European naval power — and the war ended with formal Ottoman recognition of Italian sovereignty over Libya in October 1912.
The First Balkan War of October 1912 to May 1913 was the catastrophe that ended Ottoman rule in Europe.
A coalition of Bulgaria, Serbia, Greece, and Montenegro, encouraged by the Italian victory and seeing the Ottoman state as terminally weak, declared war on the empire.
The combined Balkan armies overran Macedonia, Albania, Thrace, and most of the Aegean coast within weeks.
The Ottoman state lost almost all its remaining European territory in seven months.
Salonika — the second-largest city of the empire and the operational center of the CUP itself — fell to the Greeks on November 8, 1912.
Adrianople (Edirne) — the city Murad I had taken in 1369 and which had been the empire's working capital before Constantinople — fell to the Bulgarians in March 1913.
The empire's European frontier had collapsed.
The war ended with the Treaty of London (May 1913), which forced the Ottomans to cede everything west of a line approximating modern Turkey's European border.
They retained eastern Thrace (the Edirne province) and the Bosporus straits, and almost nothing else.

The Second Balkan War of June-July 1913 was a redistribution of the Balkan spoils — Bulgaria attacked its former Greek and Serbian allies over the division of Macedonia and was rapidly defeated by a coalition that now included the Ottoman state.
The Ottomans recovered Edirne and a slice of eastern Thrace from the Bulgarians.
This was the empire's last successful military operation.
The Edirne recovery was emotionally significant — the empire had recovered the city of Murad I — but the strategic situation remained desperate.
By August 1913 the Ottoman state had lost approximately 83% of its European territory and 69% of its European population in two wars.
The Balkan empire that had been the dynasty's territorial heartland for six hundred years was effectively gone.

The CUP's response was political consolidation: a January 1913 coup by a faction of CUP officers known as the Three Pashas — Enver Pasha, Talaat Pasha, and Cemal Pasha — established what would effectively be a triumvirate government for the remainder of the empire's existence.
The constitutional regime continued to operate formally, but real power was held by Enver as War Minister, Talaat as Interior Minister, and Cemal as Naval Minister.

The decision to enter the First World War on the side of Germany and Austria-Hungary was made by the Three Pashas in late October 1914, against the preferences of significant portions of the Ottoman political class.

The strategic calculation was clear-eyed: the empire was diplomatically isolated; Britain and France had repeatedly demonstrated willingness to support Russian and Greek nationalist threats against Ottoman territory; Germany was the only major power offering substantial military assistance and equipment; an Ottoman alliance with the Central Powers might, if Germany won, allow recovery of lost territories in the Caucasus and the Balkans.
The bet was catastrophic.
It cost the empire its existence.

The Ottoman war effort, October 1914 through October 1918, fought on multiple fronts: The Caucasus front against Russia, where Enver Pasha personally launched an ambitious winter offensive in December 1914 against the Russian army in eastern Anatolia.

The Battle of Sarıkamış (December 1914 to January 1915) was an unmitigated disaster — the Ottoman Third Army, perhaps 90,000 strong, was caught in the eastern Anatolian highlands in winter conditions for which it was not equipped, was decisively defeated by the Russians, and lost perhaps three-quarters of its strength to combat, frostbite, and starvation.
The eastern Anatolian frontier collapsed.
Russian forces would advance into eastern Anatolia for the next three years until the Russian Revolution of 1917 ended the Russian war effort.
The Mesopotamian front against the British, who landed at Basra in November 1914 and pushed up the Tigris-Euphrates valley over the next four years.

The Ottomans achieved a remarkable victory at the Siege of Kut al-Amara (December 1915 to April 1916), capturing a British force of about thirteen thousand under General Charles Townshend — the largest British military surrender since the American Revolution.
The victory was followed by British reinforcement and renewed advance.
Baghdad fell to the British in March 1917.
By war's end the British held all of Mesopotamia.
The Sinai-Palestine front against the British forces based in Egypt.
The Ottomans launched a Suez Canal offensive in early 1915 that failed at the canal itself.
The British counter-offensive moved north through Sinai in 1916–1917 under General Edmund Allenby, supported by Arab Revolt forces under Sharif Hussein of Mecca and his sons (advised by T.E.
Lawrence, the British liaison officer whose memoirs would become the most famous English-language source on the Arab Revolt).
Jerusalem fell to Allenby in December 1917.
Damascus fell in October 1918.
The Gallipoli front against the British, French, Australian, and New Zealand forces who attempted in 1915 to force the Dardanelles, take Constantinople, and knock the Ottomans out of the war.
The Gallipoli Campaign (April 1915 to January 1916) was the Ottoman war effort's one major strategic success.

Allied landings at multiple points on the Gallipoli peninsula were contained by Ottoman defensive operations under the German general Otto Liman von Sanders and his Ottoman subordinate commander Mustafa Kemal Bey (later Atatürk), who had become a divisional commander at age thirty-four and who established his military reputation in the campaign.
After eight months of trench warfare and approximately a quarter of a million casualties on each side, the Allied forces evacuated.

Gallipoli became, simultaneously, the foundational battle of Australian and New Zealand national identity (the Anzac legend), the campaign that destroyed Winston Churchill's reputation as First Lord of the Admiralty (he had championed the operation and resigned after its failure), and the campaign that established Mustafa Kemal as a national figure in the late Ottoman state.
In the middle of this multi-front war, in the spring of 1915, the Ottoman state began the systematic destruction of its Armenian Christian population.

The Armenian Genocide of 1915–1916 needs to be addressed directly and accurately, because it is one of the defining events of late Ottoman history and one of the most consequential atrocities of the early twentieth century.

The Armenian Christian population of eastern Anatolia, perhaps two million strong before 1914, was concentrated in the highlands of the Ottoman eastern frontier — provinces that were also the immediate war zone of the Russian-Ottoman Caucasus campaign.

The CUP government, particularly Talaat Pasha as Interior Minister, identified the Armenian population as a politically unreliable population whose loyalty in wartime could not be assumed and whose proximity to the Russian frontier made them a strategic liability.
The institutional precedent of the Hamidian Massacres of 1894–1896 (Chapter 10) was already established.
The wartime decision was to extend that approach to the systematic destruction of the entire community.
The genocidal program had three components.
First, the deportation orders of April 1915 onward, which directed the systematic removal of Armenian populations from their home villages and cities.

The deportees — predominantly women, children, and the elderly, since adult Armenian men had already been conscripted into the Ottoman army and many had been executed in 1914–1915 — were marched south through Anatolia toward concentration sites in the Syrian desert.

The marches were conducted under conditions deliberately designed to produce mass death: minimal food and water, no shelter, organized banditry by escort forces and local irregulars, deliberate route choices through hostile terrain, periodic massacres of marching columns.

Second, the massacres in cities and villages, conducted by Ottoman regular troops, Special Organization (Teşkilât-ı Mahsusa) paramilitary units, and Kurdish tribal forces under official Ottoman direction.

Third, the concentration sites in the Syrian and Mesopotamian desert (most notoriously Deir ez-Zor), where surviving deportees were held under conditions producing mass death from starvation, disease, exposure, and continued violence.
The death toll is contested in detail but well established in magnitude.
The standard scholarly estimate is between one and one and a half million Armenian deaths during the genocide period, out of a pre-war population of approximately two million.

Substantial Armenian populations also lived in the Russian Caucasus and (after the war) in the Soviet Armenia that became the modern Republic of Armenia, but the Ottoman Armenian community of eastern Anatolia was destroyed as a coherent population.

Many of the survivors fled to Russia, France, the United States, and the Levant, founding the modern Armenian diaspora that continues to be one of the most consequential exile communities in modern world history.
The genocide was conducted with systematic state organization.

Detailed Ottoman administrative records of the deportations and massacres survive in the Ottoman archives, supplemented by the contemporary reports of foreign diplomats (the American ambassador Henry Morgenthau Sr., whose memoir became one of the foundational documentary sources), foreign missionaries, foreign journalists, and surviving Armenian witnesses.
The institutional fingerprint of state organization is unambiguous in the documentary record.

The argument that the events were spontaneous communal violence, occasional excesses of regional officials, or unintended consequences of legitimate wartime population transfers — arguments that have been advanced by various Turkish state and academic sources from the 1920s to the present — is not supported by the primary documentary evidence.
The Republic of Turkey, since its founding in 1923, has officially denied that the events constituted genocide.
The denial is a continuing diplomatic and historical issue.
Most major academic institutions, most other state governments, and the international scholarly consensus on twentieth-century atrocities have recognized the events as a genocide for several decades.

The Turkish state's official position remains that the events were a wartime population displacement with associated casualties on multiple sides, that the death toll has been exaggerated, and that the use of the term "genocide" is historically inaccurate.
The continuing dispute has shaped Turkish-Armenian diplomatic relations, Turkish-American relations, Turkish-EU relations, and the Republic's domestic political culture for the past century.
Honest reckoning with the events is the responsibility of any account of late Ottoman history.
The Ottoman state, in 1915–1916, organized and executed the systematic destruction of one of its own constituent populations as a deliberate state policy in wartime.
The death toll was over a million people.

The institutional and political continuity between the late Ottoman state that conducted the genocide and the early Republican state that succeeded it is direct — the same individuals, the same political organization (the CUP became the political ancestor of the Republican People's Party), the same institutional culture.
The Armenian Genocide is one of the founding events of the modern Middle East.
It continues to shape the politics of the region a century later.
The Ottoman war effort collapsed in late 1918.
The Bulgarian capitulation in September 1918 opened the empire's European frontier to Allied advance.
The Allenby offensive in Palestine and Syria swept Ottoman forces northward through October.
The Russian Empire's collapse in 1917 had created a brief opportunity for Ottoman reconquest of lost Caucasus territories, but those gains were lost when German military support evaporated.
On October 30, 1918, the Ottoman Empire signed the Armistice of Mudros (named for the harbor on the Aegean island of Lemnos where the negotiations were conducted) with the Allied powers.
The terms were severe: Ottoman demobilization, Allied occupation of strategic territory, Allied control of the straits, and effective Allied supervision of the Ottoman administration.
The empire was, formally, a defeated state under Allied occupation.
Allied forces moved into Istanbul in November 1918.
The British and French naval presence in the Bosporus was the first foreign military occupation of Constantinople since the Latin Empire of 1204–1261 (Byzantine Empire Ch 9).
The Ottoman government continued to function in name, but real authority was held by the Allied High Commissioners.
The Three Pashas — Enver, Talaat, and Cemal — had fled the country on a German submarine the day before Mudros was signed.
Enver was killed in 1922 fighting Soviet forces in Central Asia.

Talaat was assassinated in Berlin in March 1921 by an Armenian Genocide survivor named Soghomon Tehlirian (in a politically targeted killing whose subsequent trial — Tehlirian was acquitted on grounds of temporary insanity, with the genocide explicitly entered as evidence — became a major international cause célèbre and contributed to the postwar international legal vocabulary of "crimes against humanity").
Cemal was assassinated in Tbilisi in July 1922.
The peace settlement was the Treaty of Sèvres (signed August 10, 1920, after extensive negotiations among the Allied powers and the Ottoman government).
The treaty was the most punitive settlement imposed on any Central Power after the war.
Its terms included: The cession of all Arab provinces to British and French mandates (Britain to administer Iraq, Palestine, and Transjordan; France to administer Syria and Lebanon).
The cession of eastern Anatolia to a planned independent Armenia and an autonomous Kurdistan.
The cession of western Anatolia (the Smyrna region, now called Izmir) to Greece.
The cession of eastern Thrace to Greece.
The internationalization of the Bosporus straits under Allied supervision.
Allied military and economic control over the remaining Ottoman state.
The treaty terms reduced the Ottoman state to a small rump territory in central and northern Anatolia.

The territorial losses were complete: the Arab provinces gone, the Greek-administered western Anatolia and eastern Thrace gone, the planned Armenian and Kurdish autonomous states carving out the eastern half of Anatolia.
What remained was less than a third of the empire's pre-war territory.
The Sèvres treaty was signed by the Ottoman government in Istanbul.
It was rejected by a different Ottoman political authority that had emerged in central Anatolia — the Turkish nationalist movement based at Ankara, led by Mustafa Kemal Pasha, the hero of Gallipoli.
The Greco-Turkish War of 1919–1922 was the war that destroyed the Sèvres settlement.

Greek forces had landed at Smyrna in May 1919 with British and French logistical support, intending to establish the Greek territorial administration of western Anatolia provided for under the planned peace settlement.
The Greek military presence in Anatolia provoked an immediate Turkish nationalist response.
Turkish military officers — primarily veterans of the Ottoman war effort, organized around Mustafa Kemal — assembled a resistance movement based in central Anatolia.
The movement was simultaneously anti-Greek (the immediate enemy), anti-Allied (rejecting the Sèvres settlement), and anti-Sultanate (rejecting the Istanbul government's signing of the treaty).
It was a Turkish nationalist movement, with explicit ethnic Turkish self-conception, articulated as a national-liberation movement against foreign occupation and Greek invasion.
The war was fought over three years across central and western Anatolia.
The Greek army initially advanced east from Smyrna, taking Bursa, Eskişehir, and Afyon, and pushing close to Ankara in the summer of 1921.
The Turkish nationalist defense at the Battle of Sakarya (August-September 1921) halted the Greek advance after a three-week engagement.
The Greek forces, overextended and undersupplied, began a withdrawal in 1922.
The Turkish counteroffensive of August-September 1922 broke the Greek army at the Battle of Dumlupınar and pursued the retreating Greek forces back to Smyrna.
The city fell to Turkish forces on September 9, 1922.
A massive fire destroyed most of the Greek and Armenian neighborhoods of the city in the days following, killing tens of thousands of civilians.

The Greek population of western Anatolia, perhaps a million people whose ancestors had lived in the region continuously since the eighth century BCE, fled to Greece in the largest single refugee crisis of the early twentieth century.
The Turkish nationalist victory in the Greco-Turkish War effectively destroyed the Sèvres settlement.
The Allied powers were unwilling to commit further military forces to enforce a treaty that had not been accepted by the de facto government of Turkey.
Negotiations for a replacement settlement opened at Lausanne in November 1922.
The Treaty of Lausanne (signed July 24, 1923) replaced Sèvres with substantially better terms for the Turkish state.
The Ottoman Arab provinces remained under British and French mandate (a non-negotiable Allied position).

The planned Armenian and Kurdish autonomous states were abandoned (with massive consequences for the Armenian and Kurdish populations of eastern Anatolia, who had been counting on international support that did not materialize).
Western Anatolia and eastern Thrace remained Turkish.
The Bosporus straits were internationalized but under conditions that allowed Turkish administrative authority.
A massive population exchange between Greece and Turkey was formalized: approximately 1.2 million Greeks deported from Anatolia to Greece, approximately 400,000 Turks deported from Greece to Turkey.
The exchange was conducted on the basis of religion rather than language or self-identification — Greek Orthodox populations to Greece, Muslim populations to Turkey, with very limited exceptions.
It was the largest single state-organized population transfer of the twentieth century before the partition of British India in 1947.
The Lausanne treaty established the borders and the demographic foundations of the modern Republic of Turkey.

Before the Lausanne treaty, while negotiations were still ongoing, the Turkish nationalist movement had taken a step that eliminated the institutional basis of the Ottoman Empire: the abolition of the sultanate.

On November 1, 1922, the Grand National Assembly of Turkey (the parliament of the nationalist movement, based in Ankara) passed a law abolishing the office of sultan and declaring the Ottoman dynasty to have no further governmental role.
The last sultan, Mehmed VI Vahdettin (ruled 1918–1922), fled Istanbul on a British warship two weeks later, on November 17, 1922.
He was the thirty-sixth and final sultan of a dynasty that had begun with Osman I six hundred and twenty-three years earlier.
The Ottoman Empire, as a continuous political institution, had ended.

The Caliphate continued briefly under Vahdettin's cousin Abdülmecid II, who was named Caliph but not Sultan in November 1922 — a deliberate institutional split between the religious and political offices that had been merged since Selim I's claim of 1517.
The arrangement was unstable.
The Republican government would eliminate it within eighteen months.
That story is the next chapter.

Cross-civ check: 1922 — the year the Ottoman sultanate was abolished — was also the year Mussolini's March on Rome installed Italian Fascism, the year the Soviet Union was formally established, the year British rule in India entered its terminal phase under Gandhi's first non-cooperation movement, the year of the Irish Free State's independence, and the year the Versailles settlement was beginning to visibly fail across central Europe.

The post-WWI dissolution of the multi-ethnic empires (Ottoman, Habsburg, German, Russian) created the political geography of the modern Middle East, central Europe, and northern Eurasia in a single concentrated period of state formation.
The Ottoman case was one of four major imperial dissolutions in the period.
Its consequences continue to shape the politics of the eastern Mediterranean a century later.

chapters.title: The Republic and What Endured
sentences: The Ottoman Empire ended on November 1, 1922.
The Republic of Turkey was proclaimed on October 29, 1923.

In the eleven months between those two events, and in the year and a half that followed, the institutional, religious, and political framework that had defined the Ottoman state was systematically dismantled by the new Republican government and replaced with a different framework on a different model.

The transformation was the most rapid and most thoroughgoing institutional change in any of the major successor states emerging from the post-WWI imperial dissolutions, and it was conducted by a single political movement under the leadership of a single figure.
The figure was Mustafa Kemal, who would adopt the surname Atatürk ("Father of the Turks") in 1934 when surnames were made compulsory.
The political movement was the Republican People's Party.
The transformation produced modern Turkey.
Its consequences continue to shape Turkish politics, identity, and foreign relations a century later.

This chapter is about that transformation, about the legacy the Ottoman Empire left across the territories it had once ruled, and about what specific elements of the Ottoman institutional and cultural inheritance continue to operate in the modern world.

Mustafa Kemal (1881–1938) was a graduate of the Ottoman Imperial Military College, a junior officer in the Three Pashas era, the divisional commander who had stopped the Anzac advance at Gallipoli in 1915, and the senior officer who had organized the Turkish nationalist resistance against the Greek invasion in 1919–1922.
He combined exceptional military and political ability with an explicit commitment to the wholesale reconstruction of the Turkish state along secular European lines.
He was not, by temperament or training, an Ottoman traditionalist.
He had no patience for the institutions of the Caliphate, the Ottoman dynastic system, or the cultural traditions of the late empire.
His project was to replace those institutions, deliberately and rapidly, with new institutions modeled on European national-state precedents.
The transformation proceeded in several stages.
In 1922 the sultanate was abolished, separating the Caliphate from the temporal monarchy.
In 1923 the Republic was proclaimed.
Ankara, the central Anatolian city that had been the capital of the nationalist movement, was made the new capital of the Republic — replacing Istanbul, the imperial capital of nearly five centuries.
In 1924 the Caliphate was abolished.
Abdülmecid II, the last Caliph, was deported to France with the rest of the Ottoman dynastic family.
The eight-hundred-year-old institutional continuity of the Sunni Caliphate (which had passed from the Abbasids to the Mamluks to the Ottomans) was definitively broken.
The Caliphate has not been reconstituted since.
In 1925 the religious-legal framework of the empire was systematically replaced.
Islamic religious courts were abolished.
Religious orders (the Sufi tariqats — the Mevlevi, Bektashi, Naqshbandi, and other orders that had been embedded in Ottoman religious life for centuries) were closed.

The traditional religious dress code was abolished — the fez (the cylindrical red felt hat that had been the symbol of Ottoman official identity since Mahmud II's clothing reforms in the 1820s) was banned, and European-style clothing was made mandatory for state officials.
The Islamic lunar calendar was replaced with the Gregorian solar calendar.
In 1926 the Civil Code of the Swiss Confederation was adopted as the basis of Turkish family and personal law, replacing the Ottoman sharia-based personal status law.

The transformation included the abolition of polygamy, the introduction of equal civil rights for women (including the right to vote and to hold office, granted in 1934 — earlier than in many European states), and the institution of secular marriage as the only legally recognized form of marriage.
In 1928 the Latin alphabet was adopted to replace the Ottoman Arabic-script alphabet that had been the standard written form of Turkish for six centuries.
The transition was rapid — roughly six months from the adoption decision to the legal mandate — and was accompanied by a state-sponsored mass literacy campaign.
The rupture with the previous textual tradition was deliberate and severe.
Within a generation, most Turks could not read documents written in the Ottoman script.

The Ottoman literary inheritance — divan poetry, court chronicles, religious texts, administrative documents, six centuries of accumulated writing — became inaccessible to the general population without specialized scholarly training.

In the 1930s the Turkish Language Society undertook a systematic project to purge Turkish vocabulary of Persian and Arabic loan-words, which had constituted perhaps half of formal Ottoman Turkish vocabulary.
The replacements were either revived archaic Turkic words, neologisms coined from Turkic roots, or in some cases European loan-words.

The result was that modern Turkish — particularly its written form — became substantially different from late Ottoman Turkish, with vocabulary differences that are roughly equivalent to the differences between modern English and Anglo-Saxon Old English.
A modern Turkish speaker reading a Tanzimat-era newspaper article requires substantial scholarly assistance.
The aggregate effect of these reforms was an unusually rapid and complete cultural rupture.
The Republican government had deliberately and systematically severed the new Turkey from its Ottoman past in matters of religion, law, dress, language, alphabet, and political structure.

The transformation was, in important respects, more thoroughgoing than the parallel modernizations in Meiji Japan, post-Tsarist Russia, or post-imperial China — each of which retained more substantial continuity with their pre-modernization cultural inheritance.
Turkey, under Atatürk, conducted what was effectively a state-organized cultural revolution against its own immediate past.
The political logic of the transformation was clear.
The Ottoman framework had been permanently associated, in the minds of the Republican leadership, with imperial collapse, military defeat, and external dependency.

The new Turkey was to be a different kind of state — secular, ethnically Turkish, European-modeled, and politically defensible against European pressures because it had explicitly adopted European institutional forms.
The strategic calculation was that Turkey could only retain full sovereignty if it stopped looking, institutionally, like the kind of state European powers expected to dismember.
What survived from the Ottoman period, despite the Republican rupture?
A great deal more than the Republican founding rhetoric acknowledged.
Geographic and demographic.
The territory of modern Turkey is, in its broad outlines, the Ottoman Anatolian core — the region that had been continuously under Ottoman rule from the early fourteenth century onward.
The cities are the Ottoman cities.
The road and water infrastructure has Ottoman foundations beneath the Republican-era and modern overlays.
The agricultural geography of grain belts, olive coasts, and fruit-growing regions follows patterns that were established under Ottoman fiscal and irrigation systems.

The Turkish population is the demographic descendant of the Ottoman Anatolian-Muslim population — modified by the population exchange with Greece in 1923 and by various subsequent migrations, but recognizably continuous with the Ottoman population.
The Sunni Hanafi Islamic tradition that the Ottoman state had patronized for six centuries remained the religious tradition of the great majority of the modern Turkish population.
The mosques continued to operate.
The five-times-daily call to prayer continued from Ottoman-era minarets.
Ramadan continued to be observed.
The hajj continued to be made.
The everyday religious life of Turkish Muslims did not undergo a Republican-era transformation comparable to the institutional transformation of religious institutions.

The Republic is constitutionally secular, but the population is religiously Muslim, and the relationship between official secularism and popular religiosity has been one of the defining tensions of Turkish political life for the past century.
The Sufi orders, formally banned in 1925, never disappeared — they continued to operate informally throughout the Republican period and have re-emerged into more public visibility since the 1980s.
Architectural.
The visual landscape of Turkish cities is unmistakably Ottoman.

Istanbul's skyline — defined by Hagia Sophia, the Süleymaniye, the Sultan Ahmed Mosque, and the network of imperial mosques and palaces built between the fifteenth and seventeenth centuries — is the same skyline that Sinan helped create.

The provincial Ottoman mosques, the kulliye complexes, the Topkapı palace, the Iznik tilework, the courtyard houses with their wooden lattice screens (the kafes and cumba of traditional Ottoman urban architecture) all continue to define the visual character of Turkish cities and many cities across the former Ottoman lands.
The Ottoman aesthetic continues, even where the Republican-era state distanced itself from Ottoman political institutions.
Linguistic.

Despite the language reforms, modern Turkish remains the descendant of Ottoman Turkish, in roughly the same way that modern English is the descendant of Middle English — substantially modified, but recognizably continuous.
Ottoman vocabulary is recoverable through scholarly training.
