The Persian and Arabic loan-words that were officially purged in the 1930s have, in many cases, returned to colloquial usage.
The literary tradition is, with effort, accessible to modern readers.

The Ottoman cuisine — kebabs, pilavs, börek, baklava, Turkish coffee, mezes, the elaborate savory and sweet pastry traditions of the imperial palace kitchens — remained essentially unchanged through the Republican transformation.
Modern Turkish cuisine is, more or less directly, the cuisine of the Ottoman court and the Ottoman commercial cities.

Many of the cooking traditions carried over to the successor states across the former Ottoman lands — the cuisine of Greece, Bulgaria, Lebanon, Syria, and Egypt is shaped by the Ottoman culinary inheritance to a degree that local nationalist sentiment has often tried to obscure but which is unmistakable to any cross-cultural diner.

Ottoman classical music (Türk sanat müziği), Sufi music traditions, the Mevlevi semazen ritual, Janissary band music (the precursor of European military marching band traditions), and various folk traditions all continued in modified form into the Republican period and remain part of contemporary Turkish musical culture.
The Ottoman legacy beyond modern Turkey is broader and harder to summarize, because it stretches across roughly a third of the modern Mediterranean and Middle Eastern world.

In the Balkan successor states — Greece, Bulgaria, North Macedonia, Albania, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Kosovo, Serbia, Montenegro, parts of Romania, parts of Croatia and Hungary — the Ottoman period left enduring marks.

The mosques and Ottoman urban architecture in cities like Sarajevo, Skopje, Sofia, and Pristina; the lingering ethnic and religious diversity (Bosnian Muslims, Albanian Muslims, the Pomak Muslim populations of Bulgaria and Greece, the Sephardic Jewish populations of the Balkan cities) that maps onto Ottoman-era millet patterns; the cuisine, music, and folk traditions; the linguistic substratum — Turkish loan-words remain common in Balkan languages, and the languages themselves were shaped by centuries of multilingual Ottoman administration.

The negative legacy is also real: the long-running ethnic and religious conflicts of the Balkans, which exploded in the wars of the 1990s, drew on grievances and identity formations that had been shaped during the Ottoman period and the wars of Ottoman dissolution.

In the Arab successor states — Iraq, Syria, Lebanon, Jordan, Israel/Palestine, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, the Hijaz, Yemen, Libya, Tunisia, Algeria — the Ottoman legacy was structurally important even where it has been politically downplayed by Arab nationalist narratives.

The administrative geography of the modern Arab states was substantially shaped by the late Ottoman vilayet (provincial) structure, with many post-WWI mandate borders following Ottoman provincial lines.
The religious institutions — the system of religious endowments (waqfs), the structure of Islamic legal scholarship, the administration of holy sites — were continuous with their Ottoman precedents.
The architecture of Damascus, Aleppo, Cairo, Baghdad, and the smaller Levantine and Anatolian cities preserved Ottoman building traditions extensively.
The Hijaz Railway, built under Abdülhamid II, continued to operate in modified form for decades after the empire's collapse.
The borders of much of the modern Middle East are post-Ottoman borders.

The borders between Turkey and Syria, Iraq and Syria, Iraq and Saudi Arabia, Saudi Arabia and Jordan, Jordan and Israel/Palestine — these were drawn after 1918 by the Allied mandate authorities, sometimes following Ottoman administrative lines and sometimes overriding them.

The various twentieth- and twenty-first-century conflicts of the Middle East — the Arab-Israeli conflict, the Lebanese civil wars, the Iraq wars, the Syrian civil war, the Kurdish conflicts in Turkey and Iraq — have all involved disputes over borders, populations, and institutional arrangements that trace, in some part, to the Ottoman dissolution.
The religious geography of the Sunni-Shi'a divide in the Middle East was shaped by the Ottoman-Safavid rivalry that began at Chaldiran in 1514 and continued for the next two centuries (Chapter 5).

The modern political tensions between Sunni Saudi Arabia, Sunni Egypt, and the Sunni Gulf states on one side, and Shi'a Iran, the Shi'a-led government of Iraq, the Shi'a Hezbollah of Lebanon, and the Alawite-led government of Syria on the other side, are recognizable extensions of the Ottoman-Safavid conflict in modern form.
The Caliphate question, dormant for nearly a century after Atatürk's abolition in 1924, has periodically resurfaced.
The early-twentieth-century pan-Islamic movements that sought to revive the caliphate failed.
The mid-twentieth-century Arab nationalist movements were largely uninterested in restoring it.

Various twenty-first-century radical movements (most notoriously the so-called Islamic State of Iraq and Syria, ISIS, which proclaimed a caliphate in 2014) have invoked the Ottoman caliphate as historical precedent.

The substantive theological and political questions raised by the abolition — about the relationship between political authority and religious authority in Sunni Islam, about the institutional form of pan-Islamic religious leadership — remain unresolved.
What was the Ottoman Empire, in the end?

It was a multicontinental polity that lasted six hundred and twenty-three years, ruled at peak about thirty million people of dozens of ethnicities and several major religions, and operated as one of the central political organizations of the Mediterranean basin from the late fourteenth century to the early twentieth.

It was the institutional successor to Byzantium — taking over Constantinople, the surviving Roman administrative apparatus of the eastern Mediterranean, and the Greek and Slavic populations of the Balkans, and running them under a different religious framework and a different ruling dynasty for four centuries.
The Roman Empire that had refused to die for eleven hundred years (Byzantine Empire Ch 1) finally received an institutional successor that, in some respects, continued its role.

It was, for two centuries, the most powerful state in its region — the empire that took Constantinople, defeated the Mamluks, conquered the Hungarian plain, dominated the Mediterranean, codified law for three continents, and produced an architectural climax in the work of Mimar Sinan that ranks among the supreme achievements of any pre-modern civilization.

It was, for three centuries, the empire that managed religious and ethnic diversity through the millet system on a scale that no contemporary Christian European state attempted, providing protected status to religious minorities under conditions that — for all their limitations — were more durable than anything available in early modern Catholic or Protestant Europe.

It was, for one century at the end, the Sick Man of Europe — the polity whose dissolution shaped the political geography of the modern Middle East, whose final wars produced one of the twentieth century's first systematic genocides, and whose collapse produced the modern Republic of Turkey along with sixteen other successor states across three continents.
Its institutional inheritance is everywhere across the former Ottoman lands.

The mosques of Sarajevo and Cairo, the bazaars of Istanbul and Damascus, the legal codifications that fused sharia and kanun, the architectural vocabulary that descends from Hagia Sophia through Sinan to the modern provincial mosque, the administrative geography of the Middle East, the Sunni-Shi'a sectarian map, the Greek-Turkish-Bulgarian-Armenian diaspora communities scattered across the world, the Sephardic Jewish heritage that traces through Salonica back to medieval Spain — all of these are Ottoman.
The Ottoman Empire fell in 1922.
Its inheritance is operating, contested, and unfinished.

Modern Turkey, modern Greece, modern Bulgaria, modern Israel, modern Lebanon, modern Iraq, modern Saudi Arabia, modern Egypt, and modern Bosnia are still working out — some peacefully, some with difficulty, some catastrophically — what the empire left them.

The empire that had ruled at peak from the Algerian coast to the Caucasus and from the Hungarian plain to the Yemeni highlands left, when it fell, an institutional and cultural inheritance that no nation-state successor has been able to absorb completely, and that continues to shape the politics of three continents a century after the last sultan boarded a British warship and sailed away from his city.
The empire is gone.
Its world is still being inherited.

Cross-civ final check: the Ottoman Empire's six centuries (1299–1922) overlap, in turn, with the Yuan and Ming and Qing dynasties of China, with the entire arc of the Mughal Empire of India, with the Safavid and Qajar dynasties of Persia, with the early modern consolidation of European nation-states, with the rise and fall of the Russian Empire, with the entire colonial period of European expansion into the Americas, Africa, and Asia, and with the emergence of the modern global system of nation-states.

Among the great early modern empires, only the Russian Empire — which lasted from approximately 1547 to 1917, with various formal start and end dates depending on definition — had comparable longevity, and the Russian Empire is itself one of the polities most directly shaped by the Byzantine inheritance that the Ottomans had simultaneously inherited and replaced.

The two great heirs of Byzantium — the Russian Empire claiming the Third Rome and the Ottoman Empire claiming Kayser-i Rûm — operated in parallel for nearly four hundred years before the Russian Empire ended in revolution in 1917 and the Ottoman Empire ended in republican proclamation in 1922 and 1923.
They were, between them, the two longest-running political continuities in early modern history.
They both ended within five years of each other.
The age of the great multicontinental empires ended with them.

chapters.title: The Safavid Order
sentences: The dynasty that turned Iran into a Shia country started as a Sunni mystical brotherhood in a small town nobody outside the region had heard of.

The town was Ardabil (ar-dah-BEEL), in northwestern Iran near the Caspian Sea, in the Persian-Turkic borderland of Azerbaijan (the historical region, not the modern republic, though the modern republic gets its name from it).
The brotherhood was called the Safaviyya (sah-fah-VEE-yah), founded around 1300 by a charismatic Sunni Sufi sheikh named Safi al-Din (sah-FEE al-DEEN).
And the dynasty that eventually grew out of this brotherhood is the Safavid dynasty, which takes its name from him.
This is one of the strangest origin stories in early-modern history.
The founders of every other major Islamic empire of the period — the Ottomans, the Mughals, the Uzbeks — were soldiers and tribal warlords.
The Safavids started as monks.

By the time they reached the throne, they had transformed themselves into the most fanatical military force in the Islamic world, claimed descent from the Prophet Muhammad (probably falsely), reversed their original Sunni identity into a militant Shia one, and inspired their followers to charge Ottoman cannons believing they could not be killed.
The transformation took two centuries.
It is the precondition for everything else in this book.
To understand the Safavids, you have to understand Sufism (SOO-fizm), the mystical and devotional tradition within Islam.
Mainstream Islam, in both its Sunni and Shia branches, emphasizes religious law (the sharia, sha-REE-ah), correct ritual, and direct individual relationship with God through prayer.

Sufism is a parallel tradition that emphasizes inner spiritual experience, the cultivation of the soul, and the role of a teacher — a sheikh or pir (peer) — who guides disciples on a path toward direct knowledge of the divine.
Sufi orders, called tariqas (tah-REE-kahs, literally "paths"), formed around lineages of spiritual masters.

Each tariqa had its own distinctive practices: certain forms of meditative chanting (dhikr, ZIK-r — "remembrance" of God's names), specific breathing techniques, sometimes ecstatic dance (the most famous example being the whirling dervishes of the Mevlevi order, founded by the Persian poet Rumi in the thirteenth century), and a master-disciple relationship that demanded absolute loyalty.
Sufism flourished across the Islamic world after the Mongol invasions of the thirteenth century (Mongol Empire Ch 5 and Ch 7).

The Mongols had wrecked the existing political order — sacking Baghdad in 1258 and ending the Abbasid caliphate — and the centralized religious authority that had legitimized the old order collapsed with it.
Into this vacuum stepped the Sufi orders, which provided spiritual direction, social organization, charitable services, and political networks at the local level.

By the time the Ilkhanate (the Mongol successor state in Iran, Mongol Empire Ch 7) collapsed in 1335, Sufi tariqas were arguably the most powerful non-state institutions across the Persian-speaking world.
This is the world Safi al-Din was born into.
Safi al-Din (1252–1334) was a Sunni Sufi sheikh, originally a disciple of an older Sufi master named Sheikh Zahid Gilani in Lahijan, on the Caspian coast.
When Zahid died, Safi al-Din inherited the leadership of his tariqa, married Zahid's daughter, and moved the order's headquarters to his hometown of Ardabil.
From Ardabil, he built the Safaviyya into one of the most influential Sufi orders in the Iranian world.
What is striking about the early Safaviyya is how mainstream it was.
Safi al-Din was a Sunni Muslim of the Shafi'i (SHAH-fee-ee) school of jurisprudence — one of the four standard Sunni legal schools, the dominant one in much of the eastern Islamic world.
He was on cordial terms with the Ilkhan court.
The historian Rashid al-Din (the same Jewish-born physician-vizier who compiled the Compendium of Chronicles, the first true world history, Mongol Empire Ch 7) was a personal correspondent.
Wealthy patrons donated land to the order.
Pilgrims came to Ardabil to receive Safi al-Din's blessing.
By the time he died in 1334 — coincidentally the same year the Ilkhanate began to fall apart — the Safaviyya was a wealthy, respected, politically connected Sunni Sufi establishment.

Nothing about Safi al-Din suggests his descendants would conquer Iran two centuries later, claim descent from the Prophet, declare themselves messianic figures, and force-convert millions of Sunnis to Shia Islam.
The transformation happened in stages, and each stage was driven by external political pressure.
The first stage was geographic and political.

The Ilkhanate's collapse left Iran fragmented among rival successor dynasties (Mongol Empire Ch 7) — the Jalayirids in Iraq and western Iran, the Chobanids in northwest Iran, the Muzaffarids in the south, and various smaller principalities.

None of these states had the strength to reunify Persia, and into this vacuum stepped a new conqueror: Timur (TEE-moor, also called Tamerlane in European sources), the Turco-Mongol warlord from Transoxiana who built one of the most violent empires of the medieval world between the 1370s and 1405.

Timur's campaigns through Iran, India, the Caucasus, and Anatolia produced massacres on a scale not seen since the original Mongol invasions — pyramids of skulls outside cities that resisted, populations exterminated, entire regions depopulated.
Timur was theoretically a Muslim and patronized Sufi orders, including the Safaviyya, but his political project was conquest, not cultural restoration.

When Timur's empire began to crumble after his death in 1405, his descendants — the Timurids — held on to a reduced version of his territory in Khorasan (eastern Iran and modern Afghanistan) for most of the fifteenth century.

The Timurid capital at Herat (HEH-rat, in modern Afghanistan) became one of the cultural jewels of the Islamic world: Persian miniature painting reached new heights under masters like Kamal al-Din Bihzad (kah-MAHL al-DEEN bee-ZAHD), Persian poetry flourished in the work of Jami (the last great classical Persian poet), and Timurid architecture pioneered the soaring blue-tiled domes that would later define Safavid building.
Much of what we think of as classical Persian high culture was codified at fifteenth-century Herat.
The Safavids would inherit it almost entirely.
Meanwhile, in northwestern Iran, the Safaviyya order at Ardabil was changing.
The second stage was the conversion to Shia Islam.
Exactly when and how the Safaviyya shifted from Sunni Sufism to Shia Sufism is one of the messier questions in the historical literature.

The standard scholarly reading is that the conversion was gradual, beginning in the late fourteenth century and accelerating through the fifteenth, driven by the order's shifting political alliances with various Turcoman (TUR-koh-man — Turkic-speaking nomadic tribal confederations) groups in Anatolia and Azerbaijan.
Many of these Turcomans practiced a folk Islam that blended Sunni and Shia elements with pre-Islamic Turkic shamanic traditions.

As the Safaviyya recruited disciples from these groups, the order's theology drifted toward Shia positions — particular reverence for Ali ibn Abi Talib (AH-lee), the Prophet Muhammad's cousin and son-in-law, whom Shia Muslims consider the rightful first successor to the Prophet, and for the line of imams descended from him.
The Safavid sheikhs also began to claim, retroactively, that their family descended from Ali himself.
This claim was probably invented in the fifteenth century — Safi al-Din's actual genealogy almost certainly does not run through Ali — but it became central to Safavid legitimacy.
If you are descended from the Prophet through Ali, you are not merely a Sufi master but a sayyid (SAY-yid), a member of the Prophet's bloodline, with a special claim to religious authority.

The Safavids would eventually push this claim further: they were not just sayyids but the legitimate heirs of the Twelfth Imam himself, the Hidden Imam whose return Twelver Shia Muslims await as the apocalyptic redeemer.
The doctrinal claims and the political claims developed together.
As the order grew, its sheikhs needed bigger justifications for their growing power.
The third stage was militarization.
The militarization happened under two sheikhs whose names matter: Junayd (joo-NAYD, sheikh from 1447 to 1460) and his son Haydar (HIGH-dar, sheikh from 1460 to 1488).
Junayd was the first Safavid leader who actively raised armies, married into ruling houses, and sought a political throne.
He was killed in battle in 1460 fighting the rulers of Shirvan (a region on the western Caspian coast).
Haydar inherited his father's project and pushed it further — and gave the movement its visual signature.
The signature was a red turban.
Haydar designed a distinctive twelve-pointed red headgear for his followers, the points commemorating the twelve imams of Twelver Shia Islam.

The red turban was simultaneously a religious symbol, a military uniform, and a political badge — anyone wearing it was identifying as a Safaviyya disciple, a Shia, a partisan of Haydar, and a soldier ready to fight at his command.
The Turcoman tribesmen who flocked to Haydar's banner were called Qizilbash (kih-zil-BASH), Turkish for "red-heads," after their distinctive headgear.
The name stuck.
The Qizilbash were the military backbone of the early Safavid project for the next century.
What made the Qizilbash extraordinary was the religious dimension of their loyalty.
They did not fight for wages, plunder, or land alone.
They fought because they believed their sheikh was a divinely guided figure — not just a Sufi master but a near-messianic incarnation of the divine, possibly the returning Hidden Imam himself.

Some Qizilbash factions reportedly believed their sheikh was literally a manifestation of God in human form, a position that mainstream Islam — Sunni or Shia — would consider heretical to the point of blasphemy.

The historian Hans Roemer described early Qizilbash religion as something closer to a millenarian cult than orthodox Shia Islam: ecstatic, charismatic, organized around personal devotion to a living messianic figure rather than around scripture and law.
This produced an extraordinary military asset.
Qizilbash warriors charged into battle believing they could not be killed, that their sheikh's spiritual power would protect them, and that death in his service was a direct ticket to paradise.
They were, in the literal sense, fanatics — but the fanaticism worked on the battlefield.
Through the 1480s and 1490s, the Safaviyya order under Haydar's son Ali (briefly sheikh from 1488 to 1494) and then Ali's nephew Ismail built a fighting force that would shortly conquer Iran.
Haydar himself was killed in 1488 in another battle in the Caucasus.
Ali was killed in 1494.

The young Ismail — Haydar's grandson, Ali's nephew, six years old at the time — was smuggled to safety by loyal Qizilbash and hidden for the next five years among friendly families in the Caspian region.
He emerged in 1499 as a thirteen-year-old leading a small army.

By 1501, fourteen years old, he would conquer the city of Tabriz and proclaim himself Shah (SHAH — the Persian word for king, the same word the Achaemenid emperors had used 2,000 years earlier — Persian Empire Ch 1).
That is where the next chapter starts.
A pause, before the chronology takes over: the Safaviyya story is the kind of origin myth that sounds invented, and parts of it almost certainly were.
The genealogy back to Ali is dubious.
The claim of unbroken Shia identity from Safi al-Din onward is anachronistic.
The accounts of Qizilbash religious extremism may be exaggerated by later orthodox Shia historians embarrassed by the founders' theology.
Modern scholars are divided on how much of the early Safavid self-presentation reflects fifteenth-century reality versus sixteenth-century reconstruction.

What no one disputes is that by 1500, the Safaviyya had transformed from a Sunni Sufi devotional order into an armed Shia messianic movement with thousands of fanatical Turcoman warriors, and that this transformation was the launch pad for one of the most consequential religious revolutions in Middle Eastern history.

A structural parallel worth pausing on: the two great Islamic empires of the early-modern Middle East — the Safavids and the Ottomans — were both born out of Sufi orders in the chaos that followed the collapse of the Mongol Ilkhanate.

The Ottoman dynasty's earliest fourteenth-century Anatolian frontier emerged from heterodox dervish networks (the Babai movement and related groups), in much the same way the Safaviyya emerged from the Ardabil Sufi establishment.
Both began as religious brotherhoods that armed themselves and turned political.

They then faced the same institutional problem from opposite ends: how to build a military force loyal to the ruler personally rather than to the tribal leaders whose private armies had founded the dynasty.

The Ottomans solved it through devshirme — recruiting Christian boys from the Balkans, raising them as Muslims, and creating the Janissary corps as a slave-soldier infantry with no kin ties to the territory they policed (Chapter 3).
The Safavids would eventually solve it the same way at one remove, importing Caucasian boys and training them as ghulam household troops (Chapter 4).
Both systems worked.

The Ottoman version came earlier, was institutionally older when the rivalry began, and was one major reason the Ottomans hit Chaldiran in 1514 with a professional gunpowder army while the Safavids were still riding into battle on the basis of religious fanaticism.

Cross-civ check: while the Safaviyya was militarizing in the late fifteenth century, the Ottoman Empire (the rival Sunni Turkic empire that would shortly become the Safavids' nemesis) was at the height of its early expansion under Mehmed II (the conqueror of Constantinople in 1453) and Bayezid II.
The Mughal Empire in India did not yet exist — it would be founded by Babur in 1526 — but Babur himself was a Timurid prince, distant cousin of the families the early Safavids were fighting.
In Spain, the Catholic Monarchs Ferdinand and Isabella completed the Reconquista in 1492, expelling the last Muslim ruler from Granada the same year Columbus reached the Americas.
In China, the Ming Dynasty was at mid-arc, with the great voyages of Admiral Zheng He completed and the country turning inward.

The world that Ismail was about to step into was the early-modern world — gunpowder armies, intercontinental trade, religious confrontation across continents — and the Safavids would shape its eastern half.

chapters.title: Ismail and the Shia Revolution
sentences: In 1501, a fourteen-year-old boy with red hair and pale skin, leading a few thousand Turcoman cavalry, captured the city of Tabriz (tah-BREEZ, the largest city in northwestern Iran) and proclaimed himself Shah Ismail I of a new dynasty.
Within a decade, he controlled most of Iran.
Within a generation, the country was forcibly converted from Sunni to Twelver Shia Islam, and the religious geography of the Middle East was permanently redrawn.
Ismail's revolution is one of the strangest political events in early-modern history.
He was a teenager.
His army was small.
The country he set out to conquer was overwhelmingly Sunni and had been for nine centuries.
He had no scholarly establishment to support the Shia conversion, no economic base outside what his Qizilbash followers could plunder, and no diplomatic recognition from any major foreign power.
What he had was charisma, fanatical followers who believed he was a near-divine figure, and a willingness to use systematic violence on a population that had not asked for any of this.
The political situation Ismail inherited was the chaotic aftermath of two centuries of Mongol-Timurid disintegration (Chapter 1).
Iran in 1500 was divided among competing Turcoman tribal confederations.

The Aq Qoyunlu (ak koy-OON-loo, "White Sheep") were the dominant power, a Sunni Turcoman confederation that had defeated their rivals the Kara Qoyunlu ("Black Sheep") in the 1460s and ruled most of western Iran, eastern Anatolia, and Mesopotamia from their capital at Tabriz.
The Aq Qoyunlu were going through their own succession crisis in the late 1490s, fragmenting into factions led by rival princes.

To the east, the Timurid princes still held Khorasan and parts of Afghanistan, while the Uzbeks under Muhammad Shaybani (shy-BAH-nee) were pushing south from Central Asia, threatening to absorb the Timurid lands.
To the west, the Ottoman Empire under Sultan Bayezid II watched the Iranian situation with mounting concern but did not yet intervene.

The Safaviyya order under Ismail's father Haydar had been on bad terms with the Aq Qoyunlu — Haydar had been killed fighting their allies — and the Aq Qoyunlu had imprisoned the boy Ismail's older brothers, eventually killing one of them.
When Ismail emerged from hiding in 1499, the Aq Qoyunlu had just collapsed into civil war and the moment was ripe.
He raised a Qizilbash army of perhaps 7,000 Turcoman cavalry, marched on the Aq Qoyunlu prince Alvand, defeated him at the Battle of Sharur in summer 1501, and entered Tabriz unopposed.
The first thing he did was declare Twelver Shia Islam the state religion.
This requires explanation.
Twelver Shia Islam is the dominant branch of Shia Islam today — the official religion of Iran, a majority in Iraq and Bahrain, a substantial minority in Lebanon, Pakistan, and elsewhere.

It takes its name from its core doctrine: that there were twelve divinely guided Imams (ee-MAHMS) descended from the Prophet Muhammad through his daughter Fatima and her husband Ali ibn Abi Talib, and that these twelve Imams are the rightful spiritual and political successors to the Prophet.
The First Imam was Ali himself (assassinated in 661 CE).

The line passes through his son Hussein (who was killed at the Battle of Karbala in 680 CE, the foundational martyrdom of Shia Islam) down to the Twelfth Imam, Muhammad al-Mahdi (al-MAH-dee), who is said to have gone into occultation (a state of hidden existence) in 874 CE and will return at the end of time as the Shia messiah figure to establish justice on earth.
Sunni Islam, the dominant branch comprising roughly 85–90% of Muslims worldwide, rejects this entire framework.

Sunnis hold that the proper succession to the Prophet was through the elected caliphs — Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman, and only then Ali — and that there is no special spiritual authority vested in Ali's descendants.
In 1501, Iran was, by the surviving evidence, somewhere around 80–90% Sunni.
There were Shia communities — Twelver, Ismaili, and other branches — scattered across the country, and certain regions like Qom and Mazandaran had significant Shia populations.

But Persia in general had been Sunni since the Arab conquest of the seventh century (Persian Empire Ch 10), and the major scholarly establishments at cities like Nishapur, Shiraz, and Isfahan were Sunni institutions teaching Sunni jurisprudence.
The Safavids' own ancestor Safi al-Din had been a Sunni Sufi (Chapter 1).
What Ismail proposed in 1501 was therefore not religious reform, not religious tolerance, not religious pluralism.
It was religious revolution.
The state would be Twelver Shia.

The official Friday prayer in every mosque would curse the first three caliphs (Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman) as usurpers of Ali's rightful succession — a practice known as tabarra (tah-BAR-ah, "dissociation") that Sunnis considered intolerable blasphemy.
Sunni religious scholars who refused to convert would be executed or driven into exile.
Public Sunni religious practice would be banned.
The country would be converted, on the timetable and by the methods Ismail's regime determined.
The conversion took the better part of a century to complete.
It was nowhere close to complete in 1501.
But the project began at Ismail's coronation, and it never stopped.
The methods of forced conversion deserve some attention, because they are often glossed over in popular accounts that emphasize Safavid art and architecture.
The basic mechanism was state violence.
Sunni judges, preachers, and scholars who refused to convert were killed.
Sunni mosques were converted to Shia mosques (which mostly meant adding the cursing of the first three caliphs to the Friday prayer and reorienting the educational curriculum).
Sunni religious endowments — properties whose income supported mosques, schools, and charitable institutions — were confiscated and redirected to Shia institutions.
Public displays of Sunni piety were banned and could be punished by death.
In some cities, particularly Tabriz and Herat (the latter conquered in 1510), Ismail's regime conducted mass executions of Sunni clerics and notables.

Death-toll estimates for Tabriz alone in the first few years of Safavid rule range widely in the scholarly literature — figures of 10,000 to 20,000 appear in various secondary accounts, with some scholars arguing for substantially lower numbers — but no surviving primary source supports a precise count, and the estimates that exist are extrapolations from chronicle descriptions of mass executions rather than firm tallies.
There was also a systematic ritual humiliation campaign.
Public preachers, called tabarra'iyyan ("cursers"), were sent through the streets of conquered cities cursing the first three caliphs.
Anyone who failed to join in could be killed on the spot.
The historian John Foran, drawing on contemporary sources, describes scenes of Sunni inhabitants being forced at swordpoint to publicly curse caliphs whom they had been raised to revere.

The cumulative psychological effect was enormous: within a generation, the social cost of being publicly Sunni had become so high that conversion was the only practical option for most of the urban population.
The conversion was therefore not a matter of theological persuasion.
It was a matter of state power applied systematically over decades.

The fact that it succeeded — that Iran is overwhelmingly Twelver Shia today, five centuries later, while Iraq and Anatolia (where Ismail's regime did not have the same staying power) remained majority Sunni — is testimony to how effective coercive religious conversion can be when sustained over multiple generations.
This is a hard thing for modern readers, raised on the principle of religious freedom, to absorb.

The Safavid conversion of Iran was one of the most violent religious transformations in early-modern history, comparable in coercion (if not in body count) to the Spanish Inquisition's persecution of Jewish and Muslim converts in the same period.
It is also the reason modern Iran exists.

The Safavid state created the Twelver Shia identity that distinguished Iranians from the Sunni Arab and Turkic populations around them, and that distinct identity is what made Iran a coherent national entity rather than just another fragment of the Sunni Muslim world.
The conversion is morally appalling and historically foundational at the same time.
The closest structural parallel to the Safavid project in this app is one that ran the opposite direction on coercion.

Ashoka of the Maurya dynasty (Maurya Empire Ch 5–6), eighteen centuries earlier, used the machinery of the Indian state to propagate Buddhism — a minority religion in third-century-BCE India — as a state-sponsored faith.

Ashoka, like Ismail, imported scholarly specialists (in his case Buddhist monks dispatched as missionaries to other regions), built new institutional infrastructure (rock and pillar edicts, monastery networks, pilgrimage circuits), and used royal authority to elevate a minority religion.

But Ashoka tried to persuade rather than coerce — his edicts emphasize moral example, tolerance of other traditions, and the merits of Buddhist ethics, with no equivalent of the tabarra'iyyan or the executions in Tabriz.

The Mauryan project did not survive Ashoka's dynasty: Buddhism remained important in India for several centuries but never became the majority faith, and within a few hundred years the Mauryan-era Buddhist establishment was in long decline.
The Safavid project, conducted with state violence applied systematically over generations, did stick.
The depressing inference is that for purposes of imposing a minority religion on a populated country, sustained coercion works better than persuasion.
The Safavid Iran of 2026 is overwhelmingly Shia.
The Buddhist India that Ashoka tried to build is not even a memory of itself.
The technical problem with the conversion was that there were almost no Twelver Shia scholars in Iran to staff the new state religion.

Twelver Shia Islam was a minority tradition with most of its scholarly centers outside Iran — at the shrine cities of Najaf and Karbala in Iraq (under Ottoman control), at Bahrain in the Persian Gulf, and at Jabal Amil (jah-BAL ah-MIL), a region in southern Lebanon that had been a Twelver Shia stronghold since the tenth century.
Iran itself had Shia minorities but no Twelver scholarly establishment of any size.
Ismail's regime needed jurists to issue rulings, preachers to staff mosques, theologians to argue against Sunni opponents, and teachers to train the next generation of Iranian Shia clerics.
The solution was importation.

Ismail and his successors paid Arab Shia scholars from Jabal Amil and Bahrain enormous sums to migrate to Iran, settle in the new Shia centers at Qom and Isfahan, and train the Iranian clerical class that would propagate the new state religion.
The migration began under Ismail himself and accelerated under Tahmasp I.

Some of the most influential Safavid-era Shia clerics — including Muhaqqiq al-Karaki (mu-HAH-kik al-kah-RAH-kee), one of the architects of Safavid Shia jurisprudence in the 1530s — were Lebanese Arabs imported for the purpose.

Their descendants intermarried with Iranian families and became the founding stock of Iran's Shia clerical establishment, the same establishment that would eventually produce Ayatollah Khomeini and the 1979 Islamic Revolution.
The mechanism is worth pausing on.
The forced conversion of Iran was not, in the first instance, a popular movement.
It was a state project that required imported labor — like building a factory before you have the workforce trained to operate it.

The Safavid state created the demand for Shia clerical expertise, the Lebanese and Bahraini scholars supplied it, and a native Iranian Shia clerical class was trained over the following century to staff the system.

By the late seventeenth century, the imported lineage had been effectively absorbed: the leading Safavid clerics were Iranian-born, trained in Iranian seminaries, and conducting their scholarship in Persian as well as Arabic.
The state religion had become genuinely Iranian.
But the seed had been imported.
Ismail's military conquests over the first decade of his reign extended the Safavid state across nearly the entire Iranian plateau.
In 1503 he defeated the last Aq Qoyunlu prince at the Battle of Hamadan and annexed western Iran.
In 1504 he took Yazd and Kerman in central Iran.
In 1507 he conquered the Caucasus principalities of Shirvan (where his grandfather Junayd had been killed).
In 1508 he marched into Iraq and captured Baghdad — bringing the holy Shia cities of Najaf (the burial place of Imam Ali) and Karbala (the martyrdom site of Imam Hussein) under Safavid control.
The Shia shrine cities became major Safavid pilgrimage destinations, lavishly patronized by the new regime.
In 1510 Ismail turned east and confronted the Uzbek leader Muhammad Shaybani, who had conquered the Timurid heartland and was threatening Iranian Khorasan.
The two armies met at the Battle of Merv (Merv — an oasis city in modern Turkmenistan) in November 1510.

Shaybani was defeated and killed; according to the bloodthirsty traditions of the period, Ismail had Shaybani's skull encased in gold and made into a drinking cup (the parallel to the Mongol drinking-from-skull tradition was probably deliberate — Ismail was claiming the political legacy of Genghis Khan as well as the religious legacy of Ali).
The Battle of Merv stabilized the eastern frontier briefly, and Ismail returned west to consolidate his rule.
By 1510 he ruled an empire that extended from the Euphrates to the Oxus, from the Caucasus to the Persian Gulf — roughly the Iranian heartland he would pass on to his son.
He had defeated the Aq Qoyunlu, the last Timurids, and the Uzbeks.
He had declared Iran Twelver Shia, begun the forced conversion, imported Lebanese clerics, conquered the Shia holy cities, and established Tabriz as the Safavid capital.
He was twenty-three years old.
What he had not yet done was face the Ottoman Empire, the rival Sunni Turkic power to his west.

The Ottomans had been watching Ismail's career with growing alarm, partly because of his religious revolution (which threatened Ottoman legitimacy as the leading Sunni state), partly because of his Qizilbash following inside Ottoman territory (the Turcoman tribes of eastern Anatolia were heavily Qizilbash and effectively pro-Safavid), and partly because of his sheer military success.
In 1512, the Ottoman throne passed to Selim I (seh-LEEM, called Yavuz — "the Grim" — in Ottoman tradition), who was determined to settle the Safavid problem by direct military action.
He would do so at Chaldiran in 1514, and the result is the subject of the next chapter.

Cross-civ check: Ismail's reign (1501–1524) overlaps almost exactly with the High Renaissance in Italy — Leonardo da Vinci, Michelangelo, Raphael, all working in Florence and Rome while Ismail was conquering Iran.
Martin Luther posted his Ninety-Five Theses in 1517, three years after Chaldiran, beginning the Protestant Reformation that would fracture European Christianity.
Cortés conquered the Aztec Empire (Aztec Empire Ch 8) in 1519–21.
The Mughal Empire in India was founded by Babur in 1526, two years after Ismail's death.
The early sixteenth century is one of the densest moments of imperial expansion and religious revolution in human history, and the Safavids are squarely in the middle of it.

chapters.title: Chaldiran and the Frontier
sentences: The defining moment of early Safavid history happened on a flat plain in eastern Anatolia, on August 23, 1514.
The battle was called Chaldiran (chal-dih-RAHN), and the Safavids lost it badly enough that the religious and political map of the Middle East was fixed for the next five centuries.
To understand Chaldiran, you have to understand what each side brought to the battlefield.
The Ottoman Empire under Sultan Selim I was, by 1514, the most militarily sophisticated state in the Islamic world.

It had spent the previous century building a standing army centered on the Janissaries (JAN-uh-sair-eez, from Turkish yeni çeri, "new soldiers") — a corps of professional infantry recruited as boys from Christian populations in the Balkans, raised as Muslims, trained from childhood in military discipline, and equipped with the latest gunpowder weapons.
The Janissaries were one of the world's first true standing professional armies.

They drilled in unit tactics, trained with muskets (matchlock firearms that had become reliable enough for battlefield use by the late fifteenth century), and were supported by the most advanced Ottoman field artillery — bronze cannons cast in centralized state foundries and dragged to battlefields on heavy wagons.

By 1514, the Ottomans had perfected a battlefield formation called the wagon-fort (Turkish tabur cengi) — a defensive perimeter of chained-together supply wagons, with cannons firing through gaps between them and Janissary musketeers firing from behind, that could withstand cavalry charges and shoot the attackers to pieces at distance.
The Safavid army under Shah Ismail was the opposite of all of this.
The Safavids had no infantry, no muskets, no artillery, and no wagon-forts.

Their entire military doctrine was built around the Qizilbash heavy cavalry charge: armored Turcoman horsemen, fanatically loyal, attacking in waves with lances and swords, relying on shock, mobility, and individual martial valor to break the enemy line.
This had worked brilliantly against Aq Qoyunlu, Timurid, and Uzbek opponents, who were equipped with similar weapons and fought similar battles.
It had not been tested against gunpowder.
Ismail also had a religious confidence problem.
His followers genuinely believed he was a near-divine figure who could not be defeated.
He had spent fifteen years winning every battle he fought.
Chronicle accounts describe Qizilbash warriors in 1514 boasting that they would brush aside the Ottoman cannons with their swords.

Ismail himself reportedly refused his commanders' suggestion to attack the Ottoman army before it could fortify its position — declaring that he would not strike like a brigand but would wait for Selim to deploy and meet him in fair battle.
This was the kind of decision a leader makes when he believes God is on his side and the result is preordained.
The two armies met at Chaldiran, on the plain east of Lake Van, on August 23, 1514.
Numbers are debated.
Modern estimates suggest the Ottomans fielded roughly 60,000 troops — about 12,000 of them Janissaries with muskets, another several thousand cannoneers, and the bulk in supporting cavalry.
The Safavids fielded perhaps 40,000 cavalry, almost all Qizilbash.
The Ottomans had numerical superiority and decisive technological superiority.
The Safavids had cavalry shock and religious fanaticism.
Selim deployed his army in the perfected wagon-fort formation: cannons and muskets behind chained wagons, Janissaries massed in the center, supporting cavalry on the wings.
Ismail attacked.
The Qizilbash cavalry charged in two wings, attempting to envelop the Ottoman army.
The right wing, led by Ismail himself, broke through the Ottoman left-wing cavalry and routed it — for a moment, the battle looked like another Safavid victory.
But the left Qizilbash wing, charging the Ottoman right where the Janissaries and cannons were concentrated, ran straight into massed musket fire and artillery at close range.
The Qizilbash cavalry — armored against arrows and swords, not against bullets — were torn apart.
The cannon fired, the matchlocks volleyed, and the charge broke before reaching the Ottoman line.
Within an hour the Qizilbash left wing was destroyed and the right wing, including Ismail himself, was caught in a counterattack.
Ismail was wounded, his horse killed under him, and only his bodyguards' efforts saved him from death or capture.
Several of his most senior Qizilbash commanders were killed.
His harem, traveling with the army in the customary fashion of Iranian kings, was captured — including one of his wives, Tajli Begum, who would later be ransomed back.
The Safavid army was driven from the field.

Selim's forces marched east unopposed, occupied Tabriz on September 7, 1514, looted the city, and held it for several weeks before withdrawing in late autumn because the Janissaries refused to winter so far from home.
The Safavids had lost the battle, lost the capital, and very nearly lost the dynasty.
Ismail recovered Tabriz after the Ottomans withdrew, but the psychological damage was permanent.
The aura of invincibility — the conviction among the Qizilbash that their sheikh-shah was divinely protected — was broken.
Ismail spent the last decade of his life in mourning, drinking heavily, and reportedly refusing to lead troops into battle again.

The chronicle accounts say he wore black, wrote melancholy poetry (he was an accomplished Turkic-language poet under the pen name Khata'i), and avoided the public ceremonies of kingship that had defined his early reign.
He died in 1524 at the age of thirty-six, leaving a ten-year-old son to inherit the throne.
Chaldiran's consequences ran far beyond the battlefield.
First, it fixed the Ottoman-Safavid frontier in eastern Anatolia roughly where it would remain for the next four centuries.
Eastern Anatolia stayed Ottoman; western Iran stayed Safavid; the border ran roughly along the modern Turkey-Iran boundary with some shifts to the north and south at various points.
This is one of the most stable frontiers in world history — the line drawn by Selim's victory in 1514 is still very nearly the line drawn on maps today.

The Ottoman Empire Ch 5 covers Selim's eastern campaign from the Ottoman side — for that narrative, Chaldiran secured the flank that allowed Selim to pivot south and conquer the Mamluks within three years.
Second, it established gunpowder as decisive in early-modern Middle Eastern warfare.
The Safavids had been a pre-gunpowder cavalry empire facing a gunpowder Janissary state, and they had been crushed.
Every successful Iranian government from Chaldiran forward would have to address this problem.
Tahmasp I (Ismail's son) made halting progress on adopting muskets and cannons.
Abbas I (Chapter 4) finally solved the problem by reorganizing the entire military around gunpowder weapons, with consequences that would let him recover most of what Ismail had lost.
Third, it ended the messianic phase of Safavid politics.
Ismail had presented himself as a near-divine figure, possibly the returning Hidden Imam, whose followers could not be killed.
Chaldiran demonstrated, in front of his entire army, that he could be defeated by ordinary mortals with better technology.
The Qizilbash continued to fight for the Safavids for another century, but the religious extremism that had powered the original conquest faded.
Subsequent Safavid Shahs would present themselves as legitimate Shia monarchs in the orthodox sense, descendants of the Prophet, defenders of the faith — but not as living gods.
The shift made the dynasty more institutionally sustainable.
It also made it more dependent on the Shia clerical establishment, which had its own ideas about the proper relationship between religion and state (Chapter 5).
Tahmasp I (TAH-mahsp, ruled 1524–1576) was ten years old when his father died, and his fifty-two-year reign was the longest of any Safavid king.
The early years were a Qizilbash regency: rival tribal factions fought each other for control of the boy-shah while Ottoman and Uzbek armies invaded the empire from west and east.
By the time Tahmasp emerged as effective ruler in his late teens, the situation was dire.
The Ottomans had occupied Tabriz repeatedly.
The Uzbeks under Ubaydullah Khan had launched five major invasions of Khorasan.
The state treasury was depleted, the military was demoralized, and the imported Lebanese clerics were just beginning the long work of building Iran's Shia establishment.
Tahmasp's contribution was survival.

He was not a great conqueror — he lost ground more often than he gained it — but he held the dynasty together long enough for the religious conversion to take root, the clerical establishment to develop, and the next generation of military and administrative reformers to come of age.

He fought the Ottomans through three major wars (1532–1555, with the Peace of Amasya finally stabilizing the frontier in 1555), held off repeated Uzbek invasions in the east, and managed the Qizilbash factions through a combination of intermarriage, executions, and strategic favoritism that prevented any single tribe from dominating the court.
His most consequential strategic decision was relocating the Safavid capital.
Tabriz had been the original capital under Ismail, but it was too close to the Ottoman frontier — captured and looted three times in the sixteenth century alone.
In 1548, Tahmasp moved the capital inland to Qazvin (kahz-VEEN), in the northwestern Iranian highlands south of the Alborz mountains.
Qazvin was further from Ottoman raiding range, defensible against Uzbek incursions, and located on the major trade routes connecting western Iran to Khorasan.
It would remain the capital for fifty years, until Abbas I moved it again to Isfahan in 1598.
The cultural and religious project also accelerated under Tahmasp.
The Shahnameh of Shah Tahmasp — one of the most spectacular illustrated manuscripts in the history of book art — was produced at the Tabriz court between roughly 1522 and 1535.
The Shahnameh ("Book of Kings") is the Persian national epic, written by the poet Ferdowsi around 1000 CE during the Samanid period (Persian Empire Ch 10).
It is over 50,000 couplets long, telling the mythological and historical story of Iranian kingship from the creation of the world to the Arab conquest.

Every Persian-speaking court before and after the Safavids commissioned its own illustrated copy of the Shahnameh — these manuscripts are some of the highest works of Persian art — but Tahmasp's was the most ambitious.

It contained 258 full-page miniature paintings by the leading masters of the Tabriz school, including the great Sultan Muhammad (one of the most influential Persian painters of any era), and the production employed dozens of calligraphers, illuminators, painters, and binders over more than a decade.
The completed manuscript was the size of a small piano, weighing roughly 75 pounds.
What is most interesting about Tahmasp's Shahnameh is what eventually happened to it.

Around 1568, Tahmasp gave the manuscript as a diplomatic gift to the Ottoman Sultan Selim II — sending the greatest illustrated manuscript of the Persian national epic to the son of the man who had defeated his father at Chaldiran.
The political message was complex: a peace offering, a display of cultural superiority, an acknowledgment that Persian culture transcended political enmity.
The manuscript stayed in the Ottoman imperial library until 1903, when it was sold to a private European collector.
It was eventually broken up — its individual paintings sold separately on the international art market through the twentieth century.
As of today, individual pages of the Tahmasp Shahnameh hang in museums from New York to London to Doha, with the bulk of the surviving folios in the Aga Khan Museum in Toronto.

The world's greatest illustrated Persian manuscript was partly disassembled by the international art trade in the twentieth century — a fate that says something about both the value of Persian art and the limits of preservation.
The Tabriz school of painting that produced this manuscript represented a major synthesis of earlier Persian painting traditions.

It combined the Herat school style developed under the Timurids in the late fifteenth century — the flat compositions, brilliant colors, and elaborate landscape backgrounds of Bihzad — with new innovations in figure drawing, narrative complexity, and emotional depth.

Persian miniature painting under the Safavids was one of the great visual arts of the early-modern world, comparable in sophistication to contemporary Italian Renaissance painting and operating on entirely different aesthetic principles.

The Mughal painting tradition that would shortly emerge in India under Akbar (after 1556) drew its initial training from Safavid masters — including two Tabriz painters, Mir Sayyid Ali and Abd al-Samad, who migrated to Delhi after Tahmasp's son tried to reverse the Shia conversion (see below).
Ismail II is one of the strangest episodes in the Safavid story.
He was Tahmasp's son, and after his father's death in 1576 he briefly attempted to reverse the Shia conversion entirely.

Ismail II had spent twenty years imprisoned by his father (the Safavids, like most early-modern dynasties, had a chronic problem with princely succession that they often solved by locking up the spare princes).
When he emerged from prison in 1576 and took the throne, he was bitter, paranoid, and apparently sympathetic to Sunni Islam.

During his eighteen-month reign he restored Sunni religious practice in many cities, persecuted Shia clerics who had prospered under his father, and reportedly considered formally restoring Sunni Islam as the state religion of Persia.
He never got the chance.

He was found dead in his palace in 1577 — officially of natural causes, almost certainly poisoned, probably by his sister Pari Khan Khanum or by Shia clerics who had every motive to prevent the reversal.
The episode is illuminating: in just seventy-five years, the Shia clerical establishment had become powerful enough that even a Safavid Shah could not openly oppose it without losing his life.
The conversion had taken root.
After Ismail II's death, his elder half-brother Muhammad Khudabanda was placed on the throne.

He was nearly blind and reportedly indecisive, and his eleven-year reign (1578–1588) descended into another round of Qizilbash factional warfare — exactly the kind of crisis the dynasty had faced after Ismail I's death seventy years earlier.

The Ottomans took advantage and launched a major invasion (the Ottoman-Safavid War of 1578–1590) that captured Tabriz, Azerbaijan, and the Caucasus, forcing the humiliating Treaty of Constantinople in 1590 in which the Safavids ceded enormous territory.

It was at this moment — the dynasty's lowest point since Chaldiran — that a sixteen-year-old prince named Abbas seized the throne from his blind father and began the most consequential reign in Safavid history.
Cross-civ check: the long sixteenth-century reigns of Ismail I and Tahmasp I (1501–1576) overlap with the rise of the Mughal Empire in India under Babur, Humayun, and Akbar.
Humayun himself spent fifteen years in Safavid exile after being driven from India by his brothers in the 1540s.

Tahmasp gave him refuge at Qazvin, supplied him with a 12,000-strong Safavid army to reclaim his throne, and required in exchange Humayun's nominal conversion to Shia Islam and the cession of the strategic city of Kandahar (in modern Afghanistan).

The Safavid-Mughal relationship would be marked by this combination of cultural intimacy (shared Persian language and high culture) and political competition (especially over Kandahar) for the next two centuries.

Meanwhile, the Ottoman Empire under Suleiman the Magnificent (1520–1566) reached its peak power, the Spanish Empire under Charles V and Philip II conquered the Americas and Portugal, the Tudor dynasty consolidated England, and Ivan the Terrible founded the Russian tsardom.
The sixteenth century is the moment when the early-modern world system took shape, and the Safavids were one of its major players.

chapters.title: Abbas the Great and Isfahan
sentences: In 1588, a sixteen-year-old prince named Abbas seized the Safavid throne from his blind father Muhammad Khudabanda with the help of a Qizilbash faction that wanted a strong ruler.

Over the next forty-one years, he transformed the Safavid Empire from a failing tribal confederation into one of the most sophisticated states in the early-modern world, recovered nearly all the territory lost to the Ottomans, broke the political power of the Qizilbash tribes that had founded the dynasty, and built a capital city that contemporaries called "half the world." Abbas I (ruled 1588–1629), known to history as Abbas the Great, is the Safavid ruler everyone has heard of, and for once the reputation is fully deserved.

He was a brilliant administrator, a ruthless politician (he had two of his own sons blinded and a third killed to prevent palace coups), a competent military commander, an obsessive city-builder, and a religious diplomat skilled enough to negotiate with the Catholic Pope while waging holy war against the Sunni Ottomans.
His reign is the apex of the dynasty and one of the great moments in Iranian history.
He inherited a disaster.

When Abbas took the throne in 1588, the Ottomans were occupying western Iran, the Uzbeks were raiding Khorasan, the treasury was empty, the Qizilbash were fighting each other, and the Mughals had taken Kandahar.

His first move was strategic retreat: in 1590, he signed the Treaty of Constantinople with the Ottomans on devastating terms — ceding most of Azerbaijan, the Caucasus, and parts of western Iran in exchange for a fifteen-year peace that gave him time to rebuild.
The treaty was humiliating.
It was also necessary.
Abbas needed the Ottoman pressure off his western frontier so he could deal with the Uzbeks, the Qizilbash, and the structural reorganization of the state.
What he did with that fifteen years is the foundation of everything that followed.
The first project was the ghulam revolution.
The Qizilbash tribal cavalry — the founding military of the dynasty (Chapter 1) — had become a chronic political problem.
The Qizilbash chiefs commanded their own tribal armies, governed major provinces as personal fiefs, intermarried with each other, and had repeatedly destabilized the state during succession crises.
They had also been crushed at Chaldiran (Chapter 3) and were no longer competitive against Ottoman gunpowder armies.

Abbas needed a military that was loyal to the crown rather than to tribal chiefs, equipped with modern weapons rather than lances, and answerable to the central state rather than to provincial power blocs.
The solution was the ghulam (GHOO-lahm) army.

The word ghulam means "slave" or "servant" in Arabic, but the institution it referred to was something specific to the Islamic world: a military and administrative corps recruited from non-Muslim populations conquered or captured at the frontier, converted to Islam, trained from childhood in royal service, and made personally loyal to the monarch.
The Ottomans had been doing this for two centuries with their Janissaries, recruited from Christian boys in the Balkans (Chapter 3).
Abbas adapted the model.
The Safavid ghulam corps was recruited primarily from the Caucasus — Georgians, Armenians, Circassians — captured in raids, converted to Shia Islam, and trained in royal palace schools.
Some came as boys taken in the devshirme-style boy levies; many more came as captives from the Caucasus campaigns Abbas conducted in the 1600s and 1610s.
The captured boys were trained in horsemanship, military discipline, palace etiquette, Persian language, and Shia religion.
The most promising were placed in elite musketeer or cavalry units.
The most administratively talented were promoted to court positions, eventually rising to provincial governorships, military commands, and even the office of vizier (chief minister).
This was the structural innovation that made the ghulam system work: ghulams could not pass their offices to their sons in the way Qizilbash chiefs did.
They served at the king's pleasure, owed everything to royal favor, and had no tribal power base to fall back on.
The Georgian boy who became commander of the Safavid army served because Abbas had made him commander, and his Georgian relatives in their Caucasus villages had no say in the matter.

This is exactly the kind of personal-loyalty mechanism that early-modern monarchs across Eurasia were building into their armies and bureaucracies — Janissaries in the Ottoman Empire, military slaves of the Mamluk sultanate before Ottoman conquest, eunuch administrators in Ming China — and the Safavid version worked with particular effectiveness.
The most famous example is Allahverdi Khan (ah-LAH-ver-dee), a Georgian boy captured in the Caucasus, converted, trained in palace service, and promoted by Abbas in the 1590s.
Allahverdi rose to become commander-in-chief of the Safavid army, governor of the strategic province of Fars, and one of Abbas's most trusted advisors.

He led the major Safavid victory over the Ottomans at Sufiyan in 1605 (which began the recovery of lost territory), recaptured Kandahar from the Mughals, and built the Si-o-se-pol bridge in Isfahan (more on which below).
When he died in 1613, he was buried in a magnificent tomb at Mashhad, his career a model of what the ghulam system could achieve.

The ghulam corps grew to roughly 40,000 men by the mid-seventeenth century — a substantial standing army, equipped with muskets and cannons, drilled in modern infantry tactics, supported by artillery, and answerable directly to the Shah.
The traditional Qizilbash tribal cavalry continued to exist as a secondary military force, but they no longer dominated the political system.
Abbas had created a centralized monarchy on the early-modern European model, with a professional army loyal to the crown rather than to feudal lords.
This was the structural foundation of everything else.
The military reform produced almost immediate strategic results.

In 1598, Abbas turned east and crushed the Uzbeks under their leader Din Muhammad Khan at the Battle of Herat, recovering Khorasan and the city of Herat (which had been under Uzbek occupation since 1588).
In 1603, he launched the major Ottoman campaign that recovered most of the territory lost in 1590.
The new Safavid army, with its musket-armed ghulam infantry and its bronze cannons, defeated the Ottomans at Sufiyan (1605), recaptured Tabriz, then Yerevan and the Caucasus.
The Treaty of Nasuh Pasha (1612) and a follow-up treaty in 1618 restored most of the pre-1578 Safavid frontier.
In 1622, with English East India Company naval assistance, Abbas captured the strategic Portuguese-held island of Hormuz at the entrance of the Persian Gulf (Chapter 6).
In 1623, he captured Baghdad from the Ottomans, restoring Safavid control of the Shia holy cities of Najaf and Karbala for the first time since 1534.
In 1624 and again in 1638, the Mughals and Safavids fought the chronic war over Kandahar that would continue into the next reign.
Within three decades, the dynasty that had been on the verge of collapse in 1588 had recovered nearly all its territory and projected power from the Caucasus to Kandahar.
The transformation was complete by the late 1610s and the building program that crowned it was already underway.
The capital of the new Safavid state was Isfahan.
Isfahan is in central Iran, on the banks of the Zayanderud (zah-yahn-deh-ROOD, the "life-giving river" that flows out of the Zagros mountains and disappears into the central desert).
It is one of the oldest cities in Iran, a pre-Islamic Sasanian city that had served as a regional capital under the Seljuks and other medieval dynasties.
It is centrally located, defensible, with reliable water supply and good agricultural surroundings — strategic strengths that Tabriz and Qazvin could not match.
In 1598, Abbas formally moved the Safavid capital from Qazvin to Isfahan and began the most ambitious urban building program of the Safavid era.
The project would consume thirty years and produce one of the most beautiful cities in the early-modern world.
The centerpiece was a vast new public square called Naqsh-e Jahan (nahkhsh-eh jah-HAHN, "Image of the World").

The square is approximately 1,750 feet long and 525 feet wide — the dimensions are deliberately chosen to be larger than any comparable public space in the early-modern world. (For context: Naqsh-e Jahan is roughly twice the size of St.

Peter's Square in Rome, which is one of the largest comparable spaces in Renaissance Europe, and roughly seven times the size of Trafalgar Square in London.) The square was used for royal ceremonies, public festivals, military parades, polo matches, and the everyday commerce of the bazaar.

The four sides were architecturally unified: the Shah Mosque at the south end, the Sheikh Lotfollah Mosque on the east, the Ali Qapu palace on the west, and the entrance to the Grand Bazaar on the north.
Two-story arcaded shops surrounded the entire perimeter.
The square was the political, religious, commercial, and ceremonial heart of the empire, expressed in a single architectural composition.
Each of the four anchor buildings deserves attention.

The Shah Mosque (now called Imam Mosque — every reference to "the Shah" in Iranian public space was renamed after the 1979 Islamic Revolution) is a massive congregational mosque built between 1611 and 1629.

It is one of the most spectacular examples of Persian Islamic architecture: a four-iwan plan (a central courtyard with vaulted recesses opening on each side), a soaring 174-foot turquoise dome, twin minarets at the front entrance (and another pair at the rear), and several acres of polychrome tilework covering nearly every interior surface.

The tilework alone is one of the great achievements of Islamic decorative art — a technique called haft rang (HAHFT RANG, "seven colors") in which polychrome glazes were fired onto large tile panels rather than assembled from small geometric pieces.
This was an innovation specific to Safavid tilework and dramatically accelerated construction of large buildings.

The Shah Mosque used haft rang panels at monumental scale to achieve naturalistic floral patterns, calligraphic inscriptions, and abstract geometric designs that could not have been produced quickly by traditional mosaic techniques.

The mosque also has a famous quirk: the entrance portal is oriented to the public square, but the prayer hall must be oriented to Mecca (the direction Muslims face during prayer, called the qibla, KIB-lah).
The two orientations differ by about 45 degrees.

The architects solved this by building a 45-degree rotation into the entrance vestibule, so that visitors enter from the square, pass through a transitional space, and emerge in the prayer hall facing Mecca.
The transition is so smoothly handled that most visitors don't notice it.
The mathematician Sheikh Bahai (Chapter 5) reportedly calculated the precise qibla direction.
The Sheikh Lotfollah Mosque on the east side of the square is a smaller but more architecturally refined building — Abbas's private royal chapel, never used for public Friday prayer.
It was built between 1603 and 1619 and is considered by many specialists the apex of Safavid decorative art.
The exterior dome is a distinctive cream color (rather than the usual Safavid turquoise) that shifts toward pink at sunrise and sunset.
The interior tilework is more intricate than the Shah Mosque's, with a mesmerizing geometric ceiling pattern radiating from a central rosette.
The mosque has no minaret and no courtyard — both omissions deliberate, since this was a private chapel, not a public mosque.
The Ali Qapu palace ("Sublime Gate") on the west side of the square was the imperial palace, a six-story tower with an open wooden terrace on the second level overlooking the square.
Abbas and his successors used the terrace to watch polo matches, military parades, and the daily life of Naqsh-e Jahan from a position of imperial elevation.

The upper floors contained reception rooms, a music chamber decorated with elaborate plaster niches cut in the shapes of vessels (designed to enhance acoustics for court concerts), and private royal apartments.
The palace functioned as both a residence and a stage from which the Shah's relationship to the public square could be visually performed.
The Grand Bazaar entrance on the north side connected the square to the main commercial district of Isfahan, a covered market that stretched for miles through the old city.

The bazaar was the economic engine of the capital, housing thousands of shops, dozens of caravanserais (the merchant inns where long-distance traders lodged with their goods), workshops for textiles and metalwork and ceramics, religious schools (madrasas), public baths, and tea houses.
The design of the entire complex was a piece of political theater.
The Shah Mosque represented religion.
The Sheikh Lotfollah Mosque represented the dynasty's private piety.
The Ali Qapu represented royal power.
The bazaar represented commerce.

The square itself was the unifying public space where all four met, where the Shah could be seen by his subjects and his subjects could see each other in the architectural setting their ruler had built for them.

It is one of the most successful pieces of urban design in the early-modern world, and it is essentially intact today — a UNESCO World Heritage site that you can still walk through, with the same buildings the same people in roughly the same spatial relationship Abbas designed five centuries ago.
The Si-o-se-pol bridge (see-oh-seh-POHL, "Bridge of Thirty-Three Arches"), built by Allahverdi Khan around 1602, completed the architectural ensemble of central Isfahan.

It crossed the Zayanderud on a long stone causeway with — as the name says — thirty-three arches, providing infrastructure (the only major bridge over the river), water management (the bridge could be partially dammed to control river flow for irrigation), and social space (the upper promenade became one of Isfahan's favorite gathering places).

The Khwaju bridge (kah-WAH-joo), built later in 1650 under Abbas II, completed the pair: a similar but more decorative stone bridge with teahouse rooms built into its piers, used as a pleasure garden and royal viewing pavilion as well as a crossing.
The Safavid bridges of Isfahan are some of the great pieces of early-modern infrastructure.
They are also some of the most photographed buildings in modern Iran, the icons of the Safavid golden age that everyone who has been to Isfahan has stood on at sunset.
Isfahan grew enormously under Abbas and his successors.

The city's population, perhaps 80,000 when Abbas moved his capital there in 1598, reached an estimated 500,000 to 600,000 by the 1620s — making Isfahan one of the largest cities in the world, comparable to Istanbul, Beijing, and (just barely) London and Paris.

Contemporary census records (the figures are debated but the order of magnitude is reliable) describe the city containing 162 mosques, 48 religious schools, 1,802 caravanserais, and 273 public baths — a staggering urban infrastructure for a pre-industrial city.
The proverb that contemporaries coined — Isfahan nesf-e jahan ast, "Isfahan is half the world" — was hyperbole, but it captured something real about the scale and beauty of what Abbas had built.
The proverb also captured something about the city's cultural diversity.

By 1620, Isfahan was home to Iranian Persians, Turkic-speaking Qizilbash, Caucasian Georgian and Armenian ghulams, an Armenian Christian merchant community at New Julfa (Chapter 6), Indian Hindu traders working the Silk Road routes, English and Dutch East India Company representatives at their trading posts, occasional Catholic missionaries (Carmelites and Augustinians) sent by the Pope, and Jewish communities both old and new.
The city was as cosmopolitan as any in the world.
The proverb that the ulama probably found most uncomfortable about all this is that "half the world" included a lot of non-Shia.
Abbas died in 1629 at the age of fifty-eight, having reigned for forty-one years and presided over the recovery of his dynasty and the building of his capital.
He was buried at Kashan (in central Iran) rather than at one of the great Shia shrines, in a relatively modest tomb whose lack of ostentation was probably deliberate.

He had been one of the great early-modern monarchs — comparable in achievement to Suleiman the Magnificent of the Ottomans (whom he had matched militarily and surpassed culturally; Ottoman Empire Ch 5 covers Süleyman's reign and the parallel achievements in military recovery, architectural patronage, and administrative consolidation), to Akbar of the Mughals (his eastern rival, whose own architectural projects at Fatehpur Sikri were less ambitious than Naqsh-e Jahan), and to his contemporaries Elizabeth I of England and Henry IV of France in Europe.
He had also done something none of those monarchs had done: he had personally killed or blinded all of his potential heirs, leaving the throne to a grandson whose competence was untested.
That grandson was Safi I, and his reign would begin the long Safavid decline.

Cross-civ check: Abbas's reign (1588–1629) overlaps with the Elizabethan and Jacobean periods in England (Shakespeare's career runs almost exactly parallel to Abbas's reign), the late Ming Dynasty in China (about to collapse to the Qing in 1644), the Mughal golden age under Akbar and Jahangir in India, the Ottoman classical age under Murad III and Mehmed III, and the European wars of religion that would culminate in the Thirty Years War (1618–1648).
Abbas was in active diplomatic correspondence with Pope Clement VIII, King Philip III of Spain, Queen Elizabeth I of England, and the Mughal emperor Akbar.

The Safavid Empire under Abbas was a fully integrated participant in the early-modern world system, exchanging silk for silver, ambassadors for ambassadors, and ideas for ideas, with civilizations stretching from western Europe to East Asia.

chapters.title: The Shia Clergy and the Isfahan School
sentences: The most consequential thing the Safavids built was not Naqsh-e Jahan Square.

It was the institutional structure of Twelver Shia Islam — the clerical hierarchy, the seminary system, the relationship between religion and state — that emerged in Iran during the seventeenth century and has continued to define Iranian Islam to the present day.
This is the chapter that connects the Safavid past to modern Iran.
The buildings of Isfahan are tourist attractions; the institutions described in this chapter are still running.
To understand what the Safavid clerical system became, you need to understand the doctrinal innovation at its core: the concept of the mujtahid.

Twelver Shia theology holds that the only fully legitimate religious-political authority on earth is the Twelfth Imam, the Hidden Imam Muhammad al-Mahdi, who went into occultation in 874 CE and will return at the end of time as the Shia messiah (Chapter 2).

In the absence of the Imam, Shia communities need some form of religious guidance for everyday matters — questions of religious law, ritual, ethics, and theology — that the Imam himself cannot answer because he is hidden.

The early Twelver Shia tradition handled this through scholarly preservation of the Imams' teachings: collections of hadith (hah-DEETH — narrations attributed to the Prophet and the Imams), commentaries on those hadith, and direct application of the Imams' rulings to new questions by scholars who memorized the texts.

This was the Akhbari (akh-BAH-ree, from akhbar, "reports" or "traditions") approach to Shia jurisprudence: religious guidance comes from the transmitted reports of the Imams, applied as directly as possible, with no independent reasoning by the contemporary scholar.
The competing approach was Usuli (oo-SOO-lee, from usul al-fiqh, "principles of jurisprudence").

The Usuli school held that contemporary scholars — qualified by training in legal reasoning, Arabic grammar, theology, and philosophy — could exercise ijtihad (ij-tih-HAHD, "independent reasoning") to derive new rulings from the foundational sources (Quran, hadith, consensus, reason) when the Imam's transmitted teachings did not directly address a contemporary question.
A scholar qualified to exercise ijtihad was called a mujtahid (mooj-TAH-hid).
And — crucially — Usuli theory held that ordinary Shia Muslims should follow the rulings of a living mujtahid, since the dead masters could not respond to new circumstances.
The implications of the Usuli position were enormous.

If ordinary Shia must follow a living mujtahid, and if mujtahids are qualified by training rather than appointment, then the senior mujtahids of any given era effectively constitute a religious authority structure independent of the state.
The mujtahid hierarchy is not appointed by the king.
It is not subordinate to the king.
It is parallel to the king, with its own legitimacy derived from religious training and recognized scholarly competence.

The eventual Usuli victory — completed in the eighteenth century, after the Safavid dynasty had ended — created the marja-i taqlid (mar-JAH-ee tahk-LEED, "source of emulation") system that defines modern Shia Islam.
The most senior living mujtahids are called marjas.
Each Shia Muslim formally chooses a marja to follow.
The marja issues binding rulings on questions of religious practice, law, and ethics.

The marjas collectively constitute a religious hierarchy with enormous social, financial, and political power — the power that ultimately enabled Ayatollah Khomeini, a senior marja, to lead the 1979 Iranian Revolution and establish the Islamic Republic of Iran.
The mujtahid system did not exist in this form when Ismail conquered Tabriz in 1501.
It was built, gradually and contentiously, over the next two centuries — primarily by Lebanese Arab clerics imported by the Safavids (Chapter 2) and their Iranian disciples.

The Akhbari-Usuli debate was not settled during the Safavid period; the Akhbaris were probably the dominant faction through most of the seventeenth century, with the Usuli school gaining strength in the late period and triumphing definitively in the eighteenth century at the shrine cities of Najaf and Karbala.

But the institutional infrastructure that made the eventual Usuli victory possible — the seminaries, the patron-shrine networks, the sponsored translations of Arabic theological texts into Persian — was Safavid construction.

The institutional center of seventeenth-century Iranian Shia learning was Isfahan, the Safavid capital, where Abbas and his successors built or expanded a network of religious schools (madrasas) attached to the major mosques.

The most famous were the Madrasa-ye Chahar Bagh (Four Gardens School, completed 1714 — covered in Chapter 7) and the Madrasa-ye Jadda-ye Buzurg (Great Grandmother School, founded by Shah Soleyman's mother).
