These schools trained the leading Iranian Shia clerics of the age, hosted advanced philosophical and theological debate, and produced the textual scholarship that would define Twelver Shia Islam for the following centuries.
The phenomenon centered on Isfahan was rich enough to deserve its own name in the historical literature: the School of Isfahan.
It is one of the great moments in Islamic intellectual history.
The School of Isfahan was a philosophical movement that synthesized three earlier traditions.
The first was Peripatetic philosophy — the Aristotelian tradition transmitted through medieval Islamic philosophers like Ibn Sina (Avicenna, 980–1037) and al-Farabi (c. 872–950).

The second was Illuminationism (Persian ishraqi) — a mystical-philosophical school founded by Suhrawardi (sue-rah-WAR-dee, executed in 1191) that combined Aristotelian logic with Neoplatonic mystical insights about the nature of light, the structure of reality, and the soul's ascent to higher levels of being.
The third was Sufi mysticism, the contemplative tradition we met in Chapter 1.
The School of Isfahan tried to synthesize all three.

The result was a sophisticated philosophical system — at once rationalist (using Aristotelian logical analysis), mystical (insisting that the highest knowledge comes through direct intellectual intuition rather than discursive reasoning), and orthodox Shia (interpreting the Imams as cosmic principles as well as historical figures).
It is one of the most ambitious philosophical systems in the history of Islamic thought, and it has been continuously studied at Iranian seminaries from the seventeenth century to the present.
The story of the school is best told through the man who was driven out of it.

Mulla Sadra (mool-LAH SAH-dra, full name Sadr al-Din Muhammad ibn Ibrahim Shirazi, c. 1572–1640) is the school's deepest philosopher and probably its most influential — and also the figure whose career most clearly exposes the tension at the heart of Safavid intellectual life.
Born in Shiraz, he came to Isfahan as a young man to study under the leading philosophers of the new capital.

He did the work expected of him, then began to push beyond it — and was driven out of the city, reportedly by hostile clerics who considered his metaphysics heretical and his teachings dangerous to public piety.
He withdrew to the small village of Kahak, near Qom, where he lived in semi-rural retreat for somewhere between seven and twelve years (the exact dates are uncertain).
It was at Kahak, far from the patronage and the persecution of the capital, that he wrote most of his major work.

He was eventually rehabilitated enough to be invited back to Shiraz to teach, but the exile was the formative episode of his career and a perfect illustration of the chapter's central argument: that the same Safavid state that funded the most ambitious philosophical synthesis in early-modern Islam also produced a clerical establishment increasingly able to exile the philosophers it sponsored.

The philosophy that Mulla Sadra developed during his Kahak years was a metaphysical system called al-hikma al-muta'aliya ("Transcendent Theosophy") whose central doctrine was the primacy of existence over essence.

The technical philosophy is hard to translate (Sadra's Arabic prose is famously difficult), but the core insight is roughly this: reality is fundamentally about existence, the dynamic process of being itself, rather than about the static essences or definitions of things.

Existence has gradations — different levels of intensity — and beings move through these gradations in a continuous process of "substantial motion." The soul ascends through levels of being toward unity with God; the world is constantly in flux; the static categories of older Aristotelian philosophy mislead us about the nature of what is.

Mulla Sadra's system has often been compared, within the Islamic philosophical tradition, to the great synthesizing systems of medieval Christianity (Aquinas) and modern European philosophy (Hegel) — figures whose works similarly tried to weld inherited rationalist traditions to a new theological or historical vision.
Mulla Sadra did not produce his system out of nothing.

He was the culmination of a generational project, and the two figures who set up his work need to be introduced — partly because their careers show what it looked like to operate inside the Isfahan establishment rather than outside it.
Mir Damad (meer dah-MAHD, c. 1561–1631) was Sadra's most important teacher and the founding figure of the Isfahan school proper.

A philosopher-theologian who combined Aristotelian metaphysics with Shia theology in elaborate Arabic treatises, he wrote in deliberately obscure prose that earned him the nickname "the Third Teacher" — Aristotle being the First, al-Farabi the Second.

Mir Damad's most famous innovation was the concept of huduth-i dahri — eternal creation in time — a metaphysical position that tried to reconcile the Aristotelian doctrine of the eternity of the world with the Islamic doctrine of divine creation.
The argument is technical and not easily summarized, but it set the philosophical agenda Sadra would inherit and radicalize.
Mir Damad himself was a court favorite who died peacefully in royal service.
The students he trained — Mulla Sadra preeminently — would not all be so fortunate.
Sheikh Bahai (BAH-hai, full name Baha al-Din Muhammad ibn Husayn al-Amili, 1547–1621) was the other senior figure of the same generation, the polymath par excellence of the Safavid court.
He was Lebanese in origin (one of the Jabal Amil clerics imported during the conversion period — Chapter 2), and he served Shah Abbas as both religious advisor and practical engineer.

His range was extraordinary: he was a senior Shia theologian, a mathematician, an astronomer, an architect, a hydraulic engineer, a poet (in both Persian and Arabic), and a designer of practical infrastructure.
He calculated the qibla orientation of the Shah Mosque (Chapter 4).
He designed the irrigation system that distributed water across Isfahan.
He wrote treatises on arithmetic, algebra, astronomy, and theology that were standard textbooks at Iranian seminaries for centuries.

He may have been the most learned individual of his century in the Islamic world, comparable to figures like Galileo and Kepler in Europe — and like them, equally at home in religion and in natural science.

Bahai's career is the inside-track version of what Sadra's might have been: a Lebanese cleric absorbed seamlessly into the Safavid establishment, employed simultaneously by the dynasty and by the religious hierarchy, dying in royal favor.
The contrast across these three biographies is the chapter's argument in miniature.
Mir Damad and Sheikh Bahai were establishment figures whose work the regime patronized and whose orthodoxy was unimpeachable.

Sadra was their student, took their methods further, and was driven into rural exile by the next generation of clerics — the same clerical establishment the Safavids had built up to legitimize their rule, now strong enough to exile the empire's greatest philosopher.
The same state that paid Lebanese clerics to publicly curse the first three caliphs (Chapter 2) also paid Mir Damad to teach and then tolerated the exile of his most brilliant pupil.
The contradiction was real.

It was also a preview: the clerical establishment that could exile Mulla Sadra in the 1610s was the same establishment that, under Majlisi at the end of the century, would be powerful enough to dictate religious policy to the dynasty itself.
The Isfahan school and the Gundishapur precedent.
This was not the first time something like the Isfahan synthesis had happened on Iranian soil.

The Sasanian-era Gundishapur Academy (Persian Empire Ch 9), founded in the third century CE and at its height under Khosrow I in the sixth, had performed almost exactly the same function — synthesizing Greek Aristotelian philosophy, Indian mathematics and medicine, and the Zoroastrian religious tradition into a working intellectual system that would outlast the dynasty that funded it.

The Isfahan school, a thousand years later and under a different state religion, was the same civilizational phenomenon recurring: an Iranian dynasty using state patronage to weld together imported philosophical traditions (here Aristotelian, Neoplatonic, Sufi) with the dominant religion of the moment, producing an intellectual synthesis that would survive the dynasty's fall.
Two empires apart, the same Iranian habit of building synthesizing intellectual institutions at the heart of the state.
Outside the philosophical schools, the Safavid clerical project also developed the shrine pilgrimage network that became the geographic infrastructure of Iranian Shia identity.
Sunni Islam has Mecca and Medina as its two great pilgrimage sites — both controlled, after 1517, by the Sunni Ottomans.

Twelver Shia Islam has Mecca and Medina too (the Prophet himself is foundational to Shia as much as to Sunni faith), but it also has additional shrine sites associated with the twelve Imams and their families.

Most of these sites are in Iraq: Najaf (the burial place of Imam Ali, the First Imam), Karbala (the martyrdom site of Imam Hussein, the Third Imam), Kazimiyah (in Baghdad, the burial place of the Seventh and Ninth Imams), and Samarra (the disappearance site of the Twelfth Imam).
All four are under Ottoman control through most of the Safavid period.
The Safavids therefore developed parallel shrine networks inside Iran.
The most important is the shrine of Imam Reza (the Eighth Imam, who died in 818 CE) at Mashhad (mahsh-HAD) in northeastern Iran.

The shrine had existed for centuries, but the Safavids — beginning under Tahmasp I and continuing through Abbas I and his successors — expanded it into one of the largest religious complexes in the Islamic world.
The shrine acquired massive endowments, multiple courtyards, monumental gateways, gold-plated minarets, and elaborate tilework.
By the late Safavid period, Mashhad was effectively the alternative Mecca for Iranian Shia, with hundreds of thousands of pilgrims visiting annually.
Qom (KOHM), in north-central Iran, was developed as the second great Iranian shrine city.
Qom is the burial place of Fatima Masumeh, the sister of Imam Reza, who died there in 816 CE.

The Safavids expanded the shrine, built religious schools (the Qom hawza, hahw-ZAH — the seminary network) that drew students from across the Shia world, and established Qom as the center of Iranian Shia religious learning.

The Qom hawza became the institutional descendant of the older shrine seminaries at Najaf and Karbala (which remained more prestigious through most of the period but were under Ottoman control), and it has grown continuously since.
The Qom hawza is where Ayatollah Khomeini was trained in the twentieth century.
It is where most senior Iranian clerics still receive their religious education today.
The institutional continuity from the seventeenth-century Safavid expansion to the modern Islamic Republic is essentially unbroken.
A third major shrine, at Ardabil in northwestern Iran, was the original Safavid family shrine — the burial site of Sheikh Safi al-Din himself (Chapter 1).

Abbas I expanded the Ardabil complex enormously, donating a massive library of manuscripts and decorative objects (including the famous Ardabil Carpet, Chapter 6), and the shrine became a pilgrimage destination connecting Safavid dynastic legitimacy to the religious identity of the country.
The Ardabil shrine survives today and is also a UNESCO World Heritage site.
The point of the shrine network was to create a religious geography that was authentically Iranian, controlled by the Safavid state, and not dependent on Sunni-controlled Arab Iraq or Arabia.
Mashhad replaced Mecca for Iranian Shia who could not (or would not) make the journey to Sunni-controlled Hejaz.
Qom became the seminary city.
Ardabil sanctified the dynasty itself.

The cumulative effect was to ground Twelver Shia Islam in Iranian soil — to make Shia identity geographically Iranian rather than diasporic — in a way that helped the religion take root permanently after the dynasty that had imposed it was gone.
The relationship between the clergy and the state was always complicated, and it grew steadily more tense as the seventeenth century progressed.

The early Safavid clerical class had been almost entirely a state creation: imported Lebanese scholars paid by the regime, granted Iranian land and offices, and supporting the dynasty's claim to legitimate Shia kingship.

By the mid-seventeenth century, a native Iranian Shia clerical establishment had developed enough independence to start asserting its own theological positions — including, increasingly, the position that the Safavid Shah was not himself a religious authority but only a temporal ruler who served the religious authority of the senior mujtahids.

The most assertive figure in this development was Muhammad Baqir Majlisi (mahj-LEE-see, 1627–1699), who served as the Shaykh al-Islam (the chief religious official) of Isfahan under the late Safavids and became the most influential cleric of the century.
Majlisi was a militant Akhbari traditionalist who pushed Iranian Shia Islam in a more legalistic, more orthodox, less philosophically open direction.

He persecuted Sufi orders (which he considered heretical), restricted Iranian Christians and Zoroastrians, suppressed popular religious practices that did not align with strict Shia legalism, and produced an enormous compilation of Shia hadith called Bihar al-Anwar ("Oceans of Lights") — 110 volumes, the most ambitious Shia hadith collection ever assembled.
The Bihar al-Anwar is still consulted today as a primary reference work in Shia jurisprudence.

Majlisi's career marks the moment when the Iranian Shia clergy became fully institutionally independent of the state — a class of religious specialists with their own legal authority, financial endowments, educational institutions, and popular following, capable of dictating religious policy to a Safavid Shah who increasingly needed their support to legitimate his rule.

The pattern that would dominate modern Iran — a king (or president) constantly negotiating with senior clerics for religious legitimacy — was established under the late Safavids and has continued, with various interruptions, ever since.
The Safavid Shahs of the late seventeenth century — Soleyman I and Sultan Husayn (Chapter 7) — were unable or unwilling to push back against this clerical independence.

They allowed Majlisi and his successors to set religious policy, restrict cultural life, and persecute non-orthodox communities, without the kind of state pushback that earlier Safavid rulers might have applied.
The result was a long-term shift in the balance of power between the dynasty and the clerical establishment that the Safavids themselves had created.
By 1700, the Iranian Shia clergy was strong enough to outlast the Safavid dynasty entirely.
When the Afghans destroyed the Safavid state in 1722 (Chapter 8), the clerical establishment survived.
When Nader Shah deposed the last Safavid in 1736 (Chapter 8) and tried to broker a Shia-Sunni rapprochement, the clerical establishment opposed him and won.
When the Qajar dynasty replaced the short-lived Afsharids in the late eighteenth century, they had to negotiate with the clergy on the clergy's terms.
When the Pahlavi dynasty tried in the twentieth century to modernize Iran on a secular model, the clergy organized the resistance that eventually overthrew them.
The chain runs from Majlisi to Khomeini, and the institutional infrastructure was Safavid construction.
The intellectual and religious flowering of seventeenth-century Iran was therefore not a side product of the Safavid state but its most enduring legacy.
The buildings of Isfahan are spectacular but they are buildings.

The clerical hierarchy, the seminary system, the legal-philosophical traditions, the shrine networks, the relationship between religion and state — these are still running, four centuries later, governing the lives of eighty million Iranians and influencing Shia Muslims worldwide.
The Safavids declared Twelver Shia Islam the state religion in 1501 because it served their political interests.
Once established, the Shia identity outgrew them.
By 1700, the Shia clerical class was strong enough to be independent of any specific dynasty.
By 1979, it was strong enough to make itself the dynasty.
This is the deepest meaning of the Safavid revolution.
They did not merely change Iran's religion.

They built an institutional structure that turned religion into a permanent feature of Iranian state-society relations, a feature with its own self-perpetuating logic, capable of outlasting any of the regimes that nominally controlled it.
The most important Safavid creation is the one that does not appear on any tourist itinerary.

Cross-civ check: the seventeenth-century philosophical flowering at Isfahan is contemporary with the Scientific Revolution in Europe — Galileo, Descartes, Newton, all working at roughly the same time as Mulla Sadra.

The two intellectual revolutions were operating on entirely different premises: European thinkers were building the experimental methodology of modern natural science, while the Isfahan school was extending the Aristotelian-Neoplatonic-Sufi tradition into new metaphysical territory.
The relationship between the two has been debated since the nineteenth century.
The European tradition produced the technological transformation that would eventually overtake the Islamic world; the Iranian tradition produced a metaphysical depth that European philosophy lacked.
Each got something the other did not.
The world would have been different if they had met more directly.

chapters.title: Trade, Carpets, and the World
sentences: The Safavid Empire under Abbas I was not just an Iranian state.

It was a node in the early-modern world economy, exporting silk and carpets to Europe, importing silver from the Spanish Americas, hosting English and Dutch trading companies, and managing diplomatic correspondence with Catholic Habsburgs as well as Protestant Stuarts.

This chapter is about the commercial face of the Safavid state — the silk monopoly, the Armenian merchant network at New Julfa, the European trading companies, the recapture of Hormuz, and the cultural products (carpets, miniatures, ceramics) that became internationally recognized luxury goods.
The economic story matters because it explains how Abbas funded the building program of Chapter 4 and the clerical infrastructure of Chapter 5.
The Safavid golden age was built on silk and silver.
The commercial backbone was silk.
Iran had been producing silk since the Sasanian period (Persian Empire Ch 9), when sericulture (silkworm cultivation) had been imported from China along the Silk Road.

By the sixteenth century, the principal silk-producing region was Gilan (gee-LAHN) and Mazandaran (mah-zahn-dah-RAHN) — the humid Caspian provinces of northern Iran where mulberry trees (the food source for silkworms) grew in profusion.
Safavid Iran produced an estimated 700,000 to 1 million pounds of raw silk per year by the late sixteenth century, making it one of the largest silk producers in the world.
The economic geography of silk had, until the Safavids, run mostly through Ottoman territory.
Iranian silk went west through Anatolia to Aleppo and Bursa, where it was sold to Italian and English merchants who shipped it to European markets.
The Ottoman state collected substantial transit duties.
The Iranian producer got a fraction of the eventual European retail price.
Abbas I attacked this system on multiple fronts.

First, in 1599, he declared a royal monopoly on raw silk export — silk could only be sold to European merchants through a single state-controlled marketing apparatus, with all revenues flowing through the Safavid treasury.
Second, he actively promoted alternative export routes that bypassed Ottoman territory.

Silk could move south through the Persian Gulf, where European trading ships could pick it up at Hormuz or Bandar Abbas; or north through the Russian-controlled Caspian and Volga route, where it reached Europe via Moscow and Archangelsk.

Third, he negotiated directly with European trading companies — particularly the English East India Company and the Dutch VOC (Verenigde Oostindische Compagnie) — to establish trading posts in Iranian ports.
The result was a substantial reorganization of the world silk trade in Iran's favor.
By the 1620s, perhaps half of Iranian silk export was moving through non-Ottoman channels, and the Iranian state was capturing a much larger share of the eventual sale price.
The silk monopoly was the single largest source of Safavid government revenue for most of the seventeenth century.
The mechanism that made the silk monopoly work commercially was the Armenian merchant community of New Julfa.

In 1604–1605, in the middle of his Ottoman campaigns, Abbas conducted one of the most ruthless population-engineering projects in early-modern history: he forcibly relocated the entire Armenian Christian population of the city of Old Julfa (on the Aras River, in the Caucasus borderland) across hundreds of miles of difficult terrain to a new settlement on the south bank of the Zayanderud River, just outside Isfahan.

Population estimates vary widely: Armenian sources of the period give figures as high as 50,000 to 100,000, while many modern historians give substantially lower numbers — perhaps 10,000 to 20,000 — and treat the higher figures as the upper bound of a contested range.
Many died on the march.
Old Julfa was burned to deny it to the Ottomans (the standard scorched-earth tactic of the period) and the survivors were resettled in the new district called New Julfa (Nor Jugha in Armenian).
The brutal logic of the relocation was economic.

The Armenians of Old Julfa had been one of the most successful merchant communities in the Caucasus — they had centuries of experience in long-distance trade, particularly in raw silk, and they had developed a network of commercial agents across the Ottoman, Mughal, Russian, and Mediterranean worlds.
By moving them inside Iran, Abbas was essentially nationalizing their trading network.

The Armenians were given commercial privileges, religious autonomy (they could maintain their own churches, schools, and Armenian Apostolic clergy), and effective control of the silk monopoly's commercial operations.
In exchange, they served as the Safavid state's commercial agents to the rest of the world.
The arrangement was extraordinarily successful.
Within a few decades, New Julfa was one of the wealthiest mercantile communities in Eurasia.
New Julfan merchants operated trading houses in Venice, Marseille, Amsterdam, London, Aleppo, Istanbul, Surat, Madras, Manila, and as far away as Acapulco and Lhasa.

They handled the bulk of Iran's silk exports and imported in exchange Spanish silver (mined in the Americas, shipped via Manila or the Levant), European luxury manufactures, and Indian cotton textiles.

They built thirteen churches in New Julfa (the cathedral, Vank, with its remarkable frescoes blending Armenian, Persian, and European Renaissance styles, still stands today and is one of the most visited monuments in Isfahan), funded a printing press (the Vank Cathedral Press, founded in 1639, was the first printing press in Iran and one of the earliest in the Middle East), and developed a distinctive Armenian-Iranian merchant culture that has been studied in detail by economic historians like Sebouh Aslanian.

The New Julfa network is one of the great early-modern merchant diasporas, comparable to the Sephardic Jewish networks of the Mediterranean, the Gujarati Hindu networks of the Indian Ocean, and the Hokkien Chinese networks of Southeast Asia.
It connected Iran to the world economy in a way that had not existed before and would not exist again after the network broke up in the eighteenth century.

New Julfa is also one of the great moments of Safavid pragmatism: the same regime that was forcibly converting Sunni Iranians to Shia Islam (Chapter 2) maintained a protected Armenian Christian community at the heart of its capital because the Armenians were commercially valuable.
The state served its economic interests over its religious ones when the two conflicted.
The Europeans the Armenians sold silk to were primarily the English East India Company and the Dutch East India Company (VOC).

The European East India Companies were a new kind of commercial-political entity — joint-stock corporations chartered by their home governments with monopoly rights over Asian trade and effectively delegated military authority to defend their commercial interests by force.
The English EIC was chartered in 1600.
The Dutch VOC was chartered in 1602.
By the 1610s, both were operating throughout the Indian Ocean and increasingly seeking to break the Portuguese commercial monopoly that had dominated Asian trade for the previous century.

The Portuguese had reached India in 1498 (Vasco da Gama's voyage) and quickly established a fortified network of trading posts (called feitorias) at strategic chokepoints across the Indian Ocean — Goa (in India), Malacca (in Southeast Asia), Mozambique (in East Africa), and most importantly Hormuz (the island controlling the entrance to the Persian Gulf, captured by the Portuguese commander Afonso de Albuquerque in 1507).

The Portuguese had used Hormuz as the linchpin of their control over Persian Gulf trade for over a century, levying customs duties on all merchant vessels and reducing Iranian commerce in the Gulf to a Portuguese tributary.
Abbas wanted Hormuz back.
The Portuguese were too well fortified, and the Safavids had no fleet capable of contesting Portuguese naval power.
The English EIC, by contrast, did have a fleet — and they wanted to displace the Portuguese to capture the Iranian silk trade.
In 1622, an Anglo-Persian alliance made the deal.
English EIC ships landed Iranian troops on Hormuz; the combined force besieged the Portuguese garrison; after several weeks of fighting, the Portuguese surrendered.
Hormuz returned to Iranian control after 115 years of Portuguese occupation.
The English East India Company received commercial privileges, including a substantial share of Hormuz customs revenues and exemptions from various duties.
The new Iranian port of Bandar Abbas (literally "Port of Abbas") was developed on the mainland coast opposite Hormuz to serve as the primary Persian Gulf trading hub.
The Persian Gulf, after a century of Portuguese dominance, returned to operating under primarily Iranian and English control — with Dutch competition added in the 1620s and 1630s.
The recapture of Hormuz is one of the most consequential strategic moments of the Safavid period.

It restored Iranian control over the country's southern maritime trade, freed Iranian commerce from Portuguese transit duties, and established the foundation of the Iran-Britain commercial relationship that would later (much later, in unfortunate ways) shape the Iranian oil industry.
Bandar Abbas remained a major Iranian port for the next two centuries, and it is still a working port today.
The other great Safavid export was the Persian carpet.

Persian carpet weaving has roots going back at least to the Achaemenid period (Persian Empire Ch 2) — the famous Pazyryk Carpet, found frozen in a Scythian tomb in Siberia and dated to the fifth or fourth century BCE, is widely considered the oldest surviving woven carpet in the world and is generally attributed to Achaemenid Persian production.
The tradition continued through the Sasanian, Islamic, and Timurid periods.

But the Safavids elevated carpet weaving to the highest level of state-sponsored art, comparable to Renaissance Italian painting in technical sophistication and significantly more widely traded as a commercial product.
Abbas I established royal carpet workshops at Isfahan, Kashan (in central Iran), Kerman (in southeastern Iran), and Tabriz in the early 1600s.
Each workshop developed distinctive regional styles.

The Isfahan and Kashan workshops produced the most refined court carpets, often in silk, with extraordinarily fine knotting (sometimes 800 to 1,000 knots per square inch), elaborate medallion-and-corner compositions, and rich color palettes including the deep madder reds and indigo blues that distinguish Safavid carpets.
The Kerman workshops specialized in vase-pattern carpets with elaborate floral motifs.
The Tabriz workshops continued the older Tabriz tradition of garden-pattern carpets.
The most famous individual Safavid carpet is the Ardabil Carpet — actually a pair of matching carpets, both commissioned around 1539–40 for the Safavid family shrine at Ardabil (Chapter 5).

The carpets are massive — 34 feet by 17 feet — with a central medallion design surrounded by elaborate floral arabesques, lamp motifs (referencing the Quranic Verse of Light), and an inscription that gives the date and the name of the master weaver, Maqsud of Kashan.

The knotting is approximately 300 knots per square inch — at the carpet's stated dimensions, that works out to roughly 25 million individual hand-tied knots (popular accounts often round this up to 26 million), requiring thousands of person-hours of skilled weaving labor.
The carpets are arguably the most ambitious surviving textile objects from the early-modern world.
Both Ardabil Carpets survive, in damaged but largely intact form.
The better-preserved one is in the Victoria and Albert Museum in London (purchased in 1893 after a complicated provenance trail through Iranian, Ottoman, and English hands).
The other is in the Los Angeles County Museum of Art.
Together they are the touchstone of all subsequent assessment of Safavid carpet art.
Persian carpets became internationally traded luxury goods on a massive scale during the Safavid period.

They appear in Renaissance European paintings — most famously in seventeenth-century Dutch still lifes and interiors (Vermeer painted Persian carpets in several of his domestic scenes) — and in inventories of European royal and aristocratic households throughout the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. (A common confusion is worth flagging here: the so-called "Holbein carpets" that appear in Hans Holbein's sixteenth-century portraits are Anatolian, not Safavid Persian — they were woven in Ottoman Turkey, and specialists use "Holbein" only as a shorthand for that earlier Anatolian pattern type.

Persian carpets in European paintings are typically the later Dutch and Italian still-life examples.) The Safavid carpet was, in its time, what a Picasso painting is in ours: an instantly recognizable luxury object that signaled wealth, sophistication, and access to global commerce.
The other great visual art of the Safavid period was miniature painting.
The Safavid miniature tradition built on the Timurid Herat school (Chapter 1), the Tabriz school of the early Safavids (Chapter 3), and the broader heritage of Persian book painting.
Under Abbas I, the dominant figure of the Isfahan school was Reza Abbasi (RAY-zah ah-BAH-see, c. 1565–1635), the leading court painter of the early seventeenth century.

Reza Abbasi's innovation was a shift toward more naturalistic portraiture, single-figure compositions, and sketch-like draftsmanship that broke with the dense, narrative-driven compositions of earlier Persian painting.
His characteristic works are not illustrations of literary or historical scenes but stand-alone images: a young dervish reading, a courtier reclining, a hunter with his dog, a lover writing a letter.
The figures are graceful, the lines fluid, the color palettes muted and atmospheric.
Reza Abbasi's style influenced Persian painting for the next two centuries and provided much of the visual vocabulary that later spread to Mughal painting in India.

Reza Abbasi also represented the social position that visual artists occupied at the Safavid court: he was a salaried royal employee, the head of the imperial painting workshop, expected to produce works for royal commissions but also free to develop independent artistic projects.

The Safavid court provided patronage on a scale comparable to the contemporary Mughal court and substantially greater than most Ottoman patronage of the same period (the Ottomans tended to fund architecture more than painting).
Persian visual culture under the Safavids was operating at the highest level of the early-modern world.

Persian poetry of the Safavid period has been less celebrated than the painting and architecture, partly because it produced no figure of the stature of the great medieval poets — Rumi, Hafez, Sa'di, Ferdowsi — whose work defined the Persian poetic canon.
The dominant Safavid-era style was called Sabk-e Hindi (SAHBK-eh HIN-dee, the "Hindi Style," because it was particularly cultivated by Persian-language poets at the Mughal court in India).
Sabk-e Hindi was characterized by elaborate metaphorical conceits, philosophical and melancholic themes, and a high degree of intellectual complexity.

Major Iranian Sabk-e Hindi poets included Saib Tabrizi (sah-EEB tab-REE-zee, c. 1592–1676), whose technical brilliance and prolific output made him one of the most quoted Persian poets in his own day.
Modern Iranian literary opinion has rehabilitated the Sabk-e Hindi poets in recent decades, but for most of the twentieth century they were dismissed as overly mannered.
The truth is somewhere in between: technical virtuosity at the cost of immediate emotional accessibility.

The cultural products of the Safavid Empire — silk textiles, carpets, miniatures, ceramics, illuminated manuscripts — became standard luxury imports in early-modern European royal and aristocratic households.
They also flowed east to the Mughal court, where they shaped Mughal taste and provided technical training to Mughal artists.

Persian-language poetry, philosophy, and scholarship dominated the literary culture of the Mughal Empire from Babur to Aurangzeb (1526–1707) — the Mughal court conducted its administration in Persian, patronized Persian poets and scholars, and considered Iran the senior cultural partner of the Persianate world.

The Safavid-Mughal relationship was therefore politically competitive (over Kandahar, where the two empires fought a series of wars across the seventeenth century — the city changed hands four times) but culturally cooperative.
Persian artists, scholars, and merchants moved freely between the two courts.
The two Tabriz painters Mir Sayyid Ali and Abd al-Samad migrated to Delhi after the chaos of Ismail II's reign and became founding figures of Mughal painting.
The poet Urfi Shirazi wrote his major work at the Mughal court of Akbar.
The Sabk-e Hindi style developed simultaneously in both empires.

The cultural traffic was so intense that by the late seventeenth century, much of the most innovative Persian-language cultural production was happening at the Mughal court rather than at the Safavid court.
This is one of the structural features of the Persianate world that distinguishes it from the European national-cultural framework.
Persian was the literary and administrative language of an enormous geographic region — from Anatolia through Iran into Central Asia and India — that contained multiple competing political states.
A Persian poet, a Persian painter, a Persian scholar could move between courts as the political winds shifted, finding patronage wherever it was most generous.
The Safavid-Mughal cultural exchange is a particularly intense example of this broader Persianate cultural mobility, but the pattern is general.
Persian culture under the Safavids was a regional civilization, not a national one.
By 1629, when Abbas I died, the Safavid Empire was a fully integrated participant in the early-modern world economy.
Silk flowed west through Armenian merchants to European markets.
Silver flowed east from Spanish America to pay for it.
English and Dutch ships called at Bandar Abbas.
Carpets and miniatures decorated the homes of European aristocrats.

The Safavid state was, on the commercial scale, one of the most important trading partners of Europe and arguably the second-richest state in the early-modern Islamic world (after the Mughal Empire under Shah Jahan, which had a much larger population and tax base).
The decline that followed is the subject of the next chapter, and the question is partly why the commercial integration that worked so well under Abbas could not be sustained.

The answer involves bad rulers, declining military discipline, religious orthodoxy at the expense of intellectual openness, and ultimately the resurgence of Afghan tribal power on the eastern frontier.
But the commercial integration was real, and the cultural-economic Iran that Abbas built was, for a period, one of the truly successful early-modern states.
The decline destroyed the political structure but it did not destroy the cultural memory.
Naqsh-e Jahan and Vank Cathedral are still standing.

Cross-civ check: the Safavid commercial integration of the early 1600s is contemporary with the rise of the Dutch Golden Age (Rembrandt, Vermeer, the VOC), the English East India Company's establishment in India (Surat 1612, Madras 1640), the Manila galleon trade that connected Spanish America to Asia via the Philippines, and the early Mughal commercial expansion under Jahangir and Shah Jahan.

The early-modern world economy was being knit together at this moment, and Iran under Abbas was one of its central nodes — a richer, more sophisticated, more globally connected Iran than the country would be again until the late twentieth century.

chapters.title: The Long Decline
sentences: In April 1629, Shah Abbas the Great died at his palace in Mazandaran.
The throne passed to his eighteen-year-old grandson, who took the regnal name Safi I (sah-FEE) and reigned for the next thirteen years.
What followed was a slow institutional decay that lasted nearly a century.

The Safavid Empire after Abbas was still one of the largest and richest states in the Islamic world, still ruling from Isfahan in palaces of extraordinary beauty, still collecting silk monopoly revenues and trading with European merchants.

But the underlying foundations — the military discipline of the ghulam army, the administrative competence of the central court, the tax base in the productive provinces, and the assertive religious leadership of the early dynasty — were eroding.
Each successive Shah was weaker than the last.
Each generation lost more territory, more revenue, and more political will.
By 1700, the Safavid Empire was a hollow shell whose decay had not yet broken into the open.
By 1722, the shell would shatter.
This chapter is the long decline.

It is unglamorous compared to the founding revolution of Ismail or the magnificence of Abbas's Isfahan, but the long decline is what most institutional histories of empires actually look like — slow, undramatic, internally driven, the kind of erosion that does not produce a single moment of crisis until the day everything finally collapses.
Safi I (ruled 1629–1642) was Abbas's grandson — Abbas had killed his own son and blinded two others (Chapter 4), leaving Safi as the only viable heir.
Safi was eighteen at his accession, inexperienced, paranoid, and reportedly cruel.

His early reign was dominated by a systematic purge of Abbas's senior officials, including the great Georgian ghulam commander Imam Quli Khan and his entire family — executed on suspicion of political ambition.

The purges removed most of the military and administrative talent that had served Abbas, replacing competent veterans with younger officials whose loyalty was certain but whose capability was untested.
The military consequences appeared almost immediately.
In 1638, the Ottomans under Sultan Murad IV launched a major campaign against Safavid Iraq — the same Iraq that Abbas had conquered in 1623 — and recaptured Baghdad after a forty-day siege.
The fall of Baghdad in 1638 was a catastrophic loss for the Safavids.
It ended Iranian control of the Shia holy cities of Najaf and Karbala.
It cut off Iranian Shia from direct access to the major shrines of the imams.
And it forced the Iranian state to negotiate from weakness with an Ottoman regime that had clearly recovered from the setbacks of Abbas's reign.
The result was the Treaty of Zuhab (zoo-HAHB), signed in 1639 and named for the small village (also called Qasr-e Shirin) where the negotiations took place.

The treaty fixed the Ottoman-Safavid frontier with extraordinary precision: the Ottomans retained Baghdad and Mesopotamia (modern Iraq), the Safavids retained the Caucasus and the Iranian plateau, and the boundary ran roughly along the line of the modern Iran-Iraq border.
The Treaty of Zuhab is one of the most enduring international borders in world history.

The line drawn at Zuhab in 1639 is essentially the line that the United Nations recognizes today, and it has survived the collapse of both the Safavid and Ottoman empires, the British creation of modern Iraq in 1920, the Iran-Iraq War of 1980–88, and the American invasion of Iraq in 2003.
There may be no other Middle Eastern frontier that has been as stable for as long.
The Ottoman Empire Ch 8 covers the same treaty from the Ottoman side — readers of either TL encounter one of the most durable geopolitical facts of the modern Middle East.
The Treaty of Zuhab also marked the end of large-scale Ottoman-Safavid warfare.
After 1639, the two empires settled into a tense but stable coexistence.
The hot war of the sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries was over.

This relative stability was one of the things that allowed both empires to persist into the eighteenth century without major external pressure — but it also meant that neither could blame external enemies for the internal decay that was setting in.
Abbas II (ruled 1642–1666) was Safi's son, and his reign is generally treated as the Indian summer of the dynasty — a brief recovery before the deeper decline.
Abbas II was capable, energetic, and reasonably ruthless in ways that made him an effective ruler if not a great one.
He was nine years old at his accession and grew into adulthood under the regency of competent ministers; he assumed personal rule around 1654 and held the throne until his death from illness in 1666.
The signature achievement of his reign was the recapture of Kandahar in 1649.
Kandahar had been lost to the Mughals in 1638 (Mughal emperor Shah Jahan, taking advantage of the Safavid disarray under Safi).
Abbas II launched a major campaign in 1648–1649, besieged the city, and captured it after defeating Shah Jahan's son Aurangzeb (then in his forties and serving as a Mughal general).
Aurangzeb mounted three subsequent campaigns to retake Kandahar — in 1651, 1652, and 1653 — and failed in all three.
Kandahar remained Safavid for the rest of the seventeenth century.
It was the last major Safavid military success.
Abbas II also continued the Isfahan building program.
The Khwaju Bridge was completed in 1650 — the second of the great Safavid bridges over the Zayanderud, with its decorative pavilions and dam-like undercroft (Chapter 4).

The Chehel Sotoun (cheh-HEL soh-TOON, "Forty Columns") palace was completed in 1647, a low pavilion in a formal Persian garden, with a wooden veranda whose twenty columns reflect in the front pool to make the "forty columns" of the name.

The interior of Chehel Sotoun is decorated with large mural paintings depicting Safavid royal scenes — Abbas I receiving the Mughal emperor Humayun, Tahmasp I hosting various dignitaries, Shah Ismail at war.
The murals are major works of seventeenth-century Iranian painting and represent a deliberate attempt by Abbas II to commemorate his own dynasty in visual form.
But Abbas II's reign also saw the beginning of the underlying decay.
The ghulam army that Abbas the Great had built was no longer being properly recruited, trained, or paid.

The captured Caucasian boys who had filled the corps in earlier generations were no longer being supplied at the same rate, partly because the Caucasus was less under Safavid control and partly because the central state lacked the administrative reach to manage the recruitment system.
The cannons and muskets that had won the battles of Sufiyan and Hormuz were not being maintained or replaced.

The frontier garrisons on the eastern approaches were understaffed, underpaid, and increasingly relying on local Afghan and Baluch tribal levies for security — levies whose loyalty would prove dangerous.
Religious orthodoxy was also becoming more aggressive.

Muhammad Baqir Majlisi (Chapter 5) began his public career under Abbas II, and the conservative legalistic Shia Islam he championed was steadily displacing the philosophical and Sufi traditions of earlier Safavid culture.
Sufi orders — including some that had been associated with the Safavid family for generations — were persecuted.
Religious minorities (Christians, Zoroastrians, Jews) faced new restrictions.
The intellectual openness of Mulla Sadra's generation was giving way to a narrower, more legalistic religious culture.
Abbas II died in 1666, probably of syphilis (the surviving symptom descriptions are consistent with late-stage syphilitic illness), at the age of thirty-three.
His death is the moment when the long decline becomes visible.
Soleyman I (soo-lay-MAHN, ruled 1666–1694), born Sam Mirza, was Abbas II's eldest son and one of the worst rulers in Safavid history.
He took the throne at age twenty, was reportedly an alcoholic by his late twenties, and spent most of his twenty-eight-year reign in the harem rather than the council chamber.

The historian Roger Savory describes Soleyman's reign as a model of institutional drift: the Shah did almost nothing, the central court did almost nothing of substance, and the empire ran on autopilot, governed by provincial officials whose competence varied wildly and whose loyalty to a king they rarely saw was correspondingly thin.
There were no major military campaigns.
There were no significant administrative reforms.
There were no important new buildings (the architectural patronage of Abbas II's reign essentially ended).
Nothing dramatic broke.
Nothing was repaired either.

The European travelers who visited Iran during Soleyman's reign — including the French jeweler Jean Chardin (zhahn shar-DAN), whose ten-volume account of his Iranian travels in 1672–1677 is one of the most detailed European descriptions of Safavid Iran — left vivid pictures of a state that was visibly decaying despite its surface magnificence.
Chardin's Voyages en Perse (published 1686) is a primary source for everything from court ceremony to commercial practice to popular religion in late seventeenth-century Iran.

His account is mostly admiring of Iranian culture, but he is unsparing about the political situation: the Shah was incompetent, the senior officials were corrupt, the army was undisciplined, and the system was clearly heading toward crisis. (Chardin was a French Huguenot Protestant who later moved to England to escape the persecution that followed Louis XIV's revocation of the Edict of Nantes; his Iranian travels were undertaken partly in connection with the diamond trade and partly out of intellectual curiosity.
His writings are a major source for European understanding of the Islamic world for the next century.) The structural problem was the harem succession system.

Safavid princes were no longer trained for active rule — earlier dynasties had sent princes out to govern provinces as young men, building administrative experience, but Abbas the Great had ended this practice (out of fear of princely revolts) by confining all royal princes inside the Isfahan palace.
The princes were raised in the harem, educated by tutors and court scholars but without practical political experience, and emerged at the moment of succession with no skills for rule.
Each generation of Safavid kings was therefore worse-prepared than the previous one.
By Soleyman's generation, the system was producing kings who could barely function as administrators.
The harem itself became the de facto government.
Real political power flowed through the network of senior eunuchs, royal wives, and queen mothers who controlled access to the Shah and managed the daily operations of the court.

This was not necessarily catastrophic in itself — well-organized harem bureaucracies had governed effectively in Ottoman, Mughal, and Chinese contexts — but in late Safavid Iran it produced a court that was insular, factional, and disconnected from the practical demands of ruling a large empire.
The Shia clergy under Majlisi filled the resulting vacuum, claiming more religious authority and progressively narrower religious orthodoxy.
The provincial governors, with little oversight from the central state, became increasingly autonomous and corrupt.
The army continued to decay.
Sultan Husayn (sool-TAHN hoo-SAYN, ruled 1694–1722) was Soleyman's son and the last effective Safavid king — though "effective" is a generous term for what he managed.
He was reportedly devout, indecisive, and dominated almost entirely by the Shia clerical establishment, particularly by Majlisi (until Majlisi's death in 1699) and by Majlisi's successors.

The historian Laurence Lockhart, in his classic 1958 study The Fall of the Safavi Dynasty, treated Sultan Husayn as the consensus low point of the dynasty — a king who combined personal piety with utter inability to govern.
Sultan Husayn's twenty-eight-year reign saw an acceleration of the trends that had begun under Soleyman.
The army continued to decay; the treasury continued to bleed; the provincial governors continued to grow more autonomous; the religious persecutions continued to intensify.

The Shah himself was preoccupied with religious devotions and large-scale construction at Isfahan — including the magnificent Madrasa-ye Chahar Bagh (Four Gardens School, completed 1714), one of the great Safavid religious buildings, which still stands as one of the most beautiful pieces of late Safavid tilework.
While Isfahan was being beautified, the empire was disintegrating.
The provinces grew more restive.

Persecution of religious minorities — Sunni Muslims (especially in the Caucasus and Afghanistan, where Sunni populations were forced to convert or face heavy taxation), Christians, Zoroastrians, Jews — produced widespread regional resentment.
The Sunni populations of the eastern provinces (modern Afghanistan and Baluchistan) were particularly bitter.

The Safavid governor of Kandahar, Gurgin Khan (a Georgian Christian convert serving as a Safavid official — the irony of a Christian-born Iranian governor persecuting Sunni Muslims is hard to overstate), conducted brutal campaigns against the Pashtun Ghilzai (gil-ZIGH) tribes around Kandahar in the early 1700s.
The Ghilzai, like all Pashtuns, were Sunni Muslims, and they bitterly resented both the religious persecution and the political domination by a Christian-born official.
In 1709, the Ghilzai chieftain Mir Wais Hotak (meer WIGH-ees hoh-TAHK) led a revolt that killed Gurgin Khan and seized control of Kandahar.
The Safavid government attempted to suppress the revolt but failed — sending three successive expeditions over the following years, all of which were defeated by the Ghilzai.
By the time Mir Wais died in 1715, the Ghilzai had established an independent Sunni emirate in Kandahar with no realistic prospect of Safavid reconquest.
This was the moment when the long decline became existential.
The Safavid army that could not subdue a single Pashtun tribal confederation in Kandahar was clearly not the same army that had captured Baghdad in 1623.
The state was no longer capable of basic military operations on its own frontier.
The Ghilzai threat metastasized over the next several years.
In 1717, the Abdali tribal confederation (the other great Pashtun tribal grouping, rivals of the Ghilzai) seized Herat from Safavid control.
By 1720, the eastern provinces of the empire were effectively independent.

And in 1721, Mir Wais's son Mir Mahmud Hotak (meer mah-MOOD) — the new Ghilzai leader, then in his early twenties — decided to push the issue further: he assembled an army of perhaps 20,000 Pashtun warriors and marched on Isfahan itself.
The army that intercepted him was the Safavid imperial force, supposedly the elite of the empire.
They met at Gulnabad (gul-nah-BAHD), east of Isfahan, on March 8, 1722.
The Safavid army outnumbered the Afghans by perhaps two-to-one and was equipped with cannons and muskets.
It was also poorly trained, poorly led, and poorly motivated.
The Afghan force was smaller but battle-hardened, well-led, and fighting with the desperation of men who had little to lose.
The battle lasted a single day.
The Safavid lines collapsed under Afghan cavalry charges, the imperial cannons were captured, and the army fled back to Isfahan in disarray.
The road to the capital was open.
What followed was the worst urban catastrophe in Iranian history.

Cross-civ check: the long decline of the Safavid Empire (1629–1722) overlaps with the English Civil War (1642–1651), the Glorious Revolution (1688), the late Tokugawa shogunate in Japan (the Edo period of stable Tokugawa rule), the Manchu conquest of Ming China (1644 and after), the rise of the Romanov dynasty in Russia, and the Mughal apex under Aurangzeb (1658–1707, reigning over the most extensive Mughal Empire ever assembled — and beginning the long Mughal decline that would parallel the Safavid one).

The seventeenth century was the moment when the early-modern Eurasian state system reached its peak, with several large gunpowder empires reaching their territorial and economic maxima at almost the same time.

The Safavid case is one example among several of how those empires began to decay simultaneously, partly under the weight of their own institutional structures and partly under the new pressures (commercial, military, ideological) generated by European expansion.

chapters.title: The Afghan Catastrophe and Nader's Restoration
sentences: The fall of Isfahan in 1722 was the most violent end any major Islamic capital experienced in the early-modern period.
The Mughal capital at Delhi survived multiple sieges.
Ottoman Constantinople was never sacked between 1453 and the twentieth century.
Even Baghdad, sacked by the Mongols in 1258 (Mongol Empire Ch 5), recovered relatively quickly.
But Isfahan in 1722 was reduced from one of the largest cities in the world to a ruin, and the Iran that emerged from the catastrophe was a fundamentally different country.

This chapter is the end of the Safavid story — the Afghan invasion, the brief Hotaki occupation, the rise of Nader Shah Afshar, the formal end of the dynasty in 1736 — and the beginning of the Safavid afterlife in modern Iran.
After the disaster at Gulnabad on March 8, 1722, Mir Mahmud Hotak's Afghan army marched on Isfahan and laid siege to the city.
The siege lasted six and a half months — from March to October 1722 — and produced one of the great urban tragedies of early-modern history.

Isfahan had a population of perhaps half a million people in 1722, including the surrounding suburbs (the city had declined somewhat from its peak under Abbas I but was still one of the world's largest cities).
The Safavid government, paralyzed by indecision, made no serious attempt to organize a relief expedition.
The provincial armies of Iran — what remained of them — either failed to mobilize, were defeated piecemeal by Afghan detachments, or simply melted away.
The city was on its own.
The Afghan force was not large enough to storm Isfahan's walls — the Hotakis had perhaps 25,000 troops and the city had elaborate fortifications.
But they could starve the city into surrender, and they did.
Mahmud's army cordoned off Isfahan, cut the food supply lines from the surrounding agricultural districts, intercepted the relief caravans, and waited.
What followed inside the city was a famine of medieval intensity.
Within two months food prices had risen by orders of magnitude.
By summer 1722, the urban population was eating dogs, cats, leather, tree bark, and grass.
By autumn, there are detailed European accounts of cannibalism in Isfahan — the Polish Jesuit Father Krusinski, who was inside the besieged city, left a primary-source account of the horrors.
Estimates of deaths from starvation during the siege range from 80,000 to 200,000 people.
The exact number is unknowable, but the order of magnitude is reliable: approximately a third to a half of the urban population died inside the walls before the city surrendered.
On October 23, 1722, Sultan Husayn personally rode out of Isfahan to the Afghan camp, dismounted, removed his royal aigrette, and placed the Safavid crown on the head of Mir Mahmud Hotak.
Husayn formally abdicated the throne.
Mahmud entered Isfahan unopposed and began an occupation that would last seven years.
The Afghan occupation was a continuing disaster.
Mahmud and his forces were small in number relative to the population they were trying to control, and they responded to ongoing resistance with progressive escalation of violence.

In 1725, Mahmud — by then mentally ill, possibly from syphilis or from the strain of governing a foreign capital with inadequate resources — ordered the systematic massacre of much of the surviving Safavid royal family and Iranian nobility, executing perhaps 3,000 people in a single afternoon at the Isfahan palace.
He died shortly afterward, possibly of natural causes, possibly assassinated by his cousin Ashraf Hotak (ash-RAHF) who succeeded him.
The Afghan occupation also failed to control most of the country.

The Safavid governor of Khorasan (the northeastern province), Tahmasp Mirza — Sultan Husayn's son, who had escaped from Isfahan before the siege — proclaimed himself Tahmasp II in 1722 and began organizing resistance from the provinces.
Russian forces under Peter the Great invaded the Caspian provinces in 1722–1723, capturing Baku, Derbent, and the southern Caspian coast.
Ottoman forces invaded from the west, capturing most of Azerbaijan, Armenia, Georgia, and parts of western Iran.
The two foreign powers signed the Treaty of Constantinople in 1724, dividing the conquered Iranian territories between themselves while leaving Afghan-occupied central Iran as a residual rump.
By 1725, the Iran of Abbas the Great a century earlier was simply gone.
The Afghans held the center.
The Russians held the north.
The Ottomans held the west.
Tahmasp II claimed legitimate Safavid kingship from the northeast but commanded almost no military force.
The empire had effectively dissolved.
The man who reassembled it was Nader Shah Afshar (NAH-der), one of the most extraordinary military commanders in Iranian history.

Nader was born around 1688 in Khorasan, in the eastern Iranian province, into the Turkic Afshar tribal confederation — one of the original Qizilbash tribes that had backed Ismail I two centuries earlier (Chapter 1).

His early life was difficult: his father died when he was young, he and his mother were kidnapped by Uzbek slavers in his teens (he later escaped), he served as a low-level tribal warrior, and by his early thirties he was leading a band of Afshar irregulars that operated as bandits, mercenaries, or both.
He was illiterate, by all accounts brutal, and unmistakably a military genius.
In 1726, Tahmasp II — the would-be Safavid Shah running the resistance from Khorasan — recruited Nader into his service.
Nader rapidly became Tahmasp's principal general, then his de facto regent, then the actual ruler of Iran while Tahmasp held the formal title.
Over the next decade, Nader conducted one of the most successful military campaigns in early-modern Asian history.
The campaign was systematic.
First Nader expelled the Afghans.

He defeated the Hotaki forces under Ashraf at the Battle of Damghan in October 1729 and again at Murche-Khort in November 1729, broke their occupation of central Iran, and chased them back to Kandahar.
By 1730, the Afghan emirate had been destroyed and Iran had a unified government again under Tahmasp II — with Nader as commander-in-chief.
Then Nader turned on the Ottomans.
In a series of campaigns from 1730 to 1735, he recovered most of the territory the Ottomans had seized during the Afghan crisis: the Caucasus, Azerbaijan, western Iran, and parts of eastern Anatolia.
The Ottoman-Safavid frontier was effectively restored to roughly the Treaty of Zuhab line of 1639.
The Russians, seeing which way the wind was blowing, signed the Treaty of Resht (1732) and the Treaty of Ganja (1735) returning the Caspian provinces to Iranian control.
Then Nader turned on the Safavids.
In 1732, he had already deposed Tahmasp II (whom he considered drunken and incompetent) and replaced him with Tahmasp's infant son Abbas III as a puppet king under Nader's regency.
In March 1736, Nader convened a council of Iranian notables on the Mughan plain in the Caucasus, formally deposed Abbas III, and had himself proclaimed Shah.
The Safavid dynasty, after 235 years, was over.
The new dynasty was the Afsharid, named for Nader's tribe.
It would last only sixty years and produce only Nader himself plus a series of successors who fought each other inconclusively after his death.

But the immediate importance was structural: Nader had restored Iranian sovereignty, expelled foreign occupiers, reunified the country under a single government, and ended the dynasty whose institutional decay had caused the catastrophe in the first place.
Nader Shah's later career was meteoric and increasingly bizarre.
In 1738–1739, he invaded Mughal India.
The expedition is one of the strangest military adventures of the eighteenth century.
Nader's army crossed the Hindu Kush mountains, captured Kabul and Lahore, defeated the Mughal emperor Muhammad Shah at the Battle of Karnal (February 1739), and entered Delhi as a conqueror.
The Mughal capital — at that point the largest and richest city in the world, the seat of the empire that controlled most of the Indian subcontinent — was occupied by an Iranian army.
What happened next was a calculated atrocity.
After a riot in Delhi during which some of Nader's soldiers were killed, Nader ordered a general massacre of the city's population.
The killing lasted roughly six hours.

Estimates of the death toll vary widely in the literature, with no figure resting on a firm primary count — most scholarly sources fall in the 20,000 to 30,000 range, while contemporary chronicles and some later accounts give much higher figures (the 100,000–200,000 numbers that appear in some popular sources are at the high end of what was claimed at the time rather than a modern scholarly consensus).
Nader's army then systematically looted Delhi for fifty-seven days, packing up the wealth of the Mughal capital and shipping it back to Iran.

The loot included the Peacock Throne of Shah Jahan (the great gold-and-jewel throne that had been the centerpiece of Mughal imperial ceremony for a century), the Koh-i-Noor diamond (then probably the largest diamond in the world, later seized from the Sikh kingdom by the British and now in the British Crown Jewels), thousands of horses and elephants, and so much cash that Nader was able to suspend taxation in Iran for three years.
The 1739 sack of Delhi is one of the most consequential events in modern South Asian history.

It crippled the Mughal Empire (which would never fully recover and would spend the following century in slow disintegration), opened the way for British East India Company political expansion (which began in earnest after the Battle of Plassey in 1757, less than two decades after Nader's invasion), and effectively transferred the wealth of the Mughal core to Iran.
It also demonstrated, beyond any doubt, that Nader was the most successful military commander in eighteenth-century Eurasia.
The wealth he brought back to Iran did not save him politically.
Nader spent his last years (1740–1747) increasingly paranoid, increasingly cruel, and increasingly disconnected from the country he had liberated.
He had his eldest son Reza Quli blinded (on suspicion of plotting against him).
He executed senior officials on minor pretexts.
He raised taxes again to fund campaigns in the Caucasus and Central Asia.
By 1747, he was so unpopular that his own bodyguard officers conspired to assassinate him — they cut him down in his tent in June 1747 in northeastern Iran.
The Afsharid dynasty fragmented within a generation.

Nader's nephew Adel Shah held part of Iran briefly; his grandson Shahrokh Shah ruled a reduced kingdom in Khorasan until 1796; the rest of Iran was contested among rival warlords for the next forty years until the Qajar dynasty finally reunified the country in the 1790s.
Nader's career is a separate story that belongs more properly to the Afsharid TL than to the Safavid one.
What matters for the Safavid narrative is that Nader expelled the Afghans, defeated the Russians and Ottomans, and ended the Safavid dynasty — but did not undo the Safavid project.

The Twelver Shia state Ismail I had built in 1501, the institutional clerical hierarchy that Majlisi had codified in the 1680s, the architectural ensemble at Isfahan, the carpet workshops at Kashan and Kerman, the Armenian merchant network at New Julfa — all of this survived the catastrophe and continued under Nader and his successors.
Nader himself attempted, briefly, to undo the Shia revolution.

In 1736 at his coronation council, he proposed a religious settlement under which Twelver Shia Islam would be reclassified as a fifth Sunni school of jurisprudence (the Ja'fari school, named for the Sixth Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq, who had codified much of the early Shia legal tradition).
The proposal would have ended the Sunni-Shia confessional divide, normalized relations with the Ottomans, and effectively rolled back the Safavid revolution at the doctrinal level.
The Iranian Shia clergy refused.

Their refusal was the moment when the institutional independence of the Iranian Shia clerical class — the institutional creation of the Safavids — definitively asserted itself against any attempt by the state to dictate religious policy.
Nader could not force his settlement on a clerical establishment that had outgrown the dynasty that created it.
The Twelver Shia identity of Iran was now permanent, regardless of which dynasty held the throne.
This is the deepest meaning of the Safavid afterlife.
The dynasty died.
The religion stayed.
The Iran that emerged from the eighteenth-century chaos was, in most cultural terms, recognizably the country the Safavids had built.
The state religion was Twelver Shia Islam.
The clerical hierarchy was the marja-i taqlid system that the Safavid-era Usuli scholars had begun to develop and that would be fully institutionalized under the Qajars.
The major shrine cities — Mashhad, Qom, Ardabil — remained the geographic anchors of Iranian religious identity.
The intellectual traditions of the Isfahan school continued at the seminaries.
The carpet industry continued in the same workshops.
The Persian-language literary tradition continued unbroken.
The country was poorer, smaller, and politically unstable for several decades after Nader's death, but the cultural identity that the Safavids had constructed persisted.
This cultural identity has now persisted, with various political vicissitudes, for five centuries.
The Qajar dynasty (1789–1925) ruled Iran on essentially Safavid cultural foundations, with the addition of significant European political influence.

The Pahlavi dynasty (1925–1979) attempted to push Iran in a more secular and Westernized direction, but their failure — the 1979 Islamic Revolution — was largely a victory for the institutional Shia clergy that the Safavids had created.

The Islamic Republic of Iran (1979–present) is, in institutional terms, the most direct heir of the Safavid state — a Twelver Shia confessional polity governed by a clerical hierarchy whose authority derives from the marja-i taqlid system, which derives from the seventeenth-century Usuli mujtahids, which derive from the Lebanese Arab clerics whom Ismail I imported in the early sixteenth century.

The thread running from Ismail's conquest of Tabriz in 1501 to the Islamic Republic of 2026 is roughly: imported Arab clerics → trained Iranian Shia clerical class → late Safavid Usuli mujtahids → Qajar-era marja-i taqlid system → Khomeini and the 1979 Revolution → the current clerical-political structure of Iran.
The dynasty whose name appears at the head of this chain ceased to rule in 1736.
The institutional structure they constructed has continued operating, in one form or another, for nearly three centuries after their formal extinction.

What survived from Safavid Iran into modern Iran is therefore extensive: the religion, the clerical hierarchy, the shrine networks, the architectural heritage, the carpet industry, the literary language, the educational seminaries, and a national-cultural identity that distinguishes Iranians from their Sunni Arab and Turkic neighbors.
The Safavid contribution to the modern world is greater in proportion to what is recognized about them than any comparably-sized early-modern empire.
Most readers of world history have heard of the Ottomans and the Mughals.
Fewer have heard of the Safavids.

But the Safavids' core innovation — the construction of a permanent Twelver Shia state with an institutionally independent clerical hierarchy — is arguably more consequential for the present-day world than anything either of the other two early-modern Islamic empires accomplished.

The Iranian thread that began with Cyrus the Great in 559 BCE (Persian Empire Ch 1) and ran through the Achaemenid, Parthian, Sasanian, and Islamic-era dynasties (Persian Empire Ch 1–10) reached its most distinctive modern form under the Safavids.

The Persian habit of absorbing whatever conquered it (Persian Empire Ch 10 — the absorption of Greek learning by the Sasanians, the absorption of Islam by the post-conquest Persian-speaking Muslim cultural world, the absorption of the Mongol conquerors by the Ilkhanate, Mongol Empire Ch 7) reached a new variation under the Safavids: instead of absorbing a foreign religion, the Safavids took a minority strand of Islam and made it the unique national identity of Iran, distinguishing Iranians from every other Muslim people in the region.

Twelver Shia Islam, which existed before the Safavids as a scholarly tradition centered in Iraq and Lebanon, became under the Safavids an Iranian state religion — Iranian in its geography, its language, its institutional structure, and its political function.

The conversion ran the other direction from the absorptions of earlier Persian history: instead of absorbing the conqueror, the Safavids absorbed a particular religious tradition into a new national identity.
The dynasty died in 1736.
The country it built lives on.

Cross-civ check: the Afghan catastrophe of 1722 and the rise of Nader Shah are contemporary with the early Hanoverian period in Britain, the regency of the Duc d'Orléans in France, the late Kangxi and early Yongzheng emperors of Qing China (the Qing was at the height of its power as the Safavids fell), and the Mughal decline under Muhammad Shah Rangila (whose capital Nader sacked in 1739).

The eighteenth century in Eurasia is the moment of the decline of the Islamic gunpowder empires (Ottoman, Safavid/Afsharid, Mughal) and the simultaneous rise of European naval-commercial power, particularly the British East India Company.

The Safavid collapse and the Iranian eighteenth-century chaos are part of this larger pattern: the early-modern Islamic world losing relative position to Western Europe in ways that would shape the political and economic balance of the next two centuries.

Iran emerged from the chaos under the Qajars in 1796 as a much weaker state than the Safavid empire it had been, and the relative weakness vis-à-vis Britain and Russia would define Iranian political life for the entire nineteenth century.
But the cultural identity the Safavids built — the Shia state, the clerical hierarchy, the literary and architectural tradition — survived all of this, and it survives still.
The Safavids were the dynasty that made Iran Iran.
Everything else is commentary.

chapters.title: Pre-Islamic Arabia
sentences: To understand how a religion founded in Mecca in 610 conquered an empire by 720, you have to understand the country it started in.
The Arabian Peninsula is roughly a million square miles of mostly desert, about a third the size of the continental United States — bigger than Texas, Alaska, and California put together.
Most of that land is uninhabitable for sustained agriculture.
Rainfall is low to nonexistent, summer temperatures routinely exceed 110°F, and the few groundwater sources are unreliable.
The peninsula's interior is a vast sand sea called the Empty Quarter (the Rub' al-Khali, ROOB al-KHAH-lee), the largest continuous body of sand on Earth, where almost no one lives even today.
Around the edges of this central wasteland, narrow inhabitable bands run along the Red Sea coast, the Persian Gulf coast, and the Yemeni highlands in the south.
The pre-Islamic Arabian population — perhaps two to three million people in the early seventh century, though estimates vary widely — was concentrated in these edge zones.

Most lived as Bedouin (BED-oo-in, from Arabic badawi, "desert-dweller") nomads, herding camels, sheep, and goats across seasonal ranges, moving between water sources, raiding rival tribes when conditions demanded.
A minority lived in agricultural oases and small commercial towns.

A few lived in the genuinely urban settlements that mattered for what came next: Mecca (MEK-ah) and Yathrib (YATH-rib, later renamed Medina) in the western highlands called the Hijaz (hi-JAHZ); San'a (SAN-ah) and Najran in the Yemeni south; al-Hira (al-HEE-rah) on the Iraqi frontier.
The Bedouin tribal society was the matrix from which Islam emerged, and it had a few features the reader needs to picture.
Authority ran through tribes and clans, not through territorial states.
A man's first loyalty was to his tribe, his second to his clan within the tribe, his third to his immediate family within the clan.

Crime was avenged by the victim's kin under the principle of blood-vengeance — a killing called for a counter-killing, sustained over generations if necessary, and the threat of perpetual feud was what kept casual violence in check.
Hospitality to strangers and protection of guests were absolute obligations, almost sacred.
Wealth was measured in camels and slaves rather than in land or money.
There was no Bedouin state, no Bedouin king, no Bedouin standing army, no Bedouin written law — and no Bedouin tradition of obeying anyone outside one's own tribal hierarchy.
This is the social material that Muhammad and the Rashidun caliphs would have to organize into an empire.
The job was harder than just persuading individuals to convert.

It meant persuading whole tribes to accept the political authority of someone outside their tribal hierarchy — and then keeping them persuaded after the original loyalty bond (to Muhammad personally) had died with him.
The Ridda Wars of 632 (Chapter 3) were what happened when the persuasion temporarily collapsed.
The most consequential settlement in pre-Islamic Arabia was Mecca.
Mecca sits in a narrow valley in the western highlands of the Hijaz, about 45 miles inland from the Red Sea coast.
It is hot, dry, and unsuited to agriculture.

What it had — and the only reason it existed as a town — was the Zamzam well (a freshwater source in an otherwise waterless valley) and the Kaaba (KAH-bah, "the cube"), a roughly cube-shaped stone shrine that pre-Islamic Arabs treated as the most important sanctuary on the peninsula.
The Kaaba in 610 was a polytheistic shrine.

Inside and around it were arrayed roughly 360 idols, representing the gods of various Arabian tribes — a deliberately inclusive arrangement that made Mecca a kind of religious common ground for tribes that otherwise lived under permanent feud.

The annual pilgrimage to the Kaaba (the hajj, which Islam later reorganized but did not invent — the pilgrimage already existed in pre-Islamic form) brought tens of thousands of pilgrims to Mecca during four sacred months in which all tribal warfare was suspended by general consent.
The sacred-month truce let the pilgrims travel safely and the merchants of Mecca conduct the most lucrative trading season of the year.
The Kaaba was also said, in pre-Islamic Arab tradition, to have been built by Abraham and his son Ishmael — the same Abraham who is the founding patriarch of Judaism and Christianity.

Whether the Abraham-and-Ishmael story is genuine pre-Islamic tradition or was retrofitted onto Mecca by the Quranic revelation is debated by modern scholars, but the story was certainly in circulation by Muhammad's lifetime and gave the Kaaba an Abrahamic monotheistic genealogy alongside its polytheistic operating reality.
Muhammad's own theological claim was that he was restoring the original Abrahamic monotheism that the Kaaba had been built to honor before the polytheistic idols got added on.
This made his religion a reform, not an innovation — at least in the way he framed it.
The tribe that controlled Mecca was the Quraysh (koo-RAYSH), and they had organized themselves around two functions.
They administered the Kaaba sanctuary — providing food, water, and lodging for pilgrims, maintaining the sacred-month truce, mediating between visiting tribes.
And they ran the long-distance caravan trade that the Kaaba's pilgrim traffic made possible.

Two great Quraysh-organized caravans left Mecca each year: the summer caravan to Syria (carrying Yemeni spices, Arabian leather, slaves, and gold north to the Roman cities of Damascus and Gaza), and the winter caravan to Yemen (carrying Mediterranean textiles, metals, and luxuries south).
The caravans are mentioned by name in the Quran — Chapter 106 ("Quraysh") opens by invoking exactly this seasonal trade pattern as evidence of God's favor toward the tribe.
The Quraysh had subdivided themselves into several clans (sub-tribal groupings), each with its own elder council and its own piece of the Mecca operation.

Two clans matter for the rest of this story: the Banu Hashim (BAH-noo HAH-shim), Muhammad's clan, and the Banu Umayya (BAH-noo oo-MAY-yah), the rival clan that would eventually found the Umayyad dynasty after Muhammad's death.
The Banu Umayya were richer and more politically dominant in pre-Islamic Mecca than the Banu Hashim.
Muhammad's revelations would temporarily reverse the relationship; the Umayyads would permanently re-reverse it sixty years later (Chapter 5).
The other Hijazi town that mattered was Yathrib, about 210 miles north of Mecca through difficult desert terrain.
Yathrib was an oasis town, fed by groundwater in a way Mecca was not, with significant date-palm cultivation and a more agricultural economy than the trader-dominated Quraysh capital.

Its population in the early seventh century included two main Arab tribal groupings — the Aws and the Khazraj — who had been engaged in a long, bitter feud, and three substantial Jewish tribes (the Banu Qaynuqa, Banu Nadir, and Banu Qurayza), which made Yathrib one of the most religiously and ethnically mixed settlements on the peninsula.
The Yathribi Jews were an old community whose origins are not fully clear.
