Tradition held they had migrated from Palestine after the Roman destruction of the Second Temple in 70 CE; the surviving evidence is consistent with that timing but does not confirm it.

By Muhammad's lifetime they were thoroughly Arabized — speaking Arabic, organized as Arab-style tribes, intermarried with their Arab neighbors, conducting their religious life in Hebrew but their daily life in the language of the surrounding population.
They had brought monotheistic religious ideas into the Hijaz that almost certainly influenced Muhammad's revelations.

After the Hijra in 622 (Chapter 2), Muhammad's relationship with the Jewish tribes of Yathrib — initially cooperative under the Constitution of Medina, later catastrophically violent — would shape the early Muslim community's self-definition vis-à-vis the older monotheistic religions.

Yathrib in 622 was, additionally, exhausted by the Aws-Khazraj feud, which had recently killed off so many of the older tribal leaders that the surviving notables were actively looking for an outside arbiter to break the cycle.

This is the practical reason Muhammad was invited to Yathrib in 622 — not because the Yathribis had become Muslims (most of them had not yet) but because he was an outsider with a reputation for honesty who could potentially adjudicate the feud.
The arbitration job was the leverage Muhammad would use to convert the city.
Beyond the Hijaz, two great empires loomed over Arabia: the Sasanian Persian Empire to the northeast (Persian Empire Ch 9–10) and the Byzantine Empire to the northwest (Byzantine Empire Ch 1–3).
By 600 CE both empires were exhausted.

Sasanian Persia and Byzantium had been at war off and on since the third century, and the most recent round (602–628 CE) was the most destructive yet — the great Roman-Persian war Heraclius eventually won at the Battle of Nineveh in 627 (Persian Empire Ch 10).
Both empires had spent their reserves fighting each other.
Both had alienated their religious minorities.
Both had bled their tax base dry.
When the Arab armies erupted out of the desert in the 630s (Chapter 3), they hit two empires that had just spent twenty-six years exhausting each other.

The empires also each had an Arab buffer kingdom on the desert edge, designed to manage the unsettled tribes and project state power into the peninsula: The Lakhmids (LAKH-mids), centered at the city of al-Hira in southern Iraq, were the Arab clients of Sasanian Persia.

Largely Christian by the sixth century — specifically Nestorian Christian, the same wing of the eastern church the Sasanians sheltered (Persian Empire Ch 9) — the Lakhmids managed the desert frontier for the Persians, escorted caravans, raided rival tribes when ordered to, and provided trained Arab warriors to the Sasanian army.
The dynasty was deposed by the Sasanians around 602 in a misguided attempt to bring the buffer territory under direct rule.
The decision left the Persian-Arab frontier without an experienced manager precisely at the moment when the Arabs across that frontier were about to become a serious military problem.
The Ghassanids (GHAS-sah-nids), centered in the Hauran region of southern Syria, were the Arab clients of Byzantine Rome.

Like the Lakhmids they were largely Christian — but Monophysite Christian, the wing condemned at Chalcedon in 451 (Byzantine Empire Ch 1) — and their relationship with their Constantinopolitan patrons was correspondingly tense.
The Ghassanids managed the Roman desert frontier, escorted caravans, fought the Lakhmids on behalf of Constantinople, and provided trained Arab cavalry to the Roman field armies.
Like the Lakhmids, they fell apart in the early seventh century when imperial mismanagement deposed their last great king.
The fall of the buffer kingdoms is one of the underrated structural factors in the Arab conquests.

Both Sasanian Iraq and Byzantine Syria entered the 630s without functional Arab clients on their desert frontiers, which meant that the early Arab raids hit imperial territories that had no early-warning system, no friendly Arab cavalry to harass invaders, and no institutional memory of how to fight in the desert.
The Arabs walked through holes that had been there for a generation.
A note on what pre-Islamic Arabs actually believed.
The standard term for the period before Islam, in Islamic historiography, is the Jahiliyya (jah-hi-LEE-yah, "the time of ignorance").
This is a polemical term coined by the early Muslim community to disparage what came before; it implies that pre-Islamic religion was barbaric darkness lit only by the Quranic revelation.
Modern historians of religion are more cautious.
Pre-Islamic Arabian religion was a varied mix of: Tribal polytheism — each tribe with its own gods, often associated with sacred trees, stones, or springs.

The most widely worshipped pre-Islamic Arab deities were Allah (already a generic Arab name for the supreme creator god, though most pre-Islamic Arabs treated him as one god among many rather than the only god), al-Lat, al-Uzza, and Manat (three goddesses sometimes called the "daughters of Allah" in pre-Islamic ritual — these are the figures behind the contested "Satanic Verses" episode in the Quranic tradition).
Each tribe had its own pantheon.

Christianity — significant in the Yemeni south (where the Aksumite kingdom of Ethiopia had briefly conquered the country in the 520s), in the northern client kingdoms (the Lakhmids and Ghassanids), and in scattered urban communities elsewhere.
Estimates of the Christian population of pre-Islamic Arabia range widely, but it was not negligible.

Judaism — a substantial community in Yathrib and the surrounding Hijazi oases, smaller communities in Yemen (where one pre-Islamic king, Dhu Nuwas, had converted to Judaism around 510 and persecuted his Christian subjects, prompting the Aksumite intervention).
Hanifs — a small, scattered group of pre-Islamic Arab monotheists who had rejected polytheism but did not formally convert to either Christianity or Judaism.
Islamic tradition treats Muhammad's grandfather Abd al-Muttalib and several other Meccan elders as informal Hanifs who were already drifting toward the kind of monotheism Muhammad would formalize.

Magic, divination, sacred trees, sacred stones, sacred animals, and a wide range of locally specific ritual — the same kind of folk religion that surrounded the formal religions of every contemporary culture.
In other words, pre-Islamic Arabia was religiously diverse.
The Quranic narrative, and the later Muslim historiographic tradition, simplified the picture for polemical reasons.
The reality was messier and more interesting.

Cross-civ check: the early seventh century in Arabia overlaps with the Tang Dynasty in China (founded 618, the great consolidator of Sui-era institutions and one of the most powerful states in world history at the time), the Gupta Empire's final disintegration in northern India (Gupta Empire Ch 7–8), the Heraclian recovery of Byzantium after the catastrophic Sasanian war (Byzantine Empire Ch 3), the Sasanian Persian Empire's last decade before destruction (Persian Empire Ch 10), and the Kingdom of Aksum in Ethiopia.

Pre-Islamic Arabia was also in active commercial and diplomatic contact with Aksum — the Ethiopian kingdom that had occupied Yemen briefly in the early sixth century and that would later shelter the first Muslim refugees from Meccan persecution under its Christian king, the Negus.
The world Muhammad was born into in 570 was a world of tired empires, bleeding frontiers, and a peninsula at the geographic center of the late antique trade system.
Almost nothing about that world looks like a launching pad for a new religion that would conquer half of it within a century.
The peninsula's role had always been to supply spices, gold, slaves, and Bedouin mercenaries to the great states around it; it had never produced an empire of its own.
The Quranic revelation and the Rashidun-era political genius would change this in two generations.

chapters.title: Muhammad
sentences: Almost everything we know about Muhammad's life comes from sources written between 100 and 250 years after his death.

The two most important early biographies — Ibn Ishaq's Sirat Rasul Allah ("Life of the Messenger of God"), composed around 770 CE, and Ibn Hisham's later edition of Ibn Ishaq, around 830 CE — are the foundation of the traditional account.
The Quran itself, while preserved with extraordinary textual fidelity (Chapter 3), gives almost no narrative biography of its prophet; it presupposes a reader who already knows the story.
Modern Western scholarship on the historical Muhammad has been arguing for fifty years about how much of the traditional biography is reliable.

The maximalist view (still dominant in Muslim scholarship and well represented in Western academia) holds that the major outlines of the traditional account — birth in Mecca, marriage to Khadija, first revelation at Hira, Hijra to Medina, conquest of Mecca, death in 632 — are reliably attested even if individual incidents and dialogue are embellished.

The minimalist view (a much smaller school, associated with scholars like John Wansbrough and Patricia Crone, particularly in the 1970s and 1980s) held that the traditional account is so thoroughly retrofitted by ninth-century Sunni-Shia sectarian disputes that very little of it can be confidently treated as history.
The current center of gravity is closer to the maximalist view than to the minimalist one, but with more caution about specific dates and dialogue than was typical in older popular accounts.
This narrative follows the standard maximalist account.

The reader should keep in mind that the level of certainty for "Muhammad fled Mecca in 622" is much higher than for "the angel Gabriel said exactly the following words to Muhammad on the night of the first revelation." Muhammad ibn Abdullah was born around 570 CE at Mecca, into the Banu Hashim clan of the Quraysh (Chapter 1).
His early life was unsentimental.
His father Abdullah had died on a trading journey a few months before Muhammad was born.
His mother Amina died when he was about six.
His paternal grandfather Abd al-Muttalib, who had taken him in, died when he was about eight.
From age eight onward Muhammad was raised by his uncle Abu Talib (ah-BOO TAH-lib), the new head of the Banu Hashim, who treated him with affection but had limited resources to spare.

Muhammad grew up materially modest and socially marginal — a Hashimite cousin in the wealthier branches of the Quraysh trader establishment, a young man with a reputation for honesty (his nickname al-Amin, "the trustworthy") but not for wealth or political clout.
He worked, like most young Quraysh men of his generation, in the caravan trade.

By his early twenties he had risen far enough to be employed as the agent of a wealthy widowed merchant named Khadija bint Khuwaylid (kha-DEE-jah, fifteen or so years his senior — the exact age difference is disputed in the sources).
Khadija evidently liked what she saw of his work, because around 595 CE she proposed marriage to him.
He accepted.

The marriage produced four daughters who survived to adulthood — including Fatima (FAH-tih-mah, the youngest, who would later marry Ali and become the matriarch of the Shia imamate lineage) — and two sons who died in infancy.
The lack of a surviving son was one of the structural problems that would shape the post-Muhammad succession crisis (Chapter 3).
For the next fifteen years Muhammad lived as a successful Meccan merchant.
The early sources describe him as a settled family man, financially secure for the first time in his life, increasingly drawn to private religious meditation.
He had a habit of withdrawing to a cave on Mount Hira, north of Mecca, for solitary prayer and reflection.
The retreats grew longer over time.
They culminated, in 610 CE, in the event that Islamic tradition treats as the founding moment of the religion.
Muhammad was about forty years old, alone in the cave at Hira (HEE-rah), when he had what he later described as an overwhelming visionary experience.
According to the traditional account, the angel Gabriel (Arabic Jibril) appeared to him and commanded him to recite.
The first revealed verses are preserved as Chapter 96 of the Quran, beginning "Iqra'!
Bismi rabbika alladhi khalaq" — "Recite!
In the name of your Lord who created." Muhammad returned home shaken, convinced he had either gone mad or seen something genuinely supernatural.

Khadija reassured him, took him to her cousin Waraqa ibn Nawfal (a Hanif monotheist who had reportedly studied Christian scripture), and Waraqa told Muhammad that what he had experienced was the same kind of prophetic call that had come to Moses centuries earlier.
From this point onward the revelations recurred.
Muhammad would receive verses periodically — sometimes in dramatic visionary states, sometimes more quietly — for the next twenty-two years, until his death in 632.
The accumulated revelations, eventually compiled and standardized by Caliph Uthman around 650 (Chapter 3), are the Quran.
A note on the Quran.
The text is about 78,000 Arabic words long, divided into 114 chapters (called suras) of widely varying length.

The chapters are arranged not chronologically but roughly by length, longest first — which makes the text difficult to read as a biography of Muhammad's spiritual development, since the early Meccan revelations (mostly short, vivid, eschatological) are at the end of the book and the later Medinan revelations (longer, more legalistic, more political) are at the beginning.

The Quran is not a story; it is a series of divine addresses, sometimes in narrative form (retellings of stories from the Hebrew Bible and the Christian gospels, often in compressed and theologically distinctive form), sometimes in legal form, sometimes in lyrical praise of God, sometimes in direct response to specific events in Muhammad's life.
The Arabic prose is famously beautiful — the Quran's claim of inimitability (i'jaz) rests on its language, which any Muslim believer holds to be impossible to match.
Translations cannot fully convey what the Arabic does.
A note on whether Muhammad was illiterate.
Islamic tradition has emphasized Muhammad's illiteracy because it strengthens the miracle of the Quran — a man who could not read or write produced a text of unmatched literary beauty.
Modern scholars are divided.
The Arabic word ummi, applied to Muhammad in the Quran (e.g. 7:157), can mean "illiterate" but it can also mean "Gentile" (a non-Jew, someone outside the People of the Book).
A Meccan caravan trader in his forties would be unusual to have zero literacy in a society that did some written commercial accounting.
The traditional interpretation may be theologically motivated rather than historical.
The current scholarly view tends toward "the question is genuinely unresolved" rather than a confident answer either way.

Muhammad's preaching at Mecca over the next dozen years (roughly 610–622) was strict monotheism, with three core demands: the worship of one God only, social-economic justice (especially toward orphans, widows, and the poor), and acceptance of Muhammad as God's messenger.

The early Meccan suras of the Quran are dominated by vivid eschatological imagery — the Last Day, divine judgment, the rewards of paradise, the punishments of hell — and by ethical injunctions that put the early Muslim community at odds with Quraysh commercial values.
The Quraysh leadership did not, at first, take Muhammad seriously.
The Hashimite cousin claiming to be a prophet was an embarrassment but not a threat.
As his small community of converts grew, the Quraysh attitude hardened.

Muhammad's monotheism was not just personally offensive to the polytheistic Meccan establishment — it was an existential threat to the Kaaba's commercial role as a multi-tribal sanctuary, since strict monotheism would eventually require dismantling the 360 idols and ending the polytheistic pilgrimage that fed the Meccan economy.

By the late 610s the Quraysh were applying pressure: a social and economic boycott against the Banu Hashim, public mockery of Muhammad's preaching, beatings and isolated killings of vulnerable converts (including the slave Bilal, who later became the first muezzin — the caller to prayer — of the Muslim community).
Two events near the end of Muhammad's Meccan period shaped what came next.

In 619 CE — what later Muslim tradition called the Year of Sorrow — both Khadija (Muhammad's wife of twenty-four years and his most important emotional support) and his uncle Abu Talib (his clan protector and political shield against Quraysh aggression) died within months of each other.
The deaths left Muhammad both personally devastated and politically exposed.
With Abu Talib gone, the Banu Hashim leadership passed to another uncle, Abu Lahab, who was unsympathetic to Muhammad's mission and refused to extend clan protection.
Muhammad was now an unprotected man in a hostile city.
In 620 or 621, a delegation of pilgrims from Yathrib met Muhammad outside Mecca during the pilgrimage season.

They had heard of his preaching, were intrigued, and were also dealing with their own urgent problem: the Aws-Khazraj feud (Chapter 1) had exhausted both tribes, and the Yathribi notables were looking for an outside arbiter who could mediate disputes the tribal elders had failed to resolve.
Negotiations followed across the next two pilgrimage seasons.

At the second meeting, in 622, the Yathribi delegation — by then including substantial converts from both the Aws and the Khazraj — formally invited Muhammad to settle in their city, accept the role of arbitrator, and bring his Meccan followers with him.
The invitation became one of the most consequential decisions in religious history.
In 622 CE, Muhammad and his small community of Meccan followers — perhaps a hundred adults plus families — left Mecca in stages and migrated to Yathrib.
The journey is called the Hijra (HIJ-rah, "the migration").
Muhammad himself left Mecca last, traveling with his close companion Abu Bakr (ah-BOO BAKR — Khadija's father, but more importantly the most senior of the early converts and a future caliph).

They evaded a Quraysh pursuit, hid in a cave for three days while search parties passed nearby (the cave incident is one of the foundational miracle stories of the early tradition — a spider's web at the entrance allegedly persuaded the searchers no one had entered), and reached Yathrib by an indirect route.
Yathrib was renamed Medina (literally "the City," shortened from Madinat al-Nabi, "City of the Prophet").

The Hijra is the foundational political event of Islam — so foundational that the Islamic calendar starts not with Muhammad's birth (around 570), not with the first revelation (610), not with his death (632), but with the year of the Hijra.
Year 1 AH ("After the Hijra") begins on July 16, 622 in the Western calendar.

Every Islamic date from then to now is reckoned from the founding of the first Muslim political community at Medina. (The choice is theologically significant: Islam dates its calendar not from the prophet's life but from the establishment of the Umma, the community.

This is one of several places where early Islam differs structurally from early Christianity, which dates its calendar from the birth of its founder.) At Medina, Muhammad's role expanded from religious teacher to political leader.

He drafted what later sources call the Constitution of Medina — a treaty among the various Muslim, Jewish, and Arab tribal groupings of the city that established Muhammad as the arbitrator of disputes, codified mutual defense obligations, and recognized the religious autonomy of the Jewish tribes within the new political framework.
The text survives in Ibn Ishaq's biography.
It is one of the earliest written constitutions in any society, and it reads — even allowing for likely later editing — as a remarkably pragmatic document.
Muhammad was not yet trying to convert the Yathribi Jews; he was trying to organize a viable city-state out of warring tribal factions.

The political community at Medina came to be called the Umma (OOM-mah) — a word that originally meant something like "the people" but which the Quranic revelation began to use specifically for the community of Muslim believers.

The Umma is one of the load-bearing concepts of Islamic political thought: the community of Muslims is, in principle, a single body that transcends tribal, ethnic, and (eventually) national boundaries.
The concept worked well at the scale of seventh-century Medina.
It would become harder to operationalize when the Umma grew to include tens of millions of people across thousands of miles (Chapter 5).
The relationship between Medina and Mecca did not stabilize.

The Quraysh continued to view Muhammad's community as a security threat — particularly because the Medinan Muslims, having lost their property when they emigrated, began conducting raids on Meccan caravans to support themselves.
The raids escalated.
In 624 the Quraysh sent a relief force to protect a major caravan returning from Syria.
Muhammad's much smaller force ambushed the relief force at the wells of Badr, in the Hijaz between Mecca and Medina, on March 13, 624.
The Muslim force of perhaps 313 men defeated a Quraysh army of perhaps 950 (the numbers in the early sources are suspicious in their precision, but the rough scale is reliable).
Several leading Quraysh notables were killed.
The Muslim losses were small.
The Battle of Badr was the founding military event of Islam.
The early Muslim community treated it as direct evidence of divine support — Quran 8 ("The Spoils of War") was revealed in its aftermath and explicitly addresses the battle.

Strategically Badr was less decisive than the early sources make it sound (the Quraysh remained the dominant military power in the Hijaz for several years afterward), but psychologically it transformed the Muslim community's confidence.
They had won a battle they were not supposed to be able to win.
A year later, in 625, the Quraysh returned with a larger force — perhaps 3,000 men — and met the Muslims at Mount Uhud, just outside Medina.

The Battle of Uhud started well for the Muslims (the Quraysh charge was repulsed by Muslim archers) and then went badly when the archers abandoned their position to seize the loot left behind by the retreating Quraysh.
The Quraysh cavalry counterattacked into the gap, the Muslim formation collapsed, Muhammad himself was wounded by a thrown stone, and rumors briefly circulated that he had been killed.
The Muslim force broke and retreated to fortified positions on Mount Uhud, where the Quraysh failed to press the assault and eventually withdrew.
Uhud is the founding cautionary battle of the Islamic tradition.

The lesson, drawn from it by the Quranic revelation in Chapter 3 (al-Imran, verses 121–155), was that even the prophet could lose, that discipline mattered, and that the community had to be prepared for setbacks as well as victories.
The early Islamic tradition was not triumphalist about military success.
It treated victories as divine favor and defeats as divine warning, a pattern that — combined with the Bedouin warrior culture's practical skill — produced an unusually adaptable military mindset.
In 627 the Quraysh tried a third time, with a much larger coalition force (perhaps 10,000 men) that besieged Medina.

This is the Battle of the Trench (or Battle of the Confederates), so named because the Muslims, on the advice of the Persian convert Salman al-Farisi, dug a defensive trench across the only approach to Medina that cavalry could use.
The trench (a Persian military innovation, novel to the Arabs) immobilized the Quraysh army.
After two weeks the besiegers ran out of supplies and morale and went home.
The Muslim community then turned on the Jewish Banu Qurayza tribe, which had negotiated with the Quraysh during the siege, executed the adult men, and enslaved the women and children.

The mass execution — variously estimated at 600 to 900 men — is one of the most morally difficult episodes in the early Muslim community's history, and Muslim and non-Muslim historiographies have read it differently for thirteen centuries.
After the Trench, the Quraysh stopped attacking.
The military momentum had shifted to Medina.

In 630, after a Quraysh treaty violation (the killing of some Muslim allies by a Meccan-allied tribe), Muhammad assembled an army of about 10,000 — a coalition of Medinan Muslims and converted Bedouin tribes — and marched on Mecca itself.
The Quraysh leadership, calculating that resistance was hopeless, capitulated without significant fighting.

Muhammad entered Mecca, declared a general amnesty for nearly all his former opponents (including Abu Sufyan, the Umayyad-clan leader who had organized most of the anti-Muhammad campaigns and whose son Mu'awiya would later found the Umayyad caliphate — Chapter 5), and went directly to the Kaaba.
He smashed the 360 idols inside and around the shrine.
He performed the first explicitly Islamic version of the pilgrimage ritual.
He rededicated the Kaaba to monotheistic worship, recovering its supposed Abrahamic identity from underneath the polytheism (Chapter 1).
The conquest of Mecca in 630 is the political event that fixed Mecca's permanent status as the holiest city of Islam.
Every Muslim has, since 630, faced Mecca during the five daily prayers (the qibla, the direction of prayer).

Every Muslim with the financial and physical means is required at least once in life to perform the hajj — the major pilgrimage to Mecca during the sacred month of Dhu al-Hijja, with the rituals Muhammad himself performed in 630 and during his later "Farewell Pilgrimage" of 632.
Mecca's holiness predated Islam (the Kaaba had been a Hijazi pilgrimage destination for centuries), but Islamic Mecca is Muhammad's reorganization of pre-Islamic Mecca around monotheistic principles.
The conquest of Mecca consolidated Muhammad's political position throughout Arabia.
Tribes that had been on the fence began converting in numbers.

By the Farewell Pilgrimage in early 632, Muhammad commanded the allegiance of most of the Arabian Peninsula, either through direct Islamic conversion or through political treaties with tribes that accepted Muslim political supremacy without yet accepting full conversion.

The exact extent of Islamic political reach in 632 is debated by modern scholars — the traditional account exaggerates it, the minimalist account understates it, the truth is somewhere in between — but in any case, Muhammad's last year saw delegations from across the peninsula traveling to Medina to pledge allegiance.
In June 632, Muhammad fell ill at Medina with what the early sources describe as a fever, headaches, and progressive weakness.
He died on 8 June 632 in the apartment of his youngest wife Aisha (AH-ee-shah, daughter of Abu Bakr), her head reportedly cradled in her arms.
He was somewhere between sixty and sixty-three years old — the precise birth year being uncertain.
He was buried in Aisha's apartment, beneath the floor where he died.
The site became part of the Mosque of the Prophet in Medina; it remains the second-holiest pilgrimage site in Sunni Islam after the Kaaba at Mecca.
He had not designated a successor.
This is the structural fact that produced the entire subsequent history of Islamic political conflict.
Muhammad had had no surviving son.

He had not, on the Sunni reading of the surviving evidence, ever explicitly designated any other man as his successor — neither Abu Bakr, nor Umar, nor his cousin and son-in-law Ali. (The Shia reading is different and is covered in Chapter 4.) He had instructed the community in religious matters, but he had left no clear instructions about who should lead the community in political matters after his death.
The succession dispute began within hours of Muhammad's death and has not been fully resolved in the thirteen centuries since.

Cross-civ check: Muhammad's lifetime (570–632) overlaps with the Heraclian recovery of Byzantium under Emperor Heraclius (Byzantine Empire Ch 3), the last great Sasanian war under Khosrow II (Persian Empire Ch 10) and the Sasanian collapse that followed, the founding of the Tang Dynasty in China in 618 (Tang-Song China — the dynasty that would become the cultural superpower of the seventh-century world, while Muhammad was preaching at Mecca and his successors were conquering Persia), the Asuka period in Japan (when Buddhism was being formally adopted as state religion), and the late Visigothic kingdom in Spain (the kingdom Tariq ibn Ziyad would destroy in 711 — Chapter 6; what Islamic Iberia became over the following eight centuries is its own narrative, al-Andalus).
The Hijra in 622 is contemporary with Heraclius's first counter-offensive against the Sasanians.
The conquest of Mecca in 630 is contemporary with Heraclius's triumphant return of the True Cross to Jerusalem (Byzantine Empire Ch 3).
Within six years, the Arab armies pouring out of Muhammad's reorganized Arabia would take from Heraclius everything he had just recovered (Chapter 3).

chapters.title: The Rashidun Caliphs
sentences: The four caliphs who ruled the Muslim community from Muhammad's death in 632 to the assassination of Ali in 661 are called, in Sunni tradition, the Rashidun (rah-shee-DOON, "the rightly-guided").
They are: Abu Bakr (632–634), Umar ibn al-Khattab (634–644), Uthman ibn Affan (644–656), and Ali ibn Abi Talib (656–661).
Each was chosen by some form of community consensus rather than dynastic succession.
Each ruled the original community at Medina, then increasingly the rapidly expanding empire that the conquests were producing.
Three of the four were assassinated.
The Sunni veneration of all four caliphs as legitimate is one of the founding markers of Sunni identity.
The Shia view, which rejects the legitimacy of the first three caliphs (Abu Bakr, Umar, and Uthman) and recognizes only Ali, is the founding marker of Shia identity.
This chapter narrates the standard Sunni chronology while flagging the Shia counter-narrative where it diverges.
The succession argument began the day Muhammad died.

A faction of the Medinan Muslims — the Ansar (ahn-SAR, "the helpers," meaning the Yathribis who had hosted the Hijra and converted in Medina rather than Mecca) — gathered at a meeting hall called the Saqifa of the Banu Sa'ida and began discussing who should succeed Muhammad.
A faction of the Meccan Muslims — the Muhajirun (moo-hah-jih-ROON, "the emigrants," the Quraysh who had migrated from Mecca with Muhammad in 622) — heard about the meeting and rushed to it.
The two groups argued.
The Ansar leadership proposed sharing the leadership role between an Ansar candidate and a Muhajirun candidate.
The Muhajirun rejected the compromise; they argued that the new Muslim community had to be led by the Quraysh (the tribe to which Muhammad had belonged) for political and theological reasons.
The argument was tense but not violent.
By the end of the meeting, the Muhajirun candidate Abu Bakr — Muhammad's father-in-law and one of the very earliest converts — had received pledges of allegiance from a majority of those present.
This is the Sunni version.

The traditional Shia counter-version holds that Muhammad had explicitly designated Ali ibn Abi Talib — his cousin and son-in-law (the husband of Fatima, Muhammad's daughter) — as his successor, in a public declaration at Ghadir Khumm (gha-DEER KHOOM, an oasis on the route from Mecca to Medina) during the Farewell Pilgrimage in 632, only a few months before his death.

The Shia hold that Abu Bakr's selection at the Saqifa was an opportunistic coup conducted in Ali's absence (Ali was busy preparing Muhammad's body for burial) by a Quraysh faction unwilling to see the caliphate go to Muhammad's bloodline.

The Sunni reply is that Muhammad's words at Ghadir Khumm — "He of whom I am the master, of him Ali is also the master" — were a personal endorsement of Ali's character rather than a formal political designation.
The two readings produce two different histories of the early Islamic period and two different theologies of religious-political authority that have shaped Muslim communities ever since.
A clean Sunni-Shia rule of thumb for reading what follows: Sunnis consider the Rashidun caliphate the proper continuation of Muhammad's mission, with all four caliphs legitimate.
Shias consider the first three caliphs usurpers and only Ali legitimate.

The split is theological, not just political — it shapes how Sunnis and Shias understand religious authority itself. (Chapter 4 unpacks the theology more fully.) Abu Bakr (ruled 632–634) was elected caliph at the Saqifa and took the title Khalifat Rasul Allah (kha-LEE-faht rah-SOOL al-LAH, "Successor of the Messenger of God").
The Arabic word khalifa — "successor," the source of the English "caliph" — became the title of the new office.
His two-year reign was almost entirely consumed by the Ridda Wars (RID-dah, "the apostasy").
After Muhammad's death, much of Arabia attempted to secede from the Muslim federation — most tribes treating their allegiance to Muhammad as a personal pact that died with him.
Several tribal leaders proclaimed themselves prophets in their own right, in deliberate imitation of Muhammad's career.
The most significant was Musaylima (moo-SAY-lim-ah), of the Banu Hanifa tribe in central Arabia, who attracted a large following and posed a genuine military threat to Medina.
Abu Bakr's response was to refuse any negotiation with the seceding tribes.

He declared that Muhammad's political authority was not personal but institutional — the Umma was a permanent commitment, not a contract that ended with the prophet's death — and that any tribe attempting to leave was in religious as well as political revolt.
He then dispatched the most gifted military commander of the early community, Khalid ibn al-Walid (KAH-lid IH-bin al-wah-LEED), to put down the revolts.
Khalid did.
Across 632 and 633, he led campaigns through central and eastern Arabia, defeating one tribal coalition after another.

The decisive battle against Musaylima at Yamama in late 632 was unusually bloody; it killed Musaylima but also killed a number of the Muslim companions who had memorized the Quran (the huffaz), which is what prompted Abu Bakr to commission the first systematic written collection of Quranic verses (the project that would later be completed under Uthman).
By the end of 633 the Ridda Wars were essentially over and Arabia was solidly Muslim.
Abu Bakr died of natural causes in August 634, having ruled for about two years and three months.
Before his death, he had personally nominated his successor — Umar ibn al-Khattab — and the leading Companions (the surviving men who had known Muhammad personally) accepted the nomination.
The Sunni view treats this as an acceptable form of caliphal succession.
The Shia view treats it as compounding the original error.
Umar ibn al-Khattab (ruled 634–644) was the second caliph and, by most reckonings, the most consequential.

His ten-year reign saw the most spectacular phase of the Arab conquests: the destruction of the Sasanian Empire, the loss of Syria and Egypt by the Byzantines, and the construction of the administrative scaffolding that the caliphate would use for the next several centuries.
Umar himself was a hard man.
The early sources describe him as physically imposing, austere in personal habit, terrifying when angered, scrupulously honest, and obsessed with administrative competence.
He took the title Amir al-Mu'minin (ah-MEER al-moo-mih-NEEN, "Commander of the Faithful"), which would become the standard caliphal title for the next thirteen centuries.
He lived modestly, slept on a mat, wore patched clothes, and carried out his responsibilities personally.
He toured his expanding empire on horseback and conducted business in person with conquered governors.
He was assassinated in 644 by a Persian slave named Abu Lu'lu'a (ah-BOO LOO-loo-ah), who stabbed him while he was leading the dawn prayer at the Mosque of the Prophet in Medina.
The slave's motive was apparently personal grievance over taxation.
The killing left no trail of conspiracy and no obvious political beneficiary; it was just one man's grudge that ended one of the most successful reigns in Muslim history.
Under Umar the conquests began.

The Arab conquests of 634 to 651 are one of the most remarkable military expansions in human history — comparable in compressed scale only to Alexander's campaigns or to the later Mongol explosion under Genghis Khan (Mongol Empire Ch 2–3).
Within seventeen years, Arab armies took Syria, Palestine, Egypt, all of Mesopotamia, and the entire Iranian plateau from two empires that had been the dominant Eurasian powers for four centuries.
The pattern was set in 636, in two battles three months apart.

In August 636, the Arab commander Khalid ibn al-Walid (transferred from the Iraqi frontier specifically for the campaign) faced the main Byzantine field army along the Yarmouk River, on what is now the Syria-Jordan border.

The Byzantine force had perhaps 40,000 to 80,000 men under the Armenian eunuch general Vahan; the Arab force was smaller, perhaps 24,000 to 40,000 (the numbers in the Arabic and Greek sources vary widely).

Khalid maneuvered the Byzantines into difficult terrain along the steep ravines of the Yarmouk gorge, exploited a sandstorm that blew into the Byzantine lines on the sixth day of fighting, and shattered the Roman army.
Vahan was killed or captured.
The defeat ended Roman power in Syria.

Within two years the Arabs had taken Damascus (occupied a second time, this time permanently), Antioch (the great Roman provincial capital that Augustus had governed personally), and Jerusalem (which surrendered in 637 to Caliph Umar in person, on terms negotiated with the Patriarch Sophronius — the holy city changing hands in a deliberately peaceful handover).

Three months after Yarmouk, in November 636, a separate Arab army under Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas (SAHD IH-bin AH-bee wak-KAHS) fought the main Sasanian field force under Rostam Farrokhzad at the Battle of al-Qadisiyyah (kah-dih-SEE-yah) somewhere in southern Iraq.
The exact site is disputed; the date is firm.
Each side fielded perhaps 30,000 to 60,000 troops.
The battle lasted four days, with each day given a name in the Arabic sources (the Day of Concussion, the Day of Battle, the Night of Fury, the Day of Decision).
On the final day, a sandstorm blew into the Sasanian lines, the war elephants panicked, and the Persian formation broke.
Rostam was killed.
The Sasanian field army was destroyed.
The Persian capital at Ctesiphon fell almost immediately afterward (Persian Empire Ch 10).

The Arabs captured the royal treasury, the throne room, and the famous Spring of Khosrow carpet — a 95-foot-long silk-and-jewel weaving depicting a Persian garden, which the conquerors immediately cut into pieces and distributed to the troops as plunder.
The Persian collapse continued for six more years.
The Battle of Nihavand in 642 destroyed the last major Sasanian field army in the Zagros mountains; the Arabs called it the Victory of Victories.

The last Sasanian king, Yazdegerd III (yaz-deh-GERD), fled east through the Iranian plateau, attempting to rally resistance, and was finally murdered at Merv in 651 — reportedly by a local miller who killed him for his clothes and jewelry (Persian Empire Ch 10).
With Yazdegerd's death the Sasanian Empire ended after 427 years.
The Egyptian conquest was a separate campaign, conducted by Amr ibn al-As (AHMR IH-bin al-AHS) starting in 639.

Amr crossed the Sinai with about 4,000 troops, took the Roman fortress of Babylon-in-Egypt (a fortress at the apex of the Nile delta near modern Cairo, not the Babylon in Iraq) in 641, and captured Alexandria itself in 642.
The Coptic Christian population of Egypt — who had been suffering under Constantinopolitan religious persecution for two centuries (Byzantine Empire Ch 1) — did not resist with any enthusiasm.
Their bishops negotiated terms.
The Greek-speaking ruling class largely fled.
Egypt has been an Arabic-speaking Muslim country ever since.
The conquests succeeded for several reasons that are worth listing because the popular narrative ("Islam spread by the sword") is a partial truth that misses the structural picture.
First, the Arab armies hit two empires that had just spent twenty-six years exhausting each other (Persian Empire Ch 10, Byzantine Empire Ch 3).
Both Sasanian Persia and Heraclian Byzantium were broke, depopulated, and militarily depleted in the 630s.
The Arabs caught them at the worst possible moment.

Second, the local populations of the conquered provinces — Coptic Christians in Egypt, Monophysite Christians in Syria, Nestorian Christians in Iraq, Jews everywhere — were alienated from their imperial overlords by decades of Constantinopolitan or Sasanian religious persecution.

The Arab terms for non-Muslim subjects (the dhimmi arrangement: protection of life, property, and worship in exchange for the jizya head tax and acceptance of Muslim political supremacy — Chapter 7) were better in most cases than what the locals had been getting from their previous rulers.
Egypt and Syria were not "conquered" in the sense of being held down by force against unified popular resistance; they were liberated, in many places, from one ruling class by another.
Third, the Arab armies were small but tactically extraordinary.
They were highly mobile — almost entirely cavalry, fast camel-mounted infantry, no slow siege trains — which let them choose their battles and disengage when conditions were unfavorable.
They were extremely well led (Khalid ibn al-Walid, in particular, is in the discussion for the most gifted commander of the seventh century, anywhere).

They were religiously motivated to a degree that surprised contemporary observers — Arab warriors fought believing that death in battle was a direct route to paradise, which produced the kind of unit cohesion most armies struggle to manufacture.

And they were strategically patient — willing to take cities through long sieges, willing to negotiate surrenders rather than insist on military glory, willing to settle conquered territories under Arab garrisons rather than retreating after victory.
Fourth — this is important and underappreciated — the conquest was rapid but the conversion was slow, sometimes very slow.
The Arab armies did not enter conquered cities and demand mass conversion.
They demanded political submission and the jizya tax.
They left religious life largely alone.
Muslim conversion was a gradual process that took centuries, driven by social-economic incentives (lower taxes, eligibility for Arab status, marriage prospects) rather than by direct coercion.
Egypt was probably not majority Muslim until the tenth or eleventh century.
Iran was not majority Muslim until the ninth or tenth.
The popular shorthand "Islam was spread by the sword" mistakes the conquest for the conversion.
The conquest was indeed largely military; the conversion was largely social and economic, conducted over many generations.
This matters for understanding what the Umayyad and early Abbasid caliphates actually were.

They were Arab military elites ruling over majority-Christian populations in Syria, majority-Coptic populations in Egypt, majority-Zoroastrian populations in Iran, and majority-Jewish populations in some pockets of Iraq.
The slow conversion of these populations to Islam over the following centuries is the deeper story; the lightning Arab conquest is just the political prelude.
Umar's other major contribution was administrative.
He created the diwan (dee-WAHN) in about 638 — a written register of Arab Muslim warriors entitled to a share of the conquest revenues, organized by tribe and seniority.

The diwan formalized the army's relationship to the state: warriors received cash stipends from the conquered provinces' tax revenues, with payments scaled by closeness to Muhammad and by service record.
The system worked while the conquests kept producing new revenue.
It would break later when the conquests slowed and the converting non-Arab population started demanding equal stipends (Chapter 8).

He also founded the garrison cities — major new urban settlements, deliberately separated from the existing populations of conquered provinces, where Arab warriors and their families lived and from which Arab governors administered the surrounding countryside.

The most important were Kufa (KOO-fah, in central Iraq, founded 638), Basra (BAHS-rah, in southern Iraq near the Persian Gulf, founded 638), and Fustat (foos-TAHT, in Egypt south of modern Cairo, founded 641 by Amr ibn al-As after the Egyptian conquest).
Kairouan (kair-WAHN, in modern Tunisia) was added later in the 670s under Mu'awiya.

These garrison cities grew rapidly into major urban centers, became the political fault lines of every later Iraqi or Egyptian rebellion against the caliphate, and produced the early scholarly traditions in Quran recitation, hadith collection, and jurisprudence (Chapter 7) that would eventually grow into the great Islamic intellectual schools.
Umar refused to let his Arab warriors permanently settle the conquered countryside.

He kept them concentrated in the garrison cities, where they could be mobilized for further campaigns and could be prevented from "going native" — assimilating into the Coptic-Christian or Persian-Zoroastrian local population.
The policy worked for two generations and broke down by the third, as Arab settlers married locally, learned local languages, and began to merge into the broader population.
He also institutionalized the Islamic calendar, dating from the Hijra (Chapter 2).
The first official year 1 AH was retroactively set as 622 CE, and Umar's chancery began dating documents this way around 638.

The Islamic year is purely lunar (twelve months of 29 or 30 days, totaling roughly 354 days), so it drifts about 11 days earlier each solar year — meaning that Islamic dates do not align cleanly with solar seasons or with the Western calendar over long stretches.
Modern Muslim countries usually use both the Islamic and the Gregorian calendars in parallel.
Uthman ibn Affan (OOTH-mahn IH-bin ah-FAHN, ruled 644–656) was the third caliph.

He had been chosen by a small electoral council Umar had appointed before his assassination — a council of six senior Companions, including Ali, Talha, al-Zubayr, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, and Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, with Uthman emerging as the consensus candidate.
Uthman was a member of the Banu Umayya, the wealthy Quraysh clan that would later found the Umayyad dynasty (Chapter 5).

He was Muhammad's son-in-law (married first to Muhammad's daughter Ruqayya, then after her death to her sister Umm Kulthum), a very early convert, and one of the most important financial backers of the Medinan community during its lean early years.
He was also old (in his late sixties at his accession), unassertive in personal style, and disposed to trust the family connections that would eventually destroy him.
His twelve-year reign began well.
The conquests continued — Cyprus was taken in 649, the Battle of the Masts in 655 broke Byzantine naval power in the eastern Mediterranean, Khorasan in eastern Iran was consolidated.
Most consequentially, around 650, Uthman commissioned the canonical text of the Quran.
The need for canonization had been visible since Abu Bakr's reign.

The Quran had originally been preserved through oral memorization (by the huffaz, the professional reciters) and through scattered written manuscripts on palm leaves, parchment scraps, animal bones, and stones.

As the Muslim community spread across the conquered provinces, regional variations in the recitation began to appear — different cities had inherited slightly different versions of certain verses from the Companions who had carried the text to them.

Uthman, alarmed by reports that his armies in Armenia and Azerbaijan were arguing about which recitation was correct, commissioned a small editorial commission led by Zayd ibn Thabit (one of Muhammad's original scribes who had also overseen Abu Bakr's earlier collection) to produce a single authoritative text.

The commission consolidated the existing collected materials, resolved variants by reference to the Quraysh dialect (Muhammad's own dialect — the criterion privileged the Meccan reading where it differed from regional ones), and produced about five master copies that were sent to the major garrison cities.
Uthman then ordered all variant copies destroyed.
The destruction order is the foundational act of Quranic textual canonization.
From 650 onward, every Quran was supposed to be a copy of the Uthmanic text.

Modern scholarship (including the comparative analysis of the very early Sana'a manuscript discovered in 1972) has confirmed that the Uthmanic codex was, in textual terms, remarkably well-preserved — the variants between the earliest surviving Qurans are minor enough that the canonical text we have today is, to a high degree of certainty, the text Uthman authorized.
This is unusual among major religious texts, which typically show much greater textual drift over comparable periods.
The Uthmanic codification is one of the most consequential editorial decisions in the history of religion, and one of the very rare ones whose textual outcome we can verify.
The codification was not universally welcomed.

Some senior Companions had their own personal Quranic codices that differed in minor ways from the Uthmanic version (the Ibn Mas'ud codex from Kufa was the most famous case), and they resented being told to destroy them.
Others objected on principle to what looked like Uthman over-centralizing religious authority in his own family.
The complaints accumulated.

Uthman, against the advice of Ali and other senior Companions, had been steadily appointing his Umayyad relatives to provincial governorships — most notably his cousin Mu'awiya as governor of Syria, and his foster-brother Marwan as his personal chief of staff in Medina.
The Umayyad governors enriched themselves and their clients.
Tax revenues from the provinces increasingly flowed through Umayyad pockets before reaching the central treasury.
The non-Umayyad Companions, who had borne the burden of the conquests, felt frozen out.
In 656, a delegation of soldier-rebels arrived at Medina from the garrison city of Fustat in Egypt, ostensibly to present grievances against the Egyptian governor (an Umayyad relative of Uthman).
After confused negotiations, the delegation laid siege to Uthman's house in Medina for several weeks.
Ali and other senior Companions tried to mediate, with limited success.

On 17 June 656, the rebels broke into Uthman's house and murdered the eighty-two-year-old caliph as he was reading his copy of the Quran — a death that, for shock value alone, would shape every Muslim political imagination for centuries.
The murder of a caliph by Muslims who claimed to be acting in the name of justice was the founding catastrophe of the Umma.
It had to be understood, theologically as well as politically, by every faction in the community that came after.
Ali ibn Abi Talib (AH-lee IH-bin AH-bee TAH-lib, ruled 656–661) was the fourth caliph.

He was Muhammad's cousin (the son of Muhammad's uncle Abu Talib, who had raised the orphan prophet — Chapter 2), Muhammad's son-in-law (the husband of Fatima), and the father of Muhammad's only male grandchildren who survived to adulthood, Hasan and Husayn.
He had been one of the very earliest converts (depending on the source, the second or third overall, after Khadija and possibly Abu Bakr).
He had been Muhammad's most trusted political and military lieutenant during the Medinan years.

The Shia tradition holds, as Chapter 2 noted, that Muhammad had explicitly designated Ali as his successor at Ghadir Khumm; the Sunni tradition rejects this, but acknowledges that Ali was a leading Companion of unique closeness to Muhammad.
Ali had been bypassed for the caliphate three times — in favor of Abu Bakr in 632, in favor of Umar in 634, in favor of Uthman in 644.
His election in 656 — by a coalition of the Egyptian rebels, Medinan Muslims who had supported Uthman until his murder, and senior Companions like Ali himself — made him caliph at last.
He was about fifty-six years old.
His five-year reign was disastrous.

The basic problem was that Ali's accession had been preceded by Uthman's assassination, and significant portions of the Muslim community held Ali at least morally responsible for not having protected the previous caliph more vigorously.

Two prominent Companions, Talha and al-Zubayr (both members of the original electoral council that had chosen Uthman), and Muhammad's widow Aisha (Abu Bakr's daughter, who had hated Uthman in life but now demanded vengeance for his murder), raised an army at Mecca and marched to Iraq to challenge Ali.
Ali met them at the Battle of the Camel outside Basra in November 656 — the battle was named for Aisha's camel-borne litter, which became the focal point of the fighting.
Talha and al-Zubayr were killed.
Aisha was captured, treated with respect, and escorted back to Medina, where she lived in dignified retirement for another two decades.
The Battle of the Camel was the first time Muslims fought Muslims in pitched battle.
The shock was enormous.
The Muslim community had been at war with various Quraysh and Bedouin opponents for two decades, but it had never before turned its weapons on itself.
The First Fitna had only just begun.

Mu'awiya, the Umayyad governor of Syria (the same Mu'awiya whom Uthman had appointed and who had done very well out of Uthman's nepotism), refused to recognize Ali's caliphate and demanded vengeance for his cousin Uthman's murder.
Ali assembled an Iraqi army and marched on Syria.
The two forces met at Siffin (sif-FEEN), on the upper Euphrates near the modern Syria-Turkey border, in summer 657.
After several days of inconclusive fighting, Mu'awiya's troops famously raised pages of the Quran on their lance tips and called for arbitration of the dispute by reference to scripture.
Ali — against the advice of his more militant supporters — accepted.
The two sides withdrew.
Arbitrators were appointed to decide who should be caliph.
The arbitration disaster broke Ali's coalition.

His more militant supporters considered the acceptance of arbitration a betrayal — the question of caliphate, they argued, could not be decided by human deliberation, only by the sword and divine judgment.
They split off, declaring both Ali and Mu'awiya unfit to rule.
They became the Kharijites (KHAH-rij-ites, "those who go out"), the first sectarian breakaway in Islamic history.

The Kharijites went on to develop a distinctive theology — they held that any Muslim who committed a major sin had ceased to be a Muslim, and that the caliphate should go to the most pious individual regardless of lineage or tribal affiliation. (A small Kharijite community survives today in the Ibadi Muslims of Oman, North Africa, and Zanzibar; modern Ibadism is theologically much more moderate than the original seventh-century Kharijites, but the genealogy is direct.) Ali fought the Kharijites at the Battle of Nahrawan in 658, defeated them militarily, and accumulated a generation of bitter enemies.
The arbitration itself produced no usable result — the arbitrators failed to reach an agreement and the question of caliphate remained unresolved.
Mu'awiya kept his Syrian governorship.
Ali kept his Iraqi capital at Kufa.
The two Muslim states existed in tense coexistence for the next three years.
In 661, a Kharijite named Ibn Muljam assassinated Ali at the great mosque in Kufa, stabbing him with a poisoned blade as he led the dawn prayer.
Ali died two days later.
He was about sixty-one years old.
He was buried at a site outside Kufa that became, over the following centuries, the city of Najaf — the burial place of the First Imam and one of the holiest pilgrimage sites in Shia Islam.
The Rashidun caliphate ended with Ali's death in 661.
His elder son Hasan was briefly proclaimed caliph by the Iraqi army at Kufa, but he had no taste for civil war.

After a few months of negotiation, Hasan formally abdicated to Mu'awiya in exchange for a substantial pension and the promise that the caliphate would revert to the descendants of Ali after Mu'awiya's death.
Hasan retired to Medina, where he died (probably poisoned, almost certainly by his wife at Mu'awiya's instigation, though the surviving evidence is contested) around 670.
The promise of caliphal reversion was not kept.
Mu'awiya designated his own son Yazid as successor (Chapter 5), turning the caliphate into a hereditary Umayyad office.
The dispute that this would shortly produce — between Mu'awiya's son Yazid and Ali's younger son Husayn — is the subject of the next chapter.

The Sunni judgment on the Rashidun period is that all four caliphs were rightly-guided successors of Muhammad, that the conquests they ran were divinely favored, and that the catastrophe at the end (Uthman's assassination, the First Fitna, Ali's death) was a tragedy that did not invalidate what had come before.

The Shia judgment is that the first three caliphs were usurpers, that Ali was the legitimate caliph from 632 onward but had been wrongly bypassed, and that the entire Sunni narrative of the Rashidun period is a piece of Quraysh propaganda designed to hide the truth.
The reader can see that two thousand years of subsequent Muslim history had to be lived inside one of these two readings.

Cross-civ check: the Rashidun period (632–661) overlaps with the Tang Dynasty at its founding (Tang and the early Tang emperors were the contemporaries of Muhammad, Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman, and Ali — the great Chinese expansion under Tang Taizong was happening simultaneously with the Arab conquest of Iran and Egypt, which is one of the great examples of geographic distance keeping two world-historical political projects from noticing each other), the Heraclian collapse of Byzantium (Byzantine Empire Ch 3), the destruction of the Sasanian Empire (Persian Empire Ch 10), the post-Gupta breakdown in northern India (Gupta Empire Ch 8), and the Asuka period in Japan.

The mid-seventh century is the moment when the late-antique world system that had been organized around Rome-Persia-China-India began to reorganize: Persia was destroyed by the Arabs, half of Rome was taken by the Arabs, India was fragmenting, only China remained intact and continued to grow.
The political geography that emerged from this period was the early-medieval one, dominated in the western half by the Caliphate, in the eastern half by Tang China.

chapters.title: The Sunni-Shia Split
sentences: This chapter is about an event that happened in October 680 and a religious division it produced that is still organizing political life across the Middle East in 2026.
The event is the killing of Husayn ibn Ali, Muhammad's grandson, at a place called Karbala (KAR-bah-lah) in southern Iraq.

The killing — the most important single event in Shia Islam — was the moment when an essentially political dispute about succession (Chapter 3) crystallized into a permanent religious division about authority, legitimacy, and the meaning of suffering itself.

This chapter will address the Karbala event itself, the formation of distinct Shia identity in its aftermath, the eventual subdivisions within Shia Islam (Twelver, Ismaili, Zaydi), and the substantive theological differences that the split produced.

The chapter is somewhat out of chronological order — Karbala happens twenty years into the Umayyad caliphate, before the architectural and conquest projects of the next chapter — but the importance of the event is great enough that it deserves its own treatment, and the chapters that follow will need to refer back to the Sunni-Shia framework this one establishes.
A note before starting: this chapter handles religiously sensitive material on which Sunni and Shia Muslims disagree fundamentally.
The narrative tries to present each tradition's view fairly, while also noting where modern historical scholarship considers one or the other claim to be uncertain.
The author is not a Muslim of either tradition.
Where the two traditions agree, the chapter treats their joint testimony as solid evidence.
Where they disagree, the chapter reports the disagreement.
To understand Karbala, you have to understand what had happened in the twenty years between Ali's assassination in 661 and Husayn's death in 680.
After Ali's killing, Mu'awiya became the undisputed caliph (Chapter 3).
He moved the capital from Medina (where Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman, and Ali had ruled) to Damascus, his old governor's seat in Syria.
He ran the caliphate for nineteen years (661–680), competently and at considerable distance from the original Medinan-Iraqi center of Muslim political life.

His major innovation was administrative continuity with Byzantine Syria — he kept the Greek-speaking Roman bureaucracy in place, used the existing Byzantine tax registers, and ran the conquered Roman cities essentially the way Constantinople had run them.

This made his caliphate functional but also estranged it from the more religiously inflected Iraqi Muslim communities at Kufa and Basra (where Ali had ruled and where Ali's sons Hasan and Husayn still lived).
Mu'awiya's most consequential decision was to designate his son Yazid as his successor before his own death.
This converted the caliphate from an elected office (with the Rashidun pattern of community consensus) into a hereditary monarchy — an Umayyad family business.
The decision was deeply unpopular among many Companions and their descendants.
Designating one's son as successor was a Byzantine and Sasanian practice; it was not how Abu Bakr or Umar or even Uthman had been chosen.
The traditional Arab tribal practice was for tribal succession to go to the most able adult male of the ruling clan, not necessarily the predecessor's son.
Mu'awiya was bringing imperial-style hereditary succession into Islamic governance for the first time.

He gathered pledges of allegiance to Yazid from the major political constituencies of the empire while he was still alive — partly through persuasion, partly through bribery, partly through veiled threats.
By the time Mu'awiya died in April 680, most of the empire had formally accepted Yazid as the next caliph.

Two prominent figures had not: Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr (the son of Ali's old ally al-Zubayr, who would shortly raise his own counter-caliphate at Mecca, prolonging the Second Fitna into the 690s — Chapter 5) and Husayn ibn Ali, Ali's surviving son, who from his home at Medina refused to swear allegiance to Yazid.
Husayn ibn Ali (hoo-SAYN, born 626 in Medina) was Muhammad's grandson — the second son of Ali and Fatima, the younger brother of Hasan.
He was the one of Muhammad's grandchildren that the Prophet had reportedly held particular affection for, and the early Muslim community accorded him significant deference on that basis.

By 680 he was about fifty-four years old, settled at Medina with his family, an experienced political figure who had stayed quiet during his older brother Hasan's brief caliphate and the long reign of Mu'awiya.
He had not made trouble.
But he had also never sworn allegiance to Yazid, and Yazid's accession in April 680 forced him to declare himself.
He left Medina, secretly, in the spring of 680, taking his immediate family and a handful of supporters.
He traveled to Mecca, where he hoped to be safe in the sacred city and could weigh his options.

While at Mecca, he received letters from Shia partisans in Kufa — Ali's old capital, where significant pro-Alid sentiment had survived Mu'awiya's twenty years of Damascus-based rule — inviting him to come to Iraq, lead an uprising against Yazid, and reclaim the caliphate for Muhammad's bloodline.
Husayn deliberated.
The political case for going to Kufa was that Iraqi pro-Alid sentiment, properly mobilized, could produce the army he would need to challenge Yazid.

The political case against was that Mu'awiya had ruled Iraq for two decades through a series of competent, ruthless governors, and that the Iraqi Shia network was probably less capable of delivering on its promises than the letters were claiming.
The case for going was that Husayn was Muhammad's grandson and that staying quiet would have been a betrayal of the family's claim.
The case against was that going might end in personal disaster.
He decided to go.
He sent his cousin Muslim ibn Aqil ahead to Kufa as an advance representative, to gather formal pledges of allegiance from the Iraqi Shia and prepare the ground.

Muslim arrived, was warmly received, gathered perhaps 18,000 written pledges — and then Yazid's appointed governor of Kufa, the formidable Ubaydullah ibn Ziyad (oo-bay-DOO-lah IH-bin zee-YAHD), arrived in the city, arrested the prominent Shia leaders, executed Muslim ibn Aqil and a handful of other organizers, and froze the Iraqi Shia network through fear.
By the time Husayn himself approached Iraq with his small family entourage in early October 680, the city that had pledged him 18,000 supporters had been intimidated into silence.
None of the Kufan Shia rode out to meet him.
Ubaydullah dispatched a force to intercept Husayn.
The two parties met at a desolate spot in the Iraqi desert called Karbala, about 50 miles southwest of Kufa, in early October 680.

Ubaydullah's force, perhaps 4,000 men under the commander Umar ibn Sa'd, surrounded Husayn's party of perhaps 70 men plus their families and cut them off from the Euphrates River, denying them water in the desert heat.
The siege lasted about a week.
Negotiations failed.
Husayn refused to swear allegiance to Yazid; Ubaydullah refused to let him leave without the oath.
On 10 October 680 — the tenth day of the month of Muharram, the date now known as Ashura (ah-SHOO-rah) — Husayn and his small band were attacked.
Husayn's male relatives and supporters were killed one by one as they made individual stands.
Husayn's half-brother Abbas ibn Ali — the son of Ali by another wife after Fatima's death — was killed trying to bring water to the women and children.
Husayn's nephew Qasim ibn Hasan was killed.
Husayn's eighteen-year-old son Ali al-Akbar was killed.
Husayn's infant son was hit by an arrow as Husayn held him in his arms.
Husayn himself was killed last, after fighting alone among the bodies of his family.
The Umayyad force decapitated his corpse, trampled his body under their horses, and stripped the dead.

The women — including Husayn's surviving sister Zaynab and his only surviving son Ali Zayn al-Abidin (ah-LEE ZAYN al-AH-bih-din, who had been too sick to fight and was therefore spared) — were taken captive and brought to Yazid's court at Damascus, with Husayn's severed head carried before them as a trophy.

The killing of the Prophet's grandson, the destruction of his family in front of him, the desecration of his corpse, the parade of his severed head through the streets of Damascus, the captive women of the Prophet's household displayed at the Umayyad court — all of this happened.
The basic events are not in dispute between Sunni and Shia tradition; the Sunni sources confirm the events with perhaps less hagiographic embellishment but with substantively the same outline.
What is disputed is the meaning.

The Shia interpretation of Karbala, formed over the following century, was that Husayn had been martyred in the truest sense — that he had gone to certain death rather than swear allegiance to a corrupt usurper, that his suffering was a redemptive act for the Muslim community, that the Umayyads who killed him had thereby revealed themselves as illegitimate, and that the obligation of subsequent generations of Shia Muslims was to mourn Husayn, remember Karbala, and resist injustice in his name.
The annual commemoration of Husayn's killing — observed during the first ten days of the month of Muharram and culminating in Ashura itself — became the central ritual of Shia religious life.

Shia Muslims gather in husayniyya (special communal halls dedicated to Husayn's memory) to listen to recitations of the Karbala narrative, weep openly, beat their chests rhythmically in time with the recitation, and process through the streets in funeral parades for an event that happened thirteen and a half centuries ago.

In some Shia communities (especially in South Asia and Iraq), the more intense forms of mourning include self-flagellation with chains or short blades — a controversial practice within Shia Islam itself, defended by some senior clerics and discouraged by others.

The deeper theological move was to elevate Husayn's killing into a structural principle of Shia thought: that the rightful religious-political authority of Muhammad's bloodline had been violently suppressed by usurper caliphs, that the suppression continued through the Umayyad and (later) the Abbasid dynasties, and that the obligation of Shia Muslims was to wait — through possibly very long historical periods of injustice — for the eventual return of legitimate rule under the Imams (the lineage of Muhammad's bloodline through Ali, Hasan, Husayn, and their descendants).
The waiting itself became a form of pious resistance.
The Sunni interpretation of Karbala was different.
Most Sunni sources mourn the death of the Prophet's grandson and condemn Yazid for allowing it.
But the Sunni tradition does not make Karbala a structural principle of religious authority.

It treats Husayn's killing as a tragic political failure — an avoidable catastrophe that Yazid handled badly — without using it to delegitimize the broader Umayyad caliphate or the Sunni framework of caliphal authority.

Sunni religious life therefore does not commemorate Ashura the way Shia life does; the day is observed in Sunni tradition primarily as an optional fast (associated with Moses's deliverance from Pharaoh, a much older tradition) rather than as a mourning for Husayn.
The cumulative effect of the Karbala memory was to give Shia Muslims a religious-emotional vocabulary that has remained politically powerful for thirteen centuries.

"Every day is Ashura, every land is Karbala" is one of the most-quoted slogans of modern Shia political mobilization — invoked in 1979 during the Iranian Revolution against the Shah, in 1980–88 during the Iran-Iraq War, in the 2000s by Hezbollah in Lebanon and the Mahdi Army in Iraq.
Karbala is not a museum-piece historical event for Shia Muslims; it is a living reference point that shapes contemporary politics.

Understanding why modern Iran behaves the way it does, why Lebanese Hezbollah operates the way it does, why Iraqi Shia politics has the particular character it does — none of this is fully intelligible without Karbala.
Beyond the Karbala memory itself, the Sunni-Shia split produced substantive theological differences that have widened over the centuries.
Five differences are most important.
First: religious authority.
Sunnis hold that religious authority after Muhammad rests with the consensus of qualified scholars (the ulama) interpreting the Quran and the hadith.
There is no divinely designated successor to Muhammad and no clergy with sacramental powers; the ulama are simply learned men whose authority derives from training and recognition.
Shias hold that religious authority rests with the Imam — the divinely designated descendant of Ali through Husayn, who possesses unique spiritual knowledge passed down through the bloodline.

After the disappearance of the Twelfth Imam in the late ninth century (in Twelver Shia doctrine — see below), religious authority passes to the senior mujtahids (independent scholarly reasoners), but the underlying structure is hierarchical and the mujtahids derive their legitimacy from the Imam's authority, not just from scholarly consensus.
Second: the imamate.
Sunnis recognize no special spiritual authority in any bloodline after Muhammad.

Shias hold that twelve (or, in other Shia traditions, seven or five) divinely designated Imams descended from Ali through Husayn possess unique spiritual knowledge and the right to lead the community.
The first Imam was Ali himself.
The second was Hasan.
The third was Husayn.

The lineage continues through Husayn's surviving son Ali Zayn al-Abidin (the only male child to survive Karbala — Chapter 4), and so on. (See the lineage subsection below for the major variants.) Third: legal sources.
Sunnis recognize four main sources of Islamic law — the Quran, the hadith, the consensus of the community, and analogical reasoning.
The four classical Sunni legal schools (Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i, Hanbali) developed in the ninth and tenth centuries and represent slightly different methodologies for applying these sources.
Shias recognize Quran, hadith (particularly from the Imams as well as from Muhammad), consensus, and aql (reason).

The Shia legal tradition (the Ja'fari school, named for the Sixth Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq, who codified much of the early Shia legal tradition) developed alongside the Sunni schools but emphasized the Imams' rulings as a continuing source of guidance.
Fourth: the Mahdi.
Both Sunni and Shia traditions await the appearance of the Mahdi (al-MAH-dee, "the rightly-guided one"), an apocalyptic figure who will appear before the end of time to establish justice on earth.
But the two traditions understand the Mahdi differently.
In Sunni eschatology, the Mahdi will be a future descendant of Muhammad, born and growing up at some unspecified later time, who will rule briefly before the end of the world.

In Twelver Shia eschatology, the Mahdi is Muhammad al-Mahdi — the Twelfth Imam, who was already born around 869, went into occultation (a state of hidden existence) in 874, and is alive but hidden until the appointed time of his return.
The difference is enormous: Sunnis are waiting for someone who has not yet been born, while Twelver Shias are waiting for someone who is already alive but hidden.
Fifth: the role of mourning and intercession.

Shia religious practice gives a much larger place to mourning rituals (especially around Husayn and the Imams), to pilgrimage to the tombs of the Imams (Karbala, Najaf, Mashhad, Kazimiyah, Samarra), and to intercessory prayer through the Imams as spiritual mediators.

Sunni practice is generally more austere, with mosque-centered congregational prayer as the dominant ritual mode and intercession discouraged in many traditions (particularly the more reformist Sunni currents like Salafism and Wahhabism).

The visible "look" of Shia and Sunni religious life — the public processions, the funeral parades, the elaborate shrines — differs in substantial ways that go back to the Karbala-shaped formation of Shia distinct identity.

Within Shia Islam, the imamate lineage produced three main subdivisions, all of which agree on the legitimacy of the first four Imams (Ali, Hasan, Husayn, and Husayn's son Ali Zayn al-Abidin) but diverge on later succession.

Twelver Shias (the largest branch today, roughly 85% of all Shias, the official religion of Iran since the Safavid conversion of 1501 — Safavid Persia Ch 1–2) recognize twelve Imams, ending with the Twelfth Imam Muhammad al-Mahdi, who went into occultation in 874.
Twelver Shia clerical authority is organized around the marja-i taqlid ("source of emulation") system, in which senior living mujtahids issue binding rulings that ordinary Shia must follow.
Ismaili Shias (sometimes called "Seveners") recognize the same imamate up through the Sixth Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (who died in 765), but split with the Twelvers over the next succession.
Ismailis hold that Ja'far's elder son Isma'il was the rightful Seventh Imam (rather than his younger brother Musa, who is the Twelver Seventh Imam).
The Ismaili line continued through Isma'il's descendants and produced, eventually, the Fatimid Caliphate that ruled Egypt from 909 to 1171 (Islamic Golden Age Ch 6).
Modern Ismailis are a smaller but globally distributed community; the Aga Khan, the hereditary leader of the Nizari Ismaili branch, is one of the most prominent contemporary Muslim spiritual figures.

Zaydi Shias (the smallest of the three main branches, concentrated today in Yemen) recognize a different fifth Imam — Zayd ibn Ali (the grandson of Husayn, who led an unsuccessful revolt against the Umayyads in 740 and was killed) rather than Muhammad al-Baqir, who is the fifth Imam in both Twelver and Ismaili traditions.

Zaydi religious thought is in some ways closer to Sunni Islam than to other Shia traditions, particularly on the question of who can be Imam (Zaydis hold that any qualified descendant of Hasan or Husayn can rise to the imamate by leading a successful revolt against tyranny, rather than the lineage being divinely fixed).
The subdivisions matter for modern politics.
Iranian Shia Islam is Twelver.
The Lebanese Hezbollah is Twelver.
The Iraqi Shia majority is mostly Twelver.
The Houthi movement in Yemen is Zaydi.
The Aga Khan's followers are Ismaili.

The conflicts among these communities, and between them and Sunni neighbors, draw on subdivisions that go back to the eighth-century lineage disputes about who was the legitimate Imam after a particular ancestor died.
A thirteen-century Shia-Sunni history in compressed form.
The Umayyad century (this narrative's main subject) was a period of Umayyad-Sunni hegemony with a Shia opposition organized around the descendants of Ali.

The Abbasid Revolution in 750 (Chapter 8) initially benefited Shia partisans (the Abbasids had used Alid loyalty as part of their revolutionary coalition) but quickly turned against them — the Abbasids were also Sunnis and had no intention of yielding power to Ali's bloodline.

Shia movements proliferated in opposition to the Abbasids: the Fatimid Caliphate in Egypt (909), the Buyid amirs who took de facto control of Abbasid Baghdad in 945, the Ismaili Assassins in Iran in the eleventh century.
The Mongol sack of Baghdad in 1258 ended the Abbasid caliphate (Mongol Empire Ch 5) and opened a period in which Sunni-Shia conflict was less politically structured.

The major reorganization came with the Safavid conversion of Iran in 1501 (Safavid Persia Ch 1–2), which made Iran a permanent Twelver Shia state and crystallized the modern Sunni-Shia geopolitical divide that runs through the contemporary Middle East.
The thread from Karbala in 680 to the Iran-Saudi rivalry in 2026 is real and continuous.
It is not the only thread in modern Middle Eastern history, but it is one of the major ones, and any account of the region that ignores it is missing structural information.

Cross-civ check: the Karbala killing in 680 happened during the Tang Dynasty in China (Empress Wu's reign, 690–705 CE), the late Heraclian period in Byzantium (Justinian II's reign, 685–711 — Byzantine Empire Ch 3, just before the Iconoclast Century), the rise of the Bulgarian Empire in the Balkans, and the Pala Empire's predecessors in northeastern India.

The closest contemporary analogue to the Karbala-shaped religious-political division is the Christological controversies in early Christianity (Byzantine Empire Ch 1) — the disputes over Christ's nature that produced the Chalcedonian, Monophysite, and Nestorian traditions and that gave Christianity its lasting denominational structure.
Both Islam and Christianity, in their first centuries, produced foundational schisms whose theological substance was real but whose political driver was a contested succession.
