The Christian schisms produced the Orthodox-Catholic-Oriental divide; the Muslim schism produced Sunni-Shia.
Both divisions are still operative in 2026.

chapters.title: Damascus
sentences: The Umayyad Caliphate, founded by Mu'awiya I (moo-AH-wee-ah) in 661 after Ali's assassination and Hasan's abdication, ran from a capital that no Rashidun caliph had ever lived in: Damascus, the old Roman provincial capital of Syria.

This chapter is about the period from Mu'awiya's accession in 661 through the reign of Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan (AHB-d al-MAH-lik), the great organizer of the early Umayyad state, who ruled from 685 to 705.
Across these forty-four years, the caliphate transformed from a Medinan-Iraqi Arab tribal federation into a centralized empire whose administrative practice owed more to Byzantium than to Arabia.
Mu'awiya, the first Umayyad caliph, was the son of Abu Sufyan, the Quraysh-Umayyad chief who had organized most of Mecca's military campaigns against the early Muslim community at Medina (Chapter 2).

Mu'awiya himself had been a late convert — his family submitted only after the conquest of Mecca in 630, when resistance was hopeless — and the early Companions had always treated him as a man of the second tier.
His rise to power was a comeback story for the Umayyad clan that had originally opposed Muhammad and now ended up running Muhammad's empire.
Mu'awiya had been governor of Syria for twenty years before becoming caliph.

He had been appointed by Caliph Umar around 640, after his elder brother Yazid had died, and confirmed by Uthman during the Umayyad-favoring nepotism that contributed to Uthman's downfall (Chapter 3).
His twenty years in Damascus had transformed him from a marginal Umayyad cousin into the most experienced provincial administrator in the empire.

He understood the inherited Byzantine bureaucracy, knew the Greek-speaking civil servants who ran it, and had built the Arab navy in the late 640s and 650s — using Egyptian and Syrian shipwrights and Coptic crews to construct fleets that defeated the Byzantines at the Battle of the Masts in 655 and made the Mediterranean an Arab-contested sea for the first time. (Without Mu'awiya's navy, the conquest of Spain in 711 and the Siege of Constantinople in 717 — Chapter 6 — would not have been physically possible.) When Mu'awiya inherited the caliphate in 661, he kept his capital at Damascus rather than returning to Medina.
The decision was deeply consequential.
Damascus was a Roman city — colonnaded streets, monumental public buildings, a functioning Byzantine administrative apparatus, a Greek-speaking civil service.
Medina was a small oasis town with primitive infrastructure and limited administrative depth.
Running the empire from Damascus meant running it through inherited Byzantine institutions; running it from Medina would have meant building a new administrative system from scratch.
Mu'awiya chose the institutional shortcut.
The choice imported Byzantine practice into Islamic governance in ways that would shape the Umayyad caliphate for the rest of its existence.

The Umayyads ran a chancery on Byzantine lines, used Greek as the working language of administration in the western provinces (and Pahlavi, the Sasanian administrative language, in the eastern provinces) until Abd al-Malik's Arabization reform of 695, employed Greek-speaking Christian civil servants from the late Roman bureaucratic class (the most famous being the Christian theologian John of Damascus, who served as a senior Umayyad financial official before becoming the major theological defender of Byzantine icon-veneration in the 740s — Byzantine Empire Ch 4), and structured their court ceremonies on a Byzantine model.
This continuity was practical, but it was also a source of legitimacy concerns within the Muslim community.

The early Companions in Medina considered the Umayyads suspiciously close to Roman imperial style — they wore silk, they sat on thrones, they were addressed in elaborate Persian-Roman court honorifics, they hunted with falcons and built palaces in the desert with Roman-style mosaics and baths.
The accusation that the Umayyads had become "Arab kings" rather than Muslim caliphs would dog the dynasty until its fall.
Mu'awiya's reign (661–680) was marked by stability, consolidation, and the gradual but unmistakable transformation of the caliphate into a hereditary monarchy.
The conquests slowed.

The Arab armies stabilized the frontiers without dramatic new acquisitions, except for the gradual conquest of North Africa westward from Egypt (Tripolitania, then Ifriqiya, eventually reaching the Atlantic by the 700s) and the unsuccessful First Arab Siege of Constantinople of 674–678 (a four-year naval blockade that the Byzantines defeated using Greek fire — Byzantine Empire Ch 4).
Mu'awiya invested heavily in the navy, in administrative organization, and in negotiating internal political stability.
He intermarried Arab clans and Byzantine-Christian elite families.
He kept the leading Companions and their descendants paid, employed, and politically managed.
His most consequential domestic decision was nominating his son Yazid as successor (Chapter 4).
The hereditary succession transformed the caliphate from an elected office into a family business and produced the Karbala crisis of 680.

Mu'awiya himself had managed the political fallout of Husayn's killing well enough — he died unexpectedly in April 680, just before the worst of the Yazid succession crisis broke open — but the structural change he had introduced was permanent.
Every subsequent Islamic dynasty, Sunni or Shia, would be hereditary.
The Rashidun pattern of caliphal election by community consensus was over.
Yazid I (ruled 680–683) lasted three years.

His reign saw the killing of Husayn at Karbala (Chapter 4) and the start of the Second Fitna — the second major Muslim civil war, this one centered on the rival caliphate of Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr in Mecca.
Ibn al-Zubayr (the son of Ali's old ally al-Zubayr) had refused, like Husayn, to swear allegiance to Yazid.
Unlike Husayn, he had remained at Mecca rather than venturing to Iraq, sheltered behind the sanctity of the holy city and his own personal political reputation.
After Husayn's death, ibn al-Zubayr declared himself caliph, gathered support across the Hijaz and parts of Iraq, and ran a counter-government from Mecca for the next twelve years.
At the height of his control, the Hijaz, much of Iraq, southern Arabia, and parts of Egypt recognized ibn al-Zubayr rather than the Umayyads.
Yazid's response was unusually brutal.
He sent an army to besiege Medina in 683 (the Battle of al-Harrah), which sacked the city and killed many of the Companions' descendants.
He then sent a force toward Mecca to besiege ibn al-Zubayr; the siege was conducted with catapults bombarding the holy city, and the Kaaba itself was damaged by stone projectiles and burned.
The bombardment of Mecca by an Umayyad army was the kind of theological catastrophe the dynasty would never live down.

Yazid died unexpectedly later in 683, his son Mu'awiya II reigned briefly and died in the same year, and the Umayyad dynasty fragmented temporarily — different Umayyad branches recognizing different candidates in different provinces.
Order was restored by Marwan I (a senior Umayyad cousin who had been Uthman's chief of staff in 656), who rallied the family and was acknowledged caliph in late 684, though he died only a year later.
His son Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan inherited the caliphate in 685.
Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan (ruled 685–705) was the second great organizer of the Umayyad state, after Mu'awiya.
His twenty-year reign accomplished the institutional transformation that turned the caliphate into a recognizably Islamic empire.
His first task was to win the Second Fitna.
In 692, Abd al-Malik dispatched his most ruthless general, al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf (al-HAJ-jaj), to deal with ibn al-Zubayr at Mecca.
Al-Hajjaj besieged the city, bombarded the Kaaba a second time (also damaging it), killed ibn al-Zubayr in battle in October 692, and crucified his corpse on the gates of Mecca.
The Hijaz was reincorporated into the Umayyad caliphate.

Al-Hajjaj was rewarded with the governorship of Iraq, where he ruled with notorious severity until his death in 714 — the Umayyad enforcer-in-chief whose name is still synonymous in Arabic-language historical memory with effective but cruel administration.
With the Second Fitna won, Abd al-Malik began the structural reforms.
The most consequential reform was Arabization.

Until Abd al-Malik, the Umayyad bureaucracy had run in inherited languages — Greek in Syria and Egypt (the Byzantine administrative language), Pahlavi (Middle Persian) in Iraq and Iran (the Sasanian administrative language).
The civil servants were the inherited Christian and Zoroastrian/Manichaean professionals from the conquered states, working in their own languages on documents written in their own scripts.
The Arab Muslim ruling class was a thin layer on top of a continuing Roman-Persian administrative apparatus.
Around 695, Abd al-Malik decreed that the bureaucracy must shift to Arabic as its working language.

The decision required creating a whole new class of Arabic-literate administrators, training them in tax accounting and law and chancery practice, and gradually displacing the inherited Greek-and-Pahlavi-speaking professionals.
The transition took a generation.
By the time of the Abbasid Revolution in 750, Arabic was the universal administrative language of the caliphate from Spain to Sind.
The shift locked Arabic in as the language of the Middle East.
The cumulative effect of Arabization was enormous.

Within two centuries, Arabic had displaced Aramaic (the previous lingua franca of the Levant for over a thousand years — Phoenicia Ch 7, Ancient Israel Ch 6), much of Coptic in Egypt (which survived only in Christian liturgy), and substantial portions of Pahlavi/Middle Persian as the everyday language of the Mesopotamian populations (Persian, however, would survive in Iran proper as a vibrant literary and administrative language and would re-emerge in Persianized Islamic form under the Abbasids — Islamic Golden Age Ch 1).

The linguistic map of the modern Middle East — Arabic from Morocco to Iraq, Persian in Iran, Turkish in Anatolia (after a later Turkic conquest) — was set in place by the Umayyad-era language policies and the slow demographic processes they enabled.
The reform required, as a side project, reforming the Arabic script itself.
Pre-Umayyad Arabic was written without dots distinguishing similar-looking consonants and without short-vowel marks fixing pronunciation.
This had been adequate for a small community of native Arabic speakers who could supply the missing information from context.

It was inadequate for a non-native scribal class learning Arabic for administrative purposes, and it was particularly inadequate for the standardized Quran text Uthman had codified (Chapter 3), where any pronunciation ambiguity was theologically intolerable.
Under Abd al-Malik and al-Hajjaj, scholars associated with the early grammar school at Basra developed the diacritical and vowel-mark systems that are still used in Arabic today.
The reformed script let Arabic be written precisely enough for administrative use across an empire of non-native speakers.
Abd al-Malik's second major reform was monetary.
The Umayyad coinage in 685 was a hybrid.
Gold coins were Byzantine solidi, struck in Constantinople or in Arab imitation, depicting the Byzantine emperor.
Silver coins were Sasanian drachms, depicting the last Sasanian shahs.
The Arab Muslim state was conducting its commerce in money minted by the empires it had destroyed.

In 696, Abd al-Malik issued the first purely Islamic gold dinar — struck at the Damascus mint, weighing about 4.25 grams (the Roman solidus standard), bearing Arabic Quranic inscriptions and no human imagery.
The same reform produced an Islamic silver dirham (replacing the Sasanian drachm) and a copper fals (for petty transactions, replacing the various Byzantine and Sasanian fractional currencies).

The new coinage standardized the imperial money supply, signaled Umayyad sovereign legitimacy, and was a deliberate visual statement that the caliphate was no longer a continuation of Roman or Persian rule but its own thing.
The aniconism — the absence of human or animal images on the coins — was theologically significant.

Islamic religious tradition was developing, in this period, toward a strict prohibition of representational imagery in religious contexts (a position that would crystallize over the following centuries and would later influence the Byzantine iconoclast movement of the 720s — Byzantine Empire Ch 4).
The dinar's aniconic design declared that Umayyad money was Islamic money in a way the Byzantine and Sasanian coins it replaced had not been.

The Umayyad gold dinar became the standard currency of the Mediterranean and the Middle East for the next four centuries, gradually replacing both Roman and Sasanian coinage in the regions the caliphate controlled and circulating widely outside it as well.
Vikings raided Frankish territories partly to acquire silver dirhams (Viking Age Ch 5).
Indian traders accepted Umayyad and early Abbasid coins.
The dinar was the gold standard of medieval Eurasian commerce.
Abd al-Malik's third major reform was architectural, and it deserves its own chapter (Chapter 7) — but the foundational project began under him: the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem, completed in 691.

The Dome was the first major Umayyad building project, the first major piece of Islamic monumental architecture, and the first piece of physical infrastructure designed to make a public statement about the religion's place in the world.

It was built on the Temple Mount in Jerusalem — the platform that had once held the Jewish Temple destroyed by the Romans in 70 CE, and that had been left in ruins for over six hundred years afterward (Christianity having abandoned the site in favor of the Holy Sepulchre church across the city).
Abd al-Malik chose to claim the abandoned Temple Mount as Islam's Jerusalem property, building a magnificent shrine over the rock from which Muhammad was said to have ascended on his Night Journey.
The project's full architectural significance is the subject of Chapter 7.
The political motivation was multiple.
The Dome was a statement against Christian Jerusalem (the Holy Sepulchre church across the city).

It was a statement against Mecca (where ibn al-Zubayr's counter-caliphate had controlled the Kaaba during much of the Second Fitna, and where Abd al-Malik may briefly have considered redirecting pilgrimage to Jerusalem instead — though the actual extent of this policy is contested in the sources).
It was a statement of Umayyad religious legitimacy, claiming Jerusalem's holy geography for the dynasty's project.
It also worked aesthetically.
The Dome of the Rock has been continuously standing since 691, with periodic refurbishments, and it remains one of the most beautiful pieces of architecture in the world.
The Umayyad state that emerged from Abd al-Malik's reign (in place by 705, when his son al-Walid I succeeded him) had a recognizable shape.
It was an Arab Muslim military elite running an empire that stretched from Spain to Sind.

It used Arabic as its administrative language, gold dinars and silver dirhams as its currency, monumental Islamic architecture as its public face, and the dhimmi system to govern its overwhelmingly non-Muslim subject populations (Chapter 7).

The political structure was hereditary monarchy with Damascus as the capital, an Umayyad family running the state, governors of the major provinces (Syria, Egypt, Iraq, Khorasan, Spain, North Africa) appointed from the family or from trusted clients.

The Arab tribal federation that had won the conquests had been largely transformed into a professional military caste paid in cash from the conquered populations' tax revenues — the diwan system inherited from Umar but increasingly bureaucratized.

The structural problem the dynasty had not solved, and would not solve, was the mawali issue (Chapter 8) — the growing population of non-Arab Muslim converts who paid the same taxes as non-Muslims and were excluded from the diwan stipend system.
Conversion to Islam had been, in the early conquests, almost incidental to the political-military project.

But by the late Umayyad period the mawali population was large and growing — Persian-speaking Iraqis and Iranians, Coptic Egyptians, Berber North Africans — and the Arab privilege built into the original Rashidun fiscal system was an increasingly visible injustice.
The Umayyads tried, in fits and starts, to address the issue.
Umar II (ruled 717–720), the most personally pious caliph of the dynasty, briefly equalized the tax system in favor of recent converts.
The reform was honest, popular among non-Arabs, and gutted Umayyad revenues.
His successors quietly reversed it.

The structural contradiction between an Arab-privilege fiscal system and a religion that proclaimed all believers equal was the slow-burning fuse that would eventually detonate the Abbasid Revolution (Chapter 8).

Cross-civ check: the early Umayyad period (661–705) overlaps with the Tang Dynasty at its height (Empress Wu's reign 690–705 — exactly contemporary with Abd al-Malik), the Heraclian convulsion in Byzantium and the loss of southern provinces (Byzantine Empire Ch 3), the Pala dynasty's predecessors in Bengal, the Mayan Late Classic period in Mesoamerica (Maya Civilization Ch 6), and the early Visigothic kingdom in Spain (the kingdom Tariq ibn Ziyad would shortly destroy in 711 — Chapter 6).

The architectural ambition of the Dome of the Rock in 691 is contemporary with the building of major Tang Buddhist temples and pagodas in Chang'an — both empires investing imperial wealth in monumental religious architecture as a statement of dynastic legitimacy.

The administrative consolidation under Abd al-Malik is contemporary with the institutional consolidation of the Tang civil service — both states moving from improvised post-conquest governance toward systematic bureaucratic professionalism.
The two empires were the eastern and western anchors of late seventh-century Eurasian state power.

chapters.title: The Conquests West and East
sentences: The Umayyad Caliphate under Abd al-Malik's son al-Walid I (ruled 705–715) and his successors hit its territorial peak.
In a single decade — roughly 705 to 715 — Arab armies conquered Spain (711), Sind (711), and Transoxiana (709–715), more than doubling the empire's geographic reach.
The conquests were extraordinary in scale, in simultaneity, and in the ease with which a relatively small Arab force could topple existing states from Iberia to Central Asia.

This chapter is about how the Umayyad conquests reached their maximum extent — and also about the decisive failure (the 717–718 Siege of Constantinople) that defined the empire's eastern and northern limits for the remainder of its existence.
Spain was conquered by accident.
In 711, a small Berber-Arab raiding party under the Berber commander Tariq ibn Ziyad (TAH-rik IH-bin zee-YAHD) crossed the strait between Morocco and Spain.
Tariq was the freedman client of the Umayyad governor of North Africa, Musa ibn Nusayr, and his expedition was probably authorized as a reconnaissance raid rather than a conquest.

He landed at the rocky promontory now called Gibraltar (a Spanish corruption of the Arabic Jabal Tariq, "Tariq's Mountain") with about 7,000 men, mostly Berbers from the recently conquered Maghreb, and marched north into the disintegrating Visigothic Kingdom.
The Visigoths had ruled Spain since the late fifth century, when Germanic tribes had taken the peninsula from the collapsing Western Roman Empire (Ancient Rome Ch 10).
Their kingdom in 711 was a fragile elective monarchy, weakened by recent succession crises and ongoing factional warfare among Visigothic nobles.
King Roderic had taken the throne the previous year in disputed circumstances.
The internal opposition was substantial.
In July 711, Tariq met Roderic and the main Visigothic field army at the Battle of Guadalete (gwah-dah-LEH-teh), in southern Spain.

The battle was decisive — the Visigothic right wing, commanded by the family of Roderic's predecessor and bitter enemy, may have defected mid-fight (the surviving sources are not unanimous on this point).
Roderic was killed.
The Visigothic state collapsed almost instantly.
Within a year, Tariq and his commanders had taken Toledo, Mérida, Córdoba, and most of the major Iberian cities.
By 718 the entire peninsula was under Muslim rule, except for a small Christian holdout in the Asturian mountains of the far north.
The conquest of Spain initiated 781 years of Muslim presence on the Iberian Peninsula, ending only with the fall of Granada to the Catholic Monarchs in 1492.

The Muslim civilization of medieval Spain — called al-Andalus in Arabic — would become one of the great cultural centers of the medieval Mediterranean, producing the Great Mosque of Córdoba, the Alhambra of Granada, the philosophical and scientific work of Ibn Sina (in the east) and Ibn Rushd (in the west), and the convivencia of Christians, Muslims, and Jews living together in al-Andalus that has been romanticized but was also genuinely productive (Islamic Golden Age Ch 6–7).
The 711 conquest is the founding moment of all of this.
The conquest of Spain also produced the strange afterlife of the Umayyad dynasty in al-Andalus.

The Umayyad survivor Abd al-Rahman I would flee the Abbasid massacre of 750 (Chapter 8) and reach Spain as the only Umayyad prince still alive, founding an independent Emirate of Córdoba in 756 that would continue under his descendants for nearly three centuries.
The Umayyad caliphate ended in the east; in the far west, in al-Andalus, the dynasty kept going for a long time after.
Sind was conquered in the same year.

In 711, the seventeen-year-old Umayyad general Muhammad ibn al-Qasim (moo-HAM-mad IH-bin al-KAH-sim) led an expedition through Baluchistan into Sind — the lower Indus Valley, modern southeastern Pakistan.
The campaign was punitive in origin, prompted by Sindhi pirates' attacks on Arab shipping in the Persian Gulf, but it expanded into a full conquest.
Muhammad ibn al-Qasim defeated the Hindu Raja Dahir at the Battle of Aror, took the major cities of Multan and Brahmanabad, and brought Sind under Umayyad control by 713.
Sind became the easternmost Umayyad province and the first foothold of Islam on the Indian subcontinent.

The Muslim presence in northwestern India would expand and contract over the following centuries, becoming politically dominant under the Delhi Sultanate in the thirteenth century and the Mughal Empire in the sixteenth (medieval-india, mughal-empire — both not yet shipped).
The 711 conquest of Sind is the founding moment of Islam in South Asia.
Muhammad ibn al-Qasim himself had a less successful afterlife.
He was recalled to Damascus in 715 after the death of his patron, the governor al-Hajjaj, and was tortured to death by the new caliph Sulayman (sool-eye-MAHN) in a court intrigue.
He was twenty years old.
The Central Asian conquest was conducted by Qutayba ibn Muslim (koo-TAY-ba IH-bin MOOS-lim), the Umayyad governor of Khorasan from 705 to 715.

Qutayba's campaigns extended Umayyad control across the Oxus River into Transoxiana — the region containing modern Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, southern Kazakhstan, and parts of Turkmenistan, called by the Arabs Ma wara' an-Nahr ("That Which Lies Beyond the River").
Qutayba took Bukhara in 709, Samarkand in 712, and pushed the Umayyad frontier to the Syr Darya River and the foothills of the Tian Shan mountains by 715.

The conquest brought into the Islamic world some of the great trading cities of the Silk Road — Bukhara and Samarkand had been Sogdian Iranian-language commercial centers for over a millennium, with thriving Buddhist, Manichaean, Nestorian Christian, and Zoroastrian communities.
The Umayyad conquest converted the local population gradually over the following two centuries into one of the great heartlands of Islamic civilization.

By the ninth century, Bukhara and Samarkand were major centers of Persian-Islamic high culture; the Persian-language poet Ferdowsi (who wrote the Shahnameh epic — Persian Empire Ch 9) and the philosopher-physician Ibn Sina (Avicenna) were both products of this Central Asian Islamic culture (Islamic Golden Age Ch 4).
Qutayba was killed in 715, in a mutiny by his own troops over his political maneuvering during the Umayyad caliphal succession crisis.

His career, like Muhammad ibn al-Qasim's, ended badly — but the territory he had conquered stayed Umayyad and then Abbasid, and the Islamic civilization that grew up there would shape the cultural history of Iran and Central Asia for the next thirteen centuries.
Three simultaneous conquests in 711 — Spain, Sind, Transoxiana, all in essentially the same year — are remarkable.
They reflect the enormous projection power of the Umayyad state at its peak, the high quality of Arab military organization, and the structural fragility of the states the Umayyads were attacking.
Iberia had a divided Visigothic monarchy.
Sind had a small Hindu kingdom outclassed by Arab military technology.
Transoxiana had Sogdian city-states with no central political authority.
None of the targets had the institutional depth to resist sustained Arab pressure.
The major Umayyad failure was at the one target that did have institutional depth: Constantinople.
The 717–718 Second Arab Siege of Constantinople is one of the most consequential battles in history.

It is also far less well-known in the Western canon than it should be — partly because the failure of the siege is harder to celebrate than the dramatic Christian victories at Tours (732) and Lepanto (1571), partly because the Greek-language Byzantine sources documenting it have been less central to Western historical memory than the Latin sources for parallel events.
The strategic logic of the campaign was clear.
By 717, the Umayyad caliphate had absorbed most of the eastern Mediterranean coast — Syria, Egypt, North Africa, Sicily was being raided regularly.
Spain had just been added.
The Byzantine Empire was reduced to Anatolia, the southern Balkans, and the Italian holdings in Sicily and southern Italy.

Capturing Constantinople would deliver the Byzantine capital, the theme system that defended Anatolia (Byzantine Empire Ch 3), the Balkan provinces, and a clear path into Europe via the Danube and the Alpine passes.
The same strategic considerations that had made the First Arab Siege of 674–678 attractive applied with even more force in 717.

The Umayyad caliph Sulayman sent his brother Maslama (mahs-LAH-mah) with what was, by the standards of the period, a massive force — perhaps 80,000 troops and 1,800 ships, in the largest pre-modern military operation ever launched against Constantinople.
The siege began in August 717.
It went badly from the start.
The Byzantine emperor Leo III had taken the throne in March 717 in a palace coup and had used the five months before the siege to prepare.
The Theodosian Walls of Constantinople (Byzantine Empire Ch 1) — the most formidable defensive system in the medieval world — held against everything the Arab army could throw at them.
The Arab fleet was destroyed in successive engagements by Byzantine Greek fire (the medieval flamethrower-equivalent that had broken the First Arab Siege in 678 — Byzantine Empire Ch 4).
The unusually severe winter of 717–718 froze the Thracian plain where the Arab army was camped, killing perhaps tens of thousands of men by exposure and starvation.
A Bulgarian army arrived from the north, bribed by Leo to attack the Arab rear, and inflicted further losses.
The Arab supply fleet, manned partly by Egyptian Christian conscripts, suffered mass desertions when sailors switched sides on contact with Byzantine forces.
By August 718, exactly one year after the siege began, Maslama lifted it and retreated.
Of the 1,800 ships that had sailed against Constantinople, only five returned to the Caliphate.
The Arab field army that had walked east into Anatolia returned to Syria depleted and demoralized.
The greatest single military operation the Umayyad state ever attempted had ended in catastrophic failure.
The historical consequences are hard to overstate.
If Constantinople had fallen in 718, the Umayyad armies would have had a clear path into Europe via the Balkans and the Hungarian plain.
There would have been no Byzantine Empire to anchor Christian eastern Europe for the next 700 years.
There would have been no eastern Christian buffer to absorb Mongol pressure in the thirteenth century.
The trajectory of European history would have been fundamentally different.
As it happened, the failure at Constantinople in 718 effectively halted Arab expansion into Europe by sea.
The Caliphate would never again attempt a serious assault on the Byzantine capital.
The defeat also contributed to internal Umayyad legitimacy problems.

After 718, the Umayyads could no longer credibly promise the conquests that had justified their rule — and the Arab military elite that had grown wealthy from those conquests had to readjust to a caliphate whose expansion was over.
The internal tensions this created were one of the slow-burning structural causes of the Abbasid Revolution thirty years later (Chapter 8).
The contrast with the Western European narrative is worth flagging.

Western European textbooks have traditionally credited the Battle of Tours in 732 — when the Frankish ruler Charles Martel defeated an Umayyad raid in central France — with stopping the Arab advance into Europe.
Tours mattered, but its strategic significance has often been overstated.

The raid Charles Martel defeated was probably a probe rather than a serious invasion; the Umayyad force was perhaps 20,000 men, not the 400,000 some early modern Western histories claimed; and the long-term impact was modest.
The Siege of Constantinople in 717–718 was much more consequential.
The Arab expansion into Europe was halted in the Balkans by Greek fire, not in Aquitaine by Frankish infantry.

The fact that the Western narrative tradition celebrates Tours rather than Constantinople reflects the West's preference for crediting Latin Christian heroes over Greek Christian ones — an old pattern in European historical memory that can be observed in many other cases as well.
After 720, Umayyad expansion essentially stopped.
The frontiers were stabilized — Constantinople in the northwest, the Pyrenees in the west, the Tian Shan in the east, the Indus in the southeast.

Some incremental gains continued (the conquest of Sicily would begin in 827 under the Aghlabid emirs in North Africa, well after the Umayyad period; raids into southern France would continue into the 730s; Caucasus campaigns against the Khazars persisted through the 730s and 740s).
But the great explosion of conquest that had begun in 634 with Khalid ibn al-Walid in Syria had run its course by 720.

The empire that remained covered roughly 5,000 miles east-to-west — about the distance from London to Beijing — and it was held together by a thin Arab military elite ruling overwhelmingly non-Arab, mostly non-Muslim populations.
The challenges of running this empire, rather than expanding it, would dominate the next thirty years and would eventually destroy the Umayyad dynasty.

Cross-civ check: the Umayyad expansion peak (705–720) overlaps with the Tang Dynasty under Empress Wu and Emperor Xuanzong (the Tang would collapse partially in the An Lushan Rebellion of 755–763, just after the Abbasid Revolution destroyed the Umayyads — both great early-medieval empires entering structural crisis at almost the same time), the early Iconoclast Byzantium under Leo III (Byzantine Empire Ch 4 — Leo III is the same emperor who saved Constantinople in 718), the late Visigothic kingdom destroyed in 711, and the early Pala dynasty in northern India.

The fact that the Tang and Umayyad armies almost met in Central Asia in this period — both empires expanding into the same general area, separated only by the Tian Shan and the Pamirs — would produce, a generation later, the Battle of Talas in 751, where an Abbasid-led army defeated a Tang force on the Talas River in modern Kyrgyzstan.

Talas was after the Umayyad period (it happened a year after the Battle of the Zab — Chapter 8), but it was the natural outcome of the simultaneous Tang and Umayyad expansions of the early eighth century.
The two expanding empires hit each other on the Talas, the Tang lost, and Central Asia was Islamicized rather than Sinicized for the next thousand years (Tang-Song China — not yet shipped).

chapters.title: Architecture and the Religion
sentences: The Umayyad Caliphate built things.
It also developed a religion.

The two activities were intertwined — the major architectural projects of the dynasty were religious buildings, and the major theological developments of the period were shaped by the building program.

This chapter is about both: the early Islamic monumental architecture (the Dome of the Rock, the Great Mosque of Damascus, the Aqsa Mosque) and the early Islamic religious tradition (the hadith, the early sharia, the dhimmi system, the early theological controversies that would later produce the great Mu'tazila debate in the Abbasid period).

The Dome of the Rock — completed by Abd al-Malik in 691, on the Temple Mount in Jerusalem — is the oldest surviving piece of Islamic monumental architecture and one of the most beautiful buildings in the world.
The site's history is layered.
The Temple Mount had been the platform of the Jewish Second Temple, destroyed by the Romans during the Jewish-Roman War in 70 CE (Ancient Israel Ch 8).
The Romans had built a Temple of Jupiter on the site after suppressing the Bar Kokhba revolt in 135.

Under the Christian emperors (after Constantine), the Jupiter temple was abandoned and the Temple Mount left in ruins — the Christians of late antique Jerusalem had concentrated their religious building on the Holy Sepulchre church across the city, which Constantine's mother Helena had built around the supposed site of the Resurrection (Byzantine Empire Ch 3).
The Temple Mount was a deliberately abandoned sacred site for over six centuries before the Umayyad conquest.
Abd al-Malik chose to claim the abandoned Temple Mount for Islam.

The theological motivation was the Night Journey narrative — the early Islamic tradition that Muhammad had been taken miraculously from Mecca to Jerusalem one night, ascended from a rock on the Temple Mount through the heavens to meet earlier prophets and God, and returned to Mecca by dawn.
The rock itself became, in Islamic tradition, the sacred point from which Muhammad's ascension had taken place.

The Dome of the Rock was built directly over this rock as a shrine — a covering for the sacred site, not a congregational mosque (the slightly later al-Aqsa Mosque at the southern end of the same platform served the congregational function).
The architecture was a deliberate piece of theological communication.

The dome itself — a large gilded hemispherical wooden dome originally covered in gold leaf, with the modern gold coating dating to a 1990s restoration — sat on an octagonal arcade that visually tied the dome to the geometry of the rock below.

The interior was decorated with elaborate mosaics in the late Roman-Byzantine style, with calligraphic Arabic inscriptions running around the inside arcade (the earliest surviving monumental Arabic inscriptions, and the oldest surviving Quranic text in any form).

The inscriptions were polemical — they include extended passages denying the divinity of Christ and the doctrine of the Trinity, addressed quite specifically to the Christian visitors who would inevitably come to see the new building.
This was an Islamic statement set down in Christian Jerusalem, with the Christians as the explicit theological audience.
Why the octagonal plan?

The eight-sided arcade has been interpreted as a deliberate echo of the eight-sided plans used in Christian baptisteries and martyria of late antiquity (the Church of the Holy Sepulchre itself had originally featured an octagonal rotunda over the supposed tomb of Christ).

The Umayyads were using a familiar Christian architectural vocabulary — central plan, octagonal arcade, gilded dome, Roman-Byzantine mosaics — to make a building that would compete with the Christian holy sites for visual and religious authority.
The form was Roman; the message was Islamic.
Why the materials?
The mosaics include depictions of crowns, jewels, and trees — luxury imagery in Roman-Byzantine convention.
Some scholars have read these as Sasanian and Byzantine royal regalia, displayed as trophies of Islamic conquest over the two empires whose treasuries had funded the building.
The polychrome marble panels lining the interior were spolia, taken from Roman buildings across the eastern Mediterranean.
The visual statement of the Dome was: this is the wealth of the conquered empires, redirected to the service of the new religion.
The Dome of the Rock has been continuously standing since 691, with repeated restorations.
It is the oldest surviving major work of Islamic architecture and one of the earliest examples of any monumental architecture from the medieval Mediterranean to survive intact.

The reason it survives is that it was kept in continuous religious use through every change of regime — Umayyad, Abbasid, Fatimid, Crusader (who briefly converted it to a Christian church called the Templum Domini in the twelfth century), Ayyubid, Mamluk, Ottoman, and modern.
Religious continuity is the best preservation strategy in architectural history.

The Great Mosque of Damascus — completed by al-Walid I in 715 — is the second great Umayyad architectural project and a different kind of building: a congregational mosque, designed for the daily and weekly communal prayer of an entire urban population.
The site's history was even more layered than the Temple Mount's.
There had been a temple to the Aramaean storm god Hadad on the site since at least the Iron Age (Ancient Israel Ch 6 — Hadad is the same god Aramean kings worshipped).
Under Roman occupation it became a temple of Jupiter.

After the Christianization of the Roman Empire, the Jupiter temple was converted into a basilica dedicated to John the Baptist (whose head was reputedly buried in the eastern courtyard, a relic Christians had honored for several centuries before the Arab conquest).

The early Umayyad conquerors had initially shared the cathedral with the Christian community of Damascus — Muslims praying in the eastern half, Christians worshipping in the western half — for about seventy years.

Around 706, al-Walid I bought out the Christian congregation (paying them substantial compensation and authorizing the construction of new churches elsewhere in the city), demolished the basilica, and built a purpose-designed congregational mosque on the site.
The construction took about a decade.
The result was the oldest surviving congregational mosque in the world that retains its original plan, and one of the most influential religious buildings in Islamic architectural history.
The Great Mosque of Damascus is structured around a vast rectangular courtyard (the sahn) with a covered prayer hall along one side.

Three minarets rise from the corners — including one (the Minaret of Jesus, in the southeastern corner) that Islamic eschatological tradition holds will be the place from which Jesus will descend at the end of the world.

The walls and the prayer hall were decorated with extraordinary glass mosaics in gold, green, and blue, depicting an idealized paradise of cities, palaces, gardens, rivers, and trees — but no human or animal figures (the aniconic prohibition).

The mosaics were Byzantine in technical execution (the workshops were probably staffed by Greek mosaicists from Constantinople, hired or sent by the emperor as part of a diplomatic exchange) and Islamic in iconographic content.
The image of paradise on the mosque walls was intended to give the worshipper a visual prefiguration of the heavenly garden the Quran promises to the faithful.
The Great Mosque set the architectural template for early Islamic congregational mosques.

Its courtyard-and-prayer-hall plan, its mihrab niche indicating the direction of Mecca (the qibla), its minbar (preacher's pulpit), its colonnaded portico — these features would become the standard elements of Sunni mosque architecture for the next thirteen centuries.
Most significant later mosques across the Islamic world descend, formally if not directly, from the Damascus prototype.

The al-Aqsa Mosque in Jerusalem — built by al-Walid I around 705, on the southern end of the same Temple Mount platform that holds the Dome of the Rock — is the third major early Umayyad religious building.
It is the congregational mosque of the Temple Mount complex, while the Dome is the shrine over the rock.
Together with the Dome, al-Aqsa makes Jerusalem the third-holiest city in Islam after Mecca and Medina.

The al-Aqsa Mosque has been damaged and rebuilt several times across the thirteen centuries of its history (most consequentially by the 749 earthquake that destroyed much of the original Umayyad structure, with rebuilding under the Abbasids producing essentially the building that now stands).
The current building preserves the basic Umayyad plan but with substantial later modification.
The phrase al-Aqsa, "the farthest [mosque]," comes from the Quran (Chapter 17, verse 1 — the verse describing Muhammad's Night Journey to "the farthest mosque" from the sacred mosque in Mecca).

Whether the Quranic phrase originally referred to a building in Jerusalem or to a heavenly mosque is debated by modern scholars; the early Islamic identification of the Quranic "farthest mosque" with the building on the Temple Mount became standard within a few decades of Muhammad's death and was certainly fixed by Abd al-Malik's time.
The naming locked in Jerusalem's religious significance for Islam in the Quranic sources themselves, regardless of the original referential intent.

The Umayyad architectural program also included the desert palaces — a series of royal estates in remote locations across Syria, Jordan, and Iraq that the Umayyad caliphs used as hunting lodges, retreat houses, and venues for less religiously inhibited entertainment than the Damascus court could comfortably support.

The most famous are Qusayr Amra (in modern Jordan, with extraordinary frescoed bath murals that include nude female bathers, the only surviving Umayyad-era figural painting), Khirbet al-Mafjar (near Jericho, with elaborate Roman-style baths and an intact mosaic floor), Mshatta (also in Jordan, with carved limestone facades that combine Sasanian, Byzantine, and Hellenistic ornamental traditions), and Anjar in Lebanon (the most fully planned of the desert palaces, laid out on a Roman city grid).

The desert palaces are the secret architectural program of the Umayyad caliphate — the buildings that show what the dynasty actually liked, as opposed to what they showed publicly in Damascus and Jerusalem.

They are deeply Roman-Byzantine in their planning and decorative vocabulary, full of figural imagery (including erotic imagery), and designed for a courtly lifestyle that was much closer to Sasanian-Byzantine royal practice than to early Medinan Muslim austerity.
The desert palaces are some of the strongest evidence for the Companion-class accusation that the Umayyads had become Arab kings rather than Muslim caliphs.

Beyond architecture, the Umayyad century saw the development of the religious infrastructure — the institutions, practices, and texts that would define what Islam was, as opposed to just what it had been when Muhammad died.

The most consequential intellectual project was the collection of the hadith — the reported sayings and actions of Muhammad, transmitted through chains of oral testimony from the Companions to their students.
The hadith would, alongside the Quran, become the second source of Islamic religious law and ethics.

The systematic compilations of the great collectors (Bukhari, Muslim, and the others whose works became canonical) lay still a century in the future under the Abbasids (Islamic Golden Age Ch 5); but the source material — the individual hadith reports, the chains of transmission (the isnad) by which each report was traced back to a specific Companion of Muhammad, the early scholarly evaluation of which transmitters were reliable and which were not — was being gathered and circulated under the Umayyads.
The hadith project posed an unusual epistemic problem.
The early Muslim community had to assess, transmitter by transmitter, whether a particular report about Muhammad was reliable.

The reports being transmitted were anywhere from one to four generations removed from Muhammad's actual lifetime by the late Umayyad period, and the hadith literature was already being heavily contested for political reasons (Sunni and Shia partisans were each circulating reports that supported their preferred caliphal candidates, and the Umayyad state was patronizing reports that favored its own legitimacy).
The discipline of hadith criticism — the scholarly evaluation of the soundness of each individual report — emerged in this period as a methodology for sorting genuine from forged reports.
The modern Western critical scholarship on hadith is, in some ways, simply an extension of methods the medieval Muslim hadith critics had already developed.
A parallel project was the development of Islamic jurisprudence (the fiqh, FIK-h).

Under the late Umayyads, scholars in the garrison cities of Medina, Kufa, Basra, and increasingly Fustat in Egypt began formalizing the methods by which religious law (the sharia, sha-REE-ah) could be derived from the Quran and the hadith.

The two main early schools were the Hijazi tradition at Medina (eventually associated with Malik ibn Anas, born around 711, founder of the Maliki legal school) and the Iraqi tradition at Kufa (eventually associated with Abu Hanifa, born around 699, founder of the Hanafi legal school).

The four classical Sunni legal schools — Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i, Hanbali — would not crystallize until the early Abbasid period, but the source materials and the methodological approaches were being developed under the Umayyads.
A third project was the early Islamic theology (kalam).

Three theological currents emerged in the Umayyad century, around questions the Quran did not directly settle: The Qadariyya (KAH-dah-ree-yah, from qadar, "divine decree") argued that human beings have free will and moral responsibility for their actions, against the strong-predestinarian Umayyad establishment view that everything happens by divine decree.

The Qadariyya position was politically dangerous because it implied that the Umayyad caliphs were morally responsible for their decisions and could be held accountable; the establishment view implied that whatever the caliphs did was God's will and could not be questioned.
The Murji'a (MURR-jee-ah, from irja, "deferral") deferred judgment on whether Muslims who committed major sins were still Muslims.

Their position was politically convenient for the Umayyad dynasty: if the Karbala killing of Husayn (Chapter 4) and the bombardment of Mecca (Chapter 5) and various other Umayyad atrocities did not strictly speaking remove the perpetrators from the Muslim community, then the Umayyad caliphs retained their religious legitimacy regardless of their political behavior.
The Murji'a were, in effect, the establishment-friendly theological school of the Umayyad period.
The Mu'tazila (moo-TAH-zih-lah, "those who withdraw") emerged late in the Umayyad period and would explode in importance under the early Abbasids (Islamic Golden Age Ch 5).
The Mu'tazila were rationalist theologians who held that reason, properly applied, could derive the truths of religion independently of (though in conformity with) revelation.

They argued for human free will against predestination, for divine justice (which they understood as committing God to act in accordance with rational ethical principles), and for the createdness of the Quran (the controversial doctrine that the Quran was God's created speech rather than a coeternal aspect of God's being).

The Mu'tazila program would become the official theology of the early Abbasid state under the caliph al-Ma'mun in 833 (Islamic Golden Age Ch 2), with violent enforcement against the traditionalist Sunni scholars who opposed it.
The seed of the entire later debate was planted under the Umayyads.

The most consequential institutional project of the Umayyad century, for the long-term character of the empire, was the dhimmi system — the legal framework for governing the empire's non-Muslim subject populations.

The Quran establishes a category of "People of the Book" (ahl al-kitab, AHL al-kih-TAHB) — religious communities that had received earlier divine revelations through earlier prophets, specifically Christians (whose revelation was the Gospels through Jesus), Jews (whose revelation was the Torah through Moses), and possibly Zoroastrians and Sabians (the categories were variably interpreted).

The People of the Book were entitled, under Quranic and prophetic teaching, to live as protected religious minorities under Muslim political authority — preserving their own religious law, their own clergy, their own places of worship — in exchange for accepting Muslim political supremacy and paying the jizya (JIZ-yah), a head tax on adult non-Muslim men.
This Quranic framework became, under the Umayyads, the dhimmi (DIM-mee) system — a legal category of "protected people" under Muslim governance.

The dhimmi: Could practice their own religion in private and could maintain existing places of worship (though new construction was generally restricted); Were governed in matters of personal status (marriage, inheritance, religious life) by their own religious authorities and laws (the foundation of the much later Ottoman millet system — Ottoman Empire Ch 6); Paid the jizya head tax and the kharaj land tax (dhimmi taxes were initially higher than Muslim taxes, which is one of the structural problems that produced the Mawali grievance — Chapter 8); Were excluded from senior military and political offices reserved for Muslims; Were subject to various social-symbolic restrictions of varying intensity (distinctive clothing in some periods, prohibitions on bell-ringing or public Christian processions in some places, restrictions on building height, and so on — the so-called Pact of Umar codified some of these, though its actual provenance is contested).
The dhimmi framework was, by the standards of contemporary Christian European treatment of religious minorities, generous.
The Christian and Jewish populations of the Islamic world generally fared substantially better than Muslims (or Jews) in contemporary Christian Europe.
The system was not equality — equality was not on offer in any premodern society — but it was a workable framework for plural religious communities to coexist under a single political authority.

The framework would continue, with various local adaptations, throughout the Abbasid period (Islamic Golden Age Ch 6), the Fatimid period, the Ayyubid and Mamluk periods, and the Ottoman period (Ottoman Empire Ch 6) — all the way to the late nineteenth century, when European-influenced legal reforms began to phase out the formal dhimmi categories in favor of equal citizenship.
A last note on dhimmi practice.

Conversion from dhimmi status to Islam was permitted and over time became attractive, but conversion away from Islam was forbidden — a Muslim who converted to Christianity or Judaism could be punished by death under the apostasy ruling (the ridda prohibition that had also justified Abu Bakr's Ridda Wars in 632 — Chapter 3).

The asymmetry — easy entry into Islam, prohibited exit from Islam — was one of the structural mechanisms by which the long, slow conversion of the Middle East to Islam was sustained over the following centuries.

Cross-civ check: the early Umayyad architectural and religious development overlaps with the Tang Dynasty's architectural ambition under Empress Wu (the Tang built their own great Buddhist cave temples and Chang'an pagodas in the same period the Umayyads were building the Dome of the Rock and the Damascus Mosque), the Iconoclast reorganization of Byzantine religious life under Leo III after 717 (Byzantine Empire Ch 4 — the Byzantine iconoclast movement was partly inspired by what the Byzantines had observed of Islamic aniconism), the early Anglo-Saxon Christian architecture in northern England (Bede's age, the same generation as Abd al-Malik), and the Pala dynasty's Buddhist architectural ambition in northeastern India.

The Umayyad development of the dhimmi system is roughly contemporary with the Coptic patriarchate's internal reorganization in conquered Egypt (the Coptic Church, under Arab rule, became less politically subordinated to Constantinople and more autonomous than it had been in centuries), the Nestorian church's eastward expansion into Tang China (the famous Xi'an Stele documenting Nestorian Christianity's presence in the Tang capital was erected in 781, just after the Umayyad period), and the development of the Byzantine theme system that gave conquered Christian peasant-soldiers a stake in defending the empire (Byzantine Empire Ch 3).

Different states, different religions, broadly similar institutional problems: how to govern multi-religious populations under unified political authority, and how to give the religion that legitimized the state a public architectural face.

chapters.title: The Abbasid Revolution
sentences: The Umayyad Caliphate was destroyed in three years.
In 747, an obscure freedman named Abu Muslim raised a revolutionary banner in Khorasan, the easternmost Umayyad province.
By 750, the Umayyad army had been defeated at the Battle of the Zab, the last Umayyad caliph had been hunted down in Egypt, and the surviving Umayyad princes had been massacred at a Damascus banquet.
The dynasty that had ruled an empire from Spain to Sind for ninety years was extinguished except for one survivor, who escaped and would shortly found a successor state in al-Andalus.
This chapter is about how that happened.
It is also about what came next — the Abbasid Caliphate that replaced the Umayyad and that would rule the Islamic world for the next five centuries — and about the Umayyad afterlife in Spain.
The detailed Abbasid story is the subject of Islamic Golden Age Ch 1 onward; this chapter ends where that one begins.
The Umayyad collapse was structurally driven.
By the 740s, the dynasty was failing in five separate ways simultaneously, and any one of them might have been survivable but the combination was not.
Fiscal failure.

The Umayyad fiscal system had been built around Arab privilege: Arab Muslim warriors received cash stipends from the diwan, paid for by the kharaj land tax that fell most heavily on non-Muslim cultivators.
The system worked while the Arab Muslim population was small and the conquered population was large and non-Muslim.
By the 740s, however, the population mix had shifted.
Conversion to Islam was steady (slow, but cumulatively significant after a century of Muslim rule).

The mawali — non-Arab Muslim converts — were paying lower taxes (since the religious tax differential favored them) but were also excluded from the diwan stipends that had originally been Arab privileges.
The result was a fiscal squeeze: tax revenues from a converting population were declining, but the cost of paying Arab military stipends and garrisoning the imperial frontiers was not.

Umar II had attempted in 717–720 to fix the problem by extending diwan privileges to recent mawali converts and equalizing the tax system; the reform had been popular and had nearly bankrupted the state.
His successors had reversed it.
The structural fiscal problem remained unsolved for the next thirty years.
Mawali grievance.

The non-Arab Muslim converts — Persians, Egyptians, Berbers, Aramaic-speaking Iraqis, Sogdians from Central Asia — had been told by the religion they had converted to that all Muslims were equal before God.
The Umayyad fiscal and political system told them otherwise.

Mawali Muslims paid the same taxes as non-Muslims in many cases, were excluded from senior military commands and provincial governorships, were paid lower stipends than Arab Muslims when stipends were paid at all, and were treated socially as second-class citizens in the Arab-dominated garrison cities.

The discontent was strongest among the Persian-speaking Iraqi and Iranian mawali, who had a particularly long memory of the Sasanian imperial culture they had lost in the 640s and a particularly developed sense of cultural-civilizational superiority over their Arab rulers.
This Persian-Iraqi mawali population was the social base from which the Abbasid Revolution recruited its supporters.
Tribal feuding.
The Umayyad caliphate was nominally an Arab Muslim federation, but in practice the Arab tribes that had carried out the conquests had carried their pre-Islamic feuds into the new state.

The two great tribal blocs — the Qaysi (north Arabian) and Kalbi/Yamani (south Arabian) — had been at intermittent war with each other since long before Islam, and they continued the feud inside the Umayyad army and provincial administration.
Different Umayyad caliphs favored different blocs.
Different governors organized their subordinates along bloc lines.

By the 740s, the tribal feuding had become so destructive of normal military function that the Umayyad army's coherence was visibly degrading — internal feuds between Qaysi and Kalbi commanders cost the dynasty more soldiers than its external wars did.
Berber and Kharijite revolts in North Africa.

In 740, the Berber populations of the Maghreb — heavily mawali and chronically aggrieved at Arab fiscal exploitation — revolted under Kharijite religious leadership (the Kharijites, the seventh-century breakaway from Ali's coalition, had migrated to North Africa where their austere theology found receptive audiences among the Berbers).
The revolt produced major Umayyad military defeats and effectively detached most of the Maghreb west of Egypt from caliphal control by the mid-740s.
North Africa would not be reincorporated into a unified caliphate; it would fragment into a series of independent emirates that the Abbasids would also fail to control.
Caliphal succession chaos.
The competent caliph Hisham died in 743 after nineteen years of stable rule.
His successor al-Walid II lasted a year before being murdered.
Yazid III lasted six months before dying of plague.
Ibrahim lasted two months before being deposed.
Marwan II finally took the throne in late 744 and tried to stabilize the situation, but he had to spend most of the next five years fighting a major Syrian civil war among rival Umayyad factions.
The dynasty was tearing itself apart from inside while its frontiers were collapsing.
By 747 the Umayyad state was structurally ready to be overthrown by anyone who could mobilize the accumulated grievances against it.
The Abbasid revolutionaries were the people who could.
The Abbasids were the descendants of al-Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib, the Prophet Muhammad's paternal uncle.
They were therefore cousins of the Prophet — close kin, but not from the Hashimite branch that Muhammad himself had belonged to and that Ali (Muhammad's cousin and son-in-law) had inherited.

The Abbasids had been politically marginal throughout the Rashidun and most of the Umayyad period; they had spent the 720s and 730s quietly cultivating a revolutionary network in the eastern provinces, presenting themselves as the rightful Muslim leaders against the Umayyad usurpers.
The Abbasid program was a coalition.
They appealed to the Shia by claiming to be members of the Prophet's family with a legitimate caliphal claim (without, however, formally committing to Shia theology).
They appealed to the mawali by promising to abolish the Arab privilege system and create a fully equal Muslim community.
They appealed to the Khorasanis by promising to restore Iranian-Persian dignity within a renewed Islamic framework.
They appealed to the anti-Umayyad Companions' descendants in the Hijaz by promising to restore the legitimate caliphate to a closer Prophet-relative.
They appealed to anyone who wanted change, while remaining vague about what specifically would be done after the Umayyads were gone.

The operational mastermind of the Abbasid network was Abu Muslim (ah-BOO MOOS-lim), an obscure freedman of probably Persian origin whose actual identity is one of the great minor mysteries of early Islamic history.

The early sources record different versions of his name, parentage, and origin; what is firm is that he appeared in Khorasan in the early 740s as a young man (probably in his twenties) representing the Abbasid family's eastern operation, and that he was extraordinarily effective at building underground political organizations.

Abu Muslim spent several years in Khorasan cultivating the local Arab settlers, the Persian mawali, the disaffected Yamani tribal clans, and various Shia partisans into a unified revolutionary coalition.
The coordination was conducted in secrecy under the cover of the Hashimiyya movement (a vague pro-Hashimite political tendency that the Abbasids had been steering toward their own claim for years).
The key revolutionary symbol — the black banner of the Abbasid family, reportedly chosen in deliberate contrast to the white banners the Umayyads used — became the visual marker of the coming revolt.
In June 747, Abu Muslim raised the black banner at the village of Sikadanj near Merv, with about two thousand armed supporters, and declared open revolt against the Umayyad governor of Khorasan.
Within months, his force had grown to perhaps twenty thousand.
By 748 the Abbasid army held all of Khorasan and was advancing west into Iran. (The black banner has had a long afterlife in Islamic political iconography.

"A black banner from Khorasan" became a recurring messianic symbol in later Sunni eschatology — invoked, not coincidentally, by various modern jihadist movements that adopted black banners thirteen centuries later.
The original was a dynastic logo, not a religious symbol.) The military campaign moved fast.
The Khorasani Abbasid army, well-led and high-motivated, defeated successive Umayyad provincial forces across Iran in 748 and 749.
By late 749, the Abbasid commander Qahtaba ibn Shabib had reached Iraq.

The Abbasid family itself emerged from underground — the senior Abbasid leader, Ibrahim al-Imam, was captured and killed by Marwan II's agents, but his brother Abu al-Abbas as-Saffah (as-saf-FAH, "the Bloodletter" — the epithet was self-chosen and self-celebratory) was acclaimed caliph by the Abbasid army at Kufa in October 749.
The decisive military encounter came on 25 January 750 at the Great Zab river in northern Iraq.
The Abbasid army from Khorasan met the main Umayyad field army under Marwan II in person.

Numbers are debated; modern estimates suggest the two armies were roughly comparable in size (perhaps 25,000 to 50,000 men each), though the Abbasid force was qualitatively superior — better led, better motivated, fighting for a cause its troops believed in, while the Umayyad army was a worn-out collection of tribal levies and the surviving regular professional units.
The battle was decisive.
The Umayyad army broke and was destroyed.
Marwan II fled west across Syria.
He did not stop running.
The Abbasid pursuit followed him across Syria, into Egypt.
Marwan was finally cornered and killed in a small Egyptian village called Busir in August 750.
He had been the last Umayyad caliph.
His death, six months after the Battle of the Zab, ended the Umayyad dynasty as a ruling power.
Then came the calculated extermination.
The new caliph Abu al-Abbas as-Saffah understood the Umayyad family's residual political danger.
As long as Umayyad princes survived, they would be the natural rallying points for any anti-Abbasid revolt.
The Abbasids therefore conducted a systematic campaign to hunt down and kill every member of the extended Umayyad family they could find.
The campaign was conducted with calculated theater.
The most famous episode is the Damascus banquet massacre.

As-Saffah's representative invited the surviving Umayyad princes — perhaps eighty men, the senior surviving members of the family — to a banquet in Damascus, ostensibly to negotiate their surrender and to receive Abbasid pensions in exchange for political quiescence.
When the princes had assembled, the Abbasid hosts had them all murdered at table.
According to the most lurid version of the story preserved in later sources, the bodies were covered with leather sheets while the new caliph and his court continued eating.

The leather-sheets detail is of disputed provenance — it appears in some later Abbasid-era chroniclers and not in others, and the contemporary Arabic sources love a good banquet massacre with suspiciously clean dating.
The banquet itself is well attested; the leather-sheets prop is the kind of theatrical embellishment that may or may not have happened.

The broader campaign it represents was real, however: the Abbasids hunted down Umayyad family members across the empire over the following years, exhuming their tombs in Damascus, dismantling their genealogical claim, replacing them with their own.
As-Saffah's nickname was not metaphor.
One Umayyad escaped.
Abd al-Rahman I (ahbd al-RAH-mahn, born 731), a twenty-year-old grandson of the caliph Hisham, fled the massacre.

The dramatic version of the escape — which appears in his own court historian's account and was probably partly true — has Abd al-Rahman swimming the Euphrates while Abbasid horsemen shot at him from the bank.

After five years on the run, traveling slowly across North Africa under the protection of Berber tribes (his mother had been a Berber concubine, and the family connection helped), he reached Spain — the westernmost province of the old Umayyad empire, where the Arab-Berber occupiers were divided into rival factions and where no Umayyad authority had been established.

In 756, Abd al-Rahman defeated the Abbasid-appointed governor of Spain at the Battle of al-Musara outside Córdoba and proclaimed himself emir of an independent Emirate of Córdoba that recognized neither Abbasid nor Umayyad authority — except his own.

The new Andalusian Umayyad state would last in various forms for another 270 years, becoming a full caliphate in 929 under Abd al-Rahman III and producing one of the most brilliant cultures of the medieval Mediterranean (Islamic Golden Age Ch 6–7).

The story of the swimming prince, dictated by Abd al-Rahman to his court historian and probably partly true even allowing for legendary embellishment, became one of the great founding myths of medieval Spanish history.
The implication was enormous: the Islamic world was now politically split, with two rival caliphal lineages — Abbasid in the east, Umayyad in the west — that would never be reunited.
The new Abbasid Caliphate was, in many ways, the project the Umayyad caliphate had failed to be.
The Abbasids moved their capital from Damascus to Baghdad, founded in 762 by the second Abbasid caliph al-Mansur (Islamic Golden Age Ch 1).
The shift from Damascus to Baghdad was a shift from a Mediterranean-oriented capital that had inherited Byzantine institutions to an Iraqi-centered capital that drew on Sasanian Persian traditions.

The Abbasid administration was Persianized — the great vizier families like the Barmakids were Persian converts, the court culture absorbed Sasanian ceremony, the bureaucracy ran on Sasanian-derived practices.
The Abbasid state was, structurally, a Persian-Islamic synthesis where the Umayyad state had been an Arab-Byzantine one.
The Abbasids fixed the mawali grievance the Umayyads had failed to fix.
Non-Arab Muslims, especially Persians, were given full equality in the new caliphate's military, administrative, and cultural life.
The Arab tribal aristocracy that had run the Umayyad state was sidelined in favor of a more meritocratic and more Persian-influenced administrative class.

The Persian language re-emerged as the literary and administrative language of the eastern Islamic provinces (Persian Empire Ch 10) — a recovery that would produce the great medieval Persian poetic tradition (Ferdowsi, Rumi, Hafez, Sa'di) over the following centuries.
The Abbasids also patronized the Translation Movement that would become the defining cultural project of the early Islamic Golden Age (Islamic Golden Age Ch 2).

The systematic translation of Greek philosophical, mathematical, medical, and astronomical texts into Arabic — building on the late Umayyad-era beginnings (Chapter 7) but operating at vastly larger scale under Abbasid patronage — is one of the great intellectual achievements of human history.

The texts that the Abbasid translators preserved would, several centuries later, be re-translated from Arabic into Latin and would form the core of the European Renaissance's scientific recovery (Islamic Golden Age Ch 2).
The Abbasids did not, however, become Shia.
Despite their use of Alid loyalty as part of their revolutionary coalition, the Abbasids had no intention of yielding the caliphate to the descendants of Ali.
The Shia partisans who had supported the revolution were marginalized after the victory.

Shia movements would proliferate in opposition to the Abbasids over the following centuries — the Fatimid Caliphate in Egypt (909), the Buyid amirs in Baghdad (945), the Ismaili Assassins in Iran (1090s), and eventually the Safavid revolution in Iran (1501) — but the central Abbasid state remained Sunni.

The Abbasid caliphate would last, in formal terms, until 1258, when the Mongol army of Hulagu Khan sacked Baghdad and killed the last effective Abbasid caliph, ending five centuries of Abbasid rule (Islamic Golden Age Ch 10, Mongol Empire Ch 5).
Long before then, the political reality had become one of nominal Abbasid sovereignty over a fragmented array of effectively independent Islamic dynasties.

But the cultural-economic synthesis the Abbasids had built — the Arabic-Persian high culture, the translation movement, the institutional infrastructure of medieval Islamic learning — would survive their political collapse and would shape Islamic civilization for centuries afterward.
A note on what 750 meant.
The Umayyad century had built the framework.
The conquests had taken the territory.
The Damascus capital had stabilized the administration.
The Dome of the Rock and the Damascus Mosque had given the religion its public architectural face.
The Quranic codification under Uthman, the Arabization under Abd al-Malik, the gold dinar, the dhimmi system — all of these were Umayyad accomplishments that the Abbasids inherited and built on.
But the Umayyad century had also been incomplete.
The mawali grievance was structural.
The tribal feuding was destructive.
The Arab-privilege fiscal system was fundamentally incompatible with a religion that proclaimed all believers equal.
The dynasty was overthrown not because Islam had failed but because the Umayyads' particular form of Arab-imperial Islam had failed.
The Abbasids would build an Islam-imperial state that worked better — for a while — by abandoning the Arab-privilege framework in favor of a more universal Muslim identity.
The cultural-economic Abbasid era — what the Western historiographic tradition calls the Islamic Golden Age — begins with the Battle of the Zab in 750 and the founding of Baghdad in 762.
It ends with the Mongol sack of Baghdad in 1258.
Five centuries.
The greatest intellectual workshop in the medieval world.
Algebra, algorithms, optics, medicine, philosophy, the preservation of the Greek classical tradition that would later seed the European Renaissance.
The narrative that picks up where this one ends is Islamic Golden Age Chapter 1.
The revolution that destroyed the Umayyad dynasty produced the empire that built medieval Islamic civilization.
The transition was violent, calculated, and complete.
The dynasty died.
The civilization began.
A final reflection on the Umayyad century.
The Rashidun and Umayyad period of 632–750 is the founding moment of Islamic civilization, and its judgments are mixed.
The conquest of an empire stretching from the Atlantic to the Indus in 118 years is one of the most remarkable military expansions in human history.
The construction of the Dome of the Rock and the Great Mosque of Damascus established Islamic architecture as a tradition of the first rank.

The codification of the Quran, the first systematic hadith collection, the early sharia jurisprudence, the development of the dhimmi system — all of these laid the institutional foundations on which medieval Islamic civilization was built.
The period is also morally complicated, in ways the early Muslim community was already aware of and arguing about.

The forced incorporation of conquered populations under Arab rule — even if accompanied by relatively generous protection of non-Muslim religious life — was conquest, and the people doing the conquering knew it.
The killing of Muhammad's grandson at Karbala was a religious-political crime that the Umayyad dynasty never recovered from morally.
The mawali grievance was a structural injustice that the religion's own egalitarian ideals indicted.
The Abbasid massacre of the Umayyads at Damascus in 750 was a calculated atrocity that the Abbasids' own revolutionary rhetoric had repeatedly condemned in the dynasty they were replacing.
The early Islamic political tradition was already capable, by the late Umayyad period, of recognizing the gap between the religion's professed ideals and the empire's operating practice.

The honest assessment is that the Umayyad century was both: it built one of the most consequential civilizations in human history, and it did so through methods that the religion itself had to keep arguing about for the next thirteen centuries.
The arguments are still going.
The buildings are still standing.
The conversation continues.

Cross-civ check: the Abbasid Revolution and the early Abbasid period (747–800) overlap with the An Lushan Rebellion in Tang China (755–763 — the catastrophic civil war that nearly destroyed the Tang dynasty and produced massive population losses, contemporary with the Abbasid consolidation), the Iconoclast Century in Byzantium (Byzantine Empire Ch 4), the Carolingian consolidation in France (Charlemagne would be crowned Roman emperor in 800, the same generation as the Abbasid caliph Harun al-Rashid — Islamic Golden Age Ch 1), the Pala dynasty's ascent in northeastern India, and the early Tibetan Empire under Songtsen Gampo and his successors.

The mid-eighth century is the moment when the early-medieval Eurasian state system reorganizes — the Tang nearly destroyed, the Byzantines reduced to Anatolia, the Umayyads replaced by the Abbasids, the Carolingians replacing the Merovingians in western Europe, the Tibetans rising in Inner Asia.
The Umayyad collapse is one element of a larger pattern of mid-century Eurasian political reorganization.

The civilization that emerged from the rearrangement — Abbasid Baghdad, Tang Chang'an, Byzantine Constantinople, Carolingian Aachen, the Lhasa-centered Tibetan Empire — would shape the early-medieval world.
The Umayyad century built the Islamic empire.
The Abbasid millennium built the Islamic civilization.

The transition happened in the seventy-five days between the Battle of the Zab and the founding meeting of the Abbasid council at Kufa — the most consequential change of dynasty in medieval Islamic history, and the moment that separates the founding moment of Islam from everything that came after.
The dynasty died.
The religion stayed.
The empire was rebuilt under new management.
The Iberian survivor founded a parallel state that would last longer than the original.

And the conversation about what Islam should be — a debate that started during Muhammad's lifetime and that Karbala had given a particular Sunni-Shia structure — would continue across the next thirteen centuries, into the present day.

The Iran-Saudi rivalry of 2026, the Hezbollah-Israel conflict of the 2010s, the Iran-Iraq war of the 1980s, the Sunni-Shia tensions in modern Iraq, Syria, Yemen, Bahrain, Pakistan: all of these are operating, in part, on theological-political fault lines that were established between 632 and 750.
The narrative you have just read is the founding moment of those fault lines.
What came after is, in significant ways, an extended argument about what the founding moment actually meant.
The arguments continue.

chapters.title: After Moche & Nazca
sentences: By 600 CE, the brilliant regional cultures of the previous chapter (Andean Kingdoms) were all in trouble.

The Moche civilization on the north coast of Peru — the warrior-priests of Sipán, the builders of the largest adobe pyramids in the Americas, the makers of the most realistic ceramic portraits in the ancient world — had spent the late sixth century being battered by a sequence of catastrophic El Niño events.
Floods washed out the irrigation canals that fed their cities.
Decades of drought followed the floods.
The southern Moche capital at the foot of the Huacas de Moche complex was abandoned.
The northern Moche shifted their center of gravity inland to a defensive site called Pampa Grande, which itself was burned in an internal revolt around 700 CE.
By 750, the Moche as a coherent civilization were gone (Andean Kingdoms, Chapter 8).
The Nazca culture on the south coast — the makers of the desert geoglyphs, the engineers of the puquios underground aqueducts — was hollowing out from a different cause.
Long-term deforestation had stripped the huarango trees whose deep root systems held the desert valleys' subsurface water.
As the trees disappeared, the wells went dry, the agricultural valleys lost productivity, and population shrank.
By 600 CE, Nazca was no longer a regional power; by 750 it had been absorbed into the southern reach of an expanding highland state called Wari (Andean Kingdoms, Chapter 8).
The Lima culture on the central coast and the Recuay culture in the northern highlands were both in similar trouble — climatic stress, regional reorganization, declining political coherence.
By around 600 CE, the entire western Andean coast was a patchwork of weakened polities.

This is the situation into which two new powers stepped, and the chapter you are about to read is in some sense the answer to the question: what do you build when the previous order has collapsed and there is room to start over?
The standard archaeological label for what came next is the Middle Horizon.

A "horizon" in Andean archaeology is a period when a single artistic style, religious system, or material culture spread across most of the central Andes, creating a layer of cultural uniformity visible in the dirt.
There are three of them.
The Early Horizon (roughly 900 to 200 BCE) is dominated by the Chavín religious complex (Early Andean Civilizations, Chapter 7).
The Late Horizon (1450 to 1532 CE) is the Inca Empire.
