The short version: Middle Horizon religion was a continuation of the Chavín tradition (Early Andean Civilizations, Chapter 7) filtered through highland-state institutional patronage and elaborated with new ritual technologies.
Three things define it.
The Staff God was the central deity image.
Hallucinogens were the central ritual technology.
The animal triad of puma, condor, and snake was the central cosmological framework.
None of these elements were Tiwanaku or Wari inventions.
All of them had Andean antecedents going back at least a thousand years.
What the Middle Horizon empires did was systematize, monumentalize, and propagate them at imperial scale.
The Staff God, you'll recall (Chapter 2), is a frontal figure standing upright, holding a tall staff in each hand, wearing an elaborate radiating headdress of feline and serpent figures.

The image first appears at Chavín de Huántar around 500 BCE on the Raimondi Stele, a 6-foot tall flat granite slab carved with the Staff God in classic Chavín kenning style — the kind of intricate geometric line-work that turns secondary features (claws, fangs, snakes, eyes) into independently legible smaller images embedded in the larger figure.
The Chavín Staff God established the visual template: frontal pose, paired staffs, fanged face, serpent hair, radiating headdress.
A thousand years later, the same image reappears on the upper lintel of the Gateway of the Sun at Tiwanaku, recognizably the same deity but rendered in the cleaner and more geometric Tiwanaku style.

The Tiwanaku Staff God has been simplified and rationalized: the kenning has mostly been stripped out, the headdress has become a sun-disk rather than a snake-and-fang nest, the attendant figures have been added to either side.
The deity is still recognizably the same Andean Staff God, but the visual vocabulary has shifted toward greater geometric clarity.
A century or so after that, the same image reappears on the giant Conchopata urns at Wari, marking the moment when Wari adopted the Tiwanaku-derived religious vocabulary.

The Wari Staff God is rendered in still another style — bold polychrome painting on ceramic rather than carved stone — but the basic iconographic elements are the same: frontal figure, paired staffs, sunburst headdress, attendant figures.
A thousand years after Wari adopted the image, the Inca were still using it.

The figure of Wiracocha (wee-rah-KOH-chah), the Inca creator god depicted holding paired staffs in a gold plaque that hung in the Coricancha temple at Cusco, is recognizably the same Staff God image with the same basic attributes.

The Spanish chroniclers who described the Coricancha in the 1530s did not know they were looking at a deity image transmitted in unbroken continuity from a stone slab carved two thousand years earlier in the northern Peruvian highlands.
This kind of iconographic continuity across two thousand years is unusual in any civilization.
The closest comparable case might be the persistence of certain Egyptian deity images — Horus, Anubis, Isis — across the three millennia of Pharaonic history.
But even in Egypt, the deity images shifted substantially over time; the Old Kingdom Horus is visually very different from the Late Period Horus.

The Andean Staff God preserved its visual template — frontal pose, paired staffs, fanged face, radiating headdress — across multiple successor civilizations and the entire central Andean geography, with surprisingly little drift in the basic iconographic vocabulary.
What allowed this stability is unknown, but it is one of the deepest features of Andean religion.
The second central element of Middle Horizon religion is the systematic ritual use of hallucinogenic plants.

The Andes have an unusually rich pharmacopeia of psychoactive species. vilca (VEEL-kah, Anadenanthera colubrina, also called cebil) is a tree of the southern altiplano whose dried seeds contain bufotenin and related tryptamine compounds; the seeds are ground into a snuff and inhaled, typically through bone or wooden tubes inserted in the nostril.
San Pedro cactus (Echinopsis pachanoi) is a tall columnar cactus of the highlands whose flesh contains mescaline; the cactus is sliced, boiled into a brew, and consumed orally.
Coca leaves (Erythroxylum coca) are not strictly hallucinogenic in everyday use but contain cocaine and related alkaloids that produce both stimulant and mild psychoactive effects.

Ayahuasca (eye-ah-WAHS-kah, a brew of the Banisteriopsis caapi vine combined with leaves of the Psychotria viridis shrub, both Amazonian) was probably also used in the highland Middle Horizon, though the evidence is thinner.
The archaeological evidence for psychoactive plant use is unambiguous.
Snuff trays and bone snuff tubes are among the most common high-status grave goods at both Tiwanaku and Wari elite burials.
The trays are typically rectangular wooden boards with small carved figures around the rim, a flat surface for grinding the seeds, and a hollow on one end for the resulting powder.
The tubes are decorated bone cylinders with one end shaped to insert in the nostril.

The combination is unmistakable, and the parallel use of snuff trays across Andean cultures from the early Tiwanaku period through the Inca is one of the most stable features of regional religious practice.
The point of all this was visionary religious experience.

The chemical effects of vilca snuff, San Pedro brew, and ayahuasca all produce, with regional variation, vivid altered states involving visual hallucinations, distorted bodily perception, intensified emotion, and (in many users) the feeling of communicating with non-human or supernatural beings.

In Andean religious context, this kind of experience was understood as direct contact with the divine — the ritual specialists who consumed these substances were believed to be traveling, in their visions, to the spirit world to negotiate with the gods on behalf of the community.
The vilca-induced vision of meeting the Staff God was the foundational religious experience that the iconography on the Gateway of the Sun was, in some sense, an attempt to make permanent in stone.
This is documented in the iconography itself.

The Bennett Monolith (the largest carved stela at Tiwanaku, 24 feet tall, standing in the semi-subterranean temple) shows a frontal figure holding a kero drinking cup in one hand and a snuff tablet in the other — the ritual implements of chicha consumption and vilca inhalation, respectively, identified explicitly as the attributes of the depicted figure.
The figure is probably a high-status priest or a deified ancestor, and the implements are not incidental.
They define what kind of figure this is and what kind of practice authorizes his depiction at this scale.
The Tiwanaku religious specialist was, by definition, the person who drank chicha and inhaled vilca in the right ritual contexts.
Cross-civ check: visionary plant use in religion is not unique to the Andes.

Soma, mentioned obsessively in the Vedic Sanskrit hymns of early India (Vedic Period, Chapter 4), was apparently a psychoactive plant or fungus consumed by Brahmin priests in ritual contexts to produce ecstatic states.
The Eleusinian Mysteries of ancient Greece almost certainly involved a psychoactive beverage (probably containing ergot alkaloids derived from infected barley) consumed by initiates.
The peyote ceremonies of the Huichol and other indigenous peoples of northern Mexico are still practiced today.

What is distinctive about the Andean case is the institutional embedding: Middle Horizon religion was not just decorated with occasional visionary use, it was structurally organized around it, with the ritual specialists, the iconographic vocabulary, and the burial assemblages all reflecting the centrality of the visionary experience to religious practice.
The third central element is the animal triad: puma, condor, and snake.
These three animals appear obsessively in Tiwanaku and Wari art.
The puma — the apex predator of the Andean highlands — represents the earth zone, the domain of the living.

The condor — the giant vulture whose wingspan can exceed 10 feet (3 meters), soaring at altitudes higher than any other bird in the Western Hemisphere — represents the upper world, the domain of the celestial and the sacred.
The snake — particularly the constrictor and venomous species of the eastern jungle slopes — represents the underworld, the domain of the ancestors and the chthonic.
Together, the three animals encode a vertical cosmology in which the universe is layered: snake below, puma in the middle, condor above.
This triadic cosmology is everywhere in Middle Horizon iconography.
The Staff God's headdress typically includes both feline and serpent elements (and sometimes condor elements), encoding the triadic structure in the central deity image.
The kero drinking cups often display the three animals in registers stacked vertically.

The semi-subterranean temple at Tiwanaku is below the surrounding plaza level (snake zone), the Akapana platform rises above it (puma zone), and the Kalasasaya gateways open toward the celestial circuits of the sun and stars (condor zone).
The architecture itself encodes the cosmology.
The Inca, six centuries later, would inherit the same triadic system — the puma, the kuntur (condor), and the amaru (snake) appear throughout Inca cosmology, in the same vertical-zone associations.
The Inca city of Cusco was reportedly laid out in the shape of a giant puma, with the fortress of Sacsayhuamán as its head.
The royal road system is sometimes depicted as a giant snake winding through the Andes.
The condor was the bird of the royal lineage.
All of this iconographic vocabulary was Wari and Tiwanaku inheritance, modified in details but preserved in fundamentals.
Where Tiwanaku and Wari differed religiously is mostly in emphasis rather than in content.
Tiwanaku, with its astronomical alignments and elaborate stone architecture, appears to have emphasized the celestial zone — the condor, the sun, the predictable cycles of the calendar.
The Kalasasaya is an astronomical observatory; the Gateway of the Sun is iconographically a sun-disk; the Akapana drainage system is a model of celestial water descending to the earth.

Wari, with its more militarized administrative apparatus and its emphasis on bounded compounds, appears to have emphasized the earth zone — the puma, the territorial state, the human institutional reach across the wamani.
Wari iconography has more puma imagery and more depictions of state ritual than Tiwanaku iconography does.

The Wari ushnu platforms — the small raised stone stages that appear in the central plazas of Wari administrative compounds, from which the local governor presumably addressed assembled subjects — are explicitly puma-zone constructions: stages for human political theater set in the middle of the bounded administrative space.
Both empires used vilca and San Pedro.
Both empires worshipped the Staff God.
Both empires built around the puma-condor-snake triad.
The differences are real but second-order.

The first-order religious system was shared across the Middle Horizon, and the shared framework is one reason the two empires could coexist for so long without violent conflict — they recognized each other as practitioners of the same fundamental religion, even when the political and linguistic frameworks diverged.

This is the lasting contribution of Middle Horizon religion: it stabilized a shared central Andean religious vocabulary that both Tiwanaku and Wari practiced in their distinctive variations, and that the Inca later inherited and propagated across an even larger imperial space.

The Inca religion that the Spanish encountered in the sixteenth century — the Wiracocha-Inti-Pachamama theological system, the puma-condor-snake cosmology, the chicha-and-coca ritual culture — was substantially the same religion that the Tiwanaku and Wari had been practicing six centuries earlier.
The dynasty that propagated it was new.
The religion was not.

chapters.title: The Collapse
sentences: Sometime around 900 to 1000 CE, both the Tiwanaku and the Wari empires collapsed.

The collapses were almost simultaneous — within roughly a century of each other, plausibly within a few decades — and they almost certainly had a common cause: a multi-decade drought that struck the central Andes across the late ninth and tenth centuries.
The drought is not a hypothesis.

It is documented in two independent paleoclimate records: ice cores from the Quelccaya Ice Cap high above the southern Peruvian highlands (the largest tropical ice cap in the world, which preserves an annual layered record of precipitation going back thousands of years), and sediment cores from the bottom of Lake Titicaca itself (which preserve a similar layered record of precipitation, lake levels, and pollen distributions).
Both records show a sharp downturn in precipitation beginning around 900 CE and persisting, with some variability, for roughly two centuries.
By 1100 CE the climate had partially recovered, but the empires that the earlier wetter conditions had supported were already gone.
What the drought did is collapsed the agricultural systems that fed the empires.
For Tiwanaku, the trigger was Lake Titicaca itself.
The lake's water level depends on the balance between rainfall in the surrounding watershed and evaporation from the lake surface.
In wet centuries, the lake rises and the surrounding low-lying plain floods (which is what the suka kollu raised-field system was designed to handle).
In dry centuries, the lake shrinks and the surrounding plain dries out.
The 900 CE drought drove the lake level down by roughly 40 to 50 feet (12 to 15 meters) over the course of several decades.
The lake shoreline retreated.
The water table beneath the surrounding fields dropped.
The suka kollu channels — which depended on capillary rise from the elevated water table to irrigate the platform tops — went dry.
The thermal-buffering effect of the channel water disappeared.
The frost protection that had made highland agriculture possible at 12,500 feet collapsed.
Without the raised-field system, the altiplano around Tiwanaku could not produce enough surplus food to feed a city of 30,000 people.
The city did not collapse violently — there are no signs of conquest, no destruction layers, no mass burials suggesting a single catastrophic event.
It de-populated slowly.
People moved out, presumably to lower-elevation valleys where dryland agriculture could still produce some crops.
The ceremonial core was left intact.
The Akapana, the Kalasasaya, the Gateway of the Sun, the Pumapunku platform — all of them were left standing.
The city emptied around them.
By 1100 CE, Tiwanaku was a ruin still consulted by pilgrims and respected as a sacred site, but no longer a functioning urban center.
For Wari, the mechanism was different but the underlying cause was the same.
The Wari empire ran on irrigation.
The wamani provincial centers were placed in valleys where state-managed irrigation systems supported the agricultural population that fed the imperial apparatus.
The 900 CE drought reduced the river flows that fed those irrigation systems, particularly in the more marginal frontier zones.
As the irrigation systems failed, the agricultural surplus shrank.
As the agricultural surplus shrank, the wamani compounds could no longer support themselves, much less send tribute back to the capital.
As tribute flow contracted, the central state's ability to maintain the road network, the storehouses, and the diplomatic feasting infrastructure (the Cerro Baúl brewery being one example) eroded.
The empire began to dismantle itself from the periphery inward.
The peripheral compounds were closed first.
Cerro Baúl was decommissioned around 1000 CE in the smashing-the-cup ceremony described in Chapter 5.
Pikillaqta in the Cusco basin was abandoned at roughly the same time, with its doorways deliberately blocked and its rooms sealed.
The northern outpost at Viracochapampa was abandoned, with the construction apparently never even completed.
As the periphery emptied, the central state at the Wari capital became less and less capable of sustaining itself.

By the early eleventh century, the capital city of Huari was being dismantled in the same orderly way the peripheral compounds had been: doorways blocked, structures sealed, the population dispersed to smaller settlements in the surrounding valleys.
The empire did not fall to invasion.
It walked away from itself.
This is one of the more poignant features of the Wari collapse.
There are no signs of warfare destroying the empire.
There are no indications of internal revolt overthrowing the central state.
The Wari elite appear to have made a series of orderly decisions to close the imperial infrastructure as the climatic conditions made it untenable.
The compounds were sealed rather than just abandoned.
The closing rituals were performed.
The state apparatus dismantled itself with the deliberation of a corporation winding down its operations rather than a regime collapsing in chaos.
When the work was done, the bureaucrats walked away from the buildings they had built, and the people who had served the imperial state went back to being members of local ayllu communities.
What followed the imperial collapse is called the Late Intermediate Period (roughly 1000 to 1450 CE) — the four centuries between the Middle Horizon and the Inca conquest.
The Late Intermediate is the most fragmented period in Andean political history.
Without the unifying frameworks of Tiwanaku and Wari, the central Andes broke into smaller polities organized at the river-valley or regional scale.

The largest and most successful of these was the Chimú (chee-MOO) kingdom on the north coast, which rose from the post-Wari fragments around 900 CE and built the adobe city of Chan Chan into the largest pre-Columbian city in South America (an estimated 60,000 people at its peak, covering roughly 8 square miles of dense urban construction).

The Chimú inherited the Wari coastal infrastructure, particularly the irrigation systems, and ran an effective regional state that controlled the north coast for several centuries until the Inca finally conquered them in the 1470s.
The central coast was occupied by the Chancay culture, a smaller polity known for distinctive painted textiles, cloth dolls, and the unmistakable smiling-face Cuchimilco figurines.
The southern coast and altiplano fragmented into a patchwork of smaller polities.

The Aymara kingdoms around Lake Titicaca — the Lupaqa, the Colla, the Pacajes, and others — fought each other for control of the altiplano grazing lands until the Inca consolidated all of them in the fifteenth century.

The Cusco basin, where Pikillaqta had been abandoned around 1000 CE, was occupied by a series of smaller chieftaincies (the Killke culture, archaeologically) that gradually consolidated into the early Inca polity sometime after 1200 CE.
The Late Intermediate is sometimes characterized as a period of decline — fragmentation, smaller political units, less impressive monumental architecture than the preceding Middle Horizon.
This is partly true and partly an artifact of perspective.
The smaller polities of the Late Intermediate were perfectly viable on their own terms; they just operated at smaller scale.

What the Late Intermediate lost was the imperial integration that Wari and Tiwanaku had provided — the long-distance road network, the storehouse system, the wamani provincial structure, the cross-Andean religious framework.

What it kept was the economic technologies (raised-field agriculture in the altiplano, irrigation in the coastal valleys, vertical archipelago colony networks at the local scale), the religious vocabulary (the Staff God remained the central deity image throughout the period), and the basic social institutions (the ayllu, mit'a labor tribute, the warrior-priest political model).
The infrastructure of empire was dormant, but the components were all still there, waiting to be reassembled.

The reassembly happened in the Cusco basin, beginning sometime in the early fifteenth century, under a series of leaders whose names eventually become legendary: Pachacuti (PAH-cha-KOO-tee, ruled c. 1438–1471), Tupac Yupanqui, Huayna Capac.

These leaders welded the small Killke-period chieftaincies of the Cusco region into the Inca state, then expanded the state outward across the central Andes in a campaign of conquest that took less than a century to absorb the entire territorial reach of the former Wari and Tiwanaku empires.
The Inca conquest is, in important respects, a redux of the Middle Horizon imperial project.

The Inca built planned administrative cities (Vilcashuaman, Huánuco Pampa, Tambo Colorado) on the Wari template — rectangular grids, central plazas with ushnu platforms, internal patio groups, perimeter walls.
The Inca built a road network (the famous Qhapaq Ñan) on top of the existing Wari road system, refurbishing and extending it.
The Inca built storehouse complexes (qollqa) at the same kind of locations the Wari had stored at, scaled up by an order of magnitude.
The Inca ran tribute through the wamani provincial system using mit'a labor, exactly the same way Wari had done.
The Inca khipu accounting system was a refinement of the older Wari knotted-string records.
The Inca state language was Quechua, which Wari had originally spread.
The Inca religious framework — Wiracocha, the puma-condor-snake triad, chicha and coca and vilca, the mountain apus and the lake huacas — was the Middle Horizon religion essentially preserved.
What the Inca did was take the Wari template and execute it on a much larger scale, with fifteenth-century technologies and a more centralized political structure.

The empire they built was the largest in the history of the pre-Columbian Americas — at its peak, in the early sixteenth century, it stretched from modern Colombia to modern Chile and contained perhaps 12 million people.
But the institutional bones of that empire were not Inca inventions.
They were Middle Horizon inheritance, dormant during the Late Intermediate Period, picked up and refurbished by the Cusco-based imperial revival.
This is the deepest legacy of the Middle Horizon.
Tiwanaku and Wari did not just rule the central Andes for four centuries and collapse.
They invented the institutional template for Andean empire, ran the first version of it, and then bequeathed it to the successor civilization that would eventually be encountered by the Spanish.

When Francisco Pizarro (1478–1541, the Spanish conquistador who landed on the Peruvian coast in 1532 and captured the Inca emperor Atahualpa within the year) marched up the Inca royal road from the coast to the highland city of Cajamarca to meet the Inca emperor, he was walking on a roadbed that Wari engineers had laid down eight centuries earlier.
He was passing storehouses that operated on a system Wari had invented.
He was traveling through wamani provincial structures that Wari had designed.
He was encountering, without knowing it, the second iteration of an imperial template whose first run had ended in deliberate orderly closure four centuries before he was born.
A pause for what does and does not appear in modern memory.
The Inca are world-famous.
The conquistadors' chronicles described them in detail.
Machu Picchu is one of the most-visited tourist sites on the planet.
The Inca road system, the Inca terraces, the Inca Sun Temple at Cusco, the Inca emperor wearing his golden ear-spools — all of this is solidly lodged in the global cultural memory.
Most reasonably educated people can name at least one Inca emperor (Atahualpa, usually) and know roughly when and how the empire fell.
Tiwanaku and Wari are not in the global cultural memory in any comparable way.
Most reasonably educated people have never heard of either empire.
The Gateway of the Sun is sometimes seen on travel posters but rarely identified by name.
The Pumapunku is a fixture of pseudoarchaeology TV but almost never appears in standard world-history textbooks.

Wari is practically invisible — even among visitors to Peru who know about the Inca and the Moche, very few know that there was an imperial state running the central Peruvian highlands seven centuries before the Inca, and that the Inca built directly on the Wari template.
The reason for the invisibility is partly about writing.
The Inca were encountered by literate conquerors who wrote down what they saw, in detail, in Spanish books that have circulated continuously since the sixteenth century.
Tiwanaku and Wari were not encountered by anyone literate.
By the time the Spanish arrived in the 1530s, both empires had been ruins for four to five centuries.

The Aymara residents around Tiwanaku in 1549, when Pedro Cieza de León (the Spanish chronicler who visited the site that year) asked about the ruins, told him the city had been built in a single night by giants, before the time of the Inca.
This was the local oral tradition four centuries after the city's abandonment.

It was not history in the modern sense, and it could not provide what the Inca chronicles provided: a continuous narrative of names, dates, events, and political relationships connecting the visible ruins to the human past.
Tiwanaku and Wari were prehistoric to the Spanish.
They have been prehistoric to most of world history ever since.
What rescued them, partially, has been modern archaeology.
Adolph Bandelier's work at Tiwanaku in the 1890s established the site as a serious pre-Columbian civilization rather than an Inca outpost.
Tello's work in the 1920s and 1930s — Andean Kingdoms, Chapter 2 — distinguished Wari from Tiwanaku as separate empires rather than a single artistic horizon.

The modern wave of Wari archaeology since the 1970s — particularly the work of William Isbell, Gordon McEwan, and Anita Cook — has reframed Wari as a true imperial state with planned administration rather than just a religious horizon.
The 2012 discovery of the Castillo de Huarmey burial complex by Polish archaeologists Miłosz and Patrycja Giersz brought Wari back into the news cycle, briefly.
The Cerro Baúl excavations by Patrick Williams and Donna Nash since the late 1980s have provided the central case study for Wari-Tiwanaku interaction.
None of this has yet made Wari and Tiwanaku into household names, but the scholarly understanding of the Middle Horizon today is qualitatively different from what it was even a generation ago.
The hope, presumably, is that eventually the Middle Horizon will get the cultural recognition that the documentary record never gave it.

The two empires that ran the central Andes for four centuries, invented the planned administrative city, built the original Andean road network, perfected raised-field agriculture, created the most precise stonework in the pre-Columbian Americas, and bequeathed almost every institution the Inca later got famous for — these empires deserve to be in the global cultural conversation alongside the contemporary Tang Chinese, the Byzantine Greeks, and the Carolingian Franks.
They are not yet.
Maybe they will be.
Cross-civ check: the simultaneous collapse of Tiwanaku and Wari around 900–1100 CE took place during one of the more dramatic climate-driven transitions in human history.

The same period saw the Maya Classic collapse in the southern Yucatán — a cascade of city abandonments across the Petén lowlands between roughly 800 and 1000 CE, plausibly triggered by similar drought conditions to those that took down the Andean empires (Maya Civilization, Chapter 7).
It saw the Tang Dynasty collapse in China in 907 CE, followed by the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period of fragmentation.
It saw the climatic shift to the Medieval Warm Period in Europe, which favored Norse expansion to Iceland, Greenland, and briefly Newfoundland (Viking Age, Chapter 3).
The end of the first millennium CE was a period of significant climate adjustment globally, and several major civilizations responded to it by collapsing.
The Andean Middle Horizon is one of the more dramatic examples of the pattern.

The Maya collapse, the Tang collapse, and the Tiwanaku-Wari collapse all happened within roughly two centuries of each other, on three different continents, with at least partly shared climatic causation.
The first millennium of the Common Era ended with imperial demolitions on a global scale.
The empires that came back — the Inca in the Andes, the Postclassic Maya states in the Yucatán, the Song Dynasty in China — built on the institutional inheritance of the empires that had collapsed.
The patterns repeat.
The Andean version is less famous than the others but no less consequential.

The Inca that the Spanish met in 1532 were the heirs of Wari and Tiwanaku, four centuries removed and a thousand years on from Chavín, executing the same Andean imperial template that the Middle Horizon had perfected and then walked away from.
That is the end of the Middle Horizon story, and the beginning of the next book in this series.

chapters.title: The Road to Sekigahara
sentences: The Edo period begins on October 21, 1600, on a foggy plain about 250 miles (400 km) west of modern Tokyo, where two armies of roughly 80,000 men each slaughtered each other for six hours in the rain to decide which of two factions would govern Japan.
The battle was called Sekigahara (seh-kee-gah-HAH-rah).
The winner was a sixty-year-old daimyo named Tokugawa Ieyasu (toh-koo-GAH-wah ee-eh-YAH-soo).
The loser was a forty-year-old bureaucrat-general named Ishida Mitsunari (ee-SHEE-dah mit-soo-NAH-ree).
The dynasty that came out of Ieyasu's victory ruled Japan for the next 265 years and shaped everything in this book.

To understand why two enormous Japanese armies were trying to kill each other on a rainy October day in 1600, you need to understand what had happened in Japan over the previous half century — the period the Japanese call the Sengoku Jidai (sen-GOH-koo jee-DYE), the "Age of Warring States," covered in the closing chapters of the Ancient Japan TL.
The short version: from roughly 1467 to 1600, Japan was a failed state.
The emperor in Kyoto (KYOH-toh) was a ceremonial figurehead with no real power.

The shogun (SHOH-gun, the military dictator who had governed Japan in the emperor's name since 1192) had become equally powerless, and the Ashikaga shogunate (ah-shee-KAH-gah, the dynasty that had held the office since 1336) had collapsed into civil war.

In place of central authority, the country was divided among roughly 250 regional military lords called daimyo (DIME-yo, "great names"), who ran their territories as effectively independent kingdoms, fought each other constantly, and built the vast hilltop fortresses that still dot the Japanese landscape — castles like Himeji (HEE-meh-jee) and Matsumoto (mat-soo-MOH-toh).
Three figures unified the country in stages, in a process Japanese historians call the Sengoku Unification.

The first was Oda Nobunaga (OH-dah noh-boo-NAH-gah), a brutal and brilliant daimyo from central Honshu who began his career with a tiny domain and by the time of his assassination in 1582 controlled roughly half of Japan.
Nobunaga was the first Japanese commander to use European-imported arquebuses (matchlock firearms, introduced by Portuguese traders in 1543) on a mass scale.

At the Battle of Nagashino in 1575, he stationed three thousand arquebusiers in rotating volley fire behind wooden palisades and shot the famous Takeda cavalry to pieces — the same kind of gunpowder-versus-cavalry mismatch the Ottomans inflicted on the Safavids at Chaldiran in 1514 (Safavid Persia Ch 3), and the Spanish on Aztec warriors at Tenochtitlan in 1521 (Aztec Empire Ch 8).
The Sengoku Unification was a gunpowder revolution as much as a political one.
Nobunaga was killed at the Honnō-ji Incident in June 1582, betrayed and forced into ritual suicide by one of his own generals.
His succession passed not to his sons but to his most capable lieutenant, a man of peasant origin named Toyotomi Hideyoshi (toh-yoh-TOH-mee hee-deh-YOH-shee).
Hideyoshi's career is one of the most extraordinary social ascents in pre-modern history.

Born into a peasant family with no surname, he rose through the ranks of Nobunaga's army to become a senior general; after Nobunaga's death he outmaneuvered the rival generals, was granted the surname Toyotomi by the emperor, and by 1590 had completed the unification of Japan.

Hideyoshi could not become shogun (the title was reserved by tradition for descendants of a specific noble lineage to which his peasant background obviously did not belong), so he took the older imperial-court title of kampaku (KAM-pah-koo, "regent") instead.

He confiscated swords from the peasantry in the Sword Hunt of 1588, fixed the four-class social order that the Tokugawa would inherit, and set in motion the conditions that would produce the Edo settlement.
He also did one disastrous thing: in 1592, he invaded Korea.
Hideyoshi's Korean invasions (Imjin War, 1592–98) are covered in detail in Ancient Korea Ch 8 and the Joseon Korea TL.
From the Japanese side, what matters is that the war was a catastrophe.
Hideyoshi mobilized roughly 158,000 Japanese troops for the first invasion in 1592 and another 141,000 for the second in 1597.

Korean and Chinese Ming forces, supported by the brilliant Korean admiral Yi Sun-sin and his armored "turtle ships," fought the Japanese to a standstill on land and destroyed Japanese supply lines at sea.
The campaigns dragged on for six years, devastated the Korean Peninsula, killed perhaps a million Koreans, drained the Toyotomi treasury, and produced no territorial gains whatsoever.
They ended only because Hideyoshi died in September 1598 and his successors withdrew the troops.
Hideyoshi's death is where the Sekigahara story properly starts.

He left a five-year-old son and heir, Toyotomi Hideyori (hee-deh-YOH-ree), and a council of five senior daimyo regents (the Go-Tairō, GOH TAI-roh) plus five administrators charged with governing in the boy's name until he came of age.

The senior regent was Tokugawa Ieyasu, lord of the Kantō (KAHN-toh) plain — the rich agricultural region around modern Tokyo where Hideyoshi had relocated him in 1590, partly as reward, partly to get him out of central Japan where he could cause trouble.
Ieyasu was, by 1598, the richest and most experienced daimyo in Japan.

He had survived since the 1540s, fought under Nobunaga, kept his independence under Hideyoshi, refused to participate in the Korean invasions (citing the need to defend his eastern domains), and used the war years to build up his treasury while everyone else burned theirs in Korea.
He was old, patient, and completely without scruples about using legal pretexts to seize what he wanted.
The Toyotomi council was the kind of arrangement that practically begged for someone like Ieyasu to break.
The break came in 1599 and 1600.
Ieyasu began arranging unauthorized political marriages between his family and other daimyo houses — a violation of Hideyoshi's last orders — and the rest of the council split over how to respond.

The bureaucrat Ishida Mitsunari, a Toyotomi loyalist who had served as Hideyoshi's chief administrator in Korea (and who was hated by many of the field commanders for his perceived favoritism toward Hideyoshi's home retainers), began organizing a coalition of western daimyo to check Ieyasu before he could consolidate power.
The other regents either died, declared neutrality, or joined Ieyasu.
By summer 1600, Japan had divided into two armed camps.
Ieyasu commanded the Eastern Army — primarily daimyo from the Kantō and northeastern Honshu, supported by several powerful western lords who had personal grievances against Mitsunari.
Mitsunari commanded the Western Army — daimyo from western Honshu, Shikoku, and Kyushu, nominally loyal to the seven-year-old Hideyori.
The Sekigahara campaign of summer and autumn 1600 was an extraordinarily fluid affair, with sieges and skirmishes scattered across the country.

The decisive action happened on a single day, October 21, on the Sekigahara plain in modern Gifu Prefecture, where Mitsunari deployed his army in the morning fog to block Ieyasu's advance toward the imperial capital at Kyoto.
Numbers are estimated at roughly 80,000 on each side, though the Western Army may have been somewhat larger.
The Western Army held strong defensive positions in the surrounding hills — on paper, the position favored Mitsunari.
The battle began around 8 in the morning and was fought ferociously through the early afternoon, with neither side able to break the other.
What decided it was treachery.
Two western daimyo, Kobayakawa Hideaki (koh-bah-yah-KAH-wah hee-deh-AH-kee) and Wakizaka Yasuharu, had entered into secret negotiations with Ieyasu before the battle.
Around noon, Ieyasu fired arquebus volleys at Kobayakawa's stationary force on the western flank as a prearranged signal.
Kobayakawa charged — not into the Tokugawa line but into the Western Army's right wing, the troops of Ōtani Yoshitsugu (OH-tah-nee yoh-shee-TSOO-goo), a leper-warlord and Mitsunari's most loyal ally.
Other secretly compromised western commanders followed Kobayakawa's lead.
Within an hour, the Western Army's flank had collapsed.
By mid-afternoon the battle was over. Ōtani committed ritual suicide.
Mitsunari fled the field, was captured three days later, and was beheaded in Kyoto along with two of his senior allies.
The casualty figures are debated — chronicle accounts give numbers ranging from 8,000 to 30,000 dead, mostly on the Western side — but the political result was unambiguous.
Ieyasu now controlled all of Japan in fact, even though he was technically still acting in the name of the eight-year-old Toyotomi heir.
It took him three more years to formalize the result.

In 1603, the emperor appointed Ieyasu shogun — reviving the office that had been dormant for half a century, and granting it (this time) to a man who actually had the military force to enforce its claims.
Ieyasu was sixty-one years old.

He chose as his administrative capital not Kyoto (the imperial capital, where the powerless emperor resided) and not Osaka (Hideyoshi's stronghold, where the Toyotomi heir still held court) but Edo (EH-doh, modern Tokyo) — at the time a small fishing village on a swampy bay, which he had been developing since Hideyoshi assigned him the Kantō in 1590.
Within a century, Edo would be the largest city in the world.
The Tokugawa shogunate had begun.
One loose end remained: the Toyotomi heir.
Hideyori was, by the early 1610s, a young adult living in Osaka Castle (the immense fortress Hideyoshi had built as his capital).
He had no political power, but he was the focal point for any daimyo who might object to Tokugawa rule, and his mother Yodo-dono (yoh-DOH DOH-noh) maintained an alternative court that worried Ieyasu.
Ieyasu manufactured a pretext in 1614 — an inscription on a temple bell at Osaka was interpreted as a curse against him — and besieged Osaka Castle in two campaigns over the winter of 1614–15.
The Sieges of Osaka were the last major military operations of the Sengoku era.
The first siege ended in a negotiated peace under which Hideyori agreed to fill in the castle's outer moats.

As soon as the negotiation was complete, Ieyasu's troops also filled in the inner moats — without authorization but with the kind of legalistic excuse Ieyasu specialized in — leaving the castle defensible only from the keep itself.
The summer 1615 siege then breached the keep within weeks.
Hideyori committed ritual suicide.
His mother committed ritual suicide.
His seven-year-old illegitimate son (Hideyoshi's grandson) was beheaded at Kyoto's Sanjō bridge as a precaution.
The Toyotomi line was extinguished.

That same year, Ieyasu issued the Buke Shohatto ("Laws for the Military Houses"), the basic legal code regulating daimyo conduct, and the Ikkoku Ichijō Rei ("One Castle Per Province" edict), requiring daimyo to demolish all but one castle per province and break the military infrastructure of the warring-states era.
He died the next year, in 1616, having lived just long enough to see the Tokugawa system safely established.

He was buried at Nikkō (NIK-koh) in the mountains north of Edo, and shortly afterward enshrined as the deity Tōshō Daigongen ("Great Avatar Illuminating the East") at the Nikkō Tōshō-gū shrine, one of the most ornately decorated religious complexes in Japan and the cult center of the dynasty.
A pause to set up what comes next: the Edo period is structurally weird in a way that takes some getting used to.
It was a feudal warrior society in which there were no wars.

The samurai class — roughly 7% of the population, whose entire social identity was built around martial skill — spent the next two and a half centuries doing accounting, collecting taxes, attending Confucian academies, and writing nostalgic essays about the warrior ethos of their ancestors.
Many never drew a sword in anger.
Some never wore real swords at all by the late Edo period (wooden practice swords were cheaper, and there was nobody to fight).
It was a hereditary social hierarchy of unprecedented rigidity.
The four-class order put samurai on top, peasants second (because they fed the country), artisans third, and merchants at the bottom (because they produced nothing — they only moved goods around).
Within a century the merchants had most of the money; the samurai were chronically broke; and the social hierarchy had inverted economically while remaining intact legally and culturally.
It was an isolated country in which foreigners were forbidden to enter and Japanese were forbidden to leave.
The death penalty applied in both directions.

Yet the small Dutch trading post at Nagasaki transmitted European medicine, astronomy, and physics, in dribs and drabs, to a small but growing community of Japanese scholars who knew that everything they were learning would be useful when (not if) the closure ended.
It was an authoritarian state in which the central government deliberately limited its own ambition.
The shogunate did not collect a national tax.
It did not recruit a national army.

It governed roughly a quarter of Japan directly and left the remaining three-quarters to the daimyo, with controls (sankin-kotai, marriage approval, castle limits) that prevented daimyo coordination but otherwise let them run their domains as they pleased.
It was, in short, a society that had decided to stop.
The next chapter explains how the stopping was institutionalized.

Cross-civ check: Sekigahara in 1600 was almost exactly contemporary with the founding of the English East India Company (1600), which would two and a half centuries later play a major role in Japan's forced reopening — and which had already, by 1600, established the trading post system on the Indian coast that would form the core of the British Empire in India.
Akbar the Great of the Mughal Empire (Mughal Ch 3) died five years after Sekigahara, having ruled India through almost the same span as Hideyoshi.

Shah Abbas the Great of Safavid Persia (Safavid Persia Ch 4) was at the height of his power in the 1610s, transforming Isfahan into a city Europeans called "half the world" while Ieyasu was building Edo into what would become the largest city anywhere.
The Ming Dynasty in China was in its terminal decline — the Manchu invasion that would replace it with the Qing was thirty-five years away.
The early seventeenth century was a moment of imperial consolidation across most of Eurasia, and Japan was joining the pattern at the eastern end.

chapters.title: The Tokugawa System
sentences: Tokugawa Ieyasu died in 1616 without writing a constitution.
There was no founding document, no Magna Carta, no formal statement of how the new regime was supposed to work.

What there was instead, accumulated over the first half-century of Tokugawa rule, was a dense web of edicts, customs, hierarchies, and physical constraints that together produced the most stable political order in Japanese history.
By the time the third shogun Tokugawa Iemitsu (toh-koo-GAH-wah ee-eh-MIT-soo) died in 1651, the system was complete.
It would last with only marginal modification until Perry's ships arrived in 1853.
This chapter walks through the components.
The first component was the bakuhan system — the dual structure that distinguished the Edo regime from anything Japan had seen before.
Bakufu (BAH-koo-foo, "tent government") was the original Japanese term for a shogunate, dating to the twelfth century when the first shogun's headquarters were a literal field tent.

Under the Tokugawa, the bakufu was the central government in Edo: the shogun, his council of senior ministers (Rōjū, ROH-joo), his junior councillors (Wakadoshiyori, wah-kah-doh-shee-YOH-ree), and the various magistracies that handled finance, religion, foreign affairs, and the territories the shogunate governed directly.

Han (HAHN) was the term for the daimyo domains — roughly 270 of them by the mid-seventeenth century, ranging in size from the Kaga han of the Maeda family (one million koku of rice, the largest non-Tokugawa domain) down to small holdings of just 10,000 koku, the technical minimum to qualify as a daimyo.

A koku (KOH-koo) was the amount of rice considered sufficient to feed one person for one year — roughly 5 bushels or 180 liters — and it was the standard unit of value, taxation, and military rank for the entire Edo period.
A daimyo's wealth was measured in koku.
A samurai's stipend was paid in koku.
The shogunate's own holdings were measured in koku (around 4 million, plus the personal estates of the shogun and the Tokugawa branch families, totaling roughly a quarter of Japan's productive land).
The genius of the bakuhan system was that it was simultaneously highly centralized and highly decentralized.

The shogunate held overwhelming military power (the Tokugawa and their direct retainers fielded the largest army in Japan by an enormous margin), exclusive authority over foreign relations, the right to confiscate or relocate any daimyo, control of the major cities and mines, and the authority to legislate for the whole country on certain matters.

But within their domains, daimyo were essentially autonomous — they ran their own administrations, levied their own taxes (paid in koku of rice, just like everyone else), maintained their own armies, and answered to the shogunate only on a narrow set of matters defined by the Buke Shohatto ("Laws for the Military Houses"), the basic legal code Ieyasu issued in 1615.
The Buke Shohatto was itself a remarkably restrained document.

It mostly told daimyo what they could not do — could not repair castles without permission, could not arrange marriages with other daimyo families without permission, could not harbor criminals from other domains, could not build large ships, could not introduce Christianity.
It did not tell them how to govern.
The shogunate's interest was in preventing inter-daimyo coordination that might threaten Tokugawa supremacy, not in dictating local policy.
Daimyo were not all equal.
The system divided them into three categories that determined their distance from the shogun, the kinds of offices they could hold, and the kinds of trouble they could cause.

Shinpan (SHIN-pan, "related daimyo") were branches of the Tokugawa family itself — the great cadet branches at Owari, Kii, and Mito known collectively as the Gosanke ("Three Houses"), and several smaller branches.

They held important domains, were ineligible to serve in shogunate ministerial offices (to prevent any dilution of their dynastic prestige), and provided the pool from which a successor would be drawn if the main Tokugawa line failed (which it did several times).
Fudai (FOO-die, "hereditary vassals") were daimyo whose ancestors had been Tokugawa retainers since before 1600.
They were generally given small but strategically located domains, and they monopolized the major shogunate offices — the senior ministers, the junior ministers, the magistracies, the inspectorates.
They were the bureaucratic operating system of the Tokugawa state.

Tozama (toh-ZAH-mah, "outside lords") were the daimyo whose families had been independent of the Tokugawa before 1600 — including many who had fought against Ieyasu at Sekigahara and had submitted only after the battle.

They held the largest domains (the great tozama houses of Maeda in Kaga, Shimazu in Satsuma at the southern tip of Kyushu, Mōri in Chōshū at the western end of Honshu, and Date in northeastern Honshu, were among the wealthiest), but they were excluded from the shogunate's central government.
Their domains were typically remote — Satsuma in the far southwest, Chōshū at the western end of Honshu, Date in the far northeast — placed deliberately far from Edo.
This three-tier system contained a long-term geological flaw.
The fudai who actually ran the shogunate were tied to relatively small, fragmented domains and depended on the bakufu for status.

The tozama, excluded from central power, ran their own large rich domains for two and a half centuries with minimal interference, accumulated grievances they could neither express nor act on, and developed independent administrative traditions, military experiments, and (in some cases) covert foreign contacts.
When the system finally cracked in the 1860s, the great tozama domains of Satsuma and Chōshū — kept out of central power for 265 years — would be the ones that overthrew the Tokugawa (Chapter 8).

The second component was the sankin-kōtai (SAHN-kin KOH-tai, "alternate attendance") system, formalized by Iemitsu in 1635, which is probably the single most consequential institution of the Edo period.
Under sankin-kōtai, every daimyo in Japan was required to spend alternate years in residence at Edo and to leave their wife, children, and immediate heir there permanently as hostages.
The standard schedule was one year in Edo, one year back in the home domain, on rotation.
There were variations (some smaller daimyo spent half-years; some Kantō daimyo had different schedules), but the basic principle applied to everyone.
The mechanism is worth thinking through, because it solved several political problems at once.
First, the hostage function.
With every daimyo's heir living permanently in Edo, no daimyo could rebel without sacrificing their family.

The hostages were not held in cells — they lived in lavish daimyo mansions in designated districts of Edo, were educated by tutors, married off to other daimyo families with shogunate approval — but they were hostages nonetheless.
This single arrangement made daimyo rebellion, the standard political problem of the Sengoku era, structurally impossible.
Second, the fiscal function.

Maintaining a residence in Edo, traveling to and from the home domain every other year with a full retinue of samurai retainers, and supporting a permanent household of family members and servants in the capital was ruinously expensive.
Estimates suggest sankin-kōtai consumed somewhere between 50% and 75% of the average daimyo's annual income.
This expense drained the daimyo treasuries that might otherwise have funded military buildup, and it transferred enormous wealth into Edo's economy.
Third, the integrative function.
The biennial daimyo processions to and from Edo — typically several hundred armed retainers walking in formation along specific routes — bound the country together physically.

The five great highways radiating from Edo (the Gokaidō, GOH-kai-doh: the Tōkaidō along the Pacific coast to Kyoto, the Nakasendō through the central mountains to Kyoto, the Kōshū Kaidō to the central highlands, the Ōshū Kaidō to the northeast, and the Nikkō Kaidō to the Tōshō-gū shrine) became the busiest road network in pre-railway Asia.
Inn towns, post stations, and carrier services flourished along the routes.
Travel guides, regional cuisine specialties, and souvenir industries developed to serve the annual flood of daimyo retinues.
The sankin-kōtai roads were the circulatory system of Tokugawa Japan.
Fourth, and perhaps most important in the long run, the cultural-economic function.
Concentrating the daimyo aristocracy in Edo for half of every year produced an enormous urban consumer market for luxury goods, entertainment, education, and services.
Edo grew explosively as a result.

Estimates of the city's population by 1700 range from 800,000 to 1.2 million people, making it almost certainly the largest city in the world at that point — bigger than London, bigger than Paris, bigger than Beijing.
This urban scale produced the merchant culture, the entertainment districts, the bookstores and theaters and brothels and teahouses that would define Genroku-era Japan (Chapter 4).
The cost-benefit calculation from the shogunate's perspective was unambiguous.
Sankin-kōtai prevented rebellion, drained daimyo finances, and built the largest city on earth at the heart of the Tokugawa state.
From the daimyo's perspective, it was a slow-motion impoverishment they could not refuse.
The third component was the shi-nō-kō-shō (shee-noh-koh-SHOH) system — the four-class social order that fixed Japanese society in legal categories for the entire Edo period.
The four classes, in descending Confucian rank: Shi — samurai (SAH-moo-rye), the warrior class.
Roughly 6–8% of the population.
Hereditary status.
The only class permitted to wear the long-and-short sword combination (the daishō, DIE-shoh).
The only class permitted to use family surnames in formal documents (commoners had given names but generally no surnames before the Meiji period).
The only class from which government officials could be drawn.

Samurai were paid in fixed rice stipends from their domain or from the shogunate, and these stipends did not adjust for inflation — which over time produced the chronic samurai indebtedness that became one of the central social problems of the Edo period.
Nō — peasants (NOH, hyakushō, hyah-KOO-shoh), the farming class.
Roughly 80–85% of the population.

They produced the rice that fed the country, paid the taxes that funded the state, and were ranked second under the Confucian principle that those who produce food are more valuable than those who only move it around.
In practice, peasant life ranged from prosperous landowners running multi-generation village holdings to landless tenant laborers ground down by famine, taxes, and natural disaster.
Farmers were forbidden to leave their villages, change occupations, or wear silk.

The shogunate's view of peasants was famously summarized in a quotation attributed to Tokugawa-era officials: peasants should be "neither alive nor dead" — kept just affluent enough to keep paying taxes, never affluent enough to demand anything else. (Whether anyone actually said this is debated; the sentiment is documented.) Kō — artisans (KOH, shokunin, shoh-KOO-nin), the producing class.
Roughly 5% of the population.
Craftsmen, builders, blacksmiths, lacquerers, papermakers, swordsmiths, carpenters, dyers.
They lived in the cities, organized in guilds, and produced the material culture of Edo Japan.
Their position above merchants reflected the Confucian principle that those who make things are more valuable than those who only trade them.
Shō — merchants (SHOH, chōnin, CHOH-nin), the trading class.
Roughly 5–7% of the population.
Bottom of the Confucian hierarchy because, in the official theory, they produced nothing — they only moved goods, lent money, and skimmed off the productive labor of others.
In practice, they were the people who ran the commercial economy, financed the daimyo, and (by the eighteenth century) controlled most of the country's liquid wealth.

Below the four classes were two excluded categories: the eta (EH-tah) and hinin (HEE-nin), the "pollution" castes who handled leather, butchering, executioner duties, undertaking, and similar work considered ritually impure under Buddhist and Shinto traditions.

They lived in segregated communities, were excluded from the temple registration system that defined Japanese identity, and faced legal and social discrimination that persisted (in attenuated form) long after the Meiji-era abolition of the formal class system.
The descendants of the eta-hinin communities, now generally called burakumin (boo-rah-KOO-min), still face residual discrimination in modern Japan.
The four-class system was meant to be hereditary and immutable.

In practice, mobility happened — wealthy merchants could buy samurai status by marrying into impoverished samurai families and adopting samurai surnames; samurai who could not pay their debts sometimes fell out of the class entirely; some peasants in commercial regions effectively functioned as merchants.
But the formal hierarchy held until 1869, when the new Meiji government abolished the four classes by decree.
The fourth component was the controlled apparatus of religion.
Buddhism became, in effect, a state-sponsored institution.

The terauke (teh-rah-OO-keh) system, formalized in the 1640s, required every Japanese household to register with a designated Buddhist temple and obtain certificates of religious affiliation that functioned as identity documents.

Originally the system was created to identify and screen for crypto-Christians (Chapter 3), but it quickly became a comprehensive population register — the first such system in any major state, predating European census-keeping by two centuries.

Temple priests issued the certificates; the shogunate used the registers to track migration, marriage, and inheritance; and the temples drew steady income from registration fees and required services.

Shinto, the indigenous Japanese spiritual tradition (Ancient Japan Ch 3), was incorporated into the system at the level of the Ise Grand Shrine (Mie Prefecture, the central Shinto shrine, dedicated to the sun goddess Amaterasu) and the various shrine networks across the country.

Mass pilgrimages to Ise — the okage-mairi (oh-KAH-geh MY-ree) movements — periodically swept through the country, with several million commoners temporarily abandoning their villages to walk to Ise in waves that the shogunate could neither prevent nor control.

The Ise Grand Shrine continued its ancient practice of ritual rebuilding every twenty years (still observed in the modern era), with the wooden shrine buildings reconstructed identically on adjacent plots in alternation.
The Tokugawa state subsidized this practice.
Christianity, by contrast, was a capital crime, and we'll spend Chapter 3 on how that came to be.

Confucianism — particularly the Neo-Confucianism developed by the Song Dynasty Chinese philosopher Zhu Xi in the twelfth century — became the official intellectual framework of the samurai class and the curriculum of samurai education.
The Tokugawa state founded the Shōheikō academy in Edo in 1690 to train officials in Zhu Xi orthodoxy, and similar academies opened in domain capitals across the country.
The Neo-Confucian emphasis on hierarchy, loyalty, filial piety, and the rectification of names provided ideological cover for the entire Tokugawa social order.
The fifth component was the controlled apparatus of foreign relations — but that requires its own chapter.

Cross-civ check: the Tokugawa system Ieyasu and his successors built was structurally similar to the Ming Dynasty Chinese system in several respects (Confucian orthodoxy, suspicion of merchants, controlled foreign trade through designated ports, tributary diplomacy) but very different in others (no civil service exam, no centralized national army, no uniform tax code).

The closest contemporary parallel is, surprisingly, the Habsburg system in central Europe — a central monarchy presiding over a federation of semi-autonomous noble territories, balancing rival aristocratic factions, controlling commerce through chartered monopolies, restricting religious heterodoxy.

The Habsburgs were no more successful than the Tokugawa at preventing the long-term erosion of their structural foundations, and both systems collapsed in the same nineteenth-century wave of modernization.
The Tokugawa held on longer than they would have any right to expect, given the structural strain.

chapters.title: Sakoku and the Christian Purge
sentences: The Tokugawa shogunate's most distinctive policy — the one that defines the Edo period in popular imagination — was its near-total isolation from the rest of the world for over two centuries.

The Japanese term for this policy is sakoku (SAH-koh-koo, "closed country"), though the term itself was not in use until the nineteenth century — Edo-era Japanese simply referred to it as the system of foreign relations.
The decision to close Japan was not made all at once.

It accumulated through a series of edicts between 1612 and 1639, driven by an escalating fear of foreign influence — specifically, the Catholic Christianity that Portuguese and Spanish missionaries had been spreading in Japan since the 1540s.
To understand the closure, you have to understand the Christian century that preceded it.
Christianity arrived in Japan in 1549, when the Spanish Jesuit missionary Francis Xavier (FRAN-sis ZAY-vee-er) landed at Kagoshima on the southern tip of Kyushu.

Xavier was one of the founding members of the Society of Jesus (the Jesuits, the Catholic missionary order founded by Ignatius of Loyola in 1540, specifically organized for global missionary work in the wake of the Reformation).
The Jesuits had a strategy: target the elites first, accommodate local customs as much as Catholic doctrine permitted, and rely on prestige rather than force to convert populations.
In Japan they applied this strategy effectively.
They learned Japanese, dressed in Japanese clothing, adopted Japanese manners, and built personal relationships with daimyo and senior samurai.
The conversion campaign succeeded spectacularly.

By the 1580s, several daimyo on Kyushu had converted to Christianity and brought their domains with them — most notably Ōmura Sumitada (the first Christian daimyo, baptized 1563) and Ōtomo Sōrin, who at his peak controlled most of central Kyushu and treated Christianity as the official religion of his domain.
The southern port city of Nagasaki (nah-gah-SAH-kee) was effectively a Christian city by the 1580s, with thirty churches, a Jesuit seminary, and a cathedral.
Estimates of the Christian population in Japan at the 1614 expulsion edict range from 300,000 to 500,000 — perhaps 2% of the country's roughly 25 million people, concentrated heavily in Kyushu.
The Spanish and Portuguese behind the missionaries also brought trade.

The Portuguese Black Ship (kurofune, koo-roh-FOO-neh — the same word later applied to Perry's vessels in 1853, and a useful label for "alarming foreign ship" in general) arrived at Nagasaki annually, carrying Chinese silk that the Ming dynasty had banned from being sold directly to Japan, plus European weapons, clocks, and curiosities.
The trade was lucrative for the Portuguese, the Christian daimyo, and the central government — when there was one to participate.
This was the situation Hideyoshi inherited in 1582.
Initially he tolerated the missionaries; in 1587, abruptly and without warning, he issued the Bateren Tsuihōrei ("Edict of Expulsion of Padres") ordering all Jesuits out of Japan.
The edict was not enforced — Hideyoshi needed Portuguese trade for his Korean campaigns, and the Jesuits stayed — but it signaled that the political weather was changing.
The change accelerated under the Tokugawa.
Ieyasu's reasons for ultimately suppressing Christianity were several, and worth distinguishing from the simplified version that emphasizes only religious intolerance.
First, theological.
Christianity made exclusive claims that conflicted with the Buddhist–Shinto–Confucian synthesis underpinning the Tokugawa social order.

Christian doctrine held that Japanese ancestors were in hell because they had not been baptized, that the emperor's sun-goddess descent was false, and that loyalty to God superseded loyalty to the shogun.
This was not a religious tradition the shogunate could simply incorporate the way it incorporated Buddhist sects.
Second, political.
The Christian daimyo in Kyushu were a coordinated subgroup with foreign backers.
Their loyalty to the Tokugawa was conditional on the Tokugawa tolerating their faith.
If push came to shove, where would they ultimately stand?
The shogunate could not afford to find out.
Third, geopolitical.
By the early seventeenth century, news had filtered back to Japan about what European powers had done in the Philippines (Spanish conquest beginning 1565) and parts of Asia.
The Spanish friar Bernardino de Avila Girón wrote candidly in his Japanese-language sermons that the missionaries were the advance guard of conquest.
Several Spanish friars were said to have boasted to Japanese audiences that the king of Spain would invade Japan if the Japanese resisted Christianity.
Whether or not these threats were real, the shogunate took them seriously.
Fourth, commercial.
As long as Portuguese trade was indispensable, the shogunate had to tolerate Portuguese missionaries.

By the early seventeenth century, the Dutch had arrived (the Dutch ship Liefde wrecked on the Kyushu coast in 1600, with the English navigator William Adams aboard — Adams became Ieyasu's adviser on Western affairs and lived out his life in Japan).
The Dutch were Protestants, had no missionary interest in Japan, and were happy to trade silk and silver without trying to convert anyone.
They offered an alternative to the Portuguese arrangement, and the shogunate eventually took it.
In 1614, Ieyasu issued the Christian Expulsion Edict, banning the practice of Christianity, expelling all foreign missionaries, and confiscating Christian properties.
The 1614 edict was followed by a series of intensifications under Hidetada and Iemitsu.
By the 1620s, the persecution had reached the level of systematic atrocity.

Christians who refused to renounce their faith were tortured by methods specifically chosen to maximize prolonged agony — suspension upside-down over a pit of excrement, scalding with boiling water from the Unzen sulfur springs, slow crucifixion.

Estimates vary widely, but somewhere between 5,000 and 6,000 Japanese Christians were executed for their faith between 1614 and the 1640s, in addition to perhaps tens of thousands killed in associated military operations.
The Catholic Church has formally recognized 188 Japanese martyrs from this period, with hundreds more under consideration.
The shogunate also developed the fumi-e (FOO-mee EH, "trampling picture") test — bronze plaques bearing images of Christ or the Virgin Mary, which suspected Christians were forced to step on.
Refusal meant arrest, torture, and likely execution.
The fumi-e test was administered annually at Nagasaki to the entire population well into the eighteenth century, and continued in attenuated form until the 1850s.
The ultimate purge was triggered by the Shimabara Rebellion of 1637–38, the largest armed revolt of the Edo period.

The setting was the Shimabara Peninsula (shee-mah-BAH-rah) and the Amakusa Islands (ah-mah-KOO-sah) on western Kyushu — historically Christian regions where forced apostasy and crushing taxation by local daimyo had produced a desperate population.
In late 1637, peasants and rōnin (masterless samurai) led by a charismatic seventeen-year-old named Amakusa Shirō (ah-mah-KOO-sah SHEE-roh) rose in rebellion.
The rebels were heavily Christian — many bore Christian banners, called themselves Christian names, and reportedly believed that Shirō was a returning savior who would lead them to victory.
They captured the abandoned Hara Castle on the southeastern Shimabara coast and fortified it.

The shogunate dispatched an army of over 100,000 troops drawn from neighboring daimyo, reinforced by Dutch warship cannons (the Dutch at Hirado bombarded Hara from the sea in support of the besieging army — buying the Dutch credit with the shogunate that would prove valuable when Catholic-Protestant distinctions were being made).
The siege of Hara Castle lasted from December 1637 to April 1638.
When the castle finally fell on April 15, 1638, the besiegers killed almost the entire population — an estimated 37,000 rebels, plus their families.
Shirō was beheaded and his head displayed at Nagasaki as a warning.
The Shimabara region was depopulated and resettled with reliable Buddhist immigrants.
The Shimabara Rebellion convinced the shogunate that residual Christianity was an existential threat, and that the Portuguese in Japan were a permanent vector for it.
Iemitsu acted decisively.
In 1639, the Portuguese were expelled from Japan, completing the closure that had been building for a generation.

To make the point unmistakable, when a Portuguese embassy from Macau arrived at Nagasaki in 1640 to negotiate reopening trade, sixty-one of the seventy delegation members were beheaded on arrival; the surviving thirteen were sent back to Macau with their colleagues' heads to deliver the message that there would be no more discussion.
The shogunate also issued the comprehensive Sakoku edicts of 1635 (banning Japanese travel abroad) and 1639 (banning Portuguese entry), formalizing the closure as a permanent policy.
For the next 214 years, Japan was effectively sealed.
"Effectively sealed" is doing some work in that sentence, because sakoku was never absolute.

There were four authorized channels of foreign contact, sometimes called the four mouths (yotsu no kuchi, YOH-tsoo NOH KOO-chee): The Nagasaki mouth — the most famous, controlled directly by the shogunate.
After 1641, all European trade was confined to a single Dutch trading station on the artificial fan-shaped island of Dejima (DEH-jee-mah, literally "exit island") in Nagasaki harbor.
Dejima was a tiny artificial island connected to the mainland by a single guarded bridge.
About twenty Dutch employees lived there at any given time, in a compound roughly the size of a city block.

They were forbidden to enter Nagasaki without permission, prohibited from practicing Christianity in any visible form (including burials — Dutch employees who died on Dejima were dropped at sea), and required to participate in elaborate annual rituals demonstrating subordination to the shogun.
They were allowed to import Chinese silk, European clocks and instruments, books on certain subjects, and they were allowed to export Japanese silver and copper.
Dejima operated continuously from 1641 to 1858, the longest-running European trading post in Asia.

Chinese merchants also had a designated quarter at Nagasaki, somewhat less constrained than the Dutch, and the volume of Chinese trade was actually considerably larger than Dutch trade through most of the period.
The Tsushima mouth — the Tsushima domain in the Korea Strait managed all Japanese-Korean diplomacy and trade through a Japanese trading post at Busan on the Korean coast.
After Hideyoshi's catastrophic Korean invasions (Chapter 1), the Tokugawa restored relations with Joseon Korea and maintained periodic exchanges of envoys.

Twelve Korean diplomatic missions to Edo took place between 1607 and 1811, each one a major political and cultural event in Japan, with the Korean delegations of several hundred people processing along the Tōkaidō to Edo and being received by the shogun in elaborate ceremony.
Trade through Tsushima was substantial — Korean ginseng, Chinese silk routed through Korea, and various luxury goods flowed in; Japanese silver, copper, and lacquerware flowed out.

The Satsuma mouth — the Satsuma domain in southern Kyushu had invaded the Ryukyu Kingdom (modern Okinawa) in 1609 and thereafter controlled an indirect channel of trade with China through Ryukyuan tributary missions to Beijing.

The Ryukyuan king was technically a Chinese tributary and technically a Satsuma vassal — a useful ambiguity that allowed Japanese trade with Ming and then Qing China to continue under Ryukyuan cover throughout the sakoku period.

The Matsumae mouth — the Matsumae domain at the southern tip of Hokkaido (then called Ezo, EH-zoh) managed trade with the indigenous Ainu (EYE-noo, the Jōmon-descended people of Hokkaido — Ancient Japan Ch 1 and Ch 8) and indirectly with the Russians who began appearing in Hokkaido waters in the eighteenth century.
The Ainu trade was small in volume but politically sensitive, especially after Russian expansion brought European powers to Japan's northern frontier.
The four mouths together represented less than 1% of the volume of foreign trade Japan had conducted in the early seventeenth century.
The closure was not a fiction.
Foreign goods became expensive luxuries, foreign news arrived in fragments, foreign techniques (especially in medicine and military technology) fell behind.
By the early nineteenth century, the gap between Japanese and Western military technology had grown so large that it could no longer be denied — but that crisis is for Chapter 8.
Cross-civ check: sakoku is sometimes presented as a uniquely Japanese eccentricity, but it was actually a recognizable variant of a broader early-modern East Asian pattern.

Ming China had operated under similar restrictions through much of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries — the famous haijin ("sea ban") prohibited private foreign trade, restricted maritime movement, and channeled all foreign relations through the tributary system.

Joseon Korea maintained an even stricter closure, conducting nearly all foreign relations through the Tsushima channel and maintaining only token contact with the Qing Dynasty — earning Korea the European nickname "the Hermit Kingdom." The Tokugawa system was actually more open than the Korean equivalent.
Within the broader pattern, what made Japan distinctive was the duration (over two centuries), the systematic enforcement, and the particular fixation on Christianity as the existential threat.

The closest religious-suppression parallel is the Spanish Inquisition's persecution of crypto-Jews and crypto-Muslims — same period, comparable methodology of forced apostasy and ritual humiliation tests, but conducted in the opposite direction (Christian state suppressing non-Christian heresies, vs. non-Christian state suppressing Christianity).
The other thing to note about sakoku is that it was not a passive choice.

It was an active policy that required continuous administrative effort to maintain — coastal patrols, the fumi-e test, the temple registration system that screened for crypto-Christians (Chapter 2), the Dejima isolation, the periodic interrogations of Dutch ship arrivals about world events.
The shogunate spent considerable resources to keep Japan closed.
They thought it was worth it.
The chapter that follows shows what the closed country produced.

chapters.title: Genroku Culture
sentences: If you had to pick one fifteen-year stretch as the moment when Edo Japan's culture became something distinctively Japanese and distinctively new, it would be the Genroku era (gen-ROH-koo), the imperial era name covering 1688 to 1704.

This is the period of Matsuo Bashō's haiku, Ihara Saikaku's novels, Chikamatsu Monzaemon's puppet plays, the early masterpieces of Kabuki, the explosion of single-sheet ukiyo-e woodblock prints, and the founding of the Osaka Rice Exchange — the world's first organized commodity futures market, eighty years before the Chicago Board of Trade would be founded in the United States.

The shogunate during these fifteen years was the eccentric Tokugawa Tsunayoshi (toh-koo-GAH-wah tsoo-nah-YOH-shee), the so-called Dog Shogun, whose reputation has fluctuated wildly over the centuries (mocked by his contemporaries, recovered slightly by modern revisionists).
What is not in doubt is that during his reign, Japanese popular culture took on the form it would hold until Perry's arrival.
This chapter is about the culture, not the politics — though the politics produced the conditions that made the culture possible.
By 1688, Edo had been the de facto capital for eighty-five years.
The sankin-kōtai system (Chapter 2) had drawn the daimyo aristocracy into permanent residence, and the city had grown to roughly a million people.
The peace had held; merchants had accumulated wealth; the technologies of urban life (water supply, fire-control, paved streets, postal services, lending libraries) had been built out.

The two other great cities — Kyoto, the ancient imperial capital and the center of refined high culture, and Osaka, the merchant capital and commercial heart of the country — had grown to several hundred thousand each.

By 1700, Japan was probably the most urbanized country in the world: roughly 10–12% of the population lived in cities of 10,000 or more, a higher proportion than any European country at the time except the Dutch Republic.
This urbanization produced a new kind of audience.

The merchant and artisan classes (the chōnin, choh-NIN, "townspeople," covering the bottom two classes of the official four-tier order — Chapter 2) had money, leisure, literacy, and an appetite for cultural products that the older Buddhist–aristocratic culture did not satisfy.
They wanted entertainment, romance, spectacle, satire, gossip, and beauty.
The Genroku culture is what emerged when a generation of Japanese artists, writers, and entrepreneurs figured out how to give them what they wanted at scale.
The aesthetic that organized this culture had a name: Ukiyo (oo-kee-YOH), the floating world.
The term itself has a Buddhist origin — ukiyo in older usage meant "the sad world" of human suffering, the world the Buddhist seeker tried to transcend.

By the late seventeenth century, the homophone ukiyo (written with different characters) had been repurposed to mean "the floating world" — the world of pleasure, transient beauty, fashion, sensual delight, and aesthetic refinement.
The shift from "sad world" to "floating world" through pure pun is the kind of thing the period did constantly, and it captured the new sensibility perfectly.

Life is short, the merchant-poet Asai Ryōi wrote in his 1666 Tales of the Floating World, so we should give ourselves to enjoying every moment of it: living for the moment, gazing at the moon, the snow, the cherry blossoms, the maple leaves, drinking sake, singing songs, drifting along the river of pleasure like a gourd carried by the current — and not letting the misery of life trouble us.
This was the antithesis of the samurai bushido ethos.
It was also, very deliberately, the cultural alternative the chōnin built for themselves.
The floating world had physical addresses.
The most famous was the Yoshiwara (yoh-shee-WAH-rah) pleasure quarter, north of central Edo.

After the Great Meireki Fire of 1657 destroyed most of the city (the worst urban disaster of the entire Edo period — somewhere around 100,000 people killed in three days, with roughly two-thirds of Edo burned to the ground), the shogunate took the opportunity to relocate Yoshiwara from its central location to a more peripheral site, where it grew into a walled and moated entertainment district housing several thousand licensed prostitutes, hundreds of teahouses, restaurants, theaters, and an entire support industry.

Yoshiwara had its own ranks of courtesans (the highest-ranked, the tayū, were closer to celebrity entertainers than sex workers — they were trained in poetry, calligraphy, music, dance, the tea ceremony, and could refuse clients they did not like).
It had its own dialect, its own etiquette, its own ceremonial calendar of seasonal events.
