The solution was to stay in the Otuken heartland — that is, in the Khangai-Orkhon region of central Mongolia — and to take what was needed from China through trade and tribute without letting the Türk court itself be drawn south.
The argument was not new (Tonyukuk's earlier inscription had made a similar case) but Bilge's version is the most articulate.

It is also notable for being the earliest surviving first-person voice from any steppe ruler — the only direct testimony, in their own language, of how the steppe leadership of any pre-modern era thought about its political situation.
Everything we know about Modu, Attila, Bumin, and Istemi comes from second- or third-hand accounts written by people from the settled civilizations they fought.
Bilge alone speaks for himself.
Bilge died in 734, poisoned by his own minister Buyruq Chor (BOO-yook CHOR).

Sources vary on the motive (palace politics, personal grievance, possibly external Tang intrigue) but agree on the manner: a slow poison administered over several days, with Bilge living long enough to identify his murderer and have Buyruq Chor and his entire clan exterminated before he himself expired.
Bilge's death deprived the Second Khaganate of its most stable leader.
The successors were a series of weak khagans who fought each other for the throne and could not maintain the political unity Bilge had built.
By the late 730s the Türk state was fracturing again.
By 742 the subject peoples — Uyghurs, Karluks, Basmyls — were in open revolt.
By 744 the dynasty was finished.
The end is the subject of the next chapter.

Cross-civ check: the Second Türk Khaganate (682-744) overlaps almost exactly with the great Islamic conquests under the Umayyad Caliphate (Islamic Golden Age Ch 4) and the early Abbasid Revolution (Islamic Golden Age Ch 6).

The Umayyads conquered Sogdiana in 705-715 (effectively closing the Western Türk legacy in Central Asia, even though the Türks had not held that territory directly since the 660s), conquered the Visigothic kingdom of Spain in 711, and reached the gates of France at Tours in 732 — the same year Bilge erected the Kul Tigin Inscription.
The Tang Empire was at its cultural peak under Emperor Xuanzong (Tang-Song China TL) but was approaching the fiscal and military crisis that would explode in the An Lushan Rebellion in 755.
The Byzantine Empire under Leo III was fighting off the second great Arab siege of Constantinople (717-718) and recovering.
In Anglo-Saxon England, Bede was writing his Ecclesiastical History of the English People (731).
The eighth century is one of the moments when the Eurasian system shifted decisively, and the Türks were participants in the shift right up until the moment they collapsed.

chapters.title: The Uyghur Take-Over and the Turkic Diaspora
sentences: In 744 a Türk khagan was killed in his own camp by one of his subjects, the imperial title passed to a different dynasty, and the Türk state ceased to exist.
That was the political end.
The cultural and ethnic consequences took several centuries to play out — and they reshaped most of Eurasia.
This chapter is about what happened after the Türks.

Where the displaced Türk-speaking peoples went, what empires they built, and how the political ethnonym "Türk" — which in 552 had been the name of one Mongolian clan — eventually became the self-identification of two hundred million people across a continent.

It is also about the four major successor traditions: the Uyghurs in Mongolia, the Karluks in Central Asia, the Khazars and Pechenegs and Bulgars in eastern Europe, and the Seljuks-then-Ottomans in the Middle East.
Each one is its own story, but they all begin in the same place: the Türk collapse of 744.
The collapse itself was political, not military.
By the early 740s the Second Khaganate was in chronic succession crisis (Chapter 7).
After Bilge's poisoning in 734, the throne had passed through three weak khagans in eight years, each one less able to hold the empire together.
The subject peoples — the Uyghurs in northern Mongolia, the Karluks in the Tian Shan, the Basmyls in the Altai — were growing in strength and becoming impatient with Ashina rule.
In 742 the three subject groups formed a coalition and revolted.
The reigning Türk khagan Ozmish (OZ-mish) was killed in battle.

His successor Bomei Qaghan survived for two more years before being killed in 744 by the Uyghur leader Kutluk Bilge (KOOT-look BIL-geh, no relation to the earlier Bilge Kagan despite the shared name).
The Uyghur leader took the imperial title, declared the founding of a new dynasty, and the Ashina line — which had ruled the steppe for almost two centuries — simply vanished from history.
There is no record of Ashina survivors continuing to claim the throne.
The dynasty that had named the Turkic peoples was extinguished.
The Uyghur Khaganate (744-840) succeeded the Türks as the dominant power on the Mongolian steppe and ruled it for almost a century.
The Uyghurs were Türk-speakers themselves — closely related linguistically and culturally to the Türks they had overthrown — but with several important differences in political style.

First, the Uyghurs converted to Manichaeism in 762, after their khagan Bögü Qaghan (BERG-oo) was introduced to the religion by Sogdian missionaries during a visit to the Tang capital at Luoyang (which the Uyghurs were occupying after rescuing the Tang from the An Lushan Rebellion).

Manichaeism (a syncretic Persian religion founded by the third-century prophet Mani, combining Zoroastrian, Christian, and Buddhist elements into a dualistic system focused on the cosmic struggle between light and darkness) was a strange choice for a steppe empire — neither Tonyukuk nor Bilge would have approved.
The Uyghurs were the only steppe empire in history to adopt Manichaeism as a state religion.

The conversion gave them a distinctive cultural identity and tied them more closely to the Sogdian commercial network, but it also distanced them from the broader Türk-speaking world that remained committed to Tengri sky worship.
Second, the Uyghurs built a city.

Their capital, Karabalghasun (KAR-ah-bahl-GAH-soon, in the Orkhon Valley near the future site of Genghis Khan's Karakorum), was a true urban center with permanent buildings, defensive walls, and a Manichaean temple complex.
This was a sharp break from Türk practice, which had kept the khagan's court mobile and rejected city-building as a Sinicizing trap.

The Uyghurs were essentially demonstrating that everything Tonyukuk had warned against — settlement, religious conversion, integration with sedentary culture — could in fact be done without immediate political collapse. (Long-term collapse was another matter.) Third, the Uyghurs rescued the Tang Dynasty during the An Lushan Rebellion of 755-763.

The Tang court, on the verge of being overthrown by the rebel general An Lushan (himself half-Sogdian and half-Türk, born of mixed parentage on the old Western Türk frontier), called on Uyghur cavalry to retake the lost Tang capitals at Chang'an and Luoyang.
The Uyghurs delivered, restored Tang authority, and in exchange extracted enormous annual silk subsidies and effective parity-of-status with the Tang throughout the late eighth century.
The relationship was enormously profitable for the Uyghurs but also entangling: every Tang internal crisis became an Uyghur problem.

The Uyghur Khaganate ended in 840, when the Yenisei Kyrgyz (the Türk-speaking forest people of the upper Yenisei basin in southern Siberia, who had been Türk subjects since Muqan's reign in the 560s) descended on the Mongolian steppe and destroyed Karabalghasun.
The Uyghurs scattered.
Some moved south into the Tarim Basin, where they founded the Kingdom of Qocho at Turfan and gradually converted from Manichaeism to Buddhism.
Others moved further south into the Tang frontier zones.

The Uyghur language and Uyghur cultural identity persisted; the modern Uyghur people of Xinjiang trace their descent and their name to this dispersed Uyghur population, though with substantial admixture from later Türk and other arrivals.
The Karluks (KAR-luks) had been one of the three subject peoples in the 742 revolt, alongside the Uyghurs and Basmyls.
After the Türk collapse they migrated southwest, settling in the Ili River valley of modern Kazakhstan and eventually pushing into Transoxiana.
They are one of the great underrated peoples of pre-modern history: a small Türk confederation that determined, through one battlefield decision in 751, the religious future of Central Asia.
The decision was at the Battle of Talas in July 751.
The Battle of Talas was a confrontation between two empires that should have known better than to fight each other so far from home.
The Tang Empire was projecting power into Central Asia from the east through its Anxi Protectorate.

The Abbasid Caliphate (Islamic Golden Age Ch 6) — which had just overthrown the Umayyad dynasty in 750 and was at the start of its great cultural and territorial expansion — was projecting power into Central Asia from the west through Khurasan.
Both empires were claiming overlapping influence in the Sogdian oases.
In 750-751 a series of local disputes escalated into open war, and the two armies met at the Talas River in modern Kyrgyzstan.
The Tang army was commanded by the Korean-born Tang general Gao Xianzhi (GOW shyen-JR), a competent commander who had already won several Central Asian campaigns.
He fielded perhaps 30,000 Tang troops plus around 20,000 Karluk auxiliary cavalry — the latter being former Türk subjects who had recently been absorbed into the Tang protectorate system.
The Abbasid army under the general Ziyad ibn Salih had perhaps 40,000 Arab and Persian troops.
The battle was indecisive for the first four days.
On the fifth day, the Karluks defected from the Tang side to the Abbasid side, attacking Gao Xianzhi's rear while the Abbasid main force pressed his front.
The Tang army was shattered.
Gao Xianzhi escaped with a few thousand survivors.
Tang power in Central Asia never recovered.
The consequences of the Karluk defection were enormous.

With the Tang army destroyed and Tang frontier governance broken (and the An Lushan Rebellion just four years away from completing the Tang collapse in Central Asia), the Sogdian oases passed under Abbasid Arab control for good.

Sogdiana, Bukhara, Samarkand, Khwarezm, Ferghana — every one of them began the long conversion to Islam that would, over the next several centuries, transform Central Asia from a Sogdian-Iranian-Buddhist-Zoroastrian-Manichaean cultural mosaic into a uniformly Muslim region.
The Karluks themselves converted to Islam in the tenth century and founded the Karakhanid Khanate (840-1212), the first Türk-speaking Muslim dynasty.
Every later Türk-speaking Islamic state — Seljuk, Khwarezmian, Ottoman — descended in some sense from the religious watershed at Talas.
The single decision of one Türk-descended people on one battlefield in 751 effectively determined that Central Asia would be Muslim rather than Buddhist or Christian or anything else.
The Karluks may not have understood the full implications, but their defection was one of the more consequential acts in pre-modern history.
Meanwhile, on the western steppe, other Türk-speaking peoples were building empires of their own.
The Khazar Khaganate (~650-969) had broken away from the Western Türks in the seventh century and established an independent state on the lower Volga, the Caucasus, and the Pontic steppe.

The Khazars are one of the great oddities of medieval history: a Türk-speaking ruling class governing a multi-ethnic, multi-religious population (Slavic, Iranian, Greek, and others) that controlled the northern Silk Road and the Volga trade route to the Vikings (Viking Age Ch 5).
Around 740, the Khazar royal court converted to Judaism — making the Khazars the only Jewish-ruling state in history outside ancient Israel.

The conversion was almost certainly a strategic choice: the Khazars sat between the Christian Byzantine Empire and the Muslim Abbasid Caliphate and converting to either would have been a political surrender to one side.
Judaism gave them a third option that committed them to neither great power.

The Khazars blocked Arab northward expansion through the Caucasus for two centuries until the Rus prince Sviatoslav destroyed their state in 969 (the Rus, the proto-Russian Viking-descended state in Kiev, are covered in Viking Age Ch 5).
The Bulgars were another Türk-speaking people who had broken off from the Western Türk system.
Under the leader Asparuh they crossed the Danube in 680 and founded the First Bulgarian Empire in what is now Bulgaria, conquering and ruling a much larger Slavic-speaking population.

Over the next several centuries the Bulgar ruling class was gradually Slavicized — they converted to Orthodox Christianity around 864, switched to a Slavic written language, and lost their Türk identity entirely.

The modern Bulgarians are predominantly Slavic-speaking and only a faint Türk political ancestry remains in the country's name. (A separate group, the Volga Bulgars, settled on the middle Volga and converted to Islam in 922; they were eventually absorbed into the Mongol successor states and became part of the ancestry of the modern Tatars of Russia.) The Pechenegs dominated the Pontic steppe (the grasslands north of the Black Sea) from the ninth to the eleventh centuries, repeatedly defeating Byzantine and Rus armies before being absorbed by the Cumans (another Türk-speaking nomadic confederation) in the 1100s.
The Cumans in turn were destroyed by the Mongol invasion of the 1230s (Mongol Empire Ch 5), with surviving Cuman populations fleeing into Hungary.
Hungarian noble families today still preserve a distinct Cuman identity and the political vocabulary of the Hungarian state retains some Cuman-derived terms.
The biggest downstream consequence of the Türk collapse, however, came three hundred years later in Iran and Anatolia.
The Seljuks (SEL-jooks) were a Türk-speaking clan from the Aral Sea region who converted to Sunni Islam in the late tenth century.

Under their leader Tughril Beg they migrated south into Iran in the 1030s, defeated the Persianate Ghaznavid dynasty at the Battle of Dandanaqan in 1040, and conquered Baghdad in 1055 (where they took the title of "Sultan" from the Abbasid Caliphate, which had become a ceremonial figurehead).

The Seljuk Empire became the dominant Sunni Muslim power of the eleventh century — the empire that confronted the First Crusade, that sponsored the great theologian al-Ghazali, that built the most beautiful mosques and madrasas of medieval Iran (Islamic Golden Age Ch 8 covers the Seljuk era from the Persian side).
The Seljuks' most famous act was the Battle of Manzikert in 1071, where Sultan Alp Arslan defeated and captured the Byzantine Emperor Romanos IV in eastern Anatolia (Byzantine Empire Ch 9).
The defeat broke Byzantine control of central Anatolia and opened the region to Türk settlement.

Within a generation, hundreds of thousands of Türk-speaking nomads had migrated into the Anatolian highlands, founded a series of competing Seljuk emirates, and begun the slow process of converting Anatolia from Greek-speaking Christianity to Türk-speaking Islam.

The cultural transformation of Anatolia (which had been a Greek-speaking Christian region for over a thousand years) into Türkiye (a Türk-speaking Muslim region) is one of the most dramatic ethnic-linguistic shifts in medieval history.

The fragments of Seljuk Anatolia eventually consolidated into a successor state called the Sultanate of Rum (room, the Türk-Arabic word for "Rome," meaning the formerly-Roman territory they had taken from Byzantium).

Rum collapsed in the late thirteenth century under Mongol pressure, and from its fragments emerged the small frontier emirate of Osman I in northwestern Anatolia around 1299 — the founding of the Ottoman dynasty (Ottoman Empire Ch 1).

The Ottomans went on to take Constantinople in 1453, conquer the Mamluks of Egypt in 1517, besiege Vienna in 1529 and 1683, and rule a multi-continental empire from the Balkans to the Persian Gulf to North Africa until the dynasty was finally dissolved in 1922 (Ottoman Empire Ch 12 covers the dissolution).
They are the latest, longest-lasting, and most influential of all the post-Türk Türkic empires.
Their continuous self-identification as Türks runs back through the Seljuks to the Oghuz steppe confederations to the Western Türk subject peoples of the 700s to the Ashina founding in 552.
Pull back and look at the whole arc.
In 552, a single Mongolian clan called itself Türk.

In 2026, two hundred million people across six independent countries (Turkey, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan, Turkmenistan) plus large minority populations in Russia, Iran, China, and many other countries call themselves Türks of one variety or another.
The Turkic language family has more speakers than French, more speakers than German, more speakers than Italian.

Every one of them traces the political ethnonym back through some chain of inheritance — Karluk to Karakhanid to Khwarezmian, Oghuz to Seljuk to Ottoman to modern Turkish, Pecheneg to Cuman to Hungarian Cuman, Volga Bulgar to Tatar — to the Ashina founding in 552.
The Ashina dynasty itself was extinguished in 744.
The political institution they built lasted just under two centuries.
But the name they invented for themselves became the master ethnonym for one of the world's largest cultural-linguistic families.
It is one of the most successful brand-extensions in human history, and one of the strangest: the dynasty that named everyone is forgotten by almost everyone the name now belongs to.
The Türk legacy is also visible in the broader steppe political tradition that follows them.

The Mongol Empire (Mongol Empire Ch 2) is in many ways a continuation of the Türk template: the same dual-wing organization, the same decimal military system, the same Tengri-based legitimating ideology, the same khagan title, the same use of Sogdian-descended administrative practice (the Mongols inherited the Uyghur script, descended from the Sogdian alphabet via the Türk Old Turkic script, as their own writing system).

When Genghis Khan declared himself khagan in 1206, he was deliberately invoking a tradition that ran back through the Khitan Liao dynasty, through the Uyghurs, through the Türks, ultimately to Bumin in 552.

The modern Mongolian nation, the Russian Federation's Türk-speaking minorities, the Central Asian republics, the Republic of Turkey — all of them are downstream consequences of decisions taken in the Orkhon Valley fourteen centuries ago.
A pause before closing.
The Türks are an unusual entry in this app's roster because they are, in a sense, more important for what they started than for what they themselves accomplished.

Their direct political existence lasted about 190 years and never produced cities, written law codes, theological systems, or distinctive material culture beyond what they inherited from the Xiongnu and Sogdian traditions.
Their legacy is not the empire itself but the ethnonym, the language family, the political template, and the institutional practices that diffused outward across Eurasia after their collapse.
In this they resemble a few other historical pivot-points.
The Phoenicians (Phoenicia Ch 7) gave the alphabet to the Mediterranean and then disappeared.
The Sogdians (Chapter 3) ran the Silk Road for centuries and then lost their distinctive identity to Arabic-Islamic culture.
The Visigoths (Ancient Rome Ch 9) destroyed the Western Roman Empire and then assimilated into the Iberian peninsula they had conquered.
The Akkadians (Mesopotamia Ch 5) created the first empire in human history and then disappeared as a distinct people.
In each case the historical legacy is structural, not material — the Türks built the road that ran from the Ashina founding to the Ottoman Empire, and the road outlasted them.
That is the Türk story.

A small clan in the Altai, a he-wolf in a cave, a revolt against the Rouran in 552, a brother running west to crush the Hephthalites, an embassy to Constantinople, a fifty-year split, a Tang conquest, a Second Khaganate, a poisoned khagan, a name that became the name of two hundred million people.
The first political community in history that called itself Türk, and the seed of every Türk-speaking community since.
Cross-civ check: the post-Türk Turkic diaspora is one of the great population-and-language stories of pre-modern history.

By 1300 — five centuries after the Türk collapse — Türk-speakers had settled in a band across all of Eurasia: the Kazakhs and Kyrgyz on the Central Asian steppes, the Uzbeks and Turkmen in Transoxiana, the Uyghurs in the Tarim Basin, the Tatars on the Volga, the Cumans in Hungary, the Pechenegs absorbed into the Slavic populations of the lower Don and Dnieper, the Anatolian Türks building toward the Ottoman state.

Add the Mongols — who were Türk-adjacent rather than Türk-speaking but inherited the entire steppe political template from the Türks — and the post-Türk world covers most of the Eurasian continent from China to the Carpathians.
No other steppe people has had a comparable downstream impact.
The Türks were the seedbed.

chapters.title: The Sahel and Its Predecessors
sentences: The Mali Empire was the second of three great West African gold empires.
Before we get to Mali, we need to understand what came before — both the people and the land.
The land first.

The Sahel (sah-HEL, from the Arabic word for "shore" or "coast" — the shore of the Sahara, the way you might say the coast of the sea) is a band of semi-arid grassland that runs east-to-west across Africa, separating the Sahara desert to the north from the wetter savanna and forest to the south.

It is roughly 600 to 1,000 miles (1,000 to 1,600 km) wide, depending on where you draw the line, and it stretches for around 3,400 miles (5,500 km) from the Atlantic coast of Senegal to the Red Sea coast of Sudan.
In Mali's territory, the Sahel band runs through the central part of what is now the modern Republic of Mali — the country named, several centuries later, for the empire we are about to meet.
The Sahel sits at a structural pivot in African geography.
To the north is the Sahara, the largest hot desert on the planet, roughly the size of the contiguous United States, and almost entirely uninhabitable except along oases.

To the south is the savanna belt, with reliable summer rains, herds of cattle, and a diversity of farming peoples; further south still are the equatorial forests of West Africa, where the rains never stop, the tsetse fly kills horses and cattle, and a different set of human cultures developed.

The Sahel is the negotiation zone — too dry for the southern savanna agriculture but too wet for nomadic Saharan life, productive enough to support millet farming and cattle but vulnerable to the long droughts that periodically rearrange the population map.

Cutting across this Sahel band, like a strangely shaped highway, is the Niger River (NYE-jer — not to be confused with the modern country called Niger to the east, which takes its name from the river).
The Niger is the third-longest river in Africa, after the Nile and the Congo, and it has the most peculiar course of any major African river.
It rises in the highlands of modern Guinea, only about 150 miles from the Atlantic coast — and then, instead of running west to the sea like a normal river, it bends north into the Sahara.

It runs north for nearly a thousand miles, brushing the southern edge of the desert at Timbuktu, before turning sharply southeast at the Niger Bend, then curving south through modern Niger and Nigeria, and finally reaching the Atlantic Ocean at the Niger Delta after a 2,600-mile (4,200 km) journey.
The shape of that arc is the single most important geographic fact in this story.

The Niger pushes north into the Sahel and then comes back south, depositing silt along an inland flood plain called the Inner Niger Delta (a strange name for a feature that is nowhere near the actual sea-coast delta — but the Inner Delta has the same braided-channel, seasonal-flood structure as a coastal river mouth, except that it sits 1,500 miles inland in the middle of the Sahel).
The annual flood is enormous — millions of acres of seasonally flooded grassland — and it makes possible an unusually dense population in what would otherwise be marginal land.
Djenné (jen-NAY), Timbuktu (tim-BUCK-too), Gao (GOW, rhymes with "now"), and the slightly more inland city of Niani (NYAH-nee) all sit on or near this Niger arc.
Every great empire of the western Sahel — Ghana, Mali, Songhai — built its political center on the Niger.
The river also runs through the structural geography of the gold-and-salt trade, which is the economic bedrock of every Sahelian empire.

Gold came from south of the Sahel, from alluvial deposits in the headwaters of the Senegal and Niger rivers — the Bambuk (BAM-buck) and Bure (boo-REH) gold fields, both on small upper tributaries of the Niger and Senegal river systems.
Salt came from north of the Sahel, from dry lakebeds in the central Sahara — the great mining site of Taghaza (tag-HAH-zah), about 500 miles north of Timbuktu, was the most important.
Camel caravans linked the two economies.
The Sahelian empires were the middlemen, and the middleman position was extraordinarily lucrative.
This is where Mali sits.
Geography is not destiny, but in the Sahel the trade routes ran where they did because the river ran where it did, and the empires grew up where they did because that is where the trade routes ran.
A pause for caveats before we go further.
When this book says Mali was "the first" or "the largest" or "the wealthiest" of anything, those claims need the same skepticism as every other "first" claim in the project.

The medieval Sahel has a particularly thin documentary record — most of our written sources are Arabic-language outsiders writing about a region most of them had never visited, or oral epics transcribed centuries after the events they describe.
The archaeological record is improving rapidly but still patchy.
The internal records of Mali's administration, if any existed in writing, have not survived.
What we know is real, but it is filtered through more layers of distance than the equivalent claims about Roman or Chinese history.
There is also an unusual political layer to the historiography.

For a long stretch of the twentieth century, European scholarship on West Africa systematically minimized indigenous achievement, attributing every sign of complexity to outside influence — Egyptian, Phoenician, Arab, anything other than African.
Modern scholarship has pushed back hard, and the corrective is correct, but it sometimes overcorrects.

The popular claim that Mansa Musa was "the richest person in human history," for example, gets repeated because it punctures a stubborn racist myth — but it is, on its own terms, essentially unverifiable, since no medieval economy produced the kind of records that would let you compare wealth across centuries.
The story of Mali is impressive enough without inflated superlatives.
Now, the people who built the world Mali emerged from.

The Ghana Empire (GAH-nah — not to be confused with the modern country of Ghana, which is several hundred miles south of where the empire actually was, and which adopted the name in 1957 as a symbolic claim on West African heritage) was the first great Sahelian empire, flourishing from roughly the eighth century CE to the twelfth.
Its own people called it Wagadu (wah-GAH-doo); "Ghana" was originally a royal title meaning "warrior king" that outsiders took for the name of the place.
The empire was founded and run by the Soninke (so-NIN-keh), a Mande-speaking people whose modern descendants still live in the region.
Its capital was at Koumbi Saleh (KOOM-bee SAH-leh) in what is now southeastern Mauritania, and at its height it was one of the largest cities in West Africa.
Ghana's political model was the model Mali would later inherit and scale up: control the gold trade by controlling the markets where the gold was sold, not the mines themselves.

The actual gold deposits in Bambuk and Bure were worked by independent miners who jealously guarded their locations from any imperial center — a pattern that persisted through the Mali and Songhai periods as well.
The empires got rich by taxing the gold as it passed through their markets on its way north, and by controlling the import of the salt and trade goods coming the other direction.
Ghana levied a tax on every load of salt entering the empire and another tax on every load leaving for the south.

One eleventh-century Arab geographer, al-Bakri (al-BAH-kree, an Andalusian scholar from Cordoba writing in 1067), described Ghana's king holding court "adorned with necklaces of gold and silver" surrounded by horses with gold harness — the kind of self-presentation that Mansa Musa would push to a much higher level three centuries later.
By the time al-Bakri was writing, Ghana was already in decline.

The traditional account, repeated for a century in textbooks, is that the empire was sacked in 1076 by a wave of Berber Muslim invaders called the Almoravids (al-MOR-ah-vids — a militant Sunni movement from the western Sahara that conquered much of Morocco and Spain in the same period).
Modern historians have pulled back significantly from this version of the story.

The archaeological evidence at Koumbi Saleh does not show a violent destruction in the late eleventh century, and the textual evidence for an Almoravid sack of Ghana comes from sources written long after the fact and may have been inferred from the general fact of Almoravid military activity in the region rather than actual events.

The current scholarly reading is that Ghana declined more gradually, weakened by some combination of Almoravid pressure, ecological change as the Sahel dried out through the eleventh and twelfth centuries, internal political fragmentation, and the rise of competitor states.
There was no single dramatic ending.
What there was, by around 1200, was a power vacuum.
Into the vacuum stepped a series of smaller successor kingdoms.

The most important of these — and Mali's immediate antagonist — was the Sosso kingdom (SOSS-oh, sometimes written Susu) under King Sumanguru Kante (soo-mahn-GOO-roo KAHN-teh, sometimes written Sumaoro).
Sumanguru emerges from the historical record around 1200, ruling a kingdom centered on the city of Sosso in what is now southwestern Mali.
Within a generation he had absorbed most of the former Ghana territory and was pressing south into the Mandinka homeland.
Sumanguru appears in the historical record both as a real king attested in the Arabic chronicles and as the antagonist of the Sundiata epic.

The two versions agree on the basic facts — that he was a powerful king of Sosso who conquered the Mandinka — but the epic builds him into something larger: a sorcerer-king who could not be killed by ordinary weapons, whose seven-storied palace had walls of human skin, who derived his power from blood sacrifice and bound spirits.

The historical Sumanguru and the legendary Sumanguru are versions of the same person seen from different angles, and the fact that the Mandinka oral tradition still remembered him in such vivid terms eight centuries later tells us something about the depth of the trauma that founded the Mali Empire.
It is worth pausing on Sumanguru's religion, because it explains part of his role in the epic.

Sumanguru was almost certainly a practitioner of traditional Mande religion, with all the ritual apparatus of pre-Islamic Sahelian kingship — sacred regalia, blood offerings, spirit shrines, the dalilou (DAH-lee-loo, the secret knowledge that gives a king his power).
The Mandinka under Sundiata were also majority practitioners of traditional religion at this point; Mali would only Islamize gradually over the following centuries.
The framing of Sundiata as a Muslim hero defeating a pagan tyrant comes mostly from later Islamic redactors of the epic, particularly the Timbuktu chroniclers of the seventeenth century.

The original Sundiata story is a contest between two ritual specialists — one a sorcerer who has bound himself to dangerous spirits, one a young king who learns to outmatch him — within a shared traditional religious framework.
The Islamic gloss came later.
The Mandinka people themselves had been on the upper Niger for centuries when Sumanguru's pressure forced them to organize politically.
The Mandinka (mahn-DIN-kah, also written Malinke or Mandingo) are a Mande-speaking people of the upper Niger River valley.

The Mande language family — to which Mandinka, Bambara, Soninke, Susu, and several other related languages belong — is part of the broader Niger-Congo language phylum, which covers most of sub-Saharan Africa. (The Niger-Congo family is roughly comparable in scale to Indo-European: an enormous group of related languages that includes Yoruba, Igbo, Swahili, Zulu, and most of the languages of Bantu Africa, all derived from a common ancestor spoken somewhere in West Africa thousands of years ago.

Mande is one of its older branches.) The Mandinka homeland — called the Manden in Mande languages — sits in the savanna belt between the upper Niger and the upper Senegal rivers, a fertile zone of mixed farming and cattle herding with access to both the Bambuk gold fields and the Niger trade routes.

Mandinka social organization, then and now, was built around named patrilineal clans — Keita, Konde, Traore, Camara, Kone, Diakite, and others — each with specific inherited occupations and social roles.
Some clans were warriors and ruling lineages (the Keita were the royal clan, Sundiata's lineage).
Some were blacksmiths (the numu, who held both economic and ritual power because metallurgy was considered to handle dangerous spiritual energy).

Some were leatherworkers, some were potters, and some were the jeli (JEH-lee, called griots in French, hereditary musicians and oral historians who served as advisors and memory-keepers for the noble clans).

The clan system also included a complex set of joking-cousin relationships called sanankuya (sah-nahn-KOO-yah) — pairs of clans whose members were entitled to insult each other in formalized ways as a kind of structured conflict-resolution mechanism.
This whole system would eventually be codified by Sundiata in the Kurukan Fuga (Chapter 2).
Crucially, the Mandinka were not yet a unified state.

They were a network of small kingdoms, each ruled by a Keita prince or related noble lineage, all paying tribute to whoever the dominant regional power was — and that, in the early thirteenth century, was Sumanguru's Sosso.

The traditional account holds that Sumanguru had executed most of the senior Keita princes, leaving only Sundiata himself — a sickly child who could not walk until he was seven years old — as the surviving heir to the Keita line.

Whether or not the specifics are historical (the inability to walk is one of those classic epic-hero motifs that tends to drift into stories regardless of what actually happened), the structural situation is real: a fragmented Mandinka world under foreign domination, with one young prince in exile around whom resistance could organize.
This is the situation Sundiata stepped into in the 1230s.
A pause for cross-civilization context, because the Sahelian world of 1200 sits inside a much larger network than is usually appreciated.
When Sundiata was a child, the Mongol Empire (Mongol Empire Ch 1) was just beginning its conquests — Genghis Khan died in 1227, the same decade Sundiata's military career was beginning.
The Mongol invasions would shortly transform the Islamic world that Mali was about to integrate into, sacking Baghdad in 1258 (Islamic Golden Age Ch 10) and ending the Abbasid caliphate.

The Almohad Caliphate in Morocco — the Berber Sunni successor state to the Almoravids — was at its peak, controlling most of North Africa and Muslim Spain, and its trans-Saharan trade contacts with the Sahel were one of the channels through which Islam entered Mali.
The Holy Roman Empire in central Europe was at the height of its conflict with the papacy under Frederick II.

Song China (Tang-Song China) was the wealthiest and most technologically advanced civilization in the world, exporting porcelain and silk along Indian Ocean trade routes that did not yet quite reach West Africa but would within a century.
The Khmer Empire at Angkor was building its great temple complexes.

In the Americas, the Late Postclassic Maya were trading along their long coastal canoe routes (Maya Civilization Ch 8), the Inca state had not yet emerged, and the future site of the Aztec capital Tenochtitlan (Aztec Empire Ch 1) would not be founded for nearly a century.
Most of these civilizations did not know Mali existed.
Mali, similarly, did not know about most of them — though Mansa Musa's hajj (Chapter 4) would shortly change that, dramatically, for a stretch of the Mediterranean and Islamic worlds.

chapters.title: Sundiata and the Founding
sentences: In or around 1235 CE — the precise date is debated by historians, with the leading candidates ranging from 1234 to 1237 — a young Mandinka prince named Sundiata Keita (sun-DYAH-tah KAY-tah, sometimes written Sunjata or Mari Djata) led an alliance of Mandinka clans against the Sosso king Sumanguru and defeated him at a place called Kirina (kee-REE-nah).
The battle ended Sosso domination of the upper Niger.

Within a year, Sundiata had been proclaimed Mansa (MAHN-sah — the Mande word for emperor or king of kings, distinct from the more limited Faama for an ordinary king), and the political entity that would become the Mali Empire had begun.
Sundiata is one of those founding figures who hovers between history and myth, and the relationship between the two is unusually well-documented in his case.

The historical Sundiata is real — multiple Arabic sources from the fourteenth century forward refer to him as the founder of the Mali state, and the dates and basic outlines of his reign are not seriously disputed.

The legendary Sundiata, preserved by the jeli oral tradition for centuries before being transcribed in the twentieth, is a more elaborate figure: a sickly child who could not walk until he stood up for the first time at seven and pulled an iron rod into a bow; an exile who learned hunting and warfare in the kingdom of Mema; a chosen king prophesied by a hunchback hunter-diviner; a magical warrior who finally killed Sumanguru with an arrow tipped with a white rooster's spur, which broke the sorcerer-king's protective spells.

Modern historians treat the historicity of these specific details with the standard caveats that apply to all founding-king stories — almost every culture has them, almost every culture builds in similar archetypal motifs (the sickly heir, the prophesied destiny, the magical weapon), and the stories tend to converge on an idealized form regardless of what actually happened.

What is not in doubt is the basic political fact of a successful Mandinka revolt against Sosso domination, the consolidation of a multi-clan Mandinka state under a Keita prince, and the founding of an empire that would dominate the western Sahel for the next two centuries.
The line between the historical and the legendary Sundiata is probably best drawn at the level of structural narrative — the broad story is real, the specific scenes are mostly myth.
The Battle of Kirina itself probably took place near the modern village of Kirina in south-central Mali, on or near the Niger River.
The traditional date is 1235; the location has not been securely identified by archaeologists.

The traditional account has Sundiata commanding an alliance of Mandinka clans plus auxiliary contingents from the Wolof (WOH-loff, a people of the Senegal River valley), Tukulor (TOO-koo-lor, a people of the same region), and various smaller groups.
Sumanguru fielded a Sosso army with iron-armored infantry and a corps of court sorcerers whose ritual specialists were said to make him invulnerable.

The decisive moment, in the epic, is a duel between Sundiata's chief jeli Bala Faseke Kouyate (bah-LAH fah-SEH-keh KOO-yah-teh) and Sumanguru's court sorcerer, in which Bala Faseke gains the Sosso king's secret (a shoe-leather amulet, or a white rooster's spur, depending on the version) and passes it to Sundiata, who fires the magical arrow.
Sumanguru is wounded — not killed, in most versions, but driven into the wilderness where he simply vanishes from the story, sometimes turning into a stone — and the Sosso army breaks.
The historical mechanism was probably more conventional: a successful Mandinka cavalry charge against a Sosso line that was perhaps weakened by defections among Sumanguru's tributaries.
But the epic version is what was remembered, and the epic version is one of the great narrative achievements of African oral tradition.
The Kouyate clan, by the way, are still the official jeli to the Keita lineage today, eight centuries later.

Bala Faseke's descendants still recite the Sundiata epic in the same villages where their ancestor first chanted it, and modern Kouyate griots like the late Sotigui Kouyate (a Burkinabe actor who appeared in films by Peter Brook and Bernardo Bertolucci) carry the lineage into international visibility.
The continuity of the jeli profession across nearly thirty generations is one of the most remarkable facts of African cultural history.

The year after Kirina, in 1236 CE according to the traditional date, Sundiata convened an assembly at a place called Kurukan Fuga (KOO-roo-kahn FOO-gah), traditionally located on a clearing somewhere on the upper Niger plain.

The assembly included representatives of all the major Mandinka clans, plus the allied peoples whose support had been essential at Kirina, plus the leaders of the various tributary peoples who now found themselves part of the new empire.
What emerged from the assembly is one of the more striking political documents of the medieval world: an oral constitution that defined the structure, rights, and obligations of the Mali Empire.

The Kurukan Fuga, also called the Manden Charter, was never written down at the time it was promulgated — Mali in 1236 had no functional writing system for the Mandinka language, and Arabic literacy was confined to a small Muslim merchant elite.
Instead, the charter was preserved by the jeli, who memorized its provisions and recited them at official assemblies.
The version we have today was reconstructed in the late twentieth century by Malian and Guinean scholars working with multiple jeli lineages to assemble a composite text.

The reconstruction is necessarily approximate — different jeli traditions preserve different versions, and there is no way to verify what Sundiata's original 1236 promulgation actually contained — but the consistency across regional traditions is high enough that the broad outlines are probably authentic.
What does the charter say?

It is structured as a series of articles, traditionally numbered as 44 in the most common reconstruction, covering topics like: The organization of the empire into clans, with formal recognition of each clan's rights and inherited occupations.
The establishment of the joking-cousin (sanankuya) relationships as a structured mechanism for inter-clan conflict resolution.
Provisions for the protection of women, including a prohibition on certain forms of mistreatment and recognition of women's role in maintaining the family.

A declaration of certain forms of slavery as illegitimate (specifically, the enslavement of free-born members of the alliance — Mali continued to practice slavery of war captives and of certain caste groups, but the charter explicitly forbade enslaving fellow Mandinka).
Rights of refuge and asylum for visitors and displaced people.
Rules for the conduct of war, including protections for non-combatants.
Procedures for selecting successors and resolving succession disputes among the Keita lineage.
Modern advocates have, with some justice, called the Kurukan Fuga one of the world's earliest charters of human rights.
The claim should be carefully phrased — "human rights" is a modern category, and projecting it backward onto a thirteenth-century West African document risks anachronism.

But what the charter does is establish a structure of inter-group obligations within a multi-ethnic empire, a constitution-like text that constrains the exercise of imperial power according to mutually recognized rules.
That is an unusual achievement for any thirteenth-century state.

UNESCO recognized the charter on its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2009, formal acknowledgment that this is a document worth taking seriously on its own terms.
A cross-civilizational comparison helps frame the achievement.
Magna Carta — the charter that English barons forced King John to sign at Runnymede in June 1215 — was promulgated about twenty years before the Kurukan Fuga and was written down, not memorized.
Magna Carta was more limited in scope (a list of legal protections for the English nobility against royal arbitrariness) but more durable as a written instrument.
The two documents were produced by completely independent political traditions, addressing quite different kinds of problem, with no contact between their authors.
They sit in the same broad category of "thirteenth-century constitutional document" without being remotely the same text.
Both are worth knowing.

Sundiata also established a new capital, on a site called Niani on a tributary of the upper Niger River, in the heart of the Mandinka homeland in what is now southern Guinea or southwestern Mali (the exact location is one of the long-running puzzles of West African archaeology — see Chapter 8).
Niani served as Mali's capital for most of the next two and a half centuries, growing from a fortified hilltop village into a substantial trading and administrative city.

Ibn Battuta, who visited the capital in 1352 (more on him in Chapter 5), described a city of mud-brick houses arranged along the river bank, with the royal compound in the center surrounded by a wooden palisade.

The mansa held audiences in a large courtyard hung with silk curtains and decorated with ornate mats; he sat on a raised throne of ebony with elephant tusks at the corners and golden vessels arranged before him.
Court ceremony was elaborate — visitors approached the throne by crawling and pouring dust on their heads as a sign of submission, a custom Ibn Battuta found theatrically excessive.
The capital was not architecturally as imposing as Cairo or Damascus, but it was the political center of a state that controlled territory comparable in size to medieval France and Germany combined.
We do not know exactly how Mali was administered.
The bureaucratic and tax records, if any existed in writing, have not survived.

What we can reconstruct from the external sources is a system organized around three concentric rings: an inner core of Keita-ruled provinces in the Mandinka heartland, governed directly by the mansa's appointed officials; an intermediate ring of allied kingdoms (Wolof, Tukulor, Songhai, Soninke) ruled by their own kings under Mali suzerainty, paying tribute and providing military contingents but otherwise autonomous; and an outer ring of trading cities (Walata, Timbuktu, Gao) whose primarily Muslim merchant communities were left to govern themselves so long as the trade flowed and the taxes were paid.

This three-ring structure was flexible — provinces shifted between rings as central control grew or weakened — and it allowed Mali to accommodate enormous cultural and political diversity within a single imperial framework.

Sundiata himself ruled from roughly 1235 until his death in or around 1255 — the date is not certain, with sources placing it anywhere from 1255 to 1260, and the cause is similarly unclear (the epic offers multiple conflicting versions, including drowning in the Niger, an arrow during a parade, and natural death).

What is reasonably clear is that the empire he founded had stabilized by the time he died and that the succession passed to his son Mansa Uli (MAHN-sah OO-lee, also written Mansa Wali or Wali Keita) without major civil war.
The institution Sundiata created had a particularly successful structural feature: it was designed to absorb non-Mandinka peoples without requiring them to become Mandinka.

The Wolof of the Senegal valley, the Tukulor of the same region, the Soninke remnants of the old Ghana population, the Songhai of the Niger Bend, the Dogon of the Bandiagara escarpment, the Bozo fishermen of the Inner Niger Delta — all became subjects of the Mali Empire while keeping their languages, religions, social structures, and most of their internal political institutions.
This is unusual.

Most pre-modern empires either tried to assimilate their subject peoples (like Rome with its Latin-speaking provinces, or Han China with its policy of Han-Chinese cultural diffusion — Han Dynasty Ch 6) or kept them in a structurally inferior position (like the Achaemenid Persian Empire's tribute hierarchy).
Mali's three-ring system did neither.
It kept subjects autonomous and culturally distinct while extracting tribute and military service.
The model was sustainable for as long as the central power could enforce the tribute relationships — and unsustainable as soon as the center started to weaken (Chapter 6).
A pause for cross-civilizational comparison.
The decades around 1235 are unusually busy in world history.

While Sundiata was consolidating Mali, Genghis Khan had been dead for eight years and the Mongol Empire was being divided among his grandsons; Ögedei Khan would launch the western Mongol invasion of Russia and Eastern Europe in 1236, the same year Sundiata convened the Kurukan Fuga (Mongol Empire Ch 4).
The Sultanate of Delhi in northern India was at the height of its early Turkic phase under Iltutmish and his daughter Razia Sultana, the only female Muslim ruler in pre-modern South Asian history.
The Latin Empire of Constantinople — the bizarre Crusader state established in 1204 after the Fourth Crusade sacked the Byzantine capital — was nearing its collapse (Byzantine Empire Ch 9).
The Hojo regents were running Japan from Kamakura, having sidelined the imperial court (Shogunate Japan).
In the Americas, the Postclassic Maya city-states of the Yucatán were operating in a world without any of the great Classic-era cities, which had collapsed centuries earlier (Maya Civilization Ch 7).
The Andes were entering the Late Intermediate Period, with no single dominant power between the collapse of Wari and the rise of the Inca (Andean Kingdoms Ch 5).
Within the Islamic world specifically, the Abbasid Caliphate at Baghdad was about to be destroyed by the Mongols in 1258 — twenty-three years after Sundiata's victory at Kirina.
This timing matters for Mali.
The fall of Baghdad ended the institutional center of Sunni Islamic scholarship, and the diffusion of Islamic learning into peripheral regions accelerated as scholars relocated.
Mali would become one of the receivers of that diffusion over the next century — culminating in Mansa Musa's project to recruit North African and Andalusian scholars to staff Timbuktu (Chapter 4).

chapters.title: The Mansas Consolidate
sentences: Sundiata's death in the 1250s passed the throne to his son Mansa Uli, and over the next half-century a series of mansas — some sons, some nephews, occasionally a freed slave-soldier — consolidated and expanded the empire he had founded.

By the time Mansa Musa came to the throne in 1312, Mali controlled the entire trans-Saharan trade network from the Atlantic to the Niger Bend and was on the verge of becoming, briefly, one of the most internationally famous states in the world.
The half-century between Sundiata's death and Musa's accession is when the institutional infrastructure of the empire was built.

This chapter is about that infrastructure: the agricultural base, the military system, the institution of the jeli, and the early successors who held the empire together long enough for Mansa Musa to inherit something worth being famous for.
Start with the agriculture.
The empire ran on grain.

The Inner Niger Delta — that 15,000-square-mile (40,000 km²) flooded grassland that the Niger creates as it bends north into the Sahel — is the single most productive piece of farmland in the western Sahel, and it was the agricultural breadbasket of the Mali Empire.
The annual flood, fed by summer rains in the Guinea highlands, raises the river level by 15 to 20 feet (4–6 meters) and turns vast stretches of normally dry savanna into seasonal swamp.

Local farmers planted African rice (a domesticated species distinct from Asian rice — Oryza glaberrima, which had been independently domesticated in West Africa around 1500 BCE, more than three thousand years before Mali emerged) along the receding flood, taking advantage of the moisture without needing irrigation.
Other crops included pearl millet (the staple grain of the drier Sahel, drought-tolerant and high-yielding), sorghum, fonio (a small West African cereal grain), cowpeas, and groundnuts.
The Inner Delta also supported one of the densest fishing economies in West Africa.

The Bozo (BOH-zoh) and Somono (so-MOH-noh) peoples — specialized fisherfolk who lived in stilt villages along the river — caught huge quantities of catfish, perch, and tilapia, which they smoke-dried and traded inland to the agricultural communities.

Smoked fish from the Niger reached as far as the gold-mining regions hundreds of miles away, providing protein in a region that did not have year-round access to fresh fish or, in many places, to cattle.
This agricultural and fishing base supported a much denser population than the surrounding Sahel could otherwise have managed.

Estimates of total Mali Empire population are speculative — there are no surviving census records — but the archaeological evidence points to several hundred populated settlements in the Inner Delta alone, with total population in the empire as a whole probably running into the millions by the early fourteenth century.
This is a substantial state, comparable in population to the contemporary kingdoms of England or France.
It is not a thinly settled tribal confederation; it is an agricultural empire.
The military rested on cavalry, and cavalry rested on horses, and horses rested on geography.
This requires explaining, because the relationship between cavalry and West African geography is not obvious to most readers.
The horse is not a native African animal; horses were introduced to Africa from Eurasia, probably initially through Egypt and North Africa, and gradually spread south.

They thrive in temperate and arid environments — North Africa, the Sahara fringes, the Sahel — but they cannot survive in the equatorial forest belt of West Africa, because that zone is the home range of the tsetse fly (TSEH-tsee), a biting fly that transmits a parasitic disease called trypanosomiasis that is fatal to horses, cattle, and humans alike.
The southern boundary of the tsetse fly belt has shifted over time and remains the northern boundary of Africa's horse-using military zone.
Mali sat in the savanna belt north of the tsetse line, which meant Mali could field cavalry.
The forest peoples to the south could not, and were militarily disadvantaged in any conflict that involved open-country fighting.

A trained Mali warhorse, imported from North Africa across the Sahara, cost the equivalent of several enslaved people in trade — making cavalry an expensive aristocratic monopoly that only the central state and its top nobility could afford to maintain.

A typical Mali field army included a core of armored Mandinka heavy cavalry (perhaps a few thousand riders at full mobilization), supplemented by larger numbers of infantry recruited from the empire's peasant population, with auxiliary contingents of bowmen from the Bambuk forest and Wolof slingers from the Senegal valley.
The combination of fast-moving cavalry and integrated infantry was effective enough to handle most local resistance and to project force across a substantial territory.
It was not, however, equipped to handle gunpowder weapons — a limitation that would prove decisive when the Moroccan Saadians arrived in 1591 (Chapter 7).
The jeli were another piece of imperial infrastructure, and one of the more peculiar.

The jeli — usually called griots in French and English, from a Portuguese loanword — were a hereditary caste of musicians, oral historians, genealogists, and political advisors who served the Mandinka noble lineages.

Every noble family had its own associated jeli family, whose members were responsible for memorizing and reciting that family's genealogy, recording its deeds, advising on diplomacy, performing music at official ceremonies, and serving as ambassadors and negotiators in delicate situations where direct noble-to-noble communication was awkward.
The relationship was mutual and obligatory: nobles supported their jeli with food, gifts, and protection; jeli served their nobles with memory, music, and counsel.
The institution was not unique to Mali — versions of it existed across the Mande-speaking world and beyond — but Mali's imperial scale gave it a particularly elaborated form.

The most senior jeli at the imperial court (the Kouyate clan, hereditary jeli to the Keita) were powerful political figures, advisors to the mansa, masters of court protocol, and the official preservers of the dynasty's history.

Their position was institutionally protected; an attack on a jeli was treated as an attack on the noble house he served, and jeli were generally not subject to the violence of civil war or succession dispute.
This gave them an unusual structural role: they were the institutional memory of the state, and their continuity across regime changes preserved knowledge that might otherwise have been lost.
The fact that the Sundiata epic survived eight centuries of political upheaval — including the fall of the empire itself — is largely down to the jeli institution.
The epic was not preserved because some library kept the manuscript safe; there was no manuscript, and there was no library.

It was preserved because every generation of Kouyate jeli trained the next generation to recite it, with checks and corrections from rival jeli lineages that knew the same material, in a system of distributed redundancy that turned out to be more robust than any single physical text could have been.
Modern oral-tradition scholarship has used Mali as a case study for what large-scale institutional memorization can achieve.
The early successors of Sundiata are sketchily documented but worth a quick run-through, because they hold the line between Sundiata's founding and Mansa Musa's spectacular reign.

Mansa Uli (also called Wali Keita, ruled c. 1255–1270) was Sundiata's son and the first mansa to make the hajj (the Islamic pilgrimage to Mecca, an obligation for any Muslim with the means to undertake it).

Uli's pilgrimage, sometime in the 1260s, established the precedent that Mali's mansas would routinely make the hajj — a diplomatic and political act as much as a religious one, since the journey through Cairo and the Hejaz brought the mansa into contact with the rulers and scholarly classes of the entire eastern Mediterranean.
Uli is also credited with extending Mali's authority over Walata and the southern Sahara trade routes, completing the absorption of the former Ghana territory.
After Uli came two of his brothers, Mansa Wati and Mansa Khalifa, both reigning briefly.

Khalifa was apparently mentally unstable (a fourteenth-century Arabic source describes him shooting arrows at his own subjects, which sounds suspiciously like a hostile court rumor but is the only specific characterization we have) and was deposed within a few years.
The throne then went to Abu Bakr, a grandson of Sundiata through a daughter, whose reign is barely documented.
After Abu Bakr came Sakura — and Sakura is interesting.
Mansa Sakura (c. 1285–1300) was a freed slave-soldier, not a member of the Keita royal lineage, who seized the throne during a period of dynastic instability.
The fact that he could do this without overthrowing the dynasty's overall legitimacy tells us something important about the flexibility of Mali's political system.
A non-royal commander could become mansa under the right circumstances, and his reign would be considered legitimate by later historians even though it interrupted the Keita succession.

Sakura expanded the empire eastward toward Gao on the Niger Bend, consolidated central control over the trade routes, and made his own hajj — but he was killed by raiders during his return journey in 1300.
The throne reverted to the Keita lineage, eventually passing to Mansa Muhammad (Sundiata's grandson through another line) and then, around 1312, to Muhammad's brother — Mansa Musa.
There is one strange story attached to Mansa Muhammad's accession that deserves a paragraph, because Mansa Musa himself reportedly told it to his Cairo hosts in 1324.

According to the Egyptian historian al-Umari, Musa explained that his predecessor — usually identified as Muhammad, though al-Umari calls him "Abu Bakr the Second" — was a king "who could not believe that it was impossible to discover the limits of the surrounding ocean." This king assembled a fleet of 200 ships, equipped them for two years of travel, and sent them west into the Atlantic.
Only one ship returned.
Its captain reported that the others had been swept away by a great river in the middle of the ocean.
Undeterred, Musa's predecessor commissioned a second expedition of 2,000 ships, which he led personally — and never returned.
The throne then passed to Musa.
This story is preserved only in al-Umari's account, transmitted through Cairo gossip about something Musa supposedly said twelve years earlier, with no corroborating sources.
Modern historians treat it as essentially legendary.

Whether Mansa Musa actually told this story, whether his predecessor actually led an Atlantic expedition, whether any West African vessels ever crossed any portion of the Atlantic before the Portuguese arrived in the late fifteenth century — none of this is verifiable, and the practical naval engineering required is daunting.

The story does, however, reflect Mali's awareness of the Atlantic Ocean (the western edge of the empire reached the coast of modern Senegal) and the broader Sahelian fascination with what lay beyond the known world.
Treat it as a curiosity, not a documented historical event.
A pause for the broader picture.

By 1310, on the eve of Mansa Musa's accession, Mali was structurally complete: an agricultural breadbasket in the Inner Niger Delta, a heavy-cavalry military system, a hereditary jeli institution preserving imperial memory, an Islamic merchant elite running the trans-Saharan trade, a three-ring administrative structure flexible enough to accommodate enormous diversity, and a sequence of successful or at least functional mansas extending across three generations.
It was, by this point, the dominant political power in West Africa and one of the major trading states of the medieval world.
What it was not yet was internationally famous outside its immediate trade contacts.
Most of the Islamic world knew about Mali in the way you know about a major trading partner of a trading partner — secondhand, through merchants and travelers.
The European Mediterranean did not yet know Mali existed as a distinct political entity, though they knew that the gold flowing into North African markets was coming from somewhere south.
That was about to change.

chapters.title: Mansa Musa
sentences: In the spring of 1324, a caravan of around 60,000 people left Mali heading northeast across the Sahara toward Egypt and ultimately Mecca.
At its head rode Mansa Musa Keita (MAHN-sah MOO-sah KAY-tah, also written Kanga Musa), the tenth ruler of the Mali Empire.

The caravan included hundreds of attendants in matching brocade silk, twelve thousand slaves carrying gold ingots, a hundred camels each loaded with several hundred pounds of gold dust, the mansa's wife and her own attendants numbering in the hundreds, an escort of cavalry, scholars, jeli, doctors, and an indeterminate number of livestock to feed the whole procession.
It was the most spectacular hajj in the history of Islam, and the most consequential single political act of any sub-Saharan African ruler before the modern era.

By the time Musa returned to Mali in 1325, the wider Islamic world knew Mali existed, the Egyptian gold market had been temporarily wrecked by a flood of Mali bullion, the Mediterranean banking system was about to absorb a substantial new gold supply, and the European cartographers of the Mediterranean had a new African king to draw on their maps.
Within a generation, Mali would be the most internationally famous African state since pharaonic Egypt.
This chapter is about Mansa Musa: how he became mansa, what the hajj actually involved, why it had the economic effects it had, and what it bought him politically when he got home.

Mansa Musa came to the throne around 1312, succeeding his brother Muhammad — the same Muhammad who, according to the Atlantic-expedition story (Chapter 3), supposedly sailed west to find the edge of the ocean and never returned.

Whether or not the Atlantic story is true, what is certain is that Musa inherited the throne under irregular circumstances, with his predecessor either dead or vanished, and that he reigned for roughly twenty-five years (about 1312 to 1337) during which the empire reached its territorial and economic peak.
We know less about the internal workings of Musa's court than we would like.

The internal Malian sources — oral tradition preserved by jeli — focus heavily on Musa's piety, his patronage of Islamic scholarship, and his hajj, rather than on the day-to-day administration of the empire.
The external Arabic sources are richest precisely on the hajj and the Cairo stay, since that is where Egyptian and Syrian observers actually saw him.
We have less detailed information about the rest of his reign.

What we can say is that Musa expanded Mali's eastern frontier, securing control of the Niger Bend cities of Timbuktu and Gao (which had been under intermittent Mali suzerainty under his predecessors but were now firmly integrated into the empire), and he consolidated control of the trans-Saharan trade routes that linked the Sahel to North Africa.

The Mali Empire under Musa stretched from the Atlantic coast of modern Senegal to the Niger Bend, north into the southern Sahara, and south to the forest fringes — an area roughly comparable in size to Western Europe.
Musa was also a serious Muslim.

Earlier mansas had been Muslims — Sundiata himself was nominally Muslim, though the practice of Islam at his court coexisted with traditional Mandinka religion (Chapter 2) — but Musa was the first who appears to have been a deeply observant practitioner.
He prayed five times a day, observed the Ramadan fast, sponsored religious scholarship, and undertook the hajj as a personal religious obligation rather than as a primarily diplomatic act.
The hajj would also turn out to be the most consequential diplomatic act of the medieval West African state, but Musa did not undertake it for that reason.

The hajj caravan departed Niani sometime in 1324 (the precise month is not recorded) and traveled northeast across the Sahara, probably via the salt-mining oasis of Taghaza and the Berber commercial center of Sijilmasa (sih-jil-MAH-sah, in southeastern Morocco), then east along the North African coast to Cairo.
The journey took several months.

The route was the standard trans-Saharan caravan path, but the scale of Musa's caravan stretched the supply infrastructure to its limits — every oasis along the route had to feed and water 60,000 people and tens of thousands of livestock for several days, an enormous logistical demand on settlements normally serving caravans of a few hundred.
The numbers in the Arabic sources should be taken with caution.

"Sixty thousand attendants," "twelve thousand slaves," "a hundred camels each carrying three hundred pounds of gold" — these are the numbers that al-Umari and Ibn Khaldun give, but medieval Arabic chronicles routinely round up extravagantly when describing wealthy royal processions, and the round numbers (60,000, 12,000) are suspicious in themselves.
The actual caravan was certainly large by any normal hajj standard — large enough to be remembered as exceptional — but the specific figures may overstate the reality by a factor of two or more.
A more sober reconstruction might put the caravan at perhaps 10,000 to 20,000 people, with the gold load running into the multiple tons but probably less than the round numbers suggest.
The exact magnitude remains disputed; what is not disputed is that the caravan was big enough to have macroeconomic effects.
The caravan reached Cairo in July 1324 and stayed for approximately three months.

Musa was the guest of the Mamluk Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad — the third reign of a remarkable Egyptian ruler who had been deposed twice and restored twice, and who would die in 1341 after a third reign of more than thirty years.

The Mamluks were a slave-soldier dynasty (originally Kipchak Turks from the Eurasian steppe, brought to Egypt as military slaves by the Ayyubid dynasty and seized power in 1250) who had defeated the Mongols at Ain Jalut in 1260, ending the Mongol westward expansion (Mongol Empire Ch 6).

Cairo under the Mamluks was the largest city in the Mediterranean world, the cultural and economic capital of the Islamic Middle East, and the point through which all the Red Sea spice trade and most of the gold trade from Africa passed.
Musa's stay in Cairo was the most important diplomatic encounter of his reign.
The encounter started badly.
Mamluk court protocol required visiting rulers to perform a ritual prostration before the sultan — to bow to the floor and kiss the ground in front of the throne.
Musa, as the senior Muslim ruler of one of the largest empires in Africa, refused.

The two courts negotiated for several days before Musa offered a compromise: he would prostrate himself, but to God rather than to the sultan, and would explain the gesture as a religious act rather than a political submission.
Honor was preserved on both sides, the sultan was satisfied, and the formal audience proceeded.
Once protocol was settled, Musa proved a remarkable guest.
He distributed gold gifts on a scale Cairo had never seen — al-Umari's informants, interviewed twelve years later, were still talking about it.
He paid every market debt he encountered.
He gave gold to every religious scholar he met, every official who visited, every shopkeeper who served his retinue.
His attendants did the same on a smaller scale.
The Mali caravan released so much gold into the Cairo economy over three months that the gold-to-silver exchange rate collapsed and stayed depressed for more than a decade.
The economic mechanism is worth pausing on, because it is one of the better-documented examples of a pre-modern monetary shock.
Cairo in 1324 ran on a bimetallic currency system: the dinar (gold coin) and the dirham (silver coin), with a roughly fixed exchange ratio between them based on the relative supply of the two metals.
When Musa's caravan dumped many tons of gold into the Cairo market, the supply of gold suddenly increased while the supply of silver did not.
Standard monetary theory predicts that the price of gold (in silver terms) should fall — and that is exactly what happened.
Egyptian sources record that the value of gold dropped sharply during Musa's stay and remained below pre-1324 levels for ten to twelve years before recovering.
The total damage to Egyptian gold-holders was substantial, though the gainers — Cairo merchants who got rich on Mali gold — generally did better than the losers.
There is a darker side to the Cairo stay, which al-Umari only hints at and which later historians have made more explicit.

Musa's enthusiasm for gold-gifting, combined with the sheer size of his caravan, created an exploitative dynamic in which Cairo merchants quickly realized they could overcharge his attendants drastically and the attendants would simply pay.

By the end of the three-month stay, the Mali caravan's purchasing power had been substantially reduced by inflation, and Musa was forced to borrow money at high interest from Cairo merchants to fund the return journey.
Some of his Cairo creditors followed him back to Mali to collect on the debts.
The hajj that started as a magnificent display of Mali wealth ended, partly, as a cautionary tale about the costs of conspicuous philanthropy in a sophisticated commercial economy.
The hajj's downstream effects on Mali's international reputation were enormous and durable.
Within a decade, Mali appeared in the historical writings of Cairo and Damascus, in the geographical handbooks of the Maghreb, and — most strikingly — on the maps of Mediterranean Europe.
The single most famous example is the Catalan Atlas of 1375, drawn by the Mallorcan Jewish cartographer Abraham Cresques for King Charles V of France.
The Catalan Atlas was one of the most important maps of the medieval world — a six-panel parchment world map showing Europe, North Africa, and as much of Asia as European cartographers knew.
Its West African panel shows an enthroned African king holding a gold nugget the size of his head, with a caption identifying him as "Musa Mali" — the king of Mali.

The image was based on Arabic sources transmitted to Christian Spain through Jewish merchant communities, fifty years after Musa's hajj, and it represents the first known appearance of a sub-Saharan African ruler on a European map.
The Catalan Atlas image is worth pausing on because it captures something true about Mali's position in fourteenth-century geopolitics.
Mali was, for the European Mediterranean of the late fourteenth century, the place where gold came from.

Mediterranean Europe in this period was suffering from a chronic shortage of precious metal — the silver mines of central Europe were only beginning to be developed, and the gold mines of Africa were the principal external source of bullion for Mediterranean monetization.
Italian banking families like the Medici would shortly build their fortunes partly on the African gold trade routed through North African intermediaries.
The image of Mansa Musa with his gold nugget was, for European cartographers, a visual representation of a real economic relationship: Mali was the continent at the bottom of the gold supply chain.

A modern callout that actually illuminates rather than distracts: when popular online lists rank Mansa Musa as "the wealthiest person in human history" — with adjusted-for-inflation estimates running into the hundreds of billions of dollars — they are running a not-quite-honest exercise.
There is no method that allows you to translate medieval state wealth into modern individual wealth on any consistent basis, because the categories are not comparable.

Musa controlled an empire's worth of gold, in the way that a pharaoh controlled Egypt's worth of grain or a Roman emperor controlled the Mediterranean's worth of taxation; whether that translates to "personal wealth" in the modern sense is a category mistake.

What is true is that Musa had access to more gold than any other ruler of his era, that the Cairo gold-crash is real evidence of this, and that his hajj was the most spectacular single display of state wealth on the medieval international stage.
That is impressive enough; the ranked-list inflation-adjusted version is unnecessary.
When Musa returned to Mali in 1325, he brought with him an entourage that would shape Mali's culture for the next century.
Most famously, he brought back Abu Ishaq al-Sahili (al-sah-HEE-lee), an Andalusian poet and architect from Granada whom Musa had met in Cairo and induced to migrate to Mali.

Mali tradition credits al-Sahili with introducing the flat-roofed mud-brick construction that became characteristic of Sahelian elite architecture, and specifically with designing the Djinguereber Mosque in Timbuktu (commissioned by Musa around 1327) and possibly a royal audience hall at the Niani capital.
Modern scholars have qualified al-Sahili's role significantly.

The Sahelian mud-brick architectural tradition was indigenous and centuries older than al-Sahili's arrival — Djenné-Djenno (Chapter 8) had monumental mud-brick architecture going back to the early first millennium CE, and the basic vocabulary of conical buttresses, projecting toron beams, and tapered minarets predates al-Sahili by hundreds of years.
What al-Sahili probably did was introduce Andalusian decorative elements (tiled or plastered surfaces, particular doorway forms, certain interior layouts) and supervise the Djinguereber commission.

He was a real figure, and his presence at Musa's court is independently documented in multiple Arabic sources, but he is best understood as one foreign expert grafted onto a healthy indigenous tradition rather than as the founder of Sahelian Islamic architecture.
Musa also brought back a substantial number of Islamic scholars, mostly from the Maghreb, whom he installed at Timbuktu, Djenné, and Niani as teachers and judges.

The recruitment was deliberate state policy — Musa was building an Islamic scholarly establishment for the empire, modeled loosely on the Islamic teaching tradition of the Maghreb — and it would mature, over the next two centuries, into the Timbuktu manuscript tradition that is one of the great achievements of medieval Islamic civilization (Chapter 5).
Finally, Musa brought back a substantial debt.

The Cairo merchants who had financed his return journey were owed money, and several of them traveled to Mali to collect, beginning the first significant North African mercantile community in the Mali capital.

Some of these merchants stayed permanently, founding lineages that would intermarry with the Mali Mandinka elite and contribute to the empire's cosmopolitan character through the rest of the fourteenth century.
Musa died in or around 1337 after a roughly twenty-five-year reign.

His son Mansa Maghan (MAH-gahn) succeeded him but ruled briefly and badly, losing control of Timbuktu to a Mossi raid sometime in the 1330s — the city was recaptured, but the loss was an early warning sign of provincial slippage.

After Maghan came his uncle Mansa Suleyman (Musa's brother, ruled c. 1341–1360), under whom Ibn Battuta visited the empire (Chapter 5) and who maintained imperial stability but was remembered, perhaps unfairly, as miserly compared to his spectacular brother.

Mansa Musa's reign is the empire's high-water mark in the most concrete sense — territorial extent, economic wealth, international visibility, religious patronage all peaked in the 1320s and 1330s and would not be matched again.
The next two centuries are a slow contraction punctuated by occasional resurgences.
But even the slow contraction took two centuries, which is a substantial historical run for any pre-modern state.
A pause for cross-civilizational comparison.
The 1320s and 1330s — Mansa Musa's hajj decade — sit inside a remarkable period in world history.
