The Mongol Yuan dynasty in China was at its peak, with Marco Polo having returned to Venice a generation earlier with his accounts of Khanbaliq (Beijing).
The Black Death would arrive in Europe in 1347, killing roughly a third of the European population in the next four years, and would reach Cairo and Damascus the following year.
The Hundred Years' War between England and France would begin in 1337, the same year Musa died.
Edward III had just become king of England.

The Sultanate of Delhi in India under Muhammad bin Tughluq was at its expansive peak, controlling most of the subcontinent — Tughluq's coinage experiments would crash the Indian economy in the same years that Musa was crashing Egypt's.
The Aztec capital Tenochtitlan had just been founded in 1325 (Aztec Empire Ch 2), the same year Musa returned from his hajj.
The most striking parallel is between Musa and Edward III's father Edward II, who was deposed and probably murdered in 1327 — exactly when Musa was building the Djinguereber Mosque.

The two royal courts existed in completely separate worlds, neither aware of the other, but the medieval European and West African political traditions were running in parallel through the early fourteenth century, and the comparison helps anchor Mali in a global frame.

chapters.title: Timbuktu and Sankoré
sentences: For most of the world, "Timbuktu" is a name for the impossibly remote — a city of legendary gold and learning that nobody has actually been to.
The name has detached from the actual geographic place and floated free as a synonym for the edge of nowhere.
Even people who know perfectly well where Timbuktu sits on a map use the name in this metaphorical way: the back of beyond, the end of the line, the place a postcard would take a year to reach.

This is a strange afterlife for a real city, and most of it is a European invention — the late-eighteenth-century European myth of Timbuktu as an unreachable Wonder, an inversion of what Timbuktu had actually been at its peak (Chapter 8).
For now, the question this chapter is going to answer is: what was Timbuktu in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, when it actually mattered?

And the short answer is: a working trans-Saharan trade hub on the southern edge of the desert, with three notable mosques, a thriving manuscript-copying economy, an Islamic scholarly community of perhaps a few hundred to a few thousand, and a population that probably never exceeded 50,000 even at the peak.
It was a real city, with a real intellectual culture, and the intellectual culture was substantially more impressive than the city itself.
Timbuktu sits about 8 miles (13 km) north of the Niger River in modern Mali, just south of the Sahara, at the point where the Niger makes its great bend east before turning south.
The location is unromantic — a flat sandy plain with a few wells, with the Niger's seasonal floodplain to the south and the desert immediately to the north.

The city was founded sometime in the eleventh or twelfth century, probably initially as a seasonal Tuareg encampment (the Tuareg, TWAH-reg, are a Berber-speaking nomadic people of the central and western Sahara whose women, until recently, did not veil but whose men did — and still do — wear the distinctive blue-dyed indigo veil that turns their skin permanently dark blue around the face, which is why Tuareg are sometimes called "the blue men of the desert").

The name "Timbuktu" is generally believed to derive from a Tuareg word meaning "place of Tin Buktu" — Tin Buktu being a reference to a Tuareg woman, possibly a slave, who was said to have minded the wells at the original encampment site.
The etymology is folk-etymological and may not be reliable.
Whatever its origin, Timbuktu was already a functioning trade settlement when Mali absorbed it under Sundiata's successors in the late thirteenth century.
What Mansa Musa did, on his return from the hajj in 1325, was transform it from a regional trading post into an imperial showcase city.

He commissioned the Djinguereber Mosque (jin-GAH-reh-bar — a Songhai word meaning "great mosque") on the western edge of the town, traditionally credited to the Andalusian architect al-Sahili (Chapter 4).
He installed a community of Islamic scholars, mostly recruited from the Maghreb during his hajj.
He built or expanded a royal palace where the mansa stayed during visits to the city.
And he supplied capital for the construction of additional religious and educational infrastructure that would mature, over the next century, into the city's three-mosque scholarly complex.

The three great mosques of Timbuktu are the Djinguereber (the largest, on the western side, founded c. 1327), the Sankoré (sahn-KOR-eh, on the northern side, founded a generation later in the mid-fourteenth century), and the Sidi Yahya (named for its first imam, founded in the early fifteenth century).

All three are mud-brick buildings in the Sudano-Sahelian style, with characteristic projecting palm-wood toron beams that double as built-in scaffolding for the regular re-plastering that mud-brick walls require after each rainy season.
The roofs are flat, supported on internal palm-trunk columns.
The minarets are conical, tapered, and buttressed.

None of the three is architecturally spectacular by the standards of Cairo or Damascus or Cordoba; what makes them remarkable is that they have been continuously maintained as functioning mosques for nearly seven centuries, in a building material that requires constant care to survive.
The intellectual life of Timbuktu was organized around the three mosques and around individual scholar-teachers who attracted students to study with them.

The system was the standard medieval Islamic teaching pattern: a student attached himself to a particular master (a shaykh), studied a particular text under that master's supervision, received a certificate (an ijaza) attesting to his completion of the text, and moved on to another master to study another text.
The collected ijazas of a fully trained scholar made up his curriculum vitae.

There was no formal "university" with a fixed curriculum, no enrollment, no graduation; there were master-student lineages that connected each Timbuktu scholar to a chain of teachers stretching back through the Maghreb to Cairo, Mecca, and Baghdad.
Modern writers sometimes describe the Sankoré complex as "the University of Sankoré" or "Sankoré University," which is misleading.
The Sankoré Mosque was the nucleus of an associated madrasa — a teaching institution attached to the mosque — but its structure was less institutionalized than the modern term "university" implies.
There was no central administration, no fixed faculty, no degrees in the modern sense.

What there was, was a community of scholars working in proximity, sharing students, exchanging texts, and producing manuscripts at a level that compared favorably to other Islamic teaching centers of the period.

By the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, Timbuktu's scholarly community was substantial — modern estimates place the resident scholar population at several hundred at the peak, with student populations of a few thousand at any given time — and it had built a manuscript collection that probably ran into the hundreds of thousands of individual works.
What were they studying?

The same things scholars in Cairo or Damascus or Cordoba were studying: the Quran and its commentaries; hadith (the recorded sayings and actions of the Prophet Muhammad); fiqh (Islamic jurisprudence, mostly in the Maliki school, the dominant Sunni legal tradition in West Africa); Arabic grammar and rhetoric; logic; astronomy (essential for determining prayer times and the direction of Mecca); medicine (mostly working from translations of the Greek tradition through the Avicennian synthesis); mathematics; and a substantial production of original local material — Sahelian historiography, biographical dictionaries of West African scholars, legal opinions on local cases, poetry.
Timbuktu was not a peripheral consumer of an Islamic scholarly tradition produced elsewhere; it was a contributing center in its own right.
The Timbuktu manuscript tradition is the most concrete physical evidence of all this scholarly activity.
From the late fourteenth century forward, scholars in Timbuktu and the surrounding region copied, composed, and collected manuscripts on a massive scale.

Modern estimates of the total surviving corpus run from the high six figures into the low seven figures — somewhere between several hundred thousand and a million individual manuscripts, scattered across private family libraries in Timbuktu and surrounding communities in modern Mali.

This is a larger surviving corpus than from any comparable medieval scholarly center outside the major Islamic capitals, and it is by far the largest surviving body of pre-colonial sub-Saharan African writing.

The manuscripts cover the full range of Islamic scholarly genres — Quranic commentary, hadith collection, jurisprudence, theology, Sufism, grammar, rhetoric, logic, astronomy, mathematics, medicine, history, biography, poetry, agricultural treatises, ethical literature.
Many are anonymous student copies of standard Arabic-language texts produced elsewhere; many are original compositions by Timbuktu scholars.
Some are in Arabic; some are in Ajami (a variant of the Arabic script adapted to write West African languages like Songhai, Hausa, and Mandinka).
Some are illuminated, with gold-leaf decoration and elaborate borders; most are utilitarian working copies.
The full extent of the corpus is still being catalogued.
The single most important fact about the Timbuktu manuscripts, in modern terms, is that they exist at all.
For most of the twentieth century, mainstream European and American scholarship of West Africa proceeded on the assumption that pre-colonial sub-Saharan Africa had no significant written tradition.
The Timbuktu corpus puts that assumption beyond reasonable defense.

There was a written tradition; it was extensive; it was sophisticated; it engaged with the broader Islamic intellectual world on its own terms; and it survived in private hands for centuries after the imperial state that nurtured it had collapsed.
The cataloguing and digitization of the Timbuktu corpus, ongoing in the twenty-first century, is one of the more important projects in contemporary African studies.

The single most valuable outside witness to fourteenth-century Mali is Ibn Battuta (ibn bat-TOO-tah, full name Muhammad ibn Abdullah Ibn Battuta, 1304–1369), the Moroccan jurist and traveler who visited the empire in 1352–53.
Ibn Battuta is a remarkable figure on his own terms.

Born in Tangier (TAN-jeer) in the western Maghreb in 1304 to a family of Berber Muslim jurists, he set out for the hajj in 1325 — exactly when Mansa Musa was returning from his — and ended up not coming home for nearly thirty years.

By the time he wrote his memoirs in the 1350s, he had visited Egypt, Syria, the Arabian Peninsula, East Africa, Persia, India, the Maldives, Sri Lanka, Bengal, Sumatra, and southern China, traveling roughly 75,000 miles by his own account.

His memoir, the Rihla ("Travels"), dictated to a court scribe in Morocco in 1355 from his own recollections (he had lost his notes), is one of the most important geographical and cultural documents to survive from the medieval Islamic world.
Ibn Battuta is the most widely traveled person of the pre-modern period of whom we have a detailed firsthand record.
His Mali visit came near the end of his career.

In 1352, the Sultan of Morocco — Abu Inan Faris of the Marinid dynasty, who had heard about Ibn Battuta's travels and wanted a complete account — commissioned a final journey: cross the Sahara, document the Mali Empire, and come back.
Ibn Battuta crossed the desert with a Berber caravan, spent eight months in Mali, met Mansa Suleyman at the Niani court, and returned to Morocco with a long set of observations.
His account is detailed, often critical, and extremely useful.

He describes the trans-Saharan crossing (brutal, well-organized by professional caravan masters); the salt-mining oasis of Taghaza ("a village with no good in it... no trees, only sand, and a salt mine... they say flies are unknown there, and the houses and mosques are built of blocks of salt"); the Niger River cities (organized, prosperous, integrated into a sophisticated commercial network); the conduct of justice in Mali ("complete and general security... neither traveler nor inhabitant has anything to fear from thief or robber"); the discipline of Mali's Muslim population ("they observe the times of prayer carefully... they fast in Ramadan and conform to its requirements"); and the elaborate court ceremonial at Niani (which Ibn Battuta found theatrical and excessive).
He was also unsparing about what he disliked.

He thought Mali's women had insufficient regard for what he considered proper Islamic modesty — many appeared in public unveiled, mixed freely with men who were not their relatives, and held positions of influence in ways his Maghrebi sensibility found shocking.
He thought Mansa Suleyman was personally miserly and noted that the great gold-distribution gestures of Mansa Musa were not being replicated by his successor.
He found certain Mandinka customs, particularly those involving public performance and humiliation rituals, distasteful.
His critical observations are valuable precisely because they make the rest of the account more credible — he is not flattering his hosts, so when he praises something, the praise registers.

The single most important thing Ibn Battuta confirms is that Mali in the 1350s was a functional, prosperous, internationally connected Islamic state — not a peripheral barbarism dressed up in Islamic ornament, as some later European writers would suggest, but a real participant in the Islamic civilization of the wider world.
By the late fourteenth century, the Mali Empire was beginning to lose its grip on the Niger Bend.

The eastern territories — Timbuktu, Gao, the Songhai-speaking population centers — had always been the most loosely integrated parts of the empire, governed indirectly through local elites under Mali suzerainty.
As central control weakened during a series of short and contested mansa reigns in the late fourteenth and early fifteenth centuries, these regions began to assert independence.
Gao, in particular, the Songhai capital on the Niger Bend, became effectively autonomous by the mid-fifteenth century.

Tuareg raiders — the same Berber-Saharan nomads from whose original encampment Timbuktu had grown — periodically seized control of the city, taxed its merchants, and either ruled it directly or extracted tribute.
When the Tuareg controlled Timbuktu, Mali's authority extended only as far as Djenné and the Inner Niger Delta.
The deepest blow came in 1468, when Sonni Ali of Songhai captured Timbuktu (Chapter 6).
After 1468, the Niger Bend was Songhai territory, and Mali was reduced to its core western and central Sahelian provinces.

The intellectual life of Timbuktu continued under Songhai rule — and indeed the city's scholarly community arguably reached its peak under Sonni Ali's successor Askia Muhammad in the late fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries — but the political imperial framework was now Songhai, not Mali.
The greatest scholar Timbuktu ever produced lived through the city's Songhai-then-Moroccan transitions and is the perfect figure to close this chapter.
Ahmed Baba al-Timbukti (1556–1627), born into a scholarly family of Sanhaja Berber descent in Timbuktu, was the leading jurist and biographer of his generation in the western Islamic world.
He wrote more than forty books on Islamic law, biography, theology, and grammar; his biographical dictionary of Maliki jurists, Nayl al-Ibtihaj, remained a standard reference for centuries.

He was also a vocal opponent of certain Saharan slave-trading practices, arguing in detail that the enslavement of West African Muslims was prohibited by Islamic law — a sophisticated legal critique of the very trade that Mali's rulers had themselves facilitated for centuries.

When the Saadian Moroccan army occupied Timbuktu in 1591 (Chapter 7), Ahmed Baba was deported with other Timbuktu scholars to Marrakesh, where he spent fifteen years in exile teaching Moroccan students before being permitted to return to Timbuktu in 1607.
He died in Timbuktu in 1627, and the Ahmed Baba Institute in modern Timbuktu — the principal institutional home of the manuscript collection in the city — preserves his name.
His career is the perfect emblem of late Timbuktu: cosmopolitan, prolific, deeply learned, internationally respected, and ultimately disrupted by political collapse beyond his control.

chapters.title: Songhai Begins to Eat Mali
sentences: Mali did not collapse.
It contracted.

The contraction took most of the fifteenth century and was driven primarily by the rise of a single rival empire — the Songhai Empire (SONG-high), based at Gao on the Niger Bend, which absorbed Mali's eastern territories province by province until the Mali state was reduced to its western Mandinka core.

This chapter is about how Songhai grew up under and then beyond Mali; about the two great Songhai rulers (Sonni Ali and Askia Muhammad) who completed the absorption; about what survived in the Mande core; and about why the rise of Songhai matters for understanding what would happen in 1591 when the Moroccans arrived (Chapter 7).

The Songhai people are a non-Mande population speaking a language that does not fit neatly into any of the major West African language families — Songhai is a linguistic isolate, or possibly a member of the broader Nilo-Saharan family (depending on which classification you accept), distinct from the Niger-Congo family that includes Mandinka.

Songhai-speakers had been on the Niger Bend, particularly around the city of Gao (GOW), for centuries before Mali existed — Gao itself was a substantial trading city by the late first millennium CE, controlling the eastern terminus of the trans-Saharan trade routes and the northern terminus of the Niger River trade.

Mali absorbed Gao in the late thirteenth or early fourteenth century, probably under Mansa Sakura around 1300, and Gao remained nominally tributary to Mali under Mansa Musa and his immediate successors.

But the relationship was always loose — Gao kept its own ruling dynasty, the Sonni lineage, paid tribute when forced to and ignored Mali when it could, and gradually consolidated its independence as Mali's central authority weakened in the late fourteenth century.

By the early fifteenth century, the Sonni rulers of Gao were effectively independent kings of a small kingdom that included most of the Niger Bend; they paid no tribute to Mali and conducted their own foreign policy.

The transition from local kingdom to regional empire happened under one ruler: Sonni Ali (SOH-nee AH-lee, sometimes written Sunni Ali Ber, "Sonni Ali the Great"), who came to the Songhai throne in 1464 and reigned until his death in 1492 — almost exactly the years of the early European voyages of discovery, with which his career ran in unsettling parallel.
Sonni Ali was a brilliant, brutal, and deeply controversial military commander.
In the popular memory of the Sahel, he is one of the great empire-builders, comparable to Sundiata as a founding figure.
In the scholarly Arabic chronicles produced in Timbuktu after his death, he is a violent tyrant who massacred the city's scholars and treated Islamic religious authority with contempt.
Both views are partly correct.
What is certain is that Sonni Ali expanded Songhai territory dramatically through twenty-eight years of nearly continuous campaigning.

He conquered the central Niger River valley from his initial base around Gao, fought the Mossi (a non-Mande, non-Songhai people of the southern savanna), pushed Tuareg raiders back into the Sahara, and — most consequentially — captured Timbuktu in 1468 and Djenné in 1473.
The capture of Timbuktu in 1468 was the structural turning point of fifteenth-century West African history.
Until 1468, Timbuktu was a Mali tributary city occasionally seized by Tuareg raiders; after 1468, it was the second city of the Songhai Empire.

The shift fundamentally repositioned Mali — the loss of the Niger Bend cut Mali off from the Saharan trade routes that had been its economic foundation, and the loss of Timbuktu's scholarly community removed the main symbolic claim to Islamic civilizational status that had grown up under Mansa Musa.
The capture itself was violent.

Sonni Ali apparently distrusted Timbuktu's scholarly class, suspected (probably correctly) that they would prefer Mali rule and would side with any anti-Songhai faction, and dealt with them accordingly.
Specific scholars were killed; the family of one prominent scholar, the Aqit family, was reportedly slaughtered nearly entire.
Other scholars fled to Walata in the western desert.

The Timbuktu chronicles produced a generation later remembered Sonni Ali with horror — the Tarikh al-Sudan calls him a tyrant who "tyrannized the scholars and saints, killing them, insulting them, humiliating them" — and modern historians have generally taken these accounts at face value, though they also note that the chronicles were written by descendants of the families Sonni Ali had attacked, which colors the description.
The conquest of Djenné in 1473 was technically more impressive and politically less brutal.
Djenné, the second great city of the Inner Niger Delta, had been a Mali commercial center for two centuries and was strongly fortified.

Sonni Ali's forces besieged it for either seven years and seven months (the chronicler-friendly version) or some shorter period (the modern-historian version), eventually starving the city into surrender.

The defenders were spared and the city's commercial and Islamic institutions were left intact, in marked contrast to Timbuktu — possibly because Sonni Ali had learned from the political fallout of his Timbuktu massacres.
By the end of Sonni Ali's reign in 1492, Songhai controlled the entire Niger Bend, the central Sahelian trade routes, and most of what had been Mali's eastern provinces.
Mali was confined to its western Mandinka core, with a reduced but still functional state structure centered on Niani and a network of tributary western provinces stretching to the Atlantic.
Sonni Ali died in 1492 — the year Columbus reached the Caribbean and the Catholic Monarchs completed the Reconquista — under unclear circumstances, possibly drowning while crossing a river.

His son Sonni Baru succeeded him but was deposed within months by Sonni Ali's senior general, Muhammad Ture, a Soninke from a non-royal background who took the throne under the regnal name Askia Muhammad (AHS-kee-ah moo-HAM-mahd, sometimes written Askia the Great or Askia Muhammad I).
Askia Muhammad ruled Songhai from 1493 until his deposition by his own son in 1528 — a thirty-five-year reign that fundamentally restructured the empire.

Where Sonni Ali had been a brilliant warrior who treated Islamic institutions with contempt, Askia Muhammad was a deliberate Islamic statesman who built his political legitimacy on religious patronage and orthodox observance.
The contrast was deliberate and self-conscious; Askia Muhammad explicitly positioned himself as the Islamic restoration after Sonni Ali's pagan-tinged tyranny.
Askia Muhammad's most famous act was his own hajj in 1497–98, which he undertook with deliberate echoes of Mansa Musa's 1324 pilgrimage.
His caravan was smaller (perhaps 1,000 attendants and a more modest gold load — Songhai never had Mali's gold supply), but the political theater was precise.

He visited Cairo, met the Abbasid puppet caliph (the Mamluks maintained a powerless figurehead caliph as a legitimacy token), received from him the honorific title of Caliph of Sudan — sudan being the Arabic word for the West African Sahel — and returned to Gao with formal Islamic credentials no Mali mansa had bothered to obtain.
The Caliph of Sudan title was largely symbolic, but it gave Askia Muhammad a religious authority within his own empire that Sonni Ali had never possessed.

Inside the empire, Askia Muhammad rebuilt Timbuktu's scholarly community, restored the patronage relationships Sonni Ali had broken, recruited new scholars from the Maghreb, and supported the construction of additional madrasas.

The greatest single document of late-medieval Sahelian Islamic political philosophy is the Replies to Askia by the Maghrebi scholar al-Maghili, written in response to Askia Muhammad's request for guidance on how a Muslim ruler should conduct his government.

The text is a sustained piece of practical political theology, addressing questions about jihad, the treatment of non-Muslims, the administration of justice, and the proper relationship between the religious scholarly class and the secular ruler.
It is one of the most sophisticated political documents to come out of medieval West Africa and a marker of how seriously Askia Muhammad's regime took the Islamic intellectual tradition.
Askia Muhammad expanded Songhai territory westward into the western Sahel, bringing the Mali core under direct pressure.
By the 1510s, Songhai control extended into territory that had been securely Mali only twenty years earlier.
The Mali Empire was being squeezed.
What survived in the Mali core, even as Songhai absorbed the eastern territories, is worth describing because it explains how the empire's afterlife worked.

The Keita lineage continued to rule the Mandinka heartland from a series of capitals — Niani survived as the imperial center into the early sixteenth century, after which the political center shifted to Kangaba and other smaller towns as the empire shrank.

The mansa institution continued to function; the Kurukan Fuga continued to govern the Mandinka clans; the jeli continued to recite the Sundiata epic; the Mande language network continued to extend across an enormous swath of West Africa from the Atlantic coast to the upper Niger, even where political authority had fragmented.
Mali in 1530 was no longer an empire in the territorial sense, but it was still the political and cultural center of a coherent Mande world.
The empire's reduced territory still included some of the most economically valuable land in West Africa.

The Bambuk gold field on the upper Senegal River remained under Mali control even after Songhai took the Niger Bend, and Mali continued to supply gold to the trans-Saharan trade through the western caravan routes that ran north to Wadan and Walata in Mauritania.

The Mali coastal provinces extended to the Atlantic, and the empire had some of the earliest contact with Portuguese traders (who reached the Senegal River coast in the 1440s and the Gambia River in the 1450s) — though the systematic Atlantic-trade reorientation of West Africa was still a century in the future and the Mali state was not yet structurally affected by it.
What weakened Mali through the late fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries was less direct Songhai attack than the slow erosion of the tributary structure that had supported the imperial system.

As Songhai grew, Mali's outer-ring tributaries (Wolof kingdoms, smaller Mandinka subordinate kingdoms, peripheral provinces) reassessed their relationship with the imperial center and increasingly chose autonomy or shifted allegiance.

By 1530, the Mali Empire was a regional power confined to the western Mandinka heartland — still substantial, still wealthy by the standards of the surrounding kingdoms, but no longer the dominant force it had been a century earlier.

Mali might have continued in this reduced form for centuries, gradually shrinking but never quite collapsing — the Songhai pressure was real but not fatal, and the Mande cultural network gave the western core a depth of political and social institutional support that buffered against rapid decline.

In a counterfactual where the Moroccan Saadians had not invaded in 1591, the Mali Empire might have survived in some form into the eighteenth or nineteenth century before being absorbed by one of the later Sahelian Islamic states or by the European colonial expansion.

But the Saadians did invade, and the structural shock of the invasion — which actually targeted Songhai, not Mali — fundamentally destabilized the entire region in ways that nobody at the time foresaw.
Chapter 7 is about that invasion.
A pause for cross-civilizational comparison.
The fifteenth century — the Songhai expansion — sits inside a remarkable global moment.

The Mongol Empire had finally fragmented, with the Yuan dynasty in China replaced by the Ming in 1368 (Ming Dynasty Ch 1) and the Ilkhanate in Iran giving way to a sequence of post-Mongol Persian dynasties.
Ottoman expansion under Mehmed II captured Constantinople in 1453 (Byzantine Empire Ch 12, Ottoman Empire Ch 2) — twenty-eight years before Sonni Ali's death.
Ferdinand and Isabella completed the Spanish Reconquista by capturing Granada in 1492, and Columbus reached the Caribbean the same year.
The Inca Empire in the Andes was at its expansionist peak under Pachacuti and his successors.
The Aztec Triple Alliance under Moctezuma I was building the largest empire in Mesoamerican history (Aztec Empire Ch 5–6).

Vasco da Gama would reach India by sea in 1498, the year after Askia Muhammad's hajj — and the resulting Portuguese maritime trade route would, within a century, fundamentally rewire Indian Ocean and African Atlantic commerce in ways that would reduce the importance of trans-Saharan trade and undermine Sahelian states like Mali and Songhai.
The structural global shifts that would shortly destroy Sahelian primacy were already beginning to unfold while Sonni Ali was still besieging Djenné.

chapters.title: The Saadian Strike
sentences: In March 1591, on the dusty plain of Tondibi (TON-dih-bee) on the Niger River about thirty miles north of Gao, an army of approximately 4,000 Moroccan soldiers — most of them carrying matchlock muskets, supported by a small artillery train of medium cannons — confronted a Songhai army of perhaps 40,000 to 50,000 cavalry and infantry.
The Songhai outnumbered the Moroccans by ten to one, fought on home territory, were better acclimatized to the climate, and were the dominant military force in West Africa.
The Moroccans were exhausted from a five-month Saharan crossing that had killed roughly half their original force; their gunpowder was damp; their horses were dying.
The Moroccans won.
The battle lasted a few hours.
The Songhai cavalry charges, of the kind that had carried the day in countless Sahelian battles for two centuries, broke and disintegrated when they hit massed musket fire and cannon shot.
The Songhai infantry could not close to use their swords and lances.
Within days, Gao had fallen to the Moroccan force; within a few weeks, Timbuktu and Djenné had been occupied.

The Songhai Empire — the great power of the western Sahel for more than a century — was effectively destroyed in a single afternoon, by a much smaller force, on the basis of a technological gap nobody in West Africa had quite seen coming.
This chapter is about how the Moroccans got there, what their muskets actually did, and why the destruction of Songhai also finished off whatever remained of Mali's regional position.
The Saadian strike was aimed at Songhai's gold supply, not at Mali — but the political collapse it triggered destabilized the entire western Sahel, and Mali was caught in the wreckage.
The Moroccan invasion of 1591 was the project of a single ruler, Ahmad al-Mansur (ah-MAHD al-mahn-SOOR, "the Victorious"), Sultan of Morocco from 1578 to 1603.

Al-Mansur was the third major ruler of the Saadian dynasty — a sharifian Berber lineage from the Sus valley in southern Morocco that had displaced the earlier Wattasid dynasty in the early sixteenth century and consolidated control of all Morocco by the 1550s.

The Saadians presented themselves as descendants of the Prophet Muhammad through Hasan ibn Ali (a sharifian claim that gave them religious legitimacy in a Maghreb increasingly preoccupied with Islamic credentials), and they styled themselves as the defenders of Sunni Islam against both the Christian Iberian powers to the north and the Ottoman Turks to the east.
Al-Mansur came to the throne in unexpected circumstances.

His older brother, the previous sultan Abd al-Malik, had just won the most famous Moroccan victory of the early modern period — the Battle of the Three Kings at Alcácer Quibir in northern Morocco on August 4, 1578, against an invading Portuguese army led by King Sebastian I of Portugal.

The battle was a Moroccan victory but an exhausting one: three rulers died on the battlefield (Abd al-Malik of natural causes during the battle, Sebastian killed in the rout, and the deposed Moroccan claimant al-Mutawakkil drowned in the river).
Sebastian's death without an heir triggered a Portuguese succession crisis that ended with the Spanish Habsburgs absorbing Portugal in 1580, fundamentally reshaping European geopolitics.
And it left al-Mansur — Abd al-Malik's younger brother — on the Moroccan throne with an enormous war indemnity from Portuguese ransoms and a powerful army flush with victory.
Al-Mansur was an unusually well-educated and ambitious ruler.

He spoke Arabic, Spanish, and Italian; he read widely in classical Islamic scholarship; he ran a sophisticated diplomatic service that maintained relations with the Ottomans, the Spanish Habsburgs, the English (Queen Elizabeth I corresponded with him about a possible joint anti-Spanish alliance), and various smaller European powers.

He used the Portuguese ransom money to build a substantial army equipped with the latest European-pattern firearms — matchlock muskets bought from the Ottoman trade and from European arms dealers, supplemented by domestic gunpowder production.
By the 1580s, Morocco had one of the more modern armies in the western Mediterranean.
What al-Mansur wanted, more than anything else, was access to the West African gold supply.

Morocco's economy depended substantially on the trans-Saharan gold trade, but the gold reached Morocco through a long chain of intermediaries — the Sahelian empires that controlled the mining regions, the Tuareg and Berber caravan operators that ran the desert crossing, the Moroccan border markets that distributed the gold.
Each intermediary took a margin, and the Moroccan state's share of the gold flow was a fraction of what it would be if Morocco controlled the source directly.
Al-Mansur saw this as a structural problem worth solving by force.
The military problem of crossing the Sahara to attack Songhai had been considered by previous Moroccan rulers and dismissed as impossible.

The desert crossing alone would consume an army through heat, thirst, and disease before it ever reached the Niger; even if the army survived, the climatic shock of moving from the temperate Maghreb to the tropical Sahel killed horses and men in unusual numbers.

No North African power had attempted a direct trans-Saharan invasion of the Sahel since the early Almoravid period in the eleventh century, and even those operations had been smaller-scale and contested.
Al-Mansur's solution was to send a small but heavily armed expeditionary force, tightly organized, with extensive logistical preparation.

The force was assembled in 1590 and consisted of approximately 4,000 troops — most of them morisco (Spanish-Muslim refugees who had been expelled from Spain after the Reconquista and who served in considerable numbers in the Saadian army) and ulj (renegade European converts, mostly captured in Mediterranean piracy and absorbed into the Moroccan military), with a smaller contingent of native Moroccan soldiers.

The morisco and ulj background of most of the force was significant: these were soldiers who knew European-style musket warfare, and they had been brought up speaking Spanish or Italian rather than Arabic, which made them exotic but also militarily competent in a specific technical way.

The force was led by a remarkable commander: Judar Pasha (JOO-dar — a Spanish-born eunuch who had been captured as a child by Saadian raiders and converted to Islam, raised in al-Mansur's household, and risen to senior military command).

Judar's appointment to lead an expedition into territory none of the Saadian high command had ever seen was a calculated gamble; the appointment of a eunuch outsider rather than a senior native Moroccan general meant that political risk would not propagate back to the Marrakesh court if the expedition failed.
The crossing took five months — from October 1590, when the force left southern Morocco, to March 1591, when it reached the Niger.
Roughly half the original 4,000 men died en route, mostly from heat, dehydration, and disease.
The horses suffered worse; almost all the cavalry mounts died, and the survivors had to be replaced from local sources after the army reached the river.
What arrived at the Niger Bend in March 1591 was a small, hardened, exhausted force with several hundred functional firearms and a few cannons.
By the standards of any conventional military assessment, it should have been crushed by Songhai.
Songhai in 1591 was ruled by Askia Ishaq II, a competent but unspectacular successor to the great Askia Muhammad.

Ishaq had a substantial army — modern estimates run from 30,000 to 50,000 men, with the cavalry forming the core — and the army was organized along the traditional Sahelian heavy-cavalry pattern that had dominated regional warfare for two centuries.
What it did not have was firearms in any meaningful number, or any institutional experience in fighting against firearms.
The technological asymmetry was the whole story of the battle.

Matchlock muskets in 1591 were not technically advanced weapons by European standards — the matchlock was the previous generation of military firearm, already being supplanted by the wheellock and the early flintlock in European armies — but they were vastly more effective than anything the Songhai cavalry could field.

A trained matchlock musketeer could fire perhaps one shot per minute, accurate to fifty yards, with a heavy lead ball that would punch through any armor a Songhai cavalryman could wear and that would knock a horse down at close range.

A line of musketeers, firing in volleys, produced a wall of lead that no cavalry charge could survive — provided the musketeers held their formation, did not panic, and had enough time to reload between charges.
The Battle of Tondibi was, by all accounts, brief.

The Songhai cavalry charged, the Moroccan line held, the muskets fired, the cannons fired (much louder than anything the Songhai had heard before, terrifying horses that had never been exposed to artillery), and the Songhai charge broke.
There was no recovery; once the cavalry was scattered, the infantry had no answer to the muskets, and the army disintegrated.
Casualties on the Songhai side ran into the thousands; on the Moroccan side, perhaps a few dozen.
Within days, the Moroccans occupied Gao.
Within weeks, they had also taken Timbuktu and Djenné.
Askia Ishaq II fled south with what remained of his court, eventually being killed by his own bodyguards.
The Songhai Empire fragmented into a series of small successor states in the southern provinces, but the imperial center was finished.

The Moroccan occupation of the Niger Bend cities was permanent in name and impermanent in practice — Marrakesh was 1,500 miles away across the Sahara, supply lines were essentially nonexistent, and within a generation the Saadian government had effectively given up on direct administration and was treating the Niger Bend as a remote tributary handled by the local commanders on the spot.
The local commanders settled in.

The Arma (al-rumat, "the marksmen" — the descendants of the original Saadian musketeers) settled in Timbuktu and Gao, married into local families, gradually became a hereditary military caste in the Niger Bend cities, and ruled the region nominally on behalf of the Saadian sultan but in practice as autonomous lords.

By the early seventeenth century, the formal connection to Marrakesh had attenuated to a periodic exchange of ceremonial gifts; by the mid-seventeenth century, the Arma were entirely independent and ruled the Niger Bend as a series of city-states.
The intellectual life of Timbuktu was substantially damaged but not destroyed.

Ahmed Baba (Chapter 5) was deported to Marrakesh with several other senior scholars, ostensibly because al-Mansur wanted them at his court but practically because the Saadians regarded the Timbuktu scholarly establishment as politically unreliable.
Ahmed Baba spent fifteen years in Marrakesh exile before returning to Timbuktu in 1607 to find the city much reduced; he died there twenty years later.
Other scholars fled to smaller centers; some were killed; the main libraries were partly looted, partly preserved by the families that had owned them.

The seventeenth-century Timbuktu chronicles — the Tarikh al-Sudan and the Tarikh al-Fattash — were composed in this immediate post-conquest environment and reflect both the trauma of the conquest and a deliberate effort to preserve Sahelian historical memory in writing for the first time.
Mali, meanwhile, was not directly affected by the Tondibi campaign.
The Saadian force did not penetrate into the Mali core; al-Mansur's strategic goal was Songhai's gold, not the dismantling of every Sahelian state.

The Mali Empire in 1591 was still a regional kingdom centered on the Mande heartland with its capital somewhere in the Niani region (the city itself had declined sharply by the late sixteenth century — see Chapter 8 on Niani's archaeological disappearance — but the imperial state continued to function under the Keita lineage from a sequence of nearby capitals).
But the structural shock of the Songhai collapse was severe.

The trans-Saharan gold trade that ran through the Niger Bend cities was disrupted; the Tuareg and Berber caravan networks that had handled the Sahara crossing reorganized around new political arrangements; the gold flow that had once gone north through Timbuktu was diverted, with substantial portions now going south to the Atlantic coast where Portuguese and Dutch traders were establishing coastal forts.
Mali's economy depended on the trans-Saharan trade; when the trade was disrupted, the imperial fiscal base shrank.

By the 1620s, the Mali Empire was a small Mande kingdom of regional importance, paying intermittent attention to its tributary peripheries and increasingly absorbed into local Mande political structures rather than maintaining the imperial framework Sundiata had built.

The Atlantic slave trade, growing rapidly through the seventeenth century, drew the focus of West African commerce southward toward the coast and away from the Sahel; the Mali Empire's traditional sources of wealth and political leverage withered in the new commercial geography.
The political empire was, for practical purposes, finished by the mid-seventeenth century.

Sometime around 1670 — the exact date is impossible to determine, since the empire's end was a gradual evaporation rather than a single dramatic collapse — what had been the Mali Empire effectively dissolved into a network of small Mande successor states, the largest of which was the Keita kingdom of Kangaba (Chapter 8).
The continuous imperial line that had run from Sundiata in 1235 was broken.
A pause to sit with what 1591 actually means.
The Battle of Tondibi was the first time gunpowder weapons decisively determined a major engagement in sub-Saharan Africa.

The technological gap that opened up at Tondibi — between Mediterranean-pattern firearm armies and Sahelian-pattern cavalry armies — would persist and widen for the next three centuries, and by the nineteenth century the same basic technological asymmetry would underwrite European colonial conquest of the Sahel.

The 1591 campaign is, in this sense, the first installment of the long African encounter with industrialized military technology, run by a Maghrebi power before any direct European conquest had begun.
It is also a cautionary tale about the limits of military success.

Al-Mansur's campaign achieved its tactical objective — the Songhai army was destroyed, the Niger Bend cities were occupied, the gold supply came under nominal Moroccan control — but the strategic payoff never materialized.

Within a generation, the Arma had gone native, the gold flow to Marrakesh had collapsed back to pre-1591 levels (and was actually lower, because the disrupted Sahelian trade routes were less productive), and the Saadian dynasty itself was failing.
Al-Mansur died of plague in 1603; the dynasty fragmented within a decade; by the 1660s, a new dynasty (the Alawites, still ruling Morocco today) had taken over.

The 1591 invasion is sometimes cited in modern military-history textbooks as a classic example of a tactical victory that produces no useful strategic result — an enormously expensive campaign that achieved its immediate objective and accomplished nothing of lasting value to the conquering power.
For the Sahel itself, however, the 1591 invasion was permanently transformative.
The great empires were finished.

What replaced them was a fragmented landscape of smaller Mande and Songhai successor states, increasingly oriented toward the Atlantic coast as European commercial expansion drew the region southward.
The Sahelian world that had centered on Mali, Songhai, and the trans-Saharan trade for half a millennium was structurally different by 1700.
Mali itself had become a memory carried in oral tradition rather than a functioning state.

chapters.title: The Long Mali Tail
sentences: This last chapter is about what survives.
Empires end, and the question of what an empire's ending actually means depends on what you count.
The political institution of the Mali Empire effectively ended in the seventeenth century, with no single dramatic moment of collapse.

The Keita ruling lineage continued in the small successor kingdom of Kangaba and is technically still in existence today, with a hereditary chief whose office is the direct continuation of the Sundiata line.

The Mande cultural network — the languages, the clan system, the jeli institution, the Sundiata epic — survived the empire's political collapse intact and is still functioning, with modifications, across a broad swath of West Africa.
The Manden Charter is on the UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage list.
The Timbuktu manuscript corpus survived in private libraries through nearly four centuries of upheaval and is being catalogued and digitized in the twenty-first century.
Whether Mali "ended" depends on which Mali you mean.
This chapter is about the long tail — what continued after the empire was no longer an empire, what was lost, and what remains in living tradition today.
Start with the Keita kingdom of Kangaba (kahn-GAH-bah).

After the imperial center at Niani disintegrated in the late sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries, the Keita royal family relocated to Kangaba, a small town on the upper Niger River in what is now southern Mali.

Kangaba was the original homeland of the Keita lineage, the place Sundiata's family had come from before the Sosso conflict drove them into exile, and the royal return to Kangaba was a deliberate cultural move — back to the ancestral source, away from the imperial capital that had failed.
The Kangaba kingdom was small.
It controlled a few villages along the upper Niger, a few thousand subjects, and no significant trade routes.

It was politically irrelevant by the standards of the broader West African world, and the larger Mande and Bambara polities of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries (the Bambara kingdoms of Segou and Kaarta, which would dominate the upper Niger from the late seventeenth century through the early nineteenth) treated Kangaba as a culturally important but politically minor neighbor.
What Kangaba had, that no one else had, was the Sundiata legitimacy — the Keita lineage and the rituals that went with it.
The most important of those rituals was, and is, the Kamabolon ceremony (kah-mah-BOH-lon).
The Kamabolon is a small mud-and-thatch shrine in Kangaba, traditionally associated with the Keita lineage and said to contain ritual objects connected to Sundiata himself.
Every seven years, the shrine's roof is reconstructed in a multi-day ceremony attended by Mande people from across the region.

During the ceremony, selected jeli of the Diabate, Kouyate, and other senior griot lineages recite the full Sundiata epic — the most authoritative version, the canonical text, performed in full, by the institutionally recognized custodians of the tradition.

The seven-year cycle has, by all accounts, continued without recorded interruption for centuries; the most recent reconstructions in the modern period have been thoroughly documented by anthropologists, who treat the Kamabolon as one of the most important living oral-tradition events in West Africa.
The Kamabolon ceremony is the institutional mechanism that has kept the Sundiata epic alive across nearly thirty generations.

Without it, the epic would still exist — there are many jeli traditions and many regional versions — but the canonical reference text, the version against which other versions are checked, would be much less stable.

With it, the epic is preserved in something like the way a religious scripture is preserved: by an institutional community whose recurring ritual obligation is to perform the full text in the presence of qualified witnesses.
In the western part of the former empire, a different successor state survived for much longer.
The Kaabu Federation (KAH-boo) was a confederation of small Mande-speaking kingdoms in what is now Guinea-Bissau, eastern Senegal, and northern Guinea.

Kaabu had originated in the thirteenth or fourteenth century as a western province of the Mali Empire, governed by Mandinka warrior families called the Nyancho (NYAN-cho) who had migrated from the Mande heartland to extend Mali authority over the local Balanta, Fula, and other populations.

After the imperial center collapsed, Kaabu continued to function as an independent federation under its own king, the Kaabu Mansaba, with a confederate structure that gave significant autonomy to the constituent kingdoms while maintaining nominal centralized authority.
Kaabu lasted for nearly two and a half centuries beyond the formal end of the Mali Empire.
Its end came through Islamic religious revolution rather than colonial conquest.

The Fula jihads of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries — a series of Islamic reformist movements led by Fula (FOO-lah, also called Fulani or Peul) Muslim clerics across the western Sahel, modeled on the earlier reform movements in the eastern Sahel — built up Fula military power across the region and eventually came into collision with Kaabu.
At the Battle of Kansala in 1867, the Fula imamate of Futa Jallon defeated the Kaabu federation, capturing the Kaabu capital and killing the last Kaabu Mansaba.
Kansala marked the end of the last Mande-speaking polity that could claim direct institutional descent from the Mali Empire.

Less than three decades after Kansala, the entire region was under French colonial rule, and the political structures that had defined West Africa for centuries were being dismantled and replaced by the colonial administrative apparatus.
The Mali Empire's political afterlife ended, as Sahelian political history more broadly ended, at the cross between Fula jihadism and European colonialism in the middle of the nineteenth century.
The puzzle of Niani's archaeological disappearance deserves its own paragraph, because it is one of the more peculiar facts of West African archaeology.

Niani, the imperial capital described by Ibn Battuta in 1352 — a substantial city of mud-brick houses along the river, with a royal compound, market, mosque, and surrounding agricultural villages — has not been securely identified by modern archaeologists.

Several sites have been proposed as the location of imperial Niani, with the leading candidate being the village of Niani in modern Guinea, just south of the Mali border, on a small tributary of the upper Niger.

Excavations at this site have revealed an occupation that spans the right period and includes appropriate material culture, but the scale of the archaeological remains is much smaller than the imperial city Ibn Battuta described, and there is no consensus among archaeologists that this is, in fact, the city Ibn Battuta visited.
The disappearance is structural, not accidental.

Sahelian mud-brick cities, when they cease to be inhabited and maintained, dissolve back into the landscape with extraordinary speed — the mud brick that requires constant re-plastering to survive a single rainy season returns to the soil within decades when the maintenance stops.

A city the size of imperial Niani, abandoned in the sixteenth century, would leave visible ruins for perhaps a generation and faint surface traces for perhaps two centuries before disappearing entirely.

By the time the first European archaeologists reached the upper Niger in the late nineteenth century, almost three hundred years after Niani's abandonment, the imperial city was simply gone — reduced to subsoil scatters of broken pottery and faint outlines of building foundations, indistinguishable from any other small Sahelian village site.
This matters for understanding what we can and cannot know about the Mali Empire.
The basic political and economic outlines of the empire are reasonably well attested through the Arabic sources and the surviving Sahelian chronicles.
The detailed urban, administrative, and material culture of the empire is much harder to reconstruct, because the cities themselves have largely vanished.

Djenné survives as a working city and has been intensively studied; Timbuktu survives as a much-reduced version of its medieval self and has substantial standing remains; Gao survives in a similar way.
But Niani, the imperial capital, is essentially a textual entity rather than an archaeological one.
We know it from Ibn Battuta's description and from the Arabic chronicles; we do not know it from excavation in any thorough sense.

The Timbuktu manuscript tradition survived everything — the Songhai conquest, the Moroccan invasion, the Arma occupation, the French colonial period, two world wars, the Mali independence movement, the Tuareg rebellions of the late twentieth century — until it nearly didn't survive the events of 2012.
In April 2012, an alliance of Tuareg separatist forces and jihadist groups associated with al-Qaeda in the Islamic Maghreb seized control of northern Mali, including Timbuktu.

The jihadists, modeled ideologically on Saudi-Wahhabi religious extremism, treated Timbuktu's mausoleums of Sufi saints, traditional shrines, and historical manuscripts as instances of unacceptable folk Islam that needed to be destroyed.
They began systematically destroying the shrines and burning manuscripts.
A Timbuktu librarian named Abdel Kader Haidara organized a clandestine rescue operation.

Over the next several months, with a network of volunteers (mostly young men from Timbuktu families with hereditary library connections), Haidara smuggled tens of thousands of medieval manuscripts out of the city — packed in metal trunks and rice sacks, hidden in donkey carts, transported by river to the safer southern city of Bamako, and stored in safe houses.
The operation was funded by emergency grants from international heritage organizations and by Haidara's personal credit.

By the time French and Malian forces retook Timbuktu in early 2013, Haidara's network had successfully evacuated an estimated 350,000 manuscripts to Bamako — the great majority of the city's surviving corpus.
The manuscripts are still in Bamako, in private storage and in the partial-rebuilding institutional facilities of the Ahmed Baba Institute.
The political situation in northern Mali remains unstable, and the manuscripts have not been returned to Timbuktu.

Cataloguing and digitization continue at Bamako; international scholarship is gradually working through the corpus; the academic field of Timbuktu studies is, as a result of the 2012 rescue, in a much healthier position than it was at the start of the twenty-first century.
The corpus that nearly burned is now better-documented than at any previous point in its history.
The 2012 rescue is, by most measures, the most important single event in the history of pre-colonial African manuscript preservation.

It is also a striking demonstration of how the institutional traditions Mali built — the network of family libraries, the multigenerational jeli memorization, the Kangaba ritual cycle — produced cultural infrastructure resilient enough to survive both the empire's political collapse and the modern crises that have followed.
The Manden Charter received international recognition in 2009 when UNESCO inscribed it on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

The inscription was the formal acknowledgment of what the jeli had been preserving for nearly eight centuries: a charter of inter-clan obligations, rights of refuge, prohibitions on certain forms of slavery, and rules for the conduct of war, promulgated by Sundiata in 1236 and transmitted by oral tradition across thirty generations.

The inscription does not give the charter legal force — it is not a binding international instrument — but it places the Kurukan Fuga in the same category of human cultural achievement as the world's other great medieval constitutional and human-rights documents.
That is appropriate recognition of what the document is.
The European myth of Timbuktu also deserves a paragraph, because it has had an unusual afterlife.
By the eighteenth century, Timbuktu had become a European synonym for the impossibly remote, a city of legendary gold and learning that no European had reached.

The first European known to visit and return alive was the Frenchman René Caillié (reh-NAY kah-YEH), who reached Timbuktu in April 1828 disguised as an Egyptian pilgrim and stayed two weeks before joining a caravan back across the Sahara.

What Caillié actually found was a sun-baked clay town of perhaps 10,000 people, dusty markets, and a faded scholarly community — much reduced from the imperial city Ibn Battuta had described five centuries earlier, and falling well short of the European legend.
The myth had outlived the imperial city by three centuries, and continued to outlive Caillié's deflating account for many decades after.
The Mansa Musa image — the enthroned king with the gold nugget that first appeared on the Catalan Atlas in 1375 — has had an unusual modern revival.
In the early twenty-first century, internet popular history rediscovered Mansa Musa, primarily through viral articles and social-media posts ranking the wealthiest people in human history.

The "richest person ever" framing is, as discussed in Chapter 4, essentially unverifiable and probably misleading — but it had the side effect of bringing Mansa Musa, and by extension medieval Mali, back into public awareness in a way that no academic effort had managed.
This is mixed news.

The popular Mansa Musa image emphasizes wealth and gold to the exclusion of almost everything else interesting about him — his religious patronage, his recruitment of scholars, his architectural commissions, his participation in the broader Islamic intellectual world, the institutional infrastructure of the empire he ruled.
The Mansa Musa of viral lists is a one-dimensional figure: rich, gold, hajj, Cairo gold-crash, end.
The historical Mansa Musa was much more interesting than that — and the historical Mali Empire was much more than its richest individual ruler.

The popular revival has at least put Mali on the mental map of a generation of readers who would otherwise have heard nothing about it; whether it will translate into serious engagement with the actual empire's history is an open question.
A final pause for the broader pattern.
What does the Mali Empire's afterlife actually look like?
Not a dramatic collapse and disappearance, of the kind that overtook the Akkadian empire (Mesopotamia Ch 5) or the Western Roman Empire (Ancient Rome Ch 9).
Not a colonial absorption that destroyed local institutions, of the kind that overtook the Aztec Empire (Aztec Empire Ch 8) or the Inca Empire.
Not a continuous imperial line that mutated into modern statehood, of the kind that connects modern China to its ancient dynastic past.

Mali ended somewhere in the middle ground: the political empire dissolved, the cultural and institutional infrastructure survived, the lineages and rituals continued, and the modern Republic of Mali — which took the imperial name on independence in 1960 — looks back to the Mali Empire as its symbolic ancestor without claiming any direct institutional descent.
This is a more common pattern in world history than the dramatic-collapse model.
Most great empires don't really "fall"; they thin out, fragment, persist in attenuated forms, and gradually become more memory than functioning institution.

What is unusual about Mali is that the memory is extraordinarily well-preserved — the Sundiata epic is still performed by jeli whose lineage runs back to the founding court, the Manden Charter is on a UNESCO list, the manuscripts of Timbuktu have just been rescued from a recent existential threat, the modern Republic of Mali named itself after the empire and treats that imperial inheritance as a central element of its national identity.
The infrastructure that Sundiata, Mansa Musa, and the long line of Mali rulers built turned out to be more durable than the political empire itself.
The empire became a cultural project that has lasted nearly twice as long as the political empire did.
In a project that is, by definition, about which civilizations get remembered and how, that is a striking achievement.
A closing cross-civilizational comparison.
As Mali was finally fading as an institutional state in the seventeenth century, the world it had helped shape was undergoing transformations none of its founders could have anticipated.
The Atlantic slave trade was reaching industrial scale, drawing West African economic and political life away from the Sahel and toward the coast (Atlantic shadow, Chapter 7).
The Manchu Qing Dynasty had just conquered Ming China (Qing Dynasty Ch 1).
The Ottoman Empire was at its territorial peak under Mehmed IV and the Köprülü viziers (Ottoman Empire Ch 9).
The Mughal Empire under Aurangzeb was about to begin its long decline.
Louis XIV was building Versailles.
Newton was working out the calculus and the laws of motion.
The Iroquois Confederation in the Great Lakes was at its peak as a regional power.

In the Andes, the colonial Viceroyalty of Peru was extracting silver from Potosí at industrial scale, doing to the seventeenth-century European silver supply something analogous to what Mansa Musa had done to the fourteenth-century Egyptian gold supply.
The world Mali had inhabited was disappearing.

The world that replaced it would not have a place for an inland Sahelian empire of the kind Sundiata had founded — but the cultural inheritance of that empire would survive into the world that replaced it, and would survive into the world that has replaced that one in turn.
Mali endured, in its strange afterlife, longer than most of the great empires that overtook it.
That is the empire's final accomplishment, and a fitting note to end on.

chapters.title: The Songhai Before Songhai
sentences: The Songhai Empire was the third and largest of the three great medieval West African gold empires.
Ghana came first, Mali came second, Songhai came third — and Songhai inherited the institutional architecture of both predecessors while building a much more centralized state on top of it.

This chapter is about the foundation: the Niger Bend geography, the Songhai people themselves, the long-running Za and Sonni dynasties at the city of Gao, and the moment in the early fifteenth century when the Songhai stopped paying tribute to a fading Mali Empire and started running their own affairs.
A word on what is not in this chapter.
The dramatic conquests, the brilliant generals, the gold-laden hajj, the matchlock catastrophe — all of that is coming in Chapters 2 through 8.
This chapter is the slow build, the geography and the institutions and the dynastic backstory that made the rest possible.
Skim it if you want; come back to it when later chapters reference something that needs grounding.
The geography first.

The Sahel (sah-HEL, from the Arabic word for "shore" or "coast" — the shore of the Sahara, the way you might say the coast of the sea) is a band of semi-arid grassland that runs east-to-west across Africa, separating the Sahara desert to the north from the wetter savanna and forest to the south.

It is roughly 600 to 1,000 miles (1,000 to 1,600 km) wide, depending on where you draw the line, and it stretches for around 3,400 miles (5,500 km) from the Atlantic coast of Senegal to the Red Sea coast of Sudan.
Songhai's heartland sat in the central part of this band, in what is now northeastern Mali and western Niger.
Cutting across the Sahel like a peculiarly shaped highway runs the Niger River (NYE-jer — not to be confused with the modern country called Niger, which takes its name from the river).
The Niger is the third-longest river in Africa, after the Nile and the Congo.

It has a famously strange course: it rises in the highlands of modern Guinea, only about 150 miles from the Atlantic coast, and then, instead of running west to the sea, it bends north into the Sahara.

It runs north for nearly a thousand miles, brushing the southern edge of the desert at Timbuktu, before turning sharply southeast at the Niger Bend, then curving south through modern Niger and Nigeria, and finally reaching the Atlantic Ocean at the Niger Delta after a 2,600-mile (4,200 km) journey.
The shape of that arc is the single most important geographic fact in the history of the western Sudan.

The Niger pushes north into the Sahel and then comes back south, depositing silt along an inland flood plain called the Inner Niger Delta (a strange name for a feature that is nowhere near the actual sea-coast delta — but the Inner Delta has the same braided-channel, seasonal-flood structure as a coastal river mouth, except that it sits 1,500 miles inland in the middle of the Sahel).
The annual flood is enormous — millions of acres of seasonally flooded grassland — and it makes possible an unusually dense population in what would otherwise be marginal land.
Djenné (jen-NAY), Timbuktu (tim-BUCK-too), Gao (GOW, rhymes with "now"), and the slightly more inland city of Niani (NYAH-nee, the Mali capital) all sit on or near this Niger arc.
Every great empire of the western Sahel — Ghana, Mali, Songhai — built its political center on the Niger.
Songhai's specific niche on this geography was the eastern leg of the arc.

Where Mali had been a Mandinka kingdom of the upper Niger and the Inner Delta, Songhai was a Songhai-speaking kingdom of the Niger Bend — the long stretch where the river runs east past Timbuktu before turning southeast at Gao and heading for modern Nigeria.
This eastern position had two consequences.

First, Songhai sat closer to the Hausa city-states of modern northern Nigeria and to the trans-Saharan caravan routes coming south from modern Algeria and Libya, which gave Songhai a different commercial orientation than Mali's western Bambuk-and-Bure gold focus.

Second, the river was navigable and predictable along this stretch, which is why Sonni Ali's war fleet (Chapter 2) could become a strategic instrument in a way that no Mali ruler had ever quite managed.
The Niger also runs through the structural geography of the gold-and-salt trade, which is the economic bedrock of every Sahelian empire.

Gold came from south of the Sahel, from alluvial deposits in the headwaters of the Senegal and Niger rivers — the Bambuk (BAM-buck) and Bure (boo-REH) gold fields, both on small upper tributaries of the Niger and Senegal river systems.
Salt came from north of the Sahel, from dry lakebeds in the central Sahara — the great mining site of Taghaza (tag-HAH-zah), about 500 miles north of Timbuktu, was the most important.
Camel caravans linked the two economies.
The Sahelian empires were the middlemen, and the middleman position was extraordinarily lucrative.
Songhai, like Mali before it, did not control the gold mines themselves.
The Bambuk and Bure miners were independent populations who jealously guarded their locations from any imperial center — a pattern that persisted from Ghana through Mali to Songhai.
The empires got rich by taxing the gold as it passed through their markets on its way north, and by controlling the import of the salt and trade goods coming the other direction.

This middleman model is essential to understanding both Songhai's wealth and its eventual vulnerability: the empire's revenues depended on the trans-Saharan trade flow, and anything that disrupted that flow — the Atlantic shift after 1471, the Moroccan strike at Taghaza in 1585, the post-Tondibi commercial collapse — threatened the foundation of state finance.
Now the people.
The Songhai (SONG-high, sometimes written Songhay or Sonrai) are a Nilo-Saharan-speaking people of the eastern Niger Bend.

Their language is part of the Nilo-Saharan language family — an ancient and somewhat controversial grouping that links Songhai to Nubian (the language of medieval Christian Nubia, Kingdom of Aksum cousin), to Maasai in East Africa, and to several scattered languages across the Sahel and southern Sahara.
Whether Nilo-Saharan is a single coherent family or a residual category for languages that don't fit elsewhere is still debated by linguists.
What matters for our purposes is that Songhai is not a Mande language — it is unrelated to Mandinka, Soninke, Bambara, and the other Mande tongues of Mali — and it is not a Berber language.
As different from Mandinka as English is from Hungarian, and from Berber as English is from Arabic.
The Songhai were a genuinely distinct people from their Mali neighbors, even though they had lived alongside the Mandinka for centuries and had borrowed many institutional patterns from them.
The Songhai homeland was a fishing, farming, and trading society along the eastern Niger long before any state apparatus had emerged.
The river supported a specialized fishing population — the Sorko, river-dwelling Songhai who lived in stilt villages and made their living from catfish, perch, and tilapia smoked and traded inland.
Other Songhai groups farmed millet, sorghum, and rice along the floodplain, herded cattle on the dry-season pastures, and traded along the river with Soninke and Wangara merchants from the west.

The political organization was loose — village heads, regional war-chiefs, traditional ritual specialists — and unified state structure did not appear until the Za dynasty established a kingship at Gao.
A note on names.
"Songhai" refers to the people, the language, and the empire.
"Songhay" is an alternative English spelling, and the spelling "Songhay" is preferred in some recent scholarly works.
"Sonrai" is an older French rendering, occasionally used in older texts.

The political entity was called by multiple names in different periods — the Gao Kingdom in the early period, the Songhai Empire after the breakaway from Mali, the Askia state in some chronicle usage.
Use whichever you like; they all refer to the same broad civilizational tradition.
The kingship at Gao goes back to perhaps the eighth century.
Gao sits on the eastern Niger Bend, just upstream from the point where the river turns south for its long run toward modern Nigeria.

The location was a natural commercial center: south-facing for Sahel trade, west-facing for the river network running through Timbuktu and the Inner Delta, north-facing for trans-Saharan caravan routes coming down from modern Algeria and Libya through the central Sahara.

Camel caravans had been crossing the Sahara since at least the third century CE — the systematic introduction of the dromedary camel to the Sahara from the Roman-Arabian world had made regular trans-Saharan trade possible for the first time, opening the gold-salt circuit that would underwrite every Sahelian empire from the eighth century forward.
Gao was one of the southern terminuses of this circuit.

Excavations at Gao-Saney, just northwest of the modern city, have revealed monumental stone-and-mud-brick tombs of Muslim rulers from the eleventh century onward — including stelae with inscriptions in Arabic, attesting royal Islamic burial practice as early as the 1080s.

The archaeology suggests a substantial commercial city by the eleventh and twelfth centuries, with stone-built royal residences, a large Friday mosque, and active trading quarters housing North African and Andalusian merchants.
By any reasonable measure, Gao was a working city well before any of the dramatic political events of this story occurred.
The traditional dynastic history of Gao starts with the Za dynasty (also spelled Dia or Dya).
The Za kings ruled Gao from perhaps the eighth century.

Their traditional founder, Za Alayaman, is a semi-legendary figure said to have come from Yemen — a typical post-conversion Islamicizing genealogical motif (after kings convert to Islam, their dynastic histories often retroactively acquire Yemeni or Arabian origins, claiming a connection to the Prophet's homeland) rather than verifiable history.
What is verifiable is that a royal lineage at Gao, which the chroniclers called Za, controlled the kingdom through the high middle ages.
The Gao kings converted to Islam around 1010 CE.

The conversion was elite and commercial — useful for trans-Saharan trade and diplomatic recognition by Maghrebi states — and coexisted for centuries with traditional Songhai religious practices among the rural population.

This is the same layered religious pattern we see in Mali (Mali Empire Ch 5): a Muslim royal court and merchant class sitting on top of a peasant population that practiced traditional religion, with intermarriage and ritual borrowing in both directions.
Gao's Islamization predates Sundiata's founding of Mali by more than two centuries.
Around 1325, Gao came under the control of Mali.
Mansa Musa's eastern campaigns (Mali Empire Ch 4) brought the Niger Bend cities into the Mali Empire as tributaries.

For roughly a century thereafter, the Songhai paid tribute to the mansas at Niani and supplied military contingents to Mali's wars, while preserving their own ruling dynasty, language, and local administration.

Gao's tributary period under Mali is poorly documented — neither Mandinka oral tradition nor Songhai oral memory had much reason to dwell on it — but it was real, and it was the political experience the Sonni dynasty would eventually overthrow.
The Sonni dynasty (also spelled Sunni — no relation to the Sunni branch of Islam) replaced the Za as rulers of Gao around the late thirteenth century.
The chronicle tradition credits Sonni Sulayman Dama as the dynasty's founder.

The Sonni held Gao through the fourteenth century as a tributary of Mali and through the early fifteenth century as something closer to a satellite kingdom — paying nominal tribute, maintaining their own administration, and watching for the moment when Mali's central authority would weaken enough that the tribute could be quietly stopped.
That moment came in the 1430s.

Mali was simultaneously losing Timbuktu to Tuareg raiders (1433), losing the western provinces to the rising Wolof and Tukulor kingdoms, and consumed by a long succession dispute among the Keita royal lineage.
The Sonni under Sonni Sulayman Dandi simply stopped paying tribute around 1430, and Mali did not have the military capacity to compel resumption.
There was no dramatic moment of rebellion; Songhai independence was a quiet fact on the ground that took several decades for both sides to fully recognize.
The Tuareg occupation of Timbuktu from 1433 to 1468 is worth a paragraph because it sets up Sonni Ali's signature military achievement.
The Tuareg (TWAH-reg, sometimes Touareg) are a Berber-speaking nomadic people of the central and western Sahara.

They speak Tamasheq, a Berber language closely related to the languages of modern Morocco and Algeria and unrelated to either Songhai or the Mande languages — the Berbers had spread south into the Sahara from the Maghreb over the previous two millennia and were the dominant pastoralist population of the desert by the medieval period.
Tuareg society was structured around camel-herding, caravan-running, and intermittent raiding of settled Sahelian populations whenever central authority weakened.

When Mali's grip on Timbuktu loosened in the 1420s, Tuareg raiders under Akil ag Malwal seized the city around 1433 and held it for thirty-five years, taxing the trade and broadly leaving the urban population alone but providing no central authority capable of restoring imperial order.
Timbuktu's Sanhaja Berber clerical families — the scholarly lineages that had run the city under Mali — adapted to Tuareg taxation while keeping the trade flowing and the manuscripts copying.
This is the situation Sonni Ali would inherit when he took the throne in 1464.
Before the curtain rises on Sonni Ali, a pause for cross-civilizational context, because the western Sudan in the 1430s sits inside a much larger network than is usually appreciated.

When the Songhai were quietly stopping tribute payments to Mali, the Ottoman Empire (Ottoman Empire Ch 2) had recently taken Constantinople — the city would fall in 1453, fundamentally restructuring the eastern Mediterranean.

Ming China was at the height of its early-fifteenth-century power, with Zheng He's treasure fleets having just completed their last voyage in 1433 (the same year the Tuareg took Timbuktu, by coincidence).
The Aztec Triple Alliance had just been founded in 1428 (Aztec Empire Ch 3), the same decade Sonni Sulayman Dandi was breaking from Mali.
The Inca Empire was beginning its great expansion under Pachacuti, who would come to the throne around 1438 and transform Cuzco into a continental capital.
Renaissance Florence was producing Brunelleschi's dome, Donatello's statues, and the first cracks of European humanism.

The Mamluk Sultanate in Egypt was at its institutional peak, the Timurid Empire was collapsing into successor states across central Asia, and the Joseon dynasty in Korea was inventing the hangul alphabet under King Sejong.
Songhai did not know about most of these civilizations, and most of them did not know about Songhai.

The Mediterranean and Islamic worlds knew that gold flowed north across the Sahara from somewhere in the western Sudan, but the political map of the Sahel was hazy in Cairo and almost entirely unknown in Florence.
Mali's reputation from the Mansa Musa era was still alive in European cartography (Mali Empire Ch 4), but Mali itself had been reduced to a regional power.
The world that would briefly turn its attention to the Niger Bend two and a half centuries later — the Saadian Morocco of Ahmad al-Mansur — did not yet exist as an organized state.

chapters.title: Sonni Ali the Great
