This chapter is about the long decay: the post-Askia-Muhammad chaos, the long stable reign of Askia Dawud as the empire's last great ruler, the post-Dawud collapse, and the structural gap between Songhai's military system and the gunpowder revolution that was about to arrive at the gates.

The chapter is shorter than the rest because the decay is unpleasant to read about and because the structural pattern is the same throughout: a short reign by a contested Askia, a coup by a brother or son, a brief moment of restored stability, another coup.
Distinct events do not stand out so much as a cumulative pattern of institutional decay.
By the time Tondibi came around in 1591, Songhai had spent two generations weakening itself.
The immediate post-Askia-Muhammad crisis ran from 1528 to roughly 1549.
Askia Musa (1528–1531), the son who had deposed his father, was deposed and killed by his own brothers within three years.
Askia Muhammad II Bonkana (1531–1537) was deposed by another brother.
Askia Ismail (1537–1539) reigned briefly before dying — possibly of natural causes, possibly poisoned, the chronicles disagree.
Askia Ishaq I (1539–1549) finally provided a decade of relative stability before being challenged by his brother, the future Askia Dawud.
The pattern was: a coup brought a new Askia to power, the new Askia faced rival claims from his brothers, palace conspiracies and outright civil war intermittent through each reign.

The empire's institutions absorbed the chaos at significant cost — the cavalry aristocracy fragmented into competing factions, the provincial governors became increasingly independent, the tribute flows from the eastern provinces became erratic.
At the same time, the Saadian dynasty in Morocco was rising to power.

The Saadians — an Arab-descended family from the Sous Valley in southern Morocco — had displaced the Wattasid Berber dynasty in 1549 (the same year Askia Dawud took the Songhai throne) and were beginning the territorial consolidation that would eventually produce Sultan Ahmad al-Mansur.

The Saadians had inherited the Wattasid commercial relationship with Songhai across the Sahara, and they were beginning to think about whether trans-Saharan commerce could be supplemented by direct trans-Saharan military projection.
Askia Dawud (1549–1582) was the empire's last great ruler.
Dawud's thirty-three-year reign restored stability after the post-1528 chaos.

He suppressed the most disruptive factional conflicts in the cavalry aristocracy, normalized the tribute flows from the provincial governors, maintained the trans-Saharan trade at peak volume, and continued the patronage of Timbuktu's scholarly community.

He repelled the first serious Moroccan raid on Taghaza (around 1556, when Sultan Muhammad al-Shaykh of the Saadians sent a small expedition to seize the salt mines, which the Songhai forces eventually drove back).
He added a personal library to the imperial court and encouraged the manuscript trade.

The chronicles treat Dawud as the last competent Askia and one of the great Sahelian rulers — comparable to Askia Muhammad in his administrative competence, though without the spectacular hajj and the founding-figure status.
Two features of Dawud's reign deserve attention.
First, Dawud's handling of the cavalry aristocracy was the most successful in the dynasty's history.

He used a combination of careful patronage, strategic marriage alliances among the noble lineages, periodic rotation of provincial governors, and occasional punitive campaigns against particularly disruptive factions to keep the aristocracy in line.
The system worked because Dawud was personally adroit at it; it did not transfer to his successors, who lacked his political skill.
Second, Dawud avoided the gunpowder restructuring that the Ottomans, Safavids, Mughals, and Saadians were all undertaking during the same decades.
The Songhai military remained a cavalry-and-fleet army, with at most a handful of personal arquebuses at the imperial court and no organized gunpowder infantry units.

The decision was probably driven by the cavalry aristocracy's resistance to a restructuring that would have devalued their status, by the geographic difficulty of producing gunpowder in commercial quantities in West Africa, and by the absence of any acute external pressure that would have forced the issue.

The Saadian raid on Taghaza in 1556 should have been a warning sign — a small Moroccan force armed with firearms had reached deep into Songhai's northern frontier — but the raid had been driven off, the threat had not materialized at the imperial center, and the cavalry aristocracy had every reason to interpret the episode as proof that the existing military system was adequate.
The structural mistake was made during Dawud's reign, not during his successors'.

By the time the Saadians came back in force in 1591, the gap between Songhai's cavalry army and the gunpowder forces of the Mediterranean Islamic world was wide enough that no quick adjustment could close it.
The institutional decision against gunpowder restructuring was a generation-long commitment that locked Songhai into a military trajectory it could not easily reverse.
The post-Dawud civil wars (1582–1588) destroyed the empire's central authority faster than anyone expected.
Dawud's death in 1582 was followed by a sequence of contested successions.

Askia al-Hajj (1582–1586), one of Dawud's sons, was deposed by his brother Askia Muhammad Bani (1586–1588) in a brief civil war that involved at least one major battle and substantial casualties among the cavalry aristocracy.
Bani was deposed in turn by another brother, Askia Ishaq II (1588–1591), in another brief civil war.

Each succession involved palace coups, the killing or exiling of competing princes, the reshuffling of provincial governorships, and the breakdown of the careful factional balance that Dawud had maintained.

The cumulative effect was that by 1588, when Askia Ishaq II took the throne, the cavalry aristocracy was fractured into competing factions, several of the largest provincial governorships were effectively independent of central control, and the standing army's morale was visibly poor.
The empire's institutions still existed on paper; in practice, they were operating at a small fraction of their capacity.
Tribute flows were down, military readiness was down, the trans-Saharan trade was still functioning but increasingly dependent on local arrangements rather than imperial authority.
This was the situation that Sultan Ahmad al-Mansur of Morocco was watching from Marrakesh.
Ahmad al-Mansur had become Saadian sultan in 1578, after the Battle of the Three Kings.

The Battle of the Three Kings (also called the Battle of Wadi al-Makhazin) at Ksar el-Kebir in northern Morocco on August 4, 1578, was one of the great Mediterranean military catastrophes of the sixteenth century.

King Sebastian I of Portugal, a young and inexperienced ruler obsessed with the idea of a crusade against Muslim Morocco, had landed an army of around 17,000 Portuguese troops and Moroccan allies (under the Saadian claimant Abu Abdallah Mohammed II, who was trying to recover the throne from his uncle) on the Moroccan coast.
The Saadian sultan Abd al-Malik met them with a larger army of perhaps 50,000 troops including a substantial gunpowder infantry contingent.

The battle was a catastrophic Portuguese defeat: the Portuguese army was annihilated, King Sebastian was killed (his body was identified the next day), Abu Abdallah Mohammed II was killed, and Sultan Abd al-Malik died of natural causes during the battle itself.
Three kings dead on a single battlefield.
Abd al-Malik's brother Ahmad — soon to be al-Mansur, "the Victorious" — succeeded immediately.

The ransom money for the surviving Portuguese nobles, the captured arms and equipment, and the political prestige of the victory gave Ahmad al-Mansur both a treasury surplus and the international standing of a major Islamic ruler.

He spent the next thirteen years building Morocco into a regional power, modernizing the Saadian army with European-trained gunpowder specialists (some of them captured Portuguese converts to Islam), and quietly developing the intelligence and logistical preparation for a project that no Moroccan ruler had ever attempted: a trans-Saharan invasion of Songhai aimed at seizing the Sahelian gold supply at its source.
Why did al-Mansur undertake this?

The standard explanation is the gold motive: Saadian Morocco was running structural budget deficits, the Mediterranean European demand for gold was high, and the trans-Saharan trade was perceived as inadequately profitable for Morocco when the Songhai were the middlemen taking most of the profit.
If Morocco controlled the source — Taghaza for the salt, the Bambuk-Bure goldfields for the gold — Saadian revenues would expand dramatically.

The calculation was probably partly correct (Taghaza was a real and sizable revenue source) and partly wrong (the Bambuk-Bure goldfields were not actually located where al-Mansur thought they were, and the Moroccan occupation never managed to control the gold supply at the source).
But there were also non-economic motives.
Al-Mansur wanted the prestige of expanding the Islamic world's southern frontier.
He wanted to demonstrate the Saadian dynasty as the dominant power of the western Mediterranean Islamic world.
He wanted to secure a southern strategic depth against Ottoman pressure on Morocco's eastern flank.
The gold was the public justification, but the broader project was political and prestige-driven.
Al-Mansur sent a series of diplomatic feelers to Songhai during the late 1580s, demanding tribute payments and presenting various claims to the Taghaza salt mines and to broader Sahelian territory.

Askia Ishaq II, on the throne from 1588, replied with the gestures of contempt that Sahelian rulers traditionally extended to upstart Maghrebi sultans: he sent al-Mansur a gift of two hundred sticks of iron and a token offering of gold dust, with a message that suggested the Saadian sultan's claims were as ridiculous as the gift was small.
The diplomatic exchange was, in effect, a declaration that Songhai did not take al-Mansur seriously.
This was a miscalculation.
Al-Mansur was already preparing the invasion.
The Moroccan expeditionary force was being assembled, the trans-Saharan logistics were being planned, the European-converted gunpowder specialists were being trained.
Ishaq's contemptuous reply removed any remaining diplomatic constraints on the invasion plan.
Within two years the Moroccan army would be marching south.
A pause for cross-civilizational context.
The 1580s were a remarkable decade across the early-modern world.
While Songhai was tearing itself apart in succession civil wars, the Spanish Armada was being built and then destroyed (1588) by the English navy and the Atlantic weather.
Philip II of Spain was at the peak of his global power, ruling a Habsburg empire that included Iberia, the Low Countries, much of Italy, and the entire Spanish New World.
Elizabeth I of England was consolidating Protestant rule and patronizing Shakespeare and Marlowe at the start of their careers.
In the Islamic world, the Ottomans under Sultan Murad III were at the territorial peak the empire would ever reach (Ottoman Empire Ch 4).
The Safavids under Shah Abbas I (taking the throne in 1588, the same year as Askia Ishaq II) were beginning the ghulam revolution that would restructure the Iranian state (Safavid Persia Ch 4).
The Mughals under Akbar were consolidating their grip on northern India, having defeated the last major Rajput resistance and integrated the Hindu nobility into the imperial administrative system.
The Saadians under Ahmad al-Mansur were preparing the invasion that would shortly destroy Songhai.
All four of these Islamic empires — Ottoman, Safavid, Mughal, Saadian — had completed their gunpowder transitions by 1588.
All four were running professional standing armies built around firearms infantry and artillery.
Songhai had not made the transition, and was about to discover what that meant.

chapters.title: Tondibi 1591
sentences: In late 1590, a Moroccan expeditionary force of around 4,000 men set out from Marrakesh on a march that no organized military had ever attempted.

They were heading south across the Sahara to invade the Songhai Empire — a thousand-mile march across some of the harshest desert on the planet, against an enemy fielding a much larger cavalry army on terrain the Moroccans had never seen, with logistics that depended on a chain of oases and salt-mining outposts that might or might not provision them adequately.
The expedition was, by any sober military assessment, extremely high-risk.
It was also a complete success.

This chapter is about the 1591 campaign: al-Mansur's calculation that produced the project, the trans-Saharan crossing of Judar Pasha's force, the matchlock-vs-cavalry showdown at Tondibi, and the long aftermath — the Pashalik of Timbuktu, Ahmed Baba's exile, the fragmentation of the western Sudan, the Dendi successor kingdom, and the structural reorientation of West African commerce away from the Sahara and toward the Atlantic that would prevent any Sahelian successor empire from emerging.
Sultan Ahmad al-Mansur's calculation was the strategic foundation.
Al-Mansur had been preparing the trans-Saharan invasion for at least five years before the 1590 expedition departed.

The preparations included intelligence gathering on Songhai's military and political condition (probably through the Taghaza salt traders and through Sahelian merchants visiting Marrakesh), logistical planning for the Saharan crossing (identifying water sources, calculating provisioning requirements, training pack-animal handlers), recruitment of European converts and Andalusian Moriscos with gunpowder expertise, and the assembly of an expeditionary force whose composition was specifically designed for the conditions it would face.
The force was small by Sahelian battlefield standards — al-Mansur knew that any larger force would be impossible to provision across the Sahara — but heavily armed.

The composition included around 2,500 musketeers (mostly Andalusian Moriscos and European converts trained in matchlock infantry tactics), 1,500 cavalry (mounted lancers serving as a screening force and pursuit element), a small artillery train of perhaps 6 to 10 light cannons, and a substantial logistics tail of camel handlers, water-carriers, and support personnel.
Total expedition size was around 4,000 fighting men and a roughly equal number of support personnel.
The commander was Judar Pasha (joo-DAR PAH-shah), a Spanish-born eunuch who had been captured as a child in Almería, taken to Marrakesh as a slave, and risen through the Saadian military hierarchy.

The choice of commander is interesting: Judar was a competent professional officer with no significant political connections in the Saadian court, which made him both a reliable executive of al-Mansur's plan and a politically expendable scapegoat if the expedition failed.
The Pasha rank was a Saadian institutional borrowing from the Ottomans — a senior military and provincial-administrative title.
The trans-Saharan crossing lasted from October 1590 to February 1591 — roughly four months across some of the most lethal terrain on the planet.

The route went south from Marrakesh through the Draa Valley, then southwest into the western Sahara, then across the central Sahara via the salt-mining oasis of Taghaza, then on south to the Niger Bend.
Total distance was around 1,500 miles (2,400 km).

The expedition had pre-positioned water and provisions at intermediate stopping points where possible, but several stretches between water sources ran 50 to 100 miles with nothing — fatal for any group that lost its way or ran short on water.
The crossing was catastrophic for the expedition.
Heat, thirst, exhaustion, disease, and accident killed roughly half of the original force before the survivors reached the Niger.
The casualty rate was particularly heavy among the camels and pack animals; equipment had to be abandoned along the route to keep the survivors moving.
Some of the artillery was lost.
By the time the column reached the Niger Bend in February 1591, Judar's effective fighting force was probably around 2,500 to 3,000 men, with the rest dead or too debilitated to fight.
That this was still enough to win the war is the great structural fact of Tondibi.
The Battle of Tondibi was fought on March 13, 1591, at the village of Tondibi (TON-dee-bee) on the Niger River about 35 miles north of Gao.
Askia Ishaq II had assembled the Songhai army at Tondibi to block the Moroccan advance.
The chronicle figures for the Songhai force vary widely — from 12,000 to 50,000 — but the most plausible estimate is around 30,000 cavalry plus a much larger but less mobile infantry contingent.
The cavalry was the strike arm; the infantry was the mass formation expected to follow up the cavalry's initial breakthrough.
Ishaq personally commanded the army, accompanied by the senior cavalry aristocracy and the imperial standing-army units.
Judar's force, by contrast, was probably around 2,500 effectives.
The Moroccans were a tiny fraction of the size of the Songhai army.
They had two structural advantages: the matchlock muskets, and the artillery.
The battle began with the standard Sahelian opening: a Songhai cavalry charge, intended to break the Moroccan formation and open the way for the infantry to roll up the broken units.
The Songhai cavalry probably numbered several thousand at the leading edge, with thousands more in supporting waves.
The charge crossed open ground toward the Moroccan position.
The Moroccans responded with organized matchlock volley fire.
The musketeers were arranged in disciplined lines, trained to fire in rotation so that one rank fired while the others reloaded.
Maintained continuous fire — perhaps two volleys per minute from the front line, sustained over the few minutes it took the cavalry to cover the open ground.
The artillery fired solid shot through the leading cavalry ranks.
The combined firepower destroyed the cavalry charge before it reached the Moroccan formation.
Songhai cavalry casualties were heavy.
The supporting cavalry waves saw the front rank shatter and either pulled up short or attempted to maneuver around the flanks of the Moroccan formation.
The flanking attempts ran into the Moroccan cavalry screen and were repulsed.
What turned the engagement into a rout was a tactical error by a herd of cattle that the Songhai had positioned on the flank to break the Moroccan formation.
The cattle, panicked by the gunfire, stampeded back into the Songhai infantry rather than forward into the Moroccans.
The Songhai infantry formation broke.
The cavalry, seeing the infantry collapse, began to withdraw.
Within a few hours the Songhai army had disintegrated entirely.
Ishaq fled south with a small bodyguard.
The Moroccans, still numbering several thousand, occupied the battlefield.
Tondibi was, in retrospect, one of the foundational early-modern demonstrations that gunpowder infantry could destroy a much larger pre-gunpowder cavalry force in open battle.
The Ottomans had demonstrated something similar at Chaldiran in 1514 (Safavid Persia Ch 3) against the Safavid Qizilbash.
The Mughals would demonstrate it again in their later sixteenth-century campaigns.
The Habsburgs and the Swedes would demonstrate it across the Thirty Years' War.
The same structural pattern was running across the entire early-modern Islamic and European military world.
Tondibi was the West African instance of a global military revolution.
The Moroccan occupation of Gao came within days.
Judar's force entered the Songhai capital without resistance.
Ishaq's bodyguard had withdrawn south down the Niger toward the Dendi region, and the city's remaining population had no military capacity for resistance.

The Moroccans found Gao less wealthy than al-Mansur's intelligence had suggested — much of the imperial treasury had been removed by the fleeing Askia — and the looting was extensive but commercially disappointing.
Gao would never recover its imperial role.
Judar then moved on Timbuktu, occupying the city in April 1591.

The conquest of Timbuktu was the strategic centerpiece of the campaign — it was the city al-Mansur had really wanted, both for its commercial centrality and for its symbolic status as the capital of West African Islamic learning.

The occupation was followed by systematic looting of the city's libraries, the deportation of leading scholars including Ahmed Baba (next section), and the imposition of direct Moroccan military rule.
Within a few months of Tondibi, the structural occupation of the Niger Bend was complete.
The Moroccans held Gao, Timbuktu, and Djenné under direct military government.

The provincial governors of the more distant provinces accommodated as best they could to the new reality — some by submitting to Moroccan suzerainty, some by quietly going independent in their own provinces, some by attempting and failing to organize resistance.
The Songhai imperial administrative structure had simply ceased to function.
The empire was over.
Ahmed Baba's exile is the single act that captures the cultural cost of the conquest.

Ahmed Baba was forty-five years old in 1591, in his prime as a Maliki jurist and scholar, with a major library, an active teaching practice at Sankoré, and a position as one of the most respected figures in the Timbuktu scholarly community.

The Moroccans arrested him in Timbuktu in 1593, charged him (probably correctly) with leading the Sankoré scholars' resistance to the occupation, and transported him in chains across the Sahara to Marrakesh.
Sultan al-Mansur intended to display him as a trophy of the conquest.
Ahmed Baba's library, possibly the largest single collection in Timbuktu at that point, was confiscated; some volumes were carried to Marrakesh, others were lost or stolen.
The exile lasted fifteen years, from 1593 to 1608.
Ahmed Baba was held under restricted conditions in Marrakesh — initially in actual prison, later under a kind of house arrest in a residence on the city's southern edge.
He continued to write, to receive visitors, to teach Moroccan students who came to study with him, and to correspond with scholars across the Islamic world.
Some of his most important works, including the biographical dictionary of Maliki jurists, were composed or completed during the Marrakesh exile.
His Marrakesh teaching had a paradoxical effect: it transferred a substantial body of Timbuktu scholarship into the Moroccan intellectual world.
Ahmed Baba's Moroccan students carried his teaching into the next generation of Maghrebi Maliki jurisprudence.
The brain drain that the occupation had inflicted on Timbuktu was partly a brain transfer to Marrakesh.
The cultural cost was real, but it was a redistribution rather than a destruction.
Ahmed Baba was finally allowed to return to Timbuktu in 1608, after Sultan al-Mansur's death.
He spent the last nineteen years of his life in his home city, teaching the next generation of Sankoré scholars and continuing the literary output.
He died in Timbuktu in 1627, near seventy years old.
The Ahmed Baba Institute in modern Timbuktu — established in the 1970s as the central archive of Timbuktu manuscripts and devastated by the 2012 jihadist occupation — preserves his name.
The Pashalik of Timbuktu — the Moroccan-officered military regime that governed the conquered territories — institutionalized within a few years of the conquest.
The Pashalik was nominally subject to Marrakesh, with the Pasha of Timbuktu appointed by the Saadian sultan and reporting back through standard imperial channels.
In practice, the Pashalik became autonomous within a generation.

The reasons were structural: the trans-Saharan distance made effective central control impossible (it took several months for messages to travel between Marrakesh and Timbuktu), the Moroccan soldiers stationed in the Niger Bend married into local Songhai and Wangara families and developed local interests that diverged from Marrakesh's, and the Saadian dynasty itself collapsed in the 1620s into a long civil war that prevented Marrakesh from maintaining any consistent imperial policy toward its trans-Saharan territories.

The descendants of the Saadian soldiers — known as the Arma (from the Arabic al-rumat, "the marksmen" or "the gunners") — settled in Timbuktu and Gao, married into local families, and gradually formed an autonomous Mande-Arabic-speaking military caste that ruled the Niger Bend cities into the early nineteenth century.
They paid nominal tribute to Marrakesh; they were independent within a generation; they operated more like a creole frontier oligarchy than an imperial garrison.

The Arma maintained the gunpowder military advantage — they continued to acquire firearms and gunpowder through trans-Saharan trade — but they did not attempt to rebuild the Songhai Empire's territorial extent.
The Arma regime was a contracted, defensive holding operation centered on the Niger Bend cities, not an expansionist successor state.
The Pashalik formally lasted until the early nineteenth century, when the Tuareg confederations and the rising Fulani jihads of the western Sudan swept it aside.

The Arma population assimilated into the local Songhai-Mandinka-Berber demographic mix and survives in modern northern Mali as the Arma ethnic identity, with its own cultural memory of descent from the 1591 expeditionary force.
The Dendi successor kingdom maintained the Askia dynasty in exile.

After Tondibi, Askia Ishaq II fled south down the Niger to the Dendi region — the eastern Niger provinces in what is now the Niger-Benin border zone, far enough from Gao to be beyond the practical reach of the Moroccan occupation.
Ishaq was deposed by his own brother Muhammad Gao within months and disappears from the historical record.

Muhammad Gao established a successor state at the city of Lulami (later moved to other capitals as the kingdom shifted across the centuries), which maintained the Askia dynasty and the imperial cultural traditions for another three centuries.
The Dendi kingdom never recovered Songhai's territorial scale.
It was a regional power, controlling the Niger frontier between the Hausa city-states and the contracting Mossi kingdoms, but it was not an empire.

It maintained the Songhai language, the Askia royal lineage, the administrative titles (the koi and fari offices), the qadi court system, and many of the religious and cultural institutions of imperial Songhai.

The institutional continuity is striking: the Askia dynasty survived in Dendi for roughly the same length of time as the imperial Songhai had existed, finally being absorbed by French colonial conquest in 1901.

The Dendi survival is one of those underappreciated historical patterns: the great medieval imperial dynasties often outlived the empires themselves by remarkable spans, in the form of regional successor states.

The Sasanian dynastic memory survived the Arab conquest in various Iranian successor traditions; the Byzantine cultural inheritance survived the fall of Constantinople in the Greek Orthodox Church; the Mali Keita lineage survived in Kangaba (Mali Empire Ch 8).
The Askia survival in Dendi belongs to the same pattern.
The empire was over; the dynasty was not.
The structural reorientation of West African commerce was the slow shadow that prevented any successor empire from emerging.
By 1591, the Atlantic slave trade was already replacing the trans-Saharan gold trade as the dominant West African commercial flow.

European trading forts dotted the coast — Elmina (Portuguese, 1482), Cape Coast (English, later), Whydah (Dutch, later) — and the African political ecosystem was beginning to reorient toward the coastal trade rather than the Saharan trade.
The new commercial centers — Ouidah, Cape Coast, the Niger Delta city-states — were positioned for Atlantic shipping, not for Saharan caravans.
The economic basis for a Sahelian empire was being hollowed out from the south.
The Moroccan occupation accelerated this reorientation by destroying the trans-Saharan commercial infrastructure that had survived the conquest.
Without the unified Songhai imperial administration, the trans-Saharan trade became more dangerous, more expensive, and less consistently profitable.
The merchant networks shifted south toward the coast.
The Wangara commercial diaspora reorganized along Atlantic-facing routes.

The gold flow that had once moved north across the Sahara to Sahelian markets and then on to Cairo and the Mediterranean increasingly moved south to the coastal forts and across the Atlantic to Lisbon, Amsterdam, and London.
The Sahel was not depopulated, the cities were not abandoned, the cultural traditions did not vanish.

But the structural conditions that had made empire-building possible in the western Sahel — the trans-Saharan trade as a concentrated revenue source, the agricultural surplus of the Inner Niger Delta, the gold supply chain running north — were all weakening simultaneously.
After Songhai, no successor state would manage to consolidate Sahelian power on a comparable scale.
The Mossi kingdoms persisted into the colonial period.
The Bambara kingdoms of Segou and Kaarta emerged in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries as regional powers, never approaching Songhai's territorial extent.

The various Fulani jihad states of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries — the Sokoto Caliphate in modern northern Nigeria, the Massina Empire in the central Inner Niger Delta, the Tukulor Empire of al-Hajj Umar Tall — were significant regional polities but operated in a fundamentally transformed commercial environment.
None of them matched Songhai's scale.
A pause for the broader picture, and the myth-puncturing that needs to happen.
Songhai's destruction is sometimes presented as evidence for "what West African civilization could have been if not for European colonialism." The framing is wrong on several counts.
First, the agent that ended Songhai was not European.
It was the Saadian Sultanate of Morocco — an Arab-Berber Islamic state with no European political affiliation, operating on its own strategic calculations.

Al-Mansur's invasion was a classic early-modern imperial expansion, motivated by the same calculations of revenue and prestige that drove Suleiman's Hungarian wars or Akbar's Deccan campaigns or Shah Abbas's Caucasus campaigns.
It was an Islamic-world geopolitical event, not a European intervention.

Second, the technology that enabled the Saadian victory — the matchlock musket, the artillery train, the disciplined volley-fire infantry — was not European in the sense that "European technology destroyed African civilization" implies.

Gunpowder weapons had been developed in China (Tang-Song China), refined across the Mongol-era trade networks (Mongol Empire Ch 8), spread through the Islamic world by the early sixteenth century, and adopted by Mediterranean Europeans in roughly the same timeframe.
By 1591, the Ottomans, Safavids, Mughals, Saadians, and Habsburg Spanish were all using essentially the same matchlock-and-artillery military system.
The Saadians acquired their gunpowder expertise partly from European Moriscos, but the underlying technology was a transcontinental Islamic-world adoption, not a European import.
Third, what European colonialism did to West Africa was structural rather than conquering.

The Atlantic trade reorientation that hollowed out the trans-Saharan gold supply was a slow shadow over the entire seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, gradually starving the Sahelian states of their economic foundation.

The actual European colonial conquest of West Africa came in the late nineteenth century — three centuries after Tondibi — and it operated on a Sahel that had already been structurally transformed by the Atlantic shift.
The "what could have been" speculation underestimates how long the Atlantic reorientation had been working before European armies actually arrived.
The honest reading of Songhai's fall is that it was destroyed by a combination of three factors.

First, internal: the long succession crisis after Askia Dawud's death had visibly weakened the central authority by 1591, making Saadian intervention attractive in a way it had not been a generation earlier.
Second, military: the gunpowder gap that Songhai had failed to close during the Dawud reign meant that even a small Moroccan force could defeat a much larger Songhai army in open battle.

Third, structural: the Atlantic reorientation was already underway, and even if Songhai had defeated the Saadian invasion in 1591, the long-term economic basis for the Sahelian empire was slowly collapsing.
Songhai was not destroyed by colonial Europe.

It was destroyed by the early-modern global gunpowder revolution, applied locally by a Moroccan sultan, against an empire that had been weakened by its own succession problems and was operating in an economy that was gradually being restructured by long-distance commercial shifts none of the participants fully understood.
The story is complex enough on its own terms; it does not need to be flattened into a colonial-grievance narrative.
Coda — What Survived The Songhai Empire ended in 1591.
The Songhai people did not, the language did not, the cultural traditions did not, and the manuscript tradition that had been Songhai's greatest intellectual achievement did not.
The modern Songhai population — perhaps several million speakers across modern Mali, Niger, and Burkina Faso — is the direct demographic descendant of the imperial population.

The language is still spoken; the traditional religion still exists in modified form; the river-fishing culture of the Sorko still operates along the Niger; the trading networks of the Wangara diaspora still connect the Niger Bend to the Mediterranean and increasingly to the Atlantic.
The manuscript tradition survived in private libraries through the centuries.

The 2012 rescue operation, led by Abdel Kader Haidara and a network of volunteers, smuggled tens of thousands of medieval manuscripts out of Timbuktu in metal trunks and rice sacks ahead of the jihadist occupation, hiding them in private homes in Bamako.

The operation rescued the largest concentration of pre-colonial sub-Saharan African writing still in existence — and most of what was rescued was Songhai-era Maliki jurisprudence, hadith collections, theological treatises, and the literary output of the Sankoré scholarly tradition.
The work of cataloging, digitizing, and translating the rescued manuscripts is still ongoing, decades after it began, and is one of the great unfinished projects of African historical scholarship.
The Tomb of Askia at Gao still stands.
UNESCO inscribed it as a World Heritage Site in 2004.
The mud-brick monument has required continuous maintenance for five hundred years, and the maintenance continues.
The Dendi kingdom maintained the Askia dynasty in exile until the French colonial conquest in 1901.

The ceremonial regalia of the Askias survived in the Dendi royal compound; some of the symbolic objects from the original Mecca-investiture of Askia Muhammad in 1497 — the green turban, the Prophet's-relic sword — are reportedly still preserved in family hands.
The three great mosques of Timbuktu still function as working mosques.
They have been re-plastered hundreds of times since they were built.
The maintenance is performed annually by the city's religious community, in the traditional Sudano-Sahelian technique that has not significantly changed in seven centuries.
The trans-Saharan caravan routes that Songhai had taxed and protected fell into long decline after 1591 but never quite vanished.

Salt caravans from Taghaza were still moving south to the Niger as recently as the late twentieth century, when the construction of paved roads and the rise of motor transport finally rendered the camel caravans obsolete.
The economic logic of the trans-Saharan trade — salt south from the desert, gold north from the savanna — had outlasted the empires it built by four centuries.
What did not survive was the imperial state.
Songhai produced no successor empire on its own scale.
The structural reorientation of West African commerce toward the Atlantic prevented any new Sahelian empire from consolidating after 1591.

The political vacuum was filled by smaller regional kingdoms — Bambara, Mossi, Hausa, Fulani — that were significant in their own contexts but never approached Songhai's territorial extent or institutional sophistication.
The largest continuous territory ever ruled by a sub-Saharan African state, the Songhai imperial peak around 1515, has not been matched by any successor.
What does it mean to call a civilization "destroyed" when the people, the language, the religion, the cultural traditions, and the manuscript archive all survive?
Songhai is a useful test case for that question.
The empire is gone — five centuries gone, with no real possibility of reconstruction — but the underlying civilization continues.
The matchlock at Tondibi ended the imperial state; it did not end the people who built it.
That is most of what can be said.

The rest is a matter of cataloging the manuscripts, walking the Tomb of Askia, listening to the modern Songhai musicians who carry the cultural memory forward, reading the Tarikh chronicles in their cramped Arabic script, and trying to imagine what fifteenth-century Timbuktu actually looked like under the Mecca-blessed regime that thought it had built something permanent.
The empire built more than it knew.
Most of what it built outlasted it.

chapters.title: The Sui Reunification
sentences: China had been broken for 369 years.
From the moment the Han dynasty officially ended in 220 CE (Han dynasty Ch 8) until the Sui armies crossed the Yangtze in 589, no single government had ruled all of China.
The Three Kingdoms split it three ways.
The brief Western Jin reunified it for a generation and then collapsed into the Disaster of Yongjia (Six Dynasties Ch 2).
The north fell to a long sequence of nomadic and Sino-nomadic dynasties; the south held out under a series of refugee Chinese courts (Six Dynasties Ch 4 and Ch 7).
For almost four centuries, "China" was a cultural memory rather than a political fact.
The reunifier was a northern aristocrat named Yang Jian (yahng JEE-en), and the dynasty he founded — the Sui (SWAY) — lasted just 37 years.
That sounds short, and it is.
But those 37 years did three things that shaped the next 1,400.
The Sui reassembled the country into a single state.
The Sui built the Grand Canal, the world's longest artificial waterway, which is still in use today.

And the Sui burned itself out so spectacularly that the Tang dynasty, which inherited the wreckage in 618, drew explicit lessons from the collapse and used those lessons to govern for nearly three centuries.
The pattern is one Chinese historians noticed early: a short, harsh, transformative dynasty reunifies the country through massive state projects, then bankrupts itself through overreach.
Then a long, successful golden-age dynasty inherits the infrastructure and refines the institutions.
The Qin did this in 221–206 BCE and the Han inherited it (Qin Dynasty Ch 7).
The Sui did it in 581–618 and the Tang inherited it (Chapter 2).

The pattern is so neat that some Chinese historians treated it as a moral lesson — harsh reunifiers are historically necessary but morally doomed — and as a governance principle: the next dynasty's job is to learn what not to do.
Yang Jian's path to the throne is one of the strangest in the dynasty-founding genre.
He was born in 541 CE into the Northern Zhou ruling class, one of several short-lived northern dynasties of the late Six Dynasties period.

The Yang family was Chinese in language and culture but had served the Xianbei (shyen-BAY) — the Inner Asian people whose Northern Wei dynasty had ruled north China from 386 to 534 (Six Dynasties Ch 6).

Like most of the northern aristocracy, the Yangs were ethnically and culturally hybrid: they held both a Chinese surname (Yang) and a Xianbei surname (Puliuru), spoke Chinese at home but Xianbei at court, and intermarried freely with both groups.
This is the world the Sui came out of.
It is also the reason the Tang founders, who came out of the same milieu, could project Chinese imperial authority into Central Asia later — they were already partially Inner Asian themselves.

Yang Jian rose through the Northern Zhou military and bureaucracy, married his daughter to the Northern Zhou emperor, and when his son-in-law died in 580 leaving a six-year-old grandson on the throne, Yang Jian became regent.
Within months he had eliminated rival princes, consolidated military command, and arranged for the child emperor to "abdicate" in his favor.
He proclaimed the Sui dynasty in 581 and took the reign name Wen (WEN — meaning "civil" or "cultured"), so he is known in the historical literature as Emperor Wen of Sui.
He was forty years old.

Eight years later, in 589, the Sui invasion force of 518,000 troops crossed the Yangtze in a coordinated multi-pronged amphibious assault, defeated the southern Chen (CHEN) dynasty in weeks, and reunified China.
The captured Chen emperor, Chen Shubao (chen shoo-BOW), was reportedly hiding in a palace well with two concubines when Sui soldiers found him.

The reunification was anticlimactic precisely because it was so overwhelming — the Sui had spent eight years consolidating the north and building the Yangtze fleet, and the Chen had spent the same period in court intrigue and luxury.
What Emperor Wen built in his 23-year reign (581–604) is the institutional foundation of everything that followed.
He commissioned a new capital in 582.
The old Han Chang'an site was cramped, polluted, and superstitiously inauspicious after centuries of dynastic failure on the location.
Wen ordered his architect Yuwen Kai (yoo-WEN KIGH) to lay out an entirely new city southeast of the old one, on a strict north-south grid plan.
The new capital was called Daxing (dah-SHING — "Great Prosperity"); the Tang would inherit it and rename it Chang'an (chahng-AHN — "Perpetual Peace").

Daxing covered approximately 32 square miles (84 km²), with the imperial palace at the north, government offices in the center, and 108 walled residential wards plus two enormous markets to the south.
It was the largest planned city in the world at the time of its construction and would become the largest city in the world during the Tang.
Its grid was copied by Japan for Nara in 710 and Heian-kyō (modern Kyoto) in 794, and by Korean capitals as well.
The architectural template of a Chinese imperial capital — central avenue, walled wards, north-south orientation, ceremonial palace at the head — was effectively codified at Daxing in the 580s.

Wen also promulgated the Kaihuang Code (kigh-HWAHNG) in 583, a unified legal code that drew on the best elements of the various northern and southern legal traditions that had developed during the Age of Division.
It reduced the number of capital offenses, distinguished intentional from accidental crimes, and ran to 500 articles in 12 chapters.
The Tang inherited it almost wholesale and revised it into the Tang Code of 624 (revised again in 653 with full commentary), which is the oldest complete Chinese legal code to survive.
The Tang Code in turn became the model for Japanese (the Taihō Code of 701), Korean, and Vietnamese law.
The legal infrastructure of all of East Asia traces back to Wen's Kaihuang reforms.
He began the civil service examination system that would define Chinese governance for the next 1,300 years.
Earlier dynasties had recruited officials through aristocratic recommendation and hereditary privilege.
The Sui introduced standardized written examinations in Confucian classics and policy as a parallel route into the bureaucracy, originally on a small scale.
The Tang would expand it dramatically (Chapter 2), and by the Song the jinshi exam would be the dominant path to high office (Chapter 6).
Emperor Wen did not invent meritocracy — but he opened the door.
He standardized weights, measures, and coinage.
He built a network of imperial granaries to stabilize the food supply across the reunified empire.

He restored Buddhist institutions that had been suppressed during a brief Northern Zhou persecution and used Buddhist relics as a propaganda instrument — in 601, he had relics distributed to thirty temples across the empire on a single day, a coordinated demonstration of dynastic reach and religious legitimacy.

He fought off the Eastern Turkic Khaganate (the dominant steppe power, occupying the same Mongolian and Inner Asian territories that the Xiongnu had held seven centuries earlier — Xiongnu-Huns Ch 8), playing different Turkic factions against each other to keep the northern frontier quiet.
Wen was not a glamorous ruler.
The historical record describes him as personally austere, suspicious of his own court, frugal to the point of stinginess, and increasingly paranoid in his later years.
But he was extraordinarily effective.

Modern historians rank him alongside Qin Shi Huang (Qin Dynasty Ch 4) as one of the two most consequential reunifiers in Chinese history — the man who reassembled what had been fragmented for centuries.
He was succeeded in 604 by his second son Yang Guang (yahng GWAHNG), who reigned as Emperor Yang of Sui and destroyed the dynasty in fourteen years.
The succession itself is one of the dynasty's mysteries.
Wen had originally designated his eldest son Yang Yong as heir.
Yang Guang, the second son, conducted a multi-year campaign of court intrigue to discredit his brother — feigning frugality and Confucian propriety while accusing Yang Yong of debauchery.
He succeeded in getting Yang Yong demoted from the position of Crown Prince in 600.
When Wen died in 604, Yang Guang inherited the throne.
Within hours, Wen's old chief minister was reporting that Yang Guang had murdered his father.
Modern historians remain divided on whether the parricide actually happened or whether the charge was a later Tang-era smear designed to delegitimize the Sui.
What is clear is that Yang Yong was killed within days of Wen's death, on Yang Guang's orders, removing the only viable rival.
Whatever the truth of the murder, Emperor Yang was now Sui.
He was thirty-five years old, intellectually brilliant, ferociously ambitious, and apparently unable to comprehend the concept of overreach.
He launched everything at once.
The signature project was the Grand Canal.
China's two great agricultural regions are separated by hundreds of miles of intervening terrain.
The Yellow River north grows wheat and millet on its loess plain (Ancient China Ch 1).
The Yangtze valley south grows rice in flooded paddies and supports enormously denser populations per square mile.

By the 6th century, the south had quietly become more populous and more economically productive than the north, partly because of agricultural advantages and partly because waves of refugees fleeing northern barbarian conquests over four centuries had pushed Chinese culture and labor south.

But moving rice from the south to the imperial capitals in the north was prohibitively expensive — overland transport of bulk grain in pre-modern conditions consumes most of what is being transported just feeding the porters and oxen along the way.
Emperor Yang's solution was to connect the existing river systems and shorter local canals into a single artificial waterway running north-south through the populated heart of China.

The Grand Canal stretched over 1,000 miles (1,700 km) in its full Sui-era form, from Hangzhou (hahng-JOH) on the south coast through the Yangtze, the Huai (HWIGH) River, the Yellow River, and on to the vicinity of modern Beijing in the north.
Sections were up to 130 feet wide, lined with stone where the soil was unstable, with willows planted along the banks for shade and to stabilize the embankments.
The canal was built between 605 and 611 — six years for over a thousand miles of waterway, much of it dug by hand.
The cost in human lives was staggering.

Contemporary chronicle accounts speak of more than five million laborers conscripted under corvée (kor-VAY — unpaid labor required by the state), with one adult male per every five households mandatorily drafted.

Death rates from overwork, exposure, and disease appear to have been very high; specific death tolls in the chronicles (one source claims roughly half the workers died) are probably exaggerated, but the underlying reality of mass mortality is not in serious dispute.
Whole villages were depopulated of their working men.
Communities fell behind schedule and were collectively punished.

Yang's Grand Canal is a piece of infrastructure on the same engineering scale as the Great Wall built four centuries earlier (Qin Dynasty Ch 4 — though the iconic stone Great Wall most tourists visit today is a Ming-era reconstruction, not Qin), and it was built by the same kind of mass-mobilized corvée system.
The political point of the canal was practical: it bound the wheat-and-millet north to the rice-growing south economically and allowed surplus southern rice to feed northern capitals and armies.
The strategic effect was permanent — for the next thousand years, control of the Grand Canal was control of China's economic backbone, and every subsequent dynasty rebuilt and maintained it.
It is still in operation today as a UNESCO World Heritage Site, the longest artificial river system in the world, with Sui-era sections still carrying barge traffic in 2026.
The political effect on the Sui itself was catastrophic.
The corvée burden fed peasant resentment exactly when the state needed peasant loyalty.

Yang made the situation worse by traveling the new canal in person on dragon-shaped pleasure barges so enormous that they reportedly required tens of thousands of laborers walking along the banks to pull them.
The image of imperial luxury floating on the bones of dead corvée workers became the defining symbol of Sui excess in later Chinese moralizing.
The Tang historians had every motive to exaggerate the picture; modern scholarship has questioned the most colorful details.
What is not in question is that the canal worked, that millions worked on it, and that many died.
The Grand Canal alone might have been survivable.
Then Yang invaded Korea.
The target was Goguryeo (go-GUR-yo, sometimes Romanized Koguryo), the powerful Korean kingdom whose territory ran across Manchuria and northern Korea (Ancient Korea Ch 6).
Goguryeo had refused to formally submit to Sui suzerainty, and Yang seems to have decided that the conquest of Goguryeo was the demonstration of Sui supremacy that would crown his reign.
He launched three invasions in three years, and all three failed catastrophically.
The 612 invasion is the campaign the historical record remembers.
Yang mobilized an army that contemporary chronicles place at over a million troops — a number that is probably inflated but that was certainly enormous by any standard.
The supply train was so vast that the rear of the marching column was reportedly leaving the staging ground when the front was already approaching the Yalu River.

The Goguryeo general Eulji Mundeok (UL-jee MUN-duck) used a classic feint-and-trap tactic — he allowed the Sui forces to advance deep into Korean territory, even pretending to surrender at one point, drawing them past their supply lines and into terrain favorable for ambush.
At the Salsu River, he had Korean engineers dam the river upstream while Sui troops were crossing, then released the dam during the crossing.
Of the 305,000 Sui troops that had crossed the Yalu, only about 2,700 returned.
Eulji Mundeok is still a national hero in Korea today.
The 613 and 614 invasions did no better.
Yang would not stop.
By 614, the empire was openly rebelling — peasant uprisings in multiple provinces, deserter bands forming armies of their own, regional governors raising private militias.
The Sui economy could not finance another mobilization, and the population could not be mobilized again without total revolt.

Yang withdrew to his southern pleasure capital at Jiangdu (jyahng-DOO, near modern Yangzhou) on the Yangtze and reportedly spent his last months in a haze of palace luxury, apparently unable to confront the disaster he had created.
In the spring of 618, Yang's own palace guards mutinied.
The story preserved in the chronicles has him on a balcony as the rebels closed in, asking what crime he had committed.
They strangled him with a silk sash.
The Sui dynasty had ruled all of China for 29 years (since the conquest of Chen in 589) and had been founded only 37 years earlier.
It was finished.
A Sui general named Li Yuan (lee yoo-EN), military governor of Taiyuan in Shanxi, had marched on Chang'an in late 617 with an army backed by Turkic cavalry.

He had taken the city in November and installed a puppet Sui emperor; when news of Yang's death arrived in 618, Li Yuan had the puppet abdicate and proclaimed himself emperor of a new dynasty: the Tang (TAHNG).
He was a Sui aristocrat, his mother had been a sister of Emperor Yang's mother, and his family — like Yang Jian's — was Sino-Xianbei in origin and Turkic in connections.
The dynasty he founded would last 289 years and become, in many later evaluations, China's greatest.
The Tang founders drew explicit lessons from the Sui collapse.
Don't overtax the peasantry.
Don't launch vanity wars before the economy can support them.
Don't build infrastructure faster than the population can endure.
Studying the Sui's mistakes became a centerpiece of Tang governance philosophy.

Wen had been the harsh reunifier; Yang had been the catastrophic overreacher; the Tang would inherit the canal, the new capital, the legal code, the granary system, the examinations, and the reunified state — and would govern with an institutional memory of what could go wrong.

Cross-civ check: while the Sui were reunifying China and building the Grand Canal, the Mediterranean world was watching the Byzantine Empire under Justinian I attempt his own reconquest of the Western Roman Empire (Byzantine Empire Ch 3).
Justinian rebuilt the Hagia Sophia in Constantinople (532–537), nearly contemporary with Yuwen Kai's design of Daxing.
Both projects involved massive imperial budgets and skilled engineering corps.
Justinian's empire reached its territorial peak in the 550s and immediately overstretched, much as Sui Yang would.

In Persia, the Sassanid Empire under Khosrow I and his successors was approaching its final century before the Arab Muslim conquest (Persian Empire Ch 10) — Khosrow died in 579, two years before Yang Jian became emperor.
In India, the post-Gupta Empire kingdoms (Gupta Empire Ch 8) were fragmenting into the regional states that would dominate medieval India.
The early Maya city-states in Mesoamerica were entering their Classic Period peak (Maya Civilization Ch 5).
And in northern Europe, the various successor kingdoms to the Western Roman Empire were still consolidating.

The 7th and 8th centuries — when the Tang would peak — became one of the most globally connected moments before the early-modern world, with the Tang at the eastern end of Eurasia trading along the Silk Road with the Sassanids, the Byzantines, and shortly the new Islamic Caliphate.

chapters.title: The Tang Founding & High Tang
sentences: The Tang dynasty was founded in 618 by Li Yuan (Chapter 1) — the Sui aristocrat-turned-rebel who took Chang'an and proclaimed himself Emperor Gaozu (GOW-zoo — "High Ancestor").
He was 51 years old, a competent but cautious general, with three adult sons who immediately began competing for the succession.
The middle son, Li Shimin (lee shih-MIN), was the family's military genius.

He had led the campaign that took Chang'an in 617, fought the unification wars that consolidated Tang control over a still-fragmented China through the early 620s, and accumulated the loyalty of the senior military commanders.
The eldest son, Li Jiancheng (lee jyen-CHENG), was the designated Crown Prince and held the political faction at court.
The younger son Li Yuanji (lee yoo-en-JEE) was allied with Jiancheng.
The brothers' rivalry was open and increasingly dangerous through the early 620s.
On July 2, 626, Li Shimin resolved the rivalry the way most Chinese succession disputes were resolved — by killing his brothers.
The episode is called the Xuanwu Gate Incident (shoo-en-WOO GAH-tuh), after the northern gate of the Chang'an palace where it took place.
Shimin and a small group of loyal officers ambushed Jiancheng and Yuanji as they rode toward the palace.
Shimin personally shot the Crown Prince dead with an arrow.
His ally Yuchi Gong (yoo-CHIH GAWNG), one of the most famous warriors of the era, killed Yuanji.

The brothers' families — including their adult and infant sons — were systematically hunted down and killed in the days that followed, eliminating any future rivals from the lines. (Shimin spared the wives and small daughters and, in a gesture of imperial magnanimity that may have been genuine or political, formally adopted some of his murdered brothers' surviving sons as his own.) Two months later, his shocked father Emperor Gaozu abdicated.
Li Shimin, twenty-eight years old, took the throne.
His reign name was Taizong (TIE-tsong — "Grand Ancestor"), and he is the figure known to history as Emperor Taizong of Tang.
He is, in most assessments, one of the two or three greatest emperors in Chinese history.
The contradiction between the bloody seizure of power and the model reign that followed is one of the things Tang historians struggled with for centuries.
Confucian historiography teaches that legitimate rule comes from virtue, and Shimin had begun his reign with fratricide.

The reconciliation the historians eventually settled on was that the brothers had themselves been plotting against him, that the Xuanwu Gate ambush was a defensive preemption, and that the subsequent quality of governance demonstrated retroactive virtue.

Modern historians are less certain — the "they were going to kill him first" version is largely supported by Tang-era sources written under Taizong's own court — but what is not in doubt is the quality of the reign.

Taizong's twenty-three year reign (626–649) is called the Zhenguan era (jen-GWAN — after the reign-name slogan "True View"), and it became the gold standard against which all subsequent Chinese reigns would be measured.
The Zhenguan reign got several big things right at once.
Taizong refined the equal-field system (juntian — joon-TYEN).
The system itself originated under the Northern Wei in the late 5th century (Six Dynasties Ch 6) as a way to distribute reclaimed farmland to peasant households after the chaos of nomadic wars.
Under Tang law (codified in 624), each adult male received an allotment of about 80 mu (roughly 12 acres) of farmland.
In return, he owed the state a fixed grain tax, a fixed cloth tax, and 20 days of corvée labor per year.
The land reverted to the state on his death and was redistributed to other households.

The system kept the peasantry tied to the land, kept the tax base broad, and kept the army supplied with men through a parallel fubing system in which militia soldiers held farm allotments in exchange for military service.

The equal-field model would underpin Tang prosperity for over a century before aristocratic estates and Buddhist monasteries quietly bought, encroached on, and inherited their way around it (Chapter 4).
Taizong expanded the civil service examination system.
Where Wen had introduced exams as a parallel track, Taizong made them the primary route to the most prestigious positions.

The most important degree was the jinshi (JIN-shr — "presented scholar"), which tested literary composition (including poetry — yes, the Tang government required prospective bureaucrats to compose poetry as part of the entry exam), Confucian classics, and policy argument.

The number of jinshi degrees granted per year was small — typically only a few dozen — but a jinshi pass became the dream of every ambitious family, and the resulting flood of literary effort is one major reason Tang poetry exploded into the form we know it as. (More on the poetry in Chapter 3.) He expanded the Tang military beyond Chinese borders.
In 630, the general Li Jing led a winter strike that captured the khagan (the supreme title of the Turkic ruler) of the Eastern Turkic Khaganate, Illig Qaghan.
The khaganate collapsed.
Taizong resettled the surrendered Turks south of the Gobi, near Chang'an, where they continued to serve in Tang armies as cavalry.

The Central Asian Turkic peoples acclaimed Taizong as Tian Kehan (TYEN kuh-HAHN — "Heavenly Khan"), an unprecedented title that explicitly combined the Chinese imperial role with supreme rulership over the steppe.
No previous Chinese emperor had claimed both.

The dual identity was real, not just rhetorical: Taizong's court included Turkic generals, Sogdian translators, and Inner Asian advisors as a matter of routine, and Tang armies continued to push west into the Tarim Basin (the great oasis-strung desert that connects China to Central Asia, today's Xinjiang).
By 657, under Taizong's successor, the Western Turkic Khaganate would also collapse before Tang general Su Dingfang, and Tang military protectorates would extend to the borders of Persia.
Taizong cultivated the image of a philosopher-king who welcomed criticism.
His most famous advisor was Wei Zheng (way JENG), a former servant of his murdered brother who had bluntly opposed Taizong's faction during the succession struggle.
Taizong, instead of executing him, made him a senior official and tolerated decades of public criticism.

The collected dialogues of their court discussions, compiled later as the Zhenguan Zhengyao ("Essentials of Government from the Zhenguan Era"), became required reading for Chinese rulers for centuries.
The famous Taizong line, addressed to his court after Wei Zheng's death in 643, runs roughly: "With a mirror of brass, you can adjust your hat.
With a mirror of history, you can understand the rise and fall of states.
With a mirror of men, you can see whether your actions are right or wrong.

I have lost a mirror." Whether or not the sentiment is exactly as recorded — the chronicles polish such moments — the Wei Zheng relationship was real and was the deliberate model Taizong wanted projected.

This combination — institutional reform, military expansion, examination meritocracy, dual Chinese-steppe legitimacy, and the philosopher-king image — defined what people meant by "the Zhenguan era" and the Tang at its early peak.
The Sui had reunified China; the Tang under Taizong made the reunification work.

Taizong died in 649 and was succeeded by his ninth son, who reigned as Emperor Gaozong (GOW-tsong, not to be confused with the founder Gaozu — Chinese emperors had complicated reign-name conventions that produced these collisions).
Gaozong's reign continued Taizong's policies, including the conquest of the Western Turks in 657.

But Gaozong's most consequential decision was personal rather than political: he married, and then politically empowered, a former low-ranking concubine of his father's named Wu Zhao (woo JOW), better known to history as Wu Zetian (woo zuh-TYEN).
She would become the only woman in Chinese history to formally hold the title of Huangdi ("Emperor") in her own name.
Wu Zetian's career is a chronicle of how an exceptionally capable woman could navigate one of the most patriarchal political systems ever constructed.
She entered the imperial palace around age fourteen as a fifth-rank concubine of Emperor Taizong.
After his death in 649, all the concubines without children were sent to a Buddhist convent — the standard fate.
Gaozong, who had apparently noticed her during his father's lifetime, brought her back to court within a few years.

She bore him sons, eliminated rival consorts (the chronicles accuse her of strangling her own newborn daughter and blaming it on the Empress, which would have been a horrifying piece of political maneuvering if true; modern historians regard the accusation as plausible but unproven), and was elevated to Empress in 655.
When Gaozong suffered a debilitating stroke in the early 660s, Wu Zetian effectively governed in his name for years.
After Gaozong's death in 683, she ruled through two of her own sons — installing one, deposing him when he proved insufficiently pliable, installing another.

In 690, judging that the political conditions were finally right, she deposed her own son, declared the Tang dynasty suspended, and proclaimed herself founder of a new dynasty called the Zhou (JOH — chosen for its association with the legendary virtuous Zhou dynasty of the early first millennium BCE, Zhou Dynasty Ch 1, not to be confused with the Northern Zhou of Yang Jian's rise).
She took the title Huangdi — Emperor — the same title used by every previous male ruler.
She was sixty-six years old.
This was, by the standards of the Confucian political order, cosmically wrong.
Confucian thought taught that the universe operated on a hierarchy of yin (female, passive, receiving) and yang (male, active, governing), and that political rule was structurally yang.
A woman ruling as Emperor was not merely improper; it was a violation of the natural order.

Wu Zetian's response to this objection was largely to ignore it — she promoted Buddhism, which offered more flexible roles for women than Confucianism, lavishly patronized Buddhist monasteries (commissioning the colossal Buddha at the Longmen Caves near Luoyang, with features said to be modeled on her own), and used Buddhist apocalyptic literature suggesting she might be the Maitreya (the future Buddha) reborn as a female ruler.
She governed effectively.

She expanded the examination system to bring in officials from outside the established northwestern aristocracy, creating a new political class of men who owed their careers to her rather than to family.
She moved the capital to Luoyang (LWAW-yang), the eastern capital first built under the Sui and Tang as a secondary administrative center.
She maintained military pressure on the Turkic peoples on the northern frontier.

And she invented around twelve new Chinese characters — most famously a new character for her own name, Zhao (照, or in her invented form 曌), composed of "sun" and "moon" above "sky." The new characters mostly fell out of use after her death; her name-character is still occasionally seen.
She was also ruthless.
She maintained a network of secret police and informers.
She was not above ordering the execution of opposition figures, including members of her own family (two of her own sons died under suspicious circumstances).

The Tang historiographical tradition that consolidated after her death vilified her with the standard misogynistic vocabulary — usurper, witch, harlot, depraved — and the picture of her in traditional Chinese histories is uniformly hostile.

Modern scholarship has substantially revised the judgment, noting that her administration was genuinely competent, that the empire was stable, that her economic and military policies were sound, and that her usurpation was no bloodier than any number of male-led successions in the same period (the Xuanwu Gate Incident, after all, was a male-led massacre that produced one of China's greatest emperors).
She abdicated in 705 under pressure from a court coup — she was eighty-one years old by then and clearly failing — and the Tang dynasty was formally restored under her son.
She died a few months later.
Her tombstone at her tomb west of Xi'an was deliberately left blank.
This is the Wordless Stele (无字碑, wu zi bei), which still stands today.
Whether the blankness was Wu Zetian's own instruction (her legacy was for history to judge) or her successors' decision (they could not agree on what to write about her) remains debated.

Either reading captures something true: she was a ruler whose actual achievements could not easily be reconciled with the moral framework that her own successors used to evaluate rulers, and the easiest solution was silence.

The dynasty that Wu Zetian had restored stabilized under a few short reigns and then settled into the long reign of her grandson, Li Longji (lee LONG-jee), who ruled from 712 to 756 as Emperor Xuanzong (shoo-en-TSONG — yet another Chinese reign name that English speakers must keep distinct from Gaozong, Gaozu, and Taizong; the Tang naming conventions were not built for foreign convenience).
Xuanzong's reign produced the Kaiyuan era (713–741), the absolute peak of the Tang.

The economy was prosperous, the equal-field system was still functioning, the examination system was producing a steady stream of capable officials, the military protected expansive Central Asian frontiers, and Chang'an was the most cosmopolitan city in the world.
The cultural flowering of the Kaiyuan era produced China's greatest poetry, most celebrated court music, and most brilliant Buddhist philosophy.
This is the High Tang that Chinese historical and literary tradition celebrates above all other moments.
Chapter 3 covers it.
The Kaiyuan era was also the setup for the catastrophe.

By the 740s, Xuanzong was in his sixties, increasingly disengaged from governance, and infatuated with a consort named Yang Guifei (yahng GWAY-fay) whose family was acquiring uncomfortable political power.
The frontier military commands had been delegated to a handful of generals who controlled standing armies far larger than the central court could match.
The most powerful of those generals was a man of mixed Sogdian-Turkic origin named An Lushan (AHN loo-SHAHN), and in December 755 he rebelled.
Chapter 4 covers what happened next.

But before the rebellion, before the catastrophe, there is the High Tang itself — the cosmopolitan capital, the poetry, the Silk Road at its peak, the absorption of foreign religions and foreign cultures into Chinese life on a scale that would not be seen again.
That is Chapter 3.

Cross-civ check: Wu Zetian's reign (effectively 660s–705) overlaps with the rise of the Umayyad Caliphate in the Middle East — the first Islamic empire, which by 700 controlled territory from Spain to Central Asia (Islamic Golden Age Ch 2).
The Umayyad-Tang frontier in Central Asia was already shaping up; the Battle of Talas in 751 (Chapter 4) would be its first major collision.
The Byzantine Empire under the Heraclian dynasty was simultaneously losing Egypt, Syria, and North Africa to the Arab conquests (Byzantine Empire Ch 5).

In Japan, the Taika Reform of 645 had remodeled the Japanese government on Tang lines, copying Tang law, examinations, and capital design (Ancient Japan Ch 7) — Nara, founded in 710 on the Daxing/Chang'an grid, is one of the clearest examples of Tang cultural projection.
In Korea, the Silla kingdom unified the peninsula in 668 with Tang military assistance (Ancient Korea Ch 6), then promptly fought Tang armies to assert independence.
The Tang influence on East Asia in this period was so deep that historians sometimes treat the entire region as a Tang-centered cultural sphere — the original "Sinosphere."

chapters.title: The Cosmopolitan Capital
sentences: There are not many cities in human history that you can say with confidence were the largest, most populous, and most culturally important on Earth at a specific moment.
Tang Chang'an in the early 8th century is one of them.
The numbers matter, so it's worth pausing on them.

Chang'an covered approximately 32 square miles (84 km²) inside its walls — the inner walled city alone was about seven times the size of contemporary Constantinople, the largest city in Europe at the time, and roughly five times the area of Baghdad after the Abbasids built it in the 760s.
The walls themselves were about 18 miles (29 km) in circumference.
The central north-south avenue, Zhuque Boulevard, was 150 meters wide — nearly 500 feet, broader than any street in any modern city.
The population at peak is estimated at over a million inside the walls, with another million in the suburbs and surrounding districts.

By comparison, contemporary Constantinople probably held 300,000–500,000; Baghdad after its 762 founding would briefly approach the same range; Rome at its imperial peak had reached around a million but had collapsed to perhaps 50,000 by the 8th century.
Tang Chang'an in 700–750 was the largest and most populous city on Earth, and was probably the largest city the world had ever seen up to that point.
It was also, by a significant margin, the most cosmopolitan.
The grid-plan structure of Chang'an, inherited from Yuwen Kai's Sui-era Daxing (Chapter 1), was a perfect machine for managing a multicultural population.
The 108 walled wards — each a city block surrounded by its own internal walls with gates that closed at curfew — could be assigned to specific communities.
Foreign quarters, religious enclaves, and residential districts for different social classes all had their own ward or cluster of wards.
This was social engineering by urban planning.
The foreign communities were extensive and visible.

Sogdian merchants from Central Asia (Iranian-speaking traders, the dominant intermediaries of Silk Road commerce) had their own quarters — Sogdian-named families show up routinely in Tang tax records, court documents, and tomb inscriptions.

Persian refugees and merchants formed substantial communities, particularly after the Sassanid Empire fell to the Arab Muslim conquest in the 650s (Persian Empire Ch 10) and the last Sassanid prince Peroz III fled east to seek Tang protection.
Arab merchants arrived after the establishment of the Umayyad and then Abbasid caliphates, traveling the Silk Road and the southern sea route.
Indian Buddhist monks and scholars came overland through the Tarim Basin or by sea through the southern ports.

Korean students came in numbers — the Tang court ran what was essentially an international university for sons of Korean and Japanese aristocrats — and Japanese delegations came on the periodic embassies known as the kentōshi (Ancient Japan Ch 7), spending years studying Tang government, law, art, and Buddhism before returning home.
The religions present in Chang'an reflected this.
Buddhism was by far the most influential foreign religion, having arrived from India centuries earlier (Six Dynasties Ch 5) and now fully integrated into Chinese life.

But the city also hosted Zoroastrian fire temples, Nestorian Christian churches (the Christian community even put up a stele in 781, the Nestorian Stele, recording the arrival of Christianity in 635 under Taizong — an extraordinary document that astonished European missionaries when it was rediscovered in 1625, since they had assumed they were bringing Christianity to China for the first time), Manichaean shrines (Manichaeism was a Persian religion that survived in Central Asia long after dying out in Persia itself), and Islamic mosques following the establishment of regular Muslim merchant communities in the 7th and 8th centuries.
This was not religious tolerance in the modern liberal sense.
The Tang state regulated foreign religions, restricted certain kinds of conversion, and would in 845 launch a major persecution of Buddhism (Chapter 4).

What the Tang state did do, especially in the High Tang period, was permit foreign communities to maintain their own religious institutions in their own neighborhoods on the assumption that this kept them stable and their merchants productive.
The framework was pragmatic, not principled.
It produced something like the most religiously diverse single city in the early-medieval world.
The economic engine driving all this was the Silk Road at its historical peak.

The "Silk Road" is a name coined by the 19th-century German geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen (a useful one-line intro: he was a Berlin geographer who traveled extensively in China in the 1860s–70s and named the trade network Seidenstrasse in an 1877 publication).
It was not a single road but a network of overland and maritime trade routes connecting China to Central Asia, Persia, and the Mediterranean.
The network had operated since the Han dynasty (Han Dynasty Ch 5), when Chinese diplomatic missions had first opened direct contact with the Central Asian kingdoms.
It had been disrupted during the Six Dynasties chaos.

The Tang military expansion into the Tarim Basin in the 630s–650s, and the establishment of the Anxi Protectorate (the Tang military command zone covering the four great oasis cities of Kucha, Khotan, Kashgar, and Karashahr) gave Chinese armies direct control over the Silk Road oases for the first time since the Han.
What flowed through the network is worth pausing on.
From China westward: silk (China was the only producer of silk for centuries, and silk remained an enormous luxury throughout the Mediterranean world), porcelain, paper, lacquerware, and silver.

Eastward from Central Asia, Persia, and beyond: horses (Tang armies depended on imported horses for cavalry, and the Tang state ran an enormous bureaucracy just to manage the horse trade), gemstones, glassware (Tang Chinese glassblowing was minimal; almost all glass was imported from Persia or further west), spices, aromatic woods, exotic foods, musical instruments, and slaves.
The trade was conducted primarily by Sogdian merchants speaking the Sogdian language, which served as the lingua franca of Silk Road commerce.

Sogdian-language documents have been found from China to the Black Sea. (Sogdian is now extinct as a spoken language; its closest modern relative is Yaghnobi, spoken by a few thousand people in the mountains of Tajikistan.) The cultural traffic was as significant as the goods.
Central Asian music, dance, food, fashion, and art flooded into Tang Chang'an.
The pipa (a four-string lute) is a Central Asian instrument that Chinese musicians adopted and that became a defining sound of Chinese classical music.

The whirling dances of the Sogdian and Central Asian performers (one famous example: An Lushan, of whom more shortly, was reportedly an enormously fat man — over 300 pounds — whose performance of Sogdian whirling dances delighted Emperor Xuanzong's court) became standard entertainment at imperial banquets.

Tang ceramic figurines from this period preserve a remarkable visual record of the era: Bactrian camels loaded with goods accompanied by bearded Sogdian merchants, foreign musicians playing Central Asian instruments, dancers in foreign dress, foreign ambassadors in their distinctive costumes.

These figurines are the single best surviving record of how visibly multicultural Chang'an was — the sancai (san-TSIGH, "three-color") glazed Tang figurines in amber, green, and cream are among the most recognizable Tang artifacts.

The maritime trade route — through the South China Sea, the Strait of Malacca, the Indian Ocean, and on to East Africa — was also active by the High Tang, particularly through the southern ports of Guangzhou (gwang-JOH) and Quanzhou (chwen-JOH).

Arab merchants established communities in Guangzhou by the late 7th century; by 879 the Arab community in Guangzhou would number in the tens of thousands (with disastrous consequences in that year — Chapter 4).
The maritime route would become dominant after the An Lushan Rebellion disrupted the overland Silk Road, and would peak under the Song (Chapter 8).
The cultural product the Tang is most remembered for is poetry.
