Tang poetry occupies a position in Chinese culture roughly comparable to what Shakespeare occupies in English — except that the Tang produced about a dozen poets of comparable stature rather than one, and the result is that contemporary Chinese schoolchildren memorize hundreds of Tang poems through their education.
Two figures dominate the canon, and they have been paired in Chinese literary criticism for over a thousand years: Li Bai (lee BIGH) and Du Fu (doo FOO).
Li Bai (701–762), called the Immortal Poet (Shixian — SHEE-shyen), was the wild one.
He was probably born in Central Asia to a Chinese family — there are theories that his family had Sogdian or Turkic connections, though the evidence is thin — and grew up in what is now Sichuan.

He never sat the civil service examinations and never had a stable government career; instead he wandered China as a Daoist-influenced poet, drinking, writing, occasionally appearing at court (he had a brief stint as a court poet under Xuanzong before being dismissed for, depending on the source, drunkenness or arrogance or political missteps), and dying in obscurity.
Legend says he drowned trying to embrace the moon's reflection in a river while drunk; the reality was probably more prosaic.
His poetry is what survives him.
Li Bai wrote with an apparent effortlessness on subjects like wine, moonlight, friendship, the natural world, and the sense of cosmic isolation that comes from being a human in a vast universe.
His best-known poem, "Quiet Night Thought" (床前明月光, Chuangqian mingyue guang), runs only twenty characters in Chinese — about a paragraph in English translation.
It is probably the most widely memorized Chinese poem ever written; virtually every Chinese schoolchild can recite it.
Its surface is minimal.
Its emotional reach is enormous.
The combination of formal compression and emotional vastness is the Li Bai signature.
Du Fu (712–770), called the Poet Sage (Shisheng — SHEE-shung), was the disciplined one.

He came from a family of scholars, sat the examinations and failed (multiple times — Du Fu's examination failures became part of his legend), spent much of his adult life in poverty, and lived through the An Lushan Rebellion as a refugee.
The catastrophe of those years shaped his work permanently.

Where Li Bai writes about cosmic isolation, Du Fu writes about national tragedy: families torn apart by war, peasants conscripted to die in border campaigns, the spring view from his windowsill turning into a meditation on dynastic collapse.

His poem "Spring View" (春望, Chun wang) — written in 757, after the An Lushan rebels had captured Chang'an and Du Fu was trapped in the occupied city — opens with the characters 国破山河在 (the country is broken; the mountains and rivers remain).
It is one of the most quoted lines in all of Chinese literature.
Du Fu also perfected the formal technical structure of Chinese poetry.

The form called lüshi (LOO-shr — "regulated verse") is a strict eight-line poem with rigid rules about tonal patterns and parallelism between paired lines; Du Fu was its supreme practitioner, and "Du Fu lüshi" became the benchmark against which all later regulated verse was measured.

The pairing of Li Bai and Du Fu — the wild Daoist transcendentalist and the disciplined Confucian witness, the sky and the earth, the wine cup and the conscience — became the structuring frame for how Chinese literary tradition organized its understanding of poetry.
They knew each other (briefly) in person; Du Fu wrote multiple poems for and about Li Bai, in tones of deep affection and deeper anxiety about Li Bai's drinking and instability.
The friendship is one of the most touching footnotes in Chinese literary history, two of the greatest poets in any language each writing about the other.

Tang poetry is enormous — the standard Complete Tang Poetry compiled in 1705 contains over 48,000 poems by more than 2,200 authors — and Li Bai and Du Fu are only the two most famous of dozens of major figures.

Wang Wei (701–761) was a court official who wrote spare, Chan-Buddhist-influenced landscape poetry that paired with his work as a painter (Wang Wei is sometimes considered the founder of Chinese literati landscape painting, though most of his actual paintings have been lost).

Bai Juyi (BIGH joo-EE, 772–846) wrote in a deliberately accessible style — legend has it he read his drafts aloud to an illiterate elderly servant and revised anything she could not understand, which is probably an exaggeration but captures something true about his voice.

His 120-line narrative poem "Song of Everlasting Sorrow" (长恨歌, Changhen ge), about Emperor Xuanzong's love affair with Yang Guifei and her death during the An Lushan Rebellion, is one of the most famous poems in the language.

Bai Juyi was also enormously influential abroad — his collected works arrived in Japan within his own lifetime and shaped the Tale of Genji (the great Heian-period Japanese novel of around 1010) and centuries of Japanese poetry.

The structural reason Tang poetry exploded in this period was partly the examination system: composing regulated verse on assigned topics was a required component of the jinshi exam, which meant that every educated man in the empire — every aspiring official, every gentleman-scholar — was practicing poetry as a professional skill from his teenage years onward.
This produced a vast amateur poetic culture out of which the great geniuses emerged.

The structural reason it eventually mattered globally is that the Chinese examination model was eventually adopted by Korea (Gwageo), Vietnam, and Japan (the Heian court adopted Chinese-style exams in modified form), spreading Tang literary forms and conventions throughout East Asia.
Beyond poetry, the High Tang produced equally important developments in religion, calligraphy, and visual art.
Chan Buddhism (CHAHN — pronounced "chan" in Chinese, transmitted to Japan as Zen, to Korea as Seon, to Vietnam as Thiền) crystallized as a distinctly Chinese school during the Tang.

Its tradition traced its lineage back to Bodhidharma (a monk said to have arrived from India in the early 6th century, though his historicity is debated; Six Dynasties Ch 5), but its mature form developed over the 7th and 8th centuries.

Chan emphasized meditation (chan is the Chinese pronunciation of the Sanskrit dhyana, "meditation") and the possibility of sudden enlightenment through direct experience rather than through textual study or accumulated merit.

The Sixth Patriarch Huineng (HWAY-nung, c. 638–713) is the foundational Chan figure; his Platform Sutra, supposedly recorded by his disciples after his death, is the only Chinese-composed text accorded the status of "sutra" (a word normally reserved for the discourses of the historical Buddha himself).

Chan would survive the Tang's anti-Buddhist persecution (Chapter 4) better than most Buddhist schools precisely because it required minimal institutional infrastructure — no large monasteries, no expensive liturgical equipment, just teacher-student transmission.
Chan would shape East Asian aesthetics for the next thousand years through its influence on tea ceremony, garden design, ink-painting, and martial arts.
Calligraphy reached one of its peaks in the Tang.

Yan Zhenqing (YEN jen-CHING, 709–785) developed a bold, structured style of regular script (kaishu) that broke from the elegant lyrical tradition of the great Six Dynasties calligrapher Wang Xizhi (Wang Xee-JEH, 303–361, often called the "Sage of Calligraphy" — Six Dynasties Ch 4).
Yan's "muscular" style emphasized structural integrity over delicacy.

He was also a model Confucian scholar-official: he organized military resistance to the An Lushan rebels in the northeast, served the Tang faithfully through decades of crises, and was finally executed at age seventy-six by a regional warlord rebel for refusing to defect.

The combination of artistic mastery and personal integrity made Yan Zhenqing the Confucian ideal of a scholar-official in posterity, and his calligraphic style became one of the four standard models taught in Chinese schools for over a millennium.
Painting developed under the Tang in directions that the Song would extend (Chapter 8).

Tang painters worked in colored mineral pigments on silk, with a specialty in horse paintings (the Tang court's Central Asian horses were prestige objects and frequent subjects), figure paintings, and decorative court scenes.
The shift to monochrome ink and to the dominant Chinese genre of monumental shanshui (mountains-and-water) landscape painting would happen under the Song.
Pottery is one of the era's most globally recognizable products.

The sancai (three-color) glazed ceramics of the Tang — usually camels, horses, court ladies, foreign musicians, and tomb guardians, glazed in amber, green, and cream — are among the most distinctive Tang artifacts.
They have been found across Eurasia.

The Belitung shipwreck, an Arab dhow that sank around 830 in the Java Sea while carrying Tang export ceramics back to the Middle East, contained over 60,000 pieces, including bowls, dishes, ewers, and the earliest known Chinese blue-and-white porcelain (which would later become the global signature of Chinese ceramics under the Yuan and Ming).
The English word "china" for porcelain comes from this trade.

Tang ceramics established the global demand for Chinese pottery that would define international trade for the next thousand years, and that would eventually drive the Ming to mass-produce blue-and-white for European markets seven centuries later.
A pause, before the catastrophe.
The High Tang of Xuanzong's Kaiyuan era (713–741) is one of those moments in human history that produces more than its fair share of cultural heritage.
China had been reunified for 150 years by Xuanzong's reign and was at peace internally.
The economy was prosperous.
The military had pushed Chinese influence further west than at any point in history.
The capital was the largest city in the world and the most multicultural city in pre-modern Eurasia.
The poetry, calligraphy, ceramics, music, and Buddhism of the era are still actively quoted, performed, and practiced in modern China.
There is a reason the Kaiyuan reign is the moment Chinese cultural memory returns to most often.
It is also the case that this moment was created by structural conditions that would not last.
The equal-field land system was already breaking down — the chronicles of the 740s record growing problems with private estates, falling tax revenues, and the corruption of local administration.

The frontier military system had drifted from the Sui-era model of fubing militia farmers to professional standing armies under regional military governors called jiedushi (jyeh-DOO-shr — "military commissioners"), each commanding tens of thousands of professional soldiers.

The court was dominated by Yang Guifei's family faction (her cousin Yang Guozhong rose to become chancellor) in growing conflict with the most powerful jiedushi, An Lushan, whose three frontier commands in the northeast controlled over 160,000 troops.
The fiscal cost of the standing armies was enormous, and the Tang had no good way to control commanders who controlled their own soldiers, payrolls, and supply networks.
Xuanzong, by the 740s and 750s, was in his sixties and increasingly disengaged.
He had been a vigorous reformist emperor in his early decades; in his later years, he delegated.
The combination — failing land system, restive professional armies, weak central control, factional war at court — was exactly the recipe for the catastrophe that arrived in December 755.
Cross-civ check: the High Tang Chang'an of the early 8th century is contemporary with the Umayyad Caliphate at its peak, with Damascus as its capital and territory from Spain to Central Asia.
The Umayyads would be overthrown by the Abbasid Caliphate in 750 (Islamic Golden Age Ch 1), shifting the Islamic capital east to Baghdad (founded 762).
The Abbasid Baghdad of the 8th–9th century would briefly approach Chang'an in size and would inherit the cosmopolitan-trade-network position the Tang was about to lose.
The Byzantine Empire under the Isaurian dynasty was wracked by the Iconoclast controversy over religious images (Byzantine Empire Ch 5).
The Carolingian dynasty in western Europe was consolidating under Charles Martel (defeated the Arabs at Tours in 732) and his grandson Charlemagne (crowned Holy Roman Emperor in 800).
In Mesoamerica, the great Maya city of Tikal was at its peak (Maya Civilization Ch 6).
In the Andes, the Wari and Tiwanaku empires were dominating their respective regions.

The 8th century Eurasian world was unusually densely interconnected — the silk that left Tang Chang'an reached Constantinople and Baghdad and was traded onward to Carolingian Europe, while Buddhist and Islamic ideas circulated along the same routes — and Tang Chang'an was the eastern anchor of the system.
The system was about to break.

chapters.title: The An Lushan Rebellion and the Late Tang
sentences: In December 755, An Lushan rebelled against the Tang dynasty, and it took eight years of warfare to suppress him.
The fighting killed something on the order of 13 to 36 million people, by the most cited modern estimate.
That number deserves some context.
The estimate comes from a comparison of Tang census records before and after the rebellion.
The 754 census recorded a registered population of about 53 million.
The 764 census, after the rebellion's end, recorded about 17 million.
A 36-million decline in registered population in a decade would imply, if taken literally, the deadliest war in human history before the 20th century — comparable in raw scale to World War II.
Modern historians treat the figure as imperfect but suggestive.

Some of the apparent decline reflects people who simply stopped being registered for taxation as the central state collapsed (many regions slid out of central control, with their populations vanishing from the imperial books while continuing to live and pay taxes to local warlords).
Some reflects refugee dispersal, with people fleeing south or to remote areas where census-takers could not reach them.
Some reflects deliberate evasion as families dropped off the registers to avoid corvée and military conscription.

The conservative range — even adjusting downward for these factors — still puts the death toll in the millions, possibly the low tens of millions, making the An Lushan Rebellion one of the deadliest single conflicts in pre-modern human history.
The Mongol conquests (Mongol Empire Ch 5) and the Ming-Qing transition (Qing Dynasty's founding) are the only competitors.
Whatever the exact number, the demographic and political impact was catastrophic.
The Tang dynasty technically lasted another 144 years after the rebellion ended in 763, but it never recovered its central authority.
The rest of the Tang story is the slow, often beautiful decay of an empire that had lost its core.
An Lushan himself is one of the strangest figures in Chinese history.
He was born around 703 in the borderlands northeast of China, of mixed Sogdian and Turkic ancestry (his father was probably Sogdian; his mother was a Turkic shamaness).
His name in Sogdian was probably Rokhshan, with An being the Sinified version of his clan name and Lushan the Sinified version of his given name.

He grew up multilingual — he reportedly spoke six languages — and entered the Tang military as a frontier officer in his twenties, rising rapidly through ability and through the patronage of the powerful Tang general Zhang Shougui.
He was also enormously fat.
The chronicles describe him as weighing over 330 pounds, with a belly that hung to his knees, and report that Emperor Xuanzong's court found his obesity comically endearing.

An Lushan exploited this — he played the role of the loyal foreign clown at court, performing Sogdian whirling dances despite his bulk, addressing Yang Guifei (despite being older than her) as his "mother," and presenting himself to Xuanzong as a barbarian buffoon whose loyalty was beyond question.
In private, he was acquiring three of the Tang's most important frontier military commands.

By the early 750s, he was simultaneously jiedushi of three of the seven major frontier zones (Pinglu, Fanyang, and Hedong) — controlling the northeast frontier from the area of modern Beijing west to Shanxi — with over 160,000 professional troops under his direct command.
Almost half the Tang's frontier military strength reported to a single man.
The political crisis that triggered the rebellion was the rivalry between An Lushan and Yang Guozhong (yahng gwaw-CHONG), Yang Guifei's cousin who had risen to become chief chancellor at court.
Yang Guozhong, watching An Lushan accumulate military power, repeatedly warned Xuanzong that An Lushan was about to rebel.
An Lushan, hearing of Yang Guozhong's accusations, became convinced that he had to rebel before being purged.

Xuanzong refused to credit the warnings — he liked An Lushan, considered him a personal favorite, and reportedly said his trust was so complete that he would believe An Lushan if he said the sun and moon had collided.

In December 755, An Lushan marched south from his base at Fanyang (modern Beijing) at the head of his frontier armies, claiming he had been sent by secret imperial decree to remove Yang Guozhong from court.
Loyalty to "Emperor Xuanzong against treacherous officials" was the conventional cover story for any Chinese coup.
Within weeks, An Lushan had crossed the Yellow River and captured Luoyang, the eastern capital.
In January 756, he formally proclaimed himself emperor of a new Yan dynasty.
The Tang response was incompetent at the highest level and brave at the operational level.
The strategic disaster was at the Tongguan Pass (TONG-gwan), the fortified mountain pass that controlled the approach to Chang'an from the east.
Tang general Geshu Han held the pass with a Tang army that, while inferior in quality to An Lushan's professionals, occupied a position so strong that the rebels could not force it.
Yang Guozhong, fearing Geshu Han's growing political importance and possibly suspecting his loyalty, pressured Xuanzong to order Geshu Han to abandon the pass and attack the rebel army in the open.
Geshu Han knew this was suicidal but obeyed.
The Tang army was destroyed.
The road to Chang'an was open.
Xuanzong fled west toward Sichuan in June 756, with Yang Guifei, Yang Guozhong, and the imperial entourage.
At a place called Mawei Station (mah-WAY), about 60 miles west of Chang'an, the imperial guards mutinied.
They killed Yang Guozhong and his sons, then demanded that Yang Guifei be killed as well.
Xuanzong, aged seventy-one, refused for a moment and then conceded.
Yang Guifei was strangled with a silk cord by the chief eunuch Gao Lishi.

The episode became one of the great tragic love stories in Chinese literature, mourned by Bai Juyi in his "Song of Everlasting Sorrow" (Chapter 3) and retold in Chinese poetry, opera, and film for over a thousand years afterward.
Xuanzong continued into Sichuan.
His son Li Heng, who had been left behind with another army at the city of Lingwu in the northwest, was acclaimed emperor by his troops without his father's approval.
He took the throne as Emperor Suzong (SOO-tsong), and Xuanzong, now in Sichuan, accepted the fait accompli and abdicated.
The dynasty had two emperors briefly, then one again.
Chang'an itself fell to An Lushan's forces in late 756.

The rebels looted the capital and conducted what amounted to ethnic-cleansing raids on the city's Persian, Sogdian, and other foreign communities — many of which were unfairly associated with An Lushan because of his Sogdian ethnicity, even though most foreigners in Chang'an had no political connection to him.
The recovery took eight years.
The Tang court, operating from refuge in the northwest, called on multiple sources of military aid.

The most important was the Uyghur Khaganate (OO-ee-gur — a Turkic-speaking confederation that had risen on the Mongolian steppe after the collapse of the Eastern Turkic Khaganate, displacing the Tang's earlier Turkic vassals).
The Uyghurs sent cavalry south in exchange for trade privileges, formal recognition, and substantial bribes.
The Uyghur cavalry was militarily decisive — the recovery of Chang'an in 757 and Luoyang shortly afterward depended on Uyghur shock cavalry assaulting positions Tang infantry could not take alone.

The price was that the Uyghurs were allowed to sack Luoyang as their reward in 762, and that the Tang court formally treated the Uyghur khagan as a peer rather than as a vassal — a major status shift away from the Tang's earlier dual-monarchy posture in Central Asia.
The rebellion itself fragmented and turned on itself.

An Lushan was murdered in January 757 by his own son An Qingxu, who had been alarmed by his father's growing erratic behavior — An Lushan was going blind, possibly diabetic, possibly mentally ill, and had reportedly been beating his entourage with sticks.
An Qingxu then ruled the rebel state briefly before being murdered in turn by another rebel general, Shi Siming, who in turn was murdered by his son Shi Chaoyi in 761.
The rebel dynasty consumed itself through patricide and assassination over four years before finally collapsing in 763.

The pattern is too neat to be entirely accidental — once the founding charisma of An Lushan was gone, the rebel army fragmented along the same lines that the late Tang frontier military had fragmented, with each commander fighting for personal power.
By the official end of the rebellion in 763, the Tang dynasty had survived but was structurally transformed.
Northern China was depopulated.
The economy was wrecked.
The equal-field land system had collapsed beyond repair — too many records had been destroyed, too many peasants had fled, too many estates had absorbed too much abandoned land.
The Tang military system based on fubing militia-farmers was gone, replaced by professional standing armies under regional military governors.
Most consequentially, the central government had largely lost control over those regional governors.

The jiedushi (military commissioners) of the old frontier zones — and a growing number of jiedushi in the interior, set up during the rebellion to fight the rebels and never demobilized after — became effectively autonomous regional warlords.
They collected their own taxes, raised their own armies, controlled their own succession (often passing the office father-to-son), and paid only nominal loyalty to the Tang court.
The Tang dynasty after 763 was no longer the centralized empire of the Zhenguan and Kaiyuan eras.
It was an emperor in Chang'an surrounded by a patchwork of semi-independent military regions, with central control most effective in the southern and central regions and weakest in the northeast.

This "fragmented Tang" lasted from 763 to 907 — 144 years, longer than the dynasty had existed before the rebellion — and produced its own art, poetry, and political innovations even as it slowly disintegrated.
The cultural life of the Late Tang was, against expectations, almost as rich as the High Tang.
Du Fu (Chapter 3) wrote his greatest work in the years after the rebellion, as a refugee.

His poems on the war's effects on ordinary people — "Song of the War Chariots" on the conscription system, "Three Officials" and "Three Partings" on the recruitment of new troops from devastated villages — are among the most powerful war poetry in any language.
He died in 770, in poverty, on a small boat on the Xiang River in Hunan.
His reputation grew slowly over the next two centuries; by the Song dynasty, he was generally accepted as the greatest poet in the Chinese tradition.
Bai Juyi (Chapter 3) wrote his "Song of Everlasting Sorrow" in 806, retelling the Yang Guifei tragedy.
He also wrote the New Yuefu poems, which used verse to critique social injustice — the corvée system, the conscription burden, the corruption of the military commissions.
His commitment to clarity over obscurity made him one of the most widely read poets in East Asian history; his collected works arrived in Japan within his lifetime.
Han Yu (HAHN YOO, 768–824) is a different sort of figure.

He was a senior official, a successful examination candidate, and a leader of a literary movement called the guwen (GOO-wen — "ancient prose") movement, which rejected the highly ornate parallel-prose style that had dominated Chinese writing since the Six Dynasties (Six Dynasties Ch 4) in favor of a return to the more direct, classical style of pre-Qin and Han writers.

Han Yu wrote a famously controversial memorial to Emperor Xianzong in 819, opposing the imperial veneration of a Buddhist relic (a finger bone of the Buddha that had been brought to Chang'an for ceremonial display).
Han Yu argued that Buddhism was a foreign corruption of Chinese values, that the cult of relics was vulgar superstition, and that the emperor was demeaning himself by participating.
The emperor was furious; Han Yu was nearly executed and was instead exiled to the southern frontier.
The memorial became one of the most famous prose pieces in Chinese literature, and Han Yu is generally counted as one of the Eight Great Prose Masters of the Tang and Song.
His anti-Buddhist Confucian revival also planted the seeds that would grow into Neo-Confucianism under the Song three centuries later (Chapter 8).

The Late Tang also produced the Diamond Sutra of 868 — a Buddhist text printed by woodblock on a 17-foot scroll, commissioned by a man named Wang Jie "for universal free distribution," and recovered from the Mogao Caves at Dunhuang (DUN-hwahng — the great oasis-city Buddhist library on the Silk Road, in the western Gansu corridor).
The Diamond Sutra is the world's oldest dated complete printed book, predating Gutenberg's first European movable-type printing by nearly six hundred years.

It was sealed in a hidden cave at Dunhuang around 1000 CE, rediscovered by a Daoist caretaker named Wang Yuanlu in 1900, and acquired by the Hungarian-British archaeologist Aurel Stein in 1907 for the British Museum.
It is now in the British Library.

Its survival is one of the great accidents of textual history — the Mogao Caves' dry desert climate preserved tens of thousands of Buddhist manuscripts, paintings, and printed texts that would have been destroyed almost anywhere else in China.
Two events bracket the dynasty's actual end.
The first is the Great Anti-Buddhist Persecution of 845, under Emperor Wuzong (WOO-tsong, ruled 840–846).
Wuzong was a devoted Daoist (in the religious sense — Daoism in this period had developed into a full religious tradition with its own clergy, monasteries, and rituals, parallel to Buddhism).

His advisors, particularly the Confucian official Li Deyu, argued that Buddhism was a foreign religion that had accumulated vast tax-exempt monastic lands and was draining the empire's economic productivity.

The economic argument was sound — by some estimates, Buddhist monasteries owned 10–15% of the productive land in China by the mid-9th century, and the monastic population was a substantial demographic loss to the tax base.
In 845, Wuzong ordered the destruction of 4,600 Buddhist monasteries and 40,000 minor shrines, the forced laicization of 260,000 monks and nuns, and the confiscation of monastic landholdings.
Bronze Buddhist statues were melted down and recoined as currency (a one-way conversion of religious art into money that historians have lamented ever since).
The persecution was carried out systematically over several years, and despite being formally rolled back after Wuzong's death in 846, the institutional damage to Chinese Buddhism was permanent.

The schools that survived best were the ones that needed least infrastructure: Chan, with its emphasis on personal teacher-student transmission rather than monastic learning, came through almost intact, which is part of why Chan dominates East Asian Buddhism today.
The scholastic schools — Tiantai, Huayan, Yogacara — that depended on large monasteries with libraries and trained scholarly clergy never recovered to their former scale.
The second is the Huang Chao Rebellion (HWAHNG CHOW), 875–884.
Huang Chao was a salt trader from Caozhou (TSAW-joh, in modern Shandong) who had repeatedly failed the civil service examinations.
When peasant uprisings broke out in the late 870s in response to floods, famine, heavy taxation, and government corruption, Huang Chao rose to lead them.
His army moved across China for nearly a decade.

In 879, the rebels sacked Guangzhou (the great southern port that hosted China's largest foreign merchant community); contemporary accounts claim 120,000 foreign merchants were massacred — a figure that is probably exaggerated but that captures the scale of the catastrophe and that effectively ended Guangzhou's role as a major international port for over a century.
In 880, Huang Chao captured Chang'an and declared himself emperor of a new "Great Qi" dynasty.
Tang loyalist forces, supported by the Shatuo (SHAH-twaw — a Turkic-speaking people of the northern frontier) cavalry under their leader Li Keyong, drove him out by 884.
Huang Chao died (suicide, or possibly killed by his nephew, depending on the source).
But Chang'an was finished.
The capital had been sacked, depopulated, looted, and partly burned.
The Tang court returned briefly but the city never recovered as a functioning capital.
The warlords who had fought the rebellion were now effectively independent.
The most powerful of them was Zhu Wen (JOO WEN), originally a Huang Chao rebel who had defected to the Tang side in 882 and been rewarded with major commands.
By 900, Zhu Wen controlled the central court, and the last Tang emperor was a hostage to his power.
In 907, Zhu Wen forced the last Tang emperor to abdicate and proclaimed his own dynasty, the Later Liang.
The Tang dynasty was over after 289 years.

Chinese historians would later count Zhu Wen's 907 coup as the beginning of the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period (Chapter 5) — fifty years of fragmentation that would only end with the Song reunification in 960.

Cross-civ check: the An Lushan Rebellion (755–763) was contemporary with the Abbasid Revolution that overthrew the Umayyad Caliphate in 750 and established the Abbasid capital at Baghdad in 762 (Islamic Golden Age Ch 1).
The two events together — the Tang's structural collapse and the Abbasid consolidation — fundamentally redrew the Eurasian power map.

The Battle of Talas in 751 had already established that the Tang and the Abbasids would share the Central Asian frontier; the An Lushan Rebellion forced the Tang to withdraw its westernmost garrisons, leaving the Tarim Basin oases under nominal Tang control but with no actual Tang military presence, and effectively ended Chinese westward expansion for nearly a millennium.

The cultural exchange continued — Abbasid astronomers, mathematicians, and physicians were absorbing Chinese papermaking technology (transmitted by the prisoners taken at Talas) and would shortly be transmitting Indian numerals and Greek philosophy to a Tang-Song China at the eastern end of the network.
In Europe, Charlemagne was crowned Holy Roman Emperor on Christmas Day 800, a few decades after An Lushan's rebellion.
In Japan, the Heian period began in 794 with the founding of Heian-kyō (modern Kyoto) — modeled on Chang'an — and produced the great Heian court culture (Ancient Japan Ch 8).
In Mesoamerica, the Maya Classic Period was beginning to collapse around 800 (Maya Civilization Ch 7), an unrelated catastrophe that took down the Maya city-states for reasons still debated.
The 8th and 9th centuries were a moment of widespread structural strain across the Eurasian and Mesoamerican civilizations; the Tang's collapse was one of the most consequential examples.

chapters.title: The Five Dynasties & Song Founding
sentences: The fifty years between the fall of the Tang in 907 and the founding of the Song in 960 are called the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period.

It is the shortest interval of significant fragmentation in Chinese history after the Han collapse, and it has the unusual characteristic that almost nothing of cultural lasting importance was created during it.
Five short-lived dynasties succeeded each other in the north, each lasting on average about thirteen years before being overthrown by its own military commanders.
Ten more stable but smaller kingdoms divided the south.

The northern dynasties — Later Liang (907–923), Later Tang (923–936), Later Jin (936–946), Later Han (947–950), and Later Zhou (951–960) — all imitated the Tang's institutional structures while controlling far less territory and far less population.
They were ruled, with one or two exceptions, by Shatuo Turkic generals who had risen to military prominence in the late Tang anti-rebel campaigns.
The single most consequential event of the Five Dynasties period is also one of the saddest: the Loss of the Sixteen Prefectures in 938.
The story is short and sordid.
Shi Jingtang (shih jing-TAHNG), a Shatuo Turkic general serving the Later Tang dynasty, rebelled against his own emperor in 936.

To win the support he needed to take the throne, he allied with the Khitan Liao dynasty — a steppe empire that had risen in Manchuria and Inner Mongolia in the early 10th century under the leader Abaoji.

Shi Jingtang offered the Liao a price for their military support: the Sixteen Prefectures of northern China, including the area around modern Beijing, the city of Datong, and the mountain passes through the Yan Mountains and the Taihang Mountains that formed the natural defensive barrier between the northern Chinese plain and the steppe.
The Khitan accepted, helped Shi Jingtang win the throne (he founded the Later Jin dynasty in 936), and took possession of the prefectures.
The strategic significance of the cession is hard to overstate.
The Sixteen Prefectures included the major mountain passes through which any cavalry-based steppe army would have to enter the Chinese heartland.

Without them, the rich agricultural northern Chinese plain — including the future Beijing region, the Yellow River corridor, and the productive farmland of modern Hebei and Henan — lay open to direct cavalry attack.
The Song dynasty would spend its entire 167-year northern existence trying to recover these prefectures, and would never succeed.
The Jurchen conquest of 1127 (Chapter 7) and the Mongol conquest of the 13th century (Chapter 9) both poured through these passes; without them, both invasions might have been delayed or blunted.
Shi Jingtang's deal is one of those moments where you can name the specific decision that produced centuries of consequence.

Modern Chinese historiography treats him about the way English-language historiography treats the figures who let the Goths into the Roman Empire: a short-term opportunist who created a permanent strategic disaster.

The Later Jin dynasty itself lasted only ten years before being overthrown by the Khitan Liao, who briefly invaded and looted central China in the late 940s before withdrawing because their tribal organization could not sustain occupation of densely populated Chinese cities.
The reunifier who emerged from Five Dynasties chaos was Zhao Kuangyin (JOW kwahng-YIN).
Zhao Kuangyin was a general of the Later Zhou dynasty, the last of the five northern dynasties.

The Later Zhou's founding emperor Guo Wei (951–954) and his successor Chai Rong (954–959) had been unusually capable rulers — Chai Rong in particular had launched a vigorous reform program and reconquered some lost territory in the south.
When Chai Rong died in 959, leaving a six-year-old son on the throne, the Later Zhou court was vulnerable to the same kind of military coup that had ended every previous Five Dynasties regime.
In early 960, Zhao Kuangyin was the senior military commander of the Later Zhou, with control of the imperial guard and most of the field armies.
The court sent him north on campaign against a reported (possibly fabricated) Khitan threat.

At a place called Chenqiao Station (chen-CHYOW), a few days' march out of the capital at Kaifeng (KIGH-fung), Zhao Kuangyin's troops "spontaneously" placed an imperial yellow robe on his shoulders and acclaimed him emperor.

The gesture was a Chinese political convention dating back centuries — soldiers acclaiming their general as emperor was the standard mechanism for legitimizing a military coup, with the implication that the general had been forced to accept the throne by his loyal followers rather than seizing it on his own initiative.

Whether the Chenqiao acclamation was actually spontaneous or was carefully staged by Zhao Kuangyin's circle is one of the standard debates of the early Song historical literature; the consensus view is that it was probably staged but that we cannot rule out a genuine soldier initiative.
Zhao Kuangyin marched on Kaifeng.
The Later Zhou court surrendered without a fight — the imperial guard was already on Zhao's side, and the regents had no military force to resist.
Zhao Kuangyin proclaimed the Song dynasty in February 960, took the reign name Taizu ("Grand Progenitor"), and began the long campaign of reunifying China.
The reunification took twenty years.

The southern kingdoms — most of them long-stable, well-governed, prosperous regions that had been quietly independent for half a century — submitted one by one through a combination of military pressure and negotiated capitulation.

By 979 (under Taizu's brother and successor, Emperor Taizong of Song — yet another Taizong, distinct from the Tang one), most of China south of the lost Sixteen Prefectures had been reunified under Song rule.
The Sixteen Prefectures themselves remained Khitan; multiple Song military campaigns to recover them in the 980s and afterward all failed.
What made the Song founding different from the Tang founding was the conscious philosophical decision Taizu made about the role of the military.
The Tang had been founded by aristocratic military families and had governed through a fusion of aristocratic and military power.
The Sui had been the same.
The Five Dynasties had been entirely a military affair, with each dynasty founded by a general who had then been overthrown by the next general.
Zhao Kuangyin had himself come to the throne through a military acclamation — and he understood, better than almost anyone, how unstable a system that produced was.
The fundamental problem of Chinese governance, as he saw it, was that powerful generals always tried to seize the throne, and there was no structural mechanism to prevent them.
His solution was the famous "exchanging military power for wine cups" episode of 961.
Within a year of taking the throne, Taizu invited his most senior generals — the men who had supported him at Chenqiao and through the early consolidation — to a banquet at the imperial palace.
Over wine, he openly told them that their military power made him uneasy, as it had made every emperor since the Tang collapse.

He offered them an alternative: surrender their commands voluntarily, accept generous lifetime pensions and large estates, marry into the imperial family, and retire to comfortable lives in the capital.
The implication was clear: refuse, and the offer would not stand.
They accepted.

The senior military command of the Song was reorganized over the following years, with field armies divided into smaller units commanded by a rotating roster of officers who held no permanent regional commands and who served at the pleasure of the central court.
Taizu went further.
He systematically subordinated the military to civilian bureaucratic control.
The most prestigious position in the Song state was no longer the military commissioner; it was the chief grand councilor (the senior civilian official).

The civil service examinations became the dominant route to power, with the Song increasing the annual jinshi quota dramatically — by the mid-Song, several hundred jinshi were being awarded each year, far more than the Tang had ever produced.
The result was a bureaucracy of unprecedented size, sophistication, and prestige.
Generals reported to civilian officials.
Provincial military commanders had no permanent regional bases.
Frontier defense was organized through a complex system of multiple overlapping commands, designed to make any single general's coup impossible.
The trade-off was real and obvious from the start.
The Song had the most stable internal governance of any Chinese dynasty and the longest peaceful reigns; it also had the weakest military relative to its size and wealth.
Song armies were large but were organized to prevent internal coups rather than to win battles.
Song frontier defense depended on bribes, diplomacy, and elaborate fortification rather than on offensive cavalry capability.
The Song would lose the Sixteen Prefectures forever, lose half the country to the Jurchen in 1127, and ultimately lose everything to the Mongols in 1279.

But the bureaucratic state Taizu built was so effective that Mongol Yuan and Ming Chinese governments after them would all be variations on the Song model, and a version of it would persist all the way to the end of imperial China in 1912.
Taizu had, in effect, traded military power for governance technology, and the technology proved to be more durable than the military.
The Song dynasty Taizu founded (the Northern Song, 960–1127) is the subject of Chapter 6.
But it is worth pausing here on what the founding represented in long-term Chinese history.
The Sui-Tang reunification of 581–589 had restored a single Chinese state after centuries of fragmentation but had governed through aristocratic military power.
The collapse of that model in the 9th and 10th centuries had produced fifty years of warlord chaos.
The Song founding restored unity again — but this time through a deliberate constitutional shift toward civilian bureaucratic governance.
The shift would shape every subsequent Chinese dynasty.
It is also one of those rare dynastic transitions that did not require a major war.
The Song reunification of the south was conducted largely through diplomacy and negotiated submission.
The casualty count from the 960–979 reunification campaigns was tiny by the standards of the An Lushan Rebellion, the Mongol conquest, or the Ming-Qing transition.

The Song emperors were able to consolidate their bureaucracy, expand the examinations, and begin the cultural and economic flowering of the Northern Song precisely because the founding war had not destroyed the productive base of the country.
This is a structural advantage that historians sometimes overlook in evaluating dynasties: the Song got to start from a relatively undamaged starting position.

Cross-civ check: the founding of the Song in 960 was contemporary with the height of the Abbasid Caliphate's cultural golden age (Islamic Golden Age Ch 4) and with the rise of the Holy Roman Empire under Otto I in central Europe (crowned 962).
The Byzantine Empire under the Macedonian dynasty was experiencing its own military and cultural revival under emperors Nikephoros II Phokas and Basil II (Byzantine Empire Ch 7).
In southern India, the Chola empire was beginning its great maritime expansion.
In Mesoamerica, the Toltec civilization was at its peak.

The Song founding marks the beginning of what historians sometimes call the "medieval optimum" — a relatively stable, prosperous, intellectually creative period across multiple Eurasian civilizations that lasted until the climate cooling and Mongol disruptions of the 13th century.

chapters.title: The Northern Song
sentences: The Northern Song dynasty (960–1127) was the most internally peaceful, economically prosperous, technologically innovative, and intellectually productive period in pre-modern Chinese history.

It is also the period that most contemporary historians of world economic and technological history return to, repeatedly, when looking for the closest pre-modern analog to a modern industrial society.

Some of the technologies the Northern Song produced — paper money, movable type, the navigation compass, weaponized gunpowder, mass-produced cast iron at industrial scale — would not be matched in Europe for between 400 and 700 years.
The dynasty was founded on the Five Dynasties' ruins (Chapter 5) by Zhao Kuangyin in 960 and inherited his constitutional commitment to civilian over military rule.
This had two large consequences.
The first was that the Song could never recover the Sixteen Prefectures in the north and would forever be vulnerable to nomadic and semi-nomadic invasion from that direction.

The second was that the resources the state did not spend on offensive military conquest were available for everything else — bureaucratic infrastructure, public works, education, scientific research, commerce, the arts.
The Song traded conquest for prosperity, and the result was a society visibly more sophisticated than anything else in the world at the time.
The Song capital was Kaifeng (kigh-FUNG), on the Yellow River in Henan.
Kaifeng was a different kind of city from Tang Chang'an (Chapter 3).
Chang'an had been laid out on a strict ward grid with internal walls and night curfews — a closed-block city designed for controlled administration.
Kaifeng broke from that template entirely.
Its streets were open.
Shops, restaurants, and entertainment quarters lined the public thoroughfares without internal walls separating them.

Night markets operated past midnight — a revolutionary departure from the Tang curfew system, and a sign of how thoroughly the Song's commercial economy had outgrown the older imperial-administrative urban model.
By 1000 CE, Kaifeng was the most populous city in the world, with over a million residents inside the walls.
The Iron Pagoda built in 1049 — a 180-foot, 13-story tower faced in 28 types of brown glazed brick that still stands today — is the most visible Northern Song monument to survive in the city.
We have a remarkable visual record of Kaifeng from a single painting.
Zhang Zeduan (jahng zeh-DWAHN), a Northern Song court painter, completed a 17-foot handscroll around 1120 called Along the River During the Qingming Festival (清明上河图, Qingming shanghe tu).

The scroll depicts the city's commercial life on the Qingming spring festival: over 800 human figures from every social class, 28 boats of various sizes navigating the canal, 60 animals (donkeys, oxen, horses, camels), 170 trees, the famous Rainbow Bridge (a single-span arched bridge of timber, with details that have allowed modern engineers to reconstruct the Song-era bridge-building technique), shops, teahouses, restaurants, brothels, fortune-tellers, and street performers.
It is the single most valuable visual record of Song urban life and is now considered a national treasure of China, held in the Palace Museum in Beijing.
Multiple Ming and Qing reinterpretations exist, but the original is the historical document.
The political life of the Northern Song was dominated by a half-century of bitter intellectual conflict between two factions — the reformers led by Wang Anshi and the conservatives led by Sima Guang.
The conflict shaped Song governance from the 1060s to the 1090s and exhausted the state at the worst possible moment.
Wang Anshi (wahng AHN-shih, 1021–1086) became chancellor in 1069 under the young Emperor Shenzong.

Wang's diagnosis of the Song's problems was that the state was financially weak, militarily inadequate, and structurally incapable of meeting the threats from the Khitan Liao to the north and the Tangut Western Xia to the northwest. (The Western Xia was a Tibetan-related kingdom that had emerged in the 1030s in modern Ningxia and Gansu, and that would harass the Song's western frontier for two centuries before the Mongols destroyed it in 1227.) His solution was a sweeping reform program known as the New Policies (新法, xin fa).

The New Policies included: government loans to peasant farmers at below-market rates (the Green Sprouts program, intended to break the power of rural moneylenders who charged extortionate harvest-time rates); state trading bureaus to stabilize commodity prices; a baojia (BOW-jya) militia system in which households were organized into groups of ten for collective security and military training; reforms to the civil service examinations to test practical policy and administration rather than literary elegance; a state-monopoly tea trade; and government direct production of military equipment.
The reforms were aggressive, comprehensive, and explicitly designed to expand state capacity at the expense of established economic interests.
Sima Guang (sih-MAH GWAHNG, 1019–1086) led the opposition.

He argued that the reforms gave too much power to government bureaucracy, undermined the traditional gentry's social role, generated corruption through the loans-and-monopolies system, and undermined the moral foundations of Confucian governance.
Sima Guang and his allies were repeatedly purged, recalled, and purged again as Shenzong wavered in his support for the reforms.

The factional warfare reached a peak in the 1080s after Shenzong's death, when an anti-reform regency reversed most of the New Policies, then was reversed again by a pro-reform faction in the 1090s, then partially reversed again in the 1100s.
The continuous flip-flopping consumed the dynasty's political energy and produced a political class that hated each other more than it feared the foreign threats on the borders.
Su Shi (Chapter 8), one of the era's great writers, was repeatedly exiled by both factions for being too independent.
Sima Guang spent his years out of power on a different project.

He compiled the Zizhi Tongjian (zih-jih tong-JYEN — "Comprehensive Mirror to Aid in Government"), a 294-volume chronological history of China from 403 BCE to 959 CE — covering 1,362 years of Chinese history.

Emperor Shenzong, despite their political differences, personally titled the finished work, framing it as a teaching device: history as a mirror in which rulers could see how their decisions had played out in past dynasties.
The Zizhi Tongjian became the second most influential work of Chinese historiography, after Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian of the Han period (Han Dynasty Ch 4).
Every subsequent Chinese emperor was expected to study it.
Modern Chinese historians still treat it as a primary reference for the periods it covers.
The Northern Song's lasting legacy, however, is technological rather than political.
Four innovations in particular reshaped the world.
Gunpowder had been recorded in Daoist alchemical texts since the late Tang (Chapter 4), but it took the Song to weaponize it.

The Wujing Zongyao (woo-JING zong-YOW — "Complete Essentials of Military Classics"), compiled by Zeng Gongliang under imperial commission in 1044, contains the earliest known weaponized gunpowder formulas, with specific proportions of saltpeter, sulfur, and charcoal alongside recipes for incendiary bombs, fire arrows, fire lances (huo qiang — bamboo or paper tubes packed with gunpowder that shot flames and shrapnel at close range, a proto-flamethrower that doubled as a proto-firearm), thunderclap bombs, and signal rockets.
By the early 12th century, Song armies were deploying gunpowder weapons on a substantial scale.

The Song would never have the offensive military strength to use gunpowder in conquest — that was inherited by the Jurchen and Mongols, who absorbed Song gunpowder technology and used it more aggressively — but the technology that ended the age of castles, transformed European warfare, and reshaped global politics over the next eight centuries originated as a Song military innovation.
Printing had emerged in the Tang as woodblock printing (Chapter 4), but the Song took it to industrial scale.

Around 1040, a commoner artisan named Bi Sheng (bee SHENG) invented movable type — small reusable individual character pieces fired in clay, set in a wax-and-resin bed inside an iron frame, used for printing and then redistributed.

Shen Kuo (shen KWAW), the great Song polymath whose Dream Pool Essays of 1088 we will return to in a moment, described the process in detail; without his account, Bi Sheng's invention might be lost to history.

Movable type was less practical for Chinese (which has thousands of distinct characters and therefore requires thousands of distinct types) than for alphabetic writing systems with twenty-six letters; for Chinese, woodblock remained the dominant printing technology through the Ming.

But the principle was independently rediscovered by Korean metalworkers in the 13th century (using metal type, an improvement on Bi Sheng's clay) and then by Gutenberg in Mainz around 1450, three to four centuries later.

The combination of printing and the Song commercial economy produced the first true mass-publishing culture in human history: Confucian classics, examination-prep texts, encyclopedias, medical manuals, agricultural treatises, poetry collections, Buddhist sutras, and government documents in print runs of thousands.
Paper money is the most consequential single Song innovation by some measures.
The story begins in Sichuan, where the local economy ran on iron coins rather than copper because copper was scarce in the region.
Iron coins were so heavy that large transactions required cartloads of money — it reportedly took 1.5 kilograms of iron coins to purchase a pound of salt.
Private merchants began issuing paper certificates of deposit in the late 10th century to avoid carrying iron coinage.
By the 1020s, the system was so widespread that the Song government took it over.

In 1024, the government began issuing the jiaozi (jyow-ZIH), the world's first state-backed paper currency, with multi-color printing to fight counterfeiting and three-year circulation periods to control the money supply.
The jiaozi system was eventually expanded to other regions and to higher-denomination notes called huizi.

The Song discovered, and the Mongol Yuan dynasty would catastrophically rediscover (Yuan Dynasty), the dangers of overprinting — Song-era inflation from excess currency was a serious recurring problem.

But the basic concept of fiat paper money, redeemable in principle for metal coin, is a Song invention that would not appear in Europe for seven centuries (Stockholm's Banco issued the first European paper money in 1661).
The magnetic compass was the fourth great innovation.

Chinese geomancers had been using magnetic lodestone for feng shui divination since the Han period (Han Dynasty Ch 6) — aligning buildings, tombs, and other structures with the Earth's magnetic field.
By the Song, the magnetic properties of magnetized iron needles were well understood.

Shen Kuo in his Dream Pool Essays (1088) described floating-needle compasses in detail and noted magnetic declination — the slight offset between magnetic north and true geographic north — about four centuries before European scientists made the same observation. (Christopher Columbus rediscovered magnetic declination during his 1492 transatlantic voyage and treated it as a novel observation; Shen Kuo had documented it in 1088.) By the early 12th century, Chinese maritime navigators were using magnetic compasses for ocean voyages, enabling the Song maritime trade revolution that would reach East Africa (Chapter 8).

The compass reached Arab navigators by the 12th century and European navigators by the 13th, and combined with improvements in shipbuilding and the astrolabe, made the European Age of Exploration possible.
Shen Kuo himself deserves a longer mention than he usually gets.

He was a Song official, military commander, diplomat, hydraulic engineer, and astronomer who, after his political career ended in the factional warfare of the 1080s, retired to a garden retreat called the Dream Pool near modern Zhenjiang and compiled his observations into the Dream Pool Essays (Mengxi bitan).

The Essays cover geology (Shen Kuo recognized fossilized seashells in mountain rocks as evidence that mountains had been undersea, four centuries before any European naturalist made the same inference), astronomy (he reformed the imperial calendar and improved the gnomon-and-armillary observatory at Kaifeng), magnetism, optics (camera-obscura demonstrations, observations on the inverted-image projection through a pinhole), pharmacology, military technology (he commanded armies on the Western Xia frontier), and the technological innovations of his contemporaries — including Bi Sheng's movable type and the magnetic compass.
His empirical method, his willingness to test claims by direct observation, and his refusal to defer to traditional authorities anticipated the European scientific method by several centuries.
He is one of those figures the broader world should know about and largely does not.
The Northern Song's economic backbone was something less glamorous than printing and gunpowder but at least as important: iron and steel.
By 1078, Song iron production reached approximately 125,000 tons annually.
To put that in context: this exceeded England's iron production at the start of the Industrial Revolution in the 18th century by a substantial margin.
The Song produced more iron in 1078 than the entire continent of Europe would produce in 1700.
Song iron was used for weapons, agricultural tools, the iron coins of the Sichuan economy, construction, and water-control infrastructure.
The technology behind the production was equally striking.
China had been producing cast iron since the 5th century BCE — Europe would not master the technique until the late medieval period — but Song-era production reached genuinely industrial scale.
Deforestation in north China had reduced the supply of wood for charcoal-fired blast furnaces, so Song ironworkers switched to coke (a refined coal product).
Europe would not adopt coke-fired blast furnaces until Abraham Darby developed the technique in 1709 — a difference of over six hundred years.
The other major Northern Song economic development was the Champa rice introduction.
In 1012, Emperor Zhenzong ordered the importation of fast-ripening, drought-resistant rice strains from Champa (the Cham kingdom in central Vietnam).
The new strains matured in 60 days rather than 120, and could grow on previously marginal hillside land.
Adoption across south China within a few decades enabled double-cropping (two harvests per year instead of one) and roughly doubled rice production.

The result was a population boom: China's population grew from approximately 60 million in 960 to over 100 million by 1100 — the first society in human history to surpass the 100-million-person threshold.

The agricultural surplus enabled urbanization (Kaifeng, Hangzhou, Quanzhou, and other cities all grew to populations the Tang capitals could never have supported), commerce (the surplus rural population moved into commercial production of silk, ceramics, tea, and metal goods), and the cultural and intellectual flowering of the Song period.

The combined picture — paper currency, mass printing, gunpowder weapons, the navigation compass, industrial-scale iron production, double-cropping rice agriculture, the largest urban population in the world — has led many world economic historians to ask why the Song did not spark a full industrial revolution six or seven centuries before Britain (why this technological leader did not industrialize first is the central puzzle of Industrial Revolution Chs 1 and 20).

The standard answers all involve some combination of: incomplete labor markets (the Song had abundant cheap labor, reducing the incentive to mechanize), missing institutional structures (no European-style legal framework for joint-stock corporations or modern banking), the catastrophic disruption of the Jurchen and then Mongol conquests (which interrupted the technological-economic trajectory before it could fully consolidate), and the cultural priorities of the scholar-gentry class (which valued classical learning over technical innovation).
The debate is alive in current economic history.
What is not debated is that the Song achieved what looks, in retrospect, like a proto-industrial economic structure five hundred years before Europe matched it.
The Northern Song also had a final emperor whose career encapsulates the dynasty's contradictions: brilliant in art and culture, catastrophic in politics.
Emperor Huizong (HWAY-tsong) — born Zhao Ji (jow JEE) — became emperor in 1100 and ruled until his abdication in 1126.
He was, by general agreement, one of China's greatest artists.

He invented a distinctive calligraphic style called "Slender Gold" (瘦金体, shoujin ti), characterized by extremely thin sharp strokes that look almost like twisted gold wire — still practiced and admired a thousand years later.
He painted bird-and-flower studies of remarkable quality, including the famous "Five-Colored Parakeet" handscroll now at the Boston Museum of Fine Arts.
He compiled the imperial art collection catalogue, which listed over 6,000 paintings, providing one of the most important pre-modern records of Chinese painting.
He was a passionate patron of court music, ceramics (the imperial kilns under his patronage produced the most refined Ru ware and Guan ware ceramics in Song history), and Daoist religion.
He was simultaneously a calamity as a ruler.
He delegated governance to corrupt favorites — most notoriously Cai Jing (TSIGH JING), who used the chancellor position to enrich himself and his network at the state's expense.
He poured money into Daoist building projects and an enormous imperial garden complex (the Genyue, "Heightened Mountain") in Kaifeng that drained the treasury.
He neglected the military at a moment when the dynasty needed military strength most.
And in 1115, he made the strategic decision that destroyed the dynasty: he allied with the rising Jurchen people against the Khitan Liao.
The Jurchen were a Tungusic-speaking forest people from Manchuria (the same region the Manchu would later emerge from to found the Qing dynasty in the 17th century).
Under their leader Aguda, they had revolted against Khitan Liao overlordship in 1114 and established their own Jin dynasty in 1115.
Huizong's calculation was that joining the Jurchen against the Liao would allow the Song to recover the Sixteen Prefectures lost in 938 (Chapter 5).
The strategic logic was sound; the execution was not.
The Song military failed to deliver on its promised contributions to the joint campaign.
The Jurchen conquered the Liao essentially on their own (the last Khitan emperor was captured in 1125), and in the process they took an accurate measure of Song military weakness.
They did not stop.
In 1125, Jurchen armies turned south against their Song allies.
In 1126 they besieged Kaifeng.

In early 1127 they captured the city, deposed Huizong (who had abdicated to his son Emperor Qinzong in panicked hopes of avoiding personal capture), and took both former emperors, the imperial court, the imperial library, the imperial treasures, and roughly 3,000 members of the imperial family and entourage north into captivity.
This is the Jingkang Incident of 1127.
It is the subject of Chapter 7.

Cross-civ check: the Northern Song was contemporary with the Crusader era in the eastern Mediterranean (the First Crusade in 1099, the establishment of the Crusader states), the rise of the Seljuk Turkic empires across the Middle East, the consolidation of the Holy Roman Empire under the Salian and Hohenstaufen dynasties in central Europe, and the early flowering of medieval European intellectual life around the universities at Bologna, Paris, and Oxford.

The Khmer Empire at Angkor in Southeast Asia was building Angkor Wat in the early 12th century, contemporary with the construction of the Song Iron Pagoda and the Northern Song's most active building period.
In Japan, the Heian court culture was at its late peak, with Murasaki Shikibu writing the Tale of Genji around 1010 (Ancient Japan Ch 8).

The Song traded with all of these regions through its maritime network and its silk-road connections; the world the Song operated in was already significantly more interconnected than any earlier period.

chapters.title: The Jurchen Catastrophe and the Southern Song
sentences: The Jingkang Incident of 1127 — named after the reign-period during which it happened — is the single most traumatic event in pre-modern Chinese national consciousness, comparable in cultural weight to the sack of Constantinople in 1204 in the Byzantine memory or the Norman conquest of 1066 in the English.

It was the moment when the world's most sophisticated civilization was decapitated and humiliated by a forest people from Manchuria that the Song had considered uncouth allies eighteen months earlier.
The Jurchen siege of Kaifeng began in late 1126 and lasted into early 1127.

Emperor Qinzong (CHIN-tsong) — Huizong's son, who had been hastily elevated to the throne in late 1125 when his father abdicated to escape personal blame — attempted the only defensive strategy still available to a militarily collapsing state: he tried to buy the Jurchen off.

The Jurchen demands escalated week by week — first an indemnity, then territorial concessions, then the surrender of imperial princesses, then the personal appearance of the emperor at the Jurchen camp.
Qinzong eventually had to comply with all of it.
In early 1127, the Jurchen entered Kaifeng, looted the imperial palace and treasury, and rounded up the imperial family, court officials, palace women, scholars, and skilled artisans.
Both former emperors — Huizong (still living) and Qinzong — along with nearly 3,000 members of the imperial entourage were marched north into captivity.
Most of them never came back.
Huizong died in northern captivity in 1135, in a cold border garrison far from the Yangtze valley he had spent his life painting and patronizing.

His son Qinzong survived in captivity until 1161, treated with the calculated humiliation that the Jurchen reserved for high-status hostages — he was at one point made to dress as a Khitan slave and parade publicly in front of the Jurchen court as a demonstration of conquest.

The captured imperial princesses, palace women, and noblewomen suffered a fate the Chinese sources record with the uncomfortable mix of moralizing horror and prurient interest characteristic of male chroniclers writing about female suffering: many were given to Jurchen officers as concubines, slaves, or lower-ranking palace servants.
The contemporary chronicle accounts of these abductions are some of the most painful documents in Chinese historical literature.
What survived was a single Song prince, Zhao Gou (jow GO), Huizong's ninth son, who had been outside Kaifeng on a diplomatic mission when the city fell.
He fled south.
In May 1127, in the city of Yingtian (modern Shangqiu in Henan), the surviving Song officials acclaimed him emperor.
He took the reign name Gaozong (GOW-tsong, yet another Gaozong distinct from the Tang one) and is known in the historical literature as Emperor Gaozong of Song.
He continued retreating south, harassed by Jurchen pursuit.
By 1138, his itinerant court had settled at Hangzhou on the Qiantang River estuary, which would serve as the Southern Song capital for the next 142 years.

The official designation was always Lin'an (lin-AHN — "Temporarily at Peace"), the Song court's polite fiction that the move south was provisional and the recovery of Kaifeng was always just a few campaigns away.
It never was.
The Southern Song of Hangzhou was a strange political entity.

It controlled only the wealthier southern half of China — roughly the Yangtze valley and points south — but this half was the half that had been growing fastest in population, agricultural production, and commercial vigor for two centuries.

The Southern Song's per-capita income was probably higher than the Northern Song's had been; its tax revenues, despite the territorial loss, were comparable to the Northern Song's at peak; its maritime trade was larger; its urban culture was as sophisticated as anything Kaifeng had produced.
Hangzhou itself became, by some estimates, the largest city in the world during the Southern Song.

It sat at the southern end of the Grand Canal, on the West Lake, with the bay of the Qiantang River producing one of the world's most spectacular tidal bores (a wall of incoming seawater up to thirty feet high that surges up the river estuary at certain phases of the moon — a tourist attraction even in the Song period, when poems and paintings recorded it).
The city's population at peak in the 13th century is estimated at over a million, with another million in surrounding districts.

Marco Polo, visiting Hangzhou in the 1270s under Mongol rule (a few decades after the Southern Song fell), called it "the finest and noblest city in the world" and described twelve thousand bridges, ten massive markets, public bathhouses on every block, and crowds of foreign merchants from Persia, India, and the Arab world.
The figure of twelve thousand bridges is probably exaggerated; the rest is roughly accurate.

Hangzhou's West Lake became one of the most painted, poemed, and culturally celebrated landscapes in Chinese tradition; the Su Causeway crossing it was built by Su Shi during one of his governorships (Su Shi appears properly in Chapter 8).
The Southern Song court at Hangzhou was politically traumatized.
The collective memory of the Jingkang Incident sat at the center of every political debate — to fight the Jurchen and try to recover the north, or to negotiate peace and consolidate the south.
The two positions divided the court for generations.
The most famous casualty of the debate was the general Yue Fei.
Yue Fei (yueh FAY, 1103–1142) is the most revered patriotic hero in Chinese history.
His story is almost too neat for history, and almost certainly has been polished by centuries of patriotic retelling, but the bones of it are well-attested.
He was born to a peasant family in Tangyin in modern Henan in 1103, just before the Jurchen catastrophe.
His mother famously tattooed four characters on his back: 精忠报国 (jing zhong bao guo — "Serve the country with utmost loyalty").
The episode is probably apocryphal in detail but captures the texture of Yue Fei's eventual reputation.

He entered the Song military in his teens and rose through the chaotic warfare of the 1120s and 1130s by sheer ability — he was a genuinely brilliant cavalry commander whose troops were known for both tactical effectiveness and unusual discipline (Yue Fei's army was famous for refusing to loot the Chinese villages they passed through, which made it dramatically more popular with the Chinese peasantry than most Southern Song armies).
By the late 1130s, Yue Fei was leading the most successful Southern Song offensives against the Jurchen Jin.
His 1140 campaign recovered substantial territory in central China and was preparing to recapture Kaifeng itself.
He famously addressed his officers with the line that has been quoted ever since: "Restore our rivers and mountains" (huan wo heshan — huan wo hé shān, "give us back our land").
The Jin armies were retreating before him.
This is where the politics destroyed everything.

Qin Hui (CHIN HWAY) was the Southern Song chancellor, a man of complicated personal history (he had been captured by the Jurchen during the Jingkang Incident and had been released to return south, leading to suspicions for the rest of his life that he was secretly working for the Jin).

Qin Hui's faction at court — backed by Emperor Gaozong, who had his own reasons to fear a successful general who might recover the north and produce inconvenient questions about whose throne the recovered emperor ought to occupy — was committed to a negotiated peace with the Jin.
A successful Yue Fei was a political problem.
In late 1141, Qin Hui issued twelve gold-embossed imperial decrees in a single day recalling Yue Fei from the front.
Yue Fei, after some hesitation, obeyed.
On returning to the capital, he was arrested on fabricated charges of plotting rebellion.
He was tortured for a confession and refused to confess.
His chief subordinate Zhang Xian was tortured to death with him.
The legal proceedings were transparently corrupt — even contemporary officials objected — but Qin Hui pressed forward.
The official Han Shizhong, another senior general, asked Qin Hui what evidence existed for the charges.
Qin Hui's reply, recorded in the chronicles, became one of the most quoted phrases in Chinese political vocabulary: "莫须有" (mo xu you, "perhaps it exists" or "it's something maybe").
Yue Fei was executed in early 1142, aged 39.
The peace treaty with the Jin (the Treaty of Shaoxing) was signed shortly afterward, ceding all the territory north of the Huai River and obligating the Song to pay annual tribute in silk and silver.
Yue Fei was posthumously rehabilitated in 1162, two decades after his execution, when Gaozong abdicated and his successor needed a heroic symbol for a renewed anti-Jin policy.
Yue Fei's tomb was rebuilt at the foot of Yuelai Mountain beside West Lake in Hangzhou.

Iron statues of Qin Hui and his wife Lady Wang — and two other officials who had collaborated in the execution — were placed in front of the tomb in the kneeling posture of contrition, where they have remained for nearly nine hundred years.
Visitors to the tomb traditionally spit on the iron statues and beat them with sticks; the statues have been replaced multiple times because visitors damaged them.
Modern signs ask visitors to express their contempt verbally rather than physically, but the ritual continues.

Yue Fei's name is the standard Chinese metaphor for patriotic loyalty betrayed by domestic political corruption, and Qin Hui's name is the standard Chinese metaphor for the corrupt minister who sells out a hero.

The closest English-language analog might be Benedict Arnold in American memory, but Yue Fei's place in Chinese culture is much more central than Arnold's in American culture — Yue Fei is taught in Chinese schools, dramatized in operas, and invoked in Chinese political rhetoric whenever a public figure wants to accuse an opponent of betraying the national interest.
The Southern Song that had executed Yue Fei was militarily limited but technologically and economically inventive.
Its defining military innovation was the Song navy.
Pre-modern Chinese dynasties had typically fielded river fleets when needed but had never maintained a permanent standing navy.
The Southern Song needed one.
The Yangtze River was the primary defensive barrier between the Jurchen north and the Song south, and Jurchen cavalry could not effectively cross it without a fleet.
The Song's strategic priority was therefore controlling the Yangtze and its tributaries.
The Song navy that emerged from this strategic imperative was unlike anything that had existed before in Chinese history.

Its warships included paddle-wheel vessels powered by foot-operated treadmills inside the hull — sailors walking treadmill drums that turned external paddle wheels, providing maneuverable propulsion against river currents that sail-powered ships could not match. (Paddle-wheel propulsion would not be reinvented in Europe until the early 19th century, when steam-powered paddle wheelers transformed Mississippi and trans-Atlantic shipping; the Song versions were human-powered, but the engineering principle was identical.) Larger Song warships could carry over 1,000 soldiers and deploy gunpowder weapons including thunderclap bombs, fire arrows, and the early proto-cannons that the Song military engineers were experimenting with throughout the 12th and 13th centuries.
The Song navy held the Yangtze line for over a century against repeated Jin attempts at large-scale crossing.

The Mongol conquest of the Southern Song in the 1270s would require, among other things, the construction of a Mongol naval force capable of matching the Song fleet on its own water — a process that took years.

The Southern Song's sustained survival despite its territorial limits depended on a combination of factors: the natural defensive line of the Yangtze, the technological advantages of gunpowder weaponry and naval engineering, the agricultural and commercial wealth of the south, and the sheer demographic weight of a population that probably exceeded the Jurchen Jin's by a factor of three or four to one.
The dynasty would last until 1279, longer than the Northern Song had survived, and would produce some of the most sophisticated cultural achievements in Chinese history — the subject of Chapter 8.

Cross-civ check: the Jurchen catastrophe of 1127 was contemporary with the First Crusade's consolidation of the Crusader States in the Levant, the Norman expansion in Sicily and southern Italy, and the rise of the Almoravid and Almohad Muslim empires in North Africa and Spain.
In northern Europe, the Holy Roman Empire was wracked by the Investiture Controversy between popes and emperors.
The Khmer Empire at Angkor was approaching its peak.
In Japan, the Heian court was in its long decline; the Genpei War of 1180–1185 would shortly establish the Kamakura Shogunate (Ancient Japan transitions to the shogunate-era TLs after this point).

The Jin-Song conflict continued for over a century in parallel with these developments, with the Song effectively ceding the role of Eurasia's most powerful state and the Jin filling part of that role in northern Asia.

chapters.title: Song Society
sentences: This chapter steps out of chronological narrative to look at four developments that crystallized during the Song and that defined Chinese society for centuries afterward: Neo-Confucianism, the printing-and-examination culture, the Jingdezhen porcelain trade, and the maritime trade revolution that connected Song China to the Indian Ocean world.
Some of these emerged in the Northern Song; some emerged or matured in the Southern Song; all of them were Song innovations that outlived the dynasty and shaped what came after.
Neo-Confucianism is the most important of them, and the hardest to summarize.

The basic problem the movement set out to address was that Confucianism — the philosophical tradition founded by Confucius in the 5th century BCE (Zhou Dynasty Ch 7), elaborated by Mencius and Xunzi in the centuries afterward, and made the official state ideology under the Han in the 2nd century BCE (Han Dynasty Ch 4) — had lost intellectual ground to Buddhism during the Six Dynasties and Tang centuries.

Buddhism offered things that classical Confucianism did not: a sophisticated metaphysical framework explaining the nature of reality, a rigorous theory of consciousness and mind, a coherent account of suffering and salvation, monastic institutions for serious philosophical study, and a path to personal spiritual transformation that did not depend on political conditions.
Confucian scholars who wanted to take metaphysics or epistemology or psychology seriously had been gravitating toward Buddhist categories for centuries.
The Tang anti-Buddhist persecution of 845 (Chapter 4) had reduced Buddhism's institutional power but had not really refuted its intellectual claims.
The Northern Song saw a series of philosophers begin to address the problem by building a Confucian metaphysics that could compete with Buddhism on its own intellectual ground.
