Zhou Dunyi (joh DUN-ee, 1017–1073) wrote a short but enormously influential treatise called "Explanation of the Diagram of the Supreme Polarity" (Taijitu shuo), arguing that the universe emerged through a series of cosmic transformations from an original undifferentiated principle.

The brothers Cheng Hao (CHENG HOW, 1032–1085) and Cheng Yi (CHENG EE, 1033–1107) developed the categories of li (LEE, "principle" — the underlying rational pattern of reality) and qi (CHEE, "material force" — the dynamic substance through which principle is realized).

Zhang Zai (jahng TSIGH, 1020–1077) elaborated the qi side of this metaphysics with the famous "Western Inscription" arguing that all humans share a common cosmic substance and therefore stand in a relationship of metaphysical kinship.
The synthesizer who pulled all of this into a coherent system was Zhu Xi (joo SHEE, 1130–1200), the most influential Chinese philosopher after Confucius himself.
Zhu Xi's career spanned the Southern Song.

He was educated in the Cheng-brothers tradition, served as a regional official, retired periodically to teach at private academies, and produced a vast body of philosophical commentary, education theory, and ritual prescription.

His central philosophical position is that all things — every rock, every plant, every animal, every human, every emotion, every relationship — contain both li (principle: what makes a thing what it is, what its proper nature and function are) and qi (material force: the substance and energy through which the principle is actually realized).

Moral cultivation, in Zhu Xi's account, consists in gewu (geh-WOO, "investigating things") — examining the principles inherent in particular cases until one comes to understand the universal principles underlying them.
The good life is the life lived in accordance with the principles that one has, through patient investigation and reflection, come to understand.
Zhu Xi also designated a specific curriculum as the canonical Confucian core.

The Four Books (Sishu) — the Analects of Confucius, the Mencius, and two short chapters extracted from the Book of Rites called the Great Learning and the Doctrine of the Mean — became the foundational texts of Neo-Confucian education, prioritized over the older Five Classics (which Han-era Confucians had treated as the canonical body).
Zhu Xi wrote definitive commentaries on the Four Books that became required reading.
He also developed an account of personal moral cultivation that emphasized xiu shen (cultivating the self) through careful study, ritual practice, and reflective examination of one's own motives.
The institutional consequences of all this were enormous.
Starting in 1313 (under the Mongol Yuan dynasty), Zhu Xi's commentaries on the Four Books were designated as the official curriculum for the Chinese civil service examinations.

They held that position until the abolition of the examination system in 1905 — a continuous run of 592 years during which every Chinese government official was selected on the basis of his mastery of Zhu Xi's interpretation of Confucianism.

The system was adopted by Korea (in modified form, with the Joseon dynasty's exams being explicitly Neo-Confucian after 1392), Japan (where Tokugawa-era Neo-Confucianism became the official ideology of the shogunate), and Vietnam.
From the 14th century to the 20th, Zhu Xi's account of the relationship between principle, material force, and moral cultivation was the dominant intellectual framework across East Asia.

Arguments about whether Zhu Xi was right or wrong continued, of course — particularly the Wang Yangming school in Ming China developed an alternative Neo-Confucianism that emphasized intuition over investigation — but the basic Neo-Confucian framework was the assumed background of all subsequent East Asian intellectual life.

The contemporary Islamic Republic of Iran, which has structured its religious-political authority around clerical hierarchies that the Safavid dynasty established (Safavid Persia Ch 5), is a good comparison case for what happens when a particular religious-philosophical synthesis becomes the state ideology and institutional foundation of an enduring civilization.
Neo-Confucianism shaped East Asian governance, family structure, education, and gender norms with comparable depth, for comparable durations.
The most consequential gender-related Neo-Confucian innovation was the increasing rigidification of women's roles.

The earlier Tang period had been notably less restrictive of elite women than later Chinese dynasties — Tang noblewomen rode horses, played polo, wore Central Asian fashions, and operated more visibly in public life than would later be the case.
Wu Zetian's reign (Chapter 2), however controversial, was at least possible.

The Song shift toward Neo-Confucian moral philosophy went along with — though not necessarily as a straightforward cause of — a tightening of the cultural norms around female seclusion, chastity, and economic dependence.

The most visible and historically painful expression of this shift was foot-binding, which appears to have begun as a fashion among Song court dancers in the 10th or 11th century and spread gradually through elite and then non-elite female populations over the following centuries.

Foot-binding involved tightly wrapping young girls' feet (typically starting at ages 4–7) so that the toes folded under the sole and the arch was forced upward, producing a permanently deformed foot a few inches long.
The practice became progressively more widespread over the Song, Yuan, and Ming periods and was nearly universal among Han Chinese women by the late Qing.
It would not be effectively suppressed until the early 20th century.
Foot-binding's exact origins, social meanings, and reasons for spread are still debated by historians; the textual record is much less specific than later moralizing makes it sound.

What is clear is that the practice originated in the Song, that it spread alongside the Neo-Confucian tightening of female roles, and that it became one of the most physically destructive cultural practices ever institutionalized at scale — affecting tens of millions of women over nearly a thousand years.
The printing-and-examination culture of the Song was the second great structural innovation that shaped what came after.
The Tang had introduced the examination system (Chapter 2); the Song massively expanded it.
By the mid-Northern Song, several hundred jinshi degrees were being awarded each year, against the Tang's typical few dozen.
Examination-prep schools, study societies, lineage academies, and private tutors proliferated across China to serve the demand.

Woodblock printing (Chapter 4) made standardized examination texts cheap and widely available — Confucian classics, anthologies of model essays, study guides, the works of admired scholars — so that ambitious families in any prefecture could prepare their sons for the exams without the resources that earlier aristocratic families had needed.
The result was an unprecedented expansion of the literate scholar class in China.

Estimates of male literacy in Northern Song urban areas run as high as 30–40% — a figure that would not be matched in Europe until the late 17th century and that, in some interpretations, was not matched anywhere else in the pre-modern world.

The Song produced a culture in which books were cheap, examinations were a real path to power for talented men of moderate means, classical literature was widely read, and intellectual debate was conducted in print in something like the volume that European intellectual debate would reach during the Enlightenment.
This is one of the major reasons world economic and cultural historians see the Song as a near-modern society.
It is worth pausing on the gender dimension here as well.
The expansion of literacy was overwhelmingly male — the examination system was closed to women, and the cultural infrastructure that supported male literary culture did not have a female equivalent.
There were exceptions: the Southern Song poet Li Qingzhao (lee ching-JOW, 1084–c. 1155) is generally considered the greatest female poet in Chinese history.
Born to a literary family and married to the antiquarian scholar Zhao Mingcheng, she shared in his collecting of inscriptions, paintings, and rare books.

Their comfortable life was destroyed by the Jurchen catastrophe of 1127 — Zhao Mingcheng died in 1129, the collection was lost in the southern flight, and Li Qingzhao spent the rest of her life as a refugee, occasionally writing poems on her displacement that are among the most directly devastating works in Chinese literature.
Her theory of the ci (TSIH) verse form — a kind of lyric poetry set to musical tunes with irregular line lengths — shaped the genre for centuries afterward.

Li Qingzhao is the major exception that proves the Song rule: she was an extraordinary female poet in a literary culture that had effectively no infrastructure for producing female poets, and her achievement says more about her individual talent than about any gender-inclusive Song literary system.
The other great Song literary figure of the period was Su Shi (SOO SHIH, 1037–1101), also known by his pen-name Su Dongpo (soo dong-PWAW).

He passed the jinshi exam at age twenty with distinction, served in various official positions throughout the Northern Song, and was repeatedly exiled by both the reform and conservative factions for being too independent.

Su Shi excelled simultaneously in ci poetry, prose essays, calligraphy (his handwritten manuscript of the prose poem "Cold Food Observance" is considered one of the greatest works of Chinese calligraphy ever produced), painting (he is one of the founders of the literati painting tradition that emphasized personal expression over technical skill), and gastronomy (Su Shi is credited with inventing Dongpo pork — a slow-braised pork-belly dish still on Chinese restaurant menus today).

His "Red Cliff Rhapsodies" — two short prose-poems written during one of his exiles, meditating on the historical battle of Red Cliffs (Six Dynasties Ch 1) and on the smallness of human life against the eternity of the river and the moon — are among the most celebrated pieces of Chinese literature.
Su Shi embodied the Song ideal of the cultivated gentleman-official: poetry, prose, calligraphy, painting, and political administration all integrated into a single life.
He also built the Su Causeway across West Lake during one of his governorships of Hangzhou, which still bears his name and is still walked by tourists nine centuries later.
The third defining Song development was the porcelain trade centered on Jingdezhen (jing-deh-JEN).

Chinese ceramics had been advancing for millennia, but the Song combination of refined kilns, high-quality kaolin clay, and large-scale commercial demand produced the first true global-scale Chinese porcelain industry.
Jingdezhen, in northeastern Jiangxi province, sat on enormous deposits of the white kaolin clay that produces the most refined porcelain when fired to high temperatures.

In 1004, the Song court designated Jingdezhen as the official imperial porcelain supplier — the beginning of a thousand-year run during which Jingdezhen would be the global capital of porcelain production, lasting through the Ming and Qing dynasties and continuing as a porcelain town today.
Song porcelain came in many varieties.

The most famous categories were the Five Great Kilns (wu da yao): Ru ware (small-scale imperial production with a distinctive sky-blue celadon glaze, prized above almost all other Song ceramics), Guan ware ("official ware," produced for the imperial court), Ge ware (with deliberate cracking patterns in the glaze), Ding ware (white porcelain with delicate molded or carved decoration), and Jun ware (with bold copper-red and blue color patches achieved through controlled firing variation).
Jingdezhen specialized in qingbai ("blue-white") ware, a transparent, slightly bluish glaze on white porcelain.
Longquan kilns produced spectacular jade-green celadon that became one of the most valued export ceramics across Eurasia.
The export trade was enormous.

Song porcelain has been excavated from sites across Southeast Asia, India, the Persian Gulf, the Red Sea, and the East African coast — the same archaeological pattern that the Tang Belitung shipwreck of c. 830 had foreshadowed (Chapter 3).
The Quanzhou shipwreck of c. 1271 (a Southern Song ocean junk that sank near the southern coastline) carried tens of thousands of pieces of porcelain among its other cargo.
Major shipwrecks recovered in modern decades from waters off Sinan in Korea and the Philippines have all carried Song porcelain in commercial quantities.

Chinese porcelain was so dominant in international trade by the late Song that European, Arabic, and Persian languages all eventually adopted Chinese names for the major ceramic categories, and the English word "china" for the material itself was the standard term in European usage by the 17th century.
The fourth Song innovation was the maritime trade revolution.

The overland Silk Road that had peaked under the Tang (Chapter 3) had been increasingly closed to Song China by the Tangut Western Xia in the northwest and by the Khitan Liao and then Jurchen Jin in the north.
The Song response was to pivot to the sea.
By the 12th and 13th centuries, Song maritime trade in the South China Sea, Indian Ocean, and beyond was operating at a scale that had never existed before in Eurasian history.
The technical infrastructure was impressive.

Song junks — multi-masted ocean-going ships with watertight bulkhead compartments (an innovation that would not appear in European shipbuilding until the 19th century), stern-mounted rudders, and the magnetic compass for navigation — could carry hundreds of tons of cargo across thousands of miles of open water.
The largest Song junks reportedly approached 100 feet in length, with crews of several hundred.
The compass made oceanic navigation reliable in conditions where coastal-only navigation had previously been required.

The trade routes ran from Song ports — primarily Quanzhou (chwan-JOH), Guangzhou, and Mingzhou (modern Ningbo) — through the South China Sea to Java and Sumatra, then through the Strait of Malacca to the Indian Ocean.

From there the routes split: northwest to India and the Persian Gulf; west to the Red Sea and indirectly to Egypt; further west across the Arabian Sea to East Africa, where Song porcelain has been excavated at coastal sites in modern Kenya, Tanzania, and Mozambique.
Song silver coins have been found as far west as the Swahili coast trading cities.

The Indian Ocean trade network of the 12th and 13th centuries was already the most globally integrated maritime economy ever to have existed up to that point, with Song porcelain, silk, and tea exchanged for Southeast Asian spices, Indian cottons, Persian glass, Arab pearls and aromatics, and African ivory and gold.
Quanzhou, the southeastern port that Arab merchants knew as Zayton, was the largest of the Song's international ports.
By the late 13th century, it was arguably the busiest port in the world.
Its harbor hosted ships from across the Indian Ocean.

Its foreign communities had their own quarters — Arab, Persian, Indian, Tamil, Southeast Asian — with their own mosques, Hindu temples (one Tamil-style Hindu temple's column fragments have been excavated at Quanzhou), and Nestorian Christian churches.
Marco Polo, visiting in the 1290s, called it one of the world's two greatest ports, alongside Alexandria.
UNESCO designated Quanzhou a World Heritage Site in 2021 in recognition of its importance as a node in the medieval Indian Ocean trade network.

The Song maritime tax revenues alone — the customs duties charged at the major ports — exceeded the entire annual income of some European medieval kingdoms (why this commercial lead did not translate into industrialization — the "Great Divergence" question — is Industrial Revolution Ch 1).
The economic gravity of the Indian Ocean trading world, in the 12th and 13th centuries, sat squarely on the Song coast.

This is the trade network that the Mongols would inherit when they conquered the Song; the Mongol Yuan dynasty that followed would maintain and extend the Song maritime infrastructure and would briefly extend Chinese influence to Cambodia, Java, and as far as Madagascar in their attempted naval invasions of the late 13th century.

Cross-civ check: the Song maritime trade revolution was contemporary with the rise of the Italian maritime republics (Venice, Genoa, Pisa, Amalfi) in the western Mediterranean, the Hanseatic League in northern Europe, and the great Indian Ocean trading networks operated by Persian, Arab, and Gujarati merchants.
The 12th and 13th centuries were a moment of unusually intense long-distance trade across the Eurasian world, and the Song was the eastern anchor of the system.
Goods moving from Song Quanzhou to Alexandria could be relayed onward to Venice and Genoa, which in turn traded with the Hanseatic ports of northern Europe.

The medieval Eurasian commercial world was already significantly globalized before the Mongol conquests reorganized it (Mongol Empire Ch 6) and well before the European Age of Exploration extended it across the Atlantic.

chapters.title: The Mongol Conquest of the Song
sentences: The Mongol Empire (Mongol Empire Ch 1) that Genghis Khan had founded in 1206 had absorbed China's northern neighbors over the course of the 13th century with terrifying efficiency.
The Tangut Western Xia was destroyed in 1227, in the campaign during which Genghis Khan himself died.

The Jurchen Jin dynasty was destroyed in 1234, after a generation of Mongol-Jin warfare that had left northern China devastated (the Jurchen had themselves devastated northern China after the Jingkang Incident; the Mongol conquest then completed what had been a multi-generational catastrophe for the population of the north Chinese plain).
The Goryeo kingdom in Korea (Ancient Korea Ch 7) submitted as a Mongol vassal in 1259.
The Dali kingdom in Yunnan was conquered in 1253.

The Mongol territorial sweep across Eurasia was, by the mid-13th century, unprecedented — from Korea to Hungary, the Mongol khanates ruled or dominated the largest contiguous land empire that had ever existed.
The Southern Song was the holdout.

The dynasty had survived in its Yangtze-valley retreat for over a century after the Jurchen catastrophe, defended by the natural barrier of the Yangtze, the technological advantages of gunpowder weapons and the Song navy, and the sheer demographic-economic weight of the wealthier southern half of China.
The Mongols had been conducting limited campaigns against the Song since the 1230s, but the systematic conquest required focused attention from a Mongol Khan who saw it as his life's project.
That Khan was Kublai (KOO-buh-lie, in the standard English transliteration), a grandson of Genghis Khan who had been the senior Mongol commander in north China for two decades.

After his elder brother Möngke died in 1259 during a campaign against the Song in Sichuan, Kublai fought a four-year civil war against his younger brother Ariq Böke for the position of Great Khan of the Mongol Empire.

Kublai won by 1264 but the cost was permanent — the Mongol Empire effectively split into four constituent khanates after this succession struggle, with Kublai's own domain centered on China and Mongolia, and with the western khanates (the Golden Horde, the Chagatai Khanate, and the Ilkhanate in Persia) operating as effectively independent powers.

Kublai responded to the political fragmentation of the larger Mongol Empire by doubling down on the project that mattered most to his personal legitimacy: the conquest of southern China and the establishment of a unified Mongol-ruled Chinese empire.
In 1271, Kublai formally proclaimed the Yuan dynasty (元, yuan — meaning "primordial" or "origin").

The proclamation was a deliberate Sinification of the Mongol position — Kublai was claiming the Chinese imperial mandate, presenting himself as a legitimate Chinese emperor in the established dynastic succession rather than as a Mongol khan governing Chinese territory.
The launching of the final Song campaigns followed almost immediately.
The decisive campaign of the Mongol-Song war was the six-year siege of Xiangyang (shyahng-YANG), 1267–1273.

Xiangyang was a heavily fortified Song city on the Han River (a major tributary of the Yangtze), commanding the corridor through which any Mongol force coming south would have to pass to reach the Yangtze valley.
The Song garrison commander Lü Wenhuan (LOO wen-HWAHN) defended Xiangyang for six years against repeated Mongol assault.

The Mongols had perfected most of the conventional siege techniques — encirclement, starvation, mining, conventional bombardment — but Xiangyang's walls were exceptional, and Mongol assaults on the walls had repeatedly failed.
The Mongol solution was to import counterweight trebuchets from the Middle East.

Two Muslim engineers — Ismail and Ala al-Din, sent by the Ilkhanate of Persia (the Mongol successor state in Iran, ruled by Kublai's relative Hulagu Khan) — built large trebuchets capable of hurling stones of approximately 220 pounds (100 kg) at the city walls from the besiegers' positions.

These were the counterweight trebuchet designs that had been developed in the Mediterranean Crusader-states context in the 12th and early 13th centuries — a Eurasian technology transfer running from the Crusader-Islamic interface through the Mongol communications network all the way to the Yangtze.
The Chinese sources called them huihui pao ("Muslim machines").
The trebuchets broke through Xiangyang's walls in early 1273.
The garrison surrendered.
The Yangtze defensive line was broken.
After Xiangyang's fall, the Mongol advance accelerated.
Kublai sent his Mongol-Chinese commander Bayan (BIGH-yahn), one of the most capable generals of the era, with a large army down the Yangtze valley.
Song defenses crumbled.
The capital Hangzhou surrendered in early 1276 under the regent dowager empress, who handed over the imperial seals along with the six-year-old Emperor Gong.

The boy emperor and most of the Hangzhou court were sent to Beijing as captives — the Hangzhou capitulation paralleled, in dynastic-trauma terms, the Jingkang Incident a century and a half earlier, except that this time the conquerors were the Mongols rather than the Jurchen.
The Song dynasty was not yet quite finished, however.
Loyalist officials had escaped from Hangzhou with two of the boy emperor's younger half-brothers and with the remnants of the Song navy.
They proclaimed one of the brothers as Emperor Duanzong in southern China and continued resisting.
Duanzong died in 1278, possibly of injuries from an accident at sea or possibly of disease.
The loyalists then proclaimed his even younger half-brother — a six-year-old named Zhao Bing — as Emperor Bing of Song.
They were now operating as a coastal-fortress and naval-resistance force in modern Guangdong, with the Mongol fleet relentlessly closing in.
The end came on March 19, 1279, at Yamen (yah-MEN), in the bay of the Pearl River estuary in modern Guangdong.
The Song fleet — by now reduced to about a thousand ships, with the boy emperor and the loyalist court aboard the largest of them — had taken refuge in the bay at Yamen.
The Mongol fleet, commanded by Zhang Hongfan (a Chinese commander in Mongol service), trapped the Song fleet in the bay.

The battle that followed lasted hours and was not really a contest — the Song ships were tactically pinned, the Mongol ships were tactically free, and the Song's gunpowder weapons could not change the outcome.
When defeat became certain, the Song minister Lu Xiufu (LOO shyoo-FOO) carried the eight-year-old Emperor Bing to the deck of the imperial flagship.
He told the boy that they could not allow themselves to be captured.
He bound the child to his back with a sash.
They jumped together into the South China Sea.
Both drowned.
Other loyalists followed.

The chronicle accounts say more than 100,000 Song officials, soldiers, palace women, and civilian followers either jumped into the sea after Lu Xiufu and Emperor Bing or refused capture and fought to the death on their burning ships.
The bodies were said to wash ashore for days afterward.
Local fishermen reportedly recognized the imperial robes on a small body that washed ashore some days later, identified it as Emperor Bing, and secretly buried him.
A small temple was eventually built at the burial site near modern Hong Kong; it still stands.
The Song dynasty was over after 319 years (counting from 960).
For the first time in Chinese history, all of China — every region, every population, every city, every political institution — was under foreign rule.

The Mongol Yuan dynasty inherited the most sophisticated economy, the most advanced bureaucracy, the largest urban population, the most innovative technology base, and the most globally connected commercial network on Earth.

The tension between Mongol military traditions and Chinese civilian governance — and the question of whether the Mongols would govern China as outsiders or be absorbed by it — would define the Yuan period that followed (Mongol Empire Ch 8 and the forthcoming Yuan Dynasty TL).
A pause, on what was lost and what was inherited.
The Sui-Tang-Song arc covered nearly seven hundred years — from Yang Jian's reunification in 589 to the drowning of Emperor Bing in 1279.

Across that span, Chinese civilization had moved through reunification, golden age, catastrophic civil war, partial recovery, second collapse, second reunification under different constitutional principles, technological revolution, Jurchen catastrophe, Southern recovery, and finally Mongol conquest.

Some of the cultural and technological achievements of the period — Tang poetry, Song philosophy, Song landscape painting, Jingdezhen porcelain, paper money, movable type, the navigation compass, gunpowder weapons, examination meritocracy, Neo-Confucianism — would shape East Asia and, indirectly, the rest of the world for the next thousand years and counting.

Some of the catastrophes — the An Lushan Rebellion's death toll, the Jingkang Incident's national trauma, the systematic Mongol destruction of north China's cities and population in the 13th century — would shape Chinese cultural memory for just as long.
The Mongol Yuan dynasty that followed in 1279 would be the first foreign dynasty to rule all of China.
The Ming dynasty that overthrew it in 1368 would self-consciously model itself on the Tang and Song, treating those dynasties as the standard for what proper Chinese civilization looked like.
The Qing dynasty that overthrew the Ming in 1644 would do the same, even though the Qing rulers were themselves Manchus (descendants of the Jurchen) ruling as foreigners.

The constitutional model of civilian bureaucratic rule with examination-selected officials, which the Song had pioneered in deliberate reaction against the failures of the Tang military system, would persist as the basic structure of Chinese governance through the entire imperial period — for nearly a thousand years after the Song's founding, until the abolition of the imperial examinations in 1905 and the fall of the Qing in 1912 finally ended the system.

The cosmopolitan Chang'an of the High Tang and the maritime-commercial Hangzhou of the Southern Song are still, in 2026, the cities that contemporary Chinese cultural memory returns to most often when imagining what Chinese civilization at its peak could look like.
The Tang and Song are not just dynasties; they are the standard against which all subsequent Chinese history has measured itself.
That standard was set during the seven hundred years this book covers.

Cross-civ check: the Mongol conquest of the Song in 1279 was contemporary with the height of the Crusader era's collapse (the fall of Acre, the last Crusader stronghold in the Levant, in 1291), the end of the Abbasid Caliphate in Baghdad (the Mongol sack of Baghdad under Hulagu in 1258, which the Mongol-Song war was effectively the eastern parallel of — Islamic Golden Age Ch 10), the rise of the early Renaissance in Italy, and the development of the Hanseatic League in northern Europe.

The 13th century was the moment when the Mongol Empire briefly unified most of Eurasia under a single political order, enabling the long-distance travels of merchants like Marco Polo (who crossed Asia in the 1270s and returned to Venice in 1295 with stories that shaped European understanding of the East for centuries) and missionaries like the Franciscans John of Plano Carpini and William of Rubruck.
The Mongol conquest of Song China was the eastern hinge of this Eurasian moment.

The world that emerged afterward — with the Yuan dynasty governing China, the Ilkhanate governing Persia, the Golden Horde governing the Russian steppes, and the Chagatai Khanate governing Central Asia, all linked by Mongol-protected trade routes — was the most globally interconnected pre-modern world that had ever existed.
The Tang-Song China that the Mongols conquered was the eastern cornerstone of that world.

Its fall in 1279 ended the dynasty but inaugurated the era of Eurasian exchange that would, four centuries later, produce the European voyages of discovery that would, in turn, produce the modern world.
The Sui-Tang-Song story ends here.
The Yuan story begins next.

chapters.title: The Founding
sentences: The dynasty began with a general who refused to follow orders.
In the spring of 1388, the Goryeo court — the dynasty that had ruled the Korean peninsula for the previous 470 years — issued a foolish command.

Goryeo's last decades had been dominated by the great Mongol-era political struggle: was Korea aligned with the dying Yuan dynasty, the Mongol-founded regime that had subjugated Goryeo in the thirteenth century (Mongol Empire Ch 6), or with the new Ming dynasty that had just expelled the Mongols from Beijing in 1368?
The Goryeo court was split.

The pro-Yuan faction, hoping to recover territory the new Ming had claimed in the Liaodong Peninsula (the southern tip of Manchuria, just across the Yalu River from Korea), demanded the army march north and attack Ming positions.
The general assigned to lead this invasion was Yi Seong-gye (yee SUNG-gay, 1335–1408), the most successful military commander of late Goryeo.

He had spent his career fighting Japanese pirates on the southern coast and Jurchen tribes on the northern frontier (the Jurchen were Tungusic-speaking forest people — a different language family from Chinese, Korean, or Mongolian, more closely related to Manchu — who lived north of Korea in what is now Manchuria).
Yi was not enthusiastic about attacking the Ming.

He thought the war was unwinnable, that the heavy summer rains would ruin a campaign, and that crossing the Yalu River into Ming territory would invite an annihilating counterattack on the Korean peninsula itself.
He marched north anyway, because that was the order, but when he reached the Yalu River island of Wihwa, he stopped.
He held the army on the island, sent petitions back to the king asking for the order to be rescinded, and was refused.
So in May 1388 Yi did the unthinkable: he turned the army around and marched on the Goryeo capital of Gaegyeong (modern Kaesong, in present-day North Korea).
This is called the Wihwado Retreat, and it was the founding act of the Joseon dynasty, four years before the dynasty actually existed.
Yi seized the king, exiled him, installed a puppet, and over the next four years systematically destroyed his rivals and reorganized the country's land tenure.
In 1392 he forced the abdication of the last Goryeo king and proclaimed himself the founding monarch of a new dynasty.
His reign name would be Taejo (TAY-joh, "Great Founder"), the same temple name used by every founding king of every Korean dynasty for the previous millennium.

The new dynasty was named Joseon (JOH-suhn) — a name with deep antiquarian appeal, since it had been the name of the legendary Gojoseon kingdom said to have ruled the peninsula in mythological prehistory (Ancient Korea Ch 2).
What Yi Seong-gye did in 1388–1392 is what generals do when the central government collapses around them.
The unusual thing is that the dynasty he founded would last 518 years.

Across the same five-century span, China would see the entire arc of the Ming dynasty (1368–1644) and the entire arc of the Qing dynasty (1644–1912) plus a few years; Japan would see the Muromachi shogunate, the Sengoku civil-war period, the unification under Hideyoshi, the Tokugawa shogunate (Ancient Japan Ch 8 — and the next Japan TL will pick this up), and the Meiji Restoration; Western Europe would go from the late Middle Ages through the Renaissance, the Reformation, the Enlightenment, the French Revolution, the Industrial Revolution, and into the early twentieth century.
Joseon, meanwhile, would stay Joseon.
One dynasty, one capital, one ideology, one alphabet, one royal palace complex, one method of selecting officials.
The unusual thing about Joseon is not how it began.
It is how long it lasted.
To understand why it lasted, you have to understand the ideology it was built on.
Joseon adopted Neo-Confucianism as its official state philosophy in 1394 — the first great act of Taejo's reign after the move of the capital.

Neo-Confucianism is a specific philosophical school that had developed in China during the Song dynasty (960–1279) under thinkers like Zhu Xi (joo SHEE, 1130–1200), the synthesizer who organized the entire tradition into a coherent metaphysical system.

It is not "old Confucianism plus some new stuff." It is a philosophical reconstruction of Confucianism that used Buddhist and Daoist metaphysical categories to give the old ethical teachings a comprehensive cosmological foundation.

The key ideas: the universe operates on li (lee, "principle" — the underlying patterns that govern all things) and gi (gee, also written "qi" in Chinese romanization — the material force or energy that gives things their substance).
Human beings have an inherently good nature derived from heaven; moral cultivation is a matter of clearing away the cloudy bits of gi that obscure the inherent li.
The proper organization of society mirrors the proper organization of the cosmos: hierarchical, ordered, ritually structured.

The five core relationships — ruler/subject, father/son, husband/wife, elder/younger sibling, friend/friend — should each be governed by the appropriate moral norm (loyalty, filial piety, propriety, deference, trust).
The classical Confucian texts, supplemented by Zhu Xi's commentaries, contain everything a person needs to know to live ethically and govern wisely.
This sounds abstract.
In practice, what Neo-Confucianism produced was a society obsessed with ritual correctness, family hierarchy, and scholarly study.
It produced civil service examinations (Chapter 3) that selected officials based on their mastery of Confucian texts.
It produced an ancestor-worship system in which the heads of households performed elaborate seasonal sacrifices to dead parents, grandparents, and great-grandparents back four generations.

It produced the yangban (YAHNG-bahn, "two orders" — the civil and military officials whose status was hereditary), Joseon's scholar-gentry class, who were exempted from taxes and military service in exchange for their dedication to ritual, scholarship, and government service.

Neo-Confucianism was not a religion in the Western sense — it had no creator god, no afterlife of judgment, no congregation, no clergy in the strict sense — but it occupied the same social space, organizing belief, behavior, ritual, and political legitimacy.
And like any state ideology, it required something to displace.
What it displaced was Buddhism.
Goryeo had been a Buddhist state.

For 470 years before Joseon, Buddhism had been the religion of kings, the patron of the arts, the owner of vast temple estates, the sponsor of the carved wooden printing blocks of the Tripitaka Koreana (the complete Buddhist canon — over 80,000 wooden printing blocks still preserved at Haeinsa Temple in southern Korea), and the institutional bedrock of Korean cultural life.
Buddhist monasteries had owned a quarter of all arable land in the peninsula.
Buddhist monks had served as royal advisors and battlefield commanders.
Buddhist iconography had defined Korean art for centuries (Ancient Korea Ch 8).
Joseon broke this comprehensively.
The new dynasty's policy of Buddhist suppression began under Taejo and accelerated under his successors.
Temple lands were confiscated.
Monasteries were dissolved by the hundreds.
The number of officially recognized Buddhist sects was reduced first to seven, then to two.
Monks were banned from entering the capital city of Hanyang (HAHN-yahng, the new name for the city we now call Seoul).
Buddhist clergy were stripped of their political role.
The state ceased to recognize Buddhist ordination.

Surviving temples were pushed out of population centers and into the mountains, where many of them still are today — the picturesque mountain temples of modern South Korea are not picturesque by accident, they are what survives of an institution that was deliberately exiled to the periphery.

This was as comprehensive a religious displacement as the Safavid conversion of Iran from Sunni to Shia Islam (Safavid Persia Ch 2), and it was carried out by similar mechanisms: state seizure of religious property, exclusion of the displaced clergy from political life, and the systematic substitution of an alternative ideology in every institution that had been religious.
The Safavid project required imported Lebanese clerics to staff the new Shia state religion.

Joseon had it easier — Korea already had a domestic Confucian scholar tradition to draw on, since Confucianism had been part of Korean elite culture since the Three Kingdoms period (Ancient Korea Ch 4).
The architect of the suppression was a man named Jeong Do-jeon (JUNG doh-JUHN, 1342–1398).
Jeong Do-jeon is the most important Joseon thinker most non-Korean readers have never heard of.
He was Yi Seong-gye's chief political theorist, the man who more than anyone else designed the new dynasty's institutional and ideological framework.
He drafted the legal code.
He laid out the city plan of the new capital at Hanyang (the rectangular grid still visible in old central Seoul follows his design).

He wrote a sustained polemical work, the Bulssi Japbyeon ("Critique of Buddhism"), arguing that Buddhism was philosophically incoherent, that its monastic life violated the natural order of family obligation, that its ascetic withdrawal from the world was a form of cowardly social parasitism, and that no proper society could be organized on its principles.

More radically, Jeong argued that the king should be a moral figurehead — a symbol of legitimacy and an exemplar of virtue — while actual day-to-day governance should be conducted by scholar-officials selected on the basis of competence and moral cultivation.
The throne was sacred but the prime minister and his cabinet of bureaucrats should run the country.

This was a recognizable strain of Confucian political thought (it traced back to the original Confucius and especially to Mencius in the fourth century BCE), but Jeong pushed it harder than any previous Korean theorist.
What this meant in practice was that the king should not act on his own initiative against the considered judgment of his ministers.
Royal decrees should be subject to scholarly review.
Royal personality should be irrelevant to royal function — a lazy or stupid king was no problem if the bureaucracy was strong.
The court would have multiple layers of remonstrating officials whose explicit job was to tell the king when he was wrong.
This vision of constrained monarchy and bureaucratic supremacy was implemented over the next century in Joseon's administrative structure.

It is one of the reasons the dynasty lasted 518 years: under this system, even a child king or a mentally unstable king could not destroy the state, because the state was not in his hands to begin with. (We will see the limits of this principle in later chapters — the system did not actually constrain Yeonsangun (Chapter 3) or completely prevent the Sedo crisis (Chapter 7) — but it meant the system could survive what would have wrecked many other monarchies.) It is also one of the reasons Jeong Do-jeon was murdered six years into the new dynasty.
Taejo had eight sons by two wives.

The succession question was therefore complicated, and Jeong Do-jeon's preference made it more so: backed by the queen, Jeong supported the youngest son, Yi Bang-seok (yee BAHNG-suk), as crown prince.
The fifth son, Yi Bang-won (yee BAHNG-WON, 1367–1422) — who had actually been one of his father's most active military lieutenants in the seizure of power — was passed over.
Yi Bang-won did not accept this calmly.
In August 1398, Bang-won staged a palace coup.
He killed Jeong Do-jeon, killed his half-brother the crown prince, killed his other young half-brother for good measure, and forced his shocked father Taejo to reconsider the succession.

Taejo abdicated in disgust, retiring to his hometown of Hamheung (HAHM-hung, in the northeast), where he reportedly had a series of envoys executed when his son sent them to ask his permission for various ceremonial matters — an episode preserved in the Korean idiom Hamheung chasa, "messenger to Hamheung," which still means "person sent on an errand from which they will not return." Bang-won did not immediately take the throne.

He installed his elder brother Jeongjong (JUNG-johng) as a placeholder for two years, during which a second coup (the Second Strife of Princes, 1400) eliminated the last serious rival, the second-eldest brother.
Bang-won then had Jeongjong abdicate in his favor and took the throne as Taejong (TAY-johng) in 1400.
This whole sequence — known in Korean as the First and Second Strifes of Princes — was bloody and traumatic and might easily have wrecked the new dynasty if the institutions had been less sturdy.
It nearly wrecked Taejo, who never spoke to his fratricidal son again and lived out his last decade brooding in the mountains.

It also produced one of the strangest features of the founding generation: the most brilliant intellectual of the new dynasty, Jeong Do-jeon, was dead in the dirt by 1398, killed by the man who would actually have to figure out how to run the country he had designed.
But Taejong was, despite the murder, an effective and farsighted ruler.

He spent his eighteen-year reign consolidating royal authority, breaking the power of the founding generation's military supporters, reforming the tax system, and most consequentially preparing the smoothest possible succession for his son.
In 1418 he abdicated voluntarily — a remarkable act in Korean royal history — passing the throne to his son Sejong while retaining shadow power as senior monarch for a few years.
The Sejong succession was the foundation for everything that followed (Chapter 2).
A pause to take stock of the new capital, because the geography of Hanyang is the geography Joseon would inhabit for the next half-millennium.
The old Goryeo capital at Gaegyeong was rejected immediately by Taejo's geomancers as ill-fated.
Geomancy (pungsu in Korean, feng shui in Chinese) was the study of how the energies of the landscape affected human fortune, and a new dynasty needed a city sited in a place of auspicious energy.

After several false starts (including a brief move to a different site that was abandoned after a year), Taejo and his planners settled on the basin we now call Seoul: a roughly oval area of perhaps 10 square miles surrounded by an unbroken ring of mountains — Mount Bugak (BOO-gahk) to the north, Mount Naksan (NAHK-sahn) to the east, Mount Namsan (NAHM-sahn) to the south, and Mount Inwang (IN-wahng) to the west — with the Han River flowing east to west across its southern edge.
This geography was geomantically near-perfect: protected, watered, defensible, with a clear axis of energy flow from the northern mountain (Mount Bugak) down to the river.
The city was named Hanyang.
It would not be officially renamed Seoul until 1946, but the place is the same place, and most of the Joseon-era street layout still underlies modern central Seoul.

The new dynasty built five major palaces in and around this basin, all of which still survive (in restored form) and all of which can be visited today: Gyeongbokgung (GYUNG-bohk-goong, 1395, the principal palace), Changdeokgung (chahng-DUHK-goong, 1405, the working palace after Gyeongbokgung was burned in 1592), Changgyeonggung (chahng-GYUNG-goong, 1418, the queen-mothers' residence), Gyeonghuigung (gyung-HEE-goong, 1623, the western secondary palace), and Deoksugung (DUHK-soo-goong, originally a royal villa, expanded into a palace in the late nineteenth century when Gojong took refuge there).

The Confucian royal ancestral shrine, Jongmyo (JOHNG-myo, 1395), was built east of Gyeongbokgung to house the spirit tablets of the kings and queens; the rituals performed there continue today and are UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage.
The royal Confucian academy, Sungkyunkwan (SUNG-gyoon-gwahn, 1398), was built northeast of the palaces and remains in continuous operation as the lineal ancestor of modern Sungkyunkwan University.
The city wall ran for 11 miles around the perimeter of the basin, with eight gates — four major and four minor — that controlled access.
Substantial portions of this wall still stand and can be hiked.

The four major gates were named for the cardinal Confucian virtues: the South Gate (still standing as Sungnyemun, "Gate of Exalted Ceremony," and now a Korean national treasure) for propriety, the East Gate (Heunginjimun, "Gate of Rising Benevolence") for benevolence, and so on.
The whole layout was a Neo-Confucian statement in stone.
The throne hall faced south, as Confucian rulers were supposed to.
The palace gates were oriented along the geomantic axis.
The royal shrine was placed on the east of the palace and the altar of grain on the west, in conformity with classical Chinese ritual prescriptions.
Even the trees and ponds were placed to reflect cosmological correctness.
The city was the dynasty's ideology rendered as urban planning.

Cross-civ check: while Yi Seong-gye was founding Joseon in 1392, the Ottoman Empire under Bayezid I was at the height of its early expansion, conquering most of the Balkans and starting to encircle Constantinople (Ottoman Empire Ch 1–2).

The Ming Dynasty in China was 24 years into its reign, with the Hongwu Emperor consolidating his rule and exterminating his own founding generation in a series of bloody purges that make the Strife of Princes look mild.
Timur the Turco-Mongol conqueror was campaigning across Iran, Iraq, and India, leaving the pyramids of skulls that are mentioned at the start of the Safavid story (Safavid Persia Ch 1).

In western Europe, the Hundred Years' War was grinding through its later phases, and the Italian Renaissance was just beginning to find its earliest footing under figures like Brunelleschi (whose famous Florence cathedral dome would not be completed until 1436, when Sejong was already creating Hangul).

In the Americas, the Aztec Empire was a generation old and rising rapidly to dominance over central Mexico (Aztec Empire Ch 1), and the Inca Empire under Pachacuti was about to begin its great burst of Andean expansion (Andean Kingdoms Ch 8).
Joseon was being founded, in other words, in a world being remade everywhere at once — but the dynasty it founded would outlast every one of these contemporaries.

chapters.title: Sejong the Great
sentences: The fourth king of Joseon is the only Korean monarch usually called "the Great" in English, and the call is not controversial.
Sejong (SAY-johng, born Yi Do in 1397, reigned 1418–1450) was Taejong's third son and an unlikely heir.
He was the third son.

He was a famously bookish child who reportedly read every Confucian classic and every Chinese history available, sometimes the same book a hundred times in a row. (His father once confiscated his books to make him exercise; the boy reportedly found one his father had missed and read it instead.) The conventional story is that Taejong's elder son, the original crown prince Yangnyeong (YAHNG-nyung), behaved so badly — drinking, womanizing, ignoring his Confucian instructors, generally embarrassing the family — that Taejong demoted him in favor of the bookish younger brother.

The rejected elder later became a wandering Buddhist monk, by all accounts content with the trade. (Whether Yangnyeong's bad behavior was performed deliberately to free his more talented brother for the throne is a romantic theory popular in modern Korean drama; the actual evidence is consistent with both a princely self-sacrifice and simple princely incompetence, and it is impossible to distinguish them now.) Sejong inherited the throne in 1418 at age twenty-one, with his father continuing as senior monarch for three more years.
He reigned for thirty-two years, until his death in 1450.

In those three decades he produced the most remarkable concentration of state-sponsored cultural and scientific achievement in any premodern East Asian reign — roughly equivalent in concentrated impact to what the Caliph al-Ma'mun had done in ninth-century Baghdad (Islamic Golden Age Ch 3), what Akbar would do in late-sixteenth-century India, or what Augustus had done for Roman literature in the first century BCE.

The list is striking: a phonetic alphabet that solved a problem nobody else in East Asia had even attempted to solve; the first standardized rain gauge in the world; the first self-striking water clock in Korea; the first state-commissioned agricultural manual based on actual interviews with farmers rather than copied from Chinese sources; the first metal-cast typeface (in the Gyemija typeface of 1403 — actually under his father, but expanded under Sejong) capable of printing thousands of pages of text; the systematic mapping of the northern Jurchen frontier and the establishment of the modern Korea-China border; and a concerted scientific program in astronomy, music theory, agricultural science, and medicine.
Most of this was done through an institution Sejong founded called the Hall of Worthies.
The Jiphyeonjeon (JIP-hyun-juhn, "Hall of Assembled Worthies"), refounded by Sejong in 1420, was a state-funded research institute housed in Gyeongbokgung Palace.
Its members were the brightest scholars in the country, recruited through the civil service exam and assigned full-time to scholarly projects rather than to administrative duty.
They lived in or near the palace, had access to the royal library, drew government salaries, and were given specific research commissions by the king.

Sejong personally participated in their work — the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty (the official daily record of the reign, see below) describe him sitting up past midnight discussing technical questions with his Hall of Worthies scholars.
The most famous member of the Hall of Worthies was probably Jeong In-ji (JUNG IN-jee, 1396–1478), who would later serve as a senior minister under three kings.
Other key figures included Seong Sam-mun (SUNG SAHM-mun) and Sin Suk-ju (SHIN SOOK-joo), both linguistic scholars who would do much of the technical work on the Hangul project.

The Hall produced the Yongbieocheonga (yong-BEE-uh-CHUN-gah, "Songs of Flying Dragons"), a 125-poem epic celebrating the rise of the Joseon dynasty and the first major literary work composed in the new alphabet; the Worin cheongangjigok (WUR-in CHUN-gahng-jee-gohk, "Songs of the Moon Reflected in a Thousand Rivers"), a Buddhist verse cycle in Hangul written by Sejong himself; the Nongsa Jikseol (NONG-sah jik-SUHL, "Straight Talk on Farming," 1429), the first agricultural manual based on Korean rather than Chinese practice; the Hyangyak Jipseongbang, a comprehensive medical reference focused on Korean herbs; and dozens of other government-sponsored books on history, ritual, music, and law.

This is the same institution-of-state-scholars idea that produced the Imperial Academy in Han China (Han Dynasty Ch 5), the House of Wisdom in Abbasid Baghdad (Islamic Golden Age Ch 3), the Translation Bureaus of Cordoba and Toledo, and the medieval European universities.

Each civilization that wants to do science and scholarship at scale eventually figures out the same answer: pay the scholars, give them somewhere to work and access to good libraries, and let them go.

The Hall of Worthies was Korea's version, and for thirty-two years it worked exceptionally well. (Sejong's grandson Sejo would dissolve it in 1456 after some of its members opposed his usurpation of the throne — one of the more depressing institutional self-inflictions in Korean history.) The Hall's most famous product is Hangul (HAHN-gool, "Korean writing").
To explain why Hangul matters, you have to explain the problem it was designed to solve.

Korean is a member of the Koreanic language family — possibly distantly related to Japanese (the so-called "Altaic" hypothesis, now generally rejected by linguists), but for practical purposes a language isolate with no close living relatives.
As different from Chinese as English is from Arabic, in linguistic structural terms.

Korean has agglutinative grammar (long words built from stacked suffixes that mark grammatical relations), a vowel inventory completely different from Chinese, and a syllable structure that allows clusters Chinese cannot pronounce.
Korean was not, however, written in its own script before 1443.
It was written in classical Chinese characters (called hanja in Korean), the same characters used to write Chinese itself.
This created a fundamental mismatch.

Educated Koreans learned to read and write classical Chinese as a separate language — like medieval European clerks learning Latin — and then composed all their formal writing in Chinese, even when the spoken language they used at home was Korean.

There were various awkward scripts that used Chinese characters to spell out Korean sounds (the idu and hyangchal systems, see Ancient Korea Ch 7), but they were clumsy, inconsistent, and required the user to already know thousands of Chinese characters.

The result was that literacy was almost entirely confined to the yangban scholar class, because learning the 3,000–5,000 Chinese characters needed to read serious texts took decades of study available only to people whose families could afford it.
The Joseon population was perhaps 5 million in 1443.
The literate population was probably under 50,000.
Government documents, legal codes, royal decrees, religious texts, agricultural manuals — everything was written in a language ordinary Koreans could not read.
Sejong saw this as a problem worth solving.

The Hunminjeongeum (hoon-MIN-jung-um, "The Correct Sounds for the Instruction of the People") was the alphabet Sejong personally designed, with assistance from Hall of Worthies scholars, and promulgated in 1443.

He published an explanatory book in 1446 (now a UNESCO Memory of the World document) that included a famous preface in his own voice: "The sounds of our country's language are different from those of China and cannot be communicated through Chinese characters.
Many among the ignorant common people, when they have things to say, are unable to express them in writing.

Pitying this, I have newly created twenty-eight letters, wishing that everyone may easily learn them and use them to advantage in their daily lives." This is, by any reasonable standard, the most explicitly democratic justification for a writing reform in any premodern document.

Sejong is saying out loud that the existing writing system serves a small literate elite at the expense of the common people, and that the new system is being created specifically so commoners can write what they need to write.
The political content is unmistakable.
The technical achievement is even more remarkable than the political one.
Hangul has fifteen consonants and ten vowels in its modern simplified form (the original 1443 alphabet had 28 letters total, including a few that have since fallen out of use).
The consonants are not arbitrary symbols.
Each one is a stylized diagram of the position the mouth is in when producing that sound.
The letter ㄱ (g/k) shows the back of the tongue rising to touch the soft palate.
The letter ㄴ (n) shows the tip of the tongue touching the alveolar ridge behind the upper teeth.
The letter ㅁ (m) shows the closed lips.
The letter ㅅ (s) shows the shape of the tooth-and-tongue configuration that produces a sibilant.
The vowels are based on three primary symbols representing heaven (a dot or short stroke), earth (a horizontal line), and human (a vertical line), combined to produce the various vowel sounds.

The result is an alphabet that is simultaneously phonetically precise (it represents the sounds of Korean directly, with very few exceptions), structurally elegant (related sounds have related letter shapes), and easy to learn (Sejong's own preface to the Hunminjeongeum says, no exaggeration, that "a wise man can acquaint himself with these letters before the morning is over; even a stupid man can learn them in the space of ten days").
Modern linguists have widely praised it.

The University of Chicago linguist Jared Diamond called Hangul "the world's best alphabet." Geoffrey Sampson's book Writing Systems devotes an admiring chapter to it, calling it "the most ingenious writing system ever invented." The Korean linguistic societies celebrate Hangul Day every October 9 as a public holiday.
The yangban hated it.
The yangban opposition to Hangul was sharp, sustained, and partly successful at slowing its adoption.
The most famous attack came from Choe Manli (CHOY MAHN-lee), a senior Hall of Worthies scholar who in 1444 submitted a long memorial to Sejong arguing that the new alphabet should be abandoned.

Choe's arguments are revealing about the worldview the alphabet threatened: using Hangul instead of Chinese characters would alienate Korea from the civilized world (meaning China); it would let common people read books they had no business reading; it would make Korea look like a country of illiterate barbarians who needed a baby alphabet because they could not learn proper writing; it would undermine the institutional position of educated Confucian scholars whose legitimacy rested on their mastery of the inaccessible classical script. (Choe did not put it quite this baldly, but the subtext is unmistakable.) Sejong's reply was sharp: he told Choe that he had clearly never thought hard about phonology, that the new alphabet was specifically designed for situations Chinese characters could not handle, and that the social benefits of mass literacy outweighed the concerns about cultural deference.
Choe was demoted briefly.
The alphabet survived Sejong's reign.
But its institutional position was never as strong as Sejong might have hoped.

After Sejong's death the new alphabet was given the dismissive nickname eonmun (UN-moon, "vernacular script") and was treated as a low-prestige writing system suitable for women, novelists, Buddhist monks, and translations of Chinese classics aimed at semi-literate audiences.
Government documents continued to be written in classical Chinese for the next 450 years.
The yangban literary establishment continued to compose all serious literature in classical Chinese until late in the nineteenth century.

Hangul was widely used — by women in private letters, by commoners for accounting and shopping lists, by Buddhist printers for religious tracts, by playwrights for popular pansori operas (Chapter 6) — but it occupied a low cultural position throughout Joseon.
What rescued Hangul was the late nineteenth and twentieth centuries.
As Korean nationalism grew under the threat of Japanese annexation (Chapter 8), Hangul became the symbol of distinctive Korean national identity — the alphabet, as opposed to the foreign script.
The Independence Newspaper began publishing entirely in Hangul in 1896.
Korean independence activists in the early twentieth century made promotion of Hangul one of their core programs.
By the time of liberation from Japan in 1945, Hangul was the official script of Korean nationalism, and both the new North and South Korean governments adopted it as the national writing system.
South Korea now uses Hangul almost exclusively (with occasional Chinese characters in historical or scholarly contexts); North Korea uses Hangul exclusively.
The five centuries of yangban suspicion have been forgotten.
Sejong's bet that ordinary people deserved a writing system they could actually learn took five hundred years to pay off completely.
It paid off.
While Sejong was inventing the alphabet, he was also running the most active scientific program in fifteenth-century East Asia, much of it carried out by a single man.
Jang Yeong-sil (JAHNG YUNG-seel, c. 1390–after 1442) is one of the most extraordinary figures in Korean history, and his story is sometimes hard to believe even though it is well documented.
He was born a gwannobi (a government-owned slave) in Dongnae, in the southeastern part of the country.
His exact ethnic background is uncertain — some sources say his father was a Chinese immigrant — but his official social status was the lowest in the kingdom.
Slaves did not receive formal education and could not hold government positions.
Slaves made bronze implements and repaired tools, which is what Jang's father did, and what Jang grew up doing alongside him.
Jang Yeong-sil's mechanical talent was so extraordinary that local officials repeatedly recommended him for higher service.
Eventually, around 1421, Sejong personally summoned him to the court, freed him from slavery, and assigned him to the royal observatory and instrument workshop.
Over the next two decades Jang produced an astonishing range of scientific instruments: The cheugugi (CHU-goo-gee, 1441) — the world's first standardized rain gauge.

A bronze cylindrical container of fixed dimensions was distributed to every county magistrate's office in the country, with instructions to record rainfall after every storm and report monthly to the Ministry of Works.
The data was used to predict harvests, plan irrigation, and adjust tax assessments.
Standardized rain gauges did not appear in Europe for another two centuries.

The jagyeongnu (jah-GYUNG-noo, "Self-Striking Water Clock," 1434) — a sophisticated automated water clock that announced the hours by automatically striking gongs, drums, and bells through a system of brass balls released by floats.
Smaller mechanical figures dressed as ministers appeared at appropriate hours to bow toward the throne hall.
The jagyeongnu was the official state timekeeper, installed in the courtyard of Gyeongbokgung Palace and used to set the bells of the city gates that opened at dawn and closed at curfew.
The honcheonui and ganui, two large bronze armillary spheres for tracking the positions of stars and planets.
The astronomical readings were used to calibrate the Korean calendar — previously dependent on the Chinese imperial calendar, which was slightly miscalibrated for Korean latitude.

A series of sundials of various designs, including the angbuilgu (ANG-boo-il-goo, the "upturned-bowl sundial"), a hemispherical sundial that could be read at any time of year by tracking the shadow against engraved hour and seasonal lines.
Several of these were installed in public spaces in Hanyang for ordinary people to use.
Improvements to metal type-casting that produced the Gabin typeface (1434), one of the most refined typefaces of the early Joseon printing industry.

The agricultural data, the astronomical observations, the time-keeping infrastructure, and the printing capacity were all integrated into a state apparatus aimed at producing useful knowledge — the most sustained scientific patronage program in fifteenth-century East Asia. (China under the Ming was actively reducing scientific work in this same period as it turned inward after the great voyages of Zheng He.

Sejong's Korea was the leading scientific producer in the region by mid-century.) Jang Yeong-sil's name appears in the Sejong Annals dozens of times, always with his title and salary noted; he was eventually promoted to a high official rank that should have been impossible for a former slave.
The institutional system that Sejong had built was capable of recognizing and rewarding extraordinary talent regardless of birth — at least when the king was personally pushing it.
After Sejong's death the system reverted to its default mode, which is what made the brief flowering under Sejong so remarkable.
Sejong's military program was equally consequential, if less famous.
The northern frontier of Korea had been an unstable boundary for centuries.

The territory north of the Yalu and Tumen rivers — what is now Manchuria, the Chinese-administered region of Jilin and Heilongjiang — was inhabited by Jurchen tribes (Tungusic-speaking forest people, ancestors of the Manchus who would conquer China in the seventeenth century).

The Jurchen had no central political organization in the early fifteenth century — they were divided into dozens of competing tribes, alternately raiding Korean villages and trading with Korean officials.
The exact line of the Korea-Jurchen frontier had wavered for centuries.
Sejong fixed it.

He sent his most capable generals — most importantly Kim Jong-seo (KIM JOHNG-suh) in the northeast and Choe Yun-deok (CHOY YOON-duhk) in the northwest — to drive the Jurchens north of the Yalu and Tumen and establish permanent military garrisons along the line.

Between 1433 and 1443, Korean forces fought a series of expeditions against various Jurchen tribes, eventually establishing the Six Forts (along the Tumen River in the northeast) and the Four Districts (along the Yalu River in the northwest).
Korean settlers were moved into the newly secured territories and granted tax exemptions.

The Korea-China border that resulted is, with minor variations, the same border that exists today between the modern Korean states (North and South) and China — a remarkable case of a fifteenth-century military campaign producing a stable international border that has lasted nearly six hundred years.

The Jurchen, displaced and pushed back, would coalesce in the late sixteenth century under Nurhaci and become the Manchus who would invade Korea in 1627 and 1636 (Chapter 5) and conquer China in 1644.
The same people who Sejong's generals had pushed off Korean territory would, three generations later, force Sejong's distant descendants to kneel and kowtow in the snow.
The international frontier, once established, lasted; the people pushed beyond it did not stay pushed.
A pause, before moving forward: Sejong's reign is the kind of historical moment that generates legend, and a fair amount of what is written about him in popular accounts is legend.

The image of a benevolent Confucian sage-king personally inventing an alphabet for his beloved subjects, sitting up nights with his Hall of Worthies, befriending a freed slave, conquering the northern frontier, and ushering in a golden age — this is the dominant image in Korean popular culture, and it has substantial basis in fact, but the substantial basis is layered with five centuries of admiring storytelling.
Sejong was also a sometimes harsh ruler who allowed an absolutist political system to take its full course.
The number of officials executed under his reign was non-trivial.
The Buddhist suppression continued in his reign, which he supported even though he personally had complex views on Buddhism.
The Jurchen campaigns were brutal, with significant civilian casualties on both sides.
Modern Korean historians have done substantial work over the past few decades to recover the more complicated Sejong who lies beneath the icon.

What is undisputed is the institutional and cultural output: the alphabet that thirty million people now read every day; the rain gauges that produced six centuries of weather data; the agricultural manual that improved Korean farming for hundreds of years; the printing technology that made Korean books cheaper and more widely distributed than European books would be until the Reformation.
Sejong's reign produced more usable, lasting, transformative cultural work than any other thirty-two-year period in Korean history.
The legend overshoots the reality, but the reality is still dazzling.

chapters.title: The Yangban Order
sentences: For roughly the next century and a half — from the death of Sejong in 1450 until the Imjin War in 1592 — Joseon settled into the shape it would keep.
This chapter is about the social order that solidified during those years, because it is the social order that would define every subsequent Korean experience until the late nineteenth century.
The defining institution was the yangban.
The word yangban literally means "two orders" — the civil officials (the munban) and the military officials (the muban).
Originally it referred specifically to people who held official posts.

By the mid-fifteenth century, however, it had hardened into a hereditary status: the yangban were the families whose ancestors had held high office and who continued to dominate the civil service exam (the gwageo, see below).

To be yangban was to be exempt from taxation, exempt from military service, and entitled to a degree of social deference verging on physical untouchability — a yangban could not be physically struck by a commoner without lethal consequences for the commoner, and could not even be addressed directly by a commoner without elaborate honorifics.
The yangban were not a tiny class.

Estimates of the proportion of the Joseon population who counted as yangban vary enormously — some early-Joseon estimates put them at 5–10% of the population, with the proportion growing through legal manipulation and forged genealogies to perhaps 30–40% by the late dynasty.
They were not a small aristocracy.

They were a substantial broad-based status group, more like the European gentry than the nobility: not the very top of society but a diffuse status-conferring class with shared expectations of education, ritual behavior, and political voice.

Below the yangban were three other classes in the formal Joseon hierarchy: The jungin (JOONG-in, "middle people"), a small class of technical specialists — clerks, translators, doctors, court astronomers, painters at the Royal Painting Academy — whose work was essential but whose social status was below the yangban.
Jungin status was hereditary and partly endogamous; their family lines often produced notable scientific and artistic talents (the great true-view painter Jeong Seon was jungin, see Chapter 6).
The sangmin (SAHNG-min, "common people"), the vast majority of the population: peasants, artisans, fishermen, small merchants.
Commoners paid the bulk of the kingdom's taxes, served the military corvées, and performed the labor that supported the yangban scholar class.

The cheonmin (CHUN-min, "low people"), the lowest stratum: includes butchers, tanners, sorcerers, traveling entertainers, certain categories of criminals, and most importantly the nobi (NOH-bee), the hereditary slaves who made up perhaps a third of the early-Joseon population.
This four-class hierarchy is conventionally compared to the Indian caste system or to medieval European estates.
It is not really like either.

It was less elaborate than caste (only four classes, not thousands of jati subgroups) and more legally formal than European estates (Joseon law distinguished sharply by class status in ways that were not common in Western Christendom).

It was also more permeable than the caste system in some respects — the Sejong-era promotion of Jang Yeong-sil from slavery to high office (Chapter 2) shows that mobility was possible — and much less permeable than the European estates in others, since slave status was hereditary and was very rarely escaped.
The most important fact about Joseon's class system is that it lasted.

Roughly the same hierarchy that solidified under Sejong's grandsons in the mid-fifteenth century was still in place when the Gabo Reforms of 1894 (Chapter 8) abolished it on paper four and a half centuries later.
The Joseon social order is one of the longest-running stable social systems in human history.
The civil service exam — the gwageo (GWAH-guh) — was the institutional mechanism that selected officials and maintained the yangban class.
The gwageo was modeled on the imperial examinations of Tang and Song China (Tang-Song China — coming in a future TL), but with distinctive Korean modifications.
There were two primary tracks: the munbang (literary track) and the muban (military track).
The literary track was vastly more prestigious.
Within the literary track there were further divisions: the saengwon exam tested mastery of the Confucian classics; the jinsa exam tested literary composition.
Candidates who passed either were considered "licensed scholars" and could enter the Sungkyunkwan academy or apply for low-level posts.
The serious goal was the daegwa exam, which had three stages — provincial, central, and palace.
The palace exam was overseen by the king himself, and the top three finishers in any year were lavishly celebrated, paraded through Hanyang, and assigned to elite court positions.
The pass rate for the highest stage was extraordinarily low.
In a typical year, perhaps thirty-three candidates would pass the daegwa palace exam, out of tens of thousands who attempted it across the country.
Most candidates spent decades — sometimes their entire adult lives — preparing without ever passing.
Lifetime study was the yangban's vocation, and the gwageo was the pretext.
In theory, the gwageo was open to all freeborn men.
In practice, it was almost entirely passed by sons of yangban families — for reasons that are obvious once stated.
Preparing for the gwageo required twenty or more years of intensive Confucian education, which required a teacher, a library of expensive imported books, and the leisure to do nothing else.
Commoners could not afford the time.
The sons of nobi were legally barred.
The sons of jungin had their own separate technical exams that produced jungin-level positions but did not lead to the high civil service.

Even within the yangban class, certain provincial families were systematically excluded from top positions — most notably the families of the northwestern Pyeongan and Hamgyeong provinces, whose exclusion would eventually produce serious revolts (Hong Gyeong-rae's rebellion, Chapter 7).
The result was a meritocratic-looking system that actually reinforced hereditary class status.
The gwageo guaranteed that the sons of officials would themselves become officials, generation after generation.

It produced both extraordinary scholarly achievement (the level of textual literacy required to pass the higher exams was simply astonishing — candidates were expected to recite long passages from memory and produce eight-legged Chinese essays in formal style on a few hours' notice) and extraordinary stagnation (the curriculum was the same Confucian canon for five hundred years, with very little variation, and the exam questions tended to recycle the same problems generation after generation).
This is the place to mention that the parallel Chinese system, on which the gwageo was modeled, had similar effects but at greater scale.
China's imperial examinations selected officials for an empire of 100+ million people; Joseon's gwageo selected officials for a country of perhaps 5–10 million.

The result in both cases was a large, stable, classically educated bureaucratic class that could administer the country competently for centuries — and that proved spectacularly ill-equipped to deal with the industrial-age challenges of the nineteenth century, when both China and Korea found that their carefully selected Confucian scholar-officials had no idea how to negotiate with steamships or design factories.
Joseon women had a different experience of the Neo-Confucian order, and not a happy one.
The pre-Joseon position of Korean women had been relatively free by East Asian standards.
Goryeo law had allowed equal inheritance between sons and daughters.
A married woman generally retained her own family name and her own property.
Widows could and routinely did remarry.
Brides moved into the husband's household only after the first child was born; before that, the couple lived in the wife's family compound, with the wife's parents providing initial support.
The kinship system was bilateral: a person traced descent through both maternal and paternal lines, and uncles on both sides were equally recognized as relatives.
The Confucianization of Joseon ground all this away over the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries.
The mechanism was the elaboration of patrilineal Neo-Confucian ritual.

Confucianism teaches that the proper organization of the family is patrilineal — descent traced through the male line, ancestor worship organized by the eldest son, inheritance flowing primarily to sons, women incorporated into the husband's family on marriage.
The Joseon court, advised by Neo-Confucian theorists, gradually rewrote the country's family law to match the Confucian ideal.
Inheritance was rebalanced toward the eldest son.

Widow remarriage was discouraged through a series of legal disabilities — a remarried widow's children were declared ineligible for the gwageo exam, which effectively closed the door for any yangban widow who hoped her grandchildren might hold office.
The bride moved permanently into the husband's household at marriage, often as a teenager.
Women were physically secluded in the inner quarters of yangban houses (the anchae or "inner room") and were not supposed to be seen by male visitors.
Women's names were not even routinely recorded in family genealogies — daughters were listed simply as "the wife of so-and-so," or by the husband's office.
The change took roughly two centuries to complete.

Modern Korean historians like Martina Deuchler (whose book The Confucian Transformation of Korea is the standard reference) have documented the slow, deliberate, multi-generational process by which a relatively flexible bilateral kinship system was hammered into a rigid patrilineal one through systematic legal change.
By the late seventeenth century, Joseon had become more strictly patrilineal than China itself — the disciples having outdone the master.
This is not the only case where a colonized culture proved to be a more enthusiastic adopter of an imported ideology than the source culture.
The Christianization of Spain in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries produced, in the Spanish Inquisition, a religious bureaucracy more aggressive than anything in contemporary Italy or France.
The Buddhist suppression that the Joseon dynasty carried out (Chapter 1) was more thorough than anything in Buddhist-origin India.
New converts, having something to prove, often go further than the originators.
The Joseon yangban's enthusiastic implementation of patrilineal Confucianism is a case in point.
A handful of women managed to leave a public mark anyway.
