Shin Saimdang (SHIN sah-im-DAHNG, 1504–1551), the mother of the philosopher Yi I (see below), was an accomplished painter and calligrapher whose paintings of grasses and insects survive as among the finest small-scale art of the period — her face is now on the 50,000-won note, the highest-denomination Korean banknote, an unusual choice for a country whose currency mostly features kings.

The poet Heo Nanseolheon (HUH NAHN-suhl-hun, 1563–1589) wrote in classical Chinese with such skill that her published work was considered the equal of any male poet of her generation, though she was severely limited in what she could publicly do as a yangban woman.

The medical and divination specialist Daejanggeum (DAY-jahng-geum, early sixteenth century) became the first female royal physician — her name and her position are documented in the Annals, even though most details about her life are now uncertain (she is the basis for the famous twenty-first-century Korean drama).
These were exceptional cases, and they remain exceptional.
The female experience of the Confucian order was, on average, severely diminished compared to the pre-Joseon period.
This is part of the cost of the dynasty's social achievement.
The yangban order was stable, ritually elaborated, and successful at what it set out to do — and it was built in part on the systematic legal reduction of half the population.
The slave system deserves separate treatment, because it was unusually large and unusually persistent.
The nobi were Joseon's hereditary slaves.
Nobi status was inherited from either parent: if your mother was nobi, you were nobi; if your father was nobi, you were nobi (the rule varied by period and by the parents' specific status).
There were two main categories: gwannobi (GWAHN-noh-bee, "official nobi"): owned by the state.
They served palace functions, provincial offices, military camps, and government workshops.
Jang Yeong-sil (Chapter 2) was born a gwannobi in a provincial workshop.
Gwannobi could rise to higher status through unusual talent, royal favor, or military service, though the vast majority did not. sanobi (SAH-noh-bee, "private nobi"): owned by yangban households.
They served as domestic servants, tenant farmers on yangban estates, and personal attendants.
Major yangban households might own dozens or hundreds of sanobi.
The wealthiest families could own thousands, organized into village-sized agricultural communities working family lands.

The proportion of the Joseon population that was nobi is debated, but figures of around one-third for the early dynasty are commonly cited, dropping to perhaps 10% by the late eighteenth century as legal reforms gradually freed various categories.

This is a remarkably high slave proportion for any premodern state — comparable to or higher than the slave populations of classical Rome, contemporary Ottoman Anatolia, or the antebellum American South.
Joseon was, on this measure, one of the most heavily enslaved societies in early-modern history.
Nobi were not chattel slaves in quite the American sense.
They had legal personhood — they could marry (other nobi), own modest property, sue in some courts.
They could not be killed at the master's whim.
But they could be bought and sold, separated from their families, willed to heirs.
Their children inherited their status.
They were forbidden from taking the gwageo exam, holding office, or entering most non-yangban professions.
They paid no taxes (the master took their labor instead) but had no legal independence.
The nobi system was gradually dismantled over the late dynasty.
King Hyeonjong (HYUN-johng, reigned 1659–74) restricted some categories.
King Jeongjo (Chapter 6) reduced the gwannobi rolls.
In 1801, after Jeongjo's death, the new regime emancipated the remaining gwannobi (about 36,000 people) by burning the slave registers — a startling unilateral act of state.
The sanobi system was not formally abolished until the Gabo Reforms of 1894 (Chapter 8), nearly a century later.
The legal traces of nobi status — restrictions on certain occupations, prohibitions on certain marriages — lingered into the twentieth century.
This is a substantial dark side of the Joseon achievement.
The Confucian order was elegant, scholarly, and stable.
It was also built on the unfree labor of a third of the population, for centuries.
Korean popular memory remembers the Hangul, the rain gauges, and Yi Sun-sin's turtle ships.
It does not always remember the slave registers.
It is fair to remember both.
The court politics of the late fifteenth and sixteenth centuries were dominated by an internal struggle among the yangban themselves, between two factions whose names are worth knowing.
The Hungu (HOON-goo, "Meritorious Officials") were the descendants of the founding-generation supporters of Taejo and Taejong.
By the second and third generations after the founding, they had become a hereditary establishment with vast estates, royal in-law connections, and effectively unbroken control of the central court.
They were Confucian, but their Confucianism was a state-power Confucianism focused on practical administration and institutional dominance.
The Sarim (SAH-rim, "Forest of Scholars") were a different stripe.
They were provincial Confucians, descendants of late-Goryeo loyalists who had refused to serve the new dynasty, gathered at private academies in the south and west away from the capital.
Their Confucianism was a moral-philosophical Confucianism focused on ethical purity, scholarly rigor, and the proper interpretation of the canon.
They had spent the first century of Joseon outside the central court system, building their institutional bases at the new private academies (the seowon, see below).
In the late fifteenth century, beginning under King Seongjong (reigned 1469–94), the Sarim began to be promoted into central government posts.
They were less compromised than the Hungu, more committed to Confucian principles, and useful as a check on Hungu power.
King Seongjong systematically appointed Sarim scholars to the censorate (the office whose job was to criticize official misconduct), where they immediately began attacking Hungu corruption.

This produced four major bloody confrontations known as the Literati Purges: First Purge (1498): King Yeonsangun, a paranoid and unstable ruler, was incensed by a draft of historical records that included veiled criticism of his great-grandfather's usurpation.

He executed several Sarim officials, exiled others, and posthumously beheaded the corpse of the late Sarim master Kim Jong-jik. (This is the only known case in Korean history of a corpse being beheaded as judicial punishment.) Second Purge (1504): Yeonsangun, having discovered the truth about his mother's execution years earlier (she had been a royal consort deposed and forced to drink poison), turned on the officials who had been involved or had failed to oppose it.
Hundreds of officials were killed or exiled.
Yeonsangun was deposed two years later in a yangban coup.

Third Purge (1519): King Jungjong, who had taken the throne after Yeonsangun's deposition, briefly favored an idealistic young Sarim scholar named Jo Gwang-jo (JOH GWAHNG-joh) and his program of radical Confucian reform.

Jo's enemies fabricated an omen — by writing the words "Jo will be king" in honey on tree leaves so that ants ate the honey and made the words appear miraculously written — and turned the king against him.
Jo was forced to drink poison.
Fourth Purge (1545): After the death of King Injong, factions surrounding the queen mothers of two competing princes turned on each other.
Several hundred Sarim officials were killed or exiled.

The Literati Purges are the dynasty's first sustained period of internal political bloodshed since the Strife of Princes (Chapter 1), and they wasted some of the most talented scholarly minds of the period.
Yet the system survived.
The institutions Jeong Do-jeon had designed at the founding (Chapter 1) were sturdy enough to absorb even four catastrophic purges across half a century.

By the late sixteenth century the Sarim had finally consolidated their position in the central government, the Hungu had been displaced, and Joseon court politics entered a new phase — the factional wars that would dominate the next two centuries (Chapter 7), as the Sarim themselves split into rival philosophical camps.
The structural irony is hard to miss.
The Sarim won.
They became the new establishment.
And then they fractured along the same fault lines that had originally divided them from the Hungu.

The pattern of insurgent scholar-purists displacing a corrupt establishment, becoming the new establishment, and then producing their own insurgent scholar-purists — this pattern would repeat across Joseon court history for the next four hundred years.
The intellectual heritage of the Sarim victory was the great philosophical flowering of mid-Joseon Neo-Confucianism, focused around two giants whose images are now on Korean banknotes.
Yi Hwang (yee HWAHNG, 1501–1570), scholar name Toegye (TWAY-gay), was Korea's most influential philosopher.
His face is on the 1,000-won note.

He spent most of his career in voluntary retirement at the country academy he had founded — Dosan Seowon (DOH-sahn SUH-won) in southeastern Korea — refusing repeated royal invitations to take high office and producing a steady stream of treatises that refined the Zhu Xi orthodoxy in distinctive ways.

His most important work was the Four-Seven Debate (sa-chil ron), an extended philosophical correspondence with a younger scholar named Gi Dae-seung (GEE DAY-sung) about the metaphysical origin of the four moral feelings (commiseration, shame, deference, sense of right and wrong) and the seven natural emotions (joy, anger, sorrow, fear, love, hate, desire).
Were the four moral feelings derived from li (principle), while the seven emotions were derived from gi (material force)?
Or were both li and gi present in both?
The debate sounds technical, and it was, but the underlying question was whether Confucian ethics had a metaphysical foundation distinct from ordinary emotional life.
Yi Hwang's answer was yes; Gi's was no.
The debate, conducted over more than a decade in beautifully written Chinese letters, is one of the great philosophical exchanges of the East Asian tradition.
Yi I (yee EE, 1536–1584), scholar name Yulgok (YOOL-gohk), was Toegye's younger contemporary and intellectual rival.
His face is on the 5,000-won note.
Yulgok was less metaphysically inclined than Toegye and more politically engaged.

He served in high government office, advised the king on practical reforms, and famously proposed a ten-thousand-soldier reform — the recommendation that Joseon train and maintain a permanent standing army of 100,000 troops to defend against the brewing Japanese threat.
The court rejected the proposal as alarmist.
Twelve years after Yulgok's death, the Imjin War vindicated him appallingly (Chapter 4).

Yulgok's philosophical contribution was a more monistic reading of Neo-Confucianism: he argued that li and gi were inseparable, that any concrete thing always involved both at once, and that the proper goal of moral cultivation was the harmonization of li and gi within the individual.
The disagreement between Toegye and Yulgok is sometimes summarized as Toegye emphasizing transcendent moral order (li) and Yulgok emphasizing immanent material reality (gi).

Their respective followers split into rival philosophical lineages that became the basis of the later factional divisions (Chapter 7) — the Easterner faction trace their philosophical lineage to Toegye, the Westerners to Yulgok, and the eighteenth-century Old Doctrine and Young Doctrine factions both descend from Yulgok-influenced lines.
Joseon politics would be shaped by the metaphysical disagreements of these two sixteenth-century philosophers for the next three hundred years.
The institutional infrastructure that supported all this scholarship was the seowon network.

A seowon (SUH-won) was a private Confucian academy combining three functions: an advanced study center, a memorial shrine to revered Confucian masters, and (eventually) a political base for a particular philosophical lineage.
The first seowon was founded in 1543 at Sosu Seowon (SOH-soo) in southwestern Korea, by a provincial official memorializing an early Korean Confucian master.
The model spread rapidly.
By the seventeenth century there were roughly 200 seowon across the country; by the nineteenth century, over 600.
The seowon were the institutional power base of the Sarim.
They provided the academic credentialing, social networks, and ritual continuity that kept the Sarim philosophical lineages alive across generations.

They also accumulated tax exemptions, slave grants, and land donations on the same model as Buddhist temples in earlier eras — the Sarim, having displaced the Buddhist establishment in central political life, gradually rebuilt the same kind of local landed institutional power base under a different ideology.
This is why the Daewongun (Chapter 8) would, in the 1860s, gut the seowon system as part of his attempt to centralize royal authority.
The seowon had become too powerful, too tax-exempt, and too independent of the central state.
Of the over 600 seowon that existed in mid-century, the Daewongun left only 47 standing.
The rest were dissolved, their lands confiscated, their political base broken.
Nine of the surviving seowon are now UNESCO World Heritage sites, including Dosan Seowon (where Toegye taught) and Sosu Seowon (the first one).
They are some of the most beautiful surviving examples of Joseon-era architecture.

Cross-civ check: while the yangban order was solidifying in mid-fifteenth-century Korea, the Inca Empire under Pachacuti was at its peak in the Andes (Andean Kingdoms Ch 8); the Aztec Empire was conducting the great expansion under Moctezuma I (Aztec Empire Ch 3); the Ottoman Empire under Mehmed II conquered Constantinople in 1453 and ended the Byzantine Empire (Byzantine Empire Ch 12); the Ming Dynasty in China was settling into the complacent middle decades of its reign; the Italian Renaissance was producing Donatello, Brunelleschi, and the early Botticelli; the Inca road system was spreading across the Andes; Vasco da Gama had not yet rounded the Cape of Good Hope (he would do so in 1498) and the European maritime expansion that would reshape the world had not yet begun.
The Joseon yangban order was being established in a world that had not yet been globalized — and it would have to confront the globalized world in the nineteenth century without much preparation.

chapters.title: The Imjin War
sentences: In April 1592, a Japanese fleet of perhaps 700 transport ships landed roughly 158,000 troops on the southern Korean coast at Busan.
They were led by some of the most experienced battlefield commanders in Japanese history.
They were armed with European-style matchlock muskets — the arquebus, called teppo in Japanese — that Portuguese traders had introduced to Japan a half-century earlier.
They had no idea what they were walking into.
This was the Imjin War, named for the year-cycle character imjin in the Korean sexagenary calendar (the same character that names the year 1592).

It is sometimes called the Japanese Invasions of Korea in English, since the war came in two phases: the initial invasion of 1592–93, a stalemated truce from 1593 to 1597, and a second invasion in 1597–98 that ended only when the original instigator died.

Across six and a half years it killed an estimated one to two million Koreans, devastated the agricultural economy, burned the great palaces of Hanyang to the ground, and triggered a civilian guerrilla resistance that would leave deep marks on Korean political memory ever after.

It was also the only major Japanese military project of the early-modern period and one of the largest amphibious operations of the sixteenth-century world — comparable in scale to the Spanish Armada (1588) and Henry VIII's Boulogne expedition (1544), but larger than either.
The man who started it was a peasant.

Toyotomi Hideyoshi (toh-yoh-TOH-mee hee-day-YOH-shee, 1537–1598) was the second of the great unifiers of late-sixteenth-century Japan, after his master Oda Nobunaga (Ancient Japan Ch 8 — and a future Japan TL will deal with him properly).

Born to a peasant family in Owari Province, Hideyoshi rose through the warrior class on raw talent, becoming Nobunaga's most able general and eventually inheriting the unification project after Nobunaga was killed in 1582.

By 1590 Hideyoshi had brought all the warring daimyo (DAI-myoh, "great names" — the regional Japanese warlords) of Japan under his control, ending the Sengoku ("Warring States") period that had wracked Japan for over a century.
This left Hideyoshi with a problem: he had several hundred thousand professional soldiers with nothing useful to do at home.
The same daimyo armies that had spent the previous century fighting each other would, with idle hands, be tempted to start fighting each other again.
Hideyoshi needed an external war.
He chose Korea.

The official justification was extravagant: Hideyoshi proposed to conquer not just Korea but China itself, install himself as emperor in Beijing, and possibly extend Japanese rule into India. (He apparently meant this seriously, at least in 1591–92.) The actual military rationale was that Korea was a stepping stone to China and a relatively soft target.
Joseon had not fought a major war in two centuries.
Its military was undertrained, its arsenals were undersupplied, and its political leadership had repeatedly rejected Yi I's recommendation to maintain a professional standing army (Chapter 3).

Korean diplomats had even reported back from Hideyoshi's court that the man was a buffoon making impossible threats — though one of the two ambassadors had actually reported correctly that Hideyoshi was deadly serious and his armies were enormous, only to be ignored by a court that wanted to hear the easier message.
The Joseon court realized its error very quickly.
Within three weeks of landing, the Japanese had taken Busan, marched north through the central peninsula, and reached the Joseon capital.
King Seonjo (SUN-joh, reigned 1567–1608) fled north toward the Chinese border, with his entire court trailing behind him in undignified retreat.
Hanyang fell on June 12, 1592, almost exactly two months after the initial landings.
Pyongyang fell shortly after.
By the end of the summer the Japanese controlled most of the populated southern and central regions of the peninsula.
The collapse of the Joseon land army was complete and humiliating.
The standing forces had been small and badly equipped.
The mobilization plans for emergency defense did not function.
Most of the country's senior generals were either captured or killed in the early battles.
Nine-tenths of Korean cities and towns south of Pyongyang fell without serious resistance.
The Japanese, in their letters home, professed surprise at how easy the invasion was proving.
The Joseon court fled to Uiju (oo-EE-joo) on the Yalu River, almost in Chinese territory, and began begging the Ming for emergency aid.
The Ming would eventually intervene (see below), but in the summer and fall of 1592 the Korean state was collapsing.
What saved it was a combination of three things: a navy nobody had expected, civilian guerrilla resistance from below, and Ming Chinese intervention from above.
The naval salvation came from one man.

Yi Sun-sin (YEE soon-SHIN, 1545–1598) was, in 1591, a relatively obscure mid-rank officer of the Joseon navy, recently appointed commander of the Jeolla Left Naval Command (the small naval district covering the southwestern part of the peninsula).
He had been a competent but unremarkable officer for most of his career — repeatedly demoted for failing to flatter superiors, twice court-martialed and stripped of rank, then reinstated.
His 1591 appointment to the Jeolla naval district was a kind of professional rehabilitation.
He used the year between the appointment and the invasion to do something almost no other Joseon officer was doing: he prepared.
Yi rebuilt the Jeolla Left fleet from scratch.
He drilled his crews aggressively.
He stockpiled gunpowder and provisioned his ships for extended campaigns.
Most consequentially, he commissioned the construction of a new class of warship — the geobukseon (GUH-book-suhn, "turtle ship") — that would become legend.
The geobukseon was a modification of the standard Joseon panokseon (heavy oared galley with a flat-deck crew platform) into something more like a floating tank.
The crew platform was covered with a curved roof of thick oak planks, studded with iron spikes pointing upward to prevent boarding.

The roof was sometimes plated with iron sheeting (the extent and exact configuration of the iron plating is debated; modern reconstructions show varying interpretations of the contemporary descriptions).
The bow was decorated with a fierce dragon head that could be rigged to emit smoke or fire from sulphur burners.

The ship's broadsides bristled with cannon ports — perhaps eight to ten cannons per side — capable of firing the heavy iron-tipped wooden bolts and stone shot that would prove devastating against the lighter Japanese transports.
The geobukseon was not the entire Joseon naval advantage.
The standard panokseon was already a heavier, more cannon-equipped vessel than anything in the Japanese fleet, which mostly consisted of armed transports designed for coastal sailing.
Korean naval gunpowder was of higher quality than Japanese gunpowder.
Korean ship construction used heavier oak with iron nails compared to the Japanese cypress with wooden pegs.

And Korean naval doctrine emphasized standoff cannon engagement, while Japanese naval doctrine emphasized boarding and hand-to-hand combat — a doctrinal difference that would prove catastrophic for the Japanese once Korean cannons started firing.
The crucial factor was Yi himself.
He combined extraordinary tactical imagination, an unusual willingness to engage in detailed reconnaissance before battle, and a kind of personal calm that his crews found inspiring.

He kept a daily war diary, the Nanjung Ilgi (NAHN-joong il-gee, "War Diary"), which survives and is read in modern Korea as a national treasure — both a primary historical source and a literary classic.

The diary entries record battles, supply problems, cabinet politics, family matters (he was tortured by news of his mother's death and his son's death during the war), and personal exhaustion in straightforward, unembellished prose.
It is the most intimate document we have of any senior commander of the period in any country.
Yi Sun-sin won every major naval engagement he fought.
There were many.
The first was at Okpo (OHK-poh) in May 1592, where Yi destroyed twenty-six Japanese ships at the cost of one wounded sailor.
He followed it with a series of smaller engagements through the early summer, picking off isolated Japanese squadrons.
The Battle of Sacheon in late May was the geobukseon's combat debut.
The new ship type appeared, fired its broadsides, drove off boarders with the iron spikes, and destroyed thirteen Japanese vessels.
Yi was wounded in the shoulder by a musket ball that he reportedly had cut out of the wound himself the next day.
He remained on station.
The defining victory came at Hansan Island in August 1592.
A Japanese fleet of seventy-three warships under Wakizaka Yasuharu (one of Hideyoshi's most experienced naval commanders) was destroyed almost completely.

Yi used a feigned retreat to lure the Japanese fleet out of a narrow channel into open water, then formed his ships into a crane-wing formation (a curved line that could converge from both sides on the enemy center) and turned and devastated the Japanese with concentrated broadside fire.
Forty-seven Japanese ships were sunk; perhaps 9,000 Japanese sailors and marines were killed or drowned.
Korean losses were minimal.
Hansan was decisive in a way single battles rarely are.
It severed Hideyoshi's seaborne supply line.
The Japanese army on land was now cut off from reinforcement and resupply by sea, just as the campaigning season was about to turn into autumn and the Ming Chinese were preparing to intervene.
Hideyoshi reportedly raged at his subordinate generals about the loss but had no way to compensate for it.
From this point on, the Japanese strategic position deteriorated.
Court politics intervened.

In 1597, halfway through the war, Yi Sun-sin was framed by political rivals at court (using accusations partly orchestrated by a Japanese double agent), demoted to common foot soldier, and tortured in prison.
His replacement, Won Gyun (WON GYOON), promptly led the Joseon fleet into a disastrous trap at the Battle of Chilcheollyang in summer 1597.
Of the 134 Joseon ships engaged, 122 were destroyed.
Won Gyun himself was killed.
The naval advantage that had saved Korea in 1592 was wiped out.
Yi was hastily reinstated as admiral.
He was given the surviving thirteen ships.

The Japanese fleet of 133 warships approached the Myeongnyang Strait in October 1597, expecting to round the southern tip of the peninsula and resume the supply route to the new Japanese offensive in the southwest.
Yi positioned his thirteen ships at the narrowest point of the strait, where the tidal current ran at perhaps eight knots — the strongest tidal current in Korean waters.
He waited for the tide to turn, then engaged.
The Battle of Myeongnyang is one of the most lopsided naval victories in history.
The narrow channel allowed Yi to engage only a small portion of the Japanese fleet at a time.
The strong current disrupted Japanese formations and prevented them from concentrating their numbers.
Korean cannon fire was, again, devastating.
Thirty-one Japanese ships were sunk, including the flagship of the Japanese commander.
The remaining Japanese fleet broke off and retreated.
Korean casualties: approximately ten dead.
Korean ships lost: zero.

Myeongnyang ranks alongside the Battle of Salamis (Persian Empire Ch 5) and the destruction of the Spanish Armada as one of the most consequential outnumbered naval victories in the history of warfare.
The 13:133 ratio is approximate but real.

Modern Korean popular culture has made Myeongnyang a national legend — the 2014 Korean film The Admiral: Roaring Currents about the battle was the highest-grossing Korean film of all time at its release.
The location of the battle has been studied by naval historians from multiple countries; the tactical exploitation of the tidal current is studied at modern naval academies.

Yi died fourteen months later, on December 16, 1598, at the Battle of Noryang — the final naval engagement of the war, when a combined Joseon-Ming fleet caught the last retreating Japanese squadrons and destroyed roughly half of them.
Yi was shot by a Japanese musket bullet during the engagement.
According to the standard account, his last words were a request to his nephew not to announce his death until the battle was won, lest his men lose heart.
The battle was won.
He died on the deck.
The Imjin War ended within weeks.
Hideyoshi himself had died three months earlier in Japan, and his designated heirs lost interest in continuing the Korean expedition.
The Japanese armies began their final withdrawal.
The naval war has tended to overshadow the equally important land war, but the land war was where most Koreans actually fought and died.
The defining feature of the land war from late 1592 onward was civilian guerrilla resistance.
Across the country, yangban scholars, Buddhist monks, and ordinary farmers organized themselves into local self-defense forces called Uibyeong (oo-EE-byung, "Righteous Armies").

The uibyeong typically operated from mountain fortresses, harassed Japanese supply convoys, picked off isolated garrisons, and occasionally fought set-piece engagements when they could mass enough fighters.

They were not a coordinated national resistance — they were dozens of separate local efforts loosely affiliated with the displaced central government — but in aggregate they made it impossible for the Japanese to fully consolidate their hold on the conquered territories.

The most famous uibyeong commander was Gwak Jae-u (GWAHK JAY-oo, 1552–1617), a yangban from southeastern Korea who fought in distinctive red robes and earned the nickname "Hong-uijeonggun" ("Red-Robe General").
Gwak's irregular forces conducted a sustained campaign of ambushes and night raids in Gyeongsang Province that tied down Japanese forces for years.

Buddhist monk-soldiers, organized by figures like the elderly monk Hyujeong (HEW-jung) and his disciple Yujeong (YEW-jung), formed disciplined units that fought in major engagements as well as guerrilla actions.

The presence of Buddhist monks in the war effort is one of the more interesting paradoxes of the period: an institution suppressed by the Joseon state for two centuries (Chapter 1) suddenly mobilized to defend the same state when foreign invaders threatened.
The most consequential land battle was the defense of Haengju Fortress in February 1593.

General Gwon Yul (GWON YOOL), with about 2,300 Korean soldiers and a substantial contingent of Buddhist monks, defended a hilltop fortress northwest of Hanyang against a Japanese force of approximately 30,000 troops.
The Japanese launched nine separate assaults on the position over a single day.
Each one was repulsed with the help of a primitive multiple-rocket-launcher weapon called the hwacha (HWAH-chah).
The hwacha was a wheeled cart mounting a rectangular grid of 100 to 200 rocket-tube holes.
Each hole held a singijeon ("magic machine arrow"), an iron-tipped arrow with a small gunpowder rocket motor at its tail.
When the propellant was ignited, all the singijeon fired simultaneously in a single dense volley, raining down on Japanese formations from a distance of several hundred meters.
The hwacha at Haengju, combined with Korean cannon fire from the walls and downhill rolling of stones, made the Japanese assaults appallingly costly.
By nightfall, the Japanese had taken roughly 10,000 casualties and abandoned the attack.
Joseon casualties were perhaps a tenth of that.

Haengju is sometimes described as one of the world's first uses of mass rocket artillery in combination with conventional gunpowder weapons in field warfare. (The Chinese had used rocket weapons earlier, but not in this kind of mass-volley configuration.) It was one of the engagements that turned the war.
The Ming Chinese intervention was the third leg of the Korean salvation.
The Ming dynasty in 1592 was 224 years old, settling into the mature middle phase of its long arc, and it had two reasons to intervene in the Korean war.

First, Korea was a tributary state of Ming China — the formal vassalage relationship had been re-established under the Joseon founding (Chapter 1) — and a tribute state in distress was a Ming responsibility.
Second, and more practically, Hideyoshi had explicitly stated his intention to conquer China after Korea.
The war was, from the Ming perspective, not a foreign distraction; it was a forward defense of the Chinese frontier.
A Ming expeditionary force of perhaps 40,000 troops under General Li Rusong (LEE roo-SONG) crossed into Korea in early 1593.
Li recaptured Pyongyang in February 1593 in a brutal three-day siege that involved Korean troops and the Ming artillery.

The Japanese forces, denied resupply by Yi Sun-sin's naval blockade and now confronting professional Ming infantry from the north, fell back from Pyongyang and concentrated in fortified positions in the southern coastal regions.
The war settled into a stalemate that would last four years before Hideyoshi's renewed offensive in 1597.
Ming participation in the war was extraordinarily expensive.
The cost is variously estimated at 8 to 25 million ounces of silver — sums equivalent to several years of total Ming state revenue.

The fiscal strain contributed to the Ming dynasty's progressive financial weakening that would help trigger its collapse a half-century later (the Ming would fall to internal rebellion and Manchu conquest in 1644).
It is not an exaggeration to say that the Ming saved Korea at a cost that helped end the Ming.

The Joseon court would maintain a fierce gratitude to the Ming for the rest of the dynasty — a gratitude that would shape the disastrous decision-making of the 1620s and 1630s when the Manchu Jurchen began rising and demanding that Joseon switch allegiances (Chapter 5).
The cost of the Imjin War to Korea was catastrophic.

Estimates of total Korean dead vary widely, but figures of one to two million seem reasonable for the seven-year war and its immediate aftermath — out of a pre-war Joseon population of perhaps eight to ten million.
Vast tracts of agricultural land went out of production.
Granaries, irrigation systems, and rural infrastructure were destroyed across the southern provinces.

The pre-war land registers — which had been the basis of taxation and military service — were lost in the fighting; for decades after the war, the Joseon state operated without accurate population or property data and lost massive tax revenue as a result.
The cultural cost was equally severe.

Gyeongbokgung Palace was burned (probably by retreating Joseon officials and frustrated Hanyang residents during the panicked 1592 evacuation, before the Japanese even arrived) and was not rebuilt for two and a half centuries.
The royal observatory was destroyed.
Many of the records of the early dynasty were lost.
The Sungkyunkwan Academy was burned.

The Bulguksa temple complex outside Gyeongju (the masterpiece of Unified Silla architecture, see Ancient Korea Ch 8) was burned, with its wooden structures destroyed though the stone foundations and pagodas survived.
The countryside lost much of its surviving Buddhist heritage.
The human and cultural transfer to Japan was, paradoxically, one of the most consequential legacies of the war — for Japan.
As they retreated, the Japanese armies systematically captured and forcibly deported Korean potters, papermakers, weavers, printers, and other craftworkers.
Estimates of the total number of Koreans abducted to Japan range from 50,000 to 100,000.

The captured potters were settled in northern Kyushu, where they founded the Arita porcelain industry (whose distinctive blue-and-white wares became one of Japan's first major export products to Europe in the seventeenth century) and the Satsuma ware tradition.
The transfer of Korean ceramic knowledge essentially launched modern Japanese porcelain.

The Japanese tea-ceremony tradition that valued the rough, naturalistic Korean stoneware bowls (the Ido and Kintsugi aesthetic that would later influence twentieth-century international design) emerged in this same period as Japanese collectors prized the Korean potter-made ware.
This is not a pleasant compensation.
Korean cultural transfer to Japan happened because skilled craftsmen were dragged from their homes at swordpoint.
Modern Japanese ceramic museums sometimes acknowledge this history in their exhibition labels; modern Korean nationalism remembers it bitterly.

But it also did something culturally productive: the Korean potters in Kyushu founded family lineages that produced ceramics in Japan for the next four centuries, some of them still active today, and the cross-cultural fertilization (in both directions) shaped East Asian ceramic art for generations.
The Imjin War defined Korean political memory for the next four centuries.

The war produced the founding myths of modern Korean military identity (Yi Sun-sin remains arguably the most revered historical figure in modern Korea — his statue stands in central Seoul and his face is on the 100-won coin).
It seared into Korean elites a permanent suspicion of Japan that would shape the response to nineteenth-century Japanese expansion (Chapter 8).
It demonstrated the value of civilian uibyeong resistance — a model that would be invoked again under Japanese colonial rule in the early twentieth century.
It also, paradoxically, deepened Korean dependence on Ming China at exactly the moment China was about to enter terminal decline.
The dynasty had survived.
It survived in worse shape than it had begun.
And forty years later it would have to do it again, against a different enemy, with even worse results.

chapters.title: The Manchu Trauma
sentences: The Imjin War had wrecked southern Korea.
Recovery took most of a generation.

The court of King Gwanghaegun (GWAHNG-hay-goon, reigned 1608–23), Seonjo's son and successor, focused on rebuilding the agricultural base, restoring the tax registers, and patching together the shattered state apparatus.

Gwanghaegun was an unusually competent ruler — a product of the wartime regency, where he had effectively governed the southern provinces while his father fled north — and the recovery during his fifteen-year reign was substantial.
Gwanghaegun's most consequential policy was a foreign-policy balancing act in the north.
By the 1610s, a new threat was rising in the Manchurian forests.

The Jurchen tribes that Sejong's generals had pushed off Korean territory two centuries earlier (Chapter 2) had been gradually consolidating under a brilliant chieftain named Nurhaci (NUR-hah-chee, 1559–1626).

Nurhaci had unified most of the Jurchen tribes by the 1610s and proclaimed his own state — the Later Jin (named to invoke the earlier Jin dynasty that had ruled north China before the Mongol conquest).
In 1618 he formally renounced his vassalage to the Ming and declared war on China.
The Ming demanded that Joseon, as a Chinese tributary state, send troops to help fight the Jurchen invasion.
Joseon's gratitude for Ming aid in the Imjin War (Chapter 4) made it politically impossible to refuse outright.

Gwanghaegun's solution was a careful piece of duplicity: he sent a Korean expeditionary force of 10,000 men under General Gang Hong-rip (GAHNG HONG-rip), but with secret instructions to surrender at the first opportunity and avoid actually fighting.
At the Battle of Sarhu in 1619 — the Ming's catastrophic defeat at the hands of Nurhaci's Jurchens — General Gang surrendered his command and explained to Nurhaci that Korea wanted no quarrel.
This was effective realpolitik.
It preserved the Korean army, kept Joseon out of an unwinnable war, and bought a few years of peace with the rising Jurchen power.
It was also viewed by hard-line Ming-loyalist yangban officials at court as treasonous betrayal of the Ming benefactors.
In 1623 these officials staged a coup, deposed Gwanghaegun, and installed his nephew Injo (IN-joh, reigned 1623–49) as a more reliably pro-Ming alternative.
The new Injo regime explicitly repudiated Gwanghaegun's policy of accommodation with the Jurchens and re-affirmed Korean loyalty to the dying Ming.
This was the decision that produced the Manchu invasions.
The First Manchu Invasion came in 1627.
Nurhaci had died in 1626.

His son Hong Taiji (HONG TAI-jee, 1592–1643) inherited the Later Jin throne and decided that the new pro-Ming Korean court at Hanyang needed to be neutralized before he could launch a major campaign against China.
In January 1627, Hong Taiji dispatched a force of perhaps 30,000 cavalry under his cousin Amin (ah-MIN) into northern Korea.
The campaign was rapid and one-sided.
Amin's cavalry crossed the Yalu in deep winter, brushed aside the local Korean defenses, and reached Pyongyang within weeks.

King Injo and the court fled to Ganghwa Island (a defensible offshore base in the Yellow Sea, which had been the refuge of choice for Korean kings under invasion since the Mongol invasions of the thirteenth century).
Negotiations followed.
The Korean court agreed to recognize the Later Jin as a "brother state," send tribute payments, and break formal diplomatic ties with the Ming.
The Jurchen forces withdrew.
The 1627 campaign was, by the standards of seventeenth-century warfare, almost surgical.
But the Korean court did not actually break with the Ming.
Injo's officials interpreted "brother state" as a nominal arrangement that did not require severing the deeper Ming alliance.
Tribute payments to the Later Jin were sometimes sent and sometimes withheld.
Korean officials continued to use Ming era-names in court documents (a gesture of continued loyalty) and continued to receive Ming envoys.
In 1636, with the Ming visibly collapsing and his own state now formally renamed the Qing dynasty, Hong Taiji decided to make Korea pay properly.
The Second Manchu Invasion of 1636 was different.

Hong Taiji crossed the frozen Yalu in person in December 1636 with a force of 120,000 troops — including substantial Mongol auxiliaries (the eastern Mongols had been incorporated into the Qing political system) and Manchu Bannermen.

The objective this time was not nominal vassalage but full submission — Korea was to repudiate the Ming completely, accept Qing suzerainty unconditionally, send hostages from the royal family, and convert its diplomatic relationships to Qing-centered terms.
The campaign moved much faster than 1627.
The Qing forces ignored the fortified positions on the northern frontier and drove straight for Hanyang.
Within ten days they were at the gates of the capital.

Injo's intended refuge on Ganghwa Island was cut off by the speed of the Qing advance — instead the king and a portion of the court took refuge in the mountain fortress of Namhansanseong (NAHM-hahn-sahn-SUHNG), about 15 miles southeast of the capital.
Namhansanseong was a defensible fortress on a 1,500-foot peak, ringed by stone walls following the contours of the mountaintop.
With supplies for a few weeks' siege, it was a temporary refuge while Korean forces gathered.
They never gathered.
The various provincial reinforcements that should have come to relieve the king were defeated piecemeal by Qing cavalry detachments.
Within Namhansanseong, supplies dwindled.
The winter cold was severe — temperatures probably below 0°F at night.
Officers and soldiers froze to death on the walls.
Food rationing was reduced to almost nothing.

The court inside the fortress argued bitterly between the Cheokhwapa ("Reject Peace" faction) and the Juhwapa ("Accept Peace" faction) — between hard-line officials who urged the king to fight on regardless of consequences and pragmatic officials who urged immediate surrender to spare the country worse devastation.
After 47 days of siege, with the king's supplies almost exhausted and a Qing victory in the field at Ganghwa Island (where the queen and crown prince had been captured), Injo agreed to surrender.
The surrender ceremony at Samjeondo (SAHM-jun-doh, "The Three Junction Crossing") on January 30, 1637, is one of the most psychologically traumatic episodes in Korean political memory.
Injo descended from Namhansanseong, dressed in plain white commoner's robes (a deliberate symbol of stripped status), and approached Hong Taiji's military camp on the southern bank of the Han River.

There, before assembled Qing nobles and Korean court officials, the King of Joseon performed the sambae gugodu — three kneelings and nine prostrations, the formal ritual of submission used by Chinese emperors' tributary subjects when receiving the imperial presence.
Injo dropped to his knees three times, and on each occasion struck his forehead against the ground three times in sequence.
Nine head-strikes against the cold ground, in the presence of foreign barbarians, before what was supposed to be the highest sovereign of the Korean state.
Hong Taiji watched, accepted the surrender, and dictated terms.
Korea would now be a vassal of the Qing rather than the Ming.
Two of Injo's sons — Crown Prince Sohyeon and his younger brother Hyojong — would go to Qing as hostages.
Massive annual tribute would be paid.
Korean troops would assist in future Qing campaigns.
Korean political documents would use Qing era-names rather than Ming ones.

The Qing erected a stele commemorating the surrender at the site, naming it the Samjeondo Monument, that survives to this day on the south bank of the Han River — a reminder that this is what happened, that no amount of subsequent embarrassed amnesia can erase.
The Qing armies withdrew.
Korea retained nominal independence, with Injo on his throne and the Joseon administrative system intact.

But the country was now a tributary of a foreign barbarian dynasty (or so the yangban regarded the Manchus), the king had personally kowtowed nine times to a foreign emperor, and the long Korean fantasy of cultural superiority over the Manchu-Jurchen peoples beyond the northern frontier was permanently shattered.
The trauma was not just political.
It produced a sustained ideological crisis in Korean Confucian thought.

Confucian doctrine held that the proper hierarchy of nations was civilizational: China, as the Middle Kingdom, was the source of civilization; Korea, as a fully Confucianized neighbor, was the most successful student; barbarians at the periphery were inferior.
The Manchus, as forest-dwelling Tungusic-speaking former-Jurchens, were unambiguously barbarians by this scheme — and now Korea was their tributary.
This was not merely inconvenient; it threatened the entire conceptual scheme of Korean identity within the East Asian order.

Korean Confucian intellectuals responded with a defensive posture that would shape elite ideology for the next two and a half centuries: they declared that the Ming dynasty was the rightful Chinese sovereign, that the Qing was a usurper barbarian state, and that Joseon Korea was the only remaining authentic Confucian civilization on earth.

This doctrine, sometimes called sojunghwa (SOH-joong-HWAH, "Little Middle Kingdom"), had Korea taking on the cultural mantle of fallen civilization — Korea was now the true heir of Chinese culture, the last bastion of authentic Confucianism while the actual Chinese capital was occupied by barbarian Manchu emperors.
This ideological position had practical consequences.
Joseon court documents continued to use Ming era-names long after the Ming had ceased to exist (privately, in court records, alongside the official Qing dating).

Annual sacrifices were performed at a special shrine — the Daebodan (DAY-boh-dahn, "Altar of Great Recompense") — built inside the royal palace specifically to memorialize the Ming Wanli Emperor (who had sent troops to save Korea in 1592).

Korean envoys to Beijing were required to wear traditional Korean court dress (which preserved earlier Ming-era styles) rather than adopt Qing-style queue hairstyles or banner clothing — a quiet but consistent gesture of refusal.
Korean intellectuals talked about the sojunghwa as a kind of underground identity, the truth maintained against the falsehood of the visible political order.
This is one of the more interesting cases of ideological resistance through cultural conservation in early-modern history.

Joseon could not militarily defy the Qing — the 1636 lesson had been comprehensive — but it could maintain a parallel ideological universe in which the Manchus were not really legitimate and Korean culture preserved the true tradition.
The same mechanism would later help Korean nationalism survive Japanese colonial rule (Chapter 8).
The Crown Prince Sohyeon hostage episode is one of the most poignant subplots of the Manchu trauma.
Sohyeon (SOH-hyun, 1612–1645) was Injo's eldest son and the designated crown prince.
After the 1637 surrender, he was sent as hostage to the Qing capital — first at Mukden in Manchuria, then at Beijing after the Qing conquest of China in 1644 — for a total of eight years.
His brother Bongnim Daegun (later King Hyojong) was sent with him.
Sohyeon's experience in Mukden and Beijing transformed him intellectually.

He was treated reasonably well by the Qing court — he had personal access to senior Manchu officials, was taken on military campaigns as an observer, and was permitted considerable correspondence with home.
He observed Qing military organization closely.

He met Western Catholic missionaries, particularly the German Jesuit Johann Adam Schall von Bell (yo-HAHN AH-dahm SHAHLL, 1591–1666), the imperial astronomer at the Qing court, who taught Sohyeon Western astronomy, gifted him books on Western mathematics, and gave him a small celestial globe and a Chinese-language Catholic catechism.
Sohyeon became personally interested in Catholicism, though he never converted.

When Sohyeon returned to Hanyang in early 1645 — after the Qing had finally permitted him to come home — he brought back books on Western science, Catholic religious texts, and a sophisticated understanding of why the Manchus had won and how the Joseon court might rationally adjust its outlook.
His father refused to see him for weeks.
When the king did receive his son, the audience was brief and cold.
Two months after his return, Crown Prince Sohyeon died suddenly.
The official cause was illness.

Contemporary court rumor and modern scholarship both lean toward poisoning — most likely by his father, or by court officials acting at the father's behest, who feared that Sohyeon's Qing-friendly and Western-curious orientation would undermine the sojunghwa ideology around which post-1637 Korean identity had been organized.
Sohyeon's wife was executed shortly after on flimsy charges.
Sohyeon's three young sons were exiled to a remote island, where two of them died.
We do not know with certainty what happened to Sohyeon.
The Joseon court record on this episode is incomplete and the surviving documents are deliberately ambiguous.

But the pattern — sudden death, hasty burial, execution of the wife, exile of the heirs, refusal to investigate — is very hard to read as anything but a political assassination ordered or condoned by the king.
The brilliant, internationally educated, scientifically curious crown prince who had spent eight years in barbarian captivity and come home with new ideas was a threat.
He was eliminated.
His younger brother Bongnim Daegun, who had stayed quieter about his Qing-era observations, succeeded as Hyojong in 1649.
Hyojong reigned for ten years.

His major project was an elaborate plot to launch a revenge expedition north against the Qing — the Northern Expedition that Joseon trained matchlock musketeers and stockpiled weapons for, but never actually launched.
Hyojong died in 1659 with the expedition still in the planning stage.
The revenge plot quietly faded.
The Manchu trauma also intensified Joseon's foreign-policy isolationism in a way that earned the country its lasting nickname.
After 1637, Joseon adopted a sea ban policy — sometimes called the Hermit Kingdom policy in nineteenth-century English — that systematically restricted foreign contact.
Private overseas trade was banned.
Foreign ships approaching Korean coasts were turned away or attacked.

The only authorized foreign presences were the Waegwan (WAY-gwan, "Japan House") in Busan, where a small number of Tsushima-clan Japanese merchants were permitted to live and trade under tight restrictions, and the annual Korean tribute embassies to Beijing, which traveled along a fixed road and were not permitted independent contact with Chinese populations along the way.
Even Catholic missionary contact, when it began later (Chapter 6), was systematically suppressed.
This isolation was not absolute.
Korean envoys to Beijing brought back Western books and ideas (sometimes via Jesuit contact at the Qing court).
Japanese merchants at the Waegwan brought European goods and information.
Shipwrecked European sailors who washed up on Korean shores were sometimes interrogated and detained for years (the Hendrick Hamel case below).

But by the standards of seventeenth-century Asia, Joseon was extraordinarily closed — more isolated than Tokugawa Japan (which at least permitted limited Dutch trade through Nagasaki), more isolated than Qing China (which permitted European trade in southern ports), almost certainly the most isolated state in early-modern East Asia.
The reasons were multiple.
The Imjin War had been a Japanese intrusion.
The Manchu invasions had been a continental intrusion.
The yangban political establishment had concluded that foreign contact brought catastrophe and the only safe response was withdrawal.
The sojunghwa ideology reinforced this by treating Korea as the last preserve of authentic civilization that needed protection from corrupting outside influences.
The result was two and a half centuries of careful, deliberate isolation.
The most famous case of accidental foreign contact during the isolation period was the Hendrick Hamel shipwreck.

In August 1653, a Dutch East India Company yacht named De Sperwer (the Sparrowhawk), bound from Batavia (modern Jakarta) to Nagasaki, was driven off course by a typhoon and wrecked on the south coast of Jeju Island.
Of the 64 crew members, 36 survived.
The senior surviving officer was a 23-year-old named Hendrick Hamel (HEN-drik HAH-mel), who served as the expedition's accountant.
The Joseon authorities did not know what to do with the survivors.
They could not be returned home — Joseon had no diplomatic relations with the Dutch — but executing them was problematic, and exporting them through China was not permitted under the strict Sea Ban.
The Joseon court eventually decided the easiest solution was simply to keep them.
The Dutch were transferred to Hanyang, presented at court, assigned military service in the royal guard, and effectively held as the king's involuntary guests.
Hamel and his shipmates spent thirteen years in Korea, slowly being moved between provincial postings as their numbers dwindled to about twenty by the mid-1660s.
In September 1666, Hamel and seven others escaped by stealing a small boat and sailing to Japan.
The Japanese authorities at Nagasaki, surprised but cooperative, eventually returned them to Batavia and from there to the Dutch Republic.
Hamel wrote a detailed report of his thirteen years in Korea — partly to claim his back wages from the Dutch East India Company, partly because he was an interesting man with a remarkable story.
The book was published in Dutch in 1668 as the Journal of Hendrick Hamel.
It was the first detailed European account of Korea ever published, and it remained the most informative European source on Korea for the next two hundred years.

Hamel described Korean dress, food, government, Buddhism, the climate, the language, the political system, Korean attitudes toward foreigners — the whole texture of seventeenth-century Joseon life as observed by an outside European witness.
Modern Korean historians use his account as one of the most detailed primary sources for everyday life under King Injo and his successors.
The remaining Dutch crew were eventually allowed to depart in 1668, after Japanese diplomatic intervention.

Their thirteen-year detention was the longest involuntary residence of European travelers anywhere in East Asia in this period, and the Hamel case remained the principal European point of contact with Korea until the nineteenth century opened the country forcibly (Chapter 8).

chapters.title: Silhak and Late-Joseon Culture
sentences: The half-century of recovery after the Manchu trauma — roughly 1660 to 1720 — was followed by a long late-dynasty period of substantial cultural achievement that the political histories tend to neglect because the political surface of the country in these years was visibly decaying.
The institutional politics of late Joseon were faction-ridden and stagnant (Chapter 7).
But beneath the surface, an intellectual movement and an artistic flowering were producing work that would shape Korean modernity.
The intellectual movement was Silhak (SHEEL-hahk, "Practical Learning").
The word silhak covers a loosely organized scholarly tendency rather than an organized school.

The basic complaint was that mainstream Joseon Neo-Confucianism had become absorbed in metaphysical disputes (the four-seven debate of Toegye and Yulgok, Chapter 3, and similar controversies that successor scholars continued for generations) at the expense of practical knowledge.

The Silhak scholars argued that scholarship should produce something usable — better farming methods, better administrative procedures, better public-health practice, better understanding of the actual material world — and that pure metaphysical disputation, however philosophically refined, was a form of intellectual luxury the country could no longer afford.
The Silhak movement was therefore not a rejection of Confucianism but a redirection of Confucian scholarship toward practical application.
Many Silhak scholars were devout Confucians; what they wanted was a more useful Confucian scholarship.
The founding figure was Yu Hyeong-won (YOO HYUNG-WON, 1622–1673), scholar name Bangye (BAHNG-gay).
Yu spent twenty years in voluntary rural retirement in the southwestern province of Jeolla, writing a sweeping reform proposal called the Bangye Surok (BAHNG-gay SOO-rohk).

The Bangye Surok argued for the redistribution of land away from the great yangban estates to actual cultivators, the abolition of slavery (a remarkably radical proposal for the seventeenth century), the establishment of a meritocratic civil service open to all classes, the rationalization of the tax system, and the reform of the military system.
Yu Hyeong-won was not in a position to actually implement any of this; he was a private scholar with no court position.
But his writings, slowly circulated in manuscript among sympathetic scholars, became the founding document of the Silhak tradition.
The Silhak tradition flowered most spectacularly in the late eighteenth century under King Jeongjo's patronage.
King Jeongjo (JUNG-johng, reigned 1776–1800) was the grandson of King Yeongjo and the son of the murdered Crown Prince Sado (Chapter 7).

He came to the throne after a difficult childhood in which his grandfather had killed his father by sealing him in a wooden rice chest, and his accession survived a major assassination plot orchestrated by the same noble faction that had been responsible for his father's death.
Jeongjo was, by any reasonable measure, the second-best king of the Joseon dynasty after Sejong.
He was scholarly, politically capable, willing to confront the entrenched factional system, and personally invested in promoting the Silhak intellectual current.
He founded the Gyujanggak (GYOO-jahng-gahk, "Pavilion of the Royal Library") in 1776 inside Changdeokgung Palace, modeled on the Hall of Worthies of Sejong's reign (Chapter 2).
The Gyujanggak was both a royal library — eventually housing tens of thousands of books — and a research institute.

Jeongjo recruited talented young officials of mixed factional background to staff it, used it as a counterweight to the entrenched yangban political establishment, and personally participated in its scholarly work.
Several of the great Silhak figures were Gyujanggak scholars or royal favorites.
The most important were Park Ji-won, Park Je-ga, Hong Dae-yong, and above all Jeong Yak-yong.
Park Ji-won (PAHK JEE-WON, 1737–1805), scholar name Yeonam (YUN-ahm), was the great Silhak essayist.

He accompanied the 1780 Joseon embassy to Beijing — one of the regular tribute embassies that constituted Joseon's main official foreign contact — and used the trip to produce his masterpiece, the Yeolha Ilgi (YUL-hah il-GEE, "Jehol Diary"), a 26-volume travelogue covering the embassy's journey across northern Korea, through Manchuria, and into the Qing summer capital at Jehol (modern Chengde).
The Yeolha Ilgi is unlike any other Korean book of the period.

It mixes journalism, natural observation, philosophical reflection, satirical fiction, technical description, and impassioned argument for Joseon to adopt Qing techniques in agriculture, water management, transportation, and manufacturing.

Park Ji-won had no interest in the sojunghwa fantasy that the Qing were barbarian usurpers — what he saw on his trip were paved roads, brick buildings, sophisticated water mills, productive farms, and a manufacturing economy generations ahead of Korea's.
He came home to argue that Joseon should learn from this rather than pretending it did not exist.
The Yeolha Ilgi is also extraordinary as literature.
Park Ji-won wrote in a fluid, witty, observational prose style that broke deliberately with the formal classical Chinese of conventional yangban writing.
He included satirical fictional sketches alongside straight reportage.
He included passages in vernacular Korean phrasing transcribed phonetically.
The book was read with delight by sympathetic intellectuals and with horror by orthodox Confucians who considered its style undignified and its enthusiasm for Qing culture treasonous.
The Yeolha Ilgi is now considered one of the great works of Joseon literature.
Hong Dae-yong (HONG DAY-yong, 1731–1783), an earlier traveler to Beijing in 1765, made his lasting contribution in cosmology.

After meeting Jesuit astronomers at the Qing court — including the German Jesuit Ignaz Kogler — and acquainting himself with telescopic astronomy, Hong returned to Korea and wrote a treatise called the Damheonseo (DAHM-hun-SUH) in which he argued that the earth rotates on its axis once every twenty-four hours (rather than the heavens revolving around a fixed earth) and speculated that there might be intelligent beings on other planets, since the universe was probably structured similarly throughout.

These conclusions were entirely his own — Western astronomy had not yet established Copernican rotation as orthodoxy and had certainly not endorsed extraterrestrial life — and they represent a remarkable leap in pre-telescopic Korean cosmological thought.

Hong argued from first principles and from analogy: if the earth was a sphere (which Western astronomy had established), then the apparent motion of the heavens was probably the earth's rotation rather than the universe's rotation, since rotation of the small body was simpler than rotation of the immense one.
Jeong Yak-yong (JUNG YAHK-yong, 1762–1836), scholar name Dasan (DAH-sahn), was the greatest Silhak polymath and one of the most extraordinary intellectual figures in Korean history.
Dasan's range was astonishing.

He served as a senior official under Jeongjo, designed the pulley crane that lifted the massive granite blocks for Hwaseong Fortress (see below), wrote treatises on smallpox vaccination (which he learned about from Jesuit-influenced sources in Beijing), produced reform proposals on land tenure and tax administration, did important work in textual criticism of the Confucian classics, wrote major studies of Korean geography and history, and produced a steady stream of poetry and personal essays.
The corpus of his collected works runs to over 500 volumes — by far the largest single-author body of work in Joseon scholarship.
Dasan's career was effectively destroyed by his connection to Catholicism.
He had been baptized as a young man (around 1784, when Catholic ideas first reached the Joseon yangban through Jesuit-influenced contacts in Beijing — see below).
When Jeongjo died in 1800 and the Andong Kim faction (Chapter 7) seized power, Dasan was caught up in the Sinyu Persecution of 1801 along with hundreds of other Korean Catholic converts.
His brother Jeong Yak-jong was executed.
Dasan himself was exiled to a small village in the southwestern province of Jeolla, where he spent the next eighteen years in rural isolation.
He used the exile to write.
The bulk of his collected works was produced during these eighteen years of internal banishment.
The Korean intellectual tradition has tended to treat Dasan's exile as a tragic waste of a great mind that should have been at the center of national policy-making.
The Silhak movement that he had inherited and extended was effectively decapitated when he was sent into exile.
The reform proposals he wrote in Jeolla were not implemented for another century.
The combination of Dasan's case and the broader Catholic persecutions essentially ended Silhak as an active political movement.

By the time Korea was forced to confront Western pressure in the mid-nineteenth century (Chapter 8), the intellectual tradition that might have provided a basis for orderly modernization had been largely silenced.
The Hwaseong Fortress is the physical monument to Jeongjo's reign and to Dasan's engineering genius.
Hwaseong (HWAH-suhng, "Brilliant Fortress") is a fortified city wall surrounding the city of Suwon (SOO-won), about 18 miles south of Seoul.

King Jeongjo commissioned its construction in 1794, partly as a fortified administrative center for southern access to the capital, partly as a memorial to his murdered father Crown Prince Sado (whose tomb is just south of Hwaseong, and whom Jeongjo had hoped to honor by making Suwon a kind of secondary capital).
The construction took 33 months — extraordinarily fast for a 3.5-mile defensive wall with four major gates, multiple bastions, command towers, and supporting infrastructure.

The speed was achieved through several technological innovations: Pulley cranes designed by Jeong Yak-yong, which could lift the massive granite blocks used for the wall's foundations using mechanical advantage rather than the gangs of human labor that traditional Korean construction had required.
Dasan's cranes drew on Western mechanical principles he had learned through Catholic-influenced sources.
Standardized brick manufacture, with the bricks fired at on-site kilns rather than transported from distant production centers.
Detailed centralized planning that documented every brick, beam, and piece of stone in the project.

The construction record book — the Hwaseong Seongyeokuigwe ("Records of the Construction of Hwaseong Fortress") — survives, and it is so comprehensive that Korean restorers in the twentieth century used it to faithfully rebuild sections of the fortress that had been damaged.
Wage labor rather than corvée, which Jeongjo introduced specifically for this project.
Workers were paid actual wages rather than being conscripted as unfree labor, with the goal of demonstrating that paid skilled labor was more efficient than corvée.

The experiment succeeded — workers paid in cash worked harder and faster than corvée laborers, and the Hwaseong project became a demonstration that Joseon's traditional labor system was economically irrational.
Hwaseong is now a UNESCO World Heritage site and one of the most visited historical destinations in South Korea.
Substantial portions of the original 1796 construction survive, and the fortress can be walked along its walls, visited at the gates, and toured at the inner palace grounds.
It is one of the most beautiful Korean buildings of the eighteenth century and arguably the high-water mark of Joseon civic architecture.
The other great cultural achievement of late Joseon was a flowering of distinctly Korean visual art.

For most of the dynasty, Korean painting had followed Chinese conventions — landscape paintings depicted imagined Chinese mountains and Chinese-style scholar pavilions, even when the painter had never seen China and never would.
This was the educated yangban convention.
In the eighteenth century, two great painters broke this convention.
Jeong Seon (JUNG SUN, 1676–1759), scholar name Gyeomjae (GYUM-jay), pioneered jingyeong sansu ("true-view landscape") painting.

Instead of imagined Chinese mountains, Jeong painted actual Korean mountains: Mount Geumgang on the east coast (now in North Korea), Mount Inwang behind Gyeongbokgung in Seoul, the Korean coastal cliffs and waterfalls and pine forests.

He developed a distinctive technique using sharp vertical brushstrokes to capture the angular granite peaks of the Korean landscape — a different visual texture from the rounded Chinese hills of conventional painting.
His Album of Mount Geumgang (1734) is one of the foundational works of Korean landscape painting.

His masterwork, the Inwangjesaekdo ("View of Mount Inwang After Rain," 1751), shows Mount Inwang from his rooftop in central Seoul as he watched the rain clear after a storm — a real place, a real day, a real moment, captured in a way that Korean painting had never quite captured before.
The true-view tradition was a kind of visual version of what the Silhak intellectuals were doing in scholarship: turning attention to actual Korean reality rather than imagined Chinese ideal.
It is not a coincidence that Jeong Seon and the leading Silhak scholars were near-contemporaries and that their projects shared intellectual roots.
Kim Hong-do (KIM HONG-doh, 1745–1806), scholar name Danwon (DAHN-won), was the great genre painter of late Joseon.

Danwon's specialty was scenes of commoner life: a wrestling match in a market square, a one-room schoolyard with a teacher swatting an inattentive student, a blacksmith's forge, a roof-tiler at work, a group of farmers eating lunch in a field.
The scenes are observational, witty, full of small human details — a bystander laughing at the wrestling match, a child crying at the school, an apprentice yawning in the smithy.
Danwon's paintings are an unmatched visual record of eighteenth-century Korean daily life.
His album of genre scenes is one of the most beloved works in Korean art.
Shin Yun-bok (SHIN YOON-bohk, 1758–1813), scholar name Hyewon (HEY-won), pushed even further.
Hyewon's genre scenes depicted yangban men with kisaeng (entertainer) women, scholars at illicit drinking parties, secret lovers meeting under the moon.
The paintings are sensual, sometimes explicitly erotic, often gently mocking the gap between yangban Confucian rectitude and yangban actual behavior.
Hyewon was eventually expelled from the royal painting academy (the Dohwaseo) on charges of indecency.
He continued to work privately for elite patrons.
His best-known work, the Album of Genre Paintings, is a National Treasure of South Korea.
The combination of Danwon and Hyewon represents a Joseon art that for the first time was looking at Korean society directly — not as a Confucian morality play, but as a human spectacle worth seeing.

The same observational impulse that produced the true-view landscapes of Jeong Seon and the practical-knowledge scholarship of the Silhak movement was producing, in painting, the first really sustained visual record of how Koreans actually lived.
A note on Joseon ceramics, since they are one of the things Korea is now most famous for and they followed an unexpected trajectory.

Joseon ceramic taste shifted decisively in the early dynasty, away from the elaborate Goryeo celadon (the jade-green glazed stoneware that had been the great glory of the previous dynasty, prized at courts as far away as China and Japan, see Ancient Korea Ch 8) and toward the rougher buncheong (BOON-chung) stoneware of the early Joseon period and then toward baekja (BAYK-jah, white porcelain).
Baekja is austere and visually plain — pure white porcelain with minimal decoration, often only a single brushstroke of cobalt blue.
The aesthetic preference for plainness was a Confucian visual statement.
White was the color of mourning and ritual purity.
Elaborate decoration was associated with Buddhist excess.
The proper yangban serving vessel was a plain white porcelain bowl, with restraint as its visual virtue.
The moon jars (Korean dalhangari) are the most famous expression of the Joseon white porcelain aesthetic.
These large round jars — typically 16 to 20 inches across, bulbous and asymmetrical, made by joining two thrown bowls at their rims — have become objects of intense modern collector interest.
The British potter Bernard Leach, who lived in Korea in the early twentieth century, popularized them in the West.
Modern Korean ceramic artists continue to produce them.

The Joseon moon jar's modest, slightly imperfect, weighty white presence has come to symbolize a particular kind of Korean aesthetic minimalism that influenced twentieth-century Japanese and Western design.

The same century that produced the elaborate cobalt-decorated porcelain of Qing China produced, just across the border, the deliberately understated white porcelain of Joseon — two different responses to similar ceramic technology, expressing two different cultural aesthetics.
Joseon's white porcelain is now arguably the most internationally recognizable Korean visual style.
The introduction of Catholicism to Korea is one of the most distinctive episodes in the history of Christianity in Asia, because it happened without any missionary involvement.
In 1784, a young yangban scholar named Yi Seung-hun (yee SUNG-hun, 1756–1801) accompanied his father on the regular tribute embassy to Beijing.

While in Beijing, he sought out the resident Jesuit missionaries — Catholic priests had been at the Qing court since the time of Matteo Ricci in the early 1600s — and was baptized by Father Louis de Grammont.
He took the baptismal name Peter (after the apostle whose name means "rock" in Greek).
On his return to Korea, he brought back Catholic books, religious medals, and an explicit project of organizing a Korean Catholic community.
Within a few years, an underground Korean Catholic church had organized itself, entirely without foreign missionary involvement.

The congregation grew rapidly — perhaps several thousand by the late 1790s, including some prominent yangban (the Silhak scholar Jeong Yak-yong and his brothers were among the early converts, though Dasan himself partially recanted under pressure) and many commoners and women.

Korean Catholics held secret meetings, read Catholic texts in classical Chinese (since no Catholic literature was yet available in Korean), and developed their own indigenous religious practice without any priest present in the country.
This is, as far as anyone has been able to establish, the only case in the history of Christianity where a substantial church was founded by indigenous lay converts without missionary involvement.
The standard pattern of Christian expansion is missionary-led: a foreign priest arrives, preaches, and gradually accumulates converts.
The Korean case ran in reverse: lay Korean converts wrote to the Beijing diocese asking for a priest.
The first priest sent — the Chinese-born Father Zhou Wen-mo (Korean: Ju Mun-mo) — arrived secretly in 1795 and ministered to a Korean church that had already been organized for over a decade.
The Joseon court reacted with predictable horror.

Catholicism violated multiple Confucian principles: it required ancestor worship to be abandoned (replaced by belief in a single creator god); it claimed the absolute spiritual authority of foreign priests over the Korean state; it was an alien religious importation comparable to Buddhism, which the dynasty had spent four centuries suppressing.
From the late 1790s onward, the Joseon government conducted increasingly severe persecutions of Korean Catholics.

The largest were the Sinyu Persecution of 1801 (which killed around 300 Catholics including Father Ju Mun-mo, and exiled Jeong Yak-yong), the persecutions of 1839 (which killed several French missionaries who had by then secretly entered the country), and the great Byeong-in Persecution of 1866 (which killed around 8,000 Korean Catholics and nine French missionaries — by some counts the largest single-year religious persecution in nineteenth-century Asia).

Many of the executed Korean Catholics were later canonized as saints by the Vatican; Andrew Kim Taegon, the first Korean priest, was beheaded in 1846 at age 25 and is now the patron saint of Korean clergy.
The persecutions ultimately failed to eradicate Korean Catholicism.
The church survived underground, kept alive by lay catechists, and emerged into the open after Korea was forced to accept religious toleration in the late 1880s (Chapter 8).

Modern South Korea has roughly 5 million Catholics — about 11% of the population — and the descendants of the first Korean Catholic generations of the 1780s and 1790s still constitute important elements of the Korean Catholic community today.
The persecutions also had a political function.
They were used by conservative court factions (Chapter 7) as a pretext to attack Silhak scholars whose intellectual openness to Western ideas made them vulnerable to charges of Catholic association.

The combination of the Catholic persecutions and the suppression of Silhak effectively closed Joseon's intellectual openness to Western knowledge for the better part of the nineteenth century — at exactly the moment when openness to Western technical and scientific knowledge would have been most useful in confronting the gunboat diplomacy that was about to arrive (Chapter 8).

Cross-civ check: while late-Joseon culture was producing its great moments — Jeongjo's Gyujanggak, Hwaseong Fortress, Dasan's exile-era writing, Jeong Seon's true-view landscapes, Kim Hong-do's genre scenes — the American Revolution had just produced the United States Constitution (1787); the French Revolution had begun (1789); Catherine the Great was completing the Russian expansion across Siberia and into Alaska; Edo Japan under the Tokugawa shogunate (Ancient Japan Ch 8) was producing its parallel cultural flowering of ukiyo-e woodblock prints, kabuki theater, and Confucian-influenced popular fiction; the Qing Empire under the Qianlong Emperor was at its territorial peak and beginning to slip into the slow decline that the nineteenth century would expose; the Mughal Empire in India was nearly extinguished, with the British East India Company consolidating its rule across the subcontinent (the Battle of Plassey in 1757 having given the Company effective control of Bengal).
The world Joseon was choosing to ignore was about to come knocking on the gates very hard.

chapters.title: Faction Wars and the Slow Decline
sentences: Joseon court politics from the mid-sixteenth century onward were dominated by sustained, sometimes bloody factional struggle.
This chapter is about why.
The factional pattern emerged in 1575 — the founding moment of what became the Eastern–Western division.
Two senior officials, Sim Ui-gyeom (SIM oo-ee-GYUM) and Kim Hyo-won (KIM HYOH-WON), feuded over a personnel appointment in the censorate.
Each had supporters at court.
Sim's house was in the western quarter of Hanyang; Kim's was in the eastern.
Their respective factions came to be called the Westerners (Seoin) and the Easterners (Dongin) after the geographic accident of where the two men lived.
Within a generation, the geographic origin had been forgotten and the factions had hardened into ideological camps with their own doctrinal positions, recruitment networks, and political agendas.
The Easterners traced their philosophical lineage to Yi Hwang (Toegye) and emphasized the metaphysical primacy of li (principle).
The Westerners traced their lineage to Yi I (Yulgok) and emphasized the practical interplay of li and gi.
The original metaphysical disagreement (Chapter 3) had now become a political identification.
Easterners and Westerners married within their own faction.
They sent their sons to seowon affiliated with their philosophical lineage.
They held different interpretations of how Confucian ritual should be performed at court.
They competed for high office in the censorate, the Ministry of Personnel, and the seats around the king.
Both Easterners and Westerners then split further.
The Easterners divided into Northerners and Southerners in the 1580s.
The Northerners further divided into Greater Northerners and Lesser Northerners in the 1610s.
The Westerners eventually divided into Old Doctrine (Noron) and Young Doctrine (Soron) in the 1680s.
The Southerners further subdivided.
