The hybrid that eventually emerged from this experimentation, called the Vesara (VEH-sah-rah) style, combined elements of both — a stepped tower with northern-style curving profiles and miniature shikhara motifs, the Deccan compromise between the two parent traditions.
The Hoysala temples at Belur and Halebidu (Chapter 6) would later carry the Vesara style to its decorative peak.
The Chalukya site at Pattadakal is the canonical place to see this experiment in progress.
Ten major temples cluster around a central courtyard.
Four are built in the Nagara north-Indian style.
Six are built in the Dravida south-Indian style.
The two traditions stand side by side, each with its own characteristic plan, tower form, and sculptural program, all built within the same century by the same dynasty's patronage.
UNESCO World Heritage; one of the most architecturally illuminating temple complexes anywhere in India.
The Chalukyas were finally overthrown in 753 CE by their own subordinates, the Rashtrakutas (rash-trah-KOO-tahz) of Manyakheta (mahn-yah-KHEH-tah, modern Malkhed in Karnataka).
The Rashtrakuta dynasty was the most powerful early-medieval Indian power.

They ruled most of the Deccan for two and a half centuries (753–982 CE), at their peak demanded tribute from the Pratiharas of north India and the Palas of Bengal alike, and conducted the most ambitious architectural project in medieval Indian history — the Kailasa Temple at Ellora.
The Rashtrakuta founder Dantidurga (dahn-tee-DOOR-gah, ruled 735–757) overthrew his Chalukya overlords through a combination of military skill and strategic marriage alliances.
His successor Krishna I (KRISH-nah, ruled ~757–774) consolidated the Rashtrakuta state and commissioned the Kailasa Temple.

The greatest Rashtrakuta king was Govinda III (GOH-vin-dah, ruled 793–814), who conducted the most successful military campaigns of the period — defeating the Pala emperor Dharmapala and the Pratihara emperor Nagabhata II in a single campaign and briefly making Kannauj a Rashtrakuta dependency.

Amoghavarsha I (ah-MOH-ghah-VAR-shah, ruled 814–878) was a long-reigning, highly cultured king who patronized Jainism, founded the new capital at Manyakheta, and is sometimes credited (probably loosely) with the Sanskrit poetic theory text Kavirajamarga.

The Arab traveler al-Masudi (vis-ah-LOO-dee, "the Herodotus of the Arabs," who wrote in the early tenth century after travels across the Indian Ocean world) called the Rashtrakuta king of his day one of the four great kings of the world — alongside the Abbasid caliph in Baghdad, the Byzantine emperor in Constantinople, and the emperor of China.
The classification is revealing of how an outside observer with a Eurasian comparative perspective ranked the political powers of the early tenth century.
The Rashtrakutas were operating in the same imperial league as the Abbasids and the Tang.
But their lasting monument is the temple at Ellora.
The Kailasa Temple at Ellora — Cave 16 in the cave-temple complex on the Aurangabad-Manmad highway in modern Maharashtra — is one of the genuine wonders of the world.
It is a full-sized Hindu temple to Shiva (in his form as Kailasanatha, "lord of Kailasa," referring to the sacred Himalayan mountain that Hindu mythology identifies as Shiva's earthly abode).

Architecturally it is a complete temple complex: a central sanctum, a multi-pillared mandapa hall, two subsidiary shrines, a Nandi pavilion (housing the bull-mount of Shiva), surrounding cloistered galleries with smaller shrines, and elaborate external sculpture covering the towers and walls.
The central tower rises 96 feet.
The entire complex measures roughly 165 feet long, 109 feet wide, and 100 feet tall.
What makes the Kailasa Temple unique is that it was carved downward out of a single basalt cliff.
Conventional construction works upward from foundations — you quarry stone elsewhere, transport it to the site, and assemble it.
The Rashtrakuta builders did the opposite.
Starting at the top of the basalt outcrop, they cut a vertical trench around the rectangular footprint of the future temple, isolating a great rectangular block of rock.
They then carved downward into that block, removing rock to leave the temple's external form — towers, walls, doorways, statues — all in their finished positions.
They then hollowed out the interior chambers.
Then they covered every surface, internal and external, with detailed sculpture.
Then they carved the surrounding cloister galleries and subsidiary shrines into the surrounding cliff face.
The total quantity of basalt removed is conservatively estimated at 200,000 tons.
The work probably took roughly twenty years to complete, with hundreds of stonecutters, sculptors, and supervisors organized around the project.

Modern engineering analyses have noted that the carvers had no possibility of correcting structural mistakes — one bad cut on a primary load-bearing element and the entire edifice could have been ruined — and that the geometric precision and structural soundness of the finished temple are remarkable given the irreversibility of every step in the process.
It is the largest single monolithic structure in the world.
It is the largest rock-cut temple anywhere.
It is one of the great engineering feats of the ancient or medieval period from any civilization.
And it stands today essentially intact, carved out of the same cliff it was carved out of in 770 CE, available to walk through and photograph on a regular tourist day-trip from Aurangabad.
UNESCO World Heritage, of course.

The standard cross-civ comparison is Petra (the rock-cut Nabataean city in modern Jordan, mostly second century BCE through second century CE) — but Petra's facades, however dramatic, are mostly tomb-fronts carved into cliff faces, not full free-standing buildings carved from isolated blocks.
The Kailasa Temple is a full Hindu temple complete in three dimensions, in the round, on a scale none of the Petra structures attempt.

The closer comparison is probably Lalibela in Ethiopia (the rock-hewn churches built around 1200 by Emperor Gebre Mesqel Lalibela), which uses the same isolate-and-carve-downward technique — but Lalibela's largest structure (Bete Medhane Alem) is roughly 110 feet long and 80 feet wide.
Kailasa is bigger.

Lalibela also came roughly four hundred years after Kailasa, suggesting that the Ethiopian builders may have been independently rediscovering a technique the Rashtrakutas had already perfected, or possibly that knowledge of the Kailasa technique had circulated through Indian Ocean trade and influenced the Ethiopian project.
The historical connection is unproven; the technical similarity is unmistakable.

The Pandya dynasty of Madurai, the third great early-medieval southern power, gets less coverage in standard histories than the Pallavas or Cholas because their inscriptional record is thinner and their architectural legacy got built over and rebuilt repeatedly through later centuries.
But they were continuously powerful in the deep Tamil south — modern southern Tamil Nadu and parts of Kerala — for most of the medieval period.

Their pearl fisheries on the Gulf of Mannar coast (between south India and Sri Lanka) had been famous since Roman times (Post-Maurya Kingdoms Ch 7) and remained one of the world's principal sources of pearls through the medieval and early-modern periods.
Their patronage of Tamil literature was generous and continuous.

The early phases of the Meenakshi Temple at Madurai — though most of the visible temple today is the result of much later Nayak-era construction in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries — go back to the Pandya period.
The Cheras of the Malabar coast (modern Kerala) were the third member of the ancient Tamil triumvirate, ruling the spice-producing west coast where pepper, cardamom, and ginger grew.

Throughout the medieval period, Arab and Persian merchants dominated the Kerala spice trade with the Persian Gulf and Red Sea, and the Chera kings — who took the dynastic title Kulasekhara in their medieval phase — grew rich on customs revenues from the foreign merchant communities at Calicut, Quilon, and Cochin.

The Chera kingdom is also the legendary setting for one of the more interesting religious establishments of the period: the Cheraman Juma Mosque at Methala in northern Kerala, traditionally said to have been founded around 629 CE by the Chera king Cheraman Perumal after he converted to Islam through contact with Arab traders.

Modern scholars debate the founding date — the present mosque structure is later, and the conversion narrative has obvious legendary elements — but the consensus is that the Cheraman Juma is genuinely ancient and is probably the oldest mosque in the Indian subcontinent.
It is also, importantly, a mosque founded peacefully through trade, not through Turkic conquest.

The two distinct stories of Indian Islam — the peaceful trader's mosque on the Malabar coast, and the soldier's mosque built from temple rubble in Delhi — both have roots in the medieval period, and they have continued to coexist ever since.

The cumulative point of this chapter is that the Tamil south and the Deccan in the period 600–850 CE were doing the kind of monumental temple-building, philosophical-poetic flowering, and dynastic state-building that the textbook image associates with later medieval India — and they were doing it while the north was still working through its post-Gupta political problems.
The Pallavas at Mahabalipuram were carving the Descent of the Ganges around 700 CE, a generation after Harsha's empire had collapsed.
The Rashtrakutas were excavating the Kailasa Temple in 770 CE, while the post-Gupta political situation in the north was still patchwork.
The Chera and Pandya ports were handling the pepper trade with the Arab world before the Arab armies had reached Sindh.
The center of gravity of medieval Indian civilization was, for the seventh and eighth centuries, in the south.

It would shift northward again in the ninth century when the Pratiharas, Palas, and Rashtrakutas began the Tripartite Struggle for Kannauj — and then shift south again in the eleventh century when the Cholas built the Brihadeeswara Temple.
The pattern of regional shifts in cultural and political weight is one of the underlying rhythms of the medieval period.
There is rarely a single center; there is a moving center.
Cross-civ check: the period this chapter covers (~600–850 CE) is the great early-medieval southern flowering.

Outside India, this is also the moment of Tang China's peak — the Tang capital at Chang'an (modern Xi'an) was the largest city in the world around 750, with possibly a million inhabitants (Sui–Tang–Song Ch 2).
It is the period of the Umayyad and early Abbasid caliphates expanding across Persia, Mesopotamia, North Africa, and Spain (Islamic Golden Age Ch 1).
It is the period of the Carolingian Frankish Empire under Charlemagne (crowned Holy Roman Emperor in 800, the same generation as Krishna I building Kailasa).
It is the period of the Maya Late Classic at Copán and Tikal (Maya Civilization Ch 6).

The medieval Indian south was operating in the same imperial-architectural league as Tang Chang'an and Abbasid Baghdad, and its monumental output — the Kailasa Temple, the Mahabalipuram complex — stands comparison with anything those contemporaries produced.

chapters.title: The Tripartite Struggle for Kannauj
sentences: By the middle of the eighth century, three regional dynasties had emerged as the dominant powers of north India, and they spent the next two and a half centuries fighting a three-way war for control of one symbolic city — Kannauj on the upper Ganges.
The war is conventionally called the Tripartite Struggle.
The three contestants were the Gurjara-Pratiharas (goor-jah-rah-prah-tee-HAH-rahz) of Rajasthan and the western Ganges, the Palas (PAH-lahz) of Bengal and Bihar, and the Rashtrakutas of the Deccan.
None of them ever held Kannauj long enough to translate dominance into a durable north-Indian empire.
The chronic warfare exhausted all three by the end of the tenth century, leaving the field open for the Turkic invasions that began with Mahmud of Ghazni in 1001 (Chapter 8).
This is one of the medieval period's structural pathologies.

Three roughly equal regional powers, each strong enough to defeat one of the other two but not strong enough to defeat both at once, fight a chronic three-way war for a prize none of them can actually hold.
The cumulative effect over multiple generations is that all three weaken themselves and the political vacuum eventually gets filled by a fourth party from outside.
The Gurjara-Pratihara dynasty originated in modern Rajasthan, in the desert and semi-desert zone northwest of the Indo-Gangetic plain.

The name Gurjara refers to a regional people of probably Central Asian origin who had settled in northwestern India between the fifth and seventh centuries and gradually been Hinduized. (Modern Indian historians differ on whether the Gurjaras were a tribe, a caste, or a regional designation; the surviving inscriptions are not specific.) The Pratihara branch traced descent from a mythological ancestor named Lakshmana (the brother of Rama in the Ramayana epic) and styled themselves as Kshatriya warriors and protectors of the Hindu social order against the Arab raids that had been pushing eastward out of Sindh since the Umayyad conquest in 711 CE.

The dynasty's founder was Nagabhata I (NAH-gah-BHAH-tah, ruled ~730–760), who repulsed Arab incursions into the Avanti region (modern western Madhya Pradesh) in the 730s and established the Pratihara state as the eastern bulwark against further Arab expansion.
His successors gradually extended Pratihara power eastward across modern Rajasthan, Gujarat, and into the western Ganges plain.
The dynasty's greatest king was Mihira Bhoja (mih-HEE-rah BHOH-jah, ruled 836–885), whose long reign coincided with the peak Pratihara empire.

Mihira Bhoja's territory at its peak extended from Sindh in the west to Bengal in the east and from the Himalayan foothills in the north to the Narmada River in the south — essentially all of north India outside the Pala-controlled east.

His army was reportedly the strongest cavalry force in the subcontinent, partly because the Pratiharas controlled the western Indian horse trade with the Arab world and could continuously replenish their cavalry from imported stock.

The Arab geographer Sulayman al-Tajir ("Sulayman the Merchant"), who wrote around 851 CE based on his own travels in the Indian Ocean trade routes, described Mihira Bhoja's kingdom in unusually positive terms for an Arab observer reporting on a Hindu state.

He praised the security of the Pratihara roads (a reliable indicator of effective royal control), the discipline of Mihira Bhoja's army, the strength of his cavalry, and — interestingly — the equity of his court justice.

Sulayman's Arab merchant contemporaries operated extensively in Pratihara territory, and the Pratiharas seem to have welcomed the trade despite being theoretically the eastern frontier defenders against Arab military expansion.
The two regimes maintained a workable relationship: the Pratiharas held the military line at the desert, the Arab merchants traded peacefully across it.
The Pratiharas captured Kannauj from the Maukhari successors around the late eighth century and held it through most of the ninth and tenth, making it their capital.

At its zenith in the late ninth century, Kannauj under Pratihara rule was probably the largest and richest city in north India — a major center of Sanskrit learning, Hindu temple sponsorship, and luxury trade.
It had also become, through Pratihara cultivation, the symbolic capital that any north Indian power needed to claim in order to be taken seriously as an emperor.
The Pala dynasty of Bengal and Bihar was the eastern competitor.

The Palas emerged in the mid-eighth century from a chaotic political situation in the eastern Ganges delta — the post-Shashanka Bengal region had collapsed into civil war between rival warlords for nearly a century, with no stable government emerging.

Around 750 CE, an assembly of leading Bengal nobles reportedly elected a man named Gopala (goh-PAH-lah) as king, partly in desperation to end the chronic warfare and partly because Gopala's personal reputation for courage and judgment was widely respected.

The election story is reported in Pala inscriptions and in the Tibetan historian Taranatha's much later account; some modern scholars treat it as legendary, but the Pala dynasty's foundation was, at minimum, unusually consensual for a medieval Indian king-making.
Gopala's son Dharmapala (dahr-mah-PAH-lah, ruled ~781–821) was the real architect of Pala power.
He extended Pala control across Bengal, Bihar, and parts of Odisha, and around 790 he attempted the ambitious move of capturing Kannauj from the Pratiharas — and succeeded, briefly.

Pala sources describe a ceremony at Kannauj in which Dharmapala installed a client king (a Maukhari prince named Chakrayudha) on the Kannauj throne while subordinate kings from across north India attended in homage.
This was the high-water mark of Pala power and the moment the Tripartite Struggle visibly began as a three-way contest.
The Pratiharas under Nagabhata II soon counterattacked, recovered Kannauj, and the see-saw began.
Dharmapala's other major contribution was the founding of Vikramashila Monastery, the second great Pala-era Buddhist university (after Nalanda, which the Palas continued to patronize lavishly).

Vikramashila — somewhere on the Ganges in modern eastern Bihar, the exact site is contested but probably near modern Bhagalpur — focused especially on Tantric Buddhist studies and produced many of the great Tantric scholars whose work would shortly migrate to Tibet (Chapter 7 for the slow disappearance of Indian Buddhism).
Vikramashila operated for about four centuries, until the Turkic invasions destroyed it around 1200.
The Palas were unusual among medieval Indian dynasties in being formally Buddhist for most of their existence.
Most Pala kings personally followed Mahayana Buddhism, sponsored Buddhist monasteries on a massive scale, and minted coinage with Buddhist iconography.
They also patronized Hindu and Jain establishments, in line with the standard medieval Indian royal practice of pluralistic patronage, but their primary religious identity was Buddhist.

The Pala period was the last great age of Indian Buddhism, and the Pala-era monastic universities were the institutional backbone that kept Indian Buddhism intellectually alive into the eleventh and twelfth centuries.
The Rashtrakuta dynasty (Chapter 3) was the third leg of the triangle, attacking Kannauj from the south.

The Rashtrakutas had to cross the Vindhya Mountains and the Narmada River to reach the upper Ganges, which made their northern campaigns logistically difficult and chronically expensive — but they conducted them anyway, repeatedly, throughout the ninth and tenth centuries, because Kannauj was the prize that distinguished an emperor from a regional king.
The most successful Rashtrakuta king militarily was Govinda III (Chapter 3), who in a single campaign around 800 CE defeated both the Pala emperor Dharmapala and the Pratihara emperor Nagabhata II.
Govinda then briefly captured Kannauj and installed his own client.

He could not hold the city — his army's logistical situation in the upper Ganges plain was unsustainable, and he had to withdraw south to defend the Deccan from a Pallava attack — but the campaign demonstrated Rashtrakuta military superiority over both rivals at the same time.
Subsequent Rashtrakuta kings repeated the pattern.
Indra III (in-DRAH, ruled ~914–928) sacked Kannauj around 916, defeating the Pratihara king Mahipala in the process.

Krishna III (krish-NAH, ruled 939–967) led the most sweeping Rashtrakuta northern campaign of the tenth century, defeating both the Pratiharas and Palas and establishing temporary Rashtrakuta dominance over north India.

The fundamental problem the Rashtrakutas faced was the same problem the Palas and Pratiharas faced from their own directions: holding a distant capital by force required a permanent army of occupation that was ruinously expensive, and any prolonged absence from the dynasty's actual heartland invited revolt back home.
The Rashtrakutas' Deccan-based capital at Manyakheta needed continuous attention.
The Pratiharas' Rajasthan-Western-Ganges base needed continuous defense against Arab pressure.
The Palas' Bengal-Bihar base was constantly threatened by smaller successor dynasties in the eastern frontier zones.
None of the three could maintain Kannauj as a permanent imperial capital because none of the three could afford to leave its actual heartland undefended for long.
The Tripartite Struggle ground on until the late tenth century.

By 982 CE, the Rashtrakuta dynasty had been overthrown by its own subordinates (the Western Chalukyas of Kalyani recovered the Deccan throne), the Pratiharas were in serious decline (Mihira Bhoja had been the last truly powerful Pratihara king, and his successors had been increasingly defeated by the rising Chandela and Chaulukya regional dynasties), and the Palas were facing increasingly assertive Sena rivals in Bengal.
Kannauj, the prize all three had fought for, was under Pratihara rule but Pratihara power was a shadow of what Mihira Bhoja had wielded a century earlier.
Then in 1019 CE, Mahmud of Ghazni (Chapter 8) sacked Kannauj.
The Pratihara king Rajyapala fled the city without fighting — a humiliation his Chandela neighbor Vidyadhara avenged by killing him shortly afterward.
Kannauj never recovered its political weight after the 1019 sack.
The city physically continued to exist (and exists today as a moderate-sized town in western Uttar Pradesh) but it ceased to be the symbolic prize of Indian politics.
Whatever the next great north Indian power was going to be, it would build its capital somewhere else.
The cumulative cost of two and a half centuries of three-way war was that all three competing dynasties had spent themselves.
None of them had built the kind of durable institutional foundations — administrative system, professional army, fiscal apparatus — that could withstand serious external pressure.
When Mahmud's mounted archers came south through the Khyber Pass in the early eleventh century, the regional dynasties of north India were not in a position to put up coordinated resistance.
The Pratiharas were already collapsed.
The Palas were preoccupied with the Senas.
The Rashtrakutas were gone.
The Rajput successor dynasties — Chandelas, Chaulukyas, Paramaras, Chauhans — fought Mahmud individually as he raided their territories and were individually defeated.
None of them tried to organize a north-Indian coalition.
None of them probably could have, given the chronic distrust that the long Tripartite Struggle had built up.
This is one of the genuinely tragic patterns of medieval Indian history.
The two and a half centuries of wasted three-way war did not just fail to produce a stable north Indian empire.
They actively eroded the political fabric that any future stable empire would need to build on.
By the time the Turkic invasions came, the regional kingdoms had been fighting each other so habitually for so long that the idea of unified resistance had stopped being plausible.
Two more pieces of medieval north Indian history are worth setting down before we leave this chapter, because they happened in parallel with the Tripartite Struggle and shaped what came next.
The first is the rise of the Chandela Rajputs of Bundelkhand (the central plateau region of modern Madhya Pradesh, between the Yamuna and Narmada rivers).
The Chandela dynasty emerged in the late ninth century as a vassal of the Pratiharas, then declared independence as Pratihara power waned in the tenth.

Their capital was at Khajuraho (kah-joo-RAH-hoh), a small town in the Bundelkhand interior, and over a century from roughly 950 to 1050 CE they built one of the most spectacular temple complexes in Indian architectural history (Chapter 6 takes up Khajuraho in detail).

The Chandelas were one of the few medieval Rajput dynasties to win a defensive engagement against Mahmud of Ghazni — Vidyadhara Chandela's army apparently caused Mahmud enough trouble in 1019 that the Ghaznavid sultan withdrew without a decisive battle.
The second is the rise of the Chaulukyas (or Solankis) of Gujarat, who emerged in the late tenth century at the expense of the declining Pratiharas.
The Chaulukya capital was at Anhilwara (ahn-hil-WAH-rah, modern Patan).

Their kingdom controlled the rich western Indian merchant ports at Cambay, Bharuch, and Somnath — making them probably the wealthiest north Indian dynasty of the eleventh century, since the Indian Ocean trade with the Arab world flowed through their territory.

The Chaulukya kings were enthusiastic patrons of Jainism (a high proportion of the Gujarati merchant class was Jain, and the patronage was politically as well as religiously useful), and their support funded the marble-clad Dilwara temples on Mount Abu in modern Rajasthan — among the most exquisitely detailed examples of medieval Jain temple architecture anywhere.

The Chaulukyas, the Chandelas, the Paramaras of Malwa under King Bhoja (boh-JAH, the polymath Rajput king who became a Sanskrit cultural reference for the ideal scholar-king), the Tomaras of Delhi, the Chauhans of Ajmer — all of these are Rajput successor dynasties that filled the political space in north India after the Pratihara collapse.
They are, collectively, the kings whose regional armies Mahmud of Ghazni and Muhammad of Ghor would face.
None of them was strong enough to stop the Turkic invasions individually.
None of them organized a coalition.
The political fragmentation that had been the dominant feature of north India since the Gupta collapse was now, six centuries later, about to have its predictable consequences.

Cross-civ check: the Tripartite Struggle for Kannauj (~750–1000 CE) overlaps with the Carolingian division of Charlemagne's empire among his grandsons (Treaty of Verdun, 843), which produced a similar long-running multi-way war for control of the central Frankish territories that no single successor could decisively win — and which similarly created the political conditions for later Norse, Magyar, and Saracen raids to penetrate deep into formerly imperial territory.

It also overlaps with the An Lushan rebellion (755–763) and the long Tang decline that followed (Sui–Tang–Song Ch 3), with the Abbasid weakening in Baghdad, with the Macedonian Renaissance in the Byzantine Empire (Byzantine Empire Ch 5), and with the early Viking Age raids across northern Europe (Viking Age Ch 2).
The late ninth and tenth centuries were a period of imperial weakening in many of the major Eurasian civilizations simultaneously.
The Indian version produced no Viking analog — no externally-based raiding power emerged to take advantage of the situation, until the Turkic invasions of the eleventh century.
But the structural pattern is recognizable.

chapters.title: The Chola Maritime Empire
sentences: While the north was exhausting itself in the Tripartite Struggle, the south was building south India's first true empire.

The Chola dynasty had been extinct as a major power since the early centuries CE, when the ancient Tamil Cholas (familiar to readers of Tamil Sangam-era poetry, Post-Maurya Kingdoms Ch 7) had declined into local irrelevance.

Around 848 CE, a regional chieftain named Vijayalaya (vi-jah-yah-LAH-yah) seized control of the small town of Thanjavur (THAHN-jah-voor, also spelled Tanjore) in the central Tamil region, claimed Chola descent, and founded what is now called the medieval Chola dynasty.

Over the next two centuries, his successors built the most powerful state south India had ever seen — and one that projected naval power across the Bay of Bengal in a way no Indian state had attempted before or would attempt again until modern times.

The medieval Cholas peaked in the early eleventh century under two extraordinary kings, Rajaraja Chola I (rah-jah-RAH-jah, ruled 985–1014) and his son Rajendra Chola I (rah-JEN-drah, ruled 1014–1044).
What they built in fifty-nine years is the central subject of this chapter.
The Chola revival began with conquest of the immediate Tamil neighborhood.

Through the late ninth and tenth centuries, successive Chola kings absorbed the declining Pallavas (the Pallava dynasty was extinct by about 897), pushed back the Pandyas to a southern rump kingdom around Madurai, and gradually consolidated Tamil Nadu under a single throne.
By the time Parantaka I (pah-RAHN-tah-kah, ruled 907–955) was on the throne, the Cholas were the dominant Tamil power.

Parantaka extended Chola rule into Sri Lanka — an expansion that would matter enormously a century later — but suffered a serious defeat by the Rashtrakutas at the Battle of Takkolam around 949 that briefly checked Chola northward expansion.
Rajaraja came to the throne in 985 CE and immediately started doing things on a different scale.

His military campaigns over the next twenty-nine years extended Chola rule across all of south India — the deep Tamil south (incorporating the Pandya kingdom), the western Chera coast in Kerala, the Karnataka highlands (taking territory from the Western Chalukyas of Kalyani), and the entire island of Sri Lanka (the Chola army captured the old Sinhala capital at Anuradhapura around 993 and held the northern half of the island as a Chola province).
The Chola navy also conducted operations in the Maldives, projecting Chola power into the Indian Ocean for the first time.

By the early eleventh century, Rajaraja ruled a state stretching from the Tungabhadra River in the north to Sri Lanka in the south and from the Arabian Sea to the Bay of Bengal — south India's first genuine empire.
Rajaraja was also a meticulous administrator.
He commissioned the first detailed land survey of the Tamil country, recording field-by-field measurements, soil quality, irrigation status, and tax assessments.
He standardized the Chola currency, the kasu copper coin and the kalanju gold weight.

He restructured the provincial administration, dividing the empire into mandalams (provinces), valanadus (subdivisions), nadus (districts), and kurrams (sub-districts), with a clear hierarchy of officials and a documented appeals procedure for tax disputes.
The medieval Chola administrative system was probably the most sophisticated of any Indian state of its period, and it was the institutional foundation that enabled what came next.
What came next was the Brihadeeswara Temple at Thanjavur, which Rajaraja consecrated in 1010 CE to mark the twenty-fifth anniversary of his accession.

The Brihadeeswara Temple ("Great Lord's Temple," dedicated to Shiva) is, by general consensus, the apex of medieval south Indian architecture and one of the greatest single buildings of the medieval world.
The numbers, first.

The central tower (vimana) rises 216 feet in fourteen stepped stories, capped by a single 80-ton dome stone (which according to local tradition was hauled up a four-mile-long earthen ramp from a site outside the city, but the actual mechanism is reasonably contested).

The temple is built almost entirely of granite — an estimated 130,000 tons of it, hauled from quarries at least thirty miles away (granite is not native to the Cauvery delta around Thanjavur; Rajaraja had it transported in deliberately, presumably for its durability and prestige value).
The main sanctum houses a 12-foot-tall stone Shiva lingam (the abstract sculptural form representing Shiva), one of the largest in any Indian temple.
The temple complex covers about 25 acres, surrounded by a double-walled enclosure with elaborate gateway towers (gopurams).

When Brihadeeswara was completed in 1010, its central vimana at 216 feet was probably the tallest structure in India and possibly the tallest Hindu temple in the world. (For context, the contemporary Imperial Cathedral at Speyer in the Holy Roman Empire, completed around 1060, was about 230 feet tall to the top of its towers — Speyer is slightly taller but was completed half a century later.
Paul's Cathedral in London, built in the late eleventh century after the Norman Conquest and destroyed in the 1666 Great Fire, was eventually about 489 feet tall to its spire — but St.
Paul's reached that height through later medieval and Tudor additions.
Brihadeeswara at 1010 was, on a global scale, an exceptionally tall building.) The architectural sophistication is more interesting than the raw height.
The vimana's structural system is essentially a stone version of the Pallava-era stepped-pyramid form developed at Mahabalipuram (Chapter 3), scaled up by an order of magnitude.
Each of the fourteen stories diminishes precisely as it rises, producing the temple's characteristic tapering profile.
The interior is a hollow shaft with internal galleries that allow access to the upper levels — the temple is not a solid pile of stone but a carefully engineered hollow tower.
The exterior is covered with sculptural niches at every level, each containing a bronze or stone deity figure, with detailed iconographic programs identifying each figure's mythological identity.
The temple also carries the most extensive surviving inscriptional record of any medieval Indian building.

The granite walls are densely covered with Tamil inscriptions recording the original endowments — the lands assigned to support the temple, the personnel hired (from the chief priest down to the temple drummers and the women who bathed the deity), the gold and silver vessels donated for ritual use, the daily food allocations, the rules for tax-free temple lands, the procedures for replacing broken ceremonial objects.
The Brihadeeswara inscriptions are one of the most detailed economic and administrative documents from any medieval institution anywhere in the world.
They tell us, for example, that the temple supported about 600 personnel directly and was entitled to revenue from approximately 250 villages in the Cauvery delta.
The temple was not just a religious monument; it was a major economic institution operating on a quasi-permanent basis with explicit royal endowments.

Brihadeeswara is a UNESCO World Heritage site — formally, "Great Living Chola Temples," a complex of three Chola-era temples (Brihadeeswara, plus the temple at Gangaikonda Cholapuram built by Rajendra and the Airavatesvara Temple built by Rajaraja II at Darasuram).

The Brihadeeswara has been in continuous active use since 1010, has survived a millennium of Sri Lankan raids, Vijayanagar, Maratha, French, and British rule, and is still a functioning Hindu temple where daily worship continues exactly as Rajaraja's inscriptions specify.
It is one of the few medieval architectural wonders of the world that you can still walk through on a normal Tuesday afternoon and watch in active operation.
Rajaraja's son Rajendra Chola I (ruled 1014–1044) inherited the throne and immediately set out to surpass his father's achievements.
His first major campaign was a land expedition across north India to the Ganges.
This was unusual.

South Indian kings rarely campaigned in the north — the logistical difficulty of marching an army across the Vindhya Mountains and the central Indian plateau was prohibitive — but Rajendra did it anyway, partly to demonstrate Chola power and partly to bring back symbolically charged Ganges water for a new temple ritual.

The campaign in the late 1010s defeated the late Pala king Mahipala in Bengal (the political situation in the north was already chaotic enough by this point that Rajendra did not face coordinated resistance) and brought the Chola army to the Ganges itself.

Rajendra had vessels of Ganges water carried back to the Cauvery delta, where he founded a new capital city named Gangaikonda Cholapuram (gahn-gai-KON-dah CHOH-lah-poo-rahm, literally "the Chola city that took the Ganges") and built a second great temple there, the Brihadisvara Temple at Gangaikonda Cholapuram, completed around 1030.
The new temple was nearly as large as his father's at Thanjavur, with a slightly shorter but more decoratively elaborate vimana.
The campaign earned Rajendra the title Gangaikonda Chola ("Chola who took the Ganges"), one of the more memorable royal epithets of medieval India.
Rajendra's second great campaign was the naval expedition against Srivijaya around 1025 CE.
This is the famous one.
It is also one of the most extraordinary single military operations of the medieval world.

Srivijaya (sree-vee-JAH-yah) was a Buddhist maritime kingdom based in modern Sumatra (the great island in western Indonesia), with a capital probably at Palembang (PAH-lem-bang) and tributary control extending across the Strait of Malacca to the Malay Peninsula.

Srivijaya had been the dominant maritime trading power in Southeast Asia since the seventh century, controlling the strategic chokepoint between the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea through which all trade between India and China had to pass.
Their navy patrolled the Strait of Malacca and the surrounding waters; their customs revenues from merchants passing through the Strait were the foundation of the kingdom's wealth.
Srivijaya was, in commercial terms, in an awkward symbiotic relationship with the Cholas.

Tamil merchant guilds — most famously the Ainurruvar (eye-noo-ROO-var, "the Five Hundred"), a powerful merchant corporation operating across south India and Southeast Asia — used Srivijayan ports for their Bay of Bengal trade.
Chola diplomatic missions had visited Srivijaya in the early eleventh century.

The Srivijayan king had even, around 1005, sponsored the construction of a Buddhist temple at Nagapattinam (a Chola port on the Tamil coast) for the use of Buddhist pilgrims traveling between Sumatra and the south Indian Buddhist sites.
What turned this commercial partnership into war is unclear.
The Chola inscriptions are propagandistic and not specific about causes; the Srivijayan side of the story is poorly documented.

The most plausible reconstruction is that Srivijaya had begun extracting unfavorable tolls or trade restrictions from Tamil merchant guilds operating through the Strait of Malacca, and the Chola merchant community had requested royal intervention.
There may also have been a religious dimension — Srivijaya was Buddhist and the Cholas were Shaivite, and Rajendra's reign was generally a high-water mark of Shaivite triumphalism.
There was almost certainly also a sheer demonstration-of-power dimension.
Whatever the precipitating cause, around 1025, Rajendra dispatched a Chola war fleet across the Bay of Bengal to attack Srivijaya directly.

The expedition crossed approximately 1,200 nautical miles of open ocean — from the Tamil coast across to Sumatra — using monsoon wind patterns to make the crossing efficient. (The southwestern monsoon, blowing from late spring through early autumn, would carry sailing vessels eastward from India to Southeast Asia; the northeastern monsoon, blowing from late autumn through early spring, would carry them back.

Indian Ocean trade had used these wind patterns for over a millennium by Rajendra's time, but military expeditions of this scale were unprecedented.) The Chola fleet captured Palembang, took the Srivijayan king prisoner, looted the royal treasury, and then proceeded to attack a series of additional Srivijayan tributary ports along the Malay Peninsula and the Sumatran coast.
Chola inscriptions list fourteen captured cities, including modern Kedah in Malaysia and other ports across the region.
The expedition then returned home.
The Cholas did not attempt to permanently occupy Srivijayan territory — that would have required sustaining an army across an ocean indefinitely, which was logistically impossible.

What they accomplished was the demonstration of Chola naval power, the temporary disruption of Srivijayan trade dominance, and the establishment of a clear Chola sphere of commercial influence across the eastern Indian Ocean.
Tamil merchant guilds operated unimpeded in Southeast Asia for the next century.

Srivijaya recovered, but its dominance of the Strait of Malacca was permanently weakened, and successor states (the Khmer Empire on the mainland, Majapahit in Java) eventually absorbed the regional power.
The Chola raid on Srivijaya is the only confirmed pre-modern Indian transoceanic military expedition.
No other ancient or medieval Indian state attempted anything comparable.
The Mauryan, Gupta, and Mughal states all had powerful armies but never used them across open oceans on this scale.
Rajendra's expedition was, by some distance, the single most ambitious naval operation any Indian state ever conducted before the modern period.

The cross-civ comparison that helps is the Athenian Sicilian Expedition of 415 BCE — comparable in scale, comparable in ambition, comparable in the specific challenge of projecting force across open water — except that the Athenians lost catastrophically and the Cholas won.

The other comparison is the early-fifteenth-century voyages of Zheng He under the Ming dynasty (Ming Dynasty), which were larger in personnel and ship count but were primarily diplomatic missions, not military expeditions.
Rajendra's was a war fleet.
The Chola Empire continued to flourish for another century after Rajendra.

Kulottunga I (koo-LOT-toon-gah, ruled 1070–1122) — actually a member of the Eastern Chalukya dynasty who inherited the Chola throne by marriage — extended Chola influence into the Andhra region, sent diplomatic embassies to Song China in 1077 (Tang–Song Ch 4), and presided over a long, prosperous, generally peaceful reign that Chola inscriptions remember as a golden age.
The Tamil merchant guilds expanded their operations across maritime Southeast Asia.
The Chola bronze sculpture tradition reached its mature peak, producing the iconic Nataraja (Shiva as Lord of the Dance) bronzes that now grace museum collections on every continent.

But the long Chola decline began with Kulottunga's successors in the twelfth century, accelerated under chronic warfare with the rising Hoysalas of Karnataka, and was effectively complete by 1279, when the last Chola king Rajendra III was overthrown by the Pandyas of Madurai.

The Cholas were south India's first true empire and remained for centuries the cultural reference point — the standard by which subsequent Tamil dynasties (Vijayanagar, the Nayaks, the Marathas) measured themselves.

Their bronze sculptures, their Brihadeeswara Temple, their merchant guild networks, and their naval reach across the Bay of Bengal became foundational elements of the Tamil cultural imagination that persist into the present.

Cross-civ check: the Chola peak under Rajaraja and Rajendra (985–1044) overlaps with the Northern Song dynasty in China (Tang-Song Ch 5), which was the wealthiest contemporary power and the destination of Chola diplomatic missions.

It overlaps with the Norman Conquest of England (1066), with the First Crusade (1095–99, Byzantine Empire Ch 7 and Islamic Golden Age Ch 9), with the Pala-Sena transition in Bengal, with the Khmer Empire at Angkor under Suryavarman I and Suryavarman II (the latter would soon commission Angkor Wat), and with the Fatimid Caliphate in Cairo at its peak.

The eleventh century is one of the genuinely dense moments of medieval Eurasian history — Norman cathedrals going up in England, Romanesque temples in northern Europe, Brihadeeswara in Tamil Nadu, the Hagia Sophia mosaics in Constantinople, and Khmer Bayon-style temples in Cambodia all overlapping.
The medieval Chola world was not isolated.
It was part of a connected eleventh-century cosmopolis stretching from London to Phnom Penh.

chapters.title: Bhakti and the Temple Kingdoms
sentences: The Chola, Pratihara, Pala, and Rashtrakuta dynasties built the political frame.
What filled the frame was a religious and cultural transformation that reshaped Hindu practice across the subcontinent and produced most of the temples on modern tourist itineraries.

The transformation has two interrelated parts: the rise of the Bhakti (BHAHK-tee, literally "devotion") devotional movement, which reframed worship as personal love between devotee and deity, and the consolidation of the temple as the central institution of Indian religious, social, and economic life.

Both processes were underway throughout the medieval period; both reached their first peak in the seventh through twelfth centuries; both would shape Hindu religious practice from the medieval period to the present.

The Bhakti movement began in the Tamil south in the seventh century with two parallel groups of poet-saints: the Alvars (AHL-vahrz), twelve devotees of Vishnu, and the Nayanars (nah-yah-NAHRZ), sixty-three devotees of Shiva.

The two groups composed an enormous body of Tamil-language religious poetry between roughly 600 and 900 CE — the Vaishnava poetry collected in the Divya Prabandham (DIV-yah prah-BAHN-dahm, "Divine Compositions") and the Shaiva poetry collected in the Tirumurai (tih-roo-MOO-rai, "Sacred Texts").
The combined corpus runs to thousands of hymns.
It is one of the great corpora of religious literature in any language.
What made the Bhakti poetry distinctive — and revolutionary in the context of contemporary Hindu practice — was its theological stance.
Mainstream Hindu worship in the early medieval period was conducted primarily through priestly ritual.
Brahmin (BRAH-min) priests, the hereditary priestly caste, performed elaborate Sanskrit-language ceremonies on behalf of the laity, who attended but did not personally interact with the deity.
The deity was approached through ritual purity, correct procedure, prescribed offerings, and the mediating expertise of the priest.
Worship was a transactional relationship — you sponsored the ritual, the priest performed it, the deity received it, and merit accrued to you in measurable quantities.
The system was elaborate, expensive, and accessible primarily to the well-off.
The Bhakti poets attacked this entire framework.

Their poetry insisted that the deity was directly approachable by any devotee who loved him sincerely — without priestly mediation, without elaborate ritual, without Sanskrit learning, without caste qualifications.

The Tamil Alvar Nammalvar (NAHM-AHL-vahr, ninth century, the most important of the twelve Alvars) wrote thousands of verses in vernacular Tamil addressed directly to Vishnu in tones of intimate personal love — sometimes as a child to a parent, sometimes as a lover to a beloved, sometimes as a friend to a friend, sometimes as a devotee to a master.

The Shaiva Nayanar Sambandar (SAHM-bahn-dahr, seventh century) composed Tamil hymns to Shiva at hundreds of specific temple sites, recording his pilgrimages around the Tamil country and his personal devotional experiences at each.
The Bhakti poets did not deny that priestly ritual had value, but they insisted that personal devotion was the higher path and was available to anyone willing to cultivate it.
The most striking single example is Andal (AHN-dahl, ninth century), the only female Alvar.

Her two surviving works — the Tiruppavai (tih-roo-PAH-vai, a sequence of thirty Tamil hymns ostensibly describing a religious vow undertaken by young women in the month of Margali) and the Nachiar Tirumozhi (NAH-chee-yar tih-roo-MOH-zhee) — are sustained love poems addressed to Vishnu in the voice of a young woman who is in love with the deity and wishes to be married to him.

Tradition holds that Andal was so devoted to Vishnu that she refused all human husbands and was finally married to the deity directly at the temple of Srirangam (where the local tradition reports that her body merged into the deity's image).
The Tiruppavai is still recited every December in Tamil and Telugu temples; Andal is still considered, in the Sri Vaishnava tradition, one of the most exemplary devotees in all of religious history.
The Bhakti movement was therefore, among other things, an early egalitarian challenge to caste-bound religious hierarchy.
Several of the most important Bhakti poets came from low-caste backgrounds.

Tiruppan Alvar was a member of the Panar caste of bards (a low caste in the social hierarchy of medieval Tamil society), and his hymn praising Vishnu at Srirangam is one of the most cherished Vaishnava devotional texts.
Tirumular, the author of the great Shaiva work Tirumantiram, was a non-Brahmin sage.
Karaikkal Ammaiyar was a married woman who became a Shaiva ascetic.

The Bhakti tradition explicitly held that caste and gender were irrelevant to devotional capacity — the deity loved the devotee, not the social category. (This egalitarian dimension can be overstated.
The Bhakti movement did not actually overthrow caste, and many Bhakti traditions in subsequent centuries gradually accommodated themselves to caste hierarchy.

But the founding poetic moment was, on the surviving evidence, genuinely radical for its period, and this radical streak would continue to surface in Bhakti revivals through the medieval and early-modern periods.

The fifteenth-century weaver-saint Kabir in north India and the seventeenth-century cobbler-saint Ravidas are direct theological descendants of the early Tamil Bhakti tradition.) The Bhakti movement spread northward over centuries.

In Karnataka, the twelfth-century Lingayat (LIN-gah-yaht) tradition founded by Basava (BAH-sah-vah) carried Bhakti devotion into Kannada-language religious literature with a similarly egalitarian theological streak.

In Maharashtra, the thirteenth-century Varkari tradition (centered on the temple at Pandharpur and the saints Jnanadeva, Namdev, and later Tukaram) developed a Marathi-language devotional poetry around the deity Vithoba (a regional form of Krishna).
In Bengal, Jayadeva's twelfth-century Sanskrit poem Gita Govinda brought a fully developed Bhakti aesthetic into elite Sanskrit literature.
In north India proper, the medieval Bhakti tradition would later (fifteenth century onward) produce Mirabai of Rajasthan, Kabir of Banaras, Tulsidas of Awadh, and Surdas of Braj.
The vernacular devotional traditions of every Indian regional language ultimately trace back to the seventh-century Tamil beginning.
The other half of the medieval transformation was the consolidation of the temple as institution.
This is genuinely new in scale.
Vedic religion had no temples; worship was conducted at fire altars in open enclosures (Vedic Period Ch 3).
Buddhism worshipped at stupas (relic mounds) and in monastery compounds, not in temples in the later Hindu sense.
Early Hindu temples, from the Gupta era and earlier, were modest structures — single-cell sanctuaries with small porches, sometimes built of brick or wood and only later replaced with stone.
The really big temples — the multi-acre complexes with multiple sanctums, surrounding cloisters, ritual bathing tanks, processional halls, and elaborate towers — are a medieval-period development.
The medieval Indian temple, at its most fully realized form, is several institutions at once.
It is a religious sanctum.
The central garbhagriha ("womb-house") contains the principal deity image, accessed through specific ritual procedures by qualified priests.
Daily worship sequences (aratis, abhishekas, prasada distributions) follow procedures often documented in inscriptions on the temple walls.

Major festivals — the deity's birthday, the spring or autumn festivals tied to the agricultural calendar, the deity's processional outings on chariot-floats — bring tens or hundreds of thousands of pilgrims through the complex annually.
It is a major economic institution.
Royal endowments granted villages, lands, and revenue rights to support the temple's operations.

The temple paid for its own staff (priests, drummers, dancers, cooks, scribes, security, maintenance workers — sometimes hundreds of people), its own ritual supplies (flowers, food, oil, cloth, sandalwood, gold and silver vessels), and its own ongoing construction and repair.

Brihadeeswara Temple's inscriptions document the scale: roughly 600 personnel directly supported by the temple, 250 villages providing the supporting revenue, an annual budget on the order of tens of thousands of kalanjus of gold.
A medieval temple at this scale was operating a significant fraction of the local economy.
It is a community center.

The temple complex housed pilgrim hostels, kitchens that distributed food daily to pilgrims and the poor, schools for Brahmin students learning Sanskrit, music and dance schools for the temple's resident performers (the devadasis, female temple dancers — a deeply complicated medieval institution), and assembly halls for political and judicial proceedings.
Town meetings, royal proclamations, marriage ceremonies for the local elite, and major commercial transactions all happened at or near the temple.
It is a piece of dynastic propaganda.
The king who built the temple (or his descendants who completed it) expected the inscription on the entrance pylon to credit him by name.
The temple's tower, visible from miles away, was a permanent visual statement of royal piety and wealth.

Plundering or destroying an enemy's principal temple, or conversely sponsoring a major restoration after a victory, was understood across medieval India as an act of high political symbolism — the religious equivalent of capturing or recapturing a national capital.
The medieval temple was, in short, the central institution around which medieval Indian society organized itself.

The cathedral comparison from Western Europe is partly apt — the Gothic cathedrals were also religious-economic-civic institutions on a comparable scale — but the medieval Indian temple complex was usually denser in personnel, more economically productive, and more central to local political life than the European equivalent.

Brihadeeswara at Thanjavur, Khajuraho's Kandariya Mahadeva, the Lingaraja at Bhubaneswar, the Belur and Halebidu Hoysala temples — these are the institutions through which medieval Indian society lived.
The single best place to understand medieval temple architecture in concentrated form is Khajuraho (kah-joo-RAH-hoh), the Chandela dynasty's capital region in modern Madhya Pradesh.
The Chandelas built eighty-five temples at Khajuraho between roughly 950 and 1050 CE, of which about twenty-five survive in good condition.

They are the canonical examples of the Nagara north Indian temple style at its mature peak — a square sanctum surmounted by a curvilinear shikhara tower that rises in a single sweeping curve, often with smaller subsidiary towers (urusringas) clustered around the main one to create a mountain-like aggregate profile.
The largest and most accomplished of the Khajuraho temples is the Kandariya Mahadeva ("Cave-of-Shiva of the Great Lord"), built around 1030 CE under the Chandela king Vidyadhara.
It stands 102 feet tall.
Its central shikhara is composed of eighty-four miniature shikhara peaks aggregated into the main tower's profile, producing the characteristic visual effect of a stylized Himalayan mountain range.

Every external surface of the temple is densely covered with sculptural figures — gods, goddesses, attendant deities, celestial beings, dancers, animals, and (notoriously) the erotic sculptures that have given Khajuraho its global reputation.
The erotic sculptures are worth pausing on, because they have been the subject of more popular misunderstanding than almost any other aspect of medieval Indian art.
Approximately 10% of the Khajuraho external sculptures depict explicitly sexual scenes — couples, groups, sometimes elaborate compositions involving multiple figures and various coupling positions.
The remaining 90% of the sculptural program is religious iconography, divine attendants, courtly scenes, and decorative figures with no sexual content.

The erotic figures appear primarily on the external walls in specific architectural zones (most often around the entrance and on the southern face), not at the deity sanctum, and they share visual conventions with broader genres of medieval Indian sculpture that depict the full range of human experience.
The interpretive question is what these sculptures meant in their original religious-architectural context.
Multiple theories exist.

One emphasizes the Tantric current within medieval Hinduism, which held that the energies of human sexuality could be channeled toward spiritual realization through specific ritual practices — the erotic sculptures may depict the Tantric rituals or the metaphysical principles those rituals invoked.

A second emphasizes the auspiciousness of the sexual couple (maithuna) in Hindu iconographic tradition, which long predates Khajuraho — the union of male and female principles is an ancient Hindu symbolic frame for cosmic creativity, and erotic figures appear on Hindu temples back to the early medieval period as auspicious motifs.

A third emphasizes the broader medieval Indian literary tradition of treating sexual pleasure as one of the four legitimate goals of human life (the others being dharma — moral duty; artha — material prosperity; and moksha — spiritual liberation; together called the purusharthas).
Sexual desire was a religiously sanctioned dimension of human experience, and depicting it was not regarded as obscene in the medieval framework.

The Vatsyayana Kama Sutra had been composed in the Gupta era as a serious technical treatise on these matters (Gupta Empire Ch 5), and its assumptions about the legitimacy of erotic life were broadly shared in medieval literate culture.
What is clear is that the Khajuraho sculptures were not regarded as transgressive by their original Chandela patrons.
They were carved openly, on the most prestigious temples in the dynasty's capital, by master sculptors working in standard workshops, with the full sponsorship of the ruling family.

Whatever embarrassment the sculptures have caused subsequent observers (especially during the British colonial period, when Victorian moralism collided abruptly with medieval Indian sculptural traditions and produced both prurient fascination and considerable censorship) is a function of those later observers, not of the medieval understanding.
The Khajuraho temples are a UNESCO World Heritage site.
Like Brihadeeswara, they are still actively used for Hindu worship and are accessible for tourists today.
They are also, despite the dramatic external sculpture, primarily experienced as serious religious monuments by the great majority of pilgrims who visit them.
The other great medieval temple-building dynasties of north and central India deserve at least brief mention.

The Eastern Ganga dynasty of Kalinga (modern Odisha) built the great temples on the Bay of Bengal coast — the Lingaraja at Bhubaneswar (eleventh century, the largest medieval temple in eastern India), the Jagannath Temple at Puri (twelfth century, one of the most sacred Hindu pilgrimage sites in eastern India), and the spectacular Sun Temple at Konark (mid-thirteenth century, just past the medieval period proper, but the climactic work of the Kalinga temple tradition).

The Konark Sun Temple was built by King Narasimhadeva I as a colossal stone chariot of the sun god Surya — twelve carved wheels representing the months of the year, seven horses representing the days of the week, and a sanctum that originally rose perhaps 230 feet before its tower collapsed in unclear circumstances centuries later.

The temple's surviving sculptural program is one of the great achievements of medieval Indian art, and the partial ruin (the main tower is gone, but the assembly hall, the carved wheels, the sun god statues, and the elaborate external sculpture all survive) is one of the most photographed structures in India.
UNESCO World Heritage.
The Hoysala dynasty of southern Karnataka (eleventh through thirteenth centuries) built their characteristic star-shaped sanctuaries with dense soapstone friezes covering every external surface.

The most famous Hoysala temples — Chennakesava at Belur (consecrated 1117 by King Vishnuvardhana to commemorate his military victory over the Cholas), Hoysaleswara at Halebidu (twelfth century, the dynasty's grandest temple), and Keshava at Somnathpur (1268, the most complete surviving Hoysala temple) — are the most ornately sculptured medieval Indian buildings, with thousands of figures carved into each square meter of external surface using the soft locally-quarried soapstone that allowed extraordinary fineness of detail.

The Chaulukyas of Gujarat sponsored the marble-clad Dilwara temples on Mount Abu — five Jain temples built between roughly 1031 and the thirteenth century, the most important being the Vimal Vasahi (built 1031 under the merchant-minister Vimal Shah) and the Luna Vasahi (built 1230).
The Dilwara temples are technically Jain rather than Hindu, but they belong to the same medieval tradition of dynastic temple sponsorship and architectural elaboration.

Their interior carving — every column, ceiling panel, and door frame densely worked with detailed figural and floral sculpture in white marble — is, by general consensus, the most exquisitely refined stonework of medieval India.
The Western Chalukyas of Kalyani (Chapter 4) developed the Vesara hybrid style at sites including the great temple at Lakkundi in modern Karnataka.
Their work was the immediate aesthetic predecessor of the Hoysala style.

In the deep south, the Pandyas continued building and rebuilding the Madurai Meenakshi Temple complex through the medieval period (most of the visible structure today is later, especially Nayak-era from the seventeenth century, but the medieval Pandya phases established the basic plan and dedicated the temple to the goddess Meenakshi as the principal local form of the divine).

The Sri Ranganathaswamy Temple at Srirangam (an island in the Cauvery River near modern Tiruchirappalli, the most important Vaishnava pilgrimage site in south India) was developed across centuries by the Cholas, Pandyas, and Vijayanagar dynasties into one of the largest temple complexes in the world by area.
This is, taken together, the visual signature of medieval India.
Almost every large stone temple you can see in a tourist photograph today is medieval.

The temple-building tradition continued under later dynasties (Vijayanagar in the south through the sixteenth century, the Nayaks in the seventeenth, various smaller polities into the eighteenth) but the core of the tradition — the developed architectural styles, the elaborate sculptural programs, the institutional template of the temple-as-economic-and-civic-center — is medieval.
Cross-civ check: the temple-building peak of medieval India (~950–1250) overlaps almost exactly with the Romanesque and early Gothic cathedral-building eras in Western Europe.
Speyer Cathedral was completed around 1060.
The Cluny Abbey reached its largest extent around 1100.
Saint-Denis (the first true Gothic) was begun in 1135.
Notre-Dame de Paris was begun in 1163.
Chartres was rebuilt after 1194.
Salisbury Cathedral was begun in 1220.

The architectural monumentalism of the high medieval period is global — Hindu India, Catholic Europe, Buddhist Burma (Pagan), and Khmer Cambodia (Angkor) are all building extraordinary religious monuments simultaneously, with no causal connection between them but with strikingly similar institutional logics.
Religious monumentalism was, apparently, what state-sponsored civilizations produced as their characteristic high-medieval cultural artifact.

chapters.title: Vedanta, Jainism, and the Slow Disappearance of Buddhism
sentences: The medieval period was the great age of Indian philosophical synthesis.

Three philosophers — Adi Shankara in the eighth century, Ramanuja in the late eleventh and early twelfth, and Madhva in the late thirteenth — each built a complete metaphysical system out of the older Upanishadic and Vedic textual tradition (Vedic Period Ch 5), and the systems they built defined the dominant strand of Hindu intellectual life for the next millennium and beyond.
In parallel, Jainism flourished under royal patronage in Karnataka and Gujarat, producing some of the most refined religious literature and architecture of the period.
And Buddhism, the religion that had defined Indian intellectual life for fifteen centuries, slowly disappeared from the land of its birth.
This chapter is mostly about ideas.
The architecture and the politics happen in adjacent chapters; this one is the philosophical heart of the medieval Indian world.
To understand what Shankara and his successors were doing, you have to understand what they were inheriting.
The core texts of mainstream medieval Hindu philosophy were a body of writings called the Vedanta (veh-DAHN-tah, literally "end of the Vedas").

The texts have three primary sources, called collectively the prasthanatrayi ("triple foundation"): The Upanishads (oo-PAH-nih-shahdz), a body of philosophical dialogues composed between roughly 800 and 200 BCE, in the late Vedic and post-Vedic Period (Vedic Period Ch 5).

The Upanishads explore questions about the nature of ultimate reality (Brahman, brah-MAHN, the cosmic principle underlying all existence), the nature of the individual self (Atman, AHT-mahn), and the relationship between them.

The major Upanishads — the Brihadaranyaka, the Chandogya, the Katha, the Mundaka, the Mandukya, and others — contain some of the deepest and most sophisticated philosophical writing of the ancient world, and they are open-ended enough that they can be read in support of multiple theological positions.

The Bhagavad Gita (BHAH-gah-vad GEE-tah, "Song of the Lord"), an interpolated philosophical episode in the Mahabharata epic, composed in roughly its present form between the second century BCE and the second century CE (Post-Maurya Kingdoms Ch 1).

The Gita is a long dialogue between the warrior-prince Arjuna and his charioteer Krishna (who is revealed mid-dialogue to be the supreme deity in human form) on questions of ethical action, devotion, and ultimate liberation.
Like the Upanishads, the Gita is open enough to support multiple theological readings.

The Brahma Sutras (BRAH-mah SOO-trahz), a terse and highly compressed text of 555 aphorisms attributed to a sage named Badarayana (bah-DAH-rah-yah-nah), probably composed between the second century BCE and the fourth century CE, that attempts to systematize the philosophical content of the Upanishads.

The Brahma Sutras are so terse that they are essentially unreadable without a commentary — and the commentaries on the Brahma Sutras by later Vedanta philosophers became the canonical statements of the rival philosophical schools.

What the medieval Vedanta philosophers did was write commentaries on these three foundational sources, each commentator arguing that his interpretation was the correct one and the rivals' interpretations were wrong.
The commentaries are book-length philosophical treatises in their own right.
The interpretive disagreements among them turn out to involve some of the deepest questions about the nature of reality, the self, and the divine that any philosophical tradition has ever addressed.
Adi Shankara (AH-dee SHAHN-kah-rah) was the first and most consequential of the medieval Vedanta commentators.

He lived for about thirty-two years — the traditional dates are 788–820 CE, though the actual dates have been debated and an alternative dating to the early seventh century has been argued by some scholars.
He was born in Kalady in Kerala, traveled across India debating philosophical opponents, and died at Kedarnath in the Himalayan foothills.
His philosophical position is called Advaita Vedanta (ad-VAI-tah veh-DAHN-tah, literally "non-dual Vedanta").
The core claim is that Brahman (ultimate reality) and Atman (the individual self) are not two but one.

The apparent multiplicity of the world — the apparent existence of separate selves, separate objects, separate processes — is a kind of cognitive illusion (maya, MAH-yah, "illusion" or more technically "superimposition") that arises from ignorance (avidya, ah-VID-yah, "non-knowledge").
When the underlying ignorance is overcome, the apparent multiplicity is recognized as illusory and the underlying unity is realized directly.

Liberation (moksha, MOH-kshah, "release") is not a state attained by ritual or by accumulating merit but a recognition of what has always been the case — the individual self is, and always was, identical with ultimate reality.
This is a radical position.

It implies that the world we ordinarily experience — with its distinct objects, its causation, its time and space — has only a kind of provisional or pragmatic reality, like the apparent existence of a snake when you misperceive a coiled rope in dim light.
The snake never existed; you just thought it did.
Similarly, on Shankara's reading, the multiplicity of the world never existed in the deepest sense; we just thought it did because we were ignorant.

It is also a position that aligns Shankara with certain strands of Mahayana Buddhism — particularly the Madhyamaka ("middle way") school developed by Nagarjuna (nah-GAHR-joo-nah) in the second century CE (Post-Maurya Kingdoms Ch 5), which had argued that all phenomena are empty of inherent existence (shunyata, SHOON-yah-tah).
Shankara's Hindu critics, both in his own time and afterwards, accused him of being a "crypto-Buddhist" — taking Madhyamaka conclusions and dressing them in Vedantic language.
Shankara's response was that he was correctly interpreting the Upanishads, which had said all this long before the Buddhists got around to it.

The accusation is interesting partly because Shankara's philosophical maturity coincided with the late phase of organized Indian Buddhism and may have contributed to Buddhism's eventual absorption into Hindu philosophical frameworks.

On Shankara's reading, the Buddhists had been roughly right about the illusory nature of conventional reality but had drawn the wrong final conclusion (annihilation rather than identity with Brahman).
Hinduism could thus claim everything Buddhism had to offer and more.
Shankara's other contributions were institutional.

He founded four monastic centers (mathas, MAH-thahz) at the four geographic corners of India: Sringeri in the south (Karnataka), Dvaraka in the west (Gujarat), Jagannath Puri in the east (Odisha), and Jyotirmath in the north (Uttarakhand).

The four mathas continue to operate today and are headed by lineal successors of Shankara called Shankaracharyas, who function as the highest religious authorities of the Smarta Brahmin tradition that traces itself to Shankara.
The four-corner placement of the mathas was deliberate symbolic geography: it made the institutional Vedanta tradition pan-Indian rather than regional.

Shankara also reformed the practice of Hindu monasticism by establishing the Dashanami (dah-shah-NAH-mee, "ten names") order of Hindu sannyasis (renouncers) — providing an organized structure for Hindu monastics that paralleled the Buddhist sangha and that gave Hinduism a permanent institutional monastic presence it had previously lacked.
The Dashanamis still exist; they are a major component of the Hindu religious establishment.
Shankara is, by some distance, the most consequential Indian philosopher of the medieval period.
The intellectual framework he built has remained the dominant theoretical position in Hindu philosophical discussions for over a thousand years.
When modern Indians think about the relationship between the individual soul and the divine, they are usually working — knowingly or not — within Shankara's framework.

The first major reaction against Shankara came from Ramanuja (rah-MAH-noo-jah, ~1077–1157 CE), the great philosopher of the Sri Vaishnava (shree VAI-shnah-vah) tradition, based at the temple at Srirangam in the Tamil south.
Ramanuja was uncomfortable with Shankara's monism for both theological and devotional reasons.

Theologically, he did not accept that the apparent multiplicity of the world was illusory; he thought the world was real, that individual souls were real, that God was real, and that they were all in genuine relationship to each other rather than collapsing into a single undifferentiated unity.
Devotionally — and Ramanuja was a leading inheritor of the Tamil Bhakti tradition (Chapter 6) — he thought Shankara's framework eliminated the possibility of love between devotee and deity.

If the devotee and the deity are ultimately identical (as Shankara held), then the love is in some sense self-love, and the rich devotional tradition of the Alvars and Nayanars becomes a temporary stage on the path to a final non-dual realization rather than the ultimate goal in itself.
Ramanuja's alternative position is called Vishishtadvaita (vih-shish-tahd-VAI-tah, "qualified non-dualism").

He held that ultimate reality is the personal God Vishnu, that individual souls are real and distinct from God but eternally united with him in the way attributes are united with a substance, and that liberation consists not of dissolving into Brahman but of an eternal devotional relationship between the individual soul and Vishnu.

The technical metaphysics is dense — Ramanuja worked out elaborate accounts of the relationship between God, souls, and matter that read as serious philosophical treatises — but the practical upshot is that personal devotion to a personal deity is the highest spiritual path, and that the personal devotee retains his or her individuality eternally rather than dissolving into divine unity.

Ramanuja's philosophical school provided the intellectual foundation for the Vaishnava devotional tradition that has flourished across south India ever since — and that would later spread to north India through later Vaishnava saints (Chaitanya in fifteenth-century Bengal, the various Krishna-bhakti movements of the medieval and early-modern Hindi-speaking regions).
Most modern Indian religious practice that emphasizes personal devotion to a personal deity is operating within a theological framework Ramanuja systematized.
The third great medieval Vedanta philosopher was Madhvacharya (MAHD-vah-CHAR-yah, ~1238–1317 CE), who took the reaction against Shankara even further than Ramanuja had.
Madhva was based at Udupi in coastal Karnataka and founded the school called Dvaita Vedanta (DVAI-tah, "dualist Vedanta").
His position was that God (Vishnu), individual souls, and the material world are three permanently distinct categories of reality — the strict opposite of Shankara's monism.
Souls and God are eternally distinct; souls do not become God under any circumstances; salvation consists of the soul's eternal blissful subordination to God, never of identification with God.
Even in liberation, the boundary between divine and human remains absolute.
Madhva was also the only major Indian philosopher to systematically reject the doctrine that all souls are ultimately destined for liberation.
He argued, controversially, that some souls are eternally damned — destined for a kind of ongoing hell — and that liberation is not universally available.

This is closer to certain strands of Christian theology than to mainstream Hindu thought, and the parallel has not gone unnoticed. (Some scholars have argued for direct Christian influence on Madhva via the Syriac Christian community on the Malabar coast, though the evidence is circumstantial.

Most scholars now think Madhva developed the position independently.) The Madhva tradition centered on Udupi remains the third major Vedanta school, less widespread than the Shankara or Ramanuja schools but very influential in coastal Karnataka and parts of the Marathi-speaking region.
Together, Shankara, Ramanuja, and Madhva constitute the three great medieval Vedanta schools.
They span the full philosophical spectrum from radical monism to radical dualism, with Ramanuja's qualified non-dualism in the middle.

They define the conceptual landscape that Indian philosophical discussion has inhabited ever since, and the language they developed — Brahman and Atman, maya and avidya, jiva and Ishvara, dvaita and advaita — is the standard vocabulary of Hindu metaphysical discourse to this day.
In parallel with the Vedanta schools, Jainism flourished under royal patronage across medieval Karnataka and Gujarat.

Jainism is one of the ancient Indian religious traditions, founded (in the standard narrative) by Mahavira in the sixth century BCE — roughly contemporary with the Buddha — though Jain tradition holds that Mahavira was the twenty-fourth and last in a long line of teachers (tirthankaras, "ford-makers") stretching back into mythological antiquity.

Jainism's distinctive doctrines include: A radical commitment to non-violence (ahimsa, ah-HIM-sah), extending not just to humans and animals but to insects and (in some Jain traditions) even microscopic organisms.

Strict Jain monks sweep the path before them as they walk to avoid stepping on insects, strain water before drinking to avoid swallowing tiny organisms, and (in the strictest tradition) eat no root vegetables because pulling them up kills the plant.
A doctrine of karma as a quasi-physical substance that adheres to the soul and weighs it down — reincarnation continues until karma is purged through ascetic discipline.

Liberation is achieved by burning off accumulated karma through extreme asceticism, especially fasting (in the most extreme Jain tradition, sallekhana, the ritual death by fasting at the end of life).

A pluralistic epistemology (anekantavada, ah-NEH-kahn-tah-VAH-dah, "the doctrine of many-sidedness") that holds that reality is too complex to be captured by any single perspective — multiple partial views can each be valid in their own context.

Jainism split early in its history into two main branches: the Digambara (dig-AHM-bah-rah, "sky-clad") branch, whose male monks practice nudity as a form of detachment from possessions; and the Shvetambara (shveh-TAHM-bah-rah, "white-clad") branch, whose monks wear white robes.

The two branches differ on doctrinal points (the Digambaras hold that women cannot achieve liberation in their current bodies; the Shvetambaras disagree) and operate on largely separate territorial bases.
The Digambaras predominated in Karnataka and central India; the Shvetambaras predominated in Gujarat, Rajasthan, and the western Indian merchant communities.
Throughout the medieval period, Jainism flourished under the patronage of regional dynasties whose courts were sympathetic.

The Western Ganga dynasty of Karnataka was the most important Digambara patron — under their minister Chamundaraya, the Gomateshwara monolithic statue of the Jain saint Bahubali was carved at Shravanabelagola (shrah-vah-nah-bel-LAH-go-lah) in 981 CE.
The statue stands 57 feet tall, carved from a single granite block, and is the tallest free-standing monolithic statue in India.
The ritual bathing of the statue (Mahamastakabhisheka) is held once every twelve years and remains one of the most spectacular religious events in modern India.
The Hoysalas continued Western Ganga patronage of Jainism in Karnataka.

The Chaulukyas of Gujarat heavily patronized Shvetambara Jainism — most importantly through the Dilwara temples on Mount Abu (Chapter 6), the most exquisitely refined Jain temple architecture anywhere.
The Chaulukya minister Vimal Shah built the first of the Dilwara temples in 1031 CE; subsequent temples in the complex were funded by other Jain merchant patrons through the medieval period.
