Jainism's medieval flourishing was helped by its strong association with the merchant class.

Jain ethical doctrines — non-violence, vegetarianism, business honesty, frugality, charitable giving — produced a distinctive merchant culture that accumulated capital efficiently and reinvested it in temple sponsorship and community charity.
The Jain merchant communities of Gujarat and Rajasthan would become, over subsequent centuries, the most economically sophisticated trading networks in India.
Modern Indian commercial dynasties from the Marwari Jain trading families to the Birlas and the Adanis trace their commercial cultures back to medieval Jain origins.
And then there was Buddhism, slowly disappearing.
The disappearance of Buddhism from India is one of the genuinely puzzling phenomena of medieval Indian history.
Buddhism had been the dominant religious tradition of north India through the Maurya, Kushan, and Gupta periods.
The great Buddhist monastic universities at Nalanda, Vikramashila, and Odantapuri operated continuously through the entire medieval period until the Turkic destruction around 1200.
Chinese pilgrims (Faxian in the early fifth century, Xuanzang in the seventh, Yijing in the late seventh, Wu Kong in the eighth) all reported flourishing Buddhist communities across north India.
The Pala dynasty patronized Mahayana Buddhism on a massive scale through the entire ninth, tenth, and eleventh centuries.
And yet by 1300 CE, Buddhism had effectively vanished from India.
A handful of small Buddhist communities persisted in the Himalayan foothills (where Tibetan Buddhism was a continuing presence) and along parts of the Bay of Bengal coast.
The major monasteries were gone.
The lay Buddhist community had been reabsorbed into Hindu practice.
The religion that had defined Indian intellectual life for fifteen centuries was no longer a significant presence in the subcontinent.
Multiple factors contributed, in proportions historians still debate: Royal patronage shift.
As medieval kings shifted their religious sponsorship from monasteries to temples, the financial foundation of organized Buddhism eroded.

Buddhist monasteries had depended on royal endowments to support their large monastic populations; without continuing royal sponsorship, the monastic establishments shrank and their intellectual leadership migrated elsewhere (most importantly to Tibet, where the Buddhism-centered political establishment was happy to receive Indian scholars).
Pala royal patronage kept eastern Indian Buddhism alive into the eleventh and twelfth centuries; with the Pala collapse, the patronage collapsed too.
Hindu philosophical absorption.
Shankara's Advaita Vedanta absorbed many of the philosophical positions Buddhism had developed, in a Hindu theological framework that did not require separation from the broader Hindu tradition.

A medieval Indian intellectual interested in Madhyamaka-style emptiness or Yogacara-style consciousness analysis could increasingly find versions of those ideas inside Hindu Vedanta, without needing to commit to the institutional Buddhist sangha.
This made the philosophical contribution of Indian Buddhism less distinctive over time and reduced the intellectual incentive to maintain Buddhist institutional identity.
Devotional competition.

The rise of Hindu Bhakti devotional traditions (Chapter 6) provided ordinary lay people with intensely personal religious experiences that Buddhist monasticism, focused on monastic practice and philosophical study, could not match.

The Buddhist lay community had always been dependent on the monastic community for its religious framework; when the monastic community shrank, the lay community had nowhere natural to go except into the increasingly devotional Hindu tradition.
The Turkic destruction.
The final blow came in the early thirteenth century when Bakhtiyar Khalji's Turkic cavalry overran Bihar and Bengal around 1200–1205 (Chapter 8).
Khalji's army destroyed Nalanda, Vikramashila, and Odantapuri, killing the resident monks and burning the libraries.
The Persian historian Minhaj-i Siraj reports the destruction of Nalanda in detail.

The Tibetan historian Taranatha, writing centuries later but using earlier sources, gives an even fuller account of the Buddhist religious establishment being systematically wiped out across eastern India.

The intellectual leadership of Indian Buddhism had been concentrated in these few major institutions; their physical destruction without functioning patron-states to rebuild them was the death blow to organized Buddhism in the subcontinent.
After 1200, what was left of Indian Buddhism gradually faded out.
Some monks fled to Tibet and Nepal, carrying the Sanskrit Buddhist textual tradition with them.
Some lay communities continued for several generations in attenuated form.

By 1500 CE, Buddhism had essentially vanished as a significant presence in India, surviving only in the Himalayan border regions where it would later be assimilated into Tibetan Buddhism's mature institutional form.
The religion that India had given to the world had stopped being practiced in any substantial form at home.
The cross-civ irony is striking.

Indian Buddhism survived everywhere it had been transplanted — Sri Lanka, Tibet, China, Korea, Japan, Vietnam, Cambodia, Burma, Thailand, and the Indonesian islands — and disappeared only in the land of its origin.
The land that produced Buddhism became, by 1500, the only major Asian civilization without a significant Buddhist presence.
Modern Indian Buddhism (the Dalit Buddhist movement founded by B.
Ambedkar in 1956, which converted millions of Dalits to a renewed Buddhism in protest against caste oppression) is a twentieth-century revival, not a continuous tradition.
A final note on medieval Indian science.

The Gupta-era mathematical tradition (Aryabhata, the decimal place-value system, the concept of zero) continued through the medieval period, extended by a series of remarkable mathematician-astronomers based at the Ujjain observatory in central India.

The most important medieval figure is Bhaskara II (BHAH-skah-rah, also called Bhaskaracharya, 1114–1185 CE), whose Siddhanta Shiromani ("Crown Jewel of Mathematical Treatises," 1150) is the most sophisticated medieval Indian mathematical-astronomical work.

Bhaskara II worked out principles of differential calculus several centuries before Newton and Leibniz — including a recognition that the rate of change of a function at a point can be defined as the limit of an average rate of change as the interval shrinks toward zero, and an early version of what would later be called Rolle's Theorem.
He computed the length of the sidereal year (the time for the Earth to complete one orbit relative to the fixed stars) to within minutes of the modern value.
He posed and solved problems in indeterminate equations (Diophantine equations) that European mathematicians would not match until the seventeenth century.
His textbook Lilavati ("Lila," named for his daughter), written in elegant Sanskrit verse, became the standard arithmetic textbook of medieval and early-modern India.
The cumulative achievement of medieval Indian mathematics was substantial.

The decimal place-value numeral system, including the symbol for zero as a number rather than just a placeholder, was passed to the Arab world through Persian polymaths like al-Khwarizmi (al-KWAH-riz-mee, ~825 CE, the Khwarazmian mathematician at the Abbasid court who wrote the first systematic Arabic treatise on Indian arithmetic — Islamic Golden Age Ch 3). al-Khwarizmi called the system "Hindi numerals" and credited the Indian source.

Arab mathematicians extended and refined the system; eventually it was passed from Arabic to Latin Europe (largely through the Italian mathematician Fibonacci in the early thirteenth century and his Liber Abaci of 1202), where Europeans called the digits "Arabic numerals" because they had received them from Arabic translations.
The Indians had been writing them this way since the Gupta era and refining them continuously throughout the medieval period.

This is one of the largest cross-civilizational intellectual debts in world history, and it is recognized in the modern formal name of the system — Hindu-Arabic numerals — even though the everyday English usage just says "Arabic numerals" and forgets the Indian source.
The number you use to count, to measure, to do arithmetic, to write programs, to do science, is in its essential structure a medieval Indian invention.

Cross-civ check: the Vedanta synthesis happened simultaneously with the Scholastic synthesis in Western Europe (Anselm in the eleventh century, Thomas Aquinas in the thirteenth) and with the Islamic philosophical synthesis (al-Ghazali in the late eleventh century, Ibn Rushd in the twelfth — Islamic Golden Age Ch 5).

All three civilizational traditions were doing the same fundamental work in the same era: taking inherited philosophical and scriptural materials and building rigorous systematic interpretations that would define their respective intellectual landscapes for centuries afterward.
The medieval Indian Vedanta tradition is part of the same global eleventh-thirteenth-century philosophical moment as Scholasticism in Paris and Falsafa in Cordoba.

chapters.title: The Ghaznavid and Ghurid Invasions
sentences: The medieval period that this book has been describing — six and a half centuries of regional Hindu kingdoms, monumental temple architecture, devotional poetry, and philosophical synthesis — ended in a series of military defeats spread across two centuries.
The first wave came under Mahmud of Ghazni in the early eleventh century.
The second and decisive wave came under Muhammad of Ghor in the late twelfth.
By 1206, when Qutb al-Din Aibak proclaimed himself sultan at Lahore, north India was under Turkic Muslim rule and the Delhi Sultanate was beginning.
The medieval Hindu period was over.
This is one of the genuine watersheds of Indian history.

From 1206 forward, the political dominance of north India would belong to Muslim-ruled imperial states for the next seven centuries — first the Delhi Sultanate (Delhi Sultanate Ch 1), then the Mughal Empire (Mughal Empire Ch 1), and after the Mughal collapse in the eighteenth century, the British East India Company, which inherited and modified the institutional frameworks the Mughals had built.

Hindu political power did not disappear — the Vijayanagar Empire dominated the south through the fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries, the Marathas built a major regional empire in the seventeenth and eighteenth, and various smaller Hindu kingdoms persisted across the subcontinent throughout the period — but the dominant imperial state was, from 1206 onward, no longer Hindu.
How this transition happened is the subject of this chapter.
To understand the Turkic invasions, you have to understand what Central Asia had become by the year 1000.

The story starts in the eighth and ninth centuries, when the Abbasid caliphate, recognizing that its native Arab armies were insufficient to defend the empire's enormous territories, began purchasing Turkic slave-soldiers (ghulams or mamluks) from the steppe peoples north of Khorasan.
These Turkic soldiers were converted to Islam, trained from childhood in royal military service, and proved spectacularly effective on the battlefield.
The Abbasids built up substantial Turkic military elites who, over generations, became the dominant power in the eastern caliphate.
By the late ninth and tenth centuries, regional governors of Turkic origin were establishing semi-independent states across the eastern Islamic world.
The most successful of these was the Samanid dynasty, which ruled most of Khorasan and Transoxiana from the late ninth through the late tenth century with a sophisticated court at Bukhara.
When the Samanids weakened in the late tenth century, their Turkic generals seized power.

Sebuktigin (sah-BOOK-tih-gin, ruled 977–997), a Turkic former Samanid slave-soldier who had risen to become governor of the city of Ghazni (GHAZ-nee, in modern eastern Afghanistan), declared himself an independent sultan and founded the Ghaznavid dynasty.
His son Mahmud of Ghazni (mah-MOOD, ruled 998–1030) inherited the dynasty and made it briefly the most powerful state in the eastern Islamic world.
Mahmud's military project had two phases.
The first was consolidating his control of Khorasan, eastern Iran, and parts of Central Asia — defeating his various Samanid and Karakhanid rivals and incorporating their territories.
The second was systematic raiding into northern India.
He conducted seventeen raids into India between 1001 and 1027 CE.
The raids were not attempts at permanent conquest.
They were, explicitly, extraction operations.

Mahmud would assemble a mounted army in the autumn (after the monsoon rains had ended and the rivers had subsided), march down through the Khyber Pass and across the Punjab, attack a series of targets — usually wealthy Hindu temples or Rajput capitals — for several months, accumulate as much portable wealth as possible (gold, silver, jewels, slaves), and march back to Ghazni before the next monsoon.

The raids generated enormous wealth, which Mahmud spent on building a magnificent capital at Ghazni and patronizing the great Persian poet Ferdowsi (fer-DOW-see) and the polymath scholar al-Biruni (more on whom shortly).
The most famous of the raids was the 1025 sack of Somnath.

The Somnath Temple (SOM-nahth) was the great Shiva temple on the Saurashtra peninsula of modern Gujarat, perched on the Arabian Sea coast and dedicated to Shiva in his form as Somnatha, "lord of the moon." It was one of the twelve jyotirlingas — the twelve most sacred Shiva pilgrimage sites in India — and one of the wealthiest Hindu temples in the subcontinent, accumulated through centuries of pilgrim donations and royal endowments.

The temple was a major economic institution: Arab and Persian travelers' accounts describe it as housing thousands of Brahmin priests, hundreds of dancers (the temple devadasis), a substantial treasury, and a constant flow of pilgrims from across north India.
Mahmud reached Somnath in early 1025, at the head of an army of perhaps 30,000 cavalry, after a difficult march across the Thar Desert.
The defending Hindu force was reportedly substantial — the local Chaulukya king Bhima I and his allies fielded tens of thousands of soldiers — but the defense was inadequately organized.
Mahmud's army assaulted the temple, broke through the outer defenses, and sacked the inner sanctum.
Persian sources describe Mahmud personally smashing the central Shiva lingam with his sword.

The destruction of the lingam was a deliberately symbolic act — Hindu sources record that Mahmud's army then carried away the temple's accumulated treasure, including reportedly several thousand pounds of gold and silver, and sold tens of thousands of captured pilgrims and temple personnel into slavery.
The 1025 sack became one of the most traumatic episodes in subsequent Hindu memory.
It would be invoked over and over across the next thousand years as the foundational image of Muslim violence against Hindu sacred sites.

The temple was rebuilt by the Chaulukyas after Mahmud withdrew; it was sacked again by Alauddin Khalji's army in 1297, rebuilt; sacked by Aurangzeb in 1665, rebuilt; and most recently rebuilt in 1951 after Indian independence as a deliberate act of national-religious affirmation.
The current Somnath Temple is the seventh or eighth structure on the site, depending on how you count.
The historical complexity that subsequent Hindu nationalist narratives have flattened is real, however.

Mahmud's raids were not motivated by religious ideology in the simple sense — he raided for treasure, and any wealthy Hindu temple was a worthwhile target whether or not the religious symbolism was particularly charged.
He also raided wealthy Muslim cities in eastern Iran when they were politically expedient targets.

His court patronized Persian poetry that included substantial Hindu mythological content (Ferdowsi's Shahnameh contains pre-Islamic Iranian material that overlaps with Indian mythological material in ways that Ferdowsi did not censor).

And the Hindu communities Mahmud raided rebuilt rather than fled — Somnath's continuous reconstruction across a thousand years is, in its way, evidence of religious resilience as much as of religious vulnerability.
What Mahmud's seventeen raids did decisively accomplish was the demonstration that Hindu north India was militarily vulnerable to organized Turkic cavalry.
The regional Rajput kingdoms — Chandelas, Chaulukyas, Paramaras, Chauhans — could fight off small raiding parties but could not coordinate against systematic invasions.
The political fragmentation that the Tripartite Struggle had produced (Chapter 4) had not been corrected.
The military lesson of the Mahmud raids was registered.
The implications would be drawn out a century and a half later by Muhammad of Ghor.

Before we get to Muhammad of Ghor, the figure of al-Biruni (al-bee-ROO-nee, 973–1048 CE) deserves attention, because he is the most thoughtful outside observer of medieval Indian civilization that any source produced.
Abu al-Rayhan al-Biruni was a Khwarazmian polymath — that is, from the region of Khwarazm in modern Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan — born in the city of Kath in 973 CE.

He was a mathematician, astronomer, geographer, ethnographer, comparative religionist, and historian, and he was unusual among medieval scholars for working seriously across all of these fields rather than specializing in one.
He had been a court scholar under several Khwarazmian and Central Asian dynasties before being captured by Mahmud of Ghazni when Mahmud annexed Khwarazm around 1017.
Al-Biruni was brought back to Ghazni essentially as a prize — Mahmud had a habit of collecting talented intellectuals from his conquests — and made a court astronomer.
What al-Biruni did with his Ghazni captivity was learn Sanskrit.

He spent years studying with Indian scholars (some of them captured during Mahmud's raids), traveled extensively in northwestern India during periods when the Ghaznavid army was campaigning there, read the Indian astronomical and mathematical literature in the original Sanskrit, and eventually wrote — around 1030 CE, the year of Mahmud's death — the book that became his masterpiece on Indian civilization.
The book is called Kitab fi Tahqiq ma li-l-Hind ("Book of Verifying What India Has," usually called Tarikh al-Hind, "History of India," in shortened form).
The Tarikh al-Hind is one of the most remarkable works of medieval cross-cultural scholarship.

Al-Biruni systematically describes Indian religion, philosophy, astronomy, mathematics, geography, social customs, literature, and history, drawing on Sanskrit primary sources he read in the original.
He compares Indian intellectual traditions to Greek (he had read Aristotle and the Greek astronomical-mathematical tradition in Arabic translation), Persian, and Islamic equivalents.

He is unusually frank about the difficulties of cross-cultural understanding, including his own struggles with Sanskrit philosophical vocabulary and his frustration with the rigidity of caste rules that excluded foreign scholars from many Hindu pedagogical settings.
He criticizes both Indian and Islamic prejudices fairly.
He praises Indian astronomical sophistication where it exceeds the Greek tradition (which he is in a position to judge accurately) and notes Indian errors where they exist.
The tone throughout is of a serious scholar genuinely trying to understand a civilization on its own terms.
The Tarikh al-Hind is, by some distance, the best outsider account of medieval Indian society from any source.

The fact that it was written by a scholar working in the entourage of the very Sultan whose army was simultaneously sacking Indian temples is one of the more interesting ironies of medieval Indian intellectual history.
Al-Biruni was, in modern terms, both an embedded observer with the invading army and a serious cross-cultural ethnographer who genuinely respected the civilization he was observing.
His book is the closest medieval India comes to having an external mirror held up to it.

The internal Indian sources of the period rarely attempt the kind of systematic civilizational self-description that al-Biruni produces; the Tarikh al-Hind fills a gap that the Indian sources leave open.
Al-Biruni died in Ghazni in 1048.

His reputation in the Islamic world remained high for centuries — al-Biruni was one of the four or five great polymath scholars of the Islamic Golden Age, alongside al-Razi, Ibn Sina (Avicenna), and Ibn al-Haytham (Islamic Golden Age Ch 4).

His reputation in Indian historiography went through a long eclipse and has been revived in the modern period; modern Indian historians regularly cite the Tarikh al-Hind as a major source for eleventh-century Indian society.
The Ghaznavid empire collapsed surprisingly quickly after Mahmud's death.
His descendants ruled a reduced version of the empire from Ghazni and then from Lahore for another century and a half, but the dynasty was no longer the dominant Central Asian power.

The new dominant power was the Seljuk Turks, who conquered Persia in the 1040s, defeated the Byzantines at Manzikert in 1071, and built one of the major Eurasian empires of the eleventh century (Islamic Golden Age Ch 9, Byzantine Empire Ch 7).
The Ghaznavids continued holding Lahore as a frontier outpost, but their major presence in the Indian heartland was over.
For a hundred and fifty years after Mahmud, north India had a respite.

The regional Rajput dynasties extended themselves across the Ganges plain — the Chauhans of Ajmer under King Visaladeva (twelfth century) became the most powerful, eventually capturing Delhi from the Tomaras around 1150.
The Gahadavalas ruled Kannauj.
The Senas displaced the Palas in Bengal.
The Chola Empire was in slow decline in the south.
The political situation looked, superficially, like a continuation of the medieval pattern.
What was different was that a new Turkic dynasty was rising in central Afghanistan.
The Ghurids (GOOR-idz) — originally a Tajik dynasty based at the city of Ghor (GOR), in the central Afghan highlands between Ghazni and Herat — had been Ghaznavid vassals.
In the mid-twelfth century they began expanding at Ghaznavid expense.
By 1186 they had captured Lahore from the last Ghaznavid prince and inherited the Ghaznavid Indian frontier.

The Ghurid sultan Ghiyath al-Din Muhammad ruled the central empire from his capital at Firuzkuh; his younger brother Muhammad of Ghor (born Muizzuddin Muhammad ibn Sam, ~1149–1206 CE) was given responsibility for the Indian campaign.
Muhammad of Ghor was a different kind of invader from Mahmud of Ghazni.
Mahmud had raided for plunder and returned home each spring; Muhammad set out, systematically, to conquer.
His first major Indian campaign in 1175 captured Multan and consolidated Ghurid control over Sindh and southern Punjab.
Through the 1180s he extended Ghurid territory across northern Punjab.
By 1190, he was ready to attack the great Rajput kingdoms of the Indian plains.
The principal Rajput ruler of north India was Prithviraj Chauhan (PRIT-vee-rahj CHOW-hahn, ruled 1166–1192), king of the Chauhan dynasty of Ajmer and Delhi.

Prithviraj was the great hero-king of Hindi-Rajasthani folklore — a young, brave, romantically charismatic figure whose court attracted poets, his marriage to the Kannauj princess Sanyogita became the subject of an entire literary cycle (the twelfth-century Hindi epic Prithviraj Raso by the bard Chand Bardai), and his military reputation made him one of the few Rajput kings genuinely respected across regional dynastic boundaries.
He was also, despite the legendary aura that subsequent centuries built around him, an actual capable military commander.
Muhammad of Ghor's first invasion of Rajput territory met Prithviraj at the First Battle of Tarain in 1191.
Tarain was a plain near modern Karnal in Haryana, about 80 miles north of Delhi — strategic ground controlling the road from Punjab into the Ganges plain.
The Rajput coalition that Prithviraj led included contingents from multiple regional Rajput dynasties (Chauhans, Tomaras, possibly Chandelas) and reportedly outnumbered the Ghurid army considerably.
Prithviraj's heavy cavalry charge broke the Ghurid line; Muhammad of Ghor was personally wounded and very nearly killed; the Ghurid army was driven from the field.
The defeat was the first major Hindu military victory over the Turkic invaders in two centuries.
It also turned out to be the last.
Muhammad returned to Ghor, spent a year reorganizing his army, recruiting reinforcements, and studying what had gone wrong at Tarain.
The next year, 1192, he came back.
The Second Battle of Tarain was fought on essentially the same ground, but the tactical setup was different.

Muhammad of Ghor used his cavalry archers more flexibly — withdrawing in the face of Rajput charges rather than meeting them head-on, harassing the Rajput cavalry with sustained arrow fire, and maneuvering the Rajputs into prolonged action where their heavier formations exhausted themselves.
By the end of the day, the Rajput army was broken.
Prithviraj Chauhan was captured.
The Chauhan kingdom of Ajmer surrendered.
Within months, Ghurid forces had occupied Delhi.
What happened to Prithviraj Chauhan after his capture is murky.
Persian sources say he was executed in Ghazni shortly after the battle.

The legendary tradition (the Prithviraj Raso) gives him a more dramatic ending — he is brought to Ghazni in chains, blinded by Muhammad, and then asked to demonstrate his archery skills in the sultan's court; using his memory of Muhammad's voice, he draws a bow and shoots Muhammad through the throat, then commits suicide along with his loyal poet Chand Bardai.

The legendary version is almost certainly invented, but it captures the cultural significance of Prithviraj's fate in subsequent Hindu memory: the last Hindu emperor of Delhi, defeated and killed by the founder of Muslim rule, becomes the romantic-tragic figure around whom the larger story is organized.
The Second Battle of Tarain in 1192 is the conventional dividing line in Indian historiography between "medieval" and "Sultanate" India.
It opened the road to Delhi for the Ghurid forces.

Within months, Muhammad of Ghor's general Qutb al-Din Aibak (kuh-TOB al-DEEN AY-bak), a Turkic slave-soldier whom Muhammad had purchased and trained, occupied Delhi and began converting it into a Turkic military headquarters.

Over the next decade, Ghurid forces under Muhammad of Ghor and his lieutenants — most importantly Aibak in north India and Bakhtiyar Khalji in Bengal — completed the conquest of the Indo-Gangetic plain.
Aibak captured Kannauj from the Gahadavala king Jayachandra around 1194.
He sacked Banaras (the holy city on the Ganges, also called Varanasi, the most sacred Hindu pilgrimage site in north India).
He pushed eastward across the Doab.
He suppressed Rajput revolts when they arose.

He began the construction of the Quwwat-ul-Islam Mosque ("Might of Islam") in Delhi, the first congregational mosque in the city, built deliberately on the site of demolished Hindu and Jain temples — twenty-seven of which were torn down, and their carved stone columns reused in the mosque's construction.
Adjacent to the mosque, Aibak began construction of the Qutb Minar, a 240-foot fluted brick-and-sandstone victory tower, which would be completed by his successors over the following century.

The Qutb Minar is still standing — UNESCO World Heritage, the tallest brick minaret in the world, and a deliberately ambiguous monument that has been read alternately as celebrating Islamic conquest, demonstrating Indo-Islamic architectural synthesis, or commemorating an interreligious complexity that has no clean ideological narrative.
Meanwhile, Muhammad bin Bakhtiyar Khalji (BAHKH-tee-yar KHAL-jee), a Khalji Turkic warlord in Ghurid service, conducted the conquest of Bihar and Bengal.
The campaign was completed in a series of dramatic raids around 1200–1205 that overran the great Pala-era monastic universities at Nalanda, Vikramashila, and Odantapuri.

The Persian historian Minhaj-i Siraj, writing his Tabaqat-i Nasiri about fifty years later, gives the standard account: Bakhtiyar's troops stormed Nalanda, killed the resident Buddhist monks who refused to convert, and burned the libraries — the Buddhist Sanskrit philosophical and religious texts accumulated over six centuries went up in smoke.

The Tibetan historian Taranatha (writing in 1608, but using earlier Tibetan sources) gives an even fuller account of the systematic destruction of Buddhist institutions across eastern India during this period.
The destruction of Nalanda is one of the great cultural losses in human history.
The library held perhaps tens of thousands of Sanskrit manuscripts — Buddhist, Hindu, and Jain — accumulated through six centuries of Indian intellectual life.
What survived was what had already been copied and exported to Tibet, Sri Lanka, China, and Southeast Asia.
The bulk of medieval Indian Buddhist philosophical literature exists today only because Tibetan monks had translated it into Tibetan in the centuries before the destruction.
The Sanskrit originals that the Tibetans were translating from no longer exist.
Modern scholars are reconstructing major Indian Buddhist works from Tibetan back-translation, supplemented by a few surviving Sanskrit fragments.
The Bakhtiyar Khalji destruction of Nalanda is the death blow to organized Buddhism in north India.

Buddhist communities continued in attenuated form for several generations afterward, but the institutional infrastructure — the great monastic universities, the trained teaching lineages, the Sanskrit textual scholarship — was effectively wiped out in a few years of military campaigning.
The religion that had been the dominant intellectual tradition of north India for fifteen centuries lost its institutional foundations.
The slow disappearance traced in Chapter 7 had its sudden, violent ending here.
Muhammad of Ghor himself was assassinated in 1206 CE at the river crossing of Damyak in modern Pakistan, while traveling between Ghazni and Lahore.
The assassins were probably members of an obscure Indian Hindu sect (the Khokars, an ethnic group in the Punjab who had been raided by Muhammad's army several times) — though the details are debated.
He left no son.
The Ghurid Empire collapsed within a few years of his death, fragmenting among rival successor commanders.
In India, his slave-general Qutb al-Din Aibak proclaimed himself sultan at Lahore in 1206, founding the Mamluk ("Slave") dynasty — the first dynasty of what would become the Delhi Sultanate.
The transition was as much an institutional as a personal one.

Aibak was a talented Turkic military leader, but the legitimacy of his sultanate did not derive from any traditional claim — he was a manumitted slave-soldier, with no royal lineage and no traditional Indian basis for rule.

What he was building was a new institutional template: a Turkic military aristocracy ruling India through its own administrative system, with its own religion (Sunni Islam), its own language (Persian, with Arabic religious vocabulary), and its own legal and architectural traditions, all imported from the eastern Islamic world.

The Delhi Sultanate that Aibak founded would last from 1206 to 1526 — three centuries of Turkic and Afghan dynastic succession (the Mamluks, the Khaljis, the Tughluqs, the Sayyids, the Lodis), each with its own peculiarities, but all sharing the basic framework Aibak had established.
The Delhi Sultanate is the subject of Delhi Sultanate Ch 1 and the chapters that follow.
What is relevant here is that by 1206, the medieval period of regional Hindu kingdoms was over.
The next chapter of north Indian history would be written in Persian and conducted from a Turkic-Muslim throne in Delhi.
What did the medieval period leave behind?
The temples.

Almost every famous Indian temple — Brihadeeswara, Khajuraho, Ellora's Kailasa, Konark, Belur, Halebidu, Madurai's medieval foundations, Srirangam, Bhubaneswar's Lingaraja, the Dilwara temples at Mount Abu — was built during this period.
They are still standing.
They are still in active use.
They are the visible, physical inheritance of medieval Indian civilization and they will probably outlast all of us.
The philosophical schools.
Shankara's Advaita, Ramanuja's Vishishtadvaita, Madhva's Dvaita — the three main Vedanta schools that define modern Hindu metaphysics — all crystallized during this period.

The intellectual frame that contemporary Indian religious discourse uses, on questions of God, soul, world, and liberation, was substantially worked out in medieval commentaries on Upanishads written between Banaras and Srirangam.
The Bhakti devotional tradition.

The Tamil Alvars and Nayanars established a template — vernacular devotional poetry directly addressed to a personal deity, accessible to all castes, theologically egalitarian — that would spread across India over subsequent centuries and shape the popular religious life of the subcontinent ever since.
Modern Indian devotional practice is overwhelmingly Bhakti-influenced, even when the Bhakti origins have become invisible.
The decimal numeral system, in its medieval refined form.

Bhaskara II at Ujjain, the Sanskrit mathematical textbook tradition, the systematic treatment of zero and place-value notation — passed to the Arab world through al-Khwarizmi and from there to Europe through Fibonacci, the system that you use to write numbers on a piece of paper today is a medieval Indian product.
The temple-as-civic-institution model.

The medieval Indian template — the temple as religious sanctum plus economic engine plus community center plus piece of dynastic propaganda — survived the medieval period and continued shaping Indian social organization through the Sultanate and Mughal eras (when Hindu temples continued to be built in many regions outside direct imperial Muslim control), through the British colonial period, and into the present.
Modern Indian temple management organizations operate on institutional templates with medieval origins.
And the political pattern.
The medieval period demonstrated, with depressing clarity, what happens to a politically fragmented subcontinent when faced with externally organized military invasion.
The lesson was registered.

The Vijayanagar Empire (which would emerge in south India in the fourteenth century, partly as a Hindu defensive response to the Sultanate's southern incursions) was deliberately built as a centralized Hindu state of a kind the medieval period had not produced.
The Maratha Empire of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries was similarly an attempt at centralized Hindu power.

Modern Indian nationalism, when it constructs a usable Hindu past, draws very selectively from medieval India — usually emphasizing the temple and philosophical achievements, often glossing over the political fragmentation that proved so consequentially fatal.
The medieval Indian period is, taken together, one of the great cultural flowerings of any civilization in any era.
Its political record is genuinely tragic — the long Tripartite Struggle, the failure to integrate after the Gupta collapse, the inability to coordinate against the Turkic invasions.
Its cultural and religious record is unmatched.

The temples, the philosophy, the devotional poetry, the mathematics, the maritime expeditions, the synthesis of Hindu and Buddhist and Jain religious traditions in a long mutual conversation — these are extraordinary achievements that coexisted with the political tragedy, and they did not prevent the political outcome.
After Tarain, north India would be ruled by Muslim dynasties for the next seven centuries.
The medieval period was over.
The Sultanate was beginning.
And the temples that the medieval period had built would still be standing, mostly intact, when the British finally lowered their flag at the Red Fort in 1947 and the modern Indian republic was born.

Cross-civ check: 1206 CE, the founding year of the Delhi Sultanate, is the same year Genghis Khan was proclaimed Great Khan of the Mongols at the kurultai on the banks of the Onon River (Mongol Empire Ch 2).

The two events would not connect for another fifty years — the Mongols would later raid the Delhi Sultanate's Punjab frontier through the thirteenth century, and the eventual Mughal dynasty would trace descent from both Genghis Khan and Timur — but the medieval period this book has covered ended in the same year that the most consequential Eurasian empire of the next century began.

The world that the medieval Indian dynasties had inhabited — a world of regional kingdoms, monumental temple-building, devotional poetry, philosophical commentary, and the Sanskrit cosmopolis stretching from Afghanistan to Java — was, simultaneously across Eurasia, ending.

chapters.title: The Restoration
sentences: The previous TL ended on a beach.

On July 8, 1853, four black ships of the United States Navy — two of them steam frigates, the largest things the lookout had ever seen — sailed into the entrance of Edo Bay, dropped anchor, and refused to leave (Edo Japan Ch 8).
The man on the lead frigate was Commodore Matthew Perry (PEHR-ee), sixty years old, carrying a letter from the American president demanding that Japan open to trade.

The Tokugawa shogunate, the warrior government that had ruled Japan for 253 years from the city of Edo (modern Tokyo), had no military force capable of resisting the steam-powered cannons in front of it.
After fifteen years of escalating crisis, the shogunate would be gone.

After fifteen years of escalating crisis, a coalition of samurai from two southwestern domains would have placed a fifteen-year-old emperor on a real throne for the first time in eight centuries, and Japan would have begun the most rapid national transformation any country has ever attempted.
This chapter covers the fifteen years between Perry's arrival and the proclamation of the Meiji Restoration in January 1868.
The story is dense, the names are unfamiliar, and the chronology is messy.
You don't need to remember all of it.

What you need to come away with is the political logic: a sealed country was forced open by a foreign power it could not resist, the regime that had failed to resist lost legitimacy as a result, a new regime built itself out of the wreckage, and the new regime then spent the next forty years making sure no foreign power would ever dictate to Japan again.

To set the scene: Japan in 1853 had been governed for two and a half centuries by the Tokugawa shogunate (toh-koo-GAH-wah SHOH-guh-nayt), a hereditary military government founded by Tokugawa Ieyasu in 1603 (Edo Japan Ch 1).
The shogun (literally "barbarian-subduing generalissimo") was the actual political ruler.

The emperor in Kyoto (KYOH-toh) was the ceremonial sovereign, descended in unbroken line — by official Japanese tradition — from the sun goddess Amaterasu, but had not exercised real political power since the late twelfth century, when the warrior class first took over (Ancient Japan Ch 7–8).
The country was divided into roughly 270 domains (han), each ruled by a hereditary lord (daimyō, DIE-myoh) who governed his fief under the shogunate's overall authority.
Below the daimyō stood the warrior caste (samurai, SAH-moo-rye), legally about 6% of the population, who held a state monopoly on weapons and on government office.
Below the samurai were the peasants (~80%), the artisans, and the merchants, in officially descending Confucian social rank.

The country had been formally closed since the 1630s under the sakoku (sah-KOH-koo, "closed country") policy: no Japanese could leave; no foreigners could enter except a handful of Dutch traders confined to a small artificial island called Dejima in Nagasaki harbor, plus limited Chinese and Korean trade through specific channels (Edo Japan Ch 3).
For two centuries this worked.
Japan was peaceful, prosperous, literate, urbanized — Edo had over a million people by 1700, the largest city in the world — and almost completely insulated from the rest of the planet.
Western technological developments were absorbed through the Dutch trickle and by rangaku ("Dutch learning") scholars who taught themselves European languages from smuggled books (Edo Japan Ch 6).
But the country had no modern military, no modern navy, and no modern industry.
Meanwhile the world outside had transformed.
Britain had industrialized.

The Opium Wars (1839–42 and 1856–60) had shown that European steam warships could dictate terms to the Chinese empire (Tang-Song China was nine centuries gone, but its Qing successor was still nominally the dominant Asian power).
The United States, fresh from the Mexican-American War, had reached the Pacific coast in California in 1848 and wanted Pacific coaling stations for steamships heading to China.
A door was about to be kicked in.

When Perry returned in February 1854 with a larger fleet, the shogunate signed the Treaty of Kanagawa: the United States got the right to enter the ports of Shimoda (on the Izu Peninsula, south of Edo) and Hakodate (in southern Hokkaido, the northern island), the right to station an American consul, and a most-favored-nation clause.
It was a treaty of friendship, not of full commerce.
Sakoku as a legal regime was over.
Four years later, in 1858, the American consul Townsend Harris negotiated the Harris Treaty (the Treaty of Amity and Commerce).

The terms were what Britain had imposed on China sixteen years earlier: extraterritoriality (foreigners accused of crimes would be tried by their own consular courts, not Japanese ones); a 5% tariff cap (Japan could not protect its own industries); five additional open ports including Yokohama, near Edo.
Within weeks, Britain, France, the Netherlands, and Russia signed near-identical Ansei Treaties (named for the imperial era then in effect).
The unequal treaty regime that would humiliate Japan for the next four decades was now in place.
The shogunate had signed without imperial sanction — the reactionary nationalist Emperor Kōmei (KOH-mei) on the Kyoto throne had refused to ratify.
The chief minister Ii Naosuke (EE nah-oh-SOO-keh) authorized the signing anyway.
This had two consequences.

First, the imperial court suddenly had political relevance for the first time in centuries, because the rapidly growing sonnō jōi (son-NOH JOH-ee, "Revere the Emperor, Expel the Barbarians") movement could rally around the emperor's refusal.
Second, Ii was assassinated in March 1860 outside the Sakurada Gate of Edo Castle by a band of nationalist samurai.
The Sakuradamon Incident demonstrated that the shogunate could no longer protect even its highest officials.
The bakufu (the shogunal government) began visibly cracking.
The opposition coalesced around three southwestern domains: Satsuma (SAHT-soo-mah), the Shimazu domain in southern Kyushu — the southernmost of the four main Japanese islands.
Wealthy from sugar and unofficial trade with the Ryukyu Islands.
Led by the reformist daimyō Shimazu Hisamitsu.
Chōshū (CHOH-shoo), the Mōri domain at the western end of Honshu, the main island.
Poor, mountainous, but home to the most active rangaku-trained reform faction in the country.
Tosa (TOH-sah), the Yamauchi domain on the island of Shikoku.

All three were tozama ("outside") domains — descendants of clans that had lost the Battle of Sekigahara to Tokugawa Ieyasu in 1600 (Edo Japan Ch 1) and had been excluded from central power for two and a half centuries afterward.

All three had spent the late Edo period quietly building modernized military forces using imported French and British weapons — much of it acquired through illegal channels routed through the Glover Trading Company in Nagasaki, run by the Scottish merchant Thomas Glover.
All three had specific reasons to hate the shogunate.

Satsuma had been forced to pay a 100,000-pound indemnity to Britain after the Namamugi Incident of 1862, when Satsuma samurai cut down a British merchant on the Tōkaidō highway for failing to dismount before their lord's procession; the British navy then bombarded Kagoshima, Satsuma's capital, in 1863.
Chōshū had fired on Western ships at the Shimonoseki Strait, leading to a four-power Western fleet bombardment in 1864 that destroyed Chōshū coastal defenses.
The bakufu, blamed for both incidents, then mounted two punitive expeditions against Chōshū.
The first Chōshū Expedition of 1864 forced the domain to back down.

The second Chōshū Expedition of 1866 was a humiliating bakufu failure: the Chōshū riflemen, drilled in Western infantry tactics by the rangaku-trained military reformer Ōmura Masujirō, outclassed every bakufu force sent against them.

The decisive political move had taken place earlier in 1866, when a Tosa rōnin (masterless samurai) named Sakamoto Ryōma (sah-kah-MOH-toh ree-OH-mah) personally arranged a secret alliance between Satsuma and Chōshū.
The two domains had been bitter enemies.
Sakamoto's alliance brought them into coordinated opposition to the bakufu.
The Satsuma-Chōshū Alliance (Satchō Dōmei) was the coalition that would, within two years, overthrow the Tokugawa shogunate.
The fifteenth and last shogun, Tokugawa Yoshinobu (toh-koo-GAH-wah yoh-shee-NOH-boo), came to office in late 1866.
He was probably the most capable shogun the Tokugawa had produced in over a century — energetic, intelligent, conversant in Western affairs.
His response to the situation was, in effect, a calculated surrender.

In November 1867 he formally returned political authority to the emperor in the Taisei Hōkan ("Restoration of Imperial Rule"), proposing that he continue to head the new government as a constitutional minister under imperial sovereignty.
He was betting that no other faction had the administrative experience to govern.
The bet failed.
Sakamoto Ryōma was assassinated in Kyoto in December 1867, removing the most influential mediator.
The Satsuma-Chōshū faction, dominated by hardliners, refused to keep Yoshinobu in any government.
On January 3, 1868, they staged a palace coup at the Kyoto imperial court and proclaimed the restoration of direct imperial rule under the fifteen-year-old Emperor Meiji.
The shogunate's military forces in and around Kyoto, refusing to accept the political settlement, marched on the imperial capital at the end of January 1868.
They were intercepted at Toba-Fushimi, just south of Kyoto, by a smaller but better-armed Satsuma-Chōshū force flying the imperial banner.
The bakufu forces broke and fled.
The Boshin War (Year of the Yang Earth Dragon War, January 1868 to June 1869) is the civil war that completed the overthrow.

Imperial forces marched east through the central highway, took Edo without serious resistance in May 1868 — Yoshinobu, surrendering his sword, ordered no defense — pursued the shogunate diehards north into Tōhoku (the northeastern region of Honshu) and into Hokkaido.

The last shogunate force, a naval contingent that had set up an independent Republic of Ezo at Hakodate under the navy admiral Enomoto Takeaki (eh-noh-MOH-toh tah-keh-AH-kee), surrendered in June 1869 after a six-month siege.
The Boshin War's casualties — perhaps 10,000 dead total — were modest compared to the Imjin War of the 1590s (Joseon Korea Ch 4) or the Sengoku-era wars of the sixteenth century (Edo Japan Ch 1).
But the political consequence was total.
The Tokugawa shogunate, after 265 years of rule, was over.
The new government was nominally headed by the fifteen-year-old emperor.

He had been born Mutsuhito in 1852, ascended the throne in early 1867 on the death of his father Kōmei (officially of smallpox, possibly of poison — the timing was suspiciously convenient), and would reign for forty-five years under the era name Meiji ("enlightened rule").

The actual administration was run by a coalition of senior Satsuma, Chōshū, Tosa, and Hizen officials — most of them under forty years old, most of them former samurai of relatively modest stipend rank, most of them rangaku-trained.

Of the founding generation, a small group would do most of the governing for the next thirty years: the Satsuma giants Saigō Takamori (sigh-GO tah-kah-MOH-ree) and Ōkubo Toshimichi (OH-koo-boh toh-shee-MEE-chee); the Chōshū intellectuals Kido Takayoshi (KEE-doh tah-kah-YOH-shee), Itō Hirobumi (ee-TOH hee-roh-BOO-mee), and Yamagata Aritomo (yah-mah-GAH-tah ah-ree-TOH-moh); the Tosa political organizer Itagaki Taisuke (ee-tah-GAH-kee TIE-soo-keh); and the court noble Iwakura Tomomi (ee-wah-KOO-rah toh-MOH-mee), who acted as the bridge between the imperial palace and the samurai oligarchs.
In April 1868, the new government issued the Charter Oath — a five-article document that the boy emperor formally proclaimed before a ceremonial gathering of court nobles and daimyō.

The articles promised public assembly and political consultation, abolition of feudal class restrictions, and "the seeking of knowledge throughout the world" so that Japan might secure "the foundations of imperial rule." It was the founding document of the new state — programmatically the diametric opposite of the late Tokugawa program, which had been about preserving the closed country at almost any cost.
The Charter Oath was the program of the open country, and of catch-up modernization on whatever terms catch-up demanded.
In September 1868, Edo was renamed Tokyo ("Eastern Capital") and designated the new imperial capital.
Kyoto, after a thousand years (Ancient Japan Ch 5–6), was demoted to a provincial city.
The young emperor moved into the former shogun's castle in Edo.
The symbolic transfer of sovereignty was complete.
The country the new government inherited was, by any external measure, a wreck.
Population around 33 million.
Agrarian economy with negligible industry.

Military — a few decentralized domain armies of varying modernization, no national navy beyond what the bakufu had begun to build, no railways, no telegraph, no modern banks, no national currency, no national tax system, no national legal code, no compulsory education, no centralized administration outside what the shogunate had loosely overseen.
The country was bound by unequal treaties to four major Western powers, all of whom regarded it as a quaint object of curiosity, a possible coaling station, and a future colony.

The Iwakura Mission of 1871–73, which we'll cover in Chapter 2, would discover that Western diplomats considered Japan roughly comparable to Persia or Egypt — interesting, exotic, fundamentally backward, and ripe for partition once the imperial powers got around to it.
The new government had to decide, very quickly, what it wanted Japan to become.
The answer it gave shaped everything that followed.
Japan would not be partitioned.
Japan would not be a client state.

Japan would build itself into an industrialized constitutional power on the European model so fast and so thoroughly that no foreign government would ever again dictate the terms of Japanese sovereignty.

Whatever institutions were necessary to achieve that — feudal abolition, conscription, mass education, centralized taxation, parliament, written constitution, national religion, modern army, modern navy, overseas empire — would be built.
Whatever institutions stood in the way — domains, samurai class, Buddhist temples, hereditary stipends, customary tariffs — would be dismantled.
The institutional Tokugawa Japan, the country that had taken two and a half centuries to build, would be taken apart in roughly fifteen years.
That is what the next two chapters describe.
A pause, before the chronology takes over.
The Meiji project is one of the most-studied transformations in modern world history, and the standard scholarly question about it is: why did Japan succeed where China and the Ottoman Empire failed?

The Ottomans (Ottoman Empire Ch 9) faced essentially the same external pressure as Japan from roughly the same period (the Tanzimat reforms of 1839 onward), wanted essentially the same outcome (industrialized constitutional power on the European model), and had a head start in size, wealth, and institutional development.
The Qing Chinese Self-Strengthening Movement of the 1860s–1890s had similar goals.
Both projects produced significant achievements but neither produced the wholesale transformation that Japan accomplished.

The standard scholarly readings emphasize several factors that the Meiji case had and the others didn't: a coherent reform faction that captured the central state intact (rather than reformers having to fight entrenched conservatives at every step); a relatively small and ethnically homogeneous population that could be administered uniformly; a literate population already accustomed to centralized authority; a commercial economy already in place from the Edo period (Edo Japan Ch 4); and — crucially — a foreign threat that was real but not immediate.
The Western powers had imposed unequal treaties on Japan but were not actively partitioning it the way they were China.
Japan had a window in which to reform without being invaded; China and the Ottomans, by the time they tried, no longer did.
Some historians add that the rangaku tradition (Edo Japan Ch 6) had given Japan a small but capable cadre of intellectuals already familiar with Western knowledge.

Others point to the Tokugawa-era development of a unified national consciousness through the kokugaku ("native learning") movement, which had argued for centuries that Japan was a unique sacred polity descended from the sun goddess — an ideological resource that Meiji nationalism could weaponize.
Whatever the right combination of factors, the result was that the Meiji oligarchs, between 1868 and 1900, accomplished something no other non-Western country has ever quite matched.

The cost was real and will appear in later chapters: the same machinery that built the modern Japanese state also built the imperial expansion of 1894–1910 and the militarist catastrophe of the 1930s.
The success and the disaster ran on the same operating system.

Cross-civ check: the Meiji Restoration of 1868 was almost exactly contemporary with the Italian Risorgimento (the unification of Italy under the House of Savoy, 1859–71); the American Reconstruction following the Civil War (1865–77); and the German unification under Prussia after the Franco-Prussian War (1870–71).
The 1860s and 1870s were one of the densest decades of nation-state consolidation in modern history.
Japan's project was a participant in, not an exception to, that broader pattern.

The crucial difference was that Japan was building a nation-state on a non-Western cultural foundation while consciously importing Western institutions — what the historian Marius Jansen called "selective borrowing" — and managing to make the imported institutions feel sufficiently Japanese that the population accepted them.
The same generation that watched the Charter Oath promulgated would, sixty years later, watch their grandsons march to war in Manchuria.
The chain from one to the other is what this TL is about.

chapters.title: Dismantling Feudalism
sentences: The new government came to power in 1868 with no actual government to govern with.
The Tokugawa bakufu had been dismantled.
The 270-odd domains still existed, each running its own administration, collecting its own taxes, maintaining its own samurai retainer corps, and answerable to its own daimyō.
The new imperial regime in Tokyo had control of about a third of the country (the former shogunal lands, plus the territories of the loyalist domains) and influence over the rest.
It had no national tax system, no national army, no national legal code, no national currency, and no national administration to speak of.
Before it could industrialize, build a constitution, or do any of the things on its program, it had to construct the basic apparatus of a modern centralized state.
That meant abolishing feudalism — the social and political system that had organized Japan for nearly seven centuries.

This chapter covers the first five years of the project (1868–1873), in which the new government dismantled the daimyō, dissolved the samurai class, established universal conscription, reformed the land tax, and dispatched half its senior leadership to spend twenty-two months in the West learning how the modernizing powers actually worked.
By the end of it, Japan looked, on paper, almost nothing like the country Perry's ships had encountered twenty years earlier.
Step one was the daimyō.

In March 1869, four of the most powerful loyalist domains — Satsuma, Chōshū, Tosa, and Hizen — voluntarily "returned" their fiefs to the emperor in a coordinated ceremonial gesture engineered by Kido Takayoshi and Iwakura Tomomi.
The other daimyō, seeing the writing on the wall, almost all followed within months.
The daimyō were then re-appointed as imperial governors of their old territories, drawing salaries from the central government rather than collecting their own taxes.
This was a polite half-measure — the same families still ruled the same regions — but it established the principle that the territory was the emperor's, not the daimyō's.
Step two came two years later.
On July 14, 1871, the government issued Haihan Chiken (HIGH-han CHEE-ken — "Abolition of the Han, Establishment of the prefectures").
The 270 domains were dissolved outright.
In their place, the country was divided into 72 prefectures (eventually consolidated to 47), each governed by an appointed prefectural official answerable directly to the central government.
The daimyō were stripped of their administrative roles, given lifetime pensions in central-government bonds, and required to live in Tokyo.
In a single edict, eight centuries of decentralized warrior rule ended.
This was an extraordinary thing to have done.
The daimyō and their senior retainers controlled Japan's only effective military forces.
They had every theoretical reason to refuse and to fight.
That they didn't — that Haihan Chiken was implemented essentially without resistance — is one of the under-explained miracles of the Meiji period.

The standard reading attributes it to a combination of factors: the daimyō's correct assessment that resistance against a unified Satsuma-Chōshū military would be suicidal; the bond pensions, which compensated them generously enough that most went along; the genuine prestige of the imperial restoration, which framed the abolition as the emperor's will rather than as an oligarchic power grab; and the fact that many daimyō were themselves bankrupt, glad to be relieved of administrative responsibilities they could no longer afford.
Whatever the right combination, the central government had, in three years, gone from controlling a third of the country to controlling all of it.
Step three was the samurai.
This took longer — about five years — and was harder.
The samurai were a hereditary warrior caste of about two million people, including dependents.
They held a legal monopoly on bearing arms (specifically the daishō, the paired long and short swords that signaled samurai status).
They were the only people legally eligible for government office.
They received hereditary stipends from their domains, paid in rice, that constituted their entire household income.
The dissolution of the domains in 1871 had left the central government on the hook for those stipends — which collectively absorbed about 30% of the new government's annual revenue.
This was unsustainable.
Between 1871 and 1876, the government dismantled the samurai class in pieces.
The 1871 imperial decree abolished the eta and hinin (the outcaste groups below the four-class system) and theoretically established equality of all subjects before the law.
The 1872 decree abolished the legal distinction between samurai and commoner; the samurai retained the social title of shizoku (warrior household) but had no legal privileges over heimin (commoners).

The 1873 Conscription Law, drafted by Yamagata Aritomo and modeled on the French and Prussian systems, required three years of military service from every able-bodied male over twenty regardless of class.
This was the act, more than any other, that ended the samurai monopoly on arms.
The samurai were no longer the country's warriors.
The country's warriors were now the conscript peasants the samurai had spent centuries despising.
In 1876 came the final blow.
The haitōrei edict (the "sword abolition order") prohibited the wearing of swords in public except by the active military and the police.
The samurai social signature — the daishō at the belt — was banned.
The same year, the government converted hereditary samurai stipends into one-time bonds, paying out roughly five to fourteen years of stipend value depending on rank.
About 400,000 samurai households received bonds.
The face value was real money, but inflation eroded it quickly, and the bonds proved an inadequate substitute for the inherited income they replaced.
Two million people had effectively lost their hereditary livelihood within five years.
Some samurai prospered in the new system.
The most adaptable became officials in the new prefectural governments, officers in the conscript army, schoolteachers, journalists, lawyers, businessmen.
The founders of the Mitsubishi and Sumitomo zaibatsu (Chapter 4) were ex-samurai.
The Meiji bureaucracy that ran the new state was, for at least a generation, almost entirely staffed by ex-samurai.
The middle-class professional caste of late-nineteenth-century urban Japan was the destination most successful ex-samurai families ended up in.
But the bottom half of the samurai class — the low-stipend warriors who had been functionally rural landlords or barely-paid retainers — slid into poverty.
Some turned to small farming, some to small business, many to the traditional Japanese remedy for hereditary disappointment: drink.
Many also turned to political resistance.
The Satsuma Rebellion of 1877 (Chapter 3) was the largest of the samurai uprisings against the Meiji government, but smaller revolts erupted across western Japan from 1874 onward.
Step four was money.

The 1873 Land Tax Reform (Chisō Kaisei) replaced the variable rice-tax of the Edo period with a fixed cash tax of 3% of the assessed market value of agricultural land, payable in money rather than in rice.
This had several enormous effects.

It established private land titles for the first time in Japanese history — under the Edo system, the daimyō had been the legal owner and the peasants the tenants; now individual farmers held title to specific plots.
It gave the state a stable predictable revenue base for industrialization.
It collected the tax in cash, which forced peasants to sell some portion of their crop on the market — which in turn deepened the cash economy across rural Japan.
And it meant that bad harvests no longer reduced the tax bill, which pushed marginal farmers into debt and eventually off the land in massive numbers.
Tenancy rates rose steadily through the Meiji period.
By 1900, roughly 40% of arable land was farmed by tenants paying rent to landlords.
The land tax that funded industrialization also created the rural underclass that would supply the labor for the new factories.

The New Currency Act of 1871 introduced the yen (literally "round object," in reference to the shape of Western coins) as a decimal currency replacing the bewildering Edo-era system of ryō, mon, and bu.
The yen was modeled on the Mexican silver dollar that was then the international trade currency in East Asia.
Japan now had a single national money for the first time.
The 1872 National Bank Act, modeled on the American National Banking Act of 1863, authorized the establishment of joint-stock banks.
The 1882 Bank of Japan (Chapter 4) would eventually consolidate national monetary policy.

The 1871 introduction of the modern postal service, organized by Maejima Hisoka after his return from study in Britain, gave the new state a national communication network at peasant scale: stamps, post offices in every village, uniform rates regardless of distance.
The 1869 telegraph line between Tokyo and Yokohama was the first link of what within a decade would be a national network reaching every prefectural capital.
The 1872 opening of the first railway, eighteen miles of British-built track between Tokyo's Shimbashi station and Yokohama, was inaugurated by Emperor Meiji riding the first train.
By 1890 Japan had roughly 1,400 miles of railway; by 1910, over 5,000 miles.
The country was being wired together as fast as foreign engineers could build the infrastructure.
Step five was the Iwakura Mission.
This deserves a longer description, because it was the diagnostic exercise on which the rest of the Meiji project depended.

In December 1871, half the senior leadership of the new government — the court noble Iwakura Tomomi as plenipotentiary, accompanied by Ōkubo Toshimichi, Kido Takayoshi, Itō Hirobumi, and roughly fifty subordinate officials and students — boarded the steamship America at Yokohama and sailed for San Francisco.

They would spend the next twenty-two months touring the United States and twelve European countries: the US (San Francisco to Washington and back, four months); Britain (four months); France; Belgium; the Netherlands; Germany; Russia; Denmark; Sweden; Italy; Austria-Hungary; Switzerland.
They visited factories, naval shipyards, parliaments, schools, prisons, hospitals, museums, banks.
They met President Grant, Queen Victoria, Bismarck, the Tsar, the Pope.

They came back to Japan in September 1873 with a 100-volume official report, written by the diplomat Kume Kunitake (KOO-meh koo-nee-TAH-keh), that became the essential reference document for Meiji policy.
The mission's official purpose was to negotiate revision of the unequal treaties.

This failed completely — the Western powers told the Japanese delegation politely but firmly that no revision would be considered until Japan had a Western-style legal code, a Western-style constitution, and a Western-style army and navy.
The unofficial purpose, which became the actual purpose, was to study Western institutions and decide which ones Japan should copy.
On this front the mission was extraordinarily successful.

The lessons the delegates drew from the trip were specific and consequential: Britain was the model for industry and naval power, but its political institutions (an unwritten constitution, a parliamentary system in which the cabinet was responsible to the legislature) were judged unsuitable for Japan — too anarchic, too dependent on local political culture.
The United States was admired for its technological dynamism but dismissed as politically inappropriate — a republic, no monarch, a constitutional structure that the delegates considered too radical.
France had had four constitutional regimes in eighty years and was undergoing the Paris Commune just before they arrived.
Politically a cautionary example.
Germany under Bismarck was the revelation.

Recently unified under Prussian leadership, with a written constitution that preserved monarchical sovereignty while granting limited parliamentary participation, with a powerful conscript army, with an ascendant industrial economy, with a strong civil service tradition — Germany looked like the country Japan wanted to become.
Itō Hirobumi in particular returned from Berlin convinced that the Prussian constitutional model was the right template.

He would later return to Germany in 1882 specifically to study constitutional law under the legal theorists Lorenz von Stein and Rudolf von Gneist, and the constitution he drafted in 1889 (Chapter 5) would be unmistakably Prussian.
The mission also taught the delegates that the gap between Japan and the Western powers was much larger than they had thought.
The shipyards at Liverpool, the factories of Manchester, the chemical works of Leverkusen, the Krupp steel cannons at Essen — these were a different order of magnitude from anything Japan possessed.
The mission's most influential consequence may have been the realization that aggressive expansion abroad was insane until aggressive industrialization at home was complete.
Which brings us to the Korea debate.
While the mission was abroad, the caretaker government in Tokyo — dominated by Saigō Takamori and Itagaki Taisuke — had decided that Japan should invade Korea.
The pretext was a diplomatic insult.

The Korean Joseon dynasty (Joseon Korea Ch 8), still nominally subject to Qing China and pursuing its own version of sakoku-style isolation, had refused to recognize the new Meiji government in 1868 on the grounds that the new regime's diplomatic note used imperial titles inappropriate to a non-Chinese power.
Saigō proposed, in summer 1873, that he personally go to Seoul as imperial envoy, deliberately get himself killed (he genuinely meant this), and thereby provide casus belli for an invasion.

The plan would have several useful effects, in the proponents' view: vindicating Japanese honor; testing the new conscript army; providing employment for the increasingly restive ex-samurai class; and projecting Japanese power onto the Asian continent.
The Iwakura Mission returned in September 1873, fresh from observing actual European military and industrial power, and immediately vetoed the invasion as suicidal.
Japan, Ōkubo argued, had no business projecting power abroad until it had built the industrial and financial base to sustain such projection.
The country could not afford a war with a Korea backed (potentially) by China.
The conscript army was untested.
The treasury was thin.
The unequal treaties had not yet been revised.
Modernization first; expansion second.
The hawks were defeated.
Saigō, Itagaki, and several other senior officials resigned from the government in October 1873 over what is called the Seikanron (sei-KAHN-ron, "the Korea Debate").
Saigō went home to Kagoshima in Satsuma.
Itagaki organized the Liberal Party (Chapter 5) and became the leader of the parliamentary opposition.
The government's center of gravity shifted decisively to the modernizers around Ōkubo Toshimichi, who served as the central architect of Meiji policy from 1873 until his assassination in 1878.

Korea would be invaded — but not until 1894, on the modernizers' schedule, when the conscript army was a fully-equipped European-style force trained in modern infantry tactics, the navy was a fleet of British-built cruisers, and the country had the industrial base to sustain a major war (Chapter 7).
Then Korea would be annexed, in 1910, on the modernizers' schedule, when the country had defeated both China and Russia in successive wars and had British backing for the annexation (Chapter 8).
The hawks of 1873 had wanted an invasion that would have failed and probably destroyed the regime.
The modernizers waited two decades and got a successful annexation that built an empire.

The cost of the wait was Saigō Takamori, the most popular man in Japan, sitting in Kagoshima nursing his grievances and gradually becoming the focal point for every disaffected ex-samurai in the country.
That is the next chapter.

Cross-civ check: the Meiji dismantling of feudalism in 1868–73 has obvious comparative interest, because the process happened — and largely failed — at roughly the same time in two other major Asian states.
The Qing Self-Strengthening Movement (1861–95) tried to modernize Chinese arsenals, shipyards, and education without touching the social structure or political institutions of the Qing dynasty.

It produced significant achievements — a modern Chinese navy, a few arsenals, the first Chinese railways, the first modern schools — but the underlying structure of imperial bureaucracy, hereditary banner privileges, and gentry-landlord rural domination was preserved.

When the modernized Chinese navy met the modernized Japanese navy at the Yalu River in 1894 (Chapter 7), the Chinese navy was destroyed (why buying machines without rebuilding institutions failed is Industrial Revolution Ch 18).

The Ottoman Tanzimat reforms (1839–76; Ottoman Empire Ch 9) were more ambitious — they aimed at legal equality of all Ottoman subjects regardless of religion, modernization of the army and the bureaucracy, and a written constitution.
The Tanzimat produced the 1876 Ottoman constitution, which was suspended within two years by Sultan Abdülhamid II.
The Ottoman Empire kept modernizing in fits and starts but never accomplished anything like the full institutional restructuring Japan undertook in the 1870s.
The closest comparison, in some ways, is Peter the Great's Russia of the early 1700s.

Peter — like the Meiji oligarchs — visited the West, returned convinced that wholesale institutional borrowing was necessary, and dragged a reluctant aristocratic society into European-style absolutism, conscription, navy-building, and a new capital city.

Peter and the Meiji oligarchs both faced the basic question of whether catch-up modernization was even possible for a non-Western state, and both answered yes, at the price of treating the existing institutional structure as raw material to be smashed and rebuilt.

The differences are also instructive: Peter modernized to the level of Sweden and ended up the strongest power in eastern Europe; the Meiji oligarchs modernized to the level of Britain and ended up briefly the strongest power in the Pacific.
Both projects used external pressure as both a justification and a deadline.
Both worked.
What Japan accomplished in the years between Haihan Chiken in 1871 and the Iwakura Mission's return in 1873 was the demolition phase.
Construction was about to begin.

chapters.title: The Satsuma Rebellion
sentences: The most popular man in Japan in 1873 was Saigō Takamori, the Satsuma samurai who had led the imperial forces at Toba-Fushimi in 1868, accepted the bloodless surrender of Edo from Katsu Kaishū later that same year, and personified, more than any other Meiji founder, the moral seriousness of the Restoration.

He was a large man — close to six feet tall and barrel-chested in a country whose average male height was below five feet five — with heavy eyebrows, a booming laugh, and a personal style of immense Confucian rectitude.
He was the one Meiji oligarch ordinary Japanese felt they understood.
He was also, by 1873, in profound disagreement with what the Restoration he had created was becoming.

In October 1873, after losing the Korea debate to Ōkubo Toshimichi and the Iwakura Mission returnees, Saigō resigned from the government and went home to Kagoshima, the Satsuma capital on the southern Kyushu coast.
Six hundred Satsuma officers and soldiers in Tokyo resigned with him and followed him south.
He was forty-six years old.
He would be dead in four years.
His death, and the destruction of the rebellion he led, would mark the end of the warrior class in Japanese politics — which was, paradoxically, the thing he was fighting to preserve.
This chapter is about the Satsuma Rebellion of 1877 and what it meant.
It is the shortest chapter in this book, because the events are simple.
But it deserves its own chapter because the political and symbolic stakes were so large.
The conscript army of peasants would defeat the last samurai army at Shiroyama.

After that, no one could pretend that the modernization of Japan was not also the dismantling of the seven-century-old warrior politics that had defined Japanese society since the late twelfth century.
Saigō, back in Kagoshima, did not initially intend to lead a rebellion.

He spent the first two years (1874–76) running a network of private military academies — the Shigakkō ("Private Schools") — that taught Confucian ethics, traditional swordsmanship, and modern European infantry tactics to roughly 20,000 disaffected young samurai.

Satsuma was the one prefecture where the Meiji reforms had only been imposed on paper; the local government, dominated by Saigō's old comrades and former retainers, had quietly maintained samurai stipends, kept domain weapons stockpiles intact, and refused to enforce the haitōrei sword-abolition edict.
By 1876 Satsuma was effectively an autonomous samurai mini-state inside a country that had legally abolished samurai status.
Smaller samurai uprisings broke out elsewhere in western Japan over the same period.
The Saga Rebellion of 1874 in Hizen, led by the disaffected ex-councilor Etō Shinpei, was put down within weeks; Etō was executed.

The Shinpūren Revolt ("League of the Divine Wind") of 1876 in Kumamoto saw a small band of 170 ultra-traditionalist samurai attack the local conscript garrison, kill several officers, and be wiped out within hours.
The Akizuki Rebellion and the Hagi Rebellion, both also in 1876, followed similar patterns: small groups of ex-samurai attacking modern garrisons, defeated quickly, leaders executed.
The pattern was clear: localized samurai resistance was futile against the new conscript army.
But the pattern would not stay localized if Saigō moved.

The Meiji government in Tokyo, watching Satsuma with mounting alarm, sent secret agents to assess the situation and (according to confessions later extracted from the agents) to assassinate Saigō if necessary.
The Satsuma Shigakkō captured the agents in late January 1877.
The agents confessed under torture.

Whether the Tokyo government had actually authorized assassination is debated — Ōkubo Toshimichi, who almost certainly would have known, denied it for the rest of his life — but the perception of assassination plot was enough.
Around the same time, the central government attempted to remove the weapons stockpiles from the Satsuma arsenals, presumably to prevent them being used in any future rising.
A Shigakkō faction raided the arsenals first to secure the weapons.
By early February 1877, both sides were committed.
Saigō, presented with the situation by his lieutenants, formally accepted leadership of the rebellion in mid-February 1877.

The official pretext was the alleged assassination plot, on which he proposed to march to Tokyo to "ask questions of the government." His actual program, insofar as he had one, was probably a kind of restorationism within the Restoration — a return to a Japan of samurai virtue, Confucian ethics, and traditional military forms, modernized only enough to be defensible.
He had no clear constitutional vision.
He had a moral stance and an army.
The army was about 30,000 strong at peak, drawn from the Shigakkō networks and from samurai sympathizers across western Kyushu.
They were armed with a mix of Western rifles (mostly older Enfield muskets, some Snider breechloaders), some artillery, and traditional swords.
They were well-drilled, brave, and absolutely committed to the rebellion's success.
They were also, at the strategic level, hopeless.
The first objective was the imperial garrison at Kumamoto Castle, the largest fortress in central Kyushu, defended by a conscript force of 4,000 under General Tani Tateki.
Saigō moved north from Kagoshima in late February with 12,000 troops and reached Kumamoto on February 22.
He laid siege.
The defenders had been alerted and had fortified the castle thoroughly.
The Satsuma siege lasted fifty-four days.
The samurai army threw itself repeatedly at the castle walls and was repeatedly broken by defensive fire.
The conscript garrison held.
