In 1894, Japan had been a recently modernized regional power with no formal colonies and unequal treaties still partially in force.

By 1905 it had a formal colonial empire (Taiwan since 1895, the Liaodong lease, southern Sakhalin), a protectorate over Korea (which would become formal annexation in 1910), an alliance with Britain, recognition as a great power in international diplomacy, and a navy that had defeated the third-largest navy in the world in a fleet action.
The unequal treaties had been substantially revised — extraterritoriality was abolished in 1899, full tariff autonomy was achieved in 1911.
The original Meiji project of equality with the Western powers had been accomplished.
But the wars had also institutionalized two structural patterns that would prove catastrophic.
First, the wars had demonstrated that aggressive foreign expansion produced political dividends: territory, indemnities, prestige, popular support.
The civilian government's career incentives now favored expansion.
The military's career incentives favored expansion even more strongly.
The popular nationalism that the Imperial Rescript had cultivated demanded expansion.
The structural pressure was constant and one-directional.
Second, the wars had given the Japanese army and navy enormous prestige and significant institutional autonomy.
The army that had won at Mukden and the navy that had won at Tsushima could not be easily controlled by civilian politicians who had not led troops in those battles.
The constitutional independence of military command (Chapter 5) became, after 1905, a political reality as well as a legal one.
The Meiji oligarchs were aging, the genrō system was beginning to decay, and the institutional weight of the victorious military was beginning to fill the resulting political vacuum.
By 1931, when the Kwantung Army would unilaterally seize Manchuria without civilian authorization, the institutional weight of the military would have become decisive.
The Sino-Japanese and Russo-Japanese wars had built the army and navy that would, a generation later, take over Japanese foreign policy.
This was not visible at the time.
In 1905, what was visible was that Japan was, for the first time in its history, a recognized great power.
The sixty-year-old Iwakura Mission delegates — those still alive — could remember being told by Western diplomats in 1872 that Japan was politically comparable to Persia.
They had spent thirty-three years building a country that was now politically comparable to Britain, France, Germany, and Russia.
The achievement was extraordinary.
The cost would not be apparent for another generation.
The next chapter is the closing of the era.
Cross-civ check: the Russo-Japanese War of 1904–05 was the first defeat of a European Great Power by an Asian power in the modern era, and its global political consequences were enormous.
Indian nationalists like Mohandas Gandhi cited it as evidence that European racial superiority was a myth.
The young Sun Yat-sen, future founder of the Chinese Republic, took it as confirmation that Asian modernization could match Western capability.
The young Vietnamese, Indonesian, Filipino, and Egyptian nationalists made similar arguments.

The 1905 Russian Revolution was triggered partly by the Russian defeats in the war — the bloodthirsty mismanagement of the army by Tsar Nicholas II's incompetent generals discredited the Russian autocracy and produced the constitutional reforms of 1905–07 that briefly made Russia a quasi-constitutional state before being reversed by the Tsar.

The Persian Constitutional Revolution of 1905–11 (Persian Empire's late successor states) was directly inspired by the Russo-Japanese War's demonstration that an Asian constitutional state could defeat a European autocratic empire.
The Young Turk Revolution of 1908 in the Ottoman Empire (Ottoman Empire Ch 9) drew similar inspiration.

For roughly fifteen years after Tsushima, the Meiji Constitution and Japanese institutional design were considered, throughout the colonized and semi-colonized world, the model for what an Asian society could accomplish if it modernized aggressively.
The model would be discredited by Japanese aggression in the 1930s and the catastrophe of 1945, but in 1905 it was the model.
Japan was, briefly, the world's leading example of successful non-Western modernization.
The implications, both inspiring and dark, would play out across the twentieth century.

chapters.title: Annexation, Death, and Legacy
sentences: The era ended with three events compressed into a few years: the formal annexation of Korea in 1910, the death of the Meiji Emperor in 1912, and the ritual suicide of General Nogi Maresuke on the night of the imperial funeral.
Each event closed a different dimension of the Meiji project.
Together, they marked the end of the founding generation and the transition to the post-Meiji Japan that would, within twenty years, slide into the militarist catastrophe.
This chapter is about the closing.
It is also, by necessity, about the legacy: what the Meiji oligarchs had built, what they had failed to build, and what the consequences would be for the Japan of the twentieth century.
The legacy is mixed — extraordinary achievement and catastrophic failure on the same operating system, as advertised throughout this book.
Both halves deserve honest accounting.
The annexation of Korea was the culmination of forty years of gradual Japanese encroachment on Korean sovereignty.
The 1876 Treaty of Ganghwa had opened Korea to Japanese trade on terms similar to the unequal treaties imposed on Japan two decades earlier.

Through the 1880s and early 1890s, Japan had built up commercial and political networks within Korea while the Qing Chinese government had attempted to maintain its tributary relationship through the resident Yuan Shikai.

The Sino-Japanese War of 1894–95 had ended Chinese suzerainty over Korea — the Treaty of Shimonoseki had recognized Korean "complete independence," meaning independence from China and de facto subordination to Japan.
The Russo-Japanese War of 1904–05 had ended Russian competition for Korean influence — the Treaty of Portsmouth had explicitly acknowledged Japanese paramountcy in Korea.
The remaining steps to formal annexation took five years.
In November 1905, Japan imposed the Eulsa Treaty on Korea, making Korea a Japanese protectorate.

The treaty stripped Korea of foreign-affairs authority — Japan now controlled all Korean diplomatic relations — and established a Japanese Resident-General in Seoul to oversee Korean internal affairs.
The first Resident-General was Itō Hirobumi, who had been the most senior figure in the Meiji Constitution drafting and was now applying Meiji-style institutional reform to Korea on Tokyo's behalf.
Itō's stated personal preference was for indirect Japanese influence over Korea while maintaining nominal Korean sovereignty — partial colonization rather than formal annexation.
He believed that gradual modernization under Japanese supervision would produce a stable pro-Japanese Korean state at lower political cost than direct rule.
Korean resistance to the protectorate was significant from the start.
The Korean Emperor Gojong, who had been forced to sign the Eulsa Treaty under coercion, attempted to appeal to the international community for support.
He sent secret emissaries to The Hague in 1907 to address the Second International Peace Conference, formally protesting that the Eulsa Treaty had been imposed by force and was therefore invalid.
The conference refused to receive the Korean emissaries (none of the great powers wanted to oppose Japanese policy in Korea, and Britain in particular was bound by the Anglo-Japanese Alliance).

Itō, learning of the appeal, forced Gojong to abdicate in favor of his son Sunjong in July 1907, dissolved the Korean army (provoking armed resistance from disbanded soldiers that fed the Righteous Army guerrilla movement of 1907–10), and tightened Japanese administrative control over the Korean state.
The guerrilla resistance was extensive.

From 1907 to 1910, an estimated 17,000 Korean fighters engaged Japanese troops and Korean police across the peninsula, and approximately 12,000 were killed before the resistance was largely suppressed.
The Japanese army deployed roughly 50,000 troops to Korea over the period.

The casualties on both sides were significant, and the brutality of the Japanese counterinsurgency campaign — including village-level reprisals, public executions, and forced confessions — established a pattern that would be repeated in Manchuria, China, and Southeast Asia in the following decades.

In October 1909, Itō Hirobumi was assassinated at Harbin railway station in Manchuria by the Korean nationalist An Jung-geun, who shot him three times during what was supposed to be a meeting between Itō and a Russian envoy.
Itō was sixty-eight years old.
He had been the Meiji oligarch most closely associated with constitutional government, restraint in foreign policy, and the indirect-rule preference for Korea.
His death removed the last senior voice in Tokyo for a softer Korea policy.
An Jung-geun was tried and executed in March 1910; he remains a national hero in modern South Korea.
The path was now clear for formal annexation.
The Japan-Korea Treaty of 1910, signed August 22, 1910, and proclaimed August 29, formally annexed Korea to the Japanese empire.
The 519-year Joseon dynasty (which had ruled Korea since 1392; Joseon Korea Ch 1) ended.
Korea became the Japanese colony of Chōsen (the Japanese reading of "Joseon"), administered by a Japanese Government-General based in Seoul.
The annexation would last 35 years, until Japan's defeat in the Pacific War in August 1945.

The colonial period would produce extraordinary economic infrastructure development (industrial plant, railways, ports, schools, modern administrative apparatus), simultaneous extraordinary cultural suppression (forced adoption of Japanese names, suppression of Korean language in education, conscription of Korean labor for wartime industry, conscription of Korean women into military sexual slavery as the comfort women system), and a legacy of bilateral antagonism that still shapes East Asian politics today.
Modern South Korean and Japanese governments continue to dispute, more than a century later, the legitimacy of the original annexation and the nature of subsequent colonial conduct.
The annexation was the formal completion of the Japanese imperial project.

The empire now consisted of the home islands, Taiwan (since 1895), the Pescadores, the Liaodong lease (Port Arthur and the surrounding Kwantung Leased Territory), the South Manchuria Railway zone, southern Sakhalin (since 1905), and Korea (since 1910).
Japan had become, in fifteen years, the only Asian colonial power.
The Meiji slogan fukoku kyōhei ("rich country, strong army") had been achieved in both parts.
The country was rich (industrially) and the army was strong (having defeated both China and Russia).
The original purpose of the Restoration — to make Japan capable of resisting Western dictation — had been accomplished.
What had been unclear in 1868 was that the project's logic would not stop at parity.
The same institutional and ideological apparatus that had produced parity by 1900 would, by 1910, have produced an empire of its own.

By 1931 it would produce the invasion of Manchuria; by 1937, the invasion of China; by 1941, the war with the United States; by 1945, the destruction of Hiroshima and Nagasaki and the end of the Japanese empire.
The Meiji Emperor died on July 30, 1912, aged fifty-nine, of complications from diabetes and uremia.
His final illness had begun in early July; the public had been informed of the seriousness of his condition only in the final days.
The nation went into formal mourning.

The state funeral, held on September 13, 1912, was the most elaborate ceremonial event in Japanese history to that point, attended by representatives of every nation that maintained diplomatic relations with Japan and broadcast by international press to the entire world.
The funeral procession through Tokyo took several hours; hundreds of thousands of Japanese citizens lined the route in silent mourning.

The Western press treated the event as the death of one of the great monarchs of the age — comparable to Queen Victoria, on whom Meiji had been measured throughout his reign by Japanese and Western observers alike.
Mutsuhito (Emperor Meiji) had been a remarkable monarch in a specific sense.

He had presided over the most rapid national transformation in modern history; he had attended cabinet meetings, signed the constitution, dressed in Western military uniform after 1872, opened the first Diet session, presided over military victories over China and Russia, accepted the annexation of Korea.
He had not, however, exercised significant personal political power.
The Meiji oligarchs had used him as the constitutional symbol of the new state without giving him operational authority over policy.

His personal preferences on most major decisions are not knowable from the surviving documents — the structural deference of the Meiji state to imperial authority masked the actual political dynamics, and most of the relevant private correspondence was destroyed during the imperial-era information control of the early twentieth century.

The historian Donald Keene's massive 2002 biography Emperor of Japan: Meiji and His World concluded that Mutsuhito was probably more politically active than the standard accounts suggest, but that the deliberate opacity around imperial decision-making makes a full reconstruction impossible.
What is clear is that Mutsuhito was the personal symbol around which the entire Meiji project had been organized.
His death closed an era in a literal sense.

The era name Meiji was retired; his son and successor took the throne as the Taishō Emperor ("great righteousness"), opening the brief Taishō era (1912–26) that would see the high tide of Japanese parliamentary government and the early erosion of the Meiji constitutional system.
Mutsuhito's body was buried at the Momoyama Imperial Mausoleum outside Kyoto.

The plans for the Meiji Shrine in the Yoyogi district of Tokyo, dedicated to his deified spirit, began immediately and the shrine was completed in 1920 — its surrounding forest planted with 100,000 trees donated from across Japan and the colonies, including the new colony of Korea.
On the evening of the imperial funeral, September 13, 1912, General Nogi Maresuke committed ritual suicide at his Tokyo home.
Nogi had been the commander at the siege of Port Arthur, where he had lost both his sons.
He had served as president of the Peers' School (Gakushūin), educating the imperial princes, in the years after the Russo-Japanese War.
He was sixty-three years old.

According to the suicide note he left, he had been preparing to die since the Battle of Kumamoto in 1877, when as a young officer he had lost his regimental banner to Saigō Takamori's Satsuma rebels — a disgrace that he had concluded could only be expiated by his death, and that he had been waiting since 1877 for a suitable occasion to perform.
The death of his emperor was that occasion.

Nogi waited until the imperial funeral procession had passed through Tokyo's central avenue, then returned home with his wife Shizuko (who had agreed to die with him), wrote his suicide notes, dressed in formal military uniform, and committed seppuku.
Shizuko cut her own throat with a dagger.

The junshi (ritual suicide following one's lord into death) was an ancient samurai practice that had been formally banned by the Tokugawa shogunate in 1663 and had not been performed publicly in Japan for over two centuries.
Nogi's revival of the practice in 1912 — at the moment of the death of the emperor who had presided over the modernization of Japan — was a deliberate symbolic statement.

He was offering himself as the last samurai of the imperial line, dying for an emperor whose new Japan had no formal place for samurai, in the traditional manner that samurai had honored their lords for a thousand years.
The reaction was extraordinary.
Japanese public opinion was deeply divided.

Many older Japanese — including ex-samurai, military officers, and traditionalists — celebrated Nogi as the noblest possible expression of imperial loyalty, the perfect samurai who had given his life for his lord even after the institutional samurai class no longer existed.

Younger and more Westernized Japanese were horrified — newspapers carried editorials denouncing the suicide as feudal anachronism, as ritual murder of his wife, as a regression to a medieval mentality the Meiji project had supposedly transcended.
The novelist Mori Ōgai wrote The Abe Family (Abe Ichizoku, 1913) explicitly in response to Nogi's death, examining the ethics of junshi from a deliberately ambivalent perspective.

Natsume Sōseki wrote Kokoro (1914), one of the masterpieces of modern Japanese literature, around a parallel story of a Meiji-era suicide motivated by guilt and honor — the protagonist explicitly cites Nogi's suicide as the trigger for his own decision to die.
Nogi's death encapsulated, in one event, the unresolved tension at the heart of the Meiji project.
The country had modernized at extraordinary speed.
The institutional structures of Edo Japan — the warrior class, the four-tier social hierarchy, the daimyō system, the closed borders — had been dismantled.

But the cultural sensibility of the warrior class — the conviction that the willing sacrifice of life for one's lord was the highest moral act, the ritual centrality of seppuku as an honorable death, the assumption that personal honor was inseparable from loyalty to the state — had not been dismantled.
It had been preserved, repackaged, and elevated to the central organizing principle of the new imperial nationalism.

Nogi was the perfect Meiji subject: a modernized military officer commanding an army with German rifles, a victor in the most modern war yet fought in Asia, a man who had read Western books and spoken European languages, who had also held within himself the absolute samurai ethic that made his suicide on the night of his lord's funeral the inevitable culmination of his life's logic.
The Meiji project had produced him.
The Meiji project would, three decades later, produce ten thousand kamikaze pilots whose willingness to die for the emperor would be the same ethic on a larger scale.
So what was the legacy?
In the narrowest accounting, the Meiji project had accomplished, in forty-four years, the most successful crash modernization in world history.

A pre-industrial agrarian feudal monarchy had been transformed into a constitutional monarchy with industrial production, modern military forces, modern infrastructure, near-universal literacy, integrated international finance, and a colonial empire.
The original strategic goal — preserving Japanese sovereignty against Western pressure — had been completely achieved.
The unequal treaties had been revised.
Japan was a recognized great power.
No country in the modern era has matched the speed of the transformation, and few have matched its thoroughness.
In a slightly broader accounting, the Meiji project had produced a model of late industrialization that subsequent non-Western states would study and partially replicate for the next century.

The South Korean and Taiwanese miracles of the 1960s–80s, the Singaporean transformation, the post-Mao Chinese economic restructuring, the late-twentieth-century Vietnamese reforms — all drew, more or less consciously, on the Meiji template of state-directed industrialization, strategic protection of pilot industries, recycled export earnings, tight integration of finance and industry, mass education at a national scale, and selective borrowing of foreign institutional designs.
The Meiji oligarchs invented out of desperation what became the standard manual for Asian late industrialization.
In a still broader accounting, the Meiji project also produced the institutional and ideological substrate for the Japanese militarist disasters of 1931–45.

The Meiji Constitution's structural separation of military command from civilian control gave the army and navy the constitutional independence to conduct foreign policy on their own initiative once the founding genrō died.

The kokutai ideology and the Imperial Rescript on Education had built a population willing to die for the imperial state in extraordinary numbers and unwilling to question the moral legitimacy of imperial expansion.
The Meiji-era zaibatsu had built the industrial base that could sustain continental aggression.

The Meiji-era army had built the institutional culture and the doctrinal framework that would, in the 1930s, conclude that controlling Manchuria was a strategic necessity, that controlling China was a strategic necessity, that controlling Southeast Asia was a strategic necessity, that war with the United States was an acceptable risk in pursuit of these necessities.
The Meiji-era navy had built the fleet that bombed Pearl Harbor in 1941.

The same institutional and ideological apparatus that had produced equality with the Western powers by 1900 would, by 1945, have produced the destruction of Japan and the deaths of millions of people across East Asia and the Pacific.
The honest accounting therefore has to hold both halves together.
Meiji Japan was an extraordinary achievement and a foundational catastrophe.
The achievements — universal literacy, industrial modernization, sovereignty, constitutional government, international standing — were real and lasting.

The catastrophes — the colonial brutality in Korea and Taiwan, the Manchurian and Chinese aggression, the Pacific War, the comfort women, the firebombings of Tokyo and Osaka and Yokohama, the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, the ten million Asian dead from Japanese military operations between 1931 and 1945 — were also real and lasting.
Both products came out of the same project.
The same Meiji constitution that built a parliament also gave the army the autonomy to seize Manchuria.
The same Imperial Rescript that built mass literacy also produced the kamikaze pilots.
The same zaibatsu industrial base that lifted Japan out of the agrarian past also built the warships that fought at Midway.
The institutional and ideological design that the Meiji oligarchs settled on between 1868 and 1900 had both the success and the disaster latent within it.
The post-1945 American occupation rewrote the constitution, dismantled the zaibatsu, abolished State Shinto's official status, and de-deified the imperial line.
The kokutai ideology was officially repudiated; the Imperial Rescript on Education was withdrawn from schools.
The post-1945 Japan that emerged — democratic, demilitarized, oriented toward economic growth rather than military expansion — was deliberately built on different foundations.

The post-1945 Japanese economic miracle of the 1950s–80s replicated many features of the Meiji developmentalist state model but in a constitutional and ideological context that ruled out the militarist outcome.
The contemporary Japan of the early twenty-first century is one of the most peaceful, prosperous, and democratic societies in the world.
But the contemporary Japan also still contains, encoded in its institutional and cultural DNA, the residues of the Meiji synthesis.
The unbroken imperial line is still there, no longer divine but still ceremonially central.
Yasukuni Shrine is still there, still controversial.
The bureaucratic state is still recognizably descended from the Meiji bureaucracy.
The keiretsu corporations are still recognizably descended from the zaibatsu.
Modern Japan is the heir of Meiji Japan in ways that are easy to underestimate.
That is the legacy.
A modernization project so successful that it produced the most rapid national transformation in history, and so flawed that it produced the most catastrophic Asian war of the twentieth century.
Both halves of the inheritance are still alive.
Both halves still matter.
The Meiji oligarchs would have understood the achievement and would not have foreseen the catastrophe.
They were building, consciously, the country that could survive in the world they saw.
They built it.
The world the country they built then went to war with — the world of 1941 — they could not have foreseen, and probably would not have approved of.
But they built the operating system that produced it, and the operating system produced what it produced.
The era closed in 1912.
The consequences are still running.

Cross-civ check: the Meiji legacy fits into a broader pattern of nineteenth- and twentieth-century state-building projects whose institutional designs produced both extraordinary achievements and catastrophic failures from the same operating logic.

Bismarckian Germany is the obvious comparison — the same constitutional design (Prussian model with strong monarchy, weak parliament, autonomous military, strong civil service), the same combination of industrial modernization with militarist-nationalist ideology, the same transition from founding-generation political control to military-bureaucratic dominance, the same eventual catastrophic war.

The German operating system produced the achievements of the Wilhelmine industrial economy and the catastrophe of 1914–18; the Meiji operating system produced the achievements of the late-Meiji industrial economy and the catastrophe of 1937–45.
Both states then rebuilt themselves after defeat under American supervision and produced second-act success stories — the West German economic miracle, the Japanese postwar miracle.
The structural parallels are unmistakable.

Soviet Russia is the more remote comparison — a different ideological framework, but the same logic of crash modernization at extraordinary human cost producing an extraordinary military-industrial state that then committed catastrophic strategic and humanitarian errors.
Republican-period China under the Kuomintang attempted a Meiji-style modernization in the 1920s and 1930s but lacked the institutional unity to execute it.
The post-1949 Chinese Communist project succeeded in the modernization where the KMT had failed but at far higher human cost.

Nasser's Egypt, Park's South Korea, Atatürk's Turkey (Ottoman Empire Ch 12), Kemalist secularism — every twentieth-century late-modernizing state has, in some sense, been working through the questions the Meiji oligarchs first put on the table in 1868.
None of them have entirely answered the questions.
The success-and-disaster ambivalence at the heart of the Meiji project is the success-and-disaster ambivalence at the heart of all of them.
That is the long arc.
Meiji is over.
What it built is not.

chapters.title: Yamen and the End of Song
sentences: The Yuan dynasty began with a child being drowned.

On March 19, 1279, in the bay of the Pearl River estuary in modern Guangdong, on the southern coast of China, the Song minister Lu Xiufu (LOO shyoo-FOO) carried the eight-year-old Emperor Bing of Song to the deck of his imperial flagship.
Lu told the boy that they could not allow themselves to be captured.
He bound the child to his back with a sash.
They jumped together into the South China Sea.
Both drowned.
Other loyalists followed.

The chronicle accounts say more than 100,000 Song officials, soldiers, palace women, and civilian followers either jumped into the sea after Lu Xiufu and Emperor Bing or refused capture and fought to the death on their burning ships.
The bodies were said to wash ashore for days afterward.
Local fishermen reportedly recognized the imperial robes on a small body that washed up some days later, identified it as Emperor Bing, and secretly buried him.
A small temple was eventually built at the burial site near modern Hong Kong; it still stands.
The naval battle that triggered the suicide was called Yamen (yah-MEN).

It was the last engagement of a six-decade Mongol war against the Song dynasty — the wealthiest and most technologically sophisticated state on Earth (Tang-Song China Ch 6 covers Song economic and technological supremacy).
The Mongol commander at Yamen was Zhang Hongfan, a Chinese general in Mongol service.
The Song fleet — by now reduced to roughly a thousand ships, with the boy emperor and the loyalist court aboard the largest — had taken refuge in the bay.
The Mongol fleet trapped them.
The battle that followed lasted hours and was not really a contest.
The Song's gunpowder weapons (Tang-Song China Ch 7) could not change the outcome.
Defeat was certain by midmorning.
The Song dynasty was over after 319 years (counting from its founding in 960).
For the first time in Chinese history, all of China — every region, every population, every city, every political institution — was under foreign rule.
The dynasty that did the conquering called itself the Yuan (yoo-AHN — meaning "primal" or "origin").
Its founding emperor, Kublai Khan (KOO-bligh KAHN), was a grandson of Genghis Khan (Mongol Empire Ch 2) and the most powerful single ruler on Earth at that moment.
The reign that began with the drowning of a child at Yamen would continue for fifteen more years and would lay the foundation of every Chinese dynasty for the next six hundred years.
This is the chapter about how the conquest finished.
To understand Yamen, you have to understand the seventy-five-year process that led to it.
The Mongol war against China began in 1211, when Genghis Khan crossed the Gobi and attacked the Jin dynasty that ruled north China (Mongol Empire Ch 3).

The Jin were not Chinese — they were Jurchen, a Tungusic-speaking semi-nomadic people from Manchuria who had conquered north China from the Khitan Liao in the 1120s and crushed the Northern Song at Kaifeng in 1127 (Tang-Song China Ch 8 covers the Jingkang Incident).
For a century the Jurchen Jin had ruled north China while the Han Chinese Southern Song held the southern half from Hangzhou.
The Mongol conquest of the Jin took twenty-three years and ended with the destruction of the Jin capital at Kaifeng in 1234.

The death toll across north China was apocalyptic — Mongol commanders had originally proposed converting the entire region to grassland by killing the Han farmers, a plan only deflected by the Khitan minister Yelü Chucai (YEH-loo choo-TSIGH), who argued that taxing live peasants would generate more revenue than letting cavalry graze the cleared land.
The Southern Song should have been next.

They were not, immediately, because the Mongol Empire spent the next three decades expanding everywhere else — into Persia under Hülegü (Mongol Empire Ch 5), into Russia under Batu (Mongol Empire Ch 4), into eastern Europe up to the gates of Vienna in 1241.
But after Möngke Khan became Great Khan in 1251, the Southern Song campaign resumed seriously.
Möngke himself led an invasion in 1258.

He died in southern China in August 1259 — possibly of dysentery, possibly of a Song-fired catapult stone — and the campaign paused for the Toluid Civil War (1260–1264), in which his brothers Kublai and Ariq Böke fought over the succession (Mongol Empire Ch 6).
Kublai won.
He was Great Khan from 1264 onward.

But by then the Mongol Empire had effectively split into four khanates — Kublai's in China and Mongolia, the Ilkhanate in Persia and Iraq, the Golden Horde in the western steppe, the Chagatai Khanate in Central Asia — and Kublai's claim to be emperor of all of them was theoretical at best (Mongol Empire Ch 7 covers the four khanates).
What he actually ruled, in practice, was north China, Mongolia, and bits of the eastern steppe.
The Southern Song still held the wealthier half of China south of the Huai River.
In 1271, Kublai formally proclaimed the Yuan dynasty.

The proclamation was a deliberate Sinification — Kublai was claiming the Mandate of Heaven (Ancient China Ch 5), the Chinese theological doctrine that legitimate rule was conferred by the cosmic order on a single dynasty at a time.

By taking the Mandate, he was claiming continuity with the long sequence of Chinese dynasties stretching back through the Han (Han Dynasty Ch 1), the Qin (Qin Dynasty Ch 1), and the Zhou (Zhou Dynasty Ch 1) all the way to the legendary Xia.
He was also claiming, implicitly, that the Southern Song no longer held the Mandate.
The Mandate moved when the dynasty changed.
The new dynasty was Yuan.
Therefore the Song had to go.
The launching of the final Song campaigns followed almost immediately.
The decisive campaign was the siege of Xiangyang (shyahng-YANG), 1267–1273.
Xiangyang was a heavily fortified Song city on the Han River, a major tributary of the Yangtze.
It commanded the corridor through which any Mongol force coming south would have to pass to reach the Yangtze valley.
The Song garrison commander Lü Wenhuan (LOO wen-HWAHN) defended Xiangyang for six years against repeated Mongol assault.

The Mongols had perfected most of the conventional siege techniques — encirclement, starvation, mining, conventional bombardment — but Xiangyang's walls were exceptional and Mongol assaults had repeatedly failed.
What broke Xiangyang was technology imported across the Mongol Empire.

In 1271, Kublai's court hired two Persian engineers — Ismail and Ala al-Din, both from the Ilkhanate, both specialists in counterweight artillery — to come to China and design siege machines that could throw projectiles heavy enough to crack the Xiangyang walls.
The engineers built what the Chinese sources called huihui pao ("Muslim machines") — counterweight trebuchets capable of hurling stones of approximately 220 pounds (100 kg) over 200 yards.

These were the same machines that European armies were beginning to deploy after a century of Crusader-Mediterranean engineering refinement, the Mongol communications network having transmitted the technology eastward across Eurasia.
The trebuchets broke through Xiangyang's walls in early 1273.
The garrison surrendered.
The Yangtze defensive line was broken.

The whole episode is a small case study in how the Pax Mongolica worked in practice (Chapter 6 will return to this idea at scale): an engineering technique developed in the Latin Crusader-Islamic interface, refined under Mongol patronage in Persia, transmitted to China by Mongol-employed Persians, and used to break a Chinese fortress that Chinese siege technology could not crack.
The Mongol Empire, even at the moment when it was disintegrating politically, was the Eurasian conduit through which everyone learned everyone else's technology.
Xiangyang fell because Persia and the Mediterranean had a better trebuchet than China did.
After Xiangyang's fall, the Mongol advance accelerated.
Kublai sent his Mongol-Chinese commander Bayan (BIGH-yahn), one of the most capable generals of the era, with a large army down the Yangtze valley.
Song defenses crumbled.

The capital Hangzhou — at the time perhaps the largest and richest city in the world, with a population of well over a million (Tang-Song China Ch 8) — surrendered in early 1276 under the regent dowager empress, who handed over the imperial seals along with the six-year-old Emperor Gong.
The boy emperor and most of the Hangzhou court were sent to Beijing as captives.
Gong would later be sent further west, become a Tibetan Buddhist monk, and die in obscurity in the 1320s.

The Hangzhou capitulation paralleled, in dynastic-trauma terms, the Jingkang Incident a century and a half earlier (Tang-Song China Ch 8), except that this time the conquerors were the Mongols rather than the Jurchen, and the Song had nowhere left to retreat to except the South China Sea.
The Song dynasty was not yet quite finished, however.
Loyalist officials had escaped from Hangzhou with two of the boy emperor's younger half-brothers and with the remnants of the Song navy.
They proclaimed one of the brothers as Emperor Duanzong in southern China and continued resisting.
Duanzong died in 1278, possibly of injuries from an accident at sea or possibly of disease.
The loyalists then proclaimed his even younger half-brother — a six-year-old named Zhao Bing — as Emperor Bing of Song.
They were now operating as a coastal-fortress and naval-resistance force in modern Guangdong, with the Mongol fleet relentlessly closing in.
That set the stage for Yamen.
The cliff suicide at Yamen demands a pause.

The Song minister Lu Xiufu is not quite the household name in the Anglophone world that the equivalent loyalist figures of Western Roman or Byzantine history are, but in the long memory of Chinese moral culture he is something close to canonical.

He, the loyalist minister Wen Tianxiang (wen tyahn-SHYAHNG, who refused to defect to Kublai's service after his capture and was executed at Khanbaliq in 1283), and the admiral Zhang Shijie (drowned in the same Yamen rout) are remembered together as the Three Loyal Subjects of the Song.
Wen Tianxiang in particular wrote a patriotic poem called Crossing Lingding Sea during his post-capture imprisonment that became one of the most quoted texts in subsequent Chinese culture.

The closing couplet — since ancient times no man has not died; let me leave a heart of loyalty to illuminate history — has been memorized by Chinese schoolchildren for the seven and a half centuries since.
What this is, structurally, is the establishment of a moral category that did not really exist in earlier Chinese political culture in quite this developed form: the dynastic-loyalty martyr.
The category had Confucian roots — the Han-era idea that a minister owed his lord total fidelity, even unto death (Han Dynasty Ch 4).

But the Song collapse, with its drowned child emperor and its mass suicides in the bay, gave the category an emotional density and a specific iconography that subsequent Chinese moral discourse repeatedly returned to.
Every later dynasty that fell — the Yuan to the Ming, the Ming to the Qing, the Qing to the Republic — produced its own loyalist-martyr figures, each consciously modeled on the Song precedent.
The image of Lu Xiufu binding the child emperor to his back and walking into the sea became one of the foundational episodes of the Chinese moral imagination.

It is worth pausing on this for the same reason it is worth pausing on the fall of Constantinople in 1453 (Byzantine Empire Ch 12) or the suicide of Cleopatra (Late Egypt Ch 8): some events are not merely historical, they are templates that subsequent civilizations reach for when they need to think about ending.

The dynasty Lu Xiufu died for had, in its Northern and Southern phases combined, presided over the most innovative society on Earth — the world's first paper money (1024), the world's first practical movable type (c. 1040), the magnetic navigation compass, weaponized gunpowder, and the most sophisticated bureaucratic state Eurasia had yet seen (Tang-Song China Ch 6).
What replaced it was a Mongol cavalry empire ruled from the steppe-and-China frontier by people who could not, in 1279, read a single line of Chinese.
That this transition produced anything other than total cultural catastrophe — which it did, eventually — is one of the more remarkable stories in Chinese political history.
The next chapter is about how Kublai began to build a state that could rule China without being absorbed by it and without destroying it.
The cost of the Mongol conquest of China deserves its own paragraph, because the surviving evidence suggests it was one of the worst demographic disasters in pre-modern history.

The systematic Mongol destruction of north China between 1211 and 1234 — the Jin war — is estimated by modern population historians to have reduced the registered population of the former Jin territories from roughly 50 million in 1207 to perhaps 8 to 10 million in the 1230s.

Some of this is plain killing, some is massacre survivors fleeing south (where they show up in Southern Song registries), some is the registry collapsing along with the state's ability to count anyone, and some is genuine demographic collapse from famine and epidemic.

The numbers are debated and probably overstated in the worst direction — early-modern estimates of Mongol massacre tolls were often inflated for moral effect — but even the conservative estimates indicate massive population losses.

The contrast with the Mongol war against the Southern Song from 1268 to 1279, by which point Kublai's policy was Sinifying and the Mongol commanders were under orders to spare cities that surrendered, is sharp.
The Southern Song was conquered with a tenth of the human cost of the Jin.
By 1279 the Mongols had learned that Chinese tax registers were more useful with Chinese taxpayers still attached.
This learning curve is one of the underrated structural facts of Yuan history.
The dynasty that emerged in 1279 was very different from the dynasty that would have emerged if Mongol policy had not changed in the 1240s and 1250s.
Yelü Chucai had won the argument for "tax don't massacre" by the time of his death in 1244 (Mongol Empire Ch 4); Kublai had absorbed the lesson by the time he was an adult.

The Yuan policy toward the conquered Han population — restrictive, discriminatory, but not annihilationist — is what allowed the south Chinese economy to survive intact and continue producing the silk, porcelain, and rice tax revenues that funded the rest of the empire.
But the Han population on which Kublai's new Chinese-style empire depended did not love its rulers.
The next chapter is about what Kublai did with that fact.

Cross-civ check: the Yuan conquest of the Song was contemporary with the height of the Crusader era's collapse — the fall of Acre, the last Crusader stronghold in the Levant, came in 1291, twelve years after Yamen.

The end of the Abbasid Caliphate in Baghdad had happened twenty-one years earlier, when Hülegü sacked the city in 1258 (Islamic Golden Age Ch 10) — the western parallel of the eastern Mongol campaign.
The Mamluks in Egypt had stopped Hülegü's western advance at Ayn Jalut in 1260 (Mongol Empire Ch 5), the only major battle the Mongols decisively lost in the thirteenth century.
Italy was approaching the early Renaissance — Dante was nine years old when Yamen was fought.
In Mali, the empire of Sundiata Keita had been founded in 1235 and was already the dominant power in West Africa.
In the Andes, the Chimú kingdom centered on Chan Chan was at its expansionary peak (Andean Kingdoms).
In Mesoamerica, the Aztec had not yet founded Tenochtitlán — that would come in 1325, forty-six years after Yamen (Aztec Empire Ch 1).
The thirteenth century, viewed from the perspective of the Mongol Empire, was the moment when Eurasia was briefly unified under a single political-military order.
The fall of Hangzhou and the drowning at Yamen completed the unification.
From 1279 to roughly 1340, the entire Eurasian landmass from Korea to Hungary was within reach of a single set of postal stations, trade passports, and inter-elite kinship networks.
That period will be the subject of Chapter 6.

chapters.title: Kublai's New Capital
sentences: The dynasty Lu Xiufu drowned for had been ruled from Hangzhou (Tang-Song China Ch 8), a southern coastal city of canals and gardens that the Italians who later visited it called the most beautiful city in the world.
The dynasty that replaced it was ruled from a city that did not yet exist when Kublai started building it.
That city was Khanbaliq (kahn-BAH-lik) — Mongolian for "city of the Khan" — known in Chinese as Dadu (DAH-doo, "great capital") and to modern history as Beijing.
Kublai began constructing it in 1267, on the site of the former Jin capital that the Mongols had destroyed in 1215, with the Han architect Liu Bingzhong (LYOH bing-JONG) as his chief designer.
By 1271, the year Kublai proclaimed the Yuan, the inner palace city was complete enough to hold court ceremonies.
By 1285 the entire urban complex was finished.
It was the most ambitious single act of urban construction in thirteenth-century Eurasia.
The choice of site is not obvious.

Beijing is far north for a Chinese imperial capital — closer to the Mongolian steppe than to the productive farmland of the Yellow River valley, much closer to the steppe than to the Yangtze south where the dynasty's tax base actually lived.
Earlier Chinese capitals had been at Chang'an (Tang-Song China Ch 2 — the Tang capital), at Luoyang, at Kaifeng (the Northern Song capital), at Hangzhou (the Southern Song capital).
All of these were further south, on the rivers, in the rice and wheat country.
Khanbaliq was in the dry north, on a plain with no major river, requiring grain to be shipped in from a thousand miles south.
The choice was political.
Kublai wanted a capital that was equally accessible from the steppe — where his Mongol political base lived — and from China — where his tax base lived.
He wanted to be able to ride out into Mongolia for the summer hunts that were core to Mongol elite identity, and ride back into the Chinese imperial palace for the winter administrative season.
He wanted a capital that the Mongol nobility would not feel had been culturally captured by China.
Khanbaliq was the geographic compromise: a Chinese city by architecture, a steppe-frontier city by location.
It was also enormously expensive.

The grain-supply problem alone — feeding a quarter-million-person capital city in a region that could not produce nearly enough grain locally — required Kublai to undertake the second great public-works project of his reign: the extension of the Grand Canal.

The original Grand Canal had been built by the Sui dynasty in the early 600s (Tang-Song China Ch 1 covers the Sui canal program), connecting the Yangtze valley to the old northern capitals at Luoyang and Kaifeng.
Kublai's problem was that Khanbaliq was further north than the canal's old terminus, and the canal itself had silted up in many sections after centuries of war and neglect.
Between 1283 and 1293, Kublai's engineers cut a new northern leg through Shandong directly to Khanbaliq, the so-called Tonghui Canal sections, with roughly 200,000 conscripted laborers.
The new route shortened the southern grain shipment by hundreds of miles.
By 1293, southern rice was reaching Khanbaliq's granaries by inland water transport.

The supplemental maritime grain transport route, launched in 1282, sent ocean convoys of hundreds of ships annually around the Shandong peninsula — an early demonstration of large-scale Chinese maritime logistics that was ancestral, a century later, to the Ming Treasure Voyages under Admiral Zheng He.

All of this — the city, the canal, the maritime route — was effectively built so that several thousand Mongols could live in Chinese-style luxury at the steppe-China interface while drawing their food supply from the Yangtze delta.

The political economy of Yuan rule was strange in just this way: a small foreign elite, supported by a vast Chinese infrastructure, maintained at enormous expense to bridge the cultural distance between rulers and ruled.
The architecture of Khanbaliq itself was a piece of political theater.

The city was laid out on the classic Chinese imperial grid — three concentric walls (an outer city, an inner city, and the Forbidden Palace at the center), oriented north-south, with nine major north-south avenues and nine major east-west avenues at grand symbolic dimensions.
The plan deliberately echoed the old Tang capital at Chang'an (Tang-Song China Ch 2).
Liu Bingzhong, Kublai's chief architect, had been trained in classical Chinese geomantic theory and laid out the city by fengshui principles.

Inside, the Mongol court conducted Confucian-style rituals — the emperor performed the Spring Plowing ceremony at a specially built altar, sacrificed at the imperial ancestral temple, and held court audiences in a hall whose proportions and furnishings could have come from any Tang or Song dynasty capital.
But the architectural surface concealed a more complicated reality.
The interior of the palace contained Mongol felt yurts erected on the inner courts so the imperial family could sleep in the structures their ancestors had used on the steppe.

The Forbidden City Kublai built was bigger and grander than any Chinese imperial precedent, but it incorporated specifically Mongol design elements — broader audience halls to accommodate large keshig contingents, a separate Mongol noble compound, designated spaces for raised platforms and large communal feasts in the steppe style.

The Beihai White Pagoda, completed in 1271, was a Tibetan-style stupa designed by the Nepali Buddhist architect Aniko (AH-nih-koh), set at the symbolic center of the imperial city — a Tibetan religious form at imperial Chinese scale, in the heart of a Chinese-style capital, designed by a Himalayan craftsman, for a Mongol emperor.
The Beihai pagoda is the visual epitome of the Yuan synthesis.
It still stands.
The city Kublai built became China's permanent capital for the next seven centuries.

The Ming would briefly relocate to Nanjing after 1368 but would move back to Beijing under the Yongle Emperor in the 1420s, rebuilding the inner palace into the Forbidden City that tourists visit today.
The Qing, who replaced the Ming in 1644, kept Beijing.
The Republic, the People's Republic — all of them ruled from the city that Kublai laid out.
Beijing as the political center of China is one of the few institutional decisions of the Yuan that survived everything that came after.
The capital that the dynasty needed to bridge steppe and China became the capital that Chinese politics has been organized around ever since.
The political problem Kublai had to solve, once Khanbaliq was built and the conquest was complete, was governance.

The Mongol Empire had inherited from Genghis a basic administrative philosophy: rule through your own hereditary military aristocracy at the top, employ specialist subject peoples for technical functions, tax everybody, spare nobody who resisted.
This had worked across the steppe and in Persia (Mongol Empire Ch 7).
It would not work in China, for two reasons.
One was scale — China's tax population was at least sixty million people, vastly larger than the Mongol nobility could administer directly.

The other was institutional sophistication — the Tang-Song administrative system Kublai had inherited (Tang-Song China Ch 6) was the most refined civilian bureaucracy in the world, with detailed tax registries, standardized weights and measures, a Confucian examination-trained official class, and centuries of precedent for every category of administrative decision.
To dismantle it would have been suicidal.
To run it required Han Chinese officials.
But the Mongol nobility had no intention of letting Han Chinese officials run anything important.
The compromise Kublai imposed in 1271 was the four-class ethnic system.
Yuan subjects were classified into four legal castes.
At the top were Mongols themselves — the conquering elite, perhaps 1 to 2 percent of the population, with first call on every senior office, military command, and provincial governorship.

Just below were the Semu (SUH-moo, "various categories" — also rendered Semu ren, "people of various categories") — a heterogeneous category covering Central Asians, Persians, Uyghurs, Arabs, Tibetans, Tanguts, and basically anyone from the western Mongol Empire who was not Han.
Semu were reserved primarily for tax administration, treasury work, and other middle-level fiscal positions.
Below the Semu were northern Han — former Jin subjects, including ethnic Khitan, Jurchen, and Korean populations along with the Han Chinese majority of north China.

Below the northern Han were southern Han — former Southern Song subjects, the populous and wealthy bulk of the empire's tax base, excluded from senior office and from most military commands as a matter of explicit policy.
The system governed taxation, judicial penalties, official appointments, military recruitment, and even seating at official ceremonies.
Penalties for the same crime varied by caste — a Mongol who killed a Han owed a small wergild, a Han who struck a Mongol could be executed.
Court positions were quotaed by caste.
The civil-service examinations (when they were running at all — see below) had separate easier exams and higher quotas for Mongols and Semu than for the two Han categories.
Intermarriage between castes was technically permitted but socially and politically disincentivized.
This is the part of Yuan governance that strikes the modern reader as most intolerable, and it deserves direct treatment rather than evasion.
The four-class system was an explicit racial-ethnic legal hierarchy imposed on a conquered population by a conquering minority.

Modern apologists have argued it was fluid in practice and porous at the edges, which is true to some degree — there were Han generals in the Mongol army, there were Han officials at high court positions, and the boundary between northern and southern Han was sometimes ignored.

But the fundamental architecture of Yuan rule was that the conquering Mongol minority sat on top of the Han majority by legal right, and that the highest positions in the state were systematically reserved for non-Han personnel.

The system was specifically designed to prevent the Mongol ruling class from being absorbed into Chinese society — to prevent, in other words, what had happened to every previous foreign dynasty that had ruled bits of China (the Khitan Liao, the Jurchen Jin, the Tangut Western Xia), all of which had culturally Sinified within a few generations until they were Chinese in everything but name.
The four-class system worked, in a narrow sense — the Mongol elite did not Sinify in the way the Khitan and Jurchen had — but it produced a permanent legitimacy crisis.
The Han majority knew it was being ruled by foreigners by explicit legal right, not by Chinese-style imperial legitimacy.
Every late-Yuan rebellion would explicitly invoke this fact.
The Red Turban rebellions of the 1350s (Chapter 7) would frame their uprising as the "expulsion of the barbarians" by the rightful Han.
When Zhu Yuanzhang took Khanbaliq in 1368 (Chapter 8), his proclamations specifically denounced the four-class system as an offense against the Mandate of Heaven and announced its abolition.
Comparison helps.

The closest structural parallel is the Spanish casta system in colonial Latin America after roughly 1500 — a legal-racial hierarchy that placed peninsular Spanish at the top, criollos below, and elaborated mixed-race castes through every gradation down to indigenous and African at the bottom.
Like the Yuan system, the casta system was about preventing the conquering minority from being absorbed by the conquered majority.
Like the Yuan system, it produced enormous resentment, periodic uprisings, and an eventual political revolution that defined itself partly as the abolition of the racial hierarchy.

The major difference is that the Spanish casta system was rationalized by the Catholic Church in theological language, while the Yuan four-class system was rationalized in pragmatic Mongol-imperial language.
The structural logic was the same.
So, in the long run, was the political outcome.
To staff the middle and upper layers of Yuan administration — the layers Mongols themselves were too few to fill — Kublai relied heavily on the Semu category.
Semu were the Pax Mongolica's bureaucratic class.
Persian astronomers came east to staff Kublai's Bureau of Mathematics.
Uyghur Turkic-speakers staffed much of the chancery in the Mongolian-language paperwork system.
Central Asian Muslim merchants — the ortoq trading partnerships — handled large-scale commerce on behalf of the imperial family.

The most powerful single Semu official of Kublai's reign was Ahmad Fanakati (ah-MAHD fah-nah-KAH-tee), a Persian who ran the Yuan finance ministry from the 1260s through 1282 and whose ruthless tax-farming made him the most hated minister of the dynasty.
Ahmad was assassinated in 1282 by a conspiracy of Han officials and disgruntled Mongol notables.

His death is one of the few episodes from Kublai's domestic governance that Marco Polo describes in detail (Chapter 4) — Polo gives a politically loaded but substantially accurate account of the conspiracy.
The use of foreign tax-farmers was a deliberate policy choice.
By inserting Semu specialists between the Mongol military elite and the Han taxpaying population, Kublai insulated the conquering aristocracy from direct Han hostility.
When taxes were too high or collections too brutal, the visible enemy was the Persian or Uyghur administrator, not the Mongol khan.
This worked, to a degree, but it had its own costs — the Semu administrators became rich, politically powerful, and increasingly resented by both Mongol nobles and Han officials.
The Ahmad assassination is one example; the late-Yuan Ispah Rebellion at Quanzhou in the 1350s and 1360s (Chapter 6) is another.
Eventually, the Han backlash against Yuan governance would target the Semu communities almost as much as the Mongols themselves.
The most consequential single decision of Kublai's domestic governance was the suspension of the civil-service examinations.
The examinations had been the central recruiting mechanism of the Chinese state since the Sui-Tang reforms of the seventh century (Tang-Song China Ch 1 covers the original Sui examinations).
They tested candidates on Confucian classics, on classical Chinese composition, on policy essays — the whole Han literati cultural inheritance.
Successful candidates entered the bureaucracy.
The examinations were the path by which a man from a modest gentry family could rise to the highest positions in the state.
Under the Song they had become enormously elaborate and competitive (Tang-Song China Ch 6).
They were the institutional mechanism by which Chinese political culture reproduced itself.
Kublai suspended them in 1271 and did not restore them until 1315 — forty-four years during which the entire Han literati class was structurally locked out of the formal civil-service career path.
When the examinations were restored under Renzong (Kublai's grandson), the quotas were ethnically rigged to favor Mongols and Semu over the two Han categories.
Even at full operation under the late Yuan, the examinations passed only a tiny fraction of the candidates the Tang or Song had passed.
For practical purposes, the Han literati class spent the entire dynasty effectively excluded from the formal scholar-official career.
The consequence was one of the most important cultural ironies of the period.

With the formal ladder of Confucian advancement pulled away, displaced Han literati turned their educational training and cultural energy toward forms that did not require state patronage: vernacular drama, vernacular fiction, ink-on-paper landscape painting, calligraphy, occasional poetry, and political-protest art.

Yuan zaju opera (Chapter 5), the earliest stable forms of Romance of the Three Kingdoms and Water Margin, the literati landscape painting tradition of Huang Gongwang and the Four Yuan Masters (Chapter 5), the calligraphic revival under Zhao Mengfu (Chapter 5) — all of these emerged because the Yuan had closed off other outlets for the Han educated class.
The dynasty's most enduring cultural legacy is, in this sense, an unintended consequence of its most discriminatory policy.
The court Kublai built at Khanbaliq became, by the 1280s, the most cosmopolitan capital in pre-modern Asia.

It contained, simultaneously: Tibetan Buddhist monks led by the Phagpa Lama (PHAGS-pah, the Tibetan religious leader Drogön Chögyal Phagpa, whom Kublai named Imperial Preceptor in 1270 with political authority over Tibet); Nestorian Christian clerks of Önggüd Turkic background; Sunni Muslim engineers and astronomers like Ismail and Ala al-Din from the Ilkhanate (the same engineers who built the Xiangyang trebuchets); Confucian scholars from north and south China; Persian astronomers like Jamal al-Din, who arrived in 1267 from the Maragha observatory carrying instruments and astronomical tables; Italian merchants like the Polo brothers (Chapter 4); occasional Catholic missionaries from the Pope; Korean tribute envoys from the Goryeo court; Vietnamese embassies; and a permanent population of foreign craftsmen of every description.
The official religious policy continued the Yassa, the Mongol legal code attributed to Genghis Khan, with its principle of religious tolerance (Mongol Empire Ch 2).

Tibetan Buddhism was preferred at court — Kublai's chief consort Chabi was a devout Buddhist and a major patron of the Tibetan Buddhist establishment, and the Phagpa script (1269) Kublai commissioned from his Tibetan tutor was supposed to be the empire's universal script, although it never displaced Chinese characters in practical use.
But no religion was systematically persecuted, and the imperial treasury supported temples of all major faiths.
Buddhists, Daoists, Confucians, Nestorians, Catholics, Sunni Muslims, Shia Muslims, Manichaeans, Jews, and Tibetan tantric practitioners all had institutional space at Khanbaliq.

The closest analogy in pre-modern history is probably the Abbasid court at Baghdad at its eighth- and ninth-century peak (Islamic Golden Age Ch 3), or the slightly earlier Sasanian court at Ctesiphon under Khosrow I (Persian Empire Ch 9).
Like those courts, Khanbaliq was the political center of an empire that spanned multiple cultural traditions and self-consciously curated representatives from all of them.
This cosmopolitan polish did not extend much beyond the court itself.
Outside Khanbaliq, the Yuan ruled China through the four-class hierarchy and the Han majority was excluded from significant political participation.

The brilliant cosmopolitanism of the court and the structural injustice of the system that funded it ran in parallel, and most contemporaries — including most Han subjects who had no direct contact with the court — saw the system, not the cosmopolitanism.
Marco Polo's enthusiastic descriptions of Kublai's tolerant, polyglot court (Chapter 4) reflect what he saw as a privileged foreign visitor with direct access to the imperial entourage.
They do not reflect what a tax-paying Han farmer in southern Anhui experienced.
Kublai died in 1294 at the age of approximately seventy-nine, having reigned as Great Khan for thirty years and as Yuan emperor for twenty-three.
He had outlived three of his sons including his designated heir Zhenjin.
The succession passed to his grandson Temür Öljeitü (TEH-moor UHL-jay-too — Chinese reign name Chengzong), who would rule for thirteen relatively stable years until 1307.
After that the dynasty fell into the succession chaos that defines the rest of its history (Chapter 7).

In thirty years on the throne, Kublai had completed the conquest of China, built a capital city, extended the Grand Canal, established the four-class governance system, presided over the most cosmopolitan court in Asia, sent two doomed invasion fleets against Japan (Chapter 3), and hosted Marco Polo (Chapter 4).

He had also failed to solve the central problem of Mongol governance in China — how to keep a small foreign elite in power over a large culturally and demographically dominant population — and had bequeathed to his successors a political system whose internal contradictions would destroy it within seventy-five years.
His reputation in Chinese historical memory is mixed and contested.
Han historians of the Ming period, writing for an explicitly anti-Mongol audience, treated Kublai as an able foreign conqueror whose dynasty was a national catastrophe.

Modern Chinese historiography is more ambivalent — the Yuan is now formally counted as a legitimate Chinese dynasty in the orthodox succession, partly because the Yuan brought Tibet, Yunnan, and large portions of Inner Asia within the Chinese imperial frame, territorial inheritances that subsequent Chinese states have built on.
Mongolian historiography treats Kublai as one of the great Khans, second only to Genghis.
Whatever the moral judgment, the institutional facts are not in dispute.
Kublai Khan was the most consequential ruler of thirteenth-century Eurasia, and he laid the foundation of every Chinese state from his death to the end of the imperial period.
The next chapter is about the most spectacular failure of his reign.

chapters.title: The Failed Japan Invasions
sentences: In the autumn of 1274, a fleet of approximately 900 ships and 25,000 to 30,000 troops sailed from southern Korea toward the Japanese island of Kyushu (kee-OO-shoo, the southernmost of the four main Japanese islands, Ancient Japan Ch 6 covers the medieval-era Japanese political geography).

The fleet was commanded by Kublai Khan's appointed generals, manned mostly by Korean sailors from the Goryeo vassal kingdom (Ancient Korea Ch 8 — Goryeo's submission to the Yuan in 1270 had made Korea responsible for ship construction and naval crews), and tasked with conquering Japan and annexing it to the Yuan empire.
The fleet failed.
Seven years later, in 1281, a vastly larger fleet — roughly 4,400 ships and 140,000 men — sailed against the same target.
It also failed.
In both cases the immediate cause of failure was a typhoon that scattered and sank the ships at sea.

The Japanese, who had expected divine intervention because the alternative was annihilation, named the typhoons kamikaze (kah-mee-KAH-zay) — "divine wind" — and incorporated the concept into their national mythology.
The two failed invasions are, by some measures, the most expensive military catastrophes in pre-modern Asian history.

The 1281 expedition is the largest amphibious operation that had ever been attempted anywhere in the world up to that date, and would not be surpassed in scale until the Allied Normandy landings of June 1944.
The cost in lives, ships, and matériel was enormous.
The strategic gain was zero.
The political symbolism was enduring — the typhoons that wrecked the Yuan fleets became, in Japanese historical consciousness, the proof that the home islands were divinely protected.
That conviction would echo for the next six and a half centuries, with consequences in 1944–45 that the thirteenth-century Japanese could not have anticipated.
This chapter is about why Kublai launched the invasions, what actually happened in the two campaigns, and what the long-term consequences were.
Kublai's motivation for invading Japan is not entirely clear in the surviving sources, and modern historians are divided.
The official Yuan justification was diplomatic.

Kublai had sent envoys to Kamakura Japan — the military government, or bakufu, that had ruled Japan since 1185 from the eastern town of Kamakura while the imperial court at Kyoto retained ceremonial supremacy — beginning in 1266, demanding submission and tribute in exchange for peaceful relations.
The Japanese had refused to respond at all.

After several rounds of escalating Mongol embassies and persistent Japanese non-response (some of the envoys were ignored, some were turned away at the harbor without an audience, and according to some accounts at least one envoy was executed), Kublai decided that military force was the only available option.
Modern historians have suggested several deeper motivations.
One is straightforward expansion — Kublai was a Mongol Great Khan, and Mongol Great Khans launched conquests as a matter of role definition.

Another is the resource argument: Japan was reputed in Chinese sources to have substantial gold and silver mines, and a successful conquest would have transferred those resources to the Yuan treasury.
A third is political — Kublai needed visible military victories to maintain his legitimacy with the Mongol nobility, who increasingly suspected him of having been culturally captured by China.

A fourth is strategic — Japan was the last significant unconquered country in the Mongol-accessible world, and leaving it independent created a refuge for Song loyalist holdouts and a base for potential anti-Yuan trade.

None of these arguments is decisive on its own, but together they account for the persistence with which Kublai pursued the project, in the face of two catastrophic failures, into the last decade of his reign.
What is clear is that the invasions were Kublai's project specifically.

The Mongol nobility were skeptical (steppe cavalry empires were not in the business of amphibious operations); the Han bureaucracy was opposed (the cost was crushing and the strategic gain doubtful); the Korean Goryeo court — required to build the ships and supply most of the sailors — was reduced to economic ruin by the construction effort.
Kublai pushed both invasions through over considerable internal resistance, which is part of why the failures hit his prestige so hard.
The first invasion, in 1274, is called the Bun'ei Invasion in Japanese sources after the regnal era then in effect.
The fleet of approximately 900 ships sailed from Goryeo in early November 1274 carrying a mixed force of Mongol cavalry, Chinese infantry, and Korean auxiliaries.

The strategic plan was to seize the islands of Tsushima (TSOO-shi-mah) and Iki in the strait separating Korea from Kyushu — both islands are visible from the Japanese mainland and command the only viable invasion route — and then land at Hakata Bay on northern Kyushu, defeat the local Japanese defense forces, and march on the city of Dazaifu, the regional administrative center.
After Dazaifu fell, additional reinforcements would arrive from China and the conquest of Japan proper would begin.
Tsushima fell on November 5, 1274.

The local defending samurai garrison of about eighty men was slaughtered to the last warrior; the civilian population was massacred in a manner the Mongols had used on continental cities that resisted (Mongol Empire Ch 3).
Survivors fled by ship to Iki, which fell a week later.
By November 19 the Yuan fleet had landed at Hakata Bay.
The defending Japanese force at Hakata was led by samurai of the Kyushu branch of the Hōjō clan, the family that effectively ran the Kamakura bakufu.

The Japanese fought in a manner that surprised the invading Mongol commanders — they expected the formal challenge-and-response duels that characterized the samurai tradition (Ancient Japan Ch 7), in which mounted warriors of comparable rank rode out, named themselves, and engaged in single combat.

The Mongol response was unit volleys of crossbow fire, group cavalry charges, and the use of explosive iron-shell bombs called tetsuhō (TET-soo-hoh) — early Chinese gunpowder grenades that produced loud explosions, blinding flashes, and shrapnel injuries.
The samurai were shocked but did not break.
Fighting continued through the day.
By evening the Japanese had been pushed back from the immediate beachhead but had inflicted serious losses on the Yuan landing force.
Then the Yuan commanders made a decision that has been argued about for seven centuries.
They withdrew their troops to the ships overnight, intending to consolidate, resupply, and renew the assault the next morning.

Some accounts suggest that the senior officers had been wounded and the chain of command was disrupted; some suggest that the troops were running short of arrows and explosive weapons; some suggest that the Mongol commanders were genuinely surprised by Japanese resistance and wanted time to reassess.
Whatever the reason, the entire force was at sea overnight when an autumn storm — typhoon-grade, by the surviving descriptions — broke over the bay.
Many of the ships were wrecked on the rocky coast or driven out to sea.
Estimates of losses range from a third to half of the fleet sunk or stranded.
The surviving ships set course back to Korea.
The 1274 invasion was over.
What the storm actually was is debated.
The traditional account is that it was a major late-season typhoon.

Some modern Japanese maritime archaeology — particularly the underwater surveys at Takashima Bay near Hakata, which have recovered substantial Yuan-era ship remains — suggests that many of the wrecked ships may have been structurally substandard, hastily built by the Goryeo Korean shipyards under Mongol time pressure.
Korean shipbuilding tradition built river barges, not ocean-going warships, and the rushed construction program produced ships with inadequate keels, poor caulking, and weak hulls.
A storm that an experienced ocean fleet might have ridden out destroyed the Yuan fleet because the ships were not built for the conditions.
This is not the romantic kamikaze story, but it has substantial archaeological support.
The Japanese had spent the seven years between the two invasions preparing.
Under the leadership of the Hōjō regent at Kamakura, the Kyushu and Honshu coastal regions raised militia, expanded the samurai mobilization, and built a major defensive infrastructure.

The signature project was a stone wall, roughly 20 kilometers long and 2.5 to 3 meters high, built along the inner coast of Hakata Bay to deny the Yuan force the easy beach landing they had used in 1274.
The wall — pieces of it survive today at Hakata as a national historic site — was the central physical defense of Japan against the second invasion.
The Yuan force that arrived in 1281, called the Kōan Invasion in Japanese sources, was much larger.
It came in two fleets.
The Eastern Route Force sailed from Korea in May 1281 with about 900 ships and 40,000 men, mostly Mongol-Korean troops in the same configuration as the 1274 invasion.
The Southern Route Force sailed from southern China in mid-summer 1281 with roughly 3,500 ships and 100,000 men, primarily Han Chinese conscripts from the recently conquered south.
Total force: approximately 4,400 ships and 140,000 men.
As noted above, this was the largest single amphibious operation attempted anywhere in the world up to that time.
The two fleets were supposed to converge at Hakata Bay in mid-July.
They did not converge cleanly.
The Eastern fleet arrived first, attempted independent landings, ran into the defensive wall and the dug-in samurai forces, and could not establish a beachhead.
They withdrew to the offshore islands to wait for the Southern fleet.
The Southern fleet arrived in early August.

The combined force then maneuvered offshore for several weeks attempting to find a landing point that the Japanese had not fortified, while Japanese small-craft raiders harassed the Yuan ships at night with fire-arrows and boarding parties.
The decisive event came on August 15-16, 1281.
A massive typhoon — a verified late-season storm well documented in the surviving Yuan, Korean, and Japanese sources — tore through the bay.
The Yuan fleet was caught at anchor or in ill-protected coastal waters.
Most of the ships were wrecked.

The chronicle accounts say tens of thousands of men drowned or were stranded ashore as the typhoon receded; the stranded survivors were systematically hunted down by samurai forces over the next several days.
Total Yuan losses for the 1281 invasion are conventionally given as approximately half the original force — perhaps 70,000 to 100,000 dead, mostly drowned or killed in the post-typhoon mopping up.
The losses were so heavy that Korean coastal communities along the shipping lanes back to the mainland reported hearing wreckage washing ashore for weeks.
It was, by raw casualty count, one of the worst military disasters in pre-modern history.

It is worth comparing scale: the Mongol defeat at Ayn Jalut in 1260 (Mongol Empire Ch 5), often cited as the most strategically significant Mongol defeat, involved perhaps 10,000 Mongol casualties on the losing side.
The Mongol losses at Hakata Bay in 1281 may have been ten times that.
The Japanese interpretation of what had happened was theological.
Buddhist and Shinto temples across Japan had spent the months between the appearance of the second Yuan fleet and the typhoon conducting elaborate prayer rituals for divine protection.

The two most important sites were the Ise Shrine (the chief Shinto shrine, dedicated to the sun goddess Amaterasu, ancestor of the imperial line — Ancient Japan Ch 5 covers Ise's foundational role in Japanese religion) and the Tsurugaoka Hachimangū in Kamakura (dedicated to Hachiman, the Shinto-Buddhist god of war and the patron deity of the samurai).
When the typhoon struck, the temples claimed credit.
Hachiman had sent the wind.
Amaterasu had defended her descendants.
Japan was the Land of the Gods (shinkoku), divinely protected against foreign invasion.
The term kamikaze — a compound of kami (god, or divine spirit) and kaze (wind) — entered the lexicon to describe both typhoons of 1274 and 1281, retroactively.
The concept hardened over the following centuries into a settled Japanese conviction that the home islands enjoyed special divine protection against external attack.

This conviction underwrote Japanese strategic culture for the next six and a half centuries, including the Tokugawa-era sakoku (closed-country) policy and, eventually, the World War II revival of the term kamikaze for the suicide-pilot squadrons of 1944–45 who were named for the divine wind in conscious historical reference.
The thirteenth-century typhoons did not cause the twentieth-century suicide squadrons, but the cultural lineage running from one to the other is direct and unbroken.
A note on the historicity of the typhoons.

Modern Japanese and Chinese historical meteorologists, working from chronicle descriptions, surviving Korean court records, and underwater archaeology of the wreck sites, have substantially confirmed that two genuine typhoon events struck Hakata Bay in 1274 and 1281.
The storms were real, though the 1274 storm was almost certainly less severe than the 1281 one and appears to have been compounded by the substandard Korean-built ships.
The 1281 storm was a major late-season typhoon that would have been catastrophic for any fleet caught offshore.
The Japanese theological interpretation — that the typhoons were specific divine interventions — is obviously not provable, but the typhoons themselves are not invented.

This is one of the cases where popular memory of an ancient event is essentially correct about the central facts (a great storm wrecked an invading fleet) and almost certainly wrong about the supernatural cause (divine intervention rather than weather-and-shipbuilding).
The consequences for the Yuan were significant but not catastrophic.
The treasury cost of the two invasions had been enormous, particularly the 1281 expedition with its 4,400 ships.

The political cost to Kublai was significant — the failures damaged his standing with the Mongol nobility, which had warned against the project, and exposed the limits of Yuan amphibious capacity to anyone who was watching.
Kublai briefly contemplated a third invasion in the 1280s but was talked out of it by his ministers, who pointed out that the cost of building yet another fleet would bankrupt the empire.
The 1281 invasion was the high-water mark of Yuan military expansion.
After 1281 the dynasty's overseas projects became increasingly modest and increasingly disastrous.
A 1283 expedition against Vietnam (the Trần dynasty) was driven off after several years of campaign in the highlands by Vietnamese guerrilla resistance under the general Trần Hưng Đạo.
A 1287 expedition against Burma captured the Pagan capital but failed to consolidate and was withdrawn.

A 1293 expedition against the Javanese kingdom of Singhasari was one of the most embarrassing in the entire Mongol record — a Javanese prince named Raden Wijaya tricked the Mongol force into helping him overthrow a rival, then turned on the Mongols and drove them off the island.
