Atahualpa sent quipu messages to imperial officials across the empire, ordering them to deliver gold and silver from the Coricancha, from the provincial Sun Temples, from the imperial treasury, and from the panaca holdings.

Llama caravans began arriving at Cajamarca with loads of cumbi cloth bundles full of worked gold and silver objects — gold figurines, silver dishes, beaten gold sheets, silver llamas, gold maize plants, silver moons, gold suns.
Each load was inventoried by Spanish notaries (the requerimiento de oro, which still exists in the Seville archives) and then melted down in field furnaces into ingots for shipment back to Spain.
The artistic loss is impossible to overstate.

The melted-down gold and silver of the Atahualpa ransom included the entire portable contents of the Coricancha, most of the major provincial Sun Temples, and much of the imperial treasury accumulated over the previous century.
Almost no Inca gold or silver objects survive in their original form because almost all of them were melted down between November 1532 and July 1533.

The few surviving Inca metal objects in modern museum collections are mostly small items that were not in the imperial treasury — capacocha grave goods, provincial elite burials, items in private possession that escaped the official ransom inventory.
Pizarro received the ransom, fixed his pre-arranged signature to the inventory, and then on July 26, 1533 — having received the full agreed-upon amount — had Atahualpa executed anyway.
The execution was a strangulation by garrotte, performed publicly in the central plaza of Cajamarca.
The justification given was that Atahualpa had been plotting a rebellion against the Spanish (a charge that he denied, and that the Spanish chroniclers themselves found dubious in retrospect).
The actual reason was that the Spanish had decided that Atahualpa alive was more dangerous than Atahualpa dead, and that with the ransom collected, there was no further reason to keep him alive.
He was forty years old.
He had ruled the empire for less than a year.

He was strangled to death in front of his court, his name forgotten by his Spanish executioners almost immediately, his body buried in a Christian ceremony that was performed largely as theater for the Cuzco nobles whose loyalty Pizarro was now trying to court.
What followed was the rapid Spanish occupation of the rest of the empire.
Pizarro marched south from Cajamarca toward Cuzco in the late summer of 1533, pausing at Andahuaylas and Vilcaconga to fight off Inca army resistance led by Atahualpa's general Quizquiz.

The resistance was substantial — several engagements with thousands of Inca warriors per side, with Spanish casualties and several losses of horses — but the cumulative tactical advantage of the Spanish prevailed.
Cuzco was entered by Pizarro's forces in November 1533, almost exactly a year after the Cajamarca ambush.
The looting of Cuzco followed.
The Coricancha was stripped down to bare stone.
The royal palaces were ransacked.
The remaining imperial treasury, the personal possessions of Cuzco's elite, and most of the moveable artistic wealth of the city were inventoried, melted down, and sent back to Spain.
The royal mummies (Chapter 5) were located and either destroyed or shipped to Lima for display and eventual disposal.
The major imperial cult institutions were demolished or repurposed as Spanish churches.
The Coricancha became the Dominican monastery of Santo Domingo, built directly on top of the Inca foundation walls.
Pizarro, looking for a stable post-conquest political settlement, installed Huayna Capac's surviving son Manco Inca Yupanqui (MAHN-koh EEN-kah yoo-PAHN-kee) as a puppet Sapa Inca in late 1533.
Manco was about nineteen years old, half-brother to both Atahualpa and Huascar, and one of the few legitimist heirs not killed in the recent civil war.
The Spanish hoped to use him as a stable figurehead through whom to govern the imperial population.

Manco initially cooperated, was crowned in the central plaza of Cuzco with the appropriate Inca ceremonies, and lived alongside Pizarro's small Spanish governing council for the next two and a half years.
The arrangement broke down in 1536.

Manco Inca had been increasingly humiliated by the Spanish — robbed of land, tribute, and women — and in early 1536 he escaped Spanish supervision under the cover of a religious pilgrimage and raised an army of perhaps 100,000 mit'a-mobilized warriors.

The size estimate is from Spanish sources and is probably exaggerated; but it was unquestionably a large army by any standard, and it was operating against a Spanish presence in Cuzco that consisted of perhaps 200 men.
The siege of Cuzco lasted from early 1536 to late 1536 — about ten months.
Manco's army surrounded the city, occupied Sacsayhuaman (which the Spanish had not yet fortified), and burned much of the city to flush the defenders out.
The Spanish retreated to a small fortified position in the central plaza and held out against repeated assaults.
The Spanish broke the siege at Sacsayhuaman in May 1536 with a desperate cavalry charge that recaptured the fortress (one of the men killed in the recapture was Juan Pizarro, Francisco's brother).

After Sacsayhuaman fell, Manco's army was forced to disperse for the planting season — the structural weakness of mit'a mobilization (Chapter 4) caught up with the rebellion at the worst possible moment.

Manco continued the war on a smaller scale through 1537 and 1538, including a notable victory over a Spanish cavalry force at the Battle of Ollantaytambo (where the Inca used flooded terraces to immobilize the Spanish horses).
But the strategic momentum had passed.
Reinforcements from Panama, Mexico, and Spain were arriving in increasing numbers.
The original 168 of 1532 had grown to several thousand Spaniards by 1538.
The military balance had shifted irreversibly.
Manco eventually retreated into the cloud forest northwest of the Sacred Valley and founded a small successor state at a remote site called Vilcabamba (veel-kah-BAHM-bah).

The Vilcabamba neo-Inca state would last for thirty-six years, ruled successively by Manco himself (until his murder in 1544), his sons Sayri Tupac (1544–1561, who eventually negotiated a partial settlement and moved to a Spanish-controlled estate where he died young), Titu Cusi Yupanqui (1561–1571, who dictated a chronicle defending the Inca position to Spanish negotiators), and finally Tupac Amaru (1571–1572).
In 1572, the Spanish viceroy Francisco de Toledo decided to end the Vilcabamba state once and for all.
A military expedition under Martín Hurtado de Arbieto captured the Vilcabamba site, captured Tupac Amaru, and brought him back to Cuzco for public execution.

On September 24, 1572, the last Sapa Inca was beheaded in the central plaza of Cuzco — the same plaza where Pachacuti had been crowned, where Atahualpa's ransom had been brought, where the imperial state festivals had been celebrated.
The execution was witnessed by an estimated crowd of tens of thousands of indigenous and Spanish residents.
Tupac Amaru reportedly addressed the crowd briefly before dying, asking them to maintain their loyalty to Christ.
The execution of Tupac Amaru I in 1572 is the conventional end of the Inca Empire as a political entity.
Forty years had passed since Cajamarca.
The independent Inca state was finally finished.
But the empire's institutional and cultural inheritance continued to operate, in modified form, through the colonial period and beyond.

The Spanish colonial administration adopted many of the Inca administrative geographies and labor systems wholesale — the encomienda system superimposed onto the Inca mit'a, with individual conquistadors granted the right to extract tribute and labor from specific indigenous communities; the repartimiento system reorganizing the mit'a labor draft for Spanish silver mining at Potosí (the giant silver mountain in modern Bolivia, which between 1545 and 1825 produced an estimated 60% of the world's silver and was worked almost entirely by mit'a-conscripted indigenous laborers); the road network maintained for Spanish use; the qollqa storehouses repurposed for Spanish supply; the Quechua language preserved as the rural lingua franca of the Andes (and continuing today as the most widely spoken indigenous language in the Western Hemisphere, with perhaps 8 to 10 million speakers across modern Peru, Bolivia, Ecuador, Argentina, and Colombia).
The cultural inheritance was even broader.
The ayllu social organization continued to function at the village level.
The reciprocal labor exchange of ayni continued.

The wak'a religious geography continued, often syncretized with Catholic saint cults — most famously the cult of Pachamama the earth-mother, who is now venerated alongside the Virgin Mary in much of the rural Andes.
The cumbi textile tradition continued in modified form, with weavers in Chinchero, Pisac, and other communities producing high-quality wool textiles that incorporate Inca-period designs.
The mountain-spirit (apu) tradition continued.
The reciprocal coca-leaf offering tradition continued.
Tupac Amaru II, born José Gabriel Condorcanqui in 1738, was a descendant of Tupac Amaru I through the line of his daughter.
He was a wealthy mestizo merchant in southern Peru, educated, fluent in both Spanish and Quechua, and embedded in the colonial elite.
In 1780 he led a major indigenous revolt against Spanish colonial rule.

The revolt expanded across southern Peru, Bolivia, and into northern Argentina, mobilized perhaps 100,000 indigenous fighters, and seriously threatened Spanish control of the southern Andes for over a year.

Tupac Amaru II was eventually captured and publicly executed in May 1781 in the central plaza of Cuzco — the same plaza where his ancestor had been beheaded 209 years earlier — by being quartered, with his body torn into four parts by horses dragging in different directions.
The execution was watched by Spanish officials and indigenous spectators, and was specifically designed as a deterrent against future revolts.
The Tupac Amaru II revolt was not the last indigenous resistance to Spanish or post-colonial rule in the Andes.
There would be others through the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.
But it was the largest and the most explicitly invoking the Inca past as a political symbol.

The name Tupac Amaru has remained a charged political term across the Andes ever since, invoked by movements as varied as the 1969–75 reformist Peruvian government of Juan Velasco, the late-twentieth-century Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) Peruvian guerrilla group, the late-twentieth-century Tupamaros Uruguayan urban guerrilla group, and (most surprisingly) the American hip-hop artist Tupac Shakur, named by his Black Panther mother for the Inca emperor.
The Inca past has remained political.
Modern Peru's national identity is built explicitly on Inca symbolism.
The national flag uses Inca-derived colors.
The Cuzco municipal flag is the rainbow-striped wiphala that may or may not have been an Inca imperial banner (the historicity is debated).
Machu Picchu is the country's primary tourist destination and primary international cultural symbol.
Quechua is one of two co-official national languages alongside Spanish.
The president of Peru regularly invokes Inca achievements in political speeches.
The same is true to varying degrees in Bolivia (where Aymara and Quechua identity is even more politically prominent), Ecuador, and to some extent in Argentina and Chile.
This is the long aftermath of the Inca empire.
The political state ended at Vilcabamba in 1572.
The institutional inheritance continued in colonial administration.
The cultural inheritance continued in the ayllu, the language, the textile tradition, the religious syncretism.
The political symbolism continued in Tupac Amaru II, in the modern Peruvian and Bolivian states, and in the global cultural memory of the empire.
The Inca are not gone.
They are, in a meaningful sense, still here.
A pause for one of the more delightful pieces of Andean trivia.

The sweet potato (Ipomoea batatas), domesticated somewhere along the South American Pacific coast probably by the Moche or earlier, appears in archaeological deposits across Polynesia by 1000 to 1200 CE.
The Polynesian languages call it kumara (or some variant — kumar, kuara, umara depending on the island), which is a direct phonetic cousin of the Quechua name kumar.
The botanical and linguistic evidence is unambiguous: there was direct contact between Polynesian voyagers and the Andean coast at least three to five centuries before Pizarro arrived.

Whether the contact was Polynesian sailors reaching Peru in their double-hulled voyaging canoes, or Andean coastal sailors blown west on balsa-wood rafts and somehow reaching the eastern Pacific islands, is debated.

The most parsimonious reading is that Polynesian sailors made the eastward voyages — they were the most accomplished open-ocean navigators in pre-modern history (Polynesian Voyagers Ch 7) and had the technology and the demographic motive — and brought sweet potato cuttings back as one of the takeaways.
This is a small thing, in the grand scale of the Inca story.
But it is one of the few pieces of solid evidence that the pre-Columbian Americas were not the hermetically sealed isolate that the standard narrative often implies.
The Andes and the Pacific island world were in contact, somehow, before any European made the connection.
The Inca did not invent this contact — it predated them by several centuries — but they were beneficiaries of it.
The sweet potato was a major crop in their highland agriculture by the imperial period.
A pause for the cumulative caveat that this whole TL has been building toward.
The Inca story, as told in the chronicles and reconstructed by modern scholarship, contains an enormous amount of "first" and "largest" and "most" claims.
The largest pre-Columbian empire by population.
The longest road network in the Americas.
The most precise mortarless masonry anywhere in the New World.
The largest single ransom in recorded human history.
The fastest pre-modern messenger relay system (chasqui) in the Western Hemisphere.
The most centralized administrative state in pre-Columbian America.
Each of these claims is accurate in its narrow context.
The cumulative effect is to make the Inca sound like a uniquely impressive civilization compared to all other pre-modern civilizations.
This is, on a careful reading, both true and overstated.

True in the sense that the Inca achievements really were extraordinary by any cross-civilizational standard, and the empire really was operating at a scale and sophistication that belongs in the same conversation as the Roman, Han Chinese, Persian, and Caliphate empires.

Overstated in the sense that "first" and "most" and "largest" claims in pre-modern history are always conditional on what survives, what was documented by the conquerors, and what later scholarship has reconstructed.
The Inca got more documentation than the Wari and Tiwanaku because the Inca were encountered by literate conquistadors.
They got more archaeological attention because the surviving stonework is so spectacular and because Machu Picchu generates global tourist interest.
They got more cultural-memory traction because Peru and Bolivia have built modern national identities around Inca symbolism.
The cumulative effect is a slight upward bias on the Inca compared to other comparable civilizations whose evidence is thinner or whose modern descendants have less political voice.

What seems clear, on the best reading of the evidence, is that the Inca were one of several great pre-modern empires that achieved a continent-scale administrative integration with limited technology — alongside the Roman Empire (Ancient Rome), the Han Chinese (Han Dynasty), the early Caliphate (Islamic Golden Age Ch 1), the Mongol Empire (Mongol Empire), the Ming Chinese, and arguably one or two others.
They did so with a more limited technological inventory than any of those Eurasian counterparts.

They built and ran their empire for less time than most of their counterparts, in part because of the catastrophic shock of European contact, in part because the empire was structurally young (only about ninety years old at the time of the conquest) and had not yet developed the institutional resilience that older empires had.

The conquest by 168 men is one of the wildest claims in history, and it is true; it is also embedded in a specific historical context (smallpox, civil war, succession crisis, Spanish accumulated tactical doctrine) that makes it less mysterious than it sounds when stated baldly.

The honest summary is that the Inca built one of the most impressive empires of the early-modern world using one of the most limited technological inventories, and they lost it to one of the most lopsided military encounters in recorded history because they had been catastrophically weakened by disease and civil war just before the encounter.
None of these statements is an exaggeration.
None of them is the whole story.
Cross-civ check: when the Spanish executed Tupac Amaru I in the Cuzco plaza in September 1572, the world he had been the last sovereign of was a world of intense imperial activity on every continent.
In the Mediterranean, the Battle of Lepanto in October 1571 had just halted Ottoman naval expansion in the western Mediterranean (Ottoman Empire Ch 5).
In South Asia, the Mughal Emperor Akbar was at the height of his reign, completing his conquest of Bengal in 1572 and consolidating one of the largest contiguous Muslim empires in history.

In Ming China, the Wanli Emperor had just acceded to the throne in 1572 at the age of nine, beginning what would become a 48-year reign during which the Ming bureaucracy would reach its peak before its long decline.

In Mexico, the Spanish colonial state was still consolidating its control over the former Aztec territories (Aztec Empire Ch 8), with the silver discoveries at Zacatecas in 1546 already producing the bullion flows that would reshape the global economy.

In Africa, the Songhai Empire in West Africa was a few decades from its 1591 collapse to a Moroccan musket army, and the Ethiopian Empire was rebuilding after the wars with Adal that had devastated its highlands in the 1530s and 1540s.
The Inca conquest was one move in a global early-modern game in which European imperial expansion was being attempted everywhere, sometimes succeeding and sometimes failing.

Spain succeeded in the Andes for the same reasons it succeeded in Mexico — the demographic shock of disease, the political weakness of recent succession crises, the technological lopsidedness of the encounter.
Spain failed against the Ottomans, against the Songhai (briefly), against the Ming (decisively), and against the Mughals (also decisively).
The pre-modern world was not yet a world of European conquest as a single uniform process.
It was a world of multiple imperial actors with varying levels of military and demographic resilience, in which the Andes and Mexico happened to be the most vulnerable available targets.
The Inca were not unique in falling to a small invading force.
They were unique in the speed and completeness with which they fell, and in the institutional sophistication of what they were running when the fall happened.
They are the strongest single demonstration in the historical record that the structural conditions of an empire matter more than its absolute size.
An empire of twelve million can fall to 168 men in a year, if the conditions are right.
The world has been a different place ever since.

chapters.title: Tamerlane's World
sentences: The empire that Timur built sat astride two civilizational worlds that the Mongol invasions of the thirteenth century had violently knit together — the settled Persianate world of Iran and Khorasan to the south, and the nomadic Turkic-Mongol steppe to the north — and the joining was uneasy.
Both worlds were in flux when Timur was born around 1336, and the political vacuum produced by their joint instability is what made his career possible.
To understand Timur, you have to understand the wreckage that produced him.
The wreckage was the legacy of the Mongol Empire (Mongol Empire Ch 1–8).
In the early thirteenth century, Genghis Khan (Mongol Empire Ch 1) had united the Mongol tribes and led them out of the steppe in the most rapid imperial expansion in human history.
By 1260 the Mongols controlled an empire stretching from Korea to Hungary.

By 1294, when Kublai Khan (Mongol Empire Ch 6) died, the unified Mongol Empire had fragmented into four successor states ruled by rival branches of Genghis's descendants: the Yuan in China (Mongol Empire Ch 6), the Ilkhanate in Iran (Mongol Empire Ch 7), the Golden Horde in the Russian steppe (Mongol Empire Ch 8), and the Chagatai Khanate (CHAH-gah-tye) in Central Asia.
The Chagatai Khanate is the one Timur was born into.

It is named for Chagatai (CHAH-gah-tye), Genghis Khan's second son, who received Central Asia — roughly the territory between the Aral Sea and the Tarim Basin — in his father's division of the empire.
The Chagatai khans ruled Transoxiana (the rich agricultural region between the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers, in modern Uzbekistan), Khorasan, and the eastern steppe from the 1220s onward.

Their core territories included the great Silk Road cities of Samarkand (SAM-ar-kand) and Bukhara (boo-KHAR-ah), which had been sacked during the original Mongol conquests in 1220 but had been rebuilt as Mongol-administered centers.
The Chagatai story through the fourteenth century is a slow-motion collapse, useful to walk through because it explains the world Timur stepped into.
The early Chagatai khans had ruled as steppe nomads, refusing to settle in the conquered cities and treating Transoxiana as grazing territory rather than as agricultural taxation base.

Through the early fourteenth century, two factions developed within the khanate: a "settled" faction that wanted to rule from the cities, intermarry with the local Persian-speaking Muslim population, and convert to Islam; and a "nomadic" faction that wanted to maintain steppe traditions and resist the lure of urban civilization.
The settled faction won, partially.
In 1334, the Chagatai khan Tarmashirin (tar-mah-SHEER-in) formally converted to Islam and tried to reorganize the khanate as a Persianate Muslim state on the model of the Ilkhanate.
The nomadic faction revolted, killed him, and the khanate fractured.

By the 1340s the Chagatai realm had split into two pieces: a western half (sometimes called Transoxiana or Mawarannahr, and centered on the agricultural cities of Samarkand and Bukhara) and an eastern half (called Moghulistan, in the Tian Shan range and modern Xinjiang).

The western half was nominally ruled by Chagatai puppet khans whose actual power was wielded by local emirs and tribal warlords; the eastern half remained more nomadic and sent periodic raids into the western settled lands.
This is a useful comparison to set up.

The Chagatai struggle between settled-Muslim and nomadic-steppe identities resembles the struggle that the Yuan dynasty (Mongol Empire Ch 6) was having in China at the same time, where Mongol rulers in Beijing were similarly debating whether to assimilate as Chinese-style emperors or maintain steppe identity.
It also resembles the struggle that the Ilkhanate in Iran (Mongol Empire Ch 7) had resolved a generation earlier when Ghazan Khan converted to Islam in 1295.

And it resembles, on the other end, the struggle the Golden Horde (Mongol Empire Ch 8) was having in the Russian steppe, where Mongol khans were converting to Islam under Berke and Uzbeg while their Russian subjects remained Orthodox Christian.

Across the Mongol successor world, the same question — to settle or to remain nomadic, to convert or to maintain steppe paganism — was being answered differently in each fragment of the original empire.
The Chagatai answer was: both, badly, with constant civil war.
By the 1340s the political authority of the Chagatai khans was a fiction.

Real power in Transoxiana belonged to a constellation of competing tribal emirs — leaders of clans like the Barlas (BAR-lass), the Jalayir, the Suldus, and the Arlat — who fought each other for control of the rich agricultural land around Samarkand, raised their own private armies, and treated the Chagatai khans as ceremonial figureheads to be installed and deposed at will.
This was the world Timur was born into.
The exact date of Timur's birth is not certain.

The standard date is April 8, 1336, given by the Timurid court historian Sharaf al-Din Yazdi in the Zafarnama ("Book of Victory"), the official Timurid history compiled in 1424 — but Yazdi was writing nearly a century after the event, his sources were partly oral, and he was producing a deliberately propagandistic text that emphasized auspicious astrological alignments.
The best estimate is that Timur was born sometime between 1330 and 1340.
The standard date 1336 is probably close enough.
He was born in Kesh (later called Shahrisabz, "Green City"), a town about 50 miles south of Samarkand in modern Uzbekistan.

His clan was the Barlas — a Mongol clan that had been settled in Transoxiana for over a century since the original Genghisid conquests, and that had Turkified linguistically (the Barlas spoke a Turkic dialect, not Mongolian, by Timur's day) while retaining Mongol tribal identity and aristocratic lineage.

The Barlas were not one of the dominant emirate clans of the period, but they were respectable: minor aristocracy in the Chagatai system, with grazing rights and tribal followers, but no political power at the khanate level.
Timur's father was Taraghai, a minor Barlas chief who appears in the chronicle accounts as a respectable but undistinguished tribal leader.
His mother was Tegina Begim.

The family was Sunni Muslim by Timur's generation — the Persianate religious culture had absorbed the steppe Mongols of Transoxiana over the preceding century, in the same gradual mechanism that had turned the Ilkhanate's Mongols Muslim during Ghazan Khan's reign.

The conversion was not pure ideological adoption but the slow accumulation of intermarriage, Sufi missionary influence, and the practical advantages of speaking the language of the people you were taxing.
Most importantly: Timur was not a direct descendant of Genghis Khan.

The Barlas clan claimed shared distant ancestry with the Borjigin (Genghis's clan) through a putative common Mongol ancestor, but the line was far enough back that no court genealogist could plausibly claim Timur as a Genghisid in the senior line.
This fact would constrain Timur for the rest of his career.
By the steppe customary law (the Yasa of Genghis Khan, Mongol Empire Ch 1), only direct male-line descendants of Genghis could legitimately claim the title Khan.
Timur could conquer, he could rule, he could massacre — but he could never legally call himself Khan.
He worked around this constraint his whole life.
The workarounds shaped the structure of his empire.
A note on the names: throughout the Persian-language sources, Timur is called Timur (TEE-moor — the Turkic word for "iron").
After his leg injury (more on which shortly), he became Timur-i Lang ("Timur the Lame"), often shortened to Timur Lang.

European sources transliterated this through Latin and Italian into Tamerlane, the form Christopher Marlowe used in Tamburlaine the Great (1587), and the form most English-language general readers know.
Modern scholarship uses Timur.
We will use Timur for the man and his dynasty (the Timurids), with occasional reminders that Tamerlane is the same person.
The next thirty years of Timur's life are sketchy in the surviving record.
Yazdi's Zafarnama gives a hagiographical account of a precocious warrior-leader gathering followers from his teens onward.
The earlier and more candid Tuzukat-i Timuri ("Memoirs of Timur"), which purports to be Timur's own dictated autobiography, is now generally considered a sixteenth-century forgery and not reliable.

What can be reconstructed from contemporary chronicle fragments and from later Timurid sources, read critically, is roughly this: In his teens and early twenties, Timur led a small band of Barlas tribal followers, conducting cattle raids and seasonal sheep-stealing operations in the borderlands south of Samarkand.

The line between "minor tribal warlord" and "bandit" in the fourteenth-century Chagatai world was almost meaningless — successful young Barlas chiefs built their followings the same way: a small armed band, a successful raid, the loot distributed generously, more followers attracted by the prospect of more loot, more raids.
Timur was good at it.
By his mid-twenties he had a band of perhaps a few hundred men.
Sometime around 1363, when Timur was in his late twenties, he was seriously wounded in a skirmish in Sistan (sis-TAN, in southeastern Iran).
The chronicle accounts vary: one tradition says he was hit by an arrow in the leg and shoulder during a sheep-rustling raid, another says he was wounded in a battle with a local emir.
The injuries were real and permanent.
His right leg was crippled — he walked with a noticeable limp for the rest of his life — and his right arm was partially withered, with reduced function.
The nickname Timur-i Lang ("Timur the Lame") dates from this period.
We know the injuries were real because of an unusual line of evidence.
In June 1941, Soviet anthropologists led by Mikhail Gerasimov opened Timur's tomb at the Gur-e-Amir mausoleum in Samarkand and examined the skeleton.

The remains were of a man about 5'7" (170 cm), muscular, in his late sixties at death, with a healed fracture of the right leg femur and damage to the right elbow consistent with an old wound — exactly matching the chronicle descriptions.

Gerasimov also produced a forensic facial reconstruction that has become the standard image of Timur in popular sources. (A famous and probably apocryphal story attached itself to the exhumation: a local tradition reportedly warned Gerasimov that opening Timur's tomb would unleash a curse, and Nazi Germany's invasion of the Soviet Union began three days after the exhumation, on June 22, 1941.
Gerasimov was a working anthropologist and not given to mysticism, but the coincidence of dates is striking enough that the story is now part of the Timur mythology.
The remains were reburied with full Islamic rites in November 1942 — and the Soviet victory at Stalingrad began the following month.
Make of all this what you will.) The injuries didn't stop Timur from leading armies.
They did permanently shape his physical movement and probably his self-image.

Contemporary observers describe him as a man who ignored physical pain to a degree that struck them as superhuman — riding through campaigns that broke other men, sleeping outdoors in winter conditions in his sixties, refusing to be carried in a litter even when his condition deteriorated.
The lameness was a constant reminder, and a constant repudiation, of physical limitation.

The political path that took Timur from raiding party leader to ruler of Transoxiana ran through one figure: his brother-in-law and partner Amir Husayn (hoo-SAYN — not to be confused with Husayn Bayqara, the much later Timurid ruler we will meet in Chapter 8).
Amir Husayn was the grandson of a previous emir of Transoxiana and had a stronger hereditary claim to leadership than Timur did.
In the 1360s, he and Timur formed an alliance: Husayn provided the political legitimacy and the senior tribal connections, Timur provided the military leadership and the personal followers.
Together they fought a series of wars against the Moghul (or Eastern Chagatai) khans who had been raiding Transoxiana from the east, and against rival local emirs.
The alliance was always tense.
The chronicle accounts describe repeated quarrels, brief separations, and reconciliations forced by external threats.
The decisive break came in 1370.
By then, Timur had built his own personal following large enough that he no longer needed Husayn, and Husayn — a less competent leader — was losing political support.
Timur turned on him: he besieged Husayn at the fortress of Balkh (BALKH, in modern Afghanistan), captured him, and executed him.
The execution was conducted by an unnamed third party — Timur was careful never to claim direct responsibility for killing his former ally, though it was understood that he had ordered it.
With Husayn out of the way, Timur was the dominant military figure in Transoxiana.

In April 1370, Timur captured Samarkand and held a tribal assembly (a kurultai — the same Mongol institution that had proclaimed Genghis Khan as ruler in 1206, Mongol Empire Ch 1) at which he was acknowledged as sovereign of Transoxiana.
He was around thirty-four years old.
He had risen from minor Barlas tribal chief to ruler of one of the richest agricultural regions in Central Asia in roughly fifteen years.
He held that position for the next thirty-five years, until his death in 1405, and used it as the staging ground for an empire that eventually reached from Anatolia to Delhi.
But he had a problem that no military victory could solve: he was not a Genghisid.
The legitimacy puzzle is the single most distinctive feature of Timurid politics, so it deserves a careful unpacking.
We will return to it constantly.

In the Mongol political tradition that had governed Eurasia since 1206, the title Khan (and especially the higher title Khaqan, "Great Khan" or "Khan of Khans") was reserved by customary law for direct male-line descendants of Genghis.
The rule was backed by the prestige of the Yasa, Genghis's customary legal code (Mongol Empire Ch 1), and by 150 years of universal practice across the Mongol successor world.
The Yuan emperors were Genghisids.
The Ilkhans were Genghisids.
The Golden Horde khans were Genghisids.
The Chagatai khans were Genghisids.
Even rebels and rival contenders within these states had to be Genghisids to claim the title.
Timur was not.
By the rules of the system he inherited, he could conquer territory and exercise power, but he could not legitimately call himself Khan.
To do so would be a usurpation that would alienate the steppe constituencies whose loyalty he needed.
He worked around the constraint in several ways simultaneously.
The first workaround was the puppet khan.

Throughout his reign, Timur formally ruled as the deputy of a Genghisid puppet — first Suyurghatmish (SOO-yer-gat-mish, ruled nominally 1370–1388), then Sultan Mahmud (1388–1402), both descendants of the Chagatai line.
The puppet khans had no actual power.
They appeared at ceremonial events, their names were inscribed on coins, official decrees were issued in their name, and friday prayers were said for them.
But the actual government — the army commands, the tax collection, the diplomatic correspondence — was Timur's.
The arrangement was a transparent fiction that nobody in the Eurasian political world was fooled by, but the form was preserved.
Timur could legitimately claim that the rightful Genghisid khan was on the throne, and that he himself was simply the chief military officer.
The second workaround was Timur's own title.
He never called himself Khan.

His official title was Amir ("commander," from the Arabic) or Amir-i Kabir ("great commander"), with the additional honorific Sahib-Qiran ("Lord of the Auspicious Conjunction" — a reference to a particular astrological alignment at his birth that Yazdi's chronicle interpreted as marking him as a world-conqueror).
These were lesser titles than Khan, but they were not constrained to Genghisids and Timur could legitimately use them.
The third workaround was marriage.
Around 1370, Timur married Saray Mulk Khanum (sah-RYE MOOLK kha-NOOM), a Chagatayid princess descended from Genghis Khan in the senior line.
This marriage gave Timur the title Guregen (gher-AY-gen) — "son-in-law of the Khan" — which was the closest approximation to Genghisid status a non-Genghisid could obtain.
Guregen was the title Timur used most often on his coinage and in his chancery documents.

Saray Mulk Khanum became Timur's senior wife, the chief lady of his court, and the namesake of the great mosque he built at Samarkand (now called the Bibi-Khanym Mosque — Bibi-Khanym being a Persian rendering of "lady" applied to Saray Mulk Khanum).
She survived Timur and lived on into Shah Rukh's reign.
The fourth workaround, developed gradually, was forged genealogy.
Timurid court historians invented an elaborate genealogy connecting the Barlas clan to a putative Mongol ancestor shared with Genghis Khan in the deep ancestral past.
The forgeries were transparent — modern historians regard them as obviously fabricated — but they served a political purpose.

By the second generation of Timurid historiography, the official line was that Timur and Genghis were cousins of cousins, sharing common Mongol ancestry, and that Timur's rule was therefore a legitimate continuation of the Genghisid project rather than a usurpation.
The Mughal court historians (working a century and a half later, in India) inherited and elaborated these genealogies into still more grandiose forms.
All of this is worth dwelling on because it shapes how the empire actually worked.
Timur could not simply rule as a sovereign Khan in his own right.
He had to conduct an elaborate political theater in which a ceremonial Chagatai khan sat on a ceremonial throne, while Timur the "great commander" exercised actual power.
Diplomatic correspondence had to be routed through the puppet's chancery.
Court ceremony had to acknowledge the puppet's nominal precedence.
This was true throughout Timur's reign, not just at the beginning.
He never escaped the legitimacy gap.
He grew the empire to stretch from Anatolia to Delhi while still formally serving as the deputy of a fiction.
The consequences for the dynasty were structural.
After Timur's death, the puppet-khan convention gradually eroded — Shah Rukh did not consistently use puppet khans, and his successors abandoned the practice.
But the underlying problem, the absence of Genghisid legitimacy, persisted.
It was one of the reasons the Timurid Empire never quite achieved the political solidity of its Genghisid predecessors.
The Uzbeks who eventually conquered the Timurid heartland in 1500–1507 (Chapter 8) were Genghisids in the senior Jochid line, and they used the legitimacy advantage explicitly against the Timurids.
The point: the most violent conqueror of the medieval world spent his entire career working around a constitutional rule he could not break.
The rule itself was a survival from the Genghisid moment a century and a half earlier.
Mongol political theory continued to constrain post-Mongol politics long after the unified Mongol Empire had ceased to exist as a functioning state.
A pause, before the campaigns begin: the world Timur stepped onto in 1370 was a world that had already been transformed by the Mongols and was still digesting the transformation.

The cities he would build at Samarkand and the architecture his successors would patronize at Herat drew on Persianate building traditions whose continuity reached back through the Ilkhanate (Mongol Empire Ch 7), the Seljuk Turks, the Samanids of Bukhara, and ultimately to the Sasanian Empire (Persian Empire Ch 9).
The administrative systems he inherited at Samarkand were Persian-Islamic systems descended from the Abbasid caliphate (Islamic Golden Age Ch 1), with Mongol-era modifications.
The literary culture he patronized was the Persian-language poetic tradition that had been refined under the Samanids and Ghaznavids in the tenth and eleventh centuries.
None of this was Mongol — it was the Persianate civilization the Mongols had conquered and then absorbed (Mongol Empire Ch 7, the Ilkhanate's transformation under Ghazan Khan).

The Mongol contributions to Timur's world were political and tribal: the Yasa code, the kurultai assembly, the Genghisid legitimacy framework, the tribal-confederation army structure, and a habit of imperial scale that pre-Mongol Persianate states had not really pursued.

The Persianate contributions were administrative and cultural: the bureaucracy, the language of high culture, the architectural vocabulary, the religious establishments, the agricultural taxation systems.

Timur synthesized both — combining Mongol political theater with Persianate administrative practice, Mongol military tradition with Islamic religious legitimacy, Turkic tribal identity with Persian high culture.
The synthesis was awkward, often contradictory, and never fully resolved during Timur's lifetime.
It would be Timur's son Shah Rukh who would let the Persianate side gradually win, producing the cultural florescence that defined the later Timurid period.

Cross-civ check: Timur's birth in 1336 places him squarely in the fourteenth century — the same period as the Hundred Years' War in Europe (Battle of Crécy 1346, Black Death 1347–51), the Ming dynasty's founding in China (1368, two years before Timur captured Samarkand), the high-medieval Mali Empire under Mansa Musa in West Africa (ruled 1312–1337), the Vijayanagara Empire's rise in southern India (founded 1336, the same year as Timur's traditional birth date), and the Aztec foundation of Tenochtitlan in 1325 in central Mexico (Aztec Empire Ch 1).

The Black Death that swept Europe and the Middle East in 1347–51 also reached Central Asia — some scholars argue the demographic damage from the plague contributed to the political fragmentation that gave Timur his opening, though the evidence is thin and the mechanism is hard to prove.
The mid-fourteenth century is one of the great inflection points of human history, with empires rising and falling on five continents simultaneously, and Timur's career falls right inside it.

chapters.title: The Conqueror's Method
sentences: What made Timur a world-historical figure rather than just a regional warlord was the systematic terror he applied to the cities and peoples he conquered, combined with the scale of military operations he was willing and able to conduct.
From his consolidation in Transoxiana in 1370 through the early 1390s, he developed a method of imperial conquest that was distinctive even by the brutal standards of medieval warfare.
The method had military components, political components, and propaganda components.
They worked together.
They worked well enough that for thirty-five years, almost nothing in the Eurasian world was strong enough to resist him.
This chapter is about that method.
The military component started with the army.
Timur's army was a hybrid force.
The core was Turco-Mongol cavalry on the steppe model: light horse archers in the Mongol tradition (Mongol Empire Ch 2), supplemented by heavy cavalry in armor for shock action.

The cavalry was supplied by the tribal levies of the Chagatai confederations — Barlas, Jalayir, Suldus, and others — and supplemented by recruited steppe nomads from the Kipchak and Moghulistan regions.
Tactically the army operated in the classic Mongol fashion: mobility-first, with feigned retreats, encircling maneuvers, and concentrated arrow volleys to break enemy formations.
What was new compared to the Genghisid armies was the integration of substantial infantry forces and siege capabilities for taking walled cities.

By the 1380s, Timur had developed siege engineering teams — captured Persian and Iraqi engineers, later supplemented by Indian craftsmen brought back from the 1398 Delhi campaign — capable of building catapults, mining tunnels under walls, and constructing siege towers.
He also experimented with early gunpowder weapons, though gunpowder artillery was not yet decisive in Central Asian warfare and would not become so until the early sixteenth century.

The Janissary musketeers and field artillery that the Ottomans would deploy at Chaldiran in 1514 (Safavid Persia Ch 3) and the matchlocks that Babur would use at Panipat in 1526 (Chapter 8) were the technologies that finally displaced the Mongol-style cavalry system.
Timur was operating in the last generation of pure cavalry-based imperial warfare.
The army's logistical reach was extraordinary.
Timur conducted campaigns on three continents.
He would assemble at Samarkand, march two thousand miles to Damascus, fight a major battle, and return to Samarkand within a single campaign cycle.

This required an enormous baggage train, prepositioned supply depots along the routes, careful seasonal scheduling, and an administrative machinery for keeping the army fed, watered, and paid across distances that European medieval armies could not have managed.

The expertise to run this logistics machinery was inherited largely from the Mongol Empire's earlier century of practice — the Yam relay system (Mongol Empire Ch 4), the steppe-distance estimation traditions, the tax collection apparatus that funded the campaigns.
What made Timur's campaigns different from Genghis Khan's was their reversibility.
Genghis and his successors had conquered to incorporate territory into a unified Mongol state.
Timur conquered, looted, sometimes massacred, and then withdrew.
He did not garrison the cities he took with permanent occupying forces.
He did not impose Timurid administrators on conquered provinces in any systematic way.
The pattern was: appear with overwhelming force, demand submission, accept tribute or punish resistance, install a local client regime, and march on.
This was raid-and-loot warfare conducted at imperial scale.
It produced enormous short-term wealth for the conquerors but left the conquered regions in a state of administrative chaos that often persisted for decades.
The reasons for this pattern are debated.

One factor is the simple administrative limit of any single ruler: Timur could not be in three places at once, and he chose to spend his time on the next campaign rather than on long-term administration of the previous one.

Another factor is the nature of his coalition: his army was made up of tribal contingents whose loyalty depended on ongoing successful campaigns and shares of loot, and a ruler who stopped campaigning would have lost his political base.

A third factor is the legitimacy gap discussed in Chapter 1: Timur could not legitimately claim the title Khan and so could not credibly claim sovereignty over conquered territory in the way a Genghisid could.
Conquering and withdrawing was politically safer than conquering and ruling.
Whatever the reasons, the consequences were enormous.

The agricultural base of the central Islamic world — the irrigated farmlands of Iraq, southern Iran, and Khorasan — was repeatedly devastated by Timurid campaigns and never properly rebuilt during Timur's lifetime.

The decline in agricultural productivity, demographic collapse in major cities, and disruption of long-distance trade caused by these campaigns is documented in the chronicle records and in modern archaeological surveys.
Some Iranian regions did not return to their pre-Timur populations for two or three centuries.
The economic damage Timur did to the world he conquered was, in the long run, larger than the wealth he extracted from it.
The terror component was the skull pyramid.

The practice of stacking the heads of massacred populations into pyramids outside the walls of cities that had resisted is documented in Timurid sources, in non-Timurid Persian chronicles, in Arab Mamluk sources, and in European accounts (Clavijo, who visited Samarkand in 1404, mentions seeing displays of skulls; later European travelers report similar sights).

The practice was not invented by Timur — Mongol armies under Genghis Khan and his successors had occasionally done similar things, and pre-Mongol Central Asian warfare had its own traditions of severed-head display — but Timur made it systematic and ostentatious in a way that previous practitioners had not.

The basic mechanism was: a city that resisted, surrendered after a siege, and was then occupied would be subjected to a population massacre, after which the heads of the dead would be collected and stacked into pyramidal towers near the city's gates.
Each tower would contain perhaps thousands or tens of thousands of skulls (the chronicle figures vary widely and are not modern-style census counts).
The towers were left in place as a permanent monument to the punishment.

Documented cases include Sabzevar in eastern Iran (1383), where the city's defenders were massacred after a prolonged siege; Isfahan in 1387, where a tax revolt against a Timurid garrison was punished with a general massacre of perhaps 70,000 people; Tikrit in northern Iraq (1393); Aleppo in Syria (1400); Baghdad in 1401, where the chronicle accounts say each Timurid soldier was ordered to bring at least two heads and the resulting pyramid was one of the largest Timur ever built; and Damascus in 1401.
There were others.

The Isfahan massacre is particularly well-documented because Isfahan was an important Persian-Islamic cultural center and the massacre's effects on the city's intellectual life were noted by contemporary Persian chroniclers who had no reason to exaggerate Timurid atrocities.
The numerical scale of these massacres is hard to pin down.

The chronicle accounts give round figures (70,000 at Isfahan, 90,000 at Baghdad, comparable numbers elsewhere) that are clearly not based on modern-style census methods — they are estimates, and they have a tendency to round up to dramatic-sounding numbers.

Modern historians have argued for both somewhat lower figures (treating chronicle numbers as exaggerations) and somewhat higher figures (when the chronicle accounts are corroborated by archaeological survey data showing depopulation).

The order of magnitude — that Timurid massacres killed people in the tens of thousands at multiple cities, totaling somewhere in the hundreds of thousands of victims across his career — is well-established.
The exact body count is not, and probably cannot be.
What is the point of pausing on this?
Two things.
First, the brutality was not incidental to Timur's career — it was central to his political method.
The skull pyramids were a deliberate signaling device.
The message they sent was: resist Timur and your city will be destroyed; surrender promptly and your city will be spared.
The Damascus, Aleppo, Baghdad, and Delhi examples all happened to cities that had been warned and had refused to submit.
The message was understood.

Cities that heard about the previous massacres were significantly more likely to open their gates without a fight, and Timur preferred this — a city that surrendered yielded its tribute and craftsmen with much less effort than a city that had to be stormed.
Second, the brutality is what produced the cultural achievement.

The skilled craftsmen — weavers, calligraphers, tilemakers, miniature painters, architects, engineers — who built Samarkand into one of the great cities of the medieval world were almost all forcibly deported from the cities Timur had massacred.
Indian stonemasons from Delhi were marched up to Samarkand to build the Bibi-Khanym Mosque.
Damascus weavers were resettled to produce textiles for the Timurid court.
Tabriz miniature painters were brought to work on Timurid manuscripts.
The cultural enrichment of Samarkand in the 1390s and 1400s was directly caused by the cultural impoverishment of every other major city Timur conquered.
He took the artistic capital of the Islamic world and concentrated it forcibly in a single capital.
The Renaissance at Herat under Timur's son Shah Rukh (Chapter 6) inherited this concentrated craft capacity.

The Bihzad miniature tradition, the Jami poetic tradition, the architectural style that the Mughals carried to India — all of this rests on a deportation infrastructure that Timur built through systematic terror across thirty years.
There is no clean way to separate the cultural achievement from the violence that produced it.
They are the same project.
This is unpleasant.
It is also true.
The political component, alongside the puppet khans (Chapter 1), was a system of provincial administration through trusted family members and tribal allies.

Timur installed his sons and grandsons as governors of major provinces — Miran Shah (Timur's third son) in northwestern Iran, Umar Shaykh (Timur's second son) in Fars, Shah Rukh (Timur's fourth son, the eventual successor) in Khorasan, and Pir Muhammad (a grandson) in Afghanistan and parts of India.
The princes had real authority within their provinces but reported to Timur and could be overruled or replaced at any time.
The system worked while Timur was alive; it produced a multi-sided succession war the moment he died (Chapter 5).

The senior tribal emirs of the Chagatai confederation — particularly the surviving Barlas, Jalayir, and Suldus chiefs — were given high military commands and shares of conquered loot but were carefully prevented from accumulating independent provincial power bases.
Timur was careful to rotate emirs between commands, mix tribal contingents in his armies, and intermarry his family with rival emirate clans.
The result was a court structure in which loyalty to Timur personally was more important than tribal affiliation.
After his death, this carefully managed balance fell apart immediately.
The first major external campaign was against Tokhtamysh (TOKH-tah-mish), khan of the Golden Horde (Mongol Empire Ch 8).
The Tokhtamysh war is worth a careful walk-through because it illustrates Timur's method in a particularly clear case.
Tokhtamysh was a Genghisid prince of the Jochid line — a direct descendant of Genghis Khan through Genghis's eldest son Jochi, the founder of the Golden Horde dynasty (Mongol Empire Ch 8).
In the 1370s, the Golden Horde was going through a chaotic period of civil war and dynastic instability.
Tokhtamysh was a contender for the Horde throne but had been driven out of the Jochid territories by his rivals.
He fled south to Transoxiana in the late 1370s and asked Timur for protection.
Timur saw an opportunity.

By backing Tokhtamysh's claim, he could install a Genghisid client on the Golden Horde throne, put one of the four major post-Mongol successor states in his debt, and gain influence across the entire Russian steppe without having to conquer it directly.
He provided Tokhtamysh with troops and supplies.

Tokhtamysh used this support to defeat his rivals and seize the Golden Horde throne in 1380, then went on to consolidate his rule by sacking Moscow in 1382 (an event the Russian chronicles record with horror) and reasserting the Horde's authority over the Russian principalities for another generation.
The arrangement worked beautifully — for Timur.
He had created a Genghisid client without expending much of his own resources, and Tokhtamysh duly acknowledged his gratitude in diplomatic correspondence through the early 1380s.
Then, in the late 1380s, Tokhtamysh turned.

The standard scholarly interpretation is that as Tokhtamysh consolidated power he began to see Timur not as patron but as rival — the Golden Horde's traditional sphere of influence included parts of the Caucasus and northeastern Iran that Timur was conquering, and a Genghisid khan ruling the Horde could not credibly accept being subordinate to a non-Genghisid amir.
Tokhtamysh raided the northern frontier of Timur's empire in 1387, then launched a major invasion of Transoxiana itself in 1388.
Timur's response was overwhelming.

In 1391, he led a Timurid army north into the Russian steppe — one of the most ambitious logistical operations of the medieval world, traversing approximately 1,500 miles (2,400 km) of steppe terrain in a single campaign — and defeated Tokhtamysh at the Battle of the Kondurcha River in June 1391, in what is now the Russian region of Samara.
Tokhtamysh escaped but lost his army.
Tokhtamysh recovered.
Three years later, in 1395, Timur had to do it again.
This time he marched even farther — through the Caucasus and up the Volga — and crushed Tokhtamysh again at the Battle of the Terek River in April 1395.

He then sacked the Golden Horde capital of Sarai (sah-RYE), pursued Tokhtamysh's retreating forces deep into the Kipchak steppe, and systematically destroyed the trading cities along the Volga and lower Don.
The Golden Horde never recovered.

Tokhtamysh fled to Lithuania, was eventually killed in 1406, and the Horde fragmented into smaller successor states (the Crimean Khanate, the Kazan Khanate, the Astrakhan Khanate, the Nogai Horde) over the following century.
The strategic consequences were enormous and largely unintended.
The Tokhtamysh wars eliminated the Golden Horde as a coherent political force.
This in turn freed the Russian principalities — particularly Moscow — from the constant pressure of Horde tribute and military intervention that had constrained Russian state-building for 150 years.

The rise of a unified Russian state under the Muscovite princes in the fifteenth century, completed by Ivan III in the 1480s when Moscow formally repudiated Mongol overlordship, was substantially enabled by the destruction Timur visited on the Golden Horde in 1391–95.

Timur did not intend this — he wanted a docile Genghisid client on the Horde throne, not a permanent power vacuum that allowed Moscow to grow strong — but it is one of his most important historical legacies.
He inadvertently created the geopolitical conditions for the rise of Russia.
A useful comparison: this is the same kind of long-tail strategic consequence that the original Mongol invasions had produced.
Genghis Khan's destruction of the Khwarazmian Empire (Mongol Empire Ch 3) created the conditions for the rise of the Ilkhanate (Mongol Empire Ch 7).

The Mongol sack of Baghdad in 1258 (Mongol Empire Ch 5) ended the Abbasid caliphate (Islamic Golden Age Ch 1) and created the conditions for the Sufi-network political restructuring that would eventually produce the Safavid Empire (Safavid Persia Ch 1).
Imperial conquest in this period regularly produced strategic side effects that lasted for centuries.
Timur's wars against the Golden Horde are a textbook example.
By the mid-1390s, Timur had eliminated the Golden Horde as a threat from the north, conquered Persia (the subject of Chapter 3), and was free to turn his attention to the south and west.
The 1398 Indian campaign and the 1402 confrontation with the Ottomans — the events that made him a household name in European history — were still ahead.
Chapter 4 will cover them.

Cross-civ check: Timur's emergence in the 1370s overlaps with the Ming dynasty's consolidation in China under the Hongwu Emperor (founded 1368, the same decade Timur captured Samarkand), the Aztec ascension to dominance in the Valley of Mexico (Aztec Empire Ch 4–5), the Catholic Schism in Western Europe (the rival popes at Rome and Avignon, 1378–1417), the rise of Vijayanagara as the dominant Hindu kingdom of southern India (Vijayanagara was founded in 1336, the same year as Timur's traditional birth date), and the Mali Empire's late medieval prosperity in West Africa under successors of Mansa Musa (Mali Empire Ch 5–6).
The late fourteenth century is a moment of broad imperial competition across Eurasia, with the post-Mongol world reorganizing into new state systems, and Timur is one of the major reorganizers.

chapters.title: Persia and the Caliphal Heartland
sentences: Through the 1380s and 1390s, Timur conducted a systematic conquest of the Iranian plateau, Iraq, and the southern Caucasus — the heartland of the post-Mongol Islamic world that the Ilkhanate had ruled until its collapse in 1335 (Mongol Empire Ch 7).
The conquest was conducted as a series of multi-year campaigns, punctuated by returns to Samarkand for resupply and reorganization.

The result was the destruction of the successor states that had emerged after the Ilkhanate's fall — the Muzaffarids, the Jalayirids, the Sarbadars, and various smaller dynasties — and the absorption of their territories into the Timurid Empire.
It was also the most demographically and economically destructive phase of Timur's career.

The agricultural infrastructure of the Iranian plateau and Iraq was devastated by the campaigns; the cities were repeatedly sacked; and the central Islamic world emerged from the Timurid wars in a state of long-term decline that did not begin to reverse until the Safavid revival a century later (Safavid Persia Ch 4).

This chapter is about the Persian campaigns — and particularly about the two sacks of Baghdad, which were the most consequential single events of Timur's career for the long-term history of the Islamic world.
A note on the political geography first.
When the Ilkhanate collapsed in 1335 (Mongol Empire Ch 7), the Iranian and Iraqi territories it had ruled fragmented into a constellation of regional successor states.
The major ones were: The Jalayirids (ruled from Baghdad and Tabriz), descendants of an Ilkhanid emir who had seized power in Iraq and northwestern Iran.
They were the largest of the successor states and held the most strategically important territories.
The Muzaffarids (ruled from Shiraz and Isfahan), a Sunni dynasty that controlled most of central and southern Iran.
The Chobanids in northwestern Iran (a rival faction descended from another Ilkhanid emir, defeated by the Jalayirids in the mid-fourteenth century).
The Sarbadars (ruled from Sabzevar in Khorasan), a small but ideologically distinctive Shia movement that had built a quasi-republican state in eastern Iran.
The Karts of Herat (a vassal dynasty that had held Khorasan under nominal Ilkhanid suzerainty).
The Injuids of Shiraz (briefly, before being absorbed by the Muzaffarids).
Various smaller local dynasties in the Caucasus, the Caspian provinces, and the Persian Gulf coast.
None of these states was strong enough to resist Timur.
They were also unable to coordinate against him.
By the 1380s, Persia was a politically fragmented but culturally rich region with no unified defense, ripe for systematic conquest by a determined outside power.
Timur was that power.
The first phase of the Persian conquest, in 1381–1387, focused on Khorasan and the Caspian provinces — the territories closest to Timur's base in Transoxiana.
He took Herat in 1381 from the Kart dynasty (who became Timurid clients), then proceeded west through Mazandaran and Gilan.
The Sarbadar state at Sabzevar in eastern Iran resisted briefly and was punished with the first major Timurid massacre in Iran in 1383.
The chronicle accounts say 2,000 men were buried alive — though the figure is uncertain — and the city's defensive walls were demolished.
The second phase, in 1386–1388, brought Timur into central and southern Iran.
The Muzaffarid dynasty was the main opposition.
Timur defeated several Muzaffarid armies, took Isfahan, Shiraz, and most of Fars and central Persia, and incorporated the region into his expanding empire under client rulers.
The Isfahan massacre of 1387 was the most notorious incident of this phase.
Isfahan had surrendered without a fight to Timur's representatives in 1387 and accepted a Timurid garrison.
A few weeks later, the city's population revolted against the Timurid tax-collection unit and killed approximately 3,000 of Timur's soldiers in a single night.
Timur's response was a general massacre.

The chronicle figures give 70,000 dead — modern historians regard the order of magnitude as plausible even if the precise figure is uncertain — and the heads were stacked into a pyramid outside the city walls.
The Isfahan massacre was the model for what became standard Timurid practice.
A city that resisted from the start might be massacred and burned.
But a city that surrendered, then revolted, would be punished with particular brutality — because the revolt represented a betrayal of the surrender agreement and could not be tolerated as precedent.
The signal was: do not surrender if you intend to revolt later.
The next time Timurid representatives showed up at your gates, they expected the surrender to be permanent, or they would burn you down twice.
The third phase of the Persian campaigns — and the one that mattered most for the long-term history of the Islamic world — was the conquest of Iraq.
Baghdad in 1393 was a much-diminished city.

The original Mongol sack in 1258 (Mongol Empire Ch 5) had killed the last Abbasid caliph, ended the eastern Abbasid caliphate as a functional institution (Islamic Golden Age Ch 8), and reduced the city from one of the largest in the world to a regional capital.

Through the Ilkhanate period and the Jalayirid succession, Baghdad had partially recovered — by the 1390s its population was perhaps 100,000–150,000, far below the million-plus peak of Abbasid times but still substantial — and it remained the cultural and religious center of the eastern Arab Islamic world.
The Jalayirid sultan Ahmad (AH-mad, ruled 1382–1410) had ruled Baghdad and most of Iraq for over a decade and had built up an effective regional administration.
Timur attacked Baghdad in October 1393.
Sultan Ahmad fled west to Mamluk-ruled Syria, abandoning the city.
Baghdad surrendered without much resistance and was occupied by Timurid forces.
Timur did not order a general massacre at this point — the city had submitted promptly — but he extracted enormous tribute, looted the wealth of the Jalayirid court, and imposed a Timurid garrison.
He also did something politically significant.
He installed a member of the Sayyid line of the Abbasid family — descendants of the last Abbasid caliphs — as a ceremonial caliph in Baghdad.
This was a transparent political theater.
The actual eastern Abbasid caliphate had ended in 1258.

The Mamluk Sultanate of Egypt had maintained a parallel "shadow caliphate" in Cairo since the 1260s, with their own line of Abbasid puppets, but no one took these caliphal lineages as legitimate religious authorities in the way the original Abbasid caliphs had been.

By installing his own Sayyid puppet caliph at Baghdad, Timur was claiming a religious legitimacy parallel to the Mamluk Cairene caliphate — a political move designed to demonstrate that the senior Sunni religious authority in the Arab world had recognized Timurid rule.
This was an Islamic-world version of the same legitimacy game Timur was playing on the steppe with the Chagatai puppet khans (Chapter 1).
On the steppe, a Genghisid puppet khan provided steppe legitimacy.
In the Arab heartland, an Abbasid puppet caliph provided Sunni religious legitimacy.
The arrangements were transparent fictions but they served Timur's political needs.
The Sayyid puppet caliph at Baghdad did not last.
After Timur withdrew, the Jalayirid sultan Ahmad returned and the local political arrangements reverted to whatever the situation on the ground produced.
But Timur had made his point.
He could install religious legitimacy as easily as he could massacre populations.
The two practices were complementary parts of the same political project.
The second sack of Baghdad, in 1401, was the catastrophic one.
After the 1393 conquest, Sultan Ahmad had returned to Baghdad and reasserted Jalayirid rule under Timurid suzerainty.

Through the late 1390s, while Timur was occupied with the Indian campaign (Chapter 4) and the Tokhtamysh wars, Ahmad gradually reasserted independence and began to support enemies of the Timurid Empire.
By 1401, with Ahmad in open opposition and Baghdad effectively functioning as an independent city, Timur returned to settle the issue.
The 1401 siege lasted six weeks.

The city resisted vigorously, partly because Ahmad's forces had repaired the walls and stockpiled supplies, partly because the population — having survived the 1393 Timurid occupation and seen what it cost — had no illusions about what surrender would mean.
The siege ended with a Timurid storming of the city in July 1401.
What followed was the second sack.
Timur ordered each of his soldiers to bring a minimum of two human heads.
The accounts describe a systematic massacre of the urban population — soldiers, civilians, men, women, children — that lasted for several days.

The chronicle figures put the dead at 90,000 (some accounts say 100,000), and the heads were stacked into a pyramid that was, by all surviving descriptions, one of the largest such structures Timur ever built.
The 1401 sack is the moment when Baghdad effectively ceased to be a major city for several centuries.
The infrastructure was destroyed.
The administrative class was killed.
The agricultural hinterland was devastated by the troops requisitioning supplies.
Surviving inhabitants fled into the countryside and to neighboring states.
The city's population fell to perhaps 20,000–30,000 by the early fifteenth century — a fraction of its pre-Timur level.
Baghdad would not recover its political importance until the Ottoman conquest in 1534 incorporated it into a long-running empire that could rebuild the urban infrastructure systematically.

The destruction of Baghdad in 1401 is sometimes treated as a continuation of the 1258 Mongol destruction — and there is a real continuity, in the sense that both events are major demographic blows to the same city — but the comparison can mislead.
The 1258 destruction ended an institutional structure (the eastern Abbasid caliphate) but the city itself recovered substantially over the following century.
The 1401 destruction occurred at a moment when the city was already weakened and pushed it into a much longer period of marginality.

The combination of the two — Mongol sack followed by Timurid sack 143 years later — is what reduced Baghdad from "former imperial capital recovering its position" to "regional town with no political weight" for several centuries.
The deeper consequence was for the Arab Islamic world's intellectual life.

Baghdad had been the center of the Islamic Golden Age (Islamic Golden Age Ch 1–4) — the great translation movement, the Bayt al-Hikma library, the philosophical and scientific establishment that had produced Ibn Sina, al-Razi, al-Khwarizmi, and the foundational works of medieval Islamic intellectual life.
The 1258 sack had damaged this; the 1401 sack effectively ended what survived.

The center of gravity of Islamic intellectual culture shifted permanently — eastward to Persianate centers (eventually to Timurid Herat itself, then to Safavid Isfahan), westward to Mamluk Cairo, and to Ottoman Istanbul after 1453.
The Arab core of the early medieval Islamic world never recovered the cultural primacy it had held in the eighth through twelfth centuries.
Some of this would have happened anyway through other historical processes — but the Timurid sacks of Baghdad were a major accelerator.
The Persian campaigns also had a structural cultural consequence: the systematic deportation of skilled craftsmen to Samarkand.
After every major sack — Sabzevar, Isfahan, the Iraqi cities, eventually Damascus and Delhi — Timur's standard practice was to spare and deport the population's skilled craftsmen.

Weavers, calligraphers, miniature painters, tilemakers, masons, metalworkers, glassmakers, papermakers, bookbinders, mathematicians, astronomers, theologians, scribes — all of these specialists, when identified among the surviving population, were marched to Samarkand to work on Timur's building projects, populate the workshops of his court, and contribute to the cultural infrastructure he was building in his capital.
The arithmetic was simple: by the late 1390s, Samarkand had absorbed the craft elite of half a dozen major Persian and Arab cities.
The cultural enrichment of Samarkand was the cultural impoverishment of every other major city Timur had conquered.
Tabriz lost much of its miniature-painting establishment.
Shiraz lost its calligraphy schools.
Damascus lost its weaving guilds.
Baghdad lost what was left of its scholarly community after the 1401 massacre.
All of these specialists ended up in Samarkand, working on the Timurid building program and training a new generation of Samarkand-based craftsmen.

The cultural florescence of fifteenth-century Herat under Shah Rukh (Chapter 6) and fifteenth-century Samarkand under Ulugh Beg (Chapter 7) — the Bihzad miniature tradition, the great architectural projects, the astronomical observatory — rests on this concentrated craft capacity.
The capacity itself was built through forced relocation across thirty years of imperial conquest.
There is no clean separation between the cultural achievement and the deportation mechanism that produced it.
Both are part of the same Timurid project.
A pause: this is an uncomfortable historical pattern, and it is worth not flinching from.
The relationship between imperial violence and cultural flowering is a recurring theme in world history.
The agricultural surpluses extracted by the Maurya Empire funded Ashoka's Buddhist patronage (Maurya Empire Ch 5–6).
The wealth taken from sacked cities funded Roman monumental architecture (Ancient Rome Ch 3).
The forced labor of conquered Mesoamerican peoples funded Aztec temple-building (Aztec Empire Ch 5).
The slave-trade profits funded the Renaissance European art markets that produced Italian Renaissance painting (more on the Italian Renaissance comparison in Chapter 6).
The Timurid case is a particularly direct version of this pattern: the cultural achievement and the violence are not just historically contemporary but mechanistically linked.
The deported craftsmen were the cultural achievement, and they were deported because their cities had been destroyed.
You can deplore this pattern.
You should deplore this pattern.
But you should also see it clearly.
Pretending that the Timurid Renaissance happened on its own merits, separately from the campaigns that built it, is a sanitization that prevents you from understanding either part of the story.
By 1395, with Persia subjugated, the Golden Horde shattered, and the Caucasus under Timurid control, Timur had built one of the largest empires in Eurasian history.
He had also conducted some of the most systematic violence the medieval world had seen.

The next phase of his career — the southern and western expeditions to India, Syria, and Anatolia in 1398–1402 — would extend the empire to its maximum reach and produce the moments by which European history would remember him.

Cross-civ check: the Persian campaigns of the 1380s and 1390s overlap with the late Yuan dynasty in China (collapsing into the Ming Dynasty in 1368, immediately before Timur's rise), the Castilian Reconquista advancing southward against Granada in Spain, the Lithuanian-Polish union through the marriage of Jadwiga and Jogaila in 1386 that produced the largest Christian state in eastern Europe, and the Aztec Triple Alliance consolidating control of the Valley of Mexico (Aztec Empire Ch 5).

Across Eurasia, the late fourteenth century was an era of regional consolidation and imperial competition; Timur's Persian conquest was simultaneous with similar consolidation projects in China, the Iberian peninsula, eastern Europe, and Mexico.

The Timurid achievement was distinctive in scale and brutality, but the broader pattern — a single ruler unifying a fragmented region through military conquest — was the dominant political form of the period.

chapters.title: India and Anatolia
sentences: Timur's reputation in European history rests almost entirely on two events: the 1398 sack of Delhi, and the 1402 capture of the Ottoman sultan Bayezid I (BYE-eh-zeed) at the Battle of Ankara.
Both happened in a four-year period at the height of his career, both produced enormous wealth for the Timurid state, and both had consequences that shaped the next century of Eurasian history.

They also produced the most lurid material in the Timur mythology — the elephants captured at Delhi, the Ottoman sultan in a wheeled cage at Ankara — and that material has dominated the European literary representation of Timur from Christopher Marlowe in 1587 to the present.
This chapter is about the southern and western campaigns of 1398–1402, what happened, and what they meant.
The Indian campaign of 1398 was Timur's most logistically ambitious operation to date.

The march from Samarkand to Delhi covers approximately 1,500 miles (2,400 km) one-way, crossing the Hindu Kush mountains in northern Afghanistan (a major mountain range that effectively separates Central Asia from the Indian subcontinent, with passes that climb above 12,000 feet — the same range Babur would cross 130 years later, Chapter 8), the Indus river valley, and the plains of Punjab.

Timur conducted the operation in a single campaign cycle — leaving Samarkand in spring 1398, fighting at Delhi in December, and returning to Samarkand by spring 1399 — which required careful seasonal scheduling to avoid the Indian monsoon, the central Asian winter, and the worst of the Hindu Kush snow conditions.

The military justification for the campaign was the standard Timurid framing: the Delhi Sultanate under the Tughlaq dynasty had been ruling as Sunni Muslims over a majority Hindu population, and Timur claimed (the chronicle accounts give several variants of the speech) that the Tughlaqs had been insufficiently zealous in promoting Islam.
The actual motivation was loot.
India was famously rich, the Delhi Sultanate was politically weak, and Timur needed the resources for ongoing campaigns in Persia and the planned western expedition.

The Delhi Sultanate had been the dominant Muslim power in northern India for nearly two centuries (founded 1206, the same year Genghis Khan was proclaimed in Mongolia — there is no causal connection, but the simultaneity is striking).
The Tughlaq dynasty (1320–1414) was the third major dynasty of the Sultanate.

Under its founder Muhammad bin Tughlaq in the early fourteenth century the Sultanate had extended deep into south India, but by the 1380s it had lost most of those territories and was reduced to a much smaller territory in Punjab and the Ganges plain.
The reigning Sultan in 1398 was Nasir-ud-Din Mahmud Tughlaq, a young and politically weak ruler in the middle of an internal succession dispute.
The Tughlaq state was structurally vulnerable.
Timur's army crossed the Indus in September 1398 and advanced through Punjab, sacking towns and gathering loot as they went.
The defending forces — provincial governors and local lords commanding fragments of the Tughlaq army — were defeated piecemeal.
By early December the Timurid army was outside Delhi.
The Battle of Delhi, on December 17, 1398, was a one-day affair.
Sultan Mahmud's army, including a large corps of war elephants in elaborate armor, deployed outside the city walls.

Timurid cavalry skirmished with the elephant force; Timur reportedly ordered camels loaded with flammable material driven toward the elephants and set on fire, panicking the elephants and breaking the Tughlaq line.
The Tughlaq army collapsed, Mahmud fled, and Timur entered Delhi as conqueror.
What followed was not the orderly tribute-extraction Timur had originally planned.

The chronicle accounts (including Timur's own apologetic version in the official Timurid history) describe a multi-day general massacre that Timur said he had not ordered — soldiers began plundering individual houses, fighting broke out between Timurid troops and Delhi residents who tried to defend their property, and the violence spiraled out of control.
By the time Timur's commanders restored discipline several days later, much of the city had been looted, large sections had been burned, and a significant fraction of the population was dead.
The exact death toll is unrecoverable.
