Contemporary chronicle estimates range widely; many give six-figure numbers (100,000 or higher) but these should be read as orders of magnitude rather than census counts.

What is well-attested is that Delhi was effectively uninhabitable for years afterward — contemporary accounts describe streets choked with corpses, the city's water supply contaminated, surviving residents fleeing to surrounding regions, and the urban infrastructure largely destroyed.

The historian Yahya bin Ahmad Sirhindi, writing several decades later, said that for two months no birds were heard in Delhi — a literary trope, but one that probably preserves something of the actual desolation.
Timur withdrew from Delhi in early January 1399, marching back to Samarkand with an enormous baggage train of looted wealth.

He also took with him a substantial corps of Indian skilled craftsmen — particularly stonemasons, who were destined to work on the great congregational mosque he was building at Samarkand (the Bibi-Khanym Mosque, completed 1404).
He took the surviving Hindu war elephants, which became part of his subsequent campaigns and were used to dramatic effect at Ankara in 1402.
The total loot — gold, silver, textiles, jewels — was enormous, sufficient to fund Timurid government operations for years.
The political consequences of the Delhi sack ran longer than Timur intended.

The Tughlaq dynasty did not formally end in 1398 — Sultan Mahmud returned to Delhi after Timur's departure and nominal Tughlaq sultans continued in office for another sixteen years — but real Tughlaq political authority was destroyed.

The provincial governors of the former Sultanate effectively went their own ways, the central administration collapsed, and the dynasty became a ceremonial fiction maintained by whichever provincial lord happened to control Delhi at the moment.

The Tughlaqs were formally replaced in 1414 by the Sayyid dynasty (a confusing name, since this Sayyid dynasty has no connection to the Sayyid puppet caliph Timur installed at Baghdad — different region, different family, same Arabic word meaning "descendant of the Prophet"), which was followed in 1451 by the Lodi dynasty, which was finally swept away by Babur at Panipat in 1526 (Chapter 8).

The 128-year arc from Timur's sack to Babur's victory is one continuous story — the gradual hollowing-out of a once-great Sultanate that had been mortally wounded by the Timurid invasion and never recovered.

Timur's grandson Pir Muhammad (peer moh-HAH-mad) was installed as Timurid governor of Punjab and parts of India in 1399, but his position was weak and the Timurid presence in India faded within a few years.
The 1398 expedition was therefore a raid, not a conquest.
The wealth was extracted, the Delhi Sultanate was crippled, and then the Timurids withdrew.
The Mughal claim to Indian sovereignty 128 years later under Babur (Chapter 8) ran partly through this 1398 precedent.

Babur, a direct descendant of Timur, framed his 1526 invasion as the recovery of territories that his ancestor had legitimately conquered — a flimsy legal argument but one that mattered in early-modern Islamic political thought.
The 1398 sack and the 1526 conquest are part of the same dynastic continuity.
After the Indian campaign, Timur returned to Samarkand for a year of consolidation, then turned west for what would become his last major external campaign.

The objective was the eastern Mediterranean — specifically the Mamluk Sultanate of Egypt (which controlled Syria from Damascus) and the Ottoman Empire (which controlled Anatolia from its capital at Bursa).
Both were major Islamic powers.
Both had refused to acknowledge Timurid suzerainty.
Both had to be punished.
The Syrian campaign came first.
Timur invaded Mamluk Syria in 1400, defeated a Mamluk army outside Aleppo, and stormed the city.

Aleppo had been a major commercial and intellectual center for centuries — a key node on the long-distance trade routes connecting the Mediterranean to Mesopotamia and Iran — and the sack devastated its commercial infrastructure.

The chronicle accounts describe the standard Timurid massacre and skull-pyramid, with the additional detail that the great congregational mosque was used as a stable for Timurid horses (a religious provocation Timur would not have done at a Sunni mosque in his own territory but apparently considered acceptable in a city he had just conquered).
The army then pushed south to Damascus, the great Mamluk regional capital.
Damascus was besieged through the winter of 1400–1401 and surrendered in March 1401 after the Mamluk garrison's counterattacks failed and supplies inside the walls ran out.

Timur extracted enormous tribute, demanded the deportation of the city's craftsmen — Damascene weavers, metalworkers, and tilemakers, all famous across the medieval Islamic world for their skills — to Samarkand, and ordered the sack to proceed.

The chronicle accounts describe widespread destruction; the Great Mosque of Damascus (the Umayyad Mosque, one of the oldest and most architecturally important mosques in the Islamic world) suffered fire damage during the sack, though it was restored afterward.

It was during these surrender negotiations that Timur met Ibn Khaldun (ib-n hahl-DOON, 1332–1406), the Tunisian historian and political theorist who was at that moment serving as a senior judicial official of the Mamluk regime in Damascus.

Ibn Khaldun is one of the most important medieval historical theorists; his Muqaddimah ("Introduction" — a long preface to his world history that has been read as a foundational text of historical sociology) had been completed in 1377, and he was already a famous intellectual in his own time.
He met Timur multiple times in early 1401 and recorded his impressions in his autobiography.
The meetings are one of the best primary-source descriptions of Timur we have.
Ibn Khaldun was struck by Timur's intelligence.
The chronicle accounts of Timur sometimes give the impression of a brutal warlord with limited political subtlety; Ibn Khaldun's first-hand description gives a different picture.

Timur was, according to Ibn Khaldun, sharp, well-informed, intellectually curious, knowledgeable about the political situations of distant regions, and capable of conducting sustained intellectual conversation about questions of history and dynastic succession.
He asked Ibn Khaldun about the political geography of North Africa (which Ibn Khaldun knew well), about the dynastic history of the Mamluks, and about Ibn Khaldun's own theoretical writings.
He was, in Ibn Khaldun's account, a recognizably sophisticated political mind — albeit one operating in service of an unflinching willingness to use mass violence.
This is worth flagging because the Marlovian image of Timur as pure brutish conqueror is misleading.
Timur was an intellectual operator as well as a soldier.
He maintained an elaborate court historian establishment (Yazdi's Zafarnama and other official histories were written under direct Timurid patronage).
He made political decisions on the basis of careful analysis of opponents and circumstances.
The brutality was a chosen instrument of policy, not an absence of policy.
Ibn Khaldun saw this clearly.
Modern historians who have read Ibn Khaldun's account carefully tend to agree.
After the Damascus sack, Timur withdrew north — back through Aleppo, into the Anatolian frontier zone, and toward his next objective: the Ottoman Empire.
The Ottoman Empire in 1400 was a rising power.

Founded around 1300 in northwestern Anatolia by Osman I (Ottoman Empire Ch 1), the Ottoman dynasty had spent the fourteenth century expanding through the Balkans and absorbing other Anatolian principalities.

By the late 1390s, under Sultan Bayezid I ("the Thunderbolt," ruled 1389–1402), the Ottomans had: Defeated a major Crusader army at the Battle of Nicopolis in 1396, halting Western European efforts to roll back Ottoman expansion in the Balkans.
Conquered most of Anatolia from the rival Turkish principalities, unifying the peninsula under Ottoman rule for the first time.

Begun a long blockade of Constantinople with the apparent intention of taking the Byzantine capital (which would in fact fall to Bayezid's great-grandson Mehmed II in 1453, Byzantine Empire Ch 12 and Ottoman Empire Ch 4).
Established a formidable military system based on the Janissary corps (Ottoman Empire Ch 3) — Christian boys from the Balkans, recruited as slaves, raised as Muslims, and trained as elite infantry.
Bayezid was widely considered the most successful Sunni Muslim ruler of his generation.

He was also, like Timur, an outsider ruler trying to legitimize a non-traditional dynasty — the Ottomans had no Genghisid lineage, no caliphal connection, no Abbasid sanction, only their military success and their growing reputation as the Islamic world's frontier defenders against Christendom.
The collision between Timur and Bayezid had been building for years.
Timurid expansion westward was bringing Timur's territories into direct contact with Ottoman territories in eastern Anatolia.
Several of the Anatolian Turkish princes the Ottomans had conquered had appealed to Timur for support against Bayezid; some Ottoman vassals in eastern Anatolia were defecting to Timur.
Diplomatic correspondence between the two rulers had grown increasingly hostile.
Bayezid's letters reportedly addressed Timur with insulting forms of address; Timur's responses warned of consequences.
By the spring of 1402, Timur's army was in eastern Anatolia, and Bayezid was assembling his forces to meet it.
The Battle of Ankara was fought on July 28, 1402, on a plain east of the Anatolian city of Ankara (then a regional center of moderate size, now the capital of modern Turkey).

The military details: Timur's army numbered perhaps 140,000 to 200,000 (the figures are disputed) and included substantial cavalry forces, elephants from the Indian campaign, and a heterogeneous mix of Turco-Mongol contingents, Persian troops, and conscripts from conquered territories.

Bayezid's army was somewhat smaller, perhaps 85,000 to 120,000, but included the elite Janissary infantry, Ottoman feudal cavalry (the sipahi), Anatolian Turkish vassal contingents, and Serbian heavy cavalry under the Serbian prince Stefan Lazarević (a vassal of the Ottomans by treaty after Nicopolis).
The Anatolian Turkish vassal contingents were a structural weakness.

Many of these troops had been incorporated into the Ottoman army less than a decade earlier, after the Ottoman conquest of their home principalities, and several of their commanders had been in clandestine correspondence with Timur.
When the battle opened, the Anatolian contingents on the Ottoman left wing defected to the Timurid side and turned on their former comrades.
The Ottoman left wing collapsed.
The center held longer.
Bayezid's Janissaries fought the Timurid center to a standstill through most of the day, and the Serbian heavy cavalry on the Ottoman right wing actually pushed Timur's left back.
But the collapse of the Anatolian left wing allowed Timurid cavalry to swing around behind the Ottoman center, and by late afternoon the Ottoman army was being attacked from front and rear.
Bayezid attempted to break out with his bodyguard but was surrounded and captured.
Sultan Bayezid I was taken alive — the first time a major Ottoman sultan had been captured in battle, and the first time any major Sunni Muslim sovereign had been taken prisoner in this manner.
Several of his sons were killed in the battle; others escaped.
The Ottoman army was destroyed.
The captivity of Bayezid is one of the famous episodes of medieval history, and the chronicle accounts of it are colorful enough that some sorting through is needed.
The widely-known story — that Bayezid was kept in a wheeled cage and humiliated at Timur's banquets, with his wife forced to serve naked at the feasts — has a mixed historical pedigree.

The cage story originates in late Persian and Ottoman chronicle accounts and is repeated in the European literature; modern Ottoman historians have generally treated it as embellished or anachronistic.

The contemporary accounts that survive (including the Timurid official sources) describe Bayezid as held under house-arrest conditions, traveling with Timur's court but not in a cage, and treated with the standard ceremonial respect due a captured but defeated sovereign.
He was given quarters appropriate to his rank, attended by his own retainers, and consulted on matters of policy.
Timur is reported to have lectured him about his political mistakes.

What is well-documented: Bayezid's psychological state deteriorated through the months of captivity, his health declined, and he died on March 8, 1403, eight months after the battle, while still in Timurid custody.
The cause of death is variously reported as illness, an apoplectic stroke, or — in some accounts — suicide by self-administered poison.
He was buried in the Ottoman capital at Bursa under a tomb that survives.

The version of the captivity story Christopher Marlowe used in Tamburlaine the Great (1587) — Bayezid in an iron cage, used as Timur's footstool when mounting his horse, finally smashing his head against the bars in despair — is dramatic but not historical.
It draws on the Italian and Latin sources transmitted through Renaissance Europe, themselves drawing on the embellished Persian-Ottoman chronicle tradition.
Marlowe's play established Timur's image in European cultural memory as the cruel oriental conqueror, and the cage in particular became one of the signature images of European Orientalism.

Modern English-language general readers' knowledge of Timur often runs back through Marlowe rather than directly to the chronicle sources, and the result is an unreliable composite picture of the actual Bayezid captivity.
What does matter, historically, is the political consequences.
The political consequences of Ankara ran for half a century.
Bayezid's death triggered the Ottoman Interregnum of 1402–1413, during which Bayezid's surviving sons fought a multi-sided civil war for the Ottoman throne.

Süleyman Çelebi, İsa Çelebi, Musa Çelebi, and Mehmed Çelebi each held parts of the Ottoman territories at various times, with Timurid forces initially backing different claimants in the early years and then withdrawing as Timur died and the Timurid succession crisis (Chapter 5) consumed Timurid attention.
Mehmed Çelebi finally defeated the last of his brothers in 1413 and was acknowledged as Sultan Mehmed I, reconstituting a unified Ottoman state.
The Interregnum cost the Ottomans roughly half a century of recovery time.
The institutional structures of the empire had to be rebuilt.
The Anatolian Turkish principalities the Ottomans had conquered before 1402 had to be re-conquered (the process was completed only under Murad II in the 1420s and 1430s).
The Balkan vassals had to be re-subjected.

The blockade of Constantinople was abandoned; the Byzantine capital, which had been on the brink of falling to Bayezid in 1402, survived for another 51 years until Mehmed II finally took it in 1453 (Byzantine Empire Ch 12, Ottoman Empire Ch 4).
It is hard to overstate the consequence of this delay.

If Bayezid had not been defeated at Ankara, the Ottoman conquest of Constantinople might have happened in the 1400s rather than the 1450s — possibly under Bayezid himself, conceivably with quite different international consequences.

The Byzantine refugees who fled west after 1453 carrying Greek manuscripts to Italy, where they fed into the Italian Renaissance's recovery of classical texts (Byzantine Empire Ch 12 details this), would have arrived half a century earlier.
The Ottoman wars of the late fifteenth century against Venice, the Mamluks, and various Balkan states would have looked very different.
The relationship between the early-modern Mediterranean and the early-modern Islamic world might have developed on a different trajectory altogether.
The Battle of Ankara is therefore one of those tactical events whose strategic consequences ramify far beyond the immediate participants.
Timur won a battle in central Anatolia in July 1402 and inadvertently shaped the political geography of the eastern Mediterranean for the next century.

The fall of Constantinople in 1453, the survival of the Byzantine remnants until that date, the Ottoman recovery and renewed expansion under Mehmed II, the eventual Safavid-Ottoman confrontation that began at Chaldiran in 1514 (Safavid Persia Ch 3) — all of this was conditioned by what Timur did at Ankara.
A useful comparison: the Ottoman Empire in 1402 was at roughly the same stage of development that the Safavid Empire would reach a century later under Ismail I (Safavid Persia Ch 1–2).
Both were Sunni-Sufi-derived imperial projects (the Ottomans drawing on the Babai dervish networks of fourteenth-century Anatolia, the Safavids on the Safaviyya order at Ardabil).
Both used cavalry-based armies built around tribal-confederation contingents.
Both faced the structural problem of building professional standing armies that could replace the founding tribal levies.

The Ottomans had gotten further with this — the Janissary corps Bayezid commanded at Ankara was already the most formally institutionalized standing army in the Islamic world, and would become the model that the Safavid Abbas the Great explicitly imitated when building his ghulam corps a century later (Safavid Persia Ch 4).

The Ottoman defeat at Ankara was therefore a defeat of one of the most institutionally advanced military systems of the period — by an army that was, in its core, still a Mongol-style cavalry confederation.
It was the last great victory of the Mongol military tradition over the early forms of the gunpowder-age standing army.
By the end of 1402, Timur had captured the Ottoman sultan, sacked Damascus, ended Tughlaq Delhi, conquered Persia, broken the Golden Horde, and built one of the largest empires in human history.
He was sixty-six years old.
His next project was Ming China.
Cross-civ check: the years 1398–1402 are extraordinarily dense with major events across Eurasia.

The Chinese Yongle Emperor seized the Ming throne in a civil war against his nephew (1399–1402, exactly contemporary with Timur's western expedition); the Aztec Triple Alliance was completing its conquest of the Valley of Mexico under Acamapichtli's successors (Aztec Empire Ch 5); the Hundred Years' War in Europe was in a quiet phase between major campaigns, with Henry IV consolidating power in England and the French monarchy increasingly dysfunctional under Charles VI's madness; the Joseon dynasty in Korea, founded in 1392, was in the early consolidation phase under Taejong (Joseon Korea Ch 1); the Vijayanagara Empire in southern India was at peak power under Bukka I and his successors.
These are years that pack four or five major historical inflection points into a single short span, and Timur's campaigns intersect with several of them.

chapters.title: The Death and the Will
sentences: In late 1404, Timur was sixty-eight years old.
He had spent thirty-five years in continuous warfare.
He had built one of the largest empires in human history and conducted some of the most violent campaigns in medieval history.
By any reasonable measure he should have settled in Samarkand, enjoyed the wealth he had accumulated, and let his sons and grandsons run the empire.
Instead, he assembled the largest army of his career and prepared to invade Ming China.
He did not get there.
He died at Otrar in February 1405, before the campaign could properly begin.

The succession that followed lasted four years, killed several of his grandsons, fragmented the empire he had assembled, and ended with his fourth son Shah Rukh (shah ROOK) emerging as the consolidator from his governorship of Khorasan.
The reduced Timurid Empire that Shah Rukh would govern — Khorasan, Transoxiana, parts of Persia — was much smaller than the empire Timur had accumulated.
But it was the empire that produced the cultural florescence that defined Timurid civilization and that the next three chapters cover.
This chapter is about the China campaign that did not happen, the death at Otrar, and the succession war that reshaped the Timurid Empire.
The China campaign needs some explaining.

By 1404, why would Timur — already past sixty-five, with an enormous accumulated wealth and territorial reach — set out on a logistically extreme expedition into the largest and richest state in the world?
The political framing was religious.

Ming China under the Yongle Emperor (yong-LUH, ruled 1402–1424) was, in Timur's framing, a Buddhist-Confucian state ruling a population that included substantial Muslim minorities (particularly in the western frontier provinces of Gansu and Yunnan).
Timur claimed his China expedition was a holy war (a jihad) to convert China to Islam.

The framing is not quite as preposterous as it sounds — there was a real Muslim community in China dating back to Tang dynasty contacts (Tang-Song China Ch 4), the Ming had inherited substantial Muslim populations from the Yuan dynasty (Mongol Empire Ch 6), and a Timurid invasion could plausibly have linked up with internal Muslim populations in the western Chinese frontier zones.
But the framing was also clearly a public justification rather than the actual motivation.

The actual motivations were probably some combination of: continuing the cycle of campaigns that had defined Timur's career and that his army required; the enormous wealth of Ming China, which would dwarf even the Indian loot; the political logic of being seen to outdo Genghis Khan, whose Yuan dynasty descendants had ruled China before being driven out by the Ming founder in 1368; and, possibly, a specific provocation from the Ming court.
The provocation, if there was one, ran back to a 1395 diplomatic incident.

The Hongwu Emperor, the Ming founder, had sent an embassy to Samarkand that interpreted Timur's response as a tributary submission to Ming overlordship — a misreading that may have been deliberate diplomatic insult, or may have been a misunderstanding of Timur's chancery conventions, but that Timur held against the Chinese state for the next decade.
He held the embassy at Samarkand for years (the chronicle accounts say various of the ambassadors died in Timurid custody) and eventually sent counter-letters framing himself as the senior partner.
By the early 1400s, in Timurid diplomatic framing, China had insulted Timur and the punitive expedition was overdue.
The military preparations were enormous.

Timur assembled an army at Samarkand in late 1404 — the chronicle figures give 200,000 men, though as with all medieval army-size figures this should be treated as an order of magnitude rather than a precise count — supplied with food and equipment for an extended winter march through the Tian Shan and Tarim Basin region.
The route was the classic Silk Road northern route: Samarkand to Tashkent, then Otrar on the Syr Darya, then up into the Dzhungarian basin and across to the Ming frontier.
The march would take many months.

The Ming court, well-informed of the preparations through their own diplomatic network and through merchants traveling the trade routes, was preparing defenses on the Gansu frontier — the Yongle Emperor, ruling China from his new capital at Beijing, ordered frontier garrisons reinforced and the relevant sections of the Great Wall strengthened through 1404.
Timur left Samarkand in December 1404 — late in the season, against the advice of his commanders, into a Central Asian winter.
He reached Otrar (in modern Kazakhstan, on the Syr Darya river) in late January 1405.
The army camped at Otrar to wait out the worst of the winter conditions before pushing east into the Tian Shan.
Timur died at Otrar on February 17 or 18, 1405.
The chronicle accounts describe a sudden onset of fever, several days of illness, and death in his tent surrounded by his commanders.

Modern readings of the symptoms (fever, weakness, eventual death within days) are consistent with pneumonia, influenza, or a similar respiratory infection — exactly the kind of illness an elderly man would be vulnerable to in winter conditions in a freezing Central Asian camp.
He was sixty-eight or sixty-nine years old.
The Yongle Emperor's defensive preparations had been unnecessary.
The largest planned military operation of the fifteenth century did not happen.
Timur's body was preserved (the chronicle accounts say it was embalmed by Egyptian techniques learned from craftsmen taken at Damascus) and transported back to Samarkand for burial.

He was interred in the Gur-e-Amir mausoleum, which his grandson Muhammad Sultan had begun building in 1403 — a domed tomb chamber in the Persianate-Timurid architectural tradition, with a high drum, a melon-ribbed turquoise dome on a square chamber, and elaborate banna'i tilework.

The completed mausoleum (finished under Shah Rukh by about 1410) became the architectural prototype for the great Persianate domed tombs of the next two centuries — including, most famously, the Taj Mahal (1648) at Agra, built by Timur's descendant Shah Jahan more than two centuries later.
The Taj Mahal's silhouette is recognizably the Gur-e-Amir's silhouette, scaled up and elaborated.
The Mughal mausoleum tradition that produced the Taj started here, in the tomb of the man whose 1398 sack of Delhi the Mughals would later struggle to live down.
The Soviet exhumation of 1941 (Chapter 1) confirmed the identity of the remains and the chronicle descriptions of the lameness and arm injuries.
The skeleton showed signs of the active life Timur had led — old wounds, healed fractures, calluses from horseback riding — and confirmed that he had died around the age the chronicles gave.
The forensic facial reconstruction Mikhail Gerasimov produced is the standard modern image of Timur, used in textbooks and museum displays from Tashkent to London to Tehran.
The succession war began immediately.
Timur's surviving sons in 1405 were: Miran Shah (mee-RAHN shah, ruled portions of northwestern Iran), Timur's third son, then in his late forties.

He had a reputation for instability and possibly mental illness, which had cost him several governorships during Timur's lifetime, but he commanded a significant army and held strategic territory in Azerbaijan.
Shah Rukh (shah ROOK, ruled Khorasan from Herat), Timur's fourth son, then about twenty-eight.
He had been a competent governor of Khorasan since the 1390s and had not been involved in any of the more contentious court politics.
He was widely respected but not a flashy military leader.
Timur's surviving grandsons in line for parts of the empire included: Khalil Sultan (kha-LEEL sool-TAHN), son of Miran Shah, then about twenty-one.
He happened to be at Samarkand when the news of Timur's death reached the city.
Pir Muhammad (peer moh-HAH-mad), son of Timur's eldest son Jahangir (who had died in 1376), then about thirty.
Timur had formally designated him as heir.
Muhammad Sultan, the grandson who had been building the Gur-e-Amir, had died of illness in 1403 — a major blow to the succession because Timur had also favored him for the throne.
Several other grandsons of varying ages, governing minor provinces.
Timur had nominally designated Pir Muhammad as his successor and made it formal at a kurultai in 1404 before leaving for the China campaign.
But the designation was contested.
Khalil Sultan, taking advantage of being on the spot at Samarkand, simply seized the Timurid capital, the imperial treasury, and Timur's body (when the funeral cortège arrived).
He then declared himself sovereign over the central Timurid territories.
Pir Muhammad, in southern Persia, refused to recognize Khalil Sultan and began organizing forces to march on Samarkand.
Miran Shah, in Azerbaijan, did the same.
Shah Rukh, in Khorasan, did not move immediately.
He maintained his governorship at Herat, did not contest the succession openly, and waited.
For the first four years after Timur's death — 1405 to 1409 — the empire fragmented into competing claimant zones.
Khalil Sultan held Samarkand and parts of Transoxiana but his rule was profligate and ineffective.
He spent the imperial treasury lavishly on his Persian wife Shad al-Mulk and her relatives, alienating the senior Timurid emirs whose loyalty he needed.
The senior emirs began deserting to other claimants.
Pir Muhammad, in southern Persia, was assassinated by his own vizier in 1407 — eliminating one major contender.
Miran Shah was killed in battle in 1408 fighting the Kara Qoyunlu Turkmen of western Iran (an early sign that Timurid control over Persia was unraveling).

The western and southern parts of the empire — Mesopotamia, western Iran, Anatolia, the Caucasus — fell out of Timurid control entirely, absorbed by the Aq Qoyunlu and Kara Qoyunlu Turkmen confederations.
By early 1409, with most of the contenders dead and the empire fragmenting, Shah Rukh finally moved.

He marched from Herat with an army of Khorasani troops, advanced on Samarkand, defeated Khalil Sultan's forces, and captured Khalil Sultan himself. (Shah Rukh did not execute his nephew — a notable display of moderation by Timurid standards.
Khalil Sultan was sent to Ray as a provincial governor, where he died of illness in 1411.) Shah Rukh consolidated control of Transoxiana, Khorasan, and parts of central Persia by the end of 1409.
He installed his son Ulugh Beg as governor of Samarkand.
He himself returned to Herat, which would remain the Timurid capital for the rest of his reign.
The reduced Timurid Empire that emerged from the four-year succession war was much smaller than the empire Timur had assembled.
Mesopotamia, western Persia, the Caucasus, and Anatolia were lost.
India was lost.
The territories Shah Rukh actually controlled were essentially Khorasan (modern eastern Iran and western Afghanistan), Transoxiana (modern Uzbekistan), and parts of central Persia.

This was still a substantial empire — roughly the same area as the original Samanid state of the tenth century, or the eastern half of the old Sasanian Empire (Persian Empire Ch 9) — but it was a fraction of what Timur had ruled at his peak.
The empire had been right-sized by the violence of its own succession.
The chapter could end here, but it is worth pausing on what Shah Rukh's strategic decision to consolidate rather than expand actually meant.
Timur had spent his career in continuous campaigning.

The Timurid army was structured around the expectation of regular campaigns — tribal contingents fighting for shares of loot, senior emirs commanding expeditions in exchange for political loyalty, the entire patronage system depending on a constant flow of conquered wealth.
A Timurid ruler who stopped campaigning would have to find a different way to keep the army loyal and the political coalition intact.
Shah Rukh chose to do exactly this.

He campaigned occasionally — there were Khorasani campaigns against the Kara Qoyunlu in the 1420s, and he conducted military operations on his eastern frontier — but he made no serious attempt to recover the territories his father had lost.

Instead, he reorganized the imperial finances, restored agricultural production in the territories he controlled (some of which had been devastated by Timur's earlier campaigns and were only now recovering), and channeled state resources into administrative reform and cultural patronage rather than into expansion.
This was a fundamental shift in the character of the Timurid project.
Under Timur, the empire was a war-making machine that produced extraordinary cultural side effects through deportation of craftsmen.

Under Shah Rukh, the empire became a Persianate state in the older medieval Islamic tradition — administered through bureaucratic structures, taxed through agricultural revenues, and oriented toward the patronage of arts, scholarship, and architecture as ends in themselves.
The cultural florescence at Herat that Chapter 6 describes was the direct product of this reorientation.
It was possible only because Shah Rukh had decided the Timurid Empire was no longer going to be primarily a conquest state.
The decision was politically risky.
The senior Timurid emirs — and many of the second-tier military commanders — had been raised in the campaign culture and resisted the shift.
There were several rebellions during Shah Rukh's reign, including by some of his own sons (Miran Shah's son Iskandar Sultan rebelled in Fars in 1414 and had to be put down by force).
But the shift held.

By the 1420s the Timurid Empire under Shah Rukh was operating as a settled imperial state in the older Persianate-Islamic tradition, with Herat as a flourishing cultural capital and a stable agricultural-tax economy.
The Timurid Renaissance was beginning.
A useful comparison: this is the same kind of generational transition from "founding warrior dynasty" to "settled administrative state" that other post-Mongol successor regimes had to navigate.
The Yuan dynasty in China (Mongol Empire Ch 6) had to make a similar shift under Kublai Khan and his successors, with mixed results.
The Ilkhanate in Iran (Mongol Empire Ch 7) made the shift under Ghazan Khan in the 1290s, more successfully.
The Golden Horde (Mongol Empire Ch 8) made the shift under successive khans through the fourteenth century, less successfully.

The Timurid Empire's version of this transition — under Shah Rukh, in 1409–1447 — was probably the most successful of the Mongol successor transitions in cultural terms, even though the political base was the smallest of the four.
Shah Rukh's deliberate de-prioritization of military expansion in favor of administrative consolidation produced Herat.
It also produced the structural weakness that would let the Uzbeks dismember the empire a century later (Chapter 8).

Cross-civ check: the Timurid succession crisis of 1405–1409 overlaps with Henry V's accession in England (1413, just after Mehmed I's reunification of the Ottoman Empire), the Council of Constance that ended the Catholic Schism in 1417, the early Hussite Wars in Bohemia (after 1419), and the founding of the Korean Joseon dynasty's new capital at Hanseong (modern Seoul) in 1392–1395.

The early fifteenth century is a moment when several major powers were going through generational transitions — and the Timurid case is one of the more dramatic, with the largest medieval empire of its day right-sizing itself through internal violence.

chapters.title: Shah Rukh and the Herat Renaissance
sentences: For the next four decades after his consolidation in 1409, Shah Rukh (shah ROOK, ruled effectively 1409–1447) governed the reduced Timurid Empire from his capital at Herat (HEH-rat) in northwestern Afghanistan.

Under his patronage, and the patronage of his remarkable wife Gawhar Shad (gow-HAR shahd) and several of his sons, Herat became one of the most important cultural centers of the early-modern Islamic world.
The miniature painting tradition that emerged at fifteenth-century Herat is the direct ancestor of all subsequent Persianate book art — Safavid, Mughal, and later.
The architectural style developed at Herat is the direct ancestor of Mughal architecture, including the Taj Mahal.
The Persian poetic tradition that culminated at Herat in the work of Jami (JAH-mee) is the closing chapter of classical Persian poetry.

The astronomical and mathematical work conducted at the parallel capital of Samarkand under Shah Rukh's son Ulugh Beg (oo-LOOG BEG, the subject of Chapter 7) was the most advanced pre-telescopic astronomy in the world.
This chapter is about the Herat Renaissance — what it was, who built it, and what made it possible.

The shift from Samarkand to Herat as the political and cultural center of the Timurid Empire is worth pausing on, because it represents the decisive turn from the empire's Mongol-Turkic founding identity toward its Persianate cultural identity.
Samarkand had been Timur's capital.
It was a Transoxianan city — north of the Amu Darya river, in the heartland of the steppe-adjacent agricultural zone that the Mongol successor states had ruled.

Timur had built the great Bibi-Khanym Mosque there, the Gur-e-Amir mausoleum, the Aq Saray palace at his nearby birthplace of Shahrisabz, and the array of formal gardens (the chahar bagh quadripartite garden tradition) that surrounded the city.
Samarkand was the political center of the empire and the architectural showcase of the dynasty.
Herat was different.

It was a Khorasani city — south of the Amu Darya, on the western edge of what had been the Ghaznavid and Ghurid empires of the eleventh and twelfth centuries, and a major center of Persian-language high culture for centuries.
The Sufi order networks at Herat ran back through the Naqshbandi (Chapter 8) to the spiritual masters of the eleventh century.
The city had been an important regional capital under the Ilkhanate (Mongol Empire Ch 7) and the Karts (the dynasty Timur had displaced in the 1380s).
It had not been Timur's capital but it had been governed by Shah Rukh as a senior provincial center for two decades before the succession crisis.
When Shah Rukh emerged as the consolidator after 1409, he kept Herat as his capital and let Samarkand become a secondary center under his son Ulugh Beg.
The choice was deliberate.
Herat was further from the steppe — culturally, geographically, and politically.
It was deeper in the Persianate world.
It was less subject to the tribal pressures from Transoxiana that had produced the political instability of the late fourteenth century.
It was also Shah Rukh's own established power base, where he had spent his entire adult life as governor and where his court establishment was based.
Moving the capital there was a way of de-prioritizing the Mongol-Turkic dimension of the empire and prioritizing the Persianate dimension.
This was a structural choice with consequences.
The Timurid Empire under Timur had been a hybrid — Mongol-Turkic political theater (puppet khans, kurultai assemblies, steppe tribal armies) overlaid on Persianate administration.
Under Shah Rukh, the Persianate side won.
The puppet khans were quietly dropped (Shah Rukh did not consistently use them).
The chancery shifted toward Persian as the primary administrative language.
The court ceremony took on Persianate forms drawn from the Ilkhanid and earlier traditions.

The patronage of arts, scholarship, and architecture was conducted on the model of older Persian-Islamic dynasties — Samanid, Ghaznavid, Seljuk — rather than in the Turco-Mongol style Timur had favored.
This was the same shift the Ilkhanate had made under Ghazan Khan in the 1290s (Mongol Empire Ch 7) — a Mongol successor state Persianizing into a recognizably Iranian dynasty.
It was the shift the Yuan dynasty in China had partially made under Kublai Khan and his successors (Mongol Empire Ch 6) — Mongols ruling in increasingly Sinified style.
The Timurid version of this shift, under Shah Rukh, was particularly successful in cultural terms.
It is what made the Herat Renaissance possible.

Gawhar Shad is the figure who deserves to be introduced first, because she is one of the most important early-modern patrons of architecture in the Islamic world, and because the conventional histories of the period have systematically underplayed her role.

Gawhar Shad ("Joyous Jewel," c. 1379–1457) was Shah Rukh's principal wife — they had married in 1388 when she was about nine and he was about ten, in a politically arranged marriage between two senior Timurid families.

As an adult, Gawhar Shad acquired control of substantial financial resources independent of Shah Rukh: she held lands in Khorasan in her own name, governed the city of Mashhad (mahsh-HAD, in northeastern Iran — the location of the great shrine of Imam Reza, the eighth Shia Imam), commanded her own household troops, and made independent diplomatic and political decisions that the chronicles record.

She also dominated court politics in ways that no other Timurid woman had done — installing her sons in key positions, intervening in disputes between Shah Rukh and his other relatives, and conducting her own correspondence with Ming Chinese officials and other foreign rulers.
Her great accomplishment was architectural patronage.
The two major projects she funded and personally directed are: The Gawhar Shad Mosque at Mashhad, completed in 1418, attached to the great shrine of Imam Reza.

The mosque is one of the masterpieces of Timurid architecture — a four-iwan plan (a central courtyard with a vaulted recess on each side, the standard form of monumental Persian mosques developed under the Seljuks), a soaring blue-tiled dome, and elaborate brick mosaic tilework throughout.
The inscription frieze around the qibla iwan, in Thuluth script, is attributed to Gawhar Shad's son Baysunghur (bye-SOON-ghur), regarded as one of the finest calligraphers of the Timurid era.
The mosque survives largely intact and is still in use as a working mosque today, the most important Shia pilgrimage destination in Iran outside the Iraqi shrine cities.
The Gawhar Shad Musalla at Herat, a much larger religious complex begun in 1417 and completed around 1437.
The complex included a mosque, a madrasa (religious school), Gawhar Shad's own intended mausoleum, and a series of monumental minarets.

It was, by all surviving descriptions and surviving fragments, the most ambitious single architectural project of the Timurid period — larger than the Bibi-Khanym Mosque at Samarkand, more elaborately decorated, more architecturally innovative.

Most of the complex was deliberately demolished in 1885 by British and Russian advisors of the Afghan Amir Abdur Rahman, who decided to clear sight lines for the city's defenses against a feared Russian invasion (the Panjdeh Incident of 1885 had nearly produced a war between Britain and Russia in Central Asia, and the Afghan defenses around Herat were being upgraded).
The destruction was one of the great architectural losses of the modern period — twentieth-century archaeologists have called it comparable to deliberate destruction at Palmyra.
Only Gawhar Shad's own mausoleum and a few minarets survive at the site today.
Gawhar Shad's career did not end well.
She survived Shah Rukh by ten years and continued to dominate Timurid court politics through the succession wars after his death.
She was finally executed in 1457 by her great-grandson Sultan Abu Sa'id (ah-boo sah-EED), then around forty-six, who saw her continued influence as a threat to his own consolidation of power.
She was seventy-eight years old at her execution.

The chronicle accounts describe her dignity in her final hours; she was buried at her own mausoleum at the Musalla complex in Herat, the surviving fragment of which is now the only place in the city where her memory is publicly preserved.
The treatment of Gawhar Shad in the conventional histories illustrates a recurring pattern in how women's roles in pre-modern dynastic politics are described.

She held independent financial resources, governed cities, commanded armies, made foreign policy, executed major architectural projects, and sustained the court patronage system through Shah Rukh's reign and after his death.
By any reasonable standard she was one of the most important rulers of fifteenth-century Eurasia.

The standard textbook treatment of the period mentions Shah Rukh and Ulugh Beg first, names Gawhar Shad once if at all, and treats the Mashhad mosque as a "Timurid building" rather than as her specific work.
This is a familiar historiographical pattern that more recent scholarship has been working to correct.
The Timurid Renaissance was at least as much Gawhar Shad's project as Shah Rukh's.
The cultural florescence at Herat in the 1410s through 1440s had several distinct components that are worth describing separately.
Architecture.

The Timurid architectural style — the soaring blue-tiled domes, the four-iwan mosque plans, the elaborate banna'i tilework, the geometric chahar bagh garden plans — reached its mature form at fifteenth-century Herat.

The masters were anonymous (the architects of major Timurid buildings are mostly unknown by name, in contrast to the famous Renaissance architects of contemporary Italy), but the style they developed was distinctive and enormously influential.

The same style was carried by emigrating craftsmen to the Safavid court at Tabriz after 1500 (Safavid Persia Ch 4), where it produced the great architectural projects of Abbas the Great at Isfahan a century later.
It was carried by Babur to India after 1526 (Chapter 8), where it formed the basis of Mughal architecture and produced — eventually — the Taj Mahal in 1648.
The technical innovation that defined Timurid architecture was the banna'i (bah-NAH-ee) tilework technique.
Earlier Persian-Islamic architecture had used full mosaic tilework, in which small tiles of various colors were assembled into elaborate patterns — labor-intensive, beautiful, but slow to produce.
Banna'i used larger glazed and unglazed bricks laid in geometric patterns, allowing whole facades to be covered with ornament at speeds previous traditions could not match.

The technique was less subtle than full mosaic but worked well at the monumental scale Timurid patrons preferred, and it enabled the rapid expansion of Timurid building activity through the fifteenth century.

Banna'i became the visual signature of late Timurid architecture, was inherited by both Safavid and Mughal architecture, and remains the standard surface treatment for Persianate-style buildings across Central Asia today.
Miniature painting.
The Herat school of Persian miniature painting developed under successive Timurid patrons through the fifteenth century.

The early generation worked under Baysunghur in the 1420s and 1430s, producing manuscripts like the Baysunghur Shahnameh (1430) — an illustrated copy of Ferdowsi's Persian national epic that contains 21 surviving miniatures of jewel-like quality and is now in the Golestan Palace Library in Tehran.
Subsequent generations refined the style further, culminating in the work of Bihzad (bee-ZAHD) at Herat in the 1480s and 1490s (Chapter 8).

The Herat school's distinctive features were: flat compositions in elaborate vertical-frame formats; brilliant colors using lapis lazuli blue, malachite green, and gold leaf as primary pigments; extremely precise figure drawing in ink before color was applied; elaborate background landscapes featuring stylized rocks, trees, and architectural elements; and increasingly sophisticated psychological characterization of the figures as the tradition developed.

The technical sophistication was extraordinary — these were tiny works (many of the miniatures are no larger than a paperback book page) painted with single-hair brushes under magnifying glasses, requiring years of apprenticeship to master.
The Herat tradition was carried into Safavid Persia and Mughal India by emigrating painters after the Uzbek conquest of 1507 (Chapter 8).
Bihzad himself moved to the Safavid court at Tabriz around 1510, where he became director of the royal library and trained the next generation of Safavid masters.
Several of his students migrated further east and trained the founding generation of Mughal painters under Akbar in the 1560s.

The technical lineage is direct and traceable: every Persianate book painting of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries — Safavid, Mughal, even some of the Ottoman work — runs back through Bihzad to the Herat school under Shah Rukh's patronage.
Persian poetry.

The classical Persian poetic tradition that had begun under the Samanids in the tenth century, peaked in the work of Rumi (thirteenth century), Hafez (fourteenth century), and Sa'di (thirteenth century), produced its closing major figure at Timurid Herat: Abd al-Rahman Jami (1414–1492).

Jami is conventionally regarded as the last great classical Persian poet — after him, the Persian poetic tradition continued for centuries but is generally considered to have moved into a different phase (the Sabk-e Hindi or "Hindi Style" of the Safavid and Mughal periods, Safavid Persia Ch 6).

He was a Sufi of the Naqshbandi order, a prolific scholar of theology and grammar as well as a poet, and the producer of roughly sixty surviving works including the seven masnavi cycles known collectively as the Haft Awrang ("Seven Thrones").

His poetic style combined the lyric elegance of Hafez with explicit Sufi mystical content, and his work was foundational to Persian literary culture both in Safavid Iran and in Mughal India for the next several centuries.
Calligraphy.
The Timurid era produced the major innovations in Persian calligraphic style that would define the Persianate tradition for the next several centuries.

Mir Ali Tabrizi (active in the late fourteenth century) is conventionally credited with the development of nastaliq (nast-ah-LEEK), the cursive Persian script that combines Arabic naskh and ta'liq elements into a flowing, asymmetric, visually distinctive form.
Nastaliq became the standard script for Persian poetry, official chancery documents, and royal correspondence — and remained so until the twentieth century.
The Timurid calligraphic establishment produced the master practitioners — Ja'far Tabrizi, Sultan Ali Mashhadi, Mir Ali Heravi — who refined the script through the fifteenth century.
Theology and scholarship.
The Naqshbandi Sufi order was the dominant religious establishment of Timurid Central Asia.

Founded in fourteenth-century Bukhara by Baha-ud-Din Naqshband (the order takes its name from him), the Naqshbandis emphasized silent meditation, compatibility with strict Sunni law, and active engagement with political and social life rather than withdrawal into monastic retreat.

The order's combination of scholarly orthodoxy and mystical practice fit the Timurid court's needs well — it provided spiritual legitimacy without challenging the dynasty's political authority — and Timurid rulers from Shah Rukh onward extensively patronized leading Naqshbandi sheikhs.

The most politically influential Naqshbandi figure of the late Timurid period was Khwaja Ubaydullah Ahrar (KHWA-jah oo-bay-doo-LAH ah-RAR, 1404–1490), based at Samarkand from the 1450s through his death.

Ahrar accumulated enormous agricultural estates, arbitrated disputes between Timurid princes, corresponded with rulers from the Ottoman court to the Indian sultanates, and effectively controlled the administration of Samarkand for several decades.

His independence from any specific Timurid ruler — combined with his religious authority and his control of land — made him the kind of religious figure that the political class proved unable to constrain.

The pattern would be reproduced in later Persianate states: the Safavid Shia clerical establishment (Safavid Persia Ch 5) developed a similar institutional independence in the seventeenth century, eventually producing the marja-i taqlid system that has dominated Iranian religious politics ever since.
A pause to set the cultural achievement in cross-civilizational perspective.
The Herat Renaissance is contemporary with the early Italian Renaissance.
The chronological parallel is striking.

Shah Rukh's reign (1409–1447) overlaps with the careers of Filippo Brunelleschi in Florence (the dome of the Florence Cathedral, completed 1436), Leon Battista Alberti (the architectural theorist whose works on perspective and proportion were appearing in the 1430s and 1440s), the early Donatello sculpture, and the early generation of Florentine humanists rediscovering classical Latin texts.
Bihzad's mature career at Herat in the 1480s and 1490s overlaps with the high Renaissance of Botticelli, the early Leonardo, and the founding generation of Venetian painting under Giovanni Bellini.
The two cultural florescences were operating on entirely different aesthetic premises.

The Italian Renaissance was rediscovering classical Greek and Roman antiquity through the recovery of Latin texts and (after 1453) Greek manuscripts brought west by Byzantine refugees from Ottoman-conquered Constantinople (Byzantine Empire Ch 12).

The Herat Renaissance was synthesizing Persian classical poetry, Islamic religious thought, Mongol political traditions, and Chinese pictorial influences (the chinoiserie elements in Herat painting are real — they reflect direct contact with Yuan and early Ming Chinese art transmitted through the Mongol successor states) into a distinctive Persianate visual and literary culture.

The two traditions were aware of each other's existence (Timurid embassies reached the Italian states; Italian travelers reached Samarkand and Herat) but were operating in essentially separate cultural systems with limited mutual influence.
What is striking is the simultaneity.

Two of the most ambitious cultural florescences of the fifteenth century happened on opposite ends of Eurasia, in different civilizations, drawing on different traditions, producing different aesthetic results — at the same moment in history.

The fifteenth century was an extraordinary period across Eurasia, with Renaissance Italy, Timurid Herat, Ming China under the Yongle Emperor (the Forbidden City was built between 1406 and 1420, exactly contemporary with the Gawhar Shad mosque at Mashhad), and the late Vijayanagara Empire in southern India all producing major cultural achievements simultaneously.
None of them was the only Renaissance of the fifteenth century.
Each was one of several.
The Italian comparison is also useful in another way.
Both the Italian Renaissance and the Herat Renaissance depended on patronage from violent political regimes whose wealth was extracted through processes nobody would defend morally.
The Medici in Florence funded their patronage through banking and commercial profits accumulated in a brutal Mediterranean trading world.
The Borgia popes in Rome funded their patronage through corruption and political assassination.
The Sforza dukes in Milan funded their patronage through condottiere warfare.

The Timurid patronage at Herat was funded through agricultural taxation in territories whose populations had been pacified by Timurid violence a generation earlier, and the craft labor that produced the great buildings was descended from craftsmen forcibly deported from cities Timur had destroyed.
There is no clean way to separate the cultural achievement from the violent extractive systems that funded it.
This is true on both sides of Eurasia.
It is part of how high cultural production worked across the medieval and early-modern world.
Shah Rukh died in March 1447 at Herat, aged about seventy.
He had ruled for forty-two years.
The empire he left was the reduced Timurid territories — Khorasan, Transoxiana, parts of Persia — but the cultural infrastructure he had built was extraordinarily rich.
The succession crisis that followed his death (which Chapter 7 covers from the angle of Ulugh Beg's astronomy) ended much of his political legacy within a decade.

The cultural infrastructure largely survived — the architectural style, the painting tradition, the poetry, the scholarship — and was carried by emigrating craftsmen and scholars into the Safavid and Mughal worlds in the next century.

Cross-civ check: Shah Rukh's reign (1409–1447) overlaps with Henry V and the early reign of Henry VI in England (the long crisis that would produce the Wars of the Roses), the Hussite Wars in Bohemia (1419–1434, the prototype of religious-political insurgency in central Europe), the early Joseon dynasty in Korea under Sejong the Great (whose invention of the Hangul alphabet in 1443 was contemporary with the late Shah Rukh period), the Yongle Emperor's building of the Forbidden City and dispatch of Zheng He's voyages from Ming China (1405–1433), and the founding of the Aztec Triple Alliance's peak phase under Itzcoatl and Moctezuma I (Aztec Empire Ch 5).
The first half of the fifteenth century was the high water mark of imperial cultural patronage across Eurasia, and Herat is one of its capitals.

chapters.title: Ulugh Beg the Astronomer-King
sentences: In Samarkand, while Shah Rukh ruled the wider Timurid Empire from Herat, Shah Rukh's eldest son Ulugh Beg (oo-LOOG BEG, "Great Lord," 1394–1449) governed Transoxiana for forty years.

Ulugh Beg's reign at Samarkand is one of the strangest episodes in the history of science: a working political ruler who was also a serious practicing astronomer, who built the largest astronomical observatory in the medieval world, who personally participated in the systematic measurement of the heavens, and who produced the most accurate astronomical handbook of the pre-telescopic era.
Then his eldest son murdered him, the observatory was abandoned, and the scientific establishment scattered.
The whole enterprise lasted four decades and ended in months.
This chapter is about Ulugh Beg, the Samarkand observatory, the Zij-i Sultani ("Imperial Tables") that came out of it, and the immediate cultural collapse that followed his murder.
Ulugh Beg was born in 1394, probably at Samarkand, into the Timurid royal family at the height of his grandfather Timur's career.

He was on campaign with Timur as a small child — the chronicles describe him being present at Timur's siege of Damascus in 1401 — and was therefore raised inside the operating military culture of his grandfather's empire.
After Timur's death and Shah Rukh's consolidation in 1409, Ulugh Beg was installed as governor of Samarkand at age fifteen, with senior advisors managing the actual administration.
He held that position until 1447.
Ulugh Beg's training was unusual for a fifteenth-century ruler.

The standard education for a Timurid prince consisted of horsemanship, military tactics, Persian and Turkic poetry, religious instruction, and some exposure to Persian historical chronicles — preparation for a life of warfare and provincial administration.
Ulugh Beg got all of this, but he was also given systematic instruction in mathematics and astronomy from boyhood.

The chronicle accounts say his interest was sparked by a childhood visit (with Timur's army during the western campaigns) to the ruined Maragha observatory in northwestern Iran — the great Mongol-era astronomical observatory built by the Ilkhanate scholar Nasir al-Din al-Tusi in the 1260s (Mongol Empire Ch 7), which had been the most ambitious astronomical institution of the previous two centuries.
Whether the story is literally true or a later embellishment, Ulugh Beg's mathematical and astronomical interests were established by his teenage years and persisted throughout his life.
He combined his astronomical interests with the political duties of governorship in a way that has no real parallel in the history of pre-modern science.
Most rulers who patronized scientific work hired specialists — astronomers, mathematicians, physicians — and let them do the work while the ruler attended to politics.

Ulugh Beg did this too (Samarkand under his patronage employed dozens of leading mathematicians and astronomers, including Jamshid al-Kashi, Qadi Zada al-Rumi, and Ali Qushji), but he also personally participated in the observational work, made his own astronomical observations using the Samarkand instruments, contributed to the mathematical reductions that produced the Zij tables, and taught astronomy at the madrasa he founded at Samarkand.
He was a working astronomer, not just a patron of astronomers.
This is unusual enough that it is worth pausing on the comparison.

The standard pattern across world history is that scientific work is conducted by specialists supported by patronage from political or commercial authorities — court astronomers under the Tang and Song Chinese emperors (Tang-Song China Ch 6), Hellenistic mathematicians supported by the Ptolemies in Alexandria (Late Egypt Ch 6), Islamic astronomers supported by the Abbasid court in Baghdad (Islamic Golden Age Ch 3).
The patrons might be intellectually engaged, might commission specific projects, might attend astronomical events, but they did not personally take observations or do reductions.
Ulugh Beg did.

The closest historical parallel might be the Mughal emperor Akbar in the late sixteenth century, who personally conducted theological and philosophical debates in his court and commissioned scholarly translations — but even Akbar was a patron rather than a participant in scientific work.
Ulugh Beg was both.
The phenomenon is rare enough in world history that it deserves to be recognized as such.
The Samarkand observatory was Ulugh Beg's signature project.
Construction began in 1424 and was completed by 1428, on a low hill overlooking the Bibi-Khanym Mosque on the northeastern edge of Samarkand.

The site is now one of the major archaeological monuments of Uzbekistan, partially excavated by the Russian archaeologist Vasily Vyatkin in 1908 (the observatory's location had been forgotten for several centuries before this rediscovery — one of the ironies of Ulugh Beg's career being that the major institution he built had to be located by archaeological excavation in the twentieth century).
The observatory was a three-story circular building, roughly 165 feet (50 meters) in diameter, containing the largest astronomical instruments yet constructed anywhere in the world.

The principal instrument was a meridian arc — a quarter-circle stone-and-marble structure with a radius of approximately 130 feet (40 meters), oriented along the local meridian and used to measure the altitude of celestial bodies as they crossed the meridian.
The arc's enormous radius was the key technical innovation: a larger arc allowed finer angular measurements, with a precision approaching one minute of arc (1/60 of a degree).
This was the highest precision achieved anywhere in the world before the introduction of telescopic measurement in Europe in the early seventeenth century.

The observatory also contained smaller instruments — armillary spheres, astrolabes, sundials, and various specialized devices for measuring planetary positions, equinox dates, and calendar adjustments.
The work was conducted by a team of astronomers led by: Jamshid al-Kashi (jam-SHEED al-KAH-shee, c. 1380–1429), the greatest Islamic mathematician of his generation.

Al-Kashi had calculated pi to sixteen decimal places (a precision unsurpassed for nearly two hundred years), produced the Miftah al-Hisab ("Key of Arithmetic"), one of the most influential mathematical textbooks of the Islamic world, and developed important techniques in trigonometry, decimal fractions, and root extraction.
He was Ulugh Beg's senior mathematical advisor at the observatory until his death in 1429.
Qadi Zada al-Rumi (KAH-dee ZAH-dah al-ROO-mee, c. 1364–1437), an astronomer and mathematician originally from Bursa in Anatolia who had migrated east to Samarkand under Timurid patronage.
He was Ulugh Beg's senior astronomer and the head of the observatory team after al-Kashi's death.

Ali Qushji (ah-LEE KOOSH-jee, c. 1403–1474), the youngest member of the team, who survived Ulugh Beg's death and would carry the Samarkand astronomical tradition to Constantinople under Ottoman patronage in the 1470s.
The observatory team operated for roughly two decades, conducting systematic observations of stellar positions, planetary motions, calendar adjustments, and trigonometric calculations.
The cumulative results were compiled into the Zij-i Sultani ("Imperial Tables"), completed under Ulugh Beg's editorial supervision in 1437.
The Zij-i Sultani is the most important scientific text produced by the Timurid Empire and one of the great astronomical works of the medieval world.
Its principal contents: A star catalog of 1,018 stars, with positions measured to a precision of one minute of arc.
This was the most accurate star catalog produced anywhere in the world between Ptolemy's Almagest (second century CE) and Tycho Brahe's observations of the 1580s.

The Almagest catalog had positions accurate to perhaps ten minutes of arc; Brahe achieved approximately one minute of arc with naked-eye instruments in the 1580s and 1590s; the Zij-i Sultani was already at one minute of arc 150 years earlier.
The intervening 1,400 years between Ptolemy and Brahe had not produced a single star catalog of comparable accuracy in any culture — except this one.
Planetary tables for predicting the future positions of the sun, moon, and the five visible planets.

The planetary tables were based on the standard Ptolemaic geocentric model with various Islamic-era corrections, but the underlying parameters had been measured fresh at the Samarkand observatory and were significantly more accurate than the previous Islamic tables (the Toledan Tables of the eleventh century, the Maragha-derived Ilkhanic Tables of the late thirteenth century).

Trigonometric tables with extraordinary precision — sine and tangent values calculated to nine decimal places, enabling accurate astronomical calculation that would not be matched in Europe until well into the sixteenth century.
Calendar adjustments establishing the precise length of the solar year and the lunar month, used to calibrate Islamic religious calendars across a multi-century range.
The Zij-i Sultani was used in Islamic astronomy for the next three centuries.

Copies were transmitted east to India (where they influenced Mughal astronomers and the work of the eighteenth-century Indian astronomer Jai Singh II at Jaipur), west to Ottoman Turkey (carried by Ali Qushji after Ulugh Beg's death and used by Ottoman astronomers through the seventeenth century), and eventually to Europe through Latin translations in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries.
The Polish astronomer Johannes Hevelius in the seventeenth century used the Zij-i Sultani's stellar positions in his own work; the English astronomer Thomas Hyde produced a Latin edition in 1665.
Modern historians of astronomy regard the Zij-i Sultani as the high point of pre-telescopic Islamic astronomy and the most accurate astronomical handbook in the world during the period 1437–1580.
This is worth dwelling on, because it is the kind of fact that gets lost in conventional Western histories of the Renaissance.

The standard story has European astronomy stagnating through the Middle Ages and then being revived by the discovery of classical Greek texts in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, eventually culminating in Copernicus, Brahe, Kepler, and Galileo.
This is not wrong, but it omits a parallel story.

While European astronomy was reorganizing itself from Ptolemaic remnants and rediscovered Greek manuscripts, Islamic astronomy was operating at a higher technical level than the Greek tradition had achieved at its peak, with more accurate instruments, better-trained practitioners, and a continuous research tradition that had been refining itself for several centuries.
The Samarkand observatory under Ulugh Beg was the institutional summit of this tradition.
The European astronomical revival of the late sixteenth century did not surpass Samarkand levels of precision until Tycho Brahe's work in the 1580s and 1590s.

The Greek tradition that European astronomers were rediscovering was technically inferior to the Islamic tradition that was operating contemporaneously — and the Islamic tradition's best work was happening at Timurid Samarkand.
The end of the Samarkand observatory came suddenly and is documented in detail.
In 1447, Shah Rukh died.
Ulugh Beg, then about fifty-three, became the senior Timurid ruler — inheriting the title of Sultan and effective control of both Samarkand and Herat.
He moved part of the court to Herat to consolidate, but the political consolidation went badly.

His relations with his eldest son, Abdal-Latif (ahb-DAHL-lah-TEEF), had been deteriorating for years — Abdal-Latif felt his father was slighting him in succession arrangements, the chronicle accounts describe several public quarrels, and other Timurid relatives took advantage of the rift to encourage Abdal-Latif's resentment.
By 1449, Ulugh Beg and Abdal-Latif were in open conflict.
In October 1449, Abdal-Latif's forces defeated Ulugh Beg's troops in a battle outside Samarkand.

Ulugh Beg surrendered and asked permission to make a religious pilgrimage to Mecca — a standard face-saving exit for a deposed ruler in the Islamic world, allowing the deposed ruler to retire from politics under religious cover.
Abdal-Latif granted permission.
Ulugh Beg set out from Samarkand, accompanied by a small escort.
A few miles outside the city, the escort stopped and Ulugh Beg was forced to dismount.

He was put on trial in a hasty proceeding by a religious tribunal Abdal-Latif had assembled, on charges of un-Islamic behavior (the astronomical work was framed as occultism and heresy), and sentenced to death.
He was beheaded on October 27, 1449.
He was fifty-five years old.
The parricide horrified contemporary opinion in the Timurid world.

In Islamic political and religious culture, a son's killing of his father was the most grievous sin imaginable, and Abdal-Latif's ordering of the execution destroyed his political legitimacy almost immediately.
He was killed by his own troops six months later, in May 1450 — assassinated in his palace by a junior officer who later claimed he had acted to avenge Ulugh Beg.
Abdal-Latif was buried in an unmarked grave; the chronicles record his death in tones of moral satisfaction.
The Samarkand observatory was abandoned within months of Ulugh Beg's death.

The political instability of the next several years — competing Timurid contenders, Uzbek raids from the north, the lack of any successor with Ulugh Beg's intellectual interests — meant that no new patron took up the work.
The observatory's instruments fell into disrepair; the team of astronomers dispersed; the building itself was eventually destroyed by an earthquake in the early sixteenth century.
By the time the site was rediscovered by Vyatkin's archaeological work in 1908, only the underground portion of the great meridian arc survived, preserved by being below ground level.
The Samarkand astronomical school continued in attenuated form through the second half of the fifteenth century.
Ali Qushji, the youngest of Ulugh Beg's senior astronomers, eventually migrated to Constantinople in 1471 under Ottoman patronage.

There, at the court of Mehmed II (the conqueror of Constantinople in 1453, Byzantine Empire Ch 12 and Ottoman Empire Ch 4), Ali Qushji introduced the latest Timurid astronomical methods to the Ottoman scientific establishment.

His proposal that the earth might rotate (in a brief astronomical treatise written shortly before his death in 1474) was debated by the next generation of Ottoman astronomers and prefigured similar discussions in the European Copernican tradition by several decades.

The Timurid astronomical legacy therefore survived in fragmentary form, transmitted east to Mughal India and west to Ottoman Constantinople, but the institutional center — the working observatory at Samarkand — was lost.
A pause: the Samarkand observatory's collapse is one of the genuinely sad episodes in the history of science.

A working research institution at the technical frontier of its field, operating at the highest standards anywhere in the world, was destroyed by a single act of family violence and the political instability that followed.
The institutional infrastructure that produced the Zij-i Sultani — the trained personnel, the calibrated instruments, the working procedures, the patronage relationships — could not be reconstructed.

A century later, under the Safavid restoration, similar institutional infrastructure had to be rebuilt almost from scratch (Safavid Persia Ch 5 covers the Isfahan school of philosophy and natural science under the Safavids, which represented a partial revival of pre-Timurid intellectual institutions).
The lesson is not that Islamic science was somehow uniquely fragile or vulnerable to political interference.
Scientific institutions across world history have been vulnerable to similar failures.
The Library of Alexandria was destroyed (probably gradually, over multiple incidents, but the cumulative effect was the same).
The Gundishapur Academy was disrupted by the Arab conquest of Persia (Persian Empire Ch 9).
The translation movement of Abbasid Baghdad ended with the Mongol sack of 1258 (Islamic Golden Age Ch 8).
The Maragha observatory tradition that influenced Ulugh Beg was disrupted by the Ilkhanate's collapse.
Scientific institutions need political and economic support to operate, and political crises that disrupt that support can destroy decades of accumulated capacity within months.
The Samarkand case is not exceptional.
It is just particularly well-documented and particularly tragic.
The astronomical work itself survived through the Zij-i Sultani, copies of which were preserved in dozens of manuscript libraries across the Islamic world.
The text was not lost.

But the institutional capacity to produce more work of comparable quality was lost, and it would be three centuries before any Islamic-world institution achieved comparable astronomical precision again.

By that point — the late eighteenth century — European telescopic astronomy had moved far beyond what naked-eye instruments could measure, and the Islamic astronomical tradition that Samarkand had culminated had been overtaken by the Western scientific revolution.
The Samarkand observatory was therefore not just the high point of Islamic astronomy but, in retrospect, the last major Islamic astronomical institution before the West took the lead.
The political instability after Ulugh Beg's death produced a series of competing Timurid claimants over the following decade.

Abdal-Latif's assassination in 1450 was followed by short-lived reigns of various junior Timurid princes (Abdullah Mirza, Sultan Abu Sa'id, others) and by the gradual loss of Timurid territory to the Uzbeks in the north and the Aq Qoyunlu Turkmen in the west.

Sultan Abu Sa'id Mirza (a great-grandson of Timur from a junior line, ruled 1451–1469) eventually consolidated most of the central Timurid territories and ruled for two decades — but his reign was less culturally productive than Shah Rukh's, and his death in battle against the Aq Qoyunlu in 1469 inaugurated the late Timurid period that Chapter 8 covers.

Cross-civ check: Ulugh Beg's reign at Samarkand (1409–1449) overlaps with the early Italian Renaissance (Brunelleschi's dome, the early generation of Florentine humanists), the Joseon dynasty's scientific patronage in Korea under King Sejong the Great (whose own astronomical projects in the 1430s and 1440s were contemporary with Ulugh Beg's — the Joseon court built rain gauges, sundials, and astronomical instruments at the same moment Samarkand was operating its observatory), the Yongle Emperor's dispatch of Zheng He's voyages from Ming China (1405–1433, partly contemporary with the early Samarkand observatory), and the Inca expansion under Pachacuti in the Andes (Andean Kingdoms Ch 6).

The first half of the fifteenth century is one of the most scientifically productive periods in pre-modern Eurasian history, with Korea, China, Central Asia, and Italy all running major scientific or technical projects simultaneously.
Ulugh Beg's Samarkand was one of these centers.
Its abrupt collapse in 1449 was a localized failure that did not stop the broader pattern of fifteenth-century scientific work elsewhere — but it was a serious local loss.

chapters.title: The Long Twilight and Babur
sentences: The half-century from Ulugh Beg's murder in 1449 to the Uzbek conquest of Herat in 1507 was the long Timurid twilight: a slow political decline punctuated by brief cultural florescence, ending in the extinction of the Timurid Empire as a sovereign state and the flight of the last Timurid prince — Babur (BAH-bur, 1483–1530) — to India, where in 1526 he founded the Mughal Empire (Persian for "Mongol"), which would rule South Asia for the next three centuries.
The Timurid Empire died in 1507 in Khorasan.
The Timurid project — the dynastic identity, the architectural style, the literary traditions, the court culture — survived in India for another three hundred years.
This chapter is about the late Timurid Empire and its Mughal afterlife.
Sultan Abu Sa'id Mirza (1424–1469) had reunified most of the central Timurid territories in the 1450s and ruled them until his death in battle against the Aq Qoyunlu Turkmen in 1469.
His death is generally treated as the moment when the Timurid Empire ceased to be a single political entity and fragmented permanently into rival Timurid principalities.
Three principal centers emerged: Herat (Khorasan), under various Timurid princes culminating in Sultan Husayn Bayqara from 1469.
Samarkand (Transoxiana), under Abu Sa'id's sons, eventually consolidating under Sultan Ahmad Mirza and his successors.
Ferghana (the small mountain valley east of Samarkand, in modern Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan), under another junior Timurid line, eventually inherited by the young Babur.

The political map was further complicated by the rising power of two non-Timurid forces: the Uzbeks (a Genghisid Turkic confederation pushing south from the Kipchak steppe, increasingly able to raid and eventually conquer Timurid territories) and, after 1500, the Safavids (the new Shia messianic empire of Ismail I in northwestern Iran, Safavid Persia Ch 1–2).
Both would prove decisive in the eventual extinction of the Timurid state.
But before that extinction, the Herat principality under Husayn Bayqara produced one last cultural florescence that deserves a chapter on its own.
Sultan Husayn Bayqara (hoo-SAYN bye-KAH-rah, 1438–1506) ruled Herat for thirty-seven years, from 1469 to his death in 1506.
He was a great-great-grandson of Timur in the senior line, an experienced military commander, and a cultivated patron of the arts.
His reign is the cultural climax of the Timurid period.

The political base was thin — Husayn controlled little more than Khorasan, and his territory was constantly under pressure from the Uzbeks in the north and the Safavids in the west — but the cultural production at his court was extraordinary, comparable to (and in some respects exceeding) the earlier achievements at Shah Rukh's Herat in the 1420s and 1430s.
Three figures define late Timurid Herat: Abd al-Rahman Jami (1414–1492), already introduced in Chapter 6, spent his last decades at Husayn Bayqara's court.
His later poetic work and his theological writings cemented his reputation as the closing major figure of classical Persian poetry.
He died in Herat in 1492 and was buried in a small mausoleum in the city that survives.
Kamal al-Din Bihzad (kah-MAHL al-DEEN bee-ZAHD, c. 1465–c. 1535), the greatest of all Persian miniature painters.

Bihzad was working at Herat from the 1480s through the 1490s under Husayn Bayqara's patronage, and the surviving works from this period — illustrations for various Persian classical texts including the Bustan of Sa'di (1488), illustrations for Nizami's Khamsa, and dozens of other manuscripts — define the apex of the Herat school.

Bihzad's innovations included: naturalistic figure grouping that broke from the more stylized arrangements of earlier Persian painting; psychologically expressive faces with distinct individual characterization; complex spatial compositions using overlapping picture planes; and a richness of decorative detail that exceeded anything in the earlier tradition.
