After the Uzbek conquest of Herat in 1507, Bihzad migrated to the Safavid court at Tabriz, where he was appointed director of the royal library (the kitabkhana) and trained the next generation of Safavid masters.
He died in the 1530s, having effectively founded both the Safavid and (through his students) the Mughal painting traditions.
Mir Ali Sher Nava'i (meer ah-LEE sheer nah-vah-EE, 1441–1501) was Husayn Bayqara's senior cultural minister and life-long friend (the two had been classmates as boys in Herat).
As a poet, Nava'i is conventionally regarded as the founder of the Chagatai-Turkic literary tradition.

His poems and prose works in Chagatai-Turkic — including the Khamsa (a five-part poetic cycle), the Mahbub al-Qulub ("Beloved of Hearts," a prose work of moral reflection), and the Muhakamat al-Lughatayn ("Judgment of the Two Languages," a critical essay arguing that Chagatai-Turkic was a literary medium equal to Persian) — established Chagatai as a serious literary language for the first time and shaped Turkic literary identity for the next several centuries.
As a patron, Nava'i funded Bihzad, Jami, dozens of architects and craftsmen, and most of the late Timurid cultural establishment.
His political role at Herat was effectively that of prime minister, conducting administration while Husayn Bayqara handled military affairs and ceremonial duties.
The arrangement worked extraordinarily well for thirty years.
The cultural production at late Husayn-era Herat is genuinely astonishing in concentration.

Bihzad's painting workshops, Jami's poetic circle, Nava'i's literary patronage, and the architectural projects funded across the city produced one of the most intense cultural moments anywhere in the fifteenth-century world.

Visiting European travelers (a few reached Herat in the late fifteenth century, including a Venetian named Iosafa Barbaro) described the city as a marvel — comparable to or superior to the Italian cities they had come from.
But the political base was crumbling.
The northern frontier was the immediate threat.

Muhammad Shaybani (moo-HAH-mad shy-BAH-nee, c. 1451–1510), the leader of the Uzbek confederation, had been pushing south from the Kipchak steppe through the 1480s and 1490s, building an Uzbek state that integrated the steppe Turkic-Mongol political tradition with Persianate administrative practice.

The Uzbeks were Genghisids in the senior Jochid line — direct descendants of Genghis Khan through his eldest son Jochi — and they used the legitimacy advantage explicitly against the Timurids, whose non-Genghisid status had been the structural weakness of the dynasty since Timur's day (Chapter 1).
Shaybani's political program was: replace the illegitimate Timurids with legitimate Genghisid Uzbek rule.
The Uzbek conquest of Timurid territories happened rapidly.
Samarkand fell in 1500.
Bukhara fell in 1500 (the same year).
Most of Transoxiana came under Uzbek control by 1503.
Herat fell in 1507.
By 1510, Shaybani had taken most of Khorasan as well.
The Timurid Empire as a sovereign state had ceased to exist.

Shaybani himself was killed in December 1510 at the Battle of Merv (in modern Turkmenistan) by the Safavid Shah Ismail I, who had Shaybani's skull encased in gold and made into a drinking cup (Safavid Persia Ch 2).
The detail is grotesque and is described in detail in the Safavid chronicles.

It is also a deliberate act of political signaling: Ismail was claiming the Mongol political legacy of Timur (skull-cup-from-defeated-enemy is documented in Mongol practice going back to Genghis Khan, Mongol Empire Ch 2) along with the Shia religious legitimacy that defined his own dynasty.
The killing of Shaybani temporarily slowed the Uzbek advance, but the Uzbek state survived as the Shaybanid dynasty ruling most of Central Asia for the next century.
The Uzbeks pushed many of the surviving Timurid cultural figures into emigration.
Bihzad fled west to the Safavid court at Tabriz.

Other painters, calligraphers, scholars, and architects scattered to wherever they could find patronage — to the new Safavid state, to the Mamluk Sultanate of Egypt (which would itself fall to the Ottomans in 1517), to the Indian sultanates, eventually to the Mughal court Babur founded in 1526.

The Persianate cultural establishment of fifteenth-century Herat was therefore not destroyed by the Uzbek conquest — it was scattered, and its scattered fragments became the founding generation of Safavid and Mughal court culture in the next century.
This scattering is one of the more remarkable cultural-transmission events in early-modern history.

The artistic, literary, and architectural template that the Mughals carried into India and that defined Mughal court culture from Babur to Aurangzeb (1526–1707) was substantially the same template that had been developed at Husayn Bayqara's Herat in the 1490s.

The Safavid court culture that took shape at Tabriz under Tahmasp I and reached full development at Isfahan under Abbas the Great (Safavid Persia Ch 3–4) was substantially an inheritance from the same Herat template, transmitted by emigrating Timurid craftsmen.

The Persianate world of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries was, in cultural terms, largely a reorganization of Timurid material — distributed across the new political map by the Uzbek conquest of the original Timurid heartland.
Babur is the Timurid prince through whom the dynasty's afterlife in India happened, and his career deserves its own detailed treatment.

Zahir-ud-Din Muhammad Babur (the formal name; "Babur" is a nickname meaning "Tiger") was born in 1483 in Andijan in the Ferghana Valley — a small mountain-walled valley east of Samarkand in modern eastern Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan, with a climate, geography, and political tradition somewhat distinct from the rest of Transoxiana.
His father, Umar Shaykh Mirza, ruled Ferghana as one of the late Timurid principalities.

Babur's mother Qutlugh Nigar Khanum was a direct descendant of Chinggis Khan through her Moghul royal line — meaning Babur was a Genghisid in the senior line on his mother's side, and a Timurid (fifth-generation descendant of Timur) on his father's side.
The combination was exceptionally distinguished by Central Asian political standards.
Babur had legitimacy from both the Mongol and the Timurid dynasties.
He emphasized this combination throughout his life.

Umar Shaykh Mirza died in 1494 in a freak accident — the chronicle accounts say a pigeon house at the family palace collapsed and he fell from the roof (Babur, who recorded the incident in his autobiography, framed it with a kind of wry detachment that runs throughout his prose).
Babur, then twelve years old, inherited the throne of Ferghana.
The next decade of his life was a series of disastrous military campaigns against rival Timurid cousins and increasingly powerful Uzbek invaders.
He took Samarkand briefly in 1497 (at age fifteen), lost it within months, took it again in 1500–01, lost it again to the Uzbeks.
He took Andijan and lost it.
He spent extended periods as a fugitive in the mountains.
By 1504, with the Uzbeks consolidating control of Transoxiana under Shaybani, Babur — now twenty-one — was driven entirely out of his ancestral Central Asian territories.
He turned south.
In October 1504, with a small army of personal followers, he crossed the Hindu Kush mountains into modern Afghanistan and captured Kabul, then a regional center under nominal Timurid suzerainty.
Kabul became his base for the next twenty-two years.

From Kabul he conducted occasional raids back into Central Asia (he made one more attempt to recover Samarkand in 1511, with Safavid help — Shah Ismail I, having killed Shaybani at Merv the year before, briefly backed Babur against the Uzbeks; Babur held Samarkand for less than a year before being driven out again).
But increasingly his attention turned south, toward India.
The reasons for the Indian orientation were practical.
Central Asia was lost.
The Uzbeks were too strong.
The Safavids were potential allies but the alliance was fragile (and required Babur to publicly perform Shia religious observances, which he found uncomfortable as a hereditary Sunni).
Kabul could feed itself but was not rich enough to sustain a major dynastic ambition.

India, by contrast, was famously wealthy, the Delhi Sultanate (now under the Lodi dynasty since 1451) was politically weak, and Babur's ancestor Timur had set a precedent for the conquest by the 1398 Delhi sack.

The southward turn took two decades to develop into action — Babur conducted raiding expeditions into Punjab from the early 1510s onward, gathering intelligence and accumulating the resources for a larger campaign — but the strategic shift was clear from his arrival at Kabul.
The decisive campaign came in 1525–26.

The Lodi sultan Ibrahim Lodi (ib-rah-HEEM LOH-dee, ruled 1517–1526) had alienated several of his senior provincial governors through arrogant treatment, and in 1525 the governor of Lahore (one Daulat Khan Lodi) invited Babur to invade Delhi in alliance with the dissident Lodi nobles.
Babur accepted.

He marched his army of approximately 12,000 men through the Khyber Pass into Punjab in late 1525, defeated several smaller Lodi forces, and met the main Lodi army at the First Battle of Panipat north of Delhi on April 21, 1526.
The numerical disparity was stark: Babur's 12,000 against Ibrahim Lodi's force of perhaps 100,000 men plus a thousand war elephants.
The disparity was offset by technology.
Babur had two field artillery batteries (acquired from Ottoman gunners hired in Anatolia, possibly through Safavid connections) and several hundred matchlock musketeers.

Neither weapon was new — gunpowder artillery had been used in European warfare for over a century, matchlocks for several decades — but neither was yet familiar in Indian warfare, where the Lodi army had no equivalent technologies.

The musketeers were deployed behind a fortified line of bullock carts (a wagon-fort tactic, similar in concept to the Ottoman tabur cengi formation that would defeat the Safavids at Chaldiran twelve years earlier — Safavid Persia Ch 3).
Babur's cavalry maneuvered around the flanks while the artillery and musketeers shot up the dense Lodi center.
The battle was decisive.
The Lodi army collapsed in a few hours.
Ibrahim Lodi was killed in the fighting.

Babur entered Delhi the same week and proclaimed himself emperor, founding the dynasty later called Mughal — a Persian rendering of "Mongol," chosen to emphasize Babur's combined Timurid-Mongol descent. (The dynasty itself called itself Gurkani — from the Persian title Guregen that Timur had used, "royal son-in-law," referring to his marriage into the Genghisid line.

The Persianate world used "Gurkani"; European observers used "Mughal," from the Persian word for Mongol; the English usage that followed was "Mughal" or, sometimes, "Mogul." All three names refer to the same dynasty.) Panipat was the strategic foundation of the Mughal Empire.

Babur conducted further campaigns in 1527–29 to consolidate control of northern India — defeating a Rajput coalition under Rana Sanga at the Battle of Khanwa in 1527, defeating an Afghan coalition at the Battle of Ghaghra in 1529 — and ruled from Delhi and Agra until his death in 1530.
He was forty-seven.
He had reached the throne late, after twenty-five years of failure, and had ruled India for only four years.
But the dynasty he founded would last.
The Baburnama is one of the great autobiographies in world literature and deserves its own paragraph.
Babur kept a personal memoir written intermittently from 1494 (when he was eleven, recording his father's death and his own accession to Ferghana) through his Indian conquests in the late 1520s.

He wrote in Chagatai-Turkic — his native language, the literary form of Turkic that Mir Ali Sher Nava'i had recently established as a serious literary medium — using a candid, observant, self-critical prose style that has no real parallel in contemporary royal memoirs.

The book describes Babur's military campaigns, his political mistakes, his romantic entanglements (he writes about a same-sex attraction in his teenage years with the kind of matter-of-fact description that surprises modern readers expecting sixteenth-century reticence), his depressions, his alcohol consumption (he describes drinking heavily through much of his career, then giving up alcohol in 1527 in a sworn renunciation, then describing the renunciation with a wry awareness that he might break it), his observations of natural history (entire chapters describe the flora, fauna, climate, and geography of every region he passed through, with the precision of a working naturalist), and his reflections on the people he met and the books he read.
The Baburnama's value as a historical source is enormous.

It is one of the most detailed primary accounts of Central Asian and northern Indian politics in the late fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries, written by a participant rather than by a court chronicler.
Its value as a literary work is also enormous — modern scholars have compared it to the autobiographies of Saint Augustine, Benvenuto Cellini, and (occasionally) Marcus Aurelius.
The English translation by Annette Beveridge (1922) is the standard reference; more recent translations by Wheeler Thackston (1996) and others have made it more accessible to modern readers.
The Baburnama is also the closing major work of Chagatai-Turkic literature.

After Babur, the Chagatai literary tradition continued — particularly at the Mughal court, where Babur's autobiography was treasured and translated multiple times into Persian — but the language was gradually displaced by Persian as the literary medium of the Persianate world and by various successor Turkic literatures (eventually modern Uzbek, modern Uyghur, modern Tatar) for the local Turkic populations of Central Asia.
By the early twentieth century, Chagatai had largely ceased to be a working literary language.
The Baburnama, written by a man fleeing the destruction of the Timurid Empire and founding a new empire in India, is the most lasting Chagatai literary work.
The political continuity from Babur's 1526 victory to the long Mughal afterlife is worth tracing briefly because it is the main way the Timurid project survived.

Babur was succeeded by his son Humayun (hoo-MAH-yoon, ruled 1530–1540 and 1555–1556), who lost the empire to the Afghan warlord Sher Shah Suri in 1540 and spent fifteen years in exile at the Safavid court of Tahmasp I (Safavid Persia Ch 3).

With Safavid military help (a 12,000-strong loan force, in exchange for Humayun's nominal Shia conversion and the strategic city of Kandahar), Humayun reconquered northern India in 1555–56 and reestablished Mughal rule.

He died shortly afterward, falling down a stone staircase in his library — Babur's posthumous comment in the Baburnama-of-his-mind would presumably have been that the family's relationship with library architecture was permanently unfortunate.
Humayun's son Akbar (1542–1605, ruled 1556–1605) consolidated the Mughal Empire as one of the great early-modern Eurasian states.

Under Akbar and his successors Jahangir (1605–1627), Shah Jahan (1628–1658), and Aurangzeb (1658–1707), the Mughals ruled most of South Asia for nearly two centuries, during which the Persianate court culture inherited from Timurid Herat reached its full elaboration.

The architectural projects of the Mughal period — Akbar's Fatehpur Sikri, Shah Jahan's Taj Mahal (1648) at Agra, the Red Fort at Delhi (1648), the Badshahi Mosque at Lahore (1673) — are all directly descended in style and technique from the Timurid architectural prototypes (the Gur-e-Amir at Samarkand, Gawhar Shad's mosque at Mashhad, Husayn Bayqara's projects at Herat).
The Mughal painting tradition, founded under Akbar by the same generation of painters that had migrated from Bihzad's Tabriz workshop, continued the late Timurid Herat tradition for another century.
The Mughal court ceremony, the literary patronage, the Persian-language administration, and the religious-political settlements all had Timurid antecedents.

The Mughal Empire as a sovereign political force ended in the early eighteenth century — the death of Aurangzeb in 1707 began a long decline, and the British East India Company gradually displaced Mughal authority over the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.

But the dynasty itself persisted as a political fiction in Delhi until 1857, when the failed Indian Rebellion against British rule produced the formal abolition of the Mughal title and the exile of the last Mughal emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar II to Burma.
The Timurid dynasty therefore had a continuous political existence — first in Central Asia, then in India — from Timur's coronation at Samarkand in 1370 to the abolition of the Mughal title in 1858.
That is 488 years.
By comparison, the Ottoman dynasty lasted from 1299 to 1922 (623 years), the Romanov dynasty lasted from 1613 to 1917 (304 years), the Habsburg dynasty lasted from 1273 to 1918 (645 years).

The Timurid dynasty is one of the longest-running dynasties of the early-modern and modern era — measured continuously across its Timurid and Mughal phases as a single political family, which is how its participants understood it.
A pause: the comparative point is worth emphasizing because it changes how the Timurid Empire should be assessed.
The conventional treatment of Timur is dominated by the violence — the skull pyramids, the Delhi sack, the Damascus sack, the 1401 Baghdad massacre, the planned China invasion.
This is appropriate.
The violence was real and is the most distinctive feature of his career.
But the conventional treatment also treats the Timurid Empire as essentially a one-generation phenomenon that effectively ended with Timur's death in 1405 and the succession wars that followed.

The reduced empire under Shah Rukh, the cultural florescence at Herat, the astronomical work at Samarkand, the late Timurid Renaissance under Husayn Bayqara, the Babur founding of the Mughal Empire, and the long Mughal afterlife are usually treated as separate stories rather than as a single continuous dynastic project.
This is wrong.
They are one project.

The Timurid identity, the Timurid claim to legitimacy through the Genghisid puppet-khan tradition (eventually transmuted into the Mughal claim to "Gurkani" descent), the Timurid architectural style, the Timurid court culture, the Timurid relationship to Persianate civilization — all of these continued unchanged from Timur's reign through the Mughal afterlife.
Babur in 1526 was conscious of being a Timurid recovering territories his ancestor had legitimately conquered in 1398.
Akbar in 1556 was conscious of being the senior representative of the Timurid dynasty in continued imperial form.
Shah Jahan in 1648, building the Taj Mahal at Agra, was building an architectural descendant of the Gur-e-Amir at Samarkand.
The line is continuous and was understood as continuous by the participants.
What this means for assessing Timur: the dynasty he founded did not end with him.
It outlasted nearly every other Eurasian dynasty of the period.
It produced one of the most successful empires in early-modern world history (Mughal India).
It carried the Persianate cultural template that emerged at fifteenth-century Herat into India and made it the dominant high culture of South Asia for three centuries.
The cultural legacy ran for five hundred years after Timur's death.
He was therefore not just a destructive conqueror; he was the founder of one of the longest-lived imperial dynasties of the early-modern world.
The destruction and the dynasty are part of the same story.
The cultural achievement and the violence that funded it are part of the same story.
There is no honest way to separate the two parts.
Both are required for an accurate understanding of what the Timurid Empire actually was.
The Timurid heartland — Samarkand, Bukhara, Herat — passed under Uzbek and later Russian control after 1507 and never recovered its earlier centrality in the Persianate world.

Samarkand under the Uzbek Shaybanids and their successors continued as a regional capital but never approached its Timurid peak; the great Registan complex (the three monumental madrasas around the central square at Samarkand, completed in 1417, 1636, and 1660 across the Timurid and Uzbek periods) is the most spectacular architectural ensemble in Central Asia today, but its institutional life was a much-attenuated continuation of the Timurid traditions.
Bukhara remained a center of Naqshbandi Sufism and Islamic scholarship through the early modern period.

Herat declined sharply after the Uzbek conquest, was repeatedly contested between the Safavids and various Afghan dynasties through the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, and emerged in the modern period as a regional Afghan city of moderate importance — its great Timurid monuments mostly demolished (the Gawhar Shad Musalla complex's deliberate destruction in 1885 is described in Chapter 6) and its Timurid cultural infrastructure lost.

The recognition of the Timurid achievement in twentieth-century scholarship has therefore depended substantially on the surviving evidence transmitted through the Mughal Indian afterlife — the architectural texts, the painting traditions, the literary works, the dynastic chronicles — which preserved Timurid material long after the Central Asian heartland had ceased to be a center of Persianate culture.
The Mughals, in this sense, are why we know what we know about the Timurids.
The deepest legacy, however, runs back through the political framework Timur himself constructed.

The structural problem of his career was the legitimacy gap (Chapter 1): a non-Genghisid trying to rule the post-Mongol world had to invent workarounds, and the workarounds — puppet khans, the Guregen title, forged genealogies, the integration of Persianate religious legitimacy through Sunni clerics and Sufi sheikhs — became the political template that the Mughals used.
Babur claimed legitimacy through both Timurid and Genghisid descent and through Sunni religious patronage.

Akbar elaborated this into one of the most sophisticated multi-religious political settlements in early-modern history (the Mughal court patronized Hindu, Jain, and Muslim religious establishments simultaneously, in a deliberate attempt to construct an Indian-imperial legitimacy that transcended any single religious community).
The Mughal political settlement was directly inherited from the Timurid solution to the legitimacy gap, applied in a different geographic context to a different demographic problem.
Even more deeply, the Timurid period established the model that distinguished the early-modern Persianate world from the European national-cultural framework.

Persian was the literary and administrative language of an enormous geographic region — from Anatolia through Iran into Central Asia and India — that contained multiple competing political states (Safavid, Mughal, Uzbek, Ottoman in the Persian-using parts of its administration).
A Persian poet, painter, scholar, or merchant could move between courts as the political winds shifted, finding patronage wherever it was most generous.
The cultural unity of the Persianate world was a real fact, sustained for centuries across changing political boundaries.
The Timurid Empire was the institutional matrix in which this Persianate cultural unity took its mature form.
The Timurid Renaissance at Herat in the 1410s through 1490s was the cultural template that the Safavids and Mughals would then carry forward in their respective geographic spheres.

In this sense, the most lasting Timurid legacy is not the Gur-e-Amir at Samarkand or the Mashhad mosque or even the Mughal Taj Mahal, but the political-cultural framework of the early-modern Persianate world itself.
Timur and his successors built the institutional and cultural infrastructure that made it possible for Persian-speaking culture to operate as a transregional civilization for several centuries.
That infrastructure outlived the Timurid Empire and the Mughal Empire alike.
It survives, attenuated but recognizable, in the contemporary cultural geography of Central Asia, Iran, and South Asia today.
The dynasty died — first in Central Asia in 1507, then formally in India in 1858.
The civilizational template it built has, in cultural terms, lasted longer than any of the regimes that nominally embodied it.

Cross-civ check: the late Timurid period and the early Mughal founding (1469–1556) overlap with the High Renaissance in Italy (Leonardo, Michelangelo, Raphael), the Reformation in Germany (Luther's 95 Theses in 1517 — eight years before Babur's invasion of India), the Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire by Cortés in 1519–21 (Aztec Empire Ch 8), the Spanish conquest of the Inca Empire by Pizarro in the 1530s, the early Tudor dynasty in England (Henry VII, Henry VIII), the founding of the Safavid Empire by Ismail I in 1501 (Safavid Persia Ch 1–2), and the early Ottoman classical age under Selim I and Suleiman the Magnificent.

The early sixteenth century is one of the most densely consequential periods in world history, with imperial expansion, religious revolution, and cultural florescence happening simultaneously across Eurasia and the Americas.
The Mughal founding in 1526 is one of these consequential events.
The Timurid dynasty's transition from its dying Central Asian phase to its long-lived Indian phase is one of the great dynastic translocations in world history.

Babur, riding south through the Khyber Pass in 1525 with twelve thousand men and two batteries of borrowed Ottoman cannons, was the last Timurid prince of Central Asia and the first Mughal emperor of India.
The two empires were the same dynasty.
The skull pyramids and the Taj Mahal are part of the same story.
The terror of Tamerlane and the cultural splendor of Mughal Agra are part of the same project.

The five-hundred-year arc from the capture of Samarkand in 1370 to the abolition of the Mughal title in 1858 is one continuous dynastic history, and it is one of the most consequential in the early-modern world.
That arc is the Timurid Empire.
Everything else is commentary.

chapters.title: The Ghurid Aftermath
sentences: The Delhi Sultanate began with a horse accident, an assassination, and a manumitted slave declaring himself king.

The horse accident happened to Qutb-ud-din Aibak (kuh-TOB ud-DEEN AY-bak), the Turkic slave-soldier whom Muhammad of Ghor (Medieval India Ch 8) had purchased, trained, and made his commander in north India.

After Aibak proclaimed himself Sultan at Lahore in 1206 — picking up the Indian provinces of the collapsing Ghurid empire after Muhammad of Ghor's assassination at the Damyak river crossing earlier that year — he ruled for four years before falling off a horse during a polo match in Lahore in 1210 and dying.
The horse fell on top of him and the saddle pommel pierced his chest.
He was buried in Lahore, where his tomb still stands beside one of the city's modern bazaars.
Four years is not a long reign, but in those four years Aibak did three things that defined the next three centuries.
He installed himself at the head of a Turkic Muslim military aristocracy ruling a Hindu population from a fortified compound in the southern outskirts of an existing Indian city.

He began construction of the city's first congregational mosque on the site of demolished Hindu and Jain temples, deliberately recycling their carved columns into the mosque's prayer hall as a visible architectural statement of religious supersession.

And he began, beside the mosque, a 240-foot fluted brick-and-sandstone victory tower that would be completed by his successors over the next century and is still the most photographed monument in Delhi.
The mosque was the Quwwat-ul-Islam ("Might of Islam").
The tower is the Qutb Minar.
Both are still standing.
To understand why the Sultanate took the form it did, you have to back up and look at where Aibak came from.
Aibak was born in Turkestan — somewhere in the Turkic-speaking belt of Central Asia north of Khorasan — sometime in the 1150s.
He was sold into slavery as a boy, a normal fate for boys captured in the steppe wars between Turkic confederations.
He passed through several owners before being purchased as a young man by Muhammad of Ghor's family, brought to the Ghurid capital in central Afghanistan, and trained in royal service.

The Ghurids, like every other Islamic dynasty of the eastern Persian world since the ninth century, had built their armies primarily out of trained slave-soldiers — mamluks (MAM-looks) — recruited from the Turkic tribes of the Eurasian steppe, converted to Islam, raised from childhood in royal military households, and bound to their owner-king by a tie that combined adoption, conversion, and military training (Islamic Golden Age Ch 6, where the system originates under the Abbasids).
The mamluk system worked because it produced soldiers with no kin ties to anyone except the sultan.
They could not run home to a tribal homeland because their tribal homeland was thousands of miles away in a place they had been taken from as children.
They had no local family to defect to.
Their entire identity — religious, military, social — was the household of the king who had purchased and trained them.
In practice, the most talented of these slave-soldiers regularly rose to positions of enormous power.
Many became governors of provinces, generals of major armies, and sometimes (when the dynasty above them collapsed) sultans in their own right.
The Ghaznavid dynasty (Medieval India Ch 8) had been founded by Sebuktigin, a manumitted Samanid slave-soldier.
The Mamluk Sultanate of Egypt would be founded by manumitted slave-soldiers in 1250, twenty years after Aibak's Indian sultanate.
The Tulunids of Egypt, the Ikhshidids of Egypt, the Ghaznavids, the Khwarazmians — the medieval Islamic east is a long catalogue of slave-founded dynasties.
Aibak fits this pattern precisely.

When Muhammad of Ghor was assassinated in 1206 with no son to inherit, Aibak — already the Ghurid commander in India, already running Delhi as a military headquarters — proclaimed himself Sultan at Lahore.
The Ghurid central empire fragmented within a few years among rival mamluk commanders.
Aibak's rivals Taj-ud-din Yildiz in Ghazni and Nasir-ud-din Qabacha (kuh-BAH-chah) in Sindh held off claims to his territory for a few years, but the Indian provinces stuck with Aibak.
The Mamluk or Slave dynasty of Delhi was founded.

The technical question of whether Aibak's Lahore proclamation in 1206 or his investiture by the Abbasid Caliph in Baghdad some years later constitutes the formal founding of the Sultanate is a debate medieval and modern historians have continued to have.
The conventional date is 1206, and the conventional founder is Aibak.

Most modern Indian historiography accepts this, though there are dissenting positions arguing that the dynasty really begins under Iltutmish (Aibak's son-in-law, who actually built the institutional state) in 1211.
The city Aibak ruled from was Delhi.

Not the modern city of New Delhi, but the older settlement layered onto the same fortified plateau on the southwestern bank of the Yamuna river — the great northern Indian river that flows southeast from the Himalayas, joining the Ganges at Allahabad about 600 miles downstream.
Delhi sits at a strategic crux.
It controls the route from the Khyber Pass and the northwestern invasion corridor down into the Gangetic plain.
It controls the Doab (DOH-ahb, "two waters"), the rich agricultural strip between the Yamuna and the Ganges.
It is far enough from the coast to be protected from naval attack but close enough to the great rivers to ship grain.

The site had been continuously settled since at least the Mahabharata epic period (where it appears as Indraprastha, the capital of the Pandava kings), through the various Hindu and Buddhist kingdoms of the first millennium, into the period of the Tomara Rajputs in the eighth century, and the Chauhans of Ajmer who had captured it from the Tomaras around 1150 (Medieval India Ch 8).

When Muhammad of Ghor's army defeated Prithviraj Chauhan at the Second Battle of Tarain in 1192 and Aibak occupied Delhi shortly after, the Chauhan citadel passed into Turkic Muslim hands and would not leave them until 1857.
The fortified compound the Mamluks built at Delhi was called Mehrauli, on the southern edge of the modern city.
The Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque and the Qutb Minar are both at Mehrauli today.

The complex would be added to and partially abandoned by successive sultanate dynasties — the Khaljis added a fortified extension at Siri, the Tughlaqs built Tughlaqabad and then Firuzabad and then Jahanpanah, the Lodis built tomb gardens north of all of these, and finally Shah Jahan built the modern Old Delhi at the very north of the cluster in 1648.
The "seven cities of Delhi" that tourist guides talk about are the six successive Sultanate capitals plus Shahjahanabad.
Each new dynasty preferred to build its own fortified city rather than inherit the moral and architectural baggage of its predecessors.
Aibak's capital at Mehrauli was the first.

The Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque deserves some attention because it is the founding statement of Sultanate architecture — and the most direct documentary evidence we have of how the new Turkic regime presented itself to its conquered Hindu subjects.
The mosque was begun in 1192 (immediately after Aibak captured Delhi for Muhammad of Ghor) and substantially completed under Aibak's own sultanate by 1198.
It was built on the site of, and using the materials of, twenty-seven demolished Hindu and Jain temples that had stood on the same plateau.
The carved sandstone columns of the destroyed temples were dismantled and reassembled into the mosque's prayer hall.

You can still see them today: rows of Hindu temple columns, each carved with images of Hindu deities, dancing figures, lotus motifs, and floral patterns, arranged into rows supporting a Muslim prayer hall whose orientation faces Mecca.
The figures of the gods were defaced — the sculpted faces chiseled off — but the columns themselves were left visibly Hindu.
This was deliberate.
The reused columns were a statement: these were temples; they are now a mosque; the new religion has built itself out of the materials of the old.
A Persian inscription on the mosque, from an enlargement built by Iltutmish in the 1220s, makes the political logic explicit.
It records that the mosque was built "out of the materials of twenty-seven idol temples" and credits the act to the divine favor that brought Muslim arms to India.
The inscription is one of the more uncomfortably honest historical documents of medieval north India: it says exactly what it did and exactly why.
What the mosque does not do, however, is destroy the Hindu artistic vocabulary it built itself out of.
The reused columns are still beautiful, still recognizably Indian, still carved with the lotus-and-floral motifs that Indian temple architecture had developed for the previous fifteen centuries.

The mosque's iron pillar — which we'll come to in a moment — is still standing in its courtyard, undisturbed, a fourth-century Gupta-era engineering marvel preserved as a kind of curiosity by every Sultanate dynasty that passed through.

Sultanate architecture across the next three centuries would proceed in precisely this mixed mode: Persian arch-and-dome construction techniques, Indian craftsmen using Indian techniques and materials, and a constant unresolved tension between the two.
The result is a distinct architectural tradition called Indo-Islamic architecture, of which the Quwwat-ul-Islam is the founding monument.
The Iron Pillar of Delhi, sitting in the Quwwat-ul-Islam courtyard, is its own astonishment.

A 24-foot, six-ton pillar of nearly pure wrought iron, originally erected at some other location around 400 CE during the Gupta Empire (Gupta Empire Ch 7) and bearing a Sanskrit inscription dedicating it to a king conventionally identified as Chandragupta II.
It has stood in the open air for sixteen centuries and has barely rusted.

Modern metallurgists have spent decades figuring out why: a combination of high phosphorus content, low sulfur, and the formation of a self-protecting hydrated iron oxide-phosphate film on the surface.

The pillar is one of the great surviving artifacts of medieval Indian metallurgy, and one of the strangest things about Sultanate Delhi is that the Mamluks chose to preserve it intact in their flagship mosque, rather than recycling it into iron weapons or pulling it down.
They didn't read Sanskrit, and they probably didn't know what it said, but they could see that it was extraordinary, and they left it alone.
The Qutb Minar — the 240-foot tower beside the mosque — is the more famous monument.
Aibak began the Minar in 1199, intending it as both a victory tower and a minaret from which the call to prayer would be sounded over the new mosque.
The first story was completed under his reign.
The next three stories were added under his son-in-law Iltutmish in the 1220s.
The fifth and final story, with its later marble cladding, was added under Firuz Shah Tughlaq after a lightning strike in 1369 damaged the upper section.
The tower thus took the better part of two centuries to reach its final form, with each major Sultanate dynasty adding to it.
It stands 240 feet tall (about a 24-story building, the tallest brick minaret in the world).
It is fluted with alternating round and angular ribs in the lower stories, gradually smoothing toward the top.
Each story is separated by a projecting balcony resting on muqarnas corbels — the honeycomb-like Islamic architectural feature borrowed from Iranian and Central Asian buildings.
The exterior is wrapped in carved Arabic and Persian inscriptions in flowing Naskhi calligraphy, including verses from the Quran and praise of the sultans who built each stage.
What the Qutb Minar means is genuinely complicated and has been debated for centuries.

The most direct reading — preferred by Sultanate-era court historians and adopted by colonial-era European scholars — is that it is a victory tower, celebrating the Islamic conquest of India and broadcasting Muslim power over the conquered Hindu plain.
There is a literal historical model: Mahmud of Ghazni's minarets at Ghazni (Medieval India Ch 8) were victory towers in exactly this sense, and Aibak would have known them.
The Quwwat-ul-Islam inscription on the mosque it stands beside makes the same Triumphalist note, so the reading is consistent.

But the alternative reading is also not wrong: the Minar is a functional minaret for the mosque, oriented to allow the call to prayer to project across the city, in the same architectural tradition as the great Seljuk-era Iranian minarets.

And the synthesis reading, increasingly preferred by modern Indian historians, is that the Minar is both at once — a deliberately ambiguous monument that combines triumphant Islamic conquest, functional Islamic worship, and (by the time Tughlaq added the marble cladding) a kind of monumental urban civic identity that no longer reads cleanly as either conqueror or conquered.
By the time the Minar was finished, Sultanate Delhi was Indo-Islamic, not just Islamic.
The monument reflects what it had become.
The Qutb Minar is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
About three million tourists visit it every year.
It is the single most recognized monument of pre-Mughal Islamic India.

To get a sense of where this puts the Sultanate in world history, the cross-civ check at the founding moment: 1206 CE, the year Aibak proclaimed himself Sultan at Lahore, is also the year Genghis Khan was acclaimed Great Khan of the unified Mongol tribes at the kurultai (great assembly) on the banks of the Onon river in northern Mongolia (Mongol Empire Ch 2).

Two of the most consequential thirteenth-century empires were proclaimed in the same year, on opposite sides of Eurasia, by two figures who never met but whose successors would soon collide on the Indus river.

The Mongol world-empire and the Delhi Sultanate are fundamentally contemporary phenomena — in fact, one of the central political achievements of the early Sultanate was being one of the few Eurasian states that successfully resisted Mongol absorption.
We'll get to that in Chapters 2 and 3.

In Europe, 1206 falls in the long reign of the great medieval-papal Pope Innocent III, who was about to launch the Albigensian Crusade against the Cathar heretics in southern France (Byzantine Empire Ch 9 covers the Crusader sack of Constantinople in 1204, two years before our story begins).
The Holy Roman Empire was contesting succession after the death of Henry VI.
Genghis Khan and Aibak were declaring empires while medieval Christendom was declaring crusades.
In East Asia, the Southern Song dynasty ruled the wealthier southern half of China (Tang-Song China Ch 7), and Genghis Khan would shortly attack its northern Jurchen Jin neighbors.
The Kamakura shogunate had been founded in Japan in 1192.
The Khmer Empire at Angkor was rebuilding after the death of Jayavarman VII.

In Africa, the Ayyubid Sultanate ruled Egypt (the dynasty Saladin had founded in the 1170s after defeating the Crusaders), and the Mali Empire had not yet been founded — Sundiata Keita's victory over the Sosso would not come until around 1235.

The Islamic world that the Sultanate was joining in 1206 was an Islamic world stretching from Morocco to the Indus, with the Abbasid caliphate technically still in existence at Baghdad but with real power held by various regional Turkic, Kurdish, and Persian dynasties.
The Sultanate, in other words, joined a world that was already mid-transformation.

The Mongols would shortly destroy half of it, the Crusader states would shortly collapse, the Song would fall to the Mongols by 1279, and the Sultanate would be the last surviving major Islamic state in the eastern half of this world by the late thirteenth century.
The Mongols never managed to take Delhi.
That fact is one of the central facts of medieval Indian history.
We'll get to how it happened in Chapter 3.
Aibak's death in the polo accident of 1210 left a problem.
His only son, Aram Shah, was politically weak and had alienated the Turkic mamluk nobility at Lahore.
The Delhi mamluks rejected him within a few months and invited Aibak's son-in-law, the governor of Badaun, to take the throne.
The son-in-law was Iltutmish (il-toot-MISH, ruled 1211–1236).
Iltutmish was the real founder of the Sultanate as an institution, and Chapter 2 is mostly about him.
Aibak founded the dynasty; Iltutmish built the state.
He defeated his rivals (Yildiz of Ghazni, Qabacha of Sindh) and consolidated all the Indian Ghurid territories under Delhi.
He secured a Khilat (formal robe of investiture) from the Abbasid Caliph al-Mustansir in Baghdad in 1229, giving the Sultanate Islamic legal legitimacy.
He built up the Chihalgani (chee-hahl-GAH-nee) — the Forty, an inner council of forty senior Turkic slave-officers who served as the dynasty's military and administrative aristocracy.
He introduced the silver tanka (TANK-uh) and copper jital (JEE-tul) as the standard coinage of the realm — units that would survive through the Mughal period.
He completed the upper stories of the Qutb Minar that Aibak had begun.

He commissioned his own tomb — the Tomb of Iltutmish — in the Qutb complex, the earliest surviving Islamic mausoleum in India, with red-sandstone walls covered in interwoven Quranic Arabic and Persian inscriptions in flowing geometric calligraphy.
And he is the figure who makes the central choice that will define his death: nominating his daughter Razia to succeed him as Sultan over his surviving sons.
That decision is where Chapter 2 starts.

Cross-civ check: while Iltutmish was building the Sultanate at Delhi between 1211 and 1236, Genghis Khan was campaigning across Persia and Central Asia (Mongol Empire Ch 3), the Magna Carta had been signed by King John in England in 1215, Frederick II Hohenstaufen was building his strange Sicilian-Arabic-Latin court in Palermo (Byzantine Empire Ch 10 touches the same period), and the Cathar Crusade was nearing its grim end at Montsegur.

The intellectual world of the early thirteenth century — Thomas Aquinas would be born in 1225, Ibn al-Arabi the Sufi metaphysician was teaching in Damascus, Nasir al-Din al-Tusi was writing his astronomical works at Maragha (Mongol Empire Ch 7), and Muhyiddin Ibn Arabi was synthesizing Sufi theology for the Islamic world (Islamic Golden Age Ch 8) — was producing some of the most important religious thought in any tradition.
The Sultanate joined this world as a frontier polity at its eastern edge, with most of its intellectual contributions still ahead of it.

chapters.title: Razia and the Slave Dynasty
sentences: Iltutmish died in April 1236 after a long illness.
He had spent the last year of his life systematically working through the question of his succession, and he had reached the most controversial conclusion he could possibly have reached.
He had four sons.
Two were dead.
The eldest surviving was Rukn-ud-din Firuz, who was an alcoholic widely regarded as politically incompetent.
The other surviving son was a child.
The Turkic nobility, by every Islamic dynastic precedent in the eastern world, expected one of these sons to succeed.
What they expected especially strongly was that Iltutmish would not nominate his daughter.
Iltutmish nominated his daughter.
Razia Sultana (RAH-zee-ah, ruled 1236–1240) was Iltutmish's adult daughter from his chief queen, Qutub Begum.

According to the chronicler Minhaj-i Siraj (whose Tabaqat-i Nasiri, written about thirty years later, is the principal Persian source for the early Sultanate), Iltutmish explained his choice publicly: he had observed Razia ruling Delhi as his regent during one of his Bengal campaigns, and she had managed the city better than her brothers ever had.
She was educated, militarily literate, politically shrewd, and willing to learn.
The sons, by contrast, were a disappointment.
Iltutmish formally proclaimed Razia as his designated successor and had the proclamation read in the mosques of Delhi.
Then he died.
The Turkic nobility immediately ignored the will and put Rukn-ud-din Firuz on the throne instead.
Rukn-ud-din lasted seven months.
His reign was, by all accounts, a disaster.

He spent the treasury on entertainment, neglected administrative duties, drank constantly, and allowed his mother (Iltutmish's other queen, who had not been Razia's mother) to assassinate Iltutmish's other surviving sons in a series of palace murders.
Within a year, the Delhi populace was in active rebellion against him.
Razia, watching from the sidelines, made her move.

The story Minhaj-i Siraj records — and it is impossible to know how much of it is accurate and how much is later legend, but the story itself is the historical fact that mattered for the next thousand years — is that Razia appeared at the Friday congregational prayer at the Delhi mosque in November 1236 wearing red robes (the color of mourning for her murdered brothers), publicly accused Rukn-ud-din of orchestrating the murders, and called on the assembled Muslims of Delhi to depose him in the name of justice.
The crowd surged forward.
Within hours, Rukn-ud-din had been arrested and Razia was on the throne.
She would rule Delhi for the next three and a half years.
What makes Razia historically remarkable is not just that a woman briefly held the throne of a major medieval Islamic empire — though that is remarkable enough on its own.
Shajar al-Durr would briefly hold the Mamluk throne in Egypt in 1250 (Islamic Golden Age Ch 9 references the same dynasty), so Razia is not absolutely unique.
But Shajar al-Durr ruled for three months; Razia ruled for nearly four years.

Empress Wu Zetian had ruled Tang China in the 690s (Tang-Song China Ch 4), and Boudicca had led the Iceni revolt against Rome in 60 CE (Celtic Cultures Ch 7), and Hatshepsut had ruled Egypt as pharaoh in the fifteenth century BCE (New Kingdom Egypt Ch 3).
Female rule in the medieval and ancient world is uncommon but not unheard-of.

What makes Razia distinctive is the combination of unambiguous formal succession (she was literally named successor by her father), formal sovereignty (she had coins struck in her own name, as Sultan Jalalat-ud-din Razia), and political engagement (she rode into battle, presided over court, and made her own foreign-policy decisions).
She also did several things that scandalized the Turkic nobility.
She abandoned the purdah (PUR-dah, the Islamic seclusion of royal women behind veils and curtains), appearing in public and at court without a veil.
She wore men's clothing — the standard tunic-and-trousers of a Turkic male warrior — at official functions.
She rode horseback in public.

She insisted on being called Sultan rather than Sultana, on the grounds that the masculine title was the legal title and the feminine form was demeaning. (Modern historians use "Sultana Razia" anyway, which is how the name has come down to us, but she herself rejected it.) And — most consequentially — she promoted a non-Turkic Abyssinian slave-officer named Yakut to the position of master of the royal stables, an enormously influential post in a court where horses were a critical military asset and where access to the royal stables meant access to the sultan.
The Turkic nobility took this as a personal insult and a sign that Razia was bypassing them in favor of a non-Turkic favorite.
The Forty mobilized.
The Chihalgani — the Forty — were the inner aristocracy of the Mamluk dynasty.
Iltutmish had assembled them as a corps of senior Turkic slave-officers who served as governors of the empire's major provinces and as the leadership of the central army.
Each was a manumitted slave, each had been raised in the royal household, and collectively they considered themselves the kingmakers of the dynasty.
They had grudgingly accepted Razia's accession because Rukn-ud-din had been impossible to defend, but they had assumed she would rule as their figurehead and let them run the state.
Razia, instead, was running the state.
She made her own appointments, ignored their advice, promoted Yakut over their objections, and was beginning to look like an actual sultan with her own power base.
In 1240, the governor of Bhatinda (Bah-TIN-dah), a Turkic noble named Malik Altunia (al-TOON-ya), revolted against her.
Razia rode out at the head of an army to suppress the revolt.
Yakut was killed in the campaign.
Razia was captured at Bhatinda.
The Forty in Delhi declared her deposed and put one of her brothers, Bahram Shah, on the throne.
What happened next is the part of the Razia story that has been most heavily mythologized.
The basic facts: Razia, captive at Bhatinda, married Altunia (whether by force, by political calculation, or by genuine attachment, the sources disagree).
The two of them then attempted to retake Delhi from Bahram Shah at the head of a combined army.
They were defeated outside Delhi in October 1240.
Razia and Altunia fled.
They were caught and killed, possibly by their own retreating soldiers, possibly by local villagers who robbed them, on the road near Kaithal in modern Haryana, on October 14, 1240.
Razia was about 35 years old.
She is buried in old Delhi at a small tomb, near the Kalan Masjid mosque, which is now half-buried in residential houses and largely forgotten by the city.
The tomb is a simple raised platform with two grave-markers, one for Razia and one (traditionally) for her sister.
The site receives almost no visitors.
The Qutb Minar that her father commissioned and that was completed under successors who actively suppressed her memory still stands ten miles south, drawing three million tourists a year.
The contrast is the point.
Razia's reign was uncomfortable in her own time and has remained politically uncomfortable since, in different ways for different audiences.

The Mamluk dynasty's official chronicles, written by Persian scholar-bureaucrats employed by sultans who came after her, treated her reign as an aberration that demonstrated the unsuitability of female rule.

Modern Hindu nationalist historiography sometimes (selectively) embraces her as a counter-example to "Islamic patriarchy." Modern Indian feminist historiography has reclaimed her as a proto-feminist hero.
Modern Muslim historiography has variously celebrated her competence, lamented her novelty, and ignored her entirely.
She remains one of the most contested figures in medieval Indian historiography.
What is uncontested is that she happened.
She really was Sultan of Delhi.
She really was an effective ruler in a period when most of her competition was less so.
And she really was the only woman to hold the throne of any major medieval Indian empire.
Her four years are a documented historical fact, however imperfectly remembered.
After Razia, the Sultanate spent the next quarter-century in confusion.
Bahram Shah, the brother who had taken her throne, lasted two years before being deposed and killed by his own nobles in 1242.
His successor Alauddin Masud Shah lasted four years before being deposed and killed in 1246.

The Forty cycled through three more nominal sultans — the child Nasir-ud-din Mahmud (whose real ruler was the regent Ghiyas-ud-din Balban), and brief usurpations between regnal periods — until 1266, when Balban himself took the throne in his own right.
The instability was the problem the Forty had created for themselves.
A corps of forty roughly equal slave-officers, each with his own retinue and provincial power base, could not produce a stable monarchy as long as it remained a real political force.
Each succession became a faction fight.
Each faction fight weakened the central state.
By the 1260s, the Sultanate was at risk of disintegration.
The Mongol raids on the northwestern frontier (more on which in a moment) were getting worse.
Bengal was effectively independent under its own Turkic governor.
Most of the Doab was held only loosely.
What the Sultanate needed was a strong central monarch who could break the Forty's power and make the office of Sultan into something more than a symbol manipulated by the nobles.
What it got was Balban.
Ghiyas-ud-din Balban (BAL-ban, ruled 1266–1287) had been one of the Forty himself.

He had come into Iltutmish's slave household as a young Turkic captive in the 1230s, risen through the ranks under the chaos of the post-Iltutmish years, served as regent for Nasir-ud-din Mahmud for twenty years, and finally taken the throne in his own right in 1266 as a man already in his sixties.
He brought to the throne a clear analysis of what was wrong with the Sultanate and a set of ferocious institutional reforms designed to fix it.
His basic insight was that the Sultanate had become weak because the Sultan had become a peer of his nobles rather than a sacred figure standing above them.
The remedy was to elevate the office of Sultan into something near-divine, to break the Forty's institutional power, and to back this up with a credible apparatus of state violence.
The first move was ceremonial.
Balban introduced Persian court ceremonial of a deliberately exaggerated kind.
Court attendance required full Persian dress; nobles approached the throne by performing sijdah (prostration on the ground) and paibos (kissing the sultan's feet).
Court was conducted in formal Persian; access to the sultan was strictly limited; even close family members had to formally request audiences.

Balban explicitly modeled this on the Sasanian Persian court (Persian Empire Ch 8), the most ceremonialized court in the eastern Islamic memory, deliberately importing its hierarchical theology of kingship — the Zilullah, "shadow of God on earth" — to elevate his own status.
The second move was political.
Balban systematically broke the Forty.
He demoted, exiled, or executed the senior surviving members of the Chihalgani over the first several years of his reign.

The most senior, his cousin Sher Khan, the frontier governor who had effectively held the western frontier against the Mongols for two decades, was poisoned in 1270 (Balban himself ordered the poisoning, by all serious accounts).
The other surviving Forty were neutralized through demotion, isolation, or selective execution.
By the late 1270s, the Chihalgani as an institution was finished.
The third move was military.
Balban built up a standing army of professional cavalry that owed loyalty directly to him rather than to his governors.
He created a new intelligence service (the barid, Persian for "courier service" — a network of professional informants reporting directly to the sultan from every district).

He suppressed banditry across the Doab with calculated terror, hanging the bodies of suspected bandits along the roads to Delhi in numbers that the Persian chronicler Barani records (with some satisfaction) as exceeding the legal proprieties of mainstream Islamic jurisprudence.

He campaigned personally against rebels in Bengal, against the Meo people of Mewat (the rural population around Delhi who had been raiding the city's outskirts), and against the various smaller principalities that had taken advantage of post-Iltutmish weakness.
By the time Balban died in 1287 at perhaps eighty years old, the Sultanate was once again a stable, centralized military monarchy.
The cost was high — Balban's reign is the most violent and most authoritarian of the Mamluk period — but the institutional state survived.
The Sultanate was structurally stronger in 1287 than it had been at any time since Iltutmish.
The question was whether Balban's successors would be able to hold what he had built.
They were not.
Balban's grandson Kayqubad (kay-koo-BAHD, ruled 1287–1290), who took the throne as a teenager after Balban's death, lasted three years before being murdered in his bath.
The Mamluk dynasty itself was over.

What replaced it was a new dynasty from a different Turkic lineage — the Khaljis, who had been settled in eastern Afghanistan for two centuries, who spoke a Turkic language but had absorbed enough Pashtun culture and intermarriage that the older Turkic mamluks of Delhi considered them slightly impure outsiders.

The Khalji takeover in 1290, which Chapter 3 covers, was a kind of revolution within the Sultanate — not a foreign conquest, but a transfer of power from one Turkic ethnic faction to another, with consequential effects on the dynasty's character.
But before we get to the Khaljis, we need to talk about the Mongols.
The Mongols were the central external threat to the Sultanate from 1221 to about 1330.
The fact that the Sultanate survived this threat is one of the most consequential military facts of the thirteenth century.
The Mongol problem started with Genghis Khan himself.

After Genghis crushed the Khwarazmian empire of Sultan Muhammad in 1219–21 (Mongol Empire Ch 3), the deposed Khwarazmian prince Jalaluddin Mingburnu (jah-lahl-ud-DEEN MING-bur-noo) fled south through Afghanistan to the Indus river, attempting to take refuge in north India.
Genghis Khan personally pursued him, and in November 1221 Genghis's army caught Jalaluddin at the Indus river.
Jalaluddin's army was destroyed; Jalaluddin himself escaped by swimming his horse across the Indus and disappearing into the western Himalayan foothills.
Genghis Khan was now camped on the Indus, looking east into India.
He sent a small reconnaissance force into the Punjab.

The force returned with reports of the climate (oppressive, with monsoon humidity the steppe-bred Mongol horses found difficult), the terrain (forested and broken), and the population (numerous and hostile).
Genghis Khan declined to invade.
He turned his army around and went back to Mongolia.
Genghis's restraint at the Indus is one of the great might-have-beens of medieval history.

Iltutmish, who was sultan at Delhi in 1221, had wisely refused to shelter Jalaluddin or to provoke the Mongols in any way. (His political judgment was excellent; he understood exactly what Mongol revenge for offering shelter would have looked like.) The Sultanate survived its first encounter with the Mongols by being too unimportant to be worth conquering.
That would not be true forever.
The Mongol threat returned under Genghis's successors.

The Chagatai khanate — the western half of the Mongol world-empire, centered in modern Uzbekistan and Afghanistan (Mongol Empire Ch 5) — sent regular raiding parties through the Khyber Pass and into the Punjab from the 1240s through the 1290s.

These raids were not full conquest attempts, but they were destructive: they would seize the harvest, burn villages, take captives back across the Indus, and demand tribute from the local Sultanate-appointed governors.
The frontier region around Multan and Lahore was repeatedly devastated.
The Sultanate's western frontier essentially became a permanent military zone, garrisoned by frontier governors whose entire career consisted of defending against Mongol incursions.

The most prominent of these frontier governors was Balban's cousin Sher Khan, who held the Multan-Lahore frontier for twenty years (1240s through 1265) and was one of the few senior Sultanate officials whose name the Mongols genuinely feared.
After Balban poisoned Sher Khan in 1270, the frontier was held by a succession of less competent governors, and the Mongol raids accordingly worsened.
By the 1280s, Mongol raids were reaching the outskirts of Lahore and beginning to threaten Multan.
Balban's response was to build up a standing frontier army at Sunam and Samana in the Punjab, garrisoned by professional troops with a dedicated supply chain from Delhi.
The system worked, but it was permanently expensive.
Balban's military budget was enormous, and the Sultanate was effectively running a war-economy on the western frontier from the 1270s onward.
The full Mongol assault was still to come.
It would arrive under the Khalji dynasty, in six separate invasions between 1296 and 1306, and its repulsion would be the central military achievement of the next chapter.
But the institutional foundation for that achievement was Balban's.

The standing army he built, the fortified frontier he maintained, the centralized command structure he created — all of these would be inherited by the Khaljis and used to win the wars Balban had prepared for.

Cross-civ check: while the Mamluk Sultanate was consolidating in Delhi between 1206 and 1290, the Mongol Empire was conquering most of Eurasia (Mongol Empire Ch 3, Ch 4, Ch 5), the Mamluk Sultanate of Egypt was being founded in 1250 by another set of slave-soldiers (Islamic Golden Age Ch 9), the Crusader states in the Levant were being progressively rolled back, the Yuan Dynasty of Kublai Khan was being established in China by 1271 (Tang-Song China Ch 9), and the Holy Roman Empire was passing through the long interregnum after the Hohenstaufen collapse.
The thirteenth century was the great Mongol century, and one of the few major Eurasian states to survive it without being conquered or restructured by the Mongols was the Sultanate.
That fact is the precondition for everything that follows.

chapters.title: The Khalji Imperial Moment
sentences: The Khalji dynasty (1290–1320) lasted only thirty years, but it pushed the Sultanate to its first real imperial peak.

Under one ruler in particular — Alauddin Khalji (al-ah-ud-DEEN KAL-jee, ruled 1296–1316) — the Sultanate defeated six Mongol invasions, conquered the Rajput citadels, projected armies as far south as Madurai, and ran the most ambitious price-control economy of the medieval world.
It also ushered in a sustained burst of Indo-Persian literary culture under court poet Amir Khusrau (uh-MEER khus-ROW), one of the most prolific writers in any medieval language.
The dynasty began with a murder.
Jalaluddin Khalji (jah-lahl-ud-DEEN, ruled 1290–1296) was a Khalji general in his seventies who deposed the last Mamluk sultan Kayqubad in 1290.
Jalaluddin was, by all the surviving evidence, a genuinely mild and pious man.
He pardoned political enemies who would normally have been executed.
He refused to plunder cities he conquered.
He maintained civil terms even with the relatives of the dynasty he had displaced.
He was, in short, the wrong personality for medieval Sultanate politics.
His nephew (and son-in-law), Alauddin Khalji, was the right personality.

Alauddin had been Jalaluddin's military commander on the southern frontier, and in 1296 he led a successful raid on the wealthy Hindu kingdom of Devagiri (in modern Maharashtra), bringing back enormous quantities of treasure.
He returned north along the Yamuna and arranged a meeting with his uncle Jalaluddin at the river port of Kara (KAH-rah) in eastern Uttar Pradesh, ostensibly to deliver the spoils.

What happened at Kara is recorded in detail by the chronicler Ziauddin Barani (zee-ah-ud-DEEN bah-RAH-nee), whose Tarikh-i Firuzshahi is the principal source for the Khalji and early Tughlaq dynasties.
Jalaluddin came down to the riverbank to embrace his nephew.
Alauddin's men cut Jalaluddin down where he stood.

Alauddin had himself proclaimed Sultan on the spot, marched to Delhi at the head of Jalaluddin's own army, distributed the Devagiri loot among the Delhi nobility to buy off opposition, and was firmly on the throne within a few months.
It is one of the most efficiently executed coups in Sultanate history.
It also set the political tone of Alauddin's reign: he would not be constrained by traditional considerations of family, piety, or precedent.
He would do what worked.
What worked, as it turned out, was a great deal.
The first thing Alauddin had to do was deal with the Mongols.
Beginning in 1296, the year of his accession, the Chagatai khanate sent six separate invasions through the Khyber Pass into north India over the next decade.
These were not the small raids of the previous century; they were full-scale armies, sometimes 100,000 strong, intent on actual conquest.
The most dangerous of them — under Targhi in 1303 — actually reached Delhi and besieged the city.
Another, in 1305 under Ali Beg and Tartaq, penetrated as far as the modern Saharanpur district.
A third, in 1306 under Kebek, reached the lower Punjab.
Alauddin's response was the most successful sustained anti-Mongol defense achieved by any non-Mongol state in the thirteenth or fourteenth century.
He restructured the army on professional lines, paying his cavalry and infantry directly in cash from the treasury rather than through the older iqta (IK-tah) land-grant system.
He built up new fortified frontier garrisons under generals like Zafar Khan, Ulugh Khan, and Ghazi Malik (the future founder of the Tughlaq dynasty).

He moved his own court within the new fortified extension city of Siri (SEE-ree), built just north of Mehrauli, after the 1303 Mongol siege of Delhi made the older Mehrauli compound look insufficient.

The walls of Siri, according to a tradition recorded by Barani, were partially mortared with the skulls of Mongol prisoners taken in the 1303 campaign — a detail that may be propaganda but that captures the calculated brutality of the project.
The defeats Alauddin's army inflicted on the Mongols were severe.
At the Battle of Kili in 1299, Zafar Khan broke the army of Qutlugh Khwaja outside Delhi.
At the battles of 1305 and 1306, Ulugh Khan systematically destroyed the invading forces and sent thousands of Mongol prisoners back to Delhi to be publicly executed.
By 1306, the Chagatai khanate had effectively given up.
The Mongol invasions of the Sultanate ceased almost entirely after 1306, and would resume only sporadically and at much smaller scale during the subsequent decades.
This is one of the structurally important facts of medieval Eurasian history.

The Sultanate was, alongside Mamluk Egypt (which defeated the Mongols at the Battle of Ain Jalut in 1260, Islamic Golden Age Ch 9), one of only two Islamic states to successfully resist Mongol absorption.
Hungary was raided in 1241 and survived but was devastated.
Russia was conquered (Mongol Empire Ch 4).
Persia was conquered (Mongol Empire Ch 5).

The Sultanate's anti-Mongol record is genuinely exceptional and is the central reason the Sultanate's Persianate Indo-Islamic culture was able to develop without being absorbed into a larger Mongol-imposed framework.
With the Mongol threat receding, Alauddin turned to internal consolidation and external expansion.
He systematically reduced the Rajput strongholds that had held out since Muhammad of Ghor's time.

The Chauhan fortress of Ranthambore (RAN-thuhm-bohr), one of the most defensively formidable hill-forts in north India, fell in 1301 after a year-long siege; the defending Hammir Dev Chauhan died in the final assault.
The Sisodia fortress of Chittor (CHIT-tohr), in modern Rajasthan, fell in 1303 after another protracted siege.

The fall of Chittor became the source of the legendary story of Padmini (pud-MEE-nee), the Rajput queen whose beauty was the stated cause of Alauddin's siege and who, according to the legend, led the jauhar (jow-har, the Rajput practice of mass collective suicide by fire by the women of a defeated fortress to avoid capture) along with thousands of other Chittor noblewomen as the gates fell.

The Padmini story comes mainly from a sixteenth-century Sufi poem (Malik Muhammad Jayasi's Padmavat) and is almost certainly fictional in its specifics, though the underlying fact of mass jauhar at Chittor is documented in multiple medieval sources.
The conquests continued: Mandu in Malwa, Siwana and Jalor in Rajasthan, all reduced over the next decade.
By 1311 the major Rajput dynasties had been militarily broken (though most survived as reduced regional states and would reassert themselves in the post-Tughlaq fragmentation).
Then came the southern raids.

Malik Kafur (KAH-fur) was a Hindu eunuch slave originally from Gujarat, captured by Alauddin's army during a raid on the Vaghela kingdom around 1297 and brought back to Delhi to serve in the royal household.
He converted to Islam, rose rapidly through the slave hierarchy, and by the early 1300s had become Alauddin's most trusted military commander.
Between 1308 and 1313, Alauddin sent Kafur on three campaigns into south India.
The first, in 1308, defeated the Yadavas of Devagiri (in modern Maharashtra) again and brought the Yadava king Ramachandra into vassal status.

The second, in 1310, attacked the Kakatiyas of Warangal (in modern Telangana) and forced their king Prataparudra to surrender his treasury, including the Koh-i-Noor diamond — the great Golconda stone that was about to begin one of the most extraordinary biographies of any object in human history.
The third, in 1311, swept through the Hoysalas of Dwarasamudra (in modern Karnataka) and reached as far south as Madurai, the ancient Pandya capital deep in the Tamil country.
Madurai is roughly 1,400 miles south of Delhi (about the distance from New York to Houston).

Kafur's army had marched across nearly the entire subcontinent, defeated four major Hindu dynasties in succession, and returned to Delhi with quantities of treasure that the Persian chronicles describe in numbers that read like fantasies — gold by the elephant-load, silver by the tonnage, jewels by the bushel — but that all surviving sources, Hindu and Muslim, agree were genuinely enormous.
What is critical to note is that these were not conquests in the modern administrative sense.
Kafur did not annex south India.
He did not station Sultanate garrisons at Madurai or Warangal.
He raided, extracted treasure and tribute, accepted formal submission, and left.
The southern Hindu kingdoms remained nominally independent, paying annual tribute to Delhi but otherwise unchanged.

The closest analogy is the Viking raids of the eighth-tenth centuries on western Europe (Viking Age Ch 4): great profitable extractions that did not — at least at first — translate into permanent territorial control.
The southern raids brought enormous wealth to Delhi but did not produce the southern administrative apparatus that, say, the Cholas had built within the south themselves (Medieval India Ch 5).
The Sultanate's actual administrative reach remained the Indo-Gangetic plain plus a few pockets in central India.
But the raids' political consequences were enormous.
They demonstrated that the Sultanate's military reach extended across the entire subcontinent.
They brought the Koh-i-Noor and a flood of southern gold into the Sultanate treasury, funding decades of subsequent imperial spending.
And they established the precedent — confirmed by the Tughlaqs and challenged again only by the Mughals two centuries later — that Delhi's authority was, theoretically, pan-Indian.
The Koh-i-Noor itself is worth pausing on.
The stone — at the time perhaps 793 carats in its uncut form, eventually cut and recut to its modern 105.6 carats — passed from the Kakatiyas to the Sultanate treasury in 1310.

It would pass to the Tughlaqs, then to Babur after Panipat, then to the Mughal treasury, then to Nader Shah of Iran after his 1739 sack of Delhi (Safavid Persia Ch 8 covers the same Nader Shah), then to the Durranis of Afghanistan, then to Maharaja Ranjit Singh of the Sikh Empire in the 1810s, and finally to the British Crown after the 1849 annexation of Punjab.
It is now mounted in the crown of Queen Mary's consort and is displayed at the Tower of London, with claims for its repatriation regularly made by the Indian, Pakistani, and Afghan governments.
The stone's Sultanate-era arrival in Delhi in 1310 is the start of its eight-century-long career in the treasuries and crowns of every major successor state to the Sultanate.
While the Sultanate's armies were marching across south India, Alauddin was conducting an entirely different kind of revolution at home: the price-control economy.
The basic problem Alauddin was trying to solve was a logistics-and-fiscal problem.
He had built a very large standing army (the chronicles give numbers around 475,000 cavalry at peak, which is almost certainly inflated, but the army was unambiguously huge).
Paying them in cash required a stable currency and stable prices.
If prices in the Delhi grain markets rose, the army's cash salaries would not buy enough food, and the army would mutiny.

The conventional medieval Sultanate solution was to assign each soldier an iqta land-grant and let them collect their own salary from the harvest, but this dispersed the army across the countryside and weakened central control.
Alauddin wanted his army concentrated at Delhi, paid in cash, and reliably fed.
The solution he came up with was to set fixed government prices for all major commodities sold in the Delhi markets, and to enforce those prices through an elaborate state apparatus.
The system was administratively breathtaking.
The chronicler Barani (whose father and grandfather had served as Alauddin's officials, so he had inside knowledge) describes the apparatus in detail.
There were three controlled markets in Delhi: one for grain, one for cloth, and one for slaves and animals.

Each had its own state-appointed superintendent, called a shahna, who reported directly to a senior court official — Malik Yaqub, the chief market controller, the most powerful non-military post in the empire.
Each merchant was registered.
Each transaction was recorded.
Spies — drawn from a network of professional informants reporting to a separate intelligence service — tracked unofficial sales and reported violations.
The prices were set very low.
Wheat was fixed at 7.5 jitals per maund (a standard weight, about 82 pounds).
Cloth, slaves, horses, cattle — all were priced at levels significantly below what an unregulated market would have produced.

To keep these prices possible, Alauddin built government granaries, requisitioned grain from the rural cultivators of the Doab at fixed below-market rates (raising the effective land tax to roughly half the harvest, the highest rate in pre-Mughal Indian history), and stockpiled enough grain to crash market prices whenever they threatened to rise.
The penalties for non-compliance were severe.

Merchants caught short-weighting or selling above the fixed prices were fined, flogged, or in extreme cases mutilated (the Persian chronicles describe the cutting off of an equivalent weight of flesh from the cheating merchant's body, which is probably hyperbole but captures the deterrent intent).
The system was understood by everyone involved as functioning by terror as much as by economics.
It worked while Alauddin was alive.
The Delhi army was reliably fed.
Prices in the Delhi market remained essentially stable for nearly two decades.
The state extracted a much larger share of agricultural surplus than any previous Indian state had managed.
The system collapsed within months of Alauddin's death in 1316, when his successors had neither the political will nor the administrative capacity to maintain the apparatus.
The price-control regime is genuinely without parallel in pre-modern Indian history, and it is one of the most ambitious experiments in medieval state economic planning anywhere in the world.
Modern economists have looked at it as an ancestor of twentieth-century command economies.
Modern historians have looked at it as evidence of how far a determined medieval state could push administrative penetration.
What it really was, structurally, was a wartime fiscal-military state that needed to feed its armies cheaply enough to pay for the Mongol wars and the southern raids simultaneously.
When the wars ended, the system was no longer necessary.
When Alauddin died, the system no longer worked.
Alauddin Khalji died in January 1316 at perhaps fifty years old.
The succession was contested.
His designated heir was the youngest of his sons, but the oldest sons immediately challenged the will.
Within months, Malik Kafur (still Alauddin's most trusted general, and now also his most trusted political confidant) was effectively running the Sultanate as regent for the infant heir.
Kafur was assassinated in his bath about a month later by Alauddin's surviving Turkic mamluks.
The infant sultan died (probably murdered) shortly afterward.

The throne passed to one of Alauddin's older sons, Mubarak Shah Khalji, who lasted four years before being murdered in 1320 by his own favorite, a converted Hindu official named Khusrau Khan (khus-ROW), who briefly held the throne for himself before being deposed by Ghazi Malik, the Khalji frontier governor.
Ghazi Malik proclaimed himself Ghiyas-ud-din Tughlaq at Delhi in 1320.
The Khalji dynasty was over.
The Khalji moment lasted thirty years and produced more sustained imperial achievement than the previous fifty years of the Mamluk dynasty had managed.
The Mongols were defeated decisively.
The Rajputs were broken.
The south was raided to a depth no previous north Indian dynasty had matched.
The price-control economy worked for as long as Alauddin lived.
Persian high culture flourished at the court under Amir Khusrau (whose long career we'll cover properly in Chapter 6, with the rest of the Sultanate's literary production).
The institutional Sultanate that Iltutmish had built and Balban had stabilized reached, under Alauddin, its first true imperial form.
The cost was high.
Alauddin's centralization required brutal enforcement.
The southern raids depopulated regions of the Deccan.
The price-control economy worked through coercion that the chronicles describe with discomfort even when their authors were Sultanate insiders.
