The army was vast but expensive.
The treasury was full at Alauddin's death but the structural underpinnings were brittle.
When the Tughlaqs took over in 1320, they inherited an empire at peak.
What they did with it is the subject of Chapter 4.

Cross-civ check: while Alauddin Khalji was running Delhi between 1296 and 1316, the Mongol Ilkhanate in Persia was at its peak under Ghazan Khan (whose 1295 conversion to Islam ended the Mongol-vs-Islam phase of the Eurasian wars, Mongol Empire Ch 7), the Mamluk Sultanate in Egypt under al-Nasir Muhammad was the rival Islamic great power of the period, the Yuan Dynasty under Kublai Khan's successors ruled China (Tang-Song China Ch 9), the Mali Empire of Sundiata Keita and his successors was establishing the great West African gold-empire that would peak under Mansa Musa in the 1320s (Mali Empire Ch 1), and the Ottoman beylik had just been founded by Osman I in northwestern Anatolia (Ottoman Empire Ch 1) — the Ottoman dynasty that would be the Sultanate's partial mirror-image across the next four centuries was being founded the same decade Alauddin was breaking the Mongols.
Marco Polo, whose travels in Asia included reports from south India that he had visited around 1290, wrote his memoir during this period.
The Hundred Years' War between England and France was decades away from beginning.
The Black Death would not strike Eurasia until the 1340s.
The world was, in 1316, on the cusp of a series of climatic, demographic, and military shocks that would reshape every major civilization.
The Sultanate, having reached imperial peak, was about to experience its own shock under the Tughlaqs.

chapters.title: The Tughlaq Catastrophes
sentences: The Tughlaq dynasty (1320–1414) is one of the most paradoxical regimes in medieval Indian history.

Under its three principal sultans — Ghiyas-ud-din, Muhammad bin Tughlaq, and Firuz Shah — the dynasty inherited the Sultanate at its peak, expanded it briefly to its largest territorial extent, and then watched it fragment into a collection of provincial sultanates that would never be reunited in its name.
The middle of the three, Muhammad bin Tughlaq, was probably the most intelligent ruler the Sultanate ever produced.
His reign was a sequence of brilliantly conceived and catastrophically executed policy initiatives that wrecked the empire he had inherited.
The dynasty began with a returning frontier governor, an elaborate welcome ceremony, and a wooden pavilion that fell down on the head of its sultan.

Ghazi Malik (gah-ZEE), the frontier governor whose defense of the Punjab had repulsed several Mongol invasions during Alauddin Khalji's reign, deposed the converted Hindu usurper Khusrau Khan in September 1320 and proclaimed himself Ghiyas-ud-din Tughlaq at Delhi.
He was perhaps sixty years old.

He spent the next five years rebuilding the central administration that the late Khalji chaos had damaged, restoring the price controls in modified form (his approach was looser than Alauddin's), reasserting Sultanate authority over the Doab, and beginning construction of a massive new fortress city, Tughlaqabad (toog-LAH-kah-BAHD), on the southern outskirts of Delhi.
Tughlaqabad is one of the most overbuilt fortresses in Indian history.
The walls run about six and a half miles around an enormous citadel-and-palace complex on a rocky outcrop.
The walls are cyclopean — twenty to thirty feet thick at the base, sloping inward at a defensive batter, built from massive ashlar masonry blocks.
The citadel includes Ghiyas-ud-din's own tomb, with its distinctive sloping walls and red-sandstone-and-marble construction (the model that would influence later Tughlaq architecture).
Construction took five years and reportedly involved tens of thousands of laborers.
Tughlaqabad was abandoned within a few years of its construction.

The official explanation, recorded in later chronicles and traditions, is that a Sufi saint — Nizamuddin Auliya, the great Chishti master at Delhi (Chapter 6) — cursed Tughlaqabad after Ghiyas-ud-din offended him, declaring that it would either be inhabited by jackals or by the Gujjar nomads.
Nizamuddin's curse, which is documented in Sufi hagiographies but not in court chronicles, became one of the famous folk-explanations for why Tughlaqabad collapsed so quickly.
The more prosaic modern explanation is that the site lacked an adequate water supply and was difficult to defend in practice despite its imposing walls.
Ghiyas-ud-din died in 1325 in circumstances that have been debated for seven centuries.
He was returning from a campaign in Bengal, and his son Jauna Khan (the future Muhammad bin Tughlaq) had built a wooden welcome pavilion at the village of Afghanpur outside Delhi to receive him.
After the welcome ceremony, Ghiyas-ud-din retired into the pavilion to rest.
The pavilion collapsed on him, killing him.

The official explanation — that the pavilion was built too quickly and the structural beams gave way — is contradicted by the chronicler Ibn Battuta, who arrived in Delhi nine years later and was told by people who had been present that Jauna Khan had engineered the collapse deliberately, having the pavilion built to fall on his father at a precise moment, in order to seize the throne.
Whether the Afghanpur incident was an accident, a murder, or something in between, Jauna Khan was on the throne within days, calling himself Muhammad bin Tughlaq.

Muhammad bin Tughlaq (ruled 1325–1351) is the most documented Sultanate ruler of the fourteenth century, partly because his reign was so eventful and partly because the Moroccan traveler Ibn Battuta spent eight years (1334–1342) at his court as a qadi (Islamic judge) and wrote extensive eyewitness descriptions of his rule.
Muhammad was, by every contemporary account, an extraordinary individual.
He had been formally educated in Persian, Arabic, mathematics, astronomy, philosophy, and medicine.
He could quote Quranic Arabic and write Persian poetry.
He had read Greek philosophy in Arabic translation.
He corresponded with intellectuals across the Islamic world, including with the Mongol Ilkhanate's surviving scholars and with Mamluk Egyptian theologians.
Ibn Battuta describes him as personally generous, intellectually curious, deeply pious, and capable of charming foreign visitors with his learning.
Muhammad was also, by every contemporary account, alarmingly volatile.
The same Ibn Battuta who praises his learning describes him spending entire afternoons watching public executions, distributing alms one day and ordering mass beheadings the next.

The Persian chronicler Ziauddin Barani, who served in Muhammad's administration for years and clearly admired aspects of his master, called him a man who "habitually mixed mercy with cruelty in proportions no one could predict." Modern historians have variously diagnosed him with everything from manic-depressive disorder to a kind of intellectual hubris that mistook clever ideas for workable policy.
None of these diagnoses can be confirmed and most are anachronistic.
What is undisputed is that his reign was a sequence of catastrophes, and that he reacted to each catastrophe with another grand initiative whose results were as catastrophic as the last.
Three episodes capture this pattern: the move to Daulatabad, the token currency, and the Khurasan expedition.
The first catastrophe was the move of the capital to Daulatabad.

Daulatabad (dow-luh-TAH-bahd) — formerly Devagiri, the Yadava fortress that Alauddin Khalji had captured and Malik Kafur had used as a base for the southern raids — sits in modern Maharashtra, about 700 miles south of Delhi (a little farther than the distance from New York to Charleston).
It is centrally located in the Deccan, on a defensible rocky outcrop that the Yadavas had fortified with concentric walls and a moat carved into living rock.

Muhammad bin Tughlaq decided in 1327 that Daulatabad would be the Sultanate's new imperial capital, on the grounds that it was geographically closer to the recently conquered south and would allow tighter administrative control of the empire's expanded territory.
The reasoning was not entirely unreasonable.
The southern raids had accumulated nominal authority over a territory the Sultanate could not actually govern from Delhi.
Moving the capital south would, in theory, allow Sultanate administration to penetrate the Deccan in a way that the periodic raiding system had not achieved.
What was unreasonable was Muhammad's chosen method.

He ordered the entire population of Delhi — not just the administrative elite, not just the army, but all of Delhi's residents, including the artisans, merchants, scholars, religious figures, families — to migrate 700 miles south to Daulatabad.
The population was given a year to move.
Those who resisted were to be forcibly relocated.
Ibn Battuta, who arrived in Delhi during this period, describes the move as a humanitarian disaster.
The migration occurred during the worst phase of a multi-year drought.
The road south crossed several hundred miles of arid country with limited water.
People died in large numbers along the route.
Those who arrived at Daulatabad found a city not yet built to absorb them — there was inadequate housing, inadequate water, no established mosques or markets, no functional bureaucracy.
Within a few years, Muhammad reversed the policy and ordered everyone back to Delhi.
The return migration killed many of those who had survived the original journey.
Delhi, when the survivors returned, was a half-empty ruin that took a generation to repopulate.

The Daulatabad episode is the most often-cited example of Muhammad bin Tughlaq's "brilliant disasters." A reasonable strategic concept (the empire needed a southern administrative center) was implemented in a way that demonstrated complete inability to anticipate the consequences.
The empire that had pushed to Madurai under Kafur's raids was not actually capable of relocating itself to govern from the Deccan, and the attempt to do so weakened the central state significantly.
The Bahmani revolt of 1347 (more on which shortly) was a direct downstream consequence: the Deccan administrators that Daulatabad had created were the same officials who would later rebel.
The second catastrophe was the token currency of 1330–1333.
The basic problem was again fiscal.
The Sultanate, by 1330, was running a chronic shortage of silver.
Alauddin Khalji's southern raids had produced enormous loot, but the loot was now being spent down on Muhammad's military campaigns and grandiose construction projects.
The mines that had supplied the silver tanka (the standard Sultanate coin Iltutmish had introduced) were not producing enough new silver to replace what was being spent.
Silver was draining out of the economy through purchases of Central Asian horses (the Sultanate had to import its cavalry mounts; India did not produce enough war-quality horses to meet demand).
Muhammad bin Tughlaq's solution was conceptually radical: he introduced a brass and copper token coinage backed by the imperial treasury.
The token coins were declared legal tender at the same face value as the silver tanka.
Each token, in principle, could be redeemed at the imperial mint for the silver equivalent.
The system would, in theory, expand the money supply without requiring new silver and would relieve the fiscal pressure on the treasury.
This was, structurally, exactly the same idea as fiat currency.
It was a brilliantly forward-looking concept.

Six hundred years before the Bretton Woods system formally divorced national currencies from gold backing, Muhammad bin Tughlaq was attempting to create state-backed paper-equivalent money in medieval India.

There are no real Eurasian precedents for this innovation; Tang and Song China had tried paper money (Tang-Song China Ch 7) but the Chinese systems were tied to deposits of metal in central treasuries and circulated only for specific commercial purposes.
Muhammad's tokens were intended as the actual coin of the realm, used for everything from soldiers' salaries to merchant transactions.
The system collapsed within four years.
The reason was forgery.
Brass and copper were available everywhere; private foundries across northern India began minting their own tokens within weeks of the official launch.
Within a few months, the bazaars were flooded with counterfeit tokens that the imperial mint could not distinguish from its own issues.
The face-value-redemption guarantee meant that the imperial treasury was obligated to convert all of these tokens — including the forgeries — into silver tankas on demand.
The treasury hemorrhaged silver.
Within four years, Muhammad had to abandon the experiment, accept all outstanding tokens (forgeries included) at the mint, and absorb the resulting losses.
The treasury was effectively bankrupted.
The credibility of the Sultanate currency was severely damaged for the next generation.
The token currency was, in its conception, ahead of its time by six centuries.
In its execution, it was a catastrophe that demonstrated that medieval administrative capacity could not police what modern central banks could.
The technology of state authentication of currency — the security features that distinguish a real banknote from a forgery — did not exist.
Without them, the experiment was doomed.
The third catastrophe was the Khurasan expedition.

In 1329, Muhammad bin Tughlaq raised an army of 370,000 troops to invade Khurasan — the eastern Iranian region that included Herat, Mashhad, and the Central Asian fringes (Safavid Persia Ch 1 covers the same region).

His stated goal was to overthrow the Chagatai khanate that had been raiding the Sultanate's western frontier, install a friendly regime in central Asia, and assert Sultanate primacy in the eastern Islamic world.
The army was paid for a year in advance, equipped at vast expense, and assembled outside Delhi.
The fiscal cost is recorded by Barani as draining most of what remained of Alauddin Khalji's treasury surplus, supplemented with the new revenues from the (still-functional) token currency.
The army never left Delhi.

The political situation in Central Asia changed in 1330 — the Chagatai khan whose territory Muhammad had intended to invade reached an accommodation with his neighbors, and the strategic opening Muhammad had counted on disappeared.
Muhammad cancelled the expedition and disbanded the army.
The disbanded soldiers, having been paid for a year and now released without further employment, formed roving armed bands across north India.
Some were absorbed into the Sultanate's existing military establishment.
Many drifted into banditry.
The internal security situation across the Doab and the Punjab deteriorated significantly through the 1330s as a direct result.

This is the third "brilliant disaster": a real strategic opportunity (overthrow the Chagatai khanate while it was internally weak) was prepared for in a way that depended on conditions Muhammad could not control, and when those conditions changed, the prepared army became a liability rather than an asset.
The treasury was drained for nothing.
The empire was actively destabilized by the disbandment.
The cumulative effect of the three catastrophes was to wreck the Sultanate's imperial position by the late 1330s.
The treasury was empty.
The central army had been disbanded and replaced by a smaller, less reliable force.

Famine struck the Doab repeatedly during the 1330s — partly the consequence of fiscal mismanagement, partly the consequence of the Little Ice Age beginning to affect Indian agriculture (the global climate shift that would also push the Norse out of Greenland and trigger crop failures across Europe in the next century).
The political consequences were what we would expect.
Provincial governors in the south, the east, and the west began revolting.

Bengal had been functionally independent for decades; under Muhammad bin Tughlaq's reign, Bengal formalized its independence by stages, and would proclaim itself the Bengal Sultanate in 1352, the year after Muhammad's death.
The most consequential revolt was in the Deccan.

In 1347, a discontented Tughlaq officer named Hasan Gangu led a mutiny of the Deccan administrators (many of whom had been displaced from Delhi to Daulatabad and back) and proclaimed himself Alauddin Bahman Shah, founding the Bahmani Sultanate (BAH-mah-nee).

The Bahmani capital at Gulbarga (later Bidar) became the seat of an independent Muslim kingdom in the Deccan that would last two centuries and produce some of the most distinctive Indo-Persian architecture of medieval India.

The Bahmanis were the first major Muslim kingdom to establish itself outside the Sultanate's authority, and their existence permanently broke the precedent that Muslim political power in India flowed from Delhi.

A few years earlier, in 1336, two brothers named Harihara and Bukka — formerly officials of the Hindu Kakatiya kingdom who had been captured by the Tughlaq army, converted to Islam, and sent south to govern the Deccan in the 1320s — re-converted to Hinduism and founded the Vijayanagara empire (vih-jah-yah-NAH-gah-rah, "City of Victory") on the Tungabhadra river in modern Karnataka.
Vijayanagara would become the dominant Hindu power of southern India for the next two centuries — a deliberate Hindu counterweight to the Sultanate north and the Bahmani Sultanate east.
Its founders are perhaps the only documented case in medieval Indian history of converted Muslims successfully re-converting to Hinduism (which mainstream Hinduism, in theory, did not allow).
The fact that they could do so suggests how much fluidity actually existed between religious identities in the Sultanate's southern frontier.
Muhammad bin Tughlaq died in 1351 while campaigning against rebels in Sindh.
His exact cause of death is unrecorded, but he had been ill for some time.
The reign ended with most of the south permanently lost, the Deccan in revolt, the treasury empty, the Doab depopulated, and Delhi itself a shadow of what it had been at his accession.
His successor was his cousin Firuz Shah Tughlaq (ruled 1351–1388), a man with diametrically opposite political instincts.

Where Muhammad bin Tughlaq had been ambitious, intellectually adventurous, militarily aggressive, and administratively reckless, Firuz Shah was cautious, religiously conservative, militarily defensive, and administratively careful.
He was, by personality, exactly what the empire needed after Muhammad: a competent housekeeper who could stabilize what remained.
Firuz Shah explicitly rejected expansion.
He made no attempt to retake Bengal, the Bahmani Sultanate, or any of the southern territories that had broken away.
He did campaign in Bengal twice (in 1353 and 1359), but both campaigns ended with negotiated settlements that confirmed Bengal's independence.
He focused, instead, on internal consolidation: rebuilding the administrative apparatus, restoring the treasury, and undertaking public works.
The public works are the most lasting positive legacy of his reign.

He built the West Yamuna Canal, the largest irrigation project of medieval north India, diverting water from the Yamuna across hundreds of miles of arid Punjab and Haryana to water previously uncultivated land.
The canal was rebuilt by Akbar under the Mughals two centuries later (it was one of the engineering inheritances Akbar consolidated) and parts of it are still in use today.
Firuz Shah also built or rebuilt several smaller canals from the Sutlej and the Jumna, and dug a network of stepwells and reservoirs across the dry regions of his empire.
He founded several new cities.
Firuzabad (FEER-ooz-uh-BAHD), in central Delhi (modern Firuz Shah Kotla), became his capital.
Hisar (in modern Haryana) and Jaunpur (in eastern Uttar Pradesh) were founded as administrative centers.

The Tughlaq architectural style — austere, fortified, built from rough stone with tapering walls — was developed across these new cities and is one of the more distinctive medieval Indian architectural traditions.
He had a particular fascination with antiquities.

He transported two Ashoka pillars — twenty-foot polished sandstone columns dating from the third century BCE, originally erected by the Mauryan emperor Ashoka (Maurya Empire Ch 5) and bearing inscriptions in Brahmi script that Firuz Shah could not read — from sites in the Punjab and Meerut to Delhi at enormous engineering effort, mounting one of them at his Firuzabad palace and another at his hunting lodge.
The pillars were preserved as imperial trophies and curios; nobody at the Sultanate court could decipher the Brahmi script.
The Ashokan inscriptions would not be read for another five hundred years, until James Prinsep of the East India Company decoded the Brahmi alphabet in 1837.
But Firuz Shah's preservation of the pillars meant that the inscriptions survived to be read.
He was also a religious conservative.

His Futuhat-i Firuzshahi, his autobiography, records with pride his suppression of various religious and philosophical movements he considered unorthodox — Ismaili Shia communities, Sufi groups he regarded as antinomian, Hindu temples that had encroached on Muslim public life.

He systematically applied jizya — the Islamic poll-tax on non-Muslim dhimmi (DHIM-mee) subjects, which most prior sultans had applied loosely or only in cities — to the Hindu population of his empire as a regular instrument of imperial revenue.
This is the period when Sultanate administration becomes most visibly distinct from the more religiously syncretic patterns that prevailed under earlier dynasties.

Firuz Shah's reign is therefore something of a hinge point in the religious history of medieval India: he is more orthodox than his predecessors, and the orthodoxy carries downstream consequences for how the late Sultanate is remembered.
He died in 1388 at perhaps eighty-three years old, having held the Sultanate together for thirty-seven years through patient administration and strategic withdrawal.
The empire he left was much smaller than the one Muhammad bin Tughlaq had inherited and much smaller than the one Alauddin Khalji had built, but it was still recognizably an empire.
It had a treasury, a functional army, an administrative bureaucracy, a network of public works.
His successors lost it within a decade.
The post-Firuz Shah period is a textbook succession crisis.
Firuz Shah had outlived his eldest son and had to nominate a grandson, Ghiyas-ud-din Tughlaq Shah II, who was deposed and killed within a year.
The throne passed through a series of cousins and minor relatives — Abu Bakr Shah, Nasir-ud-din Muhammad, Mahmud Shah — none of whom held it for more than a few years.
The Tughlaq nobility split into factions backing different claimants, the central administration broke down, and provincial governors increasingly behaved as independent rulers.

By the early 1390s, the actual political authority of the Tughlaq sultans had contracted to Delhi and a few surrounding districts, while the rest of the empire — Bihar, eastern Punjab, the Doab, Gujarat, Malwa — was being governed by ambitious provincial officers who paid only nominal tribute to Delhi.
This was the situation that Timur (TEE-moor) found when he invaded India in 1398 — and which he would shortly make even worse.

Cross-civ check: while the Tughlaqs were running their empire (1320–1388), the Black Death was killing perhaps a third of Europe and significant percentages of the Islamic Mediterranean (1346–1353), the Hundred Years' War between England and France was getting underway (1337), the Yuan Dynasty in China was collapsing into the Ming restoration (1368), the Mali Empire was at its peak under Mansa Musa (whose famous 1324 hajj passed through Cairo, distributing so much gold that prices in the Egyptian markets crashed for a decade — Mali Empire Ch 4), the Ottomans were establishing themselves in the Balkans (Battle of Kosovo, 1389; Ottoman Empire Ch 2), and the Aztecs were founding Tenochtitlan in central Mexico (around 1325, Aztec Empire Ch 1).
The fourteenth century was extraordinarily eventful across most of Eurasia and beyond.
The Sultanate's decline under the Tughlaqs is one regional manifestation of a much larger pattern of fourteenth-century crisis, climate shift, and political reorganization.

The Black Death itself probably reached parts of north India through the same Central Asian trade routes that brought it to Europe, but the documentation is poor and the demographic impact is debated.
Barani and Ibn Battuta both record famines and epidemics in this period without specifically identifying the bubonic plague.

chapters.title: The Timurid Sack and the Sayyid Hangover
sentences: In December 1398, Timur entered Delhi.

Timur — also called Tamerlane in European sources, a corruption of "Timur the Lame" (he had been wounded as a young man and walked with a permanent limp) — was the Turco-Mongol warlord from Transoxiana (modern Uzbekistan) who had built one of the most violent empires of the medieval world over the previous three decades.

His campaigns through Persia, the Caucasus, the Volga, Central Asia, and Anatolia had produced massacres on a scale not seen since the original Mongol invasions of the thirteenth century: pyramids of skulls outside cities that resisted, populations exterminated, regions depopulated.

Timur had defeated the Ilkhanid successor states (Mongol Empire Ch 7), invaded the Golden Horde, sacked Damascus and Baghdad, defeated the Mamluk Sultanate, and was about to defeat the Ottomans at Ankara in 1402 (Ottoman Empire Ch 3, where the Ottoman state nearly collapsed after this catastrophe).

He invaded India in late 1398 with a stated goal of converting the Hindu population by force and removing the lukewarm Tughlaq sultans who, in his theological reading, had been insufficiently rigorous in suppressing non-Islamic practice. (His chronicler, Sharaf al-Din Ali Yazdi, whose Zafarnama is the principal Persian source for the campaign, makes the religious-justification narrative explicit; modern historians read Timur's stated piety with appropriate skepticism, since his actual targets were almost as often Muslim cities he disagreed with as Hindu kingdoms he was nominally fighting.) His army crossed the Indus in late September.
The frontier garrisons were weak, the Punjab governors mostly fled or capitulated.
By October, Timur was outside Multan, which surrendered.
By late November, he was approaching Delhi.
The Tughlaq sultan, Mahmud Shah, fielded an army of perhaps 40,000 outside Delhi at the village of Loni on December 17.
Timur's veteran cavalry shattered them in a few hours.
Mahmud Shah fled south to Gujarat; his vizier Mallu Iqbal Khan died on the field.
Timur entered Delhi unopposed on December 18.
The next three days are among the worst-documented atrocities in Indian history.

The basic outline is clear from multiple Persian sources, including Yazdi's Zafarnama and Timur's own account in his Tuzuk-i Timuri (which is partly autobiography, partly later compilation, but reflects what the Timurid court wanted recorded).
Timur had originally promised the Delhi residents safety in exchange for tribute.
His soldiers, once inside the city, broke discipline almost immediately.
Looting began on December 19 and accelerated over the next two days.
Mass killings began on December 20.
By December 22, when Timur formally restored order, perhaps 100,000 Delhi residents — Hindu and Muslim, civilian and military — had been massacred.
The Persian sources discuss the killings as an unfortunate breakdown of military discipline; the Hindi-language sources that survive treat them as deliberate atrocity.

Before retreating north on December 26, Timur had also reportedly ordered the mass execution of perhaps 100,000 prisoners — Hindu fighters his army had captured during the campaign south, who had been concentrated in a holding camp outside Delhi.
The order was given on the grounds that the prisoners could not be safely taken back across the Indus and could not be released.
The execution was carried out over a single day.
The detail comes from Yazdi and from Timur's own memoir; modern historians generally accept it as approximately accurate, though the specific number is uncertain.
The total death toll of Timur's occupation of Delhi is impossible to determine precisely, but it was certainly in the hundreds of thousands.
The Persian chronicles — sympathetic to Timur — suggest 200,000-plus dead.

The conservative modern estimate (Yazdi and the contemporaries cannot be entirely trusted, but neither can they be entirely dismissed) is on the order of 100,000-200,000 killed across the city and the prisoner camp.

Timur left Delhi in late December 1398, marching back to Samarkand with vast caravans of looted treasure, captured artisans (the Samarkand mosque at the Timurid capital was built largely by craftsmen taken from Delhi), and the Sultanate's accumulated imperial regalia.
He died at Otrar in Central Asia in 1405, on a campaign to invade China that never reached China.
His empire fragmented among his descendants — the Timurids — who would hold central Asia and eastern Iran for the next century.

Babur, the Timurid prince who would conquer Delhi in 1526, was Timur's great-great-great-grandson and traced his Indian conquest as a kind of ancestral revisitation of his great-great-great-grandfather's expedition.
Delhi after Timur was a city of ruins.
The Persian chronicles describe a population reduced by killing, enslavement, and flight.
Most of the city's craftsmen had been deported to Samarkand.
Most of the city's bureaucratic class had been killed or fled.
The treasury was gone.
The physical infrastructure of Firuzabad and Tughlaqabad was substantially damaged.
The food economy had collapsed.
Famine and plague struck the survivors over the following years.

According to Yahya Sirhindi's chronicle (written in the early fifteenth century), the city was substantially depopulated for at least two years and did not return to its pre-Timur population until well into the fifteenth century.
The Tughlaq dynasty technically continued for another sixteen years, but it was a fiction.
Mahmud Shah returned from Gujarat to a Delhi that no longer recognized his sovereignty in any practical way.
The provincial governors — Gujarat, Malwa, Jaunpur, Bengal, the Punjab — declared full independence over the next decade.
The Bahmani Sultanate consolidated its hold on the Deccan.
Vijayanagara extended its reach across most of the south.

By 1414, when Khizr Khan (a Punjab governor who had originally been appointed by Timur as the Timurid representative for north India) captured Delhi from the last Tughlaq sultan, the territory the new "Sultanate" actually controlled consisted of Delhi and a few adjacent districts.
Khizr Khan founded the Sayyid dynasty as nominal vassals of the Timurids.
The Sayyids never controlled more than the territory immediately around Delhi.
The dynasty ruled a city, not an empire.
The Sayyid dynasty (1414–1451) is the lowest point in the Sultanate's three-and-a-half centuries.
Four Sayyid sultans — Khizr Khan, Mubarak Shah, Muhammad Shah, Alam Shah — ruled in succession, each more nominally than the last.
Real power across north India belonged to the breakaway provincial sultanates and the Hindu kingdoms beyond them.
The Sayyid sultans, lacking the resources to project military power, lacked the resources to do much of anything.
They maintained an attenuated court at Delhi, paid tribute to the Timurids, and watched their notional empire shrink to a circle on the map perhaps fifty miles across.
While the Sayyid sultans were ruling Delhi as a city-state, the rest of the subcontinent was being ruled by other people.
The Bengal Sultanate under the Ilyas Shahi dynasty had been functionally independent since the 1340s and formally so since 1352.
By the early fifteenth century, Bengal was one of the wealthiest Islamic states in the world, controlling the lower Ganges delta and the Indian Ocean trade routes through the port of Chittagong.

The Bengal Sultanate became the major patron of Bengali-language literature (the great Bengali poet Krittibas Ojha translated the Ramayana into Bengali under Bengal Sultanate patronage in the fifteenth century), built the distinctive curved-roof mosque architecture of medieval Bengal (the Adina Mosque at Pandua, the largest mosque in pre-modern South Asia), and managed a relatively syncretic religious culture in which Hindu and Muslim populations coexisted under a Muslim aristocracy.
The Jaunpur Sultanate under the Sharqi (SHAR-kee, "eastern") dynasty had broken away in 1394, when Malik Sarwar (formerly a Tughlaq governor) declared independence in the eastern Ganges plain.
Jaunpur (jown-POOR), on the Gomti river in modern eastern Uttar Pradesh, became one of the most culturally productive of the breakaway sultanates.

The Sharqis built the distinctive Atala Mosque at Jaunpur, whose pylon-style central facade has no precedent in earlier Indian or Persian Islamic architecture, and patronized Hindavi-language poetry (the Padmavat of Malik Muhammad Jayasi, a Sufi-influenced romantic epic about the legendary Padmini of Chittor, was composed in this milieu).

The Malwa Sultanate, founded in 1392 by Dilawar Khan Ghuri (originally a Tughlaq officer of central India), built its capital at Mandu (MAHN-doo), one of the most spectacular fortified cities of medieval India, perched on a defensible plateau in the Vindhya hills.

Mandu's Jahaz Mahal ("Ship Palace"), Hindola Mahal ("Swing Palace"), and the Hoshang Shah's Tomb (a marble-and-sandstone mausoleum that would directly inspire the Taj Mahal a century later) make Mandu one of the great architectural ensembles of the Sultanate-era subcontinent.
The Gujarat Sultanate, founded in 1407 by Zafar Khan Muzaffar, controlled the Indian Ocean trade routes through the port of Cambay (later Surat).
Gujarat was the wealthiest of the breakaway sultanates, with revenues from the spice and indigo trade that exceeded those of any other late-Sultanate-era Indian state.
Gujarat would survive as an independent Muslim kingdom until the Mughals annexed it in 1573.
The Champaner-Pavagadh complex (UNESCO World Heritage, modern Gujarat) is one of the most complete late-medieval Islamic urban ensembles surviving in India.
The Bahmani Sultanate, founded in 1347, dominated the Deccan from its capitals Gulbarga (until 1432) and Bidar (after 1432).

The Bahmani court was multicultural — Persian-speaking Sayyids and Iranian Shia immigrants competed for influence with the Sunni Turkic and indigenous Indian Muslim Deccani factions, and the resulting Sunni-Shia and immigrant-vs-local tensions would eventually fragment the empire.

But at its peak under Mahmud Gawan (the great Persian-Iranian vizier who ran the empire from 1466 to 1481), Bahmani built the Madrasa of Mahmud Gawan at Bidar — among the largest medieval madrasas in the Islamic world, with a three-story facade of intricate Persian-style tile-work — and fielded armies that fought Vijayanagara to a standstill across the Tungabhadra frontier.
In the south, Vijayanagara, founded in 1336 by Harihara and Bukka, had grown into the dominant Hindu power of the subcontinent.

By the early fifteenth century, Vijayanagara controlled most of southern India, from the Krishna river to Kanyakumari, and ruled a population perhaps three or four times the size of the Sayyid Sultanate's Delhi territory.

The Vijayanagara capital — modern Hampi in Karnataka, now a vast UNESCO archaeological zone covering 16 square miles — was one of the largest cities in the world in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, with detailed eyewitness descriptions from European visitors (the Portuguese Domingo Paes and the Italian Niccolò de' Conti) that estimate populations of 500,000 or more.

The empire would peak under Krishnadevaraya (ruled 1509–1529), the contemporary of Babur, before being catastrophically destroyed at the Battle of Talikota in 1565 by a coalition of the Deccan Sultanates.
The Rajput kingdoms of Mewar, Marwar, and Amber (Chapter 7) had reasserted themselves after Alauddin Khalji's reduction.

The Sisodia rulers of Mewar at Chittor held off Sultanate and later Mughal pressure for another two centuries; the legendary Rana Sanga of Mewar would lead the Hindu coalition that opposed Babur after Panipat at the Battle of Khanwa in 1527 (a defeat that consolidated Babur's victory).
The geography is the point.
By 1450, the political map of the Indian subcontinent was a patchwork of dynastic regional states, of which the Sayyid Sultanate at Delhi was one of the smaller and weaker.
The very framework of "the Delhi Sultanate" as a pan-north-Indian imperial state had ceased to exist.
What remained at Delhi was an administrative tradition, a Persianate court culture, and a memory of imperial greatness — but not the substance of imperial power.
In 1451, the last Sayyid sultan Alam Shah abdicated.

He had effectively ceded actual authority over the Delhi region to Bahlul Lodi (BAH-lool LOH-dee), an Afghan chieftain from the Pashtun Lodi tribe who had been serving as the governor of Sirhind (SIR-hind, in the Punjab) and had built up a private army of Pashtun cavalry.
Alam Shah retired to Badaun to live as a private gentleman; Bahlul Lodi entered Delhi in April 1451 and proclaimed himself Sultan.
The Lodi dynasty (1451–1526) was the first non-Turkic dynasty of the Sultanate.

The Lodis were ethnic Afghans (Pashtuns), speaking Pashto in their family circles and Persian at court, with a tribal structure quite different from the Turkic mamluk system that had defined the Mamluk, Khalji, and Tughlaq dynasties.
They will be the subject of Chapter 7.

But before we get to the Lodis, Chapter 6 covers the most consequential cultural development of the late Sultanate: the religious and cultural synthesis that produced Bhakti devotional poetry, Sufi mysticism, and the founding of Sikhism.

That synthesis happened in parallel with everything Chapters 1-5 have covered, and it is what most ordinary inhabitants of Sultanate India actually experienced day-to-day, far more than the dynastic chronologies of the kings.

Cross-civ check: while the Sayyid dynasty was holding together a hollowed-out Sultanate (1414–1451), the Ottomans were recovering from Timur's defeat at Ankara and rebuilding under Mehmed I and Murad II (Ottoman Empire Ch 3 and Ch 4); Mehmed II the Conqueror would take Constantinople in 1453, ending the Byzantine Empire (Byzantine Empire Ch 12), shortly after the Sayyid period ended.
The Mali Empire in West Africa was at the end of its peak, soon to be displaced by the Songhai Empire.
The Joseon Dynasty ruled Korea under King Sejong (the inventor of Hangul, 1443).
The Ming Dynasty in China was at the height of its naval-expansion phase under the Yongle Emperor and the great voyages of Admiral Zheng He (which reached as far as East Africa in 1417).
The Inca Empire in the Andes was just consolidating under Pachacuti.
The Sayyid Sultanate, in this fifteenth-century world, was a small kingdom remembered for being the residue of something that had once been great.

chapters.title: The Bhakti and Sufi Revolution
sentences: The political chronicle of the Sultanate is a story of dynasties, sieges, and revolts.
The cultural chronicle is something quite different.

While the Mamluks were fighting Mongols, the Khaljis were running price controls, and the Tughlaqs were moving their capital to Daulatabad and back, something more interesting was happening across north India at the level of village shrines, urban dargahs, and itinerant poets.

A series of religious and literary movements — Bhakti devotionalism among the Hindu population, Sufi mysticism within the Muslim population, and the founding of Sikhism as a deliberately syncretic third tradition — was reshaping the religious and cultural texture of the subcontinent in ways that would outlast the Sultanate by centuries.
This chapter covers those movements.
They are not the official chronicle.
They were not what the court chroniclers wrote about.
But they are the most consequential thing the Sultanate-era Indian population produced, and they shape modern Indian religious life in ways the Sultanate's military campaigns never did.
To understand what happened, we have to start with Sufism in India.
Sufism (SOO-fizm) is the mystical and devotional tradition within Islam (Safavid Persia Ch 1 covers the same tradition in its Iranian context).

Sufi orders, called tariqas (tah-REE-kahs, literally "paths"), formed around lineages of spiritual masters and emphasized inner spiritual experience, the cultivation of the soul, and the master-disciple relationship as the route to direct knowledge of God.
Each tariqa had its own characteristic practices: meditative chanting, breathing techniques, sometimes ecstatic music or dance.
Sufism arrived in India with the Ghurid armies and spread rapidly through the early Sultanate.
The four major orders that took root were the Chishti (CHISH-tee), the Suhrawardi (soo-rah-WAR-dee), the Naqshbandi (NUKSH-bun-dee), and the Qadiri (KAH-dee-ree).
Each had a different geographic center and a slightly different theological flavor.

The Chishti — austere, charitable, deliberately distanced from royal courts, focused on individual devotion and music as a path to the divine — became the most influential, particularly in north India.

The founder of the Chishti order in India was Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti (MOY-ee-nud-DEEN), originally from Sistan in eastern Iran, who settled at Ajmer (AJ-meer) in Rajasthan around 1192 — within months of Muhammad of Ghor's victory at Tarain.

Moinuddin spent the next four decades teaching Sufi devotion at Ajmer, accepting disciples from every social class (including, unusually for the period, both Hindu and Muslim followers), and emphasizing direct service to the poor as the practical content of religious life.
He died at Ajmer in 1236, the same year Iltutmish died at Delhi.
His tomb, the Dargah Sharif of Ajmer, became and remains the most visited Sufi shrine on the subcontinent.
Modern pilgrimage statistics put it at roughly four million visitors a year, drawn from every faith tradition.
Pakistani Muslim pilgrims who cannot get visas to attend in person send written prayers through the mail.
The dargah's annual Urs festival, marking the anniversary of Moinuddin's death, has been celebrated continuously for nearly eight hundred years.
The Chishti tradition Moinuddin founded is what makes Indian Sufism distinct from its Arab and Persian counterparts.

The Chishtis were unusually open to Hindu participation: their sama (devotional music) sessions could include musical forms with Hindu roots, their teaching language was Persian and Hindavi rather than Arabic, their dargahs welcomed pilgrims of any religion, and their practical emphasis on charity and service rather than theological orthodoxy made them accessible to the predominantly Hindu population around them.

By the fourteenth century, Chishti dargahs across north India were major institutions of religious, cultural, and economic life, attracting pilgrim donations sufficient to fund extensive charitable infrastructure (free kitchens, lodging for travelers, support for the poor).
The most influential of the Chishti masters was Sheikh Nizamuddin Auliya (nih-ZAHM-ud-DEEN ow-LEE-ah, 1238–1325).
Nizamuddin spent his entire long career in Delhi.

His khanqah (KHAN-kah, Sufi monastery and teaching center) at the village of Ghiyaspur outside Delhi attracted disciples from every social class — Hindu artisans, Muslim merchants, members of the Sultanate's military aristocracy, immigrant Persian scholars, and ordinary villagers.

His disciples included some of the most important figures of fourteenth-century India: the poet Amir Khusrau (more on him shortly), the historian Ziauddin Barani, the chronicler Sayyid Muhammad Mubarak, and a long line of Chishti successors who carried his teachings to other Indian regions.
His teachings emphasized universal love, the equality of all human beings before God, and the uselessness of theological dispute compared to direct devotion.
He systematically refused to attend the Sultanate court, even when summoned by the most powerful sultans.

He famously remarked, when warned that Sultan Ghiyas-ud-din Tughlaq was approaching Delhi from Bengal and might compel him to court appearance, "Hanuz Dilli dur ast" — "Delhi is still far off" — a Persian phrase that became a permanent piece of Indian proverbial wisdom (the sultan died in the wooden pavilion accident before reaching Delhi, validating Nizamuddin's calm).
The phrase is now used in Hindi and Urdu to mean any distant, possibly never-arriving fate.

His dargah in modern Delhi — Nizamuddin Dargah, in the Nizamuddin neighborhood of central Delhi, one stop on the metro from the Khan Market if you visit — is still a working pilgrimage site, with a continuous tradition of qawwali performance every Thursday evening for the past seven hundred years.
The dargah's Sufi qawwali is the same musical tradition Amir Khusrau is credited with developing in the late thirteenth century.

Modern qawwali singers — from Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan (the Pakistani master who brought qawwali to global audiences in the 1980s) back through the Sabri Brothers, the Warsi Brothers, and the unbroken traditional lineages of Delhi-Lahore-Multan — perform in a tradition continuously practiced at this dargah and a handful of others since Nizamuddin Auliya himself was alive.
Amir Khusrau (uh-MEER khus-ROW, 1253–1325) is the most prolific writer of the Sultanate period and one of the most influential cultural figures in Indian history.

Khusrau was born in Patiali in modern Uttar Pradesh, the son of a Turkic Lachin officer in the Sultanate army and a Rajput Hindu mother (a fact he proudly mentioned in his autobiographical writings, presenting himself as the perfect synthesis of the Sultanate's two heritages).
He was educated in Persian, Arabic, and Hindavi, and entered court service as a young man under Balban.

Over the next fifty years, he served as court poet to seven successive sultans — Balban, Kayqubad, Jalaluddin Khalji, Alauddin Khalji, Mubarak Shah Khalji, Khusrau Khan, and Ghiyas-ud-din Tughlaq — making him the longest-serving court figure of the Sultanate period and the only person to have personally witnessed the entire arc from Balban's iron rule through the Tughlaq founding.
He died in 1325, six months after his Sufi master Nizamuddin Auliya, and is buried at the Nizamuddin Dargah in a small tomb adjacent to his master.
Khusrau's literary output is extraordinary.
He wrote poetry in Persian (his primary literary language), Arabic, Turkish, and Hindavi (the early form of Hindi-Urdu emerging in the Sultanate's bazaars).
His Persian dīwāns total something like half a million verses.
His Khamsa ("Quintet," five long narrative poems modeled on the Persian Nizami Ganjavi's earlier Khamsa) is one of the great works of Indo-Persian literature.
His Tughluq Nama chronicles the rise of the Tughlaq dynasty in verse.

His Nuh Sipihr ("Nine Heavens") is a paean to India and Indian civilization that explicitly argues the superiority of Indian intellectual achievements (mathematics, astronomy, music, language, climate, fauna) to those of the rest of the Islamic world — written by a Muslim Persian-language poet who had never traveled outside India and considered himself fundamentally an Indian writer.
In Hindavi, Khusrau is credited with composing some of the earliest surviving examples of what would become Hindi-Urdu poetry.
His short verses — quatrains, riddles, work songs, devotional fragments — entered the popular oral tradition and survived in folk memory across north India.
Whether Khusrau actually composed all of the verses attributed to him or whether some were added later in his name (the medieval Hindavi tradition was loose about authorship) is debated.

What is uncontested is that the basic literary register of the early Hindavi tradition — playful, devotional, vernacular, mixing Persian and Sanskrit-derived vocabulary in approximately equal measure — was established in Khusrau's circle.

In music, Khusrau is traditionally credited with developing several raga (RAH-gah, the Indian melodic mode) traditions and inventing several musical forms including the qawwali (Sufi devotional song with a leader-and-chorus structure, percussion accompaniment, and rising emotional intensity that has been the standard format of Indian and Pakistani Sufi music for seven centuries).
The traditional attribution also credits him with inventing the sitar (SIT-ar, the long-necked plucked stringed instrument) and the tabla (TAH-blah, the paired hand drums).

The musicological evidence for these specific instrument-invention attributions is weak — both instruments probably emerged in their modern forms several centuries after Khusrau's death — but the broader claim that Khusrau and his Chishti circle were central to the development of north Indian classical music is well-supported.
Modern Hindustani classical music (the north Indian classical tradition) traces much of its lineage through Khusrau and the Chishti khanqahs of Sultanate-era Delhi.

The combination of Khusrau's Persian literary output, his Hindavi vernacular contributions, and his musical innovations made him the central cultural figure of his period and the reason the Sultanate produced a distinct Indo-Persian cultural synthesis rather than a simple imposition of Persian forms on an Indian setting.
The synthesis was Khusrau's lifework.
Modern Indian and Pakistani writers, musicians, and intellectuals across the Hindu-Muslim divide alike claim him as a foundational figure.
The Bhakti (BHUK-tee) movement was the parallel development on the Hindu side.

Bhakti — the term means "devotion" in Sanskrit — had begun in the Tamil south centuries before the Sultanate (Medieval India Ch 6 covers the original Tamil Alvar and Nayanar traditions of the seventh through tenth centuries).

The Tamil Bhakti tradition emphasized direct personal devotion to a chosen deity (Vishnu, Shiva, or Devi), expressed through vernacular poetry composed in Tamil rather than Sanskrit, accessible to all castes including the very lowest and to women — a deliberate egalitarianism that contrasted sharply with the Brahmin-mediated, Sanskrit-based, ritual-centric mainstream Vedic-Puranic tradition.

What happened in the Sultanate period was the spread of this Tamil-originated Bhakti tradition across northern India, in different vernacular languages — Hindavi-Hindi, Marathi, Bengali, Punjabi — and with new theological and social emphases that responded to the Sultanate's particular religious environment.
The northern Bhakti tradition produced some of the most influential poetry in any Indian language and reshaped Hindu religious practice in ways still visible today.

The major figures of the northern Bhakti movement include Kabir (kah-BEER, ~1440-1518), Ravidas (rah-vee-DAHS, ~1450-1520), Surdas (sur-DAHS, ~1478-1583), Mirabai (MEE-rah-bye, ~1498-1547), Tulsidas (tul-see-DAHS, ~1532-1623), and Guru Nanak (NAH-nahk, 1469-1539, the founder of Sikhism).
They are not a unified school.
They wrote in different languages, lived in different regions, addressed different deities, and developed different theological positions.
But they share recognizable features that distinguish the northern Bhakti tradition from earlier Indian devotionalism.
Kabir is the most striking of them.
Kabir was a weaver — a member of the Julaha caste, low-status weavers of Banaras (modern Varanasi, the great Hindu pilgrimage city on the Ganges, Medieval India Ch 6).
His parentage is uncertain: most accounts say he was raised by Muslim weavers but was probably born to a Hindu Brahmin widow who left him as an infant.
He lived his entire life as a working weaver, never adopted formal religious vows, and produced poetry in plain Hindavi that mocked both Hindu and Muslim religious orthodoxy.
His verses are some of the most ferocious anti-clerical poetry in any tradition.

He attacked the Hindu Brahmin priesthood for their caste-based exclusionary rituals, the Hindu temple establishment for confusing image-worship with God-worship, the Muslim ulama for insisting on the superiority of Arabic religious language, the Sufi orders for their veneration of saint-tombs as spiritually identical to idolatry.

His positive theology was simple: there is one formless God, accessible directly through inward devotion to the divine name (he called it Ram, but explicitly meant the term as a generic name for God rather than as a specific reference to the Hindu deity), beyond all the institutional religions and their boundary-drawing.
The verses themselves are short, blunt, and oral.
Kabir spoke (or sang) them to whoever would listen; they were passed on by his disciples and assembled into manuscript collections only generations after his death.

The major collections are the Bijak (the Kabir Panth canonical text), the Sant Kabir Granth, and the verses included in the Sikh Adi Granth (Guru Nanak and his successors compiled the first authoritative collection of Kabir's verse alongside their own).

The verses were also borrowed extensively into the Hindi-language Bhakti tradition; Kabir's two-line dohas (DOH-hahs, a couplet form) became part of the Hindi devotional vernacular and are still recited in modern north India.

His most famous verses include lines that are now Hindi-Urdu folk wisdom: "If kahte ho ki Ram hamare, kis ne dekha tum sang dekho?" — "If you say that Ram is yours, who has seen him keeping company with you?" "Pothi padh padh jag mua, pandit bhayo na koy / Dhai akhar prem ka, padhe so pandit hoy" — "The whole world has died reading book after book; nobody has become a true scholar / But two-and-a-half letters of love, whoever reads those becomes a scholar." The two-and-a-half letters are the Devanagari letters that spell prem (love).
The pun works in Hindi but not in translation.
Kabir's verses are full of these multi-layered jokes that work in Hindavi and refuse to work in any language Kabir was not actually writing in.
The fact that they have remained in continuous oral tradition for five centuries is part of what makes him so influential.
Kabir's death is also important to mention.
The standard Hindu and Muslim accounts both claim him after his death.

The legendary story goes: when Kabir died at Maghar (a small village in Uttar Pradesh) in 1518, his Hindu disciples wanted to cremate him according to Hindu rites, and his Muslim disciples wanted to bury him according to Islamic rites.
They fought outside the room where his body lay.
When they finally entered the room, his body was gone — only flowers remained.
They divided the flowers and each community performed its rites accordingly.
The Maghar village contains both a Hindu cremation memorial and a Muslim grave for Kabir, side by side, both still active pilgrimage sites today.
The story is almost certainly invented.
But it captures something the historical Kabir would have appreciated about the foolishness of religious boundary-drawing.

Ravidas, contemporary of Kabir and another Banaras weaver (specifically a member of the Chamar caste, leather-workers, ranking even lower than the Julaha Kabir came from — Chamars would later be classified as Dalit under modern caste-classification systems), wrote Bhakti devotional poetry in plain Hindavi that addressed God directly and explicitly rejected the legitimacy of caste hierarchy.
His verses are sung as devotional hymns and are included in the Sikh Adi Granth.

Mirabai, the Rajput princess of the Mewar royal family, abandoned her marital obligations as a Sisodia queen to write Krishna-devotional poetry that would become some of the most beloved Hindi devotional verse ever written.

Her songs, addressed to Krishna as her divine lover, reframed Bhakti devotion through unmistakably female-voiced longing — explicit in their bodily and emotional vocabulary, refusing to soften the romantic-erotic language that Krishna devotion in the Bhagavata Purana tradition had always made central.
Mirabai's songs are still sung as devotional standards across north India and have been recorded thousands of times by classical and popular musicians.
Surdas and Tulsidas, slightly later contemporaries, took the Bhakti tradition in a more textually disciplined direction.

Surdas (a blind poet associated with the Krishna-devotional Pushtimarg sect of Vallabha) composed thousands of Hindi devotional songs about the childhood of Krishna at Vrindavan that became core liturgical material for the Krishna-worshipping branches of Vaishnavism.
Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas ("Lake of the Deeds of Ram"), completed in 1574 in the Awadhi dialect of Hindi, retold the Ramayana epic in vernacular Hindi for an audience that did not read Sanskrit.

The Ramcharitmanas became the most widely recited religious text in modern Hindi and is the basis of every popular contemporary retelling of the Ramayana, including the famous 1980s television serial that briefly held a global record for largest Indian-language television audience.
The northern Bhakti tradition was, collectively, the largest single transformation of Hindu religious practice between the medieval period and the modern period.
It moved devotional life from Sanskrit-mediated Brahmin-controlled temple ritual to vernacular-language individual devotional practice accessible to all castes and both genders.
It gave the Hindu tradition a popular literature in every major north Indian language.

And it provided much of the cultural material that would later be deployed by Hindu reform movements (the Brahmo Samaj, the Arya Samaj, the various Vaishnava reform movements) and by the Hindu side of Indian nationalism.
In the late Sultanate, in the Punjab, the Bhakti and Sufi traditions met in the person of Guru Nanak (NAH-nahk, 1469–1539) and produced something genuinely new: the religion that became Sikhism.
Nanak was born in a small Punjabi village called Talwandi (now Nankana Sahib in Pakistan) in 1469, into a Hindu Khatri (mercantile-caste) family.

He was, by all the accounts assembled in the Janamsakhis (the early Sikh hagiographies), an unusual child from the start: spiritually precocious, indifferent to his father's mercantile ambitions, drawn instead to long meditative walks, conversations with both Hindu sadhus and Muslim Sufi pirs, and a kind of inward contemplation that none of the local religious institutions seemed to satisfy.

The pivotal moment of his biography came around age thirty, when (according to the standard Sikh tradition) he disappeared into the river at Sultanpur for three days, was presumed drowned, and re-emerged with a single declaration: "Na koi Hindu, na Musalman" — "There is no Hindu, no Muslim." The phrase was a rejection of religious boundary-drawing.

What he proposed instead was a single direct devotional path to the one formless God (whom he called Ek Onkar, "the One"), accessible through honest work, charitable sharing, and meditative remembrance of the divine name.

Over the next thirty years, Nanak traveled extensively across the subcontinent and beyond — to Mecca, Baghdad, Tibet, Sri Lanka, Bengal, the Deccan — accompanied by his Muslim companion Mardana (a rebab-player who provided musical accompaniment for Nanak's devotional songs).

The travels accumulated stories, encounters with religious figures of every tradition, and a body of verse that Nanak composed in a Punjabi that combined Sufi-inflected vocabulary with Bhakti devotional themes and his own distinct theological vision.

When he returned to settle at the village of Kartarpur (modern Pakistan) in his sixties, Nanak founded the first Sikh sangat (congregation) on three principles that would define the religion: kirat karo (honest work), vand chhako (sharing with the community, manifested in the practice of the langar or free communal kitchen open to all regardless of caste or religion), and naam japo (meditative remembrance of the divine name).

Before his death in 1539, he formally appointed his disciple Bhai Lehna (renamed Guru Angad) as his successor — the first of nine successor Gurus that would lead the Sikh community through the Mughal period.
The Sikh tradition Nanak founded is genuinely new, drawing on but distinct from both its parents.
It rejects caste hierarchy, image-worship, and clerical mediation (all Bhakti positions); it rejects ritual law, prophetic exclusivism, and saint-shrine veneration (all Sufi positions).
It accepts (in modified form) the Sufi emphasis on the divine name as the central spiritual practice.
It accepts the Bhakti emphasis on vernacular devotion and the equality of devotees.
And it adds a distinctive social-ethical dimension — the langar, the egalitarian community structure, the explicit rejection of caste — that became the Sikh contribution to Indian religious history.

The Sikh community Nanak founded would grow steadily through the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, develop a militarized identity under the tenth and final guru Gobind Singh (who founded the Khalsa in 1699), become a major political force in the eighteenth-century Punjab under various Sikh misls (confederations), establish the Sikh Empire of Maharaja Ranjit Singh in the early nineteenth century, and emerge as one of the principal religious communities of modern South Asia.

Modern Sikhism counts perhaps 30 million adherents worldwide — a small religion by global standards, but the fifth-largest organized religion in the world and one of the very few major religious traditions to have been founded in the late medieval period in a setting where its origins are well documented.
That well-documented origin is the cultural moment of the late Sultanate.
Nanak was born in 1469, ten years into the Lodi dynasty (Chapter 7), and died in 1539, thirteen years after Babur's victory at Panipat.
He lived the Sultanate's last decades and the Mughal Empire's first.
The religion he founded is a direct synthetic product of the Indo-Islamic cultural environment the Sultanate had built.
The Sultanate also produced, alongside Sufism and Bhakti, a third literary-cultural development: the emergence of Hindavi as a written literary language in its own right.

Hindavi (HIN-duh-vee — the term comes from "Hindi" plus the Persian -vi suffix, meaning "of the Hindi people") was the contact language that developed in the bazaars and barracks of Sultanate-era Delhi.
Persian-speaking soldiers, administrators, and merchants from Central Asia interacted daily with Hindi-speaking Indian subjects and had to develop a working language somewhere in between.

The language that emerged drew on local Indian (Khariboli, the dialect spoken around Delhi) for its grammatical structure and its core vocabulary, on Persian and Arabic for administrative-political-military-religious vocabulary, and on Sanskrit for philosophical-religious-literary vocabulary.
The result was a flexible, accessible street-and-court language in which Persian-Arabic and Sanskrit-Hindi vocabulary could be mixed at will depending on the speaker's audience and purpose.
By the late Sultanate, Hindavi was being written down for literary purposes.
Amir Khusrau's Hindavi verses are the earliest substantial surviving examples.

Kabir's dohas were composed in Hindavi (or in dialectical variants — Kabir's language has been variously classified as old Awadhi, Bhojpuri, Khariboli, or Sadhukkari, the so-called "saint-language" of the Bhakti tradition).

Surdas wrote in Braj Bhasha (the dialect of the Mathura-Vrindavan region, close to but distinct from Khariboli Hindi), Tulsidas wrote in Awadhi (the dialect of Awadh, the central Uttar Pradesh region).
All of these are recognizably forms of medieval Hindi.

By the end of the Sultanate, Hindavi had clearly differentiated into the family of related Hindi dialects that would later be standardized as modern Hindi, and was simultaneously absorbing enough Persian and Arabic vocabulary that, by the Mughal period, it would be called Rekhta ("mixed") and then eventually Urdu (a name from the Turkish word for "army camp," reflecting the bazaar-and-barracks origins).

The split between modern Hindi (with more Sanskrit-derived vocabulary) and modern Urdu (with more Persian-Arabic-derived vocabulary) is essentially a nineteenth-century development that came out of colonial and nationalist politics; in the Sultanate period and through most of the Mughal period, Hindavi-Rekhta was a single fluid language with regional and stylistic variations.
The cultural significance of this is hard to overstate.

The Sultanate's cosmopolitan Persian-speaking court culture (Khusrau's Persian poetry, Barani's Persian chronicles) coexisted with the rapid emergence of vernacular Hindavi literature (Kabir's dohas, Surdas's bhajans, Mirabai's pads, eventually Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas) at the popular level.
The two registers fed into each other.
The Sufi qawwali tradition combined Persian and Hindavi verse in the same musical performances.
The Bhakti devotional tradition borrowed Sufi vocabulary at the level of its key concepts (the sant, the saint-poet figure, is in part a Hindavi-language analogue of the Sufi pir).
The Indo-Islamic architectural tradition borrowed Hindu craftsmanship at the level of its decorative vocabulary while retaining Persian structural forms.

What was produced, across the Sultanate's three centuries, was a genuinely composite Indo-Islamic culture that was not Persian, not Arab, not classical Sanskrit-Indian, and not simply a sum of any pair of those.
It was something new.
The Mughal Empire that succeeded the Sultanate at Panipat would inherit this composite culture and develop it further.
Modern Indian and Pakistani culture, in their religious, linguistic, musical, architectural, and culinary dimensions, are still substantially shaped by what the Sultanate created.
The official chronicle is the dynasties.
The actual chronicle, for most people in late Sultanate India, was the dargah, the bhajan, the qawwali, and the new vernacular literary tradition that was making itself visible in the bazaars.
That second chronicle is what made the Sultanate culturally consequential.
Cross-civ check: while the Bhakti and Sufi syntheses were unfolding in India, broadly comparable popular religious movements were happening across Eurasia.

The Devotio Moderna in northern Europe (the Brethren of the Common Life, the Imitation of Christ of Thomas a Kempis, late fourteenth and fifteenth centuries) emphasized inward personal devotion over institutional religion in ways structurally similar to Kabir and Bhakti.
The Hesychast movement in Byzantine Eastern Orthodoxy emphasized contemplative inner prayer (the Jesus Prayer) in ways structurally similar to Sufi dhikr (Byzantine Empire Ch 11).
The Lutheran Reformation (1517) exploded into Europe two years before Kabir's death, with theological and sociological dimensions that paralleled the Bhakti rejection of clerical mediation.

The fifteenth century was, across Eurasia, a period when the institutional religious establishments of every tradition were being challenged by popular devotional movements that emphasized direct personal access to the divine.
The Indian variants are part of this larger pattern, though they emerged independently rather than under any cross-pollination.

chapters.title: The Lodi Afghans and the Provincial Sultanates
sentences: The Lodi dynasty (1451–1526) was the last dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate.
Three Lodi sultans — Bahlul (BAH-lool), Sikandar (sih-KAN-dar), and Ibrahim (ih-brah-HEEM) — ruled over a partial recovery of Sultanate authority before the final collapse at Panipat.

They were also the first non-Turkic dynasty of the Sultanate: Afghans, Pashto-speakers from the Suleiman mountains of the Pakistan-Afghanistan borderland, with a tribal political structure that operated quite differently from the Turkic mamluk system that had defined the previous dynasties.
The Lodis came in slowly, ruled cautiously, and went out fast.

Bahlul Lodi had been a Pashtun chief of the Lodi tribe, governor of Sirhind (in the Punjab) under the late Sayyid sultans, and the head of a private army of perhaps 30,000 Pashtun cavalry that he had built up over years of frontier service.

When the last Sayyid sultan Alam Shah abdicated in 1451, Bahlul moved into Delhi unopposed, was acclaimed by the Delhi nobility, and began the slow process of rebuilding Sultanate authority over the Doab and the eastern Punjab.
Bahlul ruled differently from the Turkic sultans who had preceded him.
His political model was not the centralized autocratic Persianate court of Balban or Alauddin; it was the Afghan tribal confederation.

He treated his fellow Pashtun nobles as something close to peers — first-among-equals rather than slaves of the throne — sitting them on equivalent platforms at court audiences, sharing decision-making with a council of senior chiefs, and refusing the elaborate prostration ceremonies that earlier sultans had insisted on.
The political culture of the Lodi dynasty was, in important respects, more egalitarian than its predecessors had been (within the Pashtun warrior class, that is — outside it, very little changed).
Bahlul's main political project was the reabsorption of the Sharqi Sultanate of Jaunpur into the Delhi orbit.
Jaunpur had broken away in 1394 under Malik Sarwar and had grown into one of the major fifteenth-century Indian states.
The Sharqi sultans had refused to acknowledge Delhi's authority.

Bahlul spent most of his thirty-eight-year reign in intermittent warfare with Jaunpur, finally defeating the last Sharqi sultan Husayn Shah decisively in 1486 and reincorporating Jaunpur's territory into the Sultanate.
The campaign expanded the Sultanate's effective reach back into the eastern Doab and Bihar, recovering territory lost since Timur's invasion almost a century earlier.
He died in 1489 at perhaps eighty years old, leaving the throne to his son Sikandar Lodi.
Sikandar Lodi (ruled 1489–1517) was probably the most capable Lodi sultan and the figure who transformed the Lodi state from a tribal confederation into something more like a centralized monarchy.
Sikandar was the son of Bahlul and a Hindu Khatri mother — the same kind of mixed-religion-and-ethnicity background that Amir Khusrau had had two centuries earlier.
He grew up bilingual in Persian and Hindavi, took the throne at perhaps thirty years old, and ruled for twenty-eight years.
His major achievements were administrative and territorial.

He continued the reabsorption of breakaway territories: parts of Bihar and the eastern Doab that the Sharqis had held, sections of the central Doab that had been independent under various local strongmen, the lower Ganges plain.
He extended Sultanate authority into northern Bihar and made gestures toward influencing Bengal (without being able to actually conquer it).
He systematized the Sultanate's revenue administration, restoring something like the iqta system that had operated under earlier dynasties, and rebuilt the central treasury that Timur had destroyed.
His most consequential decision was urban.

In 1504, he founded the new city of Agra (AH-grah), on the Yamuna about 130 miles south of Delhi, as a forward administrative capital that would allow him to govern the Doab region more closely than was possible from Delhi.
The site he chose — on the southern bank of the Yamuna, on a strategic crossing — would become one of the most important cities in subsequent Indian history.
Akbar would build the Agra Fort there in the 1560s.
Shah Jahan would build the Taj Mahal there in the 1630s.
The Mughal capital would oscillate between Delhi and Agra for the next two centuries.
Modern Agra, as one of India's major tourist cities, owes its founding to Sikandar Lodi.
Sikandar was also a literary patron and a poet himself.
He wrote Persian verse under the pen-name Gulrukhi ("Rose-faced") and patronized a circle of Persian poets at his Agra court.
He sponsored translations of Sanskrit texts into Persian (a project that would become much more substantial under Akbar).
He commissioned the construction of new mosques, madrasas, and libraries across his territory.
He died in 1517 at perhaps fifty-eight years old, having held the Lodi state together for nearly three decades and having significantly expanded its actual administrative reach.
His son and successor was Ibrahim Lodi.
Ibrahim Lodi (ruled 1517–1526) was the last Sultan of Delhi.
Ibrahim was the eldest of Sikandar's sons.

He took the throne at perhaps thirty years old and ruled for nine years — long enough to alienate his nobility, lose major battles, and finally lose his life and his throne to a Mughal prince from Kabul.
The basic problem of Ibrahim's reign was political.
He inherited from his father a nobility that operated on the older Lodi tribal-confederation model — Pashtun chiefs treated as relative peers, with significant autonomy in their own provinces.
Ibrahim attempted to centralize, demanding the kind of formal subordination that the Mamluk and Khalji and Tughlaq sultans had received from their nobles.
The Pashtun chiefs took this as an insult and increasingly resisted.
Several major nobles were imprisoned or executed for insufficient deference.
Others fled to provincial governorships and began behaving as independent rulers.
The Lodi state Ibrahim had inherited as a relatively coherent confederation became, under his rule, a sequence of internal conflicts and rebellions.
The most consequential of these conflicts was with his uncle Daulat Khan Lodi, the governor of the Punjab.
Daulat Khan had supported a different Lodi prince in the 1517 succession dispute and had never reconciled with Ibrahim.
By 1523, he was in open rebellion against Delhi from his power base at Lahore.
Lacking the military strength to defeat Ibrahim alone, Daulat Khan made the consequential decision to invite an outside power into north India: Babur, the Timurid prince ruling from Kabul.
Babur had been raiding the Punjab from Kabul for several years.
He had captured Lahore briefly in 1524.
Daulat Khan's invitation gave Babur the political cover to mount a full invasion.

In late 1525, Babur crossed the Indus with an army of perhaps 12,000 well-equipped troops including Ottoman-trained matchlock musketeers and Turkish field artillery — the first time gunpowder weapons in significant numbers had been deployed on the Indian battlefield.
By February 1526, he was approaching Delhi.
What happened next was the First Battle of Panipat (April 21, 1526), and what happened after that was the Mughal Empire.
Both are the subject of Chapter 8.
But before we leave the Lodis, we should pause on what the Sultanate as a whole had become by the time of its end.
The Sultanate that Ibrahim Lodi inherited was geographically much smaller than the one Iltutmish had built.
The territory directly under Lodi administration in 1517 consisted of the Doab, parts of eastern Punjab, parts of western Bihar, and a few central Indian districts.

Bengal, Gujarat, Malwa, Sindh, the Bahmani successor states (now five of them, after the Bahmani fragmentation), Mewar and the other Rajput states, Vijayanagara, and the various smaller principalities of the south and the Deccan were all independent.
What this means, structurally, is that the political pattern of the late Sultanate was a pattern of regional sultanates, of which Delhi was just one.
The label "Delhi Sultanate" preserves the name of the founding dynasty but understates how thoroughly the political map had reorganized into multiple roughly equal regional states.
Bengal under the late Hussain Shahi sultans was at least as wealthy as Delhi under the Lodis.
Gujarat under the Muzaffarids was probably wealthier (because of its Indian Ocean trade revenues).
Mandu under the Khaljis of Malwa rivaled Delhi in cultural sophistication.

Vijayanagara at its peak under Krishnadevaraya was unambiguously the most populous, wealthiest, and militarily strongest single state in the subcontinent — significantly bigger than the Lodi Sultanate at its peak.
The cultural and architectural legacies of these provincial sultanates are, collectively, more extensive than the Lodi Sultanate's own.

The Adina Mosque at Pandua (Bengal), the Atala Mosque at Jaunpur, the Jahaz Mahal and Hoshang Shah's Tomb at Mandu, the Champaner-Pavagadh complex in Gujarat, the Jami Mosque and Madrasa of Mahmud Gawan at Bidar (Bahmani), and the temple complex at Hampi (Vijayanagara) collectively produced more lasting architectural monuments than the Lodi sultans built at Delhi.

The Lodi Sultanate's own architectural contribution was the Lodi Tombs and Gardens in modern Delhi: the octagonal tombs of Sikandar Lodi and Muhammad Shah Sayyid in the modern Lodi Gardens park, with their distinctive double-domed construction and pierced-stone lattice screens.

The Mughals would refine this octagonal-tomb pattern into the Humayun's Tomb (1565) and ultimately the Taj Mahal (1648), so the Lodi tombs are architecturally important as the immediate ancestors of Mughal monumental tomb architecture.
But by themselves they are not on the scale of what the provincial sultanates produced.
The literary and religious figures of the late Sultanate were dispersed similarly across the regional states.
The Bhakti poets — Kabir at Banaras, Mirabai at Mewar (Rajasthan), Surdas at Mathura — operated in regions outside direct Lodi control.
The Sufi dargahs — Ajmer Sharif in Rajasthan, Nizamuddin Dargah in Delhi, Bahauddin Zakariya's khanqah at Multan — were spread across the entire late-Sultanate political map.
Guru Nanak founded Sikhism in the western Punjab outside any Lodi administrative reach.
Amir Khusrau's literary tradition flowed through generations of Persian-language poets at courts across the entire fragmented landscape.
The point is that the religious and cultural synthesis of Sultanate India was a pan-Indian phenomenon by 1500, not a Delhi-centered one.
The Lodis ruled a regional state with significant cultural and political achievements, but not a culturally hegemonic one.

When the Mughals arrived in 1526, they were inheriting not a single coherent empire but a constellation of regional states, religious networks, cultural traditions, and economic systems that would take a century to reorganize into the coherent Mughal political-cultural order.
The Mughals would inherit the framework.
The provincial sultanates would, mostly, be conquered and absorbed.
The Bhakti and Sufi traditions would continue.
The Indo-Islamic architectural synthesis would develop further.
The Hindavi-Rekhta language would develop further.
What was changing in 1526 was the dynastic top of the political pyramid.
What was not changing was the underlying religious, cultural, linguistic, and economic fabric that the Sultanate's three centuries had woven.
A pause to acknowledge the Vijayanagara alternative.
The southern Hindu empire, founded in 1336 in direct opposition to the Sultanate's southern projection, deserves more attention than this chapter has been able to give it.
Vijayanagara reached its peak under Krishnadevaraya (kreesh-nuh-DEH-vuh-RAH-yuh, ruled 1509–1529) — roughly contemporary with Sikandar Lodi and the early Babur.

The empire controlled most of southern India south of the Krishna river, ruled from a capital city (modern Hampi) that European visitors estimated at 500,000 inhabitants, fielded armies of perhaps 700,000 troops at full mobilization, and conducted Indian Ocean trade through the ports of the Malabar coast.
