Vijayanagara was, by every measure of population, wealth, military strength, and territorial extent, the largest single state in the Indian subcontinent during the late Sultanate period.

Krishnadevaraya himself was an extraordinary figure: a Telugu-speaking soldier-king who patronized literature in Telugu, Sanskrit, Kannada, and Tamil simultaneously, built the Vitthala and Krishna temples at Hampi (the Stone Chariot of Vitthala is one of the most photographed monuments of southern India), wrote a Telugu-language treatise on statecraft (the Amuktamalyada), and personally commanded armies that defeated the Bahmani successor sultanates at the Battle of Raichur in 1520 (which is conventionally dated as Krishnadevaraya's high point of imperial achievement).
The Vijayanagara story is partially the subject of Medieval India Ch 6 and would have been a substantial part of the Vijayanagara Sultanate TL had we written one.

For the purposes of the Delhi Sultanate narrative, the important point is that the southern Hindu empire was, throughout the Sultanate's late period, demonstrating that a centralized Hindu state of much larger scale than anything north India had produced was possible.
Vijayanagara's existence is one of the central facts of fifteenth- and sixteenth-century Indian history.

Its destruction at the Battle of Talikota in 1565 (by a coalition of the Deccan Sultanates, decades after the Lodi Sultanate had ended) is one of the great "what-if" inflection points of Indian history — what the subcontinent's political map would have looked like if Vijayanagara had survived and consolidated as a competing imperial center is one of the major counterfactuals of Indian historiography.

For the Sultanate at Delhi, Vijayanagara was simultaneously a competitor (the Bahmani-Vijayanagara wars across the Deccan frontier consumed enormous resources on both sides), a model of what Hindu political centralization could look like, and a constant reminder that the Sultanate's pan-Indian pretensions were never actually achieved in practice.
The Lodi Sultanate at its peak controlled less than a quarter of the subcontinent's population and territory.
In April 1526, Babur crossed into India for what would be his last and decisive campaign.

Daulat Khan Lodi had originally invited him, but had then, predictably, attempted to redirect him: Daulat Khan wanted Babur to defeat Ibrahim Lodi but then withdraw to Kabul, leaving Daulat Khan in possession of Delhi.
Babur had no intention of doing this.
By the time the campaign began, Daulat Khan had switched sides again and was attempting to fight Babur from the Punjab.
Babur defeated him outside Lahore in early 1526 and continued east toward Delhi.
Ibrahim Lodi mobilized the imperial Sultanate army to meet him.

The Lodi force was substantial — Persian and Mughal sources agree on something between 100,000 and 130,000 men, including the major war elephants of the imperial cavalry, supported by tens of thousands of camp followers and supply trains.
By comparison, Babur's army at Panipat was perhaps 12,000 to 25,000 (the sources disagree, but everyone agrees the Lodi force was several times larger).
What Babur had that Ibrahim did not was gunpowder weapons, used in a coordinated way that the Sultanate had no experience defending against.
We'll cover the battle in detail in Chapter 8.

But the structural fact at the end of Chapter 7 is that the Sultanate's military system — built around heavy cavalry, war elephants, and infantry archers, refined across three centuries of experience against pre-gunpowder armies — was about to encounter a small, mobile, gunpowder-equipped army using tactics borrowed from the Ottoman Janissary system, and was about to lose decisively.
The Lodi dynasty would not survive April 21, 1526.
Neither would the Sultanate.

Cross-civ check: while the Lodis were ruling Delhi (1451–1526), the Ottoman Empire under Mehmed II captured Constantinople in 1453 and ended the Byzantine Empire (Byzantine Empire Ch 12); Selim I then conquered the Mamluk Sultanate of Egypt in 1517 (Ottoman Empire Ch 5); the Spanish completed the Reconquista in 1492 with the fall of Granada and Columbus crossed the Atlantic the same year; the Safavid Empire in Iran was founded in 1501 by Ismail I (Safavid Persia Ch 2); the Mughal Empire that would shortly succeed the Sultanate at Panipat was founded the same year — 1526 — that Charles V was elected Holy Roman Emperor and Suleiman the Magnificent defeated Hungary at the Battle of Mohacs (Ottoman Empire Ch 5).
The early sixteenth century was the inflection point at which gunpowder armies, Atlantic seafaring, and centralized fiscal-military states collectively transformed every major Eurasian civilization.
The end of the Sultanate is one regional manifestation of this larger global transformation.

chapters.title: Panipat 1526 and the End
sentences: The First Battle of Panipat (PAH-nee-put) was fought on April 21, 1526, on a flat plain about 55 miles north of Delhi.
It lasted from sunrise to about midday — perhaps six hours of actual fighting.
By the end, Ibrahim Lodi was dead on the field, the imperial Sultanate army of perhaps 100,000 had been broken, and Babur was the new master of north India.
The battle is one of the textbook engagements in the global history of military technology.

It is the moment when the gunpowder army, used in coordinated combination with traditional cavalry tactics, definitively replaced the pre-gunpowder cavalry charge as the decisive military technology of the Indian subcontinent.

The same technological transition had happened at Chaldiran in 1514 (Ottoman gunpowder defeating Safavid cavalry, Safavid Persia Ch 3), and would happen at the Battle of Mohacs in 1526 (the same year as Panipat, Ottoman gunpowder defeating Hungarian cavalry, Ottoman Empire Ch 5).
India's version came at Panipat.
After Panipat, no Indian state could afford to fight wars without artillery and matchlock infantry.
The Sultanate's military system, perfected over three centuries against pre-gunpowder enemies, was suddenly obsolete.
Babur's army was small but technologically state-of-the-art.
He had perhaps 12,000 to 25,000 troops (sources disagree).

He had a few hundred matchlock musketeers under his Turkish gun-master Ustad Ali Quli, and a smaller number of field cannons (probably 10-20, some of them captured at recent campaigns, some manufactured at Kabul).
He had perhaps 3,000-4,000 mounted archers, primarily Mongol and Uzbek mercenaries.
He had a general staff that included Humayun (his son and eventual successor) and several experienced Timurid commanders.

Most importantly, he had read the Ottoman tactical manuals on what was called arabakorpus or wagenburg — the deployment of gunpowder infantry behind a defensive perimeter of chained-together baggage carts, with the artillery mounted on or between the carts to provide supporting fire while the infantry musketeers fired through gaps in the cart line.
The Ottomans had developed this tactic against Persian and European cavalry over the previous century.
Babur's gun-master Ustad Ali Quli had served in the Ottoman army before taking employment with the Timurids, and brought the tactical knowledge with him.
Babur deployed his force in this configuration on the morning of April 21.
He had his roughly 700 baggage carts chained together along the front of his line, gaps left at intervals for cavalry sallies.
His matchlock musketeers were positioned behind the carts.
His field cannons were positioned at intervals along the cart line.
His cavalry was held in reserve, divided into a center force and two wings, with mounted archers further forward to harass the approaching Lodi army.
Ibrahim Lodi's army arrived on the field with the standard Sultanate military doctrine of the period: massed heavy cavalry, supported by infantry archers, with war elephants on the flanks.
The Lodi general staff, lacking experience with gunpowder warfare, made the standard pre-gunpowder decision: charge.
The Lodi charge broke against Babur's defensive perimeter.
The matchlock fire from behind the carts decimated the leading ranks of cavalry.
The cannon fire shattered the war elephants (which spooked at the explosions and caused havoc in the Lodi ranks behind them).
The mounted archers harassed the Lodi flanks while the heavy cavalry was pinned at the cart line.
By midday, the Lodi army was disintegrating.
Babur's mounted reserves swept around the flanks of the broken line and completed the destruction.
Ibrahim Lodi fell somewhere on the field, along with perhaps 15,000 of his soldiers.
His body was identified after the battle and beheaded; the head was reportedly carried back to Babur as proof of victory.

Babur entered Delhi unopposed three days later, on April 27, 1526, and proclaimed himself Padshah (literally "master-king," the Persian-Turkic imperial title that the Mughal dynasty would use for the next three centuries).
The Delhi Sultanate, founded by Aibak in 1206, had ended.
What came next was the Mughal Empire.
We will not cover the Mughal story here — it is the subject of a different TL — but we should note what Babur inherited and what he had to do to consolidate his victory.
Babur did not, in fact, immediately control all of the Sultanate's former territory.

The Hindu Rajput coalition under Rana Sanga of Mewar mobilized to oppose him almost immediately, and Babur had to fight a second major battle — the Battle of Khanwa in March 1527 — to secure his northern Indian conquest.

The Afghan Lodi nobility scattered across the eastern Sultanate territories and would resist Mughal authority for the next thirty years (eventually rallying under Sher Shah Suri, the great Pashtun general who would briefly displace Babur's son Humayun from the Mughal throne and rule north India as the Sur Sultanate from 1540 to 1555).
The provincial sultanates — Bengal, Gujarat, Malwa, the Deccan Sultanates, Vijayanagara, the Sindh — remained independent for decades after Panipat.
The full consolidation of north India under Mughal rule would not be completed until Akbar's reign in the 1560s and 1570s.
But the Sultanate as a Delhi-based political institution was over.
The dynasty was extinguished.
The political continuity from Aibak to Ibrahim Lodi was broken by Babur's conquest.
The institutional and cultural continuities, however, were preserved.
The Mughals adopted, modified, and refined nearly everything the Sultanate had built.
What the Sultanate left behind, after Panipat, deserves a final tally.
The administrative framework.
The iqta land-grant system, modified into the more elaborate Mughal mansabdari system, would continue to organize Indian land revenue and military finance for the next three centuries.
The basic structure of provincial governorship (the suba under the Mughals), district administration (the sarkar), and rural revenue extraction (the pargana) all derive from Sultanate precedents.

The Persian language of imperial administration would continue as the official language of north Indian governance through the Mughal period and into the early British period — until 1837, when the East India Company finally replaced Persian with English in court and administrative use, ending a 631-year run that Aibak had inadvertently begun in 1206.
The architectural tradition.
The Indo-Islamic synthesis of Persian arch-and-dome construction with Indian craftsmanship would continue as a continuous tradition through the Mughal period and beyond.

The Qutb Minar and Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque are the founding monuments of this tradition; the Tughlaq fortresses of Tughlaqabad and Firuzabad are major Sultanate-era expressions; the Lodi tombs are the immediate ancestors of Humayun's Tomb and the Taj Mahal.
Modern Indian visual culture's sense of "Islamic architecture in India" is essentially a Sultanate-era invention that the Mughals refined to its most famous forms.
The religious-cultural synthesis.
The Bhakti devotional tradition would continue to grow through the Mughal period, eventually becoming the dominant form of popular Hindu religious practice across north India.
The Sufi dargah network would continue and expand under Mughal patronage (Akbar in particular was a major patron of the Chishti dargahs at Ajmer and Fatehpur Sikri).

The Sikh community Nanak founded would grow through the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, develop its distinctive militarized identity under Guru Gobind Singh, and emerge as a major religious community in modern South Asia.
The Hindavi-Rekhta language would develop into modern Hindi and modern Urdu.
The Indo-Islamic musical traditions — qawwali, the north Indian classical raga system — would become the foundation of all subsequent north Indian musical practice.
The demographic-religious geography.

The Sultanate's three centuries of Turkic and Afghan rule, plus the conversion of substantial portions of the rural population to Islam (especially in the eastern Bengal delta, where the Sultanate-era expansion of rice cultivation was associated with conversion to Islam, and in the western Punjab and Sindh), permanently altered the religious geography of the subcontinent.
By 1526, north India had a Muslim population of perhaps 15-20% in the cities and 5-10% in the countryside, varying enormously by region.
Bengal had Muslim majorities in many districts.
The Punjab had substantial Muslim populations.
Sindh was largely Muslim.
The Deccan and the south remained overwhelmingly Hindu.

The geographic distribution of Muslims and Hindus that would later produce the 1947 Partition of India and Pakistan is recognizably traceable to the demographic patterns the Sultanate had established.
The political precedent.

The Sultanate established that a centralized military monarchy could rule a Hindu-majority subcontinent through a Muslim military aristocracy, governed by Persianate administrative tradition, with Islamic religious law applied to the Muslim minority and customary Hindu law applied to the Hindu majority, financed by land revenue and trade taxes.

Every subsequent Indian state — the Mughals, the Marathas (Hindu but governing through similar institutional structures), the British, even in some respects modern India — has built on this institutional template.
The Sultanate is the matrix of pre-modern Indian state-building.
A few longer-term things the Sultanate gave India that are worth noting separately: Persian as the cultural common language of north Indian elites.

Persian poetry, Persian historical writing, Persian administrative documents — all of this would continue to be the central register of north Indian elite culture from 1206 through the early nineteenth century.
Mirza Ghalib (the great early-nineteenth-century Persian and Urdu poet of late-Mughal Delhi) was writing in a tradition that ran continuously back to Amir Khusrau six centuries earlier.
The Indian Ocean trading network.
The Sultanate maintained and extended the trading connections that the Cholas had built (Medieval India Ch 5), particularly through the Bengal and Gujarat ports.

The horse trade with Arabia and Iran (which the Sultanate's perpetual cavalry shortage made critical) flowed through the same Indian Ocean routes that brought Chinese porcelain, African gold, Indonesian spices, and European trade goods.

By 1500, the Indian subcontinent was more deeply integrated into the Indian Ocean trading system than it had been before, partly because of Sultanate-era developments in port infrastructure and trade administration.
The Sufi-Bhakti devotional vocabulary.

Modern Indian devotional practice, both Hindu and Muslim, draws on a shared vocabulary of devotional intensity, divine love, the inadequacy of formal religious institution, the importance of vernacular expression, and the equality of devotees before God — vocabulary that was substantially worked out in the Sultanate-era dialogue between Sufi tariqas and Bhakti sant-traditions.

The fact that modern Hindi and Urdu devotional songs (whether religious bhajans, Sufi qawwalis, or even popular film songs that mimic devotional registers) sound recognizably similar to a non-specialist listener — both languages, both traditions, both registers — is partly the product of this Sultanate-era synthesis.
The Indo-Islamic culinary tradition.

The cuisines of north India, Pakistan, and Bangladesh — biryanis, kebabs, naan, samosas, jalebi, kheer, and the entire vocabulary of urban north Indian-Pakistani cooking — are substantially Sultanate-era developments, drawing on Persian and Central Asian techniques applied to Indian ingredients.
The first reliable mentions of biryani as a distinct dish appear in late-Sultanate sources.
The samosa appears in Amir Khusrau's writings.
Modern north Indian street food is, gastronomically, a Sultanate-era invention that the Mughals codified.
The historical reputation of the Delhi Sultanate is genuinely difficult to summarize, because what you see depends on where you stand.

From the perspective of the Sultanate's Persian court chroniclers — Minhaj-i Siraj, Ziauddin Barani, Shams-i Siraj Afif, Yahya Sirhindi — the Sultanate was the legitimate political project of bringing Islamic rule and high Persianate culture to a previously chaotic Hindu subcontinent.

From the perspective of nineteenth- and twentieth-century British colonial historians — who built on the Persian chronicles plus their own ideological framework — the Sultanate was a foreign Muslim despotism that interrupted the natural development of Hindu civilization and prepared the way for the British "civilizing mission." From the perspective of twentieth-century Indian nationalist historians — particularly the secular-Marxist tradition associated with Mohammad Habib, Irfan Habib, and Romila Thapar — the Sultanate was a complex multi-ethnic state that integrated Indian and Central Asian institutions, produced significant administrative and cultural achievements, and prepared the institutional ground for the Mughal Empire and ultimately for modern Indian state-building.

From the perspective of twentieth-century Hindu nationalist historiography — the Hindutva tradition associated with figures like Veer Savarkar — the Sultanate was an extended period of foreign Muslim oppression that destroyed Hindu temples, persecuted Hindu populations, and represented an interruption of Hindu civilizational continuity that needed to be reversed in modern Indian politics.
All four perspectives have something to draw on in the historical record.
The Sultanate did, demonstrably, build a Persianate Islamic state ruling a Hindu majority.
It did, demonstrably, destroy Hindu temples in conquest campaigns and on a sustained basis under certain sultans.
It did, demonstrably, develop a sophisticated multi-ethnic administrative apparatus that absorbed Hindu officials and functioned for three centuries.

It did, demonstrably, generate cross-religious cultural syntheses (Sufism-Bhakti, Indo-Persian architecture, Hindavi-Rekhta language, north Indian classical music) that reshaped popular religious and cultural life across the subcontinent.
The Sultanate's record cannot be honestly reduced to any one of these descriptions.

Modern historians have spent decades trying to develop frameworks that hold all of them simultaneously — the Sultanate as a complex pre-modern state with both repressive and integrative dimensions, both destructive and creative cultural impacts, both foreign-imposed and locally-rooted institutional features.

The honest answer to "what was the Sultanate?" is that it was several things at once, and the same set of facts can be interpreted very differently depending on what political-religious-cultural framework you bring to the interpretation.
The actual end of the Sultanate at Panipat in 1526 is a moment of military-technological transition (gunpowder defeats heavy cavalry) much more than it is a moment of dynastic-cultural rupture.
The Lodi Afghans were defeated by the Timurid Babur, but the Indo-Islamic-Persianate cultural-administrative-religious world the Sultanate had built continued largely uninterrupted under the Mughals.
The cooks kept cooking biryanis.
The qawwalis kept being sung.
The Persian poets kept writing ghazals.
The Bhakti sants kept composing devotional songs.
The Hindu temples kept being built (the great Vijayanagara temples, the Rajput palace-temples of Mewar, the Bengal terracotta temples of the Kantanagar tradition) outside Mughal reach.
The Sufi dargahs kept attracting pilgrims.
The Indian Ocean trade kept moving Indian textiles and indigo to the east and west.
What changed at Panipat was the particular dynasty at the top of the political pyramid in Delhi.
What did not change was the underlying social, economic, religious, and cultural fabric of the subcontinent.
That fabric had been substantially woven by the Sultanate's three centuries.
The Mughals would alter it but not unmake it.
The British would alter it more but not unmake it either.
Modern India and Pakistan are still living in the long downstream consequences of the world the Sultanate built.

In the modern city of Delhi — which is to say, modern New Delhi plus modern Old Delhi (Shahjahanabad) plus the surrounding districts that have absorbed all the older Sultanate cities into their suburban growth — the Sultanate-era monuments are all still there.
The Qutb Minar at Mehrauli is the most visited tourist site in southern Delhi.
The Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque ruins, with their reused Hindu temple columns and the still-standing Iron Pillar of Delhi, sit beside it in the same UNESCO complex.

The Tughlaqabad fortress walls run for miles across south Delhi, partially inhabited by squatter villages, partially preserved as archaeological zone, mostly visible from passing cars on the Mehrauli-Badarpur road.

The Firuzabad complex (Firuz Shah Kotla) sits beside the Yamuna in central Delhi, a small archaeological park where pilgrims still come on Thursday evenings to leave letters at the ruins of the old palace, asking the jinn (Islamic spirits) believed to inhabit the site for help with various problems.

The Lodi Tombs sit in the modern Lodi Gardens in central New Delhi, an immaculate landscaped park that joggers and picnickers use daily without necessarily knowing whose tombs they are sitting beside.

The Nizamuddin Dargah is in active use as a working pilgrimage site in central Delhi, with daily qawwali performances, weekly Thursday-evening special programs, and a continuous flow of pilgrims of every faith.
Out beyond Delhi, the Sultanate-era monuments are even more numerous.

The Adina Mosque at Pandua (now Bangladesh), the Atala Mosque at Jaunpur, the Jahaz Mahal at Mandu, the Champaner-Pavagadh complex in Gujarat, the Madrasa of Mahmud Gawan at Bidar, the Chittor Fort complex in Rajasthan, the Hampi temple and palace ruins, the various provincial-sultanate mosques and tombs scattered across Bengal, the Doab, the Deccan, and Gujarat — all are still standing, mostly preserved, many on the UNESCO World Heritage list.
The Sultanate is not gone.

It is still there in the architecture, still there in the language people speak in the bazaars of Delhi and Lahore, still there in the qawwalis sung at the Nizamuddin and Ajmer dargahs, still there in the Bhakti songs and the Sikh hymns recorded from Sultanate-era sources, still there in the cuisines of north India and Pakistan, still there in the Persian-derived vocabulary of legal and administrative Hindi-Urdu, still there in the institutional template of modern Indian governance.

Three centuries of dynastic history, several hundred thousand victims of conquest, several million immigrants and converts, and a cultural-religious-architectural synthesis that has shaped the subcontinent for the nine hundred years since are all part of what the Delhi Sultanate left for the modern world to inherit.
The story that began with Aibak and his polo accident in Lahore in 1210 is still going on.

Cross-civ check: 1526, the year of Panipat, is the year Suleiman the Magnificent of the Ottoman Empire defeated Hungary at the Battle of Mohacs (Ottoman Empire Ch 5), the year Ferdinand Magellan's surviving crew completed the first global circumnavigation (their voyage having ended in 1522 but the political consequences still working through), the year Charles V of the Holy Roman Empire was at the height of his power across Spain, the Netherlands, the German lands, and most of Italy, the year Martin Luther had been excommunicated for five years and the Protestant Reformation was underway across northern Europe, and the year the Inca Empire under Huayna Capac was at peak — within seven years of being destroyed by Pizarro and the Spanish in 1533.
The mid-1520s are the global pivot point at which gunpowder weapons, Atlantic trade, religious reformation, and centralized fiscal-military states transformed every major civilization simultaneously.
The end of the Delhi Sultanate is one regional manifestation of this larger global transformation.

Babur's victory at Panipat is the same kind of event as Cortes's victory at Tenochtitlan five years earlier (Aztec Empire Ch 8) and Pizarro's victory at Cajamarca seven years later: the moment when a small, well-equipped, disciplined invading army defeated a large pre-gunpowder defending army using imported military technology that the defenders could not match.
The Sultanate joined a world in 1206 that included the Mongols, the Crusader states, and the Song.
The Sultanate left a world in 1526 that included the Ottomans, the Habsburgs, the Safavids, the Reformation, the Aztec collapse, and the global maritime trading networks.
Three hundred and twenty years is a long time.
The world had changed beyond recognition.
The Sultanate's three centuries had run their course.

chapters.title: Babur from Ferghana
sentences: The man who founded the wealthiest empire of the early-modern world spent the first twenty-one years of his life losing.
His name was Zahir-ud-Din Muhammad Babur (BAH-bur, "Babur" is a nickname meaning "Tiger" in Turkic).
He was born in 1483 in Andijan (an-dih-JAHN), a small town in the Ferghana Valley — a mountain-walled basin east of Samarkand in modern eastern Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan.

His father, Umar Shaykh Mirza, was one of the late Timurid princes — a fifth-generation descendant of Timur (TEE-moor, the Turco-Mongol world-conqueror who had built and lost a vast empire 1370–1405, Timurid Empire Ch 1–2).
His mother, Qutlugh Nigar Khanum, was a direct Genghisid in the senior Mongol royal line.
By the standards of late-fifteenth-century Central Asia, Babur had unimpeachable dynastic credentials.
His ancestors were Timur and Genghis Khan.
The combination meant nothing if you could not also win battles.
He did not, mostly, win battles.
His father died in 1494 in an absurd accident — the family pigeon house at the palace at Akhsi collapsed with him on it, and he fell to his death — and twelve-year-old Babur inherited Ferghana.

The next decade of his life was a nearly unbroken series of military catastrophes against his Timurid cousins and the rising Uzbeks (the Turko-Mongol tribal confederation pushing south from the steppe under the brilliant general Muhammad Shaybani Khan, Timurid Empire Ch 8).
Babur captured Samarkand at fifteen and lost it within months.
He took it again at eighteen and lost it again.

He spent extended periods as a hunted fugitive in the mountains, surviving on yogurt and stale bread, sleeping in caves, periodically losing his entire army and then reassembling it from whatever Timurid loyalists he could find.
By 1504, with the Uzbeks consolidating control of all Transoxiana, Babur was twenty-one years old and had nothing left in Central Asia.
He had lost his ancestral Ferghana.
He had lost Samarkand.
His mother had died.
Most of his original household troops were dead or had defected.
He was, in the literal sense, a refugee prince.
He turned south.

In October 1504, with a few hundred personal followers and whatever Timurid stragglers he could collect, Babur crossed the Hindu Kush mountains (the major mountain range that separates Central Asia from the Indian subcontinent — the same range Timur had crossed 130 years earlier on his way to sack Delhi, Timurid Empire Ch 4) and seized Kabul from a Timurid cousin who was even more incompetent than he was.
Kabul became his base for the next twenty-two years.
It was not much of a kingdom.
The city sat at the head of a valley in modern Afghanistan, with cold winters and a marginal agricultural hinterland that could feed a few thousand troops at most.
But it had three structural advantages that Babur came to understand slowly.
It controlled the Khyber Pass (the main mountain corridor between Afghanistan and the Punjab plains), which meant it sat astride one of the great trade and invasion routes of Eurasian history.
It was defensible — the Hindu Kush walls protected its north flank against the Uzbeks, who never seriously threatened it.

And it was a Persian-speaking court city with libraries, gardens, and Sufi shrine networks (the Naqshbandi Sufi order had its Central Asian heartland just north of the Hindu Kush, Timurid Empire Ch 8), which meant Babur could keep up the cultural-political performance of a legitimate Timurid prince while he figured out what to do next.
What he eventually figured out was that he was not going to retake Central Asia from the Uzbeks.

They were too strong, too well-organized, and they were Genghisids in the senior line — which gave them a legitimacy claim Babur could not match. (His own Genghisid descent was through his mother's line, which was junior to the male-line Genghisid descent the Uzbek royal family carried.

Steppe political theory cared about this distinction.) He made one more attempt to recover Samarkand in 1511, with help from a brand-new Iranian regime: the Safavid dynasty under Shah Ismail I (Safavid Persia Ch 2), who had killed Shaybani at the Battle of Merv the year before and was happy to back another Timurid against the Uzbeks.
Babur held Samarkand for a few months.
The price of Safavid support was that he had to publicly perform Twelver Shia religious observances in a city that had been Sunni for centuries.
The Sunni population of Samarkand turned against him, the Uzbeks counterattacked, and Babur was driven back to Kabul one final time.
The Central Asian career was over.
He turned, increasingly, toward the south.
India was not a new idea — Timur had sacked Delhi in 1398 and Babur considered himself the legitimate heir to those conquests by ancestral right — but it was now the only direction left.
Before we cover the conquest, the gunpowder revolution that made it possible deserves its own paragraph.
By the early sixteenth century, three distinct gunpowder-weapons traditions had developed across the Eurasian world.
The European tradition (cannons cast in bronze, used primarily for siege warfare and naval combat) was advancing rapidly under the pressure of the Italian Wars and the Habsburg-Valois rivalry.

The Ottoman tradition (the Janissary corps of professional matchlock infantry, supported by field artillery deployed behind a perimeter of chained-together baggage carts called the tabur cengi, Ottoman Empire Ch 3) was the most mature — Janissaries had decided major battles for the Ottomans against the Mamluks (1517) and the Hungarians (1526).

And the Chinese tradition (where gunpowder had been invented around the tenth century, Tang and Song China Ch 7), which by the early Ming had developed cannons and matchlocks but had not pushed military reform as aggressively as the Ottomans had.
India had effectively missed all three.

The major Indian armies of 1500 — the Delhi Sultanate's Lodi forces, the Hindu Vijayanagara Empire in the south (Medieval India Ch 8), the various provincial sultanates — were still organized around heavy cavalry charges, war elephants on the flanks, and infantry archers behind the front line.

This was the same military doctrine that had been state of the art a thousand years earlier under the Guptas (Gupta Empire Ch 4), and it was about to encounter gunpowder for the first time in a significant way.
Babur was lucky in one specific respect: his gun-master, a Turkish artilleryman named Ustad Ali Quli, had served in the Ottoman army before taking employment with the Timurids.

Ustad Ali Quli understood the tabur cengi tactic in operational detail — how to chain wagons into a defensive line, how to space cannons between the wagons, how to coordinate matchlock fire with cavalry counterattacks at the right moment.
He brought the tactical knowledge with him to Kabul and trained Babur's small artillery corps.
By 1525, Babur had perhaps a few dozen field cannons, several hundred matchlock musketeers, and a working operational doctrine for using them on a battlefield.
None of the Indian armies he was about to fight had any of this.
The decisive campaign came in 1525-26.
The Lodi dynasty, ruling from Delhi as the last Sultanate dynasty (Delhi Sultanate Ch 7), had been in slow decline for fifty years.

Ibrahim Lodi (ib-rah-HEEM LOH-dee, ruled 1517-26) had alienated his Afghan nobility through arrogant and capricious treatment — executing senior commanders on suspicion, demoting provincial governors who had been allies of his father, generally behaving like a man who believed his own coronation propaganda.
In 1525, the governor of Lahore, Daulat Khan Lodi, invited Babur to invade Delhi in alliance with the dissident Lodi nobles.
Babur accepted.
He marched his army — perhaps 12,000 to 25,000 men, sources disagree — through the Khyber Pass into Punjab in late 1525.
Several smaller Lodi forces were brushed aside on the way.

By April 1526, Babur was on the plain of Panipat (PAH-nee-put, about 55 miles north of Delhi) with the main Mughal army, facing Ibrahim Lodi's force of perhaps 100,000 men plus a thousand war elephants.
The numerical disparity was eight to one against him.
The technological disparity was the other way around.

Babur deployed his army in the perfected tabur cengi: roughly 700 baggage carts chained together along the front, gaps left for cavalry sallies, matchlock musketeers behind the carts, field cannons positioned at intervals along the cart line, cavalry held in reserve in the center and wings, mounted archers further forward to harass the approaching enemy.

This was the same formation the Ottomans had used at Chaldiran in 1514 to defeat Shah Ismail's Safavids (Safavid Persia Ch 3), and the same formation Suleiman the Magnificent would use at Mohacs to defeat the Hungarians later in 1526 (Ottoman Empire Ch 5).
India had not yet seen it.
Ibrahim Lodi made the standard pre-gunpowder decision.
He charged.
The First Battle of Panipat lasted from sunrise to about midday on April 21, 1526.
The Lodi cavalry charged into Babur's wagon-fort line.
The matchlock fire from behind the carts decimated the leading ranks.
The cannons opened up at point-blank range and shattered the Lodi war elephants — which spooked at the explosions, panicked, and trampled the Lodi infantry behind them.
The mounted archers harassed the Lodi flanks while the heavy cavalry was pinned at the cart line.
Babur's mounted reserves swept around the broken flanks of the Lodi army and completed the destruction.
Ibrahim Lodi was killed in the fighting.

Sources disagree on the precise circumstances — he may have been shot, stabbed, or trampled — but his body was identified after the battle and beheaded, the head reportedly carried back to Babur as proof of victory.
About 15,000 of his soldiers died with him.
The Lodi dynasty, which had ruled Delhi for seventy-five years, was finished.
The Delhi Sultanate, founded by Aibak in 1206 and continuous through five Turkic and Afghan dynasties for three hundred and twenty years (Delhi Sultanate Ch 1-8), was over.
Babur entered Delhi unopposed three days later, on April 27, 1526, and proclaimed himself Padshah — literally "master-king," the Persian-Turkic imperial title.

The dynasty he founded would be called Mughal in European sources (a Persian rendering of "Mongol," chosen to emphasize Babur's combined Timurid-Mongol descent) and Gurkani in its own court usage (from the Persian title Guregen, "royal son-in-law," that Timur had used to indicate his marriage into the Genghisid line).
The same dynasty under three names.
We will use Mughal because everyone else does.
The conquest was not yet complete.
Babur had defeated the Lodi army at Panipat but he had not yet secured north India.

The Hindu Rajput kingdoms of Rajasthan — particularly Mewar, under the formidable Rana Sanga of the Sisodia dynasty — had been quietly hoping a fight between the Sultanate and the Mughals would eliminate both, leaving the Rajputs as the regional power.

When it became clear that Babur had only replaced one Muslim Sultanate with another, Rana Sanga organized a coalition of Rajput rulers (Mewar, Marwar, Amber, Hadoti, and several smaller principalities) to drive Babur out of north India.
Babur met them at the Battle of Khanwa in March 1527, with the same wagon-fort and matchlock tactics that had won at Panipat.
The result was the same.
Rana Sanga's coalition was broken; the Rajputs were militarily neutralized for a generation.

Babur conducted one further major campaign in 1529 against Afghan Lodi remnants in the eastern Sultanate territories at the Battle of Ghaghra, and consolidated control of north India from the Indus to Bengal.
He died in Agra in December 1530, age forty-seven, less than five years after Panipat.

The deathbed scene is recorded in Mughal chronicles with a detail that may be partly legendary but became central to Mughal dynastic mythology: his eldest son Humayun (hoo-MAH-yoon) had fallen seriously ill, the doctors despaired, and Babur reportedly walked three times around Humayun's sickbed praying for the illness to be transferred to him.
According to the chroniclers, Humayun recovered and Babur fell ill the same week, dying within months.

Whether the prayer-transfer story is true or a later embroidery on a coincidence, Babur did die just as Humayun was recovering, and the story shaped Humayun's lifelong sense of his father as a near-saintly figure.
The Baburnama is one of the great autobiographies in world literature and deserves its own paragraph.
Babur kept a personal memoir written intermittently from 1494 (when he was eleven, recording his father's death and his own accession to Ferghana) through his Indian conquests in the late 1520s.
He wrote in Chagatai-Turkic (his native language, the literary form of Turkic that the Timurid poet Mir Ali Sher Nava'i had recently established as a serious literary medium).
He used a candid, observant, self-critical prose style that has no real parallel in contemporary royal memoirs.

The book describes Babur's military campaigns, his political mistakes, his romantic entanglements (he writes about a same-sex attraction in his teenage years with the kind of matter-of-fact description that surprises modern readers expecting sixteenth-century reticence), his depressions, his alcohol consumption (he describes drinking heavily through much of his career, then giving up alcohol in 1527 in a sworn renunciation, then describing the renunciation with a wry awareness that he might break it), his observations of natural history (entire chapters describe the flora, fauna, climate, and geography of every region he passed through, with the precision of a working naturalist), and his reflections on the people he met and the books he read.

The Baburnama's value as a historical source is enormous — one of the most detailed primary accounts of Central Asian and northern Indian politics in the late fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries, written by a participant rather than a court chronicler.
Its value as a literary work is also enormous.
Modern scholars have compared it to the autobiographies of Saint Augustine, Benvenuto Cellini, and (occasionally) Marcus Aurelius.
The English translation by Annette Beveridge in 1922 is the older standard reference; Wheeler Thackston's 1996 translation is the modern scholarly text.
What stands out to a reader coming to it cold is how little Babur sounds like a conqueror in the European tradition.
He grumbles about the Indian climate (he hated it — too hot, no melons, no pomegranates, the wrong kind of bread).
He misses Kabul constantly.
He records minor military embarrassments alongside the great victories.
He spends pages on the precise grades of melon available in different Ferghana villages.
The voice is so warm and self-deprecating that it is genuinely difficult to reconcile with the man who beheaded Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat.
Both are him.
What Babur left to his heirs was a strategic position rather than a consolidated empire.
He controlled Delhi, Agra, and a corridor of north Indian territory from the Punjab to Bihar.
He had defeated the Lodis, the Rajputs, and the eastern Afghans, but none of those defeats had produced lasting submission.

The Afghan nobility of the eastern Sultanate territories — Bihar and Bengal — were already plotting against Mughal rule and would shortly produce Sher Shah Suri, the most formidable opponent the dynasty would face for the next two centuries (Chapter 2).
The Rajputs were militarily neutralized but politically restive.
The provincial Sultanates of Gujarat, Malwa, Bengal, and the Deccan were still independent.
The peninsular south — the great Hindu Vijayanagara Empire at its peak, Medieval India Ch 8 — was beyond any Mughal reach and would remain so until Akbar's expansion fifty years later.
What Babur did leave was the institutional template.

The Persianate court culture, the Timurid architectural vocabulary (the four-iwan mosque plan, the chahar bagh quartered garden, the soaring blue-tiled domes that Timurid Herat had perfected, Timurid Empire Ch 7), the gunpowder army, the imperial title (Padshah), the dynastic claim (Timurid-Genghisid), and the personal memoir-writing tradition that his great-grandson Jahangir would continue (Chapter 4).
Plus the cultural orientation toward Persian as the language of administration and Chagatai-Turkic as the language of the family.
The Mughal Empire was Babur's institutional invention as much as it was a territorial state.
Cross-civ check: 1526, the year of Panipat, was an extraordinarily consequential year globally.
Suleiman the Magnificent of the Ottoman Empire defeated Hungary at the Battle of Mohacs four months after Panipat (Ottoman Empire Ch 5), opening the way to Ottoman expansion into central Europe.
The same year, Charles V of the Holy Roman Empire captured Pavia and held the Pope hostage at Rome (the Sack of Rome would follow in 1527).
Martin Luther had been excommunicated five years earlier; the Protestant Reformation was visibly fragmenting Western Christianity.

Hernán Cortés had completed the conquest of the Aztec Empire (Aztec Empire Ch 8) five years earlier, in 1521, and Francisco Pizarro was about to launch his expedition that would destroy the Inca Empire in 1533.
The mid-1520s are the global pivot point at which gunpowder weapons, religious reformation, Atlantic trade, and centralized fiscal-military states transformed every major civilization simultaneously.

Babur's victory at Panipat is a regional manifestation of the same phenomenon — the moment when a small, well-equipped, disciplined invading army defeated a large pre-gunpowder defending army using imported military technology.

The three great Islamic gunpowder empires of the early-modern Middle East and South Asia — the Ottomans, the Safavids, and the Mughals — were all founded or transformed within a single forty-year window: the Ottoman conquest of Constantinople in 1453 (Ottoman Empire Ch 1) and the eastern campaigns of Selim I 1514-17 (Ottoman Empire Ch 5), Ismail I's Safavid conquest of Iran 1501-10 (Safavid Persia Ch 2), and Babur's Panipat in 1526.

The three dynasties are sometimes grouped as "the Islamic gunpowder empires" and the framing is genuinely useful — all three were Turkic-origin dynasties ruling Persianate court cultures, all three relied on imported gunpowder technology, and all three came to define the political-religious geography of the early-modern Islamic world.
Their relationships were almost as important as their internal histories.

Babur's Mughals were closer to the Safavids than to the Ottomans (the Mughal-Safavid border ran through Kandahar in modern Afghanistan, fought over for the next two centuries; the Mughal-Ottoman border did not exist, since the Safavids sat between them).
All three dynasties peaked in the seventeenth century.
All three declined together in the eighteenth.
The Mughal story is one of three concurrent versions of the same early-modern Islamic project.
The most successful, in terms of wealth produced and territory ruled, was the Mughal version.
The most institutionally durable was the Ottoman version, which lasted until 1922.
The most religiously revolutionary was the Safavid version, which still defines the Iranian state today.
The Mughals split the difference: enormously wealthy, enormously consequential, and ultimately the most fragile of the three.

chapters.title: Humayun's Catastrophe and Recovery
sentences: The second Mughal emperor lost the dynasty.

His name was Humayun (hoo-MAH-yoon, "the fortunate one," a name that turned out to be ironic), Babur's eldest son, born in 1508 in Kabul, and he inherited the throne in December 1530 at age twenty-two.

He held it for ten years, lost it completely to an Afghan general named Sher Shah Suri, spent fifteen years in exile in Persia and Kabul, recovered Delhi in 1555, and died six months later when he tripped on the steps of his library carrying an armful of books.
The one Mughal emperor whose biography reads like a tragicomedy.

He is also one of the most consequential, despite the disasters, because his fifteen years of Persian exile seeded the Persianate cultural orientation that would define the Mughal court for the next two centuries.
Humayun's problems started immediately.

Babur had divided the empire among his four sons in the Timurid tradition (each son got an appanage to govern, with the eldest holding the imperial title), which meant Humayun's brothers — Kamran, Askari, and Hindal — controlled large blocks of territory and could and did rebel against him repeatedly.
Kamran got Kabul and the Punjab.
Askari got Sambhal.
Hindal got the southern districts.
The brothers spent the 1530s alternating between fighting each other, fighting Humayun, and occasionally fighting jointly against external enemies.
The Mughal Empire was, in the first generation after Babur, primarily a family civil war.
The external enemies arrived quickly.
The Sultanate of Gujarat under Bahadur Shah (an unrelated namesake of the much later last Mughal emperor) attacked Mughal Malwa in 1535.
Humayun campaigned successfully against him, seized Gujarat briefly, then had to abandon it when Bahadur Shah counterattacked while Humayun was distracted by his brothers.
The pattern was characteristic.
Humayun could win battles but not consolidate gains, because he kept having to leave half his army behind to deter his brothers.
But the existential threat came from the east.

In 1537, an Afghan general from Bihar named Sher Khan Suri (later Sher Shah Suri when he claimed the imperial title) began consolidating the eastern Afghan Lodi remnants into a serious military force.

Sher Shah was perhaps the most able military commander of sixteenth-century India, and he had a personal grievance against the Mughals: his father had served under the Lodis, his career had been disrupted by Babur's conquest, and he viewed the Mughals as foreign Turkic interlopers (the irony being that the Lodi Afghans were also relatively recent foreign conquerors, but a generation longer in residence than the Mughals).
Sher Shah took Bihar, then Bengal, then started moving up the Ganges toward Delhi.
Humayun marched east to confront him.
The two armies met at Chausa on the Ganges in June 1539, and Humayun's army was destroyed in a surprise night attack.
Humayun himself escaped by swimming the Ganges (a porter helped him stay afloat and was rewarded with the throne for half a day, in one of the more peculiar Mughal anecdotes).
The two armies met again at Kannauj in May 1540, and again Humayun's army was destroyed.
This time there was no escape route.
Sher Shah's victory at Kannauj was complete; the Mughal dynasty was driven out of India entirely.
The fifteen-year Sur interregnum is worth a brief tangent, because Sher Shah Suri's administrative reforms ended up shaping the Mughal Empire that eventually returned.
Sher Shah ruled north India for five years (1540-45) before dying in a gunpowder accident at the siege of Kalinjar fort in Bundelkhand.
His successors — his son Islam Shah and various grandsons — held on for another decade until the Suri Sultanate disintegrated into civil wars between rival heirs.
But Sher Shah's five years were administratively brilliant.

He restored the Grand Trunk Road (the great east-west highway from Bengal to Kabul, with caravanserais at one-day intervals — a road in some form had existed since the Mauryan period, Maurya Empire Ch 4, but Sher Shah's restoration was the most thorough refurbishment in centuries).
He systematized the land-revenue collection on the basis of a cadastral survey, fixing the assessment at one-third of the gross produce of each holding in cash.

He standardized the silver rupee and the copper dam as the standard coinage of north India (the rupee would survive, in a direct lineal sense, into the modern Indian and Pakistani currencies of the same name).
He built the Rohtas Fort in modern Pakistan and the great octagonal Tomb of Sher Shah Suri at Sasaram, both architectural masterpieces of pre-Mughal Indo-Islamic style.
Akbar's later administrative system (Chapter 3) would borrow nearly all of this — the road, the revenue assessment, the coinage, the standardized weights and measures.
The Sur Sultanate is, in administrative terms, the immediate prequel to the Mughal Empire's classic structure.
Sher Shah was, in the long run, more important for what he gave the Mughals than for what he took from them.
Where was Humayun during all of this?
After Kannauj in 1540, Humayun fled west toward the Indus, then across the Thar Desert, then south through Sindh, then back north through Rajasthan.

The chronicles describe years of misery: small bands of loyal followers, defeats in skirmishes, near-starvation, the death of his wife's first son in infancy, the birth of his second son Akbar (AHK-bar) in 1542 in the Sindh desert at the village of Umarkot while Humayun was on the run from his own brother Kamran. (The future Akbar the Great was born in a tent at a Hindu vassal's outpost while his refugee father was being chased by his uncle.) By 1543, with all hope of reconquest from Indian soil exhausted, Humayun made the decision that would shape Mughal cultural history: he turned west and crossed into Safavid Persia.
He arrived at the Safavid court in 1544 and was received by Shah Tahmasp I (Safavid Persia Ch 3), the second Safavid Shah and one of the longest-reigning monarchs in Iranian history.
Tahmasp received Humayun with imperial honors — banquets, hunting expeditions, robes of state, formal embraces — and then made his price clear.
He would lend Humayun a Safavid army to recover his throne.

In exchange, Humayun would publicly profess Twelver Shia Islam, permit Shia symbols on Mughal coinage, and cede the strategic city of Kandahar (in modern eastern Afghanistan, the gateway between Persia and India) to the Safavids permanently.
Humayun, who was a hereditary Sunni and not theologically Shia in any meaningful sense, accepted.
The chronicles record his acceptance with various degrees of embarrassment — some sources have him tearfully agreeing, some have him cynically pragmatic, some skip the moment entirely.
The terms were what they were.
Humayun went through whatever public motions Tahmasp required.
The Safavid loan of 12,000 troops and a senior commander followed.
The recovery campaign took eight years.

Humayun's Safavid-backed army recaptured Kandahar in 1545, immediately handed it over to Tahmasp's representative as agreed (and almost as immediately tried to reclaim it, since the actual cession had not been popular at the Mughal household), and then turned east into Afghanistan.
Kabul was held by Humayun's brother Kamran, who had been quasi-independent throughout the interregnum and who fought a long and bitter war against Humayun's reentry into the family lands.

The campaign for Kabul lasted from 1545 to 1553, with Kamran captured, blinded, and exiled to Mecca in the end. (The blinding of brothers was a Mughal innovation Humayun introduced reluctantly and that his successors would use freely; he reportedly wept when Kamran was blinded but accepted that he could not leave a politically dangerous brother alive and intact.) By 1555, with Kabul secure and the Suri Sultanate visibly disintegrating into civil war between rival Suri claimants, Humayun was finally in a position to attempt the reconquest of India.
He marched east through the Punjab, defeated a Suri army at Sirhind in June 1555, and entered Delhi in July of the same year.
The dynasty was back.
Humayun had done it — improbably, after fifteen years of exile — and at age forty-seven was poised to begin the actual rebuilding of the empire his father had founded.
He was emperor for six months.
On January 24, 1556, Humayun was descending the steep stairs of his library at Sher Mandal in Delhi (the library Sher Shah Suri had built and Humayun had reclaimed) carrying an armful of books.
The muezzin called the prayer; Humayun, devout, paused on the step to kneel; he caught his foot in his robe; he fell down the stone stairs; he hit his head and never regained consciousness.
He died three days later.

The dynasty's improbable recovery, the fifteen years of exile, the desert-tent birth of Akbar, the Persian alliance, the family civil wars, and the painstaking eight-year reconquest all ended in a fatal trip down a flight of stairs.
The family chronicler Gulbadan Begum (Humayun's half-sister) recorded the death with a kind of stunned simplicity: he stumbled, he fell, he died.

The British historian Stanley Lane-Poole would write four centuries later, in a sentence that has become famous in Mughal historiography: "He stumbled out of life as he had stumbled through it." The judgment is unfair to Humayun, who held the dynasty together against extraordinary odds and recovered the throne after a defeat that would have ended any other dynastic claim, but it captures something true about the texture of his life.
He was unlucky in ways that were genuinely his fault and in ways that were not, and the death by stairs is the perfect coda.
Humayun's Persian exile shaped the Mughal Empire for the next two centuries, in ways that were not yet visible at his death.

The most direct effect was institutional: a wave of Persian scholars, painters, calligraphers, architects, and administrators followed Humayun back to India in 1555, drawn by his patronage and by the promise of imperial employment.

Two of these were the painters Mir Sayyid Ali and Abd al-Samad, both trained at the Safavid royal atelier in Tabriz under the master Bihzad (the dominant Persian miniature painter of the late Timurid and early Safavid courts, Timurid Empire Ch 7).
The two of them set up the Mughal painting workshop under Humayun and trained the founding generation of Mughal court painters, including the masters who would work under Akbar (Chapter 3).
The greatest visual art tradition of pre-modern India was seeded by two Safavid refugees Humayun brought back.
The second effect was cultural-linguistic.

Persian had been the administrative language of the Delhi Sultanate (Delhi Sultanate Ch 6) and would have been the Mughal court language anyway, but Humayun's exile turned Persian from "the language of administration" into "the language of high culture." The Mughal court read Persian poetry, wrote Persian memoirs, commissioned Persian historical chronicles, and conducted formal correspondence in elaborate Persian rhetoric, for the next two and a half centuries.
The Mughal-Safavid cultural relationship (geopolitical rivals, cultural cousins) was established by Humayun's fifteen-year residence at Tahmasp's court.
Even Aurangzeb, the most religiously orthodox of the Mughals (Chapter 6), wrote his memoirs in Persian and corresponded in Persian rhetoric with the Safavid Shahs.
The third effect was architectural.

Humayun's Tomb at Delhi — built by Humayun's widow Hamida Banu Begum in 1572, designed by the Persian architect Mirak Mirza Ghiyas, modeled directly on Timurid royal tomb traditions — was the first great Mughal architectural project and the model for everything that followed.

Its red sandstone-and-white marble construction, its central domed chamber, its quartered chahar bagh garden setting, its octagonal floor plan — all of these became the template for Mughal imperial architecture from Humayun's Tomb (1572) through Akbar's Tomb at Sikandra (1613), through the Tomb of Itimad-ud-Daulah at Agra (1628), and finally through the Taj Mahal itself (1653, Chapter 5).
Without Humayun's Persian exile, there would be no Mughal architectural style as the world recognizes it.
The Taj Mahal is, in a real architectural-genealogical sense, the great-great-granddaughter of Humayun's stairs.
What Humayun left to Akbar was a small empire with a cultural orientation.
The actual territorial inheritance was modest: Delhi, Agra, parts of the Punjab, and a thin corridor of northern Indian land.
The Suri Sultanate's collapse meant most of the eastern Sultanate territories were up for grabs.
Most of the provincial Sultanates (Gujarat, Malwa, Bengal, the Deccan Sultanates) were independent.
Vijayanagara was at peak in the south.
The Mughal portion of India in 1556 was perhaps a quarter of what it would be at Akbar's death in 1605.
But Akbar was thirteen years old in January 1556 when his father died.
The dynasty's survival depended on the regency that would now have to govern the empire on his behalf.
The next chapter is mostly about how that regency, then the adult Akbar, took the small inheritance Humayun left and built it into the wealthiest empire in the world.
Cross-civ check: Humayun's recovery and death (1555-56) coincided with several globally significant moments.
Charles V of the Holy Roman Empire abdicated in 1556, the year Humayun died, splitting the Habsburg Empire between his son Philip II of Spain and his brother Ferdinand I of Austria.
Suleiman the Magnificent of the Ottoman Empire was mid-reign; the Ottoman peak was just past (Ottoman Empire Ch 6).
Ivan the Terrible of Russia was conquering Kazan (1552) and Astrakhan (1556) — bringing the Russian state to the Caspian for the first time.
Mary I of England was in the second year of her brief Catholic restoration; the Protestant Reformation was visibly destabilizing northern Europe.
The Ming Dynasty in China was about to suffer the great earthquake of 1556 in Shaanxi (the deadliest earthquake in recorded human history, perhaps 830,000 deaths).

Akbar's accession, in this context, was a small event in a globally turbulent year — but the dynasty he was about to build would, within fifty years, become one of the largest economies on the planet.

chapters.title: Akbar the Great
sentences: The thirteen-year-old emperor who succeeded Humayun in 1556 ruled for forty-nine years.
He expanded the Mughal Empire from a thin north Indian corridor into a state covering most of the subcontinent.
He was illiterate (the historians are confident on this point — Akbar could not read) but ran one of the most sophisticated state administrations in the early-modern world.

He abolished the jizya poll tax on non-Muslims, married Rajput princesses, founded a syncretic religion that was personal devotion and state propaganda in equal measure, and built Fatehpur Sikri — a complete planned royal city that he abandoned after fourteen years because it ran out of water.
He is, by consensus of modern scholarship, the most consequential pre-modern Indian ruler since Ashoka eighteen centuries earlier.
He is also one of the more contested figures in modern South Asian history.
To Indian secular historians, Akbar is the model of pluralistic governance — the Hindu-Muslim synthesis, the religious tolerance, the integration of the Rajput nobility into Mughal service.
To Hindu nationalists, the same record looks different — a foreign Muslim monarch whose tolerance was self-serving political calculation rather than principled pluralism.
To Pakistani historians, Akbar is a slightly embarrassing ancestor — too syncretic, too friendly to Hindus, insufficiently Islamic.
The historical record genuinely supports all three readings, depending on what you emphasize.
What no one disputes is that Akbar's forty-nine-year reign produced the institutional structure of the Mughal Empire.

Everything that came afterward — Jahangir's painting court, Shah Jahan's monumental architecture, Aurangzeb's imperial overreach, the whole eighteenth-century decline — happened inside the political and administrative system Akbar built.
Bairam Khan (BAY-ram khahn, the Turkmen general who had served Babur and Humayun) was Akbar's regent for the first four years of the reign.

He was an able commander and a loyal one — without Bairam Khan, the dynasty would not have survived 1556 — but he was also forty-five years older than Akbar and increasingly reluctant to hand over real power as Akbar grew up.
The first immediate crisis was a Hindu general named Hemu.
Hemu had served the Suri Sultans through their decline.

In late 1556, while the Mughal court was distracted by Humayun's death and the new regency, Hemu marched on Delhi, defeated the small Mughal garrison there, and proclaimed himself Vikramaditya — adopting an ancient Hindu imperial title (the legendary king-name from Gupta-period mythology, Gupta Empire Ch 3) and presenting himself as the restorer of Hindu rule at Delhi after three and a half centuries of Muslim sultans.
His month-long reign was the most serious Hindu political claim to Delhi the Sultanate-Mughal era ever produced.
Bairam Khan and the boy Akbar marched south to confront him.
The two armies met at Panipat on November 5, 1556 — the same plain where Babur had defeated Ibrahim Lodi thirty years earlier.
The Second Battle of Panipat was decided when an arrow struck Hemu in the eye while he was leading from the front.
He fell unconscious; his army, demoralized, broke and fled.
The Mughals captured Hemu, brought him before Akbar, and Bairam Khan offered the boy emperor the symbolic ritual of striking the enemy's neck (a Mughal coming-of-age ceremony of sorts).
Akbar, according to the chronicles, refused to strike a wounded man; Bairam Khan then beheaded Hemu himself.
The execution was in the standard sixteenth-century pattern; the boy emperor's reluctance was reportedly noted at the time as a sign of unusual character.
By 1560, Akbar was eighteen and ready to govern in his own right.
He dismissed Bairam Khan with elaborate honors, sent him on the Hajj pilgrimage, and ruled directly.
Bairam Khan never reached Mecca.
He was assassinated en route in Gujarat by an Afghan with a personal grudge from a long-ago military campaign.

Akbar absorbed Bairam Khan's young son Abdul Rahim Khan-i-Khanan into his own household; Abdul Rahim grew up to become one of the great Mughal nobles of Akbar's reign and a celebrated Hindi-Persian bilingual poet.
Akbar's first major political innovation was the Rajput marriage alliance.
In 1562, Akbar married a princess of the Kachhwaha Rajput dynasty of Amber (modern Jaipur in Rajasthan).
The bride was the daughter of the Raja of Amber, Bharmal — a relatively minor Rajput ruler who had decided that submission to Mughal authority was preferable to resistance.
The marriage was the first of many.

Over the next four decades, Akbar married princesses from most of the senior Rajput houses (Amber, Bikaner, Jaisalmer, Marwar) and integrated the Rajput princes themselves into the Mughal nobility as senior mansabdars (ranked imperial officers).
The Rajput rulers retained their own kingdoms, paid tribute and provided military service to the Mughal Emperor, and sent their daughters to the imperial harem.
Their sons served as senior Mughal generals — most famously Raja Man Singh I of Amber, who commanded Akbar's eastern campaigns and rose to be one of the highest-ranking nobles in the empire.
The political significance of the Rajput alliance was enormous.

The Rajputs were the most formidable Hindu military power in north India — they had resisted the Delhi Sultanate for three centuries (Delhi Sultanate Ch 7), and Babur had defeated but not subdued Rana Sanga (Chapter 1).
By integrating them as Mughal allies, Akbar transformed his most dangerous potential opponents into his most reliable military lieutenants.
The Mughal armies that conquered Gujarat (1573), Bengal (1576), and Sindh (1591) were as Rajput as they were Turkic-Persian.
The cultural significance was equally large.
The Akbar-era Mughal court became the first major pre-modern Indian state to systematically integrate Hindu and Muslim elites into a single political class.
Hindu princes attended Mughal court ceremonies.
Hindu deities appeared in Mughal court paintings.

Persian-language Mughal poetry was matched by Hindi-language Bhakti devotional poetry composed and performed at the same court (Akbar's court poet Tulsidas wrote the Hindi Ramcharitmanas, the most influential vernacular retelling of the Ramayana in north Indian Hinduism).
The Hindi-Persian-Turkic-Sanskrit cultural synthesis the Delhi Sultanate had begun (Delhi Sultanate Ch 6) reached its institutional climax under Akbar.
The Hindu-nationalist counter-reading of all this is that Akbar's tolerance was political calculation rather than principled inclusion.
The principle is moot.

What matters is that the political calculation was systematic, durable, and effective enough to govern a Hindu majority for fifty years through a Hindu-Muslim ruling coalition — which no previous Indian Muslim state had managed at this scale.
The jizya abolition in 1564 was the single boldest religious-political move of Akbar's reign.
The jizya was the per-capita tax on non-Muslim subjects that Islamic states had collected since the early caliphates.

The doctrinal justification was that non-Muslims under Muslim rule were dhimmis (protected subjects) who paid the tax in exchange for the state's protection of their religious freedom and exemption from military service.
In practice, the jizya was both a revenue source and a status marker — it formally distinguished the Muslim minority (full subjects) from the Hindu majority (subordinate but tolerated).
The Delhi Sultanate had collected the jizya throughout its 320 years.
Akbar abolished it.
The order went out in 1564, eight years into his reign, while he was still consolidating his rule.
The orthodox Sunni clergy (the ulama) at Delhi and Agra protested loudly.
The decision lost the state a meaningful revenue stream.
It also signaled, unmistakably, that the Mughal Empire was redefining its relationship with its non-Muslim subjects.
Hindus were no longer dhimmis paying for the privilege of practicing their religion in a Muslim state.
They were equal subjects of the Mughal emperor, owing the same revenue obligations and entitled to the same civil status as the Muslim minority.
This was, for sixteenth-century Islamic political theory, radical.
No previous major Islamic state had done it on this scale.
The orthodox response was that Akbar was not really a Muslim — that he had abandoned Sharia for personal preference.

The Fatawa-i-Alamgiri that Aurangzeb would commission a century later (Chapter 6) explicitly reversed the abolition; Aurangzeb reimposed the jizya in 1679 as part of his return to orthodox Sunni state policy.

The hundred-fifteen-year window of jizya non-collection (1564-1679) is the institutional core of what later historians have called the "Mughal Hindu-Muslim synthesis." Both its existence and its later reversal are central to understanding Mughal religious policy.
Fatehpur Sikri is the other great Akbar-era project that requires its own treatment.
In 1571, Akbar decided to build a new royal capital next to the village of Sikri, twenty-three miles southwest of Agra.
The site had no obvious strategic or commercial logic — it was inland, away from major trade routes, and lacked a reliable water source.
The motivation was personal and religious.

Akbar had been having serious problems producing a male heir (his early sons had all died in infancy), and a Sufi saint at Sikri named Salim Chishti had reportedly predicted that the empress would bear a healthy son.
When she did — the boy who would be Jahangir, born in 1569 and named Salim for the Sufi saint — Akbar built the new capital partly as a votive offering.
The chronicles call it Fatehpur ("city of victory") to commemorate the conquest of Gujarat in 1573, but the site is identical with Sikri.
The construction took fourteen years (1571-85) and produced one of the most architecturally significant pre-modern royal cities anywhere.
The buildings were red sandstone — the local material — quarried from outcrops on the site itself.

The architectural style synthesized Persian, Timurid, and Indian elements: the Buland Darwaza (the great triumphal gateway, 175 feet high, the largest gateway in the world at the time), the Diwan-i-Khas (the audience hall with its famous central pillar with branching brackets, like a stone tree supporting the emperor's throne), the Panch Mahal (the five-story open pavilion overlooking the harem courtyards), the Tomb of Salim Chishti (the white-marble shrine of the Sufi saint, set as a jewel in the red-sandstone courtyard of the great mosque), the Anup Talao (the central pool where Akbar reportedly heard music sung by Tansen, his court musician).

Every element of the architectural vocabulary was synthesizing — Hindu temple bracket-systems applied to Islamic palace buildings, Timurid four-iwan plans redrawn in Indian sandstone, Hindu symbolic geometry framing Persian inscriptional Arabic.
And then Akbar abandoned it.
By 1585, the city was fully built, occupied, working — and the water supply had failed.
The wells were inadequate, the artificial reservoirs lost too much to evaporation, and the surrounding countryside could not produce enough food to feed the imperial court at the volume Akbar wanted.
The capital moved to Lahore for the next dozen years (Akbar campaigned in the northwest from there) and then to Agra.
Fatehpur Sikri was left intact, mostly empty, periodically used as a hunting lodge or a way-station, slowly weathering in the Indian sun for the next four hundred years.
It is now a UNESCO World Heritage site and one of the most photographed Indian monuments after the Taj Mahal.

Its architectural significance lies precisely in its abandonment — because nobody lived in Fatehpur Sikri after 1585, the buildings survived essentially unmodified, and the late-sixteenth-century Mughal architectural vocabulary is preserved there in cleaner form than anywhere else in India.
A note on the architectural choices: every major design decision at Fatehpur Sikri had a purpose.

The Buland Darwaza's enormous height was deliberate — it was meant to humble visitors, with an Arabic inscription declaring "the world is a bridge, pass over it but build no houses upon it." The branching central pillar in the Diwan-i-Khas placed the emperor literally above all four corners of the room, with senior nobles seated below him on radiating walkways.
The location of the Tomb of Salim Chishti at the center of the great mosque courtyard inverted the usual mosque hierarchy — the saint, not the prayer-niche, was the symbolic center.
The synthesis of Hindu and Islamic architectural elements was not decorative; it was a programmatic statement about the empire's identity as a Hindu-Muslim joint sovereignty under a Muslim emperor.
The most controversial of Akbar's projects was Din-i-Ilahi (deen-ee-ee-LAH-ee), the syncretic religion he founded in 1582.
The background was the Ibadat Khana ("House of Worship"), a building Akbar had constructed at Fatehpur Sikri in 1575 for religious debates.

He convened scholars from every major faith available at his court — Sunni clerics, Shia scholars, Hindu pandits, Jain monks, Parsi (Zoroastrian) priests, and Portuguese Jesuits sent up from the Goa colony — and made them argue in his presence on Thursday evenings.
The debates were minutes.
The participants prepared scholarly papers.
Akbar (illiterate, but with an extraordinary memory) listened and questioned.

The Jesuit accounts in particular — which survive in detailed letters back to Goa and Rome — describe Akbar as exceptionally intelligent, completely uninterested in conversion to any specific religion, and pointed in his theological questions.
He was clearly trying to figure out what he himself believed.
What he eventually settled on was Din-i-Ilahi, the "Divine Faith." It was not a mass religion.
It had perhaps thirty initiated members, all senior Mughal courtiers, and it never spread outside the palace.

Its tenets were a synthesis of monotheism (one God, called by various names — Allah, Brahman, Ahura Mazda — in different traditions), abstinence from beef (Hindu), abstinence from pork (Muslim), reverence for fire and the sun (Zoroastrian), abstinence from violence to small creatures (Jain), and a sun-salutation devotional practice that Akbar performed daily.
The initiated members signed loyalty oaths to Akbar personally as the spiritual master of the order.
The whole thing was, in its actual operation, a kind of personal cult of the emperor as spiritual head of state.
Modern scholarly opinion is divided on what to make of Din-i-Ilahi.
The maximum reading is that Akbar genuinely believed himself to be a syncretic religious teacher and saw the Mughal Empire as a Hindu-Muslim universal monarchy that needed a unifying state religion.
The minimum reading is that Din-i-Ilahi was a political device to bind senior nobles to him personally through religious oaths, with the syncretic content as window-dressing.

Most scholars now suggest something in between — Akbar was personally interested in the comparative study of religions, did believe in some kind of universal monotheism, and used Din-i-Ilahi simultaneously as personal devotion and as political instrument.
The religion died with him in 1605.
None of his successors maintained it.
The orthodox Sunni reaction to Din-i-Ilahi was outrage.

The most consequential opponent was Sheikh Ahmad Sirhindi (1564-1624), a Naqshbandi Sufi reformer who argued that Akbar had crossed the line from Islamic monarch to apostate, and that orthodox Sunni Islam needed to reassert itself against the Mughal court's drift toward syncretism.
Sirhindi's letters, the Maktubat-i-Imam Rabbani, became the foundational texts of South Asian Sunni revivalism for the next four centuries.
Aurangzeb's later religious policy (Chapter 6) is in some respects a Sirhindi-tradition response to the Akbarian syncretism.
The intellectual lineage from Sirhindi through Shah Waliullah of Delhi (eighteenth century) and ultimately to twentieth-century South Asian Islamist movements is direct and traceable.
Akbar's Din-i-Ilahi inadvertently produced its own institutional opposition.
The administrative genius of Akbar's reign was the mansabdari system, formalized in 1577.
Every senior Mughal officer was assigned a numerical rank (from 10 to 10,000) called a mansab (literally "rank" or "office").
The rank specified two things: the officer's salary, and the number of cavalry he was required to maintain at his own expense and bring to imperial service when summoned.

A mansabdar of 5,000, for example, drew a salary commensurate with that rank and was required to keep 5,000 cavalry ready for service. (The actual cavalry counts were sometimes adjusted — a "5,000 zat / 3,000 sawar" notation meant rank 5,000 in personal status, with an obligation of 3,000 actual horsemen, the difference being administrative gradation.) The mansabs were paid in two main forms.
Cash salaries were drawn directly from the imperial treasury.

Jagirs (jah-GEERS, land revenue assignments) gave the mansabdar the right to collect the land revenue of a specific district, in lieu of cash, with the obligation to pass on any surplus above his entitled salary back to the imperial treasury.
Jagirs were not hereditary — they were reassigned periodically, and a mansabdar might hold one jagir this year and a completely different one next year.

This nonhereditary feature was central to mansabdari design: it prevented the formation of regional landed aristocracies that could resist central authority. (The contrast with European feudalism was deliberate; medieval European kings could not reassign their dukes' fiefs the way Mughal emperors could reassign their mansabdars' jagirs.

The Mughal system preserved central control much more effectively.) The mansabdari was layered on top of Todar Mal's revenue settlement of 1582 — Akbar's finance minister Raja Todar Mal completed a comprehensive cadastral survey of agricultural land, fixed the standard land-revenue assessment at one-third of the gross produce in cash, and standardized weights, measures, and the silver rupee.
The combined system produced a remarkable fiscal-military state.
Akbar's empire could deploy more cavalry than any European or Middle Eastern state of the period.
It could collect land revenue with precision and consistency that Europe would not match until the seventeenth century.

And it tied together a multi-ethnic, multi-religious nobility (Turkic mansabdars, Persian mansabdars, Rajput mansabdars, Afghan mansabdars, occasional Indian Muslim or even Christian mansabdars) into a single chain of imperial command in a way no previous Indian state had managed.
The system survived essentially unchanged through Aurangzeb (Chapter 6) and substantially intact into the eighteenth-century decline (Chapter 7).
The British East India Company, when it took over Bengal after Plassey (Chapter 8), inherited the mansabdari machinery and modified it gradually rather than replacing it.
The institutional skeleton of the late Mughal state was substantially the institutional skeleton of early British India.
The Akbarnama is the chronicle of all this, and it deserves a paragraph of its own.

Abu'l Fazl (ah-BUL fazl, 1551-1602) was Akbar's court historian, friend, and confidant — the third of three brothers (the others were the courtier Faizi and the poet Faizi) who had served Akbar from his early reign.
Abu'l Fazl was a Persian-language scholar of extraordinary range, fluent in Sanskrit and Hindi as well as Persian and Arabic, with broad reading in Islamic philosophy and Indian religious texts.
Akbar commissioned him to write the official chronicle of the reign, and Abu'l Fazl produced a three-volume work — the Akbarnama proper — plus an appendix called the Ain-i-Akbari.
The Akbarnama is the standard narrative of Akbar's reign — campaigns, court ceremonies, religious debates, building projects, family events.
It is also, in places, a piece of imperial hagiography (Akbar appears as a near-divine ruler whose every decision is wise, every battle inevitable, every policy beneficial).
Modern scholars have to read it skeptically as a source.
