But it is also extraordinarily detailed, by far the most detailed surviving primary account of the reign, and on questions where Abu'l Fazl had no reason to lie (the routine administration, the dates of campaigns, the personnel of the court) it remains the basic factual reference.
The Ain-i-Akbari (literally "the institutions of Akbar") is more remarkable.

It is a comprehensive administrative survey of the empire — provinces, sub-provinces, districts, populations, revenue assessments, military strengths, prices of standard commodities, costs of imperial workshop products (including the price of every type of paint pigment used in the painting workshop, the wages of painters by skill rank, and a detailed list of mansabdars by name and rank).

For modern economic and administrative historians of the early-modern world, the Ain-i-Akbari is one of the most valuable single documents in existence — a detailed statistical snapshot of a major early-modern economy, produced by a contemporary administrator with access to the records.

Abu'l Fazl was assassinated in 1602 by a Rajput bandit named Vir Singh Bundela, almost certainly on the orders of Akbar's son and rival Salim (the future Jahangir, Chapter 4), who hated Abu'l Fazl as the chronicler-confidant who reinforced Akbar's preference for Salim's deceased elder brother.
Akbar mourned Abu'l Fazl publicly and never forgave Salim for the murder, though the formal reconciliation was eventually patched together.
The killing was emblematic of the late-Akbar court — the syncretic reign producing internal feuds that the imperial succession would inherit.
Akbar died at Agra on October 27, 1605.
He was sixty-three.
He had reigned for forty-nine years.

The empire he left behind extended from Kabul in the northwest, across the entire Ganges valley, south through Gujarat and Malwa, into the Deccan as far as Khandesh and northern Berar, and east to the borders of Bengal — perhaps two-thirds of the modern Indian and Pakistani territory.
The state revenue was an estimated 99 million rupees per year — by far the largest in the contemporary world, larger than the combined revenues of France, Spain, England, and the Ottoman Empire.
The imperial nobility numbered around 1,800 mansabdars, drawn from Turkic, Persian, Afghan, Rajput, and Indian Muslim families in roughly equal proportions.
The painting workshop had produced thousands of illustrated manuscripts.
The historiographical project had produced the Akbarnama and Ain-i-Akbari.
The administrative system had been rationalized and standardized to a degree no previous Indian state had achieved.

His tomb is at Sikandra, on the Agra-Delhi road, and it is one of the more architecturally peculiar Mughal monuments — a five-tiered pyramidal structure, mostly red sandstone, with a top-tier marble pavilion containing a false grave (the actual burial chamber is below ground level, the false grave above it, the architectural sleight-of-hand a standard Mughal device).

The design represents Akbar's late-reign cultural eclecticism: the lower tiers are Indo-Islamic, the upper pavilion is Hindu-derived, the inscriptions include phrases from Din-i-Ilahi alongside the Quranic verses.
It is the most visibly syncretic Mughal imperial tomb.
Whether you read that as a fitting tribute to the syncretic emperor or as the worst architectural compromise in Mughal history depends on what you think of the syncretic emperor.
Cross-civ check: Akbar (1556-1605) and Elizabeth I of England (1558-1603) were almost exact contemporaries and the comparison is genuinely instructive.
Both inherited unstable thrones at young ages (Akbar at 13, Elizabeth at 25).
Both ruled long, transformational reigns at the head of states their predecessors had nearly lost.
Both managed religious-confessional crises through pragmatic compromise rather than principled commitment (Akbar's syncretism vs.
Elizabeth's Anglican via media).
Both presided over cultural florescence (the Akbarnama and the Mughal painting workshop vs.
Shakespeare and the Elizabethan theatre).
Both were charismatic monarchs who built personal cults around themselves while running effective institutional administrations.
The economic comparison is lopsided: Akbar's empire's revenue around 1600 was roughly thirty times Elizabeth's.
India was, by every available measure of pre-modern wealth, the dominant economy of the early-modern world, with Mughal-controlled north India alone larger than any single European state.
Elizabeth's England was, by comparison, a marginal northern European principality.

The post-1600 trajectory would invert this enormously, but at the moment of Akbar's death, the wealth gap between the two crowns was as wide as the wealth gap between modern Switzerland and Bangladesh — running, this time, in the Mughal direction.

The other concurrent monarch worth comparing is Abbas I the Great of Safavid Persia (1588-1629), who reigned at the same time and on the same model — centralizing administration, religious-political assertion, monumental city-building (Akbar's Fatehpur Sikri vs.
Abbas's Isfahan, Safavid Persia Ch 4), absorption of culturally-distinct mercenary populations into the imperial military (Akbar's Rajput marriages vs.
Abbas's Caucasian ghulam corps).
The Mughal-Safavid relationship was the dominant cultural and political relationship of the early-modern Persianate world.
Akbar and Abbas exchanged embassies, gifts, painters, calligraphers, and military theorists.
Both empires reached their cultural and economic peaks in roughly the same generation.
Both would decline together a century later (Chapter 7, Safavid Persia Ch 7).
The "two great Persianate empires" is the right framework for thinking about late-sixteenth-century Mughal India — and Akbar is the figure who built the Mughal half of the equivalence.

chapters.title: Jahangir and Nur Jahan
sentences: The fourth Mughal emperor was, by the consensus of every primary source that mentions him, an addict.
His name was Salim (sah-LEEM), born in 1569 to Akbar and the Kachhwaha Rajput princess of Amber, named for the Sufi saint Salim Chishti of Sikri who had reportedly predicted his birth (Chapter 3).
He took the regnal name Jahangir (jah-hahn-GEER, "world-seizer") when he succeeded his father in 1605 at age thirty-six.
He reigned for twenty-two years, until his death in 1627.
The empire he inherited was, on paper, the largest and wealthiest state on Earth.
The empire he ruled was, in practical terms, run for most of his reign by his Persian wife Nur Jahan (noor jah-HAHN, "light of the world").
Jahangir is one of the more honest narrators of his own reign.

His memoir, the Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri, written in Persian, describes his alcohol consumption, his opium addiction, his moods, his pleasure in painting and natural history, his political decisions, and his progressive incapacity for the actual work of governance, with a candor that has no parallel in seventeenth-century royal autobiography.

He is also a more interesting cultural figure than the addict-summary suggests — Mughal painting reached its absolute peak under his patronage, the empire he inherited held together better than it had any structural reason to, and his marriage to Nur Jahan produced the most genuinely powerful Mughal empress and one of the more remarkable political partnerships in pre-modern Asian history.
But the addict description is also accurate.
He acknowledged it himself.
The reign began with a rebellion.

Salim had rebelled against Akbar in 1599-1601, partly because Akbar's clear preference was for Salim's elder brother Daniyal as heir, partly because Salim wanted real power before Akbar was ready to delegate it.
The rebellion was halfhearted — Salim set up a parallel court at Allahabad and minted his own coins for a few years, then submitted when Akbar moved against him.

Akbar forgave him, mostly because Daniyal had died of alcoholism in 1604 (the third of Akbar's three sons to die of alcohol-related causes — the other was Murad, who died at thirty in 1599) and Salim was now the only surviving heir.
The succession in 1605 was therefore uncontested but resentful.
Akbar's senior nobles distrusted Salim.
Salim distrusted Akbar's senior nobles.

The first major political event of the reign was the rebellion of Salim's eldest son Khusrau in 1606 — the eighteen-year-old grandson, briefly the candidate of an anti-Salim party at court that thought Khusrau would be a more pliable emperor, raised an army and was decisively defeated near Lahore.

Jahangir blinded Khusrau as punishment (the first use of blinding-of-rivals as Mughal succession discipline) and held him in confinement for the next sixteen years until Khusrau's eventual murder in 1622, almost certainly arranged by Jahangir's son Khurram (the future Shah Jahan, Chapter 5) to clear a rival from the succession.

This is the texture of the Jahangir-era court — succession intrigue, blinding and confinement of rival princes, periodic outbursts of paranoid violence interspersed with lengthy periods of imperial inactivity.

The empire kept running because the institutional structure Akbar had built (the mansabdari system, Todar Mal's revenue settlement, the standardized provincial administration, Chapter 3) was robust enough to function with minimal central direction.
Nur Jahan entered the story in 1611.
She was born Mehr-un-Nissa (meh-roon-NEE-sah, "sun among women") in 1577 in Kandahar to a Persian noble family that had migrated to India during Akbar's reign.
Her father Mirza Ghias Beg rose at Akbar's court to become a senior mansabdar; he received the title Itimad-ud-Daulah ("pillar of the state") and served Jahangir as chief revenue minister.
Nur Jahan was first married in 1594 to a Persian-born Mughal officer named Sher Afgan, who served as governor of Bardhaman in Bengal.
The marriage produced one daughter (Ladli Begum, who would later be married into the imperial family for political reasons).

In 1607, Sher Afgan was killed in a confrontation with the Mughal governor of Bengal, Qutb-ud-din Khan Koka, in circumstances that Mughal sources describe variously and that have been the subject of historical speculation ever since (was Sher Afgan plotting rebellion?
Was the killing arranged by Jahangir to free his eye for Mehr-un-Nissa?
The honest answer is that the surviving evidence is ambiguous).
Mehr-un-Nissa was widowed at thirty and brought to the imperial harem at Agra as a lady-in-waiting to Jahangir's stepmother.
She and Jahangir met in 1611 — accounts vary on the circumstances, but one version has them meeting at a palace bazaar where Jahangir came across her selling textiles.
They married in May 1611.
She was thirty-four; Jahangir was forty-two.
He gave her the title Nur Mahal ("light of the palace") and within a few years promoted her to Nur Jahan ("light of the world").
What followed was the most powerful position any Mughal empress would ever hold.
By 1614, Nur Jahan was effectively running the empire.
Jahangir's increasing alcohol and opium consumption made him incapable of sustained administrative work.
He still presided at court ceremonies, still made the formal decisions, still received ambassadors and dispensed justice in the jharokha-i-darshan (the ceremonial window appearance).
But the actual flow of decisions — appointment of mansabdars, allocation of jagirs, military planning, diplomatic correspondence — passed through Nur Jahan's apartments.
She convened her own council of senior nobles (her father Itimad-ud-Daulah, her brother Asaf Khan, several other Persian-faction officers).
She issued imperial orders in her own name through a stamped seal called a mohr that Jahangir had granted her.
She struck imperial coinage with her name on it — a privilege no other Mughal woman ever received, and an unmistakable signal of her actual sovereign authority.
She negotiated military deployments.
She arranged dynastic marriages.
The most consequential of those marriages was Khurram (the future Shah Jahan) to Nur Jahan's niece Mumtaz Mahal in 1612 (Chapter 5).

The marriage initially aligned Nur Jahan and Khurram politically, but the alignment broke down in the 1620s when Nur Jahan tried to secure the succession for her own son-in-law (the marginal prince Shahryar, married to Nur Jahan's daughter from her first marriage).
The Khurram-vs-Shahryar succession struggle dominated the last years of Jahangir's reign, with Nur Jahan steadily losing influence to Khurram's faction.
The political fact of Nur Jahan's de facto rule is well-documented.
She was the only Mughal empress to wield this kind of executive power.
The structural reason was Jahangir's incapacity, but the personal reason was Nur Jahan's own competence — by every contemporary account, she was a better administrator than Jahangir had ever been.

The English ambassador Sir Thomas Roe (who arrived at the Mughal court in 1615 and stayed three years, see below) wrote home that the empress "governs him and wynds him up at her pleasure," with a mixture of bemusement and reluctant respect.
The dramatic high point of Nur Jahan's career came in 1626, when a rebellious noble named Mahabat Khan kidnapped Jahangir on a riverbank during a march from Lahore to Kabul.
Nur Jahan, traveling separately with her own contingent, organized an immediate counter-attack.

She personally rode an armored elephant into the river to attempt a rescue (the elephant was wounded, the rescue failed), then negotiated for several months until she could engineer Jahangir's release through a combination of force and bribery.

The episode is in every contemporary chronicle — a fifty-year-old empress leading an armed rescue of the captured emperor — and it captures something genuinely impressive about Nur Jahan as a political figure.
Mughal painting reached its peak under Jahangir's patronage, and the achievement deserves its own paragraph.

The painting workshop Akbar had founded under the two refugee Tabriz masters Mir Sayyid Ali and Abd al-Samad (Chapter 3) had produced thousands of illustrated manuscripts during Akbar's reign — the Hamzanama (over 1,400 illustrations of the legendary tales of Hamza ibn Abdul-Muttalib, Chapter 3), the Akbarnama paintings, illustrated Persian translations of Hindu epics.
The Akbar-era style was crowded, narrative, polychromatic, with every painting telling a story across multiple figures.
Jahangir's painting was different.
He preferred single-figure compositions — naturalistic portraits of individual courtiers, animal and bird studies, landscape studies.

The court masters of his reign — Ustad Mansur (the great animal-painter), Bishan Das (the great portraitist), Abu'l Hasan (the favored personal painter, whom Jahangir titled Nadir-uz-Zaman, "wonder of the age"), Manohar Das, Govardhan, several others — produced work that was technically extraordinary by any standard.
Mansur's painting of the dodo (the extinct flightless bird from Mauritius, brought to the Mughal court via Portuguese traders) is the most accurate surviving image of a living dodo.
His painting of a Bengal florican is a study in feather-by-feather realism that anticipates eighteenth-century European natural-history illustration.
Bishan Das's portrait of Shah Abbas the Safavid (drawn during a Mughal embassy to Isfahan in 1613, see Safavid Persia Ch 4) is one of the few life-from-life portraits of Abbas that survives.
The Jahangir-era painters worked in a deliberate ethnographic-natural-historical vein because Jahangir himself was a serious natural historian.
The Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri contains detailed observations on every region of India, its plants, its animals, its peoples, with the precision of a working naturalist.
He measured the size of the imperial menagerie's lion.
He noted the reproductive cycle of the saras crane.
He recorded the date of every fruit's ripening at the Kashmir summer palace.
The Mughal painting workshop served his curiosity.

It also served the imperial-political purpose of cataloguing the empire — the painting of a particular Persian noble at the Mughal court, executed as an accurate ethnographic portrait, was simultaneously an artwork and a political-intelligence document.

The peak was probably the years 1615-25, when the workshop combined Mansur's natural-history studies, Bishan Das's portraiture, and a group of younger painters working on smaller-format album leaves with European compositional influence (Jesuit missionaries had brought European prints to the Mughal court in the 1590s, and Mughal painters absorbed European techniques of perspective, modeling, and shading without abandoning the Persian-Indian color sense).
The Jahangir albums — illustrated personal anthologies the emperor compiled over decades — are among the most prized objects in modern Islamic art collections.
The mention of European influence is worth pausing on.
The Jesuits at the Mughal court (mostly Portuguese and Spanish, sent up from the Goa colony from the 1590s onward) brought prints of European paintings, particularly of Christian religious subjects.
Mughal painters studied them carefully.
The European technique of three-dimensional shading and atmospheric perspective entered Mughal painting in the early seventeenth century and never left.

By the late Jahangir period, Mughal portraits of courtiers and family members combined Persian-style flat color planes with European-style modeling and shadow — a unique synthesis that exists in no other Asian or Middle Eastern painting tradition.
Mughal painting is one of the very few early-modern visual cultures that absorbed European technique without becoming derivative.
Sir Thomas Roe's embassy is the third major topic of the Jahangir reign.
Roe was a courtier in the service of James I of England (the same James I who had commissioned the King James Bible translation in 1611, two years before Roe's mission was conceived).

The English East India Company (founded 1600) had established its first Indian factory at Surat in 1612 after defeating a Portuguese fleet at the Battle of Swally, and the Company directors wanted formal commercial privileges from the Mughal court — the right to trade duty-free, the right to maintain factories at additional ports, protection from Portuguese harassment.
James I dispatched Roe in 1615 as the first formal English ambassador to the Mughal court, with instructions to negotiate a treaty.
Roe arrived at Surat in September 1615 and traveled overland to Ajmer, where Jahangir was holding court at the time.
He spent the next three years (1615-18) at the imperial court, traveling with it as it moved between Ajmer, Mandu, and Ahmedabad.
He kept a detailed journal that survives as the first sustained English-language description of Mughal India — and one of the most valuable European sources on the Jahangir court generally.

He described the daily ceremonies of the jharokha-i-darshan (the ceremonial window appearance, where the emperor showed himself to subjects each morning), the elaborate court receptions, the food, the weather, the inadequacy of the English diplomatic gifts (Roe had brought a portrait of an English nobleman, several mediocre European prints, a coach, and a large quantity of red wine — none of which much impressed a court accustomed to receiving Safavid manuscripts and Portuguese telescopes).
Roe failed to achieve a formal treaty.

The Mughal court, accustomed to viewing all foreigners as petitioners regardless of their actual political standing, was not interested in formal reciprocal treaties with a small island kingdom on the western edge of the world.
But Roe did secure verbal commitments and firmans (imperial decrees) granting the East India Company commercial privileges at Surat and Ahmedabad.

The privileges were enough for the Company to expand its operations significantly over the following decades — additional factories at Madras (1639), Bombay (acquired from the Portuguese as part of Catherine of Braganza's dowry to Charles II in 1668), and Calcutta (1690).
The Roe embassy is one of those moments in early-modern history that look much more important in retrospect than they did at the time.

To Jahangir's court, Roe was a marginally interesting curiosity — a tall thin Englishman who drank too much red wine and could be persuaded into the embarrassing diplomatic-protocol mistake of bowing too low.
To the East India Company, Roe's three years secured the operational base from which the Company would (a hundred and forty years later, in 1757) take over Bengal at Plassey (Chapter 8).
The embassy is the formal beginning of the Anglo-Mughal relationship that would, over six generations, end the Mughal dynasty.
The last years of Jahangir's reign were dominated by the succession struggle.
By 1623, Khurram (the future Shah Jahan) had emerged as the most able of Jahangir's sons.
He had successfully campaigned in the Deccan against the Nizam Shahi Sultanate of Ahmadnagar (1616-21), demonstrating military competence that none of his brothers could match.
Jahangir formally designated him heir-apparent and gave him the title Shah Jahan ("king of the world").
But Nur Jahan's preferred candidate was the much weaker Shahryar, married to Nur Jahan's own daughter, who would have left actual power in Nur Jahan's hands well past Jahangir's death.
Khurram-Shah Jahan, understanding the threat, rebelled against his father in 1622.
The rebellion lasted four years, with Khurram losing battles, retreating to Bengal, then to the Deccan, and eventually being driven into formal exile near the Coromandel Coast.

The Mughal armies that fought against him were commanded by Mahabat Khan (the same noble who would later kidnap Jahangir in 1626) and by Asaf Khan (Nur Jahan's brother, who was actually Khurram's father-in-law and who switched sides repeatedly during the conflict).

The rebellion ended with Khurram's submission and reconciliation in 1626, mostly because Jahangir's health was visibly failing and Asaf Khan had calculated correctly that Khurram would be the eventual winner.
Jahangir died at Bhimbar in Kashmir on October 28, 1627, age fifty-eight.
The cause was almost certainly a combination of decades of alcohol abuse, opium addiction, and the asthma he had suffered from since childhood.
Nur Jahan, immediately after his death, attempted to install Shahryar on the throne.
Asaf Khan, having already opened communications with Khurram, betrayed his sister, seized Shahryar at Lahore, blinded him, and held the throne open for Khurram's arrival from the Deccan.
Shahryar and Khurram's other surviving rival brothers were executed within weeks of Khurram's accession.
The brutal succession was the new Mughal pattern that would continue, in even bloodier form, into the Aurangzeb generation (Chapter 6).
Nur Jahan, after losing the succession struggle, retired to Lahore on a generous imperial pension.

She lived another eighteen years, designing her father Itimad-ud-Daulah's tomb (the small white-marble jewel-box at Agra that pioneered the marble-and-pietra-dura technique perfected at the Taj Mahal a generation later), composing Persian poetry, and managing the substantial estate Jahangir had left her.
She died at Lahore in 1645, age sixty-eight, and was buried in the same tomb-complex as her parents.
Her grave is small and unornamented, with a simple inscription she reportedly composed herself: "On the grave of poor Nur Jahan, neither lamp nor rose.
Neither does butterfly's wing burn, nor sing nightingale." The tone of resigned acceptance is characteristic.
So is the rhetorical dignity.
Nur Jahan was, to the end, more eloquent than any of the men around her.
What Jahangir left to Shah Jahan was, on paper, the empire at peak.
The territorial extent in 1627 was essentially what Akbar had left in 1605, slightly modified — gains in Bengal and minor losses in the Deccan, but the same basic shape.
The institutional structure (mansabdari, jagir system, revenue assessment) was working, despite the emperor's incapacity, because Akbar had built it well.
The painting workshop was at peak.
The Persianate court culture was the most sophisticated in the world.
The state revenue had grown to perhaps 120 million rupees per year, an increase over Akbar's 99 million.
But the institutional integrity had been quietly hollowing out.
The reign had seen no major administrative reforms (Akbar had built the system; Jahangir had inherited it without modifying it).

The Deccan situation had deteriorated — the Nizam Shahi Sultanate of Ahmadnagar had outmaneuvered Mughal forces, and a Hindu general named Malik Ambar (an Ethiopian-born Habshi who had risen through the Ahmadnagar military hierarchy to become its de facto regent) had built an effective resistance using guerrilla warfare and revenue-assignment techniques borrowed from the Mughals themselves.
The European trading companies (English, Dutch, French) had established footholds along the coasts that would become problems in the next century.
The succession crisis had set the precedent that brothers would kill brothers without restraint.
Shah Jahan inherited all of this.
The next chapter is mostly about what he chose to do with it — which was, primarily, to build.
Cross-civ check: Jahangir's reign (1605-27) overlapped with the Thirty Years War in central Europe (1618-48), one of the most destructive religious-political conflicts in European history.

Galileo Galilei was conducting his telescope observations and writing his major works (the Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems would be published in 1632, just after Jahangir's death, and immediately suppressed by the Inquisition).
Shakespeare died in 1616.
Cervantes died in 1616 the same week.
Tokugawa Ieyasu in Japan won the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600 and founded the Tokugawa Shogunate (Edo Japan Ch 1) in 1603, just before Jahangir's accession.
Ming China under the Wanli Emperor was sliding toward the dynastic collapse that would come with the Manchu invasion in 1644.
The Ottoman Empire under Ahmed I and Murad IV was at the start of its long decline (Ottoman Empire Ch 6).
Safavid Persia was at peak under Abbas the Great (Safavid Persia Ch 4).

The early seventeenth century was an era of major cultural production across Eurasia — and Jahangir's Mughal court, with its painting workshop and its Persianate scholarship and its silken-textiled imperial wealth, was one of the major centers of that production, even when its emperor was too high on opium to actually run the place.

chapters.title: Shah Jahan and the Peacock Throne
sentences: The fifth Mughal emperor built the Taj Mahal, founded a new capital city named after himself, commissioned a gem-encrusted golden throne so valuable it became one of the wonders of the world, and was eventually imprisoned by his own son in a small apartment with a window facing the tomb of the wife the Taj Mahal had been built for.
The reign is the architectural climax of the Mughal Empire and the moment when the institutional cracks of the eighteenth-century decline first become visible in retrospect.
His name was Khurram, born in 1592 in Lahore to Jahangir and Princess Manmati of Marwar (a Rathore Rajput princess, demonstrating the Akbar-era marriage policy at work, Chapter 3).
He took the regnal name Shah Jahan (shah jah-HAHN, "king of the world") that Jahangir had granted him for his Deccan campaigns in 1617.
He took the throne in 1628, ruled for thirty years, was deposed by his son Aurangzeb in 1658, and lived another eight years under house arrest in Agra Fort before dying in 1666.
The thirty years of his actual reign (1628-58) were spent doing two things: campaigning in the Deccan to consolidate Mughal control of central India, and building.
The campaigning was indecisive — the Deccan never quite came under stable Mughal control, and the wars consumed enormous resources.
The building was definitive.
The architectural projects of Shah Jahan's reign produced the canonical visual icons of Mughal civilization.
The Taj Mahal alone is, by most measures, the most famous building constructed anywhere in the world during the seventeenth century.
The reign opened with the standard Mughal succession purge.

Within weeks of taking the throne in February 1628, Shah Jahan ordered the execution of every male relative who could plausibly claim the throne — his blinded brother Shahryar (executed by strangulation in February 1628), his cousins Daniyal's two surviving sons, his uncle Khusrau's surviving son.
The total was at least eight relatives killed within a few months.

Mughal succession discipline had hardened from Akbar's relatively restrained 1556 (Hemu killed, the rebellious nephews mostly absorbed) and Jahangir's 1605-27 (Khusrau blinded but kept alive for sixteen years) to Shah Jahan's 1628 (everyone who could conceivably claim the throne killed within months).

The pattern would harden further under Aurangzeb (Chapter 6) and would help explain why the post-Aurangzeb succession crises (Chapter 7) were so destructive — by then, the executive machinery for killing potential heirs had been so refined that each succession produced a wholesale purge of the imperial family.
With his rivals dead, Shah Jahan turned to the Deccan.

He had spent the late 1610s and early 1620s campaigning there, knew the political-military terrain, and viewed the unfinished Akbar-and-Jahangir-era project of southern conquest as his immediate priority.
The campaign was protracted.
The Sultanate of Ahmadnagar was annexed in 1636.
Bijapur and Golconda were forced into tributary status in 1636 but remained effectively independent for another fifty years.
The Maratha resistance under Shahji Bhonsle (the father of Shivaji, Chapter 6) was ongoing throughout.
The Deccan front absorbed Mughal armies, Mughal revenue, and Mughal attention for the entire reign without producing decisive results.
The Persian-Safavid frontier was also active.
Kandahar, the city Humayun had ceded to Shah Tahmasp in 1545 (Chapter 2), had returned to Mughal control under Akbar and was now contested again with Shah Abbas II (Safavid Persia Ch 7).

The city changed hands four times during Shah Jahan's reign — Mughal in 1638, Safavid in 1649 (after Shah Jahan's third son Aurangzeb was defeated by Abbas II in three successive battles), Mughal in attempted recoveries in 1652 and 1653, both of which failed.
The Mughal-Safavid rivalry over Kandahar was one of the great expensive unwinnable wars of the seventeenth century.
Then there was Mumtaz Mahal.
Arjumand Banu Begum (better known by her later title Mumtaz Mahal, "the chosen one of the palace") was Nur Jahan's niece — daughter of Asaf Khan, Nur Jahan's brother.
She was born in 1593 to a Persian noble family at Agra.

She was betrothed to Khurram in 1607, when she was fourteen and he was fifteen, and the marriage took place in 1612 with Nur Jahan's enthusiastic support (the marriage was the political instrument by which Nur Jahan tied Khurram into her own faction at court, Chapter 4).

Mumtaz Mahal was Khurram-Shah Jahan's third wife and, by every contemporary account, his only one of any emotional significance — the other two were political marriages with whom he had no recorded sustained relationship.
The marriage produced fourteen children in nineteen years.

Seven survived to adulthood, including Shah Jahan's four eventually-feuding sons: Dara Shukoh (the Sufi-scholar heir), Shah Shuja (the Bengal governor), Aurangzeb (the eventual victor of the succession war), and Murad Bakhsh (the youngest, briefly Aurangzeb's ally before being killed).

The sheer number of pregnancies is itself notable — even by seventeenth-century royal standards, fourteen pregnancies in nineteen years is an extraordinary toll on a body, and modern medical historians have suggested it directly contributed to Mumtaz Mahal's eventual death in childbirth.
She died at Burhanpur in the Deccan on June 17, 1631, giving birth to her fourteenth child (a daughter, who survived).
Shah Jahan was on campaign with her, as was the Mughal custom — the imperial harem traveled with the emperor on long campaigns.
He had been married to her for nineteen years.

His grief was reportedly extraordinary — he went into formal mourning for two years, refused to attend public ceremonies, gave up music and the imperial atelier's productions, dressed in white (the South Asian color of mourning), and reportedly aged visibly within months of her death.
He emerged from mourning in 1633 with a single dominant project: he would build her a tomb that would be remembered forever.
The Taj Mahal is the project, and it deserves a sustained treatment.
Construction began in 1632 at Agra, on the south bank of the Yamuna river, on a plot of land that had previously belonged to Jai Singh I of Amber (the Rajput noble in Mughal service).

The chief architect is generally identified as Ustad Ahmad Lahori (a Mughal court architect whose name appears in the imperial records), with the design probably the product of a team rather than a single individual.

The construction took approximately twenty-two years (1632-53), employed a workforce variously estimated at 20,000 to 50,000 (sources disagree), and was financed entirely from imperial revenue rather than from any single province's tax base — a deliberate choice that prevented any one region from being economically devastated by the project.
The white marble came from the Makrana quarries in Rajasthan, transported approximately 220 miles by ox-cart to Agra.

The semi-precious stones for the inlay work came from across Asia: jade and crystal from Central Asia, lapis lazuli from Afghanistan, sapphires from Sri Lanka, jasper from the Punjab, turquoise from Tibet, amethyst from Persia, malachite from Russia, mother-of-pearl from the Red Sea coast.

The total is estimated at twenty-eight different types of stone in the inlay work, fitted with the pietra dura technique that the Itimad-ud-Daulah tomb (built 1622-28 under Nur Jahan's supervision, Chapter 4) had pioneered in India.

The architectural design is, in its broad outlines, the standard Mughal garden-tomb plan — central domed mausoleum on a raised plinth, four symmetrical minarets at the corners, formal chahar bagh garden quartered by water channels, twin secondary buildings flanking the tomb (a mosque on the west, a guest house on the east, both red sandstone).
The plan derives directly from Humayun's Tomb of 1572 (Chapter 2), which derived from Timurid royal-tomb traditions (Timurid Empire Ch 7).

What makes the Taj different is the execution: the entire central building is white marble (Humayun's Tomb is mostly red sandstone with marble accents), the pietra dura inlay covers virtually every interior surface, the proportions of the dome are slightly elongated (taller and more pointed than the Humayun-Tomb dome) for visual emphasis, and the water-channel-and-reflecting-pool design is calculated so that the building's reflection appears in the central pool when viewed from the entrance gateway.
Every architectural decision was purposeful.
The minarets lean very slightly outward (about three degrees), so that in an earthquake they would fall away from the main building rather than onto it.

The central dome is double-shelled — an inner dome at functional ceiling height, an outer dome at the visually-dominant exterior height — to balance the proportions of the interior and exterior spaces.
The Quranic inscriptions in elegant calligraphic script around the entrance arches are subtly enlarged toward the top so that they appear visually consistent in size when viewed from the ground.
The garden's quadripartite plan (the four-part chahar bagh) symbolically represents the four rivers of Paradise from Islamic eschatology, with the tomb as the throne of God at the center.
The whole complex is a programmatic statement of Islamic eschatology applied to imperial mourning, with the technical execution at the limit of what early-modern construction could accomplish.
The building was substantially complete by 1648, with finishing work continuing until about 1653.
The total cost is variously estimated at 32 million rupees (a contemporary figure) to 70 million rupees (a higher modern estimate), or roughly a year's full imperial revenue.
The opportunity cost — the troops not raised, the famines not relieved, the irrigation works not built — was substantial.
Modern historians remain divided on whether the Taj Mahal was a sustainable use of imperial wealth or a self-indulgent monument that economically weakened the empire.
Both readings have evidence on their side.
The Italian-architect myth about the Taj Mahal deserves a paragraph of its own, because it is one of the more persistent pieces of misinformation about the building.

Beginning in the late nineteenth century, several British and Italian writers proposed that the Taj Mahal had been designed by an Italian architect named Geronimo Veroneo, who had been at the Mughal court in the relevant period.

The argument was based on (a) European architectural elements visible in the building, and (b) a brief mention of Veroneo in the journal of an Italian Augustinian friar named Sebastien Manrique, who passed through Agra in 1640 and reported a conversation with Veroneo in which Veroneo was credited with the Taj's design.
The Veroneo theory has been thoroughly demolished by modern scholarship.

The European elements in the building (some of the inlay work, perhaps some of the engineering of the dome) are real but secondary; the basic design is unambiguously Persianate-Timurid in its derivation.
Veroneo himself, according to other contemporary records, was a jeweler, not an architect, and the Manrique account is the only source that places him in any architectural role.

The actual Mughal court records of the construction, including the Padshahnama (the official chronicle of Shah Jahan's reign by Abdul Hamid Lahori), name Ustad Ahmad Lahori as the chief architect and identify several other Mughal court architects involved in the project, with no Veroneo credit.

The reason the Veroneo theory was popular in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries is that it served a specific political-cultural agenda — the assumption that a building this beautiful must have been designed by Europeans, since (the implicit logic ran) South Asians could not have produced something this sophisticated independently.
The theory was a piece of orientalist projection, not a serious historical claim.
Modern scholarship rejects it without ambiguity.
The Taj Mahal is a Mughal-Persian-Indian product.
The architects were South Asian (Ustad Ahmad Lahori was a Punjabi Persian-trained architect; the rest of the team was a similar mix).
The European contribution was modest at most.
The Red Fort of Delhi and Shahjahanabad are the second great Shah Jahan project.
The decision was political.
The Mughal capital had been at Agra since Babur's time, with Akbar's brief experiments at Fatehpur Sikri and Lahore (Chapter 3).
By the late 1630s, Shah Jahan had decided that Agra was too cramped, too southern, and too associated with previous reigns for what he had in mind.
He wanted a new capital city built from scratch, with himself as founder, on the model of Akbar's Fatehpur Sikri but on a much larger scale and at a more central north Indian location.

The site selected was Delhi, on the western bank of the Yamuna, north of the existing Sultanate-era Delhi (the various older Delhis — Mehrauli, Tughlaqabad, Firuzabad, Old Delhi proper — sat in scattered ruins to the south, Delhi Sultanate Ch 4 and Ch 8).
Construction began in 1639.
The new walled city was called Shahjahanabad ("city of Shah Jahan") and was occupied from 1648 onward.
It is now Old Delhi.
The city plan was grand.
A roughly six-and-a-half-mile defensive wall with twelve gates enclosed the whole.
The main commercial street, Chandni Chowk ("moonlit square"), ran east-west through the city center, connecting the Red Fort on the eastern wall with the Fatehpuri Mosque on the western wall.
Sub-streets and mahallas (residential quarters) radiated from Chandni Chowk.
The city was designed for a population of perhaps 400,000-500,000 — comparable to contemporary Isfahan (Safavid Persia Ch 4) and substantially larger than any contemporary European city.
Water was supplied by an extension of Firuz Shah Tughlaq's fourteenth-century Western Yamuna Canal (Delhi Sultanate Ch 4), modified to deliver water to public fountains and the imperial palace.
The Red Fort (called Lal Qila in Hindi-Urdu) was the imperial palace at the eastern wall of the new city, named for its red-sandstone walls.
Construction took ten years (1639-48), with the same architectural team that had been working on the Taj Mahal repurposed for the new project.

The fort enclosed approximately 254 acres, with private imperial apartments, public audience halls (the Diwan-i-Aam, "hall of public audience," with its red-sandstone and white-marble decoration), private audience halls (the Diwan-i-Khas, "hall of private audience," where the Peacock Throne stood), the imperial harem complex (the Rang Mahal, "palace of colors," with white-marble walls and inlaid water channels), the Hammam (the imperial bathhouse, with marble floors heated by water-pipe systems), and extensive formal gardens.

The architectural style was the mature Mughal idiom — red sandstone for the structural and public elements, white marble for the imperial-personal spaces, pietra dura inlay for the most intimate areas.

The Diwan-i-Khas, where the Peacock Throne sat, bore an inscription in Persian that has become famous: Agar firdaus bar roo-e zameen ast / hameen ast-o, hameen ast-o, hameen ast — "If there is a paradise on the face of the earth / it is this, it is this, it is this." The inscription is attributed to the court poet Amir Khusrau of the Delhi Sultanate (Delhi Sultanate Ch 6) but was probably written by a Mughal courtier in the Khusrau style.
Either way, the sentiment captures Shah Jahan's view of his own capital.
The Peacock Throne is the third project that requires attention.

Shah Jahan commissioned the throne in 1628, immediately after his accession, with a budget of approximately 100,000 tolas of gold (about 2,300 pounds) and a separate budget for jewels that was reportedly larger than the gold cost.
The construction took seven years; the throne was completed in 1635.
The chief jeweler was Said Gilani, a Persian master goldsmith who had worked at the Mughal court for decades.
The throne was a rectangular gold platform with a canopy supported by twelve emerald pillars.
The canopy was topped by two golden peacocks (hence the name) with bodies and tails set entirely in gems — sapphires, emeralds, rubies, and diamonds.

The most famous individual stone was the Koh-i-Noor (KOH-ee-NOOR, "Mountain of Light") diamond, which had been in the Mughal collection since Babur acquired it after Panipat in 1526 (the diamond's pre-Mughal history is uncertain — it may have come from the Golconda mines of the Deccan or from much further south).

The throne also incorporated the Timur Ruby (a Persian-acquired stone with a long inscription history including Timur's name, despite not actually being a ruby — it is a balas spinel) and dozens of other named stones.
The total value, expressed in contemporary terms, was reportedly twice the cost of the Taj Mahal.
In modern terms, the throne is essentially impossible to value because the gem prices it commanded depended on royal-prestige markets that no longer exist.
What can be said is that it represented a substantial proportion of the Mughal imperial gem treasury — perhaps a fifth to a third of the total imperial collection of precious stones.

Shah Jahan's choice to concentrate so much of the imperial wealth in a single moveable object would prove consequential a century later, when Nader Shah's 1739 sack would carry the throne off (Chapter 7).
The Peacock Throne stood in the Diwan-i-Khas at the Red Fort from 1648 (when the Red Fort was occupied) until 1739 (when Nader Shah took it).
Mughal court ceremonies revolved around it.
Foreign embassies were received in front of it.
The succession ceremonies of subsequent emperors were held at it.
Aurangzeb was crowned at it in 1658 (Chapter 6).

The throne was, for ninety years, the visible symbol of the Mughal Empire, and its loss in 1739 marks the end of the empire as a great power as definitively as any single political event of the eighteenth century.
The throne was disassembled in Persia after Nader Shah's assassination in 1747.

Some of the gems, including the Koh-i-Noor and the Timur Ruby, eventually made their way (through Afghan and Sikh possession) to the British Crown after the Anglo-Sikh Wars of the 1840s (Chapter 8), and now sit in the British Crown Jewels at the Tower of London.
The Indian, Pakistani, Afghan, and Iranian governments have all, at various times, formally requested the return of the Koh-i-Noor.
The British have, so far, declined.
By the late 1650s, the Mughal Empire was at peak.
The state revenue had grown to approximately 220 million rupees per year — roughly twice what Akbar had collected.
The territorial extent was the largest in two centuries.
The architectural projects (Taj Mahal completed 1653, Red Fort completed 1648, Jama Masjid completed 1656, Shahjahanabad occupied 1648) were the visible monuments of imperial wealth.
The Persianate court culture had reached a level of refinement that subsequent generations would view as a golden age.
Mughal painting was at peak.

Mughal music — the synthesis of Persian and Indian classical traditions that had begun under Akbar's court musician Tansen — was producing the formal raga system that defines north Indian classical music today.
Mughal cuisine — biryanis, kebabs, naan breads, the entire vocabulary of north Indian Persianate cooking — was being codified at the imperial kitchens.
It looked sustainable.
It was not.
The structural problems were substantial: The Deccan campaigns had absorbed enormous resources without producing decisive results.
The Marathas, Bijapur, and Golconda were still substantively independent.
Aurangzeb's later attempt to finish the Deccan project would consume his entire reign (Chapter 6).
The Kandahar wars had consumed enormous resources without producing decisive results.
Kandahar was lost permanently in 1649.
The Afghan frontier was insecure.
The architectural and cultural expenditure was enormous.
The 220 million rupees of state revenue went largely to (a) the imperial military, (b) the imperial nobility's salaries, (c) the imperial court's expenses, and (d) the building projects.
There was little fiscal cushion for crisis response.

The succession discipline (kill all rival heirs at accession) meant that each succession produced a destructive purge of the imperial family — and the Mughal family was now so large that the purges were getting destructive enough to weaken the dynasty itself.
In September 1657, Shah Jahan fell seriously ill.
The exact illness is not recorded in detail; he was sixty-five and had been visibly aging for several years.

The illness was severe enough that the four sons of Mumtaz Mahal — Dara Shukoh in Delhi, Shah Shuja in Bengal, Aurangzeb in the Deccan, Murad Bakhsh in Gujarat — all assumed Shah Jahan was dying and began maneuvering for the throne.
By the time Shah Jahan recovered (which he did, mostly), his four sons were already at war.
The next chapter is mostly about how that war was resolved.
Cross-civ check: Shah Jahan's reign (1628-58) coincided with several major events globally.
The Thirty Years War (1618-48) ended in central Europe with the Peace of Westphalia, establishing the modern European state system.

Cromwell's Commonwealth (1649-58) was running England after the execution of Charles I in 1649 (the year Aurangzeb lost Kandahar to the Safavids — small Mughal historical detail; the simultaneous regicide of Charles I in London barely registered at Shah Jahan's court).
Louis XIV of France was a child king under Mazarin's regency and would not begin his personal rule until 1661, after Shah Jahan was deposed.
The Manchu conquest of Ming China was completed in 1644, beginning the Qing Dynasty.
Tokugawa Iemitsu in Japan completed the sakoku isolation policy that would seal Japan from European trade for two centuries (Edo Japan Ch 3).
Safavid Persia under Abbas II was in mid-arc of its long decline (Safavid Persia Ch 7).
The world was actively reshaping.
Shah Jahan, building marble tombs and gem-encrusted thrones, was largely uninterested in any of it.

chapters.title: Aurangzeb
sentences: The sixth Mughal emperor is the most controversial figure in Mughal history.
His name was Muhi-ud-Din Muhammad (the formal name) or Aurangzeb (OR-ang-zeb, "ornament of the throne," the regnal name he took at his accession), born in 1618 to Shah Jahan and Mumtaz Mahal.
He took the throne in 1658 after killing his eldest brother Dara Shukoh and imprisoning his father Shah Jahan.

He reigned for forty-nine years, expanded the empire to its greatest territorial extent, reimposed the jizya tax on non-Muslim subjects in 1679, spent his last twenty-six years bogged down in the Deccan against the Marathas, and died in 1707 at age eighty-eight.
The empire he left was visibly fraying.
The fraying would accelerate after his death into the eighteenth-century decline (Chapter 7).
The historiographical problem with Aurangzeb is that the evidence supports two starkly different readings.

The first reading — common in Hindu nationalist historiography but with respectable scholarly defenders too — is that Aurangzeb was a religious fanatic who systematically reversed the Akbar-era Hindu-Muslim accommodation, reimposed orthodox Sunni state policy at the cost of the empire's institutional cohesion, destroyed Hindu temples and persecuted Hindu practices, and was the proximate cause of the eighteenth-century Mughal collapse through his combination of religious bigotry and territorial overreach.
The Maratha resistance under Shivaji and his successors, on this reading, was Hindu civilization defending itself against Mughal religious aggression.

The second reading — common in the Indian Marxist-secularist tradition associated with Irfan Habib and his students, and increasingly in revisionist American scholarship by Audrey Truschke and others — is that Aurangzeb was primarily a pragmatic state-builder whose religious-policy moves were instrumental rather than zealot-driven, that his Hindu temple destructions were politically targeted at specific local opponents rather than systematically anti-Hindu, that his employment of Hindu officials and generals at high levels of the imperial administration was actually larger than under any previous Mughal emperor, and that the eighteenth-century decline had structural causes (succession problems, fiscal exhaustion from the Deccan Wars, the rise of regional powers) that would have produced collapse regardless of religious policy.

Modern scholarship is, broadly, divided between these readings, with most academic Mughal historians leaning toward the second (state-builder) reading and most popular Indian historiography (especially in English-language journalistic and political writing) defaulting to the first (religious fanatic) reading.

The honest answer is that Aurangzeb was both — a personally devout Sunni Muslim who genuinely believed in orthodox Islamic state policy, and a pragmatic political actor who employed Hindus when politically useful and persecuted them when politically useful.
The proportions of pragmatism versus zealotry in any given decision are usually impossible to recover from the surviving evidence.
The historiographical wars over his legacy have, mostly, been driven by twentieth- and twenty-first-century political needs rather than by the seventeenth-century evidence itself.
What is not disputable is the basic chronology, which is the next several paragraphs.
The Mughal war of succession of 1657-59 was the bloodiest in Mughal history.

When Shah Jahan fell ill in September 1657, his four sons — Dara Shukoh in Delhi as the heir-presumptive, Shah Shuja in Bengal, Aurangzeb in the Deccan, Murad Bakhsh in Gujarat — all assumed the throne was about to come open and began organizing armies.
Shah Shuja moved first, marching west from Bengal toward Delhi.
He was defeated by Dara Shukoh's army (commanded by Dara's son Sulaiman Shukoh) at the Battle of Bahadurpur in February 1658.
Aurangzeb and Murad Bakhsh, more strategically, allied.
They marched from the Deccan and Gujarat respectively, met at the western Malwa town of Dipalpur, combined their armies, and moved north toward Agra.
Dara Shukoh, who had been holding the imperial court while his father was incapacitated, marched south to meet them.
The two armies met at Samugarh (sah-MOO-garh), about eight miles east of Agra, on May 29, 1658.
The battle was decided by what looked like Dara Shukoh's bizarre tactical choice.
He had fielded the larger and better-equipped army (perhaps 60,000 troops to Aurangzeb-Murad's combined 50,000), with strong artillery and elite cavalry.

He committed the artillery first, drove Aurangzeb's center back, and was in position to break the line — when, for reasons modern historians still debate, he dismounted from his elephant in the middle of the battle to ride a horse instead. (Some sources say his elephant was wounded; some say he wanted to be more mobile; some say he wanted to ride into the final charge personally.) The dismount was visible to both armies.
From a distance, the empty howdah looked like Dara had been killed.
His army began to break in confusion.
Aurangzeb counter-attacked.
Within an hour the battle was lost.
Dara Shukoh fled the field with a small bodyguard.
Aurangzeb entered Agra and seized Shah Jahan in his palace — formal house arrest, in the Musamman Burj of Agra Fort, the white-marble tower with the famous view across the Yamuna to the Taj Mahal.

Shah Jahan would live in that confinement for the next eight years, attended by his daughter Jahanara (Shah Jahan's daughter who chose to share his imprisonment voluntarily), watching the tomb of his wife from the window.
He died there on January 22, 1666, age seventy-four.
He was buried in the Taj Mahal beside Mumtaz Mahal.
Aurangzeb then turned to his brothers.

Murad Bakhsh, who had been Aurangzeb's ally at Samugarh, was lured to Aurangzeb's camp at Mathura under the pretense of a celebration banquet, arrested, sent to prison at the fortress of Gwalior, and executed in 1661.

Shah Shuja was defeated again in early 1659 at the Battle of Khajwa, fled east through Bengal into the kingdom of Arakan in modern Burma, and was killed there in 1661 in obscure circumstances (the king of Arakan had him killed, apparently, after some kind of palace intrigue involving Shah Shuja's daughters).
Dara Shukoh's end was the most dramatic.
After Samugarh, he fled west through the Punjab and Sindh, attempting to reach the Persian-Mughal border at Kandahar to seek Safavid support.

He was betrayed by an Afghan tribal chief named Malik Jiwan (whom Dara had earlier shown personal kindness — Malik Jiwan had been condemned to death years before, and Dara had intervened to save him — this is one of the more striking betrayals in Mughal history) and handed over to Aurangzeb's forces.

He was brought back to Delhi in chains, paraded through the streets in a public humiliation that the Italian traveler Niccolao Manucci witnessed and described in detail, then tried for apostasy by a panel of Sunni clerics on the basis of his Sufi-Hindu syncretist writings (Chapter 5), convicted, and executed in September 1659.
His execution was both political (clearing a rival heir) and religious (publicly establishing Aurangzeb's orthodox Sunni credentials by killing the Sufi-syncretist brother).
Dara Shukoh deserves his own paragraph because what he represented — the road not taken — was the Mughal Empire's most important alternative path.
Dara Shukoh (born 1615) was Shah Jahan's eldest son, his designated heir for thirty years, and a serious scholar and Sufi mystic.
He had been initiated into the Qadiri Sufi order in his twenties and developed a deep interest in Hindu philosophy.

He learned Sanskrit (most Mughals did not), commissioned translations of fifty Upanishads from Sanskrit into Persian (the Sirr-i-Akbar, "the Greatest Secret," completed in 1657), wrote his own comparative-religion treatise Majma-ul-Bahrain ("the Confluence of the Two Seas") arguing that Sufi Islamic mysticism and Hindu Vedanta were essentially expressing the same truth in different vocabularies, and patronized Sufi-Hindu joint religious gatherings.
His intellectual position was that the Hindu and Muslim mystical traditions were two valid paths to the same divine reality, and that the apparent doctrinal differences were superficial.
The political implication of this view, had Dara succeeded to the throne, would have been enormous.

Mughal religious policy would presumably have continued in the Akbarian syncretist direction (Chapter 3) — perhaps with more theological substance than Akbar's somewhat improvised Din-i-Ilahi had offered.
The Hindu majority would have remained integrated into the imperial system through religious-ideological inclusion as well as marriage-alliance and military-service inclusion.
The orthodox Sunni clergy would have been further marginalized.
Aurangzeb's victory closed off this trajectory.

The Sufi-Hindu syncretist tradition that Dara represented continued in other forms (the Bhakti devotional tradition, the Sikh community, regional Sufi-Hindu shrine networks) but lost its imperial sponsorship.
The Mughal state under Aurangzeb moved decisively toward orthodox Sunni state-religious policy.
The hundred-fifteen-year window of the Akbarian synthesis (1564 jizya abolition to 1679 jizya reimposition) was coming to a close.

Whether you read this shift as the empire returning to its proper Islamic foundations (the orthodox Sunni reading) or as the empire abandoning the inclusive policy that had made it sustainable (the Akbarian/Dara reading), the shift itself is undisputed.
The translation of the Upanishads into Persian — Dara's intellectual project — had a remarkable afterlife.
The Sirr-i-Akbar was translated into Latin by the French orientalist Anquetil-Duperron in 1801-02 and widely read in early-nineteenth-century Europe.

The German philosopher Schopenhauer read it and called it "the consolation of my life." The Upanishadic ideas in nineteenth-century European philosophy — the influence on Schopenhauer, on Nietzsche, on the early Heidegger — came largely through Dara Shukoh's Persian translation and Anquetil-Duperron's Latin retranslation.
The intellectual project Aurangzeb killed in 1659 ended up shaping European thought two centuries later.
The first decade of Aurangzeb's reign (1658-68) was, by Mughal standards, a period of relative consolidation.
He was crowned at the Red Fort in Delhi in June 1659.
He took the regnal title Alamgir ("world-conqueror," the formal regnal name; "Aurangzeb" remained the personal name and is what most historical writing uses).

He proclaimed a return to orthodox Sunni state policy: the Mughal court would now publicly observe orthodox Sunni rituals, the imperial atelier would no longer produce paintings of human or animal forms (which orthodox Sunni interpretation of Islamic image-prohibition forbade), the imperial musicians would be dismissed (Aurangzeb personally disliked music and considered it an unislamic indulgence), the imperial wardrobe would shift to plain austere costume rather than the gold-and-silk court dress of his father's reign.
The reaction at court was muted.

The senior nobility, mostly the same Persian-Turkic-Rajput mansabdars who had served Shah Jahan, accepted the new orthodoxy as a court-fashion adjustment rather than a fundamental change in their employment status.

The painting workshop was officially curtailed but unofficially continued (later Aurangzeb-period paintings exist, including portraits of Aurangzeb himself, suggesting the prohibition was honored more in theory than in practice).
The musicians dispersed to provincial courts where music continued; the great singer Nyamat Khan spent the rest of his career at the Hyderabad court.

The Persianate cultural world that Akbar, Jahangir, and Shah Jahan had built continued at Aurangzeb's court in modified form, with the surface Sunni-orthodox formality covering substantially continuing institutional practice.
The political reforms of the period were more substantive.

Aurangzeb reorganized the imperial revenue collection, tightened up the mansabdari ranks (which had inflated under Shah Jahan), reformed the karkhanas (imperial workshops that produced everything from textiles to weapons for the court and the military).

He commissioned the Fatawa-i-Alamgiri in 1675 — a comprehensive compilation of Hanafi Sunni jurisprudence, completed by a panel of around five hundred scholars over approximately a decade, that would become the standard Islamic legal reference across South Asia and the Middle East and was still cited by British colonial courts in the nineteenth century.

He had the Badshahi Mosque built at Lahore (completed 1673), one of the largest mosques in the world at the time, designed as an explicit architectural counterweight to Shah Jahan's Taj Mahal — power, not love, in stone.
The most consequential single decision of Aurangzeb's reign was the reimposition of the jizya in 1679.
The jizya — the per-capita tax on non-Muslim subjects — had been abolished by Akbar in 1564 (Chapter 3) as the institutional centerpiece of the Hindu-Muslim accommodation.
Its abolition had been enormously controversial among orthodox Sunni clerics for the entire 115-year window of its non-collection.

Aurangzeb had been considering reimposition for years and had been pressured by the orthodox ulama to do it; the actual decision came in 1679, twenty-one years into his reign, after the Maratha resistance under Shivaji had visibly hardened (see below).

The reimposition order specified that Hindu subjects would pay a per-capita tax graduated by income (the wealthy paid more, the poor paid less), with exemptions for the very poor, for women, for children, for monks, and for state officials (which exempted senior Hindu mansabdars from the personal humiliation of paying it).
The amounts were modest in absolute terms — most subjects paid a few rupees per year — but the political symbolism was enormous.
The jizya formally re-established the Hindu-as-dhimmi (protected non-Muslim subject) status that Akbar had abolished.
It signaled, unmistakably, that the empire was no longer pretending to be a Hindu-Muslim joint sovereignty.
The political consequences were predictable.
Hindu opposition to Mughal authority hardened across north India.
The Rajput rulers of Mewar and Marwar, who had been broadly cooperative since the Akbar-era marriage alliances, rebelled within months of the jizya reimposition.
The Rajput War of 1679-81 (sometimes called the Marwar War) was the most serious Rajput resistance to Mughal rule since Rana Sanga at Khanwa in 1527.
Aurangzeb won the war militarily but did not break the political-symbolic damage to Mughal-Rajput relations, and the Rajput-Mughal alliance never fully recovered.
The deeper consequence was longer-term.

The Akbarian synthesis had given the Mughal Empire its largest single institutional advantage over alternative Indian states: it was the only major Indian Islamic state that had genuinely integrated the Hindu majority into its administrative and military elite.
Aurangzeb's policy reversal eroded that advantage.
By the early eighteenth century, the Marathas, the Sikhs, the Rajputs, and the southern Hindu polities were all in active opposition to Mughal authority.
The empire's ability to govern the subcontinent depended on the cooperation of the Hindu majority.
Aurangzeb's policy made that cooperation harder.

Whether this policy reversal was the proximate cause of the eighteenth-century decline (the standard reading) or merely the most visible symbolic moment of a decline driven by deeper structural causes (the revisionist reading) remains debated.
Both views have evidence.
Shivaji and the Maratha resistance is the other major topic of the reign.
Shivaji Bhonsle (shih-VAH-jee BHON-slay) was born in 1630 to a Maratha family that had served as senior officers in the Bijapur Sultanate of the Deccan.

The Marathas were a Marathi-speaking Hindu population concentrated in the western Deccan plateau (modern Maharashtra), historically organized as cavalry-and-fort polities serving variously the Bahmani Sultanate, the Bijapur Sultanate, and the Mughals as mercenary forces.

Shivaji's father Shahji Bhonsle had been a senior Bijapur officer; Shivaji grew up in the western Maharashtra hill country with a Hindu religious education from his mother Jijabai that emphasized resistance to Muslim rule.
Shivaji built a Maratha state in the western Deccan over the course of the 1650s and 1660s.

His method was distinctive — small mobile cavalry forces operating from a network of hill forts (the Sahyadri mountain forts of the Western Ghats — Pratapgarh, Sinhagad, Raigad, Torna, several dozen others), conducting rapid raids against Bijapur and Mughal positions, withdrawing to defensible hill positions when superior forces appeared, and gradually consolidating territorial control through a combination of military victories and revenue-collection penetration of the surrounding lowland districts.

He destroyed a major Bijapur army at the Battle of Pratapgarh in 1659 (where he reportedly killed the Bijapur general Afzal Khan with a hidden tiger-claw weapon during a peace negotiation, an episode that became central to Maratha mythology).
He raided the Mughal port of Surat in 1664, looting an estimated 100 million rupees of merchant goods.
He was captured and brought to Aurangzeb's court at Agra in 1666 in a curious diplomatic experiment that ended when Shivaji escaped from house arrest by hiding in a basket of sweets.
The defining moment was Shivaji's coronation as Chhatrapati at Raigad fort on June 6, 1674.

The ceremony was a deliberate revival of Hindu sovereign-king ritual that had been dormant since the Vijayanagara period (Medieval India Ch 8) — performed by a Brahmin priest from Varanasi, with traditional Sanskrit Vedic ritual, conferring on Shivaji the title Chhatrapati ("lord of the parasol," an old Hindu sovereign title) and explicitly framing him as a Hindu king ruling a Hindu kingdom independent of Mughal authority.
The coronation was a direct political-religious challenge to Mughal sovereignty over India.
Shivaji died in 1680 at age fifty, leaving the Maratha state to his son Sambhaji.

Sambhaji continued his father's resistance against Aurangzeb, was eventually captured by the Mughals in 1689, refused to convert to Islam, and was tortured to death — eyes gouged out, tongue cut out, then quartered, over a period of weeks — on Aurangzeb's orders.
The execution radicalized Maratha resistance further.

Sambhaji's infant son was held by the Mughals; Sambhaji's brother Rajaram continued the fight from southern Maharashtra; Rajaram's widow Tarabai continued it after his death; Sambhaji's son Shahu eventually emerged as the Maratha sovereign in the early eighteenth century.
The Maratha resistance never broke.
By the 1690s and 1700s, it had become an unwinnable counter-insurgency that consumed the entire Mughal southern army.
The Deccan Wars of 1681-1707 are the immediate cause of the eighteenth-century Mughal collapse, and they need a sustained treatment.
In 1681, Aurangzeb personally moved his court to the Deccan to direct the war against the Marathas in person.
He left the imperial capital at Delhi essentially abandoned, with the imperial administration following the emperor south.
The court would not return to Delhi during Aurangzeb's lifetime.

Aurangzeb spent the next twenty-six years — from age sixty-three to age eighty-eight — campaigning in the Deccan in person, personally directing sieges, personally reading military dispatches, personally signing the orders that allocated jagirs and mansabs to officers in the field.
The first phase of the campaign (1681-89) annexed the two surviving Deccan Sultanates.
The Sultanate of Bijapur fell in September 1686 after a long siege of the capital city.
The Sultanate of Golconda (famous for its diamond mines, including the original source of the Koh-i-Noor) fell in September 1687 after another long siege.
Both sultanates were annexed directly to Mughal rule, with their treasuries seized and their ruling families brought to Mughal court detention.

On paper, this was a major Mughal victory — the entire subcontinent was now under nominal Mughal sovereignty, with only the southernmost tip and the Maratha hill country still outside imperial control.
In practice, the annexations were administrative disasters.
The two sultanates' bureaucratic-military structures were incompatible with the Mughal mansabdari system.
The local elites (Persian-Turkic in Golconda, mostly Bijapuri-Sunni in Bijapur) were absorbed into the Mughal nobility but with much-reduced status, producing chronic resentment.
The local economy of the Deccan — which had been organized around the Bijapur and Golconda fiscal systems — collapsed under Mughal mismanagement.
Agricultural revenue from the new Mughal Deccan provinces ran consistently below pre-conquest levels.
The cost of maintaining Mughal garrisons across the new territory ran consistently above local revenue.
The new Deccan provinces were a net fiscal drain on the empire.
The second phase (1690-1707) was the long Maratha counter-insurgency.
With Bijapur and Golconda absorbed, the Marathas under Rajaram and Tarabai conducted an asymmetric war from their hill forts and through cavalry raids deep into Mughal territory.
Mughal forces took Maratha forts (Sinhagad, Pratapgarh, Raigad, Panhala, Khelna — dozens of fort sieges across the Western Ghats) only to find that the Marathas had withdrawn to other forts.
The Mughal armies controlled the towns and roads during the day; the Marathas controlled the same territory at night.
The campaigns dragged on year after year, consuming armies, consuming revenue, consuming Aurangzeb's old age.
He died on March 3, 1707, at the camp at Ahmednagar in the Deccan, age eighty-eight, still on campaign, having achieved no decisive resolution.
His will instructed his sons to bury him simply at the shrine of the Sufi saint Zainuddin at Khuldabad, near Aurangabad, with no mausoleum and no grave-marker.
The instruction was honored.
His grave is, by his own request, the most modest tomb of any Mughal emperor — a simple open-air enclosure with a plain rectangular stone marker.
The contrast with the Taj Mahal is the single most striking thing about Mughal tomb-architecture.
What Aurangzeb left to his successors was an empire visibly at the limits of what its institutions could sustain.

The territorial extent in 1707 was the largest in Mughal history — roughly 4 million square kilometers, covering nearly the entire Indian subcontinent except the southernmost tip, the Himalayan periphery, and the Maratha hill country.
The state revenue had grown to perhaps 380 million rupees per year (a contemporary estimate; modern scholars vary somewhat).
The imperial nobility was the largest in Mughal history.
The architectural and cultural infrastructure built up over the previous four reigns was substantially intact.
But underneath this surface, the structural problems were severe: The Deccan was not pacified.
The Marathas continued the resistance after Aurangzeb's death, and the Maratha cavalry would shortly emerge as the dominant Indian military force.
The Hindu-Muslim accommodation was broken.
The jizya reimposition and the Maratha wars had radicalized opposition to Mughal authority across most of central and southern India.
The fiscal system was overstretched.
The imperial revenue was substantial but the imperial expenditure (military, court, administration) was substantially larger.
The empire had been running long-term deficits financed by drawdowns of accumulated treasury reserves.
The succession discipline was now wholesale family slaughter.
Aurangzeb's three surviving sons — Muazzam, Azam Shah, Kam Bakhsh — would now fight a civil war among themselves the moment Aurangzeb died.
The pattern would repeat in subsequent generations.
The provincial administration had begun to ossify.
Senior provincial governors were treating their jagirs as hereditary fiefs in practice, even though the mansabdari system formally prohibited it.
The central control that Akbar had built (Chapter 3) was eroding.
The eighteenth-century Mughal decline was not yet inevitable in 1707, but the structural conditions for it were all in place.
The next chapter is mostly about how those structural problems played out.
Cross-civ check: Aurangzeb's reign (1658-1707) was almost exactly contemporary with the personal rule of Louis XIV of France (1661-1715) — and the parallels are striking.
Both monarchs reigned for forty-plus years.
Both centralized state power and built up the largest standing armies in their respective civilizations.

Both pursued long expensive wars at the empire's periphery (Louis's Dutch Wars and War of the Spanish Succession; Aurangzeb's Deccan Wars) that drained the treasury and exhausted the institutional cohesion of the state.

Both reversed the more pluralistic religious policies of their predecessors (Louis's revocation of the Edict of Nantes in 1685 driving Huguenot Protestants out of France; Aurangzeb's jizya reimposition in 1679 alienating Hindu subjects).
Both presided over visible peaks of cultural production at their courts (Versailles vs. the late-Mughal cultural complex).
Both left successors who would preside over visible institutional decline.
The convergence is genuinely useful for thinking about the structural dynamics of seventeenth-century absolutist monarchy.
The closer comparison, though, is Charles V of the Habsburg Empire a century earlier (Holy Roman Emperor 1519-56).

Charles, like Aurangzeb, presided over the largest contiguous empire of his era (Spain plus the Holy Roman Empire plus the Spanish American colonies plus the Burgundian Low Countries), pursued aggressive wars in pursuit of confessional Catholic policy, exhausted the treasury through ambitious campaigns, and ultimately abdicated in despair.
Aurangzeb did not abdicate but he died on campaign in the Deccan having visibly failed to achieve his strategic objectives.

Both reigns illustrate the same pattern — ambitious centralizing monarchs whose territorial expansion outran their institutional capacity to govern, producing visible peaks followed by visible collapses.
Aurangzeb himself, in his last letters to his sons, expressed something close to despair.
The most famous of these letters, written to his son Azam Shah shortly before his death, reads in part: "I came alone and I go as a stranger.
I do not know who I am, nor what I have been doing.
The instant which has passed in power has left only sorrow behind it...
I have not been the guardian and protector of the empire.
My valuable time has been passed vainly...
I have a dread for my salvation and with what torments I may be punished." The letter is sometimes cited as evidence that Aurangzeb died regretting his own policies.
The reading may be too convenient — pious self-deprecation was a standard convention of late-life Mughal correspondence — but the language captures something true about how the reign ended.
The empire he had spent fifty years expanding was visibly slipping out of his control, and he knew it.

chapters.title: The Long Decline
sentences: The fifty years after Aurangzeb's death produced one of the most spectacular state collapses of the early-modern world.

In 1707, the Mughal Empire was the largest contiguous state in the world by population, with revenue larger than any single European state, and a territorial extent that covered nearly the entire Indian subcontinent.
By 1757, it had effectively ceased to exist as a sovereign state.
Bengal had broken away.
The Marathas controlled most of central and western India.
The Sikhs were on the rise in the Punjab.
Hyderabad was independent under the Asaf Jahi dynasty.
Awadh was independent under the Nawab.
Mysore was independent under the Hindu Wodeyar dynasty (and, after 1761, under the Muslim general Hyder Ali).
The Persians had sacked Delhi in 1739 and walked off with the Peacock Throne.
The Mughal emperor at Delhi was reduced to a powerless figurehead, his actual authority limited to the city walls of Shahjahanabad and the surrounding districts.
The collapse was not driven by a single decisive event.

It was the cumulative result of about a dozen interlocking structural problems — the succession-war discipline that killed potential heirs at each accession, the fiscal exhaustion of the Deccan wars, the weakening of central control over provincial governors, the rise of regional Hindu and Sikh military powers, the increasing penetration of European trading companies along the coasts, the periodic eruptions of military catastrophe (Nader Shah in 1739, the Marathas at Panipat in 1761) — none of which the post-Aurangzeb emperors had the institutional capacity to address.
The dynasty continued to exist nominally until 1858 (Chapter 9).
But the actual empire had ended fifty years earlier.
The post-Aurangzeb succession war (1707-12) set the pattern.

Aurangzeb's three surviving sons — Muazzam (the eldest, governor of Kabul), Azam Shah (the second, who had been with Aurangzeb in the Deccan), and Kam Bakhsh (the youngest, governor of Bijapur) — each declared themselves emperor within weeks of their father's death.
Azam Shah, the most senior in the Deccan, marched immediately on Delhi.
Muazzam, having a smaller initial army, retreated north and gathered Punjab and Afghan forces.
The two armies met at Jajau near Agra on June 8, 1707.
Azam Shah was killed in the battle.

Muazzam took the throne as Bahadur Shah I (bah-HAH-door SHAH the first — he was the first Bahadur Shah, distinguished from Bahadur Shah Zafar, the very last Mughal emperor a century and a half later, Chapter 9).
He then defeated Kam Bakhsh in 1709 at Hyderabad; Kam Bakhsh died of wounds shortly after.
Bahadur Shah I attempted a more conciliatory policy than his father.

He reopened negotiations with the Marathas (releasing Sambhaji's son Shahu from Mughal custody to act as a Mughal-friendly Maratha sovereign — this would not work as planned, but the attempt was real).
He toned down the orthodox Sunni rhetoric.
He began discussions with the Rajput rulers about restoring the marriage-alliance relationship that had broken down under Aurangzeb.
The reign showed promise of institutional repair.
He died in 1712 after only five years on the throne, age sixty-nine.
His own succession produced a four-way civil war among his sons that took two years to resolve.

The eventual winner, Jahandar Shah, lasted ten months before being deposed and executed by his nephew Farrukhsiyar (with the active backing of two senior nobles, the Sayyid Brothers of Barha, who would shortly become Mughal-empire kingmakers).
The pattern of repeated civil war between rival Mughal princes had now firmly established itself.
