The Sayyid Brothers — Hussain Ali Khan (the elder, who handled military affairs) and Abdullah Khan (the younger, who handled civil administration) — were two senior officers from a Sayyid family of Barha (a small district near Saharanpur in modern Uttar Pradesh) whose careers had risen under Bahadur Shah I and who had emerged as the senior power-brokers of the post-Bahadur Shah period.
They installed Farrukhsiyar in 1713 in exchange for the most senior court appointments.
They then deposed and murdered him in 1719 when he attempted to govern independently of them.

They installed three more puppet emperors in quick succession: Rafi-ud-Darjat (reigned three months in 1719 before dying of tuberculosis), Rafi-ud-Daula (reigned three months in 1719 before dying of opium overdose), and Muhammad Shah (a teenage prince installed in late 1719 because the brothers thought he would be easy to control).

The Sayyid Brothers' three-year reign-by-proxy (1719-22) is one of the more peculiar episodes in Mughal history — two non-royal officers running the empire through a sequence of imperial figureheads, openly treating the dynasty as their political instrument.
Muhammad Shah turned out to be less pliable than they had expected.
He conspired with rival nobles, particularly with the senior officer Asaf Jah I (the future Nizam of Hyderabad, see below), and the Sayyid Brothers were outmaneuvered.
Hussain Ali Khan was assassinated in 1720; Abdullah Khan was defeated in battle at Hasanpur and died in prison.
The puppet phase ended.
But the damage was done.
The empire's political authority had visibly become a contested prize among rival factions of nobles, with the imperial dynasty as a counter rather than as a sovereign actor.
Subsequent reigns would continue this pattern — formal Mughal emperors at Delhi, real political power exercised by senior nobles or by the emerging regional dynasties.
Muhammad Shah (ruled 1719-48), nicknamed Rangila ("the Colorful") for his patronage of music, painting, and refined court life, presided over the empire's most spectacular fragmentation.

He reigned for twenty-nine years — by far the longest reign of the post-Aurangzeb period, longer than several of his predecessors and successors combined — and did almost nothing to address the empire's structural problems.

He patronized music (his court included some of the great Hindustani classical musicians of the period), patronized painting (the late-Mughal painting style of Muhammad Shah's reign is distinctive — looser, more decorative, with strong European compositional influence), patronized poetry (the great Urdu poet Mir Taqi Mir was active at his court).
He held court ceremonies, received ambassadors, dispensed honors.
He did not, in any meaningful sense, govern.
Under his reign, the great regional powers broke away from Mughal authority one by one.
The Marathas were the dominant case.

After Aurangzeb's death, the Marathas under successive Peshwas (peshva, the Brahmin chief ministers of the Maratha state — by the early eighteenth century the actual governors of the Maratha confederacy, with the Bhonsle royal family reduced to ceremonial figures) expanded out of their western Deccan base into central and northern India.
Baji Rao I (Peshwa 1720-40) led campaigns deep into the Mughal heartland, raiding Delhi itself in 1737 and forcing Muhammad Shah to accept Maratha territorial demands.
By the 1740s, the Marathas were collecting chauth (one-fourth of land revenue) and sardeshmukhi (an additional one-tenth) as tribute from most of central India.
The Mughal emperor was, in effect, a Maratha tributary across most of his nominal empire.
The Nizamate of Hyderabad was the second major case.

Asaf Jah I (originally Mir Qamar-ud-Din Khan, also known as Nizam-ul-Mulk), the senior officer who had helped Muhammad Shah eliminate the Sayyid Brothers, was rewarded with the governorship of the Deccan in 1724.

Within two years, he had broken with the Mughal court and established the autonomous Nizamate of Hyderabad — nominally still acknowledging Mughal suzerainty (the Nizam continued to mint coins in the Mughal emperor's name and to have the Friday prayer recited in the emperor's name), but in practice fully independent in foreign policy, military command, and revenue collection.
The Asaf Jahi dynasty Asaf Jah founded would rule Hyderabad until India absorbed it in 1948 — making it, in dynastic terms, one of the longest-lasting Indian successor states.
The Nawabate of Bengal was the third major case.
Murshid Quli Khan, originally a Mughal revenue official of Persian origin, founded the autonomous Nawabate in 1717 while still nominally a Mughal officer.
By the 1740s under Alivardi Khan, Bengal was an independent state in all but name — and the wealthiest province in Asia.

Bengal's textile manufacturing (Dhaka muslins, Murshidabad silks), its rice agriculture, its expanding trade with the European companies (English at Calcutta, Dutch at Chinsurah, French at Chandernagore), made it the single most economically important Indian province, and its political detachment from Mughal authority meant that economic importance flowed away from the Mughal treasury rather than toward it.
The Awadh Nawabs were the fourth major case.

Saadat Khan, originally a Mughal noble of Persian descent, was appointed governor of Awadh (the region around modern Lucknow in Uttar Pradesh) in 1722 and quickly converted the governorship into an autonomous principality.
The Awadh Nawabate would last (in various forms, eventually as a British client state) until the British annexation in 1856.

The Sikh Khalsa was emerging as a serious military power in the Punjab — the Khalsa order had been founded by Guru Gobind Singh in 1699 (Chapter 6), and through the early eighteenth century the Sikhs developed a guerrilla-warfare tradition that would mature into the Sikh Confederacy of the late eighteenth century and the Sikh Empire under Ranjit Singh in the early nineteenth century.
The Rajput rulers had reverted to substantial autonomy after the Aurangzeb-era ruptures, particularly in the larger states (Mewar, Marwar, Amber, Bikaner).

They paid tribute to whoever was militarily ascendant in the region — the Mughals when Mughal forces were nearby, the Marathas when Maratha forces were nearby — but ran their own internal affairs without much interference.
By the late 1730s, the Mughal Empire was, in territorial-political terms, mostly an aggregate of regional successor states paying nominal allegiance to a powerless emperor at Delhi.
Then Nader Shah arrived.

Nader Shah Afshar (NAH-der SHAH ahf-SHAR) was the brilliant Iranian warlord who had emerged from the chaos of the Safavid collapse (Safavid Persia Ch 8) to reunify Iran in the late 1720s, expel the Afghan Hotaki occupiers, and establish himself as the new Iranian sovereign in 1736.
By 1738, having consolidated his Iranian rule, he turned east toward Afghanistan and India.
The pretext for invasion was a refugee problem.
Several rebel Afghan factions, having been driven out of Iran by Nader's campaigns, had fled into Mughal-claimed territory in eastern Afghanistan.
Nader sent emissaries to Muhammad Shah demanding that the Mughals expel the refugees or hand them over.
The Mughal court, paralyzed and unfocused, gave evasive responses.
Nader took this as casus belli (which he had been looking for anyway) and invaded.
His army of perhaps 80,000 troops crossed the Khyber Pass in late 1738.
Kabul fell.
The Mughal Punjab governor surrendered Lahore.
By February 1739, Nader's army was in the upper Punjab, and the Mughal court at Delhi finally raised an army to confront him.
Muhammad Shah personally took the field with a force of perhaps 300,000 men plus war elephants — on paper the largest army in the world at the time.
The two armies met at Karnal, about 75 miles north of Delhi, on February 24, 1739.
The result was the most lopsided Mughal defeat in two centuries.
Nader's smaller force, equipped with up-to-date Iranian-Ottoman gunpowder weapons and tactics, used speed, deception, and concentrated artillery fire to break the Mughal cavalry charges.
The Mughal field army was annihilated within a single afternoon.
The Mughal commander Khan Dauran was killed; the Nizam of Hyderabad (who had brought a contingent to the imperial army) escaped only by negotiating his own surrender separately.
Muhammad Shah fled the field.
The road to Delhi was open.
Nader Shah occupied Delhi for fifty-seven days, from March 20 to May 16, 1739.
The first three days passed in nominal peace.
Muhammad Shah formally surrendered, was confirmed in his nominal sovereignty, and accompanied Nader on a tour of the city.
Then a rumor spread that Nader had been killed in his quarters, the Delhi populace attacked the Iranian troops, and several thousand Iranians were killed in street fighting on March 22.
Nader, alive and furious, ordered systematic reprisals.
Iranian troops conducted a methodical sack of Delhi for the next several days.

The chronicles record death-toll estimates of 20,000 to 30,000 Delhi residents killed in the reprisals (some modern scholars suggest higher numbers, perhaps 50,000), though the precise count is impossible to recover.
The looting was systematic.
Nader's troops collected an estimated 700 million rupees in cash, gold, jewels, and goods — enough wealth that Nader famously suspended taxation in Iran for three years on his return.
The most prestigious individual items taken were the Peacock Throne (Chapter 5) and the Koh-i-Noor diamond.
The throne was disassembled in Persia after Nader's assassination in 1747, with the Koh-i-Noor passing through Afghan and eventually Sikh and British hands (Chapter 8).
Nader also took the imperial library, the imperial treasury contents, and a substantial portion of the Mughal court's elephant herd.
Nader withdrew from Delhi in May 1739, formally restoring Muhammad Shah to the throne (a humiliation Muhammad Shah survived for another nine years) and crossing the Indus back into Persia in June.
He had spent less than four months on Indian soil.
He had effectively destroyed the Mughal Empire as a great power.
The Mughal treasury was empty.
The Mughal field army was destroyed.

The Mughal prestige — which had been a substantial part of how the empire actually functioned, since regional governors paid attention to the Mughal court partly because of its symbolic weight — was visibly broken.
The political consequences cascaded immediately.
Within a year, the regional successor states were treating the Mughal court with open contempt.
The Nizam of Hyderabad stopped pretending to obey imperial orders.
The Marathas pushed northward more aggressively.
The Bengal Nawabate became fully independent in everything but coinage.
The Sikh military power expanded.
The Mughal emperor's actual authority shrank to the immediate environs of Delhi.
The Mughal Empire would continue to exist, in a nominal sense, for another 119 years (until 1858, Chapter 9).
But the empire as an effective political entity ended at Karnal on February 24, 1739, and was given its formal funeral in the streets of Delhi that March.
The 1740s and 1750s saw the consolidation of the post-Mughal regional order.

In 1747, Ahmad Shah Durrani (also known as Ahmad Shah Abdali), an Afghan general who had served under Nader Shah, founded the Durrani Empire (the modern Afghan state's predecessor) and immediately began conducting raids into Mughal-claimed territory in the Punjab.

Ahmad Shah Durrani would invade north India eight times between 1747 and 1767 — most consequentially in 1761, when his forces met the expanding Marathas at the Third Battle of Panipat (the third major battle on the same plain north of Delhi where Babur had defeated Ibrahim Lodi in 1526 and Akbar's forces had defeated Hemu in 1556, Chapters 1 and 3).
The Maratha army of perhaps 100,000-150,000 troops was destroyed; Maratha casualties of 60,000 to 100,000 in the battle and pursuit temporarily checked their northern expansion.
The battle is sometimes considered the moment when the Marathas lost the chance to establish themselves as the post-Mughal sovereigns of north India.
The vacuum left by the Maratha defeat would be filled, gradually, by the British.
Muhammad Shah died in 1748, age forty-six, at Delhi.
His son Ahmad Shah Bahadur (no relation to the Afghan invader of similar name — confusingly, both contemporary monarchs were named "Ahmad Shah") inherited a wreck of an empire.
He was deposed and blinded by his vizier in 1754.
His successor Alamgir II was assassinated in 1759 by his own vizier.

The vizier installed Shah Alam II as the next emperor; Shah Alam II would survive on the throne until 1806 in spite of being captured by the Marathas, captured by the British, blinded by an Afghan raider in 1788 (Chapter 9), and reduced to ceremonial status while the British East India Company took over the actual governance of the territory in his name.
The most consequential of the eighteenth-century events, in the long retrospective view, was a small obscure clash that nobody at the time recognized as significant.
In 1756, the new Nawab of Bengal, the twenty-three-year-old Siraj-ud-Daulah (sih-RAHJ uhd DOW-lah), captured the East India Company settlement at Calcutta.

The motivation was a complex mix of factors: the Nawab's irritation at Company fortifications around Calcutta (which he considered a violation of his territorial sovereignty), the Company's harboring of fugitives from Bengali political feuds, the Nawab's general inexperience and erratic temperament, and the financial pressure from court rivals who wanted to seize Company merchant wealth.
The capture itself was a quick military operation.
The Company garrison surrendered.
The Nawab's forces occupied the settlement.
What happened next is the famous (and substantially mythologized) Black Hole of Calcutta episode.

According to the British accounts that would shortly become central to the imperial mythology of the Company's Indian conquest, Siraj-ud-Daulah's troops crammed 146 captured Britons into a small cell at the Calcutta fort overnight, and 123 of them died of suffocation in the heat by morning.
The chief contemporary source was John Zephaniah Holwell, a Company official who survived the cell and wrote a detailed account that was published in London in 1758 to enormous public reaction.
Modern scholarship has substantially demolished the most extreme version of Holwell's account.
The actual numbers were much smaller — modern scholars estimate around 64 prisoners, with 18 to 43 deaths overnight depending on which secondary source you trust.
The cell was real, the suffocation was real, the deaths were real, but the scale and the deliberate-atrocity framing of Holwell's account were exaggerated.
The Black Hole story became central British justification for the conquest of Bengal, which is one reason the British accounts amplified it.

The Indian counter-narrative, that Holwell exaggerated for political effect, is broadly correct on the scale question but does not erase the underlying fact that prisoners did die of suffocation in a Bengal jail.
The political consequence was, however, enormous.
The British public reaction to the Black Hole story (whether accurate or exaggerated) created political support for a Company military expedition to recapture Calcutta.
The expedition was led by Robert Clive (KLIVE), a thirty-two-year-old Company officer with prior Indian military experience.
Clive recaptured Calcutta in January 1757.
He then began maneuvering for a much larger objective — the replacement of Siraj-ud-Daulah with a more pliable Nawab who would grant the Company expanded commercial privileges.

Clive's instrument was bribery: he negotiated secretly with Mir Jafar, Siraj-ud-Daulah's senior military commander, offering a fortune for Mir Jafar to defect during the inevitable confrontation between Company forces and the Nawab's army.
The confrontation came on June 23, 1757, on a mango grove called Plassey (PLAS-ee, a corruption of Palashi), about 95 miles north of Calcutta.
The next chapter is mostly about what came after Plassey.
Cross-civ check: the eighteenth-century Mughal collapse coincided with several major contemporaneous transformations elsewhere.

The Ottoman Empire under Ahmed III and his successors was in mid-arc of its own long decline (Ottoman Empire Ch 7 and Ch 8) — the parallel structural problems (succession instability, fiscal exhaustion, regional governors becoming autonomous, European commercial penetration) are striking.
Safavid Persia had collapsed entirely in 1722 (Safavid Persia Ch 8) and was now reorganizing under Nader Shah and his successors.

Qing China under the Yongzheng Emperor (1722-35) and the Qianlong Emperor (1735-96) was at peak — the largest single Qing expansion was happening in exactly the years the Mughal Empire was collapsing.
Tokugawa Japan continued its sakoku isolation (Edo Japan Ch 5), wealthy and stable but disconnected from the Eurasian political-economic transformation.

The British Industrial Revolution had begun in textile-mechanization (the flying shuttle was patented in 1733; the spinning jenny in 1764; the steam engine substantially developed by 1769) — the same transformation that would shortly destroy the Indian textile industry that had been the foundation of Mughal economic prosperity.

The eighteenth century was an era of profound global restructuring, and the Mughal collapse is best understood as one regional component of that larger restructuring rather than as a specifically South Asian story.

chapters.title: The Company Takes Over
sentences: The conquest of India by the British East India Company is one of the strangest events in the history of empire.

A chartered commercial corporation, founded in 1600 by a group of London merchants for the purpose of trading in Asian spices and textiles, gradually transformed itself over the course of the eighteenth century into the sovereign government of the most populous part of the early-modern world.
By 1800, the East India Company governed about 20% of the human race.
The conquest was not directed from London; the British government did not formally take over until 1858 (Chapter 9).

It was conducted by Company employees, financed by Company revenues, justified by Company commercial interests, and produced what is almost certainly the largest sustained accumulation of imperial wealth in modern history.
The conquest happened in three phases.
The first phase was the conquest of Bengal (1757-65), which produced the wealth and political base for everything that followed.
The second phase was the wars against the regional Indian powers (1767-1818) — three Anglo-Mysore Wars against the Wodeyars and Tipu Sultan, three Anglo-Maratha Wars against the Maratha Confederacy.
The third phase was the wars against the Sikhs (1845-49) that completed the Company's conquest of north India.
This chapter covers all three phases compactly.

The Mughal emperor at Delhi remained throughout — nominally still the sovereign, in practice a pensioner of the Company, his actual authority limited to the Red Fort and a few square miles of surrounding city.
The Company collected the revenue, made the laws, and fought the wars.
The emperor signed the firmans the Company drafted for him.
The arrangement was, in formal legal terms, an absurdity, but it served everyone's purposes well enough that nobody dismantled it for a century.
The Battle of Plassey on June 23, 1757, was less a battle than a stage-managed political assassination.

Robert Clive's force totaled about 3,000 men — 800 European soldiers from the Company's regular regiments, around 2,200 sepoys (Indian soldiers in Company service, mostly recruited from the Bhojpuri-speaking districts of Bihar and eastern Uttar Pradesh), about 8 cannons.
Siraj-ud-Daulah's army totaled approximately 50,000 men — perhaps 18,000 cavalry, 30,000 infantry, 50 cannons, and a substantial elephant contingent.
The numerical disparity was about 17 to 1 against the Company.
The numerical disparity didn't matter, because Clive had bribed Siraj-ud-Daulah's commander Mir Jafar to keep his troops out of the fighting.
Mir Jafar commanded approximately two-thirds of the Bengal army.
He had agreed, in a secret treaty signed with Clive in early June, to keep his forces in reserve and to refuse to engage the Company forces.
In exchange, Clive would install him as the new Nawab of Bengal, with substantial cash payments to himself personally and to several other senior Bengal officers who were also in on the conspiracy.
The battle proceeded as Clive had engineered it.

The fighting actually conducted was between Company forces and the loyal portion of Siraj-ud-Daulah's army (perhaps 12,000-15,000 men, commanded by the loyalist general Mir Madan, who was killed in the early fighting).
A heavy mid-morning rain damaged the loyalist artillery (which was not protected) but not the Company artillery (which had been covered with tarpaulins).

With Mir Madan dead and the loyalist artillery silent, Clive's Company forces moved forward, the loyal portion of the Bengal army began to retreat, Mir Jafar's contingents stood watching, and within a few hours the battle was over.
Total casualties were minimal — perhaps 500 dead on the Bengal side, perhaps 70 dead on the Company side.
Siraj-ud-Daulah fled the field, was captured a few days later, and was assassinated on Mir Jafar's orders.
Clive entered the Bengal capital Murshidabad in late June and installed Mir Jafar as the new Nawab.
The financial settlement was extraordinary.
Mir Jafar paid the Company £2.34 million (approximately £400 million in modern terms, conservatively estimated), with additional £234,000 personally to Clive himself.

The new Nawab also granted the Company the zamindari (landlord rights) over an additional 24 districts around Calcutta, effectively converting much of southern Bengal into Company-administered territory.
Plassey is conventionally taken as the starting point of British India.
The military victory was modest.
The political coup was decisive.
The Company had transformed itself from a commercial trading partner into the de facto sovereign of the wealthiest province in India.
Mir Jafar's career as Nawab of Bengal was short.
He proved (predictably) ineffective as a ruler — his court was riven by factional conflict, his revenue collection deteriorated, the Company found him uncooperative on additional commercial demands.
The Company deposed him in 1760 and installed his son-in-law Mir Qasim as the new Nawab.

Mir Qasim turned out to be more capable than the Company had expected, attempted to reorganize the Bengal military and resist Company demands, and was promptly deposed in turn (1763) and replaced with the now-old-and-pliable Mir Jafar again.
Mir Qasim's response was to ally with the Mughal emperor Shah Alam II and the Nawab of Awadh Shuja-ud-Daulah in a coordinated military effort to drive the Company out of Bengal.
The combined armies of the three Indian rulers met the Company forces under Hector Munro at Buxar on October 22, 1764.
The Battle of Buxar was a more serious military engagement than Plassey.
The Mughal-Awadh-Bengal coalition fielded perhaps 40,000 troops; Munro's force was about 7,000 (1,800 European, 5,200 sepoy).
There was no bribery this time — the Indian commanders were committed and competent.
But Company forces had now had seven years to consolidate their organizational and tactical advantages, and the Indian forces were uncoordinated.

Munro's troops broke the coalition's center, the Indian armies retreated in confusion, and within a single day the Company had defeated the most serious Indian military challenge it would face for the next forty years.
The political consequences of Buxar were enormous.
The Treaty of Allahabad in 1765 transferred the Diwani — the right to collect land revenue — over Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa from the Mughal emperor to the Company.
Shah Alam II formally granted the Diwani in exchange for a Company pension of 26 lakh rupees per year (approximately £260,000).
The Nawab of Awadh, Shuja-ud-Daulah, had to pay a war indemnity of 50 lakh rupees and accept a Company resident at his court.
The Company now legally controlled the revenue of the wealthiest province in India, with the Mughal emperor's formal endorsement.
The actual administrative arrangement was peculiar.

The Company collected the revenue but did not, initially, govern Bengal directly — it operated a kind of dual government, with the Nawab nominally administering civil and criminal justice while the Company ran the revenue collection and the military.

The arrangement was dysfunctional (the Nawab had no resources, the Company had no political-cultural infrastructure), and by the 1770s it was being progressively unwound in favor of more direct Company administration.
By 1772, under Warren Hastings as the new Governor-General, the Company had effectively become the direct government of Bengal.
The wealth that flowed from Bengal in the next four decades was, by modern estimates, the largest single accumulation of imperial wealth in early-modern history.
The Bengal land revenue collection alone produced approximately £2 million per year in the 1770s and grew steadily through the rest of the century.
The Company's customs duties at Calcutta produced additional revenue.
The Company's own commercial operations — buying Bengal cotton textiles, indigo dye, opium, and other commodities, selling them in Britain, China, and Southeast Asia — generated additional profits.

The opium trade in particular became a major revenue source: Company-monopolized opium production in eastern India was sold at Company auctions in Calcutta, transported to Canton in China by private merchants, and exchanged for tea (which the Company sold in Britain at substantial profit).

The opium-tea-textile triangle became the financial foundation of late-eighteenth-century British imperial wealth (the triangle's full arc — opium, cotton, empire — is the subject of Industrial Revolution Ch 19; the Manchester cotton machinery on the British end is Ch 3).
The Indian impact was correspondingly devastating.
Bengal's economy contracted under Company rule.

The textile manufacturing centers (especially around Dhaka, the muslin capital) declined as the Company's purchasing terms forced producers to sell at fixed low prices (the mechanized Manchester mills on the other end of this story are Industrial Revolution Ch 3).
The agricultural sector deteriorated as the Company's revenue assessment was raised to maximize extraction.

The Bengal Famine of 1770 killed approximately 10 million people — about a third of the Bengal population — partly from drought but substantially exacerbated by Company revenue policies that maintained tax demands while grain prices spiraled.
The famine was probably the worst in eighteenth-century world history, and it happened under Company rule directly.
Modern scholars have debated the extent to which "drain" of wealth from India to Britain contributed to British industrialization in the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries.
The estimates vary substantially.
The most cautious scholars suggest the drain was modest as a fraction of British GDP.
The most aggressive scholars (most prominently the Indian historian Utsa Patnaik) suggest the drain was enormous and central to British industrialization.

The honest answer is somewhere between — the drain was real, was substantial, and was probably significant in financing the British Industrial Revolution, but other factors (technological innovation, coal availability, institutional structures) were also important.
What is not disputable is that the conquest of Bengal made the Company immensely rich and made Bengal substantially poorer.

The expansion to the south came through the Anglo-Mysore Wars (1767-99), four conflicts against the Hindu Wodeyar dynasty of Mysore (succeeded after 1761 by the Muslim general Hyder Ali and his son Tipu Sultan, TEE-poo SUL-tahn).
Hyder Ali, originally a soldier in Mysore service, had taken effective control of the Mysore state in the 1760s while keeping the Wodeyar maharaja on the throne as a figurehead.

He was an able military commander who built up the Mysore army using up-to-date European military techniques (he hired French military advisors and equipped his troops with French-made muskets and artillery).
He fought the First Anglo-Mysore War (1767-69) to a draw, fought the Second Anglo-Mysore War (1780-84) inconclusively.
He died in 1782 during the Second War, leaving his son Tipu Sultan as his successor.
Tipu Sultan was a more remarkable figure than his father.

He was a serious military innovator — most famously the pioneer of military rocket warfare, deploying iron-cased rockets in the Mysore army that delivered explosive warheads at ranges of up to two miles.

The British copied the Mysore rockets directly: the Congreve rocket, developed by William Congreve in the early 1800s and used by the British army through the Napoleonic Wars and beyond, was substantially based on the Mysore rocket designs.

The "rockets' red glare" in the American national anthem refers to Congreve rockets fired by the British navy at Fort McHenry in 1814 — derived directly, in technological lineage, from Tipu Sultan's Mysore artillery.
Tipu was also a serious diplomat.

He sent embassies to Ottoman Constantinople (seeking support from the Ottoman caliph), to revolutionary France (signing a treaty of friendship with the French Republic in 1798), to various other anti-British powers, attempting to build a coalition against Company expansion.
He patronized scholarship, built libraries, modernized his administration, and in many respects was the most administratively capable of the late-eighteenth-century Indian rulers.
He fought the Third Anglo-Mysore War (1790-92) and lost about half his territory to the Company.

He fought the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War (1798-99) and was killed defending his capital Seringapatam (sih-ring-ah-PAT-am, also called Srirangapatna, on an island in the Kaveri river south of Bangalore) in May 1799.
The Company restored the Wodeyar dynasty to the Mysore throne as a Company-client kingdom and absorbed roughly two-thirds of the former Mysore territory directly into Company administration.
Tipu's defeat is sometimes cited as the moment when the Indian military challenge to the Company effectively ended.

The judgment is too strong (the Marathas and Sikhs would still produce serious wars over the next half-century), but it captures something true: by 1800, no individual Indian ruler had the military or financial resources to seriously contest the Company's territorial expansion.
The Anglo-Maratha Wars (1775-82, 1803-05, 1817-18) destroyed the Maratha Confederacy and gave the Company control of central and western India.
The Marathas had emerged as the dominant Indian military power after the Maratha-Mughal wars under Aurangzeb (Chapter 6) and the post-Aurangzeb expansion under successive Peshwas (Chapter 7).

By the late eighteenth century, the Maratha Confederacy was a loose alliance of five major chieftaincies: the Peshwa at Pune (the central authority, head of the Confederacy), the Scindia at Gwalior (the dominant force in north-central India), the Holkar at Indore (Malwa region), the Bhonsle at Nagpur (eastern Deccan), and the Gaekwad at Baroda (Gujarat).
The combined Maratha military power was the largest single Indian political-military force at the end of the eighteenth century.

The first Anglo-Maratha War (1775-82) was a Company defeat — a Company expedition to install a Peshwa-claimant was crushingly defeated at the Battle of Wadgaon in 1779, and the Treaty of Salbai (1782) restored the prewar boundaries.
The Company learned from this and prepared more carefully.
The second Anglo-Maratha War (1803-05) was the Company's decisive victory.

The young Company general Arthur Wellesley (the future Duke of Wellington, who would defeat Napoleon at Waterloo twelve years later) defeated the combined Scindia-Bhonsle army at the Battle of Assaye on September 23, 1803.

Wellington reportedly described Assaye later in his life as the toughest battle he ever fought — and the man had Waterloo to compare it to, which gives a sense of how seriously contested the Maratha military was.
The Company also defeated the Marathas at the simultaneous Battle of Argaon and the siege of Gawilghur fort.
The treaty of Surji-Anjangaon (1803) and Deogaon (1803) transferred substantial Maratha territories to the Company.
The third Anglo-Maratha War (1817-18) was the final destruction of Maratha independence.

The Peshwa at Pune attempted to organize one last resistance; the Company crushed it; the Peshwa was deposed; the Maratha Confederacy was formally dissolved; the chieftaincies were reduced to Company-client princely states.
By 1818, the Company had effective control of most of central and western India.
The Anglo-Sikh Wars (1845-46, 1848-49) completed the Company's conquest.

The Sikh Empire in the Punjab had been built up under Maharaja Ranjit Singh (ruled 1801-39), the most able Indian state-builder of the early nineteenth century, who had united the Sikh principalities of the Punjab, modernized the Sikh army using European military advisors (the Sikh Khalsa Army of the 1830s was probably the most up-to-date Indian army of its time), and built a state that controlled the entire upper Indus basin from Kashmir to Multan.
After Ranjit Singh's death in 1839, the Sikh Empire fell into a succession crisis with multiple short-lived rulers and a powerful military council that increasingly dominated state affairs.
The Company, alarmed by the proximity of the powerful Sikh state to its Bengal territories and by the political instability of the post-Ranjit succession, provoked a confrontation in 1845.

The First Anglo-Sikh War (December 1845 to March 1846) saw a series of hard-fought battles (Mudki, Ferozeshah, Aliwal, Sobraon) in which the Sikh army acquitted itself well but was eventually defeated by Company forces under Sir Hugh Gough.
The Treaty of Lahore (1846) reduced the Sikh state to client status.
The Second Anglo-Sikh War (1848-49) finished the job.
The decisive Battle of Gujrat (1849) destroyed the remaining Sikh military power.
The Punjab was annexed to British India in March 1849.

The annexation included one specific item that has become famous: the surrender of the Koh-i-Noor diamond, which had passed from Mughal possession after Nader Shah's 1739 sack (Chapter 7) through Afghan hands (the Durrani dynasty) into Sikh hands during Ranjit Singh's reign.

The diamond was surrendered as part of the 1849 settlement, transported to England, recut by Garrard's of London at Queen Victoria's instruction in 1852 (the recut reduced its weight from 186 carats to 105 carats but improved its visual brilliance), and set into the British crown.
It now sits in the Tower of London, the subject of recurring restitution claims by the Indian, Pakistani, Afghan, and Iranian governments.

The diamond's path — Mughal court > Persian conqueror > Afghan king > Sikh maharaja > British queen — is in itself a compact map of the eighteenth- and nineteenth-century political collapse of South Asian sovereignty.

By 1849, the East India Company governed effectively the entire Indian subcontinent, either directly (in the major provinces — Bengal, Bombay, Madras, Punjab, Bihar, Orissa, parts of central India) or indirectly through client princely states (Hyderabad, Mysore, Awadh, Travancore, Kashmir, Rajput states, Sikh chieftaincies, several hundred smaller princely states).

The Company had a private army of approximately 250,000 troops (mostly Indian sepoys, with a smaller European officer corps), a private revenue-collection apparatus, a private court system, and a private bureaucracy.
It was, in operational terms, a sovereign state.
The chartered commercial corporation founded by London merchants in 1600 had become the largest empire in Asia.
The Mughal emperor at Delhi remained throughout.
Shah Alam II (1759-1806) had been the Mughal emperor at the time of the Diwani grant in 1765.
His successor Akbar Shah II (1806-37) had been the Mughal emperor through the Anglo-Maratha Wars.
Bahadur Shah Zafar (1837-57) was the Mughal emperor at the time of the Anglo-Sikh Wars.
None of them had any actual political power.

They received Company pensions, presided over ceremonial functions at the Red Fort, patronized the Urdu poetry and music that was the cultural specialty of late-Mughal Delhi, and signed whatever the Company wanted them to sign.
They were, formally, sovereign monarchs of an empire that no longer existed.

The next chapter is mostly about the moment when the Company miscalculated, the sepoys mutinied, and the dynastic ceremony got dragged into the actual political conflict that ended both the dynasty and the Company.
Cross-civ check: the Company's Indian conquest happened during the same decades as several other major imperial transformations.

The American Revolution (1775-83) coincided with the First Anglo-Maratha War and the post-Plassey consolidation of Company rule in Bengal — Britain lost its American empire while gaining its Indian empire, a substitution that was not lost on contemporary British observers.

The French Revolution (1789-99) and the Napoleonic Wars (1803-15) coincided with the Third and Fourth Anglo-Mysore Wars and the Second Anglo-Maratha War — Tipu Sultan attempted to align with revolutionary France, and his death at Seringapatam in 1799 was directly relevant to British strategic concerns about French penetration of South Asia.
The Latin American independence wars (1810-25) coincided with the late Anglo-Maratha campaigns.

The Opium Wars in China (1839-42, 1856-60) coincided with the Anglo-Sikh Wars — and were closely connected, since the opium that the British forced China to import came from Company-controlled production in Bengal and Bihar.
The Company's Indian conquest was one component of a global British imperial expansion that, between roughly 1763 and 1858, made Britain the dominant power of the nineteenth-century world.
The Mughal collapse and the British rise are two halves of a single story.

chapters.title: The 1857 Rebellion and the End
sentences: The Mughal Empire ended in 1858, three hundred and thirty-two years after Babur's victory at Panipat.

The proximate cause was the Indian Rebellion of 1857 (also called the Sepoy Mutiny in older British accounts, the First War of Indian Independence in some Indian nationalist accounts, and the 1857 Uprising in most modern academic usage — the choice of name carries political baggage that is best acknowledged rather than papered over).

The rebellion began as a mutiny of Indian soldiers in Company service at Meerut in May 1857, spread across north India over the following weeks, focused on Delhi where the eighty-two-year-old Bahadur Shah Zafar was reluctantly proclaimed emperor of India by the rebels, was suppressed by Company forces over the following fifteen months at enormous cost in life on both sides, and ended with the British government formally taking over the administration of India from the East India Company and exiling the last Mughal emperor to Burma.
The Mughal dynasty died in this convulsion, after lingering for fifty years past any effective political relevance.
This chapter covers the rebellion compactly — the trigger, the spread, the ceremonial role of Bahadur Shah Zafar, the British suppression, the Delhi reprisals, the formal dissolution.
Then it spends some time on the longer question of what the Mughals actually left to South Asia and to the world — which, even after 1858, was substantial.
The trigger was the Enfield rifle cartridges.
The Company had introduced the Pattern 1853 Enfield rifle to Indian service in 1857.
The new weapon used pre-greased paper cartridges that the soldier had to bite open before loading.
The grease was a mixture of animal fats — and a rumor spread among Indian sepoys (both Hindu and Muslim) that the grease was a mix of cow tallow and pig lard.
For Hindu soldiers, biting beef-greased cartridges would be a major religious pollution (the cow being sacred).
For Muslim soldiers, biting pork-greased cartridges would be a major religious pollution (pigs being haram).

The combination of these religious offenses, applied simultaneously to two different religious communities by the same weapon, looked from the sepoy perspective like a deliberate Company plan to humiliate or even forcibly convert Indian soldiers.

The Company army administrators recognized the problem and quickly modified the cartridge greasing — switching to vegetable oil and beeswax, allowing soldiers to grease their own cartridges, withdrawing the original cartridges from issue.
The damage was already done.

The trust between the Company and its Indian soldiers had been substantially eroded for years by other grievances (low pay, poor treatment, restrictions on overseas service, the recent annexation of Awadh by Lord Dalhousie in 1856 which had stripped many sepoys of their home-state privileges).
The cartridge issue was the last straw.
The withdrawal of the cartridges did not undo the damage.

The first significant mutiny incident was at Meerut on May 10, 1857, when sepoys of the 3rd Bengal Light Cavalry mutinied after eighty-five of their colleagues had been court-martialed and sentenced to long prison terms for refusing to handle the Enfield cartridges.
The Meerut mutineers killed several British officers and the British civilians they could find, then marched south through the night to Delhi, arriving on May 11.
At Delhi, the Meerut mutineers reached the Red Fort and presented themselves to the Mughal emperor.
Bahadur Shah Zafar (bah-HAH-door SHAH ZAH-far) was eighty-two years old.
He had been the nominal Mughal emperor since 1837.
His actual authority extended only to the Red Fort and the surrounding areas of Shahjahanabad.

He was a serious Urdu poet (the pen name Zafar — "victory" — was his literary signature; his collected poetry, the Diwan-i-Zafar, is part of the canon of Urdu classical poetry) and a devoted Sufi disciple of the Chishti order.
He had spent his reign managing the elaborate rituals of the Mughal court while drawing his Company pension and signing whatever the Company put in front of him.
He was, by every contemporary account, a kind, cultured, indecisive man who had no personal interest in being part of an anti-British rebellion.
The Meerut mutineers presented him with a fait accompli.
They had killed European officers; they had killed European civilians; they had marched on Delhi expecting the Mughal emperor to lead them.
They proclaimed him emperor of India on the morning of May 11.
He, reportedly, tried to refuse.
They insisted.

He acquiesced — partly under pressure, partly because his own Mughal court was sympathetic to the rebellion (his eldest surviving son Mirza Mughal was particularly enthusiastic), partly because the alternative was being killed or deposed by the mutineers themselves.
The proclamation made him, formally, the head of the rebellion.
Whether he was a willing rebel leader or an unwilling figurehead is one of the questions that divides modern historical interpretation of the 1857 Uprising.
The British court that would later try him for treason chose to treat him as the willing leader.

Modern scholarship is more ambivalent — most historians now see Bahadur Shah as a substantially passive figure caught up in events he had no power to direct, but the dynastic-political symbolism of an actual Mughal emperor proclaimed by the rebels was undeniable, and he did sign rebel firmans and receive rebel commanders during the Delhi siege.
The rebellion spread across north India through May, June, and July 1857.

Major centers of mutiny included Meerut (May 10), Delhi (May 11), Lucknow (May 30), Cawnpore (Kanpur — June 5), Allahabad (June 6), Jhansi (June 6), Gwalior (June 14), and several dozen other smaller posts.
The geographic distribution corresponded roughly to the recruiting grounds of the Bengal Army (Bihar, eastern Uttar Pradesh, Awadh, parts of Bengal).
The Bombay Army and the Madras Army largely did not mutiny, partly because their recruiting was different and partly because their grievances were less acute.
Most of the south, west, and far north of India did not rebel.
The character of the rebellion varied substantially by region.
At Delhi, the rebellion was organized around the Mughal court and had a recognizable dynastic-political character.
At Lucknow, the rebellion was organized around the deposed Awadh royal family (Begum Hazrat Mahal acting as regent for her son, the displaced heir) and had a regional-monarchical character.

At Cawnpore, the rebellion was led by the Nana Sahib (an adopted son of the last Peshwa, with a personal grievance against the Company over his denied pension) and produced one of the most notorious atrocities of the rebellion when British civilians, including women and children, were massacred at the Bibighar after surrendering on a guarantee of safe passage.

At Jhansi, the rebellion was led by Rani Lakshmi Bai (the widowed queen of the small principality of Jhansi, whose state had been annexed by the Company under the Doctrine of Lapse, which became a martial heroine in subsequent Indian nationalist mythology).
The various regional rebellions had different leaders, different goals, and limited coordination.
The unifying feature was the breakdown of the Company-sepoy relationship.
The British civilian and military death toll across north India was approximately 6,000 in the first weeks.

The Indian death toll — both rebels killed in fighting and civilians killed in retaliatory British actions — would eventually run into the hundreds of thousands, possibly close to a million across the full eighteen-month period of the rebellion and its aftermath.
The 1857 Uprising was the bloodiest single event in nineteenth-century Indian history.
The British recapture of Delhi in September 1857 was the symbolic and military turning point.
A British force, the Delhi Field Force, was assembled at Karnal in late May and marched south to invest Delhi from the Ridge (a low ridge of high ground north of the city).

The siege ran from June through September 1857, with the British force consistently outnumbered by the rebels inside the city but maintained by a constant flow of reinforcements from the Punjab (which had not rebelled, partly because Sikh and Punjabi Muslim soldiers in Company service had no particular reason to support the Mughal emperor and were happy to fight against the Bengal sepoys who had often been their professional rivals).

The decisive assault came on September 14, 1857, with British and Sikh-Punjabi forces breaking through the city walls at the Kashmiri Gate and fighting through the streets of Shahjahanabad over the following five days.
The Red Fort was taken on September 19.

Bahadur Shah Zafar fled the fort with his immediate family and took refuge at the Tomb of Humayun (his great-great-great-great-great-great-great-grandfather, the second Mughal emperor whose tomb had been built three hundred years earlier, Chapter 2).
He was captured there on September 21 by a British officer, William Hodson.
What followed was systematic violence against the Delhi population.

The British forces conducted house-to-house searches, executed Indian men suspected of having participated in the rebellion (the threshold of suspicion was sometimes very low), expelled the surviving Muslim population of Shahjahanabad from the city for several months, looted the Red Fort and the great houses of the Mughal nobility, and demolished portions of the city to widen streets for military access.
The Delhi population in 1857 was approximately 160,000; by 1861 it had dropped to perhaps 50,000-60,000, partly from killings, partly from expulsions, partly from emigration.

The most notorious individual incident was Hodson's execution of Bahadur Shah's three sons (his heir Mirza Mughal, his second son Mirza Khizr Sultan, and his grandson Mirza Abu Bakr) on September 22, 1857, the day after their father's surrender.
Hodson had captured the three princes near the Tomb of Humayun and was escorting them back to Delhi under guard.
He stopped the convoy, ordered them to strip to their underclothes, ordered them to dismount, and shot them personally in the chest with his revolver.
The justification Hodson gave later was that crowds were assembling to attempt a rescue and he could not safely continue with the prisoners.
The actual reason was almost certainly personal — Hodson wanted to be the man who had killed the Mughal princes.
The bodies were displayed publicly at Delhi for several days.
The location of the killings, near a gateway in the Mughal city wall, was named Khooni Darwaza ("Bloody Gate") and is still called that.
The British reprisals at Delhi went on for months.
The Mughal court was dispersed, the great Mughal-era Muslim landholding families were dispossessed, and the cultural-economic infrastructure of late-Mughal Delhi was substantially destroyed.

The Urdu poet Mirza Ghalib (mir-ZAH GHAH-lib, 1797-1869), who had been the literary genius of late-Mughal Delhi and a favorite courtier of Bahadur Shah Zafar, lived through the siege and its aftermath in Delhi and recorded the catastrophe in letters and a Persian-language journal called Dastambu.

Ghalib's letters from the post-siege period are some of the most affecting documents of Indian history — he describes the streets empty of people he had known, the houses of friends torn down for British military purposes, the sense of a world he had spent his life inside ending around him.

The British retook Lucknow in November 1857, suppressed the remaining major rebellions through 1858 (the Rani of Jhansi was killed in battle in June 1858; Nana Sahib disappeared and was never captured; smaller resistance fighters held out in Awadh and Central India until late 1858), and declared the rebellion over in late 1858.

The total Indian casualties — combatants and civilians, killed and missing, including the famine and disease deaths driven by the war's disruption — are now estimated at hundreds of thousands at minimum, possibly close to a million.
The dissolution of the Mughal dynasty was made formal in 1858.

Bahadur Shah Zafar was tried by a British military commission in January-March 1858, sitting in the Diwan-i-Khas of the Red Fort (the same hall where the Peacock Throne had stood until Nader Shah took it in 1739).
The charges were treason against the Crown of England, complicity in the murder of British officers and civilians, and conspiracy in the rebellion.
The trial ran for forty days, with extensive testimony from witnesses to events at the Red Fort during the rebellion.
Bahadur Shah was convicted on all charges.
The sentence was exile to Rangoon (modern Yangon), where he was conveyed by ship in October 1858 along with his wife Zinat Mahal and his surviving family members.
He died there on November 7, 1862, age eighty-seven, four years into exile.
He was buried at an unmarked grave to prevent his tomb becoming a pilgrimage destination.
His grave was located only in 1991 and is now a small commemorative shrine.
The Government of India Act 1858 (passed by the British Parliament in August 1858) transferred power from the East India Company to the British Crown.
The Company was dissolved as a sovereign authority.
The British government appointed a Viceroy of India (the first being Lord Canning, the previous Governor-General) to administer India directly.
The British monarch was henceforth styled "Empress of India" (a title formally adopted by Queen Victoria in 1876).
The princely states that had been Company-client sovereigns now became British-Crown-client sovereigns, with substantially the same arrangements but a new sovereign at the top of the chain.
The Mughal dynasty was extinguished.
The line of Babur, Humayun, Akbar, Jahangir, Shah Jahan, Aurangzeb, and the eighteenth-century successors had ended at Bahadur Shah Zafar's exile.
The last surviving sons and grandsons of the dynasty died in obscurity in Rangoon, Calcutta, or Hyderabad over the next several decades.
The descendants who exist today have no political claim and most live private lives in India and Pakistan.
What did the Mughals leave?
The simplest answer is the architecture.

The major Mughal monuments — the Taj Mahal, Humayun's Tomb, the Red Fort at Delhi, Fatehpur Sikri, Akbar's Tomb at Sikandra, Jama Masjid in Delhi, Badshahi Mosque in Lahore, the Lahore Fort, the Shalimar Gardens at Lahore, the various provincial monuments — are still standing, mostly preserved, mostly on UNESCO World Heritage lists.
Modern visitors to north India and Pakistan encounter Mughal architecture as the dominant pre-modern visual culture of the region.
The architectural inheritance is substantively unbroken from 1530 to the present.
The cuisine is the second most visible inheritance.

The biryanis, the kebabs, the naan and roti breads, the kheer and gulab jamun and jalebi sweets, the entire vocabulary of north Indian Persianate cooking (and much of Pakistani and Bangladeshi cuisine) — these are Mughal-era developments that have been continuously practiced from the early modern period to the present.
The modern Indian-Pakistani food world is, gastronomically, a Mughal inheritance with regional and modern modifications.
The third inheritance is linguistic.

Urdu, which had emerged as a Persianate register of north Indian Hindi-Khariboli during the late Sultanate period (Delhi Sultanate Ch 6) and matured as a literary language at the eighteenth- and nineteenth-century Mughal and Awadh courts (with the great Urdu poets Mir Taqi Mir, Mirza Ghalib, Allama Iqbal, and others), is now the national language of Pakistan and one of the major languages of north India.
The Persian-derived vocabulary of Hindi and Urdu — for legal terms, administrative terms, courtly terms, romantic terms — is substantially Mughal in origin.
Even Hindi, which has been deliberately Sanskritized in independent India to distinguish it from Urdu, retains a substantial Mughal-era Persian vocabulary in its everyday spoken form.
The fourth inheritance is political-institutional.
The British Raj that succeeded the Mughals inherited the Mughal administrative-fiscal structure substantially intact, modifying it gradually rather than replacing it.
The mansabdari-jagirdari system of the Mughal nobility evolved into the British Indian Civil Service and the princely-state system.
The Mughal land-revenue assessment evolved into the British Indian land-revenue system.

The Mughal-era provincial boundaries (suba, sarkar, pargana) substantially survived as British provincial-and-district boundaries, and substantially survive in the modern Indian and Pakistani administrative geography.
The institutional template of the modern Indian and Pakistani states is, in significant respects, a Mughal template.
The fifth inheritance is the cultural-religious geography of the modern subcontinent.

The Mughals expanded the Indian Muslim community substantially through the conversion of certain regional populations (eastern Bengal, western Punjab and Sindh, parts of the Deccan), and consolidated the Indo-Persian high-cultural synthesis that defined Indian Muslim identity.

The eventual partition of British India in 1947, into majority-Hindu India and majority-Muslim Pakistan, mapped substantially onto the demographic-religious geography that the Sultanate and Mughal periods had created.
The 1947 Partition is, in some respects, the long-delayed second-order consequence of the Mughal religious-political settlement and its eventual unraveling.
The Mughal inheritance is contested in modern South Asia, and the contestation is itself worth a brief discussion.

For Indian secular-nationalist historiography (the dominant academic tradition since independence in 1947, associated with Marxist-influenced scholars at Delhi University, Aligarh Muslim University, and Jawaharlal Nehru University), the Mughals are part of the inclusive composite culture of pre-modern India — a Persianate Islamic dynasty that integrated Hindu and Muslim elements into a single state and culture, that produced one of the world's great pre-modern civilizations, and whose legacy is part of the shared Indian cultural inheritance available to citizens of all religions.
For Indian Hindu-nationalist historiography (the tradition associated with V.D.
Savarkar, K.B.

Hedgewar, and the Sangh Parivar of the late twentieth and early twenty-first century), the Mughals are foreign occupiers who suppressed Hindu civilization, destroyed Hindu temples (most famously, in this reading, the temples at Mathura, Varanasi, and Ayodhya — the Babri Masjid at Ayodhya, allegedly built on the site of Lord Ram's birthplace, was destroyed by Hindu activists in 1992 in one of the most consequential single events of late-twentieth-century Indian politics), and represent an interruption of authentic Indian civilization that needs to be reversed in modern Indian politics.
Akbar in this reading is a useful idiot whose tolerance helped Muslim political dominance; Aurangzeb is a religious fanatic whose policies are taken as paradigmatic of Muslim rule generally.

For Pakistani historiography (the tradition associated with Ishtiaq Hussain Qureshi and others), the Mughals are foundational ancestors of the Indian Muslim community and its eventual political expression in Pakistan.
Aurangzeb is a particular Pakistani nationalist hero (a serious orthodox Muslim ruler who resisted the syncretist tendencies of his predecessors).
Akbar is a more uncomfortable figure (his religious tolerance is sometimes read as departing from properly Islamic governance).

For Bangladeshi historiography, the Mughals are the dynasty under which eastern Bengal experienced its mass conversion to Islam (the demographic-religious shift that made Bangladesh majority-Muslim and that produced the eventual Bangladesh Liberation War of 1971 against Pakistan).

The Mughal period is centrally important to Bangladeshi national identity, but with regional Bengali emphasis rather than the Delhi-centric framing that dominates Indian and Pakistani Mughal historiography.

For modern American and European scholarship on the Mughals, the dynasty is increasingly viewed as one of the major early-modern world states, comparable in importance to the Ottoman Empire, Ming-Qing China, Tokugawa Japan, and the European absolutist monarchies.

The "early-modern global history" framework that has dominated academic world history since the 1990s places the Mughals as central rather than peripheral, with substantial scholarship on Mughal economic productivity, administrative innovation, cultural production, and global commercial connections.
The historiographical wars are ongoing.
They will probably continue for as long as modern South Asian politics depends on competing readings of the pre-colonial past — which is to say, indefinitely.

The honest scholarly response is the one this narrative has tried to take throughout: present the evidence, acknowledge the contested interpretive frameworks, and try to remain open to what the evidence supports without forcing it into any single political reading.
The British "civilizing mission" question also deserves a moment.

A central claim of nineteenth- and early-twentieth-century British colonial historiography (most famously in Macaulay's 1835 Minute on Indian Education, but the framework was much wider) was that British rule rescued India from Mughal-era despotism, religious obscurantism, and economic stagnation, bringing modern science, modern law, modern administration, and economic development to a backward society.
The civilizing mission was the moral justification for the colonial project.
The historical record does not support this claim.
Pre-British Mughal India was, by every available measure of pre-modern wealth, the richest of the early-modern world states.
The Bengal that the Company conquered in 1757 had a per-capita income probably comparable to or higher than contemporary England.
The textile manufacturing at Dhaka was the most sophisticated in the world.
The Mughal administrative apparatus that the Company inherited was, in operational terms, more elaborate than anything the British had built in their own kingdom.
The Mughal court culture was more refined than anything in early-modern Europe.
There was nothing for British rule to "civilize." What British rule did was extract.
The Bengal Famine of 1770 killed approximately 10 million people in part because of Company revenue policies.

The destruction of the Indian textile industry, accomplished partly through punitive tariffs in Britain that excluded Indian textiles from the British market while flooding the Indian market with Manchester mill-made cloth, deindustrialized the most economically advanced part of Asia within a generation.
The British-imposed "Permanent Settlement" of 1793 created a parasitic landholding class in Bengal that contributed to long-term agricultural stagnation.

The famines of the late nineteenth century (the Bihar famine of 1873-74, the Madras famine of 1876-78, the Indian famine of 1899-1900) killed millions of additional people under conditions of British administrative malpractice.

The Indian per-capita income, which had been close to British levels in 1757, had fallen to perhaps a fifth of British levels by 1947 — a substantially impoverished India produced by two centuries of British rule.
The civilizing mission was a story the British told themselves.
Modern scholarship — including modern British scholarship — has comprehensively dismantled it.
The Mughal Empire, for all its institutional and political failings, was not a backward society awaiting British civilization.

It was one of the great pre-modern civilizations, and its conquest by a chartered British corporation was a catastrophe for the Indian population that has been documented in modern economic history but is still imperfectly recognized in popular British and American historical memory.
The Mughal story ends, in one sense, at Bahadur Shah Zafar's exile and death.
In another sense, it continues.
The architecture is still there.
The Taj Mahal at Agra.
The Red Fort at Delhi.
Humayun's Tomb.
Fatehpur Sikri.
Akbar's Tomb at Sikandra.
Itimad-ud-Daulah's Tomb.
The Lahore Fort.
The Shalimar Gardens.
The Badshahi Mosque.
The Jama Masjid at Delhi.
Hundreds of smaller monuments scattered across north India, Pakistan, and Bangladesh — provincial Mughal-era mosques, tombs, gateways, gardens, residential buildings.
The architectural inheritance is the most visible continuous Mughal presence in the modern subcontinent.
The cuisine is still there.
The biryanis, the kebabs, the rotis, the sweets.
The tea-and-spice culture of north India.
The rich curries of the Mughal-influenced regional cuisines from Punjab through Hyderabad.
Every restaurant called "Moti Mahal" or "Karim's" or "Dastarkhwan" in the Indian and Pakistani diaspora is, in some sense, a Mughal cultural inheritance.
The language is still there.
Urdu is the national language of Pakistan and a major language of north India.
Hindi, despite its post-1947 deliberate Sanskritization, retains substantial Mughal-era Persian vocabulary in everyday usage.
The vocabulary of romance, of courtly elegance, of formal address, in north Indian Hindi-Urdu is largely Mughal-Persian in origin.
The religious geography is still there.

The Indian Muslim community of perhaps 200 million people (in modern India alone — Pakistan and Bangladesh add another 400 million Muslims) is the second-largest national Muslim population in the world.
The community's institutional, cultural, and intellectual traditions run through the Mughal period.
The Sufi shrine networks of north India and Pakistan are mostly Mughal-era foundations or expansions.
The Persian-Arabic vocabulary of Indian Islamic religious practice was substantially codified during the Mughal period.
The political inheritance is still there, in modified form.
The administrative geography of modern India and Pakistan substantially derives from Mughal provincial boundaries.
The land-revenue and tax-collection institutional template of the modern Indian and Pakistani states substantially derives from the Mughal mansabdari-jagirdari system.

The basic institutional template of the modern South Asian state — centralized fiscal-military monarchy at the top, provincial governorships in the middle, district-level revenue collection at the bottom — is, in terms of its fundamental structure, a Mughal template that the British inherited and that the post-independence states continue to operate.
The Mughal Empire ended in 1858.
The Mughal inheritance has not.
Cross-civ check: 1857-58 was a year of major imperial-political transformations globally.
In the United States, the Dred Scott decision (March 1857) and the broader sectional crisis were running toward the American Civil War (1861-65).

In China, the Second Opium War (1856-60) was being fought between Britain-France and the Qing Dynasty, with the British forces involved actively supporting the colonial expansion in India simultaneously.

In Japan, the late-Tokugawa crisis was beginning the process that would lead to the Meiji Restoration of 1868 (Meiji Japan Ch 1) — Japan's response to European pressure was, deliberately, a study in not becoming India.
In Italy, the Risorgimento (the Italian unification movement) was active under Cavour, with the eventual creation of unified Italy in 1861.
In Russia, Alexander II had ascended the throne in 1855 and would issue the Emancipation Edict of 1861 freeing the Russian serfs.

The mid-nineteenth century was an era of major political restructuring across the world, and the formal end of the Mughal dynasty was one component — the South Asian component — of the broader nineteenth-century transformation that produced the modern political world.
The closest comparison, in terms of dynastic-political end, is probably the end of the Ottoman Empire in 1922 (Ottoman Empire Ch 12).
Both empires ended through external military pressure (British in the Mughal case; Allied World War I in the Ottoman case).
Both ended with the formal deposition of a dynasty that had ruled for several centuries.
Both had spent decades before the end as substantially decayed political entities surviving on the inertia of institutional habit and ceremonial ritual.

Both left behind successor states that were defined in significant part by their relationship to the deposed dynasty (modern India, Pakistan, and Bangladesh defining themselves with and against the Mughal legacy; modern Turkey and the Middle Eastern Arab states defining themselves with and against the Ottoman legacy).
Both legacies remain politically contested in their respective regions.
The Mughal dynasty died at Rangoon in 1862 with Bahadur Shah Zafar.
The Mughal cultural inheritance is still a working part of the everyday life of perhaps 600 million people in the modern subcontinent.
Both facts are true.
Both deserve to be acknowledged.
Babur, who arrived at Panipat in 1526 with a few thousand troops and a stack of borrowed Ottoman tactical manuals, would probably be amused by what eventually came of his refugee-prince's gamble.

chapters.title: The Great Famine and the End of the Boom
sentences: The story of late medieval Europe begins not with plague or war but with the weather.
For three centuries before 1300, the climate of Europe was unusually warm.
Vineyards grew in southern England.
Norse colonists farmed cereals on Greenland (Viking Age Ch 8).
Glaciers in the Alps retreated to their highest stands.
The growing season lengthened by perhaps two weeks at the latitude of Paris.
Agricultural yields rose, the population doubled, and the high medieval boom of cathedrals and universities and Crusades was financed in significant part by the surplus calories of this warm spell.
Climate historians call it the Medieval Warm Period or, more recently, the Medieval Climate Anomaly.
Around 1300 — give or take a few decades — the Medieval Warm Period ended.

European summers cooled by roughly 1°C on average, the growing season shortened, glaciers began to advance, and the run of warm wet weather that had supported the high medieval expansion gave way to a colder, more variable, more dangerous regime.
The cooling pulse that began around 1300 and persisted for the next five centuries is called the Little Ice Age in modern climate history.
It was not an ice age in the geological sense.
It was a cooling of perhaps 1–2°C in northern hemisphere summers, with much higher year-to-year variability — exactly the kind of climate that breaks medieval agriculture.
Why did the cooling happen?

The current scholarly reading involves three overlapping causes: a clustering of major volcanic eruptions in the late thirteenth and early fourteenth centuries (whose sulfate aerosols cooled the upper atmosphere), a dip in solar output called the Wolf Minimum between roughly 1280 and 1350, and changes in ocean circulation patterns that are still being worked out.
The relative weight of each cause is contested in the climate science literature.
What is not contested is the shift itself, which shows up clearly in tree-ring records, glacial moraines, and pollen sequences from across Europe.
The relevant point for human history is that medieval Europe in 1300 was a population pushed up against its agricultural limits.
Centuries of high-medieval warmth had supported a population growth that required virtually every plowable acre to be plowed.
Marginal land that should never have been farmed — too high, too cold, too thin-soiled — had been brought into cultivation because the warmth made it temporarily viable.
When the warmth went away, the marginal land went away with it, and a population that had grown to depend on that marginal yield was suddenly in trouble.
It took fifteen years for the trouble to become catastrophe.
The catastrophe arrived in the form of three consecutive failed harvests.
In the spring of 1315, it began to rain across northern Europe.
It rained through the planting season.
It rained through summer.
It rained through what should have been the harvest.
Grain rotted in the fields.
Hay could not be cured.
Fuel could not be dried.
The 1315 harvest was the worst on record in living memory.
The 1316 harvest was worse: cooler, wetter, even less productive.
The 1317 harvest was somewhat better but still inadequate to refill the empty granaries.
The cumulative effect across northern Europe — the British Isles, the Low Countries, northern France, the Holy Roman Empire, the western Polish plain — was the Great Famine of 1315–1317.

Mortality estimates vary by region, but a credible round figure is that 10% of northern Europe's population died in those three years from starvation, malnutrition, and the diseases that prey on malnourished bodies.
In some northern German cities the death toll appears to have been higher.
Cannibalism was reported in chronicles and probably occurred.
Parents abandoned children they could not feed.
Bands of refugees roamed the countryside, broke into towns to demand bread, and were repulsed by armed citizens.
The English wool trade collapsed.
The Flemish cloth industry contracted sharply.
The price of bread tripled and then tripled again in some cities.
The Great Famine was the largest demographic shock to Europe between the Plague of Justinian in the sixth century and the Black Death thirty years later.

It is also one of the most well-documented famines in pre-modern history, partly because the late medieval European bureaucracy had finally developed the literate institutions — town chronicles, manorial accounts, royal correspondence — capable of recording it.
What the Great Famine demonstrated was that the high medieval expansion had peaked.
The land could not support the population that had grown to depend on it.
Even before plague and war began their work, late medieval Europe was demographically vulnerable in a way that high medieval Europe had not been.
A second blow followed almost immediately.
In 1319, a cattle disease — probably rinderpest (RIN-der-pest, a viral disease of cattle, related to measles, that produces near-100% mortality in unvaccinated herds) — swept through European herds.
The Great Bovine Pestilence of 1319–1320 killed perhaps 60% of European cattle and oxen.
For an agricultural system that depended on cattle for milk, meat, leather, manure, and (above all) traction power for plowing, the bovine pestilence was a second body-blow.
Fields that survived the human famine could not be plowed because the oxen were dead.
The agricultural retreat continued through the 1320s and 1330s.
By 1340, on the eve of the Hundred Years War, late medieval Europe had spent a generation contracting.
It was a continent already in trouble before plague and war made everything worse.
It is worth pausing on what late medieval Europe in 1300 actually looked like, because the chapters ahead will assume the reader can picture it.

The continent had perhaps 75–85 million people, depending on which scholarly estimate you prefer. (For comparison: the Americas in the same period had perhaps 50–60 million; China around 100 million; the Islamic world from Spain to Central Asia perhaps 50 million.) The largest cities were small by modern standards.
Paris was the biggest at perhaps 200,000 people.
Venice, Genoa, Florence, and Milan in northern Italy had populations around 100,000 each.
London was a provincial town of about 80,000.
Constantinople (Byzantine Empire Ch 10) had collapsed from its tenth-century peak of 400,000 to about 100,000.
Cordoba and Seville in Muslim and recently-Christian Spain were larger than most northern European cities.
The population was overwhelmingly rural.
Perhaps 90% of Europeans worked the land, lived in villages of 200–500 people, and rarely traveled more than 20 miles from their birthplace in their lifetimes.
The political map was a patchwork.
France under the Capetian dynasty was the largest centralized monarchy, with a population of perhaps 17 million and a sophisticated royal bureaucracy.
England under the Plantagenets was smaller (5 million people) but more administratively unified, with a parliament that already met regularly and a common-law system already a century old.

The Holy Roman Empire — the loose German-Italian federation that traced its origin to Charlemagne's coronation in 800 (early-medieval Europe) — was politically fragmented, with the emperor elected by seven prince-electors and ruling more in name than in fact.
Italy was a checkerboard of independent city-states (north and center), the Papal States (central), and the Kingdom of Naples (south).
Iberia was four kingdoms — Castile, Aragon, Portugal, Navarre — plus the surviving Muslim emirate of Granada.
Eastern Europe was a frontier zone of Polish, Hungarian, Lithuanian, and Bohemian kingdoms expanding into Slavic lands.
The Byzantine Empire held a few footholds in Greece and around the Sea of Marmara (Byzantine Empire Ch 10).
Scandinavia was a sparsely populated northern world of fishing, timber, and herring trade, increasingly tied to the Hanseatic League of north German trading cities.
The universal institutions were the Catholic Church, with the papacy in Rome (until 1309) as its administrative head, and the Latin language, used by every educated person from Iceland to Sicily.
The Church owned roughly a third of the cultivable land in most of western Europe.
Almost every village had a parish priest.
Every town of any size had a bishop.
The seven sacraments — baptism, confirmation, the Eucharist, confession, marriage, holy orders, last rites — structured the life of essentially every Christian European from cradle to grave.

The Church taxed (the tithe, one-tenth of agricultural income), educated (every cathedral had a school, every university had begun as one), regulated marriage and inheritance, ran most charity, owned most hospitals, sheltered the orphans, and provided the only realistic vertical mobility ladder open to a peasant boy of unusual intelligence.
This is the baseline against which everything in the next 200 years should be measured.
The continent that walked into the fourteenth century was Catholic, agricultural, and demographically taut.
The continent that walked out of the fifteenth century was different in every one of those dimensions.
A few high medieval names show up briefly in this chapter and the next, and the reader should know who they were.

Dante Alighieri (1265–1321), the Florentine poet, finished his Divine Comedy around 1320 — an epic vernacular poem in Tuscan Italian, structured as a guided tour through Hell, Purgatory, and Paradise.

The Divine Comedy is the founding masterpiece of Italian literature, the most-read non-Biblical text of late medieval Europe, and the best single demonstration that medieval Europeans knew the earth was a sphere.

Dante's universe is built on the Aristotelian-Ptolemaic cosmology that every educated person took for granted: a spherical earth at the center of nested celestial spheres, with Hell underneath Jerusalem, Purgatory on a mountain in the southern hemisphere ocean, and the heavens arrayed above in concentric rotating shells.
The flat-earth myth as applied to medieval people is a nineteenth-century invention.
Dante's poem is one of many proofs.
Petrarch (1304–1374), Francesco Petrarca in Italian, is conventionally identified as the first Renaissance humanist — a label so worn that it can obscure how genuinely strange Petrarch's project was.

He spent forty years rediscovering classical Latin manuscripts in monastery libraries (Cicero's lost letters in 1345 was his most famous find), writing love sonnets in Italian to a married woman named Laura, climbing Mont Ventoux in Provence in 1336 in what is conventionally called the first self-conscious aesthetic appreciation of nature in European literature, and inventing the cult of the individual genius that defined Renaissance humanism for the next two centuries.
Petrarch lived through the Black Death (Laura died in it) and through the Avignon Papacy (he hated it, calling Avignon the "Babylon of the West").
He is the bridge between high medieval scholasticism and what would later be called Renaissance humanism, and we will see his project develop across multiple chapters ahead.
The Knights Templar, a military religious order founded in the early twelfth century to protect Crusader pilgrims, were extinguished in this period in spectacularly violent fashion.

King Philip IV of France, deeply in debt to the Templars and threatened by their independent power, arrested every Templar in his kingdom on Friday October 13, 1307, extracted confessions of heresy and sodomy and idol worship under torture, and pressured the Avignon pope Clement V to suppress the order.
The Templar grand master Jacques de Molay was burned at the stake in 1314, reportedly cursing Philip and Clement from the pyre — both men died within a year.

The Templar suppression is the case where the late medieval state demonstrated, in a single coordinated action across an entire kingdom, how powerful royal bureaucracies had become and how vulnerable the universal church was to coordinated secular pressure.
