It rehearses several of the dynamics — the king-pope confrontation, the use of legal-judicial machinery to destroy political enemies, the choreography of confession and exemplary execution — that the next two centuries would replay in different keys.

The Templar story also gave us Friday the 13th as a date of bad luck — the most successful piece of late-medieval superstition still in circulation. (This is one of the few popular Templar legends that probably has a real medieval source.) Cross-civ check: in 1300, when Europe was tipping into the Little Ice Age, the rest of Eurasia was also in flux.
The Mongol Empire (Mongol Empire Ch 7) had broken into four khanates, with the Yuan dynasty ruling China under Kublai's successors and the Ilkhanate ruling Iran.

Both the Yuan and the Ilkhanate would collapse before mid-century — the Yuan to the Ming founding in 1368 (right in the middle of the Hundred Years War), the Ilkhanate to internal fragmentation in 1335 (which produced the political vacuum the Safavids would eventually fill — Safavid Persia Ch 1).
In India, the Delhi Sultanate was at its territorial peak under Alauddin Khalji, projecting power south into the Deccan for the first time.

In West Africa, the Mali Empire under its founder Sundiata's successors was beginning the trans-Saharan gold trade that would shortly produce the most spectacular royal pilgrimage of the medieval world (Mali Empire Ch 4).

In the Americas, the Aztec were a small mercenary tribe still wandering the Valley of Mexico — they would not found Tenochtitlan until 1325 (Aztec Empire Ch 1) — and the Inca were a small mountain polity around Cuzco that would not begin its imperial expansion until 1438 (Inca Empire Ch 2).
The early fourteenth century is a hinge moment in Eurasian history, and the European crisis is one node in a wider system of climate, migration, and disease pressures.
It is also worth flagging, before the next chapter takes over, that the climate stress of 1300 was a Eurasian phenomenon.

The same Little Ice Age cooling that produced European famine appears to have stressed Mongol pastoralism on the Eurasian steppe, contributing to the political instability that would eventually break the empire and to the dislocations along the Silk Road that would ferry the plague west.
The plague is the next chapter.

chapters.title: The Black Death
sentences: In October 1347, twelve Genoese trading galleys put in at the Sicilian port of Messina.
The ships had come from Caffa (KAH-fah, the modern Crimean city of Feodosiya), the major Genoese trading post on the Black Sea.
The crews were dying.
By the time the ships docked, most of the rowers were dead or dying.
Their bodies were covered in painful black swellings — buboes (BYOO-bohs) — at the lymph nodes of the neck, armpit, and groin.
They coughed blood.
Their fingers and toes turned black.
They died within days of showing symptoms.
The Messinese harbor authorities, recognizing the symptoms of a plague they had heard rumors about from the east, ordered the ships back out to sea.
It was already too late.
The disease had jumped from rats to fleas to humans on the docks within hours of landing.
Within a week, Messina was beginning to die.
Within a month, the disease had spread to mainland Sicily and across the Strait of Messina to Calabria.
By spring 1348, it had reached Pisa, Genoa, Marseille, Venice, Florence, and (via overland trade routes) the cities of central France.
By summer 1348, Paris.
By autumn 1348, London.
By 1350, Norway, Sweden, Iceland, and Russia.
In four years it killed roughly a third of Europe's population.
This is the Black Death, the worst demographic catastrophe in recorded European history.
A point of nomenclature first.
The phrase "Black Death" is not what contemporaries called it.

Fourteenth-century European writers called it the Pestilence, the Great Mortality (Latin magna mortalitas), the Plague, or sometimes "the death." The earliest known use of the phrase "Black Death" in something close to its modern sense is from a sixteenth-century Latin poem about the 1347–1351 outbreak, but the phrase did not become common in popular history until the nineteenth century, when Scandinavian and German historians popularized it.
The "black" probably referred to the metaphor of dread or to the gangrenous black extremities that characterize a minority of plague cases, not to the ordinary appearance of the disease.
Most Black Death victims had buboes, fevers, and coughing blood, but were not literally black.
Calling the disease the Black Death is therefore a modern convention.
It is so deeply embedded in popular history that abandoning it now is impossible, but the reader should know that it is not how anyone in 1347 talked about what was happening to them.
The disease itself has been definitively identified by modern paleogenomics as Yersinia pestis (yer-SIN-ee-ah PES-tiss), the bacterium responsible for bubonic plague.

DNA from Yersinia pestis has been recovered from Black Death-era mass graves at sites including the East Smithfield cemetery in London (excavated in the 1980s), the Saint-Laurent-de-la-Cabrerisse cemetery in southern France, and dozens of other sites across Europe and the Mediterranean.
The 2010s identification of Y. pestis at multiple Black Death sites resolved a long debate among historians (some had argued for anthrax, hemorrhagic fever, or smallpox) by direct genetic evidence.

The disease is the same one that causes plague outbreaks today — it has not disappeared, it is treatable with modern antibiotics, and there are still 1,000–2,000 cases per year worldwide, with mortality rates of perhaps 10% in treated cases and 60–90% if untreated.
The vector cycle is well understood.
Yersinia pestis lives in a complex ecology of rodents and fleas.
The bacterium colonizes the gut of certain flea species (notably Xenopsylla cheopis, the oriental rat flea), which feed on rodents (notably Rattus rattus, the black rat).
Infected fleas regurgitate bacteria into the rodent's bloodstream when they bite; the rodent dies; the now-hungry fleas jump to the next available warm body, which can be a human.
Once a human is infected, the bacterium spreads through the lymphatic system, producing the buboes that gave the disease its medieval name.
In a minority of cases, the bacterium reaches the lungs, causing pneumonic plague, which can spread directly human-to-human through coughing without any flea intermediary.
Pneumonic plague is much more lethal — close to 100% mortality without antibiotics — but spreads less rapidly than the flea-mediated bubonic form, since it requires close personal contact.
The arrival of plague in Europe in 1347 was not the first European plague pandemic.

The Plague of Justinian in 541 CE (Byzantine Empire Ch 2 mentions it) had been the same disease, hit the eastern Mediterranean about as hard, and continued in waves for two centuries before disappearing for reasons that are still unclear.

There are also recent suggestions of plague outbreaks in the Roman world, in Bronze Age Europe, and even in late Neolithic communities — Yersinia pestis DNA has been recovered from skeletons going back several thousand years.

What was unprecedented about the 1347 outbreak was the speed and density of its spread, made possible by the integrated trade network that linked the Mediterranean, the Black Sea, and the overland Silk Road.
The route into Europe ran through the Mongol-controlled steppes.

The current scholarly reading is that Yersinia pestis was endemic in marmot and ground-squirrel populations in Central Asia — probably in what is now Kyrgyzstan, where mass graves at the Issyk-Kul lake region show plague DNA dated to 1338–1339, several years before the European outbreak.

From its endemic reservoir, the disease appears to have escaped into the broader rodent populations of the Mongol-controlled trade routes during the political and ecological turbulence of the early fourteenth century — possibly driven by climate stress on steppe rodent populations, possibly by the breakdown of Mongol-imposed peace (the Pax Mongolica, Mongol Empire Ch 8) that had previously kept caravan traffic moving through endemic plague zones without incident.
By the early 1340s the disease was spreading along the Silk Road westward.
It hit the Mongol Khanate of the Golden Horde in southern Russia by 1346.
In that year, the Golden Horde khan Jani Beg was besieging the Genoese trading colony at Caffa when plague broke out in his army.

According to a single contemporary account by the Italian notary Gabriele de' Mussi (writing several years later, possibly without firsthand knowledge), Jani Beg ordered the bodies of his plague-dead soldiers catapulted over the walls into the besieged city — one of the first attested instances of biological warfare.

Whether Mussi's account is literally accurate is debated, but the broader story is consistent with the evidence: the plague reached Caffa, the Genoese garrison and merchants caught it, and when the survivors fled westward by ship in 1347 they carried it with them to Constantinople, the Aegean, and the western Mediterranean.
From Caffa onward the route is well-attested.
Constantinople caught it in summer 1347 — the Byzantine emperor John VI Kantakouzenos lost his thirteen-year-old son to it and wrote a clinical account of the symptoms (Byzantine Empire Ch 10).
Messina in October 1347.
Genoa and Venice by January 1348.
Marseille by January or February.
Pisa by March.
Florence by April.
Paris by July or August.
London by autumn.
Norway in 1349 (carried, according to local tradition, by a single ship that drifted into Bergen with all hands dead).
Iceland and Greenland later.

The Norse settlements on Greenland, already in trouble from the Little Ice Age, faded from contact entirely sometime in the fifteenth century — plague is one of several proposed causes (Viking Age Ch 8).
The cumulative European death toll between 1347 and 1351 is estimated by modern historians at roughly 30–50% of the population, with a third dead as the conventional round number.
Some regions did much worse.

Florence lost perhaps 60% of its 100,000 inhabitants; the Florentine writer Giovanni Boccaccio lost his stepmother and most of his friends, and used the plague as the framing device for his Decameron (deh-KAH-meh-ron) — a hundred bawdy, satirical, and tender stories told by ten young Florentines fleeing the city for a country villa, finished around 1353 and instantly recognized as the founding masterpiece of Italian prose.
Avignon lost perhaps half its population.
Some smaller villages were entirely depopulated.
Other regions did somewhat better — Milan, partly because it imposed early quarantine measures, lost perhaps 15% — but no significant region escaped untouched.
The plague returned.
The 1347–1351 outbreak was the first wave.

There were major recurrences in 1361–1362 (the Pestis Secunda, "Second Plague," which killed proportionally more children because the survivors of the first wave had partial immunity), 1369, 1374, 1390, and roughly every decade or two for the next three centuries.
The cumulative effect kept the European population well below pre-plague levels for nearly two centuries — Europe did not regain its 1340 population until around 1500.
Whole villages disappeared.
Marginal land returned to forest.
The agricultural retreat of the Great Famine became a permanent rural depopulation across much of the continent.
The social consequences of the Black Death broke the high medieval order in ways no single act of policy or rebellion could have done.
The most immediate consequence was a labor shortage.
With a third of the workforce dead, the surviving peasantry suddenly held an enormous bargaining advantage.
Wages roughly doubled across western Europe in the decades after 1351 — for agricultural workers, masons, carpenters, weavers, and most other manual trades.
Land rents fell.
Peasants who had been bound to their manorial lords by hereditary serfdom began to walk away, knowing that any landlord short of labor would take them on.

The seigneurial system — under which a peasant family worked the lord's land in exchange for the right to work their own subsistence plot — began to dissolve in western Europe over the next century, though it would persist much longer in the east.
Governments tried to legislate the labor shortage away.
In England, the Statute of Labourers of 1351 fixed wages at pre-plague levels and criminalized peasants who demanded more or moved between manors.
The French crown issued similar ordinances.
The Iberian kingdoms passed sumptuary laws restricting what newly-wealthy peasants could wear.
Almost everywhere, these laws failed.
The economic logic was overwhelming.
By 1400, English real wages were the highest they had been for centuries and would be again until perhaps 1700.
The peasantry of late medieval England was — for a couple of generations after 1351 — better fed, better clothed, and better housed than at any point before the Industrial Revolution.
This is a paradox worth pausing on.
The Black Death killed a third of the continent.
The survivors were materially better off.
The mechanism is straightforward — fewer people splitting the same agricultural surplus, plus a bargaining advantage in labor markets — but the moral implications are uncomfortable.
The standard of living of the medieval European peasantry depended, in significant part, on the demographic catastrophe of the Black Death.
This is the same kind of grim irony the next chapter will return to in connection with the Hundred Years War.
The second major consequence was antisemitic violence on a scale not previously seen in European history.
The plague was not understood by contemporaries as a bacterial disease (no one understood bacteria until the nineteenth century).

It was understood, depending on the audience, as divine punishment for sin, as the result of a corrupt miasma (a noxious vapor in the air), or — increasingly, as the death toll mounted — as the work of human enemies who had poisoned the wells.
The favored scapegoat was the Jewish community.

Jewish communities in much of western and central Europe had been targets of intermittent persecution since the First Crusade (Islamic Golden Age Ch 9), but the Black Death produced an acceleration of pogrom violence that destroyed many of the Rhineland Jewish communities altogether.

The pattern was depressingly consistent: a city would catch the plague, mortality would rise, rumors would spread that local Jews had poisoned the wells, a mob would form, the city authorities would either stand aside or actively participate, and the Jewish community would be murdered or expelled.
Strasbourg burned 900 Jews alive on Saint Valentine's Day, February 14, 1349 — before the plague had even reached the city.
Mainz, Cologne, Worms, Frankfurt, Speyer, and Basel had their Jewish communities destroyed or expelled within months.

Pope Clement VI, to his credit, issued papal bulls in 1348 condemning the pogroms, pointing out that Jews were dying of the plague in equal numbers to Christians and could not therefore be the cause, and ordering bishops to protect Jewish communities.
The bulls had limited effect outside the Papal States.
The 1348–1349 pogroms permanently shifted the Jewish demographic geography of Europe.

Many surviving Jewish communities migrated eastward — to Poland, Lithuania, Bohemia, and Hungary, where the Polish king Casimir III (1333–1370) and other eastern rulers offered relative protection in exchange for the economic services of Jewish merchants and artisans.
The center of Ashkenazi Jewish demographic gravity moved from the Rhineland to the eastern European plains over the next century, where it would remain until the twentieth century.
The Black Death pogroms are one of the underexamined hinge moments of European Jewish history.
Two other consequences of the plague are worth noting before this chapter closes.
The first is the Flagellant movement.

In 1348 and 1349, bands of penitents — sometimes thousands strong — moved through central European towns whipping themselves bloody in public processions, arguing that only voluntary self-mortification could appease God's anger and end the pestilence.
The Flagellants were a legitimately popular religious movement, drawing recruits from townsmen and peasants, with their own rituals and their own theology of sin and atonement.
They were also, by the late 1340s, well outside the Church's institutional control.

Pope Clement VI condemned the movement in October 1349, and the bishops and secular authorities suppressed it over the next year, but the Flagellant movement is a useful early sign of how late-medieval Christianity was developing forms of popular piety that the institutional Church could no longer easily channel.
The Reformation in the sixteenth century is the eventual consequence; movements like the Flagellants are early symptoms.
The second is what historians sometimes call the late medieval cult of death.
After 1351, European art and culture became preoccupied with mortality in ways earlier medieval art had not been.

The genre of the danse macabre ("dance of death") — paintings and woodcuts showing skeletal Death dancing with people from every social rank, from pope to peasant — appeared in the late fourteenth and fifteenth centuries and became a major theme of late medieval Europe.

Memento mori ("remember you must die") devotional images, transi tombs (showing the deceased as a decayed corpse rather than the idealized living figure), the Ars Moriendi (the "Art of Dying," a fifteenth-century devotional manual on how to die well), the Triumph of Death in Italian fresco painting — all of this is the cultural sediment of a society that had watched a third of itself die in four years and watched plague return generation after generation.
People who lived through the Black Death and its echoes did not need to be reminded of mortality in the way modern Western readers do, but they did need to make sense of it.
Late-medieval death culture is the result.
Cross-civ check: the Black Death was not just a European event.
The Yersinia pestis pandemic that originated on the central Asian steppe spread across the entire Eurasian world system.
Egypt under the Mamluks lost perhaps 30–40% of its population.
Syria and the Levant were devastated.
Constantinople lost perhaps half its remnant population.
Anatolia under the rising Ottoman beyliks (Ottoman Empire Ch 1) was hit hard, though the plague's effect on Ottoman expansion is contested in the literature.

China had experienced major plague-like epidemics in the 1330s and 1340s — possibly though not certainly the same disease — that contributed to the political instability that brought down the Yuan Dynasty in 1368 (Mongol Empire Ch 6, Tang-Song China context).

The Islamic world generated its own response literature: the Andalusi physician Ibn al-Khatib wrote a 1349 treatise arguing for direct human-to-human contagion against the prevailing miasma theory — one of the most modern-sounding pieces of medieval medical thinking on either side of the Mediterranean.

In West Africa, the Mali Empire under Mansa Musa's successor Mansa Sulayman appears not to have been affected (the trans-Saharan trade routes seem not to have been efficient plague vectors, possibly because of the desert's role as a biological filter).

In the Americas, where Eurasian diseases had not yet reached, the populations of the Aztec frontier and the contemporary Andean kingdoms (Andean Kingdoms Ch 8, Middle Horizon Empires Ch 8) were untouched — they would experience their own demographic catastrophe a century and a half later, when Columbus and Cortés arrived with smallpox and measles.
The asymmetric immunological history of Eurasia and the Americas is one of the structural facts of the centuries that followed.
The plague is the single largest event in late medieval European history.

Everything in the chapters ahead — the Hundred Years War, the schism, the peasant revolts, the Reformation, the Renaissance, the Age of Discovery — happens in a Europe that has just been culled, and is being culled again every decade or two, and is collectively trying to make sense of what that means.
The Hundred Years War is next.

chapters.title: The Hundred Years War
sentences: In the spring of 1337, Edward III of England — a tall, handsome, unusually competent young king of twenty-four — formally claimed the throne of France through his mother Isabella, sister of the recently-extinguished Capetian line.
Within months, an English army had landed in Flanders.
Within a decade, English longbowmen had destroyed the flower of French chivalric cavalry at Crécy.

Within a century, an English king named Henry V had been recognized as heir to the French crown, French civil war had reduced the country to three rival regencies, a teenage girl claiming divine voices had personally led the French army to break the siege of Orléans, and French artillery had ended the war by killing the last English commander on the field at Castillon.

The whole sequence is conventionally called the Hundred Years War — though the name was coined in the nineteenth century, contemporaries did not use it, and the actual fighting spanned 116 years (1337–1453) with several long pauses.
It is the longest sustained inter-state conflict in European history.

It is also the war that broke the high medieval military order, shifted the balance of power between cavalry and infantry, professionalized European warfare, and produced the early forms of national identity in both England and France.
The dynastic claim was thin.

The Capetian dynasty, which had ruled France since Hugh Capet in 987, ran out of male heirs in 1328 with the death of Charles IV, the last of the three sons of Philip IV (the Templar-suppressing king from Chapter 1).
The French succession question became: who inherits when the direct male line dies out?

The candidates were Philip IV's nephew Philip of Valois (through Philip IV's brother), and Philip IV's grandson Edward III of England (through Philip IV's daughter Isabella, who had married Edward II of England).
The French nobility, faced with a choice between a French nephew and an English grandson, chose the nephew.
Philip of Valois became Philip VI in 1328, founding the Valois dynasty that would rule France until 1589.
Edward III, then a teenager, accepted the decision at the time.
He paid homage to Philip VI for his French duchy of Aquitaine in 1329.
By 1337, Edward had changed his mind.

The reasons were complex — friction over Aquitaine, French support for the Scots (who were in chronic war with England), French confiscation of Aquitaine in 1337, English reliance on Flemish wool exports that Philip VI was trying to control — but the legal handle was the dynastic claim.
Edward unrenounced his earlier homage, declared himself the rightful king of France, quartered the French royal arms with the English on his coat of arms, and went to war.
The French sovereignty claim was the surface issue.

The deeper issue was that England had held French territory since the Norman Conquest of 1066 (high-medieval Europe context — William the Conqueror was a French-speaking duke) and the Plantagenet acquisition of Aquitaine through Henry II's marriage to Eleanor of Aquitaine in 1152.

By the early fourteenth century, the English king ruled a substantial duchy in southwestern France that he held in technical homage to the French crown — a structurally unstable arrangement that produced friction every generation.

The Hundred Years War can be understood as the long process by which this anomaly was resolved (badly, expensively, with enormous loss of life on both sides) in favor of a clean separation between an English nation north of the Channel and a French nation south of it.
The war happened in three big phases, separated by long pauses.
The first phase (1337–1360) was the period of English military shock.
Edward III's England had two military advantages the French lacked.
The first was the English longbow, a six-foot yew-staved bow that could throw a heavy arrow 250 yards (about 230 meters) and pierce most contemporary armor at 100 yards.
The longbow was not new — it had been developed in Wales over the previous century — but its systematic deployment as the core of English infantry tactics was a fourteenth-century innovation.
Trained from childhood, a competent English longbowman could shoot 10–12 aimed arrows per minute.
A force of 5,000 longbowmen could put 50,000 to 60,000 arrows per minute into the air.

The cumulative effect on advancing cavalry was devastating: horses panicked, knights were thrown from their saddles, the disordered survivors arrived at the English lines in scattered remnants where dismounted men-at-arms finished them off.
The second English advantage was dismounted men-at-arms fighting in disciplined infantry formations rather than charging individually as mounted knights.

The English had learned this approach in their long border wars with the Scots; they imported it to France, deploying the men-at-arms behind sharpened stakes and pits to break the French cavalry charge that the longbow had already disordered.
The two innovations together — longbow plus dismounted men-at-arms — were demonstrated catastrophically at Crécy on August 26, 1346.

A French chivalric host of perhaps 30,000, led by Philip VI personally, charged a smaller English force commanded by Edward III and his sixteen-year-old son Edward of Woodstock (later called the Black Prince for his dark armor).
The French sent in their Genoese crossbowmen first; the longbows outranged and outshot them, breaking their formation.
The French knights, charging through their own retreating crossbowmen, ran into the longbow storm in waves.

Estimates of French casualties at Crécy run to 4,000–10,000, including 1,500 nobles and the king of Bohemia (who was blind and asked his knights to lead him into the fight, reportedly so he could strike one blow with his sword before dying).
English casualties were perhaps 200.

The chivalric warfare of the high Middle Ages — armored mounted knight against armored mounted knight, with battlefield outcomes determined by individual valor and the social rank of the combatants — had been demolished in a single afternoon by disciplined infantry firepower.
Edward followed up Crécy by besieging Calais for eleven months.
The port surrendered in August 1347 (just as the Black Death was beginning to spread west from Sicily).
England held Calais as a continental beachhead until 1558.
The Black Death interrupted the war from 1348 through the early 1350s.

When it resumed, the Black Prince repeated his father's victory at Poitiers on September 19, 1356, where an English-Gascon army a third the size of the French force not only won but captured the French king John II alive.

With their king prisoner in London (where he was treated as a guest of honor at Edward's court), the French agreed to the Treaty of Brétigny in May 1360 — ceding most of southwestern France to England in exchange for Edward renouncing his French throne claim and releasing John.
It looked like a permanent settlement.
It lasted nine years.
The second phase (1369–1389) was the French recovery under Charles V the Wise and his brilliant general Bertrand du Guesclin (du-geh-KLAN).
Charles V (king from 1364) was a sickly, scholarly man who hated battle and favored siege warfare, harassment, and the avoidance of pitched engagements.
Du Guesclin was a Breton knight of dubious appearance (chronicle accounts describe him as squat and ugly) and unusually shrewd tactical sense.

Together, they recovered most of what France had lost at Brétigny over a long, grinding decade of small-unit warfare that never delivered a decisive battle but slowly bled English territory back to French control.
By 1380, when both Charles V and du Guesclin died, England held only a coastal strip of Aquitaine and Calais.
The 1370s and 1380s were a period of relative quiet, with both sides distracted by other things.
England was distracted by the English Peasants' Revolt of 1381 (Chapter 6) and the political instability of Richard II's minority and erratic adult reign.

France was distracted by the death of Charles V and the long minority of his son Charles VI, who would eventually descend into chronic mental illness and reduce the country to civil war between rival regency factions.
The French civil war of the early fifteenth century is essential context for the third phase of the Hundred Years War, and it deserves a brief explanation.
Charles VI of France, who became king as a child in 1380 and did not produce a stable adult reign, suffered from periodic episodes of severe mental illness beginning in 1392.
He believed at various points that he was made of glass, that his name was George, that his courtiers were trying to murder him.
During his lucid periods he ruled normally; during his mental episodes the regency was contested between two rival noble factions.

The Burgundian faction, led by Duke John the Fearless of Burgundy, was based in the powerful composite state of Burgundy (which included most of the modern Low Countries — Flanders, Brabant, Hainaut).
The Armagnac faction, led by the Count of Armagnac and rallying around the Dauphin Charles (the future Charles VII), represented the southern French nobility loyal to the Valois crown.

From 1407 (when John the Fearless had Louis of Orléans assassinated in a Paris street) through 1435 (when Burgundy switched sides), France was wracked by an internal war that ran in parallel with the English invasion.
The English gains of the third phase would have been impossible without Burgundian collaboration.
The third phase (1415–1453) opened with Henry V of England, who has had very good Shakespearean press and was indeed a remarkably effective king and battlefield commander.

Henry resumed his great-grandfather's claim, invaded Normandy in 1415, and won the most lopsided victory of the entire war at Agincourt (AH-zhin-coor or AH-jin-court) on October 25, 1415 — Saint Crispin's Day, the date Shakespeare made famous in Henry V.
Agincourt was a re-run of Crécy and Poitiers with one extra horror.
Henry's army of perhaps 6,000 (most of them longbowmen) faced a French force of perhaps 20,000–30,000 in a narrow muddy field between two woods.
The French cavalry charged through the mud — knee-deep in some places after recent rain — and were shot to pieces by the longbows before reaching the English line.
The dismounted French men-at-arms, advancing in heavy plate armor through the same mud, were exhausted before they arrived; those who reached the English line were quickly killed or taken prisoner.
The chronicles report several thousand French dead and roughly 1,500–2,000 prisoners taken.

What made Agincourt particularly grim was Henry V's order, partway through the battle, to kill the prisoners — apparently because he feared a French counter-attack and could not spare men to guard them.
English men-at-arms reportedly refused the order (they would lose ransom money if the prisoners died) and Henry sent his own archers to do it.
Several hundred to perhaps 2,000 captured French nobles were killed in cold blood.
The episode is documented in multiple contemporary chronicles.
It was controversial at the time and remains so among historians; Shakespeare omits it.

It is a useful corrective to the romantic image of late-medieval warfare — Henry V was an excellent king by the standards of his time and was also capable of mass killing of unarmed prisoners when military necessity (or his judgment of military necessity) demanded.
Agincourt opened the way for Henry's systematic conquest of Normandy over the next four years.

The Treaty of Troyes in May 1420, signed in the wake of further English military success and exploiting Charles VI's incapacity and Burgundian collaboration, was the high-water mark of English continental ambition: Henry married Charles VI's daughter Catherine of Valois, was recognized as heir to the French throne, and was effectively appointed regent for the disinherited Dauphin Charles.
If Henry had lived, the personal union of England and France might have happened in 1422.
He did not live.
Henry died of dysentery in August 1422 at the age of thirty-five, two months before his father-in-law Charles VI.
His son Henry VI was nine months old.

Charles VI's son the Dauphin, now formally disinherited but still claiming the French throne, was nineteen, holed up in a small court at Bourges south of the Loire that contemporaries jokingly called the "Kingdom of Bourges." It was the lowest point French royal authority had reached since Hugh Capet 435 years earlier.
This is where Joan of Arc walks into the story.
Joan of Arc — Jeanne d'Arc in French, Jehanne in her own time — was born around 1412 in Domrémy (dom-reh-MEE), a village on the Lorraine-Champagne frontier.
Her family were prosperous tenants — not landless peasants, as the popular image has it, but moderately well-off villagers with a substantial farmhouse and several head of livestock.

She was illiterate, devout, unusually willful, and from the age of about thirteen began to hear what she described as the voices of Saints Catherine of Alexandria, Margaret of Antioch, and the Archangel Michael — telling her, eventually, that she was destined to lead the Dauphin Charles to his coronation at Reims Cathedral and drive the English from France.
The first audacious thing she did was demonstrate that anyone listened to her at all.
In May 1428, at sixteen, she walked from Domrémy to the nearby town of Vaucouleurs and asked the local royalist captain Robert de Baudricourt for an armed escort to take her to the Dauphin.
He told her to go home.
She came back twice.

By February 1429, after she had correctly predicted a French defeat at the Battle of the Herrings before news of it reached Vaucouleurs, Baudricourt sent her with a small armed party through 350 miles (560 km) of English-held territory to the Dauphin's court at Chinon.

She arrived in early March, was examined for orthodoxy by clerics at Poitiers for three weeks (they cleared her), and was sent to relieve the besieged city of Orléans (or-LAY-ahn) in late April with armor, a horse, a small banner, and a position of effective command of part of the French army.

Orléans had been under English siege for seven months and was the strategic key to the lower Loire — if it fell, the road to Bourges was open and the English would probably finish off the disinherited Dauphin's regime within the year.
Joan reached Orléans on April 29, 1429.

Within nine days the siege was broken: the French sortied repeatedly under her presence, captured or destroyed the English siege fortifications around the city, and forced the English commander Lord Talbot to retreat north on May 8, 1429.
The relief of Orléans is the moment that reversed the trajectory of the Hundred Years War.

It is reasonable to argue, as many modern historians do, that without Joan it would not have happened — French morale, by the spring of 1429, was so broken that no other commander appears to have been willing to attempt the relief.

What followed was the Loire campaign of June 1429 — a sequence of French victories at Jargeau, Beaugency, and the spectacular open-field victory at Patay on June 18, where French heavy cavalry caught the English longbowmen before they could deploy their stakes and rode them down.
Patay was the longbow's first major battlefield defeat in eighty years.
Then the coronation.

Joan led the Dauphin and the army on a 200-mile (320 km) march through still-Burgundian territory to Reims Cathedral, the traditional anointing place of French kings since Clovis (early-medieval Europe).
On July 17, 1429, the Dauphin was anointed and crowned as Charles VII of France, with Joan standing in armor beside the altar holding her banner.

The coronation transformed the political position of the French monarchy: Charles was now the legitimate, anointed king of France in the eyes of every Frenchman who recognized the traditional ritual, and the English Henry VI was a usurper.
What happened to Joan after the coronation is the part of the story that gets less attention.
Charles VII, having got what he needed from her, became cooler toward her.
Joan's military judgment, by the second half of 1429, was no longer always sound.
She insisted on attempting to retake Paris in September; the assault failed and she took a crossbow bolt through the thigh.
She was captured by Burgundian forces at Compiègne on May 23, 1430 — Charles VII made no significant effort to ransom her — and sold to the English in November.
Her trial took place at Rouen (roo-AHN, in English-held Normandy) over the winter of 1430–31, in front of a tribunal of pro-English French clerics led by Bishop Pierre Cauchon of Beauvais.
The charges were heresy (her voices), witchcraft, and the cross-dressing she had practiced consistently since leaving Domrémy.

The transcripts of the trial survive — they are one of the most extraordinary documents of late medieval Europe, in part because Joan's responses to her interrogators are so consistently sharp. ("Asked whether she knew she was in God's grace, she answered: 'If I am not, may God put me there; and if I am, may God so keep me.'" — a theologically perfect answer that gave the tribunal nothing to convict on.) She was convicted, sentenced to life imprisonment, recanted to escape the stake, then resumed wearing male clothing in prison (probably under coercion, certainly providing the tribunal the pretext to convict her of relapsed heresy), and was burned alive in the marketplace at Rouen on May 30, 1431.
She was nineteen.
Her conviction was overturned by a posthumous retrial under Pope Calixtus III in 1456.

She was beatified in 1909 and canonized as Saint Joan by Pope Benedict XV in 1920 — half a millennium after her death — partly to consolidate French Catholic support during World War I, when Joan had become a symbol of French national resistance.

The myth of Joan of Arc — the visionary peasant girl who saved France and was burned for it — has been adapted by everyone from Shakespeare (badly) to Mark Twain to Bertolt Brecht to multiple twentieth-century films.

The historical Joan is, somewhat improbably, even more interesting than the myth: a teenage girl who, through a combination of astonishing self-confidence, real military competence, the right historical moment, and a story that translated her into the iconography of the French monarchy, genuinely turned the course of one of the longest wars in European history.
Almost nothing about her trajectory should have worked.
All of it did.
The endgame of the Hundred Years War took twenty-two more years.
After Joan, the French gradually recovered the territory the English had won.
Philip the Good of Burgundy switched sides at the Treaty of Arras in 1435, ending the Burgundian-English alliance and isolating England diplomatically.

Charles VII's reformed army — built around the compagnies d'ordonnance, professional standing cavalry units paid by the crown rather than by individual lords — slowly retook Normandy in 1449–1450 and Gascony in 1451.
The English landed a relief expedition under John Talbot to recover Gascony in 1452.

The French army, now equipped with the most advanced field artillery in Europe — bronze cannons cast in royal foundries under the direction of the Bureau brothers, Jean and Gaspard, who had standardized cannon production for Charles VII's military — caught Talbot's force at Castillon outside Bordeaux on July 17, 1453.
Talbot's frontal cavalry charge ran straight into massed cannon fire.
He was killed, and the last English army on French soil disintegrated.
Bordeaux surrendered in October.
The Hundred Years War was over.
Castillon is the symmetrical bookend to Crécy.
Crécy in 1346 had demonstrated that disciplined infantry could destroy chivalric cavalry.
Castillon in 1453 demonstrated that gunpowder artillery could destroy disciplined infantry.

The military future of Europe was clearly visible from Castillon: the cannon was now the decisive weapon, and the states that could afford to cast and deploy cannons in quantity (centralized monarchies with bureaucratic tax systems) would dominate the states that could not (feudal aristocracies with private armies).

The same year that French artillery ended the Hundred Years War, Ottoman cannons brought down the walls of Constantinople (Chapter 8). 1453 is one of those years that historians like to designate as a turning point.
It really was one.
What did the Hundred Years War actually accomplish?
At one level, it returned the French and English crowns to roughly the territorial situation of 1337, minus Calais (which England held until 1558).
The dynastic claim that started the war was abandoned by both sides as a fiction.
The territorial map that finally emerged was not radically different from the map Edward III had inherited.
At a deeper level, the war transformed both kingdoms.

France emerged with a much stronger crown — Charles VII's standing army, his royal taxation system (including the taille permanent direct tax, made permanent in 1439), his centralized command structure — that would shortly produce the French nation-state of Louis XI and Francis I.
England emerged with the opposite: a weakened, bankrupted crown that would shortly collapse into the dynastic civil war called the Wars of the Roses (Chapter 8).
The war also produced two new senses of national identity.
By 1453, men in both kingdoms had been told for a century that they were fighting for "France" or "England" against the foreign other, and the rhetoric stuck.
The early forms of French and English nationalism trace to the Hundred Years War in a way they do not trace to anything earlier.

A cross-civ note before the next chapter: while England and France were spending 116 years killing each other, the Ottoman Empire was using the same period to consolidate the conquest of the Balkans, defeat the last great Crusade at Nicopolis in 1396 (Ottoman Empire Ch 2), survive Tamerlane's near-fatal blow at Ankara in 1402 (Ottoman Empire Ch 3), and prepare the conquest of Constantinople in 1453 (Ottoman Empire Ch 4).

The Ming Dynasty in China was founded in 1368 — right in the middle of the Hundred Years War — and was launching the great voyages of Zheng He (1405–1433) at exactly the moment Henry V was conquering Normandy.
The Mali Empire in West Africa was at its mid-arc peak under Mansa Musa's successors during the early Hundred Years War (Mali Empire Ch 4–5).
The Aztec Triple Alliance was founded in 1428 (Aztec Empire Ch 2) — one year before Joan of Arc broke the siege of Orléans.
The Inca Empire's expansion under Pachacuti began in 1438 (Inca Empire Ch 2).
The Safavid order in Iran was militarizing in the late fifteenth century, two generations before its founder Ismail would conquer Tabriz in 1501 (Safavid Persia Ch 1).
The fifteenth century is one of the densest moments of imperial formation in human history, and Europe, distracted by its long civil war, was not the central event.
It would be, after 1492.

chapters.title: The Avignon Papacy and the Western Schism
sentences: The single most consequential institutional crisis of late medieval Europe was the long collapse of papal authority that ran from 1309 to 1417.

In just over a century, the Catholic Church went from being the unchallenged universal arbiter of Christian Europe — the institution that crowned emperors, deposed kings, and called Crusades — to being the divided, discredited spectacle of two and then three rival popes simultaneously claiming to be Christ's vicar on earth, each excommunicating the others' followers, each absolving the others' sins as null.
By 1417, the Church had a single pope again, but the damage to the institution's prestige was permanent, and the consequences would unfold across the next two centuries as the Reformation.

The crisis happened in three overlapping phases: the Avignon Papacy (1309–1377, when the popes lived in southern France and were widely seen as French puppets), the Western Schism (1378–1417, when there were rival popes), and the conciliar movement (the long argument over whether the papacy or a general council of bishops held supreme authority in the Church, decisively decided in the papacy's favor by 1450).
All three are essential to understanding why the late medieval Church was institutionally vulnerable to Wycliffe, Hus, and eventually Luther.
To understand the Avignon Papacy, you have to understand who Pope Boniface VIII was and what happened to him.

Boniface VIII (pope from 1294 to 1303) was the last great medieval pope in the high Gregorian tradition — the tradition that had begun with Gregory VII in the eleventh century (high-medieval Europe context) and held that the papacy was the supreme authority in Christendom, above all secular kings.

In his most famous bull, Unam Sanctam of 1302, Boniface declared that "it is necessary to salvation that every human creature should be subject to the Roman Pontiff." This was as maximal a claim of papal supremacy as any pope ever made.
It came at the worst possible time.
The king Boniface picked his fight with was Philip IV of France (ruled 1285–1314) — the same king who would shortly destroy the Templars (Chapter 1).
Philip was the most ruthless and most administratively competent French king of the thirteenth century.
He needed money, was taxing the French clergy without papal consent, and had no patience for Boniface's claim that the French king required papal permission to do anything.
The dispute escalated through the late 1290s and early 1300s.
Boniface threatened excommunication.

Philip's chief minister Guillaume de Nogaret organized a small armed force, marched to the papal residence at Anagni (ah-NAH-nyee) in central Italy in September 1303, and physically arrested the pope.
Boniface was rescued by the local townspeople after three days, but the elderly pope died a month later — broken, contemporaries said, by the humiliation.
The episode at Anagni was the inverse of Henry IV's penance at Canossa in 1077, when an emperor had stood barefoot in the snow for three days waiting for papal forgiveness.
By 1303, the king was capable of arresting the pope, and the pope died of it.
Philip IV then arranged the elections of two compliant successors: the brief Benedict XI (pope 1303–1304) and the much more consequential Clement V (pope 1305–1314).
Clement was a Frenchman, a former archbishop of Bordeaux.
He was elected under heavy French pressure.
Within a year, citing the political instability of central Italy and the difficulty of safe travel to Rome, he relocated the papal court to the southern French city of Avignon (ah-veen-YOHN) in 1309.
He never left.
Neither did the next six popes.
The Avignon Papacy lasted from 1309 to 1377 — sixty-eight years, seven popes, all of them French.
Petrarch, who hated Avignon, called it the Babylonian Captivity of the Church, drawing the parallel to the Old Testament exile of the Jews in Babylon (Ancient Israel context).
The label stuck.
How bad was Avignon?
The honest answer is: less bad than the propagandistic accounts suggest, and more bad than the apologetic accounts admit.
The seven Avignon popes were generally competent administrators.
They reformed the papal financial system, professionalized the curia (the papal bureaucracy), and developed the elaborate fiscal machinery that funded papal operations.
They also lived very well.
Avignon was rebuilt around the Palais des Papes (the Palace of the Popes), an immense fortified palace that is still one of the largest Gothic buildings in the world.
The papal court attracted artists, lawyers, and theologians from across Christendom.
Petrarch spent much of his early career there.
The musical innovations of the Ars Nova (the new compositional style that introduced rhythmic complexity into Western music) flourished at the Avignon court.

What earned Avignon its bad reputation was three things: the perception of French royal capture, the elaborate financial extraction from the rest of Christendom, and the personal venality of some of the popes' courts.
The French capture was real but partial.
All seven Avignon popes were Frenchmen.
So were the majority of the cardinals they appointed.

The papacy was clearly closer to the French crown than to the English, the Imperial, or the Italian crowns, and English chroniclers in particular complained that the Avignon popes blocked English ecclesiastical appointments and favored French diplomatic positions. (The English Statute of Provisors in 1351, which restricted papal appointments to English benefices, is a direct reaction to perceived Avignon favoritism.) But the papacy was not simply a French royal department.
The popes were capable of opposing French policy when they chose to; the relationship was structural alignment rather than control.
The financial extraction was the deeper problem.
Running the papal court was expensive — the curia, the papal household, the diplomatic corps, the construction of the Palais des Papes.

The Avignon popes funded it through a sophisticated system of payments extracted from the rest of Christendom: annates (the first year's income from any benefice the pope appointed), provisions (papal control over high ecclesiastical appointments, which generated substantial fees), indulgences (payments for the remission of sins, which were aggressively marketed), and various other levies.
The cumulative effect was that benefices across Europe paid into Avignon a significant fraction of their revenues, and bishops everywhere had powerful financial incentives to keep the curia happy.
It was difficult to look at this system from England or Germany or Italy and not conclude that the papacy was running an extraction racket.
The personal venality varied.
Some Avignon popes lived in sober monastic style.
Others did not.
The court, with its lawyers and bankers and ambitious clerics seeking papal favor, attracted the kind of corruption that any wealthy administrative center attracts.

Petrarch's polemical descriptions of "the Babylon of the West" with its "stinking, rotten old he-goats" who had reduced the holy seat to a brothel are exaggerated, but there was something to exaggerate.
The cumulative effect over sixty-eight years was that the moral authority of the papacy was significantly reduced.
By the 1370s, Italian writers were openly attacking the Avignon Church, and even Avignon-loyal clerics were calling for the popes to return to Rome.

Catherine of Siena (1347–1380), an extraordinary Dominican mystic and political activist who would later be made a Doctor of the Church, wrote letters to Pope Gregory XI that combined spiritual advice with blunt political demands: come back to Rome, restore the papacy to its rightful seat, stop the Babylonian Captivity.
Gregory eventually agreed.
He returned to Rome in January 1377.
He died fourteen months later.
The conclave to elect his successor produced the Western Schism.
The Western Schism (1378–1417) was a thirty-nine-year period in which two and at one point three rival popes simultaneously claimed the throne of Saint Peter.
It is the single most damaging episode in the institutional history of the medieval Church.
The mechanism by which it happened is depressingly simple.
Gregory XI died in March 1378.
The conclave to elect his successor met in Rome amid mob pressure from the Roman population, who demanded an Italian pope after a generation of French ones.
The cardinals — most of them French — elected an Italian, the elderly Neapolitan Urban VI.
Urban turned out to be a difficult, prickly, possibly mentally unbalanced man who immediately began alienating the cardinals who had elected him.

Within months, twelve of the French cardinals had withdrawn from Rome, declared Urban's election invalid (because, they now claimed, it had been performed under duress from the Roman mob), and elected a Frenchman, Clement VII of Geneva, as the rival pope.
Clement returned the papal court to Avignon.
Urban remained in Rome.
There was now no procedural way to determine which election was valid.
The cardinals had gone through the same procedure in both cases.
The same men had voted in both elections.
Both popes claimed legitimacy.
Both excommunicated each other.
The Christian states of Europe lined up by political affiliation: France and its allies (Scotland, Castile, Aragon) recognized Clement VII at Avignon.
England and the Holy Roman Empire recognized Urban VI at Rome.
Italy was split.
Portugal wavered.
Naples changed sides.
The lay populations of Christian Europe found themselves told that their salvation depended on choosing the correct pope, with no available means of determining which one was correct.
The Schism continued through the deaths of Urban VI and Clement VII and the elections of their successors.
Both lines maintained themselves.
By the 1390s, it was clear that the dispute would not resolve through mere persistence — both sides could keep electing popes indefinitely.

The intellectual current that emerged in response was conciliarism: the doctrine that, in cases of disputed papal succession, a general council of bishops representing the whole Church holds the authority to settle the matter, even by deposing the disputed claimants and electing a new pope.
The first attempt at conciliar resolution was the Council of Pisa in 1409, which deposed both existing popes and elected a third — Alexander V.
The two existing popes refused to accept the deposition.
There were now three popes. (Alexander V died within a year and was succeeded by John XXIII, not to be confused with the twentieth-century pope of the same name.

The fifteenth-century John XXIII was a former mercenary captain of disputed personal morality whose name was retroactively erased from the official papal register, which is why a twentieth-century pope could reuse the number.) The decisive resolution came at the Council of Constance (kon-STANCE, in southern Germany) from 1414 to 1418.
Constance was the largest church council ever held — some 600 bishops and abbots, plus thousands of theologians, jurists, and political representatives, attended at various points.
The council was convened jointly by Holy Roman Emperor Sigismund of Luxembourg and the conciliarist John XXIII.
Once it convened, it deposed all three rival popes (Roman, Avignonese, and Pisan), and elected a new universally recognized pope: Martin V, in November 1417.
The Schism was over.

The Council of Constance also did one other thing that would shape the next century of European history: it burned Jan Hus alive on July 6, 1415, despite holding a written safe-conduct from the emperor.
The Hus episode is significant enough that it gets its own chapter (Chapter 5).

Constance also issued, in its decree Haec Sancta of 1415, the most ambitious assertion of conciliarism in the history of the Church: that a general council "lawfully assembled in the Holy Spirit" holds "power immediately from Christ" and that "every person, of whatever rank or office, even the papal," is bound to obey it.
This was the closest medieval Christianity ever came to constitutional reform — to placing the papacy under the institutional check of a representative assembly.
The Council of Basel (1431–1449) tried to extend the conciliarist project further, with Frequens requiring regular general councils every ten years.
But the popes won the long argument.

Martin V and his successors patiently undermined the conciliarist movement, refused to summon councils, and by the Concordat of Vienna of 1448 had effectively re-established papal supremacy over national churches.

The conciliarist project — the road not taken in late medieval Catholicism — would have produced a more constitutional, less monarchical Church, and almost certainly would have made the sixteenth-century Reformation either unnecessary or much smaller.
The papacy's victory over conciliarism was tactically successful and strategically catastrophic, because it left the Church without an institutional mechanism for reform other than schism.
A pause to flag what the Schism era looked like on the ground.
For ordinary parishioners in (say) a Castilian village in 1395, the question was theological with practical consequences.

The local priest had been ordained by a bishop appointed by the Avignon pope (who Castile recognized) — but the Roman pope's followers said that the Avignon pope's ordinations were invalid, which meant the local priest's masses were not real masses, which meant the parishioners' confessions and Eucharist were not real either, which meant they were dying in a state of mortal sin.
From the Avignon side, the same thing was true in reverse for English and German parishioners.
There was no neutral authority to consult.
The reasonable answer — which most people, sensibly, settled on — was that this was God's problem to sort out, not theirs, and that following one's own bishop was the best one could do.
The structural effect was a long erosion of the assumption that the universal Church was actually universal.
By 1417 there had been three full generations of European Christians who had grown up in a Church with two or three popes.
Anti-clerical attitudes had hardened.
National churches had grown more administratively independent.
The idea that the pope's spiritual authority was self-evident and indivisible had been broken in lay imagination, even after Constance restored a single pope.
The institutional damage was permanent.

Cross-civ note: the Western Schism is one of those events with no real parallel in other civilizations, because no other civilization had an institutional church remotely like the Latin Catholic Church.

The closest analogies are organizational rather than religious: the Sunni-Shia split in Islam (much earlier and more theologically substantive) or the disputes over imperial succession in Byzantium (Byzantine Empire Ch 9–10), Yuan/Ming China (Ming founding 1368, Tang-Song China context), or the Mongol Khanates after Kublai (Mongol Empire Ch 7).

Late medieval European Christianity's combination of an institutional papacy with universal claims, a dispersed European political system, and a literate clerical caste capable of generating principled critiques is a unique configuration.
So is the resulting century-long crisis.
The Hus story and the seeds of Reformation are next.

chapters.title: Wycliffe, Hus, and the Late-Medieval Reformations
sentences: The standard textbook version of the European Reformation places it in 1517, with Martin Luther's Ninety-Five Theses on the church door at Wittenberg.
This is true but misleading.
The Reformation Luther started had been rehearsed for at least 130 years before he wrote a word.

The doctrinal positions Luther took — the supreme authority of scripture, the priesthood of all believers, the rejection of papal authority and clerical celibacy and indulgences and (more cautiously) transubstantiation, the demand for vernacular Bibles — had been developed in detail by John Wycliffe in late fourteenth-century England and by Jan Hus in early fifteenth-century Bohemia.
The Lollards and the Hussites were, in everything but name, the first Protestants.

They were suppressed, burned, and crusaded against — but the Hussite armies fought five papal-imperial Crusades to a standstill between 1419 and 1434, and Wycliffe's English translation of the Bible circulated underground for over a century.
By the time Luther came along, much of the doctrinal scaffolding was already in place.
This chapter traces the late-medieval Reformations that didn't quite happen, and the one that did.
John Wycliffe (1320s–1384) was an Oxford theologian, philosopher, and royal advisor.

He was, by most contemporary accounts, the most brilliant scholastic philosopher in late fourteenth-century England — the kind of intellectual eminence that had earned him the master's chair at Balliol College and a position as adviser to the John of Gaunt, Duke of Lancaster (the third son of Edward III, uncle of Richard II, and the most powerful English nobleman of the 1370s and 1380s).
Wycliffe started as a conventional Oxford academic in the 1360s.
He drifted toward radical doctrine in the 1370s.
By 1380, he was making claims that no orthodox Catholic theologian had dared make for centuries.
Wycliffe's positions, in compressed form: The supreme authority in Christian life is the Bible, not the pope or the magisterium of the Church.
Anything in Christian practice that cannot be justified from scripture is illegitimate.
The pope, if he opposes scripture, is not just wrong but — Wycliffe sometimes said — possibly the Antichrist.
The Church's enormous wealth was a corruption.
Christ and the apostles had lived in poverty.
A Church owning a third of England's land and demanding tithes from every parish was unrecognizable as the body Christ founded.
Wycliffe argued that secular rulers could rightly seize Church property when the Church fell into mortal sin (a doctrine called dominion).
This was wildly attractive to John of Gaunt and other English nobles who would have liked to seize Church property; it was also wildly attractive to the king's tax collectors.

Transubstantiation — the doctrine, formalized by the Fourth Lateran Council in 1215, that the bread and wine of the Eucharist literally become the body and blood of Christ — was, Wycliffe argued, philosophically incoherent and unscriptural.

He proposed instead a doctrine called remanence, holding that the bread and wine remain bread and wine while also becoming, in some real but mysterious sense, the body and blood. (Luther's later position was very similar.) The clergy had no special spiritual authority that distinguished them from laypeople.
Every baptized Christian was a priest.
The institutional hierarchy — pope, cardinals, bishops, priests — was a human accretion, not divinely instituted.
Indulgences (the practice of paying the Church to remit punishments due for sin) were straightforwardly corrupt.
Confession to a priest was unnecessary; confession to God directly was sufficient.
The cult of the saints was largely idolatrous.
Pilgrimage was largely a waste of time.
The Bible should be available in English — and any other vernacular — so that every Christian could read it.
In the late 1370s and early 1380s, Wycliffe and a team of his Oxford followers began translating the Bible into English.

The Wycliffite Bible (sometimes called the Lollard Bible) — translated from the Latin Vulgate, in two versions, the first stiltedly literal and the second more readable — was the first complete English Bible.
Around 250 manuscript copies survive, which is an enormous number for a banned text and suggests that hundreds or thousands more once existed.
Underground production and circulation continued through the fifteenth century.
The English ecclesiastical authorities and the papal hierarchy were horrified, but for two reasons Wycliffe was never burned.
He had powerful political protectors (especially John of Gaunt), and he died of natural causes — a stroke, in his Lutterworth parish in 1384, before the Church had fully organized to suppress him.
His followers, called Lollards (from a Middle Dutch word for "mumbler," used pejoratively), were less protected.
Lollardy was suppressed by a series of English laws beginning with De heretico comburendo in 1401 (literally "On the burning of heretics"), the first English statute making heresy a capital offense.

Lollard preachers were burned; the movement went underground; it survived in scattered communities through the fifteenth century, providing a ready-made audience for Lutheran ideas when those arrived from Germany in the 1520s.
Wycliffe's bones were a separate problem.

Forty-four years after his death, the Council of Constance — the same council that had ended the Western Schism (Chapter 4) — ordered Wycliffe's body exhumed, burned, and the ashes scattered in a stream.
The order was carried out in 1428.
Posthumous burning was the Church's way of declaring that Wycliffe's heresies were so dangerous that even his corpse could not be allowed to rest in consecrated ground.
The exhumation order is one of the more theatrical items in the Council's record.
The Wycliffite ideas migrated to Bohemia.

Jan Hus (yahn HOOSS, sometimes anglicized as "John Huss," 1369–1415) was a Czech preacher and theologian — a chaplain at the Bethlehem Chapel in Prague, where he preached in Czech rather than Latin to large lay audiences, and a master at Charles University in Prague (the first university in central Europe, founded in 1348 by the Holy Roman Emperor Charles IV).
Hus was not himself a peasant; he was a university-educated cleric of modest origins.
His native town of Husinec gave him his surname (which means "goose" in Czech — a fact Hus himself joked about).
Bohemia in the late fourteenth century was an unusually fertile environment for reformist ideas.

The Czech kingdom had several distinctive features: a strong reform-minded preaching tradition going back to Jan Milíč of Kroměříž and Matěj of Janov in the 1370s, a literate urban population in Prague that had grown rich on silver mining, a Czech-speaking peasantry that resented German and Italian Church appointments, and a royal house (Charles IV and his successors) that had at various points patronized reformist preachers as part of broader political agendas.
Wycliffe's writings reached Prague in the 1390s through scholarly networks (Czech students had begun studying at Oxford after the marriage of Richard II of England to Anne of Bohemia in 1382).
They were enthusiastically received by the Prague reform faction.
Hus adopted most of Wycliffe's positions: scriptural supremacy, attack on indulgences, attack on clerical wealth, attack on papal authority.

He was somewhat more cautious on transubstantiation and on lay communion in both kinds (the doctrine that lay communicants should receive both the bread and the cup at communion, not just the bread — the Latin term utraquism, from sub utraque specie, "under both kinds").
Hus's preaching at the Bethlehem Chapel drew enormous crowds.
By 1410, the archbishop of Prague had condemned him and had Wycliffe's writings publicly burned.
By 1411, Hus had been excommunicated.
The political tension escalated through 1412–1414, with Hus retreating from Prague to a sympathetic noble's castle but continuing to write and preach.
In 1414, the Holy Roman Emperor Sigismund invited Hus to attend the Council of Constance to defend his views.
Sigismund issued Hus a written safe-conduct guaranteeing his personal safety.
Hus accepted the invitation, traveled to Constance, was almost immediately arrested by papal authorities, was held in chains for months, and was tried for heresy.
The promised safe-conduct was held to be inapplicable on the grounds that the Council was not bound by promises made to heretics — a piece of casuistry that Sigismund accepted without protest.
Hus refused to recant.
He was condemned and burned at the stake in Constance on July 6, 1415.
His ashes were thrown into the Rhine.
The execution of Jan Hus produced the response in Bohemia that the Council had not anticipated.
The Hussite Wars (1419–1434) were the first successful military rebellion against papal authority in late medieval Europe.
They are also one of the most under-taught episodes in the popular history of the period.

In Prague in 1419, a crowd of Hussite supporters threw seven Catholic city councillors out of the windows of the New Town Hall — the First Defenestration of Prague (a tradition of Czech political action that would be repeated in 1483 and most famously in 1618, where it began the Thirty Years War).
The defenestration was the trigger.
Within months, Bohemia was in revolt.
The Czech king (Sigismund's brother Wenceslas IV) died in shock at the news; Sigismund, claiming the crown by inheritance, was rejected by the Bohemian estates as the man who had murdered Hus.
By 1420, Bohemia was at war with the empire and the papacy.

The military genius of the Hussite revolt was Jan Žižka (yahn ZHEESH-kah, c. 1360–1424), a Czech minor noble who had been blind in one eye since youth and would lose the other to a crossbow wound during the wars (and continued to command from a cart, with his lieutenants describing the battlefield to him). Žižka's tactical innovation was the war wagon (Czech vozová hradba) — armored ox-drawn wagons fitted with mounted firearms (early handgonnes and small cannons), arranged in a defensive square that could march across a battlefield, halt, and become an instant fortress.

The wagon-fort tactic absorbed cavalry charges, repelled infantry assaults, and gave the Hussites overwhelming advantage in defensive battles. Žižka also pioneered the systematic use of gunpowder firearms by infantry — Hussite armies fielded large numbers of handgonners and crossbowmen at a time when most European armies still relied on bow-and-pike infantry.
The Hussite wagon-fort tactic and gunpowder infantry doctrine would shortly be adopted by other armies (including, two generations later, the Ottomans at Chaldiran — Safavid Persia Ch 3).
Five major Hussite Crusades were called by the papacy and Sigismund between 1420 and 1431.
All five failed.
The Hussite armies, though always smaller than their crusader opponents, won repeatedly through tactical superiority and home-territory defense.

The Crusades culminated in the catastrophic crusader defeat at Domažlice in 1431, when a 100,000-strong imperial army reportedly broke and fled at the mere sound of the approaching Hussite wagons singing the Hussite battle hymn.
After Domažlice, the papacy abandoned the crusade strategy and opened negotiations.
The compromise was reached at the Council of Basel (the conciliarist council from Chapter 4) in the Compactata of Prague in 1436.
The compromise: the Hussites accepted nominal reunion with Rome and the legitimacy of Sigismund as king of Bohemia.
The papacy accepted lay communion in both kinds (the cup as well as the bread) for Hussite congregations and the right of Bohemian preachers to preach in Czech.
This was a substantial concession — it was the only time the late medieval Catholic Church formally permitted distinctively reformed liturgical practice in any region.

The Hussite Compactata held for about fifty years before later popes repudiated them, but during that period Bohemia had a semi-independent national church with reform doctrines, two centuries before the Reformation made that pattern routine.
The Hussite movement also fragmented internally.
The moderate Utraquist wing accepted the Compactata.

The radical Taborite wing — based in the south Bohemian town of Tábor, where they had built a millenarian community organized around shared property and apocalyptic expectation — was crushed at the Battle of Lipany in 1434, where the moderate Hussites and Catholic Bohemians together defeated the Taborites in a particularly grim civil-war engagement.

The surviving Taborite remnants would eventually merge with various reformist communities to produce the Unity of the Brethren (the Czech proto-Protestant church that would later become the Moravian Church), which is still extant in the twenty-first century.
Why didn't the Hussite Reformation spread?
The historical question is genuinely interesting because the Hussite ideas were essentially identical to Lutheran ideas and were defended by armies that had defeated five papal-imperial crusades.
Why didn't Bohemia's local reformation become a continent-wide one?
Several factors.
The Hussite reformation was strongly Czech-national, with the linguistic boundary between Czech and German doubling as the reformation boundary.

Hussite ideas crossed into German lands through scholarly networks but did not produce mass movements among German speakers — partly because German princes had no political incentive to break with Rome at a moment when they were busy consolidating their own power within the imperial framework.
The Hussite ideas also lacked the printing press as a mass-distribution mechanism.
They were spreading, slowly, by manuscript.

When Gutenberg's printing press appeared in the 1450s (Chapter 7), the basic Hussite-Wycliffite doctrinal package was already a century old but had not yet reached the audience that would shortly be available.
Luther got the Hussite-Wycliffite ideas plus the printing press and produced an avalanche.

There is a famous story — possibly apocryphal — that Luther himself, when accused at the Leipzig Debate of 1519 of espousing Hussite heresies, replied: "I am a Hussite without knowing it." It is at minimum a useful summary of the relationship.
Cross-civ note on religious reform movements: the late medieval European Reformations sit in a wider pattern of fourteenth-and-fifteenth-century religious reform.

Within Latin Christendom there were also the Devotio Moderna (a Dutch and Rhineland devotional movement led by Geert Groote and the Brethren of the Common Life, producing the bestselling devotional manual The Imitation of Christ by Thomas à Kempis around 1418), and the various Italian observant movements that reformed the Franciscan and Dominican orders from within.

Outside Latin Christendom: the Hesychast movement in late Byzantine Orthodoxy (Byzantine Empire context — peak in the fourteenth century), which produced its own theological controversy over the nature of divine light and the spiritual practice of contemplative prayer.

The Sufi orders across the Islamic world were entering one of their most generative periods — including the Safaviyya order at Ardabil that would eventually produce the Safavid dynasty (Safavid Persia Ch 1).

The bhakti devotional movement in late Medieval India produced regional reform traditions like Kabir, Mirabai, and the early Sikh community under Guru Nanak (Medieval India Ch 6 — the bhakti chapter).

All of these are independent developments that should not be over-assimilated to the European story, but it is striking that the late medieval centuries across Eurasia were a period of unusual religious creativity outside (and sometimes against) established institutional religion.
The peasant revolts are next.

chapters.title: Peasant Revolts and Urban Uprisings
sentences: If the Black Death produced material gain for the peasantry through labor scarcity (Chapter 2), it also produced rising peasant expectations and the political assertiveness that came with them.

The half-century after the plague saw three of the largest popular uprisings of medieval Europe: the Jacquerie in northern France (1358), the Ciompi in Florence (1378), and the English Peasants' Revolt (1381).
All three were suppressed within weeks.
None achieved their immediate political goals.

All three are, however, useful indicators of the post-plague political weather, and they share enough common features to suggest a pattern: rural and urban workers who had absorbed the Black Death's lessons about labor scarcity and were no longer willing to accept the social subordination the high medieval order had taken for granted.
This chapter is shorter than the previous ones because the revolts themselves were brief.
Their structural significance is larger than their narrative footprint suggests.
The Jacquerie of 1358 was the largest peasant revolt in French history before 1789.

It takes its name from the contemptuous nickname Jacques Bonhomme ("Jack Goodfellow") that the French nobility used for peasants — the medieval equivalent of "Joe Sixpack." The political context was the catastrophe of the Hundred Years War.
France in 1358 was reeling from the English victory at Poitiers in 1356 (Chapter 3), where King John II had been captured.

The French royal government was paralyzed: the king was a prisoner in London, his teenage son the Dauphin Charles was attempting to govern under enormous pressure, the nobility had lost prestige catastrophically (their famous chivalric host had been routed by a smaller English force), and the Estates General in Paris under Étienne Marcel (the merchants' leader) was attempting reforms that bordered on revolution.
The countryside was being systematically pillaged by routier mercenary companies — bands of demobilized soldiers who had not been paid and were living off the land.
Peasant villages were being burned, raped, and looted on a routine basis, often by the same nobility whose military protection the peasants were notionally paying for.
The revolt began in late May 1358 in the Beauvaisis region north of Paris when a group of peasants killed a knight who had been extorting them.
Within days the uprising spread across the Île-de-France, Picardy, and Champagne.

Peasants attacked noble manors, burning castles, killing knights and their families, and sometimes engaging in symbolic atrocities — chronicle accounts (mostly written by hostile noble or clerical observers) describe the rape of noblewomen in front of their husbands, the killing of children, the eating of roasted noble flesh.
How much of this is accurate and how much is later atrocity-mongering is contested.
What is clear is that the violence was directed specifically at the nobility — peasants did not attack their own villages, churches, or commoner neighbors.
The grievance was social, not anarchic.

The Jacquerie's leader, the only major figure to emerge from it, was a peasant named Guillaume Cale (sometimes called Guillaume Carle), who organized perhaps 5,000–6,000 peasant fighters into a coordinated force in the lower Beauvaisis.
Cale attempted to coordinate with the bourgeois reform movement of Étienne Marcel in Paris.
The connection never fully worked, but it was enough to terrify the nobility into a coordinated response.
The crushing happened on June 10, 1358.

Charles II of Navarre ("Charles the Bad," a French nobleman who claimed the French throne and would shortly attempt to seize it during the post-Poitiers chaos) lured Cale to a parley under safe conduct, arrested him, decapitated him on the spot, and then attacked the leaderless peasant army.
The peasants, who had no real military training or equipment, were slaughtered.
The estimates of casualties run from "thousands" to "20,000" in the next several weeks of nobility revenge across the Beauvaisis. Étienne Marcel was killed in Paris a month later.
The Dauphin Charles consolidated his control, eventually became Charles V the Wise (Chapter 3), and the reformist moment passed.
The Jacquerie achieved nothing politically.

What it left behind was a collective noble memory of how dangerous the rural population had become, and the corresponding political logic of harsh repression that would shape French peasant policy for the next four centuries.
The Ciompi Revolt in Florence in July 1378 was a different kind of uprising — urban rather than rural, and led by industrial workers rather than peasants.
Florence in 1378 was the financial and textile capital of late medieval Europe.
The city's economy was dominated by the wool industry, which employed perhaps a third of the urban population.

The political system was structured around guilds (the arti), with the seven major guilds (arti maggiori) — bankers, judges, cloth merchants, silk merchants, doctors, furriers, money-changers — holding effective control of city government.
The fourteen minor guilds (arti minori) of artisans had limited access to power.
The ordinary wool workers — the Ciompi (CHOM-pee, possibly from a French nickname for spinning workers) — had no guild at all and no political representation.
