The trigger was a confrontation between the powerful Albizzi faction and a coalition of moderate political opponents over the ammonizione (a system of political proscription that the Albizzi had been using to exclude rivals from office).
When the Albizzi-controlled regime fell in late June 1378, the resulting power vacuum gave the unrepresented working class an opening.
The Ciompi rose on July 21, 1378.
They marched through the city, burned the records of the wool merchants' guild, and demanded their own guild representation, fairer wages, and the right to participate in government.
Within days they had effectively seized control of the Signoria (the city government).
The Ciompi government — the only direct rule by industrial workers in any major medieval European city — held power for about six weeks.
It established three new guilds for wool workers, dyers, and shirt-makers, giving these previously unrepresented workers political voice.

It also confronted the structural problem that had limited every previous worker movement: it could not coordinate with the moderate guilds that had initially supported the broader anti-Albizzi coalition.
The major guilds and the surviving Albizzi faction reorganized, and on August 31, 1378, an alliance of guild masters and patrician forces overthrew the Ciompi government and restored oligarchic rule.
The Ciompi guilds were dissolved.
Their leaders were exiled, executed, or driven into hiding.
The Florentine ruling oligarchy was so traumatized by the experience that it spent the next half-century systematically excluding any possibility of working-class political participation.

The eventual settlement was the Medici ascendancy of 1434 and after (Chapter 7), which provided the urban poor with patronage, employment, and ceremonial inclusion in exchange for political quiescence.
The Ciompi episode is sometimes called the first proletarian revolution.
This is anachronistic but not entirely wrong.

The Ciompi were industrial workers in a recognizably modern sense — they did not own their tools (the wool merchants did), they sold their labor for wages, and they organized politically against the conditions of that labor.

They were also, in a recognizably modern sense, defeated by the structural disadvantages of working-class organization in a capitalist economy: the masters could afford to wait them out; the workers could not afford to stay out of work; the moderate middle classes who had initially supported them found their economic interests aligning with the masters once the immediate political crisis passed.
The Ciompi were the first test of a script that the next five centuries would replay many times.
The English Peasants' Revolt of 1381 — sometimes called Wat Tyler's Rebellion — was the largest popular uprising in medieval England.
The political context was the Poll Tax of 1380, the third in three years, levied to fund the dragging Hundred Years War.
Unlike the earlier graduated income taxes, the 1380 poll tax was a flat per-capita charge on every adult — which was massively regressive, since a poor laborer paid the same as a wealthy yeoman.
The tax was widely evaded; the government's response was to send tax commissioners to enforce collection.

The commissioners' aggressive methods (chronicle accounts describe inspectors verifying women's tax status by examining whether they were sexually mature) provoked riots in Essex and Kent in late May 1381.
Within a week, the riots had grown into an organized movement.
The leaders were Wat Tyler, a Kentish ex-soldier whose background is otherwise obscure, and the radical priest John Ball.
Ball was a Lollard sympathizer (probably — the doctrinal links to Wycliffe are debated) who had been preaching for years on the equality of all Christians and the wickedness of the social hierarchy.

His most famous sermon, preached to the rebels at Blackheath on June 12, 1381, took as its text the rhyming couplet: When Adam delved and Eve span, Who was then the gentleman? (Delved meant "dug"; span meant "spun thread.") The point was theological: all human beings descend from Adam and Eve, who worked the soil and the spinning wheel without any noble class.
The class system was therefore a human invention without biblical warrant.

Ball's egalitarian preaching reached an audience that was already economically empowered by the post-plague labor scarcity, politically radicalized by the poll tax, and ideologically primed by Lollard doctrine.
The combination was explosive.
The rebels marched on London on June 13, 1381.

They burned the Savoy Palace (the home of John of Gaunt, who was conveniently away in Scotland), destroyed the Inns of Court (where the legal records of serfdom were kept), opened the prisons, and killed the Archbishop of Canterbury Simon Sudbury (who, as Lord Chancellor, had introduced the poll tax) and the royal treasurer Robert Hales.
The fourteen-year-old King Richard II, who had taken refuge in the Tower of London with his mother, met the rebels at Mile End on June 14 and at Smithfield on June 15.

At Smithfield, in negotiations whose chronology and detail are disputed, the Mayor of London William Walworth killed Wat Tyler with a dagger — the rebels were on the point of attacking when Richard rode forward and reportedly cried "I will be your captain!", successfully calming the leaderless crowd long enough for the city militia to arrive and disperse them.

Richard II's promises to the rebels at Mile End — the abolition of serfdom, free participation in markets, pardons for the rebels — were honored for about a week, then revoked once the rebellion was clearly broken.
Royal forces hunted down the surviving leaders over the following month.
John Ball was arrested, tried, hanged, drawn, and quartered at St Albans on July 15, 1381.

The rebellion was suppressed; the poll tax was abandoned; the formal institution of English serfdom was not abolished but quietly fell into disuse over the next half-century as labor market pressures made it economically untenable.
What did the late-medieval peasant revolts achieve?
Politically, almost nothing.
None of the three major revolts produced lasting institutional change.
The Jacquerie was crushed in two weeks.
The Ciompi held power for six weeks.
The English Peasants' Revolt was suppressed in a month.
The participants were killed in large numbers.
The political demands were rejected.
The class system the revolts attacked persisted essentially unchanged for the rest of the medieval period.
What the revolts did achieve was demonstrate that the post-plague European labor force had developed a political consciousness that the high medieval order had not allowed for.

Peasants and urban workers could organize across long distances (the English revolt coordinated Essex, Kent, East Anglia, and parts of the Midlands within days), articulate political programs (egalitarian preaching, demands for guild representation, specific tax grievances), and confront royal and noble authority directly.

They could also, when crushed, contribute to a quiet structural transformation in which the formal institutions of serfdom and labor coercion eroded over the following century, not because they were abolished but because they became unenforceable.
The economic logic mattered more than the political demands.
By 1500, English serfdom was effectively extinct.
French serfdom persisted in some regions but had become much milder.
Italian urban guild systems had become more inclusive.

Eastern European serfdom — for complex reasons that include the absence of comparable post-plague labor markets and the specific political balance between landlord and peasant — went the other direction, intensifying through the late Middle Ages and into the early modern period in what historians call the Second Serfdom.
Western European peasants gained material conditions they would not lose; Eastern European peasants lost conditions they would not regain for another four centuries.
Cross-civ note on contemporary peasant uprisings: the late fourteenth century was a period of unusual rural unrest across Eurasia.

The Red Turban Rebellion in China (1351–1368) — actually not the same Red Turban as the later Qizilbash (Safavid Persia Ch 1), but a millenarian Buddhist movement — overthrew the Yuan dynasty and brought Zhu Yuanzhang, a peasant turned warlord, to the imperial throne as the first Ming emperor.
The Ming founding in 1368 was the largest peasant-revolt success in world history and the only one in the late medieval period that produced a long-term political revolution.

The contrast with the European revolts is instructive: the Chinese rebellion succeeded because the imperial system had collapsed under climate, plague, and Mongol misrule; the European rebellions failed because European royal governments, despite the Hundred Years War and the schism, had not collapsed at the same level.
Late-medieval European peasants got better wages and quietly buried serfdom; late-medieval Chinese peasants founded a dynasty.
The Italian Renaissance is next.

chapters.title: The Renaissance Threshold
sentences: The conventional story of the Italian Renaissance starts in 1401, with the famous competition for the bronze doors of the Florentine Baptistery, or in 1436, with the consecration of Brunelleschi's dome on Florence Cathedral, or in 1453, with the fall of Constantinople and the flood of Greek manuscripts west, or in some other dramatic launch moment.
The reality was less dramatic.

The Italian fourteenth and fifteenth centuries were a continuous period of artistic, intellectual, financial, and architectural innovation that emerged from late medieval foundations and produced the cultural moment that nineteenth-century historians named the Renaissance ("rebirth").

This chapter takes a thematic rather than chronological approach to that emergence — the Italian city-states, the Medici, the early humanists, the architectural and artistic revolutions of the fifteenth century, the Northern Renaissance in oil, and the printing press that would shortly change everything.
A point of definition before we start.

"Renaissance" is a term invented by the nineteenth-century Swiss historian Jacob Burckhardt in his 1860 book The Civilization of the Renaissance in Italy, on the model of language used by Italian fifteenth- and sixteenth-century writers about themselves (Petrarch wrote of a renovatio, "renewal," and Ghiberti of a rinascita, "rebirth").

The term has been heavily contested by twentieth-century historians: medievalists rightly point out that the "rebirth" framing implies that medieval culture had been dead, which it manifestly had not; that the supposed Renaissance discoveries (perspective, naturalism, classical sources, vernacular literature) were extensions of late medieval developments rather than break-throughs; and that the standard periodization (Italy in the fifteenth century, the rest of Europe in the sixteenth) flattens a much more complex regional and chronological story.

We will use the term because it is unavoidable, but the reader should hold in mind that it is a label rather than an explanation, and that "the Renaissance" is more usefully thought of as the late-medieval Italian city-state world entering its mature phase than as a sudden break with what came before.
The Italian city-states of the late Middle Ages were the world's largest concentration of urban wealth and political independence outside East Asia.
By 1400, Italy was the only region of Europe where political fragmentation and urban concentration combined at scale.
Northern and central Italy contained perhaps twenty independent or semi-independent city-states, each with its own government, foreign policy, currency, and military.

The most important were the so-called Five States that the Peace of Lodi in 1454 would formalize as the major powers of the peninsula: Venice was a maritime republic governed by an oligarchy of merchant patricians through a Doge (a ceremonial figurehead with limited real power) and a series of councils of ascending exclusivity.

Venice's wealth came from Mediterranean trade — the spice routes from Alexandria, the silk routes through Constantinople and Trebizond, the slave routes from the Black Sea, and the salt and timber trade in the Adriatic.
By 1400 Venice was probably the wealthiest city in Europe, with a population of perhaps 100,000 and a maritime empire stretching down the Dalmatian coast and into the Aegean.
Genoa was Venice's main rival, a smaller maritime republic on the western Italian coast with similar trading networks but a less stable internal politics.

Genoa had founded the trading colony at Caffa that brought the Black Death to Europe (Chapter 2) and would later, through one of its mariners — Christopher Columbus, born in Genoa in 1451 — accidentally open the Atlantic.
Milan was a powerful inland duchy in the Po valley, ruled until 1447 by the Visconti dynasty and then by their condottiere (mercenary captain) successor Francesco Sforza and his descendants.
Milan was the most militarized of the major Italian states, with the most professional army and the most aggressive expansionist foreign policy.
The Visconti were also major patrons of late Gothic art and the early universities.
Florence was the textile and banking capital of Italy and would become the principal site of Renaissance art and intellectual culture.
Florence was nominally a republic governed by elected magistrates from the major guilds, but actual political power was concentrated in a small group of wealthy banking families.

After 1434, the Medici family ran the city without ever holding formal monarchical title, through their control of the Medici Bank, their patronage networks, and their elaborate manipulation of the constitutional offices.
Florence's population in the fifteenth century was around 50,000 — half what it had been before the Black Death — but its economic and cultural weight was disproportionate.
Naples was the kingdom in the south of Italy, the only major Italian power that was a monarchy in the conventional sense rather than a city-state.
Naples was contested between French (Angevin) and Spanish (Aragonese) dynastic claims through the fifteenth century, with frequent shifts of dynasty.

The Papal States in central Italy completed the political picture, although the popes were a special case — they were both Italian princes (with significant territory and revenue) and the universal heads of Latin Christendom (Chapter 4).
The political fragmentation of fifteenth-century Italy was, paradoxically, the precondition for the cultural flowering.
Five competing capitals meant five sets of patrons, five courts seeking artistic glory, five sources of commission.
The city-state competition produced a building boom, a portrait boom, and an intellectual boom that single-state monarchies elsewhere in Europe (France, England, Castile) did not match.
When Italian artists and humanists wanted patronage, they had options — and the patrons knew it, which inflated both their prices and their prestige.
The mature Italian Renaissance was structurally the product of competitive city-state patronage, not of any single court's vision.
The most important political family of the Italian Renaissance was the Medici of Florence.
The Medici started as middling Florentine bankers in the fourteenth century.

They were not aristocrats — the Florentine constitution was officially anti-aristocratic — but a successful merchant family who had built up the Medici Bank through prudent management, papal banking concessions (a major source of their wealth was acting as bankers for the papal curia, collecting dues from across Christendom and remitting them to Rome with a profitable cut), and shrewd political alliances.

The first Medici to translate financial wealth into political power was Giovanni di Bicci de' Medici (1360–1429), who consolidated the bank's papal business and accumulated political capital without ever holding formal office.
His son Cosimo de' Medici (1389–1464) — Cosimo the Elder, Cosimo il Vecchio — completed the transformation.
Cosimo inherited the bank in 1429 and built it into the largest bank in Europe.
He was briefly exiled by a rival faction in 1433.

When he was recalled in 1434, he returned to Florence and proceeded to dominate its politics for the next thirty years through what would today be called "soft power": careful constitutional manipulation, cultivation of friendly magistrates, generous patronage of guilds and neighborhood associations, and avoidance of any formal title that would have made him a target for traditional anti-tyranny rhetoric.
Foreign visitors who asked who ruled Florence were told "the Council of Two Hundred." Foreign visitors who knew anything knew it was Cosimo.
Cosimo also patronized the early Italian Renaissance as a major project.

He founded the Platonic Academy in Florence under Marsilio Ficino (who translated Plato's complete dialogues into Latin between 1463 and 1483 — the first such Latin translation, made possible by Ficino's Greek training and Cosimo's funding).
He commissioned major works from Brunelleschi, Donatello, and Fra Angelico.
He founded the Library of San Marco, the first public library in Europe with cataloged collections open to scholars.

He hosted the Council of Florence in 1438–1439, the great failed attempt at reunion between the Latin and Greek churches before the fall of Constantinople, paying enormous sums to bring the Byzantine emperor and the Greek delegation to Italy.

The Council failed politically (it produced a paper union that was repudiated by most Greeks within a few years), but it succeeded culturally — the Greek scholars who attended brought manuscripts of classical Greek texts that the Italian humanists immediately copied, beginning the great fifteenth-century Italian rediscovery of ancient Greek literature.
Cosimo's grandson Lorenzo de' Medici (1449–1492) — Lorenzo the Magnificent, il Magnifico — completed the Medici cultural project.
Lorenzo ruled Florence from 1469 to 1492 with even less formal authority than Cosimo had used, and even more cultural impact.

He sponsored Sandro Botticelli (the painter of the Birth of Venus and the Primavera), the young Michelangelo Buonarroti (whom Lorenzo housed in his palace and treated essentially as an adopted son from the age of fourteen), the philosopher Pico della Mirandola (whose Oration on the Dignity of Man is the manifesto of Renaissance humanism), and the Greek-trained poet Angelo Poliziano.

Lorenzo also let the Medici Bank slide toward bankruptcy through a combination of bad loans (especially to Edward IV of England, who defaulted), distracted management, and political concessions that diverted bank resources to political spending.
By the time of Lorenzo's death in 1492, the Medici Bank was effectively insolvent, and the family's political position was sustained by reputation rather than by financial substance.
Within two years of Lorenzo's death, the Medici had been driven from Florence (the French invasion of 1494, see below) and the bank had collapsed.

The Medici story is the early-modern model of a family that translated financial wealth into political power and cultural patronage and back again, and ran the cycle for three generations before it broke.
Versions of the story would replay in Genoa, Augsburg, Antwerp, Amsterdam, London, and (eventually) New York.
The intellectual movement that historians call Renaissance humanism was the systematic recovery, study, and emulation of classical Latin (and increasingly Greek) literature, philosophy, and rhetoric.
The pioneer was Petrarch, whom we met briefly in Chapter 1.

Petrarch and his immediate followers — Giovanni Boccaccio (1313–1375) of Decameron fame, who was also a serious scholar of Latin literature; Coluccio Salutati (1331–1406), the Florentine chancellor who professionalized humanist Latin in government correspondence; Leonardo Bruni (c. 1370–1444), Salutati's successor and a major scholar of Greek (he translated Aristotle and Plato into much-improved Latin) — established humanism as a coherent intellectual program by roughly 1400.
The program had several components.
Recovery: searching monastery libraries across Europe for surviving classical manuscripts, copying them, and making them available for study.
Petrarch's discovery of Cicero's lost Letters to Atticus in 1345, and Poggio Bracciolini's discovery of Lucretius's De Rerum Natura in a German monastery in 1417, are the famous moments.
Editing: comparing manuscripts, identifying corruptions in the text, restoring what the original was likely to have said.
Imitation: writing Latin in the style of Cicero rather than the simpler Latin of medieval church documents.
Translation: producing Latin versions of Greek texts (and, increasingly, vernacular Italian versions of Latin texts) so they could reach wider audiences.

Education: training the next generation of humanists in classical languages and rhetoric, eventually producing the studia humanitatis curriculum (grammar, rhetoric, poetry, history, moral philosophy) that became the educational model for European elites for the next four centuries.
The humanists were not anti-Christian.
Most of them were devout Catholics.

What they argued was that classical pagan literature contained moral wisdom and rhetorical sophistication that complemented (rather than contradicted) Christian revelation, and that the medieval educational curriculum had unduly neglected this body of work.

Pico della Mirandola in his Oration on the Dignity of Man (1486) tried to argue for an even broader synthesis — combining Christian, Greek, Hebrew, and (he believed) ancient Egyptian wisdom into a single perennial philosophy.
The orthodox Church was wary; Pico's Oration was condemned by the papacy and Pico himself died young (1494, at thirty-one, of arsenic poisoning — possibly accident, possibly murder).

But the broader humanist project flourished and would, within two generations, produce the textual scholarship that Erasmus and others would use to launch the Christian humanist movement of the early sixteenth century, which would feed directly into the Protestant Reformation.
The architectural and artistic revolution of the fifteenth century is the part of the Renaissance that the lay reader is most likely to recognize.
The launching figure was Filippo Brunelleschi (1377–1446), trained as a goldsmith, who designed the spectacular dome of Florence Cathedral.
The cathedral itself had been under construction since 1296 — the immense Gothic structure of Santa Maria del Fiore designed by Arnolfo di Cambio and continued by successors.
The body of the church was finished by 1380.
The crossing, however, was open to the sky, with a yawning octagonal hole 138 feet (42 m) across that no one knew how to span.
Conventional Gothic vaulting could not handle the span.
Roman concrete techniques had been lost.
The cathedral committee stalled for forty years.
Brunelleschi won the design competition for the dome in 1418 with a proposal that astonished and offended his contemporaries.

He proposed a double-shelled brick dome — an inner load-bearing structure and an outer protective shell, with hidden iron and stone tension chains binding the structure horizontally to prevent it from spreading.

Most controversially, he proposed to build the entire dome without exterior scaffolding — the medieval method of dome construction, which would have been impossible at this scale because no scaffolding could be cantilevered from a 200-foot-high opening.
Instead, he proposed building each course of bricks as a self-supporting catenary curve, with each course locking the previous one in place.
He also designed special hoisting machinery (powered by oxen on the ground and ropes through pulleys) to lift bricks, stone, and water to the construction level.
The dome was begun in 1420 and finished in 1436 — sixteen years of construction during which Brunelleschi invented essentially every element of the project.
The completed dome was the largest masonry dome built in Europe since the Pantheon (Ancient Rome Ch 7) thirteen centuries earlier.
It is still standing in 2026 and still the largest brick dome in the world.
The lantern that crowns the structure was added by Brunelleschi's successor between 1446 and 1471.
The cathedral was finally consecrated in 1436, the year the dome was finished.

Brunelleschi also reinvented linear perspective — the geometric system for representing three-dimensional space on a two-dimensional surface that defined Western painting from the fifteenth century until the early twentieth.

His exact priority is debated, but two famous demonstrations around 1413 (Brunelleschi's perspective drawing of the Florentine Baptistery, viewed through a peephole that aligned the painted image with the actual building) are conventionally credited as the launch of the technique.

The geometric principles were codified in the 1430s by the architect-theorist Leon Battista Alberti (1404–1472) in his treatise De Pictura ("On Painting"), the first systematic theoretical text on Renaissance art.

Linear perspective was new in the technical sense — the geometric procedure for drawing accurate perspective had not been formalized before — but the broader interest in spatial naturalism had been developing in Italian painting for at least a century before Brunelleschi.

Giotto di Bondone (c. 1267–1337), painting in the Arena Chapel in Padua around 1305, had already produced figures with three-dimensional weight and emotional psychological depth that look proto-Renaissance to modern eyes.
The Brunelleschi-Alberti perspective system was the codification and extension of trends that were already present in late medieval Italian art.
The artists who applied the new spatial techniques most influentially in the early fifteenth century were the sculptor Donatello (1386–1466) and the painter Masaccio (1401–1428).
Donatello's bronze David (around 1440) was the first freestanding nude statue cast in Europe since classical antiquity.
His equestrian Gattamelata in Padua (1453) was the first such monument since the Romans.

His expressive marble figures — including the bald, intensely staring Habakkuk (the Zuccone) for the Florentine cathedral campanile — combined classical naturalism with psychological intensity that was new to European sculpture.

Masaccio painted the Brancacci Chapel frescoes in Florence around 1424–1427 with rigorous Brunelleschian perspective, modeled chiaroscuro figures, and emotional immediacy that made him, in retrospect, the founder of Renaissance painting.
He died at twenty-six, possibly poisoned, with most of his major work still ahead of him.
The Brancacci Chapel was treated as an open-air school by Florentine painters for the rest of the century — Michelangelo, in his teens, sketched there.
The Italian Renaissance was not the only late-medieval European artistic revolution.

The simultaneous Northern Renaissance in the Low Countries (modern Belgium and the Netherlands) developed independently and produced a different aesthetic, centered on oil painting, microscopic naturalistic detail, and the integration of religious and bourgeois subject matter.
The launching figures were the van Eyck brothers, Hubert and Jan.
The shared masterpiece, the Ghent Altarpiece (formally The Adoration of the Mystic Lamb), was completed in 1432.

It is a vast multi-panel altarpiece — twelve panels, hinged so they can be opened or closed depending on the liturgical calendar — that combines theological complexity with a visual realism unprecedented in European art.
Every leaf on every plant in the central panel is botanically identifiable.
The figures have individual personalities visible through facial expression, posture, and eye direction.

The Arnolfini Portrait (1434), Jan van Eyck's solo masterpiece, is a small (32 × 23-inch) double portrait of a Bruges merchant and (probably) his wife in their bedroom, with a convex mirror on the back wall that reflects the room from the opposite angle.
Every surface — the bronze chandelier, the wooden floor, the dog's fur, the orange on the windowsill — is rendered with microscopic specificity.
The painting is the founding document of the genre that would, much later, become northern European bourgeois portraiture.
What enabled the Northern Renaissance was the oil painting technique.
Earlier European painting had used tempera — pigment mixed with egg yolk on a gesso ground — which dried quickly, did not blend smoothly, and could not produce the layered translucency of oil.

Oil painting (pigment mixed with linseed or walnut oil) had been used for minor purposes in earlier medieval art, but its development as a major fine-art medium was a Flemish innovation of the early fifteenth century.
The van Eycks did not invent oil painting in the literal sense, but their refinement and systematic exploitation of the medium transformed what European painters could do.

Italian painters adopted oil over the next several decades; by the late fifteenth century, oil on panel and oil on canvas had largely replaced tempera as the standard medium of European painting, and would remain so until the twentieth century.

The Northern Renaissance also produced Hieronymus Bosch (c. 1450–1516), the Dutch painter from 's-Hertogenbosch whose hallucinatory triptychs — the Garden of Earthly Delights is the famous one, painted around 1490–1510 — combined late medieval moralist iconography with grotesque fantasy and proto-surrealist imagery without parallel in fifteenth-century European art.
Bosch's work is genuinely strange and remains genuinely strange; modern art historians have not produced a unified interpretation of what he was actually trying to communicate.

The likeliest reading is that he was a deeply orthodox Catholic moralist using the visual vocabulary of medieval marginal illumination (where grotesque hybrids and obscene puns had been a tradition for centuries) to communicate the dangers of sin and the necessity of salvation — but the reader is welcome to draw their own conclusions from staring at the paintings.

The Northern Renaissance had its own architectural and intellectual streams as well — the late Gothic flowering in Flemish and Brabantine architecture, the Devotio Moderna religious movement (Chapter 5), the early Christian humanism of figures like Rudolf Agricola (1444–1485) and the young Erasmus (1466–1536).

The conventional account that has the Renaissance starting in Italy and migrating north is therefore incomplete; the late fifteenth century had two parallel northern and southern Renaissances that were in dialogue with each other (Italian artists studied Flemish oil painting; Flemish humanists studied Italian classical scholarship) but developed substantially independently.
The single most consequential late-medieval European invention was the printing press.

The technology of movable-type printing — individual reusable metal letters that could be assembled into pages, inked, pressed against paper, and disassembled for reuse — was developed in Mainz in the German Rhineland in the 1440s by Johannes Gutenberg (c. 1400–1468) and his collaborators.
The first major book produced was Gutenberg's 42-line Bible, a Latin Vulgate Bible printed around 1455 in an edition of perhaps 180 copies (49 of which survive in 2026, in whole or in part).
The 42-line Bible is one of the most beautiful books ever printed.
It is also the founding artifact of the modern era.
Why did Gutenberg's invention matter so much?
The cost of producing a book collapsed by perhaps a factor of ten.
A skilled scribe could produce one large manuscript book in a year of work; a Gutenberg press could produce hundreds in the same period.
The labor cost per book fell roughly proportionally.

The cumulative effect over the next half-century was that books — and the literacy they enabled — became economically accessible to a much broader population than had ever had access to written texts before.
The numbers are dramatic.
By 1480, presses had been set up in 110 European cities.
By 1500, in over 200.

The total number of books produced in Europe between Gutenberg's first Bible (around 1455) and the end of 1500 — the period of incunabula, "swaddling clothes," the first half-century of printing — is estimated at roughly 20 million volumes.
This was more books than had been produced in the previous millennium of European manuscript culture combined.

The titles printed were dominated by religious texts (Bibles, devotional works, theology), but rapidly diversified into classical literature, vernacular poetry, technical manuals, news-sheets, and proto-newspapers.
The cultural and political consequences would not become fully visible until the sixteenth century.

Martin Luther in 1517 would post his Ninety-Five Theses to a church door in Wittenberg; within months, printed copies were circulating in every major German city; within a year, Luther was a continent-wide celebrity.
The Protestant Reformation was the first great revolution to use mass-produced printed text as its primary mobilization technology.

Without Gutenberg's press, Luther's theses would have stayed local; without printing, the Reformation might well have been another Hussite-style regional movement that survived as an enclave but did not transform the continent.
The press is the single technology that distinguishes Luther's potential from Hus's.
It also transformed every other domain of European intellectual life.
Classical texts became accessible to scholars and educated readers at a level they had never been before.
Vernacular literatures expanded as printers commissioned Italian, French, English, and German texts.

Technical knowledge — on shipbuilding, on navigation, on metallurgy, on artillery, on the new astronomy of Copernicus that would arrive in 1543 — circulated at a speed that pre-print Europe had not allowed.

The European voyages of discovery that begin in the late fifteenth century (Chapter 8) depended on printed maps, printed sailing manuals, and printed accounts of returning voyagers in ways that would have been inconceivable a generation earlier.
A small caveat on "first" claims: movable-type printing had been independently invented in Korea in 1234 and in China earlier than that.
Gutenberg's press was a separate European invention rather than an importation.

The Korean and Chinese versions did not produce a comparable cultural revolution, partly because of the much larger character sets required by Korean Hangul (introduced 1443) and Chinese (thousands of characters), partly because of the different political-cultural contexts in which printing operated in East Asia.

The European press's revolutionary effect depended on the alphabet (only 26 letters needed in metal type), on the highly competitive multi-state political environment that made it difficult to suppress print, and on the existing literate-but-restricted European elite that was eager for cheaper texts.
The press is one of those rare cases where a recurring invention finally produced a transformative effect because the surrounding conditions were finally right.
Cross-civ note: the late-medieval European intellectual and artistic flowering was not a unique global event.

The same century saw the Timurid Renaissance in Herat (Safavid Persia Ch 1 — Bihzad, Jami, the brilliant illustrated manuscripts), the early Joseon Korean intellectual flowering under King Sejong (who personally co-invented the Hangul script in 1443), the late Ming flowering in classical learning and the great voyages of Zheng He (1405–1433), and a generally creative period in late-medieval Indian Bhakti devotional literature (Medieval India Ch 6).
Europe was one node of an unusually generative fifteenth-century moment across Eurasia, not a uniquely creative outlier.

What would distinguish Europe in the next century — the global voyages, the Reformation, the printed scientific revolution — depended on a combination of technologies (printing, gunpowder ships, navigational mathematics) and circumstances (political fragmentation, post-plague labor markets, capital concentration) that had not yet fully converged in 1450 but would by 1500.
The next chapter is about how that convergence happened.

chapters.title: The End of an Era
sentences: In the year 1453 — the same year French artillery ended the Hundred Years War at Castillon (Chapter 3) — Ottoman cannons under Sultan Mehmed II breached the Theodosian Walls of Constantinople, ending the Roman Empire after 1,123 continuous years.
The two events happened within seven weeks of each other (Constantinople fell on May 29, Castillon on July 17).
Both used artillery as the decisive weapon.
Both ended a long-running medieval geopolitical configuration.
Both are conventionally dated as the end of the Middle Ages, though as we will see at the end of this chapter, the periodization debate is less settled than the textbooks suggest.

This chapter covers the last half-century of the Middle Ages — Constantinople 1453, the Wars of the Roses in England, the completion of the Reconquista at Granada, Columbus, the Portuguese voyages around Africa, and the long debate over when (if ever) the Middle Ages actually ended.
Constantinople in 1453 was a husk.

The city that had been the largest in Christendom and one of the largest in the world for most of its first thousand years of existence (Byzantine Empire Ch 6) had been progressively reduced over the centuries.
The Fourth Crusade's sack in 1204 (Byzantine Empire Ch 9) had broken the imperial economy.
The Ottoman conquests of the surrounding Balkans through the fourteenth century (Byzantine Empire Ch 10, Ottoman Empire Ch 2) had stripped away the last hinterland.
The repeated Black Death waves had culled the urban population.
By 1453, the city was a small Byzantine remnant of perhaps 35,000 people inside walls built to enclose 400,000, with whole districts depopulated and reverting to gardens and ruined churches.

The "Roman Empire" of 1453 consisted of Constantinople itself, a few footholds along the Sea of Marmara, and the Despotate of the Morea (the Peloponnese in southern Greece) — total population perhaps 100,000.
The empire had been a polity in name only for at least a century.

What kept it alive — to the extent it was alive — were the Theodosian Walls, the fifth-century triple-layered land fortifications that had repelled every besieging army for a thousand years (Byzantine Empire Ch 1, Ch 6).
The walls were what Constantinople still had.
The Ottoman strategy, under their young (twenty-one-year-old) Sultan Mehmed II, was to break the walls.
The instrument was gunpowder artillery.
Mehmed had commissioned a Hungarian renegade named Orban to cast bronze cannons of unprecedented size for the siege.
The largest, called Basilica (or sometimes the Dardanelles Gun), was 27 feet long, fired stone balls weighing 1,200 pounds, and required 60 oxen and 400 men to move.

Its rate of fire was perhaps three rounds per day — slow enough that defenders could repair the wall between shots by dragging up wood and earth and rubble — but the cumulative damage over weeks of bombardment was beyond what masonry walls had been designed to handle.
Mehmed's army of perhaps 80,000 — including Janissary infantry (Ottoman Empire Ch 6), feudal cavalry, gunpowder artillery, and a fleet — surrounded the city in early April 1453.

The defenders were perhaps 7,000, including the Genoese mercenary captain Giovanni Giustiniani with about 700 mostly Genoese professional soldiers and the last Roman emperor Constantine XI Palaiologos with the city's residual military forces.
The defenders were outnumbered better than ten to one and were facing the most modern siege artillery in the world.
The siege ran from April 6 to May 29, 1453.

The decisive moment was Mehmed's brilliant logistical coup of April 22: when the Golden Horn (the inlet harbor north of the city) was sealed by an iron chain that prevented Ottoman ships from entering, Mehmed had 70 of his ships dragged overland on greased logs across the ridge behind the Genoese suburb of Galata and launched into the upper Golden Horn from the inland side, opening a new front against the harbor walls and forcing the defenders to spread thin.
By late May, the cannons had reduced large sections of the Theodosian Walls to rubble.
The defenders rebuilt nightly but were running out of men.
The final assault came at dawn on May 29, 1453.
Mehmed sent in three waves: irregular Christian and Muslim auxiliaries first, to wear down the defenders; then Anatolian Turkish regular infantry; then the elite Janissaries.
The Janissaries broke through the Saint Romanus Gate in the third wave.
Giustiniani was wounded and carried from the field; his death (a few days later) effectively ended the defense.

Constantine XI was killed in the fighting, in armor, somewhere near the gate — his body was never positively identified, which produced the legend of the Marble Emperor that would survive in Greek folk memory until the nineteenth century.
The Ottomans sacked the city for three days according to the customary terms of conquest by storm.
Mehmed entered the city on May 29 and rode straight to Hagia Sophia, the Christian cathedral that had been the largest in the world for nearly a thousand years (Byzantine Empire Ch 2).
He converted it to a mosque on the spot.
Constantinople became Istanbul (an existing Greek nickname meaning "to the city," which the Ottomans adopted as the official name two centuries later).
The Roman Empire — the polity that traced its institutional continuity in unbroken succession from the city Romulus founded in 753 BCE (Ancient Rome Ch 1) — was over.
It had lasted 2,206 years.
The fall of Constantinople had immediate consequences across Christendom.
Greek scholars and clerics fled west, mostly to Italy, carrying manuscripts of classical Greek literature that fed into the Italian humanist movement (Chapter 7).

The Ottoman state inherited the Byzantine bureaucratic infrastructure, the Patriarchate of Constantinople (which Mehmed pragmatically preserved as a religious authority for his Greek Orthodox subjects within the millet system, Ottoman Empire Ch 6), and the prestige of being the new Roman emperor — Mehmed adopted the title Kayser-i Rum ("Caesar of Rome"), and his eventual successors would conquer most of the lands the Romans had once held in the eastern Mediterranean (Ottoman Empire Ch 5).
The cultural shock to western Europe was substantial but slower-moving than is sometimes claimed.

The "Greek scholars fleeing to Italy" narrative is only partially correct: the most important Greek manuscripts had been brought west in the previous half-century by traveling Italian humanists (especially during the Council of Florence in 1438–1439, Chapter 7) rather than by post-1453 refugees.

But the symbolic effect — the loss of the eastern Christian capital, the obvious threat the Ottomans now posed to the rest of Christian Europe, the end of any realistic prospect of crusade-style restoration of the Holy Land — reshaped the European political imagination in ways that took decades to fully manifest.

The Ottoman Empire ascended to the position it would hold for the next four centuries: the dominant land power in eastern Europe and the eastern Mediterranean, the principal external threat to Christian Europe, the arbiter of the Balkans and the Middle East.
The next five centuries of European geopolitics would be shaped, in significant part, by the Ottoman question.
England, meanwhile, was descending into its own civil war.

The English losing of the Hundred Years War (Chapter 3) had bankrupted the royal treasury, demoralized the nobility, and discredited the Lancastrian regime under the gentle, intermittently-mad Henry VI (Henry V's son, who had inherited the throne at nine months in 1422).
By the 1450s, with Calais the only English continental possession left, returning veterans of the French wars were arriving home with no employment, no land, and military experience.
Aristocratic feuds that had been suppressed during the war broke out across the country.

The royal court had become a battleground between rival factions led by the king's wife Margaret of Anjou (a French princess whose pro-French sympathies had been controversial since her arrival in 1445) and the king's cousin Richard, Duke of York (who claimed a stronger hereditary right to the throne than the Lancastrian line through descent from Edward III's third son).
The Wars of the Roses (1455–1485) — named centuries later from the white rose of York and the red rose of Lancaster — was the dynastic civil war that resulted.

It is one of the most narratively complex conflicts in English history, with multiple battles, several changes of dynasty, repeated reversals, and a cast of characters that includes some of the most memorable in English medieval history (Richard III being the obvious example).

The summary is that the House of York seized the throne in 1461 with Edward IV, lost it briefly in 1470–71 to the restored Lancastrian Henry VI, regained it in 1471 (with Henry VI murdered in the Tower of London a few weeks later), held it for the rest of Edward IV's reign and the brief reign of his son Edward V (the older of the famous "Princes in the Tower" who disappeared in 1483 and were almost certainly murdered), then transitioned to Richard III (Edward IV's brother, who took the throne in 1483 by declaring Edward IV's marriage invalid and the princes therefore illegitimate, then probably arranged their murder).
Richard III ruled for only two years.

The Lancastrian claim had passed through a complicated dynastic chain to Henry Tudor, a Welsh-descended exile in Brittany whose connection to the royal house was through his mother Margaret Beaufort (a great-granddaughter of John of Gaunt through John of Gaunt's eventually-legitimized affair with Katherine Swynford).

Henry Tudor invaded England in August 1485 with French and Scottish troops, met Richard III at Bosworth Field in Leicestershire on August 22, 1485, and won when Richard's allies (notably the Stanley family) defected at a key moment.
Richard was killed in the fighting.
He was the last English king to die in personal combat on a battlefield.

His body was buried hastily in a Leicester monastery whose location was lost over the centuries — until a 2012 archaeological dig in a Leicester city-council car park rediscovered his bones, complete with the distinctive scoliosis Shakespeare had described, and reburied him in Leicester Cathedral with appropriate ceremony.
Henry Tudor became Henry VII, the first king of the Tudor dynasty that would rule England for the next 118 years and produce Henry VIII, Elizabeth I, and the English Reformation.
The Wars of the Roses had killed off most of the older medieval English aristocracy and consolidated political power in the crown to a degree no late-medieval English king had achieved.
The Tudor era — and the early modern English state — emerged directly from the destruction of the medieval English aristocratic order at Bosworth.
In Iberia, the long story of the Reconquista finally ended.

The Reconquista ("reconquest") was the long Christian recovery of the Iberian peninsula from the Muslim emirates that had ruled most of Iberia after the Arab conquest of 711 CE (Islamic Golden Age Ch 7 — Cordoba and Andalusi history).

The recovery had begun in the eighth century in the Asturian highlands, accelerated through the eleventh and twelfth centuries (the conquest of Toledo in 1085, the great Almohad-Christian wars), and slowed through the thirteenth century as the Christian kingdoms — Castile, Aragon, Portugal, Navarre — consolidated their gains.
By 1300, only the small Emirate of Granada in southeastern Iberia remained Muslim, paying tribute to Castile and surviving as a satellite state for the next two centuries.
The dynastic union that finally ended the Reconquista was the marriage in 1469 of Ferdinand of Aragon (then heir to the Aragonese throne) and Isabella of Castile (then heir to the Castilian throne).
The marriage joined the two largest Christian Iberian kingdoms into a personal union that would eventually become Spain (the political entity formed by the eventual fusion of the two crowns).
Ferdinand and Isabella — known together as the Catholic Monarchs (Reyes Católicos, a title given them by Pope Alexander VI in 1494) — were exceptionally competent rulers.
They reformed the royal administration, asserted royal authority over the nobility (curbing the Castilian grandes who had dominated the previous reign), and pursued an aggressive foreign policy.
The Granada War (1482–1492) was the final phase of the Reconquista.

The Catholic Monarchs invested ten years in systematically reducing Granada's frontier fortresses, exploiting internal divisions in the Granadan ruling Nasrid dynasty, and starving the city itself through siege.

Granada surrendered on January 2, 1492, with the last Nasrid emir Boabdil (Spanish corruption of his Arabic name Abu Abdallah) handing over the keys of the Alhambra palace in a famous ceremony. (Legend has it that Boabdil's mother Aisha told him as he wept on a hilltop overlooking the city: "Do not weep like a woman for what you could not defend like a man." The hilltop is still called El Suspiro del Moro, "The Moor's Sigh." The line is almost certainly invented by later chroniclers but has stuck.) The Reconquista was over.
Eight centuries of Christian-Muslim coexistence, conflict, and gradual displacement on the Iberian peninsula had ended with the last Muslim political entity extinguished.
The 1492 surrender terms guaranteed the Granadan Muslim population freedom of religion, personal property, and language.

Within ten years, those terms had been violated and Iberian Muslims were being forcibly converted; over the next century, the Moriscos (descendants of forced converts who continued to practice Islam in secret) would be progressively persecuted and finally expelled in 1609.
The Iberian Jewish population suffered the same fate, faster.
The Alhambra Decree of March 31, 1492, gave all Jews in Castile and Aragon four months to convert to Christianity or leave.

Roughly 40,000 to 100,000 Jews left, many to Portugal (where they were expelled five years later), to North Africa, to the Ottoman Empire (where Sultan Bayezid II welcomed them as economically valuable refugees, allegedly remarking that Ferdinand had impoverished his own kingdom and enriched the Sultan's), to the Italian states, to the Netherlands, and eventually to the New World.
The Sephardic Jewish diaspora that resulted is one of the major demographic events of late medieval Europe.
The cultural loss to Iberia was immense.
The third enormous event of 1492 was Columbus.

Christopher Columbus (Italian: Cristoforo Colombo, Spanish: Cristóbal Colón) was a Genoese mariner born around 1451 who had been trying for years to find a royal sponsor for his proposed voyage west across the Atlantic to reach Asia.

His geographical theory was incorrect: he believed (relying on a misinterpretation of Marinus of Tyre's geography and an exaggerated estimate of the size of Asia) that the western route from Iberia to Japan was about 2,500 miles, when the actual distance is roughly 12,000 miles.
The Portuguese rejected his proposal in 1485 because their own geographers correctly calculated that the actual distance was much larger than Columbus claimed.

The Spanish Catholic Monarchs, after years of indecision, finally accepted his proposal in 1492 — partly out of opportunistic interest, partly because the Granada victory had freed up royal attention, partly because Columbus had reduced his demands.
Columbus sailed from Palos de la Frontera on August 3, 1492, with three small ships (the Santa María, the Pinta, and the Niña) and 90 men.
He stopped at the Canary Islands for refit, then sailed west into the open Atlantic on September 6.
On October 12, 1492, his lookout sighted land — an island in the Bahamas that the indigenous Lucayans called Guanahani and that Columbus renamed San Salvador.
The exact island has been debated; the modern consensus identifies it as either Watlings Island or Samana Cay.

Columbus and his crews proceeded to explore the Bahamas, Cuba, and Hispaniola over the next three months, encountering the Taíno populations of the Greater Antilles, before returning to Spain in March 1493 with samples of indigenous people, parrots, gold, and reports of vast new lands beyond the Atlantic.

Columbus believed until his death in 1506 that he had reached the eastern fringes of Asia — that the Bahamas were islands off the Japanese coast, that Cuba was a peninsula of mainland China, that Hispaniola was a Japanese island.

The realization that he had encountered an entirely new continent unknown to ancient geography came over the next decade, primarily through the voyages of Amerigo Vespucci (whose name would, in 1507, be applied to the new continent in a German cartographer's map: America).

Columbus made four voyages in total, was made governor of Hispaniola, was eventually arrested for misrule and shipped back to Spain in chains, was rehabilitated, and died still believing he had reached Asia.
The political and demographic consequences of Columbus's voyages would unfold over the next century.
The Aztec Empire would fall to Cortés in 1519–1521 (Aztec Empire Ch 8).
The Inca Empire would fall to Pizarro in 1532–1533.

Eurasian diseases — smallpox, measles, influenza, eventually plague — would kill roughly 90% of the indigenous population of the Americas over the next century and a half, in the largest human demographic catastrophe ever recorded (worse than the Black Death proportionally and incomparably larger in absolute terms).

The Atlantic slave trade, beginning with Portuguese coastal slaving in the mid-1400s and accelerating after 1500, would forcibly transport perhaps 12 million Africans to the Americas over the next four centuries.
Silver from the Potosí mines in Bolivia (discovered 1545) would flow through Manila to China and reshape the global monetary economy.
None of this was visible from 1492.
All of it followed.
The Portuguese were doing the same thing on a different ocean.

While Spain was finishing the Reconquista and funding Columbus, Portugal had been systematically working its way down the African coast for most of the fifteenth century, looking for a sea route to the Indian Ocean.

The project had been started by Prince Henry the Navigator (1394–1460), a younger son of King John I of Portugal, who had organized a sustained program of Atlantic exploration from his base at Sagres on the southwestern Portuguese coast beginning around 1418.

Henry trained generations of Portuguese pilots and cartographers, financed expeditions down the West African coast, and (by the 1440s) had triggered the trans-Atlantic slave trade by importing the first enslaved African captives to Lisbon for sale.
The progression down the African coast was grinding: every expedition pushed a few hundred miles further than the last, then returned to confirm the route and bring back economic intelligence.
Cape Bojador (modern Western Sahara) was passed in 1434.
Cape Verde in 1444.
The equator in the 1470s.
The Congo River in 1482.
Bartolomeu Dias finally rounded the Cape of Good Hope at the southern tip of Africa in 1488, the first European to enter the Indian Ocean by sea.
The route to Asia by water around Africa was now demonstrated to be possible.
It took another decade to actually use the route.
Vasco da Gama sailed from Lisbon in July 1497 with four ships and roughly 170 men, rounded the Cape of Good Hope in November, and reached the Swahili coast of East Africa by early 1498.

With the help of an Indian or Arab pilot (the contested attribution; possibly the famous Ibn Majid, who would have been an Arab Yemeni navigator, but the identification is disputed), da Gama crossed the Indian Ocean and reached Calicut on the Malabar Coast of southwestern India on May 20, 1498.
It was the first sea voyage from Europe to India and the founding moment of European maritime imperialism in Asia.
The Portuguese moved fast.

Within twenty years, they had established trading posts at Goa, Malacca, the Spice Islands, Macao, and Nagasaki — a maritime empire stretching from the West African coast to Japan, built on superior naval technology (heavily armed sailing ships with broadside cannons), strategic chokepoints, and the willingness to use violence.

The Indian Ocean trade that had been controlled by Arab, Persian, Indian, and Malay merchants for centuries was rapidly subordinated to Portuguese gun-armed shipping (Mali Empire Ch 6 covers the African end of this; Medieval India context covers the Indian end).

The Spanish-Portuguese division of newly-discovered territories was negotiated in the Treaty of Tordesillas of June 1494, which drew a line down the Atlantic about 1,100 miles west of the Cape Verde islands: Portugal got everything east of the line (which would include Brazil, discovered in 1500 by Pedro Álvares Cabral), Spain got everything west.

The treaty was negotiated under papal mediation; no other European power agreed to it, and within decades the Treaty of Tordesillas was effectively a dead letter as the French, English, and Dutch entered the colonial competition.
But it set the linguistic boundary in South America (Portuguese Brazil, Spanish elsewhere) that has lasted to the present.
So when did the Middle Ages end?
The answer is: there is no single date, and historians have settled on different ones for different purposes.
The major candidates are: 1453 — the fall of Constantinople and the end of the Hundred Years War.
The classic textbook answer, traditional in European historiography since the nineteenth century.

It marks the end of the medieval Mediterranean order: the last fragment of the Roman state extinguished, the dynastic war that had dominated Latin Christendom for over a century closed, the Ottoman Empire ascendant, gunpowder confirmed as the decisive military technology. 1485 — the Battle of Bosworth Field and the Tudor accession.
The conventional English answer.

It marks the end of the medieval Plantagenet dynasty, the consolidation of Tudor royal authority, and the beginning of the early modern English state. 1492 — Granada, Columbus, and the Jewish expulsion.
A popular modern choice, particularly in Iberian and American historiography.

It marks the end of the Reconquista, the beginning of the European encounter with the Americas, and the start of the global Atlantic economy that would define the early modern world. 1500 — round-number convention.
Useful for textbook purposes but not corresponding to any specific event. 1517 — Luther's Ninety-Five Theses.
The conventional Protestant choice.
It marks the beginning of the Reformation, which is the single largest religious-political rupture in early modern European history. 1648 — the Peace of Westphalia.
A more recent choice, popular among historians of international relations.
It marks the end of the Wars of Religion and the beginning of the modern state-system.
The honest answer is that none of these dates marks a clean break.
The Middle Ages did not end on a single day.

The features we associate with "medieval" — feudal lord-vassal relations, manorial agriculture, universal Catholic Church, scholastic theology, mounted knightly warfare, Latin as the only learned language — eroded at different rates in different places over the long fifteenth and sixteenth centuries.

Some medieval institutions persisted into the eighteenth century (French serfdom in some forms) or even later (the Holy Roman Empire was not finally abolished until 1806, and the Papal States persisted until 1870).

A different framing might be: the Middle Ages ended when the central explanatory institutions of medieval Europe — the universal Church, the manorial system, the scholastic university, the chivalric military order, the small Mediterranean trade economy — were no longer adequate to describe how Europeans actually lived.
By that standard, the period of transition runs from roughly 1450 to roughly 1550, with no single year decisive.

The Italian Renaissance, the Wars of the Roses, the fall of Constantinople, the Reconquista, Columbus, the Cape Route, the printing press, the Reformation, the Ottoman ascendancy, and the demographic catastrophe of the Americas are all part of the long transition.
The Middle Ages were not simply replaced by something better.

The early modern world that emerged from the late-medieval crisis had its own catastrophes — the Wars of Religion, the Atlantic slave trade, the European witch hunts (Chapter 5 mentions the Malleus Maleficarum of 1486 — the witch craze proper would be a sixteenth- and seventeenth-century event), the demographic destruction of the Americas, the entrenchment of serfdom in Eastern Europe.
The continuities are at least as significant as the breaks.
Medieval Europe was not a darkness ended by a Renaissance dawn; it was a complex civilizational order that mutated, under enormous demographic and political pressure, into the early modern world.
What is true is that the European who fell asleep in 1300 and woke up in 1500 would have found very little of his world recognizable.
The plague had culled the population by a third and recurred every decade.
The Church had been split, reformed, and discredited.
The Hundred Years War had broken the chivalric order and produced national identities.
The printing press had collapsed the cost of books.
Italian cities had reinvented painting, sculpture, banking, and architecture.
Constantinople was an Ottoman capital.
Iberia was Christian and was sending ships to America.
The Wycliffite-Hussite reformations had rehearsed the Lutheran one.

The institutions that would dominate the next four centuries — the centralized nation-state, the global maritime empire, the printed book, the joint-stock company, the gunpowder army, the Atlantic slave trade — were all in their early forms.
The Middle Ages were over in any sense that mattered.
The next chapter of European history was beginning.
A final cross-civ pause.
The world of 1500 — the world that emerged from the late-medieval European crisis — was the first genuinely global world in human history.
The Portuguese Indian Ocean trading network linked Lisbon to Nagasaki by sea.
The Spanish Atlantic system would shortly link Sevilla to Manila via Mexico.
The Ottoman Empire connected the Mediterranean, the Black Sea, the Red Sea, and the Persian Gulf.
The Ming and the early Joseon Korea were tied into the East Asian world system.
The Aztec Triple Alliance dominated central Mexico (Aztec Empire Ch 7), the Inca Empire stretched 3,000 miles down the Andes (Inca Empire Ch 3).
The Safavid order in Iran was a generation away from founding the Twelver Shia state that would define Iranian identity (Safavid Persia Ch 1).
The Mughal Empire would be founded in India in 1526.
The Songhai Empire was reaching its peak in West Africa.

In 1500, for the first time, every major continental population — Europe, Africa, Asia, the Americas, the Pacific (the Polynesian voyaging society, Polynesian Voyagers Ch 8) — was within a few decades of being interconnected.
The diseases, technologies, crops, ideas, religions, and military innovations that had previously been regional were about to become global.
The next five centuries of human history are the working-out of that interconnection.
The European late Middle Ages are the long period in which the conditions for that interconnection were assembled.
The continent walked into 1300 with a Mediterranean orientation, an agricultural economy, and a universal Church.
It walked out of 1500 with an Atlantic orientation, a partly-monetized economy, a fractured Church, and gunpowder ships ranging from Lisbon to Calicut.
The transformation was ugly, expensive, and largely involuntary.
It was also the foundation of the modern world.
The Middle Ages ended because the medieval system could no longer describe what Europeans were doing.

The early modern world that replaced it was not better in any obvious moral sense — it produced colonial slavery, religious wars on a scale the medieval Church had never managed, and the demographic destruction of the Americas.
But it was different, and the difference is what the late medieval centuries had been slowly producing.

The next civilization in this app to pick up the thread is the early modern world — the Reformation, the Wars of Religion, the global trading empires, the scientific revolution, and everything else that the late Middle Ages had set in motion.
The story does not end.
It just becomes a different story.

chapters.title: The Year 1000 and the Take-Off
sentences: For most of the early Middle Ages, western Europe had been a backwater.
The Roman cities had shrunk into provincial market towns or disappeared into farmland.
The Roman roads were still there but no one was repairing them.
The aqueducts were broken, the public baths were ruins, the great libraries of Antioch and Alexandria and Constantinople were either lost (Alexandria) or out of reach (Constantinople).
A Frankish bishop in 700 had to write to Cassiodorus's old monastery in southern Italy to ask for a copy of a basic geometrical text he could not find in his own library.
The civilization that had been the western half of the Roman Empire was running on inheritance and not generating much new of its own.
Then, somewhere around the year 1000, something changed.
The change was not a single event.

It was the accumulation of small improvements — a heavier plow, a better collar for the draft horse, a third field added to the crop rotation, a watermill on every workable stream — that compounded into a transformation of the European countryside.
Population grew.
Surplus food fed the cities.
The cities grew.
New cities were chartered.
Long-distance trade revived.
Money came back into common use.
Stone construction picked up.
Latin literacy spread.
By 1100, western Europe had been quietly turned into a different kind of place.
This chapter is about the slow undramatic infrastructure layer that made everything else in this book possible.
The Crusades, the cathedrals, the universities, Magna Carta — none of it happens without the agricultural revolution that fed the people who built and fought and studied.
Civilizations run on calories.
The High Middle Ages got more calories per acre than any previous European civilization had ever managed.
To understand the take-off, start with the climate.
Between roughly 950 and 1250 CE, average temperatures in northern Europe ran about half a degree to one degree Celsius warmer than the medieval baseline.
This sounds small.
It was not.

A temperature shift of that size, sustained over three centuries, lengthens the growing season at northern latitudes by two to four weeks a year, lifts the elevation at which grain will ripen, reduces the frequency of catastrophic frost, and pushes the boundary of viable agriculture significantly further north and higher into the mountains.
This is the Medieval Warm Period (the standard name; some climatologists prefer "Medieval Climate Anomaly" because the warmth was real in northern Europe but not globally uniform).
Vineyards reached as far north as southern England — wine production at Ely Cathedral in eastern England in 1086 is recorded in the Domesday Book — and rye could be grown in Norway.
Greenland was actually green enough in the early 1000s for the Norse to plant farms there (Viking Age Ch 7).
The warming did not cause the take-off, but it provided the floor.
Crops that struggled in colder centuries became reliable.
Marginal land became productive.
Famines, while they still happened, became less frequent and less catastrophic.
A peasant in 1100 could expect more reliable harvests than his great-great-grandfather had managed in 900.
This is the kind of background condition historians often skip past on the way to the more glamorous narrative.
It deserves attention.

The same warming that let the Norse settle Greenland was letting French peasants double-crop their fields in Normandy, German colonists push into eastern Europe with rye and oats, and English shepherds graze sheep in the Scottish borderlands.

A few hundred years later, when the climate cooled again at the start of the Little Ice Age around 1300, the European agricultural system would be running into hard limits and the demographic boom would stall — but that is the Late Medieval story, not this one.
The four technological innovations that powered the agricultural revolution all reached western Europe in usable form between roughly 800 and 1100 CE.
First, the heavy mouldboard plow.

The light wooden ard plow inherited from the Mediterranean Romans worked fine in the dry sandy soils of southern Europe but barely scratched the wet heavy clay soils that covered most of northern France, the Low Countries, England, and Germany.

The heavy plow — iron-shod, with a vertical knife (the coulter) cutting the sod, a horizontal blade (the share) slicing it from below, and a curved board (the mouldboard) turning it over — could break clay soils that had been effectively unfarmable.
Once you have the heavy plow, vast tracts of northern Europe become arable for the first time.
Forests that had stood since the end of the last Ice Age were cleared.
Land area under cultivation expanded by an estimated factor of three to five over the next two centuries.
Second, the three-field crop rotation.
The older Mediterranean two-field system left half the cropland fallow each year to recover.

The three-field system divided the cropland into three: one field of winter wheat or rye (planted in autumn, harvested in summer), one of spring oats or barley (planted in spring, harvested in late summer), one fallow.
This raised the productive share of farmland from one half to two thirds and added the spring-planted oats — a crop that could feed both humans and the new draft horses.

Three-field rotation spread across northern Europe between 900 and 1200, slowly enough that no single date marks its arrival but cumulatively enough to roughly double the food output of the average farm.
Third, the rigid horse collar.
The classical world had used the throat-and-girth harness, which let an ox pull a plow by the chest but choked a horse by the windpipe whenever it tried to pull seriously.

The rigid padded horse collar — apparently invented in China by the third century CE and transmitted west across the Eurasian steppe over the next several hundred years — let a horse pull from the shoulders, transferring all its weight into the load.

Combined with horseshoes (which protected the hooves from soft European mud) and the shoulder yoke for two-horse teams, the new harness made the horse roughly twice as efficient as the ox for plowing and hauling.
The horse moves faster, works longer hours, and handles uneven terrain better than the ox.
The substitution of horses for oxen across northern Europe between 1000 and 1300 effectively tripled the available draft power on the medieval farm.
Fourth, the watermill.
The watermill is older than the High Middle Ages — Romans had them, eighth-century monasteries had them — but the diffusion explodes after 1000.
The 1086 Domesday survey commissioned by William the Conqueror counted 5,624 watermills in England alone, roughly one for every fifty households.
By 1300 there were more than 10,000 in England and probably 30,000 across France.

Watermills were used to grind grain (the original application), full cloth (pounding wet wool to thicken it), saw timber, hammer iron, crush ore, work bellows for furnaces, and run a dozen other industrial processes.
The High Medieval watermill was the first widespread non-animal industrial power source in human history.

The closest contemporary parallel was the much later Song dynasty's use of water-powered industry in eleventh- and twelfth-century China (Tang-Song China Ch 8), running on a similar logic but applied to silk and iron rather than wool and grain.

To these four core innovations the High Middle Ages added the post mill — a wooden windmill mounted on a central post so the entire body could be rotated to face the wind, first attested in Yorkshire and Normandy around 1180 — adding wind power to the mechanical inventory wherever streams ran dry.
The cumulative effect of all this was that a peasant family in 1200 could feed itself on roughly half the land its great-great-grandfather had needed in 900.

The other half — and the new land brought under cultivation by the heavy plow — produced the marketable surplus that fed the cities, supported the merchants, paid the masons of the cathedrals, and freed enough young men from farm labor to fill the new universities.
The demographic effect was enormous.
Best modern estimates put western Europe's population at roughly 35–40 million around the year 1000 and roughly 70–80 million by 1300.
This is a doubling in three centuries.

The figures are extrapolations from incomplete tax and church records, hearth counts, and archaeological surveys, and the error bars are wide — but every serious estimate points to the same general magnitude.
The High Middle Ages were the most demographically expansive period in European history before the Industrial Revolution.
Where did the extra people go?
Some onto newly cleared land — the great forests of Germany, Poland, and Hungary were rolled back by axe and plow over these three centuries.
Some east, into the German colonization (the Ostsiedlung) of Slavic lands across the Elbe.
Some south, into the Christian advance through Iberia (Chapter 8).
And, most consequentially for the rest of this book, some into the cities.
The cities of western Europe in 1000 were small.
Paris had perhaps 20,000 people.
London perhaps 10,000.

The largest cities of the early-medieval West were dwarfed by their contemporaries elsewhere — Constantinople (Byzantine Empire Ch 5) at perhaps 400,000, Córdoba in Muslim Spain at over 100,000, Baghdad (Islamic Golden Age Ch 1) at perhaps 800,000 at its eighth-century peak.
By 1300 the picture had shifted.
Paris had perhaps 200,000 residents, Venice and Milan around 150,000, Florence and Genoa around 100,000.
These are still small compared to Hangzhou (Tang-Song China Ch 8) at over a million, but they are the largest western European cities since Rome's fourth-century population peak.
And they kept growing.
The cities were also organizationally new.

The high-medieval city was not the Roman survival of the early Middle Ages but a chartered self-governing commune with its own institutions: an elected council, a defined legal jurisdiction (the famous formula was that "city air makes you free" — a serf who lived in a chartered city for a year and a day was no longer a serf), guilds organizing crafts and trade, taxation by consent.
The northern Italian cities went furthest, becoming effectively independent republics by the twelfth century.
The German "free imperial cities" — Cologne, Lübeck, Hamburg, Frankfurt, Augsburg — answered only to the emperor and not to any local lord.
The Flemish cloth cities (Bruges, Ghent, Ypres) became some of the wealthiest urban centers in Europe.
France and England kept tighter royal supervision, but even there the chartered town with elected officers and its own court was the standard model by 1200.
This was something genuinely new.
The cities of the ancient world had been governed by the same aristocracies that governed the countryside.
The High Medieval city had its own merchant-and-artisan elite that owed nothing to the rural lords.
It is one of the structural inventions of the period and the foundation of everything else in the urban story — the merchants of Chapter 4, the masons of Chapter 6, the students of Chapter 7.
Cross-civ check: the European take-off of 1000–1100 is one of those moments where it helps to look around the world.

In China, the Song dynasty had been founded in 960, and the eleventh century saw the most spectacular economic and technological efflorescence in pre-modern world history — printed books in millions of copies, paper money, industrial-scale iron production, the magnetic compass, gunpowder weapons, water-powered textile machinery (Tang-Song China Ch 6 and Ch 8).
The Song economy in 1100 was probably four to five times the size of the entire western European economy combined.
Most of what western Europe was inventing for the first time, China had had for centuries.

In the Islamic world, the eleventh century was the late golden age — al-Ghazali was writing in Baghdad, Avicenna had finished his philosophical and medical synthesis a generation earlier, the great hospitals of Cairo and Damascus were operating, Cordoba in Muslim Spain held more books than every Christian monastery in Europe combined (Islamic Golden Age Ch 4 and Ch 7).
The translations that would carry Aristotle back to the Latin West (Chapter 5) were waiting on the shelves of libraries the West had not yet learned to read.
In India, the Chola maritime empire was at its peak, conducting naval expeditions across the Bay of Bengal and dominating the trade between South India and Southeast Asia (Medieval India Ch 5).

South Indian temple-cities were producing some of the most sophisticated stone architecture in the world, with thousand-pillared halls and 200-foot gopuram gate towers — at exactly the same time the first Romanesque cathedrals of western Europe were being built with much more modest engineering ambitions.

In Japan, the Heian court was producing The Tale of Genji (around 1010), the world's first psychological novel, written by the woman court official Murasaki Shikibu (Ancient Japan Ch 8) — at exactly the moment the rural aristocrats of northern France were largely illiterate and getting their letters dictated by clerks.
In the Americas, Cahokia in the Mississippi valley was approaching its early-twelfth-century peak with perhaps 20,000 residents — the largest pre-Columbian city north of Mexico.

The Maya of the southern lowlands had collapsed in the eighth and ninth centuries (Maya Civilization Ch 5), but Postclassic Maya kingdoms continued in the Yucatán under Chichén Itzá and later Mayapán (Maya Civilization Ch 6).
The Wari highland empire of Peru was in its final decline (Middle Horizon Empires Ch 8), and the next great Andean polity, the Chimú on the north coast, was just beginning to consolidate.
The European take-off of 1000–1100 was therefore not Europe leaping ahead of the world.
It was Europe catching up.
The Latin West in 1000 had been a back province of Eurasia; by 1300 it was at least back in the conversation.
By 1500 — which is the territory of the Late Medieval and Early Modern volumes — it had begun to diverge in the directions that would eventually produce the modern world.
But the take-off in this chapter is a recovery, not a sprint.
A few words about how this gets paid for, because the rest of the book sometimes takes the institutional infrastructure for granted.
The medieval economy ran on land.

A king or great lord granted land to a vassal in exchange for military service; the vassal granted land to lesser knights in exchange for the same; the knights granted plots to peasants in exchange for labor and a share of the crop.
This stack of obligations is what historians since the seventeenth century have called feudalism (FYOO-duh-lizm), from Latin feudum, meaning a fief — a grant of land.
