The actual term "feudalism" did not exist in the Middle Ages and the system was much messier than the textbook diagrams suggest, but the basic logic — land in exchange for military and labor service — held across most of western Europe between roughly 900 and 1300.
The man at the bottom of the stack was the serf (SURF, from Latin servus, slave).

The serf was not a slave in the classical sense — he could not be sold separately from the land, he had legal rights, he could marry and pass property to his children — but he was bound to the manor of his lord, owed labor on the lord's fields a fixed number of days per week, and could not leave without permission.
The High Medieval centuries saw two contradictory trends.
On the one hand, agricultural intensification made the serf's labor more valuable and gave many serfs better terms.

On the other, the rise of the urban economy gave serfs a way out — the chartered town's "year and a day" rule that made fugitives free was the safety valve that drained the most ambitious labor off the manor and into the city.

The manor itself — the basic unit of medieval rural economy — was a self-contained working estate with the lord's house at the center, the peasants' village around it, and the cultivated fields, common pastures, woodland, and watermill organized as a single working system.

The Domesday Book of 1086 catalogues English manors in extraordinary detail: how many plows, how many peasants, how many mills, how many fishponds, how the population had changed since 1066 (most often: it was now smaller, because William's conquest had been brutal).
The manorial economy is the engine room of the High Medieval take-off.
The cathedrals and the universities are the steeple and the tower; the manor is the foundation.
By 1300, most of the institutional pieces of the High Middle Ages were in place.

The next chapter turns to the political and religious confrontation that defined the eleventh century — the long war between the popes who were now claiming supremacy over kings and the kings who refused to accept it.

chapters.title: Pope vs. Emperor
sentences: In late January 1077, the Holy Roman Emperor Henry IV stood barefoot in the snow for three days outside the gate of the castle of Canossa (kah-NOH-sah) in northern Italy.
He was wearing only a coarse woolen pilgrim's robe over his shirt.
He was waiting for Pope Gregory VII to come to the gate and lift his excommunication.
Eventually Gregory did.
Henry kissed his ring, was readmitted to the Catholic Church, and rode home.
This is one of the most famous scenes in medieval history, and it deserves explanation.

Why was the most powerful secular ruler in western Christendom standing in the snow in his nightshirt waiting for permission from a sixty-year-old monk with a cane to be allowed back into a Church he himself was supposedly the protector of?
What had they been fighting about?
And what did it actually settle?
The answer is the Investiture Controversy, the long contest from roughly 1075 to 1122 over who could appoint bishops in western Europe — the king or the pope.
It sounds technical.
It was technical.
It was also one of the structural turning points of the entire medieval period, the moment when the western Church established itself as a power independent of the secular state.

Everything that follows in this book — the Crusades, the universities, Magna Carta, the conflict between civil and religious authority that would still be live in the Reformation and the Enlightenment — runs out of the precedent that Gregory VII set against Henry IV.
This chapter explains what was at stake.
Some setup.
Through most of the early Middle Ages, the western Church had been comfortably entangled with secular rulers.
Bishops were major landholders, and their lands came with feudal obligations to the king who granted them.

When a bishop died, the king typically chose his replacement from among candidates suggested by the cathedral chapter, then "invested" him by handing him the symbols of his office — a ring (representing his marriage to the diocese) and a crozier or staff (representing his pastoral authority).
The new bishop also received from the king the lands and revenues of his see, which often made him one of the wealthiest and most powerful men in the kingdom.
The king got a loyal noble in a key position; the bishop got land and rank; the Church got an institutional presence.
Everyone, on the surface, was happy.
There were two problems with this arrangement that grew worse through the tenth and eleventh centuries.
The first was simony (SY-muh-nee), the buying and selling of church offices, named after Simon Magus from the New Testament who tried to buy spiritual power from the apostles.
By 1000, simony was endemic.
Bishoprics were openly sold to the highest bidder.
Wealthy noble families bought the bishopric of, say, Reims for a younger son who had no particular religious vocation but who would administer the see's revenues for the family's benefit.
The Church's spiritual authority and its temporal wealth had become so entangled that the spiritual side was visibly being prostituted to the temporal.
The second was clerical marriage.
The early Church had not strictly required priests to be celibate, but by the eleventh century the Roman Church was moving toward an absolute requirement of clerical celibacy.
This was less a matter of theology than of property: a married priest had children, and his children inherited church property as if it were family property, draining the institution.
The reformers wanted celibate clergy partly for spiritual reasons (the model was the monk) and partly to keep church property from leaking out into hereditary noble lineages.
Underneath both of these specific abuses was a deeper structural tension.

If the Church's spiritual authority was higher than the king's temporal authority — and the entire medieval theology of kingship insisted that kings derived their power from God through the Church — then how could the king appoint the bishops who administered that spiritual authority on God's behalf?
It looked like the river running uphill.
The reform movement wanted the river to flow the right way: bishops would be chosen by the Church, not by the king.
The reform began in the monasteries.

The abbey of Cluny (kloo-NEE) in Burgundy, founded in 910, had been chartered with the unusual provision that it answered directly to the pope and not to any local lord or bishop — a kind of jurisdictional independence that let it pursue strict religious reform without political interference.
The Cluniac model spread.

By the late eleventh century there were over a thousand Cluniac priories across western Europe, all loosely linked to the mother house, all observing a stricter version of the Rule of Saint Benedict (the sixth-century template for monastic life, Mongol Empire era predecessor of much medieval institutional thinking — actually written in early-medieval Italy, the foundational Western monastic charter).
The Cluniacs produced a generation of reform-minded clerics who eventually started getting elected pope.
The reformers worked their way to the top of the institution between roughly 1046 and 1073.
Pope Leo IX (1049–1054) issued the first systematic decrees against simony and clerical marriage.

Pope Nicholas II (1059–1061) issued the bull In Nomine Domini in 1059 that took the election of the pope itself out of the hands of the Roman aristocracy and the German emperor and gave it exclusively to the College of Cardinals — the papal electors who still choose the pope today. (The 1059 reform is one of the Church's most consequential institutional moves and it is often skipped in popular histories.

Without it, the popes would have remained essentially appointees of whoever held Rome.) The third major figure was Hildebrand of Sovana, an Italian Cluniac monk who had been advising successive popes for twenty years before he was elected as Gregory VII in 1073 at the age of about sixty.
Gregory was the most ambitious pope of the medieval West.
In 1075 he issued the Dictatus Papae — the Dictates of the Pope — a list of twenty-seven propositions claiming sweeping papal authority.

A few examples will give the flavor: the pope alone is universally called pope; the pope can depose emperors; all princes shall kiss the pope's feet; the pope may absolve the subjects of unjust rulers from their oaths of loyalty.
This was new.
Previous popes had claimed religious supremacy.
Gregory was claiming political supremacy too.
He was saying, in effect: I can fire your king.
It would have been provocative under any circumstances.
But Gregory had picked an opponent in Henry IV, the young Holy Roman Emperor, who was not going to take it lying down.
Henry IV of the Salian dynasty had inherited the throne at age six in 1056 and reached his majority around 1065.

The German emperor was theoretically the protector of the western Church and held the right to "invest" bishops within his vast empire (which then included Germany, the Low Countries, much of northern Italy, and Burgundy).
When the bishopric of Milan came open in late 1075, Gregory and Henry both insisted on appointing different candidates.
Gregory threatened excommunication.
Henry, in January 1076, summoned a council of German bishops at Worms that issued a counter-blast declaring Gregory deposed and demanding that he descend from his usurped throne.
Gregory's reply in February 1076 was overwhelming.

He excommunicated Henry — formally cutting him off from the sacraments, which any medieval Christian believed meant being damned if he died — and, more devastatingly, he released Henry's subjects from their oaths of loyalty.
The second move was the new move.
It said, in effect: the political loyalty you owe your king depends on his being in good standing with the Church, and he is no longer in good standing.
The German nobility seized on it instantly.
Henry had been struggling with rebellious vassals throughout his reign; many of them had been waiting for an excuse to disobey him.
With the pope's release of obligations in hand, they convened at the Diet of Tribur in October 1076 and gave Henry an ultimatum: get the excommunication lifted by February 1077 or be deposed.

Henry crossed the Alps in midwinter — by the chronicle accounts, with great difficulty, his small entourage sliding down icy mountain passes on hides and ropes — and arrived at the castle of Canossa, where Gregory was staying as the guest of Countess Matilda of Tuscany, in late January 1077.
The chronicles say Henry stood barefoot in the snow, wearing only a hair shirt, for three days outside the castle gate before Gregory would receive him.
On the fourth day, Gregory accepted his penance and lifted the excommunication.
Henry kissed the pope's ring and returned to Germany.
In the short term, Canossa was a victory for Gregory.
The pope had brought an emperor to his knees.

In the medium term, it was a victory for Henry — by removing the excommunication, Gregory had taken away the legal basis for Henry's deposition, and Henry went back to Germany and quickly defeated the rebellious barons.
In the long term, the question of who had actually won would not be settled for another fifty years.
The personal struggle continued.
Gregory excommunicated Henry again in 1080.

Henry invaded Italy, captured Rome in 1084, installed an antipope (Clement III), and forced Gregory to flee south to Salerno, where Gregory died in 1085 reportedly muttering, "I have loved justice and hated iniquity, therefore I die in exile." Henry's descendants kept fighting his successors.

The contest finally ended with the Concordat of Worms in September 1122, signed between Pope Calixtus II and Henry's son Henry V, which compromised the question by separating the spiritual investiture (the ring and staff, by the pope) from the temporal investiture (the lands and office, by the emperor).
Bishops would be elected by their cathedral chapters under both papal and royal supervision.
It was a compromise.
But the compromise was on the new ground that Gregory had cleared.

The Church now genuinely was a power independent of the secular state, with its own legal system (canon law), its own judicial procedures (the church courts), its own hierarchy answerable only to itself, and its own financial system.
The Investiture Controversy did not put the pope above the king in any practical sense.
It put the pope alongside the king, as a parallel sovereign in a shared territory.

This dual sovereignty — two parallel power structures with overlapping jurisdictions — is one of the structural inventions of the High Middle Ages and one of the things that distinguishes the European political tradition from most of its contemporaries.
The structural parallel worth pausing on is the Great Schism of 1054, which had happened twenty-one years before the Investiture Controversy began, on the eastern side of the Christian world.

On July 16, 1054, Cardinal Humbert, a papal legate visiting Constantinople, walked into the Hagia Sophia during the liturgy and laid on the altar a bull of excommunication against the Patriarch Michael Cerularius.
The patriarch returned the favor a few days later.

It was, on the surface, a procedural quarrel about doctrinal differences (the use of unleavened bread in the Eucharist, the filioque clause in the Nicene Creed, papal supremacy) that had been simmering for centuries.
Neither side considered it permanent at the time.
Mutual excommunications had happened before and been retracted.
This one was not retracted.

The 1054 split between the Roman Catholic Church in the Latin West and the Eastern Orthodox Church in the Greek-speaking east hardened over the following decades and centuries, deepened by the linguistic and cultural drift between Latin Europe and the Byzantine world (Byzantine Empire Ch 7), the Crusader sack of Constantinople in 1204 (Chapter 3), and the failure of every subsequent attempt at reunion.
As of 2026, the Catholic and Orthodox churches are still formally in schism, though the mutual 1054 excommunications were lifted by Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras in 1965.

The 1054 schism and the 1075–1122 Investiture Controversy were related episodes in the same larger story — the western Church becoming a more aggressive, centralized, jurisdictionally ambitious institution under the reform popes.
The same Cardinal Humbert who delivered the excommunication at Hagia Sophia in 1054 was a Cluniac reformer who had drafted some of the early reform decrees.
The reform that produced the Investiture Controversy and the reform that produced the schism with the East were the same reform.
The Church that the High Middle Ages would build — disciplined, centralized, jurisdictionally aggressive — was being assembled at exactly this moment.

Cross-civ check: while Gregory VII and Henry IV were fighting over investiture, the Seljuk Turks had just defeated the Byzantines at Manzikert in 1071 (Byzantine Empire Ch 7), opening Anatolia to Turkic settlement and triggering the Byzantine appeals for western military help that would shortly become the First Crusade.
In al-Andalus, the Cordoban caliphate had just collapsed (1031) and Christian armies were beginning the long advance south (Toledo would fall in 1085).
In China, the Song dynasty was at its eleventh-century peak, with Wang Anshi pushing through the most ambitious reform program in pre-modern Chinese history (Tang-Song China Ch 6).
In India, the Chola navy was at the height of its Bay of Bengal expansion (Medieval India Ch 5).
The 1070s and 1080s are an unusually busy decade for institutional restructuring across Eurasia, and the European share of it is the Investiture Controversy.
The longer-term consequence was the medieval papacy as a continuous political institution.

By 1100 the popes had: Their own electoral process (cardinals, since 1059) Their own legal system (canon law, codified by Gratian's Decretum around 1140) Their own court system (the diocesan courts and ultimately the papal curia) Their own diplomatic corps (the legates) Their own international taxation system (the tithe, Peter's Pence, and the various papal levies) Their own ideological program (the reform movement) And their own demonstrated willingness to confront kings and emperors The thirteenth-century popes (Chapter 8) would push this institutional power further than Gregory had imagined possible.

Innocent III (1198–1216) would place England under interdict to bring King John to heel, depose the Holy Roman Emperor Otto IV, call the Fourth Crusade and the Albigensian Crusade, approve the Franciscans and Dominicans, and preside over the Fourth Lateran Council that codified medieval Catholic doctrine and discipline for the next three centuries.
By 1216 the medieval papacy was the most institutionally developed political organization in Latin Europe.
It was also still the Church.
This is one of the things that makes the medieval papacy genuinely strange to modern eyes.

It was simultaneously a religious institution claiming to be the body of Christ on earth, and a political-administrative apparatus collecting taxes from England to Sicily and adjudicating property disputes between Sienese banking houses.
The medieval Church's spiritual mission and its earthly machinery never separated.
They could not separate, because the institutional theory of medieval Christendom assumed that they were the same thing.
Gregory VII's reform had been about making the spiritual mission control the earthly machinery rather than the other way around.
By 1216 the popes had largely won that fight.
By 1300 they had begun to lose it again to the rising centralized monarchies of France and England, in ways the Late Medieval volume picks up.

The Investiture Controversy's most important legacy was therefore not a specific outcome but a structural principle: that there are two parallel sovereignties in Christian Europe, the spiritual and the temporal, neither of which is reducible to the other.
This is not the modern doctrine of separation of church and state — neither side in 1077 would have recognized that idea, and both would have rejected it.
But it is the medieval foundation on which the eventual modern doctrine could be built.
The dual sovereignty of pope and emperor, fought over for fifty years and compromised at Worms in 1122, is one of the structural inheritances of the modern western political tradition.
The next chapter turns to the most spectacular thing the reformed papacy did with its new authority: it called Christendom to war.

chapters.title: The Crusades
sentences: On November 27, 1095, Pope Urban II delivered a sermon in an open field outside the town of Clermont (klair-MOH(N), in central France) that called the Christian knights of western Europe to march two thousand five hundred miles overland to the Holy Land and recover Jerusalem from Muslim rule.
Within a year, tens of thousands of people — peasants as well as knights, including women, children, and the elderly — had set out east.
Within four years, an army of European knights had captured Jerusalem and slaughtered most of its Muslim and Jewish inhabitants.

Within two centuries, four Crusader states had been established and largely lost again, the eastern Christian capital at Constantinople had been sacked by western Christian crusaders (1204), and the entire enterprise had ended with the fall of the last Crusader stronghold at Acre in 1291.
The Crusades are one of the most familiar episodes in medieval history and one of the most thoroughly mythologized.

This chapter tries to do a few things at once: explain why the Crusades happened, narrate what actually happened, address some of the most persistent myths, and assess what the Crusades did and did not accomplish.
Several long-term developments converged at Clermont in 1095.
The first was the Seljuk shock.

In 1071 a Seljuk Turkish army under Sultan Alp Arslan had destroyed the Byzantine field army at the Battle of Manzikert (Byzantine Empire Ch 7), capturing Emperor Romanos IV and opening the Anatolian plateau to Turkic settlement.
Within a decade the Seljuks had pushed almost to the walls of Constantinople.

The Byzantines had been losing territory for four hundred years, but Manzikert was a different kind of loss — the Anatolian heartland that had supplied half the empire's tax revenue and most of its soldiers was gone in a single campaign season.
The second was the changing political situation in the Levant.
The Seljuks had also taken Jerusalem in 1073 from the Fatimid caliphate of Egypt (Islamic Golden Age Ch 6 covers the Fatimid context).

Christian pilgrims to the Holy Land — a stream that had been steady through the early Middle Ages, occasionally tolerated and occasionally harassed under successive Muslim rulers — found the Seljuks less hospitable than the Fatimids had been.
Stories of mistreatment of pilgrims circulated in western Europe in the 1080s and 1090s.
Some of the stories were exaggerated.
The general impression was not.
The third was the Byzantine appeal for help.
Emperor Alexios I Komnenos sent ambassadors to Pope Urban II in 1095 asking for western military assistance against the Seljuks.
Alexios was hoping for a few thousand mercenary knights to bolster the Byzantine army.
He got something quite different.
The fourth was the reformed papacy of the previous chapter, looking for ways to channel the violent energies of the Frankish warrior aristocracy into something more useful than fighting each other.
The Peace of God and Truce of God movements had been trying since the late tenth century to limit aristocratic violence by declaring various people, places, and days off-limits for warfare.
A military expedition to the Holy Land — directed against non-Christians, sanctioned by the pope, framed as a pilgrimage with spiritual rewards — was the logical next step.

The sermon at Clermont survives in five different versions written by different chroniclers years later, none of them verbatim, and historians have argued for centuries about what Urban actually said.

All five versions agree on the basic structure: Urban described the suffering of eastern Christians under Seljuk rule, called the Frankish knights to undertake a military pilgrimage to liberate Jerusalem, and promised that participants would receive remission of sins for their journey.
The crowd reportedly responded with shouts of Deus vult — "God wills it" — that became the slogan of the First Crusade.
The response far exceeded anything Urban had planned for.
He had expected to send a knightly army of several thousand under disciplined noble leadership.
What he got was a vast popular movement.

The first wave was the People's Crusade of spring 1096 — an unauthorized expedition of perhaps 40,000 mostly unarmed peasants and townsfolk, including significant numbers of women, children, and the elderly, led by a charismatic preacher called Peter the Hermit and an impoverished knight named Walter Sans Avoir (san-zah-VWAR — "Walter the Penniless").
They marched east through Germany and the Balkans toward Constantinople, sustaining themselves by foraging and by extorting supplies from the towns they passed through.
Most never reached the Holy Land.
A large fraction died of disease, hunger, or fighting along the way.

The remnant that arrived at Constantinople in summer 1096 was hustled across the Bosporus by the appalled Byzantine emperor and was almost entirely massacred by Seljuk Turks at Civetot in October 1096.
The People's Crusade also produced the first significant act of organized antisemitic violence in medieval Europe.

As bands of crusaders moved through the Rhineland in May, June, and July 1096, mobs attacked the Jewish communities of Speyer, Worms, Mainz, Cologne, Trier, and other cities, killing several thousand people and destroying centuries-old communities.
Some of the killings were carried out by crusader bands; others by local townspeople using the crusade as a pretext.
The bishops of several Rhineland cities tried to protect their Jewish populations and were mostly unable to.

The Rhineland massacres of 1096 are the largest single episode of antisemitic violence in Europe before the Black Death pogroms of 1348–1349 (Late Medieval Europe Ch 4) and they established a pattern — crusade preaching producing local antisemitic violence — that would recur on every subsequent crusade.
The official First Crusade set out in autumn 1096, several months after the People's Crusade had largely already destroyed itself.

Four major contingents marched separately: Godfrey of Bouillon with the Lotharingians, Raymond of Toulouse with the Provençals, Bohemond of Taranto with the Norman-Sicilians, and Robert of Normandy with the Anglo-Normans.

They converged on Constantinople in late 1096 and early 1097, where the alarmed Emperor Alexios extracted oaths from the leaders to return any reconquered former Byzantine territory before ferrying them across the Bosporus.
The march south through Anatolia was brutal — the summer of 1097 saw thousands die of heat and thirst — but the First Crusade reached Antioch in October 1097 and besieged it for eight months.

Inside Antioch the situation was desperate; outside, the crusaders ran short of food, with chronicle accounts describing them eating their horses, dogs, and (in some accounts) the corpses of dead Muslims after battle.
The city finally fell in June 1098 by treachery — a Christian merchant inside the walls let a small party in by night, who opened a gate.
Two days later a Turkish relief army under Kerbogha of Mosul arrived and besieged the besiegers.

The crusaders, starving and outnumbered, were rescued (according to crusader chroniclers) by the discovery of the Holy Lance — the spear that had pierced Christ's side at the Crucifixion — buried under the floor of Antioch's cathedral.
The discovery, almost certainly orchestrated by the visionary Peter Bartholomew, gave the crusaders enough morale to sortie out and defeat Kerbogha's army on June 28, 1098.
Antioch was kept by Bohemond as the Principality of Antioch, in violation of his oath to Alexios.
The breach of trust would poison Byzantine-Crusader relations for the next two centuries.
The march south through Syria took a year.
Jerusalem was finally besieged in June 1099.
The first assault failed.
The crusaders built two siege towers from timber stripped from the surrounding hills, and on July 15, 1099, they breached the walls in two places and entered the city.

Over the next two days they slaughtered most of the Muslim and Jewish inhabitants — Muslims who had taken refuge on the roof of the al-Aqsa mosque, Jews who had gathered in the main synagogue (which the crusaders set on fire).
Western chroniclers boasted that the blood ran ankle-deep in the streets; Muslim sources quoted similar figures.
Modern estimates of the death toll run from 3,000 to 30,000.
The massacre at Jerusalem in July 1099 is one of the most notorious atrocities of the High Middle Ages.

It is also somewhat anomalous — most crusader sieges did not end this way, because most cities surrendered on terms before the wall was breached, and once a wall was breached, medieval law of war considered the inhabitants forfeit.
The massacre would be remembered by later Muslim chroniclers (notably Ibn al-Athir in the early thirteenth century) as the founding act of the Crusader presence in the Levant.
It would be contrasted, repeatedly, with the very different terms on which Saladin would retake the same city eighty-eight years later.
The First Crusade established the four Crusader states in the Levant: the Kingdom of Jerusalem, the Principality of Antioch, the County of Edessa, and the County of Tripoli.

These were Christian states ruled by a French-speaking aristocracy of crusader veterans and their descendants, with Italian merchant communities (Venice, Genoa, Pisa) running the port cities and the maritime trade, and a much larger native population — Muslim, Christian, and Jewish — providing the labor and most of the inhabitants.
They survived in increasingly reduced form for nearly two centuries.
The Crusader states are sometimes presented in popular accounts as a kind of medieval European colonial project.
The comparison is partial.
They were ruled by European crusader veterans, they were religiously legitimized by the Roman Church, and they were demographically dominated by indigenous populations.
But they were also genuinely indigenous in some ways.
The crusader nobility intermarried with local Christian and even Muslim families.
They adopted Levantine architecture, food, dress, and some social customs.

Visiting western European pilgrims in the late twelfth century were sometimes appalled at how "Easternized" the Outremer (oo-truh-MAIR — French for "overseas," the standard medieval name for the Crusader states) French had become.

The crusader states were neither pure transplants nor pure indigenous polities; they were something hybrid, like the Norman kingdom in Sicily (with which they shared many characteristics) but more politically precarious because of the constant Muslim military pressure from the surrounding Levantine and Egyptian states.
The crusades did not end with the First.
The Second Crusade (1147–1149) was launched after the County of Edessa fell to the Muslims in 1144.
It was preached across Europe by Bernard of Clairvaux (Chapter 5) — the most influential preacher of his generation — and led by Louis VII of France and Conrad III of Germany.
It collapsed at the disastrous siege of Damascus in July 1148, when an ill-advised four-day attack on the city's walls failed and the crusader army withdrew in chaos.
The failure damaged crusader prestige in the Holy Land, Bernard's reputation in Europe, and the credibility of the crusading idea.
Bernard spent the rest of his life writing apologies for what had gone wrong.

The Third Crusade (1189–1192) was triggered by the most consequential single event in twelfth-century crusader history — the recapture of Jerusalem by Saladin (sah-lah-DEEN, properly Salah al-Din ibn Ayyub, the Kurdish Muslim general who had unified Egypt and Syria under his Ayyubid dynasty).

On July 4, 1187, Saladin's army destroyed the assembled crusader field army at the Horns of Hattin in Galilee — luring the heavily armored crusader force across waterless terrain in summer heat, then surrounding and methodically destroying them.
On October 2, 1187, Jerusalem surrendered to Saladin after a brief siege.
Saladin's treatment of conquered Jerusalem was conspicuously different from the crusaders' treatment of conquered Jerusalem in 1099.
Christians who could ransom themselves were permitted to leave with their property; those who could not were enslaved, but Saladin and his brother al-Adil paid the ransoms of thousands themselves.
The Holy Sepulchre church was preserved, with Christian access negotiated.

The contrast — Christian crusaders massacring Muslims and Jews in 1099 versus Muslim Saladin protecting Christians in 1187 — was widely commented on at the time and is one of the reasons Saladin became one of the very few non-Christian figures to be admired in medieval European literature, including in Dante's Divine Comedy.

The fall of Jerusalem triggered the Third Crusade under three of the most famous monarchs of the era: Frederick Barbarossa of the Holy Roman Empire, Philip II Augustus of France, and Richard the Lionheart of England.
Frederick drowned crossing the Saleph river in Anatolia in June 1190 and his German army largely went home.
Philip and Richard reached the Levant by sea in 1191.
Together they recaptured Acre after a two-year siege.
Then Philip went home, leaving Richard to fight Saladin alone for another year.

Richard won the Battle of Arsuf in September 1191 and twice came within sight of Jerusalem but never tried to retake the city — knowing that even if he could capture it, he would not have the manpower to hold it after the bulk of the crusader army went home.
The Treaty of Jaffa in September 1192 left Jerusalem in Saladin's hands while granting Christian pilgrims access to the city.
It was a draw, on terms that left the Crusader states reduced but viable.
Saladin died the next year, in March 1193, at age fifty-six.

Richard was captured on the way home by Duke Leopold of Austria (whom he had insulted at Acre), held for ransom by Henry VI of the Holy Roman Empire, and finally freed in 1194 after the English crown paid a ransom equal to roughly two years' English royal revenue.
The Fourth Crusade (1202–1204) is the worst of them.
The plan, agreed in 1201, was an attack on Egypt — the strategic move that would split the Ayyubid sultanate and create conditions for retaking Jerusalem.
Pope Innocent III approved.
The crusader army gathered at Venice in 1202 to be ferried east.
The Venetians, who had built an enormous fleet for the expedition at significant expense, expected to be paid the contracted price in full.
The crusader army that arrived was much smaller than projected and could not pay the bill.

The Doge of Venice, Enrico Dandolo — at this point in his eighties and famously blind — proposed a deal: the crusaders could work off their debt by helping Venice recapture the rebellious Adriatic city of Zara from the king of Hungary (a Catholic Christian) on the way east.
The crusaders did so in November 1202, sacking the Christian city.
Pope Innocent III excommunicated the entire expedition.
They proceeded anyway.
At Zara they were met by ambassadors of Alexios IV Angelos, the son of the deposed Byzantine emperor Isaac II, who proposed an even more lucrative side trip.

If the crusaders would help him take Constantinople and put him on the Byzantine throne, he would pay the crusaders' Venetian debt, fund the rest of their expedition to Egypt, place the Byzantine Church under Roman authority, and provide ten thousand Byzantine troops for the crusade.
The crusaders accepted.
The crusader fleet arrived at Constantinople in summer 1203, took the city in July with limited fighting, installed Alexios IV as co-emperor with his father Isaac II, and waited to be paid.
Alexios IV could not pay — the Byzantine treasury was nearly empty, the population hated him as a Latin puppet, and the promised Church union enraged the Orthodox clergy.
He was overthrown and killed in late January 1204 by Alexios V Doukas Mourtzouphlos.
The crusaders, denied their payment and now openly at war with the new Byzantine government, decided to take Constantinople for themselves.
They sacked the city on April 13, 1204.
The sack was the worst urban disaster in Constantinople's history — worse than anything the Persians, the Arabs, the Bulgarians, or the Russians had ever managed.
The crusader army looted the city for three days, methodically.
They stripped the great churches of their altar plate.
They stole the bronze horses from the Hippodrome (which still stand in front of the Basilica of San Marco in Venice).
They smashed the imperial tombs and scattered the bones.
The city's libraries, with their irreplaceable Greek classical manuscripts, were burned or looted for parchment.
Nuns were raped in the convents.
The patriarchal throne in the Hagia Sophia was occupied by a drunken prostitute who sang bawdy songs from it.

The crusaders established the Latin Empire of Constantinople that lasted until 1261, when the Byzantine successor state at Nicaea retook the city under Michael VIII Palaiologos (Byzantine Empire Ch 9).

The Byzantine Empire was permanently broken — when Constantinople was recovered in 1261 it was a smaller, poorer, less populous shadow of the city that had fallen in 1204, and the empire never recovered its former territory or military strength.
The Fourth Crusade is one of the great catastrophes of European medieval history.

Pope Innocent III, who had explicitly forbidden the attack, had no power to stop it; when he learned of the sack he reportedly wept, then conditionally approved the Latin Empire because the schism with the Greek Church was, in his view, now provably the Greeks' fault for resisting the crusader-installed Latin Patriarch.
The lasting consequence was the permanent embittering of the Greek-Catholic schism.
Greeks who might have considered the 1054 schism (Chapter 2) a procedural quarrel could not consider 1204 anything but a devastation by the Latin Church.
The schism's emotional foundation in popular memory was set by the sack, not by the doctrinal disputes that had supposedly caused it.
To this day, eight centuries later, the 1204 sack is still cited in Orthodox-Catholic dialogue as the wound that has not healed.
A few words about the popular myths.

The Children's Crusade of 1212 — the legendary expedition of thousands of children who supposedly set out for Jerusalem and were sold into slavery by treacherous merchants — is largely a later embroidery.

Two unrelated movements in 1212, a French one led by a shepherd boy named Stephen of Cloyes who marched to Saint-Denis, and a German one led by a boy named Nicholas of Cologne who led a procession south toward the Mediterranean, were merged in fifteenth-century chronicles into the legend.
Modern historians regard the original participants as mostly poor adolescents and unemployed adults from the wandering bands of the early thirteenth century.
The slavery story is largely later invention.
The legend persisted because it fit the medieval and post-medieval imagination of childhood as innocent and crusading as corrupted.

The Crusades as a "civilizing mission" — the modern claim, sometimes asserted on both political wings, that the Crusades represented an effort to civilize a barbaric Muslim world — is essentially backward.

In 1095, the Islamic civilization that the Crusaders confronted in the Levant was wealthier, more urbanized, more literate, and in most measurable cultural respects more sophisticated than the Latin Europe they came from.
Damascus was a larger city than any in northern Europe.
Cordoba and Cairo had public hospitals, public lighting, public baths, paved streets, and pharmacies; Paris in 1100 did not.

Arabic was the language of Aristotle and Galen and Euclid; Latin was a much smaller intellectual world that had only just begun, through the Toledo translations (Chapter 5), to recover what Arabic readers had had for three hundred years.
The cultural traffic between the Crusader states and the surrounding Muslim world ran overwhelmingly Islamic-to-European, not the other way around.
The crusaders learned Arabic medical practice, Levantine cuisine, irrigation techniques, glassmaking, sugar production, and much else, and brought a great deal of it back to western Europe.
They taught the Muslim world relatively little.
The Inquisition, often imagined as a feature of the crusader era, was actually only beginning at the very end of this period.

Pope Gregory IX issued the bull Excommunicamus in 1231 establishing the medieval Inquisition — papal inquisitors, mostly Dominicans, deployed to hunt down surviving Cathars and Waldensians in southern France and northern Italy.
This is the institutional ancestor of the much later Spanish and Roman Inquisitions of the early modern period.

The medieval Inquisition was smaller, more legally constrained, and less catastrophically violent than its later descendants — but it was a real and growing apparatus by the late thirteenth century, and the Albigensian Crusade of 1209–1229 had already inflicted brutal religious violence on the Cathar populations of Languedoc.
What did the Crusades actually accomplish?
Militarily: very little, in the long run.

The Crusader states established by the First Crusade survived for less than two centuries; the last stronghold at Acre fell to the Mamluks on May 18, 1291, ending the European military presence in the Levant for six hundred years.
None of the four cities the First Crusade captured — Jerusalem, Antioch, Edessa, Tripoli — has been continuously in Christian hands since.
Politically: the Crusades reinforced the medieval papacy's claim to lead Christendom but also exposed its limits.
The pope could call a crusade; he could not control what the crusade did once it left.
The Fourth Crusade was the dramatic demonstration of the limit.
The popes kept calling crusades into the late thirteenth century and beyond, but the response shrank steadily.
Economically: the Crusades vastly expanded the Italian maritime cities — Venice, Genoa, Pisa — that financed and supplied the expeditions and that established trading colonies in the Crusader ports.
The commercial revolution of Chapter 4 has the Crusades as one of its triggers.
The wealth flowing back to western Europe from Levantine trade, with sugar, spices, silk, and dyestuffs at the center, transformed the European luxury economy.
Culturally: the Crusades intensified European contact with the eastern Mediterranean and accelerated the cultural transfer that the Toledo translations had begun.

New foods, new technologies, new literary themes (the romance of the East, the figure of Saladin), new architectural styles, new diseases, and a much larger geographic imagination flowed back to Europe with returning crusaders and their followers.

Religiously: the Crusades produced the permanent embitterment of European Christian–Jewish relations through the Rhineland massacres and their successors; the permanent embitterment of Catholic-Orthodox relations through 1204; and a long persistence of holy-war thinking in European Christianity that would resurface periodically into the early modern period.
Demographically: the Crusades killed enormous numbers of people, on both sides, including very large numbers of crusader participants who never returned.
The total death toll across all the major crusades cannot be reliably estimated; figures of one to five million dead across the two-century arc have been argued.
Morally: the Crusades have been condemned and defended in every century since they ended, and they will be condemned and defended in every century to come.

The honest summary, from this distance, is that they were a religiously motivated military enterprise that achieved their stated short-term goal (reaching Jerusalem) at enormous cost, did not achieve their long-term goal (holding Jerusalem), inflicted horrendous violence on Muslim, Jewish, and Eastern Christian populations along the way, and left the world they encountered substantially less changed than they themselves were changed by encountering it.
The next chapter follows the money — the commercial revolution that the Crusades helped accelerate.

chapters.title: The Commercial Revolution
sentences: While the warriors of Chapter 3 were marching east, the merchants of Chapter 4 were quietly building something more permanent.
Between roughly 1100 and 1300, western Europe shifted from a barter-and-land economy run by lords and manors to a money economy run by merchants and banks.
The Italians invented the bill of exchange.
The Florentines invented double-entry bookkeeping.
The Hanseatic Germans built the first international free-trade zone.
The Champagne fairs in northern France became the central exchange between Mediterranean and Baltic Europe.

By 1300, a Florentine banker could issue a credit instrument in his Florence office, have it cashed in London or Bruges or Acre weeks later, and earn a profit on the currency conversion that technically did not violate the canon law prohibition on usury.
This is one of the most consequential structural inventions of the High Middle Ages.

The commercial institutions developed between 1100 and 1300 — international banking, bills of exchange, double-entry bookkeeping, joint-stock investment, international trade fairs, chartered merchant cities, a body of merchant law — are the direct ancestors of the financial system that runs the world in 2026.
Most of them were invented in Italy.
The setting was the recovery of long-distance trade, which had largely collapsed in western Europe with the Roman Empire and only began to revive in earnest after 1000.
The trade flowed along three main axes.
The first was the Mediterranean axis between the Italian maritime cities and the Levant, North Africa, and Byzantium.
Venice and Genoa were the dominant players, with Pisa important until its naval defeat by Genoa at Meloria in 1284.

The Italian cities shipped European silver, woolen cloth, timber, and slaves east; they brought back silk, spices, sugar, dyestuffs, alum, and the exotic luxury goods that the European aristocracy increasingly wanted.
The Crusader states (Chapter 3) gave the Italian merchants permanent ports and trading colonies in the Levant.

The Fourth Crusade (1204) gave Venice an outright commercial empire in the eastern Mediterranean — a network of fortified bases on the islands of Crete, Negroponte (Euboea), and the Greek mainland that Venice held for the next four centuries.
The second was the North Sea–Baltic axis dominated by the German Hanseatic League.

The Hanse merchants traded Russian furs, Baltic amber, Polish grain, Norwegian dried fish, English wool, Flemish cloth, and Rhenish wine across the entire northern European coast from Novgorod to London.

Founded informally in the twelfth century and formalized by the 1241 mutual defense treaty between Lübeck and Hamburg, the Hanseatic League grew over the next century into a self-governing trading network of more than a hundred north German and Baltic cities, with major foreign trading posts (the Kontore) at Bergen, London, Bruges, and Novgorod.

At its peak in the fourteenth century the Hanse fielded its own navy, ran its own coinage, and could blockade or wage war against entire kingdoms (it forced the king of Denmark to accept humiliating commercial terms in 1370).
The third was the continental land-trade axis between the two, running through France and Germany.
The principal exchange point was the Champagne fairs.

The Champagne fairs were six great trade fairs held in rotation in the towns of Lagny, Bar-sur-Aube, Provins (proh-VAN), and Troyes (TWAH) in the Champagne region of northern France between roughly 1150 and 1300.
Each fair lasted six to eight weeks.
The cycle ran continuously around the year.

At any given time, there was a major Champagne fair in progress somewhere in northern France, attended by Italian merchants from Florence and Venice, Flemish merchants from Bruges and Ghent, German merchants from Cologne, English wool merchants, and Iberian merchants from Barcelona and Valencia.
The Champagne fairs did several things at once.
They were the principal commercial meeting point of medieval Europe, where Italian merchants exchanged Mediterranean goods for Flemish cloth and northern raw materials.

They were the principal financial settlement point — the last week of each fair was reserved for clearing accounts, with merchants who owed each other money settling their balances by transferring credits, often with no actual coin changing hands.

They were the principal site for the development of European commercial law: the lex mercatoria (Latin for "law merchant"), a body of customary commercial principles enforced by the fair courts, became the foundation of European commercial law and the ancestor of much of modern contract law.

The Champagne fairs also nurtured a sustained relationship between Italy and northern France that exposed Italian merchants to the institutional habits of the Flemish and German trading cities, and exposed northern merchants to the financial instruments the Italians had been developing.
The technology transfer ran both ways and was continuous for a century and a half.

The fairs declined after 1300 as the Italian merchants increasingly bypassed them — first by sailing directly from Italy to Bruges and London via the Strait of Gibraltar after 1277 (the Genoese galley pioneer voyage that opened the route around Iberia), and later by relocating their main northern operations to Bruges and then Antwerp.
By 1400 the Champagne fairs were a shadow of what they had been.
By 1500 they were a memory.
The Italian banking innovations of the thirteenth century are worth pausing on because they shaped the financial architecture of the entire later western world.
Start with bills of exchange.
The bill of exchange is a written order by which a merchant deposits money with a banker in one city and has it paid out in another currency in a different city.

A Florentine wool merchant could deposit 100 florins in his Florence bank, receive a bill payable in London in pounds sterling, hand-carry the bill to London, present it at the Florence bank's London office, and collect his pounds.
This is a money-transfer instrument like a modern wire transfer.

It also let the bank earn interest on the time-and-currency conversion in a way that technically did not constitute usury — the canon-law prohibition on lending at interest that limited Christian financial activity throughout the medieval period.
This last point matters.
The medieval Catholic Church considered any loan at interest a form of theft (you were extracting payment for the use of money, which the Church held to be barren of natural increase).

Jewish moneylenders, who were not bound by canon law, supplied much of the small-scale lending market in northern Europe — and were repeatedly persecuted, robbed, and expelled when their royal protectors decided their debts were too inconvenient.
Christian bankers had to find ways around the usury ban.
The bill of exchange was one of the great workarounds.
The interest income was disguised as a foreign-exchange profit, which was permissible.
By the late thirteenth century the Italian merchant-bankers had built an entire international financial system on this single innovation.
Next, double-entry bookkeeping.

The systematic recording of every transaction as both a debit in one account and a credit in another — the foundational accounting practice that lets a business track its own financial position in real time — was developed by Italian merchants in the late thirteenth and early fourteenth centuries and codified in 1494 by the Franciscan mathematician Luca Pacioli (loo-kah pah-CHOH-lee) in his Summa de Arithmetica.
Pacioli's exposition is fifteenth-century, but the practice he was describing was thirteenth-century.
Double-entry bookkeeping is the conceptual technology that made modern corporate finance possible.
Next, branch banking.

The great Florentine houses of the High Middle Ages — the Bardi (BAR-dee), the Peruzzi, the Acciaiuoli (ah-chah-YOH-lee), and later the Medici — operated branches in London, Paris, Avignon, Naples, Constantinople, and Cyprus, all coordinated through the Florentine head office.
They handled foreign exchange, deposits, loans, papal tax collection, royal financing, and private investment, all at once.

The Bardi and Peruzzi houses were the principal bankers of King Edward III of England in the early fourteenth century — and were both bankrupted in the 1340s when Edward defaulted on his Hundred Years' War loans, one of the trigger events of the late-medieval Italian banking crisis (Late Medieval Europe Ch 1).

Finally, commercial partnerships — the commenda in Venice and the societas in Florence — that pooled investment from multiple parties for a single trading voyage, with returns distributed proportionally.
These are the medieval ancestors of the joint-stock company.

The cumulative effect of all this was to make Florence and Genoa and Venice the financial capitals of late-medieval Europe and the source of most of the institutional vocabulary the rest of the world would inherit.
The word bank comes from the Italian banca — the bench on which the moneychanger conducted business.
The word bankrupt comes from banca rotta — the broken bench, the public destruction of an insolvent moneychanger's bench in the Florentine market.
Credit is credito — what is believed about a borrower.

Florin, the gold coin first minted in Florence in 1252, became the standard high-value coin of late-medieval Europe and the first European gold coin in regular international circulation since the fall of Rome.
Cross-civ check: the High Medieval European commercial revolution did not invent international banking from nothing.
It learned heavily from the much older and more sophisticated Islamic commercial system.

The Islamic world had been operating long-distance commercial networks since the Abbasid period, with sophisticated financial instruments — the suftaja (a written order for payment in another city, the direct ancestor of the bill of exchange), the hawala (an informal value-transfer system still in use in 2026), the mudaraba (a commercial partnership pooling capital and labor), and an extensive network of merchant communities from Andalusia to China (Islamic Golden Age Ch 8).

The Geniza documents from Cairo's Ben Ezra synagogue, accidentally preserved in a storage chamber for nine centuries and discovered in the 1890s, show eleventh- and twelfth-century Jewish merchants in Cairo conducting international trade with India, Spain, Sicily, and Yemen using exactly the kind of credit instruments and partnership arrangements that Italians would be using two centuries later.
The transmission of Islamic commercial techniques to Italy ran through Sicily, southern Spain, the Crusader states, and the Italian merchant colonies in Alexandria and Tunis.
Italian merchants learned the Islamic financial instruments, modified them to fit Christian canon law, and built them into the European banking system.
The suftaja → bill of exchange translation is well-documented; many of the other innovations follow the same pattern.

In China at the same time, the Song dynasty had pioneered paper money — the first widely circulating government-issued paper currency in human history — with the imperial jiaozi notes from 1024 (Tang-Song China Ch 6).
The Song economy ran on paper currency, deep credit markets, and large-scale state-guaranteed merchant guilds.
Western Europe would not have widely circulating paper money until the eighteenth century.

The Italian banking innovations of the thirteenth century brought western Europe much closer to Song-era Chinese commercial sophistication, but the Chinese had still been doing it earlier and at greater scale.
The High Medieval commercial revolution was therefore not a European leap into uncharted territory.
It was Latin Europe catching up to commercial techniques the Islamic world and China had been using for centuries.

What was distinctive about the European version was the institutional scaffolding — the chartered merchant cities, the lex mercatoria, the professional notarial profession, the banking partnerships organized around extended families — that wrapped around the Islamic-derived financial instruments and made them durably embedded in European urban political life.
A few more cross-currents are worth flagging here.

The Mediterranean trading economy the Italians were building ran on West African gold, channeled north across the Sahara through Berber caravan networks to the North African ports — gold whose source would shortly be the rising Mali Empire under Sundiata's successors (Mali Empire Ch 1 and Ch 4).
The Italian commercial system that financed the European take-off was therefore physically dependent on a Sub-Saharan African political economy that contemporary European writers barely understood.

Eastward, the Indian Ocean trading system the Italians tapped into through the Mamluk-controlled Red Sea routes already had its own deep institutional architecture: the Chola maritime empire of medieval South India dominated the Bay of Bengal between roughly 985 and 1120 (Medieval India Ch 5), with naval campaigns reaching Sumatra and Sri Lanka and trade networks that wound from East Africa through Yemen and the Malabar coast to Southeast Asia.

By the late thirteenth century, the Pax Mongolica across Eurasia made overland travel from Venice to the Yuan court at Dadu unprecedentedly secure — which is why Marco Polo could make the trip and come back in one piece.
The same Mongol-protected corridors would carry the Black Death plague west out of Central Asia in the 1340s, but that catastrophe is the Late Medieval volume's territory.
A note on the Knights Templar, who deserve their own paragraph in any commercial revolution chapter.

Founded in 1119 by Hugues de Payens to protect pilgrims to Jerusalem, the Knights Templar were a religious-military order — knights who had taken monastic vows of poverty, chastity, and obedience while remaining trained warriors.
They grew rapidly: papal endorsement in 1129, donations of land across western Europe, exemption from local taxation and ecclesiastical jurisdiction.
Within a century they were one of the wealthiest organizations in Latin Christendom, with an international network of preceptories from Ireland to Cyprus.
The Templars also turned out to be excellent bankers.
Their network of preceptories doubled as a network of secure deposit vaults.

A pilgrim traveling from Paris to Acre could deposit money at the Paris Temple and withdraw it at the Acre Temple on a Templar credit slip, avoiding the risk of carrying large amounts of coin across Europe.
By the late twelfth century the French royal treasury was being kept in the Paris Temple.
Several French kings used the Templars as their personal financiers.
The Templar banking operation pioneered some of the same instruments — deposits, transfers, loans — that the Italian houses would soon be doing on a larger scale.
The Templars met a famously bad end.
King Philip IV of France, deep in debt to them and resenting their independence, arrested every Templar in France in a single day on October 13, 1307, on charges of heresy, sodomy, and idolatry.
Most confessed under torture.
Philip pressured Pope Clement V to dissolve the Order, which Clement did at the Council of Vienne in 1312.
The last Grand Master, Jacques de Molay, was burned at the stake in Paris on March 18, 1314.

The Templars' lands were transferred to the Knights Hospitaller (their parallel order, founded around 1099 to operate a hospital for pilgrims), but most of the cash disappeared — almost certainly into Philip's treasury.
The Templar destruction is technically early-fourteenth-century, just outside this volume's window.
But the High Medieval banking apparatus they had built was thirteenth-century, and the precedent of using a religious organization as a transnational financial network outlived them.
The commercial revolution had social consequences that ran beyond the merchant class.
The rise of the urban economy gave serfs (Chapter 1) a way out of the manor, and the cumulative drain on rural labor through the High Middle Ages helped erode serfdom across western Europe.

By 1300, serfdom had largely disappeared from Italy and was visibly weakening in France and England. (Eastern Europe followed a different trajectory — Polish, Hungarian, and Russian serfdom would actually intensify in the late medieval and early modern centuries, as the eastern European nobility tightened control over peasants who were increasingly producing grain for the western market.
The "second serfdom" of eastern Europe is one of the most striking divergences in late-medieval continental development.) The commercial revolution also produced new conceptual problems.

If a merchant could become rich without owning land, what was his place in the medieval social order, which had been structured around the three estates of those who fight (the warrior nobility), those who pray (the clergy), and those who work (the peasantry)?

The answer, which the late medieval centuries spent working out, was the rise of a fourth estate — the bourgeoisie, the chartered townsmen, the merchants and artisans and bankers and lawyers and notaries and clerks.

By 1300 this fourth estate was numerous enough, wealthy enough, and politically organized enough to demand a place in the new representative assemblies (Chapter 8) that were beginning to appear across western Europe.
The commercial revolution and the political constitutionalism of the thirteenth century were the same revolution, viewed from two different angles.
The next chapter turns to the mind.

chapters.title: The Twelfth-Century Renaissance
sentences: In 1100, an educated cleric in Paris had access to perhaps a few dozen books of classical Latin literature, no Greek philosophy except what had survived in Boethius and a few late-Roman handbooks, no Arabic science, no Roman law in any systematic form, no medical treatises beyond a thin surviving Latin tradition, and a body of Christian theology that had been worked over for centuries but had not had a serious infusion of new material since Augustine in the fifth century.

By 1200, that same Parisian cleric had access to the complete works of Aristotle in Latin translation, the major works of Plato, Euclid's Elements in full, Ptolemy's Almagest, the medical writings of Galen and Hippocrates, the philosophical works of the great Islamic synthesizers Avicenna and Averroes, the great Jewish philosopher Maimonides, the complete Roman law of Justinian's Corpus Juris Civilis, and a vastly expanded Christian theological literature including the systematic theology of Peter Lombard's Sentences, the systematic canon law of Gratian's Decretum, the first European logical treatises since antiquity, and the first vernacular literature in Provençal, Old French, German, and Italian.

This is the twelfth-century Renaissance — the recovery of the classical and Islamic learning that had been lost or out of reach for the preceding seven centuries, and the explosion of original European thought that the recovery enabled.
It was the most consequential intellectual transformation in European history before the printing press.

The phrase "twelfth-century Renaissance" was coined by the American medievalist Charles Homer Haskins in 1927 to insist that the high-medieval centuries deserved the same honorific that historians had previously reserved for the fifteenth-century Italian Renaissance.
The phrase has stuck.
Modern scholars sometimes prefer to talk about the "long twelfth century" running from roughly 1075 to 1225, but the basic claim is unchanged.
Something significant happened to European intellectual life between Anselm and Aquinas, and most of it happened in the twelfth century.
The key mechanism was translation.
When the western Roman Empire collapsed in the fifth century, knowledge of Greek was largely lost in the Latin West.

The Greek-speaking eastern Empire continued to read its own literature, and the Islamic world that conquered most of the eastern Mediterranean in the seventh and eighth centuries (Islamic Golden Age Ch 1) inherited and translated the Greek scholarly tradition into Arabic.
By 900, almost the entire surviving corpus of Greek philosophy, mathematics, astronomy, and medicine existed in Arabic translation in the great libraries of Baghdad, Cordoba, Cairo, and Damascus.

The Latin West, meanwhile, had Boethius's partial Latin translations of Aristotle's logical works (the so-called "old logic"), some Cicero, some late-Roman compendiums and encyclopedias, and very little else of Greek thought.
Latin Europeans who wanted to read Aristotle's Metaphysics or Physics or Ethics could not, because no Latin translation existed.
The translation movement that recovered this material happened in three main centers between roughly 1080 and 1200.

The first was Toledo (toh-LAY-doh), the great Visigothic capital of Spain that had been under Muslim rule since the early eighth century and had been recaptured by the Christian king Alfonso VI of León-Castile on May 25, 1085.

Toledo's surviving Arabic libraries, with their accumulated centuries of translation work, became the principal channel through which Aristotle, Greek mathematics, Indian numerals, and the work of Islamic scholars like Avicenna and Averroes were translated into Latin.
The translators were a polyglot mix of Spanish Christians, Mozarabic Christians (Arabic-speaking Christians from al-Andalus), Spanish Jews, and visiting Latin clerics from across Europe.

The most prolific was Gerard of Cremona (chreh-MOH-nah, an Italian who relocated to Toledo around 1145 and stayed until his death in 1187), who produced more than seventy translations including Ptolemy's Almagest (the most influential single text in medieval European astronomy), the medical canon of Avicenna, and Aristotle's Physics and On the Heavens.

The second was Sicily, where the Norman kings (Norman Sicily, founded 1091, see Viking Age Ch 7 for the long Norman context) ruled a multilingual Christian-Muslim-Greek kingdom and patronized translations directly from Greek into Latin without going through Arabic.
The Sicilian translations were technically more accurate (less filtered through intermediate languages) but smaller in volume.
The translation of Plato's Phaedo and Meno into Latin was Sicilian.
Much of Ptolemy's Optics was Sicilian.

The court of Roger II in twelfth-century Palermo was one of the great cultural crossroads of the Mediterranean — Greek bureaucrats, Arab geographers, Norman knights, and Latin clerics all serving the same king.
The third was Antioch in the Crusader states (Chapter 3), where Latin clerics had access to Arabic libraries in the Levant.
Antiochene translations were less systematic than Toledan ones but contributed important scientific and medical material.

The cumulative result of all this translation activity was that by 1200 the Latin West had recovered most of what the Islamic world had inherited from the Greeks, plus a great deal of original Islamic scholarship.
Aristotle was back.
Euclid was back.
Ptolemy was back.
Galen was back.

The medical canon of Ibn Sina (called Avicenna in Latin, ah-vih-SEN-uh) and the philosophical commentaries of Ibn Rushd (called Averroes in Latin, ah-VER-oh-eez) — two of the great Islamic synthesizers who had themselves been working on Aristotle (Islamic Golden Age Ch 4 and Ch 7) — were available in Latin and were being read alongside the classical texts they were commenting on.
This created a problem that would absorb European theology for the next century: how to integrate this newly recovered classical and Islamic thought with Christian theology.
Aristotle's Metaphysics contained claims (the eternity of the world, the unity of the active intellect across humanity) that contradicted Christian doctrine.

Averroes's commentaries on Aristotle were even more troubling, since Averroes had pushed the Aristotelian system in directions (the impersonal nature of intellectual immortality) that were openly incompatible with Christian belief.
The integration project — what to do with Aristotle, how much of him to accept, how to read him compatibly with Christianity — is most of what the next chapter (Chapter 7) on scholasticism is about.
The other great recovery of the twelfth century was Roman law.

Around 1080 a complete manuscript of the Corpus Juris Civilis — the great sixth-century compilation of Roman law produced by Emperor Justinian (Byzantine Empire Ch 2) — was rediscovered in northern Italy, possibly at Pisa or Ravenna.

The Corpus Juris Civilis is enormous: it includes the Digest (a fifty-book compilation of opinions by classical Roman jurists), the Codex (the imperial laws then in force), the Institutes (a textbook), and the Novels (Justinian's own legislation).
Together they represent a thousand years of Roman legal thinking, systematically organized, in usable form.
The Corpus came to Bologna, where the lawyer Irnerius (ihr-NEHR-ee-us) and his successors built a school of legal scholarship around it.
The Bologna jurists treated the Corpus as a complete and internally consistent system that could be reconciled by close reading and dialectical analysis.
They invented the gloss — the marginal commentary on the legal text — and built up over the next century a layered commentary apparatus that became the foundation of European civil law.
The Bologna school produced lawyers who staffed the courts and chanceries of every European kingdom, the papal curia, and the new town governments.
It also produced (Chapter 7) the first university.
The Bologna recovery of Roman law was paralleled by the codification of canon law.

Gratian (an obscure monk about whom almost nothing is known) compiled the Decretum (or Concordia Discordantium Canonum — Concordance of Discordant Canons) around 1140, a systematic compilation of nearly four thousand church-law texts organized by topic, with apparent contradictions resolved by Gratian's own dialectical commentary.
The Decretum became the foundational textbook of canon law for the rest of the Middle Ages and the institutional armature of the medieval Church's legal system.

By 1200, Latin Europe had two parallel and increasingly sophisticated legal traditions — the civil law (Roman, secular) and the canon law (ecclesiastical) — and a professional class of legally trained men staffing both.
This is the legal substrate of the Magna Carta moment in Chapter 8.
The figures of the twelfth-century intellectual world are worth meeting briefly.

Anselm of Canterbury (1033–1109), abbot of Bec in Normandy and then Archbishop of Canterbury, formulated the ontological argument for God's existence in the Proslogion around 1078: God is that than which nothing greater can be conceived; existing in reality is greater than existing only in the understanding; therefore the greatest conceivable being must exist in reality.
The argument is the most influential single piece of medieval philosophy and is still a live question in modern philosophy of religion.
Anselm also wrote Cur Deus Homo (Why God Became Man), the foundational medieval treatise on the theology of the Atonement.
As Archbishop he clashed with William Rufus and Henry I over the same investiture question that had launched the Investiture Controversy in Germany (Chapter 2), and was twice forced into exile.
Peter Abelard (1079–1142) was the most controversial logician of the early twelfth century.

A Breton-born brilliant young teacher who took on his own teachers in Paris and bested them in disputation, Abelard was famous (and notorious) for his confidence, his sharp tongue, and his ability to make logic sing.
He also famously fell in love with the brilliant young Heloise (HEH-loh-eez), the niece of a Paris cathedral canon named Fulbert, in whose household he was tutoring her around 1117.
They had a son.
Heloise's uncle had Abelard castrated by hired men in retaliation.
Abelard withdrew to the abbey of Saint-Denis as a monk; Heloise became a nun.

They corresponded years later from separate monasteries, and their letters became one of the great romantic correspondences in European literature — Heloise's particularly so, with her unflinching meditations on the difference between obligation and desire, between conventional virtue and what she calls the love that survives despite everything.

Abelard's theological treatise Sic et Non (Yes and No) collected 158 contradictory statements from authoritative Christian sources on theological questions and offered no resolutions, on the principle that the reader's own intellectual work in resolving them was the point.
Abelard's dialectical method became the foundation of the scholastic disputation that would dominate the next century's universities.

Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), Cistercian abbot from 1115 and the most influential churchman of his generation, was Abelard's principal antagonist and the most important religious figure of the twelfth century not to wear the papal tiara.
Bernard preached the Second Crusade.
He founded sixty-eight Cistercian monasteries.
He mediated between popes and kings.
He produced sermons and treatises that shaped western mysticism for centuries.
The papacy of his former student Eugene III ran effectively on Bernard's advice.

Bernard's hostility to Abelard's logical theology — to the application of dialectical reason to questions of faith — represented a strand of medieval thought that would lose institutional ground over the next century to the scholastics, but never disappeared.

Hildegard of Bingen (1098–1179), Benedictine abbess of Rupertsberg in the Rhineland, was the most extraordinary intellectual woman of the twelfth century and one of the most extraordinary intellectuals of any gender.

Her works include theological visions (the Scivias, the Liber Vitae Meritorum, and the Liber Divinorum Operum), a treatise on natural medicine (Causae et Curae), a treatise on the medicinal properties of plants and animals (Physica), the morality play Ordo Virtutum, the largest surviving body of medieval music by a single composer (seventy-seven liturgical songs and an oratorio), and a private correspondence with popes, emperors, and Bernard of Clairvaux.
She invented her own language (the Lingua Ignota) with over a thousand words and an alphabet.
She advised four popes and wrote sharply to the German emperor Frederick Barbarossa when she disapproved of his church policy.

She is one of the small set of medieval intellectuals whose authority — institutional and personal — actually transcended the gender constraints of the period; she was widely regarded in her lifetime as a saint, was read continuously through the late Middle Ages, and was finally formally canonized in 2012 and named a Doctor of the Church.

The new monastic movements of the twelfth century — most importantly the Cistercian Order, founded in 1098 at the abbey of Cîteaux (see-TOH) in Burgundy by reformers seeking a stricter return to the Rule of Saint Benedict — provided much of the institutional support for the intellectual revolution.
The Cistercians built sixty-eight monasteries in Bernard's lifetime and over five hundred by 1300.

They were austere, agricultural, and organized around a constitutional charter (the Carta Caritatis) that linked daughter houses to the mother in a federal structure that anticipated some later medieval institutional designs.
They pioneered medieval estate management, hydraulic engineering, and large-scale sheep farming, becoming some of the most economically dynamic landlords in Europe.
They also produced theological writing and devotional literature that fed the new urban universities.
The vernacular literature of the twelfth century is worth noting because it represents Latin's first systematic competition for European literary attention.
Until roughly 1100, all serious writing in western Europe had been in Latin.
Vernacular languages — Old French, Old English, Old High German, Provençal, Italian — were spoken everyday tongues, used for some practical writing, but not considered fit for literature.
This changed in the twelfth century.
The change began in southern France with the troubadours (TROO-buh-dorz, from Provençal trobador, "finder" or "composer").

Beginning around 1100 with Duke William IX of Aquitaine (Eleanor of Aquitaine's grandfather, Chapter 8), the troubadours composed Occitan-language lyric poetry around the new theme of fin'amor (fee-na-MOR — "refined love" — what later French and English literature would call "courtly love").

The basic conventions: the lover is a knight; the beloved is a noble lady, often married to a more powerful lord; the love is intense, refined, often unrequited; the lover serves the lady through the lyric song.

The convention spread north to the trouvères (troo-VAIR) of northern France writing in Old French, east to the German Minnesänger (MIN-eh-zeng-er), and eventually south to Italy, where it would become one of the foundations of Dante's Divine Comedy and the vernacular Italian literary tradition.
Northern France in the late twelfth century also produced the great Arthurian romances.

Geoffrey of Monmouth's Latin History of the Kings of Britain (1136) seeded the Arthur legend; Chrétien de Troyes (kray-TYAN duh TWAH) developed it in the 1170s and 1180s into the cycle of Lancelot, Guinevere, Perceval, and the Holy Grail.
The Arthurian cycle became the dominant prose-romance form of late-medieval European literature.
By 1200, vernacular literature was no longer a peripheral activity.

Latin remained the dominant language of theology, law, philosophy, and the Church, but French was the dominant language of romance and chivalric literature, German of the courtly epic, Italian of the new lyric, and Provençal of love poetry.

The thirteenth century would extend this to include Castilian (with Alfonso X's prose chronicles and law codes) and Middle English (which would not produce major literature until Chaucer in the fourteenth century, just outside this volume's window).
Cross-civ check: the twelfth-century European intellectual recovery is best understood by comparing it to the intellectual systems it was learning from.
The Islamic world was running a much more mature philosophical-theological synthesis through exactly the same period.

Al-Ghazali (al-gha-ZAH-lee, d. 1111) had just published his Incoherence of the Philosophers — the great Islamic critique of the Greek philosophical tradition — and his autobiography Deliverance from Error, which together largely redirected Islamic intellectual life away from Hellenistic philosophy and toward Sufi spirituality.

Ibn Rushd (Averroes, d. 1198) responded with The Incoherence of the Incoherence, defending Aristotelian rationalism against al-Ghazali, and produced commentaries on Aristotle that became more influential in Christian Europe than they were in the Islamic world after his death.
The Latin West that was first encountering Aristotle was therefore encountering him via Islamic commentators who had already been arguing about him for centuries.

The Jewish world of the twelfth century produced Maimonides (my-MON-uh-deez, properly Moshe ben Maimon, 1138–1204), the great rabbinic scholar and physician born in Cordoba, exiled by Almohad persecution to Cairo, where he served as personal physician to Saladin's vizier.

Maimonides's Guide for the Perplexed (written in Arabic around 1190) attempted the same synthesis between Aristotelian philosophy and revealed religion that Averroes was attempting from the Islamic side and Aquinas would attempt from the Christian side.
It was rapidly translated into Hebrew and then Latin and read across Christian Europe within a generation.

The three great twelfth- and thirteenth-century religious-philosophical syntheses — Aquinas's Christian, Averroes's Islamic, Maimonides's Jewish — were genuinely parallel projects working on the same problem (how to integrate Aristotle with revealed monotheism), within the same intellectual conversation, and largely reading each other.

In India, the twelfth century saw the great Vedanta synthesizers continuing the work of Shankara (eighth century) — most importantly Ramanuja (d. 1137) and later Madhva (thirteenth century) — building elaborate philosophical systems around the Upanishads (Medieval India Ch 7).

The temple-cities of South India in the same period were producing some of the most sophisticated stone architecture in the world (Medieval India Ch 6), with thousand-pillared halls and 200-foot gopuram gate towers.
The Cholas at this point were the dominant maritime power in the Bay of Bengal, with naval campaigns reaching Sumatra and Sri Lanka.

In China, the eleventh and twelfth centuries saw the Neo-Confucian synthesis under thinkers like Cheng Yi, Cheng Hao, and culminating in Zhu Xi (joo SHEE, d. 1200), the great Song dynasty philosopher whose systematic reading of the Confucian classics became the official philosophical framework of Chinese imperial civilization for the next seven centuries (Tang-Song China Ch 8).
