Zhu Xi and Aquinas died within a century of each other.
They were both responding to the same kind of intellectual problem — how to systematize a textual tradition into a coherent philosophical theology — in cultures that had no contact with each other.
The European twelfth-century Renaissance was therefore one of three or four parallel intellectual revolutions happening across Eurasia in the eleventh and twelfth centuries.
What was distinctive about the European version was that it was happening in a culture that had recently been intellectually impoverished and was building from a much lower base.
The Latin West in 1200 was still well behind the Islamic and Chinese intellectual establishments.
By 1300 it had largely caught up to Islamic philosophy through the scholastic synthesis.
By 1500 (which is the Late Medieval volume's territory) it would be visibly diverging in directions that the others were not.
The next chapter turns to the visible monument of the twelfth-century recovery — the cathedrals.

chapters.title: Cathedrals and the Gothic Revolution
sentences: In 1140, the Abbot Suger (soo-ZHAY) of the royal abbey of Saint-Denis outside Paris began rebuilding the choir of his church in a new way.
He used pointed arches instead of round Romanesque ones.
He used ribbed vaults that channeled the weight of the ceiling onto specific load points.
He pierced the walls with large stained-glass windows that filled the interior with colored light.

He left a written explanation of what he was doing — one of the very few surviving statements by a medieval architect about his own building philosophy — that argued the bright colored light entering the church was a direct experience of divine illumination, the worshipper's soul being drawn upward through the material light to the immaterial light of God himself.
The technical and the theological program were the same program.
Saint-Denis is conventionally dated as the birth of Gothic architecture.

The actual technical innovations Suger combined had been developed individually elsewhere: pointed arches existed in earlier Romanesque buildings, ribbed vaults existed in Norman architecture, large windows existed at scattered earlier sites.
What Suger did at Saint-Denis was combine them all into a coherent architectural and theological system.
Over the next century and a half, his combination spread across northern Europe and became one of the most successful architectural styles in human history.
This chapter is about how a small abbey choir on the outskirts of Paris turned into the dominant European architectural style for three centuries.
A bit of background on what Gothic was reacting against.

The dominant architecture of Latin Europe between roughly 1000 and 1140 had been Romanesque — a style derived from the surviving examples of Roman building, characterized by massive stone walls, round arches (the standard Roman form), barrel vaults or groin vaults, small windows, and a generally fortress-like solidity.
The Romanesque cathedral was built like a stone box: thick walls bore the weight of the heavy stone vaults above, with the windows kept small to preserve the wall's structural strength.
The interiors were dark and ponderous, decorated with painted murals because there was little light to display anything else.

The great Romanesque churches — Speyer in Germany, Pisa in Italy, the Norman cathedrals at Caen and Durham, the abbey at Cluny in Burgundy (which at its third rebuilding around 1100 was the largest church in Europe) — were imposing and theologically purposeful but structurally limited.

You could not raise the vault much above sixty or seventy feet without the walls beginning to bow outward under the lateral thrust, and you could not pierce the walls with large openings without compromising the structure.
Gothic solved both problems with the three innovations Suger combined.

The pointed arch allowed builders to vary the proportions of an arch independently — the same span could be arched at any height, by adjusting the angle of the point — which meant that vaults could be raised to whatever ceiling height the builders wanted without proportionally widening the arch.
This let Gothic vaults climb to 100, 130, 150 feet — heights that Romanesque round arches could not reach in stone.

The ribbed vault concentrated the structural weight of the ceiling onto a skeleton of stone ribs that channeled it down to specific load-bearing points — the columns and pier bundles of the nave — rather than distributing it across the entire wall as Romanesque vaults did.
This meant the walls between the load points could be hollowed out, removed, replaced with windows or with mere stone tracery, without any structural consequence.
The flying buttress, which appeared at Notre-Dame de Paris around 1180, completed the system.
The flying buttress is an external arch that transfers the outward thrust of a high vault to a free-standing pier well outside the wall of the church.
It looks (and looks better in nineteenth-century photographs than in person) like the cathedral has stone arms reaching out in all directions to brace itself.

The mechanical genius of the flying buttress is that it lets the wall of the church be reduced to almost nothing — the structural work is being done outside, by the buttresses, and the wall is freed to be replaced by stained glass.
The combination — pointed arch plus ribbed vault plus flying buttress — produced a building that looked nothing like Romanesque.
The Gothic cathedral interior is high, light, and skeletal.
Stone columns run up the inside walls and branch into the rib pattern of the vault overhead.
Between the columns, the wall is replaced almost entirely by stained-glass windows.
Light pours in through the colored glass and fills the interior with intentional theological color — blue for heaven, red for the blood of Christ, gold for divine light.
The Romanesque cathedral was a stone fortress.
The Gothic cathedral was a stone cage of light.
The major cathedrals of the High Gothic period, in roughly chronological order: Saint-Denis (begun 1140) — Suger's abbey church just north of Paris, the prototype.
The choir survives largely as Suger built it; the nave was rebuilt in the High Gothic style in the next century.
Notre-Dame de Paris (begun 1163) — Construction began in 1163 under Bishop Maurice de Sully on the Île de la Cité in Paris.
It took roughly two centuries to complete.
Notre-Dame was one of the first cathedrals to use the flying buttress, around 1180.
The fire of April 15, 2019, destroyed the spire and most of the medieval roof timbers; the stone vault and the great rose windows survived, and the cathedral was reopened on December 7, 2024.

Chartres Cathedral (rebuilt after fire 1194) — When fire destroyed most of the older church on the night of June 10–11, 1194, the bishop and chapter took the unusual decision to rebuild faster and grander than before.
The new cathedral was substantially complete by 1220 — twenty-six years from foundation to working liturgy, an extraordinarily fast pace for a building of this size.

Chartres has the densest surviving medieval glass collection on earth: 167 windows, including the deep blue glass that scholars still cannot fully reproduce (the recipe involved cobalt added during glassmaking; the exact medieval method has been lost).
The Chartres west portal sculptures and the south transept Bible windows together form the most important coherent visual program of medieval theology that survives intact in any single building.
Reims Cathedral (begun 1211) — The coronation church of every French king from the thirteenth century to Charles X in 1825.
The Reims west front sculpture is one of the great High Gothic sculpture cycles.
Amiens Cathedral (begun 1220) — The largest interior space in northern Europe, with a 138-foot vault — taller than a fourteen-story modern building.
Amiens represents High Gothic at its most engineered.
Beauvais Cathedral (begun 1225) — Beauvais pushed Gothic engineering past its limits.
The choir vault was raised to 153 feet (the highest vault in any Gothic cathedral) and partially collapsed in 1284.
The cathedral was repaired, the central tower added in 1569, and that tower then collapsed in 1573.
The rest of the cathedral was never built.
Beauvais is what Gothic looks like when ambition outruns the engineering budget.

Sainte-Chapelle (1242–1248) — King Louis IX of France built Sainte-Chapelle on the Île de la Cité in Paris to house his collection of Passion relics, including the Crown of Thorns purchased from the Latin Emperor of Constantinople in 1238 for what was reportedly more than half a year's French royal revenue.

The chapel's upper level is essentially a glass box held up by stone, the most spectacular surviving demonstration of Rayonnant Gothic — the more delicate, more glass-dominated phase of the style that succeeded the High Gothic of Chartres and Amiens.
Cologne Cathedral (begun 1248) — Construction began in 1248 to house the relics of the Three Magi (taken from Milan in 1164 by Frederick Barbarossa's chancellor).
The building was abandoned in the sixteenth century with construction roughly half complete; the choir, the south wall, and the foundations of the nave were finished.
It was not completed until the nineteenth century, when the original medieval plans were rediscovered in a granary and followed almost exactly.
Cologne Cathedral as it stands today is therefore both a medieval and a nineteenth-century building, on a thirteenth-century plan.
Salisbury Cathedral (begun 1220) — The major English cathedral entirely built in a single coherent Gothic style, over a remarkably short thirty-eight-year period to its main consecration in 1258.
Most other English cathedrals (Canterbury, York, Durham, Westminster) are stylistic patchworks of Romanesque, Early English, Decorated, and Perpendicular Gothic from successive rebuilding campaigns.
The High Gothic technical peak is reached at Amiens around 1240 and at Beauvais (briefly, before the collapse) around 1284.

After about 1300, French Gothic shifts into the more decorative Rayonnant and then Flamboyant phases that the Late Medieval volume picks up; English Gothic shifts into Decorated and then Perpendicular.
The structural innovation is largely complete by 1280; what comes after is elaboration on the established system.
The construction of a Gothic cathedral was an enormous undertaking — the largest sustained capital project most medieval cities ever attempted.

A typical High Gothic cathedral required somewhere between twenty thousand and a hundred thousand cubic meters of cut stone, quarried from sites that were sometimes hundreds of miles away and shipped by river barge.
It required tens of thousands of square feet of stained glass, made in specialized regional workshops.
It required tens of thousands of tons of timber for scaffolding, centering for the arches during construction, and the eventual roof framing.

It required the labor of hundreds of skilled stonemasons, glaziers, carpenters, and ironworkers, plus thousands of unskilled laborers, organized into traveling guilds that moved from cathedral project to cathedral project across the High Medieval period.

It typically took fifty to two hundred years to complete; many cathedrals were started in one century and finished in another by builders working from the original master plan with whatever modifications successive generations imposed.
The financing came from a combination of episcopal endowments, royal grants, papal indulgences, private donations from wealthy townsmen, and the collection plates of pilgrims.

Pilgrim relics — fragments of the True Cross, pieces of Mary's veil at Chartres, the Three Magi at Cologne, the Crown of Thorns at Sainte-Chapelle — were both spiritual focuses of the building and economic engines that drew the donations and pilgrim spending that funded ongoing construction.
The cathedral was the center of the medieval city's religious, cultural, and economic life all at once.
A common popular myth is worth addressing here: the medieval cathedrals were not built by anonymous communal volunteer labor in some kind of pre-modern collective religious fervor.
They were built by professional specialist guilds, paid in cash for skilled work, on contracts negotiated and supervised by the cathedral chapter and the master mason.

The medieval guilds — organized fraternities of masons, carpenters, glaziers, sculptors, and ironworkers — were a real and central feature of cathedral construction, and the master mason was a paid professional architect-engineer who ran the project on a contractual basis, not a pious enthusiast.
The "everyone helped to build the cathedral" image is a nineteenth-century romantic invention, not a medieval reality.

What is true is that the unskilled hauling and carrying labor sometimes drew on local volunteers as a form of pilgrimage, especially during the famous outbursts of building enthusiasm in the 1140s and again at Chartres after 1194, when chronicle accounts describe townspeople voluntarily harnessing themselves to wagons hauling stone from quarries.
But the skilled construction itself was always paid professional work.
The Gothic cathedral was not just a building.
It was a comprehensive theological program rendered in stone, glass, and sculpture.
The plan of the cathedral was a Latin cross — a long nave intersected by transepts, with the altar at the eastern end pointing toward Jerusalem.
The west portal sculptures presented the Last Judgment, with Christ as judge, the saved on his right, the damned on his left, and the resurrection of the dead in the lintel below.
The north transept sculptures typically presented the Old Testament: Adam and Eve, Moses, the prophets.
The south transept sculptures presented the New Testament: the Annunciation, the Nativity, the apostles.
The interior columns and capitals displayed scenes from the lives of saints, the virtues and vices, sometimes the labors of the months and the signs of the zodiac.
The stained-glass windows ran a continuous biblical narrative from Genesis to the Last Judgment in pictures that the largely illiterate congregation could read directly.
A medieval worshipper walking through Chartres or Amiens was walking through the entire Christian theological program rendered in three dimensions.
Some of the iconography is technical enough to be worth pausing on.

The rose window — the great circular stained-glass window typically placed above the western door, with smaller rose windows above each transept — was visual theology: the rose was a symbol of the Virgin Mary (the "rose without thorns" of the Marian tradition), and the geometric structure of the window radiating from a central medallion was understood as a diagram of the divine order radiating from the centerpoint of God.

The labyrinth inset in the floor of the nave at Chartres and several other cathedrals was a meditative pilgrimage path that the faithful could walk on their knees as a devotional substitute for going to Jerusalem.
The vault keystones at the crossing of each rib pattern were often carved with sacred images that were understood to bind the building together both structurally and theologically.

The gargoyles on the exterior — grotesque demonic figures projecting from the corners of the roofline — were both functional rainwater spouts and theological warnings: the demonic remained outside the consecrated interior of the church.

The pilgrimage circuit around the eastern end of the choir, with radiating chapels each containing a different relic and altar, was designed to let the increasing pilgrim traffic of the High Middle Ages flow through the cathedral without disrupting the daily liturgy at the main altar.
This is a piece of practical traffic engineering that the architects of Saint-Denis essentially invented and that became standard High Gothic practice.

Cross-civ check: while the Gothic cathedrals were going up across northern Europe, comparable monumental religious architecture was being built in other civilizations with very different structural and theological logics.

In South India during exactly the same period, the Chola, Hoysala, and later Vijayanagara empires were building massive temple complexes — Brihadeeswarar at Thanjavur (1010), Hoysaleswara at Halebidu (1121), the temple-city of Madurai — characterized by massive carved-stone gopuram gate towers reaching 200 feet, thousand-pillared halls (the Chola "Thousand-Pillared Hall" at Madurai actually has 985 pillars, but the figure is conventional), and façades carved with thousands of sculpted figures depicting the entire Hindu mythological corpus (Medieval India Ch 6).
The South Indian temple was an attempt at total visual representation of the divine cosmos using continuous figural sculpture.
The Gothic cathedral was an attempt at the same goal using glass, light, and structural skeleton.
Both produced spectacular monuments.
Both were, in their respective traditions, the highest forms of religious art.
In the Islamic world of the same period, monumental architecture took a very different direction.

The Great Mosque of Cordoba had been completed in stages between the eighth and tenth centuries; the Almohad-era mosques of Marrakech and Seville (the latter's minaret survives as the Giralda tower, completed 1198) were being built during the High Gothic period.

Islamic religious architecture preferred horizontal expansion (vast open prayer halls), geometric pattern decoration (because figural representation was generally avoided in religious buildings), and dome-and-minaret silhouettes inherited from Byzantine and Sassanian models.
The Gothic vertical aspiration toward stone-and-glass walls of light is essentially absent from Islamic religious architecture, which had its own quite different aesthetic priorities.

In China under the Song dynasty, monumental religious architecture was built in wood — the great Buddhist temples and pagodas of the period (the Yingxian wooden pagoda of 1056 still survives, 220 feet tall, the oldest surviving wooden tower in the world) used elaborate timber-bracket construction (dougong) to achieve heights and spans comparable to Gothic cathedrals using completely different structural logic.

Chinese sacred architecture generally avoided stone for religious building because of the cultural preference for wood and the philosophical preference for harmony with the natural materials of the site.
Tang-Song Chinese pagodas and temples could be as tall and ambitious as Gothic cathedrals; they just looked nothing alike.

In Mesoamerica, the Postclassic period (roughly 900–1521) saw the construction of major Maya complexes at Chichén Itzá and Mayapán (Maya Civilization Ch 6), with continued pyramid-building in the long Mesoamerican tradition.

The Aztec capital at Tenochtitlán would not be founded until 1325 — slightly outside this volume's window — but the Toltec-influenced architecture that would shortly inspire it was being built at Tula in central Mexico through the eleventh and twelfth centuries.

The High Gothic cathedral is therefore best understood not as a uniquely European achievement but as one of several great civilizational responses, in roughly the same period, to the problem of representing the divine in monumental architecture.

What was distinctive about the Gothic version was the structural engineering — the achievement of unprecedented vault heights and unprecedented wall transparency through the pointed-arch / ribbed-vault / flying-buttress system.
Most of the Gothic cathedrals would still be standing 800 years later.
So would most of the South Indian temples, and the Yingxian pagoda, and the Cordoba mosque.
Monumental religious architecture, when well-built, lasts.
The High Gothic moment was also the high-water mark of medieval craft guilds as economic and cultural institutions.

The guild was a voluntary association of practitioners of a single craft — masons, glaziers, weavers, dyers, goldsmiths, illuminators — that regulated training, set standards, controlled quality, restricted entry, and provided mutual aid for sick or destitute members.

The medieval guild was simultaneously a labor organization, a trade association, a mutual-aid society, a religious confraternity (most guilds had a patron saint and a guild altar in the local cathedral), and a political institution within the chartered city.
By 1300, most western European cities were governed by some combination of patrician magnates and the guilds of the leading crafts.

The cathedral construction industry sat at the high end of the guild economy: the master masons and the leading sculptors were among the most highly paid and most internationally mobile professionals of the medieval world.

A famous master mason — like Villard de Honnecourt, whose surviving sketchbook from the 1230s contains drawings of cathedral details, geometric problems, mechanical devices, and architectural elements from his travels across northern France and Germany — could expect employment offers from across the continent.
The cathedral master masons were the international rock stars of medieval applied science.
The next chapter turns to the parallel institution that emerged at the same time as the cathedrals: the universities.

chapters.title: Universities and Scholasticism
sentences: The medieval university is one of the most consequential institutional inventions of the High Middle Ages and one of the very few medieval institutions that has survived continuously into the present.

The universities of 2026 — Bologna, Paris, Oxford, Salamanca, Cambridge — are the same institutions, in the same cities, doing recognizably the same kind of work, that opened in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries.
They are older than any other continuously existing secular institution in the western world.
They are older than every modern nation-state.
The University of Bologna in 2026 is celebrating its 938th anniversary.
The university was something genuinely new in the world.

The classical world had had philosophical schools (Plato's Academy, Aristotle's Lyceum), the early-medieval cathedral schools had taught Latin and basic theology to clerics, and the great Islamic madrasas of the eleventh century were teaching Sharia and theology in formally constituted institutions.

But the medieval European university was something different from all of these — a self-governing chartered corporation of teachers and students, organized as a guild with its own legal identity, granting credentials recognized across western Christendom, with a defined multi-year curriculum, in subjects that ranged from law and medicine to theology and philosophy.
By 1300, every kingdom in Latin Europe wanted one.
This chapter is about how the universities were invented, what they taught, and what they did with the rediscovered classical and Islamic learning of the previous chapter.
The first formal European university was Bologna, traditionally dated to 1088.
Bologna grew out of the recovery of Roman law (Chapter 5).
The lawyer Irnerius had begun teaching Justinian's Corpus Juris Civilis there around 1080.
By 1088 there was a recognizable school of legal studies attracting students from across Europe.

By 1158, the Holy Roman Emperor Frederick Barbarossa issued the Authentica Habita, granting Bologna's students legal protection from local jurisdiction during their studies — one of the first imperial charters of academic privilege.
By 1200, Bologna was the leading school of Roman and canon law in Europe and the model that other universities tried to copy.
The peculiar feature of Bologna was that it was a student-run university.
The universitas ("the whole" — Latin for "guild" or "corporation," from which the word university derives) at Bologna was a guild of students, not a guild of professors.

The students collectively hired their own professors, set the curriculum, fixed the tuition rates, fined professors for showing up late or skipping difficult material, and could collectively withdraw their patronage if they were dissatisfied.

This sounds modern but produced very different institutional dynamics — the Bologna professors were essentially professional services hired and fired by their students, who were mostly older men preparing for careers in canon law or imperial administration, often already in lower clerical orders, often with money and political connections.
The second great early university was Paris, formalized around the mid-twelfth century.
Paris grew out of the cathedral school of Notre-Dame, which had been a serious teaching institution since at least the time of Peter Abelard (Chapter 5) in the early twelfth century.
The masters teaching theology and the liberal arts in Paris organized themselves into a guild of teachers, distinct from the Bologna model.
The Paris universitas was a guild of professors who admitted students into a defined curriculum and granted them credentials at the end.
King Philip II issued the first royal recognition in 1200; Pope Innocent III formally recognized the university in 1215.
By 1230 Paris was the leading school of theology and philosophy in Europe and the model for most northern European universities.
Oxford emerged in the mid-twelfth century from the migration of English students after Henry II banned them from Paris in 1167.
Cambridge broke off from Oxford in 1209 after a town-and-gown riot.

The two English universities followed the Paris model of master-led institutions and developed the distinctive English collegiate system in the thirteenth century, when wealthy donors began endowing residential colleges (Merton at Oxford in 1264, Peterhouse at Cambridge in 1284) as residential foundations for poor students.
Salamanca in Spain was founded by King Alfonso IX of León in 1218 and reaffirmed by Alfonso X in 1254, becoming the leading university of the Iberian peninsula.
Salamanca was distinctive for its connections to the Toledo translation movement and its role in transmitting Arabic and Hebrew scholarship into the Latin academic mainstream.

By 1300, the major university map of Latin Europe looked roughly like this: Bologna for law, Paris for theology and philosophy, Oxford and Cambridge for theology and the liberal arts, Salamanca for Iberian scholarship, Salerno in southern Italy for medicine (Salerno had been a leading medical school since the late ninth century, with a distinctive Greek-Arabic-Latin synthesis going back to the eleventh century), Padua founded in 1222 (after a secession from Bologna) as a rival law school, and Naples founded by Frederick II in 1224 as the first explicitly state-founded university.

Other university foundations followed across the late thirteenth and fourteenth centuries — Coimbra, Toulouse, Montpellier, Prague, Vienna, Heidelberg, Cracow — but the High Medieval template had been set by 1300.
The medieval university curriculum was inherited from late antiquity and elaborated in the cathedral schools.

A student arrived at the university typically around age fourteen or fifteen, after preparatory study in a cathedral or grammar school, and entered the arts faculty for a course of study in the seven liberal arts organized in two groups: the trivium (TRIH-vee-um — grammar, logic, rhetoric — the three verbal arts) and the quadrivium (kwah-DRIH-vee-um — arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, music — the four mathematical arts).

Students completed the trivium for the bachelor's degree (typically three to four years), then continued through the quadrivium for the master's degree (another two to three years), at which point they were licensed to teach the liberal arts themselves.
Most students stopped at this point and went off to careers in the church bureaucracy, royal administration, or the towns.
The most ambitious students continued into one of the three higher faculties: theology (at Paris and Oxford), law (at Bologna and Padua), or medicine (at Salerno and Montpellier).
The higher degrees took another five to fifteen years, depending on the field.

A doctorate of theology from Paris in the thirteenth century took thirteen to sixteen years of study after the master of arts and required defending a series of public disputations on disputed theological questions.
The medieval universities took a long time.
The teaching method was the lecture, the disputation, and the commentary.

The lecture (Latin lectio, "reading") was literally the master reading a designated authoritative text aloud, sentence by sentence, with explanatory commentary — Aristotle's Physics, Justinian's Digest, Peter Lombard's Sentences, depending on the faculty.
Students copied down the lecture as fast as they could write.

The disputation (Latin disputatio, "argument") was a structured oral debate on a specific question, with one master defending a thesis, opponents raising objections, and a master determining the answer.
The commentary was the written exposition of an authoritative text, with the master's reading of difficult passages and his resolution of apparent contradictions.
The pedagogical assumption was that authoritative texts were internally consistent and that apparent contradictions could be resolved by close reading and dialectical analysis.
This is the method that Peter Abelard had pioneered in Sic et Non (Chapter 5) and that became the standard scholastic technique.
The student was not learning to think original thoughts; the student was learning to master the authoritative texts and to defend orthodox positions in formal disputation.
This is a more constrained intellectual ideal than the modern university aspires to.
It was also extraordinarily effective at producing the trained cadre of lawyers, theologians, doctors, and administrators that staffed the institutions of late-medieval Europe.
The new institution that revolutionized university teaching in the thirteenth century was the mendicant order — specifically, the Dominicans and the Franciscans.

Dominic of Caleruega (1170–1221) was a Spanish canon who founded the Order of Preachers (the Dominicans) in 1216 with papal approval, organized for educated preaching against the Albigensian heresy in southern France (Chapter 3).
The Dominicans took theological learning as their core institutional identity from the start.
They sent their best students to the universities, established Dominican houses in every university town, and within a generation were occupying many of the chairs of theology at Paris and Oxford.
Francis of Assisi (1181–1226) had a different starting point.

Born to a wealthy cloth merchant in central Italy, Francis renounced his inheritance in a public scene around 1206 (he stripped naked in the town square and gave his clothes back to his father) and founded the Franciscan Order in 1209 around radical voluntary poverty, preaching to ordinary people in their own languages, and care for the sick and the outcast.
Within a decade the Franciscans were one of the largest religious orders in Europe.

The original Franciscan emphasis had been on simple itinerant preaching rather than scholarly study; this changed in the second generation, when the Franciscans, like the Dominicans, moved into the universities and began producing some of the period's most original theology.

Both orders together — the Dominicans (the Order of Preachers, dedicated to learned preaching) and the Franciscans (the Order of Friars Minor, dedicated to apostolic poverty) — are called the mendicant orders because they were originally supposed to live by alms (Latin mendicare, to beg) rather than by endowed monastery lands.

The mendicant orders transformed medieval religious life by relocating the most ambitious preachers and theologians from rural monasteries into the new urban universities, where they took most of the chairs of theology at Paris and Oxford in the thirteenth century.
The two greatest scholastic theologians of the High Middle Ages — Albertus Magnus and Thomas Aquinas — were both Dominicans.

The two most influential Franciscan thinkers of the period — Bonaventure and (just outside this volume's window) Duns Scotus — produced a parallel Franciscan synthesis that disagreed with the Dominican one on several major points.
Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274) is the central intellectual figure of the High Middle Ages.

Born to a noble family in southern Italy, Thomas was educated at Monte Cassino, then at the new University of Naples, and joined the Dominican Order around 1244 against the violent objections of his family (who locked him up at home for over a year trying to make him change his mind).

He went to Paris to study under Albertus Magnus (Albert the Great, the German Dominican who was the first major Christian thinker to engage seriously with the recently translated Aristotle) and followed Albert to Cologne.

He returned to Paris as a master of theology in 1256, taught there in two extended periods, and spent the rest of his life lecturing, writing, and producing the systematic theology that would shape Catholic intellectual life for the next seven centuries.
Aquinas's central project was the synthesis of Aristotelian philosophy with Christian theology.

The recently recovered Aristotle (Chapter 5) had been controversial at Paris in the 1210s and 1220s — Aristotelian texts had been formally banned by the Paris faculty in 1210 because of their apparent incompatibility with Christian doctrine on points like the eternity of the world and the personal immortality of the soul.
By Aquinas's time the bans were lapsing, but the integration problem remained.

Aquinas attempted to show that Aristotle's philosophy and Christian theology were not just compatible but mutually illuminating — that natural reason (Aristotle) and revealed faith (Christianity) led to the same God by different paths.
The result was the Summa Theologiae (begun 1265, unfinished at his death in 1274 — a working manuscript of roughly 1.8 million words).

The Summa's structure is the formal scholastic disputation taken to its furthest extension: Aquinas poses thousands of theological questions, presents the strongest objections to his preferred answer, gives his answer, then responds to the objections individually.
The five "Five Ways" (the five proofs for the existence of God in question 2 of part 1) are the most famous single section.
The whole work is a vast Gothic cathedral of structured argument, reading every theological question through both natural reason and revealed scripture and arguing for the harmony of the two.
Aquinas's project was not universally welcomed at the time.
Several of his specific theses were condemned by the Bishop of Paris in 1277, three years after Aquinas's death.
The Franciscan school under Bonaventure favored a more Augustinian, Plato-influenced theology that distrusted Aristotle as much as Bernard of Clairvaux had distrusted Abelard.
There was a continuing thirteenth-century debate, never fully resolved, about how much Aristotle Christian theology could safely absorb.
What is now obvious in hindsight, but was not obvious at the time, is that Aquinas had won.
Aquinas was canonized in 1323 and named a Doctor of the Church in 1567.
The Council of Trent (1545–1563) placed his Summa on the altar alongside the Bible during deliberations.

Pope Leo XIII's 1879 encyclical Aeterni Patris declared Thomism the official philosophical framework of Roman Catholic theology — which it remains in 2026, eight centuries after Aquinas first arrived in Paris as a student.

The structural parallel worth pausing on is that the Christian-Aristotelian synthesis Aquinas was building had two contemporary parallels — one Islamic, one Jewish — working on exactly the same problem in exactly the same generation.
Ibn Rushd (Averroes, 1126–1198), the great Andalusian Muslim philosopher, had attempted a parallel synthesis of Aristotle with Islamic theology (Islamic Golden Age Ch 7).

His position was more radical than Aquinas's would be — Averroes accepted some Aristotelian conclusions (like the eternity of the world) that Aquinas would reject as incompatible with revealed religion, and his commentaries on Aristotle were so extensive and so influential that he was simply called "the Commentator" by the medieval Latins.

Averroes's positions on the unity of the active intellect across humanity (which seemed to imply that personal immortality was an illusion) became the focus of one of the great intellectual debates of thirteenth-century Paris, with the so-called Latin Averroists (most prominently Siger of Brabant) defending Averroes's reading and Aquinas writing his treatise On the Unity of the Intellect against the Averroists (1270) to refute it.

Maimonides (Moshe ben Maimon, 1138–1204), the great Jewish philosopher writing in Cairo (Chapter 5), had attempted a parallel synthesis of Aristotle with Jewish theology in his Guide for the Perplexed (composed in Arabic around 1190, rapidly translated into Hebrew and then Latin).

Maimonides's position was closer to what Aquinas would eventually argue: that revealed religion and natural reason were ultimately consistent, and that apparent contradictions between scripture and Aristotle could usually be resolved through allegorical reading of the difficult biblical passages.
Aquinas read Maimonides extensively and cited him by name as "Rabbi Moses" repeatedly in the Summa.

The three great twelfth- and thirteenth-century religious-philosophical syntheses — Christian (Aquinas), Islamic (Averroes), Jewish (Maimonides) — were therefore parallel projects working on the same problem, within the same intellectual conversation, reading each other across linguistic and religious boundaries that did not stop the exchange of ideas.
This is one of the most striking features of high-medieval intellectual life and one of the things modern accounts often underplay.

The medieval Mediterranean was not the sealed religious-civilizational compartments that later periods would imagine; it was a connected intellectual ecology in which Spanish Jews translated Arabic Aristotle for Italian Christians, and Aquinas at Paris cited Maimonides at Cairo on a question Averroes at Cordoba had also addressed.
A common modern myth is worth addressing: the medieval university was not "open to all" in any sense the modern reader would recognize.
The student body of the medieval university was almost entirely male.
The very few documented exceptions are exceptional precisely because they are exceptional.

Women were formally excluded from matriculation across nearly all medieval universities (Salerno's medical faculty admitted some women, including the famous Trotula in the eleventh century, as the most documented exception).

The exclusion of women was not just about the formal student body but about the entire institutional structure — the universities were organized around clerical orders, since faculty members had to be in lower clerical orders even if not actually ordained priests, and women were canonically barred from clerical orders.
The student body was also socially restricted.

Latin literacy was the entry barrier — and Latin literacy was acquired in cathedral schools and grammar schools that mostly served the children of the clergy, the lesser nobility, and the urban patriciate.
A peasant boy might in theory rise into the universities (the old chronicle accounts treasure the occasional case), but in practice the social filter was heavy.
The medieval universities served a clerical-bourgeois-noble male population, not a representative cross-section of medieval society.
The universities also had a complicated relationship with the city populations around them.

The medieval town-and-gown conflict — the recurrent tension between the privileged exempt-from-local-jurisdiction student population and the resentful local townspeople — was a regular feature of university towns from the start.
The 1209 Cambridge secession from Oxford was triggered by a town-and-gown brawl.

The 1229 Paris student strike (after a tavern brawl in which several students were killed by royal troops) led to a two-year suspension of teaching and a permanent reorganization of the relationship between the university and the French crown.
The 1265 Oxford riots saw the killing of a number of students by townspeople.
The privileged status of medieval university students made them frequently arrogant, sometimes violent, and recurrently resented by the cities they lived in.

What is true is that the medieval universities created, for the first time in Europe, a credential — the master's degree — that conferred a set of legal privileges (exemption from local taxation, the right to teach anywhere in Christendom, the right to be tried in church courts rather than secular ones) recognized internationally.
A student who completed his master's at Paris could go on to teach at Oxford or Bologna without re-credentialing.
This is a small thing that turned out to be very consequential.
The international academic credential is a medieval invention.
The next chapter turns to the political and constitutional shock of the early thirteenth century — and to the equally important shock that arrived from the steppe in 1241.

chapters.title: Magna Carta to Mongol Shock
sentences: On June 15, 1215, in a meadow at Runnymede (RUN-ee-meed) on the south bank of the Thames near Windsor, King John of England put his seal to a charter that his rebellious barons had forced on him.

The charter — the Magna Carta ("Great Charter") in Latin — established that the king was bound by law, that no free man could be imprisoned or dispossessed without the lawful judgment of his peers, that taxation required the consent of those taxed, that the church had certain liberties from royal interference, and a long list of more specific provisions about wardship, inheritance, foreign mercenaries, and the conduct of royal officials.
John repudiated it within ten weeks.
He was dead within fifteen months.
His nine-year-old son Henry III's regency reissued Magna Carta in 1216 and again in 1225, and the reissued versions became the foundation of the English constitutional tradition.
The 1215 document itself is a contingent piece of medieval baronial politics.
The institutional principle it established — that even the king is under the law — became one of the most consequential ideas in western political history.

Twenty-six years after Runnymede, in April 1241, two Mongol armies under generals Batu Khan and Subutai annihilated a Polish-Moravian-Templar force at the Battle of Legnica (LEHG-neet-sah, in modern Poland) on April 9 and a Hungarian royal army at the Battle of Mohi (MOH-hee, in modern Hungary) on April 11 — two complete victories two days apart.
King Béla IV of Hungary fled to the Adriatic coast.
The Mongols devastated central Europe for a year.
They turned back in spring 1242 only because of the death of the Great Khan Ögedei (UH-guh-day) in Mongolia, which recalled Batu to the steppe for the succession kurultai (Mongol Empire Ch 4).
The reprieve was political and accidental.
There was nothing in central Europe in 1242 that could have stopped the Mongols if they had decided to keep coming.

This chapter is about the two parallel structural shifts of the thirteenth century — the constitutional shift inside western Europe, exemplified by Magna Carta and the rise of representative bodies, and the geopolitical shock from outside, exemplified by the Mongol arrival.
By 1300, both shifts had reshaped the political landscape of Latin Europe in ways the rest of the medieval period would be living with.
Start with the constitutional story.
King John of England (reigned 1199–1216) was the youngest of the four legitimate sons of Henry II and Eleanor of Aquitaine and one of the worst kings ever to reign in England.
He was also unlucky.

He inherited the throne from his older brother Richard the Lionheart in 1199 with most of the resources of the Angevin Empire — England, Normandy, Anjou, Maine, Touraine, Aquitaine — and a hostile Philip II of France actively working to dismember it.
The dismemberment proceeded faster than anyone expected.
Between 1202 and 1204, Philip II's armies overran Normandy, Anjou, Maine, and Touraine, leaving John holding only England, Ireland, and parts of Aquitaine.
The lost territories included most of the wealthy continental French heartland of the Plantagenet dynasty.
John spent the next decade trying to recover them and failing repeatedly.
His attempt at a major continental coalition with the Holy Roman Emperor Otto IV ended at the Battle of Bouvines on July 27, 1214, where Philip II destroyed the coalition army in northern France.

John was personally absent from Bouvines (he was running a parallel campaign in southwestern France that also went badly), but Bouvines confirmed the loss of the continental Angevin territories and triggered the political crisis at home that produced Magna Carta the following year.
John's domestic problems were just as bad as his foreign ones.

He had quarreled with Pope Innocent III over the appointment of the Archbishop of Canterbury — when Innocent insisted on his own candidate, Stephen Langton, against John's preferred choice, John refused to accept Langton; Innocent excommunicated John in 1209 and placed England under interdict (suspension of all church services, including baptisms, marriages, funerals, and the Mass) from 1208 to 1213.

John eventually backed down and submitted to Innocent in May 1213, accepting Langton, paying compensation, and formally surrendering England as a fief of the papacy — which he then held back from the pope in vassalage.
The submission was humiliating but politically clever; it made Innocent John's defender against subsequent baronial revolt.
The barons would later complain that the pope was protecting an unfit king against their legitimate grievances.
The grievances themselves were real.
John had taxed England punishingly to fund his failed continental wars.
He had abused royal wardship and marriage rights to enrich himself at the expense of noble families.
He had imposed arbitrary fines, sold royal offices to the highest bidder, and repeatedly violated feudal custom.
He had personally killed his nephew Arthur of Brittany (the rival claimant to the throne) in 1203, in circumstances that everyone in Europe believed were murder.
And after Bouvines, he had returned home wanting to launch yet another war that would require yet more taxation.
The barons revolted in spring 1215 under Robert Fitzwalter, captured London in May, and forced John to negotiate at Runnymede in June.
The document they presented him is what we now call Magna Carta — sixty-three clauses, a mixture of specific feudal grievances and broader principles of restraint on royal power.

The most famous clauses are clause 39 (no free man shall be imprisoned or dispossessed except by the lawful judgment of his equals or by the law of the land) and clause 40 (to no one will we sell, to no one will we deny or delay right or justice).

These two clauses, in slightly modified form, would become the foundation of the English common-law principle of due process and the foundation of the right against arbitrary detention (habeas corpus, technically a later development).
John repudiated Magna Carta within ten weeks, on the grounds that it had been extorted from him under duress.
He persuaded Pope Innocent III to annul it in August 1215.

The barons rebelled again, invited the French Prince Louis (the future Louis VIII of France) to invade England and claim the throne, and were saved from the awkward consequences only by John's sudden death from dysentery in October 1216, at age forty-nine.
The regency of John's nine-year-old son Henry III was much more politically skilled than John had been.

The regents under William Marshal reissued Magna Carta in November 1216 in modified form, as a goodwill gesture to settle the rebellion, drove out the French invasion, and reissued the charter again in 1217 and definitively in 1225 in the version that became permanently English constitutional law.
Henry III repeatedly confirmed the 1225 reissue throughout his sixty-six-year reign (1216–1272).
His son Edward I confirmed it again in 1297, in the Confirmatio Cartarum.
Magna Carta was a settled part of English law by 1300.
The institutional consequence of Magna Carta was the gradual emergence of a representative assembly in England.

Clause 14 of Magna Carta required the king to summon "the archbishops, bishops, abbots, earls, and greater barons" and the lesser tenants-in-chief through the sheriffs to consent to extraordinary taxation.
This was the seed of Parliament.
The principle — that taxation required consent — required a body to give the consent.
The body that emerged over the thirteenth century was Parliament, an assembly of the king with the magnates, prelates, and (eventually) elected representatives of the shires and the towns.
The crucial expansion was Simon de Montfort's Parliament of January 1265.

Simon de Montfort, Earl of Leicester, was an Anglo-French baron who had led a baronial revolt against Henry III, defeated the king at the Battle of Lewes in 1264, and effectively governed England as a kind of medieval parliamentary regent for fifteen months.

To shore up support against royalist resistance, de Montfort summoned a parliament in January 1265 that for the first time included representatives of the shires and the boroughs alongside the magnates and clergy.
This is the first English assembly to include elected commoners and is conventionally regarded as the institutional origin of the House of Commons.

De Montfort was killed in battle at Evesham on August 4, 1265, but his model became the structural basis of the English Parliament under Edward I (1272–1307), whose Model Parliament of 1295 — including bishops, abbots, peers, two knights from each shire, two burgesses from each borough, and elected representatives of the lesser clergy — became the standard form of English parliamentary representation for centuries.
The English development was paralleled, with significant variations, across other parts of western Europe.

The Cortes in Iberia were assembling representatives of the noble, ecclesiastical, and urban estates from the late twelfth century — the Cortes of León in 1188 was the first European assembly to include burghers from the towns, predating Simon de Montfort's parliament by seventy-seven years.
The Cortes of Castile and the Cortes of Aragon developed alongside.

The Estates-General of France would not be formally summoned until 1302 (slightly outside this volume's window), but provincial estates assemblies had been operating in various French regions throughout the thirteenth century.

The Diet of the Holy Roman Empire had been operating since the early twelfth century but was an assembly of the major imperial princes rather than a representative body in the constitutional sense; the imperial cities would not gain formal representation until the later fourteenth century.

The Hungarian Diet secured its own constitutional charter, the Golden Bull of 1222, only seven years after Magna Carta — establishing similar restraints on royal power and the right of the nobility to resist unlawful royal acts.
The 1222 Golden Bull is the parallel Hungarian document to Magna Carta and developed into the constitutional foundation of the medieval Kingdom of Hungary.

By 1300, every major western European kingdom had some form of representative or quasi-representative assembly with at least conditional power to constrain royal taxation and (in some cases) royal legislation.
This is the medieval foundation of the modern parliamentary tradition.
It was not democracy in any modern sense — the franchise was extremely narrow, the assemblies were dominated by the noble and ecclesiastical estates, and the king retained vast prerogative powers.
But it established the principle that taxation requires consent and that there must be some formal body to give that consent.
That principle would be the seed of what would eventually grow into modern constitutional government.
A note on the figure who pulled the thirteenth-century papal apparatus to its peak.
Pope Innocent III (1198–1216) was elected at thirty-seven and pope for eighteen years, the most politically ambitious pope of the Middle Ages.

His record reads like a list of medieval institutional landmarks: he placed England under interdict and brought King John to heel; he called the Fourth Crusade and the Albigensian Crusade; he approved the new Franciscan and Dominican orders; he presided over the Fourth Lateran Council of November 1215; and he pushed the medieval papacy to the height of its institutional power.
The Fourth Lateran Council is worth pausing on.

Innocent's largest single legislative act, the council issued seventy decrees that defined transubstantiation as Catholic doctrine, required annual confession and communion of every Catholic, mandated identifying clothing for Jews and Muslims (one of the dark precedents of European antisemitism — the requirement that Jews wear distinguishing dress was repeatedly enforced and reissued through the late Middle Ages and beyond), condemned the Albigensian heresy, and codified much of the medieval church's pastoral and disciplinary apparatus for the next three centuries.
The Fourth Lateran is the institutional equivalent of Magna Carta on the religious side — a single act of assembly that defined the framework for everything that came after.
After Innocent, the medieval papacy began to decline relative to the rising centralized monarchies of France and England.

Pope Boniface VIII (1294–1303) tried to repeat Gregory VII's claims of papal supremacy over kings; his clash with King Philip IV of France ended in his humiliation at Anagni in 1303, his death three weeks later, and the relocation of the papal court to Avignon in 1309 — beginning the Avignon Papacy that the Late Medieval volume picks up.
The thirteenth century was the high tide of the medieval papacy.
After 1300 the centralized monarchies began to eat the papacy's institutional space.
The other thirteenth-century strand worth following is the long Christian advance through the Iberian peninsula.

The Reconquista ("reconquest" in Spanish) was the long Christian recovery of Iberia from Muslim rule — conventionally beginning with the Battle of Covadonga around 722 (where the Visigothic refugee Pelagius defeated an Umayyad raiding force in the Asturian mountains) and ending with the fall of Granada in 1492 (Late Medieval Europe Ch 8).
The thirteenth century was its most spectacular phase.
The trigger event was the Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa on July 16, 1212.

A coalition of the Christian kingdoms of Castile, Aragon, Navarre, and Portugal under Alfonso VIII of Castile destroyed the army of the Almohad caliphate (the Berber dynasty that had been ruling al-Andalus and Morocco since the 1140s) in southern Spain.
The Almohad collapse opened the way for rapid Christian advance over the next half-century.

Córdoba — the former capital of the Umayyad caliphate of al-Andalus, one of the great cultural centers of the medieval Islamic world (Islamic Golden Age Ch 7) — fell to Ferdinand III of Castile on June 29, 1236.
Valencia — the great port city on the Mediterranean coast — fell to James I of Aragon on September 28, 1238.
Seville — the largest remaining Muslim city in Spain and the Almohad administrative capital — fell to Ferdinand III on November 23, 1248 after a sixteen-month siege.
By 1250, four-fifths of the Iberian peninsula was under Christian rule.

The remaining Muslim territory was the small Emirate of Granada in the southern mountains of Andalucia, a tributary state under the Nasrid dynasty that would survive for another 244 years before falling in January 1492.
The high-medieval Reconquista was both a military and a cultural project.
As territory was conquered, Arabic libraries were absorbed into Christian Iberia (the Toledo translation movement of Chapter 5 was the most consequential single result).

Muslim and Jewish populations under the new Christian regimes initially retained substantial legal protections — the Mudéjars (moo-DAY-har, Muslims under Christian rule) and the Mozarabs (moh-ZAH-rab, Arabic-speaking Christians) maintained their religions and communal autonomy under royal protection.
The Spanish-Jewish community of medieval Iberia was the largest and culturally most productive Jewish community in medieval Europe.
The protections eroded over the following centuries.
The Almohad-era ferocity that had driven Maimonides into exile in Cairo was paralleled by increasing Christian intolerance after the great thirteenth-century conquests.
By 1300 there were intermittent forced conversions, anti-Jewish riots, and pressure on Muslim communities to convert or emigrate.
The full collapse of medieval Iberian religious coexistence into the Spanish Inquisition of 1478 and the Jewish expulsion of 1492 is post-medieval and belongs to the Late Medieval volume.
But the trajectory had been set during the great thirteenth-century conquests.
The Mongol shock arrives now.
The Mongol Empire under Genghis Khan had unified the steppe in the early thirteenth century and expanded into Central Asia and northern China by Genghis's death in 1227 (Mongol Empire Ch 2 and Ch 3).
His grandsons divided the empire and continued the expansion.
Batu Khan, son of Genghis's eldest son Jochi, took on the western expansion.
Between 1237 and 1240 his armies systematically destroyed the cities of the Rus' principalities — Ryazan in 1237, Vladimir in 1238, Kyiv on December 6, 1240.
The destruction of Kyiv was particularly thorough: contemporary accounts and modern archaeology agree that the city was substantially leveled.

The Mongol overlordship of Rus', known to Russian historians as the Tatar Yoke, lasted in formal terms until 1480 and reoriented Russian politics decisively away from the Byzantine cultural sphere and into the eastern, steppe-oriented orbit (Mongol Empire Ch 7).
After Kyiv, Batu turned west.
In late 1240 and early 1241, Mongol scouting parties raided into Poland, Hungary, and the Balkans.
The main invasion force came in spring 1241.
The Mongols divided into two main columns.
The northern column under Baidar and Kadan swept through Poland to draw away the northern European armies that might otherwise have reinforced Hungary.
The southern and main column under Batu and Subutai marched directly on Hungary.
The northern column met the assembled Polish-Moravian-Templar force under Duke Henry II the Pious of Silesia at the Battle of Legnica on April 9, 1241.
The Mongols used their standard tactic of feigned retreat and envelopment to draw the Polish chivalry into pursuit, then closed around them with their reserve heavy cavalry.
The Polish force was annihilated.
Henry was killed; the chronicles say his head was paraded on a Mongol lance.
The Polish chivalry was destroyed as a fighting force.
Two days later, on April 11, 1241, the southern column under Batu and Subutai met the Hungarian royal army under King Béla IV at the Battle of Mohi on the Sajó river in eastern Hungary.

The Mongols crossed the river by night, surrounded the Hungarian camp at dawn, deliberately left a gap in their encirclement to encourage the Hungarians to flee through it, and then methodically destroyed the disorganized fugitives over thirty miles of pursuit.
The Hungarian royal army was effectively annihilated.
Béla escaped to the Adriatic coast and spent the next year as a refugee on Croatian islands while the Mongols devastated Hungary.
The devastation was thorough.
Mongol contingents reached the Adriatic coast and threatened Vienna.
The chronicles record the burning of villages, the slaughter of populations, and the enslavement of survivors across the Hungarian plain.
Modern estimates put the Hungarian population loss at fifteen to twenty-five percent in the year of Mongol occupation.
Then, in spring 1242, the Mongols withdrew.
The reason was not Christian military resistance — there was no Christian military resistance — but Mongol internal politics.
The Great Khan Ögedei had died in Mongolia in December 1241, and Batu had to return for the succession kurultai that would eventually elect Güyük as the new Great Khan (Mongol Empire Ch 4).
The Mongol withdrawal from central Europe in 1242 was an accident of imperial succession, not a victory by Christian arms.
The reprieve was permanent in central Europe — the Mongols never returned in force, though raids continued into Poland and Hungary through the late thirteenth century.
But the lesson stuck.

The Mongols had demonstrated that a steppe army with disciplined cavalry tactics, gunpowder weapons (Mongol Empire Ch 3), and competent generalship could defeat any European army the kingdoms could field, and could devastate any country they chose to attack.
There was nothing in 1241 between the Mongol field armies and the Atlantic coast of France that could have stopped them.
The fact that they did not keep coming was contingent — a matter of imperial succession politics, not Christian capability.
This is one of the strangest counterfactuals in medieval history.

If Ögedei had not died in December 1241, the Mongol invasion would almost certainly have continued through 1242 and 1243 into the Holy Roman Empire and France, and the political shape of late-medieval and early-modern Europe would have been very different.
The High Middle Ages as a coherent period might have ended at Mohi in 1241 rather than at the Black Death in 1347.
The Mongol shock had a second echo in the Levant.
Hülegü Khan, another grandson of Genghis, sacked Baghdad on February 10, 1258, ending the Abbasid caliphate (Islamic Golden Age Ch 10).

The Mongol westward advance was finally stopped at Ayn Jalut on September 3, 1260, by the Mamluk Sultanate of Egypt — the only major army to defeat the Mongols in a major field battle in the thirteenth century (Mongol Empire Ch 5).
The Mamluk victory at Ayn Jalut saved Egypt and the surviving Crusader states and fixed the Mongol western frontier roughly along the Euphrates.
It also produced one of the great might-have-beens of medieval European diplomacy.
The Mongol Ilkhans of Persia, who had taken the Levant up to the Egyptian frontier, were openly courting Christian Europe in the late thirteenth century as potential allies against the Mamluks.
Successive Ilkhans sent embassies to the popes and the kings of France and England proposing joint Mongol-Christian campaigns against Mamluk Egypt.
Some of the Ilkhans personally were sympathetic to Christianity (their wives and mothers were often Christian, from the Christian populations of Central Asia).
Several rounds of negotiation between the Ilkhans and the Crusader-supporting western powers came close to producing a joint campaign.
None ever did.
The opportunity for a Mongol-European alliance against Mamluk Egypt expired with the Ilkhanid conversion to Islam under Ghazan in 1295.

This is the closest the medieval Latin West came to genuinely allying with a non-Christian Eurasian power against another, and it is a measure of how far the Mongol shock had pushed European political thinking.
The most famous European to take up the Mongol opening commercially rather than diplomatically was Marco Polo.

The Venetian merchant Marco Polo traveled overland with his father and uncle to the Mongol court of Kublai Khan in 1271, spent seventeen years in China, and on his return dictated The Travels of Marco Polo while imprisoned in Genoa after capture in a Venetian-Genoese sea battle around 1298 (Mongol Empire Ch 6).

The book became the most influential European description of Asia for the next two centuries and, two centuries later, gave Christopher Columbus the vague mental geography that motivated his westward voyage looking for the Indies.
Polo is technically late-thirteenth-century, just inside this volume's window, but his cultural impact is mostly fourteenth- and fifteenth-century and belongs to the Late Medieval volume.
A few words about the legacy of the High Middle Ages, since this volume ends here.

By 1300, the institutional inventory of western Europe included things that had not existed in 1000 and that the rest of the world would eventually inherit: the chartered self-governing town, the international banking corporation, the corporate university, the constitutional charter, the representative parliament, the international religious order, the Gothic cathedral, and a body of recovered classical and Islamic learning that the rest of the medieval period would build on.

The institutions were not modern in their content (the parliament had a tiny franchise; the university excluded women; the banks ran on Catholic-canon-law workarounds; the cathedrals were funded by indulgences).

But their institutional logic — chartered corporate identity, formal credentials, written constitutional documents, separation of church and state, taxation by consent, due process — was a recognizable ancestor of what the modern western political and intellectual tradition would eventually become.

The High Middle Ages also have a legacy of darker things that the rest of medieval Europe would also build on: the antisemitic violence of 1096 and its successors, the religious-war ideology of the Crusades, the Inquisition's emerging machinery for prosecuting heresy, the gendered exclusions of the universities and the religious orders, the European idea of itself as a uniquely Christian civilization with a divine right to expand outward.
Most of these darker features would intensify in the late medieval and early modern centuries before they began to give way under modern critique.

The Late Medieval Europe volume picks up the story in 1300 with the four catastrophes of the fourteenth century — the climate cooling that started the Little Ice Age, the failure of the Italian banking houses, the Hundred Years' War, and the Black Death.
The High Middle Ages had been a long boom.
The Late Middle Ages would be a long shock.

But the institutional inheritance from the boom — the cathedrals, the universities, the parliaments, the chartered cities — would survive the shock, and would be the platform from which everything afterward was built.
Cross-civ check: while western Europe was processing its constitutional and Mongol shocks of the 1200s, the rest of Eurasia was managing its own version of the Mongol arrival.
China under the Southern Song would fall to the Mongols in 1279, ending the Song dynasty and inaugurating the Yuan (Mongol Empire Ch 6).

Persia had been under Mongol rule since the 1250s under the Ilkhanate, which would convert to Islam in 1295 and dissolve into successor states in the 1330s — the political vacuum that gave the Safaviyya order at Ardabil room to grow into what would eventually become Safavid Persia (Safavid Persia Ch 1).
Mali in the western Sudan was just beginning its rise under the founder Sundiata around 1235, the empire that would peak under Mansa Musa a century later (Mali Empire Ch 1 and Ch 4).

Aksum had long since dissolved into the medieval Ethiopian states, where the Solomonic dynasty would come to power in 1270 and consolidate the Christian Ethiopian kingdom that the European myth of "Prester John" — a legendary Christian king of the East whom the Crusaders kept hoping to make contact with — was vaguely groping toward (Kingdom of Aksum Ch 8).

In Mesoamerica, the Postclassic Maya kingdoms continued under the regional power of Mayapán (Maya Civilization Ch 6); in the Andes, the Wari empire had collapsed and the regional successor states were consolidating around Chimor on the Peruvian coast (Andean Kingdoms Ch 8 and Middle Horizon Empires Ch 8).

In the Pacific, the Polynesian voyaging culture had reached the easternmost limits of its expansion at Aotearoa (New Zealand) and Rapa Nui (Easter Island) sometime in the thirteenth or fourteenth centuries (Polynesian Voyagers Ch 4 and Ch 6).

The Mongol shock and the High Medieval European boom were both real, but they were two episodes in a much larger thirteenth-century world history that was simultaneously absorbing the Mongol arrival, building the Mali Empire across the Sahara, settling the eastern Pacific, and continuing the long Mesoamerican and Andean cultural traditions.
The High Middle Ages had been one Eurasian civilization recovering from a long slump and rebuilding its institutional base.
By 1300, Latin Europe was a player on the Eurasian stage again.
Whether the Late Middle Ages would consolidate that recovery or break it down was an open question — and the answer would turn out to be both.
But that is the next volume.

chapters.title: The Fall and the Migration Period
sentences: The Western Roman Empire ended on a specific day.
The day was September 4, 476.

The Germanic general Odoacer (OH-doh-AY-ser, of probable Scirian or Hunnic background) walked into the imperial palace at Ravenna, deposed a teenage emperor named Romulus Augustulus (ROM-yoo-lus aw-GUS-tyoo-lus, whose name contained both Rome's legendary founder and its first emperor — an irony that even contemporaries noticed), exiled him to a country villa in Campania on a generous pension, and sent the imperial regalia to Constantinople.
Odoacer informed the eastern emperor Zeno that the western half of the empire no longer needed an emperor of its own.
He, Odoacer, would govern Italy as king on Constantinople's behalf.
It is the most anticlimactic ending in world history.
There was no battle.
There was no last stand.
There was no burning of the city.
There was a man with too many soldiers walking into a palace full of paperwork and informing a teenager that his services were no longer required.
Romulus Augustulus survived for years in genteel retirement and we don't know exactly when he died.

This is the conventional end of antiquity and the conventional start of the Middle Ages. (Ancient Rome Ch 10 covers the same event from the Roman side and explains the eighty-year cascade of catastrophes that preceded it.) The actual texture of the moment, though, was not ending.
It was continuing-under-new-management.
The Roman Senate continued to meet.
The Roman bureaucracy continued to function.
The bishops of the Catholic Church continued to administer their dioceses.
Latin continued to be the language of literacy across the former Western provinces.
The aqueducts continued to bring water into cities that continued to be called by their Roman names.
The change was real and it was profound, but it was not the kind of change that announces itself with trumpets.

It was the kind that you only see clearly two or three centuries later, when you look back and realize that the imperial postal service has stopped running, the senatorial families have intermarried with Gothic dukes, the cities have shrunk to a third of their former population, and somebody is plowing a field across what used to be the forum.

This chapter is about the long century after 476 — the Migration Period (German Völkerwanderung, "wandering of peoples") in which the Germanic confederations that had been pushing across the Roman frontier for two centuries finally settled down, subdivided the western provinces among themselves, and started building the kingdoms that would eventually become the medieval European states.
The Germanic peoples who took over the West were not a single group.

They were a collection of tribal confederations speaking related but distinct Germanic languages (the same language family that would eventually produce English, German, Dutch, the Scandinavian languages, and Yiddish), arriving on the western Roman frontier from different directions over roughly two centuries.

A short roster, because the names matter: The Visigoths (VIH-zee-goths, "Western Goths") had crossed the Danube into Roman territory as refugees in 376, defeated the eastern emperor Valens at Adrianople in 378, sacked Rome in 410, and eventually settled in southern Gaul and Spain, where they founded a Visigothic kingdom that lasted until the Arab conquest of 711 (the conquest, and the eight-century Islamic civilization that followed it, is told in its own narrative, al-Andalus; the complete Gothic story from Scandinavian origins through Adrianople, the sack, the Toulouse kingdom, and the Visigothic kingdom of Toledo is the subject of the Goths narrative).
The Ostrogoths (OS-troh-goths, "Eastern Goths") followed somewhat later and ended up in Italy, where their king Theodoric ruled from 493 to 526.

The Vandals (the same Germanic word that survives in our "Vandalism" — though the connection is a 17th-century coinage, not a fair description of the actual Vandals) crossed the Rhine in 406, marched through Gaul, swept down through Spain, crossed to North Africa in 429, captured Carthage in 439, and built a Vandal kingdom in the richest province of the former Western Empire that controlled the western Mediterranean grain supply for nearly a century (the full Vandal story within the broader Migration Period collapse is told in the Migration Period narrative).
The Franks (the people who would eventually give France its name) settled in northern Gaul.

They were less mobile than the others — they expanded gradually from a homeland on the lower Rhine rather than migrating across the entire continent — and they would prove to be the most important of all.
The Burgundians settled in the upper Rhône valley and gave their name to the region of Burgundy.

The Anglo-Saxons — a confederation of Angles, Saxons, and Jutes from the North Sea coast of modern Germany and Denmark — crossed to Britain in the fifth century, displaced the Romano-British inhabitants, and founded the small kingdoms that would eventually become England (the full Anglo-Saxon story, from the last Roman withdrawal through the conversion, the Northumbrian golden age, and the eve of the Vikings, is told in the Anglo-Saxon England narrative).

The Lombards (Latin Langobardi, "Long-Beards") arrived last, crossing the Alps into Italy in 568 — almost a century after Romulus Augustulus's deposition — and undoing most of what Justinian's reconquest had achieved (Chapter 2).
These are not, despite what older textbooks sometimes implied, separate races physically distinguishable from Romans.

The Germanic peoples had been in contact with Rome for centuries, often serving in the Roman army, intermarrying with the provincial population, adopting Roman material culture, and learning Latin alongside their own languages.

By the late fifth century the visible difference between a "barbarian" and a "Roman" was sometimes a haircut, sometimes a religion (most Germanic peoples were Arian Christians at this point, while the Roman provincial population was largely Catholic), sometimes a name, sometimes nothing visible at all.
The people who replaced the Roman state were thoroughly Romanized.
They had been the Roman state's army for a generation before they took it over.
The single most consequential decision of the entire migration period was made in the small Frankish town of Reims around 496.

The Frankish king Clovis I (KLO-vis, the Latinized form of Chlodovech — the same name eventually softened in modern French to Louis, which is why French kings would carry that name into the eighteenth century) accepted Catholic baptism from the bishop of Reims, Remigius.
This was a choice.
The other major Germanic peoples — the Visigoths, the Ostrogoths, the Vandals, the Burgundians — were already Christian, but they were Arian Christians.
Arianism was a fourth-century theological position, named after the Alexandrian priest Arius, that held Christ to be a created being, subordinate to God the Father, not co-eternal with Him.

The Council of Nicaea in 325 had condemned Arianism as a heresy and adopted the Nicene Creed, which declares Christ "of one substance with the Father." But Arianism had survived and prospered among the Goths in particular, who had been converted to Christianity in the fourth century by an Arian missionary bishop named Ulfilas before the Nicene victory had become decisive on the frontier (how Ulfilas and his invented Gothic alphabet carried Arianism to the Goths, and why it proved fatal to their kingdoms, is told in the Goths and the Migration Period narratives).
When the Gothic peoples migrated west, they brought their Arian Christianity with them.
Clovis was a pagan when he came to the Frankish throne in 481.
The Franks had not yet been Christianized at all; they still worshipped the old Germanic gods (the same gods we will meet again in Chapter 7 as the Norse pantheon — Wodan, Donar, Frigg, the lot).
The story preserved by the Frankish chronicler Gregory of Tours has Clovis vowing to accept the Christian God if a particular battle went his way.
The battle went his way.
He was baptized along with three thousand of his warriors at Reims, on Christmas Day 496 (or 508 — the chronology is contested).
The choice that mattered, though, was not Christianity vs. paganism.
It was Catholicism vs.

By choosing Nicene Catholicism — the religion of the Gallo-Roman bishops, the Roman provincial population, and the Eastern Roman Empire that still claimed nominal sovereignty in the West — Clovis aligned the Frankish monarchy with the entire surviving Roman religious establishment.
Every Catholic bishop in Gaul became, in effect, a partisan of the Frankish king.
The Arian Visigoths and Ostrogoths were heretics in the eyes of their Catholic Roman subjects, which would always be a structural weakness.
The Frankish kings were not.

When Clovis defeated the Visigothic king Alaric II at the Battle of Vouillé (voo-YAY) in 507 and pushed the Visigoths back across the Pyrenees, the Catholic Gallo-Roman population of southern Gaul welcomed him as a liberator from heretical rule.
The decision to be Catholic rather than Arian is one of the great hinges of European history.
Without it, Francia would have been a heretic kingdom — a hostile religious enclave inside Catholic Christendom — rather than the eventual political backbone of Latin Europe.

The Carolingian-papal alliance of the eighth century (Chapter 4), Charlemagne's coronation as Roman emperor (Chapter 5), the entire medieval entanglement of French royal power with the institutional church — all of it traces back to a Frankish warlord's calculated decision to accept the religion of his Roman subjects in 496.
Clovis ruled until 511 and founded the Merovingian (mer-oh-VIN-jee-an, named after a legendary ancestor Merovech) dynasty that would govern Francia for the next 250 years.
The Merovingians were not an impressive lot of rulers, on the whole.

They had a chronic tendency to die early (palace politics, dynastic struggle, occasional violence at the dinner table), and the kingdom was repeatedly subdivided among multiple sons, leading to civil wars among brother-kings.
By the seventh century the Merovingians had become rois fainéants — French for "do-nothing kings" — figureheads over a state actually run by hereditary chief stewards called mayors of the palace.
By the early eighth century the mayors were the de facto kings of Francia (Chapter 4).
But Clovis's choice held.
The Frankish kingdom remained Catholic.
And it remained the kingdom in the West with the closest religious-political alignment to surviving Roman institutions.
While the Franks were settling into northern Gaul, Italy went through its own version of the same process under a king who deserves more attention than he usually gets.
Theodoric the Great (THEE-oh-dor-ik, ruled 493–526) was an Ostrogothic king who had grown up as a hostage at the imperial court in Constantinople.
