He spoke Greek, had been educated in Roman literature, and understood the eastern Roman political world from the inside.

In 488, the eastern emperor Zeno — the same Zeno who had received Romulus Augustulus's regalia twelve years earlier — sent Theodoric and his Ostrogoths west with a commission: dispose of Odoacer, take over Italy, and rule it as the empire's deputy.
This solved two problems at once: it removed the troublesome Ostrogoths from Constantinople's borders, and it brought Italy back under nominal imperial authority.
Theodoric did the job.
In 493 he murdered Odoacer at a banquet in Ravenna (the chronicle says Theodoric himself swung the sword and split Odoacer in half, though the detail is suspect) and assumed the kingship of Italy.
He then proceeded to govern the country for thirty-three years with a sophistication and lightness of touch that no later medieval ruler would match for centuries.
Theodoric's Italy was a curious hybrid.
He kept the entire Roman senatorial bureaucracy in operation — the same officials who had administered the late western empire continued to administer it under Theodoric.
He kept the Roman Senate, gave it ceremonial honors, and consulted it (more or less) on important questions.
He kept the Roman law for his Roman subjects and used Gothic law for his Gothic ones — a "personal law" system in which your legal code depended on your ethnicity rather than your geography.
He minted coins with his portrait on the reverse and the eastern emperor's portrait on the obverse, advertising the constitutional fiction that he ruled as Constantinople's appointee.
He sponsored the rebuilding of Roman public buildings — the famous Mausoleum of Theodoric in Ravenna, with its enormous monolithic dome carved from a single block of Istrian limestone, still stands.
He employed two of the great late-antique intellectuals as his ministers.
Boethius (boh-EE-thee-us, c. 480–524), a Roman aristocrat who had translated Aristotle into Latin and written treatises on arithmetic and music, served as Master of Offices at Theodoric's court.

Cassiodorus (kass-ee-oh-DOR-us, c. 485–585), another Roman senator, served as Theodoric's secretary, wrote the official correspondence (which survives — the Variae — and is one of the great primary sources for Ostrogothic Italy), and was eventually placed in charge of Roman law in the kingdom.
But Theodoric's Italy had a structural problem.
He was an Arian Christian; his Roman subjects were Catholic.
As long as relations between the kingdom and Constantinople were good, the religious gap could be papered over.
When relations broke down — Constantinople began to suppress Arianism inside the eastern empire in the early 520s — Theodoric's situation became precarious.
He grew paranoid.
He convinced himself that the Roman senatorial class was conspiring with Constantinople against him.
In 523 he had Boethius arrested on charges of treason and corresponding with the eastern emperor.
He had Boethius's father-in-law, the senator Symmachus, arrested with him.
Boethius was executed in 524 after months in prison.

While awaiting execution he wrote The Consolation of Philosophy — a dialogue in mixed prose and verse between himself and the personification of Philosophy, who consoles him by walking him through the classical doctrines about fortune, providence, the nature of evil, and the relationship of human freedom to divine foreknowledge.
The book is the deepest statement of late-antique philosophical synthesis between Plato, Aristotle, the Stoics, and Christian theology.

It would become the most widely read philosophical work of the entire Middle Ages, translated into every European vernacular — including Old English by King Alfred himself in the late ninth century (Chapter 7), and Middle English by Geoffrey Chaucer in the late fourteenth.
Theodoric died in 526, two years after Boethius's execution.
His Ostrogothic kingdom would survive him by less than three decades before Justinian's eastern Roman armies destroyed it (Chapter 2).

But the Italy he had governed — Roman bureaucracy, Roman law, Roman cities, Catholic bishops, classical learning still alive at the level of high culture — was the closest thing to a successful late-antique synthesis between the old empire and the new Germanic rulers.

It was also a preview of what the early medieval west might have looked like if the eastern Roman reconquest and the Lombard counter-invasion had not turned Italy back into a war zone for two centuries.

The Roman senator and minister Cassiodorus, who had served Theodoric and lived through the catastrophe of Justinian's wars in Italy, retired around 540 to his family estate in southern Italy and founded a monastery there called Vivarium (vih-VAH-ree-um, "fish-pond," after the artificial fishponds on the property).
What he did at Vivarium matters out of all proportion to its size or its survival.

Cassiodorus had watched the secular Roman intellectual establishment collapse — the senatorial families dying out or fleeing, the public schools closing, the government chancery shrinking, the supply of new educated men drying up.

He realized that if classical Latin literature was going to survive at all, it would have to survive inside the church, in the only institution that still had a continuous reason to keep teaching young men to read Latin.

So at Vivarium he set up a deliberately learned monastic program: monks would copy not just biblical and patristic Christian texts but also pagan classical works — Cicero, Virgil, Horace, the technical writers on astronomy and grammar — on the principle that these were necessary for a properly educated reader of scripture.
He wrote a handbook for the program called the Institutions of Divine and Secular Learning, which became the model for medieval monastic education.

The principle that monasteries should preserve the classical literary heritage — not just Christian texts — entered the medieval educational tradition through Cassiodorus's example, and it would become the institutional reason why most surviving Latin classical literature exists at all.
Vivarium itself did not survive; we don't know exactly when it closed.
But the model survived.
Two centuries later the Carolingian scholars at Aachen would adopt exactly Cassiodorus's principle and apply it on an empire-wide scale (Chapter 5).

And nine hundred years later, when Italian Renaissance humanists like Petrarch went hunting for lost classical manuscripts, the books they found in monastic libraries had survived because Cassiodorus and his successors had put the right idea into the right institution at the right moment.
The thread is that direct.
The other essential figure of the Migration Period in the West is the bishop.
Bishops are the social load-bearing structure of late antiquity in a way that is hard to overstate.
The Roman empire had organized itself, by the fourth century, around a network of city-based bishoprics.
Each major city had a bishop; the bishop had a permanent cathedral, a permanent staff, permanent property, and direct authority over the Christian community in his diocese.
When the western imperial government dissolved in the fifth century, the bishops did not.
They had landed property that nobody could easily take from them.
They had the loyalty of the urban population.
They had Latin literacy and administrative experience.
And they had the moral standing to negotiate with the new Germanic kings, who needed someone with social authority to talk to.
Across western Europe in the fifth and sixth centuries, the bishop becomes the principal figure of urban government.
In Gaul, bishops ransom captives from raiders, organize famine relief, build churches and hospitals, and manage relations between the surviving Gallo-Roman population and the new Frankish overlords.
In Spain, bishops convoke councils that issue both religious and civil legislation.
In Italy, the bishop of Rome — increasingly called the pope (from Greek pappas, "father") — emerges as the de facto civil authority of the city after the imperial administration leaves.

The institutional form of the medieval west is taking shape: a continent of small kingdoms, each with a king at the top and a network of bishops alongside him, with the bishops forming the connective tissue between the kingdoms because they all answer (more or less) to Rome.
We will pick up the popes properly in Chapter 3, with Gregory the Great.
The point for now is that when historians say "the Catholic Church inherited the Roman Empire," they don't mean the church became a state.

They mean that the Roman administrative system — the dioceses, the bureaucracy, the literate Latin record-keeping, the city-based civil authority — kept running inside the church after it stopped running outside it.

Cross-civ check: while the Western Roman Empire was dissolving into Germanic kingdoms in the fifth and early sixth centuries, the Eastern Roman Empire (Byzantine Empire Ch 1) was thriving — Justinian was about to come to the throne, the Hagia Sophia was about to be built, and the Roman state was about to attempt the western reconquest that Chapter 2 covers.
In Persia, the Sasanian Empire under the Sasanid kings was at the height of its rivalry with Byzantium, with the long Roman-Persian wars devouring resources on both sides (Persian Empire Ch 9).
In India, the Gupta Empire's classical period was tapering off into the regional kingdoms that would dominate the subcontinent for centuries (Gupta Empire).
In China, the Six Dynasties period had divided the country between rival northern and southern regimes — China would not be reunified until the Sui in 581 (Six Dynasties).
In Mesoamerica, the great pyramid-city of Teotihuacan was at or near its peak (Teotihuacan), and the Classic Maya city-states of the Yucatán were entering their golden age (Maya Civilization Ch 4–6).
The world that the early medieval west was joining was one in which it was, for the first time in five hundred years, a peripheral civilization rather than a dominant one.
It would take six centuries to climb back.

chapters.title: Justinian's Reconquest and the Plague
sentences: The story you usually get about the early Middle Ages skips Justinian.
This is a mistake.

The eastern emperor Justinian I (jus-TIN-ee-un, ruled 527–565) is the principal reason the early medieval west looks the way it does — not because of what he built, but because of what his attempted reconquest broke and what the plague that arrived during his reign did to everything else.
Byzantine Empire Ch 2 covers Justinian properly from the Constantinopolitan side.
This chapter covers what his reign meant for the western half of the former Roman world.
Justinian came to the eastern throne in 527 with an enormous ambition and a remarkable team.

The ambition was the renovatio imperii, the "renovation of empire" — the reunification of the eastern and western Roman worlds under a single emperor at Constantinople, recovering the lost provinces of the West that had been overrun by Germanic kingdoms in the previous century.

The team consisted of his wife Theodora (a former actress and possibly former prostitute who had become his closest political partner and the most formidable empress in Roman history), his commander Belisarius (bel-ih-SAH-ree-us, the great general who would conduct the western reconquest), his jurist Tribonian (who would codify Roman law), and his architects Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus (who would build Hagia Sophia).
Two of these projects were spectacular successes.
The third was a disaster.
The legal codification was the spectacular success that mattered most for the long term.
Tribonian's commission compiled the entire surviving body of Roman law — fifteen centuries of imperial decrees, juristic opinions, and case-law — into a single coherent corpus between 529 and 534.

The result was the Corpus Juris Civilis ("Body of Civil Law"), in four parts: the Code (imperial legislation), the Digest (juristic writings), the Institutes (a textbook for first-year law students), and the Novels (Justinian's own new laws).
The Corpus codified Roman jurisprudence at a level of sophistication that would not be matched anywhere in Europe for a thousand years.

It was promptly forgotten in the West (the Germanic kingdoms had their own Germanic law codes), survived intact in the East, and was rediscovered at Bologna around 1070 — at which point it triggered the rebirth of European legal scholarship and became the foundational text of every continental European legal system.
The legal code of modern France, Germany, Italy, Spain, and Latin America descends, by an unbroken chain of commentary, from the work Tribonian did in the 530s.
The architectural success was Hagia Sophia.
Anthemius and Isidore built the Church of the Holy Wisdom in Constantinople in just five years, dedicating it on December 27, 537.
Its 105-foot dome on pendentives (a structural device that lets a circular dome rest on a square base) was the largest enclosed space in the world for nearly a thousand years.
Justinian is supposed to have walked into the finished building on its dedication day and exclaimed "Solomon, I have surpassed thee" — referring to the Temple of Jerusalem.
The line is almost certainly invented, but it captures what he was doing.

Hagia Sophia is the architectural statement that the Roman Empire is not over, that its capital is now Constantinople, and that imperial Christianity can still build at a scale nothing in the West can rival.
The building still stands.
The third project — the western reconquest — was the disaster.
Justinian's reconquest started brilliantly.
Belisarius sailed for North Africa in 533 with an expeditionary force of perhaps 18,000 men and destroyed the Vandal Kingdom in a single campaigning season.
Carthage fell almost without resistance.
The Vandal king Gelimer surrendered.
The richest grain-producing province of the former western empire was back under Roman rule.

Belisarius returned to Constantinople in 534 to celebrate a triumph — the first formal Roman triumph since the early empire — with the Vandal royal treasury dragged through the streets of Constantinople behind him.
Then he was sent to Italy.
The Italian campaign opened equally promisingly: in 535 Belisarius captured Sicily, in 536 he took Naples, in 536 he occupied Rome unopposed, and in 540 he accepted the surrender of Ravenna.
The Ostrogothic kingdom of Italy seemed to have collapsed.
The Goths regrouped under a new king, Totila, who recovered most of Italy in the 540s.
Belisarius was recalled to Constantinople and Justinian's resources were stretched thin.
A second eastern Roman commander, the eunuch Narses, was eventually sent west with a larger army and finally crushed the Goths at the Battle of Taginae (552) and again at Mons Lactarius (553).
Italy, after twenty years of intermittent warfare, was nominally back under Roman rule.
But the campaigns had wrecked the country.
Italy in 535 had been the seat of Theodoric's sophisticated Ostrogothic kingdom — Roman cities still functioning, classical buildings still standing, Latin literacy still alive.
Italy in 555 was a war zone.
The cities had been besieged repeatedly, sometimes by both sides in succession.
Rome itself had been besieged five times during the Gothic War, with the population dropping from perhaps 800,000 in 400 to perhaps 30,000 in 600.
The aqueducts had been cut by besieging armies and never properly repaired.
The senatorial families had been killed, dispersed, or impoverished.
The agricultural countryside had been devastated.

The recovery Justinian's armies had achieved was a recovery only in the technical sense that the territory was now in imperial hands — there was very little left of what the territory had previously been.
A third campaign in the western Mediterranean recovered a strip of southern Spain from the Visigoths in 552.
This was Justinian's high-water mark.
The Mediterranean was once again, just barely, a Roman sea.
It would not stay one for long.

In 541, while Belisarius was being recalled from Italy and Justinian was negotiating with the Goths, the Bubonic plague arrived in Pelusium in Egypt, almost certainly carried by ship from East Africa or India along the Red Sea trade routes.
By 542 it had reached Constantinople.
Within a few years it had spread across the entire Mediterranean basin and as far north as Britain.
The first wave killed an estimated quarter to a third of the eastern Mediterranean's population — perhaps 25 to 50 million people — over the course of a few terrible years.
Subsequent waves returned at roughly fifteen-year intervals through the rest of the sixth century and into the seventh, killing more.
This was the Plague of Justinian, the first of the great Eurasian bubonic plague pandemics.

The same disease (Yersinia pestis) and the same vector (rat fleas spreading from infected rodents to humans) would return as the Black Death in 1347 and kill another third of Europe (high-medieval-europe, late-medieval-europe).
But the Plague of Justinian came first, hit a Mediterranean world already destabilized by Justinian's wars, and inflicted demographic damage that took centuries to repair.

The contemporary historian Procopius (proh-KOH-pee-us, who served as Belisarius's secretary on the western campaigns and is the principal source for the period) wrote a horrified description of Constantinople during the plague's first wave: 5,000 to 10,000 people dying per day at the peak, bodies stacked in the streets because there was no one left to bury them, the imperial guards detailed to fling corpses into mass graves, the city emptied of normal commerce and worship.
The plague did things no other event of the period did.
It crashed the eastern empire's tax base by killing the taxpayers.
It crippled the army by killing the soldiers and the men of military age.
It hollowed out the cities by killing the urban populations who paid for and lived in them.
It destroyed Justinian's ability to consolidate his western conquests — there were no longer the men or the money to hold what Belisarius and Narses had taken.

And it set up the eastern empire for the catastrophes of the seventh century: the Persian invasion of 602, the Arab conquests of 632–650 (Byzantine Empire Ch 3), the loss of Syria, Egypt, and most of North Africa to the new Islamic caliphate, the reduction of the Eastern Empire from a Mediterranean superpower to a beleaguered Anatolian-Balkan state.
For the western Mediterranean, the plague meant that whatever Justinian's armies had done to recover would not be sustained.
The men were not there to garrison Italy.
The money was not there to rebuild it.
The administrative infrastructure was not there to absorb it.
When the next wave of Germanic invaders arrived in 568 — the Lombards crossing the Alps into northern Italy — there was almost no one to stop them.
The Plague of Justinian is one of the structural reasons the early medieval west looks the way it does.
The classical world had survived the fall of the Western Empire in 476 with most of its institutional substance intact under new management.
It did not survive the plague.
The half-century from 540 to 590 is the moment when late antiquity ends and the early Middle Ages begin, and the trigger is bubonic.

The Lombards (Latin Langobardi, "Long-Beards," from a tribal legend about the god Wotan playing favorites in a battle when the women of the tribe combed their hair forward over their faces and the god mistook them for additional warriors) were the last Germanic people to invade the former Western Empire.
They had been moving for centuries from somewhere in southern Scandinavia, through the Hungarian plain, down toward Italy.

In April 568 their king Alboin crossed the Alps with an army that included Lombards, Saxons, and a substantial number of Pannonian followers, and within four years they held everything in northern Italy north of the Po valley plus most of the central Italian highlands.

The Lombards left the eastern Romans (the Byzantines — for clarity I will start using the modern term from here onward, recognizing it is anachronistic; the people themselves continued to call themselves Romans) in possession of Ravenna, the corridor running across central Italy through Rome, and the southern coastal strip and Sicily.

The political map of medieval Italy that resulted — Lombard duchies in the north, papal Rome in the center, Byzantine pockets along the coasts — would persist for two centuries and shape Italian politics into the present.

The Lombards eventually converted from Arianism to Catholicism (the process took until the seventh century) and produced the most extensive Germanic law code of the period: the Edictum Rothari in 643, codifying Lombard customary law in 388 numbered chapters in Latin.
They built a kingdom centered on the city of Pavia (PAH-vee-ah).
They gave their name to Lombardy.
They were the people Charlemagne would conquer in 774 (Chapter 5).
For the moment, what matters is that the Lombard invasion completed the unraveling of Justinian's reconquest.
The Vandals had been destroyed and the African province kept (it would be lost to the Arabs in the 690s instead).
The Visigoths had been pushed back into Spain.
The Ostrogoths had been crushed.
But Italy — the ostensible prize of the western reconquest — was now in the hands of yet another Germanic kingdom, this time one that the eastern empire had no resources to dislodge.
By 600, the Mediterranean was no longer a Roman sea.
It would not be again.
Justinian's reconquest was the last serious attempt to restore the political unity of the late-antique world.

The next emperor to even attempt something on a comparable scale — Charlemagne in 800 — would attempt it from the wrong end of the Mediterranean, on a much smaller scale, and explicitly as an outsider claiming the inheritance.

What happened to the cities is worth pausing on, because the urban collapse of the sixth and seventh centuries is one of the structural facts of the early medieval west, and most modern readers underestimate it.
A late-Roman city of 50,000–100,000 people was a substantial place: forum, basilica, theater, baths, aqueducts, paved streets, multi-story masonry buildings, public food distribution, regular trade.

By 700 most of these cities had shrunk to villages of 1,000–5,000 people, often relocated from the original Roman site to a more defensible hilltop nearby, with the old urban infrastructure crumbling or actively dismantled for building stone.
The aqueducts stopped functioning because there was no one with the engineering knowledge to maintain them and no one with the political authority to fund them.
The baths closed.
The theaters closed.
The public food distribution stopped.
The economy ruralized.

Long-distance trade survived in luxury goods (silk, spices, slaves, swords) but the volume bulk-trade in olive oil, wine, and grain that had moved across the Mediterranean for centuries dropped to a fraction of late-Roman levels — with measurable consequences in the archaeological record (fewer amphorae, fewer shipwrecks, fewer coins struck).

This is the classic "Pirenne Thesis" image of the early medieval west — the Belgian historian Henri Pirenne argued in the 1930s that it was the Arab conquests of the seventh century that broke Mediterranean trade and produced the deep ruralization of the West.

Modern archaeology suggests Pirenne was partly right and partly overdramatic: the trade collapse was real, but it had begun in the sixth century with the plague and the Italian wars, not the seventh with the Arabs.
Either way, the urban infrastructure of the late Roman west did not survive.

What survived instead were two things: the church, in the persons of bishops who continued to occupy the old Roman cities even after the cities had shrunk to a fraction of their former size; and the monastery, a new institution we will meet properly in Chapter 3 that was just becoming a major social presence in the West.
The monastery especially would carry the late-antique intellectual and administrative tradition into the early medieval centuries.
Without it, the early Middle Ages would look much darker than they actually do.
One more thing happened during Justinian's reign that turned out to matter, though nobody at the time saw it.

In 552 — the same year Narses crushed the Goths at Taginae — a pair of Christian missionary monks slipped out of China with silkworm eggs hidden in hollow bamboo canes and brought them west to Justinian's court.

Sericulture — the cultivation of silkworms and the production of silk — had been a Chinese monopoly for two thousand years, with all the profits of the long Silk Road trade flowing through Chinese and central-Asian intermediaries to reach Constantinople.
The smuggled eggs broke the Chinese monopoly.
Within a generation Byzantine workshops were producing their own silk.

The Byzantine silk industry — concentrated at Constantinople, Thebes in Greece, and a few other centers — became one of the great state-controlled luxury industries of the early Middle Ages, its products reaching western European courts as diplomatic gifts that established Byzantine prestige across Christendom.
The episode is a small reminder that the early medieval west was never sealed off from the rest of Eurasia.
The Mediterranean trade networks contracted but they did not disappear.

The wider world kept supplying western Europe with religious ideas (from the Christian East), with goods (silk, spices, slaves, silver coinage), and occasionally with technologies (the stirrup, the horse collar, eventually the lateen sail).
The west was peripheral in this period in a way it had not been before, but peripheral is not isolated.

Cross-civ check: while Justinian was attempting his western reconquest and the plague was eviscerating Constantinople, China was about to be reunified by the Sui dynasty in 581 after three centuries of division (Six Dynasties, then Tang-Song China).
The Gupta Empire in India had collapsed around 550 under Hunnic pressure (Gupta Empire Ch 8).
The Sasanian Persians were locked in their long final war with Byzantium that would exhaust both empires and leave them defenseless against the Arab onslaught (Persian Empire Ch 9).

In Mesoamerica, Teotihuacan was burning around 550 (Teotihuacan), the Maya Classic period was at its height (Maya Civilization Ch 5–6), and Tiwanaku in the Andes was beginning the long ascent that would make it one of the great Andean civilizations (andean-kingdoms).

The Plague of Justinian, by some estimates, may have reached as far as Britain by 549 and southern China by the seventh century — a genuinely intercontinental disaster that prefigured the Black Death by 800 years.

chapters.title: Christianizing the West
sentences: The early medieval west was Christianized by monks.
This is not the romantic version of Christianization — there were no soaring sermons in great cathedrals, no popular conversions en masse.

It was conducted, slowly, between roughly 500 and 800, by small groups of celibate religious men setting up communal religious houses on the frontier of pagan Europe and waiting for the locals to come to them.
The model was invented in late-antique Egypt and Syria.
It was adapted for the West by a single man — Benedict of Nursia — and then propagated by Irish missionaries from a marginal Atlantic island that the Roman Empire had never even tried to conquer.
By 800 the monastic system Benedict had outlined was the principal religious-cultural-economic infrastructure of Latin Europe.
This chapter is about how that happened.

Monasticism — the practice of religious withdrawal from ordinary society into communities devoted to prayer, manual labor, and ascetic discipline — was a Christian invention of the late third century.

It started in the deserts of Egypt with hermits like Antony the Great (the original "desert father," who lived alone in the eastern desert from roughly 270 to 356, attracting disciples who imitated his life).

It quickly evolved from solitary anchorite life into communal cenobitic monasticism — monks living together under a common rule and an abbot — pioneered by figures like Pachomius in fourth-century Egypt.
By 500 there were monastic communities scattered across the Christian East: in Egypt, in Palestine, in Syria, in Cappadocia.
The model spread to the West, but slowly.
There were monastic experiments in fifth-century Gaul and Italy, but they were small, scattered, and operated under varying rules borrowed haphazardly from the East.
What the West did not have was a single, coherent, practical monastic rule that could be adopted by any community anywhere and produce a functional monastery.
That is what Benedict of Nursia (BEN-eh-dikt, c. 480–547, "Nursia" being a small town in central Italy) provided around 530.

Benedict's biography is sketchy — almost everything we know comes from the Dialogues of Pope Gregory the Great, written half a century after Benedict's death and thick with edifying miracle stories that may or may not be reliable.

The basic outline: he was born to a moderately well-off Roman family, sent to Rome to study, dropped out in disgust at the dissolute student life of late-antique Rome, became a hermit in a cave at Subiaco for several years, attracted disciples, eventually founded the monastery of Monte Cassino on a hilltop in central Italy around 529, and spent the rest of his life there as abbot writing and refining his monastic rule.
The Rule of Saint Benedict is one of those documents whose practical impact is enormous and whose actual contents are unspectacular.

It is a short book — about 30,000 words, the length of a modern paperback — divided into 73 short chapters covering everything from how to run an election for an abbot to what kind of bread to serve in Lent.

It prescribes a balanced day for each monk: about eight hours of prayer (the eight canonical "hours" of the divine office, from Matins before dawn through Compline at nightfall), six hours of manual labor, four hours of private reading.

It requires three vows from each monk: obedience (to the abbot and the rule), stability (to the specific monastic community he has joined, for life), and conversion of life (a continual moral and spiritual reform).
It establishes the abbot's authority but constrains him by requiring that he consult the senior monks on important decisions and the entire community on the most important.

It prescribes hospitality to all strangers, "for every guest is to be received as Christ." It legislates the diet, the clothing, the punishments, the night office, the care of the sick, the admission of children, and a hundred other practical matters of running a household of religious men in a self-sufficient agricultural community.
The Rule's defining quality, in the words of the great twentieth-century Benedictine historian David Knowles, is moderation.
It is harder than the lives of the desert fathers (Egyptian monks who fasted on bread and water and slept on stone) but easier than the lives of the most ascetic Eastern monks.
It assumed monks who were ordinary men trying to live an extraordinary religious life, not spiritual athletes attempting heroic feats.
It worked everywhere it was tried.
By the seventh century it had spread across most of western monastic communities.
By the ninth century it was, by Carolingian decree (Chapter 5), the universal monastic rule of the Latin west, binding on every monastery from Ireland to Italy.

What Benedict had built was an institutional template — a portable model for a self-sufficient religious community of about 30 to 100 men that could be set up almost anywhere, would feed itself, would educate its own next generation, would maintain a library and copy books, would provide hospitality to travelers, and would serve as a stable cultural center in a region that had little else.
Multiplied across thousands of monasteries over four centuries, this template became the basic infrastructure of medieval European culture.

Almost every Latin classical text that survives — Cicero, Virgil, Tacitus, Livy, the technical writers, the entire surviving corpus — survived because Benedictine monks copied it onto fresh parchment when the original was wearing out.
Without Benedict, almost nothing of Latin literature would exist today.
He was not trying to save Latin literature.
He was trying to save souls.
The literature came along for the ride because his Rule required monks to read, and to read you have to have books, and to have books you have to have someone copying them.
Monte Cassino itself, where he wrote the Rule, has had a complicated afterlife.
The Lombards destroyed it in 577.
It was rebuilt.
Saracen pirates sacked it in 883.
It was rebuilt.
An earthquake leveled it in 1349.
It was rebuilt.
The Allies bombed it flat on 15 February 1944 during the Italian campaign of World War II, on the (mistaken) assumption that German troops were using it as an observation post.
It was rebuilt.
The original sixth-century building does not survive in any meaningful sense; the current monastery is essentially a postwar reconstruction.
But the Rule survives, and it is the same rule Benedict wrote.
While Benedict was building Monte Cassino, an entirely separate monastic tradition was developing on the absolute opposite end of the western world.
Ireland had never been part of the Roman Empire.
The Romans had looked at it from the Welsh coast, said no thank you, and gone back to Britain.
Christianity had reached the island in the fifth century, traditionally by way of St.
Patrick — a Romano-British Christian who had been kidnapped as a teenager by Irish slavers, escaped, became a priest, and returned around 432 as a missionary.

Patrick is mostly legendary in detail (he probably did not actually drive the snakes out of Ireland — there had never been any snakes in Ireland, the climate is wrong) but he is solidly historical in outline; the Christianization of Ireland really did happen in the fifth century, and it really was largely accomplished by missionaries from Roman Britain.
What happened next was unusual.
Ireland adopted Christianity but it adopted Christianity into a society that had no cities, no Roman bishops, no late-antique civic infrastructure.

The result was a distinctively Irish form of Christianity in which the basic religious unit was not the urban diocese (as in continental Christianity) but the monastery — a religious-agricultural community usually founded on land donated by a local king, often with the king's family providing the abbot.
The abbots of these Irish monasteries became the principal religious authorities in the country, often outranking the bishops.

Monastic life in Ireland tended toward the ascetic — Irish monks were famous for fasting all night standing in cold rivers, for elaborate self-imposed penances, and for peregrinatio pro Christo, "pilgrimage for Christ," which meant leaving Ireland forever to go preach Christianity in foreign lands as an act of religious self-exile.
The masterpiece of Irish monasticism was Iona (eye-OH-nuh), founded by the monk Columba (kuh-LUM-buh, also called Colmcille, c. 521–597) on a small Hebridean island off western Scotland in 563.
Iona became the mother house of an entire missionary network that Christianized Pictish Scotland and then northern England.

The monk Aidan crossed from Iona in 635 at the invitation of the Northumbrian king Oswald and founded Lindisfarne on a tidal island off the Northumbrian coast — the cradle of northern English Christianity.

The Lindisfarne community produced, around 715, the Lindisfarne Gospels: an illuminated manuscript whose dense interlaced page borders, intricate carpet pages, and zoomorphic capital letters are one of the masterpieces of Insular ("island," meaning Irish-British) art.
Other Irish monks fanned out across Europe.
Columbanus (different person from Columba) crossed to Gaul in 590 and founded a network of monasteries that included Luxeuil in Burgundy and Bobbio in northern Italy.
Irish missionaries reached Switzerland (founding St.
Gall), Germany (Würzburg, Salzburg), and even Iceland, where Irish monks were probably living before the Norse arrival in the ninth century.

The Book of Kells, made around 800 either at Iona or at Kells in Ireland (probably both — work began at Iona and finished at Kells after Vikings forced the community to evacuate), is the most spectacular surviving example of the Insular illumination style.
So the early medieval west had two monastic traditions — the Benedictine tradition rooted in Italy and gradually spreading north, and the Insular tradition rooted in Ireland and spreading south.
They eventually merged, with the Benedictine model winning out across most of the Continent.

But the Irish contribution was structural: it was Irish monks who carried Christianity to the pagan margins of northern Europe — Scotland, Northumbria, Frisia, parts of Germany — that the Roman missions had never reached, and Irish scriptoria that preserved a startling amount of Greek and Latin learning that had been lost on the Continent.
The point at which the Roman and Insular traditions had to be reconciled was northern England.

Northumbria in the seventh century was a kingdom with two competing Christianities: a Roman tradition descending from Pope Gregory's Augustine of Canterbury mission to Kent in 597, and an Irish tradition descending from Aidan's Lindisfarne foundation in 635.

The two had different ways of calculating the date of Easter (the most important feast of the Christian year), different styles of monastic tonsure (the haircut monks wore as a marker of their religious profession), and different relationships to broader Christendom.
King Oswiu of Northumbria convened the Synod of Whitby in 664 to settle the question.
The Roman side argued that the practices of the Roman tradition came directly from Saint Peter, the rock on whom Christ had founded his church.
The Irish side argued that their practices came from Saint Columba and the apostolic tradition transmitted through the Irish church.
Oswiu, asked to choose between Peter and Columba, made the political choice: he chose Peter.
The English church aligned itself with Rome.
The Irish-style monks at Lindisfarne who would not accept the Roman calendar withdrew to Iona; the rest of the English church adopted Roman practices.
The Synod of Whitby is a small event with large consequences.
It tied the English church into the broader continental Latin tradition rather than the more isolated Insular one.

It made possible the long English contribution to continental Christianity — the eighth-century English mission to convert Frisia and Germany, led by Boniface (a Wessex monk who became "the apostle of the Germans" before being killed by pagan Frisians in 754); the Northumbrian scholar Alcuin of York, who would join Charlemagne's court in 781 and lead the Carolingian Renaissance (Chapter 5); and the broader cross-Channel ecclesiastical traffic that knit the early medieval west into a single Latin Christian intellectual community.
It also helped produce the Venerable Bede (the most learned man in early-eighth-century Europe).

Bede (c. 673–735) entered the Northumbrian monastery of Wearmouth as a child of seven and never left it for the rest of his life — for the next sixty years he lived, prayed, studied, taught, and wrote at the twin monastery of Wearmouth-Jarrow.
His Ecclesiastical History of the English People, completed in 731, is the foundational source for early Anglo-Saxon history.

It is also the first major work to use Anno Domini dating systematically (counting years from the supposed birth of Christ), the convention that became universal in the Latin west and is still in worldwide use today as "AD" (or, in the modern secularized version, "CE").

Bede's textbook on the calendar — De Temporum Ratione, "On the Reckoning of Time" — taught generations of monks how to compute the date of Easter, including the standard medieval discussion of why the earth has to be a sphere (it's the only shape that produces the observed shadow of the earth on the moon during a lunar eclipse).
The flat-earth myth has Bede teaching the opposite.
Bede taught the opposite of the flat-earth myth.
While Bede was writing in Northumbria, the principal organizer of the western church was the bishop of Rome.
Pope Gregory I (the Great, ruled 590–604) is the single most important pope of the early medieval period.

Like Benedict before him and Cassiodorus before that, he was a Roman senatorial-class figure (he had served briefly as prefect of Rome before retiring to a monastic life around 575) who tried to use surviving Roman institutional skills to organize the post-Roman Christian world.
He became pope reluctantly in 590, served for fourteen years, and in that time set the model of medieval papal authority that every later pope would inherit.
Gregory's papacy did roughly four big things.
First, he organized famine relief and refugee management in a Rome that was a fraction of its former size, repeatedly besieged by Lombards, devoid of effective imperial protection.

He used the substantial papal estates (the patrimonium Petri) — agricultural land scattered across Italy, Sicily, and as far as Gaul, donated to the Roman church over centuries — to feed the urban poor and ransom captives from Lombard raids.
The papal administrative system that managed these estates became, in effect, the surviving administrative system of central Italy.
Second, he asserted papal primacy over the Western patriarchates with new clarity.

The pope had always had a special status in the Christian world as the bishop of the imperial capital and the supposed successor of Saint Peter, but the relationship between Rome and the other major patriarchates (Constantinople, Alexandria, Antioch, Jerusalem) had been one of theoretical equality.
Gregory asserted that the bishop of Rome had a special apostolic authority over the entire Latin west — over Gaul, Spain, Italy, Britain — that no other bishop possessed.
The assertion was not new but the systematic insistence was, and it set the long medieval pattern of papal centralization.
Third, he dispatched the Augustine mission to convert the Anglo-Saxons.

In 596 Gregory sent a Roman monk named Augustine (not the same as Augustine of Hippo, the great fourth-century theologian — a different Augustine entirely) and forty companions to Britain to attempt a missionary effort.
Augustine landed in Kent in 597, was politely received by King Æthelberht (whose Frankish wife was already Christian), and within a few years had baptized the king.
The Christianization of England would take another century to be substantially complete, but the see of Canterbury founded by Augustine remains the senior English archbishopric to this day.

The Augustine mission is also the structural reason the eventual English church aligned with Rome rather than with the Celtic tradition — a fact that mattered when the Synod of Whitby came to choose between them in 664.
Fourth, he codified the liturgical chant — a body of plainsong used in the Roman liturgy that became known as Gregorian chant and forms the foundational repertoire of western liturgical music.

Modern scholars are divided on how much Gregory personally contributed and how much was developed in the following two centuries by Carolingian cantors who attached his name to it for prestige; the standard current view is that "Gregorian chant" is mostly post-Gregory but that he probably did contribute to liturgical reform, and the attribution stuck for very good reasons of medieval branding.
The music is still sung today.
Gregory's papacy is the moment at which the medieval papacy comes into focus.

Earlier popes had been important figures, but Gregory was the first to combine the moral authority of the papal office with the administrative competence of the late-Roman senatorial class and to turn the combination into a coherent program of Western church organization.

He also wrote prolifically (commentaries on Job, the Pastoral Rule on the duties of bishops, the Dialogues including the life of Benedict) and was canonized as one of the four traditional Doctors of the Latin Church alongside Augustine, Jerome, and Ambrose.
By 700 the papal model Gregory had built was the organizing framework of western Christianity.
A note on what Christianization actually did, because popular accounts often conflate it with what it didn't do.

Christianization in the early medieval west did not convert the entire population overnight to a deeply held personal religious commitment of the kind that nineteenth-century Protestant readers were trained to expect.

Mass conversion in this period was a top-down phenomenon: a king accepted baptism, his warriors followed, and over the next several generations the population gradually adopted the new religion, with old practices either banned, syncretized, or quietly tolerated.

The peasant who burned a candle to a saint in 800 was often the descendant of a peasant who had burned a similar candle to a local spirit in 600 — and the saint and the spirit often had suspiciously similar attributes.
The line between "Christian practice with pagan survivals" and "pagan practice with Christian veneer" was fuzzy and stayed fuzzy for centuries.
The institutional church understood this perfectly and largely tolerated it.

What Christianization did do was put a bishop and (eventually) a parish priest in every settlement, give every settlement a calendar of religious feasts that organized the agricultural year, give every individual a baptismal record that established legal personhood, give every dispute a moral framework drawn from Christian ethics, and give the political ruler a religious authority that anointed his power.
It built the institutional infrastructure within which medieval European life would be lived.

The personal piety stuff — the deep individual conversion experience, the literate engagement with theological doctrine — would mostly come later, in fits and starts, with the high-medieval revival of urban preaching and (much later) with the Reformation.
In 700, the deep work of building that institutional infrastructure was about half done.
Kingdoms had Christian kings.
Monasteries dotted the landscape.
Bishops ran the cities.
Missionaries were still working at the pagan northern and eastern frontier — Frisia, Saxony, Bavaria, the Slavic lands beyond the Elbe.
Pope Gregory's organizational model was being applied almost everywhere from Spain to England.
The Catholic version of Christianity was on the way to being the universal religion of western Europe.
That uniformity was about to be tested by an outside force nobody had seen coming.

Cross-civ check: while the western European church was organizing itself under Gregory the Great and Bede, the Byzantine Empire was about to enter the catastrophic seventh century — the Persian invasion, the loss of Syria and Egypt, the Arab conquests, the Iconoclast controversy (Byzantine Empire Ch 3, Ch 4).
The Tang Dynasty in China had just begun its long classical period (Tang-Song China).
Buddhism was at its medieval peak in East Asia.

Aksum in highland Ethiopia was the southernmost outpost of Christian late antiquity, having converted to Christianity in the fourth century and now functioning as the only African Christian state outside the soon-to-be-conquered Egyptian and Nubian territories (Kingdom of Aksum).
The Islamic-led Arab armies were about to break out of the Arabian peninsula and rewrite the Mediterranean political map.

chapters.title: Mohammed's Wave and the Iberian Loss
sentences: In 732 — exactly a century after the death of the Prophet Muhammad in Medina — a Frankish army under Charles Martel met an Umayyad Arab raiding force on a road between Tours and Poitiers in central Gaul, and the Frankish line held.

The battle is one of the most famous events in early medieval history and the story is told in roughly the same shape in every textbook: the Arab tide that had swept across North Africa, Spain, and southern Gaul reached its high-water mark on a cold October day, the Franks held, the tide receded, and Christian Europe was saved.
That story is half right.
The Frankish line did hold and the Arab raiding force was repulsed.
But Tours was not the climax of a continental conquest project; it was a frontier raid, one of many, conducted by a regional commander rather than the central Caliphal government.
The "tide" had been receding for some time before Tours because the Umayyad center of gravity was busy with civil war.
And the long-term consequences of what had happened in the previous twenty years were so much larger than Tours that the battle is, by the standards of what it allegedly settled, almost a footnote.

The actual story of how Islam reached western Europe in the early eighth century is the story of Spain, Tariq ibn Ziyad, the Visigothic kingdom, and a permanent civilizational fault line that would not be erased until 1492.
The Islamic explosion out of Arabia between 632 (the year Muhammad died) and roughly 750 is one of the most rapid expansions in world history.
Islamic Golden Age Ch 1 covers the religious and political background from inside the new caliphate.

From the perspective of the western Mediterranean, the relevant chronology is: 632: Muhammad dies in Medina; his successors (the caliphs, "deputies") inherit a unified Arab state stretching across the Arabian peninsula 636: Arab armies destroy the Byzantine field army at the Battle of Yarmouk in Syria 637: Sasanian Persian capital of Ctesiphon falls 642: Egypt falls; Alexandria is captured; the western Roman grain breadbasket since the time of Augustus is now Muslim 670s: Arab armies push west across North Africa, founding the city of Kairouan in modern Tunisia as their base 698: Carthage falls; Roman/Byzantine Africa is gone 711: Arab armies cross from Morocco into Visigothic Spain In one human lifetime — eighty years from Muhammad's death to the conquest of Spain — Islam went from a regional Arabian movement to the dominant religious-political force of the southern Mediterranean rim, controlling territory from the Atlantic to the Indus, killing or absorbing the Sasanian Persian Empire, amputating two-thirds of the eastern Roman Empire, and destroying every Christian state along the southern Mediterranean coast.
By the time the Arabs reached Spain in 711, the eastern Mediterranean was already Muslim — Syria, Egypt, North Africa, all of it.
The southern Mediterranean was not just disputed territory; it was lost, and lost permanently.
Western Europe was being squeezed into the northwestern corner of the former Roman world.
The conquest of Spain itself was extraordinarily quick.
Spain in 711 was ruled by the Visigothic kingdom that had survived in the peninsula since being pushed out of Gaul by Clovis at Vouillé (Chapter 1).

The Visigothic kingdom was Catholic (since Reccared's conversion in 589) and reasonably sophisticated (it produced the most extensive law code of the western successor kingdoms and the great encyclopedist Isidore of Seville).
It was also riven by succession disputes and unable to mobilize effective military resistance.
In April 711, an Arab-Berber army of perhaps 7,000 men under the Berber commander Tariq ibn Ziyad crossed from Morocco at the strait that the Romans had called the Pillars of Hercules.
The strait took its medieval Arabic name from Tariq's first landing point on the European side: Jabal Tariq, "Mount Tariq" — softened in modern English to Gibraltar.
Tariq destroyed the Visigothic king Roderic at the Battle of Guadalete in July 711, killing the king and most of the Visigothic nobility in a single engagement.
Within seven years a series of follow-up campaigns had swept across nearly the entire Iberian peninsula.

Most of Spain became al-Andalus — the Arabic name for the Muslim portion of Iberia, eventually applied to Spain as a whole and the source of the modern Spanish region "Andalusia." Only a thin strip of Christian kingdoms survived in the northern mountains: the Kingdom of Asturias in the Cantabrian uplands (founded by the Visigothic noble Pelayo, who won a small skirmish at Covadonga around 722 that the later Christian Reconquista would memorialize as its founding moment), and a few Pyrenean valleys that would eventually become Navarre and the Basque country.
From these tiny mountain refuges, the Christian counter-conquest — the Reconquista — would creep south at glacial pace over the next 781 years, finally completing in 1492 with the fall of Granada.
But for the early medieval west, the immediate fact was: Spain was gone.

The largest single piece of the former western Roman Empire outside Italy, the most Romanized of the Germanic kingdoms, the home of Isidore of Seville and the most sophisticated Latin legal tradition in the West, had been absorbed in seven years into the new Islamic civilization.
The western Mediterranean was now bounded on three sides by Muslim power: the Maghreb, al-Andalus, and the sea between them dominated by Muslim raiders.

Islamic Golden Age Ch 7 covers the brilliant Andalusian civilization that grew up in conquered Spain — Cordoba, the great mosque, the philosophical and scientific work that would feed back into Latin Europe centuries later.

From the early-medieval Latin perspective, though, Spain was not yet a source of culture; it was a source of pirates, raids, and the permanent reminder that Christendom was no longer secure in its own western Mediterranean.
After Spain, the Arabs probed northward into Gaul.
They were not attempting a continental conquest in the way they had attempted Spain; the Pyrenees and the distance from Damascus made that impractical.
What they were doing was raiding — large armed forces crossing the mountains on summer expeditions, looting the wealthy monasteries and cities of southern Gaul, retreating with plunder before winter.
The Frankish kingdom these raids were probing was, by the early eighth century, a strange political entity.

Officially the kingdom was still ruled by the Merovingian dynasty Clovis had founded — but the actual Merovingian kings had become the rois fainéants, the do-nothing kings, and real power had drifted to the hereditary chief stewards of the royal household, the mayors of the palace.

The dominant family in this office was descended from Pippin of Herstal and his son Charles Martel (KHAR-uhl mar-TEL, ruled as mayor of the palace 718–741, "Martel" being a nickname meaning "the Hammer").
Charles Martel was, by every functional measure, the king of the Franks.
He commanded the army, conducted foreign policy, distributed offices, and had united most of Francia under his control by force in the 720s.

He just wasn't called "king." His grandson Charlemagne would later be called the model of the Carolingian dynasty; the dynasty itself takes its name from Charles Martel's grandfather, who was also called Charles, and the family is properly called Carolingian (kair-oh-LIN-jee-an, from Latin Carolus, "Charles").
When the Arab raiders began pushing across the Pyrenees in the 720s, Charles Martel was the man with the army to stop them.
The largest of these raids came in 732.

The Umayyad governor of al-Andalus, Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi, led a major expedition north that sacked Bordeaux and was advancing toward the wealthy abbey of Saint-Martin at Tours when Charles Martel's Frankish army intercepted him on a road south of the city.
The exact site is debated; the engagement is variously called the Battle of Tours or the Battle of Poitiers depending on which nearby town you prefer.
The battle itself, by the surviving Arab and Frankish chronicle accounts, was conventional.
The Franks deployed in a tight infantry formation on a defensive position in wooded terrain that limited the use of Arab cavalry.
The Arabs attacked repeatedly; the Frankish line held.
Abd al-Rahman was killed; the Arab army retreated under cover of darkness; Charles Martel did not pursue.
The Franks took the field.

The medieval significance of the battle was enormously inflated by Frankish chroniclers (and later by Edward Gibbon and even later by nineteenth-century textbook writers) into the salvation of Christian Europe.
The actual significance was somewhat smaller.

Tours was one of many checks the expanding Caliphate received in the 730s — the Khazars in the Caucasus, the eastern Roman defense of Anatolia, internal Berber revolts in North Africa, and eventually the Abbasid Revolution of 750 — and the cumulative effect of all these checks was that the Umayyad expansion phase ended around mid-century.
The Caliphate did not retreat from Spain after Tours — al-Andalus was Muslim for another seven and a half centuries — but it stopped trying seriously to push north of the Pyrenees.

What Tours did do, even if the salvation-of-Christendom rhetoric oversells it, was establish Charles Martel's military reputation across western Europe and confirm the Carolingian family as the dominant force in Francia.
Within a generation his son Pippin would feel confident enough to depose the last Merovingian and put on the crown himself.
The deposition happened in 751, and it required the help of the pope.
Pippin the Short (PIP-in, also called Pepin III, son of Charles Martel) had inherited the office of mayor of the palace from his father in 741.
By 750 he was the most powerful man in the Frankish kingdom, but he was not the king.
The last Merovingian, Childeric III, sat on the throne — long-haired, ceremonial, useless.
Pippin wanted the title to match the power.
He needed religious cover for the deposition.
He turned to the pope because the pope needed him.
Pope Zachary (ruled 741–752) was facing the Lombards, who were once again pressing Rome from the north and threatening to absorb the Papal patrimonium and the city itself.
The Byzantine emperor was busy with Iconoclasm and had effectively given up on protecting Rome.
The pope needed a powerful military ally.
Pippin needed religious legitimation for a coup.
The two requirements lined up.

In 750, Pippin sent ambassadors to Pope Zachary with a single carefully framed question: "Is it good or not that someone with no royal power should be called king?" Zachary returned the answer: "Whoever holds the power should be called king" — so that there should not be a discrepancy between the title and the reality.
That was the green light.

In November 751, an assembly of Frankish nobles deposed Childeric III, sent him to the monastery of Saint-Bertin (where his hair was shaved off, ending the Merovingian dynastic claim, since the long royal hair had been a symbol of Merovingian sacral kingship), and elected Pippin king of the Franks.

Pippin was anointed with holy oil — a new ritual for Frankish royal accession, deliberately echoing the Old Testament anointing of King David by the prophet Samuel, and laying the foundation for the medieval theory that Christian kings ruled by sacred consecration.
The Carolingian dynasty had its throne.

Three years later, in 754, Pope Stephen II crossed the Alps in winter to come and personally re-anoint Pippin and his sons in Saint-Denis outside Paris — the first time a pope had ever traveled to Francia, and a public ceremony that sealed the Frankish-papal alliance.
In return, in 754 and 756, Pippin marched his army into Italy, defeated the Lombard king Aistulf, and donated the conquered Lombard territory in central Italy to the pope.

This was the Donation of Pippin: a strip of central Italy, including Ravenna and the corridor west to Rome, transferred from the Lombards to direct papal rule, becoming the Papal States that would survive as a temporal sovereign entity until Italian unification absorbed them in 1870.
The Donation of Pippin matters out of all proportion to its territorial extent.
It gave the papacy its own kingdom — a temporal political base that would let popes operate as independent international political actors for the next 1,114 years.

It permanently aligned the papacy with the Franks rather than with Constantinople — a re-orientation that would become decisive in the Iconoclasm controversy and the eventual East-West religious split (Byzantine Empire Ch 4, the Great Schism of 1054 in high-medieval-europe).

And it set the institutional model of the medieval Western political order: a partnership between the Frankish-derived emperor and the bishop of Rome, each legitimating the other, both claiming to rule over the rest of Christendom on different but complementary grounds.

The arrangement Pippin made in 754 is the political DNA of the Holy Roman Empire that would survive in some form until 1806 and of the medieval papacy that would survive in altered form to the present day.
Pippin's son Charlemagne inherited the framework.
The next chapter is what he did with it.

Cross-civ check: while the Arabs were conquering Spain and the Carolingians were inventing themselves in Francia, the Abbasid Revolution in 750 was overthrowing the Umayyad caliphs in the East and shifting the center of the Islamic world from Damascus to the new city of Baghdad (Islamic Golden Age Ch 1).
The Tang Dynasty in China was at its golden classical peak (Tang-Song China).
In Mesoamerica, the great Maya cities of the southern lowlands (Tikal, Palenque, Copán) were entering their late-Classic Florescence (Maya Civilization).
In the Andes, the Wari and Tiwanaku empires were the dominant powers (middle-horizon-empires).
In Polynesia, the great voyaging expansion across the Pacific was reaching New Zealand and Hawaii within the next two centuries (Polynesian Voyagers).
The early medieval west was, for the first time since Roman Britain, a small player in a much larger Eurasian system.

chapters.title: Charlemagne and the Carolingian Renaissance
sentences: Pippin the Short died in 768 and divided his kingdom (in the standard Frankish fashion) between his two sons, Charles and Carloman.
Carloman conveniently died three years later and Charles took the entire kingdom.

Charles ruled the Franks for the next 43 years, conducted 53 separate military campaigns, conquered or defeated the Lombards, the Saxons, the Bavarians, the Avars, and the Bretons, was crowned Emperor of the Romans by the pope on Christmas Day 800, sponsored a copying program that preserved most of surviving classical Latin literature, and is, by any reasonable standard, the most consequential figure of the early Middle Ages.
He is known to history as Charlemagne (SHAR-luh-mayn, French for Carolus Magnus, "Charles the Great").
His older Frankish-language nickname was Karl der Grosse in German and Karol Wielki in Polish — the same epithet in three different languages, all meaning the same thing.
His Latin name Carolus is the source of the modern name "Charles" and gives the Carolingian dynasty its name.
This chapter is about him, about what his empire did, and — perhaps most importantly — about what his copying program accomplished that nothing else in early medieval Europe came close to matching.
The military reputation comes first because the Carolingian Empire was founded on military success.

A short list of major Charlemagne campaigns: The Saxon Wars (772–804): a brutal 32-year project to conquer and forcibly convert the pagan Saxons of northern Germany (one of the four great Germanic confederations formed in the third-century crisis; their North Sea kin who crossed to Britain are the subject of the Anglo-Saxon England narrative, and the Danish consolidation the war triggered is told in the Vendel Age narrative).

Includes the infamous Massacre of Verden in 782, in which Charlemagne ordered the execution of 4,500 Saxon prisoners taken in a single battle, and the Capitulary on the Saxons of 785, which made it a capital offense to refuse Christian baptism, to eat meat in Lent, or to cremate the dead in pagan fashion.
The Saxon Wars are the moment at which the Carolingian project of Christian universalism shows its sharpest edge: conversion was offered, but conversion-or-death was the actual policy.

The Lombard Conquest (773–774): Charlemagne destroyed the Lombard kingdom of Italy in a single campaign, taking the Lombard capital of Pavia in June 774 and adding "King of the Lombards" to his Frankish title.
He took the Iron Crown of Lombardy (a Lombard royal regalia incorporating, by tradition, a nail from the True Cross) and the kingdom became part of the Frankish realm.
The Donation of Pippin was confirmed and extended; the popes now had a Frankish king as their permanent military patron in Italy.
The Bavarian Annexation (788): Charlemagne deposed the Bavarian duke Tassilo III, absorbed Bavaria into the Frankish kingdom, and pushed the eastern frontier to the Enns river.

The Avar War (791–803): the Avars were a steppe-nomad people who had occupied the Hungarian plain for two centuries and accumulated, through tribute extracted from Constantinople, an enormous treasure.
Charlemagne's armies destroyed the Avar Khaganate between 791 and 803.
The Frankish chronicler reports that the captured Avar treasure required fifteen ox-carts to haul back to Aachen.
The Spanish March (778 onwards): Charlemagne intervened in Muslim Spain in 778 in support of one Andalusian faction against another.

The expedition itself was inconclusive (and produced the rear-guard ambush at the Pass of Roncesvalles in which Roland died, eventually mythologized into the great vernacular epic La Chanson de Roland in the late eleventh century — the foundational text of medieval French literature).
But subsequent campaigns established a Frankish-controlled buffer zone south of the Pyrenees, the Spanish March, that included Barcelona by 801 and would eventually become Catalonia.
By 800, Charlemagne ruled an empire stretching from the Atlantic at the Pyrenees to the Elbe in the east, from the Italian peninsula in the south to the North Sea coast.
It was the largest political entity in western Europe since the western Roman Empire's high-imperial period.
It included all of modern France, almost all of modern Germany west of the Elbe, the Low Countries, Switzerland, northern Italy down to Rome, and a strip of northeastern Spain.
The fragmented post-Roman west had been (briefly) reassembled under a single ruler.
The fixed capital of this empire was Aachen (AH-ken, German; Aix-la-Chapelle in French — both names refer to the city's hot springs).

Earlier Frankish kings had been itinerant — they had moved constantly between royal estates, eating up the produce of each estate for a few weeks before moving on, because the agricultural surpluses of any single estate were not large enough to support a permanent court.

Charlemagne fixed his court at Aachen in the 790s, building a permanent palace complex that included the famous Palatine Chapel — an octagonal church modeled directly on Justinian's San Vitale in Ravenna, completed and consecrated around 805.
The chapel still stands; it is one of the few essentially intact early medieval buildings in northern Europe, and Charlemagne is buried in it.
Aachen was Charlemagne's deliberate statement that the Frankish kingdom was a permanent institution with a permanent capital, modeled on the imperial capitals of late Rome.
It also gathered around itself a court of the most learned men Charlemagne could recruit from anywhere in Latin Christendom — and from a few places outside it.
The most important of these was the Northumbrian scholar Alcuin of York (AL-kwin, c. 735–804).

Alcuin had been trained at the cathedral school of York under the heirs of Bede; by 781 he was the leading scholar in northern England (he also wrote the most vivid contemporary response to the Lindisfarne raid of 793, the human hinge between two narratives).
Charlemagne met him in Italy in 781, recruited him on the spot, and put him in charge of the palace school at Aachen.
For the next twenty years Alcuin was the principal intellectual of the Frankish court, the architect of what later historians would call the Carolingian Renaissance.
The Carolingian Renaissance was not a "rebirth" in the sense the later Italian Renaissance was — there was no rediscovery of lost classical learning, no overturning of medieval orthodoxy.

What it was was much more practical: a deliberate, top-down, empire-wide program to standardize Latin grammar, copy and preserve the surviving classical and Christian Latin literature, train a generation of administrators and clergy capable of reading and writing that Latin to a high standard, and reform the liturgy and the law on the basis of carefully copied authoritative texts.
It was, essentially, an empire-scale intervention to fix the manuscript and educational infrastructure of Latin Europe before it deteriorated any further.
The mechanism was the monastery.

Charlemagne issued capitularies (royal decrees on specific subjects, the basic legislative form of the Carolingian state) requiring every monastery and cathedral school in his empire to maintain a school for boys, to teach Latin grammar and the basic disciplines, to copy specified texts, and to send their best scholars to court.

The surviving capitularies on this subject — most famously the Admonitio Generalis of 789 — read like a modern Department of Education curriculum reform memo, full of practical instructions on what to teach and how.
The monasteries complied because Charlemagne could replace any abbot who didn't.
The result was the most significant book-copying program in European history.

Across the empire, in monasteries from Tours to Reichenau, scriptoria turned out fresh copies of every classical Latin text that the previous centuries' monks had managed to preserve, plus the entire surviving Christian Latin patristic corpus, plus the standard reference works (Isidore's Etymologies, the encyclopedias, the legal texts, the technical grammars).
A single Carolingian book historian estimates that around 7,000 manuscripts survive from the ninth century alone — more than from the previous five centuries combined.

Almost everything we have of Cicero, Tacitus, Livy, Suetonius, Lucretius, the Augustan poets, the technical writers — exists today because Carolingian monks copied them in the eighth or ninth century from earlier manuscripts that have not survived.
Without the Carolingian copying program, the great majority of Latin classical literature would simply not exist.
The script those monks used for the copies is the second consequential Carolingian invention: Carolingian minuscule.
The script needs a paragraph because it is one of those small technical things that turn out to have outsize cultural consequences.
Pre-Carolingian Latin scripts had a problem.

Late-Roman cursive had fragmented after the western collapse into a half-dozen regional national hands — Insular minuscule in Britain and Ireland, Visigothic minuscule in Spain, Beneventan minuscule in southern Italy, Merovingian cursive in Gaul, and so on.
Each was difficult to read for anyone trained in a different national hand.

The letters were cramped, often joined together (so that you couldn't tell where one letter ended and the next began), abbreviated heavily (saving parchment but requiring expert decipherment), and lacked any consistent spacing or punctuation system.
A Frankish monk reading a Visigothic manuscript was reading something close to a foreign alphabet.
Carolingian scribes — first at Corbie in northern France, then at Tours under Alcuin, then across the empire — developed a new script that solved all of these problems.

Carolingian minuscule was a clean, upright lowercase letterform, with separated letters of uniform height, generous spacing between words (a genuine Carolingian innovation — earlier Latin had often been written without spaces), consistent abbreviation conventions, and clear punctuation marks (the modern question mark and exclamation point are descended from Carolingian invention).
It was easy to read.
It was easy to teach.
It could be read by any literate person anywhere in the empire.

The script became the standard book hand of the Carolingian world by 800 and remained the dominant Latin script of Europe until it was replaced (very gradually) by Gothic textura in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries.
It was rediscovered in the fifteenth century by Italian Renaissance humanists hunting for ancient classical manuscripts.
They found Carolingian copies — clean, easy to read — and mistook them for the original ancient Roman hand.

They copied the script as their model for "ancient Roman" handwriting, called it littera antiqua ("ancient script"), and Italian Renaissance typesetters then turned it into the roman type of the new printing press.

The lowercase letters of every Western book printed in roman type since around 1470 — including this one — descend in unbroken visual lineage from a script developed in northern Frankish monasteries around 780.
The "humanist" lowercase letters of Italian printing are Carolingian.
The medieval contribution to the modern visual world is right there on every page.
Charlemagne's reign culminated, in symbolic terms, on Christmas Day 800.

He had spent the autumn of that year in Rome, helping Pope Leo III (a recent appointee whose election had been disputed and who had been physically attacked by Roman aristocratic opponents) reconsolidate his position.
On Christmas morning Charlemagne attended Mass at St.
Peter's basilica.

As he rose from prayer, Pope Leo placed a crown on his head and the assembled congregation acclaimed him: Carolo Augusto a Deo coronato magno et pacifico imperatori Romanorum, vita et victoria! — "Long life and victory to Charles, August, crowned by God, the great and peace-giving Emperor of the Romans!" It was the first time a Roman imperial title had been conferred in the West since 476 — three hundred and twenty-four years.
The political theology of the moment was complicated.
The Eastern Roman Empire (Byzantine Empire Ch 4) considered the Roman emperorship its own monopoly.

There was a Roman emperor at Constantinople in 800 — a woman, the Empress Irene, ruling as senior empress after blinding her son Constantine VI to take the throne — and the Byzantine position was that there could not be another.

Pope Leo, by crowning Charlemagne, was implicitly arguing that the Byzantine throne was vacant (because of Irene's gender or her usurpation, depending on which Latin commentary you read) and that the Roman imperial title had reverted to the West.
Charlemagne, by accepting the crown, was claiming to be the legitimate continuation of Augustus, Constantine, and Theodosius.

The Byzantines were furious and refused to recognize the title for over a decade. (They eventually accepted the formula that Charlemagne could be called basileus — "emperor" — but only of the Franks, not "of the Romans," which remained Constantinople's exclusive claim.) The Carolingian chronicler Einhard, in his later biography of Charlemagne, claimed that Charlemagne would not have entered the church that day if he had known what Leo was going to do — a face-saving claim probably written to manage the diplomatic awkwardness, since the entire ceremony was so clearly stage-managed in advance that nobody could have been surprised by it.

Whether Charlemagne was surprised or not, the coronation founded a political idea that would dominate medieval European politics for the next thousand years: the Holy Roman Empire as a Christian-Roman monarchy in the West, distinct from but structurally rivalrous with the Byzantine East, ruled by the Frankish-German emperor in partnership (and recurrent conflict) with the Roman pope.

The institutional realities would change repeatedly over the next millennium; the basic idea — that there is a properly Roman, properly Christian, properly imperial sovereignty in the West, not the same as either the local kingdoms or the universal church — survived all the changes.
The Holy Roman Empire itself, as a continuous institution, dates more accurately from Otto I's coronation in 962 (Chapter 8) than from Charlemagne's in 800.
But the model is Carolingian.
Charlemagne died at Aachen on January 28, 814, at the age of about 71.
He was buried, sitting upright on a marble throne wearing his imperial regalia, in the Palatine Chapel he had built.

The empire he had assembled passed intact to his only surviving legitimate son, Louis the Pious — a pious, scholarly, well-intentioned monarch whose reign would be consumed by civil wars among his own sons over the planned succession.
The empire would not survive Louis's death.
By 843 it would be permanently divided (Chapter 6).

But the cultural infrastructure Charlemagne had built — the Latin standardization, the copying program, the Carolingian minuscule script, the network of cathedral and monastic schools, the administrative apparatus of capitularies and missi dominici (royal inspectors who toured the empire enforcing decrees), the alliance between the Frankish crown and the Roman papacy — survived.
It survived the breakup of the empire.
It survived the ninth-century crises.
It survived the century of Viking and Magyar raids.

By the time the Ottonian dynasty rebuilt the eastern half into the Holy Roman Empire in the tenth century (Chapter 8), the Carolingian Renaissance's institutional residues were what they had to work with, and they were enough to anchor the recovery.
That is why Charlemagne is not remembered primarily for the territorial empire — which fragmented within thirty years of his death — but for the cultural project, which lasted.
The empire was a moment.
The script, the curriculum, and the saved books were a permanent inheritance.

Cross-civ check: while Charlemagne was building his empire and his palace school, the Abbasid Caliphate was at the height of the Islamic Golden Age under Harun al-Rashid (Islamic Golden Age Ch 2 — al-Rashid and Charlemagne were diplomatic correspondents, exchanging gifts including, by tradition, an elephant named Abul-Abbas).
The Tang Dynasty in China was at its classical peak, with the great poets Li Bai and Du Fu writing during exactly this period (Tang-Song China).
In the Andes, the Wari Empire was the dominant power on the Peruvian highlands (middle-horizon-empires).
In Mesoamerica, the great Classic Maya cities were entering their terminal collapse over the next century (Maya Civilization Ch 7).
In Polynesia, voyagers were settling Hawaii and pushing toward New Zealand (Polynesian Voyagers).
Charlemagne's empire was, by Eurasian standards of the early ninth century, a respectable but not exceptional medium-sized state.
The Tang and the Abbasids were both substantially larger and substantially more sophisticated.

What made Charlemagne consequential was not scale; it was that his cultural project happened to provide the institutional framework on which Latin Europe would build the much larger civilization of the High Middle Ages.

chapters.title: The Treaty of Verdun and the Carolingian Inheritance
sentences: Charlemagne's empire fell apart almost as soon as he was buried.

The reason was not external pressure (the Vikings were just starting to bite, but they had not yet reached the catastrophic phase that Chapter 7 covers) and not internal incompetence (Charlemagne's son and grandsons were perfectly competent monarchs by the standards of the period).
The reason was Frankish inheritance custom, which required that a king's lands be divided among his sons.
