This had not been a problem under Charlemagne himself, because his only surviving legitimate son when he died was Louis the Pious, who therefore got the entire empire.
Louis's three surviving sons all reached adulthood, all had their own ambitions, and all expected to inherit.

The Treaty of Verdun in 843 — twenty-nine years after Charlemagne's death — divided the empire into three pieces, drew the borders that would shape the political map of western Europe for the next millennium, and is the deep structural origin of the modern Franco-German divide.
This chapter is the story of that breakup and what it produced.
Louis the Pious (Latin Ludovicus Pius, ruled 814–840) was Charlemagne's only surviving legitimate son and inherited the entire empire intact.
He was a serious, scholarly, deeply religious monarch — the epithet "the Pious" was earned, not ironic — who took his duties as Christian emperor more solemnly than his father had.

He sponsored monastic reform under the great Benedictine reformer Benedict of Aniane (a different Benedict than the founder of the order, c. 747–821, whose program of strict observance to the original Rule of Benedict was made empire-wide policy at the Synod of Aachen in 817).

He pushed for stricter Christian behavior at court, banished some of the more theatrical late-Carolingian customs, and tried to govern as a proper Christian sovereign rather than a pagan-warlord-with-a-church-veneer.
The trouble was the succession.

In 817 — three years into his reign, and well in advance of any actual succession crisis — Louis issued a planning document called the Ordinatio Imperii ("Ordering of the Empire") that attempted to do something Frankish kings had never tried before: it set up a permanent inheritance scheme that would keep the empire intact across generations.
Louis's eldest son Lothair would inherit the imperial title and the bulk of the empire.
The two younger sons, Pippin and Louis the German, would receive subordinate kingdoms (Aquitaine and Bavaria) but would acknowledge Lothair as senior emperor.
This made dynastic sense (it preserved the empire as a single unit) but it was a radical departure from Frankish tradition (which would have given roughly equal shares to all three sons).
The plan was contested almost immediately and never really stabilized.
Things got worse in 823 when Louis's second wife, Judith of Bavaria, gave birth to a fourth son, Charles the Bald.
Now there was a child son who under the old custom should have received an inheritance share, and the question of how to fit him into the Ordinatio Imperii consumed the rest of Louis's reign.
Three civil wars broke out between Louis and his elder sons over the allocation.
Louis was deposed at the Field of Lies in 833, then restored, then subjected to public penance, then deposed again, then restored.
By the time he died in 840, the Frankish nobility had been picking sides for nearly twenty years and any consensus on the succession had collapsed.

The actual division came at Verdun (vehr-DUN, an old Roman town on the Meuse river in northeastern France) in August 843, after three years of further civil war among the three surviving brothers (Pippin had died in 838).
The eldest, Lothair I, had inherited the imperial title and the central position.
The middle brother, Louis the German, controlled the eastern Frankish lands.
The youngest, Charles the Bald, controlled the western Frankish lands.

The decisive moment had come in February 842, when Louis the German and Charles the Bald — recognizing that they would each be eaten by Lothair separately if they did not combine — met at Strasbourg and exchanged sworn oaths of mutual support against their elder brother.
Each swore in the other's vernacular language so that both armies could understand the oath being taken.
The text of those oaths survives, and it is a small linguistic miracle.

Louis the German swore in Old High German (the ancestor of modern German); Charles the Bald swore in what the document calls lingua romana rustica ("rustic Roman language") — and the surviving text is the earliest substantial document in any language that is identifiably French rather than Latin.

The Strasbourg Oaths of 842 are the document with which the French language enters the historical record. (Old High German has earlier surviving documents.) The oaths also demonstrate something the chroniclers of the period otherwise mostly leave implicit: by 842 the population of West Francia and East Francia were already speaking different languages and could not understand each other in the vernacular.
The cultural division between what would become France and what would become Germany was already emerging in the ninth century.
After Strasbourg, the war continued through 842 and into 843, until the three brothers finally agreed at Verdun to formal partition.

The settlement gave each brother a share roughly proportional to his current military strength: Charles the Bald (the youngest) received West Francia — the western Frankish lands stretching from the Atlantic east to roughly the Scheldt, Meuse, Saône, and Rhône rivers.
This is, very roughly, the territory of medieval and modern France west of the Rhône and east of the Atlantic.
Louis the German received East Francia — the eastern Frankish lands east of the Rhine, plus Bavaria, Saxony, and the Frankish territories in modern Germany.
This is, very roughly, the territory of medieval and modern Germany.

Lothair I kept the imperial title and received Middle Francia — a long, awkward strip running from the Low Countries (modern Belgium and the Netherlands) south through Lorraine and Burgundy to most of Italy, including Rome and the imperial capital of Aachen.

This was the wealthiest of the three shares (it included most of the major late-Roman cities of the empire and the imperial regalia) but it was also the most strategically incoherent — a thin north-south corridor with no natural defensive frontier and bordered by both his brothers.
Verdun is the deep structural origin of the modern political map of western Europe.
West Francia became France.
East Francia became Germany.
The unstable Middle Frankish strip in between would be fought over by France and Germany for the next 1,100 years — Lorraine, Alsace, Burgundy, the Low Countries, northern Italy.

The Franco-German contestation of these lands runs through the wars of Louis XIV in the seventeenth century, the Napoleonic wars, the Franco-Prussian War of 1870, both World Wars, and ends only with the European Coal and Steel Community in 1951 and the European Union that grew out of it.

The EU itself can be read as the long-deferred political resolution of the Verdun partition: a way of governing the Middle Frankish territories without either France or Germany having to dominate them militarily.
Lothair's Middle Frankish strip did not stay a single kingdom for long.

When Lothair died in 855 it was divided again among his three sons: Louis II received Italy and the imperial title; Lothair II received the strip from the Low Countries to Burgundy (which became known as Lotharingia, the source of the modern "Lorraine"); Charles received Provence.

Lothair II died without legitimate heirs in 869 and his uncles Louis the German and Charles the Bald promptly carved up Lotharingia between themselves at the Treaty of Meersen (870), confirming the basic east-west division.
The imperial title itself bounced around among Carolingian relatives for the next several decades, mostly held by figures who controlled only fragments of the original empire.

Charles the Fat — the youngest son of Louis the German — briefly reunited almost the entire Carolingian inheritance under a single sovereign in 884–887, but he was an unimpressive monarch whose military failures (he paid the Vikings 700 pounds of silver to leave the Siege of Paris in 886, see Chapter 7) had so destroyed his authority that his nephew Arnulf of Carinthia deposed him in 887.
With Charles the Fat's death the following January, the unified Carolingian Empire as a single political entity was definitively dead.

What replaced it was a patchwork of regional successor kingdoms: West Francia (the future France), East Francia (the future Germany), the Kingdom of Italy, the Kingdom of Burgundy, the Kingdom of Provence.
Each was nominally Carolingian (most of the dynasties were descended from Charlemagne by some line) but each operated independently.
The imperial title was claimed by the Italian kings sporadically through the rest of the ninth century but had no real political content.

The Carolingian dynasty itself did not end immediately — the West Frankish kings continued to be Carolingian until 987, when Hugh Capet, the count of Paris and head of a powerful aristocratic family, was elected king after the death of the last Carolingian Louis V.
Hugh founded the Capetian dynasty that would rule France for the next 300 years (and through cadet branches — the Valois, the Bourbons — into the nineteenth century).

The East Frankish Carolingian line ended in 911 with the death of Louis the Child; the German nobility elected a non-Carolingian, Conrad I, and after his death in 918 elected the Saxon duke Henry the Fowler (Chapter 8), founding the Ottonian dynasty.
By 911–987 the original Carolingian project had completely fragmented.
The three western European political units that emerged from it — France, Germany, and Italy — were on the trajectories that would shape their entire medieval and modern histories.
France was on its way to becoming the most centralized of the major European monarchies.
Germany was on its way to becoming the loosest of them.
Italy was on its way to becoming the most fragmented, with the popes, the German emperors, the Lombard cities, and the Norman south all contesting the peninsula until Italian unification in 1861.
The Verdun partition is the deepest single fact about the political geography of western Europe.
The other Carolingian inheritance worth noting is institutional.

The Carolingian Empire never functioned as a centralized state in the modern sense — it had no permanent capital after Aachen was lost to the Lothair line, no professional bureaucracy, no standing army, no regular taxation system.

What it had was a network of counts (the local royal officials who governed individual administrative districts called counties, plural Latin comitatus), dukes (military commanders of frontier or composite regions), bishops (who exercised both ecclesiastical and quasi-secular authority over their dioceses), and abbots (heads of the great monasteries, often with substantial landed property and political influence).

The whole apparatus was held together by the personal authority of the king, the periodic visits of the missi dominici ("envoys of the lord," royal inspectors sent in pairs — usually one bishop and one count — to tour the districts and enforce royal decrees), and the network of capitularies (royal legislation on specific matters).
Under a strong monarch like Charlemagne, this worked.
Under weak monarchs in the mid- and late-ninth century facing mounting Viking, Magyar, and Saracen pressure (Chapter 7), it didn't.
The counts began converting their public offices into private hereditary fiefs.
The bishops did the same for their dioceses.
Local landowners who could afford to build fortified residences — the early castles — began controlling their immediate territory more or less independently of any royal authority.
By 900 the counts of West Francia and East Francia were no longer royal officials; they were independent regional dynasts who happened to acknowledge the king as a feudal superior.
The political fragmentation that defines the central Middle Ages was beginning.
This is the proto-feudal transition that will dominate Chapter 7.
The structural cause was the failure of Carolingian centralized authority to defend against the ninth-century triple shock from outside.
The institutional consequence was that public power got fragmented downward into private hands.

The new model — local magnates exercising public authority through privately controlled castles and warriors — would be the basic political architecture of western Europe until the centralized monarchies began re-asserting royal authority in the late twelfth and thirteenth centuries.

Cross-civ check: while the Carolingian Empire was breaking up in the mid-ninth century, the Tang Dynasty in China was at its mature golden classical period and beginning to face its own imperial overstretch problems with the An Lushan Rebellion (Tang-Song China).
The Abbasid Caliphate was at the height of its cultural and political power under al-Mu'tasim and al-Wathiq, with Baghdad as the largest city in the world (Islamic Golden Age Ch 4).
The Byzantine Empire was just beginning the long Macedonian Renaissance recovery that would restore much of its former power (Byzantine Empire Ch 5).
In the Andes, the Tiwanaku and Wari empires were beginning to weaken (middle-horizon-empires).
In Mesoamerica, the great Classic Maya cities had collapsed within the previous half-century (Maya Civilization Ch 7), and the Postclassic Toltec and Aztec successor cultures were emerging.

The world that the post-Carolingian west was joining was, in absolute terms, smaller and poorer than the worlds of the Tang and the Abbasids — but it was on a steeper upward trajectory than either, and the gap would close fast in the coming three centuries.

chapters.title: The Triple Shock: Vikings, Magyars, Saracens
sentences: The hundred-and-fifty years from roughly 793 to 955 are the closest thing the early medieval west has to a sustained external crisis, and they are often the thing modern readers know best about the period because the raiders involved have outsize cultural footprints.
From the North Sea came the Vikings — Scandinavian raiders in clinker-built longships who sacked monasteries, conquered chunks of England and Ireland, founded Russia, and reached Newfoundland.
From the Hungarian plain came the Magyars — Finno-Ugric horse archers who galloped deep into Italy, Germany, and even northern France in lightning summer raids.
And from Sicily and Spain came the Saracens — Muslim pirate fleets who sacked Rome, kidnapped the abbot of Cluny, and made the western Mediterranean a Muslim lake.
Three different enemies, attacking from three different directions, all hitting western Europe at roughly the same time.
The Carolingian state could not stop any of them.

The response — the proto-feudal transformation, the spread of the castle, the rise of the mounted knight, the conversion of public authority into private hands — defined European political structure for the next four centuries.
This chapter is about the shock and the response.
We start with the Vikings, because they came first and they are the most famous.
The Viking Age proper is treated at chapter length in viking-age — eight chapters covering the Norse world from the longship to Stamford Bridge in 1066.
This chapter covers the same material from the perspective of the European victims rather than the Norse raiders.

The conventional opening date is June 8, 793, when Northumbrian monks at the monastery of Lindisfarne on a tidal island off the northeastern English coast looked up from their morning duties to see dragon-prowed wooden boats running up the beach.
The raiders killed some of the monks, dragged others into the sea and drowned them, looted the church treasures, and were gone before any local force could react.

The chronicler Symeon of Durham, writing centuries later, called it the moment when "the heathens miserably ravaged God's church on Lindisfarne with plunder and slaughter." The Northumbrian scholar Alcuin of York, then at Charlemagne's court, wrote a horrified letter to King Æthelred: "Never before has such a terror appeared in Britain as we have now suffered from a pagan race.
Behold the Church of St.
Cuthbert spattered with the blood of the priests of God, despoiled of its ornaments." It was a small event in absolute terms.
A handful of monks dead, perhaps a dozen captured, modest plunder.

But the symbolic meaning — that the sea, which had always been a barrier protecting the Christian west, was now a highway being used by somebody on the other side — propagated through the Latin world and was the first sign of what was coming. (Viking Age Ch 2 covers Lindisfarne and the early western raids in detail.) For the next two decades the raids stayed at the small-fleet level — a handful of longships hitting an unprotected coastal monastery, looting it, leaving.
Iona was sacked in 795 and again in 802 and 806.
The Frankish coast was raided.
The Frisian coast (the Low Countries) was raided.
Charlemagne organized coastal defenses but the Frankish state had no navy in any serious sense, and a Carolingian land army could never assemble fast enough to catch a Viking raid.
Then, in the 830s and 840s — coincident with the civil wars among Louis the Pious's sons — the Vikings shifted gears.
The fleets got larger, the raiders started staying ashore over winter rather than retreating in autumn, and the targets started including not just monasteries but cities.
Dublin was founded as a Norse fortified base in 841 (and would become the largest slave market in northern Europe within a century — Viking Age Ch 7).
Paris was sacked in 845 and the Frankish king Charles the Bald paid the Vikings 7,000 pounds of silver to leave.
The Vikings came back.
They sacked Paris again in 856.
They sacked it again in 861.

By 865 a coalition of Danish armies — the Great Heathen Army, an enormous combined force probably numbering several thousand warriors — landed in East Anglia and within a decade had destroyed three of the four major Anglo-Saxon kingdoms (the Vendel-Age society that produced this army is the subject of the Vendel Age narrative; the Anglo-Saxon society it struck is the subject of the Anglo-Saxon England narrative): Northumbria fell in 867 (with King Ælla famously killed by being subjected to the "blood eagle," though the historicity of this Norse execution method is contested), East Anglia fell in 869 (with King Edmund killed), and Mercia fell in 874.
By 878 only Wessex under King Alfred survived as an independent Anglo-Saxon kingdom.

Alfred the Great (ruled 871–899) is the only Anglo-Saxon king to be called "the Great" and one of the few medieval English kings to be remembered for his administrative work rather than just his battles.
He was the youngest son of King Æthelwulf of Wessex; his elder brothers had all reigned briefly and died, mostly young, in the wars against the Vikings.
By the time he became king in 871 at the age of 22, Wessex was the last surviving Anglo-Saxon kingdom and the Danish Great Heathen Army was preparing to finish it off.
The decisive moment came in the winter of 878.

A Viking force under the warlord Guthrum launched a surprise winter attack on Alfred's headquarters at Chippenham in early January, catching the Wessex government off guard during the Christmas season when armies were not supposed to campaign.

Alfred fled with a small bodyguard into the marshes of Athelney in Somerset and spent the late winter as a hunted refugee. (The famous story of King Alfred letting a peasant woman's cakes burn while hiding in her hut is from a 12th-century life of Saint Neot and probably invented, but the underlying historical fact — that the king of Wessex was reduced for several months in 878 to hiding in the swamps with a handful of loyalists — is real.) Alfred recovered.
He summoned a small army, marched it across Wiltshire, and confronted Guthrum's main force at the Battle of Edington in May 878.
Alfred won.
He pursued Guthrum to his fortified base, besieged it, and forced Guthrum's surrender.

The terms of the Peace of Wedmore that followed were dramatic: Guthrum and thirty of his senior commanders accepted Christian baptism (Alfred standing as Guthrum's godfather), and the Danish army accepted partition of England into a Wessex-controlled south and west and a Danish-controlled north and east — the Danelaw.
The Danelaw is a fact every English speaker still encounters daily.

The English place names ending in -by (Whitby, Derby, Grimsby), -thorpe (Scunthorpe, Mablethorpe), and -toft are all Norse in origin, marking villages founded or held by Danish settlers in the ninth and tenth centuries.

The English vocabulary loaned from Norse includes some of the most basic words in the language: sky, leg, knife, ill, call, happy, the pronouns they, them, their (which replaced the Old English equivalents hi, him, hira over the late-Saxon centuries), and the verb to be in its plural form ("are" is a Norse loan replacing the Old English sind).
The word law itself is a Norse loan; the older English word was æ.
English is, in a real linguistic sense, an Anglo-Norse hybrid language, with the Anglo half winning the framework but the Norse half contributing a remarkable amount of the high-frequency vocabulary.
After Edington, Alfred consolidated.
He codified West Saxon law in his own law-code.

He built a defensive system of fortified towns called burhs (BURGS, the source of modern English "borough" and German Burg) — about 30 of them across Wessex, each within a day's march of any other so that no Viking force could move very far without being intercepted.
The burh system was financed by a tax called the burhbot assessed on landholders proportional to the length of wall they were responsible for maintaining.
He founded the English navy, building a fleet of ships specifically designed to outclass Viking longships.

And he sponsored a translation program — Latin classics rendered into Old English — that included Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy, Gregory the Great's Pastoral Care, parts of Augustine, and several others.
He claimed to have done some of the translations himself, which is at least plausible — the prefaces survive and are written in his name.
Alfred died in 899, having stabilized Wessex and laid the foundation for the gradual reconquest of the Danelaw under his son Edward the Elder and grandson Athelstan.
By 927, Athelstan had absorbed all of the Danelaw and was calling himself "King of the English" — the first ruler to use that title meaningfully.

The unification of England as a single kingdom is, in this sense, a Viking-era achievement: the Danish destruction of all the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms except Wessex made political consolidation possible in a way that the heptarchic patchwork of seventh-century England never had been.
The Frankish response to the Vikings was less successful than the Wessex response, mostly because the post-Carolingian state was too fragmented to mount the kind of coordinated defense Wessex could.

The pattern that emerged in West Francia in the late ninth century: a Viking fleet would sail up the Seine or the Loire, raid the cities and monasteries along the river, demand a payment of silver to leave, leave, come back the following year.
The king's army (when there was one) usually arrived too late.
Local counts and bishops increasingly took matters into their own hands, building castles and raising private armies to defend their districts.
The episode that crystallized this dynamic was the Siege of Paris in 885–886.

A massive Viking fleet of perhaps 700 ships and 30,000 men under the warlord Sigfred sailed up the Seine in November 885 and besieged Paris — at this time a small fortified city on the Île de la Cité in the middle of the Seine, plus two fortified bridges connecting it to the riverbanks.
The defense was led by Count Odo of Paris (later known as Odo I, king of the Franks), who held the city through a winter and spring of intermittent assault.
Emperor Charles the Fat — supposedly the senior Frankish monarch — eventually arrived in October 886 with an enormous army that should have crushed the Vikings outright.
Instead, he negotiated.
He paid the Vikings 700 pounds of silver and gave them permission to ravage Burgundy (a region currently held by his rebellious nephew).
The Vikings happily took both the silver and the permission and went off to plunder Burgundy.
Charles the Fat's settlement was so humiliating that it shattered his political authority.
Within a year his nephew Arnulf of Carinthia had deposed him; he died in disgrace in 888.
The unified Carolingian Empire died with him.
The pattern of paying off Viking raiders to leave — institutionalized in England as the Danegeld ("Dane-payment") — was the most expensive way possible to handle the problem.
The Vikings always came back for more.
The actual long-term solution was the one Alfred had pursued: build defensive fortifications, raise local forces, and when possible negotiate not just payments but settlements.
The ultimate Frankish version of the Alfred solution came in 911.

The West Frankish king Charles the Simple (a grandson of Charles the Bald, ruled 898–922) faced a Norse warlord named Rollo (REL-loh, from Norse Hrólfr) who had been raiding the lower Seine for fifteen years and was effectively beyond the kingdom's military reach.

By the Treaty of Saint-Clair-sur-Epte in 911, Charles ceded the lower Seine valley to Rollo as a hereditary fief on condition that Rollo accept baptism, hold the territory in vassalage to the Frankish king, and stop the raids.
Rollo accepted.
The ceded territory became Normandy — "Land of the Northmen" — and Rollo and his successors became the Dukes of Normandy, technically vassals of the French crown but in practice independent.

Within four generations the Normans had Frenchified completely (their language, their religion, their political customs were all Frankish by 1000) but retained the Viking aggressive military tradition.

The Normans would conquer England in 1066 (a story for high-medieval-europe Ch 1), conquer southern Italy and Sicily in the 1060s and 1070s, and become one of the most expansionist political-military groups in the high medieval world.
The chain: a Viking warlord makes a settlement deal in 911, his great-great-great-grandson conquers England in 1066.
Rollo's bones are still buried in Rouen Cathedral.
The Norse east — the Rus' — also founded states during this period.

Scandinavian traders and warriors sailing down the great Russian rivers established a fortified base at Novgorod under the legendary chieftain Rurik in 862, then moved south to take control of the strategic crossroads at Kyiv by 882.
The Kievan Rus' state that grew from this Norse-Slavic synthesis became the ancestor of Russia, Belarus, and Ukraine.

Rus' grand prince Vladimir the Great accepted Eastern Orthodox Christianity in 988, married the Byzantine emperor's sister Anna, and brought the entire Rus' state into the Byzantine cultural and religious sphere — choosing the Greek tradition over the Latin, with consequences that have shaped Russian-European relations to the present day. (The Cyrillic alphabet, the Eastern Orthodox liturgy, the political ideology of caesaropapism — all came in with the Vladimir conversion.
Viking Age Ch 4 covers the Rus' eastward thrust in detail.) While the Vikings were attacking from the north, the Magyars were attacking from the east.

The Magyars (sometimes confusingly called "Hungarians" — they are the same people, the modern Hungarian state takes its English name from a different etymology, but the people call themselves Magyar) were a nomadic confederation speaking a Finno-Ugric language.

Finno-Ugric is the language family that also includes Finnish and Estonian (and the Sami languages of the Arctic) — completely unrelated to the Indo-European languages spoken by every other people in early medieval Europe.

The Magyars had spent centuries on the Eurasian steppe before being pushed west by the Pechenegs (another Turkic steppe people) in the 890s; they crossed the Carpathians under their leader Árpád in 895 and settled in the Hungarian plain, the broad flat fertile basin where they have lived ever since.
Their conquest of the Hungarian plain probably extinguished the surviving Avar population and pushed back the Slavic peoples already there.
Almost as soon as they arrived, the Magyars began raiding deep into western Europe.

Their style of warfare was the standard steppe-nomad combination of mounted archers and lightning maneuver — armies of perhaps 5,000–20,000 horsemen, capable of covering 30–50 miles a day, hitting western European armies on terms that the western armies (built around heavy infantry and slower cavalry) could not effectively counter.
Between 899 and 955 the Magyars launched an estimated 33 major raiding expeditions into northern Italy, Bavaria, Saxony, Burgundy, and even northern France.
In 924 they reached the Atlantic coast at Provence.
In 937 a Magyar raid penetrated as far as the Loire valley in France.
They besieged Pavia (in northern Italy) repeatedly, sacked Brescia and Verona, and burned dozens of monasteries.

Frankish chronicles describe the Magyar raids in language reminiscent of the Mongol terror that would arrive 300 years later: lightning attacks out of nowhere, slaughter of populations, abduction of women and children for the slave market, withdrawal before any defense could be organized.
The Magyar raids were the eastern half of the ninth-century triple shock.
They were not stopped until the German king Otto I crushed them at the Battle of Lechfeld in 955 (Chapter 8).
Until then, the eastern German lands (Bavaria, Saxony, Franconia) and northern Italy lived under permanent Magyar threat for two generations.
And from the south came the Saracens.

"Saracen" (SAIR-uh-suhn) was the Latin medieval term for any Muslim raider — derived obscurely from a Greek word for an Arabian tribe, but used in Western chronicles to mean essentially "the Muslim pirates raiding our coasts." The Saracen problem in the early medieval west had two main sources.
The first was Sicily.
Byzantine Sicily had been a wealthy province in the early medieval Mediterranean — large grain production, important sea-lane control.

The Aghlabid emirs of Tunisia (the Muslim dynasty that controlled the central North African coast in the ninth century) began the conquest of Sicily in 827 and completed it over the next 75 years: Palermo fell in 831, Syracuse in 878, Taormina in 902.

Muslim Sicily would become one of the wealthiest and most culturally productive provinces of the medieval Mediterranean — a sophisticated Arabic-Greek-Latin trilingual society at the same time it was a base for raiding the Italian mainland.
The Saracen raids on the Italian peninsula throughout the ninth and tenth centuries were largely launched from Sicily.
The most famous of these raids was the Sack of Rome in 846.
An Aghlabid Muslim raiding fleet sailed up the Tiber in August 846, looted the basilicas of St.
Peter and St.
Paul outside the Aurelian Walls (which were outside the city's main defensive perimeter), and stripped the tombs of the apostles.
They left without entering the inner city, but the symbolic shock was enormous: the burial place of Peter, the spiritual center of Latin Christendom, had been desecrated by Muslim raiders.
Pope Leo IV responded by enclosing the Vatican Hill in a new defensive perimeter called the Leonine Wall, completed in 852.
It is the first time St.
Peter's was given fortified protection in its eight centuries of existence; previously the Aurelian Walls of imperial Rome had been considered sufficient.

The second main source was a small Muslim base on the Provençal coast at a place called Fraxinetum (modern La Garde-Freinet near Saint-Tropez), established around 887 by Muslim raiders from al-Andalus.

Fraxinetum was tiny — perhaps a few hundred fighters — but it sat in a strategic position from which raiders could strike at any monastery, town, or trade route in southern France, Provence, Liguria, or the western Alps.
Fraxinetum raiders kidnapped the abbot of Cluny (Maiolus) in 972, demanding a ransom of 1,000 pounds of silver — the kidnapping that finally galvanized the Provençal lords to act.
A coalition under William of Provence destroyed Fraxinetum in 973.
The cumulative effect of the Saracen raids was that the western Mediterranean became an unsafe sea throughout the ninth and tenth centuries.
The Italian coastal cities (other than the few like Venice that could maintain their own naval forces) saw repeated raids.
Sardinia and Corsica were repeatedly looted.
The southern French coast was lightly defended.
Maritime trade contracted.
The line between "Christian Mediterranean" and "Muslim Mediterranean" hardened, with the Italian peninsula and the islands forming a contested zone in between.
Islamic Golden Age covers the same Saracens from the Muslim side: the Sicilian Aghlabids, the Andalusian Umayyads, and the broader Mediterranean dynamics from a Caliphate-centric perspective.
From the Latin-Christian early-medieval perspective, the Saracens were one part of the three-front siege.
The response to the triple shock was the proto-feudal transformation of European political structure.
The basic mechanics: the central state could not protect against the raiders.

Local strongmen — counts who had inherited their offices from Carolingian appointees, regional bishops, ambitious smaller landholders — could, on a small scale, by building fortifications and raising local fighters.

The arrangement that emerged was a contract: a man who could afford a horse and armor would swear personal loyalty (Latin fidelitas, the source of "fealty") to a more powerful man — a lord — in exchange for a grant of land (a fief, Latin feodum) sufficient to support him.
The vassal owed military service — usually 40 days a year, fully equipped, including the cost of his horse, armor, and weapons — to his lord.
The lord owed protection to his vassal.
The arrangement was personal, sworn before God, and (in the early phase) lifetime rather than hereditary.

This is what historians eventually called feudalism, though the word itself is a 17th-century invention and modern medieval scholars are wary of it — the actual late-Carolingian arrangements varied enormously across regions and never formed the clean pyramidal "feudal system" of the textbooks.

The cleaner formulation is that in the late-ninth and tenth centuries, public authority in much of western Europe was privatized: the functions previously exercised by the king's officials (justice, taxation, military service, defense) were converted into the private property of local landed magnates, who exercised them on the lands they controlled and held them by hereditary right.
The architectural signature of this transformation was the castle.
The first true castles — privately owned fortified residences serving as both home and instrument of local political control — appeared in Frankish territory in the late ninth and tenth centuries.

They were typically motte-and-bailey structures: a wooden tower (motte, French for "mound") on top of an artificial earthen mound, with a fortified courtyard (bailey) below containing stables, storerooms, and quarters for the garrison.

They were quick to build (a few weeks for a small castle, requiring only timber and labor), defensible against the kind of raiding force that terrorized the late Carolingian world, and small enough that even a modest local lord could afford one.
Within a century the European countryside was sprinkled with thousands of them.

The landscape that the high medieval period inherits — the lord's castle on the hill, the village clustered below, the cathedral in the valley — was made by the proto-feudal response to the ninth-century triple shock.
The military companion piece was the mounted knight.

A heavily armored cavalryman, mounted on a strong warhorse, equipped with a long lance for the couched charge, capable of breaking infantry formations and outrunning raiders, was the kind of military asset that could actually contest the Vikings (on land), the Magyars (with proper deployment), and the Saracens.
But mounted knights were expensive — the horse, the armor, the weapons, and the years of training added up to a level of investment that only the landed nobility could afford.
The proto-feudal arrangement of fiefs in exchange for military service was, in effect, the financing system that paid for the new mounted aristocracy.
The lord granted his vassal enough land to support a knight's worth of equipment; the vassal showed up for military service when required.

The historian Lynn White Jr. argued in 1962 that the stirrup — introduced into western Europe via the steppe nomads in the seventh and eighth centuries — was the technological enabler that made the heavy cavalry charge possible and therefore the trigger for feudalism.

Modern scholars treat the connection as much more diffuse than White's clean causal chain — the social transformation had many causes, and the rise of heavy cavalry was gradual rather than sudden — but the technological enabler is real.
Without the stirrup, the couched-lance charge that defined medieval cavalry warfare cannot work; the rider has nothing to brace against and is unhorsed by his own weapon's impact.
By 950, then, western Europe had survived the triple shock, mostly through institutional improvisation.

The Vikings had been settled (Normandy 911, Danelaw 878 onward), the Magyars were about to be defeated decisively (Lechfeld 955, Chapter 8), the Saracen bases were under pressure (Fraxinetum destroyed 973).
The kingdoms had not been replaced by anything new; the Carolingian fragments were still the political framework.
But the social and military structure inside those kingdoms had changed permanently.

The mounted knight, the castle, the proto-feudal contract, the privatization of public authority — all of it would define European political life from 950 to roughly 1300, when the centralized monarchies began re-asserting royal power.
The next chapter is the start of the recovery.

Cross-civ check: the ninth-century triple shock that hammered the Latin West coincided with the An Lushan Rebellion (755–763) and its long aftermath that crippled Tang China (Tang-Song China), the Abbasid civil wars of the mid-ninth century that fragmented the Caliphate (Islamic Golden Age Ch 6), and the long crisis of the Maya Classic collapse in Mesoamerica (Maya Civilization Ch 7).

The mid-ninth century is, by some recent climate-history arguments, a period of unusually difficult Northern Hemisphere weather and possibly volcanic-driven cooling — with social-political consequences from China to the Yucatán.
The triple shock in Europe may have been one regional manifestation of a broader Eurasian-American crisis.
Or it may have been bad luck.
Both readings have respectable defenders in the recent literature.

chapters.title: Ottonian Recovery and the Year 1000
sentences: The eastern Frankish kingdom that had been Louis the German's share of Verdun — the kingdom that would eventually become Germany — found itself by 900 in particularly bad shape.
The Magyars were raiding annually.
The Slavic peoples beyond the Elbe were pushing back against earlier Frankish-Saxon expansion.

The royal authority had collapsed completely; the Carolingian East Frankish line ended in 911 with the death of the eight-year-old Louis the Child, and the German nobility had to elect new kings from their own ranks.
The first elected king, Conrad I, was an unimpressive Franconian who could not control the dukes and died in 918 having achieved nothing.
What followed was the Ottonian dynasty — the Saxon dukes who took the East Frankish throne in 919 and reinvented it.

Within four generations they had defeated the Magyars decisively, revived the Roman imperial title in the West, sponsored a deep monastic reform, overseen the conversion of Hungary, Poland, and Russia to Christianity, and produced what historians sometimes call the Ottonian Renaissance.
By the year 1000 the western European world had stabilized politically, religiously, and culturally.
The threshold conditions for the High Middle Ages — the urban revival, the cathedrals, the universities, the Crusades — were all in place.
This chapter is the story of the recovery.
Henry I the Fowler (HEN-ree, ruled 919–936) was Duke of Saxony and the most powerful regional magnate in the East Frankish kingdom when Conrad I died.
His nickname comes from a probably-apocryphal story about messengers finding him hunting birds when they arrived to inform him of his election as king.
He was elected by an assembly of the German dukes — the first time a non-Frankish lineage had taken the throne — and his reign establishes the Ottonian dynasty.
Henry's accomplishments were structural rather than spectacular.

He negotiated a nine-year truce with the Magyars in 924 by paying tribute, then used the pause to build a network of fortified frontier strongholds (German Burgen, related to Old English burhs — these are the fortified villages from which words like "Hamburg," "Magdeburg," and "Bamberg" derive their names) and to train his nobility in mounted warfare.
When the truce expired in 933, Henry crushed a Magyar invasion at the Battle of Riade, in central Germany — the first significant Frankish military victory over the Magyars in nearly forty years.
He brought Bohemia into nominal vassalage to the German crown.
He established the precedent that the East Frankish (German) crown would be elective among the major dukes rather than hereditary in any one family.
Henry died in 936 and was succeeded by his son Otto I.

Otto I (ruled 936–973), called the Great — the first medieval ruler since Charlemagne to earn that epithet by general consensus — is the founder of the medieval German monarchy and arguably the second-most-important political figure in the early medieval west.

He inherited his father's kingdom, faced down a series of internal revolts among his own family and the German dukes in the 940s and early 950s, defeated the Magyars decisively, conquered northern Italy, and was crowned Roman Emperor in 962.
The institutional Holy Roman Empire that would survive (in various forms) until 1806 dates from Otto I's coronation.
The decisive military moment was the Battle of Lechfeld in 955.
The Magyars had launched their greatest single invasion of western Europe in summer 955 — perhaps 50,000 horsemen sweeping across Bavaria toward Augsburg.
Otto assembled a coalition army of about 8,000 heavy cavalry from across the German duchies and met them on the plain of the Lech River (LEKH) outside Augsburg on August 10, 955.
The battle was the decisive demonstration of what the new heavy-cavalry mounted-knight tactics could do against steppe horse archers.
The Magyar archery was negated by the German heavy armor; the German charges shattered the Magyar formations; the Magyar leadership was killed or captured.
The pursuit lasted for days and accounted for most of the surviving Magyar warriors.
Lechfeld ended the Magyar raids on western Europe.
It was also a personal political triumph for Otto — he was acclaimed Imperator by his soldiers on the battlefield, the first time the title had been popularly conferred since the late Roman Empire.

More important in long-term political effect, it consolidated Otto's authority over the German dukes (who had not always been reliable) and made possible the eastern Christianization of Hungary itself: the Magyars who had survived Lechfeld returned to the Hungarian plain, abandoned the lifestyle of seasonal nomadic raiding, and within a generation began the process of conversion to Latin Christianity that culminated in the coronation of Stephen I as Christian king of Hungary on Christmas Day 1000.
After Lechfeld, Otto turned south.

The Italian peninsula was politically chaotic — the Lombard kingdom of Italy had effectively disintegrated, regional warlords were fighting over the imperial title, and the popes in Rome were being manipulated by the local Roman nobility.
In 951 and 961–962 Otto led major expeditions into Italy.

The 961 expedition was decisive: Otto entered Rome in early 962, was crowned Emperor by Pope John XII on February 2, and took the imperial title that had been effectively dormant since the death of Berengar I in 924.

Pope John promptly tried to play Otto off against other Italian factions and was deposed by Otto in 963 — establishing the precedent that the German emperor could appoint and depose popes when the popes proved disloyal.

The 962 coronation is the conventional founding date of the Holy Roman Empire as a continuous institution. (Charlemagne's 800 coronation founded the idea but the institution did not survive in continuous form between 924 and 962.) The empire Otto created was a complex constitutional artifact: an elected German monarchy whose ruler was also king of Italy, claimed the Roman imperial inheritance, exercised theoretical authority over the universal Catholic church, and balanced uneasily between papal claims and German ducal autonomy.
It would continue under the Ottonians through Otto II (973–983), Otto III (983–1002), and Henry II (1002–1024) before passing to the Salian dynasty in the eleventh century.
Otto's institutional architecture would shape it through the next eight centuries.
The other Ottonian innovation worth noting is the rise of an imperial church — the Reichskirche, "imperial church," in German historiography.
Otto's strategy for managing the German nobility was to lean heavily on the bishops and the major monastic abbots as instruments of royal authority.

He appointed loyal clerics to bishoprics and abbacies; gave them substantial landed property and political authority within their dioceses; required them to maintain knights at royal service; and used them as administrators, ambassadors, and military commanders.

The system worked because bishops were celibate and could not pass their offices and lands to legitimate sons — which meant that, unlike the secular nobility, they could not convert their fiefs into hereditary dynasties.
The Reichskirche made the Ottonian and Salian emperors substantially more powerful (and substantially more involved in church appointments) than the West Frankish kings of the same period.

It also set up the long medieval struggle between emperor and pope over who had the authority to appoint bishops — the Investiture Controversy that would consume European politics in the eleventh and twelfth centuries (covered in high-medieval-europe).
Religious life in the tenth century was being transformed by a quieter revolution — the Cluniac monastic reform.

The abbey of Cluny (KLOO-nee, in Burgundy) was founded in 910 by Duke William the Pious of Aquitaine with an unusual charter: the abbey would be subject directly to the pope, free from all secular and even episcopal control.
This independence — formally guaranteed by papal privilege — was the institutional innovation that made the Cluniac reform possible.
Cluny did not have to compromise its monastic discipline to satisfy any local lord or bishop; it answered only to Rome, which was usually willing to leave it alone.

Under a series of remarkably long-lived abbots — Odo (927–942), Maiolus (954–994, the one kidnapped by Saracens at Fraxinetum), Odilo (994–1049), Hugh (1049–1109) — Cluny pushed for stricter observance of the Rule of Benedict, longer liturgical hours (the great Cluniac liturgy eventually consumed most of the monks' day), elaborate church architecture (the great church of Cluny III, built between 1088 and 1130, was the largest church in Christendom for several centuries until the new St.
Peter's was built in Rome), and freedom of monasteries from secular interference.

By 1100 Cluny had over a thousand daughter monasteries spread across western Europe, all under the direct authority of the abbot of Cluny — a network of religious houses larger than any ecclesiastical structure had ever been before.

The Cluniac reformers also pushed for changes in the broader church: an end to simony (the buying and selling of ecclesiastical offices), enforcement of clerical celibacy (parish priests through much of the early Middle Ages had been informally married), and a clearer separation between religious and secular authority.
By the mid-eleventh century these arguments would produce the Gregorian Reform that fully established papal supremacy and triggered the Investiture Controversy with the Salian emperors.
The Cluniac groundwork laid in the tenth century is what made the eleventh-century papal revolution possible.
The other great religious-political development of the late tenth century was the Christianization of Northern and Eastern Europe.
Through the eighth and ninth centuries, the Latin Christian world had ended somewhere east of the Elbe and somewhere north of Saxony.
The peoples beyond — the West Slavs (Bohemians, Poles, Wends), the East Slavs (Russians, Ukrainians, Belarusians), the Magyars, the Norse, the Baltic peoples — were largely pagan.
By 1050 most of them would be Christian.
The conversion happened in a remarkable fifty-year burst between roughly 950 and 1050.

The Polish prince Mieszko I accepted baptism in 966 from Latin missionaries in Bohemia, marrying the Bohemian Christian princess Doubrava as part of the package, and brought the new Polish state into Latin Christendom.
Bohemia itself had begun converting earlier under Boleslav I but was definitively Christianized by Mieszko's generation.

Hungary was Christianized through the conversion of its grand prince Géza in the 970s and the formal coronation of his son Stephen I as Christian king on Christmas Day 1000, with a crown sent by Pope Sylvester II.
Norway and Denmark became Christian under Olav Tryggvason and Sweyn Forkbeard respectively in the 990s and 1010s.
Sweden followed in the eleventh century.
Iceland voluntarily adopted Christianity by parliamentary vote at the Althing of 999 — possibly the only such case in history.
The exception was Russia, which converted to Eastern Orthodox Christianity rather than Latin.
Vladimir (volo-DEE-mir, ruled c. 980–1015), grand prince of Kyiv, accepted baptism in 988 and married the Byzantine emperor's sister Anna.
The Rus' Christianization brought the alphabet, the church architecture, and the political ideology of Byzantium rather than of Rome.

The Latin-Cyrillic line bisecting modern Europe — running roughly through the Baltic, central Poland, the Carpathians, and down to the Adriatic — was drawn in the late tenth and early eleventh centuries by which missionaries got there first.
By 1050 western Christendom extended from the Atlantic to the Russian rivers, from Sicily to Iceland.
It was, for the first time, a coherent religious-political-cultural unit at continental scale.

Almost everything that the High Middle Ages would build — the Crusades, the cathedral schools turning into universities, the rise of the towns, the scholastic synthesis — assumed this Christianized continental unit as the platform.
The agricultural backdrop to all of this was an agricultural revolution that gathered pace through the early Middle Ages and reached its takeoff phase around the year 1000.

The four key innovations: The heavy mouldboard plow — drawn by oxen and later horses, capable of turning the heavy clay soils of the north European plain that the older Mediterranean scratch-plow could not work.
The north European agricultural heartland that had been marginal under the Romans became the breadbasket of medieval Europe.
The three-field crop rotation — winter grain, spring grain, fallow — replacing the older two-field system.
Increased the area planted each year from one-half to two-thirds of the total, and the spring crop (oats, legumes) added nitrogen to the soil and provided fodder for horses.
The rigid horse collar, transmitted from China and Central Asia, allowed horses to pull heavy loads with their shoulders rather than choking against an ox-yoke around their throats.
Combined with iron horseshoes and better breeds, it tripled the draft power of a working horse.
Watermills, increasingly numerous and increasingly used for purposes beyond grinding grain — fulling cloth, sawing wood, hammering iron.
The Domesday Book of 1086 would record over 6,000 mills in eleventh-century England alone.
Europe was developing a deep mechanical-power infrastructure that no other contemporary civilization quite matched.
These four innovations spread across northern Europe between roughly 800 and 1100, with most of the spread happening in the tenth and eleventh centuries.

Their cumulative effect was that European food production probably more than doubled between 800 and 1200, with corresponding effects on population (which roughly doubled in the same period from perhaps 30 million to perhaps 70 million), urban revival (the cities began growing again after their post-Roman collapse), and economic complexity.
The High Middle Ages will run on the agricultural surplus that the early medieval centuries created.
The final image of the early medieval west should probably be the most famous: the year 1000.
The approach of the year 1000 — counting from the supposed birth of Christ — produced, in some western Christian communities, a wave of apocalyptic anxiety.

Chroniclers reported popular fears that the millennium of Christ's birth or, more often, the millennium of his Resurrection (so 1033 rather than 1000) would bring the end of the world: the return of Christ, the Last Judgment, the end of human history.

The French chronicler Rodulfus Glaber (ROD-ulf-us GLAB-er, c. 985–1047), writing fifty years later, described enthusiastic rebuilding of churches and pilgrimages to Jerusalem in the years before 1000 as evidence of millennial expectation.
Other chronicles describe panicked expectations of the apocalypse.
How widespread the panic actually was remains hotly contested.
The French historian Jules Michelet (jools mish-LAY) popularized "the terrors of the year 1000" in his nineteenth-century History of France as a kind of medieval doom-spectacle.

Twentieth-century revisionist scholars, especially in mid-century French scholarship, dismissed Michelet's picture as overdrawn — most chronicles do not mention millennial fears, and the institutional church does not seem to have officially expected the apocalypse on any specific date.

Recent scholarship since the 1990s has partly rehabilitated the millennial-anxiety reading, arguing that the popular religious-cultural mood of the late tenth century did include a genuine apocalyptic strain even if the institutional church played it down.
What is not contested is that the year 1000 was, by any reasonable historical metric, a turning point.
The triple shock had ended.
The Carolingian institutional inheritance had been recovered and extended by the Ottonian dynasty.
The agricultural revolution was producing a sustained increase in population and surplus.
The Christianization of northern and eastern Europe had created a continent-scale Latin-Christian civilizational unit.
The proto-feudal order had stabilized into the recognizable medieval social structure of lords, knights, monasteries, and villages.
The pope and the emperor were both established as universal authorities.
The Cluniac reform was preparing the ground for the more radical religious transformations of the eleventh century.
The cathedral schools at Reims, Chartres, Liège, and Magdeburg were becoming the institutional ancestors of the universities.
The Italian maritime cities (Venice, Pisa, Genoa, Amalfi) were beginning to rebuild Mediterranean trade.
The Jewish merchant communities of the Rhine valley, southern France, and Spain were building the long-distance commercial networks that would feed the High Medieval economic revival.
All of these threads are about to converge.

The year 1000 is the threshold of the High Middle Ages — the period of the urban revival, the Crusades, the Gothic cathedrals, the universities, Magna Carta, and the institutional foundations of modern Europe (high-medieval-europe Ch 1).

The continent that crossed that threshold was, in 1000, far from the largest or richest civilization of Eurasia (the Tang-Song China and the Abbasid Caliphate were both demonstrably bigger and more sophisticated).
But it was the one with the steepest forward trajectory.
Within three centuries it would be building Notre Dame, founding the universities of Bologna and Paris, and writing Magna Carta.
Within four centuries it would be sending Columbus across the Atlantic.
Within seven, it would be running an industrial revolution that would absorb the entire planet.
The institutional materials of all that were assembled between 476 and 1000.
That is what the early Middle Ages were for.

Cross-civ check: at the year 1000, while the Latin west was building the foundations described in this chapter, the Tang-Song transition in China was producing a sophisticated commercial-bureaucratic society of perhaps 100 million people (Tang-Song China).
The Fatimid Caliphate in Egypt was at its cultural and political peak, with Cairo as one of the major cities of the Mediterranean (Islamic Golden Age Ch 6).
The Byzantine Macedonian Renaissance had restored most of the empire's former territory (Byzantine Empire Ch 5).
Vladimir's Rus' was being Christianized into Eastern Orthodoxy (Viking Age Ch 4).
In Ghana in the western Sudan, the trans-Saharan gold trade was financing the first of the great medieval West African empires (the Ghana Empire predecessor of mali-empire).
In the Andes, the Wari had collapsed and the regional kingdoms that would precede the Inca were emerging (middle-horizon-empires, andean-kingdoms).
In Mesoamerica, the Toltec-period Tula was the dominant power (preceding aztec-empire).
In Polynesia, voyagers had reached Easter Island and were nearly to New Zealand (Polynesian voyagers).
The world the High Middle Ages would join was the most populated, the most connected, and the most commercially active that humanity had so far produced.
The late-medieval European projection of that connectivity into a planetary system — the next 500-year story — starts here.

chapters.title: Maritime Southeast Asia Before Srivijaya
sentences: To understand Srivijaya, you have to first picture the world it grew out of: a vast island archipelago whose people had been sailors for thousands of years, sitting at the natural pivot point of a long-distance trading system that already ran from the Roman Mediterranean to Han China.
Srivijaya did not invent Maritime Southeast Asia.
It inherited it.
The geography matters.

Maritime Southeast Asia is the chain of islands and peninsulas stretching from modern Myanmar in the west to New Guinea in the east — a region the size of the continental United States, divided by hundreds of straits and seas, dominated by tropical rainforest and volcanic mountains, and almost impossible to traverse by land.
To get from one place to another in this world, you took a boat.
The geography forced everyone living here into a maritime culture, and over thousands of years it produced one of the most formidable seafaring traditions in human history.
The people who built this tradition were the Austronesians (AW-stroh-NEE-zhuns), one of the great linguistic dispersals in human history.

The Austronesian language family originated somewhere in what is now Taiwan, probably around 3000 BCE, and spread southward through the Philippines, across the Indonesian archipelago, and eventually outward in two directions: westward all the way to Madagascar off the east coast of Africa, and eastward across the entire Pacific to Easter Island.

By the time of European contact, Austronesian languages were spoken across more than 13,000 miles (21,000 km) of ocean — the widest geographical spread of any pre-modern language family on Earth, and they did it almost entirely by boat. (For comparison, the Indo-European family that produced English, Spanish, Hindi, and Russian spreads roughly 5,000 miles from Ireland to India.
The Austronesians more than doubled that range.) The Polynesians who voyaged into the central Pacific (Polynesian Voyagers Ch 1) were the easternmost branch of this same family.
The Malay-speakers of Sumatra and the Malay Peninsula were a central Asian branch.
They were linguistic cousins — distant ones by the time the Polynesians reached Hawaii, but cousins nonetheless.

The Austronesians who settled the Indonesian archipelago brought with them the technology that defined regional culture: the outrigger canoe, a hull with one or two lateral floats connected by crossbeams that prevent the vessel from capsizing in rough seas; rice agriculture adapted to wet tropical conditions; pigs, chickens, and dogs as domesticated animals; and a maritime worldview in which the village's relationship to the ocean was as defining as a Mesopotamian village's relationship to its irrigation canal (Mesopotamia Ch 2).

By the early centuries CE, Austronesian-speaking communities along the coasts of Sumatra, Java, Borneo, and the Malay Peninsula had several thousand years of coastal and inter-island sailing experience.
The infrastructure for a major maritime trading empire was there long before any state existed to organize it.
What changed in the first few centuries CE was the arrival of long-distance trade with India and China.

By around 100 CE, Chinese imperial records were already describing ships from "the southern seas" calling at Guangzhou with rhinoceros horn, ivory, pearls, tortoiseshell, kingfisher feathers, and exotic woods — the first written references to ports in modern Sumatra and the Malay Peninsula.
Han-dynasty merchants were reaching south for these goods (Han Dynasty Ch 5), and the southerners were sending tribute missions to the Han court in return.

At roughly the same time, Indian merchants were sailing east, drawn by the spice islands and by the gold their texts called Suvarnabhumi (soo-var-nah-BHOO-mee, "the land of gold") and Suvarnadvipa ("the gold island") — terms that referred most often to Sumatra.

Pliny the Elder, writing from Rome in the first century CE, complained that the Roman Empire was hemorrhaging silver to India to pay for spices that originally came from Indonesian islands he had no name for.
The economics of long-distance trade in the early common era was governed by a single physical fact: the monsoon wind cycle.
Half the year, from roughly May to September, prevailing winds blew from the southwest, carrying ships eastward from India and the Middle East across the Bay of Bengal and the South China Sea.
The other half, from November to March, the winds reversed and blew from the northeast, carrying ships home.

A merchant who set out from a port in Tamil Nadu in early summer could expect to reach Sumatra in a few weeks, and would then need to wait several months in port for the wind to flip before sailing back.
The Strait of Malacca and the surrounding ports were the natural waiting room.
A Chinese merchant heading west operated on the same cycle in mirror image.
The result is that long before any centralized political authority existed in maritime Southeast Asia, the region had become a layover zone for international commerce.
Ports along the Strait of Malacca and on the eastern Sumatran coast filled up with traders waiting for the monsoon to change.
The traders needed food, water, fresh ship repairs, lodging, and sometimes companionship.
They needed protection from local pirates.
They needed reliable currency exchange.
They needed warehousing for goods that had to be transferred from Indian Ocean vessels to South China Sea vessels (different ship designs, different crews, different sailing techniques).
The communities that figured out how to provide these services took a cut of every transaction.
The community that figured out how to monopolize these services became fabulously wealthy.
That community would eventually be Srivijaya.
But before it could exist, the regional template had to be invented.

The first major Southeast Asian state attested in outside sources is Funan (foo-NAHN), a kingdom in the lower Mekong delta in modern southern Vietnam and Cambodia, which flourished from roughly the first century CE to the mid-sixth.

Funan's capital was probably at a site called Vyadhapura, and its principal port at Oc Eo has yielded archaeological finds that document the cosmopolitan trade culture of the era: Roman gold coins from the second century, Chinese mirrors from the third, Sanskrit inscriptions, a Hindu-Buddhist religious establishment, and warehouses full of glass, gemstones, and Indian goods.

Funan was not on the Strait of Malacca route — it sat further east, on the South China Sea side of the Malay Peninsula — but it was the first regional power to demonstrate what an Indianized Southeast Asian state looked like.
What does "Indianized" mean?

Beginning around the early common era, Indian cultural elements began spreading across maritime Southeast Asia: Sanskrit, the Brahmi-derived scripts of India, Hindu and Buddhist religion, Indian temple architecture, Indian-style royal titles and coronation rites, Indian legal concepts, and the Indian cosmological framework in which a king served as the earthly mirror of a divine universal order.

Local Southeast Asian rulers adopted Sanskrit names ending in -varman ("protected by"), patronized Brahmin priests and Buddhist monks, built Hindu temples on the Indian model, and wrote royal inscriptions in Sanskrit.
The transfer was not military conquest.
India never invaded.
The mechanism was trade, prestige, and the practical utility of an existing literate religious culture for legitimizing emerging states.
This process is sometimes called the Indianization of Southeast Asia, and it is one of the most consequential cultural transfers in pre-modern history.

The closest comparison is the Hellenization of the eastern Mediterranean after Alexander, or the Sinicization of Korea (Ancient Korea Ch 4) and Japan (Ancient Japan Ch 3) under the long Chinese influence: a great civilization radiating cultural prestige across a wide region without ever conquering it.

The structural parallel to Romanization in the western Mediterranean is closer in scale but less precise, because Romanization required Roman troops and Roman administrators on the ground, while Indianization spread without a single Indian soldier setting foot in Sumatra.
Indian texts, ideas, and religious specialists traveled by ship and were welcomed by local elites who found them useful.
The result was that, by the fifth or sixth century, every emerging state in maritime Southeast Asia was building itself in Indian dress.
A few of these early Indianized states deserve names.

Champa (CHAHM-pah), on the central coast of modern Vietnam, was a Hindu-Buddhist kingdom that controlled the Vietnamese coast through medieval times and produced extraordinary brick temple complexes at My Son.
Kedah (KEH-dah), on the western coast of the Malay Peninsula, was an early Indianized port state that would later become a major Srivijayan tributary.
The Pyu city-states in upper Burma were a third.
Each of these polities adopted Indian writing, Indian religion, and Indian-style royal symbolism while remaining ethnically and linguistically Southeast Asian.
They were the regional template Srivijaya would inherit and surpass.
Funan collapsed in the mid-sixth century, conquered or absorbed by an upstart neighbor called Chenla (CHEN-lah, the predecessor state to the later Khmer empire).
The collapse opened a regional vacuum.
The trade routes did not stop — international demand for Indonesian spices and Sumatran gold was as strong as ever — but no single state was now positioned to dominate them.
For roughly a century, between 550 and 650 CE, the maritime trade of Southeast Asia was distributed among many small port-states, none of them powerful enough to extract serious tolls.
In this vacuum, a small Sumatran community at the mouth of the Musi River began to grow.
The site was Palembang (PAH-lem-bahng), a settlement set inland on the Musi about forty miles upstream from the open sea but accessible to ocean-going ships through a wide navigable channel.
Palembang's geography was almost ideal for the role it would shortly play.
The inland location made the city safe from naval attack — any hostile fleet would have to fight its way upriver through a narrow channel that local defenders could easily block.
The river itself was deep enough to take large trading vessels at high tide.
The surrounding hinterland was rich in forest products (camphor, eaglewood, dammar resin, and gold panned from the upland streams) that could be carried down to the port for export.
And, most importantly, Palembang sat just south of the Strait of Malacca — close enough to dominate strait traffic if the city ever gained the means.
Around 650 CE, by the conventional date, that means appeared.

Out of the small Palembang polity emerged a ruler named Dapunta Hyang Sri Jayanasa (dah-POON-tah HYAHNG sree JAH-yah-NAH-sah), who within a generation had conquered the surrounding territories, brought the Strait of Malacca under his control, and proclaimed a new kingdom called Srivijaya — Sanskrit for "shining victory." Within two decades, Chinese sources were writing about him.

Within fifty years, his successors were sending tribute missions to the Tang court at Chang'an, taxing every merchant ship passing through the Strait, and presiding over a Buddhist scholarly establishment that pilgrims from across Asia would soon describe.
That is where the next chapter starts.
A pause, before the chronology takes over: maritime Southeast Asia in 650 CE was a far more sophisticated and connected world than European or American readers usually imagine.

The region had several thousand years of continuous maritime tradition behind it, an active commercial network linking it to India, China, the Roman Mediterranean (via India), and the Persian world, a literate Indianized political culture across most of its emerging states, and a population of skilled seafarers with the deep-water ship technology to make long voyages routine.
What it lacked was a single state powerful enough to capture the wealth that flowed through its waters.
Srivijaya filled that gap.
The empire's growth was less an invention from scratch than the consolidation of a pre-existing system under unified management.
Cross-civ check: the world that Srivijaya was about to grow into was the seventh-century Eurasian world of the late antique transition.
The Sassanid Empire in Persia (Persian Empire Ch 9) had just been destroyed by the Arab Muslim conquests of the 630s and 640s.
The Byzantine Empire had lost Egypt, Syria, and North Africa to the same Arab armies (Byzantine Empire Ch 4).
In China, the Tang Dynasty had been founded in 618 and was about to enter its great age under Empress Wu and Emperor Xuanzong.
In India, the Pushyabhuti emperor Harsha had just died in 647 (Medieval India Ch 1), ending the brief reunification of the north.
In Mesoamerica, the Maya were entering their Late Classic peak (Maya Civilization Ch 5).
Srivijaya was a contemporary of all of these — a smaller and more invisible state than any of them, but plugged into the same Eurasian system through trade.

The story of how a small Sumatran river port became the gatekeeper to Asia's wealthiest trade route is the story of one ruling family, one strategic geographic accident, and one Chinese pilgrim who happened to write everything down.

chapters.title: The Founding
sentences: In June of the year 671, a Chinese Buddhist monk named Yijing (yee-JING, also spelled I-Tsing) boarded a Persian merchant ship at Guangzhou and sailed south for Sumatra.
He was thirty-six years old and on his way to study Buddhism in India.
The ship took twenty days to reach his destination, a port he calls in Chinese sources Foshi (FOH-shee) and which all modern scholars identify as Palembang.
He stayed there for six months.
He came back several times over the next two and a half decades.
And what he wrote about the kingdom he found is, to this day, the longest and most detailed surviving description of Srivijaya from any contemporary observer.
Yijing's account is the foundation of everything we know about early Srivijaya, and it deserves a moment of explanation.

He was a serious scholar — a member of the great wave of Chinese Buddhist pilgrims who, in the seventh century, undertook the dangerous journey to India to study the Sanskrit originals of Buddhist scriptures.

The most famous of these pilgrims was Xuanzang (shwen-DZAHNG, 602–664), who had crossed Central Asia overland to India in the 630s and returned to China seventeen years later with hundreds of Sanskrit texts and a memoir of his travels that was so detailed it later helped Indian archaeologists rediscover lost Buddhist sites.

Yijing was a younger contemporary who took the southern sea route instead, and his memoir of his Indian and Southeast Asian travels — usually translated as A Record of Buddhist Practices Sent Home from the Southern Seas — is one of the great travel books of the medieval world.
It is also, by sheer historical luck, the principal evidence for Srivijaya's existence in its first century.
Without Yijing, we would have only a few stone inscriptions and a great deal of uncertainty.
What did Yijing find at Palembang in 671?

He found a thriving Buddhist establishment with more than 1,000 monks studying Sanskrit, debating doctrine, and copying scriptures — a community he considered comparable in scale and seriousness to the great Indian monasteries he was on his way to visit.
He found a king who patronized Buddhism actively and whose realm was apparently expanding.

He found a port full of foreign merchants, with traders from China, India, the Persian world, and parts of the Indonesian archipelago all transacting business under what was clearly a regulated and orderly customs regime.

And he found enough Sanskrit instruction at Palembang that he recommended Chinese pilgrims spend a year or two there before continuing on to India, both to learn Sanskrit grammar and to acclimate to the rigorous Indian-style monastic life.
Palembang, he wrote, was effectively a Sanskrit prep school for Chinese monks heading to Nalanda.
That is a strikingly developed institutional complex for a kingdom we have no other contemporary description of.
It is also strikingly Buddhist for a region that had been, until recently, a patchwork of Hindu and animist port-states with smaller Buddhist communities scattered in.
Something had happened at Palembang in the recent past.
Yijing's account does not really explain what.
The Srivijayan side of the story comes from a small handful of Old Malay stone inscriptions, all dating to the 680s, that surface across southern Sumatra and the offshore islands.
The most important is the Kedukan Bukit Inscription (keh-DOO-kahn BOO-kit), discovered in 1920 on a hillside near Palembang.
The stone is small — about eighteen inches across — and the text is short, but its content is dramatic.

It records that in 682 CE, a king called Dapunta Hyang Sri Jayanasa set out from a place called Minanga with a fleet of perhaps twenty thousand troops, made a journey, and the next year, in April or May 683, founded Srivijaya ("shining victory" in Sanskrit).

The inscription is fragmentary and parts of the translation are debated — exactly where Minanga was, exactly what the journey accomplished, and exactly what the founding of Srivijaya consisted of are all matters scholars argue about.
But the basic outline is solid: somewhere in the early 680s, a Sumatran ruler named Dapunta Hyang launched a major military expedition that resulted in the establishment of a new kingdom.
The second inscription is the Talang Tuwo Inscription (TAH-lahng TOO-woh), dated 684 CE and also found near Palembang.
This one records the founding of a Buddhist sacred garden by the same Dapunta Hyang.

The text is longer than the Kedukan Bukit and includes elaborate Mahayana Buddhist devotional language — wishes that the merit generated by the garden's foundation should benefit all sentient beings, a list of physical comforts the king hopes will be available to those who use the garden, and praise to various Mahayana figures.
It is the earliest Buddhist text yet found in maritime Southeast Asia.

It also confirms that Dapunta Hyang's regime was already deeply Buddhist by the time it consolidated political power, which fits Yijing's contemporary description of the 1,000-monk monastic establishment.
The Buddhist character of the new Srivijayan state was there from the start.

The third and fourth inscriptions are the Telaga Batu Inscription (teh-LAH-gah BAH-too, found at Palembang) and the Kota Kapur Inscription (KOH-tah KAH-poor, found on Bangka Island), both dated to 686 CE.
The Telaga Batu is an elaborate oath text, the kind that vassals would swear to a king.
It threatens supernatural punishment — death, sickness, the destruction of one's family — on anyone who rebels against Srivijayan authority, and the punishments are described with vivid precision.
The Kota Kapur is similar in form and includes a specific reference to a planned military campaign against Java.

Together, the two inscriptions document the political mechanism of early Srivijaya: not a centralized administered state on the Roman or Tang Chinese model, but a network of vassal port-states bound to the king by personal oaths backed by religious sanctions.
This matters.
Srivijaya was, structurally, less like a territorial empire and more like a federation of harbor towns owing allegiance to a central royal court.
The king did not station governors in vassal cities or collect taxes through a salaried bureaucracy.
He extracted tribute and military service from local rulers who had personally sworn loyalty to him.
When those rulers failed to maintain their oaths, the king used naval force to discipline them.
When they failed to do even that, the empire weakened.
Most pre-modern empires worked this way to some degree, but Srivijaya's dependence on personal loyalty and naval punishment was unusually pure.
The empire had no land army of consequence and no provincial bureaucracy.
It had a fleet, a treasury, and a network of sworn vassals.
That was the system.
A pause on what we don't know about Dapunta Hyang.
The inscriptions tell us his name and his role as founder.
They tell us he commanded a substantial military expedition in 682–683.
They tell us he was Buddhist, that he founded a sacred garden, and that he claimed sovereignty over a wide swath of southern Sumatra and the offshore islands.
They do not tell us where he came from, who his parents were, what he looked like, how he claimed legitimacy beyond military success and Buddhist patronage, when he died, or what his successor did.
We know almost nothing about him as a person.
The Srivijayan king who founded one of the most consequential maritime empires in pre-modern history is, as a historical individual, almost invisible.
This is a recurring pattern with Srivijaya, and it is worth flagging early because it affects how the rest of the chapters read.
The empire's internal records have not survived.
There is no Srivijayan equivalent of the Tang dynastic chronicles, the Pala copperplate grants, the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, or the Sasanian inscription tradition.
There is no king-list.
There are no preserved royal annals.
Most Srivijayan kings are named only in passing in foreign sources — Chinese tribute records, Tamil military inscriptions, Tibetan Buddhist hagiographies — and many of them are not named at all.
We know the empire existed, we know what it controlled, and we know what it accomplished.
We know almost nothing about the specific human beings who ran it.
