There were vernacular literatures (the French chansons de geste, the German Minnesinger lyrics, the English Chaucer who was Dante's near-contemporary), but they were treated as secondary to the Latin canon.

What Dante did with the Divine Comedy was claim, with absolute confidence, that vernacular Italian could carry the full weight of an epic theological-political poem on the model of Virgil's Aeneid — and then he did it.
He even wrote a separate Latin treatise (De vulgari eloquentia, "On Vernacular Eloquence") arguing the theoretical point.
The choice of Tuscan Italian as Dante's medium would shape Italy in ways Dante did not anticipate.

The Italian peninsula in 1300 had no single Italian language — every region spoke its own dialect, often mutually unintelligible (a Sicilian and a Venetian could not easily understand each other in their everyday speech).
What Dante did with the Comedy was make Tuscan, specifically the dialect of Florence, the prestige dialect of Italian literary culture.
Every subsequent Italian writer who wanted national reach wrote in Tuscan.

By the time Italy was finally unified in 1861, Tuscan had been the de facto national literary standard for five centuries, and modern standard Italian is essentially fourteenth-century Tuscan with grammatical updates.
Dante is therefore, in addition to everything else, the founding father of Italian as a unified national language.
The Comedy is also one of the strongest pieces of evidence against the modern myth that medieval Europeans believed the earth was flat (Late Medieval Europe Ch 1).

Dante's universe is a sphere — a spherical earth at the center of nested celestial spheres, with Hell carved into the earth's interior as an inverted cone descending to the center, Purgatory as a mountain rising in the southern hemisphere ocean (where Dante believed there was no other land), and Heaven as a series of concentric rotating spheres above.

The cosmology is the standard Aristotelian-Ptolemaic model that every educated person took for granted, and Dante's geographic precision in describing it (latitudes, hemispheres, antipodal locations) is the work of someone for whom spherical earth was obvious common sense.
Dante's significance for the Renaissance goes beyond his individual achievement.
He demonstrated that vernacular Italian could be a serious literary medium.
He treated classical antiquity (Virgil) as a living presence in the Christian world rather than a discarded predecessor.
He used a first-person poetic voice to claim spiritual and political authority that the medieval tradition had reserved for institutional authorities.

And he set a precedent of the writer as autonomous individual genius, working in exile against political enemies, that would shape Petrarch's self-presentation a generation later and the broader Renaissance cult of individual creative ambition for the next three centuries.

The painter who matters most for the Trecento is Giotto di Bondone (JOT-toh dee bon-DOH-nay, c. 1267–1337), a near-contemporary of Dante (Dante mentions him by name in Purgatory), born in a small Tuscan village near Florence and trained in the Florentine painters' workshops.
Giotto worked across Italy — in Florence, Padua, Naples, Rome, Assisi — and dominated Italian painting in the first third of the fourteenth century.
The single best place to see his work today is the Scrovegni Chapel (skroh-VEN-yee) in Padua, which he frescoed around 1305.
What Giotto did was reinvent how Italian painters depicted physical and emotional reality.

The dominant style of late thirteenth-century Italian religious painting was the Italo-Byzantine — a derivative of Byzantine icon painting, characterized by flat figures, stylized facial expressions, gold-leaf backgrounds, and a deliberate non-naturalism that emphasized the spiritual rather than the physical reality of holy subjects.

The figures in Italo-Byzantine paintings are not in three-dimensional space; they float on a gold ground, conveying religious meaning through symbolic gesture and convention rather than through observed reality.
The style was sophisticated and beautiful, but it was not interested in depicting the physical world the viewer actually lived in.
Giotto changed this.
His figures have weight: you can see how their bodies bear gravity, how their robes hang from their shoulders, how their feet press into the ground.
His faces have specific psychological expressions: grief, surprise, anger, tenderness — emotions painted from observed human reality rather than copied from convention.
His compositions place figures in three-dimensional architectural settings, with rudimentary perspective (the receding lines are not yet mathematically accurate, but they convey spatial recession).
His colors are subtle gradients rather than flat blocks.

And the overall effect is that the religious narratives — the life of Mary, the Passion of Christ, the lives of the saints — feel like things that happened to real people in a real world, rather than emblematic icons floating outside time.
The Scrovegni Chapel cycle is the masterpiece.

Painted in roughly two years for the wealthy Paduan banker Enrico Scrovegni (whose family fortune came from usury, a sin that would have placed the elder Scrovegni in Dante's Hell — the chapel was probably built partly as expiation), the cycle shows the lives of Mary's parents, Mary's own life, and Christ's Passion across thirty-eight large panels.

The most famous individual scenes — the Lamentation (Mary cradling the dead Christ, painted with raw human grief that no earlier Italian painter had attempted), the Kiss of Judas (Judas embracing Christ in close-up, the composition centered on the dramatic tension between betrayal and recognition), the Massacre of the Innocents (Herod's soldiers killing Bethlehem's children, painted with horrific specificity) — became reference works for every Italian painter for the next two hundred years.
Masaccio (Chapter 3) studied Giotto.
Michelangelo (Chapter 4) studied Giotto.
The Italian pictorial tradition that the Renaissance would extend and codify is recognizably continuous with Giotto's work a century earlier.
The continuity matters because it is one of the strongest pieces of evidence against the "Renaissance as sudden break" framing.
By 1305, an Italian painter had already produced figures with three-dimensional weight, emotional psychological depth, and proto-perspectival spatial settings.
The technical refinements that the fifteenth-century painters would add — mathematical perspective, anatomical precision, oil painting — were extensions of Giotto's project, not departures from it.

Modern art historians describe Giotto as a proto-Renaissance figure, but the prefix is doing a lot of work; he is part of the same continuous Italian tradition that produced Masaccio, Botticelli, and Leonardo.
A small clarifying note: Giotto's frescoes survive but his panel paintings are mostly lost or contested in attribution.
The famous Ognissanti Madonna in the Uffizi (Florence) is reliably his.
The Assisi frescoes traditionally attributed to him (the Life of St.
Francis cycle in the upper basilica) are debated in modern scholarship — some specialists attribute them to a contemporary called the Master of the St.
Francis Cycle, possibly the young Giotto, possibly not.

The historical Giotto is therefore a slightly more constrained figure than the legendary Giotto of Vasari's Lives of the Artists (Chapter 7), whose biography of Giotto in 1550 introduced most of the colorful anecdotes (the perfect circle drawn freehand for the pope, the discovery of the boy Giotto sketching sheep on a flat rock and being invited to apprentice in the city) that have circulated ever since.
Vasari's stories are entertaining; very few of them can be independently verified.
The third Trecento figure is Petrarch (1304–1374, Italian: Francesco Petrarca, fran-CHESS-koh peh-TRAR-kah), conventionally identified as the first Renaissance humanist.
The label is so worn that it can obscure how genuinely strange Petrarch's project was — and Petrarch deserves a fuller introduction than the brief one Late Medieval Europe Ch 1 gave.
Petrarch was born in Arezzo, in Tuscany, the son of a Florentine notary who had been exiled from Florence around the same time as Dante.
The family moved to Avignon when Petrarch was a child, following the papal court that had relocated there in 1309 (Late Medieval Europe Ch 4).

Petrarch grew up bilingual in Italian and Provençal, was educated for a legal career he never pursued, took minor church orders that gave him a modest income from clerical benefices without requiring full priestly responsibilities, and spent his entire adult life as an independent scholar-poet supported by a combination of clerical income and aristocratic patronage.
He never married.
He had at least two illegitimate children.
He moved between Avignon, Vaucluse (a country retreat in Provence), Milan, Padua, Venice, and Arquà (in the Euganean Hills near Padua, where he died).
His career is one of the earliest examples in European history of someone making a living as a freelance intellectual on the strength of literary reputation alone.
The substance of his work was twofold.
The first was the systematic recovery of classical Latin literature.

Petrarch traveled to monastery libraries across Europe looking for surviving manuscripts of classical authors, copied them out by hand, edited them against other manuscripts, and built up a personal library of perhaps 200 classical texts — one of the largest classical libraries in private hands at the time.

His most famous individual discovery was a manuscript of Cicero's Letters to Atticus at the cathedral library of Verona in 1345 — a private correspondence by the great Roman orator that no medieval reader had previously seen.

Reading Cicero's intimate letters changed Petrarch's view of Cicero: the public moralist of the medieval tradition turned out, in private, to have been a vain, ambitious, frequently petty politician with strong opinions about everyone he disliked.
Petrarch wrote a famous letter to the dead Cicero complaining about his disappointing private behavior.

The exchange — a fourteenth-century scholar writing to a first-century-BCE Roman as if to a contemporary — is the founding moment of the Renaissance humanist relationship to antiquity: classical authors as living interlocutors rather than as authoritative texts.

The second component of Petrarch's work was vernacular love poetry, specifically the cycle of Italian sonnets and other lyrics that he wrote (in Tuscan Italian, like Dante) over four decades to a married woman named Laura.

He claimed to have first seen Laura in a church in Avignon on April 6, 1327, fallen instantly in love, and continued to write about her for the next twenty-one years until she died in the Black Death on April 6, 1348 — exactly twenty-one years to the day after he had first seen her.
He continued to write about her for another twenty-six years after her death.
The collected poems, called the Canzoniere (kahn-tsohn-YAIR-ay, "Songbook") or Rime sparse ("Scattered Rhymes"), are 366 lyrics that he revised and rearranged obsessively for the rest of his life.
Whether Laura was a real person has been debated; the standard scholarly reading is that she was, possibly Laure de Noves, a Provençal noblewoman.
But the literary Laura is more important than the historical one.

The Canzoniere established the sonnet form as the dominant European lyric form (Petrarch's structural innovation — fourteen lines in a specific rhyme scheme — was imitated for the next four centuries, including by Shakespeare in the 1590s), the Petrarchan beloved as the standard literary trope of unattainable idealized female beauty, and the introspective first-person lyric voice as a major mode of European literature.
Petrarch's third claim to historical importance is more diffuse: he invented the modern conception of the autonomous individual creative genius.
He wrote autobiographically.
He cultivated a personal literary reputation.

He arranged for himself to be crowned poet laureate in Rome in 1341 in an elaborate public ceremony modeled on (Petrarch claimed) ancient Roman precedent — the first such coronation since antiquity, and the model for every subsequent poet laureate in the European tradition.

He climbed Mont Ventoux in Provence in 1336 in what is conventionally called the first self-conscious aesthetic appreciation of nature in European literature (he wrote a long letter about the experience that has been one of the founding documents of European nature writing).

He saw himself as a great man living among ordinary contemporaries, recovering the lost greatness of antiquity, leaving a literary legacy for an imagined future readership that would understand him better than his contemporaries did.
The self-mythologizing was not subtle.

It was also enormously influential: the Renaissance cult of the individual creative genius — the painter, the writer, the architect as a person of historical importance comparable to a king — runs continuously from Petrarch through Vasari's Lives of the Artists (Chapter 7) into the modern conception of the artist as a privileged figure.

Petrarch's relationship to Christianity was uncomplicated and orthodox: he was a devout Catholic who took religious life seriously, wrote devotional works in Latin, and considered his vernacular love poetry trivial compared to his classical scholarship.
He was not, despite the modern framing of "humanism" as a quasi-secular movement, in any sense anti-religious.
The Renaissance humanists in general were not anti-religious.

What they argued was that classical pagan literature contained moral wisdom and rhetorical sophistication that complemented Christian revelation, and that the medieval educational curriculum had unduly neglected this body of work.
The synthesis the humanists were trying to build was Christian-classical, not anti-Christian.
Petrarch is the prototype.

The fourth Trecento figure is Giovanni Boccaccio (joh-VAH-nee boh-KAH-choh, 1313–1375), a generation younger than Petrarch (whom he met in 1350 and venerated for the rest of his life as a literary mentor) and the third great Tuscan vernacular writer after Dante and Petrarch.
Boccaccio was born in Florence (or possibly Certaldo, near Florence — sources differ), the illegitimate son of a Florentine merchant.

His father sent him to Naples in 1327 to apprentice in the Bardi banking branch there; Boccaccio hated banking and abandoned it for literary work, frequenting the Neapolitan court of King Robert of Anjou, falling in love with a noblewoman he called Fiammetta (fee-ah-MET-tah, "little flame") in his early poetry, and reading widely in classical and medieval literature.

He returned to Florence around 1340 — just in time to live through the Bardi bank's spectacular 1346 collapse (which devastated his father's finances) and the Black Death of 1348 (which killed his father, his stepmother, and most of his Florentine friends).
The Black Death is the framing device for his masterpiece, the Decameron (deh-KAH-meh-rohn, from Greek deka hēmerai, "ten days").

Written between roughly 1349 and 1353, the Decameron is a collection of one hundred prose stories told by ten young Florentine narrators — seven women and three men — who have fled the plague-stricken city for a country villa in the Tuscan hills above Florence.
Each narrator tells one story per day for ten days; each day has a thematic prompt set by the day's elected leader.
The stories range from bawdy farce to courtly romance to devotional miracle to satirical anti-clericalism, with nearly every conceivable subject and tone represented somewhere across the hundred.

The collection is the founding masterpiece of Italian prose and one of the most influential narrative works in European literature — Chaucer's Canterbury Tales (1380s) is partly modeled on it, and individual Decameron stories were retold throughout subsequent European literature.
What distinguishes the Decameron from its medieval predecessors is the matter-of-fact secularism of its narrative voice.

Many of the stories are set in contemporary Florence and feature recognizable types of Florentine social life — merchants, wives, friars, peasants, courtesans, lawyers — described with sharp observational realism and very little moralizing.

The frame story, in which the ten narrators have escaped a plague-stricken city, gives the entire collection an undercurrent of mortality: the storytellers are entertaining themselves while a third of their fellow citizens die, and Boccaccio is unsparing in describing what plague-stricken Florence actually looked like (the abandoned dead, the closed shops, the breakdown of normal social life).

The famous opening of the Decameron — Boccaccio's first-person prose description of plague-time Florence — is one of the most cited primary sources for what the Black Death looked like to people who lived through it.
Boccaccio's anti-clerical streak is worth noting.
A substantial number of Decameron stories satirize hypocritical or corrupt friars, lecherous priests, and credulous laypeople taken in by religious fraud.

The satire is not anti-religious — Boccaccio remained a Catholic — but it is anti-clerical in a way that became standard in late-medieval Italian literature and that the Reformation would amplify a century and a half later.

The institutional Catholic Church in Boccaccio's time was a wealthy, politically powerful, and frequently scandalous institution, and Italian literary realism took unflinching note of the gap between its spiritual claims and its actual operations.
In his later life, Boccaccio shifted dramatically away from vernacular fiction toward Latin scholarship.

Influenced by his veneration of Petrarch, he produced encyclopedic Latin works on classical mythology, on the genealogies of pagan gods, on famous classical women, on the geography of the ancient world.
None of these later works approaches the Decameron in literary quality, but they were standard reference works in Renaissance scholarly culture for two centuries.
He also gave the first public lectures on Dante's Divine Comedy in Florence in 1373, a year before his death — establishing the academic study of Dante that has continued unbroken to the present.
The Black Death looms over the entire Trecento, and the cultural consequences of the plague are visible across Italian art and literature for the rest of the century.

The most immediate effect was demographic: roughly half of Florence's population died in 1348, and the population stayed depressed for the rest of the fourteenth century — the city of 100,000 in 1340 was still around 50,000 in 1400.
The same was true across Tuscany and most of northern Italy.

The depopulation had ambiguous economic effects: agricultural production fell, but the survivors inherited concentrated wealth (when a third to a half of a community dies, the survivors inherit the land, houses, gold, and movable property of the dead).
Wages for skilled labor doubled in many trades.
Land prices fell.
Houses became cheaper.

The surviving merchant elite of Florence emerged from the plague richer per capita than they had been before, with more disposable wealth to spend on art commissions, family chapels, public buildings, and the trappings of social status.

Some of the great fourteenth-century Florentine art commissions — including elements of the cathedral construction that would shortly produce Brunelleschi's dome — were paid for with plague-redistributed wealth.
The cultural effect was deeper.
Italian art and literature after 1351 became preoccupied with mortality in ways earlier medieval Italian work had not been.

The genre of the Triumph of Death — frescoes showing skeletal Death harvesting people from every social rank — appeared in Italian churches in the second half of the fourteenth century and remained a major theme through the fifteenth.
The danse macabre ("dance of death") tradition was strong in Italy as in northern Europe.

Devotional art emphasized the Crucifixion, the Lamentation, the Pietà, the suffering Christ — emotionally raw scenes of death and grief — over the more triumphant Christ-in-glory iconography of the high Middle Ages.
Death is everywhere in late Trecento Italian art in a way it had not been before.

Some art historians (notably Millard Meiss in his 1951 study Painting in Florence and Siena after the Black Death) have argued that the plague produced a measurable retrogression in Italian painting between roughly 1350 and 1400 — a swing back toward more hieratic, more rigidly devotional, less naturalistic styles than Giotto's, partly as a response to the perceived spiritual failure that the plague represented.

The Meiss thesis is contested in modern scholarship — counter-examples of continuing naturalistic development across the second half of the century have been adduced — but the broader point about the plague's cultural impact is generally accepted: the Black Death changed what Italian art and literature were trying to do, in ways that pushed the cultural conversation toward more direct engagement with mortality, divine judgment, and the precariousness of earthly success.
The other long-running consequence was the strengthening of vernacular literary culture.

The plague disrupted the institutional infrastructure of medieval Latin scholarship — universities lost faculty, monasteries lost monks, ecclesiastical schools closed temporarily — at exactly the moment when wealthy plague-survivor elites were looking for entertainment and edification in their own language.
Vernacular literature in Italian (and French and English) accelerated in the second half of the fourteenth century partly because Latin literature was struggling.
Boccaccio is the key example.
Chaucer in England is the parallel case.
The cultural consequences of the plague were therefore not all retrogressive: the depopulation that emptied the monasteries also fertilized the soil for vernacular literature.
Cross-civ check: the same plague that reshaped Trecento Italy reshaped most of the Eurasian world.
Constantinople lost perhaps half its population (Byzantine Empire Ch 10).
Egypt under the Mamluks lost perhaps 30–40%.
The Ottoman beyliks in Anatolia were absorbing the disrupted refugees and consolidating power that would shortly produce the great Ottoman expansion (Ottoman Empire Ch 1).
China had experienced major plague-like epidemics that contributed to the political instability that brought down the Yuan in 1368.

Mali under Mansa Sulayman appears to have been spared (the trans-Saharan trade routes seem not to have been efficient plague vectors, possibly because of the desert's role as a biological filter — Mali Empire Ch 5).
The Americas, where Eurasian diseases had not yet reached, were untouched (Aztec Empire Ch 3, contemporary Andean polities).
The fourteenth-century Eurasian plague is one of the structural facts that shaped the rest of the millennium, and Italy is one node in that pattern.
The cultural transformation that produced the Renaissance happened, in part, on the demographic ruins of the Black Death.
By 1400, the Trecento was over.
Dante had been dead for eighty years.
Petrarch and Boccaccio were dead.
Giotto had been dead for sixty years.
The first generation of the figures who would define the Quattrocento — Brunelleschi, Ghiberti, Donatello, Masaccio, Cosimo de' Medici — were either recently born or about to be.

The cultural infrastructure was in place: vernacular Italian was a serious literary medium, classical scholarship had a model in Petrarch, naturalistic painting had a model in Giotto, prose narrative had a model in Boccaccio.
The economic infrastructure was in place: post-plague Florence and Venice were flush with concentrated wealth looking for investment.
The political infrastructure was in place: the city-state competition was producing patrons in multiple capitals.
What was about to happen in fifteenth-century Florence had been prepared, slowly and incrementally, by the previous century.
The Quattrocento is next.

chapters.title: The Quattrocento
sentences: The fifteenth century — the Quattrocento — is when the cultural shift that began with Dante and Giotto matured into something that contemporaries themselves recognized as new.
The center of gravity was Florence.
The patrons who funded it were the Medici.
The architectural symbol that announced it was an enormous brick dome rising over the Florentine cathedral that had stood roofless for forty years because no one knew how to span it.
The Quattrocento story is structurally a Florentine story.
Most of the figures lived or worked in Florence; most of the major commissions were Florentine; the Medici Bank that funded much of the patronage was a Florentine institution.

Other Italian cities produced major Quattrocento art (Mantegna in Padua and Mantua, Piero della Francesca in Urbino, the Bellini family in Venice — Chapter 5), but the energy that defined the century radiated outward from Florence.
Florence in 1400 had a population of around 50,000 — half what it had been in 1340.
By 1500, it would still be only 70,000.
That a city of perhaps 50,000–70,000 people could produce a generation of artists and architects who reshaped Western art is one of the most striking demographic-cultural facts in European history.

The single best symbol of the Florentine Quattrocento is the dome of Florence Cathedral — the Cathedral of Santa Maria del Fiore (SAN-tah mah-REE-ah del fee-OR-ay, "Saint Mary of the Flower"), the immense Gothic structure begun in 1296 by the architect Arnolfo di Cambio.
The body of the cathedral was finished by 1380.
The crossing, however, was open to the sky.
The architects had designed an enormous octagonal opening 138 feet (42 meters) across the diameter that no one knew how to span.
Conventional Gothic vaulting could not handle the span.
Roman concrete techniques had been lost.
The cathedral committee stalled for forty years.
Florentines walked past their cathedral every day and saw a hole in the roof.
In 1418, the cathedral committee announced a public competition for the dome design.
The competition was won by Filippo Brunelleschi (fee-LEEP-poh broo-nel-LES-kee, 1377–1446), a Florentine goldsmith with no formal training as an architect.
Brunelleschi's proposal was so radical that the committee initially refused to accept it.

He proposed a double-shelled brick dome — an inner load-bearing structure and an outer protective shell, with hidden iron and stone tension chains binding the structure horizontally to prevent it from spreading outward as it rose.
The double-shell design was lighter than a solid masonry dome would have been, with a hollow space between the two shells where construction workers could climb internal staircases.

He proposed to build the entire dome without exterior scaffolding — the medieval method of dome construction, which would have been impossible at this scale because no scaffolding could be cantilevered safely from a 200-foot-high opening with no central support.
Instead, he proposed building each course of bricks in a self-supporting catenary curve, with each course locking the previous one in place through the geometry of the brickwork itself.

He also designed special hoisting machinery — powered by oxen on the ground, with ropes through pulley systems, including a famously clever reversible gear that let the hoists lower loads without the oxen having to be unhitched and walked backward — to lift bricks, stone, and water to the construction level.
Most of these techniques had no contemporary precedent in Italy.

Brunelleschi appears to have worked them out partly by studying Roman ruins (he had spent time in Rome around 1402–1404 with the young Donatello, sketching Roman architecture and learning from the surviving classical buildings) and partly by sheer engineering invention.
He filed for the world's first known patent in 1421, on a boat design for transporting marble to the cathedral construction site.
He drew almost nothing for the dome itself, kept his methods secret, and supervised construction in person from the scaffold tops, refusing to delegate the structurally critical decisions.
The dome was begun in 1420 and finished in 1436 — sixteen years of construction, during which Brunelleschi invented essentially every element of the project.
The completed dome was the largest masonry dome built in Europe since the Pantheon (Ancient Rome Ch 7) thirteen centuries earlier.
It rose 376 feet above the floor of the cathedral, weighed an estimated 37,000 tons, and contained roughly four million bricks.
It is still standing in 2026.
It is still the largest brick dome in the world.
Brunelleschi's later structural lantern that crowns the dome (designed before his death, completed by his successor between 1446 and 1471) added another 70 feet of height.
The cathedral was finally consecrated by Pope Eugenius IV in March 1436, the year the dome was finished — over a century and a half after construction had begun.
Brunelleschi did not stop with the dome.

He went on to design the Foundling Hospital (Ospedale degli Innocenti) in Florence between 1419 and 1445 — a long arcaded building on the Piazza Santissima Annunziata that is conventionally cited as the first Renaissance building in the strict sense, in that it deliberately revives classical Roman architectural elements (semicircular arches on Corinthian columns, a regular geometric facade, classical proportional ratios) rather than continuing the late Gothic tradition.
He designed the Pazzi Chapel at Santa Croce, the Old Sacristy at San Lorenzo, the rebuilt church of San Lorenzo itself (the Medici parish church), and the church of Santo Spirito across the Arno.

By the time he died in 1446 (and was buried inside his own cathedral, in a tomb under the dome), Brunelleschi had effectively founded Renaissance architecture as a discipline distinct from late Gothic.
He had also reinvented linear perspective — the geometric system for representing three-dimensional space on a two-dimensional surface.

Two famous demonstrations around 1413 (Brunelleschi's perspective drawings of the Florentine Baptistery and the Palazzo Vecchio, viewed through peepholes that aligned the painted images with the actual buildings to demonstrate the geometric accuracy of the technique) are conventionally credited as the launch of the technique.

The geometric principles were codified in the 1430s by the architect-theorist Leon Battista Alberti (Chapter introduction below) in his treatise De Pictura ("On Painting"), published in Latin in 1435 and in Italian translation the following year.

Linear perspective was new in the technical sense — the geometric procedure for drawing accurate perspective had not been formalized before — but the broader interest in spatial naturalism had been developing in Italian painting for at least a century before Brunelleschi (Giotto's spatial settings in Padua are proto-perspectival, Chapter 2).
The Brunelleschi-Alberti perspective system was the codification and extension of trends that were already present, not a sudden break with what came before.
The dome and the perspective system together announce the Quattrocento.

They are simultaneously technical innovations, deliberate revivals of classical antiquity, and acts of civic and personal ambition by a man who was determined to surpass everything Italian builders had ever done.

Brunelleschi is the prototype of the Renaissance Man — the artist as engineer, mathematician, theorist, and self-conscious creative genius — that the next century would extend through Alberti, Leonardo, and Michelangelo.

Brunelleschi's near-contemporary in sculpture was Donatello (don-ah-TEL-loh, full name Donato di Niccolò di Betto Bardi, c. 1386–1466), who reshaped European sculpture in the same decades that Brunelleschi reshaped European architecture.
Donatello was a slightly younger Florentine, trained in Lorenzo Ghiberti's workshop, who had traveled to Rome with Brunelleschi as a young man to study Roman antiquities.

The two men were lifelong friends and collaborators — Donatello provided the sculptural decoration for several of Brunelleschi's buildings — though they reportedly fought constantly about everything else.
Donatello produced an astonishing volume of work across a long career, and a partial list of his innovations is extraordinary.

George for the Or San Michele guild oratory (around 1416) — a marble figure of an armored saint with an unprecedented psychological intensity, the head turned slightly aside, the eyes alert, the body relaxed but ready.

The bronze Habakkuk for the Florentine cathedral campanile (around 1427), a bald, intensely staring prophet so striking that the Florentines nicknamed him lo Zuccone ("the Pumpkin") — Vasari claimed Donatello swore at the statue, "Speak, damn you, speak!" while finishing it.

The bronze Gattamelata equestrian monument in Padua (1453) — a bronze horseman commemorating the Venetian condottiere Erasmo da Narni, the first freestanding equestrian monument cast since the Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius's bronze rider that had stood (mistakenly identified as Constantine) on the Capitoline Hill in Rome.

The wooden Magdalene for the Florentine Baptistery (around 1455) — an emaciated, leathery, terrifying figure of the penitent Mary Magdalene aged by years of desert fasting, painted to look almost like real flesh and hair.
And the bronze David for the Medici palace (around 1440), the work that is still the most discussed.
Donatello's bronze David is the first freestanding nude statue cast in Europe since classical antiquity.

It depicts the biblical David — the boy who killed Goliath — as a slim, sensuous adolescent in a feathered hat and leg-greaves, holding the sword he has just used to behead Goliath, with the giant's severed head under his foot.
The figure is a little over five feet tall.
The bronze surface was originally polished to a high shine.

The composition shows the boy in a relaxed, slightly-twisted contrapposto stance, the weight on one leg, the body in subtle counter-rotation between hips and shoulders — exactly the kind of naturalistic anatomical pose that Greek sculptors had perfected in the fifth century BCE (Ancient Greece Ch 6) and that Roman copies had transmitted to medieval Europe but that no European sculptor had attempted to recover at this scale and quality.
The statue was commissioned for the inner courtyard of the Medici palace, where it stood on a pedestal at eye level, viewable from all sides.
It remained there until the Medici were exiled in 1494, after which it was moved to the courtyard of the Palazzo Vecchio and eventually to the Bargello Museum, where it stands today.
The Davidstatue is also the first identifiable male nude in Italian Renaissance art that openly engages a homoerotic register.

The figure's languid pose, the suggestive feather running up the inside of his thigh, the sensuous polish of the bronze surface have led modern commentators to debate whether Donatello was making a deliberate homoerotic statement, a contemporary biblical allegory, a Medici political statement (the boy hero defeating tyranny), or all three at once.

The biographical evidence about Donatello's own romantic life is thin — Vasari claims he liked beautiful young male assistants, which probably means what it sounds like by modern standards but was not unusual in fifteenth-century Florentine artistic culture — and the question of authorial intent is therefore open.

What is unambiguous is that the statue introduced a new category of object into European sculpture: the freestanding pagan-style nude with classical proportions, displayed in a domestic rather than ecclesiastical setting, on a scale that had not been attempted in over a thousand years.
Donatello and Brunelleschi between them established the visual vocabulary that the Quattrocento would expand.

Painters like Masaccio (Chapter 2 covers his early death; his Brancacci Chapel and Trinity frescoes were painted around 1426–1427 and applied Brunelleschian perspective and Donatellian figural intensity to wall painting) and his successors Fra Angelico, Fra Filippo Lippi, Andrea del Castagno, Paolo Uccello (who was so obsessed with perspective drawing that his wife reportedly complained he loved geometry more than her), and the young Botticelli all worked within a pictorial framework defined by Brunelleschi's perspective and Donatello's figural naturalism.

The single most consequential individual patron of the Quattrocento was Cosimo de' Medici (KOH-zee-moh deh MED-ih-chee, 1389–1464), the Medici banker who effectively governed Florence from 1434 to his death in 1464.
The Medici story has become so famous that it can obscure how unusual their political innovation was.
They were not aristocrats.
They were not military leaders.
They had no formal title higher than membership in the Florentine guilds.
The Florentine constitution was officially anti-aristocratic, deliberately structured to prevent any single family from accumulating monarchical power.
And yet, from 1434 onward, three generations of Medici ran the city as if they owned it, without ever changing the constitution and without ever holding the formal title of king or duke.
The mechanism was money plus patronage plus careful constitutional manipulation.
Cosimo's father Giovanni di Bicci de' Medici (1360–1429) had built the family bank — the Medici Bank, founded in 1397 — into a profitable enterprise centered on the Florentine wool trade.
His genius was political: he won the Roman Curia account, becoming the bankers for the papal court.

The papal account was enormously profitable because the Catholic Church collected dues from ecclesiastical institutions across Europe and needed someone to remit those dues to Rome through international banking networks.
The Medici did this for a percentage.
By the time Giovanni died in 1429, the Medici Bank was the leading bank in Italy and one of the leading banks in Europe.

Cosimo inherited the bank in 1429 and built it further — by mid-century, the Medici Bank had branches in Florence, Rome, Venice, Geneva, Lyon, Avignon, Bruges, London, and several other major European commercial centers.

The total capitalization of the bank around 1450 has been estimated by economic historians at perhaps 90,000 florins, which translated into the largest single concentration of banking capital in Europe.

The bank was not just larger than its rivals; it was structurally more sophisticated, with a system of partially-independent regional branches (each with local managing partners and local capitalization) that limited the parent company's exposure to any single branch's failures.
The Medici Bank was, in modern financial terms, an early limited-liability multinational corporation.
Cosimo's political career began in 1433 with a brief disaster.
The rival Albizzi faction, which had dominated Florentine politics through the 1420s, exiled him in October 1433 on charges of trying to make himself a tyrant.
Cosimo went to Venice for one year.
Florentine voters, missing the tax revenue and credit access the Medici Bank had provided, swung sharply against the Albizzi faction in the 1434 elections.
Cosimo was recalled in October 1434 — and proceeded to dominate Florentine politics for the next thirty years through what would today be called soft power.
He cultivated friendly magistrates.
He bankrolled the campaigns of allied candidates.

He arranged the elaborate constitutional manipulations (changing the rules for who was eligible for the candidate lists, packing the lottery boxes from which magistrates were drawn) that ensured friendly factions controlled the major offices.
He held formal office only intermittently and reluctantly.
Foreign visitors who asked who actually ruled Florence were politely told that the city was governed by the elected Council of Two Hundred.
Foreign visitors who knew anything knew it was Cosimo.
What Cosimo did with that political position is the part of the story that matters for art history.
He patronized Brunelleschi (commissioning the rebuilt church of San Lorenzo, the Medici parish church, with the Old Sacristy where Cosimo and his immediate descendants are buried).
He patronized Donatello (the bronze David in the Medici palace courtyard, plus other commissions).
He patronized Fra Angelico (the frescoes in the Dominican monastery of San Marco, which Cosimo rebuilt and endowed).
He commissioned the Florentine Library of San Marco, the first public library in Europe with cataloged collections open to scholars.

He sponsored Marsilio Ficino to translate Plato's complete dialogues into Latin between 1463 and 1483 — the first such Latin translation, made possible by Ficino's Greek training and Cosimo's funding.

He hosted the Council of Florence in 1438–1439, the failed but culturally consequential attempt at union between the Latin and Greek churches before Constantinople's fall, paying enormous sums to bring the Byzantine emperor and the Greek delegation to Italy (Late Medieval Europe Ch 7 covers the same Council from the medieval Catholic side).
The Council of Florence is worth pausing on, because its cultural consequences exceeded its political ones.

The Greek delegation that traveled to Italy in 1438 included the Patriarch of Constantinople, the Byzantine emperor John VIII, dozens of senior Greek clerics, and scholars including George Gemistus Plethon (a Greek Neoplatonist philosopher whose lectures in Florence introduced Italian humanists to Plato as a serious philosophical alternative to the dominant Aristotelian tradition).

The Council itself produced a paper union between the Latin and Greek churches that was repudiated by most Greek clerics within a few years of returning to Constantinople and that did nothing to prevent the Ottoman conquest fifteen years later.
But the Greek scholars who attended brought manuscripts of classical Greek texts that the Italian humanists immediately copied.

Plato's dialogues, the works of the Greek Neoplatonist philosophers, the Greek tragedians, the Greek geographers — all of this was circulating in Italy by 1450, fifteen years before the Greek refugees of 1453 (the conventional textbook account exaggerates the importance of the post-Constantinople refugees and underemphasizes the Council of Florence as a transmission moment).
Cosimo's funding of the Council was one of the most consequential acts of cultural patronage of the Quattrocento, even though the political effort failed.
Cosimo died in 1464 and was given the posthumous official title Pater Patriae ("Father of the Fatherland") by the Florentine government — the same title the Roman Senate had given Cicero.
The title was carved on his tomb in San Lorenzo.
The entire Medici dynastic project to transform political dominance into something like quasi-monarchical status was visible in that gesture.

Cosimo was succeeded briefly by his sickly son Piero il Gottoso (PYAY-roh eel goh-TOH-zoh, "Piero the Gouty," because of his chronic gout), who ruled Florence for only five years (1464–1469) before dying.

Piero was succeeded by his twenty-year-old son Lorenzo de' Medici (loh-REN-tzoh, 1449–1492), who would dominate Florence for the next twenty-three years and earn the nickname il Magnifico ("the Magnificent") that has stuck to him ever since.
Lorenzo is the most famous Medici, the symbol of the Florentine high Quattrocento, and the patron whose court produced the cultural moment that the next chapter (the High Renaissance) would inherit.

He was educated by Marsilio Ficino and the Greek scholars his grandfather had brought to Florence; he was personally a competent vernacular poet (his Italian lyrics are still anthologized); he was politically shrewd, charming, and ruthless when he needed to be.
He ruled Florence with even less formal authority than Cosimo had used and even more cultural impact.
What Lorenzo did with patronage was different in kind from what Cosimo had done.
Cosimo had funded major building projects, single great commissions, and large institutional efforts (the library, the Council of Florence, the Platonic Academy under Ficino).
Lorenzo funded individuals — the personal careers of artists, philosophers, and poets whom he housed in or near his palace, supported with stipends, and treated as members of his extended household.

The list of figures who passed through Lorenzo's circle in the 1470s and 1480s is extraordinary: Sandro Botticelli (sahn-droh bot-tee-CHEL-lee, c. 1445–1510), the painter of the Birth of Venus and the Primavera; Andrea del Verrocchio (in whose workshop Leonardo da Vinci trained as a young man); the philosopher Pico della Mirandola (PEE-koh del-lah mee-RAHN-doh-lah, 1463–1494, whose Oration on the Dignity of Man is the manifesto of Renaissance humanism); the Greek-trained poet Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494, who tutored Lorenzo's children and wrote sophisticated Italian and Latin verse); the young Michelangelo Buonarroti, whom Lorenzo housed in his palace and treated essentially as an adopted son from the age of fourteen.

Botticelli's two famous commissions for the Medici extended household — the Primavera (around 1480) and the Birth of Venus (around 1485) — are the visual statements of Lorenzo's Neoplatonic court culture.

Both paintings depict pagan classical subjects (Venus and her nymphs in a flowering grove, Venus rising from the sea on a scallop shell) treated with the reverence that medieval painters had reserved for biblical subjects.

The Birth of Venus is the first large-scale depiction of the female nude in Western art since classical antiquity, and the figures' attenuated graceful proportions and rhythmic linear contours became defining features of late Quattrocento Florentine style.
Both paintings were probably commissioned for a Medici country villa as decorative wedding paintings for Medici cousins, though the precise commissioning circumstances are not fully documented.
Botticelli's later career took a darker turn under the influence of Savonarola (below), and the painter reportedly burned some of his own paintings at one of Savonarola's bonfires.
Pico della Mirandola's Oration on the Dignity of Man (1486) is the manifesto Renaissance humanism that the modern textbooks always cite.

Pico, then a 23-year-old prodigy who had mastered Latin, Greek, Hebrew, Arabic, and Aramaic, proposed to defend 900 theses in public debate in Rome — covering Christian theology, classical philosophy, Jewish kabbalah, and what Pico believed was ancient Egyptian wisdom.
The papacy condemned the theses, prevented the debate, and would have put Pico on trial had Lorenzo not intervened to protect him.
Pico was eventually pardoned by Pope Alexander VI but died young at thirty-one in 1494, of arsenic poisoning that may have been accidental and may have been murder.

Modern scholarly opinion has gradually moved away from treating Pico as the founder of modern humanism (the Oration is brilliant rhetoric but somewhat overheated philosophy) but his career remains the most striking case of the Lorenzo-era Florentine intellectual prodigy: young, polylingual, philosophically ambitious, dependent on Medici protection, and dying mysteriously young.

The other major figure of the Lorenzo years was the young Michelangelo Buonarroti, whose full career belongs to the next chapter but whose Florentine apprenticeship in the 1480s ran inside Lorenzo's household.

Lorenzo had founded an informal school for sculptors in his garden at San Marco, where promising young artists studied the Medici collection of antique sculpture under the master sculptor Bertoldo di Giovanni (himself a former Donatello pupil).

Michelangelo, then a teenage apprentice in the painter Ghirlandaio's workshop, was recruited into the garden school around 1489 and lived in the Medici palace for the next three years until Lorenzo's death in 1492.
Lorenzo's patronage was the foundation of Michelangelo's artistic education.

Lorenzo also let the Medici Bank slide toward bankruptcy through a combination of bad loans (especially to Edward IV of England, who defaulted on enormous sums), distracted management (Lorenzo himself was uninterested in banking and delegated it to subordinates who lacked his grandfather's commercial discipline), and political concessions that diverted bank resources to political spending.
He also nearly lost his life in 1478 to one of the most notorious assassination attempts in Italian history.

The Pazzi Conspiracy of April 26, 1478 was the result of a feud between the Medici and the rival Florentine banking family the Pazzi (PAH-tzee), supported by Pope Sixtus IV (who had his own grievance with the Medici over a denied loan and a contested archbishopric appointment).

The conspirators planned to assassinate both Lorenzo and his younger brother Giuliano (joo-LYAH-noh) during High Mass at the Florentine cathedral on Easter Sunday, with the murders timed to the elevation of the host.

The plan was that two Pazzi agents would knife the Medici brothers at the moment of maximum public visibility, the city would rise against the Medici, and a papal-allied Pazzi government would take over Florence.
The execution was a partial success.
Giuliano was knifed at the front of the cathedral and died of his wounds in the cathedral itself.

Lorenzo was attacked but managed to fight off the assassins, took a flesh wound to the neck, escaped into the sacristy, and barricaded himself behind the heavy bronze sacristy doors that Donatello and Luca della Robbia had cast for the cathedral.

The Pazzi rising in the city failed completely — Florentine sentiment was overwhelmingly pro-Medici, the conspirators were captured within hours, and the Pazzi family and their accomplices were systematically lynched, hanged from the windows of the Palazzo Vecchio, or executed in the public square.
The leader of the conspiracy, Francesco de' Pazzi, was hanged from a window of the Palazzo Vecchio still wearing the bishop's robes he had put on for the morning's ceremony.
The young Sandro Botticelli painted commemorative portraits of the hanged conspirators on the wall of the Palazzo Vecchio (these were destroyed when the Medici were eventually exiled in 1494).
The Pazzi Conspiracy made Lorenzo's grip on Florence essentially unchallengeable for the rest of his life.

It also produced a war with Pope Sixtus IV (who had backed the conspiracy and was outraged that Florence had hanged a bishop) and the Kingdom of Naples that nearly bankrupted Florence in the early 1480s.

Lorenzo personally negotiated the end of the war by sailing to Naples and persuading King Ferrante to abandon the alliance with the pope — one of the most famous acts of personal diplomacy of the fifteenth century, and the foundation of Lorenzo's reputation as the "needle of the Italian compass" who maintained the balance of power among the Five Powers (above) for the next decade.
When Lorenzo died in 1492, of the same hereditary illness that had killed his father and grandfather, the Italian peninsula was at the height of the fifteenth-century equilibrium.
Within two years, that equilibrium would be permanently shattered.
Two events at the end of the Quattrocento set up the High Renaissance.
The first was Lorenzo's death and the brief but extraordinary career of Girolamo Savonarola (jee-ROH-lah-moh sah-voh-nah-ROH-lah, 1452–1498).
The second was the French invasion of 1494.

Savonarola was a Dominican friar from Ferrara who arrived at the Florentine convent of San Marco in 1490 and began preaching in the cathedral against the moral corruption of Florence — luxury, classical paganism, sexual license, the wealth of the Church, the tyranny of the Medici, the worldliness of the Borgia papacy in Rome.
His preaching was apocalyptic, denunciatory, and unusually persuasive.
By 1492 he had attracted a substantial Florentine following, including some of the most prominent intellectual figures (Pico della Mirandola among them).
He prophesied — accurately, as it turned out — that a foreign army would shortly invade Italy as a divine scourge to punish Italian moral failure.
The army arrived in 1494.
Charles VIII of France, a young king with a tenuous Angevin claim to Naples, marched 25,000 men and a train of modern bronze field artillery down the Italian peninsula in autumn 1494.

The march was almost unopposed: Italian cities surrendered or paid off the French as they passed; the Italian condottiere armies that had handled Italian wars for the previous century were unprepared for French heavy cavalry and modern artillery.
The French entered Florence in November 1494.

Lorenzo's son Piero (called il Fatuo, "the Unfortunate," in dynastic memory) had mismanaged the diplomatic crisis catastrophically, agreeing to humiliating French terms that Florentines refused to accept.
Piero was driven from the city by an angry mob; the Medici were exiled.

The French passed through Florence and continued south to Naples (which they captured in February 1495), then withdrew the same year when an Italian league cobbled together by Pope Alexander VI cut off their retreat.
The political vacuum in post-Medici Florence was filled by Savonarola.

He preached that Florence had been delivered from its sinful Medici past by divine intervention and was now to become the New Jerusalem, a renewed Christian republic whose constitution he personally helped draft.

The new constitution established a Great Council of nearly all eligible male citizens — a much wider franchise than the previous Medici-era oligarchy — and Savonarola became its dominant moral and political authority, even though he held no formal office.

His most famous innovation was the Bonfire of the Vanities (Italian falò delle vanità) — public bonfires in the Piazza della Signoria at which Florentines voluntarily burned books, paintings, jewelry, mirrors, cosmetics, musical instruments, gambling equipment, and other objects considered occasions for sin.
Savonarolan youth gangs — boys recruited and organized by the friars at San Marco — went house to house collecting items for the bonfires.
Several major paintings were probably destroyed in the bonfires of February 1497 and February 1498.

Botticelli was reportedly so influenced by Savonarola that he burned some of his own paintings; his late paintings (the Mystic Nativity of 1500, the Mystic Crucifixion) shifted dramatically toward more austere religious subjects and away from the pagan-mythological themes of his Lorenzo-era work.
Savonarola's downfall came when his moral confrontation with Pope Alexander VI (Rodrigo Borgia, the most notoriously corrupt pope of the period — Chapter 4) became politically untenable.
Alexander excommunicated Savonarola in May 1497.
Savonarola continued to preach in defiance of the excommunication.

A rival Franciscan friar challenged him to a public trial by fire in April 1498 — both friars to walk through a corridor of flames in the Piazza della Signoria, with the survivor demonstrating divine favor.
The trial was canceled at the last moment due to a sudden rainstorm and procedural disagreements, but the fiasco shattered Savonarola's prestige.
A Florentine government coup arrested him.
He was tortured — he initially confessed to heresy, then retracted, then was tortured again — and was hanged and burned in the Piazza della Signoria on May 23, 1498.
The fire was set with the same wood that had been gathered for his bonfires of vanities.
The Savonarola episode is one of the strangest chapters in fifteenth-century European history.

A Dominican friar, in the most commercially sophisticated city in Europe, in the middle of the most luxurious and pagan-classical artistic moment of the early Renaissance, organized a four-year theocratic moral revolution that included voluntary mass book-burnings — and was successful enough that he had to be killed before he could be displaced.

The episode demonstrates how unstable Florentine politics actually were under the surface of Medici prosperity, how powerful late-medieval apocalyptic preaching could be even at the height of Renaissance rationalism, and how thin the separation between high Quattrocento Florence and the religious convulsions that would shortly produce the Reformation actually was.
The Reformation that Luther would launch in 1517 (Chapter 6) was, in many ways, Savonarola's confrontation with the Borgia papacy at continental scale.
By 1500, the Quattrocento was over.

Florence was in political flux — restored Republican government for fifteen years, then restored Medici rule from 1512, then a brief second Republican exile of the Medici from 1527 to 1530, then permanent Medici rule again that would last until the dynasty died out in 1737.

The architectural and artistic infrastructure that the Quattrocento had built was in place — the dome, the perspective system, the freestanding nude, the linear classical Renaissance buildings, the workshop-and-patron system that produced sustained artistic careers.
The next generation of artists was already at work.
Leonardo da Vinci, then 48, had been working in Milan for nearly two decades and was in the final stages of the Last Supper.
Michelangelo, then 25, had returned to Florence after a period in Rome and would shortly start work on his marble David (1501–1504).
Raphael, then 17, was in Urbino completing his apprenticeship.
The High Renaissance was about to begin.
Cross-civ check: the Quattrocento (1400–1500) overlaps with several major non-European events.

The Ming Dynasty in China was at mid-arc — the great voyages of Admiral Zheng He between 1405 and 1433 had reached the Persian Gulf and East Africa, and the Ming court had then turned inward (Late Medieval Europe Ch 7).
The Ottoman Empire captured Constantinople in 1453 (Byzantine Empire Ch 11), ending the eastern Roman Empire and accelerating Greek manuscript transmission to Italy.
The Songhai Empire in West Africa was reaching its peak under Sunni Ali (Songhai Empire — concurrent).
The Aztec Empire was consolidating its dominion over central Mexico (Aztec Empire Ch 5).
The Inca Empire began its imperial expansion under Pachacuti from 1438.
Portuguese voyages down the African coast progressed steadily through the century, with Bartolomeu Dias rounding the Cape of Good Hope in 1488 and Vasco da Gama reaching India in 1498.
The fifteenth century is one of the densest moments of imperial expansion and global integration in human history, and the Italian Quattrocento is one node in that wider system.

The Italian artistic explosion was structurally enabled by the same global commercial integration that produced the Atlantic voyages and the Indian Ocean trading empires; the silver from the Americas (which would not arrive until after 1545) and the spices from the East Indies were not yet flowing into Italian banking networks, but the European wool-and-banking economy that the Medici Bank symbolized was already operating at a scale that previous centuries had not seen.
The High Renaissance is next.

chapters.title: The High Renaissance
sentences: The roughly three decades between 1495 and 1527 are conventionally called the High Renaissance — a thirty-year window in which a small handful of artists working in Florence, Milan, and Rome produced the works that came to define, for centuries afterward, what the Renaissance had been.
Three figures dominate the period: Leonardo da Vinci, Michelangelo Buonarroti, and Raphael Sanzio.
They overlapped in time (all three were working simultaneously in 1505) and in patronage (all three worked for various combinations of the Medici, the Borgia, and the della Rovere popes).
They also reportedly disliked each other intensely.
The cultural moment they produced was over by 1527, when the Sack of Rome ended the artistic confidence of the era.
This chapter focuses on these three figures and the Roman papal patronage that funded much of their late work.

The political background is the Italian Wars that began with Charles VIII's invasion in 1494 (Chapter 3) and ran until the Peace of Cateau-Cambrésis in 1559 (Chapter 8) — sixty-five years of nearly continuous foreign warfare on Italian soil that progressively destroyed Italian political independence even as Italian artistic production reached its peak.
The Italian Wars and the High Renaissance are the same period.
The artistic peak was achieved by people working in war zones.

The oldest of the three figures is Leonardo da Vinci (lay-oh-NAR-doh dah VEEN-chee, 1452–1519), born in the small Tuscan town of Vinci, near Florence, the illegitimate son of a Florentine notary and a peasant woman.

He was apprenticed around 1466 to the Florentine painter and sculptor Andrea del Verrocchio, in whose Florence workshop the young Leonardo trained for roughly a decade before establishing his own independent practice in the early 1470s.

Leonardo's career is the prototype of the Renaissance Man story — the artist who is also a scientist, engineer, anatomist, mathematician, and musician — and the prototype is real but needs immediate qualification.
Leonardo was an extraordinary draftsman, a brilliant observational naturalist, and a polymath of genuine range.

He was also an unreliable employee who left most of his major commissions unfinished, an obsessive who could spend years on a single painting, an inventor whose mechanical designs were brilliant on paper but mostly never built, and a writer whose voluminous private notebooks were mostly unread for centuries after his death.
The myth of Leonardo as universal genius across all fields equally is overstated.

The reality is more interesting: he was an artist whose obsessive interest in everything else turned him, gradually, into a strange one-man research enterprise whose results survived in fragmentary notebooks and were rediscovered by later generations.
His completed paintings number around twenty — fewer, by some counts, depending on attribution disputes.

The most famous are the Mona Lisa, the Last Supper, the Virgin of the Rocks (in two versions), the Madonna of the Carnation, the Lady with an Ermine, the Annunciation, the Adoration of the Magi (left unfinished), the Madonna Litta (debated attribution), and a handful of others.
Twenty paintings is a thin lifetime output by Renaissance standards — Raphael painted at least 50 in his short 37-year life, Titian painted hundreds across his 88 years.
Leonardo's reputation rests less on volume than on the extraordinary quality and innovation of the surviving works.

The Last Supper (Italian Cenacolo) was painted on a refectory wall at the Dominican monastery of Santa Maria delle Grazie in Milan between roughly 1495 and 1498, while Leonardo was employed by Ludovico Sforza ("il Moro," ruler of Milan from 1494 to 1499).

The painting depicts Christ at the moment of announcing that one of the twelve disciples will betray him, with the disciples reacting in twelve distinct emotional registers — surprise, horror, denial, defensive self-protection, calm acceptance — that together produce one of the great pieces of psychological narrative painting in Western art.
The composition is classically symmetrical, with Christ at the center and the disciples grouped in four trios; the perspective lines converge on Christ's head; the sense of arrested time is total.
It is the work that announced the High Renaissance.
It was also Leonardo's most famous technical disaster.
He painted on dry plaster rather than wet fresco (fresh, the technique in which pigment is applied to wet plaster and chemically bonded to the wall as the plaster dries).
Fresco is permanent but unforgiving — once the plaster dries, the artist cannot revise.
Leonardo wanted the freedom to revise, so he developed an experimental technique using oil and tempera on dry plaster.
The technique allowed him to revise but did not bond chemically to the wall, and the painting began to deteriorate within years of completion.
By 1517, Leonardo himself reportedly noted the deterioration.

By 1556, Vasari described the painting as "ruined." Centuries of progressively invasive restoration efforts (the most thorough one, by Pinin Brambilla Barcilon between 1978 and 1999, removed the accumulated overpainting from previous restorations to reveal what survives of Leonardo's original) have left the surviving image about 80% restored to varying degrees, with perhaps 20% of original paint visible.
The painting that millions of tourists see in Milan today is an authentic Leonardo composition rendered through five centuries of imperfect conservation.
The Mona Lisa (Italian La Gioconda, "the cheerful woman") is the portrait of Lisa del Giocondo, wife of a Florentine silk merchant, painted by Leonardo over more than a decade beginning around 1503.

The painting was probably commissioned around the birth of the Giocondo's second son, but Leonardo never delivered it — he kept the painting with him through the rest of his life, working on it intermittently, taking it to France in 1516 when he accepted King Francis I's invitation to live at the French court.
After Leonardo's death in 1519, the painting passed into the French royal collection.
It is now in the Louvre, where it became the most famous painting in the world after a 1911 theft and recovery turned it into international news.
What makes the painting unusual is its technique.

Leonardo used a technique called sfumato (sfoo-MAH-toh, "smoked") — soft tonal transitions between light and shadow, with no sharp edges, achieved by applying many translucent layers of oil paint that gradually built up depth.
The face has no defined contour line; one tone blends imperceptibly into the next.

The famous half-smile (which is more a faint asymmetric play of expression than an actual smile) and the indeterminate landscape behind the figure (which mismatches between the left and right backgrounds in ways that draw the viewer's gaze) combine to produce a portrait that has been the subject of more interpretation than any other painting in Western art.

The interpretations range from the prosaic (a successful Florentine merchant's wife at a moment of family celebration) to the mystical (an idealized image of Beatrice or Mary or some Neoplatonic principle of feminine beauty) to the conspiratorial (the painting is a self-portrait, the painting is of Leonardo's mother, the painting encodes hidden symbols).
Most modern art historians stick with the prosaic reading.
The painting's fame is a twentieth-century phenomenon.
Leonardo's third major activity was his notebooks.

Across his lifetime he filled an estimated 13,000–25,000 pages with sketches, observations, mechanical designs, anatomical studies, hydraulic experiments, mathematical notes, art-theoretical treatises, fragmentary literary projects, and miscellaneous private musings.
He wrote in mirror-script (right-to-left, with reversed letters), partly out of left-handed convenience, partly probably for privacy.

The notebooks include studies of human and animal anatomy that no contemporary equaled (Leonardo dissected perhaps 30 human corpses, mostly in Milanese hospitals, producing anatomical drawings that anticipated discoveries Vesalius would publish in 1543); proposed designs for flying machines, helicopters, parachutes, tanks, submarines, and various weapons; observations on the geology of fossil deposits in the Italian Apennines (Leonardo correctly inferred that fossil seashells found high in the mountains had once been on a sea floor, and reasoned about the gradual processes that produced the fossil distributions); studies of bird flight, water flow, plant geometry, and the optics of the eye.
The influence-on-later-science question is where Leonardo's legend tends to overstate.
His notebooks were almost entirely unpublished in his lifetime.

The notebooks remained scattered after his death, gradually dispersed across several European collections (the largest, the Codex Atlanticus, is now in the Biblioteca Ambrosiana in Milan; the Codex Leicester was bought by Bill Gates in 1994 for $30.8 million).
Most of the notebooks were not systematically transcribed and published until the late nineteenth and twentieth centuries.

The proto-scientific insights they contain — many of them remarkable — therefore had essentially no influence on the actual development of European science, which proceeded through Copernicus, Vesalius, Galileo, and Newton without reference to Leonardo's unread private papers.
Leonardo's reputation as a pioneer of modern science is a retrospective construction by twentieth-century historians who could finally read the notebooks.
He was, in his own time, mostly a famous painter who was rumored to be doing strange experiments in private.

What is true is that Leonardo demonstrated, in his own person, that an artist could be a serious researcher in everything else as well — that the boundary between visual art and natural philosophy did not have to be policed.
The model of the artist-scientist that runs from Leonardo through Bernini and Christopher Wren to the modern artist-engineer is a real cultural inheritance.
The specific scientific results Leonardo produced are largely artifacts of curiosity.
The model is the inheritance.
Leonardo died in 1519 at Cloux (now Clos Lucé), the French manor near Amboise that King Francis I had given him for his retirement.
King Francis reportedly cradled him in his arms as he died, though the story (told by Vasari) is probably a Vasarian flourish.
He was buried at the chapel of Saint-Florentin at the royal chateau of Amboise.
The tomb was destroyed during the French Revolution and his remains were lost.
A nineteenth-century reburial in a different chapel at Amboise was based on uncertain identification of bones recovered from the chapel ruins.

The most physically impressive figure of the High Renaissance is Michelangelo Buonarroti (mee-kell-AHN-jay-loh bwoh-nah-ROH-tee, 1475–1564), born in Caprese in Tuscany, raised in Florence, and trained in two stages: first as an apprentice in Domenico Ghirlandaio's painting workshop in Florence in the late 1480s, then in Lorenzo de' Medici's sculpture garden at San Marco from around 1489 (Chapter 3).
He lived in the Medici palace as a teenager, ate at Lorenzo's table, and was raised effectively as a younger member of the Medici household until Lorenzo died in 1492.
The early Medici patronage was the foundation of his career.
Michelangelo lived to nearly 89 — extraordinarily long for the period — and his career spans almost the entire High and Late Renaissance.
He worked through six papacies.
He survived the Sack of Rome.
He died in 1564 in Rome, the same year Galileo was born in Pisa and Shakespeare was born in Stratford.
The continuity is striking: Michelangelo had been alive when Christopher Columbus reached the Americas in 1492, and was still working on St.
Peter's Basilica when Shakespeare was born.
His earliest major work is the Pietà for St.
Peter's Basilica in Rome, carved between 1498 and 1499 when Michelangelo was 23.

The Pietà (PYAY-tah, "pity") is a sculptural genre depicting the dead Christ across the lap of his mother Mary; northern European Pietàs of the late Middle Ages had typically shown a worn, aged Mary holding a tortured Christ, emphasizing grief and physical suffering.

Michelangelo's marble Pietà reverses the convention: his Mary is unnaturally young (younger than the dead Christ on her lap, though the Mary was historically perhaps fifteen years older than her crucified son), serene rather than anguished, of monumental physical scale.
The composition is a balanced triangular pyramid; the carving is technically perfect, with the marble polished to surfaces that reflect light like skin.

Michelangelo signed the work — chiseling MICHAEL ANGELVS BONAROTVS FLORENTIN FACIEBA[T] across the band running across Mary's chest — after he overheard a viewer attribute the work to a different sculptor.
It is the only sculpture he ever signed.
His most famous individual work is the marble David, carved between 1501 and 1504 for the city of Florence.

The 17-foot-tall figure was carved from a single block of Carrara marble that had been quarried decades earlier and had been roughed out (and abandoned as unworkable) by two earlier sculptors — Agostino di Duccio in 1463 and Antonio Rossellino in 1476.
The block had stood neglected in the cathedral workshop for 40 years before Michelangelo, then 25, took it on.

The completed figure depicts David before the fight with Goliath rather than after — tense, watchful, sling slung over one shoulder, eyes fixed on his target — in marked contrast to Donatello's earlier post-victory David (Chapter 3).
The political symbolism was clear: post-Medici Florence as the small, brave, free city defying the giants (papal Rome, the French monarchy, the Spanish Habsburgs) that surrounded it.

The statue was installed in the Piazza della Signoria outside the Palazzo Vecchio in September 1504, where it stood for nearly four centuries until it was moved indoors to the Galleria dell'Accademia in 1873 to protect it from weathering.
A copy stands today in the original outdoor location.
The David is one of the great pieces of marble carving in any tradition.

It is also a piece of physical engineering: Michelangelo had to design the figure to fit within the dimensions of the available block, which was tall and thin, producing the famous slightly-distorted proportions of the figure (the head and hands are slightly oversized, originally to compensate for the planned high outdoor placement that would have required these features to read correctly from below — when the placement was changed to ground level, the proportions remained as carved).
The carving demonstrated, conclusively, that a sculptor working in 1504 could match or surpass anything the Romans had carved a millennium and a half earlier.

His most ambitious project was the Sistine Chapel ceiling, painted between 1508 and 1512 for Pope Julius II (joo-LEE-uss, 1503–1513), the warrior pope who personally led armies to recover Papal States territory.
Julius commissioned Michelangelo (then a sculptor with limited fresco experience) to paint the chapel ceiling — the broad barrel-vaulted ceiling above the chapel where papal conclaves were held.
Michelangelo initially refused, reportedly arguing that he was a sculptor not a painter and that fresco was not his medium.
Julius insisted.
Michelangelo took the commission, sent his sculpture assistants away, and painted the ceiling almost single-handed (with a small team of plaster preparers and color grinders) over four years.
The ceiling covers roughly 5,000 square feet of vaulting.

The central narrative band depicts nine scenes from Genesis — the Creation of the World, the Creation of Adam, the Creation of Eve, the Fall, Noah's Sacrifice, the Flood, the Drunkenness of Noah — surrounded by ignudi (naked youths), prophets, sibyls, and biblical ancestors.
The most famous individual scene is the Creation of Adam, in which the seated God reaches across a small gap toward the languid reclining Adam, their fingertips not quite touching but about to.

The image has become so culturally familiar through reproductions that it is easy to forget how strange and original it actually is — God is depicted as a muscular bearded man flying through space surrounded by angels and a billowing cloak, in a composition unlike anything earlier Italian religious art had attempted.
Michelangelo painted the ceiling standing on scaffolding, not lying on his back.
The popular myth that he painted lying down is an error introduced by later biographers and reinforced by film.
He worked on a wooden scaffold platform he himself had designed, with his head tilted back and his arm raised to paint the surfaces above him.
The position was physically grueling — Michelangelo wrote a sonnet to a friend describing the back pain, the cramp, the paint dripping onto his face — but he was upright, not supine.
He completed the ceiling in October 1512.
The Sistine Chapel ceiling is one of the most influential pieces of Western art.

The figural style — the muscular athletic male nude as the universal compositional element, the dramatic foreshortened poses, the heroic emotional register — set the visual vocabulary for European religious painting for the next two centuries.
Mannerism would extend it.
Baroque painting would extend it further.
Twentieth-century artists from Rodin to comic-book illustrators are all working in a tradition Michelangelo's ceiling defines.

His later work includes the Medici Chapel at San Lorenzo in Florence (the New Sacristy, with the famous tomb sculptures of Day, Night, Dawn, and Dusk surrounding the Medici tombs of Giuliano and Lorenzo, completed 1534), the Last Judgment fresco on the wall of the Sistine Chapel behind the altar (painted 1536–1541, depicting the apocalyptic Second Coming with naked figures rising and falling — the nudity caused enough scandal during the Counter-Reformation that loincloths were painted over the most prominent figures, by an assistant Vasari nicknamed Il Braghettone, "the Breeches-Maker"), the architecture of the Laurentian Library at San Lorenzo, the urban redesign of the Capitoline Hill in Rome, and — finally — the dome of St.
Peter's Basilica, which he designed in his late 80s but did not live to see completed.
Michelangelo's St.
Peter's dome is the structural and visual successor to Brunelleschi's Florentine dome a century earlier.
Michelangelo had taken over the St.
Peter's project in 1546 (he was 71) after the deaths of the previous architects Bramante, Raphael, and Antonio da Sangallo had left the project in disarray.
He simplified the floor plan, redesigned the dome with steeper double curvature, and supervised construction until his death in 1564.
The dome was completed by Giacomo della Porta in 1590, with modifications that produced the soaring vertical profile that is now the visual signature of the Vatican.
It is one of the most consequential buildings in Western architecture.
A note on Michelangelo's psychology, because his is unusually well-documented for a Renaissance figure.
He was famously difficult — moody, jealous, paranoid, prone to feuds with patrons and rival artists.
He never married.

His surviving private letters and poetry suggest deep emotional attachments to several younger men, particularly the Roman nobleman Tommaso de' Cavalieri (to whom Michelangelo wrote some of his most intense surviving sonnets in the 1530s and 1540s).

The standard scholarly reading is that Michelangelo had homosexual desires that he largely sublimated into his work; the modern label "gay" is anachronistic, but the directionality of his desire is reasonably well-attested in the surviving documents.

He was also intensely religious, particularly in his old age, and his late religious sculptures (the Florentine Pietà in the Florence cathedral, the Rondanini Pietà still being carved when he died) are unusually raw and unfinished — the Rondanini in particular is one of the strangest sculptures of the period, with figures that appear partly melted into the marble block, a kind of premature modernism four centuries early.
He died in Rome on February 18, 1564, at age 88.

His body was secretly transported back to Florence by his nephew (the city of Rome had wanted to keep him), and he was buried in Santa Croce in Florence — the Florentine cathedral of national memory where Galileo, Machiavelli, and Rossini are also buried.
