He was the first Western artist to have a biography (by Vasari, in the Lives of the Artists — Chapter 7) published in his own lifetime, in 1550.
The book made him famous as a historical figure rather than just a working artist.
He is the prototype of the modern artist as celebrity.

The third figure of the High Renaissance trio is Raphael (RAH-fa-el, Italian: Raffaello Sanzio, raf-fa-EL-loh SAHN-tzee-oh, 1483–1520), born in Urbino in the Apennine foothills and dead at 37 in Rome.

Raphael's career was the shortest of the three, but his work was, in the centuries that followed, considered the most perfect of the three — the synthesis of Leonardo's psychological depth and Michelangelo's figural power, expressed with a serene formal harmony that the other two could not match.

Raphael was the son of a court painter at the small ducal court of Urbino — one of the great Quattrocento centers (Federico da Montefeltro's court, where Bramante and Castiglione had also been formed).
His father died when Raphael was eleven.

Raphael trained briefly with the painter Pietro Perugino in Perugia (whose graceful figural style Raphael initially imitated) before moving to Florence in 1504 to learn from Leonardo and Michelangelo, who were working there at that time.

He absorbed both their styles and produced, in his Florentine years (1504–1508), a series of Madonnas that combined Leonardo's sfumato modeling with the figural sweetness Raphael had inherited from Perugino.
In 1508, Pope Julius II called Raphael to Rome to fresco the papal apartments in the Vatican — the rooms now called the Stanze di Raffaello ("Rooms of Raphael").

Raphael spent the next twelve years in Rome, simultaneously frescoing the Stanze, painting altarpieces and portraits for various patrons, and (after Bramante's death in 1514) directing the construction of St.
Peter's Basilica and supervising classical archaeological surveys of Rome for the papacy.

He died on his thirty-seventh birthday — which fell on Good Friday in 1520 — of an illness that contemporary accounts attributed (with characteristic Renaissance moralism) to overexertion in his romantic life.
He was buried, by his own request, in the Pantheon (Ancient Rome Ch 7), the ancient Roman temple-turned-church where his tomb is still visible.
The Stanze are Raphael's masterpiece.

The Stanza della Segnatura (the room of the papal signing, frescoed 1509–1511) contains the four most famous large frescoes of the Italian Renaissance: the Disputation of the Holy Sacrament (representing theology), the School of Athens (representing philosophy), the Parnassus (representing poetry), and the Cardinal and Theological Virtues (representing law).

The School of Athens is the work that defined how the Renaissance imagined classical antiquity — a vast classical interior with coffered barrel vaults receding into the distance, populated by ancient Greek philosophers gathered in animated conversation.
Plato and Aristotle stand at the visual center, Plato pointing upward (toward his realm of Forms) and Aristotle gesturing horizontally (toward the empirical world).

The figures around them include Socrates, Pythagoras, Euclid, Heraclitus (with the face of Michelangelo, painted as a sullen brooding genius — Raphael's affectionate portrait of his rival), Diogenes, and dozens of others.
Raphael painted his own face into the gathered crowd at the lower right, looking out at the viewer.
The composition is one of the most carefully balanced in Western painting.
The architectural setting (probably referencing Bramante's planned new St.
Peter's, then under early construction) creates a deep perspectival recession that focuses the eye on Plato and Aristotle.
The figural groupings are arranged in symmetrical clusters across the foreground.
The colors are calibrated to maintain visual harmony across the composition.

The painting has been read for five centuries as the visual statement of Renaissance humanism: classical philosophy as the true companion to Christian theology, ancient Greece as the great age before the modern age that Raphael's Vatican was creating, the artist himself as a participant in the conversation.
The pope who commissioned it had it painted on the wall of the room where he signed papal documents, surrounding himself with the collected wisdom of Western thought.

Raphael's portraits — including the Pope Leo X with Two Cardinals (1517–1518), the Baldassare Castiglione (1515, the courtier author of The Book of the Courtier — Chapter 8), and his own self-portrait (around 1506) — established the High Renaissance portrait as a distinct genre, with the sitter shown in three-quarter-length, in a calm psychological register, against a neutral or slightly atmospheric background.
The genre would dominate European portraiture for the next four centuries.
What makes Raphael distinctive among the High Renaissance trio is the absence of struggle in his work.
Leonardo's paintings have a kind of obsessive perfectionism that often kept him from finishing them.
Michelangelo's work is full of strain, conflict, and physical effort.
Raphael's surviving paintings look effortless.
The compositions are balanced, the figures graceful, the colors harmonious, the emotional registers contained.

The contemporary phrase that came to describe his quality was grazia (GRAH-tzee-ah), "grace" — the easy elegance that the Castiglione Book of the Courtier would shortly codify as the supreme aristocratic virtue (sprezzatura, the art of making the difficult look effortless).
Raphael painted as if the painting was easy.
None of it was.
But the apparent ease became, in subsequent centuries, the ideal that academic painting aspired to imitate.
He died on his thirty-seventh birthday — Good Friday, April 6, 1520.
His funeral procession through Rome was one of the largest in the city's recent memory.
Pope Leo X was reportedly inconsolable.
Raphael's body lay in state in his studio with his last unfinished painting — the Transfiguration, completed by his assistants — propped above his coffin.
He had been working in Rome for twelve years.

The political background to all of this was the Italian Wars — the long sequence of conflicts that began with Charles VIII's 1494 invasion (Chapter 3) and continued, with various coalitions and pauses, until 1559.
The wars are too complicated to narrate fully here.

The essential pattern is: France, Spain, the Holy Roman Empire, and various Italian states fighting each other for control of the Italian peninsula, with the Papal States, Venice, Milan, and Naples shifting alliances repeatedly as the fortunes of war demanded.

The military innovations were dramatic — the bronze field artillery that Charles VIII had introduced in 1494, the Spanish tercio infantry formation that defeated the French at the Battle of Cerignola in 1503, the arquebus (an early matchlock firearm) that progressively replaced pike-and-shield infantry — and the cumulative effect was that Italian condottiere armies (the mercenary forces that had handled Italian wars for the previous century) were progressively displaced by professional national armies from France and Spain.
By 1530, the Italian peninsula was militarily dominated by foreign powers in a way it had not been since the Lombard invasion of the 6th century.
Two episodes from the wars matter for the High Renaissance.

The first was the Battle of Marignano in September 1515, where Francis I of France crushed the Swiss pike infantry that had previously been considered the finest in Europe, securing French control of Milan and ending the Swiss reputation for invincibility.
Marignano was won by combined arms — heavy French cavalry, German Landsknecht infantry hired by the French, and (above all) French bronze field artillery firing point-blank into the Swiss formation.
The battle effectively ended the medieval pike block as the dominant military formation.

It also produced the Concordat of Bologna between Francis I and Pope Leo X in 1516, which gave the French king substantial control over the appointment of French bishops in exchange for the king's acceptance of papal sovereignty — a settlement that kept France within the Catholic fold during the Reformation crisis of the next two decades.
The second was the Sack of Rome in May 1527, the event that conventionally ends the High Renaissance.

The political situation in 1526 was that Pope Clement VII (a Medici cousin of Lorenzo the Magnificent, born Giulio de' Medici) had aligned the Papal States with France against the Holy Roman Emperor Charles V, who controlled both Spain and the Habsburg German territories and was the most powerful single monarch in Europe.

Clement's diplomatic miscalculations — switching alliances at exactly the wrong moments, failing to pay imperial troops he had hired, antagonizing Charles V personally — combined with the chronic problem of imperial troops in Italy who hadn't been paid for months.

By spring 1527, an army of about 22,000 imperial troops — Spanish regulars, German Landsknechts (many of them Lutheran sympathizers who hated the papacy), and Italian mercenaries — was approaching Rome with no money, no supplies, and rapidly evaporating discipline.
They had been told they could supply themselves by sacking Rome.
The army arrived outside Rome's walls on May 5, 1527.
The Roman defenses were entirely inadequate — the city had perhaps 5,000 troops, including the famous Swiss Guard of the papacy.
The imperial commander, the German captain Charles III, Duke of Bourbon (a French nobleman who had defected to Charles V), led the assault on May 6.

Bourbon was killed by a bullet through the chest in the first hour of the attack — by some accounts, fired by the Florentine sculptor Benvenuto Cellini, who was serving as a papal artillerist on the walls and would later boast about the kill in his autobiography.
Bourbon's death removed the last figure with any authority over the imperial troops.
They breached the walls within hours, and the city was theirs.
What followed was eight days of systematic looting and atrocity unlike anything in Roman history since the Vandal sack of 455.
The German Lutheran troops, in particular, treated the sack as a religious war: they desecrated churches, killed priests, raped nuns, looted St.
Peter's, scrawled Lutheran graffiti on Raphael's frescoes in the Vatican Stanze, and ransomed every Roman they could capture.

The Swiss Guard was nearly annihilated defending Pope Clement VII, who escaped to the Castel Sant'Angelo (the fortified former tomb of the emperor Hadrian on the Tiber) along the Passetto — a narrow elevated passageway connecting the Vatican to the fortress that the popes had specifically maintained for emergencies of this kind.
Clement remained besieged in Castel Sant'Angelo for seven months while the imperial troops looted Rome.

Casualty estimates for the Sack of Rome are uncertain — modern scholarly estimates of immediate killings range from around 6,000 to 12,000, with thousands more dying of starvation and disease during the subsequent occupation, and the urban population (perhaps 55,000 before the sack) reduced to something like 10,000–20,000 within a year as survivors fled.
Substantial portions of the city's artistic heritage were destroyed or stolen.
Raphael's tapestries were looted (most were eventually recovered).
Books and manuscripts from the Vatican Library were used as fuel for cooking fires by the imperial troops.
The Sistine Chapel survived intact, but the looting of the rest of the Vatican palace was thorough.
The political consequences were enormous.
Clement VII signed humiliating peace terms with Charles V in June 1527 and was effectively reduced to Charles's puppet for the remainder of his pontificate.
The formal coronation of Charles V as Holy Roman Emperor by Clement VII at Bologna in 1530 confirmed Spanish Habsburg dominance over Italy that would last for the next two centuries.
The Italian Wars continued until 1559, but the political center of gravity had shifted permanently away from Italy.
The cultural consequences were even larger.

The Sack of Rome dispersed the Roman artistic community — many of the artists who had been working for Clement, including major figures like Parmigianino and Sebastiano del Piombo, fled the city and never fully returned.
The artistic confidence of the High Renaissance — the sense that the popes commanded inexhaustible resources to patronize the greatest art the world had ever seen — was broken.
Subsequent papal patronage continued, but it was more conservative, more defensive, more preoccupied with the Reformation crisis (Chapter 6) that had begun ten years earlier with Luther's theses.
The cultural moment that Leonardo, Michelangelo, and Raphael had defined was over.
Raphael had been dead for seven years.
Leonardo had been dead for eight.
Michelangelo lived another 37 years and continued working — but the artistic moment that had produced him was gone.
The Sack of Rome is the conventional endpoint of the High Renaissance.

Nothing in subsequent Italian art (until Bernini's Roman Baroque a century later) recaptures the confident synthesis of antiquity and Christianity, of classical form and personal psychology, of city-state pride and papal ambition that the three decades 1495–1527 had produced.
Cross-civ check: the High Renaissance (1495–1527) overlaps almost exactly with several other major early-modern transformations.

Ismail I founded the Safavid dynasty in Iran in 1501 and forcibly converted Persia to Twelver Shia Islam — Leonardo was painting the Last Supper while Ismail was conquering Tabriz (Safavid Persia Ch 2).
Cortés conquered the Aztec Empire in 1519–1521 (the same years Raphael was finishing the Stanze, Aztec Empire Ch 8).
Pizarro would conquer the Inca Empire in 1532–1533.
Babur founded the Mughal Empire in India in 1526 (a year before the Sack of Rome).
Suleiman the Magnificent ascended the Ottoman throne in 1520 and would soon be besieging Vienna.
Martin Luther posted his 95 Theses in 1517 (Chapter 6).
Magellan circumnavigated the globe in 1519–1522.
The High Renaissance was happening in the middle of one of the most concentrated periods of imperial expansion, religious revolution, and global integration in human history.
The artistic moment in Florence and Rome was structurally connected to the larger world even if Leonardo and Michelangelo did not always notice.
The Spanish silver from the Americas that would shortly fund the Counter-Reformation and pay for Bernini's Baroque was already starting to flow.
The Reformation that would split Christianity was already underway in Wittenberg.
The cultural moment the High Renaissance achieved was real, but it was also vulnerable, embedded in a wider world that was changing faster than the Italian city-states could adapt to.

chapters.title: Venice and the Sea
sentences: While Florence was building Brunelleschi's dome and Rome was raising St.
Peter's, Venice was running a maritime empire.
The Florentine and Roman Renaissance were inland phenomena, financed by textile manufacture and ecclesiastical taxation, oriented toward Italian classical antiquity.

The Venetian Renaissance was a sea-power phenomenon, financed by Mediterranean trade, oriented toward both classical antiquity and the very different world of Constantinople and the eastern Mediterranean.

The visual style is recognizably different from the Florentine: less interested in linear perspective, more interested in color and atmosphere; less monumental architecture, more painted altarpieces and palace decorations; less classical sculpture, more glittering surfaces and decorative tilework.
Venice was the great rival capital of the Italian Renaissance, and the Venetian school deserves a chapter to itself.

This chapter covers Venetian art and culture from roughly 1450 to 1600 — the Venetian century that overlaps the late Quattrocento, the High Renaissance, the Late Renaissance, and the early Counter-Reformation.
The major figures are the Bellini family, Giorgione, Titian, Tintoretto, and Veronese.

The political backdrop is Venice's long contest with the Ottoman Empire for control of the eastern Mediterranean, including the great naval victory at the Battle of Lepanto in 1571 — the moment when Italian and Spanish Catholic naval power finally checked Ottoman expansion in the Mediterranean.
The Venetian state, by 1500, was the most stable government in Europe and had been for nearly a thousand years.

The lagoon-island city had emerged in the early Middle Ages as a refuge from mainland barbarian invasions; by the eighth century it was a trading post under nominal Byzantine sovereignty; by the eleventh century it was a fully independent maritime republic; by the thirteenth century it controlled a maritime empire stretching down the Dalmatian coast, into the Aegean, around Crete, into the Black Sea (Caffa, where the Black Death entered Europe — Late Medieval Europe Ch 2 — was a Genoese rather than Venetian colony, but Venice held parallel posts at Trebizond and elsewhere).
By 1450 Venice had a population of around 100,000 and was probably the wealthiest single city in Europe.
By 1500 it had also expanded onto the Italian mainland — the Terraferma ("solid land") — absorbing the cities of Padua, Verona, Brescia, and Bergamo into a substantial inland Italian state.
Venetian culture by 1500 was therefore not just a lagoon culture but a regional Italian culture with imperial extensions across the Mediterranean.

The political system was the Most Serene Republic of Venice (Italian Serenissima Repubblica di Venezia, "the Most Serene Republic" — La Serenissima for short), governed through a series of nested councils of ascending exclusivity.

The supreme body was the Maggior Consiglio (the "Great Council"), about 1,200–2,500 male members of the Venetian patrician class drawn from a fixed list of recognized noble families (the Libro d'Oro, "Golden Book" — Venice had closed its patrician class in 1297 in the so-called Serrata ["closure"], after which membership was hereditary).

The Great Council elected smaller councils — the Senate (about 200 members, handling foreign policy and major domestic issues), the Council of Ten (a small executive body handling state security, criminal justice, and intelligence), and the inner Signoria that worked directly with the Doge.

The Doge himself was elected for life by an elaborate multi-stage process designed to prevent any single faction from controlling the choice — the procedure involved repeatedly drawing lots and electing electors until the eventual nominating committee was small enough to vote.

The Doge was a ceremonial figurehead with limited real power: he wore an elaborate brocade robe and the famous corno ducale (a horned cap), presided over state ceremonies, signed state documents, and served as the visual symbol of Venetian sovereignty.
He could not engage in private commerce, could not marry without state permission, and was watched by a constitutional system designed to prevent the dogeship from becoming hereditary or autocratic.
The system worked: in over a thousand years, Venice never once experienced a successful coup d'état or dynastic seizure of the dogeship.

The closest case (the Marin Falier conspiracy of 1355, in which Doge Falier conspired against the patrician class to seize personal power) was discovered in time, Falier was beheaded, and his portrait in the Doges' Palace was painted over with a black veil and the inscription Hic est locus Marini Falethri decapitati pro criminibus ("Here is the place of Marin Falier, beheaded for his crimes").
The black veil is still there.
The political stability allowed Venice to develop institutional infrastructure that other Italian states could not match.

The Venetian Arsenal (Italian Arsenale, from the Arabic dār al-ṣināʿa, "house of manufacture") was the state shipyard, a complex of dockyards, foundries, rope-walks, and timber yards that occupied roughly sixty acres of the eastern part of the city.
By the late fifteenth century, the Arsenal employed at peak production roughly 16,000 workers (the arsenalotti) and could assemble a galley in a single day at maximum throughput.

The Arsenal pioneered something close to assembly-line manufacturing — pre-fabricated standardized hull components, sequential workstations through which a hull moved as fittings were added, division of labor among specialized crafts — three centuries before the Industrial Revolution would make the assembly line famous in other industries.
Dante's Inferno describes the Arsenal in operation (he visited Venice around 1305) and uses it as a metaphor for the activity of the damned in Hell.
By 1500, the Arsenal was the largest industrial complex in Europe.
The Venetian fleet that the Arsenal produced was the foundation of Venetian commercial power.
Galleys — long, low-slung oared warships with auxiliary sails, descended from Mediterranean designs that ran back to the Phoenicians — were the standard Venetian merchant ship.
State-organized galley convoys (the muda) sailed in coordinated annual voyages to Alexandria, Beirut, Constantinople, the Black Sea, the Atlantic Flanders ports, and elsewhere.
Each convoy carried Venetian goods outbound and returned with cargoes of spices, silks, slaves, dyes, and luxury textiles.
The convoy system reduced piracy losses (galleys were heavily armed, and convoys could defend themselves), spread costs across multiple ships, and enabled centralized state regulation of trade.
It also allowed the Venetian state to capture the bulk of the eastern Mediterranean luxury trade.

The wealth that financed the Venetian palaces along the Grand Canal — the Ca' d'Oro, the Palazzo Ducale, the Palazzo Foscari, the Palazzo Vendramin-Calergi, dozens of others — was muda wealth, accumulated over centuries of organized maritime commerce.
Venetian painting begins to be visible as a distinct school in the fifteenth century, with the Bellini family.
The patriarch was Jacopo Bellini (c. 1400–1470), a Venetian painter trained in the late Gothic tradition who became the leading painter of mid-fifteenth-century Venice.

His two sons, Gentile Bellini (c. 1429–1507) and Giovanni Bellini (c. 1430–1516), and his daughter Nicolosia (married to the Paduan painter Andrea Mantegna, who introduced Florentine perspective and classical archaeology into the Venetian-Paduan visual world), together transmitted the Florentine technical innovations to Venice and adapted them to Venetian taste.
Giovanni Bellini is the most consequential of the Bellinis and arguably the founder of the mature Venetian school.

Across an unusually long career (he was painting into his eighties), he absorbed every major innovation of the Quattrocento — Florentine perspective, Mantegna's classical figural style, the new oil painting techniques imported from Flanders — and synthesized them into a distinctively Venetian style.

His Madonnas (perhaps fifty surviving) combined the affectionate humanity of Florentine pietas with luminous color, atmospheric landscape backgrounds, and an unprecedented sense of light pouring through the painting from a specific implied source.

His altarpieces (the San Zaccaria altarpiece of 1505 is the masterpiece) used the new Venetian preference for sacred conversation compositions — Madonna and saints arranged in a unified architectural setting rather than in the segmented Gothic panel format that had dominated earlier altarpieces.

Bellini's late portraits, particularly the Portrait of Doge Leonardo Loredan (around 1501–1502, now in the National Gallery in London), set a new standard for Venetian portraiture: the sitter painted in three-quarter pose, in rich brocade, against a flat blue background, with the kind of sustained psychological characterization that the High Renaissance trio in Florence and Rome were developing in parallel.

What Bellini transmitted to his pupils, and through them to the entire sixteenth-century Venetian school, was a particular emphasis on color and light as the primary tools of pictorial composition rather than line and figure.
The Florentine tradition (Brunelleschi, Donatello, Masaccio, Michelangelo) had emphasized disegno — drawing, line, the intellectual structure of an image.
The Venetian tradition (the Bellinis, Giorgione, Titian) emphasized colorito — painted color, atmospheric light, the sensuous physical surface of paint.
The disegno-colorito distinction would become a defining critical opposition in European art theory for the next four centuries.
It was already visible in Bellini's late work.
Bellini's most famous pupils were Giorgione (jor-JOH-nay, c. 1477–1510) and Titian (TIT-ian, Italian: Tiziano Vecellio, tee-tsee-AH-noh veh-CHEL-lee-oh, c. 1488–1576).
Giorgione is one of the great mysterious figures of Italian art.
He died young — at perhaps 33, of plague in Venice in 1510 — and only a handful of paintings are confidently attributed to him.

His most famous works are the Tempest (around 1508, now in the Accademia in Venice, depicting a young soldier and a nursing woman in a stormy landscape with no clear narrative subject), the Sleeping Venus (around 1510, in Dresden, the first reclining female nude in Western art since classical antiquity), and several enigmatic small pictures that have been the subject of decades of iconographic debate.
Giorgione's importance is that he introduced two innovations that the rest of the Venetian school would extend.

The first was the landscape with figures — paintings in which the natural setting (mountains, woods, weather) is as important as the human subjects, and in which the picture is held together by atmospheric mood rather than by narrative content.
The second was the non-narrative subject — paintings that do not illustrate a specific story but project a poetic mood without a fixed iconographic program.
Both innovations would become signatures of Venetian painting.
Titian is the giant of sixteenth-century Venetian art.

Born around 1488 (the date is uncertain), trained in the Bellini workshop alongside Giorgione, and active in Venice from the 1510s until his death in 1576 at perhaps 88, Titian dominated Venetian painting for sixty years.

His career is a kind of inverse image of Michelangelo's: where Michelangelo was famously difficult, Titian was a smooth political operator who got on with everyone; where Michelangelo's Roman commissions had run mostly through papal patronage, Titian became the favored painter of the Habsburg dynasty (Charles V and Philip II of Spain), painting more European royalty than any other Renaissance figure; where Michelangelo's late work became spiritually severe, Titian's late work became progressively freer in brushwork and looser in composition.
Titian's range across genres was enormous.

Religious altarpieces: the Assumption of the Virgin for the Frari church in Venice (1518), a vast vertical composition with Mary rising into a glowing yellow heaven and the apostles below reaching toward her, that announced his arrival as Bellini's successor; the Pesaro Madonna (1526), which broke with the symmetric Madonna-and-saints convention by placing the Madonna off-center on a high diagonal throne.

Mythologies: the Bacchus and Ariadne (1523, for the duke of Ferrara), the Venus of Urbino (1538), the late Diana and Actaeon and Diana and Callisto for Philip II of Spain (1559) — paintings that adapted classical mythology to Venetian erotic-poetic mood.

Portraits: the most famous is the Portrait of Charles V on Horseback (1548), commissioned to commemorate Charles's victory at the Battle of Mühlberg, in which the emperor in armor on a black horse rides through a misty Saxon forest with the dawn light behind him.

Charles V reportedly stayed Titian's hand from picking up a fallen brush during one of their sittings, in a famous gesture of imperial recognition: "A king is served only by another king." (The story may be apocryphal but illustrates the way Titian's social position elevated the artist as a category in sixteenth-century Europe.) Titian's late style is one of the great phenomena of European painting.
From the 1560s onward — when he was in his seventies and eighties — his brushwork became progressively looser, with paint applied in visible separate strokes rather than blended into smooth surfaces.
Up close, the late paintings look almost abstract, with patches of color and rough texture; from the proper viewing distance, the figures resolve into fully realized forms.
The technique anticipated Impressionism by three centuries and Velázquez by one.
Titian himself reportedly spoke of working with his fingers as much as with brushes in the late paintings.

The most famous late works — the Pietà he was working on for his own tomb when he died, the Crowning with Thorns in the Munich Alte Pinakothek, the Flaying of Marsyas — are among the strangest and most powerful paintings of the sixteenth century.

He died of plague in Venice in 1576, was buried in the Frari (the same church where his Assumption hung), and is conventionally given the title "the founder of modern oil painting" by later art historians who saw his free brushwork as the launch of techniques that Velázquez, Rubens, Rembrandt, and ultimately Manet would extend.
The two great painters of the Late Renaissance Venetian generation are Tintoretto and Veronese.
Tintoretto (Italian: Jacopo Robusti, called "Tintoretto" because his father was a tintore, dyer, 1518–1594) was Venice's other dominant painter of the second half of the century.

He worked at extraordinary speed (his reputation was that he could complete a major altarpiece in days rather than months) and at extraordinary scale — some of his canvases, particularly the cycle of paintings he produced for the Scuola Grande di San Rocco in Venice between 1564 and 1588, run to dozens of feet in length.

The San Rocco cycle is one of the great unified painting commissions in Western art: roughly fifty paintings on biblical subjects covering the walls and ceilings of a Venetian confraternity's three-story headquarters, executed largely by Tintoretto across two and a half decades.

The visual style is dramatic, dynamic, and often violent — figures in extreme foreshortened poses, plunging diagonals, pools of theatrical light cutting through dark backgrounds, an emotional register much more intense than Titian's measured equilibrium.

Modern critics often describe Tintoretto as proto-Baroque, with the sense of dramatic motion and theatrical lighting that Caravaggio and Bernini would extend in the next century already visible in his work.

Paolo Veronese (vay-roh-NAY-zay, 1528–1588), born in Verona but active in Venice from the 1550s onward, specialized in vast colorful banquet scenes — large architectural compositions with dozens of figures in luxurious sixteenth-century Venetian dress, set in classical buildings or grand outdoor settings, often nominally illustrating biblical subjects but actually depicting Venetian patrician life.

The most famous example is the Wedding at Cana (1563) for the refectory of the monastery of San Giorgio Maggiore, a 22-foot-long canvas with 130 figures including Veronese and his fellow painters Titian and Tintoretto in the foreground musicians and several recognizable European royalty among the wedding guests. (The painting was looted by Napoleon's troops in 1797 and is now in the Louvre, where it hangs across from the Mona Lisa.) Veronese's other famous case is his 1573 trial by the Venetian Inquisition over a Last Supper that he had populated with dwarfs, dogs, drunken Germans, a man with a nosebleed, and various other figures the Inquisition considered theologically inappropriate.

Veronese's defense — recorded in surviving trial transcripts — argued that painters had license to invent details for visual richness; the Inquisition disagreed; Veronese simply renamed the painting Feast in the House of Levi (a different biblical scene with looser iconographic constraints) and kept the figures.
The painting now hangs in the Accademia in Venice under the new title.

The Venetian school by 1600 had produced an alternative to the Florentine-Roman tradition of the High Renaissance: more colorful, more atmospheric, more interested in the visual richness of fabric and skin and light, less interested in the philosophical-classical iconographic programs that had dominated the High Renaissance.
The Venetian style would feed directly into the Baroque painting of the seventeenth century — Rubens learned from Titian, Velázquez learned from Titian, Rembrandt learned from Titian.
The Venetian color tradition is one of the most consequential transmissions in European art.
Venetian architecture and music deserve briefer mention.

The major architectural figure of the Venetian Renaissance was Andrea Palladio (pal-LAH-dee-oh, 1508–1580), a Vicenza-trained architect who designed villas (country houses for the Terraferma patriciate), palaces in Vicenza, churches in Venice (San Giorgio Maggiore, the Redentore), and (most influentially) the Villa Rotonda near Vicenza around 1567 — a perfectly symmetrical building with four identical Ionic porticos, one on each face.
The Villa Rotonda became the most imitated work in Western architecture, copied from Lord Burlington's Chiswick House to Thomas Jefferson's Monticello.

Palladio also published the Four Books of Architecture (I Quattro Libri dell'Architettura, 1570), a systematic architectural treatise with engraved illustrations that became, over the next two centuries, the most widely consulted architectural manual in the Western world.
Eighteenth-century English country houses, American Federal-style state capitols, and the Capitol Building in Washington, D.C., are all directly indebted to Palladio.
The European architectural style called Palladianism runs from his death to the early twentieth century.
He is one of the most influential architects in history.
Music is the other Venetian Renaissance achievement.

The basilica of San Marco in Venice — the immensely decorated Byzantine-influenced cathedral on the Piazza San Marco — pioneered the polychoral musical style under composers like Andrea Gabrieli (1532/3–1585) and his nephew Giovanni Gabrieli (1554/7–1612).

Polychoral music used multiple separated choirs of singers and instruments positioned at different points in the basilica, with passages tossed back and forth between the spatially-separated groups to produce stereophonic spatial effects of a kind earlier music had not attempted.

The Gabrielis' polychoral works at San Marco — the Sacrae Symphoniae of Giovanni Gabrieli is the famous collection — anticipated the Baroque use of musical space and influenced composers across Europe through the seventeenth century.
The Venetian church-music tradition would shortly produce the early operas of Monteverdi (Chapter 7) and the instrumental concertos of Vivaldi in the eighteenth century.
The political backdrop to all of this was the long contest between Venice and the Ottoman Empire for control of the eastern Mediterranean.

The Ottoman conquest of Constantinople in 1453 (Byzantine Empire Ch 11) had ended Byzantine power but had not ended Venetian commercial access to the eastern Mediterranean — the Ottomans were pragmatic rulers who maintained Venetian trading rights at Constantinople and along the Anatolian coast in exchange for Venetian recognition and tribute.
Through most of the late fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries, Venice and the Ottomans coexisted as commercial partners and intermittent military rivals.
There were wars: Venice lost Negroponte (Euboea, in central Greece) in 1470, lost the southern Peloponnese in stages, lost Cyprus in 1570–71.
There were also long periods of profitable peace.
The Battle of Lepanto in 1571 was the single largest naval engagement of the period and the moment when the long Ottoman-Venetian-Christian Mediterranean conflict reached a decisive head.

Sultan Selim II (the son of Suleiman the Magnificent, who had died in 1566) had launched the conquest of Cyprus from Venice in 1570; by spring 1571, the Ottoman army had captured the Venetian fortress at Famagusta after an eleven-month siege.

The Venetian commander Marcantonio Bragadin, who had surrendered Famagusta on terms that supposedly guaranteed safe passage out of the city, was instead seized by the Ottoman commander Lala Mustafa Pasha, tortured for two weeks, and finally flayed alive in front of the Famagusta cathedral. (His skin, stuffed with straw, was paraded around Famagusta and then sent to Constantinople; it was eventually recovered by Venice in 1580 and is now buried in the church of Santi Giovanni e Paolo in Venice.) The atrocity made the Ottomans the focus of pan-Christian outrage in a way the political conflict had not.

In response, Pope Pius V organized the Holy League of Spain, Venice, and the Papal States (with smaller contributions from Genoa, Savoy, the Knights of Malta, and several other Italian states) and put together a Mediterranean fleet of around 200 galleys under the overall command of Don Juan of Austria — the 24-year-old illegitimate half-brother of King Philip II of Spain.
The Ottoman fleet, under Müezzinzade Ali Pasha, was of comparable size, perhaps slightly larger.
The two fleets met on October 7, 1571, in the Gulf of Patras at the western end of the Gulf of Corinth, near the small Greek port of Lepanto (Naupactus).

The battle lasted about four hours and was the last major naval engagement fought primarily between oared galleys (gunpowder-armed sailing ships would dominate naval warfare for the next three centuries).

The Ottoman fleet was decisively defeated: roughly 200 Ottoman galleys captured or sunk, perhaps 25,000 Ottoman casualties, the Ottoman commander Ali Pasha killed in the fighting and his head displayed on a Spanish flagship.

Holy League casualties were much lower — perhaps 7,500 dead and 17,000 wounded — though one of the wounded was a young Spanish soldier named Miguel de Cervantes, who lost the use of his left hand at Lepanto and would later refer to it for the rest of his career as "the most memorable and lofty event the past or present age has seen." The strategic consequences of Lepanto are debated by historians.

The Ottomans rebuilt their fleet within a year (Sultan Selim II's grand vizier Sokollu Mehmed Pasha is reported to have remarked to a Venetian envoy that defeating the Ottomans at sea was "like shaving a beard" — the beard would grow back; capturing Cyprus had been "like cutting off an arm" — the arm would not).
Cyprus stayed under Ottoman control until 1878.
The Ottoman-Venetian commercial relationship resumed within a few years.
The eastern Mediterranean continued to be a contested zone for the next two centuries.
But the symbolic consequences were enormous.
Lepanto was the first major Christian naval victory over the Ottomans in over a century.
It checked the perception of inevitable Ottoman expansion that had haunted Christian Europe since the fall of Constantinople.

It produced an outpouring of Italian and Spanish commemorative art (Veronese painted Lepanto allegories, Titian painted a Lepanto allegory for Philip II, the Doges' Palace in Venice received a major Lepanto cycle from Tintoretto and his workshop).
October 7 was added to the Catholic liturgical calendar as the feast of Our Lady of the Rosary, commemorating the prayers for victory that Pope Pius V had organized.

The battle entered European cultural memory as the moment when Christendom had finally pushed back against the Ottoman threat — a memory that, in the next few decades of escalating Reformation conflict (Chapter 6), helped sustain Catholic confidence at exactly the moment when the Counter-Reformation was being institutionally consolidated.
For Venice, Lepanto was a victory that did not save the Venetian commercial empire.
The city-state's long decline had begun before Lepanto and continued after.
By 1600, Venetian Mediterranean commerce was being progressively displaced by Atlantic Portuguese, Dutch, and English shipping.

The Indian Ocean spice trade that Venice had dominated through the Mamluk Egyptian intermediary had been redirected by the Portuguese around the Cape of Good Hope (Late Medieval Europe Ch 8) — Venetian spice prices became uncompetitive against Lisbon and (later) Amsterdam direct imports.

The Venetian terraferma economy continued to function, the Venetian Arsenal continued to produce ships (though increasingly for defensive rather than offensive purposes), the Venetian patrician class continued to commission paintings and palaces.

But the Mediterranean maritime empire that had been the foundation of Venetian wealth for five centuries was contracting through the seventeenth century, and the city's role as a major European power was shrinking.

Venice would persist as an independent republic until Napoleon dissolved it in 1797 — over two centuries longer than any other Italian city-state — but its Renaissance moment was effectively over by 1600.
Cross-civ check: the Venetian Mediterranean of 1500–1600 was one node in a wider sixteenth-century world system.

The Ottoman Empire under Suleiman the Magnificent (1520–1566) reached its peak — Belgrade in 1521, Rhodes in 1522, the failed siege of Vienna in 1529, the conquest of Iraq from the Safavids in 1534 (Safavid Persia Ch 3), Cyprus in 1571 (above), and territorial control from Algeria to Yemen to Hungary (Ottoman Empire Ch 5–6).

The Safavid Persia under Tahmasp I and then Abbas the Great consolidated the Iranian Shia state and traded silk through Armenian merchants to European markets including Venice (Safavid Persia Ch 4–6).
The Mughal Empire in India was founded in 1526, expanded under Akbar from 1556, and became the wealthiest state in the world by the early seventeenth century.

Spanish silver from the Americas (mined at Potosí from 1545 onward) flowed through Manila to China and through Seville to Europe, restructuring global monetary relationships in ways that progressively disadvantaged Mediterranean trading economies (including Venice).
The Venetian sixteenth century was therefore the late, mature phase of a Mediterranean-centered commercial world that was being progressively overtaken by an Atlantic-centered global system.
Venice was at the height of its art-and-architecture achievement at exactly the moment its commercial foundations were being structurally undermined.

The contradiction is one of the structural ironies of Italian Renaissance history: the artistic confidence of the late sixteenth century was financed, increasingly, by past wealth rather than by current commercial dominance.

chapters.title: The Reformation Threat
sentences: The Italian Renaissance had been, for two centuries, a Catholic phenomenon.
The patrons were Catholic popes, Catholic city-state governments, and Catholic merchant families.
The subject matter was overwhelmingly Christian.
The institutional framework — the cathedrals, the parish churches, the monastic orders, the university faculties — was the universal Catholic Church.
By 1500, the Italian Renaissance had reached its peak in a Christendom that, despite the Wycliffe-Hus rehearsals (Late Medieval Europe Ch 5), was still institutionally unified under the Roman papacy.
By 1555, that unified Christendom was gone.
The Protestant Reformation that began with Martin Luther in 1517 had split Western Christianity permanently.
Northern Europe — Germany, the Scandinavian kingdoms, England, Scotland, the Netherlands — had broken with Rome in various combinations of Lutheran, Calvinist, and Anglican forms.
Southern Europe — Italy, Spain, Portugal, France (after the Wars of Religion) — remained Catholic.
The intellectual and cultural integration of medieval and Renaissance Europe was over.

The Catholic Church responded with the Counter-Reformation institutionally formalized at the Council of Trent (1545–1563), which reshaped Catholic doctrine, discipline, and culture in ways that would define European Catholicism for the next four centuries.
This chapter is about how the Reformation crisis hit Italy.

The story is sometimes underemphasized in textbooks because Italy itself remained Catholic — there was no Italian Reformation in the sense that there was a German or English one — but the Reformation transformed Italian Renaissance culture from the outside, restructuring papal patronage, narrowing the scope of acceptable artistic and intellectual subject matter, and (eventually) ending the Renaissance as a recognizable cultural phase.

The intellectual prequel to Luther was the Christian humanism of Erasmus of Rotterdam (eh-RAZ-muss, c. 1466–1536), the Dutch scholar who was the most famous European intellectual of the early sixteenth century and the figure who, more than any other, prepared the intellectual ground for the Reformation while himself remaining Catholic.

Erasmus was born in Rotterdam, raised in the Brethren of the Common Life (a late-medieval Dutch lay devotional movement that emphasized inward piety and biblical reading — the Devotio Moderna described in Late Medieval Europe Ch 5), trained as an Augustinian canon, and broke from monastic life in his twenties to pursue an independent scholarly career.
He moved repeatedly across Europe — Paris, Oxford, Cambridge, Rome, Venice, Basel, Louvain — supported by a combination of clerical benefices and patronage from aristocratic and royal admirers.

He was the first European intellectual since Petrarch to make a substantial living from the international book trade: his works were printed in dozens of editions across the European cities of the early sixteenth century, and he received royalties (or honorary gifts in lieu of royalties) from the Aldine Press in Venice (Chapter 3 — Aldus Manutius), the Frobenius Press in Basel, and the Estienne Press in Paris.
Erasmus's Italian period (1506–1509) is the part that matters here.

He spent three years in Italy — Rome, Venice, Bologna, Padua — at the absolute peak of the High Renaissance, working with Aldus Manutius on the Aldine editions of classical texts and absorbing the Italian humanist intellectual environment.
He was unimpressed.

Renaissance Italy seemed to him simultaneously brilliant and corrupt: the artistic and scholarly achievement was real, but the ecclesiastical institutions that ran the country were moneymaking enterprises wrapped in religious rhetoric.
He arrived in Rome to find Pope Julius II preparing to lead an army to attack Bologna in person — a warrior pope wearing armor instead of vestments, with the Sistine ceiling not yet painted and St.
Peter's not yet rebuilt but the papal court already operating as the most magnificent court in Europe.
Erasmus left Italy in 1509 and never returned.

What he produced after his Italian period was the body of work that would, twenty years later, be cited as having "laid the egg that Luther hatched." (The phrase is a sixteenth-century jab; Erasmus reportedly replied that "Luther hatched a different bird.") The major works: The In Praise of Folly (Latin Encomium Moriae, "Praise of Stupidity"), published in 1511, written during a stay with Thomas More in England (the title is a Latin pun on More's name).
Folly is a satirical mock-encomium delivered by the personification of Folly herself, ridiculing every social class but reserving particular venom for clerics, theologians, and monks.

It was an instant European bestseller — printed in dozens of editions, translated into every major European vernacular language, and read across Europe as the most successful piece of vernacular religious satire of the early sixteenth century.

The Adagia, a collected and continuously expanded compilation of classical proverbs with Erasmus's own learned commentary on each — the first edition appeared in 1500 with about 800 proverbs, the final edition (1536) had grown to over 4,000.

The Adagia was the major reference work that introduced classical learning into vernacular European literary culture: many famous Latin and Greek phrases ("between Scylla and Charybdis," "to leave no stone unturned," "to know oneself") entered modern European languages through Erasmus's compilation.

Most consequentially, the Greek New Testament of 1516 — Erasmus's critical edition of the Greek text of the New Testament with a parallel new Latin translation that corrected over a thousand errors he had identified in the Vulgate (the standard medieval Latin Bible).

The Vulgate had been the official Bible of Western Christianity since Jerome's translation in the late fourth century, and the medieval Catholic Church had treated its specific Latin wording as authoritative for theology.

Erasmus's Greek text undermined that authority by demonstrating that the Vulgate Latin contained translation choices that did not correspond accurately to the original Greek — including, most consequentially, choices that affected the doctrinal foundation of the seven sacraments. (The most famous example: the Vulgate translates the Greek metanoeite in Matthew 4:17 as poenitentiam agite, "do penance," supporting the medieval Catholic sacrament of penance; Erasmus retranslated it as resipiscite, "repent" or "be of changed mind," undermining the textual basis for the sacrament.) Luther's German New Testament of 1522 was based on Erasmus's Greek text.
The English Tyndale New Testament of 1526 was based on Erasmus's Greek text.
The King James Bible of 1611 was based, ultimately, on the line of textual scholarship Erasmus had launched.
Erasmus himself remained Catholic through the rest of his life.

When Luther's break with Rome became unmistakable in the early 1520s, Erasmus refused to follow him — instead writing a 1524 treatise On Free Will (De Libero Arbitrio) that defended traditional Catholic doctrine against Luther's reformed theology.
Luther replied with a furious On the Bondage of the Will (De Servo Arbitrio, 1525) that effectively ended any cordial relationship between the two men.
Erasmus spent his last years in Basel and Freiburg, increasingly isolated as both Protestants and conservative Catholics rejected him, and died in 1536.

The Catholic Church placed his complete works on the Index of Forbidden Books in 1559 (Chapter 7) — a posthumous condemnation that erased his immediate influence in Catholic Europe for the next two centuries.
The English-language Reformation tradition appropriated him; the modern Catholic Church eventually rehabilitated him in the twentieth century.

What Erasmus represented was the late phase of an attempt at internal reform of the Catholic Church through humanist scholarship and moral persuasion — an attempt that the Reformation crisis would shortly render impossible.
After 1521, the choice in northern Europe was between staying Catholic or breaking from Rome; the Erasmian middle position was no longer politically viable.
In Italy, where Erasmus had been widely admired in the 1510s, his works gradually became suspicious in the 1530s and were finally banned in the 1559 Index.
The narrowing of Italian intellectual freedom that the Counter-Reformation produced is in large part the story of how the Erasmian moment was closed off.

The Reformation itself began on October 31, 1517 — All Hallows' Eve — when an Augustinian friar named Martin Luther (1483–1546), professor of biblical theology at the University of Wittenberg in Saxony, posted (or perhaps mailed, the account varies) ninety-five theological propositions for academic disputation on the door of the Castle Church at Wittenberg.
The 95 Theses were not, in themselves, a manifesto for breaking with Rome.

They were a set of propositions, written in Latin, attacking the contemporary practice of selling indulgences — papal documents that promised remission of the temporal punishment for sin in exchange for monetary contributions, currently being marketed across Germany by the Dominican preacher Johann Tetzel to fund the rebuilding of St.
Peter's Basilica in Rome (Chapter 4 — Pope Leo X's New St.
Peter's project).

Luther's specific objections were theologically conservative: the indulgence trade was being misrepresented to ordinary believers; the pope had no jurisdiction over purgatory; spiritual repentance could not be purchased; the pope, if he could in fact empty purgatory through indulgences, ought to do so out of charity rather than for money.
What turned the 95 Theses into a continental crisis was the printing press (Late Medieval Europe Ch 7, Chapter 3 of this narrative — the Italian printing infrastructure).
Within months of the Wittenberg posting, the Theses had been translated into German, printed in dozens of pamphlet editions, and distributed across the German-speaking world.
The pope, the imperial court, and the Catholic theological establishment denounced them.

Luther defended them in increasingly radical terms, escalating his theological critique through 1518–1521 to the point where he was rejecting papal authority entirely, denying the validity of five of the seven Catholic sacraments, and arguing that ordinary Christians had direct access to scripture without clerical mediation.

By 1521 he had been excommunicated by Pope Leo X, condemned as a heretic by the imperial Diet of Worms, and protected from arrest by the Elector of Saxony Frederick the Wise (who had political reasons for resisting imperial authority over German princes).
He spent the next year in hiding at the Wartburg castle, where he translated the New Testament into German.
The translated New Testament — published in September 1522 in 5,000 printed copies that sold out within weeks — was the founding text of the German Lutheran Reformation.
It made the biblical text directly available to literate German laypeople for the first time.
It established Luther's German prose style as the foundation of modern standard German (in the same way Dante's Tuscan had become Italian, Chapter 2).

And it institutionalized the central Lutheran principle of sola scriptura — scripture alone as the ultimate authority in Christian belief, displacing the papal magisterium and the medieval theological tradition.

The principle was theologically radical and (over the next century) socially explosive: if every literate Christian could read scripture for themselves, the institutional mediation of the Catholic Church became unnecessary.
The Reformation in Germany spread rapidly.
Lutheran congregations and city governments adopted the new theology across northern and central Germany through the 1520s.
In Switzerland, Huldrych Zwingli (1484–1531) led a parallel reform in Zurich starting in 1519.

In Geneva, the second-generation reformer John Calvin (1509–1564) developed a more rigorous predestination theology starting in the 1530s that would shape the Reformed (Calvinist) tradition in Scotland, the Netherlands, the Huguenot communities of France, and (eventually) the New England Puritans.

In England, King Henry VIII broke with Rome in 1534 over the pope's refusal to grant his divorce, establishing the Church of England as a national church under royal supremacy that would gradually develop Protestant theological commitments through the reigns of Edward VI and Elizabeth I.
The Scandinavian kingdoms (Denmark-Norway, Sweden-Finland) adopted Lutheranism through royal decree in the 1530s.
Within thirty years of Luther's theses, perhaps a third of European Christians had broken with the papacy.
The Reformation in Italy is a different story.

There was significant early Italian sympathy for reform — Italian humanist scholars, Italian merchants who traveled north of the Alps, and several Italian noble families showed interest in Lutheran ideas through the 1530s and 1540s.

There were small Protestant communities in northern Italian cities, particularly Naples (where the Spanish reformer Juan de Valdés ran an influential reform circle in the 1530s) and the cities of Lucca, Modena, Ferrara, and Venice.
Italian writers of the period — including Pietro Aretino (the satirical poet and pornographer) and several younger humanist scholars — wrote sympathetically about reform.
But Italy did not become Protestant.

The combination of papal political authority, Spanish Habsburg dominance from the 1530s onward, and the institutional response of the Roman Inquisition (re-established under Pope Paul III in 1542 specifically to combat Protestant heresy on the Italian peninsula) systematically suppressed Italian Protestant communities through the second half of the sixteenth century.
By 1600, organized Protestantism in Italy had been effectively eliminated.

The few surviving Protestant communities — like the Waldensian villages in the Cottian Alps in northwestern Italy, who had maintained a heterodox tradition since the late twelfth century — survived only because they were defensible mountain enclaves or because they had received Genevan or Swiss diplomatic protection.
What this meant for Italian Renaissance culture was that Italy entered a period of progressively narrower intellectual and religious life through the 1540s, 1550s, and 1560s.

The Roman Inquisition prosecuted heresy; the Index of Forbidden Books (Chapter 7) restricted reading; the Counter-Reformation institutionalized at the Council of Trent (below) reshaped Catholic doctrine and practice in ways that systematically reduced the space for the kind of free-ranging humanist inquiry that had characterized the Quattrocento and the High Renaissance.
The Italian Renaissance did not end suddenly.
It slowly suffocated under Counter-Reformation orthodoxy.

The most famous individual Italian victim of the Counter-Reformation was Giordano Bruno (jor-DAH-noh BROO-noh, 1548–1600), a former Dominican friar from Naples who had developed an unusual cosmology combining Copernican heliocentrism with Hermetic mysticism and a doctrine of an infinite universe with an infinite plurality of inhabited worlds.
Bruno spent the 1580s teaching in Paris, London (where he met Sidney and the Elizabethan court), Wittenberg, and Helmstedt before returning to Italy in 1591 on the invitation of a Venetian patron.
The patron denounced him to the Roman Inquisition.

Bruno was arrested in 1592, held in the Roman Inquisition's prisons for eight years while a long legal proceeding examined his theological positions, and finally burned alive at the stake in the Campo de' Fiori in Rome on February 17, 1600.

The exact charges remain debated by modern scholars (the trial documents were largely lost in the eighteenth century), but the consensus is that he was condemned for theological heresy rather than for his cosmological speculations specifically — though those speculations contributed to the case.
Bruno is remembered today both as an early martyr of free intellectual inquiry and as a strange transitional figure between Renaissance Hermeticism and modern science.
A bronze statue of Bruno was erected in the Campo de' Fiori in 1889 — by liberal Italian Catholics and freethinkers commemorating him as a victim of papal intolerance — and stands there today.

A more famous later case (just outside the chronological scope of this chapter, but worth noting here for continuity) is Galileo Galilei (gah-lee-LAY-oh gah-lee-LAY-ee, 1564–1642), the Pisa-born physicist and astronomer whose first conflicts with the Roman Inquisition began in 1616 and culminated in his 1633 trial and house arrest.
Galileo's case will be discussed in Chapter 7 as part of the early-seventeenth-century scientific developments.

The structural point for the present chapter is that the institutional apparatus that made the Galileo trial possible was created by the Counter-Reformation between 1542 and 1563, in direct response to the Reformation crisis the previous chapter has been describing.

The Catholic institutional response to the Reformation was the Council of Trent, which met intermittently in three sessions across nearly two decades (1545–1547, 1551–1552, 1562–1563) at the small northern Italian city of Trento (TREN-toh, German Trient, in the Italian Alps near the modern Austrian border).
The Council was originally proposed in the 1530s as an attempted reunion council that might bring Lutherans back into the Catholic fold; by the time it actually convened in 1545, that hope was gone.
Trent was a Catholic-only council whose function was to define Catholic doctrine in opposition to Protestant theology and to reform Catholic clerical discipline.
The Council's doctrinal definitions formalized Catholic positions across the entire range of disputed issues.
Justification by faith alone — Luther's central doctrine — was condemned; the Council reaffirmed that justification involved both faith and good works.
Sola scriptura was condemned; the Council reaffirmed that scripture and apostolic tradition were equally authoritative, and that the Vulgate Latin text remained the official Catholic Bible.
The seven sacraments were reaffirmed against Lutheran reduction to two.
Transubstantiation — the doctrine that the Eucharistic bread and wine are physically transformed into the body and blood of Christ — was reaffirmed against Protestant alternatives.
Purgatory was reaffirmed.
Indulgences were reaffirmed (though their abusive sale was banned).
Clerical celibacy was reaffirmed.
The veneration of saints, relics, and images was reaffirmed.
The cumulative effect was to harden every contested Catholic position into formal doctrinal definition, ending the negotiating flexibility that pre-Reformation Catholic theology had permitted.
The disciplinary reforms were equally consequential.

The Council established diocesan seminaries — formal schools for training parish priests — to address the chronic problem of poorly-educated clergy that had been one of the legitimate Lutheran complaints.
It required bishops to actually reside in their dioceses (the medieval practice of absentee bishops collecting income from a diocese while living elsewhere was banned).
It standardized the Mass — the Tridentine Mass in Latin, codified by Pope Pius V in 1570, would be the universal Catholic liturgy until the Second Vatican Council in 1965.
It standardized the breviary (the daily prayer cycle for clergy).
It tightened control over religious orders.
It mandated parish records of baptisms, marriages, and burials.
It required all priests to administer the sacraments according to a uniform prescribed rite.
The cumulative effect was to centralize and standardize Catholic ecclesiastical practice in a way that medieval Catholicism had never been.
The cultural consequences for Italian Renaissance art were significant.

The Council's general decree on sacred images (issued in 1563 in the final session) reaffirmed that images in churches were appropriate but instructed bishops to ensure that images were doctrinally orthodox, modestly clothed, and devotionally appropriate.
The decree was vague in its specifics but launched a long Counter-Reformation campaign against perceived inappropriateness in religious art.
Michelangelo's Last Judgment in the Sistine Chapel (Chapter 4) had its most prominent nudes loinclothed by Daniele da Volterra (nicknamed Il Braghettone, "the Breeches-Maker") starting in 1565.
The pleasure-loving banquet scenes that Veronese painted (Chapter 5) increasingly attracted Inquisition scrutiny — hence Veronese's 1573 trial.

Italian religious painting through the late sixteenth century became progressively more sober, more devotionally focused, and more iconographically constrained than the High Renaissance work it succeeded.
The new Catholic religious orders that emerged from the Counter-Reformation also transformed Italian Renaissance culture.

The Society of Jesus (the Jesuits), founded by the Spanish soldier-saint Ignatius of Loyola in 1540, became the most influential Catholic teaching order of the period — running schools, universities, and missions across Catholic Europe and the world.

Jesuit churches like the Gesù in Rome (begun 1568) developed a new architectural style — simpler nave, larger preaching pulpit, dramatic altar lighting — that would feed into the Baroque churches of the seventeenth century.

The Capuchin Franciscan reform, the Theatines, the Barnabites, the Oratorians under Philip Neri (Roman reformer who founded the Oratorian congregation in 1575) all contributed to a religious culture that was more ascetic, more disciplined, and more pastoral than late-medieval Catholicism had been.

The Counter-Reformation Catholic Church that emerged from this period was a fundamentally different institution from the Renaissance papal court of 1500 — more bureaucratic, more theologically rigorous, more aggressively missionary, less culturally permissive.

The political settlement that ended the immediate sixteenth-century Reformation crisis was the Peace of Augsburg of 1555 — a settlement within the Holy Roman Empire that established the principle of cuius regio, eius religio ("whose realm, his religion"), under which each German prince could choose between Catholicism and Lutheranism for his own territory and his subjects had to follow.

The peace did not include Calvinism (which would not be added until 1648) and did not address the broader European question of Catholic-Protestant relations, but it stabilized the German confessional situation for the next sixty years and became a structural template for European religious accommodation.
In Italy, the political situation was more straightforward: Spanish Habsburg domination from the 1530s onward kept the peninsula Catholic, with the Inquisition handling residual heterodoxy.

The Italian Wars finally ended in 1559 with the Peace of Cateau-Cambrésis (Chapter 8), which confirmed Spanish control of Naples, Sicily, Sardinia, and Milan, and ended French ambitions on the peninsula.
The five Italian powers of 1454 (Chapter 1) had been reduced, by 1559, to a Spanish-dominated political system with Venice and the Papal States as the only fully independent states.
The Renaissance political world was over.
Cross-civ check: the Reformation crisis in Europe (1517–1563) was contemporary with several other sixteenth-century religious-political transformations.

Suleiman the Magnificent ruled the Ottoman Empire at its peak (1520–1566 — Ottoman Empire Ch 5), confronting the Habsburg-Catholic alliance from the east while the Habsburg-Lutheran conflict was dividing it from within.

Ismail I had founded the Safavid Twelver Shia state in 1501 (Safavid Persia Ch 2) and forcibly converted Persia to Shia Islam — the structural parallel to the Reformation is striking, in that both events used state power to enforce a previously-minority religious identity over an existing Sunni or Catholic majority.

Akbar the Great would become Mughal emperor in 1556 and pursue a religious-tolerationist policy unique among sixteenth-century rulers (though Akbar's heterodox Din-i Ilahi was an internal Mughal phenomenon rather than a state policy).

The Spanish conquest of the Americas (Aztec Empire Ch 8, then the Inca conquest in the 1530s) was funded in significant part by the same Spanish silver that was funding the Counter-Reformation church in Europe.
The sixteenth century is the moment when previously-regional religious conflicts became globally entangled with imperial expansion, monetary integration, and the early modern state-system.
The Italian Reformation crisis was one node in a wider pattern of state-sponsored religious hardening that affected, in different forms, every major Eurasian civilization of the period.

chapters.title: Music, Print, and Counter-Reformation
sentences: The late sixteenth century — the period between the Council of Trent (1545–1563) and the Sack of Mantua and beginning of the Thirty Years War in the early seventeenth century — is the Late Renaissance or Cinquecento.

It is the period in which the cultural world of the High Renaissance was being progressively reshaped by the Counter-Reformation, but in which several genuinely new innovations also emerged that would define European cultural life for the next two centuries: musical Polyphony at its mature peak under Palestrina, the birth of opera under Monteverdi at the turn of the seventeenth century, the consolidation of Venice as the printing capital of Europe, and the early conflicts between the Roman Inquisition and what would become the Scientific Revolution — including Galileo's first run-ins with the Church.
This chapter is about the Italian Late Renaissance — the moment when the cultural world that the previous chapters have described began to mutate into something else.
The high Renaissance moment was over; the Baroque had not yet begun.
What emerged in this transitional period set the cultural agenda for the seventeenth century.
The single most consequential Italian cultural development of the second half of the sixteenth century was, surprisingly, in music.
The visual arts of the Late Renaissance produced significant work (Palladio's villas, Veronese's banquet scenes, Tintoretto's San Rocco cycle — Chapter 5) but no fundamentally new genre.

Music produced two: the perfection of polyphonic vocal writing in the Roman school of Palestrina, and the invention of opera in the Florentine and Mantuan courts at the turn of the seventeenth century.
Both innovations would define European musical culture for the next four centuries.
Polyphony is music in which multiple independent melodic lines are sung simultaneously, with the lines weaving together according to harmonic and contrapuntal rules.

Polyphonic vocal writing had been the dominant style of European church music since the late twelfth century — the music of medieval Notre-Dame, Renaissance Burgundy and Flanders (composers like Guillaume Dufay, Johannes Ockeghem, and Josquin des Prez), and Renaissance Rome.

The technique reached extraordinary complexity in the fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries, with Mass settings using six, eight, or more independent voice parts woven together in dense contrapuntal textures.
The Counter-Reformation crisis, however, produced a problem.

Critics at the Council of Trent complained that elaborate polyphony obscured the sacred text — the words of the Mass were lost in the dense vocal counterpoint, the music was being written for the singers' display rather than for the worshippers' instruction, and the whole genre had become essentially incompatible with the Council's reforming emphasis on doctrinal clarity and pastoral effectiveness.

There was serious discussion in the 1560s of whether polyphony should be banned from Catholic worship altogether and replaced with plainchant — the ancient unison liturgical singing that had no harmonic complexity and presented the text with absolute clarity.

The composer who saved polyphonic Mass writing for the Catholic Church was Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina (jee-oh-VAH-nee pyair-loo-EE-jee dah pah-leh-STREE-nah, c. 1525–1594), a Roman musician who spent most of his career in the papal musical establishment — at the Cappella Giulia at St.
Peter's, the Papal Chapel (the Sistine Chapel choir), the Lateran, and Santa Maria Maggiore.

Palestrina's technical innovation was a polyphonic style — clean voice-leading, consonant harmony, careful control of dissonance, voice spacing that gave the text intelligibility — that demonstrated polyphony could be doctrinally appropriate as well as musically beautiful.

The famous demonstration was the Missa Papae Marcelli ("Mass for Pope Marcellus"), composed around 1562, that some accounts claim Palestrina wrote specifically to convince the Council of Trent that polyphony deserved to be preserved.

The story is probably embellished (the Council had not actually banned polyphony before Palestrina's Mass appeared; the legend that Palestrina single-handedly saved polyphony is a seventeenth-century construction), but the actual influence of Palestrina's style on Catholic church music was real.

Palestrina's mature polyphonic style — clear voice-leading, consonant harmony, balanced phrase lengths, controlled emotional register — became the textbook standard for Catholic church polyphony for the next four centuries.
Subsequent generations of composers studied Palestrina as the model.
The eighteenth-century counterpoint treatises that trained Bach and Mozart used Palestrina as the canonical example.
Modern conservatory students still learn species counterpoint through exercises modeled on Palestrina's style.
The technical-musical tradition that runs from Palestrina through Bach to Brahms (and beyond) is one of the most consequential continuities in European cultural history.
Palestrina is, in his way, as foundational a figure for European music as Donatello and Michelangelo are for European sculpture.

The same period produced parallel work in the Venetian school under the Gabrielis (Andrea and Giovanni — Chapter 5) and the Spanish school under Tomás Luis de Victoria (a Spaniard who spent his most productive years in Rome) and others.

The Renaissance Catholic polyphonic tradition reached its mature peak in roughly the period 1560–1610, just as a different musical innovation was emerging in Florence and Mantua that would shortly displace it.
The new innovation was opera — sung dramatic narrative, with continuous vocal music carrying the text rather than spoken dialogue.
Opera grew out of late-sixteenth-century discussions in Florence about how ancient Greek drama had been performed.

A Florentine intellectual circle called the Camerata Fiorentina ("Florentine Camerata"), meeting at the palace of Count Giovanni Bardi in the 1570s and 1580s, had become convinced that ancient Greek tragedy had been entirely sung — not spoken with intermittent choral interludes, as the surviving texts suggested, but continuous solo vocal recitation throughout.
The Camerata wanted to recover this lost ancient form.

Their earliest experiments — composer Jacopo Peri's Dafne (1597) and Euridice (1600), both with libretti by the poet Ottavio Rinuccini — used a new compositional technique called stile rappresentativo ("representational style") in which a solo singer delivered the text in a kind of expressive sung-spoken declamation, accompanied by simple harmonic instrumental backing.
The first opera with sustained musical life was L'Orfeo by Claudio Monteverdi (mon-teh-VAIR-dee, 1567–1643), premiered at the Mantuan court of Duke Vincenzo Gonzaga in February 1607.

L'Orfeo tells the Orpheus myth — the singer who descends to the underworld to retrieve his dead wife Eurydice — in five acts of continuous music for solo voices, choruses, and a substantial instrumental ensemble.

The work was unprecedented in its musical sophistication: Monteverdi combined the Camerata's recitative style for narrative passages with arias, instrumental sinfonias, and choral interludes that drew on the full resources of late-Renaissance polyphony and instrumental writing.
L'Orfeo was not the first opera ever written, but it was the first opera that subsequent composers and audiences agreed was a fully realized example of what the new genre could do.

Monteverdi's later operas — including L'Arianna (1608, of which only a single famous lament survives), Il ritorno d'Ulisse in patria (1640, the return of Ulysses), and L'incoronazione di Poppea (1643, the coronation of Poppea, written for the public opera houses of Venice in his late seventies) — extended opera into the genre that would dominate European musical theater for the next four centuries.
The first public opera house opened in Venice in 1637, making opera a paid commercial entertainment for the first time.

By 1700 there were dozens of opera houses across Italy and Europe; opera was the dominant form of European musical entertainment by the eighteenth century, and arguably remained so until the rise of the symphony in the nineteenth century.
The genre that began in Florentine intellectual experiments in the 1590s became, within a hundred years, the central institution of European musical culture.
A small note on Monteverdi's significance: he is the figure who bridges the Renaissance and the Baroque musical worlds.
His early works (the books of madrigals he published from the 1580s onward) are squarely in the late-Renaissance polyphonic tradition.

His late works (the Venetian operas and the Vespers of 1610, his great Marian liturgical setting) are in the new stile concertato that would shortly produce Baroque music proper — basso continuo accompaniment, expressive solo recitative, dramatic harmonic juxtapositions.
He is the most consequential single figure in the transition from Renaissance to Baroque music, and is conventionally dated as the boundary figure of the two periods.
The technological infrastructure that made all of this possible — and that had been transforming European intellectual life since the 1450s — was the printing press.
By the late sixteenth century, the Italian printing industry had matured into the most sophisticated in Europe, and Venice had become its capital.
Venetian printing began in the 1460s, shortly after the introduction of printing to Italy in 1465 (Chapter 3 — the German printers Sweynheym and Pannartz at Subiaco).

By 1500, Venice had over 400 printing shops in operation, and Venetian presses had produced perhaps a million volumes — the largest concentration of printing capacity in Europe and possibly the largest concentration of book production anywhere in the world at the time.

The economic structure that made Venetian printing successful combined the city's existing commercial-financial sophistication, its position as a trading entrepôt that could distribute books efficiently across the Mediterranean and into northern Europe, and its (relative) freedom from the censorship pressures that constrained printing in Spain, France, and even (after the 1540s) Rome.
The most famous Venetian printer was Aldus Manutius (Italian: Aldo Manuzio, 1449–1515), the founder of the Aldine Press (Chapter 3).

Aldus established Venice as the European center of classical Greek printing — between 1495 and his death in 1515, the Aldine Press published the first printed editions of nearly every major classical Greek text, often based on Byzantine manuscripts that the Greek refugees of 1453 and earlier had brought to Italy.

The Aldine editions were textually rigorous (Aldus employed Greek scholarly editors who produced authoritative critical editions), beautifully printed, and (by the standards of early printing) affordable.

Aldus also pioneered two innovations that would shape European book design for centuries: the italic type (a slanted printing typeface modeled on the Italian humanist cursive script, allowing more letters per line and more compact pages), and the octavo format (a small portable book size, roughly 5×8 inches, that fit comfortably in a reader's hand or a coat pocket — the predecessor of the modern paperback).
The Aldine octavos made serious classical literature physically portable for the first time, and the format was rapidly imitated across European printing.

Venetian printing through the late sixteenth century continued to dominate European publishing in several specialized areas: classical Latin and Greek scholarship, medical and scientific texts (including the first edition of Vesalius's De Humani Corporis Fabrica in 1543, which was actually printed in Basel but distributed primarily through Venetian merchant networks), illustrated books, music (the first major printed music collections were Venetian), and Hebrew texts (Venice was one of the major centers of European Hebrew printing, serving the Italian Jewish communities and the wider European Jewish diaspora).
