The encyclopedia was Yongle's personal project, partly motivated by a desire to assemble in one place every text bearing on Chinese statecraft, but also partly motivated by something less elevated: a desire to demonstrate that the usurper-emperor was the legitimate cultural patron of Han civilization in all its accumulated depth.
The legitimacy argument worked.

The Yongle Encyclopedia became one of the durable symbols of Ming cultural authority, and subsequent Confucian scholars who might otherwise have refused to recognize Yongle's legitimacy were able to point to the encyclopedia as evidence that the regime was genuinely committed to traditional Chinese learning.
The political utility of the project was as important as its scholarly value.
The military project was the third great Yongle enterprise.
Yongle conducted five personal campaigns into the Mongolian steppe between 1410 and 1424, attempting to break the surviving Mongol confederations that had reformed after the Yuan collapse.

The Northern Yuan court — Toghon Temur's descendants — had splintered into several rival factions by the early fifteenth century, and various Mongol warlords were competing for paramount-leader status across the Mongolian heartland.

Yongle's strategy was to march into the steppe with a large army, destroy whichever Mongol leader had most recently consolidated power, and force the Mongol nobility to submit nominal tribute to the Ming.
The campaigns were tactically successful in their immediate objectives.
Yongle's forces marched as far north as the Onon River (in modern Mongolia, near the heartland of the original Mongol homeland) and defeated several major Mongol leaders.

But the steppe was too vast for permanent occupation by a sedentary Chinese army; the Mongols simply withdrew when faced with a Chinese force, regrouped after the Chinese army returned south, and resumed their raiding within months.
Yongle himself died on the return from his fifth campaign in August 1424, near the modern city of Wuzhumuqin, before reaching Beijing.
His long-prepared sixth campaign was abandoned by his successor.
The Mongolian campaigns demonstrated Ming military reach but did not solve the northern frontier problem.

The strategic lesson — that nomadic confederations could not be permanently destroyed by punitive sedentary expeditions — would be relearned, painfully, by every later Ming emperor who attempted aggressive northern policy.

By the mid-fifteenth century, after the Tumu Crisis (Chapter 4), Ming northern policy would shift from offensive expedition to defensive Wall-building, and the offensive impulse of the early Ming would be permanently abandoned.
But the most spectacular project of Yongle's reign was not in the steppe.
It was on the ocean.
And it gets its own chapter.

Cross-civ check: Yongle's reign (1402–1424) was contemporary with the Ottoman recovery under Mehmed I after the catastrophic interregnum that followed Timur's victory at Ankara in 1402 (Ottoman Empire Ch 3); with the Council of Constance (1414–1418) that ended the Western Schism in the Catholic Church; with the English victory at Agincourt (1415) under Henry V; with the rise of Joan of Arc during the closing phase of the Hundred Years' War (Joan's intervention came in 1429, five years after Yongle's death); with the Brunelleschi dome in Florence under construction (1420–1436); with the Korean Joseon dynasty under King Sejong (whose reign 1418–1450 produced the invention of Hangul script).

The early fifteenth century in Eurasia is one of the great moments of post-medieval state-rebuilding, and the Ming under Yongle was its eastern anchor — the single largest, richest, most administratively sophisticated state on Earth at that moment, and the single most ambitious patron of imperial monumental projects.

chapters.title: Zheng He's Treasure Fleet
sentences: Between 1405 and 1433, the Ming Dynasty conducted seven gigantic naval expeditions across the Indian Ocean.
The fleets reached Java and Sumatra, India and Sri Lanka, the Persian Gulf and the Arabian Peninsula, and the East African coast at Malindi and Mogadishu.
They were the largest naval expeditions launched by any state anywhere in the world before the eighteenth century.
They preceded Vasco da Gama's voyage from Lisbon to Calicut by ninety years.
The flagships were several times larger than anything the Portuguese or Spanish would build for another two centuries.
Then they stopped.
The fleets were laid up.
The shipyards at Nanjing were dismantled.
The navigation records were eventually destroyed by the Ministry of War.
The Ming never built another deep-water navy.
China's naval projection effectively ended in 1433 and would not resume on a comparable scale for almost six hundred years.

This is one of the great counterfactual moments in world history — what would the modern world look like if the Ming had continued to project naval power across the Indian Ocean? — and it deserves a chapter to itself.
The chapter is about the voyages, the man who led them, the ships and the science that made them possible, and the political-cultural reasons the Ming chose to stop.
The man who led the voyages was Zheng He (jeng HUH).
Zheng He was born around 1371 as Ma He (mah HUH), the son of a Hui Muslim family in Yunnan province in southwestern China.

The family was prominent — his father and grandfather had reportedly made the Hajj pilgrimage to Mecca, suggesting both wealth and status — and the family name Ma was a Chinese version of Muhammad, marking the lineage as Muslim.

Yunnan in the late fourteenth century was the last Yuan-loyalist province in China; when Hongwu's army conquered Yunnan in 1381, the ten-year-old Ma He was captured, castrated as part of the standard treatment of conquered Yuan officials' sons, and sent north as a slave-eunuch to be assigned to the imperial household.
The boy ended up in the household of Hongwu's fourth son, Zhu Di — the future Yongle Emperor — at the Beiping court.

He grew up there as Zhu Di's personal servant, adopted the surname Zheng around 1404 (the name was bestowed by the new emperor in honor of military service during the Jingnan Campaign), and became one of Yongle's most trusted associates.

By the time Yongle took the throne in 1402, Zheng He was thirty-one, physically imposing (Ming sources describe him as exceptionally tall and powerfully built), militarily experienced from the civil war, and unusually cosmopolitan — a Hui Muslim with Yunnan Mongol-frontier connections, who spoke Persian and possibly Arabic in addition to Chinese, and whose religious background gave him useful credibility in dealing with Muslim courts across the Indian Ocean trade network.
In 1405, Yongle made him Commander of the Western Treasure Fleet.
The first voyage left Suzhou in the autumn of 1405.
The seventh and last returned in 1433.
Across those twenty-eight years, Zheng He commanded the largest naval expeditions in pre-modern history.
The fleets themselves require a careful description, because the dimensions are contested and the popular accounts often exaggerate.
Each voyage involved roughly 28,000 men aboard approximately 300 ships.

The ships included multiple categories: warships, supply ships, water tankers, troop transports, horse carriers, and the largest category, the baochuan (bow-CHWAHN, "treasure ships") — the imperial flagship class.
The dimensions of the treasure ships are the most famous and most contested aspect of the entire program.
Ming chronicle sources describe baochuan as up to 137 meters (450 feet) long and 56 meters (185 feet) wide, with nine masts and four decks, and crews of several hundred.

If accurate, these dimensions would make them several times larger than any contemporary European vessel — Columbus's Santa Maria was about 19 meters (62 feet) long, Vasco da Gama's São Gabriel about 27 meters (88 feet) — and possibly the largest wooden ships ever built.

Modern naval historians dispute whether ships of the stated length were structurally feasible; the engineering challenge of building a wooden hull strong enough to flex without breaking at 137 meters of length is severe, and the published structural calculations suggest the upper limit for traditional Chinese hull construction was probably significantly less.

Archaeological excavations at the Nanjing shipyards have recovered rudder posts of dimensions consistent with very large vessels (one rudder post is over 11 meters long, suggesting a hull of perhaps 60 to 70 meters), and dry-dock foundations of unprecedented scale.

The conservative modern reading is that the treasure ships were probably 60–70 meters (200–230 feet) long — substantially smaller than the chronicle dimensions, but still vastly larger than anything Europe could build for another two centuries.
Whatever the exact dimensions, the scale of the fleets is not in dispute.
Twenty-eight thousand men is a small army.
Three hundred ships is a substantial fleet by any pre-modern standard.
The total fleet displacement, even at conservative ship dimensions, exceeded the entire combined naval power of all European states at the same date.

The treasure voyages were not exploration in the European sense (the Ming was not seeking new lands — it knew the Indian Ocean trade network well from centuries of Chinese commercial contact, particularly during the Song and Yuan); they were imperial projection, on a scale calibrated to demonstrate Ming superiority to every state in the system.
The technology that made the voyages possible was substantial.

Chinese shipbuilding had pioneered watertight bulkhead compartments — segmented internal walls that allowed a damaged section to flood without sinking the ship, an innovation that would not appear in European shipbuilding until the nineteenth century.

The Ming had stern-mounted rudders (the European standard since the medieval period, but in larger and more sophisticated forms), the magnetic compass (invented under the Song, Tang-Song China Ch 6), and detailed navigational charts derived from a long Chinese tradition of coastal cartography.
Star navigation tables prepared at the Nanjing observatory allowed positional fixes by the elevation of specific stars.

The supply infrastructure included food storage adequate for 28,000 men on multi-year expeditions, freshwater management through both stored barrels and rain collection, and an advanced understanding of the Indian Ocean monsoon system that allowed the fleets to sail with prevailing winds in both directions.
The seven voyages can be summarized briefly.
The first voyage (1405–1407) sailed to Champa (in modern Vietnam), Java, Sumatra, Malacca, Sri Lanka, and Calicut on the Malabar coast of India.
The diplomatic mission was to establish Ming authority at the major Indian Ocean trade ports and secure them as tributary states.
The fleet defeated and captured a major pirate chief at Palembang in Sumatra and brought him back to Nanjing for execution.
The second voyage (1407–1409) repeated and extended the first, with stops at additional Indian ports.
The third voyage (1409–1411) was militarily more aggressive.
The fleet intervened in a succession dispute on Sri Lanka, captured the Sinhalese king Vira Alakeshvara, and brought him back to Nanjing as a prisoner.

The Yongle Emperor eventually pardoned and returned the king, after the Sri Lankan court promised tribute, which is the kind of imperial gesture that distinguishes Ming projection from European colonialism — the Ming wanted recognition and tribute, not territorial annexation.
The fourth voyage (1413–1415) reached the Persian Gulf, calling at Hormuz (Safavid Persia Ch 6 covers the later Hormuz history under the Safavids and English East India Company).
The fleet returned with envoys from over twenty foreign states bearing tribute, and — most famously — with a giraffe brought from the Swahili port of Malindi (in modern Kenya).
The giraffe was identified by Ming officials with the qilin (CHEE-lin), a mythical Chinese creature whose appearance was traditionally said to herald the reign of a sage-ruler.

A famous Ming court painting (the Tribute Giraffe with Attendant, painted by Shen Du in 1414, now in the Philadelphia Museum of Art) shows the animal being led on a leash by an African handler — possibly the earliest extant Chinese depiction of an East African person and animal.
The political symbolism was useful: a usurper-emperor whose legitimacy was contested at home received what could be officially interpreted as cosmological endorsement of his rule.
The fifth voyage (1417–1419) reached Aden in southern Arabia, returning the foreign envoys to their homes and collecting another wave of tribute.

The sixth voyage (1421–1422) sailed to Africa, with detachments reportedly reaching Mogadishu (in modern Somalia) and possibly further down the Swahili coast. (A persistent claim that the Ming reached the Americas in 1421, popularized by Gavin Menzies's 2002 book 1421: The Year China Discovered America, has been comprehensively rejected by professional historians of pre-modern China and the Indian Ocean.
The Menzies book is bunk.

There is no evidence that any Ming vessel ever crossed the Pacific or rounded Africa, and there is substantial positive evidence that Zheng He's voyages were confined to the Indian Ocean trade network.

The Ming knew about the Indian Ocean monsoons and exploited them; they had no equivalent knowledge of Pacific or Atlantic wind systems and no apparent reason to attempt crossings of either ocean.) The seventh voyage (1431–1433) was launched after a long pause caused by political shifts at court (described below).

It revisited many of the earlier ports, confirmed tribute relationships, and sent detachments as far as Mecca — where Zheng He's Muslim sailors were reportedly able to perform the Hajj on the imperial expedition's behalf, a remarkable diplomatic-religious moment for a Chinese imperial project.
Zheng He himself died at sea, probably near Calicut, on the return trip in 1433.
He was around sixty-two years old.
The political question — why did the voyages stop? — deserves direct attention, because the answer reveals one of the deepest structural tensions of Ming politics.
The voyages were a project of the eunuch faction at court.
Zheng He himself was a eunuch, as were most of the senior commanders of the fleet.

The administrative apparatus that supported the voyages — the shipyards at Nanjing, the supply networks, the personnel rosters — was managed through the imperial household, which is to say through the eunuch bureaucracy.

The Yongle Emperor, who personally sponsored the voyages, was using the eunuch apparatus partly because it answered to him directly without filtering through the regular Confucian bureaucracy, and partly because the Confucian officials were skeptical of the entire enterprise.
The Confucian officials were skeptical for both ideological and practical reasons.
Ideologically, the Confucian tradition emphasized agrarian governance, frugal court finance, and minimal state expenditure on prestige projects that did not directly benefit the rural population.
The voyages were colossally expensive.

They produced exotic tribute (giraffes, ostriches, lions, foreign envoys with strange clothes) but no tangible economic return — Ming exports of silk and porcelain were already reaching the Indian Ocean markets through private trade, and the official tribute exchanges generally cost the Ming more in return-gifts than they received in tribute.
Practically, the officials wanted state resources directed to the agricultural infrastructure (river dikes, granaries, canals), not to building 70-meter ships to take giraffes to Beijing.

When the Yongle Emperor died in 1424, his son the Hongxi Emperor suspended the voyages within months — the new emperor was on the side of the Confucian officials, who had pushed the suspension hard during Yongle's lifetime and now had a sympathetic ear at the throne.

Hongxi died after only nine months, but his successor the Xuande Emperor authorized only one more voyage, the seventh of 1431–1433, partly as a memorial to his grandfather Yongle and partly to confirm the established tribute relationships.
After Zheng He's death and the fleet's return, the voyages were never resumed.
The political coup against the maritime project went further than just suspension.
The records of the voyages — the navigation tables, the route logs, the ship designs — were progressively suppressed across the following decades.
The standard account is that around 1480, the Ministry of War official Liu Daxia ordered the surviving navigation records destroyed to prevent any future emperor from reviving the voyages.

This story may be exaggerated (the destruction was probably more piecemeal than the dramatic version suggests), but the underlying reality is documented: by the early sixteenth century, the Ming no longer had the technical capacity to build deep-water expeditions on Zheng He's scale, the shipyards had been dismantled or repurposed, and the maritime knowledge base had been allowed to lapse.
The decision to abandon the maritime project shaped Chinese state policy for the following four centuries.

The Ming would maintain the official Haijin (HIGH-jin, "sea ban") edicts forbidding private overseas trade for most of the dynasty — the ban being honored mostly in the breach, since smuggling and unofficial trade continued at large scale, but the official posture being firmly against maritime engagement.
The Qing dynasty that followed continued the same general policy.
China would not project naval power on a comparable scale until the People's Republic began building a blue-water fleet in the 2000s, almost six centuries after Zheng He's last voyage.
The deeper question — why did the political coup against the voyages succeed so completely? — is one of the most-discussed counterfactuals in world history.

The standard answers focus on Confucian ideology (agrarian priorities, suspicion of merchant wealth, distrust of eunuch power), on fiscal pressure (the voyages were expensive at exactly the moment Ming finances were strained by the Beijing capital relocation and the Mongolian campaigns), and on strategic priorities (the northern frontier required attention, and the Ming made a deliberate choice to redirect resources from maritime projection to land defense).
All of these are real factors and all are documented in the period sources.
But there is also a deeper structural point worth pausing on.
The Ming voyages were not a commercial project; they were a state project.
They did not generate revenue to fund themselves; they were funded by the imperial treasury.
Their continuation depended entirely on continued political support from the throne.

When that support evaporated — for the perfectly comprehensible reason that the next emperor was a Confucian-tradition agrarian moderate rather than an outward-projecting usurper-emperor — there was no commercial constituency capable of sustaining the project in the absence of imperial sponsorship.

The Indian Ocean merchants (Chinese, Arab, Persian, Indian, Southeast Asian) who actually moved goods across the trade network continued doing so without any need for Ming naval protection; the imperial fleet had been imposed on top of an existing commercial network rather than being functionally necessary to it.
The contrast with the European maritime projects of the following century is instructive.

The Portuguese voyages to the Indian Ocean in the late fifteenth century were sponsored by the Crown but operated by joint commercial ventures, with Portuguese merchants and the state sharing both costs and returns; the Dutch and English East India Companies of the seventeenth century (Safavid Persia Ch 6 covers the EIC's role at Hormuz) were corporate-state hybrids in which commercial profit motivation kept the maritime project running through political shifts at the home government.
The Ming voyages had no equivalent commercial-political coalition.
They were the Yongle Emperor's personal project; when his successors lost interest, they ended.
Whether things would have looked different if the Ming had continued is one of the great unanswerable questions of world history.

Some economic historians have argued that a continued Ming naval presence in the Indian Ocean would have made Vasco da Gama's 1498 arrival irrelevant — the Portuguese would have found the trade network already controlled by a much larger Chinese imperial fleet and would have had no opening to establish their own coastal-fortress empire.

Others have argued that the Indian Ocean trade network was deeply enough established by the early fifteenth century that no naval projection would have permanently controlled it, and the Portuguese would still have found their way in.
The historical record contains the choice the Ming actually made (to stop) but does not contain the alternative.
What the historical record does contain is the cultural memory.
Zheng He has become, in twentieth- and twenty-first-century Chinese popular culture, the icon of a possible China that engaged the wider world rather than retreating from it.
His statue stands at Nanjing, at Jakarta, at several Indonesian and Malaysian Chinese-community sites along his routes.
The People's Republic has invested heavily in promoting his memory as a counter-narrative to the standard Western framing of European maritime expansion as the inevitable arc of early-modern history.
The 600th anniversary of the first voyage in 2005 was a major Chinese government commemoration.
The treasure fleet has, in the modern Chinese imagination, become the symbol of what the Ming might have been if it had not turned inward.

It is also a reminder of what the Ming actually was for one extraordinary generation: the largest naval power on Earth, projecting force halfway around the world, with ships that nothing in Europe could remotely match.
Cross-civ check: the Zheng He voyages (1405–1433) ran in parallel with several other major early-modern maritime projects — though all of them at smaller scale.

The Portuguese Atlantic exploration under Henry the Navigator was beginning in the same decades — Henry founded his Sagres maritime academy around 1418, the Portuguese reached the Madeira Islands in 1419, the Azores in 1427, and Cape Bojador on the African Atlantic coast in 1434 (the year after Zheng He's last voyage).
The Korean Joseon dynasty under King Sejong was developing the geobukseon (turtle ship) gunboat designs that would later defeat the Japanese at the Imjin War (Chapter 6).
The Polynesian navigators had completed their two-millennium expansion across the Pacific (Polynesian Voyagers) and were settling into their final island cultures.
In Mali, the great empire of the western Sahel was at its commercial peak.
In the Aztec heartland, Tenochtitlan was completing its dominance of the Valley of Mexico (Aztec Empire Ch 5).

The early fifteenth century is the moment when several civilizational centers were, simultaneously, making decisions about long-distance maritime engagement that would shape the next four centuries — and the Ming made the most consequential of those decisions in the most decisive manner.

chapters.title: The Eunuch Empire
sentences: The Yongle Emperor died in 1424, on the return from his fifth Mongolian campaign.
His son Hongxi reigned for nine months.
His grandson Xuande reigned for ten years and authorized the seventh and last Zheng He voyage (Chapter 3).
His great-grandson, the Zhengtong Emperor (jeng-TONG, "Orthodox Succession"), inherited the throne in 1435 at age six.

What followed was a 130-year period in which actual political power at court drifted progressively away from the throne and toward the eunuch bureaucracy that Hongwu had tried so hard to prevent (Chapter 1).

The Tumu Crisis of 1449 was the most dramatic single moment of the period — a Chinese emperor was captured in battle by Mongol cavalry, the first such event since the Mongol Yuan conquest itself — but the underlying institutional drift was constant.

By the end of the period, the regular Confucian bureaucracy was operating in the shadow of the Directorate of Ceremonial (the eunuch office that controlled access to the emperor), the Eastern Depot (the eunuch-run secret police), and the imperial workshops (the eunuch-controlled industrial-economic apparatus that produced everything from porcelain to silk to weapons for the imperial household).

This is the chapter about the eunuch empire — the institutional period that made the late Ming what it became, the Tumu Crisis that exposed the rot, the Great Wall reconstruction that was the period's most visible monument, and the Grand Canal economy that kept the dynasty solvent through it all.
The first eunuch to dominate Ming politics outright was Wang Zhen (wahng JEN).
Wang Zhen had been the boy Zhengtong Emperor's tutor before he became emperor.

He retained a close relationship after the boy ascended the throne, and as Zhengtong grew up, Wang Zhen rose through the eunuch hierarchy to control the Directorate of Ceremonial (Si Li Jian) — the office responsible for handling memorials between the outer government and the inner palace, and increasingly the office that decided which memorials reached the emperor's desk and which were quietly filed without action.

By the early 1440s, Wang Zhen was effectively running the Ming government, with the young emperor approving documents that Wang Zhen drafted and signing off on personnel decisions that Wang Zhen had made.
In 1449, Wang Zhen made the catastrophic mistake of his career.

The Mongol leader Esen Taishi (eh-SEN TIGH-shih), the dominant figure of the Oirat (western Mongol) confederation, had been raiding the Ming northern frontier and demanding additional trade concessions.
Wang Zhen persuaded the twenty-two-year-old Zhengtong Emperor to lead a personal punitive expedition against the Mongols — the first time a Ming emperor would campaign in person since Yongle.

The expedition was hastily organized, with an army that Ming sources later claimed numbered 500,000 men (probably exaggerated but certainly very large), inadequately supplied, and led by Wang Zhen himself in his capacity as the emperor's chief political advisor.
The expedition was a disaster from the start.
The army marched into Mongol territory in August 1449, found nothing because Esen had withdrawn rather than fight on Ming terms, and turned back toward Beijing as supplies ran low.
Wang Zhen, deciding to detour the army past his hometown for a flattering display, slowed the retreat dangerously.
Esen's cavalry caught the Ming army at the Tumu (TOO-moo) fortress on September 1, 1449, while it was reorganizing for water resupply.
The Mongol attack was rapid and devastating.
The Ming army, exhausted and poorly led, broke.
Casualties were enormous — modern estimates suggest perhaps half the army was killed in a few hours, the rest scattered.
Wang Zhen was killed by his own bodyguard, who reportedly judged that he had already destroyed the empire and might as well die with it.
The Zhengtong Emperor was captured.
A captured Chinese emperor was an unprecedented diplomatic problem.
Esen attempted to use the captive emperor as leverage to extract massive concessions from the Ming court.
The Ming court — under the leadership of the brilliant Vice Minister of War Yu Qian (YOO chyen) — refused to pay.
They formally enthroned the captured emperor's brother as the Jingtai Emperor (jing-TIGH), making Zhengtong's captivity diplomatically irrelevant.
Yu Qian then organized the defense of Beijing itself against Esen's siege in October 1449.
The defense held.
Esen was forced to withdraw without taking the capital.
The captured Zhengtong Emperor, now politically useless to his Mongol captors, was eventually released in 1450 and lived under house arrest in Beijing for seven years.
The story has a disturbing coda.
In 1457, the displaced Zhengtong Emperor mounted a coup against his brother the Jingtai Emperor and reclaimed the throne (under a new reign name, Tianshun, "Heaven's Approval").
One of his first acts was to execute Yu Qian — the man who had saved Beijing from the consequences of his original capture — on trumped-up treason charges.
Yu Qian's execution is one of the most universally condemned political killings in Chinese imperial history.
Subsequent Ming and Qing emperors formally repudiated the verdict; Yu Qian's tomb at Hangzhou is a major pilgrimage site for the Confucian moral tradition.
The Tumu Crisis was the most visible single moment of the eunuch-dominated mid-Ming, but its institutional consequences were more important than the dramatic events.
The crisis demonstrated three things, each of which would shape Ming policy for the rest of the dynasty.
First, the weisuo military system (Chapter 1) was failing.
Hongwu's hereditary military households, supposedly self-supporting and ready for service, had decayed across two generations.
The army Wang Zhen led to Tumu was poorly trained, poorly equipped, and poorly motivated.
It was a hereditary peasant militia rather than the professional force the Ming would need to face actual Mongol cavalry.
Subsequent Ming emperors would gradually shift toward paid mercenary forces (mubing) as the weisuo decayed further, but the institutional transition was slow, expensive, and politically contentious.
Second, the northern frontier could not be permanently secured by offensive expedition.
Yongle's five campaigns had not solved the Mongol problem; the Tumu Crisis showed that even one badly-organized expedition could end in catastrophe.
Ming policy shifted toward a defensive posture, anchored on the rebuilt Great Wall (described below).
The shift permanently abandoned the Yongle-era ambition of projecting Ming military power into the steppe.
Third, the eunuch system had become structurally impossible to dislodge.
Wang Zhen was dead, but the institutional position he had occupied — chief eunuch of the Directorate of Ceremonial, with effective control over the flow of information to the emperor — remained.
His successors slipped into the same position.
Across the next 175 years, the chief eunuch of the Directorate would be the second-most-powerful person at court, and sometimes the most powerful, depending on the emperor's energy and competence.
The institutional logic that had created the eunuch problem under the Hu Weiyong abolition (Chapter 1) continued to operate; the Tumu Crisis did not break it.
The chief eunuch who came closest to surpassing Wang Zhen in raw power was Liu Jin (lyoo JEEN), who dominated the court of the Zhengde Emperor (jeng-DUH, reigned 1505–1521) from 1505 to 1510.
Liu Jin's tenure is usually treated by historians as the apex of pre-Wei Zhongxian eunuch corruption.

He effectively ran the government while the teenage Zhengde Emperor pursued an enthusiastic life of debauchery and military play (the Zhengde Emperor is one of the most colorful Ming rulers — he built a private military pleasure-palace in the Forbidden City called the Leopard House, rode personally into combat against Mongol raiders under the assumed military rank of General Zhu Shou, and largely ignored normal governance).
Liu Jin accumulated personal wealth that contemporary estimates put at roughly 250 million ounces of silver — possibly the largest individual fortune in pre-modern world history.
He was eventually executed in 1510 after being accused of plotting to seize the throne; the punishment, lingchi (slow slicing), reportedly took three days to administer.
Liu Jin's wealth — even allowing for considerable exaggeration in the reported figures — illustrates the scale of eunuch corruption at its height.
A single court official with no legitimate revenue source had assembled a fortune comparable to the entire annual tax revenue of major European states.

The wealth was assembled through a combination of bribes, grants of state monopolies (salt, tea, mining), and outright extortion of provincial officials who needed to pass requests through the Directorate of Ceremonial.

The Ming state had become, at the eunuch interface, something close to a pure rent-extraction apparatus — and the regular Confucian bureaucracy was institutionally incapable of doing anything about it.
The most visible monument of the mid-Ming period is the Great Wall of China that tourists visit today.
The Great Wall in popular imagination is often presented as a single ancient structure built by the Qin Dynasty under the First Emperor (Qin Dynasty Ch 4 covers the Qin-era Wall).
This is not accurate.
The Qin Wall was built of rammed earth, has mostly disappeared into the soil, and ran along a different route from the modern Wall.

The famous brick-and-stone fortification with the watchtowers, battlements, and rolling stretches across the mountains north of Beijing — the Great Wall that appears on every Chinese tourism brochure — is almost entirely a Ming construction project, undertaken between roughly 1450 and 1600 in response to the strategic lessons of the Tumu Crisis.
The decision to rebuild the Wall was a deliberate strategic shift.

After Tumu, the Ming court accepted that offensive expeditions into the steppe could not be sustained — Mongol cavalry could outpace any Ming army in the open plains, and the cost of supplying expeditions deep into Mongolian territory was prohibitive.

The defensive alternative was to wall the entire northern frontier and force any attacker to either besiege fortifications (which was difficult for nomadic cavalry) or to penetrate the Wall at specific gates that could be defended by garrison forces.
The Wall did not need to be impenetrable; it needed to channel attacks into chokepoints where the Ming could mass defensive forces.
Construction proceeded in stages over more than a century.
The earliest substantial Ming wall sections were built in the 1450s and 1460s in Hebei and Liaoning provinces.

The major reconstruction of the central sections — the picturesque mountain Wall north of Beijing, including the famous Mutianyu and Badaling sections that Western tourists visit — was concentrated in the mid-to-late sixteenth century, particularly during the reign of the Wanli Emperor (Chapter 5).
The western extension to Jiayuguan (jya-yoo-GWAHN) in modern Gansu province, the Wall's Ming-era western terminus, was completed in stages through the late sixteenth century.

The eastern terminus at Shanhaiguan (shahn-high-GWAHN, "Mountain-Sea Pass," where the Wall meets the Pacific) was built up as the major fortress facing the Manchurian frontier, the gate that Wu Sangui would eventually open to the Manchus in 1644 (Chapter 8).

The total length of the Ming Wall is contested; modern surveys have produced figures ranging from about 5,500 miles (the most commonly cited number) to over 13,000 miles (a 2012 Chinese government archaeological survey that included every fortification fragment that could be associated with the Ming defensive system).
The construction effort was one of the largest in human history — millions of conscripted laborers, soldiers, and artisans worked on the project across the century and a half of major construction.
The cost in human lives, particularly during the Wanli-era extensions, was enormous.
The Wall did not actually stop Mongol raids.

Altan Khan invaded northern China in 1550, broke through the frontier defenses, and besieged Beijing for several days before withdrawing with massive plunder — a raid roughly comparable in audacity to Esen's 1449 Beijing siege a century earlier.

The Wall slowed the Mongol raiding parties, channeled them into specific approaches, and made the raiders pay a higher cost in casualties for any given operation, but it did not exclude them from China.

The Mongols continued raiding the northern frontier for the entire Ming period; the eventual modus vivendi was not the Wall but the Longqing settlement of 1571, in which the Ming recognized Altan Khan as a tributary ruler and opened official trade markets at the frontier — what the Mongols had been demanding all along.
The Wall's most spectacular failure came in 1644.
The Manchu armies that overthrew the Ming did not, in the end, breach the Wall by force.
They came through the Shanhaiguan gate, opened from the inside by the Ming general Wu Sangui (Chapter 8).
The Wall held against Manchu attempts at frontal assault for years before Wu's defection; once the gate was opened, the Wall became irrelevant.
The lesson — that fortifications cannot stop an enemy whose internal allies will let them through — would be relearned in many later contexts.
The Ming Wall is now a UNESCO World Heritage site, the most visited monument in China, and one of the largest construction projects ever undertaken on Earth.
It is also an enduring case study in the limits of defensive engineering against a determined adversary with internal political support.
The economic backbone of the mid-Ming was the Grand Canal and the rice it carried.
The Grand Canal had been built by the Sui dynasty in the early 600s (Tang-Song China Ch 1) and extended by the Mongol Yuan to reach Khanbaliq in the 1280s (Yuan Dynasty Ch 2).
The Yongle Emperor had comprehensively rebuilt and re-cut the canal between 1411 and 1415 to support the new northern capital.

The result was a continuous internal water transport network running roughly 1,100 miles from Hangzhou in the south to Beijing in the north, capable of carrying up to four million bushels of grain per year — the logistical artery that fed the Ming capital and remained the spine of Ming state finance.
The Canal had to operate continuously for the dynasty to function.

Beijing, with a population of perhaps a million by the late Ming, did not produce nearly enough grain to feed itself; the surrounding north Chinese provinces produced wheat and millet but not the rice that the imperial court and its associated officials and military expected.

The grain shipments came from the Yangtze delta — the most productive agricultural region in the empire — and moved north through the canal in the slow procession of grain barges that defined Ming logistics.
The Canal Transport Bureau, staffed by hereditary canal workers, was one of the largest single state enterprises of the Ming period.
The Canal economy supported a thriving commercial network along its length.
The Yangtze delta cities — Suzhou (SOO-joh), Hangzhou, Yangzhou, Wuxi — became some of the wealthiest urban centers in the world during the mid-Ming period.
Suzhou by the late sixteenth century had a population of over a million, with extensive silk-weaving, embroidery, and book-printing industries.

The Canal towns connected the wealthy Yangtze south to the political capital in the north, and the economic gravity of the late Ming was concentrated along this north-south axis to a degree that persisted into the modern period (the modern Beijing-Shanghai high-speed rail line follows roughly the same route as the Grand Canal).
The Canal also supported one of the most distinctive economic-political features of the mid-Ming: the imperial workshops (yuyong jian) operated by the eunuch bureaucracy.

The Directorate of Ceremonial and its subsidiary offices ran enormous industrial operations — the Jingdezhen porcelain kilns producing the imperial blue-and-white wares (Chapter 7 describes the porcelain in more detail), the silk workshops at Suzhou and Hangzhou producing imperial robes and ceremonial textiles, the lacquer and jade and metalwork operations that supplied the court's ceremonial requirements.

These workshops were enormous economic enterprises operated outside the regular fiscal system, with their own labor forces (often conscripted artisans serving long periods of corvée), their own raw-material supply chains, and their own sales channels for surplus production.
The eunuch faction's institutional power rested partly on its control of this parallel economic apparatus.
A pause, on the institutional shape of the mid-Ming.
The mid-Ming century from Tumu (1449) to the rise of Zhang Juzheng (1572) is sometimes presented as a period of stagnation.

This is partly accurate — the dynasty did not produce major institutional innovations during this period, did not expand its territory, did not significantly reform its administrative structure, and did not produce many emperors of great competence.

The Zhengde Emperor's debauchery, the Jiajing Emperor's twenty-year absence from court to pursue Daoist alchemy in pursuit of immortality, the various Liu-Jin-style eunuch corruption episodes — these are the headline events of mid-Ming political history.
But the period was also one of institutional stability and economic growth, on a different reading.
The Grand Canal economy worked.
The Beijing capital was successfully maintained for over a century without major fiscal crisis.
The Great Wall was built.
The northern frontier was contained, expensively but effectively.
The agricultural base of the empire continued to grow.
The population recovered to and exceeded its Song-era peak.
The commercial economy along the Yangtze became one of the most sophisticated in the world.
The cultural production of the period — described in Chapter 7 — was extraordinary even by Ming standards.
The institutional pattern of the mid-Ming is one of an autopilot empire.

The institutions Hongwu had built operated by their own momentum, with the eunuch bureaucracy filling the coordination role that the abolished Chief Minister had previously occupied, and the Confucian regular bureaucracy filling the technical-administrative role of running provinces and ministries.
The system worked because the Chinese economic base was robust, the institutional infrastructure was substantial, and the threats to the dynasty were manageable.
It failed when those conditions changed in the late sixteenth century — when the Imjin War (Chapter 6) and the rise of the Manchus created stresses the autopilot system could not absorb.
But for a long generation, the autopilot empire functioned.
The next two chapters cover the late Ming era when the autopilot began to fail.

Cross-civ check: the mid-Ming century (1449–1572) was contemporary with the fall of Constantinople to the Ottomans in 1453 (Byzantine Empire Ch 12), the Wars of the Roses in England (1455–1487), the Reconquista completion in Spain (Granada 1492), Columbus's voyages to the Americas (1492 onward), the Reformation in Germany (Luther's 95 Theses 1517), the Mughal founding under Babur (1526), the Aztec conquest by Cortés (1519–1521, Aztec Empire Ch 8), the Inca conquest by Pizarro (1532–1533), the Safavid founding by Ismail I (Safavid Persia Ch 2), and the Suleiman the Magnificent Ottoman peak (1520–1566, Ottoman Empire Ch 5).

The mid-Ming was the eastern anchor of one of the most transformative centuries in world history — a century during which the Eurasian-American world system was knit together for the first time and the early-modern global economy began to take shape.

The Ming's relative inactivity during this period (the choice not to project naval power into the Indian Ocean, the choice not to engage with the Americas, the choice not to extend territorial control beyond its existing frontiers) was a strategic decision with very large long-term consequences.

chapters.title: Single Whip and the Silver Globalization
sentences: In 1572, the Wanli Emperor (WAN-lee) inherited the Ming throne at age nine.

His reign would last until 1620 — forty-eight years, the longest of any Ming emperor — and would span almost exactly the late Ming period during which the dynasty's commercial economy reached its peak, its silver-based monetary system was knit into the global economy, the great vernacular novels were written (Chapter 7), Matteo Ricci reached Beijing, and the Imjin War in Korea (Chapter 6) bankrupted the treasury just as the Manchu threat was rising in the northeast.
The reign was simultaneously the cultural apex of late Ming China and the political prelude to its destruction.

The Wanli Emperor himself, after the first decade of competent rule under the regency of the Grand Secretary Zhang Juzheng, settled into one of the strangest patterns of imperial behavior in Chinese history: he simply stopped governing.
From the late 1580s until his death, he refused to attend court, refused to fill vacant offices, refused to sign personnel decisions, refused to read most memorials.
The dynasty drifted on its institutional momentum while the throne sulked in the inner palace.
The Wanli work strike is one of the most-studied cases in the historical literature of what happens when an early-modern monarchy operates under a non-functional monarch for decades at a stretch.

This is the chapter about the late Ming silver economy, the global trade network it produced, the Wanli reign that funded all of it without governing any of it, and Matteo Ricci's arrival at the Beijing court.
The Imjin War is its own chapter (Chapter 6).
The decade before the Wanli work strike was the most administratively vigorous of the late Ming, conducted by the Grand Secretary Zhang Juzheng (jahng joo-JENG).
Zhang Juzheng (1525–1582) was a brilliant career official from Hubei province who had risen through the regular Confucian bureaucracy and reached the Grand Secretariat (Neige) in the 1560s.
When the boy Wanli Emperor took the throne in 1572, Zhang Juzheng became effective regent — chief tutor to the boy emperor, chief political coordinator, and chief reformer all at once.
His tenure (roughly 1572–1582) was the most ambitious set of late-Ming reforms.
The reforms had three main components.
First, fiscal consolidation: Zhang Juzheng audited the imperial accounts, identified massive arrears in tax collection, and forced provincial officials to make up the deficits or be dismissed.
By the late 1570s the Ming treasury had a positive surplus for the first time in a generation.

Second, land surveys: a comprehensive empire-wide survey of cultivated land in 1578–1580 identified vast quantities of land that had been quietly removed from the tax registers by wealthy households over the preceding century, restoring perhaps 30% more land to taxable status.
Third, the Single Whip Tax Reform, the centerpiece of his fiscal program.
The Single Whip Reform (Yi Tiao Bian Fa, "Single Whip Method") was implemented gradually under Zhang Juzheng's leadership across the 1570s and formalized empire-wide in 1581.
It consolidated the labyrinthine Ming fiscal system into a single payment, made in silver, per landholding.

The previous system had required each rural household to make separate payments of grain (rice or wheat depending on region), corvée labor obligations (so many days of work per year owed to the state for canal maintenance, conscription, courier service, etc.), miscellaneous local fees, and special provincial assessments.
The system was complicated, easy to manipulate, and difficult to administer fairly.
The Single Whip replaced all of this with a single annual silver payment based on land area and quality.
The reform's logic was administrative simplicity, but its consequence was monetary revolution.
The Ming had not previously been a silver-based economy.

The Hongwu founding had attempted to use paper money (jiaochao) on the Yuan-era model, but the paper currency had inflated catastrophically through the early Ming and was effectively worthless by the mid-fifteenth century.

Day-to-day commerce had reverted to copper coins (cash) for small transactions and silver bullion for large transactions, with no formal silver coinage but with weighed silver chunks (sycee) circulating as the de facto large-denomination currency.
The Single Whip Reform took this informal silver-based commercial economy and made it into the official basis of state finance.
The effects were immediate and global.
Chinese demand for silver, already enormous, became overwhelming after 1581.

Every rural household across the most populous country on Earth needed to convert agricultural produce into silver to pay their taxes — and the Chinese silver mines produced nowhere near enough metal to meet the demand.
The shortfall had to be made up by imports.
The silver imports came from two sources, and they were the gravitational center of the early-modern global economy.
The first source was Spanish America.
The huge silver deposits at Potosí (in modern Bolivia) and at Zacatecas (in modern Mexico) had been discovered in the 1540s and were producing silver at unprecedented scale by the 1570s.

Most of the silver crossed the Atlantic to Seville, where the Spanish Habsburg state taxed and minted it; from Seville it spread through European commerce, primarily to fund the Habsburg wars against the Dutch revolt and the Ottoman Empire.
But a significant fraction — perhaps a third by the late sixteenth century — went the other direction.

From Acapulco on the Pacific coast of Mexico, the Manila galleon carried silver west across the Pacific to Manila in the Philippines, where it was exchanged with Chinese merchants for Chinese silk, porcelain, and luxury goods.
The Manila galleon ran annually from 1565 to 1815, the longest-running scheduled trans-oceanic trade route in pre-modern history.
The second source was Japan.
Japanese silver mines at Iwami and Sado in the late sixteenth century were producing silver at scale, perhaps 20-30% of total global silver output for several decades.

Japanese silver flowed across the East China Sea via several channels — direct smuggling between Japanese and Chinese merchants, official trade through the Ryukyu Islands (the Okinawa-based kingdom that maintained tributary relations with both China and Japan), and after 1557 through the Portuguese trading post at Macao, where Portuguese ships shuttled between Nagasaki and Macao and Goa carrying silver one direction and silk the other.
The combined silver flows were staggering.
By the early seventeenth century, perhaps 10,000 tons of silver had flowed into China from these two sources combined — possibly a third or more of all silver mined in the early-modern world.
The Ming economy was the destination for the largest single redistribution of precious metal in pre-modern human history.

The Spanish Habsburg silver economy that funded the wars against the Dutch (Safavid Persia Ch 6 covers some parallel dynamics in the silk-for-silver trade with Iran) was the western pole of this system; Ming China was the eastern pole; and the Indian Ocean and Pacific commercial networks were the connecting tissue.
The economic consequences were profound.
China's commercial economy was deeply monetized for the first time.
Long-distance internal trade became dramatically easier because silver was a portable, durable, infinitely divisible medium of exchange.

Specialized regional production for distant markets expanded — Jiangnan silk, Jingdezhen porcelain, Sichuan paper, Shanxi salt, Fujian sugar, Guangdong iron all developed integrated commercial networks.
The late Ming commercial economy was, by the early seventeenth century, probably the largest and most sophisticated in the world.
The political consequences were almost as profound.
The Ming state suddenly had access to silver tax revenues at a scale Hongwu could not have imagined.

But the silver was also a vulnerability — disruptions to the Manila or Macao silver flows could create rapid fiscal crises, and the Ming state had no real control over either Spanish American mining output or Japanese silver production.

When the Tokugawa shogunate restricted Japanese silver export in the early seventeenth century, when Spanish silver production declined after about 1620, the Ming fiscal crisis that followed contributed directly to the dynasty's fall (Chapter 8).
The same silver flows that had built the late Ming commercial economy turned into the dynasty's strategic dependency — and when the silver dried up, the dynasty could not adapt fast enough.
The deeper structural point is worth pausing on.
China under the Single Whip Reform had become integrated into a global economic system whose central commodity it did not produce and could not control.

The state's fiscal viability now depended on the smooth operation of trade networks running from the Andes through Manila to the Yangtze delta — networks operated by Spanish galleons, Portuguese trading posts, Chinese and Hokkien private merchants, and Japanese silver miners, all outside the Ming's direct authority.
This was, in retrospect, the moment when Chinese state autonomy stopped being possible in the way Hongwu had imagined it.
The early-modern global economy had absorbed the Ming, and the Ming had not noticed.
Zhang Juzheng's reforms briefly stabilized the dynasty's finances and produced the late Ming silver economy.
He himself died in 1582, in the middle of the great land survey, exhausted from a decade of overwork.
What happened next was a political reversal that exemplifies one of the chronic Ming problems.
Zhang Juzheng had made enemies — many of them, accumulated over a decade of vigorous reform, fiscal pressure on wealthy provincial families, and ruthless personnel decisions.
After his death, those enemies organized a posthumous campaign against his reputation.
Within a few years, Zhang Juzheng had been formally disgraced, his honors stripped, his family's wealth confiscated, his sons exiled or driven to suicide.

The reforms were not entirely undone — the Single Whip continued, because no one had a viable alternative — but Zhang Juzheng himself became a cautionary example for the next generation of officials, who took the obvious lesson: do not be too vigorous, do not make too many enemies, do not push reforms that depend on personal political capital you cannot maintain after death.
The Wanli Emperor, by then in his early twenties, had personally signed off on the destruction of his former regent's reputation.
It was around this time that the emperor began his long withdrawal from active governance.

The Wanli work strike is one of the most extensively-studied episodes of Ming political history, partly because it lasted so long (roughly 1589 to Wanli's death in 1620 — over thirty years), partly because the documentary record is unusually good (the regular Ming bureaucracy continued producing memorials throughout the period, providing detailed evidence of what happens when an early-modern monarchy is run on autopilot for decades), and partly because the proximate cause was so personally trivial that the structural consequences are particularly stark.
The trigger was a succession dispute.

The Wanli Emperor's first son, born to a low-ranking palace concubine in 1582, had a stronger claim to the throne by primogeniture than the Emperor's preferred third son, born to his favorite concubine Lady Zheng in 1586.
The Confucian official class insisted that the eldest son be designated crown prince according to traditional Chinese succession law.
The Emperor preferred his third son.
The dispute became a multi-year political confrontation between the throne and the Confucian bureaucracy, conducted through escalating memorials, court arguments, and Imperial sulks.

Wanli refused to designate any crown prince at all for years, fueled the speculation that he might overrule the bureaucracy, and finally — in 1601, after nearly two decades of dispute — capitulated and designated the eldest son as crown prince.
But by then, the work strike had set in.
Some time around 1589, Wanli stopped attending court audiences.
By the mid-1590s he had stopped reading most memorials.
By the early 1600s he had stopped filling vacant ministerial offices — when a senior official died or retired, the position simply went unfilled, sometimes for decades.
By the 1610s, large fractions of the regular bureaucracy were running on understaffed skeleton crews, with junior officials handling responsibilities they had no formal authority to discharge.

The provincial governorships were unevenly staffed; the central ministries had ministers who had not had formal interviews with the emperor in years; the Grand Secretariat was filled with officials whose appointments had never been formally confirmed.
The system continued to function, after a fashion, because the institutional infrastructure was substantial.
The Grand Canal still moved grain.
The provinces still collected taxes.
The provincial military commanders still defended their districts.
The regular bureaucracy still produced its ritual outputs.
But the central coordinating function that the throne was supposed to provide — the personnel decisions, the major policy choices, the responses to crises — was simply not being performed.
When the Imjin War broke out in Korea in 1592 (Chapter 6), the Ming response was organized by the few senior officials still functioning, with minimal direction from the throne.
When the Manchu confederation began consolidating in the northeast in the 1610s, the Ming response was similarly under-coordinated.
The dynasty was running on its institutional momentum, and the momentum was slowing visibly with each year that the throne refused to engage.
There is one perfect detail worth pausing on.

The Wanli Emperor's tomb at the Ming Tombs north of Beijing — the Dingling, the only Ming imperial tomb to have been excavated by modern archaeologists (it was opened in 1956–1958 in one of the most disastrous archaeological excavations of twentieth-century China, in which most of the recovered organic artifacts were destroyed by exposure before proper conservation methods could be applied) — contained the emperor's skeletal remains.

Forensic analysis showed that Wanli had been physically incapacitated for much of his later reign; one leg was significantly shorter than the other, probably due to a chronic condition that had developed in his middle age, and would have made walking and standing extremely painful.

Some modern historians have argued that part of the work strike was simple physical inability — the emperor was too ill to attend court ceremonies that required him to stand for hours in heavy ceremonial robes.

The story is more complicated than pure royal sulkiness; but it is also true that nothing prevented him from delegating, from receiving officials privately, or from filling vacant offices through written orders.
The work strike was substantially political in character, even if physical incapacity was a contributing factor.
The cultural and intellectual life of the late Ming, paradoxically, flourished during exactly the period of Wanli's withdrawal.
This is the chapter for one major late-Ming intellectual encounter: the arrival of the Jesuit mission to China, and particularly the figure of Matteo Ricci (mah-TEH-oh REE-chee).
The Catholic missionary order called the Society of Jesus had been founded by the Spanish soldier-mystic Ignatius of Loyola in 1540, in the wake of the Protestant Reformation.
The Jesuits became the spear point of Catholic missionary expansion across the early-modern world — to Brazil, to India under the Portuguese, to Japan, and (from the 1580s) to China.

The Jesuit missionary strategy was distinctive: rather than confronting the local culture, they would master it from inside — learn the language, adopt the local elite's clothing and manners, study the local intellectual traditions, and try to position Christianity as compatible with rather than opposed to local civilization.

The strategy was controversial within the Catholic Church (the Dominicans and Franciscans favored a more confrontational approach) and would eventually lead to the Rites Controversy that closed the China mission in the early eighteenth century.
But for over a century, it was the most sophisticated cross-cultural project in world history.
The Jesuit mission to China was founded in 1583 by Michele Ruggieri and Matteo Ricci, both of whom established themselves first in Macao and then at provincial Chinese cities in Guangdong.
Ricci would become the dominant figure of the early mission.
Born in 1552 in central Italy, trained at the Roman College in mathematics, astronomy, and theology, he arrived in China in 1582 at age thirty.

He spent twenty years studying classical Chinese — eventually achieving the rare feat of foreign mastery of the language to a level where he could write substantive treatises in classical Chinese — and adapting himself to Chinese elite culture.
By 1601 he had reached Beijing and was the first European granted permanent residence at the Ming court.
Ricci's approach was ingenious.
He dressed in the robes of a Confucian scholar (after initially trying Buddhist monastic robes, which had identified him with a religious tradition the Confucian elite generally looked down on).
He studied the Confucian classics deeply enough to argue Christian theology in their vocabulary.

He emphasized the points of compatibility — the Confucian heaven (Tian) as analogous to the Christian God, the Confucian ethics of family and ritual as compatible with Christian moral teaching — while quietly setting aside the points of conflict (the Confucian veneration of ancestors, which Catholic doctrine considered idolatrous, would become the issue that broke the mission a century later).

He used his European mathematical and scientific training as currency for cultural respect — translating Euclidean geometry into Chinese (the first six books of Euclid's Elements, translated with the Chinese scholar Xu Guangqi (shoo gwahng-CHEE) and published in 1607), demonstrating European-style world maps that displaced China from the center of the world (and were enormously controversial for that reason), discussing European astronomical methods that improved on Chinese calendrical calculations.
His Chinese-language treatises shaped the next two centuries of European understanding of China and Chinese understanding of Europe.

The True Meaning of the Lord of Heaven (Tianzhu Shiyi, 1603) was the most successful Christian apologetic ever written in Chinese, arguing for a monotheistic understanding of ultimate reality in vocabulary that drew on Confucian and Daoist precedent rather than rejecting them.
The Great Western Mnemonic introduced European memory technique to Chinese scholars.

The world map he drew at Beijing in 1602 (the Kunyu Wanguo Quantu, "Map of the Myriad Countries of the World") was the first European-style world map widely circulated in China and remained influential well into the Qing period.

Ricci was personally received by the Wanli Emperor (or at least granted formal court status, since the work-striking emperor probably never actually met him in person), given a residence in Beijing, allowed to build a small chapel, and integrated into the city's intellectual life.

He died in Beijing in 1610, was buried in a state-granted plot of land outside the city walls, and was succeeded by other Jesuits — including Adam Schall von Bell and Ferdinand Verbiest — who would continue the mission well into the Qing period and would eventually direct the imperial astronomical bureau.
The Jesuit mission was the most sophisticated cross-cultural intellectual encounter of the early-modern world.

It produced genuine European understanding of Chinese civilization (Ricci's De Christiana expeditione apud Sinas, published in Europe after his death, was the first detailed European description of Ming China based on extensive direct observation), and genuine Chinese understanding of European mathematical and scientific methods (the European astronomical techniques the Jesuits introduced were used to reform the Chinese calendar in the 1640s and remained the basis of imperial calendrics for the rest of the Qing).

It is also worth noting what it didn't produce: the Jesuit mission did not produce mass conversion in China the way the parallel Catholic mission produced in the Philippines and parts of South America.

The Jesuit converts in late Ming China numbered perhaps a few thousand, mostly drawn from the educated elite (including the senior Ming official Xu Guangqi, who was baptized in 1603 and translated Euclid with Ricci); the Chinese population at large remained almost entirely uninfluenced.
The mission was a high-cultural encounter, not a popular religious movement.

What the encounter shows, structurally, is that the late Ming intellectual elite was open to engagement with foreign ideas under the right circumstances — when the ideas came packaged with mathematical rigor, ritual respect, and a willingness to operate within Chinese cultural categories.

The same Ming culture that had abandoned Zheng He's voyages and turned inward against maritime engagement was simultaneously engaged in active intellectual exchange with European scholars at the imperial capital.

The myth of a Ming China sealed off from the world by the Haijin maritime ban needs to be balanced against the reality of Matteo Ricci writing in classical Chinese in Beijing while Spanish silver flowed in through Manila and Portuguese silk-and-silver shuttles connected Macao to Goa.
The late Ming was vastly more globally engaged than the official rhetoric of cultural self-sufficiency suggested.

Cross-civ check: the Wanli reign (1572–1620) was contemporary with the Spanish Habsburg apex under Philip II (the king who built the Escorial, dispatched the Armada in 1588, and presided over the Spanish silver economy that supplied so much of Wanli China's monetary base); with the Elizabethan and early Jacobean periods in England (Shakespeare's career runs almost exactly parallel to Wanli's reign); with the Mughal apex under Akbar and Jahangir in India; with the Ottoman classical age continuing under Murad III and Mehmed III; with the Tokugawa unification of Japan (Tokugawa Ieyasu defeated his rivals at Sekigahara in 1600 and established the shogunate in 1603); with Galileo's early career in Italy (his telescope observations began in 1609); with the Dutch revolt against Spanish rule that would establish the Dutch Republic.

Most strikingly, Wanli's reign was contemporary with Shah Abbas the Great in Safavid Iran (1588–1629, Safavid Persia Ch 4) — the two rulers presided over their respective empires at the same moment, both at the height of cultural achievement and commercial integration into the early-modern global economy.

Abbas's Isfahan and Wanli's Beijing were the two great Asian capitals of the early seventeenth century, both fully integrated into the global silver trade, both producing some of the most sophisticated cultural production of the early-modern world, and both presiding over institutional structures that would unravel within a few decades.

chapters.title: The Imjin War
sentences: In April 1592, the Japanese warlord Toyotomi Hideyoshi (toh-yoh-TOH-mee hee-deh-YO-shee) — the unifier of Japan after the Sengoku period of civil wars — landed an invasion army of 158,000 men at Busan on the southern coast of Korea.
His stated goal was nothing less than the conquest of Ming China, with Korea as the staging route.
The Korean army collapsed almost immediately.
The Korean capital at Seoul fell within three weeks.
The Japanese forces drove north and east across the peninsula, sacking Pyongyang in June and reaching the Yalu River — the Korean-Chinese frontier — by the autumn of 1592.
The Ming response was the largest military intervention of the late Ming period.

Wanli-era Beijing dispatched expeditionary armies that fought a seven-year war on Korean soil, kicking the Japanese out of most of Korea by 1593, fighting them to a standstill through five years of negotiation and renewed combat, and decisively breaking their final 1597 invasion.
The war ended in 1598 only because Hideyoshi died in Japan and the Japanese armies withdrew.
The Imjin War (named after the Korean lunar-calendar year of the invasion, imjin in Korean) is one of the largest pre-modern wars in East Asian history.
It killed perhaps two million people.
It devastated Korea so thoroughly that the country took most of the seventeenth century to recover.
It exhausted the Ming treasury at exactly the moment the Manchu confederation was rising in the northeast (Chapter 8).
And it demonstrated, in the cruelest way possible, how much the late Ming dynasty's military reach exceeded its institutional capacity to sustain that reach.
This is the chapter about the war itself, the strategic situation that produced it, and the consequences for all three states involved.
The strategic situation that produced the war began with the Japanese unification.
For most of the sixteenth century, Japan had been in the Sengoku (SEN-go-ku, "Warring States") period — a long civil war in which competing warlord families fought across the archipelago.
The unification was completed in three stages by three successive figures.
Oda Nobunaga (oh-da no-boo-NAH-gah) broke the back of the central rivals between the 1560s and his assassination in 1582.
Toyotomi Hideyoshi, his most effective lieutenant, completed the unification by 1590, defeating the last major rival families.

Tokugawa Ieyasu (toh-koo-GAH-wah ee-eh-YA-soo) would consolidate the unification after Hideyoshi's death in 1598, founding the Tokugawa shogunate that ruled Japan from 1603 to 1868 (Edo Japan covers this in detail).
Hideyoshi by 1591 had unified Japan but had a serious political problem.

The unification process had concentrated enormous military power in the hands of the great daimyo (regional lords) who had submitted to him, and those daimyo retained their armies and their territorial bases.
Hideyoshi could not safely demobilize them — they had nowhere to go and no other livelihood than warfare.
He needed an external war to keep his fractious vassals occupied.
He chose Korea as the route to his stated grand ambition, the conquest of Ming China.
The choice of Korea was militarily logical and politically catastrophic.

Korea was the obvious overland route to China — the Korean peninsula reaches almost to the Manchurian frontier — and it had been the bridge through which Chinese culture, Buddhist religion, and political institutions had reached Japan for over a millennium (Ancient Japan covers this in detail).

The Korean Joseon dynasty (founded 1392, contemporary with the Ming founding) was a Confucian-tradition state that maintained vassal-tributary relations with Ming China and was militarily weak; Hideyoshi assessed, accurately, that he could overrun Korea quickly.
What he assessed wrongly was the Ming response: he assumed Beijing would either ignore the Korean war or send a token force that he could brush aside.
In fact the Ming sent successive expeditionary armies that, however dysfunctional their internal organization, were large enough and persistent enough to fight the Japanese to a standstill.
The war divides into two distinct phases separated by an extended truce.
The first invasion (1592–1593) was the catastrophic Korean collapse and the partial Ming recovery.
Hideyoshi's army of 158,000 men, organized in nine divisions under his senior daimyo commanders, landed at Busan on April 13, 1592.

The Korean army was structurally unprepared: long peace under the Joseon dynasty had hollowed out the Korean military, and the Korean government had ignored repeated warnings from observant officials about Japanese rearmament.
Busan fell on the first day.
Seoul (then called Hanseong) fell on May 19.
The Korean court fled north to Pyongyang, then abandoned Pyongyang for the northern frontier town of Uiju on the Yalu, and from there sent desperate appeals to Beijing.
The Ming response was initially small.
A first relief force of 5,000 men was sent in July 1592 and was defeated at the second Battle of Pyongyang in September.
The Ming court then dispatched a much larger force of perhaps 43,000 troops under General Li Rusong (LEE roo-SONG), which arrived in Korea in late 1592 and recaptured Pyongyang in January 1593.
The Ming-Korean force then drove south and recaptured Seoul in April 1593.
By mid-1593 the Japanese had been pushed back to a defensive perimeter around Busan and the southern coast.

The first phase also produced what is, even in cold-blooded military-history terms, the most spectacular individual achievement of the war: the naval victories of the Korean admiral Yi Sun-sin (YEE soon-SHIN).
Yi Sun-sin commanded the Joseon navy from a base on the southern coast and conducted a series of engagements against the Japanese supply convoys between 1592 and 1598.

His ships included the famous geobukseon (geo-BOOK-son, "turtle ships") — armored Korean galleys with iron-spiked roofs to repel boarders, multiple cannons, and high freeboard for defensive standoff combat.
Yi's tactics emphasized concentrating his small fleet against fragments of the much larger Japanese supply effort, defeating each fragment in detail through superior firepower and discipline.

His victories at the Battles of Hansando (July 1592, in which his fleet of 56 ships destroyed a Japanese fleet of 73 ships using a crane-wing tactical formation) and Myeongnyang (October 1597, in which his fleet of 13 ships defeated a Japanese fleet of perhaps 333 ships in the strait between Jindo and the mainland through tactical exploitation of tidal currents) are studied in modern naval academies as classic examples of inferior force defeating superior force through tactical brilliance.
Yi Sun-sin's naval campaign was strategically decisive.
The Japanese ground forces in Korea depended on supply convoys from Japan; Yi's command of the Korean Strait disrupted those supply lines repeatedly.
The Japanese army could not be reinforced or resupplied at the rate it needed.
Combined with the Ming intervention on land, Yi's naval campaign forced Hideyoshi to accept a stalemate.
The truce period (1593–1597) lasted four years and was dominated by Sino-Japanese negotiation that produced no settlement.
The negotiations were one of the more comically dysfunctional diplomatic exchanges in pre-modern history.
Both sides were lying to their own governments about what the other side had agreed to.
The Ming negotiator Shen Weijing told the Beijing court that Hideyoshi had agreed to accept Ming suzerainty as a tributary king.
The Japanese negotiator Konishi Yukinaga told Hideyoshi that the Ming had agreed to send a Ming princess as Hideyoshi's bride and to recognize Japan as the dominant power in Korea.

When the actual Ming embassy arrived at Hideyoshi's court in 1596 carrying an imperial seal investing Hideyoshi as "King of Japan" — a formal grant of Ming tributary status, which was an enormous insult to a man who considered himself superior to the Ming emperor — Hideyoshi was furious.
The negotiations collapsed.
The Japanese launched the second invasion in 1597.
The second invasion (1597–1598) was less ambitious than the first — Hideyoshi's stated goal had narrowed from conquering China to securing the southern Korean provinces — but more brutal.

Japanese forces conducted systematic massacres in southern Korea, partly as deliberate policy to depopulate the area and partly as the retaliation of soldiers who knew the war was losing political support back home.

The famous Mound of Ears (Mimizuka) at Kyoto was assembled from the noses of perhaps 38,000 Korean and Chinese dead — Japanese commanders had been required to send back ear-or-nose proof of kills, since heads were too heavy to ship across the strait.
The Mound still stands today in Kyoto and is one of the most physically grim memorials of pre-modern East Asian warfare.
The Ming response was substantial.
Larger expeditionary forces were dispatched in 1597.
Major land battles were fought at Jiksan in September 1597 (Ming-Korean victory) and Sacheon in October 1598 (Japanese tactical victory but strategic stalemate).
Yi Sun-sin's naval victories continued.
The war ended on August 18, 1598, when Hideyoshi died in Japan of natural causes.
The succession Council of Five Regents he had appointed in his last months ordered the Japanese armies in Korea to withdraw.

The withdrawal was conducted in late 1598, with the last major Japanese forces fighting their way out at the Battle of Noryang in December 1598 — the battle in which Yi Sun-sin himself was killed, struck by a Japanese musket ball while pursuing the retreating fleet. (Yi Sun-sin's last reported words, as he refused to allow his death to be announced before the battle ended, were: "The battle is at its height — beat my drum and do not announce my death.") The Japanese forces withdrew.
The seven-year war was over.
The casualties were on a scale that requires sober accounting.

Korean deaths from the war and its associated famines and epidemics are estimated at roughly 1 million people, perhaps 20% of the pre-war Korean population — one of the worst per-capita demographic catastrophes of the early-modern period.
Chinese deaths from the Ming military campaigns were probably in the tens of thousands of soldiers, plus indeterminate numbers of civilian casualties in border provinces.
Japanese deaths in Korea were perhaps 200,000 across the seven years.
Total deaths probably reached 2 million.
The economic damage was equally severe.
Korea's productive capacity was devastated — entire provinces were depopulated, cultivated land returned to scrub, urban centers were burnt out.

The Korean government printing offices were destroyed and rebuilt; the Joseon dynasty that emerged from the war was structurally weakened in ways that persisted for generations (Joseon Korea covers the post-Imjin recovery and the consequences for Korean intellectual life).

Japan's losses included the political defeat of Hideyoshi's faction; the Toyotomi family was destroyed at the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600 by Tokugawa Ieyasu, who had stayed home from Korea and emerged with his army intact — partly because the Korean adventure had broken so many of his rivals.
The Tokugawa shogunate that would rule Japan for the next 250 years was the indirect beneficiary of the Imjin War's political wreckage of the Toyotomi camp.
The Ming consequences were the most consequential for the future of East Asia.
The treasury was effectively bankrupted by the war.

The standard estimate is that the Ming spent roughly 20 to 26 million ounces of silver on the campaigns — a substantial fraction of the entire annual silver tax revenue under the Single Whip system, accumulated as a war-debt that the late-Wanli treasury could not absorb.

The financial pressure forced cuts in other budgets at exactly the moment those budgets were needed: northern frontier defense was scaled back just as the Manchu confederation was beginning to consolidate (Chapter 8 covers Nurhaci's rise during exactly this period), provincial military maintenance was deferred, and the inadequately-paid soldiers of the late Ming weisuo system began to desert in large numbers.
There is a structural argument worth making about the connection between the Imjin War and the eventual Ming collapse.
The Manchus were not a force the Ming had to face down with superior resources to defeat; they were a force the Ming could have managed with a functional northern frontier policy.

The northern frontier policy depended on an adequately-funded and adequately-paid army, on attentive coordination with the Mongol tribal allies who served as buffer states, and on competent provincial military administration in Liaoning and Hebei.
The Imjin War destroyed all three.
The same silver that should have paid for the northern frontier defense was, instead, being shipped to Korea to pay for the war against Hideyoshi.
The same generals who should have been running the northern military commands were, instead, dying or being recalled for service in Korea.
