They were placed outside, on the mound slopes and around the base, forming a kind of ceremonial boundary or guardian ring.
Some kofun have hundreds of haniwa around their perimeters; the Daisen Kofun is estimated to have originally had as many as 30,000.
The haniwa are invaluable because they show us what Kofun-period people actually looked like — or at least how they wanted to be depicted.
Warriors wear armor made of riveted iron plates, carry swords and bows, and wear helmets with visors and cheek guards.
Horses are equipped with elaborate saddle gear, stirrups, bridles, and (sometimes) full body armor.
Women wear hairstyles and jewelry that suggest court fashion: long unbound hair, beaded necklaces, decorative robes.
The figures have simplified, almost cartoon-like faces — round eyes, straight noses, small slot mouths or no mouths at all — but their clothing and equipment are rendered in careful detail.

From the haniwa, we know that Kofun-period warriors used mounted combat (a major shift from the Yayoi period, when fighting had been infantry-based), that horses were armored, that court dress included elaborate headgear, and that the military equipment of the period was heavily influenced by Korean models.

Without the haniwa we would have almost no visual evidence at all for what Kofun-period Japanese society looked like, since Japanese painting and sculpture would not arrive until Buddhism did (Chapter 8).
That Korean influence runs deep through the entire Kofun period.
The Kofun era was a time of intense interaction between the Japanese archipelago and the Korean Peninsula.

Baekje (BEHK-jeh, one of the Three Kingdoms of Korea, occupying the southwestern part of the peninsula) was Yamato Japan's closest ally and most important source of continental technology — see Ancient Korea Ch 5 for the Korean side of this relationship.
Baekje princes were sometimes raised at the Yamato court as honored hostages-cum-students.
Baekje envoys carried specialized craftsmen, scholars, and eventually religious teachers across the strait to Japan.

Korean influence at the Yamato court was so pervasive that by the late Kofun period, perhaps a third of the aristocratic clans listed in later Japanese genealogies claimed Korean ancestry — either as recent immigrants who had risen to elite status, or as older lineages whose origins traced back to the early waves of toraijin (continental immigrants) discussed in Chapter 4.
The Gaya (GAH-yah) confederacy, a group of small polities on the southern tip of the Korean peninsula between Baekje and Silla, was another critical connection point.

Gaya produced some of the finest iron in East Asia, mined and worked from rich ore deposits along the southern Korean coast, and Gaya iron was exported to Japan in large quantities through the Kofun period.
Gaya served as a cultural and economic bridge between Yamato Japan and the broader Korean and Chinese world, with diplomatic ties to both Baekje and the Yamato court.
Japanese involvement in Gaya politics during this period is documented but contested.
The Nihon Shoki, compiled in 720 CE, claims that Yamato Japan established a colonial outpost in southern Korea called Mimana (mee-MAH-nah) in the late fourth century CE.

Most modern scholars, both Japanese and Korean, consider this claim significantly exaggerated — probably a later projection of imperial Japanese pretensions onto the Kofun era, possibly with some kernel of truth in the form of Yamato diplomatic and trading outposts in Gaya territory rather than actual political control.

The honest answer is that Japan and southern Korea were deeply interconnected through trade, migration, military alliance, and royal marriage during the Kofun period, in a relationship more complex than either later Japanese nationalist historiography (which exaggerated Japanese dominance) or later Korean nationalist historiography (which denied Japanese involvement) was willing to accept.
The horse-and-armor revolution of the fifth century is a particularly revealing case.
Before about 400 CE, there is no archaeological evidence for horses or mounted combat in Japan.

After about 400 CE, suddenly there are horses everywhere — horse bones in elite burials, horse haniwa around kofun mounds, horse trappings (saddle parts, bridle bits, stirrups) in grave goods, and the distinctive riveted iron-plate armor that goes with mounted combat.

This shift is dramatic enough that one mid-twentieth-century Japanese archaeologist, Egami Namio (EH-gah-mee NAH-mee-oh), proposed that fifth-century Japan had been conquered by a wave of mounted Korean warriors who imposed themselves as the new ruling elite — the so-called "horse-rider theory" of Yamato origins.
The horse-rider theory has fallen out of favor among modern scholars, who generally argue that the change reflects gradual cultural transfer and elite emulation rather than military conquest.

But the underlying observation is sound: Korean military technology rapidly transformed the Yamato war machine in the fifth century CE, and the resulting cavalry-based military elite was visibly different from anything that had existed in Japan before.
The political organization of Yamato Japan was built around two interlocking systems: the uji (OO-jee) and the be (BEH).
The uji were extended kinship groups — clans claiming common descent from a divine ancestor (a kami of a specific place, function, or natural feature).

Each major uji had a distinctive sphere of influence: the Mononobe (moh-NOH-noh-beh) clan controlled military and weapons production; the Nakatomi (nah-kah-TOH-mee) clan controlled court ritual and divination; the Otomo (oh-TOH-moh) clan controlled the imperial guards; the Soga (SOH-gah) clan controlled foreign trade and Korean immigrant labor; and the Yamato clan itself sat at the apex, claiming descent from the highest deity (Amaterasu) and exercising overlordship through marriage alliances and ritual centrality.

The uji structure was simultaneously a religious system (each clan was identified with a particular kami), a political system (clan leaders held hereditary court positions), and an economic system (each clan controlled specific resources and specialized labor).
The uji aristocracy was the actual government of late Kofun Japan, with the Yamato chief as first among many.

The be were occupational groups beneath the uji aristocracy — hereditary specialist communities of weavers, potters, scribes, smiths, salt-makers, fishermen, brewers, and dozens of other specialized crafts, attached to particular uji or directly to the royal court.

The be system organized the working population of Yamato Japan into functional categories: the kanuchi-be (KAH-noo-chee BEH) made metalwork; the tomo-be were palace attendants; the kinunui-be (kee-noo-NOO-ee BEH) wove silk; the ama-be were fishermen; and so on.

Many be were originally Korean immigrants whose specialized skills made them economically essential — a Baekje-trained smith brought to Japan to teach iron working would establish a smith-be, his descendants inheriting both the trade and the obligation to provide finished metalwork to their patron uji.
The be system was not slavery (be members were free in personal status), but it was strongly hereditary, tied to specific occupations and specific uji patrons, and limited in social mobility.
It was the early Japanese version of the kind of occupational caste organization that would emerge in various forms across pre-modern Eurasia.
Together, the uji-be system gave the Yamato court a workable structure for governing an island society without writing, without coinage, and without a centralized bureaucracy.
Authority flowed down through clan leaders to occupational specialists.
Goods and labor flowed up through the same channels.
Rituals at the royal court bound the aristocratic clans together.

It was a clan-federal system, not a centralized empire, and it would last in essentially this form until the centralizing reforms of the seventh century (Asuka-Nara Japan Ch 1) replaced it with a Chinese-style bureaucracy.

Cross-civ check: the Kofun period covered in this chapter (~250–500 CE) overlaps with the Three Kingdoms and Western Jin periods in China followed by the Northern and Southern Dynasties (Six Dynasties Ch 1–4), the Three Kingdoms period in Korea with Goguryeo, Baekje, and Silla as fully developed states (Ancient Korea Ch 5–6), the decline and fall of the Western Roman Empire (the official "fall" date is 476 CE, near the end of our period — Ancient Rome Ch 13), the rise and consolidation of the Sasanian Empire in Iran (Persian Empire Ch 10), the Gupta Empire's golden age in northern India (Gupta Empire Ch 1–3), the Maya Classic period in full swing in Mesoamerica (Maya Civilization Ch 3–4), and the Moche state at its height on the coast of Peru (Andean Kingdoms Ch 1–2).
The Kingdom of Kush in Nubia was in its later Meroitic phase (Kingdom of Kush Ch 5–6) and would shortly fall to Aksum.

The world that Yamato Japan was emerging into was a world of consolidating territorial states and post-imperial successor kingdoms, distributed across Eurasia and the Americas in roughly comparable patterns of political development.
Japan in 500 CE was a mid-sized agrarian state organized around a clan-federal court, monumental burial, and intensive ties to neighbors across a narrow sea.
The next two hundred years would transform it into something much more institutionally sophisticated.
The trigger for that transformation arrived in 538.

chapters.title: On the Threshold
sentences: In the 520s and 530s CE, Yamato Japan was on the edge of a transformation that nobody at the court could have fully anticipated.

This chapter is about that edge — the late Kofun period, the technological and political consolidation that was happening invisibly in the background, the decline of the great tomb-building tradition, the rise of the Soga clan to dominance at court, and the moment in 538 CE when a Korean envoy arrived at the Yamato court bearing a golden Buddha statue and a set of Buddhist sutras, ending Japanese prehistory in one diplomatic delivery.

Almost everything in the chapters that come after this one — the Asuka period, the Buddhist transformation, the Nara state, the Heian court, the samurai, the shogunate, the Meiji Restoration, modern Japan — runs forward from the events of this chapter.
We are at the very edge of the prehistoric era, and the world the Yamato court is about to step into is recognizably the historical Japan that the rest of Japanese history will be about.
The first thing happening on the threshold is the slow decline of the great kofun tradition.
Through the late fifth and early sixth centuries, Kofun construction in the Kinai heartland and the major regional centers became smaller, fewer, and less ambitious.

The enormous keyhole tombs of the early to mid fifth century — the Daisen Kofun, the Ojin Kofun, and dozens of other massive monuments built for early Yamato chiefs — gave way to more modest mounds in the late fifth and sixth centuries.

Provincial elite tombs continued to be built, sometimes in forms that imitated the Kinai keyhole shape and sometimes in distinctive local variations (square mounds, scalloped mounds, double-mounded forms).
But the trend was unmistakable: tombs were getting smaller, the labor mobilized for them was decreasing, and clan-mound competition was giving way to something else.
The "something else" was political consolidation.
As the Yamato court extended its authority more reliably over subordinate clans, the great families no longer needed to advertise their status through monumental tombs.
They could rely on their position at court, their hereditary uji rank, their relationships with the imperial line, and their economic role through the be system (Chapter 7).
The kofun had been built in the first place because the early Yamato confederation was an unstable competition among ambitious chiefs, each of whom needed visible monuments to assert his standing.
By the early sixth century, the political system was institutionalized enough that visible monuments mattered less.
The decline of the kofun is the archaeological signature of a maturing state.
Late kofun did continue, in reduced form, until the early seventh century CE — well past the chronological end of our narrative.
But the great heroic age of monumental tomb-building was over by around 550.
The next century would see a different kind of monumental architecture entirely: Buddhist temples.
The second thing happening on the threshold is the continued intensification of Korean technology transfer.

By 500 CE, sueki (SOO-eh-kee) stoneware had largely replaced the older softer earthenware Yayoi tradition for elite Japanese use. sueki was a hard, gray, high-fired stoneware made on the potter's wheel in reduction-fired kilns — technology that required specialized Korean craftsmen and that produced vessels far stronger and more durable than anything previous Japanese pottery had achieved.
The introduction of sueki around 450 CE, by Korean potters who established kiln complexes in central Japan, reshaped Japanese ceramics for the next several centuries.

The local earthenware traditions did not disappear entirely (older-style Hajiki ware continued to be used for everyday cooking and storage), but for any serious or prestige use, sueki became the standard.
The Japanese ceramic tradition would never again be without high-fired stoneware.
Iron production was the other major transfer.
Through the fifth century, Yamato Japan had depended heavily on imported Korean iron (mostly from Gaya — see Chapter 7).
By the late fifth and early sixth centuries, the Japanese were beginning to produce iron domestically using techniques learned from Korean smiths.

Bloomery furnaces (a type of iron-smelting furnace that produces a spongy lump of iron — a "bloom" — that can then be worked and forged) appeared in the Chugoku region of western Honshu, using local iron sand (satetsu, sah-TEH-tsoo) collected from riverbeds and beaches.

This was the beginning of the tatara (tah-TAH-rah) iron-smelting tradition that would persist as the technological foundation of Japanese metalwork through the medieval period and that would eventually produce the legendary swords of the samurai era.
By 538 CE, Japan had iron production capability of its own, breaking the dependence on Korean imports and enabling the rapid expansion of armored cavalry forces and iron tools across the country.

Other technology arrived alongside the metal and the pottery: improved horse breeding (with the introduction of larger Korean horse stocks alongside the smaller native breeds), silk-weaving (which had been present at small scale earlier but was now scaling up under Korean instruction), specialized woodworking techniques for elite construction, and more sophisticated agricultural tools and irrigation methods.

Korean immigrants — toraijin — continued to flow across the strait in significant numbers, settling especially in central Japan around the Yamato court, intermarrying with local elite families, and providing the specialized skilled labor that the increasingly complex Yamato state needed.
By the early sixth century, perhaps a third of the named aristocratic clans at the Yamato court claimed Korean ancestry, either recent or several generations back.
The Yamato court was simultaneously becoming more institutionally sophisticated and more demographically continental.
The third thing happening on the threshold is the emergence of historically secure imperial succession.

Through the third, fourth, and fifth centuries, the names of Japanese rulers come to us only through later mythological compilations (the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki, both compiled in the early eighth century — over two centuries after the events they describe), and the historicity of any given early emperor is uncertain.

The traditional list of emperors begins with Jimmu in 660 BCE (Chapter 7) and continues through fourteen named emperors before reaching anyone whose existence is generally considered probable rather than legendary.
Emperor Sujin (SOO-jin), traditionally the tenth emperor, is sometimes proposed as a possibly historical figure of the early to mid-fourth century CE.
Emperor Ojin (OH-jin), traditionally the fifteenth emperor, is usually associated with the Ojin Kofun and dated to the late fourth or early fifth century.
Emperor Nintoku, sixteenth in the traditional list, is associated with the Daisen Kofun.
But all of these identifications are more tradition than evidence.
We have no contemporary records of any of these rulers, and the chronology in the eighth-century chronicles is internally contradictory.

The first emperor whom most modern scholars consider historically secure — meaning his reign is reasonably well documented, his dates are reasonably reliable, and his existence is not in doubt — is Emperor Keitai (kay-TYE), who reigned from approximately 507 to 531 CE.
Keitai is interesting because his accession appears to break the previous imperial line.
According to the Nihon Shoki, the previous lineage had failed when Emperor Buretsu (BOO-reh-tsoo) died without an heir.

Court factions, after considerable difficulty, eventually selected Keitai — described in the chronicle as a fifth-generation descendant of Emperor Ojin and as a regional aristocrat from Echizen province (in central Honshu, well outside the Kinai heartland).

Modern scholars are skeptical of the genealogical claim that linked Keitai back to Ojin (it looks like a later interpolation to maintain the unbroken-line fiction); the more plausible reading is that Keitai was an outside warlord brought in by Yamato court factions to fill the throne after the previous lineage genuinely died out.
Whether or not he was actually descended from Ojin, his accession marks the moment Japanese imperial history starts to become verifiable rather than mythical.
The years immediately after Keitai were turbulent.

In 527 CE, a powerful chieftain named Iwai (EE-wai) in northern Kyushu rebelled against Yamato authority — possibly with backing from Silla, the Korean kingdom that was Baekje's rival and Yamato's enemy.

The Iwai rebellion took two years of difficult campaigning to crush, and the episode revealed how thin the Yamato grip on Kyushu still was, and how deeply local clans were entangled in Korean politics.
The Yamato court was a leading power on the Japanese archipelago, but it was not yet an unchallenged one.
The fourth thing happening on the threshold is the rise of the Soga clan.

The Soga (SOH-gah) clan, possibly of Korean immigrant descent (the question is debated — the Soga claimed descent from a legendary native ancestor, but several modern scholars argue for a Korean origin a few generations back), began their rise to power at the Yamato court in the early sixth century.
Their strategy was novel for Yamato Japan.
Rather than competing for traditional uji privileges (military command, ritual priesthood, palace guard duties), the Soga focused on controlling foreign trade and Korean immigrant labor.
They established themselves as the patrons of toraijin communities in the Kinai region, channeling continental skilled workers into Soga-managed estates and Soga-allied workshops.
They became the conduit through which continental wealth (silk, sueki ware, iron, gold, exotic luxury goods) flowed into the Yamato court economy.
This was a politically smart strategy.
The other major clans — the Mononobe, the Nakatomi, the Otomo — held the traditional power positions that had defined the early Yamato system.

The Soga held something newer and arguably more important: the relationship with the continental world that was the source of all the technology and prestige goods that the Yamato elite increasingly depended on.
As Korean immigration intensified through the early sixth century, Soga influence grew.
The Soga also used the standard aristocratic tactic of marrying their daughters to imperial princes, positioning themselves to produce future emperors with Soga grandfathers.

By the 530s, the Soga were one of the most powerful clans at the Yamato court, and they were positioning themselves to champion a new technology that was about to arrive from Baekje — a technology that would justify their ascendancy and break the older clans' grip on traditional ritual authority.
That technology was a religion.

In 538 CE — some sources say 552, with the discrepancy itself an artifact of the messy early Japanese historical record (the Nihon Shoki gives 552; the older Gangoji-engi monastery chronicle gives 538; modern scholars generally accept 538 as more reliable) — King Seong (SUNG) of Baekje sent a diplomatic gift to the Yamato court that would transform Japan more thoroughly than rice, bronze, iron, sueki ware, horses, or any of the other Korean technological imports that had reshaped the islands over the previous millennium.
He sent a golden Buddha statue and a set of Buddhist sutras.
This is the moment that ends Japanese prehistory.

The reasoning is simple: from 538 CE onward, Japan begins to participate in a literate religious-political world (the Buddhist East Asian sphere) that produces continuous written records on Japanese soil — temple chronicles, sutra copies, dedicatory inscriptions, eventually the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki and the early Buddhist commentaries written by Japanese monks.
The era of Chinese chronicles describing a foreign barbarian land called Wa is over.
The era of self-documented Japanese history begins.
Everything before 538 belongs to prehistory, in the strict sense that the Japanese themselves were not yet writing about themselves.
Everything after 538 belongs to history.
The gift itself was modest.

A small Buddha statue, made of gilt bronze (probably no more than a few feet tall, though the exact size is not recorded), and a set of Buddhist scriptures (sutras) — Mahayana texts in Chinese translation, the standard textual basis of East Asian Buddhism at the time.
The statue and the sutras were accompanied by a letter from King Seong recommending that the Yamato court adopt Buddhism.
The recommendation was not casual.

Baekje had its own reasons for promoting Buddhism in Japan: a Buddhist Yamato would be a stronger diplomatic and ideological ally for Buddhist Baekje against Buddhist Silla and Buddhist Goguryeo (the two other Korean kingdoms — see Ancient Korea Ch 6).

King Seong was making a religious-political offering at a moment when Baekje needed Yamato support against rival Korean powers, and the Buddha statue was the cover note on a strategic alliance proposal.
The arrival of Buddhism split the Yamato court into two warring factions.
Both factions were already there, and the Buddha statue gave them something new and important to fight about.
The Soga clan championed the new religion.
They saw Buddhism as a source of continental sophistication, magical power, and diplomatic advantage.
Buddhist temples were impressive.
Buddhist monks were literate and educated.
Adopting Buddhism would signal to China and Korea that Japan was a civilized state worthy of respect rather than a barbarian periphery.

And — more pragmatically — Buddhism was the religion of the Korean immigrant communities the Soga patronized, so Soga sponsorship of the Buddha statue would consolidate Soga authority over those communities and over the new ideological resources Buddhism brought with it.
The Mononobe and Nakatomi clans opposed it.

They were the custodians of Japan's indigenous spiritual tradition (what would later be called Shinto, SHIN-toh, "the way of the gods" — the venerable but at that point still largely unsystematized native cult of the kami, the spirits associated with natural features, ancestors, and clan deities).
The Mononobe and Nakatomi argued that adopting a foreign religion would anger the native gods and bring disaster on the Japanese islands.
This was not just a theological position.

It was also a self-interested one: the Mononobe and Nakatomi clans derived their hereditary court influence from their roles as guardians of the indigenous ritual system, and any major shift to a foreign religion threatened to undermine their institutional power base.
The dispute was settled not by theology but by politics and violence.
Initial responses to the Buddha statue were mixed: when a plague broke out shortly after the statue arrived, the Mononobe blamed the foreign religion and threw the statue into a canal.
When the plague persisted, the Soga retrieved it.

The conflict simmered for nearly fifty years, escalating through successive generations of court intrigue, until the Soga clan, backed by military force and by the increasingly Buddhist sympathies of the Yamato royal family, destroyed the Mononobe in battle in 587 CE and established themselves as the dominant power at court.
Buddhism was in.

The native Shinto tradition would not be displaced (it would coexist and eventually fuse with Buddhism in characteristically Japanese syncretic patterns), but the question of whether to adopt Buddhism at all had been settled definitively in the Soga's favor.

That long settling process — the Soga consolidation, the Buddhist establishment, the centralizing reforms that built a Chinese-style state on top of the older Yamato clan-federal foundation — is the subject of the next narrative in this series, Asuka-Nara Japan.
From 538 forward, the story has writers.
From 538 forward, the dates are reliable.
From 538 forward, the rulers have biographies and the institutions have charters and the buildings have dedicatory inscriptions.
The Yamato court that received the Buddha statue from King Seong was still essentially a prehistoric polity, organized around clan loyalty and divine ancestry.

The court that emerged from the next two centuries of Buddhist-influenced reform was something genuinely different: a Chinese-style imperial state, with a permanent capital, a written legal code, a state-sponsored Buddhist clergy, and a court culture that produced some of the most beautiful surviving art and literature of the early medieval world.
The boundary between prehistory and history is artificial.
The people of 537 CE did not know they were living in prehistory.
The people of 539 CE did not know they were living in history.
But for the purposes of telling the story, we have to put the line somewhere, and the arrival of the Buddha statue from Baekje is the cleanest single event that marks the transition.
Before it, Japanese sources do not exist.
After it, they accumulate.
Before it, we have to read about Japan through Chinese eyes.
After it, the Japanese begin to write about themselves.
A pause, before we close the book: the fourteen and a half millennia covered in this narrative are the deep substrate of everything Japanese.
The Jomon pottery tradition is still embedded in the Japanese aesthetic relationship to clay, to natural materials, to the marks of process visible on a finished object.

The Jomon-derived spiritual sense of the sacredness of natural features — particular trees, rocks, waterfalls, mountains — survives in Shinto and in the broader Japanese cultural attitude toward landscape.
The Yayoi rice-paddy economy is still the basis of Japanese rural life and of the cultural significance of rice as a sacred and central food.

The Yamato imperial line traces back, in its own self-understanding, to the Kofun-period Yamato chiefs who built the great keyhole tombs, and the modern Japanese emperor (the longest continuously reigning monarchical line in the world by a large margin) carries that lineage forward as a living institution.
The Korean immigration of the Yayoi and Kofun periods established a continental component in the Japanese gene pool and the Japanese aristocratic genealogy that has always been there since.
None of this means modern Japan is the Jomon, or the Yayoi, or the Kofun, in any direct way.

Modern Japan is also the product of two thousand years of further transformation: Buddhism, Chinese-style centralization, the medieval feudal system, the Tokugawa peace, the Meiji modernization, and the postwar rebuild.
But the substrate that all of those transformations were built on top of is the substrate this book has been about.
Pots, rice, and tombs.

The first pots fired by hunter-gatherers as the Ice Age ended; the first rice paddies dug by Korean immigrants on a Kyushu beach; the first keyhole tombs raised by ambitious Yamato chiefs on the plains of Kinai; and the gold-bronze Buddha statue that arrived in 538 to end one chapter of Japanese history and begin the next.

Cross-civ check: 538 CE, the year Buddhism arrived in Japan, is roughly the same year as the death of Emperor Justinian's general Belisarius's campaign against the Vandals in North Africa (Byzantine Empire Ch 4 territory), the late Six Dynasties period in China (Six Dynasties Ch 5–6) just before the Sui reunification, the height of the Three Kingdoms period in Korea with Baekje, Silla, and Goguryeo balancing each other (Ancient Korea Ch 6), the Gupta Empire's late phase in India (Gupta Empire Ch 4–5), the late Maya Classic in Mesoamerica (Maya Civilization Ch 4), and the post-Roman Germanic kingdoms across Western Europe.

Japan, in 538 CE, was joining a recognizably medieval world — a world of literate religious institutions, centralized monarchies, Buddhist or Christian or Hindu state cults, and continental commerce networks.
The prehistoric Japanese archipelago — the Jomon-Yayoi-Kofun world this book has described — was about to become the medieval Japan that the next narrative is about.

chapters.title: The Buddhist Crisis
sentences: In the year 538 CE — or possibly 552, the early Japanese chronicles disagree and the discrepancy itself is a clue to how confused the surviving record is — King Seong of Baekje (BEHK-jeh, the southwestern of the three Korean kingdoms then dividing the peninsula) sent a diplomatic gift to the Yamato (YAH-mah-toh) court in central Japan.
The gift was a small gilded bronze statue of the Buddha, a set of Buddhist sutras in Chinese, and a polite letter recommending the new religion to the Japanese court.
The court was at the time housed in a series of impermanent palaces in the Asuka (AHS-koo-kah) basin, a small valley in the hills south of modern Nara that gives this entire era its name.
What followed inside the Yamato court was one of the most consequential factional wars in Japanese history.
It lasted roughly fifty years, killed several court nobles, destroyed one of the great founding clans of the Japanese aristocracy, and decided whether Japan would become a Buddhist civilization.
But it was close.

The fight is worth dwelling on, because everything that happened afterward — the Tang-modeled bureaucracy, the great Nara temples, the Buddhist grip on imperial politics that would eventually drive the capital to Kyoto — flows directly from the Soga clan's victory at the Battle of Shigisen (shih-gee-SEN) in 587.

If the Mononobe had won that battle, the Yamato state would still have absorbed continental civilization (the pressure was enormous, the Korean immigrants were already arriving in waves, the writing system was unstoppable), but it would have done so on a different theological basis, with a different priesthood at the center, and very probably without the great state-Buddhist building program of the next two centuries.
This chapter is the story of how Japan became Buddhist.
To understand the dispute, you have to understand the state of things at the Yamato court in the early sixth century.

Japan in 538 was still a network of clan-based aristocratic households, knit loosely together by their common acknowledgment of the tenno (TEN-noh — the Yamato sovereign, "heavenly sovereign," though the title itself was almost certainly not yet in use and was applied retroactively by later chroniclers) and his ritual authority.

The previous era is called the Kofun period (KOH-fun, "old mounds") after the keyhole-shaped burial mounds the great clans built for their dead, some larger by surface area than the Great Pyramid at Giza (Prehistoric Japan Ch 3).

Power inside the Yamato federation was divided among a handful of uji (OO-jee) — extended aristocratic clans, each with its own hereditary specialization, its own protected lands, and its own claim on a slice of court ritual.
Three uji mattered most for the religious crisis: The Soga (SOH-gah) were administrators and finance specialists.
Their territory lay in the Asuka basin near the seat of the court itself.

Crucially, the Soga had married into and absorbed several immigrant lineages of toraijin (toh-RYE-jin, "people who came across") — Korean and Chinese specialists who had migrated into Japan over the previous centuries with skills the native Japanese wanted: writing, accountancy, metalwork, sericulture, and increasingly, Buddhism.
The Soga's connections to the continental immigrant communities meant they were the one great clan with a working knowledge of Buddhist practice before it arrived as a state question.
The Mononobe (mon-oh-NOH-beh) were the warrior clan.
Their hereditary specialization was military command and weapons production.
They were the closest thing the Yamato court had to a national army.
They were also, by tradition, deeply tied to the cult of certain Yamato war-gods whose shrines and rites they administered.
The Nakatomi (nah-kah-TOH-mee) were the priest clan.

Their hereditary specialization was the ritual service of the kami (KAH-mee — the Japanese word for the local spirit-deities of mountains, rivers, forests, ancestors, and natural forces, in what would later be systematized as Shinto, "the way of the gods").
The Nakatomi conducted the seasonal court rites, divined imperial questions, and performed the purification ceremonies that kept the divine balance between court and gods stable.
If you accepted Yamato religious authority, you implicitly accepted Nakatomi ritual expertise.
The Mononobe and the Nakatomi together represented the indigenous religious establishment.
The Soga represented the immigrant-influenced reform faction.
The Buddhist gift from Baekje became the issue around which the long-running tension among these three clans crystallized into open war.
The first Soga leader to take Buddhism seriously was Soga no Iname (SOH-gah noh ee-NAH-meh, lived c. 506–570).
When the Buddha image arrived from Baekje, the Yamato sovereign — Emperor Kinmei, by the traditional reckoning — convened his court to ask whether to accept the foreign deity.
Iname was enthusiastic.

He pointed out that Buddhism was the religion of the great civilized states (Baekje, the Korean kingdoms, the Chinese dynasties to the west) and that adopting it would put Japan on the same cultural footing.
The Mononobe leader and the Nakatomi leader both opposed accepting it.
Their argument was simple: the kami of Japan were the gods of this land and had always given victory to the Yamato court.
To worship a foreign god would be to insult the kami of Japan, who would punish such betrayal with disasters.
The compromise the court reached was characteristic and revealing.
Iname was permitted to enshrine the Buddha image as his own private devotion, in his own household, on his own land.
The court itself would not adopt the new religion.
The other clans would not be required to acknowledge it.
If something terrible happened, it would be Iname's fault and Iname's problem.
A plague broke out shortly afterward.
The Mononobe and Nakatomi went straight to the sovereign and announced that this was exactly what they had warned about — the kami were taking revenge for the foreign image.

With the court's grudging permission, they raided Iname's compound, threw the Buddha statue into the Naniwa (nah-NEE-wah — modern Osaka) canal, and burned down the small temple that Iname had built around it.
The plague did not stop.
The argument did not stop either.
The Buddha-into-the-canal episode happened more than once over the following decades.
Each time a plague or a famine or a bad harvest struck, the Mononobe-Nakatomi faction blamed the Buddhist deviation, raided the latest Soga shrine, and disposed of the latest Buddha image.
Each time the disasters continued anyway, the Soga retrieved a fresh image from Korea and started over.

By the time Iname died in 570, the Soga had built up a small Buddhist establishment in the Asuka basin (involving Korean monks, Korean-style architecture, and steadily growing influence) that they were prepared to defend by force.
Iname's son Soga no Umako (SOH-gah noh OO-mah-koh, c. 551–626) took up the religious cause and turned it into a military project.
Umako was, by the surviving evidence, one of the most politically capable figures in early Japanese history.

He spent his career consolidating Soga influence at court — installing Soga-friendly princes as crown prince, marrying Soga women into the imperial line, and building the institutional base that would eventually make him the de facto ruler of Japan for the four decades from 587 to his death in 626.
The Buddhist question and the political question were the same question.
Whoever won the religious war would dominate the court.
Umako intended to be that person.
In 585, another plague broke out.
The Mononobe leader Mononobe no Moriya (mon-oh-NOH-beh noh MOH-ree-yah) and the Nakatomi leader Nakatomi no Katsumi went to the sovereign yet again with the same complaint.
The sovereign yet again gave permission for an anti-Buddhist raid.
The Buddha images were destroyed, the temples burned, the nuns Umako had ordained as Japan's first Buddhist clergy were stripped naked and publicly flogged.
The plague did not stop.
This was the breaking point.

When the sovereign died in 587 (suspiciously soon, some chroniclers thought, after the latest cycle of religious violence), the question of who would succeed him became inseparable from the question of which clan would dominate the court.
Umako backed one prince.
Moriya backed another.
The two factions raised armies.
In the autumn of 587, Soga and Mononobe forces met at Shigisen in modern Nara Prefecture, near the Mononobe's home estates.
The battle was a rout.
Mononobe no Moriya was killed in the fighting, reportedly shot out of a tree where he had taken refuge as a vantage point.
The entire Mononobe leadership was destroyed.
The clan was broken up, its lands distributed among the victors, and its hereditary military role transferred to Soga clients.

The Nakatomi, who had been the Mononobe's allies in the religious war but had not committed military forces to the actual battle, survived as a clan but lost their political influence at court for the next sixty years.
Buddhism became, by default, the official religion of the Yamato court.

A famous scene from the Soga side of the battle: the young Prince Umayado (OO-mah-yah-doh, the future Prince Shotoku Taishi and the subject of Chapter 2), then about fourteen years old and serving in Umako's army as a junior commander, is said to have personally carved small wooden images of the four Buddhist guardian kings before the battle, vowing to build them a temple if the Soga won.

The temple — Shitenno-ji (shih-TEN-noh-JEE, "Temple of the Four Heavenly Kings") at modern Osaka — was duly founded after the victory and is still in operation today, though the original buildings were destroyed and rebuilt many times over the centuries.
The story may be partly legendary, but it captures the kind of vow-and-fulfillment cycle that early Japanese Buddhism ran on: pray for victory, win the battle, build the temple.
The Mononobe had bet on the kami.
The Soga had bet on the Buddha.
The Buddha won.
The aftermath of Shigisen reshaped Japanese religion permanently, but not in the way either side had expected.
The pattern that emerged after 587 was not the replacement of Shinto by Buddhism.
The kami did not lose their shrines.
The Nakatomi did not lose their priesthood (though they lost their political clout).
What happened instead was a uniquely Japanese accommodation that scholars later called shinbutsu-shugo (shin-BOO-tsoo SHOO-goh, "the merging of kami and buddhas").
Buddhist temples were built next to Shinto shrines, sometimes literally on the same compound.
The native kami were reinterpreted as Japanese local manifestations of Buddhist deities.
Buddhist monks performed rituals at Shinto shrines, and Shinto priests participated in Buddhist temple ceremonies.
The two traditions interpenetrated until they became, for ordinary Japanese, almost indistinguishable in practice.
This accommodation is genuinely unusual.

In most religious histories, when an organized world religion arrives in a region with a strong indigenous tradition, one of two things happens: either the new religion suppresses the old, or the old digests the new and produces a syncretic hybrid that the new religion's foreign authorities consider heretical.
Christianity in late-Roman Europe drove out the old gods (mostly) and demonized them.
Islam in conquered Iran tolerated Zoroastrians for a generation and then squeezed them down to a marginal minority over the following centuries (Persian Empire Ch 10).

The Buddhist arrival in Tibet in the seventh and eighth centuries fused with the local Bon religion in a contested process that took five hundred years and produced multiple incompatible Buddhist schools to unsort it.
Japan did something different.
Buddhism did not destroy the kami; it absorbed them and was absorbed by them.

The two traditions coexisted for the next thirteen centuries, until the early Meiji government in the 1870s forcibly separated them as part of its modernization program — itself a remarkable piece of religious engineering in the opposite direction.
From 587 to 1868, Japan was a country in which most people did not consider a Buddhist temple visit and a Shinto shrine visit to be acts of two different religions.
They were two complementary aspects of the same religious life.
This pattern starts here, in the immediate Soga aftermath.
Umako, who had just won a war over whether Buddhism would be permitted at all, did not ban the kami cults.
He installed Buddhist statues but did not demolish kami shrines.

The reason was probably political — the surviving anti-Buddhist factions were too important to alienate, and the kami-worshipping rural population was the entire labor base — but the political pragmatism produced a religious settlement that lasted longer than most pure religious settlements ever do.
Soga no Umako spent the years immediately after the Shigisen victory consolidating his political position.
In 587 he installed his nephew Hatsusebe on the throne as Emperor Sushun.
Sushun lasted five years before Umako had him assassinated in 592 (the chronicles say Umako found Sushun was no longer pliable enough).
In 593 Umako installed his own niece — Sushun's half-sister, who had been an empress consort to a previous emperor — as the new sovereign.
Her reign name was Suiko (soo-EE-koh), and she was the first reigning empress in Japanese history.
Suiko was the first of a remarkable series of Asuka-Nara empresses regnant.
Of the eight monarchs who reigned between 593 and 770, six were women, and a seventh (Junnin) was deposed by a woman.

This concentration of female rule has no equivalent in any other major monarchy of the period — Tang China would have only one female emperor in three centuries, and her reign was treated as an aberration by every later Chinese historian (Sui, Tang & Song China Ch 2).

The Asuka-Nara pattern was not aberrational: it was simply how the Yamato succession worked when a strong adult male candidate was unavailable, when the powerful clans needed a temporarily neutral figure on the throne, or when a regent (like Umako) needed a sovereign whose loyalty he could rely on.

Whether Suiko herself was the captive of her uncle or his active partner is a matter of debate — the chronicles, written later under Suiko's family, present her as an active and learned monarch, while modern historians have variously read her as a Soga puppet or as a strong figure in her own right.
The truth was probably both at different moments.
What is not in dispute is that Suiko's reign produced one of the most consequential political appointments in early Japanese history.
In 593 she made her nephew Prince Umayado — the same teenager who had vowed to build Shitenno-ji at Shigisen six years earlier, now twenty years old — the regent of her court.
He took up his post at the Asuka palace, opposite his great-uncle Soga no Umako.
The two of them, with Suiko presiding from the throne, would govern Japan for the next thirty years.
History remembers Prince Umayado by a posthumous title: Shotoku Taishi (SHOH-toh-koo TYE-shee, "Prince of Sagely Virtue").
His regency is the subject of Chapter 2.
A pause to anchor the international moment.
The arrival of Buddhism in Japan in 538 happened in a world that had been in motion for a long time.
The Buddha himself had lived around 480 BCE in northern India (Vedic Period Ch 7, Maurya Empire Ch 1) — the religion was already over a thousand years old when it reached the Yamato court.
The great propagator-king Ashoka of the Maurya dynasty (Maurya Empire Ch 5) had used Indian state machinery to spread Buddhism across south Asia in the third century BCE.
By the first century CE, missionary networks had carried Buddhism north through the Kushan Empire (Post-Maurya Kingdoms Ch 5) and along the Silk Road to Han Dynasty China (Han Dynasty Ch 6).
By the fourth century CE, it had reached the Three Kingdoms of Korea — Goguryeo accepted Buddhism in 372, Baekje in 384, Silla last and most reluctantly around 528 (Ancient Korea Ch 4–5).
And then, in 538, the Baekje statue arrived at the Yamato court.
The journey from the Bodhi tree at Bodh Gaya in northern India to a small valley in central Japan had taken roughly a thousand years and covered well over 3,000 miles (4,800 km).
Buddhism was the most successful intellectual export in Asian history.

Cross-civ check: while the Soga and Mononobe were fighting over Buddha statues in the Asuka basin, Justinian I was rebuilding the Hagia Sophia in Constantinople (537), the Sassanid Empire was at the height of its final century under Khosrow I (Persian Empire Ch 10), the Gupta Empire in India was already past its peak and the Gupta synthesis of mathematics-and-Sanskrit-and-Hindu-revival was diffusing across south Asia (Gupta Empire Ch 5–7), and on the Korean peninsula, Baekje, Silla, and Goguryeo were the three competing kingdoms whose shifting alliances shaped Japanese policy for the next century and a half (Ancient Korea Ch 4–7).
The Six Dynasties chaos in China was just then in its closing decades, with the brief Sui reunification in 581 about to remake East Asia (Sui, Tang & Song China Ch 1).
Buddhism was diffusing from India to Japan along a route that ran through every one of these civilizations.

The fact that Japan got it last, after Korea and China and Central Asia had each had centuries to digest and reshape it, meant Japan got a particular form: a fully developed, monastically organized, image-and-sutra-and-temple religion that came pre-packaged with Korean monks, Chinese architectural plans, and a millennium of accumulated theological argument.
Japan would spend the next two centuries figuring out which parts of the package it actually wanted.

chapters.title: Shotoku Taishi and Empress Suiko
sentences: The figure who dominates the early Asuka period is a young prince named Umayado — known to history as Shotoku Taishi (SHOH-toh-koo TYE-shee, "Prince of Sagely Virtue").
He was twenty years old when his aunt Empress Suiko (soo-EE-koh) made him regent of her court in 593.
He held that post for twenty-nine years, until his death in 622 at age forty-eight.

In those twenty-nine years he attempted, with mixed success, to remake the Yamato state into a centralized monarchy on the Chinese model — and along the way he founded a temple that still contains the oldest standing wooden buildings anywhere on Earth.
Shotoku is the closest thing Japan has to a founding father.

The cult that grew up around him after his death portrayed him as a saint, a Buddhist sage, a political prophet, a mystical figure who could read ten petitions simultaneously, who heard the cries of dying ascetics from miles away, and who composed his own funeral elegy at age six.
Modern historians spend much of their time peeling back this cult to find the historical man underneath, and the picture that emerges is more interesting than the legend.

The historical Shotoku was an ambitious, intellectually voracious, politically savvy regent who used his position as the favored nephew of both Empress Suiko and Soga no Umako to push reforms that neither his patroness nor his great-uncle could have pushed alone.
He failed, in important ways.
The Tang-style centralized state he envisioned was not built in his lifetime, and his own line was wiped out by the Soga within a generation of his death.
But the direction he set held.
Every major Japanese reform of the next century was built on Shotoku's program.
The court Shotoku inherited in 593 was small, rural, and impermanent.

The Yamato sovereigns moved their palace with each new reign — partly for ritual reasons (Shinto beliefs about death pollution made it taboo to remain in a building where the previous monarch had died) and partly because the court was small enough to relocate without enormous expense.
The new palace under Suiko was at Toyura (TOH-yoo-rah) and then Oharida (oh-hah-REE-dah) in the Asuka basin, a few miles from the previous court site.
The basin itself was a small valley running roughly north-south, bordered by low hills, with the Asuka River winding through it.
The total population of the Asuka court complex was probably in the low thousands.
By Tang Chinese standards, this was barely a provincial market town.
Shotoku had been to Korea (probably as a child or young man, accompanying diplomatic missions) and would have known how primitive the Yamato setup looked compared to a real continental capital.
His response was a sustained campaign of institutional borrowing.
In 603, Shotoku promulgated the Twelve Level Cap and Rank System (often shortened to Twelve Cap Ranks), Japan's first formal court rank system.
Twelve grades of rank, marked by colored caps that officials wore at court, replaced the older system in which rank attached to the clan rather than the person.

The colors were graded — purple at the top, then blue, red, yellow, white, and black, each in two shades — and were modeled directly on the Sui (SWAY) Chinese rank system that had been promulgated in the 580s (Sui, Tang & Song China Ch 1).
The point was to give the throne a tool for elevating talented officials regardless of their clan birth.
In practice, the great clans continued to dominate the high ranks for generations, but the principle had been established: rank was a personal possession, not a clan inheritance.

The seed planted in 603 would eventually grow, by the eighth century, into a court bureaucracy in which appointment depended on rank and rank depended (at least nominally) on individual qualification.
The next year, 604, Shotoku promulgated his most famous document: the Seventeen-Article Constitution.
The name is misleading.
It is not a constitution in the modern sense — it establishes no branches of government, defines no procedures, grants no individual rights, sets no limits on royal power.
What it is, instead, is a moral handbook for court officials, a hortatory document blending Buddhist ethics, Confucian hierarchy, and a pragmatic Japanese insistence on group harmony.

Article One reads: "Harmony is to be valued, and an avoidance of wanton opposition is to be honored." Article Two: "Sincerely revere the Three Treasures of Buddhism — the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha." Article Three: "When the imperial commands are received, they shall be scrupulously obeyed." Article Twelve: "Provincial authorities and district lords shall not levy exactions on the people." The document reads, in places, like a memo from a thoughtful CEO to a fractious management team — it earnestly tries to impose civil-service norms on a court that was used to clan feuding.
Whether Shotoku himself wrote the Constitution is debated.
The document survives only as quoted in the Nihon Shoki of 720 (Chapter 7), more than a century later.
Some modern scholars argue that the Constitution as we have it is in part an eighth-century composition projected backward onto Shotoku's era to give later reforms a venerable founding document.

The current scholarly reading is somewhere in between: Shotoku probably promulgated some version of a moral-political directive, and the eighth-century text we have is an elaboration and stylization of his original.
Either way, the Seventeen-Article Constitution is one of the foundational texts of East Asian political thought, and it has been the subject of continuous Japanese commentary for fourteen centuries.

The same year, Shotoku adopted the Chinese lunisolar calendar (the Yuanjia calendar that the Sui used), enabling for the first time a standardized system of timekeeping across the Yamato court — useful for agricultural planning, taxation, and bureaucratic record-keeping, all of which were starting to matter more than they had a generation earlier.
Shotoku's foreign policy was as ambitious as his domestic reforms.
In 607, he sent a diplomatic embassy to the Sui Chinese court under the diplomat Ono no Imoko (OH-noh noh ee-MOH-koh).

The embassy was the first formal Japanese mission to China in over a century, and it carried a letter from the Yamato sovereign to the Sui emperor that opened with a famous and politically explosive greeting: "From the Son of Heaven in the land where the sun rises, to the Son of Heaven in the land where the sun sets.
We hope you are well." The phrase translated as "Son of Heaven" is the Chinese term tianzi, the formal title of the Chinese emperor — the unique earthly representative of Heaven.
By Chinese diplomatic convention, no other ruler in the world was a Son of Heaven.
Korean kings, Central Asian khaganates, Indian rajas — all were vassals or barbarians, addressed in correspondence as inferiors.
To address the Chinese emperor as one Son of Heaven to another was a frontal challenge to the entire Sinocentric world order.
To call China "the land where the sun sets" while calling Japan "the land where the sun rises" added insult to the challenge.
Sui Emperor Yangdi (the second and last Sui emperor, the disastrous overreacher whose Korean wars would shortly destroy his dynasty — Sui, Tang & Song China Ch 1) was reportedly furious.
The chronicle says he ordered his foreign-relations officials never to bring such a letter to him again.
But he did not refuse the embassy.
He accepted Ono no Imoko's gifts, sent a Chinese diplomat back with him, and the channel was opened.

The Yamato court's claim to be a peer of the Chinese empire was, of course, ludicrous on a power-arithmetic level — Sui had a population of around 50 million people and an army that had just (605–611) built the Grand Canal with five million conscripts, while Yamato had a population of perhaps 5 million and a court that lived in wooden palaces it relocated every reign.
But the diplomatic gesture mattered.

It established the principle that would define Japanese foreign relations forever after: Japan would borrow Chinese culture intensively but would not formally subordinate itself to Chinese suzerainty.
Korean kingdoms, which were physically connected to China and could be invaded overland, accepted vassal status and tribute relations.
Japan, sitting on islands a hundred miles offshore, could afford to be impudent.

Ono no Imoko's 607 mission was followed by a continuous stream of kentoshi ("envoys to Tang") — though when the Sui collapsed in 618 and was replaced by the Tang, the Japanese embassies simply switched targets.

Over the next two and a half centuries, Japan would send roughly twenty official missions to the Chinese court, some carrying hundreds of monks, scholars, and officials on dangerous voyages across the East China Sea.
The embassies were the central conduit by which Tang Chinese institutional models, Buddhist learning, art, technology, and material culture flowed into Japan.
They were also enormously expensive and lethally risky: ships sank, embassies were lost, returning students arrived decades later having forgotten which emperor was on the Yamato throne.

But the program continued for as long as the Tang was visibly a model worth copying. (We will meet the embassies several more times — Chapters 6 and 8 in particular.) Shotoku's most enduring physical legacy is a temple complex called Horyu-ji (hor-YOO-jee, "Temple of the Flourishing Dharma"), founded in 607 in the village of Ikaruga, a few miles north of the Asuka basin.
Horyu-ji is a remarkable place for several reasons.
First, it contains the oldest surviving wooden buildings anywhere on Earth.

The main hall (the Kondo) and the five-story pagoda at Horyu-ji have been standing in their current form since the late seventh century — making them roughly 1,300 years old. (There is a small archaeological complication here: the original 607 buildings burned down in a fire in 670, and the surviving structures are a careful reconstruction completed by around 711, using the same Korean-derived techniques.

Some of the timbers in the central pillar of the pagoda, however, have been radiocarbon-dated to around 594 — meaning at least some original wood was reused in the reconstruction, and parts of the pagoda may genuinely date to Shotoku's era.) Either way, no other wooden buildings in human history have stood for so long.

The cypress timbers used in the construction have proven remarkably resistant to rot, fire, and insect damage; the joinery techniques have absorbed earthquake stress that would shatter rigid stone construction; and continuous Buddhist patronage has paid for the periodic refurbishment that any wooden building requires.
Second, Horyu-ji's architectural style is a frozen snapshot of late Sui–early Tang Chinese building practice, transmitted via Baekje.

The deep eaves, the brackets that fan out from the column tops to support the roof load (called tokyo in Japanese), the use of stone podiums and wooden columns, and the layout of the temple compound all derive directly from continental models that have not survived in their original Chinese or Korean forms.
To see what a major early Chinese Buddhist temple looked like, you go to Horyu-ji.
The Chinese originals burned down centuries ago.

Third, the pagoda contains a structural innovation that Japanese carpenters would refine over the next millennium: a central pillar (the shinbashira, shin-BAH-shih-rah) that runs the full height of the structure but is not load-bearing.

Rather than supporting the floors and roof above it, the central pillar hangs from the top of the pagoda, swinging slightly as the building moves, while the actual structural load is carried by the surrounding columns.
The pillar acts as a kind of pendulum that absorbs earthquake stress by oscillating out of phase with the floors.

Whether the original seventh-century carpenters fully understood the engineering is unclear — some modern scholars argue the design was originally just symbolic, with the structural benefits noticed and refined later — but the result is real: Japanese pagodas almost never fall in earthquakes, even at scales (60-meter pagodas) that would seem catastrophically vulnerable.
Modern engineers have compared the design to a passive tuned mass damper, the kind of pendulum suspended in skyscrapers like Taipei 101 to absorb wind and seismic loads.
The comparison is retrospective, not a deliberate engineering choice, but striking.
Horyu-ji is not the only temple Shotoku founded.

He is also credited with Shitenno-ji in modern Osaka (the temple he vowed at Shigisen, Chapter 1, much rebuilt and now in a 1960s reinforced-concrete reconstruction), and his patronage helped the Soga clan complete Asuka-dera (also called Hoko-ji), Japan's first true Buddhist temple complex, which was finished in 596 with Korean architects from Baekje.
The bronze Asuka Daibutsu inside Asuka-dera, cast around 609 by the sculptor Tori Busshi (TOH-ree BOO-shee — grandson of a Korean immigrant), is the oldest surviving Japanese Buddhist statue.
Shotoku died in 622 at age forty-eight.
His mother and his consort died within months of him; the cluster of deaths in the same family at the same time was probably an epidemic but produced lasting suspicions of poisoning.
Whatever the cause, Shotoku's death cut short his reform program before it could institutionalize itself.
His son Prince Yamashiro no Oe inherited his father's temples and his father's faction at court but did not have his father's combination of imperial blood, political favor, and personal capability.
Within twenty years, the Yamashiro line would be wiped out by the Soga (Chapter 3).
The cult of Shotoku as a near-Buddhist saint began almost immediately after his death.
By the 660s, only forty years on, the chroniclers were attributing supernatural deeds to him.
By the eighth century he had become a quasi-bodhisattva, the embodiment of Japanese Buddhist learning, the first translator of the great Mahayana sutras into Japanese commentary.

The Hokke-ji nuns in Nara claimed the prince had personally written commentaries on the Lotus Sutra, the Vimalakirti Sutra, and the Shrimala Sutra — the so-called Three Sutra Commentaries, traditionally attributed to Shotoku himself.

Modern scholars are skeptical of the attribution (the linguistic evidence in the surviving texts is mixed, and the standard scholarly reading is that they were composed in the late seventh century by court Buddhist scholars in Shotoku's name), but the tradition itself testifies to the cultural weight Shotoku came to carry.
His face appeared on the 10,000-yen note from 1958 to 1986 — for a generation the most-reproduced image in Japanese history.
He has been depicted in countless paintings, sculptures, anime, manga, dramas, and elementary-school textbooks.
The Japanese imagine him roughly the way Americans imagine the founding fathers, with the same mixture of reverence, partisan reinterpretation, and selective memory.

The historical Shotoku was a real person, ambitious and intellectually serious, who pushed the Yamato court several decades further down the road toward bureaucratic centralization than it would have gone without him.
He did not finish the project — that would take another century — but he set the direction so unmistakably that everything that followed could be presented as completing his work.

Cross-civ check: while Shotoku was promulgating the Seventeen-Article Constitution and sending letters to Sui Yangdi addressing him as an equal, Justinian had been dead for forty years and the Byzantine Empire was sliding into the catastrophic Persian and then Arab wars that would shortly halve its territory (Byzantine Empire Ch 5).

The Sassanid Empire under Khosrow II was at the height of its power, about to conquer Egypt and besiege Constantinople in the 610s — and about to be destroyed by the Arab armies of the new Islamic faith in the 630s (Persian Empire Ch 10, Umayyad Caliphate Ch 1).

The prophet Muhammad was a young man in Mecca during Shotoku's regency, beginning his career as a merchant and preparing the religious career that would begin in 610 — within a few years of Horyu-ji's founding.
The world that Shotoku addressed as "the land where the sun sets" was about to be remade in ways that no one in 607 could have anticipated.
By the time Shotoku's grandnephew presided over the Taika Reform forty years later (Chapter 3), the Sassanid Empire would no longer exist.

A structural parallel worth pausing on: Shotoku's reforms — a young royal-family member promulgating a moral-political code, building monumental religious architecture, claiming a kind of equality with the dominant continental empire of the day — bear a remarkable resemblance to the program of Emperor Justinian the previous century.
Both were trying to import the institutional model of a more sophisticated neighbor (Roman tradition for Justinian, Tang China for Shotoku) into a culturally distinct local setting.

Both built a great religious building that was meant to demonstrate the new order in stone (Hagia Sophia for Justinian, Horyu-ji for Shotoku — though Horyu-ji is wood, with a different relationship to permanence).
Both worked through a strong female imperial figure (Empress Theodora for Justinian, Empress Suiko for Shotoku) whose actual role in policy is debated by modern historians.

And both ran out of time before their reform projects could be fully institutionalized — Justinian's reconquests collapsed within a century, Shotoku's centralizing program had to be re-launched in 645 (Chapter 3).
The comparison is not exact (Shotoku was a regent, not a sovereign; Justinian inherited a more developed state).
But the resemblance suggests something general about how middle-rank powers absorb the institutional templates of their dominant neighbors.
Japan and Byzantium were doing structurally similar things at the same historical moment, on opposite ends of Eurasia, in mutual ignorance.

chapters.title: The Coup of 645 and the Taika Reform
sentences: For sixty years after the Battle of Shigisen, the Soga clan had run the Yamato court.
Soga no Umako had been the de facto regent under Empress Suiko (Chapters 1 and 2).
After his death in 626, his son Soga no Emishi (eh-MEE-shee) inherited the position, and after Emishi, his grandson Soga no Iruka (ee-ROO-kah).
By 645, the Soga were not just dominant at court — they had become arrogant in a way that earlier Japanese aristocrats had been careful to avoid.
The signature of Soga overreach was Iruka's destruction of the Shotoku family.
In 643, Iruka sent troops to the Ikaruga estate of Prince Yamashiro no Oe (yah-mah-SHEE-roh noh OH-eh), Shotoku Taishi's son and a possible candidate for the throne.
Yamashiro and his entire household — wives, children, retainers — chose suicide over capture, hanging themselves inside the Horyu-ji compound.
The chronicles describe the scene in mournful detail: a great prince of Buddhist learning, the son of a saint, exterminated with his whole line, in the temple his father had built.

Even allowing for the chronicles' partisan editing (they were written under the regime that had just overthrown the Soga, with every motive to blacken Iruka's reputation), the basic facts are not seriously disputed.
Iruka had decided that no rival imperial line could be allowed to survive.
The Soga grandchildren of Empress Suiko's line were the only acceptable claimants.
This was a miscalculation.
Even the Yamato aristocracy, which had a high tolerance for political violence, considered the destruction of Shotoku's family an outrage.
The temples Shotoku had founded were national institutions.
The Buddhist establishment owed the prince's memory a debt that no Soga purge could erase.
And other princes of the imperial line — including some who were themselves part Soga — began to fear that Iruka would come for them next.
The leading edge of the resistance was a young prince named Naka no Oe (NAH-kah noh OH-eh), grandson of Empress Suiko's predecessor Bidatsu and a candidate for the throne in his own right.
He was around twenty years old, ambitious, and dangerous in the way Iruka had failed to appreciate.
He found his political partner in a court noble of the Nakatomi clan — the same clan that had backed the Mononobe in the 587 religious war and had been politically marginal ever since.

The Nakatomi heir was named Nakatomi no Kamatari (nah-kah-TOH-mee noh kah-mah-TAH-ree), about ten years older than Naka no Oe, brilliant, embittered by his clan's exclusion from real power, and reportedly the man with the actual coup plan in his head.

The two princes met, the chronicles say, at a kemari game (a kind of ceremonial kickball played at court — the standard upper-class social activity of the period) in 644, where Kamatari fetched Naka no Oe's lost shoe and the two of them began their careful conversations about how to remove Iruka.
Whether the kemari-game origin story is true or romanticized, the conspiracy was real.
By the spring of 645, they had a plan.
The opportunity came on July 10, 645 (in the modern Western calendar; the chronicles give the date in Japanese ritual reckoning).

A formal court ceremony was scheduled at Empress Kogyoku's palace at Asuka, at which envoys from the three Korean kingdoms — Baekje, Silla, and Goguryeo — would present tribute to the Yamato sovereign.
Soga no Iruka, as the dominant figure at court, was expected to attend in his full regalia.
The ceremony would draw all the senior nobles into a single hall on a single afternoon.
Naka no Oe and Kamatari intended to make sure Iruka did not leave it alive.
The attack went badly at first.
The two assassins Naka no Oe had stationed in the wings froze at the sight of Iruka and the assembled nobility.
Naka no Oe himself had to leap forward and personally cut Iruka down with a sword, in front of his stunned mother the empress, while the Korean envoys watched.
Iruka, badly wounded, reportedly crawled toward Empress Kogyoku and asked what crime he had committed; she fled the hall without answering.
He died on the floor of the audience chamber.

The next day, Iruka's father Soga no Emishi, who had retreated to the family compound at Asuka with his retainers, set fire to his own mansion and committed suicide rather than face the loyal Naka no Oe troops marching on his estate.

The compound burned, and a number of irreplaceable historical records — the chronicles say the Tenno-ki ("Records of the Sovereigns") and the Kokki ("National Records") that Shotoku Taishi and Soga no Umako had compiled together in the 620s — were destroyed in the flames. (The episode is one reason eighth-century historians had to reconstruct so much: the records the seventh-century court had assembled were ash.) The remaining Soga were rounded up and either executed or stripped of their offices over the following weeks.
The clan that had dominated Yamato politics for sixty years was wiped out in a long weekend.
This event is called the Isshi Incident (ISH-shee), after the name of the year in the traditional Chinese sexagenary cycle.
It is the most famous palace coup in early Japanese history, and it is the hinge that turns the Asuka period from its first half — the Soga era — into its second half, the era of Tang-modeled reform.
Empress Kogyoku, who had presided in shock over the assassination of her chief minister, abdicated within days.
Her brother took the throne as Emperor Kotoku (KOH-toh-koo).

The real power in the new regime was Naka no Oe, who declined the throne for himself (he was technically still a prince, not directly the heir, and taking the throne immediately after a violent coup would have looked too much like a Soga-style usurpation) but became Crown Prince and effective ruler.
Nakatomi no Kamatari was made the new Inner Minister, the senior advisor at court.
The two of them — the warrior prince and the bureaucratic minister — began work on the reform program that would define the next decade.
The first symbolic act was a calendar change.
The new regime adopted Japan's first reign-name (a Chinese-style era designation that subsequent emperors would use to mark major regnal moments) and called it Taika (TYE-kah, "Great Change").
The era name announced the political program in two syllables: this was not a continuation of the old order, this was a great change, on the Tang Chinese model.
Every reform that followed in the next four years was promulgated under the banner of "Taika," and the whole program is collectively known as the Taika Reform.
The second symbolic act was a capital move.

Naka no Oe and Kotoku abandoned the Asuka basin — too closely associated with the Soga, too rural, too cramped — and moved the court to Naniwa-kyo (modern Osaka), on the coast where the Yodo River meets Osaka Bay.
The new capital was laid out for the first time in Japanese history on a Tang-style north-south grid, with a great palace called the Naniwa Nagara-Toyosaki Palace at the head of a central avenue.

Nothing of the architectural scale survived (the palace burned down later in the century and modern Osaka has been built and rebuilt over the site many times), but the gridded urban plan was the first signal that the new regime intended to copy continental city planning along with continental institutions.
In the first month of the Taika era — January 646 — Emperor Kotoku promulgated the Taika Edicts.
The edicts are the most ambitious single piece of legislation in early Japanese history.
They proposed, in four articles, a wholesale restructuring of the Japanese state on the Tang model.
Article One abolished private ownership of land and private subjects (the be, BAY — hereditary servant-lineages attached to particular clans).
All land was to revert to the throne.
All cultivators were to become subjects of the central state.
The economic basis of clan power was to be liquidated.
Article Two reorganized the country into a system of provinces (kuni, KOO-nee), districts (gun, GOON), and townships (ri, REE), each governed by an officer appointed from the center.
The chaotic patchwork of clan territories was to be replaced with a Tang-style provincial bureaucracy.
Provincial governors and district magistrates would report through a chain of command running back to the imperial palace.
Article Three ordered the compilation of population registers (koseki, KOH-seh-kee) and tax registers, on which the new central tax system would be based.
Each adult in the realm was to be enrolled, and taxes would be levied on the basis of the registers, not on the basis of clan obligations.

Article Four replaced the older clan-based labor and tribute system with a uniform tax in rice (a fixed percentage of the harvest from each adult cultivator's allocated land), a tax in cloth and other products, and a labor obligation (so many days per year of corvée work for the central government).
The system was modeled on the Tang equal-field (juntian) system that Wen and Taizong of Sui-Tang had perfected to support their massive bureaucracies and armies (Sui, Tang & Song China Ch 1–2).
This was, on paper, a revolution.

It proposed to turn Japan from a clan-federation patched together by ritual obligations into a centralized empire on the Chinese model — with all land state-owned, all cultivators state-registered, all officials state-appointed, all taxes state-collected.
In practice, the reforms were only partially implemented.

The powerful clans — even after the Soga purge, there were several other great clans whose cooperation the throne could not do without — resisted the abolition of private land in their own territories.

The bureaucratic apparatus needed to actually run a Tang-style state did not yet exist; it had to be built up over the following half-century, official by official, register by register, province by province.

The 646 Edicts were less an instruction set that could be executed in the short term and more a manifesto: a statement of what the reformers thought Japan ought to look like in fifty or a hundred years.
Some of the proposed reforms (universal tax registration, the provincial-district system) eventually happened, by the early eighth century.

Others (true central ownership of all land) never fully happened — the Tang system itself broke down in China within a couple of centuries (Sui, Tang & Song China Ch 4), and Japan never built the institutional muscle to keep its own version intact.
But the direction had been set.
From 645 onward, the Yamato court was committed to becoming a Tang-style state.
Every subsequent law code (the Omi Code, the Asuka Kiyomihara Code, the Taiho Code — Chapters 4 and 5) pushed further down the road.
Every subsequent capital was built more aggressively on the Tang model.
Every subsequent generation of officials was trained on Confucian classics and Chinese legal precedent.
The 645 coup turned the country onto a track that it would stay on for a century and a half.

A crucial side-effect of the 645 coup was the elevation of Nakatomi no Kamatari, who had been a minor noble of a marginalized clan and who in the next twenty years became the most powerful courtier in Japan.
Kamatari served as Inner Minister to three emperors.
He drafted laws, advised on Korean policy, ran the censure courts, and built up a clientele of officials who owed their careers to him personally.

On his deathbed in 669, he was visited by Naka no Oe (by then on the throne as Emperor Tenji), who granted him a new family name as the highest possible reward for a lifetime of service: Fujiwara (foo-jee-WAH-rah), after the wisteria-flowered estates where Kamatari had lived.
The new clan was Kamatari's own line and his son's line; the rest of the Nakatomi remained Nakatomi.
This is the founding of the Fujiwara clan, which would dominate Japanese court politics for the next four centuries.
Every regent of the Heian period (Heian Japan Ch 1–3), every great Heian poet, every emperor's mother for most of the next four hundred years, would be a Fujiwara.

Kamatari's son Fujiwara no Fuhito (FOO-hee-toh, 659–720) would architect the Nara-period legal codes (Chapter 5), marry his daughters into the imperial line in three different generations, and build the political machine his descendants would inherit.
The Fujiwara were what the Soga had failed to be: a clan that controlled the throne not by murdering imperial princes but by marrying them.
The Fujiwara strategy was elegant, durable, and almost impossible to dislodge from below.
In 660, in the middle of the post-Taika reform period, an event on the Korean peninsula changed everything.

The kingdom of Baekje, Japan's closest ally on the continent and the cultural conduit through which Buddhism, writing, and most of the toraijin specialists had flowed for the previous century, was destroyed by a coalition of Tang Chinese armies and Korean Silla (SIL-la) forces.

The Tang general Su Dingfang led a 130,000-man invasion fleet across the Yellow Sea; the Silla king committed his own armies overland from the south; Baekje's smaller forces could not hold against a two-front war.
The Baekje capital Sabi fell within months.
The Baekje king was taken to the Tang court as a captive.
The kingdom was carved up between Tang occupation forces and Silla allies (Ancient Korea Ch 6).
For the Yamato court, Baekje's destruction was a strategic catastrophe and an emotional crisis.

Baekje was the kingdom that had sent the Buddha statue, whose royal family had intermarried with Yamato princes for generations, whose specialists had been arriving in Japan in steady waves for nearly two centuries.
To lose Baekje was to lose the closest thing the Yamato court had to a continental cousin.
And it raised the immediate prospect that Tang and Silla, now allied and victorious, would turn next to Japan itself.

The Baekje resistance held out in the southwest of the peninsula for three years after the fall of Sabi, led by Baekje generals who escaped the initial Tang sweep, and a Baekje prince fled to the Yamato court asking for help in reclaiming his throne.
