Naka no Oe — by 661 effectively running the Yamato state on behalf of the now-elderly Empress Saimei (who was Empress Kogyoku reigning under a new name after her abdicated brother Kotoku had died) — decided to intervene.
The decision was momentous and, in retrospect, mistaken.

The Yamato court committed an enormous expedition: an estimated 800 ships and 40,000 men, the largest military force Japan had ever assembled, sent across the Korea Strait to reinforce the Baekje resistance and contest the Tang-Silla occupation.
In August 663, the Yamato fleet met the Tang and Silla naval forces at the mouth of the Geum River, on the Korean west coast.
The battle is called Baekgang (BEHK-gahng — "White River," the Korean name for the Geum estuary).
It was a disaster.
Tang naval doctrine was vastly more sophisticated than anything Japan had experience with.
Tang ships were larger, more heavily built, and crewed with professional naval troops.
Tang fire-arrow tactics could ignite an opposing fleet at standoff range.
Tang formation discipline allowed concentrated boarding actions where Yamato ships were forced into single combats.
Over two days of fighting, the Tang and Silla forces destroyed roughly 400 Japanese ships (half of the entire fleet) by ramming, burning, or boarding.
Yamato casualties were enormous — possibly 10,000 dead, most of them drowned.
The surviving Yamato ships fled south down the coast and back to Japan with the remnants of the Baekje resistance.
The Baekje resistance collapsed within months.
Baekgang is one of the most consequential battles in Japanese history.
Its three major effects: First, Japanese military ambitions on the continent ended for nearly a thousand years.
From 663 until Toyotomi Hideyoshi's invasions of Korea in the 1590s (Edo Japan Ch 1), no Japanese government attempted to project military power onto the Korean peninsula.

The geographic logic — Japan could be defended by the sea, but offensive operations into Korea required a fleet that could decisively beat whatever continental power was paying attention — held throughout the medieval and early-modern periods.
The Yamato lesson was learned: stay home, build the islands, defend the coasts, do not try to fight Tang armies on Tang terms.
Second, Naka no Oe ordered the construction of a chain of defensive fortifications across northern Kyushu against a possible Tang counter-invasion.
The most famous was the Mizuki (MEE-zoo-kee, "water castle"), a long earthwork dike with a moat that ran across the narrow neck of land protecting the inland Dazaifu administrative center.

A network of mountain fortresses (yamashiro, yah-mah-SHEE-roh) was thrown up on key passes, with Korean Baekje refugee engineers — fleeing into Japan in the wake of their kingdom's destruction — providing the construction expertise.
Tang never invaded.

By the 670s the threat had dissipated, as Tang and Silla turned on each other in the post-conquest carve-up of Korea (Ancient Korea Ch 7) and as Tang's attention pivoted to the Tibetan Empire on its western frontier.
But the fortresses had been built, the construction labor had been mobilized, and the Yamato court had its first taste of what large-scale military mobilization actually cost.
Third, the destruction of Baekje produced a refugee wave that profoundly accelerated Japan's cultural development.
Tens of thousands of Baekje aristocrats, scholars, monks, architects, metalworkers, and military officers fled the conquered kingdom and were welcomed in Japan.
Many were given lands in central Honshu, granted court ranks, and absorbed into the Yamato aristocracy.
Their descendants would shape Japanese cultural production for generations.
The kingdom that had been Japan's mentor was gone; many of its best people now lived in Japan.
A pause to reflect on Baekgang's broader significance.
The defeat at Baekgang was the moment Japanese sovereignty became, by default, an island sovereignty.

Korea, China, and the steppe powers fought their wars over the same Eurasian landmass, with the same rules: armies marched across borders, sieges took down capitals, dynasties replaced each other through conquest.
Japan, after 663, was defended by its sea moat.
No foreign army would land on the Japanese islands again until the Mongol invasions of 1274 and 1281 (Mongol Empire Ch 8) — over six centuries of continental immunity.
This is one of the foundational facts of Japanese history.
Japan had the option, in a way that Korea or Persia or Hungary did not, to choose what it borrowed from abroad and at what pace, because the choice was never enforced by an invading army.
Naka no Oe finally took the throne himself in 661 after Empress Saimei died, and reigned as Emperor Tenji (TEN-jee) until 672.

His reign concentrated on the post-Baekgang reconstruction: defensive fortifications, the Omi Code of 668 (Japan's first comprehensive legal code, intermediate between the Taika Edicts and the later Asuka Kiyomihara Code — no copy survives, but later sources reference it heavily), the first comprehensive household and population register of central Japan (the Kogo-nenjaku of 670, taking over a year to compile and registering perhaps 5 million subjects), and the relocation of the capital from Naniwa to a new palace at Otsu on Lake Biwa, near modern Kyoto, in 667.
Tenji died in 672 after a reign of eleven years.
The succession dispute that followed was the largest civil war of the entire Asuka period: the Jinshin War.
That, and the late-Asuka regime that came out of it, are the subject of Chapter 4.

Cross-civ check: the 645 Isshi Incident was contemporary with the early Rashidun Caliphate in the Arab world — Caliph Umar had just been assassinated in 644, Uthman was in the early years of his reign, the explosive Arab conquests of Persia and Byzantine Egypt and the Levant were under way (Persian Empire Ch 10, Byzantine Empire Ch 5, Umayyad Caliphate Ch 1).

The Sassanid Empire of Persia, the dominant power of western Asia for four centuries, was destroyed between 636 and 651 — exactly the years Naka no Oe was building his Tang-modeled state in the Yamato court.
The world was being remade in two directions at once.

In the Tang Chinese capital of Chang'an, Emperor Taizong was at the height of the Zhenguan era (Sui, Tang & Song China Ch 2), governing the largest, wealthiest, most cosmopolitan empire on Earth and providing the model the Yamato reformers were trying to copy.
The contrast Naka no Oe could draw on was vivid: Tang power was real, Sassanid power was suddenly nothing, and the difference was institutional.
Centralized states with bureaucracies and standing armies could mobilize resources and absorb shocks; clan federations and nomadic confederations could not.
The Taika Edicts were partly a response to this geopolitical lesson.
A direct comparison: the Taika Reform (646) and the Tang Code of 624 were almost exactly contemporary attempts to codify Sui-derived bureaucratic models into operational law.

Tang Taizong's Zhenguan reforms in China — equal-field land system, civil service examinations, the cap-and-rank bureaucracy — are the direct model for what Naka no Oe and Kamatari were attempting to build in Japan two decades later.
Tang Taizong was twenty years older than Naka no Oe and had taken power through a similarly bloody palace coup (the Xuanwu Gate Incident of 626 — Sui, Tang & Song China Ch 2).
Both rulers used a coup-and-reform sequence to reshape their states: a dramatic seizure of power followed by an aggressive program of institutional modernization.
Taizong's reforms succeeded more thoroughly, partly because Tang inherited a far more developed bureaucratic substrate to build on.
Naka no Oe's reforms were more aspirational, partly because Japan had no comparable substrate.
But the model was the same, and the trajectory both regimes set their countries on lasted for centuries.

chapters.title: The Hakuho Era and the Jinshin War
sentences: The thirty years between Baekgang in 663 and the move to Fujiwara-kyo in 694 are a transitional moment in Japanese history.
Politically, they cover the late reign of Emperor Tenji, the largest civil war in early Japanese history, and the long consolidating reign of Tenji's brother Tenmu and Tenmu's widow Empress Jito.

Culturally, they are called the Hakuho period (hah-koo-HOH, "white phoenix"), a name applied retrospectively by twentieth-century art historians to distinguish the late-Asuka decades from the earlier Soga-era Asuka and the later Nara periods.

The Hakuho is best known for a particular style of Buddhist sculpture — fuller, more lifelike, more naturalistic figures than the angular early-Asuka work — but it is also the moment Japan stopped imitating Korean Buddhist art and started absorbing direct Tang influences brought back by Yamato monks who had spent years studying in Chang'an.

The political story of the Hakuho is the story of how the imperial line consolidated its authority after Baekgang, weathered a violent succession crisis, and emerged with the centralized power it had been trying to build since the Taika Edicts twenty years earlier.
Emperor Tenji, the former Naka no Oe and the architect of the 645 coup, finally died in late 671 after a reign that had been spent reconstructing from the Baekgang disaster.
His death immediately produced a succession crisis.
Tenji had a younger brother named Prince Oama (OH-ah-mah), who had served as Crown Prince during much of his brother's reign and was the conventionally expected heir.
He had also fathered, late in life, a son named Prince Otomo (OH-toh-moh) by a relatively low-ranking consort.

As Tenji aged, he had become increasingly favorable to making his own son Otomo the successor, even though Otomo was younger, had less experience, and lacked the network of allies that Oama had built up over decades.
Tenji formally elevated Otomo to a position of high authority in late 671, signaling — without actually changing the nominal succession — that he wanted his son rather than his brother to inherit.
Oama, sensing what was coming, did something dramatic.

He renounced all claims on the throne, shaved his head as a Buddhist monk, and retired to Yoshino (yoh-SHEE-noh), a remote mountainous region south of Asuka, where he announced his intention to spend the rest of his life in religious meditation.

The chronicles describe this as a strategic move: by making himself look completely uninterested in politics, Oama bought time and reduced the suspicion that Tenji's deathbed faction had been gathering against him.

As soon as Tenji died, however, Oama began secretly assembling allies among the eastern aristocracy — especially the warrior families of the Mino-Owari region (modern central Honshu, between Nagoya and Lake Biwa), who had grievances against the Otomo faction and who controlled key passes leading from the eastern provinces toward the capital.
In the summer of 672, Oama left Yoshino with a small party of loyal retainers and rode east into the mountains.

Within weeks, he had assembled an army of perhaps 30,000 men, marched on the Otsu capital where the Otomo faction was concentrated, and defeated his nephew's larger but less coordinated forces in a series of battles around Lake Biwa.
The decisive engagement came at the Battle of Seta, where Oama's eastern coalition broke through Otomo's defensive line on the Seta Bridge and routed his army.
Otomo, surrounded and defeated, hanged himself rather than surrender.
Tenji's son was dead, and Oama took the throne as Emperor Tenmu (TEN-moo).
This was the Jinshin War (JIN-shin, again named after the year in the sexagenary cycle).
It lasted only about a month of active fighting but mobilized larger armies and produced more casualties than any other event of the Asuka period.
Several thousand men died in the battles.
Many of Otomo's senior supporters were executed in the aftermath.

The Yamato court, which prided itself on its civilized refinement, had just gone through a violent and bloody civil war between an uncle and a nephew, both of whom were direct grandchildren of imperial mothers.
The war's lasting effect was the consolidation of imperial authority.

Tenmu — who was already an experienced political operator with a clear reform program — used his victory to break the political power of any clan that had supported Otomo, redistribute their lands and offices among his own loyalists, and centralize court rituals and decision-making in the imperial palace to a degree that no previous Yamato sovereign had attempted.
The Soga had fallen in 645.
The pro-Otomo faction fell in 672.

The two great post-Shotoku reform moments produced the same result: a court whose dominant figure was the emperor, surrounded by reform-minded officials who owed their positions directly to the throne, with the great hereditary clans permanently weakened relative to imperial authority.
Emperor Tenmu's fourteen-year reign (672–686) is when many of the institutions of the next two centuries were either invented or formalized.
He formalized the title tenno (TEN-noh — "heavenly sovereign").
Earlier sovereigns had been called by various titles, including okimi (great king) and sumera-mikoto (a Japanese sacred title roughly meaning "divine sovereign").
Tenmu adopted tenno as the official designation, with explicit reference to the Daoist concept of the heavenly emperor and the Tang Chinese imperial title huangdi.
The name change was a theological claim: the Yamato sovereign was not just the head of the senior aristocratic clan, he was a heavenly figure with cosmic significance.

From Tenmu onward, Japanese monarchs are conventionally called tenno, and the Western convention of translating this as "emperor" persists today (despite the technical implications — there was never an actual Japanese empire in the sense of a multi-ethnic conquered territory governed by the tenno).
He commissioned the writing of national histories.

Tenmu, troubled by the burning of the Tenno-ki and Kokki at the Soga compound in 645 (Chapter 3) and by the absence of any organized Yamato historical record, summoned the court reciter Hieda no Are (hee-EH-dah noh ah-REH) — said by the chronicles to have had a perfect memory and the ability to recite long oral compositions verbatim — and instructed Are to memorize a complete narrative of Yamato dynastic history from the age of the gods down to Tenmu's own day, integrating the surviving fragments of older records, oral traditions, court genealogies, and ritual chants.
The recitation, when finally written down decades later, became the Kojiki (Chapter 7).
Tenmu also commissioned a parallel historical project, written in classical Chinese for foreign-policy use, which would eventually become the Nihon Shoki (Chapter 7).

Both works were national histories on the Chinese model — official documents written by court committees under imperial direction — designed to legitimize the Yamato dynasty by tracing it back to the gods themselves.
The Kojiki begins with the creation of the world; the Nihon Shoki begins with the same creation.
Both then trace the imperial line through gods, demigods, semi-mythical heroes, and finally historically attested rulers, until the line reaches Tenmu's own court.

The traditional date of the founding of the imperial line — 660 BCE under the legendary Emperor Jimmu — was almost certainly calculated by the Tenmu-era chroniclers to align with Chinese astrological cycles, projecting an imperial pedigree backward by more than a thousand years to make the Yamato line look at least as old as China's.
He decreed a new legal code, the Asuka Kiyomihara Code (AHS-koo-kah kee-yoh-mee-HAH-rah).
The code was drafted under Tenmu but promulgated under his successor Empress Jito in 689.

It was the first Japanese legal code with the structural division — borrowed from Tang practice — between ritsu (criminal law, with prescribed penalties for specific offenses) and ryo (administrative regulations, governing the operation of the bureaucracy).
This ritsu/ryo split would become the structural template for the great Taiho Code of 701 (Chapter 5) and the Yoro Code of 718 — the operational legal framework of Japan for the next thousand years.
No copy of the Asuka Kiyomihara Code survives, but its provisions are reconstructable from later citation.
He elevated state Buddhism while strengthening the Shinto (SHIN-toh) cult of the imperial line.
Tenmu was an enthusiastic Buddhist patron — he founded the Yakushi-ji temple ("Medicine Buddha temple") in 680, vowing to build it if his wife (the future Empress Jito) recovered from illness.
She did, the temple was built, and Yakushi-ji became one of the great Asuka-Hakuho-era temples (it was relocated to Nara in 718; only its East Pagoda survives in original form).

Simultaneously, Tenmu massively expanded imperial patronage of the Ise Shrine (the great Shinto shrine on the eastern coast of Honshu, sacred to the sun goddess Amaterasu — ah-mah-teh-RAH-soo — whom the Yamato sovereigns claimed as their divine ancestor).

He instituted a regular cycle of imperial offerings at Ise, codified the rituals of imperial succession (which involved, and still involve, ceremonial visits to Amaterasu's shrine), and established the principle that one of the Yamato princesses would be sent to Ise as the Saio (sah-EE-oh), a vestal-like figure who served as the high priestess of Amaterasu's cult.
The Saio system would continue for over six centuries.
Tenmu's religious project was both/and, not either/or: state Buddhism and state Shinto, expanded simultaneously, both subordinated to imperial authority.
This is a continuation of the shinbutsu-shugo accommodation that had emerged after Shigisen (Chapter 1), now operationalized at the highest level of state policy.
Tenmu died in 686.

The succession then passed, after a brief interregnum during which a designated crown prince was forced to commit suicide on plausible-but-trumped-up charges of conspiracy, to Tenmu's widow, Empress Jito (jee-TOH).
Jito's reign (formally 690–697) finished her late husband's reform program.
She promulgated the Asuka Kiyomihara Code in 689.
She maintained the Tenmu-era policy of imperial centralization.
She held the dynasty steady until her grandson — the future Emperor Mommu, Tenmu and Jito's grandson by their daughter — was old enough to inherit.
And she made the most consequential single decision of the late Asuka period: she moved the capital to a new, permanent, Tang-modeled grid city.
The new capital was called Fujiwara-kyo (foo-jee-WAH-rah KYOH), built on the southern edge of the Asuka basin starting around 690 and occupied from 694 onward.

It is named after the Fujiwara clan estates the city was built near, not after the Fujiwara as occupants — the clan would not move its main house to the new capital until the Heijo-kyo era (Chapter 5).
Fujiwara-kyo was the first Japanese city laid out as a permanent capital with a comprehensive grid plan, on a scale that committed the state to lasting more than a single reign.

It covered roughly 4 square miles (10 km²), with the imperial palace at the geometric center (an unusual placement — Tang Chang'an had its palace at the north end), wide north-south avenues, walled residential wards, and two great markets to the east and west.
Three monarchs ruled from Fujiwara-kyo — Jito, her grandson Mommu, and Mommu's mother Empress Genmei — over roughly sixteen years.
Fujiwara-kyo did not last.

By the early eighth century, the imperial court had decided that the city's design was flawed (the central-palace placement created drainage and traffic problems), that the site was too far from the Yodo River trade arteries, and that a fresh start was needed.
In 710, Empress Genmei moved the capital again, this time to Heijo-kyo (hay-JOH-kyoh — modern Nara), in a basin a few miles north (Chapter 5).
Fujiwara-kyo was abandoned within a year of the move.
Today the site is a quiet rice-field landscape with archaeological reconstructions of the palace foundation marked out for visitors.
But Fujiwara-kyo had set the principle.
From 694 onward, the Japanese capital would be a permanent planned city, not a relocatable palace, and the design would be based on Tang grid models.
This is the moment Japan stopped being a country of itinerant courts and became a country of fixed imperial cities.
The Hakuho-era cultural production deserves a brief note before the chapter closes.
The Hakuho style of Buddhist sculpture, named after the late-Asuka decades from 645 to 710, shows the absorption of direct Tang and Korean Unified Silla artistic influences.
Earlier Asuka sculpture (Tori Busshi's work for Asuka-dera and Horyu-ji, Chapter 2) had been visibly Korean Baekje in style — angular faces, archaic smiles, frontal pose, long thin bodies.
Hakuho figures are fuller, with more naturalistic body proportions, gentler facial expressions, and more relaxed postures.

The bronze Yakushi Triad at Yakushi-ji, completed in the late seventh century, is the most famous example: three figures (the Medicine Buddha flanked by two attending bodhisattvas) in lifelike poses, with detailed jewelry and flowing robes that suggest fabric weight rather than abstract decoration.

The shift parallels what had happened in Tang China between the early and high Tang: a movement away from the abstract spiritual style of the immediately post-Buddhist-arrival centuries toward a more naturalistic aesthetic that would peak in the eighth century.
Japan, importing the new style from China within a generation of its development there, was for the first time in artistic synch with the continental mainstream rather than a generation behind.
Hakuho-era scholars and monks also became central to Japanese intellectual life.

Kakinomoto no Hitomaro (kah-kee-NOH-moh-toh noh hee-toh-MAH-roh, active around 680–710), the greatest Japanese poet of the early period and the central figure of the Manyoshu poetry anthology (Chapter 7), wrote his elegies on dead empresses and his court occasion poems during the late Hakuho.
The poet Yamabe no Akahito (yah-mah-BEH noh ah-kah-HEE-toh) was a contemporary.

The court was now actively producing literature in Japanese (using the awkward Chinese-character-as-phonetic system that would later be called man'yogana, Chapter 7), not just consuming Korean and Chinese imports.
The Hakuho is the moment Japanese culture starts producing its own art, in its own language, while still drawing intensively on continental models.
By the end of Empress Jito's reign in 697, the Yamato state had come a long way from the Asuka basin clan-federation of a century earlier.
It had a centralized bureaucracy on the Tang model (still being elaborated, but functional).
It had a permanent grid capital.
It had a written legal code (the Asuka Kiyomihara Code), and a more comprehensive code in preparation (the Taiho Code of 701, Chapter 5).
It had a state Buddhist establishment with a network of temples scattered across central Honshu.
It had a state Shinto establishment with the Ise Shrine as its imperial center.
It had two national histories in compilation.
It had defensive fortifications across northern Kyushu.
It had a strengthened sense, after Baekgang, that its job was to consolidate the islands rather than project power onto the continent.
What it was missing, still, was scale.
The capital was small.
The bureaucracy was small.
The Buddhist establishment was small.
The next phase of Asuka-Nara development would be the scaling-up.
The Taiho Code of 701 codified the Tang-modeled state at full operational detail.
The move to Heijo-kyo in 710 built a city large enough to house a real metropolitan court.
And the great Nara-period building program, culminating in the casting of the Daibutsu in 752, would put Japan's state Buddhism on the same monumental scale as anything in Tang China.
That story is the next two chapters.
Cross-civ check: the Jinshin War of 672 happened in a remarkable global moment.

The Umayyad Caliphate was just then beginning its rapid eastward and westward expansion — by 711, the Umayyads would conquer Spain, and within Tenmu's lifetime they would push Arab armies as far east as the Hindu Kush (Umayyad Caliphate Ch 1–4).
The Tang dynasty was midway between Taizong's reforms and Wu Zetian's reign as Empress (Sui, Tang & Song China Ch 2), still expanding, still the cultural and military hegemon of East Asia.
Unified Silla in Korea, having expelled Tang armies from the peninsula in 676, was beginning the golden age that would last for the next two centuries (Ancient Korea Ch 7).

The Byzantine Empire under the Heraclian dynasty had survived the catastrophic Arab and Persian wars of the early seventh century and was stabilizing on a smaller territorial base centered on Anatolia (Byzantine Empire Ch 6).
And in the Americas, Teotihuacan had collapsed around 600 (Teotihuacan Ch 8) but its successor cultures were thriving, and the Maya Classic Period was at full flower (Maya Civilization Ch 5–6).

The world Tenmu and Jito built their reformed state in was a connected one — at least in fits and starts, through the Silk Road, through Korean intermediaries, through the periodic kentoshi missions to Tang.

Japan's centralizing reforms were one piece of a larger pattern of state-formation across Eurasia in the seventh and eighth centuries, in which a number of polities were simultaneously consolidating under Tang-, Arab-, or Byzantine-influenced bureaucratic models.

chapters.title: Building the Capital
sentences: By the year 700, the Yamato court had been talking about being a Tang-style state for two generations.
The Taika Edicts of 646 had laid out the program (Chapter 3).
Tenmu and Jito had elaborated and partly implemented it (Chapter 4).
The Asuka Kiyomihara Code of 689 had codified the bureaucratic structure.
The Fujiwara-kyo capital had built the first permanent grid city.

What was still needed was the operational machinery: a comprehensive legal code that would make the system work day-to-day, a coinage that would let the state collect taxes in money rather than only in rice and cloth, and — most consequentially — a capital city large and durable enough to project the image of a real continental empire.
The first decade of the eighth century delivered all three.

This chapter covers the short window from 694 to roughly 720 — the Fujiwara-kyo experiment, the great Taiho Code of 701, the first official Japanese coinage in 708, and the founding of Heijo-kyo (Nara) in 710 that gives the next eighty years their name.
The Taiho Code of 701 (TYE-hoh, named after the Taiho era, "Great Treasure," in which it was promulgated) was the first comprehensive Japanese legal code on the full Tang model.

It superseded the Asuka Kiyomihara Code of 689 (Chapter 4) by elaborating it in operational detail across both halves of the ritsu/ryo split — the criminal code (ritsu, eleven volumes prescribing penalties for specific offenses) and the administrative regulations (ryo, eleven volumes governing every aspect of how the bureaucracy was supposed to function).
The drafting committee was led by Fujiwara no Fuhito (FOO-hee-toh, 659–720) — Kamatari's son, the second-generation Fujiwara, the architect of Nara-era institutional design.
Fuhito had spent his career studying Tang law and Tang governance, and the Taiho Code reflects his depth of understanding.

The administrative ryo sections cover the full Tang-modeled bureaucracy: a council of state at the top (the Daijokan, dye-JOH-kahn — Council of State) with the Daijo-daijin (Grand Minister) at its head; eight ministries below it (Personnel, Treasury, Civil Affairs, Imperial Household, Ceremonies, Justice, Military, and Popular Affairs), each with subordinate bureaus; a parallel Department of Worship (the Jingikan, jin-GEE-kahn) responsible for state Shinto rites; an investigation-and-censorship bureau; a national university; and a province-district-township structure extending the central bureaucracy out to the rural population.
The Taiho Code's land system was the handen-shuju (hahn-DEN SHOO-joo, "field allocation and revocation") system, adapted from the Tang equal-field system (Sui, Tang & Song China Ch 2).

Every six years, the population would be re-registered and farmland would be allocated: each adult male received about 2 tan (roughly 0.6 acres) of irrigated rice paddy, each adult female received 2/3 of that, and slaves received fractional allotments depending on category.

In return, each adult male owed a fixed grain tax (the so, SOH — typically about 3% of the rice harvest from his allocated land), a tax in textiles or local products (the cho, CHOH), labor service (the yo, YOH — typically ten days per year, often commuted to extra cloth payments), and military service in a part-time conscript army (the gundan system).
Land reverted to the state on the holder's death and was reallocated.
The system kept the peasantry tied to the land, kept the tax base broad, and (in theory) kept the army supplied with men.

The Taiho Code is the document that turned Japan into what historians call a ritsuryo state (rits-RYOH, "codes-and-regulations state") — a polity organized around a comprehensive written legal code on the Tang model, with a centralized bureaucracy, a registered taxpaying population, and an explicit hierarchy of court ranks.

Every later piece of pre-modern Japanese law — the Yoro Code of 718 (a polished revision of Taiho, formally promulgated in 757), the various supplementary regulations issued through the Heian period, even fragments cited in court rulings as late as the Edo period — derived from the structural framework set down in 701.
In practice, the ritsuryo system never worked as fully as its drafters had envisioned.

The handen-shuju land registration was supposed to be redone every six years; in reality, the great bureaucratic effort required to do it right meant that re-registrations slipped to once a decade, then once a generation, and by the late Heian era had effectively stopped.

The aristocratic estates and the Buddhist temple landholdings quietly carved off chunks of the registered tax base into legal exemptions called shoen (SHOH-en — manorial estates outside the regular tax system), which by the Heian period would consume most of Japan's productive farmland (Heian Japan Ch 2).
The conscript army system burned out within fifty years against the Emishi frontier (Chapter 8) and was replaced by warrior aristocracies that the central court could not control.
The Taiho Code was a Tang-on-paper system that Japan's actual social structure could not fully sustain.

But the framework remained the official law of the land for over a thousand years, and the language and concepts of ritsuryo governance shaped Japanese political thought down to the Meiji Restoration.
The other major operational reform of the early eighth century was the introduction of official coinage.

In 708, copper deposits were discovered in Musashi Province (modern Saitama Prefecture, near Tokyo), and the court immediately struck Japan's first official coins: the Wado Kaichin (wah-DOH KYE-chin), modeled directly on the Tang Kaiyuan Tongbao copper cash.

The coins were circular with a square hole in the center (so they could be strung on cords for transport — the standard East Asian coinage form for the next twelve centuries), inscribed with four characters reading "Wado Kaichin" ("Inaugural Treasure of the Wado [Soft Copper] Era").
Twelve more official coin issues would follow over the next two and a half centuries, mostly minted in Yamashiro and Musashi.
The coinage program was, in part, a propaganda exercise: a respectable state in the Tang model needed to issue its own currency, and Japan now issued one.
It was also a serious attempt to monetize the rural economy and ease tax collection.

The state pushed hard on the program — it required certain ranks of officials to hold portions of their salary in coin, attempted to require coin payments for certain transactions, and offered tax discounts for taxpayers who paid in coin instead of in kind.
None of this worked very well outside the capital.
Rural Japan stuck with rice-and-cloth payments for centuries.

By the late ninth century, the state had effectively stopped minting coins, and Japan would not have a functioning monetary economy again until imported Chinese cash flooded in during the Heian period (Heian Japan Ch 2).
The Wado Kaichin program is one of the clearer examples of a Tang-modeled reform that Japanese society was not yet ready to absorb at scale.
It worked for the bureaucracy in Heijo-kyo.
It did not work for the village economy.
The big political fact of the early eighth century was the move to Heijo-kyo (hay-JOH-kyoh) in 710.
This was the city later known as Nara (NAH-rah), and it gives the next eighty years of Japanese history their name: the Nara period.
The decision to move was made by Empress Genmei (gen-MAY), Mommu's mother, who had taken the throne in 707 after her son's early death.
Fujiwara-kyo had been functioning as the capital for sixteen years but had drainage problems, traffic problems, and (the chroniclers noted) a series of inauspicious portents.
The court accepted the proposal of an imperial commission that a fresh start was needed at a new site a few miles north of Asuka, in a flat basin at the southern edge of the Yamato plain.
Construction of the new capital began in 708 and was advanced enough by spring 710 to allow the imperial court to relocate.
The remaining government offices and aristocratic families followed over the next year.
Heijo-kyo was Japan's first major capital built at the scale of a Tang Chinese imperial city.
It covered roughly 9 square miles (24 km²), with a north-south axis running about 2.9 miles (4.7 km) and an east-west axis of about 2.7 miles (4.3 km).
The layout was a careful copy of Tang Chang'an — at the time the largest city in the world (population around 1 million), and explicitly the model the Japanese planners were following.
The imperial palace sat at the north end of the city (correctly placed this time, unlike at Fujiwara-kyo).
A great central avenue, the Suzaku Oji ("Red Phoenix Avenue") — about 280 feet wide, running directly south from the palace gate — bisected the city.
Walled residential wards lined either side of Suzaku Oji, organized in a grid pattern of major streets.
Two enormous markets, the East Market and the West Market, were located in the southern half of the city.
The whole thing was enclosed (in plan, though never fully in earthworks) by a roughly rectangular boundary, with a great southern gate (the Rajomon) facing south.
There was one significant difference from Chang'an.
Chang'an was a fully walled city, with massive earth ramparts protecting it against the steppe armies that periodically threatened China's northern frontier.
Heijo-kyo was not walled.

Japan's island geography meant the city did not face the threat of mounted nomad invasion — no Japanese city would be walled until the castle-building era of the late medieval period nearly nine hundred years later.
The Nara court could afford to build for prestige and beauty rather than defense.

The central avenue, the orderly grid, the great markets, the temples scattered across the city, the imperial palace at the head — all were architectural statements about the kind of state Japan now intended to be: not a fortress but a civilization.
At its peak (around 740), Heijo-kyo housed perhaps 100,000 to 200,000 residents.
By Tang Chang'an standards, this was small — Chang'an had perhaps ten times the population.
By the standards of any other city in eighth-century East Asia outside China itself, Nara was substantial.

By the standards of the previous Yamato capitals (Asuka, with its low-thousands court population; Fujiwara-kyo, with maybe 30,000), it was an order of magnitude larger than anything Japan had ever built before.
The aristocratic and government population was also vastly larger.

The Taiho Code's bureaucracy required thousands of officials — drafters, archivists, treasurers, censors, ritualists, military planners, judges, provincial supervisors, and the clerks who kept the registers and the tax records flowing.
Nara housed all of them.
The court itself, with all its concubines and nurses and household staff and attendants, was a small city by itself.

The Buddhist establishment grew correspondingly: the great temples that would dominate Nara's southern and eastern districts (Kofuku-ji, Yakushi-ji after relocation, Todai-ji built later, Saidai-ji) all had monastic populations in the hundreds, plus their lay supporters and craftspeople.

A crucial early move at Heijo-kyo was Fujiwara no Fuhito's decision to relocate the Fujiwara clan temple to the new capital and rebuild it as Kofuku-ji (KOH-foo-koo-JEE — "Temple of Flourishing Fortune").

The Fujiwara had a small clan temple in Asuka called Yamashina-dera; Fuhito moved its institutional identity, its monks, and its religious functions to a new and much larger temple compound on prime land in the eastern half of Heijo-kyo, dedicated in 710.

Kofuku-ji would become the religious headquarters of the Fujiwara clan and one of the great power centers of the next several centuries — its monk-soldiers (Heian Japan Ch 4) would be a major political force from the late Heian period onward.
The placement of Kofuku-ji in the new capital was a Fujiwara claim on the religious life of the new city, a counterweight to the imperial monasteries the throne would soon be founding.
Yakushi-ji (Tenmu's vow temple, Chapter 4) was also relocated to Heijo-kyo in 718, rebuilt on a new site west of the imperial palace.

Its East Pagoda from this rebuilding still stands today — a three-story pagoda that, because of an architectural device of three small pent roofs called mokoshi between the main roof levels, is sometimes mistakenly described as a six-story pagoda.
It is one of the most beautiful pagodas in Japan and one of only a handful of Nara-era structures to have survived continuously in its original form.

A number of other temples were founded or relocated to Nara in the first two decades of the new capital, gradually building up the institutional Buddhist apparatus that would be elaborated in the great Shomu-era projects of the 740s and 750s (Chapter 6).
Empress Genmei reigned until 715, when she abdicated in favor of her unmarried daughter, who took the throne as Empress Gensho (gen-SHOH).
This is the only consecutive mother-to-daughter imperial succession in Japanese history.
Gensho reigned until 724, when she abdicated in favor of her nephew (Genmei's grandson), who took the throne as Emperor Shomu.

The Genmei-Gensho-Shomu sequence is a single political continuity, all of them working under the umbrella of Fujiwara no Fuhito's reforms and (after Fuhito's death in 720) under the political guidance of Fuhito's four sons.
Shomu's reign would dominate the central decades of the Nara period, and his program would culminate in the casting of the Daibutsu — the next chapter.

But before turning to Shomu, one more item from the Genmei era deserves mention: in 712, Empress Genmei accepted the long-promised completion of Hieda no Are's recitation, in the form of a written manuscript prepared by the court attendant O no Yasumaro (OH noh yah-soo-MAH-roh).

This was the Kojiki (koh-JEE-kee, "Record of Ancient Matters") — Japan's oldest surviving written work and the text that would eventually be elevated, by nineteenth- and twentieth-century nationalist scholars, into the founding scripture of Japanese identity.
Eight years later, in 720, the parallel state-history project would also be completed: the Nihon Shoki (nee-HON SHOH-kee, "Chronicles of Japan"), in classical Chinese, written for foreign-policy use.
Both works are central to the literary history of the Nara period, and both deserve a chapter of their own; we will come back to them in Chapter 7.
The early Nara court was also when state-sponsored ethnographic and geographical compilation got under way.

In 713, Empress Genmei issued the Fudoki edict ordering every province to compile a local Fudoki (FOO-doh-kee — "records of wind and earth") documenting the geography, climate, agricultural products, place-name etymologies, and folk legends of the area.
The orders went out to all sixty-odd provinces; only five provincial Fudoki survive intact today (Izumo, Hitachi, Harima, Hizen, and Bungo), with fragments from a number of others.

The Fudoki are an irreplaceable source for early Japanese rural culture, preserving traditions that would otherwise have vanished into the imperial cult — local creation myths, lists of indigenous deities not absorbed into the Yamato pantheon, agricultural rituals, etymological speculations about why this hill is called what it's called and that river is named for what god.
The Fudoki edict was a small bureaucratic moment — a single court directive to provincial governors.
But it shows the eighth-century court trying to systematize knowledge of its own territory in a Tang-bureaucratic way.
The Tang state had its own gazetteer tradition (the Tang Liudian, a comprehensive encyclopedic compilation of administrative geography).
Japan was now compiling its own version.
The country was being mapped, registered, and inventoried in the categories of the new ritsuryo state.
Cross-civ check: the founding of Heijo-kyo in 710 was contemporary with one of the most consequential single decades in Eurasian history.
Umayyad Arab armies had reached the Indus River and conquered al-Andalus (modern Spain) by 711 — within a year of Empress Genmei's capital move (Umayyad Caliphate Ch 4).
The Battle of Tours in 732 (about a generation later) would mark the Umayyad expansion's western limit at the Pyrenees.
In Tang China, Emperor Xuanzong had just taken the throne in 712 and was beginning the High Tang reign that would peak in the great cultural moment of Li Bai and Du Fu (Sui, Tang & Song China Ch 3).

The Tang Chang'an that Heijo-kyo was modeling itself on was at the height of its cosmopolitan power: a million-person multi-ethnic capital where Sogdian merchants, Persian refugees from the destroyed Sassanid Empire, Indian Buddhist monks, Korean students, and now Japanese kentoshi embassies all moved through the same wards.
Unified Silla in Korea was at the start of its golden age (Ancient Korea Ch 7).
The Byzantine Empire under the Isaurian dynasty was about to enter the Iconoclasm crisis (Byzantine Empire Ch 7).

The early eighth century is one of those moments when several civilizations were simultaneously building on the institutional models inherited from a previous generation — Tang on Sui, Umayyad on early-Caliphate, Japan on its own Asuka-era reforms — and producing the operational metropolitan capitals that would define the high medieval period.

chapters.title: Nara Buddhism and the Great Buddha
sentences: The dominant figure of the central Nara period is Emperor Shomu (SHOH-moo, reigned 724–749), and his obsession was Buddhism.
Shomu was the great-grandson of Tenmu and Jito, the grandson of Empress Genmei, the nephew and heir of Empress Gensho.

Through his maternal grandfather Fujiwara no Fuhito, he was also the first emperor in whose veins ran a substantial dose of Fujiwara blood — his mother had been Fuhito's daughter Miyako, and his empress consort would also be a Fuhito daughter (his maternal aunt by half-blood, technically), the formidable Empress Komyo.

The intermarriage of imperial and Fujiwara lines was the deliberate Fujiwara strategy that would dominate Japanese politics for centuries (Chapter 3 noted Fuhito as the political architect; Heian Japan Ch 1 picks up the strategy at maturity), and Shomu's reign is the moment the strategy first paid off at full strength.
But Shomu's defining personal characteristic was not his Fujiwara connections.
It was his religious intensity.

He was a fervent Buddhist, increasingly convinced over the course of his reign that the spiritual power of organized Buddhism could protect Japan from the disasters that kept hitting it — and there were many disasters.

His twenty-five-year reign saw plague (the catastrophic 735–737 smallpox epidemic), famine, drought, an attempted Fujiwara coup that ended in 740 with the murder of one rebel and the suicide of three others, and the political collapse of the great Fujiwara generation his uncle Fuhito had led.
Shomu's response to each disaster was to invest more deeply in state Buddhism.
By the end of his reign, he had committed an enormous fraction of Japan's national resources to a Buddhist building program of unprecedented scale, culminating in the Daibutsu of Todai-ji.
The crisis that reshaped Shomu's reign was the 735–737 smallpox epidemic.

The disease had spread along the Eurasian trade networks for centuries; it appears to have entered Japan through the Korean trade in 735, from a Tang ship that reached Dazaifu in northern Kyushu carrying infected sailors.
From there it moved up through western Honshu, reached the capital Heijo-kyo by early 737, and ravaged the densely populated central provinces through the summer.
The mortality was catastrophic.
Modern epidemiological estimates put the death toll at roughly one-third of the Japanese population — somewhere between 1.5 and 2.5 million people, in a country of about 5 million.
Whole communities lost half their adults.
Tax registers from the period show massive defaults — large numbers of registered taxpayers simply gone.

The court itself was decimated: in the spring of 737, all four Fujiwara brothers — sons of Fuhito and the dominant figures in court politics for two decades — died of smallpox within months of each other.
Their deaths broke the senior Fujiwara line's grip on policy and triggered a generation of factional instability that would not really stabilize until the late eighth century.
Shomu's response to the catastrophe was not retreat but expansion of the state-Buddhist program.
He had already been a heavy temple patron.
After 737, he became something more aggressive: a sovereign convinced that only a national network of Buddhist prayer could save Japan from further calamities.

In 741, four years after the worst of the epidemic, he issued the Provincial Temple Edict: every province in Japan was to build a kokubunji (KOH-koo-boon-JEE — "provincial monastery"), with a seven-story pagoda; and a parallel kokubunniji (KOH-koo-boon-NEE-JEE — "provincial nunnery"), housing the female counterpart Buddhist establishment.

Together the kokubunji network was meant to garrison the whole country with prayer — a national infrastructure project on a religious basis, coordinated from the central court but funded substantially by provincial revenues.
The kokubunji program was a real burden on provincial finances.
It was also a massive employment program for craftsmen, sculptors, painters, carpenters, bronze-casters, and the bureaucratic clerks who supervised the construction.
Across the provinces, the project transformed the countryside.

By the late eighth century, every Japanese province had a Buddhist cathedral on the Tang temple model, with a pagoda visible from miles away, a great Buddha image, a community of resident monks, and a dedicated tax-exempt land allotment to support the operation.
Many of these provincial temples have either survived in some form (sometimes only a foundation outline, sometimes a partly reconstructed building) or are mentioned as ruins in medieval sources.
The kokubunji network is one of the most visible Nara-era impositions on the landscape of pre-modern Japan.
The crown jewel of Shomu's program was at Heijo-kyo itself: Todai-ji (toh-DYE-jee — "Great Eastern Temple"), founded in 743, and its centerpiece, the Daibutsu (dye-BOO-tsoo — "Great Buddha").

The Daibutsu was a colossal bronze seated Buddha statue, approximately 49 feet (15 meters) tall, depicting the cosmic Buddha Vairocana (vy-roh-CHA-nah — the central deity of the Kegon school of Buddhism, the meditation sutra-based tradition that Shomu favored above the other schools).
The statue was cast in eight sequential stages over multiple years, using copper, tin, mercury, and gold drawn from across the country.
The bronze itself weighed over 500 tons.
The gilding was applied as a mercury amalgam — gold dissolved in liquid mercury, painted onto the surface, then heated to drive off the mercury and leave the pure gold bonded to the bronze.

The mercury fumes from the gilding process are thought to have killed or seriously poisoned a significant number of the workmen — there is no precise contemporary tally, but the casting process was understood at the time to be hazardous, and the chronicle accounts of post-casting mortality among the bronzeworkers are not seriously disputed.
The casting consumed most of Japan's known copper reserves and a large portion of its known gold.

New gold deposits discovered in Mutsu (the northeastern frontier province) in 749 — by Korean Baekje refugee descendants who had settled the region after the seventh-century refugee waves — were specifically dedicated to the Daibutsu project; their discovery is recorded in the chronicles as a divine sign that the Buddha approved the work.
The state issued offerings asking aristocratic families to contribute personal jewelry, household bronze, and other metallic possessions to the casting; the contributions came in.
The Daibutsu casting was, in resource terms, the largest single material project the Yamato state had ever undertaken.

The official figure given by the chronicles for the labor force is 2.6 million workers — almost certainly a stylized number rather than a precise count (the figure is suspiciously close to half the country's population), but indicative of the scale at which the project was being remembered.
Whatever the actual labor numbers, the casting drew on conscript labor, hereditary craftsman lineages (many of Korean immigrant descent), corvée tax obligations, and voluntary religious donations.
The dedication ceremony in 752 is one of the great set-piece moments in Japanese cultural history.
It was held in the open-air pavilion at Todai-ji while the Daibutsuden ("Great Buddha Hall") was still under construction around the statue.
Over 10,000 monks attended.

Musicians, dancers, and ritual specialists came from Tang China, from Korea, from India, and from Central Asia — making the event the most cosmopolitan religious gathering in Japanese history to that point.

The ceremonial "eye-opening" of the statue (the painting of pupils onto the carved eye-sockets, ritually animating the figure) was performed by an Indian monk named Bodhisena (boh-dih-SEE-nah), who had traveled from India via Vietnam and China to attend, brushing the giant pupils onto the bronze face with a brush whose handle was attached to long silken cords; the cords ran out into the audience, and dozens of the assembled dignitaries (including the retired Empress Gensho and the now-retired Shomu himself) held the cords as Bodhisena did the actual brushwork — sharing in the merit of the eye-opening.
The Daibutsu sat inside the Daibutsuden ("Great Buddha Hall"), at the time among the largest wooden buildings in the world by floor area.

The original Daibutsuden was approximately 280 feet wide and 165 feet deep — wider and possibly taller than the current rebuilt version, which is itself among the largest traditional wooden structures still standing.

The original building was destroyed in fires in 1180 (during the Genpei War, Heian Japan Ch 6) and again in 1567 (during the late medieval Sengoku-era civil wars); the current Daibutsuden is an early-eighteenth-century reconstruction that is only about two-thirds the width of the Nara-era original.

The Daibutsu itself was also damaged in those fires and repaired multiple times — the head of the current statue dates to the seventeenth century, though much of the body and the lotus-petal pedestal preserve original eighth-century bronze.
The Vairocana visible in Nara today is a partial Heian-, Kamakura-, and Edo-era reconstruction wrapped around a Nara-era core.
After Shomu died in 756, his widow Empress Komyo (KOH-myoh) made one of the most generous and culturally consequential donations in world history.

She gave Shomu's entire personal collection — over 9,000 objects, including textiles, musical instruments, glasswork, calligraphy, paintings, ritual implements, weapons, mirrors, masks, and writing brushes — to Todai-ji.

The collection was housed in a raised-floor log-cabin storehouse called the Shoso-in (SHOH-soh-in), built in the azekura (ah-zeh-KOO-rah) style — interlocking triangular cypress logs that flex and breathe with seasonal humidity changes, providing exactly the right preservation environment.
The Shoso-in collection has survived intact for over 1,250 years, in extraordinary condition.
It is the most important single time capsule of the eighth-century world.

Its objects came from across Eurasia: Persian glass, Chinese Tang Dynasty mirrors, Central Asian textiles, Indian-influenced musical instruments (including a five-stringed lute called a biwa, the only surviving example of its type from the Tang era), Korean metalwork, and Japanese lacquerware.

The presence of these foreign objects in a Japanese temple storehouse demonstrates concretely what the historical record tells us in summary: that Heijo-kyo, sitting at the far eastern end of the Silk Road, was connected to a trade network stretching from the Mediterranean to the Pacific.

Some of the objects in the Shoso-in had been gifts to Shomu from Tang Chinese embassies; others were luxuries acquired through merchants traveling the kentoshi routes; still others were Japanese-made imitations of Tang and Korean originals.
The collection is opened to the public for one month each autumn, in a carefully staged annual exhibition at the Nara National Museum.
A different selection of objects is shown each year.

Visitors who attend the Shoso-in exhibition see things — eighth-century Persian rhinoceros-horn cups, eighth-century Chinese-language documents written by Korean scribes, eighth-century lutes still strung with their original silk strings — that have not significantly aged in 1,250 years.
The Shoso-in is, by any measure, one of the most remarkable surviving early-medieval collections anywhere on Earth.
The institutional structure of Nara Buddhism deserves a brief explanation because it is unusual.

By the mid-eighth century, the Nara temple complex had organized itself into the Six Schools of Nara Buddhism (the Nanto Rokushu, NAHN-toh roh-KOO-shoo): six distinct scholarly traditions, each with its own canon of sutras, its own training program, its own residential monks, and its own home temple.
The schools were: Hosso (HOHS-soh) — the "Consciousness-Only" school based on the philosophy of the Indian masters Asanga and Vasubandhu, headquartered at Kofuku-ji and Yakushi-ji.
Kusha (KOO-shah) — the school based on the Abhidharma (Buddhist scholastic) literature, primarily a sub-school of Hosso.
Sanron (SAHN-rohn) — the "Three Treatises" school, based on the Madhyamaka philosophy of the Indian master Nagarjuna.
Jojitsu (JOH-jeet-soo) — based on the Satyasiddhi Shastra, primarily a sub-school of Sanron.
Kegon (KEH-gohn) — based on the Avatamsaka Sutra, the cosmic-Buddha tradition that produced the Vairocana focus of Todai-ji.
Ritsu (RIT-soo) — the discipline-based school, focused on the precise rules of Buddhist monastic ordination, headquartered at Toshodai-ji.
These were not popular sects competing for lay followers in the way that later Japanese Buddhism would (the Pure Land and Nichiren sects of the Heian and Kamakura periods, see Heian Japan Ch 2).
They were scholarly traditions, each one essentially an academic department within the larger Nara temple complex.
A serious Nara monk would study at multiple temples and engage with multiple schools rather than belonging exclusively to one.
The Six Schools specialized the intellectual labor of Buddhist analysis, with each school maintaining the textual lineage and exegetical tradition for a different segment of the Mahayana canon.
This is one reason Nara Buddhism functioned as state Buddhism.
The organization was not designed to evangelize the rural population (which mostly continued to practice a syncretic mix of kami worship, ancestor rites, and folk Buddhism).

It was designed to maintain a sophisticated scholarly Buddhist establishment in the capital, capable of staffing the kokubunji network, conducting state rituals, advising the emperor, and producing the prayers that were supposed to protect the country from disasters.
Nara Buddhism was, fundamentally, an academic-and-bureaucratic institution rather than a missionary one.

The exception that proves the rule is Gyoki (GYOH-kee, 668–749), a charismatic monk who defied the official restrictions on independent Buddhist activity and went out into the countryside to preach Buddhism to commoners, organize voluntary labor for public works projects (bridges, irrigation channels, harbors), and run charitable services for the destitute.
The state initially persecuted him — Gyoki was, by Taiho Code definitions, an unauthorized religious teacher operating outside the licensed system.
But he proved enormously popular and had assembled a following so large that the court could not safely suppress him.

By the 740s, Emperor Shomu had reversed the relationship: he formally honored Gyoki, made him Japan's first Daisojo ("Grand Priest"), and recruited him to coordinate fundraising and labor for the Todai-ji Daibutsu project.
Gyoki's popular religious networks proved essential to the project's success.
He died in 749, three years before the Daibutsu dedication, but his organizational work made the casting possible.

The most consequential foreign Buddhist arrival of the entire Nara period was Ganjin (GAHN-jin) — the Tang Chinese name was Jianzhen (jyen-JEN, 688–763), a senior monk of the Vinaya (monastic discipline) tradition, recruited by Japanese embassies to come to Japan and properly transmit the Buddhist ordination lineage that the Japanese clergy had been doing without.
The story is one of the great narratives of Buddhist missionary history.
Ganjin was approached by Japanese envoys around 742 and agreed to come.
He attempted the voyage from Tang China to Japan five times over the next eleven years.
The first attempt was sabotaged by a jealous disciple.
The second was wrecked by a storm.
The third hit pirates.
The fourth was blown so far off course that Ganjin's party landed on Hainan Island in the South China Sea, several thousand miles away from their destination.
The fifth was abandoned partway.
By the time of the sixth and successful voyage in 753, Ganjin was sixty-five years old and had gone completely blind from exposure during one of the failed attempts.
He arrived in Kyushu in late 753 and was carried to Heijo-kyo in early 754.

In Nara, Ganjin formally ordained the leading Japanese clergy in the proper Buddhist ordination lineage. (Until his arrival, Japanese ordinations had been performed by the local clergy without the formal transmission line back to the Buddha that the Vinaya tradition required.

Strictly speaking, no Japanese monk had been a fully proper Buddhist monk before Ganjin formally ordained them.) He founded Toshodai-ji (toh-SHOH-dye-jee — "Temple of the Tang Dynasty Founder") as the new headquarters of the Ritsu school and the institutional home of proper ordination.
He spent his last decade in Japan teaching, writing, and passing on his disciplinary tradition.
He died at Toshodai-ji in 763.
The Toshodai-ji main hall (the Kondo) is the finest surviving example of Tang-influenced architecture in Japan.

Built in the late eighth century, after Ganjin's death, it shows the deep eaves, the wide proportions, the simple bracketing, and the unpainted natural-wood finish characteristic of mid-Tang temple construction in China. (Almost no original Tang wooden buildings survive in China; the few that do are in remote western provinces.

To see a real Tang temple, you go to Toshodai-ji in Nara.) A lacquer portrait sculpture of Ganjin himself, made by his disciples in his lifetime or shortly after his death, is preserved at Toshodai-ji and is shown to the public for a few days each year.

It is one of the most striking pieces of early Japanese sculpture: a portrait of a blind, elderly, deeply weathered monk who had survived five shipwrecks and crossed the East China Sea to bring Buddhism to a country he could not see.
By the 760s, the Nara state-Buddhist program had reached an apex from which only a few directions of motion were possible.
The Daibutsu had been built.
The kokubunji network was established.
The Six Schools were institutionalized.
The Shoso-in had been founded.
The Manyoshu was being compiled (Chapter 7).
And the Buddhist establishment was, by sheer institutional weight, becoming the most powerful non-imperial force in Japan — with implications for the throne that will be explored in the next chapter.
Cross-civ check: the Daibutsu dedication of 752 happened in a remarkable synchronous moment of religious-political monumentalism across Eurasia.
The Umayyad Mosque of Damascus had been completed in 715 — a massive imperial mosque sponsored by the Umayyad caliphs (Umayyad Caliphate Ch 5).
The Abbey of Saint-Denis north of Paris, the burial church of the Frankish kings, was being built and rebuilt across the eighth century.
In Tang China, Emperor Xuanzong had spent the 730s and 740s expanding the imperial palaces at Chang'an and Luoyang on the largest scale of the entire Tang dynasty (Sui, Tang & Song China Ch 3).
The Borobudur monumental Buddhist temple in Java (one of the largest Buddhist monuments ever built, see Srivijaya Ch 1) would begin construction within a generation after the Daibutsu was cast.
The Great Mosque of Samarra in Iraq (the largest mosque ever built, Islamic Golden Age Ch 3) would be built by the Abbasids in the next century.
Every major civilization of the Eurasian middle was investing enormous resources in monumental religious architecture in the same period.
The Daibutsu is Japan's contribution to this Eurasian moment of imperial religion-as-stone, and it stands well in the company.

A particular comparison is striking: the Daibutsu was dedicated in 752, two years after the Abbasid Revolution of 750 that overthrew the Umayyad Caliphate and established the Abbasid dynasty in Baghdad (Islamic Golden Age Ch 1).

The same year the world's largest Buddhist statue was being unveiled in Nara, a new Islamic dynasty was being founded that would shortly embark on its own great urban project — the building of Baghdad in 762 as the new caliphal capital, on a Tang-influenced grid plan eerily similar to Heijo-kyo's.

The two great planned capitals of the late eighth century — Heijo-kyo in Japan and Baghdad in Iraq — were being built within a decade of each other on opposite ends of Eurasia, both consciously borrowing the Chang'an model.

And one year before the Daibutsu was dedicated, in 751, a Tang army was defeated by Arab forces at the Battle of Talas in Central Asia — a battle whose practical effect was to fix the boundary between the Tang and Abbasid spheres of influence, and whose cultural effect was to transmit Chinese papermaking technology to the Arab world.
The world that the Daibutsu sat at the center of was a connected one, in which institutional templates and technologies and religious practices were diffusing rapidly across vast distances.

chapters.title: Literature, Law, and the Dokyo Affair
sentences: The Nara period's most enduring legacy is not its temples or its bronze.
It is its books.

In a single seventy-year window — roughly 700 to 770 — Japan produced its first surviving written history, its first comprehensive legal code, its first poetry anthology, its first national geography, and its first attempts at vernacular Japanese prose.
The volume of writing the Nara court generated, after centuries of Japanese illiteracy, is one of the most striking transitions in the literary history of any premodern civilization.
By the end of the Nara period, Japan had a written canon.
Almost everything Japan had not written down before was now being written down, in a sustained burst of bureaucratic-and-literary energy that would not be equaled again until the Heian period.

This chapter covers the Nara textual moment — the great chronicles of 712 and 720, the Manyoshu poetry anthology, the Yoro Code of 718 — and then turns to the most peculiar episode of the late Nara period: the Dokyo Affair, in which a Buddhist monk nearly seized the imperial throne through his influence over a reigning empress.
The two great Nara chronicles are the Kojiki of 712 and the Nihon Shoki of 720.

The Kojiki ("Record of Ancient Matters") was completed by O no Yasumaro (OH noh yah-soo-MAH-roh) in 712, on the basis of recitations from the court reciter Hieda no Are that had been commissioned by Emperor Tenmu decades earlier (Chapter 4).
It is Japan's oldest surviving written work.

It is also, despite being shorter and less polished than the parallel Nihon Shoki, the more spiritually loaded of the two Nara histories, the one that nineteenth- and twentieth-century nationalist scholars elevated into the founding scripture of Japanese identity.

The Kojiki opens with the creation of the world: the formless cosmic chaos, the emergence of the first divine couple Izanagi (ee-zah-NAH-gee) and Izanami (ee-zah-NAH-mee), the divine couple's creation of the Japanese islands by churning the ocean with a heavenly spear, the birth of the first generation of kami including the sun goddess Amaterasu, the great cosmological cycle of Amaterasu's withdrawal into a cave (a partial solar eclipse interpreted mythologically), the descent of Amaterasu's grandson Ninigi to Earth carrying the three sacred imperial regalia (the mirror, the sword, and the curved jewel), and the founding of the imperial line by Ninigi's great-grandson Emperor Jimmu, traditionally dated to 660 BCE.

The narrative then continues with a semi-mythological chronicle of the early emperors, blending genealogy, legend, ritual, and poetry, before reaching more historically attested figures and ending around the death of Empress Suiko in 628.

The Nihon Shoki ("Chronicles of Japan") was completed eight years later, in 720, by a committee that included Prince Toneri (Tenmu's son, the senior imperial figure on the project) and the same O no Yasumaro who had finished the Kojiki.

It is longer (thirty volumes versus the Kojiki's three), more comprehensively documented, written in classical Chinese (whereas the Kojiki uses a hybrid system in which Chinese characters were sometimes used for their meanings, sometimes for their phonetic values to represent Japanese syllables — see the discussion of man'yogana later in this chapter), and includes alternative versions of many myths, with the text noting "another tradition says..." or "the records of such-and-such province say..." It carries the historical narrative through 697 CE, ending with the abdication of Empress Jito to her grandson Mommu.
Why were these works compiled, and why two of them so close together?
The political motivation is reasonably clear.
The Yamato court needed a written foundation myth to legitimize its rule.
Every civilized state in East Asia — China, Korea, even the smaller polities along the steppe frontier — had official histories tracing the ruling dynasty back to divine or cosmic origins.
Japan, which had only recently acquired writing, had none.
The Kojiki and Nihon Shoki filled the gap.

They established that the emperor descended from Amaterasu, that the imperial line was unbroken since the age of the gods, that the calendrical-traditional founding date of 660 BCE was older than any rival East Asian state's foundational date, and that Japan's political order was ordained by heaven.
These claims were not neutral historical observations — they were state propaganda, composed by court officials under imperial patronage to serve imperial interests.
This is not a modern cynical reading.
It is exactly what the texts present themselves as.
The Nihon Shoki opens with explicit acknowledgment that it was commissioned to be a state history.

The Kojiki preface by O no Yasumaro discusses, with some pride, the political motivation: a written record of the ages was needed to "rectify the falsehoods" that were circulating in oral tradition and to give the imperial line a definitive lineage.
The chroniclers were not pretending to be neutral.
They were doing a state-sponsored job of legitimization.
The two-version production reflects different audiences.
The Kojiki was for internal Japanese consumption — written in the hybrid script, focused on mythological detail and ritual genealogy, composed in a style that was sometimes archaic and rhythmic.

The Nihon Shoki was for external (especially Chinese and Korean) consumption — written in classical Chinese, presented as a proper East Asian dynastic history, more conscious of comparative chronology, attempting to demonstrate that Japan was a respectable civilized state with a documented past.
Both versions were doing political work, but for different audiences.
The texts preserve enormous amounts of cultural information that would otherwise have been lost.

Mythological cycles, regional traditions, royal genealogies, ceremonial practices, place-name etymologies, fragments of pre-Buddhist religious thought — all of it preserved, even if filtered through the eighth-century court's editorial purposes.
They are propaganda and treasure at the same time, just like every other ancient national origin text from the Hebrew Bible to Virgil's Aeneid.

Modern Japanese historiography spends a great deal of effort trying to disentangle the historical from the mythological in the early sections, with mixed results — most scholars accept the chronicle accounts of late-sixth-century and seventh-century events as substantially reliable, treat the early-emperors sections as legendary, and dispute everything in between.
The Nara period's other great literary achievement was the Manyoshu (MAHN-yoh-shoo, "Collection of Ten Thousand Leaves"), Japan's oldest poetry anthology, compiled around 759.
The Manyoshu contains 4,516 poems by over 500 named authors plus many anonymous compositions, organized into twenty volumes.

The poems range across the entire seventh and early-eighth centuries, with the bulk of the material from the late seventh and early eighth centuries — making the Manyoshu a generation-by-generation snapshot of the Asuka and Nara court's literary production.
What makes the Manyoshu unusual in the world's anthologies of this period is its social range.
Most ancient and early-medieval poetry collections preserve aristocratic or scholarly poetry.

The Manyoshu does that — emperors and high nobles are well-represented — but it also includes poems by frontier guards posted to the eastern Emishi border, by anonymous farmers and fishermen, by roadside laborers, by women separated from their husbands, by mothers grieving for dead children, and by men whose names did not survive but whose verses did.
No other surviving poetry collection of comparable size, anywhere in the eighth-century world, includes commoner poets alongside emperors.

The Manyoshu's anonymous frontier-guard poems (the sakimori-uta) are among the most affecting compositions in the collection: short laments by men leaving home for years of guard duty in distant Kyushu, addressed to the wives and parents and children they were leaving behind.
The greatest poet of the Manyoshu is Kakinomoto no Hitomaro (kah-kee-NOH-moh-toh noh hee-toh-MAH-roh), a court poet active around 680–710 (Chapter 4 introduced him as a Hakuho-era figure).

Hitomaro composed elegies for dead empresses, court occasion poems for imperial banquets, travel poems written on the road between Asuka and the various provinces he visited on official duty, and personal lyrics about love, separation, and grief.
His formal sophistication and emotional intensity have caused him to be recognized for thirteen centuries as one of the great poets in the Japanese tradition.

A famous Hitomaro poem on the death of his wife — addressed to her ashes after her cremation, lamenting that he can no longer find her form in the smoke rising from the funeral pyre — is one of the foundational texts of the Japanese elegiac tradition.

The Manyoshu's principal compiler was probably Otomo no Yakamochi (OH-toh-moh noh yah-kah-MOH-chee, 718–785), an aristocrat-poet of the Otomo clan who held provincial governorships and military posts across the Nara period and who wrote 473 of the anthology's poems himself — the largest single contribution by any author.

His selections preserved the Manyoshu's social breadth: it was Yakamochi who included the frontier-guard poems, the work-songs, the regional dialects, the unpolished but heartfelt voices of non-court Japanese alongside the formal compositions of his own aristocratic class.
The result is one of the most democratic poetry anthologies in any pre-modern literary tradition.
The Manyoshu is also the greatest surviving monument of an unusual writing system called man'yogana (MAHN-yoh-gah-nah, named after the anthology itself).
Man'yogana uses Chinese characters for their phonetic values rather than for their meanings — each character represents one Japanese syllable.

Since the two languages are completely unrelated (Japanese is an agglutinative non-tonal language with completely different grammar from monosyllabic tonal Chinese), the only way to write Japanese poetry while preserving its actual sound was to strip Chinese characters of their meaning and use them purely as sound symbols.

One character per syllable, hundreds of different characters in use, no standardization on which character to use for which sound — different scribes used different conventions, sometimes within the same poem.
The system was absurdly inefficient.

Imagine writing English by repurposing Chinese numerals as sounds (一 = "wun," 二 = "too," 四 = "for") and then spelling out entire sentences that way, with each writer free to substitute different characters for the same sounds.
That's man'yogana.
It was begging to be simplified.

Within a century, by the early Heian period, Japanese scribes had simplified the man'yogana characters into the two streamlined syllabaries — hiragana and katakana — that would let Japanese be written as Japanese rather than as a tortured phonetic adaptation of Chinese (Heian Japan Ch 1).
But until the kana revolution, the Manyoshu represents the best the Japanese could do: the heroic, awkward, beautiful effort of writing native poetry in a borrowed script.
The Nara period also saw the polishing and re-promulgation of the great Tang-modeled legal code.
The Yoro Code (YOH-roh) was drafted by Fujiwara no Fuhito and his collaborators around 718, as a careful revision of the Taiho Code of 701.

The two codes were structurally identical and operationally similar; the Yoro version made textual refinements, clarified ambiguous provisions, updated some of the bureaucratic ranking, and incorporated the experience of two decades of running the ritsuryo system.

The Yoro Code was held in reserve for several decades after Fuhito's death in 720, then formally promulgated in 757 under Empress Koken — and once promulgated, it became the operational legal framework of Japan for the next millennium.
Yoro provisions were still being cited in court rulings during the Edo period in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries.
Few legal codes anywhere in the world have had a longer continuous official life.
The Yoro Code is also unusual in that nearly the entire text survives.
The Taiho Code of 701, despite being the more historically important of the two, survives only in fragments cited in later sources.
The Yoro Code survives almost intact, as a thirty-volume compilation that has been continuously preserved at imperial archives since the eighth century.

Modern Japanese legal historians have an almost embarrassing wealth of primary material on Nara-period law — the Yoro text itself, plus the Yoro commentaries (Ryo no Gige of 833 and Ryo no Shuge of around 880), plus the fragments and citations from earlier codes.
The full operational shape of the Nara state can be reconstructed in detail.
What the Yoro Code reveals, as a document, is just how far the Japanese state had pushed the Tang model into operational reality.

The Code specifies the duties of every bureaucratic post, the schedule of ranks and salaries, the procedures for tax assessment and collection, the sentencing framework for criminal offenses, the rituals of ceremonial occasions, the regulations governing Buddhist clergy, the rules for provincial governance, and the protocols for diplomatic correspondence.
It is a Tang state on paper, adapted at almost every detail to Japanese institutional realities, fully functional as a governing document.

The fact that the actual operational reach of the central state never matched the Code's ambitions — that aristocratic estates and Buddhist temple lands carved themselves out of the registered tax base, that the conscript army system collapsed in fifty years, that the handen-shuju land registration broke down by the late ninth century — does not change the fact that the framework existed and shaped Japanese political thought for over a thousand years.
The most peculiar episode of the entire late Nara period is the Dokyo Affair.
The story begins with Empress Koken (KOH-ken), daughter of Shomu and Komyo, who took the throne in 749 after her father's abdication and reigned until 758.
She was unmarried and had no children, both unusual for a Japanese empress.
After 758 she retired and her cousin took the throne as Emperor Junnin, with the senior Fujiwara minister Fujiwara no Nakamaro (nah-kah-MAH-roh) as the dominant figure at court.
In the early 760s, the retired Koken became seriously ill.
She was attended by a Buddhist monk of the Hosso school named Dokyo (DOH-kyoh — usually rendered without the long o-mark in plain ASCII).
Dokyo was a learned monk, an effective spiritual healer, and (the chronicle accounts repeatedly emphasize) personally charismatic to a degree that captured the retired empress's deep loyalty.
By the time Koken recovered from her illness in 762, Dokyo had become her most trusted personal counselor.
She moved him into senior court positions — Master of Imperial Sutras, then State Minister, then increasingly extraordinary titles invented to justify the level of authority she was placing in him.
The senior Fujiwara minister Nakamaro, watching this with growing alarm, attempted a coup in 764 to remove Dokyo and reassert Fujiwara dominance.
The Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion lasted only a few weeks — Nakamaro was outmaneuvered, defeated militarily, and beheaded with most of his senior allies.

The retired Empress Koken returned to active reign in 764, deposing her cousin Junnin (who was sent into exile and died there, possibly murdered), and taking the throne under a new reign name as Empress Shotoku (SHOH-toh-koo — confusingly the same name as the great Asuka prince of Chapter 2, but as a posthumous designation rather than an active personal name).
This was Empress Shotoku's second reign.
It was completely dominated by Dokyo.
He was given the title Hoo ("Dharma King") in 766 — an unprecedented designation that styled him as a kind of monastic-imperial figure parallel to the secular emperor.
He moved his temple base into the Heijo-kyo palace complex itself.
