His Hosso-school faction took over the Buddhist establishment, displacing rival schools.
Court appointments increasingly went to Dokyo's allies.

The chroniclers — writing later under the post-Dokyo restoration — describe the period in tones of horror, suggesting (without quite stating it directly) that Dokyo's relationship with the empress was sexual, that he was using her infatuation with him to seize political control of Japan, and that the country was on the edge of being taken over by a Buddhist priest.
In 769, the affair came to its head.

An oracle was reported from the Usa Hachiman shrine in Kyushu (one of the most powerful Shinto shrines in Japan, dedicated to the deified emperor Ojin, regarded as a war-god protector of the imperial line).
The oracle, the chronicle account says, declared that Dokyo should be made emperor.
The court was thrown into crisis.

If the Usa oracle was authentic, the throne itself was about to pass from the imperial line — descended from Amaterasu through unbroken male succession (with female intervals) for the entire history of the country — to a Buddhist monk with no imperial blood.
Empress Shotoku sent an envoy to Usa to verify the oracle.
The envoy chosen was Wake no Kiyomaro (WAH-keh noh KEE-yoh-mah-roh), a young court official who had not yet been compromised by the Dokyo faction.
Kiyomaro went to Usa, performed the ritual consultation, and returned with the opposite oracle: the throne could only pass through the imperial line, and Dokyo could not become emperor.

Whether the original "Dokyo oracle" had been a forgery, whether Kiyomaro's counter-oracle was genuine or invented, whether the Usa shrine priesthood was politically aligned with the Fujiwara faction — none of this can be resolved from the surviving sources, all of which were written by parties hostile to Dokyo.
What is clear is that Kiyomaro's report blocked the succession plan.
Dokyo had Kiyomaro exiled in disgrace.
Then, in 770, Empress Shotoku died.
She left no clear successor.
Her court faction, led by her dying preferences, had lost decisive momentum.

The senior aristocrats — primarily the surviving Fujiwara — moved quickly to install a male emperor of impeccable imperial lineage (Konin, a sixty-two-year-old grandson of Tenji, chosen specifically because he was old, conservative, and far from the Dokyo faction).
Dokyo himself was demoted, exiled to a remote temple in the eastern provinces, and died there a few years later.
Wake no Kiyomaro was recalled from exile and rewarded.
The Dokyo affair had two enormous consequences.
First, the political power of Nara Buddhism was now visible to every court faction.
A monk had nearly taken the throne.
The risk that Buddhist temples could collude with reigning empresses to overthrow the secular government had been demonstrated.
Second, and as a direct result, female imperial succession was now politically suspect.

The court that had installed Konin in 770 began an unwritten policy of avoiding reigning empresses unless absolutely necessary, on the theory that women were vulnerable to being manipulated by court Buddhist factions in the way Empress Shotoku had been manipulated by Dokyo.
This policy would harden over time into a formal exclusion that lasted, with very minor exceptions, for over a thousand years.
The next reigning Japanese empress would not appear until 1629, and the policy would not be formally reversed until the post-1868 Meiji Constitution.
A single eccentric monk had warped the gender of Japanese imperial succession for the next millennium.
The Dokyo affair is also one of the events that drove the eventual decision to move the capital out of Nara entirely.
If the Buddhist establishment in Heijo-kyo had grown so politically powerful that it could nearly seize the throne, then the obvious solution was to take the throne somewhere else.
Emperor Konin's son and successor, Emperor Kammu, would do exactly that in 784 (Chapter 8).
Two final cultural products of the late Nara period deserve mention before we close.
The Hyakumanto Darani (hyah-koo-MAHN-toh dah-RAH-nee — "One Million Pagodas with Dharani") is one of the most extraordinary printing projects in world history.

Empress Shotoku, in the wake of the suppression of the Nakamaro rebellion in 764, commissioned the production of one million miniature wooden pagodas, each containing a printed Buddhist dharani charm (a short ritual text).
The project took six years and was completed around 770.

Each of the million pagodas was a small hand-carved wooden object about three to four inches tall; inside each was a printed paper scroll bearing one of four short Sanskrit-derived dharani prayers in Chinese transliteration.
The dharani prayers were printed using woodblock printing — wooden printing blocks carved with the text, inked, and pressed onto paper.
These printed dharani are among the earliest surviving examples of woodblock printing anywhere in the world.
They predate the famous Diamond Sutra of 868 (long considered the earliest surviving printed book, found in the Dunhuang caves in western China — see Sui, Tang & Song China Ch 4) by nearly a century.
There are competing claims — Korean printing, Chinese pre-Tang printing — but most are based on fragmentary or contested evidence; the Hyakumanto Darani are not contested.

Roughly 50,000 of the original million pagodas survive in temple collections (the bulk at Horyu-ji, which received a tenth of the original distribution), and dharani prints from the project can be examined by visiting scholars.

The fact that the world's earliest substantially surviving printed texts come from late-Nara Japan — produced as a state-Buddhist propitiatory project at the height of an empress's grief and political guilt — is one of the more unexpected facts in the technological history of the medium.
And finally, the late Nara period continued the kentoshi missions to Tang China that had been the central conduit of continental influence for over a century.

The 717 embassy was particularly consequential: it included the young scholar Kibi no Makibi (KEE-bee noh MAH-kee-bee), who spent eighteen years in China (returning in 735), bringing back astronomy, military strategy, and a general intellectual sophistication that made him one of the highest-ranking non-Fujiwara officials of his generation.

The same embassy included the priest Genbo, who returned with the largest single shipment of Buddhist sutras Japan had ever received (over 5,000 scrolls), establishing the Hosso-school textual library that Dokyo would later draw on.
And the most famous Japanese figure of the entire kentoshi tradition was a contemporary: Abe no Nakamaro (AH-beh noh NAH-kah-mah-roh), sent to China at sixteen on the same 717 embassy.
Nakamaro stayed.

He passed the imperial examinations (an extraordinary achievement for a foreigner), became a high official under Tang Emperor Xuanzong, befriended the great poets Li Bai and Wang Wei, and spent his entire life in China, never managing to return home alive despite multiple attempts.

He wrote a famous poem looking eastward across the sea toward Japan and watching the moon rise: "If I could see in my homeland the same moon that rises here over Mount Mikasa..." Li Bai wrote a poem mourning him after a false report of his death.
Nakamaro died in Chang'an in 770 and was buried in China.
He is the most poignant single figure in the long story of Japan's eighth-century relationship with Tang.

Cross-civ check: the 770s — when the Dokyo Affair was unfolding and the Hyakumanto Darani was being printed — were also when the Abbasid Caliphate under Caliph al-Mansur was completing the construction of Baghdad as the new caliphal capital (founded 762, walls complete by 766).
The Abbasid revolution had ended the Umayyad dynasty in 750 (Islamic Golden Age Ch 1).

In Tang China, Emperor Daizong was struggling to recover from the catastrophic An Lushan Rebellion of 755–763, which had killed perhaps 36 million people and broken the back of the Tang dynasty (Sui, Tang & Song China Ch 4) — Tang would limp along for another 144 years but never recover its earlier vitality.

In Europe, Charlemagne had just inherited the Frankish throne (from his father Pepin in 768) and was beginning the conquests that would unify most of western Europe under Carolingian rule by the end of the century.
The Manyoshu, completed around 759, is roughly contemporary with the Old English Beowulf (composed in some form around 700–800), the great surviving Anglo-Saxon poem in alliterative meter.

The two poetic monuments are interesting to compare: Beowulf preserves a single epic narrative in the warrior aristocracy's voice; the Manyoshu preserves 4,500 lyrics across the entire social spectrum from emperors to anonymous frontier guards.
Different societies produced different kinds of monumental poetry.
Both have lasted.

chapters.title: The Move to Heian
sentences: By the early 780s, the Heijo-kyo capital had been the seat of the Japanese imperial court for over seventy years.
Three generations of emperors and empresses had reigned there.
The great Buddhist temples had grown into the most powerful religious institutions in the country — and after the Dokyo Affair of 769–770 (Chapter 7), into the most politically dangerous ones.
The Fujiwara clan had consolidated its grip on senior court positions.
The Tang-modeled bureaucracy had reached the limits of its actual operational reach into the rural provinces.
Something had to change.

The change came from a determined emperor whose mother was a Korean royal descendant, whose political program was to break the temple-court symbiosis that had built up at Nara, and who was prepared to move the capital twice in a decade to do it.
His name was Emperor Kammu (KAH-moo), and his decision in 794 to settle the imperial court at a new city he named Heian-kyo — modern Kyoto — closed the Asuka-Nara period and opened the Heian one.
This chapter covers Kammu's reign from 781 to his death in 806, the Emishi frontier wars that reshaped Japan's military system in the same period, and the legacy of the Asuka-Nara centuries.
Emperor Kammu (737–806) was an unlikely figure for the throne.

He was the son of Emperor Konin (the elderly conservative who had been installed after Empress Shotoku's death in 770) and a consort named Takano no Niigasa (TAH-kah-noh noh NEE-gah-sah), who was descended from the Yamato no Fubito immigrant clan — a lineage tracing back to refugees from the Baekje royal family who had fled to Japan in the seventh century.
Kammu was, in other words, partly Korean by ancestry on his mother's side.

This fact was discreetly noted in the eighth-century chronicles and quietly minimized through the medieval period; in 2001, Emperor Akihito of Japan publicly acknowledged the Korean ancestry in his great-distant ancestor's line, in a remark that was a small but real diplomatic moment between modern Japan and Korea.
Kammu became Crown Prince in 773 and Emperor in 781, when his father Konin abdicated in his favor at age sixty-five.
He was forty-four years old at his accession, a relatively mature emperor with clear political views and a willingness to push them through.
His twenty-five-year reign is one of the most consequential of the entire pre-modern Japanese imperial line.
Kammu's central political conviction was that the institutional symbiosis between the throne and the Nara Buddhist temples had to be broken.
The Dokyo Affair was still in living memory.
The kokubunji network had become an enormous economic burden on provincial finances.

The great temples in Heijo-kyo had become major landholders in their own right, with monastic populations of thousands, with tax-exempt estates spreading across central Honshu, and with the political reach to influence court appointments at the highest level.
As long as the imperial court remained in Nara, the temples would always be on its doorstep, with the institutional ties between them only deepening over time.
Kammu's solution was radical: move the capital, and leave the temples behind.
The aristocratic and bureaucratic court would go to a new site.

The great Nara temples could keep their existing buildings, their existing monastic populations, and their existing landholdings — but the political court they had attached themselves to would no longer be there.
The new capital would have its own temples, on the imperial court's terms, not on the temples' terms.
Kammu's first attempt was at Nagaoka-kyo (nah-gah-OH-kah-KYOH), in the Yamashiro region a few miles north of Heijo-kyo.
Construction began in 784, and the imperial court moved within a year.

Nagaoka-kyo was meant to be a permanent replacement: it was laid out on a Tang-style grid like Heijo-kyo but at a slightly larger scale, with better river access (the new capital sat at the confluence of the Yodo, Katsura, and Uji rivers), and at a sufficient distance from the great Nara temples to break their political grip on the court.
The Nagaoka project went badly almost from the start.
The construction was supervised by Kammu's chief minister, Fujiwara no Tanetsugu (TAH-neh-tsoo-goo), an architect of the relocation strategy.
In 785, just over a year after the move, Tanetsugu was assassinated at the Nagaoka construction site — shot with arrows in a coordinated attack while supervising work on the new palace.
The assassins were tracked down and executed, but the conspiracy reached high into the imperial family itself.
Kammu's brother, the Crown Prince Sawara (sah-WAH-rah), was implicated in the plot — possibly justly, possibly framed by Kammu's faction as a way of removing a rival.
Sawara was stripped of his Crown Prince title and exiled.

Refusing to eat during the journey toward exile, he died en route — possibly by deliberate self-starvation, possibly from the stress of the political destruction, possibly through assassination disguised as natural death.
The chronicle accounts are inconsistent and partisan.
Whatever the exact cause, the brother of the reigning emperor was dead, by means that would not bear close examination.
Then a series of disasters hit Nagaoka.
Plague broke out in the new capital.
Floods damaged the construction sites.
Kammu's mother died unexpectedly in 789.
His wife died in 790.
His son died in 792.
By 793, the court was convinced that Sawara's angry spirit was taking revenge on the family that had destroyed him, and that the new capital was cursed.
Kammu was prepared to move again.
The decision to abandon Nagaoka-kyo was formalized in 793, after only nine years of occupation.

The court began the search for a new site, and a third capital was selected just north of Nagaoka, in a basin protected on three sides by mountains, with the Kamo and Katsura rivers running through it.

The site was traditionally regarded as auspicious — in the Chinese geomantic system the Japanese used for capital site selection, it was considered a particularly favorable location, with mountains to the north (blocking malevolent influences), open ground to the south (allowing positive influences), and rivers framing the site (representing prosperity).
Construction began in 793.
The court moved in 794.
Kammu named the new capital Heian-kyo (hay-AHN-kyoh — "Capital of Peace and Tranquility").
The name worked.
The new city would remain the imperial capital for the next 1,074 years — until 1868, when the Meiji Restoration would relocate the imperial court to Edo, renamed Tokyo.

Heian-kyo, called Kyoto from the late medieval period onward, was the longest-serving imperial capital in Japanese history and the longest-serving continuously occupied imperial capital of any major civilization.
It is still inhabited today, with significant portions of the original eighth-century street grid preserved in the modern city's layout.

The opening of the Heian period — the brilliant aesthetic civilization of Murasaki Shikibu and Lady Sei, of The Tale of Genji and The Pillow Book, of the Fujiwara regents and the cloistered emperors and the Genpei War (Heian Japan, all chapters) — is the next narrative.
The closing of the Asuka-Nara period is the move to Heian-kyo in 794.
Kammu's reign also produced the major reorganization of the Japanese frontier military system, in the long-running campaigns against the Emishi (eh-MEE-shee) people of northeastern Honshu.
The Emishi were the indigenous population of what is now the Tohoku region — roughly the northeastern third of the main Japanese island.
They were not Yamato Japanese in language, culture, or political organization.

They had maintained a distinct culture (probably descended from Jomon-period populations who had not been fully absorbed by the Yayoi-period continental migration, see Prehistoric Japan Ch 2–3) into the historical period.
They lived in scattered settlements, organized around chiefs and clan leaders rather than centralized states, with subsistence economies that combined hunting, fishing, and limited agriculture.

They were not "barbarians" in any meaningful sense — they had complex social organization, distinctive material culture, and effective military traditions — but they were not the kind of agriculturally settled tax-paying subjects that the ritsuryo system was designed to register.

For most of the Asuka-Nara period, the Yamato court had pursued a slow expansion of the frontier into Emishi territory — establishing fortified administrative posts, settling immigrant farmers, gradually drawing border populations into the registered tax base.
This gradual process accelerated under Kammu, who was determined to definitively bring the Emishi region under imperial control.
The campaigns of the 780s and 790s were the most intensive military operations the Yamato state had ever mounted.
They went badly at first.

The Emishi had a strong cavalry tradition, knew the difficult northern terrain, and could disperse and re-form against larger invading armies in ways that the Yamato conscript forces found difficult to counter.
The campaign of 789 — sent under the general Ki no Kosami with an army of perhaps 50,000 — was decisively defeated at the Subuse River by Emishi forces under their leader Aterui (ah-teh-ROO-ee).
Ki no Kosami's army lost over a thousand men dead and several thousand more wounded, a significant defeat for the Yamato side.
Kammu reorganized.

He recruited a new general, Sakanoue no Tamuramaro (sah-kah-noh-OO-eh noh tah-moo-rah-MAH-roh, 758–811), and gave him a new title: Sei-i Taishogun (SAY-ee TYE-shoh-gun — "Barbarian-Subduing Great General").

The title is the origin of the later word shogun (which would, under different historical circumstances, become the title of the de facto rulers of Japan from the late twelfth century onward — Heian Japan Ch 6 onward).
Tamuramaro would shape it into a permanent post.
Tamuramaro's campaigns of the 790s and early 800s gradually pushed the Yamato frontier northward.
He fought the Emishi with mounted forces, professional soldiers paid out of imperial revenues, and a willingness to negotiate with Emishi leaders rather than insist on unconditional subjugation.
Aterui himself eventually surrendered in 802 and was taken to Heijo-kyo (the old capital, now the religious center of the country though no longer the political one).
The court refused Tamuramaro's request to spare him; Aterui was executed.
The campaigns continued through the early 800s and gradually subdued the Emishi region down to roughly the modern boundary between Tohoku's central provinces and Hokkaido.
The Emishi campaigns had two enduring effects.
First, they exhausted the Taiho-Code conscript army system.
Mobilizing Japanese peasants under arms for years of frontier warfare in the cold northeast turned out to be politically and economically unsustainable.
Kammu eventually abolished the conscript system in 792 and replaced it with a smaller force of professional soldiers recruited from local strongmen.

This is the institutional foundation for the eventual rise of the warrior class — the bushi (BOO-shee) and eventually the samurai — that would dominate Japan from the late Heian period onward (Heian Japan Ch 4–6).
Second, the campaigns created the first regional warrior aristocracies.

The military families that supplied generals like Tamuramaro, that provided the professional cavalry, that learned to fight Emishi-style wars in the northeastern terrain, were the first generation of what became hereditary warrior lineages.
The northeastern frontier produced tough, mounted, militarily experienced families — the Abe, the Kiyowara, the eventual Northern Fujiwara — that would matter politically for centuries.
The Emishi wars are the unromantic but real beginning of Japanese warrior culture.

The legacy of the Asuka-Nara period — the 256 years from 538 to 794 — is enormous and largely invisible to the casual modern eye, because so much of what was built in this period became simply the structure of Japan, taken for granted by everything that came after.

The imperial line that the Asuka and Nara historians traced back to the gods continued unbroken through the Heian, Kamakura, Ashikaga, Tokugawa, and Meiji periods, all the way to the present day — an imperial line of officially 126 monarchs, of which about 60 reigned after the Asuka-Nara period closed, all of them building their legitimacy on the foundation that the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki had laid.
The Japanese imperial family today is the longest continuous reigning dynasty in the world, and that dynastic continuity was textually constructed in the Asuka and Nara periods.
The Buddhist establishment that Shomu and the kokubunji network created became the bedrock institution of pre-modern Japanese religion.

Subsequent centuries layered new Buddhist schools on top of the Nara foundations — Tendai and Shingon in the early Heian, Pure Land and Zen and Nichiren in the Kamakura — but the great Nara temples never lost their importance, and many continued to operate without interruption from the Asuka-Nara period to the present.
Todai-ji, Horyu-ji, Kofuku-ji, Yakushi-ji, Toshodai-ji, and dozens of others are still functioning Buddhist institutions today, with continuous monastic traditions reaching back twelve centuries.
The Tang-modeled state that the Taika Reform and the Taiho/Yoro Codes established became the conceptual framework of Japanese political thought.

Even when the actual operational reach of the central state failed in subsequent centuries — when the Heian-period shoen estates carved up the registered tax base, when the Kamakura shogunate established a parallel warrior government, when the Ashikaga and Tokugawa periods further fragmented political authority — the language and concepts of ritsuryo governance remained the official terminology.

The Meiji Restoration in 1868 explicitly invoked the Asuka-Nara model: it claimed to be returning Japan to the original imperial-bureaucratic state that the Taika Reform had attempted to build, before the warrior governments had usurped imperial authority.

The two great chronicles — the Kojiki and the Nihon Shoki — became the founding scriptures of Japanese national identity, especially after the late-Tokugawa and early-Meiji nativist scholars (the kokugaku movement) elevated them to a quasi-sacred status.
The myths they contain were taught as literal national history in pre-1945 Japanese schools and were one of the textual foundations of the wartime emperor cult.
Modern Japan has been more careful with these texts, but they remain canonical sources for understanding pre-modern Japanese self-conception.
The Manyoshu became the foundational anthology of the Japanese poetic tradition.
Every later poetry anthology (the Kokin Wakashu of 905, the Shin Kokin Wakashu of 1205, the medieval imperial anthologies, the Edo-period commentaries) defined itself in relation to the Manyoshu.

The vernacular Japanese literary tradition — including the Heian-period explosion of court literature in kana script — built on the Manyoshu's establishment of vernacular poetry as a respectable art form.

The capital city tradition — that the imperial court resided in a permanent grid-planned capital named with auspicious Chinese characters — held from Heijo-kyo onward through Heian-kyo, Edo, and Tokyo.
Kyoto preserves substantial portions of its Asuka-Nara-derived street grid into the modern city.
The basic civic geography of Japan was set in the Asuka and Nara periods.

And finally, the Asuka-Nara periods set the precedent for the deeper cultural pattern that would define Japan for the next millennium: a society that absorbed enormous amounts of foreign cultural material, especially from China and Korea, and transformed every borrowed element into something distinctively Japanese.
Buddhism became Japanese Buddhism.
Chinese writing became Japanese writing.
Tang government became Japanese government.
Korean architecture became Japanese architecture.

The pattern was not unique to the Asuka-Nara period — Japan would later absorb European industrial science in the Meiji era, American consumer culture in the postwar era, with the same selective creativity — but the pattern was established here.
The Yamato court of the Soga era had been a small, rural, clan-based polity.

The Heian court of 794 was a sophisticated imperial court that ran a Tang-modeled state, patronized a Buddhist establishment of continental scale, produced national chronicles in two scripts and poetry in a third, and held a capital city of 100,000-plus residents at the eastern end of the Silk Road.
The transformation took 256 years.
It was the foundation of everything that came next.
Cross-civ check: the move to Heian-kyo in 794 happened in a remarkable European moment.
Six years later, in 800, Charlemagne would be crowned Emperor of the Romans by Pope Leo III in Rome — the Carolingian moment that would reshape Western European political organization for centuries.

The Abbasid Caliphate under Harun al-Rashid (786–809) was at the height of its golden age, with Baghdad as the largest city in the Islamic world and the cultural capital of the Eurasian middle (Islamic Golden Age Ch 2).

In Tang China, the dynasty had survived the An Lushan Rebellion (Sui, Tang & Song China Ch 4) but was visibly weakening, with provincial governors increasingly autonomous and the central state's revenue base shrinking.
In Korea, the Unified Silla golden age was approaching its last century, with Korean trade networks reaching as far as the Persian Gulf.

The Viking Age had just begun — the raid on Lindisfarne in 793, one year before the Heian-kyo move, opened two and a half centuries of Scandinavian expansion across the North Atlantic and Europe (Viking Age Ch 1).

And in the Americas, the classic Maya civilization in the Yucatan was approaching its mysterious collapse in the ninth and tenth centuries (Maya Civilization Ch 7), and the middle-horizon empires of the Andes (Wari and Tiwanaku) were at their peak (Middle Horizon Empires Ch 1).

The world Kammu's new capital opened onto was a connected one — through the Silk Road, through the kentoshi missions, through Buddhist-monastic networks reaching across Eurasia — and Heian-kyo would spend its early centuries quietly producing one of the most distinctive aesthetic civilizations any of those connected regions ever generated.

chapters.title: The New Capital
sentences: In 794 CE, the Japanese emperor moved his capital, and it stayed put for the next thousand years.
The previous century of Japanese political history (Asuka-Nara Japan Ch 6–8) had been a story of capital-shuffling.

The court had moved every reign or two — sometimes for ritual reasons (an emperor's death polluted the capital site), sometimes for political ones (a rival faction's power was rooted in the existing capital), and sometimes because the elaborate Chinese-style permanent capital that the Nara reformers had finally built at Heijo-kyo (modern Nara) had gotten too tangled in Buddhist political intrigue to be governable.
The reforming emperor Kammu (KAH-moo, reigned 781–806) had had enough.
Kammu's solution came in two stages.
First, in 784, he moved the capital from Nara to a new site at Nagaoka-kyo (nah-gah-OH-kah-kyoh), about thirty miles north.
That capital lasted ten years and was abandoned after a series of disasters that the court interpreted as the angry ghost of Kammu's murdered brother taking revenge.
Then, in 794, Kammu picked a second new site, ten miles further north, in a basin ringed by mountains on three sides with two small rivers running through it.
The new city was named Heian-kyo (hay-AHN-kyoh, "the capital of peace and tranquility").
In the colloquial of later centuries it would simply be called Kyoto — "the capital." It is the capital of this book.
Heian-kyo is the city Heian Japan is named after, and the name covers the next 391 years of Japanese history.
That is a longer span than the United States has existed.
Within those four centuries the Japanese court invented a literature, a script, an aesthetic vocabulary, and a political system that had no real precedent in East Asia.
It also failed at the basic governance task of keeping armed men under control, and the failure produced the seven centuries of warrior rule that followed.
Both stories are in this book.
Both started with the city Kammu founded.
The city itself was a copy.
Or, more precisely, a smaller copy of a copy.
Kammu's planners had a model in front of them: the Tang Chinese capital at Chang'an (chahng-AHN, modern Xi'an), the largest and most influential city in the early-medieval world.
Chang'an at its height housed about a million people inside walls that enclosed roughly thirty square miles.
It was laid out on a strict north-south, east-west grid.
The imperial palace was at the north end, looking south down a wide central avenue called Suzaku Avenue (in Chinese, Zhuque).
The grid divided the city into rectangular wards, each enclosed by walls.

The Sui and Tang dynasties had used this layout for two centuries (Tang-Song China, by the way, was about to enter its long decline at exactly the moment Kammu was copying its template — Tang-Song China Ch 1).
The Japanese had already copied Chang'an once at Nara in 710.
Heian-kyo was a second copy, slightly different in proportions and roughly half the size — about nine square miles, planned for around 100,000 inhabitants.
The grid was strict: nine east-west avenues, eight north-south streets, dividing the city into rectangular blocks.
The imperial compound (the Daidairi, dye-DYE-ree) sat at the north end.

From its main gate, the wide central Suzaku Avenue (soo-ZAH-koo, named after the Vermilion Bird of southern Chinese cosmology) ran two and a half miles south to the Rashomon (rah-SHOH-mohn) gate, the city's main southern entrance.
The east half of the city was nominally Sakyo ("left capital") and the west half Ukyo ("right capital") — left and right from the perspective of a south-facing emperor at the north end.
Inside the imperial compound stood the Daigokuden (dye-go-koo-den), the audience hall where the emperor performed state ceremonies and received foreign envoys.
It was the largest building in the city — a vast Chinese-style hall with a tiled roof, vermilion-painted columns, and a raised throne platform inside.

The compound also held the Chodoin (CHOH-doh-in), where officials of the various government ministries did the actual work of administration, and the Dairi (DYE-ree), the residential palace where the emperor and his immediate family lived.
By Heian convention the emperor almost never left this compound except to visit shrines or temples.
He was a sacral figure, surrounded by ritual obligations, kept indoors by the etiquette of his own court.
The grid plan was the announcement of a Chinese-style state.

Cities laid out on rectangular grids — Chang'an, Nara, Heian-kyo — say we are organized, we are bureaucratic, we are the legitimate government of a centralized empire. (Cross-civ: the same architectural argument was being made in this period by other capitals consciously imitating each other.

Constantinople under the Macedonian dynasty had its own grid of ceremonial avenues — Byzantine Empire Ch 7 — and Baghdad's round city under the Abbasids was a deliberate cosmological statement — Islamic Golden Age Ch 2.
Capital architecture in the early-medieval world was always a political claim.) The grid did not entirely work.
The west half of Kyoto — Ukyo — was on marshy ground and was largely abandoned by the late ninth century, with the population concentrating in the better-drained east half.
The full Tang-style city plan was never quite occupied as designed.
But the basic grid survived, and modern Kyoto's downtown streets still run on it.
If you walk around central Kyoto today you are walking on Kammu's plan, half-erased by twelve centuries of fires and rebuildings but still legible underneath.
Kammu's other major reform was on the military side, and it would matter more than the city plan in the long run.

The Nara state had inherited a Chinese-style conscript army from the Asuka-period reformers (Asuka-Nara Japan Ch 6) — peasants levied for military service on a rotating basis, organized into provincial regiments, equipped at state expense, deployed to garrisons.
The system was modeled on Tang military organization and it had never worked well in Japan.
Japanese peasants were rice farmers, not warriors, and the rotational system pulled them off their farms during planting and harvest seasons.
Equipment was shoddy.
Morale was nonexistent.
Frontier campaigns against the Emishi (eh-MEE-shee), the indigenous people of northern Honshu who had never been incorporated into the Yamato state, kept failing.
The conscript army was an expensive Tang Chinese affectation that did not fit Japanese conditions.
In 792, two years before he founded Heian-kyo, Kammu abolished the conscript army in most provinces.

He kept it on the frontier zones where active campaigning continued, but the rest of the country shifted to a different system: provincial defense was delegated to kondei (KOHN-day, "stalwart youths"), a smaller force recruited from the sons of local landholding officials — men who had grown up around horses and weapons and could afford their own equipment.
Tax collection and law enforcement at the local level were contracted out to provincial governors, who were given wide discretion in how they ran their territories.
This looks technocratic.
It is also one of the most consequential decisions in Japanese history.

By replacing a state-controlled peasant army with a privatized warrior caste recruited from the gentry, Kammu set up the institutional template for the samurai (SAH-moo-rye, "those who serve") class that would slowly take over the country over the next four hundred years.
The Heian court would continue to function as if it commanded the country's military.
In practice, after 792, organized violence in Japan was in the hands of the local landowners.
The court did not really notice this for two centuries.
By the time it did notice, in the eleventh century, it was too late to do anything about it.
The frontier campaigns continued.
Between 797 and 811, the general Sakanoue no Tamuramaro (sah-kah-no-WEH no tah-moo-rah-MAH-roh) led repeated expeditions into the Emishi territory of northern Honshu.
He was named Sei-i Taishogun (SAY-ee TYE-shoh-goon, "barbarian-subduing great general"), a title invented for the campaign.

The campaigns broke organized Emishi resistance, pushed the Yamato frontier deep into modern Iwate and Aomori prefectures, and established a chain of fortified administrative centers across the north.
Tamuramaro's title — usually shortened to shogun — would not be politically loaded for another four centuries.
When Yoritomo took it in 1192 (Chapter 8), he was deliberately reaching back to Tamuramaro's precedent. (The Emishi campaigns are the dark side of Heian-kyo's elegance.

While the court at Kyoto was beginning to write delicate poetry about cherry blossoms, the same state was conducting a long, grinding campaign of conquest against the indigenous people of northern Honshu, displacing them from ancestral lands and incorporating their territory into the Yamato administrative system.
The Heian aesthetic vocabulary did not extend to ethnic warfare on the frontier.) The early Heian court was a small institution.

The court ranks were inherited from the Nara system: officials were divided into nine numerical ranks, each subdivided into sub-ranks, each carrying specific privileges — what color robes you could wear, what rooms you could enter at the palace, what kind of carriage you could ride in, what salary you received in tax-grain stipends.
The top three ranks were the inner aristocracy — perhaps two hundred families at most — and effectively all political life happened among them.

The lower ranks were a buffer zone of working bureaucrats; below that were the gentry who would eventually produce the warrior class, and then everyone else, who did not exist as far as the court was concerned.

Within the inner aristocracy, the most important institution was the Council of State (the Daijokan, dye-JOH-kahn) — a small body of senior nobles who advised the emperor and ran the major ministries.
The Council was theoretically chaired by the Daijo-daijin (dye-JOH-DYE-jin, "Grand Minister of State"), an office so prestigious that it was usually left vacant when no one was qualified to hold it.

The actual day-to-day senior official was usually the Sadaijin (SAH-dye-jin, "Minister of the Left") or his slightly junior counterpart the Udaijin (OO-dye-jin, "Minister of the Right"), with various Major and Minor Counselors below them.
This Council of State was the system the Fujiwara would soon hijack from inside (Chapter 3).
They did it not by abolishing the Council or seizing the throne, but by getting Fujiwara men appointed to all the senior positions and Fujiwara women married to all the emperors.
The institutional architecture was Chinese; the political life it housed turned out to be something distinctively Japanese.

The early Heian decades — Kammu's reign and the reigns of his immediate successors Heizei (HAY-zay, 806–809), Saga (SAH-gah, 809–823), and Junna (JOON-nah, 823–833) — were a period of high-Chinese cultural seriousness.
The court wrote poetry in Chinese and held composition contests judged on Tang aesthetic standards.
The emperors took strong personal interest in Chinese-style government.
Three official imperial anthologies of Chinese-language poetry were compiled during this period.
Saga in particular was a serious calligrapher in the Chinese tradition and a patron of imported Tang-style culture.
But underneath the Chinese surface, a Japanese counter-current was already running.
The early Heian decades are also when the two foundational figures of Japanese Buddhism set up shop in the mountains around the new capital.
They are the subject of Chapter 2.

A pause to notice the historical moment: Kammu's reign and the founding of Heian-kyo (794) coincide with Charlemagne's coronation as Holy Roman Emperor in 800 (Early Medieval Europe Ch 6) and with the long Abbasid peak under Harun al-Rashid in Baghdad (Islamic Golden Age Ch 3).

Three of the great early-medieval capitals — Aachen, Baghdad, Heian-kyo — were being built or rebuilt within the same generation, by rulers consciously trying to reconstitute imperial models from earlier eras (Roman for Charlemagne, Sassanian for the Abbasids, Tang for Kammu).
None of the three knew the others existed in any detail.
The convergence is a coincidence, but a striking one.
The Tang Dynasty whose capital Kammu was copying was about to enter its long decline (Tang-Song China Ch 4).

The An Lushan rebellion of 755–763 had broken Tang central authority a generation earlier, and by Kammu's reign the dynasty was visibly weakened — though no one in 794 would have predicted that the great civilization Japan had spent two centuries learning from would be effectively gone within a hundred years.
By the time Sugawara no Michizane recommended canceling the embassies in 894 (Chapter 3), the Tang would be in its death spiral.
Heian Japan thus had the strange historical experience of growing up modeling itself on a civilization that, halfway through the Heian period, ceased to exist.

Cross-civ check: the founding of Heian-kyo in 794 happened during what historians sometimes call the Carolingian moment in Western Europe — Charlemagne's brief reconstitution of an empire in the West (Early Medieval Europe Ch 6) that would itself fragment within fifty years of his death.
In Constantinople, the Macedonian dynasty was about to begin its long brilliant century (Byzantine Empire Ch 7).
In Korea, the Silla kingdom that had unified the peninsula in the 670s was entering its late decline (Ancient Korea Ch 7).
In Baghdad, the Abbasid caliphate under Harun al-Rashid was at the peak of the Islamic Golden Age (Islamic Golden Age Ch 3).
In the Andes, the Wari and Tiwanaku empires were running parallel imperial projects (Andean Kingdoms Ch 1).
The Heian project was not alone, but it was unusually long-lived.
None of those other early-medieval institutions still existed in 1185, and Heian-kyo was still the imperial capital.

chapters.title: Saicho and Kukai
sentences: The two most important Japanese Buddhist figures of the early ninth century met as rivals, traveled to Tang China together, came back with completely different teachings, founded the two great Japanese Buddhist mountains, and reshaped Japanese religious life so thoroughly that everything that came afterward — including the Pure Land schools of the late Heian, the Zen schools of the Kamakura era, and modern Japanese Buddhism — runs back to one of them or the other.
Their names are Saicho (SYE-choh, 767–822) and Kukai (KOO-kye, 774–835).
They are the founders, respectively, of the Tendai (TEN-dye) and Shingon (SHIN-gohn) schools of Japanese Buddhism.
Tendai's headquarters is Enryakuji (en-RYAH-koo-jee) on Mount Hiei (HEE-ay), northeast of Kyoto.
Shingon's headquarters is Kongobuji (kohn-GOH-boo-jee) on Mount Koya (KOH-yah), south of the capital in the Kii peninsula.

These two mountains — Hiei and Koya — are the two great religious centers of medieval Japan, the way Cluny and Citeaux were the great monastic centers of medieval France or the way Athos and the Studite monasteries were the great centers of Byzantine monasticism.
Both Saicho and Kukai were the products of the Chinese-style state Buddhism that Nara had built in the eighth century (Asuka-Nara Japan Ch 7).
Both wanted to escape it.
Both succeeded, and the Buddhism they built was unmistakably more Japanese than what they had learned from.
To understand what they did, you have to know what they were reacting to.

The Buddhism the Nara court had patronized was state Buddhism in a literal institutional sense: temples were built with state money, monks were ordained under state license, scriptures were copied in state-funded scriptoria, and the ostensible purpose of the whole apparatus was to protect the state through ritual.

The flagship project had been Todaiji (TOH-dye-jee) and its enormous bronze Vairocana Buddha (Asuka-Nara Japan Ch 7), dedicated in 752 with the explicit purpose of generating spiritual merit for the imperial state.

The Nara schools — six recognized doctrinal traditions called Nanto Rokushu (NAHN-toh roh-KOO-shoo, "the six schools of the southern capital") — were organized around scholarly study of Indian and Chinese Buddhist texts.

They were located in the capital, run by aristocratic monks, funded by aristocratic patrons, and politically powerful enough that one of the explicit reasons Kammu moved the capital to Heian-kyo in 794 was to get away from them.
Both Saicho and Kukai started their careers inside this Nara system.
Both grew dissatisfied with it.

Both came to believe that what Japan needed was a different kind of Buddhism — practiced in mountain retreats rather than urban temples, focused on direct spiritual experience rather than scholastic textual analysis, and (this was the key strategic insight) sponsored by the new emperor at Heian-kyo rather than tied to the old Nara establishment.
Both also realized that to do this credibly, they would need to study in Tang China.
In 804, the Japanese government dispatched the seventeenth official embassy to the Tang court.
The embassy involved four ships sailing from Kyushu across the East China Sea — a dangerous voyage that often killed half the people who attempted it.
Two of the four ships in the 804 embassy made it.
Saicho was on one.
Kukai was on the other.
They had different missions and different temperaments.

Saicho was a quiet, scholarly monk in his late thirties who already had a small mountain hermitage on Hiei and had been promised official sponsorship to bring back a specific teaching he was interested in.
Kukai was an unknown thirty-year-old, with no official status to speak of, who had talked his way onto the embassy as a junior monk and was planning to stay in China for the full twenty-year tour.
They probably did not know each other before the trip.
They certainly did not travel together — separate ships, separate landfalls, separate itineraries inside China.
They became rivals, then collaborators, then rivals again.
The story is one of the great early-medieval intellectual relationships.
Saicho's destination was Mount Tiantai (tee-EN-tye), a major Chinese Buddhist center in modern Zhejiang province.

Tiantai was the headquarters of a Chinese school of the same name (the Japanese pronounce the characters "Tendai," hence the school's Japanese name) that took the Lotus Sutra as the central scripture of Buddhism and organized all other Buddhist teachings as preliminary stages leading up to it.
Saicho had been studying Tiantai texts in Japan; he wanted authoritative initiation from Chinese masters.
He spent eight months on Mount Tiantai, received the transmissions, collected several hundred volumes of texts, and sailed back to Japan in 805.

Almost as an afterthought, on the return voyage, Saicho stopped at another monastery and received initiation into a different tradition: mikkyo (MEEK-kyoh, "esoteric teachings"), the strand of Buddhism centered on mantras, mandalas, mudras, and the doctrine that buddhahood could be attained in this very life through ritual technique.
He did not have time for full training in the esoteric tradition.
He took what he could and went home.
This shortcut would later become a problem.
Kukai's mission was different.
Kukai went straight to Chang'an itself, the Tang capital, and spent two years there studying the new esoteric Buddhism that had been arriving from India.

His teacher was the master Huiguo (HWAY-gwoh), an Indian-trained monk who had become one of the great esoteric teachers of the Tang and who was looking for a successor to carry the tradition out of China.
Huiguo, on meeting Kukai, declared that he had been waiting for him.

Within months Huiguo had transmitted the full esoteric initiations — both of the two great mandalas of mikkyo, the Womb Realm (Taizokai) and the Diamond Realm (Kongokai) — and had named Kukai his Dharma successor.
Then Huiguo died.
Kukai, now the inheritor of a major Tang Buddhist lineage at age thirty-two, returned to Japan in 806 with the full apparatus of esoteric Buddhism.
Esoteric Buddhism — mikkyo in Japanese, Vajrayana ("diamond vehicle") in Sanskrit — needs explaining, because it is a strange tradition by the standards of the rest of Japanese Buddhism.

The basic assumption of mikkyo is that the universe is the body, speech, and mind of the cosmic Buddha Mahavairocana (mah-hah-vye-ROH-chah-nah, "the great illuminating one") — that everything that exists is a continuous expression of buddha-nature.

From this premise, mikkyo derives a ritual technology: if you can align your own body, speech, and mind with the cosmic Buddha through the right physical postures (mudras, MOO-drahs, ritual hand gestures), the right sounds (mantras, MAHN-trahs, sacred Sanskrit syllables), and the right mental visualizations (focusing on a mandala, MAHN-dah-lah, a geometric diagram of the cosmos), then you can become the Buddha in this lifetime, in this body.
This is a much faster claim than mainstream Buddhism, which generally said enlightenment took many lifetimes of disciplined practice.
The ritual apparatus is dense.
A senior mikkyo monk has to memorize hundreds of mantras, master dozens of mudras, and visualize complex multi-deity mandalas in precise detail.

The mandalas themselves are works of geometric art — painted on silk or rendered as three-dimensional installations in temple halls — with deities arranged in hierarchical concentric squares around a central Buddha.

The two foundational mandalas of Shingon are the Diamond Realm (representing the Buddha's wisdom) and the Womb Realm (representing the Buddha's compassion); together they describe the cosmos as Shingon understands it. (Cross-civ: Vajrayana Buddhism was simultaneously becoming the dominant Buddhist form in Tibet during this period — the Tibetan king Trisong Detsen had invited the Indian master Padmasambhava in the 770s — and would later move to Mongolia under Yuan dynasty patronage.

The technology of mantras, mandalas, and ritual visualization that Kukai brought to Japan was part of a larger Indian export that was reshaping Buddhism across half of Asia.) For an early-medieval Japanese aristocrat, mikkyo had two enormous appeals.
First, it promised quick spiritual results — buddhahood in this body, through ritual technique, without thirty years of textual study.
Second, it was visually and aurally spectacular.

Mikkyo ceremonies involved chanting in Sanskrit, elaborate altar arrangements, fire offerings (goma, GOH-mah, ritual fires that consume offerings while the priest visualizes the burning of attachments), and consecrated bronze ritual implements (the vajra, VAH-jrah, "thunderbolt" or "diamond"; the bell, the lotus).
It was sensory religion.
It made the older Nara textual scholasticism look bookish and dull.
Kukai brought all of this back to Japan in 806 and proceeded to remake Japanese Buddhism around it.
Kukai's career after his return is one of the most extraordinary in Japanese cultural history.

He arrived back in Kyushu in 806 as a still-junior monk with no official patronage, sat for several years in Kyushu temples reorganizing the texts and ritual implements he had brought back, and only in 809 was invited to the new capital.
Once at court, he moved fast.

Within a few years he had cultivated personal relationships with the emperor (Saga, who was a serious Chinese-trained calligrapher and a fellow art enthusiast), founded his first major temple in the capital area (Toji, near the Rashomon gate at the south end of Kyoto), been appointed administrator of several state Buddhist institutions, and begun teaching the full esoteric initiations to selected disciples.
In 816, the court granted him a remote mountain site for his main monastic complex: Mount Koya, in the Kii peninsula south of the capital, a thousand-meter plateau ringed by eight peaks.
Kukai chose the location for both geomantic and practical reasons.
The peaks form a natural three-dimensional mandala — the central plateau corresponding to the central Buddha, the eight surrounding peaks corresponding to the eight surrounding deities.
It was also remote enough to be isolated from the politics of the capital.
By 819 the central temple complex was consecrated.
Kukai spent the rest of his life dividing his time between Toji in the capital and Koya in the mountains.
Kukai's other accomplishments were enormous.
He was a major calligrapher, considered one of the three brushes of Heian art alongside Emperor Saga and the courtier Tachibana no Hayanari.
He was a prolific writer whose collected works run to dozens of volumes — religious treatises, poetry, calligraphic theory, dictionaries.
He founded the first commoner school in Japanese history, the Shugei Shuchiin (shoo-GAY shoo-CHEE-in), open to non-aristocratic students, in 828.
He was a credible engineer who designed irrigation works and roads.
He is traditionally credited with the development of the kana syllabary — though the actual development was probably gradual and involved many hands (Chapter 4).
He died in 835 at Mount Koya.
According to Shingon tradition he did not actually die — he entered a state of permanent meditation in the inner sanctuary of Koya, where he remains to this day, awaiting the future Buddha Maitreya.
Pilgrims who visit Mount Koya bring food offerings to his tomb on the assumption that he is still alive inside.
The posthumous title Kobo Daishi (KOH-boh DYE-shee, "the great teacher who spread the dharma") was conferred by an emperor in 921 and has stuck ever since.
Modern scholars are divided on how much of the legendary Kukai is the historical Kukai.

The legendary version is the polymath who invented kana, founded a school for commoners, designed irrigation systems, calligraphed the imperial palace gates, and entered eternal meditation rather than die.

The historical version is more modest: a brilliant, ambitious monk who imported a major foreign tradition, built it into Japan's most institutionally successful Buddhist school, and accumulated enough cultural capital that his afterlife in Japanese memory swelled to absorb every available achievement.
Both versions are real, in different senses.
Saicho's story is more subdued but no less important.
Saicho returned to Mount Hiei in 805 with his Tiantai initiation and his late-acquired dose of esoteric teaching.

He immediately ran into a problem: in eighth-century Japan, monastic ordination was strictly controlled by the Nara establishment, which licensed all new monks at one of three official ordination platforms in the Nara region.
Saicho wanted to ordain his own monks at a new platform on Mount Hiei, independent of Nara control.
The Nara schools, predictably, refused to permit this.
The dispute dragged on for years and was only resolved a week after Saicho's death in 822, when the court granted Hiei the long-requested ordination platform.
This was the institutional moment that made Tendai possible — Hiei could now produce its own monks without going through the Nara establishment.
Saicho's other problem was Kukai.
Saicho had brought back only a partial dose of esoteric teaching from his shortened study in China, and in the years after Kukai's return Saicho repeatedly approached Kukai for further initiations.

Kukai gave him some basic transmissions but eventually refused to confer the full esoteric ordinations, on the grounds that they could not be transmitted casually — they required years of supervised practice.
The two men corresponded.
The correspondence cooled.
They became opposing figures rather than collaborators.

Saicho's Tendai school continued to incorporate esoteric elements (it became a kind of hybrid: Lotus Sutra study at the core, esoteric ritual layered on top), but the fully developed esoteric tradition belonged to Kukai's Shingon.
This division — Tendai's "exoteric-plus-esoteric" synthesis on Hiei, Shingon's pure esotericism on Koya — defined Japanese Buddhism for the rest of the Heian period.
What made Hiei matter in the long run was less Saicho's specific teaching and more the institutional structure he set up.

Enryakuji on Mount Hiei was designed as a great Mahayana monastic university where monks studied multiple Buddhist traditions, lived in mountain seclusion, and produced teachers who would then go out and lead the various schools of Japanese Buddhism.
By the late Heian period, almost every major innovator in Japanese Buddhism had spent formative years on Mount Hiei.
Honen (Chapter 6), the founder of Pure Land Buddhism.
Eisai, who later founded the Rinzai Zen school.
Dogen, who founded Soto Zen.
Nichiren, who founded the Lotus-centered Nichiren school.
All of them trained on Mount Hiei before founding their own movements.
Hiei was the seedbed.
It was also a small army.

By the late Heian period, Enryakuji had thousands of resident monks and tens of thousands of armed retainers — the sohei (SOH-hay, "warrior monks") (Chapter 6) — who functioned as a private military force that could march down from the mountain to enforce temple demands on the court below.
The cloistered emperor Shirakawa (Chapter 6) famously complained that there were three things in his realm he could not control: the dice, the waters of the Kamo River, and the monks of Mount Hiei.
Saicho had built more than he intended.
The combined effect of Saicho and Kukai was that, by the middle of the ninth century, Japanese Buddhism had relocated its center of gravity.
The old Nara schools continued to exist — they still do — but the live action had moved to the mountains: Hiei to the northeast of the capital, Koya to the south.
Both mountains had built esoteric ritual into the core of their practice.
Both were generating monks, texts, and architectural patterns at a rapid clip.
Both were tightly integrated with the new Heian court at Kyoto rather than the old Nara establishment.
This restructuring was not just a religious development.
It was a cultural one.

The Heian aesthetic vocabulary — the obsession with ritual, with calligraphy, with elaborate visual arrangement, with mandalas of color and form — borrows directly from the esoteric Buddhist sensibility that Kukai had imported.

The Heian taste for the symbolic over the literal, for layered meaning rather than stated meaning, for the gesture that points beyond itself, for the resonant detail rather than the explicit declaration — all of this is mikkyo aesthetics, transposed from the temple to the court.

The Tale of Genji (Chapter 5), with its extraordinary attention to mood, color, scent, and the suggestive incomplete gesture, is among other things a courtly application of the sensibility Kukai brought back from Chang'an in 806. (The relationship between mikkyo and the Heian court aesthetic is one of the underappreciated features of Japanese cultural history.

The court did not become Buddhist in the doctrinal sense — most Heian courtiers were perfectly comfortable maintaining Shinto rituals alongside Buddhist ones, and the shinbutsu-shugo synthesis described later in this chapter made the boundary deliberately permeable.
But the courtly visual and emotional grammar, the things the court found beautiful, came largely from mikkyo.

This is one reason the Heian court aesthetic looks so distinctive against Tang Chinese taste: Tang aesthetics were based on Confucian classical models; Heian aesthetics were based on esoteric Buddhist ones, transposed into secular use.) The other religious development of the early Heian period was the slow institutional formalization of Shinto (SHIN-toh, "the way of the kami").

Shinto is the indigenous Japanese spiritual tradition: the veneration of kami (KAH-mee), nature spirits and ancestral deities associated with specific places, mountains, rivers, trees, shrines, and clan lineages.

Shinto had existed as a folk practice for millennia (Prehistoric Japan Ch 7) and the imperial cult itself was the apex of an elaborate Shinto genealogy — the emperor as descendant of the sun goddess Amaterasu, channeling divine authority through ritual rather than through the mandate of any text.
But Shinto had never been systematized.
Different shrines had different traditions; ritual procedures varied by locality; there was no central institutional structure binding the network together.
This changed in the early tenth century.

In 927, after decades of compilation work, the court issued the Engishiki (en-GEE-shee-kee, "Procedures of the Engi era"), a fifty-volume compendium of ritual and administrative regulations that included a detailed list of more than 2,800 official Shinto shrines across Japan, with their hierarchical rankings, their ritual procedures, and their specified offerings.

The Engishiki made Shinto official: the shrine network was now a recognized organ of the state, with the imperial house at its apex and the local shrines extending the imperial ritual downward into every village.
This institutional Shinto coexisted comfortably with Buddhism.
It coexisted, in fact, by interpenetrating it.

Buddhist temples maintained Shinto shrines on their grounds; Shinto shrines hosted Buddhist sutra readings; the same priests served at both; the same worshippers prayed at both without sensing any contradiction.

The doctrinal explanation that emerged was honji suijaku (HOHN-jee swee-JAH-koo, "original ground, manifest traces"), the idea that the kami of Shinto were local Japanese manifestations (suijaku) of the cosmic Buddhas of mikkyo (honji).
The sun goddess Amaterasu was a manifestation of the cosmic Buddha Mahavairocana.
The thunder kami Susanoo was a manifestation of one of the wisdom kings.
Each shrine had a corresponding Buddha.
Each Buddha had a corresponding kami.
The whole religious landscape was woven together into a single seamless system called shinbutsu-shugo (shin-BOO-tsoo SHOO-goh, "the merging of kami and Buddhas").

This synthesis lasted from roughly the ninth century through the nineteenth, when the Meiji government in 1868 forcibly separated Shinto from Buddhism as part of an emperor-centered nationalist reconstruction.
The forced separation broke a thousand-year tradition.

Most major Japanese religious sites still bear the marks of pre-Meiji syncretism — Buddhist halls inside Shinto shrine compounds, Shinto torii gates outside Buddhist temples, kami worshipped at temples and Buddhas at shrines. (Cross-civ: peaceful coexistence of two distinct religious traditions inside the same culture is rarer than the Heian case makes it look.
Contemporary medieval Europe was a one-religion zone where any deviation got you killed.

The Abbasid Caliphate of the same period — Islamic Golden Age Ch 3 — tolerated minority religions on the dhimmi ("protected peoples") legal model, but the framing was that Islam was true and the others were grudgingly permitted.
The Heian shinbutsu-shugo synthesis was different: not toleration of one religion by another, but doctrinal interpenetration to the point that the categories blurred.

The closest medieval parallel is probably the syncretism of Daoism, Confucianism, and Buddhism at the Tang court — Tang-Song China Ch 4 — but even there the three traditions remained more institutionally distinct than Heian Shinto and Buddhism became.) By the middle of the ninth century, the religious landscape of Heian Japan was set.
The two great Buddhist mountains — Hiei and Koya — were operational.
The esoteric ritual technology that Kukai had imported was reshaping aesthetic life across the court.
The Shinto shrine network was being institutionalized into a state ritual system.
The shinbutsu-shugo synthesis was emerging as the operating consensus.
What was about to happen in the political sphere was even more consequential.
The Fujiwara clan was about to take over.

Cross-civ check: while Saicho and Kukai were importing esoteric Buddhism to Japan in the early ninth century, comparable religious developments were happening across the civilizational arc that Buddhism connected.

In Tibet, the king Trisong Detsen had imported Indian Vajrayana masters (Padmasambhava and Shantarakshita) in the 770s and was establishing the Tibetan Buddhist tradition that would flower under the second diffusion in the eleventh century.

In Korea, the Silla kingdom was patronizing Hwaom (the Korean version of Chinese Huayan) and Son (the Korean version of Chan/Zen) Buddhism, and Korean monks were among the teachers that Saicho and Kukai had encountered in China (Ancient Korea Ch 7).

In Tang China, the Buddhist establishment was about to be devastated by the Huichang Persecution of 845, in which the emperor Wuzong destroyed thousands of monasteries and forcibly defrocked hundreds of thousands of monks — a disaster that ironically helped Japan, since many of the texts and ritual lineages that Wuzong destroyed in China survived only in the Japanese copies that Saicho and Kukai had brought back.
The Tang collapse meant that Tendai and Shingon eventually became the most institutionally complete versions of their traditions anywhere in East Asia.

chapters.title: The Fujiwara Regency
sentences: For two centuries, the Japanese emperor was a child.
Not always literally — sometimes the man on the throne was a healthy adult with his own opinions — but functionally.
The real power lay with whoever held the position of regent, and the position of regent was effectively hereditary in a single noble family: the Fujiwara.
This sentence understates the strangeness of the situation.
The Fujiwara never deposed an emperor.
They never claimed the throne.
They never even formally challenged imperial authority.
The imperial institution remained intact — the emperor performed state rituals, conferred court ranks, and was treated with elaborate ceremonial deference.

The Fujiwara simply made sure that every emperor, from childhood onward, was their grandson, their nephew, their son-in-law, or all three; that all senior court positions were held by Fujiwara men; and that the actual administrative decisions ran through the regent's office rather than through the emperor's personal staff.
They controlled the throne by encircling it.

This is the pattern that runs through Heian political history from the middle of the ninth century to the late eleventh: the emperor was the symbolic center, and the Fujiwara regent was the actual ruler.
The system worked, in the sense that it produced two centuries of relative political stability and a flowering of court culture without precedent in East Asia.
It also failed, in the sense that the institutional logic of marriage politics eventually broke down (Chapter 6) and left the court unable to govern.
The Fujiwara had been climbing for a long time before they got to the regency.
The clan's founding moment was 645 CE (Asuka-Nara Japan Ch 4), when the courtier Nakatomi no Kamatari helped Prince Naka no Oe overthrow the dominant Soga clan in a coup.
As his reward, Kamatari received a new family name — Fujiwara ("wisteria field") — and a permanent place at the top of the court.
For the next two centuries, the Fujiwara were one of several powerful court families competing for influence, and they did better than most.
They produced effective ministers, married into the imperial family at every opportunity, and waited.
The breakthrough came under Fujiwara no Yoshifusa (yoh-shee-FOO-sah, 804–872).
Yoshifusa had been a senior official under three emperors and had married his daughter to one of them, producing a son who became Emperor Montoku in 850.
When Montoku died in 858 leaving an eight-year-old as heir (Emperor Seiwa, SAY-wah), Yoshifusa — Seiwa's grandfather on his mother's side — was the obvious choice for regent.
He took the title sessho (SES-shoh, "regent for a child emperor"), an office that had previously been held only by members of the imperial family itself.
Yoshifusa was the first non-imperial regent in Japanese history.
The precedent stuck.
Yoshifusa's adopted son and successor Fujiwara no Mototsune extended the model.
When Seiwa abdicated in 876 and was replaced by another minor (Emperor Yozei), Mototsune was again sessho.

When Yozei was eventually deposed for instability in 884 and replaced by an adult emperor (Koko), Mototsune was given a new title — kampaku (KAHM-pah-koo, "regent for an adult emperor") — that legalized continued Fujiwara dominance even when there was no minor on the throne.
Between sessho and kampaku, the Fujiwara now had a regency office available regardless of the emperor's age.

The institutional formula was: Fujiwara man marries his daughter to the emperor; emperor produces son with Fujiwara daughter; emperor abdicates or dies; son becomes emperor; son's maternal grandfather (a Fujiwara) becomes regent.
The system rewarded fertility — the more daughters you could marry to emperors, the more likely your line would dominate the next generation — and it rewarded longevity.

A Fujiwara patriarch who outlived the emperors he was related to could end up grandfather to multiple consecutive sovereigns, regent for all of them, and the most powerful man in the country for decades on end. (This is structurally similar to several other medieval systems where formal sovereignty was separated from actual power.
The Merovingian "do-nothing kings" of seventh-century Frankia were figureheads while the Carolingian mayors of the palace ran the country (Early Medieval Europe Ch 5).
The Abbasid caliphs in Baghdad after the late ninth century were figureheads while the Buyid and then Seljuk sultans ran the country (Islamic Golden Age Ch 4).
The Heian arrangement is unusual mainly in its longevity — most figurehead arrangements eventually got resolved by someone formally taking the throne.
The Fujiwara never did.

They left the imperial institution untouched and operated through it, which turned out to be a more durable design.) The high tide of the early Fujiwara was the career of Sugawara no Michizane (soo-gah-WAH-rah no mee-chee-ZAH-neh, 845–903), and Sugawara no Michizane was not a Fujiwara.
Michizane was a brilliant scholar from the Sugawara, a family of court historians and Confucian classicists.

He rose through the literary bureaucracy on talent, became one of the leading Chinese-style poets of his generation, served as governor of Sanuki Province, and by the 880s was a senior court official.
Emperor Uda (OO-dah, reigned 887–897), who was actively trying to reduce Fujiwara influence on the throne, made Michizane his right-hand man.
Under Uda's patronage, Michizane became Minister of the Right (Udaijin) in 899, a position normally reserved for a senior Fujiwara.
Michizane is the figure who closed the door on direct cultural traffic with Tang China.
In 894, the court was preparing to send the next official embassy to Chang'an.
Michizane, who had read the recent dispatches from Japanese travelers in China, recommended that the embassy be cancelled.

His argument was practical: the Tang Dynasty was visibly disintegrating (it had perhaps fifteen years left, though no one knew that yet), the voyages across the Korea Strait were dangerous and expensive, and the cultural benefits of continued direct contact no longer justified the costs.
The court agreed.
The embassy was cancelled.
No further official Japanese embassy went to China for the next 700 years.
This was not isolationism — Japanese pilgrim monks continued to travel to China privately, and Chinese merchants continued to call at Kyushu ports — but it was a major institutional turn.
The Tang model that had structured Japanese government for two centuries was no longer the live reference.
Japanese culture would now develop on its own terms, with Chinese influences mediated through private trade rather than state embassies.

The kana writing system (Chapter 4), the vernacular literature of the women's courts (Chapter 5), the indigenous aesthetic vocabulary — all of these depend on the inward turn that began in 894. (Modern scholars have sometimes overstated this.

The cancellation of embassies was specifically the cancellation of the formal state-sponsored mission; private contact with China continued throughout the Heian period and was actively encouraged by some emperors.
But the symbolic break was real.
After 894, the Heian court no longer thought of itself as a satellite of Tang civilization.
It thought of itself as the center of its own civilization.) Michizane did not enjoy his triumph for long.
In 901, Fujiwara no Tokihira — head of the Fujiwara clan and Michizane's chief political rival — engineered Michizane's downfall.
The accusation was that Michizane was conspiring to put his own son-in-law on the throne in place of the reigning emperor.
The evidence was thin.
The new emperor (Daigo, who was Tokihira's grand-nephew through marriage) accepted the accusation and exiled Michizane to Dazaifu (dah-ZYE-foo) in distant Kyushu.
Michizane lived in poverty there, separated from his family, writing increasingly bitter Chinese-style poetry about his fate.
He died in 903.
What happened next is the strangest part of the story.
After Michizane's death, the capital was hit by a series of disasters: plagues, droughts, fires, lightning strikes on the palace.
In 909 Tokihira himself died at thirty-eight; the Fujiwara faction interpreted his death as Michizane's spiritual revenge.
Several senior Fujiwara died over the next two decades under circumstances that were superstitiously linked to Michizane.

In 930, lightning struck the Seiryoden (the imperial residential hall) during a court conference and killed several senior officials in front of the emperor; the emperor went into shock and died three months later.
The court concluded that Michizane's angry ghost was destroying the capital.
The solution was to deify him.
In 947, a shrine was established for Michizane at Kitano (KEE-tah-noh) in the northwestern part of Kyoto, and he was elevated to the status of Tenjin (TEN-jin, "heavenly deity").
The deification was complete: Tenjin was now a recognized kami, with shrines, festivals, and an official rank in the court ritual hierarchy.
The original posthumous goal was to appease his ghost.
The eventual outcome was something different: because Michizane had been the most distinguished scholar of his generation, Tenjin was reinterpreted as the patron deity of learning and scholarship.
By the medieval period, Japanese students were praying at Tenjin shrines before exams.
They still are.
There are roughly 14,000 Tenjin shrines across Japan, and the main shrines at Kitano in Kyoto and Dazaifu in Kyushu draw millions of pilgrims a year, mostly students.
This is, as far as I know, the only case in world history of a government bureaucrat being deified because his former colleagues felt guilty about firing him.
After Michizane's destruction, the Fujiwara had no serious rivals at court for the next century.

The clan went through several internal succession struggles — the Fujiwara had multiple branches, and the senior Hokke ("northern house") branch had to fight off challenges from junior Fujiwara branches every generation — but no non-Fujiwara family ever again came close to Michizane's level of influence.
The kampaku and sessho offices were rotated among senior Hokke Fujiwara men.
The empresses and imperial concubines were almost exclusively Fujiwara women.
The most senior court positions — Minister of the Left, Minister of the Right, Major Counselor, Middle Counselor — were filled by Fujiwara appointees.
The system reached its peak under Fujiwara no Michinaga (mee-chee-NAH-gah, 966–1027).
Michinaga was the fifth son of Fujiwara no Kaneie, who had been kampaku in the 980s.
He was not the obvious heir — his older brothers were ahead of him in line.
But the Fujiwara succession in this generation was unusually cursed.
Michinaga's two oldest brothers died young, his third brother died of smallpox, his fourth brother (Michikane) became kampaku and died seven days into the office.
By 995 Michinaga was the senior Fujiwara man standing, and he held effective control of the court for the next thirty-two years.
He never took the title kampaku itself.
Instead he served as nairan (NYE-rahn, "examiner of imperial documents"), a less formal position that allowed him to review and approve all official memoranda before they reached the emperor.
The actual title was less important than the network of relationships.
Michinaga married four daughters to four successive emperors.
His daughters bore the next three emperors.
His grandsons all became emperors in succession (Go-Ichijo, Go-Suzaku, Go-Reizei), with Michinaga as their maternal grandfather and de facto guardian.
By the late 1010s he was father-in-law to one emperor, grandfather to the next, and great-grandfather to the one after that.
The succession ran through his bloodline three generations deep.
Michinaga's position was unique even by Fujiwara standards.
The traditional historian's marker for it is the full moon poem he composed at a banquet in 1018, celebrating the elevation of his third daughter Ishi to the rank of empress.
The poem is short.
In transliteration it runs: Kono yo o ba / waga yo to zo omou / mochizuki no / kakitaru koto mo / nashi to omoeba.
Translation: "This world, I think, is indeed my world.
Like the full moon, I shine, uncovered by any cloud." The poem is not modesty.
It is a literal description of his political situation.
Michinaga had three daughters as imperial consorts at the moment of composition — a situation that no Japanese politician before or since has matched.
He was the most powerful man in Japan, the emperor was his grandson (and son-in-law to one of his other daughters), and he saw no political clouds.
The poem was extempore and his courtier audience reportedly received it in dazzled silence.
The diary of his rival Fujiwara no Sanesuke records the moment with a mixture of awe and resentment.

Sanesuke's diary is one of the great primary sources for Heian court history; he disliked Michinaga personally but was professional enough to record everything Michinaga did. (Sanesuke's grumbling is a useful corrective to the legend.
The full moon poem reads as triumphant, but it was composed in a court whose detailed political grievances are preserved in the diaries of men like Sanesuke.
Heian court politics were more contentious than the surviving high-cultural artifacts make them look.

Sanesuke spent his diary career documenting the petty corruptions, missed ceremonies, and procedural violations of his colleagues, and Michinaga features in the diary as a sometimes-impressive, sometimes-irritating, often-wrongheaded political operator rather than as the unchallenged moon-figure of his own poem.) Michinaga's other accomplishment was patronage.
He was the patron of the salon at the court of Empress Shoshi, his daughter.
The senior lady-in-waiting at that salon was Murasaki Shikibu (Chapter 5).
The Tale of Genji was written under Michinaga's roof.

Whether Michinaga read it is unclear; what is clear is that the world's first novel was produced inside the Fujiwara family compound, in the orbit of the most politically successful figure Heian Japan ever produced.
The high culture and the high politics of the Heian peak were the same family's productions.
Michinaga retired in 1019 and entered Buddhist orders, building a series of temples around his retirement villa.
The most famous is Hojoji (HOH-joh-jee), a vast Pure Land complex that has not survived but was the most lavish religious building of the period.
He died in 1027, surrounded by gilded Amida statues, with monks chanting the nembutsu (Chapter 6) at his bedside.
His son Yorimichi (yoh-ree-MEE-chee, 992–1074) inherited the regency and held it for over fifty years (1017–1068).
Yorimichi was a competent operator but lacked his father's combination of political dominance and dynastic luck.
The dynastic luck in particular ran out.
Yorimichi married daughters to emperors as expected, but none of those daughters produced a male heir.
The Fujiwara genealogical machine broke down.
By the 1060s, the reigning emperor (Go-Sanjo) was the first emperor in over a century who was not the son of a Fujiwara mother.
Go-Sanjo's reforms began to undermine the regency from above (Chapter 6).
The Fujiwara peak was over.
But Yorimichi left a permanent monument.
In 1053, he converted his father's villa at Uji (OO-jee), south of Kyoto, into a temple — Byodoin (BYOH-doh-in).
