The march itself was theatrically engineered.
Gandhi left Sabarmati Ashram on March 12, 1930, with 78 chosen volunteers, on a 240-mile walk to the coast at Dandi.

The route, the pace (about 12 miles a day), the stops in villages along the way for speeches and prayer meetings, the daily press updates, the photographs and newsreel footage transmitted around the world — all of it was carefully calibrated to maximize attention while remaining absolutely nonviolent and absolutely legal until the act of salt-picking at the end.
The arrival at Dandi on April 5 and Gandhi's ceremonial bending to pick up natural salt from the beach the next morning was the most photographed moment of the Indian freedom struggle.
Mass salt-defiance broke out across India in the following weeks.
Hundreds of thousands of Indians made or sold illegal salt; the government arrested tens of thousands.

The poet Sarojini Naidu led a follow-up satyagraha at the Dharasana salt works (in May 1930) where over 2,000 satyagrahis were systematically beaten by police lathis (long wooden batons) — an event covered in extraordinary detail by United Press correspondent Webb Miller, whose dispatch was the first sustained, English-language, eyewitness account of British colonial police violence to reach mass American newspaper readers.
American public opinion shifted.
The 1930s American left was already disposed against European colonialism; the Salt March made British India a specific and visible target.
Gandhi was arrested in May 1930 and held without trial under the Bengal Regulation of 1818.

He was released in January 1931 for the First Round Table Conference in London, the first of three conferences held between the British government and Indian political representatives to discuss the constitutional future.
The conferences were inconclusive.

They produced the Government of India Act 1935 (Chapter 4), the largest single piece of colonial constitutional legislation, which would frame Indian politics until 1947 — but they did not produce independence, which was the only thing the Congress now wanted.

Gandhi's negotiations with successive Viceroys (Irwin in 1931, Linlithgow later) settled various intermediate disputes — temporary truces, the suspension of various satyagrahas, the release of political prisoners — without resolving the underlying question.

By 1934, Gandhi had withdrawn formally from the Indian National Congress, declaring that the Congress had drifted from his program of village reconstruction and constructive work, while remaining its presiding moral authority.
The campaign for swaraj (self-rule) continued.

The cast of leaders who would carry it through the final phase — Nehru, Patel, Bose, Maulana Azad, the rising provincial figures who would become independent India's first state-level politicians — was already in place.

The next chapter is about the seventeen years from the Salt March to the Mountbatten Plan, during which the question shifted from whether the British would leave to who would inherit what they left behind.

chapters.title: The Path to Freedom
sentences: The seventeen years from the Salt March to independence were the most politically dense in colonial Indian history.

They contained four substantial constitutional revisions, two world wars, the rise of an alternative armed Indian liberation movement, a famine that killed perhaps three million people, the breakdown of the Hindu-Muslim political alliance the Congress had assumed it could rebuild, and finally the rushed dismantlement of the Raj under a Labour government that had run out of money and Asia-strategy.
The Government of India Act 1935 is where to start.

The Act was the largest single piece of British colonial legislation ever passed — 321 sections and ten schedules, over 1,200 pages — and was the framework within which Indian politics operated from 1937 through the formal handover.

The Act created an All-India Federation that combined British India with the princely states (though the federation provisions never actually came into effect because too few princely states acceded); restructured British India as eleven provinces with their own elected legislatures, Indian cabinets, and substantially expanded franchises (around 35 million voters, roughly 14% of the adult population); abolished dyarchy and gave full provincial autonomy to elected Indian governments in the provinces (subject to gubernatorial "emergency" override powers); and left central government — defense, foreign affairs, communications — entirely in British hands, governed by a Viceroy whose authority was now constitutional rather than purely executive.
The 1937 provincial elections, the first held under the new Act, produced Congress provincial ministries in seven of the eleven provinces.

The ministries — in Bombay, Madras, the United Provinces, Central Provinces, Bihar, Orissa, and the North-West Frontier Province — held office for twenty-eight months before resigning in October 1939 over the question of whether India had been entered into the war without consultation.
They were the Congress's first sustained experience of executive government.

Several future cabinet ministers of independent India served in them; the administrative habits formed in 1937–39 — provincial planning departments, public-works programs, rural development schemes, language policy choices in education — shaped what the postwar Indian state would look like.

Vallabhbhai Patel, who would later be independent India's first home minister and the architect of the integration of the princely states (Chapter 5), ran the Congress provincial governments as a kind of de facto coalition leader.
Jawaharlal Nehru did not hold provincial office; he stayed at the national party level, traveling, writing, organizing.

The Congress's main electoral competition in 1937 was the Muslim League — by then under the leadership of Muhammad Ali Jinnah, who had returned to active Indian politics in 1934 after a decade in London.

The 1937 results were a disaster for the League: in Muslim-majority provinces it won pluralities rather than majorities, and the Congress refused (controversially, in retrospect) to share provincial cabinet positions with League representatives in the United Provinces where a coalition might have been mathematically possible.

The League's reading of the results was that the Congress was now in effect a Hindu party, however much it claimed otherwise, and that Muslim political interests required a separate organizational vehicle.

This conclusion was the basis for the Lahore Resolution of March 1940 — the so-called "Pakistan Resolution," though the word Pakistan (coined by the Cambridge student Choudhry Rahmat Ali in 1933 as an acronym for Punjab–Afghania–Kashmir–Sindh–Baluchistan) did not appear in the resolution's text.
The Lahore Resolution called for "Independent States" — plural — in the Muslim-majority regions of British India.
What this would have meant in practical constitutional terms was deliberately left vague.

Whether Jinnah in 1940 actually wanted a separate sovereign Muslim state, or whether he was using the demand as a bargaining lever to extract better terms for Muslims within a federated India, is a question Indian and Pakistani historiography has been arguing about for eighty years.

The probable answer is that Jinnah's position changed between 1940 and 1947, that he was open to a federated solution in the early 1940s and committed to partition only after the late-war negotiations failed, but that this is a difficult question to settle definitively because Jinnah was a careful lawyer who did not write down his strategic thinking.
The Second World War transformed the political landscape.
The Viceroy Lord Linlithgow declared India at war with Germany in September 1939 without consulting any Indian political body.
The Congress demanded an immediate transfer of power as the price for cooperation; Linlithgow refused; the Congress provincial ministries resigned in October.

India spent the rest of the war under direct British rule, with Congress leadership periodically imprisoned and the Muslim League gradually becoming the official British interlocutor for "Indian opinion." The British Cripps Mission of March 1942 — led by the Labour Party's Sir Stafford Cripps, sent to India under wartime pressure from Roosevelt and the British dominions to negotiate Indian cooperation — offered eventual dominion status after the war, with the right of provinces to opt out of the post-war Indian union (an early signal of acceptance of the partition principle).
The Congress rejected the offer as deferring real power to an undefined future moment while demanding immediate war cooperation.
Gandhi described the offer as "a post-dated cheque on a failing bank." The Mission failed.
In August 1942, with Japanese forces advancing through Burma and Burma–India border attacks underway, the Congress passed the Quit India Resolution at Bombay.
The resolution demanded immediate British withdrawal and authorized a mass nonviolent rebellion.

Gandhi gave the famous "do or die" speech to the All India Congress Committee — "we shall either free India or die in the attempt; we shall not live to see the perpetuation of our slavery." Within twenty-four hours, the British arrested Gandhi, Nehru, Patel, Maulana Azad, and the entire senior Congress leadership.
They would not be released until June 1945.

The Quit India Movement that followed was the most violent of the major Congress satyagrahas, despite Gandhi's nonviolent framing — partly because the Congress leadership was imprisoned and could not enforce discipline, and partly because the issue (immediate independence from a wartime occupying power) was more existential than any previous one.
Telegraph lines were cut, police stations attacked, railway tracks sabotaged, government officials assaulted.

The British response was overwhelming: 60,000 arrests in the first months, the deployment of British and Indian army troops against Indian civilians, the establishment of parallel underground Congress committees that operated for the rest of the war.
The movement was suppressed by late 1943.
The independence question was deferred to the post-war negotiation.
The most striking single phenomenon of the war years was the alternative liberation strategy pursued by Subhas Chandra Bose.
Bose (1897–1945), Bengali, Cambridge-educated, civil-service trained, was the Congress's most charismatic and most operationally aggressive figure of the 1930s.

He had been Congress president twice, in 1938 and 1939, before being forced out of the party leadership by Gandhi's faction over the question of whether to make common cause with the British in the war or to seek alliance with Britain's enemies.

Bose's view was that the British Empire's wartime weakness was a strategic opportunity that Indian nationalists could not afford to miss; Gandhi's view was that allying with Nazi Germany or Imperial Japan would betray the moral basis of the freedom struggle and would produce, after the war, a worse occupation by a different power.

Bose, ousted, fled India in January 1941 under house arrest at Calcutta, escaped through Afghanistan to the Soviet Union (then a non-belligerent against Germany), and was passed via Berlin and Tokyo to a Japanese-occupied Southeast Asia.

From the Andaman Islands and Singapore he reorganized the Indian National Army (INA) — Azad Hind Fauj — built originally by other Indian officers from the Japanese-captured Indian prisoners of British forces in Malaya.

The INA fought under Japanese command in the 1944 Imphal–Kohima campaign — the Japanese attempt to invade British India through the northeastern hills, which failed disastrously and is generally regarded as one of the decisive land battles of the Pacific War.
Bose's eastern army crossed the Indian border at Manipur, planted the Indian tricolor on Indian soil, and was destroyed by British counter-offensives over the following months.
Bose himself died on August 18, 1945 in a plane crash in Taiwan while en route to Japanese-occupied Manchuria.

The plane crash, the death, and the body's cremation in Tokyo have been the subject of conspiracy theories in Indian political culture for eighty years; there is no serious evidence for any alternative narrative, but the political utility of Bose-as-mystery has kept the speculation alive.
The Bose phenomenon mattered politically in 1945–46 in a way the Congress had not anticipated.

The British had assumed that the INA trials — court-martials of former INA officers for treason against the Crown, held at the Red Fort in Delhi from November 1945 — would be a quiet legal exercise to reassert imperial discipline.
Instead, the trials became a massive cause célèbre.

Indian nationalist lawyers — Bhulabhai Desai, Tej Bahadur Sapru, Jawaharlal Nehru (returning to a law career briefly), and others — defended the INA officers as patriots; popular sentiment across India sided with the defendants; the Royal Indian Navy mutinied at Bombay in February 1946 in part over the INA trials; the British government commuted the death sentences and quietly dropped further prosecutions.
The trials demonstrated that the British could no longer rely on the Indian Army to enforce British authority against Indian political mobilization.
The strategic calculus shifted.
The Bengal Famine of 1943 was the war's other defining Indian event.
The famine killed somewhere between two and three million people in Bengal between summer 1943 and early 1944.
The causal chain has been the subject of extensive historical analysis (notably Amartya Sen's Poverty and Famines, 1981, which made the famine a foundational case in modern famine economics).

The proximate causes were a cyclone that destroyed Bengal's autumn 1942 rice crop; the Japanese conquest of Burma, which cut off rice imports that normally supplied 15% of Bengali consumption; and the wartime "denial policy" under which the colonial government had stripped coastal Bengal of boats and grain stocks to prevent Japanese use after invasion.

The structural cause was the inability or unwillingness of the colonial government to mobilize a wartime food rationing and distribution system that could have prevented mass starvation in the affected areas.

The colonial wartime cabinet (Linlithgow as Viceroy, succeeded by Wavell in October 1943) and the war cabinet in London under Churchill made a series of choices that the historical record now suggests were criminally negligent: continued export of rice from India during the famine peak; refusal to divert shipping from non-essential military uses to bring relief grain; and the dismissal of Bengali demands for emergency aid as exaggerated.
Churchill's personal contempt for Indian political demands was a documented factor.
The famine reshaped Bengali politics permanently.
Bengal had been the Congress's strongest province in 1937; by 1946 it was the Muslim League's stronghold.
The famine had hit the rural Muslim cultivator population hardest, and the League's wartime provincial ministry under H.
Suhrawardy had handled relief somewhat better than the British and Congress alternatives.

The League also benefited from a more general pattern: where the Congress was disabled by the wartime imprisonment of its leadership, the League had cooperated with the war effort, kept its provincial machinery intact, and emerged in 1945–46 with a much stronger political infrastructure than its 1937 results would have predicted.
The post-war settlement came under the Labour government elected in July 1945.

Clement Attlee's cabinet — committed to decolonization in principle, broke after six years of total war, facing American pressure to withdraw from imperial commitments — sent the Cabinet Mission of March–July 1946 to negotiate the constitutional form of an Indian transfer of power.
The Mission proposed a three-tier federation: provinces grouped into clusters (one Muslim-majority, one Hindu-majority, one mixed), grouped into a federal union with limited central powers.
The Congress and the League both formally accepted the plan in summer 1946, then both immediately repudiated parts of it; the negotiation collapsed by autumn.
Jinnah called for a Direct Action Day on August 16, 1946 to demonstrate Muslim political resolve.

The day became the Great Calcutta Killings — a four-day communal riot in which approximately 4,000 people died and over 100,000 were rendered homeless, primarily in Hindu–Muslim attacks across central Calcutta neighborhoods, with both communities involved in atrocities.
Calcutta in August 1946 was the dress rehearsal for what would happen across northern India eleven months later.

The plan that would actually settle the question — partition, with the Punjab and Bengal divided along religious-demographic lines, the rest of British India transferred as a single Indian Union, the princely states left to choose between the two new dominions — was announced by the new Viceroy, Lord Louis Mountbatten, in June 1947, with handover to occur on August 15, 1947.
The acceleration was extraordinary.
The Cabinet Mission had assumed a multi-year transition.
Mountbatten compressed the schedule to ten weeks.

The reasons were partly his own assessment that further delay would produce uncontrollable violence, partly the British government's recognition that it could no longer fund or staff the administration through a long transition, and partly the increasing communal violence in Bengal, Punjab, and the United Provinces, which suggested that the longer the British waited the worse the eventual handover would be.
The accelerated schedule was a catastrophe.
The next chapter is what happened in the ten weeks between Mountbatten's plan and the formal independence of the two new dominions.

chapters.title: Partition
sentences: Cyril Radcliffe arrived in India on July 8, 1947.
He had never been to India before.
He spoke no Indian language.
He had no specialist knowledge of South Asian geography, demography, religion, or history.
His career to that point had been at the English bar, where he was widely considered one of the leading commercial litigators of his generation.

He was forty-seven years old and had been chosen for his ignorance: the British government wanted a commissioner whose lack of prior Indian connections would make his determinations defensible as impartial.
He was given five weeks — five weeks — to draw the lines that would divide the Punjab and Bengal between the new dominions of India gains independence and Pakistan.

The work was done in a single small office in the Viceroy's residence in New Delhi, using out-of-date census tables, district-by-district religious-demographic data of variable reliability, and the recommendations of the two Boundary Commissions (one for Punjab, one for Bengal) whose Indian and Pakistani members had deadlocked on most contested districts, leaving Radcliffe as chairman to make the determinative calls.

The Punjab map was the hardest: in the central Punjab, in districts where Sikh, Hindu, and Muslim populations were thoroughly intermixed and where the Sikh Khalsa institutions (especially the Golden Temple at Amritsar) and the headworks of the canal-irrigation system were spread across what would become both sides of the border, no division could be drawn that did not produce massive minorities on the wrong side of the line.
Radcliffe's eventual line ran through villages — sometimes through individual fields, leaving farmers' homes in one country and their crops in another.
The Bengal map produced a smaller but equally arbitrary line dividing Calcutta from the eastern jute-growing districts that had supplied its mills.
The lines were finalized on August 12, 1947.
They were not published until August 17, two days after independence.

The reason for the delay was Mountbatten's calculated political decision: announcing the actual borders before the formal handover would have pre-empted any final political negotiation and might have triggered immediate fighting between the two states' new armies.

The cost of the delay was that the population transfers — millions of people moving between regions assigned to the "wrong" state — happened largely in ignorance of where the actual borders were, with the resulting confusion compounding the violence.
India gains independence on August 15, 1947.

Pakistan formally became independent on August 14, one day earlier, so that Mountbatten could attend both ceremonies in his capacity as the last Viceroy of British India and the first Governor-General of independent India.
The flag ceremonies in Karachi and New Delhi were attended by jubilant crowds.

Nehru's "Tryst with Destiny" speech to the Constituent Assembly at midnight August 14–15 — "long years ago, we made a tryst with destiny, and now the time comes when we shall redeem our pledge" — has remained the defining rhetorical moment of Indian independence, but the speech was being delivered in Delhi at the same hour the killing was at peak intensity in the Punjab.
The Partition of India killed between half a million and two million people in the three months around independence.

The lower estimate is approximately the British government's contemporaneous figure; the upper estimate is from later Indian and Pakistani academic studies that incorporated previously unreported village-level data and corpses recovered later from disused wells, canals, and railway sidings.
The actual number is unknowable.

The number of displaced persons is better attested: roughly 15 million people crossed the new borders in 1947–48 — Muslims moving from India to West and East Pakistan, Hindus and Sikhs moving from West Pakistan into India, Hindus moving from East Pakistan into West Bengal.
It was the largest forced migration in human history outside of war or famine.
The violence had patterns.

In the divided Punjab, the worst killings were Sikh-on-Muslim and Muslim-on-Sikh, with the Sikh jathas (armed bands originally formed for self-defense against Muslim violence in West Punjab) systematically attacking Muslim refugee columns and Muslim villages in the east, while Muslim Khaksar and tribal-irregular groups in West Punjab attacked Hindu and Sikh refugee columns and villages on their side.
In the United Provinces and Bihar, Hindu-on-Muslim violence predominated.

In Bengal, the killings were lower in intensity than in the Punjab — partly because Gandhi conducted a months-long personal fast in Noakhali district from October 1946 onward, exerting enormous moral pressure on local Hindu and Muslim leaders to restrain their followers, and partly because the Bengali rural fabric, intermixed as it was, made the kind of clean-sweep ethnic violence the Punjab saw harder to organize.
The Sindh experience was different again — relatively low-violence, but with the gradual expulsion of Sindh's substantial Hindu trader and professional population eastward into India.
Refugee columns moved by the train, by oxcart, by foot, in some places stretching dozens of miles.
The trains were attacked.
"Ghost trains" — trains arriving at Lahore from Amritsar or at Amritsar from Lahore with no living passengers, only the corpses of refugees murdered en route — became a defining image.

Both the Indian and Pakistani governments later attempted to track the death tolls on specific trains; the records are partial and inconsistent, but multiple "ghost train" incidents are documented in contemporary newspaper accounts and in the recently declassified British military records.

Rape was systematic and large-scale on all sides: estimates range from 75,000 to over 100,000 women abducted across the new border, many forcibly converted and remarried in the receiving community, with state-organized recovery missions on both sides continuing into the 1950s.
The receiving cities — Delhi, Calcutta, Karachi, Lahore — absorbed staggering refugee populations.

Delhi's pre-Partition population of about 900,000 grew to over 1.4 million within a year, with the new arrivals (mostly Hindus and Sikhs from the West Punjab) clustering in refugee camps and informal settlements that would become permanent neighborhoods.
Karachi's population doubled in a year.
Lahore lost its Hindu and Sikh middle class and gained a Muslim refugee population from the east.
The demographic and economic fabric of all four cities was reshaped within months.
The integration of the princely states ran in parallel to the Partition violence and was led by Vallabhbhai Patel as independent India's first Deputy Prime Minister and Home Minister, working with V.
Menon, an Indian civil servant whose long career in the Viceroy's secretariat had given him deep personal relationships with most of the princely households.

Of the 565 princely states, Patel and Menon secured 562 accessions to the Indian Union or to Pakistan between June and August 1947, working through a combination of personal pressure, financial inducements (privy purses paid to the former rulers in exchange for their renunciation of sovereignty), and the implicit threat that states attempting to remain independent would face political and economic isolation.
The three holdouts — Junagadh, Hyderabad, and Kashmir — each required different solutions.
Junagadh, a Muslim-ruled coastal state on the Kathiawar peninsula in modern Gujarat, with a majority-Hindu population, attempted to accede to Pakistan in August 1947.
The local population revolted.
The state's Nawab fled to Karachi.
The Indian government took over administration and conducted a plebiscite in February 1948 that confirmed accession to India.

Hyderabad, a Muslim-ruled state of 17 million people in the southern Deccan, with a majority-Hindu population and a fanatic Muslim paramilitary force (the Razakars) terrorizing the Hindu majority, attempted to remain independent.

After a year of negotiation and escalating Razakar violence, the Indian Army conducted Operation Polo in September 1948 — a five-day military operation that occupied the entire state and dissolved the Nizam's government.

The operation killed somewhere between 30,000 and 200,000 people, most in the Razakar-led communal violence that the Indian Army occupation suppressed; later inquiries (notably the Sundarlal Committee report, suppressed for decades and only fully released in 2013) confirmed substantial atrocities by both Razakar forces and the Indian Army during and after the operation.
Hyderabad joined the Indian Union.
Kashmir was different.
The Maharaja Hari Singh — Hindu, ruling a majority-Muslim population (roughly 77% Muslim, 20% Hindu, 3% Sikh in 1941) — wanted independence rather than accession to either dominion.

In October 1947, tribal Pashtun irregulars from the Pakistani side of the new border invaded Kashmir, ostensibly without Pakistani government coordination (the actual extent of Pakistani military support has been the subject of contested historical analysis for seventy-seven years; the documentary evidence suggests that Pakistani government coordination was real, but the public framing was deliberately ambiguous).
The tribal invaders reached the outskirts of Srinagar.
Hari Singh signed the Instrument of Accession to India on October 26, 1947 in exchange for Indian military intervention.
Indian Army units were airlifted to Srinagar the next day.
The First Kashmir War ran for thirteen months and was settled by UN-brokered ceasefire in January 1949.

The ceasefire line left roughly two-thirds of the former princely state under Indian administration (the Kashmir Valley, Jammu, Ladakh) and one-third under Pakistani administration (later called Azad Kashmir and the Northern Areas).
The dispute over the legal and political status of the territory has framed Indo-Pakistani relations ever since.
Gandhi's assassination completed the founding sequence.

On January 30, 1948, in the garden of Birla House in Delhi where Gandhi was conducting his daily prayer meeting, Nathuram Godse — a former member of the Hindu Mahasabha and the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, with a longer record of involvement in Hindu nationalist politics than the immediate news coverage acknowledged — approached Gandhi, touched his feet in respect, drew a Beretta pistol from his waist, and fired three rounds into Gandhi's chest at point-blank range.
Gandhi died within minutes.
Godse's stated motive in his trial was that Gandhi had been pro-Muslim.

The specific grievance was Gandhi's January 1948 fast — the second of his major late-life fasts in Delhi — to compel the Indian government to release 550 million rupees of Pakistan's share of the partition assets, which the Indian cabinet had been withholding in protest of Pakistani conduct in Kashmir.
Patel had been opposed to the release; Nehru and Gandhi had insisted on it as a matter of honoring the partition settlement.
Gandhi's fast had forced the cabinet to relent.

For Godse and the Hindu nationalist circle around him, the fast was final proof that Gandhi had structurally sacrificed Hindu and Indian interests to Muslim and Pakistani ones across decades of negotiation, and that his moral authority had to be ended by violence.
The assassination shocked the country.
The funeral procession from Birla House through Delhi was attended by perhaps two million people.

Nehru's radio broadcast from the night of the assassination — "the light has gone out of our lives, and there is darkness everywhere... the light that has illumined this country for these many years will illumine this country for many more years" — was the rhetorical moment in which independent India formally consecrated Gandhi as the Father of the Nation.

The RSS was banned (the ban was lifted in 1949 on the RSS's commitment to remain a cultural rather than political organization, a commitment whose subsequent honoring has been contested across all of independent Indian history).
Godse and his co-conspirator Narayan Apte were hanged at Ambala Jail on November 15, 1949.
The full conspiracy — the extent of involvement by the Hindu Mahasabha, by V.

Savarkar (the older Hindu nationalist theorist, tried and acquitted), and by Pune-based militant networks more broadly — has been the subject of further inquiries (the Kapur Commission of 1965–70) that documented additional networks of complicity without producing further criminal convictions.
The political question of who, exactly, was responsible for Gandhi's death beyond the two convicted assassins is one Indian historiography is still working through.
The Republic, when it was formally inaugurated two years later, would carry both the memory of the freedom struggle and the trauma of how its first months had ended.
The constitution Nehru and Ambedkar would draft, and the political settlement they would impose, was conditioned by both.

chapters.title: Nehru's Republic
sentences: The Constituent Assembly that drafted India's constitution had been elected in 1946 under the limited franchise of the late Raj.

After Partition, the assembly's remaining members — 299 representatives drawn from the provinces and the acceded princely states — sat in Delhi from August 1947 through November 1949 to produce the founding document.
The chairman of the drafting committee was B.
Ambedkar (1891–1956), the most consequential figure of independent India that the West has typically heard the least about.

Ambedkar was born to a Mahar family — a Dalit caste community in Maharashtra, in the system of social ranks that the colonial census had begun calling "untouchable" — and was the first member of his community to receive higher education at international levels.
He took degrees at Bombay University, at Columbia University in New York (PhD in economics, 1927), and at the London School of Economics, with a parallel call to the English bar at Gray's Inn.

He spent the 1920s and 1930s as the leading political voice for Dalit (literally "broken" or "crushed," the term Dalits prefer for their own community) emancipation, and the leading critic of Gandhi's framing of caste reform as a problem of Hindu spiritual reform rather than a problem of legal and economic structure.

Ambedkar and Gandhi clashed publicly across the 1930s — most famously over the Poona Pact of 1932, where Gandhi's fast forced Ambedkar to give up his demand for separate Dalit electorates in exchange for a system of reserved seats within general constituencies — and the disagreement was substantive and unresolved.

Ambedkar's later view, written down in Annihilation of Caste (1936) and in his unfinished history The Buddha and His Dhamma (1957, published posthumously), was that the Hindu social order was so structurally hostile to Dalit dignity that Dalits could only achieve full citizenship by formally leaving Hinduism.
He converted to Buddhism with around half a million Dalit followers in October 1956, two months before his death.
That Ambedkar — a Dalit, a public Gandhi-critic, a man who would convert out of Hinduism — was placed in charge of drafting the new Indian constitution was Nehru's decision, supported by Patel.
The decision is a case study in what the early Nehruvian state was.

The new republic was claiming to be a constitutional democracy with full equality before the law; placing a Dalit at the center of the founding document made the claim politically and symbolically real.

Ambedkar's authority over the constitution's text is also analytically real: the document's emphasis on individual rights and equality before the law, its abolition of untouchability (Article 17), its empowerment of the federal state to pursue affirmative-action programs (reservations) for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, and its careful balance of federal and provincial powers, reflect Ambedkar's specific intellectual project.

The Indian Constitution adopted in 1950, formally enacted on January 26, 1950 (Republic Day, chosen to commemorate the 1930 Purna Swaraj declaration of complete independence by the Congress), is the longest written constitution of any sovereign nation, then or now — 395 articles and 8 schedules in the original 1950 document (since expanded to over 470 articles and 12 schedules by numerous amendments).

It established India as a "sovereign democratic republic" (the word "socialist" was added by the 42nd Amendment in 1976; the word "secular" was added the same year); created a parliamentary system on the British Westminster model with a President as head of state and a Prime Minister as head of government; created an independent judiciary with the Supreme Court at its apex; reserved seats in legislatures for Scheduled Castes (Dalits) and Scheduled Tribes (Adivasis, India's indigenous-forest-dwelling communities); created a federal structure with substantial state-level autonomy; protected individual fundamental rights through judicial enforcement; and provided non-justiciable but politically authoritative Directive Principles of State Policy guiding the government toward economic redistribution, secular education, and welfare provision.
The constitution did several things that are easy to miss from the West.
It abolished untouchability in a way that European constitutions had never had cause to do.

It established universal adult suffrage — every Indian over 21 (later 18, by amendment) regardless of literacy, property, gender, or caste — at a moment when much of Europe and the United States had not yet extended full voting rights to all of their adult citizens.

It made Hindi (in the Devanagari script) the official language of the Union government — but added a transitional period during which English would continue as a working language, and explicitly enshrined linguistic diversity in the Eighth Schedule, which listed (originally) 14 recognized languages (now 22).
It contained no established religion.
It guaranteed the right to "freely profess, practice and propagate" religion (Article 25, where the word propagate was contested by some Hindu members because it implied a right to proselytize).
The constitution was, in 1950, the most ambitious document of universal citizenship rights anywhere in the world.
The first Nehru becomes first Prime Minister in 1947 and held the office continuously until his death in May 1964.
The seventeen years of his prime-ministership define what Indian historians call the Nehruvian Era and what the country still partly lives inside.
The Nehruvian project rested on four pillars.

The first was secular democracy — the principle that the Indian state would treat all religions with equal respect, would not establish any religion, and would not allow religious considerations to drive state policy.

The principle was tested almost immediately by Partition's communal violence and by the Hindu nationalist agitation around Gandhi's death; Nehru's specific contribution was to insist, repeatedly and at political cost, that the Indian state could not be a Hindu state, that the 35 million Muslims who had remained in India were full citizens with full rights, and that any political tendency that sought to make India a religious state would be met with the full weight of constitutional law.

This commitment was not popular with every Congress colleague (Patel's instincts on Muslim and Pakistani questions were notably harder than Nehru's), and it was bitterly opposed by the RSS and the Hindu Mahasabha.

The settlement Nehru imposed — that India would be a constitutionally secular state — held substantially until 1991 and is still the formal basis of Indian constitutional law, even as the political center has moved sharply away from it.
The second pillar was planned economic development.

The First Five-Year Plan launched in 1951 committed India to a Soviet-influenced model of state-led industrialization, with the public sector taking the "commanding heights" of heavy industry, agriculture as a private but state-coordinated sector, and consumer industries left to private capital under heavy regulation.
The Second Plan (1956–61), drafted under the chairmanship of the Indian Statistical Institute's P.

Mahalanobis, accelerated the heavy-industry emphasis: steel mills at Bhilai (Soviet collaboration), Rourkela (German), and Durgapur (British) became the symbols of the era; the First IIT established in 1951 at Kharagpur (followed by Bombay 1958, Madras 1959, Kanpur 1959, Delhi 1961) created the engineering-education infrastructure that would later staff both Indian industry and, much later, Silicon Valley; large dam projects (Bhakra Nangal, Hirakud, the Damodar Valley Corporation) physically reshaped the Indian agricultural landscape.
The performance was mixed.

India's annual GDP growth from 1950 to 1980 averaged about 3.5% — a rate the economist Raj Krishna would later call the "Hindu rate of growth" in a phrase that has been resented in Indian discourse ever since (Krishna himself was using it descriptively, not pejoratively, but the phrase has often been deployed to suggest some kind of cultural inability to grow faster).
Population growth in the same period was about 2%, so per capita growth was barely 1.5%.
India remained one of the poorest countries in the world by per capita income.

But the period also produced the institutional foundations of a modernizing economy: a steel industry, an engineering workforce, a defense-research apparatus, a higher-education infrastructure, a banking system.
The argument over whether Nehru's economic choices were correct given the constraints of the time has been a central element of Indian political economy since 1991 (Chapter 11).

The retrospective consensus is now that the planning model was too rigid and that the import-substitution framework had locked in inefficiencies that compounded; the more careful version of the same argument is that the alternatives available in 1951 — full market opening to a global economy still dominated by colonial trade patterns, or a Communist-style command economy — would have been worse, and that Nehru chose the least-bad option available to him.
The third pillar was non-alignment in foreign policy.
India would not join NATO.
India would not join the Warsaw Pact.
India would not allow foreign military bases on Indian soil.
India would maintain working diplomatic relations with both blocs.
India would lead, with Tito's Yugoslavia and Nasser's Egypt, the construction of a third pole of post-colonial states — the Non-Aligned Movement, formally constituted at Belgrade in 1961.

The doctrine was widely admired in the developing world and consistently mistrusted in Washington, where John Foster Dulles's State Department considered neutrality between the West and the Soviet Union a form of soft hostility to the West.

The doctrine produced one major strategic catastrophe (Chapter below, China 1962) and one substantial diplomatic success (the moral leadership India exercised through the 1950s on issues of decolonization and nuclear disarmament).
Whether the trade was net positive depends on how one values the two outcomes.
The fourth pillar was the integration of the princely states into modern republican structures.

Patel's work in 1947–48 had legally integrated the states; the harder work was administrative integration — converting heterogeneous princely administrations, with their own civil services and judicial systems and revenue codes, into the standardized Indian system.

The States Reorganisation Act 1956, after a long agitation in southern India for redrawing internal state boundaries on linguistic lines, reorganized the country into fourteen states and six union territories, with boundaries that broadly followed linguistic divisions (Andhra Pradesh for Telugu speakers, Tamil Nadu for Tamil speakers, Kerala for Malayalam speakers, Karnataka for Kannada speakers, Maharashtra and Gujarat eventually split in 1960).

The reorganization is now generally recognized as a major piece of state-building: it gave each major linguistic community a state in which their language was the official medium of government, education, and administration, defused linguistic separatism that had been a serious threat in the early 1950s, and produced the federal structure that has held the country together since.
The 1962 Sino-Indian War broke Nehru.

India and the People's Republic of China had recognized each other in 1950, with the slogan Hindi-Chini bhai-bhai — "Indians and Chinese are brothers" — defining the Nehruvian framing of bilateral relations.
The slogan obscured a serious territorial dispute.

The eastern border between India and Chinese-occupied Tibet — the McMahon Line drawn at the 1914 Simla Convention between British India, Tibet, and China — had never been accepted by any government in Beijing.
The western border — the Aksai Chin plateau, an empty high-altitude region claimed by India as part of Ladakh and by China as part of Xinjiang — had also never been bilaterally agreed.
China was, by the late 1950s, building a road across Aksai Chin connecting Tibet to Xinjiang.
Indian forward patrols had begun encountering Chinese road-construction crews and military posts in territory India considered its own.

The Forward Policy of 1961 — Nehru and Defence Minister Krishna Menon's response to the territorial dispute — instructed Indian troops to establish forward posts inside disputed territory, including some posts behind Chinese positions, on the theory that physical Indian presence would deter Chinese advance without provoking actual conflict because (as Indian planners assumed) the Chinese would not risk a wider war over the issue.
The assessment was wrong.
On October 20, 1962, the People's Liberation Army launched coordinated attacks across both the western (Ladakh) and eastern (NEFA, the North-East Frontier Agency, now Arunachal Pradesh) fronts.
Indian forward positions were overrun within days.

The PLA advanced 90 miles into Indian-claimed territory in the east before unilaterally declaring a ceasefire on November 21 and withdrawing to positions north of the McMahon Line — keeping all the Aksai Chin territory it claimed in the west, and demonstrating it could have advanced much further in the east if it had chosen.
The military defeat was complete.
Roughly 1,400 Indian soldiers were killed in action; 1,047 were wounded; over 3,000 were captured.
The captured included two brigade commanders and the disgraced corps commander General B.
Kaul, who had personally directed the Forward Policy implementation.
The political damage to Nehru was profound.
The Defence Minister Krishna Menon was forced out.
The intelligence and military leadership Nehru had defended for fifteen years was discredited.

The non-alignment doctrine had failed in its first major test: India had received military aid from the United States and Britain during the crisis (airlifted small arms, ammunition, and air-defense equipment) but no strategic guarantees, and the Soviet Union — Nehru's primary diplomatic partner — had been technically neutral but in practice closer to Beijing than to Delhi.
Indian public confidence in the Nehruvian project never fully recovered.
Nehru himself never fully recovered.
He suffered a stroke in January 1964 and died of a second stroke on May 27, 1964.
He had been Prime Minister for seventeen years.
His daughter Indira had been managing his political appointments and his household for years; his colleague Lal Bahadur Shastri would succeed him as PM.
The next chapter is what they did.

chapters.title: Shastri and Indira's Rise
sentences: The Congress was unprepared for Nehru's death.
There was no designated successor.

The party leadership reverted to a process — the Kamaraj Plan institutional arrangements left over from 1963, named after the Tamil party chief Kumaraswami Kamaraj — that had originally been designed to bring younger leaders into the party but now functioned as a mechanism for collective selection of a Prime Minister.

The party elders met in the days after Nehru's death and produced a consensus candidate: Lal Bahadur Shastri (1904–66), a small, soft-spoken UP politician who had served as Home Minister under Nehru and who was, importantly, acceptable to all of the major Congress factions because he did not threaten any of them.
Shastri was sworn in on June 9, 1964.
Shastri's nineteen months in office surprised everyone.
The man whose chief political asset had been his inoffensiveness turned out to have a serious independent program.

The Green Revolution begins in 1965, the foundational shift in Indian agriculture from the recurrent-famine subsistence model to one of food self-sufficiency, was launched under Shastri in collaboration with the agriculture minister C.
Subramaniam, the Indian Council of Agricultural Research, and (consequentially) the American foundations and US Agency for International Development.

The program imported and locally adapted the high-yielding wheat varieties developed at the International Maize and Wheat Improvement Center in Mexico by Norman Borlaug, combined them with chemical fertilizers, irrigated water, and pesticides, and concentrated the package geographically on the Punjab and parts of Haryana where the irrigation infrastructure and cultivator base could absorb it.
The first wheat harvest under the new package, in 1968, yielded 17 million tons against a previous best of 12 million; by 1971 India had achieved approximate food self-sufficiency in cereals.

The package was unevenly distributed (rice followed wheat by about a decade; cotton and pulses lagged longer; the eastern states with their water-logged soils and tenant-farming systems got less benefit than the Punjab and Haryana), and its long-term environmental costs (groundwater depletion, soil exhaustion, pesticide accumulation, agricultural debt and farmer suicides) would become defining issues by the 2000s.

But the short-run achievement was that the recurrent late-colonial famines of the 1870s–1940s — including the 1943 Bengal famine that had killed three million people — became, by the 1970s, a historical category rather than a recurring risk.
The Indian state could feed its population.
This had not been true since at least the 1860s.
The other defining event of Shastri's premiership was the Second Indo-Pakistani War of August–September 1965.

The war began with Pakistani Operation Gibraltar — an infiltration of Pakistani-trained irregulars into Kashmir, on the theory that they would catalyze a Kashmiri uprising against Indian administration — that failed in its immediate goal but escalated to full-scale conventional war between the two armies along the entire Punjab–Rajasthan border.
The fighting lasted seventeen days.
Both sides claimed victory; the actual military result was roughly a stalemate, with India holding more captured Pakistani territory than vice versa at the ceasefire.

The war was settled diplomatically at the Tashkent Conference in January 1966, brokered by the Soviet Union (the United States and China were both ambivalent or hostile to mediation), where Shastri and the Pakistani President Ayub Khan signed an agreement returning all captured territory and agreeing to settle Kashmir bilaterally rather than through war.
The agreement is now widely considered to have been unfavorable to India given the military situation, but it ended the war.
Shastri died of a heart attack in Tashkent on the night of January 10–11, 1966, hours after signing the agreement.
He had been Prime Minister for nineteen months.
The Indian political class again confronted the question of who would lead the country, and again chose by Congress-elder consensus.
The Congress's regional bosses — known as the Syndicate, a group including K.
Kamaraj (Tamil Nadu), S.
Nijalingappa (Karnataka), Atulya Ghosh (West Bengal), and S.
Patil (Maharashtra) — selected Nehru's daughter Indira Gandhi as the next Prime Minister on the explicit understanding that she would be a pliant figure they could control.
She was forty-eight, had served briefly as Information and Broadcasting Minister under Shastri, and had no independent political base.
She had been chosen because she was Nehru's daughter and because the Syndicate believed she could be managed.
This proved to be one of the great political miscalculations of post-independence India.
Indira Gandhi becomes PM in 1966 and would hold the office, with one three-year interruption, for fifteen of the next eighteen years.
She would also reshape the Congress in her own image, dismantle the Syndicate, and produce the most consequential single political career in modern Indian history.
Indira's first term — January 1966 to March 1971 — was a period of consolidation against the party establishment that had elected her.

The Congress lost ground heavily in the 1967 General Election, finishing with 283 of 520 Lok Sabha (lower house) seats — its narrowest national majority ever and its first major loss of state-level governments.
Non-Congress coalitions took power in nine of the seventeen Indian states.
The Syndicate read the 1967 results as evidence that Indira was electorally weak and that the party needed to return to collective leadership.
Indira read the results as evidence that the Syndicate's old-style patronage politics had run out of legitimacy and that she needed to build her own political base independently of the elders.
She did so through populist programs.

The Bank Nationalization of July 1969 — converting the fourteen largest private commercial banks into state-owned institutions in a single overnight ordinance — transferred control of the largest piece of Indian financial capital from private (mostly Bombay industrial) families to the central government and the public sector unions.
It was massively popular.

The bank-employee unions had been agitating for nationalization for years; the rural-cooperative banks and the smaller industrialists had wanted credit access the private banks had restricted; the Indian left was unanimous in supporting it.
The Syndicate had opposed it.

The split it produced in the Congress was decisive: in November 1969 the Syndicate expelled Indira from the Congress, and Indira responded by reorganizing her followers as Congress (R) — Requisition Congress, claiming continuity with the original organization — while the Syndicate continued as Congress (O) — Organisation Congress.
The split functioned as a referendum within the party: Congress (R), Indira's faction, retained the larger share of Congress MPs and won the political battle.
Indira ran the country as a minority government with support from the Communist parties from 1969 to 1971.
The Abolition of Privy Purses in 1971 was the second major populist move.

The 1947 settlement with the princely states had committed the Indian government to pay the former rulers annual "privy purses" — pensions calibrated to their former state revenues — as compensation for renouncing sovereignty.
The pensions had been guaranteed by the constitution.

Indira's government, with the support of a two-thirds Lok Sabha majority following the snap 1971 General Election (which she called early and won decisively on a single-issue "Garibi Hatao" — "Remove Poverty" — campaign, taking 352 of 518 Lok Sabha seats), passed the 26th Constitutional Amendment abolishing the privy purses entirely.
The former princes lost their guaranteed pensions and their formal recognition as princes.
The political class of the former princely states never recovered as a political force, and the symbolic break with the late-colonial settlement was complete.
The defining war of the Indira era came at the end of 1971.

East Pakistan had been part of the Pakistani state since 1947 but was politically subordinated to West Pakistan: West Pakistani officials staffed the East Pakistani administration, West Pakistani military officers held all senior commands, Urdu (a West Pakistani language) was imposed as official medium in a Bengali-speaking province, and the substantial revenue surplus from East Pakistani jute exports flowed west.

The Pakistani 1970 General Election — the first conducted under universal franchise in a unified Pakistan — produced an absolute majority for the East Pakistani Awami League under Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, on a program of substantial East Pakistani autonomy.
The West Pakistani military government under General Yahya Khan refused to allow Mujibur Rahman to form a government.

On March 25, 1971, the Pakistani Army launched Operation Searchlight — a coordinated military campaign across East Pakistan to suppress the Awami League and Bengali nationalist political organization.

The operation killed somewhere between several hundred thousand and three million Bengalis over the following nine months, displaced ten million refugees into the Indian state of West Bengal, and committed atrocities (the Bangladesh genocide) that the U.S.
State Department's Dhaka consul Archer Blood documented in real time and that the Nixon administration suppressed for Cold War political reasons.
India's strategic problem was acute.
Ten million East Pakistani refugees were a humanitarian and economic catastrophe for the eastern Indian states, which lacked the infrastructure to support the population.
The Awami League was operating a government-in-exile in Calcutta.
The Indian government recognized Mukti Bahini — the Bengali armed resistance forces — and provided training, weapons, and logistical support from Indian territory.

India also signed the Indo-Soviet Treaty of Peace, Friendship and Cooperation in August 1971 — a strategic shift away from non-alignment, providing for "mutual consultation" in event of attack — that explicitly counterbalanced the U.S.-Pakistani strategic alignment under Nixon and Kissinger and provided the Soviet veto cover for what India was about to do.
Pakistan attacked first.
Pakistani Air Force preemptive strikes on Indian airfields on December 3, 1971 gave India the pretext for full-scale military intervention.
The Bangladesh Liberation War lasted thirteen days.

Indian forces under General Sam Manekshaw — with the Mukti Bahini operating in coordination — advanced from three sides into East Pakistan, isolated the Pakistani garrison, and accepted the surrender of 93,000 Pakistani troops at Dhaka on December 16, 1971.
It was the largest mass surrender of a regular army since the Second World War.
East Pakistan became the independent state of Bangladesh.
The new country recognized Sheikh Mujibur Rahman as its first prime minister.
The 1971 war was Indira Gandhi's strategic high-water mark.

The opposition leader Atal Bihari Vajpayee — later himself Prime Minister (Chapter 11) — was widely reported to have hailed her in Parliament as "Durga", the warrior goddess (Vajpayee in later years disputed having used the exact word, but the epithet stuck to the moment).
Her domestic political authority was, for a brief moment, beyond serious challenge.
The Smiling Buddha nuclear test of May 18, 1974, in which India detonated a 12-kiloton fission device underground at Pokhran in the Rajasthan desert, was the next confirmation.
The test made India the first country outside the original five nuclear powers (US, USSR, UK, France, China) to demonstrate nuclear weapons capability.

The Indian government called it a "peaceful nuclear explosion" in a fiction that fooled no one — the test triggered Pakistani crash nuclear-weapons development and international sanctions but also definitively established India as a major regional military power.
The crown ought to have rested easy.
Instead, within twelve months, Indira would face the worst political crisis of her career — and would meet it by suspending Indian democracy.
The next chapter is the Emergency.

chapters.title: The Emergency
sentences: The political turn that produced the Emergency began with an electoral case.
In 1971 Indira Gandhi had won her Rae Bareli Lok Sabha seat against the socialist veteran Raj Narain by a massive margin.

Raj Narain filed an election petition in the Allahabad High Court alleging multiple corrupt practices: that the District Magistrate had been used for campaign work, that government officials had built election platforms, that distinct election-law violations had occurred.
The petition seemed quixotic; the violations alleged were minor and procedural.
The case ground through the courts for four years.

On June 12, 1975, Justice Jagmohan Lal Sinha of the Allahabad High Court ruled in Raj Narain's favor on two narrow technical grounds, finding Indira Gandhi guilty of electoral malpractice, voiding her 1971 election, and barring her from holding elected office for six years.
The judgment was stayed for twenty days to allow appeal.
It was the first time in Indian history that a sitting Prime Minister had been found guilty of an offense by an Indian court.
The political opposition saw the judgment as the moment to force Indira's resignation.

The Jayaprakash Narayan movement — JP, the elderly Gandhian socialist who had been agitating for what he called "Total Revolution" against the Congress since 1973, drawing on the rural distress, urban unemployment, and middle-class anger over corruption that had built up across the early-1970s economic downturn — called for a mass rally at Delhi's Ramlila Maidan on June 25 and for an indefinite gherao (encirclement) of the Prime Minister's residence.
JP also called on the police and the army to refuse "illegal" orders from the Indira government.

The call was, by any constitutional standard, an extraordinary one — JP was effectively calling for the breakdown of governmental authority — and it was made by a figure whose Gandhian moral authority gave the call weight that no ordinary political appeal could have carried.

On the night of June 25–26, 1975, the Emergency declared in 1975 was proclaimed under Article 352 of the Constitution — the provision allowing emergency suspension of fundamental rights in cases of "internal disturbance." The proclamation, signed by President Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed at 11:45 PM on Indira Gandhi's recommendation, made effective without prior cabinet discussion, was the most consequential constitutional act of independent Indian history outside of the founding itself.
What the Emergency did, over the next twenty-one months, was to suspend the operative parts of Indian democracy.
The opposition leadership — JP, Morarji Desai (former finance minister and rival), Atal Bihari Vajpayee, L.

Advani, virtually every senior opposition politician across every party — was arrested in the first hours and held under the Maintenance of Internal Security Act (MISA), which allowed detention without trial.

Press censorship was imposed within days, with prior-restraint instructions sent to every newspaper editor in the country requiring submission of front pages and editorials to government censors before publication.

Three constitutional amendments — the 38th, 39th, and 42nd — were passed by a now-purely-Congress Parliament, restricting judicial review of emergency proclamations, retroactively legalizing the 1971 election, and granting the central government sweeping new powers over states, civil liberties, and election rules.
Judges who had ruled against the government were transferred to remote benches.
Civil-service officers who had spoken inconveniently were removed.
The fundamental-rights enforcement mechanism that the Constitution had built was disabled.
The Sanjay Gandhi factor made the Emergency something more than a constitutional power-grab.
Sanjay (1946–80) was Indira's younger son, twenty-eight in 1975, with no formal political position but with extensive informal authority through his mother's confidence.

He had been running a parastatal small-car project (the Maruti project, eventually delivered as the Maruti Suzuki small car of the 1980s) that became a model of Emergency-era corruption: contracts handed to Sanjay-favored firms, regulatory shortcuts cleared by ministerial fiat, government banks pressured to lend on terms commercial banks would not have accepted.
Sanjay also directed two campaigns that defined Emergency-period popular memory of the regime more than any policy decision did.

The first was Slum Demolition — particularly the Turkman Gate demolitions in Old Delhi, where over 300,000 residents of the historic city's working-class neighborhoods were forcibly displaced from their homes to make way for what the Sanjay-affiliated Delhi Development Authority described as urban beautification.
Police killed at least twenty-five protesters in the Turkman Gate firing of April 1976; the actual death toll across the wider Delhi demolitions has never been credibly counted.

The second was forced sterilization — a coercive family-planning campaign that performed an estimated eight million sterilizations between 1976 and 1977, with administrative quotas imposed on government employees that produced widespread coercion (especially of poor men) and at least 1,800 documented deaths from infected post-surgical wounds in poorly equipped rural sterilization camps.
The two programs together represented the kind of state behavior that the Indian middle class had assumed was reserved for authoritarian regimes elsewhere.
The Emergency had defenders, then and now.

Indira's argument was that the country had been on the edge of breakdown, that JP's call for army and police disobedience was a serious institutional threat, that some democratic functioning had to be suspended temporarily so that the underlying constitutional order could be preserved.
Some elements of this argument have force.

The pre-Emergency political situation had been genuinely dangerous: industrial strikes had paralyzed major cities, the Naxalite insurgency in Bengal and Bihar was active, university students had been agitating against the government for years, and JP's specific call for police disobedience had no precedent in Indian constitutional history.

The Emergency also coincided, by coincidence or by design, with a period of partial economic recovery: inflation came down from 28% in 1974 to single digits in 1975–76, agricultural production was strong, the trains ran on time (a phrase that became famously associated with Emergency apologetics).

But the case for the Emergency rests heavily on the policy outcomes of its first six months; the case against it rests on the constitutional damage of its full twenty-one-month duration, the personal political abuses of the Sanjay period, the suppression of civil liberties, and the demonstration that the Indian constitutional system had no built-in safeguards against an executive willing to use Article 352 as broadly as Indira used it.
The Emergency ended in a way that surprised everyone.

In January 1977, Indira Gandhi announced an election — the March 1977 General Election — on the apparent assumption that the country had accepted the Emergency framework, that the opposition leadership was demoralized after eighteen months in detention, and that the Congress would win a working majority.

Why she made this assessment is still unclear; the most common interpretation is that her intelligence services had given her overoptimistic reports and that she had genuinely lost touch with public sentiment after months of staged news in censored media.
She released the opposition leaders from detention, scheduled the election for late March, and lifted most of the Emergency restrictions in the campaign period.

The opposition leaders, freed from detention but still under restrictions, met in Delhi in January 1977 and formed the Janata Party — a four-way merger of the old Congress (O), the Bharatiya Lok Dal (Charan Singh's farmer-based party), the Jana Sangh (the Hindu nationalist precursor party that included Vajpayee and Advani), and the Socialist Party (JP's network).

The merger was extraordinary: ideologically, the Janata combined Hindu nationalists, Gandhian socialists, North Indian rural conservatives, and elder Congress dissidents in a single electoral vehicle.
The unifying program was anti-Emergency.

The campaign was conducted in an unusually compressed period — about ten weeks — with the Janata's senior figures (Desai, JP himself in advisory capacity though not as a candidate, Vajpayee, Charan Singh) campaigning across the Hindi belt and into the south.
The Congress entered the campaign with all the institutional advantages of incumbency but without an effective response to the Emergency-period record.
The result was a political earthquake.

The Janata Party won 295 of 542 Lok Sabha seats, the Congress was reduced to 153 (its worst result ever), and Indira Gandhi personally lost her own Rae Bareli seat to Raj Narain — the same opponent whose 1975 election petition had triggered the entire chain of events.
Sanjay Gandhi lost his Amethi seat.
The Congress was wiped out across northern India, retaining seats only in the south and parts of Maharashtra.
The Janata's victory was the first defeat of the Indian National Congress in any general election since independence — thirty years of unbroken Congress rule had ended in a single vote.
Morarji Desai was sworn in as Prime Minister on March 24, 1977.

The Janata government would last twenty-eight months — a complicated period covered in the next chapter — before fracturing along the original ideological lines and producing the conditions for Indira's return.

But the basic point about Indian democracy had been made and would be remembered: the electorate had punished the Emergency at the ballot box, peacefully, in a process the deposed government had itself organized.
The Indian democratic system had survived its first authoritarian interlude.

chapters.title: Indira Returns
sentences: The Janata government was a coalition that had defeated the Emergency but had no plan for what came next.

Morarji Desai (81 years old when he took office) was Prime Minister; Charan Singh (the Lok Dal leader, an UP farmer-politician with deep agrarian-caste roots) was Deputy Prime Minister and Home Minister; Atal Bihari Vajpayee (the Jana Sangh's most respected figure) was External Affairs Minister.
The cabinet's ideological range was vast and the unifying program — anti-Emergency — was a one-time issue that did not generate ongoing legislative direction.
Within months, the cabinet was openly feuding.
Charan Singh pressed for agricultural-loan write-offs and farmer subsidies.
The Jana Sangh wing pressed for Hindu cultural symbols in state programs.
The old Congress (O) wing pressed for moderation and continuity.
JP, by 1978, was effectively withdrawn from active politics (he died in October 1979).
The government continued to function bureaucratically but lost political cohesion across 1978.
The Janata's most consequential single act was the 44th Constitutional Amendment of 1978 — a careful rewriting of the emergency provisions that the Indira government had abused.

The amendment narrowed the constitutional grounds for emergency declaration (replacing "internal disturbance" with "armed rebellion"), required cabinet recommendation in writing for the President to declare emergency, restored full judicial review of fundamental rights during emergencies, made the right to life and personal liberty (Article 21) non-suspendable, and reversed most of the 42nd Amendment's pro-executive provisions.

The 44th Amendment was the legal-constitutional response to the Emergency, and it has held: no subsequent Indian government has invoked the Article 352 national emergency provisions, and the procedural safeguards the 44th Amendment introduced have functioned as intended.
But the Janata could not hold its own coalition.
In July 1979, Charan Singh withdrew his Lok Dal contingent from the government over Desai's refusal to push for harder action on Sanjay Gandhi's pending criminal cases.
Desai resigned.

The Congress (R) — Indira's faction, now reconstituted under the new name Congress (I) for "Indira" — agreed to support a minority Charan Singh government, then withdrew that support before Charan Singh had survived a single Parliament confidence vote.
Charan Singh became the only Prime Minister of India never to have faced the Lok Sabha.
Parliament was dissolved.
The 1980 General Election in January 1980 returned Indira to power with 353 of 529 Lok Sabha seats — a clearer majority than she had ever previously won.
The Janata's electoral mandate had collapsed in three years.
The Congress's argument in 1980 was simple: the Janata could not govern.
The two and a half years of Janata rule had produced unstable cabinets, unimplemented promises, and ineffective administration.
Indira returned on the implicit promise that the Congress could at least manage the bureaucracy.
The argument was not, in 1980, an argument about whether the Emergency had been justified — that had been settled in 1977 — but about whether the alternative was workable.
The voters' verdict in 1980 was: no.
Indira's second term ran from January 1980 to her assassination in October 1984.
The dominant issue was the Punjab.
The Punjab crisis had been building since the 1970s.

The Akali Dal — the regional Sikh political party — had pressed since the Anandpur Sahib Resolution of 1973 for greater autonomy: a renegotiated federal settlement that would give the Punjab control over its own rivers (water-rights disputes with neighboring Haryana and Rajasthan were central), greater fiscal autonomy, and recognition of Punjabi-language and Sikh-religious symbols in state policy.
The demands were politically substantive but not separatist.

In response, however, Indira's Congress government had encouraged the rise of Jarnail Singh Bhindranwale — a young, charismatic Sikh fundamentalist preacher whom Congress strategists initially saw as a useful instrument for splitting the Akali political base.

Bhindranwale and the radical Sikh political-religious organization Damdami Taksal began advocating for Khalistan — an independent Sikh sovereign state — and conducting targeted assassinations of Hindu and Sikh political opponents.

By 1982 Bhindranwale had taken up residence inside the Golden Temple complex at Amritsar — the holiest site in Sikhism — and was operating as the de facto authority over the temple complex while continuing to direct militant activity from inside it.
By 1984 the security situation in the Punjab had deteriorated to multiple political killings per week, with the Indian state having lost effective authority over substantial parts of the province.
Operation Blue Star was Indira's response.
Between June 1 and 8, 1984, the Indian Army conducted a full-scale assault on the Golden Temple complex to remove Bhindranwale and his armed followers.

The operation involved tank fire on the Akal Takht — the Sikh political-spiritual seat — major damage to the Golden Temple's surrounding structures, and the deaths of over 500 people including Bhindranwale, around 80 Indian Army soldiers, and (the actual disputed number) several hundred to several thousand civilians who had been inside the complex at the time of the assault, many of them Sikh pilgrims who had no involvement in militant activity.
The military objective was achieved: Bhindranwale was dead, the temple complex was retaken.
The political consequence was a wound in the Sikh community that has not closed.

The Golden Temple was the religious center of every Sikh on Earth, the equivalent in religious terms of a military assault on the Vatican or the Kaaba; the Akal Takht's reconstruction was rejected by the Sikh community for years afterward because the original Indian-government rebuild had been politically tainted.
The Sikh political consensus, even among Sikhs who had been horrified by Bhindranwale's actual conduct, hardened against the Congress.

On October 31, 1984, two of Indira Gandhi's Sikh bodyguards — Beant Singh and Satwant Singh — shot her on her way from her residence at 1 Safdarjung Road to a scheduled interview with the British actor Peter Ustinov at her office.
Beant Singh fired three rounds from a service revolver; Satwant Singh emptied a Sten submachine gun magazine.
Indira died on the way to the hospital.
Beant Singh was killed in the immediate gunfight with other guards; Satwant Singh and a third co-conspirator (Kehar Singh, a civil-service officer) were captured, tried, and hanged in January 1989.
The assassination was direct revenge for Operation Blue Star.
What followed was worse.

The 1984 anti-Sikh pogrom in Delhi and several northern Indian cities — November 1–3, 1984 — killed at least 3,000 Sikhs (the official Indian government figure; later inquiries suggested 8,000 or more).
The killings were not spontaneous riots; they were organized by Congress politicians and local strongmen, with police complicity.
Voter lists were used to identify Sikh households.
Petrol and rubber tires (for the burning of victims, a method the killers had used in earlier communal violence) were distributed by trucks bearing Congress political insignia.
The Delhi police, under direct central-government authority, were instructed to stand down.
The killings stopped on November 3 only when the army was finally deployed to restore order.

The political class that had organized the pogrom included Congress figures who would go on to substantial subsequent political careers, including Jagdish Tytler and Sajjan Kumar; the legal accountability process for those killings, eventually producing a conviction of Sajjan Kumar in 2018, took thirty-four years.
The pogrom changed Indian politics in ways that are still working themselves out.
The Congress, which under Nehru had been the institutional guardian of secular tolerance, had organized communal mass violence at the center of the Indian state.
The fiction of Congress secular credibility never fully recovered.

The Sikh community's grievance with the Indian state hardened into a thirty-year alienation that produced a violent Khalistani militancy in the Punjab through the late 1980s, suppressed eventually by a brutal counterinsurgency under the Punjab Police chief K.

The Hindu-majoritarian critique of the Congress — that the party preached secularism in principle but practiced communalism in pursuit of votes — gained an empirical anchor that the BJP would use across the next thirty years.

Rajiv Gandhi — Indira's elder son, an Indian Airlines pilot with limited political experience, who had been drawn into politics only after Sanjay Gandhi's death in a small-plane crash in June 1980 — was sworn in as Prime Minister within hours of his mother's death.

The Congress called the December 1984 General Election less than two months after the assassination and won 414 of 542 Lok Sabha seats — the largest single-party majority in any Indian election before or since, driven entirely by sympathy voting.
Rajiv was forty when he took office.

He had been described variously as a "computer raja" — meaning to suggest both his interest in technological modernization and his distance from old Congress politics — and he committed his first months to a modernization agenda: telecommunications upgrades that began the conversion from analog landlines to electronic exchanges (the work of his confidant Sam Pitroda and the new Centre for Development of Telematics), the New Education Policy 1986 that expanded the role of the Navodaya Vidyalaya residential schools and shifted curriculum priorities, an end to the import-substitution restrictions on consumer electronics that would later be the cultural foundation of the IT industry.
Then came the Shah Bano case.

In April 1985, the Supreme Court ruled that Mohammed Ahmed Khan, an Indore lawyer, was required to pay continuing maintenance to his divorced wife Shah Bano under section 125 of the Criminal Procedure Code.
The ruling was a routine application of secular Indian criminal law.

It became politically charged because the parties were Muslim and because Muslim personal law (the Sharia-derived family law that applied to Muslim Indians in matters of marriage, divorce, and inheritance) does not require post-divorce maintenance beyond the iddat period (three menstrual cycles).
Conservative Muslim political organizations protested that the Supreme Court was effectively imposing secular law on Muslim religious matters.

The Rajiv government, in a major political miscalculation, passed the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act in May 1986 to legislatively reverse the Supreme Court ruling and restore the conservative interpretation of Muslim personal law.
The episode was politically catastrophic.

Indian feminists denounced the legislative reversal as the state subordinating women's rights to conservative religious leadership; Hindu nationalist organizations denounced it as an example of Congress "appeasement" of Muslims; secular liberals denounced it as a violation of the principle of equal citizenship.

The argument that the Congress practiced two different standards for Muslim and Hindu religious matters became, after Shah Bano, the central rhetorical lever the BJP would use to dismantle Congress secular credibility across the next decade.
The same period brought the Babri Masjid controversy to the center of Indian politics.

In February 1986, a district court in Faizabad — under a Congress-aligned district administration — ordered the unlocking of a small disputed mosque in Ayodhya (the Babri Masjid, traditionally identified as having been built in 1528 by a general of the Mughal emperor Babur).

The mosque had been the subject of a property dispute since 1949, when Hindu activists had placed idols of the deity Ram inside the structure overnight and the district magistrate had locked it shut to prevent further communal disturbance.
