The 1986 unlocking allowed Hindu worship inside the mosque, was politically welcomed by the Hindu nationalist Vishwa Hindu Parishad (VHP), and triggered Muslim political mobilization against the perceived state assistance to Hindu religious claims.

Both sides understood that the symbolic stakes were higher than the actual building: the Babri Masjid stood on what Hindu activists claimed was the birthplace of the deity Ram, and the construction of a Ram temple at the site would have civilizational meaning.
The VHP began organizing nationwide Ram Shila Pujan — brick-consecration ceremonies in which villages contributed bricks for the eventual Ram temple — across 1989.
The Babri site was at the center of Indian political contention for the next six years, culminating in the demolition (Chapter 11).
The Rajiv government's other defining crisis was the Indian Peace Keeping Force intervention in Sri Lanka.
The Sri Lankan civil war between the Sinhalese-majority government and the Tamil-minority Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) had been escalating since 1983.

The Tamil insurgency had political support from the Tamil-speaking Indian state of Tamil Nadu (where successive state governments had quietly provided sanctuary and training to Tamil militant groups) and direct support from Indian intelligence (RAW).

In July 1987 Rajiv signed the Indo-Sri Lanka Accord with Sri Lankan President Jayewardene, under which India would deploy a peace-keeping force to the Tamil-majority north and east of Sri Lanka to disarm the LTTE and oversee a political settlement granting Tamil regional autonomy.
The deployment turned catastrophic.
The LTTE refused to disarm.

The IPKF — committed initially as a 6,000-strong peacekeeping force — escalated to over 80,000 troops fighting an insurgency in unfamiliar terrain against the very militants Indian intelligence had previously supported.
Approximately 1,200 IPKF soldiers were killed before the force was withdrawn in March 1990.

The deployment was a strategic and political failure that defined Rajiv's defense legacy and would, in 1991, return to kill him: an LTTE suicide bomber detonated a vest at a campaign rally near Madras on May 21, 1991, killing Rajiv and fourteen others.
He was forty-six.

The Bofors scandal — corruption allegations around a 1986 contract under which the Swedish defense firm Bofors AB had supplied 410 howitzer guns to the Indian Army, with kickbacks paid to Indian political intermediaries — broke in Swedish radio reporting in April 1987.
The Indian opposition (the V.
Singh-led faction within the Congress that had been forced out, the Janata-successor parties, the left, and the BJP) made Bofors the centerpiece of the 1989 campaign.

The actual evidence against Rajiv was always limited — direct kickbacks to senior Congress figures including possibly Rajiv himself were alleged but never proved in court — but the broader perception of corruption was politically lethal.
The 1989 General Election reduced the Congress to 197 seats, costing it the parliamentary majority and producing a National Front coalition government under V.

The Bhopal disaster — the December 1984 industrial accident at the Union Carbide India pesticide plant in Bhopal, in which approximately 40 tons of methyl isocyanate gas was released into the air around the plant, killing an estimated 3,000 people in the immediate aftermath and another 15,000 to 25,000 over subsequent decades from injury and exposure — sits across this period as a separate but illustrative event.
The disaster was the worst single industrial accident in human history.

The legal and political response was a thirty-year sequence of compromises: a 1989 out-of-court settlement under which Union Carbide paid US$470 million (about US$870 per affected person) in exchange for criminal-charge dismissal, a settlement now widely regarded as inadequate; the company's eventual sale to Dow Chemical in 2001 without resolution of the residual environmental contamination at the site; the prolonged Indian inability to extradite the Union Carbide CEO Warren Anderson to face manslaughter charges before his death in 2014.

Bhopal illustrated everything about the period — a developing-country industrial economy operating dangerous facilities without effective safety regulation; a state apparatus unable to negotiate adequate compensation against transnational corporate resources; a legal system unable to assign accountability for catastrophic damage.
The site was finally remediated in the late 2010s.
Survivors are still receiving partial compensation in 2026.

chapters.title: Liberalization
sentences: The 1989 General Election produced a hung Parliament.

Singh — the former Congress finance minister who had broken with Rajiv over Bofors, joined the new Janata Dal, and unified the anti-Congress opposition outside the Hindu nationalist BJP — became Prime Minister at the head of a National Front coalition with outside support from the BJP on one side and the Left on the other.
The arithmetic was unstable.
The coalition would last eleven months.
Two issues defined V.
Singh's brief premiership.
The first was the Mandal Commission report.

The Mandal Commission had been set up in 1979 under the Janata government to study the conditions of India's Other Backward Classes (OBCs) — the broad category of mostly agricultural, mostly low-status (though not Dalit) Hindu castes that had historically been excluded from elite professions and government employment but had not been covered by the Scheduled Caste/Scheduled Tribe reservations system.
The commission, chaired by B.

Mandal, had reported in 1980 recommending that 27% of central-government jobs be reserved for OBCs in addition to the existing 22.5% reserved for SCs and STs — bringing total reservations to just under 50%.
The Indira and Rajiv governments had shelved the report.
Singh's government announced in August 1990 that it would implement the Mandal recommendations.
The political effects were enormous.
The OBC vote — perhaps 40% of the total Indian electorate — had not been a coherent political bloc; the Mandal implementation made it one.

The new OBC political parties that emerged across the 1990s — the Samajwadi Party in UP, the Rashtriya Janata Dal in Bihar, the Janata Dal (Secular) in Karnataka, the DMK in Tamil Nadu — would dominate state-level politics in the Hindi belt and substantially in the south for the next two decades.

The Congress lost its OBC vote across this period, and the BJP, which initially opposed the Mandal report on the grounds that it would split the Hindu vote, eventually adapted by building cross-caste Hindu coalitions of its own.

The Indian political landscape that resulted — caste-based regional parties controlling the Hindi-belt states, the Congress confined increasingly to coastal and southern states, the BJP organizing Hindu cross-caste coalitions at the national level — was set up directly by the 1990 Mandal decision.
The middle-class and upper-caste reaction was immediate and intense.

Anti-Mandal protests broke out across northern Indian universities; the most striking single image was that of Rajiv Goswami, a Delhi University student who set himself on fire in protest on September 19, 1990, beginning a wave of self-immolations that killed at least 159 people across the autumn of 1990.
The protests revealed the depth of upper-caste anxiety about reservations — a politics that the BJP would later mobilize but that V.
Singh's coalition could not contain.
The second defining issue was the BJP's Ram Janmabhoomi movement.
The VHP, in September 1990, organized a Rath Yatra — a chariot procession across northern India from Somnath in Gujarat to Ayodhya in UP — led by the BJP president L.
Advani, calling for the construction of a Ram temple at the disputed Ayodhya site.
The Rath Yatra was carefully theatrical: Advani traveled in a converted Toyota truck disguised as a chariot, gave speeches in towns along the route, and was accompanied by VHP, RSS, and BJP cadres.
Communal violence broke out at multiple stops along the route.
In Bihar, the state government under Lalu Prasad Yadav arrested Advani on October 23, 1990.
The BJP withdrew its support from V.
Singh's government over the arrest.
The coalition collapsed.

Chandra Shekhar, a former socialist who broke from the Janata Dal, served as Prime Minister for four months at the head of a rump government with Congress outside support, before the Congress also withdrew support and Parliament was dissolved in March 1991.

The 1991 General Election was conducted in two phases — May 20 and (after Rajiv Gandhi's assassination by LTTE suicide bomber on May 21 in the middle of campaigning) June 12 and 15 — and returned the Congress as the largest single party with 232 of 545 Lok Sabha seats.

Narasimha Rao — a Telugu Brahmin from Andhra Pradesh, former external affairs minister and home minister under both Indira and Rajiv, considered by political observers to be an ineffectual elder statesman — was sworn in as Prime Minister on June 21, 1991.
He was seventy years old.
He had no organic base in the Congress family or in any regional faction.
He had been chosen because he was acceptable to everyone and threatening to no one.
He would, like Indira before him, surprise the people who chose him.
Rao inherited a financial crisis.

The Indian rupee was overvalued; the trade deficit was widening; the Gulf War had spiked oil prices and disrupted remittance flows from Indian workers in the Persian Gulf; the Soviet Union (India's largest trading partner under preferential bilateral arrangements) was collapsing, which would shortly remove a major component of the Indian export and import structure.
Foreign exchange reserves had fallen to about three weeks of import cover by mid-1991.
The Reserve Bank of India had been forced, the previous month, to physically airlift 47 tons of gold reserves to London to be pledged as collateral for emergency Bank of England and IMF lending.
The Indian economy was about to default.

Rao's first major appointment was the Economic liberalization begins in 1991 under the new Finance Minister Manmohan Singh — an Oxford-trained economist with thirty years of senior bureaucratic experience (RBI Governor, Planning Commission deputy chairman) but no political experience.
The combination of Rao's political authority and Manmohan's technical credibility was, in retrospect, the most important Indian political partnership since Nehru-Patel.

The July 1991 budget — presented by Manmohan to Parliament on July 24 — opened the Indian economy in ways the country had not seen since independence: The rupee was devalued by 24% over the first two weeks of the new government.

The complex industrial licensing system — the so-called License Raj under which any new factory or capacity expansion required prior government permission, a system that had created decades of administrative obstruction and corruption — was abolished except in a small set of specifically restricted industries.
Foreign direct investment limits were raised from 40% to 51% in most industries, and the Foreign Investment Promotion Board was created to fast-track approvals.
Import licensing was substantially dismantled; import tariffs began a fifteen-year decline from peaks of over 200% to single digits.
Capital-market reforms allowed foreign institutional investors to buy Indian listed equities directly.
The public-sector monopoly in core industries (steel, telecommunications, banking) was retained in name but eroded in practice through partial-privatization and competition with new private entrants.

The reforms were politically possible because they had no domestic political champions and because the alternative — outright default and IMF-mandated structural adjustment — was worse than anything the reforms imposed.
Manmohan was a technical figure presenting technical solutions to a fiscal crisis.
The Congress's left wing, led by Arjun Singh, opposed the reforms but had no alternative.
The BJP, the Janata-successor parties, and the Left parties opposed individual measures but did not have the parliamentary numbers to block them.

The Indian capitalist class, which had operated under the License Raj as a small protected oligopoly, was initially divided — Bombay industrial families like the Bajaj and Birla groups had built their positions under the old regime and feared open competition, while a new generation of entrepreneurs (Sunil Mittal at Bharti, Dhirubhai Ambani at Reliance, the founders of Infosys and Wipro at Bangalore) welcomed the opening.
The IT sector, in particular, was about to discover that the new framework was an export-led boom waiting to happen.
The structural results of the 1991 reforms unfolded over the next thirty years.
India's GDP growth rate accelerated from the 3.5% Hindu-rate average of the prior decades to 6–7% for the 1990s and to peaks of 8–9% in the 2003–10 period.
Foreign exchange reserves recovered from three weeks of cover to over $600 billion by the mid-2020s.
The Indian middle class — defined by economists variously, but at the broadest definition adding several hundred million people between 1991 and 2025 — was created by the opening of consumer markets.
Poverty rates fell substantially across this period, though inequality also widened.
The Indian economy of 2026 — fifth-largest in the world by nominal GDP, third-largest by purchasing-power parity — was set up by what Manmohan Singh did in 1991–92.
The political class never gave him formal credit; the reforms were defended after the fact by every subsequent Indian government regardless of party.
The Rao government was politically defined, however, less by the economic reforms than by what happened on December 6, 1992.
The Babri Masjid demolished action that day was the culmination of the VHP–BJP campaign that had been organizing since the 1989 Ram Shila Pujan.
A rally of approximately 150,000 kar sevaks (volunteers) had gathered at Ayodhya, ostensibly for a symbolic kar seva (volunteer service) at the disputed site.
The BJP leadership (Advani, Murli Manohar Joshi, Uma Bharti) was present.
The Uttar Pradesh state government — then under BJP control, with Kalyan Singh as Chief Minister — had given the Supreme Court a sworn assurance that the rally would not damage the structure.

The central Rao government, which had legal authority to deploy central paramilitary forces in the state to protect the structure, had chosen not to do so on the grounds that the state government's assurance should be respected.
The kar sevaks began climbing the mosque structure at midday.
The senior BJP leaders, present on the rally platform a few hundred yards from the structure, did not order the crowd to stop.
By late afternoon the three domes of the 464-year-old mosque had been pulled down brick by brick.
The structure was reduced to rubble.
The BJP leaders' speeches and gestures during the demolition were televised.
Advani later said he wept when the demolition began.
Atal Bihari Vajpayee, who was not present at Ayodhya that day, expressed regret.
Uma Bharti and others were photographed celebrating on the platform.

The Liberhan Commission, established later by Rao to investigate the demolition, took seventeen years to report (it submitted its findings in 2009) and concluded that the demolition had been planned and that the BJP and VHP leaders bore primary responsibility.

None of the criminal cases produced convictions of senior BJP leaders; the principal accused were acquitted in September 2020 by a special CBI court that ruled the demolition had been spontaneous despite the documentary record.
The demolition triggered the worst Hindu-Muslim communal violence since Partition.

In Bombay (Mumbai by 1995), riots in December 1992 and January 1993 killed at least 900 people — predominantly Muslim, in attacks that the Srikrishna Commission later documented as substantially organized by the Shiv Sena political party in coordination with local police.

The 1993 Bombay bombings of March 12, 1993 — coordinated explosions at twelve locations across Bombay including the Stock Exchange, the Air India building, and major hotels, killing 257 people — were carried out by an organized-crime network (Dawood Ibrahim's D-Company) operating from Karachi with the cooperation of Pakistani intelligence in retaliation for the Bombay riots.

The bombings were the first international terror attack of major scale against Indian civilian targets and the first systematic use of Pakistani-territory-based organized crime as a vector for political violence — a pattern that would define Indo-Pakistani relations for the next two decades.
The Rao government completed its full five-year term (1991–96) — the first non-Nehru-Gandhi government in Indian history to do so — and then lost the 1996 General Election.

The Congress had been damaged by the Babri demolition (which Rao had failed to prevent), by the Bombay riots and bombings (which had taken place under partial Congress administrative responsibility), by the Bofors-era corruption legacy, and by the general perception that the economic reforms had benefited urban elites while leaving rural India behind.
The party fell to 140 seats; the BJP emerged as the largest single party with 161 seats but lacked the alliance partners to form a government.
The next chapter is the coalition decade and the BJP's slow rise to a working national majority.

chapters.title: Coalition Decade and NDA
sentences: The 1996 to 1998 period was the chaotic high-water mark of coalition politics.
Between May 1996 and October 1999, India had four Prime Ministers — Vajpayee (briefly), H.
Deve Gowda, Inder Kumar Gujral, and Vajpayee again — and three general elections.

The institutional cause was that no single party had the seats to form a government; the political cause was that the BJP was building toward an electoral majority but had not yet assembled the alliance partners to translate plurality into governing coalition.

The BJP's eventual breakthrough came through the National Democratic Alliance (NDA) — a formal coalition organized by Vajpayee in 1998, including the BJP plus a long list of regional parties (the AIADMK in Tamil Nadu, the Trinamool Congress in West Bengal, the Telugu Desam Party in Andhra, the Akali Dal in Punjab, the Shiv Sena in Maharashtra) that gave the BJP working majorities in the 1998 and 1999 elections.

The NDA's distinctive innovation was that the BJP set aside its most ideologically charged issues — the Ram temple, the abrogation of Article 370 in Kashmir, the Uniform Civil Code — in exchange for governing-coalition support from regional parties whose voters were not Hindu nationalist.

The NDA's "common minimum program" was a moderate economic-reform-and-good-governance agenda that the regional parties could accept and that allowed the BJP to learn the institutional habits of national government.
The Vajpayee government that took office in October 1999 — and held until May 2004 — was the BJP's first sustained experience of central executive authority.

Atal Bihari Vajpayee (1924–2018), the Prime Minister, was an unusual figure in his own party: a poet, a multi-decade parliamentarian (he had first been elected to the Lok Sabha in 1957), a public figure whose actual ideological commitments were softer than his party affiliation suggested.
His political success rested on his ability to project moderate consensus while presiding over an explicitly Hindu nationalist organizational machine.
The decade of his ascendancy — 1996 to 2004 — was when the BJP became a normal Indian political party.
The defining strategic event of the Vajpayee period was the Pokhran-II nuclear tests of May 11 and 13, 1998.

India conducted five underground nuclear tests at the Pokhran range in Rajasthan — the first detonations since the 1974 Smiling Buddha test — including one claimed thermonuclear device (the actual yield of which has been disputed by external technical assessments, with most foreign analysts concluding the yield was below the Indian government's claimed 45 kilotons).

The tests were conducted in tight secrecy: American satellite surveillance had been deliberately deceived by Indian operations security; the United States learned of the tests only when the underground detonations were detected by global seismographic networks; the immediate international response was sweeping sanctions from the United States, Japan, and Germany.

India's strategic rationale was both regional (Pakistan was known to be near nuclear-weapons capability and would test its own devices two weeks later, on May 28, 1998 at Chagai Hills in Baluchistan) and historical (the 1974 test had been a single-device demonstration that did not produce reliable weapons capability; the 1998 tests aimed at producing a deployable nuclear arsenal).
The Indo-Pakistani strategic balance became formally nuclear in May 1998.
The international sanctions imposed on India were largely lifted within three years as the Bush administration repositioned India as a strategic partner against China.
The Kargil War of May–July 1999 was the first armed Indo-Pakistani confrontation under nuclear conditions and a model of what subsequent Indo-Pakistani military crises would look like.

Pakistani Northern Light Infantry troops, disguised as Kashmiri irregular insurgents (the "Kargil intruders" framing was maintained by the Pakistani government for years afterward despite eventual acknowledgment of regular Pakistani Army involvement), infiltrated across the Line of Control in the high-altitude Kargil district of Jammu and Kashmir and occupied unmanned Indian military posts at altitudes of 14,000–18,000 feet.
India responded with the largest Indian Army mobilization since 1971 and with combat air operations by the Indian Air Force.
The Indian counter-offensive, conducted in extraordinarily difficult mountain conditions over ten weeks, retook the captured peaks at substantial cost (527 Indian Army personnel killed in action).
The international response — particularly American pressure on Pakistan, under the Clinton administration's Pakistan-specific channels — pushed Pakistan to withdraw.

The Pakistani military's domestic political position was substantially damaged by the operation's failure; General Pervez Musharraf, the principal Pakistani officer behind the Kargil plan, would use that domestic damage to launch a coup against the elected Pakistani civilian government in October 1999.

India's response to Kargil — measured retaliation contained within the operational area, no escalation across the international border — set the pattern for how nuclear-era Indo-Pakistani crises would be managed.
The Vajpayee government also produced the most ambitious infrastructure-investment program of any post-independence Indian government to that point.

The Golden Quadrilateral — a 5,846-kilometer four-lane (later six-lane) national highway network connecting Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai, and Kolkata, with feeder spurs to most of the major Indian cities — was conceived and substantially built between 1999 and 2006.

The Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (PMGSY), the rural roads program launched in 2000, paved or graded over 750,000 kilometers of rural roads across the next twenty-five years and substantially closed the rural-urban physical infrastructure gap.
The combined road program was the largest single physical-infrastructure investment of the Indian state since the colonial-era railways.

Its electoral consequences were direct: rural voters reached by the new roads were more likely to access urban markets, hospitals, schools, and jobs, and were more likely to vote for the party that built the roads.
The Vajpayee government also presided over the IT boom and Bangalore rises that defined Indian economic perception abroad.

The 1990s opening had created the regulatory space; the late-1990s Y2K crisis — the global panic over the 2000 calendar rollover and the need to remediate decades of two-digit-year computer code — gave Indian software services firms (Tata Consultancy Services, Infosys, Wipro, HCL Technologies) their first large-scale Western contracts.

Bangalore (Bengaluru, by then increasingly using its Kannada name), Hyderabad, Pune, and Chennai became the centers of an export-oriented software-services industry that grew from approximately $5 billion in 2000 to $150 billion by 2020.

The IT industry transformed the Indian middle class: educated young Indians could enter a global economy directly from their hometowns at wages that were Western-comparable in nominal terms (and far higher in purchasing-power terms within India).
The "back office of the world" framing was real economically and shaped Indian public-policy debate across the 2000s.
The Vajpayee government lost the 2004 General Election.

The "India Shining" campaign — built around the economic-reform success — failed to translate to the rural voter, who had not experienced the IT boom directly and who had been hit hard by the 2002 Gujarat communal violence (Chapter below).

The Congress under the new leadership of Sonia Gandhi — Rajiv's Italian-born widow, who had taken over the Congress in 1998 after a long political withdrawal — won 145 seats, the BJP took 138, and the United Progressive Alliance (UPA) — a Congress-led coalition with support from the Left parties and an array of regional partners — assembled the working majority.
Sonia Gandhi declined the prime-ministership in the face of organized BJP campaigning around her foreign birth and named Manmohan Singh as Prime Minister instead.
The architect of the 1991 reforms became Prime Minister in his own right at age seventy-two.
The 2002 Gujarat communal violence requires its own paragraph here because of its later consequences.
On February 27, 2002, a train carriage at Godhra station in Gujarat caught fire, killing 59 Hindu pilgrims returning from Ayodhya.

The cause of the fire was disputed at the time and remains contested: a state inquiry concluded it was deliberately set by Muslim mob action; an independent inquiry concluded the cause was likely accidental.

Regardless of cause, the response was anti-Muslim communal violence across Gujarat over the next three months that killed at least 1,000 people (the Indian government figure; later inquiries suggest 2,000 or more), the vast majority Muslim, with attacks documented in over a dozen Gujarat cities and with credible evidence of police and state-administration complicity.
The Gujarat Chief Minister at the time was Narendra Modi, in his first stint as Chief Minister (he had been appointed in October 2001 to that position by the BJP).
Modi's role in either organizing, condoning, or failing to suppress the violence was the subject of multiple inquiries across the next decade and is still actively contested.
A Special Investigation Team appointed by the Supreme Court in 2008 concluded in 2012 that there was no prosecutable evidence against Modi personally for the violence.
The US government revoked Modi's visa in 2005 over the 2002 violence; the visa was restored in 2014 when he became Prime Minister.

The 2002 violence shaped Modi's political identity for fifteen years — for his critics, indelibly tying him to Hindu nationalist communal violence; for his supporters, identifying him as a strong leader who had imposed order on a chaotic state and as a figure the Indian left would attempt to discredit no matter what.
The Indian Supreme Court closed the principal pending case against Modi in 2022.
The 2002 violence is now legally inert but politically active.

chapters.title: Manmohan's UPA
sentences: The UPA's first term (May 2004 to May 2009) was probably the most successful Indian government of the post-1991 period.

The combination of Sonia Gandhi as party leader (with effective coordination authority over the Congress organizational machinery and the coalition partners) and Manmohan Singh as Prime Minister (with technical competence and personal probity unmatched by any post-Nehru predecessor) produced a remarkably coherent governing program.
The defining policy of UPA-1 was the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA), passed in 2005 and operational from 2006.
The program legally guaranteed up to 100 days of paid manual labor per year per rural household, at the agricultural minimum wage, on locally proposed public-works projects.

The scheme was the largest workfare program in human history by enrollment (roughly 250 million workers registered at peak; 50–100 million working in any given year), the largest such program by spending (around 0.5% of GDP at peak), and a substantial achievement in rural welfare guarantee.

The economic-development debate around MGNREGA has been continuous since: critics argue it has reduced agricultural productivity by pulling labor out of farms and has crowded out productive private investment; defenders argue it has provided rural consumption floor in drought years, has reduced distress migration, and has built (often imperfectly) durable rural infrastructure (canal cleaning, watershed regeneration, village road maintenance).
The program is, in 2026, still operating; no government has dared dismantle it.

The second defining policy was the Right to Information Act of 2005 — a sweeping freedom-of-information law that required all government bodies at central, state, and local levels to respond to citizen information requests within 30 days, with limited exemptions for national security and personal privacy.
The RTI Act became a foundational instrument of Indian civil society activism, citizen accountability, and journalism.

The volume of RTI requests filed annually grew from a few thousand in 2006 to over six million by the mid-2010s, and the law substantially changed the operating habits of the Indian bureaucracy by introducing systematic external scrutiny of administrative decision-making.
The cost was real: RTI activists became targets of organized political and bureaucratic retaliation, with at least 100 RTI activists killed in the decade after the Act's passage.
The Act's effectiveness was eroded in later years by court rulings and government amendments that narrowed its scope.
But in 2005 it was a major piece of democratic deepening.

The third was the US nuclear deal — the Indo-US Civil Nuclear Agreement of October 2008 — under which the United States, after sustained negotiation across Manmohan's first term, agreed to lift its post-1974 sanctions on nuclear-related trade with India and to support India's exception from the Nuclear Suppliers Group export-control regime.

The deal acknowledged India's existing nuclear-weapons status outside the Non-Proliferation Treaty framework and gave India access to the international civilian nuclear market while not requiring India to sign the NPT or surrender any weapons capability.

The agreement was a major diplomatic shift: the United States, under Bush and then Obama administrations, was effectively choosing India over Pakistan as its primary South Asian strategic partner, and Indian-American relations entered a phase of substantive convergence that would shape both countries' foreign-policy positioning for the next two decades.

The agreement was nearly fatal to UPA-1 domestically — the Left parties, which had been providing outside support to the coalition since 2004, withdrew over the deal in July 2008, and the Manmohan government survived a confidence motion only by a few votes (and with significant evidence of cash-for-votes inducement, which later produced criminal investigations of multiple parliamentarians).
The deal was nonetheless ratified.

The Mumbai terror attacks of November 26–29, 2008 — the 26/11 attacks, the most deadly single terror operation against Indian civilians in decades — were the worst single security failure of the Manmohan period.

Ten Lashkar-e-Taiba terrorists infiltrated by sea from Karachi to the Mumbai waterfront on the evening of November 26 and conducted coordinated attacks at multiple targets: the Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus railway station, the Taj Mahal Palace Hotel, the Trident-Oberoi Hotel, the Leopold Café, the Cama Hospital, and the Nariman House Jewish community center.

The siege lasted 60 hours. 166 people were killed (including six Americans and several Israeli, British, and Canadian nationals); the only captured terrorist, Ajmal Kasab, was tried in India, convicted, and executed in 2012.

The Pakistani intelligence service's coordination of the attacks was extensively documented by the captured terrorist's own statements, by intercepted Lashkar-Pakistan handler communications, and by external intelligence-service intelligence sharing.

India's response was diplomatic rather than military — the Manmohan government chose not to retaliate militarily under the assessment that Indo-Pakistani nuclear deterrence made conventional escalation too dangerous, a calculation that the BJP opposition criticized at the time and that would become a point of comparison with Modi's later Balakot strikes (Chapter 13).
The 26/11 attacks crystallized Indian public sentiment around Pakistani-sponsored terrorism and reduced public tolerance for the Manmohan-era policy of dialogue with Pakistan.
UPA-1 won re-election in May 2009 with an even stronger mandate — the Congress alone took 206 seats, the UPA coalition reached 262, and Manmohan was sworn in for a second term.

The 2008 financial crisis had been navigated with relative success (Indian growth slowed from 9% to 5% but did not contract, and the public-sector banking system absorbed the global shock through partial state recapitalization rather than systemic failure).
The Indian economy was growing at over 8% annually.
Per capita income had doubled in the eight years since the IT-driven acceleration began.
The political class read the 2009 result as endorsement of the UPA model.
UPA-2 (May 2009 to May 2014) is the period during which the Manmohan settlement collapsed.
The collapse had three drivers: corruption, economic deceleration, and the rise of organized anti-corruption mobilization that the Congress could not absorb.
The 2G spectrum scandal broke in November 2010, when the Comptroller and Auditor General reported that the Telecommunications Minister A.

Raja (a DMK politician in the UPA coalition) had allocated 2G mobile-telephony spectrum licenses in 2008 at substantially below-market prices, with the alleged loss to the exchequer being approximately Rs 1.76 lakh crore (about $39 billion at then-exchange rates).
The number was politically devastating.
The scale was unimaginable.
The allocations had been concentrated among a small group of telecom firms, most of whom resold their licenses at multi-billion-dollar profits within months.
The Supreme Court in 2012 cancelled all 122 licenses allocated under the 2008 process.

Raja was tried, eventually acquitted in 2017 by a special court that found insufficient prosecutable evidence (a verdict the Congress later used to claim vindication and that the BJP described as judicial failure), but the political damage to UPA-2 was permanent.

The Commonwealth Games scandal broke in October 2010 around the New Delhi Commonwealth Games of that year — multiple investigations documented contract irregularities, cost overruns, and quality failures across the games' infrastructure.
The Games Organising Committee chairman Suresh Kalmadi was arrested in 2011 and tried over several years; the case was eventually closed in 2024 without conviction.

The political impact again preceded the legal outcome by many years: the Games had been a high-visibility national event held at a moment when the Congress was claiming managerial competence, and the corruption findings undermined that claim.

The Coalgate scandal of 2012 documented similar allocation-pricing issues in the assignment of coal-mining blocks to private firms during 2005–11, with CAG-estimated losses ranging from $33 billion to $200 billion depending on methodology.
The Supreme Court in 2014 cancelled all 204 coal-block allocations made under the contested process.
Multiple senior Congress figures (though notably not Manmohan Singh personally) were charged in associated cases; the legal proceedings have continued for over a decade.
The Anna Hazare anti-corruption movement of 2011–12 was the political vehicle that translated the scandals into electoral consequence.

Hazare — a 73-year-old former Indian Army soldier turned Gandhian rural activist from Maharashtra, with a long history of local good-governance campaigns — began a hunger strike in April 2011 at Delhi's Jantar Mantar demanding the passage of a strong Lokpal Bill that would create an independent anti-corruption ombudsman with prosecutorial powers over the central executive.
The movement attracted enormous middle-class urban support, particularly through social media and through television-news coverage that gave Hazare round-the-clock attention.
A second Hazare fast in August 2011 at the Ramlila Maidan drew sustained crowds.
The Congress government's responses — alternately conciliatory and dismissive — failed to manage the movement's political momentum.
The Lokpal Bill was eventually passed in 2013 in a substantially weakened form that satisfied few activists.
But the political consequences of the Hazare movement were larger than the legislation.

The movement produced two new political vehicles: Arvind Kejriwal, who had been Hazare's chief organizational deputy, broke with Hazare in 2012 and founded the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) — a Delhi-based anti-corruption populist party that would win the Delhi state election in 2013 and 2015 and would become a substantial regional force; and the Bharatiya Janata Party under its new leadership, which adopted the anti-corruption framing as its own and positioned itself as the natural alternative to a discredited UPA.
The economy was also slowing.
Indian GDP growth fell from 9% in 2010 to 4.7% in 2013.
The rupee fell sharply against the dollar in mid-2013, hitting historical lows.

The deceleration combined supply-side factors (deferred infrastructure investment, regulatory uncertainty around the scandals' fallout) with global factors (the slowdown in Chinese demand for Indian commodity exports, the US Federal Reserve's signaling of monetary tightening that triggered emerging-market capital outflows).
Inflation remained stubbornly above 10%, putting pressure on real wages.
The Indian middle class — the constituency that had benefited most from the 1991–2010 growth boom — was experiencing for the first time the sense that the high-growth period might be over.
The BJP organized for 2014.

Narendra Modi had been re-elected Chief Minister of Gujarat three times (2002, 2007, 2012) on a development-focused political platform that had cultivated a national-level reputation as an effective administrator.
He had also rebuilt his international position, partly through systematic outreach to Indian-American business networks and to Hong Kong–Singapore–London Indian diaspora communities.
In September 2013, the BJP formally named Modi as its prime-ministerial candidate for the upcoming general election — over the resistance of senior party figure L.
Advani, who had assumed the candidacy would go to him.

The campaign that followed was the most expensive and most data-intensive Indian election campaign to that point: heavy use of holographic 3D projections that allowed Modi to "appear" simultaneously at multiple rallies, sophisticated micro-targeted social-media outreach, sustained branding around the "Gujarat model" of economic development, and a personal cult of Modi as a decisive alternative to the perceived drift of the Manmohan years.
The Congress was unable to articulate a coherent response.
Rahul Gandhi, Sonia's son and the heir apparent, ran a hesitant campaign that did not address the corruption charges directly.
The 2014 General Election result was the first single-party Lok Sabha majority since 1984.
The BJP took 282 seats — its first absolute majority in any general election.
The Congress fell to 44 seats — its worst result ever and the lowest seat-count of any major Indian party in a general election.
The NDA total was 336 seats out of 543.
Narendra Modi becomes PM on May 26, 2014.
The Manmohan settlement had ended.
The next decade was the BJP's.

chapters.title: Modi I
sentences: Modi's first term (2014–2019) was the most ambitious legislative and administrative period of any Indian government since Nehru's first decade.
Whether the ambitions translated into commensurate outcomes is, eight to ten years on, a contested judgment.
The most consistent pattern is that Modi's first term consisted of large, dramatic interventions whose actual results often fell short of the framings.
The most dramatic single act was the demonetization of banknotes on November 8, 2016.

Modi addressed the nation at 8:15 PM on a recorded television broadcast and announced that, effective midnight that same evening, the 500-rupee and 1,000-rupee notes — comprising approximately 86% of the cash currency in circulation by value — were no longer legal tender.
The notes had to be deposited at banks for replacement with new notes (a redesigned 500-rupee note and a brand-new 2,000-rupee denomination) within fifty days.
The stated rationale was the elimination of "black money" — undeclared cash holdings — and the disruption of counterfeit-currency networks (some allegedly Pakistan-sourced) and terrorism financing.
The implementation was chaotic.

The Reserve Bank of India had not stockpiled adequate replacement notes; ATMs across the country recalibrated for the new currency at variable rates; rural and small-town banks were overwhelmed by depositor demand; cash-economy small businesses and informal-sector workers (the substantial majority of Indian economic activity, including most agricultural labor and most retail) lost their working capital overnight.
The estimated economic cost of the disruption was 1–2 percentage points of GDP growth in 2017.

The stated benefits were not realized: the RBI's eventual count, in 2018, showed that 99.3% of the demonetized notes had been redeposited at banks, meaning that virtually no black money had been destroyed and that the principal hoarders had successfully laundered their holdings through proxy depositors or through cash-to-cash conversion networks.

Counter-arguments — that demonetization had increased digital payments adoption (which is documented: UPI digital-payments volume grew from negligible levels in 2016 to over 10 billion monthly transactions by 2023), that it had broadened the tax base (also partially documented), and that the political signal of decisive action against the wealthy had electoral benefit — are real but harder to weigh against the immediate disruption costs.
The Goods and Services Tax (GST), implemented July 1, 2017, was the second major intervention.

The GST replaced a long-accumulated tangle of central excise duties, state value-added taxes, service taxes, and a dozen smaller levies with a single nationally-harmonized indirect-tax system across all Indian states.

The reform had been in legislative development since the Vajpayee period and required a constitutional amendment to allocate taxation authority between the Union and the states; both the Vajpayee and Manmohan governments had failed to assemble the political consensus required.

The Modi government negotiated the deal with state governments by guaranteeing revenue protection (with the Centre making up any state-level shortfalls for the first five years) and by setting up the GST Council as a federal cooperative body where state finance ministers vote on rate changes.

The implementation phase was again chaotic — small businesses struggled with compliance requirements, the GST Network IT infrastructure had bottlenecks, multiple rate tiers complicated reporting — but the long-term effect was a substantial simplification of the Indian indirect-tax system and the removal of internal trade barriers between Indian states.

The third broad initiative was the Swachh Bharat Abhiyan (Clean India Mission) — a public-sanitation program launched in October 2014 with the stated goal of constructing toilets for every Indian household by 2019 to end open defecation.
The program built approximately 110 million toilets at central and state expense across five years.

The construction was real (though the quality and the sustained-use rate of the built toilets is contested — multiple later assessments found that many constructed toilets were not used, that water-supply provisions for the toilets were inadequate, and that the behavioral-change campaign had only partial reach).

The political and symbolic value of the program — the Prime Minister of India personally identifying with the dignity of poor Indians' sanitation — was substantial regardless of the implementation gaps.
The Swachh Bharat framing also extended to a broader urban-cleanliness campaign that produced visibly different urban environments in BJP-governed states across the late 2010s.

The fourth was the Jan Dhan Yojana financial-inclusion program of 2014, which opened bank accounts for over 500 million previously unbanked Indians by 2020, and the related Aadhaar biometric identity system — which had been launched under the Manmohan government in 2010 but which the Modi government dramatically expanded and operationalized for delivering government benefits.

The combination of Jan Dhan + Aadhaar + mobile-phone-number registration (the so-called JAM trinity) created the digital-identity and digital-payments infrastructure for the next phase of Indian state-citizen interaction.
Welfare payments, agricultural subsidies, COVID relief payments, and pension transfers all migrated to the new infrastructure across the late 2010s.

The Aadhaar system has been controversial — civil-liberties critics have raised concerns about state surveillance and database security, and the Supreme Court in 2018 narrowed the permissible uses of Aadhaar verification — but the basic infrastructure became a permanent fixture of the Indian state.
The defense and foreign-policy story of Modi I was structured around two episodes with Pakistan and a broader strategic reorientation.

The Uri attack of September 18, 2016 — a militant attack on an Indian Army camp at Uri in Jammu and Kashmir that killed 19 Indian soldiers — produced India's first formally acknowledged cross-border "surgical strike" operation.
Indian Special Forces units crossed the Line of Control on the night of September 28–29, 2016 and attacked alleged militant launch pads inside Pakistan-administered Kashmir.

The operation's actual effects — whether it destroyed significant militant infrastructure, how many militants were killed — has been contested by Pakistani denials and by external analysts who have questioned the Indian government's specific claims.
But the political message — that India would now respond to Pakistan-based terror attacks with explicit retaliation rather than the Manmohan-era policy of strategic restraint — was the point.
The Pulwama–Balakot crisis of February 2019 was the larger test.
On February 14, 2019, a Jaish-e-Mohammed suicide bomber detonated an explosive-laden vehicle alongside a Central Reserve Police Force convoy at Pulwama in Kashmir, killing 40 paramilitary personnel.

India responded on February 26 with Indian Air Force airstrikes at Balakot, a Jaish-e-Mohammed training facility located inside Pakistan's Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa province — the first Indian air strikes inside Pakistani territory since 1971.

Pakistan retaliated with attempted strikes the next day inside Indian-administered Kashmir; in the resulting aerial engagement, an Indian MiG-21 was shot down over Pakistan and its pilot Abhinandan Varthaman was captured (and released two days later after diplomatic pressure).

The actual battle-damage assessment of the Balakot strikes has been contested — Indian claims of substantial militant deaths were not supported by external satellite imagery analysis — but the political message was again the point: India would strike inside Pakistani territory in response to terror attacks, and the Indo-Pakistani strategic equation now included formal Indian air operations beyond the Line of Control.
The Balakot strikes were also conducted ten weeks before the 2019 General Election; whatever their military effect, the political effect on Indian public sentiment was significant.

The broader strategic reorientation was toward a closer Indian alignment with the United States, Japan, and Australia — the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue (Quad), which had originated under Vajpayee and Manmohan but had been quiescent through the early 2010s.

The Modi government revived the Quad in 2017, expanded annual Indo-American and Indo-Japanese defense exercises substantially, and signed major U.S. defense-cooperation agreements (LEMOA, COMCASA, BECA) that integrated Indian military capabilities with American logistics, communications, and intelligence networks.

The strategic logic was the rising threat from China — particularly after the 2017 Doklam standoff (a 73-day Indo-Chinese military standoff at a tri-junction with Bhutan in the eastern Himalayas, ended by mutual disengagement) — and the recognition that India's southeastern and northern strategic position required American security underwriting that Indian non-alignment had previously precluded.
The 2019 General Election was a referendum on Modi's first term, and the result was a stronger BJP majority than 2014.
The BJP took 303 seats (the NDA reached 353); the Congress recovered marginally to 52 seats.

Modi was sworn in for a second term with an even stronger mandate and the political authority to pursue the BJP's core ideological program, which the coalition constraints of NDA-1 had partially blunted.
The next chapter is what he did with that authority.

chapters.title: Modi II
sentences: Modi II (2019–2024) was the period during which the BJP delivered its core Hindu-nationalist agenda after thirty years of organizing.

The three signature acts of the second term — the abrogation of Article 370 in Kashmir, the Citizenship Amendment Act, and the construction of the Ram temple at Ayodhya — completed the legislative-and-symbolic program the BJP had been promising since the 1990s.
The abrogation of Article 370 on August 5, 2019, was the boldest single act of the Modi period.

Article 370 of the Indian Constitution had granted Jammu and Kashmir special autonomous status since 1949 — separate state constitution, separate flag, restrictions on land purchase by non-Kashmiri residents, separate central-government legislative authority.

The article had been the basis of the 1947 accession terms and had become, in BJP framing, a permanent obstacle to Kashmiri integration with the Indian Union and a special privilege for Muslim-majority Kashmir that the rest of India did not enjoy.

The Modi government's procedure for abrogation was constitutionally aggressive: a presidential order on August 5 changed Article 370's operative provisions through a reinterpretation of "Constituent Assembly" (the original Kashmir Constituent Assembly having dissolved in 1957) as the Jammu and Kashmir State Legislative Assembly (which was under President's Rule and not in session).

A parallel Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act divided the former state into two Union Territories — Jammu and Kashmir, and Ladakh — converting the territory from a state under President's Rule to a centrally-administered territory with substantially reduced autonomy.

The constitutional legality of the abrogation was challenged in the Supreme Court; the court's 2023 ruling upheld the abrogation by 5–0 majority while raising questions about specific procedural aspects.
The implementation was managed with extraordinary security.
The internet was shut down in the Kashmir Valley starting August 4 and was not fully restored for over a year (the longest internet shutdown ever imposed by a democratic government).
All major Kashmiri political leaders, including three former state Chief Ministers, were placed under preventive detention; many were held for months without trial.
Substantial paramilitary deployments locked down Kashmir Valley cities and prevented public protests.

The international response was muted: Pakistan protested loudly but had no leverage; the United States and the United Kingdom expressed mild concern but did not push for reversal; China protested the Ladakh component (which included Aksai Chin, claimed by China) and would later use the protest as justification for the 2020 Galwan border clashes (below).
The Indian public was overwhelmingly supportive: opinion polls showed support for the abrogation at over 70% across all major Indian states except Kashmir itself.
The Kashmiri political consensus after 2019 was that the abrogation was a unilateral imposition that delegitimized the constitutional basis of the 1947 accession.

The integrationist counter-argument was that the special status had been a fiction since 1953 (when Sheikh Abdullah's pro-autonomy state government had been dismissed) and that the constitutional reorganization had simply formalized what had been the actual federal arrangement for decades.

The political question — whether the abrogation will permanently shift Kashmir into the normal Indian federal framework or whether it will produce, over time, a longer-running political crisis — is, in 2026, still being settled.
The Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA) of December 2019 was the second core ideological measure of Modi II.
The act provided expedited Indian citizenship for non-Muslim refugees from Pakistan, Bangladesh, and Afghanistan who had entered India before December 31, 2014.
The list of eligible religions — Hindus, Sikhs, Buddhists, Jains, Parsis, Christians — explicitly excluded Muslims.

The act, in conjunction with the proposed National Register of Citizens (NRC) — a citizenship-verification process that had been implemented in Assam and was being discussed for nationwide rollout — produced widespread opposition: Muslim political organizations argued that the combination of CAA's religious-criterion citizenship pathway and NRC's documentation-based citizenship verification was specifically designed to render undocumented Muslims stateless while protecting undocumented non-Muslims.

Mass protests broke out across the country between December 2019 and March 2020, most prominently at the Shaheen Bagh sit-in in southeast Delhi (a months-long peaceful protest led primarily by Muslim women that became the defining symbol of CAA opposition).

Communal violence in northeast Delhi in February 2020 killed 53 people — predominantly Muslim, in attacks where Delhi Police complicity has been alleged by multiple inquiries — and the protests broadly dissipated under the impact of the COVID lockdown that began in March 2020.
The Ram Temple consecrated in Ayodhya on January 22, 2024 completed the third leg of the program.

The construction of the temple at the disputed Ayodhya site — on land where the Babri Masjid had stood until December 1992 — had been authorized by the Supreme Court's November 2019 ruling resolving the land-title dispute.
The court awarded the disputed site to the Ram temple trust while allotting an alternative five-acre parcel elsewhere in Ayodhya for a new mosque.
The temple's construction began in 2020 and the pran pratishtha (consecration of the deity inside the new temple) was conducted on January 22, 2024 in a ceremony attended by Modi personally.

The opposition political parties, the Shankaracharyas (the senior Hindu religious authorities), and the Indian liberal commentariat were divided on whether to attend; most stayed away on the grounds that the ceremony was being conducted while construction was incomplete and that the political framing of the event subordinated religious to political authority.

The consecration was nonetheless a defining moment in 21st-century Indian political-religious history: it completed the symbolic project that the VHP had launched in 1986, vindicated the BJP's long-running political bet on Hindu cultural mobilization, and demonstrated the BJP's ability to deliver substantive cultural outcomes that previous Congress governments had been unwilling or unable to attempt.
The non-ideological story of Modi II was dominated by COVID, the farmers' protests, and the slow-motion strategic confrontation with China.
The COVID-19 pandemic struck India in March 2020.

The Modi government imposed one of the world's most stringent national lockdowns on March 25, 2020 — a 21-day complete shutdown of economic activity announced with four hours' notice and subsequently extended for two months.

The implementation produced a humanitarian crisis: tens of millions of urban migrant workers, suddenly unemployed and unable to access transport home, were stranded in cities without food, shelter, or medical care; many died on the long walks home; the economic disruption produced India's first GDP contraction since 1979 (an estimated –6.6% in fiscal 2020–21).

The Indian vaccine rollout, beginning in January 2021, was eventually the world's largest by total doses administered (over 2.2 billion doses by 2022); the Delta variant wave of April–June 2021 produced the worst public-health disaster of the period, with India's official COVID death toll reaching approximately 470,000 but with academic excess-death studies estimating actual mortality at 3–5 million.

The Delta wave overwhelmed Indian hospital infrastructure across multiple states; the images of crematoria operating at full capacity around the clock and of family members of COVID patients searching for oxygen cylinders defined the worst weeks of 2021.
The political consequences of COVID were mixed.

The Modi government's initial response was widely supported (the lockdown framing as decisive national action met its political moment) but the Delta wave damaged its competence reputation, particularly in states (including Uttar Pradesh) where hospital infrastructure failed under load.
The post-pandemic economic recovery was, by global standards, strong: Indian GDP growth recovered to 8.7% in fiscal 2021–22 and stayed above 7% through 2023–24.
The Indian economy in 2024 was the world's fifth largest by nominal GDP, having overtaken the United Kingdom in 2022.
The 2020–21 farmers' protests were the largest sustained protest movement against the Modi government.

In September 2020, the government passed three agricultural reform laws that opened the agricultural produce market to private buyers, allowed contract farming with private corporations, and removed price controls on essential commodities.
The laws were technically defensible from a market-economy standpoint and had been recommended by multiple economist commissions for two decades.
The political execution was poor.

Farmers' organizations from Punjab, Haryana, and Western UP — predominantly Sikh and Jat Hindu small-landowners benefiting from the existing Minimum Support Price (MSP) system and the regulated mandi (market yard) infrastructure — read the laws as designed to dismantle the price-support and market-access systems that protected them from corporate buyer concentration.
Farmers' unions organized a sustained encampment at the Delhi border, principally at the Singhu and Tikri checkpoints, beginning November 2020.
The encampments persisted through one of the coldest North Indian winters in decades and through the Delta COVID wave.
The protests included Republic Day 2021 violence at Red Fort, organized by a fringe of the movement, that produced criminal cases and political division within the protest leadership.
After fourteen months of standoff, Modi announced on November 19, 2021 that the three laws would be repealed, conceding the protesters' core demand.
The repeal was the largest single Modi-government policy reversal of the second term and a substantial demonstration of organized rural-Indian political capacity.

The Galwan Valley clash of June 15, 2020 — a hand-to-hand combat engagement between Indian and Chinese troops in the high-altitude Galwan Valley of Ladakh that killed 20 Indian soldiers and an undisclosed number of Chinese troops (later Chinese acknowledgments and external estimates suggest at least 40) — was the first lethal Indo-Chinese border engagement since 1975.
The clash followed weeks of Chinese forward deployments into multiple sectors of the disputed Ladakh frontier and produced an ongoing standoff that, six years later, has not fully resolved.

The Modi government's response was a substantial Indian military reinforcement of the eastern Ladakh region, combined with a public-relations effort to minimize the political damage from the casualties.

India's response also included the banning of dozens of Chinese mobile applications (notably TikTok), increased tariffs on Chinese imports, and broader regulatory restrictions on Chinese FDI in Indian companies.
The Indo-Chinese relationship after Galwan has been worse than at any point since the 1962 war.
The Chandrayaan-3 lands on Moon mission of August 23, 2023 was the most successful single Indian scientific achievement of the period.

The Indian Space Research Organisation's robotic lunar lander touched down at 70°S, 32°E on the lunar surface — the first soft landing on the lunar south pole region by any space agency, and the first Indian soft landing on the Moon after the 2019 Chandrayaan-2 mission's lander had failed during descent.

The mission was completed at a total cost of approximately $75 million — less than the production budget of several Hollywood space films — and demonstrated the cost-effectiveness of the Indian space program (also visible in earlier missions: the 2008 Chandrayaan-1 lunar mission, India's first lunar probe; the 2014 Mangalyaan reaches Mars mission, the first Asian Mars mission and the first to succeed on first attempt by any space agency; and the parallel scientific programs across these missions).

The political framing of Chandrayaan-3 by the Modi government — the lunar surface as Indian sovereign reach, the technical achievement as evidence of broader civilizational capability — was successful: the Indian public received the achievement as national vindication.
Modi's G20 presidency of 2023 was the diplomatic high-water mark of the second term.

India hosted the G20 summit in Delhi in September 2023 with extensive coordination across multiple national capitals and multiple sub-national working groups, produced the Delhi Declaration (a consensus document despite Russia-Ukraine war tensions), and used the presidency to substantially elevate India's diplomatic profile as a leader of the global South.
The summit's branding around "Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam" (the Sanskrit phrase meaning "the world is one family") was a successful piece of cultural-diplomatic positioning.

India's diplomatic relationships across the period of the G20 presidency were strong with the United States (which had stepped up arms transfers and intelligence cooperation), with the European Union (concluding major trade negotiations), with the Gulf monarchies (energy and labor migration), and with Russia (oil purchases sustained despite Western sanctions).

The simultaneous tensions — with China across the disputed border, with Canada over the Trudeau government's accusations of Indian involvement in the killing of a Khalistani activist on Canadian soil, with the United States over the alleged Indian government plot to assassinate the New York–based Khalistani lawyer Gurpatwant Singh Pannun — sat alongside the diplomatic successes without disrupting them.
The 2024 General Election was held in seven phases between April and June 2024 and produced a result the BJP had not expected.

The party's seats fell from 303 to 240 — a substantial loss that left the BJP short of an outright Lok Sabha majority and dependent on its NDA partners (particularly the Telugu Desam Party in Andhra Pradesh and the Janata Dal United in Bihar) to form the government.
The opposition INDIA bloc — a Congress-led coalition that had assembled across 2023 — improved substantially, with the Congress doubling to 99 seats and the bloc total reaching 234.

The 2024 result was the third Modi mandate but the first one to require coalition management rather than majority governance, and it has substantially changed the operating conditions of the second-decade BJP.

chapters.title: The Republic at Seventy-Seven
sentences: The Modi 3.0 government — formed in June 2024 with the BJP at 240 Lok Sabha seats and the NDA coalition at 293 — operates under coalition constraints that the BJP had not faced since 1999.

The early signals of the third term suggest the government will be more moderate on the ideological program than Modi II had been: the major signature legislative items have been deferred, the cabinet portfolio distribution has been more accommodating to coalition partners than the second-term cabinet, and the BJP's organizational machinery is partially focused on a generational transition (Modi is 75 in 2025; the question of who succeeds him at the next election in 2029 is unresolved within the party).
Three structural conditions will define the next decade of Indian politics regardless of who is in charge.
The first is the demographic dividend.
India in 2026 has approximately 1.43 billion people, having surpassed China in 2023 to become the world's most populous nation.
The Indian median age is 28 (compared to 39 in China, 39 in the United States, 49 in Japan).
India will add another 200 million people to its working-age population by 2050.

This demographic structure is an enormous economic opportunity — a young workforce can drive growth and innovation if the workforce is educated and employed — and an enormous economic and political risk if it is not.
India's labor-force participation rate is, by global standards, low (about 56% overall, with female participation around 33%); the formal employment rate is even lower.
The Indian state's most important medium-term question is whether it can generate sufficient employment for the demographic wave that is currently in school.

Manufacturing growth has been below targets; agricultural productivity has plateaued; the IT and services sectors have absorbed a substantial share of the educated middle-class workforce but not enough to absorb the broader labor pool.

The political economy of the next twenty years will be heavily shaped by whether India can produce 12–15 million new jobs per year for the next twenty years; the current pace is closer to 7–8 million.
The second is the China question.
The Indo-Chinese strategic competition is the defining external pressure on Indian foreign and security policy.

The Galwan-era border standoff has not fully resolved; substantial Chinese forward deployments persist along the Line of Actual Control; Chinese infrastructure construction in Tibet and Xinjiang continues to alter the disputed-border equation.
The broader question is whether India can sustainably operate as a strategic counterweight to China across the Indo-Pacific region.

The Quad partnership with the United States, Japan, and Australia is one element; bilateral defense cooperation with France, the United Kingdom, Israel, and South Korea is another; the building of indigenous defense-industry capacity (the Atmanirbhar Bharat — "self-reliant India" — initiative that the Modi government has emphasized since 2020) is a third.
Whether the combination is sufficient to manage Chinese strategic pressure is the question of the next two decades.

The economic-coupling question — India's continued dependence on Chinese imports for several critical industrial sectors, particularly pharmaceuticals, electronics, and rare earths — is parallel and unresolved.
The third is the diaspora superpower dimension.

The Indian diaspora is, in 2026, approximately 32 million people, including 5 million in the United States, 4 million in the Gulf monarchies, 3 million in the UK and Europe, and substantial communities in Canada, Australia, Singapore, and East Africa.

The diaspora's economic, political, and cultural influence on contemporary India has grown dramatically since the 1991 opening — both as a financial flow (remittances exceeded remittances exceeded $125 billion25 billion in 2023, the largest annual remittance receipt of any country in history) and as a political asset (Indian diaspora communities have substantial influence on host-country relationships with India, particularly in the United States, where Indian-Americans now hold senior positions across multiple branches of government, the corporate sector, and academia).

The "civilizational" framing that the Modi government has emphasized — India not as a post-colonial state but as a continuous civilization with global reach — is at least partly underwritten by the diaspora reality.

The diaspora is also a vehicle for the export of Indian politics back to India: the funding base for both the BJP's Hindu nationalist organizations and for the Indian liberal commentariat's institutional infrastructure includes substantial overseas-Indian components.
India in 2026 is no longer a country whose political life can be cleanly separated from the political life of its citizens and former citizens abroad.
The question of what India is becoming, in 2026, is genuinely open.
The country has, in the eighty years since independence, accomplished things that very few comparably sized post-colonial states have achieved.

It has held competitive multiparty elections at every five-year interval since 1952, including the 2024 election that reduced the ruling party's majority — a transfer of partial political authority by ballot rather than by coup.
It has produced a nuclear-armed military capable of regional deterrence and a space program capable of lunar and Martian missions.
It has lifted hundreds of millions of people out of absolute poverty, though several hundred million remain poor by any reasonable definition.

It has produced cultural and intellectual exports — films, software, academic and literary work, religious and philosophical traditions in revival — that have substantially shaped global culture far beyond Indian borders.
It has also produced things that the founding generation of the republic would not have endorsed.
The constitutional secularism Nehru defended has been substantially eroded by the BJP's reframing of Indian identity around majoritarian Hindu cultural symbols.

The press freedom that was the strongest argument against the Emergency has been eroded by a combination of corporate capture of the major media houses, regulatory pressure on independent outlets, and the criminal prosecution of journalists under various national-security statutes.

The judicial independence that survived the Emergency has been substantially worn down by post-retirement appointments of judges to executive sinecures, by the executive's increasing influence over Supreme Court appointment processes, and by selective non-enforcement of court rulings the government finds inconvenient.

The civil-society space that the Right to Information Act expanded has been substantially narrowed by the use of foreign-contribution regulation, money-laundering investigation, and direct administrative pressure against NGOs perceived as politically inconvenient.

The independent fiscal and statistical institutions (CAG, NSSO, RBI) have been substantially restructured under political direction, with documented effects on the reliability of official Indian economic and social-indicator data.

Whether the net trajectory of these changes is — in the framing of Indian liberal critics — the slow conversion of a constitutional democracy into a "Hindu Rashtra" majoritarian state, or — in the framing of Indian conservative defenders — the long-overdue correction of a Nehruvian secularism that had subordinated the country's actual cultural majority to its post-colonial elite, is the basic interpretive question of contemporary Indian politics.
The empirical evidence is rich and the disagreement is real.

The book takes no position on what comes next; the chapters that come next are being written by Indian voters, by Indian institutional actors, by the Indian diaspora, and by external pressures the country has only partial ability to control.
What the book does take a position on is the basic claim.

India in 2026 — at seventy-seven years from independence, at 168 years from the formal establishment of Crown rule, at over five thousand years from the first urban civilizations of the Indus Valley (Indus Valley Ch 1) — is a continuous historical project that has, against substantial odds, survived.
The next chapter is not yet written.
The country goes on.

chapters.title: The Manchu Conquest
sentences: The previous book in this chain ended in 1644, when the Ming Dynasty — the last ethnically Chinese dynasty to rule a unified China — collapsed under the weight of fiscal crisis, a small ice age that wrecked harvests, peasant rebellion, and a rebel named Li Zicheng who took Beijing and drove the last Ming emperor to hang himself from a tree on a hill behind the palace (Ming Dynasty Ch 8).
This book is about who walked into that vacuum, and it was not the rebels.
It was a people from the forests northeast of the Great Wall who in 1644 numbered perhaps a million souls and who would rule a fifth of humanity for the next 268 years.

They were the Jurchens (pronounced "JUR-chens"), a people of the Manchurian forest and river country, the broad zone of pine forest, fertile valley, and grassland that lies north of Korea and northeast of the Great Wall.
They were not Chinese.
They spoke a Tungusic language, a family as distant from Chinese as Finnish is from English, related to the languages of the Siberian taiga, not to anything spoken in the Ming heartland.

They lived by a mix of farming, hunting, fishing, ginseng-gathering, and horse-borne raiding, and they were organized into rival clans that the Ming had spent two centuries playing against each other so that none grew strong.

The Jurchens had a deep history here — their ancestors had ruled north China as the Jin dynasty five centuries earlier, before the Mongols destroyed them — but in 1600 they were a fragmented frontier people, nominally Ming tributaries, trading furs and ginseng for Chinese silver and iron.
What changed everything was one man.

Nurhaci (pronounced "NOOR-hah-chee"), a minor Jurchen chieftain who began, according to his own later propaganda, with nothing but his father's thirteen suits of armor, spent three decades from the 1580s onward conquering and absorbing the rival Jurchen clans.
His central institution, and the single most important thing in this chapter, was the Eight Banners.
Around 1615 Nurhaci reorganized his entire society — every household, not just soldiers — into large units each identified by a colored flag: plain yellow, bordered yellow, plain white, and so on.
A banner was simultaneously an army division, a census unit, a tax unit, and an aristocratic household.
Every Manchu belonged to one for life and inherited it.

The banners gave Nurhaci something the Ming, with its conscript peasants and demoralized hereditary garrisons, could not match: a standing professional army that was also the entire social order, fed and motivated by the prospect of plunder and land. (China would not face anything like this fusion of army and society again until the People's Liberation Army; the closest earlier parallel is the Mongol decimal army that conquered the same territory four centuries before, Mongol Empire Ch 2.) In 1616 Nurhaci proclaimed himself khan of a revived Later Jin state, deliberately invoking his Jurchen ancestors who had ruled north China.
In 1618 he issued a manifesto called the Seven Grievances — a list of complaints against the Ming, the standard ritual of declaring you are not a rebel but a wronged party — and went to war.
He took the Ming's northeastern fortress towns one after another.
He died in 1626, probably of wounds, with the Great Wall still ahead of him and the prize, China itself, still unwon.
His son Hong Taiji (pronounced "hong TIE-jee") finished building the state.

He created a Chinese-style bureaucracy with ministries, recruited Chinese and Mongol bannermen into parallel Eight Banners of their own (so the conquest army was never purely Manchu), and made the institutional decision that defines this whole dynasty.

In 1635 he abolished the name "Jurchen" and decreed that his people would now be called Manchu (the etymology is contested; the leading scholarly guess links the name to a Buddhist title, possibly invoking the bodhisattva Manjushri, but it is genuinely not settled).
In 1636 he abolished "Later Jin" and proclaimed a new dynasty: the Qing (pronounced "ching"), meaning "pure" or "clear." The renaming was not cosmetic.
"Jurchen" and "Jin" were the names of a frontier raider people and a defunct regional dynasty.

"Qing" was the name of a universal empire claiming the Mandate of Heaven — the ancient Chinese political theory that Heaven grants the right to rule to a virtuous dynasty and withdraws it, signaled by disasters and rebellion, when the dynasty becomes corrupt.
By claiming the Mandate, Hong Taiji was announcing in advance that he intended to replace the Ming, not merely raid it.
He never lived to do it; he died in 1643.
And here the conquest turns on an accident of timing so improbable that if a novelist invented it you would object.
In April 1644 the rebel Li Zicheng captured Beijing and the Ming dynasty fell — to a Chinese peasant rebel, not to the Manchus at all.

The last Ming field army, under a general named Wu Sangui (pronounced "woo sahn-GWAY"), was sitting at Shanhai Pass, the fortress where the Great Wall meets the sea and the only good road from Manchuria into China proper.
Wu was caught between two enemies: the rebel regime now holding Beijing and his family, and the Manchu army at his back.
He chose the Manchus.
He opened the pass and let them through, and the combined force smashed Li Zicheng's army and took Beijing in June 1644.
Wu Sangui's calculation — that he was inviting in an ally to restore order, who would then go home — was the worst miscalculation in Chinese history.
The Manchus did not go home.

The man who actually ran the conquest was not an emperor at all but a regent: Dorgon (pronounced "DOR-gun"), Hong Taiji's half-brother, who governed in the name of his five-year-old nephew, installed on the throne as the Shunzhi Emperor (pronounced "shwun-JR").

Dorgon made the key decision to present the Qing not as a foreign conqueror but as the avenger of the Ming — the Manchus, the official line went, had come to punish the rebels who killed the Ming emperor and to restore civilized order.
Many Chinese officials, exhausted by decades of misrule and terrified of the peasant armies, accepted this and kept their jobs.
The Qing kept the Ming bureaucracy almost entirely intact, kept the civil service examinations, kept the Confucian rituals.
To a county magistrate, very little changed except the dynasty's name and the people at the very top.
Two things made clear that this was a conquest and not a restoration.
The first was the queue order.
In 1645 the Qing decreed that every Han Chinese man must shave the front of his head and wear the rest in the long braided queue (pronounced "kew"), the Manchu hairstyle, on pain of death.
