Used with that caution, though, it is the closest thing we have to a film of the early Rus', and it is independent of every Rus' source.

The Byzantine emperor Constantine VII's manual (Chapter 1) supplies the other great external snapshot: his precise description, around 950, of the annual Rus' trade convoy assembling at Kyiv each spring, running the gauntlet of the Dnieper rapids.

He names all the cataracts twice, once in "Rus'" and once in "Slavonic," and the two columns do not match: the fourth and worst, for instance, he gives as the Slavonic Neasit (after the pelicans nesting there) and the Rus' Aeifor, which is transparently Old Norse for "ever-fierce." That single side-by-side list, written down by a Greek emperor with no axe to grind, is a tiny linguistic fossil that all by itself confirms the bilingual, Norse-and-Slav character of the trading class around 950, the assimilation of Chapter 2 caught in mid-process.
The convoy then reached Constantinople under armed escort against the Pechenegs lying in wait at the portages.
Then the windfall, and it deserves its own paragraph because it changes what we can claim.
For most of medieval Europe, ordinary people are silent: they could not write, and what was written about them was written by clerics.
Rus' has an exception so large it reorganizes the whole picture of the society.

The waterlogged soil of Novgorod preserves organic material, and from the 1950s archaeologists began pulling out of it, by the thousand, birchbark letters: everyday documents scratched with a stylus onto strips of birch bark by ordinary townspeople from roughly the eleventh century onward.
They are not chronicles or scripture.

They are debt records, business orders, a boy's school exercises (a child named Onfim's doodles of himself as a mounted warrior survive), love notes, a marriage proposal, a woman managing property, complaints, shopping lists, a furious letter from a jilted woman.

They prove, against every prior assumption, that literacy in Rus' was not confined to monks and princes but reached deep into the merchant and artisan population, including women and children, in a republican commercial town.

They are the only mass source of unmediated voices from this civilization, and they are why the picture of Rus' society in this chapter can be drawn at all below the level of princes and saints. (Other early book-artifacts confirm how early writing took hold: the wax-tablet Novgorod Codex, possibly the oldest book of Rus', whose date is debated but which radiocarbon and stratigraphy place around the start of the eleventh century, and the lavishly illuminated Ostromir Gospel of 1057, the oldest precisely dated East Slavic manuscript book, precise because it names the year in its own colophon.) The society those sources reveal was sharply stratified.

Chapter 7 used the Russkaya Pravda to make one point, that putting blood-feud and the vira into writing was itself the milestone; the point here is different, and it is what the developed code lets us see rather than when it was written: it names and prices the social ranks, so the structure of the society is documented, not inferred.

At the top, the prince and his senior retinue, who over the twelfth century settled down from a mobile war-band into a landed boyar aristocracy that increasingly checked princely power, especially in Novgorod and Galicia.

Below them, free townsmen and merchants; the free peasants, the smerdy, who worked the land and owed dues; the zakupy, debt-bondsmen working off what they owed, in a status that could shade toward unfreedom; and at the bottom the kholopy, outright slaves, whose killing the Pravda treats as a property loss to their owner rather than a vira (the blood-price for a free person, Chapter 7), a single legal clause that tells you, coldly and reliably, exactly where the law drew the line of full personhood.

The towns themselves were substantial by the standards of the age: at its twelfth-century height Kyiv may have held on the order of tens of thousands of people and hundreds of churches, large enough that western visitors compared it to Constantinople, and crowded with workshops producing goldsmith's work (cloisonné enamel, niello, the filigree kolt temple-pendants) at a level genuinely comparable to Byzantine craftsmanship.
The church was the other load-bearing institution, and its work was cultural as much as spiritual.

The conversion (Chapter 6) brought not just a religion but, through Old Church Slavonic and Cyrillic, the entire apparatus of literate civilization, because the clergy were the readers, writers, and translators.

The Kyiv Caves Monastery (the Pechersk Lavra, founded under Yaroslav, its early holy men collected in a book of lives called the Caves Paterik) was the powerhouse: it produced the Primary Chronicle itself (this whole narrative's main source was written by the very institution it describes, a fact worth holding onto), it ran an infirmary whose healer-monks combined local herbal remedies with the Greek medical learning that came in with the church, the inherited classical tradition of Galen and Hippocrates as Byzantium transmitted it (humoral theory, dietary regimens, the systematic written case, things Rus' folk healing did not have on its own), and it trained the bishops who staffed the church across the principalities.

Rus' Christianity also generated original work, not just translation: Hilarion's Sermon on Law and Grace (Chapter 7), the eloquent sermons of Cyril of Turov (called the "Rus' Chrysostom," after John Chrysostom, the fourth-century archbishop of Constantinople whose name means "golden-mouthed" and who was the most admired preacher of the entire Greek church, so the nickname was the highest rhetorical compliment available), the pilgrimage account of Abbot Daniel, who traveled to crusader-era Jerusalem around 1107 and wrote the first Rus' travel book, the calendar-calculation treatise of Kirik of Novgorod, the careful chronicle notices of comets and eclipses that modern astronomers still find usable.
And it produced its own distinctly Rus' holy figures, above all the passion-bearers Boris and Gleb (Chapter 7), whose cult was a homegrown response to the dynasty's own bloodshed.
But the conversion's reach had limits, and the sources admit them, which is itself a reason to trust them.
Paganism persisted in the countryside for centuries; the Chronicle records pagan sorcerers, the volkhvy, leading uprisings as late as 1071.
Popular religion settled into what later scholars called dvoeverie (dvo-yeh-VYEH-ree-yeh, "double faith"): Orthodox practice layered over surviving pagan custom.

Concretely, that meant a village keeping the pre-Christian spring and midsummer fertility festivals but sliding them onto the nearest saints' days, leaving food and drink for the household spirit (the domovoi) behind the stove while also lighting candles to icons, marking the farming year by old seasonal rites under new Christian names, and consulting a volkhv about a sick cow and a priest about a sick soul without feeling a contradiction.

Whether dvoeverie is a real historical phenomenon or partly a category invented by later writers is itself debated, and the honest position is that the church was unambiguously dominant in the towns and among the elite while the depth of Christianization in the deep countryside is exactly the sort of thing the sources let us see only dimly.

That, then, is the civilization: a wealthy, river-fed, fur-and-silver-and-slave economy; substantial towns full of literate people who left their own voices in birch bark; a sharply graded society codified in written law; a Greek-rooted but increasingly self-confident church that carried the alphabet, the books, the architecture, and the law; women who in Novgorod managed property and in the dynasty became queens of France and Norway (Chapter 7), and at least once, like Olga (Chapter 4), ruled.
It was, around 1200, by any reasonable measure a flourishing medieval civilization, fragmented politically but rich and creative.
It is important to feel that fullness before the next two chapters, because what comes out of the eastern steppe is going to be measured against it, and the measure is annihilation.

chapters.title: The Steppe and the First Horsemen from the East
sentences: Every chapter of this narrative has had the steppe in it as a fact of life, and it is worth gathering the thread before the steppe produces the thing that ends the story.
North of the Black Sea and east toward Asia runs the Pontic–Caspian steppe, an ocean of grass that for the entire span of Rus' history was the home of mounted nomad confederations.
The Rus' relationship with the steppe was never simply "civilization versus barbarians"; it was a permanent, intimate, two-way frontier.
The Khazars (Chapter 1) had taxed the early Slavs and then been destroyed by Svyatoslav (Chapter 5).
The Pechenegs had killed Svyatoslav at the rapids and besieged Kyiv before Yaroslav broke them around 1036 (Chapter 7).

Their successors on the grassland, arriving on the Rus' frontier around the 1050s, were the Cumans (KOO-manz, called the Polovtsy in the Rus' sources and the Kipchaks further east), a Turkic confederation that would be the Rus' world's defining steppe partner-and-enemy for nearly two centuries.

It is worth being precise about how that relationship actually worked, because the popular image of nomad raiders flattens something more interesting and the sources are unusually clear here. the Cumans raided Rus' farmland savagely and repeatedly (they crushed Rus' coalition armies at the Alta in 1068, Chapter 8, and the Stugna in 1093, and the raids were devastating enough that the southern frontier zone was a place of real danger and depopulation).

But the Cumans also traded with the Rus', and the princes married them: from the early twelfth century, sealing peace with the steppe through marriage alliances became routine, and Rus' princes increasingly had Cuman mothers, Cuman wives, and Cuman in-laws.

The line between enemy and kin genuinely blurred, and, the part that becomes tragically load-bearing in Chapter 12, Rus' princes habitually hired Cuman cavalry to fight other Rus' princes in the endless dynastic wars (Chapter 8).
The steppe was not a wall the Rus' faced outward against.

It was a third partner in Rus' politics, an arena the princes used against each other, which is precisely why they were so fatally bad at recognizing a steppe enemy of an entirely different kind when one finally appeared.
The Cuman wars also produced the literary masterpiece of the whole civilization, and it deserves a careful look both for what it is and for the question mark over it.

In 1185 a minor prince, Igor Svyatoslavich of Novgorod-Seversk (and note the confusable: this is Igor of the poem, a twelfth-century princeling, not Igor of Kyiv the early prince of Chapter 4, two and a half centuries earlier), led an under-strength, glory-seeking private raid against the Cumans without waiting for the other princes.
It went exactly as such ventures went: his army was surrounded and destroyed and Igor himself captured, an unremarkable military disaster of the kind the era produced regularly.

What is not unremarkable is that someone, very soon after, turned it into the Tale of Igor's Campaign (the Slovo o polku Igoreve), a short, dense, strange, intensely poetic prose-poem that is, by wide agreement, the supreme work of Old East Slavic literature.
It is not triumphalist; it laments.

It uses Igor's failure to mourn the disunity of the princes, calling on them by name to stop feuding and defend the land together, shot through with pagan nature-imagery and grief, including a passage where Igor's wife Yaroslavna laments to the wind, the river, and the sun from the city wall.

It also contains a precisely datable detail, a solar eclipse that frightens Igor's army at the campaign's start, and the historically attested eclipse of 1 May 1185 fits, one of those small cross-checks between literature, chronicle, and astronomy that this narrative keeps finding.

Now the honest caveat, because the rules of this app require it and the question is real: the Tale survives only through a single manuscript that was discovered in the late eighteenth century and then destroyed in the burning of Moscow in 1812, before it could be properly examined, with only a copy and an early printed edition surviving.
Because of that, a minority of scholars have argued the Tale is an eighteenth-century forgery rather than a genuine medieval work.

The mainstream scholarly view, supported by detailed linguistic analysis (notably by the linguist Andrey Zaliznyak, who argued that the text consistently obeys subtle features of twelfth-century East Slavic, things like patterns of the lost vowels and the so-called second-position clitics, that were not understood by scholars until long after 1800, making deliberate forgery extremely improbable), holds that it is authentically medieval.

The reader should know the debate exists; the working position of this narrative is the majority one, that it is genuine, while flagging that the lost-manuscript problem makes it the one major literary source here we cannot physically re-examine.
And then, from a direction and with a scale that no part of the Rus'–Cuman–Pecheneg world had a category for, came the Mongols.

In 1206, two thousand miles to the east, a man the Rus' had never heard of, Temüjin, was acclaimed Genghis Khan (the founding of the Mongol Empire is its own enormous narrative; this chapter is only its first touch on Rus').

"Acclaimed" is precise and not soft: at a great assembly of the Mongol tribes he had subdued or allied, the chiefs formally proclaimed him supreme ruler of all the steppe peoples, the title meaning roughly "universal/fierce ruler," which converted a victorious war-leader into the single sovereign of a unified nation built for conquest.

Within fifteen years his armies had shattered northern China and the great Islamic empire of Khwarazm in Central Asia, an arc of conquest faster and wider than anything since the early Arab expansion.

In 1223 a Mongol force of perhaps twenty thousand under two of Genghis Khan's best generals, Subutai and Jebe, came around the south of the Caspian on a long-range reconnaissance-in-force (a powerful armed column sent not to conquer and hold ground but to probe, fight where useful, and above all gather intelligence on terrain, routes, and enemies, then report back), smashed through the Caucasus, and burst onto the Pontic steppe from the southeast, the open back door that Svyatoslav had unbarred when he destroyed Khazaria two and a half centuries earlier (Chapter 5), the consequence finally arriving.

This is the detail the Mongol Empire narrative supplies and that makes Kalka uniquely dangerous: Subutai and Jebe had originally been sent to chase the fleeing remnants of the shattered Khwarazmian ruler, and the western sweep was an opportunistic scouting loop.

Everything they saw between the Caspian and the Dnieper, every river, army, and road, went back east in a report, and that report became the operational plan for the full invasion thirteen years later.

They began defeating the Cumans, and the Cuman khans, some of them now the fathers-in-law of Rus' princes, appealed to Kyiv for help with a warning the Rus' should have weighed: "Today they have taken our land; tomorrow they will take yours." A coalition of southern Rus' princes, with their Cuman allies, marched out to meet them, and the result was the Battle of the Kalka River in 1223, and the way it was lost is the whole tragedy of the preceding eight chapters compressed into one day.

The Mongols were masters of the feigned retreat: a disciplined cavalry force would break off and gallop away as if beaten, holding the pretended flight together for days over open ground, until the pursuers had strung themselves out into a long, exhausted, disordered line with no formation and no reserve, at which point the Mongols wheeled and destroyed them piecemeal with fresh horses.
They drew the Rus'–Cuman force into exactly that trap.

The Rus' princes, with no unified command because there was no longer any such thing as a unified Rus' command (Chapter 8), advanced in jealous, uncoordinated contingents, some fighting while others sat in their fortified camp; the Cumans broke and the rout spread; the Mongols destroyed the army a fragment at a time.

The chronicle adds a detail of pointed horror: captured Rus' princes were not given the warrior's death of the blade but were laid under heavy boards on which the Mongol commanders sat to feast, crushed slowly.

The Rus' chronicler explains this as a way of killing them without spilling royal blood on the ground, which fits a known steppe taboo against shedding the blood of royalty (the Mongols are independently reported using a similar bloodless execution for high captives elsewhere), though the interpretation is the chronicler's gloss on the act, not necessarily the Mongols' own stated reason.
Either way the Rus' could read it only as a nightmare.
Three or six princes died; the army was annihilated.
And then the strangest part: the Mongols, their reconnaissance complete, simply turned around and rode back east, vanishing as abruptly as they had come.

The principalities, with no instinct for a threat that did not behave like the Cumans they understood, treated Kalka as one more bad year on a violent frontier and went back to fighting each other over Kyiv (the city was sacked yet again in the inter-princely wars of the early thirteenth century).
They had been given the clearest possible warning, dated and unambiguous, and the fragmented system Chapter 8 explained had no mechanism left for heeding it.

They had thirteen years, and they did not even keep their steppe ally: when the Mongols returned, the Mongol Empire narrative shows them spending 1236–37 first systematically destroying the Cumans (the Kipchak confederation, the same people, under the name used further east) before turning on Rus'.
The principalities' one experienced steppe partner was shattered and scattered, some Cumans fleeing as far as Hungary, before the Rus' towns understood the storm was coming for them next.
Chapter 12 is what came back.

chapters.title: The End of the World, and What Grew After
sentences: The Mongols who came back were not a raiding party.

In 1237, fourteen years after Kalka, a full Mongol army of the western campaign entered the Rus' lands from the southeast with a stated objective the principalities had no answer to: conquest, not plunder.
The size of that army is genuinely debated.

The chroniclers' figures are unusable, and modern estimates run from perhaps 40,000 up to the 150,000 the Mongol Empire narrative cites; the honest statement is a large field army in the high tens of thousands at least, and what matters more than the headcount is its character.
This was not a local steppe raid.

It was, as the Mongol Empire narrative describes, a pan-imperial coalition force drawn from across the whole Mongol world and stiffened with conscripted Turkic auxiliaries, commanded in the field by the supreme general Subutai (the same Subutai who had won at Kalka) under the nominal leadership of Batu Khan, a grandson of Genghis Khan, and it was the same campaign that within a few years would also smash Poland and Hungary in the same season.
They came, deliberately, in winter, which is the single most important tactical fact of the whole campaign and the one that most reverses the reader's intuition.
Western armies did not campaign in the Russian winter; the cold and snow stopped them.

The Mongols campaigned because of it: frozen rivers and marshes that were impassable barriers in summer became smooth high-speed roads for cavalry, letting them move on the wooded, waterlogged northeast exactly when its defenders thought the season made them safe.

Everything Chapter 9 described as the strength of the fragmented principalities (many separate centers, each with its own prince and army) was now a fatal weakness, because the Mongols did not have to beat a Rus' army.
There was no Rus' army.
There were a dozen, and the Mongols destroyed them one at a time, city by city.

Their decisive tool was siege engineering absorbed from conquered China and Persia: catapults and counterweight trebuchets that flung stones heavy enough to break masonry, plus engineer corps who could build them on the spot.

Rus' town walls were earthen ramparts topped with timber, built to stop steppe horsemen who had no siege equipment at all, and they simply were not designed against an enemy that arrived with the demolition technology of the most advanced sedentary empires on earth.
The sequence is a list of annihilations and the chroniclers, monks watching their world end, recorded it as apocalypse.

Ryazan (rya-ZAN), the first northeastern principality in the path, refused the demand for submission and tribute; the Mongols stormed it in December 1237 and, the chronicle says, killed everyone, a destruction so total that the old city was never rebuilt on the same site.
The road into the heart of the northeast was open.

Vladimir, the proud capital that Andrei Bogolyubsky had built to replace Kyiv (Chapter 9), fell in February 1238; the Grand Prince's family and much of the population took refuge in the great Dormition Cathedral and the Mongols burned it down on top of them.
Grand Prince Yuri II, who had marched out to raise a relief army, was caught and destroyed with it at the Sit River days later.
Town after town in the northeast was taken.

The small fort of Kozelsk held out, against all odds, for seven weeks, long enough that Batu reportedly named it "the evil city" and slaughtered it to the last soul when it finally fell, the kind of doomed, total resistance the chroniclers seized on because it was the only consolation available.
After a year regrouping on the steppe, the Mongols turned on the south.
Chernigov, one of the senior old cities, fell in 1239.
And in December 1240, Batu's army reached the mother city itself.
The fall of Kyiv in 1240 is the formal end of Kievan Rus', and it is the kind of ending that earns the word.

The city that Oleg had seized in 882 and called the mother of Rus' cities, that Vladimir had baptized, that Yaroslav had rebuilt as a small Constantinople with Saint Sophia and the Golden Gate, was stormed after a siege of only about a week to ten days of concentrated bombardment and assault, the walls broken, the population massacred, the great churches looted and wrecked. ("Short" here is relative and pointed: the obscure little fort of Kozelsk had held the Mongols seven weeks the year before.

The mother city of Rus', far larger and supposedly far stronger, was cracked open in a fraction of that time, which is the measure of how completely the new siege technology had changed the math.) A papal envoy named John of Plano Carpini, a Franciscan friar sent by the Pope across the steppe to the Mongol court, passed through the ruins of Kyiv in 1246, six years after the sack, and recorded in his report what he saw: fields still littered with "countless skulls and bones of dead men lying about on the ground," and the once-great city shrunk to barely two hundred houses.
That detail is not from a grieving Rus' monk; it is from a Latin churchman with no stake in the legend, and it is the single most reliable measure we have of what happened to Kyiv.
The 882–1240 state was over.
It did not fragment further or decline.
It was destroyed.

What replaced it was the Golden Horde, the westernmost of the four great khanates into which the Mongol Empire was dividing (the others ruled China, Persia, and Central Asia; the Mongol Empire narrative tells that fourfold split).
Batu established it on the lower Volga around 1242, ruling the surviving Rus' principalities not by occupation but by overlordship.

This is the system later called the Mongol Yoke (or "Tatar Yoke," from the name the Rus' used for the Mongols), and it lasted roughly two hundred and forty years, longer than the independent Rus' state had.
Its mechanism, since this app insists on mechanisms, was indirect rule through humiliation and tribute.

The Rus' princes were left in place, but every prince now had to travel to the Horde, in the early decades sometimes all the way to the Mongol imperial capital in Mongolia, to receive a yarlik, a patent of office without which his rule was illegitimate, and to deliver tribute extracted by Mongol census and tax officials.
The Horde deliberately played rival princes against one another, granting and revoking the yarlik to keep them divided and competing for Mongol favor.

The mechanism is best seen in one case: in 1327 the city of Tver rose against a Mongol tax party and massacred it; the prince of Moscow, Ivan Kalita, led a Mongol punitive army against his Rus' rival Tver, crushed it, and was rewarded with the yarlik for the grand-princely title and the right to collect everyone's tribute.

Moscow rose by being the Horde's most reliable enforcer against other Rus' princes, which is the precise way the conquest reshaped Rus' politics for centuries: the path to power now ran through serving the conqueror better than your cousins did.
The Horde itself did not stand still while this played out.

Over the following century it converted to Islam under its khans Berke and Öz Beg, grew rich on the Black Sea trade through the Genoese colony at Caffa in the Crimea, and was the route by which the Black Death travelled from the steppe to Caffa to the Mediterranean in the 1340s; the Mongol Empire narrative follows that arc, including the Horde's own slow fragmentation, which is ultimately what let Moscow break free.
Not everywhere fell, and the exceptions are the seed of the divergence that is the whole point of this final chapter.

Novgorod, the merchant republic of the far northwest (Chapter 9), was saved by geography (the spring thaw turned its approaches to impassable swamp and the Mongols turned back before reaching it) and so it never suffered the sack, kept its veche and its Baltic trade, and submitted to pay tribute without being destroyed.

Its prince in these very years was Alexander Nevsky (NYEV-skee), and his career is the hinge of the historiographical argument that closes this narrative, so it has to be told carefully rather than as legend.
While the southeast burned, Novgorod faced pressure from the west: Swedes, and the Catholic crusading military orders of the Baltic.

Alexander defeated a Swedish force on the Neva river in 1240, which earned him the name Nevsky, and famously defeated the Livonian Order's knights on the frozen surface of Lake Peipus at the Battle on the Ice in 1242, halting Catholic expansion into the Orthodox Rus' northwest.

But the decision that made him a saint to some and a collaborator to others was the strategic one: faced with the Catholic West on one side and the Mongol Horde on the other, Alexander chose submission to the Mongols and resistance to the West.
He calculated, defensibly, that the Mongols took tribute and the yarlik but left religion and local rule intact, while the Catholic orders came to convert and to stay.

It was also a calculation the Mongols themselves would have recognized and rewarded: the Mongol Empire narrative shows the Horde routinely leaving in place any ruler who submitted fast and taxed efficiently, and the concrete institutional payoff of that bargain in Rus' was that the Mongols, by decree, exempted the Orthodox Church from tribute and taxation entirely, which is one major reason the church came out of the Yoke richer and more powerful than it went in.
He went to the Horde, submitted, secured his yarlik, even helped enforce a Mongol census, and kept Orthodox Rus' culturally intact under the Yoke.
The Russian Orthodox Church later canonized him; later still he became a Soviet patriotic icon (and a celebrated 1938 film).

Whether his submission was wise pragmatism that preserved Rus' identity or a betrayal that normalized the Yoke is a debate with no neutral answer, and it is offered here as a debate, not resolved, because the rules of this app forbid pretending a contested judgment is a fact.
Now the divergence, which is where this entire narrative has been pointing since the first paragraph of Chapter 1.
The lands of Kievan Rus' did not recover as one thing.
They split, under the long pressure of the Yoke and the different fates of the regions Chapter 9 set up, into three distinct trajectories that became three nations.

In the northeast, the principality of Vladimir–Suzdal, with its autocratic tradition and its obscure town of Moscow, became the heartland from which Moscow rose: by the bargain described above, in which Ivan I (Kalita) won the grand-princely yarlik and the right to collect everyone's tribute by acting as the Horde's enforcer against Tver around 1327 and through the 1330s, Moscow turned tax-collection into power.

It also became the seat of the Orthodox metropolitan, who had relocated north from ruined Kyiv, so spiritual and fiscal authority converged in the same town, and over the next two centuries Moscow gathered the northeastern Rus' lands, eventually threw off the Yoke, and became Russia, carrying forward the autocratic model and explicitly claiming to be the legitimate heir of Kyiv.

In the southwest, Galicia–Volhynia survived the Mongols better, kept a western-facing, Latin-influenced tradition, and was eventually absorbed into the Kingdom of Poland and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania. (Lithuania, then the last large pagan state in Europe, expanded fast in the fourteenth century into the Rus' lands the Mongols had hollowed out, taking over much of the old western and central Rus' largely without destroying it and absorbing its Orthodox population, before its own rulers converted to Catholicism and merged with Poland.) The central Dnieper lands around Kyiv itself, and the northwestern lands around Polotsk, also fell under Lithuanian and then Polish rule, developing for centuries inside a different political and religious world from Moscow's.
Out of those western and central Rus' lands, over centuries, grew the distinct languages and national identities of Ukraine and Belarus.
All three, Russia, Ukraine, Belarus, descend from Kievan Rus'.
All three speak East Slavic languages written in the Cyrillic that came with the conversion of 988.
All three are Orthodox Christian because of Vladimir's choice.
And all three claim the inheritance, which is exactly the problem the narrative opened with.
This is where the source-criticism thread that has run through every chapter pays off, because it is the same thread as the political argument.
We know early Rus' mainly through one monastery chronicle written around 1113 by men making a case for one dynasty's legitimacy and one religion's centrality.

Every later regime that wanted to claim the Kievan inheritance has read that chronicle, and the whole story, in its own favor: Moscow casting itself as the unbroken continuation of Kyiv, Soviet historians required to be anti-Normanist (Chapter 2), modern Russia in 2021 invoking the "one people" of the shared cradle to justify a war, modern Ukraine insisting the cradle stood on its soil and the rest is appropriation.

The honest historical position, the one this narrative has tried to hold from the first page, is that Kievan Rus' was a real, rich, fascinating civilization (a Norse-Slavic river enterprise that became a Byzantine-Christian world, peaked under Yaroslav, fragmented by the logic of its own succession system, and was destroyed by the Mongols), and that it belongs, intact and undivided, to no modern nation, because it predates all three of them and was not yet any of them.
It was its own thing.

The most useful conclusion is the one the rules of this app point to and that the politics make urgent rather than academic: the gap between what the sources can actually establish and what people need them to mean is not a footnote to the history of Kievan Rus'.
It is, a thousand years on, still the most consequential thing about it.

chapters.title: The Size of the Problem
sentences: Start with a number that does not behave like a number.
In 1914, on the eve of the catastrophe that ends this book, the Russian Empire covered about 8.6 million square miles (22.4 million square kilometers).
That is roughly a sixth of all the land on the planet.
It is more than twice the size of the entire United States including Alaska.

If you stood on the empire's western edge in Poland and started walking east at a steady pace, you would cross eleven of the world's twenty-four time zones before you reached the Pacific, and it would take you the better part of a year.
A telegram from St Petersburg to the Pacific port of Vladivostok in the 1890s, before the railway, could take longer to be acted upon than a letter from London to Boston.
This is not a colorful detail.

It is the central engineering problem of the entire narrative, and almost everything that follows is, in one way or another, an answer to the question: how do you govern that, with the technology of 1700, or 1800, and a population most of whom cannot read?
The answer the Russian state arrived at, and clung to with a desperation that finally killed it, was a particular machine.
It had three load-bearing parts, and you need all three in your head before Peter is even born, because he inherits them and the empire dies still trying to run on them.
The first part is autocracy (from Greek, "self-rule," meaning rule by one person answerable to no law, no parliament, and no one).
The Russian ruler was not a king in the western European sense, hemmed in by nobles with charters and assemblies that voted taxes.
The Russian ruler was the tsar (TSAR, from "Caesar," the title the rulers of Moscow had adopted to claim the inheritance of the Roman emperors after Constantinople fell to the Ottomans in 1453).
Tsarist autocracy was not a tendency or a style.
It was a formal doctrine, written into law, that the tsar's will was the only source of legitimate authority in the state, and that any limitation on it was a kind of blasphemy.

Western Europe had spent the late Middle Ages growing institutions that could say no to a monarch (Parliament in England, the Estates in France, town charters everywhere, the subject of the European narratives).
Russia had grown almost none.
When this narrative reaches 1906 and Russia finally gets something resembling a parliament, it will be 600 years after England got one, and it will arrive too late to matter.
The second part is Orthodoxy.

Russia was a Christian country, but it belonged to the Eastern Orthodox Church, the branch of Christianity that split from the Catholic (Roman) West in 1054 and looked to Constantinople, not Rome, for its model.

After Constantinople fell to the Muslim Ottomans in 1453 (the event told from the conqueror's side in the Ottoman Empire narrative), Russian churchmen developed the idea that Moscow was the "Third Rome," the last surviving seat of true Christianity, with a sacred duty to preserve it unchanged.

The claim had a dynastic prop: in 1472 the Moscow grand prince Ivan III had married Zoe (Sophia) Palaiologina, a niece of the last Byzantine emperor, so Moscow could argue it had inherited Byzantium's imperial legitimacy by blood as well as by faith just as the Ottomans took its capital.
The practical effect, for our purposes, was that the Russian church was not a rival power center that could check the tsar (as the Catholic papacy repeatedly checked western kings).
It was, increasingly, an arm of the state that sanctified the tsar's authority as God-given.

Hold that; in Chapter 4 Peter abolishes the church's leadership outright and runs it as a government department, and almost nobody can stop him, because the institution that might have had no independent ground to stand on.
The third part, and the one this entire book is really about, is serfdom.
By 1649, a legal code called the Ulozhenie (oo-loh-ZHEN-yeh) had finished a long process of binding the Russian peasant to the land he worked and to the lord who owned that land.
A serf was not technically a slave in the way a person on an American plantation was chattel property with no legal personhood whatsoever.
The distinction is real but, for the human being living it, thin.
A serf could not leave the estate without permission.
He could be bought, sold, mortgaged, gambled away, and (in practice though the law grew coy about it) sold apart from his family.
He owed the lord either heavy labor on the lord's own fields (barshchina, bar-SHCHEE-nah) or heavy payments in cash and kind (obrok, ob-ROHK), often both.
He could be flogged at the lord's discretion and conscripted into the army for what amounted to a life sentence.

By the early nineteenth century, somewhere around 23 million people, more than a third of the entire population of the empire, lived in this condition, and roughly as many again were "state peasants" bound to the crown in a milder version of the same.

To put 23 million in an American frame: it is more than five times the roughly four million people enslaved in the American South on the eve of its civil war, and that war is the bloodiest event in United States history.

Russia carried a bound population on that scale, white and Orthodox and indistinguishable by sight from the people who owned them, for two full centuries, and the question of what to do about it is the unexploded ordnance under every chapter of this story.
So here is the thesis, stated once, plainly, so you can watch it operate for the next nineteen chapters and decide for yourself whether it holds.
The Russian Empire was a machine for converting the unfreedom of the many into the grandeur of the few, and it was extraordinarily good at the grandeur.
It built St Petersburg, one of the most beautiful cities ever made, on a swamp where tens of thousands of conscripted laborers died in the building of it.

It produced, in a single century, War and Peace, The Brothers Karamazov, the periodic table of the elements, and the largest empire on earth, while the people who grew the food that fed all of it could be flogged for leaving the village.
The grandeur was real.
The unfreedom was real.
The wager of the Russian state, made over and over by tsar after tsar, was that you could keep the first without ever fully surrendering the second.
The fuse on that wager was lit, as best we can date it, on a December morning in 1825, and it burned for ninety-two years.
Now the caveats, because this is a book that would rather tell you what it doesn't know than pretend.
On measurement: this is a US-based reading app, so distances come in miles first, kilometers in parentheses.

We will anchor the genuinely alien magnitudes (the size of the empire, the length of the Trans-Siberian Railway, the body counts of the famines and the wars) in things an American reader can feel, and we will not insult you by anchoring a mile.
On certainty: Russian imperial history has the opposite problem from ancient history.
It is not that the sources are too few.
For the later period they are an avalanche: state archives, censuses, the greatest novels ever written, the memoirs of revolutionaries, the diaries of the last tsar.
The problem is that almost every important event in this story has been fought over by people who needed it to mean something.

Soviet historians for seventy years were required to read the entire empire as a doomed tyranny inevitably producing the glorious revolution of 1917. Émigré and Western Cold War historians often read the same events as a basically reformable society derailed by fanatics and bad luck.
Post-Soviet Russian historians have swung between a nostalgic rehabilitation of the tsars and a continued reckoning.
When this narrative says "this is debated," it means it, and it will tell you which way the wind is currently blowing.
A specific warning the reader should keep loaded the whole way through: some of the most vivid stories in Russian history, the ones everybody knows, are the least reliable.
Peter the Great did not necessarily personally swing the axe on the streltsy.
Catherine the Great did not die the way the cruelest joke about her says she did.
Rasputin's powers, Anastasia's escape, the precise number of Napoleon's men who froze on the retreat: the more cinematic the claim, the harder we will press it.
One last bit of scene-setting: where Peter is standing when this story opens, and what he is standing on.
The state Peter inherits is not yet the Russian Empire.

It is Muscovy, the Grand Duchy of Moscow, the principality that over roughly two centuries had swallowed its neighbors and thrown off the overlordship of the Mongol successor states (the "Tatar yoke," the long domination by the Golden Horde and its heirs, told from the steppe side in the Mongol Empire narrative).

Muscovy in 1672 is large, cold, landlocked in every direction that matters, and, by the standard of the Dutch Republic or France or even Sweden, technologically and administratively a century or more behind.

It has no warm-water port, no real navy, almost no modern manufacturing, a tiny educated class, and an army that is partly a medieval cavalry of service nobles and partly the streltsy (STREL-tsee, "the shooters"), hereditary musketeer regiments based in Moscow who double as a fractious urban militia and who are about to put a seven-year-old boy through the most formative trauma of his life.
The Muscovite tsar is already an autocrat in doctrine.
The church is already a near-arm of the state.

The peasant is already, by 1649, legally bound, the end of a process whose legal ancestors reach back to the kholopy (slaves) and tribute-owing peasants of Kievan Rus', the medieval Slavic state out of which Moscow grew, told in its own narrative.
The three load-bearing parts are all in place.
What is not yet in place is the grandeur.

The boy who will supply it, with an energy and brutality that has few parallels in the history of any country, is born in 1672, and in 1682, at the age of nine, he watches men he knows get torn apart on the spears of the streltsy in the Kremlin.
We open there.

chapters.title: The Boy Who Saw the Spears
sentences: The man this whole book turns on was born Pyotr Alekseyevich Romanov (PYOH-ter al-ek-SAY-yeh-vich), on 9 June 1672, in Moscow.

English flattens Pyotr to Peter, and he becomes, before the end, Peter the Great, but in 1672 he is just the fourteenth child of Tsar Alexei (a-LEK-say) Mikhailovich and the first child of Alexei's second wife, Natalya Naryshkina (na-RISH-kee-na).
The number of children and the two wives matter enormously, because they set up the murder Peter is about to witness.
When Tsar Alexei died in 1676, the throne went to Peter's much older half-brother Fyodor III (FYOH-der), a sickly, learned young man who reigned six years and died in 1682 at twenty, childless.

That left two candidates from Alexei's two marriages: Ivan, the surviving son of the first wife, fifteen years old, half-blind, with a serious speech impediment and what the sources describe as some degree of intellectual disability, and Peter, the son of the second wife, nine years old, healthy, and obviously bright.
Behind the two boys stood two clans: the Miloslavskys (mee-loh-SLAHV-skee), the family of the first wife, backing Ivan, and the Naryshkins, Peter's mother's people, backing Peter.

This is the Russian court's recurring disease, and you will see it again and again: with no fixed, ironclad rule of succession, every transfer of the crown becomes a faction fight, and the faction that controls the capital's soldiers wins.
Right now the capital's soldiers are the streltsy.
A council of churchmen and boyars (BOH-yarz, the old hereditary aristocracy of Muscovy) chose the nine-year-old Peter over the disabled Ivan.

The Miloslavsky clan, frozen out, had one extraordinary asset: Sophia Alekseyevna (so-FEE-ya), Ivan's full sister, Peter's half-sister, a clever, ambitious, formidably educated woman of twenty-five at a time when royal women were expected to be invisible.
Sophia and her allies spread a rumor through the streltsy barracks that the Naryshkins had murdered Ivan.
The streltsy, already furious over unpaid wages and abusive colonels, did not need much.
In May 1682 they stormed the Kremlin (the fortified palace-and-cathedral citadel at the heart of Moscow, the seat of Russian power then and now).
What the nine-year-old Peter saw over the next three days is the single most important psychological fact in this narrative, so it is worth being precise about what we can and cannot say.

The traditional account, which comes substantially from later memoirs and from a foreign eyewitness or two and has been polished by every biographer since, is that Peter was made to stand on the Red Staircase of the palace beside his mother while the streltsy demanded their victims, and that several men were thrown down onto the upraised pikes of the soldiers below and hacked apart in front of him, including one of his Naryshkin uncles and the boyar Artamon Matveyev, who had been his mother's guardian and was killed almost at the child's feet.
The broad outline (a multi-day massacre in the Kremlin, leading Naryshkins butchered, the boy present for at least some of it) is solidly attested.

The most cinematic specifics (exactly what Peter saw, his facial expression, the lifelong facial tic and convulsions later attributed to this moment) are the kind of detail that hardens in the retelling, and a careful reader should hold them loosely while accepting the core: a nine-year-old watched his family's men murdered by the state's own soldiers and was powerless.

Whatever the exact mechanism, the man who emerges from this never trusts Moscow, never trusts the streltsy, and carries a hatred of the old Kremlin world that will, twenty-one years later, lead him to build an entirely new capital 400 miles (640 km) away on an empty marsh just to get out of this one.
The settlement after the 1682 revolt was bizarre even by Russian standards.
To satisfy everyone, both boys were crowned: Ivan V and Peter I, joint tsars, a dual monarchy with a specially made double throne (it survives in the Kremlin Armory).
Ivan was the senior in title and incapable in fact; Peter was junior and a child.

Real power went to the regent: Sophia, ruling in the brothers' names from 1682, the first woman to hold power in Russia in her own right rather than as a queen consort, which the conservative Muscovite establishment found close to scandalous.
Sophia's regency (1682–1689) was not incompetent.

Her chief minister and probable lover, Prince Vasily Golitsyn (ga-LEET-sin), was a westernizing intellectual who negotiated a "Treaty of Eternal Peace" with Poland and signed Russia's first treaty with China (the 1689 Treaty of Nerchinsk, which fixed the far-eastern border and is one of the earliest treaties any European-style state signed with the Qing on something like equal terms).

But Golitsyn also led two disastrous military expeditions against the Crimean Tatars, the Muslim khanate on the Black Sea steppe whose horsemen rode deep into Russian and Ukrainian farmland to seize captives, tens of thousands a year in bad decades, and sell them through the slave markets of Crimea into the Ottoman world, and the failures weakened Sophia at exactly the moment Peter was growing up.
And how Peter grew up is the other half of this chapter.
Sophia kept him and his mother out of the way, in the royal village of Preobrazhenskoye (pre-ah-bra-ZHEN-sko-yeh) outside Moscow.
This was meant to neutralize him.
It did the opposite.
Left almost entirely unsupervised by the formal Kremlin world he hated anyway, the teenage Peter educated himself by obsession.

He raised two companies of "play soldiers" from stable boys and young nobles, drilled them with real weapons and real (occasionally fatal) mock battles, and these "play regiments," the Preobrazhensky and Semyonovsky, grew into the first units of a new model army and would become the elite Guards regiments that, for the next century, make and unmake tsars.

He fell in with the foreigners of the German Quarter (the Nemetskaya Sloboda, the walled suburb where Moscow's Dutch, German, Scottish, and English merchants, soldiers, and engineers were required to live, "German" being the Russian catch-all for "western foreigner," literally "the mute ones," people who couldn't speak Russian).

There he met the Swiss adventurer Franz Lefort and the dour Scottish general Patrick Gordon, drank enormously, learned shipbuilding from a Dutch sailor, found a derelict English sailboat in a barn and taught himself to tack against the wind on a pond, and conceived the two lifelong fixations that organize his entire reign: ships, and the West.

A Russian tsar who could sail, swing an axe, set a bone, pull a tooth, and turn wood on a lathe, and who learned almost none of it in a palace, is not normal, and Russia is about to find out exactly how not normal.
The dual monarchy resolved itself in 1689.
Peter, now seventeen, married and theoretically of age, came into open conflict with Sophia over whether she would keep ruling.
Sophia tried to rally the streltsy again; this time it failed.

Warned of a possible move against him, Peter fled in the night to the fortified Trinity Monastery, the great pilgrimage church-fortress about 45 miles (70 km) northeast of Moscow, with stone walls thick enough to stand a siege, in a famous scene of a half-dressed tsar galloping to safety that is reported consistently enough to trust in outline.
From there, with the loyalty of the foreign officers and his play regiments, he outlasted Sophia.
Her support melted.
She was forced into the Novodevichy Convent in Moscow; Golitsyn was exiled to the Arctic.
Ivan V remained co-tsar in name, harmless and increasingly unwell, until his death in 1696, after which Peter ruled alone.
He was twenty-four.

He had a country the size of a continent, no warm-water port, no navy worth the name, an army half-medieval, a treasury that strained to pay it, and an idea, formed in a German suburb and on a leaky boat, of what Russia ought to become.
The first thing he wanted was the sea.
The early try was the Azov campaigns (1695–1696).
Azov (a-ZOFF) was a Turkish fortress at the mouth of the Don river, controlling access from Russia's south to the Sea of Azov and beyond it the Black Sea.

Peter's first assault in 1695 failed, badly and instructively, because he had no ships to blockade the fortress from the sea while he besieged it from land, so the Ottomans simply resupplied it by water.
Peter's response prefigures his whole method: over a single frantic winter he built a fleet, more or less from nothing, hauling shipwrights and timber to the Don, and in 1696 took Azov.
It was a small victory over a frontier fort, but it taught Peter two permanent lessons.
First, sea power was not optional.
Second, to get it he needed western knowledge, western specialists, and western money, and he was not going to get those by reading about them.
He was going to go and see.
In 1697 the tsar of Russia did something no Russian ruler had ever done.
He left the country, in disguise, to learn a trade.

chapters.title: The Window
sentences: In March 1697, an enormous Russian diplomatic mission of about 250 people set out for Western Europe.
It was called the Grand Embassy.
Its official purpose was to build a coalition against the Ottoman Turks.
Its real purpose, only thinly hidden, was that the tsar of Russia wanted to go to the West and learn how it worked with his own hands, and he could not do that as a tsar.

So Peter went along incognito, traveling as a junior member of the delegation under the name "Peter Mikhailov." The disguise fooled no one (he was six feet seven inches tall, which in 1697 made him a giant nearly everywhere he went, and his presence was an open secret in every court).
But the fiction let him do what no reigning monarch could: skip the ceremony and go work in a shipyard.
He did exactly that.

In the Dutch Republic, the most advanced commercial and maritime society on earth at the time, Peter spent a brief, frustrated stint at the Zaandam shipyards and then four months at the great yards of the Dutch East India Company in Amsterdam, working as a common carpenter, axe in hand, learning hull construction.

He moved on to England, where he studied the more theoretical English approach to ship design, met with Quaker leaders, reportedly looked in on a session of Parliament (an institution Russia had no equivalent of and would not for two centuries; England's dated to 1265, so Russia was already more than four hundred years behind the model Peter was inspecting, and would be six hundred behind it by the time it finally got a parliament of its own in 1906), and toured the Royal Society, the Mint (where Isaac Newton was then Warden), and the Greenwich Observatory.
He recruited, by the boatload, the human capital Russia lacked: shipwrights, naval officers, engineers, mathematicians, surgeons, gunners, several hundred foreign specialists hired and shipped east.
The Grand Embassy is the moment the West stops being something Russian rulers occasionally borrow from and becomes a program Russia is going to be force-marched through.

It is also, for the thesis of this book, the founding act: Peter wants European technique at the top with a ferocity that never wavers, and he is entirely uninterested in importing the European thing underneath the technique, the slow growth of institutions and law and limits on the ruler.
He wants the cannon, not the parliament.
The Embassy was cut short in 1698 by news from home: the streltsy had revolted again.
Peter raced back.
The revolt had already been put down by his generals before he arrived, but his response is one of the defining and most contested episodes of his reign, so handle it carefully.
Peter ordered a mass investigation under torture and then a mass execution.
Over the autumn of 1698, more than a thousand streltsy were executed in and around Moscow, many hanged in long rows, some beheaded, the bodies left on display for months as a deliberate terror.
The streltsy as a force were effectively destroyed.
Now the contested part.

There is a persistent, vivid tradition that Peter personally took up the axe and beheaded streltsy with his own hands, and ordered his courtiers and nobles to do the same to bind them to him in blood.

This story comes substantially from the diary of an Austrian diplomat, Johann Korb, who was in Moscow at the time but was not an eyewitness to the executions themselves and was relaying secondhand court gossip in a work the Russian government later found so offensive it tried to suppress it.

Some serious historians accept that Peter may have wielded the axe; others regard the specific image of the tsar as executioner as exactly the kind of atrocity-detail that hostile foreign reporting inflates.

What is not in doubt, and is the part that matters: Peter ordered and stage-managed a mass political terror against the soldiers who had traumatized him as a child, and he did it with a cold thoroughness that announced what kind of ruler Russia now had.
He also, on his return, personally cut off the beards of his leading boyars at a reception, the first shot in a culture war we will get to in Chapter 4.
Then came the war that made the empire.
To understand it you need the strategic problem.
Russia in 1700 was sealed off from the Baltic Sea, and therefore from the easy maritime trade routes to Western Europe, by Sweden.

This is jarring to a modern reader who thinks of Sweden as a quiet northern country, but in 1700 the Swedish Empire was the dominant military power of northern Europe, controlling Finland, the eastern Baltic coast (modern Estonia and Latvia), and territory all around the sea, with a small, superbly trained army and, on its throne, a teenage military prodigy, Charles XII, who would turn out to be one of the most brilliant and reckless commanders of the age.
Peter formed a coalition with Denmark and Saxony-Poland to carve up the Swedish Baltic holdings, and in 1700 declared war.
This was the Great Northern War, and it ran for twenty-one years.
It began as a humiliation.
Late in 1700, Peter besieged the Swedish fortress of Narva on the Baltic.

Charles XII, eighteen years old, marched a much smaller Swedish army up to the Russian siege lines and attacked at once under cover of a blinding snowstorm blowing into the Russians' faces, drove dense assault columns straight through the over-extended Russian line before it could react, and broke the besieging army in a single short winter afternoon, its foreign officers surrendering and its raw conscripts stampeding for a collapsing bridge.
The Battle of Narva was a catastrophe that confirmed every Western prejudice about Russian backwardness.

But Charles then made the decision that loses the war and, eventually, his life: instead of finishing Russia off, he turned south to deal with Saxony-Poland, the enemy he considered more serious, and left Peter alone for six years.
Peter used every day of it.

He rebuilt the army from the ground up on the European model, melting down church bells for cannon when he ran short of bronze, drilling regular infantry, and grinding away at the Swedish Baltic garrisons while Charles was busy elsewhere.
By the time Charles turned back to deal with Russia, it was a different Russia.

And in the middle of this war, in 1703, on a set of cold, flat, flood-prone islands in the marshy delta where the Neva river meets the Baltic, on land he had just taken from Sweden and did not yet securely hold, Peter founded a city.
St Petersburg.
The decision is, on its face, insane.
The site was a malarial swamp, frozen much of the year, flooded much of the rest, on the empire's exposed northwestern frontier, far from the population and resources of the country.
Peter built his capital there anyway, and the reasons are the thesis of this book in architectural form.
He wanted a port on the Baltic, a "window to Europe," a Russian city that faced west and looked nothing like Moscow.
He wanted to be physically out of Moscow, the city of the Kremlin and the streltsy and the priests and the beards, the whole world of 1682.
So he conscripted labor on a colossal scale: tens of thousands of peasants and Swedish prisoners and soldiers were marched in to drive piles into the bog, dig canals, and die.
The death toll is one of those famous numbers the reader should hold with tongs.
Contemporary and later accounts threw around figures up to 100,000 dead "built on bones," and the phrase "the city built on bones" became proverbial.

Modern historians regard the highest figures as unverifiable and probably inflated, while accepting that the human cost of building St Petersburg in the early years was severe, with deaths from disease, exposure, and exhaustion certainly in the many thousands.
The exact arithmetic is lost; the moral of it is not.
The single most beautiful city the Russian Empire ever produced was raised, deliberately, on a swamp, by forced labor, at a cost in lives nobody bothered to count.

Peter began his own palace complexes there almost at once; the great pleasure-palace of Peterhof, with its gravity-fed fountains and gilded statuary meant to answer Versailles, was begun in this period and finished by his successors, and so was the cathedral that would hold the tombs of the emperors.
The grandeur and the bones arrived together, in the same decade, in the same place.
They always do, in this story.
The war turned in 1709.

Charles XII, having forced his way through Poland, invaded Russia itself, aiming at Moscow, then swung south into Ukraine hoping for support from the Cossacks (KOSS-aks, the semi-autonomous warrior communities of the southern steppe frontier, whom we will meet repeatedly) under their elected leader, the hetman Ivan Mazepa, a long-trusted ally of Peter who, seeing Charles ascendant and Cossack autonomy shrinking under Russian centralization, gambled on Sweden for an independent Ukraine.

He brought far fewer Cossacks than he had promised, lost the bet at Poltava, and died in Ottoman exile a few months later; in the Russian state's official memory he became the archetypal traitor, anathematized by the church for two centuries.

Peter applied the strategy Russia applies to every great invader for the next two and a half centuries, the strategy that will beat Napoleon in Chapter 10 and Hitler outside this book entirely: trade space for time, scorch the earth, let the distance and the winter do the work, and force the enemy to fight far from home, starving, in the cold.
Charles's army, weakened, supply-starved, and far smaller than it had been, finally gave battle at Poltava (pol-TAH-va) in Ukraine on 8 July 1709.
The Russians, now numerous, well-drilled, and well-supplied, destroyed the Swedish army.
Charles XII escaped with a handful of men into Ottoman territory; the bulk of his army surrendered days later.
Poltava is one of the genuine hinge-battles of European history.
Sweden's century as a great power ended on that field, and Russia's began.
The news of Poltava is the moment the courts of Europe realized a new great power had appeared in the east, and started, with some alarm, treating it as one.

The war dragged on another twelve years, because Charles XII was incapable of admitting defeat and kept fighting from Ottoman exile and then from Sweden until he was killed in 1718 (shot in the head besieging a Norwegian fortress, by whom is still argued; some Swedes have long suspected one of his own men, which is unprovable and probably unprovable forever).

Along the way Peter overreached badly in the Pruth River campaign of 1711, when he marched south against the Ottomans, got his outnumbered, thirst-stricken army surrounded on the Pruth river in present-day Moldova, and escaped total disaster only because the Ottoman grand vizier, his own troops restless and his supply lines long, preferred a quick advantageous settlement to a battle of annihilation, and let Peter march out in exchange for a humiliating treaty that handed Azov, his very first conquest, back to the Turks (a deal lubricated, by the persistent story, with a large bribe and the jewels of Peter's wife Catherine).
It was a sharp lesson that the man who would beat Sweden could still badly mismanage a war, and a useful corrective to the legend of Peter as infallible.
But the Baltic was the prize, and the Baltic he won.
At sea, the new navy he had willed into existence won its first major fleet victory over the Swedes at Gangut (GAN-goot) in 1714, proving the ships were not just for show.
Finally, in 1721, Sweden gave up.

The Treaty of Nystad (NEW-stat) ceded to Russia the eastern Baltic coast, the modern Baltic states and the territory around St Petersburg, a permanent warm-enough-water frontage on the sea, the thing every Russian ruler since had wanted and none had gotten.
Russia was now, unarguably, a European great power.

That same year, the Senate and Synod formally offered Peter, and Peter accepted, the titles Emperor of All Russia and "the Great" and "Father of the Fatherland." The state stopped being the Tsardom of Muscovy and became, in its own official self-description, the Russian Empire.
The word matters.
Muscovy was a grand duchy that had grown large.

The Russian Empire was a self-conscious imperial project on the European model, with a window on the sea, a navy, a European-drilled army, a half-built western capital, and an emperor who had personally learned to caulk a hull.
The grandeur was now undeniable.
What it cost, and who paid, is the next chapter.

chapters.title: Revolution From Above
sentences: Peter the Great is the only ruler in this book who tried to change his country faster than it could be changed, and the wreckage and the achievement of that attempt are still being argued about three centuries later.
The standard shorthand, "Peter westernized Russia," is true and useless.

What he actually did was attempt, by decree and force, to clamp a modern European-style state onto a society that had not generated any of the things such a state usually grows out of, and to do it inside one lifetime.
This chapter is about the machinery he built and the people it ran over, because both halves are the thesis.
Start with the machine, because Peter was, above all, an institution-builder.
The old Muscovite government was a tangle of overlapping departments (the prikazy) staffed by hereditary clerks and run on personal connection.
Peter replaced it, in stages, with a rationalized bureaucratic state copied substantially from Sweden and the German states.
He created the Governing Senate in 1711 as the supreme administrative and judicial body to run the country, originally while he was away at war and then permanently.

He replaced the old departments with the Colleges, a set of (eventually twelve) functional ministries, each run by a board rather than a single official, on the Swedish model: a College of War, of the Admiralty, of Foreign Affairs, of state revenue, and so on.
He carved the empire into provinces (gubernii) with appointed governors to push tax and conscription down into the country.

To make sure the new machine actually obeyed him, he created a parallel surveillance system, the fiskaly and then the office of the Procurator-General, officials whose job was to watch the other officials, the seed of a Russian habit (a state agency that secretly watches the state, and everyone else) that runs straight through this book to the Third Section and the Okhrana.
The single most consequential institution he built was the Table of Ranks, promulgated in 1722.
This is worth slowing down for, because it reorganized the entire Russian elite for the next two centuries.
The Table of Ranks was a grid: fourteen parallel ranks in the military, the civil service, and the court, from the lowest commissioned grade up to field marshal and chancellor.
The rule was that status now flowed from service to the state, not from birth.
A nobleman's son started at the bottom and rose by serving; a commoner who reached a certain rank in the army or bureaucracy was automatically ennobled.
In one stroke Peter converted the old hereditary boyar aristocracy from a class that owned its status by blood into a service class that owed its status to the crown.
This is the deep structure of the grandeur-and-unfreedom machine. the nobility's privileges, above all the right to own serfs, were tied to its service to the autocrat.
The serf served the noble; the noble served the state; the state was the emperor.
It was a pyramid of obligation with one man at the top and 23 million at the bottom, and Peter built the part of it that locked the nobility in.

Catherine, in Chapter 7, will cut the nobility loose from its end of the bargain while leaving the serfs chained to theirs, and that asymmetry is the moral crack the whole edifice eventually falls into.
To pay for the army and the navy and the wars, Peter needed money the old tax system could not raise, so he changed how Russia was taxed in a way that pressed the bond on the serf tighter.

The old tax was assessed by household, which encouraged peasants to cram many people into one taxable "household." Peter replaced it in 1718–1724 with the soul tax (the podushnaya podat), a flat tax levied on every individual male "soul" (peasant or townsman) recorded in periodic censuses called "revisions." To collect it the state had to count and fix every peasant in place, which deepened serfdom by making the serf, in effect, a permanent tax-unit registered to a place and a master.
The soul tax also, for the first time, swept up previously freer categories of rural people into the bound mass.
It funded the empire and it tightened the chain in the same act, which is Peter's whole reign in one fiscal instrument.
Now the culture war, the part everyone remembers, and the part it is easy to get wrong by treating it as comic.
On returning from the Grand Embassy, Peter set out to make the Russian elite look European, on the theory that a service class that looked and lived like the Muscovite past would think like it.

He personally sheared the beards of his boyars, then in 1705 instituted the beard tax: a Russian man who wished to keep his beard had to pay an annual fee and carry a small bronze token, stamped with a picture of a beard, proving he had paid.
This sounds like an eccentric joke.
It was not received as one.
In Orthodox belief, going back centuries, the beard was close to a religious obligation, the mark of a man made in God's image; shaving it was, for many devout Russians, something near sacrilege.

The beard tax, the order that nobles and townsmen wear Western (Hungarian, then German, then French) dress instead of the long Russian caftan, the order that women appear unveiled at the new compulsory mixed social gatherings (assemblies) Peter imported, all of it landed on traditional and religious Russia as an assault on the soul of the country by its own ruler.
To Peter's enemies, and to the Old Believers (we will get to them), he was not just a reforming tsar.
He was, literally, the Antichrist, and that belief was widespread and sincere.
The culture war was not cosmetic.

It opened a fissure, between a Westernized elite that increasingly spoke French and an enserfed mass that did not, that never closed and that Russian writers a century later (Chapter 12) would name as the country's central wound.
He also took on the church directly, and won, in the move that proves how little could check a determined autocrat.
The Russian Orthodox Church was led by a Patriarch, an office of immense moral authority.
When the Patriarch died in 1700, Peter simply did not allow a new one to be elected.

He left the office vacant for twenty-one years, and then in 1721 abolished it altogether, replacing the Patriarch with the Holy Synod, a committee of churchmen run, in practice, by a lay government official (the Ober-Procurator) appointed by the emperor.
The Russian church became, formally and openly, a department of the Russian state, and it stayed one until 1917.
No western monarch of the period could have decapitated his national church this casually; the western churches had independent ground to stand on and the institutional habit of saying no.
The Russian church did not, for exactly the reasons laid out in Chapter 1, and Peter exposed that with a single administrative stroke.

The cost fell hardest on the Old Believers (the raskolniki), Russians who decades earlier had broken with the official church rather than accept the liturgical reforms the Patriarch Nikon imposed in the 1650s, corrections meant to bring Russian practice back into line with the Greek originals: spelling Jesus's name differently, crossing oneself with three fingers instead of two, processing in a different direction, revising service books.
To devout traditionalists these were not small edits but the deliberate corruption of the only true faith, worth dying for, and many did, by the thousands, some by self-immolation.

They were now doubly hated as religious dissidents under a state church run by the "Antichrist." They were persecuted, taxed punitively (Old Believer men paid a double soul tax, and there was a tax on their beards too), and driven to the empire's edges, where, ironically, their disciplined, literate, tight-knit communities became some of its most successful merchants and frontier settlers, a pattern of persecuted minorities turned into economic engines that this book will see again with the empire's Jews.
And Peter built the apparatus of knowledge, because a modern state needs trained people and he had almost none.

He reformed the calendar, ordering Russia in 1700 to count years from the birth of Christ rather than from the supposed creation of the world and to celebrate the new year on 1 January like the rest of Europe (Russia kept the older Julian calendar itself, which by the twentieth century ran 13 days behind the West, which is why the "October" Revolution of 1917 happened, by the Western calendar, in November, a confusion that haunts every date in the last chapters of this book).

He simplified the alphabet into a cleaner civil script for secular printing, separating it from the old ecclesiastical letters, which made secular books and the first Russian printed newspaper, Vedomosti, cheaper to produce.

He founded technical and naval schools, sent young nobles abroad to study on pain of losing their status, and chartered the Russian Academy of Sciences in St Petersburg, which opened in 1725 just after his death.

The Academy is a perfect emblem of the whole reign: a world-class scientific institution, stocked at first almost entirely with imported German and Swiss scholars because Russia could not yet supply its own, decreed into existence by a state that needed the output and did not have the society underneath it.
Within a generation it would have one genuinely Russian colossus in it (Lomonosov, Chapter 5), and within two centuries it would be world-class.
The grandeur was being engineered top-down at forced speed, and it worked, and it cost what it cost.

Peter died in February 1725, at fifty-two, in agony from a urinary and bladder disease that had plagued him for years; the much-loved story that he caught his fatal chill wading into the icy Neva to help rescue drowning sailors is the kind of redemptive deathbed scene this book has taught the reader to distrust, and most historians treat it as embellishment on an illness that was already killing him.

He left no clear heir, which is itself a Petrine catastrophe: in 1722, having had his own son Alexei tortured and condemned for opposing his reforms (Alexei died in prison under circumstances the regime never honestly explained, one of the darkest and least defensible episodes of the reign), Peter issued a law allowing the reigning emperor to name any successor he chose, and then died without naming one.
He had broken the old succession custom and put nothing reliable in its place.

The throne of the largest empire on earth was now an open question to be settled by whoever controlled the Guards regiments in the capital, the play-soldiers he had raised in a village forty years before.
For the next thirty-seven years, that is exactly how Russia chose its rulers.

chapters.title: The Age of the Guards
sentences: The thirty-seven years between Peter the Great's death in 1725 and Catherine the Great's coup in 1762 are usually told as a confusing parade of forgettable rulers, and they are confusing, so this chapter will give you the through-line first and the parade second.

The through-line is this: Peter destroyed the old rule of succession and replaced it with nothing, and into that vacuum stepped the only institution in the capital with both the weapons and the proximity to decide things, the Guards (the Preobrazhensky and Semyonovsky regiments Peter had raised as a boy, now the elite household troops, stationed in St Petersburg, recruited heavily from the nobility, and acutely aware that they made and unmade emperors).
For four decades, Russian successions are settled by which faction the Guards back at three in the morning.
This is the period that proves the autocracy had a hidden dependency: the autocrat was absolute, but the autocrat was chosen by a few thousand soldiers, and everyone in the elite knew it.
It is also the period in which the nobility, the service class Peter had chained to the state, methodically negotiates its chain looser while the serf's stays exactly where it is.
The parade, briskly, with each ruler tagged so you can keep them straight.
Catherine I (reigned 1725–1727), not to be confused with the far more famous Catherine the Great who comes later.

This Catherine was Peter's second wife, born a servant of obscure Baltic peasant origin who was taken when Russian troops overran her town in the Great Northern War, passed through the households of a Russian field marshal and then Menshikov, and became Peter's mistress and finally his wife and crowned empress, one of the more improbable rags-to-throne climbs in European history.
With the backing of Peter's chief lieutenant Menshikov (MEN-shih-koff) and the Guards, she was installed as ruler in her own right after Peter's death, the first woman to rule the empire.

She was not a stateswoman; Menshikov, a man who had risen from selling pies in the street to prince by sheer ability and corruption, effectively ran the country, and a new top body, the Supreme Privy Council, ran it with him.
Peter II (reigned 1727–1730), Peter the Great's grandson, the son of the tortured Alexei, a boy of eleven at accession.

Menshikov tried to control him by betrothing him to his own daughter; the rival Dolgoruky clan outmaneuvered him, and Menshikov fell spectacularly, stripped of everything and exiled to Siberia, where he died, a textbook demonstration of how vertiginous the climb and the fall could be in this system.
The boy-emperor moved the court back to Moscow, a small symbolic victory for the old anti-Petrine party, and then died of smallpox at fourteen, ending the direct male line of the Romanovs.
With him the dynasty's succession became, for the rest of this book, a matter of cousins, in-laws, and Germans.
Anna (reigned 1730–1740), Peter the Great's niece, Duchess of the Baltic backwater of Courland.
Her accession is the single most interesting constitutional moment in the entire eighteenth century and almost nobody knows it, so slow down.

The Supreme Privy Council, dominated by great aristocratic families, offered Anna the throne only if she signed a set of written "Conditions" sharply limiting her power: no declaring war, no spending state money, no marrying or naming an heir, no executing nobles, without the Council's consent.
For a few weeks in early 1730 it looked as though Russia might get a constitutional, oligarchic monarchy a full 175 years before it got the Duma.
Anna signed.

Then she discovered that the broader nobility and, crucially, the Guards detested the idea of being ruled by a handful of magnate families more than they feared an autocrat, and within weeks she publicly tore the Conditions up and restored full autocracy to roar of approval from the Guards.

This is the autocracy's clearest near-death-and-recovery before 1905, and the lesson the regime drew from it, that the broad gentry would always back an autocrat over an aristocratic oligarchy, shaped Russian politics for two centuries.
Anna's reign is also remembered, fairly or not, for the Bironovshchina (bee-ron-OFF-shchee-na), the supposed reign of terror and German favoritism named after her Baltic German favorite Ernst Biron.
Modern historians think later Russian nationalist writers exaggerated the "German yoke" framing, but the resentment of foreign favorites at court was real and recurs.

Then a brief, grim interlude: Ivan VI, an infant great-grandnephew of Peter, proclaimed emperor in 1740 at two months old under a regency, deposed at fifteen months in 1741, and then, in one of the cruelest stories in the dynasty, kept in secret solitary confinement for the rest of his life, never told who he was, and finally killed by his guards in 1764 during a botched attempt to free him.
He is the bound prisoner at the bottom of the dynasty's own house, and a reminder that the grandeur-and-unfreedom logic could reach the imperial family itself.
