Elizabeth (reigned 1741–1762), Peter the Great's daughter, took the throne in the period's most theatrical coup.

In November 1741 she walked into the barracks of the Preobrazhensky Guards at night, in person, and led the grenadiers to arrest the infant Ivan VI's regency (the rallying line tradition gives her, to the effect of "you know whose daughter I am, follow me," is the kind of cinematic quote this book treats with caution; that she went to the barracks herself and the Guards followed her is the solid part).
The Guards made her empress on the spot.
The image, a Petrine daughter personally leading the household troops to seize the crown, is the whole age in one scene.
Elizabeth's twenty-year reign was, by the standards around it, stable and consequential.
She was vain, pious, pleasure-loving, and politically shrewder than her reputation.
She founded Moscow University in 1755 (still Russia's leading university, still named for her co-founder), at the urging of the one towering native intellect this period produced.

That intellect was Mikhail Lomonosov (loh-moh-NOH-soff), and he deserves a paragraph because he is the proof that the top-down knowledge machine Peter built had begun, by mid-century, to manufacture Russians and not just import Germans.

Lomonosov was born around 1711, the son of a fisherman from the far Arctic north, walked, by the durable story, much of the way to Moscow to get an education, and became a chemist, physicist, astronomer, geologist, historian, and poet of genuine international stature, a Russian Benjamin Franklin in range and roughly his contemporary.

He did real science (he argued for a wave theory of heat and a conservation-of-matter principle, observed the atmosphere of Venus during a 1761 transit), reformed Russian literary language and verse, fought the German-dominated Academy of Sciences for the dignity of Russian scholars, and championed the founding of Moscow University.
One generation after Peter chartered an Academy he had to staff with foreigners, it had produced a world-class Russian polymath.
The machine worked.

The question this book keeps asking is what it was worth, given who paid for it, and Lomonosov, the fisherman's son who rose through the one institution that judged talent over birth, is one of the better answers the empire ever gave.
Two more strands of this period feed forward.
First, art and stone.

Elizabeth's reign is when Russian imperial grandeur acquires its definitive look, through the Italian architect Bartolomeo Rastrelli (rah-STREL-lee), who built for her a wedding-cake Russian Baroque of blue, white, and gold: the rebuilt Winter Palace in St Petersburg (the vast imperial residence that becomes the literal target of the revolution in the last chapters), the Catherine Palace at Tsarskoye Selo with its famous Amber Room, the Smolny Convent.
Rastrelli's buildings are the architectural form of the thesis, sublime surfaces raised by a serf economy, and you should keep that double vision through every palace in this book.
Second, the army went to general European war and proved something.

In the Seven Years' War (1756–1763, the first genuinely global war, fought from Europe to North America to India), Russia under Elizabeth joined the coalition against the Prussia of Frederick the Great (Frederick II, king of Prussia 1740–1786, the soldier-philosopher who had turned a medium-sized German kingdom into a feared military power and was rated by his own enemies the finest general of the age), then the most admired military machine in Europe.
Russian armies beat Frederick's repeatedly, most crushingly at Kunersdorf in 1759, and even briefly occupied Berlin in 1760.
Frederick, the finest general of the age, was pushed to the edge of total defeat and, by the accounts of those around him, came close to despair.
Then Elizabeth died, in January 1762.
Her heir was the next ruler in the parade, and he changes everything by changing nothing more dramatically than any palace coup in the whole period.

Peter III (reigned 1762, six months), Elizabeth's nephew, a German-born grandson of Peter the Great, raised in the duchy of Holstein, a man whose obsessive hero-worship of Frederick the Great is about to alter European history.

On taking the throne in the middle of a war Russia was winning against Prussia, Peter III abruptly made peace with his idol Frederick, returned all Russia's conquests, and switched sides, an act so astonishing it is still called in German history "the Miracle of the House of Brandenburg," because it saved Prussia from destruction and arguably made possible the Prussia that becomes Germany a century later.
But the act of his short reign that matters most to this book had nothing to do with Prussia.
In 1762 Peter III issued the Manifesto on the Freedom of the Nobility, which abolished the nobility's compulsory state service.
Remember the Petrine bargain: the noble owed service to the state, and in exchange got the right to own serfs.
Peter III cut the first half of that deal.
The nobility was now free of its obligation.
The serf was not.
From 1762 the educated, serf-owning class held its privileges with no corresponding duty, and the bound peasant held his bondage with no corresponding protection.
That asymmetry, the noble freed while the serf is not, is the precise structural injustice that Russian writers, radicals, and finally revolutionaries will gnaw on for the next 155 years.
It is the single most important sentence in this chapter, and it is why a six-month emperor nobody respected gets a paragraph to himself.

Peter III himself was personally unpopular, erratic, contemptuous of Russian Orthodoxy and Russian feeling, and within six months he was overthrown and shortly afterward killed, by a conspiracy fronted by the Guards and led by his own wife, a minor German princess who had been quietly preparing for exactly this for eighteen years.
Her name was Catherine, and she is the subject of the next four chapters.

chapters.title: The German Girl Who Became Russia
sentences: She was born Sophie of Anhalt-Zerbst in 1729, in Prussian Stettin, the daughter of a minor German prince in the service of the King of Prussia, with no fortune, no great connection, and no drop of Russian blood.

She died in 1796 as Catherine II, Catherine the Great, autocrat of the largest empire on earth, the most formidable ruler Russia had between Peter and the twentieth century, and a woman who corresponded as an intellectual equal with the most famous philosophers in Europe while presiding over the harshest tightening of serfdom in Russian history.

Catherine is the chapter where the central contradiction of this book stops being a structural diagram and becomes a single person's biography, because she believed, sincerely and at length, in the European Enlightenment's program of reason, law, and human dignity, and she ruled a state that ran on the opposite of all three, and she knew it, and she chose the state.
To understand why, you have to take both halves of her seriously, which the propaganda (both the flattering and the filthy kind) never does.
She arrived in Russia in 1744 at fourteen, brought in as a bride for the future Peter III.
She did the things a foreign princess survives by doing: she converted to Orthodoxy with conspicuous devotion, learned Russian obsessively, and read.

While her husband played with toy soldiers and admired Frederick of Prussia, Catherine spent two decades in an unhappy marriage reading Voltaire, Montesquieu, the French philosophes, and the entire library of the European Enlightenment, and building, very quietly, a network in the Guards and the court.
When Peter III took the throne in 1762 and rapidly alienated almost everyone, Catherine moved.

Catherine's coup of 1762, in June, was a Guards coup of the now-classic type: the Guards regiments, organized by her allies (the five Orlov brothers, well-connected Guards officers with a following among the rank and file, the most prominent of them Grigory, who was her lover), proclaimed her empress, arrested her husband, and forced his abdication.

Peter III died a few days later, in custody, under circumstances the regime declared to be "hemorrhoidal colic" and almost nobody believed; he was near-certainly killed by his guards, with Catherine's foreknowledge probable and her direct order unproven and probably unprovable.
This matters because Catherine's entire legitimacy was a problem she never solved.

She was a German with no Russian blood and no hereditary right whatsoever, who took the throne by overthrowing and (at minimum) acquiescing in the murder of her husband, who was himself the legitimate emperor, while her own son Paul, the actual Romanov heir, was alive and a child.

She ruled for thirty-four years as, strictly, a usurper, and she knew it, and a good deal of her conduct, including the grandeur, is best read as a permanent campaign to be so magnificent and so successful that the question of right would not be asked out loud.
Now the Enlightenment half, taken at full strength because it was real.

Catherine read voraciously and corresponded for decades with Voltaire, the most famous writer in Europe and the era's emblem of rational, anticlerical, reforming thought, who flattered her extravagantly as the philosopher-empress, the proof that an enlightened absolute monarch could do more good faster than any messy parliament.
She corresponded with the encyclopedist Diderot, bought his library when he needed money and paid him to keep it as his salary, and brought him to St Petersburg for months of conversation.
She bought the art collection that became the Hermitage, one of the greatest museums on earth, founded as her private gallery in the Winter Palace in the 1760s.

She built and endowed; she founded the Smolny Institute, among the first state-run institutions in Europe for the formal education of noblewomen (a finishing-school curriculum of languages, manners, music, and some arithmetic, modest by later standards but genuinely novel as a state commitment to schooling girls), and patronized the Academy of Sciences, whose directorship she gave to Princess Yekaterina Dashkova (DASH-koh-va), an early ally from the 1762 coup and a serious intellect in her own right, and one of the first women anywhere to head a national academy of sciences.

She presented herself to Europe, with great skill, as the living argument for enlightened absolutism, the eighteenth-century theory that the fastest road to a rational, prosperous, humane society was not democracy but a wise, philosophically educated absolute monarch imposing reform from the top.
Russia under Catherine was that theory's showcase, and the showcase was not entirely fake.

It was, however, a bargain, and the philosophes were slow to see it: as the Enlightenment narrative puts it from the other side, patronizing Voltaire was a great deal cheaper than freeing a serf, and it bought a far better European press than freeing one would have, and the movement let itself be consumed as prestige by a ruler who implemented almost none of it.
By the end of the century several of the philosophes had come to see the performance for what it had been.

She secularized vast church lands, expanded schooling, reformed provincial administration, promoted inoculation against smallpox (and had herself publicly inoculated in 1768 to lead by example, which in 1768 was a genuinely bold scientific gesture), and built and beautified on a scale that announced Russia as a full member of the European cultural order.
The high-water mark of the Enlightenment Catherine, and the place where its limits become unmistakable, is the Nakaz and the Legislative Commission.
In the 1760s Catherine personally wrote an enormous treatise, the Nakaz (na-KAHZ, "Instruction"), to guide a sweeping reform of Russian law.

It was, in long stretches, lifted almost word for word from Montesquieu and from the Milanese jurist Cesare Beccaria, whose 1764 On Crimes and Punishments argued against judicial torture and the death penalty and effectively founded modern criminal-law reform.

Beccaria's book was not just an idea on the page; in these same years it was reshaping actual law elsewhere in Europe, in Habsburg Tuscany and then in Austria itself, where Joseph II abolished judicial torture outright.

Catherine quoted Beccaria approvingly and changed nothing, which is the contrast in one sentence. the Nakaz floated ideas radical for Russia: equality before the law, restraint of cruelty, the welfare of the people as the purpose of the state, even a famous passage that conceded liberty was a natural good, called the mass enserfment of human beings an evil, and stopped carefully short of saying it should actually be ended.

In 1767 she convened a Legislative Commission, an assembly of 564 deputies elected from nobles, townsmen, state peasants, and non-Russian peoples (though pointedly not the privately owned serfs, who had no voice at all) to use the Nakaz as the basis for a new law code.
It was the broadest consultative body Russia had assembled, and European observers were dazzled.
It produced nothing.

After eighteen months of debate that exposed exactly how irreconcilable the empire's interests were, especially that the nobility would defend serfdom to the death and that the Nakaz's hints against it were politically impossible, Catherine prorogued the Commission in 1768 (using the convenient pretext of a new war with the Ottomans) and never effectively reconvened it.
No new code came of it.
This is the precise hinge of the chapter and one of the precise hinges of the whole book.
Catherine had, in writing, intellectually conceded the case against serfdom, and then concluded, correctly in terms of holding power, that she could not touch it.

Her throne rested on the support of the serf-owning nobility (the same Guards-and-gentry constituency that had made her and could unmake her), and the Enlightenment program ran straight into the load-bearing wall of the regime, which was unfreedom.
She chose the wall.
The reader should resist both the cynical reading (she never meant any of it) and the naive one (she was a frustrated liberal).

The truthful reading is the uncomfortable one: she sincerely believed in reform and sincerely valued her power more, and when they collided she discovered, like every reforming Russian ruler in this book after her, that the empire was built so that you could not have very much of the first without endangering the second.
The choice is sharpest set against her fellow "enlightened despots," the other rulers Europe filed under the same label.

Frederick the Great of Prussia (Chapter 5) kept his serfs because his army needed them; Joseph II of Austria abolished serfdom in the Habsburg lands in 1781, within a few years of Catherine's Legislative Commission.
Catherine had, in effect, a working example of a contemporary autocrat doing the thing the Nakaz had argued for, and a working example of one who refused, and she chose Frederick's path.
Alexander I will discover it (Chapter 9).
Alexander II will partially break it and be murdered for it (Chapters 14–15).
Nicholas II will refuse to learn it at all (Chapter 19).
Catherine is where the pattern is set, by the most intelligent ruler the dynasty produced, which is exactly why it is so damning.
The limit she had reasoned her way to in 1768 was about to be demonstrated to her from below, in blood.

Catherine the reformer had written about the dignity of the peasant in the privacy of the Nakaz; five years later, in 1773, a Cossack claiming to be her murdered husband Peter III, come back to free the people, told her what the peasants actually wanted, with pikes, and her response set the chain tighter than Peter the Great ever had.
That is the next chapter.

chapters.title: Pugachev and the Machinery of Bondage
sentences: This is the chapter where the book stops describing serfdom and makes you stand inside it, because the largest popular revolt in Russian history before 1917 cannot be understood as anything other than 23 million people's answer to the question Catherine's Legislative Commission refused to ask.
First the machinery, in concrete human terms, because "serfdom" is a word that hides what it names.
Then the revolt.
Then the regime's response, and let that response arrive as the discovery it was for the people who lived it.
So: what was it actually like to be a serf in Catherine's Russia?
Forget the word "serf," which sounds medieval and distant, and look at the legal and daily reality.
A privately owned serf, around 1770, belonged to a noble landowner the way the land did.
He could be bought and sold.

By Catherine's reign, serfs were openly advertised for sale in newspapers, sometimes individually, sometimes alongside livestock and furniture, and although selling family members separately was officially frowned upon it demonstrably happened.

The serf owed his lord either barshchina, unpaid labor on the lord's own land (commonly three days a week, sometimes far more, and the lord set the terms), or obrok, a money or produce rent (which at least let the serf work for himself the rest of the time, and on some estates take up a trade or trade in towns), and frequently a punishing mix of both.

The lord was the serf's judge and police: he could flog him, imprison him on the estate, and, by a series of Catherine-era decrees, exile a troublesome serf to Siberia or hand him over for army recruitment, which meant a 25-year term that the village mourned like a death because the man usually never came back.

A serf could not legally marry without the lord's leave, could not leave the estate without a written pass, could not, until far too late in this book, own property in a way the law would defend against his owner, and, by a 1767 decree issued the very year of the enlightened Legislative Commission, could be sentenced to hard labor merely for submitting a petition against his own master.

To anchor the scale one more time: this was the legal condition of more than a third of the population of the largest country on earth, somewhere around 23 million people in the private serf category alone, a bound population larger than the entire population of Britain at the time, and held that way not on distant plantations across an ocean but in the villages that fed the capital.

The American reader's nearest handle is plantation slavery in the antebellum South, and the comparison is instructive precisely where it breaks: the Russian serf was the same religion, the same language, the same appearance as his owner, which made the bondage harder to rationalize and, in the end, harder for educated Russia to keep not-seeing.
Russia abolished it in 1861.
The United States abolished its slavery in 1865, by a war that killed about 750,000 people; the British Empire had abolished slavery in its colonies in 1833.

Keep those three dates side by side, because Chapter 14 turns on them, and notice the oddity already: of the three, Russia was by far the least industrial, the one with the weakest economic motive to free its labor, and yet it acted earliest and without a war.
The reason is in this chapter, not in any ledger.
It was fear of a repeat of what you are about to read.
Now add the other engine of revolt: the frontier.

South and east of the settled core lived the Cossacks, communities of free, self-governing, militarized frontiersmen, many descended from peasants who had fled serfdom to the open steppe, organized into "Hosts" (the Don, the Yaik, the Zaporozhian) that had historically traded military service to the tsar for autonomy.
Catherine's centralizing state was steadily eroding that autonomy, conscripting Cossacks into regular service, interfering with their self-rule.
The Yaik Cossacks on the Ural river were in a state of smoldering fury about exactly this in the early 1770s.

Add to that frontier the Bashkirs and other non-Russian peoples resentful of land seizures, Old Believers hiding from the state church, and serfs assigned in brutal conditions to the Ural mining and metal works (above all the empire of the Demidovs, a family that had risen from a single Tula blacksmith to own a sprawling private industrial domain of iron foundries worked by serfs bound to the factory rather than the field, Chapter 18's industrial story in its grim prehistory).
The southeast of the empire in 1773 was dry tinder.
It needed a spark, and Russian popular culture provided the standard one: the pretender.
Yemelyan Pugachev (poo-gah-CHOFF) was a Don Cossack and army deserter who, in 1773, declared that he was not Pugachev at all.

He was Peter III, Catherine's murdered husband, the true emperor, who had not died but escaped, and who had now returned to punish the wicked nobles, abolish serfdom, end conscription and the soul tax, and give the people the land.

This was not a one-off con; "the returned true tsar" was a recurring template in Russian peasant politics (in the chaotic "Time of Troubles" around 1605–1612, before the Romanovs, at least three different men had claimed to be Dmitry, a dead son of Ivan the Terrible, and one briefly took the throne; there had since been other false Peters too), rooted in a popular belief that the tsar was the people's father and that their misery must be the nobles' doing against his true will.
Pugachev's genius was to weaponize that belief at the exact moment the southeast was primed to explode.
Pugachev's Rebellion (1773–1775) became the largest popular uprising in Russian history before the twentieth century.

It started among the Yaik Cossacks, spread like fire to Bashkirs, Tatars, Old Believers, factory serfs, and finally the mass of agricultural serfs along the Volga, raised armies tens of thousands strong, briefly stormed and burned the city of Kazan, issued mock-imperial "decrees" freeing the serfs, and for the better part of two years (1773–1775) kept a vast, shifting swath of the southeastern empire in open revolt while the regime, also fighting the Ottomans, scrambled.

Where Pugachev's forces passed, serfs settled accounts with their owners directly: estate houses burned, landlords and officials were hanged, and for a season the machinery of bondage ran backward across a region the size of a large European country.
It was crushed, as it had to be once the regular army was freed up from the Turkish war and turned on it.

Pugachev's improvised peasant armies could not stand against trained troops; he was defeated, betrayed by his own lieutenants, handed over in a cage, taken to Moscow, and in January 1775 publicly executed (quartered, the sentence formally softened to beheading first, the bodily details of which are exactly the kind of thing later accounts dramatize and should be read with that in mind).
His name was to be erased; even the Yaik river was renamed the Ural and the host renamed, an attempt to delete the event from the map that, characteristically, only fixed it more firmly in memory.
Here is the chapter's whole argument, and one of the spine moments of the book.
The Pugachev terror did not move Catherine the philosopher-empress toward emancipation.
It moved her, hard, the other way.

The revolt confirmed for her and for the entire noble class their deepest fear: that beneath the serene Enlightenment surface sat a vast, illiterate, vengeful mass that, if the chain were loosened even slightly, would rise and slaughter them in their houses.

The regime's conclusion was not "this system is unjust and dangerous and must be reformed." It was "this system is dangerous and must be held down harder." In the decade after Pugachev, Catherine extended serfdom into Ukraine where it had been weaker, reorganized provincial government to put more armed force at the local nobility's disposal, and, in 1785, issued the Charter to the Nobility, which codified into permanent law everything the nobility had been winning piecemeal since Peter III freed them from service in 1762: confirmed freedom from compulsory state service and from the soul tax and from corporal punishment, guaranteed property rights including absolute property in their serfs, the right to assemble in provincial corporations, immunity from confiscation.
A parallel Charter to the Towns the same year gave the merchant class a defined, lesser set of privileges.
The Charter to the Nobility is the legal capstone of the grandeur-and-unfreedom machine.
It made the serf-owning nobleman a free man with rights against the crown itself, at the very moment it left the serf with fewer rights against his owner than ever.

The two halves of the Petrine bargain had now fully come apart: the noble was free and protected, the serf was bound and exposed, and that gap was now written into the empire's fundamental law by its most enlightened ruler in direct reaction to the peasants who had tried to close it themselves.
Every revolutionary in the last half of this book is, in some sense, a delayed echo of Pugachev, and the regime spent the next 142 years afraid of him.
A coda on conscience, because the period also produced the first Russian who said all this out loud.

In 1790 a nobleman and customs official named Alexander Radishchev, educated partly in Leipzig on Catherine's own scholarship and steeped there in exactly the Enlightenment writers she patronized, published, on a private press, a book called A Journey from St Petersburg to Moscow: a fictional traveler's account that used the form of a road trip to detail, soberly and without melodrama, the daily cruelty of serfdom and the case against autocracy.

It is generally regarded as the first frontal moral indictment of the system by a member of the privileged class itself, the genuine ancestor of the entire Russian conscience-stricken intelligentsia to come.

Catherine, the correspondent of Voltaire, read it, annotated her copy with fury (her notes call him a rebel and, by the much-repeated summary of them, a man worse than Pugachev), and had Radishchev arrested, sentenced to death, the sentence commuted to Siberian exile.

Around the same time she shut down the publisher and freemason Nikolai Novikov, who had built the most ambitious independent printing and philanthropic network in Russia, journals, cheap books, schools, and famine relief organized privately through Masonic lodges, the first sustained example of educated Russians acting on the public good without and outside the state, which is exactly why it frightened her, and imprisoned him without trial.

The message was exact and it closes the chapter: the Enlightenment was welcome in Russia as the private hobby of the empress and as a glaze on the state, and it was a crime the instant a Russian applied it to the actual condition of the Russian people.
That is the box the next century's writers and revolutionaries are born into.

chapters.title: The Empire Doubles
sentences: While Catherine the Great was tightening the chain at home (Chapter 7), she was, with the other hand, expanding the empire faster than any Russian ruler since Peter, and arguably faster in raw territory and population than anyone before her.
This chapter is about that expansion, and it carries a second strand of the thesis: imperial grandeur in the Russian system did not only mean palaces and the Hermitage.
It meant land, and it meant the systematic conversion of conquered peoples into subjects of the autocracy, which is grandeur measured in square miles and in the absence of consent.

By the time Catherine died in 1796, the empire had added something like 200,000 square miles and on the order of seven million people, and it had wiped a thousand-year-old European country off the map entirely.
That last achievement is one she shared with two partners, and it deserves the cold look it usually doesn't get.
Start with the south, because the south is where the grandeur was loudest.

Catherine fought two long wars against the Ottoman Empire (the Turkish-ruled Muslim empire that controlled the Black Sea, the Balkans, and the Middle East, the subject of its own narrative), and won both.
The first Russo-Turkish War (1768–1774) produced a victory dramatic enough to rearrange the region.

A Russian fleet did something no Russian fleet had ever attempted: it sailed the entire length of Europe, out of the Baltic, down past Britain and through the Atlantic, around Gibraltar into the Mediterranean, thousands of miles from any Russian port or base, a navy barely two generations old undertaking the kind of long-range projection only the established maritime powers were thought capable of, and burned an Ottoman fleet trapped in the bay of Chesma in 1770 while Russian armies overran the Black Sea steppe and the Crimean Peninsula.

Britain and France watched closely and uneasily: Chesma was the first proof that Russian sea power could reach the Mediterranean at all, an alarm that fed, eighty years later, directly into their decision to intervene against Russia in the Crimean War (Chapter 13).

The Treaty of Kuchuk-Kainarji (koo-CHOOK ky-NAR-jee) in 1774 was a landmark: Russia gained territory on the Black Sea, the right to a navy on it, and, fatefully, a vaguely worded claim to protect Orthodox Christians within the Ottoman Empire, a clause Russia would use as a lever against the Turks for the next 140 years and that lights the fuse on the Crimean War in Chapter 13.

The treaty also detached the Crimean Khanate, the last surviving major fragment of the Mongol successor states and a Muslim Tatar state that had raided Russia for slaves for three centuries, from Ottoman protection as a nominally independent buffer.
Nominal independence lasted nine years.

In 1783 Catherine simply annexed Crimea outright, ending the khanate, the historic completion of Russia's centuries-long contest with the steppe slave-raiders, and a strategic prize: a warm-water foothold and the naval base of Sevastopol.

From St Petersburg this was a triumph; from Istanbul, as the Ottoman narrative tells it, the same two wars were the opening of the long Ottoman decline, and the loss of Crimea, with the Black Sea turned from an Ottoman lake into an open sea Russia could sail at will, was the single most strategically devastating amputation in Ottoman history.
The same event, read as ascent from one capital and as the beginning of the end from the other, is one of the cleanest examples in this whole series of why the cross-references exist.

The man who built the new south was Catherine's most important favorite and partner, Grigory Potemkin (poh-TYOM-kin), who many historians believe she secretly married, though the marriage rests on inference and circumstantial correspondence rather than a surviving record, and belongs in the "probable but unproven" column this book keeps for the colorful claims.

He governed the conquered southern lands, christened Novorossiya ("New Russia"), and oversaw an enormous state-driven colonization: founding cities (Yekaterinoslav, Kherson, and the great port of Odessa was begun in this push), settling the empty steppe with Russian, Ukrainian, German, and other colonists, and building a Black Sea fleet from nothing.
Potemkin is also the source of one of history's most durable and instructive myths.

The story goes that when Catherine toured the new south in 1787, Potemkin had fake village façades, "Potemkin villages," erected along her route and populated with happy peasants moved from site to site, to deceive her into thinking the region was prospering.
The phrase "Potemkin village" is now permanent English for a deceptive front.

The trouble is that historians have largely concluded the story is, at minimum, hugely exaggerated and probably originated as hostile propaganda from Potemkin's diplomatic rivals; the development of the south was real, if uneven, and the lavishness of the tour was theatrical statecraft aimed at impressing the foreign ambassadors traveling with Catherine more than at fooling Catherine herself.

The myth is included here precisely because it is so satisfying and so unreliable, which is a useful reflex to keep for the rest of the book: a too-perfect story about Russian autocratic pretense is exactly the kind of thing this narrative slows down to check.

The second Russo-Turkish War (1787–1792) confirmed the conquests, made the reputation of the greatest Russian general of the age, Alexander Suvorov (soo-VOR-off), who never lost a battle in a long career and whose storming of the Ottoman fortress of Izmail in 1790 became legendary for its ferocity, and pushed the frontier to the Dniester.
The southern wars were conquest, the ordinary if brutal business of empires taking territory from a rival empire.
What happened next was something colder and, morally, worse: not the defeat of a state but its premeditated erasure.
Now the cold part: Poland.

In 1772 the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth was the largest state in Europe by area, an old, culturally rich, but politically paralyzed republic-monarchy whose constitution gave any single nobleman in its parliament the power to veto and dissolve any session (the notorious liberum veto), originally a prized guarantee that no king could ride over the nobility, which by the eighteenth century had curdled into total paralysis because any reform that might have removed it could itself be vetoed, and because Poland's neighbors actively bribed deputies to keep the country ungovernable and defenseless.
Its three powerful neighbors, Catherine's Russia, Frederick the Great's Prussia, and Habsburg Austria, solved the inconvenience of a large country in the middle of them by eating it.

In three Partitions of Poland, in 1772, 1793, and 1795, the three monarchies divided the entire Commonwealth among themselves until, in 1795, Poland ceased to exist as a state, and stayed off the map for 123 years.
Russia took the largest share, the eastern lands including most of Lithuania, Belarus, and right-bank Ukraine.

There was a desperate Polish attempt to stop it: in 1794 a national uprising under Tadeusz Kościuszko (kosh-CHOOSH-koh), who had served the American Revolution as a military engineer, designing the fortifications at Saratoga and West Point, before coming home to fight for Poland's survival (there is a Kościuszko bridge in New York and a county in Indiana named for him, the modern handle), fought the partitioning powers and lost, which triggered the final, third partition.
The destruction of Poland is the largest single act of imperial expansion in this book and the one that ages worst, both morally and strategically.
Morally, because it was the deliberate murder of a sovereign European nation by its neighbors for convenience.

Strategically, because it absorbed into the Russian Empire millions of Poles, Lithuanians, Catholic and Uniate Christians, and the bulk of Eastern European Jewry, none of whom had any loyalty to the tsar, all of whom became a permanent internal problem, and it bequeathed the empire its largest concentrated grievance: a proud nation, with its own language, church, and memory of statehood, swallowed and determined not to be digested.
Poland revolts in Chapter 12 (1830) and again in Chapter 14 (1863), and the "Polish question" gnaws at the empire until the empire is gone.
One more frontier, in the opposite direction, almost as an afterthought, which is how the empire treated it.

While the court fought Turks and partitioned Poland, Russian fur traders, the promyshlenniki, having crossed all of Siberia in the previous century chasing sable and sea otter (the Siberian fur trade was, for two centuries, one of the Russian state's largest sources of hard wealth, the reason Russia bothered with Siberia at all), pushed across the Bering Strait into North America.
In the 1780s and 1790s they established the first permanent Russian settlements in Alaska.
Russian America was a real colony, run as a commercial monopoly chartered as the Russian-American Company, reaching at its furthest down the Pacific coast to a fort in northern California.

It is the strangest limb of the empire and the most revealing about how the empire actually worked: a continent away from St Petersburg, run for fur profit by a chartered company, settled by a few hundred Russians and a much larger forced and semi-forced native labor force, governed barely at all.

It is also, for the American reader, the setup to one of the most consequential real-estate decisions in United States history, the sale of Alaska in 1867, which gets its full treatment in Chapter 17.

For now, note only the shape: by 1796 the Russian Empire ran, however thinly, from the new Polish lands in the west to the coast of California, the largest contiguous land empire on the planet, and it had been assembled, in Catherine's reign, by a German-born usurper who corresponded with Voltaire and could not free a single serf.

The empire was now enormous, and enormity in this book is never only strength: every conquest added subjects who had not consented and grievances that did not dissolve, so that each expansion made the empire at once larger and harder to hold together, bigger and weaker in the same act.
That is the imperial version of this book's whole thesis, and it had just been demonstrated on a continental scale.
In Chapter 9 the empire nearly destroys itself at the top, twice in fifteen years, while the man it most needs to fight is assembling an army in France.

chapters.title: The Mad Tsar and the Hopeful One
sentences: Catherine the Great died in November 1796, and the throne passed to the one person in the empire she had least wanted to have it: her son Paul I (PAWL).
The relationship between Catherine and Paul is the psychological key to this chapter, so set it up plainly.
Catherine had taken the throne in 1762 by overthrowing Paul's father, Peter III.
By strict hereditary right the crown in 1762 arguably belonged to the infant Paul, not to his German mother who had no Romanov blood at all.

Catherine ruled for thirty-four years anyway, kept Paul away from power and from his own children, and is widely believed to have considered passing the throne over him directly to her grandson Alexander.
Paul grew up the rightful heir, sidelined, watching, embittered, half-convinced his mother had murdered his father and stolen his crown, and increasingly erratic.
When he finally became emperor at forty-two, he ruled like a man settling scores, which he largely was.
Paul reigned only five years (1796–1801) and his reign is genuinely contradictory, which is why "the mad tsar" is a label to handle with care rather than repeat.

He did one thing of permanent, stabilizing importance: in 1797 he issued the Pauline Law of Succession, which finally abolished Peter the Great's disastrous 1722 rule (the one that let an emperor name any heir and that had produced seventy years of palace coups).
In its place Paul fixed a strict, automatic order of succession by male primogeniture.
After 1797 there were no more disputed successions and no more Guards-made emperors; every ruler from Alexander I to Nicholas II followed automatically by the rule.

It is one of the most consequential pieces of constitutional engineering in the book, and it is genuinely odd that the man usually written off as a lunatic is the one who finally solved the dynasty's single most destabilizing flaw, partly out of personal grievance at how the lack of a rule had let his mother do what she did to him.

Paul also tried to relieve some of the worst pressure on the serfs (a 1797 decree recommended limiting forced labor to three days a week, the first time the state ever tried to put any ceiling at all on a lord's demands, though it was advisory and largely ignored), curbed some noble privileges, and tried to impose Prussian-style discipline and order on a court he found corrupt and disrespectful.
But he did it with an arbitrary, paranoid harshness that made him enemies everywhere he had power, which was everywhere.

He persecuted the nobility he distrusted, reversed his mother's policies seemingly to spite her memory, banned French books and fashions to keep out revolutionary contagion, and lurched in foreign policy.

He sent the great Suvorov (Chapter 8) on a brilliant, brutal campaign through Italy and across the Alps against Revolutionary France in 1799, then abruptly switched course, reconciled with Napoleon, broke with Britain, and in his last months ordered a Cossack army to set off across the steppe toward British India, thousands of miles of unmapped desert, mountain, and hostile khanates with no supply line, roads, or accurate maps, a scheme so unworkable it was abandoned the moment he was dead and that confirmed for the elite that the emperor's judgment had failed.

He had also alienated, specifically, the officers of the Guards and the St Petersburg nobility, the exact constituency that had made and unmade every ruler of the eighteenth century, by humiliating and threatening them.
They reverted to type one last time.

In March 1801, a conspiracy of senior officers and officials broke into Paul's bedroom in the newly built, fortress-like Mikhailovsky Castle he had built specifically because he feared assassination, and killed him (officially "apoplexy"; in fact strangled and beaten).
The assassination of Paul I is the last successful palace coup in Russian history, the Pauline succession law it followed having made future ones pointless.

Its darkest feature is the part that shadows the next chapter: Paul's son and heir, Alexander, was in the palace that night, knew of the conspiracy, and had given a conditional blessing to his father's removal on the explicit understanding (the conspirators' assurance, which he chose to believe) that Paul would only be forced to abdicate, not killed.
When he was told his father was dead, Alexander, by the consistent testimony of those around him, collapsed in a guilt that shadowed him for the rest of his life.
The new emperor of Russia began his reign as a probable, if unintending, accomplice to his father's murder.
Keep that, because it explains a great deal about the strange, haunted man who is about to beat Napoleon.

Alexander I (the first emperor of that name, grandson of Catherine the Great, son of the murdered Paul, ruled 1801–1825) is one of the most enigmatic figures in this book, and contemporaries already called him that; the poet Pushkin would later nail him in a phrase as a "weak and wily ruler," and his own friends despaired of ever knowing what he actually believed.

He came to the throne at twenty-three, raised by tutors Catherine had chosen, soaked in Enlightenment ideals by Frédéric-César de La Harpe, the Swiss republican Catherine had hired (she wanted her grandson fashionably educated, not guessing how fully the tutor would take, instructing the future autocrat for over a decade in natural rights, the rule of law, and the wrongness of slavery), and he opened his reign as the great hope of liberal Russia.

He gathered a circle of young, reform-minded friends (the "Unofficial Committee") and seriously discussed, in private, things no Russian ruler had let himself discuss in public: a constitution, the rule of law, the eventual ending of serfdom.
He relaxed his father's repression, reopened the borders to books and travel, founded new universities, and reorganized the central government into modern ministries.
For a few years it genuinely looked as though the most powerful autocrat in Europe might voluntarily limit his own autocracy.
The man who turned that hope into actual blueprints was Mikhail Speransky (spe-RAN-skee), and he is the chapter's tragic protagonist because he is the empire's recurring lost chance personified.

Speransky was not a noble; he was a village priest's son who rose by sheer administrative genius, exactly the kind of talent Peter's service ladder was supposed to surface, and Alexander made him his chief adviser.

Between 1808 and 1812 Speransky drafted a comprehensive plan to convert Russia, gradually and from the top, into something like a law-governed constitutional monarchy: an elected hierarchy of assemblies rising to a national legislative body, a separation of administrative, judicial, and legislative functions, civil rights graded by property, the autocracy retained but bound by law.
It was cautious, it kept the emperor strong, and it would still have been the single largest constitutional reform in Russian history.
Almost none of it was enacted.
What survived was one institution, the State Council (established 1810), an appointed advisory body for reviewing legislation, useful but a shadow of the plan.

The rest died of the same disease that killed Catherine's Legislative Commission: the nobility hated it, regarded Speransky as a low-born upstart dismantling their world, and the international situation (the looming war with Napoleon) gave Alexander every excuse to set reform aside for safety.
In 1812, on the eve of the invasion, Alexander sacrificed Speransky to noble pressure and to whispers (probably false) that he was a French sympathizer, and exiled him.

The pattern from Chapter 6 repeats exactly: the reform was drafted, the autocrat half-believed in it, the load-bearing wall of the regime (the serf-owning nobility and the autocracy's own survival instinct) stopped it, and the moment passed.

By 1812 Russia had a hauntingly guilty emperor, a shelved constitution, an exiled reformer, and 23 million serfs, and Napoleon Bonaparte, master of Europe, was massing the largest army the world had ever seen on its western border.
A word on how that border had moved, because it sets up the trap that destroys Napoleon.
Alexander's first decade was a string of wars.

He fought Napoleon in alliance with Austria and was beaten badly alongside the Austrians at Austerlitz in 1805 (the battle Napoleon rated his own masterpiece, and a disaster for the Russian army), and then, fighting on after Austria dropped out, was beaten again at Friedland in 1807.
That second defeat forced the Treaty of Tilsit (1807).

Its setting was pure theater and a humiliation dressed as a courtesy: a raft was moored in the middle of the Niemen river, the border, and the two emperors met on it alone, Napoleon the master of Europe and Alexander the defeated party pretending to negotiate as an equal.

On that raft Alexander, having no real choice, became Napoleon's reluctant ally and agreed to join the Continental System, Napoleon's economic blockade of Britain, a concession that wrecked Russian trade and that Alexander spent the next five years looking for a way out of, which is one of the roads to 1812.
The alliance was hollow from the first day; the blockade wrecked Russian trade, neither emperor trusted the other, and both prepared for the war they knew was coming.

In the breathing space, Alexander expanded: a war with Sweden (1808–1809) took Finland, which became an autonomous Grand Duchy under the tsar, keeping its own laws, Lutheran church, and assembly (Alexander could afford generosity to a small, quiet, strategically loyal Finland in a way he never could to a large, proud, rebellious Poland that sat astride the road to the heart of the empire, which is why the two conquests were treated so differently); the arrangement, for a century, made Finland the freest corner of the empire and, eventually, a refuge for revolutionaries; a war with the Ottomans took Bessarabia (modern Moldova) in 1812; a long war with Persia, beginning in 1804, pushed Russian power into the Caucasus toward the mountain war that Chapter 17 covers.

The empire kept getting bigger right up to the moment of maximum internal failure: a guilt-ridden emperor who had let his reformer be driven out, a constitution drafted and shelved, and 23 million people still owned, the chapter's real verdict, all of it sealed in 1812.

And then, in June of that year, the largest invasion army in the history of the world to that point crossed the Niemen heading east, and the empire's size stopped being a problem to be governed and became, for the first time, a weapon.

In June 1812, Napoleon Bonaparte crossed the Niemen river into the Russian Empire with the largest army Europe had ever assembled, somewhere on the order of 600,000 men drawn from France and the entire continent it controlled, the Grande Armée. (The exact figure is debated and the round numbers should be held loosely, but the order of magnitude, the better part of two thirds of a million men, is solid.) Five and a half months later, a starving, frozen remnant variously estimated in the low tens of thousands recrossed the same river going the other way.

The destruction of the Grande Armée in Russia is one of the largest military catastrophes in recorded history, the event that broke Napoleon and made Russia, for the next forty years, the dominant land power of Europe.

It is also the most mythologized episode in this entire book, retold by Tolstoy in the greatest novel ever written about war, scored by Tchaikovsky with actual cannon, and turned by Russian memory into a sacred national epic, the "Patriotic War." So this chapter does two jobs: it tells you what happened, and it keeps flagging which famous parts are solid and which are the legend doing its work.
First, what Napoleon wanted and why it was a trap.
Napoleon did not primarily want to conquer and hold Russia; that was logistically impossible and he knew it.
He wanted to force Alexander I, by a fast, crushing battlefield victory near the border, to come back to heel and re-enter the Continental System.
His entire method, perfected across a decade of European wars, depended on bringing the enemy's main army to a decisive battle quickly and destroying it.

The Russian commanders, above all Barclay de Tolly, the cool, methodical war minister of Scottish émigré descent who commanded the main army at the start, did the one thing that defeated that method: they refused the decisive battle and retreated, deeper and deeper into the enormous country, trading the empire's vast space (Chapter 1's central problem) for time, and burning supplies behind them so the invader's enormous army could not feed itself off the land.
This was the same strategy that beat Charles XII of Sweden at the end of the road to Poltava a century earlier (Chapter 3), and it is no accident; the Russian command knew that history.
It was also wildly unpopular at the time.

To ordinary Russians and much of the army, retreating without fighting while the enemy burned his way toward Moscow looked like cowardice or treason, and the pressure to stand and fight became politically irresistible.
Alexander replaced Barclay with a commander the army and the public trusted viscerally: the old, one-eyed, shrewd, fatalistic Mikhail Kutuzov (koo-TOO-zoff), a veteran of Suvorov's wars.
Kutuzov privately understood the retreat was working and would have happily continued it.
He could not.
He had to give Russia its battle.
He gave it at Borodino (bor-oh-dee-NOH), a village about 70 miles (110 km) west of Moscow, on 7 September 1812.

Borodino is one of the bloodiest single days of combat in history before the twentieth century: roughly a quarter of a million men engaged, and casualty estimates commonly put the combined dead and wounded at around 70,000 to 75,000 in one day, though every specific number from that day is contested and the higher figures should be treated as estimates, not measurements.

The outcome was tactically a draw bleeding toward a French victory: by nightfall the Russians had been pushed back and Kutuzov, to preserve his army from annihilation, withdrew, leaving the road to Moscow open.
Napoleon held the field, which by the conventions of the age made it his victory, and it did him no good at all, which is the entire point and the deepest lesson of the campaign.
The Russian army was battered but not destroyed; it withdrew intact and dangerous.

Napoleon had won the kind of battle that always before had ended a war, and the war did not end, because the Russian state did not collapse and the Russian army did not surrender, and he was now eight hundred miles from home with winter coming.

Kutuzov then made the decision that defines him and horrified contemporaries: at a council of war at the village of Fili, he chose to abandon Moscow without further fighting, reportedly with words to the effect that the loss of Moscow was not the loss of Russia but the loss of the army would be. (The famous council and the sentiment are well attested; the exact wording, like most famous lines in this book, has been smoothed by retelling.) In mid-September Napoleon entered Moscow, the old capital and the symbolic heart of the country, expecting that taking it would force Alexander to negotiate.
He found a city largely emptied of its people.
And then Moscow burned.
The burning of Moscow, which destroyed perhaps two thirds of the city over several days, is one of the genuinely unresolved questions of the campaign and a perfect case study in why this book hedges.

Three explanations have been argued for two centuries: a deliberate Russian scorched-earth policy, most likely ordered or enabled by the city's governor Rostopchin who had removed the fire-fighting equipment; accidental fires spread by chaos, looting, and a wooden city; and French negligence.

The honest current position is that a deliberate Russian element is widely accepted as at least a major cause, that Rostopchin's role is probable, that he himself gave contradictory accounts over his life, and that a single clean answer is not available.
What is not in doubt is the strategic effect: Napoleon sat in the ashes of Moscow for five weeks, sending peace feelers that Alexander, stiffened now into total refusal, simply ignored.
There was no one to negotiate with and nothing to hold.
In mid-October, with winter closing and his army unsupplied in a burned city, Napoleon began the retreat.
The retreat is where the catastrophe actually happened, and where the legend most needs checking.
The popular memory, the one Tchaikovsky scored, is "General Winter": the idea that the Russian cold, almost supernaturally, destroyed the Grande Armée.
The truth is more brutal and more to this book's point.
The army was already gutted before the hard frosts came, by the thing this narrative keeps returning to: distance.

Hunger, disease (typhus above all), exhaustion, the disintegration of supply across hundreds of miles of devastated country, and the relentless harassment of Cossacks and armed peasants on the flanks had wrecked it through the warm autumn weeks.
Then the cold arrived and finished what the space had started, and it did so with a horror that is not exaggerated.
The nadir was the crossing of the Berezina (be-re-ZEE-nah) river in late November.

With Russian armies converging and the bridges destroyed, the army's combat engineers, the pontonniers, waded into the ice-choked river and built two trestle bridges by hand, working in water that killed many of them within days, and the army crossed under attack in a multi-day chaos of drowning, trampling, and slaughter that left tens of thousands dead and made "Berezina" a synonym for catastrophe in French to this day.
By the time the survivors recrossed the Niemen in December, the Grande Armée as a fighting force had ceased to exist.

The space had eaten it, exactly as it had eaten Charles XII, exactly as the empire's planners had always feared the space would eat them; for once the impossible size of Russia was the empire's weapon instead of its burden.
Russia did not stop at its own border, and this is the strategic hinge for the next two chapters.
Alexander I, against Kutuzov's instinct (Kutuzov wanted to let Napoleon limp home and not bleed Russia further to liberate Germany), chose to pursue the war into Europe.
The campaign of 1813–1814 turned the Patriotic War into the War of the Sixth Coalition: Russia, now joined by a recovering Prussia, Austria, and Britain, pushed west across Germany.

The decisive blow fell at the Battle of Leipzig in October 1813, the "Battle of the Nations," the largest battle in European history before the First World War, where the allied armies decisively beat Napoleon and broke his hold on Germany.

In March 1814 the allied armies entered Paris, and Alexander I of Russia, the haunted son of a murdered father who had begun his reign dreaming of constitutions, rode through the streets of the French capital as the most powerful monarch in the world and the principal author of Napoleon's downfall.
Napoleon abdicated and was exiled (he would return for the brief, final act that ends at Waterloo in 1815, but the Russian campaign is what actually broke him).
For Russia the meaning was immense and double-edged in exactly this book's way.
The empire had achieved the absolute summit of its grandeur.
It had destroyed the man who conquered Europe and now stood as the continent's arbiter, its army the most respected on earth, its emperor the figure everyone in Europe waited on.

And it had done it without changing a single thing about itself internally: the serf who had marched to Paris and seen, with his own eyes, a Europe without serfdom, came home in 1815 to a village where he was still owned.
Some of those soldiers, and some of the young officers who led them, brought the contradiction back across the border with them and could not put it down.
The summit of the grandeur and the lighting of the long fuse are about to happen in the same ten years, and they are the same story.
That is Chapter 11.

chapters.title: Gendarme of Europe
sentences: For ten years after 1815, Russia was the most powerful state in the world, and it used that power, almost entirely, to prevent change anywhere.

This chapter is short by the standards of this book because its content is essentially one argument with one demonstration, and the demonstration is the most important single morning in the whole narrative: 14 December 1825, the day the long fuse was lit in public.
But you need the decade of reaction first, because the Decembrists are its product.

At the Congress of Vienna (1814–1815), the conference where the victorious monarchies redrew the map of Europe after Napoleon, Alexander I of Russia (Chapter 10's victor, now Europe's arbiter) was the dominant figure.
Russia's main territorial gain was the bulk of what had been Poland, reconstituted as the Kingdom of Poland, usually called Congress Poland, in personal union with the Russian crown.

In a move that captures Alexander's lifelong contradiction perfectly, he granted Congress Poland a written constitution, an elected parliament (the Sejm), and civil liberties considerably more generous than anything in Russia itself, so that the autocrat of an empire with no constitution was simultaneously a constitutional monarch in his Polish province.
It pleased almost no one and it set up the explosion of 1830 (Chapter 12).
Alexander's deeper project at Vienna was ideological.

Increasingly mystical and conservative in his later years, he proposed the Holy Alliance, a treaty signed by the rulers of Russia, Austria, and Prussia pledging to govern as Christian brothers on Christian principles.
In its plain words it was a vague piece of religiose idealism that the hard-headed Austrian statesman Metternich privately mocked.

In its effect it became the ideological flag of the post-1815 order: the principle that monarchy was divinely sanctioned, that revolution and liberalism were sins to be suppressed wherever they appeared, and that the great powers had a right and duty to intervene across borders to crush them.

Russia, the strongest land power on earth, became the muscle behind that principle, the gendarme of Europe (a gendarme is an armed state policeman; the phrase, used at the time and after, casts Russia as the continent's cop).

For the next forty years, through Alexander and especially through his brother Nicholas, Russia's role in European affairs was to be the great immovable conservative weight, the army that could be marched to put down a revolution, and it did exactly that, most starkly in Hungary in 1849.

The empire that had liberated Europe from Napoleon spent the next generation as the chief jailer of European liberty, which is the foreign-policy face of the grandeur-and-unfreedom thesis: Russia could project colossal power, and the only thing it knew how to use that power for was to keep things from changing, including at home.
At home the reaction had a specifically grotesque institution: the military colonies.

This was the scheme of Alexander's late-reign favorite, the brutal artillery officer Count Arakcheyev (ah-rak-CHEH-yeff), whose name became a Russian byword for mindless harsh discipline (Arakcheyevshchina).

To make the huge standing army cheaper, whole districts of state peasants were converted into permanent military settlements where peasant families lived under total military regimentation: their farming, their dress, their houses, their daily routine, even marriage, ordered by army regulation, the men soldiers and farmers at once, the children raised to the regiment.

It was an attempt to turn a chunk of the peasantry into a self-funding army by abolishing the boundary between the village and the barracks entirely, and it was so hated that it produced brutal revolts. the military colonies are worth a paragraph because they are the regime's instinct in its purest form: faced with the cost of the grandeur (a vast army), the solution was not reform or representation but a deeper, more total regimentation of the unfree.

It is the thesis rendered as a settlement plan. (One bright thread crosses this dark decade and deserves its sentence, because the empire's grandeur was never only military: in 1820 a Russian naval expedition under the Baltic German officer Bellingshausen, sent out under Alexander I, made what many specialists rank as the first confirmed sighting of the continent of Antarctica, days ahead of a British and an American claimant in a priority dispute that has never been fully settled, an achievement of the same expansionist energy that drove the empire across Siberia, here pointed at the bottom of the world.) Now the morning.

Alexander I died suddenly in November 1825 in the southern town of Taganrog, far from the capital, of an illness (the abruptness and the remoteness later spawned a durable Russian legend that he had not really died but secretly retired to live as a Siberian holy man called Fyodor Kuzmich; this is folklore, with no reliable evidence, included here only as a classic example of the Russian "the true ruler did not really die" myth this book has flagged before, the same template that produced Pugachev's false Peter III).

His death produced a brief, bizarre succession crisis even under the Pauline law, because the next brother, Constantine, had secretly renounced his rights, and the throne therefore fell to the third brother, Nicholas, but the secrecy meant that for three weeks in December 1825 it was genuinely unclear in the capital who the emperor was, and the army had been sworn to Constantine before being told to re-swear to Nicholas.
Into that three-week gap stepped the men this whole book has been walking toward.
They are called the Decembrists, after the month.
They were not peasants and not professional revolutionaries.

They were aristocratic army officers, many of them the very men who had marched to Paris in 1814, members of the Guards regiments and the cream of the service nobility, who had spent the years since 1815 in secret discussion societies (the Union of Salvation, the Union of Welfare, the Northern and Southern Societies) reading the European liberalism their own emperor was suppressing and arguing about how to give Russia a constitution and end serfdom.

They are the precise human form of Chapter 10's closing image: the educated Russian who had seen, with his own eyes, a Europe without serfdom and an emperor bound by law, and could not come home and un-see it.
They were also not an isolated Russian eccentricity.

The early 1820s were a continent-wide wave of liberal revolt against exactly the restored order Russia was policing: the secret Carbonari societies rose in Naples and Piedmont in 1820–1821, a constitutional revolt broke out in Spain in 1820, the Greeks rose against the Ottomans in 1821.
The Decembrist officers read the same European liberal literature and knew of these movements; 1825 was the Russian beat of that drum.

The grim symmetry is that the same Russia whose officers were trying to import a constitution was, as a state, the muscle suppressing constitutions everywhere else, and would march an army to crush the next European revolutionary wave outright when Hungary rose in 1849.

Their plans were various and not fully agreed (a constitutional monarchy in the northern group's program, a radical republic with land reform in the southern leader Pestel's), but the core was constant: limit or end the autocracy, and free the serfs.
The confused succession of December 1825 handed them an opening they were not really ready for, and they took it anyway.

On 14 December 1825, the day the Guards regiments in St Petersburg were to swear allegiance to Nicholas I, a few thousand soldiers led by the conspiring officers refused the oath and assembled under arms in the Senate Square, demanding "Constantine and Constitution" (a slogan many of the rank-and-file soldiers reportedly only half-understood, some apparently told that "Constitution" was Constantine's wife, a detail that is probably partly legend but captures the gulf between the educated conspirators and the men they led, a gulf that recurs for the rest of this book).
The Decembrist revolt failed in a single afternoon.

The leaders hesitated, the planned coordination collapsed, the chosen "dictator" of the rising never showed up, and Nicholas I, on his first day as emperor, after some hesitation, ordered loyal artillery to fire grapeshot into the square.
The rebels were scattered and killed in some number; the revolt in the south was put down within weeks.
Nicholas personally involved himself in the investigation and interrogation of the prisoners.

Five of the ringleaders were hanged, among them the southern radical Pavel Pestel, who had drafted the most far-reaching republican program, and the poet Kondraty Ryleyev (a botched, horrific execution in which several ropes broke and the men had to be hanged a second time, one of them reportedly saying that in Russia they could not even do this properly, a line that is widely repeated and impossible to fully verify but has become emblematic).

Over a hundred more were stripped of rank and exiled to hard labor and settlement in Siberia, where many spent decades, followed in a famous and genuinely documented gesture by a number of their wives who voluntarily gave up their titles and went into Siberian exile with them, an act that became a permanent moral touchstone in Russian culture.
Here is why this short chapter is one of the load-bearing chapters of the entire book.
The Decembrist revolt failed completely, militarily and politically, in an afternoon.
It changed nothing in 1825.

And it changed everything afterward, because it was the first time the grandeur and the unfreedom were brought into open, armed collision by the empire's own elite, in the open, in the capital, and the regime's answer was grapeshot and the gallows.

Before December 1825 the case against the system had been a private book burned by Catherine (Radishchev, Chapter 7), a shelved plan by an exiled adviser (Speransky, Chapter 9), a conversation among the emperor's young friends.

After December 1825 it was a martyrdom, a heritage, and a permanent question that no Russian of conscience could stop asking, passed down deliberately as a torch: from the Decembrists to the writers of Chapter 12, to the radicals of Chapter 15, to the revolutionaries of Chapter 18, to the men who finally finished the empire in Chapter 20.
This is the moment the fuse is lit.
Everything after this is the fuse burning, and the next emperor's entire thirty-year reign is one long, increasingly desperate attempt to stamp it out.

chapters.title: Official Nationality
sentences: Nicholas I (the first emperor of that name, third son of Paul I, younger brother of Alexander I, ruled 1825–1855) became tsar on the morning he ordered grapeshot fired into the Decembrists in Senate Square, and that fact organized the next thirty years of Russian history.
Every other ruler in this book before him came to the throne by inheritance or coup and then decided what kind of ruler to be.
Nicholas decided in his first hours, under fire, and never wavered: his life's work would be to make sure that 14 December 1825 never happened again.
He was hard-working, personally austere, militarily obsessed, sincerely convinced that autocracy was a sacred trust and that any concession to it was the first crack in a dam holding back chaos.

He is the purest expression of the regime's central choice in this entire book: offered, at the start of his reign, the clearest possible warning that the system needed to change, he concluded instead that it needed to be defended harder, and he spent thirty years and the whole machinery of the state proving the point.

Russians and historians have called his reign the "apogee of autocracy." It is also, not coincidentally, the reign in which the Russian intelligentsia, the class of people who would eventually destroy the autocracy, is born.
The regime got an official ideology, the first time Russian autocracy explicitly stated a doctrine rather than just assuming one.
Nicholas's education minister, Sergei Uvarov, formulated it in 1833 as a triad: Orthodoxy, Autocracy, Nationality (Pravoslavie, Samoderzhavie, Narodnost).
This is the doctrine of Official Nationality, and it is worth unpacking because it is the regime's own statement of the thesis of this book, from the regime's side.
Orthodoxy: the state church as the moral foundation of Russian life.
Autocracy: the unlimited tsar as the only possible government for Russia, divinely sanctioned, the antithesis of Western constitutions.

Nationality (narodnost, hard to translate, roughly "national character" or "the people-ness"): the claim that the Russian people were uniquely, organically devoted to the first two, that the bond between the loving tsar-father and his trusting people was the special genius of Russia and had no need of the legalistic, contractual, revolutionary apparatus of the West.

Official Nationality was, in effect, a sophisticated argument that the grandeur and the unfreedom were not a contradiction at all but a harmony, that Russia's strength came precisely from not having what Europe had.

It is the most coherent intellectual defense the autocracy ever produced of itself, and the entire history of the next eighty years is the slow, grinding refutation of it, starting with the Crimean War in the very next chapter.
To enforce it, Nicholas built the machinery the regime would use, in various forms, until 1917.

He created the Third Section of the Imperial Chancery, the empire's first true centralized political police: a secret-police bureau, backed by a uniformed Corps of Gendarmes, charged with surveillance of opinion, censorship enforcement, monitoring of suspect persons, and the management of dissent. the Third Section is the direct institutional ancestor of the later Okhrana (Chapter 18) and, beyond this book, of the Soviet security organs; the Russian habit of a powerful secret state agency watching the population, traceable back to Peter's fiskaly (Chapter 4), here becomes a permanent, professional fixture.
Censorship became pervasive and capricious, administered by an "censorship terror" of overlapping agencies.

He codified the empire's tangled laws into the great Digest of Laws (the actual monumental work was done by Speransky, the reformer Alexander I had exiled in 1812, Chapter 9, now brought back from disgrace by Nicholas to organize the autocracy rather than to limit it, the one piece of his life's project that was ever realized), which imposed order but pointedly did not include a constitution; it organized the autocracy, it did not limit it.
And he confronted the empire's largest concentrated grievance head-on.
When the news of the 1830 revolutions in France and Belgium reached Congress Poland (Chapter 11), the Poles rose in the November Uprising of 1830–1831, a full-scale national war.

Nicholas crushed it militarily, then abolished the Polish constitution his brother had granted, dissolved the Polish army and Sejm, closed Polish universities, and ruled Poland thereafter as occupied territory.
The "Polish question" did not go away; it went underground and detonated again in 1863 (Chapter 14).
The pattern is the chapter's pattern: a demand for liberty answered with force and the removal of what limited liberties existed.
And here is the paradox that makes this reign the hinge of the book's cultural argument.

The most repressive reign of the nineteenth century is also the foundational age of Russian literature, the moment Russia goes from having essentially no world-class literature of its own to producing, within two generations, the greatest novels ever written.
This is not a coincidence and it is not in spite of the repression.
It is, in a specific and demonstrable way, because of it.

When every other avenue of public life, no parliament, no free press, no legal politics, no independent associations, is closed by the state, the only place a thinking Russian can examine the moral condition of the country is in literature and the "thick journals" that printed it, read between the lines past the censor.

The dynamic is not uniquely Russian (the French Revolutionary Terror, hunting its own thinkers, drove Condorcet to write his great treatise on human progress while in hiding from the guillotine, in the Enlightenment narrative); repression has a way of displacing thought rather than ending it.
But Russia ran the experiment at a scale and for a duration that made the displaced thought into a national literature.

Literature in Nicholas's Russia became the substitute for the politics the regime forbade, and Russian writers became, by default, the conscience and the opposition the country was not allowed to have any other way.

The class this produced got a name, the intelligentsia (a Russian coinage, roughly "the thinking, educated, morally engaged class"), and it is one of the most consequential social formations in modern history, the carrier of the Decembrist torch (Chapter 11) for the rest of this book.
The titans arrive in this reign.

Alexander Pushkin (POOSH-kin, 1799–1837) is the one Russians put above all the others, the writer who effectively created the modern Russian literary language and is to Russia roughly what Shakespeare is to England, an analogy Russians use themselves.
His verse novel Eugene Onegin, his historical drama, his lyric poetry, set the standard for everything after.

He had a glancing, dangerous relationship with the regime (some early liberal verse, friends among the Decembrists, personal censorship by Nicholas himself, who appointed himself Pushkin's personal censor in a gesture that was equal parts patronage and surveillance).

He died in 1837 at thirty-seven, of wounds from a duel defending his wife's honor against a French officer, a death the whole of literate Russia experienced as a national catastrophe and that many believed, then and since, the court establishment had at minimum done nothing to prevent.

The young officer-poet Mikhail Lermontov wrote a furious poem blaming high society for Pushkin's death, was promptly arrested and exiled to the Caucasus for it, wrote the first great Russian psychological novel there, and was himself killed in a duel in 1841 at twenty-six.
Two of Russia's greatest poets, dead in duels four years apart, both in their twenties or thirties, both having tangled with the regime, is itself a kind of statement about the era.

And Nikolai Gogol wrote, under this same censorship, Dead Souls (a comic-grotesque novel whose plot, a swindler buying up the legal title to dead serfs who are still on the tax rolls, is the most devastating possible satire of a society that literally counts and trades human beings, and which got past the censor partly because it was funny) and The Government Inspector, a play about provincial corruption that Nicholas I himself reportedly attended and laughed at, apparently missing that the joke was the regime.
The intelligentsia did not stay literary; it began to argue about Russia itself, and the argument it started in Nicholas's reign is still, in some form, going on.
The thinking class split into two camps.

The Westernizers held that Russia was a backward European country whose only hope was to catch up with the West: adopt its science, its law, its eventual liberty, complete the project Peter the Great had begun.

The Slavophiles held the opposite: that Peter's Westernization had been a wound, that Russia had a unique spiritual destiny rooted in Orthodoxy and the peasant commune and the organic bond between tsar and people, and that salvation lay not in copying Europe but in recovering an authentic Russian path. (Note how close the Slavophile position sits to Official Nationality, and how The Slavophiles nonetheless ended up censored too, because even loyal independent thought was suspect; that is how total the closure was.) The Slavophiles versus Westernizers debate is the master template of Russian intellectual life from then on; almost every later movement in this book, the Narodniks, the Marxists, the liberals, even the revolutionaries, is a descendant of one side or the other, and the question they were really arguing, is Russia's salvation to become Europe or to become more itself, is the same question the empire dies without answering in Chapter 20.
The regime watched all of this with mounting suspicion and a heavy hand, and one episode shows exactly how heavy.

In 1849 the Third Section arrested the members of the Petrashevsky Circle, the discussion group that gathered at the apartment of Mikhail Petrashevsky, a minor foreign-ministry official and Fourierist utopian socialist, whose actual crime was meeting to read and debate banned Western socialist writings, talk, essentially.

Twenty-one of them, including a twenty-eight-year-old writer named Fyodor Dostoevsky, were sentenced to death and taken to a public square, where, in front of the firing squad, in the last seconds, a courier galloped up with a pre-arranged imperial "pardon" commuting the sentence to Siberian hard labor.
The mock execution was theater, deliberate psychological terror staged by the state.
Dostoevsky did four years in a Siberian prison camp and several more as a soldier; the experience reshaped him and, through him, world literature (Chapter 16).
The Petrashevsky affair is the perfect closing image for this reign: men arrested for reading the wrong books, marched to a fake execution to teach the country a lesson about the price of thought.
Nicholas I had built, by 1849, the most thoroughly controlled state in Europe, an apparatus that could reach into a discussion circle and stage a man's death to frighten him.
It looked, from the inside, like total success.

Within four years it would be exposed, by a war the regime started confident of victory, as a rotten and backward shell, and Nicholas I would die a broken man, possibly by his own hand, while his army was being beaten on his own soil.
That is the next chapter, and it is the chapter where the thesis stops being an argument and becomes a body count.

chapters.title: The War That Told the Truth
