sentences: The Crimean War (1853–1856) is the shortest era this book gives a whole chapter to, and it gets one because it is the moment the entire argument of the book stops being something a reader has to take on the narrator's word and becomes something the Russian state itself could no longer deny.

For forty years, since 1815, Russia had been the gendarme of Europe, the strongest land power on earth, the showcase of Official Nationality, the proof (the regime believed) that autocracy and unfreedom produced strength, not weakness.
The Crimean War was the experiment that tested that claim against reality, and the claim failed, in public, on Russian soil, in front of the whole world.

Everything in the second half of this book, the Emancipation, the Great Reforms, the revolutionaries, the desperate late-imperial scramble to industrialize, flows from the wound this war opened, because it was the war that told Russia the truth about itself.
The causes are tangled and this book will keep them brief, because the diplomatic detail matters less than the result.

The proximate trigger was a quarrel over which Christians, Orthodox (backed by Russia) or Catholic (backed by France), had custody of the holy sites in Ottoman-ruled Jerusalem and Bethlehem, a dispute Nicholas I inflated, on the strength of Russia's old claim to protect Orthodox Christians in the Ottoman Empire (the lever from the 1774 Treaty of Kuchuk-Kainarji, Chapter 8), into a confrontation with the weakening Ottoman Empire that he expected to be a short, victorious Russian advance.
Nicholas badly misjudged two things.

He misjudged that Britain and France, despite being rivals with each other, would not tolerate Russia dismembering the Ottoman Empire and dominating the eastern Mediterranean and the route to British India, and he misjudged that Austria, whose 1849 revolution Russia had marched in and crushed for it, would repay the favor; instead Austria stayed hostile-neutral, which left Russia diplomatically isolated, the gendarme of Europe with no friends in Europe.
What had looked like a quick chastisement of the Turks became Russia, alone, at war with the Ottoman Empire, Britain, France, and eventually the Italian kingdom of Sardinia.
There is a sharp irony in the matchup that the Ottoman narrative draws out from its side.

The nineteenth century's two great "sick" empires, the one Nicholas I himself had reportedly called the "sick man of Europe" and his own, fought this war on opposite sides, and both came out of it having learned the same lesson: that their survival now depended less on their own strength than on the patronage of the industrial powers of western Europe.
Russia was about to discover from the losing side what the Ottomans already knew from long experience.

The fighting that mattered came to the Crimean Peninsula, Russia's own territory, the warm-water prize Catherine had annexed in 1783 (Chapter 8), where the British and French landed an expeditionary force in 1854 to take the great naval base of Sevastopol (se-VAS-toh-pol), home of the Black Sea Fleet.
The siege of Sevastopol lasted almost a year, from late 1854 to September 1855, and it is the heart of the war and of this chapter.

The Russian defense was, at the level of individual courage, magnificent; the city held for eleven months against the combined might of the leading industrial powers of the age, and the defenders, soldiers, sailors, and the Russian surgeon Nikolai Pirogov, the founder of field surgery in Russia, pioneering battlefield triage and the first large-scale use of ether anesthesia under fire, became a permanent Russian legend of endurance.

One of the junior artillery officers in the defense was a young count named Leo Tolstoy, who turned what he saw into the Sevastopol Sketches, a piece of unsparing war reporting that made his name and that no censor seems to have fully grasped was an indictment (Chapter 16).
The heroism was real.
The system behind it was the point, and the system lost.
Here is the mechanism of the defeat, and it is the thesis made physical.

Russia was fighting on its own soil, far closer to its own heartland than its enemies were to theirs, and it still could not adequately supply or reinforce its own army, while Britain and France could project and sustain power across the entire length of Europe and the Mediterranean.
Because the things that win industrial wars were exactly the things autocratic, serf-based, agrarian Russia had refused to grow while it was busy being the gendarme of Europe.

The British and French armies were moved and supplied substantially by railway and steamship; Russia had almost no railways (a single line between the two capitals, finished only in 1851, and essentially nothing reaching the south), so Russian troops and supplies moved to Crimea by ox-cart over dirt roads, taking longer to travel within their own country than the enemy took to cross a continent and a sea.
This was not ignorance of what railways could do.

Germany, Belgium, and France had been building state-backed railway networks since the 1830s, and the military value of rail had already been demonstrated in the Austrian and Prussian mobilizations of 1848–1849, which Russian officers had watched closely.

Russia was not vaguely behind "the West"; it was specifically behind the industrial-policy states it had spent two decades observing modernize, held back not by lack of knowledge but by the same autocratic-fiscal paralysis this whole book has been describing.
Russian soldiers carried smoothbore muskets against British and French rifled weapons with several times the effective range.
Russian industry could not produce munitions, equipment, or modern arms at anything like the rate of the industrialized West.
The Russian financial and administrative system, built for autocratic control rather than mobilization, could not raise or spend money at the necessary scale without wrecking the currency.
The serf army was huge and brave and led, with exceptions, by a promotion system that rewarded loyalty and connection over competence.

Every one of these failures traces directly back to a choice the regime had made, over and over, across this whole book: the choice of autocratic and social control over the modernization that would have threatened it.
Official Nationality had said Russia was strong because it had not become Europe.
Sevastopol said Russia was being beaten, on Russian ground, because it had not become Europe.
The war was the audit, and the books did not balance.
Sevastopol fell in September 1855.
Nicholas I did not live to see it.

He died in February 1855, in the middle of the war he had started, of pneumonia, a broken man who knew his life's certainty had failed; there is a persistent contemporary rumor, never proven and rejected by most historians, that the proud emperor, unable to bear the humiliation, ordered his doctor to give him poison.

The rumor persists not on evidence but on its narrative perfection, the man who had staked everything on the doctrine of strength choosing not to outlive its public refutation, which is exactly why this book flags it as the kind of too-shapely deathbed claim it has taught the reader to distrust.
What is not in dispute is that he died a broken man, watching the visible collapse of everything he had built his reign on, even his defenders concede that much.
He was succeeded by his son, Alexander II (not to be confused with Alexander I, the victor over Napoleon and his great-uncle), who inherited a losing war and the necessity of ending it.

The Treaty of Paris (1856) was a humiliation calibrated precisely to wound: Russia lost its right to keep a navy or fortifications on the Black Sea, the warm-water foothold itself neutralized, and the gendarme of Europe was publicly demoted in front of the continent it had policed for forty years.
This chapter is short because its meaning is single and overwhelming.

The Crimean War killed something more important than the roughly half a million men (the figure is an estimate; disease, not combat, killed most of them on every side, and Russia, defending on its own ground with the worst supply, is generally reckoned to have lost the most, on the order of a quarter to a third of a million, more than the British and French combined) who died in it.
It killed the regime's central belief about itself.

For the educated Russian, for the new emperor, for the intelligentsia, even for many conservatives, the war proved, with the unanswerable evidence of defeat on home ground, that the system, autocracy plus serfdom plus the suppression of everything that might have modernized the country, did not in fact produce strength.
It produced a giant that could not feed its own soldiers in its own country.

The whole second half of this book is the answer to one question that the smoke over Sevastopol forced onto the throne: if the system as it stands cannot even defend the empire, can the empire afford to keep the system?

Alexander II's answer, the most courageous answer any Russian autocrat gave to that question and the one that got him blown apart on a St Petersburg street twenty-five years later, is the next chapter.

chapters.title: The Tsar Liberator
sentences: This is the chapter the whole first half of the book has been building toward, because it is the chapter in which the Russian Empire finally, after two centuries, does the thing it had refused to do, and discovers that doing it badly is in some ways worse than not doing it at all.

Alexander II (the second emperor of that name, son of Nicholas I, grandnephew of Alexander I, ruled 1855–1881) was a dutiful, conscientious, intelligent man, conventionally raised by Nicholas I to revere the autocracy and genuinely devoted to the duty of the throne, with a streak of pragmatic realism his father had lacked: he could look at a verdict he did not like and accept it.
And he had just inherited one.
The Crimean War (Chapter 13) had returned its unanswerable judgment: the system as it stood could not defend the country.

Faced with the same collision every reforming ruler in this book has faced, Catherine, Alexander I, the choice between the grandeur and the unfreedom, Alexander II became the one autocrat who chose, on the central question, to give up the unfreedom.

It made him "the Tsar Liberator." It also, by the specific way it was done, lit a faster-burning length of the fuse, and within twenty years the people he had freed and the radicals who claimed to speak for them were hunting him through his own capital with bombs.
Start with the decision itself, because Alexander II's own words frame it better than any paraphrase.
Pressing the reluctant Moscow nobility to accept reform in 1856, he told them, in substance, that it was better to abolish serfdom from above than to wait for it to abolish itself from below.
The exact words vary across the sources, but the sentiment is solidly documented, and it is the strategic core of the entire reform.

This is the thesis stated by the regime itself, out loud, for the first time: the unfreedom at the bottom was no longer just unjust, it was dangerous, a Pugachev (Chapter 7) waiting to happen on a national scale, and the grandeur at the top could no longer be safely maintained on top of it.
Emancipation was not, primarily, an act of conscience.
It was an act of regime self-preservation, and understanding that is the key to understanding why it was done in the particular crippled way it was done.
The Emancipation of the Serfs was proclaimed in the Emancipation Manifesto of 19 February 1861 (3 March by the Western calendar).
On paper it freed somewhere around 23 million privately owned serfs, with the state peasants and others following over the next two decades, in total well over forty million people.

In raw scale it is the single largest act of human liberation by legislation in history up to that point, and the comparison this book has been setting up since Chapter 7 must be made here, in this paragraph, because the timing is the whole point.
Britain had abolished slavery in its empire in 1833, by act of Parliament, with compensation paid to the slave owners.

The United States abolished slavery between 1863 and 1865, by the Emancipation Proclamation and the Thirteenth Amendment, at the cost of a civil war that killed roughly 750,000 Americans, the bloodiest event in that country's history.

Russia freed a bound population several times larger than the American one, by autocratic decree, peacefully, in 1861, two years before Lincoln's Proclamation and four years before the Thirteenth Amendment.
For one moment, on the single measure of "did you legally free your unfree millions, and how violently," the most backward great power in Europe was, astonishingly, ahead of the United States.
That is the grandeur of the act, and it is real, and Russians were right to feel it.
But the mechanisms ran in opposite directions, and the difference is the whole story.

British abolition in 1833 came after industrialization, partly because industrial wage labor had made Caribbean slave-worked sugar economically marginal, as the Industrial Revolution narrative traces.
American abolition in 1865 came through an industrial war, the railways and ironworks of the North grinding down an agrarian slave society.

Russian emancipation in 1861 came before industrialization, with almost no industrial economy pressing for it; it was not the result of economic change but a political pre-emption of revolt, and it would later supply the unbound, mobile labor that Witte's factories ran on (Chapter 18).
Britain freed its slaves because industry no longer needed them; Russia freed its serfs so it could begin to industrialize at all.
Now the mechanism, because the mechanism is where the act was sabotaged, and this book's whole method is to insist on mechanism over slogan.
The serfs were freed.
They were not, in any meaningful sense, given the means to live free.
The settlement, hammered out by reform bureaucrats against ferocious noble resistance, worked roughly like this.
The freed peasant received personal liberty (he could no longer be bought, sold, flogged at a lord's whim, or denied marriage) immediately, and that was real and mattered.
But the land, the only thing a peasant could actually live on, was handled so as to protect the nobility.

The peasants received allotments of land, but typically less land than they had been farming for their own subsistence as serfs (the landlords kept the best and largest portions, and in many regions the peasants ended up with less than before), and they did not get it free.

They had to pay for it, through a system of redemption payments: the state compensated the landlords up front for the land, and the peasants then had to repay the state, with interest, over a period set at forty-nine years.
Until enough was paid, peasants were in many cases "temporarily obligated," still owing labor or dues to the former lord.

And crucially, the land in most of Russia was not given to individual peasants at all but to the village commune (the mir or obshchina), the collective village body, which was made jointly responsible for the redemption debt and the taxes and which controlled and periodically redistributed the land among its households and could refuse a peasant permission to leave.
The peasant had been freed from the lord and bound, instead, to the commune and the debt.
He could not freely leave the village; he could not freely own or sell his strip of land; he was poorer in land than before and now in decades of debt for it.
The chain had not been struck off.
It had been re-forged in a new shape and handed to a new keeper.
The result was a disappointment so profound it became one of the engines of the revolution.

The peasants, who had genuinely expected the Tsar Liberator to give them the land, their land, the land they and their ancestors had worked, free, reacted to the actual terms with bewilderment and then anger.

A persistent peasant belief held that the real emancipation, the true tsar's golden charter giving them all the land, was being hidden from them by the wicked nobles and officials, the exact Pugachev-era "the good tsar's true will is being concealed" myth this book flagged in Chapter 7, now attached to 1861.
There were hundreds of disturbances.

The most notorious came at the village of Bezdna, where peasants gathered around a man who claimed the real golden charter freed them completely, refused to disperse, and were fired on by troops; scores were killed for not believing that the emancipation they had been handed was the real one.

The educated radicals drew the conclusion that would organize the rest of this book: that the autocracy was structurally incapable of giving the people real freedom, that even its greatest reform was a fraud designed to preserve the landlords and the debt, and that the thing would have to be taken, not granted.
Emancipation, the regime's bid to defuse the danger from below, instead convinced the most determined of its critics that reform from above was impossible and only revolution would do.
That is the precise hinge into Chapter 15.

But 1861 was not the end of Alexander II's reform; it was the start of a remarkable burst of it, the Great Reforms, and this book has to give them their due, because they were the genuine article and their fate is the chapter's deepest lesson.
Freeing the serfs forced the state to rebuild institutions that had assumed serfdom.

The zemstvo reform of 1864 created elected local self-government councils at the district and provincial level, with real responsibility for schools, roads, public health, and agriculture, the first institutions in Russian history in which Russians elected representatives to manage their own local affairs.

The franchise was real but rigged in the gentry's favor: voting was by separate curiae for landowners, townsmen, and peasant communes, with the seats weighted so that the relatively few noble landowners returned a heavily disproportionate share of the delegates.
It was a small, deliberately limited school of self-government in a country that had none.

The judicial reform of 1864 was the most radical of all: it created, more or less from nothing, a modern Western-style court system with independent judges, public trials, equality of all classes before the law, and trial by jury, in the country that had had the Third Section and serf justice a few years earlier.

The military reforms of war minister Dmitry Milyutin, the reform-minded general who ran the army ministry for two decades and rebuilt it after Crimea, completed in 1874, replaced the brutal 25-year conscription of serfs with universal, all-class, far shorter military service, and modernized the army that Crimea had disgraced.
Censorship was relaxed (Chapter 16's literature pours through the gap), universities got autonomy, and the first higher education courses for women in Russia were established.

For about a decade it genuinely looked as though Russia might be reforming itself, from the top, into a modern, law-governed society without a revolution, the thing every reformer in this book had dreamed and none had achieved.
And then the chapter's iron point.
Every one of the Great Reforms stopped at the same wall, the wall this entire book is about.

Russia got elected local councils but no national parliament; the zemstvo could fix a district road but could not touch a national law, and when zemstvo liberals asked, politely, to "crown the edifice" with some form of national representation, Alexander II refused, flatly, every time.

Russia got independent courts and trial by jury but the autocracy remained legally unlimited and could, and increasingly did, simply route political cases around the new courts through administrative and military justice.

Russia got everything that modernized the country except the one thing that would have shared power, because sharing power was the line no autocrat in this book would cross, the same line Catherine would not cross with the Nakaz (Chapter 6) and Alexander I would not cross with Speransky (Chapter 9).

The Great Reforms modernized the body of Russia and deliberately left the autocratic head untouched, and that mismatch, a society being given courts, councils, education, and a freed (if cheated) peasantry, while political power stayed the absolute possession of one man, is precisely the unstable compound that the rest of this book detonates.

Alexander II had done more to dismantle the unfreedom than any ruler in two hundred years and had still refused to touch the autocracy, and for that incomplete courage the people who thought even his reforms were a lie spent the 1870s building the bombs.
The hunting of the Tsar Liberator is the next chapter.

chapters.title: Going to the People
sentences: This is the chapter where the fuse, lit by the Decembrists in 1825 (Chapter 11) and carried through the literature of Chapter 12, finally reaches the people who will spend the next four decades trying to blow up the empire, and it is also the chapter where Russia, more or less, invents modern terrorism.

The argument runs: the disappointment of the Emancipation (Chapter 14) convinced a generation of educated young Russians that the autocracy could not be reformed and must be destroyed; they tried, in sequence, three strategies, propaganda, peasant insurrection, and assassination, and the third one worked, in the narrow sense that they killed the Tsar Liberator in 1881, and failed totally, in the wide sense that his murder produced not revolution but the harshest reaction of the century (Chapter 18).
Watching them cycle through those strategies is watching the revolutionary movement that eventually wins in 1917 learn its trade.
First the cultural mutation, because the revolutionaries of the 1860s were a new psychological type and contemporaries felt it as a rupture between generations.
The men of the 1840s, the Westernizers and Slavophiles (Chapter 12), had been aristocratic, philosophical, literary, given to talk.

The new men of the 1860s were often raznochintsy (raz-no-CHEEN-tsee, "people of various ranks," educated young Russians of non-noble origin, priests' sons, minor officials' sons, the products of Alexander II's expanded schooling), poorer, harder, contemptuous of their elders' refined hand-wringing, and committed to science, materialism, and a ruthless rejection of every inherited authority, religion, the family, the state, sentiment itself.

They got their label from a novel: in 1862 Ivan Turgenev published Fathers and Sons, whose hero Bazarov, a young man who believes in nothing he cannot dissect, gave Russia and the world the word nihilist (from Latin nihil, "nothing," one who recognizes no authority, accepts no principle on faith).
The radicals embraced the insult as a badge.

Their practical bible was another novel, written in a prison cell: Chernyshevsky's What Is to Be Done? (1863), a clumsily written but incandescently influential book whose model revolutionary, the iron ascetic Rakhmetov who sleeps on nails to harden himself, became the template a generation consciously tried to live by. (The title was later deliberately reused by Lenin, Chapter 18, a direct torch-pass the reader should notice.) The literary thread of Chapter 12 has now turned operational: the novels are not describing the revolutionaries, they are producing them.
The first strategy was propaganda and the famous attempt to merge with the people.

The dominant idea among the radicals of the 1860s and 1870s was Narodism (from narod, "the people"), a distinctively Russian agrarian socialism whose central wager, inherited partly from the Slavophiles and the radical exile Alexander Herzen (a wealthy nobleman's son, hounded by Nicholas I's police for his politics until he left Russia for good in 1847 and settled in London, from where his uncensored journal The Bell was smuggled back in and became, for a decade, the first great free Russian voice), was that Russia could leap straight to socialism without a capitalist stage, because the peasant commune (the mir, Chapter 14) was already a natural socialist institution; all that was needed was to awaken the peasants.

In the spring and summer of 1874, thousands of idealistic young men and women, students, dressed as workers and peasants and went into the countryside, the movement called "going to the people," to live among the peasants, teach them, and rouse them to revolution.
It was a near-total failure and the failure is instructive.

The students arrived expecting to find a peasantry seething for revolution and instead found one that was devoutly Orthodox, monarchist, suspicious of educated outsiders who could not handle a scythe, and far more likely to want the students' land redistributed by the tsar than to want the tsar overthrown.

When agitators preached atheism or attacked the emperor, peasants were variously baffled, scandalized, and alarmed; in a striking number of cases the villagers themselves tied up the young revolutionaries and marched them to the police, the people the movement had idealized handing it over to the state.

The first secret-police mass round-ups followed, and hundreds of the "go to the people" radicals ended up in the dock in mass political trials (the Trial of the 193 the most famous), which, by giving the defendants a public platform, the regime's own reformed courts (Chapter 14) having made trials public, turned martyrs into celebrities and radicalized more people than the trials punished, a self-defeating dynamic the autocracy never solved.
The failure of "going to the people" split the movement, and the split is the chapter's pivot.

The radicals organized into a disciplined underground society called Land and Liberty in the late 1870s, and then, in 1879, it broke in two over a single question: what to do now that the peasants would not rise.
One faction (which became Black Repartition, led by Plekhanov, who matters enormously in Chapter 18) wanted to keep up patient propaganda.

The other, larger and more impatient faction concluded that since the masses could not be roused and the autocracy could not be reformed, the answer was to strike directly at the autocracy itself, to kill the tsar and his servants, on the theory that systematic assassination would either provoke the revolution or so terrorize the regime into concessions.

They called themselves The People's Will (Narodnaya Volya), and they are widely regarded as the first organization in modern history to adopt systematic political assassination as a deliberate, theorized program rather than an isolated act, the direct ancestors of a great deal of what the twentieth century would call terrorism.

The atmosphere had been prepared: in 1866 a lone student, Karakozov, had already fired the first shot at Alexander II (and missed, triggering a wave of reaction); in 1878 Vera Zasulich shot and seriously wounded the governor of St Petersburg in revenge for the flogging of a political prisoner, and a St Petersburg jury, in one of the most astonishing moments of the whole period, acquitted her, an open public verdict that the regime's own new courts would not convict a political assassin the public sympathized with, after which the regime simply stopped sending such cases to juries.

The theory of terror also had its monster-text in the Catechism of a Revolutionary (around 1869), associated with Sergei Nechaev, a young provincial schoolteacher's son whose distinctive horror was not extremism but instrumentality: he treated other revolutionaries as disposable tools, fabricated a phantom central committee to control his followers, and had a wavering member of his own cell murdered to bind the rest in blood and silence.

His cold doctrine that the revolutionary may use any means and any person without scruple so horrified Dostoevsky, basing the killing on the real case, that he built the novel Demons around it (Chapter 16).
The escalation from a missed shot in 1866 to an organized assassination bureau in 1879 is the radicalization of the entire movement compressed into thirteen years.
The People's Will then did something no one had done before: it sentenced the emperor of Russia to death and spent two years methodically trying to carry out the sentence.
They tried explosives on his train and blew up the wrong one (the imperial train had already passed; the bomb wrecked the baggage train following it).

They got a member, Stepan Khalturin, employed as a carpenter inside the Winter Palace itself, who smuggled in dynamite over weeks and detonated it under the imperial dining room; the tsar survived only because his dinner happened to be running late and the room was still empty when the charge went off, while the explosion tore through the guardroom below and killed about a dozen soldiers and wounded dozens more, the Winter Palace bombing of 1880, an attack inside the emperor's own home that announced the autocracy could be reached anywhere.

The regime's response to the terror was itself revealing of the thesis: in 1880 Alexander II created an emergency "Supreme Commission" under Mikhail Loris-Melikov, an Armenian-born general who had made his name in the Caucasus and the Turkish war and who, unusually for a soldier-administrator, believed the terror could only be beaten by pairing repression with cautious political concession, and by early 1881 the aging Tsar Liberator had actually approved a cautious proposal, the so-called "Loris-Melikov constitution," which was not a constitution at all but a modest step toward including elected representatives in reviewing legislation, the smallest possible crack toward the national representation the zemstvo liberals had begged for since 1864 (Chapter 14).
He signed off on it on the morning of 1 March 1881 (13 March, Western calendar).
That afternoon, the People's Will killed him.
As his carriage drove through St Petersburg, a bomber threw a device that wrecked the carriage and wounded the escort.

Alexander II, by the well-attested account, was unhurt and got out to attend to the wounded, the humane reflex of the man who had freed the serfs, and a second bomber, standing close, threw a second bomb directly at his feet.

The assassination of Alexander II tore the lower half of his body apart; he was carried, conscious and dying, back to the Winter Palace, to the same study, and died within hours, on the very day he had approved the first hairline step toward representative government in Russian history.

The symbolism is so total it would be rejected as too neat if it were fiction: the most reforming tsar in two hundred years, murdered by revolutionaries on the afternoon he authorized the reform they said could never come, in the palace his terror had already bombed once.

His son built a church on the exact spot where the blood fell, the Church of the Savior on Spilled Blood, and his son was the man who answered the assassination not with the dead tsar's constitution but with its incineration, who tore up Loris-Melikov's project, hanged the assassins, and turned the full machinery of the state to crushing everything Alexander II had loosened.
The People's Will had bet that killing the tsar would bring the revolution closer.
It set it back, by the most repressive reign since Nicholas I, by a full generation.
But it had also proved, to everyone watching, that the autocracy could be physically reached and physically killed, and that lesson did not die with the men who were hanged for it.
It went underground, was studied, and was inherited, like every other length of this fuse, by the people who finally used it in 1917.

Before we get to the reaction, though, the book owes the reader the other thing this same half-century produced, the thing that makes Russia matter to people who never cared about tsars at all: the greatest outpouring of art the modern world has seen.
That is the next chapter.

chapters.title: The Golden Age
sentences: This chapter breaks the chronology on purpose, because its subject does not fit on a timeline.

Across roughly the second half of the nineteenth century, the same Russian Empire that was hunting and being hunted in the chapters around this one produced what is, by very wide agreement, the single greatest concentration of literature any country has produced in any comparable span, plus world-altering music and science, and it did so while the autocracy held and the unfreedom only half-lifted.
This is not a digression from the thesis.
It is the thesis at its most uncomfortable, because the grandeur in this chapter is not palaces and conquests, which are easy to see through.

It is War and Peace and the periodic table, achievements of permanent value to all of humanity, produced by the same machine that flogged peasants and hanged students, and the honest reader has to hold both at once without letting either cancel the other.
That double vision is the whole point of the chapter.
Why here, why then, why so concentrated?
The argument this book has been building since Chapter 12 pays off here.

In a country with no parliament, no free press worth the name, no legal politics, and a censor reading everything, the novel became the only place the largest moral questions a society can ask, what is a just life, what do we owe each other, can violence ever be redemptive, what is Russia for, could actually be asked, by writers, in front of a reading public that brought to fiction the desperate seriousness other countries brought to politics and religion.
Russian literature is so heavy because it was carrying the weight of everything the autocracy forbade anyone to say any other way.

The repression did not produce the genius, but it shaped what the genius was for, and that is why the Russian novel feels different in kind from the English or French one: it is arguing about how to live, under penalty, for readers with nowhere else to take the argument.
The two giants first.

Leo Tolstoy (1828–1910), the count who had been an artillery officer at Sevastopol (Chapter 13), wrote, in the decade after the Emancipation, War and Peace (serialized from the 1860s), an attempt to put an entire society, several hundred characters across the Napoleonic Wars (his account of 1812, Chapter 10, is where most of the world's mental image of it comes from), inside one book, and Anna Karenina (1870s), commonly cited by other novelists as the most technically perfect novel ever written.

Then, at the height of his fame, in his fifties, the most celebrated novelist alive, Tolstoy fell into a crisis so total he kept a rope hidden so he would not hang himself, and came out of it a radical Christian anarchist who renounced rank, property, copyright in his own books, the Orthodox Church, the army, the courts, and the autocracy itself, and tried, not very successfully, to live as a peasant on his own estate.

He preached a literal nonviolence and non-cooperation with the state that reached a young Indian lawyer named Gandhi, who corresponded with him near the end of his life and built a movement on the idea, so that a line runs from this Russian count's late conversion to the twentieth century's largest experiment in nonviolent resistance.

The Orthodox Church, the state church of Chapter 1, formally cut him off from communion in 1901 (the "excommunication of Tolstoy," technically a declaration that he had separated himself), an event so large that the censored press could barely contain the public reaction; the most famous man in Russia, possibly in the world, openly against the church and the autocracy, and untouchable because killing or jailing Tolstoy was unthinkable.
When he died in 1910, fleeing his own home and aristocratic life at eighty-two, his death was an international event and a political one.
Fyodor Dostoevsky (1821–1881) is the other pole.

The young man marched to the fake firing squad in 1849 and sent to a Siberian prison camp (Chapter 12) came back with a shattered, religious, anti-rationalist intensity and wrote the novels that map the modern psyche from the inside: Crime and Punishment (the student who reasons his way into murder and is destroyed by his own conscience), Demons (a savage portrait of the Nechaev-style revolutionary nihilism of Chapter 15, written by a man who had himself been a radical and recoiled), and The Brothers Karamazov, his last and largest, whose chapter "The Grand Inquisitor", a parable in which a returned Christ is arrested by the Church for offering people a freedom they did not want, has been argued over by philosophers and theologians ever since.

Dostoevsky against Tolstoy, faith against reason, the abyss against the moral law, is itself one of the permanent arguments of world literature, and it happened inside one country inside thirty years.
They were not alone, which is the point of a golden-age chapter.

Ivan Turgenev (Chapter 15's source of the word "nihilist") was the great novelist of the liberal Westernizing conscience and the gentle elegist of a dying gentry world, the Russian most read in Western Europe in his own lifetime and the bridge by which Europe discovered there even was a Russian literature.

Anton Chekhov (1860–1904), a doctor and the grandson of a serf who had bought his own family's freedom (a biographical fact that is itself this book's whole thesis in one family tree), reinvented the short story and, in plays like The Cherry Orchard, wrote the long, soft requiem of the gentry order, a class talking elegantly while the estate is sold out from under it, which is also, if you tilt it, the empire itself, ten years before the end.

His plays were made by a new institution, the Moscow Art Theatre, whose director Stanislavski developed a method of psychologically realistic acting that, transmitted to America, became the dominant approach to screen acting in the twentieth century (the modern handle: the "Method" of Brando and De Niro descends, by a traceable line, from a Moscow theater staging Chekhov in the 1890s).
The same surge ran through music, and Russian music's defining quarrel rhymes exactly with the Slavophile-Westernizer split of Chapter 12.

A group of nationalist composers known as The Mighty Handful (or "The Five"), self-taught amateurs by training and proud of it, set out to build a specifically Russian classical music out of folk song and Orthodox chant rather than German technique; their monument is Mussorgsky's opera Boris Godunov, a raw, unconventional drama of a guilt-haunted tsar and the suffering Russian people that broke European operatic rules on purpose.

Against them, more cosmopolitan and conservatory-trained, stood Pyotr Tchaikovsky (chy-KOFF-skee), who became the most internationally beloved composer Russia ever produced, the man who wrote Swan Lake, The Nutcracker, the symphonies, and the 1812 Overture, the piece, complete with scored cannon fire, that gave the West its sonic image of Russia beating Napoleon (Chapter 10) and that, by a long irony, now mostly plays over American fireworks on the Fourth of July.

Painting had its own nationalist rebellion, the Wanderers (Peredvizhniki), who in 1863 walked out of the state Imperial Academy of Arts, the official body that controlled training, exhibition, and patronage and required its prize students to paint approved mythological and classical subjects, in order to paint instead what they saw, peasants, prisoners, priests, the actual Russia, and to take it directly to the provinces in traveling exhibitions rather than to the salons of the capital.

Their work was bought up by Pavel Tretyakov, a self-made Moscow textile merchant who set out deliberately to assemble a national collection of Russian art and then handed the whole gallery to the city of Moscow, where it still is, so that the definitive collection of imperial Russia's painting was preserved not by a tsar but by a merchant, which is itself this book's thesis in one bequest.
And the same machine produced world-class science, which matters to this book because science is the part of the grandeur the autocracy most desperately needed and least knew how to grow.

Dmitri Mendeleev (men-de-LAY-eff), working at St Petersburg, published in 1869 the periodic table of the elements, arguably the single most important organizing idea in the history of chemistry; its power, the detail that made the world believe it, was that Mendeleev left gaps for elements not yet discovered and predicted their properties, and when those elements (gallium, germanium) were found and matched his predictions, the table was vindicated as not a chart but a law of nature.

Earlier, the mathematician Nikolai Lobachevsky, working in provincial Kazan, had been among the independent creators of non-Euclidean geometry, a revolution that overturned 2,000 years of assumed truth about space and laid groundwork that Einstein's physics would later need.

Ivan Pavlov won, in 1904, one of the first Nobel Prizes in physiology, and then, through the experiments on conditioned reflexes in dogs that made "Pavlovian" an English adjective, founded a science of how learning physically works. (And in the same years a deaf provincial schoolteacher, Konstantin Tsiolkovsky, was quietly working out the mathematics of rocket-powered spaceflight, a thread that belongs to the next narrative, not this one.) Hold the chapter's two facts together one last time, because this is the place in the book to do it without flinching.

The periodic table, The Brothers Karamazov, Pavlov's Nobel, The Cherry Orchard, the conditioned reflex, War and Peace, all of it, was produced inside the same empire, in the same decades, by the same society, that hanged the men of Chapter 15, that ran the Pale of Settlement and the pogroms of Chapter 17, and that was, even as Chekhov wrote, marching toward the catastrophe of Chapter 20.
The grandeur in this chapter is not a fraud the way the Potemkin villages were a fraud (Chapter 8).
It is real, permanent, and given freely to all of humanity.

And it does not redeem the unfreedom, and the unfreedom does not erase it, and any honest account of the Russian Empire has to carry both without resolving them, because the empire itself never resolved them.

It produced the greatest novels ever written about the moral life and never managed to organize a moral political order, and in 1917 the second failure consumed the country that had achieved the first.
The chapters that remain are about how the consuming happened.

chapters.title: The Empire of All the Russias
sentences: So far this book has mostly told the story from St Petersburg, looking down.
This chapter turns the empire inside out and looks at it from its edges, because "the Russian Empire" was never just Russians.

The tsar's official title ran to dozens of lands, "Emperor and Autocrat of All the Russias, of Moscow, Kiev, Vladimir, Novgorod; Tsar of Kazan, Tsar of Astrakhan, Tsar of Poland, Tsar of Siberia," and on, a recited inventory of conquests.

By the empire's last census, in 1897, of its roughly 125 million people only about 44 percent counted as Great Russians in the narrow sense; even folding in Ukrainians and Belarusians as "Russian," the official habit, brought it to only about two thirds, and tens of millions were neither.

It was, like the Habsburg and Ottoman empires it competed with, a vast multi-ethnic patchwork, and the thesis of this book has a second face here: the same logic that kept the peasant unfree at home drove an expansion abroad that absorbed tens of millions of non-Russians who never consented and, in the empire's last decades, tried to make them all into Russians by force, manufacturing exactly the nationalist grievances that helped tear the empire apart in Chapter 20.
This is the empire as the largest contiguous prison-house and treasure-house of peoples on earth, and you cannot understand 1917 without it.
Take the directions in turn.
South, into The Caucasus.

The Caucasus is the wall of high mountains between the Black and Caspian seas, one of the most ethnically and linguistically dense regions on the planet, dozens of peoples and languages in an area the size of a couple of US states.

Russia spent roughly half a century (the Caucasian War, conventionally dated from around 1817 to 1864) conquering it, and the conquest produced one of the great resistance figures of the nineteenth century: Imam Shamil (sha-MEEL), the Avar religious and military leader who, from the 1830s to 1859, united the Muslim mountain peoples of Chechnya and Dagestan in a holy war against Russian expansion and held the mountains against the empire for a quarter of a century with guerrilla warfare before finally being captured in 1859.
The regime did not execute him; it pensioned him, paraded him through Russian cities to admiring crowds, and let him die on pilgrimage in the Ottoman holy cities.

The clemency was a calculated message, aimed partly at the watching mountain peoples (resistance, once over, would be forgiven rather than avenged) and partly at European opinion, which had followed Shamil as a romantic freedom-fighter; a hanged Shamil would have been a martyr, a comfortable old pensioner would not.
The conquest's darkest chapter was the fate of the Circassians of the northwest Caucasus.
In the 1860s the Russian state, having decided their coastal homeland was strategically intolerable, drove the bulk of an entire people off its land and into the sea.

Scholarly estimates of those expelled to the Ottoman Empire range from several hundred thousand to over a million, and the deaths, from starvation, exposure, disease, and drowning in overloaded boats during the deportation itself, are credibly put in the hundreds of thousands.
Many specialists describe it plainly as ethnic cleansing, and some as genocide.
It is the single worst atrocity in this book, the empire spent a century minimizing it, and the descendant communities have never forgotten it.
This is the conquest's true face, and the book states it plainly rather than leaving it as "pacification." East and southeast, into Central Asia and Siberia.

Across the middle decades of the century, Russian armies absorbed the Muslim khanates and emirates of Central Asia, Tashkent taken in 1865, Bukhara and Samarkand reduced to vassalage, the Khanate of Khiva stormed in 1873, the oasis of Merv annexed in 1884, until the empire's southern frontier ran up against Afghanistan and the borders of British India.

This brought Russia into a long, mostly cold strategic rivalry with the British Empire across Central Asia that the British called the "Great Game," and it nearly came to war at the Panjdeh incident of 1885, when Russian troops seized a contested oasis on the ill-defined Afghan frontier and Britain, treating Afghanistan as the shield of its Indian empire, came within a diplomatic hair of fighting Russia over it before the border was settled by negotiation.

Meanwhile Siberia, conquered for fur over the previous two centuries (the fur trade, Chapter 8), was being turned from a penal dumping ground and trapper's frontier into something the state wanted to actually populate and exploit, a transformation that hangs on one machine, addressed below.
The empire reached the Pacific, founding the port of Vladivostok ("Ruler of the East," the name is a small confession of the whole enterprise) in 1860.
And then the empire did something almost unique in imperial history: it voluntarily sold a piece of itself.

Russian America, the Alaskan colony (Chapter 8), was remote, barely populated by Russians, expensive to defend, no longer profitable now that the sea otters were nearly hunted out, and, the St Petersburg calculation went, indefensible against Britain (whose Canada was next door) in any future war and better turned into cash and into a friendship with the rising United States.
In 1867 Russia sold Alaska to the United States for 7.2 million dollars, about two cents an acre.
Derided in the American press at the time as "Seward's Folly" after the secretary of state who bought it, it became, after gold and then oil, one of the great bargains in the history of states.

For this book the sale is diagnostic: the empire that would not surrender an inch of autocratic power or a single serf without crisis would cheerfully sell an entire North American territory, because land at the far edge was negotiable in a way that power at the center never, ever was.
The machine that changed everything in the east was the Trans-Siberian Railway, begun in 1891 and substantially completed by the early 1900s (with a final link finished around 1916).
It is the physical answer to the problem this whole book opened with in Chapter 1, the impossible size of the empire.

It runs from Moscow to Vladivostok on the Pacific, roughly 5,700 miles (9,200 km), and remains to this day the longest single continuous railway line on earth; to anchor it for an American reader, it is more than twice the distance from New York to Los Angeles, a single rail line longer than the entire United States is wide, more than doubled.

It collapsed a journey that had taken months into a journey of about a week, made it possible to move armies and settlers across the continent, opened Siberia to mass peasant resettlement (millions of land-hungry peasants moved east along it in the empire's last decades, a relief valve for the land hunger the Emancipation had left, Chapter 14), and drew Russia into the Far Eastern ambitions, a railway shortcut across Manchuria, a warm-water naval base at Port Arthur, that lead directly into the catastrophe of the war with Japan in Chapter 19.

The Trans-Siberian is the single most impressive engineering grandeur of the late empire and, like every grandeur in this book, it carried the seed of a disaster, in this case the overreach into Asia that Japan punished in 1905.
Now the part of the multi-ethnic empire that bears most directly on the fuse, because it created millions of people with a specific reason to want the empire gone.

As the late empire grew more anxious and more reactionary (Chapter 18), it adopted a policy called russification: the active pressure on non-Russian peoples, Poles, Ukrainians, Finns, Baltic peoples, Georgians, Armenians, and others, to adopt the Russian language and Orthodox religion and surrender their own institutions and autonomy.
Polish and Ukrainian-language education and publishing were restricted.

The Ems Ukaz, a secret decree Alexander II signed in 1876 while taking the waters at the German spa of Bad Ems, banned the printing and import of almost all Ukrainian-language books and the use of Ukrainian on the stage, on the official theory that Ukrainian was not a real language but a peasant corruption of Russian invented by Polish agitators.

The Ukrainian national poet Taras Shevchenko, himself born a serf and bought out of bondage by admirers, had already, a generation earlier, been arrested and sentenced to ten years of military exile under Nicholas I, forbidden to write or paint, essentially for having made Ukrainian a literary language at all.
Finland's cherished autonomy was eroded.
The Uniate Church (Eastern-rite Catholics) was forcibly absorbed into Orthodoxy.

Russification did not assimilate these peoples; it did the opposite, it created or hardened modern nationalist movements among Poles, Ukrainians, Finns, and others by giving each of them a concrete, daily, language-and-faith grievance against the empire, and in 1917 those nationalisms helped the empire come apart along exactly these seams.
And then there is the empire's specific treatment of its Jews, which is the chapter's, and arguably the book's, sharpest single indictment, and must be stated without softening.
When Russia partitioned Poland (Chapter 8) it acquired the largest Jewish population in the world.

Rather than grant them the rights of subjects, the empire confined the great majority of its Jews, by law, to a designated western region called the Pale of Settlement, an area roughly the size of a few large US states, outside which Jews were generally forbidden to live or own land, subject on top of that to quotas on education and bans on many professions.
The Pale was, in effect, a country-sized legal ghetto, maintained for over a century.

After the assassination of Alexander II in 1881 (Chapter 15), in which a Jewish woman's marginal involvement was seized on as a pretext, a wave of pogroms, violent mob attacks on Jewish communities involving killing, rape, and the destruction of homes and businesses, swept the southwestern empire, and pogroms recurred in worse waves around 1903–1906.

The historical debate over how far the central government actively organized the pogroms versus tolerated, encouraged, and failed to punish them is genuine and ongoing; what is not in dispute, and is the point, is that the imperial state maintained the legal cage, fostered the climate, and protected the perpetrators far more reliably than the victims.

The consequences ran straight into the rest of this book and far beyond it: the pogroms and the Pale together drove the largest Jewish emigration in history, much of it to the United States (a great many American Jewish families trace their arrival precisely to the wave of flight set off by the pogroms of 1881 onward), pushed others toward the new Zionist movement, and pushed a disproportionate number of young Jews, with overwhelming reason to want the autocracy destroyed, into the revolutionary movements of Chapter 18.
The empire manufactured, by deliberate policy, some of its own most determined enemies.

That sentence is the whole thesis of this chapter, and very nearly the whole thesis of the book: the grandeur, the railway across a continent, the empire of all the Russias, was bought at a cost in unfreedom so wide that it eventually included tens of millions of people who had every reason to help light the powder, and in Chapter 20 they did.

chapters.title: The Counter-Reformation
sentences: The People's Will killed Alexander II on 1 March 1881 (Chapter 15) expecting the revolution.

What they got was his son, and his son spent thirteen years systematically destroying as much of his murdered father's reform as he could reach, on the explicit theory that the Tsar Liberator's mistake had been liberating anything at all.

Alexander III (the third emperor of that name, son of Alexander II, ruled 1881–1894) is the regime's clearest answer, after Nicholas I (Chapter 12), to the question this book keeps asking the autocracy: shown that the system is failing, will you change it or harden it?
Alexander III hardened it with a conviction and a competence that make him, in a grim way, the most successful reactionary in the book.

He was physically enormous, personally honest, domestically devoted, contemptuous of constitutions and intellectuals and everything Western, and certain that Russia's salvation lay in undiluted autocracy, militant Orthodoxy, and Russian nationalism.
His reign was outwardly stable, even peaceful (he avoided major wars and was called, with some irony, "the Peacemaker").

That outward stability is the chapter's trap, because underneath it the regime was simultaneously freezing political life solid and unleashing an economic transformation that would shatter that frozen surface from below, and the contradiction between those two policies, repression on top, capitalism underneath, is the specific compound that 1905 (Chapter 19) ignites.

The mind of the reaction had a name: Konstantin Pobedonostsev (po-be-do-NOS-tsev), Alexander III's former tutor, the lay head (Ober-Procurator) of the Holy Synod (the government department that ran the church, Chapter 4), and the most influential ideologue of late autocracy.

Pobedonostsev was not a thug; he was an intelligent, cultured, deeply pessimistic reactionary who genuinely believed that democracy, parliaments, juries, a free press, and equality were the "great lie of our time," that they led only to chaos and the rule of demagogues, and that the Russian masses needed the firm, paternal, sacred authority of autocracy and church the way a child needs a parent.
He drafted the manifesto, issued weeks after the assassination, that publicly buried Loris-Melikov's near-constitution (Chapter 15) and reasserted unlimited autocracy as God's order.

Under him and Alexander III came the Counter-Reforms: the elected zemstvo and town governments (Chapter 14) were brought under tighter bureaucratic control and the franchise narrowed in favor of the nobility; a new official, the "land captain," was created to put appointed gentry authority back over the peasants, partially undoing the personal liberty of 1861 in daily practice; university autonomy was crushed and tuition raised to keep out the poor (the raznochintsy of Chapter 15 were the explicit target); censorship tightened; the independent press was throttled.

Russification (Chapter 17) intensified, the Pale and the disabilities on Jews were enforced harder and the pogroms of 1881 went essentially unpunished, and the secret police, reorganized after 1881 as the Okhrana (the empire's last and most sophisticated political-police agency, the lineal heir of the Third Section, Chapter 12, and a direct institutional ancestor of the Soviet security state), became extremely effective, penetrating revolutionary groups with informers and double agents so thoroughly that for two decades it kept the organized revolutionary movement small, fragmented, and largely in exile or prison.
By the standard of holding the political surface still, the counter-reformation worked.
The revolutionary movement of the 1880s was nearly strangled.
And then the regime did the thing that made all the strangling beside the point.

The same state that was freezing politics decided, out of strategic necessity, to force-march Russia into the industrial revolution, eighty years after Britain, decades after Germany and the United States, and roughly in step with Meiji Japan, which had started from a comparable standing start at almost the same time.
The difference between the two, which the Industrial Revolution narrative draws out at length, is the difference that decides 1905.

Japan rebuilt its state, a constitution, a parliament, a modern bureaucracy, a broadened political class, in order to run the industrialization, so that the new economy produced a political coalition with a stake in the regime.

Russia used its unreconstructed autocratic state to own the industrialization while refusing to share a particle of political power, so that the new economy produced a working class with no voice and nothing to lose.
Same method, opposite institutional choice, and Japan would collect on the difference at Tsushima.
The Crimean War (Chapter 13) had taught the lesson; the danger of remaining a non-industrial great power in an industrial age was now an article of state faith.
The man who acted on it was Sergei Witte (VIT-te), finance minister through the 1890s, the most consequential economic statesman in the empire's history.

Witte's industrialization program was a deliberate, state-driven crash modernization, and it was not improvised: it was, almost point for point, the standard nineteenth-century latecomer playbook that Germany and the United States had already run and Meiji Japan was running at the same moment, the protective-tariff, infant-industry doctrine the German economist Friedrich List had set out for exactly this situation (the Industrial Revolution narrative traces the same playbook across all of them).

Witte put Russia on the gold standard in 1897, which both stabilized the currency and plugged Russia into the British-anchored global financial system through which capital could flow worldwide, to attract foreign investment Russia could not generate at home, which came mainly from France and Belgium, France because the 1894 Franco-Russian alliance made lending to Russia a strategic act backed by the French state, Belgium because its banks and heavy-industry firms were aggressively exporting capital; he used protective tariffs, state orders, and direct state enterprise to build heavy industry; and he made the Trans-Siberian Railway (Chapter 17) and railway-building generally the spine of the whole effort, because railways consumed the coal, iron, and steel that built the industrial base.

It worked, by the numbers, spectacularly: in the 1890s Russian industrial output grew at among the fastest rates in the world, the Baku oil fields (in the Caucasus, Chapter 17) made the empire, around the turn of the century, briefly the world's largest oil producer, before American output and Baku's own labor unrest and the 1905 upheavals knocked it back, and huge new industrial concentrations grew up around St Petersburg, Moscow, the Ukrainian coal-and-steel basin, and Baku.
The grandeur of the late empire is, substantially, Witte's furnaces and rails.
Here is the detonator the chapter has been assembling, stated as plainly as the book can.

State-forced industrialization created, very fast, a new class that the autocracy had no place for and no way to control: an urban industrial proletariat (the wage-working class of the factories, the term from the European socialist movement), concentrated in huge numbers in a few cities, working twelve-hour-plus days for low wages in dangerous conditions, packed into barracks, with no legal trade unions, no right to strike, no political voice, and, unlike the scattered peasantry, gathered together in the thousands where their grievances could be organized.
Witte built the working class; Pobedonostsev guaranteed it had no legal way to express a single demand.

The autocracy had spent a century terrified of the peasant Pugachev (Chapter 7) and the educated radical (Chapter 15), and now, by its own industrial policy, it manufactured a third and far more dangerous adversary in the one place, the modern city, where revolutionaries could actually reach them.
And the new class arrived precarious.

Russia's countryside was already being squeezed by the same force squeezing farmers across the whole industrial world: the long agrarian depression of the 1873–1896 period, when a flood of cheap American prairie wheat collapsed grain prices everywhere and gutted farm incomes from Britain to Germany to the Russian black-earth belt (the Industrial Revolution narrative covers the European side).

Elsewhere it caused emigration and political radicalization; in Russia, where the regime's relief machinery was incompetent and the peasantry already land-poor from the cheated Emancipation, the same global price collapse plus a bad harvest produced something far more lethal, the Great Famine of 1891–1892, in which somewhere on the order of hundreds of thousands of people died (the figure is debated and was deliberately obscured by the regime, which long refused even to use the word "famine"), and the government's visible incompetence in relief drove educated society decisively into opposition.
The famine is usually dated as the moment a generation of the intelligentsia gave up on the regime entirely.
One of them was a young law graduate from the Volga town of Simbirsk named Vladimir Ulyanov.

Four years earlier, in 1887, his older brother Alexander, a university student, had been hanged for his part in a People's Will splinter group's plot to assassinate Alexander III with bombs concealed in hollowed-out books; the execution radicalized the family and pointed the surviving brother, in time, toward a colder and more disciplined kind of revolution than his brother's had been.
That generation now had a new theory, and its arrival is the chapter's last movement, because it is the theory that wins in 1917.
Older Russian radicalism had been Narodism (Chapter 15), the bet on the peasant commune.

The new theory was Marxism, the European doctrine of Karl Marx holding that history advances through class struggle, that capitalism inevitably produces an industrial working class that will overthrow it, and that socialism is the scientific destiny of the industrial age.

Marxism's appeal to Russian radicals after the failure of "going to the people" was exact: Witte's industrialization was visibly creating the very industrial proletariat Marx said would be the revolutionary class, so Russia's forced capitalism could be read not as a defeat for socialism but as the necessary stage toward it.

The first Russian Marxist organization, the Emancipation of Labour group, was founded in exile in 1883 by Plekhanov (the patient-work advocate of the 1879 split, Chapter 15), who now became the founding theorist of Russian Marxism.
Out of these circles, in 1898 and effectively in 1903, came the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party (the RSDLP), the Marxist party.

At its 1903 congress (held in Brussels and London because it was illegal in Russia) the party split, ostensibly over a narrow question of membership rules, actually over a fundamental difference of revolutionary temperament, into two factions whose names come from the Russian for "majority" and "minority": Lenin's group won a single decisive vote late in the congress, after some delegates had walked out, and seized the label "majority" (bolsheviki) for good, sticking its rivals with "minority" (mensheviki) even though the names flattered one side and were never an accurate running headcount.
The Bolsheviks ("majority") were led by that same Vladimir Ulyanov, now using the alias Lenin, who argued for a small, disciplined, professional, centrally controlled party of revolutionaries.
The Mensheviks ("minority") favored a broader, more open, more democratic party on the Western social-democratic model.

This 1903 split, an obscure quarrel among a few dozen émigrés in a Brussels hall, is one of the most consequential events of the twentieth century, because the Bolshevik faction it created is the one that takes power in 1917 and runs the state that comes after this book.

Alongside the Marxists, the heirs of the Narodnik tradition organized as the Socialist Revolutionary Party (the SRs), who kept the focus on the peasantry and revived the People's Will tactic of political assassination.

By the time the elderly Alexander III died in 1894 of kidney disease, his counter-reformation looked like a complete success: the autocracy was solid, the press was silenced, the revolutionaries were in exile, the economy was booming.
Underneath, the regime had built a working class with no voice, ruined a generation's faith in a famine, and let its most determined enemies organize abroad into the party that would finish it.
He left all of it, the booming furnaces, the frozen politics, the buried fuse, to his son, who was utterly unequipped for any of it, and whose name was Nicholas.
That is the last act.

chapters.title: The Year It Cracked
sentences: Nicholas II (the second emperor of that name, son of Alexander III, the last tsar, ruled 1894–1917) is the most consequential incompetent in this book, and the word has to be used carefully because his failure was not stupidity or cruelty but something the regime could survive even less: a sincere, gentle, dutiful, devoutly Orthodox man of limited imagination who believed, with absolute conviction, that God had personally entrusted him with unlimited autocratic power and that his sacred duty was to hand that power, undiminished, to his son.

He came to the throne at twenty-six in 1894, unprepared and admitting it, and he spent his reign applying the answer Nicholas I and Alexander III had given, hold and harden, to a country that the railways, the factories, the famine, the working class, and the revolutionary parties of Chapter 18 had made completely unlike the country they had ruled.
He inherited the buried fuse and he refused, to the last possible day and past it, to believe it was lit.
This chapter is the year it became impossible not to see, and the year is 1905, the dress rehearsal that the regime survived just well enough to learn nothing from.
The omens were early and ignored.

At his coronation festivities in 1896 a crowd crush at Khodynka field in Moscow killed well over a thousand people; the new tsar, advised it would be undiplomatic to cancel, attended a French embassy ball that same evening, and the contrast, a thousand subjects trampled in the morning, the tsar dancing at night, attached itself to him permanently as a kind of folk verdict.

The deeper trouble was that Nicholas II combined his father's iron belief in autocracy with none of his father's force, and pursued, against Witte's advice, the reckless Far Eastern adventurism the Trans-Siberian had made possible (Chapter 17): pressing Russian power into Manchuria and Korea, straight into the ambitions of Japan, which had just done in forty years the institutional and industrial modernization Russia had refused to do, the Meiji transformation that is its own narrative.

Vyacheslav Plehve, the hardline interior minister who ran the empire's police and repression in these years, is supposed to have said he wanted "a small victorious war to stem the tide of revolution", a line so apt it is quoted everywhere and documented nowhere reliably, and which this book passes on with that warning attached.
Whatever he actually said, he got a war.
It was neither small nor victorious.
The Russo-Japanese War (1904–1905) is the Crimean War's lesson (Chapter 13) delivered a second time, harder, and to a regime that had spent fifty years insisting it had learned it.

Japan opened the war in February 1904 with a surprise night torpedo attack on the Russian Pacific squadron lying at Port Arthur, striking before any declaration of war, a stroke many later pointed to as the model for Pearl Harbor.
On land, the Japanese besieged and took Port Arthur and then beat the Russian army at the colossal Battle of Mukden (1905), one of the largest land battles in history to that point.

At sea came the single most concentrated humiliation in the empire's military history: Russia sent its Baltic Fleet halfway around the world, an 18,000-mile voyage, to relieve the Pacific, and the Japanese navy under Admiral Togo destroyed almost the entire fleet over two days at the Battle of Tsushima in May 1905, the decisive damage done in a few shattering hours of the first afternoon.

A European great power, the gendarme of Europe, the conqueror of Napoleon, had been comprehensively beaten on land and annihilated at sea by an Asian power the European empires had regarded forty years earlier as a quaint feudal curiosity.
The Treaty of Portsmouth (1905) ended the war on terms that confirmed the defeat.

It was mediated, tellingly, by the United States: President Theodore Roosevelt, wanting neither power dominant in the Pacific where American interests were growing, brokered the talks in New Hampshire and earned a Nobel Peace Prize for it, the first sign that the center of gravity in great-power diplomacy was beginning to cross the Atlantic.
The strategic meaning was global, the first modern defeat of a European empire by a non-European one, and it electrified Asia.

It also carried a specific lesson that the reformers in every "backward" empire of the era read at once: industrialization paired with institutional reform (Japan) beat industrialization without it (Russia).
Reform-minded Ottomans, Chinese, and Persians all absorbed that lesson from 1905; the one regime that did not absorb it was the one that had just been beaten teaching it.
The domestic meaning was that the regime had lost the last argument it had, the argument from strength, and had lost it while the new working class it had built was already in the streets.
Because by the time Tsushima sank, the Revolution of 1905 was already underway, and its trigger is one of the most precisely datable moments in the book.

On 9 January 1905 (22 January, Western calendar), a huge, peaceful, unarmed crowd of St Petersburg workers and their families, carrying icons and portraits of the tsar and singing hymns, marched toward the Winter Palace to present a humble petition.

They were led by a priest, Father Gapon, who ran a workers' organization that the police themselves had originally sponsored as a controlled, loyal, tsar-revering alternative to the revolutionary unions, the idea being a safety valve they controlled.

The valve failed because the grievances it gathered were real: when a strike at a huge St Petersburg plant escalated and the organization's tens of thousands of members looked for redress, Gapon channeled them not into revolution but, exactly as the regime had wanted, into a humble, loyal appeal to the tsar himself, and the regime then shot the loyal appeal in the street, converting its own controlled workers, at a stroke, into people with nothing left to be loyal to.
The petition was loyal in tone; it asked for an eight-hour day, a living wage, and, fatally for the regime's mythology, a popularly elected assembly to share in making the country's laws.
It addressed the tsar as "Sire" and appealed to him as the people's father, the exact Pugachev-and-1861 belief (Chapters 7, 14) that the good tsar would help if only he knew.
The troops guarding the palace approaches opened fire on the crowd.
Hundreds were killed (the exact toll is disputed and was minimized by the regime; the order of magnitude, hundreds dead, is solid).

It is called Bloody Sunday, and its real historical work was psychological and total: it killed, in a single morning, the foundational myth of the entire autocracy, the sacred bond between the tsar-father and his trusting people that Official Nationality (Chapter 12) had made the regime's whole theory of itself.
After Bloody Sunday the worker who had carried the tsar's portrait to the palace and been shot for it no longer believed the tsar was his father.
That belief had held the unfreedom together, in the peasant's head and the worker's, since before Peter.
Bloody Sunday is where it died, and once it was dead the regime had only force left.
The year 1905 then became a general convulsion.

Strikes spread across the empire; there were peasant risings, mutinies in the armed forces (the most famous: the crew of the Black Sea battleship Potemkin, pushed past endurance by being served maggot-ridden meat and then by the shooting of a sailor who protested, killed their officers, seized the ship, sailed it for days as a rebel fortress unable to find a port that would take them, and finally surrendered it to Romania, the episode Eisenstein later turned into the most influential propaganda film ever made), national revolts on the russified peripheries (Chapter 17), and assassinations by the SRs.

In the autumn a general strike paralyzed the country, and in St Petersburg the striking workers spontaneously elected a council to coordinate, the St Petersburg Soviet (soviet simply means "council"), which in its last weeks, after its first chairman was arrested, was led by a young revolutionary named Leon Trotsky, an institution invented in 1905 that the reader should mark, because the soviets are the form the 1917 revolution takes and the word that names the state that follows this book.

With the army still tied down and trickling back from Manchuria, the regime, for the only time in this book, genuinely lost control, and Nicholas II was forced, by Witte's urgent advice and against every fiber of his belief, to do the thing every autocrat in this book had refused: concede.
The October Manifesto of 1905 promised civil liberties and, decisively, an elected legislature, the State Duma, with real legislative power, without whose consent no law could be made.
On paper, on 17 October 1905, Russia stopped being an autocracy.
Six hundred years after England, the empire had a parliament.
It did not last as promised, and how it was hollowed out is the chapter's final lesson and the precise reason the fuse kept burning.

The Manifesto split the opposition exactly as it was designed to: liberals who wanted a constitutional order (organizing as the Kadet party) were partly satisfied and partly co-opted; the revolutionary left was not, and the Moscow workers' December uprising of 1905 was crushed by the army with artillery, the regime having recovered its nerve and its troops.
Then Nicholas II spent the next decade taking the concession back by increments.

The Fundamental Laws of 1906, issued just before the first Duma met, reasserted that the emperor's power remained "autocratic" and gave him sweeping authority to rule by decree, veto, and dissolve, gutting the Manifesto's spirit before it was a year old.
The first two Dumas, too radical for the regime, were dissolved within months.

Then, in 1907, the regime simply rewrote the election law by illegal decree to massively over-weight the propertied and Russian voters, engineering a compliant third Duma, an act contemporaries openly called a coup.

The lesson the regime took from surviving 1905 was not "we must share power to survive" but "we survived, therefore we need not share power," the identical conclusion Catherine drew from Pugachev and Alexander III from his father's murder, the book's deepest and most fatal pattern, made one last time, with the last chance.
There were two men in the last decade who embody the regime's final choice between its possible futures.

One was Pyotr Stolypin (sto-LIH-pin), prime minister from 1906, a tough, intelligent conservative who paired ferocious repression of revolution (the field courts-martial that hanged so many that the noose was nicknamed "Stolypin's necktie") with the most serious attempt since Alexander II to actually fix the regime's foundational problem.

Stolypin's land reforms, his "wager on the strong," tried to break up the peasant commune (the mir, Chapters 14–15), let enterprising peasants consolidate and privately own their land, and create a class of prosperous, property-owning, conservative farmers who would have a stake in the existing order rather than in burning it, the one late, intelligent attempt to undo the half-done Emancipation and turn the dangerous peasant into a contented citizen.
It needed, by Stolypin's own estimate, twenty years of peace to work.
It got about five.
In 1911 Stolypin was shot dead at the Kiev opera, in front of the tsar, during a gala performance.
The assassin was a revolutionary who was also a paid Okhrana informer, and the police security around the event had let him in.

The regime's own secret service had, in effect, delivered the killer of the one minister seriously trying to save the regime, which is as exact a picture as this book can offer of how rotten the autocracy's own machinery had become by 1911.
With Stolypin dead, the land reform lost its driver and never got another.
The regime's other face was Grigori Rasputin (ras-POO-tin), the single most mythologized figure in modern Russian history, around whom almost everything vivid is contested.

The verifiable core is this: Rasputin was a Siberian peasant holy man, a self-styled mystic of dubious clerical standing, who gained extraordinary influence at court for one reason this book can state with confidence, because it is genuinely tragic and genuinely consequential.
The heir to the throne, the Tsarevich Alexei, suffered from hemophilia, the inherited disorder in which blood does not clot and a minor injury can be fatal.
It ran through the descendants of Queen Victoria, and the empress Alexandra, Victoria's granddaughter, had carried it into the Russian dynasty.
The boy's condition was a desperately guarded state secret.
