They burned their own crops, smashed their tools, and above all slaughtered and ate their livestock rather than surrender it to the collective, which is why the USSR's livestock herds collapsed catastrophically between 1928 and 1933, cattle and horses by roughly half and some categories worse, a self-inflicted wound the economy did not recover from for decades.

The loss of horses in particular crippled the new collective farms at the worst possible moment: Soviet agriculture was still overwhelmingly horse-powered, the promised tractors did not yet exist in remotely sufficient numbers, and fields that had been worked by draft animals now had to be sown and harvested by hand or not at all, which deepened the coming famine.
There were thousands of revolts, many led by women (the regime, revealingly, often treated women's protests as less politically dangerous and used that).

In March 1930, with the countryside in near-uprising and the spring sowing threatened, Stalin published an article titled "Dizzy with Success," blaming the chaos on overzealous local officials supposedly exceeding orders, the orders having in fact come from him.

It was propaganda cover, not accountability: a few local scapegoats were reprimanded, but the officials had done exactly what the center wanted, and the article's real function was to vent peasant fury onto subordinates while the leadership kept its hands clean.
It allowed a temporary mass exodus from the collectives, and then, once the spring sowing was safe, Collectivization was driven through again, harder.
By the mid-1930s the overwhelming majority of peasant households were in collective farms.
The independent Russian and Ukrainian village, a social world a thousand years old, had been destroyed as a political force in about five years, and the state now controlled the food.
Then came the famine, and here the narrative must be at its most careful.
In 1932–1933 a massive famine struck the major grain regions of the USSR: Ukraine, the Kuban and North Caucasus, the Volga, and, with particular ferocity, Kazakhstan.

The total death toll across the entire USSR is estimated by most archival demographers in the range of roughly 5.5 to 7 million people, with some estimates higher; the range exists because the regime falsified or suppressed the vital statistics, the 1937 census that revealed the demographic hole was itself suppressed and its organizers shot, and demographers reconstruct the deaths by indirect methods that yield different totals.
What is not in serious dispute among historians is the basic mechanism: this was not a natural famine.

Harvests in 1932 were poor but not catastrophically so; people starved because the state continued to extract grain through brutal procurement quotas, requisitioned seed and food stocks, blockaded stricken regions to stop starving peasants from leaving in search of food, criminalized even the gleaning of grain from already-harvested collective fields (the August 1932 decree popularly nicknamed the "law of spikelets," under which a starving peasant, often a woman or child, picking up leftover stalks or ears, the gleaning that had fed the rural poor for centuries, could be shot or sentenced to ten years for "theft of socialist property"), and refused to acknowledge the famine or accept the foreign aid it had accepted in 1921 (Chapter 4).
The famine was, in the consensus of the field, man-made: a product of policy, not weather.
That much is not the contested part.

It is worth noting that an ideologically rationalized, policy-driven famine was not unique to communism: a century earlier, British officials, citing the political economy of laissez-faire, had restrained relief and allowed grain exports during the Irish Famine while roughly a million people starved inside the United Kingdom (the industrial-revolution narrative).

The point of the comparison is not to equate the two, the scale, the deliberate procurement, and the sealing of regions were Soviet specifics, but to show that letting doctrine override visible mass starvation had a liberal-capitalist precedent in the same century.
The contested part is Ukraine, and it must be presented as the live, unsettled, morally and politically loaded debate it is, not resolved by fiat in either direction.
Within the all-Union famine, Ukraine (and the heavily Ukrainian Kuban) suffered with exceptional severity; the Ukrainian death toll is estimated at roughly 3.5 to 5 million.
This specific catastrophe is known by the Ukrainian name Holodomor (pronounced "huh-luh-duh-MORE").
The word is built from Ukrainian roots meaning, roughly, "killing by hunger," and the name itself carries the claim that the starvation was inflicted, not suffered.

The central question, fiercely argued for decades, is whether the Holodomor was a genocide: that is, whether Stalin's regime deliberately used the famine to destroy the Ukrainian nation as such, targeting Ukrainians because they were Ukrainians, rather than peasants generally.
State that this is a genuine, ongoing scholarly and political dispute, and lay out the camps honestly.

One position, advanced influentially by Robert Conquest in The Harvest of Sorrow (1986) and developed by historians such as Andrea Graziosi and adopted as official position by independent Ukraine, the United States, the European Parliament, and many other states, holds that the famine in Ukraine was qualitatively different from the famine elsewhere: it was accompanied by a simultaneous assault on Ukrainian national institutions, language, and the Ukrainian Communist cadres, the borders of Ukraine were specifically sealed, and the intent was to crush Ukrainian nationhood, which on this reading makes it a genocide. (Raphael Lemkin, the Polish-Jewish jurist who coined the word "genocide" in 1944 and drove the drafting of the 1948 UN Genocide Convention, himself argued in a 1953 address that the Soviet destruction of the Ukrainian nation was a classic case of what he meant by the term, which is why his name carries weight in this specific dispute.) A second position, associated with historians such as R.

Davies and Stephen Wheatcroft, accepts that the famine was man-made and that the regime's policies caused mass death through criminal negligence and brutal extraction, but argues the documentary evidence does not establish a specific intent to exterminate Ukrainians as a nation rather than to break peasant resistance and extract grain across all the grain regions, including the heavily Russian Volga and the Kazakhs; on this reading it is a monstrous crime, possibly a crime against humanity, but the genocide label, requiring proven intent to destroy a national group as such, is not established by the surviving record.

A third strand, prominent in recent work by Timothy Snyder and others, emphasizes that whatever label is used, the Ukrainian dimension was real and deliberate in its severity and cannot be flattened into a generic Soviet famine.

The honest summary, which this narrative holds to: that the 1932–33 famine was man-made and lethal on a colossal scale is established; that Ukraine and Kazakhstan were hit hardest is established; whether the Ukrainian catastrophe meets the definition of genocide (which, under the 1948 Convention, requires not just mass death but a provable intent to destroy a national group as such, the intent being the hard, disputed element here) is genuinely disputed among serious historians and is simultaneously a live political claim that present-day states, including Russia (which denies the genocide framing) and Ukraine (which affirms it), use as a weapon.

Anyone who tells you the genocide question is simply settled, in either direction, is doing politics, not history, and this is exactly the kind of claim the writing rules of this whole project forbid stating as plain fact.
One more catastrophe inside the catastrophe, because it is the least known and proportionally the worst.

In Kazakhstan, the Soviet state forced the Kazakhs, a traditionally nomadic, pastoralist people, into settled collective farms while simultaneously requisitioning their herds, the only food economy they had.

The result, the Kazakh famine of 1930–33 (called in Kazakh memory the Asharshylyk, or sometimes the Goloshchekin famine after Filipp Goloshchekin, the Party boss of Kazakhstan who drove the forced settlement and herd requisition there and gave it its especially merciless local character), killed an estimated 1.5 million people, on the order of a third or more of the entire Kazakh population, the highest proportional death rate of any people in the USSR during collectivization.

It is the clearest case in the whole episode of a distinct people nearly destroyed by the forced transformation of its way of life, and it is barely known in the West, which is itself a comment on whose deaths get counted and remembered.
By 1933 the war on the village was won, and the reckoning is best stated as the honest range it is.

The price across the whole USSR in those four years was somewhere between roughly six and eight million dead by the demographers' reconstructions, the independent peasantry destroyed as a social and political force, and wounds in Ukrainian and Kazakh national memory that are, ninety years later, still open and still weaponized.
The state had its grain, its labor reserve, and its control.
It had seized them to build the factories.
That is Chapter 7.

chapters.title: The Furnace
sentences: The reason the village was destroyed (Chapter 6) was so that this could happen: in roughly a single decade, an overwhelmingly agrarian country was dragged, at terrible cost, into being the world's second industrial power, in time to survive a war that would have annihilated the agrarian version.
The Soviet industrialization of the 1930s is the regime's strongest case for itself and also a case study in what coercion can and cannot buy.

This chapter is the strongest single test of the whole book's thesis, because here the promise and the machine produced, together, something that was simultaneously a genuine achievement and a human catastrophe, and the honest reckoning has to hold both.

Start with the image, because the abstractions only mean something through it: an entire steel city raised in five years out of empty steppe, by a workforce that lived in dugouts through the Ural winter while building it.
That was Magnitogorsk (more on it below), and conjuring things like it was the entire purpose of the planning machinery described next.
The instrument was the Five-Year Plan.

In 1928 the regime launched the First Five-Year Plan, the central act of the new command economy: instead of a market deciding what got produced, a central planning agency, Gosplan (the State Planning Committee), set output targets for every major sector and every major enterprise, allocated resources by administrative order, and measured success against fulfilment of the plan rather than against profit or demand.

In practice Gosplan was a body of economists and statisticians translating the leadership's political priorities into physical targets (so many tons of steel, so many tractors), passing them down through ministries to factories; when a target was physically impossible, the factory was expected to claim fulfilment anyway, falsify the figures, or be punished, which built dishonesty into the system's nervous system from the start.

The doctrinal ancestor was Lenin's 1920 GOELRO plan (the State Commission for the Electrification of Russia, an ambitious scheme to wire the country, source of Lenin's slogan that "communism is Soviet power plus the electrification of the whole country"), but the scale was new and the spirit was a kind of economic warfare.

Stalin's slogan was that the USSR was fifty to a hundred years behind the advanced countries, with "they" meaning the hostile capitalist powers he was certain would attack a weak Soviet state, and "we must make good this distance in ten years.
Either we do it, or they crush us." The fear was both a real strategic assessment and a mobilizing instrument, and 1941 (Chapter 11) is the reason it cannot simply be dismissed as pretext.

Targets were set deliberately impossibly high, revised upward mid-plan for propaganda effect, and declared fulfilled "in four years" whether or not they were, because the plan was as much a mobilizing myth as an accounting system.
The reality was chaotic, wasteful, and astonishingly productive at the same time.
The monuments were real and the conditions building them were brutal.
Magnitogorsk (pronounced "mag-nee-tuh-GORSK") was a steel city conjured out of bare steppe at the Ural mountains around a mountain of iron ore, explicitly modeled on the U.S.

Steel works at Gary, Indiana, and built in part by imported American engineers; within a few years it was one of the largest steel complexes in the world, built by a workforce that included enthusiastic young volunteers, conscripted peasants fleeing collectivization, and deported "kulaks" living in earthen dugouts through Ural winters.

Dnieprostroi, the Dnieper Hydroelectric Dam in Ukraine, completed in 1932, was for a time the largest in Europe and a genuine engineering triumph, also built with American consulting; its power fed the new metallurgical and chemical plants of industrial Ukraine, and it mattered enough that the retreating Red Army deliberately blew it up in 1941 rather than leave it to the Germans.

Tractor plants at Stalingrad and Kharkov, the White Sea–Baltic Canal (the Belomorkanal, Chapter 8, dug almost entirely by Gulag prisoners with hand tools; its economic value turned out to be limited because, hurried and built shallow to hit a propaganda deadline, it was too shallow for the larger ships that would have justified it), the Moscow Metro (Chapter 9), and the Second and Third Five-Year Plans that followed: the physical transformation was not propaganda.

Soviet industrial output, especially in heavy industry, steel, coal, machinery, electricity, grew at rates that, in the depths of the global Great Depression when capitalist economies were contracting, looked to many foreign observers like proof that planning worked.

This is the period when significant numbers of Western intellectuals visited and came back believers; the American journalist Lincoln Steffens, after an earlier 1919 trip, had already given the genre its most quoted line, usually rendered "I have seen the future, and it works" (the exact wording and even what he was describing are debated, but the sentiment became the template for a decade of credulous visitors).
It is also the period when the famine those same visitors mostly did not see was killing millions a few hundred miles away.
The cross-civilizational comparison is the way to see what was actually happening, so make it directly.

Every industrializing society extracted a brutal price from someone: Britain's first Industrial Revolution ran on enclosed peasants, child labor, and slave-grown cotton; the American Gilded Age ran on immigrant labor, company towns, and the violent suppression of strikes; Meiji Japan (the modern-Japan narrative) industrialized fast by squeezing its own peasantry with the Matsukata land tax, driving small farmers into tenancy and their daughters into the textile mills.

The speed comparison is worth pinning exactly: Britain's industrial revolution took roughly eighty years, Germany's catch-up about sixty, and Japan's compressed catch-up, the fastest the world had yet seen, about thirty-eight years (roughly 1872–1910).
The Soviet First Five-Year Plans demolished even Japan's record, compressing a comparable transformation into roughly a decade.

What was distinctive about the Soviet case was not that industrialization had a human cost, which is universal, nor merely the speed, but the direction of the coercion: Japan achieved its compression with land taxes and rural-to-factory migration and built constitutional structures and a (narrowly held) private economy alongside it, whereas the Soviet state achieved its faster compression by consciously deciding, in a few years, to take the food and labor of its own peasants by force, abolish private property entirely, and use prison labor as a planned economic input.

The two are the twentieth century's great state-led industrialization templates, and the moral distance between Japan's severe cost and the Soviet famine-and-camp cost is the whole point of putting them side by side.
The Soviet achievement was real, and so was the fact that it was paid for in a famine and a camp system.

The honest sentence is that the USSR industrialized faster than any society had ever done and at a price in its own people's lives that no industrializing society had ever deliberately and knowingly chosen in so concentrated a form.
The regime needed the workers to want it, so it built a cult of the worker.

The icon was Alexei Stakhanov, a coal miner who in 1935 was credited with cutting many times his shift quota of coal in a single night (the precise multiple, around fourteen, varies in the sources, which is itself revealing).

The feat was a staged set-piece: Stakhanov was given the best seam, a dedicated team of helpers to clear and prop behind him, and uninterrupted power, while the propaganda stripped all of that out and presented the tonnage as one hero's solitary muscle.

The Stakhanovite movement that followed turned record-breaking output into a mass campaign, with Stakhanovite workers rewarded with apartments, bonuses, and fame, and used to ratchet up production norms for everyone else, which made the movement deeply resented on the factory floor even as it was celebrated in the press.

The cult of the heroic worker, the labor medal, the production record as a form of patriotism, was one of the genuine emotional engines of the system: for a young person from a mud-floored village, the new world of the factory, the night school, the city, the literacy campaign (the Likbez, the drive that took Soviet literacy from a minority to near-universal within a generation, a real and enormous achievement), the engineering diploma, and a place in a society that told you that you were building the future, was not a lie.

Millions experienced the 1930s as liberation and ascent at the very same time that millions of others experienced them as deportation and starvation, and both experiences were true, often in the same family.
That simultaneity is the truest single thing this book can tell you about the Stalin era, and it is why it remains so impossible to summarize.
What did the furnace actually buy, and what did it not?

It bought the industrial base, especially in metals, machine tools, and armaments, that allowed the USSR to lose almost its entire pre-war heavy industry to German occupation in 1941 and still out-produce Germany in tanks, artillery, and aircraft by 1943 (Chapter 12).

Without the brutal industrialization of the 1930s, the USSR very probably loses the war, and that is the core of the regime's self-justification and a serious argument that has to be granted its weight.

The model also became an export: newly independent India under Nehru, looking for a way to industrialize fast without colonial capital, consciously modeled its First Five-Year Plan (1951) on Soviet planning, took the "commanding heights" of heavy industry into the public sector, and built showpiece steel mills like Bhilai with direct Soviet collaboration (the modern-India narrative).

The Soviet furnace, in other words, was watched and copied across the decolonizing world as proof that a poor country could industrialize on its own terms, which is part of why its later stagnation (Chapter 16) mattered far beyond the USSR.
What it did not buy was a sustainable model.

The command economy was superb at the single task it was designed for, the crash mobilization of resources for heavy industry and war, and structurally bad at almost everything else: at consumer goods, at agriculture (which never recovered from collectivization and would import grain by the 1970s), at quality, at innovation once the catch-up phase was over, and at responding to what people actually wanted.

The very features that made it win the 1930s and the war, central command, output targets, the suppression of the market, the indifference to consumer demand, are the same features that made it stagnate and ultimately fail by the 1980s (Chapters 16 and 18).
The furnace built the thing that broke Hitler.
It also built the machine that, having no internal correction mechanism, could only run until it ran out.
While it ran, it also ran a parallel system whose entire economic logic was the unpaid labor of prisoners, and the regime had a near-limitless way of supplying them.
That system, and the Terror that fed it, is Chapter 8.

chapters.title: The Vanishing
sentences: This is the chapter the introduction warned you about most.

The Gulag and the Great Terror are the events where the gap between the Soviet promise and the Soviet machine becomes total, where the body counts are most fiercely contested, and where the writing rules of this whole project, never state a contested claim as fact, give ranges with the reason for the range, distinguish archival consensus from Cold War estimate, are not optional refinements but the only honest way to write the sentences at all.

So read this chapter knowing that the numbers are estimates, that the estimates have moved, and that the movement of the estimates is itself a story about how a totalitarian state hides its dead and how, partially, they were found.
First, the system, because "Gulag" is used loosely and should not be.

Gulag is an acronym, the Glavnoe Upravlenie Lagerei, the "Main Administration of Camps," the bureaucratic agency that ran the Soviet forced-labor camp system; by extension the word came to mean the whole archipelago of camps, labor colonies, special settlements, and prisons.

It existed under Lenin in embryo (the early camps of the civil war, Chapter 3) and was expanded enormously by Stalin from around 1929 as both a punishment system and, explicitly, an economic one: prisoners were a planned labor input for projects in places free workers would not go: the timber of the far north, the gold of Kolyma (a region of the Arctic far east so remote it could be reached only by ship through the Pacific port of Magadan, with winter temperatures below minus 40 and a survival rate so low it became the Gulag's byword for a death sentence), the nickel of Norilsk (a city built by prisoners above the Arctic Circle in Siberia, hundreds of miles from any railway), and the White Sea–Baltic Canal (Chapter 7).

The agency that ran it, the political police, went through a sequence of names you should keep straight because they recur for the rest of the book: Cheka (1917, Chapter 3) became the GPU, then OGPU, then in 1934 was folded into the NKVD (the People's Commissariat of Internal Affairs, the body that ran both the Gulag and the Terror), which after the war became the MGB and finally, in 1954, the KGB (Chapter 13).
Different initials, one continuous institution and one continuous function: the regime's instrument for doing to its own population what an army does to an enemy's.
The scale of the Gulag is the textbook example of why this narrative gives ranges.

For decades the only sources were the testimony of survivors and émigrés and the literary reconstruction of Solzhenitsyn's The Gulag Archipelago (1973), which conveyed an overwhelming, possibly tens-of-millions impression and was, the author said himself, "an experiment in literary investigation," a moral and documentary monument but not a body count.
When the Soviet archives opened after 1991, historians could for the first time count the NKVD's own internal records: the American scholar J.

Arch Getty (a leading "revisionist" social historian of the Terror) with collaborators published analyses of the camp statistics, the demographer Viktor Zemskov worked through the NKVD population registers, and, separately, the Russian organization Memorial built its victim databases from the same opening archives.

Those records show, in round terms, that roughly 18 million people passed through the Gulag camps and colonies over its full Stalin-era existence, with several million more in the "special settlements" (the deported peasants, Chapter 6, and later deported nationalities); that the population in the camps at any one time peaked at around two and a half million in the early 1950s; and that recorded deaths in the camp system over the whole period were on the order of 1.6 to 1.7 million, with the toll spiking horrifically in the war years 1941–1945 when prisoners were the first to be starved.
These archival figures are lower than the highest Cold War estimates and are now broadly accepted as the documentary baseline by most historians of all political stripes.

They are also, and this must be said in the same breath, contested at the edges and not the whole story: the archival death figure counts deaths inside the camps as recorded by the camps, and does not straightforwardly include those shot outright (counted separately, below), those who died in transit, those whom camps released when they were near death so the death would fall outside the camp's recorded mortality (a practice documented in survivor testimony and in some camp records, though its scale cannot be quantified), or the full toll of the special settlements.

The serious modern argument is not between "tens of millions" and "almost none." It is between historians who take the archival figure as essentially the answer and those who argue, with reason, that the archive undercounts a system designed to not record its own worst outcomes.

This narrative's position is the field's mainstream one: roughly 18 million through the system, recorded camp deaths in the high hundreds of thousands to under two million, the true mortality somewhat higher than the recorded figure for documented structural reasons, and the lower-than-the-legend total in no way reducing the moral weight of a state running a slave economy on its own citizens.

The Gulag and the Terror were not two systems but one circuit: the camps were the economic engine that needed bodies, and the Terror was, among other things, the machinery that supplied them on an industrial schedule, which is why the next part of the story is about the trigger that turned the flow up.
The Terror has a precise trigger, a precise machinery, and a precise, archivally documented core number that you should hold onto.

On 1 December 1934, Sergei Kirov, the Party boss of Leningrad, a Politburo member and a popular figure both among the Party rank and file (where he was seen as a more moderate, conciliatory voice than Stalin) and as a public face of the regime, was assassinated by a lone gunman. (The Politburo was the Political Bureau, the small inner committee, around a dozen men, that actually ran the USSR.) Stalin used the murder as the pretext for emergency laws accelerating political trials and executions, and a decades-long suspicion, voiced by Khrushchev in 1956 and by many historians since, holds that Stalin himself had Kirov killed to remove a potential rival and manufacture a pretext.

State this honestly: the suspicion is widespread and not unreasonable given what followed, but it has never been proven, the post-Soviet investigations did not establish Stalin's hand, and the current scholarly weight is cautious, the murder was the pretext for the Terror beyond any doubt; that Stalin ordered the murder itself is a credible hypothesis, not an established fact, and this narrative will not present it as one.
What is established is what came after.

The Great Terror, also called the Yezhovshchina after Nikolai Yezhov (pronounced "yuh-ZHOFF"), the unusually short NKVD chief who ran it at its 1937–38 peak and was then himself arrested in 1939 and shot in 1940, the executioner consumed by the machine like everyone else, which was itself part of the pattern, ran principally from 1936 to 1938 and had two faces the public mostly saw only one of.

The visible face was the Moscow show trials (1936, 1937, 1938), in which the surviving Old Bolsheviks, Zinoviev, Kamenev, Bukharin, the men who had made the revolution alongside Lenin (Chapter 5), were put before cameras and foreign journalists and made to confess, in elaborate, scripted, physically and psychologically coerced detail, to grotesque and impossible conspiracies, to having been Trotskyite-fascist wreckers and assassins in the pay of foreign powers, and were then shot.
The trials were theater, and their function was to rewrite the revolution's history so that every founder except Stalin had always been a traitor, and to terrorize the elite.

The purge of the Red Army in 1937–38 was part of the same logic: roughly the entire top tier of the Soviet officer corps, including Marshal Tukhachevsky (the man who had stormed Kronstadt, Chapter 4), was shot or imprisoned on fabricated charges of a German-linked military plot, a self-inflicted decapitation of the army's command that the Wehrmacht would exploit savagely in 1941 (Chapter 11).
The hidden face was far larger and was unknown to the public and to most historians until the archives opened, and it is where the documented core number lives.
The show trials killed dozens of famous men.
The mass operations killed hundreds of thousands of ordinary, anonymous ones.

From mid-1937 the NKVD ran secret operations, above all the notorious Order No. 00447, that set regional quotas, literal numerical targets, for the number of people in each province to be arrested and either shot or sent to the Gulag, with categories like "former kulaks," clergy, ex-tsarist officials, and "anti-Soviet elements." Who fell into a category was decided by NKVD officers working from existing surveillance files, old kulak and clergy lists, the registries of former tsarist officials, neighbors' and colleagues' denunciations, and confessions extracted under torture that named further suspects, so the operation fed itself.

The parallel "national operations" targeted people of Polish, German, and other diaspora origins identified largely by surname, recorded nationality in internal documents, and place of origin, on the blanket assumption that an ethnic tie to a foreign state made one a potential agent.
Local NKVD offices, like enterprises with a plan to overfulfill (Chapter 7), frequently requested permission to exceed their execution quotas.

The archival documentation of these operations is the firmest number in this entire chapter: NKVD records reconstructed by Zemskov and others show that in 1937–1938 these operations produced roughly 1.5 to 1.7 million arrests and on the order of three-quarters of a million executions (the central archival figure is about 681,000 recorded death sentences carried out, with the upper end of the range, near 750,000, including related operations; it is a documented count from the regime's own books, not a Cold War estimate or an émigré projection), the vast majority anonymous citizens, in roughly two years.

That figure, three-quarters of a million executions in two years, is accepted across the historiographical spectrum, from "revisionists" to their hardest critics, because it comes from the regime's own internal accounting.
It is one of the most concentrated state killings of a peacetime population by its own government in recorded history.
The cross-civilizational comparison is unavoidable and is the way to feel the years, so make it plainly and without flippancy.
The Great Terror's peak, 1937–1938, runs in the same calendar years as the New Deal in the United States, the Munich crisis in Europe, and the consolidation of the Nazi regime in Germany.

While Franklin Roosevelt was running work-relief programs and the U.S. argued about the Supreme Court, and while in 1937 the Indian National Congress was winning the first provincial elections under the Government of India Act and Gandhi was building a mass movement for independence on the principle of nonviolent civil disobedience, the Soviet state, a regime claiming to embody the will of the working class, was shooting on the order of a thousand of its own citizens, mostly workers and peasants, a day.

Nazi Germany in those same pre-war years was building its repressive apparatus and its early concentration camps but had not yet begun mass killing on anything like this scale; the Soviet peacetime state in 1937–38 was, by raw count of citizens deliberately executed by their own government, killing on a scale the Nazi state would not reach until the war and the Holocaust.

The comparison is not made to rank atrocities, which is obscene, but because the simultaneity is the only way an American reader can locate these years on a timeline they already feel: the Terror is not ancient or exotic; it is contemporaneous with their grandparents' Depression.
The chapter has to name who did this, and the answer is not only Stalin.

It could not have happened without his direct, documented authorization: he and other Politburo members personally signed the rasstrelnye spiski, lists of names submitted for sentencing in batches that ran to the thousands, marking them for shooting; those signed lists physically survive in the Party archive, so this is documentation, not inference.

But it also ran on hundreds of thousands of denunciations by ordinary citizens, the letter to the NKVD reporting a neighbor's careless remark, the colleague accusing a rival to take his apartment or his job, the subordinate denouncing a boss before the boss could denounce him, on careerism and settled scores and terror feeding terror.
That ordinary participation is the genuinely disturbing finding of the social history and the part a simple "a tyrant did it" story misses.
How we know all of this is the chapter's last and most important point, and it has a single embodiment.

The West's picture was shaped first by Conquest's The Great Terror (1968), written before any archive and attacked for decades as exaggeration, then by Solzhenitsyn's literature, then, after 1991, by the historians who counted the opened files.

But the fullest record was built by Memorial, the Russian organization that spent more than thirty years assembling the name-by-name databases of the shot, restoring an identity to each anonymous number, and that the Russian state shut down by court order in 2021–2022 while prosecuting the people who had kept the record.
Denial, then literature, then the opened archive, then the archive closed again and the rememberers in the dock: the life and death of one organization is this book's second thesis entire.
The society that lived inside this machine, and the culture it produced and devoured, is Chapter 9.

chapters.title: The New Soviet Man
sentences: So far this book has mostly described what the Soviet state did to people.

This chapter is about what it tried to make them into, because the USSR was not only a coercive machine; it was a project to manufacture a new kind of human being, the New Soviet Man (and Woman), collectivist, atheist, literate, technically minded, free of the old loyalties of religion, nation, and family, devoted to the building of socialism.

The promise and the machine run through every part of this story too: real liberation, especially in literacy, in opportunity for the lowborn, and at first in the position of women, tangled together with the destruction of independent thought, the gutting of religion, and the breaking of the artists who were supposed to be the project's voice.
Take the Church first, because the assault on it was the clearest statement of intent.

The Russian Orthodox Church had been the spiritual arm of the tsarist state, and the Bolsheviks were militant atheists who held religion to be, in Marx's phrase, "the opium of the people," a tool of class oppression to be eliminated.
From 1917 the regime separated church from state, seized church property, and during the 1921 famine confiscated church valuables.

From the late 1920s the campaign became destruction: thousands of churches, mosques, and synagogues were closed, demolished, or turned into warehouses, clubs, or "museums of atheism"; tens of thousands of clergy of all faiths were shot or sent to the Gulag, the Orthodox clergy among the hardest-hit single occupational groups in the Terror; and an organization with the candidly aggressive name the League of Militant Godless ran mass anti-religious propaganda, blew up cathedrals, and promised the elimination of religion within a five-year plan.

The supreme symbol was the Cathedral of Christ the Saviour, the largest Orthodox cathedral in Russia, dynamited in Moscow in 1931 to clear ground for a planned Palace of the Soviets, a colossal tower designed to be crowned by an enormous statue of Lenin, that was designed, partly excavated, and never built; the hole eventually became, in a detail that is almost too neat, a heated open-air swimming pool, and the cathedral was rebuilt after 1991.

The regime never did eliminate belief; it drove it underground, and in the war, needing every source of national morale against the German invasion, it would make a desperate, temporary peace with the Church, reopening parishes in exchange for patriotic support (Chapter 12), and then, under Khrushchev, attack it again (Chapter 15).

But the intent, the engineered abolition of God by the state, is one of the purest examples in the book of the promise (a rational, liberated humanity) and the machine (the secret police closing the village church) being the same act.
Now women, where the story is the book's thesis in miniature, real emancipation followed by retrenchment.
The early Bolshevik program on women was, for 1918, among the most radical on earth.

It legalized divorce on demand and civil marriage, decriminalized abortion in 1920 (one of the first states anywhere to make it legal and free on request, well ahead of most of the world), declared full legal equality of the sexes, and set up the Zhenotdel, the Party's women's department, led by Alexandra Kollontai (the revolutionary of Chapter 4, who held a cabinet post in the first Soviet government, one of the very first women anywhere to do so, and later served as a Soviet ambassador, among the first women to lead a diplomatic mission), to draw women into public life, literacy, and work.
The aim was explicitly to dissolve the patriarchal family as an economic unit.
Then it reversed.

Under Stalin from the mid-1930s, in the name of stability and population growth, abortion was recriminalized (1936), divorce was made difficult and expensive, the family was rehabilitated as a "socialist" institution, motherhood was decorated with medals for bearing many children, and the Zhenotdel was abolished.

What endured was the double burden that became the lasting reality of the Soviet woman's life: she was genuinely brought into the workforce in vast numbers, as engineers, doctors, factory workers, and after the war's male slaughter (Chapter 12) as the demographic backbone of the labor force, with a real and unusual-for-the-era presence in technical professions, and she still carried essentially all the housework and childcare in an economy that never produced enough housing, food, or consumer goods to lighten it.
Liberation into the workforce, not liberation from the second shift.
That is the honest summary, and it held until 1991.
The same pattern of liberation-then-clampdown ran through the dimension that quietly outlived everything else and detonated at the end (Chapter 20): the nationalities.

The USSR inherited the most multi-ethnic state on earth, well over a hundred nationalities, and the New Soviet Man was supposed to be made out of all of them, which made what the regime did with national identity central, not incidental, to the whole project.

Early Soviet policy was strikingly, deliberately the opposite of Russification: korenizatsiya ("indigenization") in the 1920s actively promoted local languages, schools, and national Communist cadres in the non-Russian republics, on the theory that national feeling, given cultural expression, would dissolve into socialist identity.

It went as far as commissioning linguists to create written alphabets, in Latin script, for dozens of languages that had never had a written form, so that previously unwritten peoples could be made literate in their own tongue (the same alphabets were forcibly switched to Cyrillic in the late 1930s when the policy reversed).

It was, the historian Terry Martin influentially argued (in The Affirmative Action Empire, 2001, a major post-archival study of Soviet nationalities policy), the world's first "affirmative action empire." Under Stalin this too reversed: from the mid-1930s came the rehabilitation of Russian as the binding language and Russian history as a shared heroic past, the purging of national Communist elites as "bourgeois nationalists," and, at its most savage, the wartime deportation of entire nations, the Chechens, Ingush, Crimean Tatars, Volga Germans, Kalmyks, and others, every man, woman, and child loaded onto trains and dumped in Central Asia and Siberia on collective charges of disloyalty, with death rates in transit and exile that for some peoples approached or exceeded a quarter (Chapter 12).

The federal structure the regime built, ethnically defined republics with paper rights to secede, married to a reality of Moscow control, was a contradiction it managed by force for decades and could not manage without it.
The arts are where you can watch the New Soviet Man being written, and watch the writers being destroyed for not writing him correctly.

The 1920s saw a genuine explosion of revolutionary modernism that believed it was inventing the art of the future: Constructivism (an avant-garde movement that wanted art to be functional industrial design rather than decoration, building, posters, and typography as engineering for the new society), the montage cinema of Sergei Eisenstein (whose Battleship Potemkin, 1925, is still studied in every film school), the agitational poetry of Vladimir Mayakovsky.

Then in 1932–1934 the state imposed Socialist Realism as the single compulsory doctrine for all art: art must be realistic in form, optimistic, accessible, and ideologically correct, depicting socialist reality "in its revolutionary development," which in practice meant heroic workers, wise leaders, and happy harvests, with experimentation condemned as "bourgeois formalism." The novelist Maxim Gorky was installed as figurehead of the new, all-controlling Union of Soviet Writers, membership in which was the precondition for being published at all and expulsion from which could be a death sentence.
What happened to four people is the clearest possible illustration of the machine.

Vladimir Mayakovsky, the revolution's loudest poetic voice, who had thrown himself into Bolshevik agitprop with total sincerity, shot himself in 1930, disillusioned and hounded, and was then posthumously canonized by the state he had despaired of.

Osip Mandelstam, one of the century's great Russian poets, wrote a sixteen-line epigram mocking Stalin (the "Kremlin mountaineer," with "fingers fat as grubs"), recited it to a few trusted friends, was denounced anyway, and died in a transit camp near Vladivostok in 1938; his widow Nadezhda preserved his work by memorizing it.

Anna Akhmatova, the most revered living Russian poet, was unpublished for decades and spent the Terror standing month after month in the prison queues outside the Leningrad jails where her son was held, composing in her head the cycle Requiem, which trusted friends memorized line by line and burned, because to keep a copy on paper was lethal; it could not be published in the USSR in full until the 1980s.

Dmitri Shostakovich, the country's foremost composer, was denounced in Pravda in 1936 (on Stalin's apparent prompting, after the dictator walked out of his opera), lived for years with a packed suitcase by the door for the night the NKVD came, and answered with the Fifth Symphony of 1937, presented in the press as "a Soviet artist's creative reply to just criticism," its triumphant finale heard by some as capitulation and by others as buried fury.

Whether Shostakovich was a secret dissident or a survivor saying what he had to is genuinely and unresolvably debated, and the more honest reading is that the binary is wrong: he was a man composing under a gun, and the music holds both things at once. (The same machine claimed others by the same logic.

Eisenstein ended up making the historical epics Stalin commissioned; Mikhail Bulgakov wrote his masterpiece The Master and Margarita in a desk drawer, unpublished until 1966–67, decades after his death, Chapter 17.) The avant-garde that thought it was building the future became the state's decorator or its corpse.
So pull the chapter's thesis together.
The New Soviet Man was not purely a lie.
The Likbez literacy campaign (Chapter 7) genuinely took one of Europe's least literate populations to near-universal literacy in a generation.

The Pioneers and the Komsomol were a single escalator: the Pioneers took children from about ten to fifteen in a mass scouting-style organization, the Komsomol (the Young Communist League) carried teenagers and young adults from about fourteen to twenty-eight, and membership was effectively the path to higher education, a career, and eventually the Party.
They gave millions from the bottom of the old order a structured route upward.

The Semashko system (named for Nikolai Semashko, the first Soviet health commissar, who designed it) built free, universal, basic healthcare across a vast poor country, with real gains in life expectancy and the conquest of epidemic disease, an achievement that impressed even hostile observers.
A peasant's son could become an engineer, a marshal, a cosmonaut; that mobility was real and was felt as deliverance.

And the same project required the destruction of the church, the recriminalization of abortion in the name of population growth (Stalin's regime wanted births, not the autonomy the 1920s had granted), the deportation of nations, and a literature whose greatest works had to be hidden in drawers and memorized in prison queues.

The point of this chapter is not to total the ledger; it is that there is no single ledger, that the liberation and the suffocation were the same program, and that any account that gives you only one is propaganda, in whichever direction it leans.

The hole where the Cathedral of Christ the Saviour had stood is the chapter in one image: a church dynamited for a tower to a new humanity, the tower never built, the pit turned into a swimming pool, and, after 1991, the cathedral built back, as if to insist the whole thing could be undone, which is its own kind of forgetting.
Having built this society, the regime now had to defend it against the one force in the world more violent than itself.
The road to that war is Chapter 10.

chapters.title: The Pact
sentences: In August 1939 the Soviet Union, the self-proclaimed homeland of world revolution and the implacable enemy of fascism, signed a friendship treaty with Nazi Germany and then jointly invaded and partitioned Poland with it.

To understand how the country that lost twenty-seven million people fighting Hitler had, two years earlier, shaken his foreign minister's hand over a carved-up map of Eastern Europe, you have to follow the foreign policy of the 1930s, which is a story of a regime that genuinely feared encirclement, genuinely wanted an anti-Nazi alliance, did not get one, and then made the most cynical and consequential deal of the century.
This is also a chapter where the moral accounting is contested, and the narrative will say so.

Begin with the Communist International, the Comintern, founded in Moscow in 1919 as the general staff of world revolution: an organization of Communist parties in other countries that took their line, and in practice their orders, from Moscow.

The control was concrete, not figurative: Moscow funded the foreign parties, trained their cadres in Soviet schools, approved or removed their leaderships, and issued binding strategic "lines" that every member party was required to follow on pain of expulsion.

That reach extended into the colonized world as well as Europe; the Communist Party of India, founded in 1920, also took its line from the Comintern, which repeatedly ordered Communists in colonies to treat the nationalist independence movements (in India, Gandhi's Congress) as bourgeois rivals rather than allies, a directive that often left them isolated from the very mass movements they hoped to lead.

For the regime's whole life, Soviet foreign policy ran on two tracks that often contradicted each other, the state's national interest (borders, security, trade) and the Comintern's revolutionary mission, and Stalin increasingly subordinated the second to the first, which is one of the things that made the 1939 pact possible.

In the early 1930s the Comintern's line was disastrous in Germany: it ordered Communists to treat the moderate Social Democrats, not the Nazis, as the main enemy, branding them "social fascists" on the theory that reformist socialists who propped up capitalism were a more insidious obstacle to revolution than open fascists (whose rule, some even argued, would discredit capitalism and hasten the Communist turn).
This split the German left and eased Hitler's path to power in 1933, a catastrophic misjudgment Moscow then reversed.

The reversal was the Popular Front: from 1935 the Comintern ordered Communists everywhere to ally with all anti-fascist forces, including liberals and social democrats, and the USSR pursued collective security, seeking alliances with Britain and France against Germany.
The test case was Spain.

When a fascist-backed military coup against the elected Spanish Republic touched off the Spanish Civil War (1936–1939), the USSR was the only major power to send the Republic substantial military aid: weapons, advisors, and, organized through the Comintern, the International Brigades, tens of thousands of volunteers (Communists, socialists, and antifascists from across Europe and the Americas, including Americans in the Lincoln Battalion) who came to fight for the Republic.
Britain and France stayed neutral while Germany and Italy openly backed Franco.

Soviet involvement in Spain was real anti-fascism and also a Soviet power play: the NKVD operated inside Republican Spain, arresting, "disappearing," and in some cases assassinating Trotskyists and anarchists it deemed deviationist, a brutal duality George Orwell, who fought there, witnessed and wrote into Homage to Catalonia.
The Republic lost.
The lesson Stalin drew was that the Western democracies would not actually fight fascism, which fed directly into 1939.
There was a second front nobody in the West watched, and it mattered.
In 1938–1939 the USSR fought a large, undeclared border war with Imperial Japan in the Far East.

At Khalkhin Gol (also called Nomonhan) in Mongolia in 1939, Soviet forces under a then-obscure general named Georgy Zhukov decisively crushed a Japanese army, a battle that is barely known in the West and was strategically enormous: it convinced Japan that war with the USSR was a losing proposition and pushed Japanese strategy southward toward the Pacific and the United States rather than north into Siberia, which two years later let Stalin move his Siberian divisions west to save Moscow (Chapter 11).
Hold Zhukov's name; he becomes the central Soviet soldier of the war.
Now the pact, told straight.

Through 1939 the USSR negotiated, slowly and with mutual distrust, for an anti-German alliance with Britain and France, who were lukewarm, slow, and unwilling to grant the Soviet demand to move troops through Poland (which Poland, with good historical reason, refused).
Simultaneously, secretly, Stalin opened a channel to Berlin.

On 23 August 1939 the Soviet foreign minister Vyacheslav Molotov and the German foreign minister Joachim von Ribbentrop signed, in Moscow, the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact, a public ten-year non-aggression treaty and, attached to it, a Secret Protocol whose existence the USSR flatly denied for fifty years, insisting the published copies circulating in the West were Western forgeries, until a Soviet commission under Gorbachev finally admitted in 1989 that it was real, dividing Eastern Europe into German and Soviet "spheres of influence": Germany would take western Poland and a free hand against the West; the USSR would take eastern Poland, the Baltic states (Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania), Finland, and Bessarabia.
Nine days later, on 1 September 1939, Germany invaded Poland from the west and the Second World War began.

On 17 September the USSR invaded Poland from the east, per the secret deal, presenting it not as an invasion but as the protective "liberation" of the ethnic Ukrainians and Belarusians who lived in eastern Poland (the borderlands left on the Polish side of the 1921 line, Chapter 3), an argument that recast a partition with Hitler as the reunification of kindred Soviet peoples.
The two totalitarian states partitioned Poland between them and held a joint victory parade at Brest.

This is not Soviet propaganda's version and it is not contested in outline: the pact, the secret protocol, the joint invasion are documented, the protocol's text recovered, its existence finally admitted by the dying USSR itself.

Stalin's defenders, then and in some scholarship since, argue the pact was a defensible if cynical bid for time, that the West had just appeased Hitler at Munich and could not be relied on, and that the USSR bought nearly two years and a strategic buffer it badly needed before Barbarossa.

Critics argue it freed Hitler to fight a one-front war, supplied Germany with Soviet grain and oil right up to the invasion, and shares moral responsibility for the war's outbreak and for Poland's destruction.

This is a genuine, unresolved historical and political argument, intensely so today, when the present Russian state defends the pact and the European Parliament has condemned it as a co-cause of the war; this narrative's job is to give you the documented facts, the secret protocol, the joint invasion, the deliveries to Germany, and to flag clearly that the evaluation (necessary buffer versus enabling crime) is contested and politically live, not to hand you a verdict dressed as fact.
The Soviet sphere was occupied with the machine's usual methods.

The Baltic states, Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania, three small countries that had been independent since 1918, were first forced in 1939 to accept Soviet military bases, then in summer 1940 occupied outright, presented with rigged "elections," and annexed as new Soviet republics.

The occupation came with mass arrests and the deportation of tens of thousands of the Baltic elites, officials, officers, professionals, and their families, to Siberia in the weeks around the German invasion.

This 1940 annexation is not a footnote: the refusal of the Baltic peoples ever to accept it is what makes them the first to break away fifty years later (Chapters 17 and 20), and the legal argument that the annexation was always illegal is central to how three of the fifteen successor states understand themselves.

In occupied eastern Poland the NKVD carried out the Katyn massacre: in the spring of 1940, on a written Politburo order signed by Stalin and others, roughly 22,000 captured Polish officers, police, and members of the educated elite were shot and buried in mass graves at several sites (the killings happened at three main locations and the bodies in several burial grounds; "Katyn," the forest near Smolensk where the German army first uncovered graves in 1943, became the name for the whole crime), an attempt to decapitate the Polish nation.
State the documentation precisely because it is a model case of the contested-attribution problem and how it resolves.
For fifty years the USSR blamed the massacre on the Germans; the Germans had blamed the Soviets when they found the graves in 1943; the West largely looked away for alliance reasons.
The truth was established when, in 1990 and 1992, the dying and then post-Soviet Russian state released the actual Politburo execution order and admitted NKVD responsibility.

So Katyn is no longer a "Soviets or Nazis" mystery, it is a documented Soviet crime with the signed order in the open, and it is also a textbook example of why this book insists on distinguishing the denied from the documented: the same act was a lie, then a stalemate of accusations, then, when the archive opened, a confessed fact, and the present Russian state has since moved back toward minimizing it.
The sphere's last installment misfired and is the chapter's grim foreshadowing.
In November 1939 the USSR, having failed to extract territorial concessions, invaded Finland: the Winter War.
The expected quick conquest turned into a humiliation.

The vastly outnumbered Finns, in white camouflage on skis, inflicted enormous casualties on a Red Army whose officer corps Stalin had just shot in the purge (Chapter 8) and whose performance was so poor that it advertised, to the entire world and especially to Hitler, that the Soviet military was a hollow giant.

The USSR eventually won by sheer mass, took the territory it wanted, and was expelled from the League of Nations (the post-WWI international body, the UN's weak predecessor, then near collapse, so the expulsion was symbolic more than practical) as an aggressor, but it had bled perhaps a hundred thousand or more dead against a tiny opponent and exposed a broken command.
The strategic damage was the lasting cost: Hitler watched the Winter War and concluded that the USSR could be knocked over with one hard kick.
The Soviet high command absorbed the same lesson the other way, in something like silence, and began a frantic, incomplete reform of the army it had just decapitated in the purge.
It would not be enough by June 1941.
Twenty-two months after signing the pact, Hitler tried his kick.
Chapter 11 is what happened.

chapters.title: The Catastrophe
sentences: On 22 June 1941, the largest invasion in the history of warfare crossed into the Soviet Union, and within six months the USSR had lost more territory, more soldiers, and more people than any nation in modern history had ever lost and survived.
The Soviet war, which Soviet and Russian usage calls the Great Patriotic War, is the single most important event in the country's history.

It was the regime's near-death, its supreme achievement, and the source of the legitimating myth that held the system together for its last fifty years and that still saturates Russian politics today.
It takes two chapters.
This one is the catastrophe of 1941.
Chapter 12 is the turn.

The invasion was Operation Barbarossa, roughly three million German and Axis troops attacking along a front from the Baltic to the Black Sea, the goal not just conquest but, in the explicit Nazi planning, the enslavement and partial extermination of the Slavic population and the seizure of Lebensraum ("living space," the Nazi doctrine that Germans were entitled to depopulate and colonize the lands east of them) and resources.
The intent was written down: the Hunger Plan, drafted before the invasion, deliberately calculated the death by starvation of tens of millions of Soviet civilians to feed the German army and Reich.

This is essential context: the war in the East was, on the German side, designed as a war of racial annihilation, not a conventional campaign, which is why it killed in proportions no Western front approached and why the Soviet population had, in the end, no option of a survivable surrender.
The invasion was also, on the Soviet side, a self-inflicted disaster of preparation.
Stalin had received a flood of intelligence warnings of the coming attack, from his own spies, from Britain, from defectors, and had dismissed them.

His reasoning, as far as it can be reconstructed, was that Hitler would not be insane enough to open an eastern front while Britain was still undefeated, that the British warnings were a plot to provoke a Soviet–German war that would rescue Britain, and that visible Soviet mobilization would itself hand Hitler a pretext; so he forbade his commanders to ready their forces for fear of "provoking" Germany, and the conviction was largely his own, held against the judgment of several of his own commanders.

The Red Army was caught with its aircraft parked in rows on forward airfields (most of the air force was destroyed on the ground in days), its command shattered by the 1937–38 purge (Chapter 8) that had killed most of its experienced senior officers, and its forces deployed too far forward.

What is solidly attested is this: Stalin did not address the nation himself for eleven days (the early broadcasts were made by Molotov), and around the end of June he withdrew to his dacha and was, for a day or two, not directing the government.

The more dramatic vignettes, that he was catatonic, that he assumed the Politburo had come to arrest him when they arrived to fetch him back, come largely from Khrushchev's and others' post-Stalin memoirs, which were written by men with reasons to portray him as having broken, and should be held more loosely than the documented gap itself.
The scale of the 1941 catastrophe is almost impossible to convey, so anchor it.

In the first weeks the Germans encircled and destroyed Soviet armies in clean sweeps of a scale almost without parallel: at the Kiev encirclement in September, roughly half a million or more Soviet troops were killed or captured (German records claimed about 665,000 prisoners; modern Soviet-based estimates of prisoners taken are lower, in the range of 450,000–540,000 plus the killed), among the largest single encirclements in the history of warfare.
By the end of 1941 the USSR had lost the equivalent of its entire pre-war army; total Soviet military dead and captured in 1941 ran into the millions.
What happened to the prisoners deserves its own paragraph, because it was one of the largest and least-remembered mass killings of the war.
Over the whole war the Germans captured something on the order of five to five and a half million Soviet soldiers (the totals vary by source and by how the chaotic 1941 surrenders are counted).
They were not treated as prisoners of war in any conventional sense.

In line with the war's annihilationist design, they were herded into open-air pens, marched without food, and deliberately left to starve, freeze, and die of disease through the winter of 1941–42, with many later worked to death as slave labor.

By the most-cited estimates roughly three million of them died in German captivity, the great majority in that first winter, a death rate of well over half, vastly worse than that of Western Allied POWs in German hands and a deliberate policy, not negligence.
The Germans took Ukraine, Belarus, and the Baltic, and stood at the gates of Leningrad and Moscow before the year was out.
By any normal measure the country had been defeated.
Three things stopped it from being true, and they are the substance of this chapter.
The first was the evacuation of industry, one of the most extraordinary logistical feats ever performed by any state.

As the Germans advanced, the Soviet regime physically dismantled over 1,500 entire factories, often in days and under air attack, by mobilizing the workforce itself, the machinists, their families, and conscripted labor unbolting their own plants, loading the machine tools and blueprints onto requisitioned freight trains, and shipping them a thousand miles and more east, beyond the Urals into Siberia and Central Asia, where the same workers reassembled them, sometimes under open sky in the snow before walls and roofs existed, and restarted production within months.
The tank that fought at Kursk in 1943 was often built in a factory that in 1941 had been a field in the Urals.

The forced industrialization of the 1930s (Chapter 7), with its deliberate placement of duplicate heavy industry in the deep interior, is what made this possible; the brutal command economy's one supreme competence, the crash mobilization of resources by central order, is exactly what saved the state that built it.
The second was Leningrad.

The Germans, on the northern axis, decided not to storm the city (the former Petrograd, the cradle of the revolution) but to encircle and starve it, deliberately, as policy: the Nazi plan was to let the population die and raze the city.
The siege of Leningrad lasted nearly 900 days, from September 1941 to January 1944, the longest siege of a major city in modern history.

Inside it, in the first winter of 1941–42, people died of starvation at a rate that is hard to write: the bread ration fell to a few ounces a day of "bread" that was largely sawdust, cellulose, and other fillers eked out with a little flour, people ate wallpaper paste, leather, boiled glue, and worse; the diarist Tanya Savicheva, an eleven-year-old girl, kept a notebook recording her family's deaths one by one, ending "the Savichevs are dead.
Everyone is dead.
Only Tanya is left," and it became one of the war's defining documents.

The city was kept barely alive by a supply route driven across the ice of frozen Lake Ladoga, the "Road of Life," along which trucks ran under German artillery fire and air attack, many breaking through the ice.

Estimates of civilian deaths in the siege range from roughly 800,000 to over a million, the spread arising because the city's record-keeping collapsed under the mortality and because deaths during the post-evacuation are counted differently.
The city did not fall.
That it did not is one of the central facts of the Soviet war myth, and in this case the myth and the documented record largely agree: the endurance was real and on a scale that has few parallels.
The third was Moscow, and the winter, and Zhukov.

By late autumn 1941 German spearheads were close enough to the capital that some could see the Kremlin's towers through field glasses; the government was partly evacuated, the city was in panic and partly in looting, and the regime was a few dozen miles from losing its capital.

Stalin stayed, and on 7 November held the traditional revolution-anniversary military parade in Red Square with German artillery within earshot, the troops marching straight from the square to the front, an act of theater that was also a real signal that the state would not flee.
Two things turned it.

First, the intelligence that Japan would strike south, not north (a consequence of Khalkhin Gol, Chapter 10, and confirmed by Richard Sorge, a German Communist working as a journalist in Tokyo who was secretly a Soviet agent with access to German embassy traffic and Japanese intentions) let Stalin transfer fresh, winter-equipped Siberian divisions to Moscow.

Second, General Zhukov, the victor of Khalkhin Gol, was given command of the capital's defense, held the line through the worst, and in early December 1941 launched a counteroffensive that, aided by a savage winter the Germans were not equipped for, drove the Wehrmacht back from Moscow for the first significant German defeat of the war.
Barbarossa, which had been built on the assumption of victory before winter, had failed in its central objective.
The blitzkrieg that had conquered France in six weeks had not conquered the USSR in six months, and now it was committed to exactly the long, attritional, two-front war Germany could not win.
The country had survived 1941 by a margin so thin it is still studied.
It had survived.
It had not yet won, and the cost of winning is Chapter 12.

chapters.title: The Turn
sentences: The Soviet Union won the war in Europe.

That sentence is contested only at its edges (the Western Allies' role was real and is covered in their own narratives), but the central fact is not in serious dispute: by the usual reckonings something in the range of three-quarters to four-fifths of German military deaths in the Second World War occurred on the Eastern Front, and the war against Nazi Germany was overwhelmingly decided in the East, at a price the Soviet population paid in numbers no other combatant came close to.
This chapter is the turn, from the near-defeat of Chapter 11 to Berlin, and then the reckoning with what victory cost and what the regime did with it.
The hinge was Stalingrad.
In the summer of 1942 Germany, unable to take Moscow, drove southeast toward the oil of the Caucasus and the city on the Volga that bore Stalin's name.

The Battle of Stalingrad, from August 1942 to February 1943, became the most lethal battle in human history, a months-long struggle for a ruined industrial city fought building by building, room by room, sewer by sewer, in which both sides fed in armies and both sides bled.
It was here that the Soviet command issued Order No. 227, "Not One Step Back," forbidding unauthorized retreat on pain of death.

It created penal battalions (units into which deserters and "cowards" were thrown for near-suicidal tasks as a chance to redeem themselves) and blocking detachments (armed security units posted behind the front line with orders to stop, and if necessary shoot, soldiers retreating without authorization), a measure of how close to collapse the defense was and how ruthlessly it was held together.

The turn came in November 1942, when the Red Army, no longer the broken instrument of 1941, executed Operation Uranus: a double encirclement that trapped the entire German Sixth Army, some 250,000 men, inside the city Hitler had forbidden it to leave.

The trapped army was starved and frozen and surrendered in February 1943; roughly 90,000 emaciated prisoners marched into Soviet captivity, of whom only a small fraction, by most German accounts on the order of five to six thousand, survived the camps and returned home, many not until the 1950s.

Stalingrad was the psychological hinge of the entire war: the first time a complete German field army had been destroyed, and the moment, recognized at the time on both sides, that the war had turned.

The military hinge followed at Kursk in July 1943, generally described as the largest tank battle in history by the number of armored vehicles committed, where Germany's last great strategic offensive in the East was broken against deep Soviet defenses that, thanks to excellent intelligence, knew exactly where the blow was coming.
After Kursk the strategic initiative passed permanently to the Red Army, and the war became a steady, grinding, immensely costly westward advance.

Its masterpiece was Operation Bagration in summer 1944, the destruction of the entire German Army Group Centre in Belarus, by the count of German divisions annihilated and men lost an even larger catastrophe for Germany than Stalingrad, and far less remembered in the West; timed to coincide with the Western Allies' Normandy landings, the two together broke Germany's ability to hold the war together.
The advance came with an atrocity this book will not pass over in a clause.

As the Red Army rolled through East Prussia, Poland, Hungary, and into Germany, its troops committed mass rape and pillage against German civilians and, along the way, civilians of the very countries being "liberated." This is documented, was suppressed for decades by the Soviet state, and is now established in the historical record.
Naming it does not equalize the war's moral ledger; it cannot, because the Germans had come to exterminate and the Soviets had not.
It is named because this book does not launder any state's crimes, including those of the side that was, in this war, fighting an annihilationist enemy and was overwhelmingly the wronged party.
The Red Army took Berlin in a massive, bloody assault in April–May 1945.

The famous Reichstag flag-raising photograph, like the storming of the Winter Palace (Chapter 2), was a staged and edited image; in the best-known account the photographer Yevgeny Khaldei retouched it, and a watch on a soldier's wrist is usually said to have been removed because he appeared to be wearing two (the looting reading is the common interpretation, not a certainty).
The exact details of the edit are debated, but the larger point is not: the Soviet war was both genuinely heroic and relentlessly mythologized, and the same photograph can be both at once.
Germany surrendered in May 1945.
In August, honoring a promise made at the Allied conferences, the USSR launched a colossal and devastatingly effective invasion of Japanese-held Manchuria.
It mattered far beyond 1945.

The speed of the Soviet onslaught helped force Japan's surrender in the Pacific, and the Soviet occupation of Manchuria let the Chinese Communists take over its industry, weapons stocks, and a secure rear base, a decisive boost on their road to winning China's civil war in 1949 (Chapter 13), while the Soviet–American division of Korea along the 38th parallel set up the Korean War and a partition that still stands.
The threads run forward; the chapter only plants them here.
Now the cost, and it has to be given as the range it is, because it is the single largest number in this book and one of the most fought-over.

The total number of Soviet citizens who died as a result of the Second World War is conventionally given as about 27 million, the figure most widely used since a late-Soviet and post-Soviet demographic reassessment; estimates across the serious literature run roughly from 25 to 27 million and up toward 30 million in some reconstructions.

The range exists because the deaths span battlefield, prisoner-of-war murder, deliberate starvation of civilians, the Holocaust on Soviet soil (well over a million Soviet Jews were murdered by the Germans and their collaborators, much of it by mass shooting before the death camps even opened), reprisal massacres, famine, and disease, across territory that changed hands twice with the records destroyed each time, and because demographers reconstruct the total from census gaps rather than from a body count that was never possible.

To make 27 million feelable to an American reader: it is more than the entire population of Texas, killed in under four years; it is roughly seventy times the U.S. military and civilian deaths in the same war; it is, proportionally, as if the United States today lost the combined populations of California and New York.
About two-thirds of the dead were civilians.
There was scarcely a family in the western USSR that did not lose someone.
This is the fact underneath everything that follows in this book.
Two things the regime did with the victory matter for the rest of the story.
First, it built the war into the founding myth of the system, and this is the book's thesis in its most uncomfortable form.

The October Revolution had created the state, but by the 1960s the war, not the revolution, became the central legitimating story: the Soviet system was the thing that had defeated fascism and saved the world, and therefore the sacrifices, the camps, the famine, the whole machine, were retroactively redeemed by the victory.

The cult of the Great Patriotic War, with its eternal flames, its 9 May Victory Day parades, its colossal monuments like The Motherland Calls at Stalingrad, became the one thing nearly all Soviet citizens, including dissidents and the children of the purged, genuinely shared and believed in, and it remains, today, the single most powerful and most politically exploited element of Soviet memory in Putin's Russia.

An honest account holds both that the Soviet sacrifice and contribution were colossal and real, the world genuinely was saved in significant part by Soviet blood, and that the regime weaponized that truth to launder everything else it had done.

Second, the war ended with the Red Army in Berlin, Warsaw, Budapest, and Prague, which meant the USSR ended the war controlling the eastern half of Europe and confirmed, in its own mind, that security meant a belt of subordinate states between itself and the West.

It also ended with the regime turning, immediately, on its own people: returning Soviet prisoners of war and forced laborers were treated as "contaminated" by the outside world (the regime's fear was concrete: that men who had seen Western Europe, even as prisoners, knew the West was not the poverty-stricken hell propaganda described, might have been recruited as agents, and had, by surrendering at all, committed in Stalin's eyes the crime of not dying), funneled through filtration camps, and in large numbers sent on to the Gulag, the men who had survived German camps reimprisoned by their own state for the crime of having been captured.
The wartime relaxation, the temporary truce with the Church, the loosening of terror, the appeals to Russian patriotism rather than class, was rolled back.
The country had won the most justified war in its history and its reward was the resumption of the machine.
What that resumption looked like, and how it became a global confrontation, is Chapter 13.

chapters.title: The Iron Curtain
sentences: The Soviet Union emerged from the war devastated and triumphant at the same time, its western regions a wasteland of an estimated 70,000 destroyed villages and 1,700 destroyed towns, its population missing 27 million people (Chapter 12), and yet its army standing in the heart of Europe and its prestige higher than it would ever be again.

Out of that contradiction came the Cold War, the forty-year global confrontation between the Soviet bloc and the American-led West, and at home a return of the machine to its full ferocity in the regime's last and arguably most senselessly paranoid years.
This chapter is high Stalinism's final act.
The descent into the Cold War was fast and the blame is genuinely contested, so present it as a problem, not a verdict.

The wartime alliance of the USSR, the United States, and Britain had been an alliance against a common enemy with almost nothing else holding it together; the three wartime summits had set the shape and left the contradiction unresolved.

At Tehran (1943) the Big Three agreed the broad strategy and that Poland's borders would shift west; at Yalta (February 1945) Stalin signed a "Declaration on Liberated Europe" promising free elections he had no intention of allowing; at Potsdam (July 1945), with the war won and Roosevelt dead, the disagreement over who would actually govern Poland and Germany was no longer maskable.

The unresolvable knot throughout was Poland: the West wanted the independent, London-based Polish government restored, Stalin was installing a Soviet-controlled one, and neither would yield on the country his army was standing in.

The Soviet view, defensible on its own terms, was that having been invaded twice through Eastern Europe in thirty years at a cost of 27 million dead, the USSR had an absolute right to friendly (meaning controlled) governments on its western approach.
The Western view was that Stalin had promised free elections in liberated Europe at Yalta and was now imposing one-party Communist regimes by force, in breach of his word.
Both readings have evidence.

The traditional Western account blames Soviet expansionism; a "revisionist" school blames American economic and atomic assertiveness; the "post-revisionist" mainstream concludes the Cold War emerged from a security dilemma in which each side's defensive measures looked offensive to the other and neither could afford to test the other's intentions.
