He kept the Senate sitting, the law courts open, the tax system and grain dole functioning, and the whole Roman civil administration staffed by Romans, governing as a king who left the machinery of Roman Italy essentially intact and simply ran it.

By 489 the peninsula Theodoric marched into was not a wrecked country but a working one, a going concern in Roman administrative order, and that inheritance is half the reason his own reign could become what it did.
The empire in the West did not fall in a day.
It was administered, by barbarians, into a different thing.

The Goth who replaced Odoacer was Theodoric the Great (pronounced "thee-OH-dor-ik"), of the Amali royal house of the Ostrogoths (the Greuthungi dynasty of Chapter 4), and his life is the perfect distillation of everything this book is about.

As a boy he had been sent to Constantinople as a hostage, a guarantee of his people's good behavior, and he grew up there, in the greatest Roman city in the world, absorbing Roman government, Roman culture, and Roman political thinking.

He was a Gothic king raised inside the Roman state, the same paradox as Alaric and Stilicho, but taken further than either: Alaric had grown up in Roman armies and Stilicho served the empire, yet neither had been schooled from boyhood inside its imperial capital, and neither ended up actually governing Roman territory through the Roman Senate.
Theodoric did both.
He is the paradox not just embodied but enthroned.
How he got Italy is itself a study in how the post-Roman world worked.

The eastern emperor in Constantinople, Zeno, had a problem: Theodoric and his Ostrogoths were a dangerous, restless armed nation loose in the Balkans, too strong to destroy and too disruptive to ignore.
Zeno's solution, around 488, was elegant and cynical: he commissioned Theodoric to invade Italy and overthrow Odoacer, in the emperor's name.
This solved two problems at once.

It removed the dangerous Goths from the Balkans by pointing them at Italy, and it replaced Odoacer, a ruler Constantinople had never properly recognized, with one who at least notionally held his authority from the emperor.

Theodoric marched an entire people across the Alps into Italy, beat Odoacer in a string of battles, at the Isonzo river and at Verona in 489 and again at the Adda in 490, and then ran into the obstacle every conqueror of Italy in this period ran into: Ravenna, the swamp-girdled capital, effectively unstormable.
Theodoric besieged it for three years.
It fell only by negotiation, not assault, in 493, with an agreement that the two men would rule Italy jointly.
That agreement lasted about ten days.
At a banquet held to seal the peace, Theodoric personally killed Odoacer with his own sword.

Jordanes (Chapter 1), writing decades later and never one to waste a good scene, adds a grim warrior's joke, that surveying the body Theodoric remarked the man "had no bones in him," that the blow had cut clean through.
That line is exactly the kind of too-perfect anecdote a court-flattering source invents, and its historicity is essentially nil; the murder, however, is not in doubt.

It was treachery, plain and unflinching, and this book does not dress it up; it is the founding act of Ostrogothic Italy, and it tells you that the philosopher-king's regime began, like every Gothic kingdom in these pages, with a murder.
What Theodoric then built over the next three decades is the reason he is called "the Great," and it is genuinely extraordinary.
He ran Italy as a deliberate dual state.

The Goths were the army, holding military command and the profession of arms; the Romans ran everything civil, the Senate, the law courts, the tax administration, the bureaucracy, almost entirely unchanged and staffed by Romans.

The two peoples were kept legally and religiously separate, Arian Goths and Catholic Romans, soldiers and civilians, but yoked into one functioning kingdom under a king who presented himself, carefully, as a restorer of Roman civilization rather than its conqueror.
He issued a law code, the Edictum Theodorici, applying to Goths and Romans alike to reduce friction between them.

The great Roman senatorial families, the Anicii and the Symmachi, the old aristocratic dynasties whose wealth, landholdings, and inherited offices had run Rome's civil life for generations, served as his consuls and prefects and found, to their own evident surprise, that the Gothic regime was a stable and reasonably generous patron of the traditional Roman order.

Cassiodorus's letters (the same Cassiodorus whose lost Gothic history Jordanes abridged, Chapter 1) record the regime ordering the maintenance of the great roads like the Via Appia, the repair of aqueducts, the restoration of public baths, the management of the grain supply, the protection of Rome's ancient monuments.

This was a barbarian king treating the upkeep of Roman civilization as a central duty of government and saying so loudly, framing it as proof that the Goths were carriers of civilization, not its destroyers.

It is the most thorough refutation in this whole series of the word "barbarian." The physical proof still stands at Ravenna, and architecture in this world was always purposeful, so the why matters as much as the what.
Theodoric rebuilt the royal palace, and he raised two structures that survive.

One is the basilica of Sant'Apollinare Nuovo (pronounced "sant ah-pol-ee-NAH-reh"), built as his palace church, its walls lined with mosaics of a quality that puts it among the finest buildings of the early medieval world; it was an Arian church, built to proclaim that the Gothic king's faith was as splendid and as legitimate as the Romans' own.

The other is his own Mausoleum, a massive circular tomb of pale stone whose most astonishing feature is its roof: a single colossal slab of limestone, roughly 33 feet (10 meters) across and weighing on the order of 230 tons, set in place as one piece, a dome that is one monolithic rock rather than masonry.

Where the slab was quarried is debated, with limestone from the Istrian coast across the Adriatic the leading candidate and a closer Apennine source also argued; how a stone that size was moved and lifted at all is the part nobody has fully explained.
The choice was a statement.

A Roman dome is mortared masonry, the empire's signature technology; Theodoric's is a single Gothic boulder doing the same job by sheer scale, a barbarian king's monument that borrows the Roman form and announces, in stone, that it is something else.
It still stands outside Ravenna, the only thing in this entire book the reader could go and touch.
The intellectual life of Theodoric's Italy produced one book that outlasted the kingdom by a thousand years, and the way it was produced is the dark turn that ends the reign.

The finest scholar at Theodoric's court was Boethius (pronounced "boh-EE-thee-us"), a Roman aristocrat from the Anicii who had already translated parts of Aristotle's logic and written textbooks on arithmetic and music, and who had set himself a larger project: to render all of Plato and Aristotle into Latin and reconcile them, a one-man rescue mission to keep Greek philosophy alive in a West that was losing the ability to read Greek at all.
He served Theodoric as head of the civil administration.
And then it turned.

When a senator was accused of treasonous correspondence with Constantinople and Boethius spoke up to defend him, the accusation swung onto Boethius himself: that he too had been plotting to bring back imperial rule.

The charge fell into Theodoric's last and most fearful years, and around 523 Boethius was arrested, imprisoned, and in 524 executed without the full hearing his rank should have guaranteed, condemned, as he saw it, for loyalty to the very Roman order his king had spent thirty years claiming to restore.

In prison, waiting to die, stripped of office, wealth, and reputation, he wrote The Consolation of Philosophy, a dialogue in which a figure called Philosophy visits the condemned man in his cell and argues him out of despair, on fortune, on suffering, and on the goods that no king and no executioner can confiscate.

It became one of the most widely read and beloved books of the entire Middle Ages, copied and translated across Europe for the next thousand years, the last great work of the classical mind written, fittingly, by a Roman dying at the hands of a Gothic state that thought of itself as Rome's protector.
Theodoric also executed Boethius's father-in-law, the revered senator Symmachus, on related charges.
These executions were the regime's self-inflicted wound, and the reason cuts to the heart of the book.
Theodoric's whole system depended on the trust of the Roman aristocracy and the toleration of the religious divide.
In his last years that trust curdled.

The eastern empire under a new, aggressively Catholic regime was persecuting Arians, the rift between the Arian Gothic king and his Catholic Roman subjects widened into mutual suspicion, and Theodoric, aging and increasingly fearful of Roman disloyalty and a Constantinople plot, turned on the very Roman elite his rule had courted.
He even imprisoned the pope, John I, after a failed diplomatic mission, where the pope died.
The philosopher-king ended as a frightened old man killing his best Roman servants over their faith and their loyalty, and the goodwill that had made the dual state work died with them.
Theodoric died in 526, leaving the throne to his young grandson under the regency of his daughter.

That daughter was Amalasuntha (pronounced "ah-mah-lah-SOON-tah"), and she was the most thoroughly Romanized of all the Amali, fluent in Latin and Greek, schooled in literature and philosophy, and determined to keep her father's dual state and his careful peace with Constantinople alive.
She ruled in her young son Athalaric's name and tried to raise him as an educated prince in the Roman manner, with tutors and books.

The Gothic nobility took this as exactly the wrong lesson: they wanted a king raised hard, among warriors, at the hunt and the drill ground, and they forced her to hand the boy back to a soldier's upbringing, under which he drank and sickened and died as a teenager.
With him died her only legitimate claim to rule, and the nobles who resented the drift toward Rome now had her cornered.

Politically exposed, she took a cousin, Theodahad, as co-ruler to shore up her position; he turned on her at once, had her imprisoned on an island, and in 535 had her murdered there, strangled in her bath.

It was the worst possible decision at the worst possible moment, because the murder of the Romanized Gothic queen handed the most powerful man in the world the legal and moral pretext he had been waiting for.
In Constantinople, an emperor who had sworn to reconquer the lost Roman West now had his cause.

chapters.title: Justinian's War
sentences: The Ostrogothic kingdom was not conquered quickly and cleanly.

It was killed slowly, over twenty years, in a war so destructive that the country both sides were fighting over, Italy, the original heartland of the Roman Empire, came out of it depopulated, plague-ridden, its cities broken and its aqueducts dry, never to recover its ancient prosperity.
The grim final irony of this entire book is that the people who did the most physical destruction to Roman Italy were not the Goths who ruled it but the Romans who came to take it back.
This is the story of how the Goths ended, and of what it cost.

The man who launched the war was Justinian (pronounced "jus-TIN-ee-an"), emperor of the eastern Roman Empire from Constantinople, whose great consuming ambition was the renovatio imperii, the reconquest of the western provinces lost to the barbarians and the restoration of the Roman Empire to one whole.
He had already, by his general's hand, destroyed the Vandal kingdom in North Africa and retaken Carthage.
The murder of Amalasuntha in 535 (Chapter 10), a princess Justinian had cultivated as a friendly contact, gave him exactly the casus belli he wanted.
In 535 CE he sent an army to take Italy from the Ostrogoths, and the Gothic War began.
The general was Belisarius (pronounced "bel-ih-SAIR-ee-us"), the finest soldier of the age and Justinian's instrument in every reconquest.
The opening went almost embarrassingly well for the empire.

Belisarius took Sicily in 535 against little resistance, crossed to the mainland, captured Naples in 536 by a famous ruse, sending a party into the city along a disused aqueduct channel to surprise the defenders, and entered the city of Rome itself later that year as the Gothic garrison simply withdrew.

Almost everything we know about this war comes from Procopius (pronounced "proh-KOH-pee-us"), a Greek-speaking secretary who served on Belisarius's own staff and wrote the standard contemporary history of Justinian's wars.

The aqueduct story is his, and it is good to remember that a secret-aqueduct entry is also a stock dramatic set piece in ancient history-writing, so the detail may be sharpened in the telling even if the city did fall to a surprise infiltration.
For a moment it looked like the whole thing might be over in two years.
It was not, because the Goths found a king.
The feeble Theodahad was killed and replaced by a war-leader named Witigis (pronounced "WIT-ih-gis"), who gathered the Gothic army and in 537 laid siege to Belisarius inside Rome.
The siege lasted over a year.

Belisarius held the city using the great walls of Aurelian, the third-century fortifications built during the crisis of Chapter 3, now defending Rome against the Goths who had once helped make those walls necessary.

He held, eventually went over to the offensive, and in 540 took Ravenna itself, the impregnable swamp-capital, not by storm but by a ruse: he let the Goths believe he would accept their offer to make him their western emperor, walked into the city under that pretense, and then took it for Justinian instead.
Witigis was shipped to Constantinople as a prisoner.
In 540 the war looked won, the Ostrogothic kingdom apparently finished.
It was not finished, and the reason is the structural flaw that runs through Justinian's whole project.

Belisarius had won with a small army that was never properly reinforced or paid, because Justinian, fighting Persians in the east and suspicious of any general too successful, would not pour resources into Italy once it looked won.
He recalled Belisarius, left the conquest half-garrisoned, and let the heavy taxation begin before the country was actually pacified.
Into that gap the Goths recovered.
What followed is the part of the war that makes it a tragedy rather than a conquest, and it centers on one man.
The Goths, beaten and leaderless, raised a new king who turned out to be one of the most capable leaders in their whole history: Totila (pronounced "TOH-tih-lah").

From near-total defeat in 541, Totila reconquered almost all of Italy over the next decade and held it against the full weight of the eastern empire, and he did it with a strategy that was politically brilliant and that the Roman sources, hostile as they are, cannot quite hide.
Totila understood that the war was being lost by the Romans among their own people.

Justinian's reconquest came with a tax regime far heavier than Theodoric's, run by imperial finance officials, the most notorious named Alexander "the Scissors" for the way he clipped soldiers' pay and squeezed the provincials, who treated newly retaken Italy as a source of revenue to be wrung dry rather than a population to be won over.
The ordinary people of Italy, the poor, the enslaved, the dispossessed, were discovering that imperial liberation was worse than Gothic rule.
Totila exploited this directly.

He freed slaves who joined him, cancelled or redirected the rents the great landlords extracted, recruited the dispossessed into his army, and presented the Gothic cause not as barbarian resistance but as the liberation of ordinary Italians from a predatory Roman aristocracy and a predatory imperial tax collector.

He wrote letters to the Roman Senate making exactly this argument, sophisticated political propaganda in full Roman rhetorical form, from a Gothic king, denouncing Constantinople's exploitation of Italy.

He even put together a Gothic fleet, the same way the third-century Goths had taken to the sea (Chapter 3), by controlling Italian ports and harnessing the local shipwrights and sailors he now ruled, and used it to raid Sicily and the Adriatic coast, a people of the inland steppe two centuries earlier now fighting a naval war in the Mediterranean.
He took Rome itself, more than once; the city changed hands several times in this war, was partly demolished, was at one point left almost entirely empty of inhabitants.
Totila's revival is the proof that the Ostrogoths, even at the end, were not a spent barbarian remnant but an adaptive, politically inventive power that nearly won.
Justinian ended it by changing the general.
He recalled Belisarius and in 551 sent the man who finished the war: Narses (pronounced "NAR-seez"), and the choice was as strange as anything in this book.

Narses was a castrated palace official, a eunuch, the class of men who in Constantinople staffed the most trusted positions around the emperor precisely because, barred from founding dynasties of their own, they were thought safe to hold real power.
He was by now around seventy-five, had spent his life in the treasury and the court rather than the field, and had no conventional military training at all.

What he did have was Justinian's complete confidence, and with it the one thing Belisarius had been denied through fifteen years of war: not brilliance, which Belisarius had in abundance, but a large, fully supplied, fully paid army that did not melt away for want of food and wages.
The greatest reconquest in Roman history was finished not by its finest soldier but by an old palace administrator who was finally given enough money to do the job.
The two armies met in 552 at the Battle of Taginae (pronounced "ta-JEE-nay," also called Busta Gallorum, in the central Apennines).
Narses out-thought Totila completely, anchored his line with massed dismounted archers, broke the Gothic cavalry charge, and won decisively.
Totila was killed fleeing the field.
The Gothic king who had nearly reversed the entire war was dead, and with him the Ostrogothic cause's last real chance.
The Goths fought on, briefly, under one more king, Teia, who made a last stand in 553 at the Battle of Mons Lactarius (pronounced "monz lak-TAH-ree-us," near Mount Vesuvius) and died there too.

The surviving Goths negotiated terms; most of those who were left crossed the Alps out of Italy, and the Ostrogoths as an organized people, a kingdom, an army, a name with a state attached, ceased to exist.
The Amali dynasty, the heroic Gothic royal line that Jordanes had traced back to semi-divine ancestors on the steppe (Chapter 4), simply ended.
There was no more Ostrogothic Italy.

In 554 CE Justinian issued the Pragmatic Sanction, the decree that formally reimposed imperial Roman law over Italy, returned confiscated estates to their pre-war owners, and erased the Ostrogothic legal order as though the kingdom had never been.
On paper it was the triumphant restoration of the Roman Empire in Italy, Justinian's life's ambition achieved.
In reality it was a death certificate written over a grave.
Twenty years of siege, famine, scorched earth, and the Plague of Justinian had wrecked the peninsula.
That plague was the catastrophic pandemic, probably the first great outbreak of the bubonic plague, that swept the Mediterranean from the 540s and reached Italy in the middle of the war.

Bubonic plague kills fast and in appalling numbers, swelling the lymph nodes into the black "buboes" that name it and carrying off a large fraction of an exposed population within weeks, and in a peninsula already emptied by war it removed the farmers, soldiers, and townspeople who might otherwise have rebuilt.
Cities were depopulated, the aqueducts that Theodoric had so carefully maintained were broken, the agricultural economy was shattered, Rome itself was a fraction of its former self.
Italy would not recover its pre-war population or prosperity for centuries.

And the restoration did not even last: just fourteen years later, in 568, a new Germanic people walked into a northern Italy that the war had stripped of garrisons, defenders, and people, and took most of it almost unopposed.

These were the Lombards, a frontier confederation from the middle Danube of much the same kind the Goths themselves had once been; some of them had actually fought in Narses's army against the Goths, and now they helped themselves to the prize.
The empire had bled itself white winning a country it no longer had the strength to hold, and a fresh set of barbarians simply walked into the vacuum.
Justinian destroyed the Goths and, in doing so, destroyed the thing the Goths had been preserving.
That is the end of the Goths as a power in Italy, and it is the place to step back and say what this whole book has been.

The Goths were the people who did the most to end the ancient world, and they did it not as the simple destroyers of Roman propaganda but as something far more interesting and far more consequential: the empire's most capable heirs.
They produced the first written literature in any Germanic language.
They issued some of the first written Germanic law codes, in Latin, in Roman form.

They killed two Roman emperors in the field, sacked the unsackable city after eight hundred years, and then turned around and ran Roman Italy with more care for its aqueducts and its philosophers than its own last emperors had managed.

They were Christians of the losing side, Arian heretics ruling Catholic subjects, and that single fact, planted by one bishop's mission in the fourth century, shaped and broke their kingdoms for two hundred years.
The Ostrogoths end here, in 554, completely.
But the Goths do not entirely end, and the honest close of this book has to point both forward and outward, the way the previous book pointed at this one.

The Ostrogothic destruction is one act in a much larger drama, the whole churning shattering of the Roman West, the Huns and the Vandals and the Franks and the fall of the empire, that is the subject of the wider story of the age.
And the western Goths did not die at all.
The Visigothic Kingdom of Toledo (Chapter 9) ruled Hispania for another century and a half after the Ostrogoths were gone.

In 589 a Visigothic king, Reccared, finally did the thing no Gothic ruler had done in two and a half centuries: at the Third Council of Toledo he converted his entire people from Arianism to Catholicism, healing at last the religious fracture Ulfilas had opened in the fourth century, and merging Goth and Hispano-Roman into a single Catholic people.
That kingdom of Catholic Visigoths ruled Spain until 711, when an army crossed from North Africa and took the whole peninsula in a few years, opening the next great chapter of Iberian history.
The Goths who sacked Rome are gone.

But the law they wrote down, the alphabet a bishop built for them, the idea that a barbarian king could be a restorer of civilization, and the political map their kingdoms drew across Gaul and Spain and Italy, all of that outlived them by a thousand years.
They were not the end of Rome.
They were, more than anyone, the bridge from it to everything that came next.

chapters.title: The Domino Falls
sentences: In the year 376 CE, a Roman army watching the lower Danube saw something that had no precedent in living memory: an entire nation, hundreds of thousands of people, standing on the river's far bank and begging to be let in.
These were the Goths (pronounced with a hard "g," as in "goat"), a Germanic people the Romans had known and fought and traded with for over a century, and they were not raiding.
They were fleeing.
They had their wagons, their herds, their old people and their children, and they were asking the Roman Empire, the thing they had spent generations harassing, for asylum.

Something had come up behind them out of the east, something that had broken the most powerful Gothic kingdom on the steppe with frightening speed (the sources do not tell us in how many campaigns, only that it was fast) and was still coming, and the Goths had decided that throwing themselves on the mercy of Rome was less terrifying than staying to meet it.
That something was the Huns.

This book is about what happened next: the roughly two centuries in which the western half of the Roman Empire was overrun, dismantled, and replaced, not by one invasion but by a chain reaction of peoples in motion that historians, borrowing a nineteenth-century German word, call the Völkerwanderung (pronounced "FUR-kuh-VAN-deh-roong," literally "the wandering of the peoples").
It is the story of how the ancient Mediterranean world came apart and how medieval Europe was assembled out of the pieces.
It is not, mostly, the story of the Goths themselves.
They get their own book, because their journey from the Danube to a kingdom in Spain is long enough to deserve one.

This book is about the wider shattering they were the first crack in: the Huns who started it, the Vandals who took Rome's breadbasket and then Rome itself, the Franks who would become France, the collapse of the Western emperors, and the Eastern Empire's catastrophic attempt to put it all back together.
The Goths walk through these pages constantly, but in the background.
The foreground is the system, and the system breaking.
A word, once, about how we know any of this, because it shapes everything that follows and it is more honest to say it now than to keep apologizing for it later.
Almost every written source for these two centuries was produced by Romans, Greeks, or Christian churchmen writing within the surviving (Eastern) empire.

The peoples doing the migrating, Huns, Vandals, most of the early Franks, wrote little or nothing that survives, and what little they did was usually written down generations later by their descendants once those descendants had Latin clergy to do it for them.

So when this book says a battle happened "in 451," or that a king "decided" something, the reader should hear an implied caveat that does not need repeating every sentence: the dates, numbers, and especially the motives are reconstructed from a handful of sources who were often far away, often hostile, and often writing decades after the fact.
Where a claim is genuinely contested, this book will say so.
Where it is reasonably solid, it will say that too.
The general rule is that the shape of events is well attested and the vivid details are the part to hold loosely, because vivid details are exactly what ancient writers liked to improve.
With that on the table, the place to start is with the people who knocked over the first domino, because nobody in the Roman world had any idea who they were.
The Huns were not Germani.

This is the single most important thing to understand about them, and it is easy to get wrong, because the Romans lumped almost everyone beyond the frontier under the catch-all sneer "barbarian," and a modern reader can absorb that flattening without noticing.

The Germanic peoples, Goths, Vandals, Franks, Saxons and the rest, spoke languages from the Germanic branch of Indo-European, the same vast language family that produced Latin, Greek, Persian, and Sanskrit.
They were the cold-country, forest-and-farm peoples Rome had been managing along the Rhine and Danube for four centuries (the Germanic Tribes tells that long story).
The Huns were something else entirely.

They were steppe nomads: horse-herding, tent-dwelling, cattle-driving people from the Eurasian steppe, the immense belt of open grassland that runs for thousands of miles from the plains of Hungary east across Ukraine and Central Asia to Mongolia.
Their language is essentially unknown.

We have a few personal names and almost nothing else, and scholars have argued for over a century about whether it was Turkic, related to the later Mongolic languages, something Iranian, or something with no surviving relatives at all.
The honest answer is that we cannot classify it, but it was certainly not Germanic and almost certainly not Indo-European.
To put the distance in terms a reader can feel: a Goth meeting a Roman shared a deep common linguistic ancestor with him, the way English and Russian share one, distantly.
A Goth meeting a Hun shared nothing, the way English and Chinese share nothing.
These were not cousins of the Germani.
They were strangers to everyone.
Where did they come from?
The honest answer is that we do not securely know.

A long tradition connects them to the Xiongnu (pronounced "shyong-NOO"), a steppe confederation that had menaced Han-dynasty China centuries earlier, but the link is debated and the evidence is thin enough that careful historians treat it as a hypothesis rather than a fact.
What is solid is the behavior.
The Huns appeared on the western steppe, north of the Black Sea, in the 370s, and they were a kind of military machine the Roman and Germanic worlds had never had to fight.
Their power was the horse and the bow.
Every man rode, from childhood.

Their weapon was the composite bow, a short, brutally powerful bow built up in layers of wood, horn, and sinew so that a weapon small enough to shoot from a galloping horse hit as hard as a much larger one, and they could shoot it accurately at the gallop, wheel away, and shoot again before an enemy could close.

Against this a Roman infantry unit, trained to lock shields and grind down an enemy that came to meet it, had nothing to grind down: the Huns simply rode in a wide circle out of reach, shot the formation full of arrows until it broke or charged, and if it charged they fell back faster than it could follow and shot it some more.
They did not hold ground; they had no cities to defend and nothing to besiege.
They could not be brought to a decisive battle they did not want, and they could not be exhausted by burning farms they did not own.
Roman armies were built to fight other armies that stood still and fought.
The Huns refused to be that, and for a generation no one had an answer.
The other thing the Huns did, and it is the engine of this entire book, is that they absorbed.
When the Huns broke a people, they did not necessarily destroy or replace them.
Often they incorporated them, took their warriors, their tribute, and their submission, and rolled them into a growing confederation under Hunnic overlordship.
So the thing pressing on the Danube frontier was not a fixed nation of a known size.
It was a snowball, and everyone it touched either ran or was rolled into it.
Here is the mechanism, stated plainly, because the whole rest of the book is variations on it.

The Huns hit the easternmost Gothic confederation, the Greuthungi (pronounced "groy-THUNG-ee," later remembered as the ancestors of the Ostrogoths), on the open steppe north of the Black Sea around 375, and broke them.
The shock rolled west into the next Gothic group, the Tervingi (pronounced "TER-ving-ee," later the core of the Visigoths), who did not wait to be broken and instead ran for the Danube and Rome.
That is one domino knocking the next.

The Goths' arrival inside the empire in 376, the catastrophic battle three years later at Adrianople in 378 where the Goths destroyed an entire Eastern field army and killed Valens (the emperor of the Eastern half of the empire, on the throne since 364; for an emperor to be killed in battle by barbarians was almost unheard of, a humiliation Rome had not suffered on this scale in centuries), and the uneasy settlement of the Goths inside the Balkans in 382, all of that is the Gothic story, and it is told in full elsewhere.
What matters here is the principle it established and the precedent it set.
The principle: a people pushed hard enough from behind does not negotiate over whether to move.
It moves, and the only question is who is in the way.
The precedent: faced with a whole armed nation it could not destroy, Rome did the thing it would now do over and over until it had given the empire away.
It cut a deal.

It admitted the Goths as foederati (pronounced "feh-deh-RAH-tee," from the Latin foedus, "treaty"), allied peoples settled on Roman soil who kept their own leaders and their own internal law and served in the Roman army in exchange for land, supplies, and gold.

This was not invented in 382; Rome had been settling defeated barbarians under treaty for two centuries, planting groups of beaten Germani as farmer-soldiers on emptied frontier land along the Rhine and Danube where they could work the soil and be called up to fight.
But it had always done that on Rome's terms, with broken and divided peoples.
It had never before done it with a whole intact nation that arrived under its own kings, on its own terms, having just annihilated a Roman army.

The difference between a settled prisoner population and an armed allied nation living inside your border with its own command structure is the difference, eventually, between a province and a kingdom.

This is, in fact, an old trap (Carthage had armed and settled foreign mercenaries it could not pay, and they turned on it in the savage Mercenary War and nearly destroyed the city from inside; Gaulish factions had hired Germanic Suebi who then refused to leave), seven hundred years old by the time Rome learned it the hard way.
Rome learned it anyway, because at every step the immediate alternative looked worse than the deal in front of it.
That sentence is the closest thing this book has to a thesis, and it will be true on almost every page.
The Huns had knocked over the first domino.

For the next thirty years the line of falling tiles ran mostly through the Balkans and the Gothic story, far enough from the Western capital that the men running Italy could persuade themselves it was a containable eastern problem.
It was not.

On the freezing last night of the year 406, while the Roman world was looking the other way, the dominoes reached the Rhine, and the half of the empire that had told itself it was safe began to come apart in earnest.

chapters.title: The Rhine Gives Way
sentences: The Western Roman Empire of the year 400 was held together, more than by any emperor, by one man, and the most revealing thing about him is that he was half-barbarian.
His name was Stilicho (pronounced "STILL-ih-koh"), and his father was a Vandal, one of the Germanic peoples that this chapter is about to turn loose on Gaul.
His mother was Roman.

He had risen through the army to become the supreme military commander of the West and the effective regent for the boy-emperor Honorius (pronounced "hoh-NOR-ee-us"), a weak and suspicious man who reigned, in the technical sense of occupying the throne, from 393 to 423, and who governed almost nothing.
Stilicho was the West's general, diplomat, and strongman, and the fact that the Roman Empire's survival rested on a man of Vandal blood is not an irony the book is inventing for effect.
It is the central fact of the age.

By 400 the line between "Roman commander" and "barbarian warlord" had become so blurred that the question "which side is this person on" frequently had no clean answer, including for the people asking it about themselves.
Stilicho spent the early 400s fighting fires he could not put out, only move.

In 405 a large mixed Gothic-led war host under a leader the sources call Radagaisus (pronounced "rah-dah-GUY-sus") crossed into Italy itself and drove deep toward Florence before Stilicho cornered and destroyed it and had Radagaisus executed.
It was a Roman victory, and it was also a warning, because to assemble enough troops to crush Radagaisus, Stilicho had to strip soldiers off other frontiers, above all the Rhine.

The Rhine was the western empire's oldest, most heavily fortified border, the line Julius Caesar had fixed as Rome's edge when he conquered Gaul in the 50s BCE and four and a half centuries of Roman policy had maintained since.

In the winter of 406 it was thinner than it had been in living memory, and on the far side of it, pushed west by the same Hunnic pressure churning the whole barbarian world, several entire peoples were looking for somewhere to go.
On the last night of 406, traditionally given as 31 December, they crossed.

The "New Year's Eve" date comes from a single line in Jerome, the great Christian scholar of the day, naming the night the barbarians broke into Gaul; a minority of modern historians, rereading the chronology, have argued for late 405 instead.
The year is firm; the famous midnight-on-the-river detail is best held as a memorable approximation, not a logged fact.
The Crossing of the Rhine put three peoples into Gaul more or less at once, and they are worth introducing properly, because two of them are not what the reader might assume.

The Vandals (the name is Germanic; the modern English word "vandalism" was coined from them in the eighteenth century, long after the fact, and tells you more about later propaganda than about the Vandals) were a Germanic people, Indo-European-speaking, from the forest-and-farm world east of the Rhine, the same broad cultural sphere as the Goths and the Franks.
They came in two related groups, the Hasding and the Siling Vandals.
They were, in language and origin, exactly the kind of people Rome had been managing on the Rhine for centuries.

The Suebi (pronounced "SWAY-bee") were also Germanic, a name attached to a sprawling and shifting set of peoples from deep in central Europe, the same broad Suebic world Caesar had fought when he drew that Rhine line.
The Alans (pronounced "AL-anz") were not Germanic at all, and this is the detail that matters.
The Alans were an Iranian-speaking people, originally from the steppe and the Caucasus region between the Black and Caspian Seas.

Their language belonged to the Iranian branch of Indo-European, the same branch as Persian, which makes them linguistic cousins of the Persians and only very distant relations of the Germanic peoples they were now marching alongside, roughly as distant as English is from Hindi.
They were horse people, steppe people, not forest farmers, and they had been swept up and scattered by the same Hunnic shock that started this whole book.
Some Alans had been absorbed into the Hunnic confederation; these were Alans who had run the other way and ended up bound to a Germanic migration heading into Gaul.

That a steppe Iranian people, a Germanic forest people, and another Germanic people crossed the Rhine together as allies is a perfect snapshot of what the Völkerwanderung actually was: not one nation invading, but the debris of a continent in motion, clumping into whatever traveling alliance could survive.
These three peoples poured across the frozen river and spent roughly three years devastating Gaul, the rich, long-settled, thoroughly Roman heartland that is now France.
They did not arrive with a plan to found kingdoms.

They arrived as a moving disaster looking for land and food, and the Roman state, which should have met them at the river, was not there, because its army was in Italy and its politics had just shattered in the worst possible place.
The shattering happened in Britain, and it happened because of the Rhine, not separately from it.

With the field army drawn into Italy to crush Radagaisus and the frontier left bare, the soldiers furthest from the capital concluded that the central government had abandoned them, and reached for the late Roman army's standard remedy for an absent emperor: they made one of their own.

When the Rhine collapsed, the Roman troops stationed in the diocese of Britain did what Roman armies in a panic had done for three centuries: they proclaimed their own emperor, on the theory that a local strongman was better than a distant boy who could not protect them.

After two short-lived candidates they settled on a common soldier with a promising name, Constantine III (no relation to Constantine the Great, the emperor who a century earlier had reunited the empire by force and made Christianity its favored religion, and whose name had carried the shine of victory ever since; this Constantine simply took it because it sounded lucky, which tells you something about how the late Roman army chose emperors).
In 407 Constantine III crossed from Britain into Gaul with the British garrison to make himself master of the West, fighting the barbarians and Honorius's loyalists at the same time.

This is the moment Roman Britain effectively ended, and the mechanism is worth being precise about, because the popular version ("the legions marched out and never came back") is roughly true but skips the why.
Constantine III took the mobile field troops out of Britain to fight his civil war in Gaul.
They were never replaced, because there was no functioning central authority left to replace them and every soldier was needed elsewhere.

A few years later, around 410, with Gaul in chaos and the city of Rome itself under Gothic attack, the British civitates, the self-governing Roman towns of the island, sent to the emperor Honorius asking for help against raiders.
The reply, as the Eastern historian Zosimus reports it, was essentially that the cities should see to their own defense.

Zosimus wrote his history of the empire's decline around the year 500, roughly a century after these events, and is our only real source for the moment, which means the famous "Rescript of Honorius" rests on a single, late, and somewhat garbled passage that historians still argue over.

Whatever the precise wording, the substance is not in doubt: after roughly four centuries, Roman government in Britain stopped, not with a dramatic withdrawal but with a request for help that was declined and then never followed up.
What happened on the island after that, the long fade of Roman life and the arrival of Angles, Saxons, and Jutes across the North Sea, is its own story.
For this book, Britain is the first whole province to simply fall off the map, and it fell off not because barbarians conquered it but because Rome's own civil wars drained it and then forgot it.
And while the Rhine was breaking and Britain was sliding away, Rome did the most self-destructive thing available to it.

In 408, with the frontier wide open and barbarians loose in Gaul, a court intrigue convinced the paranoid Honorius that Stilicho, his half-Vandal generalissimo, the one man who had repeatedly saved the West, was secretly plotting with the barbarians.
Honorius had him arrested and executed.

This is the chapter's hinge and its bitterest joke: at the exact moment the empire most needed the soldier of Vandal blood who kept beating barbarians, the empire killed him for having barbarian blood.
Within two years the leaderless West suffered the unthinkable in Italy itself, the sack of the city of Rome.
Constantine III's revolt collapsed not long after; he was captured and executed in 411.
The damage was now structural and permanent, and its scale is hard to take in even at this distance.

In the space of about five years a fortified river border four and a half centuries old had ceased to exist, an entire province had quietly fallen out of the empire, the Western field army had been burned up on a civil war and a Gothic crisis, and the only man who understood how to hold the system together had been killed by the government he served.
Nobody alive had a map for what came next.
The frontier was not coming back, and the peoples already inside it now had to become something, because there was no longer a Roman state in the West capable of telling them what to be.

chapters.title: Kingdoms Inside the Empire
sentences: Here is the strange thing about the fifth century, the thing that makes it different from a simple story of invasion and conquest: most of the barbarian kingdoms that replaced the Western Roman Empire were not founded by conquest.
They were founded by treaty.
Rome gave the land away, on paper, with its own seal on it, and then discovered it could not take it back.
The instrument was the federate settlement, the foederati system from Chapter 1, and by the 410s and 420s it had become the central mechanism of Western politics.
The mechanism deserves to be laid out concretely, because "Rome settled them as federates" is a result, and the reader needs the process.

When a Roman government could neither defeat a barbarian people nor expel it, it offered a deal: the people would be assigned a defined territory inside the empire; its king would keep command of his own warriors; in return that king and his army were legally Roman allies, obliged to fight Rome's other enemies (very often other barbarians) when ordered.

The Roman population in the assigned territory kept its own Roman law, its own bishops, and in principle its own property; the barbarians were quartered on it under arrangements historians still argue about.

The argument is whether the newcomers took shares of the land itself or shares of the tax revenue the land produced, and the surviving evidence points different ways in different places, so the honest answer is that it varied.
On parchment it looked like a Roman government deploying allied troops.
On the ground it meant an armed foreign people with its own king now lived permanently inside the empire, drew Roman revenue, and could not be removed by the government that had "settled" it.
Every such settlement was a Roman administrative document that was also, in slow motion, an independent kingdom.
The first peoples to turn the deal into durable kingdoms were not the most famous ones.
They were the Burgundians.

The Burgundians (pronounced "BUR-gun-dee-anz") were a Germanic people, the same broad Indo-European, east-of-the-Rhine forest-farm world as the Vandals and Franks, who had crossed in the general collapse and were settled by Roman treaty on the middle Rhine around the city of Worms (a Roman town on the river in what is now western Germany) by about 411.

Their first kingdom there left a long shadow: centuries later it became the seed of the great medieval German legend of the Nibelungs, the dragon-and-gold epic that the nineteenth-century composer Richard Wagner turned into his four-opera Ring cycle.

The historical Burgundians and the legendary ones are joined by a real thread of memory and a great deal of later invention; the saga remembered that a Burgundian kingdom on the Rhine was annihilated, which is the one true bone inside the myth, and that annihilation is the actual story here.
The first Burgundian kingdom did not last long.
In the 430s the Roman commander Aetius (the dominant Western general of the next two decades, his full story in Chapter 6) destroyed it, with Hunnic mercenaries doing a large part of the fighting.
This is the first place the Huns appear inside the story rather than behind it, and it is worth noting that Rome did not only fear them; it also hired them.

Aetius had lived among the Huns as a young man and could call on Hunnic horsemen for pay, so the same people churning the eastern frontier were, for a generation, also Rome's most effective hired muscle against everyone else, until they stopped being for hire (Chapter 5).
The Burgundian survivors were resettled by treaty far to the south, around Lake Geneva and the Rhône valley in what is now eastern France and western Switzerland, well away from the exposed Rhine.
There they built a second, longer-lasting Burgundian kingdom whose name still sits on the French region and the wine.

The Burgundians matter here less for themselves than as the clearest early demonstration of the pattern this whole book turns on: a people is settled by treaty, smashed by Rome using other barbarians, resettled by treaty, and ends up a kingdom Rome can no longer control.
The biggest treaty kingdom of all was Gothic.

After the years in the Balkans, the sack of Rome in 410, and a long migration through southern Gaul and into Spain and back (the Goths tells this in full), the Visigoths were settled in 418 by formal Roman treaty in Aquitaine (pronounced "AH-kih-tane"), the rich southwest of Gaul, with their capital at Toulouse.

This is the one to fix in mind, because it is the template: the first time the Western government assigned a major, prosperous, intact province to an armed barbarian people under its own king as a permanent home, on parchment, as Roman policy.
The Visigothic kingdom of Toulouse is the prototype of the post-Roman successor state, and what it built in Gaul and later in Spain is the Gothic book's story, not this one.
What this book takes from it is the precedent: after 418, "give a province to a barbarian king and call him an ally" was no longer an emergency improvisation.
It was the constitution of the Western Empire.
Meanwhile the Rhine-crossers were still loose in Spain.

After three years wrecking Gaul, the Vandals, Suebi, and Alans had been pushed south, across the Pyrenees into Hispania (the Roman name for the Iberian Peninsula, modern Spain and Portugal) around 409, partly under pressure from the Visigoths, who were doing exactly the federate job Rome had hired them for: fighting Rome's other barbarians on Rome's behalf.
In Spain the four groups divided the provinces among themselves.

The Siling Vandals and the Alans took the heaviest losses to Visigothic and Roman attacks; the surviving Alans, having lost their king and most of their fighting strength, gave up independent existence and folded themselves into the Hasding Vandals, which is why the Vandal kings afterward styled themselves "King of the Vandals and Alans." That is how a distinct Iranian-speaking steppe people disappears from history: not massacred to the last man but absorbed, its name surviving only as a title on someone else's king.
The longest-lived of all the Rhine-crossers' kingdoms was the quietest.

The Suebi settled the far northwest corner of Hispania, Gallaecia (pronounced "gal-EYE-kee-ah," roughly modern Galicia and northern Portugal), around 411 and built a kingdom there that, against every expectation, lasted until the Visigoths finally absorbed it in 585, outliving the Western Roman Empire itself by more than a century.
The Suebic kingdom of Gallaecia is one of the great forgotten states of European history, and its survival is the chapter's real lesson.
The peoples whose names everyone remembers, the ones who sacked Rome and terrorized emperors, mostly did not last.

The ones who lasted were the ones who stopped migrating: found a defensible corner nobody powerful wanted badly enough to fight for, settled it, and quietly became the government, until the difference between "barbarian war-band" and "the local state" had simply worn away.
Survival in this age went not to the most spectacular but to the most boring.
The Vandals were about to prove the rule by being the spectacular exception.

chapters.title: The Vandals
sentences: The Vandals are the people who proved that a migrating barbarian nation did not have to settle for a corner of someone else's empire.
It could take the richest piece, build a fleet, and become a Mediterranean power that the empire had to come and destroy in person.

The man who did it was Geiseric (pronounced "GUY-suh-rik," also spelled Gaiseric or Genseric), king of the Hasding Vandals and the Alans from 428 to 477, and he is one of the genuinely formidable political minds of the age, a fact the "vandalism" caricature has buried.
He was, by the hostile Roman sources' own grudging account, lame from a fall, cold, calculating, ruthless, and a far better strategist than almost any Roman he faced.
In 429 he made the decision that defined the western Mediterranean for the next century.
He took the entire Vandal-Alan people, by the most-cited figure around eighty thousand of them, and ferried them across the Strait of Gibraltar out of Spain and into Roman North Africa.

The eighty-thousand number comes from Victor of Vita, a North African Catholic bishop who wrote a bitter history of the Vandal kingdom and its persecution of Catholics in the 480s, two generations after the crossing. (A figure of this kind, handed down by a hostile churchman writing decades later, is the sort of detail this book treats as plausible-but-uncheckable rather than precise; modern historians use it for rough scale, not headcount.) This was not a raid.
It was a national relocation across a sea, and the target was chosen with precision.
Roman North Africa, the coastal band of modern Tunisia, eastern Algeria, and western Libya, was not a frontier backwater.
It was the breadbasket of the Western Empire, the single most valuable economic asset Rome had left.

The mechanism that made it so was the annona (pronounced "uh-NOH-nah"): the state-run food supply, a centuries-old system under which African grain was levied as tax-in-kind, loaded onto a government-organized merchant fleet, shipped across the Mediterranean, and distributed to feed the population of the city of Rome at public expense.
It was not a market; it was a logistical artery, the thing that physically kept the old capital alive, and the African tax revenue on top of it paid the Western army.
Geiseric did not march on Carthage to plunder it.
He marched on it to own the artery, and he understood, in a way few barbarian leaders did, that holding the switch on Rome's food supply was worth more than sacking Rome itself.
The conquest took ten years and it was patient.
The Vandals moved east along the African coast, and in 430 they besieged the great port city of Hippo Regius (pronounced "HIP-poh REE-jee-us," on the coast of modern Algeria).
The siege has a famous casualty.

The bishop of Hippo was Augustine (pronounced "aw-GUS-tin" or "AW-gus-teen"), the most influential Christian thinker of the entire ancient world, whose Confessions and City of God shaped Western Christianity for the next thousand years and beyond, and who had in fact written City of God partly in response to the Gothic sack of Rome in 410, arguing that the eternal city of God was not the same as the perishable city of Rome.
Augustine died inside Hippo during the Vandal siege in 430, an old man watching the Roman African world he had spent his life in being dismantled around him.
The image of the West's greatest Christian intellect dying as the Vandals battered the walls is the kind of detail that is almost too neat, and it happens to be true.
In 439 Geiseric took the prize itself.
Carthage had been, for six centuries, one of the great cities of the Roman world.

Long before that it had been something else entirely: the capital of a Phoenician-descended maritime empire that fought Rome in the Punic Wars and was annihilated by it in 146 BCE, then refounded as a Roman colony and grown into the empire's second city in the West (Carthage tells the older story).

There is a grim symmetry, which contemporaries noticed, in a sea-power barbarian kingdom rising again at Carthage to throttle Rome's grain, six hundred years after Rome had destroyed the original Carthaginian sea power for the same threat.
Geiseric took the city in 439, by most accounts through a surprise move while Roman attention was elsewhere, and he made it his capital.
The Western Empire had now lost its breadbasket not to a raid but to a permanent rival kingdom.
The economic consequence was immediate and it is one of the most underrated turning points in this whole story.
The annona, the African grain artery that had fed the city of Rome for centuries, simply stopped at the African end, because the African end now belonged to Geiseric.

Rome the city did not starve overnight, but the Western Empire's largest single source of revenue and the machine that fed its capital were both gone, and both were now in the hands of a king who could switch them on and off as a weapon.
An empire that cannot feed its capital or pay its army from its own taxes is no longer an empire in any functional sense.
After 439 the Western Roman state was, fiscally, a hollow shell with a court inside it.
Then Geiseric did the thing no one expected a Germanic land people to do.
He built a navy.
This was genuinely strange.
The Germanic peoples of this era were not sailors; their power was warriors on land.

But Geiseric grasped that whoever held Carthage and the African coast sat astride the central Mediterranean, and he built a Vandal fleet that within a year or two was raiding Sicily, Sardinia, the Balearic Islands, and the Italian coast at will.

For about a generation the Vandals were the supreme naval power of the western Mediterranean, and the Roman and East Roman attempts to dislodge them by sea repeatedly failed, sometimes catastrophically.
A barbarian kingdom had not just taken Rome's breadbasket; it had taken Rome's sea.

This is one of the genuine "firsts" of the period: no Germanic people before had ever been a Mediterranean naval power (the Gothic sea-raids of the 250s, Greek-crewed and Gothic-led, had been Black Sea and Aegean affairs), and none would be again until the Norse centuries later took to longships in a wholly different sea (the Vendel Age traces how that northern seafaring world was built).
For the Vandals it was invented from necessity in a single generation, and it worked.
The fleet made possible the most famous Vandal act of all.

In 455, after the murder of the Western emperor Valentinian III had thrown Italian politics into chaos and a complicated marriage-and-succession dispute (Geiseric had a dynastic claim through his son's marriage to a Roman princess) gave him a pretext, Geiseric sailed a Vandal army straight to the mouth of the Tiber and took the city of Rome.
The Sack of Rome in 455 lasted, by the standard accounts, about two weeks.
It is worth being careful here, because this is exactly the kind of vivid event later writers reshaped.

The contemporary evidence suggests the Vandals were systematic and thorough looters rather than indiscriminate burners; the bishop of Rome is said to have negotiated terms that spared the city wholesale slaughter and arson (the same bishop, Pope Leo, walks into the center of the next chapter, so he is left for it).

The reputation for mindless destruction, the "vandalism" that gave the word to modern languages, is largely a later French coinage from the 1790s and a great deal of subsequent bad-press, not a clean reading of what happened in 455.

What is not in doubt is the scale of the haul (the Vandals stripped imperial and religious treasure on a massive scale and shipped it back to Carthage along with high-value captives) and the symbolism. forty-five years after the Goths had sacked Rome, it had happened again, this time by a fleet from Africa, and this time the Western Empire was too weak even to retaliate.
The Vandals went home to Carthage with the loot, and they kept everything: the city, the breadbasket, the fleet, the leverage.

Geiseric had taken a beaten land people that crossed the Rhine on foot in 406 and, in one lifetime, turned it into the dominant power of the western Mediterranean and the only barbarian kingdom that could starve Rome at will.
He died in his bed in 477, undefeated, having outlasted nearly every Roman emperor he had ever dealt with.
It was the single most successful migration of the entire period, and nothing the Western Empire still had could touch it.

chapters.title: Attila
sentences: While the Vandals were taking Africa, the man who had started the whole chain reaction back in Chapter 1, or rather his people, came to a single terrifying point.

For about twenty years in the middle of the fifth century, the Huns stopped being a pressure transmitted through other peoples and became a direct force in their own right, under one ruler, and his name has outlived almost everyone else's in this book: Attila (pronounced "AT-ih-lah" or "uh-TILL-uh").
For the first two generations after 375 the Huns had been mostly a cause, not an actor.

They sat on the Hungarian plain and the steppe behind it, taking tribute, hiring out as mercenaries to Romans (the West's general Aetius, who had lived among them as a hostage, used Hunnic troops repeatedly; his full story is Chapter 6), and rolling subject peoples, above all a large body of Goths, the Gepids (pronounced "GEP-idz," an East Germanic people related to the Goths, settled in the middle Danube region), and others, into their confederation.

The Huns' power by the 430s rested as much on the Germanic and other subject warriors they commanded as on Huns themselves; this was a steppe empire, and steppe empires were always confederations of the conquered held together by a successful leader and the flow of plunder and tribute.
Remove the successful leader and the flow, and they came apart with startling speed.
Hold onto that.
It is how this chapter ends.
Attila and his brother Bleda (pronounced "BLEH-dah") became joint kings of the Huns around 434.
In 445 Attila murdered Bleda and ruled alone, removing the last internal check on a man whose entire strategy was the systematic extraction of gold by terror.

Between roughly 441 and 450 he turned that strategy on the Eastern Roman Empire, devastating the Balkans (the mountainous region between the Danube and Greece, the land bridge guarding the approaches to Constantinople) in a series of campaigns and forcing the wealthy Eastern capital to buy him off.

The size of the payments is one of the few hard numbers Priscus gives us: a treaty in 443 set the annual tribute at 2,100 pounds of gold and the back-payment owed at 6,000 pounds, and a harder treaty after the 447 campaign roughly tripled the annual figure.
To feel the scale, the higher rate was on the order of what it cost to maintain a substantial field army, paid every year, simply to make one man not attack.
This was the Hunnic system at its purest: not conquest, not settlement, but a protection racket run at the scale of an empire.
The Eastern Empire paid because, with the Vandals loose in the Mediterranean and the West collapsing, fighting the Huns to a finish looked even more expensive than the tribute.
We have, for once in this book, a real eyewitness, and he deserves a proper introduction because almost everything vivid we know about Attila as a person comes from him.

His name was Priscus (pronounced "PRISS-kus"), a Greek-speaking Eastern Roman, a trained rhetorician and minor official, who in 449 accompanied a diplomatic embassy from Constantinople to Attila's court somewhere on the Hungarian plain.

Priscus wrote up what he saw in a history that mostly does not survive, but the long passage describing the embassy was quoted at length by a later compiler and so came down to us, and it is the single most valuable primary source for the migration period: a literate, observant, slightly ironic Roman diplomat actually inside Attila's camp, recording what the place looked like.
Priscus's account is why we can say anything concrete at all about the Hunnic court rather than just relaying Roman terror-propaganda.
What he describes is not a tent of savages.

It is a large timber-built complex of halls and stockades, a royal compound, with Attila's wooden hall the grandest structure, attended by servants, with the court of subject Germanic kings and Roman renegades around him. (Priscus actually meets one of the renegades: a Greek who had been captured, prospered among the Huns, and now argued to Priscus's face that life under Attila was freer and fairer than life under Roman tax collectors.

Educated Romans crossed over because the empire's own subjects were not always better off than its enemies, and Attila's court paid and protected men who could read, write, and negotiate for him.) Priscus records a banquet in detail: gold and silver plate and rich food set before the guests and the lesser lords, and Attila himself eating plain meat off a plain wooden platter and drinking from a plain wooden cup while everyone around him used precious metal.
What Priscus reports is the contrast; he does not tell us Attila's reasons.
But the contrast is worth pausing on, because the obvious reading, and it is a reading, an inference from the scene rather than something Priscus states, is that the austerity was deliberate.

Surrounded by the looted wealth of two empires, Attila appears to have performed plainness, signaling that he, unlike the soft Romans and his own gilded subjects, did not need it, that his power came from the warrior and not the gold.
If that reading is right, a man who can make wealth grovel by refusing it is a more dangerous politician than one who merely hoards it.

What is on firmer ground is the tone of the source itself: Priscus, a Roman, clearly half-admired the man he was sent to flatter, and that complicated portrait, neither monster nor noble savage, is exactly why the source is trusted where the screaming chroniclers are not.

One more thing from the era's writers, flagged rather than repeated as fact: Roman sources describe some Huns as practicing the artificial elongation of infants' skulls by binding, and archaeology has indeed found deliberately deformed skulls across the Hunnic-period steppe and into Europe.
The practice is real and attested.

The lurid Roman descriptions of Hunnic appearance and "monstrousness," on the other hand, are ethnographic horror-writing of exactly the kind this book keeps warning about, and should be read as Roman fear, not Hunnic reality.
In 451 Attila turned west, and the chain reaction briefly ran in reverse: instead of pressure transmitted through the Germani into Rome, the Huns came directly into the heart of the West.
Attila invaded Gaul with an enormous army, the Huns themselves plus a great mass of subject Germanic peoples, and drove through the cities of the Rhine and into central Gaul, sacking as he went.
What stopped him is the most revealing battle of the age, because of who fought it on each side.
The Roman commander was Aetius (pronounced "ah-EE-shus" or "ah-EE-tee-us"), the last truly capable Western generalissimo, of whom much more in the next chapter.
Aetius did not have a Roman army that could face the Huns alone; there was barely a Roman army left.
So he did the thing the whole book has been describing: he assembled a coalition of the very barbarian kingdoms Rome had been settling for fifty years.

The decisive contingent was Visigothic, the Aquitaine federates from Chapter 3, under their old king Theodoric I (not to be confused with the later Theodoric the Great, the Ostrogoth, who appears in Chapters 6 and 7; same name, two different famous Gothic kings two generations apart).
Burgundians, Franks, and others joined too.

The Battle of the Catalaunian Plains (pronounced "kat-uh-LAW-nee-an," somewhere in the Champagne region of northeastern France; the exact site is unknown and debated) was fought in 451 and was one of the largest battles of late antiquity.
It was, in its essence, a coalition of Germanic kingdoms led by a Roman general against a Hunnic confederation that was itself mostly Germanic subject troops.
The old Roman-versus-barbarian frame had completely dissolved; this was barbarian Europe fighting itself with a Roman holding one of the leads.
And the lead was not firmly in hand.

Aetius's decisive contingent, the Visigoths, had every reason to fight the Huns and no particular reason to love Rome; the coalition held together for one battle out of shared fear of Attila, not out of loyalty to Aetius, and it would not outlive the day.
Holding such an alliance steady long enough to fight at all was itself the harder half of Aetius's achievement.
The battle was savage and indecisive in the technical sense, but Attila was checked, halted, and forced to retreat, the only major reverse of his career.

The Visigothic king Theodoric I was killed in the fighting, trampled or struck down in the chaos, and his death became a celebrated heroic legend among his own people, a measure of how hard the day had been.
The Catalaunian Plains did not destroy Attila.

The very next year, 452, he came back, this time straight into Italy, sacking the great northern city of Aquileia so completely that its refugees, by a much-loved tradition, helped found the lagoon settlements that became Venice (this is a charming origin story repeated for a thousand years; treat it as legend with a kernel, not as documented fact).
Northern Italy lay open.
And then Attila turned around and went home, and why he did is one of the famous puzzles of the period.

The legend, and it became one of the foundational legends of the medieval papacy, is that Pope Leo I rode out personally to meet Attila on the river Mincio in 452 and, by sheer moral authority, persuaded the scourge of God to spare Rome and withdraw.
Leo (pronounced "LEE-oh," bishop of Rome 440–461, later called Leo the Great) is the man the previous chapter held back.

He was one of the architects of papal supremacy, the claim that the bishop of Rome, as heir of the apostle Peter, held authority over the whole Christian Church and not merely his own city, an idea still in its early and contested days in the fifth century and one this man did much to push forward.
A pope who faced down the terror of two empires and turned him back by words alone was exactly the kind of story that claim needed, which is precisely why it should be handled with care.
Pope Leo's meeting with Attila is a real event; an embassy including Leo did go to Attila, and Attila did withdraw shortly after.
The meeting happened.

Whether the meeting caused the withdrawal is the contested part, and the papal legend leaves out the other reasons a coldly practical commander had to leave anyway: by the modern reconstruction his army was being wrecked by disease and famine in a ravaged Italy, his supplies were thin, and an Eastern Roman force was raiding the Hunnic homeland behind him. (That reconstruction is itself an assembly of clues from later sources, not a single eyewitness account, and historians debate its weighting.) The legend became powerful precisely because the Church needed it to be true: it is one of the clearest cases in this book of an event being remembered for what it was made to mean rather than what it demonstrably did.
Then the entire thing evaporated, almost overnight, exactly as a steppe empire built on one man was always going to.
In 453 Attila died, suddenly, the night after a feast celebrating yet another marriage, of, by the standard account, a haemorrhage, choking on his own blood in his sleep.

The account is usually traced back to Priscus, but Priscus's own narrative of the death does not survive; it reaches us through Jordanes, a sixth-century writer who summarized a now-lost Gothic history a full century after the event, and through still later compilers.
So the famous version is a tradition transmitted at two or three removes, not Priscus speaking to us directly, which is reason enough to hold the lurid bedchamber detail loosely.
There was no plausible Hunnic institution to replace him, because the Hunnic empire was him plus the flow of plunder and the fear.
His sons fought each other over the inheritance, as steppe heirs did, and the subject peoples the Huns had rolled up over three generations did the arithmetic and rebelled.

In 454, at the Battle of Nedao (pronounced "NEH-dow," somewhere in the province of Pannonia, in modern Hungary; the river and site are not securely identified), a coalition of the Huns' own former Germanic subjects, led by the Gepids under their king Ardaric, with Ostrogoths and others, destroyed the Hunnic army and the sons of Attila with it.
The Hunnic empire did not decline.
It vanished, inside a single year of Attila's death, and the Huns as a power simply cease to appear in the sources.

This is the clearest demonstration in the entire book of the deepest mechanism of the age: a barbarian power built purely on a successful war-leader and the loyalty he could buy with victory and plunder was, by its nature, only as durable as the man at the top.
Attila's empire reached from the Rhine to the steppe and lasted barely a generation.

The Roman Empire it had terrorized was a creaking, hollow, badly-governed wreck, and it would still be standing, in the East, a thousand years later, because it was built on institutions and not on a man.
The thing the Huns set in motion in 375 outlived the Huns by centuries.
That is the irony Chapter 6 has to live inside, because the Western Empire was about to die anyway, and not from the Huns at all.

chapters.title: The Fall of the West
sentences: The Western Roman Empire did not fall in a battle.
There is no Hunnic horde at the gates, no apocalyptic siege, no last emperor dying sword in hand.
It fell the way a company goes bankrupt: slowly, then in a single anticlimactic afternoon when someone finally said out loud that the thing everyone could already see was true.

The date is famous, 476, and the most important thing this chapter has to do is explain both why that date matters and why a great many serious historians think it matters far less than the textbooks pretend.
The man holding the West together in its last functional decades was Aetius (the general from Chapters 3 and 5, now in full).
Later writers, and a string of historians after them, called him "the last of the Romans," and the label is not unfair.
Aetius ran the Western Empire as military strongman and power behind the throne from the 430s to the 450s.
His method was not conquest; the West had nothing left to conquer with.

His method was management of barbarians by other barbarians: balancing the Visigoths against the Vandals, hiring Huns against the Burgundians, the Burgundians and Visigoths against the Huns, keeping every barbarian power in the West checked by another so that none could swallow Italy and what was left of the central state.

And what was left was thin: by the 440s the Western government effectively controlled Italy, a slice of southern Gaul, and the dwindling tax base those regions still yielded, having already lost Britain, most of Spain, and the African breadbasket.
Aetius was not defending an empire so much as a fortified remnant of one.
The Catalaunian Plains in 451 was his masterpiece, a coalition he stitched together precisely because Rome itself could no longer field a decisive army.
It worked exactly as long as Aetius personally ran it, which is the problem with strongman systems and the reason this book keeps returning to it.
In 454 the emperor Valentinian III, jealous and badly advised, murdered Aetius with his own hand at court.
There is a famous line attached to the act, in which an unnamed bystander tells the emperor he has cut off his right hand with his left.

It is a good line and it makes the point exactly, but it has the shape of a later moral epigram polished by chroniclers writing after the fact rather than a verbatim record of something said in the room, and it is best read as the judgment history passed on the killing, not a transcript of it.
Within a year, in 455, Valentinian was himself assassinated by men loyal to the murdered Aetius, and the resulting power vacuum is what gave Geiseric his pretext to sail on Rome (Chapter 4).
After 455 the Western Empire enters its terminal phase, and its shape is the single most telling fact about the fall.
From 455 to 476, the Western throne went through roughly nine emperors in twenty-one years.
Almost none of them ruled in any meaningful sense.

They were figureheads, raised up and discarded by whoever commanded the actual soldiers, and the man who commanded the actual soldiers, for most of that period, was not Roman and could not legally become emperor himself.
His name was Ricimer (pronounced "RIH-kih-mer"), and he is the perfect emblem of the end.

Ricimer was of Suebic and Visigothic royal descent, a Germanic barbarian by blood and an Arian Christian by faith. (Arianism was the rival, condemned form of Christianity most of the Germanic peoples followed, holding Christ to be lesser than God the Father rather than co-equal with him; the Roman population of the West held the opposite, and the gulf between the two ran through everything.

The next chapter is built on it; for now it is enough to know an Arian was, to Roman eyes, the wrong kind of Christian.) As supreme commander of the Western army Ricimer was the real ruler of Italy from 456 to 472.

But he could not take the purple himself, because a barbarian and an Arian was unthinkable as Roman emperor, so he became a kingmaker instead, installing pliable emperors and removing them when they showed independence.

This is the late Western Empire in one biography: real power held by a Germanic general who exercised it through a series of Roman puppets because the symbol of Roman legitimacy still mattered even though the substance of Roman power was entirely in barbarian hands.
One of those emperors deserves more than a name, because he was the last serious attempt to reverse the decline, and his failure is the chapter in miniature.
Majorian (pronounced "muh-JOR-ee-an"), emperor 457–461, was, by the testimony of even hostile sources, an able and energetic ruler.

He passed laws shielding provincials from the tax collectors and money-lenders who were stripping them, forbade the demolition of Rome's ancient buildings for their stone, reformed the revenue system, and rebuilt a fleet from nothing for the campaign that mattered: the recovery of Vandal Africa, the breadbasket whose loss had hollowed the Western state in the first place (Chapter 4).

He marched an army through Gaul and into Spain to embark it, and then, on the Spanish coast in 460, his invasion fleet was burned at anchor before it could sail, betrayed, the sources strongly imply, by men inside his own side.
The one realistic plan to restore the West died with those ships.
Majorian made peace with Geiseric on humiliating terms, marched his army home, and was met on the road by Ricimer, who could not tolerate a competent and independent emperor.
Ricimer arrested him, deposed him, and had him executed five days later, in 461.
He was, by the universal verdict of those who write about the period, the best emperor the West produced in its final century, and he reigned four years and ended in a ditch by the road.

The eighteenth-century English historian Edward Gibbon, whose History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire is still the most famous book ever written on this subject and whose framing still shapes how the period is taught, singled Majorian out as the last Western emperor who might have saved the West.
After him there was no serious attempt; there were only puppets, and a man named Ricimer choosing them.
There was one genuine pocket of continued Roman life, and it is worth a sentence because it punctures the tidy story.

In northern Gaul, cut off from Italy by the barbarian kingdoms, a Roman commander named Aegidius and then his son Syagrius (pronounced "see-AG-ree-us") held an independent rump Roman territory, the Domain of Soissons (pronounced "SWAH-sonn").

"Roman administration" there meant something concrete: Syagrius still kept a standing armed force, still collected taxes from the towns under him, still ran Roman courts in Latin under Roman law, and still styled his authority in Roman terms, simply without an emperor over him to report to.
It was a working scrap of the Roman state running on inertia, and it kept running for years after there was officially any Western Empire to belong to.
It survived until the Franks destroyed it in 486, meaning a piece of functioning "Roman Gaul" outlived the Western Roman Empire itself by a decade.
