What the graves do establish, beyond reasonable doubt, is the shape of the society: a steep hierarchy topped by a hereditary warrior aristocracy, organized around the sworn war-band, the gift, the hall, the horse, and the ship, wealthy enough to bury a usable boat and a fortune in worked metal with a single man, and stable enough to do it, in the same families, in the same cemeteries, for two hundred years.
That last point is the one to carry forward.
The boat-graves are not snapshots of chaos.
They are the archaeology of continuity: a settled, confident, deeply unequal elite reproducing itself, generation after generation, in a recovered and prospering north.

To find out what those families thought they were, and where they said they came from, we have to go to the place they made the symbolic center of their world, and to the dangerous, beautiful, mostly legendary stories that later told its story for it.

chapters.title: Old Uppsala and the Kings Who May Not Have Existed
sentences: About 40 miles (65 km) north of Stockholm, in a flat open landscape, stand three enormous grass-covered mounds in a row, with a smaller terraced platform and a medieval church beside them.
This is Old Uppsala (pronounced "OOP-sah-lah"), and for the people of the Vendel Age it was the closest thing their world had to a sacred capital.

It is also the place where this book has to be most careful, because Old Uppsala is where the firm evidence of the spade and the unreliable enchantment of the sagas collide most directly, and telling them apart is the whole job.
Take the firm part first.

The three great barrows are real and they are huge, among the largest burial mounds in Iron Age Scandinavia, each well over 200 feet (60 m) across at the base and standing two or three stories high even after fourteen centuries of slumping.

Excavation has shown they are graves, raised in the late sixth and early seventh centuries over cremated individuals of the very highest status, the burnt remains accompanied by melted fragments of gold, garnet, fine weapons, and gaming pieces, plus the bones of horses, dogs, and birds of prey burned with the dead.

Around the mounds, modern excavation has found the post-holes of monumental timber halls, one of them gigantic, rebuilt over time on the same commanding spot, along with rows of post-settings and evidence that this was a ceremonial and political center for centuries, not just a graveyard.
All of that is grave-and-ground evidence and it is solid: Old Uppsala was, demonstrably, a major cult and power center of Vendel-Age Sweden.
Now the dangerous part.
Almost everything narrative attached to Old Uppsala (who the kings were, what they did, how they died) comes from one source, and that source is a poem.
The poem is Ynglingatal (pronounced "ING-ling-ah-tahl," roughly "the enumeration of the Ynglings"), and the place to start is with what it actually says, because what it says is unforgettable.
It lists, generation by generation, a long line of kings, the Ynglings (pronounced "ING-lings"), supposedly ruling from Uppsala, and tells in a verse or two each how every one of them died.

The deaths are spectacularly grim and frequently bizarre: a king drowned in a vat of mead, one burned alive in his own hall, one pitchforked to death, one ridden to death in his sleep by a witch in the shape of a nightmare, one strangled by his own gold collar, one who simply walked off into a stone and was never seen again.
It reads like a catalogue of doom, and it is the single most vivid thing the legendary tradition hands us about Uppsala's kings.
It is also a trap, and here is the flag, which has to be a loud one.
Ynglingatal is a skaldic poem, meaning a piece of the dense, formal, allusive court poetry of the Norse world.
Such verse was composed to be memorized and recited rather than written.

The version we have survives only because around 1225 an Icelander named Snorri Sturluson (a brilliant, deeply learned thirteenth-century Christian politician and writer, and the single most important, and most problematic, source for almost everything we think we know about Norse paganism, who returns in Chapter 4 with the same warning attached) quoted it and built a connected prose history of these kings around it, at the head of his great compilation of Norwegian royal saga.

Even the generous datings put the poem's composition no earlier than the ninth or tenth century, well after the Vendel Age it claims to remember, and a strong scholarly current argues it is later still.
Either way it is not a Vendel-Age document.
It is, at best, a much-later poetic memory of dynastic tradition, and at worst a constructed genealogy designed to give later Norwegian and Swedish kings a deep and prestigious pedigree.

The Ynglings are the founding dynasty of later Scandinavian royal self-mythology in roughly the way the Trojan refugee Aeneas (the legendary Trojan prince from whom Rome's founders, and later its emperors, claimed descent) is the founding ancestor of Rome's: a charter myth a real later power told about its own origins, not a transcript of events.

Some of the names may dimly preserve real Vendel-Age dynasts, and the famous matching of certain Ynglings to certain mounds at Uppsala ("Aun's Mound," "Adils' Mound," "Egil's Mound") is old and attractive, but it is tradition, not identification, and no spade has ever pulled a name out of those barrows.
When this book says the Ynglings, it means the legendary royal line as later tradition remembered it, and you should hear the word "legendary" each time even where the sentence does not repeat it.

There is, however, independent, non-Scandinavian evidence that this heroic royal world was not simply invented whole by later Icelanders, and it matters enormously because it anchors the legend to something outside itself.
That evidence is an Old English poem.
Beowulf (pronounced "BAY-oh-wulf") is the great surviving epic of early English literature, composed in Old English and preserved in a single manuscript, and it is set entirely in Scandinavia.
There is not one English place or person in it.

Its hero is a warrior of the Geats (pronounced "GAY-ats" or "GEE-ats," most likely a people of southern Sweden); its central setting is the hall of a king of the Danes; its political background is a long, bitter, recurring feud between the Geats and the Swedes of the Uppsala dynasty; and several of its supposedly background figures, the Swedish and Danish kings name-checked in passing, recur across independent Scandinavian legendary traditions, which is the kind of cross-confirmation that suggests a shared real memory rather than one author's invention.
The dating of Beowulf is fiercely contested and the poem is heroic legend, not history, with a hall-haunting monster and a dragon in it.

But the world it describes, in its furniture and its values, is an unmistakable portrait of exactly the society the Vendel and Valsgärde boat-graves dug up: boat-going warrior kings, mead-halls, gift-giving lords, sworn retinues, ring-swords, blood-feud, and ship-funerals.
The poem opens with one such funeral and closes with the burning of a dead king on a pyre-laden ship.
Beowulf is what the boat-graves sound like.

It is the Sutton Hoo helmet with the voice turned on, which is why the discovery of that Scandinavian-style ship-burial in England in 1939 detonated a century of Beowulf scholarship: the poem and the grave illuminate each other across the North Sea.
Beowulf also lets us name the other great pole of this world besides Uppsala.

The poem's Danish kings, the Scyldings (pronounced "SHILL-dings"), rule from a famous hall under a king called Hrothgar, and tradition firmly locates the legendary Danish royal seat at Lejre (pronounced "LIE-reh") on the island of Zealand in modern Denmark.
Lejre is the Old Uppsala of the Danish legend, and, satisfyingly, the spade backs the legend up here the way it does at Uppsala.

Excavation at Lejre has uncovered a long sequence of enormous timber halls, one of them among the largest known in Iron Age northern Europe, occupied and rebuilt across exactly the centuries the legends place a great Danish royal hall there. (How do you reconstruct the size of a wooden building that rotted away a thousand years ago?

The timber posts are gone, but the holes dug to hold them are not: a buried post leaves a stain and a packing of stones in the soil, and the rectangle of post-holes an excavator maps out is the floor plan of the vanished hall, wall line, roof supports, and all.) The hall is real even though the kings who fill it are stories: Hrothgar, the host-king of Beowulf, and Hrólf Kraki, a different and even more celebrated legendary Danish king (his name belongs not to Beowulf but to a whole later Icelandic saga cycle of his own), are both firmly figures of legend rather than record.

This is the recurring shape of the whole chapter, and it is the most honest thing the period can teach us about how we know what we know: at Uppsala and at Lejre the places are real, the halls are real, the power was real, and the kings are mostly poems.
What those poems still let us see, used carefully, is not a king but an idea, and the idea is real even where the men are not.

It is sacral kingship: the belief that the king's body and conduct were ritually bound up with the fertility of the land and the favor of the gods, so that a king was not merely a war-leader but a kind of living guarantee of good harvests and victory.
The grimmest detail of Ynglingatal points straight at it.
Several of those bizarre royal deaths read like sacrifices, a king killed in legend after a run of bad seasons, his death restoring the luck of the land.
This is exactly the sort of vivid, memorable claim this book is built to distrust, so the honest version is the careful one.
We cannot prove that a historical Vendel king was ever ritually killed for a failed harvest.

What we can say is that the idea of a king answerable with his life for the land's luck runs consistently through the legendary material, fits the wider pattern of a religion in which the king mediated with the gods, and is the best available explanation for why these stories take the strange shape they do.
The idea is solid even though the individual kings are smoke.

And it points directly at the next question, because a king who answers to the gods with his body is only intelligible once you know who those gods were, and what their worshippers actually did at the bog and the grove and the hall.
That is where the firm ground gets thinnest of all.

chapters.title: The Gods Before the Vikings
sentences: Everyone knows the Norse gods.

Odin with his ravens and his one eye, Thor with his hammer, the rainbow bridge, the world-tree, Loki, Valhalla, Ragnarök: it is one of the most recognizable mythologies on earth, recycled endlessly into comics and films.

And almost all of it, as a connected system of stories, comes from two Icelandic books written around 1220–1270, in Christian Iceland, two to three centuries after Iceland itself converted away from paganism, and four to seven centuries after the Vendel Age.

This chapter is about the religion of the Vendel-Age north, and it has to begin by taking that famous mythology away from you, because the most important thing to understand about pre-Viking Norse paganism is how much of what you picture is a late literary reconstruction and how thin the evidence for the early system actually is.
The two Icelandic books are the Poetic Edda and the Prose Edda.

The Poetic Edda is a collection of older mythological and heroic poems, some of them probably composed in the Viking Age and transmitted orally for generations, but surviving only in a single Icelandic manuscript copied around 1270, so that even its old poems reach us through a late Christian filter.

The Prose Edda is the work of Snorri Sturluson (the same thirteenth-century Christian scholar from the last chapter), written around 1220 partly as a handbook so that poets could still understand the old pagan imagery their craft depended on.
They are magnificent and they are indispensable and they are also exactly the trap this book keeps warning about.

Snorri was a Christian writing about a religion neither he nor his great-grandparents had practiced, systematizing scattered older poems into a tidy narrative the way a scholar tidies anything, and possibly importing structure and meaning the living religion never had.
Reading Vendel-Age belief straight off the Eddas is like reconstructing the religion of Iron Age Britain from a medieval romance about King Arthur.
You would get something (a real tradition does run underneath), but you would also get a great deal of much later shaping, and you would have no way, from the romance alone, to tell which was which.
So this chapter does the harder thing.

It asks what we can say about the religion from the Vendel Age itself, from the graves, the art, the deposits, the place-names, and the few scraps of outside report, and treats the famous mythology as a late, cautiously usable echo rather than a description.
The result is thinner and stranger and much less story-shaped than the Marvel version, and that is the point.
What the Vendel-Age evidence actually supports is roughly this.

The north was polytheistic, with a population of gods whose Viking-Age names, Odin, Thor, Freyr and the rest, are partly traceable backward through place-names, personal names, picture imagery, and the deep Germanic inheritance the north shared, though the stories about them are mostly late.
Start with a single image rather than a list.
On a stamped bronze foil from a Vendel helmet there is a rider, spear levelled, two birds at his head, one eye sometimes rendered blind.

That figure, recurring on helmet after helmet and on the Gotland stones, is the archaeology's clearest face of a god: a war-and-rulers god, the figure who becomes Odin (pronounced "OH-din"), god of battle-fury, the chosen slain, kingship, and the runes.

Beneath that warrior god the evidence implies a rougher division of labor it supports better than any single late text: a thunder-and-protection god of the ordinary farmer (Thor, pronounced like the English word, defender against the chaotic powers), and fertility-and-prosperity powers governing harvest, peace, and increase, chief among them the god Freyr (pronounced "FRAY"), worshipped alongside a wider family of fertility deities such as his father Njörd and sister Freyja.

The honest summary is a polytheism with at least these functional zones, worshipped by a society in which the warrior elite naturally favored the war-god and the farming majority leaned on the protector and the fertility powers.
Anything more specific than that, pulled from the Eddas, should be heard with Snorri's thirteenth-century voice audible behind it.
The worship itself we can see better than the theology, because worship leaves residue and theology does not.
The central act was the blót (pronounced "blote," a Norse word for a sacrifice).

A blót was a blood offering, performed at the seasonal hinges of the year, in which animals, and according to some written sources sometimes humans, were killed, their blood collected and reddened onto images, altars, posts, and the participants themselves, the meat then boiled and eaten in a communal feast that bound the living community and the gods into the same meal.
The human-sacrifice claim has to carry its own flag.
It rests mainly on Adam of Bremen, a German churchman who around 1075 described a great Temple at Uppsala hung with the bodies of sacrificed men and animals.

Adam wrote three centuries after the Vendel Age, never visited Sweden, was reporting hostile hearsay about a paganism his Church was trying to destroy, and is corroborated only by later sagas with their own problems.
Bog bodies and scattered human bone in ritual deposits make some human sacrifice entirely plausible, but Adam's lurid scene is testimony from far away and long after, not eyewitness fact.
There was, on the present evidence, no class of full-time priests running the cult the way Mediterranean temples had professional priesthoods.

The reason is structural: a religion with no central authority, no scripture, no temples to endow, and no surplus set aside to feed a separate clerical caste has nothing for full-time priests to be paid out of or to administer.

Instead, leadership of the cult was an attribute of the lord and the king, the same men whose halls fed the war-band, which is precisely why kingship and the favor of the gods were the same problem (Chapter 3).
And the worship was largely outdoors.
The Vendel-Age north built no great roofed temples for archaeologists to find.
The sacred places were a sacred grove, a spring, a particular boulder or hill, a hall used for the feast, a bog.

The boundary between cultivated human ground and the wild was itself a religious frontier, which is part of why the animal-style art that wrapped the wild back onto the warrior's gear (Chapter 1) carried the charge it did.
The most archaeologically vivid form of all this is the practice of destroying wealth by giving it to water.

For centuries, Scandinavian war-bands that won a battle repaid the gods by annihilating the spoils: enemy weapons deliberately bent, hacked, and broken so they could never be used again, then sunk, sometimes with the enemy dead, into a bog or a lake.
The choice of weapons specifically is not arbitrary and the logic is recoverable.

The defeated army's gear was the most concentrated, most valuable, most potent thing a victory produced, and it belonged, in this theology, to the god who had granted the win; to keep it and re-use it would be to steal the god's own share of the victory.
So it was killed the way a sacrificial animal was killed, made useless to any human so it could pass wholly to the divine.

The great deposits excavated so far are mostly earlier Iron Age, with boat timbers in a few of them and the practice attenuating but still recognizable into the Vendel period; the bent swords are physically there in the peat, not a guess.
Hold the structure of that exchange, because it does not disappear when the bog deposits fade.
The same society that gave the gods their cut of every victory will, a few chapters from now, be running an economy where silver is weighed out and a portion changes hands at every transaction.
The accounting instinct, the win that owes a payment, survives the religion that first expressed it.
Now the ship, because the ship is where the religion and the rest of this book join up, and it deserves to be stated carefully rather than romantically.
The Vendel-Age north folded the ship deep into its picture of death and the cosmos.

The boat-graves of Chapter 2 are the loudest evidence: a usable vessel buried with the dead is a statement that the dead are going somewhere by water, or that the ship itself is the dead lord's power made into a monument, or both.

The other great body of evidence is the Gotland picture stones (pronounced "GOT-land," after the large Baltic island; the stones are upright carved memorial slabs, a narrative art unique to that island).

The Vendel-Age and later Gotland stones are dense with imagery, and at their center, again and again, is a ship under sail packed with warriors, and above it a scene that has become famous: a hall, a rider arriving, a standing woman holding out a drinking horn to welcome him.
Take what this securely shows first, because it is the strong part.
This is contemporary Vendel-Age carving, not a later text, and it shows, in stone, a culture that pictured the dead arriving somewhere important by ship and being formally welcomed there.
That is genuine, early, hard evidence for an afterlife belief, the single best we have.

The caveat follows, and only follows: later literature calls that hall Valhalla and fills it with Odin's chosen slain and a named mythology, and all of that naming and furniture is read back onto the carving from texts centuries younger.
Whether the people who cut these stones called the place Valhalla, and whether it looked anything like Snorri's hall of the slain, the stones cannot tell us.
What they can tell us, they tell us clearly, and it is old.
The single most important sentence in this chapter is the dull one, so it gets its own paragraph.

The Vendel-Age north was deeply, seriously religious, organized around outdoor blood sacrifice, sacred natural places, kingship as a cult office, and the ship as an emblem of power and the passage of the dead, and we know this from graves, stones, bog deposits, and place-names, not from the Eddas.
The Eddas describe a related world centuries downstream and through a Christian lens.
Where this book uses the famous names, it uses them as the best later labels for functions the early evidence already shows, never as proof that the early people told the late stories.
The richest, most-quoted Norse mythology is, almost in its entirety, evidence from a different time.
It belongs properly to the age that comes after this one.
The Vendel-Age religion is the root system that mythology grew out of, and the honest thing to do with a root system is admit you are mostly inferring it from the tree.

chapters.title: The Reach of a Cold Island
sentences: In the 1950s, archaeologists digging a settlement on a small island in Lake Mälaren, the great lake-system west of Stockholm, pulled out of the Swedish ground a small bronze statue of the Buddha.

It had been made somewhere in the broad region of north India or what is now Pakistan, in the Gandhara-Swat artistic tradition, at a date most often put somewhere in the sixth or seventh century though neither the exact origin nor the date is settled.

It had then traveled, by routes nobody can fully reconstruct, several thousand miles, and ended up on an island called Helgö (pronounced "HEL-yur," roughly "the holy island"), in a workshop community at the cold edge of Europe, in or before the seventh century.

With it, in the same broad context at the same site, were a bronze ladle of Coptic manufacture (Coptic meaning the long-established Christian civilization of Egypt, which kept its own church and language under, and after, Roman rule) and a fitting read as the crook of a bishop's staff in an Irish or insular style (insular here meaning the distinctive Christian art of the British Isles, Ireland and Britain together).

One island in a Swedish lake had produced objects from India, Egypt, and the British Isles, three continents reaching one excavation trench, in a society that wrote nothing and that most people, then and now, would have called the back of beyond.
The Helgö finds are the single most efficient way to demolish the idea that Vendel-Age Scandinavia was isolated, primitive, or waiting around to be discovered by the Vikings.
This chapter is about what those finds prove and what they do not, because the temptation to over-read a bronze Buddha is enormous and the careful version is more interesting than the romantic one.
First, the careful version of what Helgö was.
It was not a town and not a port-of-trade in the later sense; it was a settlement and, above all, a workshop.

The most important Helgö evidence is not the exotic imports at all but the industrial debris: a vast quantity of clay-mold fragments, crucibles, metal scrap, and unfinished castings, the residue of a major non-ferrous metalworking operation turning out brooches, mounts, and fittings on a scale far beyond one community's needs.
Helgö made things for export.
The exotic objects are real and they are spectacular, but the spine of the site is production, and that reframes everything.
The Buddha did not wander to a passive backwater.
It arrived at a place that was already a node, a place that made goods, moved them, and pulled others in.
Now the careful version of what the Buddha proves.
It does not prove a Swedish trader walked to India.

The honest reading is that an object can travel enormous distances through many hands, each hop short, the whole chain long, with no single person aware of the route's full length, the way a cowrie shell from the Indian Ocean ends up in an inland African or a North American site without anyone making that whole journey.
The Buddha is proof that Vendel-Age Scandinavia was connected to the long-distance exchange systems of Eurasia, not proof that it ran them.

But "connected to" is already a strong claim and it is the right one: the bronze Buddha, the Coptic ladle, and the Irish crozier together establish, beyond argument, that the late Iron Age north was plugged into networks reaching the Mediterranean, the Christian Near East, and the British Isles, two centuries before anyone in those places had heard of a Viking.
The plumbing of those networks is recoverable, and it explains how a cold island got rich without conquering anyone.
The local spine was the Mälaren basin (pronounced "MEH-lah-ren," Lake Mälaren and its tangle of connected waterways), which functioned as the economic backbone of early Sweden.
Inland, the Scandinavian forests produced two reliable, valuable commodities.

One was bog iron (iron smelted from the iron-rich nodules that form in northern bogs), which the forest communities turned into blooms and tools and which moved south as a dependable export into the Frankish and Anglo-Saxon worlds, where good iron always had buyers.

The other was fur: the pelts of beaver, marten, sable, and bear from the sub-Arctic north, the most prestigious northern export of all, the good that would eventually pull Scandinavians deep into the Arctic and, later, into Russia in pursuit of it.
Outward along the waterways went iron, fur, and amber; the river-and-lake system carried them to the coast and the coast carried them to the wider world.
Helgö sat on that spine and taxed it, in effect, by being the place that worked the metal and gathered the traffic.
The reach went both east and west, and both directions matter for what comes later.
Eastward, across the Baltic, Scandinavians were already establishing themselves on foreign shores well before the Viking Age proper.
The clearest case is Grobiņa (pronounced "GRO-bin-ya"), on the coast of what is now Latvia.

There, two separate cemeteries dug from around the seventh century hold a markedly Scandinavian, largely central-Swedish, population: not just men's warrior graves but women's burials with characteristically Scandinavian jewelry, which is the detail that pushes the reading past "traders stopped here" toward a community that lived and died on the spot.

How permanent and how large that community was is genuinely debated, the alternatives running from a true planted colony to a recurring seasonal trading-and-raiding station, but either way it is hard evidence that the eastward push, the one the Viking Age would turn into a river-highway running all the way to Constantinople, had its first roots here, two centuries early.
Westward and south, the gateway to the rich Frankish world ran through the Frisians (pronounced "FREE-zhuns").

The Frisians were a Germanic people of the North Sea coast around the modern Netherlands, and in this period they were early medieval northern Europe's pre-eminent maritime traders, the carriers everyone else's goods moved through.

Frisian merchants worked the North Sea coast and funneled Scandinavian goods into Francia, above all through Dorestad (pronounced "DOOR-eh-stad"), a great emporium on a branch of the Rhine, then one of the busiest trading places in northern Europe. (An emporium, a word the next chapter leans on, is one of the new planned coastal trading towns of the age, a place set up specifically for craft and exchange rather than farming.) Through Dorestad and the Frisian network, Scandinavian furs and amber went south and Frankish silver, wine, glass, and fine metalwork came north.

Baltic amber (fossilized tree resin, gathered on the southern Baltic shores and worked into beads and amulets) moved south too along a route that had carried it for millennia, prized far out of proportion to its weight, and finished glass beads came back north as a near-currency.

It is worth holding two of these "earliest" claims up against the rest of the world, because the cross-civ comparison is where the Helgö evidence stops being a Scandinavian curiosity and starts being a statement about how connected the early medieval world already was.

When that Indian Buddha reached a Swedish lake, the Mediterranean had been moving goods across continents for two thousand years, and the Indian Ocean trade that the Buddha's homeland sat on was already old and dense, a maritime exchange network of monsoon-sailed ships threading East Africa, Arabia, India, and Southeast Asia together long before this.
What is striking is not that the Buddha existed but that the chain reached this far up, into a region with no cities, no coinage yet, and no writing to speak of.

And the Scandinavian presence at Grobiņa, around the seventh century, is a late instance of a very old pattern: the Phoenicians (the Levantine sea-traders of the eastern Mediterranean) and after them the Greeks had been planting trading colonies on distant coasts more than a thousand years earlier, the Greeks ringing the Mediterranean and Black Sea with them.
Scandinavia was late to the city, late to the coin, and late to writing things down, but it was, on this evidence, not late at all to the long-distance network.
It was a far node on a system that was already global in everything but the name.
The Buddha, the ladle, and the crozier do not make Vendel-Age Scandinavia a great power.
They make it a connected one, a society generating exportable surplus and pulling the world's objects toward it through Frisian and Baltic plumbing.
Surplus plus connection is the precondition for the next thing, the thing that turns scattered workshops and seasonal markets into actual towns with mints.
That is where the silver enters the story.

chapters.title: Towns and Silver
sentences: Around the year 704, on the marshy western coast of the Jutland peninsula in what is now Denmark, someone laid out a market.
Not a settlement that drifted into being a market over generations, but a laid-out one: a strip of land beside a river, divided into regular, allotted plots, occupied by craftspeople, organized.
This is Ribe (pronounced "REE-beh"), and on the present evidence it is the oldest town in Scandinavia.
That claim needs the careful treatment this book gives every "first," because "town" is a slippery word and the alternatives are real.
By "town" here we mean a permanent or seasonally permanent, planned, plot-divided settlement of specialized craftworkers and traders, distinct from a farm, a hall, or a single workshop like Helgö.

By that definition Ribe wins, dated by precise tree-ring and stratigraphic work to the very early eighth century, with its regular plots and its concentrated craft debris arguing strongly for deliberate organization by a king or great lord rather than organic sprawl.

The honest qualifications: Helgö (Chapter 5) was an earlier production node but not a planned plot-divided town; sites like Åhus (pronounced "OH-hoos"), on the southern Swedish shore of the Baltic (the cold inland sea east and south of Scandinavia, the highway connecting the Swedish coast to the lands of the eastern push), show similar early-eighth-century craft-and-trade activity and belong to the same wave; and the "first" is always "first in the surviving, well-dated evidence," the caveat from Chapter 1 doing its quiet work again.
With those stated, Ribe stands: a real, planned, specialized town, on the Scandinavian coast, around 704.
The cross-civ comparison is where Ribe's date lands with its proper weight, and it cuts both ways.
On one hand, this is staggeringly late.
Mesopotamia (the civilization of the Tigris and Euphrates in modern Iraq, the world's oldest) had cities of tens of thousands by 3000 BCE.

China, Egypt, the Indus (the great Bronze Age civilization of the Indus river in modern Pakistan), Mesoamerica (the urban cultures of central America, the Maya and their neighbors), and the Andes (the civilizations of the South American mountain spine that culminated in the Inca) had all crossed the urban threshold thousands of years before a Scandinavian ever laid out a plot at Ribe.
Even nearby, Rome had been an empire of great cities for centuries, and the Frisian emporia and Frankish towns Ribe traded with were older than it was.
By the global yardstick the Scandinavian north reached the town almost last.
On the other hand, the comparison that actually matters is the local and contemporary one: Ribe is right in step with the northern European emporia of its own moment.

The early-eighth-century North Sea world was sprouting these planned coastal trading places, Frisian Dorestad and English Hamwic at modern Southampton among them, and Ribe is not a backward latecomer to that wave; it is a full member of it, founded essentially when its trading partners' equivalents were.
Scandinavia was late to the city in the deep-time sense and exactly on time for the emporium in the early-medieval one.
Both things are true, and the second is the one that explains what happens next.
What happens next is silver, and the mechanism is the part to get right, because "an economy with money" is an outcome and the chapter has to give you the process.
At some point in the first half of the eighth century, a generation or so after the town itself was laid out, the mint at Ribe began striking small silver coins.
The type is called the sceatta (pronounced "SHE-at" or "SKAT," plural sceattas).
A sceatta was a small, thick early medieval silver penny, the standard small-value coin of the North Sea trading world of the time, also struck in Frisia and in Anglo-Saxon England.
These Ribe sceattas are, on the present evidence, the first coinage produced in the Scandinavian world.
And a distinctive group of them carries an image worth lingering on, because it is one of the rare moments the Vendel Age speaks in a picture instead of a grave.
The obverse shows a stylized human face above a backward-looking quadruped, the so-called "Wodan-monster" type (Wodan being the West Germanic form of the name Odin).
A coin is, by its nature, a tiny piece of state communication, and these put the paramount god of the warrior elite onto the north's first money.
The blunt reading is the right one: at the very moment Scandinavia adopts the most Roman-and-Christian-world of economic tools, a struck coin, it stamps that tool with the face of its own pagan god.
It is a monetary instrument and an identity statement in one object, minted on the only frontier of Germanic Europe that was still entirely pagan.
Here is the apparent contradiction, stated before it is resolved: that "first coinage" sounds like the climax of the chapter, and it is not.
The coins were only the leading edge of the change, and the deeper mechanism is the part that matters most.
Coinage at Ribe did not make Scandinavia a cash economy; it stayed, for a long time yet, mostly a barter-and-gift economy in which the struck coin was one tool among many.
What actually transformed it was the slower, deeper arrival of silver as a weighed metal.

Across the eighth century, silver in every form began circulating through the trading places: foreign coins valued not by their stamp but by their weight, ingots, and hack-silver, meaning objects and coins deliberately chopped into pieces so a precise weight of metal could be paid out.

The thing being measured was no longer "one cow equals so many sheep" but "this much weight of pure silver, on a scale, by anyone, anywhere." That is the embryo of the system the Viking Age runs on, where a Norse trader at Baghdad (the great Abbasid capital in Iraq and the richest city in the western world), at Dublin (the Norse-founded port on the Irish coast), or at Kiev (the river-trade town on the route down to Constantinople) can transact with a balance and a bag of cut silver because silver-by-weight is a language understood everywhere.
The Vendel-Age towns are where the north learned to speak it.
The towns did one more thing, less dramatic than coins and more consequential: they concentrated specialists, and that concentration changed what the north could make and sell.
On the old farmstead, the basic social unit of this society, production and consumption happened in the same place, by the same people, between other chores.
The farmstead was an extended-family longhouse shared by people and animals, ringed by its own fields and forest, producing its own food and most of its own goods.
The emporium broke that apart.

At Ribe and its peers, archaeologists find dedicated craftspeople doing one thing full-time and at volume: comb-makers cutting fine-toothed combs from reindeer and elk antler in numbers far beyond any household's use, bead-makers melting imported glass into beads that doubled as adornment and near-currency, smiths casting brooches and mounts from bronze and pewter in disposable clay molds, leather-workers, amber-workers.
This is craft specialization, the structural separation of the maker from the user, and it is one of the quiet engines of everything in the next chapter.
There was another, uglier input feeding the same workshops, and it should be named now rather than dropped later as a surprise: this economy ran in part on slaves.

War in Vendel-Age Scandinavia, the constant raiding of one petty kingdom on another, produced captives, and captives were wealth: the unfree (the Norse called such a person a thrall) cut the antler, ground the grain, pulled the oar, and could themselves be sold south for silver.
A society organized for endemic small-scale war is also, structurally, a society organized for taking people, and the trading towns gave that traffic a market.
Hold that, because it does not stay small.

A society that can support full-time specialists, and feed them in part with forced labor, is a society generating a real surplus, and a society generating a real surplus, organized by competing lords, is a society with the means and the motive to build better ships and send its restless men a long way to use them.
The town, the coin, the weighed silver, the specialist, and the captive are not separate developments.
They are one development, the monetization and intensification of the northern economy, and they are loading the spring.
The last piece is the ship itself: not the rowed boat the boat-graves were buried in, but a hull that could cross open ocean and come home in a season.

The next chapter is about that hull, the mast that finally went into it, the runes the same century rebuilt, and a mass grave on an Estonian beach proving someone had already started using all of it to kill people.

chapters.title: The Ship and the Script
sentences: Everything in this book has been building toward one technological fact, and it is worth stating it bluntly before unpacking it: the Vendel-Age north did not invent the boat, and it did not invent the sail.
It put the two together, last and best, and that combination is the physical reason the Viking Age happened.
The boat the Scandinavians had was already, by the seventh century, a masterpiece.
It was clinker-built (pronounced "KLINK-er").

In clinker construction the hull's planks overlap each other along their edges like the clapboards of a house and are riveted together, the shell of overlapping planks built first and the internal frame fitted into it afterward; the point of doing it that way is the result, a hull that is light, strong, and springy.
A clinker hull flexes and works in a seaway instead of resisting it, it draws very little water so it can run right up onto a beach with no harbor, and it can be built long and lean.
The Scandinavians had been perfecting clinker construction for centuries, and the boat-graves of Chapter 2 are buried clinker boats.
But every Scandinavian vessel from the early Vendel period that survives well enough to tell was driven the same way: by oars.
It was a superb rowing boat.
It had no mast.
The honest evidence for when that changed is worth giving carefully, because "the Sail Reaches Scandinavia" is the single load-bearing claim of the entire book and it deserves its sources shown.
The argument is largely negative-then-positive.

No well-preserved early Vendel-Age Scandinavian vessel shows the structures a sailing ship requires, most diagnostically a mast-step (the reinforced timber a mast's foot locks into; without it the mast just tears the bottom out of the hull).

Then, from around the early eighth century, the diagnostic evidence appears: hulls reinforced amidships to take a mast, the keel deepened, the whole design shifting from "rowed boat that can take a sea" to "ship that can run before a wind." The picture-stones of Gotland (Chapter 4) corroborate it: the later stones, unlike the earliest, are crowded with ships under big square sails.

The current scholarly reading, on this combined negative and positive evidence, is that sail technology was adopted in Scandinavia broadly across the eighth century, almost certainly transmitted through the same Frisian and Frankish maritime contact that brought the silver and the sceattas (Chapter 6), the North Sea traders being sailing people the Scandinavians dealt with constantly.
The cross-civ comparison is the one that makes this land, and it is genuinely arresting.
The sail is not a hard idea.
Egypt was sailing the Nile before 3000 BCE.
The Mediterranean had been a sea of sailing ships for more than three thousand years before a Scandinavian stepped a mast.

The Polynesians (the Pacific island peoples who settled an ocean a third of the planet wide in double-hulled sailing canoes) were making deliberate open-ocean voyages of thousands of miles while the Vendel north was still rowing.
The Scandinavians were not behind on boats; their hulls were arguably the finest in the world.
They were, for reasons that are still debated, simply very late to put a sail on one.
And that lateness is the hinge of the whole story, because of what they put the sail on.
They did not bolt a sail onto a generic boat.
They put it onto the best clinker hull on earth, a hull that already drew almost no water and could beach anywhere and be rowed in a dead calm or up a shallow river.

Sail plus that hull is the mechanism, and it has to be spelled out because the whole Viking Age is downstream of it: the result was a single vessel that could cross open sea fast under sail, then drop the sail and row silently up a river or onto an undefended beach, strike, and be gone before any land-based response could form, and then sail home, all in one season.
No society on the Atlantic edge had a tool that combined open-water range with that landing flexibility.
The longship is not a better boat.
It is a raiding system with no defense designed for it yet.
By the second half of the eighth century the political map underneath all this had hardened enough to name, though only roughly.
There was no Norway, no Sweden, no Denmark in the modern sense.

There was a patchwork of petty kingdoms: along the Norwegian fjord coast a scatter of small kingdoms whose lords competed ceaselessly for men, ships, and cattle; across the Swedish lake-country the Uppland power around Uppsala and its rivals; and in the south, around the Jutland peninsula and the Danish islands, a Danish kingship consolidating faster than the rest, because it had the most dangerous neighbor.
These kingdoms were not peaceful with each other.

Vendel-Age Scandinavia raided itself constantly, petty kings seizing each other's ships and coasts and cattle, and the organization and seamanship honed in that internal violence was exactly the capability that would shortly be turned outward.
The thing pushing Danish consolidation hardest was at its southern door.

The Frankish ruler Charlemagne, the most powerful man in Europe, was in these decades conquering and forcibly Christianizing the Saxons (the Germanic people of what is now northwestern Germany, the Danes' immediate southern neighbors and pagan kin) through a long, brutal war across the 770s and 780s, grinding Frankish power right up to the Danish border.
A Christianizing superpower destroying the pagan people next door concentrated Danish minds wonderfully.
The clearest monument to that pressure is the Danevirke (pronounced "DAH-neh-veer-keh"), a massive earthen rampart, in places miles long, thrown across the narrow waist of the Jutland peninsula.

Jutland is the land bridge connecting Denmark to the continent, only about 25 miles (40 km) across at this neck, and a rampart there did not have to stop an army so much as channel it: a wall, ditch, and palisade across the one land approach forced any invader off the easy route and into a killing ground the defenders chose, while leaving Danish ships free to come and go by the sea the wall did not block.

Dendrochronology has dated major construction phases at the Danevirke to the eighth century (one well-known dated phase falls around the 730s), pushing serious building earlier than scholars once assumed.

It proves what it proves rather than what it stopped: a barrier on that scale, raised by organized mass labor, means a Danish authority that could command large numbers of people to dig for a collective purpose.
The petty kingdoms were no longer just war-bands.
At least one of them was becoming a state with a frontier.
The same century the north got the sail and hardened its kingdoms, it also rebuilt its writing, and the change is small, technical, and quietly revealing of the whole society.
The Germanic peoples had had a runic script for centuries, the Elder Futhark (pronounced "FOO-thark," named like "alphabet" from the sound-values of its first letters).
The older system had 24 characters and was used across the whole Germanic world for short inscriptions on objects.
Across the eighth century the Scandinavians did something counterintuitive with it: they cut it down, to a streamlined sixteen-character script, the Younger Futhark.

This is strange on its face, because the spoken language was actually getting more complex in its sounds at the time, so the new alphabet had fewer letters for more sounds and was, as a recording tool, markedly worse: a single rune now had to stand for several different sounds, and the reader had to supply the rest from context.
The exact reasons are debated and this book will not pretend otherwise.
But the most-cited explanation fits everything else in this book: the runes were never meant to be a precise recording technology in the first place.
They were for marking ownership, casting a charm, and above all raising a memorial to the dead, short public monumental statements, not archives.

A society that runs on the spoken oath, the memorized law recited at the assembly, the genealogy carried in the head, and the poet's praise-verse held in memory does not need a precise alphabet, and never did.
The Younger Futhark is a tool optimized for its real job, the runestone, and the Viking Age would raise those by the thousand.
The streamlining is not a society getting dumber.
It is a society sharpening a memorial chisel and quietly confirming that, even now, it had no intention of becoming a society of records.
All of that, the ship, the sail, the kingdoms, the chisel, is structure.
Here is the proof that the structure had already fired at least once, recent, grim, and dated decades before the history books say the violence began.

In 2008 and after, on the Estonian island of Saaremaa (pronounced "SAH-reh-mah"), at a place called Salme (pronounced "SAL-meh"), construction workers and then archaeologists uncovered two buried clinker boats packed with the dead.

The smaller held around seven men; the larger held roughly three dozen, stacked in layers with their weapons, shields, fine combs, and elaborate gaming pieces, and many of the bodies bearing the unhealed cuts and blade-wounds of men killed in a fight.
They were not local.

Isotope and ancient-DNA analysis indicates the dead came from Scandinavia, several of them close blood relatives (one pair full brothers), most consistent with central Sweden and the Lake Mälaren region that was the heartland of the boat-graves and Helgö, though the science narrows the homeland to that broad area rather than to a single district.
They are dated to around 750.

The most economical reading, and the consensus one, is that this was a Scandinavian armed seaborne expedition: a high-status war-band, kinsmen among them, that crossed the Baltic, met disaster in a fight on the Estonian coast, and was buried where it fell by survivors or by the enemy with strange honor.

Salme is, on the present evidence, the earliest physically attested Scandinavian sea-raid, and it pushes the violence the Viking Age is famous for back roughly forty years before the date the history books traditionally start it.
The longships were already going out, and already dying out, a full generation before Lindisfarne.

A monetized economy, a town network, restless competing kingdoms hardening into states, a slave economy running on captives, the best ships on earth with sails newly on them, and, at Salme, the buried proof that a Scandinavian war-band had already crossed the open sea to kill and be killed.
Salme is the system of this whole chapter, found by accident, with the men still in it.
Everything is now in place.
The last chapter is about why it went outward.

chapters.title: The Longships Sail
sentences: By around the year 780, every separate thread this book has followed was lying in the same hand, and the only question left was which way that hand would turn.

It is worth laying the threads out together one last time, because the Viking Age is not a single cause and the popular explanations (overpopulation, or greed, or pagan rage at Christian missionaries) are each a fragment of a convergence.
Here is the convergence, stated as the mechanism it was.

The north had surplus: recovery from the sixth-century die-off (Chapter 1), combined with a warming climate and better farming, had by the mid-eighth century put more food on the ground and more people on it than there had been in living memory.
Surplus produces a specific demographic problem in a specific inheritance system.

There was no written law of inheritance in this society, only custom, and the customary pattern reconstructed from later Scandinavian law and from the structure of the farmstead itself was partible: a dead man's land and movable wealth tended to be split among his sons rather than handed whole to a single heir, as it was in parts of the Frankish world.
Partible inheritance in a prospering, growing elite has a brutal arithmetic.
Every generation it subdivides estates and generates a standing crop of armed, well-born, ambitious young men with a famous name, a sword, and no land of their own and no prospect of any at home.
Those men needed a lord, and a lord needed gold, weapons, and glory to keep them (the war-band logic, running unchanged since the deep Germanic past).
The competing petty kingdoms (Chapter 7) manufactured exactly the surplus of restless aristocratic violence the system fed on.
The monetized, silver-using economy (Chapter 6) gave that violence a clear, portable, universally fungible goal: not just plunder, but silver, the one thing wanted everywhere.
And the ship-plus-sail (Chapter 7) gave it, for the first time, the physical reach to go get it and come home in a season.
Five loaded conditions.
Four of them were about pressure building inside Scandinavia.
The fifth was about a target outside it, and the target is the part that decided the direction.
We have an unusually clear window onto exactly that northern economy, and the right way to use it is to take what it says first and flag it second.

A Norwegian chieftain called Ohthere (pronounced "OAT-here"), from the far north of Norway, described his world and his wealth in his own voice, and what he describes confirms from the inside what the archaeology argues from the outside.
His wealth was not grain.

It was the far north: a herd of his own domesticated reindeer, the sea-hunt for whale and walrus, and, above all, the tribute he levied in furs, eiderdown, walrus hide, and walrus ivory from the Sámi (the indigenous reindeer-herding and hunting people of the European Arctic, called "Finnas" in his account, whom the Norse chieftains taxed as subjects).

The northern economy ran on squeezing high-value, low-bulk goods out of the wild and the far north and moving them south to where the silver was, and it ran in good part on dominating other people to do it.
Now the flag, and it is the same one the sagas got.
Ohthere is not a Vendel-Age source.

He was a real traveler who visited the English court of King Alfred (the king of Wessex who beat back the Viking armies and around 890 had a circle of scholars translating Latin learning into English), and his account survives only because Alfred's scholars inserted it into their Old English version of a Latin world-history, the Orosius.
It is therefore a single later traveler's report, recorded by foreigners around 890, describing the generation after this book ends.
Held at that arm's length, it is gold: the clearest single witness to the economic engine of the whole Viking enterprise, provided you never forget he is testifying after the fact.
They could, by now, actually get there.

With no compass and no chart, they navigated by accumulated craft taught from father to son: the sun's height and bearing, the star patterns, the set of the swell against a known course, the color of the water over a bank, the flight of land-bound seabirds at dusk.

It was not magic and it was not guesswork; it was a body of memorized practice precise enough for repeated open-water crossings, and the war-band at Salme had already shown, around 750, that it worked well enough to carry armed men across the Baltic.
What lay across that water is the fifth condition, and it is the one that aimed the spring.
Across the North Sea, on the coasts of Britain and Ireland, sat the richest soft targets in the early medieval world.

For two and three centuries the Christian kingdoms of the Anglo-Saxons and the Irish had been pouring wealth into monasteries: gold and silver altar vessels, jewelled book-covers, reliquaries, the accumulated pious donations of generations of kings and nobles.
The logic of those donations matters, because it explains why the wealth piled up where it did.

Early medieval Christians believed the prayers of monks measurably helped a soul through judgment and out of punishment after death, so endowing a monastery with treasure and land was, in the plainest terms, buying prayer: a king gave gold to a holy house and the house prayed for his soul forever.
Centuries of that left the monasteries as treasuries of portable precious metal that no one had ever needed to guard.

And the monasteries had been sited, for spiritual reasons, in exactly the worst possible places from a defensive point of view: on remote headlands and small islands, deliberately set apart from the world, far from any army, walled against nothing because nothing had ever come for them by sea.
They were undefended, immensely rich, and reachable only by a ship that could cross open ocean and land on an open beach.
Such a ship had not existed in northern hands a few generations earlier.
It existed now.
A concentration of portable, holy, unguarded silver on an exposed island is, to a society configured exactly the way Chapters 6 and 7 configured this one, not a temptation.
It is a solved equation.
The solving had, in fact, already started, and the first recorded contact reads almost like a dark joke about everything that was about to happen.
Around 789, three ships came across the sea to the Dorset coast of southern England.

A local royal official, a reeve named Beaduheard, rode down to meet them; the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle says only that he tried to compel the newcomers to the king's town, treating them, the natural assumption, as traders to be regulated, because in living memory ships from the north were traders.
They killed him.

The Portland incident, written down later in that Chronicle, is the first notice in any English source of Norsemen (the word this book has used for the Scandinavian peoples it is about, the same Vendel-Age north now turning its ships outward) on English soil, and its whole meaning is in the misunderstanding: the English official met them inside the old, peaceful framework of trade, and the framework was already dead and nobody on the English side knew it yet.
Then comes the date the world remembers, and it is the right place for this book to stop, because it is not really an ending.
It is a handoff.

In 793, traditionally dated to the 8th of June (the precise day comes from the chronicler Symeon of Durham, writing around 1100, three centuries later, not from the near-contemporary sources, which agree on the year and the horror but not the day), raiders from across the sea fell on the monastery of Lindisfarne (pronounced "LIN-dis-farn").

Lindisfarne was the perfect proof of everything this book has argued: a small island off the Northumbrian coast in northeastern England, joined to the mainland only by a sand causeway the tide covers twice a day, holding one of the holiest and richest churches in the British Isles, the home of jewelled gospel-books and a saint's shrine, with no wall, no garrison, and nothing but open water between its treasure and the sea.
They plundered the church, cut down and drowned and carried off the monks, took the treasure, and were gone before any force on land could reach a place the land could barely reach at all.
The shock through Christian Europe is hard to overstate.

Alcuin (an English scholar from York, the leading scholar of the age, then running Charlemagne's palace school in Francia) wrote letters that survive, appalled, groping for an explanation and settling on the only one his world had: that God was punishing the English for their sins.
The alternative, that a new kind of enemy with a new kind of ship now existed and nothing on any coast was safe, was almost literally unthinkable.
It was, of course, the truth.
Everything in this book is in that one June day.
The surplus that bred the restless young men.
The competing kingdoms that gave them lords.
The silver economy that told them exactly what to want.
The trade networks that told them exactly where the wealth was.

And the ship, the perfected clinker hull with a sail on it at last, that let them cross the open sea, strike a defenseless holy island, and vanish back over the horizon with the treasure before the alarm could even be raised.
The Vendel Age built every one of those pieces, slowly, over the two and a half centuries between a darkened sky in 536 and this.
None of it was a plan.
It was a convergence, and in 793 it converged.
This book has been the long fuse.
The explosion is not its story.

The longships are over the horizon now, low and fast and full of armed men, the sail up and the coast of Northumbria falling away behind them, and the age they are sailing into belongs to the Norsemen who would live it and the world that would have to survive them.
The Vendel Age is over.
The Viking Age has just begun.

chapters.title: The Mound Builder Myth
sentences: Somewhere around the year 1810, a Tennessee farmer running a plow through his field hit something that wasn't a rock.
When he dug it out, it was a small pot, and inside the pot were human bones.
He was not surprised.

Half the farms in the Mississippi and Ohio valleys turned up bones and broken pottery and carved shell when the land was first cleared, because the land was full of mounds (deliberately built hills of piled-up earth, not natural rises, ranging from low domes to flat-topped earthen platforms the size of small pyramids).
Tens of thousands of them dotted the landscape, some small enough to plow flat in an afternoon, some a hundred feet tall and covering more ground than a city block.
They were everywhere.
They were obviously made by people.
And almost every white American who looked at them refused, flatly and on principle, to believe that the people in question were Indians.
A note on words before we go further.
This book uses "Indians," "Native Americans," and "Native peoples" to mean the same thing: the indigenous peoples of North America and their descendants.
"Indian" is the older term (Columbus's geographic mistake, frozen into the language) and the one the nineteenth-century sources used; "Native American" and "Native peoples" are the modern usages.
They are not different groups.
Where this book later names specific nations (the Cherokee, the Muscogee, and so on), those are particular peoples within that whole.
This is where we have to start, because the lie came first.

Before the archaeology, before the careful excavation, before anything we now know about the people who built the mounds, there was a story that white Americans told themselves for most of a century, and it is worth understanding that story in detail, because the truth is partly the story of how it was demolished.

The story was called the Mound Builder Myth, and its core claim was simple: a vanished race of people (not Native Americans, but someone else, someone "civilized") had once lived in North America, built these magnificent earthworks, and then been exterminated by the ancestors of the Indians, who were cast as savage latecomers incapable of such works.

The identity of the vanished race was filled in differently by different enthusiasts, and the list is a tour of nineteenth-century fantasy: they were the lost tribes of Israel; they were Vikings who had sailed down from a Norse colony; they were refugees from sunken Atlantis; they were the Toltecs (a real central-Mexican people who built the city of Tula and dominated the region around 900–1150 CE, well known to nineteenth-century writers from Spanish colonial accounts) or some other civilized Mexican people who had passed through on their way south; they were Welsh, Phoenician, Hindu, or the survivors of a "white" race annihilated by a "red" one.
The specifics did not matter.
What mattered was the load-bearing assumption underneath all of them: that Native Americans could not possibly have done this.
It is important to be precise about why this myth was so popular, because it was not an innocent error.

The decades when the Mound Builder Myth was at its strongest, roughly the 1820s through the 1840s, were exactly the decades when the United States was forcibly removing the Native nations of the eastern woodlands from their land.

That is not a coincidence of timing; the myth peaked when it did because it was useful when it did. (The groundwork was laid earlier, in Washington's scorched-earth Sullivan Campaign and the shattering of Tecumseh's confederacy: Early American Republic Ch 3 and Ch 15.) As white settlement pushed west into the Southeast in the early 1800s, the federal government and southern states wanted the land occupied by five large, organized, treaty-holding Native nations: the Cherokee of the southern Appalachians, the Muscogee (Creek) of Georgia and Alabama, the Chickasaw and Choctaw of Mississippi, and the Seminole of Florida, all of them in the Southeast, all of them with their own governments and farms and (in several cases) written constitutions.
The argument for taking that land needed a moral cover, and the mounds, sitting all over the contested ground, supplied one.

The Indian Removal Act was the 1830 federal law that authorized the result: the government negotiated (and coerced) treaties under which these nations were expelled from the Southeast and marched a thousand miles west to what is now Oklahoma.

The forced march, during which thousands died of exposure, hunger, and disease, is remembered as the Trail of Tears (its full story, the removal's legal mechanism and the Cherokee court cases, is told in the American narrative; Antebellum America Ch 4).
It was being debated and executed while Americans were standing in front of the mounds insisting that no Indian could have built them.
The two facts are connected, and not subtly.

Walk the logic the way its believers did: the mounds prove a civilized people once lived here; Indians are savages who could not have built them; therefore Indians must have arrived later and exterminated the real builders; therefore the Indians are themselves usurpers who took this land by slaughter; therefore taking it back from them is not theft but the recovery of a stolen inheritance.
Every step is false, but stacked together they convert dispossession into restitution.
If the Indians had exterminated the noble Mound Builders, then removing the Indians was not theft.
It was, in a grotesque inversion, justice.
The myth was not a harmless antiquarian hobby.
It was the dispossession's alibi, and it was repeated from pulpits, in school textbooks, and on the floor of Congress.
The dismantling of the myth was slow, and it began, improbably, with a future president and a hole in the ground.

In 1784, Thomas Jefferson (the Virginia planter and revolutionary, later the third president of the United States, here a forty-one-year-old gentleman scientist) owned land near a small earthen mound on the Rivanna River in central Virginia.

Jefferson did something with that mound that essentially nobody in the Western world had thought to do with an ancient monument before: instead of digging straight down into the middle to grab whatever treasure was inside, he cut a trench through the side and looked at the layers.

He observed that the mound was built of distinct strata, that bones occurred at multiple levels in different states of decay, and that the bodies had clearly been added over a long period rather than all at once.
From the layering he reasoned about the sequence of events that had produced the mound.
This sounds obvious.
It was not.

Reading a site by its layers, what archaeologists call stratigraphy (the principle that material laid down later sits on top of material laid down earlier, so the vertical sequence is a record of time), is the foundational technique of modern archaeology.

Jefferson's Rivanna trench is widely cited in histories of archaeology as the first stratigraphic excavation conducted in the Americas and one of the earliest deliberate uses of the layered approach anywhere; the precise "world first" claim is hard to defend strictly (a few European antiquarians were also digging and observing layers in the eighteenth century), but the standard reading is that Jefferson's dig was a remarkably early and methodologically modern instance.
He published his findings in Notes on the State of Virginia, and crucially, he concluded that the mound had been built by the ancestors of the Native peoples of the region.
He was right.
Almost nobody listened.
For comparison, careful stratigraphic excavation would not become standard archaeological practice in Europe, at sites like Troy and Pompeii, for nearly another century.
The next major step was a survey.

In 1848, the brand-new Smithsonian Institution in Washington published the inaugural volume of its scholarly series, Contributions to Knowledge. (The Smithsonian is a federally chartered research and museum organization, founded in 1846 with a bequest from the British scientist James Smithson, today the world's largest museum and research complex.) That volume was titled Ancient Monuments of the Mississippi Valley, and it was the work of two Ohio men, Ephraim Squier, a newspaper editor, and Edwin Davis, a physician.

Over several years they had measured, mapped, and surveyed more than two hundred mound sites and earthwork complexes across the Ohio and Mississippi valleys, producing precise scale drawings of geometric earthworks so large and so exactly laid out that the drawings themselves became the primary record, which mattered, because most of the sites they drew were plowed away within the next two generations.
The detail in those surveys is what makes the persistence of the myth so striking.

At the Newark Earthworks in Ohio they recorded a circle joined to an octagon, each side of the octagon hundreds of feet long, the whole figure laid out with a regularity that implies a unit of measure and a survey method.

Squier and Davis put a near-perfect geometric monument on the page, in ink, at scale, and still leaned toward the vanished-race interpretation, because the cultural pressure to do so was nearly irresistible.
That is the cognitive dissonance the myth demanded: you could draw the evidence with your own hand and refuse to read what it said.
The myth survived rigorous mapping.
It would take the federal government setting out, deliberately, to settle the question.
The pressure Squier and Davis bent under was not a vague mood; it had concrete teeth.
A scholar who credited the mounds to Indians was contradicting the political consensus of the country that funded the scholarship, the textbooks that taught it, and the churches that moralized it.

The vanished-race story was the respectable position, taught in schools and preached from pulpits; the contrary position aligned a researcher with the inconvenient and unpopular claim that the people the United States was busy expelling had built the nation's most impressive ancient monuments.
It cost reputation and standing to say so, and it threatened the comfortable national story almost everyone wanted to keep believing.
That is the kind of pressure that makes careful men report what their data did not show.

The break came at the Bureau of Ethnology, the Smithsonian's research arm devoted to ethnology. (Ethnology is the systematic study and comparison of human cultures; in this period the Bureau was focused on documenting Native American languages, customs, and history under the wrong assumption that they were vanishing.) In the 1880s, Congress appropriated money specifically to resolve the mound question once and for all, and the work was handed to a man named Cyrus Thomas.
Thomas is one of the quiet heroes of this story, and what makes him interesting is that he started out a believer.
When he took the job he was confident the mounds had been built by a vanished race.

His team then spent years excavating mounds across the eastern United States systematically, comparing the construction methods, the artifacts, the burial practices, and the pottery against everything known about the historic Native peoples of the same regions. ("Historic" here means the nations that lived there in the period of European written records, as opposed to prehistoric, the eras before any written documentation.) If the mound builders had been a different, vanished people, their work should look unrelated to the historic nations'.
It did not; the techniques and artifacts lined up.
The evidence pointed in exactly one direction.

In his enormous 1894 report for the Bureau, Thomas stated the conclusion without hedging: the mounds were built by the ancestors of the American Indians, the same peoples Europeans had encountered when they arrived.
There was no vanished race.
There never had been.
Thomas had been hired to prove the myth and had instead, honestly, killed it.
Among scholars, the question was effectively closed by 1894.

In the popular imagination it would limp along for decades more, and a diluted version of it (the vague sense that the mounds are "mysterious" and that "nobody really knows" who built them) survives in roadside lore to this day.
They are not mysterious in that way.
Thomas won the scholarly argument on paper at almost the exact moment the physical evidence was being hauled away in carts.
By the time he published, much of what he was racing to record was already gone.
The destruction of the mounds is its own grim chapter, and the clearest example is a city.
The site of modern St.
Louis, Missouri, was so thick with earthen mounds that its nineteenth-century nickname was "Mound City." The largest of them was a colossal riverfront earthwork called the Big Mound.
By nineteenth-century descriptions it was a long ridge-top mound on the order of 300 feet long and roughly 30 feet high, a small city block of piled earth.

It was leveled in the 1860s, and the dirt, human burials and artifacts included, was carted off as construction fill during the city's expansion (the destruction is variously attributed in the sources to railroad grading and to street and lot leveling; the common thread is that the largest mound in St.
Louis was sold off by the cartload).
Across the Mississippi and Ohio valleys, thousands of mounds were plowed flat for farming, quarried for road and rail construction, or simply bulldozed for towns.
We will never know what was in most of them.
The myth helped here too: it is psychologically much easier to bulldoze a "mysterious old hill" than the pyramid of a known people.
So here is the thesis of this book, stated plainly so the rest of it can argue the case.
In the river valleys of eastern North America, between roughly 800 and 1600 CE, Native peoples built a civilization.
It had cities.

It had monumental architecture: flat-topped earthen pyramids larger at the base than the Great Pyramid of Giza, raised basket-load by basket-load by people with no metal tools, no wheel, no draft animals, and no writing.

It had hereditary sacred rulers, ranked classes, organized warfare, a shared art and religion that spanned half a continent, and trade networks that moved seashell, copper, and stone across thousands of miles.

When white Americans found the wreckage of it, they could have read it correctly (Jefferson did, in 1784) but instead they built a myth that erased the builders, because the myth was useful to a project of dispossession.
The builders did not vanish.

They were devastated by a catastrophe we will come to (Chapter 9), they reorganized under new names (Chapter 10), and their descendants are citizens of sovereign Native nations in the United States right now.
The mounds still stand.
People who can trace their ancestry to the people who raised them are alive and can tell you so.
One methodological note before the story, and it governs everything that follows.
The Mississippian peoples had no writing system.

Not a script, not even an undeciphered one like the Indus Valley seals. (The seals are short strings of pictorial signs carved on stone stamp seals by the Bronze Age cities of the Indus River, in modern Pakistan and India: a real script that nobody has been able to read; Indus Valley Ch 6.) The Mississippians did not even have that.
They left no inscriptions, no records, no names of their own kings written by their own hands.
This means that, unlike Mesopotamia or Egypt or China, we cannot quote a single sentence a Mississippian person said.

The contrast inside the Americas is sharper still: the Maya, far to the south in Mexico and Central America, had a fully developed writing system that modern scholars have largely deciphered, the only fully readable indigenous script in the pre-Columbian Americas.

While Maya scribes were carving dated dynastic histories into stone in the same centuries (Maya Ch 2), the Mississippian world produced monumental cities and a continent-spanning sacred art and not one readable word.
Everything in this book therefore comes from exactly four kinds of evidence, and it is worth knowing them up front so you can weigh each claim as it arrives.
They are flagged here because they are the spine of the chapter title and they govern every page after this one.

The first is archaeology: the mounds, the houses, the pottery, the bones, the trash, the seeds, the postholes, the physical residue of life, read with techniques like stratigraphy and tree-ring dating (matching the distinctive pattern of wide and narrow annual growth rings in a wooden beam to a master ring sequence built from living and dead trees, which can pin a piece of timber to the exact year it was cut).
This is the bulk of what we have, and it is silent on names, words, and motives.

The second is the de Soto chronicles: four accounts written by members or contemporaries of a Spanish military expedition led by Hernando de Soto, the same conquistador who had grown rich helping plunder the Inca Empire in Peru (Chapter 9), which marched through the Southeast from 1539 to 1543 while Mississippian chiefdoms were still functioning.
These are eyewitness, which is priceless, and they are also the testimony of an invading army that was robbing, enslaving, and killing the people it described, which colors everything.

The third is the French ethnography of the Natchez: detailed accounts written by French colonists in the early 1700s who lived alongside the Natchez of the lower Mississippi, the last society to practice something recognizably like the old Mississippian way of life into the era of European observers with notebooks (Chapter 7).

This is the one window we have onto the inside of a living Mississippian-style society, but it is a single, late, contact-altered society, and projecting it back five centuries onto Cahokia is a temptation the careful reader must resist, as the careful scholars do.

The fourth is descendant oral tradition: the migration stories, clan histories, and ceremonial knowledge of the Native nations of the Southeast and the eastern woodlands (the Muscogee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Cherokee, Caddo, and others) whose ancestors built and inherited this world.
These are not decoration and they are not folklore in the dismissive sense.
They are the testimony of the people whose history this is, and where they can be checked against the archaeology they have repeatedly turned out to be carrying accurate information across centuries.
And a final caveat that inoculates the entire manuscript, because this book will say "first" and "earliest" and "largest" many times.

In archaeology, "first" never means "the first time this was ever done." It means "the first instance for which we have found surviving evidence." Evidence survives by luck: by climate, by what got plowed under versus what got protected, by which sites a railroad happened to miss.

The eastern woodlands are humid; organic material rots; the dry desert preservation that makes the record of the Ancestral Puebloans so rich does not exist here. (The Ancestral Puebloans were the Native farming peoples of the arid Southwest, the builders of the great houses of Chaco Canyon and the cliff dwellings of Mesa Verde, ancestors of today's Pueblo nations, and the subject of this chain's previous book; Ancestral Puebloans Ch 1.

This book will compare the two repeatedly: two very different North American civilizations running at roughly the same time, one on river floods in the east, one on desert ingenuity in the west.) So when this book says the largest earthwork in the Americas, or the first city north of Mexico, read it as "the largest and first that we have found and can date," and hold the rest of the continent's unrecovered past in mind.

chapters.title: The Eastern Woodlands
sentences: Forget, for this chapter, the people.
Start with the water.
If you stand on a bluff on the east bank of the Mississippi River just below where it meets the Missouri, near modern St.
Louis, you are looking at the outflow of a drainage basin that covers roughly forty percent of the continental United States.
