None of the three uses the word "slavery"; the document carefully says "other persons," "such persons," "person held to service," which is itself evidence the framers knew exactly what they were doing and how it would read later.
The first is the Three-Fifths Clause.

The question was: when you apportion seats in the population-based House of Representatives (and electoral votes for president), do you count enslaved people, who could not vote and were held as property, as part of a state's population?
Southern delegates wanted them counted fully, which would inflate Southern representation enormously while the people being counted had no rights at all.
Northern delegates wanted them not counted, since they were treated as property, not citizens.
The "compromise" was to count each enslaved person as three-fifths of a person for the purpose of apportioning representation and direct taxes.

The mechanical effect was enormous and is often misunderstood: it did not make enslaved people three-fifths free; it gave slaveholding states extra seats in Congress and extra votes for president in direct proportion to the number of human beings they held in bondage.
It made slavery a source of national political power for the people who practiced it.

A few delegates did say so on the record at the time: Gouverneur Morris of Pennsylvania denounced the clause on the Convention floor, asking why the people of Pennsylvania should be tied to the inhabitants of Georgia and the Carolinas who held their fellow men in bondage and then claimed political power for it.

For decades, this clause tilted Congress and the presidency toward the slave states (Chapter 18); the outsized Southern weight it created outlived slavery as the Senate bloc whose filibuster killed every anti-lynching bill and nearly killed the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (the Civil Rights Era narrative, Ch 10).
The second is the slave-trade clause.
Several Southern states, especially South Carolina and Georgia, made continued importation of enslaved Africans a condition of joining at all.
The compromise was a clause forbidding Congress from banning the Atlantic slave trade for twenty years, until 1808 (Chapter 13).
The mechanism: it constitutionally protected the international slave trade from federal interference for a fixed period, in exchange for Southern agreement to other commerce powers.

The third is the fugitive-slave clause, which provided that a "person held to service" who escaped into another state was not freed by reaching free soil but had to be "delivered up" on the claim of the owner.

Mechanically, this meant the free states were constitutionally obligated to help return escaped people to slavery; it nationalized slavery's reach, making no part of the country a true refuge, and it is the seed of the bitter fugitive-slave fights of the next era (Antebellum America Ch 6).

Historians and Americans argue, genuinely and unresolvedly, about what these clauses mean about the Constitution as a whole: whether it was fundamentally a pro-slavery document, an antislavery one that contained compromises its framers expected to wither, or a document deliberately ambiguous because the alternative to ambiguity was no union at all.
This book does not pretend that argument is settled, because it is not.
It is worth seeing the framers' evasion of the word against a later constitutional choice.

When India wrote its constitution in 1950, its drafters, who had the American example in front of them as a warning, did the opposite: they named the evil they were attacking, explicitly abolishing untouchability and caste discrimination by name in the document itself (Modern India Ch 6).

The American framers' refusal to write "slavery" while building it into the structure, and the Indian framers' decision to name caste in order to outlaw it, are two opposite answers to the same question: does a founding document confront the great injustice of its society, or paper over it.

What is not in dispute about the American case, because it is in the text, is the mechanics: the Constitution gave slaveholding regions disproportionate national power, shielded the slave trade for two decades, and bound free states to slavery's enforcement.
The framers chose union over confronting slavery, and they did it knowingly.

Whether that was statesmanship that bought time for the experiment or a catastrophe that armed the worst men in the country with the machinery of the state is exactly the question the rest of this chain (and the next) is forced to answer in blood.

The American refusal to name slavery was eventually corrected, at the cost of 750,000 lives and a constitutional revolution, in the Reconstruction Amendments of 1865–70, the "Second Founding" (Reconstruction Chs 4–5).

chapters.title: Ratification
sentences: Writing the Constitution was the easier half.
The fifty-five men in Philadelphia had no authority to impose anything; what they had produced was a draft, and a draft is just paper until people agree to be ruled by it.

The fight over whether to adopt the Constitution (its ratification, the formal state-by-state vote to approve it) was a year-long argument that the Constitution's supporters won narrowly, sometimes by a handful of votes, and the terms on which they won shaped the document the country actually lives under.
This chapter is that argument, and it matters because it was a real argument about power, not a formality.
The Convention built its own approval mechanism, partly because it had no legal standing to do otherwise.

The Constitution would not go to the state legislatures (who would resent losing power to it) but to specially elected ratifying conventions in each state, on the theory that the document should be approved directly by representatives of the people.

And it would take effect once nine of the thirteen states ratified, not all thirteen, a deliberate break from the Articles' unanimity rule that had paralyzed everything (Chapter 4), and, strictly, an illegal one, since the Articles required unanimity to change.
The framers were betting that legitimacy would come from popular approval and momentum, not from following the old rules.
The country split into two camps, and their names are a propaganda victory worth flagging.
The supporters of the Constitution called themselves Federalists, which sounds reassuring and moderate.

The opponents got stuck with Anti-Federalists, a label that defines you by what you are against, and they never recovered the messaging ground, a reminder that the founders were practicing politicians, not marble statues.
But the Anti-Federalists were not cranks, and their objection was serious and, in hindsight, partly prophetic.

Their core argument was the orthodox one (Chapter 1): a republic this large, with a central government this strong, would inevitably slide toward tyranny, swallow the states, and lose touch with the ordinary people it claimed to represent.
They distrusted a distant capital, a standing army, a powerful president who looked to them like a king with a term limit, and a Senate that looked like an aristocracy.

And they made one concrete, devastating point: the proposed Constitution had no Bill of Rights, no written list of specific liberties (free speech, free worship, jury trial, protection from unreasonable search) that the government was forbidden to violate.
Several state constitutions had one; the federal document did not.

The Federalists' answer, that a bill of rights was unnecessary because the federal government only had the powers specifically granted to it, was logically clever and politically disastrous, because ordinary people, reasonably, did not want to trust their liberty to a clever argument.
The Federalists' great weapon in the argument was a series of newspaper essays, and the fact that it was newspaper essays is itself the point.

Under the shared pen name "Publius," Alexander Hamilton, James Madison, and John Jay wrote eighty-five essays, published in ordinary New York newspapers across 1787–88 and read by ordinary New York voters before being collected as The Federalist (often called the Federalist Papers).
This was unusual in the world of the 1780s.

Argument of this depth about how a government should be engineered was, almost everywhere else, conducted privately among rulers and ministers; here it was being made in the public press, for popular persuasion, because in a republic the public was the audience that had to be won.
They were campaign documents, written fast, to flip a specific ratifying vote in a doubtful state.
They are also the deepest explanation anyone produced of how the machine was supposed to work and why, which is why they are still read.
The single most important essay is Federalist No. 51 (Madison), which answers the obvious objection to the whole design: what if the people running the government are not good men?
Madison's answer is that you do not rely on their being good.
You arrange the offices so that each official's personal ambition and self-interest is set against every other official's, so that the system polices itself.

"Ambition must be made to counteract ambition," he wrote, because "if men were angels, no government would be necessary." That is the engineering principle of the entire Constitution in one line: it does not assume virtuous people; it assumes self-interested ones and points their interests at each other. (Federalist No. 10, also Madison, makes the related argument that a large republic controls faction better than a small one, Chapter 5.) The Federalist is read today as political philosophy; it was written as a get-out-the-vote operation, and both things are true at once.
The state conventions were close, contingent, and dramatic, and a few near-misses are worth naming because the outcome was not foreordained.
The small states ratified fast (the Constitution's Senate was good for them).
Pennsylvania ratified amid procedural brawling.

Massachusetts ratified only after the Federalists struck a deal (ratify now, with a strong recommendation that a bill of rights be added immediately by amendment), the "Massachusetts Compromise" that became the template for getting the big undecided states across.

Virginia, the largest state and home to half the famous founders, ratified narrowly, by a recorded vote of 89 to 79, after a ferocious debate between Madison for the Constitution and Patrick Henry against it.

Henry was Virginia's most famous Revolutionary orator, the man whose "give me liberty or give me death" speech had helped push the colony toward war in 1775, and he now turned the same thunder against a national government he feared would swallow the states.
New York ratified by an even tighter 30 to 27, essentially because Virginia had already gone in and being left outside the union alone was untenable.
North Carolina and Rhode Island held out and only ratified after the new government was already running.
The Constitution did not win in a landslide of consensus.
It squeaked through, conditionally, on a promise.
That promise was the Bill of Rights, and it is essential to see it as the negotiated price of ratification, not a gift.
To get the wavering states, the Federalists promised that the very first Congress would propose constitutional amendments listing protected liberties.
Madison, initially skeptical, made himself the manager of that promise.

The Constitution's own amendment rule is demanding by design: an amendment must be proposed by two-thirds of both houses of Congress and then ratified by the legislatures of three-quarters of the states (not all of them, the Articles' fatal unanimity trap having been deliberately abandoned, but a deep supermajority).
The First Congress proposed a set of amendments, and by 1791 enough states had ratified that the first ten took effect: the Bill of Rights.

They guarantee, among other things, freedom of speech, press, religion, and assembly (First Amendment); the right to bear arms (Second); protection against unreasonable searches (Fourth); the rights of the criminally accused, including jury trial and protection against self-incrimination (Fifth and Sixth); and, crucially for the original argument, the Ninth and Tenth Amendments, which say that rights not listed are still retained by the people and that powers not handed to the federal government are reserved to the states or the people (in practice, for most of the country's early history, this meant that ordinary matters like criminal law, marriage, property, and schooling were the states' business, not Washington's).
The Anti-Federalists lost the war (the Constitution was adopted) but they won this concession, and it is one of the most-cited parts of the document today.
American constitutional liberty is, in a real sense, a thing the losers extracted.
End this chapter on what ratification decided and what it deliberately did not.

It decided that the United States would be a single federal republic with a strong national government, an experiment in scale that the best political theory of the age said could not work (Chapter 1).
It decided how power would be divided, checked, and transferred.
It did not decide slavery.

The slavery clauses (Chapter 5) went in unaltered; the Constitution that the country ratified in 1788 was a structure built to last, with an unresolved and growing contradiction sealed inside its load-bearing wall.
Everyone involved knew it was there.
The bet was that the structure could hold long enough for some later generation to deal with it.
The rest of this book is the testing of that bet.

chapters.title: Inventing the Presidency
sentences: On April 30, 1789, George Washington stood on a balcony in New York City (the temporary national capital, chosen because the new government had to meet somewhere immediately and the permanent capital had not yet been located or built, Chapter 8) and took an oath of office for a job that had existed, on paper, for a matter of months and that no human being had ever held.
Everything about the federal government was, at that moment, a hypothesis.
The Constitution described the offices; it did not describe how to actually run them.

Here is the single thread that runs through this entire chapter, and it should be held onto through all three of its parts: nothing in these years was inherited, and everything was being made up by people arguing as they went.

The presidency, the cabinet, the federal court system, the relationship between Congress and the executive, all of it was improvised in real time and then, because it worked, frozen into permanence and treated ever after as if it had always been there.
Washington understood this more clearly than anyone, because he knew every single thing he did would become a precedent whether he wanted it to or not.
Start with why it had to be Washington and what that did.

The Electoral College (Chapter 5) chose its first president unanimously, the only unanimous presidential election in American history, and it chose Washington because he was the one figure every faction trusted not to become a king, which they trusted precisely because he had already given up supreme power once and gone home (Chapter 3).

That is the cross-civilizational point worth holding: most new republics, ancient and modern, have failed at exactly this hinge, the transition from the heroic founder to a working institution, because the founder will not let go or no one trusts him to.
The clearest example was unfolding at that very moment across the Atlantic.

The French Revolution, which began the same year Washington took office, would run through a constitutional monarchy, a republic, a Terror, and a Directory in barely a decade and then collapse into the dictatorship of General Napoleon (Chapter 9), failing precisely the test Washington was passing, because no French figure could be trusted to hold supreme power and then surrender it.
The American republic's enormous initial advantage was that its founder had already proven, before the office existed, that he would let go, and would build the office to be let go of.
Washington was acutely aware of this.
"I walk on untrodden ground," he wrote.
"There is scarcely any part of my conduct which may not hereafter be drawn into precedent." So he set precedents on purpose.

A fight broke out almost immediately over what to call him; some in the Senate, led by Vice President John Adams, wanted a grand title ("His Highness the President of the United States and Protector of their Liberties") on the theory that the office needed dignity to command respect.
Washington let the plain title "Mr.
President" win, because a republican chief magistrate who is addressed like a minor monarch starts becoming one.
The Constitution did not mention a cabinet (a group of department heads who advise the president and run the executive branch's main divisions).

Washington created one in practice by appointing and regularly consulting the heads of the new departments: Thomas Jefferson as Secretary of State (foreign affairs), Alexander Hamilton as Secretary of the Treasury (finances), Henry Knox (the self-taught former Boston bookseller who had been Washington's trusted artillery chief through the Revolution) as Secretary of War, and Edmund Randolph (a Virginia lawyer, former governor, and Convention delegate) as Attorney General, the government's chief lawyer.

The habit of a president governing through a council of department heads he picks and meets with regularly is, again, a Washington invention, not a constitutional command, exactly the pattern this chapter keeps pointing at: an institution conjured out of practice rather than text.

He guarded the office's independence in concrete ways too: when the Senate expected to advise him face to face on a treaty and the meeting went badly, he stopped coming in person and established that the president negotiates treaties himself and brings the finished result to the Senate, not the other way around, a boundary between the branches drawn by one awkward afternoon.

He served two four-year terms and then deliberately declined a third (Chapter 9), establishing by personal example a two-term limit that held as an unwritten rule for nearly a century and a half until it was finally written into the Constitution.
He kept the presidency dignified but not royal, deferred to Congress on legislation while protecting the executive's separate sphere, and treated the office as a trust to be handed on intact.
None of that was required by the text.
All of it became the unwritten constitution.
The same improvisation was happening, just as urgently, in the legislature.

The First Federal Congress (1789–91) was doing work so foundational that historians have often called it a second constitutional convention, because the Constitution had given it an outline and it had to build the actual government out of nothing.
It created the executive departments.
It passed the revenue laws that gave the government an actual income (a tariff and other duties), solving at a stroke the fatal flaw of the Articles (Chapter 4).
It debated and sent out the Bill of Rights (Chapter 6).
And it passed the Judiciary Act of 1789, which deserves its own paragraph because it built a whole branch of government the Constitution had barely sketched.

The Constitution created "one supreme Court" and authorized Congress to create lower federal courts, but it did not say how many justices the Supreme Court would have, what the lower courts would look like, or how cases would move between state and federal courts.

The Judiciary Act of 1789 answered all of that: it set the Supreme Court's size, created a system of lower federal courts beneath it, and, in a provision that became enormously important, defined the kinds of cases the Supreme Court could hear.

One clause of this very act, Section 25, would later be the basis for the Supreme Court reviewing and overturning state court decisions, and another part of it would, in 1803, be struck down by the Court itself in the case that invented judicial review (Chapter 11).

The point is the chapter's whole point: the federal judiciary that Americans now treat as a timeless coequal branch was not handed down ready-made in 1787; it was assembled by an ordinary act of Congress in 1789, the way the cabinet was assembled by Washington's habit and the presidency by his self-conscious choices.
Step back and look at what these few hundred people did in roughly two years.

They took a sketch on parchment and, by improvising, arguing, and watching each other for precedents, conjured into actual working existence a president, a cabinet, a court system, and a treasury that could collect money and make the government move, every piece of it invented in real time by men who often disagreed bitterly about what they were inventing.
The astonishing thing is not that it was perfect.
It was that it ran at all, built on the fly by people who knew the whole world expected it to fail.
And the deepest of those disagreements, the one about money and power and what kind of country this was going to be, was about to split the inventors against each other.
That fight is the next chapter.

chapters.title: Hamilton's Revolution
sentences: The new government worked, mechanically, almost at once.
What it did not have was money, credit, or any agreement about what kind of country it was supposed to become.
The man who answered the money question, and in answering it split the founders into the country's first two political parties, was the Secretary of the Treasury, Alexander Hamilton.

His financial program is the most consequential set of policy decisions in this entire book, and most Americans could not explain how a single piece of it worked, so this chapter explains the mechanisms, because the mechanisms are the history.
Hamilton's situation in 1790 was dire.

The United States owed money it could not pay: to foreign governments (chiefly France, plus the Dutch, whose Amsterdam bankers had lent the Revolution money as a commercial investment, betting on a new trading partner that would owe them and pay interest), to the national government's own domestic creditors who had lent it money or supplied the army in exchange for paper IOUs, and, separately, the individual states owed large war debts of their own.
The country's credit (its reputation for paying what it borrows, which determines whether anyone will lend to it again and at what cost) was wrecked.
The government's bonds (its IOUs) traded for a fraction of their face value because nobody believed they would ever be paid in full.
Hamilton's Report on Public Credit (1790) proposed a solution that was, by the standards of the time, audacious.
The first piece was funding the debt at par.
Hamilton proposed that the federal government honor its debts at full face value, paying off old IOUs at one hundred cents on the dollar, with reliable revenue dedicated to it.
To most people this looked like madness: why pay full value for paper everyone knew was worth a fraction?

Hamilton's reasoning is the key to his whole worldview: a government that always pays its debts in full can always borrow again, cheaply, in the next emergency, and the ability to borrow is the sinew of national power.

A national debt, properly managed and reliably serviced, was not a curse but, in the idea he is famous for, something close to a national blessing: it bound the country's wealthy creditors to the government's survival (you do not want the institution that owes you money to collapse) and it created a stock of trustworthy financial instruments the whole economy could build on.
The second and most explosive piece was assumption.
Hamilton proposed that the federal government assume (take over and pay off) the states' individual war debts as well as its own.
The mechanism mattered enormously.

If the federal government, not the states, owed the war debt and paid it, then the people the country owed money to (a wealthy, influential, nation-spanning class of creditors) would look to Washington, not to thirteen separate state capitals, for their money.
Their financial self-interest would be permanently attached to the strength and survival of the national government.
Assumption was, deliberately, a nation-binding device disguised as accounting.

It was furiously opposed, partly because states like Virginia had already paid off much of their own debt and resented being taxed to cover the debts of states (like Massachusetts) that had not, and partly because critics saw, correctly, that it was a transfer of power and loyalty from the states to the center.
That opposition had a leader and a rival vision, and this is where the first party system is born.
Thomas Jefferson (Secretary of State) and James Madison (now a leader in Congress) came to see Hamilton's whole program as a betrayal of the Revolution.
Their objection was not bookkeeping; it was a fundamentally different idea of what America should be.
Hamilton's America was commercial, urban, industrial, financially sophisticated, led by an energetic central government, modeled frankly on the institutions that had made Britain powerful.

Jefferson's and Madison's America was a republic of independent farmers: virtuous, self-sufficient, suspicious of banks, cities, debt, and concentrated power, with a small central government and most authority left to the states and the people.
They believed Hamilton's system would create exactly the corrupt alliance of government and rich financiers that had, in their reading, rotted Britain, and would in time produce an American monarchy.
This was not a personality clash.
It was a real argument about whether the United States should become a commercial great power or remain an agrarian republic, and it has, in mutated forms, never stopped.
It was also a local version of an argument already running across the Atlantic Enlightenment.

The French Physiocrats had argued that real wealth comes only from land and agriculture and that manufacture and finance are essentially parasitic; Adam Smith, in The Wealth of Nations (1776), had argued the opposite, that commerce, manufacture, and markets are the engine of national wealth.
Hamilton was, in effect, the American Smith; Jefferson was close to an American Physiocrat.
The founders were fighting Europe's economic debate with American material and American stakes.
The deadlock over assumption was broken by one of the most famous deals in American history, and the mechanism is the lesson.

In 1790 assumption was stuck in Congress and so was the question of where to put the permanent national capital, which Southerners desperately wanted on the Potomac (near Virginia) rather than in the financial North.

At a single private dinner in New York in June 1790, arranged and hosted by Jefferson, the three men (Jefferson and Madison on one side, Hamilton on the other) cut a bargain over the meal: Madison would stop organizing the votes blocking assumption and let enough Southern congressmen switch to pass it, and in exchange the permanent national capital would be built on the Potomac River, on land Virginia and Maryland would cede, the future Washington, D.C. (Chapter 12).

The account survives mainly because Jefferson later wrote it down himself, with his own spin, so the exact words are his version; what is not in doubt is that assumption and the capital's location were settled together, off the floor, at that table.
The federal financial system and the location of the capital were traded for each other over dinner.
It is the model of how the early republic actually governed: not by the machine running itself, but by a handful of men negotiating across a table because the formal mechanism had jammed.
Hamilton's program had two more pillars.

The Bank of the United States (chartered 1791) was a national bank, partly government-owned, that would hold federal money, issue a stable national paper currency, and lend to the government and to business, the financial spine a modern economy needs.
It provoked the first great constitutional argument over the limits of federal power.
Jefferson argued the Constitution nowhere authorized Congress to create a bank, so it could not (a position called strict construction: the government may do only what the document explicitly says).

Hamilton argued that the Constitution's clause empowering Congress to make all laws "necessary and proper" for carrying out its listed powers implied the authority to create instruments, like a bank, reasonably useful to managing the nation's finances (a position called broad or loose construction, the doctrine of implied powers).

Washington sided with Hamilton; the Bank was created; and that argument, over whether federal power extends only to what is written or also to what is reasonably implied, became one of the permanent fault lines of American government, settled, mostly, only by a Supreme Court decision a generation later (Chapter 17).
It is worth seeing how American the form of this fight was.

At almost the same moment, Revolutionary France was discovering the same hard truth (that a written constitution does not interpret itself) and resolving its constitutional disputes by decree, street mob, and ultimately the guillotine.
The United States fought its equivalent argument with legal briefs, cabinet memos, and eventually a court opinion.
The contrast (the same problem, settled by lawyers in one place and by violence in the other) is one of the quiet reasons the American experiment held.
Hamilton's last great state paper, the Report on Manufactures (1791), deserves a real sentence rather than a footnote, because it was the most radical of all.

It argued that the federal government should deliberately build American industry from scratch, using protective tariffs to shield infant factories from cheaper British goods and direct subsidies ("bounties") to encourage new manufacturing, a frank rejection of the idea that America should stay a nation of farmers.
Congress, dominated by agrarian interests, declined to enact most of it.
But the document became the explicit blueprint that Henry Clay's "American System" would pick up a generation later and that economic nationalists have returned to ever since (Chapter 17).

By the early 1790s the founders had sorted into two camps with names, newspapers, and organizers: the Federalists, around Hamilton and (loosely) Washington and Adams, favoring strong central government, commerce, order, and Britain; and the Democratic-Republicans (often just "Republicans" then, the ancestors of today's Democratic Party, not today's Republicans; the names and coalitions reshuffled repeatedly across the nineteenth century, which is a story for later books in this chain, not this one), around Jefferson and Madison, favoring states' rights, agriculture, France, and a narrow reading of federal power.
The framers had not wanted parties; the Constitution does not mention them; Washington dreaded them.
They formed anyway, almost instantly, because the argument they embodied (about money, power, and what kind of nation this would be) was real and could not be wished away.
The first party system was the proof that the machinery could absorb deep, organized disagreement without breaking.
Whether it could absorb the one disagreement everyone was carefully not having, over slavery, was the question being postponed, and the rest of this book is the postponement running out.

chapters.title: The World at War
sentences: The American republic spent its first decade believing it could stay out of Europe's quarrels and discovering it could not.

In 1789, the same year Washington took office, the French Revolution began, and within a few years it had plunged Europe into a generation of war that no neutral commercial nation could escape, least of all one whose two political parties each loved one of the warring sides.

This chapter is about how foreign policy nearly tore the young republic apart, and how the federal government, for the first time, used force against its own citizens, and what both of those tests proved about whether the machine could hold.
The trigger was the French Revolution.

In 1789 the French overthrew their king, declared a republic, and proclaimed the rights of man, and many Americans, who remembered France's decisive help in their own revolution (Chapter 2) and saw a sister republic being born, were thrilled.

Then it turned: the French executed their king, launched a Terror that guillotined thousands, and went to war with monarchical Britain and most of Europe (the French side of this, 1789 and the Terror, is told in the Enlightenment volume's chapters on the Revolution; this chapter is the same event seen from the American shore).
Now Americans were split exactly along the party line.
The Democratic-Republicans (Chapter 8) saw France as the embattled republic, liberty's cause, and Britain as the eternal monarchical enemy.
The Federalists saw Revolutionary France as bloody anarchy and Britain as the source of order, trade, and most of America's commerce.

Foreign policy was no longer a question of national interest argued calmly; it was a partisan passion, and each side genuinely believed the other was conspiring to sell the republic to a foreign tyranny.
The first crisis was Citizen Genêt.

In 1793 the French Republic sent a minister, Edmond-Charles Genêt, to the United States. ("Citizen" was a revolutionary affectation: the new French Republic had abolished aristocratic titles like Monsieur and addressed everyone, even diplomats, as Citoyen, "Citizen," to signal that all were equal under the Revolution; Americans found the style either thrilling or alarming depending on their party.) Citing the 1778 Franco-American alliance (Chapter 2), Genêt began, on American soil, recruiting Americans into privateering ventures (a privateer was a privately owned armed ship licensed by a government to attack and capture enemy merchant shipping for profit, a kind of legalized, government-commissioned piracy used by every naval power of the age) and military expeditions against Britain and Spain, appealing directly to the public over the head of the government.
This was an open challenge to whether the United States controlled its own foreign policy.
Washington's answer was the Proclamation of Neutrality (1793): the United States would take neither side and forbade its citizens from participating in the war.
The mechanism mattered as much as the content.

Nothing in the Constitution explicitly said the president could unilaterally declare the nation's posture toward a foreign war; Washington asserted that the executive could, and the precedent that the president leads in foreign affairs largely dates from this act. (Genêt's mission collapsed so completely that, his own government having turned murderous and likely to execute him if he returned, Washington let him stay in America rather than send him to the guillotine.) The deepest domestic firestorm of the decade was Jay's Treaty.

Britain was still doing things the Treaty of Paris (Chapter 3) had supposedly ended: holding forts on American soil in the Northwest, seizing American merchant ships and cargoes trading with France, and impressing American sailors (forcibly seizing men off American ships and forcing them into the British Navy, on the claim they were British subjects, a practice that will detonate in Chapter 15).
Washington sent John Jay, the Paris peace negotiator of Chapter 3 and now the first Chief Justice of the United States, to London to negotiate.

The treaty Jay brought back in 1795 got the British forts evacuated and avoided a war the United States could not afford, but it conceded almost everything else, won nothing on impressment, and looked, to half the country, like a humiliating surrender to the old enemy.

The reaction was the most violent partisan eruption of the era: Jay was burned in effigy up and down the country, Hamilton was reportedly pelted with stones while defending the treaty at a New York public meeting (a story that comes from later Hamilton biography and may be sharpened in the retelling, but the hostility it describes is not in doubt), and the treaty passed the Senate by the bare two-thirds required.

The lasting significance is double: the treaty probably did save the country from a disastrous early war, and the fight over it hardened the two parties into permanent, organized, mutually loathing machines.

The same period produced a parallel negotiation with the opposite mood, and the pattern connecting them is the point: in both cases a weak United States had to bargain with a European power from a position of weakness, but where Jay had little leverage against a confident Britain and came away with a bitter half-loaf, the American envoy to a distracted, declining Spain came away with almost everything he wanted.

That was Pinckney's Treaty (1795), which fixed the American boundary in the Southwest and, crucially, guaranteed American farmers the right to ship their crops down the Mississippi through Spanish-held New Orleans, the lifeline of the entire western economy and a foreshadowing of why Louisiana would matter so much (Chapter 12).

In the middle of all this, the new government's coercive power was tested at home for the first time, and the test is worth understanding mechanically because it is the answer to Shays' Rebellion (Chapter 4).

To pay for Hamilton's debt program (Chapter 8), Congress had put an excise tax on domestically produced whiskey. (An excise is a tax on a good made and sold inside the country, as opposed to a tariff, which taxes goods coming in from abroad; this was the new federal government's first internal tax, and it landed on a product, not a port.) On the western frontier, especially in western Pennsylvania, farmers distilled their grain into whiskey because it was the only way to get a bulky, perishable crop to distant markets profitably; the tax therefore fell hardest on exactly the people least able to pay in cash and most distant from the government.
In 1794 western Pennsylvania erupted: tax collectors were tarred and feathered, an official's house was burned, and armed assemblies talked of secession.
This is the Whiskey Rebellion.
The crucial difference from Shays' Rebellion was the machinery now available.
Where the Confederation had been helpless (Chapter 4), the federal government under the Constitution could act.

Washington, citing the new laws, called out and federalized a militia force of around thirteen thousand men (the figure usually given; it was, by the standards of the time, a very large army, comparable to the field forces Washington had commanded in the Revolution) and personally rode west at its head.
The rebellion evaporated without a battle; a few men were convicted and then pardoned.

The contrast with Revolutionary France is sharp and worth drawing: in the same years, the new French Republic was also putting down armed risings of its own people, above all the Vendée revolt in western France, but it did so with mass killing on a scale that radicalized the whole Revolution.
The American government used a show of overwhelming force, secured surrender almost without bloodshed, tried a handful of men in regular courts, and then pardoned them.
The point was never the whiskey.

The point, demonstrated deliberately, was that the new government, unlike the old Confederation, could enforce a law it had passed, by force if necessary, against its own citizens, and that it would do so within the law and then show mercy, rather than as a vengeful tyrant.
It was the Constitution's answer to the question Shays' Rebellion had asked, and the answer was yes, the republic can keep order.
Washington left office on his own terms, and the manner of his leaving is itself a founding act.
After two terms he declined a third (establishing the precedent of Chapter 7) and published, in 1796, his Farewell Address, drafted with Hamilton's help.
It was never delivered aloud; Washington never read it to anyone.

It was released to a newspaper and reprinted across the country as a printed open letter to the nation, which was simply how a national leader reached a continent-sized public before there was any way to address one in person.
Two warnings in it echo through the rest of this book and the next.

He warned against the "spirit of party," the danger that partisan loyalty would become so fierce that Americans would see fellow citizens as enemies and invite foreign powers to exploit the split, a warning written by a man watching exactly that happen.
And he warned against "permanent alliances" and entanglement in Europe's quarrels, advice that shaped American foreign policy for over a century.

The irony is total: the most revered figure in the country, warning against parties, was leaving a government already split into two parties that were about to fight the most poisonous election yet (Chapter 10).
The machine had survived foreign crisis and a domestic rebellion.
Whether it could survive its own partisanship was the next test.

chapters.title: The Adams Interlude
sentences: The single term of the second president, John Adams (1797–1801), is usually treated as a bridge between the two giants who bracket it, Washington and Jefferson.
That undersells it.

The Adams years contain the young republic's first true civil-liberties crisis, the first explicit articulation of the doctrine that would eventually be used to justify secession, and a decision by the president to put the country's survival ahead of his own political life.
It is a four-year stress test of whether a republic can tolerate dissent in a crisis, and the republic nearly failed it.
Adams won the election of 1796 narrowly over Jefferson.

By a quirk of the original Constitution (which awarded the vice presidency to the runner-up in the presidential vote, not to a running mate, a flaw fixed in Chapter 11), the new president was a Federalist and his vice president was the leader of the opposition party.
That alone tells you how unprepared the system was for parties.
Adams was honest, learned, prickly, and politically isolated, not fully trusted by Hamilton's wing of his own party, and loathed by Jefferson's.
The defining crisis was a near-war with France, called the Quasi-War because it was an undeclared naval conflict, never formally a war.
France, furious that the United States had signed Jay's Treaty with Britain (Chapter 9), began seizing American merchant ships in large numbers.
Adams sent a commission to Paris to negotiate.

French intermediaries, identified in the published American dispatches only by the letters X, Y, and Z, relayed a demand that, before formal talks could even begin, the Americans pay a substantial bribe to the French foreign minister Talleyrand personally and arrange a sizable loan to the French government. (The specific sums vary in the retellings; what the dispatches show is a demand for money up front as the price of being negotiated with at all.) When Adams released the dispatches, the XYZ Affair detonated American opinion: "Millions for defense, but not one cent for tribute" became the slogan, anti-French fury swept the country, the navy fought French ships at sea, and the Federalists, riding the war fever, won big in the 1798 elections.
And then they overreached, in a way that produced the first great test of the First Amendment.
In 1798 the Federalist Congress passed four laws known together as the Alien and Sedition Acts, and each has to be understood for what it actually did.
The Naturalization Act raised the time an immigrant had to live in the country before becoming a citizen from five years to fourteen, aimed squarely at immigrants, who tended to vote Republican.
The Alien Friends Act let the president deport any non-citizen he personally judged "dangerous," with no trial, on his own say-so.

The Alien Enemies Act allowed detention and deportation of citizens of an enemy nation during a declared war (this one, uniquely, was never repealed and is still on the books more than two centuries later, and it has been invoked in America's later wars to detain or remove enemy-nation nationals).

The fourth, and the one that mattered most, was the Sedition Act: it made it a federal crime, punishable by fine and prison, to write, print, or speak "false, scandalous, and malicious" statements against the federal government, Congress, or the president with intent to defame them or bring them into "contempt or disrepute." On its face it had a safety valve: truth was a defense, and a jury decided.
In practice, the administration used it to prosecute and jail its political opponents: Republican newspaper editors and even a Republican congressman were convicted for criticizing President Adams.

Whether the Sedition Act was a genuine wartime security measure aimed at French subversion, or a cynical attempt to criminalize the opposition press in an election cycle, is debated by historians, and honesty requires saying so rather than picking the most damning version.
What is not debatable is its effect and its selectivity: it was enforced almost entirely against critics of the party in power, and conspicuously not against critics of the Republican vice president.

A republic had passed a law making it a crime to criticize the government, eight years after ratifying the First Amendment. (The mechanism, the federal government jailing dissenters for their speech under a war scare, has a direct descendant in the Espionage Act of 1917 and the Palmer Raids, Roaring Twenties Ch 3.) The irony deepens across the Atlantic: Britain, the country whose liberties the founders had so often invoked, had passed almost identical wartime gag laws of its own in 1795 (the Treasonable Practices and Seditious Meetings Acts), criminalizing dissent under the same French-war pressure.
The model of liberty was doing the same thing at the same time.
The opposition's response is one of the most consequential documents in American history, and it is double-edged.

Jefferson and Madison, unable to fight the laws in a Federalist-controlled Congress and courts, did something extraordinary: the sitting Vice President of the United States (Jefferson) and the country's leading constitutional thinker (Madison) secretly wrote resolutions attacking the federal government's own laws and arranged, anonymously, to have friendly state legislatures adopt them.

Jefferson's authorship of the Kentucky resolutions in particular was concealed for years; had it come out at the time, the Vice President would have been exposed as covertly orchestrating state defiance of federal law.
The legislatures of Kentucky and Virginia passed them in 1798–99 as the Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions.

Their argument: the Constitution is a compact among the states; the federal government is the states' agent, not their master; and when the federal government exceeds the powers the states delegated to it (as, they argued, it had with the Sedition Act), a state may declare the offending law void within its borders.
The mechanism being asserted is nullification, the claim that a state can, on its own authority, refuse to obey a federal law it judges unconstitutional.
In 1798 this was deployed in defense of free speech against an authoritarian law, which is the sympathetic context, and it should be stated.
But the doctrine, once articulated, did not stay attached to that context.

No state ever actually made nullification work as law (in 1798 the other states rejected the doctrine, and every later attempt to enforce it was beaten back or ended in war), but it did not need to succeed to be dangerous; it only had to keep being available as an argument.

The principle that a state may nullify federal law became the constitutional weapon that South Carolina would pick up in the nullification crisis of the 1830s (Antebellum America Ch 3) and that the seceding states would invoke to justify leaving the Union altogether.
It is worth noting how differently another constitutional founding handled the same fear.

When India wrote its constitution in 1950, its drafters, having watched what unresolved states'-rights claims did to the American union, deliberately built a strong center with no right of a state to nullify or secede (Modern India Ch 6); the American founders left the question open and the Indian founders slammed it shut, each reacting to the other's example.

The Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions are the moment the states'-rights theory of the Constitution received its classic statement; the irony, which the rest of the chain will detail, is that it was first drawn in the cause of liberty and would be most fatefully used in the cause of slavery.
The interlude ends with a decision that destroyed Adams politically and probably saved the republic from a disastrous war.
The pressure to choose war was enormous and concrete.

The XYZ fury was still running hot, war with France would have been wildly popular, and the law had already authorized a large new army; Hamilton had maneuvered himself into effective command of that army and clearly intended to use it (some feared against domestic opponents as much as against France).
For Adams, riding the war fever meant near-certain re-election and a heroic war presidency.

He looked at it and, in 1799, did the thing that ended his career: convinced France was now genuinely willing to settle and that a war would ruin the country and possibly the Republic, he abruptly sent a new peace commission to Paris over the open opposition of his own party.
The Quasi-War was ended by negotiation, the army Hamilton wanted was never used, and the war that would have been popular never happened.

Adams, late in life, said that of everything in his career he wanted his gravestone to credit him with taking on himself the responsibility for the peace with France in 1800; the sentiment is recorded in his own later writing, and he meant it as the act he was proudest of and had paid the most for.

The political cost was fatal: he split his own party, lost the support of Hamilton, and went into the election of 1800 (Chapter 11) leading a fractured Federalist Party against a united opposition, having put the country's interest ahead of his own re-election.
That choice, like Washington's resignation (Chapter 3), is one of the quiet load-bearing acts of the early republic: a president who could have ridden a war to power chose not to.

The republic survived the Sedition crisis, barely, and the survival depended less on the machinery than on the choices of the people running it, which is exactly the fragility the next election tested to destruction.

chapters.title: The Revolution of 1800
sentences: The presidential election of 1800 is the most important event in this book, and it is important for something that did not happen.
No army marched.
No one was executed.

The party that controlled the government, including the presidency, Congress, and the courts, lost an election to a party it had spent four years calling traitors and atheists, and then it handed over power.

That sentence sounds unremarkable to a modern American precisely because of what happened in 1801, and the entire point of this chapter is to make it strange again, because measured against the history of the human race it is one of the rarest things that has ever happened.
First the mechanics of the crisis, because it nearly failed.

The election of 1800 pitted the Federalist incumbent John Adams against the Democratic-Republican Thomas Jefferson, in a campaign of genuine viciousness: Federalists warned that a Jefferson presidency would bring French-style atheism, mob rule, and the guillotine; Republicans called Adams a closet monarchist who had jailed editors for criticizing him (Chapter 10).
Jefferson's party won.

But the original Constitution had a design flaw: each presidential elector cast two votes for president, and the runner-up became vice president, with no way to distinguish a vote for president from a vote for vice president.

Jefferson's running mate, Aaron Burr (a brilliant, charming, and slippery New York politician the Republicans had put on the ticket to help carry that crucial state; before the Twelfth Amendment there was no separate ballot for vice president, so a "running mate" was simply the man the party wanted everyone's second vote to go to), was supposed to come in a deliberate notch behind Jefferson, but the Republican electors voted so disciplinedly that Jefferson and Burr tied with the exact same number of votes.
A tie threw the election, under the Constitution, into the House of Representatives, which was still controlled, until the new Congress was seated, by the defeated Federalists.
Some Federalists, rather than elevate the man they hated most (Jefferson), schemed to throw the presidency to Burr instead.

For some thirty-five ballots over several days the House deadlocked (the exact ballot count comes from the House records of February 1801); there was loose talk of the Federalists simply installing a president by statute, and of Republican-state governors arming the militia.
The republic genuinely teetered.

The deadlock broke largely because Alexander Hamilton, who despised Jefferson's politics but considered Burr a man of no principle and pure ambition, waged a private campaign by letter against Burr, writing urgently and repeatedly to wavering Federalist congressmen arguing that of two evils Jefferson was the safer, until enough of them abstained or shifted to let Jefferson win on the thirty-sixth ballot.

The Hamilton–Burr enmity hardened here did not end here: four years later Burr killed Hamilton in a duel, a death this book notes rather than narrates, since it falls outside the political story these chapters are tracking.
The structural flaw was fixed almost immediately by the Twelfth Amendment (1804), which required electors to cast separate, labeled votes for president and vice president, the system used ever since.
The machine had a bug; it nearly crashed; the country patched it.
Now the thing that makes 1800 the center of this book.
Power passed from one party to a bitterly hostile rival party, peacefully, by the result of an election.
To feel why that is astonishing, do the cross-civilizational comparison the moment demands.

In the entire span of recorded history up to 1801, the normal way a regime changed hands was violence or its credible threat: conquest, coup, assassination, civil war, revolution, or, at its most orderly, a managed succession within a single ruling family or party (a son following a father onto a throne, a hand-picked heir, a dynasty passing power inside itself, never to organized opponents).
Power passing peacefully to people who had been calling the incumbents traitors was the thing that almost never happened.
The Roman Republic could not survive its own factional transfers and died into the Caesars (Ancient Rome Ch 5).
England had cut off the head of one king, Charles I, in 1649, and driven another, James II, off the throne in the revolution of 1688.
France had just gone from monarchy to republic to Terror to a general's coup in a single decade (Chapter 9).

Even in Britain, the country with the most developed parliamentary politics on earth, governments changed by the king's choice and by maneuvering among elites, not by a national election in which an organized party lost and conceded; there was no real precedent for that anywhere, at national scale.

The idea that the people holding power would simply leave it because a vote told them to, and that the people who hated them would take over without proscriptions or reprisals, was close to unheard of.
Jefferson himself called it, accurately, "the revolution of 1800," a revolution carried out by ballots.

The peaceful transfer of power between rival organized parties, which Americans now treat as the floor of legitimate politics, was in 1801 close to a first in the modern world, and it was not guaranteed; it depended on Adams choosing to leave, on enough Federalists choosing the ballot over the scheme, and on the new Constitution's machinery holding under the most extreme stress it had yet faced.
When the thirty-sixth ballot finally went to Jefferson, the crisis simply stopped.
Adams's people did not seize the government; the militias that had been talked of did not march; the men who had spent four years calling Jefferson a traitor and an atheist let him be sworn in.
The country exhaled.

And into that strange, uncertain quiet, with the loser's party still in possession of the capital and afraid of what the winner would do, Jefferson stepped up to give the speech that turned the bare fact of a peaceful handoff into a principle.
He understood the symbolism and used his inaugural address to perform the reconciliation the moment required.
The campaign had been apocalyptic; some Federalists genuinely expected persecution.

Instead Jefferson said, in his first inaugural in 1801, "We are all republicans, we are all federalists," asserting that despite the savage fight, both parties operated within the same constitutional consensus and the loser need not fear the winner.

That sentence is the founding statement of the idea of a loyal opposition: that you can lose an election, oppose the government with everything you have, and still be a legitimate participant rather than a traitor to be crushed.
Most political systems in history did not have that idea.

The American one acquired it, in practice, in 1801, and the acquisition was the single most important thing that distinguished a working republic from the failed republics the founders feared (Chapter 1).
One more invention belongs to these years, and it came from the courts, not the ballot, and it was a partisan maneuver before it was a principle.

As the defeated Federalists left power, the lame-duck Federalist Congress created a batch of new judgeships and Adams filled them with Federalists in his last hours (the "midnight judges") to entrench Federalist control of the one branch elections could not immediately touch, the judiciary.
One commission, for a justice of the peace named William Marbury, was signed but not delivered before Jefferson took office, and Jefferson's Secretary of State, James Madison, refused to deliver it.
Marbury sued, asking the Supreme Court to order the government to give him his job.
The case, Marbury v.
Madison (1803), put the new Chief Justice, John Marshall, in a trap.

Marshall was a Virginia Federalist, a Revolutionary War veteran who had wintered at Valley Forge, a largely self-taught lawyer, and Adams's Secretary of State; Adams named him Chief Justice in his last weeks in office precisely to plant a strong Federalist mind in the one branch the election could not sweep out.

The trap was this: if the Court ordered Madison to deliver the commission, the Jefferson administration would simply ignore it, exposing the Court as powerless; if it did not order delivery, the Court would look like it had surrendered.
Marshall's solution invented the most powerful tool in the American judiciary, and the mechanism is the whole point.

Marshall ruled that Marbury was legally entitled to his commission, but that the specific law Marbury had used to bring his case directly to the Supreme Court (a provision of the Judiciary Act of 1789, Chapter 7) was itself unconstitutional, because it gave the Supreme Court a kind of power the Constitution had not granted it.
Therefore, Marshall reasoned, the Court could not act on Marbury's request, not because Marbury was wrong, but because the statute he relied on was void.

The logic underneath that result is judicial review: when an ordinary law passed by Congress conflicts with the Constitution, the Constitution wins, and it is the courts' job, when deciding a case, to say so and to refuse to enforce the unconstitutional law.
The Constitution does not explicitly grant this power; Marshall argued it followed necessarily from the Constitution being supreme law and judges being sworn to uphold it.
This was, at the time, a genuine novelty with essentially no parallel anywhere.
Britain ran on parliamentary supremacy: Parliament's word was final and no court could strike down an Act of Parliament.
France, then convulsing under Napoleon, had no such power either.

The idea that an unelected court could void a law passed by the people's elected legislature was, in 1803, close to unique to the American system, and it was not written into the document; it was reasoned into existence.

The genius of the maneuver was that he claimed an enormous power (the courts can strike down acts of Congress) in the act of declining a small one (we cannot help Marbury), so the Jefferson administration got the immediate outcome it wanted and could not defy a ruling that gave it what it wanted.
Judicial review became the keystone of the American constitutional system: it is why the Supreme Court can overturn laws today.

It was established not by the text, not by a vote, but by a Chief Justice's reasoning in a minor patronage dispute, and that, too, is how the early republic actually built its institutions: improvised by individuals in particular crises, then treated forever after as if they had been there from the start.

chapters.title: The Jeffersonian Experiment
sentences: Thomas Jefferson came into office in 1801 as the head of a party built on a clear philosophy: small federal government, low taxes, no standing army, no national bank, power left to the states and the people, a republic of independent farmers rather than financiers and factories (Chapter 8).

Then he had to actually govern, and governing forced him into the largest single expansion of federal power, national territory, and executive improvisation in the period, done by the man most committed, in principle, to doing none of it.
This chapter is about that collision between the agrarian ideal and the duty to run a country, and about the deepest contradiction in the man who embodied the founding sentence.
Jefferson governed, at first, exactly as advertised, and the change of style was visible from the first day.

Where the Federalists had cultivated ceremony, Jefferson walked to his own inauguration, received foreign ministers in a plain coat and slippers, abolished the formal levee, and sent his messages to Congress in writing rather than appearing in person to deliver them like a king opening Parliament.

Behind the symbolism the substance matched: he and his Treasury secretary slashed the federal budget, shrank the army and navy, let the hated Sedition Act expire and pardoned the men it had jailed (Chapter 10), and repealed the internal taxes, including the whiskey excise that had triggered a rebellion (Chapter 9).

The Jeffersonians did not tear out Hamilton's core financial structure (the funded debt and the Bank both survived) but they froze its growth and changed the entire register of government from energetic central direction to deliberate, frugal smallness.
For a while it genuinely looked as if the experiment could simply be the modest agrarian republic its theory described.
Then came the Louisiana Purchase, and it broke the theory open.

"Louisiana" here is not the modern state of that name; it was a near-continental expanse covering roughly the western half of the Mississippi River basin, running from the river itself up the Missouri to the Rocky Mountains, the future heartland of the United States. (The Mississippi, which has run through several chapters now as the country's western edge and economic artery, is the great river of North America, flowing north to south down the middle of the continent to the Gulf of Mexico; before railroads it was the only practical way to move a bulky harvest from the interior to the sea.) The territory was held by France, into whose hands it had just passed back from Spain.
Its strategic key was the port of New Orleans, sitting at the river's mouth.

Recall why that mattered (Chapter 9): every farmer in the entire western United States floated his crops down the Mississippi to be loaded onto ocean ships at New Orleans, so whoever held that port held the economic life of the whole American interior in his hand.
When the Spanish suspended the Americans' right to deposit goods at New Orleans in 1802, the West was enraged and war talk spread.
Jefferson sent envoys to Paris to try to buy just New Orleans and a strip of West Florida.

They arrived to an astonishing offer: Napoleon had just lost a brutal war in the Caribbean colony of Saint-Domingue, where the enslaved population had risen and, after years of fighting, destroyed a French army and won independence as Haiti (the only successful large-scale slave revolution in modern history; the full story is in the Enlightenment volume's chapter on it).
With his richest colony gone, his dream of a French empire in the Americas dead, and his European wars draining money, Napoleon abruptly offered to sell the entire Louisiana territory.
The American envoys, far beyond their instructions, said yes.

For roughly fifteen million dollars (the standard figure, working out to something on the order of a few cents an acre) the United States bought about 828,000 square miles, an area larger than today's France, Germany, Spain, Italy, and the British Isles combined, and doubled its national size overnight, in a single transaction, without firing a shot.
No European power had peacefully acquired land on anything like this scale and speed in living memory.
Now the contradiction, stated honestly because it is the chapter's point.
Jefferson's whole constitutional philosophy was strict construction (Chapter 8): the federal government may do only what the Constitution explicitly authorizes.
The Constitution says nothing about buying foreign territory or absorbing its inhabitants.
By his own stated principles, Jefferson believed the purchase required a constitutional amendment, and he drafted one.
But an amendment would take time, Napoleon might withdraw the offer, and the prize was too enormous to risk.

Jefferson swallowed his own doctrine, justified the purchase under the treaty power (the Constitution's explicit grant to the president, with Senate approval, to make treaties with foreign nations; Jefferson's argument was that buying Louisiana was simply a treaty with France, and treaties were unquestionably allowed, even if "treaties" had never been imagined to mean swallowing half a continent), and pushed it through the Senate, privately conceding he was stretching the Constitution past where his own philosophy allowed.
The strict-constructionist president had just performed the largest loose-construction act in the country's history.

It is the cleanest single illustration of this book's recurring theme: the duty to govern repeatedly forced the founders to betray their own principles, and the republic was built as much out of those betrayals as out of the principles.
The Purchase had two consequences that point straight at the rest of the chain.
First, it doubled the land available for American expansion, which meant it doubled the question of whether slavery would expand with it.

The Northwest Ordinance had banned slavery north of the Ohio (Chapter 4); Louisiana had no such line, and the fight over whether the new territory would be slave or free was now structurally inevitable; it arrived, explosively, with Missouri (Chapter 18).

There is a sharp transatlantic irony in the timing: in exactly these years the United States was doubling the ground on which slavery could grow, while across the ocean Britain's abolitionists were winning, banning the slave trade in 1807.
The two great Atlantic English-speaking powers were moving in opposite directions on slavery at the same moment.
Second, the land was not empty.
It was home to dozens of Native nations who had never been consulted and whose dispossession the Purchase set in motion over the following decades.

To find out what the country had bought, Jefferson sent an expedition led by Meriwether Lewis and William Clark (1804–06) up the Missouri, over the Rockies, to the Pacific, and back: a scientific and diplomatic reconnaissance that mapped the route, catalogued hundreds of plants and animals new to science, and recorded the Native nations along the way.

It survived in part because of the guidance and diplomacy of a teenaged woman of the Shoshone (a Native people of the Rocky Mountain and Great Basin region), Sacagawea, who had been captured as a child, sold, and was traveling with a French trader and her own infant; her presence and her ability to interpret and negotiate with mountain nations repeatedly kept the expedition alive.

Lewis and Clark are remembered as an adventure story; they were also the opening move of continental empire, the first survey of land whose Native inhabitants would, over the next century, be dispossessed of nearly all of it.
End on the man, because Jefferson is the human form of this book's spine and the contested-history rule applies directly.
He wrote that all men are created equal (Chapter 1).
He believed slavery was a moral evil and said so in print.
He also enslaved more than six hundred people over his life, freed almost none, sold human beings to pay his debts, and built his wealth and his famous house, Monticello, on their labor.
And there is the question of Sally Hemings, an enslaved woman at Monticello.

The claim that Jefferson had a long-term relationship with her and fathered several of her children was published in his lifetime, used against him politically, and for nearly two centuries was denied by most white historians and Jefferson's descendants as enemy slander.
The honest current statement is this: a 1998 DNA study established that a male in the Jefferson family line fathered at least one of Hemings's children.

DNA can only point to the family, not to one individual, so the test alone left open a handful of Jefferson relatives (notably a younger brother and some cousins who had visited Monticello) as theoretical alternatives.

But when the genetic evidence is combined with the documentary record (Hemings's children were conceived only when Jefferson was present at Monticello, the long-standing testimony of Hemings's son, and more), the historical institution that runs Monticello and the large majority of historians have concluded that Thomas Jefferson himself was the father of Hemings's children.
A minority still dissents.

What changed is important and is exactly why the contested-claims discipline matters: a story long dismissed as slander turned out, on the evidence, to be very likely true, and the long dismissal was itself a product of who got to write the history.

Jefferson is not a villain to be cartooned or a saint to be defended; he is the contradiction of the founding made into one person, the man who wrote the sentence and lived its opposite, and the rest of this chain is the country failing, for decades, to resolve what he could not resolve in his own house.

chapters.title: Cotton and the Second Slavery
sentences: In 1790 a reasonable, well-informed observer could have believed American slavery was slowly dying.
By 1820 it was the fastest-growing and most profitable institution in the country, expanding across half a continent and accelerating every year.

The thing that turned the first situation into the second was a single simple machine plugged into a global market, and the mechanism by which it happened is the most important thing in this book that is not a law or an election; every political crisis in the chapters that follow runs on top of it.
Start with why slavery looked like it might be dying around 1790.
The Revolution's natural-rights language had made it ideologically awkward (Chapter 3).
The northern states were gradually abolishing it (Chapter 3).
Tobacco, the great slave crop of the Chesapeake, was exhausting the soil and declining in profitability; some prominent Virginia planters spoke of slavery as a dying institution and an embarrassment.
The Constitution's twenty-year protection of the slave trade (Chapter 5) implied an expectation that the trade, at least, would end in 1808.
There was a plausible reading of the trend lines in which slavery slowly shrank toward irrelevance, especially in the Upper South.
Then, in 1793, a Connecticut-born tinkerer named Eli Whitney, visiting a Georgia plantation, built the cotton gin (short for "engine").
To understand why this tiny device reorganized a continent, you have to understand the bottleneck it removed.
There were two kinds of cotton.
Long-staple cotton, whose seeds separated easily, grew only in a narrow strip of the South Carolina and Georgia sea islands and coast.

Short-staple cotton grew across the whole vast interior upland South, the future cotton belt from the Carolinas through Alabama and Mississippi, but its sticky green seeds clung to the fiber and were almost impossible to remove by hand; a worker picking the seeds out by hand could clean only roughly a pound of it a day (the figure conventionally cited), which made it worthless as a bulk crop.

The cotton gin was a simple drum with wire teeth that pulled the cotton fiber through a slot too narrow for the seeds, mechanically separating fiber from seed dozens of times faster than a hand could.
Suddenly short-staple cotton, which could be grown across an immense region, was enormously profitable to produce.
And the demand was effectively bottomless, because of something happening on the other side of the Atlantic at the very same moment.

The mechanized textile mills of the British Industrial Revolution were multiplying explosively and devouring raw cotton faster than the world could grow it (the British side of this exact circuit is Industrial Revolution Ch 3, which describes the Manchester mill and the Mississippi plantation as the two ends of one machine).
British spinning machinery created the hunger; the American cotton gin and the American South's land and enslaved labor fed it.

American cotton output exploded from almost nothing to the largest single source on earth within a generation, and the two events, mechanized spinning in England and mechanized seed-cleaning in America, were really one event with an ocean in the middle.
Here is the mechanism that is the dark heart of the book.
A profitable crop that could be grown across a near-continental region created a near-infinite demand for the one input that produced it on the plantation system: enslaved labor.
Slavery did not die; it became the most valuable economic engine in the country, and the value of an enslaved human being as property rose accordingly.

This is what historians sometimes call the Second Slavery: not the colonial-era institution slowly fading, but a new, modern, expanding, brutally profitable system, integrated into the global industrial economy, that the cotton gin made possible exactly when the institution had looked vulnerable.

The single machine that, if anything, should have made enslaved labor less necessary instead made it the foundation of the national economy. (The system had a third life: after emancipation the same cotton economy was rebuilt as sharecropping and the crop-lien, Reconstruction Ch 3, still trapping Black families in the farm depression of the 1920s, Roaring Twenties Ch 5.) That is a fact about how technology and markets interact that is worth sitting with: a labor-saving invention vastly increased the demand for the most coerced labor in the country.
Now the human catastrophe inside the economics, the part the word "Cotton Kingdom" hides.
The cotton frontier moved relentlessly southwest (into Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana, eventually Texas) and it needed an enormous, growing enslaved workforce there.

After the Atlantic slave trade was closed (below), that workforce could only come from one place: the older slave regions of the Upper South, Virginia and Maryland and the Carolinas, where tobacco was declining.

The result was the domestic slave trade, a vast internal traffic in human beings: on the order of a million enslaved people (the figure historians of the trade most commonly give for the whole period from roughly 1790 into the 1860s) were forcibly moved from the Upper South to the cotton frontier of the Deep South over these decades, sold by owners in the older tobacco states for whom selling a human being had become more profitable than keeping that person laboring on the owner's own land, and marched or shipped south to be resold.
They went in coffles, columns of enslaved people chained or roped together at the neck or wrist and driven overland on foot for hundreds of miles, or packed onto coastal ships.

This was a demographic and human catastrophe inside the country's own borders, comparable in scale to a major forced migration: families were broken up by sale as a routine business practice, children sold away from parents, husbands from wives, as ordinary commerce (the full scale of this domestic slave trade, the Second Middle Passage, is in Antebellum America Ch 9).

The same world economy was grinding people on the other side of it too: The Lancashire mills this cotton fed were, in the same decades, destroying the livelihoods of millions of Indian handloom weavers who could not compete with mechanized British cloth (Industrial Revolution Ch 19).
The Mississippi plantation, the Manchester factory, and the ruined Indian weaver were three points on a single global circuit of cloth and suffering.

The American phrase "sold down the river," meaning sent to a worse fate with no way back, comes from exactly this: being sold from the Upper South down the Mississippi to the cotton and sugar plantations of the Deep South.
Finally, the closing of the Atlantic trade, and why it changed less than it sounds like.

As the Constitution's twenty-year clock allowed (Chapter 5), Congress banned the importation of enslaved people from Africa effective January 1, 1808, the earliest constitutionally possible date, and one both Jefferson and most of the country supported.
It is genuinely the case that this ended American participation in the Atlantic slave trade and that this was a real moral line.

But it did almost nothing to slow slavery's growth, and the reason is the crucial mechanical point: the enslaved population of the United States grew rapidly by natural increase, the only major slave society in the Americas where the enslaved population grew substantially from births rather than continual imports.

Closing the foreign trade therefore did not shrink slavery; it raised the value of the enslaved people already in the country and intensified the domestic slave trade, because the only legal way to get more enslaved labor for the expanding cotton frontier was now to buy it from the Upper South.

The 1808 ban looked like an antislavery victory and functioned, in the actual economy, like A protective tariff on American-born enslaved people. (A protective tariff, defined fully in Chapter 17, is a tax on a foreign import set high enough to shield domestic producers from foreign competition; cutting off the cheaper foreign supply of enslaved people raised the price and protected the market of domestic "producers," meaning the slaveholders of the Upper South who sold human beings south.) By 1820 the United States was not a country slowly outgrowing slavery.

It was a country whose single most dynamic economic sector was the production of slave-grown cotton for the world's factories, with the institution expanding westward as fast as land could be seized and broken.
That is the fact every political crisis in the rest of this book and the whole of the next one rests on.
