The slavery question was not quietly shrinking toward resolution, the way some founders had bet.
It was getting larger, richer, and more entrenched every single year.

chapters.title: Faith, Mills, and Roads
sentences: So far this book has been a story of a few hundred famous men in capitals.

But a republic is not only its government, and underneath the politics a deeper question was being answered in these years: could the loose collection of regions the Constitution had stapled together actually become a society, a place whose people shared institutions, habits, and an economy, rather than just a flag?

Three transformations between roughly 1790 and 1820 answered that question, and they belong in one chapter because they were doing the same work from three directions: a religious revival was knitting people together in shared belief and reform energy; the first factories were building a new kind of working economy; and a war on distance was physically wiring the regions to each other.
Each of the three also, fatefully, pulled the country together along an east–west axis through the free North and West while leaving the slave South increasingly on the other side of a widening seam.
The society was forming, and the line it was forming around is the one this whole book is tracking.
Start with religion, because nothing else changed daily life for more people.

Around the turn of the century the United States was swept by a wave of intense religious revival now called the Second Great Awakening. (It is the "Second" because there had been a first Great Awakening in the colonial 1740s, a wave of fiery emotional preaching, associated above all with the traveling English evangelist George Whitefield, that had crossed the colonies and then faded; the new revival was its much larger successor.) To picture it, picture the camp meeting.

In 1801 at Cane Ridge in frontier Kentucky, a crowd that contemporary estimates put somewhere in the range of ten to twenty thousand people (the figures are rough and were probably inflated, but by any account it was an astonishing multitude in a thinly settled region) gathered for days in the open air, with multiple preachers exhorting simultaneously, and worshippers falling, weeping, shaking, and crying out in mass emotional conversion.

The camp-meeting revival was a new religious technology: emotional, participatory, open to anyone, run by energetic preachers (especially Methodists and Baptists) who did not require theological education and who carried the revival on horseback into every frontier settlement.

Its theology, broadly, shifted American Protestantism away from the older Calvinist idea that God had predestined who would be saved and who damned, a doctrine no human choice could alter, toward the idea that any individual could choose salvation through a personal conversion experience.

This was a direct break with the severe Calvinism the Puritans had founded New England on (Chapter 1): the strict Protestant world of the original settlers was being overturned by a religion of personal choice.
That theological turn had a social fuse on it.

If anyone could be saved, and if society could be perfected by enough saved individuals acting together, then religion implied reform, and the Second Great Awakening became the engine of a century of reform movements: temperance, public education, prison reform, and, most explosively, abolitionism, the conviction that slavery was not a regrettable inheritance to be managed but a sin to be attacked and ended (the fuse that detonates in the next era of this chain, the antebellum decades, Antebellum America Ch 5).
The revival also gave African Americans their own institutional ground.

Richard Allen, a formerly enslaved Methodist preacher in Philadelphia, had in 1787 been physically pulled up from his knees and ordered to a segregated gallery while praying in a white church; he and others walked out and, in 1816, founded the African Methodist Episcopal Church, the first fully independent Black denomination in the United States and, for two centuries after, one of the most important institutions in Black American life.
It is worth a cross-civilizational pause here, because what was happening to American religion was structurally unusual.

In almost every country in the world at the time, there was an established church: an official state religion, funded by the government, with legal privileges, that you were taxed to support whether you believed in it or not, the Church of England in Britain, Catholicism in France and Spain, Orthodoxy in Russia. (Twentieth-century Russia would go to the opposite extreme and try to abolish religion outright by force, a later episode in this larger story.) This very question, whether the state should have an official church and whether other faiths should merely be tolerated or fully free, was one the European Enlightenment was actively arguing in these same decades, with writers in still-established-church Prussia pressing for toleration.
America did not win that argument; it sidestepped it entirely, by building a society with no establishment at all.
The American states had inherited established churches too.

But the First Amendment forbade a national one, and over these decades the states, one by one, disestablished their official churches, ending tax support and legal privilege for any denomination (Massachusetts, the last, in 1833).
The result was something close to a historical novelty: a society in which religion was entirely voluntary, funded by its own members, competing for adherents in an open market with no state backing.

Far from killing religion, as European observers expected, voluntarism made American religion more energetic, more entrepreneurial, and more pervasive than the established churches of Europe; the camp meeting was, in a sense, a product of religious free competition.
American religious voluntarism is one of the genuine institutional inventions of this period, and it ran exactly opposite to the European norm.
The second binding force was the factory, and it entered the country as a smuggled secret.

Britain had pioneered mechanized textile production (Industrial Revolution Ch 1) and guarded the designs of its machinery as strategic property; it was, in fact, illegal under British law for skilled textile workers to emigrate or to take the designs abroad, precisely to keep the technology bottled up.

Samuel Slater, a young British mechanic who had worked in those mills, slipped out of England in 1789 disguised as a farm laborer, carrying the workings of the spinning machinery in his head (he had, the standard account says, memorized the designs, since he could not have carried drawings past inspection).
In Rhode Island in 1790 he rebuilt them from memory and ran the first successful water-powered cotton-spinning mill in America.
American industrialization, in other words, began as industrial espionage; the British side of this same theft is Industrial Revolution Ch 15.

Over the following decades the factory system spread through New England, culminating after this period in the large integrated textile mills that the Market Revolution would build (Antebellum America Ch 5).
The same standardizing logic appeared in a second place.

Eli Whitney (of the cotton gin, Chapter 13) won a federal arms contract and championed interchangeable parts: instead of each musket being hand-fitted as a unique object by a skilled craftsman, every part would be made to a fixed standard so that any trigger or lock fit any gun, which let less-skilled workers assemble weapons fast and let broken guns be repaired with stock parts.

Whitney's own famous demonstration of this was, historians now think, partly staged and oversold (his workshop had not really achieved full interchangeability), but the principle was sound, and standardized interchangeable components became the foundation of mass production, later known abroad as the "American system of manufactures" (Industrial Revolution Ch 16).
The country that had declared itself a republic of farmers was quietly acquiring the machinery to become an industrial power, and that machinery was being installed in the North.

Free-labor factories spreading through one section and slave-labor cotton fields spreading through the other, each feeding the other's economy while growing politically apart, is the North–South divergence this whole book keeps tracking, now hardening into physical fact.
The third binding force was the least glamorous and maybe the most consequential: the conquest of distance.
In 1800 it could take longer, and cost more, to haul a wagon of goods thirty miles overland than to ship the same goods across the Atlantic Ocean, because the new country had almost no real roads.
A society cannot cohere if its parts cannot physically reach each other; a republic that cannot move grain, news, troops, or people between its regions is a republic on paper only.
The early answers came in two forms.

One was the turnpike, a privately built road on which travelers paid a toll at gates; the Lancaster Turnpike, running about sixty miles from Philadelphia west to Lancaster in Pennsylvania, proved that people would pay to use a good hard road and touched off a wave of turnpike building.
The more transformative answer was water.

In 1807 Robert Fulton ran the first commercially successful steamboat up the Hudson River (the navigable river running south through eastern New York from the interior down to New York City and the Atlantic).

A steamboat could carry cargo and passengers upstream against the current, which had never been practical before; this was revolutionary on the vast Mississippi–Ohio river system, where freight had previously floated only one way, downstream, and the flatboats were broken up for lumber at the bottom because they could not be brought back up.

Then, in 1817, New York began digging the Erie Canal, a man-made waterway clear across the state linking the Hudson (and therefore the Atlantic) to the Great Lakes, the five enormous freshwater inland seas (Superior, Michigan, Huron, Erie, Ontario) on what is now the U.S.–Canada border, and through them to the whole continental interior.

When it opened in the next period it cut the cost of moving goods between the interior and the East Coast dramatically, by something on the order of ninety percent in the figures economic historians give, and it pulled the growing West economically toward the Northern seaboard rather than down the Mississippi toward the South (Antebellum America Ch 5).

None of this is as dramatic as a battle, but it is the physical skeleton of nationhood: a continental republic is impossible if a farmer in Ohio and a merchant in New York inhabit separate economic worlds.
These are the years the country began, expensively and unevenly, to wire itself into one economy.

And the wiring, like the factories and the revival energy, ran predominantly east–west through the free states, not north–south across the slavery line, so that the very forces knitting the nation together were also, quietly, drawing the seam along which it would one day tear.

chapters.title: The Road to War
sentences: The republic spent the years after the Louisiana Purchase being slowly squeezed between two empires fighting a world war it wanted no part of, and being pushed, on its own western frontier, into a confrontation with a Native confederacy that was the most serious organized resistance the United States had yet faced.

This chapter is how the country talked itself, half-blindly, into a war in 1812, and the honest answer to why that war happened is genuinely contested, so this chapter sets out the causes and the argument rather than picking the tidy version.

The international vise was the Napoleonic Wars, the roughly 1803–1815 continent-spanning wars in which Napoleon Bonaparte's France fought nearly all of Europe (the French Revolution that produced Napoleon was Chapter 9; his own full story is the Enlightenment volume's).
By the late 1800s it had become a death-struggle between Napoleon's France, which dominated the European landmass, and Britain, which dominated the sea.
Each tried to strangle the other's trade, and a neutral commercial nation got crushed in between.
Britain, by far the dominant naval power, did three things Americans could not abide.
It seized American ships trading with French-controlled Europe.
It enforced rules that effectively made the United States choose a side.
And, most inflammatory of all, it practiced impressment.

This needs defining precisely because it is the grievance everything else hung on: impressment was the British Navy's practice of stopping American merchant ships at sea, boarding them, and seizing sailors it claimed were British subjects (deserters, or British-born men who had become Americans, whom Britain did not recognize as having stopped being British) and forcing them to serve in the British Navy.
In practice many genuine American citizens were also seized; the British Navy was desperate for men and not careful.
To Americans, a foreign navy stopping their ships and kidnapping their citizens was a direct assault on national sovereignty and personal liberty, the precise things the Revolution had been about.
Thousands of American sailors were taken this way over the period.
It is worth seeing the global scale of the machine doing this: the same Royal Navy manpower crisis, the same world war, was simultaneously driving Britain's expansion in India and the Mediterranean.
The hand that pressed an American sailor off a merchant ship in the Atlantic belonged to the same empire whose armies were enlarging its dominion in Asia, all of it powered by one enormous war.

The grievance turned to fury in 1807 with the Chesapeake–Leopard affair. (The name is confusing: the Chesapeake here is a ship, a United States Navy frigate, named after the bay; it is not the bay itself.) A British warship, the Leopard, demanded to search the Chesapeake for alleged deserters; when the American captain refused, the British ship opened fire, killed and wounded American sailors, and removed four men.
This was not a merchant ship; it was an attack on a United States naval vessel in peacetime.
The country erupted, and Jefferson could probably have had a war then with popular support.

He chose, instead, a strategy that is one of the clearest examples in the book of a policy mechanism backfiring spectacularly: the Embargo of 1807. the Embargo's logic was that the United States, rather than fight, would simply withhold its own trade entirely, banning virtually all American ships from sailing to any foreign port, on the theory that Britain and France depended so heavily on American goods and markets that economic pain would force them to respect American rights without a shot.
It was, in concept, economic coercion as a substitute for war.

To make it bite, the federal government had to police its own coastline against its own citizens: customs officers, the tiny navy, and eventually troops were used to stop American ships from slipping out, search vessels, and seize cargoes, an intrusive enforcement effort by the same Jefferson who distrusted federal power.
Mechanically, it failed.
Britain found other suppliers and other markets and was hurt far less than predicted.
The people it devastated were Americans.

On the New England waterfront the effect was visible and bitter: vessels lay idle and rotting at the wharves with grass said to be growing on the docks, shipwrights and dockworkers went unemployed, merchants who had owned a fleet faced ruin, sailors had no berths, and a whole smuggling economy sprang up along the Canadian border as desperate traders evaded their own government.

The Embargo inflicted more measurable damage on the United States than on either of its targets, a self-inflicted wound, and it enraged the Federalist, commercial Northeast against the Jeffersonian government to the point of open talk of resistance and even disunion (a foreshadowing of Chapter 16).
It was repealed, a near-total failure, as Jefferson left office.

Jefferson handed the problem to his successor and closest ally, James Madison, president from 1809, the chief architect of the Constitution itself (Chapter 5) now in the strange position of operating the machine he had designed under an international crisis it had never been built for.
His first term was a frustrating series of subtler economic-pressure laws that also failed and a steady drift toward a war he did not want.

Meanwhile a new generation entered Congress after the 1810 elections: young, aggressive, mostly Southern and Western politicians the older members derisively called the War Hawks, led by the Kentuckian Henry Clay.

Clay was in his early thirties, a charismatic, gambling, hard-drinking frontier lawyer and planter from Kentucky, already Speaker of the House and already the most magnetic orator of his generation; he dominates the last third of this book and the next.

They argued that submission was destroying national honor and that war with Britain was the only way to defend American sovereignty, and, not incidentally, that war might let the United States seize Canada and end British support for Native resistance on the frontier.
That last motive points at the cause this chapter has saved for emphasis, because the patriotic story tells the war as a contest with Britain over sailors' rights and that is only part of the truth.
On the western frontier, American expansion (Chapter 12) was pressing relentlessly into Native lands through a series of treaties many Native leaders regarded as fraudulent.

The fraud was structural: American officials would find a few chiefs willing to sign, often plied with goods or alcohol, and treat their signatures as binding the whole people, even though in most of these nations no chief had the authority to sell land on his own (land was held collectively, and a sale needed broad consent from the nation, not one cooperative headman).
So treaties "ceding" enormous territories were signed by men who, by their own peoples' rules, had no right to cede them.
Out of that pressure rose the most formidable Native political project of the era.

A Shawnee war leader, Tecumseh, and his brother Tenskwatawa, called the Prophet because he had undergone a dramatic religious vision and now preached a spiritual revival, a return to Native ways and rejection of American goods and whiskey, built a pan-Indian movement on a radical and coherent argument: that no single tribe or chief could sell land, because the land belonged to all Native peoples in common, and that the only defense against being dispossessed piece by piece was for the nations to unite, stop selling, and stand together.

This deserves real weight, not a paragraph of condescension: it was a sophisticated diplomatic and spiritual mobilization across many nations, building a confederacy and a religious revival from a base at Prophetstown on the Tippecanoe River, and it was the most serious organized challenge to American westward expansion the country had yet faced.

It also had deep roots: the idea of broad, pan-regional Native organization across many peoples was not new to the continent but reached back to the great mound-building and trade networks of the Mississippian world centuries earlier (Mississippian Culture Ch 10); Tecumseh was working in a long tradition of continental Native unity, not improvising from nothing.

In November 1811, while Tecumseh was away recruiting in the South, the territorial governor William Henry Harrison marched on Prophetstown and fought the Prophet's followers at the Battle of Tippecanoe, then burned the town. (Harrison would ride the fame of this single battle, decades later, all the way to the presidency, campaigning under the slogan "Tippecanoe and Tyler too.") The battle was tactically inconclusive but strategically decisive in one respect: it convinced Americans (correctly) that the British in Canada were arming and encouraging Tecumseh's confederacy, which fused the frontier war and the maritime grievances into a single case for war against Britain.
So what actually caused the War of 1812?
Honesty requires laying out that historians genuinely disagree about the weighting.
The traditional account emphasizes maritime rights: impressment and ship seizures, the assault on sovereignty at sea.

A second account, prominent in the scholarship, emphasizes the frontier and land hunger: the war as an opportunity, pushed by Western and Southern expansionists, to break the Native confederacy and conquer Canada.
A third emphasizes national honor and the survival of the Republican government's credibility after a decade of humiliating, failed economic coercion.

The honest summary is that all three were present, that the maritime grievances were the official and stated cause, that the expansionist and honor motives were real and heavily regional, and that the vote for war split sharply along party and section lines, the commercial Northeast, which actually did the shipping, mostly opposing the "maritime rights" war while the agrarian West and South, which did little shipping, mostly supported it, a paradox that by itself shows the stated cause was not the whole cause.
In June 1812 a divided Congress declared war on Britain.

It was the first time the United States, under its Constitution, formally declared war, and it did so by an unusually close vote, often described as the closest margin on any American declaration of a major war, against a divided country, for reasons Americans still argue about.

chapters.title: The War of 1812
sentences: The War of 1812 is the strangest war in this book: a war the United States entered divided, fought mostly badly, did not win, and emerged from convinced it had triumphed, a war whose most famous victory was fought after peace had been signed, and whose largest political consequence was the destruction of one of its own political parties.

It nearly ended in catastrophe; it ended in a draw that the country experienced as a vindication; and the gap between what happened and what Americans believed had happened is, itself, the most important thing about it.
It nearly went catastrophically wrong, and the reasons are the unglamorous ones the Confederation's weakness had warned about (Chapter 4).
The United States declared war with a tiny army, a small navy, no money set aside, and a banking system the Republicans had let weaken.
The opening strategy was to invade and conquer Canada, which the War Hawks had assured everyone would be easy (Chapter 15).
It was a fiasco: a series of bungled invasions in 1812 collapsed, an American army surrendered Detroit without much of a fight, and the conquest of Canada, far from being easy, never happened at all.

Then, in August 1814, with Napoleon temporarily defeated and Britain free to send veteran troops, a British force landed in the Chesapeake, scattered a hastily assembled American militia at Bladensburg just outside the city (a rout so complete it was mockingly called "the Bladensburg Races"), and marched unopposed into the United States capital.

British officers reportedly sat down and ate the dinner laid out in the abandoned President's House before setting fire to it, then burned the Capitol and the other public buildings, the seat of the national government deliberately put to the torch while President Madison fled on horseback into the Virginia countryside.

Dolley Madison, the president's wife and the capital's most prominent hostess, stayed in the President's House until the British were nearly upon it and had a large full-length portrait of George Washington cut from its frame and carried out so the enemy could not parade it as a trophy.

The President's House, scorched black, was later rebuilt and painted, which is the popular origin story of the name "the White House." The capital of the republic was a smoking ruin two years into the war.
By any sober reckoning the United States was not winning.
But the war had turning points, and they matter.
At sea and on the lakes the small U.S.
Navy did unexpectedly well in single-ship duels, which mattered more for morale than strategy.

On Lake Erie in 1813, Oliver Hazard Perry, a Navy officer not yet thirty who had built and manned a fleet from scratch on the frontier lake, defeated and captured an entire British squadron in a close, bloody battle.

He scrawled the news to Harrison in a brief field note whose opening line entered American memory: "We have met the enemy and they are ours." (The phrase comes from Perry's own short dispatch reporting the victory; it is genuine, not a later embellishment, though it has been quoted and re-quoted ever since.) Control of Lake Erie let Harrison invade Canada from the west and win the Battle of the Thames (1813), in which Tecumseh was killed.

Tecumseh's death is one of the genuinely decisive outcomes of the war: it shattered the pan-Indian confederacy (Chapter 15) and ended, permanently, the prospect of an organized Native barrier to American expansion east of the Mississippi, which is the war's most consequential and least celebrated result.

In the South, a related conflict was unfolding inside the larger war: the Creek War, a civil war within the Creek nation between an accommodationist faction and the militant Red Sticks (so called for the red-painted war clubs that were the symbol of their faction), which American forces entered on the anti-Red Stick side.

Frontier militia under a Tennessee planter and general named Andrew Jackson crushed the Red Sticks at the Battle of Horseshoe Bend (1814), then imposed a treaty stripping the Creeks, allies and enemies alike, of a vast territory and opening the future cotton lands of Alabama and Mississippi (Chapter 13).
It was an early step on the road to the wholesale removal of the southeastern nations a generation later (Antebellum America Ch 4).

And in 1814, when the British launched their main invasion from Canada, an American naval victory at Plattsburgh on Lake Champlain stopped it cold and convinced the British command that the war was not worth the cost.
That conviction produced the Treaty of Ghent, signed in Belgium in December 1814.

Its terms are almost comically anticlimactic: the war ended on the basis of status quo ante bellum, Latin for "the state in which things were before the war," meaning no territory changed hands and not one of the stated American grievances, including impressment, was even mentioned in the treaty.

On paper the war had settled nothing and won nothing, and a reasonable person could ask what the point of it had been; the answer, as the rest of this chapter shows, turned out to lie not in the treaty but in what the war did to American self-perception and to the Native nations.
And yet "nothing changed" changed everything, for reasons that are about psychology and consequence rather than the treaty text.
Britain, with Napoleon defeated, no longer needed to impress sailors or restrict neutral trade, so the grievances evaporated on their own.
Tecumseh's confederacy was destroyed.

The republic had taken Britain's best shot, lost its own capital, and survived intact, and it came out of the war with a surge of national confidence and a sense, accurate or not, of having won a "second war of independence." The thing that fixed that feeling permanently happened after the peace was signed.
Slow communications meant that neither the British army nor Andrew Jackson knew the war was over.

In January 1815 a large British army assaulted Jackson's fortified position outside New Orleans and was shattered, suffering roughly two thousand killed, wounded, and captured against a few dozen American casualties, the most lopsided result of the war, fought two weeks after the Treaty of Ghent had already ended it.
The Battle of New Orleans decided nothing militarily, because the war was already over.
What it decided was a myth and a career.
Americans, learning of the treaty and the great victory at almost the same time, fused them: they believed they had won the war and that Jackson had won it.
The reality, that the treaty changed nothing and the great victory was strategically pointless, did not matter against the feeling.

The episode manufactured a national hero, Andrew Jackson, "Old Hickory," the man who beat the British and broke the Creeks, and his entire later political rise, the populist tide that ends this book and dominates the next, runs straight out of New Orleans (Antebellum America Ch 1–2).
The war's final political consequence killed a party, with an irony this book has been setting up.
The commercial Northeast had opposed the war from the start (Chapter 15), and Federalist New England had resisted it throughout, refusing militia and undermining war finance.

In late 1814 and early 1815, delegates from the New England states met secretly at the Hartford Convention (in Hartford, Connecticut, one of the New England states), where the most extreme voices flirted with the idea that a state could nullify or resist federal war policy, and even with New England leaving the Union.
Recall the nullification doctrine from Chapter 10: the claim that a state may, on its own authority, refuse to obey a federal law it judges unconstitutional.
This is the irony, and it should be stated plainly: in 1798 it was Jefferson's Republicans who had asserted exactly that doctrine, against an authoritarian Federalist government (Chapter 10).
In 1814 it was the Federalists of New England reaching for the same states'-rights weapon against a Republican war.

The timing was, across the Atlantic, eerily parallel: the same 1814–15 months saw the Congress of Vienna in Europe burying the moderate-then-reactionary movements thrown up by the Napoleonic era, the same political tide that drowned the Federalists at home.

The nullification doctrine, it turns out, was a tool that either side would pick up when it was losing, which is exactly why it was so dangerous, and why it kept reappearing until it tore the country apart (Antebellum America Ch 3).
But the Hartford Convention's timing was fatal: its demands arrived in Washington at the very moment the news of the Treaty of Ghent and the victory at New Orleans did.
Against the euphoria of "we won," a meeting of New Englanders that had talked about leaving the Union looked like treason.
The Federalist Party, the party of Washington, Hamilton, and the Constitution's strongest defenders, never recovered, and effectively died as a national force.
For the next several years the United States would have, almost by accident, only one functioning political party (Chapter 17).

chapters.title: The Era of Good Feelings
sentences: For about a decade after the War of 1812, the United States had something it has had at almost no other moment in its history: only one political party.
With the Federalists dead (Chapter 16), the Democratic-Republicans had the field to themselves.

James Monroe, a Virginian of the founding generation (a Revolutionary officer, Jefferson's protégé, and a former minister and secretary of state) won the presidency in 1816 and again in 1820 essentially unopposed, the last of the Virginia founders to hold the office.

A Boston newspaper, watching Monroe tour even hostile New England to warm, partyless crowds, gave the period its enduring name, the Era of Good Feelings (the phrase is usually traced to the Federalist Columbian Centinel in 1817).
The name is half-true and half-irony, and the irony is the whole point of this chapter.
On the surface these were years of confident nationalism, expansion, and one-party calm.

Underneath that surface, three things were happening at once: the government was building a powerful nationalist economic and legal order, the country suffered its first modern financial crash, and the slavery question quietly loaded itself for the explosion of the next chapter.
The "good feelings" were not a resolution.
They were the deceptive quiet of a country that had not yet been forced to look at what it was sitting on.
The most striking thing about these years is that the surviving party adopted much of the dead party's program.

The War of 1812 had taught a hard lesson: the United States had nearly lost because it had no national bank to finance the war, no protected domestic industry to supply it, and no decent roads to move troops.

So the Republicans, the party of small government and strict construction (Chapter 8), turned to economic nationalism, and its champion was Henry Clay, the former War Hawk (Chapter 15), now the most powerful man in Congress.
Clay packaged a set of policies he called the American System, and its three parts have to be understood as a deliberately interlocking mechanism, because that interlock is the whole idea.

First, a protective tariff: a tax on imported manufactured goods (especially British), set high enough that American-made goods could undersell them, deliberately shielding infant American industry from foreign competition. (The word tariff simply means a tax on imports; a protective tariff is one whose purpose is not mainly to raise revenue but to protect domestic producers by making the foreign product more expensive.) Second, a national bank to provide a stable currency and credit.
Third, federally funded internal improvements (roads and canals) paid for by the tariff revenue.

The logic was a closed loop: the tariff protects Northern industry and raises money; the money builds the roads and canals; the roads and canals let Western farmers sell food to Eastern factory workers and buy Eastern manufactures; everyone is bound together by mutual economic interest into a self-sufficient national economy.

It was Hamilton's vision (Chapter 8) resurrected by Hamilton's old enemies, and it became the central economic argument of American politics for forty years. (It also carried a sectional charge that this book's successor will detonate: the South, which exported cotton and imported manufactures, came to see the protective tariff as the North taxing it for the North's benefit, Antebellum America Ch 3.) The bank part was enacted at once: the Second Bank of the United States, chartered in 1816. (The first Bank's twenty-year charter had come up for renewal in 1811 and the Jeffersonian Republicans, still distrusting Hamilton's creation, had let it die by a single vote; without a national bank to lend to the Treasury and steady the currency, the War of 1812's finances had been a catastrophe, which is exactly why the same party now reversed itself and re-created the institution.) And here the third great branch of government, the courts, stepped in to settle the oldest constitutional argument in this book.
John Marshall, still Chief Justice (Chapter 11), used the Bank to do it.
In McCulloch v.

Maryland (1819), the state of Maryland, like several states hostile to a powerful national bank competing with and disciplining their own local banks, tried to tax the national Bank's branch so heavily it would have to close; the case asked whether Congress had the power to create a bank at all, and whether a state could tax a federal institution.
Marshall's ruling answered both with a sweeping assertion of national power.

Congress, he held, did have the power to charter a bank, because the Constitution's "necessary and proper" clause grants Congress not just its explicitly listed powers but the implied means to carry them out, the doctrine of implied powers, Hamilton's old argument (Chapter 8), now made supreme law by the Court.

And a state could not tax a federal instrument, because, in a line of the opinion (Marshall sharpening an argument the lawyer Daniel Webster had made at the bar), "the power to tax involves the power to destroy," and no state could be allowed to destroy what the whole nation had created.
In Gibbons v.

Ogden (1824) The Marshall Court did the parallel thing for commerce, ruling that the federal government's power over interstate commerce (trade and navigation that crosses state lines, as opposed to business conducted wholly inside one state) was broad and overrode conflicting state grants, striking down a state-granted steamboat monopoly and clearing the inland waters for open competition.
Together these rulings did, through the judiciary, what the Federalists had failed to do through elections: they entrenched a strong, expansive reading of national power as constitutional law.
This was, by the standards of the age, an institution with no parallel anywhere.
In Britain, Parliament was supreme and no court could strike down its acts or referee the central government's reach; in France there was no such judicial power at all.

The Marshall Court was inventing, case by case, a uniquely American thing, an unelected tribunal that settled the constitution's deepest structural fights by reasoned opinion, and it used that power consistently for the nation over the states.
The same expansive national confidence reached into foreign policy and produced the era's one durable doctrine.

By the early 1820s the Spanish empire in the Americas was collapsing and most of Latin America had won independence, much of it explicitly inspired by the American and French revolutions, with leaders like Simón Bolívar citing the United States as the proof that a colony could become a self-governing republic.

The worry in Washington and London was that the Holy Alliance, the bloc of conservative monarchies (Russia, Prussia, Austria) that had declared a right to crush liberal revolutions in Europe after Napoleon's fall, might extend that principle across the ocean and help Spain reconquer its lost colonies.

In 1823 President James Monroe, in his annual message to Congress, stated what became the Monroe Doctrine: that the American continents were no longer open to new European colonization, and that the United States would treat any European attempt to recolonize the Western Hemisphere or to plant its monarchical political system there (the doctrine's "extend its political system" meant exactly this, exporting European-style monarchy or putting a European prince on a New World throne) as a hostile act, while pledging in return to stay out of Europe's internal quarrels.
It was, in effect, the American rejection of the Holy Alliance principle, applied to a whole hemisphere.

It is essential to be honest about the mechanism, because the doctrine's later reputation badly overstates its 1823 reality: the United States in 1823 had no navy remotely capable of enforcing such a claim.
What actually deterred European intervention was the British Navy.

Britain had its own commercial reason to keep the hemisphere open (it had captured the trade of the newly independent Latin American republics and did not want the old Spanish monopoly restored), and it was Britain's fleet, not American power, that stood behind the words.

The Monroe Doctrine in 1823 was a bold statement of principle riding on someone else's power; it became a real pillar of American policy only decades later, when the United States finally had the strength to back it.

As aspiration, though, it announced something striking: that the republic now thought of an entire hemisphere as its sphere, a remarkable claim from a country that, forty years earlier, most of Europe had expected to fragment within a generation (Chapter 1).
And then, against all that swelling confidence, the floor dropped.
The Panic of 1819 was the young republic's first great boom-and-bust financial crisis, and its mechanism is recognizable to anyone who has lived through a modern one.

After the war, easy credit (much of it from the new Second Bank and from a swarm of loosely regulated state banks, locally chartered private banks that issued their own paper money with little oversight) fueled a speculative boom, above all in western land bought on borrowed money by people betting prices would keep climbing.
When the Bank, alarmed, abruptly tightened credit and called in its loans, and when European demand for American farm exports slumped now that the Napoleonic Wars were over, the bubble burst.
Land prices collapsed, banks failed, debtors could not pay, farms were foreclosed by the thousands, and unemployment spread through the cities.

After chapter on chapter of the machinery working, of crises survived and a nation confidently expanding, the country's own economy turned on it without warning, and there was no doctrine and no court ruling that could undo a foreclosed farm.

The Panic left a lasting political residue: a deep, bitter popular suspicion of banks in general and the Second Bank in particular, especially in the debtor West, the grievance Andrew Jackson would ride straight to the presidency and weaponize in the next period (Antebellum America Ch 2).
And it exposed the truth the era's name was hiding.
The good feelings were a surface.

Underneath, the country was indebted, sectionally divided, and about to be asked the one question it had spent thirty years refusing to answer, the question waiting in the next chapter, when a single territory's application for statehood rang what Jefferson would call a fire bell in the night.

chapters.title: The Fire Bell and the Founders' Exit
sentences: The last chapter of the early republic is the one where the thing the founders buried in 1787 came back up through the floor.

For thirty years the slavery question had been deferred: written into the Constitution's structure (Chapter 5), made vastly larger by the cotton gin (Chapter 13), and politely not discussed at the national level by a political class that had agreed, more or less, to keep it out of national politics.
In 1819 a routine request for statehood detonated it, and the explosion frightened the surviving founders more than anything since the Revolution.
This chapter is that crisis, the compromise that contained it, and the exit of the founding generation as the country crossed into a different kind of democracy.
It started as bookkeeping.
By 1819 the territory of Missouri, carved out of the Louisiana Purchase (Chapter 12), had enough settlers to apply for statehood, and it applied as a slave state.

Until that moment the country had carefully kept the number of slave states and free states equal, which meant the Senate (two seats per state, Chapter 5) was evenly balanced between the sections, even though the slave states' three-fifths bonus (Chapter 5) gave the South extra weight in the House and the Electoral College.

Admitting Missouri as a slave state would tip the Senate balance and, more alarmingly to many Northerners, would extend slavery into the vast Louisiana territory, where the question had never been settled.
A New York congressman proposed an amendment that would admit Missouri only on condition that slavery be gradually ended there.

The proposal passed the House on a stark sectional vote (almost all Northern members for, almost all Southern members against) and the country suddenly saw, with a clarity it had been avoiding for thirty years, that its deepest political fault line did not run between parties.
It ran between North and South, along the line of slavery, and the constitutional machinery offered no automatic answer.

The crisis was contained, for a generation, by the Missouri Compromise of 1820, engineered largely by Henry Clay, who brokered this kind of sectional bargain so often (notably again in 1833 over the tariff and in 1850 over the new western territories) that he earned the title "the Great Compromiser." Its mechanism had three interlocking parts.
First, Missouri was admitted as a slave state.

Second, to keep the Senate balanced, the northern district of Massachusetts was simultaneously admitted as the new free state of Maine, so the count stayed even, one slave state and one free state added together.

Third, and most consequentially, a line was drawn across the rest of the Louisiana territory at latitude 36°30′ (the southern boundary of Missouri itself, running roughly along the line that today separates the lower Midwest from the South): north of that line, in all the remaining Louisiana territory, slavery was forbidden forever; south of it, slavery was permitted.

The transatlantic contrast is stark: in the same years the United States was drawing a continental map to manage slavery's expansion, Britain had banned the slave trade and was moving toward abolishing slavery in its empire outright, which it did in 1833.
One Atlantic power was dividing a continent to preserve the institution; the other was ending it.
The 36°30′ line was the Northwest Ordinance's idea (Chapter 4) scaled up to half a continent: a geographic fence dividing the future into slave and free.
It worked, in the sense that it postponed the explosion for over thirty years.

But it also did something ominous: it conceded, on the record, that the slavery question could only be managed by drawing literal lines on the map and balancing power section against section, that the contradiction the founders had hoped would fade was instead permanent, and could only be administered, not solved.
And it set the exact precedent that would blow up the Union when a later generation tore the 36°30′ line back up (Antebellum America Ch 14).
The man who heard the alarm most clearly was the man who had written the founding sentence.

Thomas Jefferson, in retirement, read the news of the Missouri crisis and, in a private letter written on April 22, 1820, to a Maine congressman named John Holmes, set down what has become the most quoted line in this entire book: the controversy, he wrote, "like a fire bell in the night, awakened and filled me with terror.

I considered it at once as the knell of the Union." He saw, with the clarity of an old man who had spent his life inside the contradiction (Chapter 12), that drawing a geographic line between slave and free did not settle the question but instead made it geographic, sectional, and therefore eventually irreconcilable: "a geographical line, coinciding with a marked principle, moral and political, once conceived and held up to the angry passions of men, will never be obliterated." This is the pivot of the whole chain.
The deferred question of 1787 had become, by 1820, the thing the founders themselves now believed would kill the republic.
They were right; it took forty years, and the killing is the substance of this book's successor (Antebellum America Ch 14 and following).
The early republic's great unanswered question did not get smaller as the founders had bet in Philadelphia.

It got armed, and answering it would take two attempts at Reconstruction, one abandoned in 1877 and one completed, partially, in 1965, a reckoning spanning 189 years and the full length of this chain, from the Declaration to the Voting Rights Act (Reconstruction, and the Civil Rights Era narrative, Ch 18).
The founders themselves now began to exit, and the manner of their exit is the chapter's coda.
The Era of Good Feelings' one-party calm could not survive the ambitions it had bottled up, and the presidential election of 1824 broke the single party into pieces.

Four candidates, all calling themselves Republicans, ran: John Quincy Adams (son of the second president, a brilliant, cold, experienced New England diplomat), Henry Clay, the war hero Andrew Jackson, and William Crawford (Monroe's Treasury secretary and the early favorite of the party establishment, who was partly disabled by a stroke during the campaign).

Jackson won the most popular votes and the most electoral votes but, with the field split four ways, not the absolute majority the Constitution requires, which threw the election, as in 1800 (Chapter 11), into the House of Representatives.

Clay, eliminated but powerful as Speaker of the House, threw his support to Adams, who was duly elected, and then Adams appointed Clay his Secretary of State, the office that had been the stepping-stone to the presidency for a generation.
Jackson's furious supporters called it the "corrupt bargain": the popular-vote winner denied the presidency by a backroom deal among elites.
It is important to be exact here, because this is a contested point: this was a political accusation, not a proven crime.

Clay and Adams genuinely shared a nationalist policy outlook and would plausibly have aligned anyway, and no documentary evidence of an explicit quid pro quo has ever surfaced; the standard historical view is that no such deal can be proven, not that one has been disproven.
What is not debatable is the political effect.

The charge convinced a huge part of the public that a self-perpetuating elite had stolen an election from the people, and it handed Andrew Jackson a four-year grievance and a mass movement (Antebellum America Ch 1).
John Quincy Adams's single term was a frustrated failure.

He laid out an ambitious nationalist program (roads and canals, a naval academy, a national observatory, a national university, federal support for the sciences) and a Congress controlled by his enemies and a country in an anti-elite mood rejected almost all of it; the national university, for instance, was simply never built, and most of the program died as proposals no one would fund.
The fulcrum man between the founding era and the age of mass democracy spent four years unable to govern.
Then the founders left, on a date that no novelist would dare invent.

On July 4, 1826, the fiftieth anniversary, to the day, of the Declaration of Independence, Thomas Jefferson and John Adams both died, within hours of each other, Jefferson at Monticello in Virginia and Adams in Massachusetts.
They had been revolutionary allies, then bitter political enemies (Chapters 9–11), then, in old age, reconciled correspondents whose late letters are among the finest things either wrote.

Adams's last words, as reported afterward by family and attendants at his bedside (the wording varies slightly between accounts, as deathbed quotations usually do), were that "Thomas Jefferson survives," not knowing that Jefferson had died at Monticello a few hours earlier that same afternoon.
The coincidence stunned the country and was taken, instantly, as something close to divine punctuation on the founding era.
The men who had written the sentence and built the machine were gone, and they left the contradiction unresolved exactly as they had received it, only now far larger and more dangerous.
The book ends on the threshold of a different country.

The election of 1828 swept Andrew Jackson into the presidency on a wave of expanded suffrage, mass political organization, and an explicit, electrifying claim that government should answer to the common (white) man rather than to a gentlemanly elite.
The suffrage expansion was real and worth pausing on.

Through the 1810s and 1820s, state after state had dropped the old requirement that a man own a certain amount of property or land to vote, partly under popular pressure and partly because rival politicians competed for the new voters by being the ones to enfranchise them, until something close to universal white male suffrage was the norm.
By the standards of the age this was extraordinary.
Britain in 1828 still restricted the vote to a narrow slice of propertied men and would not even begin to widen it until the Reform Act of 1832; France lurched between restrictive constitutions.

The early American republic was, by 1828, operating on a broader popular franchise than any other large state on earth, even as that same franchise pointedly excluded every woman and almost every Black American.
It was the threshold of mass democracy, and it is where this book stops and its successor begins (Antebellum America Ch 1).
So, the closing assessment, against the question the book opened with (Chapter 1).
Could a republic (no king, elected representatives, a written constitution) actually work at the scale of a continent, when every large republic in history had collapsed?
After fifty years the answer was, against the odds and the best political science of the age, yes: the machinery worked.
Power changed hands by ballot, including between mortal enemies (Chapter 11).
A written constitution held under crises that had destroyed older republics.
An army served the state and stepped aside (Chapters 3, 9).
A loyal opposition became a permanent, accepted feature rather than a treason.
The courts learned to resolve structural disputes with reasoning rather than force (Chapters 11, 17).
The continental scale that Montesquieu's theory said was impossible (Chapter 1) had, so far, not produced fragmentation or a Caesar.
By the standards of 1776, this was a stunning success, and it changed what people across the world believed was politically possible.
But the answer came with the clause this whole book has been tracking: yes, for some.

The same fifty years that built the machinery of self-government also wrote slavery into the structure (Chapter 5), made it the engine of the national economy (Chapter 13), expanded it across half a continent (Chapter 12), and, when forced to confront it, could only draw a line on a map and defer it again (Chapter 18).
The republic had proved a large republic could last.
It had not proved it could last while half-slave and half-free, and the men who built it died believing (Jefferson said so explicitly) that it probably could not.

They handed the next generation a republic that worked, a continent it dominated, and a contradiction that was no longer a footnote in a 1787 document but a loaded weapon pointed at the Union's heart.

What the next generation did with that inheritance, the fire bell ringing louder, the line on the map torn up, and the war the founders feared, is the story this chain tells next, in Antebellum America.

chapters.title: The Age of the Common Man
sentences: Start with the word, because it is doing something sneaky.
Antebellum is Latin for "before the war" (ante, before; bellum, war), and in American usage it means, specifically, the United States in roughly the four decades before the Civil War of 1861–1865.
Stop and notice how odd that is.
We do not normally name an era by a thing that had not happened yet.

We do not call the 1900s "the pre–World War years." But the entire period from Andrew Jackson's election in 1828 to the guns at Fort Sumter in 1861 got tagged, in retrospect, by the catastrophe it was sliding toward ("the antebellum South," "antebellum architecture," "the antebellum republic"), as though everything in it were a kind of long preface.
That is not how the people living it experienced it.
They thought they were living in the most exciting, most democratic, most rapidly growing country on earth, and in several measurable ways they were right.
The irony that the era is defined by its own destruction is the spine of this book, and it should make you suspicious of every "compromise" you are about to watch politicians celebrate.
Each one was sold as the settlement that would finally put the slavery question to rest.
None of them did.
Each bought less time than the last.
To see why, you have to know what the country inherited, so here is the recap in one paragraph and no more.

The United States was created by a revolution that declared all men created equal and then wrote a Constitution that protected slavery without using the word, counting an enslaved person as three-fifths of a person for the purpose of giving slave states extra seats in Congress, guaranteeing the return of people who escaped bondage, and forbidding any ban on the Atlantic slave trade until 1808 (Early US Republic Ch 6).
The three-fifths rule is worth pausing on, because its perversity is the whole pattern in miniature.
Seats in the House of Representatives, and therefore votes in the Electoral College, were apportioned by population.

Counting enslaved people, who could not vote and were legally property, inflated the population total of the slave states without giving any of those people a voice, which handed the slaveholders who owned them extra congressmen and extra presidential electors.
The enslaved did not benefit; their owners did, gaining political power in direct proportion to the number of human beings they held.
Slavery was not merely tolerated by the constitutional structure.
It was rewarded by it.

The founders knew this was a contradiction; several of them said so in writing and then did nothing about it, on the calculation that the Union could not have been formed if the question were forced and that the problem could be left to a later generation.

The first time it was forced, when Missouri applied to join the Union as a slave state in 1819, the fight was so frightening that the seventy-six-year-old Thomas Jefferson, the man who had written "all men are created equal," called it "a fire bell in the night" that "awakened and filled me with terror," because he could already hear in it the breakup of the country (Early US Republic Ch 18).

Congress patched it with the Missouri Compromise of 1820: Missouri came in as a slave state, Maine as a free one, and an imaginary line was drawn across the rest of the western territory at latitude 36°30′, slavery permitted south of it, banned north of it.
The Maine-for-Missouri pairing is the key to the next forty years of American politics, so understand the machinery.
Every state, regardless of population, gets exactly two senators.
Through the 1810s the Union had been kept at an even number of slave and free states, which meant the Senate was split evenly and neither section could pass anything over the other's objection.
Admitting Missouri alone would have given the slave states a two-seat Senate majority; admitting Maine at the same moment preserved the deadlock.
From 1820 on, states were therefore admitted in slave-free pairs to hold that balance, and the entire sectional struggle of this book is, at bottom, a fight over the day the pairing finally broke.
Remember that line.
It holds for thirty-four years, and the chapter in which a senator from Illinois erases it (Chapter 14) is the chapter the war becomes unavoidable.
That is the inheritance.
Now the country that received it in 1828.
The single biggest change in American life between the Revolution and Jackson was not industrial or territorial.
It was the franchise, meaning who could vote.

The founders' republic had been, by design, a government of property-owning white men, on the eighteenth-century theory that only a man with a material stake in the country (land, an estate) had the independence to vote responsibly.

Between roughly 1800 and 1828, almost every state quietly tore up its property and taxpaying requirements for white men, so that by Jackson's election something close to universal white manhood suffrage existed: virtually every adult white male could vote, regardless of whether he owned a thing.
This was, at the time, the most democratic electorate in the world by a wide margin.
Britain would not get close to it until 1867, France lurched in and out of it through revolutions, and most of Europe was still ruled by kings and aristocracies.

American politics became, for the first time, a mass spectator sport, with torchlight parades, campaign songs, barbecues, and turnout rates (among those allowed to vote) that would later be the envy of every modern democracy.
The man who rode this wave, and embodied it, was Andrew Jackson.
Jackson is Chapter 2's subject, so here only the shape of him.
He was not a Virginia planter-philosopher like the first generation of presidents.

He was a self-made man from the Carolina backcountry, an orphan, a duelist, a slaveholder, an Indian fighter, and a general who had become a national hero by winning a lopsided battle at New Orleans in 1815 (Early US Republic Ch 16).
He presented himself, and was believed, as the champion of the ordinary white man against a corrupt moneyed elite, and "the common man" became the era's defining phrase and self-image.
The ideology that went with it has a name historians use, Jacksonian democracy, and three pillars worth defining now because the rest of the book leans on them.

First, the self-made man: the belief, close to a national religion, that any white man could rise by his own effort, that birth and inherited rank were European corruptions, and that the government's job was to clear the track and otherwise get out of the way.
Second, the spoils system: the practice, which Jackson's people raised to a principle, of firing government employees when your party wins an election and replacing them with your own supporters.

The name comes from a senator's blunt defense of it, "to the victor belong the spoils," and the logic was genuinely democratic in intent (rotating offices among ordinary citizens was supposedly more democratic than a permanent class of officeholders) and corrupting in practice (it staffed the government with loyalists rather than competents and tied every federal job to partisan loyalty, a machine that would not be seriously dismantled until the 1880s).

Third, hostility to concentrated economic power, above all to banks and corporations that Jacksonians saw as instruments by which the few extracted wealth from the many, the conviction that detonates the Bank War in the next chapter.
Now the part that the phrase "the age of the common man" is built to make you forget.
The expansion of democracy in this era was real, and it was, with brutal precision, an expansion for white men only, and in several respects it was financed and powered by the people it excluded.
Free Black men, who had been able to vote in several Northern states in 1800, were systematically stripped of the franchise across this very period.

Pennsylvania disenfranchised them by name in its 1838 constitution; the same wave of democratization that was enfranchising every poor white man simultaneously slammed the door on Black men who already had the vote.

Women of every race could not vote, could not in most states own property or wages once married, and could not sign contracts in their own names; the law treated a married woman as legally absorbed into her husband, meaning that in the eyes of the law she had no separate legal existence at all.

Her wages were his, property she brought to the marriage was his to manage, a contract she signed was void, and she generally could not sue or be sued in her own name, because legally she was not a distinct person but a part of him (the doctrine has a name, coverture, defined in Chapter 8 where the women's-rights movement confronts it).

The roughly two million enslaved people in 1828 (about four million by 1860) were not citizens, not legally persons in the full sense, owned outright, and would be declared, by the Supreme Court in 1857, to have no rights a white man was bound to respect (Chapter 15).

The Native nations of the Southeast were, at the moment Jackson took office, about to be expelled from their homelands by the same democratic government that was being celebrated as the freest on earth (Chapter 4).
This is not a footnote to Jacksonian democracy.
It is the structure of it: a herrenvolk democracy, in the term scholars use.

Herrenvolk is German for "master people" or "master race" (Herren, masters or lords; Volk, a people), a word later twentieth-century history would attach to far darker things; sociologists adopted it for a precise structural idea.
A herrenvolk democracy is a society radically egalitarian within the dominant racial group precisely because the bottom of the social order is occupied by people defined out of it.
The two facts are not in tension; they are the same fact.
White men could be made equal to each other so cheaply, with no property qualification, no inherited rank, because the floor they all stood on was the unfreedom of everyone beneath them.

The contrast worth holding throughout this book is that the same decades in which the United States became the world's widest democracy were the decades in which it became the world's largest and most economically central slave society.

This pattern, a real democracy for the included and pure exclusion for everyone else, was not uniquely American, and seeing where else it appears sharpens what "the world's widest democracy" actually meant.

The same Britain whose 1832 reform was inching toward the franchise this chapter compares the U.S. to was, in those exact years, ruling tens of millions of colonial subjects in India who had no franchise of any kind whatsoever (Modern India Chs 1–2); the British electorate at home expanded while its imperial subjects had zero political voice, the selective freedom run on a global rather than a domestic scale.

And the structure has a sharper twentieth-century echo: the Soviet Union would call itself a workers' democracy while defining whole categories of people (the "class enemies") out of the polity entirely and applying terror to them (Soviet Union Ch 1).
The mechanism recurs across very different regimes: a political community that is genuinely participatory for its members and an instrument of total domination for those it has defined as outside it.
American herrenvolk democracy is the racial version of an old and recurring bargain.
Which raises the problem this whole book has to be honest about.

For most of American history, the documentary record of slavery was overwhelmingly the record of the people who profited from it: planters' account books, bills of sale, advertisements for the recapture of escaped people, the speeches of slaveholding politicians.
The people held in slavery were, by law in most of the South, forbidden to learn to read or write, so the written record from their own hand is thin by design.
But it is not empty, and recovering it is one of the most important things that has happened in the historical study of this period.

There are the slave narratives: book-length autobiographies by people who escaped, of which the most famous is the 1845 Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass (Chapter 10), written by a man who taught himself to read in defiance of the law and became the most formidable orator in the country.
There are thousands of others, some dictated, some smuggled out, some published by abolitionist societies.

And there is an extraordinary late source: in the 1930s, the Federal Writers' Project, a government employment program for out-of-work writers under the New Deal (the sweeping set of federal jobs, relief, and economic programs President Franklin Roosevelt launched in the 1930s to fight the Great Depression, which among many other things put unemployed people to work and is examined fully in a later narrative in this series), sent interviewers across the South to record the testimony of the last living people who had been enslaved, then in their eighties and nineties; more than two thousand interviews, the WPA ex-slave narratives, the largest body of first-person testimony from formerly enslaved Americans in existence.
These sources have problems historians take seriously.

The WPA interviewers were usually white Southerners, the people being interviewed were old, poor, and speaking under Jim Crow (the system of legally enforced racial segregation and Black disfranchisement that the white South built after Reconstruction and that was in full force in the 1930s, the subject of the later narrative in this chain) to strangers who could hurt them, and memory at seventy years' distance is memory.
But used carefully, against the planters' own records, they let us write the history of slavery from inside it and not only from the ledger.
This book uses them, and it will tell you when it is doing so.

So this is the era: a republic exploding outward and upward, drunk on its own democratic energy, genuinely the freest large society on earth for the people it counted as fully human, and resting that freedom on the largest system of human bondage in the modern world, with a question at its center that the founders had refused to answer and that every passing year made more impossible to keep answering with silence.
The next seventeen chapters are that question refusing to stay buried.
We begin with the man who gave the age its name.

chapters.title: King Andrew I
sentences: In 1832 Jackson's enemies began circulating a cartoon: Andrew Jackson in royal robes, a crown on his head, a scepter in one hand and a veto in the other, trampling the Constitution under his boot, captioned "King Andrew the First." They meant it as an insult and a warning.

The people circulating it were not cranks; they were Jackson's organized political opposition, the coalition of merchants, bankers, large property holders, and nationalist politicians who within a few years would call themselves the Whigs (Chapter 14), a name borrowed from the British party that had historically opposed an overreaching king, and the choice of name was the whole accusation: they believed Jackson was governing like a monarch.

To understand why a war hero elected as the champion of the common man got drawn as a tyrant by people serious enough to be worth answering, you have to follow the single fight that defined his presidency, the one historians call the Bank War, and you have to follow it as a mechanism, because the way Jackson destroyed the Bank, step by step, is the whole story.
First, who Jackson was, because Chapter 1 only sketched him.

He was born in 1767 in the Carolina backcountry, orphaned by the Revolutionary War as a teenager (his mother and brothers died in it; he carried a saber scar from a British officer he had refused to shine boots for, and he hated Britain for the rest of his life), and rose with no inherited advantages through frontier law and land speculation in Tennessee to become a plantation owner and the holder of dozens of enslaved people.
He was famous before he was president for two things.

He had won the Battle of New Orleans in January 1815, a crushing defeat of a British army that, through a quirk of timing, had been fought after the treaty ending the War of 1812 was already signed but before the news crossed the Atlantic; it changed nothing about the war's outcome and made Jackson the most celebrated military hero since Washington (Early US Republic Ch 16).
And he had run for president in 1824, won the most popular and electoral votes, and then lost anyway.

The mechanism by which that can happen is in the Constitution and matters for the rest of this book: a candidate becomes president only by winning an outright majority of the Electoral College, not merely the most votes, and in 1824 four candidates split the electoral vote so that no one had a majority.
The Constitution provides that when that happens, the choice passes to the House of Representatives, voting by state delegation, choosing among the top finishers.

In the House, the speaker, Henry Clay (a man you will meet repeatedly, himself a defeated candidate and so the kingmaker), threw his support to John Quincy Adams, who won the House vote and promptly made Clay his secretary of state.
Jackson's people called it the "Corrupt Bargain", proof, in their telling, that a self-dealing Washington elite had stolen the presidency from the people's choice.

Whether any actual deal was struck is genuinely unresolved; no documentary evidence of an explicit quid pro quo has ever surfaced, Clay's contemporaries knew he and Jackson loathed each other on policy and personal grounds, and most historians regard the appointment as ordinary patronage rather than provable corruption, though the timing was politically catastrophic for Adams regardless.

What is not debatable is that the grievance fueled a four-year campaign that swept Jackson into office in 1828 at the head of a new political organization built largely by a brilliant New York operator named Martin Van Buren: the Democratic Party, generally reckoned the oldest continuously operating political party in the world (a few European parties claim earlier founding dates, but most trace to organizations that dissolved and re-formed; the modern Democratic Party's institutional line back to the Jacksonians is unusually unbroken), and the direct ancestor of the modern one of the same name, though almost nothing about its policies then resembles its policies now.
Now the Bank, which requires a definition before it can be a war.
The Second Bank of the United States was a national bank, chartered by Congress in 1816 for twenty years, partly government-owned but run by private directors.
The hybrid structure is worth a sentence because its oddity is exactly what Jackson would attack.

The federal government owned one-fifth of the Bank's stock and appointed five of its twenty-five directors; the other four-fifths was owned by private investors, including wealthy Easterners and some foreigners, who chose the remaining twenty directors and effectively ran it.
So it held the public's money and exercised public power over the whole financial system, but it answered, day to day, to private shareholders chasing private profit and to no voter at all.
It is easiest to understand by what it did: it held the federal government's money, it made loans, and, crucially, it regulated all the other banks in the country.
In the 1820s and 1830s the United States had no national paper currency.
Money was issued by hundreds of individual state-chartered banks in the form of banknotes, each bank printing its own, each note a promise to pay the bearer in gold or silver coin (specie) on demand.
The system worked only to the degree that banks actually held enough specie to back the paper they printed, and many did not.
The Bank of the United States policed this by routinely collecting other banks' notes and demanding the gold, which forced reckless banks to keep their printing in check or be exposed.

It was, in effect, a privately run central bank, and its president, the brilliant and politically tone-deaf Philadelphia aristocrat Nicholas Biddle, ran it with real competence and an aristocrat's contempt for the idea that he answered to anyone.
Jackson hated it, and the reasons are a clean window onto Jacksonian democracy.
He distrusted all banks and all paper money on principle as engines by which the clever few extracted wealth from the laboring many (he was a hard-money man who believed in gold and silver).

He saw a bank that could expand or contract the entire nation's credit, that was largely owned by wealthy Easterners and some foreign investors, and that answered to no voter, as a concentration of unaccountable power fundamentally incompatible with a democracy: a "monster," "the Hydra of corruption." Whether he was right is a real historical argument.

The Bank did stabilize the currency, and its destruction arguably caused a financial disaster, but it also was genuinely undemocratic in its structure and Biddle did use its money to fund Jackson's political enemies, which made the paranoia partly self-justifying.
The point for this book is the mechanism by which Jackson killed it, because it is the mechanism the "King Andrew" cartoon was about.
Step one: the veto.

The Bank's charter did not expire until 1836, but Biddle, persuaded by Henry Clay (now Jackson's likely opponent in the 1832 election), applied to renew it four years early, in 1832, hoping to force Jackson either to sign it (a humiliation) or to veto it (an issue Clay could run against him on).
Jackson vetoed it.
That was not, by itself, remarkable; presidents have a veto.
What was remarkable was the reasoning.
Previous presidents had used the veto sparingly and almost always on the narrow ground that a law was unconstitutional.

Jackson vetoed the Bank partly on constitutional grounds but mostly on the ground that it was bad for the country and unjust to the common man, asserting that the president's judgment of the public good was as legitimate as Congress's.

This was a genuine constitutional innovation: it transformed the veto from a rare legal check into a routine policy weapon, and it made the presidency, for the first time, the tribune of the whole people against the legislature, exactly the expansion of executive power the "King Andrew" cartoon was protesting.
Every strong president since has used the veto Jackson's way.
Step two: the deposits.
Jackson won the 1832 election in a landslide, treating it as a popular mandate to destroy the Bank entirely rather than merely let it expire.
He decided not to wait until 1836.

He ordered the federal government's money removed from the Bank of the United States and deposited instead into a set of politically friendly state banks, institutions his opponents instantly nicknamed the "pet banks." This was the act that produced the cartoon, because it was legally dubious: the law gave the power to move the deposits to the secretary of the treasury, not the president, and the secretary was supposed to exercise independent judgment.
Jackson's first treasury secretary refused to do it.
Jackson removed him.
The second refused.
Jackson removed him too, and appointed a third, Roger Taney (pronounced "TAW-nee"; the future chief justice who decides Dred Scott, Chapter 15), who carried out the order.
Draining the deposits crippled the Bank well before its charter ran out and killed it as a national institution.

Biddle fought back by sharply contracting the Bank's loans to induce a recession he could blame on Jackson, which was real economic blackmail and which backfired, confirming for Jacksonians everything they had said about a private power able to squeeze the whole economy to punish its political enemies.
Step three, which Jackson did not intend and could not control: the consequences.

With the disciplining hand of the national bank gone, the "pet banks" and hundreds of others printed paper money freely against thin reserves, and a wild speculative boom followed, above all in western public land, with people borrowing paper money from banks to buy government land, then borrowing more against that land.

Jackson, the hard-money man, tried to stop the bubble he had helped inflate by issuing the Specie Circular in 1836, an executive order requiring that public land be paid for in gold or silver rather than banknotes.
Follow what that did, because it is the whole collapse in one move.
A speculator buying federal land had been doing it with banknotes, paper a bank had printed promising gold it mostly did not have.
The Circular meant the government's land offices would no longer take the paper; the buyer now had to bring actual coin.
To get coin, he had to take his banknotes to the issuing bank and demand it redeem them, exactly the thing the whole system depended on people not doing all at once.
When enough people did it at once, the banks discovered they could not pay: the paper in circulation vastly exceeded the metal in the vaults.
Banks suspended payment in specie, called in their loans to survive, and the credit that had fed the land boom evaporated overnight.

The bubble's confidence broke, and shortly after Jackson left office the country fell into the Panic of 1837, a financial collapse followed by a depression that lasted into the 1840s, with banks failing, businesses closing, and unemployment that the era had no statistics for but that contemporaries described as the worst they had seen.
The president holding the bag was not Jackson but his hand-picked successor, Martin Van Buren.
