Section 4 guaranteed the federal war debt and voided all Confederate debts and any claim for compensation for freed slaves, constitutionally bankrupting the financial expectations of the slaveholders, a clause occasionally invoked in modern debt-ceiling arguments.
The lasting architecture of Reconstruction was a moderate-Radical bargain, not a Radical dictation, which is part of why it could pass and part of why it had gaps.
The South's response to being offered the Fourteenth Amendment is the cleanest evidence of what the white South intended, and it forced the next escalation.
Congress made ratification of the Fourteenth essentially the price of readmission.
Every Southern state under Johnson's restored governments except Tennessee rejected it.
The white South was offered citizenship and equal protection for the freedpeople as the condition of full return to the Union and said no.
That refusal destroyed what was left of the moderate position and produced the most aggressive federal action of the entire era.
That "no" forced the single most aggressive act of federal power in this entire story, and it deserves to be seen, not just summarized.
In March 1867, over Johnson's vetoes and using the automatic supermajority of Chapter 4, Congress passed the Reconstruction Acts, which begin Congressional, or Radical, Reconstruction.

The acts declared the existing Southern state governments provisional and illegitimate, dissolved them as legitimate authority, and divided ten ex-Confederate states into five military districts, each placed under a U.S.
Army general with the power to govern.
Picture what that meant on the ground, because the abstraction "military districts" hides the most extraordinary thing the federal government did in the nineteenth century.
In a county seat in Alabama or Mississippi in 1867, the highest authority was no longer the governor or the local judge.

It was a Union officer, often a man who had fought the war that ended two years earlier, who could now remove a mayor, void a court ruling, halt a discriminatory ordinance, and order the army to protect a registration table.

Federal soldiers, not local officials, ran the voter rolls: army-appointed boards of registration, with troops standing by, signed up roughly 700,000 Black and 660,000 white voters, and for the first time in the history of those states a Black man's name went onto the rolls under the protection of a bayonet rather than at the sufferance of the men who had owned him.

To get back into the Union, a state now had to do exactly what the white South had just refused: hold a convention elected by all male citizens regardless of race, write a new constitution, and ratify the Fourteenth Amendment.
The army would not leave until it did.
What happened in those conventions is the payoff, and it is worth seeing concretely rather than as a phrase.

In 1867 and 1868, in statehouses across the South, men who two years earlier had been legally property, who in most of those states it had been a crime to teach to read, sat as elected delegates, in some states as majorities, drafting the supreme law of the state that had enslaved them.

They wrote, against entrenched resistance, the first public school systems the South ever had, struck out the property requirements that had limited voting and officeholding to men of means, and produced what were, by a wide margin, the most democratic constitutions the region had ever known.
This is the thing the Dunning School would spend fifty years lying about and which Chapter 7 tells in full.

End the chapter here, on the register of what had just happened: in the span of two years the Constitution had been rewritten three times over and the country had, on paper and with the army standing behind the paper, finally answered the open question of Chapter 1 in the affirmative.
Freedom meant citizenship, equal protection, and the ballot, and there were now Black men with rifles' worth of federal authority behind their names writing it into law.
It was the high-water mark of the whole story, and almost everything in the rest of this book is the tide going back out.
One man in the White House was already working with every power he had left to pull it out faster, and Congress, having stripped him of nearly everything else, now moved to take the office itself.

chapters.title: The Trial of a President
sentences: In the spring of 1868 the United States did something it had never done and would not do again for 130 years, and then, after that long gap, three more times in the quarter-century after: it put the president on trial to remove him from office.

The impeachment of Andrew Johnson is often told as a soap opera with a cliffhanger ending, and it was that, but it matters for two structural reasons this chapter has to make clear, what it was actually about, and what its outcome did and did not establish for every president since.
First, define the machinery exactly, because most people half-know it.
Impeachment is not removal.
The Constitution gives the House of Representatives the sole power to impeach, which means to formally accuse, by a simple majority vote; an impeached official stays in office.
The case then goes to the Senate, which holds a trial; removal requires conviction by a two-thirds vote of the Senate.

So impeachment is an indictment and the Senate trial is the trial, and the supermajority requirement for conviction is deliberately, almost prohibitively, high, because the framers wanted removing an elected president to be very hard.
Hold the arithmetic: in 1868 there were 54 senators, so conviction required 36 votes, and acquittal required only 19.
Now what it was about, because the surface charge and the real conflict were different and the gap is the whole point.
By 1867 Congress and Johnson were in total war (Chapters 4–5).

The army was the instrument enforcing Reconstruction in the occupied South, and the army answered to the secretary of war, Edwin Stanton, a Lincoln holdover who sided fully with Congress and the Radicals.
Johnson, as commander in chief, wanted Stanton gone so he could install someone who would soften military enforcement.
Congress, to stop exactly that, had passed the Tenure of Office Act in 1867, a law forbidding the president to remove certain officials confirmed by the Senate without the Senate's consent.
It was, fairly openly, a trap, of dubious constitutionality, designed so that if Johnson fired Stanton he would be breaking a federal law and could be impeached for it.
In February 1868 Johnson sprang the trap on purpose: he dismissed Stanton, who refused to leave and barricaded himself in the War Department office.
Within days the House impeached Johnson, 126 to 47, on eleven articles, nine of them built on the Stanton firing and the Tenure of Office Act.

Here is the part an honest account has to foreground: the formal charge was thin and most historians think the law Johnson "violated" was probably unconstitutional (the Supreme Court would say as much, about a similar law, in 1926).
The real reason Congress wanted Johnson gone was not a technical violation of a tenure statute.

It was that he was using every power of the presidency, vetoes, pardons, appointments, the bully pulpit, to sabotage Reconstruction and protect the ex-Confederate order, and a Northern majority had come to see him as, in effect, still fighting the war on the other side from inside the White House.
The impeachment was substantively about that and procedurally about a doorknob.
That mismatch is exactly what makes its outcome important.

The Senate trial ran about three months in the spring of 1868, the chief justice presiding, and a team of House "managers" prosecuting, the managers being the representatives the House appoints to argue its case at a Senate impeachment trial, in effect the prosecutors.

They included Benjamin Butler, a politically slippery Massachusetts ex-general notorious from his wartime command of occupied New Orleans, and Thaddeus Stevens, the great Radical leader of Chapter 1, by now visibly dying (he would be dead within months and had himself carried into the chamber), determined to see Johnson removed before he went.
And it came down, in May 1868, to a single vote.
The Senate voted 35 to convict, 19 to acquit, one vote short of the 36 needed.
Seven Republicans broke with their party to acquit, the most remembered being Edmund Ross of Kansas.

Johnson stayed in office, finished his term as a politically destroyed and essentially powerless man (Grant was already the certain next president), and the Reconstruction Congress simply governed around him for his last months.
Now the thing the chapter exists to establish, because it is the durable consequence and it cuts against an easy reading.

Ross's vote was mythologized in the twentieth century, most famously in Profiles in Courage, the 1956 best-seller of short biographical portraits of principled politicians published under then-Senator John F.
Kennedy's name, which cast Ross as a lone hero defying his party to save the Constitution.

Later historians, notably Ralph Roske and others working from the patronage record, have complicated that: they argue Ross used his pivotal position to extract patronage, the era's currency of politics, government jobs and contracts a powerful figure could hand to allies, in this case federal appointments Ross is documented to have sought and won for his Kansas associates around the time of his vote.

The revisionist case is itself contested, not settled fact, and the honest reading is that Ross's motives were probably mixed, principle and self-interest both, which is why this book flags the heroism as debated rather than either celebrating or debunking it.

But the structural result is not debatable and is genuinely important: the one-vote acquittal established, as a working constitutional norm that has held ever since, that a president will not be removed from office merely for pursuing policies, even disastrous and obstructive policies, that Congress hates.
To remove a president you need something the country broadly accepts as a high crime, not a policy disagreement dressed in a statutory technicality.
Every later impeachment fight in American history, and there have been several within living memory, operates inside the precedent set by these 36 votes that were not there.

The acquittal arguably saved the presidency from becoming subordinate to congressional majorities, a parliamentary system installed by the back door, at the price of leaving an obstructive president in place for ten more months.

Whether that trade was worth it is one of the genuine open arguments in this book, and the honest answer is that it cut both ways: it protected the independence of the office and it protected, for those ten months, a man using the office against the freedpeople.

With Johnson neutralized and Reconstruction's machinery in place, the camera now turns away from Washington and onto the thing all of this was supposedly for, and the thing the Dunning School lied about hardest: what the freedpeople actually did with the citizenship and the ballot once they had them.

chapters.title: Black Reconstruction
sentences: In 1860 it was a crime in most of the South to teach an enslaved person to read.

By 1867 the same people, plus their children, were registering voters by the hundreds of thousands, electing delegates, and sitting in constitutional conventions arguing the fine points of suffrage and taxation, and within three more years two of them sat in the United States Senate.
Hold that compression in your mind, because the speed of it is the single fact that refutes the libel this chapter exists to bury.
The phrase W.

Du Bois used for what actually happened, made permanent by the title of his 1935 book, is Black Reconstruction: the brief period in which Black Southerners, free for the first time, built institutions, voted, governed, and pushed the country closer to its stated ideals than it had ever been, and were destroyed for it.
The Dunning School inverted that into ignorant former slaves and thieving carpetbaggers misgoverning a prostrate South.

The writing rules require naming a contested claim and then refuting it from the sources rather than just asserting the opposite, so that is what this chapter does, and the sources are unusually loud, because for the first time in this chain the people the history is about left a vast record in their own voices.
The vehicle for the political mobilization was often the Union League.

It had begun in the North during the war as a patriotic pro-Union club of the respectable middle class, and after 1867, carried south largely by Black veterans, Bureau agents, and traveling Republican organizers, it transformed into something quite different: a grassroots network that turned Black churches and schoolhouses into political clubs, often meeting at night and armed against attack, where freedmen learned the concrete mechanics of citizenship, how to register, how to mark a ballot, what a contract bound you to, what rights the new laws gave.
It produced a disciplined, almost unanimously Republican Black electorate, which is exactly why, a few chapters from now, the League's local leaders are among the first people the Klan hunts.

The demographic fact under all of this is the one Chapter 1 flagged: in 1860 enslaved people had been a majority of the population in South Carolina and Mississippi and over 40 percent in several other states, so the instant Black men could vote, the Southern electorate was transformed and, in several states, potentially Black-majority.
That single fact, where the freedpeople actually were on the map, is why everything that follows became a war over the ballot box.
What they built with it, in the few years they had it, is concrete and worth listing because the specifics are the rebuttal.
Around 2,000 Black men held public office during Reconstruction.
Sixteen sat in the U.S.

Two became United States senators, both from Mississippi, the state with the largest enslaved population in the country in 1860, an irony so sharp it should stop you: the state that had been the densest concentration of American slavery sent, within a decade, two formerly subordinated Black men to the Senate.

Hiram Rhodes Revels, an African Methodist Episcopal minister and Union chaplain, took his seat in February 1870, the first Black member of Congress in American history, and, in a detail that reads like deliberate historical irony but is simply what happened, the Senate seat he filled was one Mississippi had once given to Jefferson Davis, the president of the Confederacy.
Bruce, born enslaved, took the other Mississippi Senate seat in 1875 and became the first Black senator to serve a full six-year term and to preside over the Senate.
In the House, Joseph Rainey of South Carolina, born enslaved, became the first Black representative and the first to preside over that chamber.

Robert Smalls had pulled off one of the war's most audacious escapes: in May 1862, an enslaved harbor pilot in Charleston, he waited until the white officers of the Confederate steamer Planter went ashore for the night, then put on the captain's hat, sailed the armed ship past the Confederate harbor forts giving the correct signals, picked up his own and the crew's families, and delivered the vessel to the blockading Union navy.
He went on to a five-term South Carolina congressional career.
Pinckney Benton Stewart Pinchback, known by his initials P.
S., briefly served as acting governor of Louisiana, the only Black governor in American history until 1990.
Jonathan Jasper Wright sat for seven years on the South Carolina Supreme Court.
In the South Carolina House, Black members were, for a time, a numerical majority.
Roughly 600 Black men served in Southern state legislatures.

This is a level of Black political representation that, after Reconstruction was destroyed, the country would not see again for a century: no Black American won a Senate election anywhere in the country until Edward Brooke of Massachusetts in 1966, ninety-one years after Bruce, and in almost the same months the movement's integrationist coalition was fracturing toward Black Power (the Civil Rights Era narrative, Ch 15).
That gap, a democracy a Black majority helped build and was then locked out of by terror and then by law, is not unique in kind.

Apartheid South Africa later excluded a Black majority from the vote by statute for forty-six years, and newly independent Ceylon stripped its Tamil minority of citizenship and the franchise in 1948–49 through nominally neutral tests of exactly the sort the post-Reconstruction South would perfect.
What was unusual about the American case was that the rights had been granted and exercised first, and then taken back.
Address the Dunning libel directly, because the writing rules require naming the contested claim and refuting it with evidence rather than just asserting the opposite.
The charge was that these governments were uniquely corrupt and incompetent.
The honest answer has three parts.

One: some Reconstruction governments did have corruption, railroad-bond graft especially, where a legislature, lobbied and bribed, would pledge the state's credit, issuing bonds the taxpayers had to repay, to subsidize a railroad whose promoters then pocketed the money and sometimes never built the line.

But that was the ordinary corruption of the Gilded Age, happening in New York, Washington, and across the white North on a far larger scale at the same time (Chapter 11), not a special Black pathology, and the men doing most of the actual stealing in the South were white.

Two: the same governments created the South's first public school systems, rebuilt the wrecked infrastructure, wrote its most democratic constitutions, and abolished property qualifications, real achievements the Redeemers immediately gutted.
Three: the Black legislators were not the ignorant figures of the caricature.

Many were ministers, soldiers, artisans, and the formally educated; Robert Brown Elliott of South Carolina, a brilliant lawyer, delivered an 1874 House speech answering the ex-Confederate Alexander Stephens, who had risen to argue that civil-rights legislation exceeded Congress's power.

Elliott took apart the constitutional argument point by point and then turned it personal and historical, noting that he, born to a people Stephens's Confederacy had called its "cornerstone" of inferiority, now stood on the House floor refuting the Confederacy's vice president on the meaning of the Constitution, the fact of the scene being itself the rebuttal of the entire libel.

The "carpetbagger" (Northern newcomer, supposedly an opportunist with everything he owned in a cheap carpet bag) and "scalawag" (white Southern Republican, the word literally meant a worthless farm animal) were slurs, coined by the people who lost, accepted as descriptive fact by historians for fifty years.
The newcomers were a mixed lot of teachers, veterans, investors, and reformers, not a uniform plague.
Now the part of Black Reconstruction that did not depend on holding office and that outlasted everything that did, because it is the human heart of the book and it survived even Redemption.
Freedpeople built, with their own hands and almost no resources, the institutions that would carry Black America through the catastrophe coming in the second half of this book.

They walked out of white-controlled churches en masse and built their own, above all the African Methodist Episcopal and the Black Baptist churches, which exploded from tens of thousands to hundreds of millions in aggregate membership over the era and became the central institution of Black civic, political, and educational life; a remarkable share of the Black political leadership just listed were ministers.

They treated literacy as the practical substance of freedom and built schools with a hunger that startled Northern observers, often funding, building, and guarding the schools themselves when the Bureau could not.

And they founded colleges that still exist and still matter: Howard University in Washington (chartered 1867), Fisk University in Nashville (1866), Hampton Institute in Virginia (1868), Morehouse College in Georgia (1867), and a whole cluster more, the historically Black colleges that would educate the Black professional class, doctors, lawyers, teachers, ministers, for the entire Jim Crow century.

Fisk's student choir, the Fisk Jubilee Singers, set out in 1871 to raise money for the nearly bankrupt school by touring the North and then, in 1873, Britain, where on that tour they performed for Queen Victoria, and carried the spirituals composed in slavery into the world's musical canon. (Their arc, an oppressed people's distinctive art reaching the dominant society's grandest stages even as that society denied the people their rights, ran almost exactly parallel to the contemporary Welsh choral movement, which carried itself from coal-mining chapels to royal command performances in the very same decades.) The Singers are an emblem of the whole pattern: a thing of value made under bondage, carried into freedom, and refusing to die when the political freedom was killed.
Keep these institutions in mind, because they are the answer to a question this book ends on, how anything survived at all.
That is what Black Reconstruction built.
The rest of the book is the organized destruction of the political half of it, and the survival, against everything, of the institutional half.

chapters.title: Forty Acres, and What Replaced It
sentences: Go back now to the thing Chapter 3 flagged as the most consequential failure of the era and give it the full chapter it deserves, because if you understand only one structural fact about why Reconstruction's gains were so fragile, it should be this one: the formerly enslaved were freed into propertylessness, in a place where the only people with property were the people who had enslaved them, and the federal government, having freed them, declined to change that.
Everything about how vulnerable Black political power turned out to be runs back to this.
State the counterfactual precisely, because it is the most important "road not taken" in the book and it was not a fantasy.

There was real confiscated and abandoned Confederate land, plantations whose owners had fled or forfeited, and there were concrete proposals to give it to the people who had worked it unpaid for generations.
Sherman's Special Field Order No. 15 (Chapter 3) had actually done it on the coast, 40-acre plots, the army's mules, some 40,000 people farming 400,000 acres by mid-1865.

In Congress, Thaddeus Stevens, the fierce Pennsylvania Radical, proposed the most thorough version: confiscate the large plantations of leading Confederates outright and distribute the land to freedpeople in 40-acre allotments, with the rest sold to fund the war debt and pensions.

Run Stevens's logic, because it was exactly right and the freedpeople had reached it independently: a Black population that owned its own land would have an economic base independent of the planters, could not be starved into signing coercive labor contracts, could not be evicted for voting Republican, and could defend its political rights because its livelihood did not depend on the goodwill of its former enslavers.
Land was not a welfare program in this analysis.
It was the material foundation without which the vote and citizenship were structurally hollow, and the people who would lose the vote said so, in advance, in plain words.
It did not happen, and the reasons are worth being exact about because they are not the reasons the Dunning School gave.

Andrew Johnson's pardons (Chapter 2) returned the Sherman land and most confiscated land to its former Confederate owners through 1865 and 1866, the news carried in person, by his own account, by Bureau commissioner Howard.
Stevens's confiscation plan was defeated in Congress, and not mainly by Southerners, who had no votes there yet (Chapter 4), but by Northern Republicans who balked at it.
The objection that killed it was the sanctity of private property.

Even most Republicans, even toward traitors, found the wholesale seizure and redistribution of land a more frightening precedent than they could accept; it looked, to nineteenth-century propertied Northerners, like an attack on the foundation of the social order itself.

It is worth knowing this was not uniquely American cowardice but the Atlantic pattern: when Britain ended slavery in 1833 it paid £20 million to the slave owners and nothing to the freed, who got no land and became a propertyless plantation labor force in the same trap.
The road not taken in the U.S. was not taken anywhere.

There is also a hard irony the book should name, because it recurs in Chapter 11: the same Congress that could not bring itself to give freedpeople 40 acres of traitors' land was, in these same years, handing railroad corporations tens of millions of acres of public land. (British India was running the identical paradox simultaneously, granting railway corridors across peasant land while refusing any land reform that would touch the great landlords whose cooperation the Raj needed.) Land for the formerly enslaved was a dangerous assault on property; land for the railroads was policy.

The Southern Homestead Act of 1866 was the fig leaf, it opened 46 million acres of public land in five Southern states to settlers including freedpeople, but the land was largely "pine barren" and swamp, sandy, acidic soil under scrub pine that grows trees but starves row crops, the freedpeople had no capital to clear and work it anyway, and the act was a near-total failure, repealed in 1876.

So what filled the space where land should have been is the system Chapter 3 laid out in full, sharecropping chained to the crop-lien, and the mechanism is not worth re-explaining; what is worth doing here is looking at what it produced over time, in aggregate and in a life, because that is the part Chapter 3 could not yet show.
Take it as a life first.
A freed couple signs on to a planter's plot in 1868.
They are good farmers, they work hard, and at the first settling the merchant's ledger says they owe a little more than the crop brought.
They sign again, because the law binds them to the creditor until the debt clears and there is no other land to go to.
They are still on that plot, owing, in 1878; their children sign the contracts now; one of them dies still in debt on land the family never owned and could never buy.
That was not an unlucky case.
It was the modal outcome.

Across the cotton South, the typical cropper family did not clear its debt in a given year, and the studies that have reconstructed plantation and merchant records find that the share of Black tenant families who climbed from sharecropping to renting to owning land was small and slow, advancing barely at all in the first generation after the war.
The aggregate fact behind the individual one: in 1880, fifteen years after emancipation, the great majority of Black Southern farm families still owned no land at all and worked someone else's.
The system also locked the whole region into cotton, and the reason is mechanical and worth stating because it is not obvious.

The lien was secured against the crop, and the only crop a merchant would reliably lend against was cotton, because cotton was the dependable cash export with a price on every exchange; a cropper could not get credit to plant something else.

So the South kept planting cotton on shrinking, exhausted soil with the same hoe-and-mule labor while the wheat-and-corn North and West mechanized, the reaper and the steel plow transforming yields the cotton South had neither the capital nor the credit nor the crop-flexibility to adopt.
The region fell behind for decades, and that backwardness was a structural consequence of how emancipation was financed, not, as racist accounts claimed, of any deficiency in the land or its people.
One more institutional betrayal belongs here, briefly, because it did specific, lasting damage.

The Freedman's Savings and Trust Company, chartered in 1865, was a bank set up to receive the savings of freedpeople, and they trusted it partly because its name and its Bureau associations made it look like a federal institution, which legally it was not.

Tens of thousands of depositors put money in, individual families, Black churches, and mutual-aid societies, the dues-funded community self-help associations, common in Black life, that pooled small contributions to cover members' funerals, illness, and widows.
The bank's white trustees then steered its deposits into reckless and self-dealing speculative loans, and it failed in 1874 in the wake of the Panic of 1873 (Chapter 11).

The precise loss is often quoted as "$3 million wiped out," and the figure should be stated carefully: total deposits at failure were roughly $3 million, and depositors eventually recovered only a fraction of that over many years through slow government payouts, so the real loss to Black families was severe but not the whole sum and not instantaneous.

The lasting damage was as much to trust as to capital: a population told that thrift was the road to freedom watched the institution that held its thrift loot and bury it, a lesson that soured Black engagement with American banking for generations.

So the economic verdict of Reconstruction, settled well before the political one, was this: freedom came without the material base that would have made it defensible, because the federal government feared property redistribution more than it valued Black security, and the system that filled the gap bound the freedpeople to the land and the merchant nearly as tightly as slavery had bound them to the master, by debt instead of by deed.
Hold that, because it is why the political destruction in the second half of this book worked so completely.
A people with no economic independence is a people whose political rights can be taken, because the man who owns your land and your debt can also control, or end, your vote.
The Klan, when it came, was pushing against a structure that had already been deliberately left without a foundation.

The same trap also explains a later exodus: the persistence of the crop-lien is what made the pull of Northern factory jobs so decisive in the Great Migration, the structural cause of the Harlem Renaissance and not a spontaneous response to wartime demand (the Roaring Twenties narrative, Ch 13).

chapters.title: The Grant Years
sentences: In March 1869 the man who had won the Civil War became president, and for the first time since Lincoln the executive branch and Congress were on the same side of the open question.
The presidency of Ulysses S.
Grant is where Reconstruction's federal protection of Black rights reaches its high tide and then, across his two terms, begins the long slide that the rest of the book traces.

Getting Grant right matters more than usual, because the Dunning School needed him to be a corrupt fool and modern scholarship has substantially rehabilitated him, and the gap between those two verdicts is itself a lesson in how this history was distorted.

Grant won the 1868 election on the slogan "Let us have peace," pledged to protect Reconstruction, and the arithmetic of his victory is worth pausing on because it explains everything about why the ballot became the thing both sides would kill over.
Grant's national popular-vote margin was narrow.
The roughly 500,000 newly enfranchised Black men who voted, almost entirely for him, were plausibly the margin of his victory.

Read that the way both parties read it instantly: Black suffrage was no longer an abstract question of justice, it was now the concrete foundation of national Republican power, which meant that to Southern Democrats, suppressing the Black vote was not incidental racism, it was the entire political strategy, and to Republicans, protecting it was self-preservation.
The fight over Black voting that consumes the rest of the book is, among other things, a fight over who controls the United States, and after 1868 everyone involved understood that exactly.

The crowning constitutional act of the Grant era was the Fifteenth Amendment, ratified in February 1870, the third of the Reconstruction amendments and the completion of the "Second Founding." It forbade denying the right to vote on grounds of "race, color, or previous condition of servitude." For a few years it did exactly what it said: Black men voted across the South in enormous numbers and elected the officeholders of Chapter 7.
But the writing rules demand precision on a "first" and this is a place to be precise about a fatal flaw, because the amendment's wording is the loophole the entire collapse runs through.
The Fifteenth does not say "everyone gets to vote." It says you cannot deny the vote because of race.
It is silent on poll taxes, literacy tests, property requirements, and "good character" clauses.

A state that wanted to disenfranchise Black men could therefore, in a few years, simply do it by a different name, a poll tax and a literacy test apply to "everyone," and if they happen to fall almost entirely on Black voters, the amendment, as the Supreme Court would soon read it (Chapter 12), does not reach that.
The radicals who wanted an affirmative, positive right to vote written into the Constitution lost that fight; what passed was a narrower negative prohibition with a hole in it the size of Jim Crow.

That loophole governed disfranchisement for ninety-five years, until the Voting Rights Act of 1965 finally closed it, not by amending the Fifteenth but by giving it the enforcement machinery, federal examiners and preclearance, the 1870 Congress had refused to write (the Civil Rights Era narrative, Ch 12).

To anchor the Fifteenth as a world "first," set 1870 against the rest of the hemisphere: Brazil would not even pass its gradual Free Womb Law until 1871 and would not abolish slavery until 1888; Cuba's slavery ran to 1886; the Ottoman reform edicts had nominally equalized Christians and Jews but touched no enslaved population resembling this one.
A constitutional ban on denying the formerly enslaved the vote, in 1870, was without parallel anywhere.
And the thing that makes Reconstruction a tragedy rather than merely an unfinished project is that this was a right won and then taken back, not a right never granted.
The Fifteenth Amendment also did something the book has to be honest about because it fractured a movement: it split the women's suffrage cause, and the split ran partly along an ugly racial line.
The amendment enfranchised Black men and said nothing about women of any race.
Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Susan B.

Anthony, leaders of the women's-rights movement that had been building since before the war (Antebellum America Ch 8), opposed an amendment that enfranchised Black men while leaving all women out, and some of their rhetoric in doing so was explicitly, unattractively racist.

Lucy Stone, a veteran abolitionist and suffrage organizer who had kept her own surname on marrying as a public statement, took the opposite side: the amendment was a real advance for Black men that should not be held hostage to the demand that women be included at the same moment.
The movement split in 1869 into two rival national organizations, Stanton and Anthony's on one side and Stone's on the other, and stayed broken for two decades.
The Supreme Court soon foreclosed the legal argument that women already had the vote under the Fourteenth Amendment, ruling in Minor v.
Happersett (Chapter 12) that citizenship did not carry a right to vote, so a state could constitutionally refuse women the ballot; and in Bradwell v.
Illinois the same year it signaled that the legal subordination of women generally was not something the new amendments would disturb.
It is a case study in how a partial revolution forces bitter triage among the people it leaves out, and the book reports the racism in the suffrage split plainly rather than smoothing it over.

The Grant years are also where the wider country crowds into the frame, and the book has to widen the lens here, not as a digression but because the same army that did or did not protect freedpeople in the South was, at the same time, the army in the West, and the two operations were competing for one finite force.

In May 1869 the transcontinental railroad was completed with a golden spike at Promontory Summit, Utah, joining the coasts by rail and remaking the national economy even as the South's future was being fought over.
That railroad ran through the Plains, and the Plains were Native nations' treaty land, which sets up the parallel that matters.

Grant's "Peace Policy" toward Native nations was billed as assimilation rather than extermination, but in practice the army kept breaking treaties to clear land for the railroad and the settlers, and Native resistance to that pressure produced the war in which, in June 1876, the Lakota and Cheyenne wiped out George Custer's cavalry detachment at the Little Bighorn, the army suffering the famous defeat, not inflicting it.
Hold the two theaters side by side, because Chapter 14 turns on it.
The post-1865 U.S.

Army was small, never more than about 25,000 to 30,000 men for the entire country, and Grant's administration was running, with that one army, two simultaneous campaigns of opposite character: a campaign of conquest against Native nations in the West, which it resourced and pursued relentlessly, and a campaign of protection for Black citizens in the South, which it resourced grudgingly and would soon abandon.
The same federal power that could be found in unlimited quantity to take the Plains could not, the country would decide, be spared to hold Mississippi.
When a Southern governor's request for troops is refused in 1875 (Chapter 14), part of the answer to "why" is that the troops, and the political will to use them, were going west.

And the first of the scandals that would corrode Grant's standing arrived early: the 1869 Black Friday gold-corner scheme, in which speculators tried to manipulate the gold market partly through Grant's brother-in-law.
Hold the scandals; Chapter 11 is their reckoning.

The point for now is that Grant himself was never shown to have stolen anything, the modern consensus is that he was personally honest and a poor judge of friends, but the wave of corruption around his administration would do real political damage to the cause he genuinely meant to protect, by handing its enemies the argument that the party of Reconstruction was rotten.
So by the early 1870s the picture is, briefly, at its best: three amendments in place, a sympathetic president, Black men voting and governing across the South, the institutions of Chapter 7 rising.

And it was, at that exact moment, under sustained armed attack, by an organization that had been founded the year the war ended and had grown into something the United States had no prior category for, a paramilitary terrorist insurgency aimed at destroying multiracial democracy by murder. (The mid-nineteenth century did know mass political violence: in the very same year the Klan trials began, 1871, the French government drowned the Paris Commune in the blood of thousands of summarily executed civilians.

But that was a state crushing a radical city; the Klan was the inverse, a stateless insurgency murdering to overthrow an elected biracial government, which is closer to genuinely new.) That is the next chapter, and it is the hinge of the book.

chapters.title: The Klan Wars
sentences: This is the chapter where the book has to name plainly what most of its second half is about: organized terrorism.
The destruction of Reconstruction was not an organic political tide.

It was, in significant and documented part, a sustained campaign of murder, arson, rape, and assassination, waged by paramilitary organizations against Black voters, Black officeholders, white Republicans, schools, and churches, with the political objective of overthrowing elected governments and ending Black political participation by force.
The book uses the word "terrorism" deliberately and accurately: the violence was organized, political, and designed to terrify a population out of exercising rights it legally held.

This chapter is the first and most famous of those organizations, the Ku Klux Klan, and, just as importantly, the proof, supplied by the federal government itself in 1871, that the terror could be stopped when the government chose to stop it.
The Klan's origin is almost absurdly small against what it became, and the smallness is itself instructive.

In late 1865 or early 1866, in Pulaski, Tennessee, a handful of bored young Confederate veterans, the founding lore says six, though that tidy number comes from the Klan's own later mythmaking and should be held loosely, started a social club.
They took the Greek word kuklos, "circle," roughed it into the deliberately strange "Ku Klux," tacked on "Klan" for the alliteration, and gave themselves nonsensical titles and outlandish costumes.
Within about two years it had metastasized, across the South, into a decentralized network of local "dens" coordinating through ritual, disguise, and night-riding.

Its probable first national leader was the former Confederate cavalry general Nathan Bedford Forrest, a name worth knowing in full: a self-made slave trader before the war, a feared and brilliant cavalry commander during it, and the officer in command at the 1864 Fort Pillow massacre, where surrendering Black Union soldiers were killed, so the man who most likely led the first Klan brought to it a documented record of killing Black soldiers who had laid down their arms.
His exact role as "Grand Wizard" is historically disputed, which is why the text says "probable," but the trajectory is not.
Its decentralization was not a weakness; it was the design feature that made it deadly and deniable.

There was no single command to decapitate, no membership list to seize; it was a method and a costume as much as an organization, which is exactly why state governments, even Republican ones with Black majorities, found it nearly impossible to suppress with ordinary policing.
Local sheriffs were often members or sympathizers; juries would not convict; witnesses who testified were murdered.

What the Klan actually did is documented in extraordinary, sworn detail, and the book should lean on that, because the existence of the documentation is itself the rebuttal to fifty years of minimizing it.
In 1871 a joint committee of Congress took thousands of pages of testimony and published a thirteen-volume report on Klan violence across the South.

As a sworn, first-person, government-compiled record specifically of organized insurgent terror aimed at destroying an electoral democracy, it has few rivals anywhere; the great atrocity records of the same era, the British famine commissions in India, the later testimony on the Congo rubber regime, document state or corporate violence against subject peoples, not a paramilitary war on a functioning multiracial franchise, which makes the Klan report unusual in kind, not just in volume.

It contains whippings, mutilations, rapes, the burning of schools and churches, and the targeted assassination of Black political leaders and white Republican officials, told under oath by victims and witnesses.
The Klan's targets were not random; they were strategic.

It went after exactly the people and institutions that made Black political power possible: Black men who voted or organized others to, Black officeholders and the white Republicans allied with them, the teachers in the freedmen's schools (Chapter 7), the schools and churches themselves.
Black Union veterans, an organized, politically conscious cohort (Chapter 1), were a particular target.
The violence spiked, predictably and by design, around elections.
This was not racial hatred venting at random.
It was a coordinated program to dismantle the electoral foundation of Reconstruction county by county, and in many places, by 1870, it was working.
Now the part of the chapter that matters most for the book's central argument, because it is the proof of the thesis.
Faced with an open insurgency the states could not suppress, the federal government, in 1870–71, did something unprecedented: it made private terrorism a federal matter and brought the army to bear.
Congress passed three Enforcement Acts.
The first (1870) made it a federal crime to use force or intimidation to deny citizens the vote.
The second (1871) put elections under federal supervision.
The third, the Ku Klux Klan Act of April 1871, was the strongest: it let the president use the army against conspiracies to deny civil rights and suspend habeas corpus to do it.

Define habeas corpus, because the suspension is the whole point: it is the ancient legal right that forces the government to bring an arrested person before a court and justify holding them, the core protection against being locked up without trial; suspending it lets the government detain suspected insurgents without immediately charging them, an extraordinary power the Constitution permits only in cases of rebellion.
Congress, in 1871, formally classified Klan terror as a rebellion against the United States.
One institutional fact in this sequence deserves its own paragraph, because it is the book's voice at its sharpest and it is genuinely almost never taught.
In 1870 Congress created the Department of Justice itself.

The federal government had had an attorney general since 1789 but no department, no organized national legal arm, and the immediate reason it built one in 1870 was, in significant part, to give Washington the lawyers and marshals it needed to prosecute the Klan.
The agency Americans now associate with everything from antitrust to terrorism was, at its founding, a Reconstruction civil-rights enforcement bureau.

No other major government in the world in 1870 had a ministry with that purpose: the British Home Office had no civil-rights remit, the French Ministry of Justice no charge to protect a racial minority from its own neighbors.
The United States built one, used it, and then spent a century forgetting why it had.
And then Grant used the powers.
In October 1871 he suspended habeas corpus in nine South Carolina counties where the Klan was thickest, and federal marshals and troops arrested hundreds of Klansmen.
Federal prosecutors brought thousands of indictments and won hundreds of convictions across the South in 1871–72.
The effect was immediate and dramatic: the first Klan, as an organized force, was broken.
It collapsed as a coherent organization by about 1872, and the 1872 elections across the South were comparatively peaceful, the calmest of the era.
Stop on that, because it is the load-bearing fact of the entire book.
The terror was not an unstoppable force of nature.

When the federal government chose to treat it as the armed insurrection it was, deployed prosecutors and troops, suspended habeas corpus, and sustained the effort, the terror dropped sharply and Black Southerners voted.

The pattern across the whole era is consistent and it is the strongest evidence for this book's thesis: where federal enforcement was energetic, the violence fell and Reconstruction functioned; where federal enforcement was withdrawn, the violence surged and Reconstruction fell.
The 1871 Klan trials are the clean experiment.
They prove that what happened next, the surrender, the collapse, the abandonment, was not because the problem was unsolvable.
It was solvable, and had just been solved, on a limited scale, in South Carolina in 1872.
What changed was not the South's capacity for terror.
What changed was the North's willingness to keep paying the price to stop it, and the reasons it stopped are the next chapter.

The same principle runs through the Second Reconstruction in both directions: federal enforcement pushed by the movement eventually broke the terror, while federal inaction prolonged it (the Civil Rights Era narrative, Chs 9 and 15).

chapters.title: The North Loses Interest
sentences: The single most important thing to understand about why Reconstruction was abandoned is that it was abandoned, not lost.
Chapter 10 just demonstrated that the federal government had, by 1872, the legal tools, the proven method, and a recent success in suppressing the terror.
What it lost over the next five years was not capacity.
It was will.

This chapter is about why the Northern public and political class, having paid in 750,000 lives to win the war and then mounted the most aggressive federal intervention in the country's history to secure its result, got tired and looked away.

The reasons are not flattering and the book should not flatter them: corruption, exhaustion, racism that had never gone away, and, decisively, an economic catastrophe that made Northern voters care about their own ruin far more than about Black Southerners' rights.
Start with the corruption, because it did specific damage to the moral standing of the cause.

The Grant era coincided with the Gilded Age, the era Mark Twain mockingly named for a society that was gold-plated, not gold, glittering and rotten underneath, and the scandals came in a relentless drumbeat.

The Crédit Mobilier scandal, exposed in 1872, revealed that insiders of the Union Pacific railroad had skimmed enormous construction profits and spread discounted stock among congressmen to buy goodwill, the recipients including the sitting vice president, Schuyler Colfax, and a future president, James Garfield.

The Whiskey Ring (1875) exposed federal officials and distillers diverting millions in liquor taxes, the conspiracy reaching Grant's own private secretary, Orville Babcock, the private secretary being roughly the era's equivalent of a White House chief of staff, the president's closest day-to-day aide.
The Belknap affair (1876) caught the secretary of war taking kickbacks on military trading posts; he resigned minutes before the House impeached him.
The Sanborn contracts, the Black Friday gold corner (Chapter 9), the looting of the Freedman's Bank (Chapter 8), the litany was constant.
Grant himself was never shown to have profited, the consensus is that he was personally honest and disastrously loyal to crooked friends, but that distinction was lost on the public.

The effect that matters for this book is specific: the party of Lincoln, the party of Reconstruction, the party that asked the North to keep spending blood and treasure to protect Black rights in the South on a moral argument, was now nationally synonymous with graft.
It is very hard to sustain a costly moral crusade abroad, or in this case in the South, when the crusading party is being exposed as corrupt at home every few months.
The scandals did not change anyone's view of racial justice directly.
They drained the moral authority of the only institution defending it.
That drain produced an open revolt inside the party, and the revolt revealed how much of the North simply wanted to be done.

In 1872 a faction of reform-minded Republicans, disgusted by Grant-era corruption and openly weary of the "Southern question," bolted as the Liberal Republicans, nominating the editor Horace Greeley, who was also endorsed by the Democrats.
Grant crushed them and won a second term decisively.
But the content of the revolt mattered more than its defeat.

A significant, respectable slice of the Republican coalition, the educated, reforming Northern elite, had announced that it considered Reconstruction a tiresome, corrupting, and probably failed project that the country should wind down.

They dressed this up in the language of "reconciliation" and "home rule" and "letting the South manage its own affairs," and the racism underneath the genteel language was real and only lightly buried: "home rule" meant white rule, and a great many Northerners were, by the early 1870s, perfectly willing to say so. (This was not a uniquely American exhaustion.

In Britain in exactly these years Gladstone's great reforming Liberal ministry of 1868–74 ran out of moral energy and fell, in 1874, to a combined assault of scandal and economic strain, the same pattern, a reform coalition spent and turned out by corruption and hard times, which suggests a structural dynamic, not just American bad luck.) The 1872 Amnesty Act restored political rights to most of the roughly 150,000 ex-Confederates still barred under the Fourteenth Amendment, and that number needs calibration: it was not 150,000 statesmen but the broad pool of former officeholders and officers, from which the South now drew back its experienced white Democratic leadership at exactly the moment Northern enthusiasm for enforcement was draining, a gift to the counter-revolution timed almost perfectly to its needs.
And then came the thing that decided it: the economy collapsed.

The crash actually began in Vienna in May 1873 and rolled west across Europe before it reached America; in September the major banking house of Jay Cooke & Company, overextended in railroad finance, failed and set off the Panic of 1873, which became the Long Depression, by some measures the longest economic contraction in American history, deep unemployment and falling wages persisting until roughly 1879.

This was a global depression, hammering Austria-Hungary, Germany, and Britain at the same time, which matters here because it drained the surplus attention and money that protecting Reconstruction required everywhere at once.
Run the political consequence, because it is the mechanism by which an economic event ended a civil-rights era.

A Northern factory worker or farmer in 1874, out of work or watching wages fall, banks failing and savings gone, was being asked to keep paying for the expensive deployment of the army to protect the voting rights of Black people a thousand miles away.
The depression made that ask politically impossible.

National attention swung hard to jobs, debt, the railroads, and above all the money question, the bitter fight over greenbacks versus the gold standard: greenbacks were the paper dollars the government had printed during the war, not backed by gold, and debtors, farmers, and many workers wanted more of them, because more money in circulation meant easier credit and rising prices that made fixed debts lighter, while creditors and banks wanted a return to the gold standard, every dollar redeemable for a fixed weight of gold, which meant scarcer money, tighter credit, and debts that held their full value.
It was, underneath the technical language, a fight over who absorbed the depression's pain, and to a ruined Northern voter in 1874 it was vastly more pressing than the South.
In the 1874 midterms, with the depression at its worst and the scandals fresh, the Democrats captured the House of Representatives for the first time since before the war.

That single election ended Congressional Reconstruction as a legislative engine: with the House in Democratic hands, no new enforcement legislation could pass, and the appropriations to fund the troops and prosecutors already authorized could be, and were, choked off.
After 1874 the federal government still had the laws of Chapter 10 on the books.
It simply stopped funding and using them.
So picture the actual end of it, because it did not look like a surrender; it looked like a clerk closing a file.

In the South Carolina up-country in 1872 federal prosecutors had filled dockets with Klan indictments; two years later the appropriations were gone, the marshals were not hired, the cases were not brought, and the men who had been afraid to ride in 1872 understood, correctly, that no one was coming.
The North had not been beaten in the field.

It had read its own ledger and decided the line item was too expensive, and turned back to its banks and its railroads, and left the South's Republicans, Black and white, alone in the dark with the people who had spent ten years promising to kill them.
What those people did once they were certain no one would stop them is the next two chapters.

chapters.title: The Supreme Court Disarms the Constitution
sentences: While the political will was draining (Chapter 11), a parallel and equally decisive thing was happening in a marble building in Washington, and it gets its own chapter because Americans are often taught Reconstruction was killed only by bayonets and bargains and not also, just as fatally, by judges.

The Supreme Court, between 1873 and 1876, took the three amendments of the "Second Founding" and read them so narrowly that the federal laws meant to enforce them were left, in practice, nearly powerless.
By the time the troops were withdrawn (Chapter 15), the constitutional weapons were already broken.
This chapter is that breaking, and it has to be precise, because the reasoning is the thing that did the damage and the reasoning outlived everyone involved.
Begin with the first cut, the Slaughter-House Cases of 1873, because it is technical and unglamorous and that is exactly why it was so destructive.
The case itself was not about race at all; it was about a Louisiana law granting a monopoly to a single New Orleans slaughterhouse, which the city's other butchers sued to overturn.

Their argument was not far-fetched at the time: the Fourteenth Amendment's sweeping language about the "privileges or immunities" of citizenship was widely read, by lawyers across the spectrum, as a broad new federal guarantee of ordinary civil rights against the states, and the butchers contended that the right to practice a lawful trade was exactly such a privilege the monopoly had taken from them.

The Court, ruling against the butchers, read the Privileges or Immunities Clause so narrowly that it protected only a tiny set of purely national rights, things like the right to travel to the capital or use navigable waters, and emphatically not the broad civil rights of citizenship against state interference.
Follow why that mattered far beyond butchers.
The drafters of the Fourteenth had loaded much of the amendment's protective force into that clause, the idea that being a U.S. citizen carried substantive rights no state could abridge.
Slaughter-House, in its first interpretation of the amendment, essentially read that clause out of the Constitution five years after it was ratified.
The protective machinery the "Second Founding" had built had its main gear removed before it was ever really used, and removed in a case the public barely noticed because it was about meatpacking.

The same Court signaled in two cases that year that the new amendments would not disturb existing hierarchies of sex either, which the book includes because the writing rules require following a "first" honestly and because it shows the limits were not only racial.
In Bradwell v.

Illinois (1873), the Court upheld Illinois's refusal to license Myra Bradwell to practice law solely because she was a woman, and one justice added a concurring opinion, a separate opinion by a judge who agrees with the result but wants to give different or additional reasons, which carries no binding force but reveals the thinking, declaring that the "paramount destiny and mission of woman" was wife and mother, by divine design.
In Minor v.

Happersett (1875), the Court ruled unanimously that the Fourteenth Amendment's citizenship did not include a right to vote, so states could constitutionally deny the ballot to women, foreclosing the legal strategy of the suffrage movement (Chapter 9) until the Nineteenth Amendment in 1920.
The new constitutional language of equality, the Court was establishing, would be read as narrowly as the justices could manage.

Now the cases that did the lethal damage to Black Reconstruction specifically, and they grow directly out of an atrocity this book covers fully in the next chapter, so meet it here only as the legal seed.
On Easter Sunday 1873, a white mob in Colfax, Louisiana, massacred a large number of Black men, many after they had surrendered, in a dispute over a contested election (Chapter 13).
Federal prosecutors, using the Enforcement Acts of Chapter 10, charged the perpetrators.
The case reached the Supreme Court as United States v.
Cruikshank, decided in 1876, and the holding is the single most consequential sentence in the legal destruction of Reconstruction, so understand it exactly.
The Court held that the Fourteenth Amendment restrains only states, not private individuals.

A state government may not deny equal protection; but a private mob murdering a hundred Black citizens is not "the state," and therefore, the Court reasoned, the federal government had no constitutional power to prosecute them, that was the job of Louisiana, the very state whose white population had just done the murdering.
The federal convictions of the Colfax killers were thrown out.
Decided the same term, United States v.

Reese arose when two Kentucky election officials refused to let a Black man, William Garner, vote and were prosecuted under the Enforcement Acts; the Court struck down the key sections those officials were charged under and held that the Fifteenth Amendment did not confer a right to vote but only barred denial on a few named grounds, leaving poll taxes and literacy tests, exactly the future tools of mass disfranchisement, untouched.
Sit with what Cruikshank and Reese together accomplished, because it is the legal hinge of the book's second half.

The federal government's entire toolkit for protecting Black Southerners, the Enforcement Acts, the Klan Act, federal prosecution of terrorists, depended on the federal government being able to reach private violence, because that is what the terror was: private mobs, not formal state action.
Cruikshank held that it could not.

In a single ruling, the Supreme Court informed every white paramilitary in the South that a sufficiently "private" massacre was beyond federal reach, and informed every federal prosecutor that the laws of Chapter 10 had just been judicially disarmed.
The Court did not need to strike the amendments down.

It simply read them so that the violence destroying Reconstruction fell precisely into the gap between what the amendments forbade (state action) and what was actually happening (private terror), and then announced that the gap was constitutional.
The bayonets had not yet been withdrawn (Chapter 15); the Court had already taken the ammunition.

None of this required striking the amendments down, and that is the point worth holding: courts have a recurring habit, well documented in this same period in Britain and across its empire, of leaving an ambitious reform statute formally on the books while interpreting it so narrowly that it loses its force, so what the Supreme Court did to the Fourteenth Amendment was a severe instance of a known judicial pattern, not a uniquely American act of bad faith.

Now walk the rest of the line in one breath, because the chapter's job is to show the architecture complete. 1873, Slaughter-House guts the Privileges or Immunities Clause. 1876, Cruikshank puts private terror beyond federal reach and Reese opens the door to poll taxes and literacy tests. 1883, the Civil Rights Cases strike down the 1875 federal law that had guaranteed Black citizens equal access to inns, theaters, and railcars (Chapter 15), ruling that Congress could bar discrimination by states but not by private businesses. 1896, Plessy v.
Ferguson completes it, upholding a Louisiana railcar-segregation law under the formula "separate but equal" and thereby constitutionalizing Jim Crow outright.
From the meatpacking case to "separate but equal" is twenty-three years and four decisions, and the line through them is straight.

The full Plessy story belongs to a later narrative in this chain, but the legal spine is built here: the "Second Founding" was hollowed out, clause by clause, while every word of it stayed on the page.

chapters.title: Redemption
sentences: Now the counter-revolution in the field, with the political will gone (Chapter 11) and the courts having disarmed the law (Chapter 12).
The white South's recapture of its state governments has a name its perpetrators gave it and were proud of: Redemption.
The word is theological and was meant to be, the white South cast itself as a fallen people redeemed from the sin of Black and Republican government, "Redeemers" as saviors.

This book uses the word because it is the historical term, while being exact about what the Redemption actually consisted of: the violent overthrow, state by state, of elected governments by organized paramilitaries, after the federal government stopped resisting.
This chapter is the open, armed phase, roughly 1873 to 1875, when the terror stopped wearing hoods and started wearing uniforms.
The change from the Klan to what replaced it is the key to the chapter and easy to miss.
The first Klan (Chapter 10) was secret, disguised, deniable, and it had been broken by federal prosecution in 1871–72.
What rose in its place after 1873 was different and more dangerous precisely because it was not secret.
The White League, formed openly in Louisiana in 1874, did not wear hoods.
It drilled in the open, in uniform, as the avowed paramilitary arm of the Democratic Party, with the publicly stated goal of overthrowing the Republican state government by force.
So did the rifle clubs and the South Carolina Red Shirts (Chapter 15).

The shift from hood to uniform is a precise index of the collapse of federal will: the Klan hid because in 1871 the federal government would prosecute it; the White League did not bother to hide because by 1874 it had correctly judged that the federal government would not.
Open paramilitarism is what terror looks like once it has concluded it is safe, and that conclusion was a direct reading of Washington's retreat.

The atrocities of this phase are not a list to skim; the book has to make you see at least the central one, because it is the one that became the Supreme Court case that ended federal protection (Chapter 12).

On Easter Sunday, April 13, 1873, in Colfax, Louisiana, in the aftermath of a violently disputed state election, a white mob with cannon attacked a group of Black men, many of them militia and freedmen, who had gathered to defend the parish courthouse.
The defenders were overwhelmed; the killing did not stop when they surrendered.

The death toll is genuinely uncertain and the honest range is wide for a specific reason, the killers kept no count and disposed of bodies; older and advocacy accounts run as high as 150, while the most careful modern reconstructions, including LeeAnna Keith's study of the massacre, settle nearer 60 to 100, most of them executed after laying down their arms.
By any of those figures it is the deadliest single act of racial violence of the entire Reconstruction era, the Colfax massacre.
Of the dozens charged, only a handful were tried, three convicted, and all convictions were thrown out by the Supreme Court in Cruikshank (Chapter 12).
A massacre of that scale producing zero punishment was itself a message, broadcast across the South, that organized mass killing of Black citizens would be tolerated.

The following year the White League gave the message an exclamation point: at Coushatta, Louisiana, in August 1874, it forced six white Republican officials to resign and then murdered them, along with Black witnesses, the killing of white officeholders signaling that the counter-revolution was now total.

A month later, in September 1874, a White League force, contemporary estimates run loosely around several thousand, defeated the New Orleans police and state militia in open street battle, the Battle of Liberty Place, and held the Louisiana statehouse for three days.
It was an outright armed coup against a state government, and what reversed it is the telling part: the League did not lose the fight, it stood down.
President Grant ordered federal troops to New Orleans, and on word that the U.S.

Army was coming the League simply withdrew and handed the building back, the Republican government restored not by combat but by the mere announced approach of federal soldiers, a measure of how much the army's presence still meant in 1874 and how much its absence would mean a year later.

Louisiana by now had rival governors and rival legislatures, two competing claimants to each, because the violently disputed elections had produced parallel sets of "winners," each with its own certification, and the federal government had to choose which to recognize and back with troops; that unresolved doubleness made the state the era's worst case of contested legitimacy and the laboratory of the violence.
Watch the map go dark, because Redemption was a sequence, not an event, and the sequence is the argument.
The border and upper South went first and earliest, Tennessee, Virginia, sometimes through less spectacular means.
Then, as the depression and the scandals (Chapter 11) drained Northern will through 1873–74, the deep South began to fall to open force.
Each state "redeemed" narrowed the territory where federal protection still reached and emboldened the paramilitaries in the states not yet taken.
By the end of 1874 the Democrats had also taken the U.S.
House (Chapter 11), so there was no longer a Washington majority that wanted to stop the sequence even if a president tried.

The pattern in the field exactly matched the pattern in Washington: federal commitment receding, terror advancing into the vacuum, in lockstep, the red of Redemption spreading precisely as fast as the federal government chose to stop resisting it, and never faster.
Stand, for a moment, where it actually landed.

A Black state legislator in 1874, a man who six years earlier had cast the first vote of his life and then helped write his state's constitution, could now read the sequence the way his enemies did: he could watch the neighboring state fall, see the federal garrison thin, hear the rifle clubs drilling openly in the next county, and know with precision that the floor was being removed under him one plank at a time, by men in Washington he would never meet, for reasons that had nothing to do with anything he had done.
The terror was advancing, but the thing that made it unanswerable was not the terror.
It was the silence behind it.

He had been promised the protection of the strongest government on the continent, and he could feel it being withdrawn in real time, deliberately, while every word of the promise remained in the Constitution.
That is the experience Redemption actually was for the people inside it: not a battle lost but a guarantor walking away.
And the coldest single demonstration of that, an entire state lost not because it could not be held but because Washington decided, in writing, not to hold it, came in Mississippi the next year.

chapters.title: The Mississippi Plan
sentences: Mississippi in 1875 gets a chapter to itself because it is the cleanest single proof of this book's central claim, that Reconstruction's collapse was a choice, not an inevitability.

In Mississippi the white Democracy openly designed, named, executed, and documented a method for overthrowing an elected government by terror; the Republican governor asked the federal government for the troops that had worked everywhere they were used (Chapter 10); and the federal government, for stated reasons, said no.
Everything ambiguous about the rest of the era is unambiguous here.
You can watch the decision get made.

The stakes are the demographic fact this book has already established: Mississippi had a Black majority, and so in any honest election it was a Republican state, and it had been governing as one, with Black legislators and officials, the two Black U.S. senators of Chapter 7, and a reform Republican governor, Adelbert Ames, a Union general from Maine, honest, committed, and serious.
To the white Democracy a functioning Black-majority democracy was both intolerable and, because of the arithmetic, unbeatable at an honest ballot box.
So they decided not to do it honestly, and, unusually, they wrote down how.
The Mississippi Plan of 1875 was a strategy, discussed openly in the Democratic press, with three coordinated components.

First, economic coercion: Black sharecroppers and laborers were told, by the men who controlled their land, debt, and jobs (Chapter 8), that voting Republican meant eviction, firing, and the merchant calling the lien, the structural propertylessness of Chapter 8 weaponized directly into vote control.

Second, open paramilitary violence: armed white "rifle clubs" broke up Republican meetings by force, paraded with cannon to intimidate Black communities, and assassinated local Black leaders, with massacres at Clinton and Vicksburg killing dozens to hundreds.

Third, and this is the chillingly modern part, deniable provocation: the rifle clubs were instructed to be the visible armed force while provoking Republicans into any act that could be framed as "Black violence" justifying the white "self-defense," a propaganda overlay that let the Northern press and public look away by pretending the aggressor and victim were unclear when they were not.
It was a designed system for stealing a state, and its designers were not embarrassed by it; they regarded it as a triumph and exported it.
Now the decision, which is the whole reason this chapter exists.

As the terror mounted through the summer and fall of 1875, Governor Ames did exactly what the law of Chapter 10 contemplated: he asked President Grant for federal troops to suppress what was, by any honest description, an armed insurrection against a state government, the same kind of insurrection that federal force had broken in South Carolina in 1871.
And the Grant administration refused.

The refusal was put in writing, and the stated reason survives in Attorney General Edwards Pierrepont's own words, conveyed to Mississippi's appeals: "the whole public are tired out with these annual autumnal outbreaks in the South." The phrase is genuine and appears in the documentary record of the episode; the further reasoning, that sending troops would cost the Republicans the pivotal Northern state of Ohio in that fall's election, is the well-attested political calculation behind the decision, drawn from the administration's own correspondence and contemporaries' accounts rather than from that single sentence.
Read what the concession amounts to.
It does not say the violence was not happening, or that troops would not work, the 1871 precedent of Chapter 10 had already proven they would.

It says, in plain administrative prose, that the Northern public was tired, and that the political cost of acting, in Ohio, in an off-year election, outweighed the value of a Black-majority state's democracy.
Mississippi was not lost because it could not be held.
It was conceded, deliberately, for stated reasons of Northern political convenience, by the administration that had the tools and the proof that the tools worked, sitting in a desk drawer.
The result followed instantly.

With no federal troops coming, and the small standing army of perhaps 25,000 men already committed to the Plains wars in the West rather than the South (Chapter 9), the Mississippi Plan worked exactly as designed.

The 1875 elections were a rout achieved by terror; Black turnout collapsed under the guns and the economic threat; the legislature flipped to the Democrats, who then forced Governor Ames out in 1876 by threatening impeachment on trumped-up charges, a sham in the sense that the accusations were political pretexts manufactured to remove a governor the new majority could not legally fault, and Ames resigned in a bargain to have them dropped rather than fight a rigged trial.
He left the state.

He lived until 1933, which is long enough that he watched the very beginnings of the historians' turn against the Dunning version, the first scholarly challenges to it were appearing in the 1920s and early 1930s, and an aged Ames, asked about Reconstruction late in life, called its defeat what it was: a national crime, in which he had been abandoned.
Mississippi became the template, written down, refined, and copied.
South Carolina's Redeemers studied it for 1876 (Chapter 15).

And it became, two decades later, the literal model for the disfranchisement constitutions, beginning with Mississippi's own in 1890, that wrote Black voting out of the South entirely through the loopholes the Supreme Court had blessed (Chapter 12).

The Mississippi Plan is the book's thesis reduced to a single state and a single refused request: the machinery to defend multiracial democracy existed and had been proven to work, and the federal government, asked to use it, chose, in writing, to be tired instead.

chapters.title: The Bargain
sentences: By 1876 only three Southern states still had Republican governments propped up by a remaining federal military presence: Louisiana, South Carolina, and Florida.

Everything else had been "redeemed." This chapter is how the last three fell, and the mechanism is fitting for a book whose thesis is that Reconstruction was traded away rather than lost: it ended not with a battle but with a backroom deal, born out of a presidential election so close and so corrupted that the country had no agreed way to decide who had won, and resolved by a bargain in which the presidency was exchanged for the abandonment of the freedpeople.
First the field, because the last three states were not handed over; they were taken, in the open, and the reader should feel that before the bargain that ratified it.
South Carolina, like Mississippi, was a Black-majority state, and in 1876 its Democrats ran the Mississippi Plan with local refinements.

Their paramilitaries were the Red Shirts, who, like the White League, did not bother to hide; they wore literal Red Shirts as a uniform and a taunt, parading behind the ex-Confederate cavalry general Wade Hampton III, the Democratic candidate for governor, in a campaign that fused torchlit parades, economic threats, and murder into open political theater.
It opened with the Hamburg massacre in July 1876.

Hamburg was a small, almost entirely Black town on the Savannah River, just across from Georgia, governed and policed by Black officials; a Red Shirt force, using a trivial road-right-of-way dispute as the pretext the Mississippi Plan's playbook called for, surrounded the town's Black militia in their armory, shelled it with a cannon brought from Georgia, and after the militiamen surrendered, selected several and executed them one by one in the night, calling out names.
The Ellenton killings, weeks of hunting that left dozens of Black residents dead, extended it.
This was not the prelude to the campaign; it was the campaign, the Mississippi Plan with a wardrobe and a body count, and it worked.

By election day South Carolina, like Louisiana and Florida, had been terrorized to the edge of, or past, a Democratic result, while the Republican state governments and federal observers contested the count.
The same violence was producing the same disputed returns in all three remaining states at once.
Now the national crisis, and you have to understand the constitutional gap to see why it became a bargain.
The 1876 presidential election pitted Republican Rutherford B.
Hayes against Democrat Samuel Tilden.
Tilden won the national popular vote outright and led the electoral count, sitting one electoral vote short of the presidency.
