The presidency turned on exactly the three unredeemed states, Louisiana, South Carolina, Florida, where the returns were genuinely disputed because the elections had been conducted amid organized terror and Republican election boards then threw out tainted returns, producing two sets of certified electoral votes from each of the three states, one Democratic, one Republican.

Here is the constitutional problem the framers had not solved: the Constitution says electoral votes are counted before Congress, but it does not say who decides when a state sends two contradictory slates.
There was no agreed mechanism.

With a Democratic House and a Republican Senate, the two chambers could not agree, and the country drifted, through the winter of 1876–77, toward March 4 with no president-elect and loose talk of a second civil war.
The improvised resolution and the deal hidden inside it are the end of Reconstruction.
Congress created a special Electoral Commission of fifteen to decide the disputed votes: five senators, five representatives, five Supreme Court justices.
The party math was deliberately built to look balanced.

The Republican Senate supplied three Republicans and two Democrats; the Democratic House supplied three Democrats and two Republicans; that left the five justices, and the design was four justices of known leaning, two from each party, plus a fifth, independent-leaning justice, David Davis, as the true swing vote.
Then Davis was unexpectedly elected to the Senate and stepped off the commission, and the only remaining justices to replace him leaned Republican.

With his exit the panel was, in effect, eight Republicans to seven Democrats, and it then awarded every single disputed electoral vote, in all three states, to Hayes, on straight 8–7 party-line votes, making Hayes president by exactly one electoral vote, the bare 185 to 184.
The 8–7 was not a coincidence of fifteen honest judgments; it was the arithmetic the commission was, by accident and then by design, constructed to produce.
A result that nakedly partisan, overturning the popular-vote winner, could not have been imposed on a furious Democratic House by procedure alone.

What made the Democrats acquiesce instead of blocking it was an informal understanding negotiated in late-night meetings, the most famous a February 1877 dinner at Washington's Wormley Hotel, a leading hotel owned by James Wormley, a wealthy free Black Washingtonian, so that the deal abandoning Black Southerners was, with a bitterness contemporaries noted, brokered over a Black man's tablecloths.
The arrangement is known to history as the Compromise of 1877.
Be precise about what is settled and what is debated, because the distinction matters at the book's climax.
What is not in serious dispute: the troops were withdrawn, the three Republican state governments fell at once, Hayes took office, and Southern Democrats got what they wanted.

What is debated by historians is the older, tidy story that the Wormley dinner was a single decisive smoke-filled-room bargain; the newer view, which this book follows, is that the explicit deal-making mattered less than a convergence both sides had already reached, the North wanting out, the Democrats wanting the South, the Wormley meeting confirming a settlement more than creating it.

Either way the substance is the same: the Democrats let Hayes take office, and in exchange the federal government withdrew the remaining troops protecting the Republican governments of Louisiana and South Carolina, plus vague promises of Southern patronage and internal improvements.
The presidency for the abandonment of the last freedpeople still under federal protection.
That was the trade, whether sealed in one dinner or arrived at over a winter.
It was paid immediately and exactly.
In April 1877, President Hayes, mockingly called "His Fraudulency" for the manner of his election, ordered the army to stop protecting the Republican statehouses in Louisiana and South Carolina.
They collapsed within days; Wade Hampton's Redeemers took South Carolina, the Democrats took Louisiana, and every Southern state was now under the control of the white Democratic Party.
The constitutional amendments of the "Second Founding" remained, every word of them, in the Constitution.

The Civil Rights Act of 1875, a last gasp pushed through Congress as a memorial to the dying Charles Sumner, the Massachusetts Radical senator of Chapter 1, beaten nearly to death on the Senate floor before the war for denouncing slavery and unbending on Black equality to the end, guaranteed equal access to inns, theaters, and transport; it too remained on the books, unenforced, until the Supreme Court struck it down in 1883 (Chapter 12).
What ended was not the law.
What ended was the willingness to enforce it.
Reconstruction did not conclude with a repeal or a surrender ceremony.

It concluded with a backroom understanding, after which the federal government simply put its weapons down and walked away from the people it had armed the Constitution to protect, and a coda fitting for the whole story: in 1875 the state of Tennessee had sent the disgraced Andrew Johnson (Chapter 2) back to the United States Senate, the only former president to date ever to serve there, the South's verdict on the 1860s rendered by returning the man who had tried hardest to stop them.
The freedpeople were now alone with the Redeemers, the constitutional promises intact on paper and dead in fact.
What that meant, and how the country then spent fifty years lying about it, is the last chapter.

chapters.title: The Long Afterlife
sentences: A book whose thesis is that Reconstruction was defeated, not failed, owes you the aftermath, because the defeat had two parts and the second one is the part most Americans, until very recently, never learned.
The first part was the destruction of Black political power in the South, accomplished by 1877 and completed over the following two decades.

The second part, and in some ways the more remarkable historical crime, was the rewriting of the story itself, so thoroughly that for half a century the country taught its children that the people who overthrew multiracial democracy by murder had been the heroes.
This chapter is both, and the long, slow, still-incomplete reckoning with them, and the bridge into the industrial America the next narratives in this chain pick up.
Take the political afterlife first, briefly, because a later narrative in this chain tells it in full.
With federal protection withdrawn (Chapter 15), the Redeemer governments moved, over the next twenty-odd years, from controlling the South to formally writing Black citizens out of it.
The Supreme Court had already shown how (Chapter 12): the Fifteenth Amendment barred denying the vote by race but not by poll tax, literacy test, or "understanding" clause.

Beginning with Mississippi's new constitution in 1890, the old Mississippi Plan made permanent and legal, Southern states rewrote their constitutions to disfranchise Black men through exactly those race-neutral-on-paper devices, and Black voter registration in some states fell from majorities to near zero within a decade.
In 1896, in Plessy v.
Ferguson, the Court completed the arc Chapter 12 began and upheld "separate but equal," constitutionalizing the system of legally enforced segregation and subordination called Jim Crow.
The name itself is telling: it came from a grotesque white blackface minstrel character of the 1830s, a mockery turned into the label for a regime.
Jim Crow was the comprehensive legal and social order of Southern white supremacy that ran from the 1890s into the 1960s.

The constitutional amendments of the "Second Founding" were not repealed, you cannot easily repeal an amendment, they were left intact and inert, sleeping in the document for sixty years until the civil rights movement woke them up, which is the subject of a later narrative in this chain.
The single most important practical legacy of Reconstruction turned out to be that the words stayed on the page, available, when the country was finally willing to mean them again.
Now the historiographical crime, which this chain's writing rules require be confronted head-on the way the predecessor narrative confronts the Lost Cause, because they are the same project.
As the political war was won by the Redeemers, a cultural war was won alongside it.

Ex-Confederate veterans' groups and, above all, the United Daughters of the Confederacy, a women's heritage organization founded in 1894 that grew to tens of thousands of members and worked through schools, textbook-vetting committees, monument campaigns, and children's auxiliaries, promoted from the 1870s onward the Lost Cause: the doctrine that the Confederacy had fought nobly for "states' rights" rather than slavery, that slavery had been benign and the enslaved content, and that Reconstruction had been a vindictive Northern tyranny of carpetbag corruption and Black misrule from which the white South had been heroically redeemed.

This was not folklore; it was an organized memory campaign, and the closest structural parallel in modern history is the German Dolchstoßlegende, the "stab-in-the-back" myth after the First World War, which likewise recast a military defeat as betrayal by domestic enemies, rehabilitated the defeated order, blamed scapegoated minorities, and was inscribed into monuments and schoolbooks, with catastrophic results.
Defeated military establishments, barred from winning the war again, set out to win the memory of it, and the Lost Cause and the Dolchstoßlegende are near-twins in method.

The Lost Cause was inscribed physically, in the wave of Confederate monuments erected mostly during the Jim Crow decades around 1900–1920 (not, mostly, right after the war), placed deliberately on courthouse lawns as statements about who controlled public space.
And it was made academically respectable.

Around 1900–1910, the Dunning School, the Columbia historian William Dunning and his students, produced scholarly state studies that put a university imprimatur on exactly the Redeemers' version: Reconstruction as a tragic era of Black incapacity and Northern vindictiveness, rightly ended.
From there it became mass culture: D.

Griffith's enormously influential 1915 film The Birth of a Nation dramatized the Dunning story with the Klan as heroic rescuers, and it was, by general agreement among historians, the clearest case in American history of a feature film directly helping to rebuild a terrorist organization, the modern Klan revival dating from the year of its release. (That second Klan could present itself as respectable and win mainstream political power in the 1920s precisely because fifty years of Lost Cause and Dunning revisionism had prepared the cultural ground; its national rise is the subject of the Roaring Twenties narrative, Ch 10.) It was screened at the White House for President Woodrow Wilson, a Southern-born admirer of the Dunning view whose own historical writing the film quoted on its title cards; the screening itself is well documented, while the much-repeated line that Wilson called it "history written with lightning" is of doubtful provenance and probably apocryphal, so the safe statement is that Wilson, the sitting president, screened the film and his administration did nothing to distance itself from it, not that he is reliably recorded endorsing it in those famous words.

That film could incite political violence was not a uniquely American discovery, governments from Soviet Russia to Weimar Germany understood and exploited the same power of mass cinema in the same era, but Birth of a Nation is the starkest case of the art directly regrowing the organization.
For roughly fifty years, this was simply what American textbooks said.
Generations of Americans, of every region and race, were taught that the chapter you have just read happened the other way around.
The correction is itself part of the story and the book should end honest about how slow and recent it was.
The first full-scale demolition came from the people the lie was about.

Du Bois published Black Reconstruction in America, a vast, documented argument that Reconstruction had been a heroic and sabotaged democratic experiment, that the freedpeople were its agents and not its problem, and that the Dunning version was propaganda.

What the white academic mainstream did with it is itself part of the historiographical crime, and the book should not soften it: the profession did not refute Du Bois, it dismissed him, on the grounds that a Black scholar writing about Black freedom was by definition too angry, too political, too partisan to be doing real history, the exact move that had let the Dunning School pass its own propaganda off as neutral scholarship.
Black Reconstruction was, for roughly thirty years, left off the syllabus and out of the citations.

Only around the 1960s, pushed by the civil rights movement and by historians such as Kenneth Stampp, a University of California historian whose 1965 The Era of Reconstruction brought the revised view into the mainstream textbook, and John Hope Franklin, the preeminent Black American historian of the era and author of the standard survey From Slavery to Freedom, did mainstream textbooks finally abandon the Dunning interpretation, roughly a century after the events and thirty years after Du Bois had already made the case, and been ignored for making it.

Eric Foner's synthesis in the 1980s established the modern consensus this book has followed throughout: Reconstruction as "America's unfinished revolution," and the three amendments as a "Second Founding" of the republic that the original 1787 compromise with slavery had left incomplete.
Be plain about the scale of the delay, because it is the final proof of the book's thesis.
It took the United States about ninety years, from 1877 to roughly the 1960s, for its official account of Reconstruction to come back into line with what the primary sources had said all along.
That is how complete the defeat was: it was not enough to overthrow the democracy; the overthrow then captured the history of itself for three more generations.
When something in this book contradicts an older story you absorbed somewhere, this is why.
End on the bridge, because this chain continues and Reconstruction hands the country forward in a specific shape.
The same April 1877 that saw the last troops leave the South saw, weeks later, those same federal forces sent to break the Great Railroad Strike of 1877.

It was the first national strike in the sense the word had not had before: not one shop or one line walking out, but rail workers stopping trains across many states at once, in a coordinated wave, so that for the first time the federal government faced a labor action it treated as a national emergency, and answered with the army, troops firing on strikers in several cities.
The federal bayonet withdrawn from protecting freedpeople was, within weeks, leveled at workers, to protect capital against labor.

The same trade-off, coalition stability and property placed ahead of Black rights, returned in the New Deal's accommodation of the Southern bloc and in the 1964 Atlantic City compromise (the Civil Rights Era narrative, Chs 1 and 11).

The contrast with the wider world is the sharpest single illustration of what kind of choice this was: in the very same years Britain was legalizing peaceful picketing and building a lawful labor movement, while the United States, fresh from abandoning racial democracy, pivoted its coercive power straight onto industrial labor.
That pivot is the whole next era in a sentence.

With the Southern question buried, American national politics reorganized around industry, railroads, immigration, money, and the conflict between capital and labor, the era Mark Twain named the Gilded Age, and the country became, with astonishing speed, a global industrial power, even as the unfinished business of racial democracy was sealed in the basement for two generations.
And here is the last turn of the knife, the one the book has gestured at twice and should now name plainly.
The Fourteenth Amendment's words did not merely sit dormant; they were taken up and used, vigorously, for sixty years, just not for the people they were written for.

Between roughly 1877 and the late 1930s, the clause drafted to shield freedpeople from hostile states was wielded overwhelmingly by corporations, which the courts treated as "persons," to strike down railroad regulation, wage and hour laws, and other protections of actual workers.
The single most successful litigant under the freedpeople's amendment, for two generations, was the business corporation.

Only in the 1930s did a sustained campaign, the NAACP's long, deliberate litigation strategy, begin reclaiming the Fourteenth for its original purpose, the work a later narrative in this chain takes up as its central drama, from Brown v.
Board in 1954 to the Voting Rights Act of 1965 (the Civil Rights Era narrative, Chs 2 and 12).

So the constitutional tools forged in these twelve years sat in the document the whole time, available but turned to other uses, until the civil rights movement of the twentieth century reopened the question this book has been about, what does freedom mean for the people slavery freed.
It did not have to invent new constitutional language.
It reached back and picked up the language written here, in the 1860s, by a Congress and a generation of freedpeople who had answered the question correctly and been defeated for it.
That is why this is called the unfinished revolution, and why the next narratives in this chain are, in a real sense, still the same story.

chapters.title: The Word and the Wreckage
sentences: Start with the label, because it is selling you something.

"The Roaring Twenties." Say it and you already see the picture: a flapper with bobbed hair doing the Charleston (the era's frantic, kicking signature dance, Chapter 14) on a speakeasy table, a Model T, a stock ticker, Gatsby's parties, jazz.

It is one of the most successful brand names any decade ever got, and it was applied, like a movie poster, after the show was over, mostly in the 1930s and after, by people looking back at the years before the Great Depression with a mixture of envy and a hangover.
That is the first thing to be suspicious of.
The people living through 1918, 1919, and 1920 did not feel like they were roaring.
They were burying flu victims, striking against wage cuts, dodging deportation, and in some American cities being burned out of their homes by mobs.
The decade did eventually produce a real, world-changing boom.

But the name flattens eleven very different years into one cocktail party, and it flattens out, almost entirely, the roughly half of the country the party never reached, the farm, the mill town, the mine, and the Jim Crow South (Chapter 5 sets out exactly who and why).
Hold the suspicion.
"Roaring" is a real description of part of this decade for part of this country, and it is also a piece of nostalgia doing a job, and this book will keep telling you which is which.

One blanket caveat, because this book makes a lot of "first" claims (the first broadcast nation, the first mass consumer economy, the first modern celebrity): "first" here means "first at national scale" or "first in the form we'd recognize," not first ever anywhere.
Radio existed before KDKA, cars before the Model T, fame before Lindbergh; what changed was scale, speed, and reach.
Chapter 5 takes up the biggest of these claims and names who was second.
Now the bridge, because there is a forty-year hole between the end of the last narrative and the start of this one, and you need it filled in or nothing here makes sense.
This is the recap, and it is a long one, but it is the only one.
The story before this story ends in 1877, when Reconstruction collapsed.

Reconstruction is the subject of the narrative that comes right before this one in the chain, so the compressed version: after the Civil War (Antebellum America), the federal government spent about a decade trying, with real but incomplete commitment, to remake the defeated South into a place where the four million people freed from slavery could be citizens, vote, own land, and be safe.
The Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments wrote birthright citizenship and Black male suffrage into the Constitution.

For roughly a decade this was not a paper promise but a working, if embattled, multiracial democracy: Black men voted across the South in large numbers, held legislative seats, and built their own churches, schools, and fraternal orders.
It was not abandoned so much as overthrown.

Organized white paramilitary violence (the first Ku Klux Klan, then the rifle clubs and the White League) systematically murdered Black officeholders and voters while the Supreme Court gutted the federal laws meant to stop it, and a disputed presidential election in 1876 was settled by a bargain in which the last federal troops were withdrawn from the South in 1877.

The Reconstruction narrative tells this as the deliberate, violent counter-revolution it was, and that distinction matters here: Jim Crow was not what the South always was, it was what a defeated experiment was replaced with by force.

With that, the South was handed back to its white ruling class, who spent the next quarter-century building the system this book calls Jim Crow and will keep calling Jim Crow: a body of state laws and customs that segregated nearly everything by race, stripped Black men of the vote they had constitutionally been guaranteed (through poll taxes; "literacy" tests on which a white registrar, who alone judged the answers, could pass an illiterate white applicant and fail a Black college graduate at will; and outright violence), locked Black Southerners into sharecropping (a form of farm tenancy that kept the cropper perpetually in debt to the white landowner), and enforced the whole arrangement with lynching, extrajudicial murder, usually by hanging or burning, often public, of which there were thousands between the 1880s and the 1920s.
The Supreme Court blessed it: in 1896 it ruled, in Plessy v.
Ferguson, that "separate but equal" facilities were constitutional, which made segregation the law of the land.

The movement that finally dismantled this system is the last narrative in the chain, the Civil Rights Era; the specific instrument was the Voting Rights Act of 1965 (Civil Rights Era narrative, Ch 12), ninety-five years after the Fifteenth Amendment had supposedly already guaranteed the vote.

This matters for the twenties because Jim Crow is the force that drives the Great Migration (Chapter 13), the movement of more than a million and a half Black Americans out of the rural South and into the cities of the North and Midwest, which begins in earnest around the World War and which builds the Harlem and the Chicago and the Detroit where this decade's most lasting culture gets made.
While the South was rebuilding white supremacy, the rest of the country was industrializing at a violent pace.

The decades from roughly 1877 to 1900 are usually called the Gilded Age (a phrase from a Mark Twain novel: a thin gold plating over cheap base metal, glittering on the surface and corrupt underneath).

It was the age of the transcontinental railroads, of steel and oil, of vast new fortunes (Carnegie, Rockefeller, the railroad and banking dynasties) and the giant monopolistic corporations called trusts that those fortunes built, and of enormous, often desperate, immigrant labor.

A trust was a specific legal trick: the stock of many competing companies was handed over to a single board of trustees, who then ran the supposedly separate firms as one combine, fixing prices and crushing rivals while technically remaining many companies, which is why "trust" became the era's word for monopoly and "trust-busting" the word for breaking one up.

The factories and the corporate organization built in the Gilded Age are the machine this decade's consumer economy will run on; the Gilded Age learned how to make enormous quantities of things, and the twenties will learn how to sell them to everyone.

Against the Gilded Age's inequality and corruption came a reaction, roughly 1900 to 1917, called the Progressive Era: a broad, contradictory reform movement that produced the federal income tax, the Federal Reserve (the national central bank created in 1913, which will matter enormously in Chapter 15), the direct popular election of senators, the regulation of food and drugs, the breakup of some trusts, and, crucially for this book, two of the constitutional amendments central to this decade's culture war: the Eighteenth, which bans alcohol (Chapter 11), and the Nineteenth, which gives women the vote (Chapter 2).

A word on what a central bank does, because the term will recur and the ending depends on it: the Federal Reserve is the bankers' bank, it holds the reserves of ordinary banks, lends to them in a crisis (the "lender of last resort"), and, above all, can make borrowing money across the whole economy cheaper or more expensive by lowering or raising the interest rate it charges banks, which is the single most powerful lever any government has over a boom.
Hold that; Chapter 15 turns on it.
The twenties will spend the whole decade living off Progressive machinery while loudly repudiating Progressive politics, a tension worth holding onto.
Two more pieces.
First, immigration.

Between roughly 1880 and 1924 something like 25 million people immigrated to the United States, the largest movement of people in the country's history, and the source shifted: where earlier waves had come mostly from Britain, Ireland, Germany, and Scandinavia, the new wave came overwhelmingly from southern and eastern Europe, Italians, Poles, Russians, Greeks, and millions of Jews fleeing the pogroms of the Russian Empire (a pogrom was an organized mob attack on a Jewish community, looting, burning, and killing, frequently tolerated or quietly encouraged by the imperial authorities of Tsarist Russia).

They were disproportionately Catholic and Jewish in a country that thought of itself as Protestant, they packed into the industrial cities, and they are the population the 1920s will slam the door on (Chapter 9) and that much of the decade's nativist politics is about.

The 1920 census was the first in American history to find more Americans living in cities than on farms, by a hair, and the rural half of the country experienced that as a loss of the nation it thought it had.
Second, the World War.

The United States stayed out of the European war that began in 1914 for almost three years, then entered in April 1917, mobilized four million men, shipped two million of them to France, fought hard in the last six months, and lost about 116,000 dead (roughly 53,000 in combat, the rest mostly to disease, much of it the flu of Chapter 2).

By the armistice of November 11, 1918, the U.S. had been transformed: it had a huge war-built industrial plant, it was no longer a debtor but the world's leading creditor, owed billions by Britain and France, and it had run, at home, a startling apparatus of repression.

The wartime Espionage Act of 1917 and Sedition Act of 1918 made antiwar speech a federal crime: the laws made it a felony to say or print anything that obstructed military recruiting or, under the 1918 expansion, anything "disloyal" about the government, the flag, or the armed forces, so a public speech urging men to resist the draft was itself the prosecutable act, no sabotage or spying required.
The Socialist leader Eugene Debs went to prison for one such speech and would run for president from his cell.

Government propaganda and quasi-official vigilante groups had whipped up "100% Americanism," anti-German hysteria (German measles became "liberty measles," and German-Americans were harassed), and a habit of treating dissent as treason.
The war ended; the machinery did not get dismantled.
It was sitting there, fully built, when the Russian Revolution gave it a new target.
That is where Chapter 3 picks up.
That is the inheritance.

A country that had let the formerly enslaved be forced back down into Jim Crow and then told itself it hadn't; that had built the world's largest industrial machine and the inequality to match; that had reformed itself and then gotten tired of reform; that had taken in 25 million immigrants and was about to decide it had made a mistake; and that had just won a war by becoming, for the duration, a surveillance state, and had not turned the apparatus off.
Now the eleven years.
One operational point before we start, because it changes how to read everything that follows.

The danger with the twenties is not too little evidence but too much of the wrong kind: the gorgeous, much-mythologized record (magazines, movies, advertising, the novels) was made by and for the slice of the country the decade was good to, while the Tulsa massacre, the lived mechanics of sharecropping, and the immigrant neighborhoods just before the door shut had to be dug back out, sometimes against active suppression, decades later.
When this book and the brand disagree, that gap is usually why.
The text will say so when it happens.

chapters.title: The Plague and the Panic
sentences: The war ended at 11 a.m. on November 11, 1918, on the eleventh day of the eleventh month, and Americans poured into the streets to celebrate.

They were celebrating in the middle of the deadliest disease event in modern American history, and many of the people in those crowds would be dead within weeks, because that is what celebrating in a crowd did in the autumn of 1918.
The 1918 influenza pandemic was a strain of influenza that did something flu almost never does: it killed healthy young adults at high rates, not just the very old and the very young.

It is usually called the "Spanish flu," not because it came from Spain but because wartime Spain, being neutral, had an uncensored press that reported it freely while the warring countries suppressed the news.

The likeliest explanation, though the details are still argued, is that it turned the body's own defenses against it: in a young adult with a vigorous immune system, the response to the virus could spiral out of control and flood the lungs with fluid and inflammatory cells until the person essentially drowned, so the very strength that protected the old and the young from this strain is what killed the people in between.
It moved along the tracks the war had laid: troopships, crowded training camps, men packed into trenches and transports.
It came in waves, the second, in the autumn of 1918, by far the worst.
It killed roughly 675,000 Americans in a little over a year.
Sit with that number against something you can feel: it is more Americans than died in combat in the World War, the Second World War, Korea, and Vietnam combined.
It killed more people worldwide, estimates run from 50 to 100 million, than the war that was ending as it peaked.

Philadelphia held a giant Liberty Loan war-bond parade on September 28, 1918, after public-health voices had warned against mass gatherings; within weeks the city's hospitals were overwhelmed and the dead outran the supply of coffins.
Cities that closed schools, theaters, and churches early and kept them closed (St.
Louis is the textbook case) fared measurably better than cities that did not (Philadelphia), a contrast that public-health historians still cite.
And then it receded, and the country more or less decided not to talk about it.

This is one of the genuinely strange facts of the decade and worth flagging because it bears on the sources problem from Chapter 1: an event that killed two-thirds of a percent of the entire population in a year left almost no mark on the decade's novels, its movies, or its popular memory.
The Roaring Twenties brand has no room for it.
It was recovered as a major subject of historical attention mostly much later, which tells you something about how the decade chose to remember itself.
While the flu was still burning through, the economy fell off the war footing with no plan.
During the war the government had effectively run the economy: it set prices, allocated steel and coal, ran the railroads, guaranteed contracts.
The armistice cancelled the war contracts almost overnight, the price controls came off, and several things happened at once.
First, a short, sharp burst of inflation: with controls gone and consumers spending wartime savings, prices jumped roughly 15 percent in 1919 and into 1920.

Second, the soldiers came home: demobilization meant the army simply mustered roughly four million men out as fast as it could, discharging them in waves with a small bonus and a train ticket and no program to find them work, into a labor market the shutting-down war industries were emptying at the same time.
Third, the inflation meant that wages which had been frozen during the war now bought far less than they had, while corporate profits stayed high.
Workers who had been told not to strike for patriotic reasons during the war were now poorer in real terms and no longer at war.
So they struck. 1919 was the largest strike year in American history: roughly four million workers, about one in five in the entire workforce, walked out at some point.
This was not, mostly, revolution, whatever the newspapers said (Chapter 3 is about what the newspapers said).
It was wage-and-recognition unionism, workers wanting their pay to catch up to prices and wanting their unions recognized, happening at enormous scale all at once.
But two of the strikes became national symbols, and the symbols are what mattered politically.
In February 1919 the entire union workforce of Seattle, some 65,000 workers, walked out in sympathy with striking shipyard workers.

It was the first general strike in American history, meaning a strike not by one trade but by essentially all organized labor in a city at once (organized labor being the workers who belonged to unions, the bargaining associations that negotiated collectively with employers, as opposed to the unorganized majority who bargained alone and lost), with the explicit aim of shutting the city down.
Seattle's strike was disciplined and almost eerily peaceful; the strikers organized their own milk delivery and kept order, and it ended in a few days without violence.

But "the workers ran the city for a week" landed in a country watching Bolsheviks (the Russian communist revolutionaries who had seized power in 1917, Soviet Union Ch 1) take over a continent, and the mayor of Seattle built a national career on having "broken" a revolution.
Then, in September 1919, the Boston police struck.

This one was genuinely alarming in a way Seattle was not: when the police walked off the job over the right to affiliate with a national union, Boston had several nights of looting and disorder, because the thing that had walked off the job was the thing that prevents looting and disorder.

The strike was broken hard. the Massachusetts governor, a tight-lipped Vermont-born Republican named Calvin Coolidge, sent in the State Guard (the emergency state militia a governor can call up when the regular National Guard is unavailable, here used as armed strikebreakers), refused to rehire the strikers, and issued a single sentence that made him a national figure overnight: "There is no right to strike against the public safety by anybody, anywhere, any time." It was the perfect line for the moment, it put his name on every front page in the country, and it is the reason an obscure state governor is on the 1920 Republican ticket and in the White House by 1923 (Chapters 4 and 5).

There was also the Great Steel Strike, about 350,000 steelworkers, the largest single strike to that point, broken over months with private guards, strikebreakers, court injunctions (judicial orders forbidding the union from picketing or organizing, so that continuing the strike became contempt of court and the strikers could be jailed by a judge without a jury), and a relentless press campaign painting it as a foreign Bolshevik plot (its lead organizer was in fact a radical, which the steel companies used for everything it was worth), and a national coal strike that a federal court shut down with an injunction.
Almost all of the 1919 strikes failed.
Union membership, which had risen during the war, fell through the entire prosperous decade that followed.
One of the quiet, important facts about the Roaring Twenties is that the boom was not shared with organized labor; it was, in significant part, built on labor's defeat in 1919.
One thing did not fail in this stretch, and it had been fought for since before the Civil War.

In August 1920 the Nineteenth Amendment was ratified, barring the denial of the vote "on account of sex." Tennessee put it over the top when a 24-year-old legislator, Harry Burn, switched his vote to yes after a letter from his mother urging him to "be a good boy" and help ratify, the kind of detail popular history loves and usually rounds off, though here the letter is real and Burn himself credited it.

Something like 26 million American women became eligible to vote (the round figure that circulates; the exact count depends on which census and which state rules you use), in time for the November 1920 presidential election, the first in which women voted nationwide.

This is the seventy-year suffrage movement's victory and it is real and it is enormous, and it needs an immediate honest qualification, because the brand version of the twenties presents 1920 as the year American women got the vote, full stop, and that is not what happened.
The Nineteenth Amendment removed sex as a legal barrier.

It did nothing about the race barriers the Southern states had built, which is why most Black women in the South, like most Black men, still could not register to vote in 1920 or for decades after, they were blocked by the same poll taxes, rigged literacy tests, and violence that blocked Black men.
Suffrage in 1920 enfranchised, in practice, white women and Northern Black women.
Black women in the South had to wait for the movement Chapter 13 starts and the later narrative finishes.

The amendment also did not, by itself, change much about women's economic and legal position fast; the campaigning split immediately into the moderate League of Women Voters and the militant wing that drafted, in 1923, the first Equal Rights Amendment, which then went nowhere for fifty years.
The vote was a real, hard-won, partial victory, which is the most honest sentence you can write about a lot of the twenties.

So the decade opened on a country burying flu victims, watching prices outrun wages, watching one in five workers walk off the job, hearing every strike described as the opening of a Bolshevik revolution, and, in the middle of all of it, doubling its electorate.
It was frightened, and frightened countries do things they regret.
The next chapter is the things it did.

chapters.title: The Fear
sentences: In November 1917 the Bolsheviks seized power in Russia and announced they intended to spread their revolution to the entire world.

To a great many Americans in 1919, looking at four million workers on strike, at general strikes and police strikes, at a wave of bombs, and at millions of immigrants from exactly the part of Europe the revolution was coming out of, it did not look like a foreign event.
It looked like the beginning.

The result was the First Red Scare, and it is one of the clearest cases in American history of a real but limited threat being inflated into a panic, and the panic doing far more damage than the threat.
There was a real threat, and honesty requires starting with it, because the standard simplification is that the Red Scare was pure hysteria over nothing, and that is not quite true.

A small movement of Italian-American anarchists who followed Luigi Galleani, an Italian agitator who had landed in the United States in 1901, edited an incendiary anarchist newspaper for immigrant workers, and openly preached "propaganda of the deed" (political murder and bombing as a tool), genuinely was committed to revolutionary violence.

In the spring of 1919 they mailed roughly thirty mail bombs to prominent men (most were intercepted before they could go off; one that did maimed the household of a Georgia senator) and then set off a coordinated round of larger bombs in several cities on a single June night, one of which destroyed the front of the Washington house of the U.S.
Attorney General, A.
Mitchell Palmer.

The bomber blew himself up on Palmer's step; among the neighbors on the same Washington block, by their own later accounts, were the future Supreme Court justice Felix Frankfurter (a Vienna-born Harvard law professor and civil-liberties advocate) and Franklin Roosevelt, then the assistant secretary of the Navy and, twelve years later, the president who would govern the Depression this book ends at.
In September 1920 a wagon packed with dynamite and iron sash-weights was detonated in front of the J.P.

Morgan bank on Wall Street, killing about 38 people and wounding hundreds, the Wall Street bombing, the deadliest such attack on American soil to that point, never solved, generally attributed to the Galleanists.
So: real bombs, real dead people, a real if tiny violent movement.

What turned that into a Scare was the decision, by Palmer, by much of the press, by employers fighting the strikes, by patriotic and veterans' organizations, to treat the tiny violent fringe and the enormous nonviolent rest (labor unionists, Socialists, immigrants, anyone foreign and to the left) as one undifferentiated revolutionary mass.

The mechanism is worth naming because it recurs in American history: a genuine security threat is used to license a sweeping crackdown on a much larger population that mostly has nothing to do with it, and the crackdown is most attractive to people who had other reasons to want that population suppressed, employers wanting to break unions, nativists wanting to expel immigrants, politicians wanting a national profile.

The Early American Republic narrative shows the first run of exactly this play, the Alien and Sedition Acts of 1798, when a war scare with France was used to jail newspaper editors and lengthen the residency wall against immigrant voters; the Palmer Raids are that 1798 machinery turned, this time, on immigrant radicals instead of opposition politicians.
Palmer wanted to be president.
In late 1919 and January 1920 his Justice Department, working through a 24-year-old aide named J.

Edgar Hoover running a new "radical division" (he ran the federal investigative bureau that became the FBI, the Justice Department's national police and domestic-intelligence arm, for the next half-century, keeping secret files on Americans the whole time), carried out the Palmer Raids: mass arrests of suspected radicals in dozens of cities, by the most-cited estimate around 6,000 people though counts vary, mostly immigrants, mostly seized without warrants, many beaten, many held for weeks in appalling conditions, many arrested simply for belonging to an organization or being in the wrong meeting hall.

Hundreds of non-citizens were deported, because deporting a non-citizen radical required no criminal trial, only an administrative hearing (an in-house government proceeding before an immigration official, with no jury, no requirement to prove a crime, and few of the protections a criminal court must give), a legal shortcut Palmer used hard.

In December 1919 the army transport Buford, which the press gleefully called the "Soviet Ark," sailed for Soviet Russia with around 250 deported radicals aboard, among them Emma Goldman, the Russian-born anarchist writer and orator who had lived in the United States since 1885 and was, after decades of agitation on labor, free speech, and birth control, perhaps the most notorious radical in the country.

The Palmer Raids are now a standard example, in American law and history, of a civil-liberties catastrophe, and they were recognized as one fairly quickly: a group of prominent lawyers (Frankfurter among them) published a damning report on the Justice Department's lawlessness, and the American Civil Liberties Union was founded in 1920, specifically in response to the wartime sedition prosecutions and the raids, to do the thing no organization had reliably done before, supply lawyers and bring court challenges on behalf of people whose speech or association the government was punishing.

Palmer then destroyed his own presidential hopes by loudly predicting a giant revolutionary uprising for May 1, 1920, which did not happen, leaving him looking like a man who had wrecked thousands of lives over a prediction that flopped.
Out of this atmosphere came the decade's longest-running legal drama.
In May 1920 two Italian immigrant anarchists, Nicola Sacco and Bartolomeo Vanzetti, were arrested for a payroll robbery and double murder in South Braintree, Massachusetts.
They were Galleanists, they were armed when arrested, and they lied to the police.

They were also tried in 1921 in front of a judge who privately called them "anarchist bastards," in a courtroom where their politics and foreignness were front and center, on physical evidence that was contested then and is contested now.
Their case became a worldwide cause; for seven years, appeals, demonstrations, and protests on multiple continents argued that two immigrant radicals could not get a fair trial in Red Scare America.
They were executed on August 23, 1927.

Here is the honest state of it, because this is one of the genuinely unresolved questions in the book: modern scholarship is divided on whether Sacco fired the fatal shots (ballistics analysis, the forensic matching of a recovered bullet to the specific gun that fired it by the marks the barrel leaves, was primitive in 1921 and has been re-run several times since, with results read both ways, and some historians now think Sacco was probably guilty and Vanzetti probably not), but it is not divided on whether the 1921 trial was fair.
The consensus is that it was not, that the defendants' anarchism and immigrant status were used against them in a way that denied them due process, whatever the truth about the gun.
"We may have shot a guilty man unfairly" is a harder and more honest summary than either side's slogan, and it is the summary the evidence supports.
The Red Scare's victims were overwhelmingly immigrants and the left.

But 1919 was also one of the worst years of anti-Black violence in American history, and it is essential not to file it as a footnote to the Red Scare, because it was its own thing and in human terms it was worse.

In the summer and autumn of 1919, white mobs attacked Black communities in more than two dozen cities and counties, Chicago, Washington D.C., Knoxville, Omaha, and Elaine, Arkansas, where a white force of hundreds, in some accounts joined by federal troops, killed somewhere between dozens and well over a hundred Black sharecroppers who had tried to organize a union.
This was not random mob fury; it was the same instrument that had overthrown Reconstruction running again.

The Reconstruction narrative documents the template, deputized white paramilitaries, the destruction of prosperous Black institutions, no prosecutions, the record actively suppressed, and 1919 followed it almost step for step.

The writer James Weldon Johnson, an official of the NAACP (the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, founded in 1909 to fight segregation and lynching through lawsuits, lobbying, and publicity, and the Black counterpart, at almost the same moment and with almost no coordination, to the white-and-radical civil-liberties work the ACLU was about to take up), named the season the "Red Summer," red for blood.

In Chicago, eight days of violence, touched off when a Black teenager was stoned and drowned for drifting across an unwritten color line at a Lake Michigan beach, left, by the figures most often cited, around 38 dead and well over a thousand Black families burned out of their homes.
A crucial difference from earlier waves of racist violence: many of the Black men in these cities were veterans who had just been to France, were armed, and fought back.

The NAACP's anti-lynching campaign (Chapter 13) gained national urgency from the Red Summer, and the violence did not stem the migration north (Chapter 13); it sharpened it, because the alternative, the rural South, produced, two years later, the single worst episode.

On May 31 and June 1, 1921, in Tulsa, Oklahoma, a white mob, deputized, and in some cases armed, by the city itself, with airplanes reportedly used to drop incendiaries, destroyed the Greenwood district, a Black neighborhood prosperous enough to be called "Black Wall Street." The trigger was the usual one: a young Black man accused, on essentially no evidence, of assaulting a white woman in an elevator, and the threat of a lynching, which armed Black veterans came to the courthouse to prevent.

The number killed is one of the genuinely uncertain figures in this book and the uncertainty is itself part of the story: contemporary official counts said about three dozen, but later investigations, including a 2001 state commission and ongoing mass-grave excavations, estimate the dead at up to about 300, and the reason the number is unknown is that the city of Tulsa actively suppressed the event for fifty years, no prosecutions, no insurance payouts, the records buried, the massacre kept out of textbooks and local memory until survivors and historians forced it back into the record near the end of the century.
Ten thousand Black residents were left homeless.

The Tulsa Race Massacre is the sharpest single illustration of two things this book keeps returning to: that the twenties did not roar for Black Americans, and that the glossy record of the decade is glossy partly because the ugliest parts were deliberately erased and had to be dug back up, sometimes literally.
The Scare burned out fast, Palmer's failed prophecy, the courts pushing back, the economy recovering, the country simply tiring of fear.
By the end of 1921 Harding had even commuted the sentence of Eugene Debs, the Socialist still in federal prison for an antiwar speech, and invited him to the White House for a chat.
But the Scare left two permanent residues.
One was a federal apparatus and a young man named Hoover who had learned how to surveil and file Americans, and who kept doing it.

The other was the political fuel for the next chapter's two great projects: shutting the immigration door (Chapter 9), and electing a government that promised, above everything, to make all of this stop.

chapters.title: Normalcy
sentences: In May 1920 a Republican senator from Ohio named Warren Gamaliel Harding gave a speech in Boston with a sentence in it that has outlived everything else about him: "America's present need is not heroics but healing, not nostrums but normalcy, not revolution but restoration." Normalcy was not, as legend later had it, a word Harding invented by mistake, it was rare but real, but the legend stuck because it fit him: a slightly fuzzy word for a slightly fuzzy promise, which was, precisely, the promise to make the previous three years stop.
No more war, no more flu, no more strikes, no more Bolsheviks, no more crusading president telling the country it had a moral mission in the world.

After Woodrow Wilson, the Progressive moralist who had taken the country into the war, fought himself to a stroke trying to get the U.S. into his League of Nations (the international body the 1919 Treaty of Versailles created; the Constitution requires a two-thirds Senate vote to ratify any treaty, and a bloc of senators who would not accept a binding commitment to defend other countries denied Wilson that two-thirds in a long and bitter fight, so the U.S. never joined the body it had invented), and left office a broken invalid, the country wanted, above all, to be left alone.

It got Harding by the largest popular-vote landslide to that point, roughly 60 percent of the vote, about 16 million to 9 million, in the first election in which women voted nationwide, a thumping repudiation not just of the Democrats but of the whole Progressive, internationalist, reforming temper of the previous twenty years.
Harding was an Ohio newspaper publisher of genuine personal warmth, limited ability, and disastrous judgment about friends.

He is routinely ranked at or near the bottom of American presidents, and the ranking is fair, but the simple "worst president, total joke" version misses what is interesting, which is that his administration contained, simultaneously, some of the most capable men of the era and some of the most corrupt, and that the policies the capable ones set in motion are the policies the boom ran on.
Start with the capable men, because their policies are the ones the boom ran on.
As Treasury Secretary, Harding appointed Andrew Mellon, a Pittsburgh banker and aluminum, oil, and steel magnate who was one of the three or four richest men in the country.
Mellon's program, pursued under Harding and then under Coolidge for the rest of the decade, was the supply-side argument in its first full American form.

Supply-side means cutting taxes on the people and firms that supply capital and goods (the rich, investors, corporations) rather than putting money in ordinary consumers' pockets, on the theory that high top rates merely drove the rich to hide money in tax-exempt shelters, while lower rates would pull that money back into productive, taxable investment and grow the economy enough that total revenue would not fall.
Over the decade, in a series of Revenue Acts (1921, 1924, the big one in 1926), the top marginal income-tax rate was cut from 73 percent to 24 percent and the estate tax was gutted.

Whether it "worked" is still argued and probably always will be, but the honest thread to pull is this: the things the policy promised, high revenue and a boom, did happen, and the things it did not promise happened too.
The income gains piled up at the very top while the farm, the mine, and the mill (Chapter 5) got nothing, and the prosperity it presided over turned out to be sitting on a hollow floor (Chapter 15).

Mellon unambiguously got what he wanted, a decade of falling taxes on high incomes and a deliberate federal retreat from using the tax code to redistribute; whether the country got what it was promised is the question the rest of the book answers.

As Commerce Secretary, Harding appointed Herbert Hoover, the famous engineer who had run Belgian war relief and the wartime Food Administration and was probably the most admired administrator in America.

Hoover turned the sleepy Commerce Department into the most dynamic agency in the government, promoting industrial standardization, trade associations, commercial aviation, and the regulation of the new radio spectrum (the finite band of broadcast frequencies on which radio signals travel; without a referee assigning each station its own frequency, powerful stations simply drown out weaker ones and nobody can be heard, which is the chaos Chapter 8 describes).

His philosophy, that government should organize and coordinate private enterprise rather than run it or leave it alone, is its own distinct thing, neither Progressive regulation nor pure laissez-faire, and it is why he, not Mellon, ends up the decade's defining administrator and its last president (Chapter 15).

As Secretary of State, Harding had Charles Evans Hughes, who hosted the 1921–22 Washington Naval Conference, which produced the first major international arms-limitation treaty by capping the battleship tonnage of the leading naval powers (the United States, Britain, Japan, France, and Italy), a real achievement and a marker of how thoroughly the country had recoiled from the war into disarmament and staying home.
The same administration was also the most corrupt the country had yet seen, and that is the part Harding is remembered for, because it was spectacular.

He had brought to Washington a crowd of Ohio political cronies and poker companions that the press came to call the Ohio Gang, and they treated the federal government as a thing to be sold off in pieces.
The pardon power is the president's constitutional authority to wipe out a federal conviction; the Ohio Gang sold it, taking cash to arrange pardons and paroles for convicted men.
They sold immunity from Prohibition enforcement and access to the government's confiscated liquor.
They sold government contracts.

Charles Forbes, put in charge of the brand-new Veterans' Bureau, the agency meant to care for the men disabled in the World War, looted it through kickbacks on hospital construction and the corrupt sale of supplies; the waste was commonly estimated at around $200 million, the kind of large round figure that should be read as an order of magnitude rather than an audited total, and he went to prison.
But the scandal that gave the decade its byword for corruption was Teapot Dome.

The Secretary of the Interior, Albert Fall, secretly leased two naval oil reserves, one at Teapot Dome, Wyoming, one at Elk Hills, California, to two private oilmen, without competitive bidding (the legal requirement that government contracts be opened to rival sealed offers so the public gets the best price and no official can simply hand a contract to a friend, the safeguard Fall deliberately bypassed), in exchange for something on the order of $400,000 in "loans," cash, and cattle, the documented value varying with how each gift is counted.
A Senate investigation, one of the great congressional investigations in American history, dragged it into the light over several years.
Fall became, in 1929, the first U.S. cabinet officer ever imprisoned for crimes committed in office.
In a verdict that became a national joke about justice for the rich, the oilman convicted of nothing was acquitted of bribing the man who was convicted of taking the bribe.
Harding seems to have begun to grasp, in 1923, that his friends were destroying him.

The line most often hung on him, recorded secondhand through the journalist William Allen White and polished in the retelling, has him saying he had no trouble with his enemies but that his "goddamned friends" were the ones keeping him walking the floor at night.
The exact words are uncertain; the sentiment is well attested.
On a western speaking tour, in San Francisco, on August 2, 1923, he died suddenly, almost certainly of a heart attack, before the worst of the scandals had broken publicly.
Because he died beloved and the corruption surfaced afterward, the country mourned him enormously, then spent the next several years discovering what he had presided over.
His historical reputation went into the basement and stayed there.
And his death did one more thing, the thing that mattered most for the decade.

It handed the presidency, at the precise moment the economy was about to take off, to the one man in the administration with no whiff of the corruption on him at all: a silent, frugal, scandal-proof Vermonter who had been kept so far from the action as vice president that he learned he was president while on vacation at his father's farm, by lamplight, in the middle of the night.

chapters.title: The Silent Man
sentences: The scene is almost too good, and it is true, which is worth saying because a lot of the best twenties stories are improved in the retelling and this one did not need it.
Calvin Coolidge, vice president, was visiting his father's farmhouse in Plymouth Notch, Vermont, in the first days of August 1923.
The farmhouse had no electricity and no telephone.
Word that Harding had died came up the valley by messenger in the dark.

Coolidge's father, John, was a notary public, a local official with the legal power to administer oaths, and so at 2:47 a.m. on August 3, 1923, by the light of a kerosene lamp, in the sitting room of a Vermont farm with no electric light, a father swore in his son as President of the United States.
Then, by his own account, Coolidge went back to bed.

It is the perfect origin story for the man, because Coolidge's entire political brand was that he was the opposite of everything the previous five years had been: not heroic, not corrupt, not eloquent, not ambitious-seeming, not modern.
He was famously, deliberately, almost aggressively silent, "Silent Cal", and the silence was a strategy, not just a temperament.

The famous exchange, a dinner companion betting she could get more than two words out of him, his reply "You lose," is told too many ways to be taken as transcript, and is best treated as the kind of legend that attaches only to a man whose silence was already proverbial.

He slept eleven hours a day and napped in the afternoon, and he understood, better than almost any politician of the era, that in a decade when the press, the radio, and the public mood all wanted the government to stop doing things and let the boom happen, the most popular thing a president could do was very little, very quietly, and let people get rich.

His actual philosophy got compressed, in January 1925, into the sentence the whole decade is remembered by, almost always shortened to "the business of America is business," which is punchier than what he actually said ("the chief business of the American people is business") and drops the more idealistic qualifications that surrounded it, but the misquote stuck because it captured the policy exactly.

The policy was: continue Mellon's tax cuts (the big 1926 Revenue Act, top rate down to 24 percent, is the Coolidge-era centerpiece), keep federal spending and the federal government small, stay out of the economy, stay out of the world, and take credit for the prosperity.

He twice vetoed the McNary–Haugen farm-relief bill, whose mechanism was that the federal government would buy up surplus crops at a high domestic "fair" price and dump them abroad for whatever the world market would pay, eating the loss to keep American farm prices up; Coolidge killed it on the grounds that propping up prices was not the government's business, a decision that tells you both the consistency of the philosophy and exactly who the philosophy was not for.

He ran for a full term in 1924 on the slogan "Keep Cool with Coolidge," against a Democratic Party that had just spent its convention tearing itself to pieces (Chapter 10) and a Progressive third-party candidate, Robert La Follette, who pulled nearly five million votes in protest and carried exactly one state, his own Wisconsin.
Coolidge won comfortably.
The country had a booming economy and a president who promised to do nothing to it, which was, in 1924, precisely the offer the country wanted to accept.
Now the boom itself, in outline, because Chapters 6 through 8 are going to take it apart system by system and this chapter just needs to establish the shape.
Between roughly 1922 and 1929 the American economy did something genuinely new in the history of the world.
Industrial output and worker productivity rose dramatically.

The gross national product, the total money value of everything the country produced in a year and the standard yardstick of the size of an economy, grew by something on the order of 40 percent across the decade (the figure varies with how it is measured, which is why the careful phrasing).

And, this is the new part, the part that makes it the first of its kind, the gains, for the urban industrial middle and skilled working class, showed up not mainly as more food and rent but as things: a car, a radio, an electric refrigerator, a washing machine, a vacuum cleaner, a phonograph, store-bought clothes, packaged food, movie tickets, all bought new, many bought on credit, all advertised relentlessly.
This had never happened at this scale anywhere, and the obvious candidate for who should have done it first sharpens the point.

Britain was the first industrial nation and had the world's largest empire and mass factory production by the 1880s, yet it did not produce a mass consumer economy then, and the reasons are precisely the ingredients America had and Britain lacked: British industrial wages were lower and far more unequally spread, so most workers had no surplus to spend on durable goods; consumer installment credit was underdeveloped, so a worker could not buy ahead of his wages; advertising was still primitive; and British industry was oriented toward exporting to the empire rather than selling at home.
America was the first place all of those came together at once, which is what "first" means here.
Germany was a great industrial power but its 1920s were the catastrophe of hyperinflation and then a fragile, debt-propped recovery.
The Soviet Union, in this same decade, was a peasant economy beginning a state-driven industrialization at enormous human cost (Soviet Union Ch 2).
Japan was industrializing fast but nowhere near American consumer levels (Japanese Economic Miracle is the chapter where Japan reaches them, decades later).

The United States in the 1920s is the first society on earth where a mass consumer economy, make enormous quantities of branded goods, pay workers enough and lend them enough to buy them, sell them through national advertising, became the way the whole system worked.
The America that comes after is, in large part, the one assembled in this decade, and it has never been disassembled.
This is the place to set down, once and at full length, who the boom left out, because the brand version stops at the paragraph above and the rest of the book will only need to point back here.
The boom was real and it was narrow, and three very large groups mostly did not get it.

Farmers, close to a third of the country, had been pushed by wartime demand to expand and borrow; the demand vanished after the war, crop prices collapsed and stayed collapsed all decade, and something like a quarter of American farmers lost their land, so the rural depression the 1930s would merely nationalize was already running in the countryside the entire time.

The "sick industries", coal, textiles, New England manufacturing, the railroads, stagnated or shrank as oil displaced coal, the South and synthetics undercut New England textiles, and labor's 1919 defeat (Chapter 2) kept wages down where the work survived; the Battle of Blair Mountain in 1921, when some ten thousand West Virginia coal miners took up arms and marched on the southern counties to break the operators' private gunmen and forced company towns and were stopped only when the U.S.
Army moved in against them, the largest armed labor uprising in American history, and the brutal 1929 Gastonia, North Carolina textile strike are bookends on a region the boom never reached.
And Black Americans, the great majority still in the Jim Crow South, were locked out by law and violence.
The three are usually told as parallel but separate stories, and the deepest point of this chapter is that for the largest group the lines actually cross.
The Black farm South was not a different misfortune from the white farm depression; it was the same crop economy with a far more brutal floor under it.

The Reconstruction narrative lays out the mechanism: when emancipation did not come with land redistribution, the formerly enslaved were forced into sharecropping and the crop-lien system, raising someone else's cotton on credit advanced at usurious terms, the debt rolled over and growing every year, with no possibility of accumulating land or capital.
Sixty years later, in the 1920s, that trap was still closed.
When cotton prices collapsed, a white owner-farmer lost equity he had built; a Black sharecropper, who had been allowed to build none, had nothing between him and ruin but the road north.
That is why the farm crisis and the Great Migration of Chapter 13 are one story, not two: the migration is the failure of Reconstruction's land promise, sixty years deferred, finally cashing out.

The "Roaring Twenties," in short, is largely the experience of the urban, white, industrial wage-and-salary class during a real boom that did not reach the farm, the mine, the mill town, or the cotton field.
That asterisk now stands; later chapters will point to it rather than rebuild it.
Coolidge, in the end, had the impeccable timing of a man who leaves the party at exactly the right moment.

On August 2, 1927, the fourth anniversary of the lamplit oath, he handed reporters a slip of paper with one sentence on it and walked away without answering questions: "I do not choose to run for President in nineteen twenty eight." Historians have argued ever since about whether he sensed the boom was hollow; the more mundane likeliest reading is that he was tired and grieving (his teenage son had died in 1924) and the famously laconic man was being laconic.

Whatever the reason, the effect was the same as Harding's death in reverse: the man who presided over the boom walked out the door before the bill arrived, and handed the presidency, and the Crash, to the famous engineer who had spent the decade being the most admired man in the government (Chapter 15).

chapters.title: The Machine That Made the Decade
sentences: If you want one object that explains the decade, it is not the cocktail or the saxophone.

It is the automobile, and specifically the way it was built, because the way the car was built is the way everything in the consumer economy was eventually built, and the way the car reshaped the country is the way the consumer economy reshaped American life.

Start with Henry Ford, who did not invent the car (Europeans did, in the 1880s) and did not even invent the moving assembly line in any pure sense, but who in 1913, at his Highland Park plant in Michigan, put the pieces together at a scale and to an effect nobody had managed before.

The assembly line as Ford perfected it works on a single principle: instead of skilled workers moving to a stationary car and building the whole thing, the car moves, on a powered conveyor, past stationary workers, each of whom does one small task, attach this bolt, fit this wheel, over and over, all day.
Break the job into the smallest possible repeated motions, never make the worker walk or fetch or think, and the time to build a car collapses.

By the standard figures, the time to assemble a Model T chassis fell from somewhere over twelve hours to roughly an hour and a half, and at peak a Ford plant was completing a car about every half-minute, the kind of vivid production statistic that gets quoted as a single number but really describes a particular plant at a particular moment.

The price of the Model T, the one model Ford built (famously available, he said, "in any color, so long as it is black," because black paint dried fastest and the line could not wait), fell year after year as volume rose, bottoming under $300 in the mid-twenties, within reach, for the first time, of a skilled worker's roughly annual earnings rather than only a rich man's.

By 1927 Ford had built around 15 million Model Ts over the model's nineteen-year run; for much of the early-to-mid twenties Ford alone built roughly half the cars made anywhere in the world, a dominance no single carmaker has matched since, though the exact share depends on how and when you count.
The line had a problem, and Ford's solution to it is the hinge of the whole consumer economy, so slow down here.

The work was so monotonous and grinding that workers quit constantly; by the company's own figures, which are the main source for the number and worth flagging as such, annual turnover at Highland Park ran several hundred percent, meaning Ford had to hire many times over his entire workforce every year just to keep the plant staffed, which was enormously expensive.
In 1914 Ford did something that looked insane to other industrialists: he roughly doubled the basic wage to five dollars a day and cut the workday to eight hours.
The immediate purpose was to stop the turnover and the labor unrest (it worked; men lined up around the block).

But the deeper logic, which Ford himself articulated and which became the founding idea of the mass-consumption economy, was this: pay the workers who build the cars enough that they can buy the cars.
A worker who is also a customer is not just a cost; he is the market.

This is the loop the entire decade runs on, mass production making goods cheap enough for the masses, and mass wages (plus, soon, mass credit, Chapter 7) putting buying power in the masses' hands to absorb the output.
It is genuinely a new economic model, and it is the exact inversion of the labor system the previous narratives in this chain were built on.

The antebellum and post-emancipation cotton South ran on the opposite principle, extract the maximum labor at the minimum cost and keep the worker with no purchasing power at all, the logic of slavery and then of sharecropping.

Ford's logic, that the worker is the market and the system fails unless he is paid enough to buy back what he makes, is why the consumer economy was Northern and urban and the cotton field stayed poor: the two halves of the country were running on opposite answers to the same question.
It is the first time a major economy is consciously organized around the idea that the worker and the consumer are the same person and the system only works if both halves are fed.
The brand version stops at "Ford was generous." The real story is that mass production without mass purchasing power is just a warehouse full of unsold cars, and Ford saw it first.
Ford's weakness was that he saw it first and then stopped thinking.
He believed the formula was permanent: one cheap, unchanging, reliable car forever.
The man who saw what came next was Alfred Sloan, who took over General Motors in 1923.
GM could not beat Ford on price, so Sloan refused to compete on price.
Instead he built what became the modern American corporation and the modern American marketing strategy at the same time.
GM offered "a car for every purse and purpose", a ladder of brands from cheap Chevrolet up to luxury Cadillac, so that as a family's income rose it could "trade up" within GM.

GM introduced the annual model change, restyling the car every year so that last year's car, though mechanically fine, looked old, which manufactured a reason to buy a new one before the old one wore out (the technique now called planned, or really perceived, obsolescence).
And GM, through its financing arm GMAC, pushed buying the car on installment credit (Chapter 7), which Ford disdained and which turned out to be how most Americans actually bought cars.

By 1927 GM's strategy had overtaken Ford's single cheap car so decisively that Ford had to shut his plants for roughly half a year, idle tens of thousands of workers, and completely retool from the Model T to the new Model A, the moment even Henry Ford had to admit that styling, choice, and credit had beaten cheapness and durability.

That defeat is one of the most important business stories of the century, because the model that won, segmented brands, annual restyling, consumer credit, marketing as the core of the enterprise, is the model the American economy has run on ever since.
Now what the car did, because the object reshaped the country as profoundly as the way it was built.
By the late twenties roughly one American family in two owned a car.

That sounds modest until you set it against the rest of the world: in Britain and France in 1929 a private automobile was still an upper-middle-class luxury, owned by a thin sliver of the population, and mass car ownership did not arrive in most of Europe or in Japan until well after the Second World War.
The American "first" here is not the car, which Europeans built, but the ordinary family's car, and the gap between America and everyone else was a generation wide.
A country where ordinary families have cars is physically a different country, and the change worth opening up is the suburb.
The car severed the old tie between where you lived and where you worked: you no longer had to live within a streetcar ride of the factory or the office.

That released a new kind of place, the planned, low-density, car-dependent residential development (Beverly Hills, Kansas City's Country Club District) built around the automobile and protected by zoning, the new municipal power, spreading fast in the twenties, to dictate by law what could be built where, banning shops and apartments and factories from designated single-family districts so the suburb stayed exactly the kind of place its developers were selling.

Zoning is what made the suburb a permanent legal form rather than just a fashion, and the suburb is the single most consequential thing the car built, the template for how Americans would live, and segregate, for the rest of the century.

The rest followed quickly and can be named more briefly: the federally funded numbered-highway system (the Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1921 put the national government into road-building dollar-for-dollar with the states, and the 1926 system included the storied Chicago-to-Los-Angeles Route 66, whose length is given variously around 2,400 miles depending on the era's routing); a whole roadside economy that had not existed (the gas station, the motel, the diner, the billboard); the national park and the family road trip as middle-class rituals; and a quiet revolution in courtship, a private space on wheels away from the parlor and the parents, which scandalized the older generation precisely because they understood what it was for.

When two sociologists ran the first deep sociological portrait of a typical American town, published in 1929 as Middletown (the town was Muncie, Indiana; the study, which recurs in Chapters 7 and 14, became the standard close reading of how the consumer decade actually changed ordinary life), they found families who would "go without clothes" before they would give up the automobile.
In one decade an object went from luxury to necessity, and the country physically rebuilt itself around it.

chapters.title: Buy Now, Pay Later
sentences: A country can only consume what it can pay for, and in 1920 most American families could not, out of current wages, pay cash for a car, a refrigerator, a radio, and a washing machine all at once.

The thing that squared that circle, that turned the productive capacity of Chapter 6 into the consumer society the decade is remembered as, was a change less visible than the assembly line and at least as important: the normalization, for ordinary middle-class and working families, of going into debt to buy things.
Buying on credit was not new; what was new was its respectability and its scale.

For most of American history, consumer debt carried a moral stigma, debt was something the poor fell into and the prudent avoided, and "neither a borrower nor a lender be" was a value, not just a line from a play.

In the twenties that stigma was deliberately dissolved, mostly by the people selling the goods, through the installment plan: buy the thing now, take it home now, and pay it off in fixed monthly amounts over months or years, with interest, the seller (or a finance company like GM's GMAC) keeping the right to repossess if you missed payments.

By the late twenties, on the economic historians' usual estimates, somewhere in the range of one in ten to one in seven of all retail sales, and the clear majority of sales of cars, radios, furniture, and major appliances, were on installment.
