Consumer debt became, for the first time, a permanent structural feature of the American economy rather than an emergency.

The phrase that did the cultural work was "buy now, pay later," and the genius and the danger of it are the same fact: it let a family consume at the level of its expected future income rather than its current cash, which hugely expanded demand on the way up and meant that a great deal of the decade's prosperity was, quite literally, borrowed.
Hold that thought; it does not stay abstract.
It is the same logic as buying stock "on margin" (Chapter 15), and the decade ends when the future everyone had borrowed against fails to arrive.
Credit gave people the money.
Advertising gave them the wanting.

The modern advertising industry, the agency, the slogan, the brand, the campaign, was substantially built in this decade, much of it on Madison Avenue, the Manhattan street where so many big agencies clustered that "Madison Avenue" became, and remains, shorthand for the advertising business itself.
What it figured out was that you do not sell a product by describing the product.

You sell it by attaching it to a fear or a desire the buyer already has: the fear of social failure, of being unattractive, of falling behind the neighbors; the desire for romance, status, modernity, youth.

The textbook case is Listerine, a mild antiseptic that the Lambert company turned into a mass product in the early twenties by pushing an obscure quasi-medical word for bad breath, "halitosis" (the word predates the campaign; Listerine's advertising is what burned it into the language), and selling the mouthwash as protection against a private flaw that was costing you romance and marriage.
Soap, cigarettes, cars, and refrigerators were sold the same way, not as objects but as the gap between the life you had and the life you feared you were missing.

The decade's emblematic advertising text is a 1925 bestseller by the ad executive Bruce Barton, The Man Nobody Knows, which recast Jesus of Nazareth as the founder of modern business, a supreme executive and advertising man who, in Barton's telling, took twelve obscure men and forged them into an organization that conquered the world (the book's argument, paraphrased; the phrasing here is not a verbatim quotation).
It was meant admiringly.

It is also, read now, an almost too-perfect confession: in a decade whose loudest public fights were about religion (Chapters 10 and 12), the thing actually being preached to the largest national congregation, every day, through magazines and soon the radio, was consumption.
Then there was the question of where you bought it, and the answer changed the American main street permanently.
The old general store ran on the storekeeper: he knew you, carried you on credit through a bad month, fetched the goods from behind the counter, and bought in small lots at prices a small buyer pays.
The chain store killed all of that on purpose.

A&P in groceries opened thousands of identical stores; Woolworth standardized the five-and-dime; Piggly Wiggly invented the self-service aisle, where the customer, not a clerk, pulled a labeled package off a shelf, which is the moment the brand on the package replaced the word of the clerk.

Buying for a thousand stores at once, a chain could undersell any single merchant and never lose, and the independent storekeeper, with him the informal neighborhood credit and the face-to-face economy, began to disappear.
The trade-off the chain store introduced at national scale, cheaper goods bought at the cost of the locally owned main street, was new in the twenties and has never been resolved since.
And underneath all of it was the wire that made the modern home a place worth filling with appliances: electrification.

In 1918 only a minority of American homes had electric power; by the end of the twenties roughly two-thirds did, though the figure conceals a brutal divide, because the two-thirds was overwhelmingly urban, and the great majority of American farms still had no electricity at all, which is one more way the boom stopped at the city limits.
But for the electrified urban home the change was total.
Electric light ended the rhythm of the kerosene lamp (the one Coolidge took his oath by, a detail that was already nostalgic in 1923).
The electric refrigerator began replacing the icebox and the daily ice delivery.

The electric washing machine and vacuum cleaner began replacing the most backbreaking parts of domestic labor, and, in one of the decade's sharper ironies, the same advertising that sold the labor-saving appliance also raised the standard it was measured against, so the time saved was substantially spent meeting the higher standard.

The vacuum cleaner is the clean example: the carpet that had been beaten outdoors a few times a year was now expected to be vacuumed weekly, and the wife who had once sent the wash out or done it on a fixed wash-day now, with a machine at home, was expected to send the family out in fresh clothes far more often.
The labor was not saved; it was reassigned and intensified, a pattern historians of housework have documented carefully.
Refrigeration plus the chain store plus the car plus national brands together rebuilt the American diet and the American kitchen inside a single decade.

Put the pieces together and you have the machine the whole decade ran on: factories that could make almost unlimited quantities of standardized goods (Chapter 6); wages and, above all, credit that put buying power in ordinary hands; advertising that manufactured the desire to spend that power; chain distribution that delivered the goods cheaply everywhere; and an electrified home to put them in.

This is the first mass consumer economy in the history of the world, not the first place with rich people who bought a lot, but the first place where the system itself depended on tens of millions of ordinary people continuously buying new manufactured things, much of it on borrowed money, in response to national advertising.
It produced a genuinely higher material standard of life for the urban middle and skilled working class than any large society had ever had.

It also built in a structural fragility that the brand version never mentions and Chapter 15 collects on: an economy that runs on continuous mass purchasing fueled by debt and confidence has a floor made of debt and confidence, and floors made of confidence do not bend.
They break.

chapters.title: The Broadcast Nation
sentences: On the night of November 2, 1920, a Westinghouse engineer in a shack on a Pittsburgh rooftop read out election returns, Harding was beating Cox, into a microphone, over a station with the call letters KDKA, to an audience of perhaps a few hundred people with homemade receivers.
It is conventionally counted as the first commercially licensed radio broadcast in the United States.
Within roughly two years there were on the order of five hundred licensed stations (the exact count moves around in the records of the new regulators).

Within the decade, radio went from a hobbyist's crystal set to a piece of furniture in roughly a third of American homes, and in doing so it did something that had genuinely never happened in human history: it let millions of people, scattered across a continent, hear the same voice, the same music, the same joke, and the same advertisement at the same instant.
That is worth stopping on, because it is one of the decade's true firsts and the comparison sharpens it.
Every previous mass medium had a delay and a copy.
A newspaper or a book or a phonograph record reached many people, but each reader read a separate physical object, at a separate time.
Radio was simultaneous and shared: a nation of strangers, in the same moment, having the same experience.
No society had ever had that.
It is the technological substrate of the modern shared culture, the national audience, and the United States in the 1920s is where it first existed at scale.

Britain built its national broadcaster, the BBC, in this same decade, deliberately as a non-commercial public monopoly funded by a license fee, the opposite institutional choice from the American one.

That contrast is worth holding, and not only because it shaped each country's media for the rest of the century: because American radio was paid for by advertisers chasing the largest possible audience, the most popular, most profitable, nationally distributed content included the demeaning imitation of Black culture that this chapter ends on, while the BBC, beholden to no sponsor and run as an instrument of national uplift, carried nothing like it.
The American structure did not merely permit broadcast minstrelsy; the advertiser model actively rewarded it.
The American structural choice was made fast and it was commercial.

The early chaos, hundreds of stations stamping on each other's signals, was resolved by the Radio Act of 1927, which created a Federal Radio Commission to license broadcasters in "the public interest" and established the principle that the airwaves were public property the government would parcel out.
But the content and the money were private and were quickly nationalized into networks.

In 1926 RCA launched the National Broadcasting Company (NBC), the first permanent national radio network, which linked local stations together with leased telephone lines so a single program could go out across the country at once.
CBS followed in 1927 and was bought the next year by William Paley, then in his late twenties, who built it into NBC's great rival.

The two-network structure created by 1928, and the model of paying for it all by selling the audience's attention to advertisers, is, recognizably, the structure of American broadcasting for the rest of the century, television included.

Radio was where the consumer economy of Chapter 7 got its national pulpit: the singing commercial, the sponsored program (whole shows were named for their sponsors), the brand jingle, all invented here.

It was also where national politics changed: the 1924 conventions were the first broadcast, and Coolidge's flat, dry, unemotional radio voice turned out to suit the new medium far better than the booming open-air oratory of the old stump speakers, an early sign that the medium would start choosing its politicians.
The other engine of the new mass culture was already running in a Los Angeles suburb.

By the early twenties the American film industry had consolidated into the studio system: a handful of large companies, many of them founded by Eastern European Jewish immigrants who had been shut out of older American industries and built a new one (a fact worth stating plainly, because it becomes a target of the nativism of Chapters 9 and 10), that controlled production, distribution, and the theaters, an integrated structure that let them dominate from the script to the ticket booth.

Movies became the country's fourth-largest industry and, more than that, its dominant storyteller: by the end of the decade weekly movie attendance ran into the many tens of millions (the figures most often cited put it well over half the population going every week, though the estimates vary widely), in a building unlike anything most of them had at home.
The lavish movie palace, the largest of them seating six thousand under marble and gilt, turned moviegoing into an opulent mass ritual, a cathedral of the new religion of Chapter 7.
The same machine that made the modern celebrity also made the modern celebrity scandal, and the scandals matter here mostly for what they triggered.

The comedian Roscoe "Fatty" Arbuckle was tried three times in 1921–22 over a woman's death at a party (the third jury acquitted him and apologized; his career was destroyed anyway), the template for the celebrity-destroying media frenzy.

When the romantic idol Rudolph Valentino, an Italian immigrant, died suddenly in 1926 at thirty-one, the public grief was genuinely enormous, a crowd estimated in the tens of thousands mobbed the New York funeral home and the press reported scenes of mass hysteria, the lurid details of which (riots, fan suicides) grew in the retelling and are hard to verify, but the phenomenon, mass mourning for a stranger known only through media, was real and new.

The studios, frightened that this drumbeat of scandal would bring government censorship down on them, censored themselves first: in 1922 they hired the Republican politician Will Hays to police screen morality, and his office grew into the Production Code that dictated what American movies could show until the 1960s.

So the decade's culture war (Chapters 10 and 12) ran inside the movies too, the moralists quietly winning the screen even as they lost the cities, which is the same split the chapter's ending turns on.
And then, in October 1927, the medium ate its own silent self.

Warner Bros. released The Jazz Singer, the breakthrough feature with synchronized singing and a few lines of spoken dialogue, the most quoted of them Al Jolson's ad-libbed "you ain't heard nothin' yet" (earlier shorts and the 1926 Don Juan had carried synchronized sound, so the precise "first words" claim is contested; what is not is that The Jazz Singer is the film that killed the silent era).
Within about three years the silent film, a global, wordless art form that had let a Chaplin be understood in any country on earth, was extinct.

It is a clean, brutal case of a new technology destroying a mature art form in a few years, and it carries an emblem the brand version never mentions: the headline performance of the first sound feature was a white star, Jolson, in blackface, performing the minstrel caricature of Black music and Black people.
Blackface minstrelsy was not a 1920s invention.

It was the most popular form of American mass entertainment before the Civil War, part of the cultural apparatus that had manufactured the fiction of the contented slave (the antebellum and Reconstruction narratives trace it), and it had survived emancipation entirely intact.

What the twenties did was put it on the new national machines: The Jazz Singer on the movie screen and network radio's first national smash, Amos 'n' Andy (a comedy built on two white performers voicing exaggerated Black "dialect" characters), broadcast the same demeaning imitation, now to the whole country at once, of the very Black culture that, uptown in Harlem, was producing the decade's most original and lasting art (Chapter 13).
The broadcast nation was born; whose voice it carried, and whose it imitated and sold, is one of the things this decade was fighting about.

chapters.title: The Door Closes
sentences: For roughly a century the United States had kept its door, for Europeans, essentially open.

There were exceptions, and they had been racial from the start (the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 had already barred Chinese laborers), but the basic fact of the country, the thing it told itself about itself, was that it took people in.
About 25 million had come between 1880 and the World War.

In a four-year span in the 1920s, Congress slammed the door, and, this is the part the brand version of the decade omits entirely, it did so explicitly, openly, on stated grounds of race and national origin, with the science of the day cited in the committee reports.
The immigration restriction of the twenties is not a shameful subtext you have to read between the lines for.
It is text.

The fuel was the nativism of Chapter 3's aftermath: the postwar fusion of anti-immigrant, anti-Catholic, anti-Jewish, anti-radical, and anti-Black feeling into a single movement that called itself "100% Americanism." Define that phrase, because it is the decade's organizing political emotion outside the cities and it powers this chapter and the next two.

"100% Americanism" held that there was one real American type, white, Protestant, of northern or western European "old stock", and that everyone else (the Catholic and Jewish immigrants of the new wave, the radicals, Black Americans, eventually the wets and the evolutionists) was a diluting, disloyal, or dangerous contaminant of it.

It is a politics of purity and of grievance, and it ran the Klan (Chapter 10), much of Prohibition's enforcement coalition (Chapter 11), the fundamentalist side of the culture war (Chapter 12), and, most consequentially in law, immigration restriction.
This is not the first American instance of the form.

The Antebellum America narrative covers its direct ancestor, the Know-Nothings of the 1850s, a mass anti-Catholic, anti-immigrant secret order with rituals, lodges, and real electoral power at the state level, which rose during the Irish and German wave and collapsed only when the larger crisis of slavery pulled the floor out from under it.

The pattern recurs almost exactly seventy years later, a rapid immigration wave, a surge of Protestant anxiety, a mass fraternal organization with secret rituals and state-level power, and a sudden collapse when a bigger scandal hits (Chapter 10).
The second Klan is the Know-Nothing structure running a second time.

The legal mechanism was the quota, and the way the quota was designed is the whole point, so follow it. the first move, the Emergency Quota Act of 1921, capped immigration from each country at 3 percent of the number of people of that nationality already living in the U.S. as of the 1910 census.

Tying the quota to the existing population mathematically favored the groups already numerous and disfavored the newer arrivals, but the restrictionists thought 1910 was still too generous, because the new-wave immigrants had already been arriving in force by then. so the permanent law, the Immigration Act of 1924 (the Johnson–Reed Act), did two things.

It cut the percentage to 2 percent, and, the decisive move, it pegged the quota to the 1890 census, deliberately reaching back to a year before the great southern- and eastern-European wave, so that the "national origins" of the 1890 population (overwhelmingly British, German, Irish, Scandinavian) would set the quotas and the Italians, Poles, Greeks, Russians, and Jews of the new wave would be cut to a trickle.
The arithmetic was the policy.
The 1924 act's quota gave Great Britain and Germany the lion's share and gave Italy a few thousand a year against the hundreds of thousands who had been coming.
And the act's "aliens ineligible to citizenship" clause barred essentially all immigration from Japan and the rest of Asia outright.

The clause worked through an older racial law: a 1790 statute had limited naturalization to "free white persons," and a pair of 1920s Supreme Court rulings held that Japanese and South Asian immigrants did not legally count as white and so could never become citizens, which the 1924 act then used as the trigger to bar them from entering at all.
It extended the 1882 Chinese exclusion to the whole continent, an insult that poisoned U.S.–Japan relations for a generation (Japanese Economic Miracle traces where that road eventually led).
The full National Origins Formula took final effect in 1929, fixing total immigration at roughly 150,000 a year.

Anchor that against what it replaced: in 1921 alone over 800,000 immigrants had entered, so the new ceiling cut the flow by something like four-fifths and was deliberately apportioned to keep America's ethnic composition frozen at 1890's.
It governed who could enter the United States until 1965.
The intellectual cover for this was a science that was entirely mainstream in the twenties and is one of the decade's hardest things to look at squarely: eugenics.

Eugenics was the belief, taught in universities and high-school biology textbooks, endorsed by respectable scientists, foundations, and politicians, and built into the immigration debate as expert testimony, that human worth was substantially hereditary, that some "stocks" were genetically superior to others, and that the state could and should improve the population by encouraging the "fit" to breed and preventing the "unfit." It was not a fringe.

Its prestige is exactly why the House and Senate immigration committees, the congressional panels that drafted the quota laws, could put eugenicists in the witness chair as expert authorities, and why, in 1927, the United States Supreme Court itself, in Buck v.

Bell, upheld the forced sterilization of a young woman deemed "feebleminded," with Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes writing the sentence that should be carved over the decade's self-image: "Three generations of imbeciles are enough." Roughly sixty thousand Americans would be forcibly sterilized under such laws across the century, the practice accelerating after the Buck decision blessed it; the ruling has never been formally overturned.

This needs saying without softening, and it also needs the specific historian's note this book owes you: it sounds, to a modern reader, like the most extreme possible projection backward of later horrors, and the natural suspicion is that the text is exaggerating for effect.

The quotation is verbatim from the Supreme Court's opinion, the law was real, the sterilizations happened, and the connection drawn at the time between American eugenics and immigration policy was explicit and proud, not hidden.
The reader's instinct to disbelieve it is itself a measure of how thoroughly the decade's nostalgia has done its editing.
One countercurrent runs the other way and belongs here for honesty's sake, though it was less an act of generosity than a closing of a different loose end.
The Indian Citizenship Act of 1924 finally granted U.S. citizenship to all Native Americans born in the country, many of whom had been excluded from it for the entire history of the republic.

It is real and it mattered, and it needs its own asterisk in the same breath: several states promptly found other ways to keep Native people from actually voting, in some cases for decades, by the same poll-tax and residency tricks used against Black Southerners.

The same Congress that was racially sorting the world's immigrants also, almost in passing, admitted the continent's original inhabitants to a citizenship many states would then quietly hollow out, which is, in miniature, the whole pattern of rights in this decade: granted on paper, qualified in practice, and never quite for everyone at once.

chapters.title: The Invisible Empire
sentences: In August 1925, somewhere between 30,000 and 50,000 men in white hoods and robes marched in formation down Pennsylvania Avenue in Washington, D.C., past the Capitol and the federal buildings, in daylight, openly, as a show of strength.

They were the Ku Klux Klan, and the single most important thing to understand about them, the thing the brand version of the twenties either omits or files under "the South", is that this was a national organization at the peak of a national mass movement, and the men marching were as likely to be from Indiana, Oregon, or Colorado as from Georgia.
This requires care, because there were three different Klans in American history and conflating them muddles everything.

The first Klan was the Reconstruction-era terrorist insurgency of the 1860s–70s, and the crucial point the Reconstruction narrative establishes is that it did not merely "dissolve", it won: its murder campaign against Black voters and officeholders helped overthrow the multiracial democracy of Reconstruction, after which it could stand down because its work was done.
The third Klan is the small, violent, segregationist resistance to the civil-rights movement of the 1950s–60s (the later narrative in this chain).
The Klan of this book is the second Klan, a different kind of animal from either.

It was refounded at a 1915 ceremony on Stone Mountain, Georgia, on cultural ground already prepared: the same year, the film The Birth of a Nation had rewritten the first Klan as heroic saviors of the white South, and it was wildly popular because it was a technical landmark of early cinema, was marketed as a prestige event with orchestral scores in major theaters, and was endorsed at the highest level (it was screened at the White House).

It did not invent that flattering story; it dramatized the version of Reconstruction that the Lost Cause and the academic Dunning School had already installed in textbooks and respectable opinion, the version the Reconstruction narrative dismantles.

The second Klan grew in exactly that soil, and after 1920 a pair of professional promoters, Edward Young Clarke and Elizabeth Tyler, who took a cut of every membership fee and ran the recruiting like a sales business, turned it into a slick, mass-marketed, multi-million-member national fraternal organization.
Its hatreds were broader than the first Klan's.

The second Klan was anti-Black, yes, but its day-to-day politics in the North and Midwest, where most of its members were, were at least as much anti-Catholic, anti-Jewish, and anti-immigrant, it was, in essence, "100% Americanism" (Chapter 9) with a costume, a fee schedule, and a national sales force.

It presented itself to its millions of members not primarily as a lynching society but as a Protestant fraternal lodge, a temperance enforcer (it loved Prohibition and saw itself as its vigilante arm, Chapter 11), a defender of "traditional morality" against the flappers and the movies and the speakeasies, and a booster of "old-stock" Americans against the Catholic and Jewish newcomers, all of which made it socially respectable in a way the first and third Klans were not.

Its violence was real, especially against Black and Catholic targets, but its mass appeal in the twenties was as a movement of cultural grievance and "decency" for ordinary white Protestants who felt the modern, urban, immigrant, wet, jazz-playing America of this very book was taking their country away from them.
Which is to say: the Klan is not a digression from the story of the Roaring Twenties.
It is the backlash half of the decade organized into a membership organization, and it has to be told beside the jazz, not after it.
How big was it?

The honest answer includes the uncertainty: the Klan lied about its numbers and the records were deliberately destroyed, so estimates of peak membership range roughly from three to six million, with four to five million the usual figure, meaning, at the mid-decade peak around 1924–25, something like one in every fifteen or twenty native-born white Protestant adult men in the country.
Numbers alone can make the second Klan sound like a respectable lodge that just happened to be huge, which is the mistake; the violence was real and worth showing rather than only stating.

In 1921, in Mer Rouge, Louisiana, two men who had spoken against the local Klan were seized by hooded men, tortured, and murdered, their crushed bodies surfacing in a lake months later; the state could not get a conviction because the Klan controlled the local courts.

Across the decade the organization ran floggings, tar-and-featherings, cross-burnings as terror, and economic boycotts against Black, Catholic, Jewish, and "immoral" targets, mostly in places where, as at Mer Rouge, no jury would convict it.
That is the thing the membership table leaves out.
It converted the membership into raw political power, especially at the state level.

It effectively controlled the government of Indiana, elected backed governors and senators across the Midwest and West, ran much of the politics of Oregon and Colorado, and was strong enough nationally to shape a presidential nominating convention.

A party's national convention adopts a platform, the official statement of what the party stands for, voted on by the assembled state delegates; at the 1924 Democratic convention in New York (so deadlocked it took a record 103 ballots over two weeks to pick a nominee), a proposed plank that merely named and condemned the Klan was fought over furiously and defeated by a margin of about one vote out of more than a thousand fractional delegate votes.
Read that twice.

In 1924 one of the two major American political parties could not bring itself, by the narrowest possible margin, to officially disapprove of the Ku Klux Klan, because too many delegates either belonged to it or feared its voters.
This was not a sudden anomaly.

The Reconstruction and Civil Rights narratives show the same party's complicity with organized white-supremacist violence running in an unbroken line from the 1870s Redemption paramilitaries through 1924 and on into the 1950s; the convention vote is one data point on a fifty-year curve, not a freak.
And then it collapsed almost as fast as it had risen, and the way it collapsed is a parable.

Stephenson held the title of Grand Dragon, the Klan's chief officer for Indiana and several neighboring states, and he was the second Klan in microcosm: he had built a personal political machine that elected the governor and much of the legislature, he posed as the guardian of white Protestant womanhood and public morality, and he was, privately, a violent predator.
In 1925 he abducted and savagely assaulted a young woman named Madge Oberholtzer; she took poison, lingered, gave a detailed deathbed statement, and died of the combined injuries and poison.

Stephenson, to whom popular history attaches the boast "I am the law in Indiana" (a line that fits him exactly and is repeated everywhere, though its sourcing is journalistic rather than documented, so it is best read as emblem rather than transcript), was convicted of second-degree murder in November 1925.

The conviction shattered the moral pretense the whole organization had been sold on, and when Stephenson, feeling abandoned by the politicians he had bought, began handing prosecutors his lists of bribed officials, the political machine came apart too.
Membership, already softening, collapsed within about two years; by the end of the decade the second Klan was a husk.

Its sudden disappearance is one reason the decade could later be remembered as roaring rather than seething: the largest hate movement in the country's peacetime history rose, briefly ran the politics of several states and nearly captured a national party, and then imploded so completely, on a single sordid crime, that the nostalgic memory of the twenties could simply leave it out.
This book does not leave it out, because it was, for several years, as much "the twenties" as the Charleston was.

chapters.title: The Great Thirst
sentences: On January 17, 1920, the United States did something no other major modern country has matched in scope: it wrote a total, nationwide ban on the manufacture, sale, and transport of alcoholic beverages into its Constitution.
The comparison is what makes the choice strange rather than inevitable.
Several countries had the same Protestant temperance movement and acted on it, but none went this far.

Britain tightened licensing and pub hours; Canada ran Prohibition province by province and mostly abandoned it within a few years; the Nordic countries used punishing taxes and a state liquor monopoly, and Sweden settled on individual rationing books rather than an outright ban.
America alone reached for the most drastic instrument available, a constitutional amendment binding the whole country at once, which is exactly why it became the textbook case.
The Eighteenth Amendment is the only amendment in American history that took a personal freedom away rather than securing one, and it is the only one that was ever repealed.

The thirteen years it lasted are the single best illustration in this book of a recurring twenties truth: a law passed to make the country more moral, virtuous, and orderly instead handed a multi-billion-dollar industry to criminals, corrupted the police and the courts that were supposed to stop them, and made the lawbreaking glamorous.
First, how a whole country bans drinking, because the mechanism explains a lot.

Prohibition was not imposed by a tipsy majority changing its mind one morning; it was the final victory of the most effective single-issue pressure group in American history to that point, the Anti-Saloon League.

The League's innovation, studied by political scientists ever since, was to ignore everything except the one issue, endorse or destroy candidates of either party solely on their "wet" or "dry" votes, and build an interdenominational Protestant church network into a disciplined voting machine.

It rode a genuine and not-crazy reform impulse (the pre-Prohibition saloon really was, often, a squalid and exploitative institution, and drink really did wreck families in an era with no social safety net), fused it with rural Protestant suspicion of the Catholic, immigrant, urban America where the saloons mostly were, and got the World War as a final gift: anti-German feeling could be turned against German-American brewers (Pabst, Schlitz, Anheuser-Busch), and grain was needed for the war, not for beer.

The amendment passed; the Volstead Act, the law that defined and enforced it, set the threshold of "intoxicating" absurdly low (anything over one-half of one percent alcohol) and then funded enforcement so feebly that for a country of 120 million people stretching across a continent the entire federal Prohibition force never amounted to more than a couple of thousand agents at a time, paid little enough that bribing them was trivial.
What followed is almost a controlled experiment in the limits of law.

Prohibition did reduce overall drinking, especially at first and especially among the poor who could not afford bootleg prices, and this is the part the "Prohibition was a total failure" cliché gets wrong and should be said honestly.
But it did not stop drinking; it drove it underground and made it criminal, profitable, and chic.
The speakeasy, an illegal bar entered by password ("speak easy" at the door), replaced the saloon, and there were more of them than there had been saloons.

The often-quoted figure for New York City, "somewhere between 30,000 and 100,000," really means nobody knew: the lower end is the Prohibition Bureau's own guess and the upper end is press exaggeration, and the honest takeaway is only that there were a great many.
An entire illegal supply chain materialized to feed them.

Ships anchored on "Rum Row" just outside the three-mile limit of U.S. jurisdiction and offloaded liquor onto fast boats; the Detroit "Purple Gang" ran Canadian whiskey across the river; rural Americans distilled "moonshine" and "bathtub gin." Some of it was lethal, and not always by accident: industrial alcohol is legally manufactured for solvents and fuel, and to stop bootleggers from rinsing it and selling it as drink the federal government ordered it "denatured", deliberately adulterated with poisons such as methanol, which causes blindness and death, and bootleggers redistilled it imperfectly anyway, so the government knowingly presided over the poisoning of thousands of its own citizens, a fact the jolly-speakeasy brand never includes.

And because the souped-up car built to outrun federal agents on back roads became a Southern subculture of its own, stock-car bootleg running is one of the documented roots (though NASCAR's own promotion has burnished the legend) of what became NASCAR, the stock-car racing circuit that is now one of the most-watched spectator sports in the United States.
A law against a drink rebuilt the country's relationship to cars, courts, and crime.
The decisive consequence, the one that outlived Prohibition itself, was organized crime.
Before Prohibition, criminal gangs were mostly local, small, and limited to gambling, extortion, and vice.

Prohibition handed them a product with insatiable demand, no legal competitor, and colossal margins, and to exploit it they had to build something new: large, coordinated, business-like criminal organizations that ran manufacturing, smuggling, distribution, and the systematic bribery of police, prosecutors, judges, and city governments necessary to protect all of it.
The modern American crime syndicate was, quite precisely, financed and organized by twenties bootleg money.

Its emblem is Al Capone, who took over the Chicago "Outfit" in 1925 and built a bootlegging, gambling, and vice empire grossing, by common estimate, around $60 million a year, while effectively owning Chicago's police and many of its politicians.
Capone was not a hidden figure; he was a celebrity, gave interviews, sat at ballgames, and styled himself a businessman serving a public that wanted what he sold, which in a sense he was.
The gang wars over territory were vicious, and the one that turned the public decisively against him was the St.
Valentine's Day Massacre of February 14, 1929: Capone gunmen, some dressed as police, lined seven members of a rival gang against a Chicago garage wall and machine-gunned them.
The shock of it (and of the realization that men disguised as the law were doing the killing) was a turning point in public opinion.

And the way Capone was finally brought down is the perfect closing irony of Prohibition: not for murder, not for bootlegging, not for owning a city, but, in 1931, for failing to file an income-tax return on the illegal millions, the one law a bootlegger could not buy, intimidate, or shoot his way around.
By the mid-twenties the failure was visible to anyone honest.

Juries in wet cities routinely refused to convict; respectable people drank openly in defiance; the poisoned-alcohol deaths mounted; the corruption was a national scandal; and a counter-movement was forming, including, devastatingly for the dry argument, Pauline Sabin's Women's Organization for National Prohibition Reform, which blew up the claim that Prohibition was what women wanted.

The dry coalition kept hardening the law as its support drained, passing the 1929 Jones Law that turned even first-offense bootlegging into a felony (a serious crime carrying more than a year in prison, as opposed to a minor "misdemeanor"), now punishable by five years.
And in 1929 Hoover appointed the Wickersham Commission to study enforcement.

Its 1931 report is the episode's perfect punchline and deserves to be said plainly: after exhaustively documenting that Prohibition was unenforceable and failing, the commission recommended that it be kept anyway, several commissioners attaching individual notes that contradicted the official conclusion.
Even the body convened to defend the law could not honestly defend it and could not bring itself to say so.
It was repealed in 1933, by the Twenty-first Amendment, in the depths of the Depression, partly because a desperate government wanted the liquor tax revenue.

But the part of Prohibition that did not get repealed is the part that matters most going forward: it had built the modern crime syndicate, normalized the wholesale bribery of police, prosecutors, and city halls, and taught a generation of Americans that the law itself could be a racket.
That machinery did not vanish with the saloons.
It went into gambling, labor, and politics, and it is one of the things the country carried, fully assembled, out of the twenties and into everything that came after.

chapters.title: God and the Monkey
sentences: In July 1925, in a small town in eastern Tennessee, a young schoolteacher was put on trial for the crime of teaching that human beings evolved from earlier animals, though, as it happens, whether he had actually taught the lesson at all was never really the point and is still debated; the trial was arranged.

The Scopes trial lasted eight days, was carried live on the radio (the first American trial broadcast nationally), drew the most famous lawyer and the most famous orator in the country to a sweltering courthouse, and settled, legally, almost nothing.

It mattered because it was the moment the decade's deepest argument, the one underneath the Klan and Prohibition and the immigration quotas, was staged in the open, in front of the whole listening country, as a single fight between two old men: the argument over whether modern America, with its science and its cities and its relativism and its jazz, was progress or apostasy.
Set the religious scene first, because the reader needs the terms.
American Protestantism in the early twentieth century was splitting along a fault that the decade widened into a canyon.

On one side were the modernists, who held that Christian faith could and must be reconciled with modern science and modern scholarship, that the Bible could be read as morally true without being literally and scientifically accurate, and that evolution and an old earth were simply facts a thinking Christian accommodated.

On the other side were the fundamentalists, a word that comes from a series of cheap doctrinal pamphlets, "tracts," short, free, mass-printed booklets of religious argument, called The Fundamentals, funded by two wealthy oilmen and mailed by the millions to ministers and seminarians across the country in the 1910s, which insisted on a set of non-negotiable doctrines, above all the literal, inerrant truth of the Bible: the world created as Genesis says, the virgin birth, the physical resurrection, miracles as historical events.

Fundamentalism in the twenties was not a fringe and was not stupid; it was a large, organized, intellectually serious (on its own premises) reaction by millions of mostly rural and small-town Protestants who experienced the modern, urban, scientific, secular culture of this entire book as a direct assault on the truths their lives were built on.

The fundamentalist–modernist controversy tore through the major denominations all decade, worst among the Presbyterians and Baptists. (A denomination is an organized Protestant church body with its own governance, doctrine, and clergy, Presbyterian, Baptist, Methodist, and so on; "which denomination" mattered because the fight was over which of these large institutions, and their colleges and pulpits, the modernists or the fundamentalists would control.) Evolution in the public schools became its battlefield because the public school was where the state itself decided which account of human origins every child would be taught, which made it, unavoidably, a fight over whose worldview the government would endorse.

Tennessee fired the first legal shot with the Butler Act of March 1925, which made it a crime to teach in a public school "any theory that denies the story of the divine creation of man as taught in the Bible." The American Civil Liberties Union (founded in the Red Scare, Chapter 3) advertised for a teacher willing to be a test case.

Boosters in the town of Dayton, openly hoping the publicity would put their fading town on the map, recruited a young, mild substitute science teacher and football coach named John Scopes, who agreed to be the defendant precisely because there was little risk: everyone, including Scopes, understood the case to be a staged test of the law, the penalty was a small fine, and the ACLU had promised to pay for his defense, so being prosecuted cost him almost nothing and made him briefly famous.
Then the case caught fire far beyond anyone's plan, because of the two men who came to argue it.

For the prosecution: William Jennings Bryan, three-time Democratic presidential nominee, former Secretary of State, the greatest popular orator in America for thirty years, a sincere Christian and economic progressive who had come to see Darwinism as the cruel ideology behind the eugenics of Chapter 9 and the social-Darwinist defense of the very business inequality he had spent his life fighting. (That is the part the famous version flattens: Bryan's anti-evolutionism was tangled up with a genuine moral horror at how "survival of the fittest" was being used to justify both racial pseudoscience and unrestrained capitalism, which does not make him right about biology but does make him something more interesting than a buffoon.) For the defense: Clarence Darrow, the most famous courtroom lawyer in the country, a militant agnostic who, the year before, had saved Nathan Leopold and Richard Loeb, two wealthy Chicago university students who had murdered a fourteen-year-old boy in 1924 to prove they could commit a perfect crime, from the gallows in a sensational trial, and who came to Dayton explicitly to put fundamentalism itself on trial.

The trial's substance was thin (Scopes had clearly taught evolution; the law clearly forbade it; he was always going to be convicted, and was, with a token hundred-dollar fine later thrown out on a technicality).
The trial's theater was historic, and it peaked when the judge would not let Darrow call scientists as witnesses and Darrow, improvising, called Bryan himself to the stand as an expert on the Bible.
Bryan, vain and unable to resist the platform, accepted.

Under Darrow's questioning, in front of the national radio audience, Bryan was pushed into defending biblical literalism in detail (where did Cain get his wife; was the whale literal; was the earth made in six twenty-four-hour days) and grew confused, contradictory, and angry.
This is the moment the legend was minted, and it is worth watching it being minted rather than simply repeating it.
The urban press, led by H.

Mencken, the ferociously witty Baltimore newspaper columnist and magazine editor who was the most quoted American writer of the decade and made a career out of mocking what he saw as American provincialism, filed copy treating the trial as civilization's war on the "yokels" of what he was popularizing as the "Bible Belt", and wrote the story as a total modernist rout and made Dayton a national shorthand for rural idiocy.
That is the version that hardened into memory, and it is, crucially, the winners' version, written in real time by the side it flattered.
Hold it at arm's length, because the next paragraph is going to take it apart.

Five days after the trial ended, still in Dayton, Bryan died in his sleep, and his death was widely read, by the same press, as the symbolic death of agrarian Protestant America itself, which made the legend feel complete and was wrong.
But here is where the brand version, the Inherit the Wind version, is most misleading, and the chapter has to say so.
The modernists won the press and lost the country.
Scopes's conviction stood.
Tennessee's law stayed on the books until 1967.

Far from being discredited, anti-evolution laws spread: Mississippi passed one in 1926, Arkansas in 1928, and, more quietly and more effectively, the major textbook publishers, frightened of the Southern market, simply removed or muted Darwin from American high-school biology books for decades.

The fundamentalists did not vanish in humiliation in 1925; they withdrew from the prestige institutions that had mocked them and spent the next half-century building their own, parallel network of churches, colleges, publishers, and, crucially, broadcasters, the new technology of Chapter 8 turned to the old-time religion.

The era's pioneering religious broadcaster was the Los Angeles revivalist Aimee Semple McPherson, who built an enormous temple seating well over five thousand and one of the first radio ministries, and who became a national tabloid sensation in 1926 when she vanished for weeks, reappeared with a story of having been kidnapped that almost nobody believed (a grand jury investigated, the evidence was contradictory, no charges ultimately stuck, and the truth was never established), and emerged, scandal and all, more famous than before, which was itself the lesson about broadcasting and celebrity religion.
The marriage of mass broadcasting and revivalism that would shape American religion and politics for the rest of the century was performed in this decade.
Scopes is remembered as the moment science laughed fundamentalism out of the room.
What actually happened is that fundamentalism walked out of that room, built its own, and came back later, larger.
The decade's culture war did not end at Dayton.
It went underground, exactly like the liquor, and for similar reasons.

chapters.title: The New Negro and the New Sound
sentences: The most lasting thing the Roaring Twenties made was not the Chrysler Building or the Model A or The Great Gatsby.

It was a body of music and writing created, in a few square miles of upper Manhattan and on the South Side of Chicago, by exactly the Americans the rest of this book has shown the decade's politics trying to suppress.

The supreme irony of the twenties is that its permanent cultural legacy was disproportionately Black, made by the children of the people Jim Crow had built a regime to keep down and the Klan had built a movement to terrorize, and that white America consumed it ravenously while refusing its makers a seat at the table, sometimes literally.
It starts with a migration, and the migration starts in the unpaid bill of Chapter 5.

The reason Black Southerners were still trapped in sharecropping in 1916, with no land and no capital to cushion them, is that Reconstruction's promise of land was made in 1865 and broken within months; the migration is that sixty-year-old failure finally forcing people onto the road.

The push was Jim Crow, debt, and lynching; the pull came when the World War and then the 1924 immigration restriction (Chapter 9) choked off the European immigrant labor Northern factories had run on, opening industrial jobs to Black workers at scale, and when the Black press, above all the Chicago Defender, advertised the North as a promised land.

The Defender had to be smuggled because white planters and many Southern towns banned or confiscated it and threatened the Black agents who distributed it, precisely because it told sharecroppers there was somewhere else to go; Pullman porters (Black railroad workers, of whom more below) carried bundles of it south and dropped them along the line to be passed hand to hand.

The result was the Great Migration: between roughly 1916 and 1930, on the conservative estimates more than 1.5 million and by higher counts well over that, Black Americans left the rural South for the cities of the North and Midwest, the largest internal migration in American history to that point.

It did not deliver the promised land, residential segregation, hostile white neighbors, the Red Summer (Chapter 3), and worse pay for worse jobs were waiting, but it concentrated, in Harlem and Chicago's "Black Belt" and Detroit, hundreds of thousands of Black Americans with wages, institutions, newspapers, churches, and audiences, at a measure of distance from the Southern terror, and out of that concentration came an explosion.
That explosion had a literary and a political wing and a musical one, and they were not equal in reach.
The writing and the organizing concentrated and trained a leadership; the music is what conquered the world, so the music is where this chapter is going to spend its weight.
But the supporting cast has to be on the stage first, briefly and in order.
The literary wing is usually called the Harlem Renaissance.

Its manifesto was The New Negro, a 1925 anthology assembled by Alain Locke, a Howard University philosophy professor and the first Black American Rhodes Scholar, whose authority and connections made him the movement's impresario; it argued that a new generation of Black Americans, urban, assertive, and unwilling to ask for white approval, was remaking American culture from Harlem outward.

Its defining poet, Langston Hughes, insisted that Black artists draw without apology on jazz, the blues, and Black speech rather than imitate white models; Zora Neale Hurston, trained as an anthropologist, salvaged the rural Southern folklore the migration was leaving behind; the Jamaican-born Claude McKay had given the movement its angriest early voice in "If We Must Die," written in the blood of the Red Summer.
The political wing, which the prettified version of "the Harlem Renaissance" tends to drop, ran in parallel.

Marcus Garvey's Universal Negro Improvement Association built the largest Black mass movement in American history on racial pride, economic self-help, and a return to Africa (its 1920 New York convention drew a crowd the UNIA put at 25,000, a figure that comes mostly from the movement's own claims and is probably high), before Garvey was convicted of mail fraud tied to his steamship line and deported.

The NAACP ran the long campaign against lynching, pushing an anti-lynching bill through the House in 1922 only to watch Southern senators kill it with a filibuster: in the Senate a senator who has the floor can keep talking, literally holding it by refusing to yield, and unless a supermajority votes to force an end to debate the bill simply never comes to a vote, so a determined Southern minority used it to strangle every federal anti-lynching measure for the next forty years.

That same weapon, the Southern bloc's filibuster, is the obstacle the movement finally breaks in 1964, when the cloture votes end the longest filibuster in Senate history and the Civil Rights Act passes (the Civil Rights Era narrative, Ch 10).

That weapon was not new in 1922; the Reconstruction narrative shows the same Senate machinery being used to block federal protection of Black citizens since the 1870s, which is the point, the 1922 defeat was the continuation of a fifty-year system, not a fresh failure.
And in 1925 A.

Philip Randolph founded the Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters, organizing the all-Black workforce that made up the sleeping-car attendants of the Pullman Company (the firm that built and operated the nation's railroad sleeping cars and was the largest single employer of Black men in America, which is why a union of porters was both possible and explosive) into the first Black-led union to win a major contract.

Mark that name and that year: the Civil Rights Era narrative identifies this same Randolph, sixteen years later, as the man whose threatened 1941 mass march on Washington forced the first federal order against employment discrimination (Civil Rights Era narrative, Ch 1), and again in 1963 as the organizer of the March on Washington (Ch 9), making him the one figure whose career directly links the Harlem Renaissance, the New Deal, and the Second Reconstruction.
The pipeline runs straight from the 1925 porters' union to that.
Now the spine.

The musical wing reached incomparably more people and traveled incomparably faster than the books or the rallies, because it had the two new machines of Chapter 8 to carry it, the phonograph record and the radio, and because one man turned a regional folk music into a fine art almost single-handedly.
Jazz had come up the river out of New Orleans's Black musical world to Chicago and then everywhere, and the figure who, more than any other, remade what it could be was Louis Armstrong.

The numbers in "Hot Five" and "Hot Seven" refer literally to the size of the band, the small studio groups Armstrong led on a run of recordings from roughly 1925 to 1928, and the point is what he did on them: jazz had been a collective music in which a front line of horns improvised together, and Armstrong pulled the improvising soloist out in front of the band as the music's center of gravity, the structural move (a brilliant individual voice taking flight over a supporting group) that organized not only jazz but most American popular music after it.
The framing oversimplifies a change many musicians were part of, but no other single player's recordings carried it as far.

Around him the rest: Duke Ellington's orchestra began its residency at Harlem's Cotton Club in late 1927, and the club's nightly radio wire carried his sound and his name into the entire country; Bessie Smith, the "Empress of the Blues," sold records by the hundreds of thousands into the segregated "race records" market (records made by Black artists for Black buyers) and was, by the usual accounts, the best-paid Black performer of the decade.

Through records, radio, and the migration that had concentrated the talent in the first place, a music made by the descendants of the enslaved became, inside a single decade, the sound of modern America, and of modern Europe, where "le jazz" took Paris.
And the Cotton Club is the symbol this chapter has to end on, because it is the decade in one room.
It was the most famous nightclub in America.

It presented the greatest Black musical artists of the age, Ellington's among them, in lavish, often grotesquely "primitive"-themed shows, to an audience that was, by the club's strict policy, whites only.
The performers entered through the back.

The decade's most original and lasting art was made by Black Americans; the decade's economy and law were structured so that white Americans profited from it and its makers largely did not, and could not even watch it from the good seats.
That is the Roaring Twenties with the asterisk attached, and it is the truer sentence than the one with the saxophone and no asterisk.
The justice did not come in this decade.

What this decade built instead was the base, the porters' union and the NAACP, the migrant cities and the money and the audiences, the confidence of a generation that had made the century's defining American music while being shut out of the room, and that base is precisely what the movement two narratives down this chain would be launched from.

chapters.title: The Lost Generation and the New Woman
sentences: The twenties got its other name, "the Jazz Age," from a young novelist who was twenty-three when he became famous and who spent the rest of his short life chronicling, and being destroyed by, the decade he had named.

Scott Fitzgerald published This Side of Paradise in 1920, became overnight the voice and the mascot of postwar youth, coined "the Jazz Age" for the era, and in 1925 published The Great Gatsby, which took the decade's bootleggers, brand-new money, parties, and hollow glamour and turned them into the novel by which the whole period is now most often understood.

It is worth a true note that cuts against the brand: Gatsby sold modestly in the twenties and Fitzgerald died in 1940 thinking himself a failure; the book became "the great American novel" only afterward, which is itself a lesson about how this decade was remembered versus how it was lived.
The point of the Lost Generation writers is that they are the decade's own internal dissent.

While the advertising of Chapter 7 told the country it had never been happier, its best young writers were saying, in the country's best prose, that the boom was spiritually empty and the official optimism was a fraud.

"The Lost Generation" is the writer Gertrude Stein's phrase, made famous by Ernest Hemingway, who used it as an epigraph to The Sun Also Rises (1926), the novel that gave the disillusioned, war-scarred postwar generation its portrait and gave American writing a new stripped-down style that influenced it for the rest of the century.

Many of these writers physically left, congregating in 1920s Paris (where the dollar was strong, the censorship was light, and the wine was legal) around Gertrude Stein's salon and the bookshop of Sylvia Beach, the expatriate American whose Left Bank shop, Shakespeare and Company, was the expatriates' clubhouse and lending library and who in 1922 published James Joyce's Ulysses when no commercial house would touch it: Hemingway, Fitzgerald, the poet Ezra Pound, and the rest.
At home, the role of professional skeptic was filled by H.

Mencken, the Baltimore critic of Chapter 12, the most quoted American writer of the decade, who founded The American Mercury in 1924 and conducted a daily war on Prohibition, the Klan, fundamentalism, and what he called the "booboisie", the self-satisfied conformist middle class that the novelist Sinclair Lewis had skewered in Babbitt (1922), a book that put a new word for that exact type into the language.

Across the decade, the people best at using its new mass media to describe it were largely in revolt against it, which is one more reason the decade's self-image and the decade's reality need to be held apart.
The decade's emblem of social change was a young woman, and she needs the same careful handling as everything else in this book.

The flapper, bobbed hair, hemlines at the knee, cosmetics in public, cigarettes in public, a cocktail in a speakeasy, the Charleston (the frantic dance, popularized by the 1923 Black musical Runnin' Wild, that traveled, like the music, from Black culture into the white mainstream), was the decade's image of liberated young womanhood, and there was something real underneath the image.

The Nineteenth Amendment (Chapter 2) had enfranchised women; more women than ever worked for wages; the open revolt against Victorian rules about female bodies, behavior, and desire was genuine, and it was a lasting change.
But the brand sells the image as the reality, and the reality was narrower.

The flapper was largely an urban, young, white, middle-class figure and substantially a media and advertising construction; most American women, especially in the rural South and among the immigrant working class and Black women under Jim Crow, lived nothing like her.
The new women in the paid workforce were overwhelmingly funneled into low-paid "pink-collar" jobs, typist, telephone operator, salesgirl, clerk, and most were still expected to quit at marriage.

The vote had not delivered economic or legal equality; the Equal Rights Amendment (Chapter 2) introduced in 1923 went nowhere; and the era's contraception movement, led by Margaret Sanger, which genuinely expanded women's control over their lives, was, like much twenties reform, entangled with the eugenics of Chapter 9.
The "New Woman" was a real and permanent loosening of one set of constraints, sold by the culture industry as a total liberation that had not, in fact, occurred.
Hold those two facts side by side, because the chapter's real subject is the tension between them.

The same decade that produced its own sharpest critics, the writers above, telling the country its prosperity was hollow, also built the most efficient machine yet invented for manufacturing the opposite message: the modern celebrity, the famous person produced at industrial scale and national speed by the tabloids, the newsreels, the radio, and the ghostwritten book.

The dissenters and the manufactured heroes are not two separate topics; they are the decade arguing with itself, the Lost Generation writing the indictment while the celebrity machine cranked out the rebuttal, and the machine had the bigger circulation.

Sport built the prototypes (Babe Ruth, whose 60 home runs in 1927 made him the closest thing to a globally famous athlete the world had yet seen and turned baseball into a power spectacle, with Dempsey, Grange, and Jones close behind), and one of them complicates the brand: Gertrude Ederle, who in 1926 became the first woman to swim the English Channel and did it nearly two hours faster than any man had, came home to a vast New York parade, the crowd put in the millions by the era's wildly unreliable estimates, for proving a woman could be a national sports hero. (Her contemporary, the heavyweight Jack Dempsey, gave the decade its emblem of the sports gate, the total ticket money a fight drew: his 1927 rematch with Gene Tunney, the famous "Long Count" bout, in which a delayed count let a knocked-down Tunney recover and win, grossed somewhere over $2 million, among the first prizefights to do so, the precise "first" depending on where the threshold is set.) The apotheosis of the whole machinery was Charles Lindbergh.
On May 20–21, 1927, the 25-year-old airmail pilot flew a tiny single-engine plane, the Spirit of St.
Louis, alone, nonstop, about 3,600 miles (5,800 km) from New York to Paris, in thirty-three and a half hours, with no radio and a periscope because the fuel tank blocked his forward view.

He was a genuinely brave man who did a genuinely extraordinary thing, and then the media did to him what they had learned to do: a crowd estimated at around four million, the standard figure, repeated everywhere and impossible to verify, turned out for his New York parade.

Lindbergh is the purest case of the decade's last invention, fame itself as an industry, the same radio-tabloid-newsreel machine that sold the cars and the soap, turned now to manufacturing a global hero overnight out of one quiet man and one good flight.
The country that could do that to Lindbergh in May 1927 was the same country that, two and a half years later, would discover what else its machinery of confidence could manufacture, and could not.

chapters.title: The Bubble
sentences: The decade ended where its psychology had been pointing all along: in a crowd of ordinary people who had borrowed against a future they were certain would arrive, discovering, over about eleven days in October 1929, that it would not.

The Crash is the perfect ending to this book not because it caused everything that came after (that is argued, and the chapter will say so) but because it was the moment the decade's organizing belief, that the boom was permanent and the prosperity general, met the arithmetic, and lost.
There was a dress rehearsal, and it is worth a paragraph because it taught the wrong lesson.
From about 1923 to 1925, Florida had a real-estate mania.

Land in and around Miami and the new town of Coral Gables was bought, often sight-unseen, often with a small "binder" down payment, and flipped within weeks at a profit to the next buyer, who flipped it to the next, on the universal assumption that the price could only rise.
It was a textbook speculative bubble, the price detached from any use the land could be put to and floating purely on the belief that someone else would pay more tomorrow.
It deflated in 1926, and then a catastrophic hurricane in September 1926 killed hundreds and physically destroyed the boom's epicenter.

The lesson available was the one American history had already taught at least three times: the Early American Republic and Antebellum America narratives walk through the speculative panics of 1819, 1837, and 1857, each the same arc of boom, easy credit, collapse, and a banking class insisting all the way down that the fundamentals were sound.
The 1929 Crash is the fourth run of a known structural failure, not a bolt from the blue.

The lesson actually drawn from Florida was narrower and fatal, that Florida specifically had been a bad bet, and the speculative money, undeterred, simply moved north to a bigger and apparently sounder market, the New York Stock Exchange.
Into this came the decade's last president.

Herbert Hoover, the famous engineer-administrator of Chapters 4 and 5, the most admired man in the government, won the 1928 election in a third consecutive Republican landslide, beating the Democrat Al Smith (the first Catholic ever nominated by a major party, against whom the campaign unleashed open anti-Catholic bigotry, the "100% Americanism" of Chapter 9 in a presidential election) on a platform that the boom was not only permanent but nearly complete; accepting the nomination in 1928 he declared, in words reproduced with minor variations across sources but consistent in substance, that America was nearer to the final triumph over poverty than any land had ever been.
He took office in March 1929.
The crash came in October.
The cruel-timing reading, that fate ambushed a decent man, is the easy one and it is the wrong one for this book.
Hoover's boosterism was not bad luck; it was the decade's central refusal speaking through its most capable spokesman.

For eleven years almost nobody with power and a platform would say the floor might be hollow, because the entire system, the credit, the advertising, the politics, the stock market, depended on no one saying it.

Hoover believing and broadcasting that poverty was nearly beaten in the summer of 1929 is not ironic timing; it is the purest possible expression of the thing this whole book has been describing, and he was as much its product as the shoeshine boy with the stock tips.

Now the machine, because the Crash is not a mood, it is a mechanism, and the mechanism is the same one the whole consumer decade ran on, applied to stocks instead of cars: borrowing against the future.
Two devices did the damage.
The first was buying on margin.

An investor could buy stock by putting down as little as ten percent of the price in cash and borrowing the other ninety percent from the broker, pledging the stock itself as collateral, the asset the lender can seize and sell if the loan goes bad.
On the way up this multiplied gains spectacularly (put down $1,000, control $10,000 of stock, and a ten percent rise doubles your money).

But it built in a trap: if the price fell, the broker issued a "margin call" demanding more cash to cover the loan, and an investor who could not pay had his pledged stock sold out from under him immediately, at whatever the price now was.
Broker loans of this kind ran to something on the order of $8.5 billion by 1929 (estimates vary, but the order of magnitude is firm).
The second device was the investment trust, a company whose only business was owning shares in other companies, often itself bought on borrowed money and often owning yet other trusts.

This is leverage, the general name for using borrowed money so that a small base of real value controls a much larger pile of assets: it multiplies the return on the way up and the loss on the way down by exactly the same factor, and stacking leveraged trusts on top of leveraged trusts meant a single dollar of genuine value was propping up many dollars of paper claims.
Both devices did the identical thing: they magnified gains on the way up and guaranteed forced, cascading, accelerating selling on the way down.
The market roughly doubled between early 1928 and September 1929 on this borrowed fuel and on a flood of new amateur investors.
"Everybody Ought to Be Rich" ran the title of a 1929 magazine article by a prominent financier; the cliché of the era, true enough to stick, was the shoeshine boy giving stock tips.
A few people said so, and the way they were treated is the chapter's bleakest point.
The economist Roger Babson predicted a crash in September 1929 and was publicly mocked.

On October 17, 1929, about a week before the collapse began, Yale's Irving Fisher, one of the most celebrated economists in the country, declared that stock prices had reached "what looks like a permanently high plateau", a line that has followed his considerable reputation ever since.

The experts who reassured the public were believed; the ones who warned it were dismissed as cranks, which is what almost always happens at the top of a bubble and is exactly why bubbles get as big as they do.
The Federal Reserve (the central bank of Chapter 1) saw the speculation and was paralyzed by a real dilemma it never resolved in time.

Its main tool was the interest rate it charged banks to borrow: raise that rate and borrowing money gets more expensive everywhere, which would have starved the stock speculators of the cheap loans feeding the mania, but the same dearer credit would also choke ordinary business and farming, which were not booming and could not stand it.
Caught between popping the bubble and crushing the real economy, the Fed dithered between its regional banks and its Washington board through 1928 and 1929, moving late and indecisively.
The debate over whether the Fed could and should have acted differently has never ended; what is not in dispute is that it did not act in time.
The market peaked on September 3, 1929, at a Dow Jones Industrial Average of 381.

The Dow is an index, a single running number built from the share prices of a small set of large companies, used as a rough thermometer for the whole stock market; the figure itself is meaningless in isolation (a modern Dow above 40,000 is not "a hundred times bigger," it is a different basket compounded over a century), so what matters is not 381 but how far and how fast it then fell from it.
It drifted and slid nervously for seven weeks while almost everyone called it a healthy correction.
Then it broke.
On Black Thursday, October 24, panic selling hit the floor; a pool of leading bankers publicly bought stocks that afternoon to show confidence, and the gesture steadied prices for one weekend.
It was the last time confidence worked.
On Black Monday, October 28, the Dow fell about 13 percent with no rescue in sight.

On Black Tuesday, October 29, 1929, the dam broke completely: roughly 16 million shares were dumped in the worst single day in the exchange's history, the ticker ran hours behind the actual prices, margin calls forced more selling which forced more margin calls, the leverage of the whole structure now running violently in reverse.

Over the worst stretch of October somewhere on the order of tens of billions of dollars in paper wealth evaporated (the figure most often quoted is around $30 billion, and like all such totals it is an estimate of unrealized losses that moves with the dates you pick).
Anchor it loosely: it was many times the entire annual federal budget of the day and comparable to the whole cost of the World War to the United States.
The decade that had named itself for its own roar ended in eleven days of falling numbers.
Two honest qualifications close the book, because the brand version oversimplifies the ending as badly as it oversimplifies everything else.
First: the Crash did not, by itself, cause the Great Depression.

This is genuinely debated among economists, but the broad consensus is that the Crash was a trigger and a symptom, and that the catastrophe of the 1930s came from deeper structural faults the brand decade had hidden, the farm depression that had run the whole decade (Chapter 5), the "sick industries," the extreme concentration of the decade's income gains at the top, an under-regulated banking system of roughly 25,000 mostly small, undiversified banks with no deposit insurance to stop a panic becoming a collapse, and the unstable circular structure of international war debt.

To these the early 1930s would add a set of specific policy failures, the Federal Reserve letting the money supply contract sharply as banks failed in waves, and the 1930 Smoot–Hawley tariff choking world trade, which are named here only so the gap is not a blank, and are the proper subject of the next narrative, not this one.
The Crash is where the Roaring Twenties ends; the Depression is where the next story begins, and this book deliberately stops at the cliff edge rather than climbing down into it.
Second, and finally: even on the way down, the men in charge would not say it.

Hoover and the bankers insisted prosperity was "just around the corner"; the market even rallied somewhat into the spring of 1930 before collapsing for real, taking, this time, the banks and the factories and the farms with it.

That is the Roaring Twenties: a decade that genuinely invented the modern consumer economy, the broadcast nation, the car culture, and the celebrity, and made, in Harlem and Chicago, a body of art that outlived everything else it produced, and that ran, on the exact same calendar, the largest peacetime nativist movement in the country's history, a failed war on alcohol that built organized crime, a racially engineered closing of the nation's doors, and a stock mania it could not bring itself to call a mania until it had ended.
The boom was real and it was narrow and it was borrowed, and it contained the Crash, and almost nobody with the power to say so would.

The Depression and the world war that followed reshaped American society from top to bottom, and returning Black veterans, the heirs of the migration and the institutions Chapter 13 described, the "Double-V" generation, helped spark the civil-rights movement that would transform the country again.
That is the next narrative in this chain, the Civil Rights Era, whose runway opens exactly here, 1929–1954 (Ch 1).
This one ends on October 29, 1929, with the ticker running hours behind the truth, which is, in the end, the most accurate possible image of the entire decade.

chapters.title: The Broken Promise
sentences: Start in 1865, even though this book is mostly about the 1950s and 1960s, because you cannot understand a single thing the movement did without knowing what it was trying to recover.
Not invent.
When the Civil War ended, the United States did three extraordinary things in five years.
It abolished slavery (the Thirteenth Amendment, 1865).

It declared, in the Fourteenth Amendment (1868), that everyone born in the United States was a citizen, and that no state could deny any person "the equal protection of the laws." And it declared, in the Fifteenth Amendment (1870), that the right to vote could not be denied "on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude." On paper, in 1870, a Black man in Mississippi was a citizen with the vote and the equal protection of the law, and for a brief period this was partly real: Black men voted in large numbers, sat in state legislatures, and sent sixteen of their number to the U.S.
Congress in the Reconstruction decades, in a national legislature of fewer than four hundred, the first Black members in American history and a number not approached again for almost a century.

That period is called Reconstruction, and the narrative immediately before this one in the chain, the Reconstruction narrative in this series, tells its story and its destruction in full. (Throughout this book, references to "the Reconstruction narrative," "the Roaring Twenties narrative," "the Antebellum America narrative," and so on point to the other books in this same American chain, read separately, not to companion volumes you need in hand here.) Here is the one paragraph this book needs from it.
It did not last, and the way it ended is the wound this entire narrative is about, so be precise about the way it ended: Reconstruction was not abandoned by inattention, it was overthrown.

White Southern "Redeemer" Democrats used organized paramilitary terror, the Klan, the White League, the Red Shirts, to murder and intimidate Black voters and officeholders off the rolls and out of office, while a Northern public and the Northern business wing of the Republican Party decided that protecting Black rights was no longer worth the cost; the Reconstruction narrative records the federal government being told, in writing, that the North was "tired." In 1877 the federal government made that an explicit choice, withdrew the last troops from the South, and stopped enforcing the amendments.
What followed, over the next quarter-century, was not a return to slavery but the deliberate, systematic construction of something new: Jim Crow.

The name comes from "Jump Jim Crow," a mocking, exaggerated caricature of a Black man performed by a white entertainer in blackface (burnt-cork makeup) in the popular minstrel shows of the 1830s; the country attached the name of a stage parody of Black people to the legal system built to subordinate them, which is its own grim summary.
It became the shorthand for an entire legal and social regime.
Jim Crow had three pillars, and the movement would spend the 1950s and 1960s attacking all three.
The first was segregation: laws requiring the physical separation of Black and white people in schools, transport, restaurants, hospitals, drinking fountains, and cemeteries.
The second was disfranchisement: a toolkit invented to take away the vote the Fifteenth Amendment guaranteed, without ever mentioning race, so that it could survive a court.
