The lesson a substantial part of the movement drew from Atlantic City was that the system could not be redeemed from inside it, and that the liberal alliance would back Black freedom only until it cost the alliance something, the same conditional support, again, that had shaped the New Deal and the Freedom Rides.
That conclusion is the bridge to Black Power (Chapter 15).
But first, in the spring of 1965, the older strategy of provoked nonviolent confrontation would win its last and greatest victory, on a bridge in Selma.

chapters.title: The Bridge
sentences: The Voting Rights Act of 1965 is, by the measure of what it changed on the ground, the most consequential law in this entire book, and it exists because the movement, having learned every lesson from Albany and Birmingham, executed the strategy of provoked confrontation with cold precision one final time, in Selma, Alabama.
This chapter is about that campaign, the violence it was designed to elicit, and the law it produced, which finally enforced an amendment ratified ninety-five years earlier.
The target was chosen the way Birmingham had been chosen.

Selma was the seat of a county where Black citizens were a majority of the population and a tiny fraction of one percent of the registered voters, because the registration machinery, run by white officials wielding literacy tests and intimidation, simply did not let them on the rolls.
And Selma had a sheriff, Jim Clark, with a reputation for exactly the violent temperament the strategy required, the Bull Connor variable again, deliberately selected.

The campaign's purpose was not, in the first instance, to register voters in Selma; it was to dramatize disfranchisement so undeniably, and provoke a response so brutal, that a national voting-rights law became politically unavoidable.
In February 1965 a state trooper shot and killed a young church deacon, Jimmie Lee Jackson, during a night march in nearby Marion.

In response, organizers, including James Bevel (who had conceived the Birmingham children's march, Chapter 8), proposed a march from Selma fifty-four miles (about 87 km) to the state capitol in Montgomery.
On March 7, 1965, about six hundred marchers set out and were stopped at the Edmund Pettus Bridge by state troopers and a mounted posse who attacked them with clubs and tear gas.
John Lewis, leading the march, had his skull fractured.

The bridge's name is the era's argument in one piece of ironwork: it was built in 1940 and named for Edmund Pettus, a Confederate general who became a Reconstruction-era Ku Klux Klan grand dragon in Alabama and was then elected by white Alabama voters to two terms in the United States Senate, serving until 1907.
The men who led the 1870s terror were not exiled for it; they were honored and returned to power, and the Reconstruction narrative in this chain documents that continuity at length.

Marchers in 1965 were beaten on a bridge bearing the name of the political tradition that had beaten their grandparents. (The name still stands, now contested, the subject of recurring proposals to rename it.) It was filmed, and that night a national audience saw the footage broadcast back into its living rooms; by the most-repeated account ABC cut into a film about Nazi war crimes to do it, a juxtaposition almost too neat, and the specific programming detail varies in the retellings, but the load-bearing fact is not in dispute: the country watched Americans in uniform club Americans on a bridge, in motion, that night.

Bloody Sunday produced exactly the national revulsion the campaign had been engineered to produce, the entire television logic of Chapter 8 at its most effective, and it is the clearest single demonstration in the book that the strategy was a designed instrument, not a spontaneous moral pageant.
Two days later, the strategy fault line cracked open in public.

A federal district judge, asked by Alabama state authorities to forbid the march and weighing whether to let it proceed under federal protection, had issued a temporary injunction (a court order forbidding a specified action) barring it for the moment, an unusual case where the federal court the movement relied on had, for now, ordered it not to move.

King, facing a column of marchers and a phalanx of troopers, led the marchers to the bridge, had them kneel and pray, and then turned them around, "Turnaround Tuesday", rather than defy the federal injunction, because his strategy depended on keeping the federal courts and the Johnson administration as allies.

To much of SNCC, this was a betrayal of the people who had come ready to march and possibly die, and it confirmed their growing conviction that the SCLC's leadership was too deferential to white federal power.
The same event read as prudent statesmanship by one wing of the movement and as cowardice by another is the internal argument of the era made visible in a single afternoon.
Under federal protection ordered by the court and enforced by federalized troops, the full march finally went from Selma to Montgomery later that month, ending with King's "How long?
Not long" speech at the capitol.

It also cost another life: Viola Liuzzo, a white mother of five from Detroit ferrying marchers in her car, was shot dead by Klansmen on the highway, and one of the four men in the Klan car was a paid FBI informant.

What the Bureau did next is the episode in miniature: rather than be exposed as having had an informant present at a murder, the FBI fed the press and Alabama officials a smear, that Liuzzo was a drug user, that she had abandoned her children, that she had been in the car with a young Black man for sexual reasons, insinuations later shown to be false and traceable to the Bureau, calculated to make a murdered civil rights worker look like a woman who got what such a woman invited.

That single sequence, an informant in the murder car and a character assassination of the victim to protect the Bureau, contains the whole story of the FBI's posture toward the movement, which the next chapter takes up in full (Chapter 15).

Eight days after Bloody Sunday, President Johnson addressed a joint session of Congress, called Black disfranchisement an American moral failure, and ended by deliberately speaking the movement's own anthem: "And we shall overcome." He then sent up the bill.

The Voting Rights Act of 1965 did what no prior law had: it suspended literacy tests, sent federal examiners physically into the South to register voters, and, crucially, imposed preclearance, a rule freezing election-law changes in covered jurisdictions until the federal government approved them, so that the South could not simply invent a new disfranchising device every time an old one was struck down.
This is the precise moment the book has been building toward since Chapter 1, and the precision of the fix is the point.

The Fifteenth Amendment of 1870 had said the vote could not be denied "on account of race," and the Reconstruction narrative in this chain argues that its drafters made it deliberately narrow, a negative prohibition rather than a positive guarantee of the ballot, and conspicuously silent on poll taxes, literacy tests, and property requirements.
That silence was the loophole.

Jim Crow's disfranchisement machinery (Chapter 1) ran through it for ninety-five years precisely because it never mentioned race: a literacy test was not, on its face, a racial denial, so the amendment as written could not stop it.
The Voting Rights Act did not amend the Fifteenth.

It built the enforcement apparatus the 1870 Congress had refused to write: federal examiners who physically registered voters where local officials would not, and preclearance, which froze the South's ability to invent the next race-neutral device.
The amendment finally had, ninety-five years late, the teeth its own framers had left out.
The Second Reconstruction's central legal task, redeeming the broken promise of 1865–1877, was in this one statute accomplished.
And the result had a human scale the book has spent twelve chapters earning.

In Mississippi, where Black registration had stood at roughly five to seven percent, the share of voting-age Black Mississippians on the rolls climbed past sixty percent within a few years (the exact baseline and pace vary across the scholarship; the order of magnitude does not).
In one Selma-area county where almost no Black resident had been allowed to register in living memory, the rolls went from a few dozen names to thousands.
Within a decade the South had more Black elected officials than at any time since Reconstruction, and the men and women who had been clubbed on the bridge could, and did, vote the sheriff out.
It is the movement's mountaintop.
And it was almost immediately followed by the discovery of how much the mountaintop did not overlook.

chapters.title: The Other America
sentences: That is the interval between President Johnson signing the Voting Rights Act and the Watts section of Los Angeles erupting into six days of fire and gunfire that left thirty-four people dead in August 1965.

The juxtaposition is the subject of this chapter and arguably the hinge of the entire book: at the precise moment the movement won its greatest legal victory, the limits of legal victory exploded into view in a Northern city the Southern strategy had never been designed to reach.
The conceptual key is the distinction Chapter 10 set up: de jure versus de facto segregation.

Everything the movement had perfected, the boycott, the sit-in, the provoked confrontation, the federal lawsuit, was a set of tools for attacking segregation that was written in law and enforced by an identifiable villain in a Southern town.
Watts had no "whites only" signs to defy and no Bull Connor to provoke into supplying the necessary footage.
Its segregation was produced by mechanisms with no single author and no statute to strike down.
The deepest of them was redlining, and it is worth dwelling on, because it is the engine of the wealth gap that runs to the end of this book.

In the 1930s federal housing agencies, the Home Owners' Loan Corporation and then the Federal Housing Administration, drew maps of every American city and color-coded neighborhoods by lending risk, marking Black and mixed neighborhoods in red as "hazardous." Banks followed the maps.

For roughly thirty years, the federal government effectively guaranteed mortgages in white areas and denied them in red ones, which meant the entire postwar explosion of homeownership, the single largest engine of middle-class wealth in American history, was routed almost entirely to white families and structurally closed to Black ones.
A white family bought a house that appreciated for generations; a Black family across the redline could not get the loan, rented, and accumulated nothing to pass on.
This was not a Southern law a court could strike.

It was a financial instrument with a race-neutral surface and a racially specific result, and it had a direct ancestor: the crop-lien system the Reconstruction narrative in this chain documents, in which debt rather than deeds tied the freedpeople to the plantation.
The lien was the nineteenth-century instrument of race-specific wealth deprivation; redlining was the twentieth.

Beside it ran the rest: urban renewal and highway construction that bulldozed functioning Black neighborhoods (the novelist and essayist James Baldwin, the era's most piercing literary voice on American race, called it "Negro removal"), employment discrimination, and a pattern of aggressive, often violent policing of Black neighborhoods.
None of that could be sued away in an afternoon, and none of it was touched by the 1964 or 1965 acts.
The movement had spent a decade building a key precisely shaped for a Southern lock and now stood in front of a Northern door that had no keyhole.
King understood the danger and tried to meet it head-on.
In 1966 he brought the SCLC north to the Chicago Freedom Movement, attacking slum housing and segregation in the country's second-largest city.
It went badly, and the way it went badly is the chapter's central evidence.

When marchers entered all-white Chicago neighborhoods like Marquette Park demanding open housing, they were met by white mobs throwing bricks and bottles; King was struck in the head by a rock, and afterward said, in remarks his aides recorded and recounted slightly differently, that he had never seen mobs as hostile and hate-filled as in Chicago, not even in Mississippi or Alabama.

The shock is more legible with the longer memory the Roaring Twenties narrative in this chain supplies: in the 1919 Red Summer, white Chicago mobs had attacked Black neighborhoods for days after the Great Migration brought Black Southerners into the city.
The 1919 riot and the 1966 Marquette Park mobs were the same phenomenon, white Northern resistance to residential integration, forty-seven years apart.
King was not encountering something new in the North; he was encountering something the North had been doing the whole time and had simply never had to do on national television.
The campaign produced a vague, largely unenforced "summit" agreement and no victory comparable to Birmingham or Selma.

Its one durable Chicago creation was economic, not legislative, and it is the payoff of the through-line that started with the Montgomery boycott (Chapter 4): Operation Breadbasket, the SCLC's economic arm, run in Chicago by a young Jesse Jackson, which used the Montgomery weapon, the organized Black boycott, to pressure white-owned businesses in Black neighborhoods into hiring Black workers and stocking Black-made products.
It was the economic-boycott-as-weapon doctrine applied to the Northern city, and it outlasted the march.

But the housing fight itself failed, and the reasons are exactly the ones the book has been laying out: there was no single segregation law to overturn, no obliging brutal sheriff to generate national footage, and the structural machinery, banks, real-estate practice, ward politics, was diffuse, deniable, and locally entrenched in a way no televised march could break.
Northern white resistance to actual integration was as fierce as the South's; it simply had no statute behind it to attack.

Johnson's response to the structural problem was the Great Society and the War on Poverty: Medicare (federal health insurance for the elderly), Medicaid (federal-state health coverage for the poor), Head Start (a federal preschool and early-childhood program for low-income children, designed to close the school-readiness gap before kindergarten), food stamps, and federal aid to schools, an enormous expansion of the federal commitment to the poor.

The scale of the effect deserves the emphasis the book usually reserves for the failures, because it makes the failure that follows sharper: the national poverty rate fell by roughly half over the decade, and Black poverty fell faster than that, the single largest reduction in American poverty in the century.
This was real, and the book credits it without an asterisk.
But it ran into two walls.
The first was structural design.

The signature anti-poverty law required the "maximum feasible participation" of the poor themselves, a clause written into the 1964 Economic Opportunity Act mandating that poor people sit on and help run the local agencies spending the money, intended to bypass the white-controlled city machines that had always captured federal funds before.

It worked well enough to start a war over control: city halls, local Black activists, and Washington fought bitterly over who actually held the money and the jobs, and many mayors moved to strangle the programs that had given their poorest residents independent leverage.
The second, larger wall is Chapter 16's subject: the money and political will required to actually attack structural poverty were, within a couple of years, consumed by a war in Vietnam.
Watts and Chicago together delivered the lesson that splits the era in half.

The Southern legal phase had succeeded at exactly what it was built to do and was finished; the destruction of de jure segregation, however vast an achievement, did not by itself change where Black Americans could afford to live, what they were paid, how they were policed, or whether their children's schools were funded.
The legal Second Reconstruction had largely won.
The economic and structural one had not even been seriously begun.

And here the book's argument turns, because the people who had been saying exactly this for years, the ones who had never believed the integrationist, nonviolent, work-within-the-system program could reach the structural city in the first place, were not new voices arriving in 1966.
They were an older tradition that had been running the entire time, in parallel, frequently armed, and largely written out of the story.
Before the narrative can show that tradition moving from the margin to the center, it has to show that it was never actually at the margin.
That is the next chapter, and it is the hinge on which the post-1965 movement swings.

chapters.title: The Longer Tradition
sentences: To understand why the movement turned the way it turned after 1965, you have to see what it turned toward, and that was not new.

This chapter doubles back across the years just covered, deliberately, because the single most distorting thing the sanitized memory does is treat the nonviolent, integrationist, church-led movement of Chapters 4 through 13 as the whole of Black politics, with everything after Watts as a late, regrettable radical turn.
That gets the history backward.

There was always a second tradition, older and continuous, Black self-defense, self-determination, separatism, and a hard skepticism that white America would ever concede equality voluntarily, and it did not appear in 1966.
It was there the whole time, under the famous one, and the post-1965 fracture is not a movement going wrong; it is a buried half of the movement surfacing.
Its most powerful twentieth-century voice, and the man whose ideas would shape everything in the next chapter, was Malcolm X.
Malcolm Little became Malcolm X in prison, where he joined the Nation of Islam, a Black religious movement led by Elijah Muhammad.

The Nation was heterodox, meaning it departed sharply from the established mainstream of the religion it claimed: orthodox Islam is a universal faith with no racial doctrine, while the Nation taught a race-based theology, that Black people were the original humanity, that its founder was a divine figure and Elijah Muhammad his messenger, claims mainstream Sunni Islam rejects entirely.

What it preached was Black separatism, rigorous personal discipline, economic self-sufficiency, and the flat doctrine that the white man would never grant Black people anything and that integration was a delusion.

As the Nation's most electrifying public speaker through the late 1950s and early 1960s, Malcolm articulated, with a clarity nothing in the mainstream movement matched, the rage and pride of the Northern urban Black population that the Southern church movement did not reach and did not speak for.

His critique of King's program was direct and is worth stating in its strongest form, because the book's honesty depends on not strawmanning it: he argued that asking your oppressor for your freedom while promising not to defend yourself was a strategy of humiliation, that "nonviolence" was a discipline demanded only of Black people and never of the mobs and police attacking them, and that "by any means necessary," explicitly including self-defense, was simple human dignity.
He mocked the March on Washington as the "Farce on Washington," a co-opted, integrated picnic.

The book does not have to adjudicate this against King to record that Malcolm's analysis, of structural and Northern and economic racism, of psychological liberation, of the limits of moral appeal, turned out to describe the post-1965 reality (Chapter 13) at least as well as King's had described the pre-1965 South.
Malcolm's last year complicates every simple version of him.

Silenced and disillusioned by Elijah Muhammad, he left the Nation of Islam in 1964, made the hajj (the Muslim pilgrimage to Mecca), embraced orthodox Sunni Islam, and began moving toward a more internationalist, human-rights framing and, in muted form, toward the possibility of selective alliance.
He was assassinated by Nation of Islam gunmen in a Harlem ballroom in February 1965, three weeks before Bloody Sunday.
The timing matters: he died just as the legal movement reached its peak and just before the post-1965 period in which his ideas, far more than his organization, would shape a generation.

The Autobiography of Malcolm X, written with the journalist Alex Haley (later the author of Roots, the 1976 family saga of slavery and descent that became one of the most-watched television events in American history) and published months after his death, became one of the most influential American books of the century and the foundational text of what came next.
But the longer tradition was not only Malcolm and not only urban and not only rhetorical; it was also, throughout the Southern movement the legend codes as purely nonviolent, armed.
This is the part most thoroughly erased from popular memory, and the book gives it the weight the erasure denies it.
Start with Robert F.
Williams, because his story is the whole argument in one life.

Williams was the NAACP branch president in Monroe, North Carolina, a Marine veteran who, after the courts and the police repeatedly failed to protect Black residents from Klan night-riders in the late 1950s, chartered a National Rifle Association affiliate and armed his chapter.

When a Klan motorcade attacked a Black doctor's house in 1957, his armed members fired back and the caravan fled, which is a fact, not a legend: organized Black self-defense worked exactly where the nonviolent appeal to law had nothing to appeal to.
The national NAACP, committed to nonviolence and terrified of the optics, suspended him.

In 1961 he was charged with kidnapping (he said he had sheltered a white couple from an angry crowd) and fled the country, living in exile in Cuba and then China for eight years and broadcasting "Radio Free Dixie" back to the South; the charges were eventually dropped and he returned in 1969.
His 1962 book Negroes With Guns, written in exile, became one of the most direct influences on Huey Newton and the Black Panther Party (Chapter 15).
Williams was not an aberration the movement disowned.
He was the movement's own suppressed half, and the suppression, by its own most respectable organization, is the point.
The pattern was institutional, not individual.

In Louisiana, the Deacons for Defense and Justice were armed Black men, many of them veterans, who guarded civil rights workers and Black neighborhoods from night-riders, and they were frequently the unspoken reason a "nonviolent" campaign could survive in a Klan county at all.

Many rural Black families who fed and housed SNCC organizers kept firearms and would have used them; the nonviolence was frequently a public tactical discipline maintained by the demonstrators while armed self-defense quietly protected the community that sheltered them.

The honest picture, the one the field has recovered over the last decades and the one this book insists on, is not "nonviolence, then a radical turn." It is two traditions running in parallel the entire time, sometimes in the same county, sometimes in the same person, with the balance between them shifting after 1965 as the structural problems the nonviolent Southern strategy could not touch (Chapter 13) moved to the center.
That shift, named, organized, and turned into a slogan and a party, is the next chapter.

chapters.title: Black Power
sentences: In June 1966, James Meredith, the man who had integrated Ole Miss (Chapter 8), set out to walk across Mississippi alone to prove a Black man could, and was shot from ambush on the second day.

The major organizations converged to continue his March Against Fear, and on that march, in Greenwood, Mississippi, SNCC's new chairman Stokely Carmichael, recently arrested again, took a platform and led the crowd in a chant of "Black Power." The phrase detonated.
This chapter is about what it meant, why it split the movement and terrified white America, and how the federal government responded to the radical turn, which was to try to destroy it.
First, what Black Power actually meant, because it was deliberately ambiguous and was heard very differently by different audiences.

To Carmichael and SNCC it meant, primarily, self-determination: Black people organizing independently, controlling their own communities, institutions, economics, and political organizations, rather than seeking integration into, and permission from, white institutions.
SNCC had already built a working model of it in Lowndes County, Alabama, an 80-percent-Black county where, before 1965, not one Black resident was registered to vote.

Rather than ask Black residents to join the white-controlled Alabama Democratic Party that had spent a century excluding them, SNCC organizers used an obscure state law to register them in an entirely new, independent party, the Lowndes County Freedom Organization, ran their own Black candidates for sheriff, coroner, and school board, and (because Alabama ballots used pictures for voters the literacy tests had kept from reading) chose a party symbol: a black panther.

That panther, and the principle behind it, that Black people in a Black-majority county should hold their own offices through their own party rather than petition white ones, was borrowed within a year in Oakland.
It also carried a psychological argument straight out of Malcolm (Chapter 14): pride, "Black is beautiful," the rejection of a self-image defined by white approval.
To the press and to frightened white audiences, amplified deliberately by both, it sounded like a threat of racial violence and a repudiation of King and of white allies.

King himself, while sympathetic to the underlying critique, publicly worried that the slogan's connotations would frighten away support and obscure the program; the older organizations, the NAACP and the Urban League, condemned it outright.
The Meredith March is where the coalition that had held, barely, through the March on Washington and Selma, visibly came apart on camera.
The institutional break followed fast.

SNCC and, somewhat later, CORE, the two organizations that had pioneered interracial direct action, voted in 1966 and 1967 to become Black-led and Black-staffed, asking white members to go organize in white communities instead, the formal end of the interracial-coalition model that the sit-ins and Freedom Rides had embodied.

To one reading this was a tragic fracture; to another it was the logical conclusion of Atlantic City (Chapter 11), the institutional expression of a hard-won judgment that the liberal coalition would not, in the end, share real power.
The book presents it as both, because the participants experienced it as both.
The era's most mythologized organization came out of this turn.

In Oakland in October 1966, Huey Newton and Bobby Seale founded the Black Panther Party, which paired armed "copwatching", legally carrying guns and law books to observe and deter police violence, with a Ten-Point Program and, increasingly, community survival programs, most famously the Free Breakfast for Children program that fed tens of thousands of children daily.
The book stresses the breakfast program for a specific reason: it is the strongest single piece of evidence about what the federal government actually feared, which is the chapter's real subject.

In a 1969 internal FBI memorandum, later declassified and entered into the public record, the breakfast program was identified as the greatest single threat to the Bureau's effort to neutralize the Panthers and the program most in need of disruption. (The exact wording is paraphrased differently across the secondary literature, often attributed directly to Director J.

Edgar Hoover; the declassified memos are the authority, and what they unambiguously establish is that the Bureau targeted the survival programs as a priority, not the guns.) The reason is the chapter's hinge: a Black organization that successfully fed its own children built exactly the kind of independent community legitimacy the state most wanted to prevent, because legitimacy, not weapons, is what the state cannot tolerate a rival institution accumulating.

That is the door into the chapter's grimmest and most important subject, and everything before it in this chapter has been the setup for it, because what the federal government did to the Black Power movement is not a coda.

It is the reason the movement could not consolidate, and the book treats it as documented fact rather than speculation, because it is documented: in 1975–76 a Senate select committee, the Church Committee, investigated and published it.

COINTELPRO, the FBI's Counter Intelligence Program, was a sustained, illegal operation that infiltrated organizations with paid informants, forged letters to set rival groups and rival leaders against each other, fed damaging fabrications to friendly journalists, pressured employers to fire activists, and worked systematically to "neutralize" Black movement leaders before, in Hoover's own internal phrase, any of them could become a unifying "messiah." It ran against the entire spectrum, from SNCC and the SCLC to the Panthers.

Against King it was personal and old: Hoover had regarded the movement as a Communist front and King as an enemy for years, and the FBI wiretapped him, bugged his hotel rooms, assembled tapes of his private life, and in 1964 mailed him an anonymous package containing a recording and a typed letter.

The letter, declassified in full decades later, told King he was a fraud and an "evil, abnormal beast," that the tapes would expose him, and closed by telling him there was only one thing left for him to do and that he knew what it was and had better do it before a set date, language read then and since as urging him to kill himself before he could accept the Nobel Peace Prize.
Against the Panthers the program escalated from disruption to complicity in killing.

In December 1969 Chicago police, acting on a floor-plan supplied by an FBI informant who had drugged him, raided the apartment of the twenty-one-year-old Illinois Panther leader Fred Hampton before dawn and shot him in his bed.

A federal grand jury found the police had fired roughly ninety shots to the occupants' one; no officer was ever criminally convicted, and the survivors and the families of the dead won a $1.85 million civil settlement from the city, county, and federal government in 1982, a settlement that is itself the official admission of what was done.

Hold the two facts together, because holding them together is the only honest way to tell the era: the same federal government the movement spent fifteen years maneuvering into enforcing the Constitution was, with the same Bureau that had stood aside while the Freedom Riders were beaten, simultaneously running a clandestine campaign to destroy the movement's most independent wing.

The radical turn was real, it had a program, and it was actively, illegally, and in Hampton's case lethally suppressed by the state, and that suppression is a large part of the answer to the question the rest of the book keeps circling, of why the post-1965 movement fractured instead of consolidating.

By 1967 the cities themselves were burning, and the man the country still thinks of as the whole movement was about to turn, decisively and at ruinous cost to his reputation, against the war and toward the poor.

chapters.title: The Fire This Time
sentences: This chapter is the end of the movement's heroic period, and it has a double structure on purpose: the cities exploding from below, and King, from the top, turning the movement toward the things, the war, capitalism, poverty, that the legal victories had never touched, and being destroyed, in reputation and then in life, for doing it.
First, the fires.
The Watts pattern (Chapter 13) was not an isolated event but the start of a wave.
The summers of 1965, 1966, and especially 1967 brought disorders to more than a hundred cities.
The two largest in 1967 were Newark (26 dead) and Detroit (43 dead, federal paratroopers deployed), the deadliest urban uprising of the decade.

Both began the way Watts had, with an ordinary policing incident in a community that experienced the police as an occupying force: in Newark, the arrest and visible beating of a Black cabdriver, John Smith, on July 12; in Detroit, a predawn police raid on an unlicensed after-hours bar, a "blind pig," on July 23.
In each case the spark was minor and the explosion was not, because the fuel, the redlined housing, the jobless rate, the policing pattern of Chapter 13, had been accumulating for decades.

The country argued bitterly about what to call them, "riots" framed them as criminal pathology, "uprisings" or "rebellions" framed them as political response to structural conditions, and the argument over the word was itself the political fight.

Johnson appointed a commission, and the Kerner Commission delivered, in early 1968, a conclusion blunter than anyone expected from an official body: the country was "moving toward two societies, one black, one white, separate and unequal," and the fundamental cause was white racism, the structures of Chapter 13 named in a government report.
Johnson, stung that the report blamed the society rather than crediting his Great Society, largely shelved it.
The official diagnosis of the structural problem was filed and ignored, which is, in miniature, the era's economic tragedy.
Now King's turn, which is the heart of the chapter and the heart of the book's argument about memory.

After 1965 King moved steadily and deliberately to the left, toward exactly the structural and economic analysis that Randolph (Chapter 9) and Malcolm (Chapter 14) had pressed and that Watts (Chapter 13) had proven.

He concluded that legal rights without economic power were hollow, that the problem was not only Southern bigotry but the structure of American capitalism and the distribution of wealth, and that all of it was bound up with the war.

On April 4, 1967, exactly one year before his death, he delivered "Beyond Vietnam" at Riverside Church in New York, condemning the Vietnam War, naming his own government "the greatest purveyor of violence in the world today," and explicitly linking what he called the three evils: racism, militarism, and economic exploitation.

His argument included a hard material point: the war was draining the money and political will that the War on Poverty needed, and Black servicemen, with less access to the student and occupational deferments that kept many college-bound white men out of combat, were dying in disproportion to their share of the population, especially in the early escalation years of about 1965 to 1967, when Black troops were roughly a tenth of the force but accounted for closer to a fifth of combat deaths; the gap narrowed later as the military adjusted assignment and draft practices, but the pattern in those early years was real and documented, not estimate.

The same linkage had been made, at enormous personal cost, by the heavyweight boxing champion Muhammad Ali, who in 1967 refused induction into the Army on religious and political grounds ("no Viet Cong ever called me" by a racial slur, he said) and was stripped of his title, convicted, and barred from boxing for three of his prime years.
The reaction is the evidence for Chapter 18's thesis, so the book records it precisely.

The "Beyond Vietnam" speech was condemned across the establishment that had praised the 1963 dream: major newspapers, including the ones that had lionized him, attacked him; the NAACP's board repudiated the linkage of civil rights and the war; the Johnson White House turned on him; his public approval fell sharply.
The King of April 1967, anti-war, anti-poverty, indicting American capitalism and American empire, was a deeply controversial and, to much of white liberal America, an unwelcome figure.

That King, the late, radical, economically focused King, is the one the later sanitized memory (Chapter 18) most thoroughly erased, and the contemporary backlash is the proof that the erasure required active work.
His final campaign followed directly from that analysis.

The Poor People's Campaign aimed to bring a multiracial army of the poor to Washington to demand an economic bill of rights, a federal guarantee of jobs or income, decent housing, an end to poverty, for all races.
It was a deliberate move from civil rights to economic class, the unfinished other half of "Jobs and Freedom" from 1963.
While organizing it, he went to Memphis to support striking Black sanitation workers.

The strike had a precise cause: in February 1968 two workers, Echol Cole and Robert Walker, sheltering from rain in the back of an old packer truck because the city did not let Black crews shelter elsewhere, were crushed to death when the truck's compactor mechanism malfunctioned and cycled.

The men marched under signs reading "I Am a Man," a demand for recognition as workers and as human beings at once, the fusion of race, labor, and economic dignity that was King's final politics in one image.
On April 3, 1968, he gave the "I've Been to the Mountaintop" speech, ending with words that read, in retrospect, like a man who knew.
The next evening, April 4, 1968, he was shot dead on the balcony of the Lorraine Motel.
He was thirty-nine.

His murder set off the largest wave of civil disorder in American history, the Holy Week uprising, so called because King was killed on the Thursday before Palm Sunday and the burning ran through the Christian Holy Week to Easter, the irony of the timing lost on no one: unrest in more than a hundred cities, federal troops occupying Washington with the Capitol dome behind columns of smoke.

Within a week Congress finally passed the long-stalled Fair Housing Act, banning discrimination in the sale and rental of housing, the era's last major civil rights statute, passed over King's coffin to address precisely the de facto, structural segregation (Chapter 13) he had died trying to confront.
The Poor People's Campaign went on without him under Ralph Abernathy.

Several thousand poor people of every race traveled to Washington and built Resurrection City, a plywood-and-canvas encampment of some six hundred shelters on the National Mall between the Lincoln Memorial and the Washington Monument, and stayed for six weeks demanding the economic bill of rights: a federal jobs guarantee, a guaranteed minimum income, and a large-scale low-income housing program.
They got none of it.

The campaign had specific bills and no leverage; the disciplined provocation that had worked on a Southern sheriff had no equivalent target in a federal budget fight, Congress was in no mood after a year of urban fires to enact a new entitlement, and the camp itself, sited on low ground, was waterlogged into mud by weeks of rain, sick, leaderless without King, and infiltrated.

Police cleared it in June 1968 and bulldozed the shelters, and the campaign ended with essentially nothing of its program enacted, the exact failure, the economic half refused, that the final chapter is about.
Two months after King, Robert Kennedy, campaigning on poverty and reconciliation and the man who had announced King's death to a grieving Black crowd in Indianapolis, was also assassinated.
The movement's heroic period did not end in a triumph.
It ended in fire, in two murders, and in a tent city in the mud, having dismantled the legal architecture of segregation and run directly into the economic structure it could not move.
What it ran into instead was a political backlash organized to make sure it moved no further.

chapters.title: Backlash
sentences: The civil rights movement did not simply wind down after 1968; it ran into an organized, durable political reaction that absorbed its momentum, narrowed its gains, and rewired American party politics for the next half-century.

This chapter is about that reaction, the busing wars, the courtroom rear-guard that put real teeth into the old rulings just as the political will to enforce them drained away, and the new kind of power the movement had nonetheless created.
The backlash had been building in plain sight.

Governor George Wallace of Alabama had built his career on it: in his 1963 inaugural he pledged "segregation now, segregation tomorrow, segregation forever," and that June he physically stood in a doorway at the University of Alabama to block the court-ordered enrollment of two Black students, stepping aside only when confronted by the federalized National Guard, a staged performance of resistance for white voters in the Faubus tradition (Chapter 5).

He then ran for president in 1964, 1968, and 1972, and the revelation of his campaigns was geographic: he drew large votes not just in the South but among white working-class voters in the North, around the very Chicago neighborhoods that had mobbed King (Chapter 13).
Wallace proved there was a national white backlash constituency, and in 1968 Richard Nixon built a strategy to capture it without Wallace's overt language.

The Southern Strategy courted disaffected white Southern and Northern ethnic voters through coded appeals, "law and order," opposition to "forced busing," states' rights, that signaled racial reaction without saying it outright.
It worked, and it completed a realignment this book has been tracking since Chapter 1, and the completeness is the point.

The Reconstruction narrative in this chain records the starting configuration exactly: in the 1860s and 1870s Southern Black men voted nearly unanimously Republican, the party of Lincoln and emancipation, while white Southerners voted nearly unanimously Democratic, and Black-majority electorates put Republican governments in Southern statehouses.

Over the decades after 1964 that arrangement did not merely shift; it inverted, almost term for term: the white Southern Democratic bloc became the white Southern Republican bloc, and Black voters became overwhelmingly Democratic, the same two coalitions facing each other across the same line with only the party labels exchanged.

The 1964 Civil Rights Act, Bill Moyers later reported Johnson saying as he signed it, had handed the South to the opposition for a generation; whether Johnson said exactly that is disputed by historians, but the arithmetic of every Southern election since has proved the prediction right.
The fiercest domestic battlefield of the aftermath was busing.
The courts, finally, were getting serious about enforcement just as the politics turned against it.

In Green (1968) the Supreme Court ruled that toothless "freedom of choice" plans were not enough and that school boards had an affirmative duty to dismantle segregated systems "root and branch", fourteen years after Brown, the Court finally supplied the deadline Brown II had withheld (Chapter 2).
In Swann (1971) the Court unanimously upheld court-ordered busing, transporting children across a district, as a permissible remedy to achieve actual integration.
And busing became the most explosive racial issue of the 1970s, in the North at least as much as the South, which is the book's de jure/de facto thesis (Chapter 13) delivered as its empirical proof.

When a federal court ordered Boston to integrate its schools by busing students between the white Irish-American neighborhood of South Boston and the Black neighborhood of Roxbury beginning in September 1974, the white resistance was not metaphorical.

Mobs of several thousand stoned the buses carrying Black children, with police escorts unable to stop the rocks coming through the windows; white crowds chanted at and assaulted Black pedestrians; a Black attorney was beaten near City Hall with an American flag as a weapon, in a photograph that won a Pulitzer; the violence ran for years and required state police and at points the National Guard.
This was Boston, the abolitionist city, in 1974, and it rivaled or exceeded what the Deep South had produced.
It was also not a surprise.

The Roaring Twenties narrative in this chain documents the 1919 Chicago riot, when white mobs attacked Black neighborhoods after the Great Migration brought Black Southerners north; the Marquette Park mobs that shocked King in 1966 (Chapter 13) were the same phenomenon; Boston 1974 was the same phenomenon again.
Northern white resistance to actual residential and school integration was not new, regional, or aberrant.
It was a continuous, century-long pattern with no statute behind it to attack, which is exactly why the movement's Southern toolkit could never reach it.
Then the Court itself drew the limit.
In Milliken v.

Bradley (1974), it ruled 5–4 that busing could not cross the line between a city and its suburbs absent proof the suburbs had deliberately segregated, which, given white flight, effectively walled off the white suburbs from integration and capped how much school desegregation the law would ever reach.
The legal Second Reconstruction had a ceiling, and Milliken was it.
A parallel argument opened over employment and what would come to be called affirmative action, and its political paternity is more tangled than partisan memory allows.
In Griggs v.

Duke Power (1971), a unanimous Court ruled that employment tests and requirements that screened out Black workers and were not genuinely job-related violated the 1964 act even without proof of intent to discriminate, establishing "disparate impact," the idea that a practice's effects, not just its motives, could be unlawful.
And the Philadelphia Plan, which imposed concrete minority-hiring goals and timetables on federally funded construction, was implemented in 1969 by the Nixon administration.

That a "law and order" president running the Southern Strategy created a landmark affirmative-action program looks like a contradiction until you see the politics: the building-trades unions were overwhelmingly white, exclusionary, and a core of the Democratic labor coalition, so a Republican plan forcing them to integrate their hiring did three things at once, it advanced a genuine civil rights goal, it embarrassed the Democrats by making them choose between Black voters and white union members, and it drove a wedge through the opposition's base.

The motive was partly principled and substantially strategic, and the book says both. affirmative action, the policy that would become the central racial argument of the next forty years, was thus born partly out of Johnson's 1965 executive order and partly out of a Republican administration's wedge tactic, a genuinely tangled paternity the book presents as tangled rather than tidy.
And here is the hinge of the whole chapter, and the reason the backlash is not the end of the story.
Busing could be walled off by a 5–4 ruling because it depended on a court order an electorate hated.
The vote could not, because once cast it elected the people who held office, and an officeholder is not a remedy a later court can narrow.
So while Milliken capped what desegregation law could reach, the other half of the movement's legal harvest was compounding, untouchable by the same mechanism, into political power.
The Voting Rights Act (Chapter 12) had re-enfranchised the Black South, and that power converted into officeholders.

Shirley Chisholm, the first Black woman elected to Congress, ran for the Democratic presidential nomination in 1972 under the slogan "unbought and unbossed," her own phrase asserting that she answered to no party machine or donor and would not be managed, a direct claim of the independent Black political agency Black Power had argued for; the Congressional Black Caucus organized in 1971 to act as a bloc; and the numbers tell it plainly: roughly five hundred Black elected officials in the entire country in 1965 became several thousand within a decade, including, in 1973, the first Black mayors of major cities, Maynard Jackson in Atlanta and Coleman Young in Detroit, in some cases governing the very cities that had burned.
This is the structural difference between the first Reconstruction and the second, and it is the hinge of the final chapter.
The first Reconstruction's Black political power was destroyed by terror and federal abandonment and did not survive.
The second's was narrowed, walled off in the suburbs, and politically out-organized, but its keystone, the vote, survived the backlash.
Whether that makes the Second Reconstruction a success, a partial success, or a betrayal deferred is the question the book closes on.

chapters.title: The Second Reconstruction
sentences: This is the last chapter of this book and the last narrative in the entire American chain that runs from the Declaration of Independence through the Early American Republic, Antebellum America, the Civil War, the first Reconstruction, the Roaring Twenties, and to here.
There is no forward chain narrative.

So this chapter does what a last chapter must: it closes the spine, the broken promise of 1865–1877, by asking what, in the end, was kept and what was not, and it confronts the strange afterlife of the movement's own memory.
Begin with the arc, stated as plainly as the book can state it.
In 1868 and 1870 the Constitution promised Black Americans citizenship, equal protection, and the vote.
The promise was not then allowed to lapse from neglect; it was defeated.

As the Reconstruction narrative in this chain documents, organized white paramilitary terror overthrew elected biracial governments while a Northern public and a Northern business wing decided the cost of enforcement was no longer worth paying, and in 1877 the federal government made that an explicit, written choice, the surviving correspondence has the Mississippi governor told in so many words that the North was "tired", and withdrew.
By 1900 the white South had built Jim Crow to nullify the amendments in fact while leaving them untouched on paper, segregation, disfranchisement, and terror, blessed by Plessy in 1896 (Chapter 1).
The first Reconstruction did not fail; it was destroyed, on purpose, and that distinction is the whole reason there had to be a second one.
For roughly two generations, the United States was a constitutional democracy whose founding post–Civil War guarantees were, for a tenth of its population in a third of its territory, a dead letter.

Then, between 1954 and 1965, a mass movement forced the country to enforce them: Brown killed Plessy; the Civil Rights Act of 1964 destroyed segregation written into law; the Voting Rights Act of 1965 finally gave the Fifteenth Amendment, ninety-five years late, an enforcement mechanism.
Historians call this the Second Reconstruction because that is precisely what it was: a second federal attempt, after a ninety-year interruption, to make the post–Civil War amendments real.
The single most important sentence in this book is that the movement was not asking for anything new.
It was collecting a debt the country had run up in 1868, defaulted on in 1877, and finally, under irresistible pressure, partly paid in 1965.
Now the ledger, honestly kept, because a triumphal close would be a lie and a despairing one would be false too.
On the side of what was kept: legal, de jure segregation, the entire "whites only" architecture, was destroyed and did not come back.

The Black franchise in the South was restored and, unlike after the first Reconstruction, survived the backlash that followed (Chapter 17), converting within a generation into thousands of Black elected officials, a structurally different outcome from the 1870s, when Black political power was annihilated.
Interracial marriage bans fell in Loving v.

Virginia (1967), the case of Richard and Mildred Loving, a white man and a Black and Native American woman who married in Washington, were arrested in their bedroom in Virginia for it, and won a unanimous Supreme Court ruling that struck down every remaining law in the country criminalizing interracial marriage.
A Black middle class expanded.

And the movement became the template, the tactical and moral grammar, for the movements that followed it: the Chicano movement (the Mexican-American civil rights and self-determination movement of the 1960s and 1970s, from farmworker organizing under César Chávez to urban youth and student activism), the Native American, women's, disability, and gay-liberation movements.
It carried abroad as well, and the specifics show the claim rather than assert it.

The Northern Ireland Civil Rights Association, founded in 1967 to protest anti-Catholic discrimination, explicitly modeled itself on the American movement, ran the same kind of marches, and sang "We Shall Overcome." In South Africa the African National Congress's youth leadership drew on the same nonviolent direct-action model, though it ultimately abandoned nonviolence after the 1960 Sharpeville massacre, precisely because the South African state, unlike the American one, faced no national television audience it needed to keep from being embarrassed, the same media-leverage logic (Chapter 8) read in the negative.
That is an enormous, world-historical achievement, and the book states it without hedging.
On the side of what was not kept: almost everything the movement turned to after 1965.

The structural segregation of the Northern and now suburban city, redlining's legacy, the wealth gap, school resegregation after Milliken walled off the suburbs (Chapter 17), survived the movement nearly intact and in some measures worsened.

The economic agenda, "Jobs" beside "Freedom" from 1963, the Poor People's Campaign, King's economic bill of rights, was never enacted; it died with him in the Memphis spring and in the mud of Resurrection City (Chapter 16).
The federal government that was finally forced to enforce the amendments was the same government that ran COINTELPRO to destroy the movement's most independent wing (Chapter 15).

The honest verdict is the one this book's whole structure has been arguing toward: the legal Second Reconstruction substantially succeeded, and unlike the first it was not violently overthrown; the economic and structural one was barely begun and then abandoned, and that unfinished half is the direct lineal descendant of the unfinished half of the first Reconstruction.

"Forty acres" is the shorthand for that older default: at the end of the Civil War there were proposals, most identified with Congressman Thaddeus Stevens, to break up the great plantations and give the freedpeople land of their own (the phrase "forty acres and a mule" comes from a wartime field order briefly carried out and then reversed), on the reasoning, which the Reconstruction narrative in this chain develops at length, that freedom without an economic base was freedom on paper only.
It was defeated, chiefly by Northern Republicans unwilling to set the precedent of seizing and redistributing property.

A century later the Poor People's Campaign's economic bill of rights was refused by, at bottom, the same mechanism: a governing coalition subordinating economic redistribution to propertied interests and its own stability.
The forty acres not given in 1865 and the jobs-and-income guarantee not enacted in 1968 are the same promise refused twice for the same reason.
The country has now deferred the same economic reckoning twice, in 1877 and again after 1968.
Which forces the book to its last subject, because it is itself part of the history: the sanitizing of the memory.

Within fifteen years of his murder, the radical, anti-war, anti-capitalist King of 1967 and 1968, the King who called his own government the greatest purveyor of violence in the world and died organizing a poor people's army, had been compressed in national memory into a single sentence from a single speech in 1963, made the subject of a federal holiday, and quoted approvingly by the political descendants of the people who had opposed him.
This narrative has treated that compression as an event, with a cause and a method, because it is one.
The mechanics are traceable.
The radical "Beyond Vietnam" King had been near-universally condemned in 1967 (Chapter 16), which made the dead King available for a different use than the living one.

The campaign for a federal holiday, fought through the 1970s and resisted for years, succeeded in 1983 only by selling Congress the safest possible King, the 1963 dreamer, not the 1968 organizer of a poor people's army; the holiday was the reduction, institutionalized.

Schools then taught the holiday's King, a single paragraph ending at the Lincoln Memorial; the one speech with the one quotable line crowded out the Letter, Riverside Church, and Memphis; and within a generation politicians whose own coalitions descended from the movement's opponents could quote "content of their character" approvingly precisely because everything that would have made the quotation inconvenient had been edited out first.

A difficult, divisive, structurally radical mass movement was easier for the country to honor once it had been reduced to one man, one dream, and a triumphal arc ending in 1965, with the foot soldiers, the women, the organizers, the radicals, the self-defense tradition, and the unfinished economic demand all edited out.

That edit is why this book spent eighteen chapters insisting on Ella Baker and Fannie Lou Hamer and Septima Clark and Bayard Rustin and the Deacons and the Panthers' breakfast program and the Letter from a jail and the speech at Riverside Church.
The flattening is not a neutral simplification.

It is the same instinct that, in the previous narrative in this chain, turned the cause of the Civil War into a myth almost before the war was over: a country managing a painful history by smoothing it.
Restoring the texture is not revisionism.
It is the repair.
So end where the chain ends.

The American story this series has followed for two and a half centuries is, at its center, the distance between "all men are created equal" and what the republic actually did, the gap the founders deferred (Early American Republic), that detonated in civil war (Antebellum America), that the first Reconstruction tried and failed to close, and that the Second Reconstruction reopened and partly, unevenly, at enormous cost, closed.
It closed the legal gap.
It did not close the economic one, and it never resolved the argument between the dream and the longer, harder tradition that doubted the dream would ever be enough.

The movement's own greatest figure spent his last year saying the legal victory was not the finish line, and he was killed saying it, and then the country built him a holiday and forgot the part where he said it.
That is where the chain ends: not at a settled triumph, but at a debt partly paid, a promise partly kept, and a country still arguing, with itself, about how much of 1868 it ever really meant.
The bell Jefferson said he heard in the night did not stop ringing at Appomattox, or at Selma.
The book ends with it still ringing, which is the most honest place to leave it.
